# Patrologia Latina, Volume 204

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library … of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III … Second Series.*

**Volume CCIV of Patrology:** Clement III, Roman Pontiff; St Stephen of Grandmont; Laborans; Henry of Castro Marsiaco, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church; Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury; Bernard, Abbot of Fountains; Stephen of Liciac; Peter Bernardi; William of Trahinac; Gerard Itherius, men of Grandmont; Reiner; Lawrence, monks of Liège; Ermengaud; Henry of Septimello.

## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library**, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all surviving monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, very carefully corrected against the most accurate editions and collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the fullest editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes appended to individual volumes or to authors of some importance; arranged with chapters suitably disposed within the text itself and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each Father wrote on any theme; the other, of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented on individual scriptural texts, and in what places in their works.

A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if the following are weighed: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the course of the work, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been issued in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The one hundred and sixty volumes of the Latin edition are sold for thirteen hundred francs; the three hundred Greek-Latin volumes for eighteen hundred francs. The wholly Latin edition embraces all authors, Western and Eastern alike; the latter, however, are supplied there only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 1188: Reiner, Monk of St Lawrence at Liège

[Col. 0009]

## Historical-Literary Notice

(Dom Bernard Pez, Preface to vol. IV of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. XVII)

Several writers have hitherto mentioned Reiner—also called Rayner or Reinerius—a monk of St Lawrence at Liège: notably Baronius, Valerius Andreas, Gerard, John Vossius, Chapeavillus, Mabillon, Casimir Oudin, and others. But they have done so very briefly, and by no means as so great a man deserved. The reason was that the greater part of Reiner’s little works, hidden in darkness, remained unknown until now. Henceforth, however, everything concerning him will be more certain and more ample, since the distinguished Father Lombard copied most of the memorials of his genius from autograph manuscripts and inserted them in our *Thesaurus*.

We know Reiner’s date with certainty—though most writers state that he flourished about the year of the Lord 1130—from his own little book *On the Lightning Strike upon the Church of His Monastery*. “In this present year,” he says, “which is the year 1182 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, on the following day—that is, after Palm Sunday—the Lord, wonderful on high, thundered over us with lightning falling amid a great and terrible crash,” and so forth. You will find chronological marks equally certain for establishing Reiner’s date in other of his little works. But the distinguished Lombard could extract from no record of his monastery the year in which he exchanged death for life.

All his works declare that he was a man endowed with outstanding and exceptionally elegant genius, written as they are in a learned, polished style scarcely characteristic of his age. Nor was he inferior in virtue and holiness of life: he was even renowned for heavenly visions, which in his little works he frequently relates as though experienced by others and interweaves with the ancient histories which he treats. He himself discusses his works carefully in Book II of *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*. From them it is pleasing to list only those which now appear for the first time in our *Thesaurus*.

### 1. Three little books, *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*

In the autograph codex these bear the following title: “A little book to his friend, on the foolishness of a certain ignorant man.” This title, undoubtedly deriving from Reiner himself, reveals the author’s remarkable modesty. In it he recounts rather carefully what each of his predecessors wrote and commended to posterity. One might wish that he had done the same for brethren contemporary with himself. But, as he confesses at the beginning of Book II, two considerations restrained him: namely, lest he be charged either with malice if he praised too sparingly those things which deserved praise, or with flattery if he paid their merits the praise due to them.

Moreover, ancient literary history will receive no small illumination from this work of Reiner, a field cultivated with such zeal by the learned men of our age. The learned John Gottfried Olearius, however, is not slightly mistaken in volume II of his *Library of Ecclesiastical Writers*, where on p. 121 he writes that Reiner’s three books *On the Illustrious Men of His Monastery*—which are precisely these three little books of ours—had been published in John Chapeavillus’s *Collection of Liège Affairs*. For in that collection one can find nothing by Reiner except the *Life of St Lambert*.

> [Note: Col. 0009: This is not by Reiner, but by Sigebert of Gembloux. See *Patrology*, vol. CLX, col. 759. — Editor.]

### 2. Little work on the nine antiphons before Christmas beginning with *O*

This is entitled, “What the nine O’s signify and what is the rationale of those days,” a title which Reiner testifies in the prologue addressed to his friend that he placed before his commentary. We have placed this little work immediately after the preceding one because Reiner treats the same subject, though more briefly, in Book III of that work; thus one may supplement the other.

This commentary was indeed published long ago, namely at Liège in 1618. But since copies of that edition are extremely rare, and since no one who has hitherto praised Reiner has mentioned it, we thought it fitting to reprint it in our collection. It will be convenient and useful to preachers of the divine word, who in various churches customarily address sermons to the people during the final week of the Lord’s Advent on these very antiphons, so full of mysteries. The reader will learn from a note by the distinguished Father Lombard why Reiner expounded nine such antiphons rather than seven, as are now sung in almost all churches.

### 3. *Mirror of Repentance*, or the *Life of St Pelagia*, in two books

Reiner is not so much the author as the reviser of this history, as is clear from his own words with which he concludes the prologue:

> “I found the record of her conversion, Pelagia’s, written by another; but the style was poorly suited to it, and moreover there was so great a confusion of barbarisms and solecisms that the obscure style seemed to have rendered a noble subject fragmentary and contemptible. Yet I suspect that this happened more through the scribe’s fault than through the author’s incompetence, since the text showed itself mutilated everywhere by four or more clauses, and also by half-lines of verse. But contemptible speech greatly detracts from glorious deeds. I have therefore taken care to refashion the aforesaid subject in somewhat better form and to test the untrained capacity of my youth. I arranged the little work in two books and gave it the title *Mirror of Repentance*. For every eye cleansed by the collyrium of goodwill may behold in it both how great a good this remedy is and how happy its result.”

Although the subject of these little books has been sufficiently celebrated, several examples of virtue which Reiner relates—either under concealment of his own name or concerning others—in Book I, chapter 4, and Book II, chapter 3, have not until now been equally well known. He does the same in his other little books of histories and lives; for this reason alone they had long deserved to be brought to light.

We know that there are people who hold all things of this kind in derision. But there are also those who, exercising discernment, draw great spiritual profit from them. If we desire by our labors to benefit the latter more abundantly, no prudent person will take this ill or impatiently in a work intended for the uses of widely differing people. Reiner himself mentions this little work in Book II of *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*, chapter 3.

### 4. *Virgin’s Palm*, or *On the Life and Passion of St Mary, the Cappadocian Virgin*, in two books

Reiner published these while still a young man, chiefly in order to flee idleness and imbue his mind with healthful studies. A vision of Blessed John, his teacher, had added an incentive to treat sacred subjects. In that vision John was said to have heard the voice and admonition of most blessed Lawrence: “How delightful and pleasant it is to direct the mind toward divine things!”

Reiner himself writes of this in the prologue:

> “For a certain brother was reading Terence to boys or youths. But theatrical reading is ordinarily more harmful than profitable to weak hearers. Meanwhile that teacher became ill, so that he was almost despaired of. Carried outside himself in ecstasy, he saw and heard many memorable things, which he afterwards committed to writing. Nor did he conceal that Blessed Lawrence had sternly directed against him the judgment which I have set out above, reproving him because he defiled himself with frivolities while employing a comic poet. For he is deemed insufficiently religious who occupies heart or tongue with shameful trifles. To treat divine and honorable matters, therefore, is most salutary. Knowledge increases, idleness is avoided, and the soul advances in virtues.

> “Indeed, we read that certain Fathers customarily wove mats or little baskets; when they had amassed great piles of them, and there was no one to sell them, they set a fire beneath them and burned them, then made others again to be reduced to the same fate. These spiritual philosophers had reasoned that idleness was the enemy of the soul, and therefore pursued it so fiercely. But I, unskilled in plaiting rushes and unfit to weave little baskets, shall at least attempt to write something, accustom my youth to worthy arts, and devote my small talent not to furnaces but to books. Thus I shall compose a little work divided into two books, entitled *Virgin’s Palm*. For it will describe the contest in which the holy virgin Mary strove and how, after defeating her enemy, she obtained the heavenly palm.”

Thus far Reiner. Although his statement is somewhat long, it seemed appropriate to reproduce it here, so that religious persons might learn by what studies they ought to exercise their minds. For in our own times there are no lack of people who devote their small talents not to books but even to painted papers and other trifles; they are also accustomed to be angry at those who consecrate good hours to copying ancient records, which they themselves judge wholly unworthy of daylight, since these records are exceedingly hostile to their own morals.

For Mary, the Cappadocian martyr and servant-woman, see Baronius in the *Roman Martyrology* for the first day of November, and Lawrence Surius, who on the same day recounts Mary’s acts from Vincent’s *Historical Mirror*. Our Reiner is nearly a full century older than Surius.

### 5. *Life of St Theobald*, in two books

Concerning these and the preceding two little works, Reiner himself says in Book II, chapter 3, of *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*:

> “Accordingly, in two little books I described the conversion of St Pelagia and gave this work the title *Mirror of Repentance*. Then I explained the passion of Mary, the Cappadocian virgin, in likewise a two-book work, calling it *Virgin’s Palm*. Subsequently, I embraced the Life of Theobald the hermit in two books as well, and called it *Flower of the Wilderness*. These works had indeed previously been written in a rough style of composition, but at the advice of certain persons I polished them, so far as I could, with the file of my small learning. For friends who enjoin pious things must be obeyed. The deeds of saints are reckoned common material, and he who exercises studies of piety ought not to be pricked with the charge of vanity,” etc.

Reiner does not disclose to whom he owes what he reports about St Theobald. But anyone who has compared, even lightly, his little work with the *Life* of that most holy hermit written by Peter, Abbot of Vangadice, and published by Surius and Mabillon in Part II of the sixth Benedictine century, from p. 156, will immediately discover that Reiner “ploughed with the other man’s calf”: he merely clothed Peter’s work in a more elegant style and, in his customary manner, embroidered the fabric with certain events of his own time. Yet all this escaped Mabillon, who otherwise would certainly not have omitted Reiner among those who had praised St Theobald.

### 6. *On the Conflict of Two Dukes and the Marvelous Revelation of Souls*, etc., in two little books

We have inserted this little work of Reiner’s, and likewise the following work, *On the Arrival of the Relics of St Lawrence from Rome at Liège*, in our collection solely in order to show the learned what Reiner could do in verse, leaving them entirely free to decide what faith, or how much faith, they wish to assign to histories of this sort.

Of the former little work, Reiner says in Book II, chapter 6, of *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*:

> “But lest the stylus fixed to the wall above the wax tablets, while they slept mouldering, should waste away with the leprosy of rust, I wrote for a certain intimate friend a little work on the notable islands of Sardinia and Sicily, arranged in two books of verse. Likewise, for another, I wrote two little books: the first *On the Conflict of Two Dukes and the Marvelous Revelation of Souls*; the second *On a Certain Captured Soldier, Liberated through the Saving Sacrifice*.”

Of the latter he writes in chapter 8 of the same book:

> “I also wrote in verse a little book *On the Arrival of the Relics of St Lawrence at Liège from the City of Rome*. Indeed, at the request of the brethren, I composed many prayers to be recited to that martyr himself and to many other saints; one metrical prayer to St Lawrence is found below in the column. Because of the same kind of prayer, I immediately appended an Office of the Holy Spirit, full of devout meaning.”

What occasion Reiner had for writing this office may be seen in the same work, chapter 8. In his metrical little work *On the Arrival of the Relics of St Lawrence the Martyr*, Reiner did scarcely anything other than render in verse what Louis the Elder had presented on the same subject in prose; for his age, he accomplished it not inelegantly.

### 7. Metrical book *On the Arrival of the Relics of St Lawrence from Rome at Liège*, etc.

This little work of Reiner’s has just been discussed.

### 8. Five little books of the *Bouillon Triumph*

Bartholomew Fisen describes at length, in Book X of his *Ecclesiastical History of Liège*, under the year 1141, the great disturbances and calamities which Hugh and Rainald, sons of Rainald, Count of Bar, inflicted upon the Church of Liège after seizing the castle of Bouillon, or Bullion. Two distinguished ancient writers committed to writing the Iliad of those miseries and, finally, the triumph of the Church of Liège after its recovery, with the aid of St Lambert the martyr, of the castle of Bouillon.

The first is Nicholas, canon of Liège, a contemporary author, whose *Triumph of St Lambert, Martyr, concerning the Castle of Bouillon* John Chapeavillus first brought to light from an old codex of Aulne Monastery in volume II of the *Writers of Liège Affairs*, from p. 577. The other is Reiner of the Church of Liège, whom we have undertaken to illuminate here and who deserves exceedingly well of that church on more than one account. He composed five highly elegant and weighty little books on the same subject, as he himself testifies in Book II, chapter 9, of *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*:

> “Moreover, in a work of five little books I wrote how, in our own days, the Church of Liège, by divine power, recovered the castle of Bouillon after three years from its invaders; and I entitled it *The Bouillon Triumph*. I also set this to a musical melody.”

The musical setting appears to have been lost, while the *Triumph* alone remains. The distinguished Father Lombard recovered it from an autograph manuscript, and we have here made it public in order to illuminate the history of Liège a little more fully.

[Col. 0013]

### 9. *Life of Evraclus, Bishop of Liège*

Reiner composed this from certain earlier records. For he discusses the matter thus in the prologue:

> “Since the deeds of Evraclus were certainly illustrious, they also had been worthy of an illustrious writer, who with skill in good expression might say to the righteous man, according to the prophet: ‘It is well; for he shall eat the fruit of his devisings.’ Certain writers did say something about him, but not very well, because not diligently or fully enough. Therefore the kindly yet insistent request of certain brethren demanded that I collect into one work the things scatteredly said by various persons and, in a more careful style, make one writing out of many writings, as I had done in describing the Life of St Wolbod, likewise Bishop of Liège,” etc.

Reiner does not mention this *Life* in Book II of *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*, where he lists his little works and the occasions and titles of each. But this passage can demonstrate that Reiner either did not list everything there or wrote further works after he had completed Book II; here he does not distinguish himself in the least from the author of the *Life of St Wolbod*, published by Mabillon in Part I of the sixth Benedictine century.

### 10. *Life of Lord Reginard, Bishop*

Nor does Reiner mention this little work in the catalogue of his little books which he compiled in Book II of *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*. Yet it is no less plain that no one other than Reiner himself should be recognized as its author. For, to say nothing now of the codex in which the *Life of Reginard* is intermixed with other certainly authentic little works of Reiner, the author brings forward in the prologue matters which can suit no one but Reiner:

> “Certain brethren also roused me, as though I were sluggish and idle, to describe Reginard, by their kindly exhortation and continual entreaty. They insistently alleged that I owed no less gratitude and no less service to our head of household, by whose benefits I had chiefly been brought up from childhood, than to the holy bishops Wolbod and Evraclus, whose lives I had already described in two books.”

These are precisely Reiner’s little works, listed by us under the preceding number.

### 11. *On the Lightning Strike upon the Church of His Monastery*

When, in the year of the Lord 1182, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, the church of St Lawrence’s monastery was struck by lightning and burned horribly, Reiner treated this tragedy in a separate book. He entitled and dedicated it to Frederick, a monk, his intimate friend, and later a monk of Stavelot, as appears from Reiner’s letter to him in chapter 7. There Reiner further complains of Frederick because, after going to Stavelot and becoming a Stavelot monk, he had sent him neither conversation nor a scrap of writing—as though the Ardennes did not possess rams, sheep, and calves, from whose skins parchment is usually made.

There is no record of this little work in Book II of Reiner’s *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*. This further confirms what was said shortly before: not all his little works were listed there. It also establishes that Reiner composed those three little books and all the works mentioned in them before the year of the Lord 1182.

### 12. Little book of thanksgiving on the new dedication of his monastery’s church

This little book follows the preceding one in natural order. For when Reiner had mourned and lamented the grievous fall and destruction of his basilica in the earlier work, in this one he believed that he should celebrate its happy restoration and leave a perpetual memorial of his grateful spirit toward Blessed Lawrence.

This little work was composed in the same year as the former, as Reiner himself teaches us in chapter 6:

> “Accordingly, 151 years are reckoned from the first dedication of this church to the second dedication, and from the year 1182 of the Lord’s Incarnation. Finally, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April we were struck by divine chastisement, but nevertheless in the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of November, we were healed by divine mercy. We celebrated the joy of this healing—that is, the solemnity of the dedication—for eight days, following the example of Solomon or the Maccabees. And, as it is written, we offered the burnt offerings of prayers and the saving offerings of praise in spiritual songs and thanksgivings, confessing the Lord as though on diverse musical instruments: ‘For he is good, for his mercies endure for ever,’” and the rest, which the reader himself may run through without loss of time.

For this is distinctive in Reiner’s little works: everywhere he joins brevity to elegance of expression, a quality which both readily draws one to reading and dismisses one from it without disgust or weariness.

### 13. *Brief Account of the Burning of the Church of St Lambert*

This little work is of the same kind as that listed under number 11. It is, namely, a lament which Reiner composed when, in the year 1188 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May—the day on which the translation of St Lambert is celebrated—at the first watch of the ensuing night, a fire burst forth from the house of a certain canon. It suddenly seized and consumed the neighboring houses, then the cloister and its workshops. The flames, excessively strengthened by demonic agitation, fell upon your monastery, holy Lambert, and, although the roofs had been most carefully covered with lead, brought down in immense conflagration and ruin both towers, the old palace with the church of the holy virgins, and several surrounding dwellings.

This writing of Reiner’s is indeed brief, but it could nevertheless have been of notable use to Bartholomew Fisen in composing his *Ecclesiastical History of Liège*, where he does not mention this memorable event by so much as a word under the year 1188, though from Reiner we learn that it occurred then.

### 14. Three little books of *Tears*

The present three little books of *Tears*, written by Reiner to Philochristus—that is, to any lover of Jesus Christ—are most elegant and surpass all the rest in devotional feeling. Perhaps they were written when he was already weighed down by old age and near death.

He calls the little books, or books, *Tears* because they set forth only those teachings and examples which may profitably shake a mind immersed in earthly things through expectation and fear of things to come, and draw bitter tears of repentance from eyes captivated by the world’s vanity. The reader will find in them no fewer historical matters than ascetic ones, although perhaps there will be no lack of persons who accuse Reiner, on the basis both of these works and of the other little books listed so far, as one who gave more weight than was proper to dreams and rather trivial stories.

But Reiner, otherwise a learned and polished man, shows us in Book II of *Tears*, chapter 1, that he handled these matters with judgment and discrimination:

> “We do not, indeed, aim at favor but at compunction; we seek instruments of tears, not arguments for frivolous boasting, especially since we speak or write only privately to the two of us. For as faces differ, so human opinions differ: what one person judges good, another supposes evil. Such a person is accustomed to object against matters of this sort with that schoolboy verse:
>
> > ‘Take no thought for dreams: for what the human mind desires  
> > while awake, it hopes for; in dreams it sees that very thing.’
>
> “And with the saying of the Wise Man: ‘Dreams have caused many to err, and those who hoped in them have fallen ….’ We do not deny this; but we add what is likewise written: ‘Dreams of evildoers are vanity, and your heart suffers fantasies like that of a woman in labor’; yet we do not conceal what follows: ‘unless a visitation has been sent from the Most High.’ For it is equally most vain and most foolish to attend to the fantasies of dreams, whose kinds, forms, and meanings no wise man or interpreter of Pharaoh, no diviner of King Nebuchadnezzar, no magician, no Chaldean—not even Muhammad, prophet and god of the Saracens, though he may have charged his Gabriel [Col. 0015] with being the master of mysteries—could have comprehended and fully interpreted. So great is the heap of fantastic dreams that it surpasses without limit the measure of the Jewish *gomer*. We set such things aside. We commend only those visitations sent from the Most High to those who are troubled in heart and humble in spirit: those who, sitting beside the rivers of Babylon, weep while remembering Zion; those who, filled with the confusion of this age, its restless and passing flux, regarding prosperity as they do adversity, say with the Apostle in tears: ‘We have here no abiding city, but seek one to come,’” etc.

This passage, as it is long, is also very useful and apt for clearing Reiner from the suspicion of excessive credulity, into which he will undoubtedly fall in the eyes of some because he rather frequently recounts visions, sometimes his own and sometimes others’.

The most learned Father Lombard, who brought these books and those following out of obscurity, carefully observed that in the codex he used Reiner’s name had been written not by the first hand but by a somewhat later one; indeed, the little books of *Tears* themselves had not been copied in the same script as Reiner’s other unquestionably authentic little works. Finally, in another copy, written in 1428 by John of Stavelot, a famous monk of St Lawrence, he found only this title: “Here begins the first little book of *Tears*, issued by a certain brother of our church.”

He further observed that the author of these little books cites Reiner himself, as author of the *Bouillon Triumph*, in Book III, chapter 4, as follows:

> “But I shall now be silent about how the aforesaid brother saw that most adorable Majesty for the third time, because this close friend of ours recounted it in the little work entitled *The Bouillon Triumph*,” etc.

From all this Father Lombard thought it could be established that these little books of *Tears* were not by Reiner but by another monk of St Lawrence who was familiar with Reiner. But these conjectures will appear groundless to everyone who compares this work *On Tears* with Reiner’s other entirely undisputed books. For the similarity in genius, style, piety, and charm is so great on both sides that one cannot deny Reiner any of them without taking all of them away from him.

Nor is our most learned friend’s final argument conclusive. It is not at all so unusual among ancient writers of visions and miracles, for reasons of modesty or fear of envy, to attribute to others things which happened to themselves. From the many examples, I shall adduce only one relevant to the present matter, from Part II of Volume III of our work.

There Othlo, dean of St Emmeram’s, in Book *On the Spiritual Course*, chapter 21, begins to relate the temptations and prodigies that confronted him when he was a young monk in the following words:

> “It pleases me here to insert writings of a faithful brother, most well known to me, who, coming to conversion and frequently reading Holy Scripture—for he had great hope in this reading—was worn out by the excessive and prolonged assault of the ancient enemy in that same Holy Scripture,” etc.


Who would not believe that this faithful brother, so well known to Othlo, was utterly different from Othlo himself? Yet nothing could be less true. For whatever Othlo relates in the cited passage from the writings of that faithful brother, he himself openly sings of himself under his own name, without any concealment whatsoever, in the metrical book *On Spiritual Teaching*, chapter 14 and the following chapter.

Let it therefore remain certain that these little books of *Tears* came from no one other than Reiner, as another, though later, hand rightly noted in the codex.

### 15. Two books *On the Advance of Death*

That the author of the books *On the Advance of Death*—which are likewise in large part historical—and of the little books of *Tears* is one and the same is clear from chapter 10 of the former. There he tells William to accept this work *On the Advance of Death* and join it to the little work which he composed a few days earlier, and to which, in accordance with the nature of the subject, he gave the title *Tears*.

There is no doubt that the little books *On the Advance of Death* are the very work which he had promised at the end of Book III of *Tears* in these words:

> “And indeed, brothers, I think I have now satisfied you with the tearful little narrative which I knew how to relate, although some matters remain which will be inserted in that little work whose completion, having been begun some time ago, your affection and exhortation impel me to undertake.”

Thus Reiner himself speaks. How splendidly he kept his promise is abundantly clear from both sets of little books, which he appears to have dedicated to William, a distinguished monk whose virtues he celebrates with the greatest praises in Book II, chapter 10.

The second little book is mutilated near the end, perhaps because he was overtaken by the death whose advance he had so steadfastly kept before his eyes and was unable to bring it to a conclusion.

These are the little works of Reiner published in our *Thesaurus*.

> [Besides the little works mentioned above, which Dom Bernard Pez made public, there is Reiner’s book *On the Life of St Wolbod, Bishop of Liège*, which he himself mentions in the above-cited lives of St Evraclus and Reginard. — Editor.]

[Col. 0015]

# REINER, MONK OF ST. LAWRENCE AT LIÈGE: THREE LITTLE BOOKS ON THE DISTINGUISHED WRITERS OF HIS MONASTERY

[Note: [Col. 0015] Manuscript title: “A little book to his friend concerning the follies of a certain unlearned man.”] Published from a manuscript codex by the distinguished Father Coelestine Lombard, librarian of the same monastery.

(D. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. IV, part III, col. 17.)

## FIRST LITTLE BOOK

### PROLOGUE

“It belongs to a man,” says Solomon, “to prepare his mind, but to the Lord to govern the tongue,” because all human ways lie open to His eyes, and the Lord is the weigher of spirits [Col. 0016–0017A] (Prov. 16). But not so, my friend—not so do the makers of scandals act: whether they fashion deceitful balances with the axe and terrifying hammer of hatred or envy, or with the smoothing plane and flattering lathe of favour and adulation, they weigh weight against weight. Giving no heed to moderation, as they judge wickedly, so they flatter dishonestly: slaves of error, that is, who knowingly call evil good and good evil. Hatred, indeed, knows no reason; envy lacks fairness.

I observed this foolishly in one of my intimates. Though he loved certain persons deeply because he believed them friends of household fidelity, he found them enemies through barbarous treachery, when at times he served the brethren in a ministry—with such labour, fidelity, and distress of spirit as the Lord Sabaoth knows, who judges with tranquillity [Col. 0017B] and disposes us with great reverence. Then, certainly without cause, the brethren hated the poor man; even his friends withdrew far from him, and he became like a portent to many, because it was difficult to discern hearts concealed beneath the fox-skin of those who say and do nothing against the will of Minerva.

It is therefore better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. For faith in many persons is unstable, and the horned moon of certain men’s friendship suffers frequent eclipses. Why, brother, do you complain of these things as though they were unusual? The hatred and envy of his brothers could not have been allayed unless, after the pit’s abyss, the Ishmaelites or Potiphar had carried Joseph away for money; nor would the persecution of the envious have ceased [Col. 0017C] unless Daniel had been thrown into the lions’ den. Malice wages unceasing war against innocence. The vices of an unwise mind are wounds; by the very thing through which a vice is satisfied, its harm is increased. Thus the ill-wisher injures himself more than another.

Yet you have repeatedly and urgently advised me not to equip a Phalarian invective of follies against my haters, but rather to weave a miscellany in which I might set forth, by enumeration, the furnishings of my poor talent. Therefore let rivals enjoy their wormwood; let patience instil its nectar into us, since it is human to be angry, but devilish always to bear malice. Accordingly, my pen shall run through what I have written thus far, on what occasions, and with what intention. Although I judge this more likely to bring envy upon me than profit to you [Col. 0017D], it will nevertheless wrong no person of good will. Yet it seems by no means unsuitable first to touch on the useful writings of the brethren of our Church who were learned in letters; for it is safer to praise what belongs to others than one’s own work.

### CHAPTER I. On Lambert, the second abbot

Our second abbot Lambert, a man of manifold usefulness, wrote in a sufficiently polished style the Life and miracles of St. Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne. He also composed certain musical pieces about him and possessed a distinguished talent for making verses.

### CHAPTER II. On Stephen, the first abbot

He himself had succeeded Stephen, who, although he left no monument of any writing [Col. 0018A], nevertheless deserves to be written about, because he was eminent in learning, but more eminent in conduct, and showed himself a worthy master of the household. The resources of the still new Church were slight; accordingly, he laboured in every way either to acquire estates or to construct buildings, and, living soberly, deprived himself of what might benefit others.

He proportioned expenditure to the poverty of the resources, and held that a little possessed by the righteous was better than the many riches of sinners. At times he would joke with his companions about Vitellius, that most voracious Cyclops of the Roman Empire, who feasted four or five times daily and who, had not death removed him in good time, would have emptied the air of birds, the sea of fish, the earth of four-footed beasts, granaries of grain, and cellars of wine. For it is written that at one banquet, besides other expenses, [Col. 0018B] he squandered two thousand fish and seven thousand birds, so that he was by no means inferior in gluttony to the Babylonian Bel—though for that mighty diner, every night, twelve artabs of fine flour, forty sheep, and six amphorae of wine were set out to be consumed by a certain abyss of a divine belly.

But Stephen, both active in doing and teaching, after he had fought lawfully, passed to the crown which his name signified. He was a man worthy of heavenly revelations, especially since, as he once grieved over the brethren’s poverty, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a vision, notable alike in face and dress, and said that Saints Lawrence and Wolbodo had received this place from Christ [Col. 0018C] into their protection, and that its foundations stood upon the holy mountains. Moreover, if its inhabitants first sought the kingdom of God, all things necessary would be added to them. This he experienced then, and we experience it to this day, through Christ’s generosity—the Wisdom of God, with whom are riches and glory, proud resources and righteousness.

### CHAPTER III. On St. Wolbodo, Bishop of Liège

But since a son who recounts glorious men is by no means wholly without glory, I shall briefly describe who the aforesaid Wolbodo was. A Fleming by birth, he made parents already distinguished in nobility and possessions more glorious by his life, and more illustrious by his eminent learning. He was first a canon and master of the schools at the church of Utrecht, and later Bishop of Liège. Our elders committed certain things about him to writing, making clear how episcopally he lived.

I should not pass over this: being uniquely devoted to St. Lawrence the martyr, he gave his whole self to our place—his care and resources while living, his body after death. For he was buried among us in the crypt of the Holy Mother of God, in a laboriously made tomb, which bears in golden letters this epitaph:

> Great was the dignity of your flesh, but greater the grace of your character;  
> the office and throne of bishop set you in your place.  
> The rich and poor alike felt how you were present for every need:  
> whence came salvation to these and food flowed to those.  
>
> [Col. 0019A] Hence the same compassion is present for us all,  
> and therefore we honour your saving tomb.

Thus the little garden-bed of our Church is beautified with the double flower of rose and lily: the martyr adorns it with some portion of his relics, and the confessor with his whole body; each does so by patronage and merits.

### CHAPTER IV. On Everard III, Abbot of St. Lawrence

After Stephen we received as our third shepherd Everard, a monk of the church of Florennes, a man powerful in experience, in whom virtues possessed, as it were, a peaceful dwelling. He fed the Lord’s inheritance in the innocence of his heart and guided it by the understanding of his hands. But the shortness of his days intervened: he died so quickly that he did not live even a full year [Col. 0019B] beyond his accession. Yet may he not lack the fruit of his bright purpose and now well-flourishing care. Let him therefore be reckoned in the days of a true year; and, enrolled with the righteous, may he receive the land of inheritance, where there is length of life and sustenance, where there is light for the eyes and peace.

### CHAPTER V. On Louis, the elder monk and deacon

Louis, of good memory, had already written how relics of St. Lawrence were brought to us from the city of Rome.

### CHAPTER VI. On Falchalin, Louis’s disciple

Falchalin too, master of the schools, had been formed by his teaching. He assisted Franco, scholasticus of St. Lambert [Col. 0019C], in little works on the squaring of the circle and on the fasts of the Four Seasons.

### CHAPTER VII. On Heribrand, the fifth abbot, another pupil of Louis

Heribrand, our fifth abbot, was likewise his pupil. In him the grey hair of wisdom matched the grey hair of his head. According to Ecclesiastes (ch. 9), his garments were white at all times: chastity girded his loins, and he held in his hands a lamp burning with the works of love of God and neighbour. He was most ready both at dictation and versification, endowed with both sacred and secular learning. He committed to writing the Life of Theodoric the Younger, Abbot of St. Hubert [Col. 0019D]. He did not keep the money of learning stored away in a napkin, but willingly taught the ignorant, always employing gentleness both of mind and voice. For a learner grasps better what is said more gently by the teacher. Minds should be handled by art rather than force.

### CHAPTER VIII. On David the monk

David was a strong ass, who into old age and advanced years placed his shoulder beneath Christ’s sweet yoke and light burden. By day and by night he toiled at ecclesiastical duties. Now he gave himself to prayer, now to reading; now his fingers took up the pen, and he copied books of learned men for the brethren to read and meditate upon. For these are the bulwarks of David’s tower; these are the thousand shields hanging from it, the whole armoury of the mighty.

Though Phalaris may have raged with his burning bronze bulls, the Sicilian tyrant did not devise a greater torment than our Methuselah, who zealously rebuked the negligent and pressed hard upon the young lest they eat the bread of idleness [Col. 0020A]. David was bent with age, indeed, but never bent in goodwill. To yield some fruit of his indefatigable labour, he composed the Passion of St. Blaise and, finally, the Life of St. Eucherius of Orléans. Though the latter had a rich subject, he began its fabric with a coarser, hempen thread, as it were.

### CHAPTER IX. On Engelbert the monk

Engelbert, an investigator and follower of computus, put together certain theorems useful to computists. For, like Boötes at heaven’s pivot, while he continually pursues this art [Col. 0020B], he makes the wagon of memory revolve but does not allow it to set. Hence he acquired much knowledge. Therefore I would celebrate him in these verses of Maro [Virgil]:

> He who knew the courses of numbers and of heaven, and the stars;  
> the varying eclipses of the sun and the moon’s labours;  
> whence comes the trembling of the earth; by what force the deep seas swell,  
> when barriers burst, and then sink back into themselves;  
> why winter suns hasten so greatly to dip themselves in Ocean,  
> or what delay holds back the lingering nights.

### CHAPTER X. On Berengar, the fourth abbot

In those days scholarly studies flourished greatly among the monks and clerics of our city, and had flourished for a long time; nor was religion less vigorous, so that this splendidly suited the condition of the churches.

> How fair are your tents, Jacob, and your tabernacles, Israel:  
> like wooded valleys, like watered gardens beside rivers,  
> like tabernacles planted by the Lord, like cedars beside waters  
> (Num. 24).

Liège flourished in virtues and learning, as also in riches. Yet a man well supplied with letters was more esteemed than one well supplied with money. And since blessed is the land whose king is noble, our Church at that time emulated the pursuits of true blessedness, while Berengar, the fourth abbot, presided—a man nobler in spirit than in flesh, humble in kinship, yet, to use the words of a certain sage: “The eye of God looked upon him for good; He raised him from his low estate and exalted his head, and many marvelled at him.” Indeed, renowned for extraordinary discernment, he was conspicuous to kingdom [Col. 0020D] and Church like a lamp set upon a candlestick.

No less would I compare the brethren living under him to lilies growing by the passage of waters, because in many of them neither the whiteness of religion nor the fragrance of good repute was lacking, while they were watered also by literary learning.

### CHAPTER XI. On Robert, or Rupert, later Abbot of Deutz

Among these Robert shone forth like a golden earring and a gleaming pearl: a man attentive to wisdom, inclining his ear to prudence, seeking her as money and digging for her as for treasures. From boyhood he was raised at our monastery, and as he happily grew in years, so he grew in virtues. As memory strengthened his natural ability, when he added knowledge he added labour. What he poured into himself by reading, he poured back upon others by teaching; yet he was diligent in prayer and contemplation, especially in the watches before dawn. The more secretly he practised these, the more devoutly he persisted in them, as his heart grew warm within him and fire kindled in his meditation.

Nor was there any lack of the richness of tears; he offered these to the Lord as a most sweet-smelling sacrifice. For truly nothing is sweeter to Him than a spirit made sorrowful, a contrite and humbled heart. Hence Robert very often enjoyed divine illumination, and a clear dawn of understanding grew within him; for, as it is written, “He rises well at dawn who seeks good things.” Thus the Wisdom of God opened his understanding to comprehend the Scriptures and to expound them with the highest ability and greatest profit. This may be seen in his little works by anyone whose eye is not offended by either the cataract of envy or the bleary sight of ignorance.

While still young, therefore, he wrote a metrical little book in praise of the Holy Spirit, progressing more by that Spirit’s inspiration than by the instruction of any master. Likewise he wrote another, *On Diverse Sayings of Scripture*, and added a third in heroic verse, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*. In one little book he also narrated the state of our Church: by whom it was built, and what good or evil it received from the hand of the Lord, from Eraclus, Bishop of Liège, to Obert. On the same subject he composed another little work in Sapphic metre. Finally, he improved the Life of St. Augustine [Col. 0021B] and that of St. Odilia the Virgin with his shining style. He composed chants for St. Theodard the martyr and Saints Goar and Severus, confessors.

After becoming a priest, he ascended to the lofty heart, for now unfurling all the sails of intention and genius toward the true south wind, he produced twelve little books *On the Divine Offices*, or sacraments, celebrated in the Church throughout the yearly cycle. Then fourteen little books *On the Gospel of John*; forty-two books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*, where one may taste every fruit of Scripture, both new and old, which the Church says she has stored up for her beloved. At the request of Frederick, archpriest of Cologne, he explained the Apocalypse in twelve books and likewise the Twelve Prophets in thirty-one books with the greatest clarity. He wrote thirteen books *On the Victory of the Word of God*, and likewise thirteen *On the Gospel of Matthew*. In the next-to-last of these, he explains how wonderfully and gloriously he received the grace of writing from above, from the Father of lights.

For Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg, strongly urged him to commit this matter to writing, having adjured him—unwilling and long resisting—by the dread name of the Holy Trinity. Cuno rejoiced generously in that divine gift, and, as a kindly yet insistent exactor, most urgently encouraged Robert to use it. He frequently discussed the Scriptures with him and delighted in his spoken and written words as in every kind of wealth. Cuno was most zealous in sacred reading; his knowledge was adorned by excellent character and religion. He later became Bishop of Regensburg.

Robert himself had already become head of the church at Deutz [Col. 0022A] after the death of that place’s abbot. Although he was intensely occupied in this ministry, anxious after the manner of Martha and sometimes troubled about many things, nevertheless, after the manner of Mary, he diligently set before himself the one thing necessary.

For he sat at the Lord’s feet and heard His word, since he kept watch also over holy meditation and the work of writing. He had this praiseworthy custom: whenever he perceived that a lesser grace was present to him—for “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things, especially external things” (Wis. 9)—he humbled himself and cast himself before the crucified Lord; and from the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens (Apoc. 2:7), he asked that what had been closed might be opened. To one humbly seeking and faithfully knocking, it was immediately opened: light was poured upon his understanding, and in a wondrous manner he heard what the Lord God spoke within him. His tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe; those who draw near to His feet receive of His teaching. So richly had He endowed His lover and so filled the treasure of his breast that scarcely two or three scribes together could take down what he dictated.

Therefore it was not superfluous that he once saw in a vision of the night the Wisdom of God, the Word of God, kissing him. Her whole body seemed formed of the purest gold, and [Col. 0022B] from it many channels projected in every direction, pouring living waters upon him with force. For the Psalmist says: “The unfolding of Thy words, O Lord, gives light and gives understanding to little ones” (Ps. 118 [119]), that is, to the humble, that they may be enriched with knowledge of lofty mysteries, due only to friends, and abundantly watered. Wisdom herself also says:

> I, Wisdom, have poured forth rivers;  
> I have flowed from the river like a channel of immense water.  
> I have gone forth from paradise like the river Dorix [uncertain reading],  
> and like a conduit of water.  
> I said: “I shall water my garden of plants  
> and make drunk the fruit of my offspring.”  
> And my channel became abundant to me,  
> and my river drew near to the sea,  
> because I make doctrine shine forth like the dawn for all,  
> and shall declare it even to what is far off  
> (Ecclus. 24).

Accordingly, Robert also wrote seven little books on the Song of Songs; fifteen books on Samuel or David; and nine books *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. He also composed a treatise of five little books entitled *The Ring*, because it contains a dispute about faith between a Christian and a Jew. He further issued four little books on certain chapters of the Rule of St. Benedict. In the first he recounts the assaults of envious persons and the vexations he endured from slanderers, who charged him with being a heretic and with rashly corrupting the sacred Scriptures through perverse interpretations.

For this reason, while still a young man, he wrote an apologetic little book to Anselm, scholasticus of Laon, and William, Bishop of Châlons, then highly renowned masters in France, *On the Will of God*. In it he opposes those who, following the heresy of the Collyridians, said that God wills evil to occur—not the evil of affliction, which plainly must sometimes be inflicted for the correction of sinners, but every evil whatsoever that is contrary to goodness and virtue.

He also published some writings either against his accusers or against certain irreligious persons. One of these, a priest—or rather a concubinary—had asserted in pamphlets that priests might lawfully have intercourse with menstruating concubines. Another, a cleric who had become a monk—or rather, a dove turned raven—defending his error with shameless arguments, preferred to toss about and be endangered in the world rather than rest and be saved with the true Noah, that is, Christ, within the ark of the monastery.

Moreover, a severe fire once seized and consumed the buildings surrounding the monastery of Deutz [Col. 0023B]. Flames raged fiercely on every side, and the monastery itself was already in danger of collapse, unless divine mercy had sprinkled it with rain. For, as some were granted to see, a figure of starry brightness stood above and, with the edge of its garment like a fan, drove away the rising balls of fire. Thus the vapours retreated, and that house shone unharmed—no doubt fulfilling what the prophet says to the Lord: “When Thou art angry, Thou wilt remember mercy” (Hab. 3).

The parish church, however, was consumed by the fire. Yet there too Christ’s right hand was gloriously magnified. For the conflagration was so great that it melted that church’s bells; nevertheless, the little wooden chest [Col. 0023C] in which the Lord’s Body was kept enclosed in a pyx could not be destroyed by burning, because the Holy of Holies preserved His own most sacred thing—He whose flesh rested in hope, whose soul was not left in hell, and to whom it was granted not to see corruption.

Indeed, a corporal which one of the brethren carried on a long pole fell directly into the flames. When it was thought burnt, it sprang back in a miraculous manner and, poised in the air, deposited itself whole and uninjured upon the ground at some distance from the fire. This was no less a marvel than when the Babylonian furnace of old grew cool for the three youths, and the beastly tyrant trembled because no corruption had harmed them: not a hair of their heads was singed [Col. 0023D], their trousers were not changed, and the smell of fire did not pass over them.

Robert himself described these things for perpetual remembrance in a golden little book full of compunction, entitled *On the Fire*, and appended another, *On the Meditation of Death*. When he had completed some part of the latter, that counsellor of heavenly philosophy—ah, that fellow-initiate in divine speech—died, full indeed of days, as had been foretold to him some time earlier by revelation in the words read in Job: “You shall enter the grave in abundance” (Job 5).

That fruitful olive tree in the house of God, alas, was scorched by the sudden breath of fever and withered. Robert, equal in learning and virtues to the greatest teachers, was added to the people of the saints; among them may he enjoy unfadingly the oil of true peace and joy, and the light of the divine countenance [Col. 0024A], according to what is written: “Those who are learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto righteousness, as stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. 12:5).

### CHAPTER XII. On Wazelin, or Waselin, the second of that name, seventh Abbot of St. Lawrence

Wazelin, our seventh abbot, was taught by so distinguished a man. Having well received the seed of learning, he produced good shoots of virtue. The simplicity of the dove made him so gentle, and the prudence of the serpent so stern, that he found favour and discipline before God and men. While he set the gems of learning in the gold of religion, he acquired a fragrant reputation, like incense giving forth scent on summer days.

A book that he wrote, *On the Harmony and Exposition of the Gospels*, demonstrates his skill [Col. 0024B]. It is certainly a clear and useful work, and the diligent reader regrets that it remained unfinished. No less do the paintings or curtains in certain churches teach this, where, through sight, one may read and, through understanding, gather the splendid and singular harmony—dictated by him—of allegorical subjects from both the Old and New Testaments.

Finally, he proved himself serviceable to St. Nicholas by revising into a more polished composition certain rusty writings concerning that saint’s life or miracles. He composed solemn chants *On the Transfiguration of the Lord*, *On the Saints of Agaunum*, and *On St. Apollinaris the Martyr*. Moreover, through his energetic care, the oratory of St. George the martyr among us was built as devoutly as laboriously, as piously as suitably [Col. 0024C], so that through the patronage of the saints he might deserve to pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God.

Set over the Lord’s household, he gave them their measure of wheat in due season. Endowed with discretion and pleasing in speech, he was especially apt, both publicly and privately, to admonish or rebuke. He had now grown old; long labour in Christ’s service and, besides, illnesses that sometimes intervened, had worn him down. Yet with the undiminished keenness of reading, prayer, and contemplation, fixing the eyes of his soul upon the true sun, he was renewed in a striking manner by a certain freshness of youth.

This was after the manner of the phoenix. When its long life has been contracted by languid decay—for it is said to live more than five hundred years—it builds a pyre of aromatic twigs [Col. 0024D], sets itself alight by the beating of its wings and the fiery ray of the sun, but after three days rises again from its own ashes and returns anew as a youthful bird, a single and unique example. Hence, fittingly, whether from its phoenix-red—that is, reddish—colour, or because it is unique in the whole world, it is called in the language of the Arabs, who call the phoenix “the unique one.”

Although these points in some measure suit our Wazelin, they suit you above all, O Jesus Christ, unique and sole phoenix. To you in particular, I say, must they be ascribed, O Isaac, only-begotten one, laughter and love of the saints: you, anointed with the spices of every grace, offered yourself upon the wood of the cross to God through the love of the Holy Spirit; but with singular renewal, with unique youthfulness, after three days you flowered again from the tomb, now immortal and restored to life.

### CHAPTER XIII. Wazelin I, Abbot of St. Lawrence

Another Wazelin had preceded him in the abbacy. Though simple in natural ability, he was diligent in religious zeal. From youth to old age he rightly performed ecclesiastical offices—now reading, now chanting psalms, now praying—like a strong ox industriously threshing in the Lord’s threshing-floor. He was gentle and approachable, imitating holy Moses rather than that Carmelite Nabal, more twisted than a camel, who never uttered anything upright or peaceable.

Let students remember Wazelin. Wazelin cherished students like a father. Free himself from bitter envy [Col. 0025B], he used sweetly and often to repeat: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of Thy house” (Ps. 25 [26]).

### CHAPTER XIV. On Lambert the monk

Lambert commented upon Aesop’s fables. Their author, indeed, had shrewdly invented them to portray human character. But our commentator, setting morality aside, laboured over allegory. In this he was not at all shrewd, wishing to forge sacred matters out of such things, as though figs could be gathered from thorns or grapes harvested from a bramble.

Accordingly, on the Kalends of March that book was read before the senate of mice; it was discussed, condemned, and received a gnawing sentence. Thus Palestinian mice rushed in from fields and villages and, with savage teeth, attacked, gnawed, and scattered the written letters [Col. 0025C]. What hope was there of recovering it? We lacked the famous resources of the Philistines, who could spend golden mice upon their vows; not even parchment was available. And Pergamum—which first gave its name to parchments through both their use and abundance—was exceedingly difficult and arduous for us to reach. Thus that Aesopic sacramentary entirely perished.

### CHAPTER XV. On Gislebert the monk

Gislebert made his agile and brilliant talent more agile through exercise and likewise more brilliant through practice. He continually occupied both mind and hand, either meditating on something or writing. Thus he wrote in heroic verse a History of Joseph and extended it into one volume. Then he composed the Deeds of David in the same metre, dividing the work into twelve little books [Col. 0025D]. He is plain and easy, yet deserving of praise because he used easy means in a difficult work, according to these verses of his own:

> I composed poems and completed them with welcome labour,  
> imposing upon myself a truly difficult rule.  
> The rule was that I should take care to render word for word.  
> Certainly this is a hard thing, most worthy of much praise,  
> and a distinguished task: from prose that walks on foot,  
> from lowly prose, to run in leaping verse,  
> and to follow the open circuit, so that anyone may hope to do the same,  
> labour much, and labour in vain.

Nor are his little works without welcome usefulness [Col. 0026A], since he adorns the field of historical narrative with the mystical flowers of allegories. Though he excelled in other arts, he most especially made sweet melodies in music, as is clear from chants which he composed on St. George the martyr, St. Ragenufla the virgin, and St. Begga.

### CHAPTER XVI. On John the monk, Gislebert’s brother

John too, his brother both in spirit and flesh, was a scholasticus in both learning and office. As a boy, I often trembled at his ferule as no one ever trembled more at Hercules’ club. Alas, how often, when he demanded or examined our little compositions and looked askance at tablets seized in his hooked hands! Alas, how often I thought that I had encountered Virgil’s one-eyed Polyphemus!

Once, when he was ill and, in a very remarkable manner, taken outside and above himself, he saw many things worthy of remembrance, which he published in writing for edification. He also composed two chants, on St. Christopher the martyr and St. Mary of Egypt; he set forth the History of Tobit and likewise the Martyrdom of St. Stephen the Protomartyr in heroic metre, and he set part of the Song of Songs to antiphonal melody.

### CHAPTER XVII. On Nizo the monk

Nor shall I omit our Nizo, whom we had as an exemplar of learning, though his natural gifts were in some sense unpromising. Though his talent was dull and almost tortoise-like, he sharpened it through exercises, until by continual meditation and reading, as though on two wings, he rose [Col. 0026C] to the height of polished advancement.

He produced fine melodies on Saints John and Paul, martyrs; Saints Nazarius and Celsus; and Lord Frederick, Bishop of Liège. From that bishop’s deeds, death, and miracles he also wrote a little book. A simple man, he could be deceived but did not know how to deceive. Thus, when we were boys being taught by him, whenever he was angry we easily outwitted him from any direction, and evaded the blows of his raised and striking hand as though they fell from the high air.

### CHAPTER XVIII. On many others not named individually

We have expressly named our brethren whom we discovered had written something, although there were also many others commendable alike for learning and religion, of whom it would be both pleasant and useful to make remembrance. But our pen has not now undertaken to write more about them.

This is what we desire with all our power; this is what we implore of you, O Christ, who number the multitude of the stars and call them all by their names, the most knowing reckoner of the saints: write upon them the name of your God, and the name of the city of the new Jerusalem which descends from heaven from your God, and your new name. Grant them, I pray, a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.

## SECOND LITTLE BOOK

[Col. 0027]

### CHAPTER I. On Reiner’s own earliest little works

[Col. 0027A]

Just as I have briefly recorded the studies or little works of those who have long since departed from the world, so, dearest friend, I wished to unfold for you the talents or writings of our brethren who still survive. But two considerations delay me: lest I be accused either of spite if I praise praiseworthy things too faintly, or of flattery if I give their merits the praise they deserve. Their own monuments will therefore make them more truly known and more convincingly manifest; for what earns favour in a man’s own person does not give offence when said by another.

Accordingly, I shall now satisfy your request—indeed, your importunity—and unfold my follies for you alone.

While still young, I published certain laments on the afflictions of the Church in diverse kinds of metre [Col. 0027B] and rhythm. I was driven by zeal for learning and, a small poet myself, I attempted as best I could to imitate the great poets.

Thus I composed a little work on the New and Old Testaments, divided into two books. I called this too *The Panther*, because it was variegated, as it were, with prose and metres.

At that time I also composed certain things *On Computus*.

Finally, I wrote in prose a little book *On the Hanging of a Certain Thief*.

I also wrote the Martyrdom of the Seven Maccabean Brothers in heroic verse.

Then I treated at greater length, in Asclepiadean metre, that chapter of the Apostle: “Do you not know [Col. 0027C] that those who run in the stadium all run indeed, but one receives the prize?” (1 Cor. 9).

But someone intimate to our household stole away these little works which I have now recalled, against my will. Copies were not available, and what I feared came to pass: I was deprived of the first fruits of my labours. For, seeking conversion, he departed to another region and carried these spoils away with him as a pledge of mutual affection.

### CHAPTER II. His melody on the saints, and its fate

Moreover, while I was being trained in musical art, I composed a melody on Saints Sixtus, Felicissimus, and Agapitus, in order that I might assign some fruit to my study. For diligent practice is the growth of talent; and the art is shown to possess a wonderful innate power, since by its sweetness it commonly produces much devotion and compunction in pious hearts.

Certain persons, however, paying no attention to this, reckoned it frivolity and wantonness when I diligently practised it. One of them, supported at that time by the tribunals of a second priorate, seized the tablets on which I had impressed my feeble thoughts and examined them for a while. Meanwhile I yawned with fear. For the grim [Col. 0028A] face of the man and his raised brows foretold coming evil to me. O judge more severe than Minos or Athamas! Reading, he growled; chanting, he bent from one side to the other. And behold: as though struck by some great affront, he began to ruin the innocent wax and, with the hostile plough of his fingernail, to obliterate what had been inscribed.

What was I to do? Should I struggle, make an outcry, hurl insults? The sickles of rods were in the chapter-house; there were many accusers, so that I had to think carefully of the tumult of Pharisees and Sadducees by which Paul had once been endangered in the council. Should I call down a plague with a murmur? An anathema clenched between the teeth would profit nothing. What then? I lower my ears like an ass of unjust disposition when a heavier burden comes upon its back, and, with the patience of hypocrites, I grow tame for calamity.

[Col. 0028B] But should I again entrust chosen pieces to wax? That crueler nail would threaten them. Should I restore them upon little parchments? I kept turning over in my mind the brazier and coals of King Jehoiakim, and the penknife of the scribe Jehudi—especially since I was no Jeremiah, nor had I Baruch for my secretary. Therefore I cooled from my undertaking. At last, a long time having passed, I began to consider whether any remnants of those same songs remained in my memory. It was recovered so readily, as though I had it written before my outward eyes, that I certainly felt in some fashion that God does not despise simple vows. Thus I gave to parchment what had been restored to memory. Nor did I pursue idleness, which is the enemy of the soul, since it was sweeter to be continually [Col. 0028C] occupied. For that saying of Solomon stirred me:

> Do not love sleep, lest poverty oppress you;  
> Open your eyes and satisfy yourself with bread  
> (Prov. 20).

And that saying of Horace:

> You will not wake in order to save yourself; yet,  
> If you refuse to be well, you will run about dropsical; and unless  
> You ask for a book and a lamp before daylight, unless  
> You turn your mind to studies and honourable pursuits,  
> Envy or love will torment you while you are awake.

## CHAPTER III. Other Works of Reiner

Accordingly, in two little books I described the conversion of Saint Pelagia, and gave this small work the title: *Mirror of Repentance*.

Then, likewise in a double little book, I set forth the Passion of the Cappadocian virgin Maria, with this prefixed title: *The Virginal Palm*.

Subsequently, I embraced the Life of the hermit Theobald in two little books as well, and called it *The Flower of the Wilderness*.

These works had indeed previously been written in the rough style of dictation; but, at the prompting of certain persons, I polished them with such small file of learning as I could command. For one must comply with devout friends when they make demands. The deeds of the saints, moreover, are reckoned common material; nor should one be [Col. 0029A] branded with vanity who pursues studies of piety.

Finally, I composed a small work entitled *A Certain Funeral Booklet on the Death of a Friend*, to whose tomb I also added an inscription of four verses.

## CHAPTER IV. Reiner’s Most Serious Illness and Health Divinely Restored

After these things, a most severe wasting sickness entered our community, and sharp fevers, made fiercer by the heat of the dog days, confined very many brethren to their beds and consigned some to their graves. Our choir was turned into mourning, while we were either sick or dying, while we were shaken by fear or grief. But you, O watchful and holy one, who neither sleep nor slumber, who keep Israel—you, O gracious Jesus, care for [Col. 0029B] us. You behold us and all our actions every day, from earliest dawn until evening.

This was then plainly shown also to one of the brethren. While he was present at the nocturnal psalmody and was dozing, a certain figure of star-like beauty stood by him and gently struck him, saying: “Why do you sleep? Watch and pray” (Luke 22). God has promised a crown to those who keep watch. He watched and observed that, standing in the midst of the choir, she indicated by a certain intelligible gesture those who were then about to depart this life. Then she ascended the steps of the sanctuary and vanished.

I, a little vessel of misery and sickness—I, mire and ignoble clay—then grievously felt the rod of God’s wrath watching over me. Struck by it, I was almost reduced to [Col. 0029C] nothing. For I was sick unto death, and the Lord turned all my bed in my sickness; he filled me with bitterness and made me drunk with wormwood. Funeral signs had now driven out hope of life, when, entirely deprived for a week of food and sleep, and with my brain almost dried up by burning fever, I was in danger, carried away by phantasies, speaking things foreign to myself. But the brethren’s devout and diligent compassion threw itself at the knees of divine mercy on my behalf, and commended this dying body of lowest corruption to him who holds the keys of death and hell, who was dead and did not see corruption, but behold, lives for ever and ever.

Accordingly, I was carried into the crypt of the holy Mother of God, to the tomb of Lord Bishop Wolbodon, whom I mentioned [Col. 0029D] above. There I lay until about midnight. The weakness that had consumed my whole little body was now creeping toward the seat of the soul, and the deadly bar was being placed upon my closing senses, when behold, I saw that holy man, flourishing in pure grey hair and splendid in the rest of his priestly attire, standing at the right side of my bed and making over me the sign of the cross for the third time. Immediately I felt the power of his blessing. For sweat burst forth, as it were, with every limb trembling; my eyes, made sour by wakefulness, received sweet sleep; and my stomach was no longer distressed by lack of food, but by fasting.

Thus, by the inestimable compassion and wondrous condescension of the blessed Mother of God—who had offered me, most unworthy as I was, the infant hanging upon the cross to adore and kiss—and also by the intercession of the holy confessor [Col. 0030A] who had blessed me unto life, I was drawn back from the very jaws of death. Yet what groans shall my soul utter? What tears shall my eyes shed? I have become trembling and afraid that this postponement of my death may prove too little a correction of my life. But I know, Lord, that a man’s way is not his own, nor is it in his power to walk and direct his steps. Correct me, therefore, yet not in judgment nor in your wrath, lest perhaps you reduce me to nothing; but you who know my frame, strengthen it as you can, for without you nothing is strong.

## CHAPTER V. Reiner’s Gratitude toward the Heavenly Physicians; A Certain Vision of Divine Judgment

After I was strengthened by restored health, I rendered such poor little gifts as I could: namely, to the very Mother [Col. 0030B] of mercy, a prayer of a contrite spirit expressed rhythmically; and a melody concerning the same confessor, elaborated into divine praises.

Finally, I do not think it superfluous to add what one brother then saw concerning another brother. One was struggling toward death; the other lay very ill. One dawn, while he was awake, he plainly saw in that same house a person of judicial authority sitting upon a raised tribunal. Before him certain men in white were conducting the cause of the dying man, answering the accusations and objections of demons raging noisily outside. By a certain divine power, indeed, these demons were kept from breaking in. Nothing was more dreadful than their appearance: their envy and malice, as it were, issued from their eyes in a sulphurous stench and horror that caused them to waste away; and they had surrounded the place as though in a hunting enclosure. At last, when the soul departed and that judge withdrew with the blessed spirits, then they pursued it with such unbearable tumult and disorderly shouting that one might have believed the whole air was being assaulted by excessive storms. O lamentable hour! O terrible judgment! O that necessity beyond all dread! How blessed is he whom a good conscience then renders safe!

## CHAPTER VI. Various Works of Reiner

For some time thereafter I had discontinued the labour of writing, because I took greater pleasure in reading, or devoted myself according to my strength to the instruction of the brethren. Yet, urged by a friend because of a certain need, I composed at length a work which I called *A Reminder of Piety*.

But lest the stylus, fixed to the wall, should waste away with the rust-disease while the wax tablets slept in mouldiness, I wrote for a certain intimate a little work *On the Notable Features of the Islands of Sardinia and Sicily*, arranged in verse in two books.

Likewise, for another man, two little books: the first, *On the Conflict of Two Dukes and a Wonderful Revelation of Souls*; the second, *On a Certain Captured Soldier Who Was Delivered through the Saving Sacrifice*.

Moreover, everyone more willingly cultivates that art which he has acquired most fully through learning and practice. Therefore, as the labour of composition had gained for me some slight capacity, I undertook a work which I myself knew exceeded my small talent—rashly transgressing, indeed, that counsel of Horace:

> You who write, choose material equal  
> To your powers, and long consider what your shoulders  
> Refuse to bear and what they can sustain. He whose chosen subject is within his strength  
> Will lack neither eloquence nor lucid order.

Thus I set forth, as best I could, in fourteen little books a history describing how, in our own time, holy Jerusalem and many other eastern cities and regions were recovered by western Christians. Its title is *The Laurel of the Jerusalemite Pilgrims*. Afterwards a severe sickness cast me upon my bed.

## CHAPTER VII. Reiner’s Second Illness, Divinely Driven Away

Now, my flesh consumed, my bone clung to my skin; now, according to the prophet, the Lord had made my skin and flesh old and had crushed my bones. Appetite for food had utterly failed, and veins deprived of moisture denied sleep as it came upon me. Therefore the eye of my soul wept before God, because his wrath passed over me and his terrors troubled me. For the soul is watered with its own tears; and, dissolved by contrition and moved by some inexpressible feeling, it stirs the very bowels of the Paraclete Spirit through most tender weeping and most powerful groaning, and so merits consolation.

One of the brethren came to visit me and directed that I have the names of the seven holy sleepers written on a slip and bound around my head. By this remedy of devout faith, the ability to sleep is sometimes restored to the sick. I put faith in it and did as he directed; and already I seemed in some manner to hear inwardly: “Your faith has made you whole” (Mark 10). For suddenly, in an ecstasy of mind, I saw myself in a certain royal hall, suffused with inestimable light and incredible fragrance. Its lamp, its glory, and its joy were the majesty of the true, uniquely desirable, blessed, and adorable Trinity. But an intemperate and presumptuous mouth must be restrained, lest, wretched man that I am, I burden my miseries too heavily. Let it suffice to have said this alone in thanksgiving: among the choirs of those clad in purple and white who were present, I recognized those saints, gloriously distinguished by golden crowns and crimson purple. There new and most sweet [Col. 0031D] songs resounded, and angelic instruments performed that responsory:

> These are the saints who gave up their bodies for God’s covenant,  
> And washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb  
> (Rev. 22).

But when I returned to myself, I looked about with astonished eyes, scarcely aware where I was. Meanwhile, a familiar brother sat beside my bed. When he urgently asked why I was looking about in that manner, since friendship owes confidence to one that has been tested, I told him the vision. I soon discovered that it had not been idle. My limbs were so weakened by sickness, so bound as though in chains by pain, that for seven days I could neither rise nor stand except with another’s assistance. Yet through the sight of that mighty and merciful one, [Col. 0032A] “who sent forth his prisoners from the pit wherein is no water, by the blood of his covenant,” I was so freed and strengthened that I then rose without any support and went with the aforesaid brother to the oratory, pouring forth thanks with all my heart. Thus health was restored to me; and to the seven holy sleepers I offered a small and wholly unequal, yet heartfelt, gift of praise and thanksgiving: namely, a melody composed concerning them.

But if anyone should take offence, if anyone should count it boastfulness that I write such things, will he forbid a miserable man to remember the mercies of the Lord?
