No well-disposed person accuses a simple and devout intention. It is indeed good to conceal the secret of a king, but honourable to reveal and confess the works [Col. 0032B] of God. Moreover, it belongs to a reverent mind not to think lofty thoughts but to agree with the lowly; for heavenly revelations are for the devout instruments not of vice but of virtue. But what benefit is it for the ungodly, such as Balaam or Nebuchadnezzar, to have seen divine things? The sun confounds diseased eyes. It is not a holy vision but a holy action that merits God.

## CHAPTER VIII. Other Works of Reiner Thereafter

I also wrote in verse a little book concerning the arrival of the relics of Saint Lawrence at Liège from the city of Rome.

Moreover, at the request of the brethren, I composed many prayers to be recited to that martyr himself and to many other saints.

Finally, I published for certain priests a little book *On the Reverence Due to Sacred Places*, sharply rebuking them because they permitted girlish choruses and other detestable acts, words, and songs to take place near cemeteries or bodies of the dead, especially at night vigils, before those bodies were carried into the church.

A sophist, however, striving to exalt his own works and depreciate ours, set before me in writing obscure questions and barbarous expressions gathered from every quarter. I thought I had encountered Daedalus’s labyrinth and the horns of the Minotaur. By what way could I escape? By what means could I be guided? The threads of subtle intellect were lacking. With what could I defend myself? There was no sword of eloquent speech. Nevertheless, I unravelled those entanglements, escaped the dreadful horned beast, and the little book received this title: *He Who Speaks Sophistically Is Odious*.

[Col. 0032D] Since it is evident that human nature is so constituted that it is refreshed by alternation and that change removes weariness, I varied my study: now prose, now verse, and at times music. For this reason I began two chants concerning the holy confessors Anthony and Jerome, especially because I wished to render some service of my smallness to such great patrons. O brutish little man that I am! O soul bent down to earth and empty of heavenly things! Yet at times, daring to lift the face of my mind, and raised as it were on the twin wings of heart and tongue, I entered the angelic mysteries. For I composed in verse three little books concerning the victory of Michael the archangel: both that victory by which he was glorified with his angels over the ancient dragon and its angels, and that by which, fighting gloriously for Christians against pagans, he made himself known when he founded and dedicated a new sanctuary on Mount Gargano. No costly heaps of metals, marbles, and cedars were expended upon that structure; rather, he opened out a rock’s hollow recess with an unpolished vault, displaying more religion than workmanship. For you, O glorious champion—for you, I say, O magnificent admirer, according to your name, of the Trinity to be glorified and admired! Indeed, “Who is like God?” Human hearts enriched with faith, hope, and charity please him more than rich material of such things.

I also composed, at the request of certain canons, some musical pieces concerning Saint Servatius and Saint Begga.

[Col. 0033B] A brother, to whose affection I was indebted and whose devotion I wished to satisfy, asked me to weave together seven hymns concerning the Holy Spirit. While he often edified me in familiar conversation, he related among other matters something venerable and memorable. Once, as he devoted himself earnestly to vigils and to invocation of that same Holy Spirit, at twilight he fell into an ecstasy. He saw himself carried into the Church by someone of utterly wonderful brightness and sweetness, clothed in a girded white garment gleaming more brightly than snow; the Church was solemnly endowed with light and fragrance. This person embraced him with most sweet affection, placing both hands upon his breast, as a loving mother is accustomed to press a nursing infant to her sweet breasts. But she hid her face whenever that brother turned himself toward her more frequently and tried longingly to look upon her. For he understood that she was the Holy Spirit; nevertheless, he saw that face for a little while—a face concerning which silence is required, since it is safer to be pierced with compunction concerning it than to speak, safer to venerate mysteries than to dispute about mysteries.

Finally, that same brother lifted from his breast the right hand of the most merciful Creator and most gracious Restorer; fitting its fingers to his own hands in order to make the sign of the cross, he impressed with that hand upon his heart, loins, and kidneys the saving seal three times, that he might be protected and strengthened against troublesome thoughts and fleshly desires, while the choir of white-clad ones present sang in melodious voices:

> Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice;  
> Seek the Lord and be strengthened;  
> Seek his face always  
> (Ps. 104).

[Col. 0034A] That brother found by experience that the vision had not been idle, as he contritely and tearfully testified that from that time he was infused with a certain light of mind and that the assaults of fleshly impulses had been greatly moderated in him.

> Blessed indeed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord,  
> And teach out of your law,  
> That you may give him relief from evil days  
> (Ps. 93).

## CHAPTER IX. The Remaining Memorials of Reiner’s Talent

Furthermore, in a work of five little books, I set down how, in our days, the Church of Liège recovered the castle of Bouillon by divine power after the invaders had been overcome; and I prefixed the title *The Bouillon Triumph* [Col. 0034B]. I also reinforced this same work with a musical setting.

At the brethren’s devout request, I also composed two chants concerning the holy martyrs Evermarus and Urban.

I wrote very many epitaphs and letters.

Thus, in such or similar trifles, I spent my wretched life; and upon the burdens of monastic life we in turn laid these burdens also on the back of our little ass. Yet far be it from me to expect the pointed critical obeli of certain men, with which they may pierce my little sheets. I judge what I have written or write to be of no importance at all—indeed, unlearned and foolish. Still, I prefer somehow to make my own things rather than appropriate another’s, to use my domestic anvil rather than a foreign one, and not to patch together poor Latin from good Latin. O praiseworthy craftsman, whoever you are, strive to become a new Tubal-cain. Practise praiseworthy things after the example of the ancient one. Let your own fire and your own tool commend you. For it belongs to a lazy craftsman always to desire another’s hammers and bellows, and ingloriously to beg continually at another’s forge. A stream is not judged to be from a spring unless it pours forth from its own vein. What is poured in from outside belongs to another. Therefore I must beware; above all I must retain that rebuke of Flaccus [Horace], in which he advises his friend:

> Let him seek private wealth and avoid touching  
> The writings which Palatine Apollo has received,  
> Lest, if ever he comes with his own property and then  
> The flock of birds brings back its feathers,  
> The little crow, stripped of its stolen colours, provoke laughter.

# THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0033]

## CHAPTER I. The Subject of the Book Is Proposed

[Col. 0033D]

Let my own trifles be marked, as it were, with a black pebble. But now I should wish for little tablets of Parian marble, now for precious pearls of milky appearance, so that a bright pebble might sort into number the matters which a close friend lately proposed for discussion. For they are worthy of inquiry and useful to know; and one person rightly obtains what he wishes to benefit many. Namely, he asked: Why are nine antiphons beginning with O sung in church over the Gospel canticle at the evening synaxis during the nine days before the Lord’s Nativity? Likewise, why is the Passion of Saint Stephen the protomartyr celebrated on the second day after the Lord’s Nativity, and the assumption of Saint John the Evangelist on the third, when—according to the tradition of the elders—the one suffered on the third day before the Nones of August [3 August], while the other was assumed to perpetual [Col. 0035A] immortality on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June], indeed by dying, but nevertheless by returning to life more quickly? Why also is the fourth day assigned to the Innocents, when it is not readily established that their passion occurred then? I shall first discuss these matters, and afterwards the remaining questions that he asked, treating them more fully at the petitioner’s desire, though I would have preferred to be more concise.

## CHAPTER II. Why Are the Nine Antiphons Beginning with the Letter O Sung at Vespers During the Nine Days before the Lord’s Nativity?

Accordingly, it is believed in the heart unto righteousness and confessed with the mouth unto salvation that the only-begotten Son of God, incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, was made man. Since, therefore, Wisdom, by the will of the Father, built itself the house of the body and hewed out the seven pillars of graces, that wondrous incarnation was formed and celebrated within the virgin’s womb during nine months. Therefore, we likewise commemorate it in a more solemn praise during nine bright days. We appoint a day in place of a month. For we must also attend to other offices, whether of seasons or solemnities, and other mysteries must also be celebrated; it would be less fitting and reasonable to be occupied continuously with one thing. Human nature tires of constant repetition; it receives more gladly what is rarer.

That these praises are performed near the end of the day, at the setting of the sun, splendidly signifies that he who was born of the Father before all ages—God from God, light from light, begotten not made—when the fullness of time came, was made and begotten of a woman: namely, when the Dayspring from on high visited us, to enlighten those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. For he himself says in the Apocalypse: “I am α and ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 22), since all things were made or created through him and in him, and all things were renewed or brought to perfection through him and from him.

These upper letters undoubtedly signify this to some extent: α is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, and ω the last. Yet observe that a mystery lies beneath more clearly. Greek letters not only form words but also express numbers; and as each letter comes later in the order, it denotes by its character a larger number. Thus α signifies one, while ω signifies [Col. 0035D] eight hundred. And truly, mercifully, graciously, he who was the Father’s only or only-begotten Son desired at the end of the ages to have with himself sons of God—not by nature, indeed, but by adoption—like eight hundred, that is, innumerable persons nobly endowed with the eight beatitudes. Therefore we in every way marvel at this work of piety, this mystery of mercy, admirable even to the nine orders of angels. Although we cannot equal with heart or mouth the thanksgivings due for so great a benefit, as the Wise Man says:

> In glorifying the Lord, exalt him as much as you can;  
> Yet he will still surpass you, and his magnificence is wonderful.  
> In blessing the Lord, exalt him as much as you are able;  
> For he is greater than all praise. When you exalt him, gather strength,  
> And do not labour in vain, for you will not attain  
> (Sirach).

Yet it would be impious ingratitude not to give thanks. Therefore we render to God glorification, blessing, and exaltation as the expression of our gratitude; and by nine antiphons let us utter a manifold petition, but one harmonious song, to the everlasting Sun, now about to illuminate the circle of the day with fullness of light. For in Christ dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity; and, like a bridegroom coming forth from the chamber of the virginal age, he displayed himself bedewed and filled with every sweetness of virtues and wondrous fragrance of every grace. Therefore, since three sets of three antiphons have been composed in praise of the thrice-holy Trinity after the pattern of the three sets of three graces, we desire, if it is granted from above, to discuss the harmony of each set.

## CHAPTER III. The Mystery of the First Antiphon, “O Wisdom,” Is Explained; An Appearance of Wisdom Granted to a Certain Person Is Related

The first of the graces which the Apostle mentions in writing to the Ephesians is the word of wisdom. The first of the antiphons, “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High,” corresponds to it even on the literal surface. But God made all things in wisdom; the Most High created the universe through the Word which came forth from his mouth, because “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32). This Wisdom indeed “reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8), because, desiring to have its delights with the children of men, it bent itself from divinity—beyond which there is nothing—to humanity, which was the last thing created among beings.

Therefore Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, after healthfully and powerfully completing the work which the Father had given him to do, ascended whence he had descended; for “his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit unto its height” (Ps. 18). For he had proceeded and come from God, crowned with the golden crown of charity and mercy, and sustained by the fullness of graces, so that even the letter which the Church utters in invoking him—namely O—may be shown to signify the complete form of his own roundness. Finally, I learned that this same thing was shown from heaven in a vision to a certain faithful person. Yet some are accustomed to make light of it and mock, objecting the saying of the wise man:

> The imprudent exalt dreams, like one who grasps a shadow  
> And chases the wind; so also is one who attends to lying visions  
> (Sirach 34).

To them the answer is that the same writer adds a little later:

> Dreams are vanity for those who act wickedly, and your heart suffers phantasies like that of a woman in labour, unless a visitation has been sent from the Most High  
> (ibid.).

For both canonical Scripture and other writings offer many examples that not every vision and not every dream is false or erroneous, and that revelations, rather than dreams, are sometimes sent from the Most High to devout persons, especially to those who, like Daniel, are men of desires. Thus Job also reads:

> In a dream, in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon men  
> And they slumber in their beds,  
> Then he opens the ears of men  
> And, instructing them, teaches them with discipline  
> (Job 33).

Apart from its more hidden meaning, this may also be understood quite appropriately in the literal sense.

The Wisdom of God, then, seemed to be seated upon a golden throne, likewise having upon her head a golden crown, which the springtime grace of jewels made distinct. Her face flourished in unfading brightness, while her eyes shone wondrously with a certain vigour of hidden light. She was clothed in exceedingly white linen and wrapped in a gilded mantle. So too the ark of the covenant shone with the purest gold within and without, and received a golden crown above it, because for the Son of God it is as a diadem or ornament of the head that, as he willed by grace, so he was able by power to assume human nature. Moreover, a wondrous fragrance breathed forth, like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed.

Around her sat men conspicuous in appearance and clothing, budding with a certain youthful bloom like lilies; rays proceeding on every side from Wisdom herself illumined them. They held in their hands lyres fashioned of snowy ivory and elaborately adorned with gold, on which they played most sweet music, those verses of the Psalm:

> The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls;  
> The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones;  
> The justices of the Lord are right, making hearts glad;  
> The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes;  
> The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for age upon age;  
> The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves,  
> More desirable than gold and much precious stone,  
> And sweeter than honey and the honeycomb  
> (Ps. 18).

[Col. 0037C] There was also a title, as though laid out in sapphire-coloured lettering:

> I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel,  
> And am present among learned thoughts.

For that aforesaid faithful man had meditated in his heart during that night and had poured out his soul within himself. Remembering the works and judgments of the Lord from the beginning of time, and also his own miserable condition, he had been greatly afflicted and humbled, and had watered his bed with tears. Through the overflowing compassion of divinity he received this vision for consolation. For the enjoyment by a devout soul of heavenly utterances is both a benefit of consolation and an incentive to devotion.

Therefore: “O Wisdom, who order all things sweetly!” For you are gracious to all, and your mercies are over all your works. Come to teach us the way of prudence: that is, teach us how the mighty angel, of whom John writes, descended from heaven clothed with a cloud, with a rainbow upon his head, his face like the sun, his feet like pillars of fire, and an open little book in his hand; teach us the mysteries of that book, so that your justifications may be songs to us in the place of our pilgrimage.

## CHAPTER VI. Mysteries of the Second Antiphon: “O Adonai”

The second grace is the word of knowledge, to which the second antiphon, “O Adonai,” plainly corresponds. For we have in [Col. 0038A] the Scriptures how the Lord—whose name is interpreted *Adonai*—was a guide in his mercy to the people whom he redeemed; how he led them about, taught them, and guarded them like the pupil of his eye. Indeed, he says that he disclosed to Moses the name which he had not disclosed to the fathers: “I am the Lord who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, and I did not disclose to them my name Adonai” (Exod. 6)—with the implication, “as I am about to disclose it to you, either by signs or by speaking face to face.” Previously he had appeared to him in the fire of the flame of the bush; and when Moses said, “I will go and see this great vision, why the bush is not burned,” he said: “Do not approach here; take the sandal from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3). Therefore, when we make for so venerable a sight, we too must put off the sandal of fleshly timidity, so that, walking in the spirit of humility, we may deserve to enjoy that living and life-giving fire.

That bush prefigured blessed Mary, who truly appears beautiful in the crimson blush of modest virginity. The bush burned but was not consumed, because when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, the virgin was enkindled with ineffable love, but was not burned up. For she conceived God, the Word of God, in her mind and bore him made flesh, while remaining inviolate after childbirth and utterly free from fleshly concupiscence. O fire of sweetness! O flame of delight! O singular blaze, in which the material of a most chaste flesh not only did not dry up but rather blossomed with a rose so special that heaven and earth are made crimson!

Finally, that fiery brightness also signified the zeal and splendid wonders which the Lord would soon perform [Col. 0038C] in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis. Yet above all it signified the humanity of Jesus Christ, burning with charity and shining with miracles. Of him John the Baptist, than whom no greater has arisen among those born of women, says: “He it is who is to come after me, who was made before me, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie” (John 1). For Christ’s sandal is his humanity, with which his divinity is shod—that is, surrounded. The sandal strap, intricate to our understanding, is the subtlety of so great a mystery. Therefore I stand back and, with Moses, hide my face. I do not dare look upon God; but, cast upon the earth, because I am dust and shall return to dust, with all the affection of my soul and the full depth of my senses I cry aloud that true praise of the true Virgin: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1).

Moreover, on the fiftieth day after Israel’s departure from Egypt—the house of Jacob from a barbarous people—the Law of Moses was given on Sinai, when the Lord descended upon it in fire and smoke ascended from it as from a furnace, and the sound of the trumpet rang out ever more loudly; when thunders were heard and lightning flashed, and a very thick cloud covered the mountain, and the people in the camp were afraid. But all these things happened to them as a figure. For they prefigured what was done on the day of Pentecost, after the true Moses—that is, Christ—had led the people of the saints out from infernal Egypt, led them through the Red [Col. 0039A] Sea of his Passion, and, lifted up from the waters of passibility and mortality, had been glorified by resurrection and ascension. For suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty wind approaching, and it filled the whole house where the apostles were sitting; and divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them and rested upon each of them; and all were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance (Acts 2). Then, as the trumpet of such resonant preaching sounded, a multitude gathered and was confused in mind, because each person heard them speaking the mighty works of God in his own language. Then, I say, the thunders sounded and the lightning flashed, as miracles shone forth and divine judgments from the Scriptures were brought against them—for example:

> The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like me. Him you shall hear according to all that I spoke to you. And it shall be: every soul that does not hear that prophet shall be cut off from the people  
> (Deut. 18).

Or this saying of Joel:

> Indeed, upon my servants and upon my handmaids in those days  
> I will pour out from my Spirit, and they shall prophesy;  
> And I will give wonders in heaven above  
> And signs on earth below:  
> Blood and fire and a vapour of smoke.  
> The sun shall be turned into darkness  
> And the moon into blood,  
> Before the great, terrible, and manifest day of the Lord comes  
> (Joel 2).

For when blood and water, contrary to the nature of dead bodies, flowed from the pierced side of Jesus of Nazareth—fastened to the cross by the hands of the wicked—after he had yielded up the spirit [Col. 0039C], then the Lord gave blood as a portent. For that blood was to some a portent of death unto death, to others of life unto life: just as formerly the blood of the lamb, when signs and wonders were sent in the midst of Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants. A bundle of hyssop was dipped in it, and both doorposts and the lintel were sprinkled; and when the Lord passed through, striking the Egyptians, he saw the blood and passed over the marked doorways, and did not permit the destroyer to enter the houses [Col. 0040A] or to harm them. Thus now also, whoever marks by faith with the sign of the cross both doorposts—that is, soul and body—or the lintel—that is, his rational faculty—so as not to take offence at Christ’s Passion, signified by hyssop, a plant lowly, bitter, yet salutary, but rather to believe from the heart, confess truly, and also worthily receive the most holy Eucharist, shall not fall into the hand of the devil who strikes; for he shall be marked by the name and protected by the sacrament of the holy Trinity.

Fire too was given as a portent, because, since it is of a shining and burning substance, it signified that the Holy Spirit would both kindle Christ’s apostles with zeal and illuminate them with understanding. Indeed, the forms of the divided tongues mystically represented [Col. 0040B] the divisions of graces. Finally, vapour of smoke was given as a portent when very many, pierced in heart by the apostles’ preaching, tearfully sought counsel for their salvation, saying: “What shall we do, brothers?” (Acts 2). For to smoke is to be pierced with compunction and to weep over sins. And where the Church’s baptism was first celebrated, three thousand were gathered, not without a great portent: divine grace plainly foreshadowing that a multitude of believers was to be gathered from the whole world into faith in the Trinity. And, just as fire may signify the illumination or ardour of believers, so vapour of smoke may signify the blindness of the Jews no less than the compunction of penitents, or the darkening of the impenitent.

[Col. 0040C] The sun, moreover, was given as a portent because, when it was darkened at the Lord’s Passion, it foreshadowed the blindness of Israel, which then befell and still endures. But although it did not plainly appear that the moon had been turned into blood, however matters may have stood, it became bloody for them, since they made their Passover—namely, that which, according to the moon’s course, they then celebrated on the fourteenth day at evening by eating the lamb as the Law commanded—bloody by killing Christ; and the bloodthirsty Synagogue received over her eyes a cloth made menstrual by so prodigious a crime.

[Col. 0039] The remainder is lacking.

[Col. 0041]

# Commentary by Reiner, Monk of St Lawrence at Liège, on the Nine “O” Antiphons before Christmas, Beginning with “O”

Reprinted here because of the extreme rarity of the booklet, after the edition produced at Liège in 1618 by the press of John Ouwer.

> **[Note: Col. 0041A]** Here is its title and prefatory matter:
>
> *A booklet, or a devout, brief, and learned commentary, on the nine antiphons beginning with O before Christmas, according to the proper use or office—namely, that of the period—of the monastery of St Lawrence; by Reiner, a religious of the Benedictine Order of the same St Lawrence; never previously published.*
>
> **A six-line poem to the most reverend and eminent lord Otger Loncin, most vigilant archimandrite of the famous and ancient abbey of St Lawrence outside the walls of Liège.**
>
> Noble Otger, revered offspring of so many heroes,  
> In no way inferior to your Fathers in religious devotion,  
> Continue to draw the deeds of the Fathers from obscuring darkness,  
> And offer the bright torch that they have deserved.  
> Whatever light you shall one day merit,  
> Posterity shall dutifully bear the light you now bring to others.
>
> **An encomiastic poem on the renowned monastery of St Lawrence, situated on the public hill in the suburbs of Liège.**
>
> Why does the Carthaginian admire the rich gardens of the Hesperides?  
> Why does he sing of an enclosure fertile in rich autumn?  
> Why does the Greek sing of the varied flowers that you nurture, Hymettus?  
> Or why does the Sicilian sing your roses, Hybla?  
> The public hill rises heavenward with a fairer yoke,  
> Superior in a nobler spring or autumn.  
> It raises its summits close beside the walls of Liège,  
> Summits nearer to the starry heights.  
> Here Lawrence planted for you fragrant gardens,  
> Which neither Boreas nor savage winter ever harms.  
> The fruitful west wind of heaven blows with joyful sound;  
> The soil is happily moistened with heavenly dew.  
> Christ cherishes what springs up with Phoebus’ light,  
> [Col. 0042A] yet he knows no setting in the western sea.  
> An urn holds twice three relics of holy saints;  
> The rich soil luxuriates in so great a pledge.  
> What wealth the earth promises through that divine pledge!  
> It shall surpass your Hybla, and surpass your Hymettus.  
> Lilies rise in comely virginal whiteness,  
> And the violet is fragrant with a sweet scent of examples.  
> Here roses gleam with Tyrian splendour, painted by the divine torch;  
> Here they smile in snowy purity.  
> Why, Muse, do you run through the various colours of flowers?  
> Their abundance will exceed all counting, and surpass song.  
> But what bees feed upon the holy fragrance of the flowers,  
> And what sweet honey do they gather to consecrate to God!  
> What songs do birds pour forth from the holy branches—  
> Songs to be ennobled by a most radiant torch!  
> From here came one who received the Virgin’s holy arts by divine gift,  
> Whom holy Tuitia revered as father:  
> Rupert, celebrated throughout the whole world,  
> Whom the Liège claims as her own light.  
> Many shoots of no slight renown come to maturity,  
> [Col. 0042B] which that sacred soil bore from fruitful seed.  
> It bore much, and shall one day bear again: thus living virtue  
> And love for ancient religious devotion promise.  
> Go forward, you younger ones, and preserve the glory of your elders:  
> No lesser palm awaits virtue.
>
> **The blessed wishes of Reiner.**
>
> Love cannot endure delay. Behold, Reiner loves;  
> The Fathers love the Divinity: delay grieves both alike.  
> “O Love, may I be joined to you!” sang the devout company of Fathers;  
> God heard, and came down from the heavenly citadel.  
> “O Love, may I be joined to you!” Reiner sings with longing voice;  
> God heard, and bore the longing man to the stars.
>
> Thus far the anonymous editor of this little work.

(Dom Bernard Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. IV, part III, col. 51.)

## Prologue to a Friend

May the gladness of your pleasant countenance graciously receive the fitting gift of friendship which our devotion offers, so that, through the appearance of this offered gift, you may diligently contemplate the image of your friend. For this is a certain form of honourable exercise in which we commonly delight when writing to any familiar friend. And now we write to you this brief work, whose title is set at its head: “What the Nine O’s signify, and what is the rationale of those days.” I have, of course, depicted for you here before your eyes, as on a small sketch, the divisions of this little work arranged by chapters, lest the sequence of discourse should appear disordered, like some shapeless face.

## Chapters

[Col. 0043]

I. Statement of the subject.  
II. On Christ’s true humanity.  
III. On observing the nine days before Christmas Day.  
IV. What is the rationale of the nine antiphons?  
V. On the correspondence of these antiphons with the individual gifts of grace.  
VI. On the first antiphon: “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High, reaching mightily from end to end and sweetly ordering all things, come to teach us the life of prudence.”  
VII. On the second: “O Adonai and Leader of the house of Israel, who appeared to Moses in the fire of the burning bush and gave him the Law on Sinai, come to redeem us with outstretched arm.”  
VIII. On the third: “O Root of Jesse, who stand as a sign to the peoples, before whom kings shall shut their mouths, whom the nations shall entreat, come to free us; delay no longer.”  
IX. On the fourth: “O Key of David and sceptre of the house of Israel, who open and none shuts, shut and none opens, come and lead the captive from the prison-house, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.”  
X. On the fifth: “O Dayspring, splendour of eternal light and sun of righteousness, come and enlighten those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.”  
XI. On the sixth: “O King of the nations and their desire, cornerstone who make both one, come and save the human being whom you formed from clay.”  
XII. On the seventh: “O Emmanuel, our King and Lawgiver, expectation of the nations and their Saviour, come to save us, O Lord our God.”  
XIII. On the eighth: “O Virgin of virgins, how shall this be? For no one like you has been seen before, nor shall you have a successor. Daughters of Jerusalem, why do you marvel at me? Divine is this mystery which you behold.”  
XIV. On the ninth: “O highest craftsman of heaven and most high ruler of the stars, descend to human beings sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.”  
XV. Brief summary of the foregoing and an appropriate conclusion to the proposed argument.

# Commentary on the “O” Antiphons before Christmas

## Chapter I. Statement of the Subject

[Col. 0043A]

A loving observance of ecclesiastical custom precedes the desired joys of the Lord’s Nativity. Its evident mystical rationale proves that it was handed down not from an abusive or improper beginning, but through heavenly teaching. For on certain days, with the new proclamation of grace, the evening Office is celebrated more solemnly by the delightful singing of certain antiphons. Flourishing in every beauty both of words and of neumes (*pneumata*), they greatly stir the Church’s sacred assembly to devotion and joy. The days of this observance are no more than nine, and there are nine antiphons of the same number, each to be sung with the Gospel canticle on its respective day. All their beginnings are marked with the same letter, O. The question arises [Col. 0043B]: what is the cause or rationale of this observance? Let those whose intellectual power is loftier explain these matters more fully and subtly; we gently gather the fruit of a simple understanding from a humble level.

## Chapter II. On Christ’s True Humanity

We know with purity of faith that the only-begotten Son of God the Father dwelt among us in the true nature of our flesh, under all the conditions of human nature; therefore we truly believe that he was brought forth through the unimpaired fruitfulness of a mother’s womb. With this exception, true human nature ran through its whole course in him, as the rule of faith handed down by the Fathers rightly maintains. For, conceived not through marital intercourse but through the divine operation of the Holy Spirit, he took form according to natural law within his mother’s womb for the full nine months [Col. 0044A]; born an infant, he cried in a manger, and chose to be raised and sustained by milk and ordinary food, altogether like our condition in every manner of life, advancing to the fullness of age by natural growth. Then he suffered a true suffering of flesh and died a true human death. We embrace and venerate with fitting devotion both the lowly acts of weakness and the magnificent works of power—such as the miracles’ glorious signs, the surpassing glory of the Resurrection, and the exaltation of the Ascension—because with firmness of faith we confess that he voluntarily endured them, not from any need of his own, but because they were necessary for our salvation.

## Chapter III. On Observing the Nine Days before Christmas Day

[Col. 0044B]

Thus we arrange the seasons of our year in an ordered way, distinguished by their variety, and mark each with corresponding devotion through the several forms of the sacraments, so that we may be struck as if by flashes of ever-approaching brightness while we rejoice in solemnities renewed in succession. This is why, before the solemn day of his Nativity, we observe the nine days immediately preceding it with joy, and are uplifted in gladness as though by the gleaming beginnings of a new light. Above all, at the hour of the evening assembly, we are raised high in heartfelt rejoicing, as we celebrate that same assembly with greater splendour and brightness through the melodies of proclamation [Col. 0045A]. By this diligent observance, ecclesiastical tradition seeks, as far as such a comparison can avail, to express that he who in the beginning commanded light to shine out of darkness now, as the world’s evening declines, mercifully shone upon those sitting in darkness and wiped away the deep night-darkness of humankind by the true light of divinity.

With a similar observance we continue through all nine days, by which we understand that the nine months during which God-man kept himself enclosed in the hidden chamber of the virginal womb are distinctly represented. Certainly this is a worthy cause and rationale for a celebrated observance. For what, or how great, was that which was accomplished in that sanctuary of all purity and holiness by the hidden operation of divinity? It is great, ineffable—indeed, incomprehensible [Col. 0045B]. For whose mind can reach, even in thought, how God was personally united to man in a woman’s womb? Divinity was not changed into flesh; rather, true humanity was assumed into God, so that from two natures there might come to be one person of the Mediator, with divinity united indivisibly and unchangeably to our flesh. Hence divinity is no longer worshipped separately in itself apart from humanity, nor is humanity alone separately proclaimed; but all faithfully adore the one Christ, true in each nature, at once Creator and Redeemer, God and man: God begotten of the Father before the ages, and man conceived and born from the Virgin in time. A joyful observance is surely worthy when it has such a great subject for rejoicing.

That we take a day for a month reasonably and appropriately abbreviates the length of time, lest the delight of this celebration appear to be interrupted by some intervening feast, or devotion, once kindled, grow cold through human weakness and weariness. Rather, continuously strengthened in fervour, it may be the purer the shorter it is, and thereby more acceptable to supreme condescension [Col. 0045C]. Therefore we gather in numbers for evening Lauds with psalms and hymns; in a new sort of gladness we anticipate the joys of the coming solemnity, and in fitting devoted service go to meet the King who is about to come forth. For he is about to come forth, to gladden those awaiting him by a new rising. What sort of one, we ask, is about to come forth? Surely one beautiful and fair, sweet and delightful, anointed with every perfume of every grace [Col. 0045D].

## Chapter IV. What Is the Rationale of the Nine Antiphons?

Those nine antiphons express the fullness of these graces by the splendid beauty of their words and the sweet charm of melody, composed fittingly and carefully. In praise of this same King and his mother the Queen, the choir of the Church solemnly raises them in heartfelt and vocal utterance with her canticle.

Nor are they unfittingly joined to the Virgin’s canticle, since this celebration is said to be dedicated to the mother as well as to the Son; and the perfection of graces overflowing in the Son is reasonably affirmed to have been fully present in the mother. For if, as the Apostle says, “in Christ are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Col. 2), and Christ is in Mary, then all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God are in Mary—indeed, the whole fullness of divinity which dwells bodily in Christ [Col. 0046A]. Therefore the angel, reverently greeting her, began with grace and said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1). He rightly declared her full of grace, since she merited to conceive in chaste entrails the only-begotten Son of God the Father, and bore for us the Lord and man, blessed for ever. Writing to the Corinthians, the Apostle divides the fullness of graces into nine parts, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge; to another faith; to another the grace of healings; to another the working of powers; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances. [Col. 0046B] But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). No believer, as has been said, doubts that the fullness of these graces flowed into the blessed Virgin, whom divinity truly filled with its whole flood and intoxicated with the full stream of delight.

## Chapter V. On Their Correspondence with the Individual Gifts of Grace

Since, then, the Apostle divides the fullness of grace by a ninefold distinction, and the ninefold number of antiphons, as stated above, distinctly expresses it, it will be most beautiful and delightful to distinguish their mutual correspondence by the discerning judgement of reason, and inwardly to hear them as different voices from a musical instrument harmonizing in an ordered symphony [Col. 0046C]. This will be very easy if we do not shrink from lingering briefly over each one and, as it were, touching the string with a light stroke of the hand, so that the attentive inward ear may discern by careful skill what relationship or harmony they have with one another.

Come then: let the first of the antiphons be compared with the first of the graces, and in the same way the remainder be compared with one another in order, so that by an unquestionable judgement of reason it may be clear that, in one and like relation, the two sets always answer one another. For just as in music the diapason, the greatest of harmonies, called the double ratio, answers with a consonance no different in kind from the low register to the note produced in the high register, according to the rule of proportions, so indeed, in equal agreement of meanings and sometimes also in an adopted kinship of words, the individual antiphons answer the individual graces in harmonious counterpoint [Col. 0046D].

## Chapter VI. On the First Antiphon: “O Wisdom, Who Came Forth from the Mouth of the Most High,” etc.

For behold: since the first of the graces is the word of wisdom, and the first of the antiphons is “O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High,” already in the very beginning the concordant resonance of language is apparent. Yet the likeness of their harmony is much clearer in meaning, since almost every word, pregnant with the fruitfulness of mysteries, plainly shows that it has been uttered not with the verbose frivolity of empty talk, but with the weight of wisdom. For the first element, O, of the proposed discussion suitably accords with the mystery, since the complete form of its roundness figuratively expresses the fullness of divinity, which, with every distribution of graces, gave its whole self to flesh and assumed the whole human being from the Virgin [Col. 0047A]. This is the Wisdom who came forth from the mouth of the Most High: namely, the Son, begotten from the Father’s substance and appearing in the beginning as Creator of all things.

He reaches mightily from end to end when, from the divinity in which he created all things, he mercifully inclines himself to the humanity which he fashioned last of all, personally uniting both natures in himself by that power of strength by which he is God, to whom every word is certainly possible.

He sweetly orders all things by that most orderly dispensation through which he providently governs created things. Hence at the end of the antiphon we faithfully and attentively pray: “Come [Col. 0047B] to teach us the way of prudence,” namely, that, appearing visibly in flesh, he may make known to angels and human beings by what way or counsel of his prudence he, being stronger, approaches the strong man armed in order to cast him out of his courtyard. Thus all the parts of the first antiphon are fittingly harmonized with the first of the graces.

## Chapter VII. On the Second Antiphon: “O Adonai and Leader of the House of Israel,” etc.

The second antiphon, “O Adonai,” likewise corresponds in a similar relation to the second grace, the word of knowledge. For what else does the name Adonai itself indicate than that God increases the grace of knowledge among his faithful with the passage of time? For he says to Moses: “I am the Lord, who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; and I did not make known to them my name Adonai” (Exod. 5). Surely he who says this declares that through the progress of time he bestows increasingly abundant gifts of knowledge, since he reveals to Moses his name Adonai [Col. 0047C], which he had not formerly revealed to Abraham.

That he appeared to Moses in the fire of the burning bush (Exod. 3) and gave the Law on Sinai (Exod. 24) is clearly most fitting to the word of knowledge in both respects. For by appearing in fire he mystically wished to instruct Moses’ discerning mind, so that he might know that he was coming then, for the temporal deliverance of his people, in great fervour of zeal and in the great and fearsome splendour of signs—and that at some future time he would come in flesh for their eternal salvation.

It is a common and celebrated teaching in the school of Christ, known even to the little ones in faith, that the bush which could burn and not be consumed signifies the blessed Virgin Mary. The fiery substance of divinity truly so filled her that it dwelt in her womb for the entire nine months, and not only did not burn or dissolve the frail material of her female nature, but also made it shine forever with greater honour of virginity, through the grace of the human being formed therefrom whom he assumed [Col. 0047D]. From the Law given on Sinai it is clear how manifold a knowledge flowed throughout the whole world.

Therefore the devout piety of the faithful Church entreats this Adonai with great desire: “Come to redeem us with outstretched arm,” namely, that with the strength of arm by which he crushed Pharaoh, oppressor of the faithful, he may crush the proud devil, of whom Pharaoh bore the type. All these things, therefore, which have been said, are reasonably harmonious with the word of knowledge [Col. 0048A].

## Chapter VIII. On the Third Antiphon: “O Root of Jesse, Who Stand as a Sign,” etc.

The third antiphon follows: “O Root of Jesse,” and it corresponds in friendly likeness to the third grace, which is faith. For Christ is the Root of Jesse according to faith; conversely, Jesse is the root of Christ according to the flesh. Finally, Jesse and Abraham alike, with the other Fathers, who in their own times flowered by the grace of virtues like little trees of a good planting, were rooted or planted in faith in the Christ to come; and, from the rich sap of this good root, they drew an abundant sweetness of good fruits, receiving all things from the fullness of grace overflowing in him [Col. 0048B].

This root rose from thirsty ground and, growing into a most beautiful tree, gave good fruit in its season: that is, Christ according to the flesh arose from the Jewish people, who lacked the moisture of faith; exalted upon the cross, he removed the bitterness of death and brought to all the sweet delight of life through his fruitful Passion. Now, raised above the heavens at the Father’s right hand, he has lifted up the wood of his cross as a sign to peoples and nations, that they may be faithfully marked by it both on their foreheads and in their minds. And now kings shut their mouths before him [Col. 0048C], humbly confessing that he rules on high in the kingdom of human beings. The nations likewise entreat him, worshipping with sacrifices and gifts. Reason proves most evidently that all these things accord with the sacrament of faith. Therefore we pray to him with the whole devotion of faith: “Come to free us; delay no longer.”

## Chapter IX. On the Fourth Antiphon: “O Key of David and Sceptre,” etc.

The fourth antiphon, “O Key of David,” no less fully accords in all its bearing with the grace of healings. For what is the Key of David in this place except royal and priestly power: the power of judging or forgiving sins, which Christ possesses as David’s son according to the flesh? Since he is God and man, King and Priest, he both intercedes and hears, reconciles and absolves. He is the sceptre of the house of Israel: namely, the royal glory of all those to whom the name Israel truly belongs [Col. 0048D].

He mercifully opens by the hand of grace the entrance of the kingdom to those who knock, and shuts it by the judgement of justice against those who despise or disbelieve. No one can shut when he opens, or open when he shuts. For who can reject one whom he has wished to gather through mercy? Or who can gather one whom he has rejected through justice? To him who possesses such and so great a power, we rightly offer the pure confession of heart and mouth, and humbly ask: “Come and lead the captives from the prison-house, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.”

## Chapter X. On the Fifth Antiphon: “O Dayspring, Splendour of Eternal Light,” etc.

[Col. 0049A]

The fifth antiphon likewise, “O Dayspring, splendour of eternal light and sun of righteousness,” is harmoniously suited in a not dissimilar manner to the fifth grace, the working of powers. For Christ is the true Dayspring, as is said through the prophet: “Behold the man: Dayspring is his name” (Zech. 6). And again in the Gospel: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1). He is the splendour of eternal Light, illuminating the heavenly homeland of the saints with the unfailing light of divinity. He is also the Sun of righteousness, as Scripture testifies: “For you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. 4). Rising in darkness, he visibly scattered some rays of your light even upon earth for the upright in heart, when by the word of his power he mightily healed every [Col. 0049B] disease and diverse infirmities. Moreover, he penetratively irradiated the apostles with the brightness of that same splendour, and through them displayed in the world signs of miracles so many and so diverse. To him is directed the devout entreaty of the Church: “Come, and enlighten those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.”

## Chapter XI. On the Sixth Antiphon: “O King of the Nations and Their Desire,” etc.

The sixth antiphon, “O King of the nations,” corresponds to prophecy, the sixth of the graces. For if we carefully attend to prophetic Scripture, we find most clearly that it speaks continually and especially of the salvation of the nations. After celebrating the mysteries in Christ [Col. 0049C] of human restoration, what else do all the divinely inspired Scriptures of the prophets proclaim but the calling of the nations and the rejection of the Jews? Therefore he is rightly called King of the nations and their desire. For the Jews, whom he healed both by his own preaching and by many works of healing, rejected him with a most importunate denial, lest he should reign over them. “We have no king but Caesar,” they say (John 19). But when the nations first received through the apostles the word of preaching, they turned to him with their whole heart and willingly sought him to reign over them in voluntary submission. He is the cornerstone who made both one (Eph. 2): that is, he unites believers in himself from each people and makes one Church of the faithful [Col. 0049D]. To him we pray with faithful devotion: “Come, save the human being whom you formed from clay.”

## Chapter XII. On the Seventh Antiphon: “O Emmanuel, Our King and Lawgiver,” etc.

The seventh antiphon, “O Emmanuel,” likewise sweetly accords with the seventh grace, which is discernment of spirits. For through Emmanuel himself—that is, through the fact that God is with us, that he is our King and Lawgiver, the expectation of the nations and their Saviour—we have discernment of spirits. We know how to distinguish sound Catholic teaching from the mad teaching of heretics; we have experience in testing the spirits to see whether they are from God; and amid every danger of life we are safe through our King himself [Col. 0050A], who remains with us until the end of the age according to his promise. Humbly ascribing to him all that we understand or can do, we faithfully pray and say that he may possess us in everlasting salvation: “Come to save us, O Lord our God.”

## Chapter XIII. On the Eighth Antiphon: “O Virgin of Virgins, How Shall This Be?”

The eighth antiphon also, “O Virgin of virgins,” harmoniously resounds with the grace called kinds of tongues. For it is the voice of faithful souls in every generation, blessing the Mother of God in every language and wondering at the greatness of such mysteries fulfilled in her, saying: “O Virgin of virgins [Col. 0050B], how shall this be?” and so forth. To them she answers in a sweet and delightful voice: “Daughters of Jerusalem, why do you marvel at me? Divine is this mystery that you behold. All that you marvel at in me is the work and grace of divine operation. God has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1). Through me he deigned to work salvation in the midst of the earth. “For behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed, because he who is mighty has done great things for me” (ibid.).

## Chapter XIV. On the Ninth Antiphon: “O Highest Craftsman of Heaven and Ruler of the Stars”

The final antiphon, “O highest craftsman,” sweetly corresponds in harmonious relation to the final grace, the interpretation of utterances. For what else do these words seem to imply [Col. 0050C] except that they open or interpret for us the hitherto closed utterances of the Scriptures and the words of the prophets? Their sum, indeed, is this: that the most high Son of the Most High will deign to descend through the womb of the undefiled Virgin to human beings, in order to raise those whom the rashness of their own pride has cast down.

He is the highest craftsman, God: namely, Creator or maker of all things, who in the beginning adorned the firmament, or heaven, with innumerable lamps—the stars—whose course he governs through the ages in unerring order. To him we pray with overflowing devotion of heart that, coming forth from the hidden dwelling of inaccessible light, he may deign to descend to us human beings sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

## Chapter XV. Brief Summary of the Foregoing and Appropriate Conclusion to the Proposed Argument

[Col. 0050D]

Behold, while we paused briefly over each of the graces and antiphons, we recognized with the faithful understanding of the mind their mutual agreement or harmony. Therefore we considered it not unfitting to say that these nine antiphons express the fullness of the graces, since they correspond to one another in every respect by such evident reasoning. The blessed Virgin fittingly ought to be endowed with the distributions of these graces as with appropriate gifts, so that she might be full of grace: she who, with the Holy Spirit coming upon her, conceived in her sound and undefiled womb the Son in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily, and, happily pregnant with such a burden, bore him in her womb through the whole nine months [Col. 0051A].

The aforementioned observance of nine days and the ninefold division of the antiphons signify this. Individual days are observed for the individual months, and individual antiphons likewise express individual graces. From this is given to us the matter of present joys; from that, the cause of the desired celebration, which ecclesiastical diligence has handed down with devout purpose in yearly recurrence. This is the fulfillment of the promises made to the Fathers; this is the accomplishment, or truth, of all that was foretold long before by the prophets. The Word which was in the beginning with God, and through whom all things were made, put on the frail form of the human condition. Divinity chose to be clothed with tender flesh in the virginal womb and, by the hidden counsel of its wisdom, to be united with our substance, so that in one and the same person the splendour of the divine nature might shine forth and the reality of assumed weakness appear [Col. 0052A]. This the clear celebration of joyful praise resounds; this the dance of new gladness and the devout joy of holy minds express. These few things we have said about so celebrated an observance in a scant supply of words, lest the work of my own devotion appear in any degree wanting to a familiar friend.

> **[Note: Col. 0051A]** By way of conclusion, you ought to know, most illustrious lord, that the ancient use of the Church of Liège has ten antiphons. For it adds to these nine a tenth concerning St Thomas, beginning, “O Thomas Didymus”; indeed, it repeats it twice, namely at both Vespers of his feast. Other Churches perhaps observe another, whether greater or smaller, number of these antiphons, according to the ancestral and religious custom of each. No one should therefore marvel at this diversity, still less lightly disapprove of it or maliciously criticize it. For just as the customs of regions—and indeed often of individual persons—are diverse, yet are not thereby uncivilized, so too the rites of particular Churches are sometimes varied, yet all praiseworthy and good. Reiner, however, deliberately expounds nine, adding two to the seven instituted by the Roman rite and still observed today, in accordance with the rationale of the proper office in use in his day; and he does so, as he says in his prologue, in a familiar manner for a friend’s benefit—and indeed, as familiarly as devoutly, soundly, and briefly. —Note by the distinguished Fr Celestine Lombard.

[Col. 0051]

# The Mirror of Repentance, or The Life of Saint Pelagia, in Two Books, by Reiner

(Extracted from a manuscript codex of the monastery of St Lawrence at Liège by the distinguished Fr Celestine Lombard; edited by Dom Bernard Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. IV, part III, col. 69.)

## The Prologue Begins

[Col. 0051B]

I have set forth Pelagia as an example of conversion and repentance: she emerged from darkness into light, from prostitution into the holiness of chastity. In her God, the Father of mercies, is blessed: he transformed a vessel of perdition and wrath into a vessel of salvation and grace. Certainly nothing is worthier than his condescension, nothing more excellent than his forgiveness; the unrepentant person offends him more than the sinner, and one who despairs offends him just as one who denies him does. No one, therefore, is so utterly evil that he who is supremely good will not pardon him, if that person duly repents. Thus Pelagia raises hope of pardon for sinners and proclaims the abundance of Christ’s mercies.

I found the record of her conversion written by another; but the style was poorly suited to it, and there was such a confusion of barbarisms and solecisms [Col. 0052B] that the obscure style seemed to have rendered an illustrious subject mutilated and contemptible. Yet I suspect that this arose more from a copyist’s fault than from the author’s lack of skill, since the text showed itself everywhere mutilated by four or more clauses, and also by half-lines of verse. Contemptible speech greatly diminishes the grace of glorious matters. Therefore I have taken care to recast the aforesaid material in a somewhat better form, while testing the unpolished talent of my youth. I have arranged the little work in two books and marked it with the title *Mirror of Repentance*. For any person’s eye, cleansed with the salve of goodwill, can also discern in it how great a good this remedy is and how blessed its result.

# Book One

[Col. 0053]

## Chapter One

[Col. 0053A]

A certain holy bishop of Antioch summoned the neighboring bishops for a matter of some importance. Eight assembled, among whom was the apostolic man and priest worthy of his office, Nonnus of Heliopolis. On account of his virtuous merits he had been taken from the monastery of the Tabennesiots and, though unwilling, had undertaken to shepherd Christ’s flock, chosen and called by Christ himself for the salvation of many. Having already freed the city of Heliopolis and thirty thousand Saracens from the devil’s yoke, he had transferred them into the service of their king.

The monastery of the Tabennesiots, situated in the Thebaid, once flourished with an outstanding vigor of religious life; through the approved men whom it trained it illuminated the entire East, so that every Church might rightly rejoice to have received one of its pupils as pastor. Five thousand or more monks there were governed by one abbot. How eagerly they obeyed him, how humbly they submitted, and with what glorious contempt they trod the world beneath their feet, I forbear to say, since it would take too long.

Accordingly, one day the bishops had set out chairs before the doors of the basilica of the martyr Julian and were seated, attentively listening while venerable Nonnus spoke on the word of life. Then, behold: the most beautiful prostitute among Antioch’s actresses passed by, seated in a carriage, wrapped in a cloak adorned with pearls and gold, and wearing a golden necklace. Because of her surpassing beauty and the brilliance of her ornaments, the people of Antioch called her “Margaret,” that is, “Pearl.” [Col. 0053C] The children of this world could never have their fill of her beauty; like a most ravenous Siren, she enticed and destroyed the wretched. Before and behind her went a great throng of boys and girls, their faces artfully arranged and their attire ostentatious, leaping about to music of various kinds; the fragrance of their perfumes filled all the air through which she passed. But the chaste eye recoils from the displays of unchastity.

## Chapter II

The priests recoiled, and, blushing with shame, turned away their eyes lest they look upon vanity. But Nonnus, a man of deeper understanding, fixed upon her his spiritual eye and watched until she had passed. Then he said to those seated around him: “Have you considered the great beauty of this woman, most blessed priests?” When they said nothing, he laid his head in his hands, bent his knees, and wept copiously. Then he asked again: “Have you not been delighted by her great beauty?” When they remained silent, he added:

“I certainly have been greatly delighted, and her appearance has pleased me; for God is going to set her before his dreadful judgment-seat, ahead of us, to judge us and our episcopates. What do you suppose? How long she must have spent in her chamber, diligently washing and arranging herself before the mirror, so that nothing might be lacking to her bodily beauty! How she strives to please all her lovers, lest she appear unattractive to those who are here today and will be gone tomorrow! But we, who have in heaven an immortal Bridegroom, granting lovers of chastity rewards of heavenly riches beyond estimation, do not present our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God. We do not, I say, purify our souls through fear of him; we do not strip off our desires or adorn ourselves with holy virtues. Instead, we lie in the dust of vices.”

Having said this, he withdrew with his deacon to the cell where he was staying. Entering its inner room, he threw himself upon the pavement, pressed his face to the ground, and wept, saying:

“Lord God, compassionate and merciful, forgive me, I beg you, a sinner; for the outward adornment of this prostitute has surpassed the inward adornment of my soul. With what countenance shall I look up to you? By what words shall I be justified in your presence? For, Lord, I cannot conceal my heart from you, since you search hearts and reins; all things are naked and laid open to your eyes. Woe to miserable me, who presume to stand at your altar and intrude upon the holy mysteries, yet do not offer a beautiful soul such as you seek. She promised to please human beings, and did so; I promised to please you, and I have lied. I am naked in heaven and on earth, Lord, because I have sinned against you and have not obeyed your commandments. Therefore I have no hope from good works; you are my hope, and I trust that through your mercy I shall be saved.”

## Chapter III

It was Saturday. When the priest had gone to rest that night, he received through a pleasant vision an oracle concerning things to come. For the benefits of divine mysteries sometimes disclose themselves beforehand to holy minds. After the morning hymns had been said, he told this to his deacon:

“Brother, I saw a dream which troubles me, because I cannot discern its meaning. I seemed to myself to be standing at the holy altar and celebrating the divine mysteries, when a black dove, wrapped in much filth, rose from the left horn of the altar and flew about me. I could not bear the horror of its stench and foulness. [Col. 0054D] When I tried to drive it away, it persisted importunately until I had completed the prayer for the catechumens. But when the deacon cried, ‘Depart, catechumens,’ it was nowhere to be seen. After the completion of the Mass, however, when I had dismissed the church and was leaving the sanctuary, it again flew around me. I seized it in my hand and threw it into the basin of water beside the church courtyard. Stripped entirely of every filthy deformity and transformed into the flower of a marvelous newness, it rose from the bath whiter than snow; [Col. 0055A] shaking its wings, it was carried upward until it vanished from the watcher’s sight.”

The next day the bishops proceeded to the greater church. Having greeted the bishop of the city, they celebrated the canon of the Mass. After the Gospel reading, the bishop of Antioch handed the book of the Gospels to the praiseworthy Nonnus and urged him to address the people. Ascending the pulpit, he spoke at length on the kingdom of God and the glory of the saints, on the places of punishments and the misery of the lost—not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the power of the Spirit and the simplicity of truth. The Lord had opened his mouth and filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding; the hearts of his hearers were pierced, tears flowed, and groans were uttered.

[Col. 0055B] Present was that notorious sinner whom I mentioned above. Drawn and led by the prompting of God’s mercy—who does not desire the death of the sinner, but that the sinner turn and live—she was pierced to repentance and gave forth most bitter weeping. For the more sin had formerly delighted her, the more grief afterwards burns away the soul of the penitent. Yet a person now cleansed is restored by a certain clear serenity of joy. For nothing is calmer, safer, or more festive than a good conscience. I shall insert some matters which, I believe, are not superfluous.

## Chapter IV

A brother familiar to me used to recount that, while still a young man, he devoted himself eagerly to the books [Col. 0055C] of the pagans and, neglecting his own soul, cared too little for divine things. One night in sleep he seemed to see that the day of universal judgment was at hand. The Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven to judge, with great power and majesty, while the world burned and trembled horribly. The revived bodies of the dead suddenly departed from their tombs. The righteous, radiant in brightness, were caught up into the air to meet Christ; the unjust, dreadful in their blackness, fled from his face, judging nothing more bitter than to behold him whom they had provoked by sins. But a cruel whirling force seized them, and bolts of lightning drove them with evil spirits down into Tartarean chaos.

[Col. 0055D] The aforementioned brother, trusting little in his conscience, sought a hiding-place, though he could not hide. [Col. 0056A] He recalled that saying of the Gospel: “Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us’” (Luke 23); and that of the Apocalypse (6): “They will say to the mountains and rocks, ‘Fall upon us and hide us from the face of him seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb; for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?’” On waking, he declared that he shook upon his bed in an indescribable manner, like a tree leaf stirred by trembling.

Finally he added that on another occasion, in a night vision, he had seen the Only-begotten of God and the Virgin hanging alive on the cross, looking upon him with a severe countenance. He blossomed with a light of inestimable beauty, fairer in form than the children of men; a ray proceeding from him pierced that brother’s heart and afflicted it with a sharper sensation. Light, which is usually most gentle and desirable to one whose conscience is good, is felt as harsh and dreadful by one whose conscience is evil.

He also described what had happened to him one night. After morning praises, the assembly of brothers was chanting psalms, as customary, for the faithful departed in the crypt of the holy Mother of God. While he sat apart from the others and fell asleep, he suddenly perceived his spirit leaving his body. He saw and heard those chanting; but he gave greater attention to the voices of demons clamoring outside, who had rushed together to drag him before the tribunal of the Judge. Since he was hemmed in on every side—for conscience accused him on one side and demons on the other—he began with all his heart to invoke the holy Mother of Christ and the blessed martyr Lawrence. [Col. 0056C] Without delay he felt himself return into his body, but gently and with a certain indulgence, lest the frail framework of his limbs be crushed by the force of his returning.

Restored to himself, he stood in dreadful amazement while soul and body were still being reconciled by their marvelous bond. With faltering steps he scarcely returned to his bed. I comforted as best I could, in feeling and in speech, the man as he recounted these and many other things with tears and trembling. I told him that divine mercy was correcting him; these were not phantasms, but at times one sees, as warnings for salvation, through a mirror and in an enigma, things which will without doubt come to pass in reality. For a dream which advances the soul is salutary. The matters I have left aside will be explained in the second book.

# Book Two

## Chapter I

[Col. 0055D] When Pelagia learned that Bishop Nonnus was staying in the basilica of Blessed Julian, she sent him a letter by two boys containing the following:

“To the disciple of Christ, from a disciple of the devil. I have heard, my lord, that your God descended from heaven to earth, not for the righteous, but to save sinners; that he whom angels long to behold was seen among human beings; that he associated with tax collectors and sinners, showing them marvelous condescension by speaking and eating with them. And you, my lord, possess great holiness, though you have not seen with bodily eyes the Lord himself, who, as I have learned from Christians, revealed himself to the Samaritan prostitute at the well. Therefore, if you are the disciple of so gracious a Master, do not despise me, miserable and sinful as I am; rather, I beg that through you I may be presented to him.”

The bishop replied: “God is not mocked, woman! Whatever you intend or think is manifest to him. Do not test my humility, for I am a sinner, the least of Christ’s servants. But if you desire salvation and wish to see me, come, and you shall see me before my fellow bishops; otherwise you cannot see me.”

Having read the letter, the woman hurried to the basilica, desiring the bath of regeneration as a deer desires springs of water. Health is desirable to one who is ill: a heart truly pierced hastens swiftly toward healing. It was announced to Bishop Nonnus, who summoned the other bishops. Presented before the holy assembly, the woman fell at the bishop’s feet and, doing penance, said with tears:

“I beseech you, holy sir, imitate Christ the Lord. Be moved in my case by feelings of piety and mercy, and make me a Christian. For I am, lord, an ocean of sins; I am the mire of uncleanness. I beg to be purified in Christ.”

When the bishop had scarcely persuaded her to rise, he said: “Daughter, the holy canons decree that a prostitute should not be baptized unless she has given a guarantor and promised that she will not again entangle herself in her former evils.” At this she again cast herself upon the ground, clasped the priest’s feet, and, after the example of the Gospel sinner, wet them with her tears, dried them with her hair, pressed kisses upon them, and with many groans earnestly implored him concerning her salvation.

## Chapter II

All were moved by such satisfaction; weeping with her, they testified that they had never seen repentance of such intensity. They therefore sent to the bishop of the city, explained the matter, and requested that one of the deaconesses be sent.

Rejoicing in the Lord, he sent Romana, the chief of the deaconesses, with this reply to Bishop Nonnus: “Rightly, honored Father, did these works await you. We know that you are the mouth of God, who says: ‘If you bring forth what is precious from what is worthless, you shall be as my mouth.’” Romana came and found the woman still clinging to the priest’s feet. She instructed her, saying: “Rise, daughter, so that you may be exorcised.” When she had risen, the bishop said: “Confess your sins.” She replied: “If, holy sir, I examine the conscience of my heart, I shall not find even a moment of good work in myself. My sins are countless, and what has been accumulated without measure cannot easily be known by number. Yet I trust that through God’s mercy I shall obtain forgiveness.”

Then, ordered to state her name, she said: “My parents called me Pelagia; but because of the splendid ornaments with which I adorned myself in the devil’s service, the citizens of Antioch call me Margaret.” The bishop said: “You are called Pelagia?” “Yes,” she replied. Then he catechized and baptized her; strengthening her with the sign of Christ’s cross, he gave her participation in Christ’s body. [Col. 0058A] Romana became her spiritual mother. Thus, in accordance with the holy man’s vision, the black dove wrapped in much filth was made white in the bath of the eternal font; she blossomed again in beautiful youth, as the eagle’s youth is renewed.

Giving thanks to God, the elder said to his deacon: “Brother, let us keep a feast-day with God’s angels for the salvation of this girl. Let us take wine and oil beyond our usual custom, because God has found his drachma which he had lost, and has restored to the flock the sheep which had perished.” While they rejoiced and refreshed themselves, voices were heard in the air as though of persons suffering violence. The prince of destruction therefore hurled these insults at the saint: “What has this decrepit old man determined against me? He takes what is mine, he plunders what is mine! I can no longer endure the insolence of this impostor. It was not enough for him to draw twenty-five thousand Saracens and all the people of Heliopolis from my kingdom, nor enough that he has made frequent raids; now, besides, he has taken a great advantage of my hope. O injurious old man!” Finally he reproached the girl with these complaints: “Come now, Lady Pelagia, what have you done? You imitate my Judas. He, raised to apostolic rank and honor, betrayed his Lord and Master; so too have you done to me.”

As he barked with this dreadful howling, the holy man diligently admonished the girl. Marking herself with the sign of the cross and invoking the Lord’s name, she blew upon the demon; and as smoke fails away, so his phantasms disappeared. Yet the deceiver of souls did not rest, but renewed his temptation. On the third night the handmaid of God was resting in the room with Romana. He came, struck the sleeping woman, and addressed her:

“What have I done to you, Lady Pelagia? In what have I grieved you, that you should leave me? Have I not enriched you with my wealth? Have I not adorned you with gold and silver, jewels and precious ornaments? Show me how I have harmed you, that I may make satisfaction to you—only do not make me a reproach to the Christians.”

Then she drove the enemy away with the sign of the cross, rebuking him thus: “May Christ almighty, who delivered me from your snares and deigned to call me to the knowledge of his name, himself resist you on my behalf.” At this the demon vanished, grinding his teeth in malice.

## Chapter III

I certainly knew a virgin illustrious in the lamp of virtues, endowed with the oil of charity which she kept in the clean vessel of conscience, and zealously striving to render herself worthy of heavenly marriage. Her modest speech accorded with her conduct, and she avoided all false speech. She confessed to me—as is characteristic of holy simplicity, which sometimes discloses some of its secrets—that demons occasionally appeared to her and were heard reproaching her because she resisted their rash suggestions and temptations. I do not speak with the tongue of a flatterer: after she had completed the course of her labors, she received the prize of righteousness; she ended blessed beginnings of life with a more blessed end.

I also saw a brother of proven life who sometimes showed me limbs swollen with livid wounds, so battered by demons visibly attacking him that he spat blood from his mouth.

Pelagia therefore devoted herself day and night to spiritual exercises. With tears she confessed her former ignorance, and with a strong spirit restrained the enticements of the flesh. Blessed is that conversion which, after repentance, admits no further cause for repentance. She clung to Bishop Nonnus’s feet, receiving instruction from the wise man; she was indeed comparable to the queen who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. That woman revered a famous king; this one Christ, or Christ’s disciple. Counting nothing precious except the desire for eternal salvation, she hastened to leave everything and follow Christ.

[Col. 0059B] Finally, having drawn up a list of all she possessed—an ample estate—she laid it at the apostolic man’s feet, begging that through him it might be distributed to Christ’s poor. He entrusted it all to the steward of the Church, binding him under an anathema neither to bring any of it to the bishop nor into the church, but to devote the whole to the needs of the poor. This was faithfully done: what had been badly accumulated was well dispersed. Pelagia also freed all her boys and girls, gave each one a gold coin, and admonished them not to neglect their salvation, but to be initiated into the Christian religion.

## Chapter IV

The eighth day was now at hand, when she was to lay aside the white baptismal garments. Rising in the night, she took off the sacred garments and, clad in Bishop Nonnus’s woolen tunic and cloak, secretly left the city. She went to Jerusalem to worship at the Lord’s tomb and to venerate the holy places.

Then, having built herself a small dwelling on the Mount of Olives, Christ’s dove entered it. There, free from the waves of the world, she gave herself to quiet contemplation and saw that the Lord is sweet. She disciplined her body through vigils and fasts; her mouth never ceased from prayers, nor her eyes from tears. Her soul burned and almost failed, hastening to the embraces and mystical kisses of her heavenly Bridegroom. Enlightened by the Holy Spirit, she enjoyed the mirror of contemplation, pondering what she would see in the kingdom of heaven—which suffers violence [Col. 0059D] and is seized by the violence of penitents.

Indeed, I heard privately from a certain brother that, when he repented of having lived too negligently and continually judged himself with mourning lest he be judged in the future, he received a marvelous consolation.
