In a vision he contemplated the holy Trinity, to whose invocation and praises he most attentively devoted himself, ineffably portrayed in a most transparent mirror beyond human artifice. From it three rays of living light shone forth and wondrously illumined him. True repentance does not lack fruit: it obtains merit if it avoids sin.

Thus, while Romana mourned Pelagia, not knowing what had happened to her spiritual daughter, the bishop forbade her, saying: “Do not weep, but rather rejoice, because Pelagia has provided well for herself. She has chosen with Mary the best part, which shall not be taken away from her.”

## Chapter V

After three years had passed, one of his deacons decided to go to Jerusalem for prayer. The elder said to him: “When, son, you have fulfilled your vow, diligently seek out a certain eunuch named Pelagius, who has lived a solitary life for a long time. If you see him, you will receive great edification from him.” He was speaking of Pelagia.

After the deacon had subsequently worshipped at the holy Resurrection, he inquired about the man of God and learned that he lived on the Mount of Olives. Going up, he saw a humble cell at the place where the Lord had prayed three times during his Passion. [Col. 0060B] There was a small window in its wall, through which the holy solitary made herself visible to visitors. The deacon knocked at it, and the recluse opened it. Seeing him, she recognized him; but he did not recognize her, because the burning sun of penitence had darkened her complexion and the flourishing flower of youth had withered. Yet she was now more beautiful in merits than in limbs, whiter in soul than in body. Her sunken eyes, with their ceaseless tears, and her pale, wasted face showed untiring abstinence. Her chaste brow expressed sobriety of mind. For the outward person is the interpreter of the inward one.

Humbly addressing her, he said: “Whence do we have you, blessed one of the Lord? Since I desired to visit these holy places, and above all wished to worship at the Lord’s tomb, the venerable elder Nonnus commanded me to greet you on his behalf, for he asks to be commended to the Lord in your prayers.” She received this reverently.

After their conversation, the deacon bowed in worship, gave thanks, and departed greatly edified. Having returned to Jerusalem, he visited the dwellings of the saints, and everywhere the good fragrance of the manner of life of the monk Pelagius spread abroad. Therefore, in the third year after receiving baptism, the happy penitent—wearied with long desire for Christ, tested by many temptations and fasts, and at last sensing that the long-desired hour of her death was near—lay prostrate on the ground, though her mind and eyes were fixed upon heaven, and surrendered her spirit to God in glory. [Col. 0060D] Having been burned upon the altar of repentance by the great fire of compunction, she ascended from the desert of this world like a wisp of smoke from spices. She gathers the cluster of heavenly sweetness, she who had borne the bundle of myrrh—that is, the weight of mortification—and, a shining pearl raised from the dust of the world, is placed in the heavenly building.

On the third day, moreover, when the deacon revisited the hut of God’s handmaid and detected no one inside, he approached and looked. Behold, she lay upon the ground, displaying death by neither sensation nor movement. He carefully sealed the window with clay and ran to announce to the city that she had departed. An honorable assembly of Fathers came forth for the burial, with monks chanting psalms. They carried the body to the place where it would be washed and uncovered it. Seeing a woman, and seeing her lifeless limbs shine more brightly than a perfectly clear mirror and give forth a marvelous fragrance, they were astonished and magnified God, who works such wondrous and glorious things even in the female sex. Finally, a great multitude of monks, virgins, and people of both sexes gathered from the whole region, with candles and lamps; they anointed the sacred body with precious myrrh and committed it to the earth.

# The Virgin’s Palm, or Two Books on the Life and Passion of Saint Mary, a Virgin of Cappadocia, by Reiner

(D. Bern. Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV, III, 83, from the manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Lawrence at Liège.)

## Prologue

[Col. 0061B] Oh, how delightful and pleasant it is to direct the mind toward divine things! This is especially relished by the faithful soul, which, poured out in affection toward God, is granted the touch of the Holy Spirit. This saying too is sweeter to us than honey, all the more because we say that it was uttered by the blessed martyr Lawrence, whose words are indeed like gems of divine oracle.

For a certain brother [Note: [Col. 0061] B. John, a monk of Liège, whose work we have given above.] was reading Terence with boys or young men. But the reading of stage-plays is generally more harmful than beneficial to weak hearers. Meanwhile that teacher fell ill, so that he was almost despaired of. Carried outside himself in ecstasy, he saw and heard many memorable things, which he afterwards put into writing. Nor did he conceal that blessed Lawrence threw the saying which I cited above threateningly in his face, rebuking him [Col. 0061C] for defiling himself with frivolities by using a comic poet. For one should be considered insufficiently religious who occupies heart or tongue with shameful trifles. To treat divine and honorable matters is therefore most wholesome. Knowledge increases, idleness is avoided, and the soul advances in virtues.

Indeed, we read that certain Fathers were accustomed to weave mats or little baskets; after they had accumulated great heaps of them and found no one to sell them, they set a fire beneath them and burned them, then made others again to be reduced to the same fate.

These spiritual philosophers reasoned in this way: idleness is the soul’s enemy, and for this reason they so vigorously pursued it. But I, a worthless man unskilled in intertwining reeds and unfit for weaving little baskets, shall at least attempt to write something and accustom my youth to good pursuits, giving my small talent not to furnaces but to books. I shall therefore compose a small work divided into two books, entitled *The Virgin’s Palm*. For it will describe [Col. 0062C] the contest in which the holy Virgin Mary fought, and how, after conquering the enemy, she obtained the heavenly palm.

# Book One

## Chapter I

[Col. 0061C] The Virgin Mary was a Cappadocian by people, native to Caesarea, born indeed of humble but Christian parents. From infancy she was instructed in divine laws and ran untiringly after Christ in the fragrance of his ointments. To him she vowed herself and her virginity; and, in accordance with the Apostle, she thought upon the things of the Lord so that she might be holy in body and spirit. She was the servant of a nobleman named Tertullus, [Col. 0063A] whose household duties she performed. But she surpassed nobility of birth by nobility of soul, and wealth by poverty. For to abound in virtues is greater than to abound in riches; the brightness of soul surpasses that of body.

When Tertullus was celebrating his son’s birthday with banquets and sacrificing victims to vain idols, she maintained her customary fast and deceived her fellow servant, who performed duties with her, by concealment so that she would not be betrayed. Yet although the other long laid snares, Mary could not remain hidden. She was summoned by her mistress, questioned as to why she abstained and what sorrow she had, and ordered to take food. When she said she was a Christian, declared that she had always observed fasts, and refused to comply, her mistress became furious, inflicted severe beatings upon her, and further threatened her with the penalty of death. While she considered these measures, [Col. 0063B] Mary resisted; then Tertullus entered from outside. Having learned the cause, he ordered the servant girl to be scourged and, after she had been severely afflicted, confined her in custody. He assigned her a small and worthless quantity of food, insufficient to satisfy hunger, so that, failing daily through lack of food, her soul might be preserved for starvation. But a mind devoted to Christ could not be broken; indeed, she gave herself to continual prayers, and her tears were her bread day and night.

## Chapter II

The thirtieth day had now come. She rejoiced in chains and tribulations, considering that saying: “Whoever perseveres to the end, this one shall be saved” (Matthew 24). She set before herself the glorious contests and palms of holy virgins, who, frail in sex but strong in spirit, [Col. 0063C] had triumphed over the world and ascended to the starry bridal chambers of their Bridegroom, conspicuous in crowns of lilies and roses, distinguished either by guarded modesty or by shed blood.

Meanwhile it was reported to the governor that Tertullus, a leading man of that city, was concealing in his house a servant girl of the Christian religion contrary to the emperors’ decrees. Tertullus was immediately brought before the tribunal. With the chief men summoned and a crowd of the people also standing by, the governor ordered the following to be read from a document:

“Hadrian and Antoninus, pious, fortunate, august, to all who live under our law. A vanity of religion, lately devised by certain persons, has come to our attention. For there are said to be some who take no delight in sacrifices or in the worship we observe. Unless fear of punishment swiftly comes to the rescue, their conduct will undoubtedly cause the ancestral belief to be erased and the veneration of our forebears to be extinguished. We therefore give this law to all peoples and propose these decrees for every judge to observe: all are to be compelled to sacrifice; rebels are to be struck with the avenging sword. For we prefer that a few be killed rather than that all should go astray, wandering like cattle instead of sharing one judgment. If anyone thinks that a person of whatever age or sex should be concealed on account of this law or cult, that person shall breathe out his life by the sword for opposing the edicts; his property, however, shall be transferred to the imperial treasury. But the informer of so great a crime shall rejoice in a grant of four hundred denarii from the public treasury, so that all may know that neither sin nor reward passes away.”

[Col. 0064A] When the imperial document had been read, the governor said: “What, citizens, are we to do? Can we oppose the decision of our lords?” The chief men of the council replied: “We beg you to permit us to be heard more humanely.” Then the governor ordered the statements to be recorded.

## Chapter III

Nithagoras the advocate then rose; endowed as he was with speech gilded by eloquence, and speaking on behalf of all, he said:

“Excellent governor of our city and ornament of the people, we beg you to hear us graciously, for the glory of your gentleness and fairness. This man, adorned with many public offices and the distinction of birth, provides great assistance to our council. He has been a priest of the Augusti and also a giver of public games for the city. Having undertaken many embassies for the public good, he gained for himself as much affection as glory. Finally, his great generosity has enlarged the commonwealth. He has expended an immeasurable quantity of money on various buildings and on heating baths. There are yet greater matters, too numerous to list. For in his earliest age, when life is unsteady and inexperienced years burn with youthful heat, he obeyed divine religion and conquered himself, restraining even nature’s own claims with the bridle of modesty.

“When, with advancing age, he began to possess a more mature judgment, he believed that he had fulfilled the divine commandments and found something pleasing to offer the people. Thus he discharged the gifts due at the opening of the year and, providing costly spectacles from his own resources, satisfied the common gaze of all the people, bringing many splendid contests to our city. Nor did he deny the citizens the rival pleasures of battle, as gladiators fought one another. He always considered his country’s interests to take precedence over his personal needs and the profits accruing to his household. Thus he pleased the gods by his priesthood and the city by his public games. Indeed—and this is greatest of all—as a young priest he taught that age may be conquered, and he showed that pleasure need not be rejected in more advanced years.”

## Chapter IV

When he had finished speaking, the governor, having summoned the advocate, said: “Why do you so extol the splendor of his past actions and fail to refute the charge at issue? He seems to acknowledge guilt who neglects to excuse himself.” [Col. 0064D] But he replied: “Nor was the girl for whose alleged crime her master stands trial given by a wife, as the dowry documents testify.” The governor said: “Is Tertullus’s wife freeborn?” He answered: “Freeborn—indeed of exceptional nobility; for her father is Cleonides, a man of high standing.” The governor said: “Was this servant girl bought, or was she taken in and raised as a home-born slave?” Tertullus said: “She seems indeed to have been born in the household, but her parents came to us by purchase.” The governor asked him: “Is your father-in-law, sir, alive, or has he now fulfilled fate’s due?” “He has already been taken from our midst,” he replied. The governor said: “Do the parents of this stubborn girl survive?” “They,” he answered, “have already gone to the gods above.” The governor asked: “Were they worshippers of the gods of this ruinous religion?” “They,” he replied, [Col. 0065A] “were held in the same madness, worshipping the Crucified One.”

The advocate added again: “You should know, excellent governor, that this girl has long been contended with, in the hope that she might be freed from error. But she could never be soothed or bent. Her heart has conceived a savage obstinacy amid punishments and terrors. Yet justice is certainly diminished if masters’ uprightness is punished for servants’ wrongdoing. It is cruel for the good to be condemned on account of the bad. Let the guilty person pay for the guilt.”

Then, after prolonged deliberation, the governor at last delivered this judgment:

“Tertullus, publicly praised, who deserves honor in return for his merits; a most excellent giver of games by birth, a distinguished senator, devoted alike to the emperor and the divine powers; one who has fulfilled both laws and cults; one whose images I myself have often seen throughout the city—let him depart free. Let him fear no accuser and no judge. Since he is to be informed of all this with untroubled ears, I order that this most wicked girl be brought before me publicly, so that crime may have its punishment and the people its example.”

# Book Two

## Chapter I

[Col. 0065B] The virgin was therefore handed over to the executioners, like a sheep exposed among wolves. She was dragged, abused, and brought before the judge. Her eyes indeed were fixed upon the judge, but her mind was set in heaven; she commended herself to Christ and prayed to Christ. Meanwhile the people cried that such a woman must be removed from the earth and perish in cruel fires. But the virgin remained fearless, because perfect love for Christ had cast all fear out of her. Thus, lifting her eyes to heaven, she invoked Christ’s name more steadfastly. The governor was astonished at this; for almost a whole hour, all watched in wonder at the girl’s great constancy.

Then the governor asked what she was called. Mary replied [Col. 0065C]: “Why do you inquire about my name and say nothing about the law? The inquiry ought to concern that for which one is summoned to answer a charge. For nature did not give me my name, but religious observance did. Therefore I answer your question first without fear: I am a Christian.”

The governor said: “Here your master awaits you, either to confer a reward if you recant or to inflict punishment if you resist. Choose which course you will follow.”

Mary replied: “He has authority over my body, certainly, but not over my soul.”

The governor said: “Why, since you are a slave, do you not follow your master’s religion?”

Mary replied: “Because from infancy I have been consecrated to Christ and endowed by him with understanding and reason, I reject vain and senseless idols, rendering worship only to him who made all things, not to those which are acknowledged to have been made by men [Col. 0065D].”

The governor said: “From what inheritance has this folly come down to you?”

Mary replied: “Thus instructed by my ancestors, I hold to it. For devout parents desire to have devout children rather than wealthy ones.”

The governor said: “Were your parents also of this sect?”

Mary replied: “They always remained in this most holy religion.”

The governor said: “Did you adopt this religion before Deucalion? Rather, sacrifice, so that you may free both yourself and your master from guilt.”

Mary replied: “For what comparison is there between a human being and God, so that God ought not deservedly to be feared more than a human being [Col. 0066B], by whose will both we and all the elements alike are governed? Therefore I shall endure whatever crosses may be inflicted upon me, whatever severity of punishments; I bear all things calmly for love of Jesus Christ the Lord, who will grant help here and reward hereafter. For the holy Apostle warned us beforehand that no distress or persecution, hunger or nakedness, sword or any danger or tribulation should separate us from his love, so that we may deserve to attain the promised prize. Hence comes that unconquered strength; hence the unyielding spirit, and a mind made loftier by the bitterness of suffering: both because the things we endure were foretold to us, and because the rewards are greater than the pains. Since, therefore, nothing ought to separate us from Christ, I call to witness him [Col. 0066C] whom I love, whom I desire, for whom I sigh, that I shall remain steadfast in his confession, and prefer death to defeat. For I hasten to abandon earthly things and attain heavenly ones.”

## CHAPTER II

The governor said: “Sacrifice, and hasten to escape the torments threatening you.”

Mary replied: “The torments with which you threaten me are temporary. I beg only that you do not delay in carrying out what you threaten. The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me.”

Angered, the governor ordered her to be subjected to punishments. She aroused such pity among the people that those standing around shed tears and loudly begged pardon for her. [Col. 0066D] But the governor’s madness pressed for the punishment to be hastened.

Again the people, stirred to an outcry, accused the judge of cruelty; for the unanimous cry of the entire crowd was that the virgin was being torn apart by the judge’s cruelty, not by punishment for a crime; that everything was being done contrary to the laws, and that the demands of equity were not being observed. Accordingly, the governor, astonished and overwhelmed by their shouts—for amid the tumult of voices he thought even the roofs were collapsing—ordered the virgin released. Then, thinking that he had satisfied the people and now more secure, he said: “What madness has seized you, citizens? Why do you cry out? Why do you press me? Why do you make such noise? Is it that the commands of the emperors may be violated and crimes go unpunished?” And there was an answering shout: yet no one thought that hands should be raised against sacred laws. “The majesty of our lords has decreed that everyone must either sacrifice or be subject to a capital sentence. This girl does not sacrifice; let her receive the punishment prescribed by the decree. Why should she be pressed by diverse tortures, by elaborate kinds of pain? You were ordered to kill her, not consume her by tearing her apart. A rational judge ought to recognize that he judges a human being, not a beast.”

When, therefore, they requested a three-day respite for the virgin, in case she might perhaps be recalled from her resolve, the governor consented: “I grant,” he said, “the time you request. You employ persuasion, since I have been unable to prevail by terror.”

But he said to the girl: “If you accept the respite you have requested, consent to sacrifice.”

She replied: “I hold fast to what is best, and seek neither delay nor human indulgence.”

The governor said: “Nevertheless, I grant you time. If thereafter I find you stubborn in this profession, I shall strike you with the harsh punishment of tortures.”

She said: “Rather, excellent governor, if any concern for my welfare moves you, I earnestly beg you to hold my master Tertullus free of this guilt and absolve him by your authority, because he has certainly done nothing in connection with this profession.”

The governor said: “He is already free, already acquitted. But if you turn to the gods with better judgment, you shall both be fittingly rewarded and granted freedom.”

Mary replied: “I have already earned freedom from Christ [Col. 0067C], so that, having subdued vices and trampled falsehood, I may devote myself to virtues and bear witness to truth. What you promise is vain and passing. For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but harms his own soul?” (Luke 9).

## CHAPTER III

The virgin, therefore, though released, was kept under guard. Once, while she was praying and had raised her eyes to heaven, and was chanting that verse of the Psalm, “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me” (Psalm 120), while her soul thirsted for God, the living fountain, suddenly, with her heart enlarged and the inner faculties of the human person illumined, she saw the glory of majesty on high and choirs of saints, distinguished according to their ranks, singing in a voice of exultation and confession [Col. 0067D] praise to the holy Trinity. She was therefore so gladdened by such joy that she considered herself already admitted into the delights of paradise. For a devout soul toward God cannot sometimes fail to see what it loves, and by strong love obtains what it desires, when even in this present age certain firstfruits of future recompense are given to the humble and afflicted.

For a certain brother, who constantly devoted himself to divine contemplation, once told me that, while he was afflicted one dawn by prayers and much grief for his sins, he was suddenly carried away in spirit to the things above. He saw the holy Trinity in an utterly wondrous appearance. The Ancient of Days, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, with snowy-white head and radiant countenance, sat upon [Col. 0068A] a sapphire throne; and in his bosom he held that consubstantial Only-Begotten One of his divinity and glory, who became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2). He also displayed him to the brother hanging on the cross, as if reminding him how greatly and in what manner he had not spared him for sinners. With what feeling, O soul, in what words can I express, O tongue, how the Father clasped and embraced him in his fatherly arms? The Holy Spirit too was seen, incomprehensibly and ineffably proceeding from the Father and the Son in the form of a dove. Indeed, an inscription in white letters was written above that great majesty: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Matthew 22). As the aforesaid brother gazed most eagerly upon this, the thought came to him [Col. 0068B] how great is the soul’s vitality and how great the frailty of human flesh. And immediately he heard one of the saints answer: “He made us, and not we ourselves” (Psalm 99).

Then, when he began to direct his attention downward, he noticed that the earth lying below, compared with the immensity of the ether, was like the small, round body of a furnace, washed on every side by the ocean. It therefore seemed clear to him how blessed Benedict, his heart expanded in God, is read to have seen the whole world brought before him and gathered as though beneath a single sunbeam. Returning to himself, he reflected sorrowfully from what light into what darkness, from what happiness into what calamity, he had returned. Perhaps someone will disdain these things, belittle them, [Col. 0068C] and object: “Dreams have led many astray” (Ecclesiasticus 34). But I do not regard as erroneous those things which bring more benefit than harm. A vision which prompts virtue is wholesome. Contrition is the spirit of devotion; confusion accompanies the spirit of vanity.

## CHAPTER IV

The holy virgin was therefore preparing to escape from the midst of a perverse nation and, like an innocent dove, to flee the fowler’s snare. Having prudently found an opportunity, she began her flight. Perhaps she had dreaded the severity of punishments. This was human, since even the Savior, on his way to the Passion, began to fear and be distressed (Mark 14), and his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the ground (Luke 22). But the heavenly Bridegroom was now preparing to crown [Col. 0068D] the faithful contest of his bride.

For when she perceived that she was being pursued by persecutors, she turned her whole mind toward him and, with tears, prayed that she might at once be worthy to be received in peace. Truly, a miracle of wondrous novelty! Yet if you consider its author, the event will not seem incredible, for no word is impossible with God. A great rock lying in her path split itself in the middle and received the virgin into its hollow as though into a mother’s womb; then, its parts drawing together solidly again, it enclosed her body, now lifeless, within itself as in a tomb. Thus the Lord deigned to accomplish for his virgin so extraordinary a deliverance; and lest wickedness should alter her understanding or deceit deceive her soul, he hastened to bring her out from the midst of iniquities, because grace [Col. 0069A] and mercy are upon his saints and his care rests upon his elect.

But the executioners, like rabid dogs, surrounding the place in their search, investigated whether the prey so suddenly snatched from them might be hidden somewhere. They found at the rock the outermost edges of the virgin’s garment. Stunned by unbelievable amazement, they reported to the governor what had occurred. Yet evil men, who ought thereby to become better, sometimes become worse. The impious judge, moved partly by anger and partly by wonder, ordered Philocomus, chief official of the city of Neochor, to gather a multitude and hurry to demolish the same rock. At once the people assembled at the herald’s call.

They had already come to the place and were laboring to accomplish the deed [Col. 0069B], when suddenly a great flashing brilliance burst forth; with a terrifying thunderclap, so that one might almost have believed the very structure of heaven had fallen, the earth was shaken, and everyone’s footing trembled as though about to collapse. And behold, two horsemen of the heavenly host, descending from above at the swiftest gallop by the eastern way, appeared for the spectacle. Their horses were whiter than snow, all their adornment was golden, and they themselves shone with starry splendor. When those present saw them, they were struck by such terror through a certain divine power that, as consciousness and life fled them, their eyes closed in death.

[Col. 0070A] But those who escaped, fleeing to the profane thresholds of idols and circling the sacrilegious altars, perished. For help is vainly hoped for from those unable to help themselves. Philocomus too breathed out his spirit before the very doorway of the temple. Finally, fire went forth from the Lord and devoured both the people and the temple. Thus perished the multitude that had served cruelty; and the more deities they had possessed there, the greater was the fuel supplied for the growth of the fire. Let them attribute their burning to their sins, and their more prolonged burning to the number of their gods. The total of those consumed both by that sudden catastrophe and by fire was 2,700. But those who happened to escape fled trembling into the city and cried everywhere in loud voices [Col. 0070B] that the God of Mary is great, that the God of Christians alone is God, and that his judgments are just.

Therefore, since the destruction of some often produces the salvation of others, many repented of their former error and turned to the truth of faith; and about three thousand people were added to God. The multitude of believers increased, because after the storm of persecution peace was granted to the Churches, when Jesus commanded the winds and the sea and there came a calm.

[Col. 0069]

# REINER THE MONK, *FLOWER OF THE WILDERNESS*, OR TWO BOOKS ON THE LIFE OF SAINT TIEBALD, MONK AND HERMIT

(D. Bern. Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV, III, 95, from the same manuscript of the monastery of Saint Lawrence.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0069C] The virtues and deeds of the saints are recounted for the glory of God and the benefit of readers and hearers, so that in them the wondrous giver of graces may be recognized and praised, and fruitful minds may bring forth the shoots of good action through the example of splendid virtue. A type for this occurs in the history where it is written that the holy man Jacob took green poplar rods, almond rods, and plane-tree rods, and partly stripped their bark; when the bark had been removed, whiteness appeared on those that had been stripped, while those left whole remained green. [Col. 0070C] He placed them in the channels where water was poured out, so that, when the flocks came to drink, the sheep might have the rods before their eyes and conceive in their sight.

In the same manner, in the Church, where the living waters of heavenly doctrine flow, by which the flocks of believers are watered, green rods and white rods have been set forth: namely, holy men, in whom dwell the greenness of faith, uprightness of life, and brightness of good works. By their sight, instruction, and examples, the sheep—that is, the simple—may, according to the Prophet, conceive and as it were give birth and travail, and bring forth the spirit of salvation upon the earth; and the Bridegroom may rejoice and say: “All with twin offspring, and none among them is barren” (Song of Songs 4).

I am indeed unskilled both in speech and knowledge: I have not, like Esau, ranged through the wild places hunting beasts, nor wandered through philosophers’ lecture halls in study; rather, like the simple Jacob, I have always remained with my mother Rebecca in the tent, continually observing the regular leisure of the Church. Yet I trust in the wisdom and Word of the eternal Father, who has perfected praise from the mouths of infants and nursing children.

[Col. 0072A] Therefore, though unworthy, I, a monk, shall praise a praiseworthy monk, and shall compose a little work in two books, bearing this title: *Flower of the Wilderness*. In it I shall set forth the life and virtues by which Tiebald the hermit and monk flourished, and shall endeavor to show how the first flowers of his still tender age and childhood grew into this fruit. For it is healthful to cultivate the heart through honorable studies. Idleness nourishes thickets of vices; to guard against them, study is beneficial, so that, clothed in black, as though garbed in the black skins of goats, I may obtain something of that blessing which the gentle brother received from his hairy brother.

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0071B] In the territory of Sens, Tiebald, a flower as it were from a noble tree, was born of an illustrious lineage. He was brought up near the castle of Provins under Henry, emperor of the Romans, and Henry and Philip his son, kings of the Franks. His parents traced their descent from Odo, once the most famous count of Champagne, he who, because of his insolence near the castle of Bar, was overcome and expelled by the forces of Lorraine.

From the earliest beginnings of childhood he gave indications of good hope, so that it should not have seemed foolish when an old woman, poor in spirit, foretold while he was still enclosed in the womb that he would be wondrous in life. Tiebald, bishop of Vienne, the uncle of his grandmother, a man of proven holiness from whom he also received his namesake’s name, had foretold this as well. Thus he was gradually formed in age and grace, adorned with remarkable purity and modesty of conduct. For a child’s sincere disposition is a great sign of future virtue. Then, as soon as he reached the strength of youth, he pursued holy studies, visited the places of saints, restrained the slippery age of youth by frugality and prayers, and was a devoted hearer of the Lord’s words.

Above all, zealous for the philosophy of the eremitic life, which flourishes in continence, poverty, and divine contemplation, he devoted himself to this purpose. Unknown to his parents, he went to a renowned hermit living on one of the islands of the River Seine [Col. 0071D], disclosed his intention, and received from him careful instruction in all things: that hermit set before the young man, about to serve as a soldier, the duties of the soldier, commended him to Christ, and dismissed him.

Thus Tiebald, forgetting what lay behind and stretching himself toward what lay before, pressed on toward the appointed prize of the heavenly calling. Leaving father and mother, brothers and servants, vast estates—in short, everything belonging to the world—he came to Reims near Easter, as though about to receive the belt of military service, with three companions: a soldier familiar to him and his own and that soldier’s squire. He lodged in the city. Then, having found an opportunity to escape from the hand of the Egyptian mistress, that is, worldly display, he left behind the cloak of all his possessions and fled. Leaving at home both horses and squires, he went out with his most faithful companion as though to bid friends farewell, and secretly departed farther on. Meeting two pilgrims dressed in excellent clothes, they stripped themselves and clothed the needy men, putting on the pilgrims’ cheap and despised hair-shirts. Thus, with their outward appearance exchanged, these merciful men travelled to a place called Ptango [Note: [Col. 0071D] In other versions: Pitango, Pitindo, and Picingo.], which was in the kingdom of the Germans. Memorable compassion! They clothed Christ in the poor, that they might escape the shipwreck of the world [Col. 0072C] naked.

## CHAPTER II

Having remained for a long time in the aforesaid place, they lived amid hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, many fasts and vigils. Indeed, as is sung in the Psalm, “Their hands served in the basket” (Psalm 80), because, made poor and pilgrims for Christ, they subjected themselves to the lowest service in order to procure necessities: cutting hay from meadows, carrying stones, cleaning the shelters of beasts of burden, and making charcoal for smiths’ work. Having earned scant wages by such labor, they set out barefoot for Galicia, seeking the protection of blessed James.

The devil envied them and rose up to oppose their progress [Col. 0072D]. Yet he did not dare to do this openly, but devised a trick. For, as Tiebald returned from prayer, he placed himself before him in the form of a man which he had assumed, lay crookedly upon the ground, and caused him to stumble. Immediately Tiebald called upon Christ and armed himself with the sign of the cross. Unable to endure this, the deceiver vanished. But the trouble of temptations is material for crowns for the righteous. Demons attack; Christ defends. Greater contests deserve greater rewards.

After this the blessed man came to Trier with his companion, and there, on finding his father, he was greatly distressed. For his father opposed him on the way of the Lord and sought to keep him in the world. But he, holding unwaveringly to what is written, “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10), clung to Christ in contempt for his father and for the world. Carrying his cross and desiring to worship the venerable tomb at Jerusalem, he went first to Rome and then to Venice, intending to cross the sea. While travelling through the regions of Italy for this purpose, he came to a place which [Note: [Col. 0073D] In other versions: Sallanica, Sallavica, and Sallaviga.] antiquity called Salanica, and he chose to remain there. Having surveyed the place, he found an extensive forest clearing and the ruins of an ancient church. With permission to dwell there obtained from the lords of the place, he began to carry out what he had long conceived in his mind: namely, to live a solitary life. Having built a small hut, he settled there as the wilderness’s new inhabitant.

It would take long to recount the crosses which this strong athlete then imposed upon himself: fasts, vigils, prayers, and mortification of the flesh. At first he abstained from meat and every kind of fat food, satisfying nature rather than his stomach with barley bread and water alone. Then, as his spirit grew strong for greater things and rose above what was human, denying himself even bread and every drink, for several years he lived only on fruits, herbs, and the roots of herbs, always wearing a hair-shirt. For the inner person was nourished by heavenly ministries and continual contemplation [Col. 0073C], so that the outer person thought less of material food; he rested wholly in God, so that he could truly say only: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song of Songs 2).

## CHAPTER III

Thus, through the dispensation of heavenly grace, as his merits grew, he was advanced by Bishop Liudecherius [Note: [Col. 0074D] In another version: Liutichericus.], a distinguished man, through the ecclesiastical ranks as far as the priesthood in the Church of Vincentia, so that he who had already become a living sacrifice to God by mortification of the flesh might offer upon the most holy altar a life-giving and acceptable sacrifice to him. For an offering is approved as more pleasing when conduct commends it as better. Yet what may edify anyone ought not to be suppressed in silence.

I heard privately from a certain priest that, while Tiebald performed the venerable mysteries in celebrations of Mass, he was sometimes touched by a kind of vapor from an invisible fire, as though he were standing beside a burning furnace. Indeed, while holding them in his hands, he felt the bread itself or the chalice grow warm in a wondrous manner, because the Word of God is truly fire; that bread is his flesh, and that wine is truly his blood.

How, too, shall I recall with sufficient feeling that he once saw upon the altar the sacrament of the true Isaac transformed into the form of a boy hanging upon the cross and smiling upon him [Col. 0074A], though glorious gray hair flourished upon him, so that in the boy’s youthfulness the newness of humanity and in the aged head the antiquity of divinity might be signified?

Nor does devotion permit me to conceal that at one twilight he beheld the holy Trinity in a vision. Two persons were of an appearance and countenance ineffably venerable, with heads whiter than snow; the third was conspicuous in the flower of youth, of beautiful and sweet modesty, and clothed in a scarlet cloak. When the other persons pointed him out and said, “Friend, do you recognize Jesus?” Tiebald fixed all his affection upon him and recognized the garment in which that same king of glory and honor—king, I say, and only-begotten Son of the King—had been clothed on the day when the reproaches of those who reproached fell upon him. When he wished to fall at his feet [Col. 0074B] and kiss them, Jesus, in marvelous condescension, extended to him for kissing his holy and venerable hands, still bloody from fresh wounds. Behold, the mind melts, the senses are astonished, speech fails, and cannot embrace in words what can be contained in affection! O how ineffable is the sweetness of heavenly delight! Fixing its mouth in kisses upon those wounds—the hills of eternal longing—the soul perceived that its mouth was, as it were, steeped in the sweetest and most merciful blood, with a wondrous and inexhaustible savor.

Nor do I think it should be passed over that the aforesaid faithful man also related that, while reading the divine page, he was several times breathed upon by a sweet warm breeze proceeding from the book he was then holding [Col. 0074C]. This is devout and serious. For Moses writes that the law of God—namely, all Scripture—was inspired and issued by the Holy Spirit, who is true fire, and is fiery; David says, “Your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire” (Psalm 118); and Solomon says, “Every word of God, tested by fire, is a shield to those who hope in him” (Proverbs 30). Therefore all things work together for good to those who love God. Truly, when through the vehemence of love they mourn with inexpressible groanings that their earthly sojourn is prolonged—especially since human life upon earth is warfare, and the weakness of the flesh, so many enemies, so many wounds, so many passions, miseries, and falls do not allow them to be secure—they are sometimes visited by divine revelation and encouraged by protection, so that they may be consoled and have confidence because Jesus has overcome the world.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0074D] Thus, the more Tiebald knew himself to have drawn near to God by a higher degree, the more he devoted himself to spiritual exercises. If you were now to see the strictness of his conduct, you would think his earlier life had been luxurious, since he often struck himself more than severely with a many-thonged whip. For he chastised his body and reduced it to slavery, lest he be compelled to serve the body.

For five years, as those close to him testified, he took sleep not lying down but sitting. So praiseworthy was his concealment of it that, when he lay down, he carefully covered himself with clothes as though he intended to rest all night; but after his attendant departed [Col. 0075A], he hurried to the duties of sacred vigils and spent the whole darkness in prayer, surely seeking upon his bed at night him whom his soul loved. When it was time to rise, however, he returned himself to the bed, avoiding human praise and desiring God alone as his witness. For the flower falls from the tree when the north wind plucks it. Good action loses its bloom through the fault of boastfulness. The rich luxury of his bed was a chest with a level surface, a linen cloth spread over it, a log for a pillow, and a woolen cap that had protected him from the heat during his pilgrimage. But when he had armed, as it were, his entire body with a hair-shirt, he laid a hair-shirt beneath himself instead of the linen cloth; and instead of the chest, he placed beneath himself a broad, planed piece of wood. Thus, wasted by daily chastisement of the body and melted by the contrition of a humbled spirit, he could truly say: “My hands dripped myrrh, and my fingers were full of choicest myrrh” (Song of Songs 5). Thus to see Tiebald practicing philosophy was a very great profit.

Two years had passed when Walter, his companion in purpose, whom I mentioned above, died a good death. For one who has lived well dies well.

Certainly I remember that some years ago I stood beside the bed [Col. 0076A] of a brother struggling in his death agony. For a while he lay unconscious, so that he was thought to have died; then he opened his eyes, looked around, consoled his weeping friends, gave kisses, and declared that he had been present at the glory of the saints. Afterwards, with great feeling and sighs, he began in a low murmur the prayer which the prophet uttered when shut up in the belly of the whale. In the midst of its words he breathed out his spirit and was raised from death’s corruption to incorruptible life. O whoever you are whose soul is distressed by the waves of temptations and miseries passing over you, attend and reflect upon the sufferings of the sick and the agonies of the dying: how they are pressed, how they sweat, at what bitterness they purchase the sweetness of that apple which the first parents seized with bloodstained teeth! Visit again [Col. 0076B] the tombs of the buried, though you cannot endure their stench; shudder also at the dreadful remains of the dead, as recently a mournful and pitiable sight showed us a human body still held together by bones and sinews, but stripped of flesh. For it greatly opposes vices to consider carefully what you shall become. But let the second book now set forth what remains.

# BOOK TWO

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0075C] Tiebald, therefore, did not lack contests with the ancient enemy, so that he might shine forth more proved through constancy. One night, as he lay in bed but was not sleeping, the tempter came. Shaking the wall of the little cell with great force, he began to reproach Tiebald for being excessively devoted to idleness, so full of sleep that he neglected to sing Matins, and said that it was now time to rise. The man of God thought that the brother who lived with him had awakened him for the morning synaxis. He went out but found no one; and when he knocked at that brother’s cell, he learned from the bolted doors that he was asleep. He therefore understood that it had been a demonic illusion. Then, making the sign of the cross and calling upon the Holy Spirit, he drove away the wicked spirit; and he heard it depart like a multitude of country people [Col. 0075D] cutting down a forest with axes. Truly a mighty warrior: since he could not conquer the hermit, he displayed that he could at least overthrow the trees of the wilderness!

At another time the holy man was undertaking a mission of peace among certain persons at variance, when the insidious enemy assailed him with a fraudulent attack, in order to wound in body the man whom he could not overcome in spirit. As Tiebald was crossing, near the castle of Leon, a river called the New, he sat in a cart because weakness prevented him from walking. Suddenly one of the vehicle’s wheels disappeared, so that the man of God might be thrown down and perish by drowning. But the Lord guarded the one who loved him and became salvation to his humble servant. Raised up by the single remaining wheel, he crossed unharmed, not even slightly [Col. 0076C] wetted. Even irrational elements, indeed, reverence the saints.

Moreover, the crafty enemy assailed him by a thousand arts of harm. But the Lord broke the arm of the sinner and the evil one, and by ever more glorious victories made his soldier more glorious. Amid his temptations, too, he sometimes refreshed him with heavenly visions. For the fervor of devotion is greatly kindled by the oil of divine consolation. Nor is there any aid more effective against temptations or evil assaults than diligent invocation of the Holy Spirit. This is the one harbor of salvation, this the unique calm, this the wondrous sweetness. When it instills a living savor into the heart, it sometimes even flourishes in the mouth with a honey-sweet taste, so that whoever has merited this rejoices to be suddenly refreshed and, when the south wind truly blows through him, puts on the flower of grateful newness.

## CHAPTER II

A certain familiar brother related to me a memorable event for the sake of edification. At dawn one day he had invoked the Holy Spirit most urgently; exhausted by prayer and tears, he fell asleep. But he awoke as a great and mighty wind came upon him like thunder. His eyes lay open, yet he was wholly unable to move. After the Spirit came a shaking, so that he felt the bed move and himself shaken like the trunk of a tree. After the shaking, fire surrounded him.

Meanwhile he recalled that something similar had occurred to the holy prophet in the cave of Mount Horeb [Col. 0077A]. After the fire, therefore, the whisper of a gentle breeze was heard, and there was the Lord. A dove, indeed, brighter than every whiteness, appeared. Flying over him and uttering the sweetest little sounds expressive of affection, it entered the brother’s mouth and, penetrating to his heart, remained there for some time. Then, beating its wings, it departed. O with what sweetness, with what delight was that heart then affected, when even the body itself became moist, as though sprinkled with oil, by the gentlest sweat. This brother truly had an unceasing remembrance of the Holy Spirit, invoking, embracing, and desiring him in a wondrous manner with all his inmost being. Hence he was often granted visitation by him.

But because a certain very dear person urges me in his prayers to write something concerning the grace and consolation of the same Holy Spirit, I shall more suitably weave into that little work the things worthy of remembrance that I have learned either from the aforesaid brother or from others, if the Father of lights gives life and ability, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift descends [Col. 0077B].

## CHAPTER III

Thus, once when Tiebald mourned his sins with a contrite heart and, following the ancient example of Achsah, longed for the upper and lower springs, a voice descended to him in these words: “Do not weep; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9). A fitting consolation indeed for a faithful soul that, in the land of pilgrimage and misery, had already received an oracle of its salvation.

At about the same time, in a vision of the night, the holy martyrs Ermagoras and Fortunatus stood before him [Col. 0077C]. The chapel of his cell was dedicated under the title of their names. They were wondrous in heavenly beauty, with fiery faces, star-like eyes, purple garments, and they gave thanks for his devoted diligence toward the worship of God and remembrance of themselves. Happy indeed were his eyes, which, while he was still placed on earth, deserved to behold heavenly things.

One of his attendants, named Odo, was afflicted by severe fever and the painful illness of a tumor. He repeatedly sought the aid of Tiebald’s prayers. At first Tiebald refused, calling himself a sinner and saying that he was not one able to resist the will of God, at whose decision illnesses are subject. But when he saw that his faithful attendant was now drawing his final breath [Col. 0077D], grieved at his departure, he ordered him carried to the church. He himself went to celebrate the sacred mysteries of Mass. The sick man received communion in the most holy body and blood, and immediately the illness was driven away and health restored. Thus he who had scarcely been carried by the hands of others returned healthy on his own feet through Tiebald’s merit, fulfilling what Truth promised to believers: “Amen, I say to you: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John 14).

The lamp, therefore, set upon its stand had spread its beams far and wide, when, as many people flocked to the man of God from every quarter, report also drew his father and mother thither with a great company of nobles. His parents rejoiced exceedingly to have found him whom they had mourned as lost, especially when they beheld their son’s so glorious [Col. 0078A] manner of life. Then the devout mother almost hesitated what she preferred: to return to her own people, country, and wealth, or to cling to Tiebald alone. But love for her son—indeed, the charity of Christ—prevailed. With all that was hers she renounced the world and followed Christ. Stripped of ambitious finery, she sought the garments of an eremitic life: a dark robe and poor attire. Thus she who had formerly been mistress of great households and broad estates now inhabited, with Tiebald, the narrow confines of a single hut; following his example, she devoted herself to fasts, vigils, and prayers. Her most devoted son served her so diligently that no cold or hardship ever caused his attentiveness to fail, recalling what is written: “Son, honour thy father and thy mother, that thou mayest be long-lived upon the earth” (Exod. 20). For the righteous man accommodated himself more to God than to nature.

[Col. 0078B] Moreover, if any guests arrived, like another Abraham or the holy Lot he hastened to meet them, rejoicing; he greeted, embraced, and kissed them. He led the little guest in, washed his feet, cooked vegetables, set the table, broke bread, and himself offered the cup. One might have seen a man disciplined by spiritual training. He was notable in conduct, speech, and bearing; his countenance was modest, his bright eyes shone, and through them, as through two mirrors, inward grace radiated. And, like holy Job, the light of his face did not fall to the ground.

## Chapter IV

For two years before his death he was free from every temptation and assault of vices; but he was afflicted with such severe illnesses and crushed by such great distress that [Col. 0078C] he could neither plant his step, nor turn himself to the other side, nor bring his hand to his mouth. For the supreme Craftsman, by the fire of tribulation and the file of infirmity, was preparing to polish the gem which He would shortly snatch from the earth and set in His diadem; He was cleansing sevenfold him whom He had judged worthy to dwell in His tabernacle. Thus that milky flower of the wilderness withered. That flowering blossom of the wilderness was scorched by the breath of illness. Tiebald lay ever intent upon heaven; nor, though he suffered no diminution of his former strictness, did he turn his mind away from prayer. For in saints the strength of the soul prevails more than bodily weakness. As the flesh wastes away, so the spirit grows strong. “For strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12).

[Col. 0078D] In the twelfth year after he had left his homeland—for he spent three years abroad and lived nine as a solitary—he came to his end. Then he summoned Peter, abbot and man of excellent fruitfulness, most intimate with him, from whom in that same year he had received the monastic habit. To him he entrusted his mother, his spiritual sons whom he had begotten and reared for Christ, his poor household goods, and the care of his cell, foretelling to the brothers that his dissolution was near.

After this, as his illness grew worse, he lay in his death-struggle and tasted the long bitterness of death. For thus was cleansed one soon to be taken up to God. That divine mercy had come to receive him was attested by an earthquake which, on the third day before his passing, shook his cell five times; some felt it before the doors, and all who stood within. Many persons of both sexes had assembled to bid him farewell, uttering groans and shedding tears.

But when one of the brothers saw the man of God wearied by his prolonged agony, moved by divine prompting he urged everyone to leave. When Tiebald had rested a little, he asked with wonderful longing for the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood; he received it and gave thanks. Then, lifting hands and eyes to heaven, and repeatedly saying, “Lord, Lord, have mercy upon thy people” (Esth. 13), as his Beloved was already knocking, he rose to open to Him, and happily rendered up his spirit, wearied by divine labours. He was thus wonderfully led on his way by angelic hands. And because here he had hungered and thirsted for righteousness, [Col. 0079B] admitted in a wedding garment to the supper of the Lamb, he feasts at the table of blessed and everlasting satiety.

[Col. 0080A] So that it might be plain to all how purely and innocently Tiebald had lived, he displayed a certain foretaste of the future glory of the resurrection and of the flesh’s transformed nature. He shone whiter than lilies and smelled more sweetly than beds of spices. After honouring him with solemn funeral rites and commending him with many tears, the faithful laid him in a worthy sarcophagus, until on the day of restoration he may bloom anew unto incorruption and receive the double robe of eternal brightness. He died on the second day before the Kalends of July [30 June], in the sixth indiction, in the reign of Henry, son of Henry, the second Augustus. The frequent miracles which are still performed through him proclaim the renown of his merits, and his memory is celebrated by crowds of people.

Finally, his sacred ashes were later translated by his sister [Col. 0080B] into Gaul, where they obtained great veneration in many places.

[Col. 0079]

# Two Little Books of the Monk Reiner on the Conflict of Two Dukes and the Marvellous Revelation of Souls, and on a Captive Soldier Freed through the Saving Sacrifice

(D. Bern. Pezius, *ibid.*, col. 109, from the same manuscript.)

## Epigram on the Following Work

[Col. 0079C]

What we write, O friend, you deem most pleasing,  
though it has very little worth in thought or expression.  
Yet why do you, who with deep heart pour golden drops in words,  
So diligently bend down to our earthenware?  
The learning of sapphire and emerald illumines you;  
Why then does the gravel of our poverty please you so greatly?  
Certainly you are drawn by affection. We are poor in talent,  
Yet we do not shrink from writing, because you take it seriously.  
Therefore accept what I have woven according to metrical rule,  
And do not doubt it. Majolus, the abbot of Cluny,  
Who shone in monastic holiness, recounted this—  
A truly marvellous event occurring between two dukes.  
For while these dukes were engaged in grievous wars,  
This Father happened to enter their borderlands;  
and while he was visiting abbeys in pursuit of his business,  
[Col. 0079D] he was seized as a captive by military guards,  
and there learned, from the reliable reports of many,  
what he related from visions of departed spirits.

[Col. 0080C]

These matters I first set forth for you in one little book.  
After it I appended another, equally worthy,  
concerning a soldier captured by enemies  
and extraordinarily saved through Christ’s sacred sacrifice.  
Favour these, then, as pledges of affection  
and most welcome hostages of mutual love.  
For I laboured over them through the course of five days,  
and put four hundred verses into the work.  
Indeed, I added twice thirty and twice ten more;  
but because you were in haste, I issued them less polished.  
And, copying each item according to your wish,  
I allowed synaloephas everywhere in poetic fashion.  
But had you delayed the leisure for writing somewhat longer,  
our poem would certainly have reached you more corrected.  
Yet whatever its quality, receive it kindly.  
[Col. 0080D] Keep it yourself, read it yourself, and conceal its foolishness.  
And you whose virtues sparkle with many gems,  
cast upon us the ray of but a single carbuncle.

## A Short Preface by the Same Author

[Col. 0081]

[Col. 0081A]

Venturing upon greater things, I first attempt smaller ones,  
and now accustom my untrained talent by a brief narration,  
lest thereafter the subject prove too broad and formidable for me.  
So a sailor tests his hand upon a narrower sea,  
[Col. 0082A] first gaining skill by practice in beginner’s work  
before he wishes to commit his sails to the billowing deep.  
Nor do I now employ ornament or elegance;  
rather, my purpose is a simple and lucid order.

# First Little Book: On the Conflict of Two Dukes and the Marvellous Revelation of Souls

[Col. 0081]

[Col. 0081B]

It is told that two dukes once flourished,  
one on Sicilian shores, the other on Sardinian.  
The latter was called Eusebius, the former Ostorgius;  
the former had greater valour, a more numerous host,  
more wealth, and more extensive power.  
But the Sardinian was superior in the endowment of morals;  
like holy Job, he lacked no virtue.  
Yet he was especially zealous for those departed from life,  
pleasing the Godhead by continual services:  
giving much to churches and to the needy,  
and causing the sacred celebration of Masses to be frequent,  
so that they might enjoy life and everlasting rest.

From the cities subject to him he had chosen one  
which surpassed the rest in cultivation and revenue;  
and he had dedicated it to Christ and to Christ’s members—  
[Col. 0081C] namely the weak, needy, and pilgrims—  
that they might flock there as to a refuge of mercy,  
there to find rest, provision, and clothing.  
He retained absolutely nothing from it for his own use;  
rather, he had all the tithes produced by the district  
brought there every year.

Nor were the life-giving offices of divine worship lacking  
from the precincts of that great and blessed city:  
by night and day, throughout its churches, the celebration of praises  
and the devout performance of Masses flourished publicly.  
Thus the illustrious man anointed Christ’s footsteps  
with the precious nard of piety,  
with the sweet unguents of devoted diligence—  
Christ who testified that what is done to the least is done to Himself,  
for they too are members of His one body.

[Col. 0081D]

Finally, as the aromatic nard of that woman of the Gospel  
spread wondrous fragrances,  
so also this memorable zeal of the righteous man  
gave forth the breath of a good breeze in every direction,  
until, penetrating the hidden retreats of heaven,  
it won the very sense of smell of the supreme Godhead.  
How great, sweet, fragrant, and pleasing it was  
is clearer than light; for it benefited not only him,  
but also brought the profit of salvation to many,  
as will now become known from the course and outcome of events.

When, therefore, the conflicts of a long quarrel continued  
and the aforesaid dukes struck one another in war,  
the Sicilian laid snares and devised treachery against him.  
[Col. 0082B] He suddenly attacked and captured the city of which we have spoken, which had been assigned to God for the aid of souls,  
and, establishing a hostile garrison, forced it beneath his rule.  
Alas—what a violent and unjust plunderer,  
who did not fear by such a base deed to injure piety  
and profane what had been dedicated to divine service!

This report struck Eusebius while he was absent;  
it gathered clouds of sorrow in his mind and face.  
For he would rather have been deprived of a part of his kingdom,  
however splendid and dear to him, than of that city  
which he himself was accustomed repeatedly to call the City of God.  
Nevertheless, casting his hope upon the Lord and considering  
that prosperous success would be granted him,  
he summoned his companions and loyal cohorts together,  
stirred them by exhortation, and strengthened the wavering by reason.

[Col. 0082C]

“What do you think, companions? What say you, friends?  
Has the wrong done to God stirred your minds?  
A greedy robber has deceitfully snatched away  
what we had bestowed upon Him, and strives to retain it by force.  
Let not the zeal of your courage endure this.  
Let us be zealous for justice and confront the enemy;  
secure in justice, we shall become victors.  
But if another outcome pleases the just Godhead,  
we shall die usefully and honourably.  
For He will raise to a state free of stain the life  
of one who falls for this cause  
and exposes mortal life to death.  
It becomes brave men, therefore, to put their hands to brave deeds.  
The graver the matter and the graver the dangers that threaten,  
the more brightly may virtue shine and courage be proved.

[Col. 0082D]

“Nor, while you fight, shall I take my ease.  
I shall carry the standards first; I shall enter the struggle first;  
I shall be present in all things and shall not spare myself labour.”

Then, just as flowers unfold beneath the sunny sky  
when murky night had bound them in its numbness,  
and the strength of friendly light’s breath revives  
what, languishing in cold shadows, had almost expired—  
so, restored by the duke’s exhortation, the men’s hearts revived;  
idle fear was driven out by reason’s rays;  
their breasts grew warm and their arms increased in strength.  
With their right hands they pledged faithful spirits for war,  
prepared to take vengeance, and gathered forces from every side.

The duke then led his formed battalions against the enemy.  
[Col. 0083A] But while he awaited their advance and an opportunity for battle,  
he himself withdrew his camp to a secure position, held it back,  
and devised ambushes with men chosen from the army,  
seeking to overcome hostile treachery by stratagem.

Meanwhile the guards watched over the camp.  
Set upon lookouts, they surveyed everything with their eyes  
and searched far and wide over the expanse of country.  
Then they saw a numerous battle-line approaching in the distance.  
They thought the arms hostile, yet stood uncertain;  
they stared intently, to recognize it more certainly.  
Now that army gradually drew near,  
of wondrous appearance and astonishing bearing.  
You would have thought that the lilies of flower-bearing fields were yielding,  
while their arms and banners shone brighter than snow  
and the horses their riders mounted blossomed in whiteness.

[Col. 0083B]

Why add more? Wherever they marched, the whole earth seemed to ripple  
with the flashing radiance of their brilliance,  
and the sunlight floated upon their shining weapons.  
The guards were amazed by this unexpected sight  
and reported it to their master, ill with pressing anxieties.  
He too was no less amazed: fear weighed him down on one side, hope raised him on the other.  
For hearing that the men’s apparel was white,  
he was called to hope of glad things by no empty interpreter;  
yet, because their weapons displayed the aspect of war,  
he anxiously feared that they might threaten him with some disaster.

He consulted his counsellors, chief men, and friends,  
and sent four mounted men ahead  
to ask who they were, whence they came, whither they were going,  
[Col. 0083C] why they had come, and whether they intended hostility or not.

As these hurried forward, four horsemen from the aforesaid company  
also came to meet them, ready to give an answer.  
They courteously returned their greetings;  
and, when asked about their arrival and the reason for their arms,  
they gently replied and thus soothed the astonished men:

“Let fear be far away; let steadfastness dwell in your hearts;  
let the anxiety of evil suspicion be removed.  
For we have come peaceably to you,  
defenders of your cause and enemies of your enemies.  
We perform a heavenly service and warfare,  
and have been sent from heaven as a consolation to you.  
Therefore, when you return, tell your lord  
to approach us confidently and fear nothing further;  
[Col. 0083D] indeed, let him clear away the cloud of fear with better hope,  
and grant us the sight and conversation of his presence.  
Now, as spring’s clear weather returns after winter,  
so, after adversity, prosperity shall return with God shining upon you.”

The envoys brought the duke this most happy message.  
Released as though from chains of sorrow and fear,  
he lifted his mind by hope and already triumphed over the enemy in hope.  
He went thither with a small retinue.  
The horsemen received him and greeted him kindly,  
eager to honour his arrival with wondrous affection.  
Then they repeated what they had said before to the envoys,  
added more, and asked whether he grieved  
that the Sicilian duke had seized so great a city from him.  
He replied that this troubled him greatly indeed,  
[Col. 0084A] especially because he had bequeathed it to Christ  
and to Christ’s members for the redemption of souls.

They said: “Set aside that care and all that grief.  
Whatever you give or have given to Christ,  
if someone defrauds, steals, or diminishes it, is not lost;  
what has been entrusted to you will assuredly never perish,  
but will remain established in heaven and be multiplied a hundredfold.  
And lest we keep you in suspense by promises,  
we shall now recover all that is yours from the enemy.  
He will restore double whatever he took from you  
and, making satisfaction, will submit to your dominion;  
or he shall be captured and handed over to you in bonds.  
Only listen to us, follow us, and do not distrust;  
prepare to lead your companies with you.”

[Col. 0084B]

Here the prince committed himself to their faith,  
followed their judgment, and obeyed without any delay.  
He returned to his camp and called troops to arms,  
not more than could be formed into one legion.  
Yet he exhorted them and went before them at their head;  
he dared to meet sixty thousand men,  
trusting in heavenly rather than earthly arms.  
For that snow-white force went before him,  
packed with forty thousand men,  
and advanced confidently against the enemy.

When Ostorgius learned this, he was utterly astonished.  
The brilliance, appearance of the weapons, and clothing of those coming  
cast him into deep amazement by their great novelty.  
Then he quickly sent to ask who they were and whence they came,  
why they threatened thus, and who was leader of so great an army.

[Col. 0084C]

Some men in white met those who had come from the host  
and declared themselves to belong to the force for which he asked.  
They said that they served Christ’s kingdom and their own king,  
and had come to capture their lord  
unless he came as a suppliant and sought peace and pardon,  
and made satisfaction to Christ and Christ’s servant,  
whom he had so greatly distressed by taking the city.

Without delay these ill tidings were reported to the Sicilian duke.  
Trembling, he urgently sought counsel from his men  
and hastened, when counselled, to go where he had been ordered.  
Men from the white-shining company likewise appeared.  
The duke asked them and heard what the envoys had said earlier;  
indeed, they further terrified him with grave threats—  
that he would undergo the punishments of divine wrath  
because, as an impious robber, he had seized from Christ the city  
[Col. 0084D] which the devout worshipper had bestowed upon Him, and dared to retain it.

He feared and trembled, begged forgiveness,  
and promised to do what they judged should be done,  
so that a correction worthy of what he had rashly committed might be made.  
He had now come to the shining multitude’s host,  
and the Sicilian sought terms of peace and pardon.  
Behold, the Sardinian duke also arrived;  
at once Trinacria [Sicily] submitted itself wholly to him,  
and he made double restitution for every loss.  
A treaty was concluded, peace was confirmed on both sides,  
and full concord made loyal friends of them all.

If Boreas on one side and Auster on the other  
have long stirred the sea with contrary raging blasts,  
at length they subside and are silent when Phoebus shines bright.

Then that white host addressed Eusebius  
[Col. 0085A] and affectionately asked whether this was sufficient for him.  
He assented, eagerly offered many thanks,  
and no longer thought it vain to learn who they were.  
He approached as a suppliant and then inquired more closely.  
Nor could they hide their secret from so great a man,  
whose merits had won them the joys of light;  
rather, it was beneficial to reveal it to him and to many others:

“We,” they said, “are the souls of the dead  
whom divine grace saved through your deeds:  
we whom you happily rescued from Satan’s snares,  
his wretched dominion, and the yoke of sin,  
and admitted into the inner dwelling-place of eternal light,  
by sharing your goods with churches and the poor  
and properly devoting yourself to works approved as pleasing to Christ.  
Do not regret, then, that you have laboured in good works for us.

[Col. 0085B]

“For thereby you have gained the love of the heavenly King  
and the favour of the saints and every righteous person.  
Indeed, continue more fully, better and ever better,  
to carry out what you have hitherto done with good will—  
a work acceptable from your own resources and intentions—  
at the prompting of our prayer and faithful service,  
so that we, delivered through you and freed from punishments,  
[Col. 0086A] may unceasingly pray with you  
for life, peace, and everlasting salvation.  
For do not doubt that you have restored all whom you see to life,  
with the Judge reconciled to us;  
and you will restore many more if devout vigilance endures.”

Thus, when the duke had been admonished and magnificently encouraged,  
that bright and blessed company requested leave to depart.  
The duke shed tears arising from the depths of his feeling,  
praised and blessed God who works wonders  
and had so marvellously disclosed His secrets to him.  
He dismissed the white-clad host, earnestly entreating them in many ways.  
They returned to the invisible citadels whence they had come.

But that devout man, that truly religious man—  
oh, what flames of holy zeal he then raised  
[Col. 0086B] in his noble heart, increased by the oil of piety!  
This cannot be told or written in our poem;  
let every thoughtful reader rather weigh it.  
He grew perfect, fulfilled better what he had well begun,  
nor lacked fruit, since he received it multiplied a hundredfold,  
becoming also possessor and inhabitant of the eternal land.

## Epilogue

[Col. 0085]

[Col. 0085C]

Perhaps, friend, you ask how things without bodies  
can assume a bodily form,  
so that souls which have now laid aside their forms  
may share in human sight as visible beings;  
or how they can have the use of limbs  
to fashion articulated measures of speech.  
My mind and intellect do not comprehend this.  
I do not believe that such a secret lies open to anyone,  
yet I do not deny that it can be accomplished by God’s will,  
for nothing is known to be impossible to Him alone.

[Col. 0086C]

For, while many authorities recount  
that a human spirit has often assumed visible form  
and uttered words, whether good or evil,  
would anyone call this false?  
You, endowed with conspicuous intelligence,  
consider with yourself how it should be understood.  
If you wish to examine it more deeply,  
use the serene writings of the Fathers as a mirror.

## Short Preface to the Second Book

[Col. 0085]

[Col. 0085D]

Behold, I sing in a nearly vernacular, unusual verse,  
and plainly and smoothly relate the brief history of Pyrgi.  
May such a memorable poem please you, friend.  
And because my pen has depicted in the former little book  
what fruits the expenditures of holy *agapē* [charity] bring forth,  
[Col. 0086D] now in the latter it will also set forth  
what the wine with bread of the divine mystical table can accomplish.  
If you yourself are not wearied by my Muse,  
it will be pleasing to write, nor shall I regret having written.

# Second Little Book: On a Captive Soldier Freed through the Saving Sacrifice

[Col. 0085]

[Col. 0085D]

Two kings joined battle against one another,  
proud of lineage, wealth, and armies.  
Both possessed great strength; therefore a most grievous slaughter  
fell upon either side. Fierce death raged here and there;  
men fell, and fatal wounds in dense succession  
broke the battle-lines, with danger nearly equal on both sides.  
For though one, after routing the enemy, bore away  
victorious eagles, they were everywhere bloodstained.  
For he lost his brother to a mortal wound,  
as well as some beloved men with part of his army.

[Col. 0086D]

Among them also happened to fall his faithful servant,  
a young man of proven worth, grievously wounded,  
already drained of blood. For the span of one night  
and likewise one day, he lay almost lifeless,  
resembling the lifeless crowd  
lying heaped around him.  
But when warmth of life slowly returned through his limbs,  
and strength returned at last with consciousness,  
he rose, sat up, and, as best he could,  
bound and tightened the deep openings of his wounds.

[Col. 0087A]

Then he gave his panting breast a little rest,  
and, though weak, raised his limbs to walk.  
He set out on his way, in case perhaps someone might meet him,  
a friendly person who would compassionately tend to him.  
But as he sought such a man, an enemy appeared, seized him,  
and brought him before his duke for examination.  
The duke asked whence he came, of what rank he was,  
and what his occupation was—free man or commoner.

The clever young man concealed what he was careful to reveal,  
and, avoiding resentment, said: “I am a poor peasant,  
with a wife joined to me in lawful marriage.  
Our means are slight, and whatever we acquire  
by service we share for the household’s needs.  
Then, good duke, since I am ignorant and unpractised in war,  
I followed the camp for no other reason on my country’s behalf  
[Col. 0087B] than to carry food supplies to the soldiers,  
as was laid upon me by royal edict and common regulation.  
Grant pardon, therefore; it is less just to punish servants  
who must obey kings and masters.”

The prince was moved by these words, grieved for and pitied the wretch.  
He took him in, summoned physicians, and supplied necessities.  
But after his strength returned and he began to recover,  
he ordered him fettered at night lest he escape.  
Yet no means could keep him bound.  
For as soon as the guard who had fastened the chains left,  
he was immediately released by an invisible power,  
greatly astonished by the marvel himself.

Now he had a brother, distinguished by an honourable life  
and holding the venerable office of priest.  
When report led this brother to believe that he had fallen in battle,  
[Col. 0087C] he diligently hurried to retrieve the dead body.  
Finding in the field the corpse of another man who happened to look very like him,  
he thought it was his brother’s body.  
He lifted it, carried it home, and buried it honourably;  
and for his repose he did not neglect to celebrate  
the offices of Mass with devout diligence.

Accordingly, as stated above, it truly came about  
that chains imposed upon the young man could not bind him.  
But lest anyone attribute this to a strange faith,  
Pope Gregory, golden in truthful speech,  
is read to recount a somewhat similar event:  
a certain captive had been carried away by enemies  
and endured very tight chains for many years.  
When his wife believed that he had died,  
[Col. 0087D] on specified days for his repose she had the mystical sacrifice  
of Christ’s saving body and blood offered at the sacred altar.  
The oaken fetters and shackles fell apart from the captive,  
and his burden and the pains inflicted on him departed.  
When at length he returned to his native land,  
he fully disclosed to his wife what had happened.  
She declared that those were precisely the hours and days  
when the sacred offering had repeatedly brought him relief.

Nor does the Doctor pass over Waracca, a sailor almost swallowed  
by the black abyss of the sea,  
who was kept safe and delivered by such protection.  
Nothing, therefore, is more beneficial or more worthy than that sacred act  
by which souls live and bodies are sustained,  
and by which, when it is worthily offered,  
both bodily and spiritual bonds slacken and burst apart.

[Col. 0088A]

Finally, who are endowed with greater honour  
than those to whom authority has been entrusted to handle and consecrate this gift—  
provided the conduct of their lives accords with their office,  
their hands are clean, and the vessel of their heart is without stain,  
so that it may fittingly retain heavenly manna?  
For God, made a victim upon the altars, makes gods.

But let us now return to begin again the matter first undertaken.
