Astonished that the young man could not be bound,  
the prince eagerly sought to learn how this occurred.  
The youth replied: “By no means, lord, regard this as a crime  
or suppose that I know magical arts.  
May such a thing be far from the heart of a Christian,  
whose brow is marked by the sign of the cross and anointed in baptism.  
This is rather the art of men driven by demons,  
[Col. 0088B] men of no reason, with grave hearts and dreadful conduct.  
They keep souls bent down in earthly dust;  
they neither fear the evils of the abyss nor desire heaven’s good things.  
Their destruction is utterly certain unless they repent.

“But I have a brother in my homeland, a priest by office.  
Thinking that I had been taken from the battle,  
he frequently performs the venerable offices of Mass for me.  
And if I were now assigned in that age to punishments  
into which all who depart from this life enter,  
I might perhaps obtain repose through their merits.

Moreover, after he had spent some time there, the young man,  
displaying the marks of distinguished character,  
was revealed not to be of common lineage,  
but rather—what he had concealed—of noble birth.  
For no one can conceal for long what long habit has taught;  
and one who is naturally inclined reveals himself diligently by signs.

[Col. 0088C]

The prince therefore called him aside and pressed him more urgently  
to reveal who he was, assuring him that he would be safe in this matter  
provided he spoke no falsehood.  
The youth replied: “I shall tell the truth even if I must be grievously tortured,  
and shall use no lies even if I must be cruelly killed.  
I was a soldier and official of the king,  
not the least among the king’s chief friends;  
my birth is not common, for I am renowned for ancestral blood.”

The prince said: “Your freeborn character, answers, and actions  
showed me that you were not lowly in origin.  
You are indeed worthy to be consumed by a bitter end,  
for by the war and grievous triumph of your king  
I lost brothers, kinsmen, and friends.  
[Col. 0088D] Yet I shall not violate what I swore to you,  
nor annul my pledged faith by punitive execution,  
nor break it by death; rather, I shall punish you by sale.”

When he had completely recovered from his wounds,  
the prince, according to the custom of selling as a slave by auction  
a person acquired in war, delivered him for a price to a Frisian.  
The Frisian wished to keep the purchased slave in chains,  
but could not restrain him by bonds or any devices,  
although he repeatedly varied their weights with fetters.  
Yet this marvel regularly occurred in the youth  
when the third hour arose,  
the customary time at which sacred Masses were solemnly celebrated.

Thus he was granted the opportunity to ransom himself,  
[Col. 0089A] if he could pay the price of freedom.  
Swearing to his master either to send the agreed sum  
or to return again, and not betray the sacred pledge of faith,  
he sought King Lothair, related his circumstances,  
and found him generous with a royal gift.  
For Lothair knew that he had flourished as his sister’s servant.  
Therefore he sent the full sum agreed to his master  
and, freed from servitude, returned to his homeland.

Nor did he conceal from his brother either the misfortunes he had endured  
or the benefits he had experienced by divine gift—  
how, amid bitter circumstances, a sweet abundance  
had comforted him by loosening his chains and relieving him.  
By the young man’s report, the priest knew with certainty  
that only at those times and on those days  
[Col. 0090A] had he deserved the help of heaven’s victorious right hand  
when, standing before God on his behalf,  
he offered the sacred mysteries of Christ at the altar.

The young man himself also observed this no less closely.  
Telling it to many, he moved many by heaven-sent mercy wrought in his own case  
to works of piety:  
that they should diligently offer wakeful prayers to Christ  
for themselves, their loved ones, and their relatives,  
whether this life held them still or the life to come;  
that they should according to their means bestow compassionate care upon the poor;  
and that, greater and worthier than the rest of good works,  
they should earnestly have the sacred rites of Mass celebrated—  
rites which benefit both bodies and souls,  
the one true good: salvation and perpetual nourishment.

## Epilogue

[Col. 0089]

[Col. 0089B]

No one possessed of reason doubts  
that the Creator of all can do all things.  
He uses created things according to His will and purpose;  
whichever way He turns them, they follow.  
It is not wonderful, then, that a captive’s chains should burst  
through the power of His sacred acts,  
when the power of some herb also prevails—  
an herb shown by the woodpecker bird.

For you will find skilled natural philosophers reporting  
that if someone places chains in this bird’s nest  
when she has gone out to seek food for her young,  
then, when she flies back and finds that she cannot enter her home,  
she seeks out and applies a certain herb,  
by which she at once loosens the whole enclosure.

[Col. 0090B]

Then one who wishes to possess it observes and gathers it,  
being now able to overcome every knot with it.  
Thus the experience of a brute bird moves me  
to acknowledge the hidden power of a herb.  
But no mind can comprehend all that the wondrous Creator has produced.  
Who could unfold all the natures of birds  
or of every race of living things;  
the names and powers of herbs, stones, and woods—  
indeed, who could explain all things?  
Truly to know or cultivate the Creator of things  
is true knowledge and the height of salvation.

[Col. 0089]

# Reiner the Monk’s Book on the Coming of the Relics of St Lawrence the Martyr from Rome to Liège, with Other Poems and Epigrams of Various Kinds

(D. Bern. Pezius, *Anecdoct.*, IV, III, 120.)

## The Preface Begins

[Col. 0089C]

The beauty of silver, jewels, and gold is diminished  
by the grime of long neglect when they lie unused;  
and rust attacks even shining steel  
if it is permitted leisure and hand or use withdraws from it.  
Thus beauty and strength, thus every art, grow dull  
when habitual care does not keep them vigorous.  
And lethargy tries the brightness of the mind with scab,  
[Col. 0090C] when one tires of studies and neglects labour—  
whether in prose or verse, as one pleases. Therefore one should often  
devote even a little effort, lest the ardour to read, meditate, and write many things  
foolishly wither.  
For a mind yielded to sloth is destined to fall into vices.

Lawrence, you shall now be celebrated [perhaps *percelebrabere*] in my verse—  
[Col. 0091A] wondrously splendid in the spring-purple of martyrdom.  
Yet I shall not sing how the cruel Caesar roasted you on a gridiron  
and blessed you, after tortures endured, with a precious end.  
Rather, I shall sing how a portion of the liquid bestowed upon us  
was drawn out by the mighty force of intense heat.  
It was not the abundance of my talent that persuaded me to undertake this;  
rather, your love compelled me to perform this devout service.  
For no relief more greatly raises one who is oppressed;  
no water more delightfully comforts one exhausted by heat  
than to recall your marvellous titles  
and dedicate to you whatever gift of writing I can offer.  
How great is your glory, how surpassing you are,  
will be understood by one to whom you deign to make yourself known—  
as you marvellously appeared in a vision to a certain man,  
shining more brightly than refined gold.

[Col. 0091B]

You were truly pure, as though tested by much fire,  
blooming in unmingled light, as though illuminated by Christ.  
Your countenance was joyful, light sparkled in your eyes,  
and you smiled, O honey-sweet hope of the wretched!  
You spoke these consoling words to the mourner:

“Behold, brother, die; for you have sought death.”

And, pointing with your finger, you indicated your picture,  
which depicted you as roasted from above.  
So may it be, holy one: may he likewise die to vices;  
so may he through you devoutly deserve the life of virtues;  
may he grow warm with the sacred fire with which you marvelously burned,  
with which you made deadly fires dew-bearing.  
How greatly you flourish in merits is abundantly proved by events,  
and it is clear that you are glorified from heaven by signs.

[Col. 0092A]

From those above we learned of a cart consumed by fire,  
which an impious farmer was threatening to load with harvest  
while he rashly violated the feast of your martyrdom.  
To his loss he paid the penalty for his fault, that he might duly be free for you.  
This event was made known to us by that same man,  
and then confirmed by the displayed coals.

Another man, revering your hallowed solemnity, feared to discover  
how great a reward he deserved through generosity toward you.  
Intending to bring the harvest under cover in a cart,  
he had raised it from the fields; but the hour of your feast-night came first.  
He stopped the work and left it bare beneath the open sky;  
then he was astonished that it was wet neither with dew nor rain,  
although that night or day had been rainy.  
Yet the dutiful power returned it unharmed.  
Thus in ancient time the fleece remained dry upon the threshing-floor [a recent manuscript: “bronze”],  
[Col. 0092B] while the earth everywhere grew wet with rain-bearing dew.

Let reverence for you, holy one, not be considered empty:  
this was also affirmed by bread which flowed with blood.  
A certain woman had baked it in violation of the feast,  
but by such an act she bore this portent through her rashness.

But who can compare you adequately in writings,  
or worthily honour your mighty deeds with praises?  
Now, however, may the sequence of the history happily be resumed.  
First published in prose, let it be recounted in verse.  
I pray: favour my vows; guide my humble Muse;  
and, leader, by your merits bring in serene light.  
Cleanse my heart, filthy with the mire of vices,  
so that my thoughts may shine with the fitting disposition of morals.

## The Little Book Begins

[Col. 0091]

[Col. 0091C]

Godefrid was a man outstanding in life, adorned with the cultivation of virtues,  
far renowned among the clergy. He flourished then in the city of Liège,  
which shone while Bishop Tiuvinus governed it,  
and was distinguished by the splendid endowment of many good things.

Though lofty in the blood of great ancestors, that cleric lived a quiet life, powerful more through humility of mind than through a rich estate. A diligent practitioner of piety, he gave much freely. He sustained some with shelter and food, many more with clothing. He frequently visited the thresholds of holy places. He prayed to the saints and offered the incense of his vows.

But you, Lawrence, were the sole hope of his heart: he entrusted himself to you, and often visited you and yours. Thus he showed himself generous and friendly to us,

[Col. 0091D] cleaving more closely and always striving to be of service. So well fitted to us, he was one of us, keeping constant watch, pondering and fearing the future judgment of the Judge—its rewards or its torments. He chastised himself, striving to punish his lapses.

By winning you, holy Peter, as a gracious patron, he softened you with vows and went as a pilgrim to Rome. There he knocked in prayer, invoked you with groaning and tears by the right of the key of supreme mercy and power, that you would grant blessings and open the enclosures of heaven.

[Col. 0092C] He persevered in dying. He renewed this practice every year. He had once come there when the Christian people were observing the sacred fast which Christ first instituted for the world by undergoing it himself, when for a full twice twenty days he dwelt in the wilderness, exalted by no ordinary food.

Having fulfilled his vows, he sought familiar thresholds—those, namely, of the abbot to whom ties of kinship commended him and affection or fellowship united him. This man too was eminent in life, adorned with much uprightness: he flourished at Rome, his name was Humbert, appointed guardian of the Church because of the worthiness of his wisdom. He enriched and consecrated it with the most precious of sacred relics, namely those of the martyr Lawrence.

This is that sacred liquid which fierce heat pressed out,

[Col. 0092D] and which the pious care of devout men gathered upon the grate on which they bore the blessed limbs. A vial contains it; none is deemed more precious in the city of Rome, nor is this holy possession considered insignificant. Care is kept diligently lest it be taken away, and the man entrusted with it is first tested as suitable.

It glows more brightly than the laurel; it surpasses sapphire and gold. Nor are vows lacking: the whole City venerates it and seeks it out. It believes this to be both its protection and its remedy, and through the saint’s merits it has very often experienced both.

[Col. 0093A] Benefits are bestowed; every adversity is relieved.

There is indeed a building there, not large in scale; yet its worship is great, upheld by the solid foundation of its works. It gleams with the colors of stones and is adorned with vaulted ceilings; it shines with crystal, radiant everywhere with metals. Variegated marble inlays embellish its pavements. There is no wood in it, nothing that fire may consume. For those who established the martyrdom took care to guard against the frequent losses caused by fires that burn cities.

It is not the consecrated church in which the martyr lies buried; nor is it one of those which Damasus built and to which he gave titles, or which Lucina, powerful in lineage or wealth, endowed; nor is it the venerable shrine, known as the Grate of the righteous man, which the laurel of the burned martyr dedicates. This instrument, this glory, this blessed memorial,

[Col. 0093B] the Roman people hold dearer than riches.

The Levite is indeed made illustrious there by so many churches. He is the morning star of the City, gleaming by merit, prayer, and crowds.

Therefore Father Humbert received his aforementioned kinsman gladly and refreshed him with humble kindness. The visitor prolonged his stay, urged this upon him, and bent him by prayer. He remained there and delayed for several days. He prayed fervently and eagerly entered the church. He pressed the Levite to grant good things and wipe away the evils of his life.

Then he asked and investigated what holy relics were there; he heard, humbly venerated them. The abbot concealed nothing, but revealed every precious thing, unfolding its marvels and disclosing the merit of the place; he also increased his fervor by showing him the saint’s liquid.

[Col. 0093C] The man listened attentively and gave thanks for so great a treasure, which was ever more worthy than gold.

His resolute mind was moved to oblige his kinsman, lest, if it were poorly guarded, the place be deprived of that possession. Such indeed was his intention, though he had not meditated it previously. For he turned over in his mind what portion he might obtain by skill, so that no one should ever know it.

The faithful man ardently desired with all his vows to acquire for us such a good, such a noble gift. Opportunity followed, because the abbot happened to be away: drawn by business, he had gone far from Rome.

But that cleric passed the night in a thousand prayers, praying for complete success and for the abbot’s absence to continue. Then he turned to deceit, rising as though to render praise demanded by the force of the nocturnal vigils.

[Col. 0093D] He proceeded from his cell and entered the venerable building. One of the brethren shared with him in the same task, a man from whom he would have concealed nothing and whom he would not have hesitated to admit. He approached the altar and found pleasure in violating it thus rashly.

The vessel that hung there contained the holy pledge. The vessel was adorned with crystal and shining metal. He seized it where it stood, placed another beneath it, and fitted it so that the liquid might safely be poured into the latter and poured back again.

But it did not drip, for its own thickness held it fast. It had thickened of itself and hardened with age. Thus he was dismayed, thus almost driven from hope. Anxiously he stood there, wondering what he should do. There was not even a small piece of wood there which he might take for himself and use to assist his undertaking. To set foot outside and then return to the building,

[Col. 0094A] he judged imprudent; he feared it and, prudently, rejected it.

Then, lest he become suspect or perhaps be exposed, he began truly to groan, to utter repeated sighs, to turn his heart, twisted with grief, toward the martyr’s merit, and to add vows, lest he depart empty-handed.

Here the pious martyr relieved the sorrowful man and removed his anguish. What he desired came to pass: he saw nearby a short piece of wood, cast down from heaven, cut, I know not from what pine, neither rough-hewn nor crudely fashioned, but quite suitable for a martyr who had been a craftsman.

He took it without delay; his face flowed still more with tears—tears summoned by affection nourished with divine sweetness! He obtained what he sought and gained the precious merchandise: the consecrated ointment, more welcome than pure balm.

When he poured it out, a new fragrance spread itself abroad,

[Col. 0094B] one that surpassed all flowers and conquered every scent; so that the breath of no beds of flowers could equal it, though the power of varied spices had steeped them. For the blessed man, when being roasted, had thus spoken:

> “Gladly by this fire I have been made Christ’s victim,
> 
> May it refresh this man with sweet dew and fragrance.”

But its discovery was less welcome to the fearful Godfrey. Had Rome perceived so great an aroma, it would have seized the matter; and he would not have departed unpunished, and the life-giving liquid would have become deadly to him.

Therefore, fearing the crowd, he left Rome by night. He deceived his kinsman by alleging a long-delayed return. He quickly ended his delay and hastened toward the borders of his homeland; he did not travel on foot, but departed on a swift horse.

[Col. 0094C] Yet the fragrance did not cease. Lest anyone pursue him from Rome, he hid it within, often looking behind him. The saint protected his journey and guided it through prosperity.

Securely he traveled the road; securely, O Liège, he reached you, to enrich you with the treasure of so great relics. When he had taken possession of them, as necessity had required and right had approved, he informed the bishop. The noble man rejoiced, adored, displayed the treasure, and offered praises to Christ. He who had sent these blessings, he who revisited these gifts, appointed these holy pledges for us, to be kept by us and venerated under a special right—those whom the protection of a good patron cherishes and joins to himself.

That devout people and the entire throng of clergy accompanied them in hymnic fashion and with solemn honor. A choir of festal monks came to meet them,

[Col. 0094D] received them, rejoiced, and resounded in affection and voice.

Then the weather was savage: it was a wintry summer. The air was bleak, and the northern gale raged. Rainstorms poured down, clouds continually followed them, the world reeled, and people thought another deluge was at hand. Christ was implored; Christ was asked for peace, for the fruit of the earth, now ruined by the flood.

Christ gave heed and granted abundant benefits. The crowd of petitioners soon experienced the martyr’s intercession, when this venerable liquid was brought into our monastery and, placed with highest favor upon the altar, began to shine forth through signs that relieved the people from Christ’s now grievous scourge.

Hence came applause, and tears mingled with rejoicing. For a month covered, the sun was immediately uncovered from cloud;

[Col. 0095A] it scattered its rays, cleared the sky of darkness, drove away the rains, and warmed the lands with fire. Clear spring shone forth; wet weather did no harm,

[Col. 0096A] because that calm face of heaven brought this about. Good things followed through the goodness of the holy patron, and thus hope of crops was restored to the grieving world.

## Epilogue

[Col. 0095]

[Col. 0095A] When, in the month of June, the sun brought forth the fourth day before the Ides, we set forth these deeds like a new star. The same annual day returns in bloom for us, while our assembly prays with vows and hymns.

[Col. 0096A] Therefore, most radiant Lawrence, first among flowers, you whose purple blossoms flourish above heaven through blood, stand by your suppliants; grant blessings, remove harmful things; through your merits save those whom you crown with relics.

## Prayer to the Same Holy Martyr

[Col. 0095]

[Col. 0095A]

Blessed Lawrence,  
look upon me in mercy,  
wretched as I am!

With sweet vows,  
when obstacles have been removed,  
show yourself favorable.

The afflictions  
by which my heart  
wastes away are without number.

Friend of salvation,  
effective physician,  
bring remedies.

Through your merit may I be  
free from the debt  
of every sin;

may I be enrolled, a fellow citizen  
and participant among the godly,  
in the kingdom of light.

Chaste Levite,  
purple-clad in heaven  
with the glory of virtues,

may your grace obtain for me, though prone to sin,  
that I may live chastely.

You cherished Christ’s poor  
with the rich price  
of treasures.

You know how I am in need;  
may I therefore flourish  
through your holy intercession.

The executioner tortured you cruelly,  
but never turned you away  
from what was right.

Vices oppress me,

[Col. 0096A] and drag me through wandering paths.  
Be present as my helper.

Fierce heat burned you,  
but the heat of the grate  
did not drive God from you.

Luxury rages in me,  
torments, tosses, and burns me;  
I call upon you earnestly.

The Holy Spirit burned you  
to the marrow,  
O victim of Christ:

may I burn with this fervor;  
may my inmost parts glow  
with so sweet a flame.

What burned within you  
was stronger  
than what burned outwardly.

Pray graciously  
that I may be warm toward Christ  
and cold toward the world.

You proved brighter than gold,  
purer than crystal,  
surpassing humankind.

Now shine down from heaven;  
now utterly cleanse  
my darkness.

Oh, from what a mouth,  
from what a heart  
you then gave thanks!

May God hear this accused man  
as he cries out,  
as he heard you when you pleased him.

## Office of the Holy Spirit

[Col. 0095]

### Hymn at Nocturns

O holy Watcher of Israel, who do not sleep!  
Awaken us from the sleep of vices, O Holy Spirit (*Pneuma*).

Grant that in the morning, Lord, we may meditate upon you;  
enlighten the eyes of our life, lest death darken them;  
and lest our enemies say, “I have prevailed against them.”  
May the Father and Son help us; govern us, Holy Spirit. Amen.

### At Lauds

The shadow of night declines; day is renewed for the earth;  
the golden sun grows young again, and the heavenly brightness increases.

Wipe away the soot of vices, the rust of sins,  
O Holy Spirit, and cleanse us utterly.

Thus may praise everlasting be yours with Father and Son,  
that, renewed through you, we may through him also be blessed. Amen.

### At Prime

In the new morning it is fitting to offer gifts of praise  
to the Holy Spirit, by whose grace we are renewed from the sacred font.

May he himself bend a gracious ear to our voices  
and command that they be joined with angelic praises.

May the Father, with the Son, show himself favorable to our prayers;  
and may the same Spirit ever render him open to entreaty. Amen.

### At Terce

Behold, the third hour shines: a happy and golden time,  
when the Holy Spirit wondrously breathed upon the apostles, giving gifts.

May that same grace graciously make us participants in him;  
may it render us fervent in love and eloquent in his praise.

Merciful holy Father, grant this to us with your Son,

[Col. 0097] your King; and you, Paraclete, console us now and always. Amen.

### At Sext

Holy Spirit, at the sixth hour we offer you praise;  
for Christ’s sake, kindly receive this service performed beneath the cross.

Make the wounds a healing remedy for us,  
and cure our sicknesses with the true ointment of blood.

May the Son himself join the Father in these pious prayers,  
and may we obtain from you and through you what we ask of you. Amen.

### At None

The ninth hour, sanctified by the life-giving death of Christ God,  
shows itself venerable to Christ’s worshippers.

Behold, with devoted service we compose for you,  
Holy Spirit, our song; in mercy bring our prayers to fulfillment.

Praise be to you with the begotten Son and with God the Father;  
join us for everlasting ages to the choirs above. Amen.

### At Vespers

There is no hymn.

### At Compline

True Light, knowing no cloud, sun that suffers no setting,  
Spirit, Paraclete! Night presses on; be yourself  
a lamp to our hearts and to our feet, guiding us safely along the way.

Lest we fall through vices, grant virtues; may we be ruled by them  
through the byways of this world, and by them deserve the joys  
of the true jubilee and the rest of eternal repose. Amen.

## Various Poems

[Col. 0097]

### Concerning the Crucifix

The cross, sign of life, subdues and drives away every evil thing:  
death and enemies yield, nor do they harm those marked by the cross.

Supported by this, strive onward, you who are crucified with it;  
then you bear the good things of life, if you rightly put evil to death.

### Concerning a Cymbal

Hunger and thirst for God, you who seek to live:  
you will soon enjoy angelic fullness.

### Epitaph Concerning a Tomb

You have been taken from the world by undergoing death’s law,  
Father Hildebrand; now the loving mother, the heavenly Jerusalem, holds you,  
where true light and rest are found.

For you lived well and cared well for your flocks.  
Now you receive your rewards and flourish again in perpetual life.  
What this stone presses down shall rise again when Christ comes.

### Concerning a Bell

May this cast sign be worthy of your praise, O God;  
may it give peoples sacred warnings to observe the rites.

### In a Stained-Glass Window

Live like a dove, but with prudent simplicity;  
be like a serpent, but with honorable shrewdness.

[Col. 0099]

## Five Books of Reiner the Monk, *The Bouillon Triumph*, or How in Our Times the Church of Liège, Having Triumphed over Invaders, Recovered the Castle of Bouillon by Divine Power

(Dom Bernard Pez, cited above, col. 129, from the same manuscripts.)

## Prologue to the Following History

[Col. 0099A] Since in our own days the holy martyr Lambert has shone forth like a new morning star by the grace of his merits and the glory of his signs; since he recovered from the hands of invaders the distinguished castle of Bouillon, which he had possessed for many years both by lawful conveyance and by free right, taking vengeance upon the invaders themselves; and since he triumphed so magnificently, I judged it not inappropriate to describe this in a few words, as something memorable.

Many people indeed say many things, and, as commonly happens in affairs of this sort, different people hold different opinions. Nevertheless, insofar as I was able diligently to investigate from those who were present, I have set down the truth.

I have also divided this work into five little books and given it the title *The Bouillon Triumph*. If anything contrary to truth has been included in it, whether this should more fairly be laid to the informants

[Col. 0099B] or to the writers, I leave to the judgment of the kindly reader. Yet truth is the friend of religion. Therefore, from those from whom I received these matters, I do not at all suspect that they invented anything, since the modesty of their persons excuses this confidence.

Moreover, an illustrious subject requires an illustrious talent, and golden thoughts ought to be illumined by gems of language. But it was only love for the saint and devotion that led me, idle and unskilled though I am, to presume to undertake so great a task. For I was indebted for the graces which I did not consider it idle to repay through so solemn a history.

For when for almost a year I was tormented by two quartan fevers, and was either burning with heat or contracting with chills, so that, weary of present misery, my very life had become burdensome to me,

[Col. 0099C] after the venerable body of the saint had recently been removed from its resting place, as will appear below, I approached amid the other ranks of the sick to seek his aid. His inexhaustible mercy deigned to hear one unworthy, and I experienced the benefit of restored health.

But in the Gospel the nine lepers who neglected to give thanks for recovered health were displeasing. Therefore, following the example of the grateful foreigner, I, humbly worshipping before kindly Jesus and magnifying God, offer this little work of praise as an acceptable sacrifice for my preservation to so great a priest. For since ingratitude is a detestable evil, it is altogether right that we should be grateful for divine benefits. Indeed, how grateful the bestower of every good thing or grace is for our devotion toward him is clearer than light.

Nor do I think it superfluous to mention here a matter full of piety and gratitude. To suppress a friend’s identity while expressing his virtues is both prudent and edifying. What is worthy of imitation is rightly made public. No good person interprets badly what is proclaimed with a good intention.

Thus a certain poor man burned with devoted service toward the Holy Trinity. He continually embraced in his heart and confessed with his mouth the triumphant name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, through which every adversity is overcome. For, as it is written: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and is exalted. The wealth of a rich man is his strong city, and like a mighty wall surrounding him” [Prov. 18]. This righteous man also often experienced the truth of this in his necessities.

[Col. 0100B] One dawn, while he had given himself to contemplation and compunction, and had returned to his bed after vigils, his bodily senses were suddenly transformed with new vigor: he was lifted into the air by a mighty Spirit and led to the church. The matter is almost incredible, but not impossible to God’s omnipotence.

Although the doors were shut, he passed through them as through some solidified body of mist.

[Col. 0100C] For the author of nature changes nature when he wills and orders it as he wills. Therefore it was not difficult for the Holy of Holies to come forth into birth from his mother’s closed womb; rather, the wondrously made-man Son willed wondrously to be such that the Virgin who bore him remained holy. Would anyone doubt that he likewise rose from the dead from a closed tomb and entered among the disciples when the doors were shut? These are indeed mysteries, yet they must without doubt be believed to be true, although they cannot be comprehended. For the apostles and certain other saints are recorded, by divine wonder-working power, to have gone out or entered through closed doors.

Accordingly, that poor man, set down at the steps of the sanctuary, was amazed at himself and felt himself with his hand, wishing to discover whether he had come there only in spirit or also bodily. Then, behold, he heard above him musical voices singing with wondrous sweetness:

> “A sanctified day has shone upon us; come, nations, and adore the Lord, for today a great light has descended upon the earth.”

Immediately so great a flash of light shone upon the sanctuary that it surpassed the brightness of the midday sun. Bathed in it, he looked toward the high altar. I tremble, wretch that I am; I shudder, unhappy man that I am, because I, a man of unclean lips, presume to utter so great a mystery.

The Holy Trinity sat there in a form truly incomparable.

[Col. 0101B] The Father, radiant in venerable appearance and clothed in royal purple ornaments, displayed through the whiteness of his hair his antiquity of days. The Holy Spirit, joyful in the bright beauty of face and garment, was surrounded by a most pure fire; he held a golden rod in his hand, since he both inflames by inspiration and teaches by touch. His white hair also suggested his timeless age.

In the middle appeared our living one, our Emmanuel, who, that we might be with God, did not disdain to be with human beings. In the middle, I say, hung upon the cross he who was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” [Ps. 44], he who was “altogether desirable” [Song 5]. O gentle one! O humble of heart! With his head bowed how reverently, he himself gave thanks to the aforementioned poor man for the affection and devotion with which he was accustomed to serve him.

[Col. 0102A] For the man had as his singular and chosen practice continually to recount the most holy Passion in vows: to adore and embrace the image of the Crucified One; to water it with tears poured forth from his heart’s depths; to wipe it with his hair; to cover it with kisses; and, in place of ointments, to offer groaning prayers and the fragrances of charity.

When, therefore, he had fallen to the ground before so great a vision and worshipped, glorifying and blessing with every voice and fiber of his soul, that glory was suddenly withdrawn. At once he was returned to his bed in the same manner by which he had come, so that he clearly perceived himself being lowered into it.

Surely, as Solomon says, you give such strong drink to the sorrowful and such wine to those bitter in spirit, O Lemuel—whose name means “in whom is God”—that they may drink and forget their poverty and remember their pain no more. Such consolation, such joy, O Christ, O Beloved One, you grant to those who mourn and are contrite of heart in humble vows, so that those who desire and love you in truth may be comforted by you and may sometimes see you, at least “through a mirror and in an enigma.”

[Col. 0102B] For your own declaration is: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Matt. 5]. But now I return to what I had set aside.

Therefore I first wished to explain beforehand from where or how the above-mentioned castle of Bouillon came into the right and possession of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert. I have also judged that the location of the place itself should be briefly described; nor do I think the poor man should be altogether blamed for his style, since matters rather than words ought to be weighed.

## First Book

[Col. 0101]

### Chapter I

[Col. 0101C]

The famous duke of Lotharingia, Godfrey, who possessed Bouillon by hereditary right from his ancestors, when he had vowed to make pilgrimage to Jerusalem—as I have more fully recounted in fourteen books in the work entitled *The Laurel of the Jerusalem Pilgrims*—transferred the same castle to Obert, bishop of Liège, for 1,300 marks of silver and three marks of gold.

Yet each party entered into a pledge upon this condition: if the duke should return to his homeland, he himself would have the right to redeem it; but if he should not return, the right to retain it would pass to his brother Eustace, count of Boulogne. If he should refrain from redemption, then it would pass into the right and lordship of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert as an eternal inheritance, in free and valid possession.

Accordingly, after the duke subsequently died at Jerusalem and his brother Baldwin was elevated as king, Count Eustace, returning from the Lord’s tomb, came to Lotharingia and turned aside to Liège. There, on the Lord’s Day of Christmas, he was received with much honor by the bishop, clergy, and people, and was treated with most ample attentions.

Therefore, whatever right he possessed in the aforementioned castle, he entirely renounced before suitable witnesses and granted, for the salvation both of himself and of his brothers and ancestors, to Saint Mary and Saint Lambert with all its appurtenances, to be possessed in future ages. The donation was made at the high altar; he further judged that it should be confirmed in every respect by legal form and written instrument, permanently forbidding every claim by any heir or blood relative of himself or of his brothers.

[Col. 0102C] Situated at the farthest edge of the bishopric of Liège, that castle forms the boundary of the kingdoms of Lotharingia and France. It is exceptional both by its natural character and human cultivation: in the extraordinary construction of its walls, in the precipices and rugged height of its cliffs, in the broad wilderness of forest surrounding it, in the River Semois flowing past it, and in access as difficult as it is impregnable.

There is no lack there either of plentiful fish or abundance of game. But the security of a place sometimes breeds in its inhabitants encouragement for insolence. Hence the men of the castle had often ranged against all their neighbors with slaughter and plundering, or with whatever form of injury they pleased, because impunity favored them.

The aforementioned bishop carefully reflected on this; and, to provide for the peace both of his diocese and of the two kingdoms, he devoted to acquiring it the total sum of money collected from the treasuries of the churches subject to him,

[Col. 0103A] thereby removing the troubles and losses of many.

### Chapter II

Accordingly, from Obert the Fourth until the episcopate of Alexander, the Church possessed that castle in quiet and free right. During Alexander’s presidency, the commonwealth of Liège was greatly disturbed by the frequent tumults of wars and the seditions of princes. The possessions of churches were seized by wicked men; dependents were oppressed and goods plundered.

Indeed, owing to impunity for crimes, the wicked were then permitted to exercise wickedness, fearing no judgment and reverencing no authority whatever. For the Roman world was shaken by a storm of conflicting divisions: Rome divided herself between two popes, two kings split one empire, and two dukes of Lotharingia asserted the duchy against one another. This undisciplined age ordained that the wicked should be exalted, the good cast down, the powerful seize, and the wretched perish. I pass over the rest.

But I shall not conceal that Godfrey, duke of Leuven, then strengthened into pride by confidence in his own power and an abundance of wealth, attacked the Church of Liège with sword, fire, and plundering. Moreover, having assembled a great army from every quarter, he advanced to battle near the castle of Dyrrachium. Yet, with God’s undefiled Mother and the holy martyr Lambert favoring their side, although the number of churchmen was far smaller,

[Col. 0103C] a considerable troop of the enemy was slain and terrified, and the broken horn of the sinner was scattered.

### Chapter III

While the same bishop was oppressed by these and various other tumults of affairs, and while the business of his own concerns drew him in one direction and the affairs of the imperial court in another, opportunity was given to enemies, both domestic and foreign, to attack the bishop.

Thus Rainald, count of Bar, a man indeed of great power but of wicked and deceitful character, seized the castle of Bouillon. He gained entry through treachery after inducing its guards with money both received and promised. Because of this, always regarding the bishop of Liège with suspicion and fearing that he might at some time prepare a siege against him,

[Col. 0103D] he took pains to fortify it with strong garrisons.

After Alexander had died, Albero, primicerius of the Church of Metz, a man born of most distinguished blood, was appointed bishop. He lodged the Church of Liège’s plea before the Apostolic See, complaining of the invader’s fraud and injustice and asking Innocent II to strike him with a sentence of anathema.

But Rainald had foreseen this too, had gone to Rome, and, having purchased the favor of courtiers with gifts, had secured that it should not be done. For among the greedy money is worth more than justice. He also asserted that the castle itself had come to him by right of kinship, and at the same time that he had wished to repay the money for which it had been pledged to the Church.

But the bishop, seeking a Roman synod a second time on the same case,

[Col. 0104A] remained unsuccessful. Finally, in three royal courts, during the reign of Conrad II, he petitioned the Roman judgment of both king and nobles concerning this matter.

Yet he made so little progress that this same ravaging boar, breathing more savage fury together with another impious vintager of the Lord’s vineyard, similarly attacked by treachery and stealth the illustrious town of Fosses, venerable for both the body and memory of the holy martyr Foillan, and proceeded to plunder and overthrow it by fire.

That night, with no one resisting—for the citizens, stunned by the unexpected event, fled in every direction—the force of the flames seized and consumed not only houses and towers, but also the sacred church of the martyr and its workshops. The hostile hand likewise destroyed the episcopal residence and the enclosure of walls.

[Col. 0104B] He also inflicted other losses on the bishop in many places. Therefore the bishop went to Rome for the third time, sought the apostolic protection, and petitioned for the pope’s judgment or sentence concerning so monstrous a mass of crimes. But when he perceived this to be of little use, he returned home and finally resolved to test the matter by himself and through his own men.

### Chapter IV

For, having secured the loyalty of his chief men, their shared consent, and their promise of assistance, he decided to besiege Bouillon. But because acting before a report of the act can sometimes be advantageous, he conducted in secret everything he was planning, wishing that his opponents should remain unaware, so that they might more easily be enclosed if taken unawares.

[Col. 0104C] Therefore, in the fifth year of his episcopate, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, he set out for the siege with certain princes and picked knights.

Two sons of Rainald had then gone out—Hugh, the elder, and the younger Rainald—to raid and plunder the bishopric; with them was a large force of armed, mobile soldiers. The bishop’s soldiers met them, engaged them, drove them into the castle, and steadfastly besieged them, ranging about with sword and fire.

Although the castle men were more numerous, they thought that more enemies than they could see were lying concealed in ambush—for otherwise they would not have presumed to undertake so arduous a task with so small a force. While they could freely have gone out or come in, they were held enclosed by fear alone.

[Col. 0104D] Likewise, trusting in the strength of the place, they so despised the besiegers that they spent the entire night in feasting and commanded boys and girls to perform dances to the cithara in mockery of them, especially because they had driven away those who had already occupied the steep slopes of the mountain and had killed some of them.

But the bishop and those with him assigned positions for the camp, established the quarters of their tents, and maintained watches and guards by night and day. They were always ready lest the besieged break out or Count Rainald suddenly attack with an army, as rumor often threatened.

They abounded in the necessary supplies, and the surrounding fields, rich in fertile soil and still bearing unharvested grain, furnished plentiful fodder for the horses.

[Col. 0105A] A mill built beside the River Semois served the enemies’ needs. Because it was suitable for supplying food, it gave them considerable hope of resistance. In order to drive its wheels with swifter motion, water retained by an ingenious arrangement of dams flowed over them in greater quantity and force. The mill itself also had its own guard to defend it against the enemy.

Therefore Henry, count of Namur, set out to seize it. Encouraging his companions, he was the first to rush into the river, in order that, after breaking the barriers holding back the waters,

[Col. 0105B] they might turn them back into their natural channel. Three crossbowmen attacked him with bolts:

[Col. 0106A] one pierced the forequarters of the horse he rode, another his own leg, and a third likewise pierced the same horse’s flank. When it collapsed, its rider fell with it into the river. A great cry arose on both sides from the onlookers, and the enemy exulted with joy.

Without delay his companions aided the count and pulled him from amid the waves. But injury is a spur to anger and indignation. Therefore, lest the enemy rejoice long, the count bound his wound and returned more fiercely to the work he had begun. He did not stop until he had scattered the obstacles and restored the waters to their free course. Thus, to the great loss of the besieged,

[Col. 0106B] he deprived that mill of its function.

## Second Book

[Col. 0105]

### Chapter I

[Col. 0105B]

Meanwhile, because no one dared approach the camp or bring in anything owing to the difficulty and dangerous narrowness of the terrain, necessary supplies began to fail the besiegers. Therefore the bishop issued orders through messengers in every direction that horsemen and foot soldiers should assemble from the entire bishopric, and that abundant provisions needed for the expedition should be brought in.

Then, as forces eagerly gathered, many assaults took place. These men attacked; those resisted. Wounds and deaths occurred on both sides. Nor did the besiegers omit anything that they believed would help against the besieged.

But because the strength and forbidding difficulty of the place defied every effort, the besiegers were brought to hope only that their enemies might be overcome by hunger,

[Col. 0105C] since human courage or ingenuity was of too little strength to subdue them. Thus they strove to block every means of exit or entrance for the besieged.

While this was happening, by the will of God, who orders all things sweetly, it seemed good to the bishop and the chief men of the Church that the venerable body of blessed Lambert should be moved from its resting place and carried to the camp. In this way the army’s courage would grow stronger by the presence and protection of so great a patron, and where human strength failed, divine omnipotence might deign to act through its martyr.

For the princes, the entire army, and indeed the people of the city who were to march out at the bishop’s command earnestly demanded this. Therefore, although there was much hesitation and much discussion in deliberation, it was at last agreed that such great necessity should be met.

[Col. 0105D] They assert that the martyr also approved this, as was sufficiently established both by the success of events and by certain revelations and signs. The custodians of the place testified that during those days the shrine in which the blessed pledges were enclosed was often shaken with such violent movements, and such divine terror came upon them, that they did not dare approach or enter it, especially at night. For carnal things are struck dumb when spiritual things flash forth.

Surely this was done to complete your glorification, O martyr, O honor and crown of Liège’s glory: you were transferred from the place of your former rest so that you might recover through yourself what was yours, since, having become a co-heir with Christ in the kingdom, you had need of no one except for the sake of your own people.

### Chapter II

[Col. 0106B]

Accordingly, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, monks and clerics assembled with a numerous multitude of both sexes and every age. Abbots and religious men entered the sacristy of the crypt that held so great a treasure, raised the sacred shrine with due reverence, and, while sweet hymns of praise resounded in the fitting voices of exultation and thanksgiving, placed it in the middle of the church.

Many vows, many prayers, and many tears were poured forth there. The power of the saint also shone forth wonderfully.

A certain woman, deafened by a pain in her head, came to the shrine and, with faithful affection and pious tears, implored help. Suddenly she felt some heavy weight fall from above upon the crown of her head,

[Col. 0106C] and as though two small iron implements [*duculos*, reading uncertain] had been thrust piercingly into each ear. Overcome, she fell to the ground; but thus, through the heavenly remedy, she fully recovered her sense of hearing and gave thanks to God and the martyr.

At last, a certain girl was pitiably afflicted by a threefold kind of suffering. Now she was shaken by fever, now by paralysis, sometimes by an epileptic disorder. Her parents, deeply distressed on her account, made a vow to the martyr and resolved to bring to his shrine an offering proportionate to the infirmity, whatever its kind might be. The merciful working of the holy Trinity attended the devout petition of the suppliants and immediately delivered the girl whole from those very afflictions.

A boy also, of wandering mind and disturbed intellect, was restored [Col. 0106D] to a sober state of reason. Other remedies and cures were likewise reported to have occurred. Yet miracles happen in order to increase the devotion of believers. Thus one advances further in devotion who is more inclined to faith. Then the foremost and wiser men, anxiously concerned in prudent fear lest something more grievous should perhaps happen to the martyr’s body if it were carried into the camp—for the outcome of wars is uncertain, and now from this side, now from that, adversity and prosperity are mingled—decided that the same shrine should be unsealed, lifted from there, and for the time being deposited in a safer place. This the religious abbots and suitable men chosen for the purpose carried out: with great fear and devotion, as was fitting, they transferred the blessed bones at [Col. 0107A] night, in silence, beside the altar of the Holy Cross situated in the oratory adjoining that basilica. Yet, placing some relics back in the shrine itself, they sealed it again, so that it might be borne and displayed in the camp.

## Chapter III

Nor did the piety of the people cease to make vows and offer gifts, until the shrine, together with an elaborately wrought panel containing a small portion of the Lord’s Cross, was taken from there into the camp. Choirs of monks and clerics followed so great a Father with due affection and reverence, conducting it in the service of song as far as the river Meuse by the public hill, through the monasteries of the saints established there, after praises had first been honorably sung in them.

Nor was there lacking a great crowd of common people: they too sounded forth [Col. 0107B] their praises and their songs. But when the venerable coffin had been received aboard a ship, the devoted flock commended their pious shepherd with many prayers and tears, that he might depart prosperously and return still more prosperously. Since they could go no farther on foot, they nevertheless followed for a long time in desire and with their eyes, and at last returned to their own homes.

From every side a multitude of both sexes came forth from hamlets and villages to meet the holy shrine; and very many healings took place, through both the power of the healing wood and the merit and prayer of the blessed martyr. When they came to the village of Nandrin, a sick man whose limbs had been disabled by a severe contraction was laid against the shrine; having implored the saint’s mercy, he was swiftly restored to health. Then, in the village of Phriere, a blind man received the light of his eyes. After the shrine had departed from there, a certain knight, who had long suffered from a quartan fever and was continually tormented by an infirmity of the head, touched the health-bringing coffin and bore it for some distance upon his shoulders; he was freed from his disorders. Immediately putting on his arms again, [Col. 0108A] and rendering thankful service in return, he followed it on the expedition.

The following night, lodging having been arranged at the village of Uphei [now Oufes], where the army of Liège was at hand, the devout diligence of the faithful, together with the inhabitants of the place, kept a solemn vigil.

## Chapter IV

When they set out thence in the morning, someone arrived to say that on the following day—that is, the third day before the Kalends of September—Count Rainald would engage in battle with five hundred horsemen and fifteen thousand foot soldiers. Therefore, hastening their journey, they came, as the sun was already declining toward sunset, to the little village of Thelim. There the citizens of Huy, who had shortly before lodged there, had been despoiled of provisions and necessary possessions by their hosts, who had abused hospitality in a hostile manner [Col. 0108B].

At midnight a messenger was sent by the army to Bishop Veredarius, that he might learn about the battle. When dawn on the next day was already breaking into light, they set out and hurried toward the village of Vilantia. A returning envoy reported to them that the battle would undoubtedly take place there that day. But an unfavorable rumor easily unnerves the fearful. Thus many were broken by foolish dread and wounded by report alone. In womanish distrust they slipped away. The rest, armed with confidence in the life-giving wood and in the holy martyr rather than with iron, hastened along narrow paths with manly courage to aid their allies.

Scouts had been sent by both armies to discover and report [Col. 0108C] how the opposing sides were disposed. When they encountered one another, they remained silent and concealed their purpose; they returned to their respective camps. The enemy, having learned from their own men how great was the number of those besieging them and of those who had then assembled, judged it better to desist from a rash attempt than voluntarily to invite danger upon themselves.

# Third Book

[Col. 0107]

## Chapter I

[Col. 0107C]

After it had been heard in the camp that the sign of the Lord’s Cross had arrived with so great a protection, the bishop and army, equipped in expectation of battle, came out under arms to meet it. Such joy then arose, such were the voices of those leading the choirs, that one would have thought Israel had then received the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord of hosts. The sacred shrine was received into a tent prepared for it in the place called the Meadow of Saint Lambert; guards were appointed, as were clerics to say the divine praises at fitting times. It immediately began, by wondrous power, to show what it contained and how great an aid it had brought, so that it became plainly evident to all that God had come into the camp.

[Col. 0107D] Indeed, at its presence, those in the castle and its garrison, who considered themselves impregnable because of the invincible position of the site, were struck by sudden dullness and fear as if by lightning. Had their mind not been perverse, they would have recognized by this that it was foretold to them that they would be overcome by such an engine. Moreover, Hugh, who had inherited the castle after his father by hereditary right, when he saw the shrine from afar and insulted it with youthful arrogance, immediately lost the use of his whole body, began to tremble, lost his senses, and fell backward: senseless and insolent, because he had not understood whose co-heir he was attempting unworthily to become. But when he gradually recovered himself, he summoned apart his brother Rainald and some of his closest companions, revealed how much terror he was suffering, and declared that his purpose was to make satisfaction to the holy martyr and restore his castle to him. His father’s will, he said, must also be sought on this matter, and the danger pressing upon himself be made known to him. He entreated them by every means to provide for him, as he perished, with a father’s compassion. They promised that they would carry out his request.

[Col. 0108D] A truce was established for a week, within which this could be reported to his father. On the third day after its arrival, the army of Liège, having celebrated Mass, received an exhortation concerning salvation and absolution of sins, and girded itself with arms, attacked the garrison that defended the mill mentioned above. It burned this, together with the mill building, by setting fire to it; many on both sides were wounded, and some fell mortally [Col. 0109A]. Indeed, a certain priest, having exposed himself too incautiously to danger, was struck through the head by a crossbowman and perished.

## Chapter II

When the days of truce had elapsed, the aforementioned young man asked his men what they had done, what they had arranged regarding his safety, and what his father’s judgment was. When he understood that nothing had been accomplished, he became violently indignant and said: “Whether they will or not, the saint shall receive what is his. But behold, I am punished by divine judgment, and behold, through your cruel obstinacy I am dying! Yet, O soldiers, O friends, if any compassion for me moves you, if you spare a wretch, at last devise a counsel beneficial both for me and for yourselves.” When [Col. 0109B] he pressed them more vehemently, they could no longer endure to see him so terribly distressed. The following night they sent, through hidden forest paths, the steward of the castle and leader of its soldiery, to carry the matter to his father and bring back his decision. He also confirmed by oath that he would without doubt return on the following Sunday, unless perhaps prevented by capture by the enemy or by death. But he disregarded his pledge and abandoned his promise. He neither performed the embassy nor returned to his companions; rather, having joined a certain knight, he engaged in plundering the goods being conveyed into the camp.

The young man, who was impatient with the slowness of delay, again asked his men on the appointed day what his father’s will or decision was. They answered that they had indeed sent a messenger, but that he had by no means returned. [Col. 0109C] Then, boiling with the keenest grief and out of his mind, he began to rage in a dreadful manner: tearing himself, biting at his hands and arms, and trying to break forth toward the saint’s shrine. But his attendants bound him and held him in a more remote place, spreading the report that he was ill. Yet, admitting no rest, he tore with bites the lips and tongue that alone remained free to him, and amid his incoherent cries repeatedly shouted: “Seek counsel, seek counsel!” Surrounded by his grief and anxiety, they decided that his brother Rainald should become the messenger of this sad affair to their father. Perhaps, at the sight of the one present, he would be moved by affection for the other absent son, and would hold cheap another’s inheritance for which he was losing so beloved an heir.

[Col. 0109D] But when they wished to provide the young man setting out with an excellent horse, the beast could neither be driven by blows nor moved by the words of those urging it, so that it seemed rooted fast like a statue. To this difficulty they added the trial of human ingenuity: they covered the horse’s eyes and drove it, in order that it might at least proceed thus. But because there is no counsel and no undertaking against the Lord, the horse remained fixed, and the cunning and ingenuity of men came to nothing. Thus the young man’s journey was obstructed.

The owner of the horse, most vexed at being deprived of the use of so great a mount, lest he should also see it die from wasting away, ordered his groom on the following day to lead it, if he could somehow do so, to water, and to hand it over at least to one of the enemy. The groom immediately obeyed the threatening man’s command and led it down from the brow of the hill to the water. One of the soldiers at once mounted the animal once it had been led across, and found it outstanding both for war and for speed [Col. 0110A].

## Chapter III

Thus the men in the castle could infer that they were being divinely hindered, and that the resistance of the horse rebuked their own rebellion and obstinacy. Nor did the saint make his power less evident among them than among those young men, who, after the quarrels of fury and contention, often armed themselves against one another with such madness that they attacked each other with swords.

A grim darkness of horror and some dreadful terror [Col. 0110B] also hung over them. For, as they themselves afterward confessed, a singular misery was then visible in them: not only were they hemmed in by the external pressure of the siege, but, what was more grievous than anything else, they tore one another’s entrails by the inward evil of discord. In contrast, a certain prisoner who had already spent a long time there in chains invoked the martyr’s power. Letting himself down from a high place in the tower, he rolled down however precipitous and rough the cliffs, and not only suffered no injury at all, but even the chains by which he was bound were loosed by heavenly favor and carried before the shrine, where they were hung up as evidence of so great a power. For faith and devotion merit grace; treachery and presumption incur displeasure.

## Chapter IV

[Col. 0110C]

Meanwhile a great engine was being built which promised the strongest hope of crushing the enemy. The craftsman’s hand constructed it so that it could be moved, with four very solid wheels fitted beneath it. Above, he carefully covered the platform that was to hold the combatants with raw oxhides, so that missiles hurled by the enemy would be frustrated by this obstacle. The route by which it was intended to draw the engine was also cleared through the wood; after the ascent of the mountain had been leveled, it was to be brought against the fortification guarding the mountain’s summit. But when fifteen hundred armored soldiers were drawing it with conspicuous effort, the ropes suddenly broke, it fell to the ground, and they were mocked by this misfortune.

[Col. 0110D] A wooden contrivance was also being prepared, to be drawn over the Simoin, which would prevent the besieged from coming down to draw water, while crossbowmen watched within, and would also serve as a shield against archers shooting from the castle. But as time passed, the people began to grow weary of the delays in building it, especially since excessive intemperance had consumed the earlier abundance of provisions and brought severe scarcity, while continual rain produced grievous bad weather.

Moreover, the soldiers who wished to display their prowess in some illustrious exploit had already begun to complain against their leaders about the delay, and that they were ordered to do nothing notable. But divine power was reserving triumphal titles for its martyr. Thus [Col. 0111A] all the ingenuity of the wise and all their deliberations fluctuated, so that what had been resolved in the evening would scarcely sometimes seem fit to be done on the following morning. [Col. 0112A] This was further compounded by the report that Count Rainald was gathering very great forces and energetically preparing war.

# Fourth Book

[Col. 0111]

## Chapter I

[Col. 0111A]

Since very many were withdrawing, some through weariness and others exhausted by lack of food, the leaders decided not to wait any longer for the completion of the engines, but rather to test an attack on the enemy’s estates with all their forces united.

[Col. 0111B] Accordingly, an order was issued in the camp that each should prepare himself for an expedition on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, the day made splendid by the glorious feast of blessed Lambert. For it was especially hoped that on that day the saint’s power would be present to aid his fighters. Then the army of foot soldiers, estimated at one hundred thousand, apart from three thousand horsemen, rushed competitively to the assault. An immense mass of timber and branches was brought from the woods. Piled up beneath the very fortification, it was set alight in an attempt to raise a fire. But because a strong wind blew violently against them, the attackers, harmed by the smoke and balls of flame alike, were forced to desist. Thus they accomplished nothing by that attempt.

[Col. 0111C] Nevertheless, there too the martyr’s hand was at work. Although many fought rashly and exposed their unprotected bodies and breasts to the enemy, not one complained that he had been injured in that assault. A troop of soldiers heavily equipped with armor climbed the steep mountain with difficulty and at a crawling pace, and halted between two fortifications which Count Rainald had built before the greater castle. This would surely have imposed no small necessity upon the enemy, since their means of going out or coming in were cut off. Yet that day had filled the miserable men with such a frenzy of dissension that, forgetful of their own defense and safety, they raged rather against one another in deadly fury. For he who strives to resist God puts on the mind of a beast. But when evening was now closing the day, the army descended from the mountain, while the armored soldiers alone pressed the enclosed enemy with greater zeal.

## Chapter II

Then Count Henry of Salm, the son of Count Rainald’s sister, came into the camp. Having asked for and obtained a truce from the bishop and the leaders, he entered the castle in order to speak with his nephew Hugh, whom he had heard to be ill, and to exhort both him and the others to surrender.

That night was made terrible by gloomy darkness, harsh storms, and a fighting south wind, peaceful calm having been driven from the sky. The raging tempest shattered the camp and the flood afflicted it; but the army’s praiseworthy endurance raised a shield against the hardship. Yet the soldiers who [Col. 0112A] spent the night on the mountain endured neither any foul weather nor the burdens of arms, because the glorious protection of their patron gave them security and concealment from storm and rain. The count, seeing the young man in so deadly a condition, recognized that it was divine vengeance; pierced to tears, he warned [Col. 0112B] the others to beware of a like fate. For the punishment of one ought to become a warning to many.

Having therefore received from all a promise that, unless their lord came to their aid within seven days, they would surrender themselves and the castle, he secured this: that the same Hugh should be carried to the martyr’s shrine, be released from excommunication by the bishop, and obtain forgiveness for what he had sinned against the saint. Yet this condition was added: until the surrender should take place, the young man himself was to be held by the bishop as a hostage. Moreover, his brother Rainald, who had stubbornly resisted the surrender, was stricken by a severe bodily illness; he was brought to the shrine, made satisfaction to the saint, and bound himself by a vow that no invasion would thereafter violate his possessions, provided that he deserved to escape the danger threatening him.

## Chapter III

Some of the enemies were also punished, each in a different manner, so that no one might think lightly of laying hands on the Lord’s saint.

Meanwhile Hugh, consumed by the prolonged anguish of his torments and crying out repeatedly the martyr’s name, closed his final day, thereby clearly showing by whose indignation he had been driven to his end.

The aforesaid count then hastened to Hugh’s father. To the astonished man he set forth the wrath of heavenly indignation, the death of his firstborn, the illness of his other son, and the miseries of his people; and he advised him at last to provide for himself and his own. Since matters were in such a strait, he said, he must yield [Col. 0112D] and relinquish what he could not retain. Thus that barbarous man, considering that to attempt to resist the divine will exceeded human power, compelled by the violence of his misfortunes consented to surrender, in the twelfth year after the seizure. O day of triumph! Then indeed, as the sun glows at its rising, so the martyr’s name shone in splendor: fighting from heaven against his enemies, divine power accomplished what human strength had been wholly unable to do.

Therefore, the enemies having been expelled from the castle on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, the venerable shrine was brought in with splendid triumph and placed in the middle of the church. This church, roofed with a vaulted structure, presents a worthy appearance. It was consecrated under the title of Saint John the Baptist, whom Lambert gloriously imitated [Col. 0113A], likewise dying for the witness of righteousness and chastity. Thus praises were sung to God according to the multitude of His greatness, and acclamations to the martyr [Col. 0114A], because he had humbled the proud man as one wounded and scattered his enemies by the strength of his arm.

# Fifth Book

[Col. 0113]

## Chapter I

[Col. 0113A]

After the enemies had been conquered and our strong man armed had regained his possessions, and all his affairs were now arranged in peace, it pleased them to return to Liège. Accordingly, after the solemn rites of Mass had been celebrated early two days later, the shrine was placed upon a wagon and conveyed to the town of Dinant; from there they proceeded to Namur. There a boy seven years old, blind from birth, received through the martyr the power of sight [Col. 0113B]. At Andenne also, a cleric exhausted by a severe bodily illness was drawn back from the very brink of death to life and health. Nor did the town of Huy pass unvisited by this healing grace. There it granted the use of new steps to a cripple whose parents testified that he had never walked.

Then, when the shrine reached Liège by ship, the whole city, crowned with triumphant joy, poured itself out to meet it, and with joyful songs and festive ranks accorded its victorious leader the ceremonial of a triumph. Received at the port of Saint James by monks and clerics with ecclesiastical solemnity, and carried through the monasteries of the island, with hymns rendered in melodious chant, it was brought back again to the greater church. [Col. 0113C] Then the body of the blessed martyr was raised from the altar of the Holy Cross, beside which it had been deposited, placed in a fitting shrine, and kept in the midst of the church with due observances. Nor did the bounty of heavenly mercy cease, deeming it worthy to repeat works of healing in proof of his merits. For when a sick man wholly possessed by illness was being conveyed in a vehicle to his martyr’s shrine, the grace of healing met his faith in the middle of the journey and saved him, after the ancient example of the ten lepers, who, when they went to show themselves to the priests at the Lord’s command, were cleansed from the affliction of leprosy before they arrived. The man leapt up, stood, and walked; and all the people, seeing it, gave praise to God.

[Col. 0113D] The merit of the pious martyr also heard a certain captive whom the barbarity of enemies had cast into chains and close confinement, when he called upon him, so as to rescue him. For the fetters by which he was bound suddenly burst apart; and thus, having obtained an opportunity to flee, he brought those same fetters to the church with thanksgiving as an indication of the miracle, that he might honor his deliverer. But the true blessedness of saints has no need of the testimony of signs. Therefore I consider it vain to add more to these matters, since utterly certain and innumerable proofs attest that nothing is impossible for the holy martyr with God. But these events occurred in the year 1141 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth indiction, during the reign of Conrad II over the Romans, in the fourth year of his reign, and in the fifth year of the episcopate of Lord Albero II. The praises of his merits and the proclamations of the wonders which he performed will be handed down to later ages, so that every generation may know them.

## Chapter II

Furthermore, while the sons of men provoked the Lord by their vanities, especially by indulging in immoderate fashions and the wanton excess of clothing, and while He visited their iniquities and sins with rod and blows, so that in certain regions of the world human bodies themselves sometimes burned while their clothing remained unharmed, and sometimes the garments themselves burned with invisible fire while the bodies remained untouched, the city of Liège, frightened by plagues so horrifying, judged it the best remedy to go beforehand to meet the face of the Lord in confession, penitence, and litanies [Col. 0114B].

For this reason it was also decided that the body of blessed Lambert should be carried through its districts and villages, so that through the merit and sanctification of so great a patron it might deserve to be guarded and preserved. This was done with great affection and solemn devotion by monks, clerics, and a multitude of the people. Yet, what I cannot say without groaning and grief, certain laymen thrusting themselves forward and irreverently touching the martyr’s shrine in an unauthorized carrying of it, provoked the martyr’s anger rather than merited his favor. For it is presumption rather than religion when unworthy persons touch holy things. This was immediately proved by adverse events.

For an accidental fire seized the city, and, having especially let loose its full force throughout the same places through which the shrine had been carried, it either consumed utterly or damaged with no slight destruction not only splendid houses and countless goods, but churches, walls, and towers as well [Col. 0114C]. No effort or work was able to withstand it, but the greatest and most beautiful part of the city fell before the devouring flames. Yet, as we afterward learned, this did not occur without divine vengeance, since the most wicked crimes of the inhabitants had kindled fires so fierce that not only things nearby, but even distant things, were inflamed by their very breath and the smallest sparks.

A memorable thing, however, shone forth: the dwelling of a certain married woman, though it was wooden, escaped danger. Great houses of masonry were burning on every side; the dreadful folds of flames encircled that dwelling in a fearful furnace, but it remained unharmed. Indeed, the fire utterly consumed the adjacent church of Saint George the martyr; harmless vapors licked the dry and almost rotten wooden structure of that dwelling’s walls, though their force was so great that they dissolved even stones. But [Col. 0115A] the good deeds of the pious are many, hidden from human beings but manifest to God. Therefore it must be believed that the woman’s devout way of life deserved this: that in her case the miracle of ancient time should be renewed, when the furnace of the Chaldeans did not harm the three boys at all, but rather glorified them.

Many nevertheless inferred that Saint Bartholomew had attended her as a protector, since she was especially devoted to him, and had offered a pallium to his church a few days earlier. Nor should it be passed over that when the fire, raging everywhere like a storm, reached a certain workshop belonging to the same apostle, it suddenly died down. At times heaps of flame rose up, as though angry to remain there, and strove to invade the building; [Col. 0115B] but they fell back upon themselves and diminished. For that glorious son of Him who suspends the waters quenched them with the streams of his merits; and danger had no rightful claim there where Bartholomew showed himself a patron.

Moreover, frequent disturbances and tumults, secret attacks and killings by the Ardennes assassins, and other misfortunes everywhere befell our city at that time. Since this class of men chiefly protects itself in the hiding places of forests and seeks impunity in the difficulty of the roads, it can sometimes do great harm, but cannot easily be caught or suppressed.

## Chapter III

[Col. 0115C] About two years after these events, the venerable body of the martyr was reinterred in the crypt beneath the altar of the Holy Trinity, with great glory and honor, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January. During this interval both the shrine and the sacristy had been splendidly decorated with gold and gems, and externally with stone panels whose elaborate carving represented the triumphs described above. It was further decreed by episcopal authority, with the approval of the Church of Liège, that the solemn commemoration of this triumph and also of his translation—for the same martyr was translated from Maastricht to Liège—should thereafter be observed on the fourth day before the Kalends of May. For the original translation had taken place on the ninth day before the Kalends of January, but on that day it could not be celebrated with due [Col. 0115D] honor because of the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. Since it is found written in many different ways how Saint Hubert formerly carried it out by divine admonition, and with how many and how great signs of power the Lord then glorified His saint, it seemed best to my insignificance to be silent about it. But I judge it fitting to add how, in the year 1153 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the martyr’s power also shone forth toward his people of Liège. [Col. 0116A] For to devote one’s labor to the praises of saints is an act of conspicuous diligence; nor will the devout praiser lack a reward, if he becomes a diligent imitator of him whom he praises.

Grave hostilities were stirred up by factious men between Bishop Henry, successor to the above-mentioned Albero, and Count Henry of Namur, so that they inflicted upon each other the evils of very great losses by plundering and burning villages and churches, and raged in mutual slaughter of men. At last the count did not fear to decide on war. Gathering a force of horsemen and foot soldiers, he came to Andenne, a town situated beside the river Meuse. The bishop advanced against him, though with a smaller number of horsemen. For when the citizens of Liège and Huy had advanced by ship, [Col. 0116B] the bishop, fearing that the enemy cavalry might attack them, did not delay to follow. Confronted by this necessity, he had had too little opportunity to gather mounted forces. But without doubt Christ had also destined this triumph to glorify His martyr.

On the Kalends of February, when the armed battle-lines met in combat, such stupor suddenly bound the enemy’s party that it wondered at its own lack of martial power, its very weapons somehow made slower to strike. Their foremost and chosen horsemen were therefore thrown down and captured; the rest sought safety in flight, some of whom were wounded or taken. The foot soldiers either fell by the sword or were dragged off with ropes, unless the speed of their feet saved them. Therefore we exult in the Church’s glorious success, and do not doubt that something like a miracle happened through God.
