For though the enemy lacked neither abundance of strength nor experience in arms, so confident were they of victory that they had even brought ropes with which to drag away the conquered, not a single ecclesiastical soldier was wounded or captured.

Thus the victors, sparing the conquered—and especially because the feast of the holy Mother of God was imminent—abandoned the pursuit of the fugitives and returned to their own people with triumphant rejoicing. Thus that Moab, whose pride the Church heard of, that he was exceedingly proud, was broken in arms but not broken in spirit, since his pride, arrogance, and indignation were greater than his strength.

[Col. 0116D] But you, humble and glorious one, victorious martyr, for whom I have woven such crown as I could of the flowers of graces and praises of this writing: with the unconquered hand of your mercy drive away all things hostile to your suppliants; and, looking with a serene countenance, behold and visit the vineyard of the Church of Liège. Watered by your blood and made fruitful by your body, protect it eternally beneath the shadow of your wings from the ungodly and from those who afflict it.

[Col. 0117]

# Life of Euraclus, Forty-Fifth Bishop of Liège, by Reiner

*(D. Bern. Pezius, Thesaurus Anecdotorum IV, 155, from the manuscript codex of Saint Lawrence at Liège.)*

## The Prologue Begins

[Col. 0117A] It is worthwhile to recall in writing how much honor and gratitude the Church of Liège owes to Euraclus, bishop of glorious memory, whom he so greatly cultivated by his character, teachings, and construction of churches: a truly diligent and industrious laborer in this vineyard of the Lord. Therefore he was not defrauded of the denarius of eternal reward. For faithful and true is the Lord of the vineyard, who made the agreement with him concerning that same denarius and renders to each according to his works.

Since Euraclus’s deeds were indeed illustrious, they deserved an illustrious writer, who, skilled in good speech, might say to the righteous man according to the Prophet: “It shall be well with him, for he shall eat the fruit of his deeds.” Some writers have indeed said something concerning him [Col. 0117B], but not well enough, because not diligently or fully enough. Therefore the kindly yet importunate request of certain brothers compelled me to gather into one what had been said here and there, and to make, in a more careful style, one composition from several writings, as I had done in writing the *Life of Saint Wolbodon*, likewise bishop of Liège.

But I, of slight ability and conscious of no learning, excused myself and resisted for a long time, turning over within myself that poetic saying:

> You who write, choose a subject equal to your powers,  
> and ponder long what your shoulders refuse to bear,  
> and what they are able to bear.  
> *(Horace, Ars Poetica 38, 40.)*

Yet because charity, according to the Apostle, is kind, does not seek what is its own but what belongs to others, and endures all things, although I judged the undertaking to be beyond my powers, I finally yielded to those who asked me, preferring to incur the reproach of incompetence rather than fail to obey the goodwill of the brothers.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 0117]

## Chapter I

[Col. 0117B]

Euraclus, the eminent glory of the Church of Liège, sprang from the illustrious blood of the Saxons. Having received his elementary literary training at Cologne Agrippina, he afterward attained such learning in sacred as well as secular subjects that he was rightly judged the equal of the greatest philosophers, especially since splendid morals adorned the beauty of his body also, and, as Solomon says, wisdom shone in the face of the prudent.

At Cisalpine Verona, commonly called Bonn, he was master of the schools. With wonderful kindness he instructed both his own pupils and all who flocked to him for the sake of learning. Adapting and accommodating himself to each, he offered solid food of doctrine to some, while to others he gave nourishment like milk from a mother’s breasts. Flaccus Rebius, describing the grammarian Donatus to his fellow student Minucius Rutilius, says: “When consulted on any question, he answered everything briefly and furiously,” [Col. 0117D] so that his pupils did not dare question him. Therefore, because he frequently raved in fury and was obscene both in body and in character, he was expelled from the senatorial order and council, although he had previously earned a senator’s cap because of his mastery of grammar. [Col. 0118C] You might think Rebius had said: “Learning suited Donatus as a golden earring would suit his ears.”

But our Euraclus was by no means such a man. He did not wait to be questioned, but pressed to be questioned; he did not grow weary or disdainful, however much or however often anything was asked of him. So zealously did he seek the advancement of others. He did not keep the money of his lord stored away in the napkin of idleness; rather, he spent it generously at interest for the increase of heavenly grace, stirring the sluggish and idle to study with that proverb of Solomon: “He who cultivates his land shall be satisfied with bread; but he who pursues idleness is utterly foolish” (Prov. 12). Likewise, he most pleasantly urged upon them these verses of the satirist:

> Robbers rise by night to murder men;  
> will you not wake to preserve yourself? But if  
> you refuse to be healthy, you will run about dropsical; and unless  
> you ask for a book and a lamp before daylight, unless  
> you apply your mind to studies and honorable pursuits,  
> envy or love will keep you awake and torment you.  
> *(Horace, Epistles, Book I, Epistle 2, lines 32–38.)*

## Chapter II
By steadfastness of faith and the brightness of his works, he was a learned man, as it is written: “Like a vessel of solid gold adorned with every precious stone” (Ecclus. 50). Although the Church of Verona set him over itself as provost against his will and despite his resistance, it experienced in his administration how great were his energy and faithfulness; so that it might rightly say with the patriarch Isaac: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 37), since he offered the good fruit of what had been well sown in him.

[Col. 0119B] Therefore it was said to him by the Lord: “Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many” (Matt. 25). For when Baldric, the first bishop of Liège of that name, departed this life, clergy and people, moved by happy zeal and the fullest concord, chose and installed Euraclus, with the favour and active support of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne. Bruno, who had found Euraclus eminently trustworthy, consecrated him bishop with solemn blessing, rejoicing that such a lamp was being placed upon the lampstand of the Church of Liège.

Thus Euraclus shone by religion and learning before all who were in God’s house, so greatly that he established schools even throughout the monastic precincts of the city, [Col. 0119C] and provided teachers for the instruction of boys, assigning them adequate salaries and annual revenues. He also pursued literary studies with such fervour that no occupations drew him away from frequently visiting the schools and imparting the disciplines of the liberal arts to pupils according to each one’s talent and capacity. But if he happened to be summoned on campaign, or detained for a long time on affairs of the realm, he vigorously urged the masters of the schools whom he had left behind toward the training-ground of learning, sending them writings composed either in cheerful prose or sweet verse. Indeed, even while following the imperial standards in Italian and Calabrian regions, he did not fail occasionally to write. Nor did he cease from this praiseworthy purpose until learning bore much fruit in many persons, with whom [Col. 0119D] he then conversed concerning mystical matters and, as he wandered through the gardens of Scripture, enjoyed with them, so to speak, the fruits “of the sun and moon”: that is, the sacraments and doctrines of Christ and the Church; and also the fruits “of the everlasting hills”: that is, the deeds and sayings of the Catholic Fathers.

## CHAPTER III

Bruno, archbishop of Cologne and archduke of Lotharingia, of whom mention has already been made, warmly cherished Euraclus’s diligence. As he was adorned with the glory of the highest nobility, so too with that of the highest religion and prudence. Together with his brother, the emperor Otto, he powerfully and energetically directed the helm of the kingdom—or empire; nor was he [Col. 0120A] so distracted by secular concerns that he did not give precedence to matters advancing the Church. Among his other magnificent works, he built the monastery of Saint Pantaleon near Cologne, installed monks and an abbot there, and most generously enriched the place with treasure and revenues.

Our Euraclus, emulating his zeal for God—for he was not inferior in devotion—founded two monasteries in this city: one of Saint Paul, the other dedicated in honour and under the title of Saint Martin; and he assigned thirty canons to each. And although he was often pressed, like a sweet grape, in the winepress of adversities, while certain armed men usurped villages or possessions of the bishopric, he nevertheless acquired for those serving in these monasteries [Col. 0120B] abundant revenues from tithes and estates, and secured them by charter to be held in perpetuity. He preferred sometimes to suffer a lack in his own household rather than fail to give to the poor, or allow necessities to be lacking to those whom he had gathered for God.

Finally, just as it is read of Jesus the high priest in Zechariah that Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him, so Euraclus was sometimes opposed even by his own fellow citizens. On one occasion they thrice broke open his wine-cellars on Mount Saint Martin and, like sons of Belial—that is, men without a yoke—poured streams of red Worms wine down the slopes into the Moselle flowing beneath. But since it is written: “The teaching of a man is known through patience” [Col. 0120C] (Prov. 19), and: “A patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own mind than a conqueror of cities” (Prov. 16), although he could have repaid evil for evil, he nevertheless strove always to overcome evil with good, and was far more ready to forgive than to exact vengeance. Thus, according to the prophet Hosea, his memorial was “like the wine of Lebanon”: so that, because *Lebanon* is interpreted “whiteness,” he might shine with heavenly brightness and enjoy the wine of everlasting gladness.

Socrates the philosopher too was deemed patient by the Thebans. Once, when his wife Xanthippe assailed him with storms of abuse, thundering that he was an utterly hideous man—bald in the forehead, with ape-like nostrils, hairy shoulders, and bowed legs—and, standing above him, drenched the man standing below with a great stream of urine, [Col. 0120D] he shook the foul rain from his clothes, hair, and beard and said: “I knew well enough that rain usually follows thunder; I had no need to be taught it by such a flood.” The philosopher considered this reply sufficient satisfaction for the injury done him.

## CHAPTER IV

Euraclus further used to relate that, while he was once in camp with the emperor Otto, who was campaigning against the Greeks in Calabria, there suddenly occurred an obscuring of the sun and a terrible eclipse. The army was struck with horror at the nocturnal darkness and unfamiliar chaos; and, as though the last day of the world were pressing upon them and the time of judgment were at hand, it began to panic. You might have seen high-spirited heroes fleeing like timid does. Some rushed competitively into wine-vessels; some hid in chests; others concealed themselves under wagons, others in caves. Alas, what confusion, what trembling there will be then, when, as the Lord foretold: “There shall be signs in sun and moon and stars, and upon earth distress of nations through bewilderment at the roaring of the sea and waves; men withering away through fear and expectation of what shall come upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven shall be shaken” [Col. 0121A] (Luke 21); or, as is read in the Apocalypse: “When heaven shall depart as a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island shall be moved from its place; when the kings of the earth, princes, commanders, rich, mighty, every slave and free person, shall hide themselves in caves and rocks of the mountains, and shall say to the mountains and rocks: ‘Fall upon us and hide us [Col. 0121B] from the face of Him who sits upon the throne, and from the face of the Lamb; for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?’” (Rev. 6).

But, to return to what I had interrupted: Euraclus, not ignorant of astronomical learning, remained undaunted. Going about among them one by one, he rebuked their womanish lack of confidence, since they trembled with fear where there was no fear. For an eclipse of the sun sometimes occurs naturally. In a little while, he said, they would see all things shining which they now vainly feared would turn black. If the enemies in whose midst they were had perceived spirits so degenerate and hearts so fearful in men who were accustomed gloriously to defeat others, these very men would shamefully have been conquered, slaughtered, and plundered by their enemies. Nor indeed was there a long delay before [Col. 0121C] light gradually began to be born anew, and the undimmed brightness of the moon’s lamp again flooded air and earth. Like ants emerging from little holes, the soldiers began to reproach one another for cowardice and, amid mocking applause, to laugh at the collapse of their own trance.

Euraclus’s learning is praised because he knew how to discern even the hidden causes of things. It is certain, according to Pliny, Macrobius, Calcidius, and many other writers, both astronomers and computists, that whenever the moon reaches the ecliptic line, if at the very hour of its conjunction with the sun—which always travels about it—it meets that line, then, by its intervention and interposition, an eclipse of the sun’s light occurs for us. Or, if, being full, it stands at that time opposite the sun across the diameter, it enters the shadow of the earthly mass and is prevented by the earth’s opposition [Col. 0121D] from the sight of the sun, and therefore necessarily suffers an eclipse.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore Euraclus stood continually by day upon the Lord’s watchtower and throughout the nights at his post: himself learned, himself, as Isaiah says, weighing the words of the law and a teacher of little ones, instructing those subject to him in whatever concerned righteousness and everlasting life and salvation. Among other observances, he decreed that, during Advent and from Septuagesima until Easter, the clergy should be clothed in dark garments, namely black copes, because black is more suited than white to penitence and affliction. Without doubt he intended that the children of the Church should display in their outward [Col. 0122A] habit what the Church says of Christ in the Song of Songs: “His locks are like lifted palm branches, black as a raven” (Song 5).

For Christ’s locks are the faithful clinging to their Head; and they are therefore compared to raised palms—that is, to shoulder-blades lifting themselves upward—because by faith and works they strive toward things above, so that they may say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Young ravens, moreover, when they begin to grow feathers, are white; and because they are unlike their parents, they are neglected by them and not fed at all. Yet, compelled by hunger, they naturally attract flies by the force of their breath; clustered around their beaks, these flies are swallowed by them. Hence also, among the other praises of God, the Psalmist says: “Who gives their food to the beasts, [Col. 0122B] and to the young ravens that call upon Him” (Ps. 146). Once they begin to turn black, however, on account of their similarity of plumage, they are fed more abundantly and lovingly by their parents.

Thus Christ’s locks are black as a raven when the faithful do not shrink from being blackened—that is, afflicted by no pressures of tribulation—for Christ, to whose blackness, to whose Passion, Isaiah sympathizes when he says: “And we saw him, and there was no appearance in him nor beauty: despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and knowing infirmities” (Isa. 53). Such locks are therefore planted in the Lordly Head by a firmer root of love. Such, I say, are the young ravens who open their mouths in calling upon God and attract the Spirit of good fragrance; they feed not on flies—that is, vices—but now on the sacraments of Christ and the Church, [Col. 0122C] and hereafter are to be fed on eternal goods, as it is written in the Prophet: “In very rich pastures I will feed them, and on lofty mountains shall be their pasture; there they shall rest in green grass, and in fat pastures they shall be fed” (Ezek. 34); and David also says: “You have prepared before me a table against those who afflict me” (Ps. 22).

Nor is it unsuitable to add that the raven desires nothing in corpses more than the eyes, to which that proverb of Solomon also seems to refer: “The eye that mocks its father and despises the birth of its mother—let the ravens of the torrents pluck it out, and let the young of the eagle eat it” (Prov. 30). False teachers, “wandering stars,” as the apostle Jude wrote, “for whom the storm of darkness is reserved forever,” [Col. 0122D] when they criticize God’s judgments, mock the Father of lights. That is, heretics are clouds without water: namely, without that water of which the Lord says, “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). When they ridicule the faith or preaching of the Church, they despise their mother’s birth, since John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2). Those who speak against the Church go forth from the Church. For them she endures pains like a woman in labour, so that she may groan with Paul: “My children, whom I am again bringing to birth until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4).

But when Catholics, abiding in the living waters of the Scriptures, refute their faithless intention [Col. 0123A] by disputation and rebuke, they pluck out, like ravens from the torrents, the wicked eye, and the young of the eagle devour it. The saints are indeed called ravens because they confess the blackness of sin in themselves; but sons of the eagle because they have been reborn from that life-giving fountain, from which He who, like an eagle, flew to heaven far beyond the sun shines in a human body. He rejected his degenerate children like an eagle rejecting chicks that turn away their eyes, dim-sighted before the sun’s ray.

But Euraclus had eyes “like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk and sitting beside fullest floods”: he dwelt continually upon the Scriptures of truth with dove-like simplicity, through which he avoided the spiritual snares of the hawk—that is, the spirit of falsehood—shunning, as the Apostle commands Timothy, [Col. 0123B] “profane novelties of speech and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some, professing, have fallen away from the faith” (1 Tim. 6).

## CHAPTER VI

And indeed he had now advanced to great age; but, according to the Psalmist, “his youth was renewed like the eagle’s.” When an eagle feels its eyes growing dim through old age and its flight impeded, it exposes itself to the most burning heat of the sun; it burns away not only the feathers of its whole body but even the pinions of its wings and the disease of its eyes, and by a wonderful effect restores therefrom the sharpness of its sight from that very source by which human vision is usually blunted and dimmed. Then it flies down to a most clear spring and immerses itself three times, [Col. 0123C] and thus restores its former youth.

By this comparison, I say, Euraclus—whose soul thirsted for God, the living fountain, and who kept the eyes of his mind fixed upon the Sun of righteousness—was in some manner renewed and flourished again through the zeal of devotion. Since, as was stated above, he had already built two monasteries in the city, he might build a third in this place to the glory of the Holy Trinity.

Thus he laid the foundations, and the wise architect did not fear that the place had an evil reputation from the hanging of thieves, was often defiled by the slaughter of wicked men, and was hateful because of the robberies of brigands, who had then made caves and hiding-places for themselves there because of the density of the surrounding wood. For he knew that [Col. 0123D] the Holy of Holies had been crucified at the place of Calvary; that the Pantheon at Rome, and countless temples of demons throughout the world, had sometimes been changed into churches and dedicated by holy [Col. 0124A] Fathers. Accordingly the work proceeded with eager zeal. The walls had already risen some distance above the foundations when, in the meantime, the bishop postponed the principal altar, which was to be Saint Lawrence’s, and ordered a smaller one to be made separately under the title of Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr. He also dedicated it, endowing the infant little church with certain estates which we possess even now.

But suddenly that construction was halted, and the craftsmen’s hands ceased, because Euraclus was taken from their midst. Christ, I say, called to Himself the labourer of His vineyard, so that, since he had worked well and borne the burden and heat of the day, He might pay him his wage: the denarius of eternal refreshment and blessed rest. The work begun accordingly remained [Col. 0124B] unfinished. The little church, now made an orphan without a father and still like a nursing infant, sat desolate and bare until Nothger, who had succeeded as bishop, finally had the walls levelled and a roof placed over them.

A certain bishop Leo, one of the noblest Greeks, fled to him. He had been driven from his see because he was accused, before Otto II—while that emperor was campaigning against the Greeks—of having betrayed Calabria. The aforementioned bishop received him humanely, established him to remain in this place, and decreed that he and his household should receive support from the goods which the venerable Euraclus had assigned. During his residence, he lived soberly, justly, and piously, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God. Later he was gloriously led forth from the exile of this world by that God, and was buried among us before the altar of Saint Gereon: no longer a stranger or foreigner, but a fellow citizen of the saints and, O holy Lawrence, a member of your household.

Finally, Euraclus, the pious householder and scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven, passed away in the year 971 from the age of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November [27 October], when John, the 134th from the blessed apostle Peter, presided over the Apostolic See; in the thirty-fourth year both of Otto I’s kingship and empire, and in the thirteenth of Euraclus’s own episcopate. Inscribed by God’s finger among the living in Jerusalem, his venerable body was buried with fitting funeral rites in the Church of Saint Martin before the high altar, assuredly joined to the choir of those of whom it was said to Daniel: [Col. 0124D] “Those who have understanding shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities.” Amen (Dan. 12).

[Col. 0125]

# THE LIFE OF REGINARD, FIFTIETH BISHOP OF LIÈGE, BY REINER

(D. Bernhard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV, III, 167, from the manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège.)

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 0125A] According to Solomon’s proverb: “A learned man is of a precious spirit” (Prov. 17). But although I am unlearned, and therefore truly of no value, I have nevertheless considered it a heartfelt and desired obligation to describe a precious man, namely the venerable bishop Reginard. Choosing you, O holy Lawrence, as his special patron, he built on earth in your name this tabernacle—that is, this church—in which God may be served forever; and through you he is believed to have deserved citizenship in the heavenly tabernacle and the Church above. For us who live under the protection of your patronage and are separated from the tumult of worldly affairs, he became as “a shelter from heat by day, a refuge and hiding-place from storm and rain.”

[Col. 0125B] Certain brethren also, with kindly encouragement and continual prayer, stirred me up as one sluggish and idle to describe him, urgently alleging that I owed no less gratitude and no less service to our householder, by whose benefits I had chiefly been reared from childhood, [Col. 0126A] than to the holy bishops Wolbodo and Euraclus, whose Lives I had previously written in two little books. But I replied that it was superfluous labour to commend in words men whom the lamp of their outstanding deeds made illustrious—as if someone should carry a torch before persons surrounded by the sun, and try by the addition of lights to assist their brightness.

Nevertheless, for the encouragement of virtues and the benefit of readers or hearers, it is worthwhile to celebrate some righteous person in writing, so that, according to the prophet, “the memory of the righteous may be with praises.” After the fruits worthy of repentance, it ought no more to be imputed to Reginard that he once made a transaction from the mammon of iniquity—that is, purchased a bishopric—[Col. 0126B] than to Matthew the apostle and evangelist that, while pursuing profit, he once sat at the tax collector’s toll-booth.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0125]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0125C] Reginard was born of distinguished stock in the territory of Cologne Agrippina; but, being committed to schools at the City [Rome], he made good beginnings both in learning and in virtue. Afterwards he became a canon in the greater church. Already as a young man he was arranging in his heart the ascents described by the Psalmist: namely, undertaking the steps by which one ascends to behold the God of gods in Zion. Thus he devoted himself to chastity and other goods; and, as someone has said, “Unless the vessel is pure, whatever you pour into it turns sour.” Into a sober and pure heart he instilled sacred readings like divine honeycombs.

Therefore the venerable archbishop Heribert, greatly admiring the young man’s diligence and mature dignity, wished him to remain by his side as his close associate, rejoicing that he was his neighbour not only in spirit but also in flesh. After Reginard had advanced through the successive offices of ecclesiastical orders, Heribert made him provost over the cathedral chapter at Verona. [Col. 0125D] Reginard managed that stewardship diligently, like the faithful and prudent servant placed over the Lord’s household: cautious in counsel, just in judgments, rendering to the Church what belonged to the Church and to the world what belonged to the world—namely, as the Apostle says, rendering to all their due. He accepted no gifts against an innocent person, nor did he favour the rich in order to oppress the poor, attending to Solomon’s saying: “A weight and a weight are an abomination before God, and a deceitful balance is not good” (Prov. 11).

Meanwhile, after the bishop of Verdun had died, clergy and people unanimously pressed for such a man to be placed over them. But Durand, bishop of Liège, also then died, and Reginard, seized by human temptation—for in human affairs better things are commonly desired—[Col. 0126D] sought the see of Liège rather than Verdun. He went therefore to the emperor Conrad and obtained by money what ought to have been obtained from God by grace. Finally, Saint Heribert consecrated him bishop. He performed the office of shepherd vigorously and watchfully, although he had climbed up by another way and had not entered the sheepfold through the door.

## CHAPTER II

At that time Poppo, abbot of Stavelot, was administering the care of this church, a duty entrusted to him four years earlier by the holy bishop Wolbodo. When he had already despaired of its condition and advancement, he resigned that care to Bishop Reginard, fifty-seven years having then passed since this church had first begun to be founded by Euraclus, a bishop of glorious memory.

Meanwhile, one of our resident servants, a poor and insignificant man of simple nature, [Col. 0127B] testified that in nocturnal visions he often heard and saw certain wondrous things, because God is sometimes accustomed to reveal great things to little ones, and His discourse is with the simple. Going about the city on feast-days, he publicly reported among the people that Saints Lawrence and Wolbodo shared a dwelling on the public hill; throughout the nights they laid out and measured their habitation, and, because it seemed too narrow to them, agreed that the old structure should be demolished and a new and more spacious one built. As he explained to those asking, “Up to this point in length, so much in breadth, so much in height, they themselves stretched out their lines,” these things were long considered foolishness and delirium, until their truth was proved by the subsequent result.

[Col. 0127C] I therefore believe that our architects, Lawrence and Wolbodo, made themselves like that architect whom Ezekiel saw measuring with cord or reed the building of the city set on a mountain and sloping southward. I also believe that the man was with them whose appearance, according to the prophet, was like the appearance of bronze, so that the place might thus be marked out for divine praise with resounding praise of God, and that the minds of those dwelling there, truly turned toward the south—that is, toward the Holy Spirit, fragrant with the breath of religion—might be breathed upon, the cold north wind being driven out, just as the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4).

[Col. 0127D] For, as was said above, after the abbot of Stavelot had transferred the care of this place into the hand of Bishop Reginard, Count Herimann, a man as illustrious in nobility as in prudence and counsel, and brother of Gozelo, duke of the Lotharingians and Mosellans, urgently petitioned the bishop to pity this orphaned and desolate Church and appoint for it a father and protector. At Verdun, he said, there was a monk very well known to him, who by religion and learning could both govern and benefit God’s house. The bishop gladly answered that he would do so, provided the man were present. The count, whose devotion toward Saint Lawrence burned with extraordinary and singular ardour, brought Stephen from Verdun as quickly as possible. Stephen had with him six monks [Col. 0128A] of commendable life; the bishop blessed him as abbot and placed him over this place.

## CHAPTER III

Thus fragrances flowed from our garden at that time—that is, from the Church in holiness and virtues—because those dwelling there had become Christ’s sweet fragrance. Their fingers, I say, were full of the most excellent myrrh, since they continually bore in their bodies and works the bitterness of Jesus Christ’s Passion and the mortification of the cross, according also to what the bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “The locks of your head are like royal purple bound in channels” (Song 7). The locks are rightly understood as thoughts, the head as the mind, and royal purple as the Passion of Christ who rules all things. Purple, therefore, is joined to channels: that is, to the faithful, [Col. 0128B] into whose minds, while they adhere by faith and love to Christ’s Passion, the living waters of the charisms of the Holy Spirit flow.

Although Stephen and the brethren under him abounded in spiritual goods, they were nevertheless greatly in need of bodily goods—namely food and clothing—because the bishop utterly neglected the place. Therefore that Father mourned for himself as though in exile and desolation, and was more distressed for his children’s need than for his own, so that his pains were like those of a woman in labour. But according to the prophet’s saying concerning the blessed mourners, “Lord, in distress they sought you; in the tribulation of murmuring your instruction was with them” (Isa. 26), he received from above an oracle of this consolation.

[Col. 0128C] One night, while keeping watch in prayer at the tomb of Saint Wolbodo, and when he had become weary from groans and tears, he fell asleep with his head bent between his hands. He saw a young man standing beside him, clothed brilliantly and with a star-like face, saying that he had been sent by the pious Father Wolbodo. Comforting him kindly, he said: “It is good, brother, to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man” (Ps. 117). “You indeed now have sorrow; but because, with a contrite spirit, you have until now cried to God as a poor man, groaning painfully, God’s salvation will receive you, so that this sorrow of yours may soon be turned into joy. For Saint Lawrence and Wolbodo have jointly undertaken before God the protection and care of this [Col. 0128D] place; and as long as those who seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness dwell here, all necessary things shall be added to them.

“And this shall be a sign to you. He who, as the Psalmist says, ‘looks upon the earth and makes it tremble, who touches the mountains and they smoke’ (Ps. 103), shall now look upon the bishop’s heart, so that he may make it tremble and smoke in salutary contrition and penitential grief for the sin of simony, by which he has grievously offended. He himself will lay in this place the foundations of his satisfaction, which through God’s grace shall be established above upon the holy mountains. Finally, brother, the man whom you are sending today to the market of Visé, to obtain a loan for purchasing clothing for the brethren’s use, will find a man sent by Saint Wolbodo, who will give him freely as much as is necessary.”

[Col. 0129A] Upon waking, the elder ordered the brother, who had already gone out and was already setting off for the market, to be summoned back at once. He disclosed the vision before them all and allowed him to go, now as one equipped with good hope. The brother came to Visé, and an unknown man standing in the market asked him why he had come and what he sought. “I have been sent by Saint Wolbodo,” he replied, “to buy clothing for the brethren, but money is altogether lacking.” The man gladly received this, quickly drew sixty solidi of tested coinage from his purse, and with liberal hand counted them out and gave them to the monk. Truly, O Wisdom, with whom are riches, proud possessions, and righteousness: meanwhile, by this act of kindness you bestowed a gift upon those who daily watch at your doors; upon those who keep watch at the posts of your doorway you conferred this small present, whose offspring are truly better than choice silver.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, that our Reginard might now make himself free from the offspring of evil commerce—that is, simony—and cleanse out the old leaven, he had made his tears day and night like unleavened bread for himself. By devoting himself to almsgiving and mercies toward the poor, he strove, according to the Apostle’s command, to become a new dough. Four years of his episcopate had now passed when, as the compassionate Jesus called Lazarus from the tomb after four days, so He called Reginard from the depth of sin and inspired him with the holy spirit of counsel, so that he might go to Rome and there be [Col. 0129C] released from the bands of simony and the napkin of blind ambition by him who exercised, in the Apostles’ stead, the privilege of binding and loosing.

He went with such a great retinue of nobles that it seemed more an expedition than a pilgrimage: some accompanied him for honour, others out of their own devotion. Yet he had conceived so great a zeal for repentance that he was not ashamed, before the numerous company of his fellow travellers, of what he intended to do.

For, entering Rome and the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, where he saw Pope John, he fell at his feet before his own people and the whole assembled crowd, roaring, as it were, from the groaning of his heart. All were moved, especially those who had come with him. The pope himself was moved and waited to learn the cause. But [Col. 0129D] the tears of the prostrate man hindered his words with sobs. At length, though scarcely, he explained the cause of such grief: he had bought his bishopric with money; therefore he felt the wrath of God like swelling waves over him; and, before being judged by the Lord, he judged himself and wished to resign the honour perilously acquired. The pope approved his purpose and declared that this course was expedient for his salvation. Reginard therefore placed his pastoral staff upon Saint Peter’s altar and, as though relieved of a great burden, gloried in the Lord with his conscience now innocent, while his followers were deeply troubled and grieved.

Meanwhile the pope, reflecting that one should deal more mercifully with a man whom he had not captured by sword or bow, but who had voluntarily disclosed his own sin and [Col. 0130A] condemned it by voice and tears, ordered him to be recalled on the third day. Receiving him kindly, he said: “Because you did not wait for Christ’s indignation and scourge, but yourself overthrew your own episcopal seat; because, to make satisfaction to the divine dove—that is, the Holy Spirit—you presented yourself to blessed Peter: behold, in Christ’s name, by the authority of the apostle Peter, receive the care and governance of the holy Church. Sit in God’s temple no longer as a merchant but as a faithful steward and lawful shepherd. And because it is written: ‘A merciful man does good to his own soul,’ and ‘he who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, and He will repay him in return’ (Prov. 19), feed the poor according to your means; assist those suffering need; and, if your resources permit, build the church of some saint, so that, when you fail, it may receive you into everlasting tabernacles.” Then he handed him the pastoral staff and, strengthened by apostolic blessing, sent him back to his own land.

Thus was fulfilled in him the saying of holy Job: “A tree has hope: if it be cut down, it shall grow green again, and its branches shall bud. Though its root grow old in the earth and its trunk die in the dust, at the scent of water it shall germinate and make foliage as when first planted” (Job 14). For you also, O Christ, restored Peter to the apostolic throne when he had denied you but, looked upon by you, wept bitterly; you, the same compassionate and merciful one, restored penitent Reginard to the episcopal chair. For you do not remain angry forever, nor threaten for eternity, overlooking sins [Col. 0130C] because of repentance.

## CHAPTER V

Reginard therefore returned safely to Liège, to the ark of the true Noah—that is, Christ’s Church—like the dove of old in the Flood, bearing an olive branch with green leaves: namely, the peace by which, amid the waves of the world, he might flourish, put forth leaves, and bear fruit in teaching and good works. As he was now descending by the public hill and caught sight of the little church located here, Count Herimann, of whom mention has already been made, somewhat privy to his secrets, approached more closely. “Behold, my lord,” he said, “Saint Lawrence; if you endeavour to make him your patron, you will have a faithful helper in times of need and will discover how great is his favour with the Lord.” Immediately, in a wondrous manner, the bishop’s heart grew warm with love and devotion for the martyr, since the oil of pious exhortation is accustomed easily to kindle a bright flame in reverent hearts.

Therefore, once he had been honourably received by clergy and people and all his affairs were at peace, on one day, as Solomon says, “He who seeks good rises early at dawn” (Prov. 11), he ascended this place at sunrise, inspected the dwellings, visited the brothers, comforted poor Stephen, and promised prosperity and joy, as the angelic oracle mentioned above had foretold to that abbot.

It was the second day of November, and therefore, because winter was at hand, he deferred the fulfilment of his purpose. But winter had not yet fully passed, rain had not yet gone away and departed, when, nevertheless, through his desire to begin your house, O Saint Lawrence, he already seemed to see spring flowers appearing and flowering vines giving forth fragrance. And behold, on the third day of February, when dawn had scarcely broken, he sent a large number of workmen. Climbing upon the church roof, they began with great eagerness and joy to dismantle the roof and demolish the wall, so that the crash left Abbot Stephen and the brethren, still sleeping and unaware of so sudden an event, as if stunned. Thus the voice of the turtledove—the voice, I mean, of Reginard’s action, issuing the good groans of repentance—began at once to be heard in our land, namely in this our place.

[Col. 0131B] The helpers and fellow-workers in building this church were Olbert, abbot of St. James and of St. Peter of Gembloux; Huneco, brother of the same bishop; and Meiner, then advocate of this city—men whom, in the Apostle’s words, I might rightly call God’s husbandry. Nor is it irrelevant to relate that a certain small tree, commonly called a *salangra*, had been left outside the circuit of the foundations. The aforementioned dreamer maintained firmly that it ought to be enclosed within the length of the church: that this was the will of Lawrence and Wolbodo; that those clear-sighted surveyors had measured it so; and that they had extended their lines thus far.

Now the walls had risen no little way above the foundations, and he persisted nonetheless in his [Col. 0131C] assertion, when the aforesaid brother of the bishop arrived. Having inspected the work, he began strongly to disapprove, saying that the measurements of the length displeased him and that his lord could complete much better what he had begun to build. Then he confidently ordered the workmen to lengthen the walls by forty feet, undertaking to supply the additional expense from his own funds if the bishop should refuse. Thus that little tree marking the boundary in Lawrence’s geometry was enclosed by the wall; and its prophet, smiling at those who had mocked him, taunted them as though vindicated in his judgment—plainly so that Solomon’s saying might be understood of this poor man: “The will of God is with those who walk simply” (Prov. 10).

With God’s favour, therefore, the work was completed; [Col. 0131D] the church was finished; and the malice of perverse men was brought to nothing. Like the Samaritans who once opposed the walls of Jerusalem, they had long and greatly obstructed the construction of this building. For its consecration the bishop wished the authority of the Apostolic See to be present; and John, bishop of Porto, sent by Pope John, together with Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, dedicated it with great honour and joy in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1034, in the second indiction, and in the tenth year of the episcopate of Lord Reginard.

## Chapter VI

From that time the martyr’s merits shone forth more brightly than the sun for the whole city. In the preceding years, while the old church here stood neglected and, as it were, orphaned, such disturbance of the air occurred on his feast [Col. 0132A] that, because of the thunder and excessive flashes of lightning, the earth itself seemed to be shaken and tremble—doubtless because malignant spirits, seeking to obscure the splendour of his celebration, were horribly convulsing even the elements. For we ourselves have sometimes experienced how fiercely those most loathsome villains are tormented by envy toward Lawrence, and how greatly they abhor the victorious fires of his gridiron. This was especially so in the year 1132 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [22 March], when lightning suddenly fell near us with a terrifying crash of clouds. By divine permission and judgment it entered through the great door of the church and ranged as far as the high altar; touching or scorching almost nothing else, it shattered into fragments the altar’s seal itself. Truly this was a wondrous miracle, since the cloth [Col. 0132B] with which that seal was covered remained unharmed. Such indeed was the fire that one might truly say of this place what is said in Zechariah: “Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?” (Zech. 3). But this subject must now be set aside, since I have discussed it elsewhere in a fuller little work.

It is therefore customary for the clergy and people of this city to assemble at this church with litanies whenever they have been alarmed either by unseasonable weather or by the hardship of any tribulation; and there is no doubt that the martyr’s merits have sometimes aided them. This appeared more clearly on the day when Godfrey, provost of the Greater Church, a man distinguished by birth and religion, brought us relics of this martyr from the city of Rome. [Col. 0132C] For there was then such an inundation of rain that a second Flood seemed imminent, since the density of the clouds had hidden the sun and withheld the benefits of its light and warmth for almost a month, while fields and vineyards promised their cultivators no good hope of produce. But when these relics had been brought into our church and placed upon the high altar, and Mass was celebrated for fair weather and peace, as soon as the cry went up, “Lord, have mercy; Lord, take pity,” a brightness appeared: the sun sent forth a radiance so clear that the Church then applauded the divine magnificence no less than the Synagogue once applauded when the glory of the Lord appeared over the tabernacle of the covenant. Nor was that sudden fair weather short-lived: it endured; ripeness followed, together with a great abundance [Col. 0132D] of crops, through the intercession of Lawrence, whose merits neither tongue can utter nor page comprehend.

How blessed you are, O Rome, in possessing his body—he whom you too wished to be honoured and made famous among you by so many basilicas and privileges. For in the Lateran palace there is a basilica of this martyr, called the *Holy of Holies*, because of the excellence of the relics kept there, both of the Holy of Holies—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—and of many other saints. There too are the heads and blood-vessels of the apostles Peter and Paul, and a great quantity of the coals and fat of blessed Lawrence. His altar there also possesses so great a privilege that no one but the pope is permitted to celebrate the sacred mysteries of Mass upon it. There too you might see the venerable [Col. 0133A] image of Christ which, when Saint Luke the Evangelist began to paint it, he wondrously found completed on the following day by that craftsman whose hands are “golden, fashioned on a lathe, set with hyacinths.”

A person of tested faith and religious devotion is accordingly set over so illustrious a place: namely, the chief subdeacon of the Apostolic See. His privilege is to use the mantle, mitre, and ring, and to present the keys of the supreme house—that is, the Lateran palace—to the newly consecrated supreme pontiff. Pope Damasus also built a basilica under the title of so great a martyr, distinguished by his relics, and named the place Damasus after himself. Moreover Lucina, a most illustrious Roman woman, built at great expense a church in Lawrence’s honour and, having procured sacred pledges, made it more renowned: [Col. 0133B] namely, the chain with which the martyr was bound; the gridiron on which he was roasted; one of the iron pincers with which he was pressed down from above; some of the coals and fat squeezed from his sacred limbs by Justin and Hippolytus; and finally, as is reported, that linen cloth with which a Roman saw an angel wipe his bloodied limbs as he hung upon the rack.

Outside the walls, moreover, he is buried under the high altar of the greater basilica together with the proto-martyr Stephen. That altar has such a privilege that, except for the six cardinals appointed for this purpose, no one is permitted to celebrate the divine mysteries upon it. Blessed place indeed! Most happy ground! Genesis praises the land of Havilah because its gold is excellent, [Col. 0133C] because bdellium—a fragrant tree—is found there, and the onyx stone. Yet more praiseworthy is the ground where such fragrant trees are planted, where gold finer than refined gold and such precious stones are found: Stephen and Lawrence. Polished by manifold pains of suffering, in accordance with the interpretation of *Havilah* as “suffering,” they have been set in your diadem, O Christ.

## Chapter VII

Furthermore, in the place called Panisperna, Pope Formosus built a basilica for Lawrence, beside the baths of Olympias themselves, where the martyr had been roasted. From their entrance there still breathes so sweet a fragrance that it surpasses the perfume which the queen of the south is read to have offered [Col. 0133D] to King Solomon. But the more the astonishing event done to Formosus bears the appearance of grief, the more should every person be moved against impiety; for the mournful tragedy of Formosus can soften even hearts of stone.

In the time of Pope John VIII, Formosus had been bishop of Porto. But he had fled from the presence of that pope after abandoning his bishopric, because the pope was deeply offended with him and accused him of seeking by some means to usurp the papacy over him. Though recalled by the same pope, Formosus refused to obey and present himself. Later, however, he made satisfaction to that pope while the latter was in Gaul; yet he did not obtain forgiveness, but was degraded even to lay status. He was compelled by oath and by a written declaration in his own hand to renounce his bishopric and thereafter to abstain from entering the city of Rome, declaring himself content, [Col. 0134A] for as long as he lived, with lay communion.

But after John’s death Martin succeeded to the apostolic office. Reconsidering the treatment of Formosus as too hasty and harsher than justice permitted, he granted him reconciliation, released him from the oath, and restored him to his dignity and see. Then, when Martin died, Formosus himself, through the favour and assent of the Romans, was raised to the papacy, being a shrewd and religious man; and during two and a half years as bishop he accomplished many things with energy.

After his death Stephen was installed in his place. Although Formosus had raised him by many benefits and, in addition, by the bishopric of the city of Anagni, Stephen nevertheless became so savage against the dead man in detestable ingratitude that, having assembled a council—or rather, a gathering of evil men—he caused him to be taken from the tomb and brought into their midst. Not as a Christian and pope, but more than [Col. 0134B] a barbarian or Scythian, he stripped from the corpse its pontifical garments while it sat in the pontifical chair and dressed it in lay clothing. Then—O monstrous deed!—after three fingers of its right hand had been cut off, its head was severed with a sword and its body cast into the waters of the Tiber. What could Nero have done more absurdly, or Decius more inhumanely? What hearts of dutiful children could endure this, and what eyes could see it? Thus, although martyrs are customarily made from the living, Formosus was made a martyr from the dead.

But because Stephen had not feared Christ’s tribunal, before which Formosus had departed to be judged, he died by the axe of an unexpected death, having held—or rather, misused—the apostolic office for only four [Col. 0134C] months. Thus, according to Scripture, “his life was cut off like that of a weaver”: while he was still beginning his weaving, he was cut down; as though from morning to evening, he was finished. Formosus’s body, however, was found by fishermen and brought in a coffin to the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles. There the images of saints carved in marble were seen openly by all to greet and adore it as that of a new martyr and a companion who had earned his reward. By a wondrous judgment, inanimate stones thought better of Formosus than did living human beings.

Theodore succeeded Stephen. Approving Formosus’s apostolic office, he held valid the ordinations Formosus had made among the clergy and the synods he had held; and he rejected and condemned the wrongful things done or written against him. [Col. 0134D]

No less did Pope John after him act likewise. He convened at Ravenna a synod of seventy-four bishops, in the presence of Frankish archbishops and King Louis, son of the emperor Arnulf; before them the synod which Stephen had held for the condemnation of Formosus was repudiated and burned. There can be no doubt, O Saint Lawrence, that your aid was present for Formosus, who was especially devoted to you, since you pursue with the greatest gratitude the benefits bestowed upon you and commend them most effectively to divine mercy. Hence devotion to you, and Reginard’s deeds through you, prospered happily.

## Chapter VIII

[Col. 0135A] Thus the Lord’s covenant was with Reginard, a covenant of life and peace. For, as the prophet says, the Lord had given him fear, and he feared Him; he stood in awe before His name. Above all he devoted himself to almsgiving and to the relief of the needy, recalling that Christ will say at judgment: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25). Therefore, when a most severe famine was afflicting this region, he supported twelve hundred poor persons by a daily allowance: three hundred at Liège, three hundred at Huy, three hundred at Dinant, and three hundred at Fosses. He also showed himself generous and most devout toward the apostle Bartholomew—whose name is interpreted “son of him who suspends the waters,” namely, of Him who at Cana of Galilee suspended the waters, [Col. 0135B] changing their nature so that they became wine—by acquiring estates so as to add eight canons to the twelve then serving him, the revenues of those estates benefiting their support.

Finally, with exceedingly difficult and costly labour, he built a very great bridge across the Meuse. Beyond the islands, in marshy places, he built two stone bridges; and likewise a third across the river Ourthe, over the impassable marshes and gulfs of water. He made passage genuinely more useful and the roads more level than Solomon, David’s son, levelled the gulf of the city when he built Mello. At that time a great multitude of both sexes and all ages had flowed into this city from western regions, driven from their homes by want and the devastations of wars. [Col. 0135C] To them the bishop extended the hand of generosity and mercy so lavishly that you would have thought him another John the Almsgiver of Alexandria.

He possessed such noble discernment that he employed in work those who were ashamed to beg. Thus, producing fragrant and incorruptible fruits of mercy, he multiplied like the cedar of Lebanon; and, as is read in the Apocalypse (chapter 22), his leaves—that is, his good deeds—were for the healing of the nations. For he spent himself wholly upon the miserable in acts of mercy and urgently exhorted those subject to him to do the same, utterly detesting avarice, which, according to [Col. 0135D] the Apostle, is the service of idols (Col. 3).

At that time Count Odo of Champagne, relying upon the aid of the Franks and Burgundians, was grievously invading Lotharingia with fire and sword. Holding divine things in as little regard as human, he devastated the vineyard of Christ’s churches like a boar from the forest and consumed it like a solitary wild beast. He captured the fortress of Bar. He surrounded with a powerful siege the city of the Leuci, called Toul, devastating the bishopric on every side by plunder and fire. Bruno then presided over it, a man renowned for holiness, learning, and birth; later honoured with the papacy of the Roman city and called Leo IX, he strove to imitate in the strength of piety and humility the footsteps of the Lion of the tribe of Judah. [Col. 0136A] I shall briefly explain why Odo broke out into such tyranny.

King Rudolph of Burgundy, long and greatly harassed and provoked by the insolence of the Burgundians, laid aside the crown and handed the kingdom to Emperor Conrad. From the time of Emperor Arnulf, kings of Rudolph’s people had held it for more than one hundred and thirty years; Burgundy was thus again reduced to the status of a province. But the aforesaid Odo demanded from the emperor, his own nephew, the kingdom of his uncle, urgently asking to govern Burgundy under him; but he did not obtain it. Therefore he began to oppose and attack the empire. Duke Gozelo of the Mosellans and Lotharingians could not endure his excessively insolent arrogance. He came to Liège and, gathering an army from every quarter, urged the bishop—who was high-spirited and clear-sighted in arranging affairs—to undertake an expedition with him for loyalty to the empire and the defence of the churches. [Col. 0136B] Reginard, commanded to render to God what belongs to God and to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, did not, like the sons of Ephraim who bent and shot the bow, turn back on the day of battle. Rather, he went up against the enemy, set himself as a wall for the preservation of Church and kingdom, and entered the camp with a chosen force of cavalry and infantry.

In the first clashes of the battle many fell on both sides, including Count Albert of Namur, while attempting to break through the enemy’s tightly packed ranks. But the Lotharingians, their spirits more fiercely inflamed by the slaughter of their own men and preferring death to defeat, dealt such havoc among the Franks that they struck down Odo himself with almost all the nobles, while the rest sought safety in ignominious flight. The duke returned in splendid victory, assigning to the bishop of Liège no small share of the triumph before the emperor and the court. The bishop decreed that throughout all the churches of his bishopric supplications should be made and sacred offerings offered for the souls of his men slain in that battle—so that Aaron of old, standing between the dead and the living, did not pray to God more earnestly for Israel or offer incense more devoutly. He himself, meditating on the Apostle’s saying, “We have no abiding city here, but seek the one to come,” sighed day and night with all his desires for the heavenly Jerusalem, where there is enduring [Col. 0136D] life and sustenance, where there is light for the eyes and peace.

Thus, in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, he was taken away from the light of this temporal life. Under Lawrence’s guidance he ascended from the valley of tears and entered into the joy of his Lord: in the year 1036 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fifth indiction, on the Nones of December [5 December], in the fifteenth year both of Conrad’s kingship and of his empire. He underwent death, but his memory lives ever among us. For in this church which he built and chose as his resting-place, buried in a conspicuous and elaborate tomb before the high altar, at the very steps of the sanctuary, he is continually before our eyes and, as though living, admonishes us to commend him by the constant services of our prayers to divine propitiation. And may [Col. 0137A] his bones sprout forth from their place together with the bones of the twelve prophets, as it is written, so that, when the end of the world is completed and the heavenly kingdom shines upon them, the new human being, rising again, may flourish in the angelic light of renewal. Amen.

## Chapter IX

Lord Abbot Everelinus distinguished his tomb with splendid workmanship and decoration, rendering an attentive service of devotion to those holy bones. He caused this epitaph, composed by himself, to be inscribed in golden letters around it, being a pontiff devoted to you, venerable one, from the depths of his heart.

## Epitaph

Flower and glory of the Church, bishop and mirror of wisdom,

Here, Reginard, you lie; in body you are now ashes.

[Col. 0137B] Since you satisfy us with the sweet richness of grain,

May the pastures of heaven be increased a hundredfold for you.

The fifth light of December carries you away from the world’s darkness;

May the sun of righteousness shine upon you in rest. Amen.

Abbot Stephen, according to the Lord’s saying through the prophet, “Behold, I have refined you, but not like silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty” (Isa. 48), lived a poor life after the bishop’s death, like an orphan without a father. For Nizo, who had succeeded his uncle in the episcopate, kept and usurped all the furnishings, including much gold and silver that Reginard had stored up for Saint Lawrence so that it might be spent in acquiring estates for this Church on behalf of his soul. Nizo did not reflect on how many good things his most pious fosterer [Col. 0137C] had done for him—I mean Nizo, a man of uncultivated intelligence and almost ignorant of letters.

Yet Stephen, inclining toward God and sustained by God, completed the monastic buildings and workshops. He had woods cut down all around, which endangered everyone passing through because of the ambushes of robbers; he worked and cultivated newly cleared land; like Noah, from the fruit of his own hands he planted a vineyard. He himself, like a sweet grape from the vineyard of Soreq—that is, “chosen” or [Col. 0138A] “excellent”—was very often pressed in the winepress of tribulations. Wazo, Nizo’s successor as bishop, also afflicted him considerably, wishing to infringe certain rights of the surrounding land, which venerable Reginard had assigned to this Church free from every exaction.

Theoduin succeeded Wazo, a peaceful star of the Church of Liège. He built the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, at Huy with as great labour as devotion. In the thirteenth year of his episcopate the aforesaid Abbot Stephen, the first father of all the monks of this Church, died in a good old age and full of days, like Abraham, father of many nations. After having governed this Church according to the rule for thirty-three years, he received from Christ, in accordance with his name—Stephen, interpreted “the crowned one”—the crown of his happy rule, that is, of righteousness, and of his labours.

He was buried in the crypt of Saint Mary, Mother of God, before the high altar, at the feet of Lord Bishop Wolbodo, with whom, because of his religious devotion and honourable character, he had enjoyed much favour and intimacy. But the most noble Count Herimannus, also called Hezelo, renounced all that belongs to the world, received the monastic habit at Verdun in the church of Saint Vitonus, and, living as a monk in goodness to the end, deserved to be joined to the fellowship of holy monks. He always honoured Saint Lawrence with faithful and singular [Col. 0138C] devotion, and generously endowed him from his treasury, household, and estate. Therefore, through the intercession and prayer of that martyr, may he receive his inheritance in the land of the living. And may our brothers who have happily departed rest in you, O Christ; when the time of resurrection comes, O firstborn of the dead, may they rise through you, live for you, and glory in you for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0137]

# Book of Reiner the Monk concerning the Lightning Strike upon the Church of His Monastery

(D. Bern. Pezius, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV, III, p. 187, from a manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Lawrence at Liège.)

## A Little Work by a Certain Man to an Intimate Friend concerning the Lightning Strike

## Chapter I

[Col. 0137C]

[Col. 0137D] I have written you this mournful little book, O Frederick, because you asked to know how we were lately struck by Him who was struck upon the cross for us; how, I say, [Col. 0138C] the crown of our head fell, cast down by Him [Col. 0138D] who wore the crown of thorns in his Passion, so that our Church may sorrowfully say with Job: “God has stripped me of my glory and taken the crown from my head” [Col. 0139A] (Job 19). Truly, as Jeremiah says: “The breath of our nostrils, Christ the Lord, was taken in our sins” (Lam. 4), because among us the gold of divine fear has been darkened, the finest colour of holy religion changed; and therefore, according to that same prophet, we have felt over us the watchful rod of God’s wrath (Jer. 1).

For in this present year, 1182 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [22 March], on the day following Palm Sunday, the Lord, wonderful on high, thundered over us when lightning fell with a great and dreadful crash. Though it fell outside, on the left side of our tower, it nevertheless entered through the main door of the monastery, striking the doors, and flying and darting to and fro threw everything into confusion with vapour, smoke, and stench, according to Job’s saying: [Col. 0139B] “Sulphur is scattered in our dwelling” (Job 18). Yet it injured no one at all, though very many were inside; indeed, it did not so much as stir the curtains, which, as is customary in Lent, hung before the crucifix in the middle of the church and before the chancel screen, almost concealed above and close to the ground below.

Yet now raising itself over those curtains, now lowering itself beneath them as if seeking whom it might strike, by the judgment of Him who is terrible in His counsels over the children of men, it penetrated as far as the high altar. There it whirled about for some time and, touching or scorching nothing else, tore but did not burn the covering with which the altar itself was covered. It broke the marble seal into seven [Col. 0139C] pieces—the sevenfold Holy Spirit, alas, having been offended by us. Then, returning by the way it had come and flying around the crucifix and the curtain hanging from it, it harmlessly passed out again through the monastery’s main door above the head of a certain little woman standing there and calling upon Saint Lawrence.

## Chapter II

There was also an astonishing occurrence which we embrace as a miracle from God. The cloth with which the aforesaid seal was covered was found unharmed by scorching or tearing, doubtless preserved by the Holy of Holies, who deigned to have His face covered in the tomb with a cloth, and who, when angry, remembers mercy.

We were therefore stunned by no small disturbance, troubled by Him of whom the prophet says: [Col. 0139D] “From the north evil shall be opened upon the earth” (Jer. 1). For from the north a brilliant flash and a whirlwind had thundered, violently hurling hail and fire, which immediately followed from the burst clouds, after a third thunderclap had preceded it.

Thus the three verses of the psalm were made clearer than daylight in their manifestation against us: “Smoke went up in his anger, and fire blazed from his face; burning coals were kindled by him. At the brightness before him, clouds passed away—hail and coals of fire. And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice—hail and coals of fire” (Ps. 21).

Perhaps, like Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, we had offered in our censers—that is, in our minds and bodies—strange fire and incense not sweetly fragrant, [Col. 0140A] which the most chaste Levite and most pure martyr could not bear. In accordance with Saint Job’s saying, he was tested as gold which passes through fire; he offered himself to God as a sweet-smelling offering. Hence we must dread terribly what the Apostle says to the Hebrews: “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10). For there is a fearful expectation of judgment and a jealous fire that will consume those who have trampled the Son of God underfoot, considered unclean the blood of the covenant by which they were sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace by approaching, handling rashly, and receiving indiscriminately the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, and eats and drinks judgment upon himself, [Col. 0140B] not discerning the body of the Lord (1 Cor. 11).

This holy, unique reality of the new and eternal covenant is far more worthy than the worldly holy thing of the old and passing covenant, since the grace of the Gospel through Christ is much greater than the righteousness of the law through Moses. Yet anyone who annulled that law died without any mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. Therefore the same Apostle, rebuking the Corinthians because they did not properly examine themselves, but rather irreverently thrust themselves into such great mysteries, says: “Therefore many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep” (ibid.). For they were wasting away with various illnesses, burning with fevers, and many were dying. Since, therefore, they did not judge themselves so as to strive for amendment, they were judged and chastened by the Lord, of whom the angel says to Moses: “The Lord—his name is Jealous—is a jealous God” (Exod. 34); while Moses says to the people: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 9).

How greatly contempt for what is accursed or for obedience commonly provokes His jealousy may be shown by two examples among innumerable others: Achan was overwhelmed with stones because of the accursed thing, and all that belonged to him was burned with fire; likewise Saul, from whom the purple of kingship was torn away because of disobedience, as the prophet said whose cloak Saul himself had torn: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you; and because you have rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord has rejected you from being king. [Col. 0140D] For obedience is better than sacrifices, and to heed than to offer the fat of rams; because rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15).

The sorrowful foundation of the matter, my brother, requires that I build sorrowful words upon it. Nor do I fear that you will reproach me with that saying of the satirist, “You have more aloes than honey,” when we fear and grieve that these were especially the evils which fed us with the bread of tears and gave us the wormwood of sorrow to drink. But I shall now continue the sequence of my narrative.

## Chapter III

When this sudden storm assailed us, we were to go into the city for the funeral rites of a certain canon. For that reason, earlier that morning [Col. 0141A] we had completed the office of several hours and the morning Mass, through the merciful providence of Him who established all things in measure, weight, and number. Thus the divine mysteries were not being celebrated on that altar at the hour of so great a divine punishment, which could not have occurred without great danger both to the ministers and to the sacraments.

Wretchedly afraid at such a violent shock, I fled into the church that I might be safer there. Then one of the brothers met me, saying that the altar coverings touched by the lightning were burning. I shuddered and trembled; yet quickly stirred by faith in the martyr, I ran there. Neglecting myself—for the vapour and stench, the gloom and terror, had not yet departed from the place—I seized the left-hand altar covering, which I thought was burning, to shake it out. By a force as if from [Col. 0141B] the wind, it had been thrown apart: partly it remained lying over the missal resting upon the altar itself, and partly had fallen onto the pavement. I was astonished that it had remained unburned, when beneath it I found a very fiercely burning spark of fire. I fixed my gaze upon it for a time and observed that it was something of lively and subtle substance; and, with the holy martyr as witness, I feared that it might leap into my face or say something savage to me. When I wished to extinguish it by shaking it out, it suddenly disappeared.

I infer that it was a demon, which by its subtle nature could creep through cracks or crevices and, by some fiery force, either demolish or burn things. For demons are as wandering as they are destructive: as cold in relation to God’s goodness as they are inflamed by their own malice. [Col. 0141C] How can it fail to be clear that we were handed over to the sentence: “He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation, indignation and wrath and tribulation, a sending forth through evil angels” (Ps. 78 [Vulgate 77])?

Finally, I found on the altar an overturned silver pyx, in which the body of the Lord was kept. The force of the heat had consumed the iron chain from which it customarily hung as though it were dry straw, so that we could scarcely find a few links of it. With groaning I took up the pyx. It was firmly locked, but blackened like ink; and it had a small hole, ordinarily present, whose maker at that time we do not know. Rubbing and scraping away the soot with my hands, I opened it and found within three whole hosts, though slightly darkened. [Col. 0141D] I showed them to those standing around, since we were in the utmost alarm that the body of the Lord might have perished.

## Chapter IV

The brothers gathered around the altar in order to extinguish any sparks of fire that might remain. They found the covering torn, as I mentioned above; the seal divided into pieces; and the cloth neither torn nor burned, except that in it, as in the pyx, there appeared a small hole, such as could be made by a needle.

Then, lifting the fragments of the seal with tears and great mourning, we moved the leaden little casket that had been beneath it, containing the relics of the saints, to a safe place behind the altar, where neither more careful attention nor continuous light would be lacking. [Col. 0142A] We do not receive it ungratefully, but honour it with earnest thanksgiving: amid so great a furnace, so to speak, neither the lead was melted, nor the relics consumed, nor the wax dissolved. In that aforesaid casket Lord Bishop Reginard of memorable fame, builder of this church, had with singular devotion placed his wax seal together with the relics.

Do you not perceive, whoever has been granted the spirit of piety, the proclamation-worthy spectacle here of the three children, whose garments, nor even whose hair, the force of the sevenfold flame could not dare to harm? Here too the victorious athlete worked with the finger of God, of whom it may truly be said: “When you pass through fire, the flame shall not harm you, and the smell of fire shall not be upon you” (Dan. 3); since he himself said from the gridiron to those roasting him: “Unhappy men! Do you not recognize that your coals provide me not burning, but refreshment?”

Before this fire—these mournful baths, if I may so call them—he had said in a vision to a certain man kneeling at the feet of his saints and supplicating: “O brother, I am coming again to be roasted.” And since the Lord threatens through the prophet, “I will search Jerusalem with lamps” (Zeph. 1), it should not be regarded as trivial that the same holy Vigil was seen to have walked by night through all the rooms of our monastery and cloister, searching with a lamp; and, angered that certain persons did not walk as children of day and light, to have driven them far away with a threatening rod. It is more lamentable that this happened to certain persons than blameworthy that anyone saw it. What then [Col. 0142C] of this also: that an image of the Lord hanging on the cross was seen, as though alive, to have shed bitter tears? Then it came to the mind of the man who saw it that, seeing Jerusalem, the Lord wept over it. He was struck by such amazement and trembling that, unable to endure the vision, he could scarcely withdraw himself with unsteady step.

But because Ecclesiastes says, “A time to speak, and a time to keep silence” (Eccl. 3), I refrain from mentioning certain visions and offences that foreshadowed so great an evil for us. To suggest to you a certain parallel, my brother—for you are devoted to learned letters—I offer that Virgilian passage:

> Often, had our minds not been perverse,  
> I remember that oaks struck from heaven foretold this evil to us.  
> —Virgil, *Bucolics*, book I, verses 16–17

## Chapter V

[Col. 0142D]

Although, therefore, we have been so enormously brought to shame—“for we have been made a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men” (1 Cor. 4)—we have nevertheless not hung our instruments upon the willows of Babylon. Rather, as it is written: “In tribulation you called upon me and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the tempest” (Ps. 80), we have increased our praises of God for the judgments of his righteousness by various forms of satisfaction. May he accept them for his own sake: he who has passed through the heavens, Jesus Christ the Son of God, who, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and was heard because of his reverence (Heb. 5).

[Col. 0143A] Furthermore, lest our chief sanctuary, that is, the high altar, remain entirely desolate, we have heeded the prophetic oracle: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise; render your vows to the Most High; call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49). And, with episcopal permission, we have until now placed upon the greater altar a lesser altar consecrated by Lord Thewin, venerable bishop of Liège. Since our church was consecrated and dedicated by holy bishops on 3 November—namely Reginard, John of Porto, legate of the Apostolic See, and Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne—it has seemed good to our humility that it should be consecrated anew on that same day, out of reverence and regard for so great a body of Fathers and for the first consecration.

[Col. 0143B] Therefore we lift up our eyes to the mountains, from which help may come to us: to you, O Mary, blessed Virgin of the blessed, from whom, as Daniel writes, was cut without hands the stone which became a great mountain and filled the whole earth; and to you, O Lawrence, mountain of the gridiron, who, the more you were worn away amid torments and melted amid flames, the more you grew until the heavenly gates of Christ, which you deserved to enter brighter than the sun. We also raise our eyes to all you Saints, whom in the Song of Songs the beloved declares to be “mountains of spices” to her beloved, that, through the fragrance of your merits, according to Zechariah’s saying, the Lord may pour out upon this house and its inhabitants the spirit of grace and [Col. 0143C] prayer, so that, according to the same prophet, we may become a blessing, though now we are judged an accursed thing by the world.
