For this scourging of ours has become a stumbling-block to many, as though that wanderer and rover over the earth, Satan, had not struck the righteous Job; as though he had not stood at the right hand of Jesus the high priest to oppose him; and as though the Psalmist had not said: “I was scourged all day long, and my chastisement was in the mornings” (Ps. 72)—with innumerable other things that might be alleged. For Satan attacked us not as much as he wished, but only as much, and in the manner and place, as he was permitted by the judgment of him whose judgments are a great abyss.

## Chapter VI

This was plainly shown to a certain man, who, on the following Good Friday, at the morning hour, after the duties of vigils and prayers, had lain down upon the ground before a certain altar to rest a little. He saw, as it were, above himself in that part of the air where the lightning had fallen, a host of angels of the brightest light opposing a demonic host utterly inflamed for our destruction. But as smoke fails away, it failed away; as wax melts before fire, so that smoking infernal brand melted away before the face of the roasted martyr.

Nor was the smoke which Isaiah saw filling the house of the Lord more dreadful than this smoke, which so enveloped the whole monastery that we ran about lamentably amid the crackling of the blaze which had set it alight. But surely the angel of the face of God—the angel whom the tyrant saw walking in the furnace with the three boys and at whom he marvelled; he, I say, who shook the flame of fire from the furnace—also drove away this conflagration and turned it back upon the demons themselves as upon Chaldeans, whose name is interpreted “fierce.”

Therefore, Lord, it is fitting to remember your mercies and for our saving mouth to speak your praise, above all that you have bestowed upon us according to the multitude of your mercies; for all that you have done to us, you have done in true judgment.

Nor, O Jesus Christ, great priest, priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, should it be passed over as superfluous that someone saw you, in priestly attire, in a heavenly vesture more glorious than Aaron’s, celebrating at the altar—which you now seem to have struck down like the tabernacle [Col. 0144B] of Shiloh—certain mystical sacraments beyond human capacity. The church’s structure had been renewed in a marvellous manner; an aromatic fragrance was diffused; there was a radiance like that of the city which, according to the Apocalypse, “has no need of sun or moon to shine in it, for the glory of God illumines it, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Rev. 21).

Therefore let all the children of light pray to him who illuminates marvellously from the eternal mountains; let the whole Church of the saints implore and obtain that our Church may receive blessing and mercy from Christ the Lord, the supreme and saving high priest. Amen.

## Chapter VII. R. to Frederick, his intimate friend in Christ

[Col. 0144C] The Apostle admonishes us “not to think high things, but to consent to the lowly.” Therefore, since I know you, like David, to be humble in your own eyes, neither puffed up by birth nor learning, and likewise not one to despise a friend’s writings, however simple their author, I have gladly and wholeheartedly undertaken to write for you a little book of tears. The subject-matter itself dictated that I should give it this title. I do not doubt that you will bestow upon this work the same favour and welcome that you usually give my other little writings, although their usefulness is slight. For in accordance with your good character you value even the smallest things highly. Kindness knows how to look favourably even upon mediocre writings by friends; malice knows not how to pardon those of strangers. The envious person turns into a fault whatever has not been sufficiently brought to the polish of correction.

But I have this against you: that you have forsaken your first love. For after you went to Stavelot, after you became a man of Stavelot, you sent me no greeting, no little sheet of writing, as though the Ardennes did not possess rams, sheep, and calves, from whose skins parchment is usually made. And what was so compelling a reason for your seeing Stavelot? Has responsibility for stabling horses there been entrusted to you, so that, detained by it, you have thus far withdrawn the service of letters from a friend? Or perhaps you will plead that there are no wild asses to carry your little books to us? Yet there are many travellers passing by. If you fear robbers, with whom the Ardennes abounds, then send them by persons whose equipment resembles that of the Gibeonites, who by their wretched appearance were able to incline even enemies to mercy. Recall:

> The traveller, empty-handed, will sing before the robber.

[Col. 0146A] But until you reply, you shall receive neither even two copper coins from the Samaritan nor, from us, a hostler’s farewell.

[Col. 0145]

# The Little Book of Reiner the Monk: An Act of Thanksgiving to Blessed Lawrence on the New Dedication of the Church of His Monastery

(D. Bern. Pezius, *ibid.*, col. 197.)

## Chapter I

[Col. 0145B]

After the voice of the great commotion with which the God of majesty thundered over us, as was set forth in the preceding little book, we must now cry out with that voice which holy Ezekiel heard behind him, likewise a voice of great commotion: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place” (Ezek. 3). For you have returned to your place, O Lawrence, from which, banished by our offences, you had been exiled for seven months and thirteen days.

Therefore, as true transgressors of the Decalogue, we have not ceased during this period of your exile to make satisfaction to the offended Trinity, to implore more earnestly the holy sevenfold Spirit, and, as it were, to punish ourselves sevenfold by various modes of repentance. Through your merits, then, avert the possibility that we may hereafter be struck by such a blow; and defend us by your patronage from the seven final plagues written of in the Apocalypse (Rev. 15), “for in them the wrath of God is completed.”

Blessed, therefore, is the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem. For though you had turned away, O gracious patron, you have nevertheless solemnly returned to your former dwelling-place, so that that most illustrious beloved of Christ did not return from exile to his seat with a more solemn spectacle or a brighter triumph, while the choirs of believing peoples proclaimed: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest” (Mark 11).

O light brighter to us than the sun’s lamp: when, on 3 November, the day of the former dedication, a great multitude of people assembled in our church with great devotion for the new dedication, and when, in the presence of monks, clergy, and religious abbots, Lord Rudolph, bishop of Liège, a man of most illustrious nobility, performed the rites of ecclesiastical consecration—with such devout movement, such splendid procession—as though you saw Jesus the [Col. 0146B] great high priest adorned with change of garments and a clean mitre.

## Chapter II

Therefore the altar that had been desolated became an altar consoled; it was renewed by most sacred mysteries and marked and dedicated with water, oil, and chrism, after the pattern of your wounds, O Christ. The little chest in which was contained the manna most sweet to us—that is, the martyr’s relics—was brought back amid the rejoicing of hearts and the devout fragrant offerings of tears. This urn, I say, more precious to us than Moses’ golden vessel, was restored to its former little sanctuary. A marble seal was placed over it, and the stone was secured: now sacred by blessing and anointing no less than the stone upon which Jacob poured oil at Bethel.

Nor do we believe that the holy angels were absent, or gracious Jesus, whom God anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. Leaning upon the ladder of reconciliation, he blessed those standing by from above; he accepted their faith and vows as the fragrant ointment of precious pure nard which the precious penitent woman poured over his head and feet, and by whose wonderful scent the whole house was filled.

Then, in a voice of exultation and thanksgiving, we sang: “This place is terrible; this is the house of God and the gate of heaven, and it shall be called the court of God.” And we offered a sacrifice of praise, an evening-like sacrifice, which, when you, O Lawrence, suffered and were buried at evening, holy priest Justin offered: the bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation. All the Christians present partook of it in tearful communion, mourning over you like doves and murmuring in their hearts.

That excellent psalmist David indeed danced with all his might, struck instruments, and offered holocausts and peace-offerings when he brought the ark of the Lord of hosts [Col. 0147A] into the tabernacle which he had pitched for it, while all Israel resounded with jubilation and trumpet blast. King Solomon likewise, when he magnificently transferred the same ark into the oracle of the Temple, into the Holy of Holies beneath the wings of the cherubim, slaughtered rams and calves. We too, in accordance with the prophet Hosea, rendered “the calves of our lips” and offered up manifold thanksgivings as the fat of rams. “You shall take a ram,” said the Lord to Moses; “when you have slain it, you shall pour its blood around the altar, and, cut up and washed, you shall offer it wholly as a burnt offering upon the altar itself. It is an offering to the Lord, a most sweet fragrance, a victim for God” (Exod. 29).

Whoever, together with the patriarch Isaac, can perceive a good fragrance will perceive that Lawrence, like this ram, gave off fragrance to the divine sense of smell. Indeed, he himself was a ram, exceedingly fattened by a contrite spirit and a contrite heart. Cut up by many torments and washed in the baptism of martyrdom, he was at last offered and sacrificed upon the altar of the gridiron to him with whom is the fountain of life, while a bloody liquid ran from his whole body in drops upon the coals. From it the Lord smelled an odour of sweetness, as from Noah’s sacrifice—Noah being interpreted “rest.”

And Decius, mocking the Saint with mockery and gnashing his teeth against him, said: “Bring an iron bed, and let the obstinate Lawrence rest upon it.” An iron bed in the form of a gridiron, with three bars across it, was brought. Upon it the unconquered champion of the Holy [Col. 0147C] Trinity said: “Look, wretch: you have roasted one side; turn over the other and eat.” The executioner, who made the carcasses of God’s servants food for the birds of heaven and the flesh of saints food for beasts of the earth, was struck by a marvellous fragrance amid the most grievous stench of burning flesh; for what was made life for the faithful became death for him.

Nor could that son of eternal night endure the gleam of the heavenly countenance; confounded and put to flight with his accomplice Valerian, Tiberian fled like one fleeing the light into the hiding-places of the palace. But Lawrence, who, as the Psalmist says, now saw light in your light, who fixed his whole attention upon Isaiah’s saying, “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who await you” (Isa. 64), flourishing with a most beautiful countenance, said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because I have deserved to enter your gates.” Thus he truly rested in that Noah; that is, he fell asleep in the Lord.

## Chapter III

This man, truly not unequal to Stephen in merits, drew that same protomartyr from Jerusalem and Constantinople alike, when fitting occasions called for it, to Rome, that they might rest in one tomb, they whose heart and soul were—indeed are—one (Acts 4). But in what sense and in what words shall I attempt to express this? Here I must use that poetic saying:

> Not if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths  
> could I offer praises worthy of so great a thing.

For Lawrence—O inestimable love of charity!—turned himself onto his side and shared one half of his resting-place, that is, half his tomb, in equal portion with so great a co-heir. It was thus shown that this inheritance was splendid for those to whom the lines had fallen in splendid places through so blessed a companionship.

But, if I may say so, O wondrous wonder! For whereas life is sometimes restored to the dead and health to the sick through the bodies or relics of saints, whoever saw Lawrence’s body so burned immediately fell as though lifeless; and within ten days no one remained alive who was not taken away by death. Why this happened cannot be investigated by human reason, for the Apostle says: “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Rom. 11). The Psalmist also says that his thoughts are exceedingly deep. It is beyond human capacity that the sons of life, whose spirit Christ has already ineffably glorified in heavenly glory, should be seen with eyes of flesh, especially by those unworthy of it. From this one may judge how much reverence and honour are owed to so great a martyr.

Nor ought I myself to conceal my misery. For when I once publicly displayed certain relics of saints entrusted to me, to be seen and handled, I was suddenly seized by such trembling in my limbs that my rashness would have exacted paralysis from me, had not the antidote of repentance promptly come to my aid.

Moreover, what the bride says in the Song of Songs—“My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5)—you too, O Rome, may likewise say: “My beloved ones are white and ruddy.” What lilies are whiter than Stephen and Lawrence? What roses are redder, planted by the perfume-makers? What beds of spices are more fragrant? They are an ointment of marvellous composition, whose maker was the Lord himself; at his command the tabernacle, the ark of the covenant, and all its utensils were anointed; Aaron and his sons were anointed with it. It is the incense which none may use as something alien, because it was the Holy of Holies: among the flowers of paradise there was none sweeter in fragrance, nor any more sacred in holiness.

## Chapter IV

For when the most sacred body of blessed Stephen was discovered, the narrator of its discovery says, “There was a great earthquake, and such sweetness and fragrance of odour came forth from it as no human being had ever been able to perceive, so that we thought ourselves placed amid the delights of paradise.” And through that very fragrance seventy-three sick persons were healed of diverse ailments. Likewise, the writer of Stephen’s translation from Constantinople to the city of Rome says: “When his tomb was opened, such an abundance of wondrous and most sweet fragrance came forth that those present thought that they had already been translated into the heavenly fatherland.”

Nor did that treasure of blessed Lawrence, which came to us by divine providence from the city of Rome in the time of Lord Diewin, bishop of Liège, and Stephen, the first abbot of this church, breathe forth and shine with a lesser grace of fragrance or with a less marvellous greatness of miracles. This matter is also carefully recorded among us; therefore I refrain from recounting again what has already been said, especially since it would be rash to obscure matters clearly set out with a lowly style. Yet, to touch on it briefly: in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1063, thirty-seven years from the day of our monastery’s first dedication, on 12 July, we were enriched by so great a treasure when this pledge, so precious and so desirable, was brought to us and bestowed upon us in the presence of a vast multitude of clergy and people glorifying God and the martyr.

Accordingly, we celebrate this day every year: a sweet and devout memorial, breathing as fragrant to pious minds as a flower of roses in spring days, and like incense fragrant in summer days.

Yet, as it is written in the Prophet, “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they, despising me, have rejected me” (Isa. 1), certain of our elders at one time made for themselves an evil resolve. Deceived by the ancient serpent, they sharpened their tongues like a serpent and said that this celebration was being held needlessly. You might have said that the dragon’s tail had drawn along part of the stars, when they so darkened and drew after themselves even lesser persons shining with a single, simple eye that, when this feast came, they deprived their patron of the honour due in worship and festal service.

Although the sky was then very clear, at evening such a storm arose that, because of the dreadful thunder and lightning, this place was thought about to be swallowed up and overthrown.

[Col. 0149C] Therefore our detractors, crushed and confounded by their stubborn ingratitude and accusing one another of guilt, resumed at the evening synaxis the offices of the feast which they had omitted; and the storm immediately moderated and ceased. Ingratitude is indeed a detestable vice. Christ the Lord himself condemned it in the nine lepers who belonged to the Jewish people, while commending the gratitude of the one who was a Samaritan and gave thanks: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one found to return and give glory to God except this foreigner?” (Luke 17).

Therefore, most gracious martyr, may you kindly receive the devotion of those who so diligently attended upon your relics, who so often embraced the chest into which they had been transferred from the altar, and pressed loving kisses upon it, bathing it in tears—as though they saw and handled the ark of the covenant, which John in the Apocalypse says was seen in the Temple of the Lord when heaven was opened. That you observed and accepted this was shown by light sometimes poured down from above.

Indeed, borne upward from the fire upon blazing stones, you ascended the holy mountain of God, from which that ancient cherub was cast down and lost. To him the Lord spoke through the prophet: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, carbuncle, and emerald” (Ezek. 28). That Lucifer, who rose in the morning, darkened through pride, lost the covering of so great a dignity; but Christ, enlightening you because of humility, placed upon your head a crown of precious stone. As Job states, neither Ethiopian topaz nor the most precious sardonyx or sapphire can equal it in any way. You have been granted a purple more precious than colours dyed by day, by that King of kings who in his Passion was clothed in a scarlet-purple cloak.

## Chapter V

And indeed, you who had said, placed among extinguished stones—that is, unbelievers—“My night has no darkness, but all things shine clearly in light”; you who had struggled through the whole night in flames, while the tyrant said, “This night will turn upon you with torments,” passed at the shining of the morning star into the true day and rest. To you spoke he whom all nations desire; to you spoke Christ, the desire of the eternal hills: “Come, good beloved; come. My angels desire you, because, roasted, you did not deny me; tested, you confessed me.”

For you deigned to show yourself to a certain person purer than refined gold and brighter than every carbuncle, since you shine and burn like a seraph. But it is written in Tobit: “It is good to conceal the secret of a king, but honourable to reveal and confess the works of God” (Tob. 12).

A young man recently related that he had been captured by certain kidnappers, who, coveting his possessions, demanded a heavy sum of money from him. They had exhausted him with chains and hunger for several days and moved him from place to place. At last they shut him up in a rather high tower, binding his feet very tightly in a stock. Thus he lay most wretchedly afflicted and sleepless. Knowing that it was then the vigil of Saint Lawrence’s Passion, he appealed to the martyr with all the concentration of his mind. Suddenly he felt the stock shake and loosen. Its mass was so enormous that it would have sufficed to confine the Minotaur once destined for Daedalus’ labyrinth.

Having drawn out his feet, he went to the tower window and looked around to see whether he could jump down without danger. He distrusted the fall, but trusted the martyr more. Therefore he cast himself down from on high and, supported by the martyr’s power and guided by his direction, though ignorant of the roads, nevertheless arrived safely among us. He recounted what had happened to him. In accordance with the Psalmist, we loudly invoked the name of the Lord “who brings forth prisoners in strength” (Ps. 67). The young man, approaching the high altar, vowed that as long as he lived he would annually pay his offering to the saint in thanksgiving.

Likewise another man, captured by wicked persons and put in fetters, was tormented with injuries unless he gave what was demanded. At length he promised to give it and, when released, left his wife as surety for him. The woman was put in fetters in place of her husband. The feast of Saint Lawrence was at hand. With lamentations and tearful grief, the miserable woman importunately called upon and entreated Saint Lawrence through almost the whole night. Suddenly she marvelled that the shackle had burst apart. Taking courage like a man, she placed it upon her shoulder and escaped with it; she immediately sent it to Saint Lawrence through her husband, who gave thanks to the saint who had loosed her bonds.

A boy also came, bringing the shackle with him, and in the presence of the saint made known, through his father, how he too had been released and rescued from enemies at the martyr’s invocation on his feast. Therefore the people together with us gave praise to God.

## Chapter VI

Thus, from the first dedication of this church to the second dedication, one hundred and fifty-one years are reckoned; and the latter occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182. Finally, on 22 March we were struck by divine chastisement, but in the same year, namely on 3 November, we were healed by divine mercy. We celebrated the joy of this healing—that is, the solemnity of the dedication—for eight days, after the example of Solomon or the Maccabees. And, as it is written, we offered burnt offerings of prayers and saving offerings of praise in spiritual songs and thanksgivings, confessing the Lord as though with diverse musical instruments: “for he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Ps. 135).

Jesus son of Sirach says: “In glorifying the Lord, do as much as you can, yet he will surpass it still; and marvellous is his magnificence. In blessing the Lord, exalt him as much as you can, for he is greater than all praise. When you exalt him, be filled with strength; do not weary yourselves, for you will not attain to him” (Ecclus. 50).

Therefore, since the crown has been restored to our head—that is, since the high altar has had its consecration restored to it—and since we cannot attain to worthy praise and thanksgiving, you, O holy Lawrence, fall down with the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse before him who sits upon the throne, and worship for us him who lives forever and ever. Cast, I say, the crown of your merits before the throne; and, joining to your prayers Stephen, who is wonderfully united to you in heaven as also in the tomb, through the supreme grace of his marvellous love for God, pray with him and obtain for us who serve in this your place that we may worthily say through every age: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” Amen.

## Epilogue

It is also fitting to remember affectionately and commemorate publicly him by whose expenditures above all, and by whose particular care, recovery was made from the necessary calamity which I have described. It would be a pious thing to recall how much our father of the household, our lord Abbot Everelin, struggled like holy Jacob with the angel, and how earnestly he persisted with Christ by prayers, tears, and, if I may say so, the arms of almsgiving. But the sincerity of good works does not require the cosmetics of flattery, since it is written: “The track of one who does good is God’s light” (Ecclus. 50).

Nevertheless, one may without rashness say of him what the prophet Hosea says of the above-mentioned wrestler: “In his strength he went straight toward the angel and prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; he wept and besought him; at Bethel he found him, and there he spoke with us” (Hos. 12). At Bethel, I say—that is, “the house of God”—he found in the house of prayer the angel of great counsel, who indeed says, “My house shall be called a house of prayer.” And there he spoke mercy with us after judgment, so that he might send to the Church of Liège an angel—that is, a bishop. For the priest is the angel of the Lord of hosts, who might restore for us, dried up by the scorching heat of our sins like Jonah’s ivy, the green and flourishing condition of a new dedication.

In this restoration you would have seen Abbot Everelin so diligent as Martha busy with Christ’s abundant ministry. Jesus son of Sirach praises Simon son of Onias, the high priest, because in his life he supported the house, in his days strengthened the Temple, and shone among his people like a rainbow amid clouds of glory. These same things may seriously be applied to our Everelin, since a lamp set upon a lampstand is visible to all who are in God’s house, and the Gospel says: “Every tree is known by its fruit.” Finally, this abbot is the ninth from the first abbot of this Church; and we desire and pray that he may be companion to the nine orders of angels.

[Col. 0151]

# Reiner the Monk’s Brief Account of the Fire of the Church of Saint Lambert of Liège

(*Ibid.*, col. 207.)

[Col. 0151D] § 1. Held by a grave and prolonged illness, I have until now delayed, my brothers, satisfying your wish and request: namely, that I should briefly sketch the malice of Satan, by which he violently attacked and shook us collectively—that is, clergy and people. The treacherous rover and wanderer over the earth, whose instability and roaming are always intent, always active, upon doing harm—he, I say, who struck holy Job so grievously—did not indeed refrain from striking us, when he contrived by the great fire which you saw to reduce our mother, the church of Saint Lambert, [Col. 0153A] almost to nothing.

§ II. In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, on 28 April, the day upon which Saint Lambert’s translation is celebrated, at the first vigil of the ensuing night a fire broke out from the house of a certain canon. It suddenly seized and consumed the neighbouring houses, then the cloister and the cloister workshops. The flames, growing exceedingly strong through demonic agitation, fell upon your monastery, O Saint Lambert; and, although the roofs were most carefully covered with lead, they cast down in a huge conflagration and collapse both towers, the old palace with the Church of the Holy Virgins, and several surrounding dwellings.

[Col. 0153B] Alas! Who could fail to grieve, who could refrain from groaning and tears, at your overthrow, O house of excellent workmanship? O noble and illustrious church, glorious in clergy, institutions, and many distinctions! Behold how you have been struck by divine judgment! Behold, bells of unique resonance and sweetness, falling to the earth, were shattered! The remarkable marble pavement is now judged fit for no use; the crown of noble workmanship that hung in the middle, while hastily and tumultuously lowered—indeed, cast down—was greatly broken apart. A lectionary splendidly made with gold and precious gems was carried out, but the more excellent of those gems were lost.

Why should I mention that the altar of the Holy Trinity and the other altars of saints were demolished and violated by fire? So greatly did Satan then prevail; so greatly did that infernal rogue, that hater of holiness, invade the sanctuary of God. Yet the principal altar, that of the holy Mother of God, remained uninjured. Flame could not profane what so great a patroness wished to preserve. Did she not also wonderfully preserve her parish church? Horrendous fires overflowed on every side, as in the Chaldean furnace into which the tyrant once cast the three boys; yet from that church the flames seemed to flee and grow numb.

§ III. But your house, blessed Peter, remained untouched and unharmed; your basilica, O Apostle, of seemly construction, was burned in the same fire together with the parish church of Saints Clement and Trudo. The cloister also, together with its cloister workshops, was consumed by the devouring fire. Alas for grief! Because of the sins of their inhabitants, God’s holy dwellings are sometimes thus destroyed; because of the offences of the undisciplined, divine sanctuaries are sometimes thus left desolate.

But you, O most compassionate Virgin Mary, mother of merciful compassion, and you glorious patrons Peter and Lambert—you most gracious shepherds, I say—drive every assault of Satan away from your flocks. Pray that your houses, that is, churches dedicated to you, may be restored for the better and protected forever by that Lord, that Holy One, whose house, as the Psalmist says, “is fittingly adorned by holiness unto length of days” (Ps. 92). Amen.

[Col. 0153]

# The Three Books of Tears of Reiner the Monk

(D. Bern. Pezius, *ibid.*, col. 211, from the manuscript of Saint Lawrence, Liège.)

## First Book

### Chapter I

[Col. 0153C]

“The righteous and the wise,” says Ecclesiastes, “and their works are in the hand of God; yet no man knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are reserved uncertain for the future” (Eccles. 9). Therefore, O lover of Christ, you who, after the example of the praiseworthy Magdalene, have so often washed with tears the wounds of the hands, side, and feet of Jesus of Nazareth crucified, wiped them with your hair, and as though from an alabaster vessel have poured over them the fragrant liquid of nard, the outpouring of a contrite spirit: therefore, I say, O lover of Christ, with whom I often have familiar conversation about such matters, “fear and trembling have come upon me, and darkness has covered me” (Ps. [Col. 0154C] 54). For I do not know when or how I shall die, though I know completely that I shall die.

Nor can I remember or speak without tears, great grief, and groaning that certain of our brothers have more than once been suddenly and unexpectedly taken from us by death; and how much the disasters of household members and of strangers alike, whether seen or heard, ought more searchingly to admonish us with fear. It is indeed plausibly written: “Whatever death overtakes the righteous, he shall be at rest” (Wis. 4). Yet to go before the face of the Lord in confession and repentance, to be anointed with holy oil, and to receive the Eucharist is both most devout and most safe.

Who can describe the diseases of soul and body? Wretched man is subject to countless calamities of suffering. All the prosperities of this world that smile upon us are vain and transitory. Better, therefore, as the same Ecclesiastes declares, is “to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting; for there the end of all human beings is remembered, and the living person considers what he shall become” (Eccles. 7). This is a fruitful reflection, for another wise man says: “In all your works remember your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7). For constantly attending to the fact that you are to die, and setting before yourself the matters concerning which you will have to render an account, greatly draws one back from sins.

But because the Lord says in the Gospel, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), and the Apostle says, “It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” [Col. 0155B] (Rom. 9), whatever good we think, speak, or do must be attributed above all to divine grace.

At last, a certain faithful man would often pierce me with the saying of the same Apostle: “We had within ourselves the answer of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead” (2 Cor. 1). He recalled how, on several occasions, while occupied either with prayer or with contemplation, he had suddenly undergone such a stupor of mind and rigidity of his whole body that he believed the agony of death to be upon him. Meanwhile a dreadful abyss pressed upon him, as though the terrors of the Lord were arrayed in battle against him. For the expectation of being snatched away to God’s fearful judgment so unexpectedly and without warning is so terrible that it exceeds the human mind, [Col. 0155C] much less the tongue. On one side stood the accumulation of sins; on the other, accusing malignant spirits; then the examination and sentence of the judge were already before his eyes. Therefore, with inexpressible weeping, he set his tribulation before God, pouring forth that prayer of blessed Job: “Leave me, Lord, that I may weep a little for my sorrow, before I go and do not return, to a land dark and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death and no order, and everlasting horror dwells” (Job 10). And also that of the Psalmist: “Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and am no more” (Ps. 38). Yet even in such distress hope in mercy did not fail him. For after some time [Col. 0155D] his soul seemed again to flow back through all his limbs, though with an unfamiliar shaking and trembling.

But why should I fear to confess what happened to me when one of our brethren was already approaching death? One Sunday, during the vigils of Matins, weighed down by sleep, I wished to rest a little upon my bed. So violently did a troop of demons rush upon me that, trembling, I fled to the church. Yet shortly afterwards I began to rebuke and be ashamed of myself, because I was of such little faith that I had been so frightened by the presence of a phantom power. Therefore, as if to amend my former flight or lack of trust, I returned to my bed, saying, “The Lord is my light and my salvation: whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26), and so forth; and, carefully fortifying myself, I surrounded myself with the sign of the cross.

[Col. 0156A] Sleep had scarcely begun to creep over me when, behold, that implacable cohort attacked with violence far heavier than before. Threatening with deadly weapons and horrifyingly assailing me, it prevailed so greatly that it seemed to lift me from the bed into the air, as though I were being snatched away. Calling aloud upon the name and aid of the Holy Spirit, and shaking myself free of so great a plague, I fled once more, a weak and sleepy combatant seeking refuge at the asylum of the church. Nor did horror fail my wretched and imperfect mind while those ghostly and exceedingly shadowy faces, which I had seen, thrust themselves upon me.

Indeed, on an earlier morning it had happened to me that, while intent on psalmody and leaning against the columns of the cloister, I saw an enormous bear emerge with a great noise from the infirmary. [Col. 0156B] Its appearance was dreadful and exceedingly grim, with flaming eyes. It filled me with no small terror as it passed directly toward me; but I cried aloud the saving name of the Holy Spirit and set before it the sign of the cross. At that sign, as smoke disappears, it failed and vanished. But I quickly left the place, so that by some other meditation I might calm my troubled heart; and I occupied myself with these verses:

> How great the evils are which demonic plagues  
> Work upon me in their frequent warfare, I can scarcely tell.  
> They press upon me with fire, threats, terrors, and scourges;  
> They shake my sleep and tear at it as with a savage claw.  
> How grievous is their force, how dire their power!  
> Who alone can overcome innumerable enemies?  
>
> [Col. 0156C] May the Holy Spirit stand against them and protect the wretched man;  
> May he strengthen his weak senses by his gift of grace.  
> With so great a guardian, all phantoms are nothing.  
> He rightly calms what the troop of sins wickedly disturbs.  
> Blessed is he whom that Spirit’s will and grace love,  
> He who is continually illumined in mind and heart!

## Chapter II

Nevertheless, I recall that two of our brethren were gravely ill. One of them, having lost all appetite for food and drink for almost a week, had also lost the relief of dying, dried up alike by fever and fasting. One night, while he lay sleepless, he suddenly saw a demon of sooty and gloomy, dreadful features standing between [Col. 0156D] his bed and that of the other brother. Both lay opposite one another in the same room. The demon turned his gaze and gestures, as though examining them, alternately toward each. Turning to the one who was awake, he said: “You indeed will now escape; but that other one will presently come with us, since he is about to die.” And so it happened. For immediately the brother grew worse and was carried out of that room itself.

The brother who remained ill heard such cries in the air as the other departed that he thought an innumerable crowd was rushing about and making an uproar. He summoned a boy sleeping before him and said: “Do you hear such loud cries around us?” “Not at all,” the boy replied. But as the same noise repeatedly grew more tumultuous, he kept waking him. The boy went to the window of the cell, [Col. 0157A] looked carefully about, and listened. “Even now,” he said, “I neither hear nor see anything.” Nevertheless, the sick man was distressed by a certain horror and trembling, reflecting upon how many assaults of demons and how many hindrances souls departing from their bodies endure. For when Christ the Lord himself, at the approach of his Passion, said, “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14); and when the blessed Evangelist John, of such wondrous grace and merit, visited by God and invited to God’s banquet, prayed, “Lord, let not the prince of darkness meet me, nor let the foot of pride come upon me” (Ps. 35), “and let not the hand of the stranger touch me”: what are we to think of the great dragon, the ancient serpent, called the Devil and [Col. 0157B] Satan—of what sort he is, and how importunately he comes with his power against others?

Greatly frightened, therefore, and deeply contrite in mind by these things and many others like them, at a certain dawn likewise I gave myself to sleep. Suddenly it seemed to me that I was before the altar of Saint Benedict in our monastery. There I found a man familiar to me, humbly prostrate upon the ground and praying. A few days earlier he had departed this life. Formerly a canon and dean in the suburb of our city, namely at Saint Bartholomew’s, he had left all things and followed Christ, that he might deserve to receive the hundredfold promised by Christ and possess eternal life. He became [Col. 0157C] a monk among us; and how earnestly he devoted himself to divine service—attending vigils, prayers, and the mysteries of the altar—we know, unless some hoopoe, follower of darkness and mire, should wish to reproach an eagle accustomed to the pure air and fixing its bright eyes upon the sun, with filth and blindness.

Indeed, as a disciple of Christ daily bearing his cross, he chastised his body and reduced it to servitude, earnestly subjecting it to disciplines. He rested upon the bare floor, or upon a cheap mat spread beneath him; and, with a stone placed at his head instead of a pillow—a stone clearly representing to us that placed under Jacob’s head at Bethel—he wore continually next to his skin a garment woven of camel hair, as an austere imitator of John the Baptist. He commonly kept fast for three days or for a week; [Col. 0157D] indeed, on one occasion he abstained from every drink throughout the whole of Lent, worthy in such preeminence of frugality to be compared with Moses and Elijah—except that they abstained from food also for the same forty days, foreshadowing by their fast the forty-day fast which Christ would fast. He had entirely banished wine and meat from himself, so that you would have thought him one of the most abstinent sons of Rechab. Whatever sustenance he denied himself, he gave to the needy and sick, either personally or through others, undoubtedly believing that he had done to gracious Jesus what he had done to one of the least of his people.

Finally, we would run to him as though to a pool of Siloam, to wash away by confession the inward filth of our eyes and our muddy deeds, as did the blind man in the Gospel. And, as it is written, “He who receives souls is wise” [Col. 0158A] (Prov. 11), he received us in a fatherly manner; like a discerning Samaritan, he was more able to pour in wine and oil and help sick minds than Hippocrates of old was to help sick bodies.

Through him, therefore, I revealed my way to the Lord, and gave the good farmer everything that needed uprooting: whatever could prick my conscience, burn it, or tear my mind. I diligently attended to that proverb of Solomon: “I passed by the field of the slothful man and by the vineyard of the foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. 24). When he was about to depart, he suffered illness for several days; but, as the breath of heavenly compassion blew upon him, the righteous man was delivered from distress and led forth from the furnace of the labours [Col. 0158B] of this world into the refreshment of eternal rest.

When he appeared to me, therefore, as I have related above, because something phantom-like had troubled me in sleep, I approached him according to custom in order to confess, recalling that saying of blessed Job: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). That is, neither awake nor asleep is he able to be safe or free from the struggles of temptations. The elder then gave absolution and bestowed a blessing, comfortingly offering me these verses:

> Keep your breast chaste, and no phantom will harm you;  
> The flame has no power if its fuel is taken away.

[Col. 0158C] He meant, of course, that just as a fire is quenched if it lacks wood for fuel, so temptation is easily weakened if it lacks the mind’s consent and delight. Then, as I asked with wholly tearful sighs what lot he had received after death, and what Christ’s dreadful tribunal had been like, he said: “I am occupied in penance. For it has been appointed to me that I should visit holy places and commend myself to the patronage of the saints.”

## Chapter III

Wholesome penance, happy purgatory, which no horror or assault of demons makes bitter, but where the hope of everlasting salvation now lightens the one being purified; where neither light is lacking nor, at times, angelic visitation! But exceedingly wretched is the soul that comes into demonic power. For as long as it is delivered over to such dreadful tormentors, it can have hope of no refreshment and no good; rather, it is disturbed day and night by the restless, until, through divine remission, it is subjected to a milder penance and will someday receive the rest of the righteous.

This was also shown to a certain brother who, during the vigils of Matins, stood in a high place, lifted his eyes toward the east, meditated in his heart, and prayed more intently. He heard a great tumult through the air. He fortified himself by invocation of the Holy Spirit and the sign of the holy cross; and, looking, he saw that an innumerable troop of malignant spirits—very black and inflamed—was driving a multitude with threats and intolerable torments. Among them one soul, namely that of a brother recently deceased—alas, [Col. 0159A] how distressed, alas, how sorrowful!—ran to the aforesaid brother, so that it could plainly be understood that it was asking his aid. But when the infernal executioners threatened with a dreadful crashing and noise, it seemed to run across to the nearby chapel of the holy Mother of God, perhaps to find some help there, because while still with us that same brother had shown himself so specially devoted to the Lady.

O how great the distance between heaven and hell! O how vast a chasm is fixed between the children of light and the children of darkness! To see and hear heavenly things is supreme sweetness and refreshment; to see and hear infernal things is supreme bitterness and exhaustion. Therefore the one who saw or heard this trembled horribly, withdrew from the place, and for a long time prayed in fraternal compassion that God’s justice might be made propitious to the brother’s soul.

Accordingly, at one Matins vigil, while he sat apart in the church, through a certain ecstasy of mind he again saw that brother among certain deceased brethren, singing psalms in alternation: “He who dwells in the aid of the Most High shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. 90), [Col. 0159B] and the rest to the end of the psalm. Their mode of penance likewise was to visit the memorial shrines of the saints. And when he asked him how he then fared, he said: “I had been handed over with some others to the most bloody power of demons, who tortured us unspeakably without any interruption. From them the Mother of Mercy rescued me by her patronage and intercession.”

[Col. 0159C] I write these things, certainly, not as trifling or imaginary matters but as serious and true admonitions to compunction and amendment. This is especially so because that same Mother of Mercy deigned personally to appear to the aforementioned brother as he sat upon his bed, worn out by tears and prayers. He was not asleep; but while he kept the bodily eyes closed, the eyes of his soul were opened to him in a wondrous manner. With such reverence as the inner man could extend, he offered that singular angelic greeting to the Lady of angels and men: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women.” When she had received it with the gesture of her most gracious countenance, she indicated that he should look at the one standing there. For there stood her captive—her own captive—oh, [Col. 0159D] if only he were freed!—worn down by the excessive cruelty of captivity. The brother looked at the brother and said: “How now, friend, does it go with you?” Weeping and groaning, he replied: “Alas, alas! How dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God! Into those hands I had fallen because of my damnable sins, unless the compassion and authority of this so great a merciful protectress, this so great a liberator, had freed me.”

Therefore, since neither the understanding nor tongues of angels and men can comprehend or express the grace, dignity, and glory of so great a Virgin and Mother, what tribute of praise can I, the lowest and most inert speck of earthly dust, render? He alone who “measured the waters in his fist and weighed the heavens with his palm,” who “weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers and balanced the mountains in a weight and the hills in scales” [Col. 0160A]—he alone, I say, the weigher of spirits both angelic and human, who distributes and apportions the streams of his graces to individual saints as he wills—fully knows how much from his fullness he measured, weighed, and apportioned to Mary. Yet, opening my mouth and drawing breath, I cry out with all the affections of body and soul: “Alas, how many evils Adam and Eve bound upon us! O how many good things Christ and Mary recovered!”

But now let me return to my wretched self. After the elder whom I saw and with whom I spoke had departed from me, I too was released from sleep; and I found myself bathed in tears and trembling throughout my whole body. [Col. 0160B] My mind’s eye therefore remained in bitterness, and my tears were my bread day and night. For I considered whence and who I was, what I would shortly become, and to whom I must render an account of my wretched life. I recalled the burdens of illnesses and the death-agonies of brethren, very many of whom had died before my very eyes. I added tears to tears, new ones to old—those, that is, which I had most bitterly poured forth at the recent funeral of certain brethren. Grey-headed elders, bright in virtues and mature in understanding; young men flourishing in character—these came back to mind, men through whom, while the vineyard of our Church flourished, the fragrance of good repute spread more widely. While such men stood at their watch, keeping the commandments of the Decalogue [Col. 0160C] and devoting themselves to the six works of mercy; while, I say, they stood every night at the Lord’s watch, cutting away vices both in themselves and in others, and wrestling “against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places,” they are rightly to be compared with those of whom the Song of Songs says: “Behold Solomon’s bed: sixty mighty men surround it, of the mightiest of Israel, all holding swords and most skilled in war. Each man has his sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night” (Song 3). It would indeed have been sweet and pleasing to me to record here the persons and set down the names of each of them. But I refrained, since I hope that they are written in the book of life, by that finger of God [Col. 0160D] by which the tablets of the covenant were written, so that they may be heirs indeed of God and fellow-heirs of Christ.

Next I shall add how grief and tears were at times no slight stimulus to me. For, as blessed Job says: “If I say, ‘My bed will comfort me, and I shall be relieved as I speak with myself upon my couch,’ then thou wilt terrify me through dreams and shake me with horror through visions” (Job 7); so too it happened to me.

## Chapter IV

In a dream I saw myself on a certain island, surrounded by a sea exceedingly violent, dreadful with black and turbulent waters. A very narrow path stretched through its midst toward another land far away, lying to the east and flourishing with every delight. [Col. 0161A] It contained a palace of marvellous and incomparable construction, and of such brightness and blessedness that it displayed the prophetic oracle: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from thee, what thou hast prepared for those who await thee” (Isa. 64). Upon its gate I read an inscription in golden letters: “Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise thee” (Ps. 83). For there the voice of praise-filled exultation and thanksgiving was heard continually. I burned with intense longing to cross there; but I feared the difficult and everywhere narrow course, rising high over the waters, lest, if I rashly attempted it, unsupported and upheld by no righteousness, my step should falter and I should fall and perish in the yawning abyss, so dreadful to behold.

[Col. 0161B] Therefore I wept greatly—indeed, all the more because I saw certain persons crossing not merely with ease but with great confidence. So I fell upon the sand and wept, as I thought, with great weeping. For the soul too has its weeping or mourning, as is familiar among mourners, of whom it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). And the Apostle says: “The Spirit prays for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8), that is, makes us pray. Thus some consolation came as well. Grant it, Jesus Christ, holy Watcher, who neither sleeps nor slumbers, who keeps Israel; grant it, I say, O guardian from the night, that I may attain in reality and effect what I saw through a dream in a riddle: namely, that I may deserve to pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even [Col. 0161C] to the house of God.

For in the vision of the night I saw myself led into our church before the high altar, and sent on pilgrimage by certain persons of the highest authority and reverence, whom I did not dare to oppose in anything. What a laborious pilgrimage! “For narrow is the way that leads to life.” I was commanded to strive toward the house of God. And I went out tearful and exceedingly afraid, since I did not know whether I could arrive; and, if I arrived, whether perhaps the door would be shut against me as against the foolish virgins, and I would be rejected and told: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25).

So I went with downcast face; relieving my labour with psalmody, I repeatedly strengthened myself by the sign [Col. 0161D] of the holy cross. I seemed to have a wallet suspended from my neck, with some kind of provisions inside; and I supported myself on the staff I held. My bare feet were unsteady, for that way was dangerous with thorns and sharp stones, and hemmed in on both sides by grim forests. Alas, how many assaults they made upon me; alas, with how many terrors did bandits leaping from hiding places afflict me! Without doubt they would have carried me off, unless a certain youth of angelic beauty had brought help when I cried upon Christ. At times I felt him accompanying me, yet did not see him, except when necessity demanded it. Light was poured down from above, such as a half-full moon is accustomed to cast upon the blind darkness of night. I had almost failed, a sorrowful and panting traveller, when behold, I saw from afar [Col. 0162A] a marvellous house; I saw a temple such as no human craftsman, but God alone, can build. Falling face down, I worshipped, greeting it and confessing that I was truly a stranger and a sojourner upon the earth.

Then, as I approached, I heard some persons singing most clearly: “This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners,” and so forth (1 Tim. 1)—the sweet and compunctive antiphon. Then, seeing the temple door opened, I entered, though with great trembling, and sat upon a pavement laid with a wondrous variety of stones and gold, so that I noticed what is written: “Thy streets, Jerusalem, shall be paved with pure gold and precious stones” (Tob. 13).

But in what words can I express my mind’s emotion? [Col. 0162B] When I looked upward, I saw “the Desired of all nations”; I saw “the Desire of the everlasting hills.” He whom the bride commends in the Song of Songs, saying, “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5)—he, I say, seemed to hang alive upon the cross, venerable in an ineffable appearance. Thus it was most fittingly said of him: “Who, in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who could save him from death, was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5). Who can equal the whiteness of his innocence? “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” he “did no iniquity, neither was deceit found in his mouth.” And oh, what redness appeared in his hands, side, and feet! When Zechariah foresaw this redness with prophetic eye, pouring out his whole soul and shaken in his inmost heart, he said: “And it shall be said to him, ‘What are these wounds in the midst of thy hands?’ And he shall say, ‘With these I was wounded in the midst of those who loved me’” (Zech. 13).

[Col. 0162C] O desirable Crucified One, O beloved Wounded One: by whom, how, and for how long will this be said to thee? By God the Father, certainly, to whom thou becamest obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; by the holy angels, who desire to gaze upon thee thus; by human beings saved by thy being nailed to the cross. With inestimable affection and unutterable wonder, throughout all ages it shall be said and asked of thee: “What are the wounds in the midst of thy hands?” And thou, truly innocent in hands, shalt answer in words that surpass [Col. 0162D] all understanding: “With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me.” Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, and the rest like them, Lord, loved thee; but their house by descent, not by faith—a sinful nation, a people burdened with iniquity, an evil seed, wicked children—hated thee without cause and thus wounded thee.

In this valley of tears also, how often and in what manner art thou questioned—or wilt thou be questioned—by thy lovers, most worthy Jesus: “What are the wounds in the midst of thy hands?” They recount to thee the martyrdoms of those wounded for thee, and the mortifications of those who crucify their flesh with its vices and desires for thee. In such persons it appears splendidly that “love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell,” since neither the many waters of temptations can extinguish their love for thee nor can the rivers of tribulations overwhelm it.

[Col. 0163A] As I sat, therefore, as I have said, in that house of refuge, behold, there came a choir, flourishing with a marvellous freshness and composed of persons of different sexes and ages, singing in measured voices: “Give praise to our God, all ye his saints, and ye who fear God, small and great, because the Lord our God omnipotent has reigned; let us rejoice and exult and give glory to him.” Having entered, they reclined upon the pavement; and just as one worn out by the excessive sun and labour of a long journey [Col. 0164A] eagerly seeks clear streams of cool water, so they thirstily fixed their gaze upon the face and wounds of the Crucified. For these wounds will be for the saints the sweetest memorials of eternal gratitude and thanksgiving; they will be lamps of fire and also of flames, by which they may burn and blaze with most blessed fire like the seraphim, when face to face they contemplate the peaceful King, the true Solomon, in the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousals and the day of his heart’s joy: the Lord whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

# Second Book

[Col. 0163]

## First Chapter

[Col. 0163B]

Now then, O lover of Christ, perform the duty that you owe: since I have related those matters about which, as a kindly inquirer, you often urged me, you in turn should relate what you have learned from certain persons truly intimate with you.

“You ask,” he said, “for an honourable return; and nothing that may furnish material for edification ought to be withheld from a friend. Nor indeed do we aim at favour, but at compunction; we seek instruments of tears, not arguments for frivolous boasting, especially since only we two speak or write our familiar concerns. For as faces differ, so human opinions differ: what one judges good, another may think evil. Such a person is accustomed to object against matters of this kind with that schoolroom verse:

> Take no heed of dreams; for what the human mind desires  
> While awake, it hopes for and sees the very same thing in dreams.

And with that saying of the Wise Man: “Dreams have caused many to err; those hoping in them have fallen.” So also that rich man marked in the Gospel, because a dream promised him longer years of life, destroyed his old barns and built and enlarged new ones to store his harvests. While he congratulated himself on the amassed quantity and looked forward to feasts and luxury for many years, he was driven into sudden death and lost what he had laid up—betraying himself because he did not know for whom he was gathering it. We do not deny this; but we add also what is written: “The dreams of evildoers are vanity, and your heart suffers phantasies like that of a woman in labour” [Col. 0163D] (Ecclus. 34). Yet we do not conceal what follows: “Unless a visitation has been sent from the Most High” (ibid.). For it is equally utterly vain and foolish to attend to dream-phantasies, whose kinds, forms, and meanings no wise man or interpreter of Pharaoh, no diviner of King Nebuchadnezzar, no magician, no Chaldean—not even Muhammad, prophet and god of the Saracens, though he claimed the angel Gabriel as his mystagogue—could have fully grasped or interpreted. Such is the heap of phantom dreams that it infinitely surpasses the measure of the Jewish *gomer*.

[Col. 0164B] We set such dreams aside. We commend only those visitations sent from the Most High to those “who are troubled in heart and humble in spirit”: those who sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep when they remember Zion; those filled with the confusion of this world’s shifting and passing things, who count adversities and prosperities alike as occasions for weeping and say with the Apostle: “We have here no abiding city, but we seek the one to come” (Heb. 13), where there is a glorious and eternally stable watchtower of happiness. Certainly those are not admitted there of whom a certain wise man writes, reporting them as thinking wrongly and being exceedingly foolish within themselves: “Our life’s time is brief and wearisome, and there will be no refreshment at the end of a human being; nor is there anyone known to have returned from the dead. For we were made from nothing, and after this we shall be as though we had not been. For the time of our life is a passing shadow, and there is no return from our end, because it is sealed and no one returns. Come, therefore, let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us quickly use creation as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of the time pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let no meadow escape our luxury; let none of us be without a share in our luxury. Everywhere let us leave tokens of rejoicing, for this is our portion and this our lot” (Wis. 2).

[Col. 0164C] Alas, what a mentality! What words for men who are to die! And what, indeed, if they were immortal? They know and confess that they will die, yet by pride and despair they make themselves equal to demons. Therefore, as Scripture says, “they descend examined into Hades,” and because they have no wisdom, “they perish through their folly” (Bar. 3). Solomon also speaks of such people: “Give not wine to kings, O Lemuel; give not wine to kings, for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments and alter the case of the children of the poor. Give strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those who are bitter in spirit. Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their sorrow no more” (Prov. 31).

[Col. 0165A] Therefore those crowned with roses of delights, those who wantonly revel in the flower of youth, those who fill themselves with costly wine and perfumes and rejoice in luxuries—these do not deserve your wine, O Lemuel, whose name means “in whom is God.” Such kings—that is, proud persons—are not worthy, O Christ, God and man, of the consolation of thy Spirit and the knowledge of the mysteries of Scripture. For where knowledge has puffed them up and intoxicated them with the cup of empty glory, there is no sobriety for speaking, because charity is lacking for edification. Truly, if such people were to drink, they would forget judgments—that is, they would judge the Scriptures wrongly—and alter the case of the children of the poor; that is, they would interpret them otherwise than is expedient for the salvation of their hearers, whom thou, poor one, hast regenerated for thyself from water and the Holy Spirit. Poor, I say, because thou art meek and humble in heart; moreover, because thou hadst nowhere in this world to lay thy head, though foxes have dens and birds of the air nests.

[Col. 0165B] For this prophetic proclamation also concerns thee: “He shall not cry out nor show partiality, nor shall his voice be heard outside; a bruised reed he shall not break and smoking flax he shall not quench; in truth he shall bring forth judgment; he shall not be sad or troubled” (Isa. 4). To thee, then, O just Lemuel, it belongs to look upon the poor and contrite in spirit, those who tremble at thy words, and to give strong drink to those who mourn and wine to those bitter in spirit. Thus, O key of David, thou mayest open their understanding, that they may understand the Scriptures; and so, drinking of thy Spirit—namely, thy singular and incomparable wine—they may meanwhile be consoled in part, until that which is perfect comes, when thou shalt wipe every tear [Col. 0165C] from their eyes and refresh them with the sweetness of thy vision.

## Chapter II

But now, brother, I shall relate what you asked. A certain poor man was grieving and bitter in spirit; amid the sighs of his prayers and tears of compunction, he frequently invoked the Holy Spirit from the depths of his heart. One evening, when he had composed himself upon his bed to rest, a pious inspiration of that same Paraclete came upon him and, with a sweet drawing, awakened him as he was falling asleep. He persisted in earnest prayers until he fell asleep again.

A second time the divine power, stronger and sweeter than before, stirred him from sleep, as though warning him to watch and pray. This occurred six times. On the seventh occasion the same brother suddenly found himself in our [Col. 0165D] monastery, before the altar of Saint Benedict. Wanting to discover more certainly whether he was there only in spirit or also in body, he touched himself and investigated by feeling; with his right hand he lifted the skin of his left hand and marvelled greatly that, though the monastery doors were shut, his real, tangible body had been brought there. Moreover, he noticed that he was dressed in the garment which he had taken off when he went to bed. He also curiously turned his eyes toward the lamps burning throughout the monastery, observing that some shone brightly and others dimly.

Because he looked toward the west, he saw at the entrance to the choir, beside the altar of Saint Mary Magdalene, someone standing like a monk. [Col. 0166A] He signed his forehead, eyes, and breast with the sign of the holy cross, in case it might perhaps be some phantom. Yet the figure he saw neither yielded place nor shrank from the life-giving sign. Then the brother, trusting in the Holy Spirit, went to him; and, reciting Psalm 66, “May God have mercy upon us and bless us”—for it is written, “Every word of God is a fiery shield for those who hope in him” (Nahum 2)—he stood beside him and looked intently at his face. But since the figure had his face, together with the entire head, pressed down and covered as though by a most grievous weight, he could not see it. He nevertheless asked who he was; the other remained silent. He adjured him by the fearful name of the holy and undivided Trinity. When he continued silent, he adjured him a second, third, and fourth time, but could obtain nothing. Therefore he was greatly astonished [Col. 0166B] and concluded that it was not without some very great cause that, even when so adjured, he could not draw from him the slightest gesture. He perceived that, as I have said, the other was pressed down and constrained from above by some unbearable weight, and perhaps therefore had no power over himself. That saying also came to mind: “My iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed me down” (Ps. 37). His colour was black and as though scorched; and, since no bodily features were evident, he seemed more spirit than body.

But burning with a fervent curiosity to know, the aforesaid brother again imposed a fifth adjuration. Unable now to bear its force, the other, as though very heavily burdened, [Col. 0166C] cast himself upon the floor. The brother too lowered himself and sat nearer, intending to embrace and hold him. When the other perceived this, he put forth something like a hand and placed it beneath the brother’s left hand. But, not wishing to weigh him down, he quickly withdrew it. For it burned like glowing iron. He also raised his head slightly and gave a sigh most sorrowful and heavy. At last the brother understood who he was; he understood the causes of his suffering. And when, through excessive compassion and grief, his soul and all his limbs began to tremble, he found himself again in his bed—how or in what manner he knew not. Nor did what he had seen and understood escape him; but, as though drunk with the wine of compunction, the wine of bitterness and contrition, [Col. 0166D] he continually pondered in his mind with what strictness, with what afflictions after death, are punished souls which have lived carnally in the flesh.

## CHAPTER III

Oh, how much lighter it is to repent here than there! How those burn there who have not here more thoroughly extinguished the burnings of carnal corruptions! Therefore every God-fearing person must ascend with Elijah—whose name means “the Lord is strong”—Mount Carmel, which in Hebrew signifies “soft” or “tender,” so that, bent low both in body and mind with that prophet, he may implore the strong Lord with strong humility to water the parched ground of his breast with the sevenfold rain of the Holy Spirit; softened by it, he may be able to say with blessed Job (ch. 23): “God has softened my heart.” Likewise, after the manner [Col. 0167A] of David, “strong of hand,” let him be made gentle by devout tenderness toward God and neighbour—David who, because of the supreme prerogative of his humble and patient soul, is written to have been like “the most tender worm of the wood” (2 Kings 23).

For the patriarch Jacob too was strong in a like power against God, as it is said of that prophet: “In his strength he directed himself with the Angel, and prevailed over the angel and was strengthened; he wept and besought him” (Hosea 12).

Moreover, friend, I wish you to recall that saying of Solomon: “Remove the rust from the silver, and a most pure vessel will come forth” (Prov. 25). A teachable mind ought not to be darkened by any rust of doubt, so as to waver in any way over those matters recorded in sacred Scripture; rather, it should give faith to venerable deeds and venerate [Col. 0167B] mysteries, even though they cannot be comprehended by human understanding.

For although it is written: “Do not raise your eyes to riches which you cannot possess, because they will make themselves wings like eagles and fly into heaven” (Prov. 23), some inquisitive persons nevertheless are not ashamed to investigate and search out how the Lord’s body, if it was real and tangible, could come forth at birth while his mother’s womb remained closed; rise when the tomb remained closed; and enter the disciples when the doors were closed. But those who search with an immoderate scrutiny fail, not considering that “as one who eats much honey, it is not good for him, so he who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25)—that is, the glory of him for whom no word is impossible. When will they fully grasp his wonders, when those heavenly eagles, those exalted [Col. 0167C] spirits or powers, fixing the un-dazzled eyes of contemplation upon the face of the highest and true Sun, will indeed attend to the height of his countenance and the depth of his mysteries, yet will never wholly and entirely apprehend them, nor be filled with sight or satiety throughout the everlasting ages?

The riches of the Trinity, the Maker, are so great that they cannot be exhausted. As though earthly human beings were sufficient even to comprehend by understanding, or attain by inquiry, the natures of all things produced either on land or in the waters! Yet there is nothing among animate or inanimate things so wonderful that the universal Author has not made it incomprehensibly, infinitely, incomparably—he himself more wonderful still—who, according to the Psalmist, “has done all things whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” [Col. 0167D] (Ps. 113). Whoever attends sincerely to such things, and with a devout heart examines in the Scriptures that are read the true works of God, will confess that it is most easy for the Almighty to have granted this to any body whatsoever: that, while solid and tangible, it might penetrate any things shut and barred. Therefore, what one cannot comprehend, let him believe through the sincerity of faith, and by merit obtain illumination, as that illustrious Chrysostom of the Latins, Pope Gregory, says: “A divine operation, if it is comprehended by reason, is not wonderful; and faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof.”

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0168A]

Indeed, I will not conceal even this from your so benevolent diligence: a certain brother, while attending the matins vigils on the Nativity of the Holy Mother of God, and while that responsory was being sung, “You have been chosen by the Lord above salvation and every beauty,” etc., sensed someone standing close by, of star-like dignity, who put forth a hand and seized his heart, and moreover conversed with him for some time in a wholly friendly touching. So great was the sweetness and force of that honey-sweet contact that the same man, who had been dozing a little, awoke; and he saw that hand, withdrawing itself immediately, to be of solid bodily substance and of a milky whiteness like the purest ivory. Then there came to mind the saying of the bride in the Song of Songs: [Col. 0168B] “My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts trembled at his touch” (Song 5).

How that brother trembled at such a touch cannot be told by one who has not experienced it; it was scarcely bearable even for one who had experienced it. Above all, it is known to God alone how, through un-torn garments and the breast of uninjured flesh, a hand of divine solidity can seize and embrace a human heart.

But no less remarkable was this: the same man, once pondering those sayings about the Lord’s Incarnation—“He who in heaven according to his divinity is in the bosom of the Father, and on earth according to the assumption of his body is in the bosom of his Mother; wholly with the Father and wholly in the Virgin”—pondering them, I say, not in doubt but in wonder, and giving himself to tears [Col. 0168C] over so omnipotent and merciful a marvel, suddenly saw himself before an image of that wondrous Virgin. Carved in stone, it bore in its lap, and seemed to nurse, that Son, God’s and its own, only-begotten and first-born. Beneath it, on the lintel, that is, of the adjoining oratory, was likewise carved the hand of the Lord, which seemed to bless those entering there. On either side were carved two saints with their scrolls: one, namely Jacob, declaring, “This is the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28); the other, namely Ezekiel (ch. 3), “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place.”

As the aforesaid brother stood there, it seemed to him that those images breathed with living and flourishing power in a marvellous way. [Col. 0168D] In reverence for the sevenfold Holy Spirit, he fell down and worshipped seven times; and he likewise repeated seven times to the glorious Mother of God that most splendid utterance of the angelic salutation, “Hail.” Then the Lord’s hand, lowered toward him, seized his heart and held it for some while with an effect truly marvellous and ineffable; though that same hand appeared above to remain whole and entire in the lintel, and nevertheless whole and entire below to hold the brother’s heart. Thus the great Lord satisfied his little one by himself; the God who is truly great and exceedingly praiseworthy taught him by himself, he who “does great and incomprehensible things, and wonders without number.”

Such things, friend, I believe are not deceptive or destructive, since they are suited to edification and rather to divine [Col. 0169A] love, and are constructive for the consolation of a soul that bears mourning and sadness because of its dwelling in this world. For, according to Ecclesiastes (ch. 7): “The heart of the wise is where sadness is; the heart of fools, where joy is.” For what wise person, mindful of the coming examination at Christ’s judgment, does not mourn and grieve, rather than laugh and rejoice? It belongs to fools to rejoice in this valley of tears; they judge laughter to be an error and say to joy, “Why are you vainly deceived?” Rather, as the apostle commands (James 4), let us be wretched, mourning and weeping over our wretchedness; let us turn laughter into mourning and joy into grief. Let us humble ourselves in the sight of the Lord, that on the day of the dead he may raise us by a blessed resurrection, and that the true Isaac may then fill our mouth with laughter and our lips [Col. 0169B] with jubilation.

## CHAPTER V

Indeed, on one occasion he gladdened the soul of a certain servant of his with desired laughter. This man, while he was a deacon, was sometimes urged by his prelates to become a priest. But he persistently maintained that his life and strength made him less fit for it. Since therefore, after David’s example, he was lowly and humble in his own eyes, repeatedly reflecting on the Apostle’s words, “No one takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5), he who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth showed him in some measure his good pleasure concerning this matter. Brother, I can no longer restrain my tears.

For Christ the Lord, of incomparable, of singular [Note: [Col. 0169D] Thus it stands in the autograph.] condescension, [Col. 0169C] appeared in a vision to that least of his servants. He met him in the church in that very cross upon which he appeared to hang alive, the cross itself being marvellously moved and borne forward by a vehement Spirit. The crucified one’s face was gracious and exceedingly gentle; his whole body was like the whitest and purest ivory, thereby indicating that chastity in such beauty is pleasing to him who had commanded through the prophet: “Be purified, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52).

Physicians commend the elephant, the animal from which this kind of bone comes, as exceedingly cold and therefore most chaste. Moreover, it has perpetual enmities with the dragon and serpents, so that it accommodates its nature to the Creator God, of whom it is written: “You shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample down the lion and the dragon” [Col. 0169D] (Ps. 90). Certainly Moses’ rod, the rod of God, changed into a serpent, devoured the serpents of the Egyptian magicians made from rods; and the bronze serpent, set up by Moses as a sign and raised in the wilderness, healed the wounds and bites of fiery serpents, restoring life and health to those who looked at it after being struck.

And indeed this happened to them as a figure of you, O Jesus Christ: you who descended from heaven, sent from the Father’s height, and were seen on earth and conversed with men; made a serpent—that is, a humble man—you who thought thus of yourself: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21); a serpent, yet without the poison of any sin whatever; a bronze serpent, that is, sounding, because you are the Word of God the Father, through whom all things were made; bronze because solid and firm, since your feet are like refined bronze, as in a furnace aflame, and your legs are marble columns founded upon bases of gold. [Col. 0170A] For who is more upright than you, who more glorious, who purer, since there is no iniquity in you? All your thoughts, all your deeds, and all your words are founded upon the most upright and pure bases of the counsels of the holy Trinity.

Therefore, after you ascended the palm-tree of the cross and victoriously took hold of its fruits—surely the fruits of human redemption and salvation—pouring forth blood from your hands and feet, and blood and water from your side, that flaming and turning sword was quenched for those predestined to life through your death, and was commanded to stand still as it guarded the way of the tree of life.
