With the cherubim it had formerly been stationed before paradise; into that paradise you triumphantly brought first your captives, whom at that time you had released “in the blood of your covenant from the pit in which there is no water,” where indeed there is weeping and gnashing of teeth but no pardon.

Finally, you deigned to smile upon the aforesaid brother and—what I say trembling greatly—to give him a kiss, while this same cross of yours bore before him the following title written in golden letters: [Col. 0170C]

> Melchizedek offered bread and wine.  
> Christ, establishing a covenant, annulled the old one.

For you offered, and daily offer for us, yourself to the Father through the Holy Spirit as an odour of sweetness, being yourself both victim and offerer, so that by a singular privilege and sovereign right you might be called by God “a priest according to the order of Melchizedek,” who first instituted so venerable a sacrifice with bread and wine. You therefore have prepared before us a table against those who afflict us: the saving sacraments of your body and blood upon the holy altar, which restrain from us the fiery serpents—that is, the demons, ministers of infernal burning and inciters of vices. And [Col. 0170D] because we who sin always need medicine, we always possess this medicine for sins, which you have established eternally in place of the former sacrifices that were according to Aaron—O Melchizedek whom we must entreat, because you are king of righteousness; O gracious king of Salem, that is, peace—since through the blood of your cross you have made peace with things on earth and things in heaven, being above all uniquely able to have compassion on our infirmities.

# THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0171]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0171A]

Since “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” than the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Acts 4), we ought, O lover of Christ, to embrace it reverently and invoke it in every way. Accordingly, we should esteem the number three more highly, so that we may gladly admit this brother, who has long desired to take part as the third in our mourning and share our tears. For you surely know what is written: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccl. 4); and, “A brother helped by a brother is like a strong city” (Prov. 18). For he is a brother well fitted to support our souls by exhortations and to fortify the stronghold of our hearts with certain devout accounts, as though with engines of war.

[Col. 0171B]

“I am troubled,” he says, “that I know and am able far too little to equal your desire or satisfy your inquiry. For according to the evangelical saying, ‘If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light’ (Luke 11), your intention is toward God, and therefore in dove-like simplicity you seek nothing but memorials of compunction and incentives to tears, by which the inward person is accustomed to be cleansed as it were with nitre.

“Therefore, in the likeness of Achsah sitting on an ass, irrational and brutish impulses must be brought under the yoke. Since her name is interpreted ‘limping’ or ‘made,’ she indicates by her name that we should not limp through vices, but should diligently consider what kind of beings we are and for what purpose we have been made. Therefore, according to the voice of one crying [Col. 0171C] in the wilderness, let us prepare the way of the Lord and make straight his paths to the father Caleb, whose name means ‘the heart of all’—that is, to that Father who has the heart to order all things—sighing that he may give us the upper spring and the lower spring: tears for love of things above and tears for fear of things below.

“Although, brothers, it is sufficiently clear that you are already inhabitants of so blessed a possession, so that I may not inappropriately claim for you what the Lord says through the prophet: ‘My covenant was with Levi, of life and peace, and I gave him fear, and he feared me, and before my name he stood in awe’ (Mal. 2). For you stand in awe not merely because you will die—for that is common to all living beings—but because you are wholly ignorant what lot you will have after death. From your mourning I infer that you too fear God and stand in awe before his name, after the example of righteous Job, who feared God as though waves were swelling above him.

“He will come to judge in a cloud with great power and majesty. Then the powers of heaven also shall be shaken; and, after the state and order of things have first been dreadfully and intolerably changed and shaken, there shall be signs in sun, moon, and stars, and upon earth distress of nations through the bewilderment caused by the roaring of sea and waves; men withering away from fear and expectation of the things coming upon the whole world” [Col. 0171D] (Luke 21). “Then heaven shall depart like a scroll being rolled up, and every mountain and island shall be moved from its place; and the kings of the earth, princes, tribunes, rich, mighty, every slave and free person shall hide themselves in caves and rocks of the mountains, and shall say to the mountains and rocks: ‘Fall upon us and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, because the great day of their wrath has come; and who shall be able to stand?’” (Rev. 6).

Although some teachers interpret these things allegorically, they can also properly be understood historically: such a chaos and such changes of air and land will be to come that all things will seem to have departed from both their places and their natures, while men, stunned by excessive fear and like drunken persons, flee in all directions and wander in search of hiding places.

The prophet Zephaniah likewise intended to depict such a terrible day: “Near [Col. 0172B] is the great day of the Lord, near and exceedingly swift; bitter is the voice of the day of the Lord, there the mighty man shall be afflicted. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and alarm against fortified cities and against lofty corners. And I will afflict men, and they shall walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord” (Zeph. 1).

The Lord’s words in the Gospel according to Matthew agree with this: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days; for then there shall be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor shall be. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days shall be shortened. Immediately [Col. 0172C] after the tribulation of those days, the sun shall be darkened, the moon shall not give her light, the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven shall be shaken. Then the sign of the Son of Man shall appear in heaven. For as lightning comes from the east and shines even to the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be. Then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn, and they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he shall send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they shall gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest parts of heaven to their farthest boundaries” (Matt. 24).

Likewise John in the Apocalypse: “Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him. Yes. Amen” (Rev. 1).

[Col. 0172D]

And indeed, the portents of such unprecedented marvels were prefigured for a certain person in a night vision. For he saw the Son of Man coming to judge the living and the dead, as the Psalmist also says: “God shall come openly; our God shall not be silent; fire shall blaze before him, and around him a mighty tempest” (Ps. 49). The same Psalmist, foreseeing in the spirit how the ungodly would dread his face, flee, and seek to hide themselves, though utterly unable to do so, and with what despair they would waste away, says: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered; let those who hate him flee from before his face. As smoke fails away, so let them fail away; as wax melts before fire, so let sinners perish before the face of God” [Col. 0173A] (Ps. 67).

## CHAPTER II

Furthermore, one of our brothers, who had conducted himself rather negligently, suddenly and unexpectedly departed this life—alas, having experienced what is written in the Apocalypse (ch. 3): “If you do not watch, I will come as a thief, and you will not know at what hour I shall come to you.” He appeared in a vision to a religious man; and when asked how matters stood with him, he replied: “Although I labour under harsh and mournful penance, nothing afflicts me more heavily, nothing terrifies me more bitterly, than remembrance of that sentence pronounced upon the reprobate: ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels’” (Matt. 25). “Therefore I adjure you by that most dreadful Judge: pray earnestly for my [Col. 0173B] miseries, and yourself be watchful; always remember that ‘the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil tidings’” (Ps. 111).

Therefore, friends, let us now hear this evil report, this report so desolate, from the Gospel in such a way that we may not fear it at the judgment. Let us send an embassy to so great a King while he is still far away, while he delays the onset of his coming, and let us ask for terms of peace. For even if a force of ten thousand supports us, it is fearful to engage one who comes against us with twenty thousand—especially God and man, the Lord of hosts, the King of glory—who can readily crush our single force with his double force. For Job says, that man who was simple, upright, God-fearing, and turning away from evil even by God’s own testimony: “Truly I know that a man is not justified in comparison with God. If he wishes to contend with him, he cannot answer him once in a thousand. He is wise in heart and mighty in strength: who has resisted him and had peace?” [Col. 0173C] (Job 9).

Likewise Isaiah, most illustrious of the prophets (ch. 64), says: “We have all become as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses as the cloth of a menstruating woman; we have all fallen as a leaf, and our iniquities like the wind have carried us away.” But if our righteousnesses are such, what then are our unrighteousnesses like?

Therefore, brothers, let us send beforehand hostages of a peaceful embassy: the precious gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Let us offer gold to the King, governing ourselves according to the golden rule of his ordinances; frankincense to God, sacrificing ourselves upon the altar of compunction, because “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise”; and myrrh, by always carrying about in our body the mortification of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus too may be manifested in our bodies.

According to Ecclesiastes (ch. 9), I say, “let our garments be white at all times, and let oil not be lacking from our head,” so that lilies of snow-white chastity may continually adorn us, and the oil of the heavenly olive—that is, the anointing of the Holy Spirit—may enrich the head of the inward person, namely our heart. For thus renewed in the spirit of our mind in the Apostle’s sense, and clothed with the new person, who according to God [Col. 0174A] is created in righteousness and holiness of truth, we shall be worthy to enter, in the wedding garment, the marriage feast of true incorruption which that highest King, holding dominion over heaven and earth, made for his Son. And by eating the flesh and drinking the blood of the paschal Lamb, we shall not fear Egypt’s death-dealing destroyer, but shall be preserved for eternal life by that promise of the Lord: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6).

This is indeed a mystery of marvellous and ineffable efficacy, through which we become gods with God and are incorporated into Christ, as he himself declares: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me shall himself live because of me” [Col. 0174B] (ibid.). Truly this is the one portion, greatly to be desired: whoever worthily partakes of it will without doubt find the coming King peaceable; and, in accordance with the name Levi, there shall be added to those who fear him the blessing written of them: “For you who fear my name, the Sun of righteousness shall arise.”

## CHAPTER III

And for your advancement, brothers, I shall relate to you an occurrence which I learned had once happened to a familiar acquaintance of ours. He was a priest and, as he had the desire, so he also practised the ministry of the sacred altar, devoutly and faithfully repeating that supplication of the Church to God: “Grant us, we beseech you, O Lord, frequently to celebrate these mysteries, because as often as the memorial of this sacrifice is celebrated, the work [Col. 0174C] of our redemption is performed.”

One morning, then, he was performing this work so desirable. During the canon—that is, after he had consecrated the Lord’s body and blood—he suddenly saw before him, with both spiritual and bodily eyes, in a manner that I am wholly unable to convey in words, a boy hanging upon a cross, from whose side blood and water seemed to drip, as though from a wound, into the chalice. But when he came to the Lord’s Prayer, the vision was suddenly changed: he beheld the same boy no longer hanging upon the cross, but seated upon the throne of majesty, according to the apostolic saying: “We see Jesus, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour” (Rom. 2). How those sacraments tasted then to the recipient upon the palate of heart or mouth [Col. 0174D] is beyond me; he knows to whom it was granted thus to taste and see that the Lord is sweet.

But how you receive what is said, and how it tastes to you, is revealed by the tears your eyes shed when you recall that verse: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. 80), and that the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, died and brought forth much fruit. Your desired and chief delight is to be fed with this fat—that is, to be nourished at the holy altar with Christ’s body and blood—and to be satisfied with honey from the rock, that is, to fill the desiring stomach of the soul with the Word of God, as the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” [Col. 0175A] (Ps. 118).

And indeed, through the divine gift you are now such persons as have no need of milk but of solid food, since you dwell about the clearest springs of the holy Scriptures and direct the eyes of a simple and pure mind toward that saying from the Song of Songs (ch. 5): “His eyes are like doves beside streams of waters, washed with milk and sitting beside most abundant streams.” Thus you see more clearly that the rock struck twice by Moses’ rod prefigured Christ: that rock from which waters came forth in greatest abundance, so that the people and the beasts drank. For from the same Christ twice struck—when living, fixed upon the cross, and when already dead, pierced by a soldier’s lance—flowed the sacraments of blood and water [Col. 0175B] and the most abundant streams of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

Yet, as this striking is venerable, so it is now dear to my heart to raise heart and tongue to it, in accordance with the exhortation given to the faithful soul: “Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, in the openings of the rock, in the hollow of the wall” (Song 2). Christ was struck twice, namely by outward suffering as well as inward anguish. For he says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26); and, “He began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark 14); and “his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (Luke 22).

Likewise, this is suggested by what the widow of Zarephath said to Elijah: “Behold, I am gathering two pieces of wood” (3 Kings 17), which undoubtedly symbolized the cross composed of two beams. Since Christ was stretched both in breadth and in length upon them, because he bore fastening in his hands and in his feet, he is rightly said to have been struck twice [Col. 0175C].

Finally, let us also apply the lamp of Gospel truth to the feet of our attention, and it will become clearer that that true Job, that man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness, who truly bore our infirmities and carried our pains, was struck twice: for he was crucified by the tongues of the Jews at the third hour and by the hands of soldiers at the sixth hour. Therefore, corresponding to the four-sided form of the cross, from which the benefits of true and eternal peace with God came to the fourfold world, I have set before you four senses by which he himself granted that I should strike your souls into compunction—he of whom the Father says: “For the crime of my people I struck him” [Col. 0175D] (Isa. 53).

Thereupon, in baptism consecrated in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, that prophetic saying was fulfilled: “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13); and that saying of the Lord: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” “This,” however, “he said of the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (John 7).

## CHAPTER IV

Moreover, since mention of so great a majesty—the Holy Trinity—now suitably occurs, and you have marked the opening of this third book with this name, I shall relate some memorable and devout matters concerning it.

[Col. 0176A]

A certain man held this name in continual remembrance, invoking it so frequently with such affection and tears, and privately performing for it the night and day offices of those who sing psalms, that at times he sensed not only in his heart but even in his mouth a certain divine taste sweeter than a honeycomb. A triumphant name! An invisible power which no adverse thing can resist. For, as it is written: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and shall be exalted. The substance of the rich is the city of his strength, and as a strong wall surrounding him” (Prov. 18). Nor is it less high or less fortified than the tower of David, “which is built with bulwarks; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armour of the mighty” (Song 4). And if we look at the tower of Lebanon that faces Damascus, this likewise is praiseworthy: for it looks down upon the strong man armed, namely the devil,

[Col. 0176B] who, in accordance with the name Damascus, interpreted “a people of blood,” always thirsts for blood—that is, for the death of souls.

Therefore, while that brother devoted himself to whiteness—such is the interpretation you know of Lebanon—and to purity of soul and body, he saw himself in a night’s rest placed in a certain church, whose sanctuary was filled with wonderful light and wonderful fragrance. There the Holy Trinity sat upon a golden throne, shining with gold more than gold itself, even the purest gold; for, because it shines brilliantly, it received that name. While he worshipped it and poured himself wholly into thanksgivings, he suddenly returned to himself, believing that he had seen this rather in an ecstasy of mind than in a dream.

[Col. 0176C]

Nor is it frivolous that the Holy Trinity was seen in this form, since in the Song of Songs (ch. 5) the Church proclaims that the head of Christ—that is, his divinity—is most excellent gold, because this metal is more precious and desirable than all metals.

The same man again saw this great majesty above a certain altar before which he was accustomed to pray often and devoutly, but in a different appearance. For, as is read in Daniel and in the Apocalypse, the antiquity of the divinity was indicated by the whiteness of radiant brightness: the Father’s garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool. In the same appearance the Holy Spirit flourished. Between them the Son hung upon the cross in a marvellous [Col. 0176D] and ineffable manner, both new parent and ancient, for his head and hair also were like white wool and snow.

Falling down before so reverend a majesty, he worshipped and blessed it, repeating three times this expression of thanksgiving: “To you be praise, to you glory, to you thanksgiving, O blessed, blessed, and glorious Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” And he felt himself favoured by the sweetest inspiration of the Holy Spirit. This inspiration, brothers, is sometimes so vehement and strong that, unless the Inspirer himself, who is strongest, sustains the soul into which he breathes, it is dissolved and as though melted away. If he finds a clean breast and a mind practised in compunction, tears, and devout deeds, he is felt to be gentle and sweet, and he bathes it in the grace and light of his love. But if the defilement of some sin [Col. 0177A] or negligence has settled upon it, he shows himself more severe, burning out by a sharper force and heat that which displeases him.

But how the aforesaid brother saw this most adorable majesty a third time I shall now pass over, because our close friend recounted it in a little work entitled *The Boulogne Triumph*. I shall also pass over certain other matters which we know that he recorded here and there in his writings. You seek things unknown; I shall briefly state what I know. Oh, how happy, how blessed is one who by good living has deserved the grace, touch, and sweetness of the Holy Spirit! Whether awake or asleep, he is secure, possessing enlightened senses and the modest restraint of a disciplined mind and tongue. Alas, how unhappy and wretched is one possessed and driven by an evil spirit! To see and hear such a person is exceedingly horrifying, as I once encountered one in whom you would have been horrified by that Virgilian description of a possessed woman: “Her face, her colour, her ordered hair did not remain the same; but her body gasps, her savage heart swells, and she appears greater, speaking with a voice not mortal” [Col. 0177B].

## CHAPTER V
Finally, a certain brother, grievously ill, greatly desired to be released and to be with Christ. He had spent all the time of his health in good religious observance, persevering in prayers and tears so as to deserve this. About the middle of one night he felt, as it were, his spirit departing from his body for the tribunal of the Judge. Nor were demons absent: like vultures, they prepared to swoop down and pursue him as he departed [Col. 0177C]. Terrified by their infernal appearance, he began to be exceedingly distressed, like a little sheep exposed among wolves; when suddenly he found himself again in his body. Thus, having learned by experience how difficult and severe that departure is, he was weighed down more by sorrow than by illness.

But on the evening of the next day, as he lay with his mind fixed upon God, he saw two glorious citizens of heaven standing before him: namely, Saint Paul the Apostle and Saint Nicholas. In their presence and sight such an atmosphere of sweetness and refreshment surrounded him that he seemed to experience something of paradise’s serenity; for the burning fever from which he had been suffering severely was immediately extinguished, and sound health succeeded it. For there is nothing that the merits of the saints cannot accomplish in God.

[Col. 0177D] And truly, according to the Psalmist, “The judgments of God are a great deep” (Ps. 35 [Vulgate]). From the beginning of the world He allowed the human beings of so many generations to remain ignorant of Him and to go to damnation. Very many of them, anticipating this by a blind and utterly misguided contempt for death, voluntarily cut short for themselves a longer span of life by different modes of dying. Thus among the Indians it was held to be the highest philosophy, when old age came, to light pyres into which they might cast themselves and burn.

No less wretched—indeed, more cruel and more inhuman than beasts—were those who impiously slaughtered and feasted upon their own parents while they were still vigorous and their flesh tenderer, as though it were an act of filial devotion to free them from the burden of old age and thus to incorporate them into themselves: plainly bestial and most dreadful murderers. While they recklessly and precipitately counted it strength or virtue to die, imagining that, borne in the little boat of some Charon across the Styx or Acheron, they would inherit the starry dwellings or the Elysian fields, they fell into the fires of Gehenna, to be torn and gnawed not by the Cerberus whom they invented but by Satan whom they did not know; and “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.”

That Horatian line also comes to mind:

> While Empedocles, coldly seeking to be regarded  
> > as an immortal god, leapt into burning Etna.  
> > (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, 464–466.)

It is also related that Leonidas, king of the Spartans, when Xerxes king of the Persians intended to invade Greece, attacked almost countless forces at the narrow pass of Thermopylae with only six hundred men and fell there. Though he could have avoided the enemy, he devoted both himself and his men to death; and before they fought he urged them to refresh themselves: “Excellent comrades,” he said, “eat your lunch as men who will dine among the dead.” Alas, what an exhortation! What contempt for death! How different is the dinner of the dead from that of which it is said: “Blessed are those called to the wedding supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19). Doubtless that magnanimous man did not know this—he who judged it a happy thing to die bravely for his country, a glorious and everlasting badge of courage—and thus, by dying, was to sit with his companions at an unhappy table.

But since it is fruitless to linger over such matters, I proceed to things you would rather hear.

## CHAPTER VI

A certain grave happened to be opened so that a recently dead man might be buried in it. The one who had been buried there before remained with his body almost whole, except that the softer parts of his belly had been consumed by worms. O mournful and tearful spectacle! The bones still held together, the ribs and sinews, the hollow sockets of the eyes, the row of teeth stripped of flesh—all miserably showed to what a man comes, however handsome, however strong, of whatever nobility or dignity.

The brother mentioned above was present. Finding in this much matter for affliction and sorrow, he invoked the Lord’s name more frequently [Col. 0178D], continually pondering what is read in Job:

> “In a dream, in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon men and they sleep in their beds, then He opens the ears of men and instructs them with correction, that He may turn a man away from what he has done and free him from pride; rescuing his soul from corruption and his life from passing into the sword. He also rebukes him with pain upon his bed and makes all his bones waste away. Bread becomes abhorrent to him in his life, and food once desirable to his soul; his flesh wastes away, and the bones that were covered are laid bare. His soul has drawn near to corruption, and his life to deadly things.”  
> (Job 33.)

And likewise that of the Psalmist:

> “In the morning it flourishes and passes away; in the evening it falls, hardens, and withers. For we fail in Your anger and are troubled in Your wrath.”  
> (Ps. 89 [Vulgate].)

Thus wholly occupied in contemplating such things, he laboured in his groaning: “Every night I washed my bed; with my tears I drenched my couch.” And because what a man meditates upon while awake sometimes also appears to him in sleep, he reported that in a vision of the night Job himself was seen by him, both as he had been on the dung-heap and as he afterwards flourished again in health. Clothed with royal splendour and glorious with a diadem, Job sat among friends who consoled and feasted with him, while each gave him one sheep and one gold earring—precious gifts surely fitting for his innocence and obedience.

Yet I shall add this: as the Gospel relates, he saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain, displaying how great and what kind of glory the elect will shine with at the resurrection, when He “will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of His glory” (Phil. 3); when “the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of His people and heals the wound inflicted by His blow” (Isa. 30). He is truly the physician who knows all things and can do all things. In that same majesty of light and beauty the whole Church of the saints will behold Him through the ages—the glory which He had with the Father before the world existed; which, I say, He had when the Father, with the Holy Spirit working through Him and with Him, made the world in six days and rested on the seventh.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0179C]

Indeed, O beloved, the fruit of wisdom is better than gold and precious stone, and its produce than choice silver; for the sober and humble soul, whatever grace it receives from the Father of lights from above, attributes wholly to heavenly beneficence and condescension.

For it is written in the Lamentations of Jeremiah—whose own name accords with the pre-eminent grace of sanctity and prophecy, since in Hebrew it means “the exalted one of the Lord”:

> “It is good to wait silently for the salvation of the Lord. It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself. He shall put his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope.”  
> (Lam. 3.)

Therefore, not for the wise man who is high-minded, but for him who fears God and seeks the solitude and silence of holy meditation—so that, in silence, he may attend more freely to that exceedingly grievous, burdensome, and lamentable yoke and sentence laid upon Adam and his children:

> “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work. In labours you shall eat from it all the days of your life; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the earth. By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”  
> (Gen. 3.)

The Lord’s visitations ordinarily awaken hope in the Lord’s salvation and lift the humble man above himself.

Conversely, Dinah shows how greatly curiosity often harms and how deeply the worldly desire for companionship depresses. Weary of the seclusion of her chaste tent, she went out to see the women of the region; but, badly supplanted, she bore for her father Jacob—indeed, for the good supplanter—a great evil of scandal. In accordance with her name, which means “judgment,” she suffered this judgment of corruption and defloration from Shechem son of Hamor. Their names too signify brutish men burdened with vices: for *Hamor* means “ass,” and *Shechem*, “labour.”

But Wisdom—that is, Christ—preaches abroad, raises her voice in the streets, cries out at the head of the crowds, and speaks her words at the gates of the city, saying:

> “How long, little children, will you love childishness? How long will fools desire things harmful to themselves, and the imprudent hate knowledge? Turn at my rebuke.”  
> (Prov. 1.)

And:

> “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light.”  
> (Matt. 11.)

And indeed, brothers, I think that I have now satisfied you by recounting the little tearful narratives I know. If anything remains, it will be included in that work which your affection has encouraged and urged me to complete, having begun it some time ago. And because this little work in which we now converse takes its beginning from Ecclesiastes, fittingly it will also take its ending from the same book, so that we may hear, not without tears, the saying:

> “Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole man.”  
> (Eccl. 12.)

For every human being was truly created for this, and by this is brought to true being: if he fears God and keeps His commandments. For Proverbs likewise says:

> “Keep the law and the commandment, and they shall be life to your soul and grace to your throat. Then you shall walk confidently in your way, and your foot shall not stumble. If you sleep, you shall not fear; you shall rest, and your sleep shall be sweet.”  
> (Prov. 3.)

Therefore the true Noah, uniquely righteous, restores to eternal things those who fear Him: He who, made drunk with the most potent wine of His Passion, slept the sleep of death upon the cross; who rested in the tomb and lay down in sleep like a lion and like a lioness; who alone could powerfully say, “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again” (John 10). For on the third day He awoke: Christ the Lord, author of life, prince of strength, supreme sweetness, the everlasting and true rest of the saints. Amen.

[Col. 0181]

# TWO BOOKS OF REINER THE MONK, ON THE PROGRESS OF DEATH

(D. Bernhard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV, III, p. 249, from the manuscript codex of St Lawrence at Liège.)

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0181A]

No one who considers in thought—or experiences in miseries—the prison of this present life and the heavy yoke laid upon the children of Adam from the day of their coming out of their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all, can possibly fail to know how greatly bodily death contributes to the salvation of souls. Such persons groan with the Apostle as he says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7.) They find tribulation and pain, and likewise say in a contrite spirit with the Psalmist: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion” (Ps. 136 [Vulgate]).

For Adam the transgressor ceased to contemplate and possess the highest good when, wickedly examining the fruit of the forbidden tree, he attached himself to the highest evil, so that at the woman’s urging he might importunately eat from it. Yet the Apostle says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression” (1 Tim. 2). Adam therefore sinned knowingly. Not content with the delights of paradise, he undertook to seek higher things by robbery, refusing obedience because he aspired to be made equal to God.

But because “when he was in honour he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48 [Vulgate]), deprived of God’s likeness and drawn and enticed by fleshly desire and now unbridled irrational impulses, he fell. For, according to the saying of the Apostle James, “Desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, brings forth death” (Jas. 1).

And alas, how bitter for the human race has that bite of the slaves of sin become! This may especially be seen in the dying. Wretched man that I am, I confess that, as I often sat beside the beds of very many persons, I sorrowed bitterly and was greatly troubled by their pains, distresses, and sweats, since I too must die and feared like things. To pass over many cases: I saw one of our brothers so oppressed by pains for nearly forty days that he took no food at all, except that he sometimes asked for water to be given him, more by a sign than by speech.

Indeed, Eve prepared such a banquet for us and mixed such wormwood for us, when, wandering with her feet and eyes, she walked freely through that place of delight and, passing beyond the bounds of radiant loveliness, looked out with unchecked curiosity to see what kind of world there was outside.

[Col. 0182A] Thereupon that ruined adversary Satan, having found an opportunity to oppose her, entered the serpent—which was “more cunning than all the animals of the earth which the Lord God had made”—and, seeking to capture sweetness by honeyed words, insinuated himself nearer the enclosure. For it is absurd to believe that he was in paradise and spoke there with the woman, especially since the serpent had been possessed by the devil, who had certainly already been expelled from the kingdom of God and its holy dwelling-places by an irrevocable punishment for pride.

But if serpents crawled there, why should lions, wolves, or other animals not also have been admitted? Why should she-goats with shaggy beards or he-goats not have wounded the fragrant shrubs with their bites, leapt through the flower-bearing fields, and caused owls and Sirens to answer one another, troubling the angelic melody as in a temple of pleasure? Far be it that digging moles should undermine and excavate that land of the living, or bats fly about there, when perpetual day there never darkens into evening.

That inviolate and special dwelling received none of such things. It was a unique gift of God bestowed upon human beings alone; nor could the evil beast—the treacherous Behemoth—have had any power whatsoever to pass through it. Rather, he himself who had said, “I shall ascend into heaven; I shall exalt my throne above the stars of God; I shall sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High; and I am God, and I sat upon the throne of God,” and had made his heart like the heart of God (Isa. 14)—he, now wholly animal according to his name, for *Behemoth* means “animal,” is cast down to the lowest depths and descends into an irrational creeping thing. He besieges the heart and tongue of the wandering serpent, through whose mouth, now wholly irrational, he speaks—or rather hisses—these apparently rational words to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat of every tree of paradise?” (Gen. 3).

How he lies! How that crafty rogue dissimulates and distorts the words of God! Of him it has been most truly said that he “was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him; and when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8)—that is, the father of falsehood. For God had granted Adam all the trees of paradise, with one alone excepted. The woman herself indeed confesses: “We eat of the fruit of the trees which are in paradise; but concerning the tree which is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat of it and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die” (Gen. 3; the source prints “Gen. V”).

O woman, now already of a subverted and reckless mind! For she violated by falsehood the truth of the divine decree, daring to add what God had not added at all: “and not to touch it.” Finally, what had been established with the gravest threat and most certain wording—“On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death”—she accounted very slight and, as though uncertain, thus added: “lest perhaps we die.”

[Col. 0183B] How mournful and lamentable is that “perhaps”! To what great and dreadful result it came must be conceived more by grief than by speech, more by groaning than by composition. Without doubt, he who was now speaking outwardly through the serpent had already inwardly assailed the minds of the dwellers in paradise, and found them headlong and inclined to agree with him. Thus also blessed Pope Gregory says: “Unless they had first swelled inwardly through pride, they would not so easily have yielded when tempted outwardly.”

Accordingly, that detestable presumer, contriving to be believed and regarded as truthful and benevolent while God was regarded as a liar and envious, again said to the woman: “You shall not die the death. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER II

Thus Leviathan, whose name means “their addition,” thus that poisonous serpent led those miserably infected to death and drew them to destruction. While he promises divinity, he adds disaster in accordance with Eve’s name; he adds infinite woe. She should more properly be called death than life, and more truly the mother of all the dying than of the living. For through her every Adam dies miserably unless he is made alive through Christ.

So the woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance; “and she took of its fruit and ate, and gave to her husband, who ate; and the eyes of both were opened” (ibid.). Before the serpent’s conversation the woman had certainly seen the tree but had not violated the command. Now, however, she is marked as having looked and gazed curiously precisely so that she might experience its conspicuous character for herself and judge by her own taste which was truer, God or the serpent, since they had presented contrary and opposing claims.

For, though endowed with reason, she did not fail to know that the serpent, like the other animals, was irrational and could obtain articulated words of speech only through an alien spirit. Yet, as though led in an animal manner by a divine oracle, she believed omnipotent the one who addressed her through such a marvel, who cared for her and wished to give her counsel. Therefore she assented, stretched out her hands to plunder, rashly plucked the apple, satisfied her deadly appetite, and, moreover, through womanly importunity, shameless and insolent insistence, drove the man also to this act. For wretched Adam obeyed the wretched woman; he submitted his manly mind to be softened, unwilling, in a most foolish compassion, to abandon his partner or to be separated from her.

Therefore he transgressed unto his own death and ours. Alas, alas, alas! Disobedient to true life—that is, to the Holy Trinity. For Augustine, the most august of teachers, says in the book entitled *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*:

> “After the deceived woman had eaten from the prohibited tree and gave Adam some to eat with her, he did not wish to grieve her. He believed that she would waste away without his comfort if she were alienated from his affection, and that she would altogether perish through that discord. He did this not because he had been overcome by fleshly lust—which he had not yet experienced in the law of his members resisting the law of his mind—but through a certain friendly goodwill, by which God is often offended lest a man become an enemy from a friend. Therefore in another way he too was deceived; but I do not think he could in any way have been deceived by that serpent’s fraud by which the woman was deceived. The Apostle called that specifically deception by which what was urged, though false, was thought true: namely, that God had prohibited them from touching that tree because He knew that, if they touched it, they would become like gods, as though He who had made them human begrudged them divinity. But even if, because of some exaltation of mind which could not be hidden from God, the searcher of inward things, a desire to make an experiment tempted the man when he saw that the woman had not died after receiving that food, I nevertheless do not think that, if he had a spiritual mind, he could in any way have believed that the Lord had prohibited them from the food of that tree out of envy.”  

## CHAPTER III

When you were at Liège, O William, we often studied this and other opinions of the doctors. In diligent investigation and fraternal debate we sprinkled one another, as it were, with the little flowers of fragrant questions. Nor, though a scholar, did you disdain to learn from me—ignorant though I was—what I thought. Even when absent, you regularly pressed me with letters [Col. 0184D]; you considered me sleepy and lazy if I did not reply at once. You welcomed your friend’s little ability so kindly that you blamed nothing, however hurriedly my style might have written or however crudely it might have lapsed into barbarism.

I therefore devoted myself wholly to your goodwill and tasted of it; and in return I drew profit from you, since you were richly adorned with the philosophy of divine and human things, and your manner of life made knowledge bloom. Though young in years, you fashioned yourself an old man in morals. For, as a certain elder says, “The gray hairs of a man are understanding, and a spotless life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4).

Indeed, you said to wisdom, “You are my sister,” and called prudence your friend, since you so diligently avoided the companionship of little women—a shrewd kind indeed, and effective at seducing—and carefully attended to Solomon’s saying: “A woman captures a man’s precious soul” (Prov. 6). Although, as it is written: “Grace upon grace is a holy and modest woman; and as the rising sun in the heights of God, so is the beauty of a good woman for an ornament” (Ecclus. 26). Nevertheless, like a prudent and cautious creature, you avoided the pit and restrained yourself with the bridle of chastity. You did not despise the female sex; rather, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11), you feared guilt and vice, because “from woman sin had its beginning, and through her we all die.”

Nor could we speak without sobs and a certain groaning of the heart about the fall of that friend of ours whom you knew. While he lived in community with us, he zealously honoured by a religious and celibate life the habit of holy religion which he wore. But he was assigned charge of a certain cell in the wilderness, where that eremite, far from idle, still pursued the duties of good discipline to which he had been accustomed.

Later, however, trusting in his own maturity and failing to consider that the devil himself tempted even the Son of God in the wilderness, he rashly gathered frivolous women and more rashly wished them to dwell with him. Worldly dances were performed in the place of penance; the enticements of songs rang out, so that even the wild beasts themselves, I suppose, fled in astonishment as the unfamiliar echo resounded through the woods.

But can a man hide fire in his bosom without his clothes burning? Or walk upon coals without the soles of his feet being burned? Nor is it safe to dispense with vigilance, however advanced one may be in years. For disordered heat can creep even into limbs cold and decayed with old age. The careless and sleeping person lies open to snares. Therefore the hostile rival of virtues must always be watched for. Indeed, the more remote the place, the more convenient it is for fools to sin there.

Accordingly, things took place there in church, in sacred places, and in dwellings which ought far more to be mourned than written. In a spiritual man, my brother, the spirit indeed is ready; but the flesh, since it is weak, immediately grows wanton and moves if the mind relaxes even a little. A certain chattering law implanted in the members rebukes the law of the mind. Truly “the people are grass.” How unstable, how weak is man! Even Samson, strongest in pre-eminence, an unconquered hero against a thousand cohorts of enemies, was conquered by the charms of a seducing prostitute and driven to death by ruinous love. He learned bitterly by experience that “the lips of a prostitute are indeed a dripping honeycomb and her throat shines with oil, but her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword; her feet descend to death, and her steps penetrate to hell. For she has cast down many wounded men, and all the strongest have been slain by her.”

## CHAPTER IV

But who could fully recount, throughout all nations, the incentives to how many evils women have been? Let it suffice to insert this one point: about the time of that same Samson, on account of the infamous abduction of a single young woman, 38,200 men, and also sixteen hundred thousand, were killed in the ten-year war of Greeks and Trojans, as Dares the Phrygian, who was present, wrote. Clearly, for what great virtue and glory, for what great privilege of courage, were the powers of Europe and Asia then so shattered! So many mighty men of old, famous men, perished!

Do you not recall, charioteer of the schools, that poetic saying:

> Whatever madness kings commit, the Achaeans pay the penalty;  
> > through sedition, treachery, crime, lust, and anger,  
> > men sin within the walls of Troy and outside them.  
> > (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.14–16.)

“But Sheol has enlarged his appetite and opened his mouth without any limit; and his mighty men, his people, and his lofty and glorious men have descended to him.” “Woe to the world because of scandals!” (Matt. 18.) There is no harbour here of perfect peace. The little boat of human life is always tossed about by the waves of temptations. At times the force of a storm moves even a rock from its place; and the onslaught of temptation moves even the righteous from the state of righteousness.

David, the most excellent psalmist of the Holy Spirit, upon whom the oil of spiritual grace was poured forth from a full horn—of whom God said, “I have found David son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will do all my wills” (Acts 13)—was himself driven and overthrown through Uriah’s wife and fell; yet the Lord received him when he repented.

Solomon, of whom it is written, “The Lord loved him, and sent word through the hand of Nathan the prophet; and he called his name Jedidiah, that is, beloved of the Lord” (2 Sam. 12), was wiser than all human beings, so that the breadth of his heart was compared with the sand on the shore of the sea. To him God said: “Behold, I have done according to your words and given you a wise and understanding heart, so that none before you has been like you, nor shall any arise after you” (1 Kgs. 3). That man, I say, who is proclaimed wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman [the Vulgate: *Emal*], and Calcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol (1 Kgs. 4), so horribly and without precedent made himself foolish through the loves of little women that he became an idolater and built shrines for the idols of the nations. Yet his praise rises so high that he is said to surpass the greatest patriarchs.

For *Ethan* means “most hard”; *Ezrahite*, “eastern.” He is Abraham, a man most resolute in spirit, because of his firm faith and steadfast righteousness, illustrious in lineage and mighty in strength, since in one military expedition he defeated four kings and was born in the eastern land of Chaldea.

*Heman* means “faithful”; and he is Moses the lawgiver, concerning whom the Lord said, speaking to Aaron and Miriam: “If there is among you a prophet of the Lord, I shall appear to him in a vision or speak to him in a dream. But not such is my servant Moses, who is most faithful in all my house; mouth to mouth I speak with him, openly, and not by riddles and figures does he see the Lord” (Num. 12).

*Calcol* means “governing”; and he is Joseph, the increasing son: “an increasing son,” who, after God had turned Jacob’s shoulder away from burdens and after his hands had served at the basket, increased so greatly that because of his supreme skill in prudence and government he was called by the Egyptians “saviour of the world”—clearly wise and understanding, possessing the reins of government because of his innocence and his distinction in chastity.

*Darda* means “generation of knowledge”; *Mahol*, “indulgence.” We understand the generation to mean the patriarchs and prophets, namely the sons of Jacob, a man especially indulgent; and Solomon is set above all these in wisdom.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, William, since, according to the saying of the Apostle Peter, “our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5), every chaste and sober person must take great care to avoid the scandals, gatherings, whisperings, and deceits of little women which violate purity and chastity. The number of those whose condition has been shaken or overthrown by them is indeed excessive, since even the great multitude of monks—“strike yourself upon the breast and beat yourself,” O tearful man, after the example of the evangelical Publican—has agreed to this practice. No writings or examples can obtain that brothers should not be more liberally generous to sisters, and sisters to brothers, than is right.

Moreover, I remember one who was splendidly regarded and highly esteemed among laypeople, yet who in our own age fell more than secularly. Under the pretext of sanctity, which he feigned, he was constantly visited; very many things were given to him in abundance, as he imitated those to whom the Lord said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour the houses of widows while making long prayers. Therefore you shall receive a greater judgment” (Matt. 23).

He sometimes used to leave his cell secretly, especially on feast days. Since he lived alone upon a mountain, he hid in any hollowed-out place, pretending that he was burdened by disturbance and that contemplation or prayer was hindered. But death entered through his windows, because he leaned too much toward a young woman serving him and therefore attaching herself to him with greater licence. He did not restrain her wantonness from his mouth, ears, or eyes, nor from the window of his cell—blind and foolish though he should have seen and known that his soul’s peril was at stake.

Therefore, ensnared and entangled in the cords of sins, he became both a violator of chastity and a deserter of his profession. With that concubine of his—or rather, himself a night-owl, fleeing the day by night—he fled from his enclosure, laden with the money he had amassed.

You yourself also knew, most valiant man, certain religious people who forcefully exposed the smallest faults of others but wanted to cast a shadow over their own great faults, as though with a double cloak of goat-hair or a sackcloth mantle. They were men of strength who brandished against those subject to them, like Hercules’ club, that saying of Solomon: “He who neglects small things shall fall little by little” (Ecclus. 19), as though Christ had not said of such people: “Blind guides, straining out a gnat but swallowing a camel” (Matt. 23). And elsewhere: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of all uncleanness. So you too outwardly indeed appear righteous to people, but inwardly are full of hypocrisy and iniquity” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER VI

That ancient enemy, who suffered a great fall with his followers, does not only openly make assaults like a lion. Since he is also the serpent who deceived Eve, since he is the great Dragon who poisons the world, he secretly watches for the ruin even of good persons and applies every art of harm, pressing both the wakeful and the sleeping with countless devices of fantasies.

Once, as a brother and I were discussing such matters together and turning over a book of the deeds of the saints, we came upon an account stating that there were two brothers, Victorinus and Severinus, natives of the province of Picenum. In the flower of youth, after the death of both their parents, they sold all the property left to them and distributed it to the poor, so that, like the apostles, by leaving everything they might be rewarded with the apostolic reward.

They therefore built themselves a cell in a remote place, where they lived together. Nothing was their own, yet nothing necessary was lacking them. One served the other, and they built one another up by their virtues. Never separated, they trained themselves through mutual guardianship, so that this could rightly be said of them: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132 [Vulgate]).

But Victorinus, striving for higher things and considering that to enjoy even brotherly cohabitation, comfort, and fellowship was a descent rather than an ascent in perfection, judged solitary life more valuable. Although Ecclesiastes says, “Two together are better than one; for they have the benefit of their companionship. If one falls, he shall be supported by the other” (Eccl. 4), he left his brother and withdrew to the wilderness.

A river flowed past a cliff of steep height; there the cliff enclosed a very narrow cave. He rejoiced to possess without payment the walls which creative nature had constructed. They were such that he could take rest in sleep only sitting, not lying down. If he admitted a guest, the host had to stand. A little door, secured by woven wicker, guarded the entrance. He diligently practised the duties of vigils, prayers, fasts, and sacred readings. But he who had begrudged Adam and Eve paradise also begrudged Victorinus this palace of such strenuous discipline. That prowler over the earth laid snares, went about, and devised a deception by which he might deprive this stranger—his adversary—of heaven.

He who is accustomed to transform himself into an angel of light transformed himself into a girl; and, as if feeling her way, striking against the doors, she knocked at the hermit’s dwelling. She complained of the dark night, raised lamentations, and feigned tears, saying that she had lost her way amid the trackless paths of thorn-bushes, that she feared the teeth of wild beasts, and that she sought lodging for one night only. [Col. 0189A] The man pitied the wretched woman and feared to incur guilt should he refuse a guest hospitality; for he could not believe her to be an enemy, but a guest. He therefore opened the door and received her.

Not even an hour had passed when she who was thought to be a girl, while the tempter meanwhile kept moving about with continual motion, devising shameless schemes (for demons are wholly incapable of rest, as Isaiah testifies: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” [Isa. LVII]), brushed the man—whom he had already disturbed with impious thoughts—with her outstretched foot. Poisoning him like a stinging scorpion, she kindled in him a warmth hitherto unknown, especially since her face blossomed with a most carefully composed beauty and her sparkling eyes glimmered even in the darkness. Then seductive, soft speech drew him into contamination. Who can trust in himself? [Col. 0189B] Holy Spirit, how unlike your heat is such heat! How can the harmful fire in anyone’s body be extinguished except by your dew? Yours alone is the gift of continence and the safeguard of purity.

But Victorinus was overcome; and before he was humbled, he sinned, because he had to be taught through himself not to think more highly than he ought to think, but to think soberly. For the ancient seducer himself, a fallen apostate, mocked at his downfall, pouring out upon him these bursts of laughter:

> “What now, most exemplary hermit, to whom even the companionship of a brother was burdensome? Behold, you have entered into fellowship with another, and among the cliffs of the forest you have lost the chastity which you preserved amid the winding paths of the world. Did you imagine modesty impregnable even among solitaries? Caution is needed everywhere—both in the world and in the desert. Holiness can be tempted. This I always assail; sometimes I overcome it.”

Then, like foul smoke, he vanished from the embrace.

## CHAPTER VII

But the Lord, who has mercy upon all and hates none of the things that he has made, who overlooks human sins for the sake of repentance and spares men because he does not will the death of the sinner but that he should be converted and live, had mercy upon Victorinus and turned him to repentance that he might live. For, returning to himself after the temptation, he delayed no longer, went back to his brother, and, although shame’s blush had long suspended his voice, at last made known to him his lamentable deed. Thinking as a Christian and hoping as a Catholic, he relied upon the words: “With [Col. 0189D] the Lord is mercy, and with him is abundant redemption” (Ps. 129); and: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11). He appointed himself judge and avenger of himself, that he might condemn himself by so severe a sentence.

He split a tree and inserted his hand; then he shut the cleft so firmly with wedges that he could neither withdraw nor move it at all—imprisoning his whole body by the imprisonment of one member.

Severinus reported both his brother’s offence and the harshness of his punishment to the bishop of that diocese. The bishop came, wishing to release Victorinus from the fastening and bring the measure of his penance into moderation. But Victorinus would by no means consent, strengthened by the apostolic oracle: “We know that, if our earthly house of this dwelling [Col. 0190A] be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in heaven” (2 Cor. 5). Nor did the bishop judge that he should be troubled further—for he was episcopal both in life and learning—but blessed the good end of his endurance and departed.

Thus Victorinus presented his body as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God, his rational service, by praying, keeping vigil, and fasting. For on every other day he abstained entirely; only on the Lord’s Day did he take a little bread and water, even then compelled by his brother, who, with an affection truly worthy of praise in a brother, did penance with the penitent, receiving no food or drink other than what his brother received.

Compare, William, the meals of John the Baptist and of these men. The desert was John’s cook, preparing locusts in the sun [Col. 0190B], which he ate with wild honey. Would you doubt that these penitents were more delicate, who with the Psalmist ate ashes as bread and mingled their drink with weeping? Compare with some of our abstinent men and lawyers those who, like John, were arrayed in soft purple of camel’s hair and girded with leather belts about their loins. A decalogue of ten courses would scarcely suffice for them, and ten changes of clothing—the blessing which Naaman the Syrian offered to the prophet Elisha.

## CHAPTER VIII

My friend, how quickly is committed that for which one must repent long! In a moment a wound is inflicted which must long be healed. For one abuse arising from diabolical stealth [Col. 0190C], Victorinus afflicted himself so greatly! Nor can so arduous a kind of penance easily be described, if one considers the inconveniences and necessities endured by a man fixed in this manner.

Let those who sin in many ways, confess lukewarmly, and repent feebly take notice of this: those who, while they complain that confessors pour upon them oil and wine without proper discernment, yet imagine that by some trifling penance they can be freed from any sin more swiftly than Samson broke cords or bonds. Nor indeed do they cease to sin; but they repeat, even to nausea, what must be repented of—not venial sins, indeed, but criminal ones—although it is written: “Cursed is he who sins in hope.” They abuse God’s patience, rashly appropriating the saying, “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, long-suffering [Col. 0190D] and greatly merciful” (Ps. 103), as though it were not also said elsewhere: “I have kept silence; I have always been silent; I have been patient. Shall I speak like a woman in labour?” (Isa. 42).

You have read of a priest from the district of Abricantum, who, given over to fleshly desire, lived abominably and, like the sons of Eli, sons of Belial, showed by his incontinence that he knew neither divine matters nor a priest’s duty toward the people. Through him, therefore, men spoke disparagingly of the sacrifice of the Lord; for where a man’s conduct is shameful, it follows that his ministry is condemned by the people. Yet he was sometimes contrite. But because he had no firm roots of compunction, he was quickly tossed about at desire’s prompting and quickly departed from sobriety in time of temptation.

[Col. 0191A] Nevertheless, because of his enormities, he made a pilgrimage to Rome every year and visited the thresholds of the Apostles Peter and Paul. But what good did this do him when he did not amend himself? After he had returned home, like a dog to its vomit and a sow to the wallowing in mud, he returned to uncleanness, foolishly failing to reflect that repentance is of no value unless the fault is corrected. “He who is baptized after touching a dead body,” says the Book of Wisdom, “and touches it again, what profit is there in his washing? So too, what does a man gain who fasts for his sins and then does the same things again? What does he gain by humbling himself? For who will hear his prayer?” (Ecclus. 34).

In the ninth year, therefore, when that irritant had returned from Rome, he died a horrible death; for, shameful even to tell, amid the embraces of foul pleasure he breathed out a soul to be thrust into the stench of hell.

You are not unaware that the same thing happened among us in recent times. A certain soldier, very worldly and incestuous, while at night making his way to a brothel, suddenly perceived a foul—indeed unbearable—stench, and cried out to the armour-bearer accompanying him. Since he had long abused such enticements, he deserved to receive such a warning and to know beforehand what delight of scent awaits the voluptuous; that same night, while committing fornication, he too was suffocated.

“But how long, sons of men, will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4). How many are blackened by lust; and since “the number of fools is infinite” (Eccl. 1), how many are there who shine white in chastity? Yet the frailty of human condition is put forward as an excuse, as if grain arose without labour and virtue of such golden worth came free of charge. The Fathers showed beforehand with what chastisement of mind and body chastity is gained: they, flourishing in white simplicity, yearned that wings might be given them from heaven like a dove’s, so that they might fly from earthly things and find rest. Therefore they fled afar and remained in solitude, like that most illustrious of solitaries, of whom we sing:

> In your tender years, fleeing the crowds of citizens,  
> you sought the caves of the desert,  
> lest you should be able to stain your life  
> even by a slight hunger.
>
> O most happy man, of exalted merit,  
> [Col. 0191D] knowing no blemish of snowy purity!

To see and hear worldly things is very often greatly harmful. How can chastity be preserved amid luxuries and crowds of women? On this subject you used diligently and sweetly to admonish your pupils, while I, occasionally arriving, rejoiced in their honourable studies and stammered out among other things those verses of the poet:

> The master truly trains the horse, obedient in neck,  
> to go by the road which the rider points out. From the time  
> when the hunting puppy barked at a stag’s hide in the hall,  
> he serves in the woods. Now, boy, receive words with a pure  
> heart; now devote yourself to better things.  
> What a fresh vessel has once absorbed will long retain its scent.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.64–70

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0192A] Victorinus was by now wasting away on his three-year gibbet, but only in flesh, not in spirit. Thus there was truly seen in him that saying of the saint: “My flesh is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust; my skin is dried up and shrivelled; I am compared to mud and made like ashes and cinders” (Job 7). Then the venerable bishop whom I mentioned above, together with all the neighbourhood round about, struck with compunction by the earnestness and mortification of so great a satisfaction, rushed to the place and freed him from that tree, though he was unwilling and resisting—Victorinus being surely more victorious than he who so shamefully bound us to the forbidden tree in Paradise by presuming to touch it.

Yet elsewhere I have read of a penance harsher than the one I described, and of a more wonderful manner of release: namely, that he shut both hands within the hollow of the aforesaid [Col. 0192B] tree and hung there for three years without his feet touching the ground. When the people wished forcibly to take him down, he asked that a three-day fast be held for this purpose. At last the fastening was loosened by fire falling from heaven with thunder; the knots by which he had been bound were burned away. This was no lesser sign, plainly, of propitiation toward God than when the acceptable burnt offerings of the Fathers were taken up by a certain heavenly fire.

Having conquered human nature itself by patience, he lived in conspicuous holiness and in the manner of angels; apostolic in his working of miracles and victorious against demons, for the hand of the Lord was with him. Therefore, by the eager agreement of clergy and people, he was raised to be bishop of the city of Amiternum [Col. 0192C]—for “he who humbles himself shall be exalted,” says the Lord (Luke 14)—and, like the gentlest Moses, governed those subject to him as a sanctuary of mercy and indulgence, because through his own fall he had learned to forgive the sins of the fallen. Under the Emperor Nerva he also attained martyrdom; and while serving the second Adam, that is, Christ, he passed with the victorious palm into Paradise.

Nor did Severinus, his brother, shine with lesser holiness: a modest man and a severe tamer of his own body, who, because of the prerogative of grace, was appointed bishop in the city of Septempeda. More brilliantly than his predecessors, he adorned that church both with regular discipline and with the splendour of sacred ornaments. “Though consummated in a short time, he fulfilled many years” (Wis. 4); for by living perfectly and in the manner of an old man, he died, like the patriarch Abraham, “in a good old age and full of days,” and was gathered to the people (Gen. 25) of the saints. He had his tomb where he had also had his monastery. There he was frequented by peoples, to whom he showed himself living through the patronage of prayers and the benefit of healings, as one who was written in life, in Jerusalem.

Accordingly, a certain priest was once travelling to his feast, a man whose life corresponded to his name. He was called Innocentius: a true Israelite in whom there was no guile. He possessed only one little ewe. When her master was leaving, she followed him and came to a river called Flosor, then swollen by rain. But the shepherds had thrown a little beam from bank to bank, [Col. 0193A] so that one might cross. Innocentius crossed somehow; the little ewe, distrusting herself to trust so narrow a bridge, began to run this way and that, signaling her distress with trembling movements of her tail and shaking her sad fleece. At last, amid her plaintive bleating, there sounded the articulated harmony of a paternal voice, crying: “To whom have you left me, poor little thing?” “In the name of Jesus the Lord,” he said, “cross safely.” You would have thought the little creature supported by a certain faith: so steadily and swiftly did she cross, without turning uncertainly to either side.

“Now, disciplined man, do not in astonishment admire the speaking tongue and eloquent throat of the ass, which rebuked Balaam, tyrannizing over her with bloody kicks and striking her with a barbarous stick, by the trumpet-blast of a reproof unheard until then. But since your ear is pure and tranquil, what would you have heard more gladly: Balaam arguing with his little ass, or Innocentius conversing with his little ewe?” In both cases the audience was magnificent; but you will rightly be judged a detractor unless you favour the ewe more, since, by not abandoning obedience, she did her guide no harm, whereas the little ass, by resisting her rider, almost broke his foot.

## CHAPTER X

Finally, you, William, zealous for evangelical perfection, at last sold all your possessions and gave them to Christ in the poor; and, bearing your cross, you deserved to be Christ’s disciple, having left the teaching of the schools. [Col. 0193C] What, moreover, were you doing behind barred doors, when I sometimes arrived unexpectedly, knocked, and was admitted only with difficulty? “Your secret is yours, your secret is yours”: I grant you it; well for you! For you imitated Christ like the glorious martyr Laurence: girding yourself with a linen cloth, pouring water into a basin, washing the feet of the poor while pouring tears over them, and drying them with the towel and with your hair. Did you not also perform the offices of generous Mary, and, as though fragrant nard had been poured from the alabaster of charity, anoint Jesus when you abundantly refreshed the least of Jesus?”

It quickly became clear, therefore, that you belonged to the number of those concerning whom the Lord says through Hosea: “I will draw them in the cords [Col. 0193D] of Adam, in the bonds of charity” (Hosea 11). For, seeking Fusmacum, you professed monastic philosophy, that you might take Christ’s yoke upon yourself—he who said: “Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls; for my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11).

Indeed, it is now many years since, with the Lord’s inspiration, you went out from your land, from your kindred [Col. 0194A] and from your father’s house; nor have you ever gone back to visit your people. Perhaps this is because it is written: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9); and because Lot’s wife, forbidden by the angels to look behind her, was turned into a pillar of salt when, in tasteless curiosity, she looked back to see the sulphurous fires of the incestuous region.

Not long ago, a brother of excellent reputation came to me from the monastery of Sept-Fontaines, because I was his kinsman, and asked me to accompany him in greeting his parents or friends. But on the journey, suddenly startled and shrinking from encounters and conversations with women, he began to say that the city had changed greatly since he saw it as a boy: that the houses were different, the citizens different, and scarcely any of his relatives remained; that he regretted having come; and that it was safest not to leave the enclosed bounds of the cloister. For the wolf always lays snares for the lamb, and the fish must seek the recesses of springs in order to escape the net. Thus our man of Fontaines departed not slowly but, as it were, in flight, declaring courageously that he would not return again.

But you, although you had resolved not to impose your presence upon friends uninvited, why did you not at least sometimes send letters to show that you remembered your former affection and literary friendship—unless someone should venture to call a little letter of good seed superfluous? Yet it is fitting to offer spiritual writings to spiritual friends. Therefore in loving and [Col. 0194C] in writing I may rightly be judged more commendable than you: I send books to one to whom not even little letters have been sent.

But perhaps you will plead the great distances between places, the difficulties of the roads, and the scarcity of carriers. The negligent man gladly seeks side-paths of excuse. Yet receive this little work, *On the Progress of Death*, and add to it the work which I composed a few days ago, to which, in keeping with its subject, I prefixed the title *Tears*. What I write may indeed be insufficient and useful to no one; nevertheless I gain this benefit from it: I exercise my small talent and in some degree overcome the vexations of idleness, as you know someone says:

> Rule your mind: unless it obeys,  
> [Col. 0194D] it commands. Restrain it with reins; restrain it with a chain.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.62–63

And because the narration of deeds is welcome to you, just as a flowering plain painted with grass delights someone, I distinguish the field of this composition with the varied colours, as it were, of events. But what I began to write at the beginning of this book I shall now continue in the following book.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0195]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0195A] Thus the eyes of both, namely Adam and Eve, were opened when they opened their mouths, hitherto closed to the praise of God, for gluttony. Ungrateful for benefits—that they had been made in the divine image and likeness; that they had been set over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts of the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves on the earth; that they had been sprinkled with blessing when God said, “Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it” (Gen. 1); that they had been granted the garden of delights—what solemn offerings of love and thanksgiving did they render? What sacrifice of proclamation was offered in that tabernacle of God’s bounty? What sacrifice of praise did they offer?

Indeed, when they saw and understood that, through the serpent’s deceits, they had been miserably cast down from so great an elevation and reduced to the desolation of their former purity and innocence—for sin now reigned in their mortal body, so that they obeyed its desires, and, ashamed of each other’s nakedness, sewed fig leaves and made themselves coverings—they not only failed humbly to tremble and penitently to hasten to meet the voice of the Lord God walking in Paradise in the breeze after noon. To him, who at that moment seemed to them profoundly asleep and grievously dissembling, they ought rather to have cried something like: “Awake, why do you sleep, O Lord? Awake, and do not cast us off forever” (Ps. 44). But they hid themselves in the midst of the tree of Paradise.

[Col. 0195C] Was there, then, some hollow in the middle of that tree in which those two might hide? Rather, such hiding must be understood as of the mind more than of the body. O unhappy hiding-place of condemnation, dark and bringing forth the night of death! Fugitives from eternal brightness and parents of our blindness, they hid themselves in the midst of the tree because, in obstinate pride, they preferred to conceal from God, who knows all things, their usurpation of it rather than confess it—already swallowed up, as they were, by the vice of concupiscence which they had contracted through that act.

[Col. 0196A] Therefore, because they had “turned their heart to words of malice, to make excuses for sins,” and did not hesitate to cast their transgression upon God, Adam saying, “The woman whom you gave me as companion gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3), and the woman saying, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (ibid.), that righteous Lord who loves righteousness, whose countenance beholds equity, now more moved and more severe, said: “Behold Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now therefore, lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, eat, and live forever” (ibid.)—where one must understand, “let us send him out.”
