But the historian immediately supplies for us this sorrowful incompleteness of the divine utterance, this mournful expression of most bitter judgment, saying: “The Lord God sent him out of the Paradise of delight, to cultivate the earth from which he was taken” (ibid.). No mind can sufficiently weigh, no tongue express, how much gravity and weight there is in this saying of the Holy Trinity: “Behold Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.” For through pride, transgression, and impenitence he had rather been united to the devil, and was now compelled, by most wretched experience of evil, to know how great the good was that he had lost.

For he who had been clothed in beauty and glory far surpassing the grace of lilies—whose adornment Truth also commends in the Gospel, saying, “Not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these” (Matt. 6)—now shamefully stripped, required the use of skins, both because of the discomfort of cold and to cover the shame of lost celibacy, as it is written: “The Lord God also made for Adam and his wife garments of skins and clothed them” (Gen. 3). That is, he involved them in the necessity of making things; since it would have been wholly unfitting for supreme Majesty to strip skins from animals and sweat at the craft of tanning, especially when the things necessary for this purpose could be found in the workshops of angels.

[Col. 0195] The remainder of this book is lacking in the manuscript.

[Col. 0197]

# LIFE OF SAINT WOLBODO, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

By REINER, monk of Saint Lawrence at Liège. From Jacques Chapeaville and the Bollandist April volume.

(D. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, sixth century, part I, p. 174.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

1. Many authors indeed committed to writing the deeds of the blessed Wolbodo, bishop of Liège; but none seems to me older than Reiner, monk of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège, where that holy man is buried. This Reiner, whom Valerius Andreas in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, Chapeaville, and Vossius in their works on Latin historians consider to have flourished about the year 1130, compiled his little work from various writers who had written about blessed Wolbodo, as he himself attests, so as to satisfy the pious desire of his brethren.

But who those authors were who had written on the subject before him, he does not state, nor have they been found elsewhere. Henschenius does indeed produce an encomium of blessed Wolbodo taken from an ancient martyrology of the monastery of Saint Lawrence, which appeared to him older than Reiner. But since it is nothing other than an abridgment of what Reiner narrates more fully, it matters little whether it preceded or followed Reiner. Besides this author, Anselm, canon of Liège, and Giles of Aurea Vallis, a Cistercian monk, wrote more concerning blessed Wolbodo in the thirteenth century; Chapeaville published these writings, with various annotations, in the first volume of *De gestis pontificum Leodiensium*. Yet it has seemed sufficient, omitting the others, to present Reiner’s work, from which those later writers drew the matters that they recount.

2. Henschenius flatly denies that Wolbodo should be assigned to the Benedictine Order, relying principally on the argument that, in the Life published by Reiner, Wolbodo is said to have been from boyhood a canon of the Church of Utrecht, and that after administering various offices in that church he was finally set over the Church of Liège. Nevertheless, the monks of Stavelot endeavour to claim him for themselves. Both ancient and modern writers, Benedictines and outsiders alike, unanimously acknowledge that he was a monk. This is explicitly affirmed by Giles of Aurea Vallis, a Cistercian monk who flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century:

> “After the death of Bishop Baldric, the forty-eighth bishop of Liège, there succeeded a religious monk, a man of great virtue and chaplain of Emperor Henry—namely, blessed Wolbodo.”

That the same opinion was received in the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège is evident from barbarous verses composed under Henry XXVI, abbot of that place. It has seemed appropriate to cite some of them here from Molanus and Chapeaville:

> Wolbodo is marked out, distinguished in lineage and shining in virtue;  
> formerly provost of Utrecht and also its ruler,  
> because of his celibate state, afterwards he received monastic profession.

Those authors do not report in what place the devout bishop received the monastic habit. But I should judge that one need seek no other place than the Church of Utrecht itself, in which, according to Reiner’s own testimony, Wolbodo was trained. For it is more than probable that the observance of the Rule of Benedict, established there by Saint Willibrord, was still flourishing at that time.

Nor ought Reiner’s calling Wolbodo a canon to be an obstacle; for monks established in cathedral churches could be honoured with that name, as could be shown by many examples. Indeed, the first author of Wolbodo’s encomium, whom Henschenius himself, as we have just said, suspects to have been contemporary with the saint, does not use the title “canon,” perhaps employed by Reiner by measuring former times with those of his own day. Rather, he asserts that Wolbodo grew up under religious Fathers in ecclesiastical disciplines of cloistered life. A little further on, the same author writes that the holy man was unwillingly led away from the quiet of the cloister by the emperor, who wished him to remain for some time with him in the chapel. All this seems to prove that Wolbodo was devoted to monastic institutions.

3. Nearly all authors agree that Wolbodo departed this life in the year of Christ 1021, and there seems to be no difficulty about that point. With equal agreement they have recorded his death on 21 April. But Henschenius maintains that ancient authors assigned the deposition of Wolbodo in the church of Saint Lawrence—not his death, which he thinks occurred on the preceding day—to 21 April; later writers of martyrologies, insufficiently attending to this point, attached the death of the same holy man to 21 April.

Indeed, if Wolbodo died in 1021, and his death occurred on a Thursday, as Saint Lawrence had promised him, he must be said to have died on the twentieth; for in 1021 that day fell on Thursday in the second week after Easter. But if the blessed bishop’s death is assigned to the year 1021, as some hold, then Thursday after Easter, namely 21 April, must be said to have been his last day, which seems sufficiently consistent with Reiner’s narrative. Yet since Reiner himself, the ancient Chronicle of Liège, the catalogues of the bishops of that city, and all the other older writers consistently assert that Wolbodo died in 1021, the opinion of Henschenius has seemed preferable.

4. John Molanus testifies in his *Natalia Sanctorum Belgii* that he saw Wolbodo commemorated in more than thirty martyrologies; there he gives a brief encomium of him together with the verses quoted above. He also mentions him in the Belgian calendars. It is therefore not surprising that later compilers of martyrologies—Arnold Wion, Hugh Menard, Dorganius, Bucelinus, Ferrarius in his general catalogue of saints, and others—entered Wolbodo’s name in their calendars. Meyer treats him at length in the *Annals of Flanders* under the year 1020, as do Placentinus, Bartholomew Fisen in the *Flowers of the Church of Liège*, and similar authors, whom it would be superfluous to enumerate.

Yet one must not omit the outstanding testimony that Baldric, bishop of Noyon, a weighty man and Wolbodo’s contemporary, gives concerning him in book three, chapter 14 of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, in these few words:

> “Endowed with every religious virtue, he furnished his people with a rule of justice and left examples of innocent conduct and life.”

The monastery of Saint Lawrence near Liège, in which blessed Wolbodo was buried, owes its origin to Eraclius, bishop of the same city. Eraclius left it, after beginning it, to his successor Notger; it was eventually continued by Baldric and Wolbodo and completed by Reginard, successor of Durand, who died in 1036, according to Miraeus in the *Origins of the Benedictines*. It remains famous even today under the Rule of Benedict, as does the other monastery of Saint James in the same city.

5. The blessed man’s body remained in its own marble tomb until the year 1656. On 29 October of that year it was raised from there by Joseph Sanfelice, archbishop of Cosenza, then nuncio of Alexander VII in the region of the Rhine; it was finally deposited in a most magnificent mausoleum which William Natalis, abbot of Saint Lawrence, caused to be constructed, where it is still devoutly preserved.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0199]

[Col. 0199A] “Golden apples in silver settings,” says Solomon, “is one who speaks a word in its proper time.” For just as it somehow feeds the eyes of those who look upon it if the crafted silverwork of some setting is adorned with golden apples, so that art skillfully imitates the forms which nature produces and the metal seems, as it were, to bear arboreal fruit; so too—indeed more truly—teaching, appropriately formed and suitably expressed either from the gold of spiritual understanding or from the silver of moral experience, nourishes the minds of students.

Although I have scarcely attained anything of this teaching, nevertheless the kindly judgment of certain brethren urged me for some time to record something concerning Lord Wolbodo, the bishop who rests among us: that is, taking only the matter from the various writers in whom things concerning him are scattered [Col. 0199B], I might gather it by my own composition and make one writing from many. But what has been attempted beyond one’s powers achieves its effect poorly; rather, in the poet’s words, it is right for each person to measure himself by his own measure and capacity. Therefore I diligently set before myself that Gospel saying: “Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost necessary to complete it?” (Luke 14:28). Measuring myself, I wholly declined to begin what I could not suitably finish.

Nevertheless, the fervent and pious insistence of those asking did not grow cool. Therefore I finally accepted what the spirit of piety imposed through the voice of brethren, yet by its own prompting, lest I incur the fault of being undevout if I did not in some measure obey devotion. And because I had pledged the hand of my own promise to a reverend confessor, I discharged the word of this present little work. Would that I have spoken it in its proper time—that is, that it may be profitable to readers and hearers. Yet if it displeases anyone, let him consider how strongly I was pressed, and he will bear my lack of skill more patiently if he considers not the words but the subject matter. For he who seeks profit from the virtues of saints does not concern himself too much with verbal ornament.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0199]

[Col. 0199B] 2. Wolbodo’s family was of illustrious nobility from Flanders [Note: [Col. 0199C] John Meyer, under the year 1020, asserts that Wolbodo’s father was Godfrey, count of Mons, and [Col. 0200C] his mother Joanna, daughter of Baldwin the Younger, count of Flanders; but on what basis?]. Yet he adorned the brightness of his lineage with a still brighter life, learning, and episcopal dignity. From the first bloom of childhood, like a white lily, he began to breathe forth the fragrance of a good disposition. Entrusted to schools, he eagerly aspired of his own accord to every good lesson; teachable in understanding, gentle in disposition and intellect, he already made it clear through his studies that his works would be pure and upright.

Thus, as he advanced in age, so he advanced in literary attainments, practising without sloth that poetic precept:

> Now, boy, receive words with a pure  
> heart; now devote yourself to better things.  
> What a fresh vessel has once absorbed will long retain its scent.

A jar, long … (HORACE, *Epistles* I.2.67–70.) Nor indeed was the care of his devout parents lacking. Holding him dearer than all their possessions, they entrusted him to modest and distinguished tutors and teachers, that they might adorn so precious a sapphire to themselves with the bright gold of a noble education—he who, in the serenity both of mind and countenance, seemed in some measure to emulate the serenity of the heavenly firmament. For good parents owe their children this care: that they should be well educated.

Philip, king of the Macedonians, outstandingly powerful alike in letters and in military achievements, wrote to Aristotle the philosopher when Alexander had been born to him: “Indeed, I give thanks to the gods,” he said, “not so much because he has been born, as because it has happened that he was born during your lifetime. For I hope that, brought up and instructed by you, he will prove worthy both of us and of undertaking royal affairs. Yet it is implanted in human nature that one undertakes the toil of teaching more willingly if benefits compensate the labor. It is written that the laborer is worthy of his hire, and that the mouth of an ox treading out grain is not to be muzzled; and the good arts are more happily stimulated by the spur of rewards. Therefore gratitude ought to be shown to good teachers, because they form their pupils not only in letters but—what is more commendable—even in good morals.”

Hence Symmachus, a man of highest rank and prefect of the city of Rome, wrote to the Emperor Theodosius: “Among the foremost public concerns it has often been deemed necessary that philosophical teachers from Attica should be sought for the education of nobles. Thus public law and authority have admitted some into the service of our city, lord Emperor; now the beneficence of your age has of its own accord claimed for the Roman schools a foremost nobleman of wisdom. For Celsus, son of Arthemius—whom literary remembrance agrees was the equal of Aristotle—offers himself as a teacher of the liberal arts to our young people, seeking no profit from his profession. He therefore deserves to be admitted to the most distinguished order, so that we may reward with the honor of rank a spirit free from the vices of avarice. It is worthy of the eternity of your divinity to adjudge to this man, commendable in birth, learning, and inclination, the pledge of noble rank, namely with consular prerogative; lest, if we demand public duties from one who promises gratuitous instruction, we appear, not without the reproach of avarice, to have sought his expenditure rather than his teaching.”

[Note: [Col. 0201D] He seems to have been the very celebrated orator sent by the Roman senate to Constantinople to petition on behalf of the children of Theodosius that the Vestals should not be destroyed by Christians. His speech was refuted by St Ambrose and Prudentius.]

### 3.

Accordingly Wolbodo, a modest young man, well educated and always stretching himself toward what lay ahead, went from virtue to virtue. Devoting himself most earnestly to sobriety and chastity, he was as constant at the church or cloister as Samuel in the tabernacle of the Lord; and, lest he should reek of worldly seductions, this Nazarite of Christ utterly refused to wander abroad.

For, as it is written: “Whoever touches pitch shall be defiled by it” (Ecclus. 13:1). So one who pursues curiosities and does not withdraw from the world will not remain untouched by contagion. Then, in a splendid youth flourishing like a palm tree—for he was tall of stature and straight of limb—he surpassed all the clergy of the church of Utrecht, in which he had also been a canon from boyhood. At that time it flourished equally in religious observance and in sacred and secular learning.

At last he was made master of the schools and instructed many; for, like holy Job, “the lamp of the Lord shone upon him,” and, drawing near to the Lord’s feet, he received from His teaching. Thus, according to the rank, age, and capacity of each, he was gracious and kind, becoming all things to all men according to the Apostle. Afterwards promoted to the provostship of the greater church, he labored, like the faithful and prudent steward commended by the Lord in the Gospel, to give his brethren their measure of wheat in due season. Not even Joseph, that fruitful son, had once been more diligent in administering Pharaoh’s granaries.

Yet his concern for outward matters did not make him neglect inward ones. Piously severe and judiciously strict, he checked every kind of disorder: intent upon the practical life like Martha and upon contemplation like Mary. Therefore, since “regular canon” is the proper interpretation of his office, he reproved his subjects in season and out of season, and urged them to be regular both in conduct and in habit, attending to Solomon’s saying: “Hold fast instruction, my son, and do not let it go; guard it, for it is your life’s way” (Prov. 4:13).

### 4.

Emperor Henry—

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Henry, surnamed the Saint, who with his most holy wife Cunigunda founded the bishopric of Bamberg in 1007. The first bishop established there was Eberhard, who administered that see piously until 1042.]

—who, because of the marks of his virtues and the splendor of his lineage, was surnamed the Glorious, held Wolbodo in high esteem and counted him among his foremost friends. He sometimes kept him with him at court, enjoying his companionship, counsel, and piety.

This orthodox prince, uniquely devoted to St Lawrence, endowed and exalted with most munificent liberality the church of Bamberg, constructed and dedicated under that saint’s title, with possessions and wealth, so that an episcopal see might be established there. Having no heir of his own body, he appointed Christ and His martyr heirs of his property and patrimony; for before his kingship or empire he had been the mighty duke of the Bavarians.

### 5.

Meanwhile, when Bishop Baldrick—

[Note: [Col. 0202D] Baldrick, successor of Notger and bishop of Liège, is said to have departed this life in 1017. In that same year Wolbodo was substituted for him by Emperor Henry. The Magdeburg chronicler, together with Sigebert, records both events under the following year.]

—illustrious alike in lineage, life, and memory, died, he who had advanced the churches of his diocese everywhere by many kinds of benefactions and had finally founded on an island of this city the monastery of St James, brother of the Lord, an embassy was sent from the church of Liège to the emperor. By letters and capable men it requested that another shepherd be appointed.

For at that time it belonged to royal power or right to invest bishops, elected at its own discretion, with ring and pastoral staff, and to assign them to churches with its recommendation. Yet religious princes took care to choose for this honor men able to benefit the kingdom and its subjects, as many did at different times and places. Thus the Glorious Emperor, who sought Christ’s glory, considered whom he should give the people of Liège as shepherd. He assigned Wolbodo to them, judging none worthier.

Wolbodo declared himself unworthy and resisted with prayers and tears; yet at last he consented, lest he should grieve a prince to whom he owed profound devotion, or rather incur the loss of obedience or the reproach of stubbornness. Sent with imperial authority, he was received with great assent and joy by clergy and people. For he did not take this honor upon himself through ambition, but was called by the Lord, like Aaron. Therefore, because the Lord caused him to grow among His people, he received a blessing from the Lord; and, that he might perform that priestly office, clothed according to Aaron’s holy garment for glory and beauty, he was consecrated bishop by St Heribert, archbishop of Cologne.

### 6.

Since this shepherd entered through the door into the sheepfold, the doorkeeper opening it to him—that is, Christ—he fed the Christian Israel after the pattern of David. He fed, I say, Christ’s inheritance in the innocence of his heart, and guided it with the understanding of his hands. Indeed, he first did what he would afterwards teach. Therefore, as the Apostle exhorts Timothy, he gave attention to reading, exhortation, and teaching, exercising himself above all in godliness, which, as the same Teacher of the Gentiles defines it, is profitable for all things, holding promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come.

His charity toward the poor was so exceedingly generous that, if at times he lacked something to give away, he secretly took for himself tapestries, little vessels, cloaks, or any other ornaments of the episcopal residence, and especially at night distributed them among the needy. These, of course, then had to be redeemed from the chamberlains and household officers.

Why should I recount his persistence in prayer and vigils? He frequently spent even winter nights without sleep, either walking about the oratory of the saints or bestowing works of mercy on the sick and poor, who watched him more secretly through the familiar byways, he himself directing them. He walked as a son of light by night because he was tending toward the true day; that is, he walked in darkness because he hated the brightness of vain display, according to the Lord’s saying: “When you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does, so that your alms may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. 6:3).

A certain man particularly close to him used to testify that, while washing his feet, he found them scorched by cold and by the icy harshness of the roads, and found blood driven from within hardened into calluses on the surface of the skin. Thus he imitated Christ’s radiant brother James, who, praying to the Father of lights, is said to have acquired on his knees calluses like those of a camel through constant kneeling.

### 7.

The Lord said to Moses: “Fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall feed it, laying wood upon it every morning, and, after the burnt offering has been placed upon it, shall burn upon it the fat of the peace offerings” (Lev. 6:12). This is the perpetual fire that shall never fail upon the altar.

Wolbodo, then, burning with the fire of charity toward God and neighbor, fed it like a dutiful priest upon the altar of holy meditation. Placing upon it the wood of good works and above it the burnt offering of alms, he burned, as it were, the fat of peace offerings. Nor were his meals devoid of dishes from his abundant generosity: whatever richer or more delicate things were set before him, he shared with Christ by sending them here or there to sick and needy people, while he himself refreshed himself with ordinary bread and common food, though far short of satiety.

Therefore the praise of holy Job might rightly be applied to him: “If I denied the poor what they desired, if I caused the eyes of the widow to wait; if I ate my morsel alone and the orphan did not eat of it” (Job 31:17). Yet he especially commended by words and honored with gifts those whom he knew to fear God and keep His commandments, although he withheld no hand of compassion from anyone, saying with the Apostle: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the unwise” (Rom. 1:14).

Nor do I think it altogether tasteless to insert here an anecdote seasoned with Greek salt. Herodes Atticus, a consular man of cultivated and pleasant civic character, was approached by a certain man in philosopher’s cloak, with long hair and a beard grown down to his breast, who asked for money. Herodes asked who he was. The man declared himself a philosopher, reproaching him by look and tone of voice, and wondered why he thought it necessary to ask what he could see.

“I see,” said Herodes, “a beard and a cloak; I do not yet see a philosopher. But, with your good leave, tell me: by what proofs do you think we can ascertain that you are a philosopher?” When the other became angry, those present said that he was a wandering fellow and good for nothing; indeed, that he frequented filthy brothels and, unless he received what he asked, was accustomed to assail people with shameful abuse. “Let us give this man,” said Herodes, “some money, whatever he may be. Let us give it as men, though not to a man.” And he ordered that he be given the price of thirty days’ bread.

### 8.

But, to return to our Wolbodo: certain slanderers turned away from him the former favor of the Augustus, sowing the tares of detraction, of whom it is said: “A whisperer and double-tongued man is accursed, for he has disturbed many who were at peace” (Ecclus. 28:15).

Nevertheless, as a pursuer of peace, who faithfully rendered to Caesar what was Caesar’s and to God what was God’s, on the counsel of his faithful friends he prepared a gift worthy of Caesar, in order to calm the emperor’s mind against him. He did not forget the saying from Proverbs: “Fear the Lord and the king; for as the roaring of a lion, so is the terror of a king” (Prov. 20:2). Nor that saying of the Apostle Peter: “Fear God; honor the king. For this is grace, if anyone, because of conscience toward God, endures sorrow while suffering unjustly” (1 Pet. 2:17).

Moreover, reflecting on the saying, “The heart of the king is in the hand of God; wherever He wills, He shall incline it” (Prov. 21:1), he judged that, once the heavenly King had been placated, the indignation of an earthly king could more easily be borne. Therefore, to shake his hands free of this gift as of every other, he scattered and gave to the poor whatever money he had amassed, retaining not even a single small coin from it.

Then he went to Cologne, where the emperor was then celebrating the Lord’s Nativity, and presented himself before him. The emperor expected from Wolbodo great talents of gold and silver. Asked about it, Wolbodo replied with subdued and grateful countenance that, through the hands of the poor, he had bestowed on the supreme Emperor whatever he had brought, so that He might always protect that emperor and his empire.

Caesar, in imperial graciousness, received this calmly and cheerfully because Wolbodo had imitated St Lawrence, to whom he himself was most devoted. At once every cloud of offence or scandal was wiped away; rejoicing with him and embracing him, he had him sit down. Thus Wolbodo was held in greater favor by giving nothing than were the other bishops who had given much, seeking the frivolous favor of courtiers or the applause and witticisms of mimes.

### 9.

For it is written: “He who preserves purity of conscience, because of the grace of his lips, shall have the king as friend” (Prov. 22:11). Yet this same emperor had long been bitterly hostile to Archbishop Heribert, and it is fitting to state the reason.

Otto III, emperor of that name, defeated in battle at Rome Crescentius, patrician of the Romans, who had rebelled against him. He captured him as he fled, after he had been brought back from flight; after condemning him, he had him placed backwards upon a wretched beast and led around the City, then gradually mutilated limb by limb, and finally ordered him hanged before the walls.

Crescentius’s wife, hoping to rule, had enticed the emperor to her love. But when she grieved that he was returning home and that she was disappointed of marriage, she secretly sent poison and infected him. Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, is said to have been diminished in wisdom; but I would say that this emperor was no less diminished in sense, since he trusted and yielded himself to an insolent and wanton little woman whose husband he had treated so disgracefully, and whose relatives and the Roman commonwealth he had utterly ruined with losses and deaths.

The following saying from the Book of Wisdom escaped Otto: “There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and there is no wrath above the wrath of a woman. It will please one to dwell with a lion and a dragon rather than to live with a wicked woman. A woman’s wickedness changes her face and blinds her countenance like a bear” (Ecclus. 25:22).

By this bear Otto was driven to death. In his last extremity, he entrusted the insignia of empire to Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, who was then present and in whom he especially trusted, so that he might assign them to the man whom the common election and assent of the princes should establish in the kingdom, for Otto had no sons.

When the Transalpine soldiers were carrying the deceased emperor’s body into Gaul, they were harassed by many plots and attacks of Italians, but forcefully made their way by arms. Yet, when affairs were thought already secure, Henry—the emperor now under discussion, then duke of Bavaria—rose against the archbishop, to whom they belonged and whom all obeyed. After Henry had been treated by him with excessive insolence, he forcibly wrested from the archbishop the same insignia, saying that they were his by hereditary right; for his grandfather, Henry, had been the brother of the first Emperor Otto.

This was the seedbed of Caesar’s hostility and discord against the archbishop, whom he several times persecuted more harshly than was just. At length, however, pierced by divine fear into repentance, and through the mediation and labor toward concord of Wolbodo—highly esteemed by both—he was reconciled, as already stated, at Cologne, where he was then staying, to that same archbishop with most humble satisfaction.

### 10.

When he afterwards celebrated the Lord’s Passover at Liège, he was approached by the brothers of Bishop Baldrick, mentioned above, men highly pleasing to the Augustus because of their nobility and capability. They asked him to provide with imperial piety for the monastery of St James, which their brother had founded but had left unfinished when death overtook him and desolate for lack of any guardian’s care.

Accordingly the emperor came to the place with a great throng of nobles and common people. He entered the crypt built in the name of St Andrew the Apostle and consecrated with relics, which he himself, the Augustus, had given to venerable Baldrick as a precious pledge of their mutual affection. After reverencing there Baldrick’s tomb, where his body rested, he said: “To you, Bishop Wolbodo”—for he was present—“to you, beloved by us, I entrust in our stead this poor place, this church. Be a father to this orphan girl and a diligent guardian; and from the goods with which your predecessor endowed her, complete the unfinished work.”

Then he made a generous offering upon the altar. Therefore, although held by many other cares, the bishop nevertheless watched over that place with a father’s care. He also placed over it Olbert, abbot of the church of Gembloux, a man most distinguished in virtue, religious observance, and wisdom. With watchful zeal, and with the bishop’s cooperation, Olbert labored to complete the monastery; and there, after his blessed departure from the world, he received burial as an old man who had completed his service.

### 11.

At the same time Count Theodoric of Ghent was waging war against the Frisians—

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Sigebert’s *Chronicle* contains some material on this war under the years 1018 and following. On the family of this Theodoric and of the counts of Ghent, see André Duchesne, *History of the Families of Guînes, Ardres, and Ghent*, preface to Book II.]

—because they had killed his father Arnulf. To restrain him, the emperor sent Duke Godfrey of Lotharingia with an army. When peace could not be achieved, both sides advanced to battle on an appointed day. The battle lines were already rushing against one another when, suddenly, a terrifying voice thundered forth in a new and strange portent, from no one knew where: “Flee, flee!”

Struck with amazement, the duke and his men fled, driven by a dizzy terror. The Frisians, however, stood firm, and the few killed many of their opponents. They moreover captured the duke himself, because they believed that he had withdrawn from battle through trickery and treachery. The emperor was deeply moved when he heard this, and sent Wolbodo to Frisia with envoys, because he was held in honor there on account of his lineage and holiness.

And Wolbodo, as Solomon says, proved himself a faithful envoy: “A faithful messenger is health; and as the cold of snow in harvest time, so is a faithful messenger to him who sends him: he refreshes his master’s soul” (Prov. 13:17). By his own diligence he brought it about that the duke was released from captivity and that the injury inflicted upon the duke and kingdom was forgiven by the emperor to the Frisians.

### 12.

Returning from there to Liège, he celebrated the Lord’s Passover with his customary devotion and spiritual joy. It was his practice to celebrate the Paschal mysteries at the holy altar on as many days as possible, and to eat the flesh of the true Lamb, roasted in the fire of the Passion. He ate it indeed as with unleavened bread and wild lettuces—exceedingly bitter, surely—for his tears were his bread day and night. Speaking to God in the bitterness of his soul, “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5), he was free from the leaven of malice and wickedness.

Then, about to be summoned from the Egypt of this world to the true and everlasting Passover—summoned, I say, from darkness into God’s marvellous light—he began to be pressed toward death by a pain in the stomach contracted through excessive abstinence. Lying down with haircloth spread over coarse straw and ashes scattered upon him, he devoted himself earnestly to prayer, psalmody, and the reading of Scripture, which he had read aloud to him. He sighed for the time when he might come and appear before the face of God.

Finally, he fatherly admonished those sitting beside him always to remember their last things and, while the days of salvation remained, to provide for their own salvation. He ordered that no one be prevented from entering to him, so that in his own strait of death they might contemplate in their bishop the bitterness of death—how bitter, how sour for their posterity, compared with the sweetness of that fruit which the first parents rashly tasted in the garden of delights.

Nor were the snares of the ancient serpent absent, seeking whether he might find in Wolbodo anything that was his own. Though sick, Wolbodo repelled him, standing by on account of those traces, with the sign of the cross and sprinkling of blessed water. For every word of God, according to Scripture, “is a shield of fire to those who hope in Him” (Prov. 30:5). Armed with it, Wolbodo said: “Depart, baleful inhabitant of darkness. I have no part with you; Christ is my portion in the land of the living.”

Blessed hope, happy expectation, of this sick and suffering man, who could confidently say to God: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, Your consolations have made my soul glad” (Ps. 93:19). For blessed Lawrence appeared immediately to him with inestimable sweetness and glory, consoling him: “On Thursday you shall be with me.”

Refreshed by this consolation, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, and by this promise as by divine nectar, the sick man explained it, more joyfully than was fitting, to the chief men of the church and certain clergy. While they rejoiced with him, he fortified himself with holy anointing and the viaticum of Christ’s sacraments. Finally, he entrusted the care of this place to Poppo, then very renowned abbot of the church of Stavelot, because no abbot or monks had yet been established there to serve God.

This church had indeed begun to be built by Bishop Eraclus, of glorious memory, who had already constructed in this city the basilicas of Saints Paul and Martin with outstanding liberality. But when he died a few days later, it was left unfinished. Both were endowed, indeed, but presented a lamentable appearance because they were not even roofed—until Notger, his successor as bishop, finally caused a roof to be placed upon them when their walls had been completed and brought to equal height: O Liège, your splendid crown.

### 13.

Thus, when the promised and desired day came, that man of desires was disappointed of his desire. For it had been his fault that the vision of so great a dignity had become known to the unworthy as well as to the worthy. Therefore, greatly distressed, he examined his own heart. Finding fault in himself, he adjured Wieland, a cleric of good conduct and his familiar, by the dread majesty of the Godhead, to bind him with cords and subject him to strict lashes.

The Lord did not despise His bound servant, whom you might observe speaking like holy Job: “I myself rebuke myself, and I do penance under the lash, in ashes and cinders” (Job 42:6). Therefore Wolbodo’s prayer as a penitent ascended like incense in the Lord’s sight; that is, the lifting up of his hands, as he drew toward the evening of death, was like an evening sacrifice before the Father of mercies and God of all consolation.

For by the Spirit he perceived that he was about to be released from the bonds of flesh. With deepest humility he urged those around him to pray more earnestly, himself beginning the antiphons for the psalms and, after their completion, himself adding the collects. In order to do this more effectively, he sometimes had his tongue, already dried by approaching death, moistened with water.

Then, on Thursday of the following week, about to depart, he received the Lord’s cross in his hands. With marvellous sweetness and inexhaustible affection he embraced it for a long time, kissed the feet, hands, and side of the Crucified, and yielded up his spirit to Christ crucified. That he might receive the reward of his labors, he was led by a wonderful way; for, with Lawrence as guide, he passed “to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God.”

His venerable body was brought with great honor and a great gathering of clergy and people to this place, to this house of the martyr whom he had made his special patron. It was laid in an elaborate and splendid tomb, upon which, so far as it can be seen, the following was inscribed in gilded letters:

> Great is the honor of the body, but greater the grace of his character;  
> His office and throne place you among bishops.  
> Rich and poor alike knew that you were present in every need:  
> From you came salvation to these, and to those food flowed.  
> Hence these same things are present to all, and compassion to us;  
> Hence we venerate the life-giving tomb.

### 14.

He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1021, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April], when Benedict, the 144th from the blessed Apostle Peter, presided over the apostolic see; in the twentieth year of the glorious Henry’s kingship and empire; and in the thirtieth month of Wolbodo’s own episcopate.

Beyond doubt an heir of the land of the living, he generously made St Lawrence heir from his own property. Moreover, he left three hundred marks of silver for completing the church, stored up for you, holy martyr, with marvellous affection. For had he lived longer, how far he would have extended his devotion toward you you know more fully with God, who measures human hearts.

Finally, he bestowed seven mother churches and many estates and revenues in Flanders, left to him by his forebears. From these we have been disinherited by violent men and covetous invaders of others’ property, Satan opposing us, despite our futile protests against their malice and against the injustice of this age.

### 15.

Nor should I omit that, loving the beauty of the Lord’s house, he instituted the stations or processions which the whole clergy of the city make together to the greater church on stated solemnities throughout the year. By such assemblies, a harmony of charity may, so to speak, continually remain in the choir of Liège: that is, the privilege and fitting subjection owed to the greater church by the lesser churches, as by daughters to their mother, may be preserved. This is ordered by Him who makes those of one mind dwell in a house, while the Apostle exhorts that the unity of the Spirit be carefully kept in the bond of peace.

The distinguished book of Psalms reminds us of that bronze basin made by Moses, in which Aaron and his sons washed their hands and feet when they were about to enter the tabernacle of witness or approach the altar to offer incense to the Lord. Wolbodo wrote this book with his own hand; to each psalm he appended a prayer composed from that psalm and dictated by himself, bringing good things out of the good treasure of his heart.

It has been carefully preserved by us to this day. In it we may wash our hands and feet—that is, the motions of our actions and intentions—with tearful compunction, chanting with a bronze-like resonance unto God, as we prepare to enter the Holy of Holies. Among other things, we cherish this memorial too of most devout Wolbodo, whose custom it was every day, before celebrating the divine mysteries, to recite the entire Psalter afresh: incense acceptable to Christ, an odor of sweetness.

### 16.

Durandus succeeded him in the bishopric, harsh enough toward our church. For he took away the many goods which Wolbodo, his predecessor, had given us: some he retained for the episcopal table, and some he granted as benefices to soldiers.

He was indeed of ignoble birth, being from the household of Godescalc, provost of the greater church; but he flourished in the splendid nobility of intellect and learning. This Godescalc built the church of St Bartholomew and established twelve canons from his own sufficient freehold estates, aided by the counsels and benefactions of the most liberal Wolbodo.

Yet Durandus, though born in servile condition, commended himself nobly even in this: he did not allow Godescalc either to swear fealty to him as bishop, as was customary, or to perform homage. Acting honorably and candidly, he considered not what he then was but what he had once been. Though no longer a slave, he nevertheless offered himself to Godescalc in service as though he were one.

Thus it was as though a play upon the theatre of the world that a man from so poor and humble a family ruled over his own former masters, while the Lord makes poor and makes rich, humbles and exalts. Because of Durandus’s modest life and excellence in learning, kindly Wolbodo held him most dear. Therefore, when Emperor Henry sought a cleric learned in letters, Wolbodo had presented and strongly commended him. The Augustus held this recommendation in such esteem that, upon Wolbodo’s death, he raised Durandus to the episcopal chair of Liège.

For Durandus, appointed by the same Augustus, had already illuminated the church of Bamberg with the bright star of learning and religious observance. But many forget benefits received, and worldly concerns sometimes corrupt even good minds. Thus Durandus, forgetful of Wolbodo’s mercy toward him, deprived the almsgiving of mercy, as stated above, which Wolbodo had assigned to Lawrence in this place; he thought it a small matter to take it away when no one opposed him.

### 17.

For this reason he was rebuked by a most severe vision, once and then a second time. The same saint appeared to him and sharply demanded back his almsgiving. When Durandus, greatly shaken along with his household, recounted this, they said—especially those upon whom he had bestowed the stolen property—that he ought not heed dreams: dreams follow many cares; a sleeping person sees what, while awake, he turns over in his mind; it is the part of a wise man to regard dream-phantoms as smoke.

The tongues of such flattering dogs, so to speak, readily licked from his mind the drop of fear conceived there. Wolbodo had indeed come once and twice in a spirit of gentleness; but now, for the third time, he was present with the rod of wrath. Terribly threatening, he said that, because he had not been heard and Durandus had not corrected his fault, the axe was already laid to the roots of the tree.

He struck Durandus down very severely, and at once he was seized by a sickness that foretold death. The household was troubled by his extreme anguish and cries; the archdeacons and also the leading men of the city were summoned in haste. He made known what he had seen and heard.

“And behold,” he said, “I am now dying. Carry me to the mercy of my lord Wolbodo, and bury me opposite him, that is, outside the church of St Lawrence, beside the wall.”

He then granted to St Lawrence the estate at Wasegga, which he had recently bought from Robert the archdeacon, and the four marks of gold alone remaining to him. He solemnly promised that, if time were granted him, he would restore in full everything he had taken away. Perhaps, according to Zacchaeus’s vow, he would have restored what he had taken fourfold; but he died before this could be expected. And he was buried outside the church, as he had requested.

There he lay exposed to the open air until a new church was built. Then he was enclosed within its wall and admitted beneath its roof. Out of reverence for the episcopal office, Abbot Stephen—

[Note: [Col. 0209] Stephen governed this monastery from 1026 until his death in 1059.]

—had the gravestone, which may still be seen, laid over him and ordered the following epitaph inscribed:

> Here lies Durandus, who for a little more than three years  
> Nobly ruled the see of Tongeren.  
> Born and reared in the nest of a poor inheritance,  
> By intellect he soared to the highest nobles.  
> Those masters whom he had borne, he found serving him:  
> What a play it was in the theatre of the world!  
> The seventh day was passing around the globe as he poured forth his urn,  
> When the old man bade a sorrowful farewell to earthly things.

### 18.

Finally, whoever has sought in faith at the body of Wolbodo, beloved by God, has been restored from various illnesses; and we have sometimes experienced the efficacy of his merits both in ourselves, who enjoy his benefactions, and in others. Of innumerable examples, I shall briefly touch upon only two.

Adelard—

[Note: [Col. 0211B] There were two abbots of St Trudo bearing this name. The first governed the monastery for thirty-five years and died in 1039; the other from 1055 until 1082, as is recorded in the published chronicle of that monastery, vol. VII of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*.]

—the second abbot of that name in the church of St Trudo, had been driven out of his mind by a most violent frenzy. When he was brought to the tomb of our Wolbodo and lay there for some time, through the saint’s aid he recovered the full soundness of his senses.

Likewise, another of our brethren fell gravely ill and was carried to the saint’s mercy. Wolbodo appeared to him graciously and made over him the sign of the holy cross for the third time. As though drawn back from the very jaws of death, he recovered without delay.

19. But bodily healings sometimes bring about infirmities of the soul, when miracles that ought [Col. 0212A] to stir people to devotion are claimed by the undisciplined as material for dissipation—especially since secular crowds are not conducive either to monastic observance or to quiet. Therefore it was not reprehensible that, as our elders related, Stephen, the first abbot of this place of pious memory, once adjured this saint by the divine Name to moderate his miracles [Note: [Col. 0212B] An outstanding example of zeal for regular observance. Would that certain persons today attended to it, who so avidly seek gatherings of secular people in order to make their churches, or their saints, famous.]; for the brethren suffered so much inconvenience, by reason of the sick, night and day. Yet, although miracles began from that time to become rarer, Wolbodo is always with us through the presence of his merits: for he has also sometimes been seen by certain religious persons at your altar, O holy Lawrence, wonderfully in the presence of the most holy Trinity, performing the hidden mysteries [Col. 0212B] of the hidden divine mysteries for the welfare of this church—a priest whose prayers are heard, according to the order of Melchizedek. May the same triune and one God, to whom be glory now and unto the day of eternity, accept, and eternally continue to accept, his offerings and the oblations of your fragrant prayers. Amen.

## A.D. 1188. HENRY OF CHÂTEAU-MARÇAY, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, LATER CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH AND BISHOP OF ALBANO

[Col. 0211]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(UGHELLI, *Italia Sacra*, I, 254, under the Bishops of Albano.)

Henry of Château-Marçay, a Frenchman, Cistercian monk and abbot of Clairvaux, was unwillingly consecrated cardinal-bishop of Albano by Alexander III on 15 March 1179, the second day after the Lateran Council had begun to be held. Born of very noble parents, he fled while still a boy to the monastery of Clairvaux under Abbot Blessed Robert, who had succeeded St Bernard. Having made remarkable progress under his discipline, Henry undertook the governance of Hautecombe, the famous abbey in Savoy. From there, after the martyrdom of Blessed Gerard, he was transferred to the care of Clairvaux. Having there trained men perfected in every virtue, he became equally renowned at court and with Pope Alexander III; he was judged worthy to be numbered among the Fathers of the Council, to be adorned with the senatorial purple, and to shine in the dignity of Albano.

This dignity certainly did not make him so idle that, as apostolic legate, he did not stir up the most noble provinces beyond the sea for the holy war [Col. 0213] and apply a saving remedy to peoples infected by the dreadful plague of heresy. He performed the same service most fully in Gaul when he exercised there the same office of legate. For, after inspecting everything pertaining to divine worship, he found the archbishops of Lyons and Narbonne conspicuously negligent concerning their flocks, and, unmoved by any entreaties, deprived them both of their rank. Then, taking up arms against the heretics, he attacked the very strong castle of Vaux, their stronghold, and finally captured it by divine rather than human counsel.

He was present at Verona when Pope Lucius was dying; soon afterward, at Ferrara, he rendered the final office of charity to Urban III as he struggled with death. When the senate of cardinals, freely and willingly, offered the apostolic see to Henry, he did not assent to those offering it, but transferred the honour to Gregory VIII, whom he accordingly secured as the choice for supreme pontiff, a man without equal. After Gregory had then appointed him legate to all Christian princes with the greatest authority, Henry fulfilled that office, as was his custom, so abundantly that he reconciled Frederick himself—though he had so often treacherously relapsed—with Clement III, and personally marked with the military cross sixty-nine most illustrious warrior-princes.

A very learned man, while still abbot he wrote a discourse against the Albigensian heretics then beginning to spring up in Gaul; Baronius reports it in his *Annals*, vol. XII. Finally, this excellent and outstanding man was so universally esteemed that the author of the *Life of St Peter of Tarentaise* calls him the chief pillar among the pillars of Christ’s Church. And deservedly so, since he laboured for the Church until his last breath. Lastly, to place a fitting crown upon his most brilliant achievements, while undertaking his final legation in Belgium under Clement III, he brought peace by his prudence and counsel between the count of Flanders and the Church of Arras, who were fighting in an almost inextricable quarrel. Stricken himself by an incurable illness, when he sensed that the fateful hour was approaching, he ordered himself carried before the altar of St Andrew in the cathedral church. There, fortified by the sacraments, he breathed out his soul in the hands of the priests, on 4 July 1188. By his will, his body was carried back to Clairvaux and buried by the bishop of Langres between St Bernard and St Malachy, with this epitaph:

> Beneath this stone lies Henry, once well known to the world,  
> An abbot worthy of the Roman pivot;  
> Despising the slippery joys of the vain world,  
> He gave his mortal frame to earth and sent his soul back to heaven.

Many wrote the life and deeds of this most illustrious man, including Caesarius, his contemporary, in the *Book of Miracles*; the *Great Exordium of the Cistercian Order*, book II, chapters 3 and 21; and Vincent of Beauvais, book XXX, chapter 31. In the Cistercian Calendar he is entered among the blessed on 14 July. Besides Baronius, he is mentioned by Crantz, *Saxony*, book VII, chapter 5; Sirmond in his notes on Peter of Celle; Chrysostom Henriquez in the *Fasciculus of Saints of the Cistercian Order* and in the *Menologium* for this day; Montalvus; and many others. Henry wrote against the Albigensian heretics. His work is extant in vol. XII of Baronius’s *Annals*.

[Col. 0213]

## ANOTHER NOTICE

(D. BERTRAND TISSIER, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, Bonfontaine, 1660, folio, vol. III, at the beginning.)

This distinguished prelate, born to noble parents at Château-Marçay near Cluny, assumed the religious habit at Clairvaux while still a boy. Before four years had passed, he was first elected abbot of Hautecombe and, after several years, abbot of Clairvaux. He arranged for the body of St Bernard, whom Alexander III had shortly before numbered among the saints of heaven, to be placed in the marble tomb where it still rests. As the renown of his virtues spread far and wide, he was beloved by all—by kings and princes no less than by religious persons and prelates.

He was elected bishop of Toulouse and shortly afterward head of the Cistercian order, but declined both dignities. Personally summoned by Clement III to the Lateran Council, he was unwillingly made cardinal and consecrated bishop of Albano; he was immediately sent as legate, with full authority from the Holy See, to the provinces beyond the mountains. He deposed the archbishops of Lyons and Narbonne and reformed, insofar as he could, the black monks and many prelates of churches. He captured, not without a miracle, the exceptionally fortified castle of the heretics called Vaux; he apprehended and convicted the leaders of error and compelled them publicly to abjure heresy.

Thereafter he visited and bestowed gifts upon his beloved Clairvaux. Having returned to Rome, not long after the death of Urban III, when by the votes of many cardinals he was designated supreme pontiff, he could not be induced to consent to his election. Instead, taking up the office of preaching the cross, he left the city and signed with the cross the emperor, sixty-nine princes, many others, and also the kings of France and England—that is, by conferring the badge of the cross he bound them to holy war and to the relief of the Holy Land.

When he came to Liège, more than sixty-six clerics, moved and compunct by his preaching, resigned their benefices to him for fear of their simony. Then, so that every stain of simony might be absent, he restored those benefices to the same men, by his full authority, as though they had been newly conferred. Finally, setting out for Flanders, he restored peace between the count of that province and the Church of Arras. There he was taken ill; having received the sacraments of the Church before the altar of St Andrew at Arras, to which he had wished to be carried, he piously fell asleep in the Lord. From there his body was conveyed to Clairvaux, as he had commanded, and placed between the altars and tombs of Saints Malachy and Bernard. These facts are from a tablet hung on his tomb, which does not specify the certain year of his death, but reports that he died about 1186. Yet since his friend Geoffrey wrote him a notable letter, extant in Baronius under the year 1188, he seems to have survived for several years thereafter.

[Col. 0215]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 211.)

Henry of Château-Marçay, abbot of Hautecombe in Savoy in 1161 and of Clairvaux in 1177, of the Cistercian order, afterward bishop of Albano, or Albanensis, in the Roman Campagna under Alexander III in 1179, and cardinal and apostolic legate under Gregory VIII, died in 1188. On him see Ughelli, vol. I, p. 254 ff.; the Sammarthani, vol. IV, pp. 31 and 256; and Oudin, vol. II, p. 1559.

The following writings of his are extant in the third volume of Bertrand Textor, or Tissier’s, *Cistercian Library*: *Commentary, or Sermons, on the Pilgrim City of God*; *Declaration against the Albigensians*, also extant from Baronius under the year 1178, nos. 29–37, in book II of Chrysostom Henriquez’s *Fasciculus of Saints of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 25; and *Letters to Various Persons*, to be compared with the eleven letters which Edmund Martène published from a Clairvaux manuscript in vol. I of his *Anecdota*, p. 576 ff.

There has recently been added *Censure of the Morals and Corruption among Clerics and Priests of His Time*, published by Johann Peter von Ludewig in *Reliquiae manuscriptorum et diplomatum ineditorum*, vol. II, pp. 437, 441; and the letters in which he summons the prelates of Germany to an assembly to deliberate concerning holy war against the Saracens, ibid., pp. 449–452. Among the letters published by Martène in vol. I of the *Vetera Monumenta* is likewise read his edict, subsequently published by Johann Peter von Ludewig in vol. II of his *Reliquiae*, under this title: *Censure of the Morals and Corruption among Clerics and Priests of His Time*. In Ludewig, however, these letters are fuller than in Martène; conversely, Martène’s texts are much more correct than Ludewig’s. It should further be noted that Ludewig’s letters are not complete, but have attached at their end another fragment of a letter, perhaps by another author and written on a different subject. MANSI.

[Col. 0215]

## LETTERS OF LORD HENRY, FORMERLY ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, LATER BISHOP OF ALBANO

(D. TISSIER, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, vol. III, p. 252.)

### I. To Pope Alexander III

*Sent to preach the holy war, he reports that Count Henry of Champagne has taken the cross, and commends the count’s land or principality to the pope.*

[Col. 0215A]

That you may reap in joy and exultation what you have sown in pious concern, we bring to your notice, holy Father, that the charge entrusted to us by apostolic authority has, through the merit of your faith, produced in some persons fruits sweet and acceptable to God. Thus, the execution of a good work delights us, and you certainly ought not to regret so useful and saving a command.

For the illustrious Count Henry, our most special prince and lord of the land through which we travel, touched with compunction and inspired by the Lord, [Col. 0215B] was the first to take up the banners of salvation. Offering the Lord the sacrifice worthy of a voluntary oblation, he has made himself a leader to the rest in emulation of this pious undertaking. Already joyful shoots are springing afresh in the garden of his heart; already the sunny greenery of his future fruitfulness [Col. 0216A] is growing bright. We who perceive in him the fragrance of good hope therefore exult and rejoice in him, as in the scent of a field full of blessing, which the Lord has blessed.

Recently, at the approaching sacred observances of the Lord’s Nativity, he received with pious devotion from the hand of your legate the sign of the life-giving cross, and anticipated the joy of the public solemnity with a festival of unexpected gladness. Thus it might deservedly be sung also concerning him: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). Behold, therefore, we humbly prostrate before you prayers of most earnest devotion on his behalf, asking that you remember to surround with the protection of apostolic defence his land, which he has entrusted to your patronage with great confidence. Thus, whoever should devise any injury against it during the prince’s absence [Col. 0216B] may be assured that he will incur your indignation. For the care of the holy apostolate is bestowed upon no one more justly than upon him who takes up his cross and, through so many perils by sea and land, follows the Lord of the cross.

### II. To Abbot Buscalon

*He desires Buscalon to come to Clairvaux, and asks him to meet him at Hautecombe, where Henry had been abbot.*

[Col. 0217A]

Behold, I, your persistent lover, keep watch at the door of your heart, crying out in letters and troubling you with prayers, so that your disposition may rise, even overcome by importunity, and open to us the bolt of its hidden will. For we believe that this will is ready through virtue, though delayed by an obstacle; it longs to find a way to come forth, if the hardness of a resisting impediment does not stand in its way.

But I cannot understand what it means that, though I have often written to you, I have not merited even once a reply from you—unless I greatly fear that you have utterly forgotten me, since no letter at least from the beloved returns to my affection as it seeks the one [Col. 0217B] it loves. Yet, impatient of delay, I overlook your delays and silence, flattering myself, perhaps, that while you postpone these wishes, you are arranging the expedients of the best recompense.

Whatever it is that torments me while you delay, meanwhile our mind neither sleeps nor grows cold in affection, seeking him whom my soul loves, that, holding him, I may hold him and not let him go until I bring you into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me. Then my beloved shall see and flow toward her; he shall marvel, and his heart shall be enlarged, when Clairvaux goes out to him, rejoicing and exulting in her children, and meets him like an honoured mother. Then perhaps he will even mock me, saying: “We no longer believe because of your speech” [Col. 0217C] (John 4), for “as we have heard, so have we seen.” We have seen and known her of whom our fathers told us.

Awaken, then, at last the grace that you have within you, lest what was given you for the gaining of nations and multitudes of peoples be buried in one corner of the mountains. He will come who demands the profit of his talents, assuredly requiring an account, should he find the quantity of the precious gift lying idle beneath the buried turf of Bulcoldon [reading uncertain; perhaps Buscalon]. Therefore, if there is in you any compassion, any fellowship of spirit, any praise of discipline, meet me at Hautecombe when I come, that there at least the secret chamber of a mind may be opened—a mind that has grown stiff through so great a slowness of delay.

### III. To Pope Alexander

*He asks the pope not to make him bishop of the Church of Toulouse.*

[Col. 0217D]

The authority of the Doctor of the Gentiles proves, and our own weakness continually experiences, that “no one knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit that is within him” (1 Corinthians 2). Yet even that spirit is darkened in discerning its own inner things unless it is assisted by another Spirit—namely, that of which the Apostle says: “The Spirit helps our weakness” (Romans 8). For he alone, who searches all things, even the depths of God—he alone, I say—understands the hidden things of the human heart and distinguishes the powers and capacities of individuals by a singular and proper virtue.

I say this, most loving Father, so that you may believe no one concerning me when he says what is above me, since my own spirit bears witness to me—[Col. 0218A] the intimate examiner of my own insufficiency, neither ignorant of my powers nor unaware of my feeble weakness. Know, therefore, Father, and believe, that whatever grace or strength is in me to any degree, or is supposed to be in me, is wholly to be attributed to the merits of those over whom, in preserving the law of the Lord, I confess myself unworthily set in authority. Everything that I can do is owed to their benefit; whatever I have received shall be assigned to their use. If by any usurpation I defraud them of any part of it, I fear that what is taken from them in part may more deservedly be taken from me in full.

It is therefore far better and safer for me continually to fulfil among them the duties of the service laid upon me than, taking what belongs to them, to roam in wandering change from nation to nation. When would I become fit to govern untamed nations ignorant of the divine law, when I am not sufficient even to administer those who confer more upon me through discipline than they receive from me through teaching? These men, running swiftly along the paths of justice, willingly make their way toward the paths of life; those others, however, have made a covenant with death and summoned it with their hands and words.

Nevertheless, even to die for those others will be most ready for me at your command: I am prepared, according to my strength, for everything that may be enjoined against the heresies of that region, provided only that I be spared the election to the episcopate which they imagine for me there. Therefore I ask and entreat, through the gentleness of our Redeemer, that whatever others may suggest to you—perhaps hastening to remove farther from their manner of life the stings of customary correction—your fatherhood nevertheless not separate me from those to whom I seem to be joined by divine ordination, [Col. 0218C] nor compel me again to look toward the heights of this world, since long ago I chose to consent to the lowly in the house of the Lord.

May I find mercy in your sight, I pray, so that I may not be delayed from attending this council through the occasion of fear; that I may be able to lay before you, as vicar of Christ Jesus and supreme watchman of the tower of David, certain matters especially discovered, which, God willing, may redound to the benefit of all. Is it so important to direct attention only to converting the three Toulousain tribes and the dregs of Gascony that many other matters are neglected—matters for which you can, if you believe, and ought to provide, even to the ends of the earth, for the salvation of many peoples? Indeed, the Church of Toulouse itself, unless help is provided for it from elsewhere, will meanwhile suffer serious loss; for if you compel me, I shall flee as far as I can, even though I shall not escape your hands.

### IV. To the Same

*He asks the pope to grant the bearer of this letter as bishop to the Irish.*

There is in the island of Ireland a man venerable in life, Christian both in faith and name, who has hitherto exercised the highest priesthood among that barbarous people and remotest nation, and is further distinguished with titles of legation. Now, worn out by infirmity and old age, he has conceived a desire for rest and release from office, alleging, indeed, his failing age, since he sees the end of life standing at his door. Thus, a mature soldier, discharged after the various triumphs of lawful combat, seeks to conclude the week of his former labour with the Sabbath of rest and finally to dedicate what remains of his life to spiritual leisure.

Having therefore resigned the episcopal office which he held, he desires that the venerable man—namely, the bearer of this letter—be ordained his successor, so that he may not leave without consolation the nation among which he has laboured hitherto. The clergy, people, and magnates of his land have elected this man. Although we desire to be such helpers in the observances of the Order, and by no means to become bishops in ecclesiastical functions, we are nevertheless induced not to withhold our consent from this present matter. We fear for that barbarous nation lest their natural savagery easily revive if, from the fervour of spiritual men, they grow cold into the sluggishness [Col. 0219B] of laxer discipline. Therefore, if this also seems good to you, we ask that you effectively assent to the wishes and desires of the aforesaid bishop, both in granting his release and in ordaining this man. Whatever must be done, know that both the length of the journey and the scantiness of his resources prevent him from making a longer delay.

### V. To the King of England

*He praises the king of England, among other things because he had resolved to roof the church of Clairvaux with lead, and for this purpose sends him the measurement of the church.*

From the day when, God inspiring you, it pleased you to open the bosom of royal [Col. 0219C] favour for the redemption of our friendship, and when the summit of so great an eminence stooped down, an unceasing and uninterrupted remembrance of you has occupied the seat of our heart. It allows us neither to grow cold in our love for you nor to cease from proclaiming your glory.

Gascony and the noble city of Toulouse, which we recently visited at the direction of your magnanimity, bear witness how, through our mouth on every occasion of public and private discourse alike, the splendid virtue of your majesty resounded; and how amid the spread darkness, so to speak, of a wandering multitude, the brightness both of your faith and of your piety shone forth. Then, having returned to our own place, we set forth the kindness of this same piety of yours in familiar account to our household; and, when abbots had assembled from various parts of the world, we announced with a certain solemn [Col. 0219D] and festive joy the abundance of royal generosity.

Among the other acts by which you have hitherto preserved and continue to preserve the enlargement and security of the Order, we made a point of recounting not only what you had bestowed but also what you had promised, so that favours already received might be remembered more gratefully, while greater things might be hoped for in the future from your generous promise. In particular, we proclaimed with greater praise that most ample gift which you promised in our hands for our Clairvaux: namely, that through a sheet of lead, supplied at your expense for the roofing of our oratory, the devotion burning in your breast might shine above our roofs.

All accepted this and rendered worthy thanks to God. After deliberation, we resolved to send you the measurement of our oratory, without measure of prayers, [Col. 0220A] earnestly beseeching and crying to the Lord that, in return for the beauty of his house which you enlarge on earth, he may restore to you an eternal house not made by hands in heaven.

### VI. To the Same

*He says that St Bernard was commemorated at his first feast, that the king’s presence was desired, and sends him a finger of St Bernard.*

A day honourable and solemn was celebrated among us, joyful because of a new feast and festive because of its abundant joy. For the elevation of the most sacred body of Blessed Bernard made it most celebrated for us and suffused it with brighter light. Oh, how we wished for the presence of your majesty at those joys, which were indeed more heavenly than earthly, so that the splendour of so great a festival might gain an increase of principal glory for us, and that a more abundant outpouring of richer blessing might flow to you from the merits of that most illustrious confessor.

But since the vast distance of a most remote region denied us this, we turned our desires to a spiritual remedy and, God being gracious, ensured that, although your presence was absent, your remembrance there was not without effect. For we solemnly impressed your name, with the distinctions of your piety, upon the affections, as was fitting, of your brethren and the hearts of your sons. Receiving it with great devotion, they might in a manner offer it to the gaze of the holy Father and present it in the secret chamber of the heavenly court.

Moreover, lest the occasion of bodily absence should deprive the royal treasuries of participation in the gift discovered, we send you an honourable portion from the treasury [Col. 0220C] of his relics, judging it altogether unworthy that the piety of so great a prince should be deprived of participation in such sanctity. Receive, therefore, a finger of that sacred hand. Because the righteous man shook from it every gift of earthly profit, God, as was fitting, filled it with the most abundant supply of heavenly blessing. I mean that hand whose touch healed the sick, strengthened the weak, made people firm, and put demons to flight. That hand laid the first stone in the foundations of our Clairvaux, whose roofs you propose to provide.

It has been our care carefully to seal what is sent in a little vessel, lest either the treasure deposited there be exposed to harm by frequent openings, or some deceit of pious fraud creep in through an impulse of devout theft [Col. 0220D].

### VII. From the Lord of Cîteaux to Henry and the Abbot of Morimond

*Henry and the abbot of Morimond are appointed by the lord of Cîteaux to visit the monastery of La Colombe.*

The contentions and quarrels which the fury of evil desire has stirred up in the monastery of La Colombe have come to our notice and that of our brethren, striking us with a most grievous wound—both because serious danger consequently threatens the administration of that house and because the honour of our Order has been violated, an honour which abhors in all its professed members the plague of familial dissension and domestic hostility.

Therefore, desiring a suitable remedy for so great an evil to be brought speedily, [Col. 0221A] we charge and command your diligence that both of you go together to the place and, with the strictest care, perform our office in the visitation. In the presence of Abbot I., first punish each person’s wickedness among the rebellious and disobedient members of his house, imposing on each an appropriate penalty according to the measure of the fault. Thus zeal for the Order may commend you yourselves, and the rash perversity of the proud may learn no longer to kick uselessly against the goad of the Order.

In particular, let the sentence of deposition be directed principally against the prior of that house, who was not afraid to retain the priorate contrary to the command of his Father; for he is not worthy to preside over others who has contumaciously withdrawn himself from the will of the abbot. But since, taking account of the man’s character, we judge that the abbot himself ought to be released, we wish both of you together, privately and carefully, to admonish him to ask humbly, in his chapter and before you, for dismissal from the office that he bears. Let him, as it were, bind you by his own importunity, so that by a kind of compulsion he may obtain the remedy of release.

### VIII. To the Community of Savigny

*He exhorts the monks of Savigny to frugality because of the apparent present poverty of their house.*

Blessed be God and Father of lights, from whom all good things proceed, who has granted your Father, Lord Abbot W., full faith in obedience and strength in action. Thus, with a father’s care for you, he is diligent and labours in every way [Col. 0221C] that your house may not suffer hardship beyond its accustomed measure. The Lord has clothed him with power from on high and strengthened his hand with might, so that, when we compare the past with the present, we are plainly given to understand that what he feared belonged to human faint-heartedness, whereas what is proving strong in action belongs to a heavenly gift.

We therefore ask you and admonish you as dearest sons to support his hand with the aid of prayer and obedience, yourselves running after him in the fragrance of his virtue and following his footsteps with a peaceful step. Act so that his soul may be pleased in you and his heart delight in your deeds; for then the cloudiness of lukewarmness is easily dispelled, if the serenity of charity breathes upon us.

Moreover, if it should be necessary for something to be restricted even in your daily provisions, do not immediately embitter the spirit of the man of God by murmuring over the expense of a diminished allowance. Rather, anticipate him yourselves by an unasked offering of monastic frugality. For it is never sufficiently raised to the summit of its profession unless, after every superfluity has been cut away, it is confined within the limits of utmost necessity. That community serves spiritual progress which, for the sake of the common good, renounces the harmful desires of its own will even in matters that seemed necessary. This is what you must now especially emulate and do, when nothing else is sought by this restraint except that your house may hereafter be enlarged for your abundant use.

### IX. To Pope Alexander

*He protests concerning the monks of Dol, who had extorted tithes by armed force from the monks of the House of God, of the Cistercian Order, and had even wounded some of them.*

[Col. 0222A]

Unpunished rashness rises without measure, and licence not restrained by the rule of law always struggles against just claims. The grossly savage presumption of the monks of Dol demonstrates this. During the past harvest they burst into the field of the brethren of the House of God, inflicting plunder upon their crops and injury upon the brethren, without first giving any warning that, if anything was due to them by right of tithe, it might come to them peacefully or by judicial process.

But these men trusted in arms rather than laws. They violently entered, amid the clash of weapons, upon those industrious brethren who rejoiced before the Lord beneath the burden of the day and heat, like men in harvest. They enjoyed, indeed, the dangerous delight with which plunderers exult when, after seizing booty, they divide the spoils. Some of them laid violent hands upon lay brothers and monks and polluted with the blood of the poor those sacred right hands which they had come to profane by the sacrilege of tithes.

And what will you do concerning these things, most blessed Father? While you preside, can that remain uncorrected among monks which the sacred canons most severely punish in tyrants? Can any justice in the exaction of these tithes belong to men who have not feared to anticipate justice and judgment by a bloody wrong? Indeed, even previously they had no justice at all in this matter, since long ago, after receiving an adequate exchange, they possessed a permanent commutation for this tithe, recorded in documents and confirmed by the subscription of the founder of the house.

We therefore beg the renowned mercy of your clemency to exact such punishment upon these evildoers that they shall no longer harass our brethren by any demand for this tithe, nor dare again to take up arms against unarmed souls.

### X. To the Same

*He complains that the abbot of Dijon disregards the pope’s decrees concerning a certain house of the Order, and asks him to increase his severity against the contumacious man.*

The ground of ambiguity and distrust is opened up if the Church, which is the mother of faith, is despised in her ordinances. Let Rome cease to promulgate what it decrees if it is permitted to oppose her decrees with impunity. We remember, most merciful Father, and recall with thanksgiving, how diligently and effectively you promoted the affair of the little house of Morans. By now the case would have reached its conclusion had not the notorious obstinacy of the abbot of Dijon overstepped the bounds of your command.
