But behold, a man has been found who prefers to perish rather than yield, preferring to be separated from divine functions rather than defeated in his factions. Yet we trust in the Lord and in the steadfastness of your strength that iniquity will at last lie to itself, and that continual vexation will grant understanding to one from whom accursed greed removes counsel. This man has now received a third letter of command from you, in which every appeal is removed from him, lest the pursuit of her right be taken from that poor little house. Through the bishop of Langres he is now held under sentence of interdict by your justice, since he refuses to relinquish what he is convicted of holding through his injustice.

But what are we doing? He does not believe the word of the first sign unless he is still struck by the blow of a heavier wound in a mighty hand. Therefore, gracious Father, grant to your voice a voice of power, and work again with us a sign for good, so that the rebellious may be ashamed and unbelievers confounded; and so that they may alike know and understand how perilously and foolishly they resist apostolic decrees. If any of them should irreverently thrust themselves into your presence, remember the sentence of excommunication under which [Col. 0223B] they lie, so that they may be either admitted by you or dismissed by you only as befits you.

### XI. To the Same

*He laments certain vices of Gaul which the cardinal of St Chrysogonus has begun to uproot, and prays that the time allowed him for returning may therefore be extended.*
Among the other evils by which the ancient splendor of the Church has grown foul in the regions of Gaul, we lament the collapse of chastity and the ruin of faith. For we see that in these evil days the chaste simplicity of devout belief is excluded, while the spotless purity of the simple is polluted by vices pouring in from every side. One remedy alone remains against these deadly monstrosities: that the rigor of apostolic discipline may not grow slack, and that, amid the abounding wickedness of others, the charity of the Roman See may not grow cold. [Col. 0223C]

For if a spirit coming from the south should revive this charity with the warm breath of gentle fervor, the whole body of the Church would immediately be warmed by a heavenly fire; and, shaking off the sloth of harmful torpor, its languishing members would recover strength unto the glory of their own vigor. Meanwhile, therefore, let the gaze of your holy contemplation, from the lofty watchtower on which it stands, attend carefully to the tunic of the true Joseph. Let it consider whether this is indeed that garment which the Father made for him, wholly untried by stain and untouched by any tearing. In our regions this garment is stained and torn, because it is subjected to a twofold mockery, dishonored alike by the blemish of depravity and by the wrinkle of error. By a kind of two-headed river, both heresies and vices have flowed into it, so that, while in many places it is defiled through the impurity of life, in others it is torn by the rending of unbelief. [Col. 0223D]

For from the ashes of Sodom there has arisen the worm of ancient lust, which, emerging from the lake of damnation after rains of fire and showers of sulphur, infects the western regions with the blasts of its stench. Arius too has revived in the western lands: though condemned in his own person by an eastern judgment, he has now occupied the furthest regions in his successors. “Outside, the sword slays; and within, there is death likewise.” For heretics publicly dispute against the faith; and many do in secret what would wound both the modesty of the writer and the decency of the reader. But why do we say “in secret”? They proclaim their sin like Sodom, and, as though in the suburbs of Gomorrah, invite the companions of their lusts to sin. Shall not your zeal be indignant at these things? Shall they sin with impunity, [Col. 0224A] while you remain silent?

It is time for the friend of the Bridegroom to avenge the injuries done to the Bride, and for the sword of Phinehas the priest to be drawn against the incest of the Israelite and the Midianite woman. Behold: in your days, by the Lord’s authorship, schisms have been calmed. Well done, good shepherd: see that heresies too are lulled to rest. For in the regions of Gaul you have a man whom we have found to be a friend of justice and truth, Lord P., cardinal of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. In one election alone, as I myself can testify, he vigorously refused five hundred marks of silver, lest under the pretext of a gift he should turn aside from the path of truth.

Therefore, having drawn from him a remedy of very great consolation, we glorify God and the Father; and in him we also magnify you, seeing that the favor of illustrious dignities, which flows from the fountain of your fullness, is by apostolic discernment bestowed upon persons such as these—persons proved worthy of lofty honors by the merit of their lives. [Col. 0224B] Hence arises matter for your joy; hence springs the source of consolation for the Church of God: that you admit to a share in your solicitude men who honor in you the fullness of power. This man proves what we have said: that your judgment concerning him has not erred, since he shows himself as fit for the weight of the burden as he is found to be free from ambition for honor.

He is one whom humility exalts and frugality enriches; burdensome to none, he has become dear and useful to all. He fights steadfastly with the beasts at Ephesus, putting on Simon Peter against the Simon Magi; and, offering a new Elisha to Syria’s lepers, he uproots and destroys, builds and plants. Thus he drives out from the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts the little foxes that destroy it, [Col. 0224C] so that he also excludes from Solomon’s own wardrobe the moths that consume it. Blessed be God, whose Church, with you acting as midwife, has brought forth such a son: one who accords with his Father’s honor and does not fall away from his Mother’s nobility.

We therefore ask that you permit him to remain against the aforesaid pests for a longer period of time. Most of our leading men agree in this request: until care has been provided for the wounds just mentioned, this man should not be withdrawn from our regions, since for this very purpose he ought to have been sent even to the most distant parts. This is especially so since the Lord has at this time touched the hearts of kings, who, their covenant of peace having been confirmed among themselves, agree in nothing better or holier than in pursuing the heretical multitude, clothed with the breastplate of faith. [Col. 0224D]

But because, according to the Gospel’s word, it is necessary that there be two swords here, we consider it worthy and honorable for you that your own emulation should accompany the zeal of secular princes, lest their pious purpose fail through some occasion, should it not receive timely support from your cooperation. It is expedient, therefore, that, by granting the said cardinal suitable extensions of time, you give him special instructions to arm himself magnanimously against the enemies of charity and faith. For in many regions wickedness has now overflowed so greatly that “as is the people, so is the priest”; or rather, the pestilence of the flocks spreads from the contagion of the shepherds themselves.

Let the consideration of so great a necessity excuse the delays of the man of God and the postponement of his appointed return. For although his presence would not undeservedly be pleasing to you, such an absence makes him welcome to all who fear God. [Col. 0225A] By God’s favor, he will return to you when a suitable time has been secured; and he will bring spiritual mandrakes from the field of this world, which already spread fragrance at our gates and will exhale abundant sweetness for you, to the envy of Rachel herself. Meanwhile, let him pursue, as he has most excellently begun, the sinners of Amalek and drive the ancient Jebusites from the city of the Lord, so that, when he comes to you and knocks, they may immediately open to him, and he may enter into the joy of his great Lord.

## XII. To the Black Monks of Flanders

He endeavors to soothe their disturbed feelings over the withdrawal of the abbot of Ham to a monastery of the Cistercian order.

[Col. 0225B]

My soul is troubled within me, wasting away in the bitterness of inborn grief, because, as is said, a storm of grave agitation has stirred your minds against us, and a great spirit of tempests has roared in the depth of devout hearts. First, therefore, the south wind must be entreated to come: may it cool, with the tempering of a gentler breeze, the pot of indignation set ablaze by the blowing north wind; and, spreading charity in the midst of Solomon’s chamber, may it bring the storm of holy minds back to the level ground of tranquil peace.

But if anything has now been done, whether in deed or word, by which your kindness has been provoked or your advantage diminished, I shall defend no guilt by a shameless excuse. I submit myself to your judgment in voluntary satisfaction. Especially because, when a case is determined before merciful judges, it is not so dangerous to pay the debt of punishment as wickedly to deny the offense. Therefore it belongs to you to weigh the burden of examination in the just balance of discernment, so that pardon may be granted to one who confesses, while offense is not imputed to the innocent. [Col. 0225C]

This is true, and I do not deny it at all: when I was formerly staying in your region—where, as I recount with thanksgiving, the abundance of your charity showed itself toward me more generously—the venerable man G., abbot of Ham, came to visit us in order to establish friendship with me, and bound me to himself, as I gladly consented, in the bond of mutual love. And when conversation concerning spiritual advancement passed between us, he disclosed the secret of his intention, saying that he had conceived in his mind the plan of joining a colony of our order and bringing with him others who would follow him.

Thereupon he also offered the house which he governed, judging, evidently, that he had not taken sufficient thought for himself unless he raised, with an equal religious commitment, the house he had governed thus far to the eminence of the order to which he himself would migrate. I hesitated, I confess, and was astonished at the consideration of the difficulty. Then, having reviewed every obstacle in my mind, I advised against pursuing the undertaking. Finally, softened by the abbot’s insistence, I suspended the whole matter through an uncertain delay. [Col. 0225D]

Moreover, I both avoided the presence and declined the conversation of the count of Flanders, whom the abbot had summoned concerning this business, both to promote it and to prevent it, lest through the arrival of his encouragement I should, unawares, commit something hasty and later needing correction. In all this, judge for yourselves what sin I have committed—unless perhaps it was that I did not immediately report the beginnings of the case to your notice, so that what ought to have been prudently brought to completion by me with your counsel was later rashly undertaken, as is known, by Abbot G. in devout zeal.

Yet in this matter also God is my witness: it was neither done through me nor on my behalf that he rashly occupied that house, which he soon vacated by dying. Thus, if we have something in him that might move us to anger, we nevertheless do not lack something that may incline us to pardon. Especially because fault ought to be punished gently when zeal for religion could urge on a work of danger. [Col. 0226A] He should therefore be spared by you also, because—to speak as one addressing spiritual men—what he intended for the benefit of those brothers he did not believe would harm you.

Now therefore, best Fathers and most beloved brothers, remove, I beg you, anger from your hearts and sadness from ours, lest any root of bitterness springing up between us corrupt the claims of charity recently begun or hinder the abundant fruits of grace growing on both sides. For I am yours in the inward affection of Christ Jesus, intending to give you no offense, always ready and prepared for reconciliation.

## XIII. To the Bishop of Chalon

He congratulates him upon his recent elevation to the bishopric of Chalon and commends to him a certain business concerning the monastery of Longivadi.

[Col. 0226C]

A good word proceeding from the Lord fittingly gladdens us concerning your election, since it also exalts us together in your love. For we rejoice when those whom we love ascend to higher things, especially those from whose manner of life we may presume that lofty heights of dignity come to them as a sign of grace and an operation of virtue. But from you we draw a special joy in this promotion: for it offers material for exultation by which the merits of preceding grace may be joined in a bond of closer friendship.

For that Church receives you as its shepherd, through which the mother of the order will have you as bishop; so that, through the kinship of spiritual grace descending in the line of subjection, [Col. 0226D] we shall henceforth possess the heart of a kindly Father in one in whom we have hitherto had the goodwill of a simple friend. Moreover, as we confidently hope, you will assist our aforesaid Mother all the more and preserve all her rights, inasmuch as from the infancy of your life you have learned from her to emulate the purpose of devout religious life.

Therefore the power of heaven must be invoked for you in devout prayers: may it advance the beginnings of this work in enduring well-being; and, where it has multiplied the weight of the burden, may it also enlarge and extend the increase of virtue. But that these very first beginnings of your advancement may be supported everywhere by happy omens, we ask your prudence to remember both our connection and your own honor in the affair of Longivadi, providing, at our intercession, that this affair may be directed to the peace and benefit of that house. [Col. 0227A]

If, therefore, you have received any letters, whether from us or from others, which set against the aforesaid house the exception of a dissolved agreement, return them to us as a great favor. You will do what is pleasing and acceptable to our heart if you free the house of Longivadi from the peril of this lawsuit.

## XIV. To Lord Hyacinth, Cardinal

He excuses himself for not yet having shown him honor, apparently by letter.

We, who have hitherto greatly neglected to seek your friendship and favor, humble ourselves in every way before your honor, so that pardon ought to be granted for our neglect. Yet every suspicion of contempt is far from us. [Col. 0228A] For although we are such that, amid many occupations, we sometimes neglect certain things, may God avert from us such great madness as to despise any of those set over us.

Among others, however, we honor you with so much the humbler reverence as we have never, with any doubt born of feigned uncertainty, questioned that your excellence surpasses very many others. Therefore, asking at the feet of your glory pardon for our past neglect, we beg that at last the entrance to your friendship be opened to us. If it please you, let it grant us this first fruit of its favor: that it remove the burden and vexation of the election that has been made concerning you. Indeed, you will bind me to yourself anew if you free me from this danger. May your exalted station flourish.

[Col. 0227] The following letters were published by Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 570, from a Clairvaux manuscript.

## XV. Petitionary Letter to a Prelate

He commends his order to him, and especially the house of Al.

[Col. 0227B]

To the venerable man and his friend Christian R., by God’s grace subject of the Holy Roman Church and bishop-elect of Lausanne, Henry, servant of the poor of Clairvaux, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

It was grievous and distressing to us that we were absent when your presence was once shown to our house. We had long desired both to be refreshed there by your conversation and delighted by your sight. May the Lord grant us the recompense we desire, so that what we then lost through our absence we may make good with the interest of a long presence. We also greatly desire that place and time may be given to us in which what is inwardly felt by affection may at last be shown toward you by deeds of affection. [Col. 0227C]

Furthermore, we ask you to remember the hope which we have conceived chiefly in and concerning you: that you too ought to love with hereditary charity our order, which the lord pope—who is your father—loves and protects with such piety; and that, by the example and imitation of so great a pontiff, you should show yourself to us as his successor in this favor.

We especially commend to you, with repeated prayers, the house of Al. We ask by every means that you show yourself such a patron to it that it may all the more happily call itself blessed as it rests more singularly under the protection of him whom it had desired. But if any matter of litigation or cause of dispute has arisen between you and it because you believed that certain vineyards which it possesses should be recalled to your control, grant the brothers a suitable delay until we speak together and establish a settlement without setting any limit to charity. [Col. 0227D]

## XVI. Petitionary Letter to a Bishop

He commends to him the monasteries of his order within the bishopric of León.

To the dearest lord and Father, D., by God’s grace bishop of León, [Col. 0228B] H., servant of the poor of Clairvaux: greeting, and such prayers as he can offer.

With a distinguished man of kindly merits, such as we trust you to be, there is no need of a long preface or many flattering words in order to obtain what is justly requested, especially where God is recognized as concerned in the matter. Therefore we do not wish to delay you longer with elaborate persuasion; rather, we lay before you in simple and unadorned speech what we ask of your holiness.

It is known that within your bishopric there are very many new foundations of our order, which greatly need the continual watering of your protection and assistance. We desire, therefore, that all of these be commended to your fatherhood—especially those known to belong more particularly [Col. 0228C] to our own house. Let it therefore be the concern of your piety and prudence to love, cherish, and uphold these monasteries for the love of God and in response to our supplication. For if you attend to them graciously and piously, all their progress will surely redound to your own honor and glory.

And that we may find you more helpful and more devoted in such praiseworthy diligence, we grant you a share in the prayers and benefactions that are to be performed in our house until the end.

## XVII. Petitionary Letter to a Prince

He commends to him the monastery of Perosa.

Our poor and humble daughter, the house of Perosa, [Col. 0228D] begs from the generosity of a more fertile soil the fruits which harsher ground among rocks does not produce. Since it has nothing near at hand by which it may be sustained, it is compelled to seek the alms of its livelihood from afar. Therefore, when it found under the shadow of your wings some remedy, however slight, for its support, it established itself with great anxiety beside you, less secure in the fertility of the soil than concerned with the abundance of your love that is to be extended.

[Col. 0229A] For it has perceived in you the fragrance of sweetness and grace, like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed. We therefore ask and entreat that, considering with due compassion both its poverty and its trust, you do not drive it away from your side. Thus, with mercy triumphing over judgment, you may the more confidently lay claim to heavenly things in proportion as you relinquish earthly things even where they are not owed. Let it know with Ruth the Moabite that it has come into the field of mighty Boaz, who did not merely refrain from driving away the foreign and unknown woman from gathering grain, but also granted her the means of fuller gain.

## XVIII. To …

He excuses himself for being unable to attend on the appointed day to settle the affair of Vallis-Lucentis.

[Col. 0229B]

We would gladly come, in accordance with your wish, on the day which you have appointed for the affair of Vallis-Lucentis, especially since affection for that house drew us and we had much to discuss with you. But that same day has been set for us at Langres to deal with the controversy of the monks of Dijon, a matter which you too desire to have settled with suitable speed. A guarantee has been given of equal submission to arbitration, to arbitrators whom we have determined to appoint for deciding the case. Thus we are not a little grieved that, because of the business mentioned above, you withdraw from us the abbot of Quincy, to whom the matter had been submitted along with the others.

We ask you to bear patiently our necessary retention of our two other abbots on the day of the case, especially since without them, being the appointed arbitrators, we cannot proceed in our matter. [Col. 0229C] But if after that day an opportunity permits us to be present at your aforesaid business, we shall not withhold our bodily presence from those from whom we are not absent in the earnestness of our will.

## XIX. On This Affair, to the Abbot of Trois-Fontaines

He entrusts him with his place in settling the affair of Vallis-Lucentis.

To his beloved and venerable fellow abbot A. of Trois-Fontaines, Henry, your servant among the poor of Clairvaux, greeting and every good.

Both the command of the lord of Cîteaux and the intimacy of that house itself had directed us to show our presence in the affair of Vallis-Lucentis. But because the day appointed for that affair had also been fixed for us for making peace between the monks of Dijon, we were compelled by our own necessity to leave undone what we acknowledge that we owe to fraternal charity. Yet one who provides a suitable representative through the care of a deputy does not altogether fail to discharge what he owes. Therefore, at the intervention of the abbot of Vallis-Lucentis, we ask your fraternity to fulfill our office: an undertaking all the more justly entrusted to you as, with God’s help, you will more diligently embrace every precaution for restoring peace and order. [Col. 0229D]

## XX. Petitionary Letter to the Pope

That he restrain religious outsiders and the nuns of Bellecombe, whose proximity impeded the pastures of the animals of Bénédiction-de-Dieu.

[Col. 0230A]

To the most holy Father and lord, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: H., little as he is.

Our poor house called Bénédiction-de-Dieu has been founded in a dry place of barren land; it is narrow in resources and weighed down by poverty, so that if it should lack pasture for its animals, it would at once also lack nourishment for its souls. But certain people of another religious observance and a different order have recently arisen. Though they have sheep and cattle abundant in their own holdings, they have brought in diverse herds and plentiful livestock to destroy the few sheep by which [Col. 0230B] our aforesaid house sustained, however poorly, its poverty.

Not only outsiders, but also the nuns of Bellecombe, heavily raid the pastures of the aforesaid house with their own herds and build new dwellings along the boundary of its granges. Therefore our brothers of that house beg, through our intercession, your clemency: by open letters addressed generally to all and specifically to the aforesaid nuns, let the incursions of such importunity be restrained, and let the pastures of the aforesaid brothers, under your protection, be free both from invasion and from the burden of that new building.

## XXI. To a Prelate

On the same matter.

[Col. 0230C]

To the dearest lord and friend, reverend Father [Note: [Col. 0229] Wichard, who was elevated from abbot of Pontigny to the see of Lyon in the year 1161], W., by God’s grace archbishop of Lyon: H., father of Clairvaux, greeting, and little as he is.

Your sons, our brothers of Bénédiction-de-Dieu, are distressed by the oppression of a new burden, because through the intrusion of many alien flocks of another religious observance and order their pastures are preoccupied; and in order to drive away the little sheep of those brothers, intolerable herds are amassed against them. But among the rest—or rather, before all the rest—the nuns of Bellecombe trouble the aforesaid brothers by a new building, erecting the structure of a recent dwelling on the boundary of their grange. Therefore we ask and entreat that the force of your authority [Col. 0230D] remove the pressure of this importunity and not permit the rights of our sons to perish at the hands of outsiders.

## XXII. To the Pope

That he alter an agreement, contrary to the institution of the order, made by the brothers of Fontenay with the monks of Flavigny.

To the lord pope.

Our brothers of Fontenay, harassed by the monks of Flavigny with continual disputes, were drawn by their desire for peace into a certain agreement, which, without consulting us, they accepted to the burden and prejudice of our order. The institution of our order does not permit us to render half-shares of dues from our own labors. Therefore we earnestly ask [Col. 0231A] your clemency to aid the brothers’ simplicity as shall seem fitting to you, writing to the monks of Flavigny that the unlawful agreement, which the institution of our order does not allow, be exchanged for the settlement of a suitable convention.

We especially commend the bearer to you with supplication, begging that you mercifully hear him in his just claims.

## XXIII. Petitionary Letter to a Prince

He complains of the vexations inflicted by the lord of Vangionis-Rivus.

Since I see myself as a pilgrim and exile in a foreign land, stripped of my former wealth and honors and deprived of all aid from relatives, this one remedy remained for the consolation of my old age: that the almighty Lord had allowed me to come and dwell in the place under your lordship, in which I had promised myself peace and security. [Col. 0231B] For as I love you from my heart, and as I trust in your piety and protection more than in any human being, so I had presumed that no evildoer would attack me while I lay hidden beneath the wings of your protection, as long as the Lord preserved you safe and sound.

But behold: as my sins deserve, one of your men strives to drive me from your land—a man who neither reveres God nor, as he should, values your request and command. The lord of Vangionis-Rivus displays his power against a leaf driven by the wind and pursues dry stubble; he continually persecutes my pitiable old age without compassion. [Col. 0231C] He daily destroys in every way, both personally and through his men, that little grange which your poor men of Clairvaux gave me for the use of my necessity and on whose construction I had expended every care and effort. He plunders and consumes the sheep, cattle, and all possessions there; he does not cease to afflict the brothers, servants, and residents with insults and blows. Finally, he recently took three horses from me, which, as I hear, he has already sold.

When the lay-brother who was master of the little grange was going to the market at Bar-sur-Aube the day before yesterday, that lord’s servants beat him on the public road—not without injury to your honor—and took his horse. If these things displease your nobility—indeed, since they do displease it—then, for the sake of your honor, restrain his malice and, according to the power granted you by God, compel him both to restore the losses and henceforth keep peace with us. [Col. 0231D] Otherwise I must make haste to flee and migrate anew, as a captive and fugitive, from this land, which out of all the world I had chosen as the place in which to die and rest, into another land.

## XXIV. Petitionary Letter to a King

He commends to him the house of M. in Ireland.

[Col. 0232A]

Although we do not doubt that the ears of your majesty are occupied with many great affairs, yet the many urgent needs arising among our brothers perhaps compel us to knock at your door more often than seems good in your eyes. Nevertheless, considering you a minister and cultivator of justice, and trusting that we have some access to your serenity, we confidently perform an embassy for our sons and brothers living under the hand of your protection.

We are therefore moved to lay before your excellence a lamentable complaint on behalf of the house of M., which is situated in the parts of Ireland subject to your rule. [Col. 0232B]

## XXV. A Friendly Letter to a Companion

It is certain, dearest friend, that our mortal and corruptible bodies are separated from one another by a most extensive stretch of lands, so that we are unable by any means to approach one another, speak with one another, console one another, or be concerned and pray for one another. Yet surely, if we are faithful in love and truthful in speech, it is our spirits that carry out every such matter: they approach; they speak with one another; they pray and are concerned for one another.

For when can my spirit forget yours? [Col. 0232C] When can the remembrance of you, of your love toward me, and of your tears for me be torn from my heart, even for a moment? Dearest friend, you have entered into my very heart and will not easily be drawn out. Even if at dawn you should take your wings, fly farther away, and dwell at the ends of the sea, I shall follow you there in spirit. There I shall visit you with whatever visitation I can: namely, with prayer and devout concern before him who has saved us because of the utterly certain hope that we have, and will save us because of the entirely true reality for which we hope.

Finally, though I am not permitted to visit you in this body as I would wish, I do not neglect to visit you by these written characters, through which I truly make known that you are today as dear to me as you were when you departed from us—dear then, and no less dear now. [Col. 0232D] You were welcome then, and are no less pleasing and welcome today, especially because, as I have learned from the mouth of the lord abbot, you make yourself acceptable to God and commendable to men.

I beg you, my dear friend: entangle yourself in these concerns, occupy yourself in these pursuits, exercise yourself in these cares. For the fruit will not be empty, nor will the reward be corruptible but incorruptible, if you persevere in them.

[Col. 0233] Chesne published the following four letters in *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, vol. IV, p. 485.

## XXVI. To the Bishop of Chalon

A letter of congratulation.

[Col. 0233A]

My spirit has regained strength in the Lord at the auspice of your happy promotion, which I judge to be acceptable to God, beneficial to you, useful to the Church, and shared by us both. For, if the union of charity between us is considered, I myself may in some way be understood to have been promoted, since through the bond of your love I am joined to your fatherhood in one heart and one soul.

Therefore we pray for happy progress and abundant success for the dignity bestowed upon you from heaven. We wish that it may claim for itself not private ambition but public benefit, and that through it we may be granted to carry sheaves of joy from the seed of justice. [Col. 0233B] And this, with divine grace going before, will come to pass for you if you accustom yourself more to benefit others than to rule over them, and if, in a spirit of emulous imitation, you show yourself a solicitous successor to your predecessor. For his liberality of mercy toward the needy overflowed so greatly that the severity of justice was always ready against tyrants.

I trust, dearest friend, that this very office was granted you by divine providence so that you might succeed in the work of care one whose example, both in life and action, would serve you as a mirror of holiness. You must therefore undertake the protection of churches, care for the poor, and defense of orphans. For by such sacrifices God is won.

And because what lies closer to the heart presses more urgently upon affection, [Col. 0233C] we make special mention of our Alta Cumba. Pour out prayers for it, and useful intercessions on its behalf, so that you may take upon your affections the care of it which I cannot lay aside at all. Know without any uncertainty that whatever favor and patronage you bestow upon it through your support will be regarded as bestowed particularly upon me.

## XXVII. To the Same

That he assist him in the election at Cîteaux.

Necessity proves a friend, and the splendor of help rendered makes clear the ardor of intimate charity. Therefore, if ever, now especially grant us proofs of your love, when Clairvaux is in pressing need and is threatened as well as we ourselves; here you may show both it and us the goodwill of your heart. [Col. 0233D]

For the urgency of the election at Cîteaux deeply distresses us, and surely must distress you too, lest, while many great persons compete for the Mother’s dignity, the Daughter fall into loss and harm. The brothers of that house press upon us, fearing that after we believed we had sailed our intact ship through the waves of the Toulouse storm, we may suffer shipwreck within sight of our harbor.

We therefore ask you, and in the cry of so great a necessity entreat you, to set aside every care and interrupt them for a time, and hasten your arrival to us, so that within the octave of the Nativity of the Lord we may enjoy your counsel and assistance in the Lord for this work. It seems to us—unless perhaps you think otherwise—that you ought to urge and persuade Durand to watch over the preservation of our peace with piety and prudence, and not incline his assent to contrary suggestions. [Col. 0234A]

## XXVIII. To Louis, King of the French

Concerning the Albigensian heretics.

To his most pious lord Louis, by God’s grace king of the French, Henry, poor [Col. 0234B] servant of the men of Clairvaux: an unfading crown of the eternal kingdom.

Among the other marks of faith and piety by which, among the other princes of the world, the summit of your eminence shines with singular and almost unique devotion, we embrace and praise in you the purpose of Christian zeal which you have conceived for eliminating the uncertainty of the heretics; so much so that, as we have heard, you have also drawn the mind of the king of the English to the same pious purpose.

Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift, from whose bounty it comes that, although placed on earth, you think of heavenly things. In these our days one man has been found in whom, contrary to the custom of princes, the remembrance of eternal things is especially awake. Therefore we, your poor men of Clairvaux, do not cease diligently to pray to God for you: may he make the desires of your magnanimity pleasing, confirmed, and acceptable, and may he advance, order, and dispose all the endeavors of your royal purpose to his glory and your salvation. [Col. 0234C]

Especially in this work of Christian religion and faith, may he grant you an abundance of heavenly grace, through which you may be found worthy of the crown of justice, both as a promoter of the faith and as a conqueror triumphant over defeated unbelievers. We ourselves, recently intending to travel to those regions to visit our houses, had resolved also to go before your presence for this very purpose, so that we might first free some of those unbelievers from their errors, and then from the mouth of the threatening sword.

But after deliberation among ourselves, we perceived that it was better for us to desist altogether, lest perhaps through our warnings they become more cautious in their unbelief. The victory of this contest is more suitably entrusted to you: with the Most High’s favor from above, you may either restore them to the bosom of the Church or drive the obstinate from the bosom of the kingdom. [Col. 0234D]

Furthermore, we wish you to know, whatever others may perhaps tell you, that on the day when Count Henry took the cross, although summoned from there, we refused to be present. We doubted, in view of what had been done the day before, lest they should turn toward some useless counsel that would be in some degree dishonorable to us. Yet on that same day neither the prayers [Col. 0235A] of our brothers nor our letters were absent. Through them, by God’s grace, the prince was encouraged to receive the cross, and his counselors proceeded along the straight path of truth.

## XXIX. To All the Faithful of Christ

Concerning actions undertaken by himself and his companions during their legation against the Albigensians.

Hear, O heavens, what we lament; let the earth feel the groaning of our heart. Let Catholic Christians grieve for the fortunes of Christ, and let the faithful people groan over the injury done to the faith. Let all earth-born men and children of men deplore the losses of human salvation, and let the general overthrow of their life be universally mourned by all living beings. A new Philistine of our time stands against the ranks of Israel: the order of heretics, the army of the perverse, which irreverently reproaches the battle-lines of the living God and, in impious presumption, blasphemes the Lord of majesty. Why do you hesitate, O David? Why do you tremble, faithful man? Take up sling and stone; let the blasphemer at once be struck in the forehead, and let the wicked head, insolently raised, be removed by your sword in your own hands. For if Christ’s party is defeated in this contest, if Mother Church is trampled even for a little while and for a moment, we know surely that our cause lacks not merit but a patron. We know that triumph will not be denied to our champion, if he goes forth to fight in the love of Christ.

But because, according to the word of the Lord, who is Truth, the harvest indeed is abundant while few labourers have entered it, the despoilers of your fields, good Jesus, boldly stand ready like deceitful labourers, more prepared to uproot the bitter plants than to reap the ripe crop, and to anticipate the day of your harvest by their ravages. Where, then, are now your husbandmen, appointed over the fertile and pleasant field, made to flourish by your blood and watered by the sprinkling of holy blood? Let them arise and help us; let them protect us in necessity; let them set themselves as a wall of defence against the bloody beasts. Rise, I say, rise, men, Fathers, leaders of nations, princes of peoples. Drive away the most evil beasts whom we have seen and whom we point out; or at least put to flight the little foxes. To capture them would indeed be better; but who is fit for this? They have no fixed approaches; they tread circular paths; [Col. 0235D] and, in a kind of labyrinth of their deceits, these latter-day monsters lie hidden. They flee like a little doe from the hand, and, like a twisting serpent, the more tightly you bind them, the more easily they escape. Yet thanks be to God: although they cannot be captured, they can be driven away, so that, when what they were destroying in us has been betrayed, they may be confounded and perish within themselves. How easy this is, we prove by what we have seen and handled, so that henceforth, if it is not done, we should lament not so much their wickedness as our own shortcomings and the negligence of our people.

For it happened recently, at the command of the lord pope and at the urging of the most pious princes Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English, that the venerable Peter, legate of the Apostolic See, the discreet men the bishops of Poitiers and Bath, and we ourselves in their company, came to the city of Toulouse. As it was a city of very great population, so it was also said to be the mother of heresy and the head of error. We therefore proceeded there in order to discover whether its affliction corresponded to the outcry which had risen up. And behold, its wound was found to be exceedingly great, so that from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there was no health in it. Truly, not a third part had been reported to us of all its evil abominations, which that noble city cherished in the bosom of its unbelief. The abomination of desolation had found a place there for itself, and the likeness of the prophetic creeping things held its dwelling in its hiding places. There heretics ruled among the people and held sway over the clergy, because, as was the people, so was the priest; and the life of the shepherd itself fashioned the destruction of the flock. Heretics spoke, and all marvelled. A Catholic spoke, and they said, “Who is this?” They considered it a wonder and a marvel if there were anyone among them who dared even to utter something concerning the word of faith. Meanwhile the pestilence had gained such strength in the land that they had not merely made priests and bishops for themselves, but had also evangelists, who, having corrupted and erased evangelical truth, coined new Gospels for them and preached to the deceived people recent doctrines from their wicked heart.

I lie if there was not among them a certain man, advanced in age, wealthy in possessions, surrounded by brothers and friends, and a great man among the greatest of the city, [Col. 0236C] whom the devil, as his sins deserved, had so blinded that he called himself John the Evangelist and separated the Word which was in the beginning with God from another first principle of things, as though from another God. He was the head of the lost in that city and prince of the heretics. Although, as an unlearned layman, he understood nothing, nevertheless among them he poured forth the streams of perdition as though he were a fountain of diabolical wisdom. Dark night-owls assembled to him by night; and he, clad in a garment resembling a tunic and dalmatic, sat among them like a king with an army standing around him, both being and acting as the preacher of fools. He had entirely filled the whole city with his disciples and doctrine, since no one in the city dared, because of his power, to resist him.

At our very entrance, moreover, the heretics’ licence everywhere was so great that, as we proceeded straight through lanes and streets, they mocked us with words and pointed at us with their fingers, shouting that we were apostates, hypocrites, heretics. But as time passed and we had been granted rest for a few days, one of us was invited to undertake a word of exhortation and dispute before the unbelieving multitude concerning the rule of the true faith. When a discourse of orthodox preaching had been delivered to the people, sinners in Zion were terrified and trembling seized the hypocrites, so that those who had formerly stopped the mouths of speakers no longer dared to appear before them. At once you might have heard or seen foxes transformed into moles: those which had formerly run about in public now plunged themselves into hiding places in the earth, into cavernous cells; and the sacred shoots, which they no longer dared to gnaw in the open, they gnawed away and killed beneath the bowels of the earth. Yet, lest that spotted leopard betray itself by the variety of its skin, they buttressed their evil teaching with cunning inventions, so that, when brought to examination in controversy, they falsely claimed to believe whatever we believe, in order to feign likeness to our conformity.

From that day, therefore, the lord legate and we others, who believed ourselves to be contending with savage beasts, turned all our zeal and labour to searching out those whom fear and shame had thrust down into the lowest parts of the earth like a base creeping thing, so that they might be forced to come forth in public and cast off in the light the works of darkness. [Col. 0237B] Accordingly, at the legate’s command, the bishop, certain members of the clergy, the consuls of the city, and other faithful men not yet touched by any report of perfidy, were made to swear that, whoever they had hitherto known, or might thereafter come to know, to be either accomplices or agents of this heresy, they would disclose their names to us in writing, sparing no one whatsoever out of love, payment, or any consideration of relationship.

As countless multitudes entered day by day in the register of that enrolment, among the others was named the great Peter Moranus, whom, as we have said above, they called John the Evangelist. After taking counsel together, we all resolved to begin judgment with him, so that the faithless crowd in the remaining cases might tremble, when the simplicity of the true Gospel had condemned the craftiness of the false evangelist. Therefore, after his officers had been sent, the count of Saint-Gilles, who faithfully stood by us, ordered him summoned. But he, trusting in the abundance of his wealth and the number of his relatives, evaded the summons at the first citation through the contrivance of a haughty delay. On the next day, therefore, the said count, employing entreaties rather than threats, gently summoned that same Peter through friends and acquaintances; and, after very great difficulties, he finally presented him to us, mixing entreaties with fear.

Then one among us who spoke began to admonish him in this way: “Come now, Peter: your fellow citizens accuse you of having rejected the rules of sound faith and fallen into the perversity of the Arian heresy; indeed, through the subtleties of manifold errors, you both lead others astray and are led astray by others.” To this he replied with a sigh from the depths that he was not such a person—a lie at first sight. Asked whether he would prove this by oath, he maintained that his simple assertion ought to be believed, as that of a noble and distinguished man.

But when we all together insisted upon requiring an oath, he at once promised that he would swear, lest he be discovered a heretic precisely in this matter, should he obstinately refuse an oath according to the established custom of that error. The relics of the saints were immediately brought forth with honour and received with such solemn reverence and devotion that the faithful people were moved to tears, while the heretics who had assembled would have preferred hiding places to such a spectacle. Yet visible trembling and pallor covered Peter himself during the chant which, with tears poured forth, we sang to invoke the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that much colour fled from him and his strength of mind failed. For how could the spirit remain in the adversaries of the Holy Spirit when the Holy Spirit came? One could see a man as though stricken with paralysis, retaining neither speech nor understanding, although all said that he possessed such eloquence that he had been accustomed to surpass everyone in speaking.

Why say more? The wretched man swore before all present that, concerning every article of faith which we should ask of him, he would declare the truth of his belief. A marvellous thing, and, in such a spectacle, most welcome with pious delight! The book upon which he had sworn was brought; and when one of those standing round, a religious man, sought the omen of the letter which met his eye at a certain place, this text of Scripture occurred: “What have you to do with us, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” Truly, Lord Jesus, you have nothing to do with those whom your Father, having cut them off from you, the true vine, as unfruitful branches, had cast outside to wither.

But when we pressed him to confess to us without fraud his faith concerning the sacrament of the altar, he neither believed in his heart unto righteousness nor confessed with his mouth unto salvation. Instead, contrary to his decision to lie about everything, he disclosed the truth of his falsity and, by a new doctrine, maintained that the holy bread of eternal life, consecrated by the ministry of the priest in the word of the Lord, is not the body of Christ. Then all arose, as it were overwhelmed with tears, drawn forth both by contempt for the sacraments and by Christian compassion for the wretched man. No more need be said. The accused was handed over to the count and, adjudged a heretic, was immediately committed to public custody under a solemn undertaking from his relatives. News of the deed flew through the lanes and streets of the great city; the mouths of the faithful were opened, and the lips of the Catholic people broke forth into your praises, O Christ, as though then for the first time the splendour of faith had burst forth in that city and a city long despairing of eternal salvation had begun to breathe again in hope. From then onward the word of faith grew and multiplied daily, so that the whole face of the city appeared happier, escaping from the darkness of error into the brightness of shining virtue.

Meanwhile Peter came to himself; and, pierced with compunction as the Lord looked upon him, seeing himself altogether worthy both of present and future death, he sent many mediators and sought a way to make satisfaction. He promised a desire for conversion, that he might be rescued from the destruction of impending death for the fruit of a better life. He came, was received, and was set before the surrounding people, naked in body, casting off the perversity of his former perfidy. There, acknowledging himself before all as a heretic, he gave his hand to the faith; there he renounced error, having sworn before all with his right hand and furnished sureties—both the count himself and many leading men among his fellow citizens—that he would submit himself to every command of the lord legate and carry out his order in all things. Then the people were summoned to assemble together on the next day in the church of Saint Saturninus, to hear and see solemnly what form of penance that Peter would be ordered to undertake.

All therefore gathered on the following day, as they had been warned: indeed, such a great and dense crowd that scarcely any unoccupied space remained even beside the horns of the altar for the lord legate, celebrating the solemnities of Mass, without extreme crowding. And behold, before that exceedingly great multitude, this Peter, now ours, was led naked and barefoot through the very doors of the church, being beaten on either side by the bishop of Toulouse [Col. 0239B] and the abbot of Saint Saturninus, until he prostrated himself at the legate’s feet on the very steps of the altar. There, in the face of the Church, he was reconciled by the Church’s sacraments, after he had abjured every heresy and anathematized the heretics.

Then, after all his possessions had been confiscated and proscribed, this penance was imposed upon him: within forty days he was to depart into exile from his homeland and remain for three years at Jerusalem in service to the poor. Meanwhile, every Sunday he was ordered to go naked and barefoot around the churches of the city of Toulouse with penitential rods; to restore the property of churches which he had taken; to repay all the usury he had received; to make good the losses of poor persons whom he had afflicted; and to overthrow from its very foundations a certain castle of his, which he had profaned by heretical conventicles. Good God, how many tears did holy joy pour forth! What thanksgivings and praises did the jubilant and devout people add to the heavenly choirs, when such a mole was drawn from the cave of perfidy and a most ravenous wolf was remade into an Israelite sheep!

After he had been dismissed, the lord legate turned his hand against others, intending to examine those whom either public suspicion or private accusation had marked in great number. We, however, only with difficulty at last obtained permission, drawn forth with tears, to return, because the pressing demands of our chapter now required our return. The requested leave was granted to us with the condition that we enter the diocese of Albi and admonish the prince of the land, namely Roger of Béziers, to release the bishop of Albi, whom he held in chains under the guard of heretics, and, in accordance with the lord legate’s command, cleanse all his land by expelling the heretics.

Accordingly, when we entered that utterly lost region together with the aforesaid bishop of Bath—a region which, like the sink of all wickedness, had received into itself the entire filth of heresy flowing thither—the said Roger withdrew to the remotest and most inaccessible borders of his territory, a fugitive alike through an evil conscience and through merited despair of his cause. For the worker of wickedness hated the light of truth and could not endure an approach for conversation with us, since he had wholly withdrawn into works of darkness. Nevertheless, we came to one of his very strongly fortified castles, which the inhabitants called, properly and distinctively, simply “the Castle.” There his wife lived with a great military retinue [Col. 0240B] and a very numerous household. Almost all the inhabitants of that castle were either heretics or accomplices of heretics, although restrained by the power of the Lord alone, so that they dared neither to undertake nor utter anything against the faith which we preached. For although we too were placed in their hands and surrounded on every side, as it were, by a heretical multitude among accomplices of their power, nevertheless the word of the Lord was not bound, so that we did not strike them with continual denunciations and rebukes.

Since we saw that they dared make absolutely no reply, we judged the said Roger a traitor, a heretic, and a perjurer for violating the peace and safe-conduct of the bishop; and, treating him as condemned by public excommunication, we confidently formally defied him in Christ’s name, on behalf of the lord legate and the aforesaid kings, in the presence of his wife and his soldiers. Behold, it is now sufficiently apparent how great and evident an opportunity lies open to Christian princes to avenge Christ’s injuries and make that desert like the garden of the Lord, and its wilderness into the delights of paradise. And lest they plead that they can do little or nothing against them, let all know that there was a general judgment in the city of Toulouse that, had this visitation been delayed another three years, scarcely anyone would have been found there still invoking Christ’s name. Moreover, over and above all this, the aforesaid count of Saint-Gilles confirmed by an oath given before the people of the city that henceforth he would neither favour heretics by entreaty nor by payment [Col. 0240D], nor tolerate them further in his land.

> **[Note: Col. 0239D]**
>
> Thus far the historical letter or declamation of Henry, abbot of Clairvaux. For a fuller knowledge of the history, it has seemed appropriate to add what follows from letters of Peter, cardinal and legate of the Holy See, reported by Baronius and others:
>
> “We therefore held valid the indulgence granted to them—although, as we have said, the aforesaid count of Toulouse and other noblemen had already issued an edict that they were to be expelled from their lands. With the same bishop of Poitiers, the aforesaid count of Toulouse, and some three hundred other clerics and laymen assembled with us in the church of Blessed Stephen, we ordered them to set forth their faith to us and, returning to the truth of the Catholic faith, to remove by a saving confession of the true faith the infamy incurred both by the whole land and by themselves through their damnable preaching. Among other words which passed to and fro, they produced in the midst a certain document in which they had written their articles of faith, and read it through in its full written length.
>
> “When we found in it certain words which seemed suspect, and which, unless more fully explained, could conceal the heresy which they had preached, we required them to answer in Latin and defend their faith: first, because their language was not sufficiently known to us; and secondly, because the Gospels and Epistles by which alone they wished to confirm their faith are known to have been written in Latin. Since they did not dare to do this—as became clear in the words of one of them, who, wishing to speak Latin, could scarcely put two words together and failed entirely—and since they were wholly ignorant of the Latin language, it was necessary for us to accommodate ourselves to them and, because of their ignorance, however absurd this might be, discuss the ecclesiastical sacraments in the vernacular.
>
> “They therefore, publicly before us and the aforesaid men, denied that there are two principles and confessed and firmly asserted that one most high God created all things visible and invisible; and they demonstrated this, as was true, from evangelical and apostolic Scriptures. They also confessed that our priest, whether good or bad, just or unjust, even one whom they knew beyond doubt to be an adulterer or otherwise criminal, could make the body and blood of Christ; and that by the ministry of such a priest and the power of the divine words uttered by the Lord, bread and wine are truly transubstantiated into the body and blood of Christ. They further asserted that infants or adults baptized with our baptism are saved, and that no one can be saved without that baptism, wholly denying that they possessed another baptism or an imposition of hands, as had been alleged against them.
>
> “They likewise affirmed that a man and woman joined in marriage, if no other sin prevents it, are saved and excused for the good of marriage even though they carnally render the marital due to one another, and are never damned for this reason. They affirmed that archbishops, bishops, priests, monks, canons, hermits, Templars, and Hospitallers are to be saved. They said also that it is fitting and just to visit with the greatest devotion churches founded in the honour of God and the saints; to show honour and reverence to their priests and other ministers; to pay them first-fruits and tithes owed; and to render faithfully and devoutly all parochial dues. Among other commendable assertions, they maintained that alms should be given to churches, to the poor, and indeed to every petitioner. Although they had previously been said to deny all these things, they asserted that they understood them in accordance with our sound interpretation.
>
> “After we had thus examined them and they had confessed voluntarily what we have said, we entered the church of Saint James, where an innumerable multitude of people assembled with us, as though prepared for a spectacle; and it heard in the vernacular their confession of faith, which had been written in the aforesaid document. When they had been heard by us and by all the people assembled there with complete patience and without any disturbance, and had themselves voluntarily ended their speech—because their exposition of faith appeared sufficiently commendable and Catholic—we again asked them, in the hearing of the whole people, whether they believed in their hearts what they had confessed with their mouths, and whether they had ever preached the contrary, as they had repeatedly been accused of doing.
>
> “They replied that they so believed and likewise denied ever having preached otherwise. Then the noble count of Toulouse and many other clerics and laymen who had heard them preach otherwise, moved by strong astonishment and inflamed with zeal for the Christian faith, rose up and convicted them most clearly of having plainly lied to their own condemnation. Some firmly declared that they had heard certain of them say that there were two gods, one good and the other evil: the good one made only invisible things and things unable to change or decay; the evil one created heaven, earth, man, and other visible things. Others affirmed that they had heard in their preaching that Christ’s body is not made through the ministry of an unworthy priest or one entangled in certain crimes. Many likewise testified that they had heard them entirely deny that a man is saved with his wife if each renders the marital due to the other. Others firmly charged to their face that they had heard from them that baptism does not benefit infants, and that they had uttered many other blasphemies against God, holy Church, and the Catholic faith—blasphemies which, because of their abominable enormity, we preferred to pass over rather than report.
>
> “Whatever they may have said in their earlier confession, which seemed sufficient for salvation if they thus believed in their heart unto righteousness and spoke with heart and mouth, they nevertheless, as men of twisted mind and crooked intention, refused at last to abandon heresy where the gross and benumbed understanding of theirs seemed to find support in the surface of a certain authority. Taking occasion from the word which the Lord is said to have uttered in the Gospel, ‘Do not swear at all; but let your speech be Yes, yes; No, no’ (Matthew 5; James 5), they said they ought not to swear—although the Lord himself is often recorded to have sworn, as it is written: ‘The Lord has sworn’ (Psalm 109), etc.; and elsewhere: ‘By myself I have sworn, says the Lord’ (Genesis 22); and the Apostle: ‘An oath is the end of every controversy’ (Hebrews 6). Many passages of this kind present themselves and occur to readers in the divine Scriptures, by which we are permitted to swear because of the weakness of those to whom we commend something.
>
> “But they, as unlearned men who did not understand the Scriptures, fell into the snare which they had hidden. For although they had previously abhorred an oath as an execrable thing forbidden by the Lord, they were convicted of having sworn in the very document of their confession when they said: ‘In the Truth which is God, we so believe and declare that this is our faith.’ They did not know that to call upon Truth and the Word of God as testimony to a true assertion is beyond doubt to swear, as we read of the Apostle when he said: ‘For this we say to you in the word of God’ (1 Thessalonians 4); and elsewhere: ‘God is my witness’ (Romans 1). Other similar passages, which those who understand and have read the divine Scriptures can more easily find, prove the same thing.
>
> “When they had been convicted by many adequate witnesses and many others were preparing to bear testimony against them, we more diligently admonished them—because the Church is accustomed not to deny the bosom of mercy to those who return—to lay aside every heretical perversity and return to the unity of the faith. Since they had been excommunicated by the lord pope, by our venerable brothers the archbishops of Bourges and Narbonne, by the bishop of Toulouse, and by ourselves on account of their perverse preaching and sect, we instructed them to come to us for reconciliation according to the form of the Church. But, turned into a crooked bow and hardened in a lost mind, they refused to do this. Therefore, before the whole people, who continually shouted and raged against them with great fierceness, we, with lighted candles, together with the aforesaid bishop of Poitiers and other religious men who had stood by us in all matters, again declared them excommunicated and condemned them with their author, the devil.”]

.

### XXX. Judgment of Henry, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, delivered in 1188 against the abbot of Saint-Sever in favour of the monastery of Holy Cross at Bordeaux; it mentions several councils.

*(Marten, Amplissima Collectio, vol. VII, col. 87, from the archives of Holy Cross, Bordeaux.)*

[Col. 0241A]

HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved sons in Christ ARNAULD, abbot, and the brothers of Holy Cross at Bordeaux: greetings and the affection of sincere love.

The case which was pending between you and the abbot of Saint-Sever and his monastery concerning the church of Saint Mary of Soulac was committed to us by Pope Alexander III, under a fixed form and with appeal removed, for determination. Desiring therefore to carry out the apostolic mandate, we summoned both parties before us, appointing the day of the octave of the Nativity of Saint John. On that day, you, beloved son abbot of Holy Cross, came prepared and furnished for the hearing before us at the castle of Descura, which is in the diocese of Albi; but the abbot of Saint-Sever did not come, nor did any representative appear for him or for his monastery willing to undertake the case, although they were the initiators of it and had raised the same cause before the Roman pontiff.

Nevertheless, the abbot of Hautepont and two clerics came without letters from the abbot or chapter. Saying that they had been sent by the abbot of Saint-Sever, they alleged that he was detained by serious illness and for this reason had not come on the appointed day. But they gave us no proof of this. Although you, abbot of Holy Cross, earnestly requested through your advocates that expenses be awarded you because of the default of the opposing party, we nevertheless decided to defer both the question of expenses and the whole cause, assigning both parties the octave of the Nativity of Saint Mary as a peremptory day.

On that day at Le Puy, you again came before us prepared and equipped with witnesses and instruments, despite great difficulty, labour, and expense; but neither the party of Saint-Sever came nor did a representative appear who would make a case for it, or even allege a reason for its absence. After we had detained you for several days awaiting your adversaries, you urgently requested, through your advocates, that you might set forth your arguments and allegations both concerning the principal cause [Col. 0243C] and the question of expenses, so that we might give a definitive judgment on all matters. After taking counsel with our venerable brothers, the bishops of Poitiers, Le Puy, Maguelonne, and Lodève, and with other persons learned in both laws who were assisting us, we condemned the abbot and monastery of Saint-Sever to pay you the expenses which you had incurred in prosecuting the case to that term.

Although the greater part of our assessors agreed that we should determine the whole cause, since we had assigned a peremptory day and the party of Saint-Sever, which had brought the monastery of Holy Cross into litigation, appeared contumaciously absent—since no representative appeared to excuse its absence—nevertheless, treating that party more gently, we assigned another peremptory day: the octave of the Kalends of December, believing that we would then be in that region and might there be more fully informed concerning the case.

On that day at Bazas, where our venerable brother the archbishop of Auch, his suffragans, and the prelates of that province had assembled for the council which we held there, both parties appeared before us. The abbot of Saint-Sever, acting through his advocates for himself and his monastery, brought the case and asserted that formerly, while the monastery of Saint-Sever peacefully possessed the church of Saint Mary of Soulac through its prior and monks, the monks of Holy Cross at Bordeaux had violently expelled them. He claimed that they had made many complaints concerning that expulsion before Roman pontiffs and in synods, and had joined issue in law by letters. They therefore requested that possession of the same church be restored to them.

You answered through your advocates, firmly denying both the violence and the expulsion, the complaints and the joinders of issue. You asserted instead that the church of Soulac had been adjudged to the monastery of Holy Cross through Amatus, formerly bishop of Oloron, and Hugh of Die, then legates of the Apostolic See, in a council which they held at Bordeaux, and afterwards by Pope Paschal; and you said that you had the documentary evidences of these judgments in hand. You added that after these judgments the church of Saint Mary of Soulac had been peacefully possessed and held by the monastery of Holy Cross not only for forty years, but beyond the memory of men. But before all else, you wished the expenses which we had awarded you at Le Puy to be restored to you.

After there had been lengthy argument on both sides and the facts remained wholly uncertain to us because of their mutual denials, we ordered each party to produce witnesses to prove its contention. There the abbot of Saint-Sever produced four witnesses, and you subsequently produced a very large number. After these had been produced, the abbot of Saint-Sever requested a delay in order to produce other witnesses, alleging that through the machination [Col. 0244C] and intimidation of the abbot of Holy Cross his witnesses had been taken away from him. Although you, abbot of Holy Cross, firmly denied this, arguing that after two peremptory days had been assigned to him no further delay ought to be granted, we nevertheless set another peremptory day, the third day after Epiphany, so that then you might come fully equipped on both sides for judgment.

On that day, when both parties had come before us at Saintes, the party of the abbot of Saint-Sever again firmly alleged that you, abbot of Holy Cross, had carried out the aforementioned removal of witnesses. On this point it produced as witnesses a certain monk and two of his servants. After they had sworn an oath, been received, and carefully examined, they gave us no confidence in this respect, since they did not agree about the facts and were insignificant and suspect persons. Yet although you and your advocates requested publication of the testimony and the delivery of judgment, and our assessors advised that we should do this, we nevertheless received from the abbot of Saint-Sever, at his petition, an oath written upon a document in the monks’ hand: that he would not maliciously seek a delay merely as it seemed expedient; that on whatever day we assigned him he would receive our judgment on the case without evasion; and that he would observe it and cause his brothers to observe it inviolably. To overcome every malice, we assigned him a fourth peremptory day, the third Sunday of the following Lent [Col. 0245A]; and by our letters, under penalty of excommunication, we strictly admonished the witnesses whom he claimed had been removed from him to give testimony to the truth in the same case.

And meanwhile, after persons had been chosen from the respective sides, we entrusted to them the taking of the testimony of those witnesses. When the appointed day arrived, both parties appeared before us at Limoges, where we held a council of the prelates of the provinces of Bourges and Bordeaux, duly prepared; and the abbot of Saint-Sever produced three sworn witnesses. After receiving and examining them, we published the depositions with the consent of both parties. When the parties had copied out these depositions and debated them at length, the party of Saint-Sever requested that further time again be granted them, in order to produce witnesses concerning the interruption of the peaceful and very long possession which the party of Sainte-Croix appeared to have proved by many witnesses that it had held with regard to the aforesaid church of Soulac. [Col. 0245B]

To this your advocates, abbot of Sainte-Croix, replied that no further delay whatsoever ought to be granted; since we had already granted them four peremptory adjournments, entirely beyond the ordinary course of law—especially since the abbot and brethren of Saint-Sever were the plaintiffs—and since, at the first encounters of the litigation, they had alleged both a violent expulsion and a consequent interruption of possession, and witnesses concerning the violence and interruption, whose depositions had been published, had been produced and examined. They added this also against the witnesses of the abbot of Saint-Sever: namely, that some of them testified only from hearsay concerning the alleged violence and interruption, not because they had themselves seen it happen. Certain others, who testified that they had seen the violence, were both unsteady and so mutually contradictory in their depositions that their testimony was altogether to be rejected and disregarded; and therefore, because they had failed in proving the violence, they ought not to be admitted to prove the interruption which they alleged had followed upon the violence that they had been unable to prove. [Col. 0245C]

You also delivered to us the privilege of Amatus, formerly bishop of Oloron and then legate of the Apostolic See, sealed with his seal. It contained the following: before him and Hugh, bishop of Die, likewise a legate, at a council which they held at Bordeaux—where the archbishops of Bordeaux, Auch, Tours, and Dol sat with their suffragans—a dispute had been argued between Arnaud Trencard, formerly abbot of Sainte-Croix, and Arnaud of Saint-Sever, concerning the already mentioned church of Saint Mary of Soulac. It was finally determined as follows: since at that council of Bordeaux it had been proved by many canonical testimonies that Gregory, abbot and predecessor of the said Arnaud of Saint-Sever, had been so convicted at Rome before Pope Alexander of the wrong which he was doing to Arnaud, abbot of Sainte-Croix, concerning the church of Saint Mary of Soulac, that Abbot Gregory himself surrendered that church into the hand of the same Roman pontiff, firmly promising [Col. 0246A] that he would not again lay claim to it; and since the same Pope Alexander had reinvested the aforesaid Arnaud, abbot of Sainte-Croix, with that church of Saint Mary: supported by apostolic and conciliar authority, he adjudged the church of Saint Mary of Soulac, with all appurtenances, to the said Arnaud, abbot of Sainte-Croix, and to his successors, to be possessed in perpetual right; he reinvested him accordingly and caused a privilege bearing his seal to be made for him.

You also presented to us a privilege of Pope Urban, in which that same judgment is expressly confirmed. You likewise produced another privilege of Pope Paschal, in which it is plainly declared that, when a complaint concerning the same church of Saint Mary of Soulac had again been brought and long argued in the Lateran palace between Suavius, abbot of Saint-Sever, and Fulk, abbot of Sainte-Croix, and when the documents of both churches had been read and more carefully investigated by the bishops and cardinal-priests then present, it was judged that the aforesaid determination made at the above-mentioned council of Bordeaux ought to retain perpetual force. Pope Paschal himself, confirming the same determination by his own affirmation, decreed by apostolic writing that the often-mentioned church of Blessed Mary of Soulac, as had been determined, should be peacefully possessed in perpetuity by the monastery of Sainte-Croix; and by that same document he prohibited any complaint concerning it from thereafter being heard. [Col. 0246B]

Accordingly, after hearing the arguments, allegations, and depositions of both parties, carefully inspecting and sufficiently understanding the instruments, and after full deliberation with our venerable brethren S., bishop of Limoges; G., bishop-elect of Auxerre; the abbot of Saint-Martial; and many other honourable persons learned in divine and human law: by their common counsel, since it was established to us by many sworn witnesses, against whom nothing was alleged, that the church of Saint Mary of Soulac had been peacefully possessed by the monastery of Sainte-Croix not only for forty years but for seventy years and more, by the judgment of Amatus, formerly bishop of Oloron, and Hugh, formerly bishop of Die, legates of the Apostolic See, and by Pope Urban’s confirmation and Pope Paschal’s decision; and since no credibility had been established for us concerning the violent ejection alleged by the abbot of Saint-Sever, apart from the wavering, contradictions, and suspicious character of his witnesses—even though we had assigned him four peremptory days for producing witnesses, and knew that no further adjournment ought to be granted him—having considered the terms of the commission concerning this case imposed upon us by Pope Alexander III, we absolve, by definitive judgment, the abbot and monastery of Sainte-Croix from the claim of the abbot and monastery of Saint-Sever concerning the church of Saint Mary of Soulac. We adjudge that same church to be possessed in perpetuity by the abbots and monastery of Sainte-Croix, without disturbance from the abbots and brethren of Saint-Sever, imposing perpetual silence upon the abbots and monastery of Saint-Sever concerning recovery of that church. [Col. 0246C–0247A]

Given at Poitiers by the hand of Raymond de Capella, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1182, on the Kalends of April [1 April].

### XXXI. Letter of Henry, Bishop of Albano, to all prelates of the Church

—He exhorts them to moderation, humility, and penitence. (Year 1187.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 975, from the Hemerode manuscript.]

To the venerable archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of the Church, his dearest beloved in the Lord: Henry, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, wishes that they may attain, through the glory of the life-giving Cross, to the joys of everlasting light.

> [Note: [Col. 0247D] Henry appears to have written this letter on the occasion of Saladin’s victory over the Christians. Accordingly, so that they might be able to appease the divine power, he exhorts those signed with the cross to humility and penitence. [Col. 0248D]]

Tax collectors and sinners forcibly seize the kingdom of God, rejoicing that it suffers violence at their hands; while those who ought to have been leaders do not even follow. Therefore ecclesiastical persons especially must take heed lest, God forbid, the princes of darkness begin to repair, through the damnation of clerics, the losses which they suffer through the conversion of laypeople. Care must also be taken lest the sea speak, so that Sidon may blush. Care must be taken lest the dumb beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, begin to rebuke the folly of the prophets.

Therefore, beloved friends, in these days it is necessary not merely to inscribe upon your foreheads the sign of Tau—the sign of the Lord’s Passion—but especially to imprint it upon your hearts. Black is the ink; grim is the ink-horn that hangs from the loins of him who comes clothed in linen, of singular whiteness such as no fuller on earth could produce, marked and distinguished with every kind of mercy, which no impenitent person may attain. He had considered this ink, this height, this blackness, who said: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53). I beseech you, beloved friends, do not be ashamed to be conformed to this disfigurement. Emulate his humility: for your sake he assumed the poverty of infant years; he did not refuse to undergo the disgrace of the Cross; he did not shrink from being reckoned among the dead. Put off the old man with his deeds, and strip off the cast skin of the old serpent—the serpent whose prudence was commended by the Saviour’s mouth. [Col. 0247B–C]
