This time does not suit splendour; it does not suit mourning. Spurs should not shine more brightly than altars, when perhaps even the altars ought for the present to be covered with haircloth. The same judgment should be made concerning remarkable saddles, bridles, and trappings that display empty brilliance. In their clothing let clerics lay aside what even kings reject and what the whole company of those marked with Christ’s sign is known to renounce. Let them cast away variegated garments, grey furs, sables, and pelts of such great price—yet of still greater danger before God, and in truth of no lesser disgrace—when a human being created in God’s image believes himself adorned by the skins of mice.

At least in these days let Peter be heard—he who ought never to have gone unheard. Let him be heard, so that men may be ashamed to desire, and clerics ashamed of, what their chief, tonsured both for their glory and for their reproach, forbade even to women. Neither their sleeves nor their shoes should be excessive. If these need daily stitching by those who serve them, let not the fineness of the thread bind their hands and feet into heavier chains, or make them seem to weave cords by which, with hands and feet bound, they may be cast into outer darkness. Do not fail to cast away hooded cloaks with sleeves, which, by their double construction from cloak and tunic, rebuke the duplicity of souls. He who prohibited a garment woven from linen and wool would not have approved, had he seen in his day garments made from cloak and tunic. [Col. 0247D–0248A]

The first transgression of humankind took place in heaven; Christ, fasting, won his first and threefold victory over the adversary. For he conquered the world in its objects of desire: in the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—triumphing over pleasure, idleness, and ambition. The laity have now imposed upon themselves a limit in food, being content with two dishes; if you were told to be content with one, perhaps certain Germans would not be pleased. Yet, if the prescribed frugality seems sufficient as regards quantity, it will be worthy of your imitation to add something further by avoiding the follies of luxury.

Indeed, your mother, the most holy Roman Church, has established and decreed that on every Friday, and during the Advent of the Lord, clerics and laity alike are to fast on Lenten food; and that on Wednesday and Saturday they are to abstain from meat and animal fat, decreeing that transgressors of this constitution shall be guilty under the sacred canons.

> [Note: [Col. 0248D] Baronius published that decree under the year 1187.]

Likewise, there at Rome, the supreme pontiff and his brethren have imposed upon themselves and their households the same abstinence from meat on Monday; and it is fitting that you, at least the greater prelates, should emulate this by voluntary devotion. Wines flavoured with spices are not suitable, above all in this time of mourning, which ought not to be forgotten. Clerics must never engage in trade, nor buy cheaply what is to be sold at a higher price. Since this has always been sacrilege, it is now especially more grievously detestable. Quarrels among clerics seem worse even than such business dealings; thus you ought rather to bear with and forgive one another, if anyone has a complaint against another. [Col. 0248B–D]

The fire of ambition is insatiable, nor is the dropsy of avarice checked by acquired riches. Why does the camel add hump upon hump through its various dignities and multitude of prebends? Such things do not provoke God’s mercy toward humankind; rather, they deserve his wrath. A camel’s hump could well suffice to deny it entry into the heavenly kingdom through a needle’s eye. Do you lack more honourable pursuits, so that you are not ashamed to amuse yourselves with birds or occupy yourselves with hunting? While the excess of your sins is being cut away, remember rather to abstain from such vanities. Cato advised the avoidance of dice, even for pagans; and for your example let the soldiery of those signed for God suffice, whom you see renouncing such games.

For the present, simple chant should suffice in churches, and organs, which with less … [lacuna] … solemnity, should fall silent. Let us fulfil what we read: “Let the organ be turned into the voice of those who weep, and the harp into mourning.” Forgive me if I say that it ought to be regarded as more healthful than sweet. The licence of the *Janicalia*, banished from churches by the peoples, has returned. What has festivity and frivolity to do here—or, to address you in apostolic language, “what agreement has Christ with Belial?” Nor are you unaware that in some churches certain enormities formerly customary have to some extent been cut back, while they still take pleasure in silken caps offered by those who bear staffs. As though the matter before God concerned conduct less than clothing; as though he delighted more in silks than in serious things. Nevertheless, no general edict concerning these and similar matters is issued, nor is a perpetual edict proposed, but only one that ought to burden no one. [Col. 0249A–B]

### XXXII. Letter of Henry, Bishop of Albano and Apostolic Legate, summoning the prelates of Germany through its bearer to an assembly for deliberation concerning holy warfare against the Saracens, the avenging of the Cross, and the places consecrated by Christ’s feet

(Ludewig, *Reliquiae mss.*, Frankfurt and Leipzig, 1720, octavo, vol. II, p. 449.)

To his dearest brothers and friends in Christ, the venerable archbishops, bishops, abbots, provosts, and other prelates of churches; and to the beloved noblemen in the Lord—dukes, counts, margraves, and all other princes established throughout the German kingdom—to whom these letters shall come: Henry, by the same grace bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, greeting in the Lord. [Col. 0249C]

Since that voice of the turtle-dove—a voice of groaning, a voice of grief—has lately spread through our lands, in the lamentable novelty of rumour, who would not groan at so great a slaughter of the Christian people? Who would not grieve to see that holy land which the very feet of the Lord consecrated for our redemption exposed to the filth of pagans? Who would not mourn the saving Cross captured and trampled by the heathen, and the Lord’s sanctuary profaned? Alas, alas! At the report of a somewhat similar event, when the Cross itself received the nail-piercings, the earth shook, the sun was afraid, rocks were split, and, we believe, tombs were opened. Whose breast, then, however stony, would not this report soften, when the wondrous Cross—the healing of our wounds, the restoration of health, the sweet wood, the sign of life, the standard of Christian warfare—is spat upon, pierced, and subjected to insults?

We must confess that, though we suffer lesser things, they are greater than anything we could have feared. Nevertheless, since all the ways of God are mercy and truth, we must not cast ourselves down so far as to cease hoping that he who, because of sins, chastised in judgment the Christian people—who had already set their eyes upon the earth, turning aside after their own desires—has reserved redemption for us in his mercy. For how would he permit the wood of the Cross to be carried away by heathens, unless he were to be crucified by them anew? [Col. 0249D–0250A]

Behold, we see the mystery of our redemption repeated: for our sake he has now spared neither his own name nor his Cross, he who once did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all. The Lord’s hand has not been shortened, nor has the Lord’s arm been weakened, so that he cannot save; rather, the unsearchable height of God works his mercy in order thus to awaken the sluggish devotion of the world and, through the service of you and others whom he deigns to choose for this, to triumph—salutarily for us and gloriously for himself—over the hostility of the barbarian nation.

Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Would that the soldiers of Christ would cast off the works of darkness and not delay to put on the armour of light, assuming the breastplate of faith and the helmet of salvation, in order to avenge the injury done to the Cross. It was wickedness, not soldiering, that until now, while intent upon the slaughter, plundering, and abominations of Christians, earned them unquenchable fire and the torments of immortal worms. A blessed warfare is at hand for them, in which victory is glory and, still more, death is gain. Today he invites us to it, he who loves souls and did not spare even his own injury, so as to impose upon his faithful the necessity compelling them into this warfare. He is present to set upon those grieving over such great evils the sign of life, for escape from an intolerable blow; and although, because of sins demanding it, manifold vessels within may already be held subject to blows that have gone forth, [the passage is corrupt] those blows will harm only those who refuse the sign of life divinely offered to them. [Col. 0250A–C]

Therefore the most serene lord F., emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, and we likewise—who by command of the Apostolic See labour for this same cause as far as, with the Lord’s help, our ability permits—have appointed a solemn court at Mainz. On the Sunday upon which “Laetare Jerusalem” is sung, let all who love her keep the feast day and assemble there.

Since, therefore, that court is especially dedicated to the Lord Saviour, as the imperial majesty summons you by its authority, so we, on God’s behalf and by the authority of the legation with which we are entrusted, summon all of you to the same court. And lest any of you should fail, without a lawful and certain necessity, to present yourselves at the aforesaid council of Christendom, we strictly enjoin and command it. We direct you, venerable bishops, to be diligent in summoning the abbots and other prelates subject to you, together with the bearer of these letters, who may perhaps be unable to visit everyone. We have also thought fit to make known to you all that you should strive to come to the court of Jesus Christ with the gravity and moderation appropriate to it, setting aside the need for mounts and every curiosity and temporal display, yet unanimously aflame with the fire of charity and obedience for the exaltation of the Christian name, so that your dress, household, and manner of life may confess the faith which our tongue professes. [Col. 0250D–0252A]

[Col. 0251]

# Treatise of Lord Henry on the Pilgrim City of God

(Dom Tissier, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, III, 1.)

## The Author’s Preface to the Monks of Clairvaux

To his dearest and spiritual sons serving the Lord at Clairvaux, Henry, a sinner and monk, wishes the overflowing consolation of the Paraclete. [Col. 0251B]

From the love by which I know that I am bound to you, I delight to measure and weigh the affection that you bear toward me. Hence, just as I am troubled by continual concern for your outward progress, so I do not doubt that you, with filial affection, share in my paternal anxieties and in turn are troubled by anxious thoughts concerning my condition. Since I see that for the present my wishes cannot be fulfilled, so that I might have you present and might more fully learn in person all that concerns you, I desire at least, though absent, to satisfy your longings; and I wish to disclose to you, as best I can, what has happened around me since I left you, and what is happening today. [Col. 0251B–C]

After I had been sent forth, by the disposition of the supreme Noah, from the ark of regular discipline and exposed to the storms of rains and winds, my foot could find no rest, to tell the truth. I, who had been accustomed to remain steadfast within the ark, when placed outside began to be tossed among things that slip away. Thus, weary from long and frequent searching for rest in all things, and instructed by those very afflictions, I finally returned into myself and said:

> “I will return to my house, from which I came” (Luke 11).

What have I to do with worldly things? What have I to do with transitory things? Let these hold their own lovers; let them occupy their own followers. I who stripped off my tunic—how shall I put it on again? I who washed my feet—how shall I defile them? (Song 5). If I am led by the Spirit, then certainly I am not under the law. “For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” Am I not free? (2 Cor. 9). Am I not a monk? If some are free to depart from God, shall I not be free to return to him?

While I silently turned such things over in my heart and strengthened my resolve still more in them, I suddenly heard the voice of one speaking:

> “When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished. But when you grow old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (John 21).

At this voice I trembled throughout, and at last, in confusion, acknowledged myself grievously bound by the chains of the divine sentence. Though I had formerly thought myself free like a wild ass (Job 39), I learned with utter certainty that a man’s way is not in himself and that a person’s steps are directed only by the Lord (Prov. 20). For who has resisted him and had peace? He himself declares disobedience to be like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit like the crime of idolatry (1 Sam. 15). Considering these and many other matters, and carefully pondering them in mind, I was disturbed by such thoughts and no way out appeared anywhere. [Col. 0251C–0252C]

At last I turned my whole self to the Lord, and, crying out to him from the inmost marrow of my heart, said:

> “Am I the sea, or a sea-monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?” (Job 7).  
> “The deep surrounded me, and the sea covered my head. Do you think that I shall see your holy temple?” (Jonah 2).  
> “Do you think that I shall ever return, released from the bonds of the episcopal burden, to that Clairvaux of mine—indeed, yours? Do you think that, restored to my most beloved sons—rather, yours—I shall joyfully sing with them to you: ‘You have broken my bonds, O Lord; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise’?” (Ps. 110 [Vulgate numbering]).  
> “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. 110 [Vulgate numbering]).

Am I separated from those without whom to live is death to me, and with whom to die is life? Who will grant me to enjoy and be refreshed by their presence? Their merits would strengthen me when I tremble; their examples would rouse me when I sleep; their humility would restrain me when I presume; their virtue would strengthen me when I falter; their counsels would confirm me when I hesitate; and their spiritual consolations would gladden me when I am sad. [Col. 0252C–D]

As I turned these thoughts over within myself more and more often, I did not cease to strike at the ears of my Lord Jesus with tears, frequently repeating with the prophet:

> “As the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are my eyes upon the Lord my God, until he has mercy upon me” (Ps. 122 [Vulgate numbering]).

And, with the patriarch Jacob, I steadfastly declared:

> “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Gen. 32).

In response, he who never forgets to show mercy at last deigned to hear me, his servant, crying out; to look upon me weeping; and to open to me as I knocked. He revealed the eyes of my heart and flooded them with the light of his grace, enabling me to know the state of that city which Ezekiel—who had himself first heard, “Behold, chariots have been given over you” (Ezek. 2)—saw inclining toward the south; which John saw descending from heaven (Rev. 21); and which the prophet David beheld as being built upon the holy mountains (Ps. 86 [Vulgate numbering]). [Col. 0253A–B]

In that city I found present the brethren and sons of Clairvaux whose absence I had mourned; in it I found enrolled as citizens all good people who are pilgrims in this world. What then appears to remain, except that, after the many and various waves described above, having at last found the city of our dwelling, we should endeavour to sow fields, plant vineyards, and produce the fruit of increase? (Ps. 106 [Vulgate numbering]). I did not believe that this could be better done by me than by committing to writing the things which I received from the Lord concerning the aforesaid city, leaving the fields of my studies to be harvested by my special and beloved sons of Clairvaux—or, should they judge a hoe necessary, entrusting them with the task of clearing away what is superfluous.

I do not fear that they will regard their father’s nakedness as something to laugh at. Rather, I trust that they will compassionately cover and at the same time adorn it with that cloak sufficient to cover both [sons]. Nor do I know that they will judge my unadorned discourse naked because it is less polished, since they approve fertility rather than eloquence. For they have surely been persuaded by the Apostle that they should attend more to the virtue than to the speech of those who are puffed up (1 Cor. 4), and that the kingdom of God consists in the power of meanings, not in elegance of words. [Col. 0253B–C]

I therefore ask you, my most beloved brethren, when you enter into your father’s labours, to judge them not alien but your own; to weigh with devout consideration the fruits dedicated to you; and, if their abundance is not such as to seem worthy of a sickle, at least not to disdain to gather and rub by hand whatever ears of grain you find. Let the heat of the sun excuse before you the barrenness of my little field; and, to use Solomon’s words:

> “Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me” (Song 1).

For this reason my discourse retains neither the flavour it once had among you nor my conduct the colour you once saw in me. May the Sun of righteousness, who is accustomed not so much to burn as to anoint, through your merits and prayers restore both its flavour to my words and its former colour to my work. [Col. 0253C–0254A]

Blessed Augustine treated in a mixed manner, in his book *The City of God*, of both cities: the one pilgrim on earth and the one reigning in heaven—if indeed they ought to be called two, since they are only one, the city into which the Prophet rejoiced that he would go when he said:

> “I rejoiced at the things said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’ Our feet stood in your courts, O Jerusalem. Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose sharing is in the same thing” (Ps. 121 [Vulgate numbering]).

Behold: the Prophet said both that it is built on earth and that it shares in the same thing in heaven. On earth it has beginning and progress, where there are “was,” “is,” and “will be”; where there are yesterday, today, and tomorrow (Heb. 13). In heaven it has consummation, where “will be” and “was” do not produce a shadow of change; but it is always the same, and whatever is there is, in that which it itself is, unfading.

I therefore leave discussion of that part of the City of God which now triumphs, crowned in heaven, to the more learned and spiritual, who judge all things. I, who do not fail to recognize my imperfection and always wish to know what I do not know—so that, if I am ignorant of anything, my ignorance may be my own—undertake to treat of the City of God militant upon earth, leaving it to the reader’s judgment whether anything in this treatise is worthy of acceptance. If he judges the whole work fit to be rejected, I ask that he read it first and despise it afterward, lest, in the words of blessed Jerome, or rather to put it more mildly, he seem improperly to condemn what he does not know before reading it. [Col. 0254A–C]

# On the Pilgrim City of God

[Col. 0253]

## First Treatise: On the Preparation of the Material of the City of God

[Col. 0253D]

Desiring with my whole heart to obey the word of the Lord who says, “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John 6), nothing seems more fitting for the present purpose than to endeavor to render some service to the city of the Lord of hosts, one part of which journeys on earth while another, crowned, triumphs in heaven. For although I may be unable to offer gold or precious stones, yet if I have at least offered goats’ hair (Exod. 25), I shall be found to have contributed something to the work of the Lord. And because “the labouring husbandman must first partake of the fruits” (2 Tim. 2), it seemed expedient to me first to linger long in contemplation of that city itself, so that by such abiding I may at last, through God’s mercy, deserve to be found its citizen. Thereafter, by zealously describing its condition, I intend also earnestly to summon others to dwell in it, so that, if the Lord grants it, I may be found to have gathered some citizens for it.

But who is sufficient for these things, unless you, Lord, make him worthy by your grace? For no one is found worthy who has not first been anticipated in his unworthiness by that grace. I confess, Lord, I confess that I am unworthy; I know that I am insufficient; nor do I undertake this work trusting in anything but your grace. The sole ground teaching me to trust in it is that ineffable abundance of your mercy by which, beyond my merits, I have proved through countless experiences that I am always forestalled in whatever good I do and advanced therein. Therefore I now flee, as is my custom, to you, Father of lights. I call upon you, my God: God, truth, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that are true are true; God, wisdom, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that rightly possess wisdom possess it; God, true and supreme life, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that truly and supremely live do live. Grant that, by knowing truly and rightly, I may enjoy you, the true and supreme life—departing from whom is to die, returning to whom is to live again, dwelling in whom is to live.

By abiding in you, may I live from you, and may you, Life, abide in me, so that I may bear from you, not from myself, fruit that remains. From you came what was revealed to your prophet David concerning your city, and what is revealed to me concerning it through him. If it should also be revealed through me to others, it will not come from me, but from you. Let us therefore hear what David, abiding within, heard from you; what he saw in your presence; and what, going forth to us, he poured out: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains,” he says (Ps. LXVI).

We set this psalm as the foundation of our work, lest we deviate in any respect from the rectitude of the prophetic and catholic rule. This psalm, then, is divided into seven verses, by which the sevenfold progress of our city is expressed. The first and second verses deal with the foundation of the city itself and the glorious completion of its gates or walls; the third, with the placing of a common asylum in the midst of the city; the fourth, with the population of the city; the fifth, with its instruction; the sixth, with its confirmation; the seventh, with the joyful dedication of the completed city. All these are found separately in the building, without rebuilding, of Jerusalem in the Old Testament.

In the building under David and in the rebuilding under Ezra and Nehemiah, we read that foundations were laid, walls built, and gates set up with bolts and bars. The common asylum, apart from the cities of refuge, is believed to have been the Jerusalem Temple, not a place to which the impunity of crimes might gather the wicked of every kind—as the asylum of Romulus is said to have been established—but a place in which wicked people, making satisfaction for their sins, might be cleansed from their iniquities, according to the prophet’s saying: “Turn the wicked man, and he shall not be” (Prov. 9).

Concerning its population, Ezra reads as follows: “After the wall had been built, and I had set up the gates” (2 Ezra [Neh.] 7), etc., “God put it into my heart, and I assembled the nobles, the magistrates, and the common people, that I might enroll them” (ibid.). Concerning instruction, the history of Nehemiah reads:

> Ezra opened the book before all the people; for he stood above all the people; and when he opened it, all the people stood. And Ezra blessed the Lord, the great God; and all the people answered, “Amen, amen,” lifting up their hands; and they bowed down and worshipped God with their faces to the ground. Moreover, the Levites kept the people silent so that they might hear the law; and the people stood in their place. And they read from the book of the law of God distinctly and plainly, so as to give understanding; and they understood when it was read. (2 Ezra [Neh.] 8)

And later:

> On the twenty-fourth day of the month, the children of Israel assembled in fasting and sackcloth, with earth upon them. And the seed of the children of Israel was separated from every foreigner; and they stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers. And they rose to stand, and read from the book of the law of the Lord their God four times in the day; and four times they confessed and worshipped the Lord their God. (2 Ezra [Neh.] 9)

Concerning confirmation, the following is read in the same books: “Over all these things we make a covenant” (ibid.), etc. Again: “The princes of the people dwelt in Jerusalem; but the rest of the people cast lots, that one part in ten should dwell in Jerusalem, the holy city, while the nine parts dwelt in the cities” (2 Ezra [Neh.] 11).

By “confirmation” here we mean not only that by which the people are bound to their Lord, but also that by which the Lord is bound to his people through promises of certain immunities, as we read was done under Moses, where it is said:

> Hear, O Israel: today you have chosen the Lord, that he may be your God, and that you may walk in his ways and keep his ceremonies, commandments, and judgments, and obey his command. And today the Lord has chosen you, that you may be his own peculiar people, as he has spoken to you, and that you may keep all his commandments; and that he may make you higher than all the nations which he has created. (Deut. 16)

Again: “Every place upon which the sole of your foot shall tread shall be yours. From the wilderness, and Lebanon, and the great river Euphrates, unto the western sea, shall be your boundaries” (Deut. 13). The Lord is said not only to have promised these things to the people of Israel through Moses, but also to have sworn them to the fathers, as in the saying: “By myself have I sworn, says the Lord” (Isa. 45; Jer. 49).

The Jewish people once gloried in being fortified by such a privilege. But the Christian people is marked by a far more worthy privilege, concerning which, should the Lord grant it, we shall speak in its place. We read that Ezra and Nehemiah dedicated the wall and the entire city in this manner: “At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem they sought the Levites from all their places, that they might bring them to Jerusalem and perform the dedication” (2 Ezra [Neh.] 12), etc.

We have thought it necessary to set down these matters from the history of the Old Testament, in order that we may build securely upon a solid foundation. Therefore, because of this sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, the Church speaks praise to the Lord seven times in the day (Ps. 118 [119]). And just as Wisdom is read to have hewn out seven pillars in the building of her house, so the Church is known solemnly to praise God by commending the seven aforesaid matters at fixed and distinct seasons of the year, so that she may be found supported, as it were, by seven pillars through these proclamations of divine praise. We reserve fuller explanation of each matter for the individual verses of the psalm proposed. But before approaching the beginning of the psalm, something should apparently be said concerning the psalm’s title.

[Col. 0257A] The title is: “A psalm of a song for the sons of Korah” (Ps. 86 [87]). What does it mean for a psalm of song to belong to the sons of Korah, except that those who strive to be sons of Korah—that is, of the bald one, for this is what *Chore* means—who hung in the place of Calvary, must fulfill in deed what they sing with their voice? They strive to be his sons not only through the sacrament, but through the reality of the sacrament; not only through adoption, but also through imitation: making themselves bald and cutting away every superfluity.

Such sons of Korah—pure and upright in heart and fervent in work—are indeed fittingly called to praise, so that neither life may differ from voice nor voice from purity of heart. Otherwise, “praise is not comely in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). Another point to observe from this title is that, just as the title precedes the psalm, so certain preparatory matters preceded the foundation of the city described at the beginning of the psalm, in fulfillment of Solomon’s saying: “Prepare your work outside, and diligently cultivate your field, that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. 24).

We see this both mystically prefigured and actually represented every year in the Church, which is itself that city. For, about to celebrate the mysteries of her foundation in Christ’s Nativity, she customarily anticipates the venerable memorial of the Lord’s Nativity by the foregoing consideration in four Sunday offices.

If we carefully consider the mystery of this, we find that the Lord’s advent was prepared and foretold in many ways and by many means through four ages: namely, from Abraham to Moses; from Moses to David; from David to the Babylonian Captivity; and from the Babylonian Captivity to John. For the two ages which preceded these, being as it were the infancy and childhood of the world, were found less apt and less capable of knowing the truth. Or, if one prefers, following the Gospel, to count one age from Abraham to David (Matt. 1), we shall say that four ages preceded from Noah to Christ.

What preparation of his city was made for the Lord during these four ages we shall explain more fully later, when the matter of the book begins to appear more fully. Meanwhile it is enough merely to taste the matter itself in advance, so that our work may not lack some preparation by which the reader’s mind, aroused to understand what follows and retain it in memory, may be prepared. Therefore, of all that is known to have been prepared during the four aforesaid ages, we select for the moment one matter, sufficient to explain the continuation of the title.

For in those ages sacred Scripture is known to have been prepared by God, to occupy in the construction of the whole city the place of mortar, for the equalizing of unequal elements and the binding together of those that are at variance. For bitumen has no place in the city of the Lord, though the Babylonians used it as mortar in their own work. Bitumen, which naturally springs from the earth, is natural cunning: that prudence of the flesh which is hostile to God. But the prudence of the Spirit, generated from the composition of sacred Scripture as from divine mortar, is life and peace.

And because mortar is made from diverse kinds of materials, God willed in each of the aforesaid ages to gather together one thing that seemed necessary for preparing this mortar. What these things are is plainly declared by the mortar made by the hand of the pontiff in the consecration of an altar. It is customarily made from water, wine, lime, and ashes. We have not thought salt, which is mixed with the water, to be counted among these, since it is known to be nothing other than congealed water. Let us therefore consider how God, the supreme pontiff, prepared these things at different times and finally fitted what had been prepared to his work.

From Abraham to Moses, by weaving the history of passing good and evil actions, he seems, as it were, to have gathered flowing waters into one place, in the single book of Genesis. Hence, although those actions, like flowing waters, passed away with their age, nevertheless they are known still to remain whole in the memory of readers through the repeated reading of Scripture, as part of the mortar of sacred Scripture. And although wine of spiritual understanding is found mixed with this water, wine is spiritually assigned to the following age, from Moses to David, in which the biting precepts and prohibitions of the Law, delivered by the Lord and received by the people, are read to have brought the harshness of wine through their very novelty.

From David to the Babylonian Captivity, perfect men, like living stones baked by the fire of the Holy Spirit, foreshadowing future things through their deeds and proclaiming coming things by the prophetic spirit, prepared through the memorials of many books the firmness of the lime of Christian faith. With this lime the apostle Peter wished his disciples to be formed and made firm in faith, saying: “You have the more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to give heed, as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1).

From the Babylonian Captivity to John, ashes were sifted, when the remnant of the Jewish people, afflicted by many straits of tribulation and transmitting their miseries to posterity through the sequence of Scripture, seem to have indicated nothing other than that things like the end of our age have been prepared. Thus we may always be found humble in prosperity through remembrance of the ashes of the past, and strong in adversity through expectation of the future. For ashes, although a lowly material, do not have a lowly effect in mortar, since they make it more durable and more tenacious.

Using this mortar in the building of his city, the Lord endeavored to fit nearly all his words and deeds to it. Thus he said: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also; for he wrote of me.” And again: “Search the Scriptures, for they bear witness concerning me” (John 5). Because it would take long to recount all that is taken in the Gospel from the Old Testament, or all that is found there foretold concerning his own birth, circumcision, manifestation, *hypapante* [Presentation/Meeting], baptism, preaching, death, burial, and resurrection, it is enough for the present to give the passage in which he is read expressly to name the four aforesaid elements:

> These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you: that all things must be fulfilled which are written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms. For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. (Luke 24)

Behold, here he plainly concludes the whole of the old Scripture by distinguishing it into the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa under the name of Psalms. We have, therefore, wine in the Law, lime in the Prophets, ashes in the Hagiographa, and water of history mixed with each of these. Indeed, it is shown that these several elements are mixed and bound together with one another through the water of history, making one mortar. And perhaps this is the wheel that Ezekiel saw, having four faces and moving in four directions.

### On the wheel having four faces and moving in four directions

History, by recounting human actions in human fashion, plainly presents the face of a man. The Law of Moses, wearing down the necks of subjects beneath the yoke of precepts and prohibitions, represents the face of the tethered calf. Prophecy, touching higher matters through threats and promises, imitates the keenness of the eagle. The Hagiographa are plainly known to express the lion’s roar through severe denunciations and harsh rebukes, such as are repeatedly set forth in the Psalms—for example, “Sons of men, how long are you heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4)—and in Daniel and Ezra.

That these are said to move in four directions plainly indicates that history looks only to things past, like water failing and flowing away as it passes into the abyss. But according to the spiritual sense, the whole Scripture of the Old Testament, looking forward to future things, stretches itself toward what lies ahead, foretelling the threefold advent of Christ: the first, hidden and humble, which is already past for us; the second, present, inwardly felt daily by the saints, and sweet; and the third, manifest and terrible, awaited at the end of time.

These three advents are found so inserted into the old Scripture that it sometimes seems to suit all of them together, sometimes to touch each separately. This is plainly seen in the Lamentations of Jeremiah. By dividing them with a fourfold alphabet, he seems to have directed one to the ruin of earthly Jerusalem, and the remaining three to the threefold fall of the Church. For just as earthly Jerusalem is read first to have fallen from the glory of kingship, afterward from the glory of priesthood, and thirdly from observance of the legal ceremonies; and just as the Temple is found first to have been destroyed by the Chaldeans, secondly profaned by the Greeks, and thirdly utterly wiped out by the Romans: so spiritual Jerusalem, which is the Church, must first be humbled from the glory and dignity of priestly authority, secondly fall from the strength of Christian religion and the simplicity of holiness, in accordance with the Apostle’s prophecy:

> In the last days men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, proud, lovers of pleasures more than of God, having indeed an appearance of godliness but denying its power. (2 Tim. 2)

Thirdly, she will abandon even the appearance of godliness and reject also the outward form of the whole ecclesiastical order. Perhaps the Church herself prefigures this in showing herself inglorious, unbeautiful, and sorrowful during the three days before the Lord’s resurrection, because she undoubtedly expects such things to precede the common resurrection of all and Christ’s final advent.

### On the three days preceding the Lord’s Resurrection, and the seven solemn antiphons of the Lord’s Advent

This is plainly recognized as prefigured by the fact that, on the three aforesaid days, the canonical hours are said without their customary beginning and ending. For a musical form is judged by its beginning and end. The omission of “The Lord be with you,” “Let us pray,” and “Kyrie eleison” indicates a failure of holiness. The complete silence of the *Gloria*, which the Church now possesses, indicates that the summit of glory is at some time to be taken away from her midst.

Nevertheless, this glory will not be hidden suddenly, but will gradually diminish over the course of time, just as, from the Sunday of the Lord’s Passion onward, it first begins to be omitted only in the Mass, where priestly glory especially shines. This distinction is also found in the aforesaid Lamentations: in the second alphabet, the polluted kingdom, the cast-down princes, and every broken horn are lamented; in the third, the prophet laments that he is a man seeing poverty; in the fourth, he laments that gold is darkened and its finest colour changed.

Although these matters are understood to have been spoken especially concerning Christ’s final advent, many things in the same alphabets refer more particularly to the first and second advents. And just as the resurrection of the Lord and the things preceding it are celebrated in the Church in preparation for the last advent, so too the things that preceded Christ’s first advent were done in preparation for it; and the things solemnly commemorated each year concerning his first advent are known to be preparations for the middle advent.

This appeared in the seven solemn antiphons sung in preparation for the Lord’s Nativity. In the first four, the cries and desires are expressed of those fathers who produced the Scriptures in the four aforesaid ages. In the three that follow, the threefold advent of Christ, foreseen and desired by those same fathers, is indicated. In the four aforesaid antiphons, moreover, four preparations for the second advent are shown. By the first, the hearts of the sluggish are stirred to rise, according to the saying: “At midnight a cry was made: behold, the bridegroom comes” (Matt. 25). The second warns those who have risen to adorn the place where the bridegroom is to be received, according to what follows in the Gospel: “Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps.” The third calls them to go out to meet him, according to the saying: “They went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.” The fourth calls them to enter, as it is said: “Those who were ready entered with him to the wedding, and the door was shut” (ibid.).

The keeper of the key of this door is both key and key-bearer: closing to whom he wills, so that none may open; opening to whom and when he wills, so that none may close. He is the one called to come in the fourth antiphon and named the key of David. A diligent reader will readily assign the other three antiphons to the other matters we have mentioned.

It is plain, then, that the things which preceded Christ’s first advent were only preparations for our city; but by Christ’s first advent the city itself was founded and fortified. By his second advent it is daily gathered together and instructed; by his third advent it will at last be fully confirmed by him and dedicated, amid the rejoicing of all, both angels and men. For these things seem in some fashion to have been prepared rather than completed by Christ’s first advent. They will be completed when, all signs passing away, the realities succeed: faith will pass into sight, shadow into truth.

Meanwhile, while the shadow endures, Christ, knowing that signs are necessary and preparatory to the realities themselves, willed to perform such things as were both the realities of preceding signs and signs of future realities. For in his Nativity he prefigured the foundation of his city; in his circumcision, its initiation; in his manifestation, its gathering together; in the institution of the sacraments, its instruction; and in his Passion, its confirmation, according to the Apostle’s saying:

> Where there is a testament, the death of the testator must necessarily intervene. For a testament is confirmed in the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while he who made the testament is alive. Therefore neither was it dedicated without blood. (Heb. 9)

Just as this dedication was threefold in the Old Testament—the first of the tabernacle, the second and third of the city and Temple—so two dedications in the New Testament are known to have preceded and prefigured the final and complete dedication of our city. The first was at the Lord’s Purification, or *hypapante*, which among us is also called the Feast of Lights; under this name we read that dedication was called among the ancients. The second was in the sending of the Holy Spirit, when the Apostles, gathered together in one place, are read to have been baptized in the Holy Spirit (Acts 2).

And because those who journey and serve as soldiers especially use signs, signs are rightly given to the city that journeys and serves as soldiers. For “while we are in the body, we are pilgrims from the Lord” (2 Cor. 6); and while “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7), we must use the ladder of visible signs toward invisible realities, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The invisible things of God are understood through the things that have been made from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1). He says, “from the creation of the world,” not “of heaven”; for heaven, already possessing the throne, does not need that ladder.

But the sons of Korah, who have *Thau* marked on their foreheads (Ezek. 9), who regard themselves as called to ashes and baldness, who know that the things appearing at first sight—that is, visible things—are temporal, and stretch themselves toward eternal things and those ahead, as blessed Augustine says: such bald men, pilgrims, and strangers upon earth, citizens of the pilgrim city, recognize the signs of their warfare; and, about to sing the song of their city, they take up the psaltery of the active life in such a way that they continually strive to pass into the contemplative life.

Its end and its blessed satisfaction is the Trinity, one God, by whose enjoyment alone people are made blessed. Since, while we journey from the Lord, this Trinity cannot be seen as it is by weak-sighted persons, the Lord willed to set before his city a certain visible Trinity, through which human weakness, rubbed warm in exile by things learned through use, might at last rise and arrive at things it has not learned.

Understanding this, that disciple whom Jesus loved set forth two trinities in his writings: one in heaven and another bearing witness on earth, indicating that one would vainly aspire to testimonies if one did not possess the testimony of the imperceptible Trinity. Concerning this he says: “There are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one” (1 John 5). For, as blessed Augustine says, we know that three things came forth from the Lord’s body as he hung on the wood: first, spirit, according to the saying, “Bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John 10); then, when his side was pierced with a lance, blood and water.

These three, each having its own different substance, are not one. But if we consider what is signified by them, the blessed Trinity, one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—comes to mind: under the name Spirit we understand God the Father to be signified, according to “God is Spirit” (John 4); under the name blood, the Son, because “the Word was made flesh”; and under the name water, the Holy Spirit, as the Evangelist says: “But he said this of the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (Luke 7). Thus Augustine.

Therefore, in order to prepare himself as a way for us to this Trinity, the Lord Jesus instituted three sacraments in these three things, by which the weak-sighted soul might meanwhile be cleansed and exercised; by exercise it might be enlarged; and, enlarged, might finally contain what it could not contain while idle. In water he instituted the sacrament of baptism; in blood, the sacrament of the altar, saying, “This cup is the new testament in my blood” (1 Cor. 11); and in the Spirit, the sacrament of confirmation—a sacrament which the Lord willed to be commended by signs of diverse tongues, when the Holy Spirit visibly confirmed and strengthened the Apostles with fire, as they imparted that same Spirit to others by the laying on of hands. By the fire of his presence he purifies every defilement, renews the human being, and transforms him.

Although these three sacraments are not one, the operation of the Trinity is one in the three, and threefold in each. In baptism a special operation of the Spirit appeared through the dove; the Son especially consecrated the mystery of the Eucharist by his Passion; in confirmation the Father was especially seen to act, who, sending the Spirit, invisibly illumined the hearts of the Apostles by his power. Therefore in confirmation the Father strengthens; in the handing over of the Eucharist, the Son wisely illumines the darkness of that night in which the flesh of the old lamb was eaten; in baptism the Holy Spirit, by the fire of his presence purifying every defilement, renews and transforms the human being.

And because the operation of the Trinity is inseparable, the whole Trinity performs these same three things in each sacrament. Therefore there are three who are shown to operate in the three sacraments, and the three are one; for in another way the whole Trinity is commended to us through these same substances. The Spirit, who makes people pray and intercedes for us with unutterable groanings (Rom. 8), commends the devotion of prayer. Almsgiving, interpreted as “the water of God,” plainly signifies water. Blood, by signifying blushes, shows the shame of confession and repentance.

These are the things that bear witness on earth, because by these fruits people are recognized on earth. They also outwardly bear witness to virtues hidden within: prayer to humility, abstinence to chastity, almsgiving to charity. How expressly the trace of the Trinity appears in these virtues will become plainly clear from what follows.

Meanwhile, outside the gate of old and earthly Jerusalem, and in the place of Calvary—that is, in newness of life—let the sons of Korah, marked with the threefold image of the aforesaid Trinity, set the seal upon their forehead, their heart, and their arm, as upon the lintel and the two doorposts, namely those of action and knowledge: so that with the heart one may believe unto righteousness, faith may work through love unto God’s glory (Rom. 10), and upon the forehead—that is, openly—confession may be made unto salvation (ibid.).

Let them also contemplate, in the first Trinity, the unity of a threefold signification; in the second, the unity of a threefold operation; and in the third, the threefold effect of one affection or intention. For the Lord teaches us to direct our intention to one end in those three matters, when he says in the Gospel, “When you pray, enter into your chamber” (Matt. 6), etc., plainly showing that prayer, almsgiving, and fasting must be referred to him who sees in secret, saying: “He who sees in secret will repay you” (ibid.).

But if it should please us to investigate the mystery of this testimony still more deeply and subtly, let this discourse end here for the present, lest, if it becomes too lengthy, it also become tedious. Therefore may he who is always Alpha and Omega be the beginning and end of our discourse: he who is the beginning and end of all things and remains without beginning and without end for ages of ages. Amen.

## TREATISE II. ON THE MARK, TITLE, AND TESTIMONY BY WHICH CHRIST WILLED HIS CITIZENS TO BE DISTINGUISHED

[Col. 0263D]

After the first man, earthly from the earth, had filled the world with earthly cities and inhabitants who minded earthly things, the new Man, heavenly from heaven, came; and, wishing to build a heavenly city on earth, he willed that his citizens, who minded heavenly things, should be distinguished from earthly citizens by the sign of his own character, marked beforehand by a title, and strengthened by a testimony. The sign was being made bald; the title, sonship; the testimony, the certainty of approved friendship through a more secret intimacy.

For the sign and image of the earthly man was to increase, multiply, and rule among earthly things. Thus indeed it was said to the first-created humans: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it; and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts of the earth, and every creeping thing [Col. 0264A] that moves upon the earth” (Gen. 1). But the new Man, granting to his followers the sign of newness, says: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). And again: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16). Also: “Whoever has left father or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 17).

See how our bald one wishes his own to be made bald of all temporal things, so that with an unencumbered face and open brow they may desire eternal things and raise their eyes to heaven without hindrance. The earthly citizens “have been multiplied by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil” (Ps. 4). Christ’s co-heirs, established uniquely in hope, “sleep and rest together in peace” (ibid.). For although many of them seem to abound in temporal goods, not at all shorn bald, but even to have their brow covered and burdened by many superfluities, nevertheless those who are true fellow-citizens of Christ use such things as though they did not use them; they place no hope in the uncertainty of riches, nor delight in luxurious pleasures, but, keeping death before their eyes, do not doubt that they will very soon be deprived of them. Nothing, indeed, mortifies in a human being the love of the world as does meditation upon death. Hence it is written: “Remember your last things, and you shall not sin” (Ecclus. 7). Nothing is more certain than death; nothing more uncertain than the hour of death.

Such people I would call ministers rather than [Col. 0264C] sons or friends in the house of the great householder. Such seem to have been the fathers of the Old Testament, who received the sign of circumcision, not the title of sonship or the testimony of special friendship. For although it was said to them, “I am the Lord your God” (Lev. 23), and “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3), yet we never read that it was said to them: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke 6); or, “Your heavenly Father will give the good Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 6). And although Abraham received the divine testimony, “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22), he nevertheless did not deserve to hear what was said to the apostles: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all things that I heard from my Father” (John 15).

This is the title of sons: “Everyone born [Col. 0264D] of God does not sin, because the divine generation preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him. By this the children of God and the children of the devil are made manifest” (1 John 5). And again: “What is born of God conquers the world” (John 3), so that victory over temptation is the title of heavenly birth; and, just as he who is Son by nature triumphed over the world together with its prince, so all who are sons by adoption are conquerors of the world.

The testimony of a friend is the bridegroom’s voice, giving joy and gladness to the hearing of the friend: whether it is directed to the friend, as in: “Rise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song 2); or spoken about the friend to others, as the Lord says concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matt. 11), and so forth. This twofold testimony of the friend [Col. 0265A] we shall pursue more fully later, if first the testimonies of ministers and sons have been sufficiently explained.

The distinction we have made between signs, titles, and testimonies rests on the fact that not all testimonies can be called signs or titles. Signs and titles, however, are rightly called testimonies insofar as they testify to something. Hence also, in the Roman Church, cardinal deacons, as certain ministers of the Lord’s table, do not assign titles in the devices of their seals; this has been granted only to cardinal presbyters, as to sons. Bishops, on the other hand, act in the place of friends: the nearer they are to the bridegroom, the more familiarly they hear his voice, and rejoice in the testimony of a more secret intimacy.

To each, then, the bridegroom renders testimony according to merits; and lest this testimony appear unstable, the whole Trinity supports it. There are therefore three things known to bear testimony, as it were on earth, to ministers occupied with transitory things: spirit, water, and blood. By these, if it is not tiresome for the reader to repeat what has been said, we have said that almsgiving, fasting, and prayer are denoted.

These testimonies are strengthened by countless testimonies of Sacred Scripture, Old and New. The words of sacred utterance are themselves called testimonies, because they bear witness that God’s commandments are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and abundant precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 18). And lest they be thought impossible, they also bear witness that many have kept them. Hence it is added: “For your servant keeps them” [Col. 0265C] (ibid.). And lest he seem to have kept them without profit, Scripture also does not keep silent concerning reward: “In keeping them there is great reward” (ibid.). And because, just as reward awaits the obedient, so condemnation awaits transgressors, they are rightly also called judgments.

The Prophet delighted in the testimonies of these commandments or judgments of God as in all riches, saying: “I have clung to your testimonies, O Lord” (Ps. 118). And: “Your testimonies are my meditation, and your ordinances my counsel” (ibid.). If we too search these testimonies more diligently through meditation, the aforesaid testimonies are commended by countless testimonies of Sacred Scripture.

Concerning fasting and prayer the Prophet says: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth. I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. 34). Concerning almsgiving: “The sinner borrows and does not repay, but the righteous shows mercy and gives” (Ps. 36). And: “He has scattered; he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111). Joel likewise speaks thus of fasting and prayer: “Return to me with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning” (Joel 2). Of almsgiving: “Break your bread for the hungry; bring needy wanderers into your house; when you see one naked, cover him” (Isa. 58). In Tobit likewise we read: “Prayer with fasting and almsgiving is good” (Tob. 2). And: “If you have much, give abundantly; if little, nevertheless share it willingly” (Tob. 4).

We refrain from setting forth every word and example commended in the Old and New Testaments, lest the accumulated abundance produce weariness. Yet I did not think that the things Jesus is read to have begun both to do and to teach should be omitted. For he, who was to accomplish the salvation of the human race in the midst of the earth, immediately after his baptism began with prayer and fasting. Thus it is read that, when he had been baptized and was praying, and the heavens had been opened above him, he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness; there, after he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he afterward hungered (Matt. 3).

Thereafter, until his passion, never abandoning these practices, he exercised them in alternating turns, so that one should not be confused with another: assigning the night to prayer, and the day to fasting, preaching, and healing, he passed through [Col. 0266B] “doing good and healing those oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10). Nor did he strive to invite us to these things by example alone; he also took care to commend them in words, saying: “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17).

For the sweetness of prayer and the inward affection of compunction are accustomed to beat down the falsely sweet affections of the flesh and the assaults “through evil angels” (Ps. 77). Fasting, however, resists by confronting temptations and occasions of sin brought to bear outwardly. Almsgiving obtains the joys of health and the gifts of graces for those purified by fasting and prayer, as the Lord says: “Give, and it shall be given to you. For with the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke 6). And the Apostle: “He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings” (2 Cor. 9).

For prayer directed to God then penetrates the heavens without obstacle, when, raised from lowly things by fasting and almsgiving as by two wings, it is supported by fasting as by the left wing, and advances and is guided by almsgiving as by the right and stronger wing. The wing of fasting has three principal feathers: one must fast from an unlawful deed, from a seductive impulse, and from an enticing affection. Likewise there are three principal feathers of almsgiving: that one should assist one’s neighbor by speech; assist from one’s own resources; or serve that neighbor, or pray for him.

These are what first bear testimony on earth: testimony before human beings, testimony for each person before himself, and testimony before God. Before human beings, it is the testimony of righteousness on which that Pharisee relied when he said: “God, I give you thanks, because I am not like other people—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers. I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke 15). For proud and arrogant, he gloried not merely in being righteous, but in appearing more righteous than others; and, content with human testimony, he was unwilling to consider his own. For the aforementioned actions bear testimony to each person concerning himself.

To say nothing of other matters, consider how far you have progressed in the virtue of abstinence, which is the beginning of all and the foundation and nurse of the virtues, without which there is no access to the rest. Enter and investigate every recess of your conscience: how your inner and outer condition stands; whether perhaps necessities—not to mention superfluities—are lacking. Whether the same expression, the same eyes, speech not different, and the same tranquillity of mind remain as when they were present. From this it will be clearer to you than light how constant and firm you are in the purpose of virtue.

Before God, however, these things afford us the testimony of confidence, so that we may confidently approach his throne of grace, we who vigorously fulfil his commandments. Hence it is written: “Almsgiving gives great confidence before God” (Tob. 4). And elsewhere: “By this we know that we have been translated from death to life: because we love the brethren. For if one who has the substance of this world sees his brother in need and closes his bowels against him, the love of the Father—which is true life—is not in him” (1 John 3).

But these testimonies of virtues, which are given toward merit, however firm they may appear, are signs of virtues rather than virtues themselves. For they are common to good and bad alike, and thus are practiced by foolish virgins—indeed, sometimes even more vigorously than by the wiser ones. For if the fasts, prayers, and almsgiving of heretics are compared with the efforts even of religious persons, these latter will seem either nonexistent or slight beside theirs. “But if I should hand over my body so that it might burn, and if I should distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I should have all faith so as to move mountains, but should not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13).

This first and visible trinity, therefore, is a sign of the supreme Trinity rather than an image: through the first, one recognizes that it is; through the second, rather what it is not than what it is. For one who approaches God must first believe “that he is, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him” (Heb. 11). By this faith the hearts of those approaching are first cleansed, according to the saying, “cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15), so that, with cleansed hearts, they may understand Truth itself, as it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7); and, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). The first step, therefore, is, believing that he is a rewarder of those who seek him, to inquire what he is not; then, with the heart cleansed, to understand what he is.

Therefore the Teacher of truth, wishing gradually to lead his disciples to the understanding of truth, appearing visible to the world, set visible things before his citizens; and in them he established the material of his whole city and expressed its form: so that the entire material of that city might proclaim God as three and one, its form might commend him, and the life of its citizens might confess through conduct as well as speech—until, with the image of the Trinity restored in them, they would no longer wander abroad seeking what they possessed inwardly in themselves.

Hence we see the imperfect, who still pursue visible things, perform outward works more earnestly and endure harsher things than the perfect: for “he who is diminished in action shall receive wisdom”; nor ought the sons of the bridegroom mourn while the bridegroom is with them. Let those mourn and go about the city who seek him and do not find him; let tears be their bread day and night (Ps. 41), while daily it is said to them, “Where is your God?” (ibid.). Let them seek, I say, outwardly by good works, or by examining outward things more diligently, so long as inward stillness neither pleases nor is permitted them.

Let them strive, by imitating him outwardly through fasting, prayer, and giving alms, to imprint upon themselves some image of the Trinity, though far dissimilar; nor in these three let them depart from the simplicity of unity, so that love may be wounded in a single eye; so that there may be one intention in the three, and one virtue of righteousness from the three—indeed, so that the three virtues themselves may be one virtue of righteousness—according to the Apostle’s saying: “There are three who bear testimony on earth, and the three are one” (John 3).

To such persons the Psalm, though not yet the Psalm of a Canticle, is fitting; for it does not belong to one laboring in groaning, sitting and weeping by the rivers of Babylon, and eating the bread of sorrow in a strange land, to sing the Lord’s song. Yet bread is not lacking even to such persons, although the song is lacking. For it ought not to be lacking to ministers, since it is lacking neither to hired servants nor to slaves. Hired servants too abound in bread; and to a slave are supplied work, discipline, and bread. But the Lord has compassion on ministers, who have already been made free from slaves; and, lest they fail on the way because of a three-day waiting—perhaps signified by those three days in which Saul, blind and taking neither food nor drink, awaited the Lord’s promise (Acts 9)—he is accustomed to set before them bread in threefold form.

The Lord already seemed in the Prophet to be weary of this bread and to long for the bread of sons, when he said: “How long will you be angry against the prayer of your servant? You will feed us with the bread of tears” (Ps. 79). This bread is sometimes made from tears of grief conceived through remembrance of past evils, such as Peter’s tears when, remembering the word of the Lord Jesus, he wept bitterly (Matt. 26). Sometimes from tears of shame, such as Hannah’s tears when, because her rival reproached her that the Lord had closed her womb, she wept abundantly (1 Sam. 1); or Susanna’s, when accused by the elders, she looked to heaven, was silent, and wept (Dan. 13). Sometimes from tears of fear and weariness, such as the tears of Elijah fleeing from Jezebel, when he said: “I beseech you, Lord, take away my soul; for I am no better than my fathers” (3 Kings 19); or of the Lord himself, who, when he began to fear and be wearied, had sweat like drops of blood falling upon the earth (Luke [Col. 0268D] 22).

The Lord himself therefore wished to be fed with this bread, lest his weaker members shrink from taking it. Hence he says through the Prophet: “I ate ashes as bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101). Yet to many it seems that this bread of ministers, although less sweet than the bread of sons, is set before them more abundantly than before sons, because the bread of sons is made from more hidden and more precious ingredients, that of ministers from cheaper and familiar kinds. The farther people are still removed from the bridegroom, the surer the reason and the greater the material they have for grieving over sins committed, blushing for things neglected, and fearing things to come.

But now, filled with so many tears, let us pass to the song of sons, which the title of the psalm seems to mark with the titles of nativity themes. For a title is accustomed to declare the subject matter of the following work and the dignity of the thing treated; this is sufficiently shown by the title set over the cross, of which it had been prophesied long before: “Do not destroy the inscription of the title” (Ps. 74).

Whoever, redeemed by the blood of the Crucified, and once made a son of the bald one, afterward degenerates from paternal morals, is corrupted in the inscription of this title within himself; and, estranged through dead works from the name of salvation, which is Jesus, and from the newness of life, which the name Nazarene signifies, is excluded also from the glory of the kingdom. Of such it is written: “Alien sons have lied to me; alien sons have grown old and have limped from their paths” (Ps. 17). But the sons of the kingdom do not limp, because “the Lord our God is upright,” and his sons are upright, and praise is fitting for the upright.

For knowledge of invisible things and love of eternal things make persons upright, just as care for and desire of earthly things make them crooked and lame. Therefore those who are perfectly bald, freely raising their brow toward eternal things, adorned with the titles of paternal likeness and royal freedom, sing to the bridegroom the bridal song, the new song, saying: “The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself in beauty” (Ps. 92). And: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115).

The Psalm of a Canticle is rightly said to suit these people, who no longer act from sadness or necessity, but “sing in the ways of the Lord, because great is the glory of the Lord” (Ps. 137). They do not act from fear, since fear has punishment; and to act from fear of punishment belongs more to slaves than to sons, who act from love and desire—not, however, for the Father alone, but rather for the paternal inheritance.

These I would first call heaven, in which Father, Word, and Holy Spirit are said to bear testimony, and the three to be one. For in them the image of the Trinity in unity, and of unity in Trinity, shines forth more clearly, just as the likeness of the father’s face customarily appears in his own children. But where there is an image or likeness, in human matters it is not the face itself that is more distinctly expressed, nor Truth itself, but an image. This image, therefore, must be sought in sons; Truth is reserved for friends.

I would call this image the three virtues of the now spiritual soul: chastity, humility, and charity. The three aforementioned practices of these virtues—fasting, prayer, and almsgiving—may rightly be called their bodies or, as it were, their garments, since these practices must be nourished and vivified by the virtues; nor do the virtues appear before human eyes except through them, delighting those eyes by their beauty.

These virtues are nothing other than certain affections of the soul, moderated and ordered by the Holy Spirit, so that they may be directed to what they ought to be and exist as they ought. Amnon’s affection for his sister, although it was directed toward what it ought to have been, because it was not as it ought to have been, was neither a virtue nor from the Holy Spirit.

Let us therefore consider how the image of the Trinity shines in these virtues. Chastity, which is love of incorruption, represents to us a likeness of eternity. [Col. 0270A] For what is nearer to eternity than incorruption? Of it Scripture says: “Incorruption makes a human being near to God” (Wis. 8). Humility, which proceeds from a true knowledge of one’s own weakness, bears in us a likeness of the highest Truth. For in what can anyone be nearer to truth than, through the truest knowledge of himself, by attributing to God not merely every good that he possesses, but also the goodness of his very being; and by attributing to himself every evil, not only what he suffers but also what he has done?

From this charity arises. For while through humility a person becomes contemptible in his own eyes and no longer finds rest in himself or in any other creature apart from God, God becomes sweeter to him than all things; and the more the creature becomes contemptible, the more sweetly the Creator shines forth. Yet the creature begins also to please in the Creator, although it ought rightly to displease in itself. What is more like the highest goodness than this charity, by which enemies are loved for God’s sake, friends in God, and God only for his own sake? Through it, indeed, we are made like him who, solely through his own goodness, “makes his sun rise upon the good and evil, and rains upon the just and unjust” (Matt. 5).

Thus, indeed, Father, Word, and Holy Spirit bear testimony in heaven—that is, in a human being illumined by such lights of virtue—that he is a son of his Father who is in heaven. For the Spirit also bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God and co-heirs with Christ, and that we have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, crying within us: “Abba, Father” (Mark 14).

We find in ourselves the image of the Trinity; it remains to discover unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity by some likeness in ourselves, though one far dissimilar. What then are these three virtues but, as we have said, three moderated and ordered affections? And what are these affections in a human being but the one human will, which, although it has the impulses of these three affections in outward action, nevertheless remains one inwardly—so much the more one as it is more closely joined to the one God; so much the more removed from unity as it is divided among diverse things, according to the saying: “You are anxious and troubled about many things, whereas one thing is necessary” (Luke 11).

The Prophet gloried that he possessed this unity when he said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek” (Ps. 26). Human will is therefore one in one way by nature, and in another by grace. Insofar as it is one by nature, it represents the image; insofar as it is one by grace, the likeness of God. By a certain substantial image it seems to imitate divinity, in that it was created such as to endure eternally. Although it had a beginning, yet because it does not know an end, what is more like eternity, while not itself eternity?

The mad, infants, and even sleepers are not without rational will, though they lack the exercise of discernment. What is more like divine power than rational will, created so free that it can be compelled by no force and changed by no necessity? For no one fails to will what he wills, or wills what he does not will.

Peter’s denial, therefore, arose not from necessity but from will—a will that endured the force it imposed upon itself, from no one but itself. Though he denied Christ sorrowing and compelled, he nevertheless did so only willingly, because he wished to avoid death: with a weak will indeed, but still with a will. For those whose will was sound could be killed, but could not be bent. See how free rational will is, whether in good or evil: it remains immovable even in hell. For the devil and anyone condemned with him in hell can no longer will good, not because violent or alien oppression makes this so, but because of their own will, obstinately fixed in evil. Likewise, an angel in heaven cannot will evil, not because necessity causes this, but because of a will firmly fixed in good and a voluntary steadfastness.

The will, therefore, is free for either course; but this freedom in the evil person is wretched and weak. Although it does not wholly depart from the image of God, according to the saying, “Man passes in an image” (Ps. 38), it is nevertheless far removed from it. For although it is free for him to will—because, having been created good, according to “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1), it received from creation both the ability not to sin and the ability to sin—yet by sinning it deserved that, because when it could it would not, it could not by itself even will rightly, nor, even if it should will, be able not to sin.

It is not liberated from this misery except by the grace of him who says: “If the Son sets you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8). By his grace the image deformed by sin is reformed in the good, so that it which in paradise received the ability not to sin and the ability not to be disturbed may meanwhile receive, in place of these, the ability to be overcome neither by sin nor by misery. For though it does sin and is disturbed vainly and miserably, this is no longer imputed to it, because “there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh” (Rom. 8).

At last, however, the image so reformed will be confirmed and conformed to divine freedom in such a manner that it will be unable either to sin or to be disturbed. In another respect also the will of rational humanity was made in the image of God and its Creator (Gen. 1). For as the one God moves all things, governs all things, and orders them according to his will, and so presides over all things that he is wholly in each individual thing, so the rational will, throughout its whole body as in a certain world of its own, is everywhere entire. Though one in itself, by its mere command it moves individual limbs, commands the senses, produces desires, and changes itself almost at every moment into various affections.

Now it raises itself to confidence; now it casts itself down into distrust. Now it is led by hatred, now by love; now it is torn by joy, now by grief. It suddenly detests what it had approved and vehemently desired; and it suffers with the whole body in such a way that, in individual limbs, it seems not so much that the limbs as that it itself is suffering. See how like it is to him of whom we read: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world; and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wis. 1). For he is “the artificer of all things, possessing all power, beholding all things” (Wis. 7).

But see how deformed this image is so long as human will disagrees with the divine will: “You have set me in opposition to you,” he says, “and I have become a burden to myself” (Job 7).

[Col. 0272A] And again: “Who has resisted him and had peace?” (Eph. 2). For no one can have peace until he agrees with that adversary who willed to become our peace, “making both one,” giving peace to those far off and peace to those near. When, through this one’s grace, human will has been raised from the dust and cleansed, and begins by agreeing with him to will the good, then good will, reconciled to peace, returns to the glory of the Most High. And no glory for this is owed to another than him whose grace alone works it in the converted person. Agreeing with this, Paul said: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15).

From this point, a human being is made a son of God by grace, according to the saying: “He willingly begot us by the word of truth” (James 1). Formerly, by consenting to the flesh through his own will, he had been his own by nature; or, by consenting to the devil through an evil will, he had been the devil’s. By willing the good, therefore, not only is the image deformed by sin reformed through grace, but the likeness of God, previously lost, is also superimposed upon the image.
