In this likeness, lesser than the image, the lost sheep or drachma is found; the unit is added to the ninety-nine (Luke 15); the possession is restored to its lord; and it becomes so like him that, by willing the same thing, it becomes one spirit with him, according to the saying: “Whoever cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6).

This likeness will be complete when it shall fully appear, according to the saying: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). Meanwhile, so long as we know in part, we are made like in part; and we shall approach likeness more closely in proportion as we shall behold more clearly with a purer heart. But this perfection is reserved for friends and initiated in ministers. It advances gradually in sons; in ministers it is initiated, or rather prepared, by poverty of spirit and meekness. In sons it advances and is tasted beforehand through hunger for righteousness and the practice of mercy. It advances through hunger of desire; it is tasted beforehand through the attainment of mercy, which is a foretaste of satiety. In friends it is perfected through purity of heart and peace, which embrace one another with an eternal bond, so that, once perfected, they cannot be separated from each other.

For in the one, namely purity of heart, the image is restored; in the other—that is, the other part—the likeness is renewed. The image is in freedom, as has been said; the likeness in uprightness. For freedom imitates divine power; its corruption is pride, the punishment of its corruption weakness, and its restoration humility, through which purity of heart is acquired, according to the saying: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50). Hence Augustine well says: “What does pride seek except power? If we refer this to facility in doing good, it is found only in a soul perfectly subject to God and turned toward his governance with the highest charity.”

Behold, the perfection of freedom in the present is freedom from the slavery of sin, which is purity of heart, to be consummated more fully in the future, when creation itself “will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8). This will be the freedom of glory; the second is that of grace; the first, that of nature.

[Col. 0273A] It remains to find likeness in uprightness and uprightness in peace. For we read that God made the human being upright, but he himself entangled himself in infinite questions (Eccles. 7). So long as he was upright, neither zeal nor knowledge was lacking to him; for if either were lacking, uprightness would undoubtedly limp. For if he either knew and did not will, or willed to act rightly and did not know, how would he be upright? Thus, by knowing, uprightness imitates divine wisdom; by willing well, it imitates divine goodness. Therefore, by knowing and willing the good, a human being becomes upright, rightly made like him of whom it is written: “The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. 91).

As we have said that this likeness has twofold advancement, so it is clear that it has a twofold corruption. Knowledge is corrupted by curiosity. Hence blessed Augustine: “What does curiosity seek except knowledge which is not true, knowledge of things eternal and always remaining in the same manner?” Zeal, however, is corrupted by pleasure of the flesh. Hence the same author cited above: “What does bodily pleasure seek except rest, which is not true save where there is no want and no corruption?”

To wish to know things that are always changing and never remain in the same state, or to wish to delight in the flesh, whose need and weakness the whole world cannot satisfy—what else is this but to fall away from uprightness, to entangle oneself in infinite questions, and miserably to withdraw from the stability of true rest, as from divine likeness, into a region of dissimilarity?

[Col. 0273C] This, then, is the corruption of uprightness; and the punishment of corruption is vain and wretched disturbance. Hence it is that a human being is vainly and miserably disturbed, and “passes in an image.” It rightly says “passes,” because, content with the freedom of nature alone, he passes by the glory of true freedom—which is freedom from sin—through contempt. It rightly says “vainly,” because a human being is disturbed from no other cause than that, deceived through ignorance, he either seeks things that seem good but are not truly good, or flees evils that are not truly evil. While he pursues the former and does not attain them, and flees the latter and does not escape them, in either case he is vainly and miserably disturbed.

These two matters seem distinctly expressed in the Canon of the Mass, where we say: “That, helped by the aid of your mercy, we may be always free from sin and secure from every disturbance.”

From this twofold punishment and twofold corruption a human being is restored to rectitude by the two things already mentioned: namely, hunger for righteousness and the practice of mercy. By these one rises to purity of heart and to the haven of the peace spoken of above, where, although a person may sometimes seem to be troubled, he is nevertheless not broken by disturbance, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. VIII). And: “I am certain that neither death nor life, nor the rest that follows, shall be able to separate us from the charity of Christ” (ibid.). This is that peace which surpasses all understanding: it is nothing other than the enjoyment of the highest good; it is true rectitude, true wisdom, true goodness. Whoever has reached this peace, choosing with Mary the better part [Col. 0274A] (Luke X), now refuses to be occupied with many things; nor does he any longer wish to involve himself in diverse questions, since it delights him to cling to the one supreme good. This belongs to friends, to whom it is said: “All things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV). And: “Because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will set thee over many: enter into the joy of thy Lord” (Matt. XXV). For God is fire; whoever clings to him through charity becomes fire himself—not merely most like him, but absorbed into fiery charity. “Blessed therefore are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God” (Matt. V), and from children they shall become friends.

Let what has been said suffice for the present, as testimony that the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit bear in heaven, working according to three proper effects [Col. 0274B] and yet in no respect departing from the simplicity of unity. Something should now be said about the testimony borne in the golden resting-place of friends, as though in a second heaven, to those to whom the Word now announces the Father not in parables but openly. But it would be unworthy to confine so great a subject within the narrow limits of this discourse; nor should children be left hungry, to whom we have not yet allotted their bread, when we have given three loaves to servants, while that of children ought to be more abundant and more delightful. Thus the Lord said that the bread of children ought not to be taken away and cast to dogs (Matt. XV). In this, perhaps, he intimated that the bread of servants need not be withheld from dogs. Accordingly, he also approved the word of the little woman [Col. 0274C] who said that the puppies eat of the crumbs falling from their masters’ table. Would that we might deserve to receive even crumbs from the children’s table, if we are unable fully to distribute whole loaves. For we are little children, and are unable not only to break whole loaves, but even need them to be broken for us by others. Yet if the Lord blesses and breaks them, the blessing will drive away want, and the breaking will remove every harshness of difficulty.

Let us therefore ask our heavenly Father to give his children the good Spirit, who cries, “Abba, Father” (Gal. IV), and bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. From such testimony conscience glories; the oil in the vessels is enlarged; the soul delights with ineffable joy in the hope of the glory of God’s children; and perhaps that [Col. 0274D] joy is the bread of children. In making this bread from the seeds which servants, going forth and weeping, cast into good ground, children lift up their sheaves with exultation and gather joy from the patience of faith and hope: rejoicing in hope because they were patient in tribulation. This joy, then, which as a kind of firstfruits of the Spirit is poured out through the Holy Spirit so that hope may act more confidently, is the bread of children, “because the expectation of the righteous is joy” (Prov. X). Nor does the number of loaves differ from the number of testimonies, since every testimony of the divine Spirit is for the human spirit both cause and matter of joy. The Lord desired his own to rejoice from no other source when he said: “Do not rejoice in this, that demons are subject to you; but rejoice in this, that your names are written [Col. 0275A] in heaven” (Luke X). This cannot be known except through the testimony of the Spirit. Let the first bread of children, therefore, be joy in contempt for the world; for we assign chastity as the first testimony of the Spirit.

True chastity of soul is to love nothing except God, or for God’s sake. Every other spiritual love is fornication of the soul. This chastity is given as merit and is an undoubted testimony of virtue. Therefore the joy which arises from such testimony may rightly be called bread, bread strengthening the human heart; otherwise every grace which virtue has not brought forth is suspect. The second bread of children is joy in contempt for oneself. For when someone sees himself despised, because he knows himself to be truly contemptible, [Col. 0275B] he rejoices together with truth. What is more solid than such joy? What strengthens the mind more, so that, while through contempt for the world it now scorns hardships, through contempt for itself it also embraces lowly things? The apostles were strengthened by this bread when they departed rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been judged worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus (Acts V).

Let us call the third bread of children joy in love for one’s neighbour. For so long as a person has not yet approached the lofty heart, it is not enough to love God in himself. Yet if he loves him perfectly in his neighbour, he rejoices no less in that neighbour’s good than in his own, and finds as many reasons for joy as occasions arise for rejoicing in the successes of his neighbours. What bread is stronger than this? At its most sweet taste, the stings of envy [Col. 0275C] are lulled, the heats of anger and indignation are calmed, and the bites of consuming sorrow and suspicion are destroyed. The Prophet lamented that this bread had been withdrawn from him when he said: “I am smitten like grass, and my heart is withered, because I have forgotten to eat my bread” (Ps. CI). Strengthened by these loaves, the soul already delights in the hope of the glory of God’s children with a certain assurance of the reality itself—not content merely with the limits of faith or hope, but confirmed by the testimony of conscience, so that it may rightly say with Paul: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). Hope supported by this testimony does not in the least bring shame, especially when such testimony is upheld by the merits of the works mentioned above, the gifts of the virtues mentioned above, and the rewards of the consolations mentioned above, by which the Father of mercies and God of all consolation feeds and consoles his children in all their tribulation [Col. 0275D].

May he therefore always be the Alpha and Omega of our discourse: he who is the beginning and end of all things, and remains without beginning and without end unto ages of ages. Amen.

## TREATISE III. ON THE TESTIMONY WHICH THE HOLY TRINITY BEARS TO FRIENDS: WHO ARE HERE DISTINGUISHED FROM CHILDREN AND SERVANTS

Taking occasion from the fact that a psalm of song is attributed to the sons of Korah, we find in the house of the great householder not only children, but also servants and friends. And just as a psalm of song is assigned to children, so we have thought fit to assign a psalm to servants. Yet if we assign a song of psalm [Col. 0276A] to friends, this too will not be unfitting, once the reason for this distinction has been understood. A psalm of song belongs to those who labour to attain the song of spiritual joy, fearing the Apostle’s threat: “He who does not work shall not eat” (II Thess. III). And Solomon’s saying: “Sloth brings on sleep, and the idle soul shall hunger” (Prov. XIX). Likewise, a song of psalm seems to belong to those who, giving thanks for the benefits received in spiritual joys, can find nothing else to render to the Lord except to take the cup of salvation; and, as Christ’s sufferings abound in them, so spiritual consolation through Christ may abound in them.

This is known to belong especially to friends, who [Col. 0276B] now act not out of fear of punishment like servants, nor out of hope for their father’s inheritance like children, but solely out of charity, anointed with the unction of the Spirit. We undertake to say something about them, lest we should rightly be blamed for having passed over the testimony of those who are foremost in the city of the Lord and occupy the place of the second heaven. In them the Father, the Word, and the Spirit bear testimony brighter than light, so that, with the face of the Lord now unveiled, they behold his glory and are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord. In these words of the Apostle the testimony of the Trinity is clearly expressed. For when he says, “From glory to glory” (II Cor. III), he seems to indicate what the Lord is recorded to have promised: “The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in proverbs, but [Col. 0276C] shall announce to you openly concerning the Father” (John XVI). For what else is it for the Son openly to announce concerning the Father than to advance from the glory of the Word to the glory of the Father? Hence it is written: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI). But the Son makes this revelation through the Spirit, whom he sends to us from the Father. Therefore it is added: “As from the Spirit of the Lord” (ibid.), so that the whole Trinity may be shown to effect in us the revelation of this testimony.

I judge this testimony to be nothing other than that coming of the Trinity promised to friends in these terms: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word,” etc. (John XIV). What testimony is stronger than this, when the Father, coming, powerfully strengthens the weak soul; [Col. 0276D] the Son wisely enlightens the foolish one; and the Holy Spirit vehemently kindles the lukewarm one? The Prophet lamented that this testimony had been withdrawn from him when he said: “My strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes—this also is not with me” (Ps. XXXVII). Wisdom seems to invite us to it where she says: “Learn where wisdom is, where strength is, where the light of the eyes is, and peace” (Baruch III). Such testimony belongs especially to a friend, who is now upright enough to stand in love for invisible things with the bridegroom and, having conceived immeasurable joy at the bridegroom’s voice, is made more certain through the intimacy of a more secret address that he is reckoned by the bridegroom among his friends, according to the saying: “I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV).

I would rightly call such persons the second [Col. 0277A] heaven, for the third seems rather to belong to the most dearly beloved. The most dearly beloved are rightly understood as those who, now stripped of the body, have been taken up by the Lord, lest malice change their understanding or deceit deceive their souls (Wis. IV). Drawn out from the midst of iniquities, they now happily experience how great are God’s grace and mercy toward his saints, and his regard for his elect. To such persons it is said: “Be intoxicated, dearly beloved” (Song V). For what they experience is intoxication in comparison with that delight which friends enjoy. Thus Paul too, who was reckoned among the foremost friends, when he was caught up into the third heaven of the dearly beloved, declares that he heard ineffable words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak (II Cor. XII). They are proved to exceed the measure of human sobriety, which a human being [Col. 0277B] cannot contain. Therefore Paul declares rather that he was snatched up by divine mercy than led by human reason.

The inhabitants of this third heaven need no testimony, since they see all things nakedly and openly. For faith has already passed for them into sight; what is received in reality and truth is no longer believed or hoped for. But in the present life, so long as one walks by faith, testimony is necessary even for friends, where ignorance and uncertainty have a place. Ignorance is driven away by the clarification of testimony; uncertainty is removed by the authority of witnesses. Friends therefore have, as testimony of divine love, the very presence of the Trinity. But the testimony of children consists in the various gifts of virtues and graces of God, [Col. 0277C] which the Apostle enumerates when he says: “There are diversities of graces; but it is the same God who works all things in all. To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another workings of miracles,” and the rest that follows (I Cor. XII).

From these gifts of God they receive from the Holy Spirit testimony of their sonship. From these pledges and firstfruits of the Spirit they now confidently presume upon receiving their paternal inheritance. But he who works such varied things in children presents to friends himself, one and the same, and all other things in himself, as he promises them in the Gospel, where it is said: “And I will manifest myself to him” (John XIV). Happy manifestation, where the Trinity is known in unity and unity in Trinity; where the threefold effect of the Trinity is perceived in [Col. 0277D] one operation; and where the one operation of the Trinity is proved by the testimony of three effects. By this testimony a human being is raised to the heights, snatched up to divine things; indeed, he becomes heaven itself, or what is greater, God and Lord of heaven, according to the saying: “I have said: You are gods” (Ps. LXXXV). What is more blessed than this testimony, by which nothing in low things now pleases; nor even in heaven does anything suffice except the Lord of heaven, according to the Prophet’s saying: “What have I in heaven? And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII). “My heart said to you: My face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I will seek” (Ps. XXVI). And: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek” (ibid.). Behold: by asking, seeking, and thirsting for the one, the Prophet, made one spirit with God, happily deserved to experience [Col. 0278A] what the Lord prayed to the Father for his own in the Gospel: “That as we are one, so they too may be one in us” (John XVII).

Friends are refreshed swiftly and in alternation in their own heaven by this testimony, by which the dearly beloved are most fully satisfied in their own heaven. Of this satisfaction the Prophet, addressing the heavenly Jerusalem, says: “Who has made your borders peace and satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. CXLVII). It has peace for its bounds, since it possesses peace without end. For the end there has no end, where eternity is the end. The peace of the heavenly Jerusalem, therefore, because it is without end, lacks alternation and rejoices in continuity. Conversely, in the present life, in which the mind must go outward to provide for its body, when it returns to itself from concern for so many necessities—as from a certain road of anxieties—a person scarcely finds within himself [Col. 0278B] what he may set before it. Therefore he is compelled to knock importunately at the door of his friend and scarcely at last deserves to receive even three loaves on loan.

Here one must carefully observe that a loan entails alternation: what is lent is granted for use for a time, not given for permanent possession. Continuity, therefore, is in the homeland; alternation, on the journey. Nor is alternation alone present, but want accompanies it, as the request so pressing and importunate demonstrates. To complete the evil, there is also the division of the loaves, which proves their threefold distinction, separation, and imperfection. But the heavenly Jerusalem is shown to have neither, for it is satisfied with the fat of wheat. There the fat of wheat [Col. 0278C] prevents the alteration of husk and indicates perfection of purity. Satisfaction excludes every want: so that neither does satisfaction produce disgust, nor has any want a place there; fullness crushes want, and the delightfulness of complete savour drives away disgust. Nor is any division found there, where after the seventh sevenfold period of the present life one arrives at that monad which is supremely and immutably one and admits neither alteration nor the shadow of alternation. The nearer one approaches that supremely one, the farther are removed all alternation, all need, every change of alteration and division.

Here the servant is compelled to knock, the child to ask, and the friend to seek his bread. [Col. 0278D] Knocking is fittingly assigned to the servant, whose condition of servitude commands him to apply himself insistently to manual work, according to Solomon’s saying: “Fodder, a whip, and a burden for an ass; bread, discipline, and work for a servant” (Ecclus. XXXIII). Asking befits the child, who prays to the Father, who judges it unworthy to take the children’s bread and cast it to dogs. Nor does he ordinarily give a stone to the child who asks for bread, a serpent for a fish, or a scorpion for an egg. For the heavenly Father knows that the child needs the egg of humility, from which is born the chick of obedience and submission, lest, deceived by the scorpion of pride—whether by empty promises, a pleasant appearance, or ostentation prepared beforehand—or crushed and overcome by threats and terrors, as though by armed hind-parts, he should be defeated. He also knows that the child needs the fish of chastity [Col. 0279A], unharmed by the cold and waves of temptation, lest that slippery serpent, whose strength is in his loins and whose power is in the navel of his belly, pour in the poison of carnal pleasure. He knows likewise that the child cannot lack the bread of charity, lest he fail or, hardened through avarice, remain with a dry and hard heart because he has forgotten to eat his bread.

This bread the friend seeks and finds. For although he too is sometimes compelled to knock and ask, seeking and finding are nevertheless proper to the friend, who, from the confidence received through love, trusts that he will conceal nothing which he seeks from his friend. The Lord himself put this forward as evidence of love when he said: “I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV). Yet it is not enough for him [Col. 0279B] to make known to his friend what he has heard from the Father; he also promises the vision of himself, saying: “I will love him, and I will manifest myself to him” (John XIV). The special testimony of love, therefore, is the vision of the beloved. And I would call this vision the bread of friends, for whom nothing now has savour except the beloved, for whom “to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” But because this vision varies in three ways, we have also said that this bread must be distinguished threefold.

The first is received and tasted by dilation of the mind, the second by elevation of the mind, the third by alienation. Dilation extends itself more broadly than usual, because it reaches beyond one’s own knowledge, yet does not exceed the measure of human effort. Elevation transcends that measure, though fear does not wholly depart from the senses. In alienation [Col. 0279C] the memory of present things falls away from the mind, and the human spirit, as far as is permitted in the present life, passes wholly into the beloved. But because the human mind is also accustomed, in contemplation, to be enlarged, raised, or even alienated concerning invisible created essences, we call only that contemplation the bread of friends by which the mind, in love and knowledge of the supreme and creative essence, is enlarged and raised above the measure of its own awareness and effort, or is even alienated above the capacity of all human nature and effort.

Since this is granted only to friends, a friend is rightly invited to this banquet when it is said: “Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song II). That soul, I say, which the brightness of chastity has made beautiful, the groaning [Col. 0279D] of humility has made a dove, and the vehemence of charity has made a friend, is summoned to rise and hasten from contemplation of every visible and invisible creature to the vision of the uncreated and invisible essence. And let her who is now perfected in those three virtues glory in the Lord of virtues alone, taught not merely through the prophet but also hearing and understanding with the prophet that the Lord of virtues himself is the King of glory. In him alone, I say, one must glory: from him comes every good gift; from him, all good gifts—the gifts of nature; from him, better gifts—the charisms of grace, which the Apostle enumerates when he says, “To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge,” etc. (I Cor. XII); and finally, from him come the best gifts, namely, the virtues of the age to come, which the Apostle says are tasted even in the present age [Col. 0280A], because in the present age they are exercised in act and tasted in affection, while in the future age they will exist in affection alone and be possessed in unending actuality.

Meanwhile, let us strive to practise them with most fervent action and desire most ardently to taste them in affection, so that, although we cannot be satisfied here, at least we may never cease to hunger and thirst. Perhaps by hungering and thirsting we shall merit his presence more easily than by investigating or disputing: he who is accustomed to satisfy in good things the desire of his friend, and whose presence knows how to fill with joy and, when he appears, to mark the friend with glory. For when he appears to a friend, he makes him like himself; and the Lord of virtues makes the lover—indeed, the imitator—of virtues, so that those who cannot be equals may at least be alike. And let the bride, who [Col. 0280B] cannot be equal to the bridegroom, endeavour by beholding and imitating to become at least like him, and become for young women a model of virtues, she who has already deserved through love to be betrothed to the Lord of virtues.

Such a soul proclaims not her own virtues but those of the beloved; she glories no longer in herself or about herself, but in the beloved and about the beloved, saying: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song V). As though she said: Whatever whiteness I have comes from him who alone is truly white—indeed, who is true whiteness: the whiteness, I say, of eternal light, which makes those whom it illumines not only white in action but radiant in understanding. But what comparison is there between one who is white and whiteness itself? It is no other than that between illumination and light, a streamlet and a fountain.

[Col. 0280C] Thus it is rightly said that no fuller upon earth can imitate the whiteness of his garments (Mark IX). And if I seem ruddy, let it be imputed not to me but to him whose blood has adorned my cheeks, who is not merely ruddy through charity but is redness itself—indeed, fire: an anointing, not consuming fire, which by gently touching those whom it has licked makes them also burn outwardly in works of piety and inwardly in the affection of compassion or, what is sweeter, in the flame of devotion. Therefore, if I seem to you white through chastity or ruddy through charity, I perceive and confess that I have my whole self from the beloved—indeed, from the chosen one—whom I chose to love from among thousands, indeed above thousands, that is, above all things embraced by number. For he is above number, creating all things in number, weight, and measure; but of his wisdom there is no number, and of his greatness there is no end. [Col. 0280D] Him I chose, him I loved, and with him—indeed, from him—all good things came to me together (Wis. VII). From him I have the lily of chastity, from him the rose of charity, from him the violet of humility. The garden itself produced such flowers for me; the gardener himself plucked them for me and showed them to be gathered and chosen. But first he taught that the violet was to be chosen, himself choosing it first, so that, as pride had been first in humankind’s fall, humility might be first in restoration.

Therefore, choosing humility for the salvation of human beings, humble Jesus was deservedly chosen, from the small number of the elect, above the great number of the reprobate. Chosen to be imitated, chosen to be relied on, chosen to be loved. He was made wisdom for us to be loved; [Col. 0281A] righteousness to be imitated; sanctification and redemption to be relied on. Wisdom in preaching; righteousness in conduct; sanctification and redemption in suffering. He was made the way to be imitated, truth to be relied on—for, according to Solomon, one must not rely on falsehood (Prov. X)—and life to be loved, because whoever does not love him remains in death (I John III). He offered himself to all for imitation through humility; to some he offered himself as support for chastity, saying: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. He who can receive this, let him receive it” (Matt. XIX). As though he said: Whoever cannot do so, let him trust in me, and through me he will be able to do what he cannot do through himself. For no one can be continent unless God grants it (Wis. VIII). He taught that he must be loved above all when he said: [Col. 0281B] “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X). And: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Matt. XXII).

In the first there is pain, in the second labour, in the third rest and the end of labour. Pain brings shame; labour afflicts; love renews and transforms, bringing all former labours into forgetfulness. Pain indeed brings shame because, when the soul first girds itself to imitate Christ’s humility through poverty, patience, and obedience, hindered either by weakness of nature, by a fault of nature, or by the force of evil habit, it often falls back—even unwillingly—into things it has already renounced. Thus, troubled, grieving, and ashamed within itself, it is compelled to cry out with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me [Col. 0281C] from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII). Nevertheless, such sorrow does not produce death but rather brings in the hope of salvation, hope which does not bring shame, because Truth does not lie when it says: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John XVI).

Labour too afflicts, because when the soul, despairing of itself, has begun to rely upon the beloved alone, it begins, now forgetful of its own weakness, to afflict the flesh beyond human strength, knowing that the mortification of the flesh produces the quickening of the spirit, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit” (I Pet. III). Finally, that love renews, and that rest is the end and reward of labours, is known by the friend who is accustomed to experience this joy of tranquillity. Established in this haven, therefore, the friend [Col. 0281D] ever seeks new testimonies of his friend, delighting in them with the Prophet more than in all riches (Ps. CXVIII). Thus he is not ashamed when it happens that he speaks of these testimonies in the presence of spiritual kings. A friend, I say, can speak without shame of God’s testimonies when personal experience teaches him the things he speaks, and neither his life nor his conscience reproaches him as he speaks.

Hence God’s testimonies have become exceedingly credible: so credible that he does not now believe about himself on another’s testimony, nor even on his own, saying with the Apostle: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified. He who judges me is the Lord” (I Cor. IV). Nor does he trust himself on the basis of all the Lord’s own testimonies, knowing that the Lord sometimes commends some persons for the sake of others, not for their own sake. [Col. 0282A] Thus he says that to certain persons, to whom a word of wisdom has been given for usefulness, who will say at the end, “Have we not prophesied in your name, and done many mighty works in your name?”, he will answer: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. VII). Therefore, whether a friend receives a word of wisdom, a word of knowledge, prophecy, or kinds of tongues; whether all mysteries are revealed, or even faith is given that removes mountains—however a friend may appear to smile upon a friend—he does not trust himself on account of all such testimonies unless he feels the testimony of charity.

This testimony alone is the bridegroom’s voice, on account of which the friend rejoices with joy. Though he may rejoice at the voice of teacher, master, brother, or father, he rejoices with a special joy [Col. 0282B] at the voice of the bridegroom. For as father he admonishes; as master he threatens and terrifies; as teacher he instructs; as brother he rejoices together; as bridegroom he clings closely. As brother he embraces; as bridegroom he is united. In each there is sweetness; in each, love; but between brother and sister it is more familial, between bridegroom and bride more ardent. There is a bond of nature; here, of grace. The bond of nature is indeed more conformable to nature, but that of grace is sweeter and more powerful, so that a man leaves father and mother and clings to his bride. Between brother and sister there is an embrace of like-mindedness, making one will and one refusal between two persons; between bridegroom and bride there is the adhesion of mutual intermingling, by which the bride, melted, passes wholly into the bridegroom and is transformed into the same image, [Col. 0282C] so that, as in carnal union they are no longer two but one flesh, so in spiritual union they may be no longer two but one spirit.

This unity is produced not merely by the single agreement of two wills, but by one enjoyment and one effect of twofold love. Although the brother’s left hand is beneath his sister’s head and his right embraces her, nevertheless no one rises to the singular grace of the bridegroom except the bride; nor does anyone rejoice with joy at the bridegroom’s voice except either the bride or the bridegroom’s friend—and not even the friend always. For it is not joy of joy to him when the bridegroom’s voice is addressed to him on account of the bride; he rejoices with joy only when it is addressed to him as to the bridegroom’s own bride. For he is a friend when he promotes the bride’s advancement; he is the bride when, free for the bridegroom alone, he gathers all his affections and directs them toward [Col. 0282D] the bridegroom, desiring that one thing and seeking that one thing in the bridegroom: that he may show himself to her.

I believed these things concerning divine testimonies should be said before I approached the discussion of the foundations, so that from such testimonies each person may readily recognize either what state he possesses or what rank he holds in the city of the Lord of virtues. If he finds himself among servants, let him strive to be numbered among children, for the Lord is able even from stones to raise up children to Abraham (Luke III). But if he knows, through the Spirit crying “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII), that he has reached the rank of children, let him strive also to ascend to the prerogative of friends, so that, founded in this way upon the firm rock, he may read the solidity of the city’s foundations in himself rather than in our written characters. For we do not intend to teach friends [Col. 0283A] who have the anointing as their teacher; would that we might be able to minister something of this sort even to servants, so that we may be worthy at least of the name of servants in the city of the Lord.

Drawing nearer now to the city itself, let us endeavour not so much to lay foundations as carefully to investigate those laid by the Lord of virtues himself. May he always be the Alpha and Omega of our discourse, who is the beginning and end of all things and remains without beginning and without end unto ages of ages.

## TREATISE IV. ON THE FOUNDATION OF THE CITY OF GOD

“Her foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI). Many kings and prophets desired to see what we see and did not see it, and to hear what we hear [Col. 0283B] and did not hear it (John VIII). But some desired to see, as the Lord says of Abraham: “They saw and rejoiced.” David must be believed to have been among these, for he declares concerning himself in the Psalm: “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of our God; God has founded her for ever” (Ps. XLVII). Therefore, wishing faithfully to communicate to present and future readers what he had seen in that city, he begins to describe it from its very foundation, saying: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains.” “Her,” he says—the city which he beheld inwardly in the spirit—as distinct from that which is openly seen outwardly. For there are two cities: one of God, the other of the devil; one spiritual, the other carnal. The foundations of both are in mountains. The foundations of the carnal city are in the mountains of Gilboa, where there is neither dew nor rain [Col. 0283C], in the northern mountains; those of the spiritual city are in holy, warm mountains, where is the dew of Hermon, where the Lord commanded blessing and life. The city is planted that inclines toward the south; when the south wind blows, its spices flow forth.

Of these things one reads in the prophet Isaiah: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it” (Isa. II). We must inquire more carefully what this mountain is and upon the summit of what mountains it is prepared. This mountain is Christ, the mountain of God, a rich mountain. The patriarchs and prophets are the mountains that prepare this mountain. [Col. 0283D] The hills alongside this mountain, above those same mountains, may rightly be called Mary and Joseph, who were manifestly more eminent in proportion as they were more closely joined to him. It is pleasing to behold a kind of new and recently founded city in one house: Mary and Joseph and the infant laid in a manger. Do they not seem already to say to you: “The high mountains are for the harts” (Ps. CIII)? We are being prepared; we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. The foundations are visible, but the towers and walls are not yet visible.

But because the beginning is usually the chief part of anything, the foundations must be investigated more carefully, since from them perhaps we shall better know how great a structure of buildings should rise. Certainly, in the little Jesus I see the foundations of humility; in Mary, those of chastity; and in Joseph, their nourisher and guardian, I find the perfection of charity [Col. 0284A]. These are the most precious and firmest foundations of the city of the Lord of virtues, upon which every building constructed grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Although the persons just named are each called foundations, Christ is nevertheless the one foundation. From his fullness all receive; and what others have severally by grace, he possesses wholly by nature. He who, born a man upon earth, became the foundation and pattern of humility, is in heaven, abiding in his divinity, light to angels and nourishment of truth. He who displayed the pattern of chastity not only in himself but also in his mother is, in his own nature, immutable eternity. He whose goodness and humanity were shown to us in his birth, and first rendered back to him with deepest devotion by Joseph, [Col. 0284B] is eternal and true charity, dear and true eternity, eternal and dear truth.

O Lord, how great was that charity by which you became a foundation in the city of human beings through humility, you who through charity confirmed the orders of angels. How great is the power of this foundation, which carries a human being from the truth of humility, by the vehicle of charity, to the rest of eternity! Behold how greatly, through the merit of the foundation, every building constructed upon it rises.

Thus, thus by the spirit of fear one arrives at the spirit of wisdom; thus the stone cut out without hands—that is, not by human work or skill, but by the fear of the Lord inspired in a human being through grace alone—shatters and overturns the statue of pride and vanity, and grows into the mountain of perfection. For the more humility grows, [Col. 0284C] the more vanity declines, and the statue of Babylon, the statue of the Babylonian city, is overthrown. For that city too has foundations opposed to the foundations of our city. For as the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, so pride is the beginning of every sin; and the punishment of pride is lust and avarice. Rightly indeed does anyone lose everything who, wishing to delight in something outside his own good, so far as lies in him cuts off the part from the whole, since every lesser good is less in itself than it is in its whole.

Therefore, by pride a human being abandons the good which he was made to be; by lust he finds himself rebellious and contrary to himself; by avarice he either pursues with toil things that flee from him, or guards with fear and anxiety those he has pursued. [Col. 0284D] By pride he opposes God; by lust, himself; by avarice, his neighbour.

These are the foundations of the earthly city, which are found laid already in Paradise itself, in the first-created humans and in the serpent, as though in certain earthly mountains. Pride is marked in the serpent, when it incites them to love of their own excellence, saying: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). In the woman is found the pleasure of fleshly desire, where it is read: “Seeing that the tree was beautiful to behold and pleasant for food, she took of its fruit and ate” (ibid.). Avarice is especially displayed in Adam, where he is condemned to cultivate the earth even in the sweat of his brow. Behold: these lay hidden in the root, but afterwards they sprang up far and wide and with great power in the branches.

[Col. 0285A] Hence Cain’s fratricide arose from pride: by it, hating and envying the grace and glory bestowed by God upon one younger than himself. Hence in that same man came wandering from the lust of the flesh, because, according to Solomon, lust makes the person it has subjected to itself talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet, unable even to remain standing at home, but now lying in wait outside, now in the streets, now beside the corners. Finally, avarice makes him a fugitive, because the miser, regarding every person as suspect, no longer trusts anyone securely; in fearing and avoiding all, he somehow flees them all.

Behold how greatly these destructive foundations advanced in the earthly city—so greatly, without doubt, that they could not even be eradicated. For not long after the Flood, Cush, son of Ham, begot [Col. 0285B] Nimrod, who began to be mighty upon the earth; whence came the proverb: “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord” (Gen. X). Babylon was the beginning of his kingdom, where, because of the tower of pride, the language of the whole earth was confused. Fittingly, moreover, the sin of pride was punished in speech, because pride is chiefly detected in words, according to that saying of James: “The tongue is a little member and boasts great things; and a little fire kindles a great forest” (Jas. III).

Yet human beings could not be corrected even by so great a punishment. Rather, adding lust to pride, they perished terribly in Sodom by fire and sulphur. Finally, at the end of the third age, the third plague also—namely avarice—was punished, but by no means healed, by those most famous plagues in Egypt: the death of cattle and beasts of burden, and the devastation of crops and trees. [Col. 0285C]

Therefore, seeing that three ages had now passed—the first destroyed, the second weakened, the third scourged—yet that none had been corrected and that all their thought was directed to evil at every time, the Lord did not say, as before: “I repent that I made man; I will destroy the man whom I created from the face of the earth” (Gen. VI). Rather, he said: “I will restore the man whom I created; I will seek the drachma which I lost; I will bring back to the flock the sheep that perished.”

But because the first man, being earthly from the earth, easily flowed down toward earthly things, it was necessary that the second man, being heavenly from heaven, should come to be, so that by testifying to what he had seen and heard he might make human beings heavenly and wise in heavenly things. Therefore, when God wished to reveal to his saints, at the time pleasing to himself, the mystery [Col. 0285D] of his purpose, which according to the Apostle had been hidden from ages and generations, and when, with the fourth age now succeeding, he was about to build the heavenly city on earth, he began to prepare what was necessary for this work.

The wisdom of God, moreover, had to observe in his building what he would later say through Solomon: “Prepare your work outside, and diligently cultivate your field, so that afterwards you may build your house” (Prov. XXIV). Therefore, outside—that is, in Egypt—he prepared his work; and from Egypt he miraculously brought it through the Red Sea into the wilderness. There, testing the very stones by many blows and rejecting a great part of them, he fitted to his work certain ones whom he found worthy. These are those whom John saw sealed from every tribe of the children [Col. 0286A] of Israel. Yet some were sealed for the establishment of the kingdom, as was the tribe of Judah; others for the shaping of the priesthood, as the tribe of Levi; and others for the preparation of the city, as were the remaining tribes.

In them, therefore, God composed, as it were, a most beautiful poem from certain antitheses: not seeking beauty of language by setting opposites against opposites, but composing the beauty of his city through the opposition of contraries, by an eloquence not of words but of realities. First he established priestly and judicial authority, so that by each the people might be instructed and compelled to humble submission. By priestly authority they were taught to be subject to God; by judicial or royal authority, a human being was compelled to become subject to another human being. [Col. 0286B] Priestly power, threatening from the chair of royal teaching, stirred him to reverence for God. Judicial power from the tribunal, or royal power from the throne, thundering terribly, restrained both prudently and strongly the swelling pride and obstinacy of the people.

But as the people in the wilderness were being clothed and instructed, by certain coverings already, for voluntary humility—because they had previously been sufficiently trained in forced humility in Egypt—so in the office of priestly dignity the virtue of chastity was already shadowed forth in figures and commended in explicit commandments. For then the divine command concerning chastity was first proclaimed, saying: “The high priest, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, shall take a virgin as wife; a widow, a divorced woman, [Col. 0286C] a defiled woman, or a prostitute he shall not take, but a maiden from his own people” (Lev. II). And concerning priests generally: “They shall be holy to their God and shall not profane his name. For they offer the incense of the Lord and the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy” (ibid.).

Virginity was already commended in this: that the high priest alone was commanded to marry a virgin, and a woman who was not a virgin was denied him as defiled. Chastity too was already prescribed in this: that although the high priest was not wholly excluded from a wife, he was excluded from a corrupted woman; and that he was commanded to abstain even from his own wife, if not always, yet at certain times. And although the other virtues are symbolized in the pontifical vestments—in the gleam of gold, the splendour of gems, and the manifold variety of colours—the brightness of chastity is nevertheless especially expressed in the shining whiteness of fine linen, which also seems to stand out among the rest. [Col. 0286D]

Now in judicial or royal authority what shone forth more than charity? Its office was to render or preserve to each person what was his due; to restrain or calm the people’s disturbances; to defend the people from the enemy’s assault; to go forth first to war; and to expose itself to death for the people. Thus Moses, the first leader and judge of that people, is recorded to have been the meekest of all. And truly meek: for although he was very often nearly stoned by the people, he nevertheless burned with such charity for them that, when the Lord said to him, “Let me be angry with this people, and I will make you into a great nation,” he replied: “If you do not forgive them, blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. XXXII).

Elsewhere also, [Col. 0287A] when he judged the people standing before him from morning until evening, forgetful as it were of himself—which he did out of excessive charity for the people—he humbly yielded, out of that same charity, to Jethro’s counsel when he said: “You will be consumed by foolish labour, both you and the people who are with you. The matter is beyond your strength; you alone cannot sustain it. Be for the people in matters pertaining to God; but choose from all the people able men who fear God, in whom there is truth and who hate avarice, and appoint them judges of the people” (Exod. XVIII). For charity, which before urged him to wear himself out by service to the people, afterwards persuaded him that it was more beneficial to the people for their affairs to be settled more quickly and easily by many persons.

And Moses, whose name is said to mean “from water,” fittingly signifies charity; Aaron, whose name is said to mean “mountain of strength,” chastity. [Col. 0287B] For charity is poured forth through him of whom it is written: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John VII); and the Evangelist testifies that this was said concerning the Spirit, whom believers were to receive. But he is the mountain of strength who excels through the virtue of chastity. Hence it is written: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good tidings to Zion” (Isa. XL). The people also, who were urged toward humble submission by hunger, thirst, every sort of distress, and the desolation of the wilderness, are rightly called Jews, or a Jew, because the name is interpreted “confessing.”

Thus, thus from Moses to David, from David to the Babylonian captivity, and from the captivity to Christ, there were not lacking among that people men of virtue [Col. 0287C] who foreshadowed the virtues mentioned above by signs, foretold them in words, or taught them by their examples. If we wished to enumerate them all, time would fail sooner than material. The books of Judges, Kings, Chronicles, Daniel, Judith, Esther, and Maccabees remain; whoever wishes to review them will find them full of such persons.

Thus, when those three ages, like a certain infancy, childhood, and youth, which had preceded, had now passed and been, as it were, consigned to oblivion; when the human race had now multiplied, grown strong, and become capable of reason; God, seeing the fullness of time draw near, when he was to send his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, wished to prepare such mountains as we have described, upon which in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord [Col. 0287D] might be prepared, so that upon that mountain the city of which we speak might be founded.

For it was necessary to prepare long beforehand whatever was needed for so great a work, so that when the builder of the city himself came, everything might be ready; and, once the foundations had been laid, the whole structure might receive its increase without delay and attain completion more quickly and without difficulty. And so it came to pass. For although we have not yet passed beyond the foundations of that city itself—indeed, have not even yet fully laid those foundations—nevertheless in the foundations themselves there already appears so great a fullness of perfection that nothing can seem to be lacking to the city for strength, nothing for beauty, nothing at all for usefulness.

For these things are especially considered in every building of a city and in every structure: [Col. 0288A] they are sought by those wishing to dwell there and praised by passers-by—namely, how suitable it is for utility, how beautiful for delight, and how fortified for defence. If these are considered spiritually in the city of the Lord of virtues, what can be found stronger than charity? For of it the Song of Songs says: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell. Many waters could not quench charity, nor shall rivers overwhelm it” (Song VIII). Hence Paul declared himself certain that neither death nor life, neither things present nor things to come, neither angels nor any other creature, could separate him from the charity of Christ.

Behold how strong, how stable—indeed, how eternal—it is: though prophecies shall be made void and knowledge [Col. 0288B] shall be destroyed, charity not only does not fail but is brought to completion. It is the beginning and end of this city; it is found as the foundation of Christ’s city at Christ’s birth, and at Pentecost it becomes the completion of that same city.

And what is more beautiful than chastity, which makes heavenly those human beings who live in flesh beyond the flesh, and makes like the angels of God in heaven those who through lust had once been likened to irrational beasts and had rotted in their own filth—where, according to the Gospel, they neither marry nor are given in marriage? Finally, as is read in the book of Wisdom, the incorruption of chastity makes a person close to God and a participant in wisdom, which is “the brightness of eternal light, the spotless mirror, and the pure emanation of the glory [Col. 0288C] of almighty God,” into which nothing defiled enters.

Accordingly, the bride is rightly described as beautiful by the Holy Spirit: she is beautiful who is chaste in body; and she is called beautiful again who is chaste also in heart, where it is read: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves” (Song I). And fittingly, where the beauty of chastity is praised, the eyes are especially commended, because the first corruption of chastity occurs in the gaze. Hence, when the Lord handed down to the Apostles the Gospel’s perfection of chastity, he said: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V).

Dovelike eyes, indeed, are not opened for lust or for harm; but, [Col. 0288D] enlightened and unveiled by the Holy Spirit, they are likened to doves over streams of water, washed with milk and resting beside flowing waters in their fullness. Such beauty is also commended in the Apostles by the prophet Isaiah, where it is read: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LX). And in Jeremiah: “His Nazarites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than old ivory.” Oh, how great is the beauty in the dove’s eyes, which Scripture pursues with such praise, or rather which is so wonderfully rewarded by the Holy Spirit.

For behold, in snow is the whiteness of heavenly grace; in milk, the brightness of effort cooperating with grace; while in ivory appears the redness and perseverance of natural modesty. Snow, which comes from above, has a pure whiteness. Milk is not assimilated to flesh, from which [Col. 0289A] it draws a certain dregginess; it approaches more nearly to an earthly brightness than to heavenly whiteness. For among things on earth that are naturally white, some shine more brilliantly through an artisan’s effort: silver through the goldsmith, cloth through the fuller. Hence the Lord’s garments are said to have been white as snow (Mark IX), such as no fuller can make white upon earth.

Behold, here in the whiteness of snow and the fuller’s operation, the whiteness of grace and the brightness of effort are clearly expressed. If they cooperate with one another reciprocally, so that effort answers grace as much as grace assists effort, one quickly reaches an incredible beauty of comeliness.

But if to these is added also nature’s good, nothing seems then to be lacking to perfection: neither the strength [Col. 0289B] of ivory bone, nor the blush of modesty, nor the endurance and gravity of antiquity. Having briefly tasted these matters concerning the strength and beauty of the city of the Lord of virtues, let us now proceed to consider its usefulness. In a human city people today attend to this more than anything else, being more readily content with the useful benefit of convenience even without the other qualities than with those qualities without convenience.

And what is more convenient than humility? By it the Lord invites us, as labourers, to rest; as burdened and oppressed persons, to relief; as captives and subjects, to the freedom of his yoke, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find [Col. 0289C] rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). For humility, like a certain convenient shortcut of a path, avoiding the winding course of the public road, easily leads to rest and quickly arrives at quiet.

For what is more peaceful than, from the inmost humility of the heart, to wish rather to be conquered than to conquer; to endure injuries rather than inflict them; to prefer poverty to riches, disgrace to glory, and a thorny crown of pains and sufferings to bodily ease and pleasures? Behold how great is the usefulness in humility, how great the delight of its sweetness, through which crooked things are most easily changed into straight and rough things into level ways (Luke III).

These things said for the present concerning the foundations of the pilgrim city may suffice, so that each of you may plainly infer from them whether he is enrolled as a citizen in it, whether he is a member of [Col. 0289D] this city, and how far he has advanced within the city if he finds those foundations already laid in himself or feels that they have already grown higher. For how can one count himself as belonging to that city who is not yet ashamed and humbled for his sins, who not only does not resolve to have recourse to penitential lamentations, but moreover piles sin upon sin, boasts when he has done evil, and exults in most wicked things? (Prov. II.) How, I ask, can such a one either believe himself, be believed, or be called a citizen of the city of the Lord—he who has not yet merited to attain either the purpose of chastity or even the first root of charity, which is fear of the Lord?

Oh, how true, and yet how miraculous, we experience today that saying of the Lord: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. [Col. 0290A] XX). Oh, how much we must fear lest we belong rather to the multitude of chaff than to the small number of grains; rather to those of whom it is written, “Many were with me” (Ps. LIX), than to those of whom it is said, “I will praise you among a weighty people” (Ps. XXXIV). Let us therefore examine our ways and our pursuits, and with anxious investigation inquire to which of the cities mentioned above we belong: to the city of the Lord or that of the devil; to the city of spiritual persons or the city of carnal persons; to the city reached by the broad and spacious way, or to that reached by the narrow way through which few enter (Matt. VII).

For the former, as it is written, is full of shouting, a crowded city, an exulting city, noble in filth, great in destruction, a city of blood, whose pyre shall be [Col. 0290B] great. Of the latter it is written: “Your eyes shall see Jerusalem, a wealthy habitation, a tabernacle that can never be moved; its pegs shall not be removed forever, and none of its cords shall be broken. For there alone the Lord our God is magnificent: a place of rivers, broad and open streams. No oared vessel shall pass through it, nor shall a great trireme cross it. For the Lord is our judge; the Lord is our lawgiver; the Lord is our king; he himself will save us. Your cords are slackened, but they shall not prevail. So shall your mast be, that you shall be unable to spread the banner” (Isa. XXXIII).

Whom would such great promises not delight? Who would not desire to share in joys so great? Who would not hasten with all desire to be enrolled as a citizen in a city so wealthy, so stable, so free, so well-watered, so spacious, so [Col. 0290C] full of justice, so saving, so renowned? And who would not seek, with all the heart’s affection, that each of us should become not merely a citizen, but rather the city itself?

But if this perhaps seems too arduous and difficult to someone, if he despairs of being able to attain the foundations which we have set forth and to be placed upon the summit of the mountains, let him at least draw near to the preparatory mountains, so that little by little he himself may become a preparatory mountain. For we judge that the preparatory mountains are now found among Christian peoples just as they were formerly among the Jewish people. That people was barred from ascending Mount Sinai, but was permitted to approach the mountain’s foot and touch the boundaries established by Moses. What else do we believe was prefigured in this, except what was later foretold by the prophet and today we see fulfilled among Christian peoples? “The mountain of the house of the Lord,” says the prophet, “shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains” (Isa. II).

[Col. 0290D] In these words, that which Moses had foreshadowed seems clearly distinguished: the mountain is understood to be placed upon the summit of mountains, a mountain which the common multitude cannot ascend, whereas it is permitted to approach the mountains in whose elevation its summit lies; and these mountains are the boundaries which it may not presume to cross. These lower mountains, preparatory to the city to be built upon the higher mountain, we interpret, not inappropriately, I think, as faith, the sign of faith, and reverence for the sign.

The Apostle expressly affirms that these preceded in Abraham, the father of faith, saying: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness; and he received the sign of circumcision, that he might be the father of all believers” (Rom. IV). The Apostle rightly calls Abraham the father of believers, since in him were spiritually prefigured the things necessary to those who would follow for the preparation of salvation. For circumcision was given to him as a sign of his faith and was received by all his offspring with such reverence and veneration that the Jews expected salvation through circumcision just as Christians expect it through baptism.

[Col. 0291A] Yet neither reverence for the sign without receiving it, nor reception of the sign without faith, benefited the Jews unto salvation. Nor today does veneration for baptism without receiving it, nor receiving the sacrament without faith, bring about one’s own salvation or that of others. Therefore we rightly call these three preparations for salvation. Although they suffice for salvation in those who lack the time to act rightly, they bring only hope rather than the reality of salvation to those who have the time but refuse to act rightly.

Where these have preceded, certain preparatory mountains already appear, upon which the city of the Lord of virtues ought to be built and in which the foundations we have set forth can be laid. For the foundations mentioned above seem to have a certain correspondence with these mountains: faith fittingly corresponds to chastity; reception of the sacrament to humility; and devotion to the sacrament to reverence for Christ. Thus these mountains too can almost be called foundations, as can those others; but these are first and lower foundations, those higher and loftier ones: [Col. 0291B] these belong to beginners, those to persons making progress; these are common to good and evil alike, those are special to the good alone.

Those who build wood, hay, and stubble upon these may fear a fire all the more burning the farther they have withdrawn from the foundation; but they may find it more tolerable the nearer they return, through penitence, to the foundation of faith. Let these things be said for those who, content with the modest city of Zoar, do not climb the steep places of the mountain and, together with the Jewish people, do not strive to cross the boundaries established by Moses.

Turning our pen toward those who endeavour to build gold, silver, and precious stones upon the foundations mentioned above, let us, now that we have passed beyond the foundations, search by careful inquiry into the walls and gates of the city itself. For the conclusion of the verse which we have cited invites us to this, where it adds after the preceding words: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI). But, insofar as the Lord grants us, we shall discuss these things under another discourse. May he who is always the Alpha and Omega of our discourse, who is the beginning and end of all things and remains without beginning and end unto ages of ages, be with us. Amen.

## TREATISE V. ON THE GATES OF THE CITY OF GOD

The prophet David, wishing to communicate without envious diminishment to present and future generations what he had seen in the city of the Lord of virtues, after commending the foundations of that city, turns to describe its gates and expound its name, so that from those things which appear at first glance even to those standing outside, it may be more plainly known how great and delightful are the things within.

But first it seems worthy of wonder that, when the Prophet was about to describe the glory of the city, he omitted neither its gates, its name, its people, its rulers, nor even its foundations, yet is found not to have made even mention of its walls. But the answer to this is easy: the Prophet did not at all pass over the walls, whose foundations and gates he so studiously wished to commend. For where so precious a foundation is laid, a most precious structure of walls is expected to rise.

Before, therefore, approaching the gates of the city, let us hear what another prophet said concerning its walls: [Col. 0292A] “Zion is the city of our strength,” says Isaiah, chief among the prophets; “the Saviour shall be set in it as wall and outer wall” (Isa. XXVI). He whom elsewhere he calls a precious stone laid in the foundation, here presents as the wall and outer wall of the same city. For he who is Alpha and Omega gave, or was, the beginning of his city, and will give its completion. He who wished to be the head of the body and the foundation of the city also distinguished and ordered the members in the body, and arranged in the city various kinds of fortifications and offices.

For as in one body there are many members, but all members do not have the same function; and as among those members some are more honourable and some weaker, to which we give more abundant honour; so in the one city of the Lord there are various civic ranks, diverse ministries and offices, although there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism (Eph. IV), one Spirit, and many divisions of graces, administrations, and operations. [Col. 0292B] For the same Spirit, dividing to each person as he wills (I Cor. XII), gave some indeed as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the edification of the body of Christ (Eph. IV), which is the very city of which we speak.

And as one spirit gives life to and, by giving life, joins together the diverse members of one body; and as many stones are cemented together in one wall by one mortar, so in the city of Christ all parts of that city are governed and fortified by the one Spirit of Christ. He who wished in his own person to become the foundation of his city also wished to be not only a wall in himself but, in certain of his members, a wall; in others, an outer wall; to make some stand forth like most steadfast towers; and to make others repel enemies like most beautiful portions, while standing open to citizens and friends. Hence it is said of the bride in the Song of Songs: “If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements; if she is a door, let us enclose her with cedar boards” (Song VIII). This will be expounded better later in its proper place.

Meanwhile, pursuing what we began, let us first see how Christ is in himself the wall and outer wall of his city, and then how he is so in his members. [Col. 0293A] If, then, we attend carefully, a wall serves not only for protection but also for outlook, while an outer wall serves for encouragement. Citizens are encouraged to resist their adversaries more ardently to the degree that they can advance more securely as far as the outer wall.

Thus Christ is for his city a protection not only through the presence of his divinity or the infusion of spiritual grace, but also through the merit of his Passion; an outlook through the teaching of Gospel preaching; and an encouragement through the examples of his common life. Whom does not the acquittal of the thief in the Passion itself free from grievous fear, not to speak of Christ’s Passion? Whose ears do not rise to the trumpet of Gospel preaching? Who does not open his eyes and ascend to look out more loftily? Whom do Christ’s poverty, fasting, vigils, snares, and reproaches not move to endure like things most patiently? Thus, thus Christ is in himself both wall and outer wall of his city.

That he is the same in his members seems plainly indicated by those three most celebrated feasts which follow the feast of the Lord’s Nativity. [Col. 0293B] Blessed Stephen encourages by his example; blessed John invites to contemplation; the most blessed Innocents fortify by merit alone. Blessed Stephen seems to have built gold upon Christ the foundation; blessed John, silver; and the holy Innocents, precious stones.

O glorious city, of which such glorious things are spoken—or rather, in which such glorious things are done—that in the very wall gold, silver, and precious stones, distinguished by a wondrous diversity and bound together by the one cement of the Holy Spirit, are found adhering to one another. Nor is such a superstructure remote from the foundations: for in Stephen the gold of charity gleams; in John the silver of chastity shines; and in the little Innocents the solidity of humility shines forth like a most precious stone.

For what is more solid than humility? Like a most precious stone, it is broken by no fire of adversity and changed by no exaltation of prosperity; but remaining one and the same in all circumstances, it retains moderation in prosperity and courage in adversity. Who could express more plainly the correspondence of chastity and silver than the Prophet, who says: “The words of the Lord are chaste words, silver [Col. 0293C] tried by fire” (Ps. XI)?

For he judges the speech of philosophers, the speech of rhetoricians, and the speech of those who seem to wish through the wisdom of language to empty the cross of Christ of its force, to be not chaste but adulterated, as the Apostle says: “We are not like certain persons adulterating the word of God” (II Cor. II). Only that which belongs to the Lord he judges chaste and comparable to silver—and not to any silver, but to silver tried by fire, which is known to be the more resonant and the brighter the more thoroughly it has been tested.

And what is dearer than charity, which, as gold surpasses all metals, is known to surpass all virtues? O what harmony, what unity, what a gathering appears at first sight in this city of the Lord, where there is no discrepancy in the walls from the foundations, [Col. 0294A] no gap, nothing found unbecoming; but all things are found distinctively united, uniformly distinguished, and wonderfully adorned by the one Spirit of Christ.

For with one and the same Spirit of Christ working all things for the edification of his body, apostles were set as certain most beautiful gates of that city; then prophets, as certain loftiest towers; thirdly evangelists, as most vigilant watchers of the towers; and finally pastors and teachers, as prudent counsellors and most wise instructors of the whole people—pastors to console and refresh in tribulations and distresses; teachers to drive away the darkness of ignorance in doubts and the perils of temptations. All these matters will be discussed more fully in their places.

Meanwhile, it is pleasing to cry out and say with the Prophet: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy in the city of our God” (Ps. XLVII). Great, I say, because he could build such a city; exceedingly praiseworthy because he both knew and willed to order it thus. Great in himself through omnipotence; exceedingly praiseworthy through mercy in the gifts bestowed upon his elect.

Let us compare, if you please, this city of ours—or rather, of the Lord—with the earthly, worldly, Babylonian, or Romulean city. For those who wished to exalt that city without measure in their praises are recorded to have left in their poems:

> Rome, head of the world, holds the reins of the round globe.

And this:

> Nothing is equal to you, Rome, though you are almost wholly ruin.

[Col. 0294C] “And how great you were when whole, you teach now that you are broken.” What, I ask, is found to have been like ours in this city that is so greatly praised, while it was still whole? For Romulus is described as having laid its foundation, whereas Christ is set forth as the foundation laid in ours. Romulus surrounded it with a wall; Christ willed to be both wall and outer rampart in ours. That man, a parricide, defiled it with his brother’s blood; Christ, marking the doorposts and lintels of his city with his own blood, fortified them against every deceit and power of enemies. He restrained a seditious people by laws and somehow checked the people’s quarrels; Christ, writing his laws in the hearts of his own by the Holy Spirit, united them by incorporating them into himself. That man was established as a god by his own people; Christ, God born of God, [Col. 0294D] made all his own children of God—indeed, his co-heirs and heirs of God. He did not fear to have a co-heir in his inheritance, but adopted all his own as brothers, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Romulus left his city built of brick; Augustus left it of marble. Christ fashioned and adorned his, as has been said, from gold, silver, and precious stones. Romulus named his city after his own name, so that it was called Rome from Romulus; Christ has distinguished not only his city but also each of its citizens by his own name, so that each is called a Christian from Christ. This too had long before been foretold through the Prophet, who says: “I shall call my servants by another name, in which he who is to be blessed shall be blessed in the Lord. Amen.” Augustus [Col. 0295A] subjected the whole world to that city; Christ subjected even demons, whom the Romans worshipped as gods, to his servants; and, teaching them to tread underfoot all transitory things, opened to them the kingdom of heaven.

O my brothers and fellow citizens, what more ought he to have done for us and did not do? How greatly Christ ought to be loved by Christians! If Romulus was so greatly loved by the Romans that they said, “Would that he had either never been born or never died,” how greatly ought Christ to be loved by us, for whom he was born and suffered, and gave us eternal life? If Brutus called his sons, who were preparing to wage new wars, to death for Roman liberty, lest proud Tarquin should rule in it, so that this is read concerning him:

> Love of country prevailed, and an immense desire for praise.

[Col. 0295B] If likewise another Roman leader, surnamed Torquatus, killed his son—not because he had fought against his country, but even though he had fought for his country, because, when challenged by an enemy, he had fought in youthful ardor contrary to his father’s command—although he had won, lest there be more evil in the example of authority despised than good in the glory of an enemy slain: how much more ought we to despise and renounce all earthly things for the rulers of our city, who have countless sons? If Marcus Regulus, rather than deceive his most cruel enemies by breaking his oath, returned to them from Rome itself and preferred to be put to death under the most grievous tortures by the Carthaginians, rivals of Roman power—because in the Roman senate he had argued against exchanging their captives for his own countrymen’s captives—rather than violate his pledge: what tortures are not to be despised for Christ’s faith and endured for the glory of our city?

Or how could a Christian dare to exalt himself on account of the voluntary poverty he has undertaken, so that he may walk more lightly, in this life’s pilgrimage, along the way that leads to the homeland whose true riches are God himself, when he reads that Lucius Valerius, dying during his consulship, wished to be so poor that his burial had to be provided for from money contributed by the people? Or when he reads that Quintus Cincinnatus, possessing four acres and cultivating them with his own hands, was taken from the plough to become dictator, in which office he was greater than a consul, and, after conquering the enemy and obtaining immense glory, remained in the same poverty?
