If these men, and many others, did such things—and far more—in an earthly city and for an earthly [Col. 0295D] city, how great are the deeds and sufferings that Christians ought to undertake for the eternal homeland?

But see: while we have turned our eyes briefly toward the earthly city, we have wandered far from the walls and gates of our own city. And since we have lingered longer over the walls than we had hoped—and to those desiring to enter the city the gates are opened all the more desirably the later they are reached—let us now approach the gates themselves more closely and knock, in season and out of season, that they may be opened to us. Once they have been unbarred and we have carefully inspected what lies within the city, may we linger there longer and with greater delight.

Since this city has many gates, four principal ones seem, among the others, to stand out. Wishing to distinguish them from the rest, the Prophet, under revelation of the Holy Spirit, says: “Lift up your gates, O princes” (Ps. 23). As though he said: There are indeed many gates, as we have heard and seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts; but let the chief and pre-eminent ones be raised above the rest, lest anything lowly, earthly, or fleshly be able to defile or corrupt them, and so prevent the King of glory—whom only glorious and exalted things befit—from entering through them.

[Col. 0296A] I take these four principal gates to be the chief sacraments of God, through which the various kinds of human beings, like citizens of that city, have diverse exits and entrances according to their different offices. Some enter the city from the east in order to dwell there; some leave from the west in order to pass over. And because the world brings a double battle-line against Christ’s soldiers, flattering in order to deceive and terrifying in order to break them, let the most valiant and battle-trained soldiers of our city continually go forth to fight against their adversaries: some from the south, some from the north, or, in the Apostle’s words, “on the right and on the left” (2 Cor. 6). From the south, or from the right, that, bearing the marks of Jesus, they may resist the pleasures of the flesh and the prosperities of the world; from the north, or from the left, that with the shield of patience and the weapons of righteousness they may strive to repel harsh and grievous things far away.

The eastern gate, then, is the sacrament of baptism, through which one enters the city and, if one enters rightly, is enrolled as its citizen. This gate is rightly called eastern, either because through it “the Dayspring from on high” first visited the world, when, at the baptism in the Jordan of the Lord whose name is Dayspring, the heavens were opened, the Father’s voice was heard, the Holy Spirit appeared above him in the form of a dove, and the whole Trinity became known to the world for the consecration of his baptism and the commendation of this sacrament; or because those baptized in Christ, like infants newly born, dead to the world and buried with Christ through baptism, rise to the Father of spirits and pass into a new creation.

Thus the gate of those entering is the sacrament of baptism. The western gate, however, I would not unreasonably call the sacred anointing of the sick: by this sacrament those about to die are fortified, as though they were now about to pass from the militant [Col. 0296D] city to the triumphant one. The gate from the north I confidently define as the sacrament of confirmation, or laying on of hands, which is given for strengthening those who are about to fight, when after baptism someone advances to a perfect man, like a ewe coming up from the washing, bearing twin offspring, and is confirmed by the princely Spirit.

For the sacrament of confirmation is not a recent invention, since long before this the Prophet is read to have distinguished between the renewing spirit given in baptism, the confirming spirit given in the laying on of hands, and the sanctifying Spirit given in the sevenfold anointing of sacred oil. Of the latter it is said: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50). Of the confirming Spirit: “Confirm me with a princely Spirit” [Col. 0297A] (ibid.). Of the renewing Spirit: “Renew a right spirit within my inmost parts” (ibid.).

There remains the southern gate, which I would not unreasonably call the sacrament of the altar: there it is no longer oil soothing the sick, but bread strengthening and wine gladdening the one who triumphs. Hence it is read in the Prophet: “You who inhabit the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread” (Isa. 21). Whoever approaches the delights of the flesh and the prosperities of the world—not to fight against them but drawn and enticed by them—intends to flee from the city of the Lord of hosts. This especially tends to happen to those afflicted by hunger for the divine bread: because they do not dare to touch consecrated loaves, they turn to common bread. For they are not permitted to touch consecrated loaves unless they are clean, especially from women—that is, fleshly pleasures.

Those, therefore, who inhabit the land of the south, whose garden the south wind frequently breathes upon in visitation so as to bring bread forth from their land, are rightly commanded to meet fugitives with bread, so that, refreshed by the bread of life and understanding, they may strive to remain in the city and retain their place. Rightly, then, we call the southern gate the Eucharist, which is especially set against the allurements of the flesh and whose power those who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires frequently experience (Heb. 13). It is indeed the altar from which those who serve the tabernacle of the flesh have no authority to eat.

For this reason Christ also willed to suffer outside the camp: so that whoever, fleeing from the camps of the Babylonian [Col. 0297C] city, wished to return to the camp of our city might have his passion as a gate and through it might re-enter the city; but if anyone wished to pass from ours to that city, he would find that same passion an obstacle. These are the gates of Christ’s city, of which the Prophet says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. 86).

Here he uses Jacob, not Israel, and says “the tabernacles of Jacob,” not Israel. He seems to intimate to us that he speaks of those tabernacles which were to be changed and to have an end, just as Jacob’s name was changed into Israel, so that he was not even to be called Jacob any longer, the Lord saying: “You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name” (Gen. 32). And just as, according to their interpretation, Israel is known to be a far worthier and better name than Jacob—for Jacob means “wrestler,” while Israel means “one who sees God,” and it is far better to rest by seeing God than to wrestle in seeking God—so the sacraments of the present Church are incomparably better and worthier than the tabernacle and ceremonies of the old Synagogue. In those there is shadow; in these, truth. In these, permanence; in those, obsolescence and oldness. Hence the Apostle says: “Whole burnt offerings and offerings for sin did not please you; then I said, ‘Behold, I come.’ In saying that you did not will sacrifices, whole burnt offerings, and oblations, then I said, ‘Behold, I come to do your will, O God’; he removes the first in order to establish what follows” (Heb. 10).

The Lord is therefore rightly said to love the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob, since he is not even said to have loved those tabernacles. Thus the Apostle, agreeing with and confirming the Prophet, asserts that they did not please [Col. 0298A] him. But he is known to love the sacraments of the Church so greatly that through the sacrament of baptism, as through the eastern gate, he brings persons in to the Father.

O how greatly these gates ought to be loved, raised on high, and revered by us! The King of glory loves and frequents them for no other reason than that he may make all who enter through them glorious. Whoever keeps watch for him from dawn will find him seated at these gates. Zion, whose gates are so greatly loved by the Lord, is aptly named. For Zion means “contemplation,” because it now beholds the glory of its future blessedness not through shadows of figures but through the truth of the sacraments, as through certain gates that are nevertheless still closed.

But because from contemplating the gates and naming the city its knowledge has begun to shine upon us more and more, an examination of its name should not be hurried over in passing or confined within the narrow limits of a discourse now ending. Let it therefore be reserved for the beginning of another discourse, since it seems to invite us to contemplation of some mystery. May he himself always be the Alpha and Omega of our discourse, who is the beginning and end of all things and remains without beginning and end for ages of ages. Amen.

## TREATISE VI. ON THE NAME OF THE CITY OF GOD

When the Prophet had been carried beyond himself in mind toward God, wishing to return sober to us and faithfully disclose what he had seen in his ecstasy, after describing the foundations and commending the gates of the city of the Lord of hosts, he does not afterward state by what name he heard it called. For, knowing that a name is commonly imposed from a thing and a thing recognized from its name, and that many other prophets who rejoiced in the same vision had called it by various titles, he wished rather to set down the name which he understood to fit the city’s proper character most closely.

Isaiah, wishing to express the name of this city but unable to do so fully as he desired, said: “You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate; but you shall be called My-delight-is-in-her” (Isa. 62). And in the same place: “A new name shall be called for you,” he says, “which the mouth of the Lord has named” (ibid.). Other prophets too are found to have written various things about the naming of this city.

David, wishing to make use of a brief expression, calls it Zion, in order to invite his hearers to contemplate and carefully investigate its glory and power. Hence in another Psalm: “Surround Zion and embrace her; recount her in her towers. Set your hearts upon her strength” (Ps. 47). Surround her by searching; embrace her by desiring; recount her by praising. And lest it seem sufficient merely to look upon outward things—the foundations, walls and ramparts, towers and gates—he says: “Set your hearts upon her strength,” so that not so much the city’s glory as its virtue may be regarded, because all glory which virtue has not produced is deceptive.

Therefore, attending to the power and proper meaning of this name, let us more keenly contemplate not what is outwardly seen but what lies hidden within. For the city of the Lord seems to have derived this name from the fact that its Creator is proposed for contemplation in all its parts, offices, and workshops. Simeon, knowing this in the Spirit, rejoiced and praised because of his contemplation, saying: “My eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples” (Luke 2). Simeon is rightly said to have come into the temple in the Spirit. For he seems to have known through the Spirit that the one he saw was his salvation—indeed, the Lord’s salvation—prepared to grant salvation before the face of all peoples, so that the right of human salvation might consist in beholding him.

Just as formerly the Jews were saved from the bites of serpents by looking upon the bronze serpent, so Simeon saw this salvation prepared before the face of all Christians, that their salvation might consist in beholding him. Knowing this also, the Psalmist said: “Show your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79). Jacob, moreover, after seeing the Lord face to face, professes that his soul was saved.

Thus Zion, holding the reality of its name through contemplation and sharing through contemplation in the effect of the name Jesus, does not cease to be saved and, once saved, to contemplate its Salvation—not as Rome bears merely a bare name from Romulus, but as it cleaves in contemplation to its Savior, so far as this is granted it by him. Yet in the present life vision is not full, nor can salvation here be perfect. For I would not call that salvation perfect which, while twilight remains, can be diminished or corrupted. But in that city which is above and free, [Col. 0299C] just as vision is manifest, so peace and salvation are perfect. It is therefore rightly called Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace.” But our city, which still fights and is a pilgrim upon earth, ought rather to be called Zion than Jerusalem, because for the present it sees in a mirror, in an enigma, him whom, after the end of its pilgrimage, it shall see face to face.

Let our Zion therefore meanwhile contemplate King Solomon, if not yet in the diadem of glory, at least in the diadem of human nature, so that it may find in the gates him whom it has already found in its foundations and walls. For we have said that the gates of our city are the sacraments of salvation. Those who rejoice only in the use of the sacraments possess these gates, but still closed. They are opened to those to whom the mysteries of the sacraments are disclosed. But those who truly enjoy the mysteries and sacraments, having entered the city with the gates of righteousness opened to them, confess the Lord with the Prophet.

The good and the evil alike can have use of the sacraments and knowledge of the mysteries. Hence the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, and know all mysteries, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). But only the good receive the reality of the mysteries and sacraments. Thus even the children of this age approach the gates and find them open; but only the children of light, the children of God, who are led by the Spirit of God, are admitted among the number of friends or citizens. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep is a thief [Col. 0300A] and robber” (John 10).

Some, then, seem to enter through the gates who do not enter through the door. Clearly, that is so. A gate is commonly shut by a door, and when the door is opened, the gate lies open.

The gate, as we have already said, is the visible sacrament; the door of this gate is Christ, who is not only the institutor but also the reality of the sacrament. The bolt of this door is the hidden mystery of the sacrament itself. The key of this bolt, or the doorkeeper, is not other than Christ, because it is Christ’s Spirit. May Christ therefore deign, by the finger and key of his Spirit, to unbar for us the bolt of this mystery, so that we may know how he himself is the door in each of the gates, and how he is the very reality of the mysteries and sacraments.

Let us see this in the sacrament of baptism, where it will appear more clearly and readily. The visible sacrament of baptism is a gate through which both good and evil enter—but the good as citizens, the evil as thieves and robbers. For they do not enter through Christ the door, nor do they possess the reality of the sacrament. To them also the bolt of the hidden mystery is often unbarred by the key of the Spirit, according to the Apostle’s words: “For the Lord revealed it to them” (Phil. 3); nevertheless, they are not introduced by the doorkeeper, because they do not attain the reality of the mystery, Christ. And although they enter by knowledge, they do not enter by conscience. They seem indeed to be within through knowledge that puffs up, but they are not within through charity that comes in addition to knowledge.

But when the good receive the visible sacrament, even if they do not know the mystery, they nevertheless enter through Christ the door; and they possess Christ the door and the reality of both mystery and sacrament. For Christ is the reality of both. He is the reality of the sacrament, because he is the salvation and sanctification conferred through it. Baptism is received in order to obtain salvation and sanctification, not for veneration of the element; for no veneration is due to it except that conferred through the sanctification of the word. For when the word is joined to the element, it becomes not water itself, but from water and the word a sacrament.

Christ, therefore, is the reality and cause of baptism. Whoever does not possess him undoubtedly has no salvation from baptism, because he says, “I am the salvation of the people,” and the Prophet says: “Say to my soul: I am your salvation” (Ps. 34). Let us also see how he is the reality of the mystery.

The mystery is the hidden sanctification of the visible [Col. 0300D] sacrament itself, and different persons have assigned it different meanings. Ambrose (ch. 6, on Romans; Gregory, book I, epistle 41) understood water to signify that, just as water washes dirt from body and clothes, so baptism, cleansing the stains of the soul and the defilements of the inner person, wipes them away. Gregory, however, understood the three immersions to signify the persons of the Trinity, and the single immersion, where that is the custom, the unity of the Godhead. He added that we who are immersed three times also signify the sacrament of the Lord’s three-day burial.

Augustine (*Sermon on the Mysteries of Baptism*, in the *Supplement*) likewise states that the rite of baptism is celebrated with a twofold mystical meaning:

> “Rightly,” he says, “were you immersed who received baptism in the name of the Trinity. Rightly were you immersed three times who received baptism in the name of Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day.”

See: these writers maintain that the three days of the Lord’s burial are signified in the threefold immersion of baptism. The second meaning of baptism, therefore, is that, as Christ was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, so those baptized in Christ ought to die to the world and be buried with respect to deed, word, and affection, that they may be able to say with the Apostle: “Yet I live, no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). Wishing to disclose this mystery, the Apostle says: “You have been buried with Christ through baptism into death” (Rom. 6). And elsewhere: “For as many of you as were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3).

If it is permissible to understand those three days differently, we may call the first day of spiritual burial the renunciation made in baptism, when Satan and all his pomps are renounced; these pomps are nothing other than the vanities of the passing world. The second is the ardent and diligent carrying out of this renunciation. The third, which is also the true Sabbath, is the rest of tranquil contemplation, when even good works are set aside so that God may be seen; when a person is lessened in activity in order to receive wisdom; when one is hidden in the secret place of God’s face from the disturbance of human beings.

On the first day the act of sin dies, when the Egyptians are submerged through baptismal grace. On the second, the inclination is mortified, when sins are not so much punished as the members are put to death through love and imitation of Christ. For then, as it is written, punishment is most beneficial when it does not [Col. 0301C] punish sins. On the third day the affection of sin dies and is buried, when the human spirit, cleaving to the divine Spirit, is one spirit, and the soul, melted by the voice or sight of the beloved, passes into that beloved.

See how Christ is the reality both of the mystery and of the sacrament: the sacrament confers salvation, which is Christ, and the mystery signifies and reveals that same salvation. He himself is therefore the door through which a person is introduced, the way along which one is led, and the life to which one is brought. He rightly says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10). Properly introduced, he shall both enter—to me, the Word, led by me, the human being—and go out—from me, the Word, brought back to me, the human being—and he shall find rich pastures: abundant in humanity, more abundant in divinity, and most abundant, once brought to the homeland after the present pilgrimage, in both.

The Prophet therefore not without reason joined the city’s name to his commendation of the gates, since he who is the door of those gates is especially proposed for contemplation in the city which he calls Zion. For, as the Apostle says, he has become to that city “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1). Redemption is in baptism, by which a person is redeemed from slavery to sin, so that natural desire without consent is no longer imputed to him for condemnation, according to the Apostle: “There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who does not walk according to the flesh” (Rom. 8), that is, who do not follow fleshly desire. And elsewhere: “If I do what I will, it is no longer I who do it” [Col. 0302A] (Rom. 7).

In baptism, therefore, the redeemed person receives the grace to turn from evil; in the laying on of hands, the grace to do good. There one is cleansed from sins; here, advancing through the merits of virtues, one has one’s fruit unto sanctification. There the head is made rich with oil; here the face is rightly made glad with oil. This perhaps not inappropriately signifies the fact that in baptism a person is anointed with chrism upon the crown of the head, while in confirmation one is sealed on the forehead.

For in baptism free choice, as the highest head of the inner person, is poured over and enriched by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, so that what before baptism was free to be able to sin but not free to be able not to sin mortally may after baptism, through cooperating grace, be free not to sin damnably. Before baptism, as Augustine says, a person is pressed down and conquered by desire and has weakness toward evil but not grace toward good; therefore one can sin and cannot refrain from sinning, even damnably. After baptism, however, one is pressed by desire but not conquered; one does indeed have weakness toward evil, but grace toward good, so that one can sin because of freedom and weakness, and can refrain from sin unto death because of freedom and assisting grace. Yet one does not have the ability wholly not to sin, or the impossibility of sinning, because weakness has not yet been fully absorbed and grace has not yet been perfectly completed.

Thus in baptism the will is freed; and because willing is not enough unless ability is also present, in confirmation the capacity for doing good is granted, so that, with a glad countenance, one may now sing: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118). But because, while we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord, and because the corruptible body weighs down the soul and depresses the mind that thinks many things, the eye of reason being meanwhile darkened, we often depart from righteousness, calling good evil and evil good, making light darkness and darkness light.

Against this disease, therefore, the antidote of the sacrament of the Eucharist has also been appointed. Through it, as through a gate that ought truly to be called beautiful, we contemplate Christ, wisdom. This antidote relieves the disease of ignorance; hence the eyes of the disciples are read to have been opened in the breaking [Col. 0302D] of bread. For in that we believe and confess an invisible reality to lie hidden beneath a visible appearance, we are taught that the visible appearances or forms of things are not alone to be regarded; rather, the invisible things, which are the causes of visible things, must be sought and loved. For the things that are seen are temporal and therefore to be held cheap; but those that are unseen are eternal and therefore to be desired and embraced with the whole heart.

Concerning visible appearance it is thus read in Daniel: “Appearance deceived you, and desire subverted your heart” (Dan. 13). At first appearance deceives the sight through its likeness to the true good; then desire subverts the affection. See: desire comes from ignorance; through the desire of the flesh, the strength of the spirit is exhausted, so that [Col. 0303A] it does not do what it wishes but unwillingly endures what it does not wish, and is compelled to cry with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Truly a body of death: while it lives, neither is weakness perfectly absorbed nor ignorance removed; weakness drives toward desire and freedom is hindered through ignorance, so that neither can reason judge without error nor can the will seek the good without difficulty, unless it is freed by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

This grace is necessary daily, because the failing of human weakness through ignorance and desire is daily. Therefore we say daily: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 2), and daily, as a help to human salvation and assistance for weakness, we repeat the sacrament of the Eucharist. The other two sacraments, baptism and confirmation, are not repeated, because once a person has been freed from the bond of desire in baptism and from weakness in confirmation—so as now to have both willing and ability—nothing remains but that one know the way to go.

This way is therefore shown more and more every day through the sacrament of the altar, and in daily use is opened more certainly the more frequently it is employed. But through this sacrament we are not only illumined by the light of wisdom in order to hold to the way and pass from visible things to invisible, from appearances and forms, as it were accidents, to substances; the other two things also, which we said are conferred through the sacraments of baptism and confirmation, are granted by the power of the sacrament of the altar, just as they are strengthened and increased in those sacraments and by their use—something which does not occur in them.

This is also shown, clearer than light, to be signified in the three substances from which the sacrament itself is made: namely bread, wine, and water. In bread, which strengthens a person, is signified the grace by which weakness is made strong; in wine, which makes glad and intoxicates, is shown the grace which estranges people from desire for visible affections; in water, which makes the eyes clear by washing them, is expressed the brightness of wisdom. Hence Isaiah says: “He gave him to drink water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 14). These are the three things which philosophers called prudence, courage, and temperance, and in their perfection located human justice.

But because, presuming on their own powers and wishing to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to God’s righteousness, and therefore, ignorant of God’s righteousness, became vain in their thoughts, claiming that they could make themselves wise, brave, temperate, and just from themselves and by themselves. But the city of Zion, philosophizing more truly, contemplates its gates differently and proclaims differently in preaching, saying: “It is good for me to cling to God; to place my hope in the Lord God, that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 72).

At the eastern gate it proclaims that no one can be continent unless God gives it (Wis. 8). At the northern gate: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Ps. 117). At the southern gate: “All wisdom is from the Lord God” (Ecclus. 1). At the western gate, when not only the outer person fails but the inner person also dreads the iron gate of death, it proclaims in confession, and in proclaiming cries out with the Prophet: “In you, O Lord, I have hoped; let me never be confounded; deliver me in your righteousness” (Ps. 30).

Now certainly distrustful of its own righteousness and setting itself before itself, it reckons all its righteousness as a menstrual cloth; and, turning to Christ’s merits, it recalls his righteousness alone and presents it before the Father’s eyes. Seeking nothing further than the oil of mercy, as it confesses that there is no health in itself from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, so it believes and glories that from the sole of the foot to the crown it is anointed not only with visible oil but that the entire inner person is suffused with the anointing of mercy.

[Col. 0304B] Such things it proclaims in its gates; such things it beholds more clearly by contemplating the gates. But since, for those eager to enter, lingering so long around the gates may perhaps seem tedious, I leave the many things that occur for discussion concerning these gates to readers for their contemplation, giving only an occasion to the wise, that they may become wiser.

Let the reader therefore see and judge whether the first of these gates is prefigured in Ezra by the Fish Gate (2 Esdr. 3), on account of what was said to Peter: “I will make you become a fisher of men” (Matt. 4). Let him see whether the second should be called the Sheep Gate, on account of what was said: “His people and the sheep of his pasture, enter his gates in confession” (Ps. 99). Do not certain flocks seem to gather at the gate when the people, panting, hurry to be confirmed by the bishop? Let him see whether the third can be called the Dung Gate, when the dung of sin is now abandoned and the little body of earth is commended as most worthless dung. Let him see whether the fourth ought to be called the Judgment Gate, at which those who approach unworthily eat and drink judgment to themselves.

Let him also see whether it may fittingly be applied to these gates, and whether by contemplating their height one may grasp what breadth, length, height, and depth are: whether breadth corresponds to the restraint of temperance, according to the words “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4); whether length corresponds to the long-suffering of courage; height to the watchfulness of prudence; and depth to the two-sided and uncertain conclusion of justice, because “a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccles. 9), but all things are reserved uncertain for the future.

Let these remarks on the principal gates suffice for the present. There may perhaps be other secondary gates, to which the other five named in Ezra (Ezra 3) may not unsuitably be applied; but that belongs elsewhere. Now, then, as we enter the city with the Prophet, let us hear from him and with him what he heard and what he saw within.

## TREATISE VII. ON THE LIBERTY, DOMINION, AND GLORY OF THE CITY OF GOD
“Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Ps. 86).

From what has been said, we seem now clearly to have grasped the strength in virtue, beauty, and usefulness of the city of the Lord, as the Prophet describes them—or rather, as the Holy Spirit reveals them through the Prophet [Col. 0305A]. For these are the qualities which, as was said above, are especially considered in every city and are chiefly accustomed to be commended. Therefore, wishing to display these things, the Prophet set forth its firmness more expressly in its foundations, its beauty in its walls, and commended its usefulness in its gates. Since this seems sufficiently clear from what has preceded, we have thought it superfluous to repeat it.

The Prophet, then, knowing that the perfection of eternal happiness in the city does not consist in these things alone, and wishing to lead us from earthly things to the measurement of heavenly things, through visible things to behold invisible things, and through familiar things to things unfamiliar, goes on, after what we have said, to describe that which is especially desired in an earthly city—namely glory [Col. 0305B] and dominion—in the city of the Lord, saying: “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God.”

First, let the city of Rome itself teach us how great glory and dominion are today among the citizens of an earthly city, and how great they were among the ancients. For Augustine says of it as follows (*City of God*, V.12):

> “The ancient and earliest Romans, as their history teaches, were eager for praise, liberal with money; they desired immense glory and honourable riches. They loved glory most ardently; for its sake they wished to live, and for it they did not hesitate even to die. By their immense desire for glory they repressed their other desires. Finally, because it seemed inglorious to serve and glorious to rule and command, they first desired with every effort that their country should be free, [Col. 0305C] and that it should be mistress. Hence, unable to endure royal dominion, they established annual offices and two consuls for themselves; and they were called consuls from their taking counsel. Thus, when King Tarquin had been expelled and consuls established, the city attained an incredible freedom, and in a short time grew as greatly as the desire for glory had impelled it. Therefore eagerness for praise and desire for glory accomplished those many marvellous and glorious deeds, according to human estimation.”

Augustine also shows what sort of eagerness for praise and desire for glory they possessed in those great and distinguished men, Marcus Cato and Gaius Caesar, who are reported to have been great in their time through mighty virtue, though differing in character. Speaking first in praise of Caesar, he says:

> “There a great command, an army, and a new war were desired, where virtue might shine forth: this was brought about by eagerness for praise [Col. 0305D] and desire for glory.”

He then reports that Cato praised those who strove after glory, honour, and dominion by the true road—that is, by virtue itself. Thus, introducing Cato’s words, he says (*ibid.*):

> “Do not suppose that our ancestors made the commonwealth great from small by arms. If it were so, we should possess it far more splendid than they did. For we have a greater abundance than they had of allies and citizens, and likewise of arms and horses. But other things made them great, things which we do not possess: industry at home, just rule abroad, a spirit free in counsel and subject neither to wrongdoing nor to passion. In place of these we have luxury and greed, public poverty and private wealth. We praise [Col. 0306A] riches and pursue idleness; among the good and the bad there is no distinction; ambition possesses all the rewards of virtue. Nor is this surprising, when each of you separately takes counsel for his own interest, when at last you are slaves to pleasures, money, or favour. The result is that an attack is made upon an empty commonwealth.”

We have cited these words of Augustine, or of those whom he introduces as speaking, so that from them it may plainly be understood how greatly the Romans first sought freedom, then dominion, and also praise and glory. Yet ambition rather than greed first exercised their minds; and this vice was nevertheless closer to virtue. Even those, however, who sought honour neither through ambition nor greed but through virtue, as Cato did, and judged that one should strive not by deceits and frauds but by the true road, still made honour the end of virtue. Hence they set up the temples of Virtue and Honour side by side. Thus it was also said of Cato that, the less he sought glory, the more it followed him, because glory always accompanies virtue.

From these matters we briefly gather that the Romans sought, first, the glory of freedom; second, the glory of dominion; and third, the glory of praise, by three ways: some by ambition, some by greed, and some by the true way, that is, through virtue. But, judging it inglorious to serve human beings, they wished to be free from human slavery. The citizens of our city, however, rejoicing in the true freedom by which Christ has made us free, glory in being free from slavery to sins, vices, and demons. For they are not [Col. 0306B] children of the bondwoman, but of the free woman.

And because they are led by the Spirit of God, they are sons of God. And if sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God, and fellow-heirs with Christ (Rom. 8). And although they are free from all, they make themselves servants of all for Christ’s sake, subject to every human creature for God’s sake, thereby serving him alone whose service is to reign.

There is also another glory of freedom, by which the citizens of our city glory that they are free not only from the servitudes mentioned above but even from slavery to the elements of this world itself, so that they no longer serve in the oldness of the letter but are perfected in the newness of the spirit. For they do not need to be taught what are the elementary principles of the sayings of God; rather, leaving behind the elementary teaching [Col. 0306D] about Christ, they are borne toward perfection, hearing from the Apostle: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father” (*ibid.*).

For these are the elementary principles of the sayings of God: rudiments, that is, and teachings of divine fear, proposed as certain first elements to beginners, who need milk rather than solid food and are still unpractised in the word of righteousness. Solomon set these before his son, saying: “Hear, my son, the instruction of your father. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 1). “Fear the Lord and depart from evil. It shall be well with him who fears the Lord at the end” (Prov. 3). “The fear of the Lord drives out sin.” And: “Without the fear of the Lord no one can be justified” (Ecclus. 1).

Some citizens of our city serve under this fear, being already free in this very respect: that they so serve willingly, freely, and gladly, hoping through this service to advance into the freedom of the glory of the sons of God. Indeed, they too are already free, although, so long as they are children, they differ in nothing from a servant, though they are lords of all; but they remain under guardians and stewards—those of fear and obedience—until the time appointed by the Father [Col. 0307A]. When, by the Father’s grace, they have arrived at that point—or when they have already arrived there by the Father’s gift—they not only cease to serve the elements mentioned above, but, as it were escaping into the breezes of freedom by a certain liberty of spirit, they transcend even the elements of figures and the sacraments of all things old and new through the life-giving power of the Spirit. They are no longer weighed down by the burden of figures, but are borne toward the perfection of truth.

There are also other elements which the Apostle mentions in a third sense, reproving some for serving “weak and needy elements.” “Elements,” or things constituted from elements (*elementata*), are whatever can be perceived by bodily sense; and they are rightly called weak and needy because they can neither preserve human nature from corruption nor suffice for its need. Those who seek health or satisfaction in them are deceived and willingly serve vanity. Free from this slavery are those who serve unwillingly, according to the Apostle, being meanwhile subjected to vanity in hope, for the sake of him who subjected them. Subjected, I say, not enslaved; but free, and at last to be wholly set free even from corruption.

Let this suffice for the present concerning the glory of freedom. Let us also hear how glorious are the things that glorious men have spoken, and how gloriously they have spoken, concerning the glory of dominion [Col. 0307C].

Isaiah, chief among the prophets—or rather, the Lord through Isaiah—says concerning the glory of the city of Zion:

> “Behold, I have inscribed you upon my hands. Your walls are always before my eyes. Your builders have come; those who destroy and lay you waste shall go forth from you. Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these are gathered together; they have come to you. As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament, and bind them about you like a bride. The children of my barrenness shall yet say in your ears: ‘The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell.’ And you shall say in your heart: ‘Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and did not bear, exiled and captive; and who has reared these? I was left forsaken and desolate; where then were these?’ Thus says the Lord God: ‘Behold, I shall lift up my hand to the nations [Col. 0307D] and raise my standard to the peoples. They shall bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. Kings shall be your foster-fathers and queens your nurses; with faces bowed to the ground they shall worship, and they shall lick the dust of your feet’” (Isa. 49).

In these words the glory of freedom is first commended, then that of dominion. For where the Lord says that he has inscribed Zion upon his hands, he shows that she is subject to no one’s dominion, bowed beneath no one’s yoke, entered upon no one’s tax-roll, but owes worship (*latria*) to himself alone. For although he said to the citizens of his city: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22), and although the Apostle—one of those builders of whom it is said below, “Your builders have come” [Col. 0308A] (Isa. 49)—sings in harmony with this when he says: “Render to all what is due: honour to whom honour is due; revenue to whom revenue; tribute to whom tribute” (Rom. 13), nevertheless the Lord teaches that sons are free from such dues, saying to Peter: “From whom do the kings of the nations demand tribute—from their sons or from strangers?” When Peter answered, “From strangers,” he said: “Then the sons are free” (Matt. 17).

In this way he proves that the citizens of his city, as sons of God and his fellow-heirs, are free from Caesar’s tribute. For although Caesar encompassed the whole world in his census and impressed his image upon his coinage, “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and those who dwell in it” (Ps. 23). All things should more rightly be called his, who spoke and they were made, commanded [Col. 0308B] and they were created (Ps. 32). Indeed, even Augustus’s power to do this proceeded from God’s ordering, because “there is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13).

Therefore, when the things that are Caesar’s are rendered to Caesar, God’s own things are rather rendered to God, by whose grant they are Caesar’s—though they are not so much Caesar’s as they are called or thought to be. And when the things that are God’s are rendered to God, even those things rendered to Caesar for God’s sake are offered not so much to Caesar as to God. The aforesaid builder agrees with this when he says: “Servants, obey your carnal masters as Christ; not serving merely before the eye, as those who please men, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with good will as the Lord and not men” (Eph. 6).

See how the census-maker and the builder agree. If the world obeyed Caesar, who was merely its census-maker and not its builder, and received the coin bearing his image, how much more ought the citizens of Christ’s city to obey Christ and be marked with his image, in order, free from every yoke, to serve him alone—him who, in his works as though in his own hands, gave them the pattern of life and discipline, and mercifully impressed his image upon them through his apostles and evangelists, as through his own builders [Col. 0308C].

They are rightly called his builders, for they say to their fellow-citizens: “Be imitators of us, as we also are of Christ” (1 Cor. 4). Their merits and examples are our walls, which are said always to be before the Lord’s eyes because through their merits we are protected and fortified by him.

As for what follows—“Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these are gathered together; they have come to you; and you shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament and bind them about you like a bride” (Isa. 49), and the rest that follows—all of it commends the glory of freedom. For citizens gathered from every side so freely, so marvellously foreordained, bestowed, begotten, and reared by God, and so multiplied and magnified, glorify and adorn the city of Zion. Like certain garments of glory, they make her like a bride who, leaving father and mother and cleaving to her husband, now lays claim to the glory of freedom. How plainly the remaining words express the glory of dominion needs no exposition, but rather admiration.

[Col. 0309A] For who would not marvel, who would not delight to hear—or rather, who would not now glory in having seen—that nations have hastened to the Church from every region of the world; that they have brought the sons of the Church in their arms and carried her daughters upon their shoulders; that kings have been her foster-fathers and queens her nurses; that they have worshipped in the Church with faces bowed down, and have most devoutly wiped with lips and tongue the dust, at the thresholds of apostles, martyrs, and other saints, of those entering and departing? The lips of emperors reverently kiss the thresholds of fishermen.

Behold how great is the glory of power and dominion belonging to the city of Zion, which rules not only nations but also kings and emperors. Indeed, kings and princes glory in serving her. And, to say something greater still, even demons are subject to her [Col. 0309B], and she receives from her king the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions (Luke 10): some of these sting with the tail, others with the tongue; and she has power over all the enemy’s force, which consists wholly in these two things, namely, the suggestion and consummation of sin.

By the gift and grace of her emperor, she rules also over all other visible creatures of the world, and deserves to hear from him: “Let your fear and dread be upon every living thing of the earth and upon every bird of heaven, together with all things that move upon the earth” (Gen. 9). Although this seems common to good and bad persons, it belongs in a special way to the good, who are read to have ruled not only living creatures but even the elements themselves with mighty power, so as to have shut heaven, halted the sun, and calmed with a word alone stormy air and tempestuous sea [Col. 0309C].

To them Paul says particularly: “All things are yours, whether Cephas, or Paul, or Apollos; but you are Christ’s” (1 Cor. 3). They rightly ought to belong to Christ, to whom Christ has subjected all invisible things and whom he has enrolled as citizens of his city to reign with him; whereas the world was called Augustus’s, though he did not create it but merely enrolled it in a census for his own service.

Having briefly tasted of the glory of dominion, let us pass on to consider the glory of praise. Blessed Augustine defines it as the judgment of men who think well of men. Although our citizens glory more in the testimony of their conscience than in human opinion, they nevertheless do not wish to lack the reputation of a good opinion. They commend themselves to every human conscience [Col. 0309D], providing things good not only before God but also before men. They desire to have a good testimony even from those who are outside, so that not they themselves but their Father who is in heaven may be glorified from the light of their works.

For they know that, in praising the Father, praise will not be lacking to them also; rather, according to Solomon, they will be given of the fruit of their hands, and their works will praise them in the gates (Prov. 31). They despise deceptive favour and vain beauty, knowing that the woman who fears the Lord shall more rightly be praised. The Lord did not wish this glory of praise—true rather than vain, stable rather than deceptive or fleeting—to be lacking to his city. Therefore he willed it to be woven into her by many memorials of lips, sending [Col. 0310A] prophets, wise men, and scribes to proclaim her; and, lest anything should be wanting to this glory, he stirred up even the glorious kings David and Solomon by his Spirit to sing of her.

If we wished to recount the sayings of all of these on this subject, time would fail sooner than material. But, omitting the others, it is enough to turn only to Solomon’s praises, which he is read to have uttered concerning the strong woman as a type of our city. There, after many statements found in praise of her, we read: “Her husband is noble in the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31). And likewise what was stated earlier: “Her works shall praise her in the gates” (*ibid.*).

For there are some gates in which what is outwardly apparent is commended, and others in which testimony is demanded not from works but from conscience, by him who examines hearts; who, when he sits to judge, will judge even acts of righteousness, and will search Jerusalem with lamps. There the righteous man is scarcely saved, and even the prudent virgins scarcely have enough oil for themselves, so that from it they may be able to help the foolish virgins even a little [Col. 0310B] (Matt. 25).

In those gates the glory of our city will appear more openly. There her husband will reveal the glory of his nobility. For her sons will arise and call her most blessed, and her husband will praise her (Cant. 6), saying: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov. 31). In those gates she will be given of the fruit of her hands, though meanwhile she seems in other gates to labour and work without fruit, receiving fruit not so much as hoping for it, according to the words: “You have established me singularly in hope” (Ps. 4). This will be in contrast to the opinion of those who will say in other gates: “We fools accounted their life madness and their end without honour. Behold how they have been counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints” (Wis. 5).

Those will be gates of glory, in which our city will be praised so marvellously and gloriously not only by her sons, not only by her husband, but even by her enemies. The gates of righteousness, however, may suitably be called those in which she is meanwhile praised for works of righteousness, concerning which it is read in the Psalm: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered through them, I will confess the Lord” (Ps. 117).

Very many writings of the doctors testify that these gates of righteousness are four. The first is the sorrow of compunction [Col. 0310D]; the second, the voice of confession; the third, satisfaction through works; the fourth, confession of praise or thanksgiving. These gates are opened in different ways.

First, they are opened when what is inwardly taking place within us is outwardly disclosed to human beings through them. The force of sorrow is revealed through tears; victory over sin through the humbling of confession—for as pride is the beginning of sin (Ecclus. 10), so sin is triumphed over by the humility of confession. Through satisfaction in works the ardour of zeal is shown, as is read of Mary Magdalene (*Homily* 33): “She considered what she had done, and did not wish to moderate what she did.” Through thanksgiving appears the advance of charity, which, the more perfect it is, glories in the Lord with greater peace and security.

These gates are opened in another way when, at the voice of a preacher or through divine inspiration alone, the hearts of sinners—previously hardened in the evil desire of the world, closed and barred against every admonition—are opened to repentance and torn by the pain of compunction. Thus the fruits worthy of repentance, which consist in confession and satisfaction, follow after every barrier of difficulty has been removed [Col. 0311A].

Thus the Prophet asked that the gates of righteousness might be opened to him, so that, entering into them—that is, entering by them—he might confess the Lord. He did not wish to remain in them, but to pass through them to that gate of which it is said: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. 117). For sinners enter the former gates; the latter is entered by those justified from sins, to whom Paul says: “Having been justified from sin, let us have peace with God” (Rom. 5). These are those who say with the Prophet to the Lord: “Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may sing your glory, your greatness all the day” (Ps. 79), because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15).

Behold the gates of righteousness through which the citizens of our city enter into grace, whereas through the four above-mentioned gates, which we called principal, they enter into pardon. Those principal gates are rightly so called, because they are of such necessity that without them one reaches neither pardon nor grace.

And, if the twelve gates which Ezekiel saw in the spirit (Ezek. 46) are to be assigned spiritually to our city, there are also four gates of glory through which one arrives at the homeland. Of these I would rightly call three the twelve apostles, who disseminated the faith of the Holy Trinity through the four parts of the world and, handing to the world the first rudiments of faith, became its gates of Christian doctrine [Col. 0311C].

When the Lord comes to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, they are believed to be the gates of the future unto Christ: gates, I say, to be shut against the condemned and opened to the saved. Through them all who have entered into faith will be admitted to the reward of faith—judged by them and presented to the Lord through them. To one of them, speaking for all, the Lord is recorded as saying: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16). And again: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

Then in these gates her husband will appear noble to his city, when he appears glorious in his saints and wonderful in his majesty. Then the glory of these gates will be revealed, which did not appear when they were crowded by the multitude entering into faith and shattered by the injuries of those who pressed upon them, although even then the apostles were by no means wholly without glory. For it was no small glory that the sick were laid in the streets and, overshadowed by Peter’s shadow alone, were healed of every infirmity (Acts 5) [Col. 0311D].

And if anyone wishes to consider not only Peter’s but the others’ miracles also, no one will suffice to admire such an immensity of glory. I omit the other glorious gifts of God by which he willed to be glorified in them. Enumerating them, the Apostle says: “To one is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues” (1 Cor. 12), and the rest that follows. Whoever wishes to consider these more carefully will be compelled to cry out with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11).

But lest the narrow compass of this discourse, now to be concluded, should confine so great a height of glory and such treasures of spiritual riches, they are better reserved for another beginning, so that by the newness of the beginning the hearts of readers may be renewed unto newness of glory. May he always be the Alpha and Omega of our discourse, who is the beginning, etc.

## TREATISE VIII. ON THE GLORY OF THE APOSTLES

[Col. 0312B]

Something now seems to be said concerning that devotion and glory which the faithful daily render to the apostles. It is sufficiently well known not only to those present who frequently celebrate festive rejoicings in their honour by sight and hearing, but was also foreseen in the Spirit by the fathers of the Old Testament, and was foretold and commended by them in many ways and by many modes.

Among these, to omit the sayings of the rest, which would take long to recount, the prophet David is read to have burst out in wonder into these words: “But to me your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured; exceedingly strengthened is their principality” (Ps. 138). Gregory applies this also to the other blessed ones, saying (*Homily* 27):

> “Behold, God’s elect tame the flesh, strengthen the spirit, command demons, and shine with miracles. They despise present things; by character and life they preach the eternal homeland; by dying they love it, and through torments reach it. They may be killed, but they cannot be bent: so strengthened is their principality.”

Yet it applies especially to the blessed apostles, who beyond all others have been honoured by the Lord and endowed with a more powerful principality, as the same Prophet says elsewhere: “Sons have been born to you in place of your fathers; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44) [Col. 0312C].

Does not their principality seem exceedingly strengthened when they have been appointed princes over all the earth? What earthly ruler ever possessed the entire earth, even though some are said to have held a monarchy? Indeed, who could traverse even half of it, either in person or through his agents? But the blessed apostles have been established as princes over all the earth in such a manner that no one rejects the yoke of their dominion; rather, there is no prince or subject who does not gladly and gratefully bow a devoted neck beneath their rule, rejoice in their patronage, and reverently seek their assistance. Their principality, therefore, has been made exceedingly powerful and strong.

That is a sufficiently powerful principality which guards its own court so strongly that all that it possesses remains in peace and no one can violently take anything from it. More powerful is that against which no one can defend or protect either himself or his possessions. Most powerful is that which no creature can resist or harm. But that is an exceedingly strengthened principality which is bounded by no end and troubled by no assault [Col. 0313A].

Foreseeing that the apostles’ principality would be strengthened in this way, and that the bars of our gates would thus be strengthened, the Prophet gloried in wonder and wondered in glory. And lest so great a principality should appear to lack its due honour, he prefaced it by saying: “Your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured” (Ps. 138).

Great honour is shown to a friend when he is admitted to a friend’s secret counsels and to any of his mysteries, as the Lord said to his apostles: “I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15). And the Prophet, giving thanks to the Lord, said: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. 50).

Greater honour is shown when a friend shares his own possessions with his friend; greatest when he entrusts all his possessions to him and sets him over and before all. Thus Pharaoh is read to have honoured Joseph (Gen. 41), thus Nebuchadnezzar Daniel (Dan. 2), and thus King Ahasuerus, wishing to honour Haman, placed his throne above all the princes he had, so that all the king’s servants bent the knee and worshipped him (Esther 11) [Col. 0313B].

But because that man, having abused so great a glory, could not remain in it long, we may call that honour very great, or excessive, which is not found momentary or passing: when the one whom a friend has set over all his possessions he also adopts as a son and makes his heir.

Thus Christ, wishing to honour his friends, having himself become the firstborn among many brethren and wishing to have fellow-heirs, nevertheless desired to set the blessed apostles above his other brethren and friends. To them he said in particular:

> “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke 22).

I pass briefly over these matters, giving only an occasion to the wise man to become wiser. Yet perhaps some will think it insufficiently explained why we said that the twelve apostles are to be included under the number of three gates. Let him therefore consider another point, perhaps not to be despised. For the apostles hold office in the city of the Lord, and perform the function of gates, in three ways.

For at first, the Church at its birth had gates leading to faith; as it made daily progress, it has gates leading to the righteousness of faith; and, when it is at last to be crowned, it will have gates leading to the reward of righteousness. This is not without reason perhaps signified by the fact that the teachings of apostolic doctrine are distinguished by only three modes of writing: first, in the Acts of the Apostles, the history of their deeds and sayings is woven together; second, by the Epistles, the virtues of the Church at its birth are commended and vices corrected; third, in the Apocalypse it is prophesied what punishments await the impious and what rewards await the just. The fact that a threefold festival of the Prince of the Apostles is celebrated in the Church seems likewise to refer to this: [Col. 0314A] the first concerning the chair, the second concerning the chains, the third concerning the triumph. For when we hear that he triumphed so gloriously over the persecutor, the world, and death, we rightly trust in so great a power in him, that by the merits of so great a patron we may obtain what we cannot by our own powers. But when we hear that he was bound with two chains and handed over to a cruel prison, we are incited to endure like things for righteousness’ sake. What shall I say concerning apostolic doctrine, which is signified through Peter’s chair, except that, when Christ’s faith had filled the whole world, that chair enclosed its four regions by its own four feet? For they confessed His testimony before kings and rulers, peoples and nations, bearing the name of Christ in four ways: by word, by conduct, by miracles, and finally by death. Resting on those [Col. 0314B] four feet, supported by such pillars, they established their chair, as had been foretold them by the Lord, when they became His witnesses in Jerusalem, in Judaea, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.

This is that chair in which, when David’s mighty men were counted and named, the first is read as sitting without a name: the wisest prince among three, like a most tender wood-worm, who slew eight hundred in one onset (2 Kings [= 2 Samuel] XXII). There thirty among David’s mighty men are named; then three mightier men; finally three mightiest men are counted, who, with David himself added, make thirty-seven in all. In the thirty mighty men is expressed the strength of good married persons: strong in faith by the multiplication of mighty works, they declare that the faith of the Trinity lives in them. For faith without works is proved dead. In the three mightier men is signified the faith of the continent, who are content not merely with the light of good works and with unfeigned faith, but also strive to offer the Lord a pure heart and a good conscience: a pure heart, that nothing be loved except that which ought to be loved; a good conscience, by which, through right living, they scent with sure hope what they love and also hold by unfeigned faith. For the invisible goods which we hold by unfeigned faith, we scent through the hope of a good conscience and taste through charity from a pure heart (1 Tim. I). Supported by these three—faith, hope, and charity—and holding them unwaveringly, a person has no need of Scriptures except [Col. 0314D] to instruct others; thus many have lived in solitude by these three without books. Hence, as blessed Augustine says, what was spoken seems already fulfilled in them: “Whether there be prophecies, they shall be abolished; whether tongues, they shall cease; whether knowledge, it shall be destroyed” (1 Cor. XIII). Yet in them there has arisen through these engines, as it were, so great a formation of faith, hope, and charity, that, possessing something perfect, they do not seek the things which are in part—perfect, indeed, insofar as this can be in the present life.

These men are said to have been so strong that, among the other mighty deeds they are reported to have performed, they are said also to have struck down three lions on snowy days. This is no different from what is read of Daniel, whom lions could not harm when he was cast into the pit (Dan. VI): because in the time of wrath and tribulation, [Col. 0315A] which is the day of snow and darkness, vices not only did not subdue him, but were rather subdued beneath him by divine help. The fact that seven lions are said to have been with Daniel, but only three here, is rightly understood thus: in the number seven all kinds of vices are signified, just as seven demons were cast out of Mary by the Lord; in the three lions, those three greatest vices from which all others arise—namely pride, lust, and avarice. These three are aptly expressed by the name of lions, because the lion is said to be an animal most proud, most lustful, and most ravenous. These three, therefore, are rightly called mightier than the thirty mighty men; nor did this escape those who assigned the thirtieth fruit to Job and the sixtieth to Daniel.

But however strong Daniel may feel himself to be, he should by no spiritual reasoning dare compare himself to Noah. For although, according to Daniel, “the learned,” who instruct many unto righteousness, shall be “as the stars for everlasting eternities,” and therefore the hundredfold fruit is assigned to them alone, because teachers are often granted understanding through the merits of those subject to them, to which they are never raised either by their own studies or by their own contemplation. Therefore David’s mightiest men are rightly understood as teachers, who deny themselves to themselves and become all things to all men for Christ, that they may gain all for Christ and may do all things in Him, Christ, who strengthens them. Foremost and chief among all these were the blessed apostles. Of their prince Peter it is said that he was in the chair the wisest [Col. 0315C] prince among three. Nor are they called three without reason though they are twelve; rather, a threefold office of teachers seems to be indicated here for us. The first is that of doctrine, the second of conduct and spiritual life, the third of divine contemplation.

These three are signified to us in those three whom the Lord, taking them apart from the other Apostles, led with Him onto the mountain and, transfigured, showed them His glory: I mean Peter, James, and John. In Peter, the grace of doctrine is especially expressed, as is plainly shown by what is recorded as said to him alone by the Lord: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI); and, “And thou, once converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luke XXII); and likewise by the fact that the vessel let down from heaven was shown beforehand to him, and that he merited to hear from the Lord: “Slay and [Col. 0315D] eat” (Acts X). In James, whose name is interpreted “wrestler,” is understood the struggle of spiritual exercise. Holy teachers experience this not only as they wrestle daily against vices, but often also in the spiritual exercises themselves, as they pass from one thing to another. For it is no slight struggle, as those who have experienced such things know, when a man is compelled by the obligation of pastoral office to pass from the sweetness of inward compunction, from diligence in divine offices, from wakeful scrutiny of his own deeds, to care for brotherly compassion and the solicitude owed to spiritual children. Hence what was said seems fitting also to such persons: “Martha, Martha, thou art anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke X).

In John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper and to whom [Col. 0316A] heavenly secrets were revealed, is plainly expressed that kind of contemplation which is especially accustomed to be given to teachers from divine revelation alone, rather than from human meditation or inquiry. Such were Paul’s ecstasies, which he recalls when he declares that such a man was caught up, not led up (2 Cor. XII). Such also was that of Peter, mentioned above, concerning the vision of the sheet; and such, as the very account of them makes clear, were John’s revelations. Although individual aspects of these three stand out in each of the aforesaid three apostles, nevertheless it must be believed that all three were fully and perfectly present in each of them and also in all the other apostles.

They are therefore rightly understood through David’s three mightiest men: they are read to have been strong against men, mightier against demons, and mightiest even against God, prevailing by prayers to appease His wrath and by their merits to move Him to mercy. Nor are all understood only in the three; they can also all be understood in their one prince Peter himself, when it is said: “Sitting in the chair, the wisest prince among three.” For apostolic doctrine, which is also called canonical, shines forth above that of the Roman pontiffs and doctors not only by greater authority, but also by the light of wisdom. Therefore the one sitting in the chair is not named, because apostolic doctrine was inspired into them not by themselves but by Christ through the Holy Spirit; it should be called not theirs but rather His, who, [Col. 0316C] remaining with them, promised them, saying: “When the Paraclete shall come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, he shall teach you all truth” (Luke XXI); and elsewhere: “When ye stand before kings and governors, do not premeditate how ye shall answer: for it shall be given you in that hour what ye shall speak” (Matt. X); and: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist” (Luke XXI). Paul also, professing this concerning himself, says: “The Gospel which I preached is not from me, neither did I receive it through man, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. II).

Peter’s chair, then, is Christ’s rather than Peter’s. But Christ, ascending to the throne of His kingdom, promised him a tribunal, or throne, of judicial power; He entrusted to him the chair of Christian doctrine. And [Col. 0316D] although the sacred canons of the succeeding Roman pontiffs and the most wise teachings of ecclesiastical doctors do not differ from the chair of apostolic doctrine, nevertheless they can by no reasoning be made equal to that chair. Rather, like a footstool adhering to the feet of the chair, they always humbly serve it; and in their midst Peter sits, presiding by authority, most wise through the illumination of divine revelation, prince by the power of grace and majesty.

Let us hear what certain Romans and what leading ecclesiastical doctors declared in their judgment on this matter. Pope Gelasius says (in the synod of seventy bishops): “The holy Roman Church, after those Scriptures of the Old and New Testament which we receive as canonical, does not forbid the reception also of these: the holy Nicene Synod of three hundred and eighteen Fathers, held through the intervention of the most great Emperor Constantine Augustus, in which Arius was condemned; the holy Constantinopolitan Synod, held through the intervention of the elder Emperor Theodosius, in which the heretic Macedonius received his deserved condemnation; the first holy Ephesian Synod, in which Nestorius was condemned with the consent of the most blessed Pope Celestine, through the intervention of his legate; the holy Chalcedonian Synod, held through the intervention of Emperor Marcian, in which Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus with their accomplices were condemned. But whatever other councils were instituted by the holy Fathers, after the authority of these four we command both to be observed and received.” Again: “The decretal letters which the most blessed popes at different times issued from the city [Col. 0317B] of Rome for the consolation of various Fathers are to be received with reverence.”

Again, Pope Leo (Epistle 89): “Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, the Saviour of humankind, ordained that the truth formerly contained in the proclamation of the Law and the Prophets should go forth through the apostolic trumpet for the salvation of the whole world, as it is written: ‘Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world’ [Ps. XVIII]. But the Lord willed that the mystery of this office should pertain to the duty of all the apostles in such a way that He established it principally in the most blessed Peter, the chief of all the apostles, so that from him, as from a kind of head, He might pour out His gifts into the whole body; and so that whoever dared to depart from Peter’s firmness might understand himself to be excluded from the divine ministry. For, having taken him into partnership in indivisible unity, He willed him to be named what He Himself was, saying: ‘Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ [Matt. XVI]. Thus, by the wonderful gift of God’s grace, the building of the eternal temple might stand firm in Peter’s solidity; and He strengthened His Church with this firmness, so that neither human rashness might assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it. But whoever attempts to break its power by failing to follow what he received from his elders wishes, with excessively impious presumption, to violate the most sacred firmness of this rock, constructed, as we have said, by God the builder.”

Again, Urban: “There are some who say that it has always been lawful for the Roman pontiff to make new [Col. 0317D] laws. We do not deny this; indeed, we strongly affirm it. But it must be known that he can make new laws where the evangelists have said nothing. Where, however, the Lord Himself, or His apostles and the holy Fathers who followed them, have expressly determined something, there the Roman pontiff ought not to enact a new law, but should rather confirm, even to life and blood, what has been preached. For if he should strive—God forbid!—to destroy what the apostles and prophets taught, he would be proved not to pronounce judgment but rather to err.”

Again, Augustine, *On the One Baptism* (Book II, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, ch. 3): “Who does not know that holy canonical Scripture, both Old and New Testament, is contained within fixed limits, and is so preferred to the later writings of all bishops that there can be no doubt or dispute whatever whether anything found written in it is true or right? But the letters of bishops, written or being written after the canon was confirmed, may be reproved if in them anything has departed from the truth, whether by the perhaps wiser discourse of someone more skilled in the matter, by the weightier authority of other bishops, by the prudent judgment of more learned persons, or by councils.”

Again, to Vincentius (Epistle 48): “Do not wish to collect calumnies from the writings of bishops—whether ours, Hilary’s, or those of Cyprian and Agrippinus before the party of Donatus separated itself—against so many, so clear, so unquestionable testimonies of God. First, because this kind of literature must be distinguished from the authority of the canon. For such writings are not read as though testimony were to be produced from them in such a way that one might not be allowed to think otherwise, should they perhaps think otherwise than truth requires. For we are of that number that we do not disdain also to accept what was said by the Apostle: ‘And if in anything ye think otherwise, this also God shall reveal unto you.’”

See how humbly Roman pontiffs and ecclesiastical doctors submit themselves to apostolic doctrine and lay themselves beneath the feet of the chair as a footstool, openly professing that the Roman pontiff may not make new laws where the Lord or His Apostles have expressly determined something, but must rather confirm, even to life and blood, what they preached. Nor do the doctors wish their own writings to be read as if testimony could be drawn from them in such a way that it would not be permissible to think otherwise, should they happen to think otherwise than the truth of apostolic doctrine requires.

But lest this footstool remain on the ground in a contemptible fashion and be defiled in any way by dust, beneath it is placed, as it were, a royal and noble covering: the secular laws, called either Justinian’s or imperial laws. In those laws Justinian himself does not blush to profess, saying: “Our laws do not disdain to imitate the sacred Canons.” Likewise Emperor Valentinian, when, coming from the East to the western regions, he wished to ordain a Catholic bishop at Milan, summoned the bishops and addressed them thus: “You know from the divine utterances what kind of [Col. 0318D] bishop ought to be: that he ought to show himself an imitator of every virtue, and have good conduct as a witness to his teaching; one to whom we also, who govern the empire, may sincerely submit our heads, and whose admonitions, when we sin as men, we must receive as remedies from a physician. Such an election belongs to you, for, having obtained divine grace and shining with that splendour, you are better able to choose.”

Pope Nicholas, considering this, says: “The emperor’s law is not above God’s law but beneath it. This is not because we say that imperial laws—by which the Church is often defended against heretics, often against tyrants, and against every kind of wicked person—are wholly to be rejected; but because we maintain that they cannot prejudice apostolic, evangelical, and canonical decrees.” [Col. 0319A]

But lest the rivals of the chair criticize what has been said concerning the chair because of the length of the discourse, though much more still occurs to be said about it, we reserve these matters for another beginning, so that, refreshed by a little rest in the meantime, we may approach briskly what remains to be said. May He Himself, the Alpha and Omega, be the beginning of our discourse, who is the beginning of all things, etc.

## TREATISE IX. ON PETER’S CHAIR AGAIN

No one should wonder or be troubled if we linger rather long over the gates of our city, or if, intending to treat of gates, we discuss at length the chair. For streets are commonly found near gates, and in them chairs are commonly prepared for wise men, so that from them, according to Solomon, fountains of wisdom may flow outward [Col. 0319B] and streams of spiritual waters may be divided in the streets (Prov. V). Thus, when Job went forth to the gate of the city, as he himself testifies (Job XXIX), a chair was prepared in the street, where young men hid themselves when they saw him, and old men rose and stood; the ear that heard him called him blessed, and the eye that saw him bore witness to him.
