It is not surprising, then, if we too, having found the broader expanse of the Scriptures, wander somewhat around the gates of glory, and, in the manner of those playing in the streets, leap from gates to chair, from chair to footstool, from footstool to a painted carpet from Egypt—lest perhaps that Gospel saying of the Fathers be reproached to us: “We sang to you, and ye did not dance” (Matt. [Col. 0319C] XI). For the Book of Kings has sung to us pleasantly and wonderfully of David’s mighty men; and their names and deeds have been described together as a type of the apostles, to whom it was said: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

For the fact that the name of the first among them is not stated perhaps signifies that whoever is assumed to the office of teaching and to the pastoral chair should not strive to make a name for himself. Even if he bears a name resembling the name of the great men who are on earth, he should not rejoice in that, but in this: if he trusts that his own name is written in heaven. With the Prophet he should say to the Lord: “Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” (Ps. CXIII); thus he should always ask and desire that the Lord’s name, not his own, be hallowed.

Hence it is that the Roman pontiff, who is Peter’s successor on earth, when he is installed, lays aside his former name and is distinguished by the name of one of his holy predecessors, so that he may no longer lead the common life or manner of living of ordinary people, but, changed into another man, may no longer be what he was; and, made one of the saints, may say with the Apostle: “I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” (Gal. II). Thus Peter alone among the others received a name from the Lord as a sign of his primacy, by which not so much he himself as Christ might be recognized. For, though He is called the Rock, from the Rock He named Peter, saying: “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI).

The first of David’s mighty men therefore fittingly prefigured Peter, not only because his name is not given [Col. 0320A], but also because he is said to have sat in the chair, to have been the wisest among three, to have been like a most tender wood-worm, and to have slain eight hundred in one onset (2 Kings [= 2 Samuel] XXIII). Enough, however, seems already to have been said concerning Peter’s chair and wisdom.

But if it is pleasing still to hear other things about it, we read of three chairs especially commended in the Scriptures: the chair of Moses, the chair of Elisha, and the chair of Peter. Of the first it is written: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses” (Matt. XXIII). Of the second, that the Shunammite woman made Elisha a small upper room, in which she placed for him a bed, a chair, a table, and a lampstand (4 Kings [= 2 Kings] IV). Of the third: “Thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build [Col. 0320B] my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI).

The chair of Moses, then, was the doctrine of the Law; the chair of Elisha was prophetic doctrine; Peter’s chair is evangelical and apostolic doctrine. The doctrine of the Law imposed the righteousness of the flesh, as the Apostle says: “The law cannot make perfect, as touching the conscience, him that serveth, only in meats and drinks and divers washings, and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of correction” (Heb. IX). This righteousness of the flesh consisted in sacrifices and offerings and various baptisms. Although these could not make the worshipper perfect according to conscience, nevertheless many were called righteous according to the righteousness of the Law, even before the Lord, walking blamelessly in the commandments and ordinances of the Law. Thus the Gospel also relates of Elizabeth and her husband Zacharias (Luke I).

Prophetic doctrine enjoined not right offering, but right doing. Hence Isaiah: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the Lord. I am full. Offer no more sacrifice in vain. Incense is an abomination unto me. New moons, Sabbaths, and other feasts I will not endure. Your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves; be clean; cease to do perversely; learn to do well. Seek judgment; aid the oppressed; judge for the fatherless; defend the widow; and come, and rebuke me, saith the Lord” (Isa. I). Behold, prophetic doctrine first removes vain hope and deceptive confidence in sacrifices, burnt offerings, and carnal ceremonies; second, it commands that perverse conduct cease; third, it enjoins learning to do good; fourth, it declares which among good works are more powerful and nearer to salvation. All prophecy agrees with this; all the prophets aim to persuade this: that the perverse turn away from evil and do what is good.

This is Elisha’s chair. Though it may appear uncultivated and woven, as it were, from rough and unpolished material by obscure speech, it is nevertheless found solid, firm, and immovable, according to the word of the Prince of the Apostles: “We have the more sure prophetic word, whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. I). Behold, Peter’s chair does not overthrow Elisha’s chair or Moses’ chair, but stands above them, resting upon them as upon most firm pillars. For of the Law He says: “I came not [Col. 0321A] to destroy the Law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. V). Of the prophets He says: “Beginning with Moses and the prophets, he interpreted to them the things written concerning him” (Luke XXIV). This too agrees with the fact that Moses and Elijah appeared speaking with Christ on the mountain.

Among these, therefore, Peter’s chair holds the middle place, as more worthy and higher, and as fittingly belonging to him who is called wisest among three. For as Peter’s chair is manifestly higher than the two aforesaid chairs, so Peter, as Christ’s vicar and the first of David’s mighty men, was manifestly more eminent in wisdom. For his wisdom recognized and taught that not only the righteousness of the flesh, like Moses, nor merely uprightness of works, like prophetic speech, but purity of heart must be sought. As he had learned from the mouth of Truth, he proclaimed: “Cleanse first that which is within the cup or the dish, and that which is without shall be clean” (Matt. XXIII); and: “Not that which entereth into the mouth defileth a man, but that which proceedeth out,” and the rest. “For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders” (Matt. XV), and the rest that follows. Likewise: “Ye have heard that it was said to the ancients, Thou shalt not kill” (Matt. V), and the rest.

In these and many other things which the evangelical and apostolic forest brings forth for us, we are taught to restrain not only unlawful acts, but also wanton movements of the body and irrational affections of the heart. He is therefore rightly called wisest among three, because he is known to have issued precepts of a more perfect life and a more abundant righteousness, the most perfect among those already mentioned. But that the dignity and firmness of this most wise chair may be more fully known, let us consider how many and what feet support it.

The Lord seems to have expressed its three feet in the Gospel when He said to the disciples: “Were not these things written in the Law, and the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning me?” (Luke XXIV). There He says that the Law, Prophets, and Psalms bear testimony concerning Him: namely, that He must suffer, rise from the dead on the third day, and that the Gospel must be preached among all nations (ibid.). There He proves that the Law, Prophets, and Psalms support the Gospel, and that the Gospel rests upon them as upon three props. To add a fourth prop, the Scriptures called Hagiographa are joined to those aforesaid: [Col. 0321D] such as the books of Job, Solomon, Daniel, and others who, no less clearly than the rest, prophesy Christ by foretelling Him.

Or, if with Jerome we count the Psalms among the Hagiographa, we may call the fourth foot that Scripture which Jerome himself calls apocryphal: namely, the Book of Wisdom, Jesus son of Sirach, Tobit, Judith, and Maccabees, in which likewise we find the times of Christ and the apostles prefigured. If the spiritual sense is sought in all these Scriptures of the Old Testament, so that a mystical understanding may be drawn forth, that most tender wood-worm, mentioned immediately after the chair, will be found no less wonderfully than fittingly.

For what is more like that little worm than spiritual understanding? That worm is produced from some moisture of wood, as though from a certain hidden matter within it, and from incidental heat applied outwardly, by a hidden force of nature. This spiritual understanding is brought forth from a likeness drawn out of the hardness of the letter, as from a kind of moisture found there, while the heat of the Holy Spirit inflames and illuminates together the mind of the beholder, as the sun kindles the air. Like a most tender wood-worm, it uses not the violence of any blow but serves as an anointing: by a hidden and subtle examination it bends and softens the hardness of the letter, and by a certain voluntary power it tenderly pierces and compuncts the mind of the beholder.

Paul wished this worm to be produced in the hearts of his hearers when he said: “The letter kills, but [Col. 0322B] the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. III). Peter expresses the same thing in other words: “No prophecy comes by private interpretation. For prophecy was not at any time brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet. I). It is as though he said: If you receive prophetic words according to your own interpretation, you will grasp the hardness of wood—indeed rather of stone—than understanding. But if you are guided by that Spirit by whom the prophets were inspired, you will find Spirit and life in their words, and from them you yourselves will gain life, so that, in the manner of a wood-borer, the word of God may work in you, and, if not with swift movement, yet by unceasing effort soften whatever is hard in you and change it into a quality like itself.

With this wood-borer, therefore, as our guide, let us investigate the remaining things joined in the same letter, so that, receiving some life-giving thing from them ourselves, we may soon experience in ourselves the extraordinary power of that most tender worm. It follows, then, that this wisest man slew eight hundred in one onset (2 Kings [= 2 Samuel] XXIII). What benefit, I ask, comes to believers from this letter when it is read, since they are forbidden not only to kill but even to be angry with a man without cause? But let the Spirit of the Lord come forth now into the light for us: He who inspired the writing of these things, and who, hidden in the heart of the writer like a most tender little worm, prepared for Himself even this hiding-place in the letter. With every hardness and obscurity removed, let Him declare what He willed to be prefigured in this deed.

First, then, without prejudice to the higher mystery, if we compare this man’s bodily strength with Peter’s spiritual power, we shall find Peter’s power incomparably superior. For he is read to have slain for the world not merely eight hundred but also three thousand men, baptized in one day by a single onset of his speech. He also slew eight hundred in one onset when in Simon he condemned all Simoniacs, saying: “Thy money perish with thee” (Acts II); because “thou hast thought that the gift of God may be possessed with money” (Acts VIII). It is as though he said: You wished to turn the grace of the Holy Spirit, signified by the number seven, toward gain represented by the number eight, judging gain to be godliness. “But thou hast neither part nor lot in this word. For I see thee to be in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (ibid.), [Col. 0323A] while you strive to multiply the number eight of worldly things, which subsist through the four elements in the four quarters of the world, and contemptuously judge saleable the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, which has no bitterness or weariness.

Apostolic speech also slays eight hundred in one onset when, by condemning every heretic, it cuts him off from the Church. Thus the Nicene Synod, in Arius, condemned all Arians by one sentence; the Constantinopolitan Synod, in Macedonius, all Macedonians; the Ephesian Synod, in Nestorius, the Nestorians; and the Chalcedonian Synod, in Eutyches, killed the Eutychians with one blow of the spiritual sword. Peter’s sword does not cease to do this even today throughout the whole world, when, according to the prophet, it does not cease to devour flesh (Deut. XXXII), either correcting or cutting off the vices of carnal people. Behold, this sword is found most harsh to the carnal, most tender to the spiritual, and most splendid to those sitting in the chair and wielding it from there.

These are the things that especially befit those sitting spiritually in the chair: the light of discernment, zeal for uprightness, and the affection of compassion. In accordance with these, the sword of God’s word must be varied in dealing with the impious according to the different merits of those subject to them. Hence blessed Benedict, who is read to have been full of the spirit of all the righteous, describing in his Rule what a pastor ought to be, says thus (ch. 2): “He must be learned in the divine law, that he may know whence to bring forth things new and old.” And further on: “Let him exhort the obedient [Col. 0323C] and meek that they may progress to better things. But we admonish him to rebuke and correct more sharply those hard of heart and wicked.” The Holy Spirit too, appearing above the apostles in fire, seemed spiritually to have figured these same things. Fire has the brightness of light, the sweetness of warmth, and the harshness of burning.

The same things seem also to be signified in the three faces of the living creatures, so that those who undertake the office of pastors and, in place of the living creatures, draw the wall of the Church, may show the face of a lion to the perverse, the face of a man to the simple and gentle, and the face of an eagle to the spiritual and instructed (Ezek. I). Thus Paul, assuming the eagle’s face, spoke wisdom among the perfect; using the face of a man, he gave milk to little ones to drink; he wept with those who wept and rejoiced with those who rejoiced (Rom. XII). But whenever it was necessary, though always under compulsion, he put on the face of a lion: he handed the Corinthian over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh; he stood ready to avenge every disobedience; and he did not hesitate to cast down every height exalting itself against the knowledge of Christ.

He knew how to use these faces in turn and without confusion, so that, having more of the lion, he did not wish to have less of the man; or, wishing to have more of the man, he did not have less of the lion; or, putting off the face of both, he did not wish to appear wholly eagle. Blessed Pope Gregory also taught others to use this same discernment, saying (Homily 32): “We owe compassion to the person, uprightness to the vices, so that in one and the same person we may love the good which he has become and pursue the evil which he has done, lest, while we imprudently remit faults, we seem no longer to have compassion through charity but to have indulged through negligence.” That is, lest we offer not so much a man to a human being as an ox.

But if we seem to say that something bovine is present in the saints, let us not attribute to them the vice of bovine sluggishness; rather, let us consider how fitting this animal is for divine sacrifices. We show the face of this animal to God alone, not to a human being, when upon the altar of the heart we sacrifice ourselves to the divine eyes. The Beloved commands this face to be shown to Him in the Song of Songs, saying: “Show me thy face” (Cant. II). It is as though He said: I count as yours that face which you form for yourself from what is your own, because within yourself you find the material of weakness and the cause of fault, whereby you are rightly pierced with compunction. And I will that you show this face to Me alone, [Col. 0324B] who alone can grant the remedy for weakness and alone suffice to abolish fault.

Nor should what follows seem contrary to this meaning: “For your face is beautiful” (ibid.). For the more unattractive any soul is to itself, the more beautiful it appears to the eyes of the Bridegroom. Blessed Benedict taught superiors to show these faces to their subjects when he said (Rule, ch. 28): “If the abbot has applied poultices to an offending brother, if ointments of exhortations”—this is to show the face of a man; “if remedies from the divine Scriptures”—this is the face of an eagle; “if, finally, the blows of rods, the burning of excommunication”—this is the face of a lion; “let him at last employ what is greater, his own prayer and that of his brethren” [Col. 0324C]—this is to apply the face of an ox. Although in this manner these faces are displayed toward one’s neighbour, nevertheless the face of the ox through prayer, and the face of the eagle through contemplation, are owed particularly to God; the face of the lion and that of the man, to one’s neighbour.

Accordingly, these latter two—the man’s face, namely, and the lion’s—are not unfittingly represented in those two mighty men of David who are first appended among the mighty men. At first sight Eleazar represents for us the face of the lion, both in fact and in name, in that he is said to have struck down the Philistines until his hand grew stiff upon the sword (2 Sam. 23). For what is it for the hand to grow stiff upon the sword, except to exercise, without any relaxation, the zeal of justice inflexibly against sins and vices, and, whether in governing subjects with an iron rod or repressing unlawful impulses, to employ the lion’s unconquerable severity? But God’s help is necessary for doing this, which is the meaning of *Eleazar*; and one must trust not so much in one’s own strength as in God’s assistance, so that such a person may say: “The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me” (Ps. 117 [118]). For, according to the Apostle, nothing will be able to harm us if we are zealous for what is good (1 Pet. 3).

But Eleazar must beware lest, while exercising the lion’s severity, he incur the lion’s harshness. The latter, when present, makes him hateful; the former, when absent, contemptible. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: “Do not be like a lion in your house, overturning your household and oppressing those subject to you” (Ecclus. 4). Conversely, it is written of Judas Maccabaeus: “He became like a lion in his deeds, and hunted down the wicked, searching them out [Col. 0325A]; and those troubling his people he burned with flames. Enemies were driven back in fear of him; he embittered many kings, and made Jacob rejoice in his deeds. Deliverance was directed through his hand, and he gathered together those who were perishing” (1 Macc. 3). Thus it is also said of this Eleazar that, after great deliverance had been wrought through him, the people who had fled returned to strip the slain of their spoils. See how greatly the lion’s face in a teacher benefits the people. For just as, where there is no governor, the people fall; and just as woe to the land whose king is a child and whose rulers are effeminate, so a wise king scatters the ungodly and bends them beneath the wheel. For while Rehoboam ruled, the people gathered under David were divided (3 Kings [1 Kings] 16); when Judas or Eleazar triumphs, those who had perished are gathered together [Col. 0325B], and those who had fled return to strip the slain of their spoils (2 Sam. 23).

After Eleazar, among David’s mighty men, follows Shammah, of whom it is written that, when the people fled from before the Philistines, he stood in the middle of a field full of lentils, defended it, struck down the Philistines, and the Lord wrought a great deliverance (ibid.). This Shammah is interpreted as “hearing”; in him we clearly discern the face of a man when we see a superior incline compassionate ears toward his subjects, effectively hear the cry of the poor, rescue the one crying out from the hand of those stronger than he, and the needy and poor from those who plunder him (Ps. 34 [35]). But lest we suspect some deficiency in this Shammah, or in the eleventh gate, because of the eleven goats’-hair curtains and the eleventh psalm, which laments a falling-away from holiness [Col. 0325C], let us investigate his deed carefully under another beginning. May he always be the Alpha and Omega of our discourse, who is the beginning and end of all things, and remains without beginning and end unto ages of ages.

## TREATISE X. ON THE THREE ORDERS OF PRELATES, AND THE EXALTATION OF THE CLERGY ABOVE THE PEOPLE

As we are about to approach the eleventh gate, before entering the field full of lentils which Shammah defends there, it is pleasing to consider, in these three strong men among David’s mighty men—by whom, we said, prelates are signified—the three distinct orders of prelates expressly represented. Just as they are distinguished in the Church today, so we find them distinguished among the pagans, among the Jews, and in the New Testament by the Lord. Among the Gentiles there were the ordinary temple-priests, the *flamines*; the greater *archflamines*; and the highest *protoflamines*. In the Old Testament likewise, high priests entered the Holy of Holies once a year. Lesser priests entered the tabernacle daily and completed the sacrifices. The Levites, as the least among them, ministered in subordinate service.

But in the New Testament James, Cephas, and John, who according to the Apostle were pillars above the others, gave the right hand to Paul (Gal. 2). The Lord also, taking Peter, James, and John, led them up a high mountain and showed them his glory (Matt. 17). In their place, primates [Col. 0326A] and archbishops have today been instituted in the Church; in the place of the other apostles, bishops. Besides the apostles, there were also seventy-two others designated by the Lord and sent into every city and place where he himself was to come; to them he said particularly: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10). In their place priests today are set over congregations. This Shammah seems properly to signify them, just as perhaps the two higher orders set forth above manifestly signify the others.

The first man, who sits in the chair and is declared most wise, represents primates and archbishops; for the higher they are above the rest, the more fitting it is that they should also be wiser. For the eagle, which is said to excel other birds, is also known to keep its eyes fixed more clearly than all others upon the light. Eleazar [Col. 0326B], who was most stern, represents bishops, just as that other man was most wise. For as the lion is known to excel other beasts in strength, so bishops ought to appear sterner and more steadfast than lesser priests. To the lesser clergy, indeed, to whom it was said, “Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves” (Luke 10), mercy and gentleness especially belong, so that no unrest of seditious peoples and no wickedness may provoke them to bitterness or hatred; rather, like most gentle lambs enduring the rabies of wolves, they should tirelessly imitate him who “was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and was silent as a lamb before its shearer” (Isa. 53).

Let them examine Shammah’s deed closely, in which they are more fully taught what they ought to do. For he is said to have defended a field full of lentils from the Philistines [Col. 0326C]. What is this field but earthly life, a field of which Cain first, and then Esau, became a cultivator? In contrast, Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Jacob a simple man dwelling in a tent (Gen. 4; Gen. 25). Our priesthood is fittingly prefigured in Abel, who first offered, and was himself offered, as a sacrifice to God; and in Jacob, who first anointed a stone, raised it as a pillar, and poured oil upon it. That priesthood is known to have been established especially by these two sacraments: the offering of the incorruptible victim and the anointing with sacred chrism.

Yet it is more particularly prefigured in Jacob, who, by offering tithes, by the death of two kids—as if by a twofold mortification of the flesh’s and the spirit’s wantonness [Col. 0326D]—and by the alteration of his own name, is known, as it were historically, to have expressed those things which now prevail in the Church. But in Cain and Esau the earthly people are rightly prefigured. The former, consumed by envy and the crime of fraternal hatred, was cast out from the Lord’s presence; the latter, while hunting in the field, was supplanted at home by his brother, and, returning from the field exceedingly weary, willingly gave up his birthright for a red lentil stew.

Let priests not wonder when they see laypeople today driven by the goads of envy. But let laypeople who recognize themselves as such fear lest they be expelled from the Lord’s presence with Cain. And if they experience themselves as cast out from the light of divine wisdom, let them nevertheless not resort to the noose of despair; but, humbly subjecting themselves to God, let them strive to turn aside from iniquity. Nor should they be troubled and grieve, though they are older by birth, if they see the clergy placed above them. For the Lord ordained that it should be so, and foreshadowed what he had ordained in Jacob and Esau.

For when Isaac blessed Jacob, he said by the Lord’s inspiration: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth an abundance of grain, wine, and oil; may peoples serve you and tribes bow down before you. Be lord of your brothers, and may your mother’s sons bow down before you. Cursed be whoever curses you, and whoever blesses you, may he be filled with blessings” (Gen. 27). Conversely, Esau was told: “In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be. You shall live by the sword, and serve your brother” (ibid.). See how plainly the Holy Spirit has expressed in these words the condition of both clergy [Col. 0327B] and Christian people. To the clergy he granted not only the dew of heaven, as some blasphemously allege, but also a fuller abundance of the fatness of the earth. He also expressly granted them the service of peoples, the reverence of tribes, lordship over their brothers, and their bowing down. In all these things we understand not *latria*, the worship owed to God alone, but *dulia*, the honour also shown to angels and holy human beings, and to any successors of the saints.

But upon the people he imposed service to the clergy; he foretold that they would live by the sword and be blessed in the fatness of the earth. For although he granted them the dew of heaven, he nevertheless did not grant an abundance of heavenly dew; and he foretold that they would not possess the dew itself within themselves, but would receive it from above through the clergy, and after the fatness of the earth [Col. 0327C]. Yet let us attend not only to what the Lord foretold through Isaac, but also to what was done between the brothers themselves. Esau first willingly yielded his birthright to his brother, lightly esteeming it as of little value. But afterwards, grieving that he had yielded it, he turned to the tyranny of persecution.

So Constantine at first devoutly offered to the Roman pontiff the insignia of empire, namely the crown and royal purple—prefigured in Esau’s very fine garments, which the mother granted to Jacob. But in his successors he later inflicted exiles upon that same pontiff, even threatened death, and inflicted many injuries. Yet Esau, overcome by Jacob’s patience and long-suffering, submitted, though unwillingly, to the divine sentence and offered him an escort and protection, though more from pretense than devotion. Jacob wisely and prudently refused it, saying: “You know that I have tender little children and pregnant sheep; if I make them travel too hard, they will all die in one day” (Gen. 33). All these things need no exposition for those acquainted with sacred Scripture, but only recollection.

But the point which seems especially to require attention is by what right, and for what reasons, the younger was set above the firstborn. At first sight the right seems evident: Jacob did not grant the lentils which he had cooked to his brother, though urgently asking for them, until Esau voluntarily yielded his birthright. Thus the clergy too were set above the people by the same right, when, casting away the works of flesh and blood as a red lentil stew—sweet in taste indeed, but harmful to the sight—they yielded them to the people. The latter, however, being as it were animal men and receiving by no means the things of the Spirit of God, retained those same works of the flesh as something supreme. They preferred involvement in carnal and secular affairs to serving God and walking in the Spirit.

But the clergy willingly embraced the apostolic saying: “Walk in the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh” (Gal. 5); and they also heard with no deaf ear: “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die”; “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. 8); and “She who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5). They chose to mortify by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh, in order to live. Justly, therefore [Col. 0328B], as spirit is set above flesh, so those who live spiritually are set above those whose wisdom is carnal.

Behold the birthright: not Esau’s eating of the lentils, but his desire for them, took it from him; Jacob’s contempt for the same lentils conferred it upon him. The clergy earned their primacy from the chastity of continence, which they valued more highly than the pleasure of carnal desire, as though it were a certain red lentil stew. There is another cause of this reversal: namely, the pious deception of our Jacob, who, taking on the flesh of sin as if it were a kid’s skin, willed to come in the likeness of sinful flesh, tempted in every respect according to that likeness, yet without sin (Heb. 4). The Jewish people, with mother Grace at work, unknowingly fulfilled in Christ by deed this pious deception—just as the blind father, Isaac, unknowingly gave Jacob by word the blessing. “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

By the merit, therefore, of this our true Jacob—who became for us a true king and priest on the cross, crowned and offered, not so much by anointing a stone as by presenting himself as the Anointed Stone, “anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44 [45])—those also who exercise his priesthood are rightly called and made “a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2), possessing by hereditary right the paternal blessing as spiritual sons of Aaron.

But amid these things let our Shammah remember that he ought to use, not glory in, the power he has received for edification and not for destruction. Let him know that he has been given the task of defending the field full of lentils, rather than harvesting it; that the eating of lentils—the pleasure of carnal works—has been forbidden him; and that the defense of the field has been entrusted to him [Col. 0328D]. Let the spiritual Shammah therefore strive to protect the carnal people, as a field full of lentils, at least from criminal sins: if not from desiring a neighbour’s wife, then at least from committing adultery with her; if not from desiring his property, then at least from seizing it; if not from hatred, then at least from murder. Let him protect the poor from the injuries inflicted by the rich, and the rich from the snares of demons, teaching them not to think proudly nor put their hope in the uncertainty of riches, and telling them that “those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare” (1 Tim. 6).

Yet let this same Shammah beware lest, while retaining only Jacob’s voice, he be found not merely to feign but actually to possess Esau’s hands—crafty through tricks and deceits, as though by the roughness and subtlety of hair [Col. 0329A]. For the Holy Spirit seems to have intimated from that deed that there would be some such priests; and the Lord rebuked precisely this in the scribes and Pharisees: “The scribes and Pharisees,” he says, “have sat upon Moses’ seat. Therefore do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). What else does he seem to say in these words but: “The voice indeed is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands”? (Gen. 27). Nevertheless, because of reverence for the priesthood, honour should be given to the chair and obedience to the voice.

But let priests fear lest those who deserved blessing because of Jacob’s voice and their contempt for lentils should incur, because of Esau’s hands and their desire for lentils, the curse of death along with the Babylonian elders. For the first of them, condemned for fraudulent and unjust judgments, heard: “Now have come to light your sins, which you formerly committed, judging unjust judgments, oppressing the innocent, and acquitting the guilty” (Dan. 13). Hence he received the sentence of his condemnation, the Holy Spirit declaring through Daniel and saying to him: “May you perish beneath the holm oak.” For the holm oak retains the perpetual green of its leaves, but bears fruit fit rather for swine than for human use. What is the greenness of leaves but the integrity and vigour of sound words? And what is the fruit of swine but the works of the flesh, which the Apostle, after shameful deeds and even crimes, enumerates when he adds: “Sorceries [Col. 0329C], enmities, strife, jealousies, wrath, quarrels, envy, murders”? (Gal. 5). And what is meant by “May you perish beneath the holm oak” but what the Apostle adds: “Those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God”? (ibid.).

Finally, the second elder, condemned for disgraceful conduct as though for eating lentils, heard: “Your beauty has deceived you, and desire has perverted your heart” (Dan. 13). Hence this was added in the sentence: “The angel will crush you into a lentil” (*in lentem comminuet te*; the wording plays on *lens*, “lentil”) (Dan. 13). Rightly, he who had yielded lentils to others, and had preferred spiritual and heavenly things, as the highest goods, to carnal foods as certain least things, returns to those small things and is crushed among them, so that he may now relish nothing but what is low and cannot rise to grasp heavenly things.

What has been said for the present concerning David’s three mightiest men might suffice, if we did not thirst with David for the water of Bethlehem, and if our thirst could seem not to be satisfied unless that same water, not to be drunk, but poured out in libation, were offered to the Lord. What was then accomplished according to the letter through the mystery of these three mightiest men was afterwards accomplished spiritually by the spiritual mighty men of the spiritual David. The apostles, namely, and their successors—whom we said are understood through David’s three mightiest men—drew from the cistern of the Mosaic Law, elsewhere called a pool and having five porticoes, the water of spiritual understanding no less bravely than subtly. Pressing strongly, in accordance with Solomon, the breasts of the Law (Prov. 30), they expressed not only the milk of moral knowledge but also the butter of allegorical meaning.

And this appears to have been done by them all the more bravely because that same cistern was more diligently besieged and guardedly closed by David’s enemies, the scribes and Pharisees, who understood the Law carnally [Col. 0330A]. For the apostles broke into the enemies’ camp when, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, the rulers, elders, and scribes were gathered in Jerusalem, along with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and all who were of the priestly family. They set Peter and John in their midst and questioned them: “By what power, or in what name, do you do this?” Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: “Rulers of the people and elders, hear: In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, by him this man stands before you whole. This is the stone rejected by you builders, which has become the head of the corner” (Acts 4).

“But God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has thus fulfilled it. Moses indeed said: ‘God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren; you shall hear him as you hear me. And every soul that shall not hear that prophet shall be exterminated from the people.’ And all the prophets, from Samuel onwards, announced these days. You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant which God established with our fathers, saying to Abraham: ‘In your seed all the families of the earth shall be blessed’” (Acts 3).

Paul also, passing through the midst of the enemy ranks and boldly proclaiming Jesus to them, said: “We proclaim to you the promise made to our fathers, because God has fulfilled it to our children by raising Jesus, as it is written also in the second psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ He says elsewhere as well: ‘You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption’” (Acts 13). When the Jews contradicted this and were filled with jealousy, Paul and Barnabas said boldly: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (ibid.).

Behold, the water of spiritual understanding taken away from the Jews and offered by the apostles to the Gentile people; and in them is David himself, who derived his origin from the Gentile people through Ruth of Moab. She too gives us water when spiritually understood. But as we are tending to other matters, let us briefly continue what we began [Col. 0330D]. Certainly, in judging the desired water worthy not to be drunk but poured out in libation to the Lord, David undoubtedly signifies in us that our David, Christ, sought the water mentioned above not as a remedy for the human weakness he had assumed, but as a proof of the divine nature which had bent itself down to humankind.

For what surer proof is there of our faith than that we know the things which we believe Christ did for us to have been foretold long beforehand by the prophets, and find them stored in the Old Testament—as in the cistern of Bethlehem—as most limpid water? Thus Isaiah says: “Declare what is to come in the future, and we shall know that you are gods” (Isa. 41). We too, if we thirst through desiring the water of spiritual knowledge [Col. 0331A], should not seek it for the deceptive and fleeting glory of this present life. Rather, we should ask it from the Lord, as James says, in order to make God favourable to us and to instruct our neighbours; and we should ascribe to him everything we have obtained in ourselves, saying with the Apostle: “We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3).

David judged this water to be blood, because just as the life of the flesh is in the blood, so the life of the soul consists in the warmth of wisdom. That this cistern is described as having been beside the gate of Bethlehem seems to signify nothing other than the Old Testament, in which ancient histories are as waters of clouds; and that it is not so much a cistern or a well as a spring-well, and that Bethlehem is the open gate of our city, is proved by the inhabitants of that city themselves [Col. 0331B]. Most fittingly I would call this gate the blessed Mary, from whom Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judah: like a spring rising from the earth and watering the whole surface of the earth; and like the river proceeding from the place of delight to water Paradise (Gen. 2), divided into four Gospels as into four heads, and making the whole world fruitful.

Concerning this twelfth gate of our city—the subject is weighty for us—the more readily it may be expounded, the more eagerly we trust our hearers will be to hear it. But the worthier this subject is, the more fitting it is recognized that a new beginning should be assigned to it, so that the hearts of readers, refreshed by a brief repose, may prepare themselves more ardently for so great a subject [Col. 0331C]. May he always be the Alpha and Ω of our discourse, who, etc.

## TREATISE XI. ON THE TWELFTH GATE OF THE CITY OF GOD: THE BLESSED VIRGIN, MOTHER OF GOD

As we are about to treat of the most glorious incorruptible Mother and Virgin of our Lord God, we humbly beseech her most glorious Son, our Lord, that he may deign to reveal to us those things which he willed to be gloriously recorded of her in the sacred Scriptures; and teach us to speak of her in ways which, even if they do not correspond to her dignity, may at least suit our unworthiness, satisfy our devotion, and suffice even for the reading of little ones.

Therefore, observing how variously and in how many ways God, who formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets, willed magnificently to commend her, one man burst forth in this metrical play:

> Many prophetic foretellings have spoken of you;  
> Not unaware that you were to be enriched with singular grace.  
> For he who willed to be born and nourished from your flesh,
Nor did she keep silence concerning your praises, either in the Scriptures or in figures. But before we approach what is said and prefigured of her by prophets and fathers, it seems necessary to observe and state more carefully that this twelfth gate of our city, of which we must treat, is the first and highest of the gates already set forth. First in order, highest in dignity. From her the other gates received their beginning; in her they possess their support; through her they receive completion. Situated in the more eminent part of the city [Col. 0332A], she supplies the others with light, confers the dignity of glory, and brings their consummation. For from her all the sacraments flowed forth to us; in her the charisms of every grace and the examples of virtues shone no less delightfully. Finally, even to the Apostles themselves the beginnings of our redemption were first made manifest through her, as through the eastern gate. For from whom could those who were to write and preach throughout the whole world concerning the infancy of our Redeemer learn more fittingly or more faithfully than from her who had seen and heard all things, had handled them with her own hands, and faithfully kept them, pondering them in her heart? (Luke 2.) Whence, unless through her, did that angelic “Hail,” so sweet to the world, become known to them? Whence came the entire sequence of that angelic salutation, each word of which [Col. 0332B] is a divine oracle, as though from a divine letter brought by an angel but dictated by the Holy Spirit? Whence came the Virgin’s response itself, the angel’s instruction as to how the things spoken by him should come to pass, and Elizabeth’s conception—both the angelic prediction made to Zechariah and the annunciation delivered to Mary? Whence came Mary’s ascent into the hill country; Elizabeth’s prophetic reply to her greeting; and Mary’s own song, no less prophetic than profound? Whence, finally, came the astounding and venerable birth of our Lord, wondrous even to the heavenly powers: his being wrapped in swaddling-clothes, laid in a manger, the narrowness of the lodging, the angels’ appearance to the shepherds, the proclamation of great joy [Col. 0332C] that would be for all the people, and the glorious chanting of the angelic hymn?

Keeping and pondering all these things in her heart, Mary presented herself to the world as a closed gate until the eighth day of the Circumcision—a gate already opened by the Holy Spirit for the Son of God, and shining more brightly than light itself when revealed not only to Gabriel but also to the multitude of the heavenly host. On the eighth day of her Son, she too began gradually to open herself to the world, lest, if she suddenly opened herself wholly, she should bring to eyes not yet sound not so much light by her splendour as blindness. Therefore, on that day, giving her Son the name sweet to the ears, sweet to the mouth, rejoicing in the heart—the name which she alone and first had learned from the angel—she brought light into the world like the morning star of the newly rising sun. Does she not seem, by conferring this name, to say to each and to all: “There is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved”? (Acts 4.) “He who is to be blessed in it shall be blessed in the Lord. Amen” (Isa. 65).

For this name is found effective not only for obtaining salvation, but also for meriting blessing; it not only saves but sanctifies. It saves from the weight of sins, from the snares of temptations, and from the varying dangers of temporal things. “At this name every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). The power of infernal wickedness bends, so that it may not harm by tempting; the pride and covetousness of earthly human beings bend, so that they may not consent to sin; even the power of heavenly spirits bends at the invocation of this name, so that they may condescend to assist those in peril [Col. 0333A]. Thus, yes, thus the worshippers of this name are saved and delivered from evil.

In this name they are also blessed, advanced, and confirmed in good, according to the priest’s prayer in the canon of the Mass, that God may deign to make his offering blessed, enrolled, and ratified. Blessed for sanctification, enrolled for perfection, ratified for confirmation. For so it commonly happens in grants of princes or in the provisions of testators. First, before a prince, through petitions or by some other means, the bare grant of something is obtained; then, in order that the grant may be put into writing, labour is expended toward its completion; finally, that the document may be strengthened for confirmation by the prince’s seal. In the same way, if the Lord’s blessing is to be full, he first sanctifies by making fruitful; then he multiplies by perfecting; finally, he confirms by strengthening. But the blessing of anyone accomplishes this only in the name of the Lord.

Job is read to have blessed the Lord, but by praising the Lord’s name, saying: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1). The Lord is read to have blessed Abraham, but by revealing and commending his own name to him: “I am God Almighty; walk before me and be perfect” (Gen. 17). Isaac is read to have blessed his son Jacob, but in the name of the Lord: “May God give you of the dew of heaven,” etc. (Gen. 27). This threefold blessing is frequently found in Scripture.

[Col. 0333C] The first is that by which we bless God, saying, “Blessed be the name of the Lord”; and this is signified by the beginning of the episcopal blessing, which is first made upon the breast, because God must first be blessed for the gifts already received within, so that we may say with the Prophet: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name” (Ps. 102). Secondly, we must ask and wait for that grace which we do not yet possess, from his blessing and assistance. For without his aid we can do no good; and we must not only believe this in the heart but confess it in the face of the Church, according to the saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). This is shown when the bishop fortifies his face with the sign of the cross and says aloud in confession: “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” Thirdly [Col. 0333D], signing the people themselves, he concludes his blessing with the invocation of the Holy Trinity.

The first of these blessings may be called one attributed to the Lord; the second, one returned by the Lord; the third, one distributed among the people. Grace and blessing should indeed be attributed to his name for his gifts, so that we may say with affection and devotion: “Blessed is God in his gifts.” He must also be blessed in all his works, according to the Prophet: “Let all your works give thanks to you, O Lord” (Ps. 144). And as is read in the same psalm: “The Lord is faithful in all his ways, and holy in all his works” (ibid.). He must likewise be blessed in his majesty. The Prophet seems to have preserved this order when he said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone works wonders; and blessed be the name of his majesty for ever” (Ps. [Col. 0334A] 71). For, blessing him for his gifts, he had first said: “Blessed be his name; his name endures before the sun; and all tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him” (ibid.).

But those who thus bless God receive in return God’s abundant blessing: sometimes in an abundance of temporal goods, sometimes in the eminence of outward graces, sometimes in the bestowal of spiritual virtues. The Apostle seems to have commended this last blessing as preferable to the others when he says: “Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Eph. 1). For the other blessings are given alike to good and evil persons—indeed, more often to evil than to good. Yet they must not be hidden or withheld by the good out of envy or avarice, since “he who hides grain shall be cursed by the peoples” [Col. 0334B]; rather, as they have been freely received, so they should piously be freely given and distributed.

A spiritual blessing is distributed by a greater person to lesser persons either by praying for them the goods they do not yet possess, as in what Rebecca’s parents said to her: “May you grow into thousands of thousands, and may your offspring possess the gates of their enemies” (Gen. 24); or by rejoicing with them over goods they already possess, as Raguel said to Tobias: “Blessing be upon you, my son, because you are the son of a good and excellent man” (Tob. 7); or by prophesying, as was Moses’ blessing upon Joseph: “May his land be blessed by the blessing of the Lord, with the fruits of heaven, with dew, and with the deep lying beneath; with the fruits produced by sun and moon; with the summit of the ancient mountains; with the fruits of the everlasting hills [Col. 0334C]; and with the produce of the earth and its fullness” (Deut. 33).

In these words, while preserving their higher mystery, the aforesaid threefold blessing is expressed. From the fruits and dew of heaven, and from the deep lying beneath, blessing proceeds when a person, from the innermost affection of the heart, blesses God for freely bestowed benefits, saying with the Prophet: “I shall cry to God Most High, to God who has done good to me. He sent from heaven and delivered me. God sent his mercy and his truth” (Ps. 56); and through these, like sweetest fruits of heaven, he delivered me. From the fruits of sun and moon a human being is blessed by God when he is heaped with spiritual gifts and temporal goods. But from the summit of the ancient mountains, or from the fruits of the everlasting hills, blessing descends to earth full of produce when subjects are enriched from the sublimity of the life or teaching of orthodox doctors; or when [Col. 0334D] all who are lower and weaker are aided by the merits and prayers of spiritual persons who seek eternal things alone.

Yet certain more sublime mysteries lie hidden in these words, which, if subtly unfolded, will reveal more fully the dignity and glory of the gate of which we speak. Joseph, indeed, plainly prefigured our Lord Jesus Christ, not only by his name but by his sale by his brothers, his rule in Egypt, and his prophetic interpretation of hidden matters; no one can doubt this. His land, however, is the flesh of the immaculate Blessed Virgin Mary, from whom Christ’s flesh proceeded, conceived solely through the Lord’s blessing, by the operation of the Holy Spirit. Moses, wonderfully foreseeing in the Spirit the mysteries of this blessing [Col. 0335A], took care to foretell them still more wonderfully beneath so great a covering of words, saying: “From the fruits and dew of heaven, and from the deep lying beneath,” etc.

The dew of heaven is the grace of the Holy Spirit. A certain emanation, as it were, of the deep lying below is the power of human nature and the animation of animal sense. Made fruitful by these two, the Virgin’s flesh, like good and most excellent soil, brought forth not the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, but the fruit of the tree of life: not to be forbidden to herself, but to be set forth for all. God at once prefigured the mystery of this fruitful generation—that is, Christ’s incarnation—in the first creation of heaven and the deep, and prepared it like fragrant fruits for spiritual persons. Nor was he content to store up these fruits only for his friends, but he also wished to reveal to them the mysteries of Christ and the Church, like fruits produced by [Col. 0335B] sun and moon.

For what else does the Prophet seem to have meant when he says, “The sun was lifted up and the moon stood in its order,” except that, Christ having been lifted up at the Father’s right hand, set at midday as the sun of righteousness, the state of the Church was established and the order of the Christian religion made firm? What else does he mean who says, “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling-place” (Hab. 3), except that, righteousness and peace kissing one another, Christ and the Church, after many heresies, have established the dwelling-place of their habitation in unity of faith? Moses too seems to have scented no other fruits than the outstanding fruits of Christ and the Church, commending them as fruits of sun and moon sweetly fragrant.

[Col. 0335C] To these fruits, for the fullness of blessing, are added the summit of the ancient mountains, the fruits of the everlasting hills, and finally the produce of the earth and its fullness. The ancient mountains are rightly understood as the patriarchs and prophets: mountains, because of the sublimity of their virtue and divine revelation; ancient, because of the incontrovertible and supreme authority of their deeds and sayings. But the most eminent summit of all patriarchal promises and visions, and of all prophetic utterances and revelations, was Christ’s humanity; and their supreme purpose was to announce in words, and foreshadow in figures and enigmas, what they foresaw in the Spirit concerning Christ’s birth, baptism, preaching, burial, resurrection, and glorious ascension into heaven. Desiring to ascend this summit and wishing to see how [Col. 0335D] the bush burned without being consumed, Moses humbly confesses his checked presumption when he reports hearing: “Do not come near here. Take off the sandal from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3).

What, therefore, he could not fully see, he foresaw that many ordinary people would plainly see; and he wished them this blessing—yet without envy. By these words he invited all later generations to embrace so great a sweetness of blessing. He seems also, if not to have tasted beforehand, at least to have scented the fruits of the everlasting hills, which he foresaw would not only be smelled but tasted by the blessed: either when they hear, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25): “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you [Col. 0336A] a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22); or even now, when a person ascends to the lofty heart, so that God may be exalted, and no longer knows Christ according to the flesh, but, clinging to eternity and thereby becoming already in part eternal, knows Christ as God’s Word and God’s Wisdom, consubstantial and coeternal with God; and, according to the Apostle, enjoying God, becomes one spirit with him, so that, like an everlasting hill, he not undeservedly bears incorruptible fruits.

But lest our Joseph should seem to feed only on heavenly and mountainous things, and to rest only among the mountains, he is also said to accept the produce of the earth: whatever fruits are worthy of repentance, and those fuller fruits which are fruits of righteousness. These words could also be expounded otherwise; but since we are hastening toward other matters, we shall run through them briefly, touching rather than explaining them.

[Col. 0336B] Therefore Moses, blessing our Jesus in Joseph (Gen. 49), and in blessing proclaiming his praises beforehand, first traces the anointing of the head, then describes how it was diffused into the members, descending even to the hem of the garment. Foreseeing upon the head an abundance of ointments poured down from heaven beyond his companions, he denotes in the fruits of heaven the heavenly fragrance of Christ’s chastity and the undefiled brightness of his celibacy; in the dew, the sweetness of his most fruitful love; in the deep lying beneath, his submissive and most gentle humility. That our head was fragrant with these choicest ointments at his very rising, and that they flowed down from the head into the members, has been sufficiently shown when the foundations were previously treated. But what were fruits of heaven in the head are called fruits of sun and moon in the members, because what his companions possessed by grace and effort Christ possessed by nature [Col. 0336C].

They are therefore rightly called fruits of sun and moon, since they are possessed changeably under the instability of sun and moon. For Christ’s virtues are steadfastly affirmed to have been established unchangeably above sun and moon. And lest these fruits, so new and unfamiliar, should perhaps seem unripe or perishable, they are presented as coming from the summit of the ancient mountains and from the summit of the everlasting hills. [Col. 0336D] The summit of the ancient mountains was the promise concerning Christ formerly made to the Fathers. Hence the Apostle says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed” (Gal. 3). That the sum and, as it were, summit of all those promises was the one made concerning Christ is proved when he adds: “He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as concerning many, but as concerning one: ‘and to your seed,’ who is Christ” (ibid.).

The Apostle calls this promise a testament, confirmed by God through the Law and the Prophets. For the promise does not come from the Law; rather, the Law was imposed because of transgressions, like a pedagogue, for the confirmation and furtherance of the promise, ordained through angels who performed many great signs to confirm it. Nor was the testimony of the aforesaid promise confirmed only through angels, but also through the sayings of the prophets. For, understanding the promise made concerning Christ and foreseeing it in the Spirit as though already fulfilled, they beheld past and future things as present [Col. 0337A] and obtained a certain likeness of eternity, according to Isaiah’s saying: “Announce to us the things that are to come, and we shall say that you are gods” (Isa. 41). Therefore, as many memorials of Christ’s coming as they left us in their Scriptures, so many exceedingly fragrant fruits, so many everlasting hills, did they produce; and they stored them up for Christ, enclosing them like fruits kept in baskets of figures and enigmas.

For they knew, according to Solomon, that every fruit, new and old, was to be kept for Christ: old fruits, that they might be fulfilled in him, opened through him, and distributed by him, according to the saying, “He gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. 67); but new fruits, that he might always create, sanctify, enliven, bless, and bestow them as good things. The new fruits are those of which the Apostle says that the Lord spoke through the Prophet [Col. 0337B]: “Behold, I shall establish upon the house of Israel a new testament, placing my law in their minds; and no one shall teach his neighbour, saying, ‘Know the Lord.’ For all shall know me, from the greatest to the least” (Heb. 8). “In saying ‘new,’” says the Apostle, “he has made the former old; and that which grows old and ages is near destruction” (Heb. 8).

For when the priesthood was changed, it was necessary that the Law too should be changed; and when the preceding commandment had been set aside because of its weakness and uselessness, since it brought nothing to perfection, a better one had to be introduced, which was promised by oath to endure forever (Heb. 7), as the Prophet says: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” [Col. 0337C] (Ps. 109). Therefore, the things belonging to the new priesthood and testament according to the order of Melchizedek are always good; and, as the priesthood is eternal, so they too were created by God as unchangeably good when he established them according to the power of indestructible life; sanctified when Christ’s death made them efficacious for propitiation; and enlivened because through Christ’s resurrection they were blessed by God not only to receive but also to confer the power of indissoluble life. Hence it is said in the Canon: “You bless and bestow for us”—that is, you bless things that are blessed in themselves, that they may possess this blessing; you bless them that they may confer life upon us.

[Col. 0337D] But lest only the nearer members should seem sprinkled with the head’s ointment, the devout acts and pious affections of simple and ordinary people are also said to belong to the blessing of our Joseph, like humble fruits proceeding from flatter and lower places. Yet because before Christ’s coming these fruits were found only half-full in those who awaited his future advent, the “fullness of the earth” denotes those more fully displayed after his coming by the peoples who believe in him.

Therefore the fullness of this whole manifold blessing—like a heavenly ointment compounded by a heavenly perfumer from diverse spices—has been poured out upon us through the Blessed Virgin, as through a gate brighter than light. Hence the angel called her “blessed among women”: not only because through her Eve’s curse was changed into blessing [Col. 0338A], but also because through her mediation we have merited to receive spiritual blessing from God, and through Jesus have received authority to bless those below us—until at last, at the end, filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, we shall have only to praise and bless the Lord, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117); and, as Elizabeth said to Mary: “Blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1).

For the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day; and, as though on the eighth day of the Resurrection, when the universal Circumcision is completed—so that they neither marry nor are given in marriage, and the function of the sexual member, which was shown in Abraham by the cutting away of the foreskin, is wholly removed from the midst, having meanwhile been kept under discipline—then it shall appear clearer than light to all how blessed, to be adored and praised, is the name of Jesus above every name [Col. 0338B]. Then truly this name will be “poured-out oil,” which, first poured into Mary through the archangel Gabriel, remained shut up within her for seven days, and on the eighth day was not so much poured out by her as revealed. For as yet there were few vessels sufficient to receive such fullness of oil, and the hour had not yet come when, after her husband’s death, she would find many empty vessels on loan, into which the poured oil would increase until it overflowed.

To this day Mary does not cease to pour this oil into empty vessels, and to instil into those who have not experienced it the sweetness of this name, divinely revealed, like the sweetness of milk from a mother’s breasts. And although young maidens anointed with this oil are said to love him exceedingly and to confess that his name is poured-out oil [Col. 0338C], still, while we are away from the Lord on pilgrimage, it must be confessed rather as oil poured in than poured out; and the maidens must be said to run rather in its fragrance than in the ardour of ointment emptied out and of perfected love (Song 1). Nor will this oil cease until the vessels fail, and every wise virgin, with the doors of her conscience opened, redeems herself from her creditor with this oil; thereafter such fullness of oil shall suffice for sustenance and life.

This, O blessed Mary, first flowed to us from your womb and afterward from your mouth. You who, by giving birth, were first to bring forth salvation to the lost world, were also first, by naming him, to disclose the grace of that same salvation. You became the gate for the Saviour of the world as he entered the world; you opened as the gate to the shepherds approaching him. Through you the Magi entered to him with gifts, the star leading and showing the gate. Through you, to this day, all faithful persons approaching him glory in having you as gate, mediator, and teacher. For you introduce them into faith by bearing witness to faith; you are mediator for the forgiveness of believers’ sins by interceding with your Son; you are teacher in finding grace by showing all people examples of life and discipline.

May you deign to be my gate to your Son: first by revealing the mysteries of his Incarnation and of his pilgrim city, then, when I approach the city that reigns and triumphs in heaven after Leah’s bleary eyes, by showing me—not Rachel’s beauty, but yours and your Son’s—with unveiled face, without mirror or enigma (2 Cor. 3). But behold: although, now entering through her into the city of the Lord by the twelfth gate, we seem to have arrived at the city, astonished by the glory, beauty, and dignity of this gate itself, we have exceeded the accustomed measure of discourse. We ask the reader’s pardon if, in yet one further discourse, contemplating this gate’s glory, we delay him a little before the city’s entrance [Col. 0339A]. For afterward nothing more glorious will appear in the whole city, except him who is the foundation and founder of the gate and city itself, the beginning and the end, creator and ruler. May he always be the Alpha and Omega of our discourse, etc.

## TREATISE XII. ON THE GLORY OF THE TWELFTH GATE, THE VIRGIN MARY

Since we are about to speak of the glory of the twelfth gate, and recall to memory the glorious things said concerning it, let us first bring forward Moses, who first removed his sandals in order to write of it; then let us carefully consider, in order, the others who wrote of it, and what each one, according to his office and to the place and time, contributed toward completing the beauty of that gate [Col. 0339B]. Moses first, then, received as it were a measuring rod for measuring the rod, and offered it to mark out the spaces of the gate. Joshua second caused the sun, now declining, to stand still, so that this designation might be more fully completed and more clearly understood. From the Book of Judges Gideon supplied the threshing-floor for building and the fleece for drying out the ground of the threshing-floor before cleansing it (1 Chron. 29). From the Book of Kings David is shown to have supplied an immense abundance of stones, gold, silver, iron, bronze, and timber. Solomon supplied an ivory throne for resting upon (1 Kgs. 10). [Col. 0339C] Hezekiah diverted the water of the upper pool by a watercourse beneath, and caused it to flow into the inner pool of the city, for the use of those at rest or at work (2 Chron. 32). Isaiah portrayed a flower of singular beauty, which would surpass every other carved ornament in adorning the gate (Isa. 11). Jeremiah bought for thirty silver pieces the potter’s field, where all necessary things might be gathered and, when gathered, adapted to the gate’s use; he offered it when purchased for this purpose, as the Lord had appointed him (Jer. 32). Ezekiel saw four wheels, full of eyes all around, ready and movable for carrying and conveying whatever was needed (Ezek. 1).

For brevity’s sake we omit the others: that is, the twelve prophets [Col. 0339D], Daniel, and the others counted among the Hagiographa, all of whom most zealously offered to the work of this gate the best that they were able to offer. We too, according to our small measure, desiring not, I will not say to exalt, but at least to behold from afar the glory of this gate, shall run through, with the Lord’s help, the matters we have briefly touched upon, explaining them still more briefly.

What, then, do we better understand by Moses’ rod (Exod. 3) than the Blessed Virgin Mary: straight in faith, pliant in humility, whole in virginity, concerning whom it is written, “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11)? From this rod came forth that serpent who, lifted up on the cross, prepared, through the sight of him, a remedy for those wounded by the ancient serpent; who finally, having conquered death and, as it were, bound the tail of mortality, restored by his resurrection to the straightness of the rod human nature twisted by many miseries and corruptions. [Col. 0340A] By this rod the Egyptians were afflicted with diverse plagues. Through it was fulfilled that burden concerning Egypt which is read in Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord shall ride upon a swift cloud and enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be shaken, and its heart shall melt within it” (Isa. 19). Through it the children of Israel, delivered from the Egyptians, crossed the sea on dry ground. Through it the waters of the sea were divided, the bitter waters made sweet, and waters struck forth from the rock.

At the touch of this rod the assaults of temptations are divided, when infant thoughts are seized and dashed against Christ the rock. The waters of sacred utterance are also sweetened when the book held in a human hand becomes sweet as honey in the mouth of the one eating it [Col. 0340B]. Waters too are drawn from the rock when, Christ looking upon anyone hardened in sin, tears of compunction are produced, according to the prophetic word: “His spirit shall blow, and the waters shall flow” (Ps. 147). By this rod, wonderfully producing leaves and nuts from itself, Aaron’s priesthood was confirmed and the mystery of the pastoral rod foreshadowed. Moses rightly placed this little rod within the ark of the covenant together with the manna and the tablets, the Holy Spirit foreshadowing that the manna of divine goodness and the knowledge of spiritual teaching would be ministered to us by the Lord through the rod of discipline. The Prophet seems to have desired and requested these three things when he said: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 118).

[Col. 0340C] The form of the pastoral rod likewise presents the same lesson: we are admonished to prick the sluggish with the point of the rod, as with the correction of discipline; to draw back those fleeing, or draw those refusing to come, by the sweetness of teaching, as with its upper hook; and finally to sustain or raise those who fall by the kindness of human compassion, as by a staff. The mystery of this rod is commended to us in many ways in various places of sacred Scripture. For Esther is read to have been strengthened by kissing the tip of the golden rod (Esth. 15); the Lord is promised to rule his subjects with an iron rod (Ps. 2); and “the rod of uprightness” is described as the rod of his kingdom (Ps. 44). We also read that the rod of his strength is to be sent forth from Zion (Ps. 109).

To touch these things briefly rather than expound them: the golden rod is Christ’s uprightness of nature; the iron rod, uprightness of life; the rod of uprightness, uprightness of teaching; and the rod of strength, uprightness of power. Although he could have used this power freely and openly, he chose to hide it beneath the humility of human weakness until, coming for judgment, he should not only strike with the rod of power those who refused correction and conformity to his uprightness, but also most justly crush and confound them with the hammer of final judgment. Yet, lest it be wholly unknown and therefore less feared, he partly made it known to the world by miracles; to hell, more fully, through his despoiling of it; and he will show it to the world most fully and openly by his resurrection, when “from Zion the beauty of his form appears: our God shall come manifestly and shall not be silent. Fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest around him” (Ps. 49) [Col. 0341A].

Meanwhile, the rod of his teaching directs the ignorant; the uprightness of his life, which was inflexible toward sin like an iron rod, corrects and urges the resistant. Although the uprightness of his nature can be called a golden rod because of his royal lineage, or because such an upright human nature was assumed—one as straight as the nature created by the upright God in the first human being—it is more properly called a golden rod especially because of the soul’s incorruptibility. For as the rod of the golden urn was joined in the ark of the covenant, so in Christ’s one person this uprightness was joined to divinity. And the fact that in Jeremiah a rod is joined to an earthenware pot (Jer. 1) [Col. 0341B] seems to signify that in that same person the flesh was joined to the spirit and, like pottery beneath iron, was subject without any opposition from fleshly desire.

But as the iron rod crushes and breaks the resistant, so the golden rod raises those who are crushed and humbled to hope of life and restores the obedient to grace. David rightly calls it iron (Ps. 2), while Jeremiah declares that he sees it awake, because Christ is found neither bent toward fault in anything nor ever asleep, nor even drowsing in the least toward sin. Rather, as the Watcher and Holy One in Daniel commands that the tree be cut down (Dan. 4), so in Jeremiah the waking rod and the boiling pot, and in David the iron rod breaking the potter’s vessel, are attested.

[Col. 0341C] The Blessed Mother of God may likewise be called both a golden and an iron rod. Golden, either because she was born of royal ancestors; or because, as a golden rod, she came forth from Eve, the first mother, as a blossoming rose; or because, full of grace and blessed among women, through the blessed fruit of her womb she is joined, in the flesh of her Son, to divinity. Thus the angel’s words to her, “The Lord is with you” (Luke 1), while common to all the faithful, were special in her case. For God is said to be present in others by grace, but into her he poured the essence of his divinity in such a way that he also united human nature to himself from her. Therefore the phrase “The Lord is with you” (Luke 1) is rightly said of her by antonomasia, since in her he was present not only by grace, but “the fullness of divinity itself dwelt bodily,” as the blessed Apostle says (Col. 2).

[Col. 0341D] Hence he is read to have come forth from her like a bridegroom from his chamber (Ps. 18). For he had previously been in her by grace, as also in the others—indeed, the Angel had testified that she was enriched with grace singularly beyond the others, saying, “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1), as if to say: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov. 31). She herself was more mature than Sarah, wiser than Rebecca, more fruitful than Leah, more pleasing than Rachel, more devout than Hannah, and chaster than Susanna. She is believed to have received in their entirety the fullnesses of grace which the others possessed separately, and to have possessed them continually, without interruption. Or she was called full of grace because she was so filled with the gift of charity—without which every grace is deceptive and beauty vain, without which nothing can be of use—that in this perfection [Col. 0342A] she appeared to have had no equal before her and none to follow her.

The Church, like another Esther, daily kisses the tip of this golden sceptre at the altar (Esth. 15); and by kissing it merits that Haman, in Antichrist, may not long prevail against the people of the saints, and that Mordecai—or rather Peter in Mordecai, or in Peter the bishop of the Roman Church, his paternal cousin—who alone will not bend the knee before Haman, may be found worthy of royal honour. Or, if one prefers to understand the tip of the golden sceptre as the consummation of secular rule and the end of royal power, we may suppose that near the end of the age, once Antichrist has been removed from the midst, such unity will exist between secular and ecclesiastical authority that they will seem to kiss one another, and Mordecai rather than Ahasuerus will rule [Col. 0342B] in the kingdom which Christ will shortly hand over to God the Father.

We also call blessed Mary an iron rod: iron not in showing mercy, but in supporting; not iron in coming to aid, but in bearing aloft. For she is not merely a reed staff, but indeed more than wooden; for as iron exceeds wood in strength, so blessed Mary was endowed from on high with power beyond every human measure, when the Holy Spirit came upon her—that is, descended upon her beyond His customary manner of coming to human beings—and the power of the Most High overshadowed her.

I gladly linger over these rods, which I find placed by the true Jacob in the channels of the Scriptures, that by contemplating them I may conceive spiritual meanings; lest perhaps, by conceiving through carnal desire, that very desire, once it has conceived, should bring forth sin; and lest my Gibeonites bring me not so much the water of compunction (Josh. 9) as fill my loins with delusions by introducing the works of old age, becoming deceivers not merely in name but in fact. Oh, how often I remember having been deceived by the Gibeonites of my imaginings, and, without consulting the mouth of the Lord, having accepted their provisions: so that, when the light of contemplation had set for me, as though some sun of righteousness were declining, I could scarcely at last obtain by unceasing prayers that the sun might stand still over Gibeon; and, if the light of contemplation did not advance, at least that the warmth of devotion might not fail. May my Beloved remain with me, constrained more by [Col. 0342D] the persistence of prayer than delighted by purity of affection.

Alas, then the conceptions of my sheep were late-born. For those of the first season, with Jacob’s aid (Gen. 30), appeared sprinkled with the varied and diverse colours of mystical senses. For then, seeing light in the Lord’s light, I beheld not only the rods mentioned above, but also green poplar rods, almond rods, and plane-tree rods placed in those same channels; and, delighted by such variety, I contemplated in those rods examples of Noah, Daniel, and Job. In Noah, like a plane tree raised beside water in the public places, I admired the straightness of doctrine. In Job, like an almond tree rejoicing in the easy-falling flowers and abundant fruit, I delighted in the rectitude of faith. In Daniel, like a green poplar, I rejoiced in the rectitude of understanding.

Moreover, lest likeness—the mother of satiety—produce some weariness, a fuller variety was added.
