In the peeled and stripped rods, stripped of the garment of worldly care, appeared the whiteness of chastity; in that which had not been peeled, the greenness of humility; and in all, the gentle tenderness of charity, whether toward compassion for one’s neighbour or toward a purer love of God. And that one royal rod which came forth from the root of Jesse brought forth for me all these varieties of rods: she whom David saw standing at the King’s right hand, surrounded with variety (Ps. 44); whom Solomon saw ascending like a column of smoke from spices of myrrh and incense (Song 3); whom Moses saw, like the rod of the bush, burning and not consumed (Exod. 3).

She was rightly seen standing at the King’s right hand, for of the whole mass of human nature corrupted and bent downward in Eve, she alone, and first of all, was able to turn and change Eve’s ill-omened name into that sweet “Ave.” For, wholly abandoning the left hand which Eve had chosen, she turned herself entirely toward the right. Rejecting earthly and carnal pleasures, and laying aside the image of the earthly person, she clothed herself with the image of the heavenly by choosing heavenly and eternal things. The likeness of God in herself—which the first human being, made upright by the upright God, had received in uprightness—she restored, the Holy Spirit repairing in her that same uprightness and most fully renewing a right spirit within her.

Thus she is said to stand upright because she was made so upright; and at the King’s right hand because she became as near to the King as she was conformed to Him. She is also in raiment embroidered with gold [Col. 0343C], because she shines, irradiated like gold by the light of wisdom. Thus John saw her clothed with the sun and having the moon beneath her feet (Rev. 12). She had the moon of human reason as the foundation of natural affection beneath her feet, because her human affections were not carried away by chance or violent impulse, but were governed by the moderation of illumined reason. This was so below, in the course of the present life, like the moon in the night. Above, however, at the right hand of contemplation, she was clothed with the sun as in the day; elsewhere she is described as having been placed in the sun itself, because she not only used the light of wisdom as a garment, but was united with it, placed and founded in it as upon a foundation.

Or she may be said to have been placed in the sun because, just as we make a gnomon project from a sundial so that, extended as it were toward the sun, it may mark the hours of the day by its course, so divine Wisdom established the blessed Virgin as a most straight rod, a gnomon for humankind, so that through her human nature might recognize how far it had fallen away from the light of wisdom and might find in her the path of return to the first point of its origin.

There are twelve hours of the day. To complete its tenth hour divine Wisdom’s sun established human nature, so that, once the nine orders of angels had been illuminated, and humankind had at last been illumined as the tenth hour, it might always return through the Holy Spirit to the Father as to its own principle—thereby completing in itself the perfection of the number twelve: remaining in Him so that there may be no excess; going forth from Him so that there may be no departure; returning to Him so that there may be no approach. From [Col. 0344A] the brightness of so great a light, although humanity had been placed in such honour, it was driven out by the foot of pride and could not stand; compared with senseless beasts, it was cast down from the day of divine brightness into the deepest night of human blindness.

Through this night passed all the beasts of the forest, and from Adam until Mary darkness remained upon the face of the abyss. At last, when the fullness of time had come, the sun of divine Wisdom—who in His own brightness could not be seen by humankind—joined Himself to blessed Mary as to a gnomon of the human clock. From our gnomon He received the shadow of flesh, which He did not possess by His own nature, so that He who could not be seen by us in His own splendour might at least be apprehended in the shadow of our weakness; and so that, according to the Prophet, [Col. 0344B] we might live in such a shadow, or, according to Solomon, sit in the shadow of Him long desired (Song 2).

This is the day which the Lord made by being born of the blessed Virgin, wonderfully completing it by passing through its twelve hours and marking them for us upon our gnomon:

1. The first hour was Christ’s Annunciation.
2. The second, His Nativity.
3. The third, His Circumcision.
4. The fourth, His manifestation.
5. The fifth, His Presentation.
6. The sixth, His flight into Egypt.
7. The seventh, His Baptism.
8. The eighth, the calling of the Apostles.
9. The ninth, the Transfiguration.
10. The tenth, the institution of the new Passover.
11. The eleventh, the Passion.
12. The twelfth, the despoiling of hell.

In this twelfth hour [Col. 0344C] Christ the sun was seen to set and, having been buried, to return to His place—that is, to the earth from which He had taken flesh. Hence this visible sun, terrified, itself appeared to set by withholding its light. Therefore a certain wise man says: “It was no wonder that there was darkness among those above when the Sun had descended to those below” (St Maximus, Homily II for the feast of Easter).

By these twelve hours the day of righteousness was completed, succeeding the day of guilt and preceding the day of glory. Of these days it seems to be written: “After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up” (Hos. 6). Concerning the third—that is, the day of glory—Solomon seems, after speaking of the day of righteousness, to have added: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; there it is born again, circles through the south, and turns toward the north” (Eccl. 1).

For Christ the sun, reborn in the Resurrection when the day of power had been completed, began the day of eternity for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death; indeed, the day of eternity shone upon those wandering in the day of mortality. The first hour of this day was the Resurrection, from which Christ the sun began to return ten lines through the steps by which He had descended. He completed the first line in humanity, appearing to the disciples for forty days and speaking of the kingdom of God. He completed the nine other lines in the nine orders of angels; and thus, circling for ten days from Ascension Day until Pentecost, He is believed to have reached the highest south.

At last He will turn toward the north when, coming for judgment, He first utterly casts down the one who chose the sides of the north; afterward, cleansing His own threshing floor and consigning the chaff to unquenchable fire [Col. 0345A], He will gather the grain into His barns and, handing over the kingdom to God the Father, will appear in a light plainly equal to Him in all things.

Meanwhile, “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest at noon” (Song 1): You who, sending out Your rays from Your south upon the Apostles, enriched them with diverse tongues, and who show us the various adornments of the Queen standing at Your right hand, whether in the variety of rods or in the multitude of stars. For after the other things mentioned above, she was also seen to have on her head a crown of twelve stars (Rev. 12).

I believe this crown to be the glory and honour with which the blessed Virgin is crowned and honoured in the present Church, where she is venerated and glorified, both in herself and in her Son, by twelve feasts, like so many stars. The first of these is the Nativity of the Virgin herself; the second, the Annunciation of her Son; the third, His birth; the fourth, His Circumcision; the fifth, His manifestation through the star. Although the star is described as appearing only at this feast, nevertheless no other feast is known to lack its own star, through which some stage of human salvation is made manifest. The sixth is the feast of Purification; the seventh, eighth, and ninth are the three days of the Passion; the tenth, the Resurrection; the eleventh, the Ascension; the twelfth, her own Assumption.

Or, if one wishes to understand these stars morally, let us call them the twelve virtues which the Apostle enumerates as the fruits of the Spirit: “Charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity” (Gal. 5). By accumulating the merits of these virtues [Col. 0345C], the Virgin is believed to have been crowned by God with their rewards, as with an equal number of stars.

By chastity, indeed, she renounced unlawful desires; by continence, she denied herself superfluities; by modesty, she moderated even necessities; by faith, she looked rather to eternal than to present goods; by gentleness, she made herself companionable; by kindness, generous; by goodness, she preserved simplicity in acts of service, according to the saying, “He who gives, let him give in simplicity” (Rom. 12). By long-suffering she displayed perseverance; by patience in persecutions, that she might not be broken; peace, that she might not be disturbed; joy, that she might not become slothful. Finally, by charity, which is the bond of perfection, she bound together and completed the virtues mentioned above—as precious stones are commonly bound together with gold in a crown—taking care that the brightness of her crown should not be darkened by any private love.

Or, thus: she was chaste in disposition, continent in action. For a person may be continent in action without being chaste in disposition; and may be chaste in disposition without refraining in action, as Abraham is to be believed to have been. She was modest in food and clothing; faithful, without the wrinkle of pretence; gentle, lest she be unapproachable; kind, lest she be inexorable; good, lest she be implacable; long-suffering, lest she be inconstant and changeable; patient, lest she be irascible; peaceable, lest she be perturbable.

By these ten virtues the circle of the crown is completed; perhaps this is the denarius given as wages, once the work is finished, to those labouring in the vineyard of moral action. For as the King’s coin bears His image, so peace, placed in the tenth position [Col. 0346A], makes a human being a child of God and represents in the child the image of the Father, according to the Gospel saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5). Elsewhere the Gospel teaches what this peace is, when it says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). Behold: humility produces this rest; indeed, this peace is nothing other than humility itself.

For what can harm one who emulates goodness? What can disturb a person who thinks lowly of himself, rejoices in lowliness, and glories in injuries and insults inflicted upon him? Thus the teacher of humility, when assailed by insults and torments, could neither be disturbed by insults nor overcome by torture. A good denarius is humility: while attributing all that it is to the supreme Giver, it offers not only a tenth but also the firstfruits of its goods to the supreme Priest, joining the beginning of the crown of the denarius to its end, so that alpha and omega may meet in one.

Chastity holds the beginning of the crown, because through incorruption it makes a human being near to God and like Him; humility completes its end, because it is chastity of soul. Through humility, when God alone is recognized as worthy to be glorified, the human will is disposed toward peace; and not only the image of God but also His likeness is restored in the human being. This crown is perfected in the present life by God’s grace at work and by the human being cooperating with God’s grace; and according to the Prophet it is called “a crown of glory” (Isa. 61).

The things which follow—namely joy and charity—are added like the two hemispheres of a sphere to the circle mentioned above and complete the diadem of the kingdom. Yet in the present life they can scarcely not only be perfected but even be halved. Hence there is said to have been silence in heaven for about half an hour (Rev. 8).

The Prophet calls those days half-days, in which the work is cut off while it is still being begun. Therefore these things, joined together at the top so as to meet in a circle, diverge from one another below and each fittingly occupies its allotted place. Joy, extending from the left toward the right, displays in its hemisphere the knowledge of truth. Charity, extending in its hemisphere from the back toward the face, rises above all the rest; and surpassing the others like the principal spirit [Col. 0346D], it confirms and strengthens them in the love of virtue.

At the summit joy is joined to charity: joy which the knowledge of truth produces, because above, where the soul clings to Christ, it is one spirit with Him. Love itself is knowledge, and there the one supreme virtue is to love what one sees and to see what one loves. Thus through charity the soul is united to the Word, as the crown is united to the jewel from which it is seen to hang entirely. It is therefore rightly called a crown “of precious stone,” not because it is wholly made from the substance of that stone, but because, from the fullness of Christ, the most precious Stone, it is believed to have received whatever preciousness or beauty it possesses.

For from Christ flows into the soul whatever joy it receives from knowledge of truth, and whatever merit it has from love of virtue. From Him comes the joy poured into a human being by contemplation of invisible created being; this joy passes beyond the mire of temporal goods and produces contempt for the world. From Him likewise flows, as an ineffable joy, that which is poured into a human being by contemplation of invisible uncreated being; this joy embraces the right hand and produces contempt of self. This is indicated by the fact that the ark was covered by the mercy-seat, and the mercy-seat by the wings of the cherubim. And just as love for visible creatures is aroused by contemplation of invisible creatures, so, by contemplation of the creative essence, love of one’s own spirit and of all created things is moderated.

Blessed is the soul who has temporal goods beneath her head like the left hand of the Beloved as a pillow, for whom spiritual joy conceived from contemplation of truth produces contempt [Col. 0347B] for all temporal things. Through contempt for all things it prepares leisure, renews zeal for seeking, and unceasingly invites the soul to be still and see how sweet the Lord is. This inquiry, at once so free from business and so busy, begins the hemisphere of spiritual joy from its earthly regions, according to the Prophet’s saying: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Ps. 104).

Hence the perfected soul, taking advantage of the leisure of the bed and the opportunity of nocturnal silence, ascends by seeking and circling toward higher things until, passing beyond itself, it passes into the Beloved. Enjoying Him, it glories that it has found what it sought and determines to hold Him more firmly lest He fly away and escape. But if it hears the voice of the Beloved saying, “Turn your eyes away from me, for they make me fly away” (Song 6), it obeys humbly, though unwillingly. Yet longing to retain the right hand, it meanwhile gives itself wholly to thanksgiving, sweetly pouring forth remembrance of the abundance it has tasted, according to the saying: “The thought of man shall confess to You, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival for You” (Ps. 75).

For thought, at the summit, confesses to the Lord alone; below, recollection is said to celebrate a feast when it delights in giving thanks with many people. This is not joy arising from vanity, from the lust of the eyes, or from the pride of life—the joy of which the Lord said, “The world shall rejoice, but you shall be sorrowful”—but that of which He immediately adds: “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16). It is the joy of which the Prophet says: “The light of Your countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us; You have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4). And elsewhere: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming, they shall come with exultation, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125).

Such sheaves of exultation as we have described are brought forth from the field of pious action by the laborious exercise of spiritual study. Hence the Apostle says: “All discipline for the present does not seem to be joyful but grievous; yet afterward it will yield to those exercised by it the most peaceable fruit” (Heb. 12). We have heard the fruits of joy; let us seek the fruits of charity.

The hemisphere of charity is said to extend from the back to the face. Burdens are placed on the back, and the back is also commonly worn down by whips. Hence the Prophet says: “Sinners have built upon my back” [Col. 0348A] (Ps. 128). Charity extends itself through compassion even to such builders, suffering far more with persecutors than from persecutors. This appears most clearly in St Stephen—to pass over the incomparable charity of Christ, who prayed for His persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23). Not content with praying, He also added an excuse.

Stephen, compassionating his stoners by prayer, reveals the zeal of his compassion by rebuking them with harsh reproof: “Uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7). Therefore whether charity rebukes or entreats, it is shown to carry out the office of compassion. The more it is afflicted by compassion in the depths, as from behind, the more refined and pure it is expanded toward the heights, and the more closely it is fitted to Christ, the supreme cornerstone, who truly became the head of the corner.

But because earthly habitation does not permit the mind, occupied with many thoughts, to remain long there, charity extends itself downward into the face of the flesh, when through congratulation it humbly agrees with those who strive to reach forward: from the back, weeping with those who weep; from the face, rejoicing with those who rejoice. Thus charity, the queen of all virtues, and her sister spiritual joy, seated at the summit, are united in mutual embraces, exchanging kisses ineffable and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Thus they are no longer to be called two, but one enjoyment of the supreme good: truly the end of the commandment, the end of the law, the end of all consummation, the end of labour, and the harbour of rest. If, however, one wishes to interpret this crown morally, we reserve that for the place where we shall take care to adorn the face of this gate with golden crowns.

In all these varieties there is no departure from the simplicity of the Trinity shown in the foundation, since everywhere one Trinity and a threefold unity are found expressed. For, to continue the rest, in the little rod of smoke we have the myrrh of chastity, whose action is mortification; incense of humility, whose action is prayer; and the fire of charity. Set ablaze by this fire, the aforesaid spices emit a most subtle, sweet, and pure smoke, by which stains are cleansed, those who smell it are delighted, and [Col. 0348D] those who behold it are illumined.

Likewise, in the little rod of the bush we have, through its redness, the modest shame of chastity; through its thorns, the humility of continual penitential suffering; through the fire which does not consume, the most sweet ardour of charity. Enkindled by this fire, blessed Virgin Mary never ceases, like a gate of light, to purify, delight, and illumine our city through the smoke [perhaps “flame”] of her most excellent renown: purifying it by her merits, delighting it through her benefits, and illuminating and inflaming it through her examples.

Let these things be said concerning the measuring rod and the standing still of the sun, which Moses (Exod. 4) and Joshua are said to have offered for the glory and adornment of our gate (Josh. 10). Habakkuk seems to have noted both in his canticle when he says: “He stood and measured the earth” (Hab. 3). For where Christ our sun, by dying, measured out the bounds of human mortality, there He truly stood; and, piercing the jaws of Leviathan with the hook of divinity hidden beneath the bait of flesh, He cast out the devil and is shown to have conquered the roaring lion as the Lion of the tribe of Judah.

This same sun also stands for us at this gate, because we who cannot long remain in contemplation of His divinity—hindered by the mass of the body which corrupts and weighs down the soul—rest sweetly in the humility of His humanity. In His deeds and words, as in the rays of the sun, we find the brightness of light and the warmth of devotion, beholding Solomon’s saying: “My Beloved is white and ruddy” (Song 5). And in this vision of the sun we measure ourselves more exactly, when by comparison with His works or inquiry into His words [Col. 0349B], we recognize how far we have advanced toward Him or how far we still stand from Him.

The constraint of now bringing this discourse to its end presses upon us and commands that the remaining matters be passed over briefly.

What else do we understand by Gideon’s fleece (Judg. 6) but blessed Mary, who is known at last to have been given as a covering and adornment to human nature, like the hundredth sheep that had perished by wandering? Into her the dew of divine grace poured itself with such fullness and gentle descent that she was deservedly called “full of grace” by the angel; and through her fullness the whole threshing floor of human nature, which until that time had remained dry and arid, without the moisture of charity, was found drenched.

For whatever spiritual grace the Church spread throughout the whole world receives in its greater or lesser members, it humbly acknowledges that all of it comes to it from the fruitfulness of this fleece, and that the shell of its capacity is filled with dew pressed from the fleece. Thus He who descends like rain upon the fleece set apart this voluntary rain for His inheritance; and by His descent He washed, purified, and dried the fleece from every moisture of carnal desire, in order to wipe clean and cleanse the threshing floor, soaked by such moisture, with the dryness of the fleece—He who bore the iniquities of us all and was afflicted for our crimes.

If one wishes to seek in these things a trace of the proposed Trinity, we have in the fleece, which derives its origin from flesh yet possesses none of flesh’s sensibility, the beauty of human chastity [Col. 0349D]; in the threshing floor, where every height has been levelled when all roughness is turned to flatness, the equality of human humility; and in the rain, the most sweet sweetness of divine charity, which grants beginning, progress, and consummation to human chastity and humility.

But this rain did not come upon the mountains of Gilboa, upon which the Lord rather rains snares, fire, sulphur, and a tempestuous wind (2 Sam. 2). The diligent reader will readily find the same things in the gold, silver, and precious stones prepared by David. If bronze, iron, and cedar wood are added, it will not be incongruous to understand by bronze, which is more enduring than the other metals, that charity which never fails; by iron, which is harder, that chastity which melts under no softness [Col. 0350A]; and by cedar wood, the most patient and unconquerable gentleness of humility.

For Isaiah’s saying, “Instead of bronze I will bring gold; instead of iron, silver; instead of wood, bronze; and instead of stones, iron” (Isa. 60), may suitably be understood as referring in bronze, iron, and wood to the aforesaid virtues insofar as they exist only in action, in place of which God gives those which exist in inward disposition. Nor is Solomon’s saying, spoken in the persons of the angels concerning the blessed Virgin, unsuited to this sense: “What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken for? If she is a wall, let us build upon it silver battlements; if she is a door, let us enclose it with cedar boards” (Song 8).

She was a wall as long as, through humility, she concealed the excellence of her holiness. But because true humility never knows how to be idle, this wall also had silver battlements when she exercised herself in works of piety through charity and shone with the brightness of perpetual chastity. She also became a door, though she had formerly been a wall, when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her: what she had formerly concealed through humility, preserving and pondering it in her heart, she revealed through charity to those found worthy to know it.

This door was also fastened together with cedar boards, because in humility she possessed the flatness of boards, and in the integrity of virginity retained the incorruptible nature of cedar. It is rightly said, “Let us fasten together,” because once these virtues have passed from outward practice into the disposition of the heart, they are found so united with one another [Col. 0350C] that humility or chastity is no longer anything other than charity, and all the other commandments are fulfilled in the one commandment of charity.

It is otherwise with virtues that exist in outward action: now one and now another must be exercised, and the work itself must vary according to place, person, and time. Their outward practice must sometimes be interrupted, so that it may extend itself more widely, according to the saying: “He who lessens activity shall gain wisdom” (Sir. 38). For this reason we too judge that we should rest a little from the labour of writing, so that, refreshed by a brief repose, we may explain more easily the matters remaining.

The ivory throne which first presents itself for description also invites us to pause. Of it we read that “no such work had been made in all the kingdoms” (1 Kgs. 10). We ask the reader’s pardon because, contrary to our promise, we have not brought all the preceding matters to conclusion in one discourse, since we follow the guiding Spirit; and wherever He leads, there too the wheel of our inquiry must follow. For, to confess the truth, while He stands, it stands; while He goes, it goes; and when He is lifted up, it is lifted up with Him. He Himself, moreover, is always alpha and omega, etc.

## TREATISE XIII. DIGRESSION IN WHICH THE AUTHOR LAMENTS JERUSALEM CAPTURED BY THE UNBELIEVING

Since we behold the glorious things gloriously foreseen by David and foretold and prefigured by many kings and prophets concerning the city of the Lord, now more clearly [Col. 0351A] the nearer we gaze; and, touching the thresholds of the twelfth gate, strive to enter through it, we are suddenly struck with amazement by the glory and beauty of that same gate and the excessive radiance of its unfamiliar splendour. Enticed by the wonder of so many varieties, we gladly stop our steps; and, like the queen of Sheba, having no breath left because of excessive astonishment, we cry out: “Not half was told me by the prophets” (1 Kgs. 10). What is seen is incomparably greater than the report which is heard; nor is it now enough to say with the Prophet, “As we have heard, so have we seen” (Ps. 47), but we now behold in the city of the Lord things far greater than we had heard.

But alas, alas! While we begin, we are cut down; and while we hasten to enter into rest, suddenly a violent wind rushes in from the desert region, and our whole city is shaken. The columns and towers themselves tremble; the very foundations seem to totter. The gates of glory are found not so much shut as obstructed. Finally, that very gate of light, whose glory we had shortly before contemplated with such delight—that eastern gate, through which the Dayspring from on high had been accustomed to illuminate His city—hides the rays of its light. With the light of glory removed from the city of the Lord and thick darkness of grief and sorrow gathered, the joy of the tambourine ceases; the sweetness of the harp falls silent; so that our harp seems turned into mourning and our organ into the voice of those who weep.

The laughter with which the whole city was smiling upon us as we entered—alas, alas!—is now mingled with pain; and mourning occupies not only the end but even the very beginning of our joy [Col. 0351C]. Praise no longer fills the gates of our city; it can no longer rightly be called an exultant city, a populous town, full of shouting—unless perhaps it be that cry which was heard in Ramah, the weeping and wailing of Rachel mourning for her children (Matt. 2), or Naomi saying: “Do not call me Naomi, that is, beautiful, but call me Mara, that is, bitter; for the Lord has filled me with bitterness” (Ruth 1).

What other voice should the Church have today than Rachel’s, whose name means “sheep”? Having lost her fruitfulness, and with Naomi’s beauty darkened, she should mourn her ruins and describe them fourfold with Jeremiah. Let her write with an iron stylus and an adamantine point, lest her grief be easily erased or quickly pass away as though momentary. Ever holding her own description before her eyes, let her not spare herself tears, even should her eyelids swell from weeping and her very eyes be covered in dimness, until the Lord—who for the present seems to have forgotten mercy—remembers mercy in His wrath.

First, therefore, let her lament the ruin of earthly Jerusalem, although the ruin of spiritual Jerusalem preceded it; nor could any adversity have harmed the earthly Jerusalem unless iniquity had first held dominion in the spiritual Jerusalem. But because faith today seems dead, and there is now no one who, with the eyes of faith opened, seeks the evidence of things hoped for and not seen, people of our time are moved more by visible than invisible things. They grieve more at being deprived of what they possess than at the loss of what they merely hope for [Col. 0352A], although visible and possessed things are transitory, while unseen and hoped-for things are eternal (2 Cor. 4).

Therefore, in the person of the Church, let us lament the temporal fall of visible Jerusalem—we who have been judged worthy to be members of the Church. If we are true members, we ought to sympathize and grieve with one suffering member of the Church; indeed, we ought to feel no less the force of its pain than the thing that the suffering member itself endures.

We read in the Old Testament that the temple was profaned by Antiochus: the golden altar, the lampstand of light, the table of the Presence, the libation vessels, bowls, golden mortars, the veil, the crowns, the golden ornament on the front of the temple, and all the vessels of the temple were broken up by him. Let us also hear what those stiff-necked people—the Jews—did and said concerning these things. “There was,” says Scripture, “great mourning in Israel. The rulers and elders groaned; young men and virgins grew faint, and the beauty of the women was changed. Every husband took up lamentation, and those who sat upon the marriage-bed mourned. The earth was shaken over its inhabitants, and the whole house of Jacob put on shame” (1 Maccabees 1).

Let us also hear what Mattathias said when he saw the evils Antiochus was inflicting on the people. “Woe is me,” he says. “Why was I born to see the ruin of my people and the ruin of the holy city, and to sit there while it is given into the hands of enemies? Its holy things have fallen into the hands of foreigners; its temple is like an insignificant man. The vessels of its glory [Col. 0352C] have been carried away captive; its elders have been slaughtered in the streets, and its young men have fallen by the sword of enemies. What nation has not inherited its kingdom and seized its spoils? All its adornment has been taken away. She who was free has become a slave. And behold, our holy things, our beauty, and our splendour have been laid waste, and the nations have defiled them. Why then should we still live?” And Mattathias and his sons tore their garments, covered themselves with sackcloth, and mourned greatly (1 Maccabees 2).

If those carnal men, thinking only carnal things and reverencing carnal ceremonies, grieved so inconsolably at the profanation of their holy things, what should Christians do—who serve not in the oldness of the letter but walk in the [Col. 0352D] newness of the Spirit (Romans 7); who have been called not to the bondage of so many and such unbearable ceremonies, but to the freedom of grace; who have received not the spirit of slavery in fear, but the Spirit of adoption, in whom they cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8)? To them the Lord, bringing His word to a brief completion upon earth, established one new commandment of love in place of all those old and burdensome commandments of the Law. This commandment lightened every burden for those who keep it and gently renewed them from the oldness of carnal desire. In place also of the savour of diverse sacrifices, He established one bloodless sacrifice, of which He Himself willed to be both author and consecrator, offering Himself to God for His own as a sacrifice of sweet savour [Col. 0353A] (Ephesians 5).

Nor did He will the sacrifice to differ from the commandment: by offering Himself, He first showed us in Himself that love than which no one has greater (John 15); and He willed that this same love should be shown to Him by us through the same sacrifice. For what else does that sacrifice set before us and proclaim, except that we should love with all our heart and all our strength Him who loved us so greatly that He was willing to die for our sins, leaving not only an example and remembrance of His Passion but also applying a remedy for our weakness? In that sacrament we are not merely urged to imitation, but are also cleansed for sanctification. These are the Holy of Holies of Christians: they can be erased by no antiquity, changed by no variation of times, and defiled by no profanation of enemies.

Yet the inscrutable height of the divine counsel willed to grant Christians certain visible holy things, so that those devoted to visible things, who have not ascended to the invisible Holy of Holies, might behold them visibly and make for themselves a ladder to invisible things. They possess them as evidence for faith, an incentive to love, a sign for remembrance, a cause for veneration, a remedy for sanctification, and finally a secure and common aid against every tribulation. Whoever understands himself understands these holy things: the Lord’s cross and tomb. These were not displayed to Christians only in this last age; in preceding ages they were foreseen and prophesied in many ways and by many means by the patriarchs [Col. 0353C]. Of these, Isaiah says: “His tomb shall be glorious” (Isaiah 11). And elsewhere: “I shall glorify,” he says, “the place of my feet” (Isaiah 60). Habakkuk also says of the Lord’s cross: “Horns are in His hands; there His strength is hidden; death shall go before His face” (Habakkuk 3). And David the prophet: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm 21). Jeremiah also, in the person of the Jews: “Let us put wood into His bread” (Jeremiah 11).

It is clear how greatly Christians venerate those things which even the Jews long beforehand themselves foresaw and foretold with wonder and reverence. Men of my time mourn with me that these holy things have been trampled underfoot in our days. If the Jews mourned the momentary violation of their holy things with such irreparable tears, what consolation can there be for us, who see these our holy things not merely violated but carried away captive?

Behold: the ark of the Lord’s covenant—the ark of the New Testament, namely Christ’s cross, the glory of the Christian people, the medicine of sins, the healing of wounds, the restoration of health—has been carried captive to Damascus. Our ark, I say, does not merely contain in one place the rod, the tablets of the covenant, and manna, enclosed within a small space. Rather, embracing the four quarters of the earth with its four arms, it is throughout the whole world a rod for correction, a book for instruction, and manna for consolation to those who honour it. By it the perverse are corrected, the erring instructed, and the obedient and learned consoled; they possess [Col. 0354A] the golden vessel of spiritual understanding, by which, with all the saints, they comprehend the breadth, length, height, and depth of the cross.

It is not only an ark of mysteries, but also the common ladder of all sinners, through which Christ, King of heaven, has drawn all things to Himself. The two sides of this ladder are the two beams of the cross: contempt for pleasure and contempt for vanity. When questioned with insults and torments, He embraced insults and taught all His own to despise the vanity of glory; refusing to yield to torture, He willed that every carnal pleasure should be renounced. What is happier than this blessed perfection, by which a person, fearing neither humiliation nor hardship—indeed, desiring to suffer such things for Christ—has already ceased both to hope and to fear while enjoying angelic abundance? [Col. 0354B] For he does not hope for prosperity who rejoices in insults, nor does he dread adversity whom adversity either delights or exercises.

Alas, O good cross, all these things have been taken from us together with you! Or rather, to speak more truly: since these your powers were long ago removed from us, we have become barren of your fruits and unworthy even of your dwelling among us. It was not fitting that you should remain for us like a shelter in a vineyard or a hut in a cucumber-field; for, since such structures are usually made to guard fruit, when the fruit is removed they too are abandoned. Who would grant me to have been removed from the midst along with you? Who would grant me, with those new martyrs who defended you, to have given up my life for you and expended my body in your service? O thrice and four times blessed are they who, in following you and defending you, chose rather to fall than to spend their days prosperously without you!

Does Christ not seem in these persons to have come to be crucified again? Indeed, He comes to be crucified anew by the pagans, He who was once crucified by the Jews. Perhaps this was prefigured in the first Passion. For He is read to have been crucified at the third hour by the tongues of the Jews, and at the sixth hour by the hands of the pagans. Therefore the sixth hour of our day appears already to have begun, in which the Lord’s Passion must be completed; and the Son, crying again, “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Psalm 21), may deserve, because of His reverence, to be heard—so that tombs may again be opened, rocks split (Matthew 27), and many of those who had fallen asleep in sin may rise again.

Was it not necessary that the Christian faith, confirmed by the death of the testator and now lying everywhere upon the earth not only dead without works but also rotten and stinking with dead works, should be raised from death by His repeated Passion? Thus that ancient dragon, who was made to be mocked, had to be deceived—the dragon who, having swallowed a river without wonder, was now rejoicing that even the Jordan flowed into his mouth. Thus, yes, Leviathan had to be caught again with a hook: he who was formerly deceived by the bait of the Lord’s flesh and ensnared by the iron of divinity must now, enticed by the bait of the Lord’s cross—that is, of human propitiation—at last feel his jaws pierced by the iron of the divine sentence; and he must not only vomit out those whom he had swallowed, but also lose those whom he had prepared to devour and destroy. For it was [Col. 0355A] divine justice that Christians who, abandoning Christ, had voluntarily subjected themselves to the devil by sinning should also be handed over to him for punishment.

But this justice of God, like a certain iron rod, seems bent and curved, since by His hidden judgment power has been granted to the raging adversary over the Lord’s cross—indeed, over the very consecrator of the cross—so that, having justly received power over Christians, he may deserve to lose it when he abuses against Christ the power he received. Through his ministers he rages anew against Him: Christ’s name is blasphemed disgracefully by pagans; His glorious tomb—alas!—is most shamefully trampled, spat upon, and reviled; and the wood of the saving cross, consecrated in His body and adorned with His members as with pearls, is not only captured, mocked, and dishonoured by all the filth of enemies, but finally even offered to Muhammad, so that Muhammad may be glorified by Christ’s disgrace, and that Muhammad may be wickedly proclaimed by his followers to have triumphed not only over Christians but over Christ Himself.

These things happened not because Muhammad was able, but because Christ willed them—willing to give Christians an opportunity to be zealous for their Lord’s glory, to avenge the Father’s injury, and to reclaim their own inheritance. Behold the acceptable time, in which those who are proved may be made manifest; in which the Lord may test who are His, who are faithful to Him and who faithless, who are alien children and who His own. Faithful soldiers will follow their king [Col. 0355C], promptly expose themselves to enemies for their king, and prefer bravely to die for him rather than preserve their lives by cowardly flight and bring disgrace upon their king. If Christians act so for a mortal king, how much more faithful ought they to be to their heavenly and immortal King?

Conversely, lying alien children will be shown to be children of so great a Father in name alone, not in reality. For alien children, according to the Prophet, “have grown old and limped from their paths” (Psalm 17). The old Adam is earthly, being from the earth; but the new is heavenly, being from heaven (1 Corinthians 15). The new taught that eternal things should be preferred to temporal; the old, abandoning eternal things, chose fleshly and earthly ones. False Christians, becoming imitators of the latter and abandoning Christ’s newness, have put on the old man; and so, having become old and lied to Christ, they have become alien children. Hence they have “limped from their paths” (Psalm 17): weak in carrying out God’s commandments, strong in fulfilling carnal and worldly desires.

Alas! Children honour their fathers according to the flesh and contend even unto death to avenge their father’s injury and preserve a narrow inheritance; they yield neither to words nor blows. But the children of their spiritual Father, wholly degenerate, are shown neither to grieve over their Father’s sufferings nor to be worthy of their paternal inheritance. O truly blessed are those now found to be true children, who do not now deny their Lord or blush for their Father when they behold so grievous a blow dealt Him that truly blessed is whoever is not scandalized by Him.

Yet whatever the occasion for scandal may be, true children are never scandalized, nor do they mock their Father’s shameful condition. Rather, they walk backward, with faces turned away, and cover it with the cloak of a devout interpretation, recognizing that they gave their Father the cause of this drunkenness (Genesis 9). For our crimes, our wicked deeds, have made Him drunk with wormwood, so that after long sleep, long feigned inaction, and a slow waiting for our correction, He seems at last to have awakened like a mighty man overcome with wine (Psalm 77): like a waking rod that may shatter and overturn the cauldron of earthly desire fiercely kindled by the devil. But children are not frightened by their Father’s rod, knowing that “the Lord chastens those whom He loves, and scourges every son whom He receives” (Hebrews 12). Rather, they fear that dreadful threat of the Lord: “My jealousy has departed from you; I shall no longer be angry with you” (Ezekiel 16).

True children prove that it is their Father’s rod and not a judge’s hammer if correction follows the rod and consolation accompanies correction. Thank You, good Jesus, who never cease to perform these three things for Your children. Your children enjoy this privilege and hold this unwavering assurance from Your Father’s promise. For He says through the prophet David: “If My children forsake My law and do not walk in My judgments; if they profane My statutes and do not keep My commandments, I shall visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges. Yet I shall not take away My mercy from him, nor harm My truth; I shall not profane My covenant, nor make void the things that proceed from My lips” (Psalm 88 [89]).

And lest anyone should hesitate over a bare promise, it is strengthened even by an oath: “Once have I sworn by My Holy One: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain for ever; and his throne as the sun before Me, and as the perfect moon for ever. Where then are Your ancient mercies, Lord, which You swore to David in Your truth?” (ibid.). Do You not heed the reproach of Your servants, laid up in the bosom of Your Christ, from the many nations who reproach not only the alteration but even the diminishment—indeed, the emptying—of Your Christ? And if, Lord, You have cast off and despised Your people and delayed Your Christ because of their sins, have You also taken Him away? Have You overthrown the covenant of Your servant, when His sanctuary is seen profaned upon the earth? You have exalted the right hand of those who oppress Him and made all His enemies rejoice. You have turned aside the help of His sword and have not assisted Him in battle. You have destroyed Him (ibid.) in His members: have You done so without cleansing them?

Far be it, Lord—far be it—that in wrath You should not remember mercy, and that so harsh a chastisement of Your children should not be followed by amendment and cleansing, or that consolation should not accompany cleansing. You have shown the Father’s blows to Your children; do not, I pray, forget also to show the Mother’s breasts. Grant, Father of mercies and God of all consolation, that Your children may profit by Your rod and more swiftly rejoice in Your consolation. Bring to fuller completion what You have already begun to do; accomplish, God, what You have begun to work in us.

Behold, through Your working we see in the midst of the earth men who were utterly lost now being cleansed: running to confession, doing penance, making satisfaction for past sins, seeking and promising amendment for the future. Not content with the moderate penance customary to them, they flock from every side toward perfection, putting their hand to mighty deeds, taking up the cross, and, leaving all things, following Christ. Nor do only persons of low estate or middling rank attempt this: the highest also fasten the cross upon themselves—indeed, glory in being fastened to the cross.

We see and testify that the Roman emperor, his son, and nearly all the princes of Germany have done this [Col. 0357B], saying with the Apostle: “What we have seen and heard, and what our hands have handled concerning the word” (2 Timothy 2) “of the cross, this we testify and proclaim to all who shall hear these things.” O good God, how many cries were there sent up to heaven, how many groans, how many sighs drawn forth from the deep, how many tears poured out, with what a rain of tears that land was drenched—you alone, Lord, know, You who alone could perform such things, bringing water again from the rock and leading waters down like rivers! (Psalm 77.)

There one might again see the cross exalted, drawing all things to itself; and, now that the scandal of the cross had been emptied out, one might see not its captivity mourned but its glory proclaimed. Nearly all, great and small alike, having received the cross from our hand, now gloried in the cross alone. What shall I say of the illustrious—and now truly glorious—kings of France and England? What of the princes of both kingdoms, among whom very few remained who had not become standard-bearers of the heavenly King? They must indeed be called standard-bearers, since they first undertook a work so arduous and so praiseworthy. Hence it may deservedly be said of them what is read in the praises of blessed Stephen: if anything distinguishes the martyrs, those are greatest who are known to have been first; yet it especially contributes to the glory of those whose emulation stirred up others and who, in the fragrance of their ointments, cause others, drawn after them, to run to salvation (Song of Songs 1).

What more need be said? Every nation, every rank, every age is encouraged by their example [Col. 0357D] to like deeds. The grain of mustard seems to have grown hot for the threshing; and from that by which the ancient enemy presumed to scandalize the faithful, a more abundant harvest is seen to have arisen; from that source faith, once dead, is known to have revived with greater fervour. This faith is proved all the more glorious and of greater merit before God because no human reasoning furnishes it with evidence. For now, as at the beginning of the Church’s birth, the blind do not see, the lame do not walk, lepers are not cleansed, the deaf do not hear, and the dead do not rise (Matthew 11). Rather, no such signs now appear, so that it may truly be said: “We have not seen our signs; there is no longer a prophet” (Psalm 73 [74]); and: “You do not go forth, O God, with our armies” (Psalm 59 [60]). Therefore those who now have not been scandalized must be called not only blessed [Col. 0358A] but most blessed.

Nevertheless, if anyone has the eyes of faith unveiled, new signs may be seen, all the more welcome because more abundant, all the more worthy because more effective for the salvation of the immortal soul than of the perishable body. For those who were formerly blind to truth, lame in good works, leprous in virtue, deaf to the prompting of the Spirit, and dead to love receive healing not through Christ’s hands, not through touching the hem of His garment, not through the presence of the life-giving wood, but through His shadow alone. Behold, those who did not reverence Him when He was present glory in the shadow of His name alone. What miracle is this, brothers? What else do we see fulfilled in these days than what we heard prophesied long ago? “Renew signs and change wonders. Glorify Your hand and right arm. Raise up the adversary and afflict the enemy” (Ecclesiasticus 36).

Behold, as we have said, we see old signs renewed, ancient wonders changed, and the right hand and arm of the Lord glorified. For the healings bestowed in aid of this present life seemed to belong to the left hand. “In His right hand is length of days; in His left, riches and glory.” Therefore this glorious change is of the right hand of the Most High (Psalm 76 [77]): we see the most vicious made chaste, the fiercest gentle, the proudest humble, the most grasping generous, kings and princes made despisers of the world, and tyrants made martyrs.

Are they not true martyrs who, giving least thought to themselves, their possessions, or their people, do not fear the long desolation of exile; the harshness of the climate; the instability of the stormy sea; the confusion of its roar and waves; the countless perils of road and wilderness; hunger and thirst; or even death itself; who do not fear even to be deprived of burial? This alone troubles them most: that they are compelled to rush upon Christ’s enemies and provoke adversaries against themselves—aspiring no less to the crown of righteousness if they fall than to the palm of victory if they prevail. Does not the Lord’s right hand alone work such mighty power, by which, temporal things being despised, eternal things alone are sought and loved with such longing?

Behold, those who used to glory only in having the left hand of temporal goods under their head now rejoice to embrace the right hand. This left hand raised up the adversary; but behold, the right hand afflicts the enemy. For Saladin’s spirit was puffed up and lifted high by transient and momentary prosperity, because he was especially eager, beyond all pagans, to oppose Christians.

But the means by which this adversary has been lifted up is also, through the working of grace, the means by which the ancient and wicked enemy of humankind is afflicted. Saladin opposes Christians in order to possess their rights; but the devil, pursuing them through Saladin and his other members with wicked hatred, hastens utterly to erase Christ’s name. Therefore he is afflicted all the more sharply because the power of ruling Christians is now being taken from him and countless vessels of captivity are snatched from him. Peoples of diverse languages and nations renounce [Col. 0359A] that most cruel robber; and scarcely anyone is now found among Christians who does not resist tyrannical laws. The impious fury of the despoiled enemy therefore rages, and he seeks new profit because he feels he has lost his ancient right. Already, I think, he regrets this contrivance of his, caught in the snare that he set.

He believed Christians could thus be made headless if, once the Lord’s tomb and cross were profaned and handed to enemies, they could no longer flee to that common refuge of all sinners or turn to that final remedy of the most wicked. But behold, frustrated in this hope and lamenting that the result has turned to the contrary, does he not seem to say in amazement to you, together with his attendants: “O cross, deceiving our joys and bringing forth our losses, why did we show you to Pilate? Why did we hand you over to Saladin? As often as we contrived your disgrace and destruction, so often we experienced your glory and our own injury. As many assailants as we raised against it, it always found defenders all the stronger. The Jew, at our persuasion, even buried it; but when Helena unearthed it, Constantine exalted it wonderfully. Chosroes captured it with our aid; but Heraclius raised it to greater glory. Our pagan people at one time, with our assistance, occupied that whole land, always hateful to us; but Charles came from the West and freed it from its enemies with mighty hand and outstretched arm. Yet when Christians were again driven out, our people were once more defeated and expelled by certain Westerners, far fewer and far inferior to our own.”

“What then are we now to hope or do? Similar events should plainly now be expected, except that our hour seems already to have come: that hour, I say, of which the Crucified One foretold that there would be tribulation so great as had not existed since nations began. There too, introducing Daniel’s prophecy, He said: ‘When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place—let him who reads understand’ (Matthew 24). Therefore, understanding this, let us cause this desolation which we have brought about in the holy place to remain there longer. And if Christians perhaps gather to relieve the desolation of their own people, let us prepare stumbling-blocks for them, construct obstacles, and lay snares. Let us sow disputes and quarrels among them. They may seem for the moment to have escaped our bonds and domination, but they will easily relapse into their habitual condition; nor shall we long endure repulse among them once we set before them, on the one hand, carnal delights, affection for friends, the sweetness of their native soil, abundance of goods, and the pleasures of life, and, on the other, frighten them with dangers of the roads, difficulty of passage, scarcity of provisions, the severity of heat and winter, and the terrible multitude of enemies.”

“Come then, my fellow-soldiers: what are we doing? Why do we delay? Let us go about the earth and walk through it; let us divide regions and kingdoms among ourselves; let us scatter scandals everywhere, stir up dissensions and wars. Let some occupy themselves with Germany, others with France, [Col. 0360A] others with England; and let each attend to those connected with them, whom they know best, whom they have more often deceived, and among whom they have made greater progress in corruption.”

Alas, alas! We are now taught by the events themselves that such things have been said—and even done—by the enemies of the cross. For we see servants of the cross, who had dedicated themselves to the cross and vowed to serve none but Christ, returning to their vomit; and we grieve that they have taken up arms against one another so soon after so recent a vow. Now cross fights against cross, and one crucified person attacks another crucified person. Those who seemed to savour heavenly things alone are proved, behold, to hunger insatiably for earthly things. The injuries inflicted upon Christ by pagans had troubled and stirred them like drunken men; but behold, graver injuries are inflicted by His children. By unbelievers, the cross has been captured as though by enemies of Christ; but by friends and believers, the cross has been most wickedly denied.

Does Christ not seem to say to you again: “If my enemy had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it. But now the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has magnified his treachery against me” (Psalm 54 [55])? Do friends not seem to have magnified their attack? Have they not harmed more than enemies themselves? Are they not convicted of adding iniquity upon iniquity, increasing Christ’s pain beyond the pain of His wounds? Alas! We lately mourned Christ suffering in His members in the East; but now in the West He suffers more detestably from His members. Contrary to the order of nature, members take up arms against members, attack one another, and strike each other down.

Alas, alas, alas! [Col. 0360C] Lord God, how the gold has grown dim; how its finest colour has changed! By Your strength and power it seemed transformed into gold, into refined gold, shining and aflame. O how that gold gleamed; with how many rays it irradiated the world, so that golden ages seemed to have returned! Whichever way one turned, one saw standard-bearers of the cross and found Christ’s martyrs, who lacked nothing for perfection in virtue and desired nothing further than the palm of victory or, in glorious death, the radiance of an unfading crown.

Alas, alas! This golden colour has turned pale, and heavenly gold has changed into bronze. Would that it may not turn into dross, found useful for nothing save to be cast out and trampled underfoot by men! O most valiant soldiers of Christ, you were running well: who has bewitched you? Is it not enough for you to be troublesome to people, unless you are troublesome also to your God? Behold, you have become a spectacle to God, angels, and people—fit to be judged, mocked, and made a show of by all—unless you bring to a still stronger completion what you began so valiantly.

Otherwise the Lord rebukes you through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: “I called my friends, and they deceived me” (Lamentations 1). For the Lord had called you as special friends to the Lamb’s supper, and, invited by a friend, you had kindly assented. Why do you deceive your friend—indeed, why do you deceive yourselves? At the hour of supper He called you, saying, “Behold, all things are ready” (Luke 14), and you seek frivolous excuses? If you say that you do not deny Him but only delay, do you not know that, once the hour of the supper has passed, you will be a burden to your friend rather than an honour? Why do you say to your friend, “Go and return, and tomorrow I shall give to you” (Proverbs 3), when you can give at once?

Do not, I pray, betray your Lord with a kiss; do not obtain a place with Judas the traitor. Judas sinned more by handing over his Lord than Pilate did by killing Him. Likewise, you will now be incomparably worse than Saladin if, regarding Him whom Saladin persecutes as an enemy, you who pledged yourselves as friends are found not merely false but traitors. Do not flatter yourselves by saying, “It is safer to protect one’s own inheritance than to seek another’s.” Rather, expect Judas’s end if you choose Judas’s lot.

For because Judas did not will blessing, he deserved such a curse: “Let his days be few, and let another receive his bishopric. Let his children be orphans and his wife a widow. Let his children be driven about and beg, and be cast out from their dwellings. Let the moneylender search out all his substance, and strangers plunder his labours. Let there be none to help him, nor one to pity his fatherless children. Let his offspring perish; in one generation let his name be blotted out” (Psalm 108 [109]). It is just that the name of those through whom God’s name is blasphemed everywhere should be blotted out in one generation. It is just that their dwelling should become desolate, with none inhabiting their tents: for, seeing Him struck and humbled by God, they added to the pain of His wounds and expelled Him even from the dwelling-places of their hearts.

It is surely fitting that those who preferred affection for wives and children to love of Christ should be denied by the Son of Man before His Father, left without children and wives. It is altogether fitting that their days should be few and their offices or dignities be received by others, since, enticed by the glory of dignities, they preferred the shortness of days to eternity of ages. Let imitators of Judas expect such things along with Judas; and if they shrink from Judas’s name, let them rather shrink from his deeds and avoid so dreadful a curse of Judas. Without delay let them render to their Lord what they so freely and devoutly vowed; let them seek no pretext for their apostasy, knowing that God is not mocked [Col. 0361D], and that there is neither wisdom, counsel, nor strength against the Lord. Therefore, He working and confirming this declaration, whoever apostasizes from this vow, being given over to everlasting reproach, let him be anathema—maran atha (“the Lord comes”).

## TREATISE XIV. ON THE SIGNIFICANCE OF SEPTUAGESIMA, AND ON THE MATTERS READ DURING IT.

[Col. 0362A] The order of the Church’s offices seems to correspond to the order of the human condition; and the things performed in the Church seem to have been prefigured in the first-created humans themselves and in their successors. For the Church’s customary solemn celebration, at the beginning of the year, of Septuagesima, then Sexagesima, likewise Quinquagesima and Quadragesima, appears to correspond to the first four ages. We must investigate with subtle inquiry to which of these they correspond, and what meaning may be drawn from one or another of them; and first let us consider Septuagesima.

For it corresponds with the first age because, when Adam was cast out from Paradise into the changeability of this exile, he seems to have descended from the stability of the number eight to the changeability of the number seven. For, just as solidity of permanence is shown through the number eight, which is a square and solid number, so the instability of the present life is signified through the number seven, by which present time revolves. Septuagesima is therefore fittingly set first, and the things written about the exclusion of the first-created humans from Paradise are rehearsed by being read in the Church, so that, as a person learns from them whence and whither he has come, [Col. 0362B] and whither he must return, he may thereby be admonished. For at the beginning of Septuagesima the book of Genesis is read, in which both the happiness of Paradise and the changeability or mortality of the present life are plainly expressed. It is not only read, but, so that it may be more usefully impressed upon human hearts, the same tragedy is also lamented in song.

And this is done at night, so that the things which possess the more prolonged darkness of night may be illuminated by night-long study, and the night of human ignorance may be enlightened and blindness driven away. But once day has come, the words of the New Testament are set forth, together with those things that correspond to the preceding words of the Old Testament; so that by day we may understand the time of grace, and by night the time of guilt, transgression, and punishment; and from the words of both Testaments [Col. 0362C] may learn how great is their difference and their agreement, so that every word may be established in the mouth of two or three witnesses. The Mass begins from the Old Testament itself; then the Apostle is introduced; thirdly, the Gospel is proclaimed with the reverence due to it. And because that for whose proof witnesses are introduced is important, those admitted to so great a testimony ought likewise to be great.

Therefore, first is produced as a witness the one to whom God bears testimony that He found him a man according to His own heart. Both royal authority and prophetic dignity support him; and, lest he who is first introduced and begins to speak before so great an assembly of the whole Church should offend the ears of his hearers in any way, he comes in the ten-stringed psalter, [Col. 0362D] chanting and blending sweet-sounding songs, and draws all the hearts of those present to himself by sweet melody. Thus, supported by royal authority and upheld by the firmness of prophetic speech, like a burning lamp in a dark place, dispelling the darkness of all uncertainty, he bears witness to the truth, saying: “The sorrows of death encompassed me,” etc. (Ps. XVII).

In these words I seem to behold David as another Janus, embracing, as it were, in one little verse both what precedes and what follows with prophetic vision. For this utterance seems especially fitting alike for Adam departing from Paradise; Cain wandering over the earth; Lamech introducing bigamy; Nimrod, the mighty hunter; Noah tossed amid the waves; Abraham dwelling as a stranger in Egypt; and Moses [Col. 0363A] likewise oppressed in the desert amid the murmurings of his people; indeed, for anyone coming from Adam’s progeny in any of the preceding ages. How aptly it applies to Christ and to every Christian is superfluous to explain. David is therefore rightly introduced first in the Church of the faithful: to him the voice of preceding ages extends, and to him the light of the grace that follows is more clearly disclosed. To him the building of the temple is shown, and the establishment of the kingdom in Solomon is promised; and it is sworn that the kingdom of Christ and of the Church will be propagated from him and prepared for ever.

Paul the Apostle follows, whose praise is declared not by a human being nor through a human being, but by God, where it is said: “This man is for me a chosen vessel, [Col. 0363B] to bear my name before kings and nations” (Acts IX). He is therefore rightly heard out of reverence for him, since the office of bearing witness to God’s own name and carrying His testimony is specially entrusted to him by God Himself. Finally, the Gospel is added, which receives no testimony from a human being; even if He who gave it bears testimony to it, that testimony is true, because He does not bear it alone, but also the Father who sent Him.

We have heard, then, who and what manner of witnesses are introduced; let us now inquire in what they agree. First let us observe wherein the new things agree with the old, and then wherein the new things themselves agree with one another. [Col. 0363C] Blessed Gregory shows how the Gospel of Septuagesima agrees with the first age, or with the nocturnal reading from Genesis itself, saying (Homily X):

> Who more rightly bears the likeness of the householder than our Creator, who governs those whom He created and possesses His elect in this world as a master possesses subjects in his house? He has a vineyard, namely the whole Church, which, from righteous Abel to the last elect person who will be born at the end of the world, has produced as many saints as it has sent forth shoots. This householder, therefore, hires labourers to cultivate His vineyard at early morning, at the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, and the eleventh; because from the beginning of the world to its end He does not cease to gather preachers for the instruction of the faithful people.

Humbly following in His footsteps, we too add that the same householder went out to cultivate the same [Col. 0363D] vineyard at different times and for different reasons. First He went out to plant; second, to prune; third, to dig; fourth, to manure; fifth, to propagate; sixth, to fence it; seventh, when He built a winepress in it, He went out to harvest. And, so that some ears of grain may remain for Ruth the Moabitess to glean, we leave it to the diligent reader to assign these things to each age.

But let us inquire whence or whither God, who is everywhere, may be said to have gone out, and how He, who is always the same, may be said to have gone out. Before the establishment of the world, God remained hidden in Himself, since there was neither anyone to whom He might make Himself known, nor anything through which He might appear. John the Evangelist seems in some fashion to have grasped this [Col. 0364A] in understanding when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John I); as though he said: the Word was in the Father, as begotten by Him, and was with the Father, as hidden in Him. Wishing also to show whence or whither He went forth, he adds: “All things were made through Him” (ibid.).

Thus, by creating invisible things, He made beings to whom He might appear; and by creating visible things, He made that through which He appears. For “the invisible things of God are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world” (Rom. I). Therefore, remaining in Himself as unchangeable truth, He could not be seen in the nakedness and purity in which He is. Accordingly, going forth in a manner from the splendour of His brightness and the unapproachability of His light, and clothing Himself, as it were, in a garment of creatures, He assumed this first garment for Himself in order that He might be seen.

This is said to have happened at the first morning, [Col. 0364B] when it is clear that the sun of righteousness had not yet shone, nor had the morning star arisen in human hearts. For human beings, loving darkness more than light, forsook the Creator and opened their eyes only to the beauty of creatures, as though merely to the radiance of the divine garment; and, abandoning the Maker, they unhappily clung to love of created things. Seeing this, and mercifully wishing to provide for created things, the Creator wove for Himself also a second garment: namely, the wonderful fabric of Holy Scripture, through which truth might present itself not only to the eyes of those who see, but also to the ears of those who hear. He wove this garment for Himself at various times through the ministry of diverse persons, “speaking in many portions and in many ways to the fathers through the prophets”; and He testifies that He Himself also sent not only prophets [Col. 0364C] but wise men and scribes for this purpose (Matt. XXIII).

But human beings divided even this garment among themselves, as they did the other garments, drawing the meaning of Scripture itself in different directions, rending its unified fabric into diverse pieces, not seeking from it the knowledge of God but desiring to glory in its learning. Thus, “claiming to be wise, they became fools; they became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. I). Therefore, seeing that He had still not made sufficient progress, He prepared for Himself a third garment also: namely, the spotless flesh which He ineffably assumed from the undefiled Virgin. By a wondrous and incomprehensible design for healing human weakness, He appeared to humanity [Col. 0364D] in such a form that nothing but He Himself could be either seen or loved in it, and that He could neither be divided nor separated from it. For in this assumption such a union of human and divine nature took place that, once they had been united, neither could be separated from the other.

In this garment of my nature I gaze upon Him without fear, no longer dreading either the wantonness or the rebounding of my eyes. For the beauty of creatures, enticing the eyes of the beholder, delayed them from the knowledge of the Creator rather than drawing them to His love. Likewise, the obscurity of the Scriptures had customarily rebounded upon the eyes of readers rather than enlightening them with the knowledge of God. But now, who would not willingly and patiently look upon God made human, when the Godhead presents itself bodily [Col. 0365A] to human sight and in some manner makes itself tangible by miracles and examples, by words and deeds? O wondrous and incomprehensible depth of the divine counsel! God became human so that, while we know Him visibly, we may be carried away through Him by love of invisible things.

And in this form He went out about the eleventh hour to hire workers for the vineyard. For, seeing that the time of harvest had arrived, He adapted for Himself a garment suited to that work, a garment which, according to the prophet, He wholly stained with that very vintage. But the more soiled He appeared in this garment, the more beautiful and radiant He afterwards shone in His robe (Isa. LXIII).

Let Septuagesima, if you please, be compared with the first hour of the day; this time of grace with the first age of the world; [Col. 0365B] with the operation of nature [lacuna]; and let us see in what they agree or differ. Those who come at the eleventh hour, though they labour for only one hour, nevertheless receive their reward first; and not only first, but as great a reward as those who came at the first hour and bore the burden and heat of the day. This is not from the merit of the labourer but from the grace and good pleasure of the one who hires.

Likewise, those who came in the morning are said not only to have laboured longer, but also more strenuously; yet they seem to have received less reward, since those who come at the eleventh hour taste by harvesting what the others had only set in order, and, as it were, enter into their labours while enjoying the fruit of those labours. For “many kings desired to see what we see and did not [Col. 0365C] see it, and to hear what we hear and did not hear it.” Thanks be to You, Lord Jesus, who have reserved this harvest for us and have reserved us for this harvest, setting before us all fruits, new and old, and making for us a feast of rich marrowed foods, a feast of rich wines, a feast of refined wine.

Since, then, so many benefits are heaped upon us in this time of grace, what does it mean that the Church, according to her usual custom, does not sing *Glory to God in the highest* at this time, when this final age ought, beyond all the others, to offer greater praises to God and to exalt His glory more abundantly? But we must observe that, just as the day on which the householder is said to have gone out into the vineyard is differentiated by different hours, and the body of our mortality by different ages, so it is varied by the divisions of Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, and Quadragesima. [Col. 0365D] And whereas the time of Quadragesima ends within Good Friday, Septuagesima extends to the Saturday in White, where the double *Alleluia* is sung; once Septuagesima is finished, nothing remains except the octave of Easter, called the closed Easter. Thus, just as through the demand of sin the number eight is said to have descended into the number seven, so through the working of grace the number seven seems to return into the number eight.

*Glory to God in the highest* and *Alleluia* are therefore rightly reserved for the end of Quadragesima, when the first Easter begins on Holy Saturday, the second is awaited with joy, and is even sometimes tasted beforehand in the present. What the third, sixth, and ninth hours signify between the first and eleventh hour, Septuagesima, Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, and Quadragesima signify between the beginning and [Col. 0366A] end of Septuagesima. And by as much as the eleventh hour is brighter and warmer than the first, by so much is the end of Septuagesima known to be more festive and more abundant than its beginning.

Seeing this in the Spirit, and wondering at this ordered progress of the Church, Solomon said: “Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle?” (Song VI). She advances from Septuagesima to Sexagesima, and from there rises like the dawn to Quinquagesima. There she is chosen, adorned like the moon, so that in Quadragesima she may be likened to the sun; and finally, made brighter and whiter than the sun, she may appear terrible to her enemies, and may be arrayed against them by angels as an army.

[Col. 0366B] And, applying this to the edification of conduct while preserving the higher mystery, let us say that a person begins Septuagesima when, admonished by the changeability of the present life and the instability of the human condition, he at last returns to himself from the region of unlikeness and resolves firmly to renounce the filth of sins. But because all who desire to live godly lives in Christ suffer persecution, and one who approaches God’s service is warned to prepare his soul for temptation, he must pass to the Sexagesima of labour, lest prolonged rest provide nourishment for vices and thorns of pleasure and indulgence, springing up at the same time, choke the seed of good resolve.

Thus the children of Israel, first wearied in Egypt by mud and brick, at last came to themselves and resolved to leave Egypt. But, as they departed, they immediately experienced the pursuing Egyptians, [Col. 0366C] who shut them in amid the narrow confines between Migdol and the sea. Yet, when the sea was divided, they crossed it on dry ground, saw the Egyptians drowned, and celebrated Quinquagesima on the shore with festive rejoicing.

The Egyptians are habitual carnal sins, sins which have become, as it were, a settled disposition. When people wish to depart from them, these sins strive importunately to pursue and retain them, and hem them in amid many great straits of opposition. If they cry to God with their whole heart, He makes the Red Sea passable for them by dividing it. For the Red Sea is the bitterness of repentance and the redness of shame, arising from confession of sins and the unaccustomed harshness of food and clothing; to those newly converted, [Col. 0366D] it is at first usually seen as unbearable and impassable. But the Lord knows those who are His; and, not permitting His little nursing children to be tempted beyond what they can bear, He provides an outcome with the temptation, so that those things which seemed obstacles begin to be a wall on the right hand and on the left.

They fortify on the right when, in a day of good things, a person does not forget the evils he has endured. They fortify on the left when, in a day of evils, he does not forget the good things he has tasted.
