Thus God, sending forth His mercy and His truth, rescued the tossing soul from among the lion cubs, leading it in a cloud by day and in the light of stars by night; preceding it by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud.

The Prophet seems to have desired this crossing of the Red Sea [Col. 0367A] and the destruction of such pursuers when he said: “See my humiliation and my labour, and forgive all my sins” (Ps. XXIV): the humiliation which I endure from remembering sins, and the labour which I endure from the pain of satisfaction; the sins which do not cease to pursue me as I flee from Egypt to You. Thus the soul, delivered from the slavery of sins, as though from the yoke of the Egyptians after crossing the sea and drowning its mortal enemies, now arms itself also to subdue carnal impulses; and, hastening to reduce its rebellious members to servitude, completes its course by celebrating Quinquagesima.

Thus, after the many resistances of Pharaoh in Egypt, when the resolve to turn aside from evil has been formed and tested by the changeability of Septuagesima and by Egypt’s many plagues; [Col. 0367B] when actual sins have been ended through the laborious struggle of Sexagesima; when the movements of sin have been restrained by mortification of the senses—indeed, when the senses themselves have now been subdued by the exercises of Quinquagesima—what remains except that the person should flee far away and remain in solitude? There, observing Quadragesima on the plain with the children of Israel, he may be refreshed with them by heavenly food; or, with Moses on the mountain, abstaining altogether from every human support, he may deserve to receive tablets inscribed by the divine finger.

These points, I think, are sufficient for the present to recognize wherein the new things agree with the old. Let us now observe in what respects the new things themselves harmonize with one another. For in the production of witnesses, [Col. 0367C] natural reason teaches us to inquire not only who the witnesses are, but also in what the testimonies themselves agree.

The outstanding Apostle, blessed Paul, says: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize?” (1 Cor. IX). Just as the Lord in the Gospel invites the vineyard workers to a denarius, so the Apostle invites those running in the stadium to a prize, and those contending in the contest to a crown. The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance. First comes running; second, fighting; third, cultivating the vineyard. A person must first be trained in the stadium of good action; second, proved in the furnace of tribulation; finally, the soul is fashioned in the renewal of the inward person, which is renewed the more as the outward person is corrupted day by day through the exercises mentioned above. Therefore one first runs through obedience, [Col. 0367D] second fights through patience, and finally is brought into the wine-cellar.

Three things usually hinder runners: weight, a fall, and the length or uncertainty of the course. Therefore, if anyone wishes, in accordance with the Apostle, so to run that he may obtain, let him first be unburdened of every anxiety and love of lower things, so that, thus unburdened, he may hasten toward the prize. But while hastening, let him with all diligence avoid a fall, so that he may continue his course without interruption. And by the persistent practice of continuity, let him set before himself some certain goal, lest, if he runs without a fixed destination, he become exhausted by the length of the course and lack perseverance.

These are the things most necessary to those running in the stadium of obedience: haste, diligence, perseverance. Haste, [Col. 0368A] lest they be sluggish; diligence, lest they be soft and undisciplined; perseverance, lest they be without reward. For the reward is promised to those who persevere, not to those who merely begin; and every praise is said to be enclosed in the end.

Likewise, three things are usually necessary for combatants: skill, by which they know how both to defend themselves against the enemy and to outwit him; strength, by which they can endure the enemy’s blows bravely and weaken him more forcefully; sobriety, lest, weighed down by gluttony or drunkenness when the fight comes, they provoke laughter from their enemies rather than win triumph over the foe. The Apostle seems to have expressed these three things when he says: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in the faith” (1 Pet. V).

Knowing that our adversary is strong, he called him a lion: [Col. 0368B] “the lion, strongest among beasts, fears the encounter of none” (Prov. XXX). Knowing also that he is cunning, he said that he goes about; and knowing finally that he is malicious, he said that he wishes to devour us. Wishing, therefore, to arm and encourage us against such an enemy, he taught us to be strong in faith, so that the strong may bind the strong. He also admonished us to watch, so that the vigilant ingenuity of a watchful person may detect the tricks of a cunning enemy, and thus skill may outwit skill. Finally, he commands us to be sober, so that, when the enemy’s malice finds us fasting and afflicted by hunger, it may have nothing with which to satisfy its own voracity upon us.

But it must be observed and carefully noted that, although the things we have mentioned are plainly necessary for runners and fighters, [Col. 0368C] the Apostle names only two, saying: “Thus I run, not as toward an uncertain goal; thus I fight, not as striking the air, but I chastise my body” (1 Cor. IX), etc. For even if the other things are lacking, these two are sometimes known to suffice. We see even the sluggish and less diligent obtain success through perseverance alone; likewise, the less strong and less cunning overcome the adversary through abstinence alone. Hence he says: “Everyone who contends in the contest abstains from all things” (ibid.).

What he adds, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and the other matters that follow, sends us back to the old things, so that he may prove the new by those prefigurations, and show that the new are the reality of the old, just as the old were the shadow of the new. For what the cloud did for them against the heat, the exercise of good works [Col. 0368D] does for us against the burning of carnal desires; and what the division of the sea did for them, a measured trial of tribulation does for us. And just as they are said to have been baptized under Moses through those two things, so through these we are washed and cleansed under the spirit of fear; and thus, with a clean heart, we pass on to eat spiritual food and drink spiritual drink, Christ the rock ministering to us, according to the Prophet’s words: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. LXXX).

For Christ, the power of God and wisdom of God, is food for the more capable, and those who eat Him will still hunger; He is drink for the less capable, and those who drink Him will still thirst. These remarks on the Apostle’s words seem sufficient, except that something still remains to be said about the prize and the crown. [Col. 0369A] To those who run in the stadium of obedience through zeal for good works, there is customarily given as a prize a certain boldness of security and the pleasant confidence of a good conscience. This is nothing other than that of which the Apostle boasts, saying: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. I).

Likewise, for those who fight in the contest there is laid up a crown of righteousness, which is the consolation of divine joy. Those who mourn are accustomed to receive it unto blessedness, according to the Prophet’s words: “According to the multitude of my sorrows, your consolations made my soul glad” (Ps. XCIII); and the Apostle’s: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Him our consolation also abounds” (2 Cor. I), along with many other sayings of this kind.

Having briefly tasted these things from the Apostolic reading, [Col. 0369B] let us now approach the Gospel vineyard and, in accordance with the Apostle’s counsel, as a good husbandman let us first partake of the fruit of our vineyard. Every righteous person who tends toward perfection is, indeed, a householder. His household consists of the senses of the outward person and the affections of the inward person. A person ought to preside over them as a householder in his house, so that when he says to one, “Go,” it goes, and to another, “Come,” it comes (Matt. VIII).

His vineyard is his own conscience, which remains uncultivated and fruitless so long as it lies neglected and disordered. The vine of this vineyard is virtue, whose branches are all the particular exercises of each virtue. Such branches bear spiritual perceptions as certain clusters of grapes. [Col. 0370C] If these are strongly pressed in the winepress of subtle inquiry and diligent reflection, [Col. 0369C] by means of the screw of strict examination, the wine of sweetest affection is drawn out: wine “which gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII), which bursts old wineskins and preserves new ones by filling them.

Such fruits are described in the book of Wisdom, where it says: “I, like a vine, brought forth the sweetness of fragrance; and my flowers are fruits of honour and uprightness” (Ecclus. XXIV). When it says that it produced fragrance, which proceeds only from a flower, and asserts that its flowers are fruits, it indicates that one whose vineyard has already flowered is by no means without fruit; and it intends to show how delightful the fruits are, if the flowers alone refresh by their scent.

[Col. 0369D] We should certainly observe how great the sweetness of the wine is in tasting, if the power of the flower is so great in scent that every poisonous thing flees at its fragrance alone. The fruits gathered from such a vine are not base, contemptible, or ordinary fruits, for they are said to be fruits of honour and uprightness. They are fruits of honour because by such fruits He is honoured to whom alone belong honour and glory (1 Tim. I); from whom they proceed, and to whom all proclamations of thanksgiving and praise ought to return, so that they may flow forth again. The giver of such fruits, I say, is rightly honoured through them; and through Him, the one who has received is also made honourable.

That is not true uprightness which is not attributed to God’s grace; nor is that praise worthy of God which uprightness does not accompany. The former is judged transitory, the latter flattering. But in the works of wisdom uprightness is said to be without failing (Wis. X). Hence wisdom is said to have completed the labours [Col. 0370A] of the one whom it is said to have made honourable in his labours. Uprightness, therefore, pertains to grace; honour, to glory.

Such are the effects of this vine’s fruits. What the fruits themselves are follows where it says: “I am the mother of fair love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope” (Ecclus. XXIV). Love and knowledge are fruits; fear and hope are the flowers of those fruits. For just as love is the keeping of the laws and charity is said to be the end of the commandment, so “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX). And just as fruit drives out the flower, so perfect charity is accustomed to cast fear out; and likewise knowledge casts out hope. “For what a person sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience” (Rom. VIII). Therefore, to await in hope through patience what we do not see is to tend through the flower of hope toward the fruit of vision.

See whether these flowers are not rightly called fruits, since that which has so flowered seems in some way already to have borne fruit. Observe also how rightly they are called fruits of honour and uprightness. [Col. 0370B] For love is fair when only that which ought to be loved is loved, and is loved in the manner in which it ought to be loved. Amnon, indeed, loved his sister Tamar, whom he ought to have loved, but not in the way he ought to have loved her. You see therefore, I think, how great an uprightness fair love bestows upon a person, and how much honour it attributes to God: through it God is loved above all things, while all other things are loved only for God’s sake or in God.

I confess that the fruits of this vine seemed so delightful that we have strayed far from our subject. Let us now return to the sequence of the Gospel reading.

The householder is said to have gone out at first morning when a person, leaving the active life as though from his own house, and as though from his land and his kindred, strives to transfer himself to the contemplative life. Then first morning dawns upon him when, at the beginning of his watches, truth first shines more clearly upon him. Then sorrow and confession, as certain workers hired for the vineyard, are sent forth. These first work in the vineyard of conscience: sorrow by uprooting and destroying harmful things, saying, “What fruit had I in those things of which I am now ashamed?”; and also by building and planting useful things, saying, “How long, sluggard, will I sleep?” Confession, moreover, works by digging and working upon hidden things, [Col. 0370D] because “the righteous person is the first accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech.”

Then, about the third hour, once truth has become more fully known, zeal and circumspection are sent. These know how to prune and manure: zeal by cutting away superfluities, circumspection by setting before the eyes the baseness both of nature and of guilt, as so much filth. About the sixth and ninth hour, when the sun is now at its height, meditation and prayer are sent to propagate and fence the vineyard. Meditation enlarges the mind by propagating virtues; prayer, so that the propagated virtues may flourish, commends them by supplication to Him who alone gives increase. Finally, about the eleventh hour, when the heat of carnal desire has begun to cool, affection and understanding must be rebuked and invited to harvest.

[Col. 0371A] For these enter into the labours of others and receive by tasting what others perceive by labouring and smelling: affection receives the fruit of fair love, while understanding receives the fruit of knowledge. Others plough, work out their salvation in hope and fear, and seem only to pluck flowers and draw from them the sweetness of fragrance. But these, now established in the reality itself, are intoxicated with the purest wine of wisdom. Hence they are rightly said to have worked one hour, because in the sweet savour of this hundredfold fruit one can scarcely remain even, as it were, half an hour. Thus it is elegantly said by someone: “The hour is slow, and the delay small.”

But the others are said to have borne the burden of the day because there is labour and affliction of spirit there, whereas here there is the completion and end of labour. Yet they too reach the same taste, though late, when, because of such great sweetness, all that is within a person [Col. 0371B] blesses the Lord. And it is rightly said to be paid in the evening, because it is received late. Of this evening it is written in Job: “If I sleep in the sleep of contemplation, I shall say, ‘When shall I arise for the exercise of action?’ and again I shall await the evening” (Job VII) of tranquil contemplation.

This is the hundredfold fruit, reached at last late, after the thirtyfold and sixtyfold, and it is rightly compared to a denarius. For the image of the king is stamped on the denarius. To the King one returns through the grace of contemplation, [Col. 0371C] when the image and likeness according to which the human being was created are restored in him through love and knowledge. For the image consists in knowledge of truth; the likeness, in love of virtue. The steward who distributes this denarius is the spirit of discernment, which subtly considers what is fitting for each person and from whom each should receive what he deserves.

This spirit discovers that, though many are called, few are chosen (Matt. XX), because, though many things are necessary in the present, it recognizes that one thing is sufficient in the future. This one thing is deferred to the evening of the day, and, like the denarius for those labouring in the vineyard, the prize for those running in the stadium, or the crown for those striving in the contest, is reserved until the end of Septuagesima.

## TREATISE XV. ON THE SIGNIFICANCE OF SEXAGESIMA, AND ON THE THINGS READ DURING IT.

With the office of the entering Septuagesima thus concluded, let us now proceed to the office of the following Sexagesima. Since, as we have said, it signifies the toil and pain of tribulations and temptations, fittingly at its beginning there is set forth a psalm in which the Lord is, as it were, awakened from sleep—he who seems to have slept amid so many and such great scourges of his own. These scourges are variously expressed when the same psalm says: “You gave us over like sheep for food, and scattered us among the nations. You sold your people for no price; you made us a reproach to our neighbors, the mockery and derision of those around us. You made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples” (Ps. 43).

Where it says, “You gave us over like sheep for food,” the affliction of the flesh is expressed; for sheep intended for food are kept only for death. Where it says, “You sold your people for no price,” it shows the darkening of their very condition: [Col. 0372A] for when a free person is sold, he is assigned to slavery. In what follows, “You made us a reproach to our neighbors,” etc., it shows that he suffered not only severe losses to his person but also injuries to his reputation; and that he was subjected to examination not only by torments but by insults as well.

Fittingly this psalm is set before those who are tempted, so that, by comparison with such numerous and great tribulations, each tempted person may take comfort in his own troubles. And lest anyone silently reply within himself that those people deserved to suffer such things because they always persisted in rebellion and unbelief, blessed Paul the Apostle is immediately introduced, declared to have labored more not only than they, but than all. Wishing to show how he endured in himself the labors of Sexagesima, he sets before us six tribulations, not merely in his reading but in his own suffering—perhaps with a subtle eye to that saying in Job: “In six tribulations I will deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not touch you” (Job 5).

Besides the mystery of the number six, which is customarily suited to labor and tribulation, there are also six kinds of tribulation by which the saints are daily worn down in the present life. The first is inflicted by the enemy; the Apostle expresses it when he says: “In prisons, in beatings” (2 Cor. 11). There too he testifies that he received from the Jews five times forty lashes less one, was beaten with rods three times, and stoned once. The second is brought about by the event of fortune—or, to speak more canonically, by the changeability of this life—which the Apostle adds when he says: [Col. 0372C] “Three times I suffered shipwreck; a night and a day I was in the depth of the sea. In dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own race,” etc. (ibid.).

Another is that by which the righteous voluntarily afflict themselves, indicated by the Apostle when he says: “In labors and hardships, in many fasts” (ibid.). And because they not only bear the cross outwardly through affliction of the flesh, but also inwardly through the compassion of the mind, he adds: “Besides the things that are outward, my daily pressure: concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (ibid.). The fourth is imposed by the weakness of nature; it is especially shown in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and frequent nearness to death. Hence he also says: “I will boast of the things that belong to my weakness” (ibid.).

[Col. 0372D] The fifth is supplied by the testing of divine chastisement, which is especially wont to be exercised through false brethren, or through unjust prelates, whom the Lord sometimes permits to rule in order to correct and test his people. They are significantly represented by the governor of Damascus, who, it is related, guarded the city in order to seize innocent Paul. The sixth, finally, is that most troublesome suffering which the good endure from the spur of carnal desire. It is perhaps placed last where he says: “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me” (ibid.), because it is finally destroyed with death; and then for the first time comes to pass the saying written: “Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15).

By these six tribulations the righteous are in the present life cleansed, tested, and [Col. 0373A] delivered. They are cleansed for pardon, tested for grace, and delivered for glory, so that they may rightly boast and say with the Prophet: “You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 116), hoping and trusting that in the seventh tribulation the evil of dreadful condemnation will not touch them.

Moreover, what is said at the beginning of the apostolic reading—“You endure it if anyone reduces you to slavery, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you in the face” (2 Cor. 11)—if carefully considered, seems to accord with the things we expressed in the psalm. Let us now therefore approach the Gospel reading and see how it too harmonizes with what has been said.

First, then, we must observe that when a voice comes from the firmament, the cherubim themselves are said to stand still and lower their wings (Ezek. 1). By the two cherubim we rightly understand the prophetic discourse and apostolic word that have preceded, because they seem to contain fullness of knowledge and to surpass all human knowledge. But if the Apostles and Prophets themselves fear at the voice of divine thunder, and, when the voice comes from above the firmament that rises over the heads of the cherubim, humbly lower the wings of their efforts, what should human weakness do where Truth speaks through itself?

For what else is it for the Lord Jesus, the power of God and wisdom of God, to explain the word to his disciples, than to give a voice from the firmament? The firmament, indeed, is his divinity. Thus a voice is given as often as divine things are disclosed to human beings. At this voice the cherubim stand still: there is nowhere further for them to go, because “the friend of the bridegroom stands and rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice.” But when the Bridegroom is silent, the cherubim spread their wings and, extending the investigations of their searching, fail in their effort: they search by searching, crying out with the Prophet, “I remembered God and was delighted, and my spirit failed” (Ps. 76).

Therefore, lowering their eyes from the firmament, they are invited to look toward the propitiatory with faces turned toward each other. The propitiatory is the customary mode of human speech that Christ chose to use in the Gospel. Although by it he seems to adapt himself and condescend to human weakness, beneath it, nevertheless, he is shown to conceal heavenly secrets in the ark of the Gospel and to preserve what is concealed. For there are the tablets of commandments; there the rod of threats; there, in the urn of divine wisdom, as a kind of manna, is the sweetness of promises.

Writing to the Hebrews, the Apostle did not wish to reveal these three things to them, lest he give what is holy to dogs, saying: “Of these things we cannot now speak individually” (Heb. 9). Yet at another time, writing to the Romans, he disclosed them in expounding them, when he said: “For I am not ashamed of the Gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith. The wrath of God also is revealed from heaven against every impiety and injustice of men who hold the truth of God in injustice. For wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, shall be upon every human soul that does evil; but glory and honor and peace upon everyone who does good” (Rom. 2).

Power refers to commandments, because it is no small strength to practice them, and they cannot be fulfilled except by divine power. Hence the Prophet says: “In your favor you bestowed strength upon my beauty; you turned your face from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. 30). Righteousness refers to promises, according to that saying of the Apostle: “I have completed the course; I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness,” etc. (2 Tim. 4). The wrath of God is also revealed from heaven, where no longer a temporal penalty but eternal condemnation is threatened: the Gospel threatens its transgressors no longer with tooth for tooth, eye for eye, bodily death for bodily death, but with the casting of body and soul into Gehenna.

[Col. 0374B] As for the statement that righteousness is revealed “from faith to faith,” it seems to have been said because, just as the faith of earlier persons is proved by the fulfillment of what follows, so too from the reception of present gifts there arises a firm expectation of future ones. Or: from the faith of the One who promises to the faith of the one who believes. For there is no place for distrust where the God who promises is not merely truthful but Truth itself, not merely powerful but omnipotent.

That the things we have mentioned are enclosed in Gospel teaching as in a kind of ark of testimony is shown by the Lord when the Apostles ask what this parable means and he says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables” (Luke 8). It is as if he said: To you it has been given to approach the ark more closely, to know the secrets of the Gospel, and to have, as it were, entrance into the Holy of Holies; while the others remain far off, with a veil set between them, astonished at the horned face of your Moses and unable to endure because of its excessive brilliance.

Let us therefore also strive to approach more closely, to understand more profitably what is said, and to retain firmly in the ark of memory what we understand. He says, then: “The seed is the word of God” (ibid.). For what else does the word of God intend—whether it terrifies by threats or soothes by promises—except that a person receive God’s commandments as a kind of seed through consent, retain them through the attention of diligent study, cherish them through the performance of good works, and strive to make them flourish through contempt of the world and compunction?

“Be in agreement with your adversary while you are with him on the way” (Matt. 5), he says. The word of God opposes us as long as we repel it; but when we consent to it, we receive the seed like earth. Yet we must beware lest that same seed fall beside the way. For the way is a heart through which good and evil thoughts pass indiscriminately, which is bound by no law of discipline, enclosed by no hedge of fear, but, employing a harmful liberty, wanders everywhere in restless curiosity. What seed, I ask, can such a heart retain, when, like a beaten path trampled by demons, it cannot resist their suggestions?

But even if restless curiosity has been overcome by study in reading and watchfulness over oneself, and the seed of God’s word has been firmly retained, the cultivator still ought not yet to be secure, since the thorns of pleasures and the anxieties of riches remain to be uprooted. If, springing up, they are freely allowed to grow, the retained seed is wholly choked. Let the mortification of vigils and fasts, therefore, be set against the desire of the flesh; and let it, like a prophet’s hoe, root out every temptation of the flesh.

Yet even then the cultivator must not rest, since the pride of life remains to be overcome. Unless this is brought low by contempt of the world and the humiliation of compunction, it makes the soil of the heart stony and dry, so that although the seed may now seem rooted, it immediately dries up when the heat of temptation comes. These are the three bands which the Chaldeans set against those approaching God (Job 1); and unless they too set against them, with Jacob, the three bands we have mentioned (Gen. 32), they are easily defeated by them. But the person who, supported by divine help, has fought bravely amid so many temptations will at last receive a hundredfold fruit from his seed.

But perhaps these matters are better reserved for the ensuing Quinquagesima or Quadragesima. For the present, let the fruit of Sexagesima suffice for Sexagesima; and while the aforesaid bands oppose one another, and now these, now those, are separated from the others, let tribulation produce patience in a person. Through patience, as a person learns to rule himself, he begins to possess that very self which he is.

But since we have briefly touched on some matters concerning the ark of testimony, and have said that Gospel teaching is to be compared with it, let us complete what remains on the same [Col. 0375C] subject in order to relieve the weariness of the present Sexagesima.

Once the Gospel has been read and the ark of sanctification has, as it were, been placed in the midst, what remains except that the priest, now drawing nearer, should hear the Lord himself speaking to him from above the propitiatory and from between the two cherubim? Drawing near to the exalted heart, he should see God raised even above the cherubim; and thus, now mingled with the assemblies of the heavenly spirits themselves, desiring always and everywhere to give thanks to God, he should sing with them in one voice: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” etc.

For one who hastens to approach God must transcend not only the cherubim but absolutely every creature, so that, no longer knowing even Christ according to the flesh, he may, by clinging to God, become not merely two in one flesh, but one spirit with him. Where the body of the Church is joined to its Head, the two, I say, are not to be called two, but one flesh; there the lowest things are joined with the highest, earthly things united to heavenly.

What is more delightful than this sight? What bread is sweeter? What better thing can be sought than such refreshment? What more fruitful thing can be found? It is good to go about this ark, this altar, with frequent inquiry, and, sacrificing upon it the victim of a loud cry, to cry aloud with the Psalmist: “Rise, Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification” (Ps. 131).

For this ark is called the ark of sanctification, the ark of testimony, the ark of the covenant. It is called the ark of the covenant because of reconciliation; of testimony because of the incorruptibility of faith; of sanctification because of purity of cleanness. This ark, moreover, is said to have been covered round about with gold on every side (Heb. 9), because Gospel teaching shines everywhere with the splendor of truth. Though it is found divided by four corners, such unity of harmony and solidity of truth is found in it that the two walls seem not so much to meet in one as both to become one.

If it pleases us to investigate these corners more carefully, we may understand by the two walls the strictness of Gospel judgment and the gentleness of dispensation. How they meet in a single corner will become clearly evident upon a more subtle examination of the Gospel. From the rigor of severity it says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). Elsewhere, from the dispensation of mercy: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11); and, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16). And again from the gentleness of mercy: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6).

These walls guard the ark on the eastern and southern sides. For when the Sun of righteousness begins to rise for us, the Gospel commandments must then be observed with all the rigor of strictness. But when he has led us on to the highest perfection, action must be moderated so that contemplation may be expanded; and, once the bow has been broken and the shield and other weapons shattered, we must now be still and see that the Lord is sweet. For “he who is diminished in action will receive wisdom” (Ecclus. 38). You see, unless I am mistaken, how rigor and dispensation meet without distinction in the corner of one harmony.

Since, therefore, the decrees of the commandments occupy the eastern and southern regions, the ordinances of the sacraments hold the western and northern. Some of these are matters of necessity; others of dignity or usefulness. Some are imposed; others are commended. Those that are necessary oppose the setting of sins; those that are useful are set against the northern blasts of the devil. Thus the Gospel is read toward the north, so that from there the enemies of truth, terrified by the voice of divine thunder, may flee away.

These two walls also make a single structure, since they cooperate effectively for human salvation and effect one reconciliation of God and human beings. As for the ark’s having four corners and four rings at the corners, I leave this to be distinguished by the reader’s diligence, for brevity’s sake and to avoid weariness. Yet this must not be passed over: just as harmonious union is signified in the corners, so consummate perfection is signified in the rings. For as a ring is round and equally surrounds one central point, so the perfection of Gospel teaching nowhere strays far from the definition of one simple truth. Thus it possesses the highest harmony in matters that it seems to express variously, and the highest perfection in matters that it commands.

The law of Moses is not so, for it brought no one to perfection, and its gifts and sacrifices could not, as regards conscience, make perfect the worshiper. [Col. 0377A] But the Gospel sacraments heal perfectly, and its commandments justify perfectly. To omit other instances: of the sacrament of baptism it is said, “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16). Of the commandments it is likewise said: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15).

Perhaps the rings are said to be four because, for both the outer and the inner person, the sacraments bring perfect salvation and the commandments perfect justification. In the rings are two poles, by which the ark is either set down to the depths or lifted to the heights. These are devotion and discernment: devotion especially concerns the sacraments, discernment the commandments. The Apostle wished these poles to be enclosed beneath these rings when he said: “May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds” (Phil. 4).

It is as though he said: May the peace of reconciliation between God and human beings, which the Gospel sacraments and commandments effect—and which by its perfection surpasses every angelic and human understanding, so that the end of this ring, as it were, cannot be comprehended by the understanding of a creature—nevertheless enclose and guard your hearts and minds; so that you may refer hearts to devotion and minds to discernment. These poles help one another, because devotion grows from discernment’s understanding, and understanding advances through devotion’s enlargement.

By these also the ark is set down or lifted up. For when these things are entangled with lower matters, the living creatures are seen, as it were, standing, and the wheels likewise upon the earth. But when the living creatures are lifted up, through devotion to desire higher things or through discernment to investigate them, the wheels of Gospel wisdom are lifted up as well. It is rightly compared to wheels, both because of the roundness of its perfection and because of the swiftness of its subtlety.

You see how old things harmonize with old, and are also shown to foretell the new; so that the new and old may rightly be said to be kept in reserve for the beloved. What the rings prefigure in Moses (Exod. 25), the wheels prefigure in Ezekiel (Ezek. 1); what the living creatures prefigure in the latter, the poles prefigure in the former. But what both these and those things signify is presented to us by the grace of the Gospel.

[Col. 0377D] What the four corners are in the ark, the four faces are in the wheel; and these signify in the Gospel the four distinctions mentioned above. Around this ark four bands pitched camp: the first to the east, the second to the south, the third to the west, and the fourth to the north (Num. 2). Nor was the ark raised until the eastern and southern bands set out. Then, after the ark had been raised and was proceeding, the others too set out. What do these things mean except what we see enacted in the Church even today?

First the priest, approaching the altar, turns toward the east, as though about to invite the one who is in the east, that, forgetting what lies behind, it may stretch itself toward what lies before. Then he turns toward the south, that he may summon the southern band also to rise. Then, with the ark now raised, he turns toward the west; and courteously greeting the western band, he urges it to follow, saying, “Let us pray.” And lest perhaps they should be found sluggish, as often happens, he repeats the same thing after the Gospel has been read, as though the ark were now proceeding farther. Then, turning toward the north, he invites the northern band to follow more by his silence than by trumpet-calls.

All these things, examined more carefully, yield no small savor of sweetness. For the sun rises for us whenever the brightness of truth begins to shine upon the eyes of our heart. In such an east dwells the band of spiritual desires. The south is where the aforesaid sun, ascending higher, has grown intensely hot; and there is the band of spiritual joys. When these two bands have gone before, and the affections of hope and joy have now stretched themselves toward what lies ahead, nothing remains except that God should now rise into his rest, with the ark of his sanctification.

For he rises when he lifts us toward higher things and reveals to us the mysteries of Gospel wisdom, bringing us into his chamber—not now, in the appearance of a stranger on the road, interpreting the Scriptures to us, but, our eyes having been opened, making himself known to us within the house of conscience through the breaking of bread. When the ark has thus been lifted up, may affections of grief follow like a western band, and may affections of fear accompany these same affections like a northern band; so that nothing from the past may now please us except to weep for sins committed before, and so that, from the remembrance of past things, we may fear future things too. This fear, however, is aroused in the soul rather by silent reflection than by clamorous voices.

Or, if it pleases you more, let those who are steadfast in virtue be said to be in the east, and those perfect in charity in the south. The priest ought first to turn toward them, so that he may be stirred both by their examples and supported by their prayers. After them the ark is lifted up when spiritual things are compared with spiritual things. But even if in considering these persons one is carried beyond oneself in mind toward God, one must nevertheless be sober also toward lesser people, so that, after day has uttered speech, one may turn even toward those in the west, and, like night to night, declare knowledge to them.

In the west are those who willingly serve some sin; in the north, those who, though unwilling, are still overcome by sin. Let these follow the ark from afar and not presume to mingle with those who have gone before, until, freed from sin through the prayers of the priest himself and the power of the sacrament, and having become servants of God, they may deserve to be incorporated into Christ, “having their fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life.” For such persons God must be entreated by their mediator silently, with a certain reverence of fear and a blush of shame; God who, speaking through the Prophet, declares that he has kept silence, been patient, and wearied himself by enduring such persons.

Once all these preparatory matters have been completed, the priest—now adorned with good actions as with garments of righteousness and with rational contemplations as with splendors of gold and gems—should follow Christ his leader with Peter, James, and John onto a high mountain, apart from the crowd of lower thoughts (Matt. 17). Thus, having heard him speaking with Moses and Elijah, he may now see him transfigured; and, struck with amazement at the splendor of his face and whiteness of his garments, may fall down from every human exaltation. So, brought into the cloud and hearing the Father’s voice, he should strive rather to preserve and ponder in his heart those ineffable words silently and reverently than to report them to others.

Consider the most beautiful connection of the Scriptures and their wonderful harmony of every sweetness. What, we said, is signified in the Old Testament by the ark between the two cherubim is shown in the New Testament by the Gospel between the Psalmist and the Apostle, and also by Christ between Moses and Elijah. And what in the old tabernacle is signified by the cloud covering the ark, in the Church is signified by the smoke of incense swirling about the altar, and in the perfected soul by the bright cloud overshadowing it.

Yet if you wish to distinguish among these clouds according to degrees of religion and holiness, observe that the first was dark, the second fragrant, and the third bright. In the Old Testament, therefore, a cloud of ignorance hid truth from that blind people. Thus the ark did not proceed except when the cloud withdrew, because the religion of ceremonies increased only so far as it was ministered by God to Moses and through Moses to the people.

But in the Church a misty vapor is customarily raised from incense, which is wont to refresh those present by its fragrance. Foreseeing this smoke, the Prophet says: “And the house was filled with smoke” (Isa. 6). What else shall we call this smoke but the vapor of a certain good hope, through which human beings are drawn to the Church as by the fragrance of ointments? Some come to the Church in hope of obtaining pardon, and they are refreshed by good hope; some in hope of obtaining grace, and they become participants in holy hope; some to earn eternal glory, and they rejoice in expectation of blessed hope.

Perhaps it is for this reason that incense is offered three times in the Mass: beginners bring good hope, those advancing bring holy hope, and the perfect bring blessed hope. However varied the vows of those who hope may be, the priest gathers them all, as it were, into one vessel in memory of Christ’s humanity, placing his deeds and words in that vessel like coals; and, placing his whole hope and that of his people in these things, he says to the Lord with the Prophet: “I will enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. 70).

What is it to remember the righteousness of God alone when entering, except at one’s very entrance to the altar to take hold, in the hand of discernment, of the memory of Christ’s deeds as a kind of golden censer, and through it to commend oneself and one’s people to God the Father? At last the cloud of hope passes into the cloud of reality; the smoky cloud into the bright cloud, which does not so much obscure as overshadow. Yet it obscures in relation to human things, enlightens in relation to divine things, and overshadows against adversities.

What is this cloud except divine contemplation, and a certain enjoyment of the divine presence, no longer in hope but in reality itself? It is rightly called a cloud so long as it is apprehended not as it is, but through a mirror and an enigma. For although Christ is recognized by the disciples within the house in the breaking of bread, and is transfigured before them on the mountain; although his face appears like the sun, he is nevertheless not seen as he is, since he incomparably surpasses the sun’s brightness, being “the brightness of eternal light and a certain pure emanation of the glory of almighty God,” and therefore nothing defiled comes upon it.

Having briefly treated these matters on the occasion of Sexagesima, let us now proceed to the chants of Quinquagesima, which begin thus.

## TREATISE XVI. ON QUINQUAGESIMA, AND ON WHAT IS READ IN THE CHURCH DURING IT

“Be to me a God who protects me, and a place of refuge, [Col. 0380B] that you may save me; for you are my firm foundation and my refuge, and for your name’s sake you will be my guide and will nourish me” (Ps. 30).

As we are about to celebrate Quinquagesima, we rightly seek our guide and nourisher, like persons entering a desert who neither know the way nor have provisions. For a desert is a land without roads and without water. In such a vast solitude, what place is there for songs? What cause of joy can there be? Surely the cause that arose when the children of Israel saw the Egyptians dead upon the shore of the sea, and saw the mighty hand that the Lord had exercised against them. Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord and said: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored,” etc., continuing through: “You stretched out your hand, and the earth swallowed them. In your mercy you were a guide to the people whom you redeemed” (Exod. 15). Mary the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, and all the women after her, with timbrels and dances, sang the same refrain.

See: the guide whom they boasted of having, we trust to have in our Quinquagesima not only as guide but also as nourisher. For Quinquagesima, as has been said, signifies fivefold restraint of the senses, by which the Decalogue of the law is fulfilled, and thus Quinquagesima is brought to completion in us. To it we turn after our departure from Egypt, passage through the Red Sea, and forsaking of mortal sins; yet lest we suffer a relapse, let us not neglect to abstain even from lawful things and to subject our senses to servitude.

[Col. 0380D] We know that this has happened to many who, having come as far as Quinquagesima, unwilling to advance further, unhappily returned to Egyptian darkness. Therefore, having come this far, let us proceed with the five prudent virgins and strive to meet the Bridegroom, so that we may please him by the restraint of all the senses, as by a kind of incorrupt virginity.

Virginity is fittingly compared to the desert, because, as the wilderness is desolate and waterless land, so the human body, removed from the pleasures of food—indeed fasting even from things necessary—and human life, inaccessible to strife, contention, every greed, and every iniquity, and waterless through renunciation of drink, luxurious bathing and ointment, and every superfluous moistening, clearly seems to be a desert.

[Col. 0381A] But who can endure the harshness of this desert? Who can explore the trackless ways of so great a wilderness unless he has God as guide and nourisher? Perhaps this is why the foolish virgins are not admitted by the Bridegroom: trusting in their own virginity and integrity of works, they lean upon themselves rather than the Bridegroom. Blessed, however, are those found prudent in this respect: though their lamps shine with splendid works, they never trust in that brightness, but always strive to be supplied with oil and to fill their vessels (Matt. 25).

For this purpose blessed Paul is immediately introduced, saying: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity,” etc. (1 Cor. 13). In Quinquagesima, in the fivefold restraint of the senses, as in a vast and harsh wilderness of bodily mortification, the Apostle wishes to show the way and to offer those wandering through it the guidance of his teaching like a cloud. What the Lord shows to be beneficial for virgins in the Gospel—oil—he shows to be charity for travelers in the wilderness.

Nor without reason did he compare charity to oil. For just as ointment customarily heals, adorns, and soothes, so among the gifts of the Spirit some things aid, some adorn, and some delight. Wishing to distinguish and clearly set forth these things, the Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels.” The tongue of angels is the discourse of wisdom; the tongue of human beings, the discourse of knowledge. In the former there is sound; in the latter, ringing. The former is compared to bronze, the latter to a cymbal.

These gifts of the Spirit adorn the one to whom they are given; and perhaps they are those “varieties of ministries” which the Apostle previously mentioned in the same Epistle (1 Cor. 12). They are ministries because they are bestowed for the manifestation of the Spirit unto usefulness; varieties because they must be ministered in different ways: so that, speaking wisdom among the perfect, we may set forth spiritual things to spiritual persons and, as it were, let day utter speech to day; but by giving milk to little ones to drink, we may teach knowledge to humanity and, as it were, let night declare knowledge to night (Ps. 18).

Then he adds: “If I have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and have all faith, so as to move mountains.” How much these things delight their possessor is unknown to no one, except one wholly lacking the spirit of delights. Perhaps the Apostle calls these “varieties of graces,” either because they are freely given or because they soothe through the poured-out sweetness of grace.

He continues:

> “If I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn.”

Those who have redeemed their sins by mercies to the poor and have received mercy, and those who have obtained renewal of the inner person through mortification of the outer person, know how beneficial and healing these things are. Perhaps these are called “varieties of workings,” because, while the other things can exist in the soul alone, these consist in action alone. But whoever possesses them without charity, they neither confer true being upon him nor avail him for true being. For just as the body derives life from the soul, so these things receive their being from charity; indeed, without charity they should not even be said to exist.

He continues:

Love is patient, is kind. The Apostle has commended love from those features which it has in common with the good and the evil; but here he begins to commend it from those which are proper to the good alone. Wishing to enumerate its benefits more fully, he first gathers them all under a certain twofold summary, and afterwards distinguishes this twofold division by subdividing it. He says, therefore: “Love is patient, is kind.” Patient, in enduring the evils inflicted by others; kind, in repaying good. And because the wicked also in some manner pretend outwardly, in deed, to possess these qualities, he shows that they are rather to be possessed inwardly in disposition, saying: “It is not envious”; it does not grieve at another’s happiness; and if it grieves because it does not itself possess something, it does not grieve because another possesses it, but in a sense rejoices that it possesses it in him. Hence it does not act perversely—which it would undoubtedly do if it strove by word, deed, or any means to deprive him of what he possesses, or at least to prevent his seeming or being believed to possess it. For certain envious persons, believing themselves diminished by the praise they hear bestowed upon others, even if they do not wish those others to lose what they possess, nevertheless do not wish them to possess it or themselves to believe that they possess it, nor do they want others to believe that they possess it. Hence they wish to interpret everything perversely, and by perversely interpreting it they distort it.

But love not only does not envy another’s goods; it is not puffed up by its own. Hence, he says, “It is not inflated.” For it does not attribute to itself what it has; rather, it praises him from whom it has received it, saying: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4). It not only does not impute to itself what it has, but does not endure that it should be imputed to it by others, because it is not ambitious. For just as it does not wish vainly to glory within itself, so neither does it seek glory or boast ambitiously outside itself. It does not seek its own things; nor does it beg outwardly for what it possesses better inwardly, by cleaving to truth. For some, departing from truth, because they do not truly retain it inwardly where they are, begin vainly to seek it outwardly where it is not. But love, always cleaving to truth, just as it does not seek what is not its own, so it can never lack what is its own. For it is a spring of its own, to which no foreign spring communicates.

It is a spring flowing continually through benevolence, [Col. 0382D] yet not overflowing through boastfulness; and, like a turned drinking-bowl, it presents itself as common and equal to all, yet never needs cups, neither envies in others what it does not have, nor seeks from others what it possesses more fully within itself. We have heard how true kindness gushes forth; we have also heard to what height the vein of patience springs. “It is not provoked,” he says: to what greater height can the vein of patience rise? But what can be more divine in a human being than that, when provoked by injuries, one is not angered; when challenged by insults and torture, one not only endures with equanimity, but even despises them, as it were trampling upon them or glorying over them? Thus indeed the Apostle says: “Not only so, but we also glory in tribulations” (Rom. 5). And the apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been deemed worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus [Col. 0383A] (Acts 5).

But whence came this to them? Because love “does not think evil”: it does not suppose that those who inflict such things do so with an evil intention, but rather that they either do not know what they are doing, or that the Lord has commanded them to curse David. Hence love also “does not rejoice over iniquity”: it does not rejoice that one who unjustly inflicts evil upon the innocent should be condemned; but it rejoices together with the truth, by which it is justly ordered that such things occur. And therefore it “bears all things,” because it believes that all things are ordered by God; it “hopes all things” to be recompensed. Hence, by awaiting them long-sufferingly, it endures them.

Behold, love has been commended by the surpassing power of its strength. It is also commended by its permanence. Hence he says: “Love never fails.” For when the other virtues, which now consist in faith and hope, are rendered void upon the arrival of the reality hoped for or believed in, [Col. 0383B] then love will be brought to fuller perfection. Therefore, while faith and hope remain for the present, as certain servants of love—where they exist without love they are of no benefit, but where they serve love they grow like branches from a root—it is plain that the root is incomparably greater than the branches, since the branches both have what they are from it and, when cut off from it, are not even anything at all. The root, however, remains in its integrity without the branches; it is not borne by the branches, but bears them; nothing is contributed to it by them, but whatever is produced in them comes from it.

Behold, lest we wander in a waterless wilderness and, failing to find the way to an inhabited city (Ps. 106 [107]), hunger and thirst, and so, having neither God as protector nor a house of refuge (Ps. 30 [31]), our soul fail within us: the Apostle has shown us the more excellent way of love, [Col. 0383C] which we are to hold.

And perhaps beside this way sits begging that blind man whom the Lord enlightens in the Gospel (Luke 18). For what is it for a blind man to see Jesus, follow him, and glorify him, except to find a way previously unknown? O good Jesus, what light, what joy, what security arises for those newly converted when you first begin to appear to them; when the joy of salvation is poured into them; when the name of Jesus begins to grow sweet to them; and, through the sweetness of this name, formerly sweet but evil affections begin to become bitter, while bitter things are changed into sweetness, so that now with great delight they gladly sing: “The people of the Gentiles who walked in darkness saw a great light; upon those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. 9).

Without doubt this light, this sweetness conceived from Christ’s humanity, is that wood which changed the waters in the wilderness and made them sweet and drinkable. Those three days signify the threefold condition of those making progress. For after conversion, when beginners have begun to advance, the novelty of things commonly brings them into a certain stupefaction of mind. And, as those who have experienced it know, when they are compelled to leave familiar things and apply themselves to unfamiliar things, they are troubled and tossed like a drunken man, and all their wisdom is swallowed up (Ps. 106 [107]). Hence from such stupefaction of disturbance, the soul is shaken by excessive trembling and, as though about to fall at any moment, is hemmed in on every side by fear alone; then, purged by this terror, it begins at last to recognize and grieve over the deficiency which it suffers.

[Col. 0384A] The Prophet appears plainly to have expressed these three things when he says: “They saw and thus were amazed; they were troubled and shaken; trembling seized them. There were pains like those of a woman in labour” (Ps. 47 [48]). Behold, he sets down the first day of astonishment, the second of trembling, the third of sorrow. These are those three days during which blessed Paul, struck down by the Lord on the road and blinded, remained without sight, neither eating nor drinking (Acts 9). After these three days, when the man was now almost failing, Ananias is sent, whose name means “sheep”; he is none other than the Angel of Great Counsel, who “was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer was silent” (Isa. 53). This sheep, after those three days, gave the milk of his humanity to his little ones to drink, and changed the bitterness of contrition, like *Marah*, into the sweetness of milk.

Therefore, what is understood here by the sheep is understood there by the wood; and what the sheep accomplishes here, the wood accomplishes there. This is not the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, but of the knowledge of good alone: the tree of life, the tree planted beside streams of water (Ps. 1), which will send forth its branches toward the moisture of human devotion and will not fear when the heat comes. O sweet wood, bearing sweet nails and a sweet burden: may your memory never depart from my mouth; may the sweetness of devotion to you always flourish in my affection; and thus may the waters of *Marah* become sweet to me, and the tears of contrition the milk of wisdom, however bitter they may previously have been.

For this reason these things are proposed today to the twelve disciples; and because, understanding none of them, they are still outside the way, the blind man calling upon the Son of David is enlightened [Col. 0384C] (Luke 18), and now, taking the road with him, follows him and accompanies him with joy. By this way one comes to Elim, where the Lord’s Passion is no longer revealed privately to the twelve disciples, but twelve open and most limpid springs are found with seventy palm trees. This occurs when Christ now accompanies his own upon the way and, delighting them wonderfully, interprets what is written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. And though their eyes are held so long as they remain outside the house and on the road, nevertheless through the warmth and savour of such discourse they are intoxicated, as it were, by certain delightful streams.

The palms are rightly said to have been with the springs, because then for the first time the victorious mind is crowned with the glory of triumph; [Col. 0384D] and from the testimony of conscience most sweet fruits, as it were dates, are tasted, when, through the revealing anointing of the Spirit, the mind is enlarged unto understanding of the Scriptures. And all this is rightly said to occur in Elim, which is interpreted “ram,” because all these things are supplied by that ram who, although he seemed for a time to have been caught by the horns of his cross in the briars of sins, is nevertheless known to have broken and consumed the bonds of sins, and by the victorious outpouring of his blood to have prepared for us most sweet food and drink—a fact now unknown to no believer.

And rightly twelve springs and seventy palms are said to have existed there, because there were twelve apostles who scattered the teaching of faith and faith in the Trinity through the four quarters of the world. There are likewise seven things promised to the seven churches in the Apocalypse [Col. 0385A] for fulfilment of the Decalogue (Rev. 1), which is victory over sin. Thus the number twelve is aptly assigned to teaching, the number seven to victory, because they receive such things in Elim from the ram. They rightly grow ardent at the words of the stranger upon the way; but they must remember that they are not to remain on the road, but, before night and the countless perils of night overtake them, must hasten to the house of lodging. This house is doubtless reached when one advances by passing from Pentecost to Lent.

## TREATISE XVII. ON LENT, AND ON THOSE THINGS WHICH ARE READ IN THE CHURCH DURING IT

To observe Lent is indeed for transgressors [Col. 0385B] to return to their heart, to examine the innermost secrets of the heart by a searching scrutiny, and, by moderating and ordering disordered and perverse affections, to make crooked, uneven, and rough places into level paths. This is to fulfil the Decalogue of the Law by the four faces, or four wings, of the spiritual creatures. For the four faces of the creatures are the four disordered and ordered affections of the saints, by which they tend toward God and are distinguished from him. The four wings are the four principal virtues by which they fly toward God and are directed by him.

But what is it to pass in this way from Pentecost into Lent, except to come from Elim to the wilderness of Sin, which is interpreted “vessel” or “jar”? We find indeed a jar, but an empty one; we enter a house, [Col. 0385C] but a solitary one, when, intent upon exploring and knowing our inward parts more closely, we find at first sight a heart that is crooked and inscrutable, like a certain uninhabitable and trackless land, a land of thirst and an image of death, a land through which no man has walked and in which no human being has dwelt. Therefore, being about to traverse such a wilderness, explore such a jar, and enter such a house, we compel the Lord to enter and remain with us, saying and repeatedly urging: “Stay with us, Lord, for it is toward evening” (Luke 24).

O how many we know who devoutly observe Pentecost, frequently mortify their members, chastise their body and reduce it to servitude (1 Cor. 9), circumcise their senses, and regulate every movement of the outward person, yet who, neglecting to this day the countenance of their inward person, are like tamarisks in the wilderness. And if perhaps they enter their heart at some time, finding nothing but dryness and a salt land, they immediately fall back into their accustomed ways. Because these do not compel the Lord, by calling upon him, to enter and remain with them, suffering not so much evening as night, they do not merit to see the length of days.

But those who, by observing Pentecost, intend to keep their heart with all vigilance and to taste the fruits of life which proceed from such a vine, trusting in the Lord’s help and grace, and as though now certain of his promise, sing gloriously: “He called upon me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation,” etc. (Ps. 90 [91]). For to invoke is to call inwardly; and those alone truly invoke God who, cleansing the eyes of the inward person, desire to see God and to worship him who is Spirit in spirit and truth (John 4). To such persons—that is, to pure eyes—God, revealing his face in the lodging-place of a good conscience, shows himself in the breaking of bread.

I believe that the same thing was prefigured by the manna first sent to the children of Israel in the wilderness of Sin. For what is manna but the sweetness of divine knowledge, which possesses, with fine flour, the honey-sweetness of devotion, and, with coriander seed, the whiteness of spiritual understanding? It is aptly called manna because what it is can be wondered at more than expressed. And it is indeed first gathered in the wilderness of Sin, not because those who are intent upon taming and subjugating the outward senses do not also taste the sweetness of divine contemplation, [Col. 0386B] but because they do not taste it unto satisfaction or endurance. For to them that hour is slow and the stay short. But to pure hearts it is given unto satisfaction—as the Prophet hoped when he said, “I shall be satisfied when your glory has appeared” (Ps. 16 [17])—and unto endurance, as the same Prophet had experienced when he said, “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93 [94]). For those who have altogether renounced human consolations ought not, and cannot, be without divine consolations.

For this reason, in Lent, apart from the course and custom of other times, new offices are sung daily, so that from the daily Introit and the daily reading of the Old Testament and Gospel, manna of unusual sweetness may be gathered. Nor should manna for one day be stored for another, lest someone, doubting the Lord’s grace, despair of it, or, trusting in his own ingenuity, be confident that he will find this manna. Otherwise it will begin rather to rot and to swarm with foul worms. For that which was first felt as sweet and living appears to rot and swarm with worms when the living and efficacious word of the Lord, which is felt through the infusion of grace and is more penetrating than any two-edged sword (Heb. 4), having been presumptuously taken hold of by human cleverness, begins to be treated with disgust and to swarm, as it were, with worm-like questions.

For as many questions as are raised, so many worms seem to arise. But the fact that no manna was gathered on the Sabbath must by no means be understood to mean that the Sabbath of spiritual rest lacks the manna of divine consolation, [Col. 0386D] on which manna is especially accustomed to abound. Rather, it means that there is no longer labour in gathering where what is desired is ready at hand; nor is there toil over the figure where the truth is present; nor is the shadow anxiously sought where the reality is possessed with delight. Perhaps this is also signified by the fact that no proper office is assigned to the Thursday of Lent. For on that day not only was the form of the sacraments, but Christ’s very body itself, first delivered to the disciples; and that day, irradiated by the splendour of truth itself, requires no other aids, lest the Church seem to labour in superfluous expenditure if she attempted to assist the sun with torches.

The Lord appears to promise this manna through the Prophet to one entering Lent, as is added in the verse mentioned above: “I will glorify him; I will satisfy him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation” (Ps. 90 [91]). For he glorifies the one whom he causes to glory in the testimony of conscience; and, lest the joy of this testimony seem momentary, he promises length of days as well. This he is accustomed to grant not only in eternity but also in the present life, when the shadows decline and the night of ignorance expires, and the day of grace begins to breathe forth—not now a wintry, rainy, and brief day, but a summer day, bright and long. Therefore, lest these longer days seem less healthful and unbearable, it is added: “I will show him my salvation.” The Prophet desired the manna of such a vision when he said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Ps. 50 [51]).

Behold how great and pleasant are the things promised. [Col. 0387B] Yet the things promised must be carefully weighed: “I am with him in tribulation, and I will deliver him” (Ps. 90 [91]). For “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom” (Acts 14); and no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully (2 Tim. 2). Discipline, according to the Apostle, does not at first seem to bring joy but sorrow; afterwards, however, it yields most peaceful fruits to those trained by it (Heb. 12). A reading from the Apostle consonant with this is then added, saying: “We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 6). This is that grace of which the same Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “God offers himself to you as to sons” (Heb. 12).

There he has shown, from what precedes, what paternal grace he wishes us to understand that God offers to his children, saying: “Consider him who endured such things,” etc.; “he scourges every son whom he receives” (ibid.). This is the grace of a father toward a son: that he scourges the one whom he loves, and that in a son scourged and chastened, or proved, the father is, as it were, pleased with himself. Some regard this discipline of the father not as grace but as wrath, and avoid it by every means they can; or, if they cannot avoid it, they kick against it with murmuring, becoming alien children, who confess to the Lord when he does them good (Ps. 48 [49]), but who are proved false in the time of temptation, though they seemed to believe in prosperity.

Some receive it patiently and endure it with strong devotion; but because they are given over to outward things and do not seek the grace of inward consolation, they run as though uncertainly and, as it were, in vain. [Col. 0387D] For whoever, like a foolish virgin, is outwardly afflicted but does not store oil inwardly in the vessel, experiences the failure of his lamp (Matt. 25), like an empty but sealed vessel. But he does not receive this grace in vain who, making progress through tribulation, is worthy to say with the Prophet: “In tribulation you have enlarged me” (Ps. 4), and: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93 [94]); and with the Apostle: “As the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (2 Cor. 1); and: “Blessed be God, who consoles us in all our tribulation” (ibid.).

The Lord also promises this consolation to those who mourn in the Gospel; the Apostle exhorts us to seek it, as though saying: I can urge you toward it, but I cannot give it. Rather, I send you to him who says: “He cried to me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation; I will deliver him and glorify him” (Ps. 90 [91]). For he who says this through the Psalmist is the same one who said through another prophet: “In an acceptable time I have heard you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you” (Isa. 49). I heard you when you were failing away from me and crying to me; I helped you as you laboured, lifting your eyes not to the mountains but to me, a helper in fitting times, in tribulation. For anyone who is striving and making progress needs to be heard in order to obtain pardon, and helped in order to find grace.

For this reason the Lenten season is called an acceptable time and a day of salvation (2 Cor. 6): acceptable [Col. 0388B] for sinners, to obtain pardon for sins and to destroy the kingdom of vices; a day of salvation, to merit the grace of good works and receive the glory of rewards. For “the Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83 [84]). Therefore let those who seek such things give offence to no one; let them become a stumbling-block or rock of scandal to no one (1 Pet. 2). Let them not become an occasion of stumbling to the weak through their example, nor a scandal to the stronger by seeking things above themselves or presuming things too strong for them. Let them beware of scandalizing the little ones; let them beware of hindering the robust; so that, according to blessed Benedict, the strong may have what they desire and the weak may not flee away, lest our ministry be blamed (2 Cor. 6).

And because it is not enough to turn away from evil, to avoid reproach from one’s neighbour, and to preserve one’s reputation before one’s neighbour, the Apostle admonishes us to present a pure conscience to God, saying: “But in all things let us present ourselves as ministers of God” (ibid.). If we cannot minister temporal things to others, we can offer ourselves as a sacrifice to God, according to the words: “In me, O God, are your vows” (Ps. 55 [56]); “With me is prayer to the God of my life” (Ps. 41 [42]); and: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. I will fulfil my vows to the Lord” (Ps. 115 [116]). We drink this cup either when we ourselves impose hard things upon ourselves by mortifying our members, or when we endure with equanimity injuries inflicted upon us by others.

Wishing to distinguish these, the Apostle first sets forth what is inflicted by others: necessities concerning food and clothing, distresses of fear and loneliness, [Col. 0388D] beatings, imprisonments, and riots raised against us. Patience amid these things is rightly called great, because “many are the tribulations of the righteous.” Hence: “You have shown me many and grievous tribulations” (Ps. 70 [71]). Then he sets forth those things which we impose upon ourselves, voluntarily sacrificing to the Lord: the labours of the hands, fasts, and vigils. And because bodily exercise is useful for little, lest we place the anchor of our hope in it, the Apostle sends us, after the aforesaid labours, to the renewal of the inward person to be achieved through outward exercise, saying: “In chastity,” which is of the heart just as continence is of the flesh; “in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in the word of truth, in the power of God” (2 Cor. 6).

These are the fruits of the Spirit, gathered from the vineyard of a good conscience; this is the hidden manna, which no one knows except the one who receives it. But the one who receives it has not received his soul in vain, has not run in vain, nor received the grace of God in vain (ibid.).

There is also to be observed in these words of the Apostle a certain distinction among the virtues of the inward person. For virtues are possessed one way on the journey and another way in the homeland. On the journey they are held with labour and interruption; in the homeland, without difficulty or change. The same Apostle calls these the virtues of the age to come, and asserts that even in the present they are possessed rather than merely tasted. He first sets down, therefore, the virtues of the journey, saying: “In chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering.”

True chastity of the soul is to cleave above every creature to the Word, according to the saying: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication by departing from you. But for me, it is good to cleave to God” (Ps. 72 [73]). For the one who cleaves in love to any thing for its own sake—not for God, but apart from God—commits fornication away from God. But knowledge is necessary for guarding this blessed chastity, so that such a person may know how to reject evil and choose good (Isa. 7). If, in his judgment, he calls good evil and evil good, then undoubtedly, being unable to choose between them through ignorance, he will fall away from the aforesaid chastity, approving true evil rather than rejecting it and disdaining true good rather than choosing it. Thus, falling from the highest good to a lesser good—and since to one who knows the good and does not do it, it is sin—long-suffering is also necessary, lest a person, overcome by faint-heartedness, condemn himself in that which he approves by discernment.

To attain these things, the spiritual soul must seek God the Word: by consenting to him for correction, it is made chaste; enlightened by him, it is filled with knowledge for reflection; leaning upon him, it is made strong unto long-suffering. But, wishing also to distinguish by adding the virtues of the age to come, the Apostle first says: “In kindness, in the Holy Spirit” (2 Cor. 6). For there is a pleasantness of this present life, of which it is written that wisdom is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly (Job 28). Such pleasantness of dying flies tends rather to destroy the sweetness of spiritual ointment. But the pleasantness which is in the Holy Spirit, like an anointing teaching concerning all things, heals every weakness and drives out every weariness and every bitterness.

And he subdivides further, to express in what—or rather in whom—this pleasantness consists, saying: “In unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God.” Unfeigned and unmade love is the Holy Spirit himself. He is the author in us of our love; he is its maker—or rather its former—who alone knows our formation.

Or perhaps our love, which is possessed on the journey, is rightly called “feigned,” because now we see through a mirror in an enigma, and it is rather a shadow of that love which will exist in the homeland than the reality. Therefore, what will exist in the homeland can be desired and tasted beforehand on the journey, but can by no means be possessed. Likewise, the word of truth—indeed, the Word who is truth—is seen and heard on the journey in the guise of a stranger, [Col. 0390A] but in the homeland will be known as he is. There too, blessed persons enjoy the power of God—indeed, enjoy God as power—not now ascending from strength to strength, but cleaving to the one supreme and unchangeable Power, made incorruptible and impassible through participation in him.

Therefore there is there one supreme Power, God: he himself is power, he himself truth, he himself the way, he himself all things, and God in all things. He is power for might, truth for knowledge, life for joy. And while there, in the blessed life, all blessed spirits are satisfied by the appearing glory of the Lord, here meanwhile these same things are only tasted beforehand, with difficulty and fleetingly. For here power is perfected in weakness. Here one ascends from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion. Here Jacob wrestles with the angel and, after [Col. 0390B] a long struggle, scarcely at last merits a blessing.
