Having thereby become strong against God and men, and even distinguished by the name Israel, then he began and learned to fail from himself and to become weak within himself. For the more anyone begins to lean upon his beloved, the more, deprived of the footing of human strength, he feels himself, as it were, to limp. But the more the outward person is corrupted, the more the inward person is renewed day by day and clothed more and more with power from on high.

In this manner, according to the Apostle, a person presents himself as a minister of God: first amid tribulations through much patience; then in spiritual sweetness through the overflowing fragrance of fervour and devotion. But it often happens that those whom adversity does not cast down, nor prosperity lift up, are nevertheless troubled by frequent alternations of circumstances and shifting reversals. Hence in Ezekiel the king of Babylon is said to sit at a crossroads and to mingle arrows (Ezek. 21), so that those whom he cannot harm either by “terror by night” or by “the arrow flying by day” may at least be shaken by the perplexity of temptations; for Leviathan is also said to have tangled sinews. Knowing this, the Apostle, to whom Satan’s wiles were not unknown, and wishing to arm and warn us against this as well, adds: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left.”

This alternation of vicissitudes was not lacking even in our Lord himself: now he heard from the children and people of the Hebrews, “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21); now, “Crucify, crucify,” and “his blood be upon us and upon our children” (ibid., ch. 27), from those same people. Paul himself too, now caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12), now buffeted by the thorn of the flesh, thrice begs the Lord that it may depart from him, and is by no means heard. Elsewhere likewise, now he is beside himself for God, now, sober for men, he rejoices with those who rejoice and weeps with those who weep; he is weak with the weak and burns for those who are scandalized. He is also restrained by chains, yet the word of the Lord is by no means bound in him; rather, he speaks wisdom among the perfect.

At one time, forgetting what lies behind and stretching himself only toward what lies ahead, he says: “Yet I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). But not even thus is he secure, nor does he rest in high-mindedness, but fears; knowing that the king of Babylon, though, according to Ezekiel (ch. 21), he does not imitate the Sabbath rest and seems to have consulted the oracle in vain by examining the entrails, will nevertheless remember iniquities for the purpose of taking captive. But in all these things Christ’s soldiers overcome, on account of and through him who loved them and armed them with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left.

What, then, are these weapons of righteousness, whether of the right hand or of the left? The aforementioned psalm, agreeing throughout with the Apostle, either previously cited or introduced by him, indicates them when it says: “He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you shall hope. His truth will surround you with a shield; you shall not fear the terror by night, nor the arrow flying by day. A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand” (Ps. 90 [91]).

For where the Apostle says, “In sweetness, in the Holy Spirit,” [Col. 0391B] there the Prophet says, “He will overshadow you with his shoulders.” For what is it for God to overshadow a person with his shoulders, if not to protect every righteous person from the heat of temptations through the sweetness of the Spirit and the infusion of grace, as though hiding him in the secret place of his face from the disturbance of men? Hence in another psalm the same Prophet boasts, saying: “You overshadowed my head in the day of battle” (Ps. 139 [140]). And because burdens are usually borne upon shoulders, God’s kindness of patience and long-suffering is rightly denoted by his shoulders: by it he cherishes and supports his little ones while waiting for them, according to the words, “He spread his wings and took them up, and bore them upon his shoulders” (Deut. 32); and Isaiah’s words, “Their children shall be carried on shoulders” (Isa. 66), [Col. 0391C] until, having grown into a perfect man, they no longer need to be carried, but are themselves sufficient to carry others.

Wings too are joined to such shoulders, because those whom he bears patiently he also warms and forms with the feathers of spiritual consolations, like a hen cherishing her chicks beneath her wings, and like an eagle urging her young to fly and hovering over them (Deut. 32). But lest a person, hoping and hiding beneath these wings, should grow numb through security and suppose that he must always rest there, the Apostle sends us to the weapons of righteousness, while the Prophet, harmonizing with him, also warns us of battle: “His truth will surround you with a shield.”

For after the innermost consolation of divine grace, when a person returns to his own weakness, he is taught more truly by experience itself how far he is from truth and how greatly transitory goods [Col. 0391D] differ from true goods. Surrounded by this knowledge of truth, as though by a shield broad above and narrow below, he is fortified to despise transitory things as things that do not truly exist and are narrow, and to desire eternal things, which truly are. Thus Peter, after the angelic vision, his release from prison, and the iron gate’s opening of its own accord, finally coming to himself says: “Now I know truly” (Acts 12). Elsewhere, after the vision of the sheet containing every kind of quadruped and creeping thing, the same Peter, returning to himself, says: “In truth I have discovered” (Acts 10). Behold: there he testifies that he truly knows; here, that he has discovered in truth things which he is not believed to have previously been ignorant of. Rather, having been made certain by divine revelation, he is shown to be surrounded by the shield of divine [Col. 0392A] truth.

Wishing also to show against what things this shield provides protection, the Prophet comprehends all temptations in a fourfold division, saying: “You shall not fear the terror by night.” By this is rightly understood the lust of the flesh, because, according to the Apostle (1 Tim. 5), “she who lives in pleasures is dead while living.” For just as death alienates the senses of the flesh from present things, so the sleep of carnal pleasure renders the senses of the soul dull toward knowledge of eternal things. Hence, “those who sleep sleep by night, and those who are drunk are drunk by night”; and the very mightiest of Israel are girded with a sword upon their thigh because of the terrors of the night.

It follows: “The arrow flying by day”; and by this we rightly understand the pride of life, which especially tends to steal in during the daylight of worldly [Col. 0392B] prosperity—a day which the Prophet confesses that he did not desire. But in “the business walking about in darkness,” which is placed third, there is clearly expressed the commerce of avarice, or the wantonness of the eyes, which is satisfied by no abundance of acquisitions; for, according to Solomon, “the eye is not satisfied with seeing” (Eccl. 1). These indeed attack us from the left.

But if we are surrounded by the shield of truth, a thousand fall at our side; and lest we seem unarmed on the right, he adds: “And ten thousand at your right hand.” Perhaps not without reason he intended the ten thousand previously mentioned to be understood as the “incursion and the noonday demon.” For the noonday demon is suitably interpreted by the Fathers when Satan’s angel transforms himself into an angel of light. Since he cannot incline a person to perverse and manifestly evil things, he turns to subtle arguments; and, as though counseling what is right, persuades him to seek loftier things, investigate stronger things, or even, by revealing certain hidden matters to him, to know more than he ought to know.

And this temptation is rightly called noonday, when a person is offended by an excess of light. It injures all the more ruinously and is guarded against more slowly, because it is more difficult to detect and more rarely discerned. Although it differs from the other temptations as much as ten thousand from a thousand, and as much as the right hand from the left, nevertheless, just as, fortified by the shield of truth, we overcome the thousand on the left, so, holding in the right hand the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, we put to flight even [Col. 0392D] the ten thousand on the right. For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the dividing of soul and spirit (Heb. 4), dividing and discerning even the most spiritual and subtle temptations of demons.

Perhaps this temptation of the noonday incursion is denoted in the following verses of the same psalm by the asp. For just as the asp stops its ears lest it hear the voice of enchanters, so those deceived by this transformation of light and pretence of good become deaf to every sounder counsel and warning. The remaining temptations perhaps are expressed by the other animals: in the lion, the pride of life; in the dragon, the lust of the flesh; in the basilisk, which harms by its gaze, the lust of the eyes. If these things may rightly be understood in this manner, we leave it to the inquisitive reader.

Enough has now been said, I think, concerning the points on which Prophet and Apostle agree: how these two cherubim have their faces turned toward one another. It now seems necessary to say how, with their faces turned, they look upon the mercy-seat of the Gospel reading. But lest by repeating what has been said either in the Psalm or in the Apostle we burden the reader or the page, let us briefly gather it together and seek to find it in the Gospel.

For the Lord Jesus, wishing first to begin doing before teaching, as was said above concerning Prophet and Apostle, began with patience; and he first wished to be exercised in patiently enduring those tribulations which the saints impose upon themselves, so that by his own [Col. 0393B] example he might teach us that one cannot easily overcome others through patience if one has not learned to rule oneself, according to the saying: “The patient man is better than a mighty man, and he who rules his own spirit than one who takes cities” (Prov. 16). For afterwards he was to teach this in words and proclaim in the Gospel: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21); because, according to blessed Gregory, when we learn to rule ourselves, we begin to possess what we are.

Wishing to fulfil these things, the Lord first imposed upon himself the necessity of solitude and scarcity, the desolation of the wilderness, the horror of fasting, and the torment of hunger. For he knew that these were especially necessary at the outset for those wishing to return to God: first, that a person fleeing and renouncing every convenience of sin and [Col. 0393C] the abundance of temporal things might remain far off in solitude, lest perhaps convenience itself should more readily cause him to relapse; then, that he should not merely lack what delights him, but should also have something at hand to dread, so that, with earthly affections softened or even driven away by that very dread, he may more gladly and easily seek heavenly things.

Thus, when the Psalmist had said that he had fled far away, he immediately added, “I waited” (Ps. 54 [55]); as though he were saying: “Provoked by the squalor of solitude itself and the horror of desolation, I immediately turned myself toward awaiting and seeking divine consolation.” Finally, the enemy must also be afflicted by bodily fasting, and the body reduced to the servitude of the spirit, so that, as the outer person is corrupted, the inner may be renewed. These things have been said because the Lord Jesus is said to have been led into the wilderness by his Spirit and, after fasting forty days and forty nights, afterward to have hungered.

It follows: “And the tempter came” (Matt. 4); as though it were said: He imposed the preceding things upon himself through his own Spirit; he endured the things that follow from an alien spirit. Those three very well-known temptations inflicted upon the Lord by the tempter have been discussed with the greatest subtlety by the Fathers. But it seems necessary to show how they correspond to the matters already mentioned.

Therefore, when the tempter said to him, “Command that these stones become loaves” (ibid.), and he is recorded to have opposed a word of Sacred Scripture to him as the shield of truth, he seems to have trampled down the dragon. For the ancient serpent attacked the Lord in the wilderness by the ancient deceit which he had employed against the first-created humans in Paradise. Seeing that flesh was close to humanity—indeed inseparable from it—he first set before them things pleasing to the flesh and delightful to it, and, deceiving them through the lust of the flesh, cast them down. So now too, seeing the Lord hungry, and wishing to enlist his very hunger as his helper, he began to tempt him through the appetite of the flesh—indeed, lest I say, through its concupiscence—saying, “Command that these stones become loaves.”

Behold how plainly the wilderness is a suitable place for penitence. For because in the wilderness he found neither fruit pleasing to him nor any other food that might drive hunger away, he turned to stones, which could not be lacking; not, as before in Paradise, saying, “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3), but using a subtler stratagem, saying, “Do as God does.”

[Col. 0394B] As though he were saying: “If you truly are God, you can do this; and if you can, you ought to sustain the life of your body, if not to gratify it, at least by necessary food.” Yet this great fraud was detected in the wilderness by one who was hungry, though the happy first-created humans, lacking no necessity whatever, were unable to perceive it even in Paradise.

Thanks be to you, Lord Jesus, because as you once overcame the dragon in yourself, so through your own people you do not cease daily to overcome him. For now, as a member of so great a head, every one of your little ones, having eyes in the head, stirred by your example, instructed by your teaching, and strengthened by your aid, recognizes the wickedness and cunning of that same dragon and makes light of his attempt. Yes, yes: through the midwifing hand of yours, the twisting serpent has been drawn forth from the cavern of deceit in which it had lain hidden until your coming.

Seeing, therefore, that he made no progress in the form of a dragon, he turned to the lion’s skin, saying: “All these things”—namely, the kingdoms of the world and their glory—“I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4). Behold, just as a lion regards itself as king of the beasts, so this one proudly believes himself lord of earthly kingdoms, which he promises to give so readily if he is worshipped. But by one word alone the lion too is easily rejected and trampled down. The Lion of the tribe of Judah conquered the lion of the nations; the Lamb, the dragon; the Dove, the basilisk.

For in this second temptation I discern not only the lion’s arrogance but also, in the basilisk’s eyes, the avarice of insatiable greed: in the showing of the kingdoms, the lust of the eyes is expressed; in their glory, the pride of life. For what follows—that he set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple and said: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down; for it is written, ‘He gave his angels charge concerning you, and they shall bear you in their hands,’” etc. (Matt. 4)—may perhaps not inappropriately be referred to the asp, the incursion, and the noonday demon. Here, transforming himself as though into an angel of light, he seeks by the testimony even of Sacred Scripture, which the Lord had opposed to him, to persuade what he had counseled.

But the Lord teaches us that we must not depart from Sacred Scripture; and he refutes Satan’s perverse interpretation of Scripture by opposing another Scripture, saying: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid.). As though he were saying: “I would be proved to wish to tempt God if, trusting in his grace and promise, I presumed beyond what is human without any necessity or benefit.”

It follows:

“Then the devil left him” (ibid.). Whoever is not seduced by any of these four modes, the devil, confounded, undoubtedly leaves him unharmed. “And behold, angels came and ministered to him” (ibid.). Where, in the Apostle, after the various troubles of tribulation have been enumerated, there is added, “In sweetness, in the Holy Spirit” (2 Cor. 6), followed by a multiple distinction of gifts of grace, here the Gospel reads: “And angels came and ministered to him.”

For by angelic ministry the manna of divine consolation is ministered in the wilderness of this present exile to mourners, pilgrims, and the contrite of heart, as to those who receive the inheritance of salvation. But this manna of divine [Col. 0395B] sweetness sometimes precedes temptation, sometimes accompanies it, sometimes follows it. It preceded in Elijah, to whom it was said, “Eat, for a great journey remains for you” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19); and after he had eaten, in the strength of that food he laboured by travelling for forty days and forty nights without any food.

In Daniel, a meal was offered in the very tribulation, while he was in the den amid the lions, brought through the prophet Habakkuk by angelic ministry (Dan. 14). But our Lord, who had come to be tempted for us, chose what was harder: after fasting had been completed and the various trials of tribulation overcome, he would finally enjoy angelic ministry, so that it could deservedly be said of him: [Col. 0395C] “You have heard of Job’s patience, and you have seen the Lord’s end” (Jas. 5).

Job’s patience, indeed, was preceded by many benefits but rewarded by more numerous ones. Hence we are directed to consider his patience alone, not the end of his patience. But we are admonished to contemplate the Lord’s end: he who, with the joy of the kingdoms of the world and their glory set before him, endured the cross, despising shame (Heb. 12). Here too, having rejected bodily food, he patiently awaited angelic delights until the end.

Having said these things concerning the Office of the Lord’s Day called the First Sunday of Lent, it is fitting, in order that the progress made from the beginning of Septuagesima may be more fully understood, briefly to recapitulate certain matters stated above, so that what must be said concerning the end of Septuagesima may be fitted more suitably to what has already been said concerning its beginning.

## TREATISE XVIII. RECAPITULATION OF WHAT HAS BEEN SAID CONCERNING SEPTUAGESIMA, ETC.

Sacred Scripture, historically speaking, commemorates two Septuagesimas: the first, namely, of times or ages, extending from Adam to the end of the world; the second, of years, which the children of Israel spent for seventy years in Babylonian captivity. In representation of these and in signification of the spiritual advances of every holy soul, the Church is accustomed to celebrate two Septuagesimas: one of weeks, divided by seven Sundays, the last or seventh of which—its virtual boundary—is the Sunday on which *Laetare, Jerusalem* is sung; the other of days, which has its end and boundary on the Saturday when the double *Alleluia* is sung.

The first signifies the progress of the active life, which has its perfection in this life and is brought, by advancing, to the end of completion: so that, when the week of Leah’s union has been completed, one finally arrives at the desired marriage with Rachel. The second signifies the rest of the contemplative life. It is measured not so much by weeks as by days—indeed, not by whole days or hours, but rather received in half-hours. It is counted only after the first Pascha has ended and the second begun.

But because these two lives are mingled together, serve one another reciprocally, and succeed one another in turn—so that now Leah envies Rachel her Jacob, now Rachel Leah, and now one snatches him from the other in excessive eagerness—these two Septuagesimas are also celebrated in the Church and connected to one another in such a way that they seem not so much two as one, and very few recognize that there are two. Yet this mystery could not remain unknown to the Roman Church, which established its observance throughout the universal Church. And it marked the seventh Sunday of the first Septuagesima, through which, as we have said, the completion of the active life is signified, by the carrying of the golden rose. But the mystery of this rose must by no means be treated lightly; it is better reserved to be explained on the day to which it is known specially to belong.

Meanwhile, let us discuss, as the Lord grants, the other Sundays [Col. 0396C] preceding it, lest, forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead, we upset the proper order. First, therefore, renouncing the world and departing from Egypt—the life of instability and darkness—we rejected the fruits of the flesh, like the seven thin ears of Egypt blighted by scorching wind; and embraced the fruits of the Spirit, like the other seven full and beautiful ears, on the one stalk of charity. Thus, intending spiritually to understand and fulfil the Decalogue, we began Septuagesima.

Second, wishing fully to renounce mortal sins and enduring in this no small straits and bitterness from the habit of those very sins, as though from the persecution of certain Egyptians, we finally crossed, by God’s miraculous aid and not without much labour, the redness and pain of that bitterness as though it were a Red Sea. And thus, striving to fulfil the Decalogue by the number six of the active life, we labour to celebrate Sexagesima.

Third, wishing not merely to resist sins but also to rule the bodily senses themselves, and thus taking care to fulfil the Decalogue by the voluntary mortification of the five senses, we rejoiced, now having crossed the sea, in celebrating Quinquagesima. Although wandering in a waterless wilderness we did not find a city of habitation, yet, passing through Marah and delightfully refreshed by the sweet draught of waters made sweet, we finally reached Elim, where, having become victors over ourselves, we found the palms of victory and [Col. 0397A] received the sweeter fruits of that victory.

But unable to remain there longer, because neither the twelve springs nor the seventy palm trees sufficed for satiety, and desiring to pass beyond those who go around the city, we crossed into the wilderness of Sin. There, examining more subtly the jar of conscience, we advanced from outward things to inward, from visible things to invisible, from the sense of the flesh to the spirit, becoming now spiritual persons. Led by the Spirit into the spiritual wilderness, flying over the Decalogue with the four wings of the virtues, we were granted to begin Lent with the Lord and taste heavenly manna.

These things fittingly begin in Sin, which means “jar,” where, to those wishing to enter the city of the inner person, there meets a man carrying a jar of water; he also shows the great furnished upper room where the Pascha is prepared (Luke 22). For those seeking God first encounter the God-man, so that through the God-man they may ascend to God the Word; and through God the Word human beings may become gods, according to that saying of the Word himself: “If he called those gods to whom the word of God came,” etc. (John 10).

This man, then, meets, aids, and goes before whom he wills, when he wills, and as he wills. He meets those who seek, helps those who fail, goes before those who hesitate and tremble, saying, before he is called, “Behold, I am here.” He appeared beforehand to Mary while she was still trembling and seeking the dead body; yet not carrying a jar of water, but as a gardener (John 20), signifying that there yet remained in her many things to be uprooted and broken up which required the aid or labour of a gardener.

He appeared to those going to Emmaus, sad and almost failing, to help them; but as a traveller (Luke 24), not carrying a jar of water. All these, still devoted to outward things, find him outside, kiss him outside, and receive outward gifts from him. Only to those striving to enter the chamber, and now seeking the secret place of the bed and the rest of the Sabbath—that is, wishing to celebrate the Pascha—does he meet carrying a jar of water.

But because the divisions of waters are with him, and divisions of graces flow forth from his various springs, his jar must not be thought always to contain one and the same water; rather, according to his will, he offers each person whatever he knows to be necessary [Col. 0397D] for that person. To one, water of refreshment; to another, water springing up into eternal life; to another, the waters of Siloam, which flow silently; to another, water flowing out from the Temple; to another, water from the open fountain for washing the house of David and the menstruous woman; to another, water from the sealed fountain; to another, waters of fountain and well flowing impetuously from Lebanon.

I pass over the water of the cistern and the streams of the living well that are led outward and divided through the streets; likewise the waters of the Jordan, in which Naaman, immersed seven times, is cleansed from leprosy (4 Kings [2 Kings] 5); and the waters of Marah and the waters of Elim, which are the tears of penitents and the baptized. All these are outside and are customarily received before the spiritual Lent. Yet our Moses, whose name means “drawn from water,” because he was conceived of the Holy Spirit, fills his jar from these waters whenever he wills and gives to each as he wills, distributing to each according to his will.

And because it would take too long to discuss all of them, let us ardently thirst for that water of his, whoever drinks which shall never thirst. This is the water of charity, of which the Evangelist says, “which those believing in him were about to receive” (John 7). The Lord displayed it to us during his human life as though in an earthen vessel, and does not cease daily to display it to those making progress: pouring his charity into them and inviting them to contemplate and imitate his manner of life, saying, “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, because love is strong as death” (Song 8).

If one wishes to inquire into the effects and properties of this water, we find it cleansing, cooling, contemplative. Of the first it is written: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50 [51]); and, “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1). Of the second: “Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16). Of the third: “He led me beside the water of refreshment” (Ps. 22 [23]). Of the fourth: “The water was stirred, and one was healed” (John 5). Of the fifth: “I shall wet my bed with my tears” (Ps. 6); and Solomon is recorded to have built pools of water in order to irrigate the forest of growing trees (Eccl. 2). Of the sixth: “The waters of the Jordan were sanctified” (the Church). Of the seventh, Solomon says: “As faces of those looking are reflected in waters, so human hearts are manifest to the wise” (Prov. 27). And in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like doves beside streams of waters, washed with milk and sitting by very full streams” (Song 5).

For doves in streams of water observe not only their own faces but also the hawk, so that they may more easily escape it when it is seen from afar. The diligent reader will readily find all these effects and properties in the water of charity. For it is the living spring to which no stranger has access. It is the living water which the Lord promises to the Samaritan woman (John 4). Indeed, it is the living water of which the Apostle says: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ” (Col. 3). This life kills and gives life: it kills [Col. 0398D] to the world, because it is strong as death; it gives life to God, because “he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4).

Because this charity is contained in four commandments—namely, “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole strength; and your neighbour as yourself” (Deut. 6; Matt. 22)—and upon these four hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Luke 23 [probably Matt. 22:40]), it is fittingly represented by the forty-day period, so that only the person who has striven to show charity in word and deed may rightly be said to celebrate Lent. Thus Lent is enclosed within the double Septuagesima described above; thus charity, advancing on the wings of the active and contemplative life and stretching itself forward as it advances, expands unto the end.

[Col. 0399A] Hence Solomon’s litter is described as having a purple ascent, a golden reclining-place, and an interior paved with charity (Song 3). What is signified there by the litter, I think, is signified in the Gospel by the great furnished upper room (Luke 22). For the litter, or upper room, is a heart elevated and illumined by divine contemplation. It has a purple ascent of laborious action and is great through the multiplicity of good work; it is furnished with the charity of heavenly desire as with a more excellent and lofty adornment, so that at last it may rest sweetly upon the golden couch of divine wisdom.

Thus Lent holds the middle place between the two Septuagesimas; thus, through charity, sleeping between the two lots—between, as it were, the active and contemplative life—it is exercised beneath itself through the active life and raised above itself through the contemplative. Through the exercise of good work it is raised from lower things; through devotion to contemplation it abides in the heights. And the more charity expands in action, the more sweetly it subsequently delights in contemplation. For charity is merited through the fruit of good work, whence it is afterwards rewarded through the taste of contemplation.

Therefore the merit of charity is patience in labour, and the reward of tribulation is knowledge of truth. If anyone aspires to the reward, let that person first procure the merit. If anyone delights in the embrace of truth, let that person first undergo the path of labour. If anyone desires to receive the sweet fruits of charity, let that person not shrink from the roughness of the bark or flee the bitterness of the root; [Col. 0399C] for “the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree and shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91 [92]). If anyone wishes to say meaningfully, “I will climb the palm tree and grasp its fruits” (Song 7), let that person know that one must begin from the root; for, according to the Apostle, the branches and everything else in the tree do not bear the root, but are borne by the root (Rom. 1 [probably Rom. 11:18]).

We must therefore ask what this root is, from which trunk, branches, and fruits proceed. For there are three commandments of charity: love of God, love of neighbour, and love of oneself. Where it is said, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22), it is shown that a person must first love himself rightly. For one does not rightly love oneself who loves iniquity; rather, according to the Prophet, such a person undoubtedly “hates his own soul” (Ps. 10 [11]). Therefore, in order to love oneself rightly, one must hate one’s vices with perfect hatred, laying aside “all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and every evil speaking” (1 Pet. 2), and anything else opposed to charity.

This first commandment, namely love of oneself, first not in dignity but in order, is fittingly understood as the root of charity. From it proceeds [Col. 0400A] the trunk of fraternal love, which spreads into the manifold branches of good works; and the fruit of divine love, which, at last, after many tribulations and ascents established in the valley of tears, is most sweetly tasted through knowledge of truth by the pure in heart.

And it should be noted that these are so connected with one another that there is no fruit without the trunk, nor does the trunk live without the root. Yet neither the one who plants nor the one who waters gives life to root or trunk; God alone gives the growth (1 Cor. 3). So too there is no true love of God in a person without love of neighbour; nor is love of neighbour pure without self-love; nor, again, is self-love right unless it is enlivened and, as it were, animated by some love and knowledge of God. For knowledge of truth is, as it were, the soul of charity [Col. 0400B]: truth is loved in proportion as it is known, and as one advances in love, one is enlarged in knowledge; for love itself is knowledge.

A person first knows truth in himself through humility; then in his neighbour through compassion; finally, in the very nature of truth through revelation. See how charity is everywhere animated and made alive by the knowledge of truth. For a person to love himself rightly, he must know himself without deception. To love his neighbour truly, he must recognize that neighbour’s weakness and stoop to him in compassion. To love God purely, he must see and know with a pure heart, insofar as this can be done in this life, the purity of God’s nature.

The courses of the aforesaid Forty Days and Seventy Days are bounded and brought to completion by these ends [Col. 0400C]: the end and completion of the spiritual Forty Days is love of God; the end of the Seventy Days, which we have called the contemplative life, is knowledge of God. Love of neighbour is perhaps commended in that part of Lent called Passion Sunday, so that a person may then rightly gird himself to love his neighbour in Christ, when he begins to hear and reflect how great were the things Christ did and suffered for him. During the remaining preceding time of the spiritual Lent, it is clearly shown to a person in what order he ought to advance and make progress in love and knowledge of himself. First, therefore, a person ought to know what he is by fault; then what he is by grace; thirdly [Col. 0400D], what he is by nature. The first seems fitting for the beginning of Lent, the second for the third Sunday; for the second Sunday is called the “vacant Sunday” and is found, from the original institution of Lent, to have lacked a proper office. The third plainly suits the fourth Sunday, called Mid-Lent, on which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung.

> [Note: [Col. 0399D] Thus far Cardinal Henry of Albano proceeded. He did not put the finishing hand to this work, as is plainly evident from its final words. No doubt hindered by undertakings for holy Church and by the several legations imposed upon him by the Apostolic See, and finally overtaken by death, he was unable to commit to writing what he had conceived in his mind.
>
> Some things also appear to be missing [Col. 0400D], and perhaps much, after Treatise 13. For when, at the beginning of that treatise, he had said that he was already touching the thresholds of the city of the Lord and was soon to enter it through the twelfth gate; that, struck dumb by the splendour and glory of that gate and by its exceeding radiance, he stood amazed and, with the Queen of Sheba, was breathless with astonishment; and that what he saw of that city of the Lord was incomparably greater [Col. 0401A] than what he had heard of it—when, I say, he had said these and similar things, had indicated that he would report great matters concerning the same city, and had raised the reader’s expectation of hearing marvels and unheard-of things, he immediately digresses to lament the earthly Jerusalem, captured by unbelievers at the time when he was writing. He begins the following treatise with the office of Septuagesima, without any prefatory notice showing the connexion of this and the following treatises with those preceding, and without thereafter making any mention of the gates or of the glory of the city of the Lord.
>
> Therefore it appears that this and the following treatises had already been carried by the author as far as the point at which we here leave off with him. It should also be known that in the Clairvaux manuscript there is no title except at the beginning of the whole work, where the author sufficiently identifies himself and makes his purpose clear. We have supplied titles to the individual [Col. 0402A] discourses, and have preferred to call them treatises rather than sermons, lest anyone infer from the name “sermon” that they were addresses delivered and pronounced in church. The author merely wrote what is written here; he did not deliver it. For this reason he sometimes addresses his reader, not his hearer.
>
> To each treatise through the twelfth he appended this conclusion: “May He Himself be the Alpha and O of our discourse, etc.” Since he did not write “Alpha and Omega,” as is now commonly written and read, we have likewise printed it so, especially since Estius, together with others whom he cites, learnedly demonstrates that one should read and write not *Omega* but simply *O*, as the ancients always read it. We have been unable to discover the sermons of this author which Ciaconius and others say that he delivered before popes; nor do we know whether they still exist.]

There the spiritual joy of freedom is commended both by words [Col. 0401A] and by delightful signs. All these matters will be explained more fully in their proper places, as God provides [Col. 0402A]. Let us therefore proceed first with the first matter.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1188: Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury

[Col. 0401]

## Notice

D. Bertr. Tissier, *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, Bonofonte, 1662, folio V, p. 1.

The Venerable Baldwin, surnamed the Devonian, an Englishman by nation, born at Oxford in humble circumstances, was entrusted by Bartholomew, bishop of Oxford, to masters for instruction in letters. Having made no small progress in the liberal arts and theology, he was appointed archdeacon of that same church. But, inflamed with zeal for the religious life, he assumed the monastic habit in the Cistercian abbey of Ford; he was then chosen abbot of that house. Afterwards he was raised to the bishopric of Worcester and, finally, to the archbishopric of Canterbury in the year of the Christian era 1184. Lucius III honoured him with the pallium and the legateship of England.

At an assembly of nobles, by an eloquent speech he persuaded Christians to provide both arms and supplies against the Saracens. He himself took the badge of the cross and associated with himself certain Cistercian abbots as companions. He ordered a nobleman named Oeneus, formerly excommunicated by St Thomas, to be exhumed and cast into the sea. He was appointed, with certain other prelates, arbiter for establishing peace between the kings of France and England. At length he crossed into Syria and overthrew the Saracens in a great defeat. Dying in that region, he bequeathed the money he had gathered to be distributed for the use of the holy military expedition.

These are the statements of our Angelus Manrique in his *Annals*, taken from the authors of Baldwin’s life. He wrote much, as we learn from Arsfeldius, the principal writer of his life, from Pits, from Manrique himself, and from others.

While still abbot, he wrote to Bartholomew, bishop of Oxford:

*On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, one book: “Great and profound, of the new and true.” A manuscript at Oxford, in Lincoln College. And I believe this is the same work as that held in manuscript at Cambridge, in the College of St Benedict, under these titles:

*On the Sacrament of the Altar*; or *On the Inestimable Sacrament of the Old and New Testament*; also in manuscript at Louvain, in the College of the Society of Jesus.

*On the Sacraments of the Church*, one book: “Reverend names of Master …”  
*On the Commendation of Faith*, one book: “All the covenants of human society …”  
*On Orthodox Doctrines*, one book: “The teaching of the holy councils …”  
*On the Sects of Heretics*, two books: “The mystery of the Christian faith …”  
*On the Unity of Charity*, one book: “The institution of the common life …”  
*On Love*, one book: “Love is strong as death …”  
*On the Priesthood of John Hyrcanus*, one book: “The lineage of the great Herod …”  
*On the Instruction of Gerald*, one book: “Your work, archdeacon, which …”  
*Thirty-Three Sermons*, one book: “Whiter than snow, more shining …”  
*On the Histories of the Kings*, four books.  
*Against Henry of Winchester*, one book.  
*On the Commendation of Virginity*, one book.  
*On the Angel’s Announcement*, one book.  
[Col. 0403] *On the Cross*, one book.  
*On Mythology*, one book.  
*A Poem of Devotion*, one book.  
*A Book of Letters*, one book.  
And many other works.

The writings thus far listed alone readily prove to us that Baldwin was an eminent man, even if all his other works had perished.

The principal works are those mentioned first, which we now publish: namely, the *Sermons*, or rather various *Treatises*, the first of which begins: “The sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.” This is followed by the book *On the Commendation of Faith*; finally comes the work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which he dedicated to his patron Bartholomew of Oxford. Those are mistaken who set down as though they were the beginnings of distinct little works the words “Great and profound,” etc., and “Reverend names,” etc.; for the latter are words of a preface, while the former is the beginning of the book or treatise which follows the preface. These small works are held in the library of Clairvaux, except *On the Commendation of Faith*, which is held at Longpont with others, written in an elegant hand.

[Col. 0403]

# Various Treatises of Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury

## Treatise I. On the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist

[Col. 0403A] The sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, by reason of its dignity and reverence, deserves to be treated worthily by worthy persons, worthily consecrated, worthily received, and worthily administered. Great and inestimable is the dignity of this sacrament; and who can attain to it? It is great beyond every measure of our understanding, beyond every capacity of our comprehension. Great indeed is the price of the world: a price beyond price, a priceless price, incapable of valuation by any assessment.

“Great,” says the Apostle, “is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3). This sacrament is a sacrifice of truth: nothing in it is feigned, nothing pretended, nothing coloured over [Col. 0403B], nothing shadowed forth by magical tricks; but it is true sincerity and sincere truth—truth in what is manifest, truth in what is hidden. The visible and true appearance of bread is manifest.

> [Note: [Col. 0403B] Add: the true body and blood of Christ are hidden.]

Before consecration there is indeed there the true substance of bread; but in the consecration, by the mighty power of the words, it is transubstantiated and changed into the true flesh of Christ. After consecration, the whole Christ is hidden beneath the visible appearance—He who “made darkness His hiding-place.” The prophet addresses Him, saying: “Truly Thou art a hidden God, O God of Israel, the Saviour” (Isa. 45). Christ was hidden from the beginning in the bosom of the Father; afterwards He was hidden in the form of a servant which He assumed; and [Col. 0404A] now He is hidden in the sacrament which He Himself instituted.

Faith finds Him hidden in the Father’s bosom; faith likewise finds Him hidden in the man; faith itself also finds Him hidden in the sacrament. The great power of faith has a great privilege of intimacy with God. Wherever it finds Him, it has access to Him; and with a certain bold confidence of household familiarity, it bursts into the inner chambers and the very bedchamber itself. It does not think itself to be shut out by those who guard the court—not by the doorkeepers, not by the chamberlains. It enters securely and joins itself, confidently yet reverently, to the mysteries of God’s counsels.

And what wonder if God entrusts His counsels to the faith of His faithful ones? Do not kings and rulers of peoples communicate the secret of their counsels to their faithful servants? “God is faithful and without iniquity” (Deut. 32); and faithful friends are likewise without iniquity when they keep faith with Him and serve in faith. “All His works are in faith” [Col. 0404B] (Ps. 32); and “without faith it is impossible to please Him in any respect” (Heb. 11).

God tests His faithful and chosen ones in order to find them worthy of Himself. He tests their faith, their hope, and their love. But we are now concerned with faith, which is tested by God in many ways and is especially exercised in this sacrament for its proving. God decreed by His eternal counsel to save the world through the death of His only-begotten Son, and to send into the world both the Saviour and salvation—no salvation other than the Saviour Himself. What He decreed, He also promised, and He revealed His counsel to His faithful ones. The faith of the saints assented; they believed and awaited the fulfilment of the promise.

But God delayed His Christ. Why He delayed Him, He alone knows, being conscious of His own secret. Meanwhile the faith of the righteous was exercised. What God promised, He willed in many ways to shadow forth for the testing of faith, and to prefigure through diverse significations of things and sacrifices. For that solemn observance of legal sacrifices, established by the Law and approved by the prophets, was a kind of remembrance of the promise made and a mystical signification of its future fulfilment. Thus the thing wonderfully promised and afterwards to come wonderfully, having testimony from the Law and the prophets, might never fall from memory amid the unceasing repetition of sacrifices. For in these signs of things to come [Col. 0405B], faith was exercised in the service of divine honour, lest it languish in idleness, grow cold from the fervour of its devotion, and fail in its hope of expectation through the inroad of forgetfulness.

And if some faithful person considered within himself what these things meant, the devotion of piety would always have something certain that remained hidden within the conscience of faith. Such was the case until the shadow gave way and truth succeeded it. For He who was to come came: the Holy One of Israel came; He became man, was seen upon earth, and conversed with men (Baruch 3). He made known to the world the ways of life, and, having completed the dispensation for which He had come, ascended into heaven, where He now is, sitting at the right hand of God.

Before He ascended into heaven [Col. 0405C], lest the disciples and other believers thereafter to come should lose confidence or despair of His assistance when His bodily presence was withdrawn from their eyes, He comforted them, saying: “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Therefore our Jesus is with us. Why should I not call Him ours, when He exists for us? For “a Son has been given to us.” He who said, “But I will rejoice in the Lord and exult in God my Jesus” (Hab. 3), claimed some right for himself in this Jesus.

This our Jesus, with whom God has given us all things, cannot bear to be absent from us. He loves us so greatly that He Himself, the Father’s Wisdom, says: “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8). He was with us, clothed in flesh, before He died for us; He was with us in death also, insofar as His body had not yet been removed from the earth; after death He was with us, appearing to the disciples in many proofs; and He is with us even now until the consummation of the age, until we are with Him, because “we shall always be with the Lord.”

See how greatly Jesus loves us. Neither death nor life can separate Him from us in the love by which He loves us. Therefore neither death nor life ought to separate us from His love. For whom should we love if not Him? Indeed, whom ought we so to love as Him? For, to pass over other things, if we are not ungrateful and wicked, this ought to suffice: that He Himself loves us. Nothing is owed more to one who loves than a return of love; and the one who loves wishes to be loved—and this is altogether just. Yet it would be strange if one who wishes to be loved but does not wish to love were acquitted even by his own judgment, so as not to be unjust [Col. 0406A]. But by true judgment, one who does not love the person who loves him is himself unworthy of love.

Whoever does not love Jesus does this at great peril to himself, being worthy of the Apostle’s curse and anathema: “If anyone does not love our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema, Maranatha” (1 Cor. 16). Conversely, the same Apostle prays: “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption” (Eph. 6). Jesus indeed loved us first; and lest He not be loved by us, He is always with us until the consummation of the age. “The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector” (Ps. 45).

Since the God of Jacob—the supplanter and wrestler—became our protector by assuming our flesh, the Lord of hosts is with us. Thus He Himself says of the righteous: “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. 90); and the righteous says to Him: “Though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, because Thou art with me” (Ps. 22). Emmanuel is with us against those who trouble us and those who rejoice in our misfortunes. He is with us in the moment of necessity, in the help of protection, in every benefit of consolation and support.

He was with the righteous of old in these ways; but now He is with us through the mystery of the Incarnation, in the sharing of our common nature. Jesus was not content with this degree of love, merely to be with us. He binds us in a closer embrace and wonderfully unites us through the sacrament of communion, so that He may be in us and we in Him [Col. 0406C], as He says: “He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood abides in Me, and I in him” (John 6).

Christ, who abides in us, lives in us, according to the Apostle’s saying: “I live; yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). And if Christ lives in us, the Spirit of God dwells in us; and, according to the same Apostle, “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not His.” But if Christ is in us, “the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of righteousness.” And if the Spirit of Him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in us, He who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will give life also to our mortal bodies because of His Spirit dwelling in us (Rom. 8). The Lord Himself also says: “He who eats My flesh and drinks My blood [Col. 0406D] has eternal life” (John 6).

Therefore in this sacrament our life is hidden with Christ in God. Here are hidden eternal life and true salvation, promised to the ancients and given to us. They will be revealed in us when God comes to be glorified in His saints and made wonderful in all who have believed. The Lord has magnificently done for us what He promised to the ancients; in great part He has already granted it to us. In this sacrament there has been granted to us the truth of the ancient counsel of which the prophet says: “Lord, let Thy ancient counsel become true.” This is the truth of God’s promises, the truth of signs, the truth of sacrifices, the truth of shadows and figures.

Finally, this truth is Christ Himself, who says [Col. 0407A]: “I am the truth” (John 4). Pilate did not know this truth when he said: “What is truth?” and went out (John 18). Let one who went out remain outside; and if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. But let us enter the sanctuary of God, lest we remain outside and our portion be with unbelievers. With Him no word is impossible; His word is omnipotent and always true, and the power to act is always present to Him whenever He wills.

For the testimony of this faith, it is enough for us that Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, said to His disciples: “Take; this is My body” (Matt. 26). If human wisdom murmurs in our heart, let the piety of faith restrain its murmuring. Let us render honour to God’s words in the humility of faith; let us offer every reverence to so venerable a sacrament [Col. 0407B] and so excellent a grace, in purity of hands and holiness of life. For this pledge of His love the most gracious Jesus left us when His hour came to pass from this world to the Father. Wishing to test the faith and love of His own, He established in this sacrament, as it were, a place of contest in which those whom He wished to prove might be exercised.

First of all, divine faith and human reason fight one another; and their contest is so conducted that one must tear out the other’s eye, nor is there any end to this struggle except the blinding of one of them. Human reason has its own eye, and faith has its own. The eye of reason is bleary and often cannot see visible things close at hand [Col. 0407C]. But the eye of faith is keen: by it the invisible things of God, understood, are beheld.

The mind is dull regarding the power of this sacrament, the eye of reason is darkened, and every bodily sense is numbed. The curious hand, diligent in handling, can discover by no effort of its own anything except what bread of this kind usually is. The experience of taste and the attentive observation of the eyes suggest to thought, from flavour and colour, inscription and shape, and all other circumstances, that it is bread and not flesh. Consulted reason answers what it has been persuaded of by carnal thoughts and verified by bodily senses.

For the eye of human reason cannot comprehend the invisible things of God unless it is anointed with the eye-salve of grace and illumined by that true light of which it is written: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 17). “If thine eye,” says the Lord, “causes thee to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from thee” (Matt. 18). This may suitably be understood of the eye of human reason, which is often a stumbling-block to the piety of faith; but when it causes stumbling, it must be plucked out. For it is better to enter into life having one eye of sound faith than, having two eyes—one of faith and the other of human reason—to be cast into Gehenna [Col. 0407D].

Indeed, the person who is guided by human wisdom and receives faith only insofar as it seems consistent with human arguments has, as it were, two eyes. But our faith has a testimony greater than that derived from human reason. It rests upon divine authority, which is itself the highest reason [Col. 0408A], incomparably surpassing all human reason. Nor should that be held more certain which human reason suggests to the heart than that which the Spirit of God suggests, who suggests all truth and imparts it by hidden inspiration. For He opens the ear of the heart; in a gentle whisper He speaks of the simplicity of piety and the mystery of faith, and His discourse is with the simple. “He who is of God hears the words of God.” It was not flesh and blood, not carnal wisdom or animal perception, that revealed the mystery of faith to Peter, but the heavenly Father who is in heaven.

Our faith therefore rests upon truth, having its beginning from the true God Himself, to whom it was said: “The beginning of Thy words is truth” (Ps. 118). God does not deceive, because He is highest truth; He is not deceived, because He is highest wisdom; He is not weakened, because He is highest power. Whatever He has said or foretold, that will also happen. To Him doing is as ready as speaking so that it may be done. As He has purposed, so it shall be; all His counsel shall stand. If He has decreed, who can weaken it?

Our faith therefore ought to rest upon certainty. It does not err through conjectures, nor doubt as concerning a doubtful matter; it does not hesitate as concerning something uncertain; it does not stagger, waver, or fluctuate, but stands upon the firm rock, upon the foundation which no one can overturn: Christ Jesus. If faith is the knowledge of salvation, why should it not be believed to have certainty? “I know,” says Job, “that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19). “I know,” says Martha, “that whatever Thou askest of God, God will give Thee” [Col. 0408C] (John 11). And, speaking of her brother, she says: “I know that he will rise on the last day” (ibid.). “I know,” says the Apostle, “whom I have believed, and I am certain” (2 Tim. 2). The same Apostle, speaking of Abraham, says: “He did not waver through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, knowing that whatever God promised, He is also able to do” (Rom. 4).

Then does the conscience of faith lack certainty? Who would say this except one who does not believe, or believes lukewarmly? Since faith rests on highest authority, truth, and certainty, it excludes pretence by authority, error by truth, and doubt by certainty. But one who doubts impiously is close to the unbeliever. For the sin of unbelief and the crime of apostasy in humankind seem to have begun from doubt.

When the tempter approached the woman, he began thus, bearing the question of doubt: “Why did God command you not to eat?” etc. (Gen. 3). Once the question struck the woman’s mind, as though puffed by the serpent’s hiss and swollen with its venom, she became inflated and hesitated; and soon she inclined her heart to doubt, saying: “Lest perhaps we die” (ibid.). She expressed in words of doubt the doubt conceived in her mind; she called into question the word which God had spoken; and, as it were, a case was argued in the woman’s heart.

The woman’s proud reason sat as judge upon the tribunal, or in the chair of pestilence. The word God had spoken was brought forward as the accused; the accuser approached and charged the word with falsehood, saying: “You shall not die at all” (ibid.). It was as though he said: “The threatening word by which God foretold death is false” [Col. 0409A]. Then the woman, still doubtful—not yet wholly driven to fall, but wavering, like a leaning wall and a shaken fence (Ps. 61), uncertain what to believe between God’s threat and the devil’s suggestion—meanwhile looked at the tree in question. She saw that it was good for eating, beautiful to the eyes, and pleasing to behold (Gen. 3).

The alluring appearance of the tree served altogether, as it were, as evidence in favour of the accuser. For no sign of death appeared in the tree from which one might suppose either that the accuser had spoken falsely or that God had not spoken falsely. Added to this was that the woman naturally loved the life which the serpent promised and likewise did not love the death which God threatened. Having experience of life but none of death, she more readily followed where love and experience drew her; and thus, at last overcome, she stretched out her hand to iniquity.

Thus she was deceived and brought first to doubt and from doubt to unbelief, so that she believed false what God had foretold. Thus persuaded, beginning from concupiscence and reaching consent, she presumed to do what God had forbidden.

Meanwhile proud reason, seated upon the tribunal, acquitted the woman from fear of death. It did not justify God in His words, but by a proud judgment condemned Him as false. Thus the woman transferred to the glory of the tempter the honour of faith which she ought to have rendered to God’s words [Col. 0409C], believing him and not believing God. Proud will sat beside proud reason: it withdrew from God the honour of obedience and voluntarily subjected itself to the tempter through disobedience.

Therefore reason in the woman was corrupted by pride, because she doubted the truth of God’s word. For it is wickedness to doubt God’s words, and impiety not to assent to His sayings. A human being, made in the image and likeness of God through the judgment of reason and freedom of will, ought in natural equity to be subject to God in such a way as always to wish to be subject to Him from whom he began to be: humbling reason before Him so as to believe all His words, and likewise humbling will so as to obey all His commands. The piety of faith humbles reason in a person; obedience humbles will.

The pride of human reason [Col. 0409D], which rejects piety and does not know how to humble itself beneath faith, is a condemnable blindness of heart, hateful to God, when it refuses to believe what it cannot sufficiently comprehend. When the Lord had given sight to the man born blind, the unbelieving Pharisees were more blinded, and their eyes were darkened lest they should see. But the Lord, directing against them the novelty of so great a miracle, said: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9): that those who do not see through pride may see through the grace of humility, and those who see through pride may not see when grace is withdrawn.

But He adds in what follows: “If you were blind, you would not have sin; but because you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains” (ibid.). It is a good blindness not to see great things in oneself [Col. 0410A], and devoutly not to know what it is not permitted to know. Therefore, in heavenly mysteries and divine sacraments, every impious doubt must be driven far from our heart and every curious investigation restrained, so that faith, which possesses the consciousness of truth, may also possess devout ignorance.

For God’s wisdom is incomprehensible; it cannot be confined within the narrow limits of human reason. Therefore in this sacrament all human reason must be humbled beneath the piety of faith. So it was necessary, and the order of our restoration required it: the image of God, deformed through the pride of reason, ought in the very sacrament of our redemption to be re-formed through humility of reason.

Let a person, then, humbling all his reason to God, believe concerning this sacrament what the Lord instituted for belief, saying: “This is My body” [Col. 0410B] (Matt. 26). Let him believe it firmly, without doubt, and confess it faithfully. If it appears impossible according to human reason, if incredible according to human wisdom, still let it remain ever true and certain in the conscience of faith, on account of reverence for the divine word. Let a person believe God more than himself; let him entrust himself to God, lest God not entrust Himself to him. Let him entrust his spirit to God, so that his spirit may be trusted by God (Ps. 77). Let him entrust his reason to God, deny himself, and judge as he hears from God, following Him who says: “As I hear, I judge” (John 5).

Christ therefore set before us in Himself an example of a twofold benefit: humility of judgment and humility of will [Col. 0410C]. Of humility of judgment it is written: “As I hear, I judge.” And through the prophet He says: “In humility His judgment was taken away” (Isa. 53). Of humility of will He says: “I came not to do My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me” (John 6). Christ is not from Himself and does not act from Himself, but from the Father, as He says: “I can do nothing of Myself” (John 5). As the Son is from the Father, so from the Father He has judgment and will to act; yet in these He is equal to the Father.

From this let the person who is not from himself but was made by God learn to judge nothing from himself but from God; to will nothing from himself; to do nothing from himself, especially in those things that work or cooperate toward salvation.

This sacrifice of which we now speak is not only a sacrament for sanctification, but also contains in itself an example for imitation [Col. 0410D]: sacrament through the mystery of faith, example as a pattern of life; sacrament for humility of will. The sacrament benefits those who imitate the example; it does not benefit those who do not imitate the example.

This pattern of life was not prescribed only by this sacrifice; it was long beforehand shown in the figure of this sacrifice. In the Law of Moses, on the tenth day of the seventh month a solemn victim is commanded to be offered, whose flesh is burned outside the camp and whose blood is brought into the Holy Place (Lev. 16). For, as the Apostle says: “The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places are burned outside the camp” (Heb. 13). The day of affliction is a day of propitiation for sin.

How is a day of affliction a day of propitiation? Is affliction propitiation? Or how is affliction not propitiation, if every soul that has not been afflicted on that day is to perish? Certainly it is better to be afflicted on this day than to perish from among one’s people. “The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places are burned outside the camp.” Those who refuse to be afflicted here through discipline cannot have their souls received into heaven. For then blood is brought into the Holy Place when the soul is received into heaven.

That the soul is signified by blood is common in Holy Scripture; Scripture itself does not conceal the reason for this signification, saying: “The soul of all flesh is in the blood” (Lev. 17). Hence the Lord says to the watchman of the house of Israel who does not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, signifying the soul by blood: “I will require his blood from thy hand” [Col. 0411B] (Ezek. 3).

No one is exempted or excused from the necessity of Christian discipline: no condition, sex, advanced age, rank, dignity, or power. For every soul that is not afflicted on this day shall perish. This agrees with what is written in the psalm: “Lay hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way” (Ps. 2). Certainly the one who does not lay hold of discipline is to perish. Hence the Apostle says: “If you are without discipline, then you are adulterers” (Heb. 11): you are not Christ’s, but the devil’s, who is an adulterer and not a bridegroom.

Through discipline, moreover, we suffer with Christ, just as through penitence we suffer with our neighbour. Compassion of mercy is always benevolent, even if, because of lack of material resources, it is not always beneficent; therefore it sometimes consists in will alone. For a person unable to afford it is excused from works of mercy. But compassion of discipline is not to be assessed by bare intention; rather, those who profess the Christian name must undertake it for Christ in actual fact and in the experience of affliction [Col. 0411C].

For because “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3), as no one is free from guilt, so no one can be free from punishment; everyone who offends by guilt owes punishment. But one who owes a penalty and does not pay it, like one who practises deceit, denies the debt.

[Col. 0411D] And, just as in civil judgments, as the adjudicators of disputes determine, a lawsuit is sometimes doubled through denial, so it is also in divine judgments—except that those to be judged by God are not judged merely twofold, but will pay eternal penalties in destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty. The neglect of repentance is, as it were, a kind of denial of the penalty. God indeed overlooks a person's sins on account of repentance, but the person neglects repentance. From this other dissimulation hostility arises; and as time passes, perpetual enmities begin beneath the covering of concealed hatred, and thus persist.

We are debtors to Christ, who, conducting the common business of all, paid on our behalf, as he himself says: “Then I paid what I had not seized” (Ps. 68). What he paid for us, he demands from us; and who will be able to exact it? [Col. 0412A] A certain great sum of sufferings was owed to God for the liberation of the human race. And, as Blessed Augustine says, each of us must contribute toward this sum, until it is completed by the contribution and paid to God. Owners of fields or estates customarily pay into the commonwealth or treasury a fixed tax, each according to the extent of his possession. So we too must pay, as if into a certain commonwealth, the due tribute of sufferings—each a greater or lesser amount, according to the measure of his strength and the fitness of his age, rank, and station. For what is more just than that a human being should suffer for Christ, for whom Christ suffered? Hence the Apostle says: “I fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 1).

Therefore we are debtors, not [Col. 0412B] to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. “For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die” (Rom. 8). Behold, the sentence of death has been threatened against those who live according to the flesh, but it has not yet been pronounced: it can still be averted through repentance and discipline. But once it has been pronounced, it cannot be stayed by an appeal through some hidden art, nor avoided or evaded by legal quibbling.

And since Christ suffered for us, it ought to be not only a cause of fear but also of shame to us if we live delicately and make provision for the flesh in its desires. For if the Lord—and such a Lord—hangs on the cross, and hangs there for a servant, while an evil servant, deserving stripes, lives in pleasures, is this not deserving of shame? Is it not ridiculous? If Christ on the cross says, “I thirst” (John 19), while our hearts are burdened daily with gluttony [Col. 0412C] and drunkenness, is this not disgraceful? Is it not shameful? As the common saying goes, this game has not been divided on equal terms. Certainly Christ’s passion is neither a game nor like a game. Yet we regard our life as like a game, as though it were some art devised for play.

We still move about in the world as on a field of combat, where Christ our Lord was slain. Whoever leaves this field having within himself neither wound nor swelling will be reckoned inglorious. We indeed “were healed by his bruise” (Isa. 53). If the Lord was slain in battle for us, and we escape unharmed, sound and whole in body, shall we not be judged guilty of treachery and guilty of Christ’s death? Guilty of Christ’s death were both its authors, those who consented to his death, [Col. 0412D] and the ministers who crucified him. In some sense, too, one is guilty of Christ’s death who, by living wickedly, nullifies in himself the power of his death.

For although he did not act so that Christ should die, he nevertheless acts so that, so far as he is concerned, Christ died without benefit. Christ’s death does not work salvation for him, nor does the Savior’s cross profit one who, not carrying the cross, destroys himself. If Christ’s cross, which is imposed upon us to be borne, is contrary to pleasure, and pleasure is contrary to the cross, how can lovers of pleasure be excused from being judged persecutors of the cross? Of such people the Apostle says: “Enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction; whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things” (Phil. 3).

These, as has been said, are guilty of Christ’s death—not [Col. 0413A] as its authors, supporters, or ministers, but as despisers of his death, who nullify in themselves the sacrament of the divine dispensation, frustrating the counsel of the Most High; who make themselves unworthy of the heavenly blessing and ineffable grace; who, living in pleasures, mock the mystery of the cross; who trample upon the Son of God, regard as defiled the blood of the covenant by which they were sanctified, and insult the Spirit of grace. The fleshly life is an injury to God, a reproach to the cross, and amounts to an insult against the whole Trinity. It is an injury to the Father that the Son is trampled upon; an injury to the Son that his blood is treated as though defiled; an injury to the Holy Spirit that grace is despised.

You, O priests of the Lord, guard yourselves from pleasures of the flesh and from the vain conduct of the world. Honor your ministry, [Col. 0413B] you who shine as lights in the midst of the world. Pursue righteousness; embrace discipline (Ps. 2), for you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your bodies (1 Cor. 6), carrying about the mortification of Jesus. In all things present yourselves as ministers of God, bearing the marks of Jesus in your body and the badge of his military service: in abstinence and self-control, in chastity and sobriety, in patience and humility, and in every holiness and sanctification (2 Cor. 6), so that all who see you may know whose you are, and the prophetic saying may be fulfilled in you: “You shall be called priests of the Lord, ministers of our God” (Isa. 61). And again: “All who see them shall know them, [Col. 0413C] because they are a seed which the Lord has blessed” (ibid.).

Bless the Lord, O priests of the Lord (Dan. 3); bless him who has blessed you with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, who has blessed the house of Aaron. May God be sanctified in you, so that in you he may appear as he is: holy, undefiled, and unstained (Heb. 7). Let not his name be blasphemed because of you; let not your ministry be reproached because of you. Let your conduct in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation be such that those who see you may say: “Truly these are priests of the Lord; truly these are ministers of our God; truly these are disciples of Jesus Christ, vicars of the apostles; truly these are the seed which the Lord has blessed.”

Consider the dignity of the priesthood entrusted to you, to be performed and dispensed. [Col. 0413D] Let your hands, to which it is granted to handle so venerable a sacrifice, be clean from every defilement of filthy gifts, lest your portion be with those “in whose hands are iniquities, and whose right hand is full of gifts” (Ps. 25). Approaching the altar with washed hands, approach with him who says: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will compass your altar, O Lord” (ibid.).

Keep your mouth clean, to taste how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 33), and to receive the Eucharist—the living bread, namely, which came down from heaven (John 6). It is not fitting for a priest’s mouth to be defiled by perjury, [Col. 0414A] false testimony, lies, filthy or idle speech, or jesting words irrelevant to the matter; nor should it be enlarged in reproaches and detractions against enemies. Let there be in the priest’s mouth thanksgivings and the voice of praise, prayers, petitions, and supplications. Let no evil speech proceed from it, but good speech that bestows the grace of edification upon its hearers; and let what the Lord says come to pass: “With my praise I will bridle you, lest you perish” (Isa. 48). Hence one bridled by praise says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33). The mouth must be bridled by the praise of God, lest through unbridled freedom of speech it be loosened toward what is dishonorable and shameful. A mouth that is to touch [Col. 0414B] the sacred banquet ought not to be unclean and common.

Most beloved brethren, let us hold most firmly and believe without hesitation what the authority of God himself and of the holy Fathers prescribes for our belief concerning this sacred communion. This sacrament contains the power of our restoration and the price of our redemption; hidden truth for the exercise of our faith; and Christ’s discipline is set before us as an example for our life. Therefore, when the Lord instituted this sacrifice and delivered it to his disciples, he said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). Do what I do; offer what I offer; live as I teach. Receive from this the pattern of living and dying which I hand down to you by my example.

This sacrament brings it about for us that Christ may live in us, and we in him. [Col. 0414C] It brings it about in us that, just as Christ died for us, so we too may die for Christ. But all who die in Christ or for Christ have a pious falling asleep and the best grace laid up for them (2 Macc. 12). The glory of that resurrection is promised and kept in store, of which a worthy reception of this sacrament is the saving restoration; by its power God will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory (Phil. 3).

What worthy return shall we make to the Lord for so great a grace bestowed upon us? What shall we repay him for so great an honor? It is vain to ask whether he loves us, since, as a sign of inestimable love, he gives us in himself the bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation. It is therefore just that, insofar as human [Col. 0414D] weakness permits, we receive so splendid a gift of God and so exceptional a benefit worthily and reverently; that we keep it as the pupil of the eye—or rather, more than the pupil of the eye—as our life, as the hope and reality of our resurrection and glory. Whatever we have hitherto sinned through negligence against the reverence due to so great a sacrament, let us amend in the future by more exact and more earnest diligence; and let us compensate for the losses of former time and past life by a more honorable purpose and more mature counsel, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

## SECOND TREATISE: ON THE CORRUPTED MORALS OF CLERGY AND PEOPLE

[Col. 0415]

[Col. 0415A] Behold how perilous are our times, how corrupt and abominable the children of men have become in their pursuits. The earth is filled with iniquity; and, as in the days of Noah all flesh had corrupted its way (Gen. 6), so it is now. And then, before the waters of the flood came upon the earth, a spiritual flood preceded in the reprobate morals of human beings; and in human guilt there was prefigured what the punishment of judgment would be. For torrents of iniquity overflowed, and those who were in the flood of many waters did not draw near to God; therefore the depths covered them, and they descended into the deep like a stone (Exod. 15).

And while the abyss of sins called upon the abyss of God’s judgments, and the cry entered the ears of the Lord God of hosts, [Col. 0415B] the fountains of the great deep were broken open and the floodgates of heaven opened (Gen. 7); and the Lord wiped out flesh from the face of the earth, and set the bow of the covenant in the clouds, so that humanity might no longer fear for itself from the waters of a flood—yet let it fear nevertheless. For God has bent his bow and made it ready, giving a sign to those who fear him, that they may flee from the face of the bow (Ps. 59). In remembrance of the judgment that has passed, terror of the judgment to come is introduced; and with the bow itself, which God set in the clouds, a sign of terror appears in varied colors: the judgment of water and the judgment of fire. He has absolved us from the judgment of water; but “a fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire which shall consume the adversaries” remains (Heb. 10).

Behold, already now the image of the future judgment has preceded in human morals.
