For the fire of greed, lust, and malice, [Col. 0415C] kindled in the midst of the peoples, devastates the inhabitants of the earth far and wide, as though the conflagration of the world were already near. When it comes, punishment will be conformed to guilt. For as guilt is now, such will punishment be. The life of the wicked is fire, and the punishment of the wicked will be fire. The life of the righteous also is fire, and so fire will be their glory. The righteous now burn with the fire of divine love—the fire which the Lord came to cast upon the earth, and how he wills that it should burn! (Luke 12). For there is a fire in Zion, and a furnace of fire shall be in Jerusalem (Isa. 31).

The righteous will burn in the future, but as seraphim: they will burn and shine like the sun in the sight of the Lord, and shine in the splendors of the saints. This will be the glory of those who, like lamps [Col. 0415D] shining and burning through charity, burn inwardly for themselves and shine outwardly as an example to others. The wicked also will burn in the future, but differently. Of them the Prophet speaks to the Lord: “Make them as a furnace of fire in the time of your countenance” (Ps. 20). They already burn now, of whom it is said: “All adulterers, their hearts are like an oven” (Hos. 7). And of the wicked the Psalmist says: “Fire has fallen upon them, and they did not see the sun” (Ps. 57). The fire in which they burn does not enlighten but blinds, so much so that it does not permit them to see the sun. Therefore, in their last days, groaning within themselves because of anguish of spirit, they will say: “The light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun of understanding did not rise for us” (Wis. 5).

The signs, too, that will precede the day of judgment will be foreshadowed in our present morals; and such as they will visibly be in the future, such they already appear spiritually in us. It is written: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2). What the sun and moon are in the firmament, the order of rulers and the life of subjects are in the Church of God; likewise ecclesiastical authority and secular power. The moon is lower than the sun and does not shine from itself, but from the sun. So too the life of subjects [Col. 0416B] is lower than the life of prelates, by whom they ought to be kindled and enlightened. For to them it was said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5).

But in those rulers who are ignorant and erring, who are blind and guides of the blind, the sun is turned into darkness; and therefore in the life of subjects the moon is turned into blood—the blood, that is, of corruption and cruelty. For behold, the charity of many grows cold and iniquity abounds. Blood has ascended from the winepress as high as the horses’ bridles (Rev. 14), even to the rulers of peoples, and blood has touched blood (Hos. 4). The laity do not find in us what they ought to imitate; they find what they wish to persecute. They persecute us with calumnies; they persecute us with injuries; they persecute us with losses, denunciations, and reproaches; at last they persecute [Col. 0416C] us even with swords.

For recently the fury of persecutors wounded us in the head: they pursued our most blessed prelate Thomas, the Lord Christ’s own, even unto death, because of his outstanding defense of ecclesiastical liberty. And if what public report has spread concerning the matter is true, and what many consciences fear, our undisciplined life was the seedbed of so great an evil and supplied the tinder for such great hatred. For people did not regard us as ministers of God and stewards of God’s mysteries; but whoever he is, he shall bear God’s judgment. Perhaps we seemed unworthy of the ancient privileges that, through the indulgence of Roman pontiffs and noble kings of old, were granted for the peace and liberty of clerics. Let due reverence be present [Col. 0416D] for them; certainly we were unworthy—altogether unworthy according to the merit of our lives. Nevertheless, in whatever priest it may be, the priestly ministry is always holy and the sacrament of priesthood honorable.

Let the time come now to our minds when Doeg the Edomite struck down with the sword eighty-five priests clothed in the ephod (1 Sam. 22). Recall the former days, and the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, who was slain between the temple and the altar [Col. 0417A] (Matt. 23). Our times too have some notable instances of sacrilegious cruelty; but the magnitude of many crimes is absolved by comparison with one deed. God knows how grievously the enemy acted wickedly against the holy one. All the wickedness of our time, though it now abounds greatly, has been justified by one act. It was indeed one act; but in that one act there are many crimes. For ingenious malice, ingenious to its own ruin, so that nothing might be lacking to perfect wickedness, brought the whole business of iniquity to completion in its uttermost malice.

But if our disordered and undisciplined conduct is, by a plausible opinion, to be regarded as having afforded occasion for so great an evil, what counsel remains except that we cry to the Lord our God until he has mercy upon us? For he is compassionate [Col. 0417B] and very merciful. What is more salutary, or more honorable, than that we restore our life to order and discipline, and in all things present ourselves as ministers of God, so that those who persecute us and speak evil of us as evildoers, seeing our good conduct, may themselves be edified by our example unto repentance?

For if the very light is darkness, how great will the darkness itself be? (Matt. 6). If we, appointed in the Church of God so that our life may shine for others in good works, still walk in works of darkness, what wonder if our subjects, not knowing and not understanding, walk in darkness—blind, and made still blinder by our example? Will not their blood be required from our hands? Will not that most blessed martyr, who laid down his life for us, bring a complaint against us? Will not the voice of his blood cry from the earth against us, and shall we not all stand guilty before the tribunal of the strict Judge? Did he not die because of our fault? Did he not die through our fault? Though it did not furnish the cause of his death, it did afford the occasion. If we persevere in sin, as it is reasonable to suppose, he will no longer be a patron for righteousness, but an accuser or witness for vengeance, not an intercessor for pardon.

In the evils which we suffer by God’s just judgment, there is no one against whom we can rightly be angry except ourselves. We ourselves deserved heavier things, and we do not yet suffer what is proportionate to our deserts. It must deservedly be imputed to us, and redounds to [Col. 0417D] our peril, that secular power claims ecclesiastical judgments for itself; that it is not governed by ecclesiastical authority; that it does not employ or rely on the counsel of the Church, but resists it; that Peter’s sword [Col. 0418A] is blunted, that Peter’s keys are not respected; that the sacraments of the Church are despised; that the holy and terrible name of God is taken in vain in contempt through perjury; that due reverence is not shown to most holy churches; that due honor is not rendered to ecclesiastical persons; that the honorable name of holy religion is brought into contempt. All these things, and very many of the same kind, are to be required of us, because they are to be attributed to our sins. For our ways and our iniquities have done these things to us.

God, however, is able, when he wills, to free from the hands of persecutors his bride, for whom he is jealous. He was angry for a little while, but they have assisted in evil. That power seems to be acting so as to keep the Church subject, lest it should itself be subject. [Col. 0418B] But what does Scripture say? “The multitude of nations fighting against Ariel shall be like a dream of a night vision” (Isa. 29). Astonishment and wonders have occurred today upon the earth. For in the perverse order of things, the moon has been exalted above the sun and does not stand in its own order.

But what does Scripture say? “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order.” Let the sun be lifted up and restored to its own place; let the life of priests return to its proper order—let it be ordered, let it be disciplined—and then the moon will stand in its order. From that time the life of subjects will be ordered and disciplined, and content with its own bounds. What is more fitting for the ordained than to live in an orderly manner? For how great an abuse, both of things and names, it is if those who are called ordained are found disordered! When the prophet says, “The moon shall stand [Col. 0418C] in its order,” he signifies that the moon, which is lower than the sun, has an order. For order of discipline is required in the life of subjects; how much more in the life of rulers? For it belongs to them to do all things in order and to order others’ morals by their judgment.

For they are God’s throne, in whom God sits and pronounces his judgments. Of this throne the Father, speaking of the Son, says: “And his throne shall be as the sun before me” (Ps. 88). And it is added: “And as the moon perfect forever” (ibid.). In this order God will bring the glory of the righteous to completion. God’s throne in prelates and the perfect will be like the sun, the moon far more splendid and far higher; and the moon in subjects, who are now less perfect, will then be forever, yet perfect in [Col. 0418D] its own order. May God, who is blessed above all things for ever and ever, bring us, each one in his own order, to that glory. Amen.

## THIRD TREATISE: ON THE LOVE OF GOD

[Col. 0417]

On the words: “You shall love your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with all your strength,” etc. (Matt. 22).

[Col. 0417D] We may be moved—and not without reason ought to be moved—to ask what is meant by this amplification of words, this so careful, so precise, so exact, so earnest reiteration within a single commandment. For it is one [Col. 0418D] commandment, not several. Of it it is written: “This is the first and greatest commandment” (Matt. 22). When it has been said, “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart,” as though this were too little, there is added, “and with your whole soul”; and as though still not enough had been said, there is joined, “with all your strength”; and as though all that has been said were not yet sufficient, there is added, “and with all your mind.” What do these things mean? Were they written so carefully idly and without cause? Who would believe this except one who does not rightly believe? If a leaf does not fall from a tree without the Father’s counsel, how much more is the word of God—and that word which is first and greatest among the words of his commandments—not spoken without God’s counsel, so that not one stroke nor one iota ought to be passed over? (Matt. 5).

Therefore we must seek most earnestly and investigate most diligently what God was so careful to have both commanded and written. For nothing is sought more salutarily, nothing found more usefully, provided that those who seek and find do what is commanded. As we may suppose, because of the hardness of our heart God took care to command this word so carefully and, by commanding it, as it were to impress it more deeply—just as commonly happens with harder wood into which a nail must be driven. Because of the hardness of the wood, the whole nail is not immediately driven in; rather, by frequent blows it is forced in and made to enter until it is wholly fixed. This saying is like a nail to be driven into our hearts.

For if, according to Solomon’s saying, “The words of the wise are goads, and like nails deeply driven” (Eccl. 12), how much more is the word of God a goad and nail, since it is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword? God, wishing with this nail of divine speech and divine love [Col. 0419C] to transfix and penetrate our whole heart, says: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart”; and, driving it in more deeply, he added, “and with your whole soul”; and that it may be admitted still further within, he adds, “and with all your strength”; and that it may reach the innermost depths, he finally joins, “and with all your mind.” Thus he commanded exceedingly this commandment which he exceedingly wished to be kept.

But another reason also seems fitting for this fourfold division of one commandment. Since love of the world occupies our entire heart and fills all its chambers, love of the world must be cast out from the whole heart, so that the prince of this world may be cast out and the love of God may enter, claiming the whole heart for itself; so that God may be known in the furthest bounds of our heart, and “all the ends of the earth may remember and turn to the Lord” [Col. 0419D]—so that God may possess the whole heart, and the heart possess God, and one may be able to say with the Prophet: “God of my heart, and God is my portion forever” (Ps. 72).

### That God Is Not Perfectly Loved in the Present Time

According to the condition of the present life, as God is known imperfectly and in part, so he is loved imperfectly and not fully. For whatever knowledge of God there may be in the present, compared with that most complete knowledge when God will be seen in his glory, when he will show his face and we shall be saved, it is like the entrance of morning light into a house through the thinnest crack compared with noonday brightness, when [Col. 0420A] the sun shines in its strength. Likewise, the love of God that can be possessed in the present is like a tiny spark of fire compared with the great conflagration of love in which the righteous will burn in Jerusalem among the hosts of seraphim. For there is a fire now in Zion, but a furnace of fire shall be in Jerusalem (Isa. 31).

Meanwhile, according to the measure of your imperfection, God must be loved with your whole heart. But how with your whole heart? How can this be, unless it is because your heart is not yet wholly yours, but strangers plunder it? Hence one man, among other things that he laments, says with groaning: “My thoughts have been scattered, tormenting my heart” (Job 7). And another says: “My iniquities have taken hold of me, and I could not see. They are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me” [Col. 0420B] (Ps. 39). Forsaken by the heart, they are left as though heartless.

Meanwhile we do not have our whole heart for loving God; indeed, we do not even have a heart for praying to God that he may restore our heart to us for loving him. Hence David says in one place: “Your servant found his heart, to pray this prayer to you” (2 Sam. 7). To speak of myself: at the time of prayer I do not find my heart. Where is it? Or rather, where is it not? While I seek where it is, I find no place where it is not. Thus it flies away, flies back, runs out, wanders about, and returns. When it returns, it does not stay; when it is held, it is not retained; when it is gripped, being slippery, it slips from the hands of the one holding it.

Human being, if perhaps you experience these things in your heart—indeed, because you are human, without doubt you experience them to some extent—you have in yourself the experience that you do not yet love God perfectly with your whole heart: I mean that measure of perfection with which he wishes to be loved by you. But if you truly love God and offer your heart to God insofar as it lies in your power, by giving it to God you make it yours; indeed, he to whom you give it makes it not yours, nor can it be yours unless he has made it not yours. Yet whatever amount you give from your heart, that much he makes yours.

But if you could direct all your thoughts, all your affections, and all your intentions immovably toward him, retain them immovably in him, and always burn inwardly with the fire of love in all your marrow, you could indeed love God more perfectly with your whole heart. But because human weakness does not permit this, if you cannot love as much as you ought, as much as you are bound [Col. 0420D] to love, nevertheless love as much as you can, as much as you are able, as much as suffices for you: so that, beginning here to love God with your whole heart, when that which is not yet wholly yours has become more perfectly yours.

> [Note: [Col. 0419] It seems that this should be added: “you may then love God more perfectly.”]

And do not wish to imitate the unjust debtor who, if he cannot pay all that he owes, refuses to pay what he has, as though the fault of paying nothing and of not paying everything were equal. But God is a gracious creditor, and to one who pays what he can, he mercifully gives so that he may be able to pay more.

### That God Must Be Loved with the Whole Heart in His Benefits

In the fourfold distinction of this commandment, four principal affections of love are suggested to us, or four modes. Although these four affections are gathered into a fixed number, they nevertheless contain within themselves innumerable differences of modes and divisions of affections. God must be loved in his benefits with the whole heart; he must be loved in his promises with the whole soul; he must be loved in his judgments with all one’s strength; God must be loved in his commandments with all one’s mind. From these four kinds—namely, benefits, promises, judgments, and commandments—those four affections of divine love are formed in us through God’s inspiration.

Just as in the present God is known in his creatures through a mirror and in an enigma, until he is more fully known in himself as he is, so in the present God must be loved in his benefits and in the other things named above, until he is more fully and perfectly [Col. 0421B] loved, as it were, in himself. Now some benefits of God are benefits of creation, others of restoration, and others of daily consolation.

The benefits of creation are these: that we were made in God’s image and likeness; that “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28), and are his offspring; that, through his gift, we possess soul and body and every sense of body and soul in their proper number and integrity. For whatever good we have from creation, we have received by God’s generosity; and all our goods are nothing but God’s gifts.

The benefits of restoration are the sacrament of the incarnation and the mystery of Christ’s passion, and all the sacraments which Christ either undertook in himself for us or instituted for us [Col. 0421C] to receive—such as the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, the sacrament of baptism, and all the other ecclesiastical sacraments, to which the merciful God has given grace and power for the remission of sins and the salvation of believers.

The benefits of daily consolation are those which the Father of mercies and God of all consolation mercifully bestows on us daily, he “who consoles us in all our tribulation” (2 Cor. 1). For our Father knows how many things we need—we, unworthy servants, yet sons through his gracious condescension. From our Father we have the ability to desire, ask, and pray. From him we must await comfort for all our sorrows, aid for all our necessities, remedies for all our weaknesses. From whom else should we hope for all these things? “From where,” says the Prophet, “will help come to me? My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120).

Behold how the Lord has magnified his dealings with us. He has overwhelmed us with a multitude of benefits and seeks by benefits to draw love from us. For these benefits, so many and so great, God must be loved with the whole heart. And rightly, worthily, and most justly, whatever he deigns to ask ought to be given to him. But he does deign to ask. For he says to a human being: “Give me your heart” (Prov. 23). He who asks that the heart be given to him wishes to be loved from the heart. God wants our entire heart for himself, that it may be drawn back from love of the world and of the things that are in the world, and turned toward him; so that he may please us above all things, and whatever displeases him may wholly displease us.

But iniquity and vanity displease God. For he hates iniquity and despises vanity. Hence the Prophet says: “You have hated all who work iniquity” (Ps. 5). And again: “You have hated those who observe vain things to no purpose” (Ps. 20). Therefore the love of God begins with a shared hatred and contempt. For what God hates or despises, he wishes us likewise to hold in hatred and contempt. So long as we love what God hates, we have no peace with God. But then we love God with the heart, if we are found in accord with God in hatred of evil.

We love God with the heart if, remembering the good things we receive from God and the evil things we do against God, we are reconciled to God by giving thanks for the good things and doing repentance for the evil, and return after discord to concord. This is the first [Col. 0422B] step of love: the conversion of the heart from evil to good, from vanity to truth, from things that displease God to things that please him. Hence the Prophet, desiring that what God hates might become vile to him, says: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice” (Ps. 118). And the Apostle, showing the conversion of his heart through contempt for vanity, says: “The things that were gains to me, these I counted as losses for Christ. Indeed, I count all things to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord, for whom I have made all things loss and count them as dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3).

The first affection of divine love can be signified by the name of heart when it is said: “You shall love the Lord [Col. 0422C] your God with your whole heart” (Deut. 6). And rightly so. By this we begin to come into accord with God and to give our heart to God. He has bestowed upon us the grace of benefits; he demands from us that we not repay injury for grace, that we not sin against him who is beneficent to us. Therefore we love God, according to our imperfection, with the whole heart when we detest with the whole heart the evil that he hates. Hence the Prophet says: “You who love the Lord, hate evil” (Ps. 46).

### God Must Be Loved with the Whole Soul in His Promises
God is to be loved with the whole soul in his promises; he who has given us great things has promised us greater ones. He has promised us rest from labor, freedom from servitude, security from fear, consolation from sorrow, resurrection from death; and, in the resurrection, full joy—supreme and unfailing joy. Finally, he has promised us himself, as he swore to our fathers that he would give himself to us (Luke 1). Great, therefore, and beyond estimation are the promises of God; and for them and in them he wishes to be loved by us in some measure. If you ask for the measure, an ardent longing for the promise is the measure of love. This measure somehow has measure, yet is without measure. For God’s promises surpass every desire. What is surpassed is exceeded, has an end to its magnitude, and therefore a limit at that end. However greatly God’s promise may be desired, it is desired less than it ought to be; and our capacity is too slight to enable us worthily to desire that which surpasses every desire. Therefore holy desire has its measure in what it can do, not in what it ought to do. For however much it has advanced, it still ought to do more. Thus ardent longing is, in a sense, without measure, since it cannot be excessive. Whereas impatience is usually blamed in other matters, in awaiting so great a promise an ardent impatience at delay is praiseworthy. For the one who loves and desires more is more grievously tormented by impatience at delay. “Hope deferred afflicts the soul.”

Thus the bride, wishing that her desire might be commended to God by the merits and prayers of holy souls and heavenly powers, says: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love” (Song of Songs 5). Likewise the Psalmist, as though unable patiently to bear delay, says: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41). Paul too, burning with a similar desire and seeming almost impatient, says: “I am constrained by the two: having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1). Yet this same Paul, who is now so impatient that he would rather die than be held in suspense by delay, says elsewhere: “Through patience we wait” (Romans 8).

Hence is shown the wonderfully patient impatience of holy and ardent desire: the righteous are tormented with long-suffering while they wait, yet do not murmur; and, while tirelessly enduring torment, they preserve unshaken hope and bravely bear whatever adversities arise. This affection of holy desire may be denoted by the name *soul*, when it is said: “You shall love with your whole soul” (Deuteronomy 6). Nor without reason. For the soul is spirit; breathed upon by the Holy Spirit, it always longs and sighs until it breathes its rest in that toward which it aspires. Thus, in expressing the longings of the saints, mention of the soul is very often made. Hence the Prophet says: “My soul has thirsted for you” (Psalm 62). Again he says: “My soul longs for and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 83). And another prophet says: “Your name, O Lord, and your memorial are the desire of the soul. My soul will desire you in the night; and also my spirit within me” (Isaiah 26).

## That God is to be loved with all one’s strength in his judgments

[Col. 0423D]

In his judgments God is to be loved by you with all your strength. Judgment concerning God’s judgments is difficult, for “the judgments of God are a great deep” (Psalm 35). Yet it is clear that one judgment is that of which the Prophet says to the Lord: “Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name” (Psalm 118); and another is that judgment of which the same Prophet says: “Enter not into judgment with your servant” (Psalm 142).

In that judgment by which those placed in hell have already been condemned, no one loves God; nor does anyone there love himself. But in this present life God exercises his judgments in various ways, both upon the reprobate and upon the elect. For in them he now wonderfully conceals and now reveals his mercy and wrath, so that what is wrath appears to be mercy, and what truly is mercy appears to be wrath. Hence the Prophet says: “Who is wise and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Psalm 106). And concerning wrath he says to God: “Who knows the power of your wrath?” (Psalm 88).

For by a hidden judgment God permits certain wicked persons to follow their own will, and gives them over to the desires of their hearts, so that they may go after their own devices. He exalts and honors his enemies and daily heaps good things upon their good things; nor does he scourge them as he does other human beings. By doing this, he adds iniquity to their iniquity, so that those who are filthy may become filthier still, until their iniquity is complete. But in this judgment God conceals his wrath, as it were under the appearance of mercy, for those who turn his mercy into judgment, so that their prosperity may become their ruin, and they may most justly perish through those things for which they do not love God. Hence it is written: “The prosperity of fools shall destroy them” (Proverbs 1).

Yet fools rejoice in their destruction, not knowing what the One terrible in counsels toward the children of men purposes concerning them, and not understanding the deep thoughts of God, of which it is written: “How magnified are your works, O Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep. A senseless man will not know, nor will a fool understand these things” (Psalm 91). But what the Most High purposes concerning them they will understand when sinners have sprung up like grass and all workers of iniquity have appeared, that they may perish for ever and ever. This, indeed, is the end of that hidden judgment by which God conceals his wrath from those who are not in the labors of men and are not scourged with men.

There are other wicked persons, however, whom God scourges here; yet the scourges do not cleanse them, because through impatience they blaspheme or murmur, and when corrected show no reverence and accept no discipline. Because in God’s judgments they do not love God, through impatience at judgment they make judgment heavier for themselves, to be led from punishments to punishments. But when the good are scourged by God, some love God amid the scourges; others love the scourges themselves for God’s sake. The former glorify and praise God amid the scourges; the latter glorify and praise God because of the scourges. The former, patient in tribulation, love God in his judgments; the latter, rejoicing in tribulation, thankfully receive God’s judgments as certain benefits and exult in them. Of such it is written: “Let the daughters of Judah exult because of your judgments, O Lord” (Psalm 96).

The daughters are most rightly understood as souls confessing God, which always glorify God in adversities and accuse themselves, saying: “All that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment, because we sinned against you and did not obey your commandments. But give glory to your name and deal with us according to the multitude of your mercy” (Daniel 3). There are others who so love God’s judgments that, without waiting for the Father’s discipline, they judge and punish themselves, and daily demand punishment for their daily sins, from which human weakness cannot be free. Of such the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11).

But the person who judges and punishes himself as guilty is at once defendant, judge, and minister of the judge. He is a just judge because he prosecutes the guilty person; and because he himself is guilty, he suffers justly; and while he justly prosecutes himself, he hates his soul and keeps it unto eternal life. In his judgments God tests and instructs his elect unto patience, trains them in endurance of sufferings, and strengthens them through hope. “Tribulation works patience; patience, testing; and testing, hope. And hope does not put to shame” (Romans 5). Therefore the Prophet says to God: “In your judgments I have hoped exceedingly” (Psalm 118), signifying that in God’s judgments patiently endured or loved there is established not merely any hope, but a firmer and surer confidence of more abundant glory.

The certainty of hope and the greatness of glory lighten the weight of tribulation, so that it may be borne calmly or even loved. For, as the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8). Again he says: “That which is at present momentary and light in our tribulation works for us beyond measure in sublimity an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17). How worthy God’s judgments are of love is known by him who says to the Lord: “Your judgments are delightful” (Psalm 118). Again he says: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves; more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 18).

These words show that every delight in possessing gold and silver, and every sweetness of this present life, however like honey and honeycomb, is less than that delight by which God’s judgments become sweet to souls that desire God above all things. To such a soul, all that it suffers is little; it counts it all joy when it falls into various trials. “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” Great indeed—and it cannot be said how great. For you are sweet in your judgments; but not yet to the one who says: “I was afraid of your judgments.”

## That God is to be loved with the whole mind in his commandments

The mind is that which rules in a human being, holding the highest and chief place. For as a master of a household disposes all things in his house according to his will, arranges services, commands servants, judges concerning all things, wishing in all things and from all persons to be served and obeyed; so the power of the mind ought to govern at its discretion every movement and sense of body and spirit: to order, judge, and diligently ensure that it is obeyed in everything. But just as the mind knows itself to be set over all that is beneath it, so it ought to remember that it is bound by necessity to obey God. It rightly renders to its superior the obedience which it exacts from its inferior. Woe, however, to the person who does not obey God. For the overpowering penalty of disobedience will be death itself.

And as death is terrible, so it is hateful; and because it adheres to disobedience, disobedience itself is equally worthy of hatred, just as death itself is. For death entered this world through the sin of disobedience. But if disobedience is as hateful as death because death proceeds from it, why is obedience not as worthy of love as life, because life proceeds from it and life persevered in it? For obedience submits to God and to his will, and life is in his will.

The love of God and obedience embrace one another in an inseparable bond and cannot be separated from one another. For the Lord shows that love does not exist without obedience when he says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14)—that is, he will keep my commandments and, in keeping them, obey me. He also shows that obedience does not exist without love when he says: “He who does not love me does not keep my words” (ibid.). Therefore, if the one who loves obeys and the one who does not love does not obey, it follows that love is not without obedience, nor obedience without love.

Through love, obedience looks to God in the commandment; through the commandment, love directs obedience toward God. God sets forth his will through the commandment; love imposes the commandment upon obedience. But whoever truly loves God also loves his commandment. For just as no one can love God without loving his will, so no one can love him without loving his commandments, in which his will is made manifest and known. Therefore love of God is always joined with love of his will and love of his commandments, and also with love of obedience. For whoever loves God’s commandment and his will loves obedience. For God wills what he commands to be done; and, when he commands it to be done, his will is that he be obeyed. Therefore, whoever loves God’s will, by which he commands something to be done, loves to be commanded. But no one loves to be commanded unless he also loves to obey. Therefore, if obedience toward God is not without love—that is, love of God—and if love of God is not without love of his will which he commands to be done, that is, not without love of the commandment, nor love of the commandment without love of obedience, what follows except that obedience toward God is not without love of obedience, nor without love of the divine commandment to which obedience is owed?

Let us further see whether this is so, and first attend to what is taught us by the Psalmist’s words concerning love of God’s commandments: “I will meditate on your commandments, which I have loved. And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I have loved; and I will exercise myself in your justifications” (Psalm 118). He shows in three ways that he loves God’s commandments: by meditation, by lifting up his hands—that is, by action—and also by exercise. God’s commandments are to be loved in meditation, according to the saying: “Always consider the things which the Lord has commanded you” (Ecclesiasticus 3). For in meditation God’s commandments become sweet to those who consider how saving, honorable, and faithful they are; how they are established for ever and ever, made in truth and equity (Psalm 110).

But to some they are sweet and pleasant in meditation, while in action they seem burdensome and bitter because they themselves are slow to act. He removes this sluggishness from himself when he says: “I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I have loved” (Psalm 118). There are also some who seem to love and delight in God’s commandments through meditation and action, yet prove faint-hearted and less steadfast in exercise. He removes this from himself when he says: “I will exercise myself in your justifications” (ibid.). There is a certain exercise in doing or meditating upon God’s commandments; but here the exercise meant is that which resists some difficulty of temptation, persecution, or adversity that endeavors in any way to draw us away from the righteousness of God’s commandments. Thus love of God’s commandments is completed in the love of meditation, action, and exercise.

Love of obedience proceeds from love of the commandments; and those who do not love the commandments do not love obedience. What then shall we say? Are there not many who keep the commandments but would not wish to be commanded, and would rather desire the commandments to be abolished? Are there not many who do not commit fornication, do not steal, and do not persecute their enemies, yet wish that God had not commanded that these things not be done? Many indeed wish that God had issued no command concerning these matters; nevertheless, because he commanded that they not be done, they abstain from them, fearing the one who commanded, lest he punish them if they do what he forbade. Such persons appear to keep God’s commandments and obey God, yet not to love obedience. If this is so, then not all who obey love obedience, and not all who keep God’s commandments love them. How, then, is obedience the inseparable companion of love? And how is this true: “He who does not love me does not keep my words” (John 14)?

But we must consider that intention and affection distinguish one obedience from another. According to intention, there is true obedience and simulated obedience. True obedience is that which establishes its hope of reward in truth—that is, in God. Simulated obedience pretends to obey God, yet through covetousness places the hope of its labor outside truth. According to affection, there is compelled obedience and voluntary obedience. Fear extorts the former; vehement love urges the latter. If affection and intention are considered together, there is a certain obedience that is compelled and true—namely, that which is rendered from fear of God and directed toward God. Such obedience has in one person more fear and less love; in another, more love and less fear. Yet it always has something of both. For just as it is never compelled without fear, so it is never true without love.

There is a certain obedience that is compelled and simulated, rendered through fear alone and not directed toward God. There is a certain obedience that is voluntary and simulated, such as that of hypocrites. There is a certain obedience that is voluntary and true, proceeding from love and tending toward God through love. This is the obedience God seeks, loves, and commends by his commandment and example; as he loves it, so he rewards it.

But compelled obedience which is also true, though it lacks the freedom of love in the affection of fear through which it is drawn where it does not wish to go, nevertheless possesses something of the freedom of love in the intention by which it directs itself where it wishes. For just as it unwillingly experiences the affection, so willingly it directs the intention. Therefore such obedience is not to be rejected altogether, but is to some degree approved. For one restrained from sin by fear of punishment avoids the punishment he fears, since he does not commit the sin for which punishment is due. Because he directs his intention toward God, he merits something from God, to whom he entrusts his hope. While restrained from sin by fear of God, he renders reverence to the fear of God and, in a sense, consecrates his fear to God and honors God in it.

But obedience that is voluntary and true is owed to God by the most equitable right. For it is fitting that a rational creature should be subject to its Creator in such a way that it wills what he wills, and because he wills it; and further, that it wills him to will the things that it wills. I shall state this more plainly. If I will what God wills, but not because God wills it, my will—because it is only my own—is not yet formed in God’s will. But if I will what God wills, and because God wills it, my will has its beginning and cause in God, so that it may be good—especially if I also will him to will what he wills. But if I were to wish that he did not will what he wills, even though I willed what he wills and because he wills it, I would not yet will with my whole will that thing which I will him not to will, so that I too might be allowed not to will it.

For example, if I love my enemy because God commands and wills this, then in some way what pleases God pleases me, and pleases me because it pleases him. Yet it does not please me entirely, because I do not yet freely love my enemy; rather, I force myself, divided within myself: in part willing, because it is good and worthy of reward to love one’s enemy; but in part unwilling, because it is difficult not to recall an injury received and to restrain the mind from every murmur. And although I am resolved in no way to seek vengeance, although I even have a heart ready to bestow a benefit upon one who needs or asks for it, nevertheless, if with a heart still grumbling and muttering I wish that God did not command and did not will an enemy to be loved, I do not yet fully and perfectly will what God commanded. I lack as much of perfect obedience as I lack of perfect love.

For love and obedience to be perfect, whatever is recognized as pleasing to God for a human being to do ought to please that human being to do himself; it ought to please him for this reason, because it pleases God; and for this end, that he himself may please God. For the end of obedience and love is one: to please God—but in those things which please God. I added this because the wicked wish to please God, but in things that please themselves and displease God. Therefore many who do not love God believe that they love God, observing that they wish to please God; they observe also the benefits and promises in which God pleases them, but do not observe the matters in which they wish to please God, and in which God displeases them. For they do not judge love by the power of obedience, but by the opinion of their own wisdom.

But obedience, the companion of love, resists its own will and always rests upon God’s will. In that supreme and principal norm of righteousness and form of equity—that is, in God’s will—the will of a rational creature is formed, so that it itself may be, and not without reason be called, God’s will: for it begins from God by the prevenience of grace and tends toward God by the direction of its intention. For just as a human being does not have the power to do good from himself, but from him who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), so he does not have the will to do good except from him who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good will (Philippians 2).

And just as “the power of God” is said not only of that power which is in God and is God, but also of that which is given by God to a human being and is in the human being; so “the will of God” is said both of that which is in God and is God, and of that which is in a human being, though not from the human being but from God. Further, the will of God is called that which he wills to be done through a human being, whatever work of righteousness or mercy it may be. Thus there is God’s will which commands, God’s will to whom it commands, and God’s will which it commands to be done. In the first resides authority; in the second, ministry; in the third, the proof of love.

Therefore obedience wholly consists in love of God, because from God’s will, through God’s will, it tends toward God’s will and returns to God’s will. For God’s will in God, through God’s will in a human being, works God’s will in the commandment, for the sake of God’s will in God. Therefore God’s will in God is the beginning and end of obedience. Whoever obeys in love, as though toward an end, sighs toward him who inspires from the beginning; inspired by him and sighing toward him, the person rests without end from the labor which he devises in the commandment.

## Fourth Treatise: On the Twofold Resurrection Obtained through Perseverance in Obedience

[Col. 0429]

“My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory. Awake, psaltery and harp; I will arise at dawn” (Psalm 107).

[Col. 0429B] What obedience can do, what it avails, toward what it tends, where it arrives, what its end is, and what its fruit is, is shown by the glory of the Lord’s resurrection. The fruit of obedience is resurrection, and life through the obedience of Christ, who is resurrection and life. Christ died once and rose once. A single resurrection corresponds to a single death. But one resurrection cannot suffice for us. We have been cast down to the depths by the debt of a twofold death; so cast down that we cannot be blessed through one resurrection. A twofold resurrection is necessary for us: the first and the second. “Blessed is he who has a part in the first resurrection” (Revelation 20).

The first resurrection is partial: it belongs to the soul more than to the body, though in some sense also to the body; and because it is imperfect, it is partial. But something is always lacking to imperfection. “When that which is perfect has come, that which is partial shall be abolished.” The second resurrection will possess absolute perfection, lacking nothing whatever. These two resurrections are distinguished by the Lord’s words: “The hour comes, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live” (John 5). Present life, compared with eternity, is as it were an hour. The dead are those separated through disobedience from God, who is the life of the soul. And because in the hour which now is time for repentance is granted, those who hear the divine voice by obeying will live, raised from death to blessed life.

For concerning the second resurrection he adds: “The hour comes when the dead who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God” (ibid.). This hour will be when the Lord descends from heaven “with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4), and gives to his voice “a voice of power” (Psalm 67). Then those who have done good will go forth to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment (John 5). In the future there will be a resurrection of life for the good, who are to be raised to eternal life, and a resurrection of judgment for the wicked, who have no part in the first resurrection because, in the hour which now is, they do not rise in order to judge themselves. “For the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous” (Psalm 1). The ungodly are those who do not believe; and whoever does not believe is already judged. Sinners, even if they believe, because they live ruinously, have no part in the first resurrection because they do not rise in the council of the righteous.

“What,” you ask, “is the council of the righteous?” Hear the Prophet saying to the Lord: “Your justifications are my counsel” (Psalm 118). Our case is tightly constrained. We must be judged. We cannot evade judgment at all: either we must be judged here, by ourselves, and therefore more gently; or in the future, by God—and by God in wrath—and therefore more severely. But what does the Apostle say? “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11). For the Lord does not judge twice for the same thing.

Thus the resurrection of life is the second resurrection. But the resurrection of judgment appears to be neither first nor second: not first, because none follows it; not second, because none preceded it. Christ’s resurrection is the cause and form, example and sacrament, of both our resurrections, first and second. For by faith in and imitation of Christ’s resurrection, we have been re-formed, justified, sanctified, and raised from death, so that, dead to sins, we may live to righteousness, walk in newness of life, and await the adoption as children of God—the redemption of our body. For in the second resurrection Christ will refashion the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory.

The first resurrection begins from obedience and is completed by perseverance. The second begins from glory and is made stable by eternity. Whoever has persevered in obedience to the end will persevere in glory without end. Perseverance is in some manner like eternity. For as eternity is, as it were, a perseverance of glory, so perseverance is, as it were, an eternity of obedience. “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew 10). Perseverance is the praise and completion, and as it were the strength, of all virtues. Love, much praised and greatly to be praised, is the life and strength of the other virtues; but the strength of love is patience, and the strength of patience is perseverance. Love without patience is not true love but feigned love. Feigned love pretends in prosperity but yields in adversity. Patience without perseverance is inconstant and weak: it begins amid adversities, but fails with time and succumbs to prolonged weariness. Perseverance neither pretends, yields, fails, nor succumbs. All the other virtues run, as it were, in the stadium; but perseverance alone receives the prize. Obedience persevering to the end experiences in the first resurrection what it can accomplish in merit; in the second it will experience what it avails in reward. In the first it tends toward the place to which it will arrive; in the second it arrives where it had previously been tending.

## On Christ’s obedience

[Col. 0431C]

Christ himself taught this order of obedience, perseverance, and glory. For when he was in the bosom of the Father, knowing himself—and willing us to know—how good obedience and perseverance in obedience are, he considered and purposed in his heart to submit himself to the yoke of obedience, to assume the garb of humility, to clothe himself in sackcloth, to cover his soul as in fasting, to make haircloth his garment, to give himself up to reproach, to promise obedience, and to persevere in obedience unto death. What he contemplated, he also did.

And just as Abraham departed from his land, kindred, and his father’s house into the land which God promised him (Genesis 12)—and he departed in order to obey God’s voice—so the Son of God departed from highest heaven and from his Father’s house into the land which the Father promised him, saying: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Psalm 2).

Coming into the world, he was clothed in a seamless tunic, woven from above throughout, which his mother gave him, which she wove by the hand of wisdom in the finger of God, and which the Father fitted to him. Yet his mother also cooperated: the strong woman who “put her hand to strong things, and whose fingers grasped the spindle.” She sought wool and flax so that from chosen material there might be made a singular work: by a new manner and a new craft, a new garment such as no human being can make upon earth.

Jesus, clothed in the assumed habit, as though girded for every obedience and earnest and devoted to every service of humility, speaks to the Father, saying: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Psalm 107). He says that his heart is ready, yet does not state what it is ready for, so that the saying, although repeated, seems incomplete. But the repetition of the saying is the confirmation of obedience, and the incompleteness of the saying reveals perfect obedience. By professing his heart ready to obey, and absolutely declaring it ready, he shows it unready for nothing. As though he said: “Father, command what you will. If you will that I do anything, my heart is ready” (Psalm 56); “if you will that I suffer anything, my heart is ready” (ibid.); “if you will that I be scourged, behold, I am ready for scourges” (Psalm 37); “if you will that I keep your commandments, I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Psalm 118).

Peter did not speak in this way when he said: “I am ready to go both to prison and to death” (Luke 22). But Christ, who [is materially uncertain: *petis*, perhaps “is”] firmer in obedience than Peter, became obedient to the Father unto death. His heart, ready to hope in the Lord, was made firm; “it shall not be moved until it looks down upon its enemies” (Psalm 111). After professing obedience, Jesus reveals his glory to us, saying: “I will sing and make melody in my glory; awake, psaltery and harp” (Psalm 107). The psaltery and harp are joy and exultation in the glory of the resurrection. Song and psalm are praise and thanksgiving for that same glory.

Christ will sing in his glory. This is he of whom the Apostle says: “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1). God’s wisdom speaks of the Father, saying: “Before he made anything, I was with him, arranging all things; I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times” (Proverbs 8). O what a spectacle! What sweet and ineffable joy: to see in heaven the Son of God playing before the Father and to hear him singing, where the morning stars sing and all the sons of God shout for joy. Who that is faithful in hope of so blessed a vision would not clap his hands, dance in heart, and cry aloud in a voice of exultation?

Jesus sings in glory. But to whom does he sing, and what does he sing? He sings to the Father; he sings also to the angels; will he sing to us as well? To the Father he sings the everlasting proclamation of praises, triumphal psalms and heralding psalms, and a new song—the Song of Songs—which no one but Jesus alone can sing: “I will exalt you, O Lord, because you have received me” (Psalm 29). He will also sing this: “You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow; O Lord my God, for ever I will confess you” (ibid.).

To the angels he will sing: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and keep festival, all you who love her” (Isaiah 66). That great angel, falling from heaven like lightning, made a great ruin; his tail drew away a third part of the stars (Revelation 12). But Christ, rising from the dead, will fill the ruined places, build Jerusalem’s walls, and complete the number of its citizens; and from this the angels will have joy and exultation. For if they rejoice over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15), how much more will they rejoice over the thousands of thousands who are to be joined to them and become like them? “The chariot of God is manifold by ten thousand, thousands of those rejoicing” (Psalm 67).

Finally Jesus will sing to us also a song of joy, a delightful song, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the origin of the world” (Matthew 25). This voice will be in the ears of those who hear it like a musical song, sung with sweet and pleasant sound. O that it might be granted us to hear this voice! O that it might caress our ears! O that it might come to us! O that it might belong to us! May we not deserve to be strangers to the hearing of so great a good.

Meanwhile, let the voice of inviting Jesus grow strong in our hearts. Even now he sings us the invitatory, saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9). The author of life invites us to life, calls us from labor to rest, continually crying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11). Those who hear this voice, even if they have died, shall live. Your voice, uttered once—“Lazarus, come forth” (John 11)—was able immediately to raise the dead man, exhausted by the earth and four days dead. Woe to those found deafer than a four-days-dead man while the Lord cries to us: “Come to me, all you who labor,” and so forth.

Let us call to one another, encouraging one another by mutual examples: “Come, let us exult in the Lord; come, let us worship and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm 94). And let whoever hears say: “Come.” While Jesus sings, let us also sing together in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord.

## On the spiritual creature
Christ, rising from the dead, raises up the psaltery and the harp. He raises them for himself, and for us as well. For whence would the psaltery and harp come to us, unless he raised them up? Whatever is in us from ourselves deserves lamentation; it is material for grief and sorrow. For from the days of Adam’s transgression our harp has been turned to mourning; joy fails in our heart. Lamentation befits our misery, not song. Like the children of the Exile, in the midst of Babylon we have hung up our instruments (Ps. 136). According to the condition of our first birth, the human voice says: “I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. 38). But if we rise with Christ, immediately in the first resurrection glory is given to us; the psaltery and the harp are raised up.

In a harp many strings are arranged in their proper order, and by the art of harpers are so fitted and tuned together that, when the harp sounds, amid differing notes there is one harmony, one sweet consonance, one pleasant accord. And if perhaps some string sounds too harshly and makes a discordant noise by itself, disturbing the peace of the others and interrupting their concord, it is immediately, by the skill and plectrum of the player, artfully tightened, so that it may sound sharper or looser, until it returns to peace and is reconciled with the others from which it had formerly differed. For this is always the aim of the player’s skill: that nothing unmusical or discordant may be heard which could offend the ear.

So it is in the individual dispositions of each one of us. For in us, like strings upon a harp, are the senses of the body and the senses of the heart. There are senses, movements, and exercises of the heart, just as there are bodily members and their movements or functions. In the heart are diverse thoughts, affections, and intentions; diverse counsels and judgments; diverse vows and desires. These are what in us sound together or clash, disagree or agree, are discordant or harmonious.

At the dawn of our resurrection—that is, at the beginning of our conversion from the vain manner of life of the world—all these things begin to be ordered and composed within us by the laws of holy obedience, the exercise of daily discipline, and the instruction of reason. And if anything disorderly or undisciplined suddenly breaks forth, whether through remembrance of an old habit [Col. 0434B] or through the condition of human weakness, it is immediately bent back to rectitude by the plectrum of penitence and discipline, so that everything in us may be ordered, tranquil, and peaceful, and all things may obey one reason; until, through the obedience of the flesh subjected to the spirit, there may be, as in a spiritual harp, spiritual harmony and spiritual joy—namely, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

This joyful consonance and harmonious joy is the voice of harp-players playing upon their harps. Whoever strives for another’s peace while having no peace in himself does not yet play upon his own harp, although he may seem to play upon another’s. He who is not at one with himself, with whom will he be at one? He who is divided against himself and disagrees with himself is always discordant with himself and always his own opponent: with whom can he be harmonious? He who is always turbulent and restless, like the boiling sea which never rests, with whom can he be peaceable? “There is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. 48). Therefore not every wicked person plays upon this harp.

But this exultation is “the voice of exultation and salvation in the tents of the righteous”; to them it is said: “Exult, righteous ones, in the Lord” (Ps. 32), and, “Give praise upon the harp” (ibid.), “upon the harp and with the voice of a psalm” (Ps. 97). What is the force of this doubling? Is there one harp in the individual dispositions of each of us, and another in the reciprocal dispositions of one person toward another?

Certainly, just as a harp has many strings, while not all the strings have one sound, yet its many sounds grow together, through the concord of sounding together, as if into one sound: so we, though many, are as it were one harp; individually, however, we stand toward one another as string toward string. And whenever, through zeal for holy emulation, one makes himself worthy for another to imitate, or shows himself lovable in every service of charity and humility, then, as in a sounding harp, string answers string.

Nor is any most pleasing melody in an instrument of joy more delightful than the welcome and joyous fellowship of a community of holy brethren: a fellowship which, in Christ and for Christ, mutually moderates itself through reciprocal endeavors and, in all things, adapts itself by humility and patience in reciprocal conduct in order to preserve peace. There pride does not puff itself up, envy does not waste away, anger does not blaze up, discord does not quarrel, impatience does not murmur; there suspicious hostility does not dispute, and no shameful thing is even named in it [Col. 0435A]. “Behold,” says the Prophet, “how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132).

They are wholly mistaken—indeed, altogether mistaken—who judge there to be greater delight in the vanity of the world than in the truth of Christ. “Let them exult,” says the Lord, “and rejoice, who desire my righteousness” (Ps. 34). Whoever experiences this will not deny it, but will say: “Surely there is fruit for the righteous” (Ps. 57). The whole recompense of the righteous for keeping God’s commandments is not deferred to the future; rather, “in keeping them there is great reward.” For “the ordinances of the Lord are right, making the heart glad” (Ps. 18); and “at his right hand are delights unto the end” (Ps. 15). His right hand is generous and liberal: it distributes delights which the world does not know, and gives the peace which the world cannot give—but to those who do not love the world.

Behold, already in the present, already manifestly in part, it appears how good and pleasant, useful and salutary, agreeable and sweet it is for brethren to dwell together in unity (Ps. 132). But those whom Christ’s love has gathered into one love each other mutually and obey each other in turn, if by mutual examples and exhortations they daily kindle one another to love God; if with one shoulder they serve God and, with purified speech, unanimously sing him eternal praises; if all will the same thing and reject the same thing; if all think the same and have the same mind, possessing one heart and one soul. Do not all, upon this spiritual harp, rejoice before God and rejoice among themselves? “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88).

## On the Spiritual Psaltery

[Col. 0435C]

At the dawn of our resurrection Christ raises up for us not only the harp but also the psaltery—and first the psaltery, although I have first spoken of the harp because that seemed to me what ought now to be said: “Awake, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56). As Augustine maintains, the psaltery sounds from above, the harp from below.

The harp, as has been shown, is joyful concord either within ourselves or with our brethren. The psaltery is peace and harmony toward God and in God. Of this peace the Apostle says: “Therefore, being justified by faith, let us have peace with God” (Rom. 5). Through the sin of disobedience man began to disagree with God and with himself. And, by God’s just judgment, he did not find peace in himself because he refused to have peace with God. Hence it is written: “You have set me contrary to yourself, and I have become burdensome to myself” (Job 7). Thus man is divided within himself because he refused to be joined to God. For disobedience separates man from God and is the death of the soul.

But in the first resurrection this death is swallowed up in victory. For through obedience the soul is restored to life and joined to God. The soul therefore occupies a kind of middle place between God, to whom it is joined above itself, and the flesh, to which it is joined below itself. One union can be dissolved by force, but not by will; the other can be dissolved by will, but not by force. The soul cannot leave the body even if it wishes, unless it is wrenched out by the force of a more violent pain. But a soul more perfectly united to God cannot be separated by any force, violence, or severity of pain.

“Who,” says the Apostle, “shall separate us from the love of Christ? For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, neither things present nor things to come, neither strength nor height nor depth nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God” (Rom. 8). All these things—or any one of them—could separate Paul’s soul from his body; but not all of them could separate it from the love of God. See, dearest brethren, imitators of God, how firm and indissoluble this union is in every circumstance, save only through the will of the soul itself. “For he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6).

It is written that Jonathan’s soul was knit to David’s soul, and that Jonathan loved him as his own soul. “For Jonathan stripped himself of the robe which he wore and gave it to David, and the rest of his garments, even to his sword, his bow, and his belt” (1 Sam. 18). If Christ is the true David, why should Jonathan, David’s friend, not be understood as the true imitator of Christ—the one who, leaving all things for God, gives his garments to him to whom he has proved himself? This is the sign of the covenant made with David. Does Christ not know how to make a covenant? Does he not himself say of some through the prophet: “I will give their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them” (Isa. 61)?

Jonathan’s soul was knit to David’s soul. By what glue, unless by the glue of love? By the glue of charity the soul of the righteous is joined to God, so that it adheres to him inseparably. Hence the Psalmist says: “But for me it is good to adhere to God” (Ps. 72). Considering both the union of soul and body and that of soul and God, he says of the former: “My soul has adhered to the pavement” (Ps. 113); of the latter, toward God: “My soul has adhered after you” (Ps. 62).

The flesh is the floor of the clay-built house which we inhabit, we who have an earthly foundation. The soul adheres to this foundation by affection; and if it adheres too much, it is dead, subjected to it and more remotely separated from God, so that it no longer holds the middle place but the lowest, as though already buried in the earth and entombed beneath the pavement. Therefore, when the Prophet had said, “My soul has adhered to the pavement,” he added: “Give me life according to your word” [Col. 0436D] (Ps. 118). It is made alive, however, when it is subjected not to the flesh but to God, so that the righteous person may truly say: “My soul has adhered after you.” It has adhered after you by preferring you to itself and placing itself after you, so that it loves you more than itself; loving not merely you for its own sake, but itself more for your sake, O Lord God of my salvation.

Here I would pray: draw me after you, so that my soul may thus adhere after you. This union of soul and God is far tighter, closer, and as it were far more inward than that other union. For God is in the soul, and the soul is in God; the soul also is in the flesh, but the flesh is not in the soul. The soul is in the flesh, lives in the flesh, and feels in the flesh. But the flesh is neither in the soul, nor lives or feels in it, although it receives from the soul the power both to live and to feel [Col. 0437A].

The soul gives life to the flesh, granting it movement and sensation: movement for doing something and rendering the soul service in carrying out the desires which it accomplishes through the ministry of the body; sensation, by which it can feel its own pleasures or sufferings, whether painfully or pleasurably. For the five bodily senses, each according to its own property, possess knowledge of sensible things and the use of them, together with an experience of pleasure or pain.

Moreover, both the flesh and the soul possess their own sufferings or pleasures, which each feels in itself with delight or pain; and reciprocally they suffer together or rejoice together in each other’s alternating goods or evils. For from the things which the flesh suffers anxiously, the soul wastes away pitiably; in those things which delight the flesh more sweetly, it becomes more cheerfully glad. Yet the soul, emulous of what is honorable, often feels illicit pleasures of the flesh through the affection of pleasure, yet dissents from those same pleasures through the moderation of reason. In a wonderful way it in some sense wills, or desires to will, what it does not fully will because it does not consent. Marvelously and ineffably, while the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, it seems divided within itself: it desires that the will of the spirit be fulfilled, and equally desires that the will of the flesh be fulfilled, sorrowful and anxious within itself because it longs for the will of the flesh to be accomplished while restraining itself from connivance in consent. For it loves the flesh so greatly that it grieves over its lot, bearing with difficulty that its will is not fulfilled—the very will which it itself wills not to be fulfilled.

But the soul wonderfully united to God through the love of obedience lives and feels in him and from him; and, drawing as it were a likeness from the bodily senses known to it, through the grace of inward inspiration it spiritually touches God, whom it feels in itself, by faith; smells him by hope; tastes him by charity; hears him by obedience; and sees him by contemplation.

## On Spiritual Touch

Touch belongs to faith, for faith grasps. Thus in the Gospel, when the woman suffering from an issue of blood believed that she would be healed if only she touched the fringe of Jesus’ garments, and when she touched in faith and perhaps unknowingly represented the touch of faith, the Lord said: “Who touched me?” (Luke 8). When the disciples wondered, as it were, that he said he had been touched while crowds pressed upon him, he added: “Someone touched me” (ibid.).

And when he had risen from the dead, he said to Mary: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20). He did not forbid spiritual touch, but rather bodily touch, lest spiritual touch should be hindered on its account: if Mary touched him merely as a man and trusted too greatly in bodily touching, she might not believe Jesus equal to the Father. For Jesus had not yet ascended in her heart to equality with the Father, since she did not yet believe him equal to the Father. Had he then ascended in her heart to the Father, without doubt Mary would already then have touched Jesus with the hand of faith. But because Mary was to touch Jesus spiritually, the touch by which faith could be weakened or impeded was forbidden.

Nor was permission to touch altogether withheld; it was postponed until the time of the visible or spiritual ascension, so that Mary might know that she truly touched Jesus when she began to touch his divinity, equal to the Father, with the hand of faith. For faith’s touch apprehends not only Christ’s humanity but embraces in devout handling his full divinity.

Mary was not unaccustomed to touching Jesus, nor was she conscious of any recent offence committed against Christ which might lead her to suppose herself prohibited from such familiar access. Nor is “Do not touch me” said to Mary in the same manner in which it is said to some: “Do not touch my Christs” (Ps. 104). Malicious intent is one thing; the service of devotion is another.

In the sinful Mary, we sinners receive consolation in both respects: both when she is permitted to touch Jesus and when she is forbidden to touch him. Let us not despair of pardon. We have indeed sinned greatly, and “in many things we all offend” (Jas. 3). Mary sinned, and yet she is permitted to touch Jesus and admitted into the grace of familiarity. Behold, here our hope is raised up. We have not been granted to see Christ in the flesh or to handle him with our hands; nevertheless, let us not despair. For Thomas was told: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20).

Mary too is told: “Do not touch me.” Behold, here also our hope is raised up and our consolation abounds. Thomas’s handling was allowed in order to drive away doubt and establish faith in the resurrection. Mary’s handling was forbidden, and in some way consoles us, to whom it is not granted to touch Jesus. It was allowed for him as necessary, since he did not yet believe; it was forbidden to her as unnecessary, since she already believed. For Mary already believed in the resurrection, but did not yet believe that Jesus’ glory, in equality with the Father, would be proclaimed to the world through the marvelous ascension. She therefore had to be led from faith to faith. Hence the glory of the ascension is now foretold to her, so that she who knew of the accomplished resurrection might also know beforehand of the future ascension.

Thus bodily touch, by which she might touch Jesus’ feet—though she was permitted to touch them when Jesus said to the women, “Greetings” (Matt. 28), for the sake of some mystery—is not required of Mary. Rather, spiritual touch is required: that by which she touches his head, namely his incomprehensible divinity, in which he is in every respect equal to the Father.

It is clear from what has been said that spiritual touch belongs to faith; and this is one of the five senses by which the soul joined to God feels God. For the soul feels God in five ways, and God feels the soul in five ways. From these five and five modes—thus from ten—the ten-stringed psaltery of the heart is fitted together: “A pleasant psaltery with the harp” (Ps. 80). It is added: Christ, rising from the dead, raises these together with himself, saying, “Awake, psaltery and harp; I will arise at dawn” (Pss. 107; 56).

The soul feels God by touching, as has been said, with the hand of faith. God feels the soul by touching with the hand of manifold grace: he touches it, as it were, unto tearful penitence and humbles the swelling of pride, as though it were a mountain. Hence it is written: “Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke” (Ps. 143). In the contrite and humbled heart is a vapor most sweet to the Lord; smoke bitter to the eyes draws forth the tear of compunction. He touches the place of leprosy in order to cleanse it. He touches and caresses the head by manifold consolation; touches the eyes for illumination; touches the cheeks by the flush of shame; touches the neck, that it may be like necklaces; touches the breasts, lest they be dry and without milk; he puts his hand through the opening, so that her inward parts tremble.

Finally, the bridegroom, with what is as it were marital liberty, touches the bride entirely: he mingles speech, joins kisses, tightens embraces. Yet his touch is most chaste, and by touching he makes chaste; and her whom he touches he preserves wholly whole, inviolate, and untouched [Col. 0439B]. For he is the bridegroom, jealously guarding the bride betrothed to him in faith, as it is written: “I will betroth you to myself for ever; I will betroth you to myself in righteousness and judgment, in mercy and compassion; and I will betroth you to myself in faith” (Hos. 2).

## On Spiritual Smell

By smell too the soul feels God and is felt by God. It smells his sweetness through hope and expectation of God. For hope is to the fulfillment of the promise what the flower is to the fruit. In the flower, scent is the hope and expectation of fruit; and through hope we await the promises of God, which are fragrant and sweet-smelling like ointments. We draw in their fragrance for our consolation amid the pressures of the present life; and by their scent we are drawn on to persevere tirelessly to the end, lest, by failing, we be drawn back from the purpose of the journey we have begun.

Hence the bride says to the bridegroom: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1). The bride also smells the bridegroom’s virtues as precious ointments. She smells them through the hope of imitation. For, stirred by the bridegroom’s example, she hopes in some manner to follow his footsteps; nor does she presume in any manner to follow by herself, as though from herself. Rather, sensing the fragrance of his knowledge, she hopes to be helped and says: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments.”

But if a living sacrifice pleasing to God is offered as a sweet fragrance; if the incense of devotion or the incense of pure prayer is kindled in the censer of the heart by the coals of charity; if the smoke of spices rises before God—then he smells a most sweet fragrance, perceiving the devotion of a soul burning within itself with holy desire; and he too is smelled by that soul.

## On Spiritual Taste

Through love, as through taste, God both feels and is felt. For Christ says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). And showing elsewhere what the Father’s will is, he says: “This is the will of him who sent me, the Father: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me” (John 5). Hence it appears that God is fed and refreshed by love for our salvation; and the soul is fed and refreshed by love of him, tasting how sweet God is.

## On Spiritual Hearing

[Col. 0440A]

Through hearing God feels and is felt, when he hears and is heard. He is heard through obedience; and if one obeys, he hears and answers prayers, petitions, supplications, vows, and desires. Man says to God: “Give ear to my words, O Lord” (Ps. 5). And God says to us: “Incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Ps. 77). For he who hears one who listens does not hear favorably one who does not listen. Hence it is written: “He who stops his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer shall be an abomination” (Prov. 28).

## On Spiritual Sight
