God feels and is felt through sight. For it is said of the righteous: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. 33). And the righteous person says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 24). But the wicked do not see God, walking in darkness; concerning them it is written: “They have not set God before their sight” (Ps. 53). Yet the eyes of the Lord behold the good and evil in every place. But with a gracious and gentle gaze they look upon the righteous; while to the wicked he says: “My eyes are upon you for evil, and not for good” (Amos 9).

As was shown above, the spiritual harp is fitted together from the bodily senses and the senses of the soul, mutually harmonizing through the obedience of the flesh subjected to the spirit. But from the five spiritual senses by which the soul feels God and agrees with God, and from the five ways by which God spiritually feels the soul, is fitted, as from ten strings, the spiritual ten-stringed psaltery. In it God, touching the five upper strings, plays to the soul; while the soul, touching the five lower strings, plays to God—delighting God and being delighted in God.

God touches the psaltery when he inspires grace; for he is spirit, and breathes where he wills, and the soul hears his voice (John 3). And so that the lower string may answer the upper string, grace anticipated returns grace: touching the one who touches, smelling the one who smells, tasting the one who tastes, hearing and contemplating the one who hears and contemplates.

God indeed goes before and sings the first note; and, as a psalmist, draws the psaltery into harmonious melodies, saying: “Let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet” (Song 2). For God works both willing and accomplishing (Phil. 2), and inwardly moves the soul to believe, hope, love, obey, and always see him whom it loves—feeling the one who feels, that is, always consenting to God’s will.

Therefore it is not without purpose, not without reason, that the Psalmist exhorts us five times to sing psalms, when he says: “Sing psalms to our God, sing psalms; sing psalms to our king, sing psalms; for God is king of all the earth; sing psalms wisely” (Ps. 46). There is some reason why he adds at the end, “wisely.” “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110); and he sings psalms wisely who exults in the Lord, yet always fears the danger of ruin. “Blessed is he who is always fearful” (Prov. 28). Hence the Prophet says: “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Ps. 85). And again: “Serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling” (Ps. 2).

Although the soul feels God through fear, fear is nevertheless not to be separated from the five spiritual senses mentioned above. For it is joined to each of them and tempers and preserves the whole spiritual harmony, lest through the laxity of false security it fall back into the danger of discord.

To return to the beginning of the discourse: the voice of Christ professing obedience and rendering submission to God the Father is this: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready” (Ps. 107). In this repetition a twofold obedience can be shown: one according to the soul subjected to God, the other according to the flesh humbled even to the shame of the cross. But the voice of Christ exulting in the glory of the resurrection is that which follows: “I will sing and make psalm in my glory; awake, psaltery and harp” (ibid.).

Christ had a twofold glory and a twofold joy: one from the glory of the soul, which is the psaltery upon which he plays; the other from the glory of the flesh, which is the harp upon which he sings, confessing to God upon the ten-stringed psaltery with a song upon the harp.

But for us, rising with Christ, this first voice can be applied according to our first and second resurrection. It is the voice of the penitent returning to obedience and promising obedience: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready.” Ready to do good things; ready to endure evil things; ready to begin; ready to persevere; ready for the obedience of the soul that will serve you, O God; ready for the obedience of the flesh that must be subjected to the spirit.

To the obedient person who serves God there is poured in a twofold joy for a twofold obedience: one from the obedience and peace of the flesh toward the spirit, and this is called the harp; the other from the peace and obedience of the spirit toward God, and this is called the psaltery. In these spiritual instruments a person justified by God through penitence and raised from death to life sings and makes psalm, but “in my glory.” “I will sing,” he says, “and make psalm in my glory.”

The first resurrection has its own glory: the glory of the flesh and the glory of the soul. Let us consult the Apostle concerning each glory. Concerning the present glory of the flesh he says: “But far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). Again: “If I must glory, I will glory in the things of my infirmity” (2 Cor. 11). But concerning the glory of the soul he says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). Again: “We glory in the hope of the adoption of the children of God” (Rom. 5).

But the second resurrection will have its own glory: the glory of the soul in the vision of God, when it sees God in his glory; and the glory of the flesh in its incorruption, when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption and this mortal shall put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15). Each of the saints will have a twofold robe; clothed in robes and in white, holding psaltery and harp, they will sing and make psalm in their glory, sounding forth eternal praises to God. Their mouth will be filled with joy and their tongue with exultation, to the praise and honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

# Fifth Treatise: On the Rest Which Christ Sought and Prepared for Himself and for Us

[Col. 0441]

On Ecclesiasticus 24: “In all things I sought rest, and in the inheritance of the Lord,” etc.

[Col. 0441C] The Wisdom of God, in whom all things were renewed and restored, is introduced in Ecclesiasticus as speaking and recounting certain works of her power—indeed, wonderful and astonishing works—and then adds: “In all these things I sought rest.” Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. God, moreover, is a certain supreme peace and supreme rest, being always the same, immutable and unchangeable; with him there is no change (James 1), because he does not change from what he was; nor “a shadow of turning” (ibid.), because he will not change from what he is. For change is the mutable condition of a mutable thing, and it cannot at all be predicated of God. He is not affected in turn by varying passions, nor is he found subject to alternating alterations; but as he always is what he is, [Col. 0441D] so he always is as he once is. Therefore he is always stable and at rest; nor does he need to seek rest for himself in himself, since he cannot be at variance with himself.

Again he says: “In all things I sought rest.” For whom, then, did he seek rest? For himself, or for us, or rather for himself and for us? It is plainly so. In all that he worked from the beginning for [Col. 0442C] our sake, he sought rest for himself in us, and for us in himself. For in all that he created, established, or made for humankind, he was acting so as to glorify humanity in himself, or to glorify himself in humanity; and so that they might have rest, sought in many ways, in one another: God being pleasing to humanity in all things, and humanity displeasing to God in none.

If we consider the course of time from the beginning, God is found now to be working and not labouring; now labouring and not working; now working by labouring and labouring by working. In the creation of the world God works and does not labour; and on the seventh day he rests, not from labour but from work. In this he set before humanity an example: before sin, to work without labour; afterwards, to rest. For this reason he placed the human being in paradise, to work and keep it.

[Col. 0442D] But after sin God labours in the perverse conduct of human beings and does not work. For he is not the author of iniquity but its detester. Thus, against the deeds of certain wicked persons, although they may even seem to pertain to his worship, he says in Isaiah: “I have laboured in enduring” (Isa. 1). And elsewhere in the same [Col. 0443A] prophet: “You have made me serve in your sins, and have given me labour in your iniquities” (Isa. 43).

But in his coming into the world God both works and labours. He works salvation in the midst of the earth, and labours unto death; by that death an end is imposed alike upon his labours and upon ours. Thus there is the labour of enduring our sins, and there is also the labour of suffering for our sins. God rests from the labour of enduring when that is fulfilled in us which is commanded through the prophet: “Cease to do perversely” (Isa. 1). For in our conversion we begin to humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, to be still before the Lord, and to tremble at his words. Hence he too rests in us, as he testifies, saying: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except [Col. 0443B] upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66.) And we rest in him, as he again says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

God rests from the labour of suffering, as he himself says: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4). And we too shall rest from our labours after death: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From henceforth,” says the Spirit, “let them rest from their labours” (Rev. 14).

Therefore, “In all things I sought rest.” As if he said: “In all my works I sought rest for myself—indeed, for myself in all, and for all in myself, so far as lies in me.” For God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to [Col. 0443C] the knowledge of truth (1 Tim. 2); yet he does not find rest in all, although he says to all: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened” (Matt. 11). But he finds rest in those who are foreknown to belong to the Lord’s inheritance. Hence he adds: “And in the inheritance of the Lord I shall abide.” “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord; the people whom he chose for his inheritance” (Ps. 32).

This is the inheritance of which it is written: “For the Lord chose Zion; he chose her for his dwelling-place. This is my rest for ever and ever” (Ps. 131). The Father gave this inheritance to him at his request, saying: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2). But the Son’s petition was the lifting up of his hands on the cross, [Col. 0443D] and that prayer of which it is written: “Let my prayer be directed as incense before you; the lifting up of my hands, an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140).

The Son therefore acquired this inheritance for himself by his blood, the Father thus commanding and directing. For this reason he now says: “Then the Creator of all commanded and said to me.” “Then” belongs to time, not eternity. As though he said: “When the fullness of time came, so that I might acquire the inheritance in which I should abide, I, awaited and desired, said: ‘Behold, I come’” (Ps. 39). “Then the Creator of all commanded and said to me.” He commanded as to a servant, as to one lesser according to humanity; he spoke as to a Son, as to one equal according to divinity.

What he commanded or what he said is not expressly stated, but is inferred from what follows. [Col. 0444A] So also elsewhere it is said: “Command, O God, your power” (Ps. 67). It does not state what God the Father wished to command his power—that is, Christ—but it is understood from what follows: that he may strengthen what he has worked in us. And elsewhere it is written: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148). What he spoke and what he commanded is shown from the accompanying words, though it is not expressly stated.

So in this passage we understand that God the Father, the Creator of all, commanded and said to Christ that he should be created according to his humanity. Hence Isaiah says: “And let righteousness spring up together: I, the Lord, created him” (Isa. 45). And the Son here, mentioning the Father as Creator of all in order to make known to us the form of the command, says of him: [Col. 0444B] “He who created me rested in my tent.” As though he said: “The Creator of all, by commanding me, created me and rested in me.” Of him he also says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3).

By his “tent” he means the humanity assumed, in which he fought mightily and defeated the powers of the air; and in that tent the Father rested. “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” The Father rested in the Son in order to establish the beginning of the rest sought, and afterwards to bring the sought-for rest to completion through the mystery of the Incarnation.

How rest is to be prepared for the Son by the Son himself in his inheritance, he shows when he says: “And he said to me: Dwell in Jacob, inherit in Israel, and strike your roots among my elect.” [Col. 0444C] The Son shows three things said and enjoined to him by the Father. If one prefers, the preceding words—“Then he commanded and said to me”—may be referred to these three. For, after the insertion concerning his Incarnation, he now at last adds what the Father commanded or said to him. And although above he used both expressions, “commanded” and “said,” nevertheless, because of the intervening passage, he repeats “and said” in order to set out what was said or commanded to him, for preparing rest for himself in his inheritance.

There are therefore three things—faith, hope, and charity—by which the hearts of the elect are prepared for Christ to rest in them. To these three correspond, in a most beautiful order, the three expressions distinguished here: “Dwell,” “inherit,” [Col. 0444D] “strike your roots.” “Dwell” pertains to faith, according to the Apostle’s words: “May he grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inward person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. 3). “Inherit” pertains to hope. For the inheritance promised is not yet seen, nor yet possessed in actuality, but is obtained by hope alone. Christ is the inheritance of the righteous, and is meanwhile inherited through hope; to him the Father says: “Inherit in Israel,” that is, “Be yourself the inheritance of Israel.”

He adds: “Strike your roots among my elect,” which pertains to charity. Hence the Apostle says: “Rooted in charity” (ibid.). By these three virtues God prepares rest for himself in his inheritance, and in the people whom he chose as his inheritance (Ps. [Col. 0445A] 32). “But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob, the line of his inheritance.” Therefore have faith, hope, and charity, and you will be of the house of Jacob, of the people of Israel, and of the number of the elect. Christ will inherit in you and be inherited by you; and he will strike his roots in you, so that he may remain in you for ever and rest in you as in his inheritance.

“In all things I sought rest,” etc. The Wisdom of God, who works all things in all, is Christ; he also works in us, most often without us, and sometimes as though we were assisting him, because “we are God’s fellow-workers.” He works with us in us those things which we work through him in him; similarly, he speaks in us those things which we speak through him in him. Thus the works and words of the righteous are the works and words [Col. 0445B] of Christ. Hence Peter says: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the utterances of God. If anyone ministers, let him do so from the strength which God supplies” (1 Pet. 4).

Whatever is rightly suggested to our heart for thought or to our mouth for speech is God’s and not ours; or, if it is in any manner ours, it is by no means from us. He knew this who said: “We have such confidence through him toward God—not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3). Hence the Psalmist says: “In God I shall praise my words” (Ps. 55). And again: “There is no speech on my tongue” (Ps. 138). As though he said: “It is not in my tongue, but rather in God, that I may utter fitting speech.” For whatever is worthily uttered is spoken by him who grants that it be [Col. 0445C] uttered. “Do you seek proof,” says the Apostle, “of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Cor. 13.) Therefore Christ speaks in his saints; Christ works in his saints, as it is written: “Lord, you will give us peace, for you have worked all our works for us” (Isa. 27). And the Apostle says: “He works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will” (Phil. 2).

Thus this utterance, “In all things I sought rest,” belongs so truly to Christ working and speaking in all the righteous that it also belongs to all the righteous; and it belongs so truly to all the righteous that it nonetheless belongs to Christ.

For when the righteous person seeks rest for himself, Christ seeks rest for himself in that righteous person, granting him this very thing: that he may seek rest for himself in Christ. Rest, [Col. 0445D] wherever it may be, is something greatly desirable and sought after. It is demanded by the prayers of all; it is pursued by the desires and sighs of all, both good and evil; it is sought amid every human toil. For all the pursuits of all people, all the inventions of craftsmen, all the exertions of workers, according to the desire of those who seek, tend toward rest and direct themselves toward rest; but they do not always attain rest in accordance with the outcome of their search.

Those who practice agriculture, those who pursue military service, those who engage in trade—indeed, those who pursue various kinds of study and labour and exert themselves in them—all desire rest in these things, seek rest, and strive toward something that delights them and in which they may delightfully rest. All human [Col. 0446A] business and leisure alike, all occupations and freedoms from occupation, turn to this and look to this. Often prolonged rest turns into weariness, and after weariness with rest, rest is again desired in the exercise of labour; and in this way rest is sought even while it is fled from. It is sought in labour, through labour, and after labour; and there is no end of labouring or seeking rest for those who do not enter upon the way of finding it.

The wicked, therefore, seek rest in all things but do not find it. “For destruction and unhappiness are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Ps. 13). But the righteous seek rest in all things, and, in order to find it, first find where rest is, and say: “In all things I sought rest,” etc. Behold, here is rest: namely, in the Lord’s inheritance, where the righteous purpose to abide in rest. What is the Lord’s inheritance except the congregation of the saints, of which it is written: “But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob, the line of his inheritance” (Deut. 32)?

When one thinks of abiding in the Lord’s inheritance, God the Creator—and therefore the merciful one—meets him as one returning from the path of error; he receives the fugitive servant returning to him, subjects him to his Lord, and lays upon him a command, that through obedience he may find rest. Therefore he says: “Then the Creator of all commanded and said to me.” He will shortly state in what follows what he commanded and said. But now he inserts certain matters and says: [Col. 0446B] “He who created me rested in my tent.”

Great is the righteous person’s hope of finding the rest he seeks. For at the very beginning of conversion to God, God, delighted by the purpose of a better life, rests in the heart of the one converting to him, in order to make the convert rest in himself. No one can rest in God unless God has rested in that person, and unless the Spirit of the Lord has rested upon that person. Hence he says: “And he who created me rested in my tent,” that is, in me as in a tent. For the righteous person is, as it were, God’s dwelling, according to the voice of the Son: “My Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). Or: “He rested in my tent,” that is, in my heart. For the righteous person dwells in the tent of the heart, where God also dwells. But the wicked, who do not remain with themselves, are exiles from their own heart. Hence they are recalled to their heart through [Col. 0446D] the prophet, who says: “Return to the heart, you transgressors” (Isa. 46).

“He who created me rested in my tent.” Although this utterance belongs to each righteous person, there is no doubt that in a special way it befits the most blessed Mother of God, who, bearing within her womb God—the Creator of herself and of all—claims this utterance for herself by a unique right, so as to say: “He who created me rested in my tent.” For “a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86).

But the righteous person converted to God has God dwelling and resting within through grace, so that, reverently receiving his commands and obeying him, that person may deserve through obedience to rest in him. For by obedience to the commandments the desired rest is prepared, [Col. 0447A] and after the labour which God has fashioned into the command, it is obtained by the merit of obedience. Therefore, in order to find rest, he is told: “Dwell in Jacob,” that is, in the people whom I loved: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1). As though it were said to him: “Let your way of life be among the good, and your dwelling among the righteous.” For among the wicked there is no rest, as it is written of some: “They mingled among the nations and learned their works; they served their carved images, and these became a snare to them” (Ps. 105).

Therefore the company of the wicked must always be avoided in spirit, though not always in body; always by dissimilarity of conduct, though not always by bodily separation. For often, while good and evil people live together, the wicked become more amendable, or the good become better and purer. [Col. 0447B] A lily springs up among thorns; so the righteous person grows like a lily among the wicked, is pricked amid thorns, and suffers tribulation from the wicked, as Jacob from Esau—the innocent from the harmful, the righteous from the unrighteous. Yet, so far as lies in that righteous person, he has peace with all, so that he may say: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119).

A file is indispensable in the workshop of smiths, scraping the rust from iron so that it may shine more brightly when polished. So too, in common life, an evil companion—even though he harms himself and intends to harm others—polishes and purifies those whom he persecutes. What then? Does the righteous person who says, “I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (ibid.), dwell here also in Jacob? He does indeed dwell there, if not in body, yet in spirit. For he walks simply, like Jacob (Gen. 25).

Jacob was a simple man, yet nevertheless prudent—so prudent that he supplanted Esau by purchasing his birthright, and supplanted him a second time by taking away his blessing (Gen. 27). Nor did he do so unjustly. For the blessing was lawfully due to him, and Esau despised his birthright: after selling it, he went away making light of it. And though, being born first, he hastened at the beginning toward the inheritance, in the end he lacked the blessing (Prov. 20). For “desiring to inherit the blessing, he was rejected” (Heb. 12); “for he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears.”

Whoever, therefore, acts simply in all things so as to harm no one, and prudently in all things so that no harm be done to him, that he may not be supplanted by anyone or defrauded of his [Col. 0447D] right, is Jacob: one who, so far as lies in him, keeps unimpaired and inviolate the right of fraternal fellowship. A peaceable manner of life amid one’s brethren is therefore commended to us. For the good among the wicked it is less pleasant, though often more useful; for the good among the good it is both useful and exceedingly sweet. Nothing is better in human society than mutual love; nothing sweeter than holy fellowship. To love and be loved is a sweet exchange, a fountain of life, a delight, and the reward of blessedness.

For how can a good and pleasant dwelling not be sweet, where God dwells and rests? “God is in his holy place; God makes those of one manner of life dwell in a house” (Ps. 67). The unity of social life is a figure and a kind of signification of that heavenly fellowship, where, through the communion of love, what belongs to each individual becomes common to all. Here is merit; there, reward. Here is figure; there, truth—yet this figure is not without truth. Here rest is begun; there it is perfected. [Col. 0448A] Perfect rest cannot be found in this place of affliction, this place of pilgrimage. Outside our inheritance there is no full rest for us.

Therefore there is added: “Inherit in Israel.” Jacob himself is Israel; he is the Lord’s inheritance, and the Lord is his inheritance. Every righteous person who supplants Esau—that is, the malignant one who hates his brother—so that the malignant person becomes as nothing in his sight, is Jacob. But the one who is strong against God, acting manfully and enduring God; who always sees God in fear, desire, hope, and intention, is Israel.

Jacob, as Israel, is himself the Lord’s inheritance. For of Israel it is written: “Israel, the work of my hands, my inheritance” (Isa. 19). And of Jacob: “He chose for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved” (Ps. 46). “For us,” he says, because what he chose benefits us; but he chose his own inheritance. What inheritance, except the beauty of Jacob whom he loved? This is Jacob’s beauty: namely, the form of faith and righteousness which Jacob displayed for all to set before themselves and imitate. He consented to dwell in Egypt for a time, where he did not wish even to remain after death, but wished to be carried to the land received in promise (Gen. 47), showing beforehand that the inheritance is not to be sought in [Col. 0448C] Egypt—that is, in the world—nor in this life, but when “God gives sleep to his beloved” (Ps. 126).

Israel’s inheritance is nothing other than that of which the Prophet says: “My portion, O Lord” (Ps. 118); and again: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15). But Esau, and those figured in him—the lovers of the world—despise and lose their right of inheritance for the food of the basest pleasure, for one meal only, soon to be ended. Of such it is written: “They regarded the desirable land as nothing” (Ps. 105). But Jacob despised the food and prudently acquired the right of the firstborn; hence he inherited the blessing. This inheritance is acquired through the love of God. Outside it, rest is sought in vain.

Therefore the person who seeks rest is told: “Inherit in Israel,” that is, “Strive and labour to be made an heir in Israel—not in Egypt, not among the nations that do not know God, but among the people Israel.” Therefore the inheritance of Israel alone is to be sought by those seeking rest, and sought perseveringly. “For the one who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10). Hence there is added: “Strike your roots among my elect.”

As covetousness is the root of all evils, so charity is the root of all goods. Of the former it is said: “I saw a fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty” (Job 5). A fool is one who places temporal things before eternal things. He has a firm root, but according to his own estimation and that of persons like him. For “he trusts in his own strength and glories in the multitude [Col. 0449A] of his riches” (Ps. 48), and: “They called blessed the people to whom these things belong” (Ps. 143). “Immediately,” he says, “I cursed his beauty.” The Psalmist agrees, saying: “God will destroy you utterly, pluck you from your tent, and uproot you from the land of the living” (Ps. 51).

Therefore, lest the love of God through instability of mind fall back into worldly covetousness, and lest love of neighbour, stirred by certain injuries, decline into hatred or contempt for one’s neighbour, the lover of God and neighbour is rightly told: “Strike your roots among my elect.” By these words one is admonished to stand with unshaken roots in both loves and to persevere to the end, that one may someday say: “And I took root among an honoured people.”

For the people of the righteous are indicated in three ways and, as it were, by three names: in Jacob, in Israel, and in my elect. Jacob is according to simple prudence: he walks simply and overcomes every stratagem, lest he himself be supplanted and lose his right. Israel is when he is strong enough to endure God, or blessed enough to see him. He is elect because, when he did not yet love, he was loved first. He is beloved and elect for the rest prepared for him, which will be given him in its time and completed in threefold felicity: namely, the communion of most blessed fellowship, the vision of the divine majesty itself, and the stability of endless eternity. Hence it is written: “In their land they shall possess double things; everlasting joy shall be theirs” (Isa. 61).

Love of neighbour corresponds to the first felicity; love of God to the second; and steadfastness in persevering—that is, loving to the end—to the third. [Col. 0449C] Let us therefore love our neighbour: in God, if that neighbour is good; for God’s sake, if that neighbour is evil. Let us love him so that we may dwell in Jacob—that is, remain in communion with the righteous and always be kept far from communion with the wicked—lest we ever belong to them, not even when we live among them or with them.

The law of this dwelling in Jacob is love of neighbour, through which the unity of brotherhood is preserved among the righteous, so that one may attain the communion of heavenly fellowship. Let us love God with all our heart and all our soul, so that we may inherit in Israel and seek no inheritance other than the vision of God himself, who swore to Abraham our father that he would give [Col. 0449D] himself to us (Luke 1). Let us persevere in love of God and neighbour to the end, so that our rest in the kingdom of God may endure without end.

### On threefold unrest

Let us consider here the threefold unrest which prevents the rest we desire, and which the frequent experience of troubles compels us almost unceasingly to consider. We are disturbed by the evil of time, that is, by all this mutability; by the evil of the heart, that is, our own covetousness; and by evil upon evil—the second upon the first, and a third still upon the second. “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6). The evil of time might indeed suffice to make us miserable enough; but the perversity of others and our own iniquity burden us beyond measure, so that we are more than sufficiently [Col. 0450A] miserable. What do I call us—miserable? Rather, worse than the miserable and utterly most miserable.

Where shall I turn away from misery so manifold and so great? Where shall I turn, that I may find rest? “In all things I sought rest,” but what I sought I found nowhere. O rest, where are you, and where shall I find you? I know that I shall not find you unless you come to me. Lord God, you alone are the rest of souls; and from all this misery there is no peace for us except through you and in you.

For my part, in order to find rest in you, I turned to your inheritance, where you rest, and said: “In the inheritance of the Lord I shall abide.” I said this by purpose of mind, desire of heart, and vow of profession. Now grant me to be able to say: “He who created me rested in my tent.” Make in me your tent and rest in me, [Col. 0450B] that I may rest in you. For this is your rest: the working of our rest.

Work, therefore, in me, that before all things and above all things I may love you; that I may desire nothing outside you, nothing except you or for your sake. Then there will be peace for me, and rest in my heart from evil covetousness, from the evil of my heart, from cares so many, so evil, so bitter, which devour my heart like birds with a most bitter bite. O how blessed I should call myself—indeed, feel myself in my heart—if, inflamed, burning, and sighing with desire for you alone, I could say with the Prophet: “Behold, what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. 72.)

If I could say this, why should I not immediately add in rejoicing: “Depart, depart, my most vain cares and [Col. 0450C] disturbances; for every human being is vainly troubled. Depart, my anxieties, and make room for my peace and rest, because God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever” (ibid.).

Lord God, rest of souls, if you grant me rest from evil covetousness, which is the root of all evils, what can another’s perversity harm me, when my own iniquity does not rule me? If Esau says, “I shall kill my brother”; if he persecutes Jacob and, leaving father, mother, and homeland, compels him to cross this Jordan with a staff, to ask and hope from God alone for bread to eat and clothing to cover himself, and to live in exile and servitude so many years far from his own borders—what can he do against Jacob? For you are a mighty helper, O God of Jacob.

Strengthen me, [Col. 0450D] Lord, in love of you and love of my neighbour, whom you have taught me to love for your sake. Strengthen me, I pray, so that for your sake I may be able to love even those who hate me. Even if my own brother is my enemy, so that I fear him greatly, may I nevertheless never hate him; but may I endeavour to appease him in his anger with gifts, repay good for evil, have him appeased instead of angry, find favour with him, draw him by services into loving me, and make a friend out of an enemy—never overcome by evil, but overcoming evil with good.

If, through you, so strong a love grows strong in me, Lord, then no human malice will henceforth disturb me. But when will the evil of time cease? How long will it last? So long as we are subject to time and to this mutability, there will be no peace for us from that evil. For not even the righteousness of the perfect can free them from the disturbance of time, until through death every deficiency of this mortality is consumed.

[Col. 0451A] Yet in the strength of your charity, Lord, those whom you have perfectly justified have peace already in the present from human evil and from the evil of the heart. “For righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84). But the evil of time has not yet failed; it is, however, sufficient for the righteous. Whatever is more is from evil and belongs to the wicked. For while the wicked seek vain, superfluous, and harmful things, they make their fetters heavier; and upon the evil of the day, the misery of common frailty, and the common necessity, they add the misery of an evil will and of superfluous and harmful anxiety.

For it is grave, burdensome, and miserable to seek necessities for the consolation of our common misery; but misery is multiplied when, amid affliction of flesh and spirit, one toils after useless and harmful things. This misery of one’s own will burdens most heavily those whom their own [Col. 0451B] will most delights; whereas the other misery belongs to common necessity and is therefore common to good and evil alike. It endures through the course of this time until the end, so that in it we may be exercised in your love, Lord, persevering to the end.

But when the evil of time fails with time itself, you will crown the perseverance of love with the permanence of eternity; and those who fail in time only until time shall then rest fully and unchangeably in you and shall fail no more. “For you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101).

I beseech you, Lord, at the end hear this small petition of mine, most useful to me and not difficult for you. Hear it, and do not put my face to shame. This is what I ask: do not place my portion with those to whom you swore in wrath, saying: [Col. 0452B] “If they shall enter into my rest” (Ps. 94); but grant that I may rest in the day of tribulation and ascend to our girded people (Hab. 3). On the day of my death say to my soul: “Rest in peace. Amen.”

## TREATISE SIXTH

[Col. 0451]

On the words of the Apostle: “The word of God is living and effectual, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword,” etc. (Heb. 4.)

[Col. 0451B] How great the power and how great the wisdom in the Word of God are is shown by these words of the Apostle to those who seek Christ, who is the Word, the power, and the wisdom of God. This Word, coeternal with the Father in the beginning, was revealed to the apostles in its appointed time, [Col. 0451C] proclaimed through them, and humbly received in the faith of believing peoples. Thus there is the Word in the Father, the word in the mouth, and the word in the heart. The word in the mouth is a sign of the Word that is in the Father; it is likewise a sign of the word that is in the human heart. The word in a human heart is either understanding of the word, faith in the word, or love of the word, when the word is understood, believed, or loved. When these three meet in one heart—so that Christ, who is the Word of the Father, is at once understood, believed, and loved—then he dwells there through faith. With wondrous condescension, God descends from the heart of the Father even to the heart of a human being, so that there he may be conceived and formed in a new manner, as the Apostle says to the Galatians:

“My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV).

When Christ is preached, the Word of God is heard—that is, understood—and thus believed, because faith comes by hearing; and thus loved. For there is no love of the word without faith in the word, nor faith in the word without hearing the word. For the one who loves believes, and the one who believes hears the words, either by the Spirit inwardly revealing them, who breathes where he wills, as it is written, “You hear his voice” (John III), or outwardly through a human preacher, while the Spirit nevertheless speaks within. Unless there is one who teaches inwardly, the speaker’s tongue labours in vain.

Understanding must be considered in two ways: either with respect to the beginning of faith, or [Col. 0452B] with respect to its end. For when the word is preached, it is not believed unless it is in some manner understood. The Spirit inspires this understanding, and it is called hearing, concerning which the Apostle says: “Faith comes by hearing” (Rom. X). That “hearing” is to be understood as “understanding” the same Apostle shows [Col. 0452C] when he says: “He who speaks in tongues speaks not to men but to God” (I Cor. XIV). “For no one hears,” that is, no one understands. For one who speaks in an unfamiliar language is like a barbarian to those who do not understand it; nor does he edify those who do not understand. Therefore understanding is necessary at the beginning of faith, so that what is announced as needing belief may be understood.

There is another understanding concerning the end—that is, the consummation—of faith, of which it is said: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. VII). Although this appears to concern future knowledge, it may also rightly be understood of the growth of faith in those who have their senses trained to know more fully the reason of faith, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks a reason concerning the faith and hope that are within us (I Pet. III).

[Col. 0452D] This Word of God, of which we are speaking, is living: the Father gave it to have life in itself, just as he himself has life in himself (John V). Therefore it is not only living, but also life, as it says of itself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). Since it is life, it is living in such a way as to give life. For, as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills (John V). It gives life when it calls the dead man from the tomb and says: “Lazarus, come forth” (John XI). When this Word is preached, it gives to its voice, heard outwardly in preaching, a voice of power perceived inwardly; through this voice the dead return to life, and from these stones children of [Col. 0453A] Abraham are raised up.

Thus this Word is living in the heart of the Father, living in the mouth of the preacher, living in the heart of the believer and lover. Since this Word is so living, there is no doubt that it is also effective. For it is the omnipotent Word. When it said, “Let there be light” (Gen. I), light was immediately made. When it said, “Let there be lights” (ibid.), the lights were immediately made. There is no delay before whatever it says to be done is done. For this Word runs swiftly, and in its swiftness the heights of the heavens, the expanses of the lands, and the depths of the waves suddenly came into being. For with this Word no word is impossible.

It is effective in the creation of things, effective in the government of the world, effective in the redemption of the world. What is more effective, what more powerful? “Who shall utter his mighty acts, and make all his praises heard?” (Ps. [Col. 0453B] CV). It is effective when it acts, and effective when it is preached. For it does not return empty, but prospers in all things to which it is sent (Isa. LV). It is effective, and “sharper than any two-edged sword” (Heb. IV), when it is believed and loved. For what is impossible to one who believes, or difficult to one who loves?

When this Word speaks, its words pierce the heart like the sharp arrows of a mighty man (Ps. CXIX); they enter like nails driven deep, and enter so far as to penetrate the innermost parts. For this Word is sharper than every two-edged sword: stronger than every force or power in cutting, subtler than every acuteness of human intelligence, and keener than the subtlety of all human wisdom and learned discourse. For a two-edged sword is the force of authority; a two-edged sword is also the sharpness of reasoning or the subtlety of discourse. If we inquire concerning force or authority, the explanation is plain.

For there are two powers by which this world is governed: royal power and priestly authority. Of these it was said: “Behold, here are two swords” (Luke XXII). A king bears the sword. The Lord shows how much this sword can do when he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X). And again: “Do not be terrified by those who kill the body, and after this have nothing more that they can do” (Luke XII). This sword is two-edged, cutting on both sides. It cuts and kills the body; it cuts the soul by the force of pain, but [Col. 0453D] does not kill it. For it separates the soul from the body with pain, but does not separate it from the life hidden in God. It dissolves the union of body and soul, but does not dissolve the union of God and soul.

“Who,” says Paul, “shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or persecution, or the sword?” (Rom. VIII). As though he said: Not even the sword. This sword can do much, but not this. Sharper than that sword, then, is the Word which, namely through the authority granted to the Church, can destroy both heart and soul in the hell of fire (Matt. X). For the rulers of the Church possess a sword in the power of the Word of God. Is it not written: “Two-edged swords are in their hands” (Ps. CXLIX)? Is it not written: [Col. 0454A] “A sword is in their lips, for who has heard?” (Ps. LVIII)? And if it is said of evil men, “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. LIV), how much more is Peter’s tongue a sword—and a sword sharpened on both edges?

Moreover, the sharpness of human intelligence and judgment, and the subtlety of discourse, like a two-edged sword of the finest material, by discernment divide truth from falsehood, good from evil, honourable from dishonourable, and the other opposites subject to ingenious and technical inquiry.

From this all worldly philosophy and human wisdom have flowed. Ignorant of the limit of their own possibility, they dared to attempt matters beyond themselves, to which, left to themselves, they could in no way attain. For while exercising themselves in lofty and profound inquiries [Col. 0454B] concerning God’s nature, the origin of the world, the condition of the soul, and the character of justice and blessedness, they did not find the way of truth and could not reach the wisdom of God hidden in mystery. Therefore the wisdom of God says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the prudence of the prudent” (I Cor. I). And again: “I will catch the wise in their own craftiness” (I Cor. III). And the Prophet says: “The wicked have told me fables, but not according to your law, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII).

Whatever the wise of this world have wrought by the most subtle investigation differs from truth just as much as it disagrees with the Word of God; and, like fabulous tales, contains nothing in itself but falsehood or vanity. But the Word of God [Col. 0454C] is truth; and, like a two-edged sword—indeed, sharper than every two-edged sword (Heb. IV)—it searches all things with discernment both most subtle and most true, even the depths of God. Therefore, whether we consider the two-edged sword in terms of power or wisdom, it is clear that the Word of God, which can do all things and searches all things, is sharper; for it is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

Although this Word works all things wonderfully in all things, it works more wonderfully in the hearts of the saints through the effect of its grace—that is, through fear and love and the other holy virtues—as through certain inward words; and it displays its power and wisdom by penetrating all inward things and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit.

[Col. 0454D] That this may shine forth more clearly, it must be observed that “soul” and “spirit” are spoken of in three ways: according to nature, according to fault, and according to grace. They are spoken of according to nature when they must be understood according to what they naturally are, or according to what they naturally possess from the origin of their creation. When it is said, “The first man Adam was made into a living soul” (I Cor. XV), or when it is said in the Athanasian Creed, “A rational soul and flesh are one human being,” “soul” is here understood according to nature. When it is said, “Who knows what belongs to a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him?” (I Cor. II), “spirit” is understood according to the nature of its essence.

When it is said, [Col. 0455A] “He who hates his soul in this world preserves it unto eternal life” (John XII), “soul” is understood not only according to nature but also according to fault. When it is said, “He remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII), “spirit” is understood according to fault. When it is said, “He who loves iniquity hates his soul” (Ps. X), it is not to be understood according to the hatred of fault, but of nature or grace. But when it is said, “The Lord preserves you from every evil; may the Lord preserve your soul” (Ps. CXX), “soul” is understood according to nature and grace. When it is said, “If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live” (Rom. VIII), it is understood according to grace.

Although soul and spirit are the same in the nature of their essence, they are sometimes distinguished as though different, as in the Apostle’s words: “May God himself sanctify you wholly; and may your spirit and soul and body be preserved entire, without reproach, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Thess. V). And in the present passage: “Reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. IV). Here, because soul and spirit are joined together as things divided, the very conjunction appears to call for some distinction. And, as it seems to me, spirit belongs to the worthier and better part, namely to the life by which one lives to God.

The soul indeed, since it too is spirit, lives to God when it lives well, according to the Prophet: “My soul shall live to him” [Col. 0455C] (Ps. XXI); and this is the life of grace. When it lives badly, it lives for itself, since it serves the fulfilment of its own will; and this is the life of fault. There is also the life of nature, which the soul imparts to the body through the functions of the limbs, giving it movement and sensation. Life according to nature is common to good and evil persons; life according to fault belongs only to evil persons; life according to grace, by which one clings to God, belongs only to good persons.

According to this life by which one clings to God, “spirit” is not inappropriately understood in this passage, since it is written: “He who clings to God is one spirit” (I Cor. VI). “Soul” in the present passage is not inappropriately understood either as temporal life, according to which both good and evil persons naturally live; or as the culpable [Col. 0455D] and undisciplined life, according to which people live badly, though only evil persons do so.

Thus two kinds of martyrdom are suggested here, where the living and effective Word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword, is said to reach even to the division of soul and spirit. For now the flesh itself is sacrificed for Christ, now the will of the flesh that desires against the spirit. When the flesh is sacrificed and killed by the persecutor’s sword, does not the living Word of God, through fear and love of God, reach even to the division of soul and spirit? Does not Christ say, “I lay down my soul for my sheep” (John X)? Does he not also say, “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII)? Does not Stephen, the first martyr, when he laid down his soul for his friends, say: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” [Col. 0456A] (Acts VII)? Does not Paul also say: “Bonds and tribulations await me; but I fear none of these things, nor do I make my soul more precious than myself” (Acts XX)?

He said “myself” on account of the spirit that clung to God; “soul,” on account of the temporal life which he despised for God. This is the soul of which it is said: “Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat” (Matt. VI). And again: “Is not the soul more than food?” (ibid.). Therefore, when the persecutor’s sword rends the bodies of martyrs and divides and separates them limb by limb, the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God, inwardly divides between soul and spirit; because fear or love of God grows strong inwardly and stands immovably, even to contempt for the soul, for the confession of truth or the defence of justice.

[Col. 0456B] A similar cause, though not an equal glory, is found in spiritual conflict, when resistance is made to the flesh desiring against the spirit, and one renounces one’s own will. Whoever lays aside the pride of self-will lays down his soul for God. This is the soul of which it is written: “He who does not hate his soul cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). Do you see how the Word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaches even to the division of soul and spirit?

There are certain wills which cling to the soul slightly and only on the surface, having not struck roots deeply; they can easily and painlessly be scraped away, like the hairs of the flesh by a razor drawn over them. [Col. 0456C] Yet, when one renounces such a will for God, God repays some reward for this; because not a hair of the head shall perish. But other wills are driven in more deeply and cling more firmly; without bloody pain they cannot be cut off at all, or scarcely can be. Therefore, just as this visible sword, handled by the hand, when it cuts and divides things joined together, makes a wound of pain and the pain of a wound, so the sword of the Spirit, cutting on the one side through love and on the other through fear, divides things commonly loved as though they were joined together, when it compels that to be despised which is loved, lest that be lost which is loved more.

One loves God, and one also loves one’s flesh, which no one ever hated (Eph. V). These are commonly loved by the righteous, [Col. 0456D] but not equally: God is loved more and the flesh less. Therefore, when a persecutor presses, the life of the flesh is despised lest the life hidden in Christ be lost. Nevertheless, when concern for preserving the body is cast aside through love or fear of God, it is as though a limb firmly attached were cut off with severe pain. So too, when one’s own will—which through appetite, though not through consent, is loved together with God—is cut off for God’s sake, the spirit divides things joined together and inflicts a wound by the force of pain.

### On the division of the soul by itself

In the manner already set forth, this sword reaches to the division of soul and spirit, dividing soul from spirit, natural or [Col. 0457A] carnal life from spiritual life. This sword also reaches to the division of the soul by itself, and likewise to the division of the spirit by itself; but more needs to be said concerning the division of the soul.

The soul is a simple nature, indivisible in essence, united to each body in unity of person: one alone to one alone, one to one; and therefore it is rightly called the unique soul of a unique person. Nevertheless, when this soul loves according to God those whom it knows should be loved for God’s sake, it joins itself to those whom it embraces in charity through the affection of charity. Divided within itself by the affections of love, it lives not only in the body to which it is personally united, but in some way also extends life and feeling beyond itself to those to whom it joins itself through love. Therefore it feels not only its own goods and evils, but gives itself over to feeling what belongs to others, by rejoicing with them or suffering with them. Thus the sword of the Spirit cuts not only through the pain of one’s own suffering, but also through compassion for another’s pain. And the pain of the compassionate person may be harsher than that of the sufferer.

For often, when a child is ill, the grieving mother is more tormented than the child who suffers. Love does this: it transfers another’s pain into itself and, with an increase of pain, makes one suffer more compassionately than the other suffers. Sometimes one wishes to suffer alone, so that the other may not suffer. In the suffering of compassion, however, the compassionate soul is in some manner divided from itself and within itself. For when the one who is loved suffers, the soul yields itself to that person and pours itself forth beyond itself, in order to make that person’s pain common to itself. Through the service of compassion it unites itself to that person, so as to suffer in that person’s place; and in a certain sense makes itself belong to the one into whom it has poured itself through compassionate affection, as though living with the one whose torment it feels.

Thus, when the aged Simeon prophesied concerning Christ and said, “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign which shall be contradicted” (Luke II), he immediately added, speaking to the Blessed Virgin: “And a sword shall pass through your own soul” [Col. 0457C] (ibid.). That is: a sword shall pass through your soul as though it were his own. It may also be understood thus: “your own soul,” that is, your proper soul, shall be pierced by a sword. In this manner of speaking, used by certain holy teachers, the Apostle says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. II), that is, your proper salvation.

For the Mother of God, who loved more than all others—as she was also loved more than all others—so compassionated her dying Son as though she truly suffered. For the measure of her pain corresponded to the measure of her love. Since she loved her Son more than herself, the wounds he received in his body she bore in her mind with an inward feeling of pain. Christ’s Passion itself was martyrdom to her. For Christ’s flesh was in some sense her flesh—that is, flesh from her flesh. She loved more in Christ than her own flesh in herself the flesh he had taken from her. The more she loved, the more she suffered; she suffered more in mind than a martyr in body. Therefore she shines forth with the singular privilege [Col. 0458A] of a glorious martyrdom.

Other martyrs were brought to their martyrdom’s completion by their own death. But she supplied flesh from her own flesh, destined to suffer for the salvation of the world; and in Christ’s Passion, and from that Passion, the force of pain so possessed her soul that, as though consummated in martyrdom in Christ, she is believed to have merited the highest glory of martyrdom after Christ.

### Again, on the division of Mary’s spirit and soul

There is another point to consider here, as belonging to the division of soul and spirit. For when the Mother of God knew that the salvation of the world would result from the death of her only-begotten Son, she both willed and grieved over his death. She willed it for her own salvation and ours alike; yet she grieved because she was [Col. 0458B] a mother—the mother of Christ’s weakness, and weak herself. Therefore, between the sorrow of her soul and the joy of her spirit, which rejoiced in God her Saviour, the sword of the Spirit made division: that sword which divided father from son, brother from brother, bridegroom from bride, friend from friend, soul from spirit, soul from soul, spirit from spirit, love from love, hatred from hatred, love from hatred, peace from peace, war from war, and peace from war.

“I came not,” the Lord says, “to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). Who can know all the divisions of soul and spirit which those wounded by charity cannot fail to feel within themselves, yet cannot count because of their multitude? For the division of soul and spirit is manifold; and as the Word of God touches the heart in many ways, so in many ways it reaches to the division of soul and spirit.

### On the division of the spirit by itself

Although from what has been said concerning the division of the soul by itself one may discern what the division of the spirit by itself is, nevertheless, so that an occasion may be given to the wise person to become wiser, I wish briefly to touch upon this division of the spirit itself.

God is spirit; and “he who clings to God is one spirit” (I Cor. VI). But the human spirit, since it cannot gather and unite all that is divided and scattered within it unless it joins itself to the one and simple God, nevertheless divides itself toward God [Col. 0458D] when it joins itself in various ways and, in joining itself, seeks in various ways to join more closely and to be joined. And who is sufficient for these things? Who can count all the excesses of fear, wonder, amazement, meditation, and contemplation? Who can count the stings of compunction, the joys of devotion, the measures of jubilation, the drawn-out sighs, the sobs of groaning, the heats of longing, and the intentions of prayer? He alone can count these who counts the days of the age and the drops of rain. He can comprehend and number them.

For the mind fixed in the love of God is subject to innumerable passions of love and affected in innumerable ways. While it wondrously alternates the changes of its affections, it nevertheless loves steadfastly and immovably. While it varies itself in manifold ways, [Col. 0459A] it divides itself toward God, but does not divide itself from God; nor does it separate from itself the one whom, amid so great a variety, it persists in loving.

Therefore the sword of the Spirit reaches to the division of the spirit. This sword pursues the old man in such a way that it is too little merely to kill him unless it also cuts into pieces the one it has killed, utterly crushes him, and reaches even to the division of joints and marrow, until the body of sin is wholly destroyed. Thus Samuel’s sword not only killed Agag, the very fat one, but also cut him into pieces (I Kings XV). Let us therefore attend more carefully to how this sword divides the joints, and then how it reaches the division of the marrow.

Whether the life of a sinner is considered limb by limb, as it were, through its individual sins, or is brought as a whole before the eyes of the heart, it is found to have both joints and marrow. For an evil life is joined together from many sins just as one body is joined from many limbs. The joints of the limbs are the connections of the parts. One sin is joined to another either by the movement of one’s own will or by the judgment of divine severity. For one who sins and plans to remain in sin by living wickedly commits certain sins through other sins; some for the preparation of later sins, some for the concealment, excuse, or defence of earlier ones; some after delay and deliberation held within oneself, others through the impulse of a sudden will, as though by the occasion of a present temptation [Col. 0459C] and the accidental occurrence of an available opportunity.

The connections of sins, arising both from premeditated and sudden causes, are like the joints of limbs, from which the sinner’s life, like one body, grows and advances toward its own increase, until iniquity is completed. For, as the merits of sins demand and the equity of divine judgments ordains, when a sinner despises repentance and resists the divine will, that person is sometimes abandoned to his own will and permitted to fall from sin into sin: neglect of repentance for earlier sins becomes the cause of later offences. Thus, while iniquity is added to iniquity, the sinner is excluded from both justice and the kingdom.

Hence it is written: “Add iniquity [Col. 0459D] to their iniquity, and let them not enter into your justice. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the just” (Ps. LXVIII). This is the end of those who abuse the riches of God’s goodness and, while piling sins upon sins, store up God’s wrath for themselves, until the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all their injustice.

Repentance, then, must not be neglected. Through it the living and effective Word of God, by the fear of the dreadful and terrible judgment, dissolves the joints of the old life and the connections of the former manner of living, as though they were the joints of one body. It reaches such a degree in dividing the joints that it breaks all the bonds of sins, lest sin cling to sin by any bond. Thus the prophet says: “Loose the bonds of impiety; remove the burdens that weigh down” [Col. 0460A] (Isa. LVIII).

Therefore the Word of God divides the joints when, through contrition of heart, it tears apart piece by piece everything wickedly connected in our depraved habits; when it crushes it “like a calf of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII); when it pulls apart from one another all things that cling persistently together; when it tears every limb of the old man from its joints, and, once the joints are loosened, leaves no limb undivided from the rest. These limbs are those the Apostle mentions when he says: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, covetousness” (Col. III).

Though a single sin is a limb of the body of sin, or of the body of the old man, it may nevertheless itself be called a body, because it is completed by its parts just as one body is made whole by its joints. That sin is called a body is shown by the Lord’s saying: “If your eye is evil, your whole body also will be evil” (Matt. VI). This may not improperly be applied to the sinner’s whole life, which is understood to be wholly dark when the purpose of living is directed toward self by one who lives for self. Yet this also is rightly believed to apply to some single sin, because, when the intention of an action is distorted by the fault of error or iniquity, even that which appears rightly done is reckoned among works of darkness.

[Col. 0460B] This body, however, is dissolved by the division of its joints when the entire structure of sin is examined by the testimony of a faithful conscience; when the quality, quantity, manner, and cause of the sin, and every circumstance of it, are accused as before God; when the whole heart is shaken within itself by everything that brings shame and terror; and when, in hope of pardon, it is wholly kindled to love God, and, broken into small pieces, is offered wholly to God as a holocaust, like a sacrifice cut into pieces.

Therefore the sword of the Spirit reaches even to the division of the joints. It also reaches to the division of the marrow (Heb. IV). Bones are moistened by marrow, and in the whole body nothing is found more inward than marrow. Therefore that which is most inward in our thoughts, affections, and actions is the marrow of the body. What is more inward in our desire than that which is especially desired? [Col. 0460D] What is more inward in our hope than that which is hoped for? What is more inward in our love than that which is especially loved? What is more inward in all the thoughts and affections of the heart than that which is thought and desired above all else?

If one asks what this most inward thing is, then, speaking of sins, nothing else occurs than the pleasure of sin. For sinners, at the beginning, progress, or end of their sins, desire and seek nothing more than the pleasure which is felt in sinning or hoped for in feeling. Often one wishes to sin apart from present pleasure, but never except mediately or immediately for the sake of pleasure. Often one wishes to sin when pleasure is present; but one never wishes to sin except so that pleasure may be present. What, then, is more inward in sins, or what should more truly be called the marrow of sin, than pleasure, which is chiefly sought in every sin, even where it is not found?

To turn our discourse from sin to justice: what should more properly be called the marrow of justice than the inward richness—that is, the inward delight—of justice itself?

### On the threefold fatness of the good

If we consider the bodies of animals and their fatty parts, there appears a certain fatness adhering outwardly to the flesh itself; then another, inner fatness adhering to the vital organs, which is usually called *adeps*; and then another fatness filling the bones, which is wholly fatness, and this is marrow. Likewise, even in the first beginnings of justice, the soul of the righteous has a certain fatness within itself, insofar as it delights in the law of God; but this is as though clinging to the flesh, because, weighed down by the former habit of the flesh, it does not yet freely aspire to the perfection of justice.

[Col. 0461B] But when, having ascended certain steps of justice, it begins to feel that it has advanced in its progress, it desires to be filled with an inward fatness which adheres to the vital organs, as is shown by the one who says: “May my soul be filled as with *adeps* and fatness” (Ps. LXII). It desires, indeed, to be filled with *adeps*, and thus to be made inwardly and completely fat, so that its holocaust may become fat, until, with the perfection of justice fulfilled and with fullest delight in its love, it may at last, as though made rich to the marrow, say: “I will offer you holocausts full of marrow” (Ps. LXV), etc.

There are righteous persons who use this world in such a manner that, in unlawful and forbidden things, they prefer to lack rather than possess; but in lawful things they prefer to possess rather than lack. Thus they use, by permission, whatever has been allowed: wives, possessions, and the other things granted to human weakness, which may be used without danger to salvation if one wishes to use them. There are others who, from zeal for perfection, renounce all things, even those allowed, as far as human weakness permits. In accordance with the Apostle’s counsel, having food and coverings, they are content with these (I Tim. VI). In spiritual goods they are richer by as much as, for God’s sake, they are found poorer in the goods of this age.

Therefore justice has outward fatness, and inward fat or marrow; and it is inward in proportion as it is deeper [Col. 0461D] and more perfect. For according to another line of consideration, delight in justice may be called marrow not only in the justice of the perfect, but also in the justice of beginners and those making progress. For no justice is so moderate or so slight that it does not have some strength attached to it according to the measure of its moderation, and delight in that strength, as marrow is in bone.

### On the threefold fatness of the evil
Iniquity too has its own richness, fatness, and marrow: in those who grow fat alike through love of, and abundance in, temporal things, and, lifted up in pride, kick against the goad, obeying God less; and who, as iniquity grows through an unrestrained use of the very things in which they abound and through luxurious habit, grow fatter still. [Col. 0462A] Then, by a greater pride through the practice of vices, they are fattened by the very love of iniquity; finally, through an arrogant estimation of themselves, they expand and swell, as it were with the fullest fatness of presumption, even to open contempt of God, so that they forsake God their maker and depart from God their saviour, as it is written: “The beloved grew fat and kicked against the goad; grown fat, made stout, enlarged” (Deut. 32). And again: “They have enclosed themselves in their fat; their mouth has spoken pride” (Ps. 16). And again: “Their iniquity came forth as if from fat; they passed into the desire of their heart. They thought and spoke wickedness; they spoke iniquity on high” (Ps. 72).

Thus iniquity, as though beginning from the surface of the heart, gradually [Col. 0462B] and gently enters into its inward parts, until the marrow of iniquity becomes like oil in its bones. For there is in the soul that which desires evil; there is also in it that which consents that what is desired should be done; there is in it that which moves the members of the body, like weapons of iniquity unto iniquity, to accomplish the deed according to the desire of that which desires and consents. There is in the same soul that which takes delight in the very deed that is desired, consented to, and toward which it moves itself—so much so that it moves even its body into the service of ministry, that what delights it may be fulfilled. For all these things are directed toward delight.

Moreover, in the soul itself there is that which presides over all these things and to which are pleasing, first desire, then consent, then movement toward the deed, and [Col. 0462C] finally delight in the deed. But when these four—namely desire, consent, movement toward the deed, and the deed resulting from movement—are pleasing together, they have as both the reason why they please and their end the delight which is sought and desired in the deed. Therefore there are five things: desire, consent, movement toward the deed, the deed resulting from movement, and delight in the deed. Yet four of these are found in the soul: desire, consent, movement toward the deed, and delight in the deed. The deed itself, however, is not in the soul; rather, by the power and will of the soul voluntarily moving the body, it is outwardly performed through the service of the body for the sake of delight, which is sought in the deed itself or from it.

By “from it” I mean on account of some deed which perhaps does not delight, but which is nevertheless performed for the sake of something else that does delight. When [Col. 0462D] these three—desire, consent, and movement toward the deed—are pleasing together for the sake of the deed or of the delight of the deed, one may observe that delight is not joined to the deed alone, but also to the three preceding elements, which are pleasing because of that very delight in the deed. Desire, therefore, has its own delight when the act of desiring itself pleases.

### That the Desire for Evil Is Not in Human Power

These persons often desire what they wholly do not will and from which they wholly dissent; they fully feel the desire for evil, yet do not consent to it. Though they are granted power to restrain desire from proceeding, they cannot prevent it from arising, nor command it to rest. For the desire for evil is not in a person’s power in such a way that, at his choice, it does not arise while at rest, or rests when it has arisen, or even ceases to grow to some extent. Therefore the righteous person, though he is the Lord’s freedman and has been delivered from the yoke of sin, is nevertheless not yet free in this respect, because he has not yet been wholly liberated from the concupiscence of the flesh, which is stirred by the desire for evil.

But he is free insofar as he has evil concupiscence in his power: through the grace of God, by whom he has been freely justified, he can restrain it so that it does not reach consent to the deed. For this grace is given to the justified person. Yet the justified person, though established in this freedom with God’s grace assisting him, may, when tempted by concupiscence, refuse consent; but, as has been said, before concupiscence is stirred through unlawful desire, he cannot restrain it from arising. Nor does he have it in his power that it should not [Col. 0463B] grow at least somewhat, or that it should immediately subside. For grace of such power is not yet given to a human being, even one justified.

Nevertheless, a righteous person can, by long practice and exercise of discipline, obtain grace such that this concupiscence arises less often, increases less, and subsides more quickly. But the sinner, who through consent to sin is a slave of sin, binds himself all the more and more tightly in the chains of this slavery insofar as he more greatly desires concupiscence to stir within him, even when it is not stirred.

For some, plunged into the depths of iniquity, provoke it by elaborate means and procure incentives to sin, in order to satisfy their will, by which they desire the effect of their habitual foulness even when they feel no present inclination. They love sin so greatly [Col. 0463C] that they wish to sin when they cannot sin. So greatly do evil concupiscence itself and its movement—namely evil desire or inclination—please them that they are unwilling to lack them, but desire them to increase in themselves more and more. This is profound iniquity.

Concupiscence is the cause and beginning of the sin that follows, just as delight is the end toward which the desire and consent of sin tend. Concupiscence is hateful as death, because through the delight of sin it leads to death, as it is written: “When concupiscence has conceived, it bears sin; but sin, when it is completed, brings forth death” (Jas. 1). Therefore the righteous person rightly hates concupiscence as death and rightly fights against it with all his strength and with the whole discipline of spiritual warfare, in order at least to weaken what he cannot wholly uproot. The more a righteous person hates this concupiscence, the more he loves righteousness. The more the concupiscence of the flesh, which desires against the spirit, decreases, the more the concupiscence of the spirit, which desires against the flesh, increases. As injustice begins from the concupiscence of the flesh, so righteousness takes its beginning from the concupiscence of the spirit. Therefore to hate the concupiscence of the flesh and to love the concupiscence of the spirit is a kind of righteousness, without which neither one who begins can be righteous, nor one who advances, nor one who arrives at perfection. And one advances and approaches perfection all the more insofar as one hates the former and loves the latter more.

### That Three Things Bring the Delight of the Concupiscence of the Spirit to Completion

[Col. 0464A]

Three things bring to completion love of the latter and hatred of the former: desire for righteousness, purpose, and the execution of both. Desire alone, without purpose and execution, is empty desire and does not touch the sinner’s heart; it pierces for an hour, but in the time of temptation it becomes empty through its own frivolity. Such perhaps was the desire of Balaam the diviner, when, beholding the tents of Jacob, he was moved and said: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last things be like theirs” (Num. 23). Many criminal, disgraceful, and wicked people have a desire of this kind: they are uselessly moved for an hour toward righteousness because they damnably return to guilt.

Some have [Col. 0464B] a desire for righteousness together with a purpose of a better life; but what they plan they defer far into the future, either setting no limit to their delay or, after a deadline, appointing another deadline; and when that arrives, they seek yet another occasion for endless postponement after postponement. If they should happen to be overtaken, neither desire nor purpose for the delayed righteousness frees them from the punishment of injustice. Therefore, for those who desire and purpose the way of righteousness, execution of their desire and purpose is necessary.

It is one thing, by going, already to be making one’s way to Jerusalem and to have the face of one going to Jerusalem; it is another thing, through idle desire, to plan the journey, always to defer it, and never to set out. The execution of holy desire and holy purpose is the exercise of body and soul according to the concupiscence of the spirit against the concupiscence of the flesh: consenting to the former unto righteousness and never giving assent to the latter against righteousness.

But desire and purpose for righteousness, together with the tireless pursuit of both, bring to completion holy hatred against the concupiscence of the flesh, which begins injustice through desire and purpose for evil, without the desire and purpose for good having been brought to completion. Desire and purpose for evil suffice to make a person evil; but desire and purpose do not suffice to make a person good. Yet without them no one is good, and no one is most evil without their absence. For those who have neither purpose nor desire for good love evil concupiscence beyond all measure, not as persons drawing an evil inclination into themselves through a temptation of the mind, [Col. 0464D] but as persons who, apart from temptation, willingly pass into that inclination. Of them it is written: “Their iniquity came forth as if from fat; they passed into the desire of the heart” (Ps. 72). And again: “They desired a desire in the wilderness” (Ps. 105).
