This concupiscence, if it is not resisted, first deprives a person of consent to good, then of purpose and desire for good, until it subjects to itself the entire will and the entire reason, so that no movement of the will toward good even stirs, nor does any spark of reason present even a little light; rather, the whole heart is hardened and darkened, and the lamp in Israel is extinguished. But when neither the will moves toward desire for good nor reason moves toward purpose for good, victorious concupiscence triumphs gloriously over both, having subjected them to itself. One who is thus conquered by victorious concupiscence and so blind as to love it must consequently hate the concupiscence of the spirit, which stands opposite it.

For he hates righteousness; he hates consenting to righteousness; he hates even desiring righteousness; he hates not desiring evil; he hates not consenting to evil concupiscence; he hates not sinning; he hates leaving sins; he hates repenting; he hates truth that reproves; he hates wisdom that urges useful things; he hates the discipline of peace; he hates the grace of God; he almost hates God himself—indeed, as iniquity advances, he even hates him gratuitously, always falling into worse things until he falls into the unforgivable sin, which will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Victorious and ruling evil concupiscence hurls its subject from sin into sin [Col. 0465B] until it leads him from love of itself to hatred of God, until the pit closes its mouth over him. Yet the cause of so great an evil is delight in sin in one way and concupiscence of sin in another. The latter is the cause for which it happens; the former, that through which it happens. The former begins; the latter completes. The former draws one away from good through unlawful appearances of things and entices one to evil; the latter captures and encloses the person drawn away and enticed. The former causally precedes consent to sin; the latter follows it.

### On the Body and Soul of the Old Man

As body and soul are distinguished in one human being, while the body is seen to possess flesh and bones, and marrow in the bones, and the soul is believed to hold the power of moving the body, so, in the composition of a single sin, our old man—who may not inappropriately be called the man of sin or the son of perdition—has concupiscence as the flesh of sin, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5). He has consent, in which lies the strength of sin, as the bone, just as the strength of the body lies in the bone; and he has delight as the marrow.

He has as the soul that which is supreme and excels in the mind, and presides over that which desires, over that which consents, and likewise over that which delights—so that desire, consent, and delight can please or displease it. Without its connivance, neither is desire carried as far as consent, nor is the body moved to act, nor is the deed completed from that movement, in which the sought-after delight is pursued. But when all things please that which presides over all in the mind, and it delights in all of them, delight is felt not in the deed alone: besides delight in the deed, there is delight of the mind in desire and consent—yet in desire then, when it is in consent. For when one is unwilling to consent, one is either wholly unwilling, or less willing, to desire. But when one is willing to consent, one is also willing to bring the act to completion. Whoever finds all these things pleasing delights in them all.

The delight that is in desire, though it seems to belong more to desire itself than to consent—that is, more to the richness of the flesh than to the marrow of the bone—nevertheless is known to belong to consent for this reason: without consent, desire itself does not entirely please. Therefore among the marrows are found, together with delight in the deed, delight in desire, delight in [Col. 0466A] consent, and every delight of the mind, by whose motion the whole evil enterprise is arranged.

But who, or whose sword, can divide these marrows, hidden more deeply in bones so densely enclosed, save his who can crush the bones of sinners and break their horns? He is indeed the one who humbles the proud to ashes and dust, who scatters mist like ashes; who sends forth his ice like morsels; who brings forth prisoners in strength, likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs (Ps. 67). He assuredly is the one who can raise the dead; he alone prevails to turn all harmful delights into the bitterness of repentance, so that everything which wickedly pleased becomes displeasing, until the body of sin is consumed to its very marrow.

“And [he is] the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and no creature is invisible in his sight: to whom is our account” (Heb. 4).

[Col. 0466B]

The Lord knows the thoughts and intentions of our heart—without doubt, all of them to himself, but to us those which he causes us, through the grace of discernment, to distinguish according to what they are. Yet the spirit that is in a person does not know all that is in the person; and of its own thoughts, which it feels while consenting or not consenting, it does not always perceive them as they truly are. Even those which it sees before the eyes of the mind, it does not, with its darkened eyes, discern subtly.

For something is often suggested by one’s own thought, by another human being, or by the tempter, under an appearance of piety, which does not merit the reward of virtue before [Col. 0466C] God’s eyes. There are certain resemblances of true virtues, and likewise of vices, which deceive the eyes of the heart and, as it were through certain illusions, so dazzle the mind’s vision that the appearance of good frequently seems present in something not good, and likewise the appearance of evil in something not evil. This is a part of our misery and ignorance, greatly to be lamented and greatly to be feared. For it is written: “There are ways which seem right to a person, whose end leads down to hell” (Prov. 14:16). To avoid this danger, blessed John admonishes us: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4).

But who can test whether spirits are from God unless discernment of spirits has been given him by God, so that he may examine spiritual thoughts, affections, and intentions by a subtle and true judgment? Discernment, moreover, is the mother of all virtues and is necessary to each one, whether in governing another’s life or in directing or correcting one’s own. No discourse can truly impart it to our minds except that living and effective Word which is the discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

This Word establishes our entire life according to a definite pattern and directs it to a definite end. Under its instruction, in all that we arrange to do we must always think of God, so that it may be done according to him and nevertheless for his sake. Do you ask how it may be according to him, and how for his sake? Hear both. Every action of ours must be directed to the end of God’s promises. We are not permitted to do anything except what he commands, permits, or counsels; [Col. 0467A] nor is it fitting for us to hope for anything except what he promises, and because he promises it. For our righteousness is formed at the beck of the one commanding or counselling; our hope is raised up from the truthfulness of the one promising.

Right is the thought of things to be done which is governed by God’s will; pious is the intention which is directed simply to him. Thus at last the whole body of our life, or of any action of ours, will be full of light if the eye is single. The single eye is both an eye and single: through right thought it sees what must be done, and through pious intention it simply does what ought not to be done in twofold fashion. Right thought admits no error; pious intention excludes pretence. This, then, is true discernment: the union of right thought and pious intention.

Do not be surprised that I have called discernment a union, although *discretio* indicates division. For this union does not exist without division. Whoever joins these two things divides between light and darkness. For error and pretence are darkness; but righteousness and piety are light in the Lord. But one who strives to separate from one another, in choosing what is to be done or in the end to be hoped for, right thought according to God and pious intention for God’s sake, because his eye contains some part of darkness, either walks in darkness or does not know where he is going. For he walks in darkness who acts wickedly; he does not know where he is going who does not tend toward God. Therefore evil things must not be done for God’s sake, nor good things done apart from God’s sake. An intention of vanity corrupts a work of piety, and piety of intention does not excuse the iniquity of the work.

Therefore all things must be done in the light of discernment, as in God and before God, because no creature is invisible in his sight. No bodily creature, no animate creature, no spiritual creature: nothing made by God for the human being or in the human being; nothing made in a human being or by a human being against God. For however many things are in a human being, some of which the person sees and some does not see, all are manifest to God. The human heart is a great abyss; all hidden darknesses are in its secret places. There are creeping things there without number. But God, who sees in secret and who also illuminates the hidden things of darkness so that thoughts may be revealed from many hearts, fails to see none of all visible and invisible things: “For all things are naked and open to his eyes” (Heb. 4).

Many things are now covered and concealed by secret silences and counsels, contrivances and inventions, fraud and deceit, the artifice of words and things, evasions and excuses, pretences and dissimulations. [Col. 0468B] But nothing is covered that shall not be revealed. For the Word to whom is our account will strip every covering from all things that are now ingeniously concealed. To him an account must be rendered, even concerning reason itself, to which the ordering of our whole life has been entrusted.

Thus the Lord considers each person’s ways and numbers his steps, so that not even the tiniest thoughts, in his judgment, nor the slightest words, which have become cheap among us through common use, remain unexamined. What word, then, can answer for me, or what account can I render for myself? Only that I may say with the Prophet: “You have understood my thoughts from afar; you have searched out my path and my cord, and you have foreseen all my ways, because there is no word on my tongue” (Ps. 138). Good Jesus, I am unable to render an account; receive prayer in place of an account, and do not enter into judgment with your servant, because “no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142).

## TREATISE SEVEN: ON THE ANGELIC SALUTATION

[Col. 0467]

“Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women” (Luke 1).

[Col. 0467C] The work of our salvation begins from a salutation, and the announcement [Col. 0467D] of peace consecrates the beginning of reconciliation. For the messenger of salvation and angel of peace, sent by God and entering in to the Virgin—himself a friend of virginity—greets her with a new, unprecedented salutation, unheard from the beginning of the world until then, bringing at once the service of new salvation and the proclamation of new praise.

It is new, or at least rare, for a woman to be greeted by an angel. Neither Hagar nor Manoah’s wife was greeted by an angel, though each enjoyed angelic sight and speech. But now a woman is greeted by an angel; now the time approaches when women shall be greeted by the Lord himself and be told: “Hail” (Matt. 28). The Virgin was pondering what this salutation might be. Let us also consider, as far as we are able, what it is.

This is not a salutation on the road, but a salutation restoring one to the homeland. “Greet no one on the road,” says the Lord (Luke 10). If someone, wishing to ingratiate himself with you by unfeigned flattery and crooked adulation in matters of vanity, displays himself as well disposed toward you or presents himself as your admirer, he is one who greets you on the road. Beware for yourself—beware of those who say to you, “Hail.” For woe to you if you become the servant of such people. Woe to you if those who seek your life rule over you. Nor should you love greetings in the marketplace. The witness of your conscience and the faithful witness in heaven suffice for you, to whom you may say: “My praise is with you in the great assembly” (Ps. 21).

One salutation is distinguished from another because one salvation is distinguished from another. For there is a vain salvation, of which it is written: “For the salvation of man is vain” (Ps. 59). And there is a true salvation, of which it is written: “Hear me in the truth of your salvation” (Ps. 68). But this salutation, whether it is a votive prayer for desired salvation or an announcement of salvation given or to be given, neither feigns the goodwill of the one greeting nor proclaims false praise of the Virgin. Rather, as virginity is ever beloved by angels, the angel commends the Virgin with faithful praise and begins his praise from the fullness of grace, saying: “Hail, full of grace.”

O saving salutation dictated by an angel and set before us as the model by which to greet the Virgin! O rejoicing of the heart, sweetness of the mouth, seasoning of love! What place is there for wrath where there is fullness of grace? For fullness of grace is the emptying of guilt and the restoration of nature. Guilt had corrupted nature and provoked wrath. But God did not restrain his mercies in his wrath. He poured out grace and turned away wrath. The sex which the sentence of curse had condemned in the first woman (Gen. 3), he now fills with the grace of blessing and with the oil of mercy in the blessed Virgin.

This is the flask of oil; this is Gideon’s bowl full of dew; this is the golden urn containing manna of supreme sweetness and heavenly rain. Who can sufficiently conceive what sort, or how great, was the grace with which she was full—she who is designated first among women and alone “full of grace,” she who bore the only-begotten Son, full of grace and truth? We read that the protomartyr Stephen was “full of grace and strength” (Acts 6). But she is believed to be fuller by as much as she was more capable of grace: she who was able to contain, alike in heart and mind, the very author of grace, so great and so boundless that the whole world cannot contain him.

We have heard that blessed Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit; recognizing the greater grace in the Virgin, she marvelled that she herself was visited and greeted, saying: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1). Rightly does she who was greeted greet in return, through whom salvation was to be communicated, so that through her thanks might be rendered to God, who gives salvation to kings and commands salvations for Jacob. For this was why she was full of grace—as a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing—that through her the grace of God might abound in us.

For God uniquely chose her beforehand and made her pleasing to himself, endowed with threefold grace: grace of beauty, grace of favour, and grace of honour, so that she might become beautiful, gracious, and glorious.

### On the Threefold Grace of God

The grace of beauty shines forth in a fair countenance. A fair countenance, according to the definition of blessed Augustine, is proportionately measured, brightly coloured, and cheerfully disposed. Proportionate measurement, according to equality, resemblance, composition, and the tempered and commensurate harmony of parts, is no small part of beauty. Dissimilar or unequal eyes, mismatched features, or discordant lips do not fit together; nor, conversely, does any part fit beautifully which, through its deformity or excessive size, departs from harmony with the remaining part. Whatever falls short of or exceeds due measure, or does not approach resemblance to its counterpart, diminishes the grace of beauty.

The praise of true beauty belongs more to the mind than to the body, though in some manner also to the body. For what is inwardly conceived through the chaste counsel of the heart is often outwardly fittingly administered through the ministry of the body. But whatever is not born from purity of heart is conducted impurely. “For all the glory of the king’s daughter is from within” (Ps. 44), though not all her glory is within. For from the inward parts there often proceeds that by which the King of glory, who is in heaven, is glorified outwardly.

This inward beauty loves proportion among corresponding things. Dissimilarity is unbecoming where no reason for dissimilarity appears. If you judge your own good or evil differently from that of another, your eyes are dissimilar. If you are proud before God and humble before people, you have mismatched features. If you bless your neighbour in his presence and detract from him in his absence; if you praise God in prosperity and murmur in adversity, your lips are discordant.

All this deformity proceeds from the vice of pride, which always loves inequality and dissimilarity in conduct; whereas, conversely, humility reduces even unequal things to equality. We ask what proportionate measurement may be found in the countenance of this Virgin—so good and praiseworthy that none better or more praiseworthy can be found among all the daughters of Zion. What can more rightly be called proportionate measurement than the equality of humility and honour, condescension and dignity? Thus it is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:18). If you are outstanding, yet be one of the flock. If you preside over all, do not disdain to be subject.

Consider yourself; consider also your Master, and in what work he professes himself truly to be Master. For he truly is. Consider what he said and what he did: “I came,” he says, “not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20). This is what he said: “Let the one who is foremost be as the servant, and the one who is greater among you as the younger” (Luke 22).

See what he said. Do you know what he did? He humbled himself even to the feet of his disciples. Who did this? He whose footstool is the earth. He who says: “I am the first and the last” (Rev. 1): first in dignity, last in humility. Therefore he gave us an example, that we might follow his footsteps, worshipping in the place where his feet stood. Come, let us worship and fall down before God; let us humble ourselves beneath him and with him, because he will save the humble in spirit—those, namely, who worship in spirit and power.

The place of worship is the virtue of humility. There his feet stood. How did they stand? He came in humility and persevered in humility. He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; and, Lord though he was, he bore the reproach of the cross for servants, becoming obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. 2). What is the summit of humility, if this is not it? How beautiful the proportion of supreme dignity and supreme humility!

O faithful soul, if you are fortified against pride by this example, so as to follow your Master’s footsteps through humility, it is said to you: “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince” (Song 7). “Hear, daughter, and incline your ear,” that you may be humbled; “and the king shall desire your beauty.” What king, except he who alone is king? You will become desirable, worthy of longing, and lovable to him if you incline your ear, if you humble yourself—and all the more as you are greater.

The more you humble yourself, the more you magnify the Lord. Hence she who is believed humbler than all others in proportion as she is more worthy, she who uniquely says, “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1), magnified him more because she was more magnified; and she was made more exalted, so that she could uniquely say: “He who is mighty has done great things to me” (ibid.). More magnified, she magnified God more because she humbled herself more. She herself is witness to her humility, humbly saying: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (ibid.).

Elizabeth also is a witness: when the Mother of God came to her, she marvelled alike at her own happiness, at the Virgin’s dignity, and at humility amid such great dignity. For great humility in great dignity is always wonderful; great humility in great power; in wisdom, eloquence, and virtue, great humility. In short, amid every greatness, great humility is the proportionate measurement that composes the countenance and shapes and fits all things together so that all things harmonize with all.

### On the Grace of Beauty

The grace of colour adorns the grace of this loveliness: whiteness together with redness. Colour is modesty. There is a twofold modesty: chaste modesty and bashful modesty. Chastity and bashfulness are the white lily and the red rose. Chastity affects the countenance with its whiteness; bashfulness bathes the cheeks in its redness. Bashfulness is the guardian of chastity, as well as its beauty and ornament.

Each sense, of both mind and body, has its own chastity and its own bashfulness. There is chastity of the eyes and also their bashfulness; chastity of the ears and also their bashfulness; and in the other senses bashfulness is usually the companion of chastity. The chastity of all the senses is assessed from their incorruption. Hence the Apostle says: “I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by its cunning, so your senses may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity which is in Christ Jesus” (2 Cor. 11).

Holy bashfulness is to blush at shameful things; holy chastity is to keep oneself undefiled. See how chaste were the eyes of him who said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not so much as think of a virgin” (Job 31). But one who looks upon a woman in order to desire her—what has he but an unchaste eye? An unchaste eye is the messenger of an unchaste mind. Corruption of the senses is the companion of unchastity; integrity of the senses is the seal of chastity.

But so great was the integrity and chastity of mind and body in this Virgin that she was wholly virgin, wholly unstained, wholly immaculate: corrupted in no sense, defiled in no sense. She wholly blushed at what is shameful, wholly rejected what is evil, wholly willed what is chaste, wholly renounced what is dishonourable. For this is full virginity: uninjured integrity in every sense. Every impairment of integrity is a certain deflowering of virginity.

This is the bright colour, compounded of the whiteness of chastity and the redness of bashfulness, shining in this Virgin’s countenance and increasing the grace of beauty. She is therefore brightly coloured, at once chaste and bashful, so that in her is fulfilled what is written: “Grace upon grace: a holy and modest woman” (Ecclus. 26). “Full of grace.” To grace is added the fact that she is cheerfully disposed: her face is gladdened with the oil of exultation because, wholly full of devotion and of the fervour of charity, she offered herself to God as an odour of sweetness. Before all the daughters of Zion, who rejoice in their King, her spirit rejoiced in God her saviour.

See how beautiful is the countenance which the grace of proportion has formed, the grace of whiteness and redness has illumined, and the grace of cheerfulness has made glad. Nor is she beautiful in face alone, but wholly beautiful, as he who was pleased by her bears witness, saying: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4). See how full she is of the grace of beauty.

### On the Grace of Favour

Nor is the grace of favour inferior in her. For she is loved, praised, and honoured by all: after God, she is the first love, praise, and glory of human beings and angels. The whole Church of the saints proclaims her praises: “The daughters of Zion saw her and declared her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her” (Song 6). She herself does not keep silent concerning this grace of such great favour when she says: “All generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1).

### On the Grace of Honour
How great the grace of honour conferred upon her was is beyond our power to declare. For, since all things in her are worthy of praise—both those which are proper to her and those which are shared—both kinds commend her with special praise. For she possesses shared things in a singular way, because she possesses beyond all others those things which she has in common with others. And it is singular that she is not alone. She is chaste, humble, gentle, and kind. There are others with like virtues, but not in the same manner or degree. She surpasses all: in all things lady of the world and queen of heaven, of human beings and angels; mother of God and daughter, sister and bride, friend and neighbour. Mother through the fruitfulness of virginity; daughter through the grace of adoption; sister through the grace of communion; bride through the faith of betrothal; friend through the mutual exchange of love; neighbour [Col. 0472D] through the nearness of likeness: more beautiful than all, more lovable than all, surpassingly beautiful, surpassingly gracious, surpassingly glorious.

“The Lord is with thee.” What distinctive glory is contained in the words “The Lord is with thee,” when the angel said to Gideon, “The Lord be with thee, most valiant of men”? (Judg. VI). And the Psalmist says: “The Lord of hosts is with us” (Ps. XLVI). Christ also says to us: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the end of the world” (Matt. XXVIII). And Isaiah says of Christ: “His name shall be called Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us” (Isa. VII). Yet before saying this he prefaced it: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (ibid.). For how could he come to us, in order to be with us, unless he came to the Virgin—whom he also preceded [Col. 0473A] so as to be with her, and in her, and from her, and to be through her in us—since God of Jacob is our protector? For this purpose God of Jacob took our nature from her: that he might always be with us, saying, “My delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. VIII). But if it is God’s delight to be with the children of men, how great, do you suppose, is his delight in being with his one chosen woman, whom he selected beforehand for the ministry of such great delights?

Therefore, that great gift and great good which consists in his being with us, sharing our nature and making us sharers in his grace, so that we may be sons and heirs of God, and brothers and co-heirs of Jesus Christ—this was said to her in a singular manner: “The Lord is with thee.” Made the minister and co-worker of so great a dispensation, she gave us the salvation of the world. Yet, because she could not do it alone, but supplied her ministry, performed the office of mediatrix, and brought forth into the midst the Mediator who could accomplish it, it is rightly said: “The Lord is with thee.” You are about to perform a magnificent work; through you the salvation of the world is to be effected; the sceptre of the oppressor is to be overcome, as in the day of Midian. But that for which you have been chosen is beyond all human power and wisdom; yet the Lord is with thee, to whom no word is impossible.

Thus it is said to Gideon, when he was about to deliver the children of Israel from Midian: “The Lord is with thee, most valiant of men” (Judg. VI); where strength is mentioned, and strength was needed, God granting strength, who is the helper of the strong. In this work too of our salvation, which is begun by most abundant grace [Col. 0473C] and consummated in most abundant grace, the fullness of grace is mentioned; and praise is ascribed to the author of grace, who, with the Virgin cooperating, is shown to be the author of the work.

## The Blessing of the Virgin

After God, the author of so great a benefit, the first praise is due to the Virgin, so that she is deservedly blessed by all. Therefore the angel says to her: “Blessed art thou among women” (Luke I). And Elizabeth says to her: “Blessed art thou among women” (ibid.). Eve, through pride and the fault of disobedience, received in herself the sentence of a curse; and through her we are liable to the curse. For a curse is due to pride, since “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace to the humble” (I Pet. V). Hence it is written: “The beginning of all sin is pride; and whoever holds fast to it shall be filled with curses” (Ecclus. X). But Mary humbled herself and deserved the blessing.

Let us consider, insofar as we can, how greatly she humbled herself and how blessed she was. There is a humility under a command, one under counsel, one under an example, one under a resolve or vow, and one under a curse. A command imposes necessity; counsel stirs free will; example provokes emulation; a holy resolve or vow increases devotion; a curse brings shame. Humility under counsel is greater than that under a command. We are commanded not to seize another’s goods; we are exhorted to leave our own. This is the greater good, though the former is more necessary. The former is more common, this more restricted.

Humility under an example, without command and without counsel, seems farther removed from the swelling of pride and the haughtiness of arrogance. For it is a sign of great humility, with no one compelling or urging, to prefer to oneself another who acts rightly, and not to disdain whatever is worthy of imitation. Often, moreover, without command, counsel, or example, some good is apprehended through a hidden prompting of the mind and undertaken as a resolve or vow: this is a remarkable humility. For it is a virtue of great strength to renounce common freedom and subject oneself to holy necessity.

Sometimes, however, what is known to be acceptable to God is found shameful among human beings and liable to a curse. For this reason some, overcome by fear of disgrace, are often ashamed of the pursuit of perfection which they desire; and while they fear human tongues, they flee the goods for which they long. But others approve and pursue justice and holiness in such a way that they despise human curses and reproaches, counting it glorious to suffer insult for the name of Jesus, and esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt. This form of humility, the less it fears human curses for God’s sake, the more abundant a grace of blessing it merits before God.

Christ himself did not omit this form of humility. Desiring to fulfil all righteousness, he “was made a curse for us,” as it is written: “Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree” (Deut. XXI; Gal. III). How he was made a curse is shown by the one who says: “Rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God” (I Pet. II). And this agrees with the other saying: “They shall curse, but thou shalt bless” (Ps. CVIII).

Let us judge from what has been said what was the humility of this Virgin, who consecrated her virginity without a command of the Law, under the Law’s curse, because she who left no offspring in Israel was accounted cursed. If God in the beginning both blessed those whom he said, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I), giving them the grace of fruitfulness as a blessing, how is she not excluded from that blessing who lacks fruitfulness? If fruitfulness is a blessing, how is barrenness not a curse? What is more barren, more unfruitful, more fruitless than virginity? Nothing whatever—before the fruitful Virgin. For nothing is more fruitful than fruitful virginity.

The holiness of virginity is above the Law. No law reduced it to a command; rather, evangelical perfection set it forth as counsel, the Lord saying: “He that can receive it, let him receive it” (Matt. XIX); and the Apostle: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (I Cor. VII). Thus no command of the Law preceded this Virgin’s resolve; nor, as some think, did any counsel from the Law; nor was there an example from the Law, which would have to be taken more from women than from men. For Elijah, Jeremiah, and Daniel are thought to have preserved the chastity of virginity. But among women, whether before the Law or under the Law, no example is found of virginity preserved and dedicated to God.

[Col. 0475A] For the fact that Jephthah’s daughter obtained a respite of two months to bewail her virginity (Judg. XI) can be interpreted in various ways. Scripture does not say with what disposition she did this. For if the reason for bewailing virginity was that, being as though barren and without fruit, she would leave no seed in Israel, this thought of mind and outpouring of tears are far removed from the resolve of holy virginity. Nevertheless, she seems to have contemplated something profound—whatever it may have been, known to the searcher of hearts—she who said to her father: “My father, if thou hast opened thy mouth to God, do to me whatsoever thou hast promised, now that vengeance and retribution against thine enemies have been granted thee” (ibid.).

But from where could our Virgin even have believed that virginity would please God, when it was so liable [Col. 0475B] to the curse, so near to barrenness? Yet she could have read in Isaiah: “Let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree’; for thus saith the Lord to the eunuchs: ‘I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters’” (Isa. LVI). She could also have read: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. VII).

Since honour, “better than sons and daughters,” was promised to eunuchs—that is, to virgins—and since the Saviour of the world was foretold as to be born of a virgin, the Virgin, divinely inspired, could by the same Spirit that inspired the prophet to say these things, and that suggested them to her mind, have understood that virginity was exceedingly pleasing and dear to God: for it was reserved to her, a Virgin about to bear, to conceive God, an honour so great. Whether, then, instructed by the prophet’s oracle concerning the merit of virginity, or inwardly taught of it only by divine prompting, she loved virginity, embraced virginity, offered it to the Lord as a most sweet fragrance, and consecrated it, while despising the reproach of the curse.

But from virginity hitherto barren she received fruitfulness; for the curse she had despised she found the grace of blessing. For other women, iniquity in conception, pain in childbirth, and in some cases fruitless barrenness served as a curse. But she conceived without sin, gave birth without pain, and brought forth fruit from virginity. And what sort of fruit? Surely a singular fruit, a fruit more precious than all the fruit of marriage. For what is the fruit of marriage except all Adam’s posterity, this entire multitude of the children of men? [Col. 0475D] Even those born of fornication derive from the first parents, joined in marriage.

But all fruit of carnal intercourse is condemned beforehand, as born from an evil tree and corrupted from a diseased root; for “an evil tree bringeth forth evil fruits” (Matt. VII; Luke VI). What, you ask, is the evil tree? Certainly evil concupiscence, the concupiscence of the flesh, which all draw with them who are begotten according to the law of the flesh, all who are propagated from the stock of sin. This is the original evil in us: the seedbed of evils, the leaven of the whole corrupted mass, and the beginning and completion of universal condemnation.

For this original evil, so harmful and deadly, a remedy had to be provided through an original good, preserved in those being born from the state of the first creation, even after the first transgression and the corrupted law of birth. For God so tempered his sentence against sinful humankind that nature, corrupted by vice, should partly feel the evil it deserved and partly recall the good it had possessed. Thus, because of the sin of disobedience, corrupted propagation brought upon those being born the law of disobedience—that is, the vice of concupiscence; and yet the original creation retains in those being born some wholeness of incorruption.

For all are born virgins; and virginity, having emerged from the womb, accompanies the growth of the ages and retains the grace of flourishing incorruption until the corruption of the flesh, which does not restrain the movement of concupiscence, extinguishes the name of integrity, and corrupts the flower of blossoming virginity. Yet what the embrace of man and woman loses in intercourse, the origin of birth restores in childbirth.

But virginity, the common integrity of all who are born, has the name and praise of virtue especially in those who, together with bodily integrity, preserve chastity of mind. Bodily virginity without chastity of mind, even though it contains in itself no reproach of guilt, nevertheless has no commendation of true virtue. But the virginity of this blessed woman possesses singular praise of virtue, because it obtains singular grace of blessing; and to her it was deservedly said: “Blessed art thou among women.”

Blessed indeed: first, by immunity from the common curse; then, by absolution from a just accusation; finally—and this is greatest—by the turning away of due condemnation. For the general curse encompasses other women, both those who give birth and those who are barren. Exempted from it through grace, she obtained in this respect a certain share of blessing, because alone she lacked the general misfortune and remained immune. This is what we have called immunity from the general curse.

A sinful man could accuse woman of sin and say: “Through thee, O cursed woman, rightly cursed and deserving to be cursed, I too am cursed. Through thee I was cast out of paradise; through thee I lost these and these goods; through thee I found these and these evils. Woe to thee, because it happened through thee; woe to me!” To this no woman could answer a single word; to this she could only be confounded with shame and distressed with perturbation. Hence the whole female sex could be hated and most deserving of public reproach. And so indeed it was before this Virgin’s childbirth.

Now, however, it is far otherwise. Woman now has something to answer; in the blessed Virgin she has that which she may oppose to this reproach. This is what we have called absolution from a just accusation. This Virgin herself was free from that accusation, and by her own merit absolved the rest. Since she brought forth the Saviour of the world, who destroyed death and turned away the condemnation due to us, after God we owe her everything in our deliverance from the curse; and in our being blessed with every spiritual blessing in heavenly places. Thus, as she is always blessed with God, so she should always be blessed by us.

## Blessed Is the Fruit of Thy Womb (Luke I)

[Col. 0477A]

To this angelic salutation, with which day by day we greet the most blessed Virgin with such devotion as is granted us, we are accustomed to add: “and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.” Elizabeth added this clause after she had been greeted by the Virgin, repeating it as though it were the conclusion of the angelic salutation: “Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.” This is the fruit of which Isaiah says: “In that day the branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted” (Isa. IV).

Who is this fruit, if not the Holy One of Israel, who is himself the seed of Abraham, the branch of the Lord, and the flower rising from the root of Jesse—the fruit of life, which we have shared? Blessed indeed in the seed, blessed in the branch, blessed in the flower, blessed in the gift, and finally blessed in thanksgiving and confession.

Christ became Abraham’s seed, made from David’s seed according to the flesh. But if the Virgin betrothed to Joseph, of the house of David, was herself David’s seed, why should it not devoutly be believed that Christ was made from David’s seed when he was made from the woman from whom he was made without seed—namely, from David’s seed without seed? (Matt. I). And why without seed, except because the Virgin “was found with child of the Holy Spirit,” conceiving in a wondrous manner and not receiving from a begetting father? For she supplied from herself the substance of his flesh; nor was he defiled in assuming flesh from her.

This, therefore, is the blessing of the seed: where there is no obligation of sin, where there is no origin of propagated or contracted iniquity. The assumption of the form of a servant without servile condition, and immunity from sin in the one born, are a double liberty and free nobility, by which he alone is free who absolves the guilty and makes them free.

To this blessing, which is immunity from fault, is joined the blessing of the branch, which is fullness of grace and perfect righteousness. For he alone among human beings is found complete [Col. 0478A] in every good, because he remained immune from every evil. To him the Spirit was given without measure, so that he alone might fulfil all righteousness. For every righteousness of the saints, compared with his, is found wanting. “There is none holy as the Lord” (I Sam. II). The righteousness of each person can scarcely suffice for that person; but his righteousness suffices for all nations, according as it is written: “As the earth bringeth forth her bud, and as a garden causeth its seed to spring forth, so the Lord God shall cause righteousness and praise to spring forth before all nations” (Isa. LXI).

For this is the branch of righteousness, increased by blessing and adorned by the flower of glory. But of how great a glory? Of as great a glory as can be conceived—or rather, as cannot in any way be conceived. For the flower rose from the root of Jesse. How far? Surely to the summit: for Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father. His magnificence has been raised above the heavens, that the branch of the Lord may be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted.

But what fruit have we in this fruit? What except the fruit of blessing from the blessed fruit? For from this seed, branch, and flower comes the fruit of blessing; it reaches even to us: first, as it were in the seed, through the grace of pardon; then, as it were in the branch, through the growth of righteousness; and finally in the flower, through hope or attainment of glory. For he is blessed by God and in God—that is, so that God may be glorified in him—and he is blessed also for us, so that we who are blessed by him may be glorified in him. Through the promise spoken to Abraham, God gave him the blessing of all nations [Col. 0478C], so that in the gift of blessing he himself may be blessed for us; and, for the gift, always to be blessed by us in thanksgiving and confession of praise. Therefore let the name of his majesty be blessed for ever, and let the whole earth be filled with his majesty. Amen, amen.

# EIGHTH TREATISE: ON THE WOUND OF LOVE WHICH THE BRIDE INFLICTS UPON THE BRIDEGROOM

[Col. 0477]

“Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; thou hast wounded my heart with one of thine eyes and with one lock of thy neck” (Cant. IV).

[Col. 0477D] In many ways God commends his love toward us: now by deeds, now by words; now by benefits, now by promises; now by the endearments and persuasions of words, now by likenesses drawn from things. A likeness is taken from forms and effects of love not unknown to us, so that our mind, reminded by things familiar to it, may always think upon him whom it ought to love with its whole mind, whom it ought always to remember, when it considers love in those things which are customarily loved, or which love, whether naturally, socially, or chastely.

For there is natural love, by which not only human beings but every living creature that feels in itself the force of love loves the nature of its own kind and, by a certain instinct, assents to the laws of love. There is also social love, by which people live in fellowship through the movement of their own choice with those with whom they consent to dwell. There is also chaste love, which strengthens and adorns marriage.

Thus the eagle loves as it flies above its young; the hen also loves as she gathers her chicks beneath her wings and, through the greatness of her love, grows weak, her feathers and affections alike loosened. A father loves his children, his sweetest pledges; and a mother cannot forget the son of her womb. Brother and sister, sweetest names of kinship, when reciprocally spoken and heard, revive the affections of love that were dead. A pair of friends are joined by the indissoluble bond of friendship. Bridegroom and bride set aside the domestic affections of their kindred in order to serve the chaste embraces and delights of love.

Yet more powerful than all these is Christ’s love: deeper, more inward, keener, more penetrating, more compassionate, sweeter, stronger, more fervent. No comparison with any love can surpass, equal, or even fully express its force. Nevertheless, Christ does not disdain to be compared with an eagle or a hen; in this is commended the wonderful love of Christ, his wonderful humility, and the admirable sweetness of each.

He is father when he says: “Henceforth thou shalt call me, My Father, thou art the guide of my virginity” (Jer. III); and: “Thou shalt call me Father, and thou shalt not cease to follow after me” (ibid.). He abounds more richly in the bowels of maternal compassion when he says: “As a mother comforteth her children, so will I comfort you” (Isa. LXI). He is brother when he says: “A garden enclosed is my sister” (Cant. IV); and again: “Go to my brethren” (Matt. XXVIII). He is friend when he says: “Thou art wholly beautiful, my friend” [Col. 0479B] (Cant. IV); and when it is said of him: “Such is my beloved, and he is my friend” (Cant. V). He is bridegroom when he says: “The bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride, and thy God shall rejoice over thee” (Isa. LXII). And now he is both brother and bridegroom when he says: “Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my bride.”

When he calls her sister, he indicates communion both of nature and of grace. This is the exchange of love: he took nature and communicated grace. When he calls her bride, he indicates the faith of betrothal and the sacrament of an indissoluble union. But she who is called sister and bride—why is she said to have wounded the heart of her brother and bridegroom? Does love also have its wounds? It certainly does. Some wounds are salutary, others deadly.

What wounds are more deadly than those endured by the author of death himself, wounded by the dart of envy and the sword of sorrow? Of him it is written: “Thou hast humbled the proud one as one wounded” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Nor was he alone wounded in this way; through him many wounded fell. For of them it is written: “As wounded men sleeping in the graves, whom thou rememberest no more” (Ps. LXXXVII).

But salutary are the wounds by which the bride was wounded: the wound of love and the wound of sorrow; and still more salutary are the wounds of the bridegroom: likewise the wound of love and the wound of sorrow. Of the wound of sorrow the bride says: “They struck me and wounded me” (Cant. V). Of the wound of love she says: “I am wounded by love.” And if, in a matter so sacred [Col. 0479D] and reverent, it is permitted to introduce the opinion of an eminent poet, so that it may serve the truth, the poet himself bears witness that there is a wound of love, saying:

> But the queen, long since wounded by grievous care,  
> Nourishes the wound with her veins and is consumed by hidden fire.  
> —Virgil

In Daniel likewise it is written concerning the two elder judges: “Both were wounded by love of her” (Dan. XIII), that is, of Susanna. But this was an unholy love. Holy love, however, is far more effective and far stronger in wounding.

Let us consider, therefore, how the bridegroom says that his heart has been wounded by his sister and bride. Nor does he say it once, but twice, repeating it: “Thou hast wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; thou hast wounded my heart.” Clearly, because of the exceeding love with which he loved us when we were dead in sins, he desired life for us and death for himself. Hence his wounds as he hung upon the cross; hence the wounds of our sins were healed; hence salvation was supplied to us.

The desire for our salvation and, for our salvation, the desire for his own death are two wounds, one of love, the other of sorrow—or rather, both of love. For both desires proceeded from the love by which the bride was anticipated, so that, beloved beforehand by one who loved her thus, she might love him; and might preserve herself for him unstained in all the truth of holy love and holy fear.

Now she is said to have wounded the bridegroom’s heart with one of her eyes and one lock of her neck, as though he who loved the ugly woman in order to make her beautiful had been drawn to love by the beauty of these. But in their beauty it appears that she herself has been chosen through love. For love’s intention was directed to this end: that she might become beautiful, she who was loved so greatly before she became beautiful; so that, through the magnitude of his love, he says that his heart is wounded at the sight of those things by which she became beautiful.

For bridegroom and bride wound one another with mutual wounds; but the bridegroom wounds only after being wounded, while the bride wounds even when she has not been wounded. Yet what does it mean that, in all the bride’s beauty—she who is called wholly beautiful—he is wounded only by one of her eyes and one lock of her neck? He loves and praises her whole person—her cheeks and lips, her breasts and the jointure of her thighs, and all the rest—so why is he not wounded by her cheeks and lips and the other objects of admiration in her beauty, but, as though captured by love, is wounded by the beauty of one eye and one lock? Does some singular grace of beauty shine forth in these which pleases him above the rest? Certainly it does.

Before all else, those things please him for the sake of which all else pleases him. And what are they? The purity of holy love and the purity of holy fear. The former is understood in one of the eyes; the latter in one lock of the neck. In the prophet Zechariah, concerning the ephah or impiety—that is, cupidity or love of the world—it is said: “This is their eye in all the earth” (Zech. V). This eye looks at earth, not heaven; at the world, not God; at temporal things, not eternal; at visible things, not invisible things. Nor indeed can it do otherwise, for it is impure and dark.

But when the love of God is perfect and undivided, it is a single, pure eye, conspicuous in its own beauty, which with wonderful subtlety contemplates not the things which are seen but those which are not seen. This is Rachel’s gaze, she who is described as beautiful in face and lovely in appearance (Gen. XXIX). This is the eye by which Mary sees the best part that she chose, which shall not be taken away from her (Luke XI). This eye is not the only eye, but one of the eyes. It is truly one, because, intent upon one thing, it loves one thing and cares for one thing.

There is another eye of the bride, by which she no longer contemplates the bridegroom’s beauty, but descends into herself and, more unwillingly than willingly, sees herself poor and miserable, exposed to many needs and infirmities, not only her own but also those of others, as though they were her own. Hence comes the domestic care of daily need, the disturbance of the mind, the anxiety of the heart, and the affliction of the spirit. Hence the mind is divided among many things and stretched out over many things; hence Martha is anxious and troubled about many things.

Therefore Martha is “Martha, Martha,” not once but twice, while Mary is Mary once, because she once chose the one thing that is henceforth necessary. But “Martha, Martha” is anxious and troubled by care for present things and provision for future things. For she must see many things and provide for many things necessary to the needs of herself and her own. Nor can she do so from just anywhere, but only from what is permitted and most honourably fitting.

How can this eye, which sees earthly things, avoid being sprinkled with the dust of earthly thought? How can it avoid being troubled? Therefore this is not the eye whose beauty wounds the bridegroom, but that one of the eyes which sees the bridegroom purely and, in order to cling to him, abhors all else. For if a man leaves father and mother in order to cling to his wife, how much more rightly does Christ’s bride leave behind all things to be despised in order to cling to her bridegroom?

But by what does she cling more than by the eye? For where love is, there the eye is. And because the eye can see and be seen, it is customarily both the sign and the enticement of love. For it provokes love by its beauty and announces love by hidden signification. I mean beauty that is faithful and true, not made up and counterfeit. For she who paints her eyes with antimony feigns a beauty that she does not possess; and the eye of intention, strengthened by falsehood, is painted in vain before the eyes of God. For he is not pleased by simulated virtues, but always loves truth, since he himself is truth.

The eye’s signification too sometimes deceives, as it is written of some: “They hated me without cause; they made signs with their eyes” (Ps. XXXIV). But God is not mocked. By its signification the eye wins love when it frequently turns toward the same object, or is fixed immovably upon it, or is formed without deceit. The bridegroom loves the eye that turns away and often returns.

But do you wonder that I said “turns away”? Hear him speaking to the bride: “Turn thine eyes away from me, for they have made me flee away” (Cant. VI). In the rapture of contemplation, when the unsearchable God is sought unsearchably beyond what is permitted, it is good to turn the eyes away; otherwise he himself will flee away and say: “Turn thine eyes away.” And through the Wise Man he will admonish: “Seek not things higher than thee, and search not things stronger than thee” (Ecclus. III).

At times, however, he does not love the eye that turns away, but he loves it when it returns. Often a person in tribulation cries to God and lifts the eyes to God; then, delivered from tribulation and relaxed in security, looks elsewhere and turns the eye away from the Lord. But soon, struck and chastened by the rod of the Lord’s discipline, that person looks back and desires to be regarded, saying: “Look upon me and have mercy on me” (Ps. XXIV).

Hence it is often written in one and the same psalm: “They cried unto the Lord when they were in tribulation, and he delivered them often” (Ps. CVI). Often the righteous are not visibly delivered from present tribulation, as it is written of some: “They were stretched out, not accepting redemption, that they might find a better resurrection” (Heb. II). Often they despise present consolation so greatly that they do not even desire to be delivered. Often, too, they desire it but do not hope for it, trusting that God will provide better for them; or perhaps, struck for a time by faint-heartedness, when after persistent prayers they do not obtain what they urgently seek, their hope gradually weakens and fails, as though he who is able did not wish to deliver them. Hence one says: “My eyes have grown dim through poverty” (Ps. LXXXVII); and again: “My eyes have failed while I hope in my God” (Ps. LXVIII).

Therefore, when hope fails, the eye turns away; when hope rises again, the eye returns. Let this be said concerning hope for temporal consolation or deliverance, which for various reasons now increases, now fails in turn. But the hope of eternal salvation is not so. It remains unmoved amid extreme perils and amid diverse kinds of temptation. This salvation may neither lawfully be undesired nor ever despaired of. That eye, therefore, is fixed immovably, from which it never turns away. It always clings there where it never ceases to adhere. Hence the Prophet says: “My eyes are ever toward the Lord” (Ps. XXXIV).

Nor should it trouble you that these are called “eyes,” as though many, when the bridegroom’s heart is wounded by one of the eyes. For there is one eye, because there is one love wholly intent upon one thing. Yet the affections of one love are various; by them one tends in many ways through desire and hope toward the one object, where the eye is fixed irrevocably.

The eye is fixed when, by a stealthy and almost furtive glance, it does not disclose all of itself but closes itself off, speaking the mystery of thought by a gesture alone. Holy love has gestures suited to itself, not like those of whom it is written: “Because the daughters of Zion are lifted up, and walk with outstretched necks, and go with gestures of the eyes” (Isa. III), but mystical gestures conscious of holy modesty, by which the bride makes a sign to and assents to the bridegroom as he makes a sign and assents to her.

For the bridegroom makes a sign when he secretly suggests what he wishes; he assents when he hears the prayers of the suppliant. The bride assents when she obeys God’s commands laid upon her. She makes a sign when, in her hidden goods, by a hidden intention, she sees as though secretly him by whom alone she desires to be seen. She makes a sign when, in the humility of prayers, she secretly and reverently sets forth the gesture of her desire.

Do not wonder that the eye is said to be “formed” in the signification of this love of which he now speaks, although holy love has nothing counterfeit. For *fingere* (“to form”) does not always mean to simulate or lie, but sometimes to compose, shape, or conceal; and in these ways—that is, by composing, shaping, or concealing—God is found and understood to “form.” For it is written that “Jesus made as though he would go farther” (Luke XXIV). And again: “He who formed each of their hearts” (Ps. XXXII); and: “He who formed the eye, shall he not consider?” (Ps. XCIII). And in the same place: “Thou who formest labour in the commandment” (ibid.).

## On One of the Eyes and One Lock of the Neck
“Thou hast wounded my heart,” he says, “with one of thine eyes [Col. 0483A], and with one lock of thy neck” (Song of Songs IV). Both before and after, the Bridegroom, as though looking all round the Bride, sees what pleases him; and in both places unity is commended—namely, in one of her eyes and in one lock of her neck. Consider, then, how a single lock is arranged. At the crown, where the summit of the head is, the hairs turn in various directions: some descend toward the forehead, others toward the back of the head, and others on either side toward the ears and temples. In women who are accustomed to let their hair grow, the hair, when dressed and becomingly combed out into a beautiful evenness, is parted from the crown down to the forehead; then it is brought back on either side past the ears, to the neck and shoulders, where it is gathered into one lock. For one lock is gathered from many hairs and fastened in one knot, lest the hairs, loose and wandering and scattered without order [Col. 0483B], hang down here and there and, by hanging down, become unseemly. By this art women dress and arrange themselves who think of the things of this world, anxious how they may please those who look at them.

The Bride of Christ also does not neglect the care of her hair, in order that she may please his eyes. For he is not delighted with just any sort of lock. It is written: “God shall crush the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of those who walk in their sins” (Ps. LXVII). And Isaiah says: “The Lord shall make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord shall lay bare their hair” (Isa. III). A little later he threatens baldness in place of curled hair. And the Apostle says: “Not with braided hair” (1 Tim. II). On the other hand, the religious consecration and sanctification of the Nazarites, and Samson’s strength, are in the hair.

Accordingly, the subtle thoughts of holy [Col. 0483C] intentions and affections are divided, from the summit of the mind—that is, from the knowledge of God—into four parts, and are parted by the comb of discernment. Some concern eternal goods, and descend toward the forehead; others concern eternal evils, and look backward; others concern temporal goods [Col. 0484A] or evils, and divide themselves to right and left on either side. These hairs are shown to please the Bridegroom’s eyes, because he says: “Put away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes” (Isa. I). Again it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. I). He grants assurance to his elect, saying: “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke XXI). All their hairs are numbered by him, because their thought is before the Most High.

But all the Bride’s hairs are drawn back to the neck, where is the yoke of obedience, and are bound into one lock by the knot of fear; because in all things obedience must always be considered in the fear of God, as it is written: “Always consider what God commands” (Ecclus. III). And again: [Col. 0484B] “Fear God and keep his commandments; this is the whole of man” (Eccles. XII). Therefore the one lock upon the neck is the unity of harmonious thoughts under the yoke of obedience: the fear of God gathers these into one and binds them indissolubly together.

This is the holy fear that endures for ever and ever: not the fear which love casts out, but that which preserves humility and strengthens love. This fear gathers what is scattered, unites what is dispersed, drives out what is evil, nourishes what is good, and guards what it has nourished. Finally, it makes the heart pure and unstained, and diligently seeks to keep it with every safeguard. The first safeguard is that no evil should issue into action; the second, that no evil word should proceed from the mouth; the third, that nothing evil should remain in the heart whereby the Bridegroom’s gaze might be offended. From this the Bridegroom’s heart [Col. 0484C] is wounded; from this the Bride is praised, because “the woman who fears God shall herself be praised.”

O Lord, grant that we may have enduring fear and love alike for thy holy name. Amen.

## NINTH TREATISE. ON THE EVANGELICAL BEATITUDES

[Col. 0483]

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” etc. (Matt. V).

[Col. 0483D] The promises of God are various and diverse, according to the merits of the righteous and their acts of justification. For to every act of justification its own recompense belongs; and every virtue has its proper praise and proper reward, according to the dignity of its rank and the quality of its kind. Let the poor see and rejoice. Let them see what their portion is, what manner of inheritance: not earthly, not perishable, but undefiled, unfading, reserved in heaven. Let them see and rejoice, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. It is indeed theirs, to possess and to share; that is, that they may have it for themselves and admit others with them, according to what is written: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, that, when you fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings” (Luke XVI).

Here the poor are received into houses, to be refreshed at the tables of the wealthy, like beggars and needy persons, so that the want of the poor may be supplied from the abundance of the rich. In the kingdom [Col. 0484D] of heaven the rich must be received by the poor, so that the need of the rich may be supplied from the abundance of the poor. For their own righteousness does not suffice them to obtain the kingdom of heaven. Poverty is the way to heaven. Some love it for Christ’s sake, emulating Christ’s poverty; and theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Others do not love it, but endure it patiently; and they are purified in the furnace of poverty, so that, having been proved, they may enter the kingdom of heaven. Others, however, neither love poverty for themselves nor endure it—though they do not lack opportunities to be in need—but they love the poor for Christ’s sake; they give readily, share with others, do not hope in the uncertainty of riches, but lay up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on eternal life. These also shall enter the kingdom of heaven by the merit of poverty; but they must be received by the poor and, in happy exchange, shall receive a return for the consolation which they gave the poor.

But if all the good are to enter the kingdom of heaven—those who love poverty, those who endure it, and also those who console it—what does it mean that the kingdom, which is to be shared by all, is promised only to those who embrace voluntary poverty, if only such persons are judged poor in spirit? This makes a difference: it is not said of them, “They shall enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXV), but, what seems more: “Theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” For although all those blessed by God who are to be blessed will receive the kingdom of heaven prepared for them from the origin of the world, and although all are believed to enter the kingdom of heaven, yet of some it is specially said: “Of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX).

There is another point which may trouble us. Whereas the other promises in this sequence of evangelical distribution are deferred to the future, this promise is suspended by no delay, but is displayed as though already granted; so that it seems rather an attainment of present benefit than an expectation of future recompense. A similar form is added concerning those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. For of both these and the former it is pronounced that the kingdom of heaven is theirs, as though the reward had already been rendered without delay, hindrance, or postponement. But the meek are not yet said to possess the earth; rather, it is said that they shall possess the earth. The merciful shall obtain mercy; those who mourn shall be comforted; those who hunger for righteousness shall be filled; peacemakers shall be called sons of God; and the pure in heart shall see God (Matt. V). Yet all these things are in the future.

[Col. 0485C] Some explanation of this difference seems to be required. Perhaps these two acts of justification, the first and the last, whose reward is not deferred, belong to the perfect: those who are tested in the furnace of poverty or in the fire of persecution, as silver is tested, and are refined to purity—those who build upon the foundation gold, silver, and precious stones. Leaving this world, they carry with them neither wood nor hay nor stubble, which might burn in them; but as soon as they depart, they fly to heaven, not delayed from the kingdom, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

Without these virtues by which the weaknesses of the other virtues are purified—for “all our righteousness is like a menstrual cloth” (Isa. LXIV)—whatever good persons may be found seem in some respect to build [Col. 0485D] upon the foundation wood, hay, and stubble, which must burn in them; they are indeed saved, yet so as through fire. Even those who are pure in heart, to whom the vision of God is promised, still need purification. For who shall boast that he has a chaste heart?

### On the acts of justification of martyrdom

There are two kinds of martyrdom: one in the flesh, the other in the spirit. By these two acts of justification the perfection of the others seems to be consummated; and when the perfection of the remaining virtues has reached its completion, it ought deservedly to be ascribed to these, because through them it is completed. For all the righteous must suffer for Christ, either in the flesh or in the spirit, if they are to attain the glory of perfection.

Who the poor in spirit are is more fully understood if spirit is distinguished from spirit. The Prophet gives us an occasion for easier understanding when he says: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and the humble in spirit shall be saved” (Ps. XXXIII). And the Apostle says: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit which is from God” (1 Cor. II). The spirit of this world may fittingly be understood as the prince of this world, concerning whom the same Apostle says elsewhere: “When you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit which now works in the children of unbelief” (Eph. II).

When the spirit of a human being is breathed upon by this spirit of the world, it is immediately puffed up; and, made like him by whom it is breathed upon, it may itself be called the spirit of this world, when it desires the things that belong to the world. [Col. 0486B] This spirit, however, is proud and vain, presumptuous and ambitious, always setting its mind on high things and despising humble things. But those who are led by the Spirit of God, the more they are breathed upon by him, the less they are puffed up and the more they are humbled: like the poor in spirit, who do not set their minds on high things but condescend to the lowly.

Therefore the virtue of the poor in spirit must be assessed from a deficiency of their own spirit and an abundance of the Spirit. The less a person has of his own spirit, the more abundantly the Spirit of God is in him; and the more he fails from his own spirit, the more abundantly he advances according to the Spirit of God. Therefore, if it is asked according to which spirit they are pronounced poor in spirit, it seems more correct to understand this according to the Spirit of God, who makes poor and makes rich, humbles and lifts up. For those whom he makes poorer, [Col. 0486C] he also makes richer; and those whom he makes humbler, he also makes more exalted—not according to the height of self-exaltation, but according to the summit of perfection.

Yet if anyone thinks that “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V) is said as though by privation, that is, of persons having less spirit or lacking spirit—namely, their own spirit or that of this world—just as those are called poor in goods who do not possess material wealth: this does not conflict with sound doctrine. Rather, through interpretation it arrives at nearly the same understanding as the preceding sense. Nevertheless, the first interpretation seems preferable, because “humble in spirit” and “poor in spirit” are more suitably said on the same principle. The humble in spirit are so called according to a habit or disposition, [Col. 0486D] and not according to privation: that is, according to the spirit which they have, not according to that which they lack.

That those who advance according to the Spirit of God fail from their own spirit is shown by the Prophet speaking to God: “Thou shalt take away their spirit, and they shall fail, and return to their dust. Thou shalt send forth thy Spirit, and they shall be created” (Ps. CIII). The south wind does not perform its course while the north wind does not cease from its own blast. The former does not breathe in its gentleness while the north wind endures in its violent wind. Therefore it is written: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song of Songs IV).

### On the human spirit

The human spirit swells and grows within itself in three ways; and in the same number of ways it fails from itself and is deflated. It swells through vain opinion, vain hope, and vain desire—all these three being vain. For swelling and inflation are vanity; and whoever swells is empty and void, as full of nothing as he is full of the wind of pride.

### On false opinion

A person swells in vain opinion—that is, false opinion—in three ways. Trusting in the pride of his own spirit, he now invents false things concerning God, now entertains proud thoughts concerning himself, now finds room for uncertain suspicion or evil thought against his neighbour. False opinion concerning God is admitted most dangerously. For it is not permitted to discuss by the uncertainty of human opinion those things of God which are hidden and secret, nor to believe anything of God other than what he himself has deigned to reveal concerning himself. He himself is his own witness; he has willed that people be conscious of his secrets only to the extent [Col. 0487B] to which the assurance of faith reaches—a faith established from the testimonies of Scripture and, supported by their reasoning, fixed and made stable without wavering.

For Holy Scripture is divinely inspired. In it the pattern of faith has been written for us; whatever is sought beyond it is not found. Every human invention which opposes the piety of faith and the prescribed pattern must be reckoned an act of presumption by the spirit. For the presumption or inflation of the spirit can be healed only by the humility of faith, which blows out whatever the spirit of pride has breathed in—a spirit ever opposed to God, whom God ever resists, while giving his grace to the humble.

This humility of faith claims the foremost place in the virtue of the poor in spirit. It shows worthy reverence to God’s words, believing them and content with them. Whoever possesses it perfectly does not trust himself, but entrusts his spirit to God, so that his spirit may be entrusted with God. God also entrusts himself to such a person, committing to him, as to one faithful to him, the mysteries of his counsel. And the human spirit is formed by the Spirit of God through inspired grace, so that it may be faithful in believing the faithful God, who is faithful in all his words.

While every impious error is removed from our heart by the Spirit of God and nothing false or unworthy is believed concerning God, the Holy Spirit bears witness to our spirit, so that our spirit in this respect retains nothing from itself. Renouncing and denying itself, it fails from itself, lest it presume to hold some opinion concerning God as if from itself. For every human opinion [Col. 0487D] concerning God is pious when it is from God, but not pious when it is from man. Therefore there is a good failure of the spirit when, failing from its own opinion, it dares nothing concerning God to which the Spirit of God does not bear witness in the words of God. Let the poor in spirit therefore say, whenever he remembers God and delights in this meditation: “I remembered God and was delighted, and my spirit failed” (Ps. LXXVI).

### On vain opinion

A person thinks proudly of himself when he ascribes to himself the good things which he has, or seems to have; when, great in his own eyes, he supposes himself to be more than he is and able to do more than he can. No less proudly does he think of himself when he judges himself unworthy of the evils he suffers, or when he conceals, excuses, [Col. 0488A] or even praises the evils which he commits and regards them as praiseworthy. He swells against his neighbour through proud opinion when, in anger, he accuses or condemns his neighbour’s evils more harshly—as anger proceeds from anger—or when, from envy, he diminishes and disparages his neighbour’s goods.

But just as the swelling of the spirit in judging oneself or one’s neighbour is evil, so the failure of the spirit from both kinds of swelling is praiseworthy; and it belongs to those who, through humility of spirit, please God and displease themselves.

### On vain hope

The human spirit swells through vain hope when, too secure in its own righteousness, it extends its hope of heavenly recompense beyond its merits. The human spirit ought to fail from presumptuous hope in expectation of heavenly recompense—not through the violence of utter despair, nor through the faint-heartedness of grievous anxiety, but through the moderation of hope mingled with and tempered by fear. For hope without fear belongs to vain security; fear without hope belongs to perverse desolation.

But concerning one overwhelmed by fear and sorrow so as to despair of salvation, judge himself worthy of punishment and unworthy of mercy, and say, “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve to be forgiven” (Gen. IV), it may be asked whether he is proud and, if so, what kind of pride it is—since it does not seem to raise the mind on high, but rather to drive it down to the depths by excessive dejection. This makes the question more difficult, lest something be called pride which, as it is written, is “the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X).

[Col. 0488C] A similar question arises concerning faint-heartedness of spirit, of which the Prophet says: “I waited for him who saved me from faint-heartedness of spirit and from the storm” (Ps. LIV). For, since despair or faint-heartedness of spirit seems to be a corruption of humility, an excessive abasement and immoderate depression, it is strange if that which seems contrary to exaltation belongs to pride; or, if it does not belong to pride, it seems equally strange how pride can be called the beginning of every sin.

But since it is not our purpose here to debate these questions, we leave it to others to investigate whether such despair or faint-heartedness of spirit belongs to the sin of pride or only to the punishment of pride. Let us instead approach the poor in spirit, among whom belong neither the proud [Col. 0488D] nor the faint-hearted in spirit nor the despairing; but the faint-hearted in spirit and the despairing must be distinguished from the proud.

### On vain hope and pride

Through vain hope, too, that person is proud and swells who trusts in himself—that is, in his own strength, wisdom, eloquence, earthly substance, reputation, nobility, human favour, or any other basis—rather than in God alone, who alone can deliver in the time of tribulation. He does not abandon those who hope in him. To him the Prophet says: “O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in thee” (Ps. LXXXIII). Again: “O Lord, thou art my hope from my youth” (Ps. LXX). Again: “God is my helper, and my hope is in God” (Ps. LXI).

But hope, when humbly placed in God, does not disappoint, because God is truth and deceives no one. “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. XVII). A human being sometimes can deliver but will not; sometimes wishes to do so but cannot. God, however, as he always can, so he always wills to save those who hope in him—not in themselves, nor proudly presuming upon him or upon themselves. The Prophet says: “Those who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of their riches—a brother shall not redeem” (Ps. XLVIII). Behold: those who trust and presume in themselves are estranged from the grace of redemption.

### On evil and good security

There are some who are secure in vain hope and add sin to sin, saying: “The mercies of the Lord are many” (Ps. XXI). Flattering themselves with God’s mercy and seeming to place their hope in it, they are the prouder the more secure they are. True security, however, is the fear of the Lord.
