This fear makes one secure rather than swollen. Those who lack it while promising themselves God’s mercy deceive themselves, so that they may be confounded in their expectation. For mercy is promised not to those who sin securely, but to those who fear God and cease from sinning.

Let us consult the testimonies of Scripture concerning these matters. The Prophet says: “As high as heaven is above the earth, he has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him” (Ps. CII). And: “As a father has compassion upon his children, the Lord has had compassion upon those who fear him” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “His salvation is near to those who fear him” (Ps. LXXXIV). And the most blessed Mother of mercy says: “His mercy [Col. 0489C] is from generation to generation upon those who fear him” (Luke I). See how the fear of God and the mercy of God are joined, so that God’s mercy ought not to be hoped for without the fear of God.

For as fear without hope is dangerous, sending one into despair, so hope without fear is destructive, drawing one toward obstinacy. Therefore it is written in the Law: “Thou shalt not take the lower and upper millstone as a pledge” (Deut. XXIV). The upper millstone is hope, and the lower is fear. Between them whatever is healthfully ground is ground. But one without the other is useless; and when taken as a pledge, either by itself benefits neither the giver nor the receiver. A pledge, however, is received for security, because it makes secure.

What the pledge is, the Apostle teaches when he says: “God who anointed us, sealed us, and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Cor. I). This is addressed to the Corinthians. But to the Ephesians he says: “You have been sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Eph. I). Therefore the pledge is the Holy Spirit, who grants us true security in the conjunction of fear and holy hope. For without fear security is vain; without hope there is no security; but together in these there is true security.

Therefore the fear of God ought to restrain hope, so that it may be deflated from its presumption, lest it become empty in its vanity and be confounded in its expectation. For it follows that the human spirit should advance by praying and hoping in God; yet it should so fail from itself by its presumption of hope that it may say with the [Col. 0490A] Prophet: “With my voice I cried unto the Lord; with my voice I made supplication unto the Lord. I pour out my prayer in his sight, and declare my tribulation before him, as my spirit fails from me” (Ps. CXLI). And again: “Hear me speedily, O Lord; my spirit has failed” (Ps. CXLII).

God is not granted delay in answering, but is asked to answer speedily when the human spirit fails in the fear of God: so that it may hope wholly neither in itself, nor in its strength, wisdom, skill or cunning, nor in any of its resources, but in God alone and in the things which belong to God because they belong to God. In our good things, since they are from God—for example, faith and works of righteousness and mercy—hope must indeed be placed after God, but so that all confidence is withdrawn from ourselves, although the good things are ours, and cast upon him whose gifts they are. For the one who draws to himself the confidence which ought to be placed in God because of God’s gifts does God an injury. And since aid is usually invoked from the quarter where it is hoped for, the one who hopes for aid from himself invokes himself rather than God. Therefore he cannot yet say: “Hear me speedily, O Lord; my spirit has failed.”

### On desire and pride

Through vain desire the mind grows great in two ways: through love of using or possessing what is possessed, or through desire to possess what is not possessed. Desire itself, however, is a kind of love. For to desire is, in some way, to love. Desire (*cupiditas*) is love of the world, just as charity is love of God. [Col. 0490C] Desire seeks its own things, not those of Jesus Christ; and it seeks them thus: now through love of earthly possession, now through love of slippery and transitory pleasure, now through love of dominion, now through love of ambitious honour, now through love of admiration, favour, and praise.

These are the things which desire proudly and insatiably seeks against God. These are the things which charity nobly despises for God’s sake and, if I may say so, by its own mode of pride. For charity has, if it is permitted to say so, its own pride, by which it nobly despises pride itself and everything proud against God. Hence it was said to the apostles: “You shall consume the strength of the nations, and shall glory in their glory” [literally, “shall be proud”] (Isa. LXI).

To despise God for the sake of things that ought to be despised, and to love things to be despised more than God, is base pride and worthy of confusion. But to despise the glory of the world for God’s sake is noble pride. Nobler still is it if even confusion itself is despised for Christ’s sake without shame: he who, “for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame” (Heb. XII). For it is better to be ashamed of dignities and honours in this world than of Christ’s cross, Christ’s poverty, or Christ’s humility. “Whoever,” he says, “shall be ashamed of me and my words, of him shall the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his majesty and that of the holy angels” (Luke IX). “The servant is not greater than his lord” (John XIII). What Christ was not ashamed of for us ought not to be ashamed of by us for Christ’s sake.

[Col. 0491A] Whoever is restrained by shame from imitating or emulating the humility of Christ still has something of his own spirit. Such shame is vain; and as far as it withdraws from humility, so far it approaches pride. Holy poverty, however, is to be judged more by humility of mind than by scantiness of possessions. Those who have no lofty self-estimation ought more to be called poor in spirit than those who have a small income. For persons who think proudly, even if poor in material things, belong less to the poor in spirit than those who possess in such a way as though they possessed not.

Therefore holy poverty, despising the world and what belongs to the world, renouncing possessions held, possessions to be held, and the desire of possessing, and restraining itself from every presumption of the spirit, is so acceptable to God that he says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). It is so lovable and dear to God that a poor person may glory in God’s concern for him and say: “But I am a beggar and poor; the Lord is concerned for me” (Ps. XXXIX). If all the honours of the rich were brought together, what could equal this honour? Which rich person would dare to presume to say, “I am full and wealthy; the Lord is concerned for me”? The rich person is sufficient to himself and does not seem to need the Lord’s concern for him.

This is the poor person’s voice and glory: “Bow down thine ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am needy and poor” (Ps. LXXXV). If any poor person approached a very rich and powerful man and said, [Col. 0491C] “Bow down your ear and hear me,” who among those standing by would endure it patiently? Would he not be driven away and hissed at by all? Would he not be regarded and despised with a proud eye by the powerful man himself? Would he not be ordered to be cast and thrust shamefully from the house itself?

Who would dare say to his Lord: “Bow down thine ear”? Who would dare say this to the Lord of lords? Who but the poor person, and the poor in spirit? For this is his voice: “Make glad the soul of thy servant, for unto thee, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul” (ibid.). If he savoured the things upon the earth rather than those above, he would not say, “Unto thee, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.” Therefore the poor in spirit, who do not abase their hearts among low things but desire, long, and burn after heavenly things—these lift their souls to God. There their life is hidden with Christ; there are their eye and their love; there are their heart and their treasure.

O happy poverty, to be rewarded not only in the kingdom of heaven but with the very kingdom of heaven! O happy poverty, though contemptible to the world, yet honourable to God! “For he shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the poor; and their name shall be honourable before him” (Ps. LXI). O unhappy riches, to be exchanged for everlasting want! O miserable prosperity, to be recompensed with eternal calamity! The rich man buried in hell and the poor man resting in Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI) settle the case of poor and rich by a certain judgment. The rich man burns and thirsts in torment, and receives no comfort from the poor man because he gave no comfort to the poor man, because he received good things in his lifetime.

[Col. 0492A] Nevertheless, let not the rich despair. Let them observe that Abraham was rich, in whose bosom Lazarus rested. But let them look to Abraham in such a way that they possess riches as Abraham did: let them possess them from just causes, for lawful uses, and for the grace of offering hospitality, as Abraham did. Finally, let them possess them not to retain for themselves but to share with the poor, by whom they may be received into eternal dwellings. For the salvation of the rich is the glory of the poor.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (ibid.).

The promises of God are various and diverse, according to the merits of the righteous and their acts of justification. To every act of justification its own recompense belongs, [Col. 0492B] and every virtue has its proper praise and proper reward, according to the dignity of its rank and the quality of its kind. To the meek possession of the earth is promised. The virtue of the meek is gentleness, so that what the Prophet says is true: “But the gentle shall inherit the earth” (Ps. XXXVI). If the meek are blessed, then surely the gentle also are blessed. Let the gentle hear this and rejoice (Ps. XXXIII). Let them hear that they now are, or shall be, blessed; let them hear also why they are blessed: “For they shall possess the earth.”

There are those who fight and contend for land: unmerciful persons oppress others and rule over the meek. Why are not these blessed, since they possess the earth? Rather, how can they be blessed if the earth shall devour them? O earth, earth, earth: with how much vanity are you loved by the children of men, who were taken from the earth, shall be consumed by the earth, and are themselves nothing but earth! Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love the vanity (Ps. IV) of this world, where there is nothing but the lust of the eyes and the pride of life?

Know, all you earthborn and children of men, that we have no abiding inheritance upon earth except the clod of our body, which is earth from earth. What, then, does this promise mean: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth”? What does it mean that God promises earth to the meek when he promises the kingdom of heaven to others? “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Why does he promise earth who warns that earth should be despised? Is not heaven promised to all the righteous and to sinners doing penance? Hence it is written: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. III). Will it not be said at the end to all who are to be placed at the right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the origin of the world” (Matt. XXV)?

[Col. 0492D] Is the virtue of the meek, then, of such middling quality and of such slender merit that its reward is assigned on earth? Yet let us hear how great is the praise of meekness. The Lord sets himself before us as an example for learning it, saying: “Learn of me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). And he shows where his Spirit rests, saying: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, but upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?” (Isa. [Col. 0493A] LXVI).

If, therefore, the Spirit of God rests upon the meek, so that they too may rest in him, as finding rest for their souls, we may be moved even more to ask why earth is promised by the Lord to a virtue of such praise and merit—he who pleads the cause of the meek of the earth, directs the meek in judgment and teaches the meek his ways (Ps. XXIV), and will rise in judgment (Ps. XXXIV) in order to save all the meek of the earth (Ps. LXXV).

### That we ought to depart from Ur of the Chaldeans

To Abraham, to whom the promises were given, the Lord promised land, saying: “To thee I will give the land of Canaan, the portion of thine inheritance” (Ps. CIV). In order to lead him into the land which he had promised him, he first brought him out of the land in which he had been accustomed to dwell, saying: “Go out from [Col. 0493B] thy land, and come into the land which I shall show thee” (Gen. XII). He brought him out of the land of the Chaldeans, from the place of his birth. By this example we too are admonished to leave Ur of the Chaldeans—that is, the burning of vices, the place of our captivity.

For our flesh, conceived in sin and liable to sin, is the land of the Chaldeans and the place of our birth. And we, because we belong to Christ, are Abraham’s seed. For those who are according to the spirit are reckoned as seed, like the children of promise together with Isaac, who was born through the promise. Abraham dwells, however, in his seed, in the land of promise, after the Canaanites have been driven out of it by the children of Israel. And they did not possess the land by their own sword; rather, the Lord drove the nations out from before them, divided the land to them by lot according to the line of distribution, and caused the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents (Ps. LXXVII).

### On the threefold state of our flesh
The land of the Chaldeans, the land of Canaan, and the land of promise signify the threefold condition of our flesh. For before the resolve of conversion, our flesh is the land of the Chaldeans, from which Abraham is commanded to depart. At the beginning of conversion, when vices have not yet been subdued, it is the land of Canaan, still possessed by the Canaanites, against whom the children of Israel declare war. The land of promise is that already possessed by the children of Israel, when, with vices driven out, the flesh has been chastened by the practice of discipline; and chastened so that sin may not reign in the mortal body (Rom. 6). It is flesh reduced to servitude and subjected to the spirit [Col. 0493D], flesh not presenting its members as weapons of iniquity for iniquity, but presenting its members as weapons of righteousness for sanctification. This flesh is land once Canaan, no longer possessed by the Canaanites but, with carnal desires expelled, now cleansed and possessed by the children of Israel. Even a Canaanite, though rarely, dwells there, but does not rule. For carnal inclination can be restrained, so that consent is not given to it.

But this land, once the land of Canaan, differs greatly from the land of the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans remain in their own land and are not driven out by Abraham’s seed; rather, Abraham is commanded to depart from there. For there are some to whom it is said: “You shall die in your sin” (John 8). These are they who dwell in the land of the Chaldeans, from whose midst Abraham departs, in order to drive out the Canaanite and possess the land flowing with milk and honey [Col. 0494A]. Consider whether perhaps this is the land promised to the meek for their possession. Meekness is the beginning of virtue. But observe that one kind of meekness is a person’s meekness toward himself, another toward his neighbour, and another toward God. Let that which is set first be considered first.

### On a Person’s Meekness toward Himself

For these three things are in a human being: flesh, will, and reason. By “flesh” I here mean that which desires against the spirit; and to it belong not only vices of the body but also vices of the soul, of which the Apostle says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, lust, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, contentions, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies [Col. 0494B], murders, drunkennesses, revelries, and things like these” (Gal. 5). You see how many vices of the mind he enumerates, such as anger and envy; how many vices of the body; and yet he calls them all works of the flesh—without doubt, of that flesh which desires against the spirit.

Thus “flesh” here means that which in us desires irrationally. Between this flesh and reason, the will is placed in the middle; and it is rightly in the middle when it agrees with reason, having reason above it, ruling it, and flesh beneath it, serving it. But if it agrees with the flesh and disagrees with reason, it is already under the flesh: not ruling the flesh, but, in a shameful and wretched servitude, serving its own handmaid contrary to the proper order of a mistress.

When flesh and will agree with one another [Col. 0494C] and disagree with reason, the will itself, as though untamed and unmeek, rejects the yoke of obedience: it is not softened by command, does not yield to counsel, and is not gentled by persuasion. Rather, like a brazen and contentious woman, it now fights against reason, now disputes, now murmurs; and there is no peace in the house in which it dwells. Whoever walks according to the flesh, serving fleshly passions while sin rules in the mortal body, when the law of sin is inscribed in sin’s kingdom so that the servant of sin is subject to it—does such a person possess the land of his body or the land of his heart? Is he not rather possessed by the land, having no freedom by which to free himself, extricate himself, or shake off what presses and weighs him down? For he is buried beneath the earth and, as it were, entombed [Col. 0494D] in the earth among those who sleep in graves, “whom God remembers no more” (Ps. 87), unless perhaps He looks upon him who makes the earth tremble.

For what can reason do when it has been abandoned by the will and stands alone, because it is alone? “Woe to one who is alone” (Ecclus. 4). But if the earth is moved from before the face of the Lord (Ps. 113), so that the awakened will may rise again, then, when it begins to agree with reason, it is restored to its order, its freedom, its peace, and thus to itself. It is restored to order, indeed, because, subjected to its superior and now set over its inferior, it finds itself there by grace from which it had voluntarily withdrawn through fault. It is restored to freedom when, on the one hand receiving obedience and willing to render it, and on the other imposing obedience and now demanding it almost by a kind of right, it does not move according to the flesh but moves the flesh according to itself [Col. 0495A], urging the members into its service in works of piety and salvation, in works of righteousness and mercy, in doing, carrying out, and enduring all that the authority of reason, with the will’s consent, has decreed either to be done or borne.

But if the members begin to move according to the flesh, the will, agreeing with reason and using its freedom, resists lest they advance; and it commands them to rest within themselves and to have peace. Then the land begins to be possessed, because the mind is humble and quiet, gentle and meek, consenting to be possessed by reason so that it may possess the land and have authority in it. This possession of the land is, as it were, a reward of meekness. Those who are meek in the manner described [Col. 0495B] begin to be restored to peace and to themselves, and to be made blessed in their peace, because “peace is for people of good will.”

A person, first disagreeing with reason and, as it were, departing from himself, began to be deprived of possession of his own land and to be exiled within himself—as though outside himself, in a foreign land and a land of forgetfulness, in a region of unlikeness. Returning to his heart after transgression, he finds himself at home with himself; and lest he lack himself, he is restored to himself, and his possession is restored to him as though in the year of Jubilee, so that he may rest beneath his vine and fig tree and possess the land in peace, because he is meek. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 26 [an apparent citation error for Matt. 5]).

This is the land of promise, once the land of Canaan, which God promised to Abraham while he was still living in the land of the Chaldeans, in a foreign land [Col. 0495C], where neither the Lord’s song nor a hymn from the songs of Zion is sung. This is the holy land, where, in spiritual senses and affections, Abraham’s seed—the temple of the Lord—dwells, and where God is adored and worshipped. Therefore the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. 6). And again: “For the temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3).

This land is not yet fully possessed, because complete meekness is not yet found in our will. In some matters we resist reason, and in some matters the flesh resists us. What we do against reason, we suffer through the flesh in corresponding fashion. Yet the will is in part subject to reason, and in part has the flesh subject to itself; yet the flesh also in part contradicts and barks against it. For the undisciplined motions in our heart or body are like the barking of a dog: more troublesome to travellers in their barking than in their bite. Barking is indeed troublesome and alarming, but biting is harmful; and barking can serve for watchfulness and caution. For dogs sometimes bark for us, not always against us; God so ordering it that we may walk carefully and be aroused to watchfulness, lest we ever fall asleep in death through complacency. If dogs bark about a house, is the house not nevertheless possessed in peace? And if there is some contradiction in our flesh, contrary not only to reason but also to our will, do we therefore fail to possess the land? Rather, we possess it—not yet wholly as we wish, but as for the time being we can [Col. 0496A].

Even in a father’s kingdom robbers are found; but, once detected, they are either hanged or condemned to other punishments, so that the kingdom may be established in its peace through judgment and justice. For without justice there is no peace in a kingdom, no peace in a house, no peace in our heart, no peace in our flesh, no peace in our land. “For the righteous shall inherit the land.” If the land is possessed in justice, it is possessed also in peace; nor is it possessed in peace without justice. Hence it is written: “Justice and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84).

This land, which is not yet completely possessed and yet is possessed in some measure, will then be completely possessed when the whole corruption of the flesh has been consumed by the glory of the resurrection, and neither the will will resist reason nor the flesh [Col. 0496B] the will in any respect. This will happen when all the seed of Canaan is exterminated from the land, when every curse of Canaan is removed from us. For Canaan is cursed and subjected to servitude; but creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Then “the meek shall inherit the land and delight in an abundance of peace.” And those who now hope in the Lord and do good shall then inhabit it and be fed by its riches. The land will surely be exceedingly rich and abundant, flowing with milk and honey, free from every evil as the reward of former obedience.

The virtue of a person’s meekness toward himself consists in patience and obedience: both the obedience of the will to reason [Col. 0496C], and that of the flesh to the will. For reason imposes upon the meek will, and the will upon meek and subdued flesh, now certain hard things to be endured—and there is the virtue of patience, because they are endured patiently; now certain good things to be done—and there is the virtue of obedience, because they are humbly performed. Thus the milk of consolation, through freedom from evil, will be the reward of patience; and honey, through the fullness of every good, will be the reward of obedience.

### On a Person’s Meekness toward His Neighbour

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the land” (Matt. 5).

The land is promised to the meek—the land, certainly, of promise. The land of promise, however, seems to be understood figuratively in four ways. First, with respect to the whole body of believers, the land of promise is [Col. 0496D] the multitude of the faithful, gathered throughout the world in the righteousness of faith and obedience in which Abraham pleased God, and to be gathered at the end into Abraham’s bosom. Hence, according to the Apostle, it was promised to Abraham that he should be heir of the world (Rom. 4), because he was to become the father of many nations.

Second, according to the particular hope of individuals, the land of promise in each person is the land of his own heart and body, given to each for possession, to be possessed in peace through meekness. Third, the land of promise is also the land of the living, where is the fellowship of the blessed, where no one dies, where is that Jerusalem “built as a city, whose inhabitants are at unity”; no uncircumcised or unclean person shall pass through it; Canaanites do not dwell there; malignant spirits have been excluded from it [Col. 0497A], and they have neither part nor lot in the land of the saints. Possession of this land is promised to the meek, because participation in the blessed fellowship is acquired by meekness.

For every holy fellowship is established by peace, and peace is not preserved without meekness. Just as an unruly beast does not pull in harness but disrupts it, so an unmeek person in a congregation of good people disturbs peace, breaks the covenant of friendship, loosens the bonds of fellowship, speaks ill of his neighbour, and brings reproach against his neighbour. Now he fights, now disputes, now murmurs; now, amid disputatious thoughts and suspicions concerning others, he judges—as an untamed and stiff-necked young bull rejects the yoke. His mind rushes toward anger, his eye toward envy, his tongue toward insult. He does not live socially, but often separates himself from fellowship and community through the singularity of his own pursuit [Col. 0497B]. Harmful to himself and disturbing to others, he does not aid the work of common salvation by his example, but dissipates unity; and like a perverse companion he obstructs the common work shared by all.

But the virtue of meekness, as it is always free from all these evils, is always intimate and friendly with peace. Its proper characteristic is neither to inflict nor to return an injury: that is, neither to harm without cause nor to seek vengeance; that is, neither to be an enemy nor an avenger. Yet both the enemy and the avenger are enemies of God; and He himself will destroy them, that “out of the mouth of infants and nursing children he may perfect praise because of his enemies” (Ps. 8). Who are nursing children and infants, if not those who are small, humble, simple, gentle, meek, patient, and who do not overcome good by evil but overcome evil by good?

An infant does not utter words; a nursing child sucks milk. Yet listen to the infant speaking: “I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me” (Ps. 38). If cursed, he does not curse; if struck, he does not threaten. For he is mute in the face of injury and says: “I became as one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth” (Ps. 37). But to nursing children it is said: “Putting away all malice, all deceit, pretences, and all detractions, desire rational milk like newly born infants, that by it you may grow into salvation” (1 Pet. 2). For in such persons the Lord is well pleased, and “he will exalt the meek unto salvation.”

Is not the land of the living rightly that place where the most blessed fellowship of the elect is promised to the meek [Col. 0497D], who in the present fellowship of the good live socially through innocence and patience, preserving unity in the bond of peace? A fitting reward for the meek is this peaceful possession of the land, where blessed fellowship is established in peace, which cannot be retained without meekness. Therefore the Prophet says to God: “Let peace be in your strength” (Ps. 121). What virtue, Lord, could I call more fittingly yours than that of which you set forth an example in yourself, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11)?

Thus peace is made by meekness and retained by meekness, so that we may first possess our souls in patience, soon to be transferred into the kingdom of peace, where eternal rest is prepared for the restful [Col. 0498A], and abundance in your towers, O Lord, as in little and humble ones. If we seek an abundance of milk and honey, let us hasten our steps toward this land. For we have heard that this region abounds in milk and honey, being free from every evil as the reward of former innocence and full of every good as the reward of former patience. A person’s meekness toward his neighbour consists, indeed, of innocence and patience; and the reward of patience will be like honey, through every abundance of good.

### On a Person’s Meekness toward God

If, according to the fourth sense, we understand the land of promise in Christ, who is the end of the promises, then it may seem difficult for those inquiring how the seed of Canaan dwelt [Col. 0498B] in that land to find an answer. For what place can a curse find where the fullness of grace dwells? Christ, conceived of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, separated from sinners, made higher than the heavens, was as full of every grace as he was free from every fault.

Yet a devout investigator may perhaps satisfy himself faithfully, if he does not dispute with himself but devoutly considers the unity of the head and body of Christ, and the condition of our mortality in Christ. For because he willed to be our head, in order to commend more deeply to his beloved the love by which he joined us more closely to himself as members, transforming us into himself because of the ineffable unity, he pleads our cause before the Father and says: “Why [Col. 0498C] have you forsaken me? Far from my salvation are the words of my sins” (Ps. 21). He calls our sins his own—sins to be imputed to us, yet not reckoned against us by him. They were ours and alien to him, who had no consciousness of personal iniquity but felt compassion for another’s misery, in order to reconcile us to God; he who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: “Cursed is the man who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. 21; Gal. 3). But the curse has now reached its end, because Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6). Therefore we hold the land of promise—not the land from Dan [Col. 0498D] to Beersheba, not from the great river Euphrates to the river of Egypt; not from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. Rather, we understand the promises made to Abraham to have been fulfilled in Christ, when the Prophet says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you are he who will restore my inheritance to me. The lines have fallen to me in splendid places; indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me. I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding” (Ps. 15).

Therefore in Christ is our inheritance and our portion; and, according to the dispensation of the nature assumed for us, there is the land of promise—the land of which it is said: “You have blessed your land, O Lord” (Ps. 84), and of which it is again written: “That glory may dwell in our land [Col. 0499A], mercy and truth have met each other” (Ps. 84). In order that the Lord might give this land to the meek, he who sits upon the cherubim came meekly, seated upon an ass, meek in all obedience and patience. In him God has set before us an example of meekness, so that in obedience and patience we may bear Christ our rider, and that we, being meek, may bear the meek one.

O our confusion, O our shame! A mute beast of burden rebukes our folly, and an ass is appointed our teacher of meekness, so that we who are more foolish may learn wisdom from a foolish animal. Woe to us, because we have wandered thus, because we have become so foolish in our folly. And whence comes this to a human being, unless because, “being placed in honour, he did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts and made like them” [Col. 0499B] (Ps. 48)? Would that we might be beneficially ashamed by this example, lest it be said of us: “The ox has known its owner and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me!” (Isa. 1).

Let us therefore show ourselves meek toward God. For the Lord, who receives the meek, both commands and counsels us to become meek to him under his yoke and burden through obedience and patience. In these two virtues, namely obedience and patience, is displayed that meekness which is toward God. Obedience fulfils what we are commanded to do; patience bears what God imposes upon us to endure. Obedience does not kick back; patience does not murmur. Obedience stands ready in commandments; patience remains steadfast [Col. 0499C] in judgments. Obedience is a yoke without a yoke, because it removes slavery and restores freedom. Patience is a burden without a burden, for it does not weigh down but lifts up. Whatever is burdensome to the impatient is lightened through patience; in patience, as in a spiritual vehicle, every burden is carried more easily. And just as the multitude of down and feathers seems to burden a bird and yet lifts it high, so patience raises tribulation upward and does not press it downward.

Those who become meek beneath Christ’s yoke and burden have God gentle even in his wrath, by which here he corrects offenders, lest they be judged more severely. Hence it is written: “Meekness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected” (Ps. 89).

Through these virtues, then—obedience, I mean, and patience—the meek rider, Christ, is borne and sustained by the meek [Col. 0499D]. With what reward? “But those who wait upon the Lord shall inherit the land” (Ps. 36): the land, indeed, flowing with milk and honey, where Christ, God and man, shall be seen in his glory—sweetly and delightfully in the glory of glorified humanity, and more sweetly and delightfully in the glory of glorious divinity.

Then, beholding this glory, they will overflow with milk and honey; for streams of both milk and honey shall flow even to them. For how would they reach them unless they flowed? Whatever delights them in the contemplated appearance of divinity, of supreme beauty and supreme sweetness, will be sweet as honey. Then it shall be said to each: “You have found honey; eat what is enough” (Prov. 25). For there will be full satisfaction, when the vessels of mercy are filled from the torrent of delight [Col. 0500A]; when it is said to the servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25), so that, surrounded by joy, wherever he turns he finds himself in joy, finds joy around him, and says: “My inheritance is above honey and the honeycomb” (Ecclus. 24).

Then honey will be good for one who has eaten much, and the contemplator of majesty will not be overwhelmed by glory. But in the meantime it is not good for one who eats much, because the searcher of majesty will be overwhelmed by glory. “I shall be satisfied,” says the Prophet, “when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). But from what shall those who are to be satisfied be satisfied? If they are to be satisfied with honey, whence will the honey flow? “From the rock,” he says, “he satisfied them with honey” (Ps. 80). “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Honey, they say, is gathered from flowers steeped in heavenly dew; hence, according to some, honeys are called *roscida* (“dewy”), as though gathered from falling dew. Thus the poet also said:

> Straightway the heavenly gifts of aerial honey,  
> > (Virgil, *Georgics* IV.1)

—whether dew grows sweet in flowers, or flowers through dew, or each in turn. Would that we might be flowers among those to whom it is said, “Bloom, you flowers” (Ecclus. 39), and of whom it is said, “Sustain me with flowers” (Song 2); and that the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion, might be made sweet in us, and we in it, and that there might be formed in us such honey as is found in the land of promise. Tasting it now beforehand and later tasting it more fully, tasting and seeing that the Lord is sweet, may we say from experience: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden [Col. 0500C] for those who fear you, and accomplished for those who hope in you” (Ps. 30).

Not honey alone abounds in the land of promise; milk also abounds. Milk has its origin in the seed of the flesh, by which a mother comforts and nourishes little children unto life, who would have no life without milk. For this purpose the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1): that we might drink milk and be satisfied from the breasts of its consolation. Therefore it is said: “As a mother comforts her children, so I will comfort you; and you shall be comforted in Jerusalem” (Isa. 66). In that heavenly Jerusalem, indeed, where there is the vision of peace, there is the milk of consolation.

Whatever will delight those beholding the revealed glory of the God-man in God will soothe them and be like milk, by which they are nourished unto life; without it they would not have that life of which he who is life himself says to the Father [Col. 0500D]: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).

The wisdom of God and the wisdom of this world differ in their judgments concerning the estimation of things; they do not weigh the importance of things on the balance of a single scale. For the wisdom of the world highly values what the wisdom of God judges fit to be rejected and despised. The wisdom of the world likewise condemns by its judgment what the wisdom of God judges precious and great.

The wisdom of God says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 6). The wisdom of the world says: Blessed are the rich, because they now rule the world. The wisdom of God says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (ibid.). [Col. 0501A] The wisdom of the world says: Blessed are warriors and the merciless, because they possess the land. The wisdom of God says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (ibid.). The wisdom of the world says: Blessed are those who laugh, because they are already now comforted.

The wisdom of the world approves, praises, and loves wealth, laughter, and the joy of the present life because they bring present consolation; it hates and condemns poverty and mourning because they bring present desolation. The wisdom of God judges the joys of the present life vain and harmful, as nourishments of vices and hindrances to salvation. But it commends and loves poverty and mourning as purgatives of vices and preparations for unending happiness.

The wisdom of God and the wisdom of this world so oppose one another in their judgments that they judge each other and are judged by one another [Col. 0501B]. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, and the wisdom of God is foolishness with the world. For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish. And the word of poverty and mourning is, in a certain sense, a word of the cross; for poverty or mourning is a kind of cross.

But the wisdom of God has been justified by her children, and by the children of light. The children of this age, however, are more prudent in their generation than the children of light. Therefore the children of this age and the children of light reckon one another foolish and mad. The former look to vanities and false madness; the latter love, as light, the foolishness of preaching by which God decreed to save believers, though the natural person does not receive it: for it is foolishness to him and he cannot understand it.

This dispute between the wisdom of God and that of this world shakes the foundations of faith itself in the hearts of many and grows so strong that, if possible, even the elect are moved. Hence one of the righteous says: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, because I was jealous of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 78). Yet when he understands their latter end, he marvels and says: “How have they been brought into desolation! They suddenly failed; they perished because of their iniquity” (ibid.).

By Solomon’s judgment laughter is condemned and mourning is preferred to feasting. “I judged laughter,” he says, “to be error; and I said to joy, ‘Why are you deceived in vain?’” (Eccl. 2). And again: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7). This is Solomon; behold, here is one greater than Solomon [Col. 0501D], who says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).

Vanity and truth distinguish one kind of mourning from another. Some mourn things that ought not to be mourned and are therefore themselves to be mourned, because they mourn vainly, just as they believe vainly. Others mourn devoutly and savingly and will be blessed because they mourn in this way, as the Lord himself, speaking to his disciples, says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice; you shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 15). And the Psalmist: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seed. But coming, they shall come with exultation, bearing their sheaves” (Ps. 125).

By this devout mourning, as by a shower of heavenly grace, our seeds are watered, that, moistened by rain, they may rise more abundantly for harvest. This is the voluntary rain [Col. 0502A] which God set apart for his inheritance. In this valley of tears, in which we were born, abundant cause for mourning is available to us, where all that meets us, whether it is within us or outside us, is scarcely anything but matter for mourning. Thus we are altogether wretched: born in misery, reared in misery until now, thereafter to live in misery, and finally to die in misery. Within, full of misery; without, surrounded by misery.

Hence one says: “My soul has been filled with evils” (Ps. 87). And: “Evils without number have surrounded me” (Ps. 39). What can we do amid these evils but groan, lament, and grieve over the evils that we feel unceasingly, and desire the goods that we do not yet feel? Or if perhaps we feel some small good, that very thing reminds us of our misery, because we feel it rarely, faintly, and not fully. Whence come to us these evils, so many and so great, unless because “we have sinned with our fathers, acted unjustly, and committed iniquity”? Our ways and our iniquities have brought these things upon us.

### On the First Cause of Mourning

The first cause of mourning, therefore, concerns evils committed and goods omitted. Who can number the evils we have committed? “My iniquities,” he says, “have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head” (Ps. 39). Who can number the goods we have lost? “I considered the days of old,” he says, “and I had eternal years in my mind” (Ps. 76). For we lost both: the days of old in which Adam was created good and blessed by God, so that he might never die; and the eternal years with which he was to be endowed, had he not sinned, so that he could never die.

These things we lost in Adam. But how many good things do we rob from ourselves in ourselves! How many good things could we have done but did not do! How many courses of time have we consumed in vain! How innumerable days have passed while we acted badly or did nothing, and swept us along with themselves in their unstable course! O where are you, fountains of waters—where are you now, fountains of tears—that I may mourn the losses of my life and likewise the losses of my innocence? Would that the floodgates of heaven might be opened above! Would that the fountains of the great deep might burst forth, and a flood of many waters overwhelm the land of my heart, so that those who dwell in it may perish [Col. 0502D], and all my senses, prone to evil from my youth!

And behold, my days have failed in vanity and my years in haste. Who will comfort me except one who grieves as I do, one who is himself penitent and says: “I have laboured in my groaning” (Ps. 6)? For while I rejoiced, playing and laughing amid worldly things and applauding various successes—while I did that in order not to groan or labour—I then truly laboured in my groaning, as I have now learned by experience. For in a true assessment, things that must be exchanged for labour and groaning are here worth what they are worth. They are truly what they are to those whom they harm.

This is indeed the late night, late for those who groan: “We have grown weary in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we have walked difficult paths” (Wis. 5). A common saying has it: “The groaning of a woman in labour is laughter a year later” [Col. 0503A]. While I walked where I wished, doing that for which I should groan—yet not in order to groan, but rather in order not to groan—woe is me: I laboured in my groaning. For what I thought and willed—that is labour before me. Then I conceived pain and gave birth to iniquity; therefore I shall wash the bed of my pain, in which I lay sick and unclean according to the uncleanness of a woman giving birth.

The bed of pain is weak flesh, evil pleasure, evil conscience; it must be washed by me in the secret silence of night, where God sees in secret, and through each individual offense. Since I bear a divided conscience—both concerning evils that I have done and concerning any goods that I have done—I will wash the bed of conscience, in which I toil in sickness; I will soak with my tears the couch of conscience which I spread for myself, so that I might rest there. I will wash the stains of my life; I will water the barrenness of my soul [Col. 0503B], if perhaps, like a rain-soaked threshing-floor, it may germinate.

For innocence, with regard to evils I did not commit, and my conscience, with regard to goods I did perform, have both become fruitless to me through the evils I did commit. Where I wish to spread a bed for myself, where I wish to rest, there I find matter for grief and cause for tears. For through those things by which I have not been corrupted—what am I saying, “where I have not been corrupted”? For where am I uncorrupted? Indeed I often think my uncorrupted qualities such that I am corrupted all the more by them. As I consider them, I say to myself: “I am not like the rest of humanity, like this man or that; I am such a one, and not like him.” And while I judge myself superior, I am often uncertain whether I ought to grieve more over my uncorrupted qualities, which exalt me in this way, or over my sins, the anxious recollection of which humbles me.

### On the Second Cause of Mourning

[Col. 0503C]

While I mourn sins as I mourn them, and seek the consolation of the remedy of repentance, another cause of mourning is also present: temptations sent, though not accepted, which besiege and surround me on every side, so that no opening for escape appears. For thousands of temptations rise up against me: some above me, some within me, some about me, and all against me. When one leaves me, another immediately seizes me; as one yields, another succeeds; and amid them there is no peace for my spirit.

For what I see, hear, do, think, will, what pleases me, what displeases me—in short, all that I live—is temptation to me, as it is written: “Human life upon earth is temptation” (Job 7). Amid these temptations, so many, so evil, so importunate, so perplexing and inextricable, from which I cannot extricate myself, life itself is often wearisome to me. And while I seek consolation, I find it more in the weakness of the saints than in my own strength.

For I hear Paul, so confined amid temptations that he is compelled to cry: “Unhappy man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). O how great is the consolation which God, in his ordering, has provided for our weakness! For the weaknesses of the saints sometimes strengthen us more than their virtues. Their virtues kindle desire; their weaknesses raise hope. When Paul, to whom it was said, “Strength is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12), himself says of himself, “When I am weak, then I am stronger” [Col. 0504A] (ibid.), I too can say: “When Paul is weak, I am stronger.” Therefore Paul’s weakness helps me in my own case, as his strength helps me before God, that he may rescue me from temptation—my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling.

### On the Third Cause of Mourning
Besides the evils that stain our life, and the evils that tempt us toward guilt, other evils press upon us which purge guilt. I rightly call them “other,” because there are kinds of temptations which are resisted by refusing consent, and kinds of suffering and tribulation in which we are exercised by endurance. And although in the same things we are commonly tempted toward guilt and exercised by punishment, nevertheless what we fear in temptation is one thing, and what we suffer [Col. 0504B] in tribulation another. Here guilt is the cause; there, punishment. These evils by which we are afflicted also have their weariness and their tears. Elijah is a witness, who threw himself beneath the shade of a single juniper tree and asked for his soul to die, saying: “It is enough for me; take away my life” (3 Kings 10). Paul too is a witness, who himself says: “We were weighed down beyond measure, so that we were weary even of living” (2 Cor. 1). Jonah too is a witness, who says: “I am angry even unto death” (Jonah 4). Let this suffice concerning weariness. For groaning and tears, he proves it who says: “Every creature groans and labours in birth until now. Not only it, but we ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves” (Rom. 8). And the Psalmist: “Through the strength of your hand I have failed under rebukes; because of iniquity you corrected man” [Col. 0504C] (Ps. 38). And he adds concerning tears: “Hear my prayer, O Lord, and my supplication; give ear to my tears” (ibid.).

But if these are the tears of all the righteous, how is the contrary not true: “They went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5)? And Paul says: “Rejoicing in tribulation” (Rom. 12); and James: “Count it all joy, brethren, when you fall into various temptations” (Jas. 1). Yet those who are weak suffer in tribulations, whereas those who are perfect even rejoice in tribulations—that belongs to strength; and nevertheless they suffer—that belongs to weakness. For the perfect are not without weakness [Col. 0504D]. For their strength is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12). In a wonderful way God strengthens his saints through weakness and humbles them through strength. Hence the righteous man says: “I ate ashes as bread, and mingled my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101). As though he said: The remembrance of my weakness and condition, by which I remember that I am ashes and dust, is my bread and refreshment, strengthening and fortifying me; the spiritual drink of joy, that which gladdens me, is not without bitterness, because joy is tempered by grief. But if there were strength without weakness, there would also be joy without sorrow. Now, however, weakness has advanced toward strength—this is: “I ate ashes as bread”—and strength toward humility through weakness—this is: “I mingled my drink with weeping” [Col. 0505A].

And indeed it ought to be so. For a little wine is necessary for us because of frequent weaknesses (1 Tim. 5). And if wine were not diluted, who would not be drunk? Whose head would not ache? Who would not have that spirit of dizziness which the Lord mixed in the midst of Egypt? It is fitting, therefore, that the cup be mingled with weeping, that joy be tempered with sorrow, and that strength be humbled in weakness.

### On the fourth cause for mourning

But if that which presently presses upon us is so grave that it wrings out tears, how much more should that which terrifies us in the future draw forth tears? For that is eternal, this transitory. This is scarcely, yet somehow, endurable; that is wholly unbearable. “For who shall be able [Col. 0505B] to dwell with devouring fire? Or who shall dwell with everlasting burnings?” (Isa. 33). What wonder, then, if this fear has its own mourning? For who is wise and does not desire to extinguish with tears the unquenchable fire? “Your wrath has passed over me,” says the righteous man (Ps. 87): this concerns the temporal punishment that now presses upon him. “And your terrors have troubled me” (ibid.): this concerns the eternal punishment which terrifies more. And blessed Job says: “The arrows of the Lord are in me; their indignation drinks up my spirit, and terrors wage war against me” (Job 6). What he says, “The arrows of the Lord are in me,” is “Your wrath has passed over me”; what he says, “Terrors wage war against me,” is “Your terrors have troubled me.”

The Prophet indicates this cause of sorrow when he says: “I mingled my drink with weeping, because of your indignation; for, having lifted me up, you dashed me down” [Col. 0505C] (Ps. 101). See what the lifting up is and what the dashing down. Man was made in the image and likeness of God; since he is capable of reason, he can therefore also be a sharer in blessedness. This is the lifting up. But because he can be saved and can be damned, this is the dashing down. Brute animals, however, since they cannot be saved, cannot be damned either; nor are they obliged to render an account, since they were not born to possess reason.

These are the four causes of sorrow: the first, fear concerning the sins we have committed; the second, danger from the temptations we endure; the third, the weight of tribulations by which we are now oppressed; the fourth, the judgment of condemnation by which we are terrified. The Prophet presents them to us in a different order: “The sorrows of death surrounded me, and the torrents of iniquity troubled me. The sorrows of hell surrounded me; the snares of death came upon me beforehand” [Col. 0505D] (Ps. 17). The sorrows of death are sorrows in death and before death, which unceasingly hasten death and, like forerunners of death, continually announce it to us. For we have within ourselves the answer of death. The torrents of iniquity are the flooding assaults of sins, which, like torrents, always rush toward a precipice and drag us with them. What the sorrows of hell are is evident from their very name. The snares of death are temptations, which he who tempts prepares, in the manner of a fowler or hunter, in order to capture souls.

These are four measures, or four jars; if two are added, there will be [Col. 0506A] six stone jars, each holding two or three measures, according to the purification of the Jews (John 2). The Jews, indeed, are penitents and confessors, who by their tears signify the purification of the Jews, to whom drink is also given in tears by measure (Ps. 79). And because temporal or eternal punishments are to be feared and mourned by us for temptations admitted and sins committed, which we have performed by will and deed, and sometimes also by habit, therefore each of these jars holds two or three measures. And if someone sins by will alone and, pierced by repentance, takes from this a cause for mourning, even in these cases two or three measures are not lacking. For appetite, consent, and the pleasure of consenting, if they are present, [Col. 0506B] make up this or that number. They are stone jars either because of the hardness of the heart hitherto stony, or because of the firmness of a better purpose, which is necessary for those who mourn devoutly. For concerning hardness of heart the Lord says through the prophet: “I will take away the stony heart from your flesh” (Ezek. 1). But concerning firmness of mind it is said: “I have set my face like the hardest rock” (Isa. 50).

### On the fifth cause for mourning

Our tears arising from the aforesaid four causes are always bitter to us, or like tasteless water, since they proceed from hatred, weariness, grief, or fear; and they concern things which we hate, which weary us, grieve us, or frighten us. Such was the disposition of him who said: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged!” [Col. 0506C] (Ps. 119). But just as those tears descend from hatred of evils, so there are certain sweeter tears which burst forth from desire for good things. By “good things” we now mean either things that are spiritual and make one good, or things that are eternal and make one blessed. Both kinds of good are objects of our desire, and each desire has its own tears. For we are often pierced by desire for the good which may justify us on the way; often by desire for the good by which we may be made blessed in our homeland. Both have been promised to us by God and must be sought with tears and unutterable groanings. Hence the Prophet says: “You have set my tears before you, as also in your promise” (Ps. 55). And: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God? My tears have been my bread day and night” [Col. 0506D] (Ps. 41).

Our righteousness lies either in the inclination of a good will, or in the inclination toward action, as in beginners; or in the practice of a good habit, as in those trained in it. For each of these its own reward is hoped for, desired, and awaited. Therefore these jars too each contain two or three measures. Yet all these tears which flow from weariness of evils or desire for goods can be common to the good and the bad. For the good are pierced for all these causes, and so are the bad. The good weep, and the bad weep; but the good beneficially, the bad uselessly. For Esau, as the Apostle testifies, “desiring to inherit the promise, was rejected. For he found no place [Col. 0507A] for repentance, though he sought it with tears” (Heb. 12). Judas too, moved by repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver (Matt. 27); and Balaam was uselessly pierced toward righteousness when he said: “May my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my last things be like theirs” (Num. 23).

Thus evil persons can grieve and fear evils that ought to be mourned and feared; they can also hope for and desire spiritual or eternal goods; and, through hope or desire for the latter, and grief and fear concerning the former, be pierced even to tears—so much the more fruitlessly as it is more vainly. For it is sufficient for no one to mourn evils and hope for or desire goods unless he adds: abandoning sins, correcting errors, and laying hold of the goods by which he may become good. For it is one thing to hope for or desire these goods, another [Col. 0507B] to possess them. No one becomes good merely by hoping or desiring, or by supposing that he possesses the goods by which he is good, but rather by possessing them. Many suppose that they possess repentance and forgiveness of sins, by which they may cease to be bad; or they hope that they can possess them whenever they wish. So too they suppose concerning charity, humility, and the other goods by which they may become good. But their hope is vain, as are also their desire and opinion; and their heart is vain. Therefore they are sometimes pierced toward righteousness to no purpose, just as the good are harmlessly tempted toward guilt.

Do not those count themselves good who judge more proudly concerning their own merits, so that they trust they will judge together with the Lord? Of such persons it is written: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand” (Ps. 90). Therefore those who are of this kind, although they rejoice more abundantly in their hope, and although they flow in tears through the desires, sighs, and sobs of their soul, are nevertheless strangers to this promise: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Col. 0507C] (Matt. 5).

### On the tears peculiar to the good

The hope of the righteous rests upon humility, and their desire upon charity. From charity and humility, as though from the fountains of the Saviour, the holy waters of tears are drawn. For he weeps devoutly who, after sin, is beneficially pierced, humbled in the fear of God, and detests iniquity; who always grieves to have done what he does not consent to do again. These are devout tears, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Streams of waters have run down from my eyes, because they have not kept your law” [Col. 0507D] (Ps. 118).

He weeps devoutly who, dissolved by spiritual desire and joy, pours himself out and melts into tears; who in the remembrance of his beloved things wonderfully pours himself out inwardly, so that he can say: “I remembered these things, and poured out my soul within me; for I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Ps. 54). That woman sick with love experienced the sweetness of these tears when she said: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 3). She rightly says, “when my beloved spoke,” for he is beloved because he spoke. For one to whom he is beloved, as soon as he has spoken, “his words are softer than oil, yet they are darts” (Ps. 54). See whether she whom he loves is not softened, whether she is not dissolved and melted at his words, since it is written: “He will send forth his word and melt them; his Spirit will blow, and the waters shall flow” [Col. 0508A] (Ps. 147).

Therefore, when the Beloved speaks and the Spirit blows, she who loves melts away, and waters flow, by which the garden of delights is watered—the garden stirred by the south wind, so that its spices may flow. These tears are honey-flowing. For “the heavens dropped,” that is, the drops by which the sprouting earth rejoices, and the voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance. Yet this rain is often withheld from the righteous; and when it is possessed, it is not retained; when it is desired, it is not obtained. For they are often forsaken: weakness knocks, strength wholly hides itself; they are filled with bitterness, afflicted with weariness, waste away amid evils, and burn with thirst. The rains are forbidden from heaven; neither dew nor rain falls upon them. Unless God helps them, their soul begins almost to dwell in hell [Col. 0508B].

But what wonder if the righteous descend for an hour, as it were, into hell, where they are given wormwood and gall-water to drink, when it is beneficial for them to know from what they are to be delivered, so that when delivered they may rejoice more and their consolation may abound to the glory of God? “They descend unto the depths; their soul wasted away in evils” (Ps. 106). But shall God forget to show mercy? Far be it! For when the Spirit of the Lord, sweeter than honey through hope and desire for that inheritance which is above honey and the honeycomb, has breathed upon the minds of the righteous and in inestimable sweetness filled every inward part and secret recess of the languishing soul, then, through the coming grace of inward sweetness and deepest delight, [Col. 0508C] everything bitter will be swallowed up in joy of heart; and waters of tears will flow like streams of honey.

And when the mother of Jesus suggests, “They have no wine” (John 2), the water of sorrow will be changed into the wine of joy—but when what Jesus commanded has been fulfilled, saying: “Fill the jars with water” [Col. 0508C] (ibid.). For the jars must first be filled with water; that is, our hearts must be more fully satisfied with abundant outpourings of tears; worthy satisfaction must be made for sins committed; things to be mourned must be sufficiently mourned; and then we may receive within ourselves the consolation of inward devotion and joy in the Holy Spirit, and exchange the sorrow of our heart for gladness. For [Col. 0508D] because we have not yet worthily wept over what ought to be mourned, we often experience losses of devotion; and because we have not yet paid what we owe, we obtain more slowly what we desire. But when God has given us drink in tears by measure, we shall experience, in the attainment of the goods for which we anxiously long, manifold present consolation, proving this consolation true: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). Yet we shall experience it more fully in the future, when God shall wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints (Rev. 21), when our mouth shall be filled with joy and our tongue with exultation (Ps. 125), to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5).

[Col. 0509A]

Many hunger more for money than for righteousness, and for no other purpose than to be filled and, once filled, to spend their days amid good things. For those who abound in money are counted blessed, as it is written: “They called the people blessed who have these things” (Ps. 143). “They called,” he says, reporting another’s opinion, not setting forth his own judgment. For according to his own judgment he says: “The rich have lacked and hungered” (Ps. 33). They have lacked indeed, because what they possess is not enough for them; and they have hungered because they insatiably seek what they do not possess. True fullness, however, does not come from money but from righteousness.

There is, nevertheless, a certain fullness of the rich, because it is written: “The abundance of the rich does not [Col. 0509B] allow him to sleep” (Eccl. 5). But this fullness is an excess in using, not an end of need; an oppression of the sick man, not an extinction of his illness; a stimulus to vice, not a fulfillment of desire. Empty, therefore, is this fullness, which does not refresh the hungry because it never suffices. This is the water from the well of Samaria, of which it is written: “Whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again” (John 4). “He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1). Who are these hungry persons who are filled with good things, and therefore fully and well satisfied, except those of whom it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness”? Or what is the righteousness which makes blessed and satisfies, except Christ, who “was made for us wisdom from God and righteousness”? This is indeed [Col. 0509C] the wisdom which says: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. 24).

Christ was made righteousness for us: freely justifying us, freely granting righteousness, and abiding in us through righteousness—the author of the gift together with his gift. He is our food, who gives righteousness; and our food is the righteousness which he gives. Hence he who by falling lost righteousness and mourned for what he had lost says: “I forgot to eat my bread” (Ps. 101); and because he strove to be restored through repentance, he adds: “I ate ashes as bread” (ibid.). This is the food of the righteous, which none hungers for except one who eats it. By tasting it one hungers; by hungering one tastes it; and the more it is tasted, the more it is hungered for; the more it refreshes, the sweeter it becomes. For it attracts by its own flavour, so that desire continually grows in the tasting and the tasting continues without disgust.

Is love of righteousness, then, insatiable like love of money? If hunger always grows and increases through the increments of righteousness, when will it end, and when will fullness be found? Let the Prophet answer and say: “But I shall appear before your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” [Col. 0509D] (Ps. 16). Therefore hunger belongs to the present time, but fullness to the future, when those who now hunger shall be filled. But who are they who now hunger? Are all who desire righteousness? Or only those who love righteousness? For to desire in some fashion is one thing, to love another. Love, indeed, is not without desire; but desire also precedes love.

For there are some who are still evil and yet resolve and desire to be righteous; but they defer the time of repentance and postpone the beginnings of conversion. Bound and conquered by delight in sin, and burdened by the habit of sinning, they still love what they desire not to love, and have not yet laid hold of that for which they sigh. They are pierced toward righteousness, but embrace the pleasure of sin; they cling to evil yet burn toward good with the heat of desire. But the settled course of evil has more power to make them evil than the mere ardour for good has to make them good [Col. 0510A].

Conversely, when good persons are tempted toward guilt, the settled course of good, by which they retain righteousness, has more power than the unconsidered heat of the soul by which they suddenly burn toward evil. The good always have the settled course of good: sometimes with ardour for good, sometimes, without consent, with ardour for evil. There are indeed two desires, both in the good and both in the bad: the desire of the flesh and the desire of the spirit, which oppose one another. “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). In the good, the desire of the flesh is moved toward sinning but does not proceed as far as consent to sin, for the desire of the spirit rules in them. So too, in the bad, compunction toward righteousness is felt but not consented to, for the desire of the flesh rules in them. Emulation for good in the bad, together with a resolve and desire for a better life, is a certain grace of God; but it is the grace of inward calling, not of justification. For righteousness is not to be measured by inclination alone, but by consent [Col. 0510B].

“What participation,” says the Apostle, “has righteousness with iniquity?” (2 Cor. 6). Therefore no one consents to righteousness unless he dissents from unrighteousness, unless he abandons it and leaves it without delay. But one who consents to righteousness already begins to love, already hungers for righteousness, already desires worthily; nor does he wholly lack what he desires, but desires to possess more of it. He has already set his foot on the right way and desires to be directed further inwardly upon it, saying: “Would that my ways were directed to keep your statutes” (Ps. 118). Already that voice of the righteous applies to him: “My soul has longed to desire your statutes at all times” (ibid.). Already desiring and longing, and not satisfied with the measure of his desire, he desires to desire more, panting toward perfection or sighing toward progress, so that he may increase good within himself and remain in good at all times [Col. 0510C].

Righteousness is increased through its own stages of growth and ordered by appointed steps: consent, inclination, effect, practice, habit, and fruit. For righteousness begins with consent. When the mind has conceived hatred of iniquity and has begun, through love of good, to consent to righteousness, it is disposed to act well. When effect follows inclination, delighted by good work it strives to grow accustomed to good works; then it seeks to strengthen that habit by perseverance; and amid these things, and especially after them, it delights to share in the most sweet fruit of righteousness. The fruit of righteousness is not simple. There is the fruit of the future time: the very fullness promised here; and there is the fruit of the present time: a certain foretaste of future sweetness, received meanwhile in delight in righteousness. [Col. 0511A]

Of this delight the Prophet says: “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches” [Col. 0510D] (ibid.).

Future fullness, however, embraces two desirable things: eternal life and everlasting joy. Righteousness acquires and renders both. For concerning the fullness of eternal life it is written: “I will fill him with length of days” (Ps. 90), undoubtedly the righteous man. Concerning the fullness of everlasting joy it is written: “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35), undoubtedly the righteous. Righteousness, therefore, which [Col. 0512A] gives life and gladness, is food and drink. It is food and the bread of life when it bestows life and preserves it for ever. For righteousness is the acquisition of immortality. It is drink and the wine of gladness when it grants joy and keeps it without end. Blessed, therefore, are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; and blessed are those who desire to live and rejoice, not in this age but in Christ. For they shall obtain fullness when our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever, fills their desire with good things. Amen.

## Tenth Treatise

[Col. 0511]

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell” (Song 8).

[Col. 0511B] God, loving us and desiring to be loved, fashioned a seal bearing the engraved image of love, by which he more closely impressed our heart, so that, conformed to the image, it might receive within itself the likeness of that image and express it in corresponding form. Understand “seal” both as that which seals and as that which is sealed. For, speaking of that which seals, the Apostle says to the Romans: “Abraham received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith which is in uncircumcision” (Rom. 4). But concerning that which is sealed, he says to the Corinthians: “You are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord” (1 Cor. 9). And it is said through the prophet to the angel distinguished by the beauty of divine likeness: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28).

Christ both seals [Col. 0511C] and is sealed. “For God the Father sealed him.” The Father sanctified him and sent him into the world. The Father distinguished him from all others by singular grace. “For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, undefiled, unstained, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens” (Heb. 7). Through him God also sealed us, as it is written: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4). He sealed us on the day of our creation, when he formed us in his image and likeness. He sealed us on the day of our redemption, when he re-formed us according to his image.

For iniquity and death divided God and man. God hates iniquity, and man hates death. Man hates death in proportion as he loves life. What is sweeter in life than life itself, or more lovable? What is more bitter than death, or more hateful? What, therefore, is more detestable than iniquity, through which the joy of life is to be lost and the necessity of dying has been imposed upon us? What can be loved more than life—above all immortal life—and God, its promiser and giver, the fountain of life and life itself? But righteousness, as it is written, is the acquisition of immortality. Therefore righteousness is to be loved no less than the life acquired through it, and without which immortal life is not retained [Col. 0512B].

Man, however, was in some measure immortal from the beginning, so that by preserving righteousness he could be able not to die: in this respect and in part like God. But now, in the condition of dying, he is like the irrational beasts; yet through the obligation of sin and danger of perishing he is inferior to them—now as much more degraded as he was formerly more dignified. Therefore iniquity is as hateful as death, and more hateful than this death. For it is more expedient to die than to sin. Sin is the sting of death, wounding with its barb unto destruction. “The wages of sin is death,” and the reward of iniquity is perdition. Sin is an injury to God, provoking zeal; the judgment of death is the sentence of God condemning sin.

But sinful man is justly delivered over to death, and, experiencing God’s wrath through many miseries, could scarcely even weakly hope in God’s love [Col. 0512C]. For his own thought could suggest to him that he should say: “How am I to believe myself loved by God, when he afflicts me thus? What good am I to hope from him who has poured out his indignation upon me and has not even spared me from death? If he loved me, he would not oppress me thus in his judgment; he would not restrain mercy in his wrath, but would remit the indignation I deserved, grant pardon, and absolve me from the decree of death.” God seemed to hate man when he brought wrath upon him and pronounced the sentence of death against him. He seemed to have loved him when he endured death for the abolition of sin and death.

Death, therefore, became a sign of hatred and of love: of hatred toward the guilt committed by man; of love toward the nature created by God. Through the death inflicted upon man, God poured out his wrath and indignation upon all nations, as it is written: “I have trodden them in my fury, and trampled them in my wrath” (Isa. 63). Through the death undertaken for man, he poured out his mercy and love upon all nations, as it is written: “Our God is the God of salvation, and the ways out of death belong to the Lord God” (Ps. 67). Therefore death is wrath and mercy; judgment and benefit; condemnation and absolution [Col. 0512D]; indignation and reconciliation.

God so ordered and tempered the remedy of our restoration that he turned the fury of his indignation into the sacrament of redemption and the help of deliverance. Hence he says: “My arm has saved for me, and my indignation itself has helped me” (Isa. 63). Therefore, that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world made subject to God, let no human being now say: “God does not love me, since he does not spare me from death”; but rather let him say, and be astonished: “How greatly God loves me, since, in order to spare me, he did not spare himself from death!”

Let us therefore compare death with love, and it will appear that love is strong as death. Who doubts the strength of death? What force, power, rank, nobility, wisdom, prudence [Col. 0513A], skill, or cunning can resist it?

[Col. 0513B] It claims all its debtors; demands tribute from all; enfolds all; spares no one; rules in every region of the earth; makes all equal; commands all; and, itself unconquerable, conquers conquerors of cities. Witnesses to this are all who sleep in the dust of the earth, and the tombs of the dead themselves are testimonies to this truth.
