Even the most powerful, kings and princes who spread their terror in the land of the living, have themselves experienced what death can do. All the world’s wise men, who contemplated the stars of heaven and calculated months and days, have been overtaken by the sudden accident of death and caught in their own cunning. This twofold strength of death is seen in the fact that it could seize or capture all, and could also hold all, and there was none who could rescue them from its hand.

But the love by which God loved us dissolved by its strength the bonds with which death bound those it had captured, so that death can retain only for a time those whom it is permitted to assail for a time. For Christ rose as the firstfruits of those who sleep, confirming our confidence in resurrection by the sacrament, example, and testimony of his resurrection, and by the word of his promise [Col. 0513C].

Strong is death, which can deprive us of the gift of life. Strong is love, which can restore us to the enjoyment of a better life. Strong is death, which can strip us of the covering of this body. Strong is love, which can seize the spoils of death and restore them to us. Strong is death, which no human being can resist. Strong is love, which can triumph over death itself, blunt its sting, quell its contention, and confound its victory. For the time will come when it will be mocked and said: “Where is your sting, O death? Where is your contention, O death?” (1 Cor. 15). Love is strong as death because Christ’s love is the death of death. Therefore he says: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13).

The love by which Christ is loved by us is likewise strong as death, since it is itself a kind of death: the extinction of the old life, the abolition of vices, and the laying aside of dead works. This love of ours for Christ is a kind of return, though unequal to his love for us, and a likeness conformed to his [Col. 0514A]. For he loved us first, and through the example of love which he set before us he became for us a seal, by which we may be made conformed to his image—putting off the image of the earthly man and bearing the image of the heavenly—as we have been loved, so loving him in return. “For in this he leaves us an example, that we may follow his steps” (1 Pet. 2). Therefore he says: “Set me as a seal upon your heart” (Song 8).

As though he said: Love me as I love you. Have me in your mind, memory, desire, sighing, groaning, and sobbing. Remember, O man, what I made you, how much I preferred you above other creatures; with what dignity I ennobled you; how I crowned you with glory and honour; how I made you a little lower than the angels [Col. 0514B]; how I subjected all things beneath your feet (Ps. 8). Remember not only how great were the things I did for you, but how harsh and how unworthy were the things I endured for you. See whether you do not act unjustly against me if you do not love me. For who loves you as I do? Who created you except I? Who redeemed you except I? Who, as defender of your life, underwent the peril of combat except I?

Therefore, to render me love in return, stretch out your arms; exercise your strength; set me as a seal upon your arm. Fight for me as I fought for you. Do not flatter me with feigned adulation by saying, “Lord, I love you.” If you love me, show that you love me. Love not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. I conquered the world by fighting for you; but the world and the prince of this world still oppose you, and the flesh also opposes you, so that you may fight against them for me—or rather, for yourself. For your own danger is at stake; the battle is for your soul, for your salvation. You cannot be conquered except through yourself, nor conquer except through me. Therefore do not trust in yourself, but in me. For it is not by your sword that you will overcome the enemy, nor will your arm save you, but by my right hand, my arm, and the illumination of my countenance [Col. 0514C]. If you set me as a seal upon your arm, victory will fall to you.

Fight thus, not as one beating the air; chastise your body and reduce it to slavery (1 Cor. 9); abstain from all things, like one competing in the contest. If this seems hard to you, what charge can you bring against me? I too kept hard paths. If you wish to emulate me, know that emulation is hard as hell [Col. 0514D]. You must drink the cup that I drank. I thirsted and I drank; I tasted death; I descended to hell; but, the pains of hell being loosed, I rose again. If, through zeal for emulation and in willing imitation of me, you feel yourself burdened and tortured as though in hell, this is what I require of you, this is what I warn, this is what I counsel: that you be tortured for a little while, as though in hell, lest you be tortured without end in hell. For emulation is like hell, resembling a place of punishment; yet this is the way that leads to entrance into the kingdom. For it is necessary to suffer these things and thus enter into life.

Accordingly, my martyrs too are true emulators of me, now sharers in the kingdom; but first they cast down their bodies and bones upon the earth in death, and before death were subjected to disgrace, saying: “Our bones have been scattered beside hell” [Col. 0515A] (Ps. 140). See how those loved me who chose to follow me beside hell and refused to be swallowed up by hell. If you suffer adversity and are therefore, in others’ estimation, regarded as a sinner and near to hell, you have grounds to say with me: “My soul has been filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell. I have been counted among those going down into the pit” (Ps. 87).

Set me as a seal upon your heart, that you may love me with your whole strength; set me upon your arm, that with your whole love you may accomplish what is pleasing to me. Set me upon your heart through the affection of love; set me upon your arm through the effect of action. Have me as the example and aid of loving purely and sincerely; as the example and aid of acting well and suffering bravely. Set me upon your heart, above everything that you think, [Col. 0515B] love, or hold dear, so that you may put aside everything precious and always place me above it, always love me more—not only more than what is outside you, but more than whatever is within you. Finally, love me more than yourself, so that you may love yourself for my sake, not merely me for your own sake. Let love of yourself according to me be at the summit of your heart; let love of me be above that summit.

But since the proof of love is the performance of a work, set me upon your arm. So fight and exert yourself in working for me that you may work from me. Let me be your hope, your confidence, your strength, your patience. Say to me: “Lord, my hope from my youth” (Ps. 70). Say to me: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17). Say to me: [Col. 0515C] “For you are my patience” (Ps. 70). Say to me: “My God, my mercy” (Ps. 58). Do not make flesh your arm; rather say to me: “Be our arm in the morning and our salvation in the time of tribulation” (Isa. 33).

I demand love from your heart in things inward, emulation in things outward. But, in order that you may know whether love is true, consider strength of spirit: for love that is not strong and like death is not true love. Consider first my love toward you and my death for you. When I laid down my life for you, neither the malice or power of my persecutors nor the violence of death wrung my life from me against my will; rather, love itself drove me, compelled me, forced me. What death could accomplish in others, love could accomplish in me, and death obeyed that love. See also in others what death can do and what love can do, so that you may know that love is strong as death. Death separates names most dear and bonds most closely joined; love also separates them. For whoever leaves house, brothers, sisters, father, mother, wife, or fields for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life (Matt. 19). Death separates soul and flesh; love also separates them. For whoever does not hate his own soul cannot be my disciple (Luke 14).

But zeal in outward things does not show itself: it is genuine if it is not harsh. For one who does not remain with me in temptation can pretend in prosperity. Therefore strength of spirit in the severing of affections [Col. 0516A] is the sign of the love that is inward; while the harshness of tribulation is the sign of the emulation that is outward. These are the marks impressed by the seal.

Lord, you who say, “Set me as a seal upon your heart,” do what you command. For whence have I the power to set you upon my heart? How can I do this? Yet unless in some manner I could do it—still only through you—you would not say to me, “Set me.” O your condescension, Lord! O my dignity and freedom, Lord! For you do not disdain to be set by your servant upon the heart of your servant! You judged me worthy enough and gave me free choice, by which I could reject whatever displeases you, choose the good that pleases you, and by choosing the good please you or cleave to you, share in you, have you within me, and love you above myself, as you are worthy to be loved.

Take from me, Lord, the heart [Col. 0516B] of stone; take away the congealed heart; take away the uncircumcised heart. Give me a new heart, a heart of flesh, a clean heart! You who cleanse the heart and love the cleansed heart, possess my heart and dwell in it, containing and filling it, higher than my highest and more inward than my inmost being! You, the form of beauty and seal of holiness, mark my heart with your image; mark my heart beneath your mercy, O God of my heart and God my portion for ever (Ps. 72). Amen.

## On human misery and need because of guilt

By the guilt of disobedience, man, departing from God, pays the most just penalty for his offence. For, failing away from the unchangeable God, he also fails within himself; and through the stages of his falling-away he continually grows old and decays, [Col. 0516C] until he is dissolved by the final death. For what is becoming obsolete and growing old is near destruction. Man, withdrawing from God, who is always one and the same, has been divided by the wrath of His countenance; and he is divided within himself, so that he is not always one and the same to himself, but always one thing and then another, and the saying written may be fulfilled: “A fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27).

Thus he is at odds with and remote from himself; thus he dissents and is discordant, that scarcely can one person be found more opposed to another than a single man is to himself. He wills and does not will; in turn he both hates and loves, considers and reconsiders, approves and condemns, seeks and rejects, attends to and neglects. Often, after undertaking a business, he tires of what he undertook; after doing something, he regrets what he did. His vows and desires, pursuits and plans, thoughts, affections, and intentions—being as it were always displeased with himself—he changes in many ways, and in all these things he himself is changed. Indeed, “a double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas. 1).

What peace has miserable man amid so great a succession of changes, amid such flightiness of an inconstant mind? “There is no peace for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. 57). A perverse mind, opposed both to God and to itself, is its own torturer and torment: it continually exacts penalties from itself and continually pays them; and the one who opposes God through the guilt of sin is, as it were, God’s minister in exacting punishment. See how the wicked are divided by the wrath of God’s countenance: they so oppose themselves that they persecute themselves. As much as they are contrary to God, so also are they contrary to themselves; they find no peace in their own will because they offend in the will of God.

[Col. 0517A] But are the wicked alone divided? What of the mind of the righteous person, occupied with the administration of temporal matters, stretched thin by a multitude of cares and therefore less attentive to God—is it not also divided? Is not Martha told: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10)? What does this doubling mean? Was it not enough to say “Martha” once, unless it was said by repetition, “Martha, Martha”? Does this repetition signify division? “Martha,” he says once, and again, “Martha.” Martha surely divided, Martha anxious, Martha troubled—troubled by provision for the time to come, troubled by care for present necessity. “You are anxious and troubled about many things.” Many things indeed trouble one; for the needs of miserable man are many.

[Col. 0517B] For necessity always clings to misery, and one who is miserable is always in want. But human necessities are so many and various, so inextricable and entangled, that they can in no way be discharged during the whole of human life. The tireless change of things and times always brings a new need and gives birth to a new anxiety; and while one necessity departs, another succeeds it. One necessity draws another to itself; and, while the one following drives out the preceding, it thrusts itself into yet another that follows; and while one need is met and relieved, another immediately arises. Like one who borrows from one person and pays another, he binds himself precisely where he frees himself. Thus, throughout human life, while one knot of necessity is untied, another is tightened; and miserable man, who is always striving to free himself, is always ingeniously contriving [Col. 0517C] to bind himself.

For the paths of man are strewn with thorns. In this manner necessity is always fled and always encountered; and abundance is continually sought to avoid need, yet poverty is found. For concerning the rich themselves, who glory in the abundance of their riches, what else should be thought than what Scripture says: “The rich have lacked and hungered” (Ps. 33)?

For those who have much always need much; and where there are many riches, there are many who consume [Col. 0518A] them. Often those who extort from unwilling people suffer similar things unwillingly; often they give unwillingly what they receive from unwilling people. But those who possess riches and do not distribute them, because they always wish to keep them safe lest they lack, are in greater need: for they equally need both what they have and what they do not have. Their disease is always increased by its own remedy, and their need is incurable because their covetousness is insatiable.

These necessities, suffered by wretched and pitiable human beings, are produced by love of unnecessary things; in many unnecessary things they seek consolation and do not find it. Yet “one thing is necessary” (Luke 10). Truly one thing is necessary, without which nothing is necessary: the one highest and common good. This one can suffice for all; without it, [Col. 0518B] not even all things can suffice for one person. For this one thing Peter left everything, that in the one he might possess all things, lest, lacking the one, he should possess neither one thing nor all things. “One thing,” he says, “have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek” (Ps. 26).

Whoever seeks this one thing shall not be deprived of any good. Whoever does not have this one thing lacks himself; poor in mind, he possesses neither his reason nor his heart in his own power. But what does one poor in mind possess, when he does not possess himself? Indeed, if one who does not have God does not possess himself, then by true reckoning he has nothing except sins. By God’s wondrous judgment, the wicked person who, in his own estimation, has much is truly empty precisely where he seems to himself full; and from the source from which he hopes for abundance he suffers want.

[Col. 0518C] Scripture, speaking of God, cannot be broken: “He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty” (Luke 1). Elsewhere Scripture says of the rich: “They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75). If the rich sleep their sleep and dream that they have much in their hands, though possessing no riches at all; and if a vain opinion deceives them into judging themselves good when they are miserable, are they truly of sound mind?

## ELEVENTH TREATISE

[Col. 0517]

### On the Apostle’s words: “Our old man has been crucified,” etc.

[Col. 0517D] “Our old man has been crucified, that the body of sin may be destroyed, so that we may no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6). On the threefold cross: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow his steps” (1 Pet. 2). He suffered on the cross, so that through the mystery of the cross the virtue of patience might be established in us. For we must suffer, in order to receive what is due to our deeds. Therefore Christ imposes upon us the duty of carrying a cross, saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9; Matt. 16). “His cross,” he says—not mine.

For Christ’s cross is consecrated by his body, and Christ alone ascended it, he alone free among the dead: neither bound by sin nor held under the debt of death. In him, the one who held the power of death had absolutely nothing; but he was offered because he himself willed it (Isa. 53). Christ’s cross, therefore, is the cross of the innocent and righteous one, not of one cleansed or justified through a cross, but of the one who cleanses and justifies through the cross.

There is another cross: not that of the God-man, but of the guilty person who murmurs and suffers impatiently. There is yet another cross of a guilty person, but one who repents, confesses, and hears: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 22). No one is absolved or excused from the necessity of taking up a cross. The wicked bear their cross: “Many are the scourges of the sinner” (Ps. 31). The good also bear [Col. 0519A] their cross: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. 33).

The wicked sometimes bear their cross willingly, gladly, and cheerfully. For in seeking, increasing, and preserving the empty things that they love most vainly, they voluntarily undertake many and great labours, many grievous tribulations. But because they prefer suffering for the world to suffering for Christ, their patience is empty; before God they have neither the name of merit nor hope of reward. For “contrition and unhappiness are in their ways, and they have not known the ways of peace” (Rom. 3). They would indeed be happy if they turned toward truth what they plan for vanity. But now they are voluntarily miserable, and are the more miserable because they judge themselves happier. Since they think themselves blessed, they do not avoid the misery that they willingly endure, like Ephraim, “a heifer trained to love threshing” (Hos. 10). Because of hope for empty chaff, the heifer loves the labour of threshing.

This generation is rightly compared to senseless beasts, horse and mule, which have no understanding, whose jaws are restrained with bit and bridle because they do not draw near to you, O God; you shall cast them into fire, and they shall not endure amid miseries (Ps. 31). From miseries they run to miseries, and by punishments they deserve punishments. “You, O Lord, will save us and preserve us from this generation for ever” (Ps. 11).

The wicked sometimes bear their cross under compulsion. Scourged by God, they kick against the goad and murmur; by their own judgment they excuse themselves and accuse God’s justice. Like crushed serpents, they hiss in complaint. They judge themselves better than others who do not suffer similar things, and consider themselves undeserving of such scourges. Of such persons it is written: “The inward parts of a fool are like a cartwheel” (Ecclus. 33): it carries hay and murmurs. The cart’s creaking does not lighten its burden: it creaks, but carries it nonetheless. So too a fool, oppressed by the burden of tribulation, is through impatience himself a burden to himself; and he is truly hay, which exists today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace (Matt. 6). The fool speaks folly, and the mouth of fools boils over with foolishness.

[Col. 0519D] What could be more foolish than to exalt oneself in adversity, set one’s mouth against heaven, fail even in weakness to recognize one’s own weakness, and provoke God’s wrath to wrath? How much more rightly do those proclaim who say with blessed Job: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1). Of such persons it is written: “They shall still be fruitful in old age, and shall endure well, that they may proclaim that the Lord our God is upright and there is no injustice in him” (Ps. 91).

### On the old earthly, fleshly, and natural man

The cross borne by the wicked, whether unwillingly or willingly, is on the left: a cross worthy of those worthy of the cross. Upon this cross the old man is crucified. For after speaking beforehand of Christ’s cross, the Apostle added: “Our old man has been crucified with him” (Rom. 6), showing that the old man must be crucified with Christ—that is, for Christ. Who is the old man except he who says: “I have grown old among all [Col. 0520A] my enemies” (Ps. 6)? Who are the enemies among whom he has grown old, except his own household? The new man, certainly, has the same household as friends: they are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household.

For I too have grown old among all my enemies. Nor do I speak only of those enemies who are outside me, among whom “I have dwelt with the dwellers of Kedar”; rather, I now mean especially those enemies who are within me, who inhabit the land of my heart and the land of my flesh. For Canaanites, Jebusites, and Perizzites dwell there, and they have become my enemies. I myself also, as an evil man and a man of iniquity, am an enemy to myself, so that I may rightly pray both for myself and against myself, saying: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; deliver me from the man of iniquity” (Ps. 139).

[Col. 0520B] Deliver me, O Lord, from myself. For after you, Lord, there is no one whom I ought to fear as much as myself. Who so lies in wait for my soul as I do? Who so opposes my salvation as I do? Who is so ingenious in contriving my ruin as I am? Who so deceitfully flatters me in order that I may perish, as I do? Who so seeks my soul in order to take it away? Who devises rejection of my ransom? Who, Lord, labours to take from me that splendid inheritance promised by you, as I do? Who hates my soul with an unjust hatred more than I do? And I do so gratuitously. For what evil have you done to me, my soul? It is yours that I live, yours that I hear, see, flourish, and have health; yours that I feel, understand, and have wisdom—if indeed I have wisdom and do not rather lack it.

[Col. 0520C] Am I not ungrateful, malicious, and ill-disposed because I love iniquity and hate you? For “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10). O my soul, is it not great iniquity if I hate you who love me? But if I hate you, how do I not hate myself? Are you not my soul and my life—or rather, what are you but my soul and my life? By what right can I fail to love you, my life and my only one? Woe to me if by my fault you are to perish for ever, and I for ever with you. If you are to perish, to whom can I more rightly impute it than to myself? If I am to perish—which God avert—to whom should I impute it: to myself or to you? If to myself and to you, woe alike to myself and to you. If through your fault I am evil and worthy to perish, on what grounds can I love you, the cause of my destruction? If this was to be my lot, it would have been better for me not to have been born.

[Col. 0520D] What counsel remains to me before I perish, that I may not perish? For if I should perish once—far be it!—what more could I do but continue perishing? Lord God, from then on is your wrath; from then on there is no counsel, no prudence, no wisdom, no reason. Whoever happens to perish once will persist in perishing. I know what I shall do before I perish—indeed, lest I perish. I shall cry to God Most High, to God who has done good to me (Ps. 56). God is Most High, and I am in the depth of iniquity; I need a loud cry, otherwise he will not hear me, because he is Most High. I shall tell my iniquities to God, who freely justifies the ungodly. “I will give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” [Col. 0521A] (Ps. 117).

Like a penitent pierced by sorrow, I shall speak in the bitterness of my soul; I shall say to God: “Do not condemn me” (Job 10). I myself shall judge myself; I myself shall condemn myself. Do not condemn me, Lord. Allow me to labour in this matter. Once you laboured for our salvation, considering the labour and pain, so as to deliver us into your hands. Good Jesus, it is not the work of your name to condemn one who condemns himself, to destroy one who judges himself. The world calls you Saviour, not destroyer. You will indeed destroy the wicked grievously—but those who persist in their wickedness. I do not wish to persist in it. Say therefore to my soul: “I am your salvation” (Ps. 34).

My soul, though you are greatly guilty and greatly afraid because of great guilt, does not hope of pardon smile upon you in the most sweet name of most gracious Jesus? Why are you consumed with grief? Why do you waste away in bitterness? “Is there no counsellor for you? Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there?” (Jer. 8). “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him, the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Ps. 41).

While I desire to console myself in my soliloquy, “my soul chose hanging, and my bones death. For my soul is weary of my life.” Nor is it surprising. For my life is evil; I am the old man and near to death: an evil man and a man of iniquity; an earthly man, bearing the image of the earthly; a fleshly man, sold under sin; a natural man, not receiving the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2); a man guilty of death and worthy of a cross [Col. 0521C]—and not of one cross only. For one cross is due to the earthly man, another to the fleshly man, another to the natural man. I, one man, am all these men; and all these are in me alone; and all my thoughts are against me for evil. “They will dwell and hide themselves; they will watch my heel” (Ps. 55).

O harsh and heavy, O wretched and miserable human condition! For our enemies live and have prevailed over us; and our enemies are ourselves: earthly, fleshly, natural. We have neither peace nor security from ourselves until, hanging on the cross with Christ, we are crucified, so that the body of sin may be destroyed in us, that we may no longer serve sin but, dead to sins, live to righteousness (1 Pet. 2); and, delivered without fear from the hand of our enemies, [Col. 0521D] we may serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days (Luke 1).

### On the earthly man

First the earthly man in us must be crucified; then the fleshly man; afterward the natural man; and afterward the man created according to God must be put on. Speaking of the earthly man, the Apostle says: “The first man is of earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15). And again: “As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of the heavenly” (ibid.). Therefore the earthly man is the old man. For he began from the days of Adam’s transgression.

Those bear his image who savour earthly things, who think only upon what belongs to the world and how they may please the world, who love earthly wealth and earthly glory too greatly. What the image of the earthly [Col. 0522A] man is, the Psalmist shows, saying: “Man is like vanity” (Ps. 143). For man, turned away from God, loving vain things and doing vain things, himself also becomes vain—indeed, vanity itself. As his works are, such is their maker. As man is outside himself in the work he makes, such he is within himself in his heart, where he plans what is to be done. For in his work the author is expressed as in a mirror.

Before sin, there was in man an image, namely that of God, who is truth. But after sin the image of truth in man was disfigured, and the image of vanity was painted in him. For he was made like vanity, and because he did not stand in truth, his days pass away like a shadow. “Man passes through in an image” (Ps. 38). Do you not see how the earthly [Col. 0522B] man, pursuing avarice and setting aside the image of God, began to love the image on a coin, whose value consists in error and the foolish opinion of human beings? A coin bearing a human image and inscription, man makes as it were in the image and likeness of man, changing the image of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man, serving the creature rather than the Creator through the error of love of money, which is idolatry (Eph. 5).

For what are silver and gold, stamped with the mark of public currency, except certain images of kings and works of human hands? These, miser, these are your gods: you love them with all your heart, all your soul, all your mind; you worship them with special honour; you trust in them; you place in them your entire hope in every necessity. “For where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. 6). But a time shall come when such persons will be told: “Where are their gods, in whom they trusted, whose sacrifices’ fat they ate and whose drink-offerings’ wine they drank? Let them arise and help you, and protect you in need” (Deut. 32).

The earthly man’s citizenship is not in heaven but on earth. He does not look toward heaven, but fixes his eyes so as to turn aside toward earth; he licks the earth, eats earth all the days of his life; his belly is glued to the earth; he is fixed in the mire of the deep, and has no firm standing. For he has not set his feet upon the rock. He always enters the lower regions of the earth until [Col. 0522D] he is swallowed by earth, like Dathan and Abiram. He quarrels for earth and fights for earth, until a pit is dug for the sinner and he is covered by earth, to be dissolved into the earth from which he was made.

Yet all his life he exults in his own glory. He envies another’s prosperity, as alien from charity as he is full of covetousness. He is not kind, nor patient; rather, he is ambitious, jealous, and acts perversely, seeking his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. His heart is heavy; he loves vanity and seeks falsehood; his mouth abounds in malice, and his tongue devises deceits. He is from the earth and speaks of the earth. He always fears poverty, and, as he continually saves things to be increased for provision against the future, so he continually increases things to be saved. Against every eventual future necessity [Col. 0523A] he provides for himself; his nostrils are always filled with the scent of gain and his right hand with gifts. He calls every skill in increasing profit prudence; he mocks poverty, and in his estimation the name of poverty is a reproach. He places all his possessions in security and always promises himself hope of a longer life, until it is said to him: “Fool, this night they shall demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose shall they be?” (Luke 12). Thus, when this man perishes, he shall not take all things with him, nor shall his glory descend with him (Ps. 48).

This man is a friend of the world and is made an enemy of God. This is the man who cries against Christ, saying: “Away, away, crucify him” (John 19). They were earthly men, indeed, who said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). The earthly man’s envy against Christ has not yet ceased. For he persecutes Christ in us lest Christ live in us. Therefore, if anyone belongs to Christ, let him arm himself with zeal for vengeance against Christ’s persecutors. Let us cry to one another for Christ against Christ’s enemy: “Away, away, crucify him.”

But what accusation shall we bring against this man? “Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the multitude of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. 51). Away, away, crucify him. If you release him, you are not God’s friend. As he has done, so let it be done to him. He crucified: let him be crucified. For he is worthy of the cross and guilty of death.

“What,” you ask, “is the cross of this man?” I judge it to be contempt for the world. This cross is fashioned, as it were, from two pieces of wood: contempt for earthly wealth and contempt for earthly glory. For the earthly man loves two things: because he trusts in his own strength and glories in the multitude of his riches. He trusts in the world; let it deliver him, if it can. Let him be stretched upon the cross by those who despise the world, and let him be stretched out wholly in length and breadth. In contempt for earthly glory—that is, in voluntary lowliness—let his height be stretched out. For this is his height: earthly glory, in which he seeks to be exalted. In contempt for earthly wealth—that is, in voluntary poverty—let his breadth be stretched out. For this is his breadth: earthly wealth, in which he seeks to expand to the right or to the left.

[Col. 0523D] Upon this cross let the earthly man be hung: here let him be stretched out; stretched out, let him die; dead, let him be buried; and let him not be added again so as to rise. Rather, may God destroy him utterly, pluck him from his tent, and uproot him from the land of the living (Ps. 51); and may his memory perish from the earth, because he did not remember to show mercy but persecuted the poor and needy man (Ps. 108).

### On the fleshly man

There is another cross upon which the fleshly man must be hung. For although the same man is earthly and fleshly, nevertheless, according to the basis of the name and the difference in love, there seems to be some distinction. Speaking of the law of sin that is in the members, the Apostle says among [Col. 0524A] other things: “I am fleshly, sold under sin” (Rom. 7). Whoever is sold under sin is in some sense a slave and not wholly free. For he does not do the good that he wills, but does the evil that he does not will. And if he wholly wills evil and does evil, he is now a slave of sin because he himself commits sin. For “everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8): he is now wholly sold under sin, receiving the coin of unlawful pleasure in return for his will’s consent.

For sinful passions work in our members so as to bear fruit for death; and we all feel these passions in common, whether good or bad, although not equally; but we do not all consent to them. Yet one who feels them and does not consent is not entirely free [Col. 0524B] from fault. For he does the evil that he does not will. In feeling the passion of concupiscence, he desires what is evil and does not wish to desire what is evil. He therefore does the evil that he does not will, for desiring evil is evil. But one who desires evil and does not consent does evil in some manner, insofar as he desires evil; and because he does not consent, in some manner he does not perform it, because, tempted by concupiscence, he suffers against his will what he does not wish to suffer.

Thus the Apostle, desiring but not consenting, says both that he does the evil which he does not will and that he does not perform it: “The evil that I do not will, that I do”—that is, I desire it, and I do not wish to desire it—“and now it is no longer I who perform it, but sin that dwells [Col. 0524C] in me” (Rom. 7). It is as if he said: I do not wish to desire, and I do not consent to concupiscence; but against my will I feel the law of sin that is in my members. For it moves within me so that it is felt by me; but it does not move me so far that I consent to it.

Therefore, when the righteous person is tempted by his own concupiscence, he has some excuse, though not a sufficient one by which to be wholly free from fault. For when asked why he feels the flesh’s titillation in the flesh when he does not consent, he has an answer: “It is no longer I who perform it, but sin that dwells in me.” But it is not always in our power to feel or not feel the passions of the members; to consent, however, is in our power, just as it is not without our will.

[Col. 0524D] At times, one who feels but does not consent has it firmly fixed in his heart not to consent at all, and desires not to feel the temptation at all. But that he feels it belongs to weakness; that he does not consent belongs to virtue; that he desires not to feel it at all is an endeavour after peace and security. At other times, one who has resolved not to consent nevertheless wishes to feel a passion of this sort, because some gain is hoped for and expected from the temptation itself. For victory is judged more glorious the stronger the temptation resisted. Hence some wish to feel what they do not wish to consent to, so that, feeling without consenting, they may resist when tempted.

But it is dangerous voluntarily to seek such temptation and even, when it comes, not immediately to repel it insofar as possible. [Col. 0525A] For it is safer not to be tempted than to engage in conflict with temptation. The outcome of war is variable, and victory under the risk of battle is uncertain. Therefore the Lord teaches us to pray thus: “Pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26). But when the Prophet says, “Test me, O Lord, and try me” (Ps. 25), this concerns that temptation by which the righteous are tested by God, who tests his elect in order to find them worthy of himself.

But the person tempted by the flesh who yields to temptation is one who feels the passions and consents wholly to them. He is the more fleshly a man the more he fulfils care for the flesh in its desires, not consenting with the spirit against the flesh but yielding to the flesh, which desires against the spirit. This man loves wine and rich foods, ease, security, [Col. 0525B] and fullness; to be clothed in purple and fine linen, to feast splendidly each day; whatever his eyes desire is not denied them. He releases all his desires into the impulse of will. Whatever does not serve the flesh’s pleasures, he considers worthless; and he reckons it his portion if he enjoys his goods during his life, and has nothing more from all his labour under the sun.

The end of the fleshly man is shown in the Gospel parable of the rich man and the poor man, where it says: “The rich man died and was buried in hell” (Luke 16). And it is written of Babylon: “As much as she exalted herself and lived in pleasures, so much give her torment and mourning” (Rev. 18). Therefore it is better for us to deliver such a man to death, for the destruction of the flesh, than to be dragged with him into the pit of destruction.

[Col. 0525C] Therefore our flesh must be put to death and crucified, so that the body of sin may be destroyed, in accordance with the Prophet’s words to the Lord: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118). And because it was said to the fleshly man, “But you have hated discipline” (Ps. 51), no cross is found more fitting than the austerity of regular discipline, by which the fleshly man is crucified—for discipline, which he hates, is a torment to him. Regular discipline is a cross constructed, as it were, from the two pieces of wood of the laws of abstinence and continence. Abstinence restrains gluttony, and the law of continence checks excess in all the senses of mind and body; and in these consists the whole fleshly man.

Likewise, from above.

[Col. 0525D] Lust within us and gluttony can be restrained in such a way that we do not consent to the sinful passions dwelling in our members; but not in such a way that we do not feel at all the law that is in our members. For concupiscence, which is inborn and innate in us, can through the long practice of discipline and the constancy of spiritual exercise be weakened and enfeebled in righteous persons, so that it does not prevail; but it cannot be utterly uprooted—while preserving, nevertheless, the freedom of God’s Spirit, whose grace is bound by no law from being able to abound or even to superabound in whomsoever it wills and to whatever extent it wills.

But just as nations were left among the children of Israel, so that the Lord might train Israel by means of them, and the Jebusite could not be driven out of Jerusalem; so the concupiscence of the flesh always dwells in the land of our body or heart, [Col. 0526A] so that we may be trained through it, and we never lack an enemy against whom to fight. “For the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7). This concupiscence is our weakness, continually presenting us to ourselves, lest we put confidence in ourselves. For it shows us what we are in ourselves and of ourselves.

But one who is tempted by weakness and overcome is found himself weak beyond measure; for by that very weakness through which he is overcome, he is proved to be weaker still. Yet one who is tempted by weakness and is not overcome is weak in so far as he feels weaknesses; but in so far as he does not consent to weakness, he feels that strength is present to him. For “strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12).

But if it has been granted from above to any of the saints—as is devoutly believed of the most blessed Virgin, especially [Col. 0526B] after the coming of the Spirit—that in this mortal flesh he feels absolutely no evil concupiscence, then, just as this grace is rare or unique, so also is the glory rare or unique. If anyone is such a person, he no longer fights but triumphs; indeed, he reigns, possessing peace upon peace: peace from consent, peace from sensation; no longer girded for battle, but ungirded in triumph. “Let not him that is girded boast himself as him that is ungirded,” says the king of Israel (3 Kings 20). But “who shall boast that he has a chaste heart?” If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

Now, just as one who is overcome by weakness deserves shame, so one who conquers weakness appears to be without glory. For what is weakness but what its name denotes? What is weakness but [Col. 0526C] feebleness, but infirmity? What glory or what strength is there in conquering weakness? It is indeed great glory and great strength if, although we are weaker than weakness itself, we conquer weakness. Yet this glory and this strength are not ours, but belong to the Lord of hosts, who is the King of glory, who is glorified in His elect and makes His mercies wonderful in the weaknesses of the saints; and to Him it is said: “For thou art the glory of their strength” (Ps. 88).

If we consider what we can do of ourselves, since we are not sufficient by our own strength even to resist weakness itself, we possess no strength whatever. But the Prophet says: “Hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened” (Ps. 25). And again: “The Lord is the strength of his people” [Col. 0526D] (Ps. 27). But if our God is our strength and our might, our strength is greater than we ourselves are; indeed, what can we ourselves not do in Him who can do all things? What can we not do in omnipotent strength? Paul says, “I can do all things in Him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4).

Therefore, when weakness is conquered, since it is not our strength, neither is the praise ours; since it is not our power, neither is the glory ours. Glory is most rightly ascribed to Him by whose power victory is won. For “the Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory” (Ps. 23): the Lord glorious in triumph, the Lord mighty in battle. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Ps. 117): strength in battle, praise in victory. For the Lord is He who fights for us; the Lord is He who conquers [Col. 0527A] in us. But when weakness is felt in us, and we do not consent to it, “the body of sin is destroyed, that we may no longer serve sin.”

If by “the body of sin” the consent to sin is rightly understood, then the body of sin is truly destroyed when consent is not given to tempting concupiscence. But the carnal man, because he is “the man of sin” and “the son of perdition,” has a body of sin, to which concupiscence is, as it were, its soul, and consent its body. When full consent is given to concupiscence, the body of sin is, as it were, quickened, and sin is then served.

Perhaps someone will think that concupiscence, since it belongs to that flesh which “lusts against the spirit,” ought rather to be likened to flesh; while consent ought rather to be likened to soul than to flesh. For consent belongs to the will, and the consenting will belongs to the soul. [Col. 0527B] This is indeed so in the spiritual man, in whom sensuality is governed by reason and, as an inferior, is subjected to its superior. But it is not so in the carnal man. For, with the order reversed and perverted, the will of the spirit is subjected, by consenting, to the concupiscence of the flesh; and that which consents is found inferior to that to which it consents.

For concupiscence moves the soul to feel what it did not previously feel. When, having been moved, it feels, and, being stirred, consents, it degenerates from its dignity; leaving its proper place, it subjects itself to its inferior and is, as it were, given life by that by which it is moved. It no longer acts as spirit but suffers as flesh. Hence it is not undeservedly likened to a body. But through the law of discipline consent is checked, [Col. 0527C] and the body of sin is destroyed; the flesh is chastised, so that the mind may not be subject to the flesh under the law of the flesh, but that the flesh, under the law of the mind, may serve the mind. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Cor. 9). Let this suffice concerning the carnal man.

## On the Animal Man

Who the animal man is may be learned from the Apostle’s words. For he says: “The animal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are examined spiritually. But the spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2).

The carnal man appears to differ from the earthly man by the object of his love: the latter loves the earth; the former loves the works of the flesh. But the animal man is known either by understanding or by affection. He is animal in understanding if he does not savour the things that are of God’s Spirit. He is animal in affection if the things that are of God’s Spirit do not please him. For the examination of the animal man takes place in spiritual matters; there everyone who is animal is tested.

The animal man hears God’s words and perhaps does not understand because he is animal; or perhaps, if he understands, immediately turns his ear away through weariness, hatred, or contempt. For it is foolishness to him because he is animal. Hence the Apostle says: “The word of the cross is foolishness to them that perish” (1 Cor. 1). To one who does not believe the cross, the word of the cross is foolishness because he is animal in understanding, walking in the vanity of his understanding and having his intellect darkened. But to one who believes the cross and does not imitate the example of the Crucified, the word of the cross—that it must be borne for Christ—is foolishness, [Col. 0528A] because he is such an animal man, no longer in understanding but in affection.

He who is animal in understanding is ignorant and errs; he walks in darkness and does not know where he is going; his foolish heart is darkened. He regards as foolishness God’s wisdom hidden in mystery; he calls the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness before God, prudence. He approves one thing for another; calls good evil and evil good; makes darkness light and light darkness; makes sweet bitter and bitter sweet.

He who is animal in affection is without affection: he does not feel within himself the affection of divine love. For with a hard, untamed, and insensible heart, he is either lukewarm, rigid, sluggish, or numb. He either hates, loathes, despises, or neglects the exercises of spiritual warfare. At the beginning of his watches [Col. 0528B] he does not rise before the presence of the Lord his God; he does not pour out his heart like water; he feels no fiery compunctions or secret exultations in his heart; he does not pant with holy sighs or burn with devout desires. He does not delight in God’s law, is not inflamed by holy meditations, and is not lifted up in contemplation. He does not sit alone and in silence, that he may raise himself above himself. He does not ask that he may receive, seek that he may find, or knock that it may be opened to him. He does not occupy himself with divine praises; nor does he speak to himself “in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs,” among those singing and making melody in their hearts to the Lord.

Like a sick person languishing in the stomach and, through a bitter mouth, loathing food, he rejects spiritual food: the food that does not perish but remains unto eternal life. “His soul abhors all food, [Col. 0528C] and he has drawn near even to the gates of death.”

The animal man is recognized more by the soul than by the body. For not only animal men but also spiritual men, while dwelling in this mortal flesh, possess an animal body. Our body, according to its present condition, receives this from the soul: it is made sentient by it, as are the bodies of other animals. Pressed down by its own mass, it is heavy and weighty; subject to diverse sufferings and corruptions; bound by the necessity of dying; and, in order to live for a brief time, in need of food, remedies, and medicines. Now it gains strength, now it fails; and in its very growth it inclines toward decline—like an old garment which, while it is patched, grows ever older [Col. 0528D] and more worn.

But the Apostle says: “If there is an animal body, there is also a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15). We must not suppose that he said this in doubt. For what ought to be doubtful to no one was not uncertain to the Apostle. It is established that there is an animal body, and it ought likewise to be established that there is a spiritual body. The one is taught by experience itself and our common weakness; the other is commended by the consciousness of faith and the example of the resurrection of Jesus Christ. But not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animal; afterward that which is spiritual.

Our body, however, will be spiritual when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption; when what is mortal shall be swallowed up by life; when our tabernacle shall be completed; when the temple of God, which we are, shall be dedicated and the faces of the temple adorned with golden crowns; [Col. 0529A] when our flesh shall be made firm as bronze and hardened as the strongest rock, impenetrable and inaccessible to every cause of injury, every violence of suffering, and every force of temptation.

Then the spiritual body will be glorious in its own strength, light and agile; no longer needing food, as it did after sin and before sin; but free from every servitude of corruption and necessity. It will not be transformed into the nature of spirit, but, in supreme freedom and without any resistance, subjected to the spirit.

Meanwhile, the animal man and the spiritual man alike possess an animal body; they are distinguished from one another more by the state of the mind than by that of the body. For in his heart the animal man is spiritually crucified by the spiritual man. The cross is zeal for God according to knowledge. For knowledge and zeal are the weapons of our warfare, not carnal weapons, but mighty through God for the destruction of strongholds; with them we arm ourselves, “destroying counsels and every height exalting itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity unto the obedience of Christ” (2 Cor. 10).

Observe that, in the Apostle’s words, a height exalts itself against the knowledge of God. But what is this height except that of which it is said, “Do not be high-minded” (Rom. 11)? This is the height of the animal man, who walks in the vanity of his understanding. But the height of the cross is the knowledge of God, which brings every understanding into captivity unto Christ’s obedience. The breadth of the animal man is his animal affection: he wanders through unlawful things on the broad way that leads to destruction. [Col. 0529C] But the breadth of the cross is the affection of devotion in the breadth of charity.

There are some who have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; and others who have knowledge of God, but not zeal. Yet, if the stature of the cross is to be joined together from two pieces of wood, zeal must be joined to knowledge and knowledge to zeal, lest devotion be undiscerning or discernment undevout. For a clean animal is one that both chews the cud and divides the hoof.

Undiscerning devotion often puts God to the test through the temptation of impossible things; and, through ignorance of useful things, either presumes what is not expedient or neglects what is expedient. But undevout discernment, though it does not err in knowing useful things, nevertheless errs in choosing them. It sees and approves the better things, while following the worse. It is no smaller an error to choose what is worse than to be ignorant of what is better. By his own judgment he condemns himself who by his choice approves what he rejects in judgment; and he convicts himself of folly on one side or the other who, apart from compulsion of necessity, chooses one way and thinks another.

For beholding some visible form, the inner light of the eyes is insufficient without the aid of outward light; just as, conversely, that outward light does not assist sight without the inner light, if a visible thing is to be seen. The closed eye does not see at [Col. 0530B] midday; the open eye does not see in the dark night. Discernment without devotion, or devotion without discernment, has something similar to this.

We desire and hope to be led to contemplate the form of the invisible God. We need two eyes, which he asks the Lord to enlighten when he says: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12). The eye of discernment without the light of devotion, or the eye of devotion without the light of discernment, sees less—like an eye closed in the light or opened in darkness. Therefore discernment must be joined to devotion and devotion to discernment, so that charity may abound in us with knowledge, and knowledge with charity, according to the Apostle’s counsel: “May your charity abound more and more in knowledge and in all understanding, that you may approve the better things, that you may be sincere and without offence in the day of Christ” (Phil. 1).

But he who has knowledge and does not have charity has been made foolish by his knowledge. For without charity neither greatness of knowledge, nor contempt for the world, nor the chastening of discipline has any value before God. Charity alone claims for itself the glory of the cross, through which we ought to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is above all to be loved and blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## Twelfth Treatise, or Exhortation to Priests

[Col. 0529]

On Acts 20: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock,” etc.

[Col. 0529D] “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired by his blood.” The apostolic word is addressed to you, O priests of the Lord, ministers of our God. To you it is said: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock.” First to yourselves, then to the flock. Those who undertake the business of another’s salvation must have regard for their own salvation. It is fitting that those entrusted with the censure of moral discipline should live with reformed morals. They must begin with themselves and not neglect themselves, since they must first render an account for themselves. “Take heed,” he says, “to yourselves.”

[Col. 0530D] Take heed to what you are according to the nature of your weak condition; what you are according to the office of the commission laid upon you; what you are according to the dignity of the authority received; and what you are according to the humility of the service owed. Take heed to what you are with others, for others, above others, and finally below others.

What are you with others except human beings like other human beings: subject to suffering, conceived in sins, bound by the necessity of death, though through grace freed from sins; not yet inaccessible to temptations, not yet incapable of being overcome? For you can still be tempted and overcome by temptations, being clothed with weakness so that you may be able to sympathize with the weaknesses of others. Such ought high priests to be: men who know how to be compassionate because they themselves are subject to suffering. Therefore, because you are human, you are weak as human beings, according to the nature of your weak condition.

According to the office of your commission, you are for others angels of peace, in whom God has placed the word of reconciliation, so that with the Apostle you may say: “We act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 6). Malachi shows that you are angels when he says: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2).

But if you are angels, your conversation is in heaven. For you are not in the flesh but in the spirit, like ministering spirits sent into service for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation. You are sent by God, who “makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire.” And you, as ministers of God, are rightly called not only burning fire but also consuming fire: burning like the seraphim, as those near to God; consuming and enlightening the hearts of those subject to you, so that, kindled by the warmth of fiery speech, they may burn together and not hide themselves from its warmth.

Each of you has been appointed to guard many, and none of those subject to you is without a guardian angel to preside over and guard him in all his ways. Thus the Prophet speaks from God to the righteous man: “For he hath given his angels charge over thee, that they may keep thee in [Col. 0531C] all thy ways” (Ps. 90).

Nevertheless, though priests of the Lord may be likened to angels by the similarity of their office and may be called angels, as fellowship with good angels must always be sought, so likeness to evil angels must always be avoided. For evil priests, since they are not good angels, are more rightly compared to evil angels, who fell from heaven, did not stand in the truth, and lost the honour of angelic dignity.

If the heavenly manner of life of holy priests can be compared to heaven, do not those who have fallen from the lofty life worthy of priests to the unworthy things of a baser life appear to have fallen as angels fall from heaven? Even if they were never upon that sublime summit of virtues, they have nevertheless lost the place which they could and ought to have possessed but did not deserve. For they seem to have fallen from the place where they would be if they were not evil, and where those are who are not such as they are.

Therefore that prophetic threat appears to apply to them as human beings, no longer worthy of the name of angels: “But you shall die like men, and shall fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81). One of the princes fell, to whom many adhered, as many members adhere to one head. Therefore, lest you too fall like one of the princes, take heed: for you are not only angels for others, but gods above others; and this according to the dignity of the authority received.

Thus, when the Prophet was about to threaten evil men with ruin along with evil angels, he first said concerning the good: “I have said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” [Col. 0532A] (Ps. 81). Is your authority from heaven or from men? It is not from men but from God. For who can forgive sins but God alone? Yet the power of forgiving sins has been given to you, because the Lord, God of gods, has spoken and said: “Whatever you shall loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18).

In this authority of yours God is represented on earth by you. Through your representation of the one true God, you are called gods and are gods, so that through your ministry God may always be present to those who seek Him—not merely by the presence of His majesty, but by the representation of His authority and power. Take heed how great is the honour that you owe to Him who has given you so honourable a name. In this name you are to be feared and honoured: feared as judges, honoured as fathers; feared because of your power, honoured because of your holiness.

If holiness is lacking in any of you—which God forbid—let him fear, because God is judge. Let him fear, because “God stood in the midst of gods, but judges gods in their midst.” For when He distinguishes heavenly kings—that is, those who ought to govern themselves and others—He judges gods. He knows those who are His; nor can those who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ lie hidden from His eyes.

For those who love the first places at feasts, the chief seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men; who are hirelings, thieves, and robbers; who do not enter through the door; who are money-changers and sell doves in the Temple; who are dumb dogs; who are evil workers; who are violent, quarrelsome, not sober, or not chaste—all this class of gods appears to be reckoned among false gods. They are images of priests, like images of gods or idols of abomination in the Temple. For just as the worship belonging to the one true God is wrongly paid to an idol through idolatry, so those who take honour to themselves, not having been called by God as Aaron was, wrongfully usurp the honour owed to gods—that is, to holy priests.

This seems to be the point of what is written: “He who gives honour to a fool is like one who throws a stone into Mercury’s heap” (Prov. 26). Nevertheless, in whatever priest, the ministry is holy and the sacrament of the priesthood honourable; nor is it lawful for us to touch the Lord’s anointed or to judge judges appointed by God. There is One who searches and judges: God, who judges gods.

All vices, in and of themselves, are subject to public reproof, as already condemned by divine judgment. Yet it is not indiscriminately permitted publicly to accuse persons on account of their vices, or vices in particular persons, or publicly to condemn them. But you, priests of the Lord, who, as befits Christ’s ministers, show reverence to divine authority, take heed in all righteousness and holiness to the greatness of your dignity. For you are more than human beings, because you are angels of God; and like the angels who are reapers, to remove from His kingdom all scandals. Yet you are still more than angels, because you are gods, exalted both in name and in honour.

[Col. 0533A] You have considered your dignity, and that you are above others. Now consider—and again I say, consider—your humility, the necessity of your service, and what you are below others. If you wish to hear it, let the Prophet first tell you, lest I seem insulting to you, what you are. Speaking to the Lord, he says: “The earth shall be filled with the fruit of thy works, bringing forth grass for cattle and herb for the service of men” (Ps. 103). Behold what you are: cattle and the service of men. You have been cast down from so high to so low, as it is written: “They mount up to the heavens and descend to the depths” (Ps. 106).

For elsewhere it is written: “The giants groan beneath the waters, and they that dwell with them” (Job 26). You are like giants, of stature more lofty than others in the pre-eminence of dignity, [Col. 0533B] yet you groan beneath the waters of the peoples, weighed down by manifold care and anxiety. As the heavens are raised above the earth, so gods are raised above cattle—that is, you above yourselves.

You gods, rulers of souls, among other matters demanding your attention, give especially careful attention to how difficult it is to govern souls, serve the dispositions of individuals, and conform yourselves to all, so as to differ in nothing from servants while being lords of all. Therefore, “let him that is greater among you become as the younger”; nor is he ashamed to be called “servant of the servants of God.”

The Apostle shows the nature of this service when he says: “Though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all. I became all things to all, that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9). To demonstrate the rule of this service belongs also what is written: “The greater thou art, humble thyself in all things” (Ecclus. 3). It is as though he said: Let the measure of humility equal the greatness of dignity.

Humility in honour is the honour of honour itself and the dignity of dignity. Every dignity is unworthy of the very name of dignity if it disdains humble things. For humility is both the cause and the safeguard of honour. Every advancement in honour which proceeds in its proper order begins from humility and is completed in exaltation. For “he who humbles himself shall be exalted,” provided that he does not humble himself in order to be exalted, but rather humbles himself lest he be exalted—I mean, exalted in the world, but not in God.

For one who is truly humble does not seek honour. When he receives honour, he does not seize it through ambition; rather, because of humility he is seized and carried away to honour, so that he may not be a plunderer of honour but, as it were, honour’s prey. Humility without honour is itself sufficient for its own honour; but honour without humility brings itself to disgrace. Thus humility both worthily precedes honour and worthily preserves it.

Therefore let those who are in honour see that they show themselves humble in all things after the example of Christ. Though He was the master of humility, when He was foremost He became as one who ministers; though He was first, He became as the last, stooping to the feet of His disciples. By the example of His humility Christ presses you, as with a great weight, down to lowly things, so that you may be subject even to those subject to you.

Therefore, “let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus.” Though He was God in the form of God, [Col. 0534A] He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant. And you are gods: empty yourselves and take the form of a servant, so that for the present you may become like human beings for the sake of human beings, weak for the weak, taking upon yourselves all necessities and weaknesses, as he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11).

You must labour more than all others because you labour for all. Therefore you are not merely servants of human beings but the very service of human beings, like oxen treading grain, like cattle that serve human needs by their labour. If you seek a gift, the land of the peoples subject to you produces grass and herbage for you in their due seasons: things owing to you and which you have and possess. But if you seek fruit rather than a gift, as the Apostle says, “I seek not the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. 4), the fruit of righteousness ought to abound in your land, as in God’s husbandry.

Through your ministry, grass and herbage are due to you; but what do you owe? First, all that is yours; then yourselves: all that you can do, all that you are. Finally, your souls for the souls committed to you—and most willingly—like him who says: “Most willingly will I spend and be spent myself for your souls” (2 Cor. 12). Therefore you are debtors, not as though entrusted to one part of the flock, but to the whole flock: to all alike and to each individually, to wise and foolish alike. For an account must be rendered for all. Therefore take heed to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has [Col. 0534C] appointed you.

For this word applies to those who do not take honour to themselves, but are called by God as Aaron was. Those who are driven by the spirit of this world have not been appointed by the Holy Spirit, nor chosen by God as Aaron was, whom He Himself chose; rather, they “called their names in their lands.” What names are these? Perhaps names of honours, names of dignities: archdeacon, bishop, archbishop, and the like—great names. Many who do not yet possess these names and desire to possess them, although they are not yet theirs, have called them, as it were, to themselves that they might become theirs. They have called with a loud cry: perhaps by services, perhaps by gifts, perhaps by flattery, or by other means by which those who are not called to these things customarily call for them.

These are the men driven by the spirit of this world, the spirit of dizziness. God has not called them and therefore has not justified them, nor will He glorify them. For they seek glory from human beings, not the glory that is from God. Even if they are found pleasing and glorious before human beings, before God they are confounded, because God has rejected them.

But you are not such, you whom the Holy Spirit has appointed bishops to govern the Church of God. Your name and the reason for your name remind you of your office: that you may do nothing negligently in the care entrusted to you, but may be abundantly attentive and intent upon governing God’s Church. For this purpose the Holy Spirit appointed you. This is your office: according to the twofold manner of governing, to direct and correct in righteousness and judgment, [Col. 0535A] since by these virtues the throne of God is either prepared or corrected, as it is written: “Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of thy throne” (Ps. 88); and elsewhere: “Righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne” (Ps. 96).

For your chair, or your throne, is the people subject to you, over whom you preside, though only for a time: as vicars of Christ, who presides over you and sits in them as upon His own throne, while you sit in them as upon your throne—yet more truly as His. Therefore you sit as a throne in judgment, because “righteousness and judgment are the preparation of his throne.”

By your righteousness and judgment the throne of God must be prepared in the setting upright of virtues, His grace cooperating, to whom it is said: “Thou hast prepared the upright paths” (Ps. 98). By your righteousness and judgment the throne of God must be prepared in those [Col. 0535B] who have not yet made themselves fit for God who sits upon them; that is, in those who have not yet begun to be subject to God through obedience. It must also be prepared in those who have begun, lest they fail, but rather advance, until they complete what they have well begun. It must also be prepared in those who have fallen, that, with God’s help, they may be raised up, because the Lord puts His hand beneath them.

The eyes of all look to your righteousness and judgment. Upon these depend the salvation of those subject to you and the life of many. Your life is a mirror of holiness, an example of integrity, a seal of righteousness. The persons of many different faces in the Church see there either the grace of their own beauty or the stain of their deformity. There they see what they ought to imitate and to what they should desire to conform themselves. The life of those subject to you is marked out like softer wax, so that it may receive the image impressed by the seal of holiness.

[Col. 0536A] “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth.” If you love Christ, love righteousness also. For He was made for us wisdom from God and righteousness, when He who knew no sin was made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him. Christ was made a sacrifice for sin and, as the good shepherd, laid down His soul for His sheep, leaving you an example that you should follow His footsteps.

Christ acquired the Church with His blood. To show His exceeding charity by which He loved her, He poured out His blood for her and thus poured out charity. This Church, so acquired, so dear and beloved, He commended and entrusted to you, as though trusting in you, so that through you the heart of her husband may trust in her. Therefore, as you love Christ and as He can trust in you, preserve His bride in your faithfulness, being zealous for her—not for yourselves, but for Him—so that you may present her as a chaste virgin to her bridegroom, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is God above all, blessed for ages. Amen.

## Thirteenth Treatise, or Sermon

[Col. 0535]

On these words: “The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

[Col. 0535C] The charity of God, by which He loved us before the foundation of the world and chose us in His beloved Son, is itself the fountain and origin of all the good things bestowed upon us on the day of our creation, on the day of our redemption, and on the day of our justification and sanctification; and, further, of those things to be bestowed upon us on the day of our glorification, when God shall be glorified in us and we in Him.

God did not love us slightly, moderately, or scantily, but more fully and more richly; not falsely or feignedly, but purely and sincerely; not outwardly, merely in appearance or at the surface, but inwardly and from the marrow; not in word and tongue, but in deed and truth. If you consider its condition, this charity is rich and full of marrow. For whence have all God’s mercies toward [Col. 0535D] us proceeded, except from His ingrained kindness? Except from sheer generosity? Except from pure grace? Except from most abundant goodwill? Whatever power our merits have is His grace; and what is above merits is grace upon grace: grace accumulating and more abundant still.

If you seek the measure of this charity: because it is great, it is measurable indeed for Him, but for us immense and immeasurable. Yet if somehow we are able, with all the saints, to comprehend what its [Col. 0536C] dimension is, how great it is can scarcely—or cannot at all—be comprehended; for beyond what we can either say or think, it is high and deep, and likewise long and broad.

His height is the sublime glory which God has prepared for those who love him: that which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man (Isa. LXIV). His depth is the self-emptying of the only-begotten Son of God, and the bending-down of so great a majesty from the bosom of the Father as far as the reproach of the cross; from the beginning of life to the end of life, from the highest point to the lowest, from heaven even to hell, from end to end. But who is sufficient to contemplate end and end? Who can comprehend from how great a height he came, or how great is the distance between the summit from which he descended and the depth to which he descended? The height, therefore, of this love [Col. 0536D] is humanity’s advancement; its depth is God’s condescension; and, as has been said, it extends from the highest to the lowest, from the beginning even to the end.

But its length is without beginning and without end. For just as his love toward us does not cease, so neither does it begin. “For his mercy is from everlasting and unto everlasting upon those who fear him” (Ps. CII). Its breadth is wide and expansive, through the common and universal benefit of his goodwill and beneficence. For he “wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II): this belongs to goodwill [Col. 0537A]. And “he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII): this belongs to beneficence. His beneficence, moreover, is to be judged the greater because it extends not only to all, but also through all things. For he who gave us his own Son, how did he not also, with him, give us all things? (Ibid.)

This love was enclosed before the foundation of the world in God’s counsel and purpose; but in its due order it was revealed, poured out and shed abroad, infused and diffused. It was lavishly poured out when God created man in his own image and likeness; it was poured out more lavishly and abundantly when, through the death of his only-begotten Son, he redeemed man. It was infused when he enlightened the human heart, through the grace [Col. 0537B] of faith, to understand so excellent a love. But it was then diffused when, by the purpose of emulation, the desire of imitation, and the zeal of responsive love, he filled the breadth of the enlarged heart.

This is the diffusion by which he confirms our hope, so that we need not fear shame. “Hope,” says the Apostle, “does not put to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts” (Rom. V)—that love which is God’s toward us. For that is what the Apostle commends in that passage; yet through this love, diffused from God, that love also which is from us toward him is diffused in our hearts. And this latter is diffused through the former and in it, just as the light of eyes illuminated by the sun is diffused in the light through which they are illuminated.

Listen more carefully to the likeness in this comparison, so that the argument may lead from bodily light to spiritual light. [Col. 0537C] There is illuminating light, by which something sees or is seen. There is illuminated light, so that the appearance of each thing may be seen; and there is illuminated light that sees. The illuminating light, by which something sees or is seen, is the light of the sun: at the very eyelid of dawn it is poured forth, so that it may first itself be seen; then it spreads more widely, so that in it the various appearances of things may be seen—the things which, with their colours, forms, and shapes, are presented to our eyes. Illuminated light, so that it may be seen, consists in those visible appearances which, while they are in darkness, cannot be seen there; thus they are, as it were, darkness—formless through indistinct confusion. But when they are in the light, they are, as it were, a kind of illuminated light, so that they can be seen. For, as the Apostle says, “everything that is made manifest is light” [Col. 0537D] (Eph. V). A visible appearance is thus seen in the light in such a way that the light is at the same time seen in the mind; and the more clearly, the brighter the light is than the appearance.

The illuminated light which sees is the light of the eyes, which spreads widely in the diffused light when the eyes stand widely open and are illumined by a more widely diffused brightness. But the spiritual light which illumines our eyes is God’s love toward us. God’s many and great benefits, displayed and granted to us, as it were receive in themselves the light of his love and show it to our eyes. For in them it appears how greatly God loves, and how greatly he ought to be loved.
