For while the greatness of his benefits spreads itself before our eyes, the immense love of God, broadly extended, becomes openly known; and in its contemplation the sight of our mind also [Col. 0538A] spreads more widely. And while the love by which God loves us is considered more deeply according to a worthy estimation of his benefits, it becomes sweet through being made inwardly known to the deepest senses; with the wondrous sweetness of reciprocal love it moves the heart, enlarging it further, so that it may become capable of God. In accordance with the mutual exchange of love, it adapts and conforms itself to his love—according to height and depth, length also and breadth.

Love toward God is high when the height is hoped for and the sublimity of glory desired—not in this age, but in God, who says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John XII). To him the bride also says: “Draw me after you” (Cant. I). It is deep when, for God’s sake, truth is sought and abasement chosen, after the example of him who says: “I chose to be abject” [Col. 0538B] (Ps. LXXXIII); where it is shown that one who has himself chosen abasement does not wish to be chosen for honour. Love is long when it perseveres unto the end—indeed, rather, without end. For “love never fails.” It is broad when, mindful of God’s goodwill and beneficence, amid adversity and prosperity it always delights in him, rejoices in him, exults and sings joyfully to him: as broad as it is joyful, without the narrowness of faint-heartedness and murmuring. For the breadth of love is itself the enlargement of the heart, which is also the delight of righteousness.

This diffusion of love in our enlarged hearts is wrought by the love of God—that is, of the Father or of the Son—and it is wrought through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us, and who himself is the love of Father and Son, the bond joining both. To pass over God’s other benefits for the present: how great, for drawing love from us, is the fact that he gave us his only-begotten Son, that in him he might make us pleasing to himself; and also gave the Holy Spirit, who might prepare our heart, so that the Father himself, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, might come and make his dwelling with us! There are indeed diversities of graces, and among them all love excels. It is not without reason, and not without cause, that its diffusion is said to take place through the Holy Spirit and that the Spirit himself is given. Great and outstanding is the gift of grace when the author of the gift gives himself together with it, not allowing himself to be divided from this gift of his, or this gift from himself. Whoever, therefore, has received love as a gift may rightly glory in God and [Col. 0538D] say: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. VIII).

But one who possesses a word of wisdom, or a word of knowledge, or kinds of tongues, or interpretation of utterances, or the grace of some administration or activity—although these gifts are of the Holy Spirit—nevertheless, if he does not have love, he no more has the Holy Spirit in himself than this is true which is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful” (Wis. I).

Love, however, both constricts and enlarges our heart in contrary ways. Often you can feel how the stomach constricts and tightens itself against disgusting foods which it rejects. For what is not willingly received scarcely enters through a constricted throat. You may likewise feel how it relaxes and enlarges itself for desirable foods, and with what ease that is swallowed which is received with great eagerness. So too love constricts the heart against worldly desires which it does not admit; toward all that is healthful and holy it enlarges the will and relaxes the freedom of its desire. But cupidity enlarges itself toward transient things to the extent that it constricts itself toward heavenly things; and the more it draws the heart back, the more it compresses it toward trivial things. Great and expansive are the things that are eternal; small are those which are soon shut up within the narrow limits of time and quickly ended by brief pleasure.

Cupidity has its own height in its affected [Col. 0540A] ambition for honours; its own depth in feigned humility or affected exaltation; its own length in unremitting continuance; and its own breadth in insatiable capacity. Therefore we, who have renounced the world, who have received not the spirit of this world but the Spirit who is from God, so that the love of God may remain poured out in our hearts, should, as our religious profession requires, love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, while that same Spirit works within us—the God who is blessed above all things for ever. Amen.

## Fourteenth Treatise, or Sermon

[Col. 0539]

On these words: “He brought me into the wine-cellar; he set love in order within me. Sustain me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Cant. II).

[Col. 0539B] Love is a languor, a passion of the infirm soul. If, for establishing this truth, the authority of a poet who says,

> Alas for me, because love can be cured by no herbs,

seems unworthy and insufficiently suitable, the voice of the bride should suffice for religious minds. She speaks what she feels and says: “I languish with love.”

Let us therefore see whether every love is a languor. There is natural love, by which parents and children love one another; and it exerts its force even among brute animals. For they too are variously affected toward their offspring. The bear murmurs tenderly over her cubs, and the hen is made weak over her chicks. What but love caused Jacob to weep and say: “A most evil beast has eaten my son; a wild beast has devoured Joseph” (Gen. XXXVII)? What but love impelled David to weep, saying: “My son Absalom, Absalom my son! Who would grant that I might die for you, Absalom, my son, my son Absalom?” (II Kings XIX)?

There is social love, by which bonds of friendship are joined. By this love David and Jonathan loved each other; David was tormented by its grief when he said: “I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan, most beautiful and lovable beyond the love of women; and as a mother loves her only son, so I loved you” (II Kings I). There is conjugal love, by which bridegroom and bride chastely love each other, and are often more bitterly separated than sweetly united. There is incestuous love, or love otherwise unchaste. This love has its own passions and the straits of sorrow. Amnon’s love for Tamar proves it; Jonathan said to him: “Why are you so wasted with thinness, son of the king, day by day?” [Col. 0539D] (II Kings XIII). Shechem too proves it: he loved Dinah, and his soul was joined to hers.

There is vain love, the love of this world, by which one loves what can hinder blessed life and cannot benefit it. The Prophet rebukes this love, saying: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity?” (Ps. IV). This vain love, like unchaste love, is not only languor but also a vice and death of the soul.

There is holy love, by which God is truly, chastely, and purely loved; and this too is a languor. For she who says, “I languish with love,” labours in anxious longing. [Col. 0540B] But if love of God is charity, and charity is a virtue—the greatest among the virtues—how is love of God languor? Is the love of God, or charity, weakness? Is virtue languor, health disease, and medicine? How is that not health or medicine by which one is healed of sickness? Of this it is written: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke VII). How is charity not health, when it heals the wounds of the languishing soul and covers a multitude of sins? But if charity is health, how is it languor? And if it is languor, how is it not an incurable languor, when it is written: “Charity never fails” (I Cor. XIII)?

Or is love possessed one way in the desire to enjoy, and another in the enjoyment of what is desired? Precisely so. For the time being, love is languor while it burns, pants, and sighs for what it loves; while that which is desired is not possessed; while she who is delayed from the desired embraces of the bridegroom is tormented—and tormented because she is delayed. But he “who heals all your infirmities,” O bride, will heal this languor of yours also, when the bridegroom offers himself to be seen, possessed, and enjoyed: that is, when you see him as he is, eye to eye, face to face, once united to him and never again separated from his conversation, sight, kiss, and embrace. From that time your languor will fail, but your love will never fail. You will no longer be able then to say, “I languish with love,” but rather, “I rejoice with love.” And your joy will arise from this: that the bridegroom will rejoice over the bride, and your God will rejoice over you. This is [Col. 0540D] the end of languor, but not the end of love.

But meanwhile, what happens? The bride is more grievously weakened and, languishing, lies confined to her bed: “May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his pain” (Ps. XL). What aid, counsel, or consolation will be given her? For the remedy for love is not now in question. It is far away, beyond the ends of the earth, and is not found under heaven. But she who cries out and feels the force of her passion, because she cannot hope for the remedy at this time or in this place, at least asks consolations from her household, by which they may comfort her until her weakness passes away. And, after the manner of the sick, she first declares its beginning, cause, and course, and then seeks consolation, because she does not yet hope for the remedy which she knows must be delayed for some time.

As though asked, “O languishing woman, whence comes this weakness to you?” she replies: “He brought me into the wine-cellar.” Who brought you in? “I sat indeed beneath the shadow of him whom I had desired; and he who fed me with his fruit, which was sweet to my throat, brought me into the wine-cellar, so that he might give drink to one already fed, from the cup of love which he mixed for me, drawn from the wine-cellar. And when I had tasted it, I wished to drink.” In this manner I languish with love.

You who desire the cup of salvation—for this languor is salvation—attend, together with the bride, to what the wine-cellar is, that you may be brought into it. And, if you wish to hear it, the chamber of the heart itself is the wine-cellar, where the wine of love is. The chamber, I say, is that of the heart—but of those who return to their heart. For those who wander outside themselves, walking in the desires of error and having become far from their own heart like men out of their minds, who look toward vanities and false madness—these are outside the wine-cellar. Through the prophet they are called back to themselves: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. XLVI).

Perhaps not all who return to the heart are at once brought into the wine-cellar. The bride first sits beneath the shadow, desires, praises the sweetness of the fruit, and afterward is brought into the wine-cellar. There are indeed many who first make lawful use of this world, sit beneath the shadow, desire, praise the sweet fruit of righteousness, deliberate within themselves concerning the way of perfection, and, pierced by the grace of divine mercy, resolve for Christ’s sake to leave all things and cling to him alone in all purity of heart. They enter the wine-cellar when for Christ’s sake they judge all things worthy of contempt and estrange them from their heart.

Nor does the bride enter as though by herself, but is brought in; for no one rightly enters the way of perfection or returns to the heart unless the voice of him grows strong in the heart—the one to whom it is said through the Prophet: “You said, ‘Return, sons of men’” (Ps. LXXXIX). And again: “He converted my soul” (Ps. XXII). The bride, then, is brought into the wine-cellar when, through contempt for the world, love of the world is wholly excluded from the whole heart. Therefore, once brought in, having set aside every desire, and now forgetful of the world through the estrangement of a sober mind produced by the wine of compunction, feeling nothing within herself but love, she says: “He set love in order within me.”

Understand here both kinds of love: love of God and love of neighbour. For love of neighbour is brought back to the love of God, since one must love one’s neighbour only according to God, in God, or for God’s sake. Love, moreover, is the order of virtue; but virtue is the order of love—though in different ways. Virtue is the order of love in the sense that it is ordered by love; charity is the order of virtue in the sense that, having first been ordered itself, it orders virtue so that it may be able to order.

Love is ordered by estimation, emulation, and choice. It is ordered by estimation when, by the true judgment of the mind, it is reckoned better, worthier, and more precious than all things [Col. 0542A]. Consult the Apostle concerning the estimation of love: he will tell you how worthily and magnificently it ought to be valued. “I show you,” he says, “a yet more excellent way” (I Cor. XIII). And again: “Now faith, hope, charity—these three—remain; but the greatest of these is charity” (ibid.). And again: “To know the charity of Christ which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. III).

But it is too little to think thus of charity and prefer it to all things merely by estimation, unless it is also set above all things by the affection of emulation, so that it is desired before all things and above all things. Peter exhorts to this when he says: “Above all things, having continual mutual charity among yourselves” (I Pet. IV). And Paul, when he says: “Emulate the better gifts” (I Cor. XII); and again: “Above [Col. 0542B] all these things, have charity” (Col. III).

Since some approve charity by estimation or emulation, yet do not approve it by choice or pursuit, it must also be ordered by choice, so that it may be sought, possessed, and retained. To obtain charity, some sort of emulation combined with estimation is not enough without the zeal of pursuit. Some aspire and sigh after it who never draw breath in it. For they desire and do not lay hold of it. Therefore they desire vainly; and vainly because, not employing counsel, they disapprove by their conduct what they approve by judgment and some sort of desire, but not by counsel.

Estimation belongs to the judgment of reason; emulation, to the desire of the will; choice, to the counsel of discernment. But there is no discernment of choice where the worse thing is chosen. Therefore the Apostle says: “Pursue charity” (I Tim. VI). For through pursuit—that is, through using God’s counsel—charity is laid hold of. This is the counsel: to renounce unlawful things for the love of Christ, that charity may be possessed; and to abstain, as far as possible, from lawful things, that it may be possessed more perfectly. This is the counsel: that cupidity may be wholly cast aside, so that charity may thus be acquired.

He intimates this counsel who says: “If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as though it were nothing” (Cant. VIII). Love for eternal things is acquired by contempt for things that pass away. The gold of charity is bought by contempt of cupidity. “I have counted all things as loss,” says the Apostle, “and have regarded them as dung, that I might gain Christ” [Col. 0542D] (Phil. III).

When charity has been placed in the first place in your heart by the judgment of worthy estimation, by the whole desire of emulation, and by every zeal of pursuit, it has been established in its proper place and therefore set in order. For that place is due to it. Thus ordered, it orders all things, so that all things are done according to order. For since the Apostle says, “Let all things be done among you according to order” (I Cor. XIV), and the same Apostle says, “Let all your things be done in charity” (I Cor. XVI), it may be inferred that those things which are done in charity are done according to order, and that those not done in charity are outside order.

Charity orders the angels in their offices and ministries; it orders the lives and morals of the righteous in their professions and pursuits; it orders the ranks of virtues in their stations [Col. 0543A], so that the ordered choir of virtues—that is, the ordered battle-line of the camp—may be neither broken into nor disturbed by enemies. In charity the law was ordered through angels by the hand of the mediator. For as Christ’s virtue shines in the charity which he commended to us, after the spirit of fear we received the Spirit of adoption as sons, so that we might serve him not in fear, as under the law, nor from sadness or necessity, but from inward love, in joy of heart and freedom of spirit.

In charity the covenant is ordered above the sacrifices of good works, because over every good that we do the covenant of God’s promise is set, while through love of God eternal recompense is always contemplated and reckoned superior to all our merits. “For the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII).

Charity ordered the mystery of our redemption: it, as it were, removed God from the place of his dignity and placed him in the place of his condescension; made him a little lower than the angels, and set man among men. “From eternity,” says the Wisdom of God, “I was ordered” (Prov. VIII), doubtless as equal to the Father, so that she is rightly above all things, through whom all things were made. Yet “she reaches from end to end” (Wis. VIII): from the end which is the fountain of life to death, which is the end of life. Strongly indeed, because by dying she destroyed death; and sweetly disposing all things, in humility and charity she ordered all things, making peace, restoring, and bringing into harmony, so that all things might be subject to her. For all things were then ordered when they were under him from whom they are.

He abandoned his own order who refused to stand in his place, wishing to coexist with God through equality rather than be subject to him through humility, saying: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). “By your ordering, O God, the day endures” (Ps. CXVIII): by yours, certainly, not by each thing’s own ordering. Therefore he did not endure, because he presumed to disturb the ordering, paying no attention to the fact that all things serve you. Thus the angel of light, who was like the day of heaven, became prince of darkness and the gloom of night.

But charity, which through obedience has subjected all things to God, orders all things according to its own judgment: now it counsels what is more perfect; now it commands what is necessary; now it permits what is not unlawful [Col. 0543D]; now it chooses what is better; now it accepts what is necessary.

For although freedom is joined to charity, charity nevertheless yields to necessity when it sometimes passes over what is better in order to avoid what is worse. Often, while we emulate the good that is better, worthier, and more perfect, we are hindered by the authority of a superior power, by the force of some difficulty, or by the weakness of our own infirmity. Thus it comes about that what was first in emulation is later in choice and pursuit. In arranging, therefore, those things which must be done, charity now uses the order of freedom and worthiness, now the order of dispensation and necessity.

For when neither the force of greater authority or of some difficulty, nor the trembling of faint-heartedness, stands in the way [Col. 0544A], charity freely chooses and pursues what is worthier and more perfect. But when freedom of choice—or rather, the choice of what is better—is impeded in some way, then, in an inverted order but still in an order, charity accepts what necessity imposes or infirmity suggests. For when charity uses its freedom, it approaches what is better; when it yields to necessity or gives way to infirmity, it subjects itself to an inferior good. Hence, when it emulates what is better and is compelled by some force of circumstances toward what is inferior, it sometimes hesitates in its choice and does not know what it should choose; yet it does not fail to know what it desires more.

Thus Paul, desiring more greatly to be with Christ, “for it is much better,” yet needing to remain in the flesh because of his brethren, is constrained by the ambiguity of choice and says: “What I shall choose, I do not know” [Col. 0544B] (Phil. I). But in all righteous persons—whether those who freely choose better things or those who accept inferior goods—charity itself is always ordered, always first in estimation, emulation, pursuit, or choice. For no one is more good or less good, provided he is good, who does not place charity itself before all other things, even if in choice he postpones what in love ought to be preferred.

But when charity has been ordered, and has itself ordered, and has ordered in whatever way, all things alike are ordered. For it is itself the order of things to be done, and nothing done in charity is outside order. But the bride, now despising the world, now possessing ordered charity, now unable through the magnitude of love to endure the burning of her breast—by what passions, do you suppose, is she anguished? By what pains is she tortured? How is she tormented amid scandals by hatred and weariness; how grievously is she held in suspense, through delay and expectation, by hope and desire! Who could explain all the distresses of the languishing bride, which she suffers for the beloved, and for whom all that she suffers is too little?

Her languor includes what she says of herself: “Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me” (Cant. I). But where Christ’s sufferings abound, do Christ’s consolations not abound? On the contrary, they abound. The bride therefore has her consolations, both in her own good qualities and in the examples of others who are good. For among the number of the good she sees some beginning and, as it were, flourishing in the first stages of virtue; she sees [Col. 0544D] others too attaining, through maturity of conduct, the summit of perfection.

But what are the examples of those who love and languish with love, in the beginnings and fulfillments of virtues, in the first rudiments and more mature exercises of patience, except flowers and fruits of honour and uprightness? The bride rejoices to surpass those who are beginning; she rejoices also to equal those who are stronger. She rejoices to have the former beneath her, so that, supported as it were by flowers, she may rest more softly. She rejoices also to have the latter at her side and beside her, so that, surrounded and enclosed as it were by apples, she may turn herself neither to the right nor to the left, but may be strengthened unturningly and steadfastly toward strong things. Therefore she says: “Sustain me with flowers; surround me with apples.”

It is as though she said to her household: “O my inmost thoughts and affections [Col. 0545A], comfort me; do this within me: that, with flowers laid beneath, I may recline more softly, and that, surrounded by apples placed about me, I may not turn elsewhere. It is pleasant to be sick in this way, when those who suffer with me and languish in like sorrow are a consolation to me.”

Moreover, the bride has consolation for her languor from her merits and the rewards of those merits. She considers that three things are promised to her as a reward by the Lord, who says: “No one has left this or that for my sake and for the Gospel’s sake who shall not receive a hundredfold now in this time, with persecutions, and at the end of the age eternal life” (Mark X). After she has advanced long through the growth of virtues and has vigorously exercised herself in the pursuits of spiritual discipline, she at last finds the hundredfold in the heart’s peace and tranquility, serenity and security, delight in righteousness, and the sweetness of ineffable spiritual joy. These are the apples; these are the fruits of righteousness which spring from the flowers of discipline begun.

Not only these, however, but also the apples of tribulations and persecutions, which God sometimes grants as an example of patience to those desiring to suffer—or even to die—for the name of Jesus. Hence patient Job says: “Let him who began crush me. Let him loose [Col. 0546A] his hand and cut me down; and let this be my consolation, that in afflicting me with pain he does not spare me” (Job VI). And again: “If he scourges, let him kill at once, and not laugh at the punishments of the innocent” (Job IX). Does not one who says this seem to call down the scourges themselves upon him, and as it were to say: “Surround me with apples”? He would certainly not say this unless he had been sustained by the flowers of virtues. For he was simple and upright and departed from evil.

Thus the bride, who emulates perfection, counts not only the charisms of virtues and the joys of inward peace among God’s benefits, but recognizes God’s gifts in her tribulations and gratefully receives his scourges as certain benefits. “It has been granted to you,” says the Apostle, “for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. I). But if the bride desires to be surrounded by these apples as by certain fruits of righteousness, how much more does she sigh for those inestimable fruits of righteousness reserved for the future! For she can mean these fruits too when she says: “Surround me with apples.” With these apples, at least in hope for the present, she consoles herself amid every tribulation and pain of evils, until she sees him whom she loves, her bridegroom Jesus Christ, who is God above all things, blessed for ever. Amen.

## Fifteenth Treatise on Cenobitic, or Common, Life

[Col. 0545]

[Col. 0545C] “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be always with you all” (II Cor. XIII).

The institution of common life is supported and sustained by authority neither small, slight, nor mediocre. The Church was founded in the primitive common life; the infancy of the Church at its birth began from common life. Common life received from the apostles the example of its profession, the title of its honour, the privilege of its dignity, the testimony of its authority, the protection of its defence, and the foundation of its hope.

The apostles, whom God established as princes over all the earth; princes of the peoples gathered together with the God of Abraham; mighty gods of the earth, greatly exalted; friends of God, exceedingly honoured [Col. 0545D], whose rule was exceedingly strengthened; senators of heaven and judges of the world, to whom the promise was made that they should sit upon twelve thrones and judge the twelve tribes of Israel; enrolled fathers, to whom swords were given in their hands to execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes upon the peoples; to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles, that they might execute upon them the judgment written—these men, so great, powerful, and illustrious, clothed with power from on high, undertook at the prompting of the Holy Spirit to observe common life. They confirmed it by their example, approved it by their practices, and handed it down for us to observe [Col. 0546C], so that, while placed on earth, through the likeness of common life we may begin to be conformed to the angels of God, with whom we are to be associated in eternal life and to become equal and like.

Common life was instituted according to the patterns of heavenly things, brought down from heaven and conveyed to us from the heavenly manner of life of the holy angels. If it is too little for the commendation of common life that it came down to us from the apostles, and to the apostles from God’s angels, there remains something to add which surpasses all its praise. For common life flowed from the very fountain of life itself. I speak now of that fountain of which it is written: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV). Common life is indeed like a certain radiance of eternal light, a certain emanation of eternal life [Col. 0546D], a certain derivative stream from the perennial fountain, whence flow living waters springing up unto eternal life.

## On the Common Life of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit
God is life; the holy and undivided Trinity is one life. The Father is not one life, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; rather, these three are one life. And just as their essence and their nature are one and common, so their life is one and common. For God is neither single nor solitary, since God is three and one. Nor is God’s life non-common, since it is one life, undivided and indistinguishable, for three persons. Perhaps, without injury to the piety of faith, God’s essence or power, or his wisdom, may seem singular to someone, because it is incomparably pre-eminent and surpassing; and therefore, although it is common, it may be thought to be, as it were, uniquely common, and hence perhaps singular. But lest what is certain be made doubtful through ambiguity of a word, it is unquestionably established that God’s life is not so singular a life that it is not common; for it is written: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 6).

It was not fitting that God should be solitary; it did not accord with his dignity, glory, and blessed life to have no companion. According to the faith of the holy Fathers, the true confession, true affirmation, and true profession of faith is that God is three and one, not solitary; and reason itself in some manner rises in support of this faith. For God, [Col. 0547B] who dwells in inaccessible light, lest he be wholly unknown and, through ignorance, not loved, causes a certain light of his own, though faint, to sparkle in our hearts. And he opens himself to us more, and discloses his nature to us, in that respect in which it is more expedient for us to know his nature—whom, according to the measure of knowledge granted us, we ought to love with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength.

Now God is love; and, as the Apostle says, “His love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). The love which is in us through grace represents to us in some way what that incomprehensible love is like which is God, whose nature is both love and goodness. This is the nature of love, as an inward perception of love itself makes known to us from the depths: both to love and to will to be loved. For just as fire cannot fail to burn, so love cannot fail to love. Love is fire, and to love is to burn. And just as fire does not contain itself within itself, but seems moved always to reach things it may kindle, so that it may not live in itself alone but communicate its heat to things touched or set alight, so love, with a kind of perceptible striving, longs to pour itself out, to convey to another—one loved with complete affection—the good it possesses, to bring that good into common ownership, and to admit the other as a partner in its possession. For every good shines forth more beautifully by the valuation of love when it is fittingly made common. [Col. 0547D]

Among those goods which can suffice for a lover and for one loved with full affection, love desires fellowship and prefers to possess in common with the beloved what may suffice for both, rather than possess it alone. But in goods which cannot suffice for each alike, love often chooses to go without them itself, lest the friend whom it knows needs its kindness should lack them. In conferring benefits, love always seeks that the one loved may love in return, lest love be one-sided. For, as was said, it always loves to be loved; nor does love of fellowship suffice for the lover if there is no fellowship of love. Since it wishes its goods to be common, it wishes its love itself still more so. Love does not know how not to be generous; it hates to be solitary.

[Col. 0548A] In the abundance of its giving, love strives, as it were through a love of fellowship, to obtain fellowship of love. For what is love’s generosity, if it wishes to keep its goods for itself alone and does not wish to share them? Or what consolation is there for one who loves, if he is not loved in return and loves alone? It is written: “Woe to one who is alone!” (Eccl. 4). Solitary love is a torment to itself and in some fashion hates itself, since it wholly refuses to be solitary lest it not be mutual. And just as it cannot be deprived of its generosity and nature, so it cannot fail to love the fellowship of good and fellowship with itself.

Therefore two things are inseparably joined to the love that is in us, so far as love’s own desire is concerned: shared love and fellowship of love. If either is lacking, love is not yet blessed, since it seeks nothing but blessedness in fellowship of good and fellowship with itself. But if common good is present and shared love absent, love lacks something which it itself wishes to be present. If shared love is present and common good absent, love lacks something which it itself does not wish to be absent. Such is the case with that love which is ours, in us, and among us: through it we are not yet fully blessed, but shall be made blessed in the future, in fellowship of the highest good, which can suffice for all, and in fellowship of mutual love, through which nothing will be unshared among us.

See, my mind, and consider: your experience of the love known to you demonstrates to you concerning God’s nature precisely what God himself reveals concerning himself through the grace of faith. You could indeed, O mind, if you were not darkened by sin, know God intimately in the very nature of yourself, as in his image. But now you are almost blinded, so that neither in yourself nor through yourself can you fully discern either God or yourself. How then am I not blind? I confess that in this respect, so far as lies in me, I am blind; so that this may truly be my utterance: “My strength has forsaken me, and the light of my eyes itself is not with me” (Ps. 37).

Since I have begun, I shall speak further to you, my mind. I believe that you desire to see God and to go into God, and that you need a guide because you are blind. If you follow the guidance of faith, you will not go astray; indeed, in the very light of faith you will already now be able to see God. But is God seen in faith alone? Is he not seen in love? Yes: in love, and more especially in love. For love itself is a luminous commandment, enlightening the eyes. Nothing in us is more like the love which is God than the love which is in us from God. Through this the image of God in us is re-formed; through this God is seen and perceived in us, and known much more fully than in faith alone. Therefore, if “the invisible things of God are perceived in what has been made in us” (Rom. 1); if it is permitted to judge God’s nature from his grace; if from a gift one may know the giver of the gift: beyond doubt, love of fellowship and fellowship of love accord with God’s nature.

For one whose nature is love and goodness naturally loves and wills to be loved; and as much as he loves, so much does he will to be loved. [Col. 0549A] Nor does he endure that full fellowship in his blessedness should be lacking to the one by whom he wills to be loved as much as he is worthy to be loved, lest fellowship of love be less than love of fellowship. So great is the Father’s love that he gave the Son to have in himself the life which he himself has in himself, so that the Son might be one life with the Father, equal to the Father and a sharer in the Father’s glory in all the fullness of eternal honour and undivided power.

For blessed love is not without a companion, and therefore is not without fellowship. Blessed love is blessed life; blessed life is blessedness; and blessedness is the highest good. The highest good is naturally common. For every good, precisely because it is good, is also praiseworthy; and if it is both good and common, it possesses a more abundant glory both of goodness and of fellowship. For the supreme goodness of a good is fellowship itself. Therefore the highest good cannot be deprived of the praise of fellowship, lest it not be the highest good if so great a power of praise, and the praise of power, were lacking to it. But the highest good is a full and perfect good, from which no worthy praise of goodness can be lacking at all. Hence it is naturally common and communicable through grace, as the fountain and origin of all goods.

This is eternal life: blessed life, common life, infinite and incomprehensible love, common to God the Father and his only-begotten Son. For, as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself. The Son has in himself the life which the Father also has, because he is one life with the Father. Yet the life which the Son has in himself—because it is life—he does not have from himself, but from the Father. For whatever the Son is said, according to substance, either to be or to have, he is and has in common with the Father; that is, he has it from the Father. From the Father he has that he is the living God, blessed, omnipotent, and wise; that he is life itself, blessedness itself, power itself, and wisdom itself. From the Father also he has that he is Son; nor did he begin to have what he received from the Father, because in being born he received what the Father gave by begetting.

For he is coeternal, consubstantial, and coequal with the Father, and in all things like him: God from God, light from light, the radiance of his glory, the imprint of his substance, and the image of the invisible God. [Col. 0549D] The Father, who gave the Son to have life in himself just as he himself has life in himself, loves the Son as himself; and the Son loves the Father as himself. Their love is the Holy Spirit, the bond and fellowship of both. Their love is so indivisible that whoever loves the Father also loves the Son; and whoever is not loved by the Son is not loved by the Father. Their love is one and their honour undivided; their power is one and their operation undivided; and their fellowship is so great that the Son says to the Father: “All that is mine is yours, and all that is yours is mine” (John 17). John the Baptist also says: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 3). The Lord himself again says: “The Father loves the Son and shows him all things which he himself does” (John 5).

## On the Fellowship of Angels

[Col. 0550A]

A certain representation of this common life—which is in God and is God—is the common life of the angels, which the Holy Spirit establishes in the highest peace, as love, bond, and fellowship. For “by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32). The heavens are angels, who live harmoniously and happily in his love. Each loves all, and all love each; all will the same thing and reject the same thing. What pleases one displeases none; what one wills, none does not will. One is the judgment of all, one their will; all think the same and understand the same.

There pride does not puff itself up, envy does not waste away, anger does not blaze, discord does not quarrel, impatience does not murmur, [Col. 0550B] and the deceitful tongue does not slander. All things there are peaceful, ordered, tranquil; nothing is disorderly, nothing undisciplined, nothing contrary to order or obedience. Nothing is secretly stored away as an occasion for possessing private property; all things are manifest, all clear. What belongs individually to each belongs commonly to all through fellowship of love and love of fellowship. All rejoice together before God in one temple; all read, meditate upon, and contemplate together in the book of life; all are refreshed together at one table. They rest together in the place of outward quiet. Nothing is done by anyone individually that can disturb or offend the common peace, obedience, or order.

Such is that most delightful and blessed society of the heavenly citizens who live in common. We who still dwell on earth must continually represent their life through the likeness of common life, so that we may deserve to be joined more intimately to their fellowship in proportion as we have been granted from above more closely to imitate their life, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## On the Fellowship of Nature, to Which Fellowship of Guilt Is Joined

Fellowship makes life common. There is a fellowship of nature, a fellowship of grace, and a fellowship of glory. In the fellowship of one nature the whole human race is gathered, [Col. 0550D] propagated from one parent together with the transmission of sin and dispersed far and wide through the multitude of humankind. To this fellowship of nature is joined a fellowship of guilt and wrath. For nature, corrupted in its root, is propagated together with the corruption itself, with original guilt and original wrath. For by nature we are children of wrath. We are all born both evil and miserable.

Human nature is so infected by the stain of sin that it cannot be purified by nitre, by borith-herb, or by any kind of washing or cleansing, except in the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, into whose death we have been baptized. For “all of us who have been baptized have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6). But the wrath of God’s indignation, coming forth from hidden justice as an arrow from a quiver, has been driven deep into human nature, [Col. 0551A] has reached the innermost recesses, and clings so firmly that it cannot be drawn out by any force except by the mighty hand of almighty God.

Of this arrow the prophet says: “He has sent the daughter of his quiver into my loins” (Lam. 3). In the zeal of his justice God conceived indignation against sin and poured out wrath. This wrath is innate in us, whose children by nature we are. This is the daughter of the quiver, taken, as it were, from the quiver of God’s hidden justice: conceived there, and born here in us—innate and connate to us, the daughter of the quiver, yet like a uterine sister of our nature. The prophet says that it is in his loins—and rightly in the loins, for there is the seat of desire, from which the infirmity of nature is propagated.

This fellowship of corrupted nature, in which all of us, sharing one nature, are subject to sin and held bound under the debt of death, imposes on us a threefold obligation: love, humility, and compassion. The Lord says: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Deut. 6). If an explanation of divine commandments must be given to human curiosity—although, for restraining every curious inquiry, it ought to suffice that God has commanded, whose commands are all faithful, made in truth and equity—nevertheless faith will not lack an answer for one excessively concerned to know why God wills this commandment to be kept.

The conscience of faith knows that God loves one consubstantial with himself, a sharer in his nature. By this example it can answer the human being: “Go and do likewise” (Luke 10); love the sharer of your nature, one who will share in the glory promised to you. [Col. 0551C] Love your nature; love what you were born, lest, by not loving in another the nature which is in you, you fail to love yourself. Thus we are drawn by God’s own example to love the sharer of our nature; we are pressed by the authority of his command; we are bound by fellowship of nature. And in consciousness of common weakness we ought to humble ourselves toward one another and have compassion upon one another, lest proud boasting divide those whom a single weakness of condition makes equal.

One does not yet know how to love oneself who presumptuously scorns the common nature in another; one wrongs one’s own condition who does not recognize one’s own right in the image of God. One violates the law of human society who does not honour fellowship of nature in one’s neighbour. One shuts off to oneself the entrance to mercy who does not extend even compassionate feeling toward a brother’s need. So much for fellowship of nature.

## On the Fellowship of Grace

There is a fellowship of grace that generally embraces all who are counted under the Christian profession, good and bad alike, in one confession of faith and participation in the sacraments. This is the field in which tares and wheat grow (Matt. 24). This is the threshing-floor whose grain is mixed with chaff. This is the net containing good fish to be chosen into vessels and bad fish to be cast out. This is Noah’s ark, in which are clean and unclean animals, the raven and the dove.

For faith belongs even to those who do not have works befitting faith; and those participate in the Church’s sacraments who, by unworthy conduct, render the power of the sacraments ineffective in themselves. Accordingly, those who share in the sacraments under the confession of faith are divided from one another as good people are divided from evil people. Among these may be counted schismatics, who reject the yoke of canonical obedience, and false brothers, who simulate the humility of Christian profession rather than observe it.

But all the righteous who participate, in faith and in obedience befitting faith, in the Church’s sacraments have one particular and special fellowship, in which a stranger has no share. Nor does anyone found in this fellowship share with strangers, so that with the Prophet he may say: “I will not share with their chosen ones” (Ps. 140). This fellowship of the righteous is the unity of the Church, which in [Col. 0552B] all Christ’s members preserves the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. This is Christ’s seamless tunic, which is not divided; concerning it Christ says: “They divided my garments among themselves” (John 19), “and over my garment they cast lots” (Ps. 21).

Under the profession of one faith and participation in the sacraments, people are divided from one another, as has been said, as though dividing Christ’s garments. For some receive ecclesiastical sacraments worthily and others unworthily, and the faith of some is dead without works (Jas. 2), whereas “the righteous lives by faith” (Heb. 10). But lots are cast over the garment which is not divided. Whoever joins himself to ecclesiastical society in Christ’s love and obedience belongs to that lot of which it is written: “The Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous” (Ps. 124).

Wherever the righteous may be, whether they live separately or in common, through the unity of ecclesiastical peace and fellowship of obedience and love, like members of one body they do not admit division. For the birds—the turtledove and the dove—were not divided when, at the Lord’s command, Abraham took a heifer, a goat, and a ram, divided all these in the middle, and placed the two parts opposite one another (Gen. 15). The Apostle indicates this fellowship of the righteous when he says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4).

Obedience is owed to one Lord, as Christ plainly shows when he says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6). And obedience is the inseparable companion of love, as he himself testifies, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14); and: “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words” (ibid.). Therefore obedience to one Lord, one faith, and one baptism constitute one fellowship of the righteous. Whoever remains in this fellowship to the end will have his lot among the elect and will not perish from the people of God.

Yet many in this fellowship, because they live too laxly and indulgently, though not ruinously—because they do not build upon the foundation which is Christ with gold, silver, and precious stones, but with wood, hay, and straw—will be saved by the merit of the foundation, but only as through fire (1 Cor. 3). This fellowship of grace, [Col. 0553A] of which we have now spoken, though necessary for establishing the life commonly called common life, cannot by itself in any way suffice for the religious purpose of common life.

## On the Fellowship of Grace Which Makes Common Life

There is also a fellowship of those who live in common, concerning whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; and no one said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4). Thus one heart, one soul, and a fellowship of all things make common life. On earth, so far as human weakness permits, this represents the life of angels.

For those who have one heart and one soul, and all things in common—concordant and of one mind in all things, always preferring public benefit and common good to private advantage—renounce themselves and their own concerns so thoroughly that whoever belongs among them must not, whether in judgments or deliberations, presume stubbornly to defend a private opinion; nor rashly seek to carry out a private will in the desires of his heart; nor possess even the smallest thing under the title of ownership. Rather, like servants of God under the hand of their fellow servant, for God’s sake they humble themselves so that the judgment of all depends upon one person, upon whom and in whom all authority has been conferred; by his decision their will is ordered and their necessity moderated. He alone may will, because he also can refuse; the rest renounce their own freedom and power, [Col. 0553C] so that they may not be permitted to will what they will, to do what they can do, to think what they think, to be what they are, or to live by their own spirit, but by the Spirit of God by whom they are led, that they may be children of God.

He is their love, bond, and fellowship. The greater the love, the stronger the bond and the fuller the fellowship; and conversely, the greater the fellowship, the stronger the bond and the fuller the love. By love I now mean that love by which God is to be loved before all things and above all things. It forms every good life, whether of those living separately or in common, so that it may be good. No life which the love of God has not made good should be thought good, or even called life; it should instead be called an image of death. For people who love themselves and serve their own desires are dead while living, as the Apostle writes of the widow living in pleasure: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while living” (1 Tim. 5).

But the person who consents to God’s will truly lives, because life is in his will. The person who consents to God’s will truly loves God. For God wills to be loved in such a way that one consents to his will; and we likewise wish to be loved in such a way that others consent to us in harmonious will, and those who agree with us more are regarded as greater friends. Love certainly always loves agreement, because it loves fellowship, to which agreement also belongs; for one who agrees thinks in common with another.

But since a human being can have either a good will [Col. 0554A] or an evil will, a person can certainly be loved well or badly. Yet it is better to be well hated than badly loved, just as it is better to hate well than to love badly. To love well and to hate well are both good, and both are owed to one’s neighbour. Therefore we are commanded to love our enemies and to hate our friends. Thus—yes, thus—it had to be commanded and must altogether be enjoined, lest our will, too headlong in hatred of enemies and favour toward friends, exceed in either direction the proper measure of its affection, rush into what is forbidden, and extend itself without limit.

Favour toward friends must be tempered by hatred, so that “the sinner is not praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 10), even if he is a friend. For no one loves a neighbour well unless one hates well. But in the love of God the principle is entirely different. For just as he is to be loved with all the heart, all the soul, and all the mind, so he himself is to be loved wholly. For he is wholly lovable, wholly desirable; nothing can be found in him worthy of hatred or unworthy of love.

O good God, O gracious God, O lovable God, O God to be loved, O desirable God, O God who are love, O God who are charity, O God of sweet nature: how great is the wickedness of those who hate you—and without cause! For you have not deserved it. Why has the wicked man provoked your name? What benefit, profit, or advantage is there for those who provoke your name? Surely there is great peace for those who love your name. But those who hate you—what do they hate except life, except salvation? What except goodness, except mercy? What finally except [Col. 0554C] love? For you, God, are love.

O how far from salvation is one who hates love and whom Love itself hates! O how great a folly it is to hate love; for this is to hate wisdom itself. You, Lord, are supreme wisdom, and to know you is perfect understanding—but to know you through love, because love itself is knowledge. Whoever does not love you does not know as he ought who you are, however proudly he may boast in the glory of flourishing eloquence, however much he may exalt himself in knowledge of marvellous things, however much he may overflow with the abundance of desirable things. He is foolish and senseless if he does not love you; he is needy and poor if he does not love you. For wisdom and knowledge are the riches of salvation; but that wisdom by which one who loves you is wise is more precious than all wealth, [Col. 0554D] and all things that are desired cannot be compared with it.

Keep me, Lord, as the pupil of the eye. Keep me from the grave sin which I greatly fear: from hatred of your love; lest I sin against the Holy Spirit, who is love and bond, unity, peace, and concord; lest I fall away from the unity of your Spirit, from the unity of your peace, by committing the sin which will be forgiven neither here nor in the world to come. Preserve me, Lord, among my brothers and neighbours, that I may speak peace concerning you; preserve me among those who keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

Most beloved brothers, let us diligently attend to what pertains to the profession of common life, preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love [Col. 0555A] of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. From the love of God proceeds unity of spirit; from the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the bond of peace; from the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, that fellowship necessary for those living in common if they are to live in common.

The love of God works unity of spirit: for the one who is joined to God becomes one spirit. The love of God—that, namely, by which God ought to be loved—is necessary in one way for those living separately and in another way for those living in common. And the love that accords with common life is like the love which is God. For God loves justice, and loves greater justice more; he also hates iniquity, and hates greater iniquity more.

But temporal things, in which and for which human [Col. 0555B] pride commonly boasts, malice envies, greed quarrels, and pleasure takes delight—these temporal things, I say—God wills us to despise rather than love, in comparison with love and desire for eternal things. Yet he permits us to use them in moderation, as human necessity requires, when every luxury of superfluity has been rejected; for he surely hates those who heed vain things needlessly.

But if the love of God that is in us agrees with the love by which God loves us, so that it loves what he loves; if, emulous of perfection, it always pursues the better things, approving the higher; if, always watchful even in avoiding lighter sins, it also judges contemptible what God wills to be despised: then this very love of God works in us unity of the Spirit. And just as the only-begotten Son of God lives with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit—for the Father and the Son have one Spirit—so we, as adopted children under God the Father, live in unity of spirit, in which we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8).

We cry indeed as from afar off, since we are greatly and widely inferior and unequal, though in some manner similar; not as the only-begotten Son of God, who is at the Father’s right hand, equal in all things. For he is said rather to invoke than to cry, as it is written: “He himself shall call upon me: You are my Father” (Ps. 88). This unity, which the love of God works in us, is preserved in the bond of peace through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is our peace, who made both one; [Col. 0555D] at whose birth the angels sing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). When about to ascend into heaven, he says to his disciples: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14).

What is this peace given to us by Christ, in whose bond unity of spirit is preserved? It is mutual love, by which we love one another, which is not broken if we all say the same thing and there are no schisms among us. Blessed Peter exhorts us concerning it: “Above all, maintain continuous mutual love” (1 Pet. 4). What is mutual love except love which is mine and yours, so that I may speak from it to the other whom I love? But if I love you without being loved by you, or if, being loved by you, I do not love you, love is not yet mutual, since it is either not mine or not yours. Mutual [Col. 0556A] love is common and does not lack fellowship of love.

And what is mutual must also be continuous; otherwise it will not be the bond of peace or the tie of love. Continuous love is made firm by truth; it is interrupted neither by hatred nor suspicion; it is always fostered and nourished by mutual services and mutual patience; lest it fail, it is guarded diligently and carefully; and it is not shadowed by any pretence. This is the love of those who truly love one another in Christ, not in word or tongue but in deed and truth. Christ impresses, fixes, and inscribes this love more deeply upon our hearts by word and example, saying: “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 15). In this love, as in the bond of peace, unity of spirit is preserved.

[Col. 0556B] This, therefore, is the law of common life: unity of spirit in the love of God; the bond of peace in the mutual and continuous love of all the brothers; fellowship in communicating all goods; and every occasion for acquiring private ownership banished far from the purpose of holy religious life. That these things may be in us and remain in us, as among those having one heart, one soul, and all things in common: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with us all. Amen” (2 Cor. 13).

## On Mutual Love among Those Living in Common
Let us take counsel from our own nature, from the nature of our body, concerning the harmony of mutual charity; for it itself admonishes us to preserve peace. Though we are many, we are one body [Col. 0556C], and members one of another. One spirit, moreover, gives life to our whole body through its members, joints, and ligaments, and brings about their mutual peace, in which the unity of the spirit itself is preserved; and it brings this about through the members’ mutual services and mutual forbearance. Observe and see how the things proper to each individual part serve the advantage of the whole. The eye does not see only for itself: it directs the feet in their steps and the hands in their work. The mouth does not eat only for itself, nor does the stomach digest only for itself; rather, a common task is performed: what suffices and benefits the nourishment of the whole body is taken in by the mouth and digested by the stomach. Does not the tongue, when some part of the body is injured, as though taking on the feeling of one who suffers with it and the voice of one who suffers, cry out against the injurer, [Col. 0556D] “Why do you hurt me?” Does not the heart, solicitous for the common good, devise counsels within itself both for others and for itself? Do not the hands, born to minister and devoted to service, as daily experience teaches, humble themselves to serve the feet? What if, as sometimes happens, one hand is wounded by the other? Does the injured hand arm itself with zeal for vengeance and, having been struck, strike back? Does not the hand that caused the injury, as if conscious of its guilt and pierced by the pain of repentance, hasten, by way of satisfaction, to apply to its wounded sister the best healing remedy it can? Does it not beg forgiveness by the very humility of its service, and entreat that it may be pardoned? Does it not, by devoted diligence and the earnestness of its kindness, excuse every suspicion of malice [Col. 0557A]?

There is another consideration that can edify us. If the eye foresees a threatening sword being brandished to strike the head, at once the hand, as though heedless under the heat either of love or of frenzy, interposes itself and opposes—or even meets—the sword. Hurrying into its own danger, while it fears for the head it does not fear for itself; and, that the head may be spared, it does not spare itself. Brothers most beloved in Christ, to what do these examples draw us, if not to mutual forbearance, mutual humility, and mutual charity? Has not God written within us a law of love, to teach us by ourselves? May he who gave the law also give us blessing; may he feed us in the innocence of our hearts and guide us by the understandings of our hands into the way of peace: to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace; to [Col. 0557B] preserve the love of God in love of neighbour.

If, with one mind and in harmony, according to the purity of our profession, we love God, then without doubt the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, and the one Spirit of God gives life to all of us as though to one body: so that none of us may live for himself, but for God; and so that all of us together may live, through the one spirit who dwells in us, in unity of spirit. This unity of spirit, which is found in us in the love of God, is preserved in us through love of neighbour, so that we may remain together in the love of God; and, remaining in this love, may remain in God, and God in us. In the love of God, the love of God becomes known, grows strong, and is knit together.

[Col. 0557C] God indeed can be content with himself; in every good he is sufficient to himself, and he has no need of our goods. Nor can anyone harm him by failing to love him, nor benefit or enrich him by loving him. Therefore, when we have done all things well, we must say, “We are useless servants” (Luke 17). For whatever good we do benefits us more than him. Yet, because God must be loved not in word or tongue—as those loved of whom it is written, “They loved him with their mouth, and with their tongue they lied to him” (Psalm 77)—God, who has no need of benefits for himself, has, as it were, entrusted to us our brothers and neighbours who are in need, that they may receive from us the benefits to be rendered in his stead. Let no one, therefore, flatter himself concerning love of God; let no one deceive himself by thinking that he [Col. 0557D] loves God when he does not love his neighbour. If a person has no means by which to test himself and prove himself—if he does not love the neighbour whom he sees, whom he has present before him, as one entrusted to him by God, to whom he ought to pay the debt of charity—how can he love God, whom he does not see, who does not present himself before him, since God has no need? In what other way can he render benefits to God except by rendering them to the one in whom God is needy, though not needy in himself? For God asks and receives in his members; he is loved and despised in them. Therefore, in love of neighbour, as through the tie of love and bond of peace, the charity of God and the unity of the Spirit are retained by us and preserved in us. For whoever does not love his brother departs from the unity of the Spirit, and [Col. 0558A] neither loves God nor lives by God’s Spirit, but by his own spirit, because he now lives for himself and not for God.

### Likewise, on the communion of grace

Communion belongs to love of neighbour; and where love is full, communion is full. But communion is not full unless there is communion of all things, as it is written: “All things were held in common” (Acts 2). Yet what follows may trouble us: “It was distributed to each according as anyone had need” (Acts 4). What has communion to do with distribution? What has communion to do with ownership? If it was distributed to individuals according to each one’s need, that which each person’s necessity required passed into that individual’s use and ownership. If individuals had differing needs, and therefore resources proper to those needs; if they had infirmities peculiar to themselves, and remedies suited to them; [Col. 0558B] if someone had some private desolation and comfort proper to it: how were all things common to them, when certain things belonged individually to each?

The Apostle makes this question weightier, saying: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for profit” (1 Corinthians 12); and: “Each has his own gift from God, one indeed in this manner, another in that” (ibid.). Again: “There are divisions of graces, divisions of ministries, and divisions of workings” (1 Corinthians 7). How, then, can there be communion of all things where there are so many divisions of graces, where individuals possess their own gifts? What shall we say to these things? And who is sufficient for these things? This is a labour before me. Yet let us see whether the knot of love, which ought not to be untied, [Col. 0558C] can untie the knot of this question. It certainly can. For charity knows, at its own discretion, how to bring ownership into communion—not so that ownership ceases to exist, but so that ownership serves communion, does not hinder it, and does not obstruct the good of communion.

A division or ownership that impedes the good of communion is foreign to charity. For charity loves communion; it also loves ownership that advances the good of communion or does not impede communion. For communion cannot exist without ownership, though communion may exist without the good of communion. How can anything be common, unless ownership distinguishes one person from another, among whom something is common? Even in that highest and indivisible Trinity [Col. 0558D] there is one unity, one eternity, one power, one wisdom, one life, one essence, common to three persons. Yet by personal property one person is distinguished from another, to whom one blessedness is common. Nor is the common good obstructed by the fact that the Father alone is Father: for the Father is not Father to himself, but to the Son, whom he begot from his own substance and to whom, in begetting him, he gave life in himself.

To turn the discussion to matters more familiar to us through ordinary experience: the property by which a man is a father does not impede the communion of human nature. Rather, through generation, nature is propagated from one person to another; nor does the property of generation prejudice the communion of nature. The power of grace is no less than that of created nature. But charity is an outstanding grace [Col. 0559A] poured out in the hearts of the saints. For the Holy Spirit, through whom charity is poured out, loves outpouring, since he himself is poured out. “I will pour out,” says the Lord, “of my Spirit” (Joel 2).

Therefore, whoever has a gift proper to himself from God should possess it not for himself alone, but for God and for his neighbour: for God, indeed, so that he may seek from God’s gift not his own glory but the glory of God; and for his neighbour, so that he may always seek the common advantage, not his private one. For charity does not seek its own interests, but those of Jesus Christ. It loves communion, not ownership without communion. Indeed, it loves communion so greatly that it sometimes does not wish to reclaim goods belonging by right to itself when another possesses them. For charity is generous and avoids lawsuits; it does not seek its own interests and does not wish to contend in court where charity itself is endangered. It prefers to suffer fraud rather than perish itself; to suffer loss rather than its own detriment. [Col. 0559B] Why should it contentiously reclaim what it does not possess, when it is ready to give what it does possess?

For each person’s own gift draws toward the good of communion, so that what belongs to one person by the ownership of a received gift may become another’s through the usefulness of a shared good. Hence blessed Peter says: “As each has received grace, administering it to one another. If anyone speaks, let it be as the words of God; if anyone ministers, let it be from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be honoured” (1 Peter 4). Paul likewise says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for profit” (1 Corinthians 12). What is this manifestation [Col. 0559C] of the Spirit given for profit, except a gift of grace given to make known, and to publish as is fitting, the benefit of neighbours? Let the wise person not be wise for himself, but say: “Without guile I learned, and without envy I shared” (Wisdom 7). Let one who has something share it with one who does not have it, as he exhorts who says: “Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6). For avarice, which keeps to itself in an unwillingness to share what it possesses, is as contrary to communion as it is hostile to charity.

If, in a pagan poet, a pagan man—without true faith, without the true God, without true hope of a true resurrection and true blessedness—is praised to the point that the poet says of him:

> He believes himself born not for himself, but for the whole world;

how much more among Christian people, and especially [Col. 0559D] among religious men professing the common life, must the principle of communion be observed in all things and preferred above all things! Thus one who is good to himself may also be good to others and not burdensome to them; one who has a word of wisdom or knowledge, a grace of activity or administration, or any other greater or lesser grace, should possess it as though given by God to him for the sake of others. He should always fear that the grace received may harm him if he does not endeavour by it to benefit another. For God’s grace is received in vain if the glory of God and the advantage of one’s neighbour are not sought through it. Then indeed God’s grace is turned into God’s glory when the gift given by God to each person is brought into the common good. And the communion of the Holy Spirit is truly with us when the gift given separately to each individual [Col. 0560A] is possessed communally through the communion of love.

### Likewise, on the communion of grace and the communion of glory

The Holy Spirit is communion, and he loves communion so greatly that he wills to be given himself. For he is goodness itself. Nor is he content to give his own gifts unless he also gives himself; but he gives himself to those whom he himself has made worthy to receive so great a gift. For he is a gift, and from eternity has been the highest good and the highest gift.

Whoever truly shares with his neighbour, in use and usefulness, the grace received from God truly possesses what he has received; and “to him who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound.” But from him who does not have, even what he seems to have shall be taken away. Grace entrusted and received from God passes, as it were, into the name and condition of a loan. [Col. 0560B] It obliges the recipient to God and to his neighbour: to God, indeed, for the rendering of glory; to his neighbour, for the sharing of grace. Whoever shares grace has mercy on his neighbour. Whoever renders glory gives it to God. This is the righteous person, who has mercy and gives. For he would be unjust if he did not pay his debt, if he violated the faith of the agreement and the rationale of that which was entrusted and received. Hence it is written: “The sinner borrows and does not repay” (Psalm 36). He borrows when he receives; he does not repay when he does not restore. And in this he is a sinner, because he borrows and does not repay. He does not repay because he neither shares with his neighbour nor glorifies God.

For God demands from bestowed grace even what he has not yet given. He requires interest; he reaps where he has not [Col. 0560C] sown and gathers what he has not scattered. He reaps among the wicked and gathers among the good. At the end he will send to the wicked reaping angels, whom he will condemn for their unreturned gain, when “the angels shall gather the tares and bind them into bundles to burn” (Matthew 13). But he will gather the good, like wheat into his barn, rewarding in them what he himself gave and receiving the returned gain. He gathers what he did not scatter, that is, what he did not himself scatter apart from those to whom he gave. But those who shared their received gifts with their neighbours scattered them, going forth and bearing fruit, like those of whom it is written: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Psalm 125).

Nor does the saying appear to refer to the Lord’s harshness in relation to the good, but in relation to the wicked. But if both clauses can be understood of [Col. 0560D] the wicked, or both of the good, then, while preserving God’s mercy, the Lord must in some way be shown to be harsh—he who, to display his harshness in one or both cases, says two things: “I reap where I have not sown; I gather where I have not scattered” (Matthew 25). Is God then a harsh lord? Who would dare say this? But who would dare contradict the Spirit of God? Does not the Prophet, speaking in the Spirit, say: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverse?” (Psalm 17). And when the Prophet said, “How good God is to Israel,” he added, “to those who are upright in heart” (Psalm 72), indicating to whom he is good. The Lord will appear harsh to those hard of heart. These he himself also hardens by a just, though hidden, judgment.

[Col. 0561A] Perhaps I seem to destroy what I previously built up. For, having begun a discourse on the goodness and charity of God, I have resumed the discussion in order to show the severity of his indignation against the wicked. Yet truth sometimes shines more clearly through a comparison of opposites. For since it is written, “The Spirit of wisdom is kind, and will not acquit the evil-speaker for his lips” (Wisdom 1), lest God’s goodness be made an occasion and security for sinning, as though he did not wish strictly to punish sins, this statement, “The Spirit of wisdom is kind,” is preceded or joined to, “he will not acquit the blasphemer of his lips.” Yet he is kind to those who, zealous for communion, love the good of sharing; he is kind to the person who possesses the good he has for another; and he is kind also to the person who loves, in another who possesses it, the good he does not have.

[Col. 0561B] Divisions of graces are brought into communion in two ways: when gifts given separately to individuals are held in common through the communion of love, and when they are loved in common through love of communion. For grace is in some manner common to the one who has and the one who lacks: the one who has it has it for another because he shares it; and the one who does not have it has it in another because he loves. The communion of the Holy Spirit also draws the individual necessities and infirmities of persons into communion. For as charity is patient, so it is compassionate; and one who suffers with another who suffers makes another’s necessity his own, so that one necessity becomes common to both. For one person’s need is his through the suffering of pain, the other’s through the affection of shared grief. If the necessities of the righteous are common, it follows that their consolations also are common. [Col. 0561C] For one who knows through the affection of charity how to weep with those who weep also knows how to rejoice with those who rejoice.

Oh, how the Apostle abounded in the affections of love and the bowels of charity when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Corinthians 11). What he himself does, he exhorts others to do, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6); nor does he contradict himself when he says: “Each one shall bear his own burden” (ibid.). For this is rightly understood of the burden of sin. Sin alone is not admitted into the communion of charity. Whatever good we do benefits all in common, though not every good is equally shared by those who love in common. [Col. 0561D] For we hope to be mutually assisted before God by mutual prayers and mutual merits; and through the merits and prayers of the saints whom we love and by whom we desire to be loved, we gain great confidence for obtaining pardon of sins and meriting glory before God—especially if, recalling their merits and beholding their faith, charity, patience, and piety, we are zealous, love them, are stirred to emulation, and are inflamed to imitate their virtues.

If each person were to be judged by his own merits so that the merits of others could not assist through the communion [Col. 0562A] of charity, who could bear the weight of divine judgment? For our iniquities are many and great, and the Prophet says: “If you should mark iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” (Psalm 129). Our good works too are insufficient, and all our righteousness is like the cloth of a menstruating woman. And, as it is written: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Romans 8). Shall we then despair? Far be it—utterly far be it! For God is charity.

O God, charity, I am under constraint: answer for me; what shall I say, or what answer will he give me? Or if I have reached an age—indeed, because I have reached it—when I ought to speak for myself, with my mouth I profess what I believe in my heart. I believe, Lord, in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church [Col. 0562B], and the communion of saints. This is my hope, this is my trust, this is my confidence, this is whatever small security I possess in the confession of my faith: in the goodness of the Holy Spirit, in the unity of the catholic Church, in the communion of saints. If it is granted me from above to love you and to love my neighbour, then, though my merits are small and few, I have a hope greater than my merits. I trust that, through the communion of charity, the merits of the saints will benefit me, so that the communion of saints may supply my insufficiency and imperfection.

The Prophet consoles me, saying: “I have seen an end of all completion; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm 118).
