[Col. 0562C] O broad and enlarging charity, how great is your house and how vast the place of your possession! Let us not be cramped in our own hearts; let us not be confined within the bounds and limit of our however small righteousness. Charity enlarges our hope toward the communion of saints, in communion of merits and communion of rewards. But the communion of rewards belongs to the future time: that is, the communion of glory which shall be revealed in us.

Since, then, there are three communions—the communion of nature, to which are joined the communion of guilt and the communion of wrath; the second, of grace; and the third, of glory—through the communion of grace the communion of nature begins to be restored and the communion of guilt is excluded; but through the communion of glory the communion of nature will be restored most perfectly, and the communion of wrath will be entirely excluded, when God [Col. 0562D] “shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints.” Then all the saints will have, as it were, one heart and one soul; and all things will be common to them, when God shall be all in all. That we may all attain this communion and come together into one: may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the charity of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be always with us all. Amen (2 Corinthians 13).

## SIXTEENTH TREATISE

[Col. 0561]

Containing an encomium of perfect religious persons upon the words: “Whiter than snow, brighter than milk, ruddier than old ivory, more beautiful than sapphire” (Lamentations 4).

[Col. 0561D] The prophetic utterance describes the beauty of the Nazarites, which it extols with marvellous praises, exalts, and highly exalts under marvellous titles of commendation. For it praises in the Nazarites whiteness; it praises brightness; it praises redness. And although these three qualities belong to beauty and increase the grace of beauty, at last [Col. 0563A] it nevertheless praises beauty itself by name. It praises all these things not simply, but by comparison, so that through comparison with praiseworthy things they may become increasingly clear; not because they are assigned an equal quality with those things, but because they are set before them in the honour of surpassing dignity. The glory of praise is fuller when that which is eminent is pre-eminent; when what excels surpasses; and the glory of praise is complete when a thing, upheld by its own power and merits and praiseworthy in itself, excels even things worthy of praise more praiseworthily.

In the Nazarites there is praised beauty not of body but of character; not the glory of flesh but of mind, virtue, and moral excellence. The glory of flesh indeed has some grace in the eyes of flesh, but it is vain and deceptive, as it is written: [Col. 0563B] “Grace is deceitful and beauty is vain” (Proverbs 31). What is vain beauty but beautiful vanity? Or what is deceptive grace but pleasing deception? It is pleasing, yet deception; it is deception, yet pleasing. It pleases those who behold it magnificently, but deceives those who gaze upon it, and mocks the eyes of its observers as if by certain illusions. For if the inward recesses of the human body are penetrated by the sharpness of the inner eye, what is bodily beauty but a covering of ugliness? A kind of cloak for hidden shame and disgrace? Beneath the glory of flesh lie concealed things of dishonour that shame forbids one to name and that horrify a person even to think about.

For man is decay, and the son of man a worm. If this is so—indeed, because it is so—what is the beauty of the son of man except the beauty of a worm? [Col. 0563C] And what is a beautiful human being but beautiful decay? Finally, what is a proud person but a noble offshoot of the most worthless corruption—one who can say with blessed Job to decay, “You are my father,” and to worms, “My mother and my sister” (Job 7)? Bodily beauty, therefore, may have glory among human beings, but not with God, since it lacks the virtue of merit and has no hope of reward. God, the inward judge and examiner of hearts, loves inward beauty. The Prophet addresses the king’s daughter, saying: “The king shall desire your beauty” (Psalm 44); and, lest anyone fail to know where that beauty lies because it is within, he adds: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, in golden fringes” (ibid.).

[Col. 0563D] But the beauty of the Nazarites is within, not without. They are thus named from the flower of sanctification, not from the flower of grass, the flower of flesh. “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.” It is written: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Psalm 91); and again: “Planted in the house of the Lord, they shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God” (ibid.). Another Scripture says: “Bloom, flowers, like the lily, and put forth leaves in grace” (Ecclesiasticus 39). Where does the lily bloom? Christ is conceived in Nazareth: the flower in the flower of virginity and sanctification. For concerning Christ the Father says: “Upon him my sanctification shall blossom” (Psalm 131). And Christ says of himself: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 1). In the book of Wisdom we read: “Bloom, flowers, like the lily” (Ecclesiasticus 39). Christ says: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus 11). All Nazarites breathe and give forth the fragrance of this lily.

[Col. 0564A] For the Nazarites who lived in the time of the Law, consecrated to the Lord, went before as a figure of Christ; by their abstinence and conduct they foreshadowed Christ’s future imitators, abstaining from wine, strong drink, and everything that can intoxicate. The sons of Jonadab also abstained from wine. For Jonadab commanded his sons not to drink wine, and they obeyed their father’s voice. Therefore the Lord says: “There shall not fail from the stock of Jonadab one standing before me all days” (Jeremiah 35). If, according to the word of the Lord, there does not fail from Jonadab’s stock one standing before him all days, then in our own days also there are sons of Jonadab: imitators of Christ, standing before the Lord. For Christ is the true Jonadab, spontaneous and willing in all obedience; [Col. 0564B] this is what the name Jonadab signifies. He is spontaneous who says: “Willingly will I sacrifice to you” (Psalm 53).

He is Nazarite and spontaneous whose is that saying of the Psalm: “And my flesh has flourished again; and of my own will I shall confess to him” (Psalm 27). The phrase “of my own will” pertains to the Spirit, because “where the Spirit is, there is freedom.” The preceding phrase, “and my flesh has flourished again,” does not refer to the present glory of pampered flesh, which is the flower of grass; rather, it refers to the hope of the glorious resurrection and the flower of sanctified flesh, which is mortified with its vices and desires.

### On the whiteness of the Nazarites

The abstinence of the Nazarites and the sons of Jonadab was a mystery, an example, and a sign. For them it was a mystery unto sanctification; [Col. 0564C] for us, an example for imitation and a sign for instruction. In this we are spiritually shaped toward a threefold abstinence. For there are three things that estrange human minds from the love of God through drunken forgetfulness and forgetful drunkenness: love of the soul, love of the flesh, and love of the world—that is, love of one’s own will, love of fleshly pleasure, and love of worldly vanity. Love of the world is vain; love of pleasure is sweet; love of one’s own will is obstinate. For the more stubbornly and perversely the soul loves itself and in a certain fashion clings to itself, the more difficult it is for it to be torn or separated from itself. The soul can scarcely love anything more than its own will and its own judgment. Therefore, [Col. 0564D] when it is drawn away from its own will, it is, as though torn from itself, bloodied by a wound inflicted.

Love of one’s own will is wine that intoxicates the mind and disorders all its senses: hearing, so that it does not hear obedience; the eyes of discernment, so that they do not see truth; and it deprives the remaining senses of their functions, mingling in their midst a spirit of dizziness. This is not the wine which is commanded to be given to those who mourn. Those who mourn and lament the sins of their own will are intoxicated with the wine of compunction, and are given to drink of the wine that gladdens the human heart in the promise and hope of pardon. For “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5). Of such people it is said: “Give wine to those who mourn, and strong drink to those who are bitter in spirit” (Proverbs 31). Conversely it is said: [Col. 0565A] “Give not wine to kings, O Lemuel, give not wine to kings; for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget the judgments of God” (ibid.).

The wine of one’s own will was filtered and pressed in the winepress of disobedience, from the sour grape which our fathers ate and which set the teeth of their children on edge. Adam, the father of disobedience, mixed this wine of his own will and offered the cup of death to his descendants alone, as though he said: “Drink of this, all of you” (Matthew 26). All sinners still drink from it. Christ, on the contrary, who came not to do his own will but the Father’s, offered the cup of obedience even unto death, saying to us: “Drink of this, all of you.” “Of this,” he says, “which I administer, not that which Adam administered.” The unbelieving and disobedient Jews offered the Lord, hanging on the cross and thirsting for their salvation, wine such as was found in their reprobate conduct; and when he had tasted it, he would not drink (Matthew 27). For he did not approve it, abstaining from wine as a Nazarite. It was from the grape of gall, from the vine of Sodom and the fields of Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 32).

This wine of self-will and disobedience is forbidden to the Nazarites and the sons of Jonadab, lest they drink it. For it is good for a person not to drink this wine. Those know this who regard every movement of their own will with suspicion; who do not trust themselves, but entrust themselves to be governed by another’s judgment; who always tremble at themselves and at seeming to will anything by themselves. Therefore they bind themselves [Col. 0565C] with the bonds of obedience, constrain themselves under the laws of regular discipline, turn their will into necessity, and reduce freedom to servitude. Yet they do all this for Christ’s sake, so that in Christ servitude may be free and necessity voluntary. For they are freer in Christ in proportion as they have made themselves more bound, by their own undertaking, to obey him. This is the first and chief abstinence of the Nazarites.

Strong drink of fleshly pleasure is likewise pressed in the winepress of disobedience, as though from the fruit of the forbidden tree. For the woman saw that it was beautiful to behold and pleasant for eating (Genesis 2). There arose the pleasure of gluttony, the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes. Nazarites abstain from strong drink, [Col. 0565D] when they do not make provision for the flesh in its desires and when, through abstinence, continence, and discipline, they bear about in their flesh the mortification of Jesus. They also abstain from everything that can intoxicate, because they flee the manifold errors of secular life, put no faith in perishing things, and tread every glory of the world, as it were, under their feet, seeing the earth from afar.

The whiteness of the Nazarites consists in this perfection of threefold abstinence, and this whiteness exceeds the whiteness of snow. Snow is the whiteness of those who abstain; but one abstinent person differs from another, and one whiteness from another, as perfection differs from imperfection. Hence it is written: “When the heavenly one distinguishes kings over her, they shall be made white as snow in Salmon” (Psalm 67). Those who use the world lawfully are, as it were, whitened like snow [Col. 0566A]; but those who do not use the world are whiter. The former’s whiteness is abstaining from unlawful things; the latter’s whiteness is restraining themselves even from lawful things. The former are troubled and anxious about many things because they love many things besides God and not for God, even though they love nothing more than God; and their love is divided. For as much love as is bestowed upon perishing things is withdrawn from the perfection of divine love. What is scattered is always less than what is gathered into one. Water divided among many streams is diminished in each; so too is love.

Hence someone, though speaking of vain love, yet speaking of love, says:

> When the mind, divided in two, runs hither and thither,  
> One love diminishes the strength of the other.

Let us therefore gather all love into one, lest it be scattered [Col. 0566B] among many things; let us recall all the affections and intentions of love from many things, so that the whole force of love may run into one thing and toward one thing: namely, toward that one thing which is worthy of complete love, to which all love is due, and which, even when worthily loved, can scarcely be sufficiently loved with all one’s love. For some injury is done when anything is partly withheld from the one to whom the whole is due. This is whiteness beyond the whiteness of snow. Perhaps this is the whiteness desired by the one who said: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Psalm 50).

### On the brightness of the Nazarites
### On the Brightness of the Nazarites

The Nazarites are honoured with this title of praise, that they are said to be whiter than snow; and, that praise may be heaped upon praise, it is added: “More lustrous than milk.” Oil, milk, fat, and rich grease possess both richness and brightness. This is mercy, concerning which the Lord says: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI). Those possess the brightness and sweetness of milk who mercifully assist the needs of the needy, so that they may drink from their milk and be satisfied from the breasts of their consolation.

Now some needs are bodily and some spiritual. For the body needs many aids in its necessities and many remedies for its infirmities. The soul too needs those things necessary to it for spiritual consolation and true salvation. Often those righteous persons who are weak according to the flesh are moved with greater compassion and affection concerning their neighbours’ bodily needs, and are more diligent to feed the hungry person than to bring one who is wandering back to the way of truth. [Col. 0566D] I think they are more tenderly affected regarding those things which they themselves feel too weak to endure, and, taught as it were by a domestic example, they love for Christ’s sake to sympathize with poverty.

But those who love their neighbours’ souls more perfectly than their bodies endure suffering for Christ’s sake, are zealous for God, are moved more affectionately concerning spiritual needs, become weak with the weak, and burn for those who suffer scandal. Amid secret tears and secret conversations with God, they pray and weep for their enemies; they grieve and mourn over others’ sins; and, in the bowels of charity and the inmost marrow of compassion, they commend to God—whom they serve in their spirit—their neighbours who are ignorant and wandering, with tearful sighs.

Yet they often seem harsh and without feeling concerning bodily needs; perhaps because they voluntarily endure poverty in themselves, they sympathize with it less in others. Nor do they regard poverty as misery, but as a way of salvation; and they consider it safer to be moderately in need than to abound in superfluities. They judge the rich, perishing amid their abundance, more pitiable than the poor who are beneficially in want for a time.

True mercy, however, has compassion for each sort of need, but greater compassion for the greater need and lesser compassion for the lesser. It is great mercy to grieve with neighbours because they lack what they need; but it is far greater to take care that they do not perish. It is a great movement of mercy to grieve over the evils that human beings suffer. Christ showed in himself an example of both mercies. For, seeing the crowd nearly exhausted, he said: “I have compassion upon the crowd” (Mark VIII); and, by multiplying the loaves, he represented in a bodily benefit the mystery of spiritual grace. But when he saw the city of Jerusalem, he wept over it, saying: “If thou too hadst known” (Luke XIX). And he added why he himself wept, or why they ought to weep: “And now indeed in this day, the things that are for thy peace.”

When the Lord was being led to his passion, he turned to the women who stood by and wept, and said: “Do not weep over me, but over yourselves and your children” (Luke XXIII). Greater, therefore, is zeal for souls than compassionate concern for bodily sufferings. That is the brightness of milk; this, that of oil, which surpasses all liquids. The former is like exterior fat in a sacrifice; the latter is inward richness. The former belongs familiarly to the rich, who distribute their possessions mercifully; the latter is more fitting for Nazarites. [Col. 0567C] For there is the inmost marrow of sincere love for one’s neighbour. For why ought neighbours, sharing one nature, to be loved more than so that they may become partakers of the common glory?

Accordingly, Nazarites, preferring zeal for souls while in no way despising bodily needs, possess before God the brightness of grace and glory, as though shining with a double lustre and whiter than milk—God who says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). Those who have professed the common life, for whom all things will be common in the future life, meanwhile share their own possessions in such a way that they desire nothing to remain for themselves which could benefit others. They reckon wholly superfluous whatever has not been brought into the grace of common possession; they take no pleasure in having anything as their own, just as it is not lawful to usurp what belongs to another.

### On the Ruddy Colour of the Nazarites

In describing the face of the Nazarites, colour is added to colour: ruddiness is joined to whiteness and brightness, so that their face may be conspicuously coloured by the grace of whiteness and cheerfully disposed by the grace of ruddiness. Ruddiness in the face usually indicates either warmth or modesty. Nazarites are ruddy, fervent with the warmth of devotion and modest through reverence for honourableness. For, zealous with zeal in God’s law, they not only burn with zeal for the pursuit of virtue, but ardently love the beauty of honourableness.

Their senses are delicate: they blush at every shameful thing. They abhor everything dishonourable; they are ashamed at everything unbecoming; their senses are chaste and modest. They are ashamed to see shameful things; ashamed not only for themselves but also to hear shameful things about others; ashamed to speak shameful things, and ashamed even to think them, as one says: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think of a virgin” (Job XXXI). They are ashamed also of having done shameful things, as the Apostle says of certain persons: “What fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. VI).

It is too little for the praise of the Nazarites that they should be called ruddy unless they are also set above ancient ivory. Ivory, as they say, is the bone of an elephant. The elephant is an animal constructed with bones, robust and firm, so that it is able to bear engines of war and fortified structures erected upon it. Such is the strength of the saints: like ivory among bones, it possesses eminent glory of solidity, firmness, [Col. 0568B] and beauty. If flesh is weak, so that it may signify the weakness of the saints, why may not bone proclaim their strength? Of them indeed it is written: “The Lord keeps all their bones” (Ps. XXXIII).

Ancient ivory is the strength of the righteous, such as existed in the righteous men of old under the Law, and such as exists now in those who imitate them. In the ancients there was great gravity of character, great maturity, great constancy of an unshaken mind, and an immovable, unconquerable strength of spirit in enduring harsh and undeserved things for their law. No adversity of circumstances, no perversity of men, no injuries, no insults, no terror, no shame could separate them from reverence for holy religion.

Thus one man, representing all the other saints in himself, says: “All day long my shame is before me, and the confusion of my face has covered me, because of the voice of him who reproaches and slanders, because of the face of the enemy and persecutor. All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten thee, nor have we acted unjustly in thy covenant, nor has our heart turned backward” (Ps. XLIII).

These things were indeed under the Law, which nevertheless brought no one to perfection. Evangelical perfection was still lacking. It had not yet been said: “If thou wilt be perfect, go, sell all that thou hast, and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX). It was still said: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, bruise for bruise” (Exod. XXI). That had not yet been said: “If anyone strikes thee on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Luke VI).

The secret counsels of consummate perfection, brought down from heaven through Christ and to be disclosed in Christ, had not yet become known to the world: counsels—which not all can receive—concerning preserving and dedicating virginity to God; embracing voluntary poverty for Christ; loving lowliness; despising rank; not seeking vengeance; forgiving every injury; not recovering one’s own property even through litigation; hating father and mother and all friends, and even one’s own life; loving enemies; laying down one’s life for friends, even should they be enemies to us; and bearing, for Christ’s honour and love, whatever injuries, insults, abuse, reproaches—in short, whatever harsh or undeserved things may occur—and bearing them cheerfully in the joy of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “They went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer insult for the name of Jesus” (Acts V).

Although these and similar counsels of Christian perfection may have been divinely inspired in some righteous persons of old, they were not made public through the Law. They were reserved for Christ, who would give perfection to the Law and yet not dissolve the Law.

Good Jesus, if it may be permitted to inquire with thy leave, why hast thou done this to us? We hoped that, on coming into the world, thou wouldst lighten burdens and soften thy wrath, and that, having become man, thou wouldst become humane—or more humane than usual. But now thou addest burden to burden and layest grievous things upon grievous things. Were Moses’ hands not heavy enough? Hast thou come in order to beat us with scorpions? Hast thou not come rather to make our yoke heavier? Are we forbidden to love friends and forbidden to hate enemies? O Founder of new laws, who can hear thy words? Dost thou seek an occasion to destroy us? Is not Jesus thy name? Art thou not our God, the God of salvation? Art thou then a God of destruction? Far be it!

Why dost thou command me not to hate my enemy—indeed, to love him? How can I do this? Behold, if I am provoked by a slight insult, inwardly I burn and blaze up; my heart boils for vengeance, and my tongue rushes headlong toward abuse. Meanwhile I do not know God, I do not know thy laws, and thou sayest: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V). If I say to my brother, “Raca” or “Fool” [ibid.], thou terrifiest me still more; for I am liable to the council or to the fire of Gehenna. Truly, thou hast commanded that thy commandments be kept exceedingly [Col. 0569C] (Ps. CXVIII).

To confess the truth: I may be forgetful of benefits, but I cannot be forgetful of injuries. By nature I am a child of wrath, so that I cannot help being angry. But thou, Jesus, art angry, and under thee I am forbidden even to be angry, to be moved even slightly against an enemy, or to mutter in my heart? Whence comes this to me: that I should so establish my heart as never to be moved and become insensible to every injury? Whence comes it to us that we should do what thou wilt have us do and endure what thou wilt have us endure, unless thou, O lawgiver, hast given the blessing? Whence comes it to us unless thou hast preceded us with the blessings of sweetness, unless we abide in the charity of thy sweetness? In that charity even bitter things become sweet, and hard things become mild; in it alone thy yoke is sweet and thy burden light (Matt. XI).

For what is difficult to one who loves? Whatever is more strictly enjoined is less burdensome through the devotion of charity. Charity is patient; charity is strong; it is neither wearied by labour nor weighed down by a burden. It bears all things and sustains all things; and, though conscious of holy modesty, it is reverently, as it were, shameless. It blushes indeed at shameful things, but not at Christ’s words, Christ’s reproach, or Christ’s example.

Christ, who added perfection to the Law, fulfilled in himself, to the full extent that he taught, what he taught ought to be done, and set himself forth as an example. Whatever Christ both did himself and taught ought to be done, although it seems contemptible to the world, cannot lack the grace of true honour. Christ’s poverty and humility are base in the world’s eyes. Indeed, the world itself is base to Christ’s poor; and in mutual contempt they despise one another, while the world despises that by which it itself is despised.

But what the world despises is the arrogance of pride; what is despised is the nobility of humility. For Christ’s true humility seems to contain in itself the noble loftiness of pride. It disdains to serve under the yoke of sin and dares by its own strength to trample underfoot every arrogant swelling of vanity and swollen pride. The perfect imitator of Christ, mindful of his condition, in which he was made in God’s image and likeness, and mindful too of the price by which he was redeemed by the Son of God, nobly takes pride, out of reverence for his own dignity, against pride—which is unworthy of every dignity. He judges it unworthy of his nobility to love the vanity of worldly honour and not to love God’s promises, which surpass every desire.

Thus it is written of the Church: “I will make thee the pride of ages” (Isa. LX). And it is said of God’s ministers: “You shall consume the strength of the nations, and you shall take pride in their glory” (Isa. LXI). What is the strength of the nations, or what their glory, except that which those love “who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of their riches”? (Ps. XLVIII). Their glory is in their shame, for they savour earthly things.

It is written: “As many as possessed lands sold them and laid the prices at the feet of the apostles” (Acts IV). Rightly at their feet, as things to be trampled underfoot, since it was unworthy even to touch them with the hands. Peter’s words are: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts III). A worthy utterance for the primacy of the prince of the apostles, the prince of the Church. What had Peter to do with silver or gold? Does not Peter say: “Behold, we have left all things and followed thee. What then shall we have?” (Matt. XIX). To one asking about the reward, silver is not promised, nor gold. He despised these things because he took pride in the glory of the nations.

Paul also despised them, saying: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these.” He was not ashamed of Christ’s poverty, eating no bread freely and working night and day. He was not ashamed of Christ’s humility, saying: “We have become like the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things until now.” And again: “We have become a spectacle to God, to angels, and to men” [ibid.].

Therefore the Nazarites, the perfect disciples of Christ, are so much ruddier through a twofold shame—both ruddiness and ancient ivory—as they are more perfect than the righteous persons of old; and so much stronger as they have become truer imitators of Christian discipline.

### On the Intention of the Nazarites

Praise is still added to praise, and honour piled upon honour. “More beautiful than sapphire,” he says. The beauty of perfection is commended in a most beautiful order. The first degree of perfection is to preserve oneself undefiled from every corruption of the present life, insofar as human frailty permits. The second degree is never wholly to neglect care for one’s neighbour, insofar as one has the means either to help or to advise. The third degree is, in the warmth of holy devotion and with the ruddiness of holy modesty, to endure courageously harsh and undeserved things, insofar as human weakness allows. The fourth degree is, in doing good and enduring evil, always to direct the eye of intention to God and refer all things to his glory, insofar as human capacity prevails.

The first virtue is perfect innocence toward oneself; the second, full mercy toward one’s neighbour; the third, unconquerable patience toward one’s enemy; the fourth, toward God, the pure and simple conscience of sincere intention. Either a pious hatred of self or an equally stern mercy toward self produces the first virtue; kindly charity, charity toward one’s neighbour, produces the second; patient charity, charity toward one’s enemy, produces the third; surpassing charity, charity toward God, produces the fourth. This last gives form to the others, so that they may be virtues; it strengthens and fulfils them, so that they may not be empty.

For however much good a person may do, and however much evil he may likewise endure, all will be reckoned empty, neither sound nor worthy of praise, unless he directs the eye of intention so as to please God in the land of the living (Ps. LV), unless he so attends to God’s honour that he does not seek his own glory.

In the heart of the Nazarites there is such purity of intention as there is beauty of the eyes in a comely face. Nothing increases the grace of loveliness and glory of such a face more than the beauty of the eyes. For in a beautiful face the grace of the eyes is the beauty of beauty and the ornament of ornament itself; and the chief beauty of a good work is purity of will itself. This is the beauty of sapphire. Sapphire has the colour of heaven; it imitates the appearance of a pure and serene sky. It imitates heaven’s purity, indeed, but does not entirely attain it, for it is surpassed by that which is above it. The purity of heaven is more beautiful than sapphire.

Thus pious and upright intention, accompanied by hope and desire for heavenly things, has in some persons the purity of sapphire, which imitates heaven’s appearance; but in others it expresses, with greater beauty, the purity of the purest heaven. For there are persons who love God most purely, not merely together with other things, but above other things. Others love him above other things, but together with other things. In these the love is sole; in those it is supreme. Supreme love does not exclude another love; sole love admits no partnership with another love. For that is purer in its kind which receives no admixture of an inferior kind.

Those who love God above all else, but together with other things, often look, amid their sufferings and actions, with the eye of pure intention toward God, who holds the chief place in their love. They confidently hope that God’s promises will be fulfilled in them, and desire them before and above all things. Yet because they love certain vain things in which they do not love God—because they do not rightly love them for God’s sake—they often turn the eye away from an intention toward heavenly reward, namely toward that which they love vainly. For where love is, there the eye is. Accordingly, they hope, desire, and pray that their desires may be fulfilled as they wish in the things they love; and, while the whole heart is not raised upward, it bends at least a little toward lower things.

But those who purely love God alone and the things that are God’s are shown to be more beautiful than sapphire in proportion as they are found purer in sincere intention, always meditating upon heavenly things, with the Prophet saying to the Lord: “The meditation of my heart is always in thy sight” (Ps. XVIII). Desiring that the eyes of his intention should not turn back to vain things, he says: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. CXVIII). Explaining the purity of his desire, he says: “My heart said to thee: My face has sought thee; thy face, O Lord, I will seek” (Ps. XXVI). Declaring the purity of his hope, he says: “The Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, and according to the purity of my hands in the sight of his eyes” (Ps. XVII).

Established in such purity of intention, desire, and hope, the Nazarites see God as it were always, and in the glory of their beauty are always seen by him, like the works of his hands—he who always rejoices in his works. Thus they behold one another with mutual gaze and delight in mutual vision. For the Prophet says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII). And the righteous man says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. XXIV). Behold, even now, in the present, the Nazarites in some manner see God eye to eye. Behold, they now anticipate the joys of future vision. Behold, they now taste the first sweetness of that future satisfaction in which they shall be more fully satisfied when the glory of God appears—God who is above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0571]

## Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury: Book on the Commendation of Faith

All covenants of human fellowship and the laws of friendship, in order that they may endure in their stability, are strengthened by the sincerity of faith and, once strengthened, are preserved by it. All people desire faith to be kept with them, even those who do not wish to keep it themselves. A friend demands faith from a friend, a companion from a companion, a master from a servant, an emperor from a soldier, a husband from a wife—everyone who lives from the person with whom he lives. Without faith neither the governance of affairs can be administered, nor human duties or services dispensed, nor pairs of lovers joined together; neither kingdoms nor cities, nor the homes of individual families, nor any greater or lesser gathering of human beings living together socially, can endure without faith or remain in the state of their happiness.

If you remove faith from the midst, the bond of love will be broken and every covenant of peace dissolved. There will be no people who love one another and have peace among themselves unless there are people who believe one another. In every fellowship of social life among human beings, faith standing between them brings together the grace of love and peace. Among household members and servants, it is immediately sought that someone should be found faithful; and one whose faith has been proved by experience to be sincere and true is considered worthy of intimacy and praise. Without true friendship there is never true peace; for when false peace is pretended, faith likewise is feigned and friendship simulated.

Since the good of peace with and among human beings is desirable, and since this good is most rightly attained through true faith and friendship, we are thereby admonished that, if we hope to attain the peace of God which surpasses all understanding, we must keep faith with God and seek his friendship, so that, made partakers of his friendship, we may deserve to have peace with him and in him.

The unity of fraternal fellowship has these three things: faith, charity, and peace. The Apostle teaches this when he says: “Faithful is God, by whom we were called into the fellowship of his Son” (I Cor. I). He established that this fellowship with his Son must be sought, possessed, and retained without end through faith, charity, and peace. By faith, moreover, God was pleased by all who from ancient days became partakers of his friendship. “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI).

### On Faith toward One’s Neighbour

Faith is owed to one’s neighbour, so that we may speak with him simply and act simply in all things, walking without malice and deceit—that is, without a will to harm and an intention to deceive. These two things, iniquity and deceit, corrupt the sincerity of faith which must be kept in social life. Whoever deliberately strives to deceive or injure his neighbour violates the law of human fellowship, because he does not observe the faith owed to the common brotherhood.

The law of not violating fellowship is this: it is naturally impressed upon every person not to do to another what he would not wish done to himself. If someone, deceived by excusable ignorance, says or does in his simplicity something by which another is harmed or deceived, without intending to harm or deceive him, it must be said of him that he does not abandon faith so long as he keeps simplicity of heart. But whoever acts in order to deceive, even though he is prevented by some circumstance from actually deceiving, does not keep faith, because he abandons simplicity.

For simplicity of conscience, apart from any will or intention to deceive or in any way harm, is itself the companion and guardian of faith, by which one person is faithful to another in every kind of living together and common intercourse. In matters faithfully said or done, faith is not to be assessed by the outcome of good or evil things that may happen, but by the simplicity of conscience whereby those who speak and act faithfully are conscious that they wish to be believed and do not wish to deceive or harm. Faith, therefore, never intends to deceive by word or deed, though it may itself happen to be deceived. This occurs because it does not always rely upon the judgment of truth, but sometimes upon the uncertainty of opinion. For it makes an estimate of what it does not know and, erring, approves one thing in place of another.

In matters which may lawfully or excusably be unknown, when someone is deceived through ignorance of the truth and consequently does to another what he would not wish done to himself, simplicity of heart in some measure excuses the erring person before God, although the deed itself displeases God. Thus the Lord, coming by night in a dream to Abimelech, who had taken Abraham’s wife, reproves the act in a remarkable manner yet excuses its author. Reproving the deed and threatening punishment, he says: “Behold, thou shalt die because of the woman whom thou hast taken” (Gen. XX). Excusing the author and preserving him from sin, he adds: “I know that thou didst this with a simple heart, and therefore I kept thee from sinning against me and did not permit thee to touch her.”

This mutual fellowship which exists among us requires faith, by which we may worthily be believed. The person who believes another is said to have faith in the words of the person whom he believes. Such faith must be assessed according to the opinion of the believer, when he thinks that the one whom he believes is not lying. But the one who is believed must keep faith with the one who believes him; and this faith must be assessed according to the simplicity of conscience.

### That God Does Not Deceive

No one is deceived by God, just as he himself is not deceived by a name. Yet God, through a hidden dispensation, does and says many things, changes and conceals many things; and thus those ignorant of the hidden dispensation come to think false things true and uncertain things certain, and so are led astray. Hence Jeremiah dares to say: “Thou hast deceived me, O Lord, and I have been deceived; thou hast been stronger than I, and hast prevailed” (Jer. XX).

The holy prophets, indeed, although enlightened by the Holy Spirit to see or foresee certain things, were nevertheless permitted, as human beings, to be ignorant of many things which God in a sense concealed from them because he did not reveal them. Thus they often hoped and expected things that did not happen. Accordingly the same prophet says: “We hoped for peace, and there is no good; for a time of healing, and behold, disturbance” (Jer. VIII). And when the Shunammite woman came to the prophet Elisha with her son dead, he said: “Her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has concealed it from me and has not told me” (IV Kings IV).

What wonder is it if prophets were permitted to be ignorant of something and to suppose differently in some matters than was then the case or would later be the case, when it is written of Jesus’ parents: “The child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it; but supposing that he was in the company, they came a day’s journey and sought him” (Luke II)?

God, however, says or does nothing deceitfully. Rather, by a just judgment or by another purpose of dispensation, through withdrawing grace or not bestowing it, he permits—and sometimes does not prevent—those worthy of deception to be deceived. Thus, as it is written in the book of Kings, he says: “Who will deceive King Ahab for me?” (III Kings XXII). And Isaiah says to the Lord: “Why hast thou caused us to stray, O Lord, from thy ways? Hast thou hardened our heart, so that we do not fear thee?” (Isa. LXIII). Again Isaiah, speaking of Egypt, says: “The Lord has mingled in her midst a spirit of dizziness, and has caused Egypt to err” (Isa. XIX). And the Psalmist, speaking of sinners raised up and cast down, says: “Yet because of their deceits thou hast set things for them; thou hast cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. LXXII). Job, speaking of the Lord, says: “He changes the heart of the princes of the people of the earth, and deceives them, so that they wander fruitlessly through a pathless place; they grope as in darkness and not in light, and he causes them to wander like drunken men” (Job XII).

These and similar passages, frequently found in Holy Scripture, must be referred to the judgment of strict justice or the counsel of divine dispensation. God is said to do these things because he judges or dispenses in this way. But when, by God’s judgment or dispensation, evil persons fall into the snare of error, or when things hoped for from God do not happen to good or evil persons, this is God’s justice or mercy, in which there is no iniquity or deceit. He speaks simply and acts simply in all things, “faithful in all his words and holy in all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).

### That Faith Is Owed to God in Two Ways

Faith, therefore, is owed to God, because he neither knows how to deceive nor can be deceived. For he is truth and wisdom: truth does not deceive; wisdom is not deceived. Faith is required from us in two ways: first, in his words to us; then, in our words to him.

Faith is owed to God’s words, so that we may worthily believe concerning God and the things of God which he has deigned to reveal in the Holy Scriptures. There is also the faith of a pledge in our promises and vows offered to God, by which we are bound to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires and, obediently serving, to serve God alone faithfully. To this faith of a pledge belongs what the Apostle said when speaking of younger widows: “When they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have made void their first faith” (I Tim. V).

Those who make void the faith of a right pledge by living badly, although they believe or appear to believe, are improperly designated by the name of the faithful, as it is written: “They lied to him with their tongue, but their heart was not right with him, nor were they found faithful in his covenant” (Ps. LXXVII). But those who faithfully believe and faithfully serve by obedience are most rightly called faithful: possessing faith by which they believe rightly, and keeping faith by which they render faithful obedience.

Faith by which God is believed is necessary before all else for obtaining salvation; but by itself it is insufficient without fidelity to the obedience promised, which must be kept uninjured or, if injured, restored through repentance. The one who believes and serves professes by conduct the faith that he confesses with his tongue. The one who believes and does not serve denies by deeds the God whom he confesses in words. Thus the Apostle says to Titus concerning the defiled and unbelieving, whose mind and conscience are defiled: “They profess that they know God, but by deeds deny him” (Tit. I). Again, in the First Epistle to Timothy: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V).

### That Vices Diminish or Extinguish Faith

Whoever denies God by deeds always diminishes faith and loses the merit of faith; sometimes, moreover, through the vice of unbelief, he extinguishes faith itself. Hence the Apostle says in the same Epistle concerning those who had rejected a good conscience by evil living: “Wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, certain persons have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have delivered to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme” (I Tim. I).

Observe that, after first saying, “holding faith,” he added, “and a good conscience,” wishing to show that faith is insufficient without a good conscience, and that shipwreck of faith occurs—which seems to pertain to blasphemy against God—as follows from the subsequent words: “that they may learn not to blaspheme.” Again, in the same Epistle, he shows faith endangered through covetousness, saying: “Covetousness is the root of all evils; some, desiring it, have fallen away from the faith” (I Tim. VI).

Showing yet another cause of failing faith, he says in the same Epistle: “Avoiding profane novelties of speech and the contradictions of falsely named knowledge; by professing this, some have fallen away concerning the faith” [ibid.]. From the Apostle’s preceding words it may be established that profane novelties of speech, which lead into error, violate faith; so too falsely named knowledge, which sets itself against the simplicity of faith and exalts itself against the knowledge of God; and not only these, but also a bad conscience, covetousness—the root of all evils—and lust; likewise evil deeds, by which those who confess God in words deny him, though they are abominable and unbelieving, and reprobate toward every good work.

Hence it is clear that without a good life or conscience, faith either does not advance or fails. How indeed does that not fail, or how is it not extinguished, which is dead? “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. II), because it has neither movement nor feeling: it is not moved through the effect of a good work, nor does it feel through the affection of love.

### On Faith That Works through Love

But “the righteous lives by faith” (Heb. X), not by faith that is dead, but by faith which works through love. This is what gives life; this is what is truly and worthily called faith, by which what is said is done and what is promised is fulfilled. This true faith rests upon the truth of belief and the truth of a pledge. Holy Scripture commends it with the greatest earnestness; the whole life of the righteous confirms it. God requires it from us, and graciously accepts it when offered.

The faith of heretics is feigned, for they invent from their own heart what they believe. Feigned too is the faith of those who promise false obedience, who promise and do not perform, offer vows and do not pay them. But faith which works through love is not feigned, because it is written: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I).

This faith, which is proved to please God, is free from error, pretence, and hesitation. It is free from error and pretence because it assents to truth and obeys in sincerity. It is free from hesitation because it admits no ungodly doubt but remains unmoved in the firmness of its conviction. Thus it is written of Abraham: “In the promise of God he did not hesitate through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, most fully knowing that what he had promised he was able also to perform” (Rom. IV). And the Apostle James says: “Whoever lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach. But let him ask in faith, hesitating in nothing. For whoever hesitates is like a wave of the sea, moved by the wind” (Jas. I).

### On Hesitation in Faith
Doubt arises from impiety when one is uncertain of the truth of faith or distrusts God’s permission. Abraham is set forth as an example of not distrusting; of him Paul says in the Epistle to the Romans: “He did not waver through unbelief” (Rom. IV). We are given counsel not to doubt concerning faith when James says: “Let him ask in faith, wavering nothing” (Jas. I). For one who is instructed to ask is instructed not to waver, whether in faith or in asking. Wavering in faith is contrary to piety. For one who wavers in faith [Col. 0577C] fluctuates and is like a wave of the sea, neither fully assenting nor fully dissenting. Just as one who dissents from the faithful by holding a contrary opinion must be said not to believe, so also one who, wavering in doubt, does not agree with the faithful must be judged not to believe. Truth itself says: “He who is not with me is against me” (Luke XI). Therefore, insofar as one doubts, one does not believe; for one does not assent or acquiesce.

But just as that doubt is impious by which matters are held doubtful that ought to be believed most firmly, so that doubt is not impious by which matters are held doubtful that may permissibly be unknown. That wavering by which we tremble amid dangers, or fear, while praying, that we shall not be heard—and often fear all the more that we shall not be heard the more greatly we desire to be heard—that doubt, I say, does not always arise from condemnable impiety, but sometimes from human weakness, faint-heartedness, or an imperfect faith. For the righteous often pray when they are not heard; they are often heard when they do not know themselves to be heard; and they often do not know what they ought to pray for, as is fitting. That the righteous are not always heard is shown by Paul’s words in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “There was given to me a thorn, an angel of Satan, to buffet me; on account of this I asked the Lord three times that it might be removed from me; and the Lord said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, Paul’” (II Cor. XII). The same is shown by the Lord’s words to Samuel: “How long will you mourn for Saul, when I have rejected him?” [Col. 0578A] (I Sam. XVI). And again by what he says to Jeremiah: “Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul is not toward this people” (Jer. XV). Behold: Paul prays for himself and is not heard; Samuel and Jeremiah pray for others and are not heard.

That they are heard when they do not think that they will be heard is shown by blessed Job’s words: “Though he hears me when I call, I do not believe that he has heard my voice” (Job IX). But that the righteous sometimes do not know what they ought to ask, as is fitting, Paul plainly shows when he says to the Romans: “The Spirit helps our weakness. For we do not know what we should pray for as is fitting; but the Spirit himself pleads for us with unutterable groanings. And he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, [Col. 0578B] because he pleads for the saints according to God. And we know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. VIII).

But when the Apostle says, “We do not know what we should pray for as is fitting” (ibid.), he does not seem to mean this generally of all things requested by the saints. For they ask for things that are good in themselves and bring about salvation unto eternal life. They also ask for eternal goods promised as a reward; and they ask for things which are not good in themselves and do not make people good or bring about salvation, but only sometimes cooperate for good. With respect to those things which cooperate for good, however, the righteous do not know what they ought to pray for, as is fitting. For when they ask that a necessity or tribulation be relieved, or [Col. 0578C] that a temptation be removed, they do not recognize the fruit of that necessity or tribulation, or the outcome of the temptation. They do not know whether it is more advantageous for their salvation to possess or to lack what they desire.

Nevertheless, because they have two wills, one of weakness and the other of strength—one according to which the flesh desires against the spirit, the other according to which the spirit desires against the flesh—a definite form of prayer has been prescribed for such circumstances: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI). This will of strength, which is according to the spirit and by which they will that God’s will be preferred to the will which is according to the flesh, is suggested and wrought [Col. 0578D] by the Holy Spirit. Therefore he says: “The Spirit helps our weakness” (Rom. VIII). As what follows makes clear, he helps when he desires and pleads for the saints. He desires and pleads when he kindles our hearts in the fervour of holy desire and causes us to ask for what is pleasing to him and salutary for us.

The human spirit too, breathed upon by the Holy Spirit, in its own way helps weakness, because it does not pray definitely for what weakness desires, but, committing everything to God, asks and desires that what may please him and be expedient for us should come to pass. This may be what blessed Job means when he says: “Though he hears me when I call, I do not believe that he has heard my voice” (Job IX). It is as though he plainly said: Although he hears the spirit’s prayer according [Col. 0579A] to God for salvation, I nevertheless do not believe that he hears my voice, because he does not hear it according to my will: “He who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God” (Rom. VIII). For he knows what pleases himself and what is expedient for a human being. But when a person asks and does not know these things, that person does not know what to request. Hence it was said to the sons of Zebedee: “You do not know what you ask” (Matt. XX).

But if anyone thinks that the Apostle’s words, “We do not know what we should pray for as is fitting” (Rom. VIII), should be understood generally, the following may support that general interpretation: the Apostle does not simply say, “We do not know what we should pray for,” but adds, “as is fitting.” We know that the things we are instructed to ask in the Lord’s Prayer must be sought from God; but he gives to whom he wills, [Col. 0579B] and as much as he wills, and when he wills, and how he wills, and does not always disclose to those who ask the reason, measure, and manner of his gift. Therefore, when we ask God for wisdom, charity, humility, patience, and tranquillity of mind—things which most certainly ought to be requested—we know what we ask, yet we do not know what we ask insofar as it is best for us to receive it or for him to give it.

For Paul too wavers in a matter that is certain. Knowing that it is much better to live with Christ than to remain in the flesh, yet considering how necessary his presence in the flesh was for those to whom he spoke, he does not know which alternative should more be prayed for and desired at that time: to be with Christ or to remain in the flesh for the brethren. Therefore he says: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if to live in the flesh is for me fruit of labour, then what I shall choose I do not know. Yet I am constrained by the two, having a desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” [Col. 0579C] (Phil. I).

In so great a darkness of uncertainty and ignorance, in which the righteous do not know whether they will be heard, or what ought fittingly to be asked by them; knowing the certainty of their own weakness and not having complete confidence in their own righteousness, although they trust steadfastly in God’s mercy, they nevertheless tremble and waver because of their frailty. They do not hope without fear, just as neither do they tremble without hope. If they feared only, how would they not despair? If they hoped only, how would they not relax themselves through excessive security? Yet, placed between hope and fear, when they pray, how do they ask in faith, “wavering nothing”? They do not waver in the faith which they do not doubt to be true in all things and through all things. But in prayer, although they doubt because of uncertainty whether they will be heard or whether their request is timely, they do not waver through distrust. For such doubt—the doubt which the Apostle also denied of Abraham when he said, “He did not waver through unbelief” (Rom. IV)—is always dangerous, contrary to true faith, and always foreign to those who pray faithfully.

For who prays and does not hope? One must therefore believe and hope; yet it is permissible to fear and doubt piously. But it is altogether impermissible to waver through distrust in God’s promises [Col. 0580A]. From this it is evident that pious doubt, arising from permissible ignorance and necessary for the righteous as a restraint and safeguard of humility, does not destroy the piety of faith or overthrow confidence of mind into despair. Rather, just as it is pious to believe without doubt what God has shown ought to be believed, so it is not impious simply to be ignorant of, and simply to doubt, what God has hidden without revealing it.

It makes a great difference whether someone doubts God’s power or his will. The man who brought his son to Jesus seems to have doubted his power, when he said in Mark: “If you can do anything, help us, having mercy on us.” But Jesus said to him: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.” And he said: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX). Those men doubted his power who said: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” [Col. 0580B] (Ps. LXXVII). The leper, however, doubted his will, not his power, when he said to Jesus in Matthew: “Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.” He immediately heard: “I will; be cleansed” (Matt. VIII). Observe this: he who doubted concerning will alone received certainty concerning that will together with the grace of healing. But he who doubted power and said, “If you can do anything,” immediately heard addressed to himself: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes” (Mark XIV). This shows that the grace of the mercy sought depends upon faith in his omnipotence, when the petitioner doubted whether he could do anything in this respect.

### On Wavering in Dangers

That doubt by which one wavers in dangers seems to pertain to a diminution of faith, since the Lord said reprovingly to Peter: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” [Col. 0580C] (Matt. XIV). He is reproved for having doubted, either because he doubted his safety when, seeing the strong wind coming, he became afraid, or because, disturbed, he doubted the Saviour’s presence. For when the Lord was walking on the sea, and those who saw him were disturbed and said, “It is a phantom” (ibid.), and cried out in fear, he said: “It is I” (ibid.). Peter ought not to have doubted the presence of the Saviour, who revealed himself and declared that he was present, especially when he said: “Take courage; do not be afraid” (ibid.).

Peter, along with the others, was commanded to have confidence and not to fear; and he was also commanded, as he himself had asked, to come to the Lord who was walking upon the waters. He too walked upon the waters, [Col. 0580D] and amid so many safeguards of faith and security he ought not to have been afraid. Yet he was afraid as a human being; nevertheless, he did not altogether despair or altogether lose faith. For he said: “Lord, save me” (ibid.). How could he call upon one in whom he had not believed? Peter’s doubt, then, appears to have been of such a kind as to disturb the steadfastness of confidence, but not altogether to extinguish faith.

Just as Peter’s doubt is reproved in Matthew, so the fearfulness of certain persons is rebuked in Mark. For when a great storm arose and they awakened the Lord, sleeping on a cushion in the stern, saying, “Master, does it not concern you that we are perishing?” he rose and said to the sea: “Be silent; be still.” And when calm had come, [Col. 0581A] he said: “Why are you fearful? Do you not yet have faith?” (Mark IV). His words, “Do you not yet have faith?” may be understood as a question, as though he were saying in order to stir up their faith: “Do you not yet have faith?” This agrees with the account in Luke, where, when some said, “Teacher, we are perishing,” the Lord is read to have answered: “Where is your faith?” (Luke VIII).

But if in Mark, to those reprovingly asked, “Why are you fearful?” the words “You do not yet have faith” were addressed not interrogatively but as an assertion, we who tremble in dangers through fear must greatly fear lest, losing steadfast confidence and security of mind, it should also be said to us: “You do not yet have faith.” Yet someone may think that those people were rightly rebuked and justly reproved because, being in danger, they had him with them, saw him present, and therefore ought not to have feared. But how are we too, who tremble in dangers, not to be reproved, since we trust that the Lord always remains with us—not through the presence of flesh, as with them, but through the presence of divinity? Thus the Lord himself says of the righteous: “I am with him in tribulation; I will deliver him” [Col. 0581B] (Ps. XC). And in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

How great our confidence in the Lord’s presence should be is shown by one who says: “Though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, because you are with me” (Ps. XXII). And again: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation: whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: before whom shall I tremble?” (Ps. XXVI). But if this is the voice of the righteous—“I will fear no evils, because you are with me”—what is the meaning of that other voice in the Psalms, likewise the voice of the righteous or martyrs: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy” (Ps. LXIII)? And elsewhere: “My heart was troubled within me, and the dread of death fell upon me. Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” [Col. 0581C] (Ps. LIV).

But we must know that the righteous are now raised above themselves through an excess of contemplation into a certain security of mind and steadfastness of confidence; consequently, they recognize that all present evils and dangers of death are to be despised in God, and, recognizing this, they despise them. But at other times, left to their own weakness, they fear amid dangers as human beings; and by fearing they recognize their own weakness, the more humbly, the more truly. Hence it is written of them: “They ascend even to heaven, and descend even to the depths” (Ps. CVI). They ascend through an excess of contemplation and security in God; they descend through an excess of dread and faint-heartedness in themselves.

Thus Elijah met King Ahab as though fearless (III Kings XVIII), yet fled from Jezebel’s face not without fear (III Kings XIX). Thus Jacob, having wrestled with an angel and having been told, “If you have been strong against God, how much more will you prevail against men?” (Gen. XXXII), nevertheless prayed in fear, saying: “Deliver me from the hand of my brother, for I greatly fear him” (ibid.). Accordingly, as God dispenses these alternating changes, [Col. 0582A] the righteous are secure and yet fearful in themselves; just as, by his same marvellous ordering, they rejoice in God and are sorrowful in themselves. Writing to the Philippians, Paul admonishes them: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV). The same man, writing in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, says concerning himself: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning our tribulation which occurred in Asia, because we were burdened beyond measure, so that we were even weary of living” (II Cor. I). The Psalmist says: “My soul shall exult in the Lord” (Ps. XXXIV). The same says: “My soul was troubled within me” (Ps. XLI). And again: “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (ibid.).

The righteous are often assailed by fear but are not moved from the stability of hope, as it is written: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Sion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” [Col. 0582B] (Ps. CXIV). Yet they are often assailed by fear and shaken to such a degree that hope itself is weakened and they almost incline into the danger of despair. For God, who tests the elect in order to find them worthy of himself, as he is a helper in times of tribulation, so he overlooks them in times of tribulation. He overlooks them when he does not look upon them amid evils, when he does not grant the prayer of one crying amid tribulation according to that person’s desire. This happens beneficially, so that the righteous, left to themselves, may discover what they are in themselves.

But when, weighed down beyond measure by excessive fear, they are often weakened so greatly that, unless God’s grace comes quickly to their aid, they incur the danger of impending despair, then that rebuke applies to them: “Why are you fearful? Do you not yet have faith?” (Mark IV). Yet by a hidden dispensation God sometimes permits the faith of the righteous to be weakened, even to the guilt of unbelief, so that they may be more deeply humbled and rise again stronger. Hence it is written in the book of Numbers: “When Moses had raised his hand, he struck the rock twice with the staff, and most abundant waters came forth, so that the people and the cattle drank. And God said to Moses and Aaron: ‘Because you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I have given them.’ This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel contended before the Lord” [Col. 0582C] (Num. XX). Behold how unbelief is charged against Moses and Aaron by the Lord and shown as deserving punishment.

Again through Isaiah the Lord says to the people of Israel: “Your first father sinned, and your interpreters transgressed against me, and I defiled the holy princes” (Isa. LXIII). The words, “Your first father sinned,” may be understood of Abraham, if perhaps he too doubted when, in reply to the Lord promising him the land of promise, he said: “By what shall I know that I shall possess it?” (Gen. XV). Or this may be understood of the fathers in the wilderness, who spoke wickedly about God: “Can he give bread, or prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. LXXVII). Of them it is also written: “Because they did not believe in God or hope in his salvation” (ibid.). The words, “Your interpreters transgressed against me” (Isa. LXIII), are rightly understood of Moses and Aaron, who, standing between God and the people, as has been said, transgressed [Col. 0583A]. God defiled the holy princes by a hidden dispensation, permitting them to be defiled and, by a just judgment, showing them to be defiled.

The righteous may also despair of certain things without danger to faith or loss of hope. For what one may rightly not desire, one may also rightly not hope for; and what one may rightly despise, one may despair of and place no hope in. Hence blessed Job, raised from temporal to eternal things, as one despising and mortifying the fleshly life, says: “My soul chose hanging. I have despaired; I shall live no longer. Spare me, Lord, for my days are nothing” (Job VII). Consider that he did not despair of the Lord, who said, “Spare me, Lord”; yet neither did he in no way despair, who said, “I have despaired.” Therefore he despaired of that from which, through holy contempt [Col. 0583B] and holy hatred, he withdrew his hope, not of that to which he transferred all his hope and all his desire.

From what has been said, it must be concluded that doubt now lightly strikes the heart, now strikes it more forcefully and inclines it toward unbelief, and now, with greater disturbance, casts it down into the guilt of unbelief. But the doubt which approaches unbelief or casts one into it is a certain defect of faith, diminishing or extinguishing the light of faith, until the mind, its disturbance’s darkness having been scattered and itself strengthened by God’s grace, rises again.

### On the Certainty of Faith

Because through faith we trust in God and believe God, and because God is truth, that faith ought to be supported by such certainty and such firmness of undoubting assent that it may rightly be called knowledge. For it surpasses every experience of the senses and transcends every conjecture of human reason, most truly and certainly apprehending things which can neither be investigated by sense nor in any way discovered by human reason. Since God is to be believed more than bodily senses or human reasoning, the dignity of faith surpasses all worldly wisdom: it sees the invisible, senses the imperceptible, and comprehends the incomprehensible. For it is a certain apprehension, most firmly strengthened by the authority of unchangeable Truth itself.

Although faith can in some respect be aided by sense or reason, as will be shown below [Col. 0583D], faith, advancing without offence, proceeds beyond the point which sense, imagination, or reason can reach by inquiry or attain by intention. The light of reason, by which the mind is naturally illuminated so as to understand, is surpassed by the incomparably brilliant splendour of the light of grace, by which the mind is illuminated so as to believe what it does not understand, until, by a certain order of grace, it understands what it now believes. Therefore, since true cognition of comprehensible things is called knowledge, and still more is the most true cognition of incomprehensible things, granted to us by God’s revelation, rightly called knowledge because of its certainty and infallibility, it must be ranked not only above the uncertainty of opinion but above all human knowledge and above the judgment of reason—knowledge to be preferred, as it were, to knowledge. [Col. 0584A] Yet it is not comparable in any respect to knowledge belonging to the time to come.

This is the knowledge of salvation which enlightens and saves, concerning which it is written: “For you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people, for the remission of their sins” (Luke I). If there is any cognition through faith in the unlearned or those making progress, it is so moderate and slight that it is not yet worthy of the name of knowledge. Yet in the advanced and perfect, who believe most firmly and certainly and more fully understand the rationale of faith through the inspiration of more abundant grace, cognition through faith is called knowledge with all the more certainty because Sacred Scripture more frequently says that those things are known which are perceived by faith alone.

Commending Abraham’s faith, the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans: “He did not waver through unbelief even at God’s promise, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, most fully knowing that whatever he promised he is also able to do” [Col. 0584B] (Rom. IV). Observe that he did not say merely “knowing,” but “most fully knowing,” so that he might commend to us the certainty of faith more profoundly through the fullness of knowledge. The same Apostle says in the Epistle to Timothy: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit unto that day” (II Tim. I). Again, to the same person: “But know this: that in the last days dangerous times shall come” (II Tim. III). He instructed Timothy to know what he had foretold must be believed. Blessed Job says: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth” (Job XIX). Martha said to Jesus: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day” (John XI).

When the Apostle says to the Romans, “I reckon that the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII), this must not be referred to the uncertainty of opinion, although he says that he reckons it; rather, it is to be referred to the consciousness of knowledge and certainty. This is proved by the Epistle to the Corinthians, where he says: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” [Col. 0584C] (II Cor. V). Behold: concerning matters pertaining to the state of the future time, the Apostle both says that he reckons and that he knows, so that we may not separate the reckoning of faith from the certainty of knowledge.

### On What Is Written: “Faith Is the Substance of Things Hoped For, the Evidence of Things Not Seen”

[Col. 0584D]

Wishing to show how great the certainty of faith is, and at the same time not wishing to pass over how great its usefulness is, the Apostle, first setting forth its usefulness and then adding its certainty, says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. XI). Things hoped for are of three kinds: temporal goods, which we need for the support of the body; spiritual goods, which we need for the formation of the mind; and eternal goods, which will be enjoyed in the state of blessedness. These are to be sought and hoped for from God, who has also promised all these things to us.

For concerning temporal things necessary for the use of this life, he says: “All these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI). Concerning spiritual things he says: “Your Father from [Col. 0585A] heaven will give the good Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke XI). By “Spirit” he understands the gifts of spiritual charisms which are to be given. He promises eternal things when he shows that we shall be made blessed in his kingdom, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V), and the other things which follow. All these are obtained by the merit of faith. Thus faith’s usefulness is rightly displayed when it is said: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for.”

The substance of faith is better than earthly substance, than treasures of money that grow old and fail. For faith is the means through which we obtain from God, either in possession or in hope, the things that are to be sought, hoped for, and desired from him. Indeed, the righteous person lives by faith, having from it every sufficiency of life, the grace of virtues, and the glory of rewards. The righteous person is one whom faith justifies precisely because he believes in God. For what is more just than to believe in him? Or to whom ought one more to give belief than to him? Or what ought to be more certain than what he says or promises? Faith, therefore, does not rest upon human reason in assenting to truth; rather, assenting to God’s words, it is sufficient in itself for certainty of truth. It is therefore called the evidence of things not seen, because it approves things not seen by true and certain assent.

### On Faith’s Argumentation

The evidence which is faith itself is one thing; the evidence by which faith itself is established is another. For Christ, appearing to his disciples in many proofs during forty days (Acts I), and wishing to establish faith in his resurrection, displayed many outward proofs by which he wonderfully formed the disciples’ hearts in faith in his divinity and resurrection from the dead. Thus it came about that what was outwardly displayed in a wonderful manner was evidence strengthening faith; and nonetheless faith itself was evidence, establishing things not seen by infallible assent [Col. 0585C].

### On Things Not Seen

By “things not seen,” understand things that are not apparent either to bodily senses or to the mind’s natural reason. Things contemplated by faith are called “not seen,” although they are perceived by faith, because they are comprehended neither by sense nor by reason. Even when the same things are perceived by sense or reason and by faith, faith still in a certain way comprehends things not seen, because it raises itself higher than sense or reason can rise. For through visible things it beholds invisible things, and in the very things that appear it apprehends things that do not appear.

For when the thief on the cross confessed God, he saw the suffering of a man but recognized the suffering of God, which sense or reason could not do. The same suffering, which belonged both to God and to man, appeared to the eyes of faith insofar as it belonged to God, and did not appear to the eyes of flesh. Likewise, Christ’s works, wonderfully performed in the flesh, and the weaknesses which he endured, belonged both to man and, through the power of God wonderfully at work, to God; they belonged to God in the weakness of the man who suffered wonderfully. Faith, however, apprehending Christ as God and man and discerning God’s mighty acts and man’s weaknesses, sees that both—the weak things and the mighty things—belong to God, because it recognizes the man as God [Col. 0586A]. Sense or reason cannot in any way attain this.

### That Faith Is Aided by Sense

Faith nevertheless knows that it is aided by sense. When Thomas said to his fellow disciples, “Unless I see, I will not believe” (John XX), the Lord later appeared and invited him both to see and to touch. Because he saw, he believed, as the Lord testifies when he says: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (ibid.). Those slow to believe are led to faith by seeing signs. The Lord showed this when, according to John, he said to the royal official: “Unless you see signs and wonders, [Col. 0586B] you will not believe” (John IV). Therefore, when the apostles preached, the Lord confirmed their word by signs following, so that, having seen signs, those who would not believe without signs might believe.

But many saw signs and nevertheless did not believe, just as many did not see signs and nevertheless believed: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII). Faith can therefore exist without sight, though not without hearing. Hence the Apostle says to the Romans: “How shall they believe in him whom they have not heard?” (Rom. X). And below: “Therefore faith is from hearing, but hearing through the word of Christ” (ibid.).
