The word is heard either outwardly when it is preached, or inwardly when it is believed through the Spirit’s revelation.

### That Faith Is Preceded by Thoughts

[Col. 0586C] In order that the word may be believed, the mind, by God’s inspiration, is preceded by thoughts which wonderfully incline it toward belief. For while it considers either God’s works, God’s judgments, God’s commandments, or God’s promises—as the Holy Spirit suggests to it—it is stirred within itself, marvels, and, marvelling, trembles and believes. Faith enters through wonder and fear, and fear through belief. Thus one begins to believe and to fear in such a way that by believing one fears and by fearing one believes. Faith does not come before fear, nor fear before faith; rather, each is a beginning. For it is written of fear: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX). And in the book of Wisdom it is written thus concerning fear and faith: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of his love” (Ecclus. XXXIV). The beginning of faith [Col. 0586D] must be joined to it. By “the beginning of faith,” understand faith as a beginning.

Our justification begins from faith. The demons would not tremble unless they believed. They believe and tremble, but neither does their belief justify them nor their fear sanctify them. Yet for us, whom faith justifies in holy fear, both are given by God: to fear and to believe, in righteousness and holiness. For we are not sufficient to conceive that by which we may fear God or believe in him, unless it is given to us from above. Therefore the Apostle says: “But we have such confidence through Christ toward God—not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (I Cor. III). Faith, then, is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ, when the word is preached and heard and, as God suggests [Col. 0587A] and works, is so considered that it is believed. Faith is therefore God’s gift and God’s work.

### That Faith Is God’s Gift

That faith is God’s gift the Apostle shows in the Epistle to the Ephesians, saying: “For by grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift, not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them” (Eph. II). And again, to the Philippians: “It has been granted to you for Christ, not only that you should believe in him, but also that you should suffer for him” (Phil. I). From these passages it is clear that faith is given to us not by the merit of preceding works but by grace alone, lest anyone boast in faith as though he had it from himself or had received it through his own merit [Col. 0587B].

### That Faith Is God’s Work

That faith is God’s work is shown by Christ in John. Asked by those seeking, “What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?” he answered: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John VI). Asked concerning God’s works as though they were many, he answered concerning the one work which he himself accomplishes in us, in which the good works we perform are formed by him so that they may be good, pleasing to God, and salutary for us. Thus it is written: “All his works are in faith” (Ps. XXXII).

By this answer of the Lord, those asking, “What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?” are instructed to have faith, which is God’s work and without which they cannot work God’s works. It is as though he said: Have faith, which works the works of God through love. God works this work by drawing us, as it is written: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John VI). One comes to Christ who believes in him. But one comes drawn—not because one is unwilling, but because one is weak; no longer unwilling, but unable by oneself. Hence the bride in the Song of Songs, recognizing her weakness and needing the aid of grace, says: “Draw me; we shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song I).

The one who believes comes drawn: drawn away from error, attracted by love of truth, drawn by the force of grace, drawn by the fervour of holy desire. One who is drawn is released from unwillingness and admitted not unwillingly. One is drawn by the hand of the mighty, by the voice of one inviting, and by one inwardly admonishing and teaching, as John himself shows when he says: “It is written in the prophets: ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” [Col. 0587D] (John VI). One taught by God is one who hears and learns from him and comes to Christ. One hears when one diligently attends to God’s word, pondering it more deeply and turning it over in one’s mind. One learns when one acquiesces and does not contradict in one’s heart. One comes when, by true confession and profession in word and deed, one approaches Christ’s discipleship.

Through faith we are drawn to Christ when, although the judgment of sense or reason resists, the mind, stunned in wonder by the power of God’s words or signs, is amazed and no longer dares to trust itself. Then, in a certain manner renouncing itself, it is humbled all the more toward the grace of faith and prepared more fittingly for it, [Col. 0588A] the more it judges itself, from what it hears or sees, to be inferior to and weaker than itself.

### That Hardening Is Blindness and Deafness

But the hardening of mind which is not led to faith either by the power of words heard or by the power of signs seen is rightly called deafness and blindness, according to Isaiah’s saying: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy” (Isa. VI).

### That faith is light and word

Faith, whether through words or through signs, opens the ears and eyes of the heart. Therefore those who believe are said to see and hear, because faith is light and word: light indeed, according to the Apostle’s saying: “God, who commanded light to shine out of darkness, has himself shone in our hearts, for the illumination of the knowledge [Col. 0588B] of the glory of God in the face of Christ Jesus” (2 Cor. 4).

God said that light should shine out of darkness when he called us out of darkness into his marvelous light; when, scattering the darkness of ignorance, he said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. Faith, moreover, is word, according to the saying of the apostle James: “Receive with meekness the implanted word” (James 1). The implanted word is that placed within the heart while God speaks inwardly; concerning it the Apostle says: “But what does Scripture say? ‘The word is near in your mouth and in your heart’” (Rom. 10; Deut. 30).

### On what is written: “The word is near,” etc.

This is the word of faith. You ask how it is near in the mouth and in the heart. Hear what follows: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness; but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” [Col. 0588C] (Rom. 10). It is therefore near because it is implanted; and it is implanted because it has been placed there by grace. If, therefore, you have faith in your heart and confess it with your mouth, “the word is near in your mouth and in your heart.”

It is near in usefulness because you are close to salvation. “But salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118). You, however, are lowly, and live by faith. “You are not far from the kingdom of God”; “the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Now you call upon God in truth: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144). Now you fear God: “His salvation is near to those who fear him.” Therefore, if you believe, “the word is near in your mouth and in your heart”—near in usefulness, because salvation is close to you through the confession of faith in the mouth and the consciousness of faith in the heart.

But if you do not yet believe and are able to believe, it is near—not as though it is already in the heart, but near so that it may be in the heart; and it is as near as it is easy for you to believe. It is near, not yet in present usefulness, but in the possibility, even the ease, of believing. For faith, except in those who by their own fault have been corrupt beyond cure, is not far from our nature, which is capable of reason and can share in righteousness and blessedness through faith.

That some cannot believe the Lord shows when he says in John’s Gospel: “How can you believe, who receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory which is from God alone?” (John 5). And again in the same Gospel: “Where I am going, you cannot come” (John 8). For he was going to glory, to which they could not come because, confirmed in error, [Col. 0589A] they were unable to believe. John himself says: “Therefore they could not believe” (John 12), because Isaiah again said: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, so that they may not see with their eyes and understand with their heart” (Isa. 6).

But for those who can believe, the word is near not only through the possibility of belief but through the preparation of grace. “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). Everything necessary for the calling of the Gentiles has been prepared. The Word became flesh; the carnal observance of the law was abolished. The Gospel has been preached to the world; the sacrifice for the world’s salvation has been offered. Nothing remains except that the word of faith be received in the heart, through which blessedness is attained. Hence it is written in Matthew: “All things [Col. 0589B] are prepared; come to the wedding” (Matt. 22).

Rightly, therefore, it is written in Deuteronomy: “The word is near in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. 30). God does not require the carnal practices of the Jews or the superstitious practices of the scribes and Pharisees, but faith: faith purifying hearts. He loves purity of heart, which is sufficient for our salvation.

### On what is written: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ that is, to bring Christ down.”

Faith has a twofold benefit: to escape the punishments of hell and to obtain the gifts of the heavenly kingdom. The Apostle shows this when he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “But the righteousness which is from faith speaks thus: ‘Do not say in your heart, Who will ascend into heaven?’ that is, [Col. 0589C] to bring Christ down; or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’ that is, to call Christ back from the dead” (Rom. 10).

The meaning of these words is this: the righteousness which is from faith urges us to consider and firmly hold that Christ ascended into heaven and descended into hell, in order to free the righteous from the punishments of hell and to bestow upon them the rewards of heaven. This must be denied by no one and doubted by no one. Therefore he says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” For if you say that no one has ascended into heaven, it follows that you say Christ also has not ascended. But if you say that Christ has not ascended, then, so far as lies in you, you bring Christ down from heaven.

And just as someone would be guilty because of an impious intention [Col. 0589D] and worthy of condemnation if he wished to bring Christ down from heaven, even though unable to do so, so one who denies that Christ ascended is worthy of certain condemnation; and, as though envying Christ’s glory, he wishes him not to be there where he denies that he is. For every impiety, in devotion to its own error, hates the truth that resists it and envies the glory of the author who lays the foundation of true faith and overturns the foundations of impiety.

Hence comes the Jews’ hatred against Christ, whom they persecute alike by impious denial and impious will. Hence they bring down from heaven him whom they do not believe to have ascended into heaven. Yet they bring him down through the guilt of their sin, not through the effect of their will.

Similarly, one who says, “Who descended into the abyss?”, believing that no one descended, or believing that Christ did not descend to free the righteous—such a person, so far as lies in him, calls Christ back from the dead, since by impious will and impious denial he maintains that Christ did not descend to free the righteous [Col. 0590A].

These words of the Apostle concerning Christ’s ascent and descent may be understood piously not only against unbelievers, as has now been said, but also in favor of believers, as will be said. For just as the impious, through impious will and denial, bring Christ down—but down from heaven—so the righteous, by the devout service and confession of faith, bring Christ down—but into heaven.

That “bringing down” may be understood in a good sense is shown by the Psalmist’s words: “You held my right hand, and in your will you led me down, and with glory you received me” (Ps. 72). But this refers to Christ’s members. Of Christ himself it is written: “Your right hand shall lead you down wondrously” (Ps. 44). Therefore, if you do not say in your heart, “Who ascended into heaven?”, this is a devout bringing-down. For not saying what it is impious to say is to bring Christ down devoutly.

Therefore those justified by faith follow Christ as he ascends into heaven with devout favor, and by following bring him down into heaven. But those who do not believe that he ascends into heaven pursue him in the hatred of their malice and, by pursuing him, bring him down from heaven. The former’s devout service is a devout bringing-down; the latter’s impious denial is an impious bringing-down.

Likewise, those who do not say, “Who descended into the abyss?”, and who believe that Christ descended, devoutly call Christ back from the dead, believing that he rose from the dead. Those call him back impiously who oppose the resurrection [Col. 0590C] and deny his descent.

### On what is written in Jeremiah: “Who has ascended into heaven?”

We must ask what is meant by the passage written concerning wisdom in the book of Jeremiah: “Who has ascended into heaven and received her, and brought her down from the clouds? Who has crossed the sea and found her, and brought her above choice gold?” (Baruch 3).

How do these statements agree: “Who has ascended into heaven?” and “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” The wisdom of which these things are said is Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God. A little later in the same book it is added concerning him: “This is he who found out every way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his chosen [Col. 0590D]. After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (ibid.).

No ruler of this world, as the Apostle says, knew this wisdom; no wise person of this world was able to discover it. For those seemed to excel among the wise of this age who, to use Isaiah’s words, contemplated the stars and calculated the months, so as to announce from them things to come (Isa. 47). One of their poets says of them:

> Happy the souls to whom it first befell  
> To care to climb into the homes of heaven.

But which of these, guided by his own intellect, ascended into heaven, received wisdom there, and brought it down from the clouds? Certainly none of them perceived true wisdom there for himself or conveyed it to others’ knowledge. Rather, all their wisdom, enclosed in their obscure sayings or writings as water is enclosed in clouds, was far from the way of discipline which God gave to Jacob his servant and Israel his chosen [Col. 0591A].

Nor did those find this wisdom who pursued learning through lands and seas throughout the whole world. Plato was among them. Of such persons it is said: “Who has crossed the sea and found her, and brought her above choice gold?” “Found and brought” is like what was said previously, “received and brought down.”

This wisdom, then, did not flow from the school of the Academics, the Stoics, or another sect of similar error; rather, they did not find the way of discipline, and therefore they perished. And because they did not possess wisdom, they perished through their folly.

Therefore God’s wisdom is neither discovered by the subtlety of human reason raising itself to lofty things, nor acquired through the labor of distant navigation and brought from remote regions. Rather, coming from heaven, it teaches us to despise earthly things and love heavenly things. To despise the world is to cross the sea and leave it behind once navigated. To love heavenly things is to strive toward heaven in hope and desire.

But none of the righteous, whether despising the world or longing for heavenly things, preceded this wisdom by his own merit or plan, so as to receive, bring down, find, and bring it above choice gold. “For who has been his counselor?” (Isa. 40), or “who has first given to him, and shall be repaid?” Wisdom itself, coming to us according to the counsel of its own will, chose, as it willed, [Col. 0591C] those to whom it would give itself, that they might love it above choice gold. For it is more precious than all riches, and all things desired cannot be compared with it (Prov. 3).

Therefore neither Enoch, nor Elijah, nor Paul, by preceding wisdom through his own merit, ascended into heaven in order to receive and bring down wisdom already attained there; neither did the children of Israel who crossed the sea on dry ground, nor Jonah, delivered from the sea and the belly of the whale, nor Peter walking upon the sea, nor Paul rescued from the depth of the deep, precede this wisdom so as to find it. Rather, all these, and all the other righteous figured in them, were preceded by God’s wisdom in order that they might become righteous and perform wonders.

It is not contradictory, therefore, that Paul recalls, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend [Col. 0591D] into heaven?’” (Rom. 10), and that the book of Jeremiah says, “Who has ascended into heaven?” There the denial of Christ’s ascent into heaven is forbidden; here neither Christ’s ascent nor our future ascent through Christ is denied. Rather, this is shown: if wicked persons are concerned, true wisdom is not apprehended by the pursuit of human curiosity; if good persons are concerned, it is indicated that this same wisdom is not preceded by merit of holiness.

Instead, wisdom itself, preceding all who were to be sanctified, revealed wisdom in the righteous of old, showing the way of discipline in the law and prophets, where it lay hidden, like water in clouds, until it was poured out in its own time, with the grace and glory of the resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ [Col. 0592A] our Lord shining forth. He was made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption.

### That Christ, the author of faith, indicated the power of his divinity by miracles and figured the efficacy of faith

This wisdom is Christ, who revealed himself and the Father to us through faith; and he is the author and perfecter of the faith through which he manifested himself to us, as the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Let us run with patience the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Heb. 12).

He is rightly called the author and perfecter of faith because he himself works faith in us, beginning and completing it. The miracles which Christ visibly performed in order that faith in his divinity might be received indicated the power of his divinity and figured the efficacy of faith. For by giving sight to the blind, opening the mouth of the mute and the ears of the deaf, directing the steps of the lame, healing the sick, cleansing lepers, and raising the dead, he signified through these signs the power of faith: faith opens the eyes of the mind for understanding, opens the ears for obedience, unseals the mouth for confession, governs the affections, washes away sins, cleanses offences, and gives spiritual life to those mortified in the flesh.

### On the new creation

Faith is, as it were, a new creation, changing from non-being into being. For unbelievers, because they are not in God, are said to be non-existent. When they are converted to faith, they begin to be, because they receive being from God [Col. 0592C]. Isaiah shows that before conversion to faith they are nothing, when he says concerning the unbelieving nations: “All nations are as though they were not before him; they are accounted by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40).

As soon as faith begins, a new creation begins. Thus the Apostle, after saying to the Ephesians, “You are saved by grace through faith” (Eph. 2), shortly adds: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (ibid.). Again, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “From now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5).

For when persons are renewed in Christ’s faith, oldness passes away and newness comes. And in the Epistle to the Galatians: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but a new creation” (Gal. 6). We are therefore God’s creatures by nature, but a new creation by grace. What we are by nature was changed for the worse through sin; but through the grace of faith we are restored for the better, so that we begin as though anew because we are renewed from oldness. Hence the Psalmist says: “And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76). “I said, ‘Now I have begun,’” he says, as confessing to God, rendering praise, and understanding that my present beginning is not from my own strength. For it was not my hand on high, but the Lord’s right hand, that performed power; therefore I said: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.”

### That through faith we become children of God

[Col. 0593A]

Through faith, moreover, we are not only changed into a new creation, but also made children of God. Hence John says: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God—to those who believe in his name” (John 1). He says that he gave them power to become children of God, not a power by which they might only someday become God’s children, but one by which, as soon as they believed, they became God’s children.

This power given to believers, therefore, does not lie in an awaited future outcome, but in the present effect of powerful grace. For one who begins to be justified through faith is immediately adopted as a child of God and at once honored with the name of child. Those who do not yet believe do not yet have this power given to believers. For this power is not of nature but of grace. Yet believers are so given power to become God’s children that they are born of God.

### That through faith we are born of God

How they are born of God is shown by blessed James, who says: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of beginning of his creation” (James 1). By “a kind of beginning of creation” he means, as it were, a beginning of creation in a new and singular way. To have a beginning through the condition of creation is common and frequent; but to receive a beginning through the grace of preparation is new and singular in humanity.

To be a kind of beginning of God’s creation, therefore, is both newness and dignity. That we might be this, God voluntarily begot us by the word of truth—voluntarily indeed, because freely and not by our merit. Yet he begot us not as he begot the Son consubstantial with himself, whom he did not make but begot. Rather, he made us, whom he created, from non-children into children through faith, and so begot us.

Hence also the saying in Deuteronomy: “You have forsaken God who made you, and have forgotten the Lord your Creator” (Deut. 32). He begot us by the word of truth. For the word of God, like seed in the heart, if mixed with faith through the mind’s assent, advances to divine generation, so that we may be children of God, according to the saying: “For we are the offspring of God” (Acts 17). But if the word heard is not mixed with faith, it does not advance to the beginning of new generation. Thus the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning certain unbelievers: “The word which they heard did not profit them, because it was not mixed with faith” (Heb. 4).

### That faith is the beginning of his substance

[Col. 0593D]

Faith, therefore, makes us a kind of beginning of God’s creation; and it is a beginning because it itself is “the beginning of his substance.” Hence the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For we have become partakers of Christ, if only we hold firm unto the end the beginning of his substance” (Heb. 3).

By “the beginning of his substance” he means faith, which is the beginning of all good things and our substance from God—namely, “the substance of things hoped for,” as was said above. Our substance is called both what we are and what we have. Concerning what we are, it is written in the Psalm: “Remember what my substance is” (Ps. 98). This is addressed to God, who knows our formation. Concerning what we have, it is written: “Honor the Lord from your substance” (Prov. 3).

Our whole substance, both in carnal goods and in spiritual gifts, proceeds from God’s gift. But among the spiritual gifts that work salvation in us, faith itself holds first place; therefore it is called the beginning of substance. Our substance includes both the natural goods received in creation and the gratuitous gifts by which we are renewed in restoration.

In the Gospel according to Luke, the younger son says to his father: “Father, give me the portion of substance that belongs to me” (Luke 15). What, then, is our substance except our nature, which we received from God, or grace and glory, which we likewise receive from him, as is written: “The Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 33)?

That glory may be called substance is shown by the Apostle, who says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “As I have said, be ready, lest when the Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—not to say you—should be ashamed in this substance of glory” [Col. 0594B] (2 Cor. 9). The Apostle exhorted the Corinthians to works of charity. He boasted of their charity before the Macedonians. Thus by “substance of glory” he means their earthly substance, charitably bestowed or to be bestowed, which was their glory in the Lord, or the Apostle’s glory on their behalf among the Macedonians.

Or he calls glory itself substance, because good boasting—whether the Apostle’s on their behalf or theirs in God—was spiritually true substance. Again, in the same epistle, commending himself and setting himself before those who boasted according to the flesh, he says: “What I speak, I do not speak according to God, but as in foolishness, in this substance of glory” (2 Cor. 11). He calls glory of the flesh substance, as it appeared to those who valued it highly. But by a true evaluation, glory in God is good substance.

Faith, therefore, is the beginning of substance because in our restoration it is the beginning for us of both grace and glory. Through it God has made us pleasing to himself in his beloved Son and glorified us in him. He glorified us so that we might be children of God; and not only this, but even gods, as is written:

### That through faith we are children of God

“I said: You are gods, and all of you are children of the Most High” (Ps. 81). It does not yet appear what we shall be, nor even what we now are. But when Christ, our life, appears, then we also shall appear with him in glory [Col. 0594D] (Col. 3); and then it will appear how great is the dignity and honor of being gods or children of God.

When we enjoy the most beautiful vision of the divine substance, when we see him as he is, then it will appear what the end and fruit of faith are—the faith which is the beginning of knowing God’s substance. Nothing is more blessed or sweeter than this knowledge.

How faith is the beginning of his substance, that is, of God, and of that substance which is the nature of God and in itself has neither beginning nor end, blessed Peter shows in both respects in his Second Epistle, saying: “All things of his divine power which have been given to us for life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and power; through whom he has given us the greatest and precious promises, that through these we may become partakers of the divine nature, escaping the corruption which is in the world through desire” (2 Pet. 1).

Understand from these words that, through knowledge of him who called us—that is, through faith in Christ—all the gifts of divine power necessary for us to attain life in the future and to preserve godliness in the present have already been given to us. God’s promises have already been fulfilled in us, so that through them we may become partakers of the divine nature: partakers not in unity of substance, but in participation in grace.

By changing person when he says, “he gave promises to us,” namely to the Jews, “that you Gentiles might through these become partakers of the divine nature,” he indicates that the promise was fulfilled among the Jews but that its fruit is shared also with the Gentiles [Col. 0595B].

### That faith is foundation and seal

Faith, which is the beginning of substance, must be held firmly to the end, so that it may itself be a firm foundation that can in no way be overthrown. Hence the Apostle says in the Second Epistle to Timothy: “Some have overthrown the faith. But the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal” (2 Tim. 2).

He calls faith the foundation laid by God and not by man; therefore it is called God’s. This is the foundation which no one can alter. This is the rock upon which the Church was founded. This is the foundation of the apostles and prophets, in which every building, constructed together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Eph. 2).

This foundation stands firm when, against every assault of temptations, steadfast perseverance remains unshaken and does not fail before the end. “Having this seal,” he says. The constancy of faith itself is the seal by which God has sealed us and distinguished the elect from the reprobate. Therefore those who believe for a time and withdraw in the time of temptation are not sealed with this seal. Rather, it belongs to those to whom it is said: “But you are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 22). For no surer sign of salvation appears in us than that of which it is written: “Whoever perseveres unto the end, that person shall be saved” (Matt. 10).

### That through faith we are God’s dwelling-place or temple

Upon this foundation we are built into a temple and dwelling-place of God in the Holy Spirit. Where is God’s dwelling through faith? Hear the Apostle saying in the Epistle to the Ephesians: “That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power by his Spirit in the inner person; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” [Col. 0595D] (Eph. 3).

If, therefore, strength in us is strengthened through God’s Spirit in the inner person, and if Christ dwells in us through faith, then we are the dwelling-place and temple of the living God. The foundation stands firm because Christ dwells within, the Holy Spirit strengthens power, and God seals us, as the Apostle says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “God anointed us, sealed us, and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Cor. 1).

Peter shows more clearly in his Second Epistle how faith is beginning and foundation: “But you, bringing all diligence to bear, supply in your faith virtue; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, self-restraint; in self-restraint, patience; in patience, godliness; in godliness, brotherly affection; and in brotherly affection, charity. For if these things are present in you and abound, they will not make you empty or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever does not have these things is blind and groping with his hand, having received forgetfulness of the cleansing of his former sins” [Col. 0596A] (2 Pet. 1).

When weighed by careful reflection, these words plainly declare that the whole structure of the spiritual edifice rises from faith as its beginning and foundation. The prophet Ezekiel corresponds to this, speaking of the building set on a mountain and saying: “And its ascent was by eight steps” (Ezek. 40). Explaining this parable, Peter distinguishes here eight steps of virtues: faith, virtue, knowledge, self-restraint, patience, godliness, brotherly affection, and charity.

“Supply in your faith virtue,” he says (2 Pet. 1). We should not understand this generally as every virtue. For knowledge, self-restraint, and the other things that follow are virtues. Rather, “virtue” here must be understood specifically as that virtue which aids our first endeavors against former sins, so that they may not prevail against us again and we may not again be conquered where we were conquered.

Thus virtue here is called not the only virtue, but the first virtue. The first thing in a new way of life is to flee “the corruption which is in the world through desire,” of which the same Apostle had just spoken. Of this virtue it is written in the Psalm: “You have girded me with strength for battle, and have cast beneath me those who rose up against me” (Ps. 17).

Knowledge here means not the knowledge that understands the good and neglects it, but that which approves the better things and chooses what is wholesome. This knowledge has praise and merit with God and is rightly ordered after virtue, because rejecting evil and choosing good are both virtue and knowledge. In abolishing the old life, virtue is needed; in beginning the new way of life, knowledge is especially necessary, so that after a fall we may learn to walk more cautiously.

To this is joined self-restraint, namely that by which we restrain ourselves even from certain lawful things. For that self-restraint by which unlawful things are abstained from belongs to the virtue previously mentioned. Patience is joined to these, by which the evils of the present life are borne with equanimity.

We owe these four virtues to ourselves for our own preservation, so that, avoiding evils, doing good, using this world temperately, and remaining patient amid adversities, we may be kept unstained from this age. We owe the next two virtues—godliness and brotherly affection—to our neighbors: godliness to those needing our help, but brotherly affection also to those who do not need it. For the affection of love extends to all, whereas the affection or action of godliness is bestowed on the needy.

But we owe faith and charity to God, in whom we are most strictly bound to believe and to love, alone before all things [Col. 0597A] and above all things. Faith is at the bottom; charity at the top. This is the ladder Jacob saw, whose summit reaches heaven (Gen. 28). One ascends by it who has arranged ascents in his heart, who advances through the increase of virtues and grows into a perfect man. Thus the life of the faithful is ordered upon the foundation of faith; thus the temple of God is built, if the foundation is stabilized immovably in its firmness.

### On the testing of faith

For it to be established, faith must be tested. Of this testing Peter says in his First Epistle: “Though now, if necessary, you are grieved for a little while in various temptations, so that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold—which is tested by fire—may be found unto praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” [Col. 0597B] (1 Pet. 1).

Faith is tested by temptation so that its character and measure may become known—either to others, as an example and testimony of faith, or to the one tempted, for consolation in labor, strengthening of hope, and zeal for perseverance. Before temptation, a person does not even know his own faith. Hence it is written in the book of Wisdom: “He who has not been tempted, what does he know?” (Ecclus. 34). And shortly afterward: “He who has not had experience knows little” (ibid.).

But God, who does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, makes with temptation a way of escape, that we may be able to endure it (1 Cor. 10). This outcome is the manifold benefit arising from temptation. For when the testimony of faith is rendered in tribulation through the strength of constancy, one’s neighbor is edified; within us the merit of faith is increased, confidence in making progress is strengthened more powerfully, charity is kindled more ardently, the name of God is honored more magnificently, and his mercy is made glorious and is glorified more wonderfully.

God tests faith not so that he himself may begin to know—he who knows all things before they occur—but so that he may make known in us his power, to the magnificence of his grace and glory. Yet he is said to know when he causes us to know what he deigns to reveal to us concerning ourselves. Hence the saying: “Test me, O God, and know my heart” (Ps. 138): as though saying, “By testing, make my heart known to me.”

Testing is either testing by temptation, while one not yet proved is still being tempted, or testing by commendation, when one found faithful in temptation is worthily praised. Of the former it is said: “Test me, O Lord, and tempt me” (Ps. 25). Of the latter it is written: “It is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends” [Col. 0597D] (2 Cor. 10). One is the testing of one who seeks; the other, of one who finds.

God tests differently when he seeks patience in us and when he finds patience in us. He tests differently when he examines and corrects us and when he commends us after examination and correction. Differently it is said, “Who do you think is the faithful and prudent servant?” (Matt. 24), and differently, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matt. 25). Differently it is said, “Peter, do you love me?” (John 21), and differently the answer is given, “You know, Lord, that I love you” (ibid.). Differently testing produces patience, and differently patience produces testing.

For both are written. James says: “The testing of your faith produces patience; and patience has a perfect work” (James 1). But Paul says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Tribulation produces patience; but patience produces testing” [Col. 0598A] (Rom. 5). What James says, “The testing of your faith produces patience,” is what Paul says, “Tribulation produces patience.” For tribulation is the testing of faith: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the fire of tribulation tests righteous men.”

What James says—“patience has a perfect work”—helps us understand what Paul says, “patience produces testing.” For since patience has the praise of perfect work and completed labor, the one found faithful in tribulation is shown to have been proved through patience [Col. 0598B].

### That faith and the faithful bear testimony to one another

Those who are found faithful are said to have been proved by the testimony of faith. Thus Paul, having spoken in the Epistle to the Hebrews of the temptations of the righteous of old, adds: “And all these were proved by the testimony of faith” (Heb. 11). And, speaking of faith in the same place, he says: “In this the elders obtained testimony” (ibid.).

For faith, tested in temptation, bears testimony to those who persevere that they are righteous and worthy of reward. Nevertheless, they themselves bear testimony to faith that it is true, must truly be held, and must by no means be abandoned in a time of tribulation.

### That faith and prayer aid each other reciprocally

[Col. 0598C] Faith grows in tribulation, and through suffering and prayer overcomes the weight of tribulation. Faith is aided by prayer, that it may not fail and may have strength to overcome the force of temptation; above all, by the prayer of him who said to Peter: “I will pray for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22).

Prayer, moreover, is always made in faith, both for faith itself and for whatever deliverance or consolation is obtained through faith against pressing tribulation or need.

### On the passages written in the Gospel concerning moving a mountain and the fig tree
If the power of faith thus advances through tribulation, just as the strength of mustard grows and is sharpened by crushing, no difficulty resists righteous desires; no mass of adversity, pressing us down like a mountain, [Col. 0598D] that cannot be moved by the urgency and perseverance of prayer—either so that it may pass away, or so that it may not harm us. This is what the Lord says in Matthew: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Pass from here,’ and it will pass; and nothing will be impossible for you” (Matt. XVII). Again, when they wondered that the fig tree had immediately withered, He says in the same Evangelist: “If you have faith and do not waver, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree; but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Pass away and cast yourself into the sea,’ it will happen” (Matt. XXI).

Although the power of faith may suffice to move these visible, bodily mountains, which have been placed so as to stand fixed by their great mass, if it were necessary or expedient that this be done—an example of which is related in the *Dialogues* of blessed Gregory concerning Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus—nevertheless [Col. 0599A] these words of the Lord ought rather to be understood spiritually, by those who compare spiritual things with spiritual, concerning spiritual mountains. These are moved by the greater power of faith more powerfully and wonderfully than if the immense masses of visible mountains were removed from their places.

Mountains, therefore, are the heights of vices and, conversely, the loftiness of virtues. Mountains are also the high and weighty trials and temptations. The good mountains are likewise those who excel in the sublimity of virtues, such as the apostles and others exalted by the merit of holiness. Mountains, too, are human beings or evil angels puffed up by the swelling of pride. With respect to such mountains is fulfilled what the Lord says here, and what is written in the Psalm: “The mountains shall be moved into the heart of the sea” (Ps. XLV).

Therefore, when the devil, together with the vice by which he possessed some sinner, leaves the heart of one who believes and repents after faith has been preached and received, and attacks another person in the world—which the sea signifies—then, by the power of faith, the mountain has been moved from its place and casts itself into the sea. When one who seemed to possess the greenness of good works, after truth has been preached and not received, is found fruitless or becomes manifestly worse, then the fruitless fig tree is changed into barrenness. Such was the unbelieving Synagogue: it bore no fruit and withered, deserving the curse. In each case the power of faith is recognized: when faith not received condemns the fig tree, and when faith received casts the mountain into the sea.

Beautifully, after the fig tree has been condemned, the Lord’s words show so great a power of faith as can move a mountain, [Col. 0599C] because through the faith of the apostles, which was to be preached to the world, Judaea was to be blinded, and the mountain was to be moved from its place—that is, the devil was to be expelled from Gentile lands—in such a way that he would cast himself into the sea, that is, into the depth of the Synagogue. This Synagogue was formerly dry land but is now sea, just as the Gentile world is now dry land though it formerly was sea.

What Job says while speaking of the Lord—“He moved mountains, and they did not know whom He overthrew in His anger” (Job IX)—is understood of the apostles, who are mountains, as it is written of them: “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. XXXV). The Lord moved these mountains from the Jews to the Gentiles. The Jews did not know this, being submerged in it, since they thought it a cause for joy that they had lost the light. Of these mountains thus moved to the Gentile world, one may rightly understand what was stated a little earlier and taken in another sense: “The mountains shall be moved into the heart of the sea” (Ps. XLV).

Mountains, therefore, are moved when impediments to righteous desires, and the burdens of temptations and tribulations, are removed by the help of God’s grace. Mountains are moved when holy preachers are sent away from some who are to be blinded to others who are to be enlightened by grace. Mountains are moved when demons are expelled from possessed bodies. Mountains are moved when the swollen hearts of evil persons are transferred from their places—that is, from corrupt habits. Thus mountains are also said to melt away, when the hearts of sinners, melted by repentance, dissolve like wax. Hence it is written: “The mountains melted like wax [Col. 0600A] before the face of the Lord; before the face of the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. XCVI).

Faith accomplishes these things in the conversion of sinners. The contrary commonly happens in the turning away of the good. For when faith fails in temptation, those who are or are thought to be lofty in merits fall headlong and are moved from their place. Hence Job also says: “A falling mountain melts away, and a rock is moved from its place” (Job XIV), when the purpose of holiness is abandoned under sudden temptation.

What the Lord says concerning the moving of a mountain through the power of faith is in some respect like that passage of Isaiah where it is written: “Is it not yet a very little while, and Lebanon shall be changed into Carmel, and Carmel shall be reckoned as a forest?” (Isa. XXIX). For what does this transformation of mountain into mountain, and this reckoning of mountain as forest, signify except the alternating reversal of faith and impiety in circumcision [Col. 0600B] and uncircumcision? For what was formerly uncircumcision through unbelief is now circumcision. What formerly was circumcision through the piety of faith is now uncircumcision through the change of faith.

According to Jerome on Isaiah, Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia. Carmel, called *Chermel* in Hebrew, overlooks Ptolemais on the border of Palestine and Phoenicia. Another mountain is also called Carmel in the Holy Scriptures, where Nabal the Carmelite lived. Again, on Isaiah Jerome says: “It is the idiom of the Scriptures always to compare Carmel—the excellent and wooded mountain overlooking Ptolemais, where Elijah prayed—to fertility and abundance.” Therefore this transformation of Lebanon into Chermel, and the reckoning of Chermel as a forest, is to be understood, as said above, of uncircumcision and circumcision according to the change of faith. “Where transgression abounded, grace abounded yet more” (Rom. V). Where there was then fertility, there is now found barrenness.

## That the power of faith is sometimes exercised through evil persons

So great is the power of faith that it can prevail to move mountains and command demons even through evil persons. This is shown from the Apostle’s words and the words of the Gospel. For the Apostle, commending charity to the Corinthians, says: “If I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (I Cor. XIII). Do you not see from this how faith without charity can prevail to move mountains?

In Matthew’s Gospel it is said in the person of certain people, who must certainly be understood as evil: “Have we not prophesied in your name, cast out demons, and performed many mighty works?” (Matt. VII). Luke’s Gospel shows that someone who did not follow Christ cast out a demon in His name. John said to Jesus: “Lord, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he does not follow us” (Luke IX). Jesus said to them: “Do not forbid him; for whoever is not against us is for us” (ibid.).

See what faith can do even through evil persons who, invoking Christ’s name, cast out demons. They would not invoke Him unless they believed, as it is written: “How shall they call upon Him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. X). But if those who cast out demons in Christ’s name did not believe, nor invoke Christ’s name [Col. 0601A] from faith, but merely named Christ in order to test the power of His name, then the power which followed should be attributed to that name: it was able to command demons even though it was invoked not from faith but merely named for trial. This cannot be ascribed to their faith, if those who did it did not believe.

## The power of faith shown by the powerlessness of unbelief

The power of faith exercised against the malice of demons is also shown by the contrary powerlessness of unbelief. In Matthew, where a father presented his moon-struck son, he said to Jesus: “I brought him to your disciples, and they could not cure him” (Luke IX). When he had been cured and the demon cast out, the disciples asked, “Why could we not cast it out?” Jesus said to them: “Because of your unbelief” (ibid.). Those who could not do so because of unbelief are shown to have been able to do so if they had believed. Therefore the Lord immediately adds: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Pass from here,’ and it will pass; and no word will be impossible” (Matt. XVII).

## Whether the power of signs is always joined to faith

In many passages the Lord commends faith as though the power of working signs were always inseparably joined to it. In one place He says: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes” (Mark IX). Elsewhere in Mark He says: “These signs shall follow those who believe” (Mark XVI), and so forth. Again, in John He says: “He who believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John XIV).

These and similar words concerning the power of faith seem to be spoken by the Lord as though one who believes can do everything, and as though one who cannot do everything does not believe. Yet it is plain and credible that faith has been given to many to whom the power of miracles has not been given. Many prophets performed no signs, among them John the Baptist, who was not merely a prophet but more than a prophet. Of him it is written in John’s Gospel: “Many came to Jesus and said, ‘John indeed performed no sign’” (John X). They seem to have said this in wonder, as though it had been worthy of great astonishment that a man of such holiness performed no sign.

Those who are to become enemies of the faith are shown to possess the power of signs [Col. 0601D] by the Lord’s statement in Matthew’s Gospel: “False Christs and false prophets will arise, and will give signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. XXIV). The Apostle, speaking in the Epistle to the Thessalonians of the son of perdition, says: “The Lord will destroy him by the brightness of His coming, him whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in all power and signs and lying wonders, and in every deceit of iniquity” (II Thess. II). It says “lying wonders” because they will be performed to deceive, so that falsehood may be believed; or because they will not be true signs but appearances. For perhaps he will perform certain false signs, that he may deceive by whatever means. This seems indicated by the Apostle’s added words: “in every deceit of iniquity.”

## That faith and prayer have a similar commendation

[Col. 0602A]

If, therefore, faith is bestowed without the power of signs, and the power of signs has been and will be bestowed without faith, what is the point of this so great and emphatic commendation of faith? But we must observe that in many places prayer receives a similar commendation. The Lord says to His disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, He will give it to you” (John XVI). In Mark’s Gospel: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it shall come to you” (Mark XXI). In Matthew’s Gospel: “If two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

Observe from these words that divine things are accessible to one who prays, just as all things are said to be possible to one who believes. Faith and prayer are known to possess similar power, and each is in turn assisted by the other. Thus in Mark, when the Lord shows His disciples the power of faith, He immediately adds the power of prayer and shows it joined with faith by a certain likeness, saying: “Have faith in God. Amen, I say to you: whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast into the sea,’ and does not waver in his heart but believes that what he says will happen, it will happen for him. Therefore I say to you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you will receive it, and it shall come to you” (Mark II). Consider from these words how powerful faith is to bring about all things which are spoken without wavering; and how equally powerful prayer is to bring about all things which are asked in faith.

## Whether it is within our power not to waver concerning impossibilities

But someone will say: Who can tell this mountain, without wavering, “Be lifted up and cast into the sea”? Does it not seem equally impossible not to waver about this as to do it? But if both—doing this and not wavering about it—belong not to our power but to divine power, such a promise may seem unworthy of God: He promises that a mountain will be moved by speech alone if there is no wavering in speaking, whereas wavering itself, so far as lies in our power, is as immovable from our heart as this mountain is from its place.

What, then, shall we say to this? Did the Lord mean to show that impossible things can be done through the power [Col. 0602D] of faith and prayer if our wavering does not oppose them? Or is even wavering concerning an impossible matter, after God’s promise, not without our own fault, if this too is a hardness of our heart? Are we powerless to do impossible things because we are slow in faith to believe them? After the Lord has said, “All things are possible to one who believes, and nothing is impossible for him” (Mark IX), ought there to be such certainty of this saying that every wavering concerning its truth must be called an imperfection of faith?

If wavering concerning impossibilities is an imperfection of faith, how much more so is wavering concerning possibilities? If wavering in faith concerning impossibilities is an imperfection of faith, which saint, placed in this weakness of the flesh, cannot say: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX)? Who is there who does not sometimes waver? Who is there who does not need his faith to be increased? For the apostles too asked for their faith to be increased. Thus it is written in Luke’s Gospel: “The apostles said to the Lord, ‘Increase our faith.’ And the Lord said, ‘If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, “Be uprooted and transplanted into the sea,” and it would obey you’” (Luke XVII).

By these words the Lord seems to approve and commend the holy desire of the apostles. For since the Lord had said shortly before, “It is impossible that scandals should not come” (Matt. XVIII), the apostles, desiring their faith to be increased so that, being strong in faith, they might not yield to scandals, heard from the Lord what has here been said of the mustard seed and the mulberry tree—as though He said to them: You rightly desire faith to be increased, because if, amid scandals, it is increased so as to be like a grain which gains greater power through crushing, then by its power this tree can be uprooted and transplanted into the sea. Hence it ought to be certain that scandals cannot prevail against it.

Mystically, this tree, whose fruit is red with blood, can signify Christ, to be reddened with the blood of His Passion. When persecution was raging, against the faith of the apostles—which was to grow through crushing like mustard—He was to be transferred from the Synagogue to the Gentile world, as a tree uprooted from the earth and wondrously transplanted into the sea. For this transplantation to occur, the apostles’ faith had necessarily to be increased against the scandals which, as the Lord foretold, could not fail to arise.

Christ thus signifies Himself through this mulberry tree, just as He signified Himself through this rock when He said: “You are Peter, and upon this Rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI), and through this temple when He said: “Destroy this temple” (John II). Therefore, instructed by the example of the apostles, who asked that their faith be increased against coming scandals, we too always need, while we walk by faith, to pray and say: “Lord, increase our faith” (Luke XVII), lest we fail when tempted by wavering. Moses was assailed by this temptation at the waters of contradiction; the apostles too were assailed, when, because of their unbelief, they could not cast out the demon from the moon-struck man, although the Lord had given them authority [Col. 0603D] to heal the sick and cast out demons.

We too are assailed by this temptation, though not concerning the performance of signs as they were. Yet we are tempted by wavering amid many pressing needs which drive us, amid many difficulties which draw us back from the good, amid many impediments to good purpose or holy desire, amid many dangers to our life and salvation. Although the Lord promises us His help, although He says that not even a hair of our head will perish and says this to make us secure, who nevertheless is altogether firm in faith and secure everywhere? Who always stands firm? Who does not sometimes totter? Who never wavers?

Accordingly, since we have scarcely even a small faith, we need our faith to be increased; and we are always bound to offer God a confession of faith and to beseech Him without ceasing to help our unbelief, saying: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark IX). “Help my unbelief” is said in the same way as the Apostle says, “The Spirit helps our weakness” (Rom. VIII), and the Prophet says, “My God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. XVII). He enlightens darkness when He gives us understanding of what we understand too little. He helps weakness when He gives us power for what we are too weak to do. He helps unbelief when He makes us believe what we believe too little.

## That the power of signs does not make holiness, but shows it

[Col. 0604B] Faith, therefore, is always to be sought from God, not the power of signs. Faith justifies us; the power of signs sometimes displays holiness, but never produces it without faith. Let those who believe and do not perform signs not become fainthearted when they read, “John performed no sign” (John X). Let those who perform signs not become proud on that account, since the Lord says: “False Christs and false prophets will arise and will give great signs” (Matt. XXIV). Let those who perform signs not glory, lest perhaps, puffed up, they fall into the judgment of the devil. Let them heed what is written in Luke’s Gospel: “The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.’ And He said to them, ‘I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven’” (Luke X). And below: “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you” (ibid.).

## On vain security

But he who tempts, and who himself fell through pride, seeks to seduce by the presumption of security those whom he cannot deceive by the wavering of faintheartedness. Therefore many, not through the piety of faith but through the security of rashness, boldly attempt arduous and impossible things, though it is written: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. VI). Thus they are unwilling to avoid dangers which they could avoid, while arrogantly believing themselves worthy persons whom evils cannot harm. And because they will great things, measuring strength by willingness and failing to recognize their weakness, they believe themselves able to do what they know themselves willing to do.

Thus Peter, not understanding his weakness but considering his own willingness, presumed and said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. XVI). Later he was afraid and denied Him. In both cases he was tempted: here by the wavering of faintheartedness, there by the presumption of excessive security. We too experience both temptations of faith within ourselves: now vainly fearful, now vainly secure; now failing through faintheartedness, now presuming through security. This is the wonderful dispensation of God, by which He permits His elect to fall for a time, that they may rise stronger, become more cautious, trust less in themselves, know their weakness more perfectly, cling more firmly to God, and hold His grace—without which they can do nothing—in greater esteem.

## How all things are possible to one who believes

[Col. 0605A]

Since many people, being unbelieving, tempted by wavering or presumption, and hindered in other ways, can neither perform signs nor obtain everything they desire, it is rightly asked how the Lord’s saying is to be understood: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes” (Mark VII). But Jesus, who said, “If you ask the Father anything in my name, He will give it to you” (John XVI), resolves this question by showing that those things are to be given us by the Father which we ask in His name—that is, in the name Jesus. These are the things beneficial to us, useful for our advancement, and suited to our salvation. These are the things expedient for us to receive and the only things we ought to ask for.

Therefore all things are possible [Col. 0605B] to one who believes when the power of faith and prayer extends to everything that is rightly desired and beneficially requested. One who believes has power for all these things in Him who can do all things. Hence the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Philippians: “I can do all things in Him who strengthens me” (Phil. IV). Thus all things are possible to one who believes, because believers can do all things in God. Nor only this: God too can do all things concerning believers. But not so concerning unbelievers. For the benefits of God are sometimes hindered by the sin of unbelief, so that God is in some sense said not to be able to do what He is prevented from doing by unbelief.

Hence it is written in Mark’s Gospel: “Jesus went to His own country; and He could not perform many mighty works there, except that He healed a few sick people by laying His hands upon them; and He marveled because of their unbelief” (Mark VI). “He could not,” it says, because their sins prevented God’s grace from reaching them, according to Jeremiah’s words: “Our sins have withheld good things from us” (Jer. V). “He marveled,” it says, because He showed that we should marvel at their great unbelief, on account of which He could not perform signs there.

## On the text: “These signs shall follow those who believe”

What is written—“These signs shall follow those who believe” (Mark XVI)—if understood literally, concerns not all believers generally but certain persons specifically, especially those to whom, at the beginning of the nascent Church, the power to perform mighty works was given, so that those who would not otherwise come to faith might receive faith through signs. For those who proclaimed new things had fittingly to perform new things, with the Lord cooperating and confirming the word through the signs that followed.

But when faith had been received far and wide, and the novelty of signs had confirmed it, signs, being less necessary, began to cease. A multitude of witnesses and the testimonies of peoples succeeded them; these could suffice in place of and before signs for the affirmation of faith. Hence the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers; prophecy, however, is not for unbelievers but for believers” (I Cor. XIV).

This too must be understood spiritually: “He who believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these” (John XIV). [Col. 0606A] The phrase “will do greater works than these” can be understood in two ways: either, “He will do the greatest things that I have done,” or, “He will do greater things than I have done.” If it concerns greater things, the healing effected by Peter’s shadow seems greater, and that effected by the hem of Christ’s garment lesser.

Although faith is shared by more people than is the power to perform bodily signs, those who cannot visibly perform signs outwardly nevertheless work wonders inwardly through faith. Hence it is written: “Blessed is the man who has been found without blemish, who has not gone after gold or placed hope in treasures of money. Who is he? We shall praise him; for he performed wonders in his life” (Ecclus. XXXI). Those who live wondrously in Christ, surely, perform wonders in their life. For it is greater than performing signs to live without blemish amid the corruptions of this life. It is greater not to desire gold and to extinguish within oneself worldly covetousness than to heal a dropsical man. It is greater to avoid the leprosy of the mind and the vices of the soul than to cure bodily diseases. It is greater for one hardened by the habit of sinning to rise through repentance than to raise from the dead one who has been dead four days.

All the righteous work these spiritual signs through faith. Compared with bodily signs, they are found greater and are judged worthy of greater wonder. Both these and those signs are wrought by God, wonderful in His saints, who always works wonders in one way or another, renewing signs and changing marvels.

## What is wondrous concerning faith

Faith itself is not a work of human ability but of divine power and will, [Col. 0606C] and among God’s wonderful works it occasions great astonishment. For who, contemplating and carefully weighing the incomprehensible mysteries of faith, does not marvel that they can be believed, since they surpass all sense and transcend every reasoning of human wisdom? Who can believe things so marvelous, profound, and unsearchable unless power to believe is given from above? Who does not marvel concerning faith itself that it is given to some and not to others; and that among those to whom it is given, it is given to some through signs and to others without signs?

Likewise, among those to whom it is not given, it is withheld from some amid signs and from others without signs. Some saw signs and believed; others saw them and did not believe; some did not see and believed; others neither saw nor believed. Since all signs are performed either through faith or for faith, faith itself is more wonderful than the signs that are performed around us or within us.

It is also marvelous that signs were displayed to some who saw them and refused to believe, while they were not displayed to others who might have believed had they seen them. Hence it is written in Matthew’s Gospel: “Then He began to reproach the cities in which most of His mighty works had been performed, because they had not repented, saying: ‘Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida. For if the mighty works which were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Yet I say to you: it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you perhaps be exalted to heaven? You will descend to hell. [Col. 0607A] For if the mighty works performed in you had been performed in Sodom, they might perhaps have remained until this day. Yet I say to you that it will be more tolerable for the land of the Sodomites on the day of judgment than for you’” (Matt. XI). Who does not marvel in these things at God’s hidden justice? Who is fit to investigate them? But let us refrain from seeking what God has not willed to reveal.

## How the Lord commends the faith of some

We should also observe that the Lord commends the faith of some before a healing takes place, but that of others after the healing has occurred. Sometimes He requires faith, or even a confession of faith, before healing. He also performs some signs on account of another’s faith, and some on account of a person’s own faith.

Commending the centurion’s faith, He says: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. VIII). Then He adds: “Go, and as you desire, so let it be done to you” (ibid.). Here the commendation of faith comes first, and the healing of the servant subsequently follows from the Lord, through the support of another’s faith and intercession. But the question arises how the Lord could say that He had not found such great faith in Israel. Who indeed would dare prefer the centurion’s faith to the faith of Jacob and the prophets? And if the matter concerns the people of that time, who would dare prefer it to the faith of John the Baptist or the blessed Virgin, of whom it is written: “Blessed are you who believed, because those things which were spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled” (Luke I)?

But this seems to be understood of the greater part of the Israelite people of that time, since among those to whom the oracles of God had been entrusted, greater faith ought to have been found than in a Gentile man. He came to faith when Christ called him inwardly, without law and prophets, and prefigured the faith of the Gentiles. The centurion’s faith, therefore, is itself the faith of the Gentiles; compared with Israel’s faith, it is found greater in that its calling is more wonderful and its multitude of believers more abundant. Hence the Evangelist prefaces the account: “Jesus, hearing this, marveled” (Mark VIII), and adds: “I have not found such great faith in Israel” (ibid.). Jesus is described as having marveled precisely in order that, from His wonder, the calling of the centurion—that is, of the Gentiles—may be shown to us worthy of great amazement.

In Matthew it is written concerning the paralytic: “They brought Him a paralytic lying on a bed. [Col. 0607D] And Jesus, seeing their faith, said to the paralytic: ‘Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you’” (Matt. IX). Observe here what another’s faith can accomplish. It so benefited the paralytic that “Take courage, son” was said to him, in order that, taking courage through faith, he might gain for himself the name of son, and forgiveness of sins might immediately follow. If this was said to one who did not yet believe, he was admonished to begin; if to one who already believed, he was admonished to persevere.

So it was said to the woman suffering from an issue of blood: “Take courage, daughter”; and it is added, “Your faith has made you well” (ibid.). Here is shown what one’s own faith can accomplish. Similarly, in Luke, the sinful woman in the Pharisee’s house is told: “Your faith has made you well” (Luke VII). To the two blind men crying, “Have mercy on us, Son of David,” [Col. 0608A] Jesus said: “Do you believe that I can do this for you?” They said to Him, “Certainly, Lord.” Then He touched their eyes, saying: “According to your faith let it be done to you” (Matt. IX), and their eyes were opened. Here He requires a confession of faith from those who believe. Having heard it, He commands that it be done for them according to their faith.

To the Canaanite woman He says: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you have asked” (Matt. XV), and her daughter was healed from that hour. Observe here too that the daughter is healed by the mother’s faith, which is proclaimed great for the reason stated above concerning the centurion’s faith. In Luke He says to the ruler of the Synagogue concerning his dead daughter: “Do not fear; only believe, and she shall be saved” (Luke VIII). Here He requires faith, which He shows alone sufficient for salvation to follow. In John, when Martha, Lazarus’s sister, said, “Lord, by now he stinks, for he has been dead four days,” Jesus said to her: “Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?” (John XI). From the preceding examples observe how mercifully the Lord invites some to faith and how magnificently He commends the faith of others.

## How the Lord rebukes unbelief and shows that it displeases Him

Observe from other passages how He rebukes unbelief and shows that it displeases Him. In Mark, when they watched Jesus to see whether He would heal on the Sabbath a man with a withered hand, so that they might accuse Him, it is written: “Looking around at them in anger, grieved at the blindness of their hearts, [Col. 0608C] He said to the man: ‘Stretch out your hand’” (Mark III). In the same Gospel, when one of the crowd said, “Teacher, I brought my son to you, who has a mute spirit; and I told your disciples to cast it out, but they could not” (Mark IX), He answered them: “O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you?” (ibid.). Again, in the same Gospel: “As the eleven reclined at table, He appeared to them, and reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they did not believe those who had seen Him risen” (Mark XVI).

## That faith is seed

From the parables in which Christ spoke, the power, growth, and failure of faith, and the diversity of believers, are shown to us by analogy. “A sower,” He says, “went out to sow his seed” (Luke VIII). The seed is the word of God—that is, the word of faith. The seed beside the road, which the birds of heaven eat, is the word of faith when it is preached but not received, the devil working to prevent belief. The seed upon the rock, which sprang up and withered, is the faith of those who believe for a time but fall away in time of temptation. The seed among thorns is the faith of those who are choked by the thorns of anxieties concerning riches and the pleasures of life. The seed in good ground is faith with patience in the hearts of those who do not live barren lives but bear fruit.

Conversely, the tares are heresies, schisms, and scandals, which the enemy—the devil—sowed over the field while people were asleep. For through negligence in life and doctrine [Col. 0609A] the devil does not cease to stir up these things to overthrow faith.

## That faith is a grain of mustard seed

Faith is a grain of mustard seed, the least of all seeds. But when it has grown, it is greater than all herbs and becomes a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches (Matt. XIII). The seeds and herbs are the doctrines of philosophers, human traditions, that is, plantings which the heavenly Father has not planted. Compared with these, the simplicity of faith seems contemptible. But when it has grown in the multitude of believers, it is raised on high through the mystery of the cross, like a tree, so that the righteous may dwell in its protection.

## That faith is leaven
[Col. 0609B] Faith is the leaven of divine righteousness, which a woman takes and hides in three measures of flour, until the whole is leavened (ibid.). This woman is understood as the faithful soul; the three measures of flour are the three gifts which, by God’s gift, we received in our created condition: the ability to do good, knowledge of the good, and the will to do good. From these is made the bread of life and understanding, by which those who hunger for righteousness are satisfied. Yet these things in us have been corrupted by the stain of sin, as though by the leaven of malice and wickedness. For the ability to do good without difficulty, knowledge of the good without error, and the will to do good without sluggishness, have been changed into their opposites in relation to those things which are good and useful to us—either by deprivation or by diminution.

By deprivation, indeed, with respect to those good things which, owing to the weakness of the flesh, we are altogether unable to do; or which, owing to the blindness of the mind, we altogether fail to know; or which, owing to perversity of will, we altogether refuse to will. [Col. 0609C] By diminution, however, with respect to those good things which we can do less freely, know less fully, or will too lukewarmly. This is what our corruption does: in place of the ability for good, it brings upon us impossibility or difficulty. Therefore, in place of knowledge of the good, it introduces ignorance or lack of discernment. In place of the will for good, it pours in weariness of good, or even hatred. Consequently, neither strength, nor knowledge, nor will is available to us for loving the good as it ought to be loved.

How can we love the good as we ought, unless we worthily love God himself, the author of good? In him and for whose sake all good things are to be loved; he himself is to be loved in all things and before all things, [Col. 0609D] because all things are from him, through him, and in him. You love him worthily if you love him as much as you will, know, and are able to love anything. For this is to love with the whole heart; this is to love with the whole soul, the whole mind, and the whole strength. This is to love with the whole will, the whole discernment, and the whole capacity. But how can this happen unless the woman receives from God the leaven of faith and hides what she has received in the bosom of her conscience, so that by faith’s fervour strength may be restored, the light of knowledge may return, and the enkindled will may grow warm again, until the whole is leavened and Christ is loved with the whole heart?

### That Christ, or faith in Christ, is a treasure and a good pearl

Christ is the treasure hidden in a field, [Col. 0610A] that is, in a heart to be cultivated with every care. That person finds this field who returns from concern for the world to concern for himself. He hides the treasure once found who thereby aims to please God alone. He sells everything and buys the field who, through the commerce of faith, leaves everything behind and recovers his own heart to possess it himself. Thus he buys his own heart who despises external things, just as he sells his soul who loves in preference to his inward things.

Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Nothing is more wicked than to love money. For such a man has his own soul for sale, because in his lifetime he has cast away his inward parts” (Ecclus. 10). When the field has been bought, the treasure hidden in the field is possessed: for, once possession of the heart has been gained and the treasure of money abandoned, a better treasure is held within—namely, the good pearl, which is acquired by selling everything; [Col. 0610B] for by contempt for earthly things, love for Christ is perfected. Faith itself also is a hidden treasure and a good pearl, acquired by selling everything; for the more perfectly that which one possesses is relinquished, the more perfectly Christ himself is possessed.

### That the Church, or faith, is a dragnet
