But because not all who in some manner have faith possess such fervour and strength of faith that they are willing to leave everything—since many do not even wish to renounce unlawful things—the kingdom of heaven, which is the Church, is rightly compared to a dragnet. Cast into the sea of this age, under the one confession of faith and profession of the Christian name, it draws good and bad alike to the shore, that is, to the end of life [Col. 0610C].

For in the Church there are good and bad alike who have faith: some possess it unto salvation, others to their own harm. Those who possess it to their own harm are those who, having recognized the truth, do not stand in the truth but turn back. For, as Peter says in the Second Catholic Epistle: “It would have been better not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment which was delivered to them” (2 Pet. 2).

### That those who have faith unto salvation leave everything, or renounce everything

Those who desire to have faith unto salvation must renounce everything if they are to be Christ’s disciples. He says: “Every one of you who has not renounced all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” [Col. 0610D] (Luke 14). But it is one thing to leave everything and another to renounce everything. The first belongs to the perfect, who, with the Apostle, count all things loss for Christ so that they may gain Christ; who, abstaining even from lawful things and wishing to have nothing in this world, can say with Peter: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matt. 19). To one wishing to undertake the way of this perfection it is said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (ibid.).

When he says, “If you wish to be perfect,” he leaves the matter to the will; he does not impose necessity. But when he says, “Whoever has not renounced all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14), he binds us by a necessity through which we are compelled to renounce everything if we wish to be his disciples. Therefore the rich, [Col. 0611A] who, according to the Apostle’s counsel, know not to be high-minded nor to place hope in the uncertainty of riches; who strive to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share; to store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on eternal life—such persons are not outside the number of Christ’s disciples.

They must therefore be understood to renounce everything, though not to leave everything. For they renounce everything in respect of unlawful gain and unlawful use, which they condemn in all things, since they are resolved neither to acquire from unlawful sources nor to employ things acquired for unlawful uses. They use this world as though not using it: clinging neither to transient things nor wishing to retain passing goods, but readily giving [Col. 0611B] and sharing with their neighbour for Christ’s sake; they set Christ before all things and love him more ardently than all things.

### That faith conquers the world in the good

Both groups, whether those who leave everything perfectly or those who less perfectly renounce everything, conquer the world by faith. I mean that world of which John says in the Catholic Epistle: “Do not love the world, nor the things which are in the world. For everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). This is the world of which it is written: “The world lies in evil” (1 John 5); and, “The world did not know him” (John 1)—undoubtedly, God.

But Christ, who said, “Take courage, for I have conquered the world” (John [Col. 0611C] 16), also conquered the ruler of this world, so that we who believe in him may, through faith in his victory, conquer the world as well. “For this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5). Yet faith is not our victory, but Christ’s. For Christ conquered the world and its ruler in such a way that he triumphed over us and subjected us to himself through faith. Therefore our faith is the devil’s confusion and Christ’s victory. It is plainly evident that faith conquers the world in those who obey faith and by faith overcome the world’s desire.

### How faith conquers the world also in the wicked

But how does faith conquer the world in Jews, pagans, and heretics who oppose it and always persecute it with their tongues and, when able, with their swords? [Col. 0611D] How does faith conquer the world in false brethren and pretended Christians, who profess to know God but deny him by their deeds? Does it conquer all: both those whom it overcomes by subjecting them to itself and those whom it convicts by their resistance to it? Certainly so.

For Christ says of the Paraclete: “When he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment: concerning sin, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no longer; concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged” (John 16). Three things accumulate the condemnation of unbelievers: the sin of their own unbelief, by which they do not believe in Christ; the righteousness of those who rightly believe, which is despised by those who do not imitate them; and the judgment of the devil, which the unbelieving do not heed.

This is the judgment [Col. 0612A] of which it is written: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12). In conversion to faith the ruler of the world is judged, whether by Christ, by whom he is cast out, or by those themselves who are converted to faith when they renounce the devil altogether. The life of the righteous and the devil’s expulsion bear witness for faith that it is true, accepted by God, and opposed to the devil. Because unbelievers do not heed this, they are to be condemned not only for the guilt of this offence, because they do not believe, but also by the testimony of faith—that is, by the life of the righteous and the casting out of the devil—which they do not believe.

For just as the devil’s dominion among the wicked, and their unrighteousness by which they live wickedly, increase the merit of the good, who, though tempted to evil by their example, are not deceived; so the devil’s expulsion and the righteousness of the godly [Col. 0612B] increase the judgment of the wicked unto evil, because, though urged by examples toward better things, they do not imitate the righteous. The unrighteousness of the wicked harms the wicked themselves and benefits the good. For the temptation of the good is conquered when it is despised. Righteousness, conversely, benefits those who possess it and harms those who do not imitate it. It is an incitement to emulation, an example toward salvation, and a judgment unto condemnation.

Hence it is written in Matthew: “The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching; and behold, one greater than Jonah is here. The queen of the south shall rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it,” and so forth; “and behold, one greater than Solomon is here” (Matt. 12). You see that the world is convicted concerning righteousness. If concerning righteousness, then also concerning faith, for righteousness [Col. 0612C] is from faith (Rom. 10). For it is written: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. 1).

Christ took care to indicate this when he said: “Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no longer” (John 16). It is as though he said: “When my bodily visibility is withdrawn by my ascent to the Father, it remains that, through that same ascent, I should be believed in the world to be equal to the Father; through faith in my equality with the Father, believers are to be made righteous.” For faith in Christ’s equality with the Father, made known through the Ascension, is the cause of the righteousness by which those who believe in Christ live devoutly in him. This righteousness will be a testimony against those who despise faith in Christ or neglect the righteousness which is from faith.

But the devil’s expulsion, which is his judgment, is made known [Col. 0612D] through confession of Christ. Those who reject that confession in unbelief are to be convicted concerning the devil’s judgment, because in his judgment, which is his expulsion, they do not acknowledge Christ’s honour and the devil’s humiliation. Therefore the devil’s judgment, made manifest to the world by the confession of believers, will be a testimony against unbelievers, so that those who refuse to believe other believers may rightly be convicted.

Faith therefore conquers the world even in those who do not believe, or in believers who live wickedly, because the Paraclete Spirit will convict them for not possessing the faith through which the ungodly person is made righteous and the devil is cast out. But faith conquers the world in those who never conquer faith, though they always attack it. For all their efforts against faith are frustrated and reduced to nothing, because “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16).

### That faith has praise and glory by comparison with impiety

Because good things always become clearer in contrast with evil things, faith, considered in this respect, possesses not only the glory of praise from its own virtue, but also a more abundant grace of commendation by comparison with impiety. Thus the serenity of the heavens pleases by its own beauty, but it pleases still more after the horror of a violent storm. The light of day shines more agreeably after black darkness. You will find the same principle in other contraries as well, one evil and the other good.

Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Good is opposed to evil, and life to death; so also the sinner to the righteous man. And thus look upon all the works of the Most High: two against two, one against one” [Col. 0613B] (Ecclus. 33). Therefore, whether two goods are set against two evils in comparison, or one against one, evil does not diminish the grace of good; rather, it commends it more magnificently and increases it more abundantly. Thus impiety, by opposition, exercises and increases faith; by comparison, commends and adorns it; by persecution, endows it with grace and glory. Faith, when it suffers contradiction, advances; when it undergoes comparison, it is greatly afraid; when it endures persecutions, it is loved more graciously and crowned more gloriously.

### God wonderfully blinds some and enlightens others

Impiety, therefore, not only harms unbelievers but also benefits believers; and while it is for some a cause of destruction, for others it is turned into an occasion of salvation. Hence the Apostle says of the Jews who stumbled at Christ: “Did they stumble so as to fall? By no means! But through their offence salvation has come to the Gentiles” (Rom. 11). It is as though he said: Their offence did not merely have the effect that they themselves should stumble and fall, but also that through their fall the Gentiles should believe. For their offence is the riches of the world, their diminution the riches of the Gentiles, and their loss the reconciliation of the world.

It is indeed wondrous why God, whose nature is goodness, blinds, hardens, and condemns some. It is wondrous also why he, who could by just judgment destroy all, enlightens some, changes them from hardness of heart, and saves them. But more wondrous than either is why [Col. 0613D] he condemns or saves these rather than those. Yet in the profound depth of so astounding a wonder, what else can we do but cry out and say with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (ibid.).

He who divided light from darkness himself knows why he condemns or saves this person rather than that. But he has not granted us to know this, nor permitted us to investigate it. Rather, he has revealed in the Holy Scriptures what we must believe: that, since the whole mass of the human race is corrupt and liable to deserved condemnation, no one is delivered from it except by gratuitous mercy, and no one is condemned except by the most righteous judgment of justice.

### On witnesses against faith and for faith

Since faith is not everyone’s possession, but many believe and many do not believe, it follows that faith itself endures much contradiction from those who do not believe, so that even among those called faithful many are found wavering, who are not ashamed to say: “We do not know whom we ought rather to believe: those who defend faith, or those who contradict faith.” For just as many are strengthened in faith by the multitude of believers, so many are weakened in faith or confirmed in error by the number and example of unbelievers.

All unbelievers are witnesses of their own error against the truth of faith, just as all believers are witnesses of faith against the impious unbelief of faithlessness. But a comparison of the witnesses will plainly show whom one should believe more. For the impiety of unbelievers is divided against itself by its own contrariety, whereas faith is made firm within itself by indivisible unity. There is one faith which steadfastly resists many varied errors. But the variety of errors, divided manifoldly within itself, does not abide in the simplicity of unity.

For those who contradict the true faith judge what they do not know from their own hearts and invent from their own understanding what they devise; and, since one thing seems right to some and another to others, those who hold contrary views disagree among themselves. Yet the enemies of faith, while opposing one another and being enemies to our enemies, act on our behalf and fight with us for truth whenever they condemn falsehood with us in some respect. Nevertheless, insofar as they err, they fight against us. Even in this, though unknowingly and unwillingly, they serve our advancement; for faith advances through persecution, grows through tribulation, and shines more brightly through contradiction. The stronger the conflict, the more glorious the victory; the more the contention of unbelievers prevails, the more brightly the glory of believers shines.

While heretics oppose, our people are exercised; the elect are tested, so that those who have been tested may become manifest and not remain hidden. Hence the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11). And the Psalmist says: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples, that those proved by silver may be excluded” (Ps. 67). Therefore contention against faith is useful to believers. For by it believers are tested and the tested are made manifest, so that, tested and made manifest, they may be found and recognized as worthy and unquestionable witnesses of faith.

### That three bear witness in heaven and three on earth

[Col. 0614D]

If the witnesses of faith and their testimonies are brought forward and examined more carefully, they will show us most plainly how great is the authority of faith and how certain, firm, and solid its truth is. John says in the Catholic Epistle: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood” (1 John 5).

The Father bears witness in heaven: he who formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets and, in these last days, has spoken to us in the Son. He bears witness when he reveals the Son in the Scriptures; he bears witness when he reveals the Son in us. Paul says of this revelation: “He who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, that he might reveal his Son in me” [Col. 0615A] (Gal. 1). And the Lord said to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood have not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16).

“Flesh and blood,” he says, “have not revealed it”: that is, not the tradition of parents—namely, mother and father—not carnal wisdom, not the natural man, but the heavenly Father. Surely the mother may be signified by flesh and the father by blood, because the father supplies seed and the woman is understood as the man’s flesh. Hence the saying in the Gospel: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man” (John 1). By “flesh” may also be signified the sense of the flesh, that is, any bodily sense. Since the soul is in the blood, the soul—or the soul’s faculty of perception—may not improperly be understood by “blood.” But the mystery of faith is not perceived through sensory experience or comprehended by the soul’s perception; rather, it is known through the Father’s revelation. Therefore it was rightly said: “Flesh and blood have not revealed it, but the Father who is in heaven.”

The Father bears witness when, as Jesus was baptized and came up from the water, the heavens were opened and a voice from heaven was heard saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). And again, at the Transfiguration: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 17). Peter says in the Catholic Epistle concerning this voice: “Such a voice came to him from the magnificent glory: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’; and we ourselves heard this voice when we were with him on the holy mountain” (2 Pet. 1).

The Lord himself likewise says of the Father’s testimony in John’s Gospel: “The Father who sent me has himself borne witness concerning me” (John 5). And John says in the Catholic Epistle: “If we receive the testimony of human beings, the testimony of God is greater. For this is God’s testimony, which is greater: that he has borne witness concerning his Son” (1 John 5).

The Son bears witness by teaching, by performing signs, and by making known who he himself was. Thus, when he said, “I am the light of the world,” and the Pharisees said to him, “You bear witness about yourself; your testimony is not true,” he answered: “Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, because [Col. 0615D] I know where I come from and where I am going” (John 8). Again he says: “It is written in your law that the testimony of two men is true. I am one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me.”

But when he says, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (ibid.), this must be understood to mean that his glory would be nothing if, without the Father’s testimony, he glorified himself as most people usually do. Lest this be believed of him, he immediately adds: “My Father is the one who glorifies me, he of whom you say, ‘He is our God’; and you have not known him” (ibid.). Likewise, the saying, “If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true” (John 5), must be understood, certainly, as meaning “without the Father’s testimony.” Therefore he immediately adds: “There is another who bears witness concerning me, and I know that the testimony which he bears concerning me is true” [Col. 0616A] (ibid.).

The Son bears witness, when death is imminent, by not denying the truth. Thus Paul says in the First Epistle to Timothy: “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who under Pontius Pilate rendered the good confession, that you keep the commandment unstained and irreproachable until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Tim. 6). The Son bears witness by rising again and, after the resurrection, revealing himself by many proofs. The Son bears witness by ascending to the Father and returning to the Father while the disciples watched, as it is written: “While they were watching, he was lifted up” (Acts 1).

The Holy Spirit bears witness when, from the beginning, he is borne over the waters, later to sanctify the waters and himself to become through water the author of sanctification for nature. He bears witness when he inspires prophets, foretells future things, and prefigures mysteries. For through the utterances of prophets and figures of things he signified that the way of the saints had not yet been made manifest but would be made manifest in its own times. He bears witness when he chooses and anoints kings and priests, foreshadowing Christ’s kingship and priesthood.

In the New Testament he bears witness when, coming upon the Blessed Virgin, he sanctifies and impregnates her; when he rests upon Christ and descends from heaven upon him like a dove and remains. He bears witness when, appearing over the disciples, he distributes tongues of fire and unites languages in the unity of believers. He bears witness when he himself is given to believers, when he himself distributes the gifts of graces, when each believer receives his own gift—one in this manner and another in that manner; when, according to varieties of graces, varieties of ministries, and varieties of workings, to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills [Col. 0616C] (1 Cor. 12).

He bears witness when he is sent to testify by teaching all things, suggesting the truth, and announcing things to come. Hence Christ says in John’s Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15). Again: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and remind you of all that I have said to you” (John 14). And again: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you things to come” (John 16).

Therefore there are three in heaven who bear witness: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one: one, indeed, in the essence of one nature; one in the concord of one testimony. For they speak concordantly one and the same thing, and work concordantly. There are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit, water, and blood [Col. 0617A] (1 John 5).

It has been shown how the Creator Spirit bears witness: he is always in heaven, even when he is sent to us from heaven. But created spirit bears witness on earth, when ministering spirits are sent for service on behalf of those who receive the inheritance of salvation. Angels bear witness in the Old Testament when they are sent to the fathers. Gabriel, sent by God to the Blessed Virgin, bears witness. Angels bear witness by announcing Christ’s birth. Angels bear witness when, after the Lord’s temptation in the desert, they approach and minister to him. An angel bears witness when he appears to the Lord before his Passion and strengthens him. Angels bear witness when they announce the Lord’s resurrection to the women and, at the Ascension, foretell Jesus’ coming again to the disciples as they marvel and look into heaven.

What is to be said of evil angels? Do these also bear witness for faith? Matthew writes: “When Jesus had crossed the strait into the region of the Gerasenes, two having demons came out from the mountain to meet him, exceedingly fierce, and cried out, saying: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?’” (Matt. 8). Behold: demoniacs through demons, or demons through demoniacs, proclaim Jesus to be the Son of God.

Mark says: “There was a man in their synagogue with an unclean spirit, and he cried out [Col. 0617C] saying: ‘What have we to do with you, Jesus the Nazarene? Have you come before the time to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God’” (Mark 7). Again he says: “As many as had afflictions and unclean spirits, when they saw him, fell before him and cried out, saying: ‘You are the Son of God.’ And he sternly charged them not to make him known” (ibid.). Again he says: “A man in an unclean spirit came from the mountain to meet him; and, seeing Jesus, he worshipped him, cried with a loud voice, and said: ‘What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me’” (ibid.).

Luke says: “In their synagogue there was a man who had an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Leave us alone. What have we to do with you, Jesus the Nazarene? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God’” (Luke 4). Again he says: “Demons came out from many, crying out and saying, ‘That you are the Son of God.’ And rebuking them, he did not permit them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ” (ibid.). Again he says: “A certain man who had a demon met him,” and so forth; “when he saw Jesus, he fell before him and, crying with a loud voice, said: ‘What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me’” [Col. 0617D] (Luke 8).

And it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists attempted to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying: ‘I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches.’ But the evil spirit answered them: ‘Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize; but who are you?’” (Acts 19).

Observe from the preceding scriptural testimonies how demons profess Jesus to be the Son of God, or Son of the Most High God. If they speak the truth, they do not merely suppose but rather know who he is: the Holy One of God. Observe how they complain against him that he had come before the time to torment them; how they adjure him by God and beg him not to torment them. Observe how Jesus charged them not to make him known and, rebuking them, did not allow them to speak. Why did he rebuke them, unless because they were unworthy to announce the truth? For God said to the sinner: “Why do you recite my righteous acts and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49). If sinful human beings are unworthy, how much more demons?

Whether Christ is proclaimed through evil angels, through evil human beings, through pretext, or through truth—through pretext, indeed, by the evil; through truth by the good—the confession of truth is always useful, if not to the evil persons themselves, yet always to the good, who rejoice in truth even when Christ is proclaimed by their enemies [Col. 0618B].

### A righteous person, or even a wicked person, can be called a spirit

But if the spirit which bears witness on earth can be understood as a righteous person who lives spiritually, let us search the Scriptures to see how this may be proved and confirmed. Paul says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6). John says in the Catholic Epistle: “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God. By this the Spirit of God is known: every spirit which confesses that Jesus has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit which divides Jesus is not from God” (1 John 4).

Here blessed John warns us to test the spirits to see whether they are from God, and he gives the sign by which one may know which spirit is from God and which is not from God. Likewise, he indicates that “spirit” is said not only of one who confesses Jesus and is from God, but also of one who divides Jesus and is not from God. Who, then, is the person who divides Jesus, except one who denies Jesus and separates him by denying him? But different persons deny him in different ways. Some deny that he is true God and separate divinity from him. Some deny that he has a soul or true flesh and separate true humanity from him. Some deny him in words; others confess him in words but deny him in deeds.

All these pronounce anathema upon [Col. 0618D] Jesus and divide Jesus, because through disobedience and unbelief they separate themselves from Jesus and, as far as lies in them, divide him, since they in some manner break the Church’s unity when by their own separation they sever themselves from the unity of the elect. But you will say, “Has Christ been divided?” By no means. Yet those who divide themselves from him in some manner divide and sever him. But one who does not separate himself from God, but clings to God, is one spirit. And this is the spirit which bears witness on earth, confessing Jesus in speech and life; of this spirit John again says: “It is the Spirit who bears witness, because Christ is truth” (1 John 5).

Water bears witness. For not only are the righteous, who live spiritually and keep themselves unstained after receiving the grace of baptism, witnesses of the truth; sinners also, who, having fallen after baptism, return through repentance and wash themselves in the water of devout mourning, likewise confess and testify that Christ is truth. Blood bears witness. The martyrs testify to this: those who shed their blood for Christ’s name and most gloriously undertook to defend the truth of faith even unto death.

Therefore the spirit of the righteous, the water of penitents, and the blood of martyrs bear witness on earth, because all the righteous—whether through their righteousness, their repentance, or their steadfastness—make us certain that they believed the faith to be true: the faith from which they lived righteously, through which they repented of sins, or for which they did not fear to die [Col. 0619A].

### That a multitude is a witness

[Col. 0619B]

Therefore the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as well as the angels of God and all righteous human beings, bear witness to our faith that it is true and not feigned. This multitude of witnesses, like a cloud laid upon us by God, protects and overshadows us, lest the harmful heat of impiety concerning the mysteries of Christ and the Church burn us, as it is written: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120). Christ is the sun, who by the light of his wisdom illumines the life of the apostles and prophets as though it were day; the Catholic Church itself is the moon, which illumines the ignorance of the simple as though it were night, by the word of preaching and the example of holy conduct. Yet Christ says: “False prophets will arise” (Matt. 24). Therefore, lest false Christs be accepted in place of Christ, or false prophets in place of true prophets, we have witnesses approved by God, upon whose testimony faith rests. Therefore the Church is not found in the conventicles of heretics, nor are Donatus and Arius, and the other heresiarchs, princes of the Church; rather, “we have been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2). There is no Gospel other than that preached by the apostles; no Christ other than he who was proclaimed; and no Church other than that built by Christ through the apostles. Therefore Christ forewarns us and says: “If anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or ‘there,’ do not believe it” (Mark 13). And the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Galatians: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should proclaim to you something other than what has been preached, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1). If, then, the persecution of enemies burns fiercely against our faith, we have a cloud of witnesses placed over us by God, to cool us from the heat in “the Church of the living God, which is the pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Tim. 3).

Therefore, O Christ, I confess you as the author of my faith; and I know that, following you as shepherd, I shall not be put to shame. You are “the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Your prophets and apostles are children of light. If I do not follow them after you, behold, I have rejected the nation of your children (Ps. 72). They are your witnesses, heralds of truth, guides of the blind, light for those who are in darkness, instructors of the nations, teachers of peoples. Under their shadow we are protected; beneath their protection we are cooled as beneath a cloud. Of them Isaiah says: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60). And Paul says to the Hebrews: “Since we have so great a cloud of witnesses laid upon us . . . let us run the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith” (Heb. 12).

## Scripture shows who the witnesses are

The witnesses of truth, therefore, are those of whom Isaiah says: “Truly you are my witnesses, says the Lord, and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me, and understand that I myself am he” (Isa. X). John the apostle is a witness of truth, saying: “What we have seen and heard we proclaim to you” (1 John 1). Peter too is a witness when he says of himself and the other apostles: “God raised him from the dead and made him manifest, not to all the people, but to witnesses preordained by God—to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness” (Acts 10; printed citation: Apoc. X).

## What the testimonies are

Since we have heard who the witnesses of faith are, let us hear what their testimonies are. Their testimonies are their words and their works. Christ instructs us concerning both. Concerning works, when he says: “The works which the Father has given me to accomplish—the very works that I do—bear witness concerning me that the Father sent me” (John 5). But concerning words, whether written or spoken, he shows this when he says: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me, for he wrote concerning me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (ibid.).

The testimonies of our faith, then, are the works of the righteous: works of righteousness and piety which all righteous persons performed from the beginning, in order to please God and glorify God in themselves. The powers of signs and miracles which God performs in certain righteous persons, through which he has magnified himself and made them wondrous, are testimonies. The testimonies of our faith are the words of the Law and the prophets, of the apostles and evangelists, of the orthodox Fathers, and the words of individual faithful persons in confession of the faith. The renown of the righteous also bears testimony to our faith. For when the life of the saints, their humility and patience, are proclaimed in the Church of God, those who hear the report of their holiness are built up in faith and confirmed in faith. Hence it is written of the apostles: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). For what the word of teaching accomplished among those who saw the apostles, the sound of their renown accomplished among those who heard of them.

The testimonies of faith are the words of God, which he spoke from the beginning, and the works of God, which he performed from the beginning, in order to make himself known to us in accordance with the fitness of the times, as he willed and as was fitting. But the words and works of the righteous, which they spoke and performed in God, are human among the words and works of God, because God—without whom they could do nothing—spoke and acted in them.

## The supports of faith are referred back to the authority of Holy Scripture

[Col. 0621A]

The works of God—those which he performed in creating all things, those which he performed in redeeming us, and those which he performs in calling and justifying us—are set out in sequence in the course of Holy Scripture. There also the words of God, which he spoke either directly or through the ministry of angels or human beings, are most faithfully arranged. It must therefore be established that the supports of our faith are referred back to the authority of Holy Scripture. If Scripture is true, the witnesses of faith are true, the testimonies of faith are true, and consequently faith itself is true.

Who could doubt that Holy Scripture is true, if it is established either that the word contained in it is God’s, or that those who wrote spoke in the Spirit of God? For who does not believe whatever God has said, if it is established that the Lord has spoken? Someone will therefore say: “You preach to me the word of faith and urge me to believe it as the word not of a human being but of God, written and handed down to us by holy prophets through the revelation of the Holy Spirit. From what, I ask, do you prove to me that the Lord spoke this word, or that the Holy Spirit revealed it to those called prophets? Prove this to me, I say, and there will be no hesitation: I shall immediately believe and make confession of faith.”

What is to be said in reply? Certainly, if any worthy answer can be found in that Holy Scripture itself, of which we are now speaking, it must not be withheld from one who believes such things; for Peter says in his first catholic epistle: “Sanctify the Lord Jesus Christ in your hearts, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you” (1 Pet. 3).

## The ways in which God formerly made himself known

It must therefore be considered that, as Holy Scripture says, God formerly made himself known to the righteous of old “in many portions and in many ways” (Heb. 1): by visible appearance and present speech; by vision; by declaration of his name; by the power of signs; by hidden inspiration; by the prediction and fulfilment of future events; and by whatever other ways he wished to make himself known to those to whom he deigned to reveal himself.

For he appeared and spoke to some in a form which he chose for this purpose, as to Abraham and Moses. Of some it is written: “Then he spoke in vision to his holy ones” (Ps. 88). Speaking to others, he made himself known, as it were, from his name, saying: “I am God Almighty,” or “I am who I am” (Gen. 17), or “I am the God of Abraham” (Exod. 3). Concerning the power of signs it is written: “Remember his wonders which he has done, his prodigies, and the judgments of his mouth” (Ps. 104). Concerning hidden inspiration it is written: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84).

Many works which he was going to perform, before they came to pass, he foretold as future, so that the words might be believed on the authority of the one predicting them, and so that, for those who believed, faith in these words might be reckoned as righteousness. The things foretold were delayed for a time before their fulfilment, and after the delay were fulfilled in their own time, so that faith might be tested by delay, shown true by fulfilment, and made readier to believe greater things still further in the future.

God foretold to Noah the coming flood. He foretold to Abraham the blessing of all the kindreds of the earth in him, the sojourn of his seed in Egypt, and its return from Egypt. Through the angel speaking to Hagar he foretold Ishmael’s birth. He also foretold Isaac. He foretold too the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah. And Jacob the patriarch, by God’s revelation, foretold what would happen in the last days, saying to his sons: “Gather together, that I may tell you what shall happen in the last days” (Gen. 49).

In faith in the promise made to Abraham, Joseph foretold what would happen and said to his brothers: “After my death God will visit you and cause you to go up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Carry my bones with you from this place” (Gen. 50). The Lord foretold Moses the wonders which he would perform in Egypt and at the Red Sea for the deliverance of his people (Exod. 3); he also foretold many things which he would perform in the wilderness. He likewise foretold many things which he would perform in the land of promise through the hand of Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ minister. After Joshua’s death God raised up judges for Israel’s deliverance, and foretold many things which he would perform through them (Judg. 1); and, as he spoke, so he fulfilled.

In the days of Samuel, God foretold many things concerning Eli, Saul, and David (1 Sam. 3). Through Nathan the prophet he also foretold future things concerning David himself and his son who would reign after him. Through other prophets he foretold many things concerning other kings, concerning the captivity of the Israelite people under the king of Babylon, and concerning the return of that same people; and, as he spoke, so he fulfilled.

But these works, and many others which God performed from ancient days until Christ’s advent—by whom could they have been foreknown and foretold except by God, the author of those very works, who knows all things before they happen, or by those to whom he deigned to reveal them? Those to whom God spoke could know without doubt that the word addressed to them was not human but divine. By this word they were so enlightened that they became aware of divine mysteries and foreknowers of future things; hence they were called prophets or seers.

Those to whom prophets sent by God spoke ought to have believed without doubt that the prophetic word preached to them was God’s word: first, because of the holiness of the prophets’ lives, since faithful and truthful men would not wish to lie; and secondly, because the truth of the matter itself was repeatedly shown to them when they often saw fulfilled what they knew the prophets had predicted. Those who preached the word said that it was not their own word but God’s, adding: “Thus says the Lord,” or “The mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. 1), or something similar. Therefore, when people saw some things fulfilled which had been foretold by these men, they held those who had foretold them to be prophets of the Lord with the utmost certainty; and through the things which they saw fulfilled, they awaited with greater certainty those things which they heard proclaimed by the prophets as to come much later.

## How the prophets were found faithful

The prophets, then, were found faithful and truthful because their word came in its time and did not fall unfulfilled upon the earth, like the word of an earthly person which, spoken falsely, is recognized, when it proves false, to have gone forth from earth and not from heaven. Hence it is written of Samuel: “Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and none of all his words fell to the ground. And all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord” (1 Sam. 3). A little later it is added: “The word of Samuel came to all Israel” (ibid.).

Observe from this passage how Samuel was recognized as a faithful prophet of the Lord. He was recognized, namely, because none of all his words fell to the ground, and because his word came to all Israel. The statement, “None of all his words fell upon the earth,” can be understood in the sense in which it was said: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth; but he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 1). The one who is of the earth is of the earth in seeking earthly things, is of the earth in thinking earthly thoughts, and speaks of the earth in teaching earthly things. But the one who comes from heaven is above all who seek and think earthly things and teach others in the same way.

When the earthly wisdom of those who are of the earth and speak from the earth predicts as future things which are not going to happen, then, when its word begins to appear false, it falls, as it were, to earth, because through the evident falsity it falls back to the place from which it had gone forth through the craft of fabricated falsehood or through conjecture founded on false opinion. Thus a word falls to the earth when it returns empty to its author and is found to be an earthly person’s word. Conversely, the Lord says: “The word which shall go forth from my mouth shall not return to me empty” (Isa. 55).

The saying, “None of all his words fell to the earth,” may also be understood differently. Since Samuel’s prophetic threats against the house of Eli and the house of Saul were like arrows sent forth to strike, it was fittingly said, by analogy with arrows which strike what they aim at and do not fall uselessly to the ground: “None of all his words fell to the earth.” Just as Samuel was recognized as the Lord’s prophet because the word he spoke came to pass, so Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the other prophets were recognized because the Lord fulfilled what he spoke through them.

Attend to the reading of the prophets, and consider diligently what and how great were the things they prophesied against the ten tribes of Israel, against Judah and Jerusalem, against the various surrounding nations and kingdoms; and you will find that they were fulfilled just as they are known to have been predicted. After such certainty of manifest truth, who should doubt that the prophets spoke in the Spirit of God, and that the word which came to them and was proclaimed to us through them is the word of God? For God revealed it to them through his Spirit. “For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit which is within him? So too no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God.”

## The diviners and gods of the nations do not know times and seasons; God alone does

Neither the wise men of Egypt, nor the astrologers of heaven, nor the gods of the nations could announce the conditions of times and the changes of affairs from the world’s foundation. Hence Isaiah, speaking to Egypt, says: “Where now are your wise men? Let them announce to you and make known what the Lord of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt” (Isa. 19). You see how the prophet, foreknowing and proclaiming the evils that were to come upon Egypt, derides the wise men who could neither announce nor make them known.

The same prophet, when prophesying against Babylon, says: “You have been wearied by the multitude of your counsels; let the astrologers stand and save you, those who observed the stars and calculated the months, that from them they might announce what would come upon you” (Isa. 47). Deriding the gods of the nations, he also says: “Let them draw near and announce to us whatever things are to come. Tell us the former things that were, and we shall set our heart upon them and know their last things. Announce what is to come in the future, and we shall know that you are gods” (Isa. 41).

“Tell us,” he says, “the former things that were, and we shall set our heart upon them.” It is as though he said: Tell us, if you can, the former things which occurred from the beginning of the age, when you did not yet exist; and if you do this, we shall set our heart upon you, so as to worship you as gods. And from the former things announced to us we shall know their last things—that is, the things after the former things which are to come at the end. If, after announcing the former things, you have also announced these to us, they will be known to us.

The prophet adds: “Announce to us what is to come in the future, and we shall know that you are gods.” By these words he shows that the true God may be known from the announcement of future things, since it belongs to him to know times or seasons. Hence the same prophet speaks in the Lord’s person: “Behold, the former things have come to pass; and I announce new things; before they spring forth I shall make you hear them” (Isa. 42). It is as though he said: Believe me, who have fulfilled what I foretold. This is plainly apparent, because the things first announced by me to Noah, Abraham, and Moses, who were before you, have come to pass. I also foretell to you the new things which are still to come, so that you may believe that I am God and receive the words of the prophets as the words of God.

Again he says: “I am the first, and I am the last; apart from me there is no God. Who is like me? Let him call and announce and set the order before me. From the time when I established the ancient people, let him announce to them the things to come and the things that shall be” (Isa. 44). It is as though he said: Who among the gods of the nations is like me? If anyone is thought like me, let him do what I do: let him call things that are not, that they may be, as I also call them; let him announce things done and things to be done; let him set before me the order of events, and what came later, from the time when I established the ancient people—either the human race in Adam or the Israelite people in Abraham’s seed. “Let them announce to them,” he says, “the things to come and the things that shall be.” If they cannot do this, while I can, it remains for you to believe that apart from me there is no God.

How much the prediction and fulfilment of future things contributes to recognizing the true God and holding fast faith in his words, the Lord frequently indicates through the same prophet: now inviting inquiry of himself concerning future matters; now declaring that he has not spoken in secret; now recalling predictions and fulfilments, or announcing things to come. Isaiah says: “Thus says the Lord: Ask me about the things to come, concerning my children; and command me concerning the work of my hands. I made the earth, and I created humanity upon the earth” (Isa. 45). It is as though he said: Ask me, and no other, concerning what I shall do, for I can do all things and my works cannot be hidden from me.

Again he says: “I am he, and there is no other; I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth” (ibid.). It is as though he said: I have spoken to you from heaven, not in secret, from where demons are accustomed to deceive, or deceitful people to give answers for idols. Again, speaking of the captivity of the children of Israel under Nebuchadnezzar, or their liberation under Cyrus, he says: “Who made this heard from the beginning? From that time I foretold it. Is it not I, God, and is there no God besides me?” It is as though he said: From the truth of prediction, through the evident fact of fulfilment, recognize in me not the conjecture of divination but the foreknowledge of divinity.

Again he says: “Remember the former age, for I am God, and there is no God besides me, nor is there one like me, announcing the last things from the beginning, and from the outset the things not yet done” (Isa. 46). And again: “I foretold it from that time; before they came to pass I declared it to you, lest perhaps you should say, ‘My idols did these things’” (Isa. 48). It is as though he said: You first heard my words and afterwards saw my works, so that you might attribute those works to me and not to idols, because idols could not predict my works or do anything like them.

Since it is established from the predictions already mentioned that the Holy Spirit foretold future things through Moses and the prophets, it must consequently be established that they wrote true things: both concerning past events, which they reported after being taught by God about things foretold and accomplished by him; concerning future events which they predicted and which were afterwards fulfilled; and concerning future events which they predicted but which have not yet been fulfilled. It must likewise be established that the authority of the Holy Spirit confirms faith in Scripture, so that it should be certain that whoever presumes to oppose prophetic speech plainly contradicts the Holy Spirit.

Hence blessed Peter says in his Epistle: “You have the more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place”; “holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet. 1). The prophetic word is a lamp, as the Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. 118). This lamp shines in a dark place, illuminating the darkness of human ignorance, until Christ, glorified in the world, shines like day, and until that same Christ rises through faith in our hearts like the morning star. We must therefore understand that prophecy is not an interpretation of human understanding, nor an invention or tradition of human will, but a revelation of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore God, so that all may know that he himself is the surveyor of the ages, claims for himself, rightly, foreknowledge of future things by predicting the future through his servants the prophets. The lying spirit, which did not stand in truth, falsely usurps this foreknowledge for itself. For he is the author of lying, whose iniquity first lied to itself and then to the human being. It lied to itself when it said in its heart: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars I will exalt my throne; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). It thought these things in its heart, but falsely, because it was frustrated in its hope and deprived of its desire. Hence Isaiah, who writes these things concerning it, says in mockery: “Nevertheless, you shall be brought down to hell” (ibid.). It is as though he said: Although your plan is to ascend to heaven and do this and that, yet it will not be so; rather, you shall be brought down to hell. Behold how iniquity lied to itself, predicting in its own heart as future what was not going to happen.

Nor is it enough for it to be deceived unless it also attempts to deceive. For when the tempter came to the woman, he said: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” She replied: “We eat of the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat it or touch it, lest perhaps we die.” But the serpent said: “You shall by no means die. For God knows that, on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3).

God foretold that death would follow if the human being did not obey. He foretold this so that by obeying the human being might avoid death and possess immortality. But the devil, promising immortality in order to take immortality away through belief in a false promise, said: “You shall by no means die.” He heaps promise upon promise, adding: “Your eyes will be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” By this promise he seems to promise foreknowledge of future things, addressing the woman’s ignorance, since she seems to have said doubtfully: “Lest perhaps we die.” It is as though he said: Do not doubt, as one ignorant of what will happen; rather, be certain that when you have eaten, your eyes will be opened to knowledge of hidden things, and you will have divine knowledge like gods, by which you will foreknow the good things that will come to you, or the evil things that will not come to you.

He said that God knew this, as though in order to arouse suspicion of envy against God: as though God had maliciously forbidden the human being to eat this tree so that he might not become immortal and possess knowledge of good and evil. Therefore, in order to be believed, the devil wished to persuade the woman that he himself foreknew future events; by his false prediction of the future he seduced her and introduced the impiety of unbelief, through which God would not be believed.

## The word of faith stands in the mouth of prophets and apostles

But God, countering the snares of his malice in a more fitting manner in order to destroy the evil of impiety and establish faith through true prediction of future things, inspired prophets, whom he sent beforehand into the world before he himself came, so that they might announce his advent and bear witness concerning the works he would perform in the world. When he himself came into the world, he chose apostles as the successors of the prophets, to announce the fulfilment of what the prophets had long before foretold.

Since one Spirit filled the prophets and apostles, witnesses of Christ, the word of faith rightly stands in their mouth, as it is written: “Every word stands in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19; Matt. 18). He says “in the mouth,” as though in one mouth. For those who speak in agreement, who agree with truth and with one another, speak with one mouth. Otherwise they are not witnesses if they think different things and utter different things, because they are not conscious of the truth.

## The agreement of witnesses and testimonies, and the comparison of words and deeds

[Col. 0627B]

The agreement of witnesses is the agreement of testimonies; and the agreement of testimonies is the agreement of words with words, works with works, and words with works. For, as has been said, words and works are the testimonies. The words of the prophets and the words of the apostles agree: the latter announced as fulfilled what the former had foretold as future. Hence Christ says in the Gospel of John: “In this the saying is true: one sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others labored, and you entered into their labors” (John 4).

The prophets labored by teaching some, warning and rebuking others, and suffering persecution from unbelievers. They labored to destroy superstition and call back those who had gone astray to worship of the true God. The fruit of this labor was reserved for the apostles, who, reaping the fruit of the prophets’ labor, gathered the nations into faith, as had been foretold by the prophets. For this very calling of the nations through the apostles had been announced by the prophets. Since the apostles proclaimed the fulfilment of what had been announced beforehand, the words of the apostles agree with the words of the prophets, and the works of fulfilment with the words of prediction. By this agreement of witnesses or testimonies, the word of the prophets and apostles is shown to be true.

For the word stands in that wherein it is shown to be true. Three things concur for it to be shown true: awareness of the truth, the voice of the one testifying, and the agreement of the corroborating witness. Therefore the prophets and apostles are true witnesses, and their testimonies are found concordant and sufficient, because, taught by the Spirit and made conscious of the truth, they both attested that truth by steadfast confession and spoke in agreement in all things.

The extent of their agreement in words is shown by the fact that the apostles confirmed their preaching by the sayings of the prophets. The agreement of works will appear plainly if those things which went before in figure are compared with those now fulfilled in truth, as the Lord says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up” (John 3). And again: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man shall be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Mark 12). The books of the apostles and orthodox Fathers are full of comparisons of this kind between figure and truth; in them the harmony of the two Testaments is shown, so that the rationale of faith may be more clearly opened.

Whether, therefore, words are compared with words, or words and works with works, all that is written concerning Christ in both Testaments will be found harmonious; and no opposition can weaken what is recognized as strengthened by such harmonious testimony. Of this comparison it is written: “But Mary kept all these words, comparing them in her heart” (Luke 2). For what were the things she compared in her heart, except those which she herself had seen and heard: things foretold by the prophets, announced by angels to the shepherds, or reported by the shepherds themselves to others?

Of this comparison she herself also says: “He has taken up Israel his servant, remembering his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his seed for ever” (Luke 1). Of this comparison Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “God, who foretold through the mouth of all the prophets that his Christ would suffer, has thus fulfilled it” (Acts 3). And again he says: “All the prophets from Samuel onwards, as many as spoke, announced these days” (ibid.).

## That so great an agreement of witnesses comes from the Holy Spirit

So great an agreement among the prophets, who in different places and at different times foretold concordant things concerning Christ—by whom or how could it have been brought about, except by the Spirit of truth? He taught them one truth in such a way that they thought, spoke, and wrote the same things concerning Christ, and did not disagree with one another. This Spirit also revealed to them concerning the apostles that they would come after them and publicly proclaim to the world what the prophets had foretold. The same Spirit dictated to them what was to be written, so that through the enduring character of Scripture the things foretold by the prophets might reach our time, when they were announced to us as fulfilled through the apostles. Therefore the reading of the Law and the prophets is necessary for us and worthy of diligent meditation, so that we may know that what is proposed to us for belief was long ago revealed by God.

## Those who neglect the Law, or do not understand Christ in the Scriptures

Therefore to those who neglect to read or hear, so that they may be without excuse, it is said: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luke 16). But to those who read Moses and the prophets and do not understand, it is said: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and they are those which bear witness concerning me. Yet you are unwilling to come to me, that you may have life” (John 5). They are admonished to search the Scriptures, which bear testimony concerning Christ, so that they may seek and find Christ in them, and thus have life. Christ is indeed revealed in the Scriptures to believers, but hidden from unbelievers. Therefore those who do not know Christ err in the Scriptures.

Hence Truth itself says to the Sadducees, who say that there is no resurrection: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matt. 22). It is as though he said: You err because you do not know the Scriptures; and therefore you do not know the Scriptures because you do not know the power of God. But Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Accordingly, those who do not know Christ do not understand the Scriptures, for they are those which bear testimony concerning Christ. Hence Philip, when he had found Nathanael, said to him: “We have found Jesus, son of Joseph, of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the prophets” (John 1).

## Various opinions concerning Christ among those who saw him present in the flesh
Those who saw Christ present in the flesh held differing opinions about him: some did not know him, while others did; and those who knew him called him [Col. 0629B] a prophet, a righteous man, and the Son of God. Those who did not know him denied or doubted one or another of these things concerning him. Nathanael confessed and said: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the king of Israel” (John 1). Nicodemus also confessed, saying: “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God. For no one can do the signs which you do unless God is with him” (John 3). The Samaritan woman, who came to draw water, said: “Lord, I see that you are a prophet” (John 4). And many from that city believed in him and said: “We ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Savior of the world” (ibid.). But certain Jews sought to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God (John 5). Some, [Col. 0629C] when they saw the sign he had performed with five loaves and two fishes, said: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6). But others said: “Is this not Jesus, Joseph’s son, whose father and mother we know? How then does he say, ‘I came down from heaven’?” (ibid.). Peter, however, said: “We have believed and known that you are Christ, the Son of God” (ibid.). They sought him during the feast and said: “Where is he?” And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd (John 7). Some said, “He is good”; but others said, “No, rather, he leads the crowds astray” (ibid.). Some wondered, saying: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” (ibid.). Others said: “When Christ comes, will he perform more signs [Col. 0629D] than this man does?” (ibid.). When they heard his words, they said: “This is truly the prophet”; others said: “This is the Christ.” But some said: “Does the Christ come from Galilee?” (ibid.). Others said: “Never has a man spoken in this way” (ibid.), as this man speaks; but others did not believe, because he called God his Father (John 8). Others said: “Do we not rightly say that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” (ibid.). Others said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.” Others said: “How can a sinful man perform these signs?” (John 9). Again they said: “We know that this man is a sinner” (ibid.). Dissension again arose among the Jews because of his words. [Col. 0630A] Many of them said: “He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?” Others said: “These are not the words of one possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” (John 10). Some said: “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy; because you, being a man, make yourself God” (ibid.). Martha said: “I have believed that you are Christ, the Son of God, who came into this world” (John 11). The Pharisees said: “Do you see that we are getting nowhere? Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12). Again it is written: “Many of the rulers believed in him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess it, lest they should be expelled from the synagogue” (ibid.). The disciples said: “Behold, now you speak openly and use no parable. By this we know that you came from God” (John 16). [Col. 0630B] The Jews said to Pilate: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18). Again they said: “According to the law he must die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19).

These things are written in the Gospel of John. But in Matthew it is written thus: “His reputation went throughout all Syria” (Matthew 4). Having seen the miracles, some said: “Nothing like this has ever appeared in Israel” (Matthew 9). Others said: “He casts out demons by the prince of demons” (ibid.). And again: “This man casts out demons only by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Matthew 12). Some said: “Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us?” (Matthew 13). Herod the tetrarch heard the report concerning Jesus and said to his officials: [Col. 0630C] “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead” (Matthew 14). When Christ questioned his disciples and said: “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16). The centurion said: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matthew 27).

In the Gospel of Mark it is written thus: “The crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat bread. And when his own people heard it, they went out to restrain him, for they said: ‘He has gone out of his mind’” (Mark 3). The scribes who had come down from Jerusalem said: “He has Beelzebub” (ibid.). Some said: “Is this not the son of the carpenter and of Mary, brother of James, Joseph, Judas, and Simon?” (Mark 6). In Luke it is written thus: They marvelled at the words of grace proceeding [Col. 0630D] from his mouth, and said: “Is this not Joseph’s son?” (Luke 4). But some said: “Blessed is he who comes as king in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest” (Luke 19).

### That Christ Is Shown to Be Righteous

Observe from what has been set forth above how various were the opinions concerning Christ: some saying that he was good; others, that he was not. While different people held differing views and uttered differing judgments according to their views, Christ is shown to be good and righteous by his life and teaching. For, beginning to do and teach, by word and example, everything holy, chaste, honorable, pleasing to God, and fitting for good morals, he acted and preached in such a way that, amid the snares of enemies [Col. 0631A] who watched him, no occasion for a just reproach could in any way be found, whether in his words or in his conduct.

Who displayed and preserved in his works humility, patience, love, and the pattern of every holiness as he did? Who was a more perfect lover of holy poverty and despiser of earthly vanity than he? Who persecuted pride, envy, hatred, anger, covetousness, avarice, lust, gluttony, injustice, falsehood, the shameful acts of crimes, and every kind of sin as he did? Who took greater care to do God’s will in all things, and who sought his glory more than he? Therefore the Father says of him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3). Who was freer from sin [Col. 0631B] and from the dominion of the ruler of this world than he? Therefore he says: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). Who among human beings was holier and more innocent than he? Therefore he says: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John 8). Who more powerfully commanded unclean spirits, even winds and sea, than he?

How could such power of signs, such wisdom of words, such grace of virtues, such purity of life, and such manifest truth of teaching meet in one man, unless he were from God, unless he were good and righteous? When he was accused before Pilate as though guilty of death, those who had handed him over out of envy accused him of the confession of truth as though it were blasphemy. Yet when they had [Col. 0631C] nothing to object to him, or plausibly to fabricate against him, compelled by the lack of a true accusation and the scarcity of plausible lies, they were forced to say: “If this man were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18). As though anyone who did not please them were wicked.

They searched out iniquities in order to find something to object against him; but those searching their search failed, since they had nothing by which to convict him. “The arrows of little children have become their wounds; their tongues have been weakened against them” (Psalm 63). Their accusations became empty and ineffectual, so that the judge said: “I find no cause in him” (John 18). Thus acquitted by the judge, who judged that he should be released, he was unjustly judged by those who had accused him out of envy. Such an accusation and condemnation, therefore, do not prove Jesus to have been unrighteous; rather, they admonish us to believe him righteous, since even before the judge his life could not be defamed by the envious. [Col. 0631D] Indeed, his holiness is thereby more highly commended: his life did not please such people, whereas it is a great praise of the righteous to displease the worst.

But what reason can those who said of Christ that he was evil give for their assertion? And if they can give none—indeed, because they can give none—let them come and say with us that he is good: not merely good, as are others who are called good; nor good in the sense apparently supposed by the man who said: “Good Master, what shall I do to possess eternal life?” [Col. 0632A] Jesus answered him: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18). God, however, is good essentially: his nature is goodness, and for him to exist is to be good. In this sense he alone is good. Christ, according to the assumed nature, is human; and he is good in a singular manner—innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens (Hebrews 7), “who committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2). Since, therefore, it is established that Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God, is holy, righteous, good in a singular manner, and free from every sin, let us see whether he is also a prophet.

### That Christ Is Shown to Be a Prophet

[Col. 0632B] That he is a prophet is proved by his foretelling of future things: things concerning himself, his disciples, the destruction of the city of Jerusalem, and matters which were to occur in the world after his ascension. He foretold them most truly, just as they were afterwards fulfilled.

Before his passion he foretold concerning himself, saying to his disciples: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death. And they will deliver him to the Gentiles to be mocked, scourged, and crucified. And on the third day he will rise again” (Matthew 20). Those who were present with him saw these things fulfilled in him. The women who came to the tomb, as Luke relates, when two men stood beside them in shining garments, were reminded to remember how the Lord [Col. 0632C] had spoken to them, so that through recollection of the prediction they might believe the resurrection announced to them: “Why do you seek him who lives among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he spoke to you, saying: ‘The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinners, be crucified, and rise on the third day’” (Luke 24). And they remembered his words; and, returning from the tomb, reported all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.

Concerning this prediction, the chief priests and Pharisees said to Pilate: “Lord, we remember that that deceiver said, while he was still alive: ‘After three days I will rise again’” (Matthew 27). In Matthew, the angel said to the women: “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him. Behold, [Col. 0632D] I have foretold it to you” (Matthew 28). But in Mark it is said: “He will go before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he told you” (Mark 16).

Observe how the prediction is repeatedly impressed upon them to be retained in memory, so that, through remembering it, faith may more readily admit its fulfillment. Thus Peter, through remembering his foretold denial, is recalled to repentance, as Matthew writes: “Peter remembered the word which Jesus had spoken: ‘You will deny me three times’; and he went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26). When the Lord had foretold to his disciples his ascension to the Father and his future coming, he repeated what he had foretold in order to confirm the prediction in their memory; and consequently he showed that the truth of a prediction is effective for faith in its fulfillment. “You have heard,” he says, “that I told you, ‘I go and come [Col. 0633A] to you’” (John 14). And shortly afterwards he adds: “And now I have told you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe” (ibid.). For his ascension, visibly displayed to the disciples’ eyes, when the prediction was recalled to them, ought to have sufficed to establish their faith in the things they had heard foretold but had not seen fulfilled.

In Luke, when he had eaten before the disciples after the resurrection, he said to them: “These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you: that all things written concerning me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms had to be fulfilled” (Luke 24). Concerning the disciples, he said: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves. For they will hand you over in councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you, and you will be led before kings and governors on account of me” [Col. 0633B] (Matthew 10). The world has known and bears witness that these things were fulfilled in the disciples after the Lord’s ascension.

Concerning the destruction of the city of Jerusalem he said: “Days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart, cast you and your children who are within you to the ground, and will not leave in you one stone upon another,” etc. (Luke 19). It is plain that all these things were fulfilled as the Lord foretold them.

The Lord also foretold that his Gospel would be preached throughout the whole world; that the nations would be baptized in his name; that his faith would be received in the world; that repentance and forgiveness of sins would be preached in his name; and that the memorial of his death would be celebrated and frequently observed in the offering of the true sacrifice. For it is written: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep whatever I have commanded you” (Matthew 28). These words plainly foretell that all nations will be baptized with Christ’s baptism and will keep evangelical teaching as the Lord delivered it to the apostles.

It is written: “Why do you trouble this woman? She has done a good work for me. Amen, I say to you: wherever the Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what she has done shall also be told in memory of her” (Matthew 26). These words show that the Gospel is to be preached throughout the world and that the woman’s good work, in her memory, is to be proclaimed everywhere through the preaching of the Gospel. We now see these things visibly fulfilled exactly as they were foretold. [Col. 0633D] That Christ’s faith was to be received in the world, he himself showed in saying: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12). And when the crowds cried out, as Luke relates, “Blessed is he who comes, the king of Israel, in the name of the Lord,” and the Pharisees said to him, “Teacher, rebuke them,” he answered: “I tell you, if they keep silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke 19). This he said concerning the nations who would believe in him, concerning whom he says in the Gospel of Matthew: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruit” (Matthew 21).

That repentance and forgiveness of sins were to be preached in his name, he showed when speaking to the disciples after the resurrection; as Luke relates, he said: “Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day; and [Col. 0634A] that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations” (Luke 24). That the memorial of his death was to be solemnly and frequently observed in the offering of the true sacrifice, he showed in saying: “This is my body, which will be delivered for you; do this in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11).

Behold, all these things have been fulfilled before the eyes of all nations just as the Lord foretold them. When they were being foretold and recorded, they could still have seemed impossible and unbelievable. For who at that time, unless inspired by God to see this, could have believed that all nations, devoted to the worship of demons, would cast aside their idols; that they would know the one true God; that they would believe Jesus of Nazareth—crucified, dead, and buried—to have risen from the dead [Col. 0634B] and ascended into heaven; and would worship him as true God and serve him as true God?
