This transformation, before it occurred so unbelievable, and now, after it has occurred, so marvelous and so plainly visible to all, by whom could it have been accomplished except by him who foresaw and foretold that it would occur? What human being could accomplish it? What demon, even if able to do so, would wish to accomplish it? The faith of Christ has indeed gained possession of human kingdoms and destroyed the dominion of demons.

And these things were accomplished not by force, not by sword and spear, not by the strength of martial toil and sweat; but by the humility of Christ, the gentleness of Christ, the cross and death of Christ, the patience of the righteous, [Col. 0634C] and thousands of martyrs confessing Christ and dying for Christ. They were accomplished not by wisdom of speech, not by sublimity of discourse, not by persuasive words of human wisdom, not through the mighty and exalted things of this world, lest Christ’s cross be made void; but God chose the foolish, weak, and ignoble things of this world to accomplish these things, so that through simple people he might confound the wise of the world; through apostles overcome philosophers; and through fishermen triumph over emperors.

### Christ the Son of God; Signs of His Coming

It is therefore most certainly and firmly to be believed, and most steadfastly confessed, that Jesus Christ, a holy man and prophet, is also the Son of God, who came forth from the Father and came into this world. For he himself said this concerning himself, nor did he falsely usurp such honor. For who, if he were holy and a prophet, would make such a claim? Therefore the saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1). The most certain signs of this coming are these: the blinding, dispersal, and removal of the Jews; the calling and illumination of the nations; the overthrow of idolatry; and the establishment of true religion, by which the true God is worshipped in spirit and truth, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

This transformation among the nations is the shaking of the earth, concerning which the Psalmist says: “Bring to the Lord, O kindreds of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor,” etc. (Psalm 95). And shortly afterwards: “Let the whole earth be moved at his presence; say among the nations [Col. 0635A] that the Lord has reigned” (Psalm 115). This transformation is the setting-right of the world, of which it is further said: “For he has set right the world, which shall not be moved” (ibid.).

Although the signs of Christ’s coming written in the prophets appear to concern some marvelous transformation among these created things—mountains, valleys, waters, trees, animals, and other such things—they must nevertheless be understood mystically and spiritually with reference to this shaking of the earth and setting-right of the world. Let us consider this by comparison with similar passages. In the prophet Malachi the Lord says: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet, and he will turn the heart of fathers to children,” etc. (Malachi 4). And in Luke the angel speaks to Zachariah concerning John, saying: “He will turn many of the children of Israel to [Col. 0635B] the Lord, that he may turn the hearts of fathers to children,” etc.; “to prepare for the Lord a perfect people” (Luke 1). In the forerunners of Christ’s first and second comings, you see what is the reason and office of their going before: namely, to turn hearts to the Lord. From this understand that this very thing is the purpose of Christ’s coming: he came into this world to save sinners and, through faith and repentance, to turn them to the Lord their God.

He came into this world not to judge the world, as he will judge it on the last day, but that the world might be saved through him. Yet in this first coming he came saving and, in a certain manner, judging: saving those who believe in his coming, judging those who do not believe. The cause of his coming, therefore, is mercy and judgment. Thus the prophet Habakkuk says: “The Lord answered me and said: Write the vision and make it plain upon tablets, that he who reads it may run; for the vision is for a distant time, and it will appear at the end and will not lie. If it delays, wait for it, for it will surely come and will not be late. Behold, the soul of one who is unbelieving will not be upright within himself; but the righteous shall live by his faith” (Habakkuk 2). [Col. 0635C] See and consider how plainly the prophet foretells that those who do not believe in Christ’s coming are not justified, whereas those who are justified live by faith.

Thus the Lord himself says in the Gospel of John: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). The Jews, who formerly believed, now do not believe; but the nations, which formerly did not believe, now believe. This judgment, therefore, is against the Jews, whose boasting has been excluded, and against demons and idols, whose worship has been abolished. Hence we who confess Christ ought to rejoice, as it is written: “And the daughters of Judah rejoiced because of your judgments, O Lord” (Psalm 96). And again: “Then all the trees of the forest will rejoice before the Lord, because he comes to judge the earth” (Psalm 95). For we who have been called from among the nations, who formerly were like the trees of the forest, ought to rejoice in this and give thanks to the Lord for it: when the Jews were blinded and the demons cast out, we were illuminated through faith. Through it we understand that the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens.

Having therefore recognized the cause of Christ’s [Col. 0636A] coming, we must investigate from it the signs of his coming—his marvelous works, for whose accomplishment he came and which he marvelously performed in coming. Concerning these, the Psalmist says: “Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done marvelous things” (Psalm 97). Tell us, prophet of the Lord: what are the marvelous things the Lord has done? “His right hand and his holy arm have brought him salvation” (ibid.). Speak still more plainly: “The Lord has made known his salvation; before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness. He has remembered his mercy and his truth to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God” (ibid.).

These are the marvelous things which the Lord has done, by which he remembered his ancient promise in order to fulfill it in its own time. The word of the promise is this: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22). This is the blessing of all nations in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ: through it the Lord had mercy upon all peoples, turning away the wrath of the first curse and restoring grace by illumination through faith in the Savior’s coming, whom God made manifest to every people. Concerning this mercy and blessing, the Psalmist says: “May God have mercy on us,” etc.; “that we may know your way upon earth, your salvation among all nations. Let the nations be glad and rejoice” (Psalm 66). This, then, is the sign of Christ’s coming: the testimony of all nations, by which, as had been prophesied concerning them, they confess that they have been freed from the error of idolatry and the power of the devil, acknowledging [Col. 0636C] the salvation of God which God has revealed before all nations.

### On the Blinding of the Jews

Concerning the blinding of the Jews, the Psalmist says: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see” (Psalm 68). Their eyes are darkened with respect to the law, which they do not understand; with respect to the time of their visitation, which they do not recognize; and with respect to their own blindness, which they do not notice. For spiritual understanding of the law has been taken away from the Jews. Hence the Apostle says in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “To this present day, when Moses is read, a veil is laid over their heart” (2 Corinthians 3). Isaiah says: “The vision of all things will be to you like the words of a sealed book: when they give it to one who knows letters, they will say, ‘Read this’; and he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed.’ And the book will be given to one who does not know letters” (Isaiah 29). [Col. 0636D]

By these words it is plainly shown that the law is not to be understood by those to whom it was given, but is to be transferred to the nations to whom it was not given from the beginning. Again he says: “I will do a marvelous work among this people, a great and astounding miracle; for wisdom will perish from its wise men, and the understanding of its prudent men will be hidden” (ibid.). He calls it a great and astounding miracle that wisdom has perished from them and understanding has been hidden from them. And again: “Will not Lebanon shortly, in a very little while, be turned into Carmel, and Carmel be reckoned as a forest? In that day the deaf shall hear the words of the sealed book, and from darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind shall see” (ibid.). By these [Col. 0637A] words he signifies the conversion of uncircumcision into circumcision through the change of faith, and of circumcision into uncircumcision; and the grant to us, once deaf and blind, of the grace of understanding the law.

And again: “Jacob shall not now be ashamed, nor shall his face now grow pale; but when he sees his children, the works of my hands, in his midst sanctifying my name, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and proclaim the God of Israel; and those who err in spirit will know understanding, and murmurers will learn the law” (Isaiah 29). He signifies the time of our calling, in which we now are. For behold, we believers from the nations, formerly erring and murmurers, are learning the law transferred to us; and we profess ourselves to be children of Jacob according to the spirit, while we proclaim the works of Israel. This is their shame and confusion.

And again: “Where is the man of letters? Where is the one who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little children?” (Isaiah 33). Jeremiah says: “But my people have not known the judgment of the Lord. How do you say, ‘We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us’? Truly, the lying pen of the scribes has wrought falsehood” (Jeremiah 8).

The Lord rebukes the Jews’ blindness concerning the time of their visitation, saying to the city of Jerusalem: “They will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19). And in the Gospel of Matthew, when the Pharisees and Sadducees tested him and asked him to show them a sign from heaven, he answered: “When evening comes you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red’; and in the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is glowing red and gloomy.’ You know how to discern the appearance of the sky, but you cannot know the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign; and no sign will be given it except the sign of Jonah the prophet” (Matthew 16). [Col. 0637C]

Jeremiah also rebukes this blindness when he says: “The kite in the sky knew its appointed time; the turtledove, swallow, and stork observed the time of their coming; but my people did not know the judgment of the Lord” (Jeremiah 8). This is the judgment which they did not know, concerning which, as was foretold, the Lord says: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). This judgment, however, is for us and against the Jews. The Apostle explains the reason for this judgment, insofar as it is against the Jews, in the Epistle to the Romans: “The nations, which did not pursue righteousness, obtained righteousness, namely the righteousness which is by faith. But Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not by faith, but as though by works. For they stumbled at the stone of stumbling” (Romans 9). And below: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Romans 10).

Therefore, stumbling at Christ and wishing to establish their own righteousness so that they might be regarded not only as righteous but also as authors of righteousness, they have been blinded by God’s just judgment and do not know the Lord’s judgment. They are the more blind inasmuch as they understand their blindness less; if they understood it, they would not have sin. Thus, when the Lord had said: “I came into the world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind,” the Pharisees heard and said: “Are we blind too?” He answered: “If you were blind, you would not have sin; but now, because you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains” (John 9). [Col. 0638A]

There must be no doubt that what Truth says is true. For if, in their own judgment, they were blind and humbly confessed their blindness, they would seek one to enlighten them and would thereafter no longer have the sin of blindness. But their sin remains because, while they were blind, they claimed to see. Because of this sin they were scattered throughout the whole world and removed from the former dignity which they lost, to the great reproach of their shame. Concerning their dispersal and removal, the Psalmist says: “God has shown me over my enemies: do not kill them, lest my people at any time forget. Scatter them in your power, and cast them down, O Lord, my protector” (Psalm 58). Therefore they have been cast down among the nations and scattered through regions. They have lost the holy land and the holy city Jerusalem, the place of their dwelling. They have lost the altar and the temple, the place of sacrifice and prayer. They have lost the anointing of kingship and priesthood. Finally, they have lost even the law, which they carry as a testimony against themselves and do not keep. Yet they preserve it for us, so that by preserving it they may serve us, and so that through them we may know that the law was given by God—a law in which the grace given to us in Christ was testified.

### On the Calling of the Nations and the Overthrow of Idolatry

Moses prophesied of the calling of the nations together with the rejection of the Jews, saying: “They provoked me by that which was not God and angered me by their vanities. And I will provoke them by that which is not a people; by a foolish nation I will anger them” (Deuteronomy 32). By “not a people” and “a foolish nation” he means the multitude of nations once devoted to idolatry, whom God called through his grace after rejecting the Jews, by whom he himself was rejected.

Isaiah says concerning the illumination of the nations: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isaiah 9). And again: “It is too little that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes [Col. 0638D] of Jacob and to bring back the dregs of Israel. Behold, I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49). And again: “Those who did not formerly ask for me sought me; those who did not seek me found me. I said: ‘Behold me, behold me,’ to a nation which did not call upon my name” (Isaiah 65). And again: “I will send from among them those who have been saved to the nations—to the sea, to Africa, to Libya, to those drawing the bow, to Italy and Greece, to distant islands—to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. And they will proclaim my glory to the nations” (Isaiah 66).

Concerning the overthrow of idolatry and the casting down of idols, Isaiah writes: “In that day the idols shall be utterly crushed” (Isaiah 2). And again: “In that day a man will cast away his idols of silver and his images of gold, which [Col. 0639A] he had made for himself” (Isaiah 2). And again: “In that day a man will bow toward his maker, and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel; and he will not bow toward the altars which his hands made and his fingers fashioned; he will not look to sacred groves and shrines” (Isaiah 17). And again: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt; and Egypt’s images will be moved at his presence” (Isaiah 19). And the Psalmist says: “Let all who worship carved images and glory in their idols be put to shame” (Psalm 96).

### On the Establishment of the New Law

Concerning the establishment of the Christian religion, in which God is worshipped not through the carnal observances of the law but in spirit and truth, Jeremiah writes in the person of the Lord: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it upon their heart; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And no one shall teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31). And concerning the abolition of carnal sacrifices, he says in the person of the Lord: “Why do you bring me incense from Sheba and sweet-smelling reed from a distant land?” (Jeremiah 6). “Your burnt offerings are not accepted, and your sacrifices do not please me” (Isaiah 56).

Ezekiel says: “I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will cause you to walk in my commandments” (Ezekiel 36). Isaiah says in the person of the Lord: “To whom shall I look, except to one who is poor and contrite in spirit and trembles at [Col. 0639C] my words? He who sacrifices an ox is like one who kills a man; he who slaughters a beast is like one who brains a dog; he who offers an oblation is like one who offers swine’s blood; he who remembers incense is like one who blesses an idol” (Isaiah 66). By these words God shows that humility, contrition of spirit, and holy fear—that is, purity of heart—are pleasing to him, not the carnal sacrifices of the Jews, which are not acceptable to him.

These and very many other things concerning the blinding of the Jews and the enlightenment of the Gentiles, concerning the abolition of the old and the establishment of the new, are written so plainly in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms [Col. 0640A] that they could neither be denied nor ignored by the Jews at all, unless malice had wonderfully and miserably blinded their hearts. Truth is poured into their ears, and they do not hear; truth is presented to their eyes, and they do not heed it. Like blind men, they carry the law of God as a lamp in their hand and do not know the way. O impious, envious Jew, why do you begrudge the glory of God and the salvation of the nations? Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also the God of the nations? Is God to be worshipped by Jews alone? Is it not written: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him” (Ps. 21)? Is it not written: “All the nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and [Col. 0640B] shall glorify your name” (Ps. 85)? Why do you confine God’s mercy and God’s worship within the narrow limits of one nation and one place? Are the nations not permitted to call upon God? Let them do what Isaiah foretold: “On that day there shall be a root of Jesse, standing as a sign for the peoples; the nations shall entreat him” (Isa. 3). And the prophet Joel says: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2). Isaiah testifies that the house of prayer is shared also by the nations. For he says in the person of the Lord: “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56). Is there not an altar of the Lord in Jerusalem? Isaiah says: “On that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a monument of the Lord beside its boundary; [Col. 0640C] it shall be a sign and a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt” (Isa. 19). Therefore God’s worship and God’s mercy are shared also by the nations. For God has shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all. All have sinned and lack the glory of God. But in the Jews was fulfilled what Jeremiah says: “This is the nation that has not listened to the voice of the Lord its God, nor received correction. Faith has perished and has been taken from their mouth” (Jer. 7). But the faith taken from their mouth has been given to us, that we may believe and confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

[Col. 0641]

# Book on the Sacrament of the Altar, or Letter to Bartholomew, Bishop of Oxford, by Baldwin, Bishop of Canterbury

[Col. 0641A] To his most beloved lord and Father B., by God’s grace bishop of Oxford: Brother Baldwin, servant of the monastery of Ford, eternal greeting in the Lord.

The revered titles of master, lord, and father, each separately, claim their due over me in relation to you; and through the manifold necessity of obedience they almost take me away from myself, so that I am not my own but yours—for after God I owe you all that I am and all that I can do. Yet in this very necessity of obedience my will is free from necessity, since necessity yields to will, not will to necessity. For what is necessary by will is not voluntary by necessity. This freedom restores me to myself, so that I am my own although I am yours—and more my own than yours; for I am more master [Col. 0641B] of my own purpose when I obey your will.

For fear and love, and the reverence mingled from both, have long possessed my heart, so that I had determined not to refuse what you might wish, nor reject what you might command. Yet when your authority pressed me and charity urged me to dictate some writings about the inestimable sacrifice of truth, and to commit what I had dictated to writing, for the edification of faith, I was so divided in my thoughts that, while fearing not to obey, I feared still more to obey. For on both sides fear of a certain danger constrained me; but what was more dangerous to me was also more astonishing to me. The subject is great and far above me—how shall I attain to it? [Col. 0641C] A profound sacrament, veiled by a sacred covering, ineffable, unthinkable, incomprehensible! Who am I, that I should be able to speak of it in chaste and pure language, as is right, fitting, and expedient? Before the darkness of such profundity sense is not admitted, reason is dulled, understanding is stunned, the mind cannot extricate itself in its efforts, and speech fails. This unsearchable mystery is above every sense, reason, and understanding; above the tongues of human beings and angels. Yet the tongue is easily prone to error, and uttered speech easily runs beyond bounds. It is nearly impossible to observe every word with careful caution [Col. 0642A] and to weigh every expression in the balance of judgment, so that nothing may emerge incautiously, nothing suspiciously. A single expression, carelessly uttered or not purely understood in so holy a matter, sometimes gives rise, even without error, to a suspicion of error.

To avoid this danger, I repeatedly offered your affection a true excuse and frequent delay, hoping that you would not persist in your decision. But finding you immovable and overcome by your perseverance, lest I fail in obedience and wound your charity, at last, like one who avoids danger by danger, I yielded to fear against fear. For I was not free stubbornly to refuse what you so earnestly desired. Trusting, therefore, in God’s help, I shall endeavor to undertake what I accept unwillingly, though not without devotion; and what necessity [Col. 0642B] imposes, devotion will somehow bring to completion. Compelled beginnings may indeed sometimes have voluntary continuations. Horses driven by whips often, once they have begun to run, burn with desire to run; and little children compelled to literary studies, once they have progressed, glow with love of learning. I too burn for the undertaking, but I am unequal to it. For willing lies close at hand to me, but I do not find the ability to accomplish. I ask that my insufficiency be aided by your prayer, anticipated by your blessing, and that your goodwill, as I trust, be content with my modest capacity. If I cannot equal what you hope for and accomplish what you desire, let it count toward my pardon that I reverence what you command. Farewell.

## What the order is

[Col. 0642C]

The great and profound mystery of the new and true sacrifice can neither be reliably appraised by the conjectures of human reason nor worthily explained in the persuasive words of human wisdom. But the institution of this sacrament, its cause, truth, power, dignity, and also the significance of its figures, must be investigated by devout inquiry from the words of God himself and of those in whom God has spoken, according to what the sacred authority of both Testaments hands down. Thus the conscience of faith may not depart from the line of truth, and the confession of the mouth may be free from every [Col. 0643A] suspicion of falsehood.

I judge this order of inquiry better suited to making the truth manifest: that the truth of the New Testament, which is first in dignity, should be set before the figures of the Law; that the Testament of new grace may be arranged above the sacrifices; and that, with the light of truth shining beforehand, the darkness of the figures may grow thin and become more easily and clearly visible. As it is written: “For you light my lamp, O Lord; my God, illuminate my darkness” (Ps. 17). For the one who says, “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. 13), indicates that new things are sometimes to be set before old ones. And the voice of the bride agrees when she says: “I have kept for you all fruits, new and old” (Song 7).

First, therefore, it must be considered—so far as he grants who suggests all truth—how old things have been transferred into new; then how the truth of new grace is presented to us in bread and wine; finally, how that same truth was formerly prefigured in the lamb and manna. For if this order is preserved, the image will appear more clearly in the truth than truth formerly appeared in the image. And may he who said that light should shine out of darkness make even the darkness itself shine through light, as it is written: “Night shall be illuminated like day” (Ps. 138). I know indeed that no discourse adequate to this is in my tongue; but, as the Apostle says: “We have such confidence toward God, not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3).

## What is contained in the Old Testament

According to the testimony of the Apostle, those who offer gifts according to the Law serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things. But Christ “is the mediator of a better testament, enacted upon better promises” (Heb. 8). The completion of this testament is shown by the same Apostle, who takes testimony from Jeremiah’s prophecy: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I shall make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah; not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers, on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. 31).

Four things are principally to be considered in the Old Testament: promises, judgments, commandments, and sacraments [Col. 0643D]. Because these four were imperfect and deficient, they had to be changed or perfected through the New Testament. It seems fitting to speak first of the change of promises.

## On the change of promises

In the New Testament it is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). In the Old Testament it is said: “He gave them the lands of the nations, and they possessed their labors” (Ps. 4). There the reward of divine worship seems to be established in the allotment of lands, abundance of grain, wine, and oil, plenty and glory of temporal goods, the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth. Here, however—that is, in the New Testament—no earthly possession or glory is promised, but an eternal inheritance; and it is promised not to the rich, but to the poor. For when Christ was poor, the poor receive the Gospel; and he pronounces judgment upon the rich, saying: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). Therefore what was then promised is now declared to be despised, because the New Testament has been enacted upon better promises.

Yet in those promises made to the ancients, the eternal goods now promised were prefigured. For all things happened to them in figure; and everything given or promised to them was a sign of the better promises upon which the New Testament has been enacted. Thus, when the little son of some exceedingly rich and powerful man is introduced into the inheritance of his deceased father, a most beautiful branch from a tree, with its fruits, may be given him as a sign of possession or investiture. If it is given, because he still thinks as a child and reasons as a child, he rejoices and smiles eagerly at the present beauty and pleasure of the fruits; but his undiscerning age does not know how to consider the extent of the estate or the dignity of the honor he has received.

Accordingly, to the still unformed people of Israel, who were being gradually withdrawn from idolatrous worship and were unaccustomed to heavenly promises, temporal goods were both promised and given, so that they might have some consolation from things known to them by experience; and so that those unable to grasp heavenly things might desire and seek earthly things from God rather than idols. Thus God wished to provide for the weak among his people. But the more perfect persons who then existed judged temporal goods to be despised because of their desire for heavenly things; and in God’s promises they conceived something inestimable, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). One of these, as though drawing forth the sighs of all the righteous from his inmost heart, says: “Behold, what have I in heaven? And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth?” (Ps. 72).

But all those to whom the promises had been made died without receiving what was promised, seeing and greeting it from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth (Heb. 11). Those who say these things show that they seek a homeland. And if they had remembered that from which they had gone out, they certainly had time to return. But now they seek a better one, the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore the reward of divine worship—that is, the recompense of faith and obedience—is not of this present time; rather, “when he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 126). But Christ is the end of the promises, in whom all God’s promises shall be fulfilled, and all hope, expectation, and desire of the righteous shall be completed.

## On the change of judgments

What is to be understood concerning promises must likewise be understood concerning judgments. For in the New Testament it is written: “Those who have done evil shall go into eternal fire” (John [Col. 0645A] 5). But in the Old Testament temporal punishments are established for transgressors, though eternal punishment is figured in them. And as the new promises are expected to be incomparably better than the old, so the threats of the New Testament must be believed to be far, far more terrible than all the judgments of punishments threatened in the former Testament.

## On the change or addition of commandments

Once the promises had been changed for the better, it was right that obedience should be increased, so that, as the reward for divine worship increased, the measure of divine service might also increase. Obedience lies in commandments, and the honor of divine worship consists in observing God’s commands. Now the Law of Moses contained certain moral commandments, such as: “Honor your father and your mother. You shall not kill. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false testimony” (Exod. 20), and others of this kind, which prescribe moral simplicity and a pattern of uprightness. These were not changed in the New Testament but increased. For some things lacking for perfection were added. The Law brought no one to perfection.

Other commandments were mystical, pertaining to sacrificial rites and the solemnity of ceremonies. They shadowed forth by figurative types the mysteries of heavenly sacraments to be revealed in their time; and by mystical signification they contained inwardly hidden and enclosed the grace of spiritual understanding. But the ceremonial things which served as a shadow of things to come were transferred from their former state, so that henceforth [Col. 0645C] we may not know the letter, but enter into the powers of the Lord; and so that, with the letter dying, it may not kill us, but, living by the Spirit, we may also walk by the Spirit. God is no longer to be worshipped in carnal and figurative observances, but adored in spirit and truth; for he seeks such as worship him in spirit and truth.

## On the change of sacraments

The sacraments of the Old Testament contained a certain sanctification in themselves, and the signification of a greater sanctification; the Holy Spirit thereby signifying that the way of the saints had not yet been revealed. They could not make perfect, in respect of conscience, the one who served. Existing only in foods and drinks, various washings, and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of correction [Col. 0645D], they contained sanctification in such a manner that perfection was lacking to them. They possessed mystical signification in such a manner that full truth was not yet present. Therefore sacraments had to be instituted which would sanctify fully and perfectly, and would contain within themselves the present truth of their signification, so that sanctification might lack neither fullness of grace nor signification the presentation of truth. Therefore, with promises, judgments, commandments, and sacraments changed, the Law had to be changed and the New Testament completed in fullness of form and presentation of truth, through new promises and judgments, new commandments and sacraments.

## That Christ is the end of the promises

In the promises of the Law love is suggested; in its judgments fear is instilled; in its commandments obedience is required; in its sacraments grace is concealed; and in all these Christ is prefigured. For Christ is our love, himself the promiser and our promise. Christ is our fear, our lawgiver and our judge. Christ is the pattern of obedience and the command of the Father, whom he commanded us to hear, receive, and love. For in him he commanded blessing and life. Thus Christ himself says: “The Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment, what I should say and what I should speak; and I know that his commandment is eternal life” (John 12).

This same Christ is our mercy, in whom is every grace of the way and truth, and every hope of life and power. For God has bestowed grace upon us in his beloved Son; and every grace hidden in the sacraments [Col. 0646B] is revealed and given by him, who is the power of the sacraments and their sanctification. For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. But grace is attested by the Law, which was changed through grace, according to the state of the person transformed through grace.

## On the change of the Law

As a human being consists of flesh and soul, so the Law consists of letter and spirit. Before receiving the Law, the human being was fleshly, sold under sin, devoted to superstition, and ignorant of true religion. Having received the Law, he began to be instructed in true religion; and, as the order of correction required, he was commanded to offer God what he had previously been accustomed to sacrifice to idols, so that he might turn God’s injury into honor and most rightly condemn himself by his own judgment, rejecting what he had formerly approved and confessing his error by that very change.

But those who before receiving the Law had faith in the one God and did not sacrifice to idols—if they survived after the Law—they could be confirmed by the authority of the Law in persevering in what they had begun. The Law indeed provided that carnal victims should be offered not to idols but to the true God, until the one true sacrifice should put an end to every sacrifice, not only of the Jews but also of the nations. For among all nations it was customary to offer victims to their god. The custom of sacrificing, having begun long before the Law, whether through natural instinct, divine inspiration, parental tradition, or the example and imitation of others [Col. 0646D], became so established that every religion and every superstition was persuaded that God could be appeased by sacrifices; and it held firmly that prayers are heard and crimes can more readily be expiated by the death of victims and the shedding of blood.

Countless books, even of the Gentiles themselves, remain which declare most plainly that among the nations the chief hope of their deliverance and the granting of their vows was placed in the religious practice of sacrifice. Whence this opinion arose, or how, having begun from whatever source, it advanced to become the religion of all, both Jews and Gentiles, is not easy to state. But when the matter is considered more carefully, it brings strong amazement and astonishment: God wonderfully so ordered it that the common opinion of all human beings, who placed hope of their salvation in the religious practice of sacrifice, should serve the future dispensation, later proving effective in bringing all to faith through the death of the one victim—those to be delivered from death by death—and in changing humanity for the better.

The Law was given and was itself to be changed for the better. It was so tempered and conformed to the carnal human being that it condescended to his weakness and, as it were, became weak with the weak. For the person walking according to the flesh was as though he were flesh alone, thinking fleshly thoughts and ignorant of the things of the Spirit. Yet through the Law he had to be led from fleshly understanding and affection to spiritual understanding and affection, so that one who was flesh might cease to be flesh and, spiritually cleaving to God, might become one spirit. This change in the womb of the human being, from flesh into spirit, was figured in the change of the Law [Col. 0647B] from letter into spirit. In the letter—that is, in the carnal observances belonging to the letter—the Law was adapted, in its weakness, to the weak human being. But as the human being grew strong from his weakness, the Law was changed for the better, advancing with the one who advanced and ascending with him from lower things to higher, as it is written: “When the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up with them” (Ezek. 1).

## On the mystical meaning of the legal victim

The mystical meaning of the Law, in its carnal sacrifices, principally prefigured three things: the human being’s guilt; punishment for guilt; and the grace of deliverance. For in carnal sacrifices the human being was shown to himself as he was through sin, and what punishment he deserved because of sin. Since through the guilt of disobedience he was liable to death, condemned to death by God’s sentence, and thus owing death, he was nevertheless not instructed by the Law to kill himself or pay the due penalty of his own death. Instead, the human being was commanded to offer, as it were, the price of his redemption. He was rightly valued as a sheep for slaughter, because through foolishness he resembled cattle and deserved death more than the animal slaughtered in his place.

Do you see, O human being, made in the image and likeness of God, how far you have been devalued, how vile you have become? If you consider the indignity into which you have been cast from before God’s eyes, then a goat, ram, or some other animal—provided it is clean—is, as it were, your fitting valuation and just price. Perhaps in this one small respect some honor is accorded you, because you are commanded to offer a clean animal; or does even this rather contribute to your shame, because the animal offered for you is called clean while you yourself are unclean? For you need to be cleansed by sacrifice precisely because you are unclean.

But if you consider the original dignity of your first creation, your price will no longer be a goat or a ram, to which you were likened through foolishness, from the time you were first deformed. Rather, it will be the only-begotten Son of God, through whom the image of God was formed in you. He himself will be your price, by whose blood you are to be redeemed, so that the image of God may be re-formed in you through the same Son, who is the image of the invisible God. Therefore, in the irrational animals offered in place of the human being and slaughtered as though in vicarious death for the human being, the human being was shown to himself as he was through guilt, and that he was worthy of death because of guilt.

There the human being could—if indeed he were human and not altogether cattle—be reminded of his fallen and mortal condition, so that, his heart inflamed and his inward parts changed, pierced by repentance, he might return to God and, never departing, might always be with God, saying: “My heart was inflamed and my inward parts were changed; I was reduced to nothing and did not know it. I became like cattle before you, and I am always with you” (Ps. 72). But what is more commonly rendered in another translation, “I became like a beast of burden before you” (ibid.), accords with that passage of the Psalm where it is written: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with irrational beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48).

Moreover, through the victims slaughtered for him, the human being could be instructed not only toward knowledge of his condition; a pattern of repentance and amendment of life was also secretly suggested to him. From the death of animals and their nature, a certain likeness of spiritual life or spiritual death was communicated to him. Of spiritual death: that he might slaughter the old life within himself, so that he might no longer be lustful and wanton like a goat; unwilling to bear the yoke of obedience like a stiff-necked bull; armed with the horns of pride like a ram—for God breaks the horns of sinners. Nor, finally, should he be carnal or animal-like, but spiritual, examining all things spiritually; having nothing beastlike in himself, but slaughtering and killing within himself every irrational thought and brutish affection.

A pattern of spiritual life was also set before the human being from the nature of animals: that through discernment he might divide the hoof, knowing what is between right and left, what is permitted, what is fitting, and what is expedient; and that through devotion and observance of God’s commandments he might continually chew over, as though his food, the law of his God. In ordering his conduct, he was to be shaped from the simplicity and gentleness, warmth and patience of animals toward the pursuit of like virtues in himself. Thus, yes, thus after sin God subjected the human being to the instruction of brute animals, to his shame, so that the human being might learn to regulate life and order conduct as though in a school of those without understanding.

Thus, yes, thus the human being is sent to the school of the ant to learn wisdom, as Solomon says: “Go, sluggard, to the ant; consider her ways, and learn wisdom,” etc. (Prov. 6). Thus, yes, thus God, who is before the ages, humbled the human being. At the beginning he crowned him with glory and honor and set him over the works of his hands. He subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field (Ps. 8). But now he has overwhelmed him with shame; and he who was made a little lower than the angels is now found inferior to the beasts of the field.

The human being is commanded to sacrifice a lamb for himself, to signify the grace of deliverance and the mercy of the Deliverer, who by death would free the human being from guilt and death. For human folly—that is, guilt—is the cause of death. But in the fact that the lamb was commanded not only to be slaughtered but also eaten, it was foreshown that Christ would give himself to us both as a price and as food. How he gave himself as food must be considered by us both from the words of the four Gospels and from the words of the Apostle, beginning, as the order requires, with the words of the Evangelist Matthew, who writes thus concerning the institution of the new sacrifice:

> From the Gospel according to Matthew: “While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, gave it to his disciples, and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from this, all of you. For this is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for [Col. 0649B] many for the forgiveness of sins. But I tell you: I shall not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father’” (Matt. 26).

## On casting away the old things

Our Lord Jesus Christ, on the day before he suffered, duly completed the old and mystical Passover with his disciples. He thereby set a limit to the legal ordinances, bringing with honor to their proper end what then had to end and thereafter be cast away. For those things that could not suffice of themselves for complete amendment had indeed to cease, so that, once grace had shone forth, eternal redemption had been discovered, and the one true sacrifice for many had been introduced in place of these figurative rites, multiplicity might yield to unity, figure to truth, shadow to light, and oldness to newness. For when new things arrive, old things must be cast away; and the very oldest of the old things must be eaten, so that the human being may eat the bread of angels, which from ancient days God in his sweetness prepared for the poor.

## What are the very oldest of the old things

The old things are the sacrifices of the Old Testament, which the Law of Moses commands to be offered, such as Aaron and his sons offered, who were accustomed to slaughter young rams and pour out the blood of goats and calves for human sins. The very oldest of the old things are what Melchizedek offered, prefiguring Christ’s priesthood. Of him God the Father swore, saying: “You are a priest forever” (Ps. 109).

Now Melchizedek was priest of God Most High and king of Salem. He met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and, “bringing forth bread and wine, blessed him and said: ‘Blessed be Abraham by God Most High, who created heaven and earth’; and he gave him tithes of everything” (Gen. 14). In the reading of Genesis, Melchizedek is suddenly introduced as though without father or mother, having neither beginning of days nor end of life. His name is interpreted “king of righteousness,” and he was called king of Salem, that is, king of peace. From the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Apostle interprets, it clearly appears that all these things belong to Christ, who is king of righteousness and king of peace, as it is written of him: “In his days righteousness shall arise and abundance of peace” (Ps. 71). He was born from a Father without a mother, and born from a mother without a father; he is beginning and end, without beginning of days [Col. 0650A] and without end.

## On the rite of sacrifice

What Melchizedek offered—namely, bread and wine—were sacraments of Christ’s sacraments. The Church observes this rite of sacrifice, namely in bread and wine, Christ having instituted it thus, for he is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. And although the saving victim was prefigured in the sacrifice of the patriarch Abraham and in the other sacrifices of other righteous persons, nevertheless the form of the true sacrifice which Christ wished to be observed in the Church is expressed more plainly in the sacrifice of Melchizedek bringing forth bread and wine.

But if anyone thinks that Melchizedek brought out bread and wine for the refreshment of Abraham and his companions, rather than offering them to God in sacrifice, let him know that in the Canon, after the gifts of the boy Abel and the sacrifice of the patriarch Abraham have been commemorated, that which Melchizedek offered is also commemorated: “a holy sacrifice, an immaculate victim.” The reading of Genesis itself plainly declares the same. For when Melchizedek, king of Salem, is introduced as bringing forth bread and wine, it is immediately added: “For he was priest of God Most High” (Gen. 14). He could certainly have brought these things out for refreshment even had he not been a priest; but the role of offering sacrifice and of blessing is shown when he is called priest, to whose office it belongs to sacrifice, bless, and receive tithes.

## Proof from the words of Ambrose

[Col. 0650C]

What was said above—that the things Melchizedek offered are meant by “the very oldest of the old things”—can be proved from the words of Saint Ambrose (ch. 8), who says in his treatise *On the Mysteries*:

> “The sacraments of the Church are older than those of the Synagogue. For the Synagogue took its beginning from the Law of Moses; but Abraham was much older. When he had defeated his enemies and recovered his own nephew, when he possessed the victory, then Melchizedek met him and brought forth those things which Abraham received with reverence.”

In these words of Ambrose the following points must be carefully noted: Abraham received with reverence, as holy things, what Melchizedek brought forth; the Synagogue took its beginning from the Law of Moses; and the sacraments of the Church are older than those of the Synagogue, [Col. 0650D] since Abraham, who received what Melchizedek brought forth, came before it. Likewise, the Church is evidently older than the Synagogue, since it began with the first righteous person. Therefore what Melchizedek offered may be called “the very oldest of the old things” in comparison with the sacrifices of the Synagogue, which began with the Law of Moses.

Nevertheless, they cannot so absolutely be called “the very oldest of the old things” as though no older gifts or sacrifices had preceded them. For Scripture says thus of Abel: “Abel also offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat” (Gen. 4). Of Noah it is written: “Noah built an altar to the Lord, and, taking from all the clean animals and birds, offered a burnt offering to the Lord upon the altar; and the Lord smelled an odor of sweetness” (Gen. 8).

From the foregoing it appears that, when new things arrive, the very oldest of the old things are to be eaten in such a way that, in the offering of the new sacrifice, the communion of the heavenly table, and the participation in spiritual nourishment, the form of sacrifice is renewed which is known to have begun with Melchizedek’s sacrifice—older than the Law and far worthier than the legal rite of sacrificing. Therefore, carnal sacrifices having been rejected and cast far away as old things, bread and wine, as the very oldest of the old things, are to be offered and spiritually eaten by us.

## “While they were dining, Jesus took bread”

After the apostles had asked the Lord, “Where do you wish us to prepare the Passover for you?” (Matt. 26), as they were preparing it and were already dining, though that food was not enough, the Lord prepared their food, since this is his manner of preparation. And he prepared it thus: he took bread and blessed it, etc. He took it, as is written in the Canon of the Mass—although this is not read in any of the Gospels—“into his holy and venerable hands.” The word “took,” in the proper force of its meaning, almost plainly indicates that he took it in his hands; for thus we take something when we grasp it with our hands.

What he took is shown by what follows: he took bread, which before being taken still had the appearance and substance of bread, bread to be wonderfully changed into Christ’s true flesh by powerful virtue. It is believed that he took unleavened bread. For on the fourteenth day of the first month, after leaven had been removed, the lamb was sacrificed in the evening. Hence the Church customarily offers [Col. 0651C] unleavened, not leavened, bread. Yet the Greeks are said to offer leavened rather than unleavened bread, lest they appear to Judaize. Now in unleavened bread there was a figure of truth, as the Apostle says: “Therefore let us feast, not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5). But the figure, as the Greeks are thought to maintain, ought to have ceased when truth arrived, so that we do not offer unleavened bread, lest we appear, like the Jews, to celebrate the Passover with unleavened bread.

## Against the reasoning of the Greeks
The Roman Church has preferred to offer unleavened bread, following Christ’s example: for, when he inaugurated the new Passover, he is believed to have instituted the mystery of the new sacrament in unleavened bread. Nor does the aforesaid reasoning of the Greeks [Col. 0651D] possess such force that it can compel us to offer leavened bread, lest, after receiving the grace of truth, we should seem, together with the Jews, to serve the shadows of figures.

For although truth has now come, not every religious use of signs and figures has altogether ceased in the New Testament. Fire and water, incense, wine and oil, the anointings of kings and priests, and many other things which were in use in the Old Testament and represented something mystical, are still customarily employed in sacraments and sacramentals, both to magnify the honor of divine worship and to signify the power of spiritual realities. And so long as the sacraments are necessary to us, figures and signs cannot be wholly rejected. [Col. 0652A] For the sacraments themselves are certain signs. We anoint kings and priests, burn incense, are washed and sanctified in waters, offer and pour out wine; yet we neither Judaize nor intend, in doing this, to Judaize. Nor, therefore, should these things be rejected lest we seem to favor or agree with the Jews.

### On what is written in Amos: “Sacrifice praise from leaven”

What is written in Amos, “Sacrifice praise from leaven” (Amos 4), neither supports the Greeks nor opposes our custom. In place of “praise,” as St. Jerome says, Aquila interpreted *eucharistia*, that is, thanksgiving; as though it said: “Sacrifice eucharist from leaven.” But it is clear that this is said by the Lord through the prophet not as a command but, as it were, as a reproach, [Col. 0652B] both from the tenor of what precedes and follows and from the Law of Moses itself. For leaven, according to Moses’ commandment, is never offered to God.

Now Amos writes thus: “Come to Bethel and act wickedly; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression” (ibid.). To act wickedly and multiply transgression, to come to Bethel and Gilgal—all these are evils, more to be prohibited than commanded. For Bethel and Gilgal were places of idolatry. Through Hosea the Lord says: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal” (Hos. 9). And again in the same prophet: “They were vain in Gilgal, sacrificing oxen” (Hos. 12). At Bethel, moreover, Jeroboam set up a golden calf for the people to worship. Therefore, to come [Col. 0652C] to Bethel and Gilgal with intent to worship was evil; and “Come to Bethel” is spoken as if in the indignation of one permitting it and refusing to forbid it. After certain other evils enumerated in the prophet Amos, which seem, as it were, to be commanded, he adds: “Sacrifice praise from leaven; call out voluntary offerings and proclaim them. For thus you have desired, children of Israel, says the Lord. Therefore I also gave you numbness of teeth in all your cities, and lack of bread in all your places” (Amos 4).

Sometimes in the prophets, things appear to be commanded through the imperative mood which are nevertheless not commanded, but are shown, from the circumstances of Scripture and from the very manner of speaking, to be more prohibited [Col. 0652D] than done. Such is what is said to Judas: “What you are doing, do more quickly” (John 13). Such is the passage in Isaiah: “Take counsel, and it shall be frustrated; speak a word, and it shall not come to pass” (Isa. 8). Such also is the passage now under consideration: “Sacrifice praise from leaven.” Therefore the holy Roman Church has not presumed to alter the form of consecrating in unleavened bread which Christ is believed to have introduced; rather, supported by such great authority, it has wished to preserve it immovably.

### Certain matters are set forth differently by different persons

In Matthew we read: “He took bread and blessed it” (Matt. 26). But in Luke it is thus: “Having taken bread, he gave thanks and broke it” (Luke 22). In the Epistle to the Corinthians it is thus: “He took bread and, [Col. 0653A] having given thanks, broke it” (1 Cor. 11). In the Canon, however, it is thus: “Lifting his eyes to heaven, giving thanks, he blessed and broke.”

Accordingly, from Matthew’s statement it is certain that Jesus blessed; from Luke’s statement, with which Paul agrees, it is certain that he gave thanks. Hence both are rightly joined in the Canon, so that it says: “Giving thanks, he blessed.” But the words added in the Canon, “lifting his eyes to heaven,” are not found at this point in any Evangelist in the translation we use. Elsewhere, however, he is read to have prayed or given thanks with uplifted eyes. In John, when he was about to raise Lazarus: “But Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said: Father, I give you thanks because you have heard me” (John 11). Again elsewhere: “Having lifted his eyes [Col. 0653B] to heaven, he said: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17). And when, with five loaves and two fish, he was about to satisfy about five thousand people, according to Luke he looked to heaven and blessed (Luke 6). Yet the words inserted into the Canon, “lifting his eyes to heaven,” have rightly been received both by the faith and practice of the Church as handed down from the elders, to whom this became known beyond doubt from some source, although we cannot readily say from what source it became known to them.

For we cannot give a reason for everything handed down by the elders; but, for things not handed down without reason, the authority of the elders itself ought to be a reason for us. For our faith itself, without which [Col. 0653C] it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11), rests more upon authority than upon human reasoning. When Peter says that an account of the faith and hope within us must be given to every person who asks, no stronger account of faith can be offered than the authority of the Scriptures or the authority of the elders—those, that is, who are found never to have erred in respect of the faith itself and are known to have pleased God by that faith.

### On the taking of the cup

In speaking of the taking of the cup, Matthew writes that the Lord gave thanks, but does not state that he blessed; just as, in speaking of the taking of bread, he writes that the Lord blessed, but does not state that he gave thanks. But because, in the taking of bread, where Matthew says, “He blessed” [Col. 0653D] (Matt. 26), and Mark, “Blessing, he broke” (Mark 14), there Luke, without mentioning blessing, says, “He gave thanks” (Luke 22), and Paul, “Giving thanks, he broke” (1 Cor. 11), someone may think that in this place “gave thanks” and “blessed” are the same: so that, when it is said, “Jesus took bread and blessed,” it may be understood that he blessed God—that is, gave thanks to God.

This interpretation would indeed be straightforward if it said, “He blessed God,” or “the Lord,” or something of that kind. But because “He took bread” comes first, and immediately follows, “And he blessed and broke,” it seems rather that he blessed the bread which he had taken and, while blessing it or after blessing it, broke it. Yet from the testimony of Luke and Paul it is certain—though Matthew and Mark do not say it—that Jesus, having taken bread, [Col. 0654A] gave thanks.

Therefore, in the order of Mass, after the bread has been taken and placed upon the altar, and likewise the cup, after the secret prayers the solemnity of consecrating the sacrament rightly begins with thanksgiving: the priest begins, “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God,” and the choir answers, “It is fitting and just.” Then the priest continues, “It is truly fitting and just,” and so forth, through to the praises which we are to sing without end to God together with the angels.

### He blessed

Priests now customarily give blessings by pronouncing words and making the sign of the cross; and they bless and sanctify things which are to be consecrated by them. For, as the Apostle says, God’s creature “is sanctified through the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. 4). [Col. 0654B] But Scripture does not say that Christ made the sign of the cross when giving the blessing.

God, however, is often read to have blessed and to have spoken certain words in blessing. For when he had created every living and moving creature which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every winged creature according to its kind, he blessed them, saying: “Increase, multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply upon the earth” (Gen. 1). When he had created male and female, he blessed them and said: “Increase, multiply, and fill the earth” (ibid.). After the flood he also blessed Noah and his son and said: “Increase and multiply,” etc. (Gen. 11). God is also read to have blessed and said nothing, [Col. 0654C] as where it says: “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (Gen. 1); and where Jacob says to Laban, among other things: “God blessed you at my coming” (Gen. 30). When he multiplied five loaves in the wilderness, it is said: “He looked to heaven and blessed” (John 5). In the account of another miracle concerning seven loaves and a few little fish, it says: “He blessed them and commanded them to be set before the people” (Mark 8). And when, before the disciples’ eyes, he ascended to heaven: “Lifting up his hands, he blessed them; and it came to pass, while he was blessing them, that he departed from them” (Luke 24).

But at the supper he is reported to have said these words: “This is my body” (Matt. 26). By these words he either substantially changed the bread and showed it changed, or merely showed it already changed. For if, before Christ spoke these words—as indeed, if he wished, he could—he substantially changed the bread, whether before the breaking or in the breaking, at the place where the Evangelist says “He blessed,” which may be understood as “he changed,” then the change was not made by these words but was only the manifestation of a change made earlier. But if the order in the event was the same as that found in the Gospel narrative, so that one must understand that one thing happened after another in sequence and distinctly, then taking the bread preceded the blessing, blessing preceded breaking, and breaking preceded the giving and the utterance of the words. If this is granted, then, if the change was effected by these words, breaking preceded the change—whereas at the altar consecration precedes breaking, not breaking consecration. [Col. 0655A]

But it may be said that all, or some, of these things could have occurred simultaneously, although they could only be narrated distinctly. Yet the order of words used by Matthew, Mark, and the Apostle seems to suggest that the change took place before the utterance of the words, “This is my body,” or “This is my blood” (ibid.). In Matthew, indeed, “Take and eat” comes first, which must surely be understood of that which the Lord wished to be taken and eaten. In the same Evangelist, “Drink from this, all of you” comes first; then follows: “For this is my blood.” When it has been said that the Lord wished it to be drunk by the disciples, Mark first says, “Take” (Mark 14), and then adds: “For this is my body.” [Col. 0655B] In the same Evangelist the order of words regarding the cup is: “Having taken the cup, giving thanks, he gave it to them; and they all drank from it. And he said to them: This is my blood.” In the Apostle, “Take and eat” (1 Cor. 11) comes first; then follows: “For this is my body.”

But the Evangelists and the Apostle could have altered the order of events and words used by Christ, if perhaps they were concerned only to disclose what was done and said, and not the order in which it was done or said. Therefore it is difficult to prove that Christ effected the change by these words; but it must be believed without doubt that Christ spoke these words and substantially [Col. 0655C] changed the bread and wine, either when he spoke them or earlier, when he willed and as he willed. Yet by the priest, who is the minister and not the author of so great a change, the mystery of consecration can in no way be accomplished without Christ’s words, just as the sacrament of baptism cannot in any way be administered validly without its solemn verbal form.

Consider how great is the power of the divine blessing; consider how wonderfully effective its force is. God’s blessing, conferred upon our first parents for the multiplication of the human race through sexual fertility, had effect (Gen. 1). God’s blessing had effect to multiply Laban’s goods. By the power of God’s blessing the five loaves were wondrously multiplied in themselves (John 5). But this blessing, of which we now speak, did not multiply bread within its own kind or increase it in number or quantity; rather, with greater wonder, while its form remained unchanged, it changed one substance into another substance—not a substance then beginning to exist, but one which had existed before. [Col. 0655D]

“This has been done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes” (Ps. 117); but in the eyes of the heart, not in the eyes of the flesh. For these things are hidden from the eyes of the flesh; they are also closed to the eyes of human reason, yet wonderfully visible to the eyes of faith alone. The magnitude of astonishment and intensity of wonder cannot exist without some faith; they move faith itself so that it marvels equally that this is done by God and believed by a human being. Both are wonderful. For just as it is wonderfully effected by God, so it is wonderfully believed by a human being. Hence those who do not believe it happens marvel still more that it is believed. But God is the one author of both matters—the deed which is believed [Col. 0656A] and the faith by which it is believed—wonderful in both: in the power of the deed and in the grace of faith.

Such a wonderful and astonishing novelty, because it exceeds humanity, could not be believed by any reasoning if any other author of so great a novelty were proclaimed than he who alone performs great wonders. What cannot he do who can do all things? What cannot he do, to whom power itself is subject when he wills? He calls into being things which are not; he changes things which are into what he wills, and as he wills, through countless modes of transformation subject to his will. He turned the sea into dry land (Ps. 65 [104]); striking the Egyptians, he turned their rivers into blood (Ps. 77); he turned their heart so that they hated his people (Ps. 104). He turned Moses’ rod into a serpent, [Col. 0656B] and restored the serpent into a rod (Exod. 3); he turned the rock into pools of water and the crag into springs of water (Ps. 113). He is the one who blessed bread and said: “This is my body” (Matt. 26). No room remains for us to doubt either the power of the one acting, the faith of the deed, or the truth of what was said. For he who did it and said it is mighty in deed and word.

### And he broke

If, by the power of blessing, the bread’s change into Christ’s body occurred before the breaking, then according to ecclesiastical custom the bread is rightly blessed first at the altar and broken afterward. Yet by breaking the body is not diminished, but remains whole in its fullness. It is indeed divided in truth, but in the sacrament it nevertheless remains undivided in itself: though distributed to many through several portions of breaking, it is found whole in each and received whole by each. It is not greater in a larger portion nor smaller in a smaller; for the whole is equally contained in the greater and the lesser part, neither greater nor lesser.

A sign of this matter formerly preceded it when the Lord rained manna for the children of Israel to eat. For he who collected more than a gomor, and he who prepared less than a gomor, did not have more than a gomor, nor did he find less than a gomor. Thus it is written: “He who collected more had no excess; nor did he who prepared less find less” (Exod. 16). And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “He who had much did not abound, [Col. 0656D] and he who had little did not have less” (2 Cor. 8).

### On the foregoing words: “He took, He blessed, He broke”

Since it is pleasing to apply these three things—the taking of bread, the blessing, and the breaking—to mystical signification or to the edification of faith and morals, they must be considered individually in sequence, so that the whole series of the deed may contribute to our sanctification and instruction.

### On the taking of bread

The assumption of our nature may fittingly be understood as a certain taking of bread. Christ took that by which he would feed us when, through the mystery of the Incarnation, he united humanity to himself, turning the hay of our flesh into grain, that he might feed us with the fat of wheat and satisfy us with the marrow of grain. He became for us the grain of wheat to be sown in good soil [Col. 0657A] and multiplied more abundantly. He became for us bread which strengthens the human heart: bread as the food of teaching, bread in the example of life, bread in every gift of spiritual grace, bread in every consolation of our misery; bread sustaining our life and strengthening us in the toil of the way, so that in his strength we may reach Horeb, the mountain of God.

### On the blessing

Here he received blessing from the Lord; and God gave blessing to himself as man. He gave it not merely that he might be blessed, but that he might be able to bless all who bless him, because those who bless him shall inherit the land. For God gave him the blessing of all nations and confirmed the covenant of his promise upon his head, upon which he wore the crown of thorns, that he might become a curse for us, [Col. 0657B] as it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. 12). Therefore he was cursed by human beings and for human beings, but blessed by God. Thus it is written: “They shall curse, but you shall bless” (Ps. 108). The covenant which God established with Abraham was confirmed in this man: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 12), so that all nations might be blessed in him. He is blessed above all others in every fullness of grace; and from his fullness we have all received. For the ointment upon the head descends to the beard, Aaron’s beard; it descends also to the hem of his garment, because there the Lord commanded blessing (Ps. 137).

### On the breaking

Would that God may acknowledge us in his blessings, so that we too may acknowledge him in the breaking of bread. Breaking belongs to distribution. He broke, that he might give to many, that he might communicate his grace to many. For there are divisions of graces, and each has his own gift: one in this way, another in that; one more, another less (1 Cor. 12). One sits at a great table; others, like little dogs, eat of the crumbs falling from their masters’ table (Matt. 15). If Jesus had not broken, how could even a crumb have reached us? He broke and distributed. He scattered; he gave to the poor. He broke through grace, in order to break his own wrath and his Father’s wrath. For God said, in order to destroy us, “unless his one chosen one had stood in the breach before him, [Col. 0657D] to turn away his wrath” (Ps. 105). He stood indeed and made atonement by invincible constancy; he stood unbroken in the breach. Yet he himself broke, when of his own will he exposed his flesh to the passions as if to be broken—that is, crushed.

There he shattered the powers of the bows; there he shattered the heads of the dragon; there he shattered all our enemies in his wrath. There, in a certain manner, he shattered the tablets of the former covenant, so that we might not be under the law. There he shattered the yoke of our captivity. In short, he broke everything by which we were broken, that he might restore whole everything broken in us and set free those who are crushed. For we were bound in poverty and iron; and still, good Jesus, although you have broken your wrath, although you have broken bread for us in our poverty, [Col. 0658A] nevertheless we still suffer want and still hunger. Surely you said: “Those who eat me shall hunger still” (Ecclus. 24): still, that is, until iniquity passes away. For they do not yet cease to hunger; a time will come when they shall hunger no more and thirst no more.

Meanwhile, day by day break this bread for the hungry. For today and daily we gather some crumbs, and today too we need daily bread. “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11). Unless you give it, who will give to us? In all our destitution, want, poverty, need, and tribulation, there is none to break bread for us, none to restore us, except you, our God. In all our consolations we gather crumbs of broken bread and experience, through their benefit, how sweet your mercy is. Yet we still are in need; and through a sweetness tasted our appetite, as though provoked, hungers ever more and more.

[Col. 0658B]

### Recapitulation

If the taking of bread at supper, the blessing, and the breaking ought to be understood according to mystical signification, then, in the manner set forth above, Christ took bread when he united humanity to himself; he blessed when, for humanity’s sake, he sanctified himself; he broke when he communicated to human beings the grace of sanctification, as he himself said: “For them I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth” (John 17). Now let the discussion proceed, following the order of the words, to what follows.

### He gave

Jesus broke and gave to his disciples; [Col. 0658C] nor need one inquire what he gave, for he himself makes it clear, saying: “This is my body.” Therefore he gave his own body, and not apart from himself. For this purpose he assumed a body: that he might give himself to us. For he was born for this purpose: to bear witness to the truth; to raise up the prayers spoken in his name by the earlier prophets; to fulfill the promises in the manifestation of truth, according to the oath which he swore to Abraham our father—that he would give himself to us (Luke 1).

O best gift and perfect gift, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1). Christ was given to us to be clothed with, eaten, and offered: as clothing, as nourishment, as a price. To be clothed with, indeed, as it is written: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” [Col. 0658D] (Rom. 8). To be eaten, as he now says: “Take and eat.” To be offered for us and by us: for us, to be offered through the bitterness of his passion and death; by us, to be offered through commemoration of that same passion and death, as he instituted, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 12). Here, however, he is remembered to have given himself in the manner in which he gave himself to be eaten. Let us now carefully observe to whom he gave himself in this manner.

### To his disciples

In giving to his disciples who were present, he showed beforehand that the grace of this sacrament belongs to those who will be numbered among [Col. 0659A] his disciples. Therefore those outside discipline, those not subject to Christ’s teaching, those who order their lives according to their own judgment rather than Christ’s doctrine—these are as alien to this grace as they are unworthy of the name of disciples.

### And he said, “Take”

The preceding words, “Jesus took bread,” and so forth, down to the word “Take,” are the Evangelist’s words (Matt. 26), reporting what Jesus did; then what he said immediately follows: “Take,” he says. Those are rightly said to receive to whom he says, “Take”: those to whom he himself gives, to whom the authority of the giver grants permission to receive, rather than the presumption of their own will. For those who thrust themselves forward shamelessly and irreverently seize rather than receive. Thus “Take” seems spoken against their presumption, since it has first been stated that he gave.

Hence, when this sacrament is dispensed to the unworthy, it is more seized than given, because permission to receive is not granted to those to whom receiving is unlawful. For they do not have authority to receive, as it is written: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat” (Heb. 13). Yet in a certain sense it may be said both to be given to the unworthy and received by the unworthy; but received as a sword is received by those of whom it is said: “All who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26). For whoever receive the authority to judge, which may be signified by the sword, not as entrusted to them by a superior authority but through themselves—that is, through their own presumption—[Col. 0659C] shall perish by the sword, because they turn the presumption of receiving into judgment against themselves.

### And eat

This sacrifice was instituted by the Lord not merely to be offered but also to be eaten. Therefore it now says: “Eat.” For concerning its offering, Luke and the Apostle report the Lord to have said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22; 1 Cor. 11). The typological lamb is first killed and then eaten, signifying by its death and consumption the death and eating of the true Lamb. Yet the true Lamb is eaten before he is killed. The new sacrifice had to be instituted before Christ’s passion, because the old sacrifice also had to be ended beforehand. For what was not to be repeated after Christ’s passion had to be concluded before his passion. [Col. 0659D]

When the old sacrifice came to an end, the new had immediately to have the beginning of its institution.

Likewise, before Christ’s passion the disciples who were to suffer scandal at Christ’s death had to be fortified by the power of this sacrament, lest their faith utterly fail and lest the tempter, who demanded them, should triumph as victor over conquered foes. Finally, while Judas was still among the disciples, an example was to be set down for the future concerning tolerating evildoers in the Church while they remain hidden.
