That Judas, tolerated by the Lord because he was not accused, received the sacrament of his body and blood is evident both from Luke the Evangelist’s words and from the words of St. Augustine, who in Sermon 62 on John says:

> “After the bread Satan then entered into [Col. 0660A] him. Therefore he had entered earlier, by putting into his heart the thought by which he would betray Christ.”

And below:

> “But now, after the bread, he entered into him, not so as to tempt one who belonged to another, but to possess his own. Yet Judas did not then receive Christ’s body, as some who read carelessly suppose. For one must understand that the Lord had already distributed to them all the sacrament of his body and blood, among whom Judas himself was present, as blessed Luke narrates with the utmost plainness. Then they came to the point where, according to John’s narrative, the Lord most clearly identifies his betrayer by the dipped and offered morsel, perhaps signifying the latter’s deceit by the dipping of the bread.”

[Col. 0660B] For the three aforesaid causes, or whatever other causes there may be, the eating of the true Lamb—an observance to be continued in the Church after Christ’s death—was instituted before that death and immediately put into use in the very manner in which it was to be used. But according to the order of nature itself and, as it were, the law of eating, the eating of the typological lamb followed the death of the victim, which it ought not—and could not—precede; and eating a victim already dead was customary not only according to nature but also according to the Law. Although its death could signify the Liberator’s death, neither its death nor its eating—of an animal consumed by death and eating—could give life or deliver from death.

But the eating of the true Lamb preceded his death, not according to the order of law or nature but according to a certain order of grace, [Col. 0660C] so that the victim, still living, soon to die, and to live again, might indicate the order of grace which he works in us. By its power we are enabled to live soberly, justly, and piously before death; by its power we are fortified so that we may receive the sleep of death with piety; by its power we are delivered from death and raised to life, once we have first paid the death which we owe. For this is the order of grace: good life, precious death, blessed life.

### This is my body

Jesus Christ showed by speaking what he had done, and announced the power of his work in words. For he did and said: “This is my body” (Matt. 26). But in the creation of things, he said and did. For when light was to be created, God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made [Col. 0660D] (Gen. 1). After the light was made, he is not read to have said, “This is light”; nor was this necessary, because the power of the speaker was manifested by the evident resulting and obedient work. The word remained hidden until it became plain through the indication of the appearing work. When he spoke for things to be made, what was made immediately came into being; and in the things made it became known that he who was able to make by speaking had said that he would make them. In this way “the invisible things of God are clearly perceived, being understood through the things that have been made,” together with his eternal power (Rom. 1).

Thus in created things the power of God, by which he commands that the things made should be made, is understood and in a certain way seen. But in this most wonderful change it is far otherwise. For a deed so hidden and so remote from human knowledge [Col. 0661A] could not be made known except through a word. Therefore he blessed and said: “This is my body.” By this word the omnipotent Word of God made known one work of his power, at which we all marvel. For he did and spoke, so that, once it was spoken, it might be believed.

Although Christ may be called, by resemblance, a vine, a lamb, a rock, or something similar, which can fittingly belong to him by signification, let no one suppose that this statement too is figuratively uttered by him when he says: “Take and eat: This is my body.” What he says is to be taken and eaten is called Christ’s body not figuratively or according to the logic of resemblance, but according to the truth of its proper nature: it truly is Christ’s body, given for us, as he is reported [Col. 0661B] in Luke to have said: “This is my body, which is given for you” (Luke 22). Therefore what Christ says, “This is my body,” is explicit truth, not a figure.

This word of truth, which is not to be taken utterly from my mouth, ought not to be obscured by a figure, but ought to bring the figures of the Law to an end. Nor should one seek a figure of speech in the truth, where words alone must reveal what until now lay hidden under figures of things. Therefore let no one, through suspicion of a figure or another meaning, become darkened in his own opinion, like one who gropes at noon or seeks a shadow in the light. The interpretation to be expressed in these words of Christ, as also in the deed, is that recognized as ecclesiastical interpretation, [Col. 0661C] confirmed by the authority of the orthodox Fathers and commended by the faith of the catholic and apostolic Church.

For Christ built the Church upon the rock of faith; Christ revealed to the Church the mysteries of heavenly sacraments; in order to unite the Church more closely to himself, he instituted this sacrament; he inspired the Church with faith in this sacrament, instructed that faith by words, and gave the Church understanding of the words, that he might feed her with the bread of life and understanding (Ecclus. 15), giving her understanding according to his utterance. Therefore as the Church believes and understands, so Christ wished to be understood; thus the Spirit of truth, who suggests all truth, enlightened her; and she received it thus; and as she received it from him, so she handed it down to us.

In the Apostles she received the word of faith [Col. 0661D]—which is the word of God—when she heard Christ saying, “This is my body.” Hearing the word of faith, she conceived faith in the word, because faith comes from hearing, and hearing through Christ’s word. Faith in this word is either the very same faith in the invisible deed or is inseparable from faith in the deed. For as soon as the word is heard, the deed too is believed in the word. But the deed is invisible: the bread’s change into Christ’s body occurred invisibly. Yet the more obscure the deed, the more clearly it was said: “This is my body,” the speech declaring what was hidden. For the declaration of speech gives light and grants understanding to the little ones (Ps. 118): that is, to the humble, who are not puffed up by their own wisdom but think devoutly concerning matters of faith.

If the change had occurred visibly, or if, having occurred invisibly, [Col. 0662A] it had not been declared by an unambiguous statement, faith would have had no place. But now faith has been established between the obscurity of the deed and the declaration of the word, so that through faith, in Christ’s word—which is believed to be God’s word—the invisible deed may be seen, though it cannot be seen in itself. It is seen only insofar as it is believed. For God’s power is revealed from faith unto faith: because faith in this sacrament must proceed from a person’s faith when what he said is believed true, because he who said it is believed to be God. Faith, therefore, enlightens faith, so that faith proceeds from faith as the brightness of light from light.

Those who look carefully at what Jesus Christ received and what he gave are shown that a change of bread took place: for he received bread, bread in reality and in name; and, blessing and breaking it, he gave his body. Hence it is believed, in accordance with the devoutness of faith, that a change of the bread occurred, even though the Evangelist did not express it by the very name of “change.” And since “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10), so that, just as the change truly accomplished is held most firmly in the faith of the heart, it may likewise be held steadfastly in the confession of the mouth: the Church confesses—as is unquestionably evident from the tradition of the orthodox Fathers—that bread, by the power of the divine blessing, is made, or becomes, the body of Christ; and is transubstantiated, changed, or converted into the body of Christ; and in many other modes of speech it more fittingly expounds the doctrine established by faith. And although there is great diversity of words in this confession of faith, [Col. 0662C] there is nevertheless one devout faith and an indivisible unity of confession.

And although these terms, “change,” “conversion,” and the rest like them, signifying change or conversion, may seem, as regards this confession of faith, to be more a matter of new invention than of evangelical or apostolic tradition: nevertheless it pleased the holy doctors, for the devout confession of faith, to use words of this kind—words which God gave them for the ministry of faith and the perfecting of the saints. Nor should the novelty of terms be judged profane when it has been introduced by the authority of the holy Fathers, the devoutness of faith, and the necessity of confession itself. In some manner, surely, that which had altogether to be believed had also to be said.

What we say is not without precedent. For the term *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, “of one substance”) and the term “person”—the former for faith in the consubstantiality of the Father and the Son, the latter for faith in the Trinity, and both for the assertion of truth and the profession of faith—were adopted by the holy Fathers, although they have no authority from either the New or the Old Testament. Yet the word “person” is found in Isaiah, where he speaks of Christ, saying: “He shall bring forth judgment to the nations; he shall not cry out, nor accept a person” (Isa. 42). But this is understood of partiality in judgment, unless perhaps someone should draw the prophet’s words in another direction, as though the Son of God, in assuming a human being, had not assumed a person but a nature.

## AND TAKING THE CUP

He took the cup, not without wine, although the Evangelist does not expressly mention the wine—unless perhaps it is understood to have been expressed shortly afterward, where he says: “I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine” (Matt. 26), and so forth.

The taking of the cup may, through its mystical signification of the event immediately to come, be understood as the ready devotion and voluntary acceptance of the death to be endured. Concerning this cup the Lord asks the sons of Zebedee, saying: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20). Therefore he took the cup because he voluntarily accepted death. For “he was offered because he himself willed it” (Ps. 53).

Moreover, by the name “cup” may be signified not only the vessel that contains, but also that which is contained within it; just as, conversely, by the name *poculum* (“cup” or “drinking-vessel”) there is commonly signified that which contains, and not only that which is contained. He gave thanks. As we said above, Matthew writes that, upon taking the cup, the Lord gave thanks, and does not state [Col. 0663B] that he blessed it; just as, upon taking the bread, he writes that he blessed it and does not state that he gave thanks. Hence someone may think that one expression is used indifferently for the other, especially because, in the taking of the bread, where one Evangelist says, “He blessed” (Matt. 26), another says, “He gave thanks” (Mark 14).

Thanksgiving can indeed be called blessing. For we also bless God when we render him thanks for benefits bestowed. Every act of thanksgiving has regard to the cause of a benefit. Yet although conferring grace comes before rendering thanks, sometimes, because of the certainty of a future event, a benefit is anticipated by thanksgiving.

Therefore Christ, knowing how great is the grace of this ineffable sacrament and how great the goods which are to be bestowed upon us by him through it; and knowing likewise how great the evils which he himself was shortly to endure for us, gives thanks to the Father for both causes: namely, for the good things to be granted and for the evil things to be suffered. For both benefit us. Jesus Christ loves us so greatly that he gives thanks for our goods as though they were his own; and indeed our goods are nothing but his gifts. Yet he who bestows the gifts gives thanks, as one who receives does. For he reckons that something is given to himself, and that thanks are owed by himself, when something is bestowed upon us. He regards himself as having received a gift when he has given one.

This is done by that inward charity through which he joins us to himself as members, so that he may receive in us whatever he has given us. Therefore the Prophet addresses him who gave gifts to humankind and says: “You received [Col. 0663D] gifts in human beings” (Ps. 67). Therefore he gives thanks for our goods, which are his gifts, teaching us to render thanks for his gifts, which are our goods. He gives thanks for the scourges of another’s wickedness, teaching us not to murmur amid the scourges of our own wickedness. He gives thanks for the salvation of the world, which he purposed to give to the human race: giving his flesh as food and his blood as drink, that he might fill our desire with good things; giving himself as the price, that he might redeem our life from destruction.

Therefore, as has been said, he gives thanks for us. What then? Does he not also give thanks for himself, to whom it has been given to redeem the world, so that at his name every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2)? For what does even the Virgin’s son possess that he has not received? [Col. 0664A] For just as the Son of God is, by condescension, Son of Man, so the son of man is, by grace, Son of God—not, however, as an adopted son, or as though adopted from not being a son into being a son, but, as the Apostle says, “predestined Son in power” (Rom. 1).

By what words he gave thanks, whether for us or for himself, is not evident, because the Evangelist does not say. If he is to be believed to have given thanks in words, perhaps he used these very words, “I give thanks,” or others having a similar force, as elsewhere, where, rejoicing in spirit, he says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11).

## AND HE GAVE TO THEM, SAYING: “DRINK FROM THIS, ALL OF YOU.”

First it is shown what he gave; then for what purpose he gave it. He gave it, therefore, to be drunk, and said: “Drink from this, all of you” (Matt. 26). The phrase “from this” can be understood thus: “From this, now,” that is, henceforth, so that the beginning of so great a grace and gift may be shown; or rather thus: “From this cup,” or “from this which I give.”

That he does not say, “Drink this,” but “from this,” as though indicating a part, may refer to the distribution of graces, such as is displayed in the breaking. For when the cup is worthily drunk, it does not bestow every benefit on every person, but distinct benefits upon distinct persons: lightening temptations for some, increasing virtues for others, and bestowing innumerable other gifts upon each according to what each needs. And lest anyone be left out, he calls all. For all believers are commonly called to this cup: it is the communion of the faithful.

It is death to anyone who does not drink; and, as the Apostle says, it is judgment to anyone who drinks unworthily. What then is the fornicator, adulterer, or anyone entangled in mortal sin to do, if drinking unworthily brings death, and not drinking at all also brings death? In either case there is danger of death, because he himself is dead. What, then, is he to do? For this is what those who are such ask. The counsel of salvation lies ready for anyone willing to accept it: let him turn and live; and, between the twofold danger of death, let him choose the life that lies between, examining and judging himself, and thus let him eat of this bread and drink from the cup.

## THIS IS MY BLOOD OF THE NEW TESTAMENT

Here it is shown what he gave; and, as the catholic Church believes, one must understand that wine was changed into the blood of Christ, into the most pure blood of the grape. [Col. 0664D] Of this blood—or wine, for wine is called blood by signification, as it is written, “He shall wash his robe in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. 49)—he says: “This,” he says, “is my blood.” “Blood,” by the truth of its nature, not merely by a resemblance of some signification; “my,” by ownership—not the blood of goats or calves, such as under the Old Testament was more commonly shed than drunk; but “this is my blood of the New Testament.”

Mark says similarly; Luke, however: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood” (Luke 22). Paul says almost the same: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood” (1 Cor. 11). Therefore, according to Matthew and Mark, “This is the blood of the New Testament”; according to [Col. 0665A] Luke and Paul, “This cup is the New Testament.”

It should be considered that “testament” is understood in various ways in sacred speech. The Apostle says: “No one rejects or adds to a human testament” (Gal. 3); and elsewhere: “A testament is confirmed in the dead” (Heb. 9). Here “testament” means the solemn ordinance of a testator, in which an heir is usually instituted.

A testament is also called the covenant made between Jacob and Laban to establish peace between them. A testament is likewise called an agreement made among the wicked against God, as in: “The tents of Edom and of the Ishmaelites have made a testament against you” (Ps. 82). A testament is also called a covenant with death, with hell, or even with the world. This befits sinners and lovers of this world, who, by the obligation of their wickedness, make themselves debtors to death and hell. Thus it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Remember that death will not delay, and the testament of hell, which has been shown to you” (Ecclus. 14). For the testament of this world works death.

A testament is also called that which God ordained for his elect: namely, the covenant with David, concerning which he himself says: “I have made a testament with my elect; I have sworn to David my servant: I will prepare your seed for ever” (Ps. 88). Likewise, the covenant with Abraham: “He remembered for ever his testament, the word which he commanded for a thousand generations, which he made with Abraham, and his oath to [Col. 0665C] Isaac” (Ps. 104).

From this it may be gathered that the law of God is rightly called a testament, because an inheritance is promised to us in it, and in many places it shows who are heirs; and because it contains God’s promises and commandments, as certain covenantal terms for establishing friendship between God and humankind. God, indeed, voluntarily binds himself, as it were, even by an oath, to fulfill the promises; human beings are bound by necessity to fulfill the commandments.

The testament between the devil and a human being was confirmed, as it were, by the human being’s sin or death as blood. Of this testament Isaiah speaks in the person of certain people: “We have made a covenant with death, and have made a pact with hell” (Isa. 28). The devil, moreover, is called death and hell; and the covenant struck with him is the testament of hell which has been shown to humanity.

But this testament, as we said above, was confirmed by the death of a human being—yet this is so as regards the human being himself. For by no power or wisdom of his own can a human being be freed from death, “since there is none to redeem, nor one to save” (Ps. 7). Therefore Abel’s innocence did not suffice, nor Noah’s righteousness, nor Abraham’s faith, nor Moses’ meekness, nor Job’s patience, nor, finally, the holiness of any of the saints, to free them from death or dissolve the testament of hell without, or before, the death of the mediator.

Therefore one says: “I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. 38); another says: “Hell is my house, and in darkness [Col. 0666A] I have spread my bed” (Job 17); another says: “I shall go down mourning to my son into hell” (Gen. 37); and again: “You will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the lower regions” (Gen. 42). But he who says, “I rejoiced at those things which were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121), shows in what power he trusts in the following words, addressing the author of salvation, who established the testament of peace: “Let peace be in your strength” (ibid.). For he is our peace, who opened heaven to us and shut hell; and in the blood of the New Testament dissolved the testament of hell. Hence he also says in Isaiah: “Your covenant with death shall be blotted out, and your pact with hell shall not stand” (Isa. 28).

The New Testament stands, as it were, opposite the testament of hell. For that testament was confirmed, as it were, by blood—that is, by the sin or death of a human being—because through sin the human being consented to the devil and could not free himself from the bond of the obligation he had entered, either through death or after death. But the New Testament was confirmed by Christ’s blood, freeing the human being from sin, prescribing for him a new manner of life, and making him heir of eternal life. Therefore this blood is called the blood of the New Testament, because through it the New Testament was dedicated and the promise of the eternal inheritance was confirmed.

Therefore the earlier testament, which went before in figure, was not dedicated without blood, because of the mystical signification of this sacrament. For, as the Apostle says: “When every commandment of the law had been read by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: This is the blood of the testament which God commanded unto you” (Heb. 9). See how fittingly Moses foretells the words which Christ used at the supper.

See how the Old Testament looks in two directions: toward the New Testament and toward the testament of hell—the one through the signification of the death of the God-man, the other through the representation of the death of the guilty human being. For the death of the legal victim, by which a human being is shown deserving of death, represents the death of the human being who through sin deserves death but is nevertheless to be freed from death through grace. The death of the victim also prefigures [Col. 0666D] the death of Christ, by which the human being was to be freed from death. Therefore both testaments, the Old and the New, avail to destroy the testament of hell: the one through signification, the other through the presentation of truth.

Therefore this blood of Christ is the dedicating blood of the New Testament, according to the new promises: because, on account of the excessive charity with which God loved us—a charity which he also commended in the blood shed for us—it is instilled into our minds by the hidden movements of inspiring grace, and suggested, as it were, by the living voice of the blood itself, so that we may love his commandments from the depths of our heart and confidently hope in his promises.

## WHICH SHALL BE SHED FOR MANY FOR THE REMISSION OF SINS (Matt. 26)

Every occasion for impious doubt is cut off when the truth of faith is opened by the very mouth of Truth. Lest anyone should think that Christ says by mere signification of something, “This is my blood,” he himself plainly shows what he said, what he understood, and what he wished us to believe. Nor may we, under pretense of simplicity, fail to know what he understood, since we must both believe what he understood in these words and confess what he said.

For in this article of common faith and testimony of public confession, it is not enough simply to believe that what Christ said in these words is true, whatever he understood in them, while not understanding what he said. Rather, the understanding and faith of the words are required of us all the more exactly because Christ states more clearly and expressly what must be believed. For the matter, although hidden, is revealed [Col. 0667B] and impressed upon us as it is in truth, so that ignorance has no excuse whatever and impiety can scarcely find an occasion for error.

For he said: “This is my blood of the New Testament,” and reinforces it: “which shall be shed for you for the remission of sins” (Luke 22). As though he said: “That which I give you to drink under the appearance of wine is not wine according to its nature, but according to truth is my blood—the very blood which shall be shed for many.”

Let this, therefore, be our faith and this our confession: that the selfsame blood is given us to drink which we undoubtedly believe was shed for us. Luke says: “Which shall be shed for you,” as though it were spoken only for the disciples. Matthew [Col. 0667C] says: “Which shall be shed for many” (Matt. 26). Although these statements appear different, they are not opposed. For it may devoutly be believed that Christ said both, either one separately after the other, or one as understood within the other. For in a certain manner, that is said which is understood in what is said.

The fact that the Apostle says, “Christ died for all” (Rom. 6), whereas he says that his blood would be shed not for all but for many, may trouble us. But one appears to consider the outcome of a definite benefit, the other the sufficiency of an infinite power. For, so far as that blood itself is concerned, it is so powerful for redemption that it can suffice for the salvation of all; it is a price so incomparable that the entire human race can be restored by it. For it is more precious than every valuation of those to be redeemed and than any number whatsoever of captives.

But those who, by living wickedly, regard the blood of the testament as defiled, because they despise the sacrament of redemption, do not receive the benefit of common grace. For Christ does not redeem one who voluntarily excludes himself from the communion of general grace, as it is written: “Those who trust in their strength and glory in the multitude of their riches: a brother does not redeem” (Ps. 48). What benefit, then, is there in the blood of Christ for those who descend into corruption? It would have been good for them had they not been born. It would have been good for them had Christ’s blood not been shed. For this blood will be a testimony against them: “You have come,” says the Apostle, “to the sprinkling of blood, speaking better than [Col. 0668A] Abel” (Heb. 12). Certainly, for those who have approached it, this blood speaks for pardon; but against the wicked it speaks for vengeance.

Therefore the blood shed for the remission of sins does not profit all, but many. Hence it was said: “It shall be shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26). Do not be disturbed by what is written, “Few are chosen” (Matt. 20), as though it were not shed for many because it benefits only the elect. For although the elect are called few in comparison with the multitude of sinners, they are nevertheless many, and are to be multiplied beyond the sand. For it is written: “Many shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8).

Again, he says, “It shall be shed for the remission of sins.” Those who shed Christ’s blood neither acted nor thought for this purpose, that the sins of the world might be taken away. For, so far as they were concerned, they worked their own destruction rather than our salvation, and condemnation for themselves rather than remission for us. Yet unknowingly they served the saving dispensation. For the salvation of the world that followed was not the work of their power, will, intention, or deed, but of God’s power, will, intention, and deed. For in that shedding of blood not only did the wickedness of the persecutors work; the charity of the Savior also worked. But wickedness effected the work of wickedness; charity completed the work of charity.

It was not wickedness but charity that worked salvation. Yet wickedness shed Christ’s blood, and poured itself out, that the human being might know how greatly he was loved by God, who “did not spare his own Son” (Rom. 8). “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3). That only-begotten Son was offered, not because the Jew had power to do so, but because he himself willed it; and, having loved his own, he loved them unto the end. The end is death undertaken for enemies. This is the end of every consummation, the end of consummate love. “For no one has greater charity than that one should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

This charity of Christ in Christ’s death was stronger than the wickedness of the Jews; nor could wickedness act except insofar as charity permitted. Judas, or the Jew, delivered Christ to death, [Col. 0668D] and this through malicious wickedness. The Father delivered the Son, and the Son delivered himself; and this out of charity. Charity is not guilty of the handing-over; rather, it is innocent even in the death of Christ. For charity alone is permitted, with impunity, to do whatever it wills. Charity alone can compel God, as though it were imperious. This brought God down from heaven; this placed him on the cross; this, as innocently as it did savingly, shed Christ’s blood for the remission of sins.

Therefore all thanksgiving for the salvation of the world is owed to charity, which so presses us by the force of its reasoning that it is fitting for us to love Christ as much as the Jew was able to hate him. I say “fitting,” perhaps, because of the weakness of our heart. For one is unworthy of the name of friend who loves less than an enemy hates. One is unworthy of remission of sins who does not repay, by loving in return, some return of love to one who loves so greatly—not an equal return, but such as one can give. For who can make an equal return? Let not our own blood be more precious to us than Christ’s love. For in order that the God of our salvation might free us from bloodguilt, he first loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood.

> “But I say to you, I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26).

At this point one must carefully consider how the Evangelist Luke seems to differ from the other two, namely Matthew and Mark. That this may appear more clearly, let us set out Christ’s own words in their order from Luke’s Gospel:

> “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I say to you, [Col. 0669B] that from this I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. And, having taken the cup, he gave thanks and said: Take it and divide it among yourselves; for I say to you that I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes” (Luke 22).

Thus Luke. Here it should be noted that after the typical Passover, or at its end, and before the true Passover, the Lord appears to have said two things: one concerning not eating, when he says, “From this I shall not eat it”; the other concerning not drinking, when he says, “I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine.” Luke alone records that the Lord said these two things, as though before the true Passover was celebrated; and he then adds these words concerning the true Passover: “And, having taken bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: This cup is the New Testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you” (ibid.).

Thus far Luke, who alone records that Christ said something about not eating, and that, as has been said, seemingly before the true Passover. But although he is not alone in giving Christ’s words about not drinking, he differs from the others in placing them before the true Passover, as though they concerned the typical Passover; whereas Matthew (ch. 26) and Mark (ch. 14) place Christ’s words about not drinking in another position, namely after the true Passover.

When these matters have been carefully considered, it is evident that Matthew and Mark omitted Christ’s words about not eating altogether. And since they give his words about not drinking, but in a different place than Luke, one may infer one of two things: either the Lord spoke words about not drinking on both occasions—where Luke alone places them, before the celebration of the new Passover, and where Matthew and Mark place them, after the celebration of the new Passover—or, if Christ said the words about not drinking only once, one of them, or two of them, altered the order of the narrative.

But an inverted narrative order does not prejudice the truth of what occurred. Nor is it impious to doubt which altered the order, if it was altered; or to doubt whether Christ spoke the words about not drinking a second time and again. In doubts of this kind the devoutness [Col. 0670A] of faith is not endangered, nor does faith in the Gospel waver, provided that we believe without doubt the things reported as done or said. For faith is necessarily due to the Gospel narrative, not to its order or chronology, except when these are incorporated into the narrative.

## BUT I SAY TO YOU

The words which Christ speaks here are not to be considered cursorily or heard negligently, especially since he prefaces them: “But I say to you.” By prefacing this, he appears to demand attention, that with attentive ears we may hear both what he says and what he says that he says. We must consider with weight: “But I say to you,” so that the weight of the words and the authority of the speaker may be weighed.

“I will not,” he says, “drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.” Three things at once must be understood in these words: that he will not drink of this fruit until a certain time; that he will then drink that with them in the kingdom of the Father; and, before these two, that he drank of this fruit either then or earlier. For “henceforth” seems to indicate a change of state: either that something which existed before will not exist henceforth, or that something which did not exist at a certain time will exist henceforth. For who says, “Henceforth I shall not do this,” unless one who has done it, or is doing it, and will not do it thereafter? Likewise, who says, “Henceforth I shall do it,” unless one who did not do it at some time?

The reasoning for this understanding is derived not only from common usage of speech; it also seems to have testimony from the usage of Holy Scripture itself. For when the Lord says to certain persons, “You shall not see me henceforth until you say: Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 23), he signifies that they see or had seen him—either with the eyes of the flesh, among the unbelieving portion, or with the eye of faith, among the believing portion who then were, or had previously been, in that people—but that afterwards, once his presence had been withdrawn, they would not see him until the veil is removed from their hearts and they acknowledge that he has come, blessing him who comes in the name of the Lord.

If it were not tedious, it would not be difficult to produce more examples; but because a plain matter does not require a multitude of examples, we must rather ask of what fruit of the vine he says this: whether of the cup belonging to the Old Testament, of which he says in Luke, “Take and divide it among yourselves” (Luke 22); or of the cup belonging to the New Testament, of which he says in the same Luke, “This cup is the New Testament in my blood” (ibid.). That is: whether of the wine believed to have been in the cup belonging to the old sacrifice, or of the blood itself which, after supper, he gave them to drink under the appearance of wine, as though it were the fruit of the vine, in the cup belonging to the new sacrifice.

For this inquiry, I think it useful first to state what food and drink Christ uses and delights in using. Concerning food, he plainly says what it is: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). And elsewhere he says what the Father’s will is: “This is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life” (John 6). Therefore Christ’s food is the salvation of the world. For this he hungers and thirsts, because it is his drink.

Therefore, when he sat beside the spring, he said to the Samaritan woman: “Give me to drink” (John 4); and, to show that he thirsted rather for the living water to be sought from him, so that he might give it to the one seeking, he says: “If you knew the gift of God and who it is who says to you, Give me to drink, perhaps you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (ibid.). Behold what he thirsted for: to be asked for water and to give it, so that in the recipient it might become a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. Who can have this water unless he gives it? Or who can be saved unless he saves that person?

The salvation [Col. 0671B] of the world which he thirsts for, he also works: partly in those things pertaining to its restoration, partly in those things pertaining to its supreme consummation. To the preparation belong all things which he worked from the beginning of the world among his elect, until the time of his coming, as prefiguring the restoration to come. To the restoration belong all things which Christ accomplished in the flesh, whether good things he did or hard things he endured, until the hour of his passion or resurrection. To consummation belongs the whole glory of the resurrection. Of this he himself says: “I perform cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am consummated” (Luke 13).

The salvation of the world, according to the sequence of times, was arranged and ordered in preparation, action, and fruit: that is, in figure, grace, and glory. First God the Father commanded salvation for Jacob in the promise of the Savior. Then he gave salvation to kings—that is, to all the righteous—in the advent of the Savior. Finally, he completed the work of salvation in the resurrection of the Savior, magnifying the salvations of his king and showing mercy to his Christ David and to his seed for ever.

Christ worked this work of our salvation, beginning from ancient days. The entire dispensation of events and times was directed by his governance to this end; and in all things conducive to this cause, he, the author of all things, delighted. And this was for his glory, as it is written: “You shall renew the face of the earth; may the glory of the Lord endure for ever; the Lord shall rejoice in his works” (Ps. 103).

Moreover, he did not delight only in the things which he did before his coming or at his coming; coming into the world, he gladly received the scourges of our wickedness. Gladly, do I say, or sadly? More correctly, I should say both. For it is written of him: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18). And he himself said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26). He not only felt bodily pain in the bitterness of his sufferings and in the severity of the laborious discipline undertaken for us, but also had real sorrow in his soul—yet willingly. For he gladly willed truly to be sorrowful; nor was that sorrow without joy, since he had joy in that very sorrow.

Therefore he says: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover” (Luke 22). The working of our salvation, ordered in its proper sequence, is the will of the Father. This is Christ’s food, what he hungers for. This is what he says on the cross: “I thirst” (John 19). This is the healing draught, this wine of joy, this fruit of the true vine: that is, of Christ himself, who says, “I am the true vine” (John 15).

Therefore, looking to the fruit and end of his work and dispensation from the beginning, he says: “I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine,” and so forth. As though he said: “Until now I delighted in working the salvation of the world, as was hitherto fitting; and, delighting in these things, I drank the wine of joy, because ‘my delights were to be with the children of men’ (Prov. 8). But it was not yet the new wine, sweeter as it is; rather, it was wine whose sweetness was mingled with the severity of the discipline which I still feel. It remains that, henceforth—after the passion now at hand—I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day of my glorification, when I shall drink it new with you: having nothing of severity, wholly filled with sweetness, and this in the kingdom of my Father, that is, in my glorified body or in the kingdom of heaven, and with you. For you too will drink with me when I have given you to drink from the torrent of my delight.”

By that day we may understand the glory of resurrection and glorification, a day which has no end. Of it is said: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117). For we shall exult and rejoice in Christ’s brightness when the body of our humility is conformed to the body of his glory.

Although, therefore, Christ is the firstfruits of those who sleep and, as the first to rise from the dead, drank this new wine before the disciples were immediately to drink it, nevertheless what is said is true, and true in the manner in which it is said: Christ did not drink of this fruit of the vine until that endless day of his glorious brightness, in which he is to be seen by his elect, so that they may exult in his presence and delight in joy.

What he says, therefore—“I will not drink henceforth until that day, when I shall drink with you”—must be referred to the duration of the interval, not to the beginning of the day; so that “when I shall drink with you” is understood as though it said, “on the day on which I shall drink with you.” But if the words “until that day” are referred to the passing day of the resurrection, having morning and evening, it will be difficult to understand his saying: “I will not [Col. 0672D] drink until that day, when I shall drink with you,” since the disciples were not to drink on that day—unless one understands simply: “I will not drink until that day, when the reason for drinking with you shall have been fulfilled.”

For the completed resurrection is the reason for drinking together the wine of joy, according to a manner of speaking whereby things that are to come are said to be already present when the cause from which they follow has arisen. In this manner may be understood: “He who believes in me has eternal life” (John 6), and: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Thus many other future things are anticipated and said to exist, because, once the cause by which they exist is already present, nothing remains except that they should be.

[Col. 0673A] That Christ says that he drinks, not “this,” but “of this fruit,” while he will drink, not “of that,” but “that,” can signify the future fullness of joy already tasted beforehand. Inquiring, according to the line of reasoning set forth above, of what “fruit” Christ is speaking—namely, of the wine of the first cup or of the second—one may answer that the expression concerning the fruit is figurative: what was said is to be understood of the meaning of one, the effect of the other, and the end of both. For Christ’s blood produces in us the joy of eternal salvation, which is the wine of gladness; and this is also signified, by a certain analogy of resemblance, in the wine of the earlier cup, because “wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103). Thus the joy of eternal salvation is signified by one cup and is the effect of the other; it is the end of both [Col. 0673B] and the fruit of both.

Therefore, when the Lord, at the consummation of the one and the institution of the other, speaks figuratively and alludes to the figure of the Law, he does not set the end of the old sacrifice merely in the substitution of the new sacrament. Rather, he directs both toward one end, beyond which there is no end. Therefore, when he says, “Of this fruit,” although by the demonstrative gesture either finger or eye is directed toward the present object, so that nothing other than what is displayed before the eyes seems intended, nevertheless the manifest truth of the matter and the piety of faith urge that something else be understood. For it would not be worthy of faith that this very thing, unless in its effect or signification, is to be drunk by Christ with the disciples in the kingdom of heaven.

Thus, in “this fruit,” although the cup or finger makes the thing apparent, another wine may without presumption be understood; just as, when water is indicated, another water is signified, the Lord saying: “Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again” (John 4). By this water shown to the Samaritan woman is understood the water of worldly pleasure or desire, which does not extinguish thirst; it is opposed by the water of saving wisdom, of which the Lord says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (ibid.).

Here one must take the greatest care that the differing placement of demonstratives in Christ’s words does not create a scruple against faith. For when above he said, “This is my body,” and then, “This is my blood” (Matt. 26), in each case he indicated [Col. 0673D] precisely what he intended to be understood—and rightly so. There the faith of this sacrament had to be established, and the form of our faith and confession had to be prescribed in plain words, without the veil of a figure. But when it is said, “Henceforth I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine,” he suggests that, in the fruit apparently indicated, something else is to be understood—what is figured in this fruit. Thus it had to be.

For since the full consummation of both Testaments had to be indicated by familiar, though less strictly proper, words, he also wished, through objects equally familiar and relevant to the matter, to signify what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). It should not therefore seem strange that the expression is figurative, so that the thing may somehow be understood—a thing which no propriety of words can [Col. 0674A] express, yet which must in some manner be understood.

### Another interpretation of the foregoing

Christ’s words are like breasts overflowing with milk: the more they are pressed, the more abundantly they pour forth milk. A grape, more firmly trodden, strains out wine after wine. Divine utterances have their storehouses, full and overflowing from one thing into another. There is found there the wine of gladness, David saying: “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103). Christ drinks of this; and all who belong to Christ will drink of it as well.

There is also found there the wine of compunction, the same David saying: “You have shown your people hard things; you have given us wine of compunction to drink” (Ps. 59). Let us see whether Christ drank of this wine, since it is written concerning his persecutor—whether Judas or the Jew: “He persecuted the poor and needy man, and the one pierced in heart, to put him to death” (Ps. 108).

He was indeed pierced in body, as it is written: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Acts 2). But how was he pierced in heart? For it is written of the repentant in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were pierced in heart.” Such compunction does not apply to Christ. But is compunction found only in the repentant? By no means. For concerning the impenitent and hard of heart, according to the Apostle, it is written: “God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear” (Rom. 2). For good things are often grievous to the wicked, and in anger or hatred they are stung against justice and truth. Wicked hatred has its own goads; and as there is a good compunction arising from [Col. 0674C] love and devotion, so there is an evil one arising from hatred and wickedness.

There is, as we have already noted, a compunction arising from the sorrow of repentance, which belongs to sinners converted to God. There is also a compunction arising from the harshness of discipline, imposed by God on all the righteous through many tribulations. “Many are the tribulations of the righteous”; and no one is righteous who does not suffer. Through this disciplinary compunction, as through an infusion of wine, the wounds, if any, of the righteous are healed; their weakness is cured, or their humility preserved, or their patience exercised. This is the wine of compunction, or, according to another translation, the wine of stimulation.

For however many righteous persons there are, although they serve God in joy and exultation because the spirit is willing, nevertheless, because the flesh is weak (Mark 16), they groan and travail until now amid the affliction and sorrow caused by evils. Eating their bread in the sweat of their face, they are fed with the bread of tears and given the wine of compunction to drink. “Our fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.” From this sour grape—that is, from the swelling of self-will—this wine has been pressed; and from this fruit of the vine has proceeded the entire penal condition of our mortality.

Christ himself, having become a participant in our mortality, “drank from the torrent in the way” (Ps. 109); and the discipline that brought us peace was upon him, until he drank the cup of suffering, thereby bringing to an end both the discipline he endured and the misery he healed. He who drank the cup of suffering drank the wine of compunction: for he was not only pierced in body, but inwardly in the sorrow of his heart, because it repented him that he had made man. Therefore the Father showed him hard things; for he did not spare him until, rising from the dead, having torn apart the sackcloth of mortality and been clothed with the robe of immortality, he said to the Father: “You have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced” (Ps. 29).

But because Christ had first to suffer and thus rise from the dead, now that the hour of his passion was near, being about to drink the cup of suffering and thus pass from this world to the Father, he says: “Henceforth I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine,” and so forth. As though he said: Until now I have drunk of this fruit of the vine—that is, I have endured the grievous things belonging to the weakness of assumed [Col. 0675B] mortality. Now sorrow has come to an end. Henceforth I shall not drink this bitter cup, but the wine of gladness in the kingdom of my Father, when he has changed my mourning into joy. And you, who will drink my cup, will grieve; but your sorrow will be turned into joy, so that I may drink new wine with you.

The expression is figurative in this way, if the new wine is the same as that which he had previously drunk, yet new; but this manner of speech is sufficiently suited to our ordinary usage, as one commonly says: “What a man has sown, that he shall also reap.”

### Another interpretation, as above

“Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?” (1 Cor. 3). The Lord planted a vineyard. What vineyard is this? “The vineyard,” says Isaiah, “of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5). As vineyard differs from vineyard, so wine differs from wine. The Lord’s vineyard is distinguished from an alien vineyard. The latter is the Gentile world, estranged from the worship of God and devoted to idolatry.

But the Synagogue, which ought to belong to the Lord’s vineyard as planted and cultivated by him, is, in respect of the righteous, the Lord’s vineyard and the vineyard of Sorech, that is, the chosen vineyard. Yet in respect of the wicked and unbelieving, it has turned into the bitterness of an alien vine. For it is a perverse generation and unbelieving children. They have become like the nations that do not know God. This vineyard has borne impiety instead of faith, distrust instead of hope, envy or hatred instead of love.

Moses also foretold this: “Their vineyard is from the vineyard of Sodom and from the districts of Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, and their clusters are exceedingly bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. 32). What are these three—grape of gall, gall of dragons, and incurable poison of asps—but impiety, distrust, and inexorable hatred, or whatever vices resemble such utterly evil things? As the vineyard is, so is its wine. It is vinegar, of which he says: “And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68). It is myrrhed wine, which, when the Lord had tasted it, he refused to drink. He tasted it, indeed, testing by experience how great their malice was; but he would not drink it, because he did not approve it; because he rejected what displeased him.

But the faithful Synagogue, which pleased God through obedience like a delightful shoot and was like a chosen vineyard—of this Isaiah says: “The vineyard of pure wine shall sing to him” (Isa. 27). God took delight in the obedience of the ancient righteous under the legal commandments, judgments, promises, and sacraments. This obedience had its time until Christ’s passion. Then new obedience and new righteousness succeeded it, more pleasing to God by a greater perfection.

Therefore he now says: “Henceforth I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine,” and so forth—as though he said: Henceforth I shall not take delight in the obedience which has existed until now under the Law. That day is at hand—that is, the time of grace—when the shadow will be done away with, religion will be enlarged through new promises, new commandments, and new sacraments, and obedience will be perfected by the example of my humility. In this obedience I shall take greater delight with you in the kingdom of my Father, that is, in the Church.

[Col. 0676B] His words, “Until I drink it new,” signify that in one respect the obedience of the Law and that of the Gospel are the same, and in another respect renewed—that is, changed and enlarged. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “I have not come to destroy the Law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5). The highest fulfilment of the Law is obedience unto death. This is perfect love; this is the end of righteousness and of every consummation.

This obedience was enclosed in the Law in the first and greatest commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind” (Deut. 6). It was also enclosed in sacrifices and covertly indicated in the death of victims. But now it has been openly revealed in the example of Christ’s death and imposed upon Christ’s imitators and lovers. This obedience is the saving cup, the cup of Christ’s passion. This is the new wine of which he says: “Until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father.”

What, then, is drinking that new wine except suffering out of the love of obedience? What is “I shall drink it with you,” except that you too will suffer with me out of the love of obedience? What is “I shall drink it, but new,” except that it was new for the cup of suffering to be drunk in place of the fruit of the vine? It was new for a man to be sacrificed in place of a lamb. “I shall drink it new with you,” because I shall delight in this newness of the cup, and you will delight in it; and “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9) because of this gladness of mind.

But obedience unto death is to be understood not only in bodily death, [Col. 0676D] but in a sense in every perfect mortification and chastening of the body, and above all in every perfect renunciation of one’s own will. For one sacrifices oneself who cuts down one’s own will; who withdraws from unlawful pleasures for God’s sake; who hates one’s soul for God’s sake and, by hating it in this world, loses it, and by losing it preserves it unto eternal life. He who, in gladness of mind and sweetness of love, setting aside his own will, prefers by the judgment of discernment the will of his brother—such a one lays down his life for his brother.

In every form of martyrdom there is obedience unto death, whether the sword of the persecutor kills us or the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. This is perfect obedience, such as was not found in the Law, because the Law brought no one to perfection. [Col. 0677A] This is the new wine which Jesus Christ drinks with his disciples. Whoever delights in this obedience drinks with Jesus Christ, drinks from his cup the spiced wine and the new wine of pomegranates.

To summarize what has been said at greater length: Christ is the true vine according to the fullness of grace; the wine of this vine is the salvation of the world and the shared joy of all the righteous. He himself drinks this wine—at the beginning, not new; at the end, new—that is, free from every harshness and full of every sweetness.

Again, Christ is a vine according to the condition of assumed weakness. The wine of this vine—that is, of assumed weakness—is the bitterness of sufferings and tribulations. It is wine not new, because it comes from the sour grape and from the propagation of the old man, that is, Adam—not according to guilt, but according to penalty. This wine is bitter from age and old in bitterness, but is soon to be changed into new wine.

Again, the Church of the righteous is called a vineyard according to the grace of faith and love. The wine of this vineyard is the obedience of the Law or of the Gospel; but the obedience of the Law was a figure of the obedience of evangelical perfection. The obedience of the Law was to sacrifice a lamb; new obedience is to sacrifice oneself. That is wine not new; this is new wine, of which the Lord says: “Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is spilled, and the wineskins perish” (Matt. 9).

### Another interpretation, as above

[Col. 0677C] A simpler interpretation is sought by some. These words may partly be taken literally. Because he celebrated this final Passover with his disciples and would not celebrate another thereafter, he says: “Henceforth I shall not drink,” and so forth. It is as though he said: I shall not drink of this fruit according to the rite of Passover observance; rather, I invite you to another banquet, “that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.”

Nor is this interpretation prejudiced by the fact that after the resurrection he ate and also drank with his disciples, as appears from the Acts of the Apostles, Peter saying: “We ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10). For he does not deny that he will drink at all, but says: “I shall not drink of this [Col. 0677D] fruit,” that is, I shall not repeat the solemnities of Passover observance by drinking from this cup. Rather, I shall fulfil the mysteries of this feast in the kingdom of my Father—that is, in the kingdom of heaven or in the Church.

Hence in Luke he says: “I tell you, I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God” (Luke 22). He did indeed eat with his disciples after the resurrection, but he did not eat “of this” nor drink “of this”; that is, he neither ate the Passover nor poured out wine as is customary in sacrifice. Yet he ate in order to establish faith in the resurrection; and the believing disciples were flooded with the new joy of the resurrection, so that in a sense he then drank new wine with his disciples—that is, he shared with them new joy in the glory of his resurrection, and in himself as though in [Col. 0678A] the kingdom of his Father.

For the disciples, saddened by his death, rejoiced at seeing the Lord beyond what can be expressed, as it is written: “Weeping will tarry at evening, and gladness at morning” (Ps. 29).

### On the reality of the change

The change of bread into Christ’s body is real and mystical. Consideration proper to each aspect—that is, to its reality and its mystery—can build up either faith or love. But let us first attend to the reality of the change. The change is real, I say, not according to figure but according to substance. For the bread is not transfigured but transubstantiated. In a new and unprecedented manner, the appearance remains while the substance is changed.

In transfiguration, however, this is not so. For when Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, his nature is not altered so that one nature is transferred into another. When the Lord was transfigured on the mountain (Matt. 17), what was glorified did not change its substance but put on beauty, so that it was not of another nature but of another glory.

It is not within our power either to state or to conceive how Christ, whether before the resurrection or after it, appearing in a glorified form, now displayed one appearance, now another, as though in order not to be recognized, although he always acted so as to be recognized. For who is sufficient for these matters? Who can explain whether in the transfiguration he put off his earlier appearance, or whether, retaining it and concealing it from the eyes of the disciples present, he put on over it that glorious appearance? Who can explain how, glorified in the resurrection, he did not appear in the splendid appearance of his glory, but in an appearance now seemingly known and now seemingly unknown, allowing himself to be recognized, or for a time not recognized, as he willed? Was the cause in himself that he was not recognized, because, as it is written, he was shown “in another form” (Matt. 16 [uncertain citation]); or was it in those who recognized him, because their eyes were held? At one time he was thought to be a phantom, at another he appeared as a gardener (John 20), at another as though a traveller (Luke 24), revealing and concealing himself in turn to whom he wished and as he wished.

What else can we affirm concerning such matters except that Jesus is God, possessing authority over every form and matter, every appearance and substance, all of which serve at his command?

Now concerning these matters—form and matter, or appearance and substance—the brilliant minds of philosophers have laboured greatly. By the most subtle inquiry they attempted to investigate the nature of each thing: whence it was, what it was or was not, where it was, and finally what it could do. What seemed right to them according to the conjecture of human reason they regarded as determined and certain; and they thought that, according to the acuteness of their own minds, they could enclose the law of nature within fixed limits and mark it out with indisputable definitions, as though whatever opposed their definitions must disagree with truth.

Certainly, according to nature’s regular order and course, they explained many things both wonderfully and faithfully; but they also worked out many matters plausibly which were as foreign to truth as they were alien to the piety of faith. Whatever they have truly and faithfully grasped and defined is not theirs but belongs to him who is Truth and who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1), through whom some portion of the light of truth shone upon them. For truth, wherever it is found, belongs to God, not to man, because “every man is a liar, but God is true” (Rom. 3).

But whatever they held and asserted against the truth of faith and the form of piety was theirs; they said it from themselves and spoke from what was their own. Ignorant of heavenly sacraments and of God’s wisdom hidden in mystery, “they became vain in their reasonings, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became foolish” (Rom. 1). And by the wondrous judgment of God, those who were esteemed among human beings as above other humans—as though alone wise, or wiser than the rest—now appear to us, through the grace of God who called us from darkness into his wonderful light, more foolish than the rest.

For true indeed is the saying written: “Every man has been made foolish by wisdom.” Therefore our faith, immovably founded upon the words of God himself, is not tossed about uncertainly, wavering and fluctuating with human opinions. Supported by truth and firmly established upon the solid rock of divine authority, it stands unshaken and unshakable. If it contains anything contrary to philosophers’ definitions, opinion must yield to truth, so that the truth of faith may triumph in all things, “destroying every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity to the obedience of Christ.”

Whatever in the mysteries of faith, by its depth, exceeds the measure of human understanding and transcends the limits of human reason must be entrusted and reserved to God, who at the fitting time will reveal mysteries now veiled to those who, offering due reverence to his words, believe firmly and faithfully, without wavering concerning the truth of those words even though the rationale of their manner does not yet appear. For God wills that his secrets should be believed by us and on our account, but that their manner should for a time remain unknown, so that faith may have merit and what is now hidden may be reserved as a reward.

Thus the simplicity of faith has a devout awareness in matters which God has commanded to be believed, and a devout ignorance in matters which he has hidden as not to be investigated. Both, moreover—devout awareness and devout ignorance—have glory and praise before God, when the human mind humbles itself before God so as to believe what he has said, and is restrained from proud and curious inquiry so as not to seek what he has not said. Thus faith advances toward merit in both respects, and in either simplicity confidently longs for reward: “He who walks simply walks confidently” (Prov. 10).

Therefore, simply and confidently, firmly and steadfastly, let us hold, believe, and confess that the substance of bread is changed into the substance of Christ’s flesh, while the appearance of bread nevertheless remains—marvellously, ineffably, and incomprehensibly. We believe without doubt that it is so; but how it is so we still simply do not know. We do not yet know the manner; but we shall know it later, when the power of this mystery has been perfected in us.

The conversion of bread into Christ’s body itself indicates that consummation. For it is mystical, signifying the very grace which it works in us.

### On the mystical significance of the change of bread

Let us therefore consider what bread is before conversion. Daily experience teaches what it is. It sustains life, but a passing life: neither the bread itself nor the life it sustains endures. Bread is consumed through use, and life passes away as it fails. It cannot grant eternal life; it can scarcely sustain temporal life for a short time. Therefore daily refreshment is necessary; daily life depends on divine refreshment. We who need nourishment every day can scarcely and painfully endure even to the third day.

Our body is weak and fragile, subject to many corruptions and ailments. While it is refreshed, it fails; while it is daily restored, it wastes away. Mortal life, while sustained by food, slips away; while nourished, it diminishes; and it continually rushes headlong toward death, even while daily nourishment postpones death. And, as experience shows, food sought as the cause of health generates causes of illness; where life is sought, there death is found.

Therefore this bread is destroyed and perishes; it does not remain unto eternal life. Likewise the body is destroyed and perishes. “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them.” When death has been swallowed up in victory, when this mortal has put on immortality, then eternal life will be given to the body—not by this food which perishes, but by the food which remains unto eternal life.

Consider the power of the sacrament. God decreed to clothe this mortal body with immortality and to transfer mortal life into eternal life. Therefore he changed food into food: the bread of life into the bread of life, but the bread of passing life into the bread of eternal life. Thus, through the change of food into food, the change of mortal life into immortal life may be believed, understood, hoped for, and awaited; so that, while the changing succession of times draws us toward death, we may not fear death itself as a change for the better, because our hope is full of immortality.

For a human being who is weak and is to be completely healed of weakness, food had to be changed, so that by life-giving food the evil of the forbidden and deadly food might be healed and the insufficiency of permitted food restored. Forbidden food could only bring death; permitted food could only postpone death, unless through Christ’s blessing it is changed into food capable of taking death away.

The substantial change of true bread into the true body of Christ in some sense both brings about and signifies the change of mortal life into immortal life, although it is dissimilar in one respect and similar in another. For, as the Apostle says: “We, though many, are one bread, one body—all who partake of the one bread and of the one cup” (1 Cor. 10). The whole Church, in the entire multitude of the elect, is one bread, and the whole Church itself is Christ’s body. Whoever belong in and to the body of the Church are one bread and members of Christ; and through a certain change we shall be, as it were, other than we now are, because it has not yet appeared what we shall be.

Yet the change which is to occur in us will indeed be a change of nature into another glory, but not into another nature. It will nevertheless be so great and such a change that it can in some measure be likened to that substantial change. For if our conversion from evil to good in the present time accomplishes in us that we are some beginning of God’s creation and, as it were, a new creation in Christ—on account of which the Prophet says, “And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76)—what shall we then be? What, I say, shall we be when what is mortal is swallowed up by life; when, beholding with unveiled face the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord?

As children of the resurrection and equal to God’s angels, we shall be so unlike ourselves that one might suppose we are scarcely anything less than what we now are. The power of this mystical change, therefore, is the consummation of blessed life. But because the consummation of blessed life is most rightly attained through the consummation of righteousness—that is, of a good life—the consummation of the good life is likewise suggested to us through the conversion [Col. 0681C] of wine into blood, and, if one takes pleasure in observing it, is beneficially intimated.

That this may become clearer, something must be added concerning other conversions, to prepare the way for understanding.

### On the mystical significance of the change of wine

We read of one conversion of water into blood among the Egyptians, as it is written: “He turned their rivers into blood” (Ps. 77). We read of another conversion, of water into wine, at the wedding held at Cana of Galilee. And we read of this third conversion, of wine into blood, which occurred at the Lord’s Supper and is repeatedly performed daily in the Church.

The first conversion can signify that the water of death-bringing wisdom—the wisdom of this world or prudence of the flesh—is turned into blood, that is, into death, for those who walk according to the flesh and do not set their minds on things above, but on things upon the earth. For it is written: “The prudence of the flesh is death; and the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. 8). Hence the prophet says in rebuke: “And now what do you seek on the way to Egypt, to drink turbid water? And what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river?” (Jer. 2).

All earthly wisdom, hateful to God, of which the Egyptians drink—that is, the friends of this world, who are enemies of God—is the water of Egypt, which is turned into blood. For its blood is upon whoever drinks from it.

The second conversion, that of water into wine, can signify the conversion of fear into love of righteousness. For there is a water of saving wisdom, and “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110). To fear God is to be wise; but fear without love does not yet possess the taste of wine, but is like tasteless water. For fear has punishment, and one who fears in some manner feels, or anticipates, the punishment that one fears. But love of righteousness is the wine of gladness which gladdens the heart of man (Ps. 103): for the judgments of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts.

This conversion occurs at a wedding because the Church is betrothed to God in faith and righteousness—namely, that righteousness which is from faith in Christ Jesus. This is a righteousness of love, not of fear alone, as is the righteousness of the Law. Therefore the Apostle says: “You have not received again the spirit of bondage in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom. 8).

Love of righteousness forms a good life so that it is good, but it does not bring it to completion unless it is perfect. For what consummation or perfection is there except that of which it is said: “No one has greater love than that one lay down one’s life for one’s friends” (John 15)? Therefore wine is changed into blood when righteousness delights, and delights so greatly that one resolves to resist injustice even unto blood. This is the perfection of righteousness. For, writing of the opposite, namely imperfection, the Apostle says: “You have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin” (Heb. 12).

Therefore, if righteousness is turned into judgment; if the righteous person girds a sword upon his thigh against temptation or persecution; if one judges it more advantageous to die than to turn away from righteousness; if one says, “It is better to fall into the hands of men than to abandon the law of my God” (Dan. 13); if with the Apostle one says, “It is better for me to die than that anyone should make my glory void” (1 Cor. 9); if one who is to be judged before human beings for confessing truth or defending righteousness is found faithful, being with Christ to judge in the future; if an emulator of Christ’s passion thirsts for Christ’s cup and says, “I shall take the cup of salvation” (Ps. 115)—then the power of this sacrament has reached its consummation, and wine is changed into blood.

One who is such is worthy of the name martyr and is found a faithful witness, giving testimony on earth, because “there are three that give testimony on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood” (1 John 5): the spirit of the righteous, the water of penitents, and the blood of martyrs.

Thus far we have noted from Matthew’s Gospel how the sacrifice of truth was instituted by the Lord. It remains for us to consider, from the Gospels of the evangelists Mark and Luke, the manner and order in which this same sacrifice was instituted.

### From the Gospel of Mark (chapter 14)

“And while they were eating, Jesus took bread and blessed it,” and so forth, down to the words: “I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine.”

Where Matthew says (chapter 26), “Take and eat,” Mark says, “Take,” using one word in place of two—and not without reason. For one who receives takes, and one who eats takes. Everything else in Matthew and Mark is not merely the same, but is stated in almost the same words, except that Mark alone adds: “And they all drank from it.”

### From the Gospel of Luke (chapter 22)

“And he said to them: With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you,” down to the words: “Which shall be poured out for you.”

The Lord, desiring to inaugurate the new sacrifice, desires that the old Passover be brought to an end. Therefore, emphasizing the greatness of his desire, he says: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” For, wishing to complete what had to be completed before the Passion, he seems to hasten toward the Passion, in order to hasten our salvation. Thus it is of the old sacrifice that he says, “With desire I have desired,” and so forth. Indicating the completion and change of that old sacrifice, he says: “For I tell you that from now on I shall not eat it, until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God” (Luke 22). As if he said: From this time forward I shall not eat that old sacrifice, nor repeat the solemn observances of the Passover; but what the figure lacks I shall fulfil, by the sacrament of truth, in the kingdom of God.

He then adds concerning the cup: “And having received the cup, he gave thanks and said: Take and divide it among yourselves” (ibid.). This Evangelist alone mentions two cups: one belonging to the old sacrifice, the other to the new. Having mentioned that which belongs to the old Passover, he adds concerning its transfer: “For I tell you that I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes” (ibid.).

As we mentioned above [Col. 0683C], where Matthew has (chapter 26), “He blessed and broke,” and where Mark has (chapter 14), “Blessing, he broke,” Luke has, “He gave thanks and broke” (Luke 22); and Paul, agreeing with Luke, has: “And giving thanks, he broke” (1 Cor. 11). But what Luke has, “Which is given for you” (Luke 22), neither Matthew nor Mark says; in its place Paul says, “Which shall be delivered for you” (1 Cor. 11). Likewise, what Luke says, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22), neither Matthew nor Mark says—unless “Do this in remembrance of me,” which Luke says (chapter 14 [an apparent erroneous chapter reference]), and “take,” which Mark says (chapter 14), and “take and eat,” which Matthew says (chapter 26), are understood as equivalent.

But because Paul gives both, namely, “Take and eat” (1 Cor. 11), for which Matthew says, “Take and eat” (chapter 26), and also what Luke says, “Do this in remembrance of me,” it appears that there is some difference between what Matthew says, “Take and eat,” and what Luke says, “Do this in remembrance of me.” It is certain, therefore, that the words written, “Do this in remembrance of me,” concern the making of a memorial of the Lord’s death and its frequent celebration in the Church. For the Apostle explains this, giving Christ’s words concerning the cup in this form: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me” [Col. 0684A] (ibid.). He then adds: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (ibid.).

“Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me.” By these words Christ instructs us to offer ourselves, to eat him, and to be transformed into him.
