As if he said: Offer what I offer; eat what I give; finally, do what I do; endure for me as I endure for you. Give your bodies and your blood for one another, and lay down your souls for one another, just as I give you my body and my blood and lay down my soul for you. Accordingly Solomon says: “When you sit at the table of a rich man, carefully consider what is set before you; and put forth your hand, knowing that you must prepare such things” (Prov. 23).

Luke continues and says (chapter 22): “Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: This is the cup,” and so forth. Speaking of the bread, he had previously said: “He broke it and gave it to them.” This is what he refers to when he here says, “Likewise also the cup”; as if to say: He gave the bread; likewise, he gave the cup. But the addition, “after he had supped,” might seem to refer to both—the bread given and the cup given—unless, when the bread was being discussed, Matthew had first said (chapter 26), “While they were supping,” and Mark (chapter 14), “While they were eating.” From Matthew’s and Mark’s words, therefore, it appears that he gave the bread while they were supping or eating. From Luke’s words it appears that, after he had supped, he gave the cup.

Matthew and Mark [Col. 0684C] therefore seem to signify that the Lord gave the disciples the bread and cup while they were still supping, as though something of the supper yet remained. This is rightly said and rightly understood if the eating of the typical lamb together with the reception of the sacrament which replaced it is regarded as one supper. But Luke, who alone mentions two cups, as it were brings the supper to an end with its own cup at the point where the Lord begins a new supper with its own cup. Therefore, “after he had supped” may be understood thus: after he had completed the solemn rites of the old sacrifice. He seems to say this in order to distinguish the Lord’s supper from the preceding supper, just as he indicates that the cup must be distinguished from the cup.

Luke continues and says: “This cup is the New Testament in my blood” (Luke 22). As we said above, Matthew and Mark [Col. 0684D] (chapter 26) say: “This is my blood of the New Testament.” Thus this is apparently said to distinguish the prior cup, which Luke (chapter 14 [apparently an erroneous reference]) records that the Lord spoke of. For the Lord had previously offered another drink, whether in the same vessel or another, concerning which he also said: “Take and divide it among yourselves” (Luke 22). But not that cup: rather, “This,” he says, “is the cup”—that is, the drink now in this cup—“the New Testament.”

The words of this Evangelist, “This cup is the New Testament in my blood,” may be understood in the same sense as Matthew’s words, “This blood is the New Testament.” But if the different form of speech suggests some difference in meaning, let us seek in similar passages a way of speaking and a principle of understanding.

The Apostle, speaking to the Hebrews and commending their endurance, says among other things: “You received with joy the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have a better and abiding substance” (Heb. 10). Then, showing after a few intervening words what that better substance is, he says: “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for” (Heb. 11). By these words he signifies that faith is the cause by whose power and merit we may obtain substance, resources, and sufficiency of every good thing—temporal and spiritual, present and future—which is necessary for us and which must be sought and hoped for from God.

Love likewise is called the fulfilment of the law: the cause and power by which the law is fulfilled consist in it, and without it nothing in the law is savingly fulfilled. From these examples it may be gathered on what grounds the Lord’s saying, “This cup is the New Testament,” may rightly be understood. The New Testament, indeed, is the new law, containing the new covenant, promised repeatedly. For he imposed a new obedience and promised anew a new inheritance. This is obedience unto death; that is eternal life after death. But through faith in this cup and worthy reception of it we are helped and strengthened to fulfil this obedience and obtain this promise; and the cause and power of both are established in this cup, so that it may truly be said: “This cup is the New Testament.”

The blood of Christ, who suffered for us, leaving us an example that we should follow in his footsteps (1 Pet. 2), requires from us obedience unto death [Col. 0685C]—that is, that we die and die together with him. He who turns death away from us requires from us a return for his return, and death for death. O marvellous and astounding thing! From that by which we are released from death and made free through death, we are bound as debtors liable unto death. From that by which the debt of death is discharged, a debt of death is incurred. Thus we are now debtors to death through a new cause: although from the old guilt, nevertheless through new grace.

But the death of sinners is a most evil kind of payment of the penalty due; yet no absolution from ingratitude follows. The precious death of the saints is a kind of thanksgiving for Christ’s death and some likeness of a return [of like for like]. For no one is adequate to answer humility with an equal return; but because he is gracious, he is content to receive, in thanksgiving, whatever likeness of his own death is offered. “For if we have been made one with the likeness of his death, we shall also be [one with him] in the resurrection.” This likeness of death is obedience unto death, belonging to this cup which is here called the New Testament.

Hence the Prophet says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I shall receive the cup of salvation” (Ps. 115). To this same cup belongs the obtaining of the new promise, which is the reward of this new obedience. Hence the same Prophet says: “My inebriating cup, how splendid it is! And your mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22). [Col. 0686A] For how long? “All the days of my life” (ibid.). To what end, to what fruit? “That I may dwell in the house of the Lord unto length of days” (ibid.).

“This,” he says, “is the cup of the New Testament”; as if he said: Here are established the cause, power, and principle for fulfilling what is commanded in the New Testament and obtaining what is promised. This is the end and fulfilment of the law. This is the fullness of grace and truth; this is the mystery of faith, the foundation of hope, the witness of our love, the example of our obedience, the pledge of our inheritance, the sacrament of our renewal, the confirmation of our religion. For the New Testament is confirmed in my blood and is never thereafter to be changed by any rite, so that it may be an everlasting ordinance.

This cup is a love-potion, which Christ has prepared for us by an art known to himself. In shedding this blood he poured out his love; in pouring it into us he instils his love, washing us from our sins in his blood. For this was necessary for us: those defiled by blood had to be cleansed by blood. For whoever has been born of bloods, and of the will of the flesh, and of the will of a man, and not yet of God, must say: “Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50).

Jerusalem, under the figure of a woman, is told in Ezekiel: “Passing by you, I saw you trampled in your blood; and I said to you, while you were in your blood: Live. I said, I say, to you in your blood: Live” (Ezek. 16). And below: “You became joined to me by covenant, and I washed you with water, and cleansed your blood from you” [Col. 0686C] (ibid.). And Isaiah says: “When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the blood of Jerusalem from its midst, in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. 4).

But the blood of the sinner, in which the righteous person washes his hands, is not a sacrament of washing but an example of judgment and fear. Christ’s blood, however—holy and sanctifying, righteous and making righteous—makes clean and white those polluted by blood and conceived from unclean seed; but especially and pre-eminently those who drink the cup of the Passion and, for Christ’s blood shed, shed their own blood. Among the rest, they are so conspicuous and marvellous that it may be said of them: “Who are these clothed in white robes, and from where have they come? These are they who came out of great tribulation, and washed their robes [Col. 0686D] and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7). Not in their own blood, however clean or righteous it may be, but in the blood of the Lamb, who takes away the sins of the world.

For no saint believes his own righteousness or passion sufficient for his cleansing. Rather, however many saints there are, they have been sanctified by Christ’s blood, and they set his covenant above sacrifices. This is the covenant to be set above all carnal sacrifices of the Old Testament and all spiritual sacrifices of the New Testament. For from it comes all their praise and all their power; from it comes the righteousness now given to us. From it must be hoped for the glory that shall be revealed in us, so that in obtaining the promise also the covenant may be set above sacrifices. “The sufferings [Col. 0687A] of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8).

If, therefore, we have any faith, hope, love, patience, or humility; if there is in us any grace, power, or praise before God, it is all poured out from this cup. For from it flows every distribution of graces; therefore to it let every thanksgiving return.

## From the Gospel of John (chapter 6)

“Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. For him God the Father has sealed,” and so forth, down to the words: “He who believes in me shall never thirst.”

## Concerning food which perishes and food which does not perish

Every creature that has life also has food suited to its life. Consider all living creatures and all things that grow on earth: how they live, how they are nourished, how each feeds on nourishment suited to it, as though on food tempered for it. Fire also, although it has no life, on what does it feed and by what is it nourished? What it consumes and devours is food for fire, according to the Prophet’s saying: “A garment mixed with blood shall be for burning and food for fire” (Isa. 9).

The bodily senses also feed upon their delights. A desirable appearance and a beauty to be coveted are the desire of the eyes; nor is the eye satisfied by seeing, nor the ear by hearing. The faculties of the mind have their own delights in their enjoyments, apart from those pleasures which they draw from bodily senses. By what are memory, understanding [Col. 0687C], and will nourished and fed, delighted and strengthened?

Every rational creature—whether a good or evil angel, or a good or evil human being—is fed by its own food, according to the quality of life by which it lives happily or unhappily, well or ill. Good angels feed upon the praise, love, and vision of God. This is their life-giving refreshment, preserving their life for ever; it always refreshes and never fails, and from it they receive the power never to fail themselves.

But the food of the apostate angel is his iniquity, by which he is always proud against God, and his malice, by which he is always ill-disposed toward us. These please him, just as humility and love, conversely, always displease him; of these he is always as hungry as he is empty. His food, of which we have spoken, is like a hunger by which he always hungers for the destruction of human beings, so that he may devour those whom he has captured and transfer them, as it were, into his own body, to agree with him. Therefore he feeds on human sins, or on sinners themselves; and more avidly if he can find any righteous people against whom he may prevail. Hence it is written: “His food is choice” (Hab. 1).

He himself, however, is swallowed by evildoers when the counsel of his suggestion is received into the belly of the inmost sense, as it is written: “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Ps. 73). And whoever join themselves to evil men, whether broken or led astray by fraud, are swallowed both by the devil and by the evil persons themselves. Hence the Psalmist says: “Unless the Lord had been in us—let Israel now say—unless the Lord had been in us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” [Col. 0688A] (Ps. 123). And again: “Let them not say in their hearts, ‘Well done, well done, for our soul!’ nor let them say, ‘We shall devour him’” (Ps. 34).

Those also who tear and bite one another through envy and strife eat one another in turn. Thus the Apostle says to the Galatians: “But if you bite and devour one another, beware lest you be consumed by one another” (Gal. 5). By such food—namely, iniquity and malice—the life of the wicked, an evil life, is nourished and strengthened. But the good life of good persons, as far removed as it is from iniquity and malice, is sustained and strengthened by very different foods. For the food of the righteous is, first, righteousness, as it is written: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5); and second, Christ himself, the author of righteousness, who says: “I am the living bread” (John 6).

All righteous people eat this bread so that they may be righteous and live righteously; without it there is no good life and no blessed life. Those also who, by the word or example of the righteous, gain persons for Christ and bring them into the company of the righteous are their food, through whom they come to Christ, according to what was said to Peter: “Slay and eat” (Acts 10). Temporal food, by which bodily life is sustained, strengthens and preserves the body’s powers and senses so that they may be sound and vigorous; but it is consumed in use. Spiritual food, however, strengthens and preserves the powers and faculties of the soul and is not consumed in use; rather, while nourishing and increasing what is good, it consumes the contrary things—that is, vices and sins.

Hence the righteous, because sins are consumed in them and by them, are said in some manner to eat them, according to what is written—if it is understood in a good sense—“They shall eat the sins of my people” [Col. 0688C] (Hos. 4); in the same way the saying, “You gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Ps. 73), may be understood in a good sense. But to that food by which the good life is nourished and sustained so that through it one may attain the blessed life, the following words of the Lord belong; how they are to be understood must next be stated.

“Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. For him God the Father has sealed.”

After the miracle of the five loaves and two fishes, the crowds came to Capernaum seeking the Lord. When they unexpectedly found him across the sea, they said to him: “Rabbi, when did you come here?” Jesus answered and said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: You seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled” (John 6). They had indeed seen signs by which they could have known his divinity; but because they followed him on account of temporal refreshment rather than devotion of faith, he disclosed their very intention to them, so that they might thus come to know God. Immediately he showed for what food, and for what kind of food, one must work more earnestly, saying: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life.”

This may be understood of righteousness, upon whose love the righteous feed, and which the Son of Man freely gives, freely justifying the ungodly [Col. 0689A]. Righteousness endures unto eternal life, according to the saying: “His righteousness endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 111). And: “But the righteous shall live for ever” (Wis. 5). All who work iniquity work for food that perishes; so do those who do what they regard as good apart from faith in Christ, and those who follow Christ merely for an occasion, not for truth.

But the food that does not perish is righteousness—the righteousness which is from faith in Christ Jesus—and Jesus Christ himself, the giver of this righteousness. While he was with the Father as the bread of angels, he chose to become a man among human beings, so that man might eat the bread of angels. By giving faith, which works through love, he gives that one may believe in him, love him, and serve him as the true God. Finally, he gives himself to be eaten, but gives himself to us while we work. Therefore he says, “Work,” even though, preceding all our merit, he gives freely. Hence the Apostle says: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is the gift of God—not from works, lest anyone should boast” (Eph. 2).

The Son of Man gives food enduring unto eternal life through the sacrament of the dispensation by which he chose to become the Son of Man. Nor is he unable to give it because he is the Son of Man, for God the Father has sealed him. The Father has marked him out from all others by his own mark of singular holiness, so that he might give us such food, anointing him with the oil of gladness above his companions.

This phrase, “The Father has sealed,” should be expounded in this way according to blessed Augustine. But if an exposition is required according to blessed Hilary, his own words should be set down in their unaltered integrity. Thus he says in Book Eight of *On the Trinity*:

> “The only-begotten Son of God, and through the sacrament of our salvation the Son of Man, wishing to signify to us in himself the form of the Father’s own nature, says that he has been sealed by God the Father. And this is because the Son of Man would give the food of eternal life, so that by this the power in him to give food unto eternity might be understood: because he contained in himself the whole fullness of the Father’s form, of God who seals, so that what God had sealed might bring forth from itself nothing other than the form of God who seals.”

When the Lord had said, “Work for the food that endures unto eternal life,” [Col. 0689D] they understood that they were being admonished to do the works of God. They therefore ask what they might do in order to work the works of God. Jesus answered and said to them: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John 6). They asked about works as though they were many; he answered about the work of God as though it were one, in order to show that all good works proceed from one [work]. This resembles what the Psalmist says: “Direct the works of our hands over us, and direct the work of our hands” (Ps. 89).

Faith working through love is itself the work of God and the beginning of good works in us: “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Therefore, when they asked what the works of God were, because they did not yet have faith, without which they could not work the works of God, they are invited to faith, which is the work of God—namely, to believe in him whom God sent.

Understanding that he said this concerning himself, they said to him: “What sign, then, do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What work do you do?” (John 6). Behold, the Jews ask for signs, and the sign of the five loaves does not suffice them. It seems too little to establish belief that Christ is powerful enough to give food enduring unto eternal life because he gave barley loaves, since Moses promised nothing so great, through whom manna was given to them from heaven. They therefore compare the sign done through Moses with this sign of the five loaves, as though the greater to the lesser, as though what he had said of himself were unworthy of belief. Thus they say: “Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat” [Col. 0690B] (ibid.).

To their statement that bread from heaven was given to the fathers, Christ responds by showing that true bread from heaven was not given through Moses but is now given by the Father. Therefore he says to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven; but my Father gives you bread from heaven. For the true bread is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world” (ibid.). My Father gives you the true bread. For the bread of God is that which comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.

But they, understanding these things carnally, said to him: “Lord, always give us this bread” (ibid.). So too the Samaritan woman, to whom it was said: “Whoever drinks of the water which I shall give shall never thirst” [Col. 0690C] (John 4), immediately understood this bodily, wishing to lack no bodily necessity: “Lord,” she says, “give me this water, that I may not thirst or come here to draw” (ibid.). Likewise these men say, “Lord, give us this bread”—namely, bread which refreshes and does not fail; for this reason they wanted to make him king after the miracle of the five loaves.

But he calls them back to himself and makes clearer what bread he meant, saying: “I am the bread of life. He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6). “He who comes to me” means what he says in the words, “he who believes in me”; and “shall not hunger” means that he shall never thirst. For each expression signifies eternal satisfaction, where there is no want.

Yet Wisdom says: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. 24). Christ, who is the wisdom of God, is not eaten in the present life in satisfaction of desire, but in desire for satisfaction; and the more his sweetness is tasted, the more desire is stimulated. Therefore, those who eat me shall still hunger, until satisfaction comes. But when desire has been filled with good things, then they shall hunger and thirst no more.

The saying, “Those who eat me shall still hunger,” and so forth, may also be understood of the future state. For in that eternal satisfaction there is, as it were, a kind of hunger—not of need, but of blessedness—where those who never wish to cease eating always desire to eat and never grow weary in satisfaction [Col. 0691A]. For there is satisfaction without weariness and desire without sighing. Christ in his beauty is always wondrous and always desirable; the angels desire to look upon him. Therefore, even when he is possessed, he is desired; and when he is held, he is sought, as it is written: “Seek his face always” (Ps. 105). For he is always sought whom one loves in order always to possess him.

Thus those who find still seek; those who eat still hunger; and those who drink still thirst. But this seeking removes every anxiety; this hunger drives away every hunger; this thirst extinguishes every thirst. It is not hunger of need, but of consummate blessedness. For of hunger that is need, it is said: “He who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst.” But of hunger that is blessedness it is said: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst.”

Hunger and thirst, moreover, may be understood as the same thing, whether in need or in blessedness. But if some distinction is required, the Psalmist gives occasion to those seeking it when he says: “Bread strengthens the heart of man, and wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103). Christ is food and drink, bread and wine, to those who believe in him: bread, when he strengthens and establishes, concerning whom Peter says: “The God of all grace, who has called us into his eternal glory in Christ Jesus, after you have suffered a little, will himself perfect, strengthen, and establish you” (1 Pet. 5). He is drink or wine when he gladdens. To him the Prophet says: “Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul” [Col. 0691C] (Ps. 85).

Whatever in us is strong, vigorous, steadfast, glad, or joyful—in fulfilling God’s commands, enduring evils, carrying out obedience, or defending righteousness—all this strength and support comes from this bread, or this gladness from this drink. Blessed are those who act courageously and cheerfully. And because no one possesses this from himself, blessed are those who eagerly desire to pursue what is just and honourable, and in all things to be strengthened and gladdened by him who says: “Blessed are those who hunger for righteousness” (Matt. 5).

If Christ is bread and drink according to the present strength and joy of the righteous, how much more will he be so in the future, according to what he will then be for the righteous? In the foregoing words of Christ it may be observed that this food which endures unto eternal life is called bread from heaven, true bread, bread of God, and bread of life; and its benefit is shown in that it gives life to the world and forever excludes hunger and thirst.

It is called bread from heaven in order to show whence it comes and distinguish it from earthly bread, which perishes. It is called true bread in contrast to manna, which preceded as a figure of this truth. It is called bread of God in order to distinguish it from bread made and prepared by the art of a human baker. For this bread has been made and prepared by God, as it is written: “You prepared their food, for such is its preparation” (Ps. 64). It is called bread of life in order to distinguish it from this corruptible bread, which neither is life nor gives life, but only preserves life with difficulty and for a time [Col. 0692A]. But this bread is life, gives life, and preserves a life owing nothing to death or to the cause of death.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: He who believes in me has eternal life,” and so forth, down to the words: “He who eats of this bread shall live for ever” (John 6).

Christ is the bread of life for those who believe in him. To believe in Christ is to eat the bread of life; it is to have Christ within oneself; it is also to have eternal life. Wishing to show this, Christ says: “He who believes in me has eternal life.” Explaining what he has said, he adds: “I am the bread of life” (ibid.). It could have been said briefly: He who believes in me has me; therefore he has eternal life. He has it indeed in its cause, in its merit, in hope, in pledge; he has that from which he may have it.

Finally, whoever has Christ in himself has eternal life—not yet revealed in himself, but hidden in Christ, whom he has in himself. For our life is hidden with Christ in God. Therefore this supreme grace, which is laid up for us in Christ, is already possessed in Christ because Christ is possessed as the promiser and giver of this grace, and as its faithful guardian, keeping it deposited with himself and to render it on the day of the revelation of the glory of the children of God.

“I,” he says, “am the bread of life.” He had said this earlier, and its repetition is confirmation—or perhaps a distinction among his gifts—so that he alone may be understood as giver and author of both lives: the one which is now good and the one which shall be blessed [Col. 0692C]. “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died” (John 6). This must be understood of spiritual death. Why did they die? Because they believed what they saw and did not understand what they did not see. Therefore they are your fathers because you are like them: unbelieving fathers of unbelieving children.

As regards this bodily death, we too die who eat the bread descending from heaven. As regards spiritual death, Moses ate manna, Aaron ate manna, and many also ate who pleased God and did not die. Why did they not die? Because they understood spiritually, hungered spiritually, and tasted spiritually, that they might be satisfied spiritually. “This,” he says, “is the living bread that came down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die” [Col. 0692D] (ibid.).

This same bread—that is, Christ—who was speaking to unbelievers, was signified by manna, but has greater power than manna. For manna could not grant even to believers, much less to unbelievers, that they should not die spiritually. But Christ, who was signified in manna, whom the ancient righteous understood in manna and believed would come, grants to all who believe in him that they shall not die spiritually. Therefore he says: “This is the bread that came down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die.” This bread that came down from heaven is now on earth, now before the eyes not of your heart but of your flesh. And immediately he reveals that he himself is this bread, saying: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”

Behold, the bread which was previously called bread of life is now called living bread. It is living bread because it has abiding life in itself, and because it can take away spiritual death and confer life. For he first speaks of removing death, saying: “So that if anyone eats of it, he may not die.” Then, speaking of conferring life, he adds: “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever.”

“And the bread that I shall give is my flesh,” and so forth, down to the words: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.”

The Word of God gives food to some; to others he himself is food. For he gives food, as it is written: “All things wait upon you, Lord, that you may give them food in due season” [Col. 0693B] (Ps. 103). And again: “The eyes of all hope in you, Lord, and you give them food in the fitting season. You open your hand and fill every living thing with blessing” (Ps. 144).

But to the rational creature, which alone can share in righteousness and blessedness, provided that it has not turned away from him through its own will but has turned to him through the love of obedience, so that it lives not for itself but for him—to such a creature he gives food by which it may live, so that he may be its food, by participation in whom it may live well and blessedly.

Therefore, after saying that he is the living bread who came down from heaven and can give eternal life—thereby signifying that he is God and the life of angels and humans—he next shows, so that they may marvel still more, that the flesh he assumed is life-giving food and is given by him for the life of the world. He says: “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh, for the life of the world.”

The body of Christ is flesh according to the proper character of its nature; and it is called bread either because it is offered under the appearance of bread or because it is sometimes signified by bread on account of the likeness of its power. “Therefore the Jews disputed” (John 6). How could flesh grasp what he said—that bread was flesh? That which flesh cannot grasp is called flesh, and flesh understands it all the less precisely because it is called flesh. For this horrified them; this, they said, was too much for them; this they considered impossible. Thus they disputed with one another, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” [Col. 0693D] (ibid.).

At one time “How?” signifies the devout inquiry of a believer, as there: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1); at another, the impious denial of an unbeliever, as here. Therefore Jesus said to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” As if he said: Although you do not know, although you refuse to believe, nevertheless it is true that unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you shall not have life in yourselves. This must be understood of the spiritual life by which one lives righteously and of the eternal life by which one lives blessedly. Whoever does not eat will have neither.

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6).

What he had said that the person who does not eat does not have, [Col. 0694A] he now shows that the person who eats does have, saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” He has it already now, as we said before, according to the spirit, though not according to the flesh. For the spirits of the righteous, cleaving to God, will never be separated from his love; and therefore they will always live. Hence it is said: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22). And again it is written: “They seemed to the eyes of the foolish to die, but they are in peace” (Wis. 3). From these words they might have imagined that one who ate this flesh would not die a bodily death. He meets this thought by saying: “And I will raise him up.” As though he said: I do not deny that the one who eats my flesh will die a bodily death. [Col. 0694B] He will indeed die according to the flesh, but I shall raise him up, so that the flesh too may not be deprived of eternal life; but this will be on the last day.

Then, to show that this food is sufficient to remove every need and to confer life and every sufficiency, he adds: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Since people seek food and drink in order to live and not hunger or thirst, this is truly supplied only by this food and drink, which makes those who receive it immortal and incorruptible. This, therefore, is truly food, because it truly provides what is sought in food; hence it can give both body and soul life and every sufficiency, so that it needs nothing further. Thus the Prophet cries out for the removal of the need of both: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh also [thirsted] for you” (Ps. 62). [Col. 0694C]

“WHOEVER EATS MY FLESH.” Christ is eaten in two ways, because he is participated in two ways. One participation is through faith—not the faith now meant which is dead in the dead, that is, in sinners, but that by which the righteous person lives, concerning which it was said above: “Whoever believes in me has eternal life” (John 6). This faith, however, is not without charity. Through faith we are justified and made participants in God’s friendship; through faith Christ dwells in our hearts, grants himself to be known by us, and to be participated in by us.

The angels know by sight the Word coeternal with the Father, the one true God with the Father; through faith we eat the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, sent down from heaven to us and incarnate for us—the living bread which came down from heaven. Knowing through faith the flesh assumed for us and given to us as food, we eat Christ’s flesh. [Col. 0694D]

There is therefore faith of unity, faith of union, and faith of communion. By the faith of unity we believe that the Son is one with the Father, as he himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). Joined to this faith is faith in the Trinity. For no one fully possesses faith in unity in God—that is, in one divinity—unless he believes that each of the three persons is one God, and that all three together are not other than one God. For the mystery of unity in the Trinity contains the mystery of the Trinity in unity. Without faith in the Trinity, faith in the one God is not complete, because the Trinity is one God. [Col. 0695A]

By faith in the union, we believe that the only-begotten Son of God has united human nature to himself in the unity of his person through the mystery of the Incarnation. Joined to this faith is the faith of unity, by which we believe that there is one person in two natures. For one does not have full faith in this union who believes either that the two natures are not united in one person or that the person is divided between two natures.

By faith in communion, we believe that Christ’s most holy, life-giving, and sanctifying flesh is dispensed and communicated to us for the remission of sins, God wonderfully ordering this: he willed that we should receive as nourishment precisely that which he willed to assume from us and for us. Joined to this faith is faith in the Passion, which is represented in the offering of holy communion, where also the Lord’s death is proclaimed. [Col. 0695B]

The sum of our faith is to know Christ in the Father, Christ in the flesh, and Christ in participation at the altar. All mysteries of faith are gathered into this sum, and whatever is written in the Law, Psalms, and Prophets is directed to this end: that Christ may be known and, being known, loved. Therefore whoever, justified by faith, thinks worthily, devoutly, and faithfully concerning the sacrament of unity, the sacrament of union, and communion—such a person eats the bread of angels which is in heaven, the living bread which came down from heaven, and the flesh of Christ. Such a person participates in him by eating him and eats him by participating in him.

This has been said concerning one way of eating, by which Christ is eaten by the righteous through faith. [Col. 0695C] Yet within this one, three modes may be distinguished, according to faith in unity, union, and communion. For it is one thing to believe concerning Christ’s divinity what is fitting; another, concerning his humanity, what is true; and another, according to the grace of the dispensation by which he willed to be clothed with our flesh; or according to the grace of the dispensation by which he willed us to be fed with his flesh. Nevertheless, the several modes are gathered into one general mode, because Catholic faith is one and contains the mysteries of Christ’s divinity, Incarnation, and holy communion. Of this mode blessed Augustine says: “Believe, and you have eaten.”

The other mode occurs when Christ is received or possessed in our heart not only through faith and the power of holy communion, but through eating, use, and reception of his very body and blood within us; so that he may be in us not only through the presence of the divinity by which we were created, but also through the presence of the body by which we were redeemed, as he himself promised and said: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). [Col. 0695D] Thus he says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6).

“AND DRINKS MY BLOOD.” As Christ’s flesh is eaten in two ways, so also Christ’s blood is drunk in two ways: namely, by drinking that blood itself in the sacrament and by the power of faith, by which the righteous person lives and which is also the power of the sacrament.

As regards the proper nature of the substance, flesh is one thing and blood another. As regards the sacrament, one visible species signifies Christ’s flesh and contains flesh not without blood; another visible species signifies the blood and contains blood not without flesh. As regards the representation of the deed accomplished, Christ’s flesh offered under the species of bread represents itself as offered in another manner on the cross; and the blood offered under the species of wine represents itself as shed from Christ’s body on the cross. [Col. 0696A] This at once admonishes us to understand that Christ, who shed his blood for us, laid down his life for us. For, as it is written in Leviticus: “The life of all flesh is in the blood” (Lev. 17).

Therefore, though Christ’s flesh and blood are different, signified under different species, and represent themselves in different ways, the power of both is shown to be one by his saying: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life”; and by the later addition: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him.” [Col. 0696B] Whoever is made alive by faith in Christ’s Incarnation and Passion, so as to live righteously—that is, not for himself but for Christ and in Christ—eats Christ’s flesh with the mouth of faith and drinks Christ’s blood. Flesh is not eaten by the power of faith unless blood also is drunk; nor is blood drunk unless flesh is eaten, because the power by which both are participated in is one, and the benefit of both, obtained through faith in each, is one.

For eternal life is given to the believer, as Christ says: “Whoever believes in me has eternal life.” It is given to the one who eats and drinks, as he again says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” That faith also pertains to drink is shown by his saying: “Whoever believes in me shall never thirst.” Therefore Christ’s flesh is eaten through faith, and Christ’s blood is drunk through faith. For through faith we venerate the remedy of our salvation in both Christ’s flesh and blood; nor are they divided in faith which are not separated in power. [Col. 0696C] This is the faith which justifies and gives life, of which the Apostle says: “The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe” (Rom. 3).

[Col. 0696D]

“HE REMAINS IN ME, AND I IN HIM.” Above he showed how great a benefit Christ’s flesh confers if eaten, and his blood if drunk; now he shows how great a grace of intimacy and honor it confers. For it brings about this: that the one who eats is in Christ, and Christ in him. It is a great and inestimable grace to have one’s dwelling in Christ and to provide Christ a dwelling. As by believing we eat, so by loving perseveringly we remain in Christ. For God is charity; and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him. Hence Christ himself says: “Remain in my love” (John 15).

Therefore that person remains in Christ who does not turn back in temptation, but acts courageously in all things, with confidence of victory and constancy in perseverance. Hence comes the enduring fruit of righteousness, which the righteous bear because they remain in Christ, like branches in the vine, which cannot bear fruit unless they remain in the vine. [Col. 0697A]

There is a love by which we are loved by God, and a love by which we love God. We remain in both if we persevere in loving Christ. For the Lord preserves those who love him. There is also a love by which we love our brothers and neighbors in Christ as Christ’s members and members of his body, which is the Church. All members of this body are made alive by one Spirit, namely the Holy Spirit, just as all the members of a human being live by that person’s one spirit. But those who do not live by Christ’s Spirit are not of his body, are not his members, and do not remain in Christ.

But those who preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace; who inviolably preserve the right of brotherhood and spiritual fellowship; who do not separate themselves from ecclesiastical unity by heresies, schisms, or faults of life or conduct—these remain in Christ’s body and in Christ. For they truly participate in Christ and, by participating, eat him. [Col. 0697B] Therefore he says: “Whoever eats my flesh remains in me.” And he adds: “And I in him” (John 6). We have been strengthened; he continually works in us, that we may remain and be strengthened in him, “because his mercy has been confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains for ever” (Ps. 116).

Hence he himself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14). He who says, “I love those who love me” (Prov. 8), makes his dwelling in those who persevere in loving, so that they may remain, while he himself remains in those who remain in him. [Col. 0697C]

But what does he mean when he says, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him,” as though Christ were loved by us before we are loved by the Father, or before the Son comes to us and makes his dwelling with the Father, when John says: “In this is charity: not that we loved God, but that he first loved us” (1 John 4)? The answer is easy for those who consider both that he loved us and chose us in the Son, according to the purpose of his grace, before the foundation of the world; and that he loves us by calling and justifying us, increasing his grace, leading us through the progress of righteousness to perfection, and confirming us in his love.

For just as the wicked are hardened through the progress of malice and made obstinate by the habit of sinning, so the good are confirmed unto perseverance by a certain order of beginning and increasing grace: God goes before, comes, and remains. [Col. 0697D] By this order they come to eternal life. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10). Therefore Christ goes before by loving and loves by going before. Whoever loves him will be loved by the Father through the showing of love and the bestowal of more abundant grace.

It can also be understood differently when it is said: “My Father will love him.” “If anyone loves me,” he says, “he will keep my word” (John 14), that is, he will persevere in keeping it. For it is too little if he keeps it but will not continue to keep it. For the sole praise of one whose love is neither pretended nor self-flattering nor lukewarm or superficial is perseverance. Hence the Prophet says: “I will love you, O Lord”—that is, I will persevere in loving you. That I may do this, I am not sufficient without you; rather, you are “my strength” (Ps. 17).

“My Father,” he says, “will love him”: that is, he will continue to love the one who perseveres in obedience. This is not because God’s love is slight or changeable—for he loved his elect before the foundation of the world, and Christ, having loved his own, loved them to the end—but because he loves perseveringly those whom he preserves to remain in his love; and he withdraws his grace from the one who makes himself unworthy of that grace. [Col. 0698A]

Thus when Christ says, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6), he plainly indicates that the person who believes in him and eats him is strengthened only by eating him, so as to remain in Christ until he comes to eternal life. Hence the righteous person prays: “Confirm, O God, what you have worked in us” (Ps. 67). Therefore, when this food is eaten with full faith and worthy veneration, it grants righteousness, perseverance, and eternal life, so that, justified by faith and rooted in charity, we may remain securely in him who has become for us a house of refuge and a fortified place, because he remains in us without end, as it is written: “Let all who hope in you rejoice; they shall exult for ever, and you shall dwell in them” (Ps. 5). [Col. 0698B]

“As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father; so whoever eats me will live because of me.”

[Col. 0698C]

According to blessed Augustine, these words are understood thus. In Sermon 26 on John he says: “For his sending is his emptying of himself and the taking of the form of a servant.” This is rightly understood while preserving the equality of nature which the Son has with the Father. For the Father is greater than the Son considered as man, but he has the Son as equal God, since he is both God and man, Son of God and son of man, the one Jesus Christ.

If these words are rightly understood in this sense, he said: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me”; as though he said: My emptying, in which he sent me, brought it about that I live because of the Father—that is, that I refer my life to him as greater. But participation, by which one eats me, brings it about that anyone lives because of me. Therefore I, humbled, live because of the Father; that person, raised up, lives because of me. [Col. 0698D]

But if it was said, “I live because of the Father,” because he is from the Father and not the Father from him, it is said without prejudice to equality. Yet in saying, “And whoever eats me will live because of me,” he did not signify equality between us and himself, but displayed the grace of the Mediator. These are Augustine’s words.

What, then, is intimated to us in these words of Christ except that he was sent by God the Father and came into the world for this purpose: that those who eat him—that is, believe in him—may live because of him, as he lives because of the Father? Christ lives because of the Father—or, as blessed Hilary has it, through the Father—because he is from the Father: God from God, life from life. For as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself. This applies to the life by which he lives with the Father.

But according to the life by which he lived among human beings as man, he lived because of the Father, because he glorified the Father in his life, doing his will and rendering him honor in all things. [Col. 0699A] We, however, live because of him if we refer all our living to him, by whose gift it comes that we live righteously and by whose power we hope to live most blessedly. Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall praise the Lord in my life” (Ps. 145). And again: “O God, I have declared my life to you” (Ps. 55).

In the comparison Christ now uses, the two pairs correspond reciprocally. Sending and eating can be compared through a similar efficacy. For the sending causes Christ to live through the Father, insofar as he is less than the Father; eating causes us to live because of Christ, who, as Mediator of God and humankind, reconciles to the Father those who live because of him, as he lives because of the Father. Christ’s life because of the Father and our life because of Christ correspond through a similar cause, intention, and end: by proceeding, tending, and arriving. For both return to that from which they begin; each is referred to him by whom it is conferred and rendered to him from whom it is received. [Col. 0699B]

Christ’s statement, “Whoever eats me will live because of me” (John 6), is rightly understood in two ways: either in terms of disposition or in terms of sign. For this eating brings about our living because of Christ—that is, through his grace unto his glory; and our living because of Christ is a sign that we eat Christ. Likewise, the preceding statement may be understood in two ways: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid.). For remaining in Christ is both the effect and the sign of eating; as if it were said: It is a sign that one eats and drinks—that is, that one remains in me and lives because of me. [Col. 0699C]

“This is the bread which came down from heaven—not as your fathers ate manna and died. Whoever eats this bread will live for ever.”

[Col. 0699D]

Observe how often Christ repeats the same things, how often he impresses upon us that the Father gave this bread, that this bread came down from heaven, and that this bread gives eternal life. Why is this? Certainly to establish faith in his divinity: that he may without doubt be believed to be God who has God as Father; who was in heaven and came down from heaven; who wills to be eaten and cannot be consumed; who can give eternal life and raise the dead on the last day. Therefore, as if repeating himself, he says: “This is the bread which came down from heaven.” And to show that this bread is greater and can do more than manna, he adds: “Not as your fathers ate manna and died. Whoever eats this bread will live for ever.” [Col. 0700A]

“He said these things while teaching in the synagogue,” etc., up to: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6).

Many of those present were scandalized because they did not understand; and many who heard these things—not his enemies, but his disciples—said: “This saying is hard. Who can hear it?” If the disciples considered this saying hard, what of his enemies? They understood that Jesus intended to distribute his flesh to those believing in him as though it were cut into portions.

“But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were murmuring about this” (ibid.)—for they said these things among themselves so that he might not hear them; but he who knew them within themselves heard them in himself—“answered and said: Does this scandalize you?” [Col. 0700B] Because I said that my flesh is given to eat and my blood to drink? This indeed scandalizes you: “What then if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?”

What is this? In this he resolves what troubled them; in this he makes clear that over which they were scandalized; in this, plainly, if they understood. For they thought that he would distribute his body by division; he said that he would ascend into heaven, undoubtedly whole. When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before, then surely you will see that he does not distribute his body in the manner you suppose; then surely you will understand that grace is not consumed by bites.

Elsewhere Christ says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). Hence it is understood, according to the unity of person, that he who is now said to be about to ascend into heaven for the exaltation of his humanity was then in heaven and had been there before.

Then he adds: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” O Lord, good teacher, how does the flesh profit nothing when you have said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in yourselves?” (John 6). Does life profit nothing? And for what purpose do we exist except to have eternal life, which you promise through your flesh? [Col. 0700C] What then does it mean that flesh profits nothing? How are these not contradictory: “My flesh is truly food,” and “the flesh profits nothing”?

In accordance with Christ’s clemency and kindness, it might have seemed fitting that those who were scandalized at his words through unbelief should be recalled from the error of their unbelief to knowledge of truth and the piety of faith by an explanation of the sayings—an explanation which enlightens and gives understanding to little ones—so that they might think worthily concerning Christ’s flesh, as he willed himself to be believed and as it is expedient for us to believe. But now, to those who were scandalized, as though intending to leave them in their error, he says: “The flesh profits nothing.”

For who, thinking unworthily concerning Christ’s flesh, would not gladly hear: “The flesh profits nothing”? For the unbeliever may perhaps take this as testimony for his own assertion, by which he presumes to oppose the benefit of so great a sacrament. [Col. 0701A] But true is what was written of him: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many” (Luke 2). His teaching is to some an aroma of life unto life, to others an aroma of death unto death.

Knowing, therefore, to whom he was speaking, he said what was appropriate—as it was appropriate to say it to persons who, after miracles and manifest proofs of his divinity, refused to believe his words. They thought of flesh carnally, not spiritually, according to the sense and wisdom of the flesh. But carnal understanding profits nothing. Even flesh itself, when conceived impiously, irreverently, and carnally—as flesh torn apart in a corpse or sold in a market—is of no benefit to those who think in that way, that is, who do not believe.

When he was about to say, “The flesh profits nothing,” he first declared, “It is the Spirit who gives life”: the latter for the good, the former for the evil. [Col. 0701B] For God’s Spirit, through spiritual understanding—that is, true faith in Christ—and through spiritual wisdom—that is, true love of Christ—gives life to the righteous, so that they may understand spiritually and live spiritually. To them belongs what is said here, “It is the Spirit who gives life,” as well as what was said before: “My flesh is truly food.”

But those who are alien to spiritual understanding—that is, to faith in Christ—or who, having faith, are empty of spiritual wisdom—that is, Christ’s charity—are not made alive by God’s Spirit; nor do they eat Christ’s flesh spiritually, namely in such a way that they live and remain in him and he in them. Therefore to those for whom flesh profits nothing it is said: “The flesh profits nothing.”

Thus, when Christ appears to say contradictory things about the flesh—as though it profits and does not profit—the meaning is that it profits spiritual persons made alive by Christ’s Spirit, but profits carnal persons, who are not led by God’s Spirit, not at all. [Col. 0701C]

The Apostle speaks in this manner concerning the Law. In one place, wishing to portray the Law as useless or evil, he says: “The letter kills” (2 Cor. 3). Again: “The Law works wrath” (Rom. 4). And: “The power of sin is the Law” (1 Cor. 15). But these things are said because of, and against, the wicked, in whom desire is increased on the occasion of the commandment and the Law is despised through transgression of the Law. For the Law identifies and provokes the enemy, but does not assist against the enemy; it forbids desire and excites it; it adds and punishes transgression.

Elsewhere he says: “The Law is holy and good” (Rom. 7); and again, “The Law is spiritual” (ibid.). This is said because of the good. Thus speech concerning faith and knowledge varies, because they can benefit some and not benefit others. Christ says: “Whoever believes in me has eternal life” (John 6). The Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13). The Prophet says: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 118). [Col. 0702A] The Apostle says: “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8).

Therefore, just as faith or knowledge alone without charity, and just as the letter of the Law without the spirit of the Law, profits nothing, so flesh without the Spirit—that is, without the grace of faith and charity—profits nothing. And as the Apostle says, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3), so Christ says: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.”

Then, wishing to show how the Spirit gives life, he adds: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” What does “they are spirit and life” mean? They are to be understood spiritually. If you have understood spiritually, they are spirit and life; if you have understood carnally, they are still spirit and life, but they are not so for you. They are spirit and life because, through the inspiration of spiritual grace, they grant and preserve the life by which one lives well. [Col. 0702B]

“Some of you do not believe,” etc., up to: “We have believed and have known that you are Christ, the Son of God” (John 6).

Among Christ’s disciples were some believers and some unbelievers; and among the unbelievers was Judas, who was to betray him. Christ knew them all: who were believers and unbelievers, who would betray him, and who would depart from him. But before those who were to depart departed, he showed that faith does not belong to all, but to those to whom it is given by his Father to come to Christ. For the mystery of faith can be revealed not by flesh and blood but by the Father who is in heaven. He gives to some that they may believe and does not give it to others. Why he does not give it to some, he himself knows. We are not given to know this; and in a matter so incomprehensible and so hidden from our sight, we can do nothing but cry out in wonder and say: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). [Col. 0702C]

But many disciples who did not believe went back—not after Christ, but after Satan. When Peter advised the Lord not to die, the Lord said to him: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not think the things of God” (Matt. 16). The Lord did not drive him away to go after Satan; rather, because Peter wished to go before the Lord, he called him Satan and made him go behind himself, so that he might not be Satan.

To Peter it is said, “Get behind me”; but concerning these persons it is said, “They went back,” and this means after Satan, as the Apostle says of certain women: “For some have already turned back after Satan” (1 Tim. 5). While they went after Satan so that they no longer walked with Christ, Judas still remained in order to lie in wait. Jesus therefore said to the twelve who remained: “Do you also wish to go away?” Simon Peter answered him: “Lord, to whom shall we go?” (John 6). If we depart from you, where shall we find life, truth, the author of life, a teacher like truth? “You have the words of eternal life.” [Col. 0702D]

Your words, reverently heard and stored in the bosom of faith, bestow eternal life. In your words you promise eternal life in the ministration of your body and blood; and we, having faith in your words, say: “We have believed and have known that you are Christ, the Son of God”—that is, you yourself are eternal life, and you give in your flesh and blood nothing other than what you are. “We have believed,” he says, “and have known that you are Christ, the Son of God”: that is, this very thing we have believed and known, that you are the Son of God. It follows that you have words of eternal life and that all you have said is true.

Or otherwise: Whatever you said concerning your flesh to be eaten and your blood to be drunk, we have believed and known to be true because you are Christ, the Son of God. He did not say, “We have known and believed,” but “We have believed and known.” This may refer to the knowledge which reaches understanding through the progress of faith, concerning which it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7). [Col. 0703A]

Faith itself is a kind of knowledge, even in those who believe simply and do not understand the reason for faith. But knowledge progressing as far as understanding belongs to those who have trained senses for more fully knowing the rationale of faith, always ready to give an answer to anyone who asks for a reason for the faith and hope that are in us. The fact that many disciples were scandalized in faith by Christ’s preceding words while others were built up to faith provides great consolation, by God’s dispensation, for those preaching God’s word, should unbelieving hearers perhaps be scandalized by their words and turn backward after Satan. Nevertheless, great caution must be used, and God’s word must always be sown with fear. [Col. 0703B]

We have expounded these words of Christ, which we have taken from John’s Gospel, following Father Augustine. Where it seemed suitable, we have at times taken care not to pass over points which he set out in his own words, nor to set them out either more fully or more briefly. Now, after the testimony of the four Evangelists, let us turn our attention, having examined with such diligence as we could marshal the matters establishing faith in this ineffable sacrament, to the words of the Apostle Paul concerning this sacrament. Thus may the confession of our faith, supported by the testimonies of evangelical and apostolic teaching, stand as an immovable mass founded in its stability; and may no force of invented or curious questions be able to shake it from its firmness. [Col. 0703C]

## On the words of the Apostle

“To eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (Matt. 18). This may be understood concerning food, which cannot cleanse a person, and concerning hands, which without guilty conscience are found unwashed every day so that they may be washed every day. But it is unfitting and unlawful to approach the Lord’s table and the flesh of the spotless Lamb with unwashed hands, and it is by no means safe. “I shall wash my hands among the innocent,” he says, “and I shall encompass your altar, O Lord” (Ps. 25). The abhorrence of crimes and the righteousness of good works: this is true cleanliness of hands.

But one who has clean hands must beware of touching what is unclean. For “whoever touches an unclean thing shall be unclean. Whoever touches pitch shall be defiled by it” (Sir. 13). Let the person not bound by the guilt of personal sin take care not to be defiled through consenting to another’s wickedness. Hence the Apostle, instructing Timothy, says: “Do not share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure” (1 Tim. 5). [Col. 0704A]

Writing to the Corinthians, he rebukes them because they did not remove from among them a public fornicator, as though by tolerating him they became participants in so great an offense. For he says: “It is reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles: that a man has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this might be removed from among you” (1 Cor. 5). And shortly afterwards: “Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass? Purge out the old leaven” (ibid.).

See: even if they appeared good in other respects, he calls their boasting—notably concerning their life, reputation, or conscience—not good, because consent to another’s crime through sinful tolerance corrupts their other good qualities, and one person’s example proves destructive to many. Therefore, desiring to draw them away from such an offense, though he could terrify them in many ways, he chose rather to exhort them by setting before them an example from the Law of Moses, to render due reverence to the paschal sacrifice. Thus, considering the dignity of so great a sacrament, they might recoil from approaching unworthily and from tolerating among themselves one unworthy to approach. [Col. 0704B]

For what is more terrifying to a sinful person approaching the Lord’s table, yet possessing true faith in this sacrament, than to consider how unclean and deserving of wrath that person is who approaches, and how holy, undefiled, and righteous is he whom that person approaches? Therefore, setting before them the remembrance of Christ’s death and the sacrifice of the Lamb, he urges them to purge out the old leaven and to feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth—unlocking what had been closed in the Law and illuminating what had been foreshadowed in the type. [Col. 0704C]

“Purge out the old leaven,” etc., up to: “With the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

In Exodus the children of Israel were commanded to sacrifice a lamb, eat its flesh roasted with fire, and eat unleavened bread with wild lettuce. And concerning the unleavened bread it is written: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, [Col. 0704D] you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month,” etc. (Exod. 12). And below: “They made for themselves unleavened cakes baked under the ashes. For it could not be leavened, because the Egyptians were forcing them to depart and permitting them to make no delay” (ibid.).

The children of Israel were forbidden to leaven bread both by the authority of the divine command and by the pressure of time. But the necessity of time, serving the divine dispensation, did not permit what God did not will to be done. As they began to depart from Egypt, abstinence from leaven was enjoined upon them; and, with the Lord commanding and the Egyptian pressing them, they could not refrain from abstaining, even if they wished not to abstain. But once they had departed Egypt, the same abstinence was enjoined in eating the lamb; necessity of time gave way to obedience, and free will entered in. [Col. 0705A] Thus, when one departs from the kingdom of sin and from the vain manner of life of the world, abstinence from sin—which God imposes—is often nevertheless observed through the necessity of circumstances; but as time goes on, what may at first perhaps have been forced becomes wholly voluntary.

Sin is the old leaven, from which one must abstain throughout this whole number of seven days. By this leaven the entire mass was corrupted in Adam’s transgression, and in his descendants. Hence it is called old, and belongs to the old man; utterly unlike it is the leaven of righteousness, concerning which it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal” (Matt. 13). That old leaven corrupts and puffs up, and is contrary to the new dough. Now dough is flour [Col. 0705B] bound together by liquid without leaven—likewise unleavened bread. But the new dough, or unleavened bread, is Christ, free from every corruption of sin.

And if we have been ground down through fear and humility; if we have been mixed with the waters of baptism or repentance, drenched with the liquid of heavenly grace, and bound together through charity so that we may not be divided by the various desires of error—then we are new dough, or unleavened bread. Having purged out the old leaven and abandoned the corruption of our life, we too, with the Corinthians, are admonished to be new dough (1 Cor. 5): that is, to remain without leaven, as through grace we have been made unleavened, that is, free from sin; or to be new dough by walking in newness of life through works of righteousness, just as we have been freed from the corruption of our old life.

For if, according to the Law, one had to abstain from leaven in eating the paschal Lamb, which came before as a figure, how much more must one now abstain spiritually from leaven: “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (ibid.). Passover is the name both of the feast and of the solemn victim. Christ was signified in each. For he himself is our feast, our joy, and the day of our gladness and exultation; he is our victim, offered for us and prepared by God for food. Therefore, let us feast. If we are new dough and unleavened loaves, how is it said to us, or by us, “let us feast,” unless because we ourselves are both the banquet and the guests—refreshed by Christ, who is bread to us and who is himself refreshed by us? Of him it is written [Col. 0705D] that “he feeds among the lilies” (Song 2). And in the Apocalypse he says of himself: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I shall enter to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3).

Therefore let us feast in God’s sight and delight in gladness, “not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness” (1 Cor. 5). For the Lamb is innocent, who takes away the sins of the world. Wickedness (*nequitia*) and malice (*malitia*) may be distinguished in this way: one may be understood as what is done against God, the other as what is done against one’s neighbor. But however they are distinguished, every iniquity must be avoided as malice and wickedness; and incorruptness of life must be pursued, so that we may feast on the unleavened bread “of sincerity,” keeping ourselves [Col. 0706A] undefiled by every iniquity, “and of truth,” doing every good thing without deceit or pretense.

From the same Epistle: “Our fathers were all under the cloud,” etc., as far as the words: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

“To Abraham the promises were spoken” (Gal. 3). They were indeed spoken, but not immediately fulfilled; rather, they were deferred for a long time. Faith in the promises, while they were awaited, was confirmed by frequent signs and mighty works—signs wrought by God—through which God made his power known, lest he should not be believed able to do what he had promised. In the signs visibly displayed to the ancient fathers, God proclaimed the power of his works, those which he was to perform [Col. 0706B] in a later generation. For the works he was to perform in fulfilling the promises were like those he did before fulfilling them: like them, I say, but not the same—similar works, able by resemblance to their own figure to foreshadow and prefigure the fruit and end of the promises.

The promises were many and one: many in one, and one in many. For the one Christ is the end of the promises, since all the righteous desired and awaited him, hoping that he would deliver his people from every evil as though from an enemy’s hand, and would grant blessing and salvation. This is what Zechariah says: “He spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old: salvation from our enemies” (Luke 1), etc. The fruit of the promises is grace, which is given in baptism; likewise grace [Col. 0706C] given in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. There is forgiveness of sins in the former; here is saving preparation for attaining eternal life. There Christ is put on; here he is eaten. These are the first fruits to be received meanwhile, until what is partial is done away with and what is perfect comes, so that we may see the God of gods in Zion.

But Christ himself—both the one promised and the one who promises—at length came, just as he himself had formerly promised together with the Father; and he instituted two sacraments, namely baptism in water and the mystery of his body, by which he might sanctify us and, having sanctified us, make us blessed. Signs of these sacraments came before in the sea and in manna. There was the figure; here is the truth. Observing this, the Apostle [Col. 0706D] says: “Our fathers were all under the cloud” (1 Cor. 10).

In Exodus we read that, setting out from Succoth, the children of Israel encamped at Etham, on the outer boundary of the wilderness. The Lord went before them, showing the way by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire, so that he might be their guide on the journey at both times. “The pillar of cloud by day never failed, nor the pillar of fire by night, before the people.” And below: “The angel of the Lord, who went before the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them; and with him the pillar of cloud likewise moved, leaving the front and standing behind, between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel. And the cloud was dark, yet it gave light by night, so that they were unable to approach one another” (Exod. 14).

In the historical sense, all who [Col. 0707A] departed Egypt were under the cloud, because the pillar of cloud never failed by day. In the spiritual sense, however, all the ancient righteous were under the cloud. The cloud is the obscurity of figures; the cloud is Christ or the Holy Spirit, protecting and overshadowing. Again, the cloud is Christ, as still hidden and not yet openly revealed. The cloud also is faith enfolded in typological mysteries and held in suspense by expectation of things to come.

Yet if those were under the cloud who faithfully and spiritually understood the promises and deeds wonderfully made known—of whom it is written: “He fed them in the innocence of his heart, and guided them by the understandings of his hands” (Ps. 77), that is, by his works—how much more were those under a cloud, though one of blindness and ignorance, of whom it is written: “Our [Col. 0707B] fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders” (Ps. 105). And again: “They forgot God, who saved them, who did great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, terrible things in the Red Sea” (ibid.). And again: “They did not believe his word” (ibid.).

Some, therefore, understood God’s works and words; others did not understand. Some believed; others did not believe. The signs of God’s works were, as it were, certain words, according to what is written: “He placed among them the words of his signs” (Ps. 104). Those who spiritually understood the meanings of words and signs, and those who did not understand spiritually, were under the cloud. For the one cloud which stood between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel was dark [Col. 0707C] and gave light by night. Christ, by a just judgment, blinds some and mercifully enlightens others. To some he is a stone of stumbling and rock of offense; to others, the cornerstone (1 Pet. 2). To some God is the Son of God; to others he is a sinful man, reckoned with those who go down into the pit (Ps. 87).

“And all passed through the sea” (1 Cor. 10).

Historically, the children of Israel walked on dry ground through the midst of the sea, and the water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained (Ps. 105). This is the form of baptism, in which the spiritual Pharaoh and all his cavalry are drowned. That this spiritual understanding was evident to the ancient Fathers is clear from many passages of Scripture. For in the Song of Songs the bridegroom speaks to the bride, saying: “I have likened you, my beloved, [Col. 0707D] to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song 1). And in Ezekiel the Lord says: “I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36). And in the same prophet it is written: “The waters descended on the right side of the temple, beside the middle of the altar” (Ezek. 47). And below: “Every living creature that moves, wherever the stream comes, shall live” (ibid.). And in Micah: “He will put away our iniquities and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Mic. 7). And in Zechariah: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of Jacob and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13). And below: “On that day living waters shall go out from Jerusalem: half of them to the eastern sea, [Col. 0708A] and half of them to the western sea” (Zech. 14).

If a moral interpretation is sought in the Apostle’s preceding words, see and consider how all the righteous who existed from ancient days were protected beneath the cloud of divine mercy, and how they crossed the sea—that is, this world, so turbulent and fluid, where all who live in the Egyptian manner are involved in the depths of vices, among the desires of error, amid the waves of a slippery life. But the righteous pass through, amid the divisions of temptations on the right and on the left, with dry foot and an undefiled path.

“And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10).

They were baptized from the same source from which they were purified. For God, purifying [Col. 0708B] their hearts through faith, was accomplishing this through the mighty deeds performed by Moses and concerning Moses, and through the display of signs which he wrought in the cloud and the sea: that they might be purified from the error of Egyptian superstition, and that the true God might be believed—the God who had sent Moses, “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3). This too he was accomplishing in all his wonders: that, confirmed in faith in the one true God, they might unhesitatingly believe and await the one who would someday come to give blessing and salvation according to faith in the promises spoken to Abraham and his seed.

Therefore, in all the benefits bestowed upon the ancient fathers, God remembered his covenant which he had made with Abraham his servant, so that they too, mindful [Col. 0708C] of the same covenant, might confess the remembrance of his holiness, and might receive present consolation from the benefits granted them in such a way as to perceive in them the signification of the promised blessing. For what could a long delay and no consolation in the meantime be except despair of the promise? But the frequent display of signs and the repeated consolation of blessings were reminders of the promise spoken, and prefigurations of future things.

Moses, therefore—the liberator, teacher, and lawgiver of the people—prefigured Christ, who is our judge, king, and lawgiver.
