The cloud too prefigured Christ: veiled in faith, hidden in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, to be veiled in flesh. Finally, it is written: “They called upon the Lord, and he answered them; in the pillar of cloud [Col. 0708D] he spoke to them” (Ps. 98). But these things happened to them as a figure. Declaring the truth of this, the Apostle says: “In many and various ways God spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1).

The sea, as was said above, prefigured baptism—indeed, that baptism which is called baptism uniquely and principally, of which the Apostle says: “One baptism” (Eph. 4). Among the Jews, to be sure, there were various baptisms according to various kinds of washings, as the same Apostle indicates when he says: “In foods and drinks, and various baptisms” (Heb. 9). They were baptized into Moses, but we into Christ; yet they were not baptized into Moses in the same way as we are into [Col. 0709A] Christ.

Moses, God’s servant sent by God, proclaimed God’s words to the people, as he himself said; and he confirmed faith in both his own words and God’s words by the signs that followed. Yet the signs shown in Moses’ hand were performed not by Moses’ power but by God’s power. By them faith either began or increased in those who believed; and, purified by faith, they pleased God. Therefore they were assisted through Moses’ ministry and example so as to believe; but the author of the faith which they held, moved by amazement at the signs, was not Moses but God, in whom they believed and by believing pleased him.

We thus possess faith in the one true God, called “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3), by whom Moses also was sent to them. Possessing likewise faith in the Savior to come, according to the promise spoken to Abraham, [Col. 0709B] Isaac, and Jacob, and according to the example of their faith, they were baptized not by Moses but into Moses. For they were baptized by him, but purified by the one by whom they were divinely inspired to believe. Therefore they were baptized spiritually, not washed outwardly but sanctified inwardly. They were baptized spiritually just as we are spiritually circumcised.

Accordingly, they were baptized by Christ’s power and grace, as we also are, because through faith in Christ—of which he is author and perfecter—they were sanctified, as we also are. For Christ was then sanctifying them through faith, just as he sanctifies us. For he was not absent, who says of himself: “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8). The Apostle too, speaking of Moses, says that “he considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure [Col. 0709C] of the Egyptians” (Heb. 11).

But since mighty, wondrous, and terrible deeds were done through Moses, by which faith might be initiated or strengthened so that believers might be sanctified, what does it mean that the Apostle mentions those signs done in the cloud and sea, while passing over the others displayed in the ten plagues against Pharaoh and Egypt? Perhaps by saying “into Moses” he intended all the other things he did not expressly mention to be understood. He mentioned the cloud and sea, however, for some particular reason. Perhaps he named the cloud because it is a sign of mercy. For water turned into blood, frogs, flies, and the other kinds of plagues indicate wrath rather more. But the cloud, protecting and overshadowing [Col. 0709D] the children of Israel, now preceding and now following them, signified that they were protected and surrounded by divine mercy, and figured Christ the protector. The Apostle names the sea because, as we have already touched upon, it is a sign of baptism.

“And all ate the same spiritual food” (1 Cor. 10).

How can that visible manna be called spiritual food? Because it was prepared not by human skill or labor but by God, perhaps through the ministry of angels. Hence it is called the bread of angels and the bread of heaven, as it is written: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77). And again: “He gave them bread from heaven” (ibid.). This food given from heaven nourished and strengthened bodies. It is truly bodily food, [Col. 0710A] but may be called spiritual according to the reason already stated; or because it signifies spiritual food, namely Christ, who is truly the food of spirits and the resurrection of bodies.

He is food for spirits just as he is their life. The righteous who live spiritually are spiritually fed and sustained by that from which they receive the ability to live spiritually. But the righteous person lives by faith, insofar as he lives righteously. Therefore, by faith one partakes of that which enables the righteous to live spiritually and righteously. To eat Christ is to receive from him the sustenance of spiritual life; this is to believe in him; and this is to live from him, as those live in him.

This spiritual food is eaten in two ways: by the taste of faith and by reception of the sacrament. One way began with the institution [Col. 0710B] of the new sacrifice; the other immediately from the beginning of our faith itself. For all who have been righteous ate this spiritual food, because they believed in Christ, lived spiritually, and received participation in him in order to live spiritually. But many ate visible manna and died—namely, by spiritual death—because they did not live spiritually. And many did not eat visible manna, yet lived spiritually, and therefore ate spiritual food.

Visible manna was a sign of this sacrament of ours and of the spiritual food contained in this sacrament. Our sacrament, under a visible species, contains in itself the spiritual food, namely Christ, and has power to confer upon those receiving it the spiritual [Col. 0710C] grace by which one lives spiritually. Visible manna, however, neither fully contained spiritual grace nor bestowed the grace of spiritual life; rather, it signified the spiritual food which could give spiritual life.

Therefore those who received visible manna but neither believed nor understood spiritually—and consequently did not live spiritually—ate bodily food for bodily refreshment, not spiritual food. But those who had the same faith as we do, and believed that the spiritual manna, namely the bread of heaven and bread of angels, was Christ to come from heaven, and who, justified by that faith, lived spiritually—these ate the same spiritual food as we do. Yet we receive the same spiritual food alike by mouth and heart; they tasted visible manna with their mouths, but believed with their hearts in the invisible and spiritual manna, that is, Christ. Therefore, with the mouth we and they have different things; with the heart, however, we and they have the same.

This spiritual food, that is, Christ, is the bread of heaven and the bread of angels. The angel eats this bread in heaven in a manner still unknown and untried by us; the pilgrim human being eats this same bread according to his measure, as it is written: “Man ate the bread of angels.” [Col. 0710D]

“And all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10).

Just as the manna given from heaven signifies the spiritual food by which all the saints are fed so that they may live spiritually, as befits saints, so the water which [Col. 0711A] flowed from the rock signifies the spiritual drink by which all who become participants in grace are spiritually given drink. “And the rock was Christ” (ibid.). Behold, through the Apostle’s interpretation we have learned what the rock which brought forth water signifies. Let us inquire from the words of the Lord himself, and likewise from the Apostle’s words, what is spiritually the water flowing from Christ as from a fountain of life, and what is the spiritual drink by which all who believe in Christ are given drink.

“He who believes in me,” Christ says, “as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly. Now he said this concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7). And the Apostle says: “We were all given drink from one Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). Behold the water which flowed from the rock; behold the spiritual drink [Col. 0711B] which all the righteous drank. By this drink the burning of thirst is quenched; by the gift of this Spirit the desire of the saints is happily fulfilled. For the Spirit is the Comforter, and gladdens grieving hearts. All the righteous rejoiced in this Spirit; all received this Spirit; and for that reason all drank the same spiritual drink.

“But they drank from the spiritual …” (1 Cor. 10).

The Apostle, first speaking of spiritual drink, then adding that the rock followed them, and inserting between the two, “But they drank from the spiritual …,” has left it uncertain how his words “But they drank from the spiritual …” are to be understood: namely, whether from the spiritual drink or from the spiritual rock. But if someone wishes to refer this to the drink, it scarcely appears how a distinction can be made between “they drank from spiritual drink” and “they drank spiritual drink.” If it is greater to drink spiritual drink than to drink from spiritual drink, why was it necessary, after what is greater, to add what is less? If it is the same, why repeat the same thing?

Yet repetition is sometimes made in order to add something. If, then, the repetition was made for the sake of addition, though the words were partly changed, it may be understood as if the words had not been changed and as though that change had no force—just as if it were said: They drank spiritual drink; but they drank from the spiritual, that is, spiritual drink, from the rock which followed them. For this is added to show whence the spiritual drink which they drank flowed. [Col. 0711D]

Further, as it seems preferable to refer this to the rock, so that they are said to have drunk from the spiritual rock which followed them, this is a manner of speaking; just as one says that a person drinks from a cistern or vineyard when he drinks water from the cistern or wine from the vineyard. The spiritual rock is Christ; the spiritual drink is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from Christ and is given by Christ, according to the distribution of diverse gifts, to those who believe in him.

Spiritual drink may also be understood as the cup. The cup of Christ is spoken of in three ways: either Christ’s own blood, shed for many, which we too drink at the altar; or Christ’s passion, which binds us to suffer with him; or imitation of his passion, by which, according to our measure, we render a return and thanksgiving to him who suffered for us by suffering with him. [Col. 0712A] Thus they drank spiritual drink not only who were given drink by the draught of the Lord’s blood in receiving the sacrament itself, but also all the righteous who, from ancient days, had faith in Christ’s passion and lived spiritually in that faith, mortifying their flesh with its vices and desires and displaying the likeness of Christ’s passion in patiently enduring their own tribulations. For no one is righteous who does not suffer.

“The rock which followed them.”

According to the historical interpretation, the rock followed them—that is, it met and complied with their will—because, as some think, wherever they went, overflowing waters followed, as it is written: “He brought water from the rock and led the waters down like rivers” (Ps. 77). And again: “He broke open the rock, and waters flowed; streams ran in dry places” (Ps. 14).

This may also be understood differently. After Miriam died, when water failed in the wilderness of Zin, at the place called Kadesh, the people murmured against Moses. Their murmuring was so effective that Moses himself seemed to have yielded somewhat. Hence, when abundant water came forth from the rock struck twice, he heard from the Lord: “Because you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I shall give them” (Num. 20). Therefore the people, turned to sedition, had almost fallen away from God’s worship and were near to fleeing from the Lord and their God, unless they had been restrained by the sign that was given and, as it were, apprehended as fugitives by the rock [Col. 0712C] following them, lest they depart, and in a sense calling them back so that they might return.

According to the mystical interpretation, Christ accompanies his own in the wilderness of this world and does not abandon those who hope in him.

“But the rock was Christ.”

A thing which signifies is customarily called by the name of the thing which it signifies. It was Christ not in substance but in signification. In the signs wonderfully wrought by God before the ancient righteous there was a mystical signification of the truth to follow—manifest to the greater and more perfect, perhaps hidden from the simpler. Yet all who possessed the piety of faith venerated the divinely wrought signs as holy, and, moved by the novelty and wonder of venerable things, were strengthened in the fear or love of God and in devotion of faith.

Nor does it prejudice the piety of faith if some perhaps simply did not know what manna signified, what the cloud, sea, or rock signified, provided that they piously believed what the order of that time required, those things which concerned faith in the one God and the coming Savior. For knowledge of mystical signification was not required of everyone; rather, piety of faith was reckoned as righteousness, and ignorance of the one God and Savior of the world was imputed to every unbeliever. Hence it is written of certain unbelievers: “A fire was kindled in Jacob, and wrath rose against Israel, because they did not believe in God nor hope in his salvation” (Ps. 77).

To believe in God and to have a confident hope of salvation in Christ his Savior [Col. 0713A] were necessary for salvation then, as they are for us now. But the signification of signs was imparted by hidden inspiration to the more perfect; reverence for signs was set before the simpler, so that they might acknowledge God’s power in his wonders, that he is able to do what he wills and as he wills.

Likewise, how many now are there in God’s Church who do not know the meaning either of the signs that then existed or of the sacraments that now exist, but who, simply adhering to the Church’s faith and holding no impious opinion concerning God, worship God in the sacraments instituted by him, believing divine power and sanctifying grace to be present in them, so that they may benefit unto salvation those who believe in God. Therefore not all who have faith need be skilled in mystical discourse or penetrate the depths of signs or sacraments. Understanding of mysteries is more necessary to those entrusted with the ministry of teaching and governing. Hence the Lord, speaking to the disciples, says: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables” (Luke 8).

“But the rock was Christ.” This is the rock of which Christ himself says: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16). This is the rock of which it was said: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. 39). And again: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (Ps. 103). Christ, therefore, is the rock because he is the firmness of the saints, strengthening them in his power through the immovable constancy of faith, the immovable confidence of security, and the unending perseverance of love.

Christ is the rock, as one firm in his promise and firm in his love; at times inexorable in his wrath, often immovable in his judgment, often, as it were, hard in our tribulation. Lord God, if I may speak without offense to your peace: how often in my prayers concerning my tribulations and temptations, even when I do not call you hard, I nevertheless think you hard. How often I turn over in my heart, “But the rock was Christ”; how often I say, “Why, Lord, do you reject my prayer, turn your face from me?” (Ps. 50); “How long will you be angry at the prayer of your servant?” (Ps. 79).

Nevertheless, because you said, “One ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18), and because you do not despise the boldness and persistence of seeking, asking, and knocking, I shall not let you go unless you bless me. With your help I shall try whether I may suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone; and, if you give me the rod of discipline, by which, through uprightness of action and direction of heart, I may be able to strike twice the flint of your wrath and break its hardness, I know abundant waters will come forth, so that the people may drink, and the beasts, and I among the beasts. Yet from Moses’ example I fear the wavering of heart which you detest. For I must ask in faith and not waver. You, Lord, who test faith, help my unbelief; preserve what pleases you, remove what displeases you.

From the same epistle, below: “Beloved, flee from the worship of idols,” as far as these words: “You cannot be partakers of the Lord’s table and of the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10).

[Col. 0714A]

The fellowship of human life and the sweetness of mutual love, although they may be reciprocally signified by many indications and understood from signs in turn, are made known in a more intimate and explicit manner by the custom of eating together and sharing one table. For since food is, as it were, life for life, those who commonly share one food indicate that they share life itself through mutual goodwill, while they jointly take the very support of life for the use of life, since they have life’s use in common.

Human intimacy is customarily nourished in shared living by shared food. Either the person who eats with one is a friend, or he pretends to be a friend so that you may believe it. Such pretense increased Judas’s sin: by eating with Christ he did not reveal himself, so that he might betray his Master. To him it was said: “But you, a man of one mind, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food: in the house of God we walked with one accord” (Ps. 54).

After the life which is shared in common, and after death, by which life is loved in fellowship both for oneself and for another, nothing is more suited to communion than the nourishment of life, whose sharing signifies the communion of friendship. For it is not fitting that one who knows himself to lack the love required for eating together should become a participant in a common table.

But the communion of the Lord’s table has, beyond the bodily table which ought to be common to those in need, this further quality: it not only indicates but accomplishes and perfects communion in true friendship. The Apostle shows how great the power and grace of this communion are, wishing to withdraw us from the table, fellowship, and friendship of demons and invite us to Christ’s table, fellowship, and friendship.

Every friendship—whether among human beings, between God and human beings, or between human beings and demons—is cultivated in its own way by the offering of a proper gift or service, or by delight in a desired gift. That proud and apostate angel, having desired to be like the Most High and being unable truly to attain likeness to that height, wished to obtain it in the foolish opinion of human beings: that he might at least be thought God and worshiped as God. Therefore, those whom he deceived he led to this: that in idols made by hands they should worship him, entreat him for safety, offer vows to him, sacrifice to him, taste what had been sacrificed in his honor, and become participants in his table—all this in order that they might have him propitious and become sharers in his friendship.

Thus he, because he wished to appear what he could not be—the exemplar of pride—instituted idolatry. True religion in Christ later destroyed it among Christ’s true worshipers, who are called into his fellowship and invited to his table, by participation in which they become participants in friendship with God. As the Apostle is about to commemorate the praise of this table, he first warns us to flee the worship of idols. “For what agreement has Christ with Belial?” (1 Cor. 10). Idolatry must be fled in order to approach Christ’s table. The likeness of idolatry must likewise be fled: namely, spiritual fornication, every delight in sin which separates one from God. For whatever is preferred to the true God—whatever is first in love and first in the mind—is worshiped as God and counted as an idol.

“I speak as to prudent people: judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ?” (1 Cor. 10).

As though about to say something profound, the Apostle asks from those to whom he speaks the judgment of discernment, as from prudent persons, so that they may carefully judge what he is about to say and consider what the Lord’s cup and the participation in Christ’s body are and can accomplish. [Col. 0715B] First he shows what the cup is, beginning with the cup; then he adds concerning the bread. It is surprising why he did this, or why he reversed the order of the Evangelists, when he himself elsewhere puts the bread first and then adds the cup. Perhaps the reason for this change is as follows. A little earlier he had spoken of spiritual food and spiritual drink, and finally of drink; and so, after inserting a few words, he joined the matter of the cup, saying: “The cup of blessing which we bless,” etc.

Understand “cup” here as drink. This cup is blessed by God; for this reason it is called the cup of blessing, and we who partake through it are blessed—that is, multiplied in spiritual gifts. For this reason also it is called the cup of blessing which we [Col. 0715C] faithful bless, by giving thanks, praising it, exalting it above all cups, and saying: “My cup, which makes me drunk—how excellent it is!” (Ps. XXII). Clearly, this cup is splendid above all others. No drink is so sweet, so health-giving, so intoxicating, so gladdening, or so beneficial in transforming the mind.

Or, we priests bless it: by a mystical prayer we consecrate it, representing Christ as the one who blesses. For he is the one who blesses; while we minister, he works invisibly. He changes mightily, commands the creature effectively, and where power commands, the effect follows without delay. What worthy thought can we have concerning this cup? For what is it? Is it not the communion of Christ’s blood? What faithful answer is possible except that it is the communion of Christ’s blood? [Col. 0715D] For this cup, which we bless and in which we are blessed, is Christ’s blood communicated to us—that is, given jointly to us and for us: to us as the cup of salvation, for us as the price of redemption. The cup of blessing, whether at the Lord’s Supper or at the Lord’s table—that is, at the altar—is nothing other than Christ’s blood, poured out for the common salvation.

By this authority of the Apostle, this drink may bear the name of communion, so that it is called Holy Communion. *Communicatio* may be understood because it is given or received in common; *communio*, because it is held in common. It may also be called communion for another reason. This blood produces charity in us, through which all things become common, and what belongs individually to each person becomes common to all.

“And the bread which we bless, is it not a participation in the Lord’s body?” (I Cor. X)

[Col. 0716A]

Having shown what this cup is, he immediately shows what the bread is which we break in the sacrament. We have said above what seemed necessary concerning the breaking. But we must have no doubt whatever, for the certainty of faith, what this bread is. Hence the Apostle says: “Is it not a participation in the Lord’s body?” As if to say: It is manifest that it is a participation in the Lord’s body. For which believer could doubt it?

“Participation in the body” must be understood as the body given to us for participation. Although the Apostle says, “communion of the blood” and “participation in the body,” as though indicating some distinction, it may nevertheless devoutly be said, “communion of the body” and “participation in the blood.” For by communicating in both we participate, and by participating we communicate. Yet, if some distinction is required, it may devoutly be said that participation corresponds to breaking, just as participation corresponds to the bread which is broken. For it is divided so that each person may receive his own portion. Yet this bread remains always whole in substance; nevertheless, it is broken in the sacrament, to signify that it accomplishes different things in different persons. For there are divisions of gifts.

The sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is grace. Hence it is also called Eucharist, that is, “good grace.” This sacrament is received whole and entire, equally, by each recipient; but it does not work equally [Col. 0716B] in every recipient. Thus the grace which works is common to those who receive worthily; but by the effect it has in individuals, it apportions graces to some and to others. Therefore communion of the blood may refer to the sharing of operative grace, while participation in the body refers to the participation in diverse graces.

Although this distribution of graces is dispensed by Christ through the power of his flesh and blood—for the power of both is one—it can nevertheless be represented more fittingly at the altar by the breaking of bread than by the sprinkling of blood. For sprinkling of blood cannot occur there without danger and irreverence toward the sacrament; sacramental breaking can occur.

“For we, though many, are one bread, one body,” etc.

After showing what the cup of blessing and [Col. 0716D] the bread which we break are, he consequently adds what they can accomplish in us—that is, what they effect in us, and what their power and effect are. Since they contain within themselves one common operative and dispensing grace, and through their efficacy bestow on many persons the distributions of many graces, they effect spiritual unity in us, so that we may all be one in Christ.

By the division of graces, indeed, we are many: some having a greater grace, others a lesser; some this grace, others that; some beginning, others advancing; some simple, others prudent; some like little children, others like adults, others mature in perfection as though old men—so that through many persons of many kinds many works of grace may be performed. The unity of the Church, composed of innumerable persons of different [Col. 0717A] sexes, different conditions, different ranks, and different degrees of perfection, is commonly signified in many ways. But here the Apostle signifies it through the unity of bread and the unity of the body. One bread is made from many grains; one body is composed of many members.

Through love of neighbour, we who are many are one bread; through love of God, one body. We are one bread for God, who delights in the brotherly love by which we love one another and is, as it were, refreshed by us. We are also one bread for one another. For our mutual love is mutual consolation and mutual refreshment to us. Hence each of us is a member of the other, because we suffer together and rejoice together, reckoning our evils as well as our goods—which seem individually our own—as common through the affection [Col. 0717B] of brotherly love.

We are one body through the love by which Christ is loved as the bridegroom, and he loves the Church as his own body. Hence the Apostle says to the Ephesians: “Christ is the head of the Church; he himself is the saviour of his body” (Eph. V). And below: “Men ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ also does the Church, because we are members of his body, of his flesh, and of his bones” (ibid.).

The Church, then, as Christ’s bride, is also Christ’s body and lives by his Spirit, just as the human body is made alive by the human spirit. Therefore the unity of Christ and the Church is rightly signified [Col. 0717C] through the unity of the body. Christ’s love produces this unity—the love by which he is loved by the Church, he himself loving first in order to be loved by his beloved.

Love of God unites and joins us to God more closely than love of neighbour does, just as our body is more closely joined to us than bread is, not only before it is consumed but even when it is changed into the body and received within the body. And as bread is necessary for the body and nourishes it, so love of neighbour is necessary for nourishing and increasing love of God. Yet love of God is prior both in cause and in dignity and must always be preferred. Hence it sometimes happens that one rightly offends one’s neighbour lest one offend God.

Therefore we who are many are one bread, one body. Who are the many? [Col. 0717D] “All who partake of the one bread and the one cup.” Here it is shown that participation belongs to the cup just as it does to the bread. Nor without reason: for the power of each is one. As the sacrifice, which is called both bread and body, brings about in us that we are one bread and one body, so too does the cup. But while the rationale of the likeness by which we are called and are one bread, one body, concerns bread or body alone, we must nevertheless believe that both participation in the cup and participation in the bread confer the grace by which we are one bread, one body. Participation, then, applies to both; but the symbolism is more fitting to one than to the other.

In these words the Apostle shows that participation in the one bread and one cup effects in us the unity of brotherly fellowship, by which we live socially for Christ’s sake and [Col. 0718A] are members one of another; and likewise the unity of Christ and the Church, by which we are also members of Christ, who is our head, in whom we are all one. Thus the Apostle, writing to the Galatians, says: “There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. III).

Those belong to this unity who partake of the bread and cup not with the mouth alone but with a devout heart: that is, those who live in Christ and have Christ dwelling in their hearts through faith. For one who lives by faith lives not for oneself but for Christ and in Christ; by believing, one eats and participates, and by participating one remains in Christ together with the many, because we who are many are one bread, one body.

For this is the participation [Col. 0718B] of which the Apostle speaks. Those who receive Christ’s body and cup with the mouth alone, but do not receive Christ into their hearts so as to live from him and in him, are strangers to the faith by which the righteous person lives and alien to the fellowship of the righteous. They do not have with them one heart and one soul; and therefore they are not members of Christ and do not belong to his body, although they seem to be in the Church, which is his body.

Hence, after the question, “The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the Lord’s body?”, the Apostle adds: “For we, though many, are one bread and one body, all who partake of the one bread and the one cup.” As though he plainly said: The bread which we break truly is a participation [Col. 0718C] in the Lord’s body, because its effect proves this. For it produces what no other food can produce, except the Lord’s body alone. What is this? Namely, that we who are many are one bread, one body.

Faith in the flesh assumed from us, the blood shed for us, and the granting of both to us for use, instils in us love for Christ and, for Christ’s sake, love of neighbour. This love, once instilled, unites us to Christ and in Christ, so that what he himself asks for us may be fulfilled: “I ask not for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John XVII).

“See Israel according to the flesh. Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What then? Do I say that what is sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? But what the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (I Cor. X).

[Col. 0718D]

An analogy is introduced from the sacrifices of the Law, to make understood what he wishes to be understood concerning food sacrificed to idols. Those who ate the victims consented to the religion of sacrifice and showed that consent of their will by the very eating of the things sacrificed. For if they did not consent, they would not eat. Therefore those who ate were participants in the altar. They received a portion of the offerings, and by receiving and eating that portion showed that they were joined to that religion.

This is what the Apostle says: “See Israel according to the flesh.” As if he said: You who are Israel according to the Spirit, seeing God and understanding spiritual things, see Israel [Col. 0719A] following the fleshly precepts of the Law. “Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?” As though he said: There is no doubt that they are participants in the altar, not merely by receiving a portion from it but also by consenting to those rites.

From what has been said concerning participation in the new and true sacrifice and concerning the use of legal victims, one may infer conversely that worship of an idol and eating food sacrificed to idols, by consent to superstitious error and impiety, join worshippers and eaters to the devil and transform them into his members. The Apostle, about to speak of this fellowship, first states that neither what is sacrificed to idols nor an idol is anything. And this is not without reason. A little earlier he had forbidden the worship of an idol as an evil and harmful thing. One who misunderstood might therefore have thought that the Apostle was suggesting that an idol was something, or that it could do something and had power to harm or do evil. He removes this impression by saying that an idol is nothing.

A person’s own impiety can indeed harm that person; the demon who presides over an idol can also do evil. But the idol itself cannot; rather, beneath the covering of the idol is concealed the mystery of iniquity. “And what is sacrificed to idols is sacrificed to demons and not to God.” Therefore the worship of idols, being in fact the worship of demons, must be avoided.

The Apostle, therefore, wishing that the worship of idols should be considered more deeply as what it truly is, the worship of demons, after saying above, “Flee from the worship of idols,” added: “I speak as to prudent people; judge for yourselves what I say.” As if he said: Think more subtly, [Col. 0719C] judge more deeply what the worship of idols is. For it is the worship of demons. “Judge,” he says, “what I say.” In what I say, let what I do not say be understood no less than what I say.

What then do I say? “That what is sacrificed to idols is anything?” As if he said: I do not say this, nor is it to be understood in what I say. Rather, I say something deeper. For this reason I said, “Judge for yourselves what I say.” But this is what I say and what I wish to be understood in what I say: “What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God.”

The whole reasoning of the Apostle, then, aims to make it understood that in idol worship not only are man-made and visible idols honoured, but in the idol the devil is worshipped, who is worse than the idol; and the worshipper is brought into fellowship [Col. 0719D] with him who is adored in the idol.

It may trouble us that the Apostle in this place suggests that an idol is nothing, when he also said above in the same Epistle: “Concerning foods that are sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world” (I Cor. VIII). Yet the Psalmist says: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold” (Ps. CXIII), and silver and gold are not nothing, at least in the estimation of those devoted to avarice, which is the service of idols.

How the Apostle’s statement is to be understood can be seen from the words of the prophet Isaiah, from whom the Apostle seems to have taken what he says about the idol. Thus Isaiah, reproaching idols, says: “Declare what is to come in the future, and we shall know that you are gods. Do good or evil also, if you can; let us speak and see together. Behold, you are from nothing, and your work is from that which is not. He who chooses you is an abomination” (Isa. LI).

From Isaiah’s words it is shown that the idol is not what it is believed to be, and that it is vainly worshipped as God, since it has neither foreknowledge of the future nor power to do good or evil, to speak, or to see. For it is a lie. Though it is the work of an artisan, fashioned by hands, it is not what error has fashioned it to be.

In sacred discourse, “not to be” or “to be nothing” is understood in various ways for various reasons. In one way, it is so said when something is one thing in opinion and another in truth. In this sense the Apostle says: “If anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. VI). In this sense [Col. 0720B] an idol can be understood to be nothing, because it is a lie and the fabrication of a fool, as it is written: “The heart of a fool worshipped it” (Isa. XLIV).

In another sense, that is said not to exist, or to be nothing, which does not have God as its author. For as God’s goodness is the cause that all good things are good, and as God’s wisdom is the light that enlightens all who rightly understand, enabling them to understand rightly, so God’s essence is the cause of all things that are, granting them existence. For all things are from him, through him, and in him. Hence Dionysius the Areopagite: “The being of all things is the Divinity’s transcendent being; for that which gives being to all is above every being.”

Therefore, whatever is not from him, through him, and in him is itself nothing. In this sense an idol is nothing; what is sacrificed to idols is nothing; sin is nothing, because it does not have God as its author. Thus Isaiah says: “All makers of an idol are nothing” (Isa. XLIV); and, concerning nations that do not believe: “All nations before him are as though they were not, and are reckoned by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. XL); and: “He makes the searchers of secrets as though they were not; he has made the judges of the earth as emptiness” (ibid.). And Esther: “Do not hand over, Lord, your sceptre to those who are not, lest they laugh at our ruin; but turn their counsel against them” (Esther XIV).

In another sense, all nations, searchers of secrets, and judges of the earth, although they appear to be something great according to the power and wisdom of this world, are nothing in comparison with him who says: “I am who I am” [Col. 0720D] (Exod. III). Again, something is said to be nothing contemptuously because of its uselessness; in this sense too an idol is nothing.

In this sense the Apostle says: “If I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and have all faith so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (I Cor. XIII). In another sense, those are said to be reduced to nothing whose designs, counsels, and efforts are frustrated—both they themselves and their works. Thus it is written concerning the righteous person: “The wicked one has been reduced to nothing in his sight.” Similar is: “You will reduce all nations to nothing.”

Everything contrary to God, insofar as it falls short of true being, so far does not exist. Sinners themselves and their sins, insofar as they are not from God or in God, are nothing. Hence, according to a change from a good life to an evil one, a person who is so changed is rightly said not to be. But “not to be” is understood far more wonderfully in the change from an evil life to a good one, or from a miserable life to a blessed one, as in: “Turn the wicked, and they shall not be” (Prov. XII); and again: “Refused to be comforted, because they are not” (Jer. XXXI).

For “they are not” is said wondrously when they are happily existent; and it is said wondrously concerning the conversion of the wicked, “they shall not be,” when they begin to be from the beginning of conversion. Hence one says: “Behold, I said: now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI).

“But I do not want you to become companions of demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be participants in the Lord’s table and in the table of demons” (I Cor. X).

[Col. 0721B]

Inviting us to fellowship with Christ, which is ratified and confirmed by participation in the true sacrifice, he draws us back from fellowship with demons, which is entered upon and maintained by idol worship; and further, by consent to and practice of crimes, and by habitual vices. For vices are dear to demons and contrary to God’s will. When they are loved, they are worshipped; by consenting to and practicing them, God is despised, demons are honoured, and intimacy with them is acquired.

Therefore, in order that their fellowship may be avoided, we must abstain from whatever is known to please them. For demons are not of our communion, nor can we share [Col. 0721C] their table or drink their cup, if we desire to attain fellowship with Christ and participate in his table or cup. This is what the Apostle says: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be participants in the Lord’s table and in the table of demons.”

As we have already said, “the cup of the Lord” is used in three ways: either for Christ’s blood, according to: “This cup is the new testament in my blood” (Luke XXII); or for Christ’s passion, according to: “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (John XVIII); or for imitation of Christ’s passion, according to: “You will indeed drink my cup” (Matt. XX). Conversely, “the cup of demons” may be understood as that which is offered to demons; or as that which those who are to drink from them through the bitterness of punishment will drink; or as that which is administered for the seduction of error, in insult to Christ’s passion, through love of pleasure and iniquity.

The Lord’s table is the altar, where Christ is eaten in the sacrament. Of this table it is written: “You have prepared a table before me, against all who afflict me” (Ps. XXII). Likewise, the Lord’s table is Holy Scripture, in which the bread of life and understanding is set forth. For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from God’s mouth. This too may be understood of the table of which we have just said: “You have prepared a table before me,” etc.; and of: “Even the little dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table” (Matt. XV).

This table is for the present, until we reach that table [Col. 0722A] of which it is written: “And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII). The table of demons is either the altar of idols or the perverse doctrine of heretics, where bread is served in secret, concerning which it is written: “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread more pleasant” (Prov. IX).

The Apostle’s statement, “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons,” seems to raise a question if “the cup of the Lord” is here understood as Christ’s blood. For many criminal and shameful persons drink the Lord’s cup to their own judgment, alienated from Christ’s fellowship and destined to be joined to demons. But the words “you cannot” must be understood as: you cannot do so beneficially, or lawfully. Thus it is shown not what does not happen, but what it is not expedient or lawful to do. Many similar expressions occur in Holy Scripture, such as: “No one takes the honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. V).

Likewise, concerning the cup.

“The cup of the Lord” is sometimes understood as Christ’s cup in one of the three modes stated above; but sometimes it means the measure of divine justice, according to: “A cup of pure wine, full of mixture, is in the hand of the Lord” (Ps. LXXIV). For God’s wisdom, disposing and governing all things by its own judgment, distributes good and evil to good and evil persons, in mercy and judgment, according to the measure of its justice, [Col. 0722C] as it knows to accord with the beauty of the universe and the salvation of those predestined for life.

This cup is said to be “of pure wine, full of mixture,” which seems contradictory. How can it be a cup of pure wine if it is full of mixture? Or how can it be full of mixture if it is a cup of pure wine? But if we consider carefully what God’s justice is in itself, it will plainly appear that all the good we do ought to be ascribed more to him, as the giver and author of all things, than to ourselves. It will likewise appear that the evils we suffer, and also the evils we do, must be imputed more to us than to him—indeed, wholly to us and not to him. But all our good proceeds from his sheer generosity and kindness.

If God’s justice is bitter or burdensome to a person, human injustice makes it so, so that one may rightly say: “My ways and my iniquities have done this to me.” Man was created simple and upright by God, but he has entangled himself in innumerable questions. Therefore, when God repays a person’s way upon that person’s head, the person drinks a draught which that person has mixed for himself. If sin did not exist, God’s justice would be sweet to everyone. But now it is both sweet and grievous: sweet through its own seasoning, yet grievous in judgment on account of sin.

The cup of the Lord, then, tempered from sweet and bitter—that is, full of mixture from mercy and judgment—is nevertheless not without pure wine, because in its own goodness it is nothing but sweet. Hence it is written: “The judgments of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts” (Ps. XVIII). Therefore God’s judgments are unmixed, and his mercy is unmixed. Accordingly, the wine of mercy and the wine of wrath are each pure; and if pure is mixed with pure, the mixture itself is nothing but pure.

The cup is over all his works and is full of mixture, because the Lord is sweet and upright, giving mercy and repaying the punishment of iniquity. To the city Jerusalem, which had once been a faithful city and full of judgment, the prophet says: “Your wine is mixed with water” (Isa. I), signifying that the unmixed justice it had formerly possessed was corrupted by an admixture of iniquity. Hence he also says: “Righteousness dwelt in her, but now murderers” (ibid.).

From this cup the Lord gives to the good both bitter and sweet things: the consolation of mercy and the bitterness of discipline. For concerning the bitterness of discipline it is written: “You have shown your people hard things; you made us drink the wine of compunction” [Col. 0723B] (Ps. LIX). But concerning the consolation of mercy it is written: “Give wine to those who mourn, and strong drink to those of bitter spirit” (Prov. XXXI).

From this cup also the Lord gives good and evil to the wicked. Justice toward the wicked is not wholly without mercy. For peace or prosperity, or an opportunity for repentance, is granted to them so that, being stirred by benefits, they may keep God’s ordinances and seek his law. But they, rejecting God’s grace, turn mercy into judgment for themselves; and from the very thing from which they should have been taught righteousness, they learn to do injustice, as it is written: “Let the wicked be shown mercy, and he will not learn to do righteousness” (Isa. XXVI). Therefore God’s wrath remains upon them, and the mercy granted to them for a time is soon justly withdrawn from the ungrateful.

Hence the Lord, wishing to show mercy and, as it were, seeking how he might show mercy, says through the prophet: “What shall I do to you, Ephraim? What shall I do to you, Judah? Your mercy is like a morning cloud, and like dew that passes away in the morning” (Hos. VI). The morning cloud and the dew cease to moderate the heat when the heat burns more fiercely. So too is mercy which is given to the wicked for a time and withdrawn in due time. Hence blessed James says: “The sun rose with its burning heat and dried up the grass; its flower fell, and the beauty of its appearance perished. So also the rich person will wither in his ways” (Jas. I).

The Lord holds this cup in his hand, because he is judge; and from the same cup—whether from the mixture or from the pure wine, which in interpretation is the same thing—he distributes his mercy or wrath, having mercy on whom he wills and hardening whom he wills, pouring when he wills and as much as he wills into vessels of mercy and vessels of wrath. When, therefore, a vessel of mercy or wrath receives from the vessel of the cup what the Lord pours into it, then the Judge inclines from that which he fills, as though transferring wine from vessel to vessel. In this manner of speaking may also be understood: “Their storehouses are full, pouring forth from this into that” [Col. 0723D] (Ps. CXLIII)—that is, from vessel to vessel; or perhaps from one kind into another kind of cup.

The Psalmist’s saying can also be understood otherwise. God often takes away grace offered or bestowed upon one person and gives it to another. Conversely, he turns away wrath that was due and directs it toward another. For he resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas. IV). Thus the Publican, humbled as it were by consideration of his sins, was justified in the temple (Luke XVIII); but the Pharisee was lifted up into pride, as it were, by the greatness of his merits. For there is a righteous person who perishes in his righteousness (Eccl. VII). And who more than the one who is overly righteous, trusts in himself, and despises others?

Hence the people of the Jews were blinded in their pride and hardened in unbelief, while the people of the Gentiles were enlightened by grace. The grace of promise taken from the former was given to the latter. God’s wrath, turned away from the Gentiles, was turned toward the perversity of the Jews. This is so because God is judge, who humbles one and exalts another. Transferring the wine of mercy and wrath, he inclines from this to that: namely, from the vessel of wrath to the vessel of mercy, and conversely from the vessel of mercy to the vessel of wrath. Hence: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI); and: “To everyone who has, it shall be given; but from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away” [Col. 0724B] (Matt. XIII).

But God acts justly in all things: he directs some, corrects others, and leaves others, uncorrected and incorrigible, to themselves and in error, to be punished more severely afterward, enduring with great patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. God’s permission or patience, though undeserved by the wicked, is always just in relation to God himself, since it accords with his kindness and befits his holiness; and therefore it does not belong to the dregs of the cup.

But the life or conscience of those who misuse God’s patience for pride deserves the name “dregs”: polluted, filthy, and impure. These are the dregs of which the Prophet says: “He brought me out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs” (Ps. XXXIX). And Isaiah: “It is too little that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the dregs of Israel. Behold, I have given you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. XLIX). And Jeremiah: “Moab has been fertile from his youth; he has rested on his dregs, has not been poured from vessel to vessel, and has not gone into exile. Therefore his taste has remained in him and his smell has not changed” (Jer. XLVIII).

These dregs ought to be emptied out, consumed by the fear of God, and wholly annihilated, because God is judge. Yet while repentance is despised, the fear of God is emptied out, but the dregs are not emptied, because the dregginess of error and the uncleanness of an evil conscience remain upon those who are not corrected, in everlasting guilt and everlasting torment.

The dregginess or corruption of sin, from which all sinners of the earth drink, may be called the wine of error. It is not merely dregs, however, but dregs of pure wine. For it is a corruption of righteousness, in comparison with which it becomes the more worthless the farther it departs from its purity. Thus one may speak of “the dregs among companions,” when a person alone is evil among good people. Thus the unbelieving Synagogue is called the dregs of Israel.

But the wine of error is administered by the prince of Babylon through human wisdom and eloquence, and through the varied beauty [Col. 0725A] of things, unto every allurement and pleasure of vices. Concerning it it is written: “Babylon was a cup in the hand of the Lord, making the whole earth drunk” (Jer. LI).

This golden cup shines only to the extent that it gives pleasure; and therefore it is golden, because it is precious to those whom it pleases. This cup is the whole vanity of this world, in which there is nothing except the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. This vanity is confusion, and is therefore called Babylon: that is, the city in which the children of this age dwell, who walk in vanity and conduct themselves in vanity. Of them it is written: “They shall receive their cities in vanity” (Ps. 128).

This cup is in the Lord’s hand, not because God gives the wine of error to drink—for he tempts no one in order to deceive—but because he leaves those worthy of deception to the desires of their hearts, that they may go after their own devices. This, therefore, is the cup of demons. Those who drink from it cannot drink the cup of the Lord. But the cup of the Lord, which is full of mixed wine, contains within itself no wine of error, but either wine of mercy or wine of wrath. For of mercy it is written: “My cup that inebriates me, how splendid it is! And thy mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22). But of wrath Isaiah writes: “Arise, Jerusalem, thou who hast drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath; thou hast drunk to the bottom of the cup of stupor, and hast drunk even to the dregs” (Isa. 61). And below: “Behold, I have taken from thy hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of my indignation. I will no longer add that thou shouldst drink it again” (ibid.) [Col. 0725B–C].

What we cited above—“Babylon, a golden cup,” etc. (Jer. 51)—may also be understood of this wine of the Lord’s indignation and wrath, so that, according to this interpretation, it does not concern the cup of demons. For the king of Babylon—that is, the prince of this world—is a minister of God’s wrath; and he scourges sinners whom he has deceived, so that the whole earth may be made drunk with the wine of the Lord’s fury: that is, all who set their minds not on things above but on things upon the earth. Yet this cup is golden, as precious to God as it is dear to him: for his own justice pleases him even in the punishments of sinners. That famous city Babylon drinks from this cup, Babylon which was destroyed in the wrath of the Lord’s indignation, as a figure of this world, which will be destroyed. Thus it is written in the Apocalypse: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon, the great city” (Apoc. 14). And shortly afterward: “All nations drank of the wine of her fornication” (Apoc. 18). And below: “Repay her double according to her works. In the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double. As much as she glorified herself and lived in delights, give her so much torment and mourning” (ibid.) [Col. 0725C–D].

Sinners are sometimes scourged for their sins; and their very injustice serves God’s justice, when iniquity itself, guilty as it is, becomes the minister of vengeance. Hence the Psalmist says: “Fire, sulphur, and a spirit of storms are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10). The fire of desire by which they now burn, the sulphur of an impure conscience by which they now stink before God and themselves, and the spirit of storms by which they are now tossed through the restlessness of their minds—these three are their portion and their cup. Or “a portion of their cup” is said as though it were not the whole cup, because this is a part of their punishment and not all of it. Therefore, when the wicked sin, they drink the wine of error from the cup of demons. When they are justly punished, whether on account of their sins or for their sins, they are made drunk from the cup of the Lord’s fury [Col. 0726A].

### Again, concerning the cup of the New Testament

But the cup of the New Testament is a cup of unmixed wine, and in a manner contains within itself mercy and judgment: mercy, indeed, for those who do not drink the cup of demons, who do not walk according to the flesh, who have been made conformed to the likeness of Christ’s death, that they may obtain mercy; but judgment for those who do not judge themselves, who walk according to the desires of error, drunk with the wine of error from the cup of demons.

The whole dispensation of God’s grace and mercy, and likewise the zeal of his indignation and wrath, seems in some manner to flow or to be administered from this cup. For it is the life of the world in those who are saved; but it is the judgment of the world in those who perish. From it God has poured out the fullness of his most profound love. From it he will pour out the whole indignation of his incomprehensible wrath. For the world will be convicted of sin in those who perish; nor does it appear why those destined to perish perish more than because they prove ungrateful for so great a grace.

Woe to that man for whom the salvation of the world is judgment; for whom life is death, absolution condemnation, grace wrath, the cup of propitiation a cup of indignation, and unmixed wine dregs. Christ died for us: was it for nothing? What shall we render in this age? What shall we answer in the age to come? Let Stephen, the first martyr, say: “For thee my flesh was stoned, O my God.” Let Lawrence also say: “For thee my flesh was burned, O my God.” Let anyone who received in his body a mortal wound for Christ say: “This befell me because I sought thy ordinances.” Let anyone who has crucified his flesh with its vices and desires say: “For thee my flesh was put to death, O my God.”

But what shall the impious and the sinner say, those who make no account of Christ’s death, who with hateful irreverence regard the blood of the utterly unmixed grape as though it were dregs, and trample underfoot the Son of God? For what dregs that have not been emptied are more grievous than an unworthy estimation and shameless irreverence toward so great a sacrament and so great a benefit—never to be wiped away, never to be forgiven? Certainly this cup contains nothing defiled, nothing impure, nothing dreggy. But just as those who are corrupted, defiled, and profaned in these things through their own fault are said to defile God’s covenant, pollute God’s holy name, and profane God’s ordinances, so also those who do not esteem so great a grace worthily, and, in their baser contempt, regard unmixed wine as dregs, become worse through what is good and, in place of unmixed wine, are made drunk with dregs [Col. 0726B–D].

Listen, fornicators; listen, adulterers; listen, all who live in pleasures and love the vanity of this age. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You who are drunk with the wine of stupor, wake at last, digesting the wine with which you are now soaked. Rise from sleep before the Lord rises against you like one asleep, like a mighty man overcome with wine. For he who now overlooks and still waits is like a sleeping Lord; but at last he shall arise as one mighty and overcome with the wine of fury, to awaken those who sleep, who are now overcome with the wine of error. From then on, the Mighty One will be able and the Prevailing One will prevail, as it is written: “Thou art terrible, and who shall resist thee? From then on is thy wrath” (Ps. 75) [Col. 0727A].

### From the same First Epistle: “When you come together,” etc., as far as: “Therefore whoever shall eat this bread or drink the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11)

[Col. 0727B]

The Apostle, instructing in many ways the Church of God which was at Corinth in true religion, among the other teachings of saving instruction handed on this teaching concerning the Lord’s supper—that is, the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood—which can benefit the edification of all churches, and which he received from the Lord. He shows how and in what order this supper was instituted, what it is, what it can do, how it benefits, and whom it harms.

There were among the Corinthians some deserving rebuke concerning their reception of this sacrament. They showed it less reverence than was fitting, as though they either did not know the worthiness of so great a grace or did not value it worthily. On this occasion he prescribes how magnificently the dignity of this sacrament ought to be esteemed, and by restrained reproof checks those deserving blame in their irreverent presumption. Rebuking, then, the evil of dissension, he says: “When you come together in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it.”

One cause of dissension is thought to have been that, in the church where they gathered for the sake of unity, they claimed their offerings for themselves, while the rest, receiving no share, were humiliated. This cause alone, even if there were no others, could suffice to mean that they ought not to eat the Lord’s supper. Therefore he says: “When therefore you come together into one, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper”; as if he said: “On this ground alone it is not lawful to eat, because divisions are among you.” Or otherwise: “Already now, in the present, this is a loss to you: you are not permitted to eat the Lord’s supper. If you do not guard against it, it will be worse for you in the future.”

He adds another cause: each one takes beforehand his own supper—that is, bodily refreshment—to eat before the Lord’s supper, rather than to distribute it to the poor. He calls the reception of the Eucharist the Lord’s supper; it ought to be received fasting, not after a meal, in honor of so great a sacrament. Christ indeed gave it to his disciples after supper, in order to commend it more forcefully, wishing to impress this last thing upon their hearts and memories. But he left it to the apostles to teach the order in which it should thereafter be received.

The Apostle does not explicitly state the cause we have mentioned concerning the appropriation of offerings, but plainly expresses the taking of supper beforehand. Perhaps for this reason he said, “I hear that there are divisions,” and, after inserting that there must also be heresies, added: “When you come together into one, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper.” Giving the reason, he adds: “For each one takes beforehand his own supper to eat” (1 Cor. 11). He then rebukes them because they gave nothing to the hungry, because they were drunk when they ought to have been sober, and because, though they had homes, they did in church what should be done in homes: that is, they ate and drank; they despised the Church of God, which is a house of prayer; and before those people they ate and drank, gave them nothing, and humiliated those who had nothing. Therefore he says: “What shall I say to you?” To speak more briefly: “Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you” (ibid.) [Col. 0727C–0728B].

“I do not praise you because it is the body of the Lord that you receive irreverently; and you ought to receive it in remembrance of him, as I learned from him: ‘For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you’” (ibid.). He received from the Lord what he was to hand down to the churches concerning this sacrament, just as he received the Gospel that was preached by him. Hence he writes to the Galatians: “I make known to you, brethren, the Gospel which was preached by me, that it is not according to man; for neither did I receive it from man nor was I taught it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ. On the night in which he was betrayed” (Gal. 1).

As the Passion was impending, “he took bread and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me’” (1 Cor. 11). The words, “On the night in which he was betrayed he took bread,” must be referred to evening, because on the evening of the fourteenth moon the lamb was sacrificed: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (ibid.). Because the Lord had said, “Do this in remembrance of me,” the Apostle explains what this remembrance is: namely, the continual proclamation of Christ’s death to be observed in the present Church and not to cease until Christ’s coming. This remembrance or proclamation of Christ’s death is made by believing, confessing, representing—that is, sacrificing—eating and drinking, and imitating [Col. 0728B–D].

“Therefore whoever shall eat this bread or drink the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” He is guilty of both things when they are received unworthily: that is, guilty because he received them unworthily; guilty of the body crucified for him and of the blood shed for him—that is, guilty of Christ’s death. Although he did not cause Christ to die, nevertheless, as far as lies in him, he acts so that Christ died in vain. For he obstructs his own salvation, regards as profaned the blood of the covenant, tramples underfoot the Son of God, and by evil living renders void in himself the power of Christ’s death. Therefore those of this kind are guilty of Christ’s death and will render an account both of their own life and of Christ’s death.

### “But let a man prove himself, and so let him eat of the bread,” etc. (1 Cor. 11)

[Col. 0729A]

Because so great a danger threatens one who eats and drinks unworthily, let a man prove himself: let him examine his conscience, question his whole life, search his memory, judge and accuse his heart closely, submit himself to the law of penance or discipline, and, that he may be found approved, exercise himself in it over a period of time; and then let him eat of that bread and drink from that cup.

In order more sharply to fix in memory the danger of receiving unworthily, and to impress it on others and thus deter them from so great presumption, he says: “For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself” (ibid.). He does not say “not worthily,” but “unworthily”: for who is worthy in every respect? Even when anyone receives, however just or perfect he may be, it is more the Lord’s condescension than the servant’s worthiness. But when the unjust person receives, the unworthiness of the sinner and the indignation of the Judge increase the danger. For he eats judgment to himself.

Why does he eat judgment to himself? Because it is a judgment of death for one who eats thus, on account of what he eats. Why does he eat judgment? Because he eats the Judge rather than the Savior, “not discerning the body of the Lord” (ibid.). Therefore he must be judged because he does not discern: through the complacency with which he receives, he does not distinguish the Lord’s body from other foods, nor does he consider how holy and venerable is that which he receives, and with how much fear and trembling it should be received.

Emphasizing the danger of those who receive unworthily, he adds: “Therefore there are among you many infirm and weak, and many sleep” (ibid.). The judgment for such great presumption is not always wholly deferred to the future. Even now, in the present, many are sick in mind and become weak in body because they receive unworthily; and, overtaken by death, they incur the loss of life. The first of these three evils seems common to all who receive unworthily. The other two, though they do not happen to all, happen to many, for the correction of others, so that from others’ misfortune they may learn to fear more deeply and show greater reverence for so great a grace.

This seems to suggest—though the Apostle does not expressly say it—that those who receive worthily are strengthened in mind; that many become stronger in bodily vigor insofar as it benefits them; and perhaps that they are granted, or at least not deprived of, the gift of a longer life. Nevertheless, we dare not rashly affirm what the Apostle does not say, just as we ought not impiously deny what he does say [Col. 0729B–D].

Among the three evils that threaten those who receive unworthily, there is surely one counsel for the faithful person: to judge himself with fitting severity. Therefore he says: “If we judged ourselves,” namely according to the law of penance or discipline, “we should certainly not be judged” (ibid.), that is, by the Lord according to the zeal of his fury or wrath. “But when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord” (ibid.). The judgment by which good persons judge themselves in the present is in some manner the Lord’s correction and is not alien to his sentence. For he himself commands and counsels it, wishing to spare one who does not spare himself.

Both the person who imposes discipline upon himself for Christ and the person who willingly or patiently accepts discipline imposed by the Lord is judged by himself; in both cases he is corrected by the Lord, so that he may not be condemned with this world, so that he may not have his portion with unbelievers, who have already been judged. For one who approaches thoughtlessly is like an unbeliever.

The words “When we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord” may also be understood differently. Before saying them, he said: “Therefore many are infirm and weak, and many sleep,” signifying that the presumption of some is sometimes punished by the Lord for the correction of others. Then, numbering himself with the others, he added: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged.” After this he adds: “But when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord”; as if he said: We faithful people, invited to so great a grace, are sometimes judged in the persons of those among us who become infirm, weak, and fall asleep; and when we are thus judged, we are corrected by the Lord—we, namely, the others, who benefit when judgment upon some is made for the correction of others.

According to this manner of understanding, “to be judged” and “to be corrected by the Lord” must by division be referred to different people, even though they seem to be said of the same people. Many expressions of this kind occur in the sacred writings, as in: “When he slew them, they sought him; they returned and came to him early” (Ps. 77). For those who were slain were one group, while those who sought him and returned were another.

By “the world” understand either unbelievers or, more generally, the wicked, among whom are many who are like unbelievers or worse than unbelievers. The teacher of truth plainly foretells to us, like a prudent helmsman, the exceedingly fearful danger of our voyage, one to be fled from alike by sail and by oar. He himself fears for himself that, unless he is corrected, he may be condemned with this world. Hence, too, he chastises his body and reduces it to servitude, lest he become reprobate. By his own fear he strikes our deeply trembling hearts, so that we may fear more greatly. For what sound-minded person would not fear where Paul fears? What can the reed of the desert do where the cedar of paradise trembles? Our cause is set in a narrow place. For we must be judged either by ourselves, and thus more gently, or by the Lord in wrath, and thus more severely. Let us therefore fear the danger so that we may flee it, avoiding judgment by judgment: restraining our sins by voluntary chastisement, let us rather be mortified for a time than assigned to eternal punishments [Col. 0730A–D].

### What is the order of what follows

The sacrament of the altar was principally prefigured in the bread and wine offered by Melchizedek, in the paschal lamb, and in manna. But because bread and wine have been discussed above, as the subject required and as the order of time and of the sacrifices themselves demanded, something must be added concerning the lamb and manna; first concerning the lamb, of which it is written in Exodus, chapter 12:

“The Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: ‘This month shall be for you,’” etc., as far as: “For it is the Passover, that is, the passage, of the Lord” (Exod. 12).

[Col. 0731A]

Just as truth now proclaimed openly once lay hidden beneath the veil of figures, so now the darkness of figures, with truth shining upon it, is made manifest as in light, according to what is written: “Night shall be illuminated as day” (Ps. 138). Everything that is made manifest is light. Manifest truth so illumines the figure that truth itself shines forth more beautifully by comparison with the figure. For the comparison of figure and truth, through a marvelous correspondence of mutual likeness, elucidates the mystical meaning of the figure and confirms the assured faith of the truth. The figure so agrees with the truth that what was set forth as a sign contributes to the testimony of the truth. The truth so answers to the figure that it can be confirmed by that very thing by which it was fitting for it to be prefigured. Let us therefore consider how the new sacrifice agrees with the old, and how wonderfully it is conformed to that by which it was long ago prefigured.

“This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first in the months of the year” (ibid.).

The first month, according to the Hebrews, is called Nisan. It is the month in which the world is believed to have been created, and its full moon must always be observed after the vernal equinox. In this month the people of Israel are delivered from Egyptian slavery, and the legal Passover begins. In this month the human race is delivered by Christ’s blood from the power of the devil and restored to life in Christ’s resurrection; in it, too, the new Passover is instituted by Christ himself. Therefore this month, distinguished by so many titles, is rightly called first in the order and numbering of months according to Jewish reckoning [Col. 0731B–C].

“Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them: On the tenth day of this month let every man take a lamb for his families and houses” (ibid.).

The lamb is commanded to be taken from the flock on the tenth day and kept until the evening of the fourteenth. This is a figure of Christ, who came to Jerusalem on the tenth day of the first month, where he was received by the crowds with palm branches and divine praises. On the tenth day of this month the lamb is taken; on the fourteenth it is sacrificed. The number ten signifies the Law because of the Decalogue; the number four, the four Gospels. Therefore Christ, who came not to abolish but to fulfill the Law, came on the tenth day to the place of his Passion, to be delivered on the evening of the fourteenth moon to those who were to crucify him, because he first fulfilled obedience to the Law and then, by laying down his life for his brethren, added the obedience of evangelical perfection [Col. 0731C–D].

“But if the number is too small to suffice for eating the lamb, he shall take his neighbor,” etc. (ibid.).

The literal sense is plain, while mystically it indicates the calling of the Gentiles, who have now been received to eat the lamb. The people of Israel alone was not sufficient to eat the lamb, because this lamb was not sufficient for Israel alone: it was sufficient for both them and the Gentiles. The people of the Gentiles was neighbor and joined to the house of Israel, because both peoples have one Father, God, by creation; both descend from Adam or Noah in the origin of the flesh; and both, according to the purpose of grace, were to be gathered into one house, that is, the Church—though the Gentile people was to be gathered through the Jewish people. Therefore the Israelites themselves are commanded to take their neighbor; and this was done in the reception of the Gentiles through the apostles.

Alternatively, if there are simple brethren in one house or congregation who are not sufficient to eat the lamb—that is, who are not sufficient to understand this sacrament of our faith—they are warned to take not a stranger, that is, a heretical person, but their neighbor, one joined to their own house, that is, a Catholic person possessing sound doctrine. With his assistance they may be able to eat the lamb: that is, devoutly to grasp in faith the sacrament of the true Lamb [Col. 0731D–0732A].

“The lamb shall be without blemish, a male of one year” (Exod. 12).

According to the command of the Law, a lamb without blemish was to be chosen: one without physical defect, neither lame nor otherwise impaired. All these things fit Christ. For he is the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found. He is male because he possesses nothing effeminate, but acts manfully in all things. He is one year old because he belongs to the year of which it is said: “Thou shalt bless the crown of the year of thy goodness” (Ps. 64), and of which he himself says through Isaiah: “That I might proclaim the year acceptable to the Lord” (Isa. 61). He is therefore one year old through the newness of grace, possessing nothing of the antiquity of preceding years: that is, nothing of the oldness of guilt [Col. 0732B–C].

“According to which rite you shall also take a kid” (ibid.).

Here it appears to be shown that, if a lamb is lacking, a kid must be taken to celebrate the Passover. Augustine seems to contradict this when he says that the Jews try to understand that a kid is to be taken to celebrate the Passover if a lamb is lacking. But Augustine seems to use another translation, as though it were written that a lamb was to be taken from sheep or goats. For he says: “Why should one be instructed to take a sheep or lamb from sheep or goats, unless he were being prefigured whose flesh was taken from the righteous and sinners?” But according to the translation we use, it seems to be commanded that a kid be taken according to the rite prescribed for the lamb. Nor is it absurd that Christ should be signified by the kid, because of the likeness of sinful flesh [Col. 0732C–D].

“And you shall keep it until the fourteenth day,” etc. (ibid.).

This must be understood of both, namely the lamb and the kid. For this was why either lamb or kid had to be taken on the tenth day: that it might be kept until the fourteenth day of this month and sacrificed at evening, because Christ was sacrificed by the Jews at the end of the ages and was betrayed and seized at evening to be killed. Christ is also sacrificed by us, as it were at evening: that is, after his death, as it were at the setting of the sun.
