For although he has already risen, nevertheless in the sacrifice of the altar the death of Christ is continually proclaimed, and what was done at evening is represented [Col. 0732D].

“And they shall take of the blood of the lamb,” etc. (Exod. 12).

[Col. 0733A]

The houses in which we dwell are ourselves, provided that we remain with ourselves and are not led outside ourselves through desires of error. The doorposts of the houses are the firmness of heart and body in courage and patience. Therefore the blood of the lamb is placed upon both doorposts when one imitates Christ’s Passion by sharing through affliction in the sufferings of both mind and body. For it is not enough to place the blood on one doorpost, because a Christian needs the discipline of chastising both mind and body.

For when it is said through the prophet, “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2), it does not forbid the rending of garments—that is, the affliction of bodies—but shows that it is not sufficient by itself. So too, when the Lord says, “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. 6), he indeed requires mercy above all, without which sacrifice is not sufficient. The lintel is devout intention, upon which blood is placed when the intention of thought is directed toward imitating Christ’s Passion.

Blood is also placed upon the lintel in another way, when the cross of the Passion is borne on the forehead. Hence the Lord says to the one who was seen by the prophet Ezekiel in the midst of the lampstands, like the Son of Man: “Pass through the midst of the city Jerusalem, and mark *tau* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are in its midst” (Ezek. 9). And to the six men who stood by the bronze altar he said: “Pass through the city after him and strike” (ibid.). And shortly after: “Do not kill anyone upon whom you see the *tau*; and begin from my sanctuary” (ibid.). In the Apocalypse we read: “Having his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads” (Apoc. 14). And in Exodus: “You shall make a plate of the purest gold, and on it you shall engrave, with a craftsman’s work, ‘Holy to the Lord’; and you shall bind it with a blue ribbon, and it shall be upon the turban, projecting over the high priest’s forehead” (Exod. 28) [Col. 0733B–C].

What is more rightly understood by the forehead than the public and unashamed confession of Christ’s cross? For Christ’s servant must be unashamed of Christ’s humility, not only in preaching it but also in imitating it, just as Christ himself was unashamed when he endured the cross, despising shame. Hence the Apostle admonishes Timothy: “Take care diligently to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed worker” (2 Tim. 2).

This is faithful confession: to proclaim Christ with tongue and life, word and example, speech and conduct alike; to endure Christ’s reproach; and not to be ashamed of humility, poverty, or every lowly condition for Christ’s sake. Hence it is said through the prophet: “I have set my face like a very hard rock, and I know that I shall not be ashamed” (Isa. 50). Far removed from those who place the blood on the lintel, who have *tau* or God’s name written on their forehead, are those who not only are not ashamed to be praised for shameful things and on account of shameful things, but even desire it. Their glory is in their shame: from that by which they ought to be ashamed they count themselves glorious; and, in the manner of a prostitute, they harden their forehead, not blushing at what they should blush for, as it is written: “The forehead of a harlot woman has become yours; you were unwilling to blush” (Jer. 3) [Col. 0733C–0734A].

In another way also we place the lamb’s blood upon both doorposts and upon the lintel, when we receive Christ’s blood with the mouth of body and heart, and mark with the blood of this lamb all our hope that is above, placing it not in our own strength. For even those found more perfect than others, namely Christ’s martyrs, did not wash their robes in their own blood but made them white in the Lamb’s blood. Their blood, however innocent and pure, was not sufficient for the cleansing of sins.

Thus we place the lamb’s blood upon both doorposts when we fortify body and soul by receiving the Lord’s blood. We place blood upon the lintel when we believe that we are saved by the power of this blood, having no confidence in our own righteousness [Col. 0734A–B].

“And they shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire” (Exod. 12).

We eat the lamb at night because we now receive the Lord’s body in a sacrament. For the mystery is deep and covered by a sacred veil. We eat at night because we do not yet see one another’s consciences, nor fully understand our own sins or the character of each person who approaches. For who understands sins? We eat flesh roasted with fire if we think worthily of Christ’s flesh: conceived from the Holy Spirit, united through the fire of love by the working of the Word of God, exposed to suffering for the salvation of the world, and burned by the fire of the Passion like a whole burnt offering into a most sweet odor for the Lord.

Fire may also refer to the love by which we must love Christ, without which no one approaches the lamb’s flesh worthily. Therefore we are commanded, and rightly so, to eat the flesh with fire. For that which is ardently loved is turned over in the heart by continual meditation and is, as it were, roasted in the heart by the heat of love. Therefore it is eaten roasted when the example of Christ’s Passion is eagerly received and taken inwardly through the love of imitation [Col. 0734B–C].

“And unleavened bread with wild lettuces” (ibid.).

In every word something useful is suggested to us and some grace of edification is contained. Behold, here we are instructed to eat unleavened bread with wild lettuces. Why is this? Or what are unleavened breads and wild lettuces? Pure and uncorrupted righteousness is itself bread and life-giving refreshment, by which a person may live righteously. Of it it is written: “Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5). And the man who long ago deserted righteousness through disobedience, but now returns to his heart through repentance, says: “My heart has dried up because I forgot to eat my bread” (Ps. 105).

Unleavened breads, then, are all the virtues of a well-ordered mind, if they are true and sincere; likewise the works of righteousness themselves, if they are done without pretense and without an admixture of sin. Thus he eats bread without leaven who performs upright works without the corruption of vainglory, who takes care not to lose through an evil intention the good he rightly administers. For the intention of vanity corrupts a work of piety. Conversely, a pious intention does not excuse the iniquity of a work. Hence this rebuke: “Offer praise from leavened bread” (Amos 4). For one offers praise from leaven who prepares a sacrifice for God from plunder, who seeks favor from an evil work.

Wild lettuces are very bitter, and they rightly signify penance and discipline. The former bitterly laments past sins; the latter bitterly restrains unlawful desires. Therefore, because we ought not approach the Lamb’s flesh without righteousness, penance, and discipline, we are rightly instructed, while eating the lamb’s flesh, also to eat unleavened bread with wild lettuces [Col. 0734C–0735A].

“You shall not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted with fire” (Exod. 12).

[Col. 0735B]

The very words of the historical account partly exclude the historical sense, since it is not customary to eat a lamb raw. Mystically, however, three classes of eaters are indicated here, containing four groups. For some have zeal for God according to the knowledge of piety; others have zeal for God not according to the knowledge of piety; others have knowledge but no zeal; others have neither knowledge nor zeal. These four differences are comprehended under three categories. Some indeed eat something raw, others something boiled in water, others only what has been roasted with fire.

To begin with the last: what is roasted with fire has been cooked by the heat of faith and love. Those eat what is roasted with fire who have zeal for God according to knowledge—that is, according to the piety of faith itself: those who believe devoutly in Christ and faithfully love him with an inflamed heart. Those eat what is boiled in water who have zeal for God but not according to knowledge—that is, not according to Christ’s teaching. For there are some who have zeal for knowing truth but, still persisting in error, do not believe as Christ taught. And there are some who have in purpose and desire a zeal for a better life, but who, still acting more laxly, do not live as Christ ordained. Both eat what is boiled in water: cooked indeed through the heat of zeal, but in water through the slippery life and uncertain conjecture of their error.

The pleasure of a fluid and slippery life is customarily signified by water, as in: “Whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again” (John 4). Likewise, erroneous conjecture or doctrine is commonly signified by water, as in: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9). There are others who have faith or knowledge but no zeal. These eat raw, because, without any heat of faith or good zeal, they cook by neither water nor fire what they conceive in their heart. There are those who have neither knowledge nor zeal, whether for knowing truth or pursuing virtue, and these eat raw. Among those who eat raw must be counted those who believe Christ to be a mere man, and those who think that the consecrated bread on the altar is only what it appears to be according to the species of bread [Col. 0735B–D].

“You shall devour the head with the entrails and feet” (ibid.).

[Col. 0736A]

The head is the loftiness of divinity, concerning which it is written: “His head is most fine gold” (Song 5). And the Apostle: “God is the head of Christ” (1 Cor. 11). Or the head is the beginning of all things, which belongs to Christ, who says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8); or it is the preeminence of dignity by which he presides over the whole Church. Hence the Apostle: “He gave him as head over all the Church” (Eph. 1). The feet are the lowly things of humanity, of which the Prophet says: “Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98). Or the feet by which he came to us are charity and humility. The inward parts are the bowels of mercy by which the Dayspring from on high visited us.

What, you ask, are the bowels of mercy? The purpose and counsel of our deliverance: purpose in the disposition, counsel in the choice. What he had determined to do, though he could have done it in innumerable ways, he chose beforehand to do in one definite way, more wonderful than the rest. Or the inward parts are the hidden mysteries which he instituted for us to receive: the sacrament of baptism and the other remedies of our cleansing and sanctification; and likewise the secret mysteries which he fulfilled in himself, namely, the sacrament of the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. We are therefore instructed to devour the head with the feet and inward parts: that we may turn into food for ourselves, and eagerly receive, what is written concerning Christ’s divinity, humanity, and mysteries; and with every desire strive to live spiritually from these things and nourish the good that is within us, by believing devoutly, venerating most devotedly, and fervently imitating what is to be imitated. For the more abundantly we do these things, the more eagerly we devour them.

**Nothing of it shall remain until morning; if anything remains over, you shall burn it with fire** (ibid.).

Morning after night will come when we apprehend in manifest truth what is now veiled in a sacrament; and when he himself will be manifest to us, or, conversely, we to him. While we still eat in the night, all that is written of Christ must be held most firmly with certain and unshaken faith. No impious doubt ought to remain in anyone’s heart, causing him to postpone until morning—that is, until the time of manifest knowledge—what he is now commanded to believe, and to say: “Unless I see, I will not believe” (John 20). For whatever remains impiously doubtful remains uneaten. Lest this happen, it is said: “Nothing of it shall remain until morning.”

But if, after a neighbor joined to the household has been taken in, the whole lamb still cannot be eaten—that is, if, even with a Catholic teacher expounding it, the whole depth of this mystery cannot be penetrated—what is to be done except what follows, wherein provision is made for our weakness: “If anything remains over,” he says, “you shall burn it with fire”? We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly commit to the power of the Holy Spirit that which we cannot penetrate, so that no one may presumptuously dare to despise what he does not understand. Thus we burn with fire what we leave to the Holy Spirit. Likewise, we burn the remainder with fire when we humbly venerate, with the fervor of devout devotion, what we are unable to comprehend. Therefore everything must either be eaten or burned with fire, lest anything of those things which we are bound or exhorted to believe remain uneaten or unburned.

**And thus you shall eat it: you shall gird your kidneys** (Exod. 12).

We have learned how the Passover is to be eaten; I shall now proceed to say by what sort of persons it ought to be eaten. Through the kidneys is propagated concupiscence, which is original evil; and therefore it is signified by the kidneys. They gird their kidneys who restrain evil desires by the belt of continence. The Lord also enjoins this upon us in the Gospel, saying: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). For chastity is imposed in the first place upon those approaching the flesh of the Lamb, as supremely necessary—indeed, so necessary that the Apostle says: “Pursue peace with all men, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12). Continence is frequently called holiness because it sanctifies. Hence the same Apostle says: “Let each one know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, as do the Gentiles who do not know God” (1 Thess. 4).

And in the first book of Kings, when David came to Nob, he said to Ahimelech the priest: “If you have anything at hand, give me five loaves, or whatever you find” (1 Sam. 21). The priest answered David: “I have no common bread at hand, but only holy bread—provided that the young men are clean, especially from women.” David answered the priest and said to him: “Indeed, if the matter is women, we have kept ourselves from them since yesterday and the day before yesterday, when we set out, and the vessels of the young men have been holy” (ibid.). From this passage it is shown that continence is called sanctification. It likewise indicates that, when sanctification was required of David’s young men in order that they might eat the holy bread, it is required much more of all believers in order that they may eat the bread of life which came down from heaven. Therefore let those who have chastity give thanks to God, the giver of so great a grace; those who do not have it should ask it from God, and should not think that they can possess it unless it has been given them from above by him, according to what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “When I knew that I could not otherwise be continent unless God gave it—and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was” (Wis. 8).

**You shall have sandals on your feet** (ibid.).

Those set ready for the journey are instructed to protect their feet with sandals, whether against the roughness of the road or against the dangers of the wilderness, lest the serpent which lies in wait for the heel bite secretly. This signifies that all who are to be delivered from Egypt—that is, from the vain manner of life of this world—by eating the true Lamb ought to protect the feet of their affections with the testimonies of Scripture, namely, the precepts and counsels of God and the examples of the holy Fathers, as with certain sandals. Thus they may not presume either to live otherwise or to think otherwise concerning Christ than Scripture’s testimonies prescribe and the examples of their elders exhort.

Hence the apostles are commanded to be shod with sandals. And the Apostle says: “Your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6). And in praise of the Bride it is said: “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince” (Song 7). But what does it mean that God says to Moses, “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exod. 3), and that the apostles are told, “Carry neither bag nor wallet nor sandals” (Luke 10)?

Sandals are understood in two ways: in a good sense, according to the foregoing passages; and sometimes in an evil sense, because they are like bonds and burdens upon the feet. The bonds of evil habits and burdens of sins in ourselves and others; the examples of dead works; and the fortifications of defenses and excuses for our chosen ways—these are like certain sandals by which our senses, through which the soul is moved, are bound, weighed down, or wickedly fortified. The apostles are commanded not to carry these; Moses is commanded to remove them. Otherwise he cannot stand upon holy ground—that is, in the Church of the saints—and approach God.

**Holding staffs in your hands** (ibid.).

There is a staff of support, and there is also a staff of correction. Weak limbs, or limbs wearied by the labor of the road, are supported by a staff. Thus the younger Tobias, for his weak parents, already as if exhausted by the labor of living, was called the staff of their old age. But for us the staff of support ought to be that of which it is said to the Lord through the Prophet: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22). This is Christ, who strengthens and supports us by his strength amid the labor of this pilgrimage. Hence it is written of the Bride: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8).

This staff must always be held in the hands, because in all our works we must lean solely upon the hope of his grace, so that our steps may not be moved. That he said “staffs,” as though there were several, if this creates any difference, may refer to this: although Christ is one, he does not distribute grace uniformly, but supports each person in the manner fitting for him, as he wills each to be supported. Or they hold staffs in their hands who, amid all the changes of this life, lean in hope upon the two pieces of wood of the cross and are supported more strongly in proportion as they lean more firmly.

In contrast, Pharaoh, under the figure of the devil, is told: “Behold, you trust in this broken reed staff, in Egypt; if a man leans upon it, it will enter into his hand and pierce it. So Pharaoh king of Egypt is to all who trust in him” (Isa. 36). As we have said, there is also a staff of correction. For a staff or rod is the emblem of authority. Hence those who preside over others in the Church are seen to carry a pastoral staff or rod, in the figure of Christ, by whose power and authority they ought to govern those subject to them: correcting some when they sin and directing others, when they have begun well, toward better things.

Thus, according to Luke, the apostles are commanded to carry a rod (Luke 9): the rod of direction, or justice, or discipline. Of this the Apostle says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4). The rod of support is likewise granted to prelates, because they may be supported by their subjects in temporal matters, and ought to support them in spiritual matters and, if possible, in temporal matters. But that, according to Mark, a rod is not to be carried (Mark 6) relates to the fact that perfect disciples of Christ are not granted the power of self-defense, according as Truth itself says: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5), and the rest that follows. Hence also the Apostle: “Beloved, do not defend yourselves” (Rom. 12).

Elisha is read to have possessed a staff, by which might be figured the severity of the law, which could not raise the dead (2 Kings 4). But Christ, or his power or justice, is signified by a rod or staff in many passages of Scripture, as there: “The Lord shall send forth the rod of your strength from Zion” (Ps. 109); and again: “A rod of direction is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. 44); and in Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. 11); and in Jeremiah: “I see a watchful rod” (Jer. 11). For this the Septuagint translated, “a nut-wood staff.”

Not only shepherds of others, to whom the administration of ecclesiastical government has been entrusted, ought to carry staffs in their hands. All who are admitted to eat the true Lamb must spiritually hold staffs in their hands, so that in all their works, whenever they encounter anything undisciplined or disordered, they may strike it, as with a staff, by the censure of rigor and the strictness of discipline. For each person ought to have care of himself, so that in Christ’s stead he may restrain himself when he sins and correct his own transgressions. This manner of self-chastisement is indicated where it says: “Each one’s sword upon his thigh; all holding swords, most skilled for war” (Song 3).

**And you shall eat in haste** (Exod. 12).

Those who live devoutly in Christ always eat the food which is Christ, because they continually receive from him in order that they may live in him. This food is necessary to all if they are to live rightly. Since it is not permitted to delay conversion to righteousness, nor, after conversion has been begun, to act sluggishly, it is said: “And you shall eat in haste,” so that those who do not yet live from Christ or in Christ may begin without delay or hesitation to live according to Christ, and thus have Christ as food. Those who already live in Christ should nevertheless strive to eat hastily—that is, eagerly to make progress toward better things.

But when Christ is eaten in the sacrament of the altar, he must be eaten promptly. This does not mean that the solemn rites of Mass should be performed hastily or precipitately, without gravity and reverence. Rather, when the very hour of reception has arrived, that which must be eaten with so great a desire should be received promptly. For this food must be received as by one who desires it with his whole desire and longs for it with entire eagerness. Whoever approaches ought to receive it as a hungry person receives food, or a thirsty person drink—unwilling to endure delay or to be deferred from so great a grace.

“For it is the phase—that is, the passing-over—of the Lord.” Why it is called the Lord’s passing-over is shown when it is added: “I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from man even to beast.” And below: “I shall see the blood and pass over you, and there shall be no destroying plague among you.” And again: “It is the victim of the Lord’s passing-over, when he passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt, striking the Egyptians and delivering our houses.”

This passing-over of the Lord is the cause of the deliverance by which the children of Israel passed from slavery to freedom, from Egypt to the land promised them. It is also the sign of that passing-over which he will make in the future, striking some and delivering others, as it is written: “Passing by, he will minister to them” (Luke 12). Christ, moreover, the victim of our passing-over, himself passing from the world to the Father, opened for us the way of passing over and showed us the manner of it, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but shall pass from death to life” (John 5).

For us there is a twofold passing-over: either from an evil life to a good one, or from a good life to a blessed one. The Hebrews’ passing from Egypt is the sign of both passages; Christ’s passing from the world to the Father is the cause of both.

**This is the religious observance of the phase. Every foreigner, etc., up to the words, “who sojourns among you”** (ibid.).

Here the name of religious observance is introduced, where the condition or character of those who are not admitted to eat the lamb is distinguished. This shows that the principal concern of religion is that not everyone, without discrimination, be admitted to eat the true Lamb, but that it be most carefully discerned who is worthy and who unworthy.

Four classes of persons not to be received are here distinguished: the foreigner, the purchased slave, the resident alien, and the hired servant. The foreigner, in its signification, denotes a Gentile or Jew, a heretic or schismatic, and an excommunicated person: people who are manifestly outside, and therefore ought not to share in the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood. The purchased slave is one who is in the Church only in name and is restrained by servile fear from doing harm openly, and is therefore a slave. He is rightly called purchased, because one who serves unwillingly has sold his freedom, that is, alienated it from himself. The resident alien is one who comes from elsewhere to the faith and pretends to believe, for he is not of us. The hired servant is one who serves for temporal gain.

Thus the foreigner is openly unbelieving or rebellious; the resident alien secretly unbelieving; the purchased slave secretly evil; the hired servant falsely good. What was said of the slave—“He shall be circumcised, and then he shall eat”—may be understood also of the foreigner, resident alien, and hired servant. For all evil persons, if cleansed by spiritual circumcision, may be admitted to eat the Lamb. In the circumcision of the slave, who is to be added to the people of God and then received to eat the Lamb, is indicated the calling of the Gentile people, who through circumcision not made with hands are to be joined to the ancient righteous, so that from both peoples there may be one Church, concerning which it is added: “It shall be eaten in one house.”

For outside the Church, in the conventicles of heretics, there is no place of sacrifice. Hence it is rightly added: “You shall not carry any of its flesh outside.” This sacrifice must not be communicated to those who are outside and are not of this house; nor should the secret of this sacrament be revealed to unworthy hearers, because what is holy must not be given to dogs, who are prepared rather to bark, ridicule, or attack than to receive reverently.

But what is added—“You shall not break a bone of it”—John explains, saying: “When they came to Jesus, seeing that he was already dead, they did not break his legs” (John 19). And shortly afterward he adds: “That the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of it’” (ibid.). Thus the bone of the Lamb, which according to the command of the law was not to be broken, foreshadows Christ’s legs, which were not to be broken on the cross. In both cases we are instructed by mystical signification to preserve, spiritually, the Lamb’s bone unbroken and intact in the conscience of faith.

The unbroken bone signifies Christ’s divinity, which could not suffer; or the power by which he could rise from the dead; or the strength of endurance by which he himself was willing to stand for truth even unto death. This is the bone of which he says: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret” (Ps. 138). Therefore he breaks the bone who denies Christ’s divinity, or affirms that divinity suffered in Christ. He breaks the bone who denies that Christ possessed such power that he could rise from the dead, or such endurance that he would willingly undergo death.

But when Christ himself says, “While my bones are being broken, my enemies who afflict me reproached me” (Ps. 41), this must be understood of his stronger members. It seems contrary to what is said in another psalm concerning the righteous: “The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them shall be broken” (Ps. 33).

Yet attention should be paid to the various possible meanings of the words, “While my bones are being broken.” Some are bones only in appearance, are truly strong, and are truly broken; some are truly bones but are broken only in appearance; and some are truly bones and truly broken, but in body, not in spirit. For breaking must be considered in two ways: bodily breaking, which comes alike upon good and evil people; and breaking of spirit, which belongs only to evil people—except that good people too are sometimes permitted to stumble in spirit for a time, so that they may rise again stronger.

The breaking of the legs of the evil and blaspheming thief, whose spirit was broken, can indicate the double breaking that occurs in the wicked: that of bodies and of spirits. The breaking of the legs of the repentant and confessing thief can indicate the breaking of bodies among the righteous, whose bodies God permits to be crushed and killed, and whose bones he permits to be broken and scattered. Hence is that cry of the martyrs: “Our bones have been scattered beside hell” (Ps. 140). Christ’s unbroken legs signify the invincible steadfastness of himself and his members. Hence it is also said of the Bridegroom: “His legs are marble columns, founded upon bases of gold” (Song 5).

Having shown who are not to be admitted to eat the Lamb, he consequently shows who are to be admitted, declaring generally that the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall do this—that is, sacrifice or observe the phase—of which he has spoken above. What he had said concerning the slave alone, he now indicates should be understood also concerning the foreigner, resident alien, and hired servant, using the name “sojourners” to indicate all who are not of the assembly of the children of Israel.

“If,” he says, “any of the sojourners wishes to enter into your settlement”—that is, into the worship of your religion—and to perform the Lord’s phase, “all his males shall first be circumcised,” that is, every male of his household. This shows that, if any unbeliever chooses, with his followers, to enter into the name and number of the faithful, both he and every one of his followers must be spiritually circumcised in order to perform the phase with us.

But even if someone called a believer is a sojourner, separated from the assembly of the good, he must have all his male element circumcised if he is to be worthy of celebrating the phase with them. For he must cleanse in himself everything strong that is directed to evil, and everything that belongs to the world; he must turn strength toward good and toward the things of God. Then, when circumcised, he will rightly celebrate and will thus be a native of the land. But if anyone has not been circumcised, he shall not eat of it, because he ought not to approach holy communion unless first cleansed by spiritual circumcision. “The same law shall be for the native and for the settler who sojourns among you,” because Jew and Gentile, gathered into one Church, are bound by one law of sacrifice.

**From the book of Numbers. The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel: Any man who shall be unclean because of a soul, etc., up to the words, “It shall be an ordinance among you, for the stranger as for the native”** (Num. 9).

The first Passover was observed on the fourteenth day of the first month. But those who were unclean because of a soul, and those who were far away on a journey, performed the phase on the fourteenth day of the second month. The first month is the time of the law. The first Passover is that of the Jews under the law. The second time is the time of grace; the second Passover is ours. For we, called from the Gentiles, were unclean because of a soul, worshipping wood and stones and walking in the way of error, made far from God.

The phrase “unclean because of a soul” may refer specifically to the uncleanness resulting from contact with a dead body, or generally to every uncleanness which, under the law, needs purification. The things said concerning the first and second months may also be understood differently. The first month may signify the time of original innocence and the state of incorrupt life after baptism and before a fall. The second month may signify the time of repentance after a fall.

Unimpaired innocence and an age of youth uncorrupted and undefiled amid the temptations of this life possess a singular dignity. Nevertheless, those who have fallen after baptism are not excluded; restored through repentance, they can celebrate the phase, but as it were in the second month. For they were unclean because of a soul: defiled by their own sins, or contaminated through consenting to another’s wickedness, as though by contact with a dead person; or because they were far away on the journey, though among their own people.

For the words, “whether on a journey far away in your nation,” indicate that even a Jew among Jews could not sacrifice the phase far from the place which the Lord had chosen for this purpose. Just as a fixed time was appointed, so too a fixed place was appointed for sacrificing the phase. For concerning the time it is written in Exodus, as we showed above; and again in Deuteronomy, where it says: “Observe the month of new fruits and the first season of spring, that you may perform the phase to the Lord your God; for in this month the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt by night” (Deut. 16). Likewise, concerning the place, Deuteronomy says: “You shall not be able to sacrifice the phase in any of your cities which the Lord your God will give you, but in the place which the Lord your God chooses, that his name may dwell there” (ibid.).

The time could be changed for certain reasons, namely from the first month to the second; but the place could not be changed. One who was far from the place appointed for this purpose could not sacrifice the phase. This shows that it is not lawful to offer the immaculate sacrifice in a profane place. Yet something higher is also intimated to us. The place which the Lord chose for sacrificing the phase is the Church of faithful people, but of righteous faithful people. Even a believer who is not righteous is far from that place.

Therefore an evil person, if he is on the journey through faith and among his own people through the common profession shared with believers, yet is far from the house because, through dissimilarity of conduct, he is separated from the number of the righteous—such a person cannot celebrate the phase, because he is not in the unity of the righteous, that is, in the place which the Lord chose for himself. But when he has returned, he can celebrate the phase in the second month, because pardon is granted to those who return through repentance and communion is not denied them.

Perhaps in this passage “journey” may more suitably be understood as the path of error, so that the difference in mystical interpretation may appear more clearly between one called unclean because of a soul and one far away on a journey. Thus, in order that they may be distinguished from one another, one unclean because of a soul may be understood as one who has already committed sin, while one far away on the journey is one who intends to commit crimes. The former is unclean in the conscience of an accomplished offense; the latter is far away on the journey through a purpose and desire to sin. He is rightly said to be on the journey because in mind he goes where he tends through the intention of his heart. But one who is clean according to his past life and is not on a path by which he abandons righteousness is worthy to celebrate the phase in the first month. For the purity of innocence is more worthy than the usefulness of repentance.

The rest of what follows in this chapter has been explained above, up to the passage: “But if anyone is clean and was not on a journey, and nevertheless did not perform the phase, that soul shall be cut off from its people.” These words show how perilous it is for a good person to neglect what an evil person wickedly appropriates. An evil person may not eat the phase. For, as the Apostle says: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11). A good person may not fail to perform the phase at its proper time, for here it is written: “He who did not offer sacrifice to the Lord at its proper time shall bear his own sin.”

What follows—“The stranger and resident alien, if they are among you, shall perform the Lord’s phase according to its ceremonies and ordinances”—and likewise what is added—“The same ordinance shall be among you, for the stranger as for the native”—agrees with what is written in Exodus, as we quoted shortly before: “The same law shall be for the native and for the settler who sojourns among you” (Exod. 12).

The order of the subject warns us to add a discussion of manna, according to what is written in Exodus, where it reads:

**The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel, etc., up to the words, “They were nourished with this food until they reached the borders of the land of Canaan; now a gomor is the tenth part of an ephah”** (Exod. 16).

One face appears differently in a painting, differently in a mirror, differently in water, and differently in itself. Three images or likenesses, unlike and unequal to one another, represent one face. It is seen separately in each, but not perfectly known until it is seen in itself. So truth, which is Christ—the face of the Father and image of the invisible God—while it is still seen through a mirror and in an enigma, has principally three figurative images in a certain respect: in bread, lamb, and manna. Through these it is known in part, until it is seen more fully.

Truth itself, however, always consistent with itself, is neither unlike nor unequal to itself; but it is figured and represented differently or unequally in one image and another. Nor does the whole reality belonging to the proper nature of truth appear in a single figurative likeness. Although each likeness has its own expression of signification, which in part supplies what the others lack, nevertheless all images of figures and likenesses of shadows do not attain the full manifestation of truth and cannot equal the contemplation of truth itself when it is revealed in itself.

Among all these created things are certain mystical likenesses in which the invisible things of God are perceived, and that which is known of God is manifest in us. Some make God’s power known in some respect; others his wisdom, goodness, mercy, or justice; others his indignation and wrath; others show that he is lovable; others that he is terrible; all show that he is wonderful. In these mystical likenesses the wisdom of God wonderfully hides itself and wonderfully discloses itself. In them it is sought in the present life; in them is engaged the contemplation of the saints, who delight to see in some manner, in a likeness, him whom they desire with their whole longing to see in his own proper reality.

These likenesses are distinguished in divine discourse when the saints delight, through likenesses familiar to them, to magnify and praise God and to edify readers or hearers. This is their meditation and contemplation; this is their speech, teaching, and preaching. Concerning these things it is written in the Song of Songs, according to one translation: “We shall make for you likenesses of gold with ornaments of silver” (Song 1).

The three aforesaid likenesses are distinguished from one another. Bread grows from the earth, according to the words: “That he may bring forth bread from the earth” (Ps. 103); and, “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84). The lamb is sacrificed, and it is written of Christ: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter; and as a lamb before its shearer was silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). Manna descends from heaven, and Christ says of himself: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). We must now speak of the likeness of this figure, in which Christ was figured through manna, and of what is the “ornament of silver,” that is, the instruction of sacred discourse.

**I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel. Speak to them: In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. The quail came up** (Exod. 16), etc.

The people, ungrateful for God’s benefits, murmured against Moses and Aaron out of a craving for meat. They did indeed have flocks of sheep and herds of cattle, from which they could have eaten; but they are thought by some to have murmured because they desired the birds with which Egypt abounded. The Lord, however, wishing to restrain their murmuring, to satisfy their present desires, and to prefigure what would at some time come to pass among them, gave them meat in the evening—namely quails—and in the morning gave them manna, that is, on the fifteenth day of the second month, when Passover is celebrated according to the Law [Col. 0745D]. This day is shown to have been the Lord’s Day, because manna was gathered for six continuous days, and on the seventh, which is the Sabbath, gathering ceased.

What the Lord says to Moses—“I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel”—indicates that God makes known to Moses, that is, to the ecclesiastical teacher, in order that through him it may be made known to others, that not only deeds done openly but also the murmurings of heart and mouth come to His knowledge and belong to His judgment; He hears these in order to punish them. Conversely, He hears the prayers of the righteous in order to spare them. He heard indeed, but delayed; He did not punish at once, but first bestowed benefits. Afterwards, however, in the place called “the graves of craving,” they were struck with a very great plague because of their murmuring [Col. 0746A]. Or, He heard their murmurings—that is, the petitions of those who murmured—of whom it is written: “And they tempted God in their hearts, that they might ask food for their souls” (Ps. 77).

What He says, “Speak to them: In the evening you shall eat,” etc., indicates that the promises of God, like His threats, are to be made known to the people through the Law or through an ecclesiastical teacher. What He says, “You shall know that I am the Lord your God,” indicates that God is known in His benefits through mercy, as He is known in judgments through wrath. When it says, “The quail went up,” it uses the singular number for the plural, as there: “He spoke, and the locust came, and the caterpillar, of which there was no number” (Ps. 104). What it says, “It covered the camp,” the Psalmist explains, saying: “And they fell in the midst of their camp, around their tents” (ibid.) [Col. 0746B]. And in the Book of Numbers it is written: “A wind went forth from the Lord, carried off quails from across the sea, and let them fall into the camp” (Num. 12), etc.

Meat and manna are each understood in different ways. By meat may be signified the fleshly sacrifices and the other carnal observances of the Law, imposed until the time of correction. The children of Israel were nourished by these and ate this meat, but in the evening, to signify the decline and end of carnal observances, which were at some time to cease. Conversely, by bread may be understood the institutions of the New Testament, by which the children of Israel were satisfied in the apostles and in others from the same people who were converted to the grace of Christ; and this in the morning, that is, at Christ’s coming, or from the time of Christ’s resurrection [Col. 0746C].

Again, by meat may be signified the Jews’ carnal understandings of the promised mysteries and commandments, concerning Christ and His coming. The Jews are now nourished by this meat, namely those among them who do not believe; and they have it in the evening, because it is now evening for them, the day’s end—that is, the failure of the faith which had gone before in the ancient righteous. But morning will then come when they are satisfied with the breads of life and understanding, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel is saved (Rom. 11). For at the end of the world the remnant will be converted. Of this conversion the Psalmist says: “They shall return at evening” (Ps. 58). Here he calls the end of the world “evening,” at which, when the Jews are converted, morning will come through the illumination of beginning grace [Col. 0746D].

Again, by meat and breads may be understood two kinds of God’s benefits, which He often confers upon those who murmur and are unworthy. There are carnal goods, which we all need because of the weakness of the flesh and life’s deficiency, signified by evening. There are spiritual goods, which we need for the salvation of the soul: such as God’s gifts in the word of life, in the sacraments, and in the other charisms of grace, given in the morning according to the beginning of grace. The latter are denoted by breads, the former by meat. The wicked, however, misuse carnal goods through manifold corruptions of life; they turn God’s mercy into wrath against themselves, eating and drinking and spending their days in prosperity, until death comes upon them and they go down alive into hell [Col. 0747A].

Of such people the Psalmist says: “They ate and were exceedingly filled, and the Lord brought them their desire; they were not deprived of their desire. Their food was still in their mouths, and the wrath of God came up against them” (Ps. 77). And Isaiah says: “Behold joy and gladness, killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating meat and drinking wine: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.’ And the voice of the Lord of hosts was revealed in my ears: ‘This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die,’ says the Lord” (Isa. 22).

Their transient, trifling, and unlawful desires may be signified by quails, or feathered birds, because they are winged and pass swiftly away. This is the meat which the Lord rained down: not only the carnal goods [Col. 0747B] which He Himself gives, raining upon good and evil alike; but He also rains snares upon sinners and abandons them to their heart’s desires. This meat is rightly compared by the Psalmist to dust and sand: both because of the abundance of riches in which they abound, as it is written, “Behold, these sinners, prosperous in the world, have obtained riches” (Ps. 72); and because those who possess these temporal things badly are defiled by the dust of earthly thinking, and the more damnably they possess them, the more barren and fruitless is their possession.

The wicked also often misuse spiritual goods. They are signified by those wicked persons who ate manna, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and died” (John 6).

Again, meat may be understood otherwise, as may be gathered from the words of Blessed Augustine on the Psalm passage: “And He rained meat upon them as dust.” There are certain good people in the Church who are weak and, as it were, carnal, unable to grasp and comprehend the profound mysteries of faith and the institutions of a more perfect life. Yet, content with the least commandments and with a small faith, they simply believe and live innocently. Upon such people God rains meat, or feathered birds, because from the clouds—that is, from preachers—there are ministered to them signs of uttered voices, passing through the air like birds. They are nourished, as it were, by meat: by words of preaching suited to those who are carnal, to small faith, and to innocence of life [Col. 0747C]. Hence Paul says: “I speak in human terms [Col. 0747D], because of the weakness of your flesh” (Rom. 6). And again: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal” (1 Cor. 3). According to Origen, however, meat signifies the doctrine of perfection, and evening the end of perfection; or meat in the evening signifies the Word incarnate in the evening of the world.

“Also in the morning there lay dew around the camp” (Exod. 16).

Although every good gift and every perfect gift, descending from above from the Father of lights (Jas. 1), may be signified by manna, Christ is nevertheless principally signified in it: whether as He is in heaven; as He was in the flesh, a man among human beings; as He is in the sacrament of the altar; as He is in the Law [Col. 0748A] and the prophets; as He is in the word of preaching; as He is in the hearts of the elect through faith; or as He is wherever He is by grace.

Therefore dew lay around the camp in the morning when, through Christ’s resurrection accomplished in the morning and the beginning of grace revealed to the Gentiles, the word of God was spread around the circle of peoples and nations, or of churches, or of believing hearts, and lay scattered, as it were, around the camp, humbly and reverently received by believers. It lay there where it remained. The churches established far and wide throughout the world are camps, around which Christ was preached as the apostles carried the word of God about. Hence the Apostle says: “In the power of the Holy Spirit, so that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have filled up the Gospel of Christ” (Rom. 15) [Col. 0748B]. That the word of God is dew is shown by the one who says: “Let my speech flow like dew” (Deut. 32).

“And when it had covered the surface of the ground, there appeared in the wilderness something small,” etc. (Exod. 16).

Although dew and manna, as said above, may commonly signify Christ, or the grace of Christ, or the word of Christ, in this passage the word of Christ is distinctly signified in the dew. This dew, spread everywhere by the preaching of the apostles, covered the earth, according to Isaiah: “The earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea” (Isa. 11). Then manna appeared in the wilderness: that is, Christ became known to the Gentiles, according to the words: “Drop down, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Righteous One” (Isa. 45) [Col. 0748C].

The Church, or the faithful soul, may be compared to a wilderness according to its earlier condition, because before conversion only beasts lived in it: that is, in Gentile life, human beings resembling beasts in the character of their morals; or, in the soul, beastly affections. But according to its present condition, wilderness may be said of either the Church or the soul, because, fleeing the tumult and crowd of errors and vices, it turns itself to peace of mind. Hence the penitent says: “I have become like a pelican of the wilderness” (Ps. 101). And again: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in the wilderness” (Ps. 54).

Manna was small because everything believed or preached concerning Christ, on account of His inestimable humility, is subtle and incomprehensible, as though because of excessive littleness [Col. 0748D]; and this is so among believers, whereas among unbelievers it is contemptible and small. Thus in Daniel Christ is called a small stone cut from the mountain; and He Himself compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed. Manna was as though shorn with a pestle, not only because Christ exposed Himself to the beatings of His persecutors, but because He was set as a sign to be contradicted. And the word of faith is pounded by the pestle of contradiction, because it is attacked by many; in that very pounding it is stripped of its literal sense, as grain, millet, or something similar is commonly stripped of its husks when it is ground with a pestle in a mortar. Thus Christ, by the pounding of His Passion and the pestle of the cross, was stripped of mortality.

Christ may be signified by hoarfrost for various reasons [Col. 0749A]: because He has whiteness through the purity of holiness; because He enriches and makes fruitful the soil of our heart; because by the rigor of discipline He restrains the flow of vices in us; and because through the coolness of grace He extinguishes the incitements of carnal desires.

“And when the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, ‘Manhu,’” etc. (Exod. 16).

The faithful say *manhu* in one way, unbelievers in another; those who do not believe and ask, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6), in one way; and those who believe, marvel and are astonished, saying, “Who has ever heard such a thing, or who has seen its like?” (Isa. 66), in another. Therefore, whenever in Christ, or in His words, works, or sacraments, we grasp something true, or through the infusion of heavenly grace experience something sweeter, we say in wonder and astonishment: “*Manhu*,” meaning, “What is this?” Those to whom visible manna appeared did not know what it was. In this ignorance was prefigured the blindness of the Jews, who do not know Christ hidden in the Law and prophets, in assumed flesh, and in the sacrifice of the altar [Col. 0749B].

But in what Moses says to them—“This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat” (Exod. 16)—it is signified that Moses himself is the witness of the true bread, namely the true bread given from heaven to eat. Hence Christ says to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also, for he wrote of me” (John 5). This very passage of Scripture pertains to Christ, when Moses says: “This is the bread,” etc. For this bread, first promised by God and afterwards given from heaven, signifies Christ, promised in the Law and given to us in the time of grace. Thus, by pointing out the bread which was given, he shows that it is the same one who was promised, saying: “This is the word which the Lord commanded” (Exod. 16): namely, to hope and to desire; as though it were said: This is the fulfillment of the word by which the Lord promised bread when He said, “In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with breads” (ibid.) [Col. 0749C].

It may also be taken simply and referred to what follows: “This is the word of God.” For it continues:

“Let each one gather from it as much as is sufficient to eat,” etc. (Exod. 16).

[Col. 0749D] From this passage it may be observed that a *gomor* is a measure sufficient for one person per day. A *gomor*, as is stated later, is the tenth part of an *ephah*. Jerome shows what an *ephah* is in Book XIV of his exposition of Ezekiel, in these words:

> “A *cor* contains thirty modii and is the principal measure for both dry and liquid goods. A tenth part of a cor, in things measured by the modius, is called an *ephah*, that is, three modii; and a tenth part of a cor in liquid kinds is called a *bath*, or *vadus*, so that the ephah and bath are of the same measure.”

Thus Jerome. In this passage it should be noted that, although he first said *ephi*, he later said *epha*, because, as he himself shows shortly beforehand in the same book, *epha* is corruptly called *ephi* in Greek [Col. 0750A]. In the same book, a little later, he also says that the *cor*, which in Hebrew is called *homor*, is called *gomer* by the Septuagint. We mention this so that the difference between *gomor* and *gomer* may be evident.

What it says, “Let each one gather a gomor for each head,” is to be understood as “for each person,” so that the principal member of the body is taken for the person. What is then added, “According to the number of your souls who live in the tents, so shall you take,” seems to mean that a gomor was to be taken for each household according to the number of persons living in it. Yet, if one carefully considers how much each person found or had after the gathering, it is clear that each had a gomor, from what is written: “They measured by the measure of a gomor”; and from what follows: “He who gathered more had no excess, nor did he who had prepared less have less” [Col. 0750B]. Therefore, after the gathering there was equality in what was possessed or found.

But for those asking how much each gathered, a certain suspicion of contradiction seems to arise from apparently contrary words. For, since it is written, “Let each one gather from it as much as is sufficient to eat, a gomor for each head,” if the gathering was made according to the form of the command, then a gomor was gathered for each head. The same seems to follow from what comes next: “Each gathered according to what he was able to eat.” How much that was is shown where it says: “As much as is sufficient to eat, a gomor for each head.” If this is so, there was equality in gathering. But the contrary seems to be said: “Some gathered more, others less.” What then shall we say?

First, it must be noted that the statement, “Some gathered more, others less,” can be understood in two ways. In one way, it compares the gatherers with one another, as though one gathered more or less than another. In the other, it compares what was gathered with a gomor, as though one gathered less than a gomor and another more than a gomor. If, then, the comparison is made among the gatherers, it may be understood without any contradiction that each one, according to the form of the command, gathered at least a gomor; yet some gathered [Col. 0750C] more than a gomor, and after gathering found no more than a gomor. But if comparison is made between the gathered amounts and the gomor, so that one is understood to have gathered less than a gomor, the exposition of the letter will be difficult, since they were commanded to gather a gomor, and Scripture says, “And the children of Israel did so”; and adds later, “Each gathered according to what he was able to eat.”

What is written, “They measured by the measure of a gomor,” may mean either that while gathering they used the measure of a gomor, lest they gather less than a gomor; or that after gathering they measured by a gomor, so that each might determine whether he had gathered a gomor; or that they measured what had been gathered and brought into a heap, so that each might receive a gomor. For it could have happened that they first gathered a gomor by estimation alone, and then tested whether it truly was a gomor [Col. 0750D].

Now let us consider, as far as we are able, what grace for edification this passage of Scripture contains. By the gomor may be signified the measure of Christ’s gift, or the measure of grace given to us according to the measure of Christ’s gift. The measure of Christ’s gift may be understood either in terms of the grace that gives or the grace that is given. For with God, in predestination, there is a determination of how much He wishes to give to each person, more to one and less to another; and therefore one gathers more, another less. Yet a gomor is given to all the righteous, because one norm of believing and living rightly is set before all from God’s Law, or suggested through hidden inspiration. And although one person’s faith is greater in knowledge or devotion, another’s less, and one is more righteous than another, nevertheless there is one faith, one law of righteousness, which is charity, and one form of believing and loving, common to all the righteous and to them alone. Likewise, because of the righteousness of faith, the one hope of eternal life is common to all [Col. 0751A]. Thus one denarius is promised to all (Matt. 20), although there is diversity of rewards according to diversity of merits.

The Apostle appears to draw from this place of Scripture what he writes to the Corinthians: “He who had much did not abound, and he who had little did not lack” (2 Cor. 8). Urging the rich to provide relief from their goods for those in need, he says: “At the present time let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be equality” (ibid.) [Col. 0751B]. In speaking of equality, he seems to allude to the measure of the gomor.

But it may seem strange that the Apostle says equality is brought about, when the rich receive more in the sharing of spiritual things and the poor less in the sharing of temporal things. Yet equality, as it presently occurs to us, is understood in three ways: according to equity, according to parity, or according to quality, that is, some sort of likeness.

Equality of equity is when evil is rendered for evil, as the Old Testament prescribes: eye for eye, tooth for tooth, bruise for bruise; and when good is rendered for good, as in the reckoning of giving and receiving. Writing to the Philippians, the Apostle says of this: “No church shared with me in the reckoning of giving and receiving, except you alone” (Phil. 4) [Col. 0751C]. Of this equality the Apostle says, “That there may be equality.” Such equality of equity can also be equality of parity. Hence the Apostle: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9). It is not a great thing to reap carnal things, although it is a great thing to sow spiritual things.

Of equality of parity it is written: “For they are equal to angels and are children of God, since they are children of the resurrection” (Luke 20). Equality according to likeness may be understood in what is written: “Have mercy, Lord, on your people, over whom your name has been invoked, and on Israel, whom you have made equal to your firstborn” (Ecclus. 39) [Col. 0751D]. This making-equal is not according to equality of complete parity, but in accordance with some degree of likeness in the name of honor and the honor of the name. For the Son of God is called the Firstborn, and God says of Israel: “Israel is my firstborn” (Exod. 4). The Son of God is called the image of God, like God in every respect; and we, insofar as we are conformed to the image of the Son of God according to our measure, are like Him, and shall be more so when we see Him as He is (1 John 3) [Col. 0752A]. We say this so that the one measure of the gomor may be understood in all according to some kind of equality.

“And Moses said to them, ‘Let no one leave any of it until morning’” (Exod. 16).

This is similar to what he had said above concerning the lamb: “Nothing of it shall remain until morning.” For in the present life each person ought to believe what is preached and do what is commanded, and not postpone it until morning—that is, until the time when he is overtaken by death or judgment, when morning will come: namely, clear and manifest knowledge of merits.

But those who did not listen to Moses and left manna until morning, so that it began to swarm with worms and rot, signify the Jews of the present time. They keep badly the word of God ministered to them through Moses in the Law; it breeds for them the worms of sins, rots for them, and turns into corruption [Col. 0752B]. Christ, however, is called a worm in three ways. First, because of true humility; hence David is said, in a figure of Christ, to be “the tenderest little worm of the wood” (2 Sam. 23). Likewise, what Isaiah says may be understood as a figure of Christ’s humility: “Do not fear, worm Jacob” (Isa. 41). Second, because of lowly rejection, as in the Psalm: “I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and despised by the people” (Ps. 21); this too can be understood of humility. Third, because of biting severity, as moths are spoken of. Hence in Hosea He says: “I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like rottenness to the house of Judah” (Hos. 5) [Col. 0752C].

That manna is said to have begun to swarm with worms, as though with many worms, may mean that Christ is grievous in many ways to those who do not believe in Him. By this example of manna the evil of avarice is condemned: money wickedly hoarded turns into a worm for its possessor, a worm which does not die. Likewise, the grace of faith does not work in one who hoards it; and the grace of wisdom or knowledge, or the grace of speech, when it is possessed fruitlessly and not put to good use, turns like manna into a worm, because God’s good gift results in evil for the one who possesses it badly [Col. 0752D].

Some hold that Christ, born from Mary, is a worm from manna. This seems strange, since by the worm from manna the dissidence and disobedience of certain persons has been shown. Nevertheless, it may not impiously be said that Mary is manna hidden in the figures and testimonies of the Law that concern her. But because the Jews preserve in their books what is written concerning her, yet neither understand it nor believe it devoutly, Christ, who was born of the Virgin, becomes a worm to them [Col. 0753A].

It follows: “And Moses was angry against them.” This shows that the Law, or the lawgiver, rebukes and foretells punishment by threatening those who leave manna until morning in any of the ways mentioned above. But those who gathered in the morning as much as could suffice for food signify vigorous workers, eager to work for the food that does not perish, beginning in the morning—that is, at the beginning of their faith or conversion. Of such persons it is said in the Psalm: “The sun arose” (Ps. 103); and shortly afterwards: “Man shall go forth to his work and to his labor until evening” (ibid.).

“And when the sun grew hot, it melted” (Exod. 16).

This may be understood in many ways. Christ, the sun of righteousness, grew hot when, ascending the cross for us at the sixth hour, He poured out the fervor of His love. He who is the sun insofar as He shines is Himself manna insofar as He grants Himself to us to be enjoyed and shared. When He was dissolved into death by the desire of love and the affections of compassion, then manna truly melted. For He ceased to appear when for a time He withdrew Himself from human sight. Hence He said: “A little while, and you shall no longer see me; and again a little while, and you shall see me” (John 16) [Col. 0753B].

In us the sun grows hot when our heart burns with desire for divine love; then manna also melts, when the word of God causes our heart to melt through Christ’s love. Hence the bride says: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5). And in the Psalm: “He shall send forth His word and shall melt them” (Ps. 147) [Col. 0753C]. Manna—that is, the word of God—is said to melt by its effect because it melts things, just as speech is called fiery because it kindles, and words are called softer than oil because they soften the heart.

Or manna is said to melt because Christ, when received in the heart, in a certain manner undergoes dissolution through compassion. For how is the sinner’s heart dissolved from its hardness unless Christ is relaxed from the hardness of a judge? When He loosens sins as ice melts in clear weather, He is then loosened from the security of a judge, so that the mind, touched by His word, may melt more softly in hope of pardon and desire of love.

This sun sometimes grows hot over the righteous, as though in wrath, and melts manna; as if causing it to fail, when it temporarily withdraws the sweetness of bodily or spiritual consolation. Thus Jonah, when the consolation of his shady plant was taken from him by the withering of the ivy, grieved deeply, when the sun beat upon his head and he was sweltering, and he asked that he might die (Jonah 4) [Col. 0753D]. The sun of righteousness grows hot over good and evil alike, and there is none who hides from its heat; but over the good it does so through the heat of love, or as though through indignation, and over the wicked through the heat of wrath and fury. Hence the unbelieving Synagogue, over which God has poured out His wrath, now has no manna of true faith, because the faith of the ancients has first been blinded in it and has vanished and failed.

But in us, in the future, the manna of faith will cease, melted through complete illumination, when faith is made void and all understanding is laid open [Col. 0754A]. In a remarkable way, as will appear from what follows, manna which melted in the sun became hard in the fire. This shows that a mind turned toward the sun of righteousness, when it is dissolved and melted through desire of love, is then strengthened for the fire of suffering through the virtue of patience. This is shown by the one who says: “My heart has become like melting wax in the midst of my body. My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21).

“But on the sixth day they gathered double food, that is, two gomors for each person.”

All the righteous, from the beginning of the world through five ages until Christ, possessed the hope of eternal life through the righteousness of faith; and this is the one gomor gathered through each day until the sixth [Col. 0754B]. But in the sixth age, as on the sixth day before the Sabbath—that is, before the rest of souls—we gather two gomors, because we have both the hope and the pledge of eternal life: namely, Jesus Christ Himself, the author and finisher of our faith, who is with us in the sacrament of the altar until the consummation of the age. They, however, gathered one gomor because they had hope, but not yet the thing itself. We have hope and hold the thing itself, though not yet as we shall after this life. For although Christ is our refreshment in the present life and is eaten in the sacrifice of the altar, He does not yet refresh us unto satiety [Col. 0754C]. Rather, by this manner of eating, by which we receive Him for the present, we are prepared to attain eternal life; and we gather, as it were, a second gomor on this sixth day, so that on the seventh day—that is, on the Sabbath of souls—we may be refreshed unto satiety.

On the sixth day one gomor is gathered and consumed; the other is gathered and kept. The hope of eternal life which is held in the present fails with this life. For when the thing itself is fully seen, hope is entirely abolished. “For what a man sees, why does he hope for it?” But the other gomor is gathered and kept. Nor does it oppose this interpretation that the bread of eternal life is eaten on this sixth day, while the gomor to be kept for the Sabbath was not eaten on the sixth day. For present refreshment, compared with future refreshment, is scarcely more than a tasting beforehand and rather a preparation for future refreshment. For as we now eat, we taste beforehand through the efficacy of this food—that is, we gather and keep. We gather manna when, through the grace of this sacrament, we make daily progress so as to be able to eat more fully in the future. We keep manna when we persevere to the end in worthy veneration of this sacrament [Col. 0754D].

The Jews, who still wait like wild asses in their thirst, gather on this sixth day only one gomor, if indeed even one; and therefore on the Sabbath day they shall remain hungry, because on the Preparation they did not make provision for themselves.

This passage may also be understood differently. In the five books of Moses is contained instruction in a simple and innocent life: either through examples of the righteous, as in Genesis, or through commandments for right living, as in the other four books. These are the five days on which one gomor is gathered. The sixth day is the teaching of the New Testament, in which two gomors are gathered: that is, in the lesser commandments, the righteousness of the imperfect, such as existed in the Law, which brought no one to perfection; and in the greater commandments and counsels of perfection, the righteousness of the perfect [Col. 0755A]. Perfect righteousness, however, is the gomor of the Sabbath. For those who attain it possess a sabbath-rest of heart in joy and exultation.

These same matters may be understood differently. There are five virtues which may be signified by the five days. These are the five kinds of continence customarily denoted by the five virgins. The guarding of the five senses is necessary for us, so that, walking in innocence, we may be kept unstained by this world. The beginning of righteousness, namely turning away from evil, is to restrain the hand from works of iniquity, close the eyes lest they see evil, stop the ears lest they hear bloodshed, and hold the remaining senses back from unlawful things. Each abstinence, however, provides a single benefit: immunity from the punishment which the contrary transgression may bring. For one who does not steal, commit adultery, or kill avoids the punishment due to such deeds. Therefore one gomor is gathered on each day until the sixth day [Col. 0755B].

This sixth day is godliness (*pietas*), which not only hates evil but works righteousness and mercy. On this day two gomors are gathered, because godliness gives us a double benefit: immunity from punishment and hope of glory. This is what the Apostle says: “Bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but godliness is useful for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4). Godliness is useful for obtaining eternal life; it is useful for multiplying spiritual goods in this life; and it is useful also for obtaining carnal goods insofar as they are necessary [Col. 0755C]. One benefit belongs to the present time, namely the sixth day; the other belongs to future time, that is, the Sabbath. The benefit of fivefold continence, consisting in immunity from the temporal punishment established by laws against evildoers, belongs to the present time.

“And all the leaders of the multitude came and told Moses,” etc. (Exod. 16.)

[Col. 0755D] The leaders of the multitude, who came to Moses and reported the gathering, the melting, and the double gathering, are the teachers of the Church, who compare the reading of the New Testament with the reading of Moses. For the Law and the Gospel, as it were, converse with one another, because they mutually explain and disclose one another, and mutually approve and confirm their testimonies. Therefore, when ecclesiastical teachers unfold the Law concerning Christ through the words of the Gospel, then the leaders of the multitude announce to Moses about the manna. But when the Law unfolds the words of the Gospel, then Moses speaks and says: “This is what the Lord has spoken.” As though he said: The event fittingly corresponds to the words of God. And Moses adds: “The Sabbath-rest shall be holy to the Lord.” The Lord loves rest, that he may rest in us and, through this, we in him.

Now there is one rest of the future age, of which it is said: “From henceforth, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labours” (Rev. XIV). There is also a rest of the present age, of which the prophet says: “Cease to do perversely” (Isa. I). One comes to the rest of the future age through the six works of mercy enumerated in the Gospel, where it says: “I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,” etc. (Matt. XXV); or through the number six of perfection, according to the measure of each person’s greater or lesser righteousness. For there are six days in which one must work; then comes night, that is, death, in which no one can work. After the six days comes Sabbath, because after the completion of good works comes the rest of souls.

And because good works must be pursued throughout the entire time of this present life, as it is written, “Whatever your hand is able to do, do earnestly,” there is added: “Tomorrow, whatever is to be done, do,” etc. (Eccl. IX). By this he instructs us to do what must be done and to bake what must be baked. The one relates to works of righteousness and mercy, which ought unceasingly to be done insofar as we can; the other to the infirmities of our character and deeds, which must be baked by the fire of repentance. Or, the one relates to lesser good works, which can be done more easily; the other to more perfect pursuits of virtue, which ought to be thoroughly baked by the fire of more fervent devotion.

What he says, “Tomorrow,” should be understood as if it said: Henceforth, let this be kept as a law for the future: let the things just mentioned be done. “But whatever remains, you shall set aside until morning.” This must be understood of manna kept for the Sabbath. “And they did so,” etc. That what was put aside for the Sabbath did not spoil is a sign that good works done for the future rest remain whole for the future. But things done for the sake of the present life and love of the world spoil; worms swarm from them. “And Moses said: Eat,” etc.

It is rightly said: “Eat it today, because today is the Sabbath of the Lord.” For in the future life there will be a time for eating, not for gathering. Whatever you gather here, you will then eat as the fruit of your labours; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you. It is rightly added: “Today it will not be found in the field,” because after this life it will not be permitted to work, nor will manna then be found from the exercise of working, which may be signified by the field. “Gather for six days,” he says: that is, live in the perfection of good works. “But on the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord; therefore it will not be found”: that is, after this life there will be rest for souls, and manna that can be gathered will not be found.

“The seventh day came.” This does not seem to be understood of the first Sabbath, since it was previously said: “Eat today, because it is the Sabbath of the Lord.” Rather, Moses took care to show that manna was not found on only one Sabbath. Thus, by two examples he makes clear that this is to be understood of the Sabbaths that followed; and he seems to add the second Sabbath in order to rebuke the people’s unbelief. For after the example of the first Sabbath—if this is to be understood of the second—and after Moses’ words about gathering a double supply of food, “they went out to gather, and did not find any.” But if the words, “The seventh day came,” etc., are to be understood of the first Sabbath, then what Moses says, “Today it will not be found in the field,” may be confirmed by the statement that “they went out to gather, and did not find any.”

### And the Lord said to Moses: “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments?” etc. (Exod. XVI)

Even brute animals love leisure and fullness, and in these lies whatever happiness they possess. But true blessedness is constituted by holy leisure and holy fullness; these two are signified by the Sabbath and manna. Therefore, after the Lord had bestowed leisure and fullness upon his people in manna and the Sabbath, and had thereby prefigured the true blessedness that he would give to those obedient to him, he rebukes their disobedience, through which they can be estranged from the things most to be desired. He says, therefore: “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?” As though he said: Although I provide you with the Sabbath’s leisure and bread from heaven, and by this invite you to better things, it is too little that you should be willing to keep my commandments.

This question, by which he asks, “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments?” etc., corresponds to that question by which, later coming in the flesh, he asked: “O unbelieving generation, how long shall I endure you?” (Mark IX). After the Lord’s question, Moses invites them to consider God’s benefits, exhorting them to notice that the Lord has given them the Sabbath and a double supply of food on the sixth day, so that they may be willing to serve him. This signifies that he will give his elect rest from labour, together with consolations in the present life and the future life.
