Two lives are here suggested to us: namely, the active life, in which we must now labour, and the contemplative life, for which we must labour and in which there will be leisure for the contemplation of God alone. Although that contemplative life belongs especially to the future age, it must nevertheless be represented in this age by holy leisure, which is prefigured in the Sabbath. Concerning this leisure Moses adds: “Let each one remain where he is; let no one go out from his place on the Sabbath day.” As though he said: Let each person rest in his own house and not go out to any work on the Sabbath day. By this we are admonished, in the time of contemplation, to remain within ourselves and not go out through unlawful desires, but to gather our whole attention, in purity of heart, toward thinking upon and loving God alone.

“And the house of Israel called its name Man,” etc. Since the name *Man* signifies a question—for it is interpreted, “What is this?”—it does not convey a definite designation. Therefore Moses took care to show some knowledge of it from its incidental qualities, for the sake of a definite mystery: by its appearance, where he says, “Like coriander seed”; by its colour, where he says, “white”; and by its taste, where he says, “its taste was like fine flour with honey.”

Yet according to the literal wording, manna seems to be compared to coriander seed in colour, if one reads without distinction: “like white coriander seed.” According to this understanding, coriander seed must be white somewhere in the world, so that manna may rightly be compared to it in whiteness. But if the words must be read distinctly and understood without the comparison, manna is said to be white, while in comparison it is “like coriander seed”; this may be understood of its appearance, quality, or form.

Manna is rightly said to be like coriander seed, because the word of God has something of a vegetable, by which the weak may be nourished. Hence the Apostle says: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV). For Christ condescends to the weak even to the minuteness of a small seed, in light and very small commandments, so that one who cannot receive him in the loftiness of a more perfect life may receive him in the moderation of an easier life; and that one who cannot receive him in the depth of mysteries may receive him in the simplicity of faith.

Manna is called white because the word of God is clean and pure from every stain, according to the saying: “The words of the Lord are chaste words” (Ps. XI). And Christ, though he himself is white and ruddy, cleanses and whitens his own, according to the saying: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L). That the word of God is sweet as honey is shown by him who says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII). That its taste is like fine flour with honey is shown by him who says: “The Lord fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. LXXX).

### And Moses said to them: “This is the word which the Lord commanded” (Exod. XVI)

Moses’ command to fill a *gomor* with manna, so that it may be kept for future generations, signifies Christ, who is the true manna and in whom is the form and standard of all righteousness, preserved for us and for every generation to come, so that we may know the bread by which those who were brought out of the land of Egypt were fed in the wilderness. For we have been justified by faith in Christ; those who come after us are to be justified; and all the righteous before us were justified and brought out of the land of Egypt—that is, liberated from the slavery of the devil.

### And Moses said to Aaron: “Take one vessel,” etc., to be kept in the tabernacle (ibid.)

[Col. 0758D]

What the Lord spoke to Moses, Moses speaks to Aaron, so that by the ministry of the priest the manna may be placed in its proper place.

Aaron therefore places manna in a vessel when the priest, taking from the law of God what ought to be done or said, preaches Christ as conceived in the blessed Virgin by the Holy Spirit, so that she may be believed to be *Theotokos* (θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”), and as a golden urn containing manna; and when he places Christ, who is to be preached, in the heart of a hearer who receives Christ in himself by faith; and when he teaches that Christ is in the unity of the catholic Church, not in the synagogue of the Jews or in the conventicles of schismatics or heretics.

The vessel of this manna, which is placed in the tabernacle, is the small number of the elect, or the faithful synagogue of the Jews. But the tabernacle itself is the multitude of those called, or the universal Church of Jews and Gentiles. What is said, “Aaron placed it in the tabernacle to be kept,” is said here by anticipation, because it was done later, after the tabernacle had been constructed.

That the Lord first commanded that manna not be kept, and then commanded that manna be kept in a vessel and the vessel in the tabernacle, may relate to the fact that the word of God is sometimes to be hidden and sometimes not to be hidden. For he who says, “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII), himself says: “I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart” (Ps. XXXIX). The word of God must be hidden in the bosom of love and in the bosom of memory, lest it slip away through negligence or forgetfulness; it must also be hidden from human praise and from unworthy hearers. But when the matter requires it, it must not be hidden out of favour toward, or fear of, human beings.

### And the children of Israel ate man for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land (Exod. XVI)

The word of God, or the body of Christ, according to this mode of use by which we presently partake of it, is our food until, leaving this wilderness, we come to the inhabited land, namely the land of the living.

The number forty serves various mysteries. In this number of days God poured out his indignation upon all flesh, so that it perished in the waters of the flood, except for the few preserved and saved in the ark. By this number, following the example of Moses, Elijah, and Christ himself, fasting was consecrated, through which the wrath and indignation of God may be appeased. By this number of years God trained his people in the wilderness, alternating the changing seasons with benefits and punishments, being appeased or angered. Hence it is written: “For forty years I was near to this generation” (Ps. XCIV); or, according to another text: “For forty years I was offended by this generation.” By this number disobedience is punished or corrected; by this number obedience is exercised. Thus this number signifies wrath and grace.

Its meaning must be considered in its parts: namely, ten and four. Ten, because of the Decalogue, signifies obedience to the Law; four signifies obedience to the Gospel. The first consists in the simplicity of innocence; the second in the perfection of righteousness. To the first belongs not to kill and not to take what belongs to another; to the second, not to be angry and to distribute one’s own possessions.

The number four is to be understood in the four Gospels, or in the four principal virtues, whose perfection is prescribed in the Gospel, or in the four sacraments of Christ’s nativity, passion, resurrection, and ascension. By the power of these we are conformed to Christ, by being reborn, suffering with him, rising with him, and ascending from strength to strength. The four virtues are attained through the instruction of the four Gospels and the power of the four sacraments. Therefore, since our whole life must be spent in obedience to the Law according to its moral precepts, and the strength of the soul must always be increased through obedience to the Gospel, the time of our life is rightly prefigured by this number, as though ten were multiplied by four.

### They were fed with this food until they touched the borders of the land of Canaan (Exod. XVI)

We shall touch the borders of the land of Canaan when, leaving this life, we begin to enter the land of the living, as it is written: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. CXXVI). But when this mortal nature has put on immortality, then, having advanced beyond its borders, we shall dwell there securely, because “the Lord will save Zion; the seed of his servants shall possess it, and those who love his name shall dwell in it” (Ps. LXVIII).

The land of Canaan is the land of promise, of which it was said to Abraham: “I will give you the land of Canaan, the portion of your inheritance” (Ps. CIV). Why that visible land was called the land of Canaan is readily explained: it was possessed by the seed of Canaan, who was cursed by Noah and subjected to servitude. But three reasons occur why the land of the living, signified by the land of promise, may spiritually be the land of Canaan.

For, after evil spirits have been cast out according to the saying, “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X), it is to be possessed by the children of Israel—that is, by us. Again, all of us in Adam were cast out of paradise, as the seed of Canaan was cast out of the land of promise; but, changed into children of Israel and beneficially moved—for *Canaan* is interpreted “moved” or “movement”—we shall obtain it. Again, the Jews may be called Canaanites because, having become a perverse generation and unbelieving children, they are the seed of Canaan and not of Judah. The promised land was promised to them, but was taken from them because of their unbelief; it has been given to us, who according to the Spirit are reckoned among the children of Abraham, according to the saying: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruit” (Matt. XXI). And again: “Many shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness” (Matt. XVIII).

### But a gomor is the tenth part of an ephah (Exod. XVI)

[Col. 0760D]

By the measure of the ephah, which is completed in ten parts, may be understood the measure of Christ’s gift, by which he distributes to the whole rational creation—that is, to the nine orders of angels and to human creation—as he wills and in the measure he wills. And since a human being holds the tenth place in the order of rational creation, which alone is capable of righteousness and blessedness and therefore alone can participate in Christ, the tenth part of the ephah rightly belongs to him.

For by the ephah is rightly understood the fullness of grace, sufficient for all; but by the gomor, the distribution of grace found in each individual. Although this distribution of grace is unequal, it is nevertheless brought back, through the communion of charity, to the unity of equality, since charity brings it about that what belongs to each individual may be common to all.

### From the Book of Numbers

“Our soul is dry; our eyes look upon nothing but Man.”

When the mixed multitude that had gone up with the children of Israel burned with desire for meat, sitting and weeping together with the children of Israel who had joined themselves to it, it said: “Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish that we ate in Egypt for nothing. Cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic come to mind. Our soul is dry. Our eyes look upon nothing but man” (Num. XI).

This is a pattern for our own time. For the children of Israel, joined to those who murmur, signify good people corrupted by association with evil people, as it is written of some: “They mingled among the nations and learned their works” (Ps. CV). And the Apostle says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV).

Many who have left secular life, as though departing from Egypt, and have undertaken the path of a better life, recall the foods of Egypt, their seasonings and incitements—that is, the vices of their former way of life and the delights attached to them. They miserably wither and waste away in desire for such things, and they loathe the spiritual manna of God’s word, saying: “Our soul is dry.” Of such people it is written: “Their soul abhorred every food” (Ps. CVI).

Often, moreover, people of this kind, inwardly joined to evil people yet placed among good people, hate doing good; they also loathe hearing good things and seeing good things in others. While they search in the life of the good for examples and consolations of their own error, and find nothing except the good things they loathe, they say: “Our eyes look upon nothing but man.” And whenever heretics among true church people, Jews among Christians, laypeople among clergy, clergy among religious persons, or those around them, see nothing except things that are holy, chaste, honourable, of good repute, and fitting to their order and profession, then those who loathe such things and look at them unwillingly say: “Our eyes look upon nothing but man.”

Yet the disgusted say, “Our eyes look upon nothing but man,” just as the righteous person says with rejoicing: “The testimony of Jesus Christ, whatever I saw” (Rev. I); and as is said of the bride: “What will you see in the Shunammite but the dances of the camps?” (Song VII).

What the *man* was like he shows when he says: “The man was like coriander seed, of the colour of bdellium.” He had said this in Exodus, except that there he explicitly mentioned the colour white and did not use the name bdellium. Bdellium, as they say, is an aromatic tree.

That the people went about gathering manna signifies the devotion of believers, who mentally survey what is preached concerning Christ so that they may receive spiritual refreshment. Manna was broken in a mill because, when the word of God is examined between the two Testaments, or between letter and spirit—that is, spiritual understanding and exposition of the letter—it is ground and crushed so as to be understood more subtly.

Alternatively: the mind, in its mobility, goes around and surveys many things that can be thought either for faith or against faith, and thus turns in a circle like the upper millstone. When beneath it stands the firmness of unshaken faith, the word of faith is broken into small pieces and understood more subtly. Both millstones are found in the mind: one in the steadfastness of faith or a good resolve; the other in the survey—that is, the consideration—of things to be believed or done. Or one is in the will, which lies beneath reason in obedience; the other in reason’s judgment, which moves about in inquiry and crushes in discernment. Or one is in fear and the other in hope. In these the word of God is crushed, so that no smallest command may be despised and not one iota or one stroke neglected.

Manna was pounded in a mortar. The mortar is our heart, where the word of God is struck as though by a pestle. In Solomon it is shown that a fool is not stripped of his folly even if he is pounded in a mortar like groats—that is, even if he is troubled in his folly or conscience while the pestle of harsh rebuke strikes from above. Thus it is written: “If you pound a fool in a mortar like groats, striking from above with a pestle, his folly will not be taken from him” (Prov. XXVII).

But just as the fool is pounded by those who hate folly, so the word of God is pounded by those who hate wisdom, either by the pestle of contradiction or of persecution. Some, by their tongues; others, by swords; others, by examples of evil deeds, wear down the word of God in persecuting it and crush it bit by bit. For through the exercise of contradiction and persecution, the word of God is always investigated more subtly and understood more subtly. Indeed, many mysteries of faith have been disclosed to us which would still have remained closed if the faith had not endured so many adversaries.

Thus manna is pounded by the pestle in the mortar when, through the beating inflicted by adversaries, the word of God is considered in the heart more discerningly and subtly. And if perhaps adversaries are lacking to attack the word of God, nevertheless through the exercise of Christian discipline, by which each person ought to oppose himself, the word of God is pounded in the heart as though by a pestle; through the practice of discipline it is always discerned more subtly. While we examine these words, what are we doing except breaking manna in the mill or pounding it in the mortar?

But however much we examine it, however much we crush this, as it were, coriander seed by diligent meditation, it can still be crushed, broken into more divisible parts, or ground more finely. For through participation it always advances in increase, and what has been crushed grows. Manna is broken or ground in two ways: either when the word of God is diligently examined so as to be understood more subtly, or when, in our zeal for progress, this is done so that it may be kept more strictly.

A distinction may be made between breaking manna and grinding manna: the former concerns matters more difficult either in understanding or in practice; the latter, matters easier in one or the other respect. The people ground manna in a mortar and baked it in a pot.

There is a pot of tribulation, of which Jeremiah says: “Behold, I see a boiling pot” (Jer. I). In the pot of tribulation manna is baked by the fire of suffering or charity, when amid the evils we endure we are made more and more firm in the good that is within us. This happens when God is loved more amid afflictions, and, for God’s sake, even the one who persecutes us is loved.

A *torta*, or in its diminutive *tortula*, seems to derive from *torquere*, “to twist.” Whether bread is called this generally because it is shaped by twisting and twisted in shaping, just as a cheese-mould (*formella*) is generally named from shaping (*formare*); or whether some kind of bread is so called from a particular art of twisting: we must believe that the little cakes are not mentioned here without purpose, nor should it be taken without reason that Scripture took such care to say that manna was broken and ground and that little cakes were made from what had been broken and ground.

Perhaps this very word now under discussion, because it is the word of God and therefore manna, may, if it can worthily be broken and ground, be shaped into little cakes, so that what is written may be turned toward the edification of faith and charity. For if the love through which faith works is the fulfilment of the Law (Rom. XIII), and if the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon the one commandment of charity (Matt. XXII), why should it not be permissible to turn toward the edification of charity or faith all things that have been beneficially written, since all things have been written for charity’s sake, for whose sake also all things have been made?

Therefore, when a word of God from the Law is taken and, as it were, appropriated for a testimony of faith or the edification of charity to something other than that for which it seems to have been originally set down, remember that the people of God made little cakes from ground manna. It is therefore permissible, for the grace of faith or charity, to turn the historical, literal, and simple sense into a mystical understanding and spiritual sense, and from things written and done anywhere to conceive of things that ought beneficially to be done.

Indeed, it is also fitting to form, from the words of God placed anywhere and in whatever manner, counsels of salvation for our times, necessities, infirmities, and habits—always preserving the charity by which God must be loved immovably and which all Scripture serves. To preserve this charity, one must make provision in manifold and various ways amid innumerable perils of temptations, so that a compelling necessity may often force one, for righteousness’ sake, to attempt certain things seemingly against righteousness.

For the preservation of this charity, the strictness of righteousness must often be bent into the moderation of mercy; what has been granted from a consideration of mercy must often be restored to the severity of discipline; and a lesser evil must often be tolerated in order that a more serious crime may be avoided. For this reason Moses, considering the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, permitted a bill of divorce to be given, lest the crime of homicide be committed.

Often we must lose a neighbour’s favour lest we lose God’s favour. Often, when Christ and one believed to act in Christ’s stead command contrary things, Christ’s precept, “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X), must be administered with such moderation that one obeys God as though against obedience. Often, when unlawful promises or oaths have been made, the word of God concerning the choice of truth must be turned to such an understanding that, out of reverence for truth, a work of wickedness is not presumed. For in such a necessity it is more prudent for an error to be recalled by repentance than for God’s ordinances to be overturned and the reverence due to them to be denied.

Just as dispensation is to be admitted when danger presses from both sides, in choosing the lesser evil, so a command or counsel of God must sometimes be bent, because of human weakness, toward the choice of a lesser good. Hence Paul, showing that he condescends to human weakness, although good people ought to devote themselves more eagerly to the service of righteousness than evil people ordinarily devote themselves to wickedness, says: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and lawlessness leading to lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification” (Rom. VI). In this place he does not invite them to what is perfect, but bends the counsel toward what is suited to our weakness.

Likewise, although in one place he says: “I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain thus,” etc. (I Cor. VII), writing to Timothy he bends the counsel, saying: “But I will that the younger women marry” (I Tim. V).

All the righteousness of good people in the present life is, as it were, a certain bending away from the highest perfection and highest rectitude; and, if weighed faithfully, it is found to possess less. Even the righteousness of the perfect is more an effort and a running toward the goal of consummation than a grasping of perfection. For however much anyone has advanced and progressed by running, righteousness nevertheless still walks before him, not yet fully grasped; but one who holds fast to righteousness will finally grasp it.

Paul shows this in himself when he says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if somehow I may lay hold of that for which I too have been laid hold of by Christ Jesus” (Phil. III). Therefore our life must be arranged and directed in such a way that, since we are not free immediately to grasp what is perfect, we bend the commandments of God from what exceeds our strength toward what is possible for us. I say “bend,” not by changing them, but by approaching them and observing them according to our strength.

For although we are unable to direct all our thoughts, affections, and intentions toward God as chastely and purely as is worthy and right, so as to love him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind, it is nevertheless wiser to love according to the measure of our weakness than not to love at all. And if we cannot offer God prayers as pure as we desire, it is nevertheless better to pray as we are given and as we are able than not to pray at all.

Therefore, when perfect things are imposed upon us, lest we do nothing because we cannot do everything, they must be bent toward what we can do, so that we may in some measure be found excusable in what we ought to do but cannot, according to the Lord’s word concerning the woman who served him: “She has done what she could” (Mark XIV).

Thus all counsels prescribed for us in the words of God must be understood and received so that they may be turned into an occasion of our heavenly salvation, as the reason of circumstances dictates—circumstances in which one must either yield to necessity or make some more lenient concession to weakness. But in everything that we order concerning others, even though it is sometimes necessary to proceed more strictly, we must keep mercy in mind, so that we too may obtain mercy from God. Thus the little cakes made from manna will have a taste like bread made with oil.

After Scripture had shown how they broke and ground manna, and made little cakes and baked them, it took care to add that manna descended with the dew. When the word of God moistens, it is dew; when it refreshes, it is manna. When it is preached, it moistens; when it is worthily received and kept, it refreshes. Manna therefore descends with the dew, because the word of God reaches the hearts of believers through the preaching of prophets and apostles. Hence the Apostle says: “How will they believe in him of whom they have not heard?” etc. (Rom. X). And shortly afterward: “Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (ibid.).

Thus the word in the heart is manna; the word in the mouth is dew, though it is nonetheless manna as well. Dew descends at night, as it is written: “While all things were held in quiet silence, and night in its course had reached the middle of its journey, your almighty Word leaped down from heaven, from the royal thrones” (Wis. XVIII).

### Again, from the Book of Numbers: “They began to be weary of the journey” (Num. XI)

Many who have been devoted to divine service and professed a stricter life eventually grow weary of laborious discipline, which can be ended only with the end of life. They murmur against Moses—that is, against God himself, the giver of the Law, or against his Law—as though it were unbearably unpleasant. Having no hidden bread in the wilderness, which is sweeter, nor stolen waters, which are sweeter, they say: “There is no bread; there is no water.” Excessively loathing heavenly manna, they add: “Our soul now nauseates at this very light food.”

For after the initial fervour of a conversion begun, these people become lukewarm and worse than the cold. The Lord vomits them from his mouth, because after first allowing them to be, as it were, incorporated into himself, he then permits them by his just judgment to return to their own vomit. Hence he says: “Would that you were hot or cold; but now, because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you from my mouth” (Rev. III).

The disgusted called that food “very light,” either because God prepared it for them without any labour of their own, or because it was purchased at no price, or because its excessive abundance made it taste less pleasant to them and thus caused it to be despised. So, too, through ease of understanding and desire for the foods of Egypt, the word of God sometimes becomes cheap in disgusted minds and turns to weariness. The bread of life and understanding, and the health-giving water of wisdom, are not enough for them; muttering, they say: “There is no bread; there is no water.”

### In Deuteronomy: “He gave you food,” etc. (Deut. VIII)

Hear now, O Jew, and understand from your Law; if you are willing to believe it, learn carefully what manna is. [Col. 0766A] Do not say any longer, “What is this?” You and your fathers—unbelieving like yourself, and therefore your fathers—did not understand this food: what it was, and for what purpose it had been given to you. Search the Scriptures, in which you suppose that you have life; search the Law in which you put your trust. Behold, it shows you—not obscurely or enigmatically, but plainly and openly—what the true manna is and for what purpose God gave you the food of manna. For no other reason than what is written here, inserted in your writings, often impressed upon your ears, and set before your eyes: “That he might show you,” it says, “that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord.” Manna was given to you in vain if you do not yet see the showing given to you in manna. It was given as a showing; it shows something.

A human being indeed lives, according to this bodily life, by bodily bread—that is, bodily food—to which bodily manna belongs. For, as Scripture testifies, loaves were made from manna. But according to the spiritual life, a person does not live by this bread, to which bodily manna belongs, but by every word of God which was shown in manna. For how is it shown through manna that a person lives by the word of God, unless the Word itself is also shown to you through manna? Yet what you refuse to believe is shown to you in vain; you cannot see it, as Isaiah says concerning you: “Who is blind but my servant, and who is deaf but he to whom I sent my messengers?” (Isa. 42).

But God has shown us [Col. 0766C] what he hid from your eyes, hiding his face from the house of Jacob: namely, that the true manna is that which proceeds from the mouth of God, Christ—the power of God and the wisdom of God—who says in Sirach: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 34). This is the Word of which God spoke: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and all things were created” (Ps. 148). This is the Word to which the Law and the Prophets bore witness. And because the prophets, in whom God spoke, are called the mouth of God, every word by which this Word is proclaimed by the prophets proceeds from the mouth of God, so that a human being may live in it.

“Word proceeding from the mouth of God” is said in three ways: the Word in the Father, begotten from the Father and coeternal with the Father; the word in the mouth of the preacher; and the word in the heart of the believer. The word in the heart [Col. 0766D] of the believer is faith or charity, or any virtue of the soul that may be called an implanted word. But God speaks the word of faith in the heart in a hidden whisper, as it is written: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood have not revealed this to you, but my Father” (Matt. 16). Every word proceeding from the mouth of God is shown in manna. For Christ is manna; the word of preaching is manna; the inward word which God speaks in the heart is manna. Both of these are manna in Christ, and Christ is manna in each of them.

From the Book of Joshua: “The manna ceased after …” (Josh. 5).

The children of Israel, leaving the wilderness and coming up from the Jordan, encamped on the tenth day of the first month [Col. 0767A] at Gilgal. There, purified by a second circumcision, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, in the plains of Jericho; and on the next day they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened bread and parched grain of that same year. Then the manna ceased.

Manna is the word of God in the Law and in the Gospel. But the manna of the divine Word according to the figurative observances of the Law ceased when Christ, on the fourteenth day of the moon at evening, celebrated the true Passover with his disciples and gave them the fruit of the promised land to eat. For by the produce of the land Christ himself may be signified, of whom it is written: “Our land shall yield its fruit” (Ps. 44); or the fruits of evangelical righteousness and perfection. When this began, manna ceased according to the righteousness that came from works of the Law. Thus the Passover and the eating of the land’s produce rightly brought manna to an end, because Christ’s death and the law of the Gospel put an end to the figures of the Law.

From the Book of Wisdom: “You commanded your people to be nourished with the food of angels …” (Wis. 16).

It is written in Exodus concerning manna that its taste was like fine flour with honey (Exod. 16); in the Book of Numbers it is written that it tasted like cakes baked with oil (Num. 11). But here it is said that it contained every delight and the sweetness of every flavor, and that, accommodating itself to each person’s wish, it changed into whatever anyone desired. Because of so great a variety, doubt may arise concerning the flavor of manna. For if it tasted for each person according to that person’s wish, [Col. 0767C] how can it be shown to have had a definite flavor like fine flour with honey, or like cakes baked with oil? Or why would they have needed to loathe manna and desire melons, cucumbers, onions, and garlic, if the flavor of all things was presented to them in manna?

But it may be said that manna properly and naturally had the flavor of fine flour with honey, and in one respect that of cakes baked with oil—just as one seasoning, made from different ingredients, can present several flavors at once. Or perhaps when uncooked it tasted like fine flour with honey, but when cooked like cakes baked with oil. Scripture mentions the latter where it speaks of cooked manna. But for those to whom these two flavors did not suffice, manna—whether in the twofold manner just described, mixed or distinct—seems, from this Scripture, to have reproduced whatever other flavor they desired.

Just as those who taste sweetness of honey in a honeyed cup may nevertheless desire to taste the sweetness of honey more fully as it is in the comb, so they could desire melons, cucumbers, onions, and garlic, although they had experienced the flavors of all these in manna. Perhaps they desired to perceive them exactly as they were accustomed to perceive them in their own proper kinds; or, overcome by weariness of sameness—as human curiosity always delights in variety—they might wish, from frivolity, to taste in other things the flavors they had tasted in manna. So lovers of wine often, through the fault of frivolity or curiosity, seek the flavor of the same wine in one cup after another.

Thus manna appears to have had definite flavors, [Col. 0768A] which Scripture specifies, and nevertheless to have tasted in many ways according to varying desires. Yet its tasting in many ways was not in the manna itself, but in those for whom it tasted differently. This opinion may be supported by the fact that one and the same fruit, as experience proves, tastes differently to different persons: one insists it is less sweet, another more sweet, another not sweet at all. Something similar is said—if the opinion is true—of a single discourse spoken through the apostles in whatever language: in the ears of the hearers it sounded differently, according to each person’s understanding, in that person’s own language.

Nevertheless, this opinion seems opposed by Scripture’s statement: “It changed into whatever anyone desired” (Wis. 6), so that it seems to place the cause of the variety in manna itself. Unless perhaps “it changed” was said because it appeared so to those tasting it.

Since what is uncertain is usually exposed to various opinions, it should suffice for us, in a doubtful matter, to consider a way in which what Scripture says could have been possible, lest faith in Scripture waver in our hearts because of some conjecture of impossibility. We may still say otherwise: namely, that manna had such a grace of flavor that it could surpass or equal any pleasantness of taste and satisfy every desire for anything desired in food. If this is true, manna changed into whatever anyone wanted, not by reproducing the desired flavor but by an equal or greater compensation, [Col. 0768C] just as a drink of water or of wine can quench thirst for water: one according to desire, the other beyond desire.

But spiritual manna, which lacks nothing in any grace of flavor, tastes so much sweeter and more delightful as it more fully surpasses every desire. God, who is goodness, whose substance is charity and whose essence is loving-kindness, willing to show what a sweet nature his substance has, and how sweet was his love for his children—how supremely gracious it is because of the exceeding charity by which he loved us—sent his Son, the bread of angels, into the world: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3). This is the true manna which the Lord rained down for eating. “For the heavens distilled before the God of Sinai” (Ps. [Col. 0768D] 67). This is the voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance; this is what God in his sweetness prepared for the poor.

Christ, descending for all and condescending to all, draws everyone to himself by the ineffable grace of his sweetness; he rejects no one, receives all to repentance, tastes most sweetly to all who receive him, and alone suffices and satisfies every devout desire. Having in himself every delight and seasoning and the sweetness of every flavor, he adapts himself differently and in different ways to different persons, according to each one’s desire, appetite, and affection. For the ordinances of the Lord are right, rejoicing hearts (Ps. 18): as many, indeed, as there are ways in Christ toward Christ. This tastes good to each person according to what that person chooses and loves.

There are diverse ranks and manners of the righteous, diverse professions and ways of life, diverse vows and pursuits. To all these Christ’s kindness yields itself: he who is sweet to all, imparting himself to everyone and distributing to each the seasonings of his own flavor. For he tastes differently to the penitent and beginner, differently to the one advancing, and differently to the one who has arrived; differently in the active life and in the contemplative; differently to one using this world and to one not using it; differently to the celibate and to the married; differently to the abstainer who distinguishes one day from another, and differently to the one who regards every day alike.

Manna tastes sweet when it relieves necessities, heals infirmities, moderates temptations, assists endeavors, and strengthens hope. Jesus is sweet, and sweet is his name, and his memorial is in the desire of the soul. He is sweet when he receives vows, [Col. 0769B] restrains sobs, ends sighs, and wipes away tears. Sweet in purity of life; sweet in peace of conscience; sweet in hope of the vision of himself. Sweet in prayer, sweet in speech, sweet in reading, sweet in contemplation, sweet in compunction, and in the heart’s rejoicing. Sweet in the mouth, sweet in the heart, sweet in love: love itself is the love of sweetness, and sweetness the sweetness of love. His inestimable delight is first among gifts and supreme among delights: those who have tasted will still hunger; those who hunger will be satisfied; and, filled, they will always pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness.

Again, from the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “When you come together in one place …” (1 Cor. 11).

[Col. 0769C] After teaching concerning matters pertaining to upright conduct, he proceeds consequently to those necessary for salvation: that is, the sacrament of the altar, in which the Corinthians especially erred. For they gathered in church to eat and drink, and afterward, filled and drunk, communicated in Christ’s body and blood. In this they are reproved on two counts: first, because they did not invite the poor to their meal; second, because, having eaten and not fasted, they communicated in so great a sacrament.

Christ truly gave his body and blood to the disciples after supper, as blessed Augustine says, in order to commend it more strongly, wishing to imprint this final act more firmly upon their memory. Or, as is said elsewhere, after celebrating the Passover with his disciples according to the Jewish custom, he began the new Passover, giving his body and blood to his disciples in the sacrament of bread and wine; signifying that the former Passover was no longer to be observed, and instituting and commanding that which he performed at the end to be retained.

“It is now not to eat the Lord’s supper” (ibid.); that is, you do not gather to eat as for the Lord’s supper, but as for your own, since you give nothing to the poor. He proves this: “For each one takes beforehand his own supper.” Or otherwise: “When you come together, it is now not”—that is, it is not permitted—“to eat the Lord’s supper”; that is, to communicate in the body and blood of the Lord. And he adds why it is no longer permitted them: because each one takes his own supper beforehand—that is, eats before the Lord’s supper—and thus, having eaten, you partake of the Lord’s supper. But this is no longer permitted; it is permitted only to those who are fasting. According to this reading we have here the Apostle’s clear authority that we ought to receive this sacrament only while fasting. Elsewhere in the whole Apostle it is not found so plainly: “Because the Lord Jesus.”

Since our salvation rests upon this sacrament, and no sacrament in the Church is greater, apart from the apostolic succession, certain questions are customarily raised here which ought not to be omitted because they are necessary to faith.

First, however, it should be noted and rightly understood that at the end of a certain gloss on this passage it is said that “Christ’s flesh is for the salvation of the body, his blood for our soul.” Do not both—Christ’s flesh and blood—work both in us, namely salvation of soul and body? Why then does it divide them, as though each were not effective for the salvation of both? Elsewhere the Apostle says: “Christ died for our offences and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 5). Yet both Christ’s death and his resurrection work both things in us: remission of sins and our justification. Similarly, it is said that Christ’s flesh works salvation of the body and his blood salvation of the soul, although both work both kinds of salvation in us. Flesh is more properly referred to the body, blood to the soul, because the seat of the soul is in the blood. Further, flesh is received under the species of bread, which is food and sustenance for the body; while blood is received under the species of wine, which produces gladness of mind. For bread strengthens the human heart, and wine gladdens it. Under each species the whole Christ is received. But if he were received under only one, it would signify efficacy only for the salvation of the other—that is, of soul or body.

But it is asked why the sacrament is celebrated under the species of bread and wine rather than of other things. This is because the author and giver of this sacrament consecrated and gave it under these species; and because it is under the species of bread made from wheat, since he called himself the grain of wheat, which is more worthy and more useful than other grains.

There are three things to be considered regarding this sacrament: things signifying only; things both signified and signifying; and things signified only. The things signifying only are the visible species, which are called sacraments, according to the statement: “A sacrament is a visible sign of the invisible grace of God.” Things both signified and signifying are Christ’s body and blood themselves. Christ’s body is signified there by the species of bread, and his blood by the species of wine. Again, Christ’s body received there signifies the body of the Church, while the blood signifies charity, the property of signifying being taken from the nature of the visible species under which they are received, as has been said in this Epistle. Things signified only are Christ’s body, which is the Church, and charity, by which it is united to its head, Christ, and in which, as in blood, lies the life of this body.

Again, it is asked whether the substance of bread passes into Christ’s body, and the substance of wine into his blood. This must altogether be believed. Therefore, if the material substance of bread passes by priestly blessing into Christ’s true body, and wine into his blood, the substance of bread will be Christ’s body; therefore some substance not born of the Virgin will be Christ’s body. This is not true. Human substance is God, yet not every substance which is not eternal is God, nor is anything not eternal God.

It is customarily asked in what subject those accidents remain which are seen and sensed after consecration. Some say that they are grounded in the air; some, in the eyes of those looking upon them; and some believe that they remain without a subject. The last seems more probable, although this may appear contrary to their nature. For the order of nature is not to be sought here, where everything is done above nature.

It is also customarily asked what is broken in the breaking, and what the portions of that breaking signify. Some say that only the sacrament is broken, because Christ’s body is impassible and receives no breaking or division of parts. But then how will that confession of Berengar, made and written at Rome before the pope in the presence of 113 bishops, be true? For he confessed that the bread and wine placed on the altar after consecration are not only a sacrament but also Christ’s true body and blood; and that they are sensibly handled and broken by priests’ hands and ground by the teeth of the faithful—not merely sacramentally, but in truth. Behold, he says that Christ’s body is truly broken [Col. 0771C] and ground by the teeth of the faithful. By the same reasoning it also truly appears there, not only to the eyes of the heart but to bodily eyes.

Berengar’s error was that after the consecration of bread, bread remained, and only the sacrament of Christ’s body—not his true body—was present there. But in his confession he expressed the truth of faith, saying that not only the sacrament, as he had formerly believed, was subject to that breaking, but Christ’s body in truth. For Christ’s body is truly that which is seen, broken, and ground by the faithful’s teeth.

“But,” you ask, “how is what is impassible broken, and what is indivisible divided?” We answer: How could God die, if he was immortal? How could he be comprehended, if he was incomprehensible? You speak according to one respect and another, yet he is one and the same. So the same body is impassible and yet is broken; but according to one respect and another—both nevertheless truly. What in itself and according to itself is impassible is divided in the sacrament, seen in the sacrament, and ground by the teeth of the faithful. Yet all this is truly so, and nothing is phantasmal.

That it is divided into three portions is for the sacrament of Christ’s body, that is, of head and members. One of the two portions remaining outside the chalice signifies the head of this body, already impassible and glorified. The other signifies those members of this body who are already impassible and glorified, united in rest to their head. The third portion, mixed with the blood, represents those members of this body who have not yet [Col. 0772A] escaped death and are still held amid the labors of this life.

It is asked concerning water why it is added in this sacrifice, and whether it is converted into blood together with wine. It is not added, as some perhaps suppose, because it flowed together with blood from Christ’s side. That water signified the water of baptism, which has the power to cleanse through Christ’s blood. But blood and water flowed together because there is no salvation without blood and none without baptism. The water placed in the chalice, they say, signifies the people redeemed through Christ’s passion. Hence, if anyone offered wine only, Christ’s blood would begin to be without us. For if anyone offers wine only without water, whether simply or through ignorance, he does consecrate, but ought to do penance.

But it seems to us that the water is converted into blood. For if the Jewish people are signified by wine, as often occurs, and the Gentiles by water, and both belong to Christ’s body, then both wine and water seem to be converted into blood.

It is also asked whether it ought to be granted that Christ is daily immolated. On this Augustine says: “Christ was immolated once in himself, yet is daily immolated in the sacrament; and the very immolation of the flesh performed by the hands of the priest is called Christ’s passion, death, and crucifixion—not in the truth of the thing, but in the mystery of what is signified.” This immolation is not one of killing, but of signification and representation.

It is further customarily asked whether Christ’s body received by us goes into the stomach or something of that kind. Would that no one asked such a question! Yet St. Ambrose answers the person who asks it: “This is not the bread that goes into the body; it is the bread of eternal life, which sustains the substance of our soul. If it becomes moldy, if it is gnawed by mice, or if something less honorable happens concerning it, nevertheless the sacrament, even if it appears to suffer such things, is contaminated by nothing of the sort. For no filth of uncleanness touches it, even though such things may appear to happen to the sacramental species.”

This chalice: container for contained thing, “chalice” for blood, because blood is in the chalice. In Scripture “chalice” is understood in several ways. Sometimes Christ’s blood is signified by the chalice, as here and in the Psalm: “My inebriating chalice, how excellent it is!” [Col. 0772D] (Ps. 22). Sometimes it signifies Christ’s death and that of his people, as in: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20). It is called a cup because it is measured, so that its bitterness does not exceed the patience of the one who endures it. The cup is also called the punishment of the wicked, as in: “He will rain snares upon sinners; fire, sulphur, and a tempestuous wind are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10), because their kinds of torment are measured out to them.

“This chalice is the new testament,” that is, the confirmation of the New Testament, because it is confirmed by the death of the testator. Why is this called the New Testament and the other the Old? It may be said that this is called new by likeness to a new garment, which has color and brightness: the warmth of charity and the brightness of good work. The Old Testament resembles the old garment in deformity and coldness. Beyond doubt, those observances and sacrificial rites of the Old Testament have deformity. They also have coldness, because they are done from fear and not from love.

“He shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord”: that is, he shall incur the guilt of the Lord’s death. For the one who places him in an unclean vessel does him no less injury than the one who fastened him to the gibbet of the cross. Or, “guilty of the body,” etc., because, as far as in him lies, he renders void the benefit of Christ’s death, so that Christ appears to have died in vain.

“But let a person prove himself,” by questioning conscience. Its answer should always be that one is not worthy to approach so great a sacrament. Yet there is a difference in the manner of this. If conscience accuses one of a grave sin and one receives it, one eats and drinks judgment upon oneself. But if one does not find oneself in mortal sin—for no one is without daily sins—one should repent of those sins and communicate, saying with the centurion: “Lord, I am not worthy,” etc. (Matt. 8).

What then? Is that person not worthy to communicate? Does that person not communicate worthily? Otherwise one eats and drinks judgment upon oneself. And if one is worthy but says that one is unworthy, one lies and thus becomes unworthy. How, then, did the Apostle not lie when he said, “I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15), although he was worthy? Nor does the one who says one is unworthy to communicate, although one is worthy. For one considers the excellence of so great a sacrament and one’s own merits, which cannot be equated with so great a thing. Thus it is by God’s mercy that one is worthy: he counts a small good as a greater one, as he counted Abraham’s faith to him for righteousness, as was said there.

It should be noted that St. Augustine assigns two ways of eating Christ: one by which both good and evil eat him, [Col. 0774A] and another by which only the good eat him. One is sacramental, the other spiritual. Thus he also says: “Whoever is at variance with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood, although that person daily receives the sacrament of so great a thing unto judgment.” Unless these words have a cautious and Catholic interpreter, they can easily deceive the simplicity of faith. The meaning of sayings must therefore be drawn from the reasons for saying them. He says that one at variance with Christ does not eat Christ’s flesh because by this eating that person is not incorporated into Christ. This has its cause, but its effect does not follow. Such a person does not eat because he does not eat to his own benefit. Likewise, one is not said to have what one does not have for one’s own benefit, as in: “To him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken from him” (Matt. 25).

“But if we judged ourselves …” St. Augustine, in the book of homilies, *On Penance*, shows in these words how a person ought to judge oneself:

> “Let the image of the future judgment turn before one’s eyes, and let a person ascend against oneself to the tribunal of one’s mind. Let one set oneself before one’s own face; and, judgment having been established in the heart, let thought be present as accuser, conscience as witness, and fear as executioner. Then let some blood of the confessing soul flow forth through tears. Finally, let such a sentence be pronounced by the mind itself that a person judges oneself unworthy of participation in the body and blood of the Lord, so that one who fears being separated from the kingdom by the final sentence may for a time be separated, through ecclesiastical discipline, from the sacrament of the heavenly bread. For one receives unworthily if one receives at the time when one ought to be doing penance.”

But this seems to have been said of public penitents—that is, of those undergoing penance outside the Church. Others may and ought to communicate at the appointed times, even before their penance has been completed.

## In the Year of the Lord 1190. Bonacursus, from Heretic a Catholic

[Col. 0775]

## The Life of the Heretics, Revealed by Bonacursus, Formerly a Heretic but Now a Catholic

(*Spicilegium*, folio edition, vol. I, p. 208.)

## Exposure of the Heresy of the Cathars

[Note: [Col. 0775B]

The Cathars discussed here differ greatly from those ancient Cathars or Novatians who arose in the times of the emperor Gallienus and Pope Stephen I. You may learn this, reader, if you compare the ancient heresy with the more recent one. The Cathars attacking the Church of Milan are mentioned in *Italia sacra* by Ughelli, in the account of Galdinus, archbishop of Milan:

> “Moreover, when Galdinus, by divine help, had restored his church almost to its former splendor … and, full of charity, had attacked the revived heresy of the Cathars,” etc.

Ughelli gives this under the year 1173, but says absolutely nothing about Bonacursus, who perhaps lived a little later.

Trithemius, in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, under the year 1163, recalls certain Cathars whom Abbot Eckbert of St. Florin attempted to refute at Cologne—“so that they were wholly unable to contradict him, [Col. 0776B] etc. But since they persisted most obstinately in their purpose, they were entirely expelled from the Church and handed over to laymen, who led them outside the city and delivered them to the flames,” etc. Against these Cathars St. Hildegard, inspired by the Holy Spirit, wrote a letter to the canons of the greater church of Mainz, etc. “They were called Cataphrygians or Cathars,” says Trithemius, “because they claimed to be pure and the only Christians.”

Later, in 1216, the Albigensians embraced the Cathars’ most abominable heresies. They began to infect the county of Toulouse and many cities of Gaul with their poison and to rage like madmen. Acherius adds that this little work was copied by Dom Jacques Lannoy from a manuscript of a Cistercian monastery. Baluze observes that a specimen concerning Bonacursus may be seen in Labbe’s *Ancient Readings*, p. 206.]

## Which Bonacursus, Who Was Formerly Their Teacher, Delivered at Milan before the People

[Col. 0775A]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who always and everywhere protects and governs his Church and confirms and preserves the Catholic faith, wished in his holy mercy to disclose and expose the errors of those called Cathars. He mercifully illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit a certain bishop and teacher named Bonacursus, and by grace renewed him into the bosom of holy Mother Church. Therefore let us render immense praises to God and to all the saints.

Their heresy is not merely dreadful, but altogether terrible and detestable to speak or hear. For some of them say that God created all the elements; others say that the devil created those elements. Yet all agree that the devil divided those elements. They also say that the same devil made Adam from the clay of the earth and forcibly enclosed in him a certain angel of light, concerning whom they believe the Gospel says: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho,” etc. (Luke 10). They say that he made Eve, with whom he had intercourse, [Col. 0776A] and from this Cain was born. From Cain’s blood, they say, dogs were born, and for this reason they are so faithful to human beings. Adam’s union with Eve, they say, was the forbidden fruit.

They introduce another error: namely, that everything made in the air, sea, and earth—human beings, animate and inanimate things alike—was made by the devil. From Eve’s daughters and demons they say giants were born, who learned through the demons that their father, the devil, had created everything. Therefore the devil, grieved that they knew this, said: “I repent that I made man” (Gen. 6). Since Noah did not know it, he was delivered from the flood; and they say that the devil said to him: “Enter the ark” (Gen. 7). They say that Enoch was taken away by the same being.

[Col. 0776B] Again, they assert that whatever was done or said to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob was said and done by a demon. They also say that the devil appeared to Moses in the bush and spoke with him. Further, the miracles performed before Pharaoh through Moses; the crossing of the Red Sea by the children of Israel; their being led into the promised land; God’s speaking to Moses himself; and the Law which God gave him—all these, they say and believe, were done by the devil, [Col. 0777A] their master.

Concerning the sayings of the holy prophets, they say that some were revealed by the Spirit of God and some by an evil spirit. Hence the Apostle: “Test all things; hold fast what is good” (1 Thess. 5). They condemn David because of adultery and homicide. They say Elijah was borne in a chariot by the devil. They assert that the angel sent by God to Zechariah was an angel of the devil. They also condemn John himself, than whom, as the Lord testifies, none is greater. Why? Because the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Matt. 2 [as printed]). And because he doubted concerning Christ when he said: “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect another?” (Luke 7).

They believe that Mary, the mother of our Lord, was born … They say of Christ that he did not have an animate body, [Col. 0777B] did not eat or drink, and did not do anything according to human nature, but merely appeared to do so. They say that the thief on the right is in hell. They do not believe that Christ’s body rose again or was taken into heaven, nor do they believe in the resurrection of the flesh or that Christ descended into hell. They do not believe the Son equal to the Father, because he said: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). They say that the cross is the mark of the beast mentioned in the Apocalypse and the abomination standing in the holy place. They say that blessed Sylvester was the Antichrist, of whom the Epistles say: “the son of perdition,” “who exalts himself above everything that is called God” (2 Thess. 2). From that time, they say, the Church has been lost. They believe that no one can be saved in marriage.

[Col. 0777C] They condemn all the doctors: Ambrose, Gregory, Augustine, Jerome, and all others universally. If anyone eats meat, eggs, cheese, or anything of animal nature, that person thereby eats condemnation for himself. They by no means believe that the Holy Spirit can be received through baptism in water, nor that any visible substance can in any way be converted into Christ’s body. They also believe that everyone who swears will be damned, and that no one can be saved except by a certain laying on of hands of their own, which they call baptism and the renewal of the Holy Spirit. They believe that the devil is the sun; they say that the moon is Eve; and every month, they say, they fornicate like a man with a prostitute. They believe that all the stars are demons. Finally, they say that no one can be saved without them. Behold such is the heresy of the Cathars, from which may God turn away the whole body of Catholics. Amen.

## Against the Heretics Who Are Called Cathars
Christ, the Son of God, our Lord and Redeemer, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one God, foreknowing the error that would come, fortifies his disciples in this manner: “See,” he says, “that no one deceives you; for many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am Christ,’ and they will deceive many” (Matt. 24). And, after a few intervening words, he adds: “And many false prophets will arise and deceive many. And because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold” [Col. 0778A] (ibid.). And again: “False Christs and false prophets,” he says, “will arise, and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (ibid.). The Apostle Peter also says in his Second Epistle: “There were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among us, who introduce sects of perdition and deny that he who purchased them is God; bringing upon themselves sects of perdition—rash, self-pleasing men, who form sects while blaspheming. But these are irrational, like cattle. Blaspheming in matters which they do not understand, naturally destined for capture and destruction, they shall perish in their corruption” (2 Pet. 2). Paul likewise, in the Third Epistle to Timothy, says: “The Spirit,” he says, “plainly declares that in the last times [Col. 0778B] some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy,” etc. (1 Tim. 4).

And who is of such slight understanding as not to recognize most plainly that this is the time of which the foregoing prophecies speak? Do we not already see cities, suburbs, villages, and fortified places full of false prophets of this kind? Trampling beneath their feet the seed of the Word, they do not cease to sow the tares of their error, and they strive, with excessive importunity, to corrupt with deadly poison the bride of Christ—that is, the holy Church. Therefore, let us rise promptly and delay no longer; but, swiftly taking up the sword of the Spirit, let us meet them and resist manfully, and let us show most plainly, by the testimony of Holy Scripture, how deadly their doctrine is. Let us go up against them and set ourselves as a wall for the house of Israel against the enemies of Christ’s cross, lest, lying under the prophetic curse, we hear: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48). Let us take up weapons and shield, and rise to the Lord’s aid. Let us pour out the sword and overthrow those who persecute and strive to scatter the Lord’s sheep, trusting in the aid of him who said: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21). Let us cast down these deceivers, whom we see confirming some of their errors by the testimony of Scripture, perversely understood, while inventing others [Col. 0778D] through a corrupt mind and the prompting of demons rather than supporting them by Scriptural authority. Whatever, then, they try to maintain by the testimony of Scripture, let us wholly destroy by that same testimony. But what they seem to put forward as ravings, let us trample underfoot as things unworthy of an answer.

## Chapter I. That all things, visible as well as invisible, were created by almighty God

John, chapter 1: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Likewise: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (ibid.). Paul, in the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2: “For in him all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were created—whether thrones, dominions, powers, or [Col. 0779A] principalities; all things were created through him and in him.” To the Hebrews, chapter 1: “And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands; they shall perish, but you shall remain for ever.” Likewise, chapter 3: “Every house is built by someone; but he who created all things is God.” In the Acts of the Apostles: “But you, Lord, made heaven and earth, the sea and all things that are in them; grant to your servants to speak your word with confidence” (Acts 4). Likewise: “What house will you build for me, or what is the place of my rest? Has not my hand made all these things?” (Acts 7). Likewise, chapter 17: “I, Paul, proclaim to you God, who made this world and all things that are in it; in whom we live and move and stand.” In the Apocalypse: “You are worthy, O Lord [Col. 0779B] our God, to receive glory and honour and power, because you created all things; and by your will they existed and were created” (Rev. 4). Likewise: “Fear the Lord and give him honour, because the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth, and all things that are in them, and the springs of waters” (Rev. 14).

## Chapter II. That almighty God created Adam and Eve, and the whole human race

Matthew, chapter 19: “He who made them from the beginning made them male and female. And he said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife,’” etc. Mark, chapter 10: “From the beginning of creation God made them male and female.” Luke, chapter 3: “And he himself, Jesus, was beginning to be about [Col. 0779C] thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph, who was of Heli,” down to, “who was of Adam, who was of God.” Likewise, chapter 11: “Fools, did not he who made what is outside also make what is within?” Paul, in the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 1: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb,” etc. Matthew, chapter 5: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.” In the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 14: “Yet he did not leave us without testimony, doing good, giving rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, [Col. 0779D] filling our hearts with food and gladness.”

## Chapter III. Concerning the law of Moses, the servant of God: that it was given by almighty God

Matthew, chapter 5: “Do not think that I came to abolish the law or the prophets; I came not to abolish the law, but to fulfil it.” Likewise: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them. For this is the law and the prophets” (Matt. 7). Likewise, chapter 19: “And behold, one came to him and said: ‘Good Master, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?’ He said to him: ‘Why do you ask me concerning the good? One is good—God. If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.’ He said to him: ‘Which?’ And Jesus said to him: ‘You shall not commit murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; nor shall you speak false testimony [Col. 0780A]. Honour your father and your mother; and you shall love your neighbour as yourself.’” Luke, chapter 2: “And when the days of her purification were fulfilled according to the law of Moses, they took him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord.” Likewise, chapter 16: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe even if someone rises from the dead.” Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 7: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good.” In the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 3: “What then? Was the law set down because of transgression?” Likewise, subsequently: “The law was our pedagogue unto Christ” (ibid.).

## Chapter IV. That John the Baptist, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses are elect and friends of God

[Col. 0780B]

Luke, chapter 1: “The angel of the Lord said: ‘Do not fear, Zachariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. He shall be joy and exultation to you, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he shall be great before the Lord; he shall drink neither wine nor strong drink, and shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb, and he shall turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. And he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah,’” etc. In Matthew the Lord said to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare [Col. 0780C] your way before you.’ Amen I say to you: among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist. But he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Matt. 11). Likewise, Luke, chapter 13: “When you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the prophets, in the kingdom of God, while you are cast out. And they will come from east and west, north and south, and recline in the kingdom of God. Behold, there are last who were first, and there are first who were last.” In the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 3: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Son Jesus.” And below: “You are the children of the prophets and of the covenant which God established with our fathers, saying to Abraham: ‘In your seed [Col. 0780D] all the families of the earth shall be blessed’” (ibid.). In the Apocalypse, chapter 15: “And I saw, as it were, a glassy sea mingled with fire, and those who overcame the beast, and its greatness, and the number of its name, standing upon the glassy sea, holding harps and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying: ‘Great and wonderful are your works, O Lord God almighty.’”

## Chapter V. That marriage was instituted by God, and that we may be saved within it

Matthew, chapter 5, it was said: “Whoever dismisses his wife, let him give her a bill of divorce; but I say to you that everyone who dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, causes her to commit adultery; and whoever marries a dismissed woman is an adulterer.” Likewise, chapter 19: [Col. 0781A] “And Pharisees came to him, testing him and saying: ‘Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatever?’ He answered and said: ‘Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And he said: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate.’ They said to him: ‘Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given and that she be dismissed?’ He said to them: ‘Because of the hardness of your heart Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives; but from the beginning it was not so. But I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, except for the cause of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries the dismissed woman,’” [Col. 0781B] etc. Paul, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 7: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let every man have his own wife and every woman have her own husband. Let the husband render to the wife what is due, and likewise the wife to the husband. A woman has no authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise the husband has no authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same union, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.” Likewise: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned. [Col. 0781C] He who gives his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not give her does better. A woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives. But if her husband falls asleep, she is released from the law of her husband; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my counsel. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7). To Timothy, chapter 5: “I wish younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no occasion for reproach” (1 Tim. 5).

## Chapter VI. That the Son of God assumed true flesh, in which he slept, ate, and drank, even after the resurrection

Matthew, chapter 1: “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.” [Col. 0781D] Likewise, chapter 8: “But he was sleeping, and they came and awakened him.” Likewise, chapter 11: “The Son of Man came eating and drinking.” Luke, chapter 24: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that I myself am he; touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet. But while they still did not believe, and wondered for joy, he said: “Do you have anything here to eat?” And they offered him a piece of roasted fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, he took what remained and gave it to them. John, chapter 1: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.” [Col. 0782A] In the First Epistle of John, chapter 4: “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is Antichrist, of whom you have heard that he is coming, and now is already in the world.” In the Apocalypse, chapter 1: “Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood.”

## Chapter VII. That the bread placed upon the altar and the wine are converted after consecration into the body and blood of the Lord, and that no one is saved unless he eats

Matthew, chapter 26: “While the disciples were eating supper, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat: this is my body.’ And taking the cup, [Col. 0782B] he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink all of this, for this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins.’” Behold, O heretic, that bread and wine are converted after the blessing into the body and blood of the Lord. For what is called bread before the blessing, after the blessing he plainly declares to be body and blood; and he who has not eaten it shall not have life, but he who has eaten it shall obtain life. Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel according to John: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has life; [Col. 0782C] and I will raise him on the last day. For my flesh is true food and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6). The Apostle likewise, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 10: “The cup of blessing which we bless—is it not communion in the Lord? And the bread which we break—is it not participation in Christ?” And below, chapter 11: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night on which he was betrayed, took bread and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat: this is my body, which shall be given up for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also, after supper, saying: ‘This is the cup of the new [Col. 0782D] covenant in my blood; do this in remembrance of me. Whenever you drink,’” etc., down to: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.”

## Chapter VIII. Concerning the resurrection of the dead on the last day

Luke, chapter 20: “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage; but those judged worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor take wives, nor can they die any more; for they are equal to angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection. And Moses too showed that the dead rise, at the bush, when he spoke of the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; for God is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him.” John, chapter 6: “This is the will of my Father who sent me: that of all that the Father has given me I should lose nothing of it, but raise it up on the last day. And this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life; and I will raise him on the last day.” Paul, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 15: “If Christ is preached as risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead, nor has he risen? But if Christ has not risen, our preaching is empty, and your faith also is empty.” And many other things which the Apostle says in this chapter concerning the resurrection, down to: [Col. 0783B] “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed,” etc.

## Chapter IX. That flesh, cheese, eggs, and milk may be eaten without sin

Matthew, chapter 15: “Hear and understand now.
