What enters into the mouth does not defile a man; but what proceeds from the mouth, that defiles a man.” Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 14: “Let him who eats not despise him who does not eat; and let him who does not eat not judge him who eats.” Likewise: “I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean [Col. 0783C] through itself; except that to him who considers anything unclean, to him it is unclean.” Likewise: “All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats so as to give offence.” Paul, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 10: “Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking no questions for conscience’ sake; for the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.” Likewise: “If any unbeliever invites you to dinner, and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you.” To the Colossians, chapter 2: “Let no one judge you in food or drink.” To Timothy, chapter 4: “The Spirit plainly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their own conscience branded, forbidding [Col. 0783D] marriage and commanding abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.” To Titus, chapter 1: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, since their mind and conscience are in iniquity.”

## Chapter X. That swearing truthfully, when necessity requires it and desire has been excluded, is not damnable

Concerning your assertion, O branded fool, that it is a mortal sin to swear because the Lord says, “Do not swear at all; let your speech be, ‘yes, yes’; ‘no, no’” (Matt. 5), we answer as follows: he said this not by commanding [Col. 0784A], but by exhorting and admonishing; nor did he then impose the necessity of a precept, but gave counsel. Nor does one who swears truthfully under compulsion of necessity, with desire excluded, do anything damnable. And what is swearing except confirming, in words, the mind’s certainty for a manifestly useful purpose? For the Lord himself swore when he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John 1). And the Apostle, when he says in his Epistle: “I call God and my soul as witness” (2 Cor. 1). And again: “God is my witness” (Rom. 1). Likewise, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 6: “For when God made promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Unless I bless you with blessing and multiply you with multiplication.’ And thus, patiently enduring, he obtained the promise. For men swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is the end of every dispute among them for confirmation.” Likewise, in the Apocalypse, chapter 10: “And the angel of the Lord, whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth, raised his hand to heaven [Col. 0784B] and swore by him who lives for ages of ages, who created heaven and the things in it, earth and the things in it, and sea and the things in it, that time shall be no more.” From these authorities, therefore, we can plainly gather that not swearing is counsel, not a precept. Hence you are manifestly proved a liar, O heretic, [you] who maintain that an oath is a mortal sin; because, just as everything decreed in the form of a command brings death when it is not fulfilled, [Col. 0784C] so things that are [advised] rather than commanded are beneficial when done, and [do] no harm when not done.

# Against Heretics Called Pasagii

What the error of those called Pasagii is, and how abominable their faith and doctrine are, is now evident not merely to a few but to very many. But since there are some to whose knowledge it has not yet come, both for the caution and safety of these and for the shame and disgrace of the others, I do not hesitate to write what I think concerning them, so that the more their madness is known, the more it may be despised and trampled underfoot by all. For just as good things ought to be known in order to be practised, so too it is fitting to know evils in order to avoid them utterly.

[Col. 0784D] Therefore observe, you who do not know, how perverse their faith and doctrine are. First, they say that the Mosaic law must be observed literally, and that the Sabbath, circumcision, and other legal observances ought still to remain in force. They also say that Christ the Son of God is not equal to the Father, and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—these three persons—are not one God and one substance. Moreover, to increase their error, they judge and condemn all the doctors of the Church, and universally the whole Roman Church. But because they strive to [establish] this error of theirs by the testimony of the New Testament and the prophets, let us, with Christ’s grace aiding us, choke it with their own sword, as David did Goliath.

## Chapter I. That the Mosaic law is to be observed spiritually

[Col. 0785A]

In Matthew: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them; for this is the law and the prophets” (Matt. 7). Likewise, Luke, chapter 16: “For all the law and the prophets [were] until John, through faith without works of the law.” Likewise, to the Romans, chapter 6: “For you are not under the law, but under grace.” Likewise, in the following chapter: “Do you not know, brethren—for I speak to those who know the law—that the law has dominion over a person as long as he lives? For a woman subject to a husband is bound by the law to her husband while he lives; but if her husband has died, she is released from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man. Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man. Thus, my brethren, you also have been made dead [Col. 0785B] to the law through the body of Christ, that you may belong to another—to him who rose from the dead—that we may bear fruit to God. For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins which were through the law worked in our members, that we might bear fruit to death. But now we have been released from the law of death, in which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and in the oldness of the letter” (Rom. 7). Likewise, chapter 10: “But being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness; for the end of the law is righteousness to everyone who believes.” And below: “He who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law” (Rom. 13). Paul, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 5: “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new.” In the same Epistle, chapter 3: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” Likewise, to the Galatians, [Col. 0785C] chapter 3: “What then is the law? It was set down because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom he had promised,” etc. And below: “Thus the law was our pedagogue unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith; but when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue” (ibid.). Likewise, chapter 5: “For the whole law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself.’” And below: “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (ibid.). In the First Epistle to Timothy, chapter 1: “But we know that the law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully, knowing this: that the law is not laid down for the just person, but for the unjust and disobedient, the impious and sinners,” etc. In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 7: “Indeed, the previous commandment is rejected because of its weakness and uselessness.” Likewise, chapter 8: “Behold, days are coming, says [Col. 0785D] the Lord, and I will establish over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt.” By saying “new,” he made the former old; and what is becoming old and aged is near destruction. Likewise, chapter 7: “For,” with the aforesaid “priesthood transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law also occur.”

### The cessation of the Sabbath: that it is not to be observed literally

John, chapter 5: “Those who were with the man who had been healed said to him: ‘It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your bed.’ He answered them: ‘He who made me well said to me: “Take up your bed and walk.”’” Likewise: the Jews [Col. 0786A] “therefore persecuted Jesus because he did these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them: ‘My Father works until now; therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God’” (ibid.). Paul, to the Colossians, chapter 2: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or concerning participation in a feast day, a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is Christ’s.” Isidore: “If it is a crime not to observe Sabbath rest, why did Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ disciple and successor, at the Lord’s command, for seven continuous days—including, surely, the Sabbath—bring forth the army and its arms and, while the ark went around and trumpets sounded, overthrow the walls [Col. 0786B] of Jericho?”

Why, then, should I speak again of the Maccabees, of whom it is written: The Jews were unwilling on the Sabbath day to defend themselves against foreigners; afterwards, having received counsel, they fought on the Sabbath day and triumphed over their enemies. By whatever testimony, we are taught that this elementary Sabbath day does not pertain to faith, but rather another, special Sabbath. For this carnal Sabbath was given not for purification but for testing, the Lord saying: “That I may test them, whether they walk in my ways or not; for six days you shall gather manna, but on the seventh you shall not gather it” (Exod. 16). Therefore he says, “that I may test them,” so that it may appear that it was not a command for justification but for testing. Hence he speaks through the prophet [Col. 0786C] Ezekiel, saying: “I gave them commandments that were not good” (Ezek. 20), that is, commandments which, when observed carnally, do not preserve their observers. Certainly, some things to be done carnally were permitted to a carnal people; yet these ceased upon the coming of the Gospel, as he says through the prophet: “I will make all her joy and her Sabbaths cease” (Hos. 2). But the question is raised: if, they say, the Sabbath is not to be kept, why was it said among the Lord’s commandments: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. For six days you shall work and do your works; but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it” (Exod. 20)? For in the work of the six days six thousand years were signified. For a thousand years are compared with the span of one day before God, as [Col. 0786D] the Prophet testifies: “For a thousand years in your sight are as one day” (Ps. 89). The Sabbath of those days is the time of the seventh thousandth year, and the rest of the kingdom and age to come, where there will no longer be any work of things, but only the rest of the saints. For there is another Sabbath, of which Isaiah says: “And there shall be month from month, Sabbath” (Isa. 63; probably an erroneous citation). “Month from month,” that is, from the perfection of good work comes the perfect joy of eternal life. And there shall be Sabbath from Sabbaths, because whoever here ceases from perverse work will there rest in heavenly recompense. But the question is again raised why Jeremiah said: “Guard your souls, and do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day” (Jer. 17). Hear, therefore, the mystery of this same prophecy. He carries burdens on the Sabbath who, [Col. 0787A] believing in Christ, does not cease from sin; for he himself is the rest of souls, as he says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). A third question is still raised: why was the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath day so cruelly slain by the people at God’s command? Let them understand, therefore, that all these things happened to them as figures; for they were written for our correction. For that former and carnal person is he who says that the Sabbath is violated while wood is being gathered; and because of this [he] was punished, he indicates the figure of one who, when found with carnal work on the day of judgment, must be driven away by all the angels and immediately punished with the final death. Thus, whatever befell those Jews through the law must be understood figuratively.

### Concerning circumcision: that it is to be observed spiritually, not literally

[Col. 0787B]

Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 2: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly; nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh. But he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision of the flesh is in the spirit, not the letter; whose praise is not from men but from God.” Likewise, Galatians, chapter 5: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.” In the Epistle to the Colossians, chapter 2: “You have been circumcised with a circumcision [not] made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of the [sins of the] flesh, [in the circumcision of Christ].”

### The reason circumcision was given to Abraham, and what it signified

[Col. 0787C] Isidore: Receive now the first reason for circumcision. Since Christ was to be born according to the flesh, in whom the blessing of all nations had been promised, and since many ages were yet to intervene from Abraham to Christ, God foresaw that Abraham’s race might mingle with the other nations and that its descent might gradually become uncertain. He therefore marked the Jewish people with the sign of circumcision, so that among Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, or Chaldaeans, it might be distinguished by this seal from them and from the other nations. Accordingly, for forty years in the wilderness no one was circumcised, since there they lived without intercourse with another people; but when the Israelite people crossed the channel of the Jordan and came into the land of promise, the sign of circumcision anticipated the error that would arise [Col. 0787D] from mingling with the nations. We believe that it was reasonably to be observed until Christ should be born, who had been promised from Abraham’s seed, so that he might cleanse the hearts of all nations, no longer by circumcision of the flesh but by cutting away vices. Hence Moses says: “In the last days he will circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed” (Deut. 30). And the Lord proclaimed through Isaiah, saying: “Do not remember the former things, and do not look upon the ancient things; behold, I shall make new things which will now spring up, and you shall know them” (Isa. 43). And circumcision was rightly performed with stone knives, for the second stone is Christ, through whom believers are cleansed by spiritual circumcision from every enticement of vices.

## Chapter II. That Christ is God, equal and consubstantial with the Father

[Col. 0788A]

John, chapter 1: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Likewise, chapter 5: “Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill Christ, because he not [only] broke the Sabbath but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God.” Likewise, chapter 14: “Philip said to him: ‘Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father. How then do you say, “Show us the Father”? And the Father is in me.’” And below: “All things whatever the Father has are mine” (chapter 16). Likewise, chapter 20: “Thomas answered and said: ‘My Lord [Col. 0788B] and my God.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.’” Likewise, in the final chapter, chapter 21, Peter said to him: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.” In the Apocalypse, chapter 1: “I am Alpha and Omega (Α and Ω), the beginning and the end.” And below: “I am the first and the last; and I was dead, and behold, I am living for ages of ages” (ibid.).

## Chapter III. That Christ is begotten, and that he is the same as the Father
Isidore: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109). “From the womb,” therefore, that is, from that innermost and incomprehensible substance of the Father. And again: “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44). And elsewhere: “You are my Son [Col. 0788C]; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). Kings obey him, nations serve him, and the kings of the earth shall worship him: “All nations shall serve him” (Ps. 11). That impious king, beholding this Son of God in Daniel, said: “Behold, I see four men, unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3).

If it is objected that in Daniel the Son of God is also above called an Angel, I agree; for Christ the Son of God is called an Angel as well. For, as the prophet says concerning him: “The ruler whom you seek shall come to his holy temple, and the Angel of the Covenant, whom you desire” (Mal. 3). Christ, insofar as he is begotten of the Father, is called the Son of God; insofar as he is read to have been sent by the Father to announce to the fathers, he is announced as an Angel. “The voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies” [Col. 0788D] (Isa. 66), namely to those Jews who do not believe. “Before she travailed, she gave birth; and before her labour came upon her, she bore a male child” (ibid.). It is as though he said openly: Before the Virgin bore Christ in the flesh, he begot the Son in divinity, as it is written concerning him: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5). And again: “His name endures before the sun, and before the moon and stars” (Ps. 71).

The Son of God himself—Word, power, and wisdom—also confirms this concerning his own birth, saying: “The deeps did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the fountains of waters had not yet burst forth, nor had the mountains been established with their heavy mass; before the hills I was brought forth; he had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the bounds of the earth’s circle. When he was preparing the heavens, I was there; when he enclosed the deeps with a fixed law and circuit, when he suspended the foundations of the earth, I was with him, ordering all things” [Col. 0789A] (Prov. 8).

Again the question is raised how he is begotten, since neither the Apostle speaks of the secrets of his sacred birth, nor the prophet discovers them, nor angel knows them, nor creature recognizes them. Isaiah bears witness when he says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). Therefore, if his birth could not be declared by the prophet, who claims to know when the Son could have been begotten by the Father? Hence also that saying in the book of Job: “Where will you find the wisdom of God the Father? For it is hidden from the eyes of human beings and concealed from the bird of heaven” (Job 28), that is, unknown even to the angels themselves. For Christ shone forth from the Father as radiance from light, as a word from the mouth, as wisdom from the heart [Col. 0789B].

Likewise, Isaiah declares that Christ is God, showing the two persons to be one God. “You,” he says, “are God, and God is in you” (Isa. 45). In saying, “You are God,” he indicates the Father; in adding, “God is in you,” he declares the Son. Yet, in order to show the same Father and Son to be one God, he adds: “There is no God apart from you. Truly you are the hidden God, the God of Israel” (ibid.). Elsewhere, too, Isaiah, comprehending the whole Trinity in the number of the fingers, thus proclaims: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and who has weighed the heavens with his palm? Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” (Isa. 40). In the three fingers, indeed, the prophet declared the threefold person of divine omnipotence and the unity which is one and the same in the Trinity.

Likewise Jeremiah shows that Christ is God in the book of Baruch, where he says: “This is our God, and no other exists besides him. He found every way of knowledge and showed it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved; afterwards he was seen upon earth and lived among human beings” [Col. 0789C] (Bar. 3). Yet they do not think that Christ is God because they have heard the voice of the Lord thundering on Mount Sinai: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6). And again: “I am God, and besides me there is no other” (Deut. 32). And: “I am the Lord God, and I do not change; I will not give my glory to another” (Mal. 3). Therefore, when these faithless persons, blinded by error, read this, they do not believe Christ to be God. Let them accordingly acknowledge that these words were foretold to them at that time lest, perhaps, withdrawing from the unity of faith, they should turn to many imaginary gods and worship the idols of the Gentiles—which indeed they did.

## CHAPTER IV. That the Holy Spirit is God, and that the same Spirit is one substance with the Father and the Son; and that he is one almighty God, not three gods.

In the Gospel of John, chapter 4: “The Spirit is God.” Job 33: “The Spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life. Behold, God made me as he made you.” In the Second Book of Kings: “David son of Jesse said: The man has spoken to whom it was appointed concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob, the excellent Psalmist of Israel: ‘The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was upon my tongue’” [Col. 0790A] (2 Kings 23). And he added who this was: “The God of Israel spoke to me, the mighty one of Israel, the just ruler of all” (ibid.). For by saying “the Christ of the God of Jacob,” he shows both the Son and the Father. Likewise, by saying, “The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me,” he clearly reveals the Holy Spirit.

Likewise in the Psalms: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their strength” (Ps. 32). In the person of the Lord we understand the Father; in the Word we believe the Son; in the spirit of his mouth we understand the Holy Spirit. In Genesis too, an equal indication of the Trinity is expressed through plurality of persons, where God says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Yet, to show the unity of the Godhead, he immediately added: “And God created man in his own image” [Col. 0790B] (ibid.).

In Isaiah too the Trinity is declared, the Son himself saying: “And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 36). Behold two persons—the Lord and his Spirit—who send, and a third person of the same Lord who is sent. Elsewhere the same Isaiah, comprehending the whole Trinity in the number of the fingers, proclaims thus: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the heavens with his palm? Who has weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers?” (Isa. 40). In the three fingers, indeed, the prophet declared the threefold equality of divine omnipotence, weighed in a certain balance of mystery, and the equality of power, its correspondence, and unity—the unity which is one and the same in the Trinity.

Likewise John, in the First Epistle, chapter 5: “For it is the Spirit who bears witness [because the Spirit is], because Christ is truth; because there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit, and these three are one” [Col. 0790C].

## CHAPTER V. What carrion is, and that certain things in the law were forbidden for eating by way of signification.

By carrion, moreover, I understand that which human use does not admit as food, because it is the dead flesh of animals which died rather than were killed, and is not fit for the preservation of the body, for which purpose we take food. For the command given to the ancients figuratively concerning the eating of blood—that flesh should not be eaten with its blood, but that the meat should be eaten after the blood has been drained—Saint Augustine admits in Book XII *Against Faustus* to prefigure this: that one’s former life should not be held, as though suffocated, in the conscience, but should find an outpouring through confession [Col. 0790D].

In the Acts of the Apostles (ch. 15) I read that the Apostles commanded this: that the Gentiles should abstain only from fornication, from things sacrificed, and from blood; that is, that they should by no means eat meat whose blood had not been poured out. Others do not understand it in this way, but hold that abstention from blood was commanded lest anyone defile himself by homicide; or perhaps the Apostles then found some easy requirement which Gentiles might observe together with Israelites. But now that pronouncement of Truth must be firmly held by all: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a human being, but what proceeds from the mouth of a human being defiles a human being” [Col. 0791A] (Matt. 15).

Likewise Isidore: By those animals which neither chew the cud nor divide the hoof are signified unbelievers, because they neither distinguish good from evil nor chew over God’s commandments by reflection; by ravens are represented those who shed human blood; by hawks and kites, those who seize what belongs to another; by swans, the proud; by fish lacking scales and fins, those who lack the scales of virtues and the fins of heavenly conduct. Therefore they cannot leap upon the waters, that is, they are unable to penetrate heavenly things.

## AGAINST THE ARNOLDISTS

Concerning their assertion that, because of the wickedness of clerics, the sacraments of the Church must be avoided: incline your ear and hear; open your eyes and see; cleanse your heart and understand. As Noah’s ark contained clean and unclean animals [Col. 0791B], so no one ought to doubt that in the present Church the evil are mingled with the good. But if, while evil persons are tolerated or unknown, an ecclesiastical office has been entrusted to them, or if perhaps a good man begins to be evil after receiving a benefice, who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own lord. He does not lose the authority of the office which he received until he has been condemned by the judgment of the Church through his prelate.

Therefore, if you receive ecclesiastical sacraments from him worthily, receive them as profitable to yourself, not to him, although he administers them unworthily. Hear, then, testimonies written on this very matter from the Old and New Testaments, and authorities from the writings of the holy doctors—namely Gregory, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and others—drawn from the Old and New Testaments.

In the First Book of Kings you will find that Eli the priest sinned grievously because he tolerated his delinquent sons. Likewise Saul “did evil in the eyes of the Lord” (1 Kings 15); David was privately anointed king by Samuel; the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul and was directed to David; and nevertheless David obeyed Saul as king, regarded and endured him as king, so long as Saul lived. In the Second Book of Kings, Uzzah stretched out his hand to the ark of God and held it; and the Lord was angered with indignation against Uzzah and struck him for his presumption, so that he died there beside the ark.

Matthew, chapter 7: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged.” Likewise chapter 13: “Let both grow until the harvest; and at the time of harvest I shall say to the reapers: Gather first the tares and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn” [Col. 0791C]. Likewise chapter 13: “So shall it be at the consummation of the age: the angels shall go forth and separate the evil from among the just, and shall cast them into the furnace of fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” Likewise chapter 23: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat. Therefore observe and do all things whatsoever they tell you; but do not act according to their works, for they say and do not do.”

Mark, chapter 1: “Go, show yourself to the priests, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” John, chapter 2: “Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said to them: ‘You know nothing, nor do you consider that it is expedient for us that one man die for the people and that the whole nation not perish.’ But he did not say this of himself; rather, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied” [Col. 0792A].

Augustine: If the minister is just, I count him with Paul, who does not seek his own glory, saying: “I planted, Apollo watered, but the Lord gave the increase” (2 Cor. 3). But if the minister is proud, he is counted with Zebulun [perhaps “the devil,” *Zabulon*], yet Christ’s gift is not defiled, because a pure stream passes through him and reaches fertile ground. I know also that a stone cannot bear fruit from water, but water passes through stone channels to the beds. Nothing grows in the stone channel, but the garden bears much fruit. For such is the special power of the sacrament: the pure law is received for the enlightening of persons, but is not defiled by impure passages.

Likewise, in the book *On the Body of the Lord*: Within the Catholic Church, in the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing greater is accomplished by a good priest and nothing less by an evil priest, because it is accomplished not by the merit of the consecrator but by the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. For if it were by the merit of the priest, it would not belong to Christ. But now, just as he himself is the one who baptizes, so he himself through the Holy Spirit makes this flesh his own and pours forth the blood. For one must believe that the sacraments are performed through Christ’s words, and that what is first created by his command is surely recreated for the better by him [Col. 0792B].

Likewise, in Book II *Against the Letter of Parmenian*: Although all sacraments harm those who handle them unworthily, they nevertheless benefit those who receive them worthily through such persons, just as does the word of the Lord. Hence it was said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.”

Gregory: The wickedness of a bishop does no harm either to the baptism of an infant or to the consecration of a church, because baptism is given by God and does not come from man. Thus the Eucharist and whatever else is placed upon the altar receive sanctification not from man but from God.

Augustine, in the book *On the Word of the Lord*: “Withdraw and go out from among them, and do not touch what is unclean”—but by contact of the heart, not of the body. For what is it to touch the unclean, except to do, so far as each person’s rank and position allows and as can be done without violating peace, what pertains to their correction? You were displeased that someone sinned: you did not touch the unclean; you rebuked, reproved, admonished, and, if the matter required it, applied fitting discipline that does not violate unity: you went out from among them [Col. 0792C]. Moses cried out these things; Isaiah cried out; Jeremiah cried out; Ezekiel cried out. Let us see whether they abandoned the people of God and transferred themselves to other nations. How greatly and forcefully Jeremiah rebuked sinners and criminals! Yet he remained one among them; when he entered the Temple, he celebrated the same sacraments and lived in the same congregation of criminal people, but by crying out he went out from among them. This, therefore, is to go out from among them: this is not to touch the unclean, not to consent to their will, and not to spare them with one’s mouth [Col. 0792D].

## ABOUT THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1190. BERNARD, ABBOT OF FONT-CHAUDE, OF THE PREMONSTRATENSIAN ORDER

[Col. 0793]

# BOOK AGAINST THE WALDENSIAN SECT

(Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, XVI, 520)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0793A]

I. While the lord Lucius, of illustrious memory, presided over the holy Roman Church [Note: Lucius III began to occupy the see in 1181.], new heretics suddenly raised their heads. By a certain foreknowledge of future things, they acquired the name Waldensians, doubtless from the “dense valley” (*vallis densa*), since they are enveloped in deep and thick darknesses of error. Although condemned by the aforesaid supreme pontiff, they rashly spewed the poison of their faithlessness far and wide throughout the world.

II. Therefore, on behalf of God’s Church, Lord Bernard, archbishop of Narbonne, distinguished by religion and honour before God, zealously defending God’s law, set himself against them as a strong wall [Col. 0794A]. Having summoned many clerics and laypeople, religious and secular alike, he called them to judgment. Why say more? The case having been investigated most carefully, they were condemned.

III. Nevertheless, afterwards they dared, both secretly and publicly, to scatter the seed of their wickedness. Hence, again—though this was more than sufficient—they were called to a disputation [Note: Bossuet mentions this disputation and the abbot of Font-Chaude (*History of the Variations*, book XI, nos. 75–79) in these words:

“The pontificate of Pope Lucius III began in 1181, that is, after Waldo had appeared in Lyons. It required a full twenty years for the movement to spread and form a sectarian body worthy of notice. Lucius III then condemned them; and, since his pontificate lasted only four years, this first condemnation of the Waldensians must have occurred between 1181, when this pope was raised to the chair of Saint Peter, and 1185, when he died. . . . After this pope’s death, since these heretics were spreading widely despite his decree, and Bernard, archbishop of Narbonne, who again condemned them after a thorough examination, could not arrest the course of the sect, several pious persons, ecclesiastics and others, arranged a conference in order to bring them back amicably. Both sides chose as arbiter of the conference a holy priest named Raimond of Daventrie, a man illustrious by birth but still more illustrious by his holy life.

“The assembly was very solemn, and the disputation was long. On both sides passages of Scripture were produced upon which they claimed to rely. The Waldensians were condemned and declared heretics on every count of the accusation. From this it may be seen that, although condemned, the Waldensians had not yet severed every tie with the Roman Church, since they agreed upon a Catholic priest as arbiter. The abbot of Font-Chaude, who was present at the conference, set down in writing, with much clarity and sound judgment, the points disputed and the passages employed by either side. Thus there is nothing better for understanding the entire state of the question as it then stood [Col. 0794B], at the beginning of the sect.

“The dispute chiefly concerns the obedience owed to pastors. It is evident that the Waldensians refused it to them and, despite every prohibition, believed themselves entitled to preach, both men and women. Since this disobedience could be founded only upon the unworthiness of the pastors, the Catholics, by proving the obedience owed to them, prove that it is owed even to those who are bad, and that, whatever the channel may be, grace nevertheless continues to flow over the faithful. For the same reason, it is shown that slanders against pastors . . . are forbidden by the law of God. Subsequently, the freedom taken by laypeople to preach without the pastors’ permission, and even despite their prohibitions, is attacked; and it is shown that such seditious preaching tends to the ruin of the weak and ignorant. Above all, Scripture proves that women, whose portion is silence alone, ought not to involve themselves in teaching. Finally, the Waldensians are shown the wrong they commit in rejecting prayer for the dead, which had so much foundation in Scripture and such evident support in tradition. Since these heretics withdrew from churches in order to pray privately together in their homes, they are shown that they ought not abandon the house of prayer, whose holiness all Scripture and the Son of God himself had so strongly commended.”], through certain clerics and laypeople. And, lest the dispute be prolonged any further, a certain priest, Raimond of Daventrie, was chosen as judge by both parties—a religious man who feared God, noble in lineage but nobler in manner of life [Col. 0795A].

IV. Accordingly, when the appointed day for the case arrived, the parties gathered together, along with many other clerics and laypeople. The Waldensians were accused by true Catholics of certain articles in which they held erroneous views. As they responded point by point, a long debate was conducted on both sides, and many authorities were produced by each side. Having heard the allegations of the parties, the aforesaid judge gave a definitive written judgment and pronounced them heretics on the points upon which they had been accused.

V. We have woven into this present little work the authorities and arguments by which they defended their assertion; what response was made to them by us Catholics; and the testimonies of Scripture by which we upheld the Catholic faith [Col. 0795B]. We have also added certain other treatises against other heresies. We did all this chiefly to instruct or admonish certain clerics who, burdened either by ignorance or by lack of books, have, through failing to resist the enemies of truth, become an offense and scandal to the faithful over whom they preside. For they neither strengthen them in the Catholic faith nor refresh them with the nourishment of the holy Scriptures. Thus, as though hungry on the road of this present age, they fail through want of spiritual strength and cannot return to their homeland, that is, paradise.

Indeed, it is a just cause of the greater evil previously described that ravening wolves—namely heretical and tyrannical demons—are not driven from the sheepfolds of Christ’s sheep, either by the voice of preaching or by the staff of discipline or severity [Col. 0795C].

VI. Therefore, I ask that they accept from our smallness, if they please, the slight gift of this little work, and commit the authorities of the holy Fathers to memory, so that, through God’s mercy, they may have impenetrable weapons against the rulers of darkness, against fabricators of lies, against worshippers of perverse doctrines—that is, heretical demons. Thus, with God’s grace preceding them, they may be able to triumph over these also, and may deserve to receive from the supreme shepherd an unfading crown of glory for the governance and instruction of their subjects.

# CHAPTER ONE. Against their assertion that the supreme pontiff and other prelates ought not to be obeyed.

[Col. 0795D]

I. First, therefore, they are accused of disobedience, because they do not obey the Roman Church, which possesses the fullness of the power of binding and loosing, and the dignity of ordering the other churches.

II. Moreover, they obey neither bishops nor priests, although, as blessed Gregory testifies, bishops hold the place of Christ’s disciples and possess the authority of binding and loosing, since they receive the office of governance. By this authority, therefore, the Roman Church and the other bishops, to whom it was said, “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” [Col. 0796A] (Matt. 16), bound the aforesaid heretics with the bond of excommunication, “being ready,” with the Apostle, “to punish every disobedience” (2 Cor. 10).

“Nothing,” however, as Augustine says on John, “ought so to be feared by a Christian as separation from Christ’s body.” For if one is separated from God’s body, one is not a member of it and is not given life by his Spirit. “But whoever,” says the Apostle, “does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8). Likewise, from *On the Words of the Apostle*: “Every Christian, beloved, who is excommunicated by priests is said to be handed over to Satan. How? Namely, because the devil is outside the Church, just as Christ is in the Church. And thus one who is removed from ecclesiastical communion is, as it were, handed over to the devil. Hence the Apostle demonstrates that those whom he then declares handed over to Satan had been excommunicated by him.”

Hence also the same Apostle says to the Thessalonians: “If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed” [Col. 0796B] (2 Thess. 3). Behold: the Apostle commands that one disobedient to him be rebuked and expelled from the fellowship or society of the others, so that, rejected in this way, he may be ashamed.

III. He also says to the Hebrews: “Obey your leaders and be subject to them. For they keep watch as those who will render an account for your souls” (Heb. 13). He also says to Timothy: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in word and teaching” [Col. 0796C] (1 Tim. 5). The double honour due to presbyters consists in obeying their commands and providing outward support with due reverence.

The Lord too, to show that obedience ought to be rendered to prelates, says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat. Therefore observe and do all things whatsoever they tell you” (Matt. 23). And again: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

IV. Therefore, since Christ and the Apostles command obedience to bishops and presbyters, whoever do not obey them are consequently disobedient to Christ and his Apostles. But every transgression and disobedience, according to the Apostle’s testimony, “receives a just recompense” [Col. 0796D] (Heb. 2). How, then, will those escape who neglect the commands of Christ and his disciples? Since, therefore, they are disobedient, they must be regarded as Gentiles and tax collectors, the Lord saying: “If anyone will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18).

V. Moreover, one must abstain from their fellowship, as is evident from the Apostle’s words to the Thessalonians cited above. For even under the Mosaic law, if anyone did not obey the command of the priest, he was to be put to death, lest the people be corrupted by the evil of disobedience. Hence in Deuteronomy: “The man who acts proudly, refusing to obey the command of the priest who ministers at that time to the Lord your God, or the decree of the judge—that man shall die; and you shall remove evil from the midst of Israel. And all the people, hearing, shall fear, so that none thereafter may swell with pride” [Col. 0797A] (Deut. 17).

Behold from this how great a crime disobedience is, since one who did not obey the priest was killed by the bodily sword. But in the time of grace, because God does not will the death of the sinner but that he turn and live (Ezek. 33), the offender is not physically killed, but struck by the spiritual sword when, through the sentence of the bishop, he is separated from the communion of the faithful, so that, rejected in this manner, he may be ashamed and come to his senses.

VI. All who are disobedient are also proved to be unbelievers, Samuel saying: “To resist is the sin of divination,” and, “To refuse assent is like the crime of idolatry” [Col. 0797B] (1 Kings 15). On this passage blessed Gregory says: “Obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it each person is proved an unbeliever, even if he appears to be a believer.” The Apostle also reckons the vice of disobedience among mortal crimes, saying: “The Gentiles are filled with every injustice, wickedness, fornication, and avarice” (Rom. 1). And after a few words: “Inventors of evils, disobedient to parents” (ibid.)—to carnal or spiritual parents, as orthodox teachers explain. And shortly afterward: “Those who do such things are worthy of death; and not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” [Col. 0797C] (ibid.). To consent, according to Ambrose, is to remain silent when one can rebuke, or, on hearing such conduct, to flatter it.

VII. Nor is it surprising that those disobedient to ecclesiastical authorities are worthy of eternal death. For the Apostle testifies: “There is no authority except from God, and those which exist are ordained by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance; and those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves” (Rom. 13). Let the aforesaid erring persons, therefore, and those who agree with them, hear the Apostle’s command: “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities” (ibid.). For “the Holy Spirit,” as the Apostle says in the Acts of the Apostles, “appointed bishops” over his flock “to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” [Col. 0797D] (Acts 20). Whoever, therefore, resists bishops through obstinacy sins against the Holy Spirit.

For when the Jews murmured against Moses and Aaron, they received the answer: “Your murmur is not against us, but against God” (Exod. 16). Hence Jude, brother of James, says: “Woe to those who perished in the rebellion of Korah!” (Jude 11). For Korah and his accomplices rose up against Moses and Aaron, priests of the Lord, and were immediately consumed by fire sent from heaven. Therefore, those perish in the rebellion of Korah who contradict the command of priests, and for that reason are burned in the blaze of eternal fire. Hence “woe,” that is, eternal damnation, is theirs.

VIII. Moreover, through Adam’s disobedience many were made sinners; through Christ’s obedience—he who was obedient to the Father unto death—many were made just. Therefore all who are disobedient bear the image of the old man. Against this the Apostle says: “As we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us bear the image of the heavenly one” [Col. 0798A] (1 Cor. 15), putting on the virtue of obedience, so that we who were expelled from paradise through disobedience may return through obedience, as by another way, and more fully.

“For obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening more than offering the fat of rams” (1 Kings 15), because in sacrifices another’s flesh is slain, whereas in obedience one’s own will is slain. And Solomon says: “An obedient man shall speak of victories” (Prov. 21), because, while we humbly submit to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in the heart [Col. 0798B]. From all these things it is clear how great is the virtue of obedience and how great the crime of disobedience.

# CHAPTER II. On the dignity of prelates, and that deference and obedience must be rendered to them.

I. That it may be clearer than light how far priests surpass others, and that deference and obedience must be rendered to them, may be seen from the words of the Saviour. To a man cured of leprosy he said: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded as a testimony to them” (Luke 5). For it belongs to priests to distinguish and judge who are Catholics and who are infected by heretical contagion. Hence, although the Lord healed many sick persons, he sent lepers alone to the priests. For the varied colour in a leper’s body signifies, in a heretical person, truth mingled with falsehood [Col. 0798C].

Plainly, the Lord did not wish a leper, even though cleansed, to be joined to gatherings of people without the priest’s judgment, so as openly to show that one who has strayed from Catholic unity, even if perhaps he has recovered his senses, is in no way to be joined to gatherings of the faithful without priestly judgment. And, as a sign of devotion and humility, he is commanded to make an offering to the priest, so that he may at once declare himself subject to him, whose hand he kisses with a religious intention while offering the sacrifice.

II. Likewise, clerics feed others; others, like sheep, are fed. The former live from the altar; the latter ought to make offerings. The former can hand sinners over to Satan; the latter must sit before them and must not transact God’s affairs without their counsel. Hence Jerome, to Heliodorus: “The case of a monk is one thing; that of a cleric, another. Clerics feed sheep; I am fed. They live from the altar; for me, an axe is laid as it were to the root of an unfruitful tree. If I do not bring a gift to the altar, I am not permitted to sit before a presbyter. If I sin, they are permitted to hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” [Col. 0798D].

The same author, to Rusticus: “The Church has a senate, an assembly of presbyters, without whose counsel monks may do nothing. Rehoboam son of Solomon lost his kingdom because he would not listen to his presbyters. The Romans also had a senate, by whose counsel they did everything; and we have our own senate, the assembly of presbyters” [Col. 0799A].

III. Moreover, when anyone doubts concerning divine law, he ought immediately to run to the priests and ask them. For they are those through whom the Creator of all determined to feed the peoples of the faithful. Hence the Lord gave five or seven loaves to his disciples, that they might set them before the crowds. He entrusts spiritual doctrine to priests, who have succeeded to the place of the disciples, so that, like good stewards of God’s household, they may dispense nourishment to souls, lest these faint from hunger on the road of this age.

Hence it is written: “Who, do you suppose, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season?” Hence too the Lord throws Paul, still Saul, to the ground on the road, but does not teach him what he must do; rather, he sends him into the city to be taught by the disciple Ananias [Col. 0799B]. Nor did the angel who appeared to the devout centurion give him the rule of faith; instead, he ordered Simeon to be summoned, so that through him the centurion might be instructed what he ought to do.

IV. From these things it is plainly understood that no one ought to presume to teach anyone the way of perfection unless he is in the city—that is, in the holy Church—and is Christ’s disciple. For Christ and his angel did not wish to teach Saul or the centurion, in order to show that the teaching office of the Church must be preserved inviolate and attempted by absolutely no one except those who have succeeded to the place of the disciples: that is, bishops and ecclesiastical men to whom the Lord entrusted this office. As is written, Malachi testifying: “The lips of the priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” [Col. 0799C].

Behold how great is the dignity of the priest. For he is, as is read in Ezekiel, the treasury in the house of the Lord: he keeps the treasure of wisdom and knowledge in his breast, and the law is to be sought from his mouth at the Lord’s command. The Lord himself, as the Gospel testifies, taught this by example: he sat in the Temple among the teachers, listened to them, and questioned them. Thus he teaches at the same time that heavenly doctrine is especially to be learned in the holy Church, not in the marketplace or the streets, so that it may be received and committed to memory all the better because in the Church one devotes more attentive care not to temporal matters but to divine things [Col. 0799D].

V. How great a thing it is that a priest is called an angel of the Lord, that is, a messenger! For he is sent to announce the heavenly Judge; and therefore, although he may be contemptible in himself, he is nevertheless to be revered because he bears the person of the Lord. For, as blessed Gregory testifies: “A powerful person often has a despised servant, through whom he conveys some reply to his own people or to strangers. The person of the speaking servant is not despised, because reverence for the sending lord is preserved in the heart.” Thus, although any priest may perhaps deservedly be despised by someone, nevertheless the person to whom he is sent ought in his own mind to preserve reverence for the Lord who sent him.

[Col. 0800A] VI. Sinners also ought to confess their wicked deeds to priests, so that they may be released from the bonds of their guilt. Hence the Lord said to one who had been dead four days: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11). When he had come forth alive, he was, at the Lord’s command, loosed from his bonds by the disciples, who were told: “Loose him, and let him go” (ibid.). The dead person comes forth when the sinner confesses his fault. The disciples loose the one who comes forth, because the preachers of the Church ought to remove from him the penalty he deserved, since he was not ashamed to confess what he had done. Judas indeed confessed his sin, not to Christ’s disciples but to the Jews, saying: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27). Yet his confession did him no good.

VII. Priests not only loose the guilty, but also bind them [Col. 0800B] and hand them over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved. Hence the Lord says: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (Matt. 16). For, according to Gregory’s testimony, the disciples—whose place bishops hold—retain the sins of some and remit those of others in God’s stead. The Apostle likewise says concerning the fornicator: “I have judged, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, in his stead or for his glory, “to hand such a one over to Satan, that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 5). He hands him over to Satan so that Satan may afflict him bodily and he may thus come to his senses. Or, according to some, the death of the body is meant; alternatively, to excommunicate is to hand over to Satan. For just as the devil has no claim upon a person after that person has been justified through faith, so, once a person is separated on account of guilt from the Church’s sacraments—which are his weapons against Satan—he is thereafter bound again beneath Satan’s yoke.

VIII. Moreover, the Holy Spirit often considers the dignity of the priesthood rather than personal merit, and provides an equal gift with the elect. Thus, when Caiaphas was high priest, he prophesied. Here the Evangelist plainly ascribes the gift of prophecy to the divine sacrament, saying: “Since he was,” that is, because he was, high “priest” (John 11). Water passes through channels of stone to beds of aromatic plants: that is, the irrigation of spiritual grace sometimes waters and pours into the souls of believers, planted with fragrant virtues, through the hard and unfeeling minds of those who preside.

[Col. 0800D] IX. Blessed James also shows how necessary and useful the order of priests is when he says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him call in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him” (James 5). Behold: the priest’s prayer saves; through it God raises the sick person and forgives sins. It saves in this way: the prayer of presbyters benefits body and soul, relieving infirmity and forgiving sins. Here likewise he rebukes those who summon heretics and abandon presbyters, since the Apostle commands that presbyters, not heretics, be summoned. He also silently rebukes certain [Col. 0801A] Christians who, when they fall ill, send not for priests but for physicians—or, in an inverted order, send for priests only afterward—although weakness of the soul is often the cause of bodily infirmity. Thus the Lord first forgives the sins of the paralytic brought to him, saying: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5), and afterward heals his body. “For when the cause is removed, the effect is removed.”

X. It also belongs to priests to decide questions arising concerning the Christian religion. Thus Moses, ascending the mountain, said to Israel’s elders: “Wait here until we return. You have Aaron and Hur with you; if any question arises, you shall refer it to them” (Exod. 24). Questions arising among believers concerning faith or Christian worship are to be referred to bishops [Col. 0801B] and presbyters. This is why, for this and other necessary reasons, bishops are appointed by the apostles in every city and presbyters in every church. Accordingly, the Apostle says to Titus: “For this reason I left you in Crete: that you might correct what is lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you” (Titus 1). The Acts of the Apostles also relates that Paul and Barnabas appointed presbyters in every church.

XI. It should be noted, however, that by the name “presbyters” bishops are meant, as shortly before in the passage addressed to Titus, and ordinary priests are meant, as in the passage above from the Acts of the Apostles. Conversely, lesser priests are sometimes called bishops, [Col. 0801C] as in the Epistle to the Philippians, where the Apostle says: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons” (Phil. 1). For there are not several bishops in one city; nor, while speaking of bishops and passing over priests without mention, would he insert a lower order, namely that of deacons, unless he had called priests “bishops.” At other times bishops, by a term reserved for them, are called the greater priests, as common usage also shows.

XII. Having said this by way of digression, it must be known that in the New Testament, when the question arose whether believers ought to be circumcised and observe the law of Moses, Paul and Barnabas determined that the believers should remain as they had believed; and that the same apostles, together with certain others from among the rest, should go up to the apostles and presbyters in Jerusalem concerning this question. “The apostles and elders assembled to consider this matter” (Acts 15). The apostles and elders together decided the question and, in response to the believers’ request, sent a decretal letter about it, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles.

XIII. From this example it is clear that, when doubt arises concerning the practice of the Christian faith, recourse must be had to the supreme patriarch, who acts in the place of blessed Peter, and to the others: both archbishops, who bear the persons of the apostles, and bishops, who hold the place of the other disciples, whom Luke above in Acts calls now presbyters, now elders. For if [Col. 0802A] the apostles Paul and Barnabas did not presume to decide so great a question except after consulting with the apostles and elders and making careful inquiry, one must diligently consider how great is the presumption and folly of seeking from others, and not from Christ’s priests, answers concerning matters that pertain to faith in God and to its established order—especially from heretics or wicked Catholics.

XIV. To this end, the Apostle tells the Corinthians that believers ought not to bring lawsuits concerning transitory matters before unbelievers, but before saints: “Does any one of you, having a case against another, dare to be judged before the unrighteous and not before the saints? Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, secular matters? If the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy [Col. 0802B] to judge the smallest matters?” (1 Cor. 6). And afterward: “Is there then no wise person among you who can judge between brother and brother? But brother litigates with brother, and that before unbelievers? Indeed, it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another” (ibid.). Therefore, if saints—that is, believers—and not unbelievers ought to judge a dispute concerning the least matters, much more, when the issue or doubt concerns faith and spiritual things, must it be considered and judged by holy believers, not by heretics or unbelievers. And if unbelievers are unworthy to judge the least matters, they are much more unworthy to judge Christian religion and faith. Especially since Moses admonishes every person, saying: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32). Who are the father and elders whom we ought to ask, if not the rulers of souls, who, instructing us in holy conduct, beget us as spiritual children? And because they surpass us in dignity or merit, they are called “our elders” [majores nostri], who are also called by another name “seniors” [seniores]. To them blessed Peter also speaks when writing to believers: “I exhort the elders among you, I who am a fellow elder and witness of Christ’s sufferings: feed the flock of God that is among you” (1 Pet. 5); and shortly afterward: “Likewise, younger persons, be subject to the elders” (ibid.).

XV. Behold, he plainly states by whom the flock of believers ought to be fed: namely, by its elders. For, as [Col. 0802D] blessed Gregory says, “Holy Scripture calls those people old who mature through gravity of character, not through length of time, as it is written: ‘Venerable old age is not long life, nor is it reckoned by the number of years; but the gray hairs of human beings are understanding, and the age of old age is an unstained life.’” Those are also called young who are not weighed down by any seriousness of counsel. The chief of the apostles commands them to be subject to elders, so that the lightness of the frivolous may be weighed down by the gravity of the serious, according to the saying: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will be innocent” (Ps. 17). These words rebuke those who do not obey the commands of their elders, that is, their prelates, and who thus prove disobedient to the Apostle Peter.

XVI. Finally, it belongs to priests, as the Lord says to them in the person of the priest Aaron [Col. 0803A] and his sons, “to distinguish between holy and profane, between clean and unclean, and to teach all the ordinances which God commanded the children of Israel through the hand of Moses,” as is found in Leviticus: “The Lord said to Aaron: You and your sons shall not drink wine or anything that can intoxicate when you enter the tabernacle of testimony, lest you die; for it is an everlasting commandment throughout your generations” (Lev. 10). And: “so that you may have knowledge to distinguish between holy and profane, between polluted and clean, and may teach the children of Israel all my ordinances which the Lord spoke to them through the hand of Moses” (ibid.). From this it plainly appears whose duty it is—not that of others—to distinguish who are holy, that is, Catholics, and who [Col. 0803B] are profane, that is, heretics; and who are clean from the stain of sin and who are unclean, that is, guilty of crimes. Indeed, it belongs to them to teach believers God’s commandments. Therefore it is blameworthy for others, who are not of the tribe of Levi—that is, not of the clerical order—to usurp their office in judging or teaching.

XVII. We have gathered these few examples from among many to show how great the dignity and authority of bishops and priests is. Once this is recognized, those who have until now been rebellious against them should humbly obey them.

## CHAPTER III. Against those who speak ill of the rulers of souls

I. But since there are some who speak ill of these rulers of souls and rebuke them at the peril of their own souls, let us say at least a few things for their correction. Let such persons therefore hear that, as the Apostle testifies, “slanderers hateful to God, whisperers, and the insolent are worthy of death” (Rom. 1). A slanderer is one who, as far as he can, diminishes his neighbor’s good qualities and attributes to him evils that are not in him. A whisperer is one who secretly conveys evils about one neighbor to another. An insolent person is one who willingly inflicts upon his neighbor some shameful dishonor, whether in word or deed. The same Apostle also says to the Corinthians: “If one who is called a brother is abusive,” that is, a slanderer, “with such a person do not even take food” (1 Cor. 5). And again: “The abusive shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6).

[Col. 0803D] II. Therefore, since a slanderer or abusive person ought not to be received into the communion of believers and is worthy of death, as one who shall not possess the kingdom of God, it is nevertheless especially forbidden to anyone to curse the ruler of the people. Thus, when Paul, unaware that Ananias was the high priest, was ordered by him to be struck on the mouth, he said: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall.” And those standing by said: “Do you curse God’s high priest?” Paul answered: “I did not know, brothers, that he was the ruler of the priests. For it is written: ‘You shall not curse the ruler of your people.’” Behold: he says that the ruler of the people, although openly acting contrary to the law and ordering him to be struck while he was being judged, must not be cursed, and he proves this by Scriptural authority. Hence those who curse the rulers of churches should consider [Col. 0804A] what great condemnation they deserve: if the Apostle refrained from cursing an unbeliever acting contrary to the law once he learned that he was ruler of the people, and said that he had cursed him because he did not know that he was ruler of the people.

III. Moreover, Ham saw the exposed private parts of his father Noah and laughed; and therefore he was condemned in his posterity, Noah saying: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Gen. 9). For no one ought rashly to rebuke or publicize the faults of his superiors, or to rejoice while seeing them; otherwise he will be condemned hereafter, that is, in the future. But Noah’s good sons cover their father’s shame, throwing a cloak over their backs and coming toward him backward. “For good [Col. 0804B] subjects, as blessed Gregory says, are displeased by the faults of their superiors in such a way that they nevertheless conceal them from others. While judging the deed and reverencing the office, they do not wish to see what they cover.”

IV. Let these aforementioned slanderers also consider that holy David humbly obeyed Saul—proud, yet king and chosen by the Lord; a persecutor who wished to kill David; finally, because of his sins, rejected by God, while David had been chosen by the Lord to govern the kingdom. Though all this was so, David obeyed the wicked king in such a manner that it was written of him: “Who in all things has been found like David in your kingdom, going in and going out and proceeding at the king’s command?” Again, when he could have struck the king who persecuted him, he cast himself down before him in a humble declaration, saying: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog and a single flea.” From this subjects should learn that, although humble and innocent, they ought to show deference—not slander—to the powers set over them by God, even if those powers rage against them; to obey, not contradict. David likewise, when his servants urged him to strike Saul after Saul had entered the cave where they were, restrained them by his words, because he ought not to lay his hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Yet he secretly rose and cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak. Because he had done this, David’s heart smote him afterward. Behold: considering that Saul was anointed by God and set above him, David refuses to kill him, even though Saul was seeking to kill him; and he repents because he cut off even the outermost [Col. 0804D] edge of Saul’s cloak. Saint Gregory says on this passage: “The deeds of a superior are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are judged rightly deserving of rebuke. But if the tongue ever slips against them, even in the smallest matters, the heart must be burned by the affliction of repentance, so that it may return to itself. And when a governing authority sins, it should fear the judgment against itself of him by whom it was set above it. For when we sin against those set over us, we oppose the ordinance of him who set them over us.”

V. Behold, by the authorities of holy Scripture and by the examples of saints, we have demonstrated how great a reverence must be shown, with detraction set aside, toward prelates; and that deference, not slander or cursing, must be shown them. Otherwise, we offend against God’s commandments and do not follow in the saints’ footsteps.

## CHAPTER IV. Against the practice of all persons, including laypeople, preaching; and what they say in its defense and what we say against them

I. Secondly, all preach everywhere, without distinction of rank, age, or sex. Since many of those who are called Christians merely in outward appearance are led astray by this error, let us, with God’s help, for the sake of recalling them and confirming the rest, consider the arguments or authorities upon which they rely; what Catholics say to weaken and utterly refute these arguments; and, thirdly, what Catholics adduce in support of their own position.

[Col. 0805B] II. First, then, they say that everyone who knows how to sow the word of God among the people ought to preach. For James says: “To one who knows to do good and does not do it, it is sin” (James 4). Why, then, if we know how to evangelize and refrain from doing so, do we sin grievously? When a certain heresiarch cited this Scripture on his own behalf, he was answered: We read in the Gospel that the devil said to the Lord Jesus: “I know who you are, the Holy One of God.” And Jesus rebuked him, saying: “Be silent” (Mark 1). Behold: the Lord did not wish to be preached through the devil’s mouth, although the devil said that he knew him, lest perhaps, by presenting falsehood as truth, he should deceive the simple, as he deceived the woman in the beginning. Thus, thus, answer: Christ’s name is not to be proclaimed from your mouth, even if you knew it, lest, in the manner of a poisoner, while you seem to offer honeyed cups to some simple person, you pour in mixed poison. For it is written of the wicked: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32). The incurable venom of asps is the doctrine of heretics, because whoever drinks it—that is, receives it willingly by listening—without doubt does not escape death.

III. Moreover, the Apostle did not say, “To one who knows how to teach good,” but “to do good” (James 4). It must therefore be understood of one who does not accomplish the good he understands and therefore sins, not of one who does not teach the good that he knows how to teach. For not every person sins who does not teach what he knows; rather, he sins if he teaches while he himself is a transgressor. For David says: “God said to the sinner: Why do you [Col. 0805D] recount my just ordinances and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49). The Apostle says: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who glory in the law, through transgression of the law do you dishonor God?” (Rom. 2).

IV. Again, in support of their error they cite: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22). Blessed Gregory says on this passage: “Let the one who has received in his heart the voice of heavenly love also give to his neighbors outwardly the voice of exhortation.” And Gregory again says there: “To the extent that you are sufficient through divine generosity, give your neighbors cups of good speech.”

V. We reply that, if these passages are carefully considered, they do not aid them in their erroneous practices. For when he says, “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come,’” it follows that one who does not inwardly hear in his heart the voice of brotherly love—or who does not hear the voice of God with the ear of the body or of the heart, even though he has bodily hearing—or who does not fulfill it in deed, must not say to another, “Come.” For with what face can one who does not obey God’s word invite another to the same obedience which he himself does not fulfill in deed? Or how can he build obedience in another when he destroys it in himself? Therefore those who do not hear God’s word—indeed, who are disobedient to it, as has been shown above—ought not to teach others. In the same homily blessed Gregory also says: “To the extent that you consider yourselves to have made progress, draw others too, and desire to have companions on God’s way.” From these words it is clear whom blessed [Col. 0806B] Gregory exhorts to encourage their neighbors: namely, those who had progressed and were on God’s way. He admonishes them to draw others according to the measure of their progress. But heretics have not progressed; indeed, they have fallen away. They are not on God’s way; rather, as it is written: “He caused them to wander in a trackless waste, and not in a way” (Ps. 106). Therefore they ought not to exhort others. For works without faith are like great strength and very swift running apart from the road.

VI. Again, in support of their assertion they cite what is said in Mark’s Gospel: John answered the Lord, saying: “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name who does not follow us, and we forbade him. But Jesus said: Do not forbid him. For there is no one who performs a miracle in my name and can soon speak evil of me; for whoever is not against you is for you” (Mark 9).

VII. “Behold,” they say, “this man did not follow the apostles; yet because he cast out demons in Christ’s name, the Lord commanded them not to forbid him. Therefore, if we preach Christ’s name, though we do not follow bishops and other priests, they ought not forbid us.”

VIII. But we reply that this authority does not help them; it harms them. For that man performed a good work, because he cast out demons in Christ’s name; thus he had faith and did not speak evil. Therefore, although he did not bodily follow the apostles, he was not to be forbidden from his good work, [Col. 0806D] because by living spiritually through faith and works he followed the apostles and introduced no perverse doctrine. But these people are unbelievers and are without obedience, “which alone possesses the merit of faith”; and, according to the Apostle, “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Consequently their works carry them away from the way of faith; through them they do not draw near to God but withdraw from him. They are makers of falsehood and worshippers of perverse doctrines. Therefore they must be forbidden, because they are opposed to Christ’s priests. Catholic teachers have also written on this passage that, in heretics and wicked Catholics, we must detest and forbid not the sacraments held in common, in which they are with us rather than against us, but the division contrary to peace [Col. 0807A] and truth, by which they are against us and do not follow the Lord with us.

IX. Again, they say that the Apostle supports them when he says: “Some indeed preach Christ out of envy and contention; others out of good will” (Phil. 1). Some envied the Apostle’s glory and contended to obtain it, seeking to equal him through the renown of preaching. Others preached Christ because they wished all people to come to knowledge of the truth. And shortly afterward: “What then? Provided only that in every way, whether from pretext or from truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, indeed, and shall rejoice” (ibid.). “Behold,” they say, “the Apostle rejoices that Christ is preached in whatever manner, whether by the envious or the good, from a good intention or a bad one. Why, then, do bishops likewise not rejoice when Christ is preached by us, but oppose us?” We say in reply that it matters greatly by whom Christ is proclaimed: by Catholics or by non-Catholics. Christ is sometimes preached by good Catholics and sometimes by evil ones—that is, by the envious or those who hate their brothers. Thus Christ’s sheep are fed sometimes by good shepherds and sometimes by hirelings. Of these it is said: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat; do what they tell you, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). Of good persons the Apostle says: “Remember your rulers, who have spoken God’s word to you; considering [Col. 0807C] the outcome of their conduct, imitate their faith” (Heb. 13). But of non-Catholics, that is, heretics, it is said: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. 7). And as though someone asked how true prophets may be distinguished from false ones, the Lord adds: “You shall know them by their fruits” (ibid.). For they oppress believers and blaspheme God, if not in words then in deeds. Above all, they are distinguished by impatience in times of adversity. Fasts, prayers, and such things belong to hypocrites as well as good people. Therefore they are distinguished not by leaves—that is, by words alone—but by fruits. Hence the Apostle says: “I shall come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I shall know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power. For the kingdom of God does not consist in speech but in power” (1 Cor. 4). As though he said: I shall know not their leaves but their fruits.

X. Moreover, Christ is truth, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Therefore one who invents and proclaims a perverse doctrine does not preach Christ. The Apostle, then, speaks of wicked Catholics—that is, hirelings—who nevertheless proclaim Christ, that is, truth. But these people make up their own falsehoods; and therefore, in accordance with the Lord’s command, they are to be watched—that is, carefully guarded against. We do not rejoice at their preaching, because they preach not Christ but falsehood. And because they are neither rulers nor hirelings, but wolves, [Col. 0808A] whereas shepherds must both be heard and imitated, as we have already shown through the Apostle. Hirelings must be heard in what they teach by word, so that it may be done, but must not be imitated in their conduct, as the Lord says; wolves must be watched and avoided. Hence the Apostle says: “I urge you, brothers, to watch those who cause dissensions and offenses contrary to the teaching which you have learned, and turn away from them. For such persons do not serve Christ our Lord but their own belly, and through sweet words and blessings deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. 16). Behold that such people are to be avoided; and why? Namely, because they cause dissent, drawing believers away from the understanding of the faithful and also causing offense against one’s neighbor, although it is written: “Be without offense toward Jews, Gentiles, and the Church of God” (1 Cor. [Col. 0808B] 10). In matters that may be done or not done, take care to “please all in all things” (ibid.), whether by doing or by not doing.
