Or perhaps he joins dissensions and offenses together because all who think otherwise than the other faithful offend by “striking against the stone of offense and rock of stumbling.” Hence the Apostle also says: “By sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience,” namely through the example which they see, “you sin against Christ” (1 Cor. 8), whose members they are. Therefore the Apostle commands dissensions to be avoided when he says: “I urge you, brothers, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you; rather, be made perfect in the same mind,” that is, willing the same thing, “and the same knowledge” (1 Cor. 1), that is, believing the same thing. And he likewise commands offenses to be avoided when he says: “Judge this instead: never to put a stumbling block or offense before a brother” (Rom. 14).

XI. Therefore heretics, who cause dissensions and offenses, are contrary to apostolic doctrine and must be avoided.

XII. Again, they cite for themselves Moses’ answer to Joshua. When Joshua wished to restrain two men who had remained in the camp and were prophesying, Moses said to him: “Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord might give them his Spirit” (Num. 11). “Behold,” the heretics say, “Moses did not envy those prophesying; indeed, he desired all the people to prophesy. But the clerical [Col. 0808D] order opposes us and envies us as we prophesy—that is, expound the mysteries of God’s word. Prophecy is the foretelling of future things, the disclosure of hidden things, or the exposition of concealed mysteries. Therefore the clergy resemble not Moses but Joshua. Since they do not follow in the saints’ footsteps but those of the envious, they sin and ought not to be listened to when they oppose us.”

XIII. To this we say that, like Moses, we would wish all the people to prophesy and that the Lord might give them his Spirit, so that every mouth might proclaim the truth which we are unable sufficiently to speak. “But each has his own gift from God, one in one way and another in another. For he gave some as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers” (1 Cor. 7). Similar is what the Apostle says: “I wish all people to be as I myself am” (ibid.), namely continent, “but each has his own gift from God,” and so forth. But God is not a God of dissension, but of peace, as the Apostle teaches in all the churches of the saints. Therefore prophecy has not been given to everyone. And we say that it has not been given to them. For prophecy is a gift of God; but these people cause dissensions and offenses, as stated above. Therefore God is not in them, for he dwells among those who are peaceful and concordant. Hence the Apostle says: “Have peace, and the God of peace and love will be with you” (2 Cor. 13). And elsewhere: “Bearing with one another in charity, take care to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Col. 0809B] (Eph. 4). But these people neither possess nor love Catholic peace; instead, they produce dissension and discord among the Christian people. Hence some follow them, while others hesitate whether they ought to follow them or rather Catholic men. Therefore the unity of the Spirit, which is preserved in the bond of peace, is not in them.

XIV. We do not, then, envy them as they prophesy, because they are not prophets—unless perhaps false ones, of whom the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets,” etc. (Matt. 7). Jeremiah says of such people to the people of Israel: “Your prophets saw false things for you; they did not expose your iniquity so as to call you to repentance” (Lam. 2). Such are these people, who have seen and preach false things to the Christian people. And although it is written: “Cry aloud; do not cease; declare to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. 58), these people, on the contrary, do not declare to believers the crimes committed by some, nor do they call them to repentance. They are rightly rejected as false prophets. And certainly the Lord says: “False Christs and false prophets will arise, and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error” (Matt. 24). In the last times false Christs will give signs and thus deceive many. Nor is it surprising when these people, who perform no signs at all, overthrow the faith of many and deceive innocent hearts with sweet words.

XV. In response, they say that many laypeople have disseminated God’s word among the faithful people, such as blessed Honoratus and Saint Equitius, whom Saint Gregory mentions in the book of *Dialogues*, and, in these times, Saint Raymond, surnamed Paul, in confirmation of whose sanctity many miracles occur. Finally, the first apostles were “unlearned and unlettered” (Acts 4). All these, though laypeople, preached God’s word. Therefore, as imitators of their deeds, we ought not to be rejected but heard.

XVI. But we reply that the apostles were indeed unlearned before their calling; yet “the Lord opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24), poured the Holy Spirit into them, [Col. 0810A] and himself sent them to preach God’s kingdom. Furthermore, they preached not errors, but the Catholic faith and the Lord’s commandments. Through God’s grace they performed new and unheard-of miracles, “the Lord working with them and confirming the word through accompanying signs” (Mark 16). But these people do not understand the sacred writings. As the Apostle says, “certain persons, having wandered away, have turned to empty talk, desiring to be teachers of the law without understanding either what they say or the things about which they make assertions” (1 Tim. 1). They do not understand because they lack faith, without which no one can possess the gift of understanding, as it is written: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7). Again, they do not understand because they do not act. If they did what is written, they would understand well, as it is written: “Good understanding belongs to all who do it” [Col. 0810B] (Ps. 110). This is the same point as the vineyard taken away from tenants who did not render its fruit and given to other cultivators who will render its fruit in its seasons; and as the talent taken from the lazy servant who would not put it to use. Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “The kingdom of God”—that is, understanding of the sacred Scriptures—“will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21). They do not possess the Holy Spirit because they have departed from the holy Church, outside which it is given to no one. Thus the Lord says to the disciples: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24). For the Church is the city of the great King, in which those who sit—that is, the humble—are clothed with the power of the Most High. Thus a mighty wind “filled the whole house where they were sitting” (Acts 2), that is, the holy Church, where the humble receive the Holy Spirit. For it is written: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). But they are not humble, since they set themselves above the rulers of churches. By contrast, humble David placed the proud king above himself, saying: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog and a single flea” (1 Sam. 26). Note how humbly he thought of himself when he called himself a dead dog and a single flea. And what did he call Saul, though rejected by God? “King of Israel.” Hence both heretics [Col. 0810D] and other proud Christians should consider how much deference they owe ecclesiastical and secular authorities, whose merits before God they do not know, if holy David so greatly revered a proud king whom he knew to be rejected by God, while knowing himself to have been chosen to govern the kingdom.

XVII. Moreover, they live restlessly, “doing no work,” as the Apostle says of those like them, but “busying themselves,” namely, with other people’s affairs. The Apostle commands such persons “that, working quietly, they should eat their own bread” (2 Thess. 3), that is, bread earned by their own labour, not another’s. Since, then, they are proud and restless, the Holy Spirit, who dwells in the humble and the quiet, will not rest upon them.

[Col. 0811A] XVIII. As for what they allege concerning holy laymen—that they preached the word of God—they would by no means make this objection if they attended to the words of Saint Gregory. For he says of Saint Honoratus that he shone by the power of abstinence, humility, and other virtues, and moreover by miracles. Likewise, when a huge mass of rock was coming down upon his cell and was about to kill the brethren, he halted it by invoking Christ’s name and setting against it his outstretched right hand marked with the sign of the cross. Gregory testifies that he had not heard that this man belonged to any discipline or religious rule. Here the heretics seize upon the point, saying that, like him, they have disciples after them although they have had no teacher. But let them consider what Saint Gregory adds. He says: “It is the practice of right conduct that one who has not learned to be subject should not dare to preside.” And again [Col. 0811B] he says: “This freedom is not to be drawn into an example, lest anyone, presuming himself likewise filled with the Holy Spirit—that is, taught not by human instruction—should disdain to be a disciple of a man and become a teacher of error,” etc. And again: “These things are to be venerated by the weak, not imitated.”

XIX. Saint Equitius also was taught and sent by an angel. For by night a handsome young man appeared to him in a vision, placed a lancet upon his tongue, and said: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; go forth to preach.” This saint shone in chastity, prayer, zeal for souls, learning, humility, prophecy, and power in driving out unclean spirits. It is therefore no wonder that this man, taught [Col. 0811C] and sent by God, and endowed with so many virtues, preached although he did not possess sacred orders. Yet by this man’s example let heretics learn that they ought without delay to obey both the supreme pontiff and the bishops. For when he was summoned by the Roman pontiff through the defensor Vitalianus, he immediately gave thanks to God; and at once commanded that the beasts of burden be made ready that very hour, and began urgently pressing Vitalianus that they ought to depart at once. But because Vitalianus was tired from the journey, they remained that night at his request. In the morning, however, the supreme pontiff sent word through another messenger that the servant of God Equitius was not to leave the monastery. On hearing this, the servant of God, though grieved because they had not gone, remained. Behold: this saint obeyed the Roman pontiff both in going and in [Col. 0811D] remaining.

XX. Likewise, Bishop Cadorius asked this same servant of God to receive into his community a certain Basil, who, foremost in magical arts, had fled Rome and sought Valeria in a monastic habit. When asked, Saint Equitius replied to the bishop: “Father, I do not see this man whom you commend to me as a monk, but as a devil.” The bishop said: “You are seeking an excuse not to grant what is asked of you.” Saint Equitius replied: “I indeed declare him to be what I see him to be; nevertheless, lest you think that I am unwilling to obey, I shall do what you command.” He was therefore received into the monastery. But a few days later, in the absence of the servant of God, this same Basil, by his [Col. 0812A] magical arts, drove mad one of the consecrated virgins over whom Equitius presided. The virgin also began to suffer a fever and said that she would immediately die unless Basil the monk came and cured her. A message was therefore swiftly sent to the servant of God, who immediately cured the virgin and, once the brethren clearly learned that Basil was a sorcerer, caused him to be expelled from the community. Behold: he proved obedient even to the bishop in receiving Basil, although through the spirit of prophecy he knew him to be a sorcerer. By these examples, therefore, let heretics learn to obey both the Roman pontiff and the other bishops.

XXI. Certainly, what they allege concerning Saint Raymond of Paul—that he preached while he was a layman, and that the Church received him—is true. But, as is said, he was a man of Catholic conduct; he preached honourably with the permission of the bishops, introducing no error, orthodox in all things, obedient to the rulers of the churches, ardently devoted with all zeal to gathering souls for God, and, according to his knowledge and ability, a most vigorous opponent of heretics. Over the very swift river called the Durance, he built from the alms of the faithful a bridge and redeemed its passage from every levy, as is said, making it free for pilgrims and all travellers. At the place called Bonpas he devoted himself, along with other needy persons, to this pious work as occasion allowed. Let heretics therefore cease to invoke this Catholic man in defence of their error, since they are known to stray so far from his footsteps.

[Col. 0812C] XXII. We have said these things in order to refute the arguments of heretics, showing also how the authorities of the holy Scriptures—which, as the Apostle Peter testifies, they distort to their own destruction—are to be understood. Now, with the Holy Spirit’s assistance, let it be our task to bring forward authorities and arguments by which it may be clearer than light that they ought not to preach the word of God, nor ought they to be heard by the faithful.

## CHAPTER V. That they are not permitted to minister the word of God to the faithful.

I. Since the question concerns laymen—whether they can sow the word [Col. 0812D] of God among the people—a distinction must be made: whether they are Catholics or not. Certainly, if they are Catholics and are commended by an honourable life; if their speech is seasoned with the salt of wisdom; if they know how to dispense the measure of the word according to each person’s capacity; and if they preside in a definite place, or are subject in obedience to a true Catholic, then, according to the extent of their own advancement in knowledge or conduct, they may, in my judgment, exhort their neighbours at the direction of the bishops or priests in whose territory they are, provided that they are not bound by wives and are not oppressed by the burden of earthly care. But if their life is blameworthy, there is no necessity to hear them. For when the Lord says, “Do what they say,” this was said only of those who sit upon the [Col. 0813A] chair of Moses—that is, of the masters and teachers of the divine law whom God set over his people. “But God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous acts, and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. 49.) Hence David too was told: “You shall not build a house for me, because you are a man of blood” (2 Sam. 16 [citation as printed]). A man of blood is forbidden to build God’s temple, because one who is still absorbed in carnal deeds must necessarily be ashamed to form the minds of his neighbours spiritually.

II. “Let your speech always be in grace, seasoned with the salt of wisdom,” according to the Apostle, “that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. 4): one way, namely, to an unlearned person; another to a learned one; and differently again to other persons. But when will a layman be able to make this distinction, when even clergy scarcely attain such knowledge? Food is not fit unless seasoned with salt; nor is speech useful without the teaching of wisdom. Hence in Leviticus: “In every offering you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2); that is, in all words or deeds possess apostolic wisdom. If, then, he does not possess apostolic wisdom in words and deeds, his speech is useless and therefore to be avoided. For the Apostle says to Timothy: “Avoid profane”—that is, heretical—“empty talk” (2 Tim. 2), that is, talk without fruit, even if not so evil as to be profane. “For they make much progress toward impiety,” that is, against the worship of God, “and their speech spreads like a cancer” (ibid.), gradually corrupting what is sound.

[Col. 0813C] III. Furthermore, one who teaches must attend to the capacity of the hearers, so as to dispense the measure of wheat—that is, of the divine word—“as God has apportioned to each the measure of faith” (2 Cor. 10 [citation as printed]). Hence the Apostle commands prophecy, that is, the revelation of hidden things, to be ministered according to the proportion of faith—that is, the measure of faith of those to whom hidden things are to be disclosed—lest an immature person be overwhelmed by higher matters, or an adult person be deprived of what would perfect him. Otherwise, if a hearer is offended by his teaching, the teacher will be held guilty before God. Hence it is written in the Law: “If anyone opens a cistern, or digs one and does not cover it, and an ox or an ass falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall pay the price of the animals” (Exod. 21). To open a cistern is to penetrate by understanding the hidden mysteries of sacred Scripture. But one covers it who conceals by silence the lofty meanings of Scripture before those unable to comprehend them. Whoever does not cover it before the brutish hearts of hearers incurs guilt of punishment if, through his words, either a clean or an unclean mind is ensnared into scandal.

[Col. 0813D] IV. Moreover, if they preside in a certain place or are subject through obedience, it becomes more plainly known that they are obedient to the holy Church; for nearly every place belongs to some diocese, and nearly every diocese has its own boundaries. Nor is this all: churches established within each diocese are also distinguished in diverse ways by their own boundaries, so that neither a bishop may exercise episcopal rights except in his own diocese, nor a priest possess authority in another parish. For it is written: “Let no one put a sickle into another’s harvest”; that is, let no one presume to judge faithful persons entrusted to another. And the Apostle says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own master” (Rom. 14). If, therefore, a bishop cannot regularly exercise his authority outside his diocese, nor a priest outside his parish, [Col. 0814A] how much less can an unknown man and layman put the sickle of the word, without the permission of the bishop or priest to whose care it belongs, into another’s harvest—that is, among a people entrusted to another? Certainly, according to the Gospel’s testimony, no one laboured in the vineyard unless hired by the householder. Elsewhere it is recorded that the householder leased his vineyard to husbandmen, who would render him its fruits in their seasons. And certainly, although they did not render fruits to the lord, but instead beat, killed, and stoned his servants, and finally killed his son, nevertheless no one presumed to appropriate the vineyard to himself so long as the master endured their uselessness and wickedness. Thus, among a people entrusted to another—even to one useless or wicked—so long as he is tolerated by the Church, no one, without the direction and permission of the person to whom it has been entrusted, presumes to labour: that is, to cast out unfruitful vines and plant fruitful ones, to apply the hoe of the word, to prune the vineyard of superfluities, or to propagate what is necessary.

[Col. 0814C] V. Finally, who is so mad as to attempt to pasture another’s sheep without consulting their master? By that very fact he is suspect, because he intrudes himself, especially if he is unknown. Such a man is the one who “does not enter through the door, but climbs in another way, and is a thief and a robber. The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy” (John 10). And certainly, as the teachers say, one enters through the door by believing in the Son of God, by imitating his humility, and by preaching to others from love of him rather than for payment. Otherwise, if he is unbelieving, proud, or seeks his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2), he is a thief, calling what belongs to another his own, and a robber, because he kills.

VI. From all these things it appears that neither cleric nor layman whose dwelling is unknown (indeed, even if it is known where he lives) is permitted to cultivate the vineyard—that is, another’s people—or pasture another’s flock without the permission of the bishop or priest to whose care it belongs. [Col. 0814D] And if anyone perhaps presumes to do so, this may be objected to him: “Who appointed you ruler or judge over us?” (Acts 7). The Gospel relates that someone from the crowd said to Jesus: “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12). And if in temporal matters it is required that a judge be appointed, so that no one may intrude himself of his own accord, how much more in divine matters? The Apostle likewise testifies: “No one takes this honour for himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5). Therefore, wishing to show that faith in God’s calling comes from hearing the word of God, and that preaching flows from the fountain of divine grace, he says: “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher? But how will they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10.) [Col. 0815A] This sequence proves that no one calls upon God unless he believes in him; no one believes unless he has heard; no one hears unless someone has preached to him; and no one ought to preach unless sent. One must first be sent by God, from whom every good thing proceeds; then each must obey God who sends and preach. Thus Moses is sent by God to the children of Israel and, after making many excuses against being sent, obeys God, who persists in his will. Thus Isaiah and the other holy prophets taught God’s people only when sent.

[Col. 0815B] VII. In the New Testament also, the apostles and other disciples were sent by the Lord to preach the word of God. For this reason they are called apostles, that is, persons sent. The apostles Paul and Barnabas were likewise sent by the Holy Spirit, while the disciples fasted, prayed, laid hands on them, and set them apart for the work to which they had been appointed; nor did they receive the office of preaching until these things had been done by God and by the disciples. Afterwards the apostles appointed presbyters in each church. Saint Paul also commands Titus to appoint presbyters—that is, bishops—in every city.

VIII. From these things it is evident that some are sent by God alone, some by God and man, and some neither by God nor man. Sent by God alone were Moses, John the Baptist, and the aforementioned Saint Equitius. [Col. 0815C] As Saint Gregory testifies: “The freedom of life of such persons is not to be drawn into an example by the weak, lest anyone, presuming himself likewise filled with the Holy Spirit, disdain to be a disciple of a man and become a teacher of error.” They are sent by God and man, as the apostles were by Christ, who is God and man, and others by the apostles or bishops holding their place. Hence the Apostle says to bishops whom he himself had appointed: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has made you bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired by his blood” (Acts 20). Behold: as the book of Acts reports, he himself had appointed them, yet calls them sent by the Holy Spirit. There are others who are not sent by God, but come of themselves in the extremity of presumption, and, that they may seduce more subtly, falsely claim to have been sent by God. To them that prophetic saying may truly be applied: “Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart, who walk after their own spirit, who say, ‘The Lord says,’ and the Lord has not sent them” (Ezek. 13). Of them the Saviour speaks in the Gospel of John: “All who came before me are thieves and robbers” (John 10): those who came, not those who were sent. For he says: “They came, and I did not send them.” In those who come is the presumption of rashness; in those sent is the obedience of service. Woe, therefore—that is, eternal condemnation—is upon those who say that they are sent when they are not: as liars, thieves, robbers, and presumptuous persons. But those sent by God possess the clearest signs: virtues, namely charity, [Col. 0816A] peace, patience, continence, kindness, humility, and obedience, its inseparable companion. Hence blessed James says: “The wisdom that is from above is first chaste, then peaceable, modest, persuasive, assenting to good things, full of mercy and good fruits, not judging, without pretence” (Jas. 3). Behold the manifest signs of wisdom given by God!

IX. Those who are sent by God and man have open testimony that they have been sent. But those who come of themselves are not sent and possess neither the testimony of a sending man nor that of God if they lack charity, humility, and obedience—which, according to Bede, is humility’s inseparable companion.

X. From all these things it is more certain than certain that those who do not possess sacred orders are not readily to be heard among God’s people, unless they have manifest signs that they are sent by God. And if they are not obedient to the rulers of the holy Church, it is plain that they have not been sent but have come of themselves. For “all authority is from God; and the authorities that are from God are ordained. He who resists authority resists God’s ordinance; but he who resists God’s ordinance acquires condemnation for himself” (Rom. 13).

XI. Furthermore, those who have wives or are burdened by earthly cares are not suited to spread the word of God. For, according to the Apostle: “He who is with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided” (1 Cor. [Col. 0816C] 7). A preacher of God’s word must have a heart free from every earthly concern, so that he may discern with proportionately greater clarity the things others must avoid as he himself more truly shuns them by knowledge and life. An eye weighed down with dust does not properly see a blemish in things. Hence the Lord said to the first teachers of the holy Church: “Do not carry a purse or a bag” (Luke 10). But what is signified by the bag except the burdens of the age? Hence the first shepherd of the Church said: “It is not fitting that we should leave the word of God and serve tables. Let us appoint,” he says, “over this work men of good repute, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom; but we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6).

XII. Since, therefore, all the things stated above must be considered in a teacher of the divine [Col. 0816D] word, it is fearful to entrust the talent of the word to a layman, especially since this charge has been entrusted to priests: namely, to teach all the lawful ordinances which God commanded the children of Israel through Moses. Malachi says: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). These things have been said on the assumption that the layman is Catholic: namely, that without the permission of the bishop or priest he should not put the sickle of the word into that person’s harvest—that is, his people; should not give a measure of wheat to a household over which the Lord has not appointed him; should not, by intruding himself, pasture another’s flock; nor labour, uncalled, in another’s vineyard.

## CHAPTER VI. A reply to the objection in which they say with the Apostle: “We must obey God, not men”; and concerning certain other matters.

[Col. 0817A]

I. Certainly, whether layman or cleric has fallen into heresy, he is not to be heard by the faithful but avoided. A heretic is one who follows an ancient heresy or another person’s heresy, or invents a new one. Such are those who say that bishops, priests, and—even more horribly to say—the holy Roman Church ought not to be obeyed. That such persons are heretics or unbelievers is evident from what has been stated above: “Obedience alone possesses the merit of faith”; without it, anyone is proved an unbeliever, even if he appears to be a believer.

[Col. 0817B] II. “But,” they say, “we obey God, not men,” following Peter, who said: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). For the Lord had commanded the disciples, saying: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). But the chief priests, the officers of the temple, and the elders had forbidden them to teach or speak in the name of Jesus. Peter therefore, seeing that Christ had commanded them to teach every creature and that, conversely, the Jewish rulers had forbidden it, said: “We must obey God rather than men.”

III. But the aforementioned heretics cannot defend their error from this Scripture. For they have not been commanded by God to teach. Those whom the Lord sends [Col. 0817C], as has been said, have manifest signs of humility—whose inseparable companion is obedience—of charity, other virtues, and miracles: “the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16). They do not have these signs; therefore they have not been sent by God and ought not to speak. Thus, when blessed Job called his friends, under the figure of heretics, “fabricators of falsehood and cultivators of perverse doctrines,” he adds: “Would that you kept silence, that you might be thought wise!” (Job 13.) Again: “Does God need your lie, that you should speak deceitfully for him?” (ibid.) Again: “Will windy words have an end?” (Job 16.) And again: “My wrinkles [Col. 0817D] bear testimony against me, and a liar rises up against my face, contradicting me” (ibid.). Again: “My friends are full of words” (ibid.). Again: “Attend to me and be astonished, and put your finger upon your mouth” (Job 21). Again: “Your answer has been shown to oppose the truth” (ibid.). The Lord also said to Eliphaz the Temanite: “My anger is kindled against you and against your two friends, because you have not spoken rightly before me as my servant Job has” (Job 42). According to Gregory, Job bears the type of the holy Church and his friends the figure of heretics. They are called friends because they share with the holy Church in certain sacraments; but in the errors which they follow or invent they are called fabricators of falsehood. Because they labour [Col. 0818A] to defend those errors, they are called cultivators of perverse doctrines. Since their malice is hidden, they are called wrinkles, which bear testimony against the holy Church while at the same time attacking it, not by arguments but by false and useless words. Hence they are called liars and wordy persons, and their words are windy. They therefore ought to keep silence. Thus Job both wishes them to be silent and wishes them to put a finger upon their mouths, and to heed the rulers of the holy Church speaking and fulfilling James’s saying (ch. 1): “Let every man be swift to hear and slow to speak.”

IV. They provoke God’s anger against themselves because they teach otherwise than the holy Church. Therefore God accepts neither their sacrifices nor their prayers; but if, [Col. 0818B] when they repent, the holy Church offers or prays for them, he accepts them. Thus the Lord says to Job’s friends: “Take for yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job; and let him offer a holocaust for you. But Job my servant shall pray for you; I shall accept his person, so that it may not be imputed to you as folly. For you have not spoken rightly before me as my servant Job has.” And they did as the Lord had spoken to them; and the Lord accepted Job’s person and was turned to Job’s repentance when he prayed for his friends (Job 42).

V. Let heretics, therefore, cease their wordiness; abandoning their proud leadership, let them return in repentance to the holy Church, as though bulls and rams had been sacrificed. That Church intercedes for their errors by sacrifices and prayers, because the sacrifice or prayer of an outsider is accepted from no one.

[Col. 0818C] VI. The apostles’ honourable lives, the novelty of their miracles, and the integrity of their teaching bore witness that they had been sent by God. Therefore, when unbelieving Jews—the crucifiers of the Lord and persecutors of the disciples—commanded something else, namely that the Lord’s name should be extinguished, they were, as it were, blaspheming God; the apostles ought not to obey them, but rather the Lord who worked with them, confirmed the word by the signs that followed, and had sent them. But, on the contrary, those aforementioned persons do not obey God at all, and moreover obey unbelieving men—that is, heresiarchs; some indeed obey neither God nor men. That they do not obey God is evident because they do not obey those whom the Lord commanded to be obeyed: namely, those who sit upon the chair of Moses—that is, bishops and priests, who hold Moses’s place while they preside over and govern God’s people, teach God’s commandments, and rebuke the perverse. Thus it is written: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon the chair of Moses; therefore observe and do all things whatever they tell you” (Matt. 23). Furthermore, the Apostle says: “Obey your leaders and be subject to them” (Heb. 13). And Peter: “You younger persons, be subject to the elders” (1 Pet. 5). By elders he means the shepherds of the flock, concerning whom he had previously said: “Feed the flock of God which is among you” (ibid.).

VII. From these things it appears with complete certainty that the previously named [Col. 0819A] heretics obey neither God nor the apostles. Some, handed over to a reprobate mind, obey faithless men such as heresiarchs, despising Catholic pastors. Others, like sheep without a shepherd, are subject to no obedience; the law of God calls them “sons of Belial” (3 Kings 21), that is, “without a yoke.” Yet when the Lord was about to ascend into heaven, he did not leave without a shepherd the sheep whom he had fed himself; rather, he entrusted them to blessed Peter, saying: “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these? Feed my sheep” (John 21). Instructed by this example, the apostles and apostolic men took care, throughout successive ages, to set shepherds over God’s faithful. For a flock without a shepherd perishes; an army without a leader, a city without a lord, and a kingdom without a ruler are scattered, as it is written: “[Col. 0819B] Where there is no governor, the people fall” (Prov. 11).

VIII. From these and similar things let the enemies of truth consider how greatly they are foolish, who presume to exist without a governor, whether God or man. Thus, by the words of blessed Peter through which they strove to establish that they obey God rather than men, they are slain, like Goliath, by their own sword, since they are proved to obey neither God nor Catholic men. Therefore, as unbelievers and anathematized persons, they are to be avoided: neither greeted nor admitted to communion, but fled from and removed from the midst. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What concord [Col. 0819C] has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. 6.) Again the same Apostle says: “But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone should preach to you besides what you have received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1). And again: “Avoid a heretical man after a first and second correction, knowing that such a man is subverted”—that is, lost—“and sins, condemned by his own judgment” (Tit. 3).

IX. Some are cast out from the Church by its judgment on account of their crimes; but heretics depart from it by their own judgment. The same Apostle commands the Thessalonians: “Do not associate with one who does not obey the word” (2 Thess. [Col. 0819D] 3) of the same Apostle. Hence blessed John says: “Everyone who departs and does not remain in Christ’s teaching does not have God” (2 John 9). And shortly afterwards: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into the house, nor say ‘Greeting’ to him. For he who says to him, ‘Greeting,’ shares in his evil works” (2 John 10). Hence blessed Paul says: “We charge you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us” (2 Thess. 3). And again: “Avoid profane and empty talk, for they make much progress toward impiety,” etc. (2 Tim. 2). Again: “Do not be led away by diverse and strange doctrines” (Heb. [Col. 0820A] 13). Again: “Remove the evil from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5), which is done when an evil man is expelled from the Church’s communion through ecclesiastical discipline. Again: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth? Consent to no one. For this persuasion is not from him who calls you,” namely God, “but from the devil. A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Gal. 5). Again: “Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, rebuke them” (Eph. 5). Again: “Let no one deceive you by loftiness of words” (Col. 2), which exists, namely, only in words. Again John says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” (1 John 4). And blessed Peter says: “Our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given him, wrote to you, as also in all his Epistles, in which are certain things hard to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own condemnation. Therefore, brethren, knowing this beforehand, guard yourselves lest, led away by the error of foolish persons, you fall from your own steadfastness” (2 Pet. 3).

X. We have excerpted these words of the holy Scriptures as salutary admonitions for Christ’s faithful to ponder and retain in memory, so that they may clearly know that there should be no participation or fellowship with faithless heretics; that they are not to be heard, as though anathematized, but avoided as lost and manifestly incorrigible persons; that one must not associate with them, [Col. 0820C] as disobedient persons; and that they are neither to be greeted nor received into one’s house, as antichrists, but avoided as profane persons given to empty talk. For they lead toward impiety and, like a cancer, gradually corrupt sound members—that is, the faithful. Like leaven, they puff up in pride those who participate with them, as though they were a lump of fine flour, depriving them of the natural sweetness of Catholic unity; and they make them sour—that is, conformed to themselves in mind, yet also corrupted in mind, as the Apostle says, and deprived of the truth, supposing gain to be godliness, because they preach for gain, not for the things to come. Hence one must not associate with them but rather rebuke them.

[Col. 0820D] XI. Therefore the Apostle, using Isaiah’s words, says as though to children: “Come out from among them and be separated, says the Lord; touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you. I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty” (2 Cor. 6). He separates himself from evil people who does not imitate their works. He does not touch the unclean thing who does not consent to sins. He goes out who does not spare with his mouth but corrects, as far as he can. This is the heavenly voice which John heard saying: “Come out of her, my people, lest you participate in her sins and receive of her plagues; for her sins have reached unto heaven, and the Lord has remembered her iniquities” (Rev. 18). In these two ways they do not defile us if we do not consent to them but rebuke them: as workers of darkness, [Col. 0821A] distorters of the holy Scriptures, unbelieving and foolish persons, corrupters of minds, and spiritual wolves who seize and scatter the Lord’s flock, as it is written: “Within are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7). They possess a venomous disposition and intention, and, if opportunity is given, persecute outwardly and corrupt inwardly; and like thorns or briars they make bloody and tear apart those who approach them, as it is written: “Do they gather grapes from thorns, or figs from briars?” (Matt. 7).

## CHAPTER VII. It is explained whom they chiefly seduce, and whom they do not.

I. Having shown how greatly heretics harm God’s people, let us see, with the Holy Spirit’s assistance, whom they chiefly seduce.

[Col. 0821B] II. They seduce women; men who act not manfully but womanishly; the unlearned; liars; those who do not obey the truth but assent to iniquity; the greedy; and finally those who do not bear a sign upon their foreheads—that is, charity in their hearts. They first seduce women, and through them men, just as the devil first seduced Eve and through her Adam. Thus he also wished to overthrow Job through his wife, who said: “Do you still remain in your simplicity? Bless God and die” (Job 2). Likewise through Pilate’s wife, who said to him: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man; for today I have suffered much in a dream because of him” (Matt. 27). He wished to hinder the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, lest through Christ’s death [Col. 0821C] he should lose his dominion. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy concerning false Christians and heretics: “Having indeed the appearance of godliness, but denying its power; avoid these. For among them are those who enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins, who are led by various desires” (2 Tim. 3).

III. Behold, it is clear that they seduce not the steadfast but seducible women, worthy of being seduced, as burdened with sins. They also seduce men of womanish weakness, as it is written: “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Ps. 67). He calls the heretics bulls: proud and untamed in their vices, who gather among the cows of the peoples—that is, among those who can easily be seduced.

[Col. 0821D] IV. They also seduce the unlearned. Hence in Proverbs: “The foolish and clamorous woman, full of the enticements of vices and knowing nothing whatever,” says: “Whoever is simple, let him turn aside to me” (Prov. 9). The foolish and clamorous woman is heretical perversity: foolish through a senseless understanding, clamorous through loquacity, “full of the enticements of vices and knowing nothing at all,” she says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn aside to me.” Every fool, deficient in understanding, is simple.

V. They also deceive the innocent, that is, the simple. Hence the Apostle: “By sweet speeches and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. XVI). They also deceive those humble of heart; hence in Proverbs: “A generation that has swords for teeth, and [Col. 0822A] gnaws with its molars, in order to devour the needy from the earth, and the poor” (Prov. XXX). Heretics, above all others, have swords for teeth, because their perverse teachers know how to strike rather than heal, to kill rather than give life. They devour the needy from the earth when, by deceiving persons slower in understanding, they lay hold of them in their own body as though dead. Likewise, they attempt to overthrow the poor above all others—that is, those humble of heart—from the congregation of the faithful.

VI. They strive to deceive the upright in heart. Hence: “Behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, that they may shoot in the dark at the upright in heart” (Ps. X). Sinners—that is, heretics—have bent the bow: that is, they have twisted the Scripture of the Old [Col. 0822B] and New Testament toward themselves, interpreting it in accordance with their own error. They have prepared their arrows—that is, poisonous words—in their heart; and this in order that they may shoot at the upright in heart in the dark, that is, amid ambiguities. Or thus: “in the dark,” that is, in the simple sense, obscured on account of the carnal and unlearned. Or, in the darkened moon, that is, the Church, which was darkened at the beginning of the faith, or which is darkened by the clouds of blasphemers, or when it is stained with the slaughter of martyrs. In this darkness heretics shoot, because they know these times are suitable for deceiving the weak. Once these have been overthrown, they suppose that they can thus draw in the upright in heart as well. Or, the children of the Church are called the darkened moon while they sin; and heretics shoot within it when, through such ministers of the Church, they administer the sacraments [Col. 0822C] and deceive certain weak persons by suggesting that they should attend to the merits of the ministers.

VII. From these things it is clear that they deceive the weak and the ignorant. To prevent this, the Apostle warns, saying: “That we may now no longer be children tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the wickedness of men, by cunning, unto the circumvention of error” (Eph. IV). Let us not, he says, be babbling in understanding, tossed to and fro—that is, now acting well, now badly—and carried about, one being driven this way, another that way, by every wind of doctrine. The teaching of the perverse, like a storm wind, drives the ignorant and weak toward destruction, that is, shipwreck. This teaching is carried on in the wickedness and cunning of men: that is, through men wicked in themselves and crafty for the deception of the simple; their teaching is always directed to the circumvention of error, that is, so that by some deceit they may lead people into error. Therefore elsewhere he says: “Do not become imprudent, but understand what the will [of God] is,” etc. (Eph. V). And again: “Brothers, do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice, while in understanding be perfect” (I Cor. XIV).

VIII. But they do not deceive the wise and strong. Hence in Proverbs: “A net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. I). The eyes of winged creatures are the souls of the blessed, supported by the wings of virtues; contemplating heavenly things with keen sight, they fly upward to the things above. Before their gaze the net of deception is spread by the impious in vain, because, aided by God, [Col. 0823A] easily passing beyond all their snares, they proceed to higher knowledge.

IX. They also deceive those who do not receive truth, or charity; or, if they receive it, do not receive it so as to be saved; and those who consent to iniquity. Hence the Apostle, wishing to show concerning the devil, who already works the mystery of iniquity through false Christs, whom he will deceive through Antichrist, says: “[The Lord] will destroy him by the brightness of His coming, whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in all power and signs and lying wonders, and in every deception of iniquity among those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. Therefore God will send them the working of error, so that they may believe a lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe truth, [Col. 0823B] but consented to iniquity” (II Thess. II).

X. And the Lord says in the Gospel of John: “I have come in the name of my Father, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him” (John V). Behold: whoever does not receive the truth, which is Christ, by the severe judgment of God believes a lie and receives the worker of error; and whoever did not believe the true signs of God believes lying signs, so that one who has removed himself from truth and its signs is joined to falsehood through deceptive signs. Hence David says of the reprobate: “Render to them according to the works of their hands; repay them their recompense, for they did not understand the works of the Lord; and in the works of their hands you shall destroy them and shall not build them up” (Ps. XXVII).

[Col. 0823C] XI. Finally, they deceive those in whom there is no sign of God—that is, charity, or the power of faith. Hence, in the Apocalypse, locusts, representing heretics, are commanded not to harm the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree, but only those people who do not have the sign of God on their foreheads. What does the earth signify here except the holy Church, as it is written: “The earth stands forever” (Eccles. I)? The grass of this earth consists of beginners, still fearing the heat of tribulations, but nevertheless clinging with all their roots, as far as they can, to the faith and unity of the Church. And what does the green thing signify except those who display their own freshness, who manifest the life of faith by the progress of their works? And what does the tree signify except those exalted by contemplation and by the excellence of works or virtues?

[Col. 0823D] XII. Heretics, therefore, do no harm to these three classes of the faithful, but to those who do not have “the sign of God,” that is, charity. “By this,” as blessed John says, “the children of God and the children of the devil are made manifest” (I John III). And the Lord says: “By this they shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII). Or the sign of God is the power of God, concerning which the same John says: “This is the victory that conquers the world: your faith” (I John V). Those who do not possess this sign deserve to be harmed, so that “those who are filthy may become still more filthy” (Apoc. XXII), and “the wickedness of sinners may be brought to completion” (Ps. VII). They deserve to have such teachers, since they have despised God, their one Teacher, so that through them blind men, led by the blind, may fall into the pit. Thus it is said in Hosea to heresiarchs: “You have become a snare for those who keep watch, all of you, and a net spread upon Tabor” (Hos. V). They are a snare and a net through which those lacking the sign of God are entangled in the contemplation of heavenly things which they promise them.

XIII. Heretics are rightly denoted by locusts—unstable, leaping, and more harmful to crops with their mouths than other small creatures. For “they did not stand in the truth, but went out from us, because they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us.” And when engaged in disputation, they leap, as it were: when convicted of one error, they flee—or rather leap—to some shadow of an argument, lest they seem defeated. They harm with their mouths because, as it is written: “They sharpened their tongues like serpents; [Col. 0824B] the venom of asps is under their lips” (Ps. XIII). They sharpened their tongues like serpents in order, by sweet speeches and blessings, to deceive the hearts of the innocent. Therefore the venom of asps is not on their lips but beneath their lips, because they harm not openly but secretly, and, in the manner of serpents, inject through the bite of the tongue the incurable venom of error. Thus, more than other wicked persons, who are represented by small animals, they harm crops with their mouths—that is, the works and virtues of some believers. For what they do not wholly take away, they sometimes damage and corrupt, so that people are either entirely deprived of the Catholic faith or waver in faith. How great an evil this is appears from the words of blessed James, who says: “But whoever [Col. 0824C] wavers”—namely, in faith—“is like a wave of the sea driven by the wind,” etc. “Therefore let that man not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord” (Jas. I).

XIV. Indeed, the avaricious also, often because their sins require it, deserve to be deceived. Thus we read that the devil said concerning King Ahab, an idolater: “I will deceive Ahab.” And it was said: “How will you deceive him?” He answered: “I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets” (II Chron. XVIII). King Ahab, because of the great sins that had preceded, deserved to be condemned by such deception, so that he who had often willingly fallen into sin might at some point be unwillingly caught for punishment. By hidden justice, permission is given to evil spirits, so that those whom they strangle willingly in the snare of sin [Col. 0824D] they may drag unwillingly into the punishment of sin.

XV. Likewise, one who does not change his reprobate life and does not turn his mind away from committing sins, when he seeks something from a prophet, hears—by God’s ordering—what he deserves to hear as one to be condemned. Behold, the house of Israel had departed from the worship of God into the service of idols, yet it came to the prophets by whom it was accustomed to be deceived, seeking a favorable hope. When, while acting perversely, it heard favorable things from the mouths of the prophets, what else were the judgments from above doing but ensuring that the sinful people should be caught in their own heart? Thus, having sinned by following faithlessness, they were deceived by the flattering words of their prophets, so that they would no longer fear because they had sinned; and thereafter they would be carried off all the more harshly [Col. 0825A] for punishment, the more securely they now lived in sin.

XVI. But behold, through God’s bounty, the human race publicly confesses the true faith and refuses to submit in worship to any creature. Therefore anyone established in the faith consults a prophet securely, because he will hear what it is fitting for faith to hear. I say confidently: if he has withdrawn from other impurities and perverse acts, he is secure. For since Paul cries out, “and covetousness, which is the service of idols” (Gal. V), whoever is still subject to covetousness is not free from the worship of idols. Therefore, if one who pants after avarice seems indeed to be established in faith, but covets what belongs to another, desires worldly honors, lusts after temporal glory, and consults a prophet about that very glory, it is altogether just that, by the merit of his sin, he should hear favorable things from the prophet’s mouth. Thus, if he was unwilling to hear God’s words in sacred discourse so as to despise earthly things and love heavenly things, by God’s judgment he hears from the mouth of his prophet that by which he falls more deeply bound.

XVII. Behold, from these things it is clear that the avaricious are not free from the worship of idols, although they appear to be established in the faith. Therefore, by God’s judgment, they hear from the mouth of their prophet that by which they fall bound. And, to speak generally, whoever does not change a reprobate life will, by God’s ordering, hear what he deserves to hear as one to be condemned, so that blind men may thus be guides of the blind.

## CHAPTER VIII. Against their assertion that women may preach

[Col. 0825C]

I. Besides the errors already mentioned, they err grievously because they permit women, whom they admit to their fellowship, to teach, although this is contrary to apostolic teaching. For it is written: “Let women be silent in the churches. For it is not permitted to them to speak. But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church” (I Cor. XIV). Behold, the Apostle commands women to be silent in material churches, or in congregations of believers, not indeed with regard to prayer or the praise of God, but with regard to teaching; and that they should not ask anything in church under the pretext of teaching, but ask their husbands at home. Hence elsewhere he says more plainly: “Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I do not permit a woman to teach, [Col. 0825D] nor to exercise authority over a man, but to be in silence. For Adam was formed first, then Eve. And Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression” (I Tim. II). Behold, the Apostle plainly says that a woman must be silent even while learning, and must not question a teacher of the Church. She is likewise not permitted to teach or exercise authority over a man for two reasons: namely, because she was formed after the man, and because she was deceived into transgressing the Lord’s commandment—as though he had said, “and not the man.”

II. Therefore, by reason of the order of time and the sin that requires it, she is not permitted to teach, or to exercise authority over a man, or to question a teacher, because, on account of the sin which she herself introduced, she ought always to be ashamed and to flee public view rather than seek it. Blessed [Col. 0826A] Peter likewise says: “Let women be subject to their husbands, so that even if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, observing your holy conduct in fear” (I Pet. III). Behold, here it is plainly stated how believing women ought to win unbelieving husbands: namely, by the example of holy conduct, without the word of preaching. From this it follows that, if she cannot teach her husband by word but only by deed, much less can she teach others by word. For one must fear that the ancient enemy, employing his former art, may seduce a man through a woman’s word. Thus he said to Job through a woman: “Do you still remain in your simplicity? Bless God”—that is, curse him—“and die” (Job II). But the man, perfect in calmness and tribulation, rejected her, saying: [Col. 0826B] “You have spoken as one of the foolish women would speak” (ibid.). And so, seated upon the dung heap, he conquered the one who had overthrown the first man in paradise. Hence in the Law it is said to the woman: “You shall be under the power of your husband” (Gen. III). Hence also, according to the Apostle’s testimony: “If a woman grows her hair, it is a glory to her, because hair has been given her for a covering” (I Cor. XI). Behold what a woman’s glory ought to be: namely, to veil herself as a sign of subjection, for “the man is the head of the woman” (Eph. V). And again: “Every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head” (I Cor. XI). And again: “Man was not created for woman, but woman for man. Therefore a woman ought not to have authority over [her] head, [Col. 0826C] and because of the angels” (ibid.), to whom this sacred and devout signification is pleasing.

III. With what rashness, then, does a woman presume publicly to teach the words of God, when she ought not even to pray to God or prophesy except veiled? And if man is the head of woman, with what face does she dare teach a man, namely, her own head? And if she ought to have a covering as a sign of subjection and modesty, let her remember the sin for which she was punished in the first transgression and made subject to man; being subject, let her not presume to teach the law of liberty. Hence in the Decrees, distinction 23, the Sixth Council of Carthage commands: “A woman, however learned and holy, must not presume to teach men in an assembly. Nor may a layman teach in the presence of clerics, unless they ask him to do so.”

[Col. 0826D] IV. Moreover, the glorious Mother and Virgin of God, who “kept all the words” shown to her, “pondering them in her heart” (Luke II), is not recorded as having preached. Nor is Mary Magdalene, or any of the women who followed the Lord.

V. But the enemies of truth say that women ought to teach because the Apostle says to Titus: “Older women likewise”—namely, exhort [them] to be—“reverent in behavior, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teaching what is good, so that they may teach the young women prudence: to love their husbands, to love their children, to be prudent, chaste, sober, caring for the household, kind, subject to their husbands, so that the word of the Lord may not be blasphemed” (Tit. II). Concerning this, it must be noted that the Apostle does not say that older women should publicly [Col. 0827A] teach men, but privately teach younger women, and only that prudence which he subsequently sets forth. Nor does he permit anyone but older women to teach—those who surpass younger women in maturity of character as well as age—so that, besides the qualities they share with old men, which the Apostle mentioned above, namely, that they should be sober, chaste, modest, sound in faith, love, and patience, they should possess the qualities which the Apostle adds as proper to that sex, saying that they should be “reverent in behavior,” etc. Therefore women who savor of heresy are forbidden to teach; according to the words just cited, they must not teach unless they are older women in character and age, nor unless they teach younger women. Indeed, they are altogether forbidden to teach, namely because they are not sound in faith, without which anyone who is not obedient is shown to be, [Col. 0827B] as was demonstrated above.

VI. Likewise, they strive to confirm this error by the example of Anna the prophetess, who, as the Gospel testifies, came up at the very hour when the Lord was presented in the temple, gave thanks to the Lord, and spoke of him to all who awaited the redemption of Israel.

VII. But let them consider what Anna was like. After her husband’s death, she was a widow up to the age of eighty-four, “who did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and supplications night and day” (Luke II). Thus, on account of such long abstinence, continence, and continual prayer, prophecy was rightly given to her. Let someone produce such a woman, and I shall gladly hear her, [Col. 0827C] not teaching, but confessing her sins to God, or confessing the Lord with a confession of praise. Nor is it said here that she preached or taught, but that “she spoke of Christ to all who awaited the redemption of Israel” (ibid.). Preaching and speaking are not the same. Everyone who preaches or teaches speaks; but not everyone who speaks preaches or teaches. For one speaks while praying, yet is not said to teach. Therefore she spoke of Christ by confessing—that is, by praising or prophesying—not by teaching. For prophecy and teaching are different gifts of the Spirit, as may be seen from the Apostle’s words: “Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what shall I profit you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, [Col. 0827D] or in teaching?” (ibid.). And again: “When you come together, brothers, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has an apocalypse, has a tongue, has an interpretation. Let all things be done for edification” (I Cor. XIV). And again: “You are the body of Christ, and members one of another. And God has set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; then miracles; then gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues” (I Cor. XII). And again: “To one, indeed, is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another the gift of tongues; [Col. 0828A] to another the interpretation of utterances” (ibid.). Since, therefore, the gift of prophecy is one thing and the word of teaching another, I readily grant that Anna, or certain women, prophesied; nevertheless it does not consequently follow that they also taught. Otherwise the Apostle wrongly set them forth as different things.

## CHAPTER IX. Against their assertion that alms, fasts, Mass solemnities, or other prayers of the living do not benefit departed believers

I. And since it is the custom of those who err wickedly, unless they immediately recover their senses, to fall into worse things—“so that those who harm may harm still more, and those who are filthy may become still more filthy, and the wickedness of sinners may also be brought to completion” (Apoc. XXII)—these mad heretics now dare to tell those whom they [Col. 0828B] deceive that the alms, fasts, prayers, and even Mass solemnities or prayers offered for them by the faithful living confer no benefit on the departed. This heresy must first be refuted by canonical authorities, then by the writings of the Catholic Fathers and by Catholic arguments.

II. Thus we read in the book of Maccabees “that the very valiant man Judas, having made a collection, sent twelve thousand silver drachmas to Jerusalem, that a sacrifice might be offered for the sins of the dead,” etc. (II Macc. XII). Behold, a man full of faith, inflamed with zeal for God’s law, praying much for God’s people, devoted to God, resisting tyrants, and fighting for the law of his God even unto death, sent twelve thousand drachmas to Jerusalem for those “who had fallen asleep in godliness” [Col. 0828C] (ibid.), that they might be offered. The Catholic Church reads this devoutly, proclaims it publicly, and observes it as an example, offering [sacrifice] for departed believers so that, absolved from all guilt, they may rejoice with God without end.

III. Certainly, we read in the New Testament that circumcision and certain other institutions of the Old Testament ought to cease; but nowhere do we read that sacrifices for departed believers have been forbidden. For it is most certain that certain sins of some believers are loosed here, and certain others in the future. Hence the book of Maccabees says: “It is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the departed, that they may be loosed from sins” (ibid.). The Lord likewise says: “But whoever speaks [a word] against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, [Col. 0828D] either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. XII). This sentence gives us to understand that certain sins may be forgiven in this age, and certain others in the future. For when something is denied in the case of one, the consequential sense is clear: it is granted in the case of some—namely, small and very minor sins, such as continual idle speech, immoderate laughter, the sin involved in care for household affairs (which scarcely can be conducted without fault even by those who know how they may avoid sin), or an error of ignorance in matters not serious. Hence blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “It must not be denied that the souls of the departed are relieved by the piety of their living relatives, when sacrifice is offered for them to the Mediator or alms are given in the Church.” And again: “When sacrifices, whether of the altar or of any alms, are offered for all the baptized, they are thanksgivings for the very good; for the very bad, though they are no help to the dead, they are whatever consolations the living may have; for those not very bad, they are propitiations. For those whom they benefit, they either result in full remission or at least make the condemnation itself more tolerable.”

IV. Moreover, that the prayers of the living benefit departed believers is established by not a few examples. For, as blessed Gregory testifies, Germanus, bishop of Capua, entered the baths at Angulana on doctors’ orders for the health of his body. There he found Paschasius, deacon of the Apostolic See, already dead—a man of remarkable holiness, especially devoted to works of almsgiving, a servant of the poor, and despising himself—standing and attending him among the hot springs. When Germanus asked what so great a man was doing there, Paschasius answered that he had been assigned to that place of punishment solely because he had sided with Laurentius against Symmachus, wishing that, Symmachus having been rejected, Laurentius should be made supreme pontiff, while other believers took the opposite view and prevailed. “But I beg you,” he said, “pray to the Lord for me; and by this you will know that you have been heard: if, when you return here, you do not find me.” Therefore Germanus, the man of God, devoted himself earnestly to prayer. After a few days he returned, but no longer found the aforesaid Paschasius in that place.

V. In the same book, when Peter asked what might benefit the souls of the dead, blessed Gregory answers: “If faults are not incapable of being loosed after death, the sacred offering of the saving Victim is often of great help to souls even after death, so that the souls of the departed themselves sometimes seem to seek it.” For a certain priest in the diocese of the city of Centumcellae regularly bathed in hot waters whenever bodily necessity required it. An unknown man, attended by a great retinue, would remove his shoes from his feet, receive his clothes, provide towels when he came out of the hot springs, and perform every service. When this had happened frequently, one day the priest offered the attendant two loaves of the offering as a blessing, asking him kindly to receive what he offered in charity. [Col. 0829D] Declining the offering humbly, he said among other things: “If you wish to assist me, offer this bread for me to almighty God, that you may intercede for my sins; and then you will know that you have been heard when you come here to bathe and do not find me.” At these words he vanished; and the one who had seemed to be a man showed by vanishing that he was a spirit. That priest then afflicted himself in tears for him through an entire week, offered the saving Victim daily, and, returning afterward to the bath, no longer found him there. From this it is shown how greatly the immolation of the sacred offering benefits souls, when even the spirits of the dead themselves ask it from the living and indicate by signs that they seem to have been absolved through it.

[Col. 0830A] VI. Likewise, a monk in the monastery of Saint Gregory, in his final illness, was despised by the brethren on account of three gold coins which he had hidden as his own property. They refused to be present at his death, and he was denied burial among the brethren. But after thirty days had passed from his death, at blessed Gregory’s direction, the saving Victim was offered for thirty consecutive days. After this, appearing to someone in a vision by night, he said that things were well with him because he had received communion, when on the preceding day the thirtieth offering had been completed for him.

VII. Behold, these examples show that prayers and the immolation of the saving Victim greatly benefit the spirits of the departed, since the aforesaid Paschasius was absolved through these from the sin of dissension or schism, and the aforementioned monk from the sin [Col. 0830B] of possessing private property, after the bitterness of mind he experienced at death and after the torment of purgatorial fire for thirty days.

VIII. This is also strengthened and, with every scruple of doubt removed, confirmed by the testimony and very long custom of the Catholic Church, which, according to the Apostle’s testimony, is “the pillar and foundation of truth” (I Tim. III). For it prays for departed believers not only at other times, but also during the sacred solemnities of Mass. Certainly, if no other authority, example, or reason were available, the custom of the holy Church, approved over so long a time, ought to suffice. For if “every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (II Cor. XV), how much more when the whole Church throughout the world proclaims this in agreement? For, as the Lord says, the Holy Spirit teaches it all truth. He has filled the world—that is, the holy Church, which is throughout the world—and therefore does not permit her to err. This is the seven lamps above the lampstand of the tabernacle. For the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit illumines the Catholic Church, lest it be enveloped in the darkness of errors.

IX. Catholic arguments likewise support these things. For, as Augustine says: “There is a manner of life neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that these things do not benefit it after death. Yet there is a condition so good that it does not require them; and again one so bad that, when it has passed from this life, it cannot be helped by them. Therefore they are propitiations for those not very bad, thanksgivings for the very good; for the very bad they are no help to the dead, but whatever consolations the living may have.”

X. Nor is it strange if the benefits or prayers of the living benefit those bodily dead in the remission of certain sins, since they also benefit those dead in soul, to remove the stain of unbelief or other crimes. Blessed Stephen prayed for those stoning him, and Paul was converted. They prayed for the paralytic whom four men carried, and his sins were forgiven and bodily health restored.

XI. Likewise, Christ, bodily laid in the tomb, descending in spirit into hell, brought his own out from there. What wonder then if the elect, descending to places of purification, are afterward brought out from there when that Victim is immolated for them which uniquely saves the soul from eternal destruction, and which restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten through mystery? And if prayer offered for another benefits him, what wonder if almsgiving or fasting performed for another benefits him? For these are the Apostle’s words: “Pray without ceasing” (I Thess. V). Saint Augustine says: “The just person never ceases to pray unless he ceases to be just. Whoever always acts well always prays.”

XII. Likewise: “As in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another; and God has tempered the body so that there may be no schism”—that is, discord—“in the body” (Rom. XII), that is, in the Church, where unity ought to exist. “But the members are concerned for one another in the same way” (I Cor. XII). Let them, I say, be concerned with the same concern, that it may be the same—that is, impartial—so that one labors no less for another than for oneself. “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (ibid.).

XIII. From these things it is clear that, just as different members live and are joined together through one soul, so different members of Christ are governed through his one Spirit and preserved in unity. Hence all believers established in Christ’s body are concerned for one another, so that, if one suffers, the others suffer with him. Therefore, while believers suffer in purgatorial fire, the others, sharing their suffering, are concerned for them; not “slothful in [their] concern” (Rom. XII), but laboring for their absolution as though for themselves. Hence, by fasting, keeping vigils, devoting themselves to alms and other pious acts, persevering in prayers, the Church endeavors to assist by such remedies both living and departed persons established in Christ’s body through the unity of faith and the bond of love.

XIV. And indeed, “the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts, who has the keys of death and hell, hears the desire of the poor, and his ears [are attentive] to their prayers” [Col. 0831D] (Apoc. III), in order to loose those whom the Church looses and bind those whom the Church binds, as he himself says: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI). Therefore, if the Church looses any on earth, they are loosed also in heaven, whether living believers or believers who are dying. For he says: “Whatever.”

XV. It is also read in the book of the *Dialogues* that blessed Benedict excommunicated two consecrated women because of the fault of their tongues, unless they corrected themselves. Their former habits unaltered, they died shortly afterward and were buried in the church. But whenever the Eucharistic Victim was being offered, they appeared to leave the church. This was then reported to blessed Benedict, who [Col. 0832A] immediately gave with his own hand an offering and ordered that it be offered for them. When it had been immolated for them, they were no longer seen leaving the church. For they had received communion from the Lord through the servant of the Lord. Behold, this also shows how greatly the offering of believers benefits departed spirits. That flesh might be able to pass judgment upon spirits, he deigned to grant this, becoming God made flesh for humankind.

XVI. But the enemies of truth object to this that, after this death, the things mentioned above benefit no one. To establish their error, they bring forward these testimonies. For the Lord says: “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John XII). And the Apostle: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI). And again: “While [Col. 0832B] we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. VI). And Solomon: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly, for there shall be neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld, whither you hasten” (Eccles. IX). And David: “For his mercy is forever” (Ps. CXVII). From these words it is clear that after death one who has despised walking in the way of God in this light is enveloped in the darkness of punishments. For in this life God’s mercy is bestowed upon those who do good works. But for the wicked, after this life, there will be not mercy but God’s judgment, because then they can acquire for themselves no aid or salvation. Therefore the departed cannot acquire salvation or settle their account through the benefits of the living. Likewise, according to the Apostle’s testimony: “We must all be made manifest [Col. 0832C] before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (II Cor. V). Behold, according to these words, each person will receive in judgment the good or evil which he has done in his own body. From this it is understood that what another has done for him after the dissolution of the body does not benefit him.

XVII. It must therefore be understood that these authorities indicate that after death no one can acquire any merit for himself. For no one who has neglected this in the present life will be able, after dying, to win God’s favor. Nevertheless, if anyone closes his last day in faith working through love, he may be helped by the prayers of the faithful or by pious acts. For here he earned [Col. 0832D] the right to be helped by those faithful persons, because, by living faithfully among the faithful, he kept the faith and was a member among the members of Christ’s body. Hence blessed Augustine says: “Here all merit is acquired, by which someone may after this life be either relieved or burdened. Let no one who neglected this prepare himself to win God’s favor once he has departed.”
