Therefore those observances which the Church frequently performs in commending the dead are not contrary to that apostolic statement in which it was said: “We shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal, that each may receive according to the things he did through the body, whether good or evil” (Rom. XIV). For while each person lived in the body, he also acquired for himself this merit: that such things might be able to benefit him. For they do not benefit everyone. And why do they not benefit everyone [Col. 0833A], unless because of the difference in the life each person led in the body? Hence blessed Gregory too says: “This must be known: there, at least, no one will obtain any worthy purification even from the least sins, unless, while still placed in this life, he deserves by good deeds to obtain it there.” Thus he says that the aforementioned Paschasius “obtained through the abundance of his almsgiving that he might then merit pardon, when he could no longer do anything.” But when the Apostle says “through the body,” this must be understood as meaning: through the time during which he lived in the body.

## CHAPTER X. Against those who deny purgatorial fire and assert that spirits released from the flesh immediately go either to heaven or to hell

[Col. 0833B]

I. There are certain heretics who maintain that souls released from the flesh immediately ascend to heaven or descend into the punishment of hell. For they deny the fire of purification. Authorities, examples, and Catholic reasoning speak against them. For the Apostle says that Christ is the foundation, and adds: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, the fire will test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work which he built upon it remains, he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned up, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (I Cor. III). This may be understood of the fire of future purification.

[Col. 0833C]

II. It must therefore be carefully considered that he said that the man may be saved through fire—not the man who builds upon this foundation iron, bronze, or lead, that is, greater sins and therefore harder sins, then incapable of dissolution; but wood, hay, and stubble, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which fire easily consumes. Likewise Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*: “It is not incredible that there may be found, or may remain hidden, some faithful persons who are saved through a certain purgatorial fire more slowly or more quickly according as they loved perishable goods more or less; yet they are not such persons as those of whom it was said that they shall not possess the kingdom of God, unless those same crimes are remitted through fitting repentance. And I said ‘fittingly’ so that they are not barren in almsgiving.”

Likewise blessed John the Baptist [Col. 0833D] says to the people concerning Christ: “He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Mark I). For the Lord purges sins in baptism and in the fire of temporal tribulation, or in the fire of purification. Likewise it is written: “Set the empty pot upon the coals until it grows hot and the bronze melts, and the rust is consumed” (Ezek. XIV). The pot is any faithful soul, now full of virtues and good works, now empty, that is, imperfect. And because it is plainly not perfect in holy desires and works, but is stained with the rust of venial sins, it is therefore commanded to be placed upon the coals of purgatorial fire until it is tortured by the burning heat of fire and the defilements of light sins are consumed in the fire. For the duration of its remaining in the fire will be as great as the rust of its sin.

## CHAPTER XI. Against those who say that, before judgment, the same spirits of the dead enter neither heaven nor hell, but are kept in other receptacles

[Col. 0834A]

I. There are, on the other hand, others who say that souls enter neither heaven nor hell before judgment, but that the souls of the righteous are kept in peaceful receptacles and the spirits of the reprobate in places of punishment. They call the receptacles of the pious “paradise,” just as they call the punitive places of the wicked “hell.” But after judgment, they say, the elect will possess the starry dwellings, and the reprobate will be tormented by the pains of hell.

II. But these too are mistaken in their assertion. For there are three places which receive spirits released from the flesh. Paradise receives the spirits of the perfect; hell, the very wicked [Col. 0834B]; and the fire of purification, those who are neither very good nor very wicked. Thus the very good are received by a very good place; the very wicked by a supremely bad place; and the moderately wicked by a moderately bad place—that is, a place lighter than hell but worse than the world.

The Apostle was among the very good when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). But Christ is at the right hand of God the Father, where he also intercedes for us. Therefore, he who desired after the dissolution of the body to be with Christ undoubtedly desired to be in heaven, where Christ is. Hence he says more explicitly to the Corinthians: “We know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal in the heavens” (II Cor. V). Behold: [Col. 0834C] without any ambiguity the Apostle knows that, after the dissolution of the earthly house—that is, the body, which is from earth—he has in heaven an eternal house not made by hands, that is, not by another’s ministry, but from God, that is, by divine operation.

Hence the Lord also says: “Where the body shall be, there the eagles also shall be gathered” (Luke XVII). For spiritual souls, freed from the mass of the body, ascend to heaven, where Christ is not only according to his divine nature but also according to his human nature, in which he bodily ascended into heaven.

III. Again: “If anyone ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also shall my minister be” (John XII). And again: “If I go and prepare a place for you, I come again and shall receive you [Col. 0834D] to myself, that where I am, you also may be” (John XIV). And again: “Father, those whom thou hast given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory which thou hast given me” (John XVII).

Great, therefore, is the reward of love and good work: to be with Christ. Truly it is an inestimable honor, that the adopted son should be with the Only-begotten; that he should be where the Only-begotten is—not as equal to the divinity, but joined to eternity.

IV. Of the very wicked the Apostle says: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the covetous, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers shall possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI). And in the Apocalypse the Lord says: “The fearful and unbelieving, the abominable and murderers, [Col. 0835A] fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars shall have their portion in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death” (Apoc. XXI). Behold: those who commit grave crimes shall not possess the kingdom of God, but shall be cast down into hell.

V. Indeed, those who commit light sins pass to purgatorial fire in order to be purified, provided that, while still placed in this life, they obtain by good acts the grace to go there; these are the persons whom the Apostle says are saved, yet “as through fire” (I Cor. III), as was stated above.

## CHAPTER XII. Against those who refuse to pray in church and maintain that it should not be called a church. Here it is proved both that it ought to be called a church, that prayer ought to be offered there, and that it must be held in great reverence. Here also an objection of some of these same heretics is answered: from the words of blessed Stephen they say that the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands (Acts VII), and therefore not in a church either

[Col. 0835B]

I. Moreover, they add iniquity to iniquity; despising the house of God—the house, that is, of prayer—they prefer to pray in stables, private rooms, or bedchambers rather than in church. And, to increase their contempt, they endeavor to persuade women and fools that there is no church and that it ought not to be called such.

II. Against them we bring forward the testimony of Holy Scripture: “That the faithful, knowing this beforehand,” as blessed Peter teaches, “may keep themselves from being led away by the error of the foolish and falling from their own steadfastness” (II Pet. III). It must therefore be observed that [Col. 0835C] the house of God is called a house of prayer and a church. And Scripture records how great a reverence should be shown to it: the Lord found in the Temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and money-changers sitting there; and, having made something like a whip of cords, he drove all of them from the Temple, the sheep also and the oxen; he poured out the money of the money-changers and overturned their tables. To those who sold doves he said: “Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (John II). This is John’s account. But Mark says that the Lord did not allow “anyone to carry a vessel through the Temple; and he taught them, saying: Is it not written, My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations? But you have made it a den of thieves” (Mark [Col. 0835D] XI). And, after these actions, according to Luke, “he was teaching daily in the Temple” (Luke XXI).

III. Behold, it is plainly clear that he calls the Temple his Father’s house, his own house, and a house of prayer—not for himself or the Apostles alone, but for all nations, that is, for the elect from Jews and Gentiles. But heretics call it neither the house of God nor a house of prayer, nor do they take care to pray there with the elect. Instead, they prefer to pray in their own houses rather than in God’s house. In this it is clear that they follow the Lord Jesus Christ neither in word nor in deed: while they blaspheme the Temple which he so greatly reveres in both speech and action, and do not pray in the place where he foretold that the nations ought to pray.

For they follow—that is, imitate—the Beast, namely Antichrist [Col. 0836A], who, as the Apocalypse says, “opened his mouth in blasphemies, to blaspheme his name, and his tabernacle, and those who dwell in heaven” (Apoc. XIII).

IV. They blaspheme God’s tabernacle when they say that one ought to pray in private rooms or stables rather than in the house of God. They blaspheme God’s name when they say that he did not create or govern the world. They blaspheme those who dwell in heaven when they say that the Apostles, martyrs, and citizens of heaven can offer no help to those who pray.

V. Moreover, he taught in the Temple, as was said: “And he was teaching daily in the Temple” (Luke XXI). There he listened to teachers, as is written of his parents: “They found him sitting in the Temple [Col. 0836B] in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them” (Luke II). When they said, “We sought thee in sorrow,” he answered: “Why was it that you sought me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that are my Father’s?” (ibid.). Behold: found in the Temple, he replies that it belongs to his Father and that he must be there.

VI. Again, the Gospel of Luke writes concerning the Lord’s disciples after the Ascension: “They were continually in the Temple, praising and blessing God” (Luke XXIV). And after the coming of the Holy Spirit, as is found in the Acts of the Apostles: “They continued daily with one accord in the Temple” (Acts II). Again: “Peter and John went up into [Col. 0836C] the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer” (Acts III); and then they restored the lame man from his mother’s womb.

VII. Likewise, the angel of the Lord, bringing the Apostles out of prison, said: “Go, stand in the Temple, and speak to the people all the words of this life.” When they heard this, “they entered the Temple at daybreak and taught” (Acts V). Likewise: “While Paul was praying in the Temple, it came to pass that he fell into a trance of mind and saw Jesus” (Acts XXII). Anna also, a widow, “did not depart from the Temple, serving night and day” (Luke II). Simeon too was “righteous and God-fearing, awaiting the consolation of Israel; and the Holy Spirit was in him. And he came in the Spirit into the Temple; and he took Jesus into his arms and blessed God” (ibid.).

VIII. From these passages it is clear that the Apostles pray in the Temple [Col. 0836D] and praise God; that Paul sees Jesus there; and that, by an angel’s command, they teach there. Anna also did not depart from the Temple, serving the Lord day and night. Likewise the holy man Simeon, full of the Holy Spirit, came in that same Spirit into the Temple, received Jesus, and gave blessing. Why then do impious heretics boast that they keep the Gospel and follow the Apostles, when they do not pray in the Temple but in the bedchamber, and do not teach there but in the marketplace—and some secretly in a house?

IX. O senseless men! Is it burdensome to you that God should have a house in every city, village, and castle, that he may be honored by his own people, when many of you have not one house but several for your own purposes? Likewise, you have houses—one for eating, [Col. 0837A] another for sleeping, another for other uses. Why do you begrudge the Christian people a house in which to pray to God, praise him, or teach the words of life? Likewise, because God belongs to all, not to one person alone, he must be prayed to by all in common.

X. That the house of prayer is called “church” is proved both by authority and by reason. For *ecclesia* is called now the assembly of the faithful, now a congregation of evil persons, now the house of God, to which commonly both the former and the latter assemble. *Ecclesia* is called an assembly of the faithful; thus it is written: “Paul, prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon our beloved and fellow-worker, and to Apphia the dearest sister, and to Archippus our fellow-soldier, and to the Church which is in his house: grace to you and peace from God [Col. 0837B] our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Phil. II).

*Ecclesia* is called a congregation of evil persons; hence David says: “I hated the assembly of evildoers” (Ps. XXV). *Ecclesia* is also called a house of prayer. Thus the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “When you assemble in church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and I partly believe it” (I Cor. XI). And a little later: “When you assemble into one, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each person takes beforehand his own supper to eat; and one indeed is hungry, while another is drunk. Do you not have houses for eating and drinking? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing?” (ibid.).

He says openly that the Corinthians, some of whom were good and some evil, assembled in the church [Col. 0837C], that is, in the house of prayer, as authoritative interpreters say. Therefore he adds: “When you assemble into one.” What is it to “assemble into one,” except to come together into one place, which place he had above called *ecclesia*, “church”? And because they refreshed themselves in that place—that is, in church—he rebukes them, saying: “Do you not have houses for eating and drinking? Or do you despise the Church of God?” That is: do you not have other places in which to take refreshment? Or, though you have other places, do you despise the Church of God—that is, the house of prayer—by eating or drinking there? It is as if he said: church is not a house for eating or drinking, but for prayer. Therefore, if you have houses [Col. 0837D] for eating or drinking, take your refreshment there, not in the house of prayer, that is, in church. Accordingly, anyone who eats or drinks in God’s church despises it, especially if he has a house in which to eat. For God’s church is not a house for eating and drinking, but a house of prayer.

XI. From this it is clear that in this passage “the Church of God” means the house of prayer. Otherwise, if someone says that “the Church of God” here means the faithful, let him consider what absurdity follows. For the Apostle here rebukes the Corinthians for eating in the Church of God. If “the Church of God” is here understood as the assembly of the faithful, he will consequently appear to rebuke those who eat in an assembly of believers; and thus [Col. 0838A] the Lord, who ate and drank with his disciples, will be blameworthy. Moreover, it would follow that one must not eat with anyone, or that one may eat only with unbelievers—to think which is utter madness.

It remains, therefore, that we understand “the Church of God” there as the house of prayer. Hence also, by etymology, *ecclesia* is called the dwelling of clerics—not because they alone assemble in it, but because they do so more frequently than the other faithful, and because it belongs to them to guard it, close it, open it, and celebrate the divine mysteries there.

XII. Nor is it surprising that “the Church of God” is said both of the assembly of the faithful and of the place of prayer where they gather; just as “house” is said both of a dwelling and of those dwelling in it. For when one reads that the Lord entered the house of a ruler of the Pharisees to eat bread on the Sabbath [Col. 0838B] (Luke XIV), “house” means the dwelling-place. But when one reads concerning the royal official that “he himself believed, and his whole house” (ibid.), “house” means those dwelling in the house.

Likewise, “city” signifies both the place belonging to certain citizens and the citizens dwelling there. It signifies the place when it is said: “Seeing the city, Jesus wept” (Luke XIX). It signifies the citizens when it is said: “When Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, saying, Who is this?” (Matt. X). For neither the circuit of walls nor the place itself said, “Who is this?” but the citizens dwelling within it.

XIII. “Synagogue,” too, is called the place of prayer in which the Jews assembled. Thus the Jews themselves say to the Lord concerning the centurion: “He himself built us a synagogue” [Col. 0838C] (Luke VII), indicating by the name “synagogue” the house which he had built for them to pray in. John also says to the angel of the church of Smyrna: “You are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan” (Apoc. II). In this place, without any doubt, he calls the Jews a synagogue of Satan.

XIV. It is manifest, therefore, both by the authority of the Apostle and by the comparison of the foregoing similar examples, that “the Church of God” denotes both the house of prayer and the assembly of the faithful. In a material church, the variety or multitude of stones and timbers signifies the diverse orders of the faithful; the pavement and roof, subjects and prelates; the windows through which the light of heaven is poured, the teachers through whom the other faithful are illumined—teachers themselves illuminated by the light of God’s word. The foundation, which supports the whole weight of the Church, is Christ, who sustains our conduct; the door is faith; the altar, God; the breadth of the church, charity; its height, hope; its length, perseverance; lamps or candles, Scriptures or virtues; cymbals, the sign of jubilation.

Since, therefore, the material church signifies the spiritual Church, it fittingly takes its name; for often a sign is designated by the name of the thing of which it is a sign. Hence the Prophet says of manna: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII)—not because it was the bread of angels, but because it signified it. And the Apostle says of the rock which poured out water for the Jews: “The rock followed [Col. 0839A] them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X)—not because the rock was Christ, but because it signified Christ, who waters with the dew of the water of wisdom.

XV. But when we say that prayer ought to be made in the house of prayer, that is, in church, the enemies of truth bring forward against us that Gospel saying: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber, and having shut the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, shall repay you” (Matt. VI). From this they say that one ought to pray in the chamber, not in church.

XVI. But if one must pray in a chamber and not in church, Jesus Christ—in whose mouth no deceit was found—was mistaken when he called it a house of prayer, if prayer is not offered there. But if he spoke truth—indeed, because Truth [Col. 0839B] spoke truth—it is a house of prayer because prayer ought to be offered there. Likewise, if one must not pray in church, Peter and John sinned when they went up to the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer. Paul also sinned; Anna sinned, who did not depart from the Temple, serving with fasts and prayers night and day. To think this, certainly, is extreme madness. Let it therefore be established that one ought to pray in church, both by Christ’s authority and by the examples of the Apostles and other saints.

XVII. Nevertheless, one must pray everywhere, as the Apostle says: “I will that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands, without anger and contention; likewise also women” (I Tim. II). And the Prophet says: “In every place of his dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul” [Col. 0839C] (Ps. CII). Therefore, although one must pray everywhere, God willed that there should be a place specially assigned for prayer—namely, a place solely for praying and serving God—so that prayer might be made there more attentively, insofar as one is occupied there with God alone and no other activity is undertaken. Other places, for the most part, are involved in many business affairs; and therefore, if someone prays there, willingly or unwillingly he is sometimes interrupted.

“For dead flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccles. X). For temporal concerns, like flies, intruding through their importunity, confuse the hearts of those praying, so that prayers which in themselves would be fragrant like spices may not yield a sweet odor to God in those who pray.

XVIII. Therefore, when the Lord says that one intending to pray should enter into a chamber, he does not establish that the material bed is [Col. 0839D] the place of prayer; for nowhere did he do this, nowhere did he call a bed or bedchamber a house of prayer. But he does call the Temple the house of God and a house of prayer. We must not, therefore, understand this of the marital bed, but spiritually. He calls the chamber the secret place of the heart, where, if the conscience is good, a person rests sweetly, but if it is evil, he is grievously burdened.

Thus a person intending to pray must enter into the secret place of the heart, so that he may pray not only with his mouth but also with his heart. Let him enter the chamber of the heart, lest a mind dispersed among external things lose the fruit of prayer. But, returning into itself, it more readily obtains through prayer insofar as, despising all else, it strives to occupy itself with God alone. Therefore, so long as one persists in prayer, the door must be shut—that is, [Col. 0840A] the hearing of the heart must be fortified by watchfulness, so that unlawful desires are restrained and carnal lust is not admitted, but the heavenly Father is prayed to with the entire intention of the heart, all the more attentively because, once the entrance of the heart is shut, it is not interrupted by intruding cares.

This is the prayer that penetrates heaven. This knocks upon the ears of the heavenly Father. This obtains whatever it asks. Hence it follows: “And your Father, who sees in secret, shall repay you” (Matt. VI).

XIX. Moreover, because they refuse to pray in church, they put forward excuses for sins against us and cite what blessed Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Solomon built God a house; but the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands, as the Prophet says: Heaven is my throne, but earth is [Col. 0840B] the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, says the Lord? Or what is the place of my rest? Has not my hand made all these things?” (Acts VII). And they say: if the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands, he does not dwell in churches made by human hands. But if he does not dwell there, why should we go there to pray?

XX. To this we reply: “God does not dwell in things made by hands” must be understood thus—that is, he is not shut up or contained in things made by hands. For God is immeasurable, uncircumscribed, and not spatially located; therefore he is not circumscribed or contained in a place. For he whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is earth—how could he be contained in any house? When you dwell in your house, you are enclosed there and are nowhere else [Col. 0840C]. God does not so dwell in temples made by hands that he is enclosed there in such a way as to be nowhere else.

XXI. Moreover, “God is spirit” (II Cor. III), as the same writer says; and therefore he is not contained by a bodily place, but dwells through grace in the hearts of the elect. Hence the Apostle says to the Ephesians: “May the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ grant that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. III). For your faith concerning Christ is Christ in your heart. Hence also the Prophet says: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle, where he dwelt in human beings” (Ps. LXXVII). Behold how God dwelt in his tabernacle: he dwelt there in human beings.

Thus God dwells in churches by dwelling in people, and therefore he dwells there rather than elsewhere, because sometimes [Col. 0840D] more people gather there and come together with greater devotion and more fervent faith; God is served there through prayers and through reception of the sacred nourishment—that is, Christ’s body—and of the divine word. Therefore, although God is always and everywhere in the hearts of the elect, he fills them more fully and perfectly in churches when he sees them more ready in his service. Yet, although God is everywhere, when he says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Isa. XXIII), he is in things made by hands, containing and governing them; but he does not dwell there as he does in the hearts of the elect. For in these he dwells also through grace; in the former he is present through essence, power, and presence.

# ABOUT THE YEARS OF THE LORD 1191–1192: HENRY OF SEPTIMELLO

[Col. 0841]

## NOTICE

(Polycarp Leyser, *Historia poetarum et poematum medii aevi*, Halle in Magdeburg, 1721, octavo, p. 450)

Henry of Septimello, a native of Etruria, came from a certain village in the Florentine district, encountered by travelers going toward Lucca seven miles from the city of Florence; this was noted by Marquard Gudius in a manuscript copy of the *Elegy*. He is elsewhere called Samariensis, and commonly Henry the Poor, in a manuscript codex of the Pauline Library of the University of Leipzig. [Note: [Col. 0841] See Joachim Feller’s *Catalogue*, p. 289, no. 9.] He is called Florentine in a manuscript gloss of the Helmstedt codex. The author himself admits that his family was rustic and poor. [Note: [Col. 0841] See Henry’s *Elegy*, book II, v. 205.] He devoted himself to studies at Bologna. [Note: [Col. 0841] See Henry, loc. cit., book III, v. 71.] He is reported to have been so poor that, when paper was lacking, he was compelled to write his verses on old, worn parchment. [Note: [Col. 0841] See Michael Neander, *Ethice vetus et sapiens*, Leipzig ed., 1590, part III, p. 259.]

Christian Daumius considers him a poet of the thirteenth century. [Note: [Col. 0841] Letter to Johann Gebhard in the *Epistolae philologico-criticae*, Chemnitz ed., 1709, p. 184.] He wrote the poem to be mentioned in the year 1191 or 1192, as is evident from book II, verses 61–64. For in 1193 Henry VI conquered all Sicily, having previously attempted it unsuccessfully; the author alludes to that adverse expedition. He also mentions [Note: [Col. 0841] *Elegy*, book III, v. 164.] as a recently performed event the captivity suffered by Richard, king of England, in 1192.

He wrote an *Elegy on the Diversity of Fortune and the Consolation of Philosophy*, as it is entitled in a manuscript codex of the Pauline Library of the University of Leipzig. [Note: [Col. 0841] See Feller, loc. cit.] Having formerly enjoyed the highest prosperity and later been reduced to the utmost poverty, he composed this poem. [Note: [Col. 0841] See the manuscript gloss of the Helmstedt codex.] He wrote this book to the bishop of Florence. [Note: [Col. 0841] See the cited manuscript gloss.] The *Elegy* contains a thousand verses. [Note: [Col. 0841] See the cited gloss and Henry, *Elegy*, book IV, v. 245.] The poem is divided into four books. In the first, Henry complains of his misery and of the adversities of this world. In the third, he introduces Philosophy sharply rebuking him. In the fourth, he introduces the same Philosophy consoling him. [Note: [Col. 0842] See the cited gloss.]

Christian Daumius published this work [Note: [Col. 0842] See Daumius’s *Epistolae philologico-criticae*, pp. 163–64.] from a manuscript codex of the Leipzig Library, which nevertheless supplied only half of it, [Note: [Col. 0842] See Daumius, loc. cit., p. 178.] and from Florentine parchment manuscripts. [Note: [Col. 0842] See Daumius, loc. cit., p. 184.] Perhaps he also used Marquard Gudius’s manuscript. [Note: [Col. 0842] See Daumius, loc. cit., p. 178.] The Daumius edition was printed in 1684 or later. [Note: [Col. 0842] See Daumius, loc. cit., p. 257.] The editor had lacked the manuscript copy of Marius Florentinus, knight of Lucca; Bartholomew Beverinus compared that manuscript with some obscure passages in the printed text and sent the results to Daumius. [Note: [Col. 0842] See Daumius, loc. cit., p. 265.] He also lacked a certain manuscript codex at Padua. [Note: [Col. 0842] See Daumius, p. 163.] Christian Daumius promised that he would add notes to the text. [Note: [Col. 0842] Loc. cit.] In any event, the work exists with a manuscript commentary in the Library of the University of Leipzig. [Note: [Col. 0842] See Feller’s *Catalogue*, p. 289, no. 9.]

I undertook a new edition of Henry of Septimello, not knowing at the time that Daumius had already published it in print. Although I was later informed of Daumius’s edition, I shall nevertheless persist in my purpose, since it occurs more rarely and perhaps is less corrected than ours; and I shall give the poem entire.

For this purpose I used two codices. The first is preserved in the older academic library at Helmstedt; the second in the distinguished ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, into which it was brought from Marquard Gudius’s collection. Of these, the latter codex serves in place of various other manuscript codices against which it was corrected.

[Col. 0843]

# HENRY OF SEPTIMELLO’S ELEGY ON THE DIVERSITY OF FORTUNE AND THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0843A]

How solitary sits integrity? It weeps, and *aleph* groans. [Note: [Col. 0843C] *Aleph* is the first letter, representing by its sound one who groans.]

Made like a widow, though she had formerly been a wife.

To whom shall I complain of you, Fortune? To whom? I do not know. Why  
do you, treacherous one, compel me to endure shameful disgrace?

[5] I am the nations’ reproach and the common subject of the crowd’s talk.  
The whole street knows my dishonor.

They point at me with the finger. All mock me with their teeth.  
I, dishonored, am displayed as a monster.

I am bitten by reproaches. Of me the crowd sings wicked songs;  
[10] I am to it a dreadful psalm. [Note: [Col. 0843C] For *ipsi*, “to it.” The reflexive pronoun is, of course, frequently used by medieval writers.]

[Col. 0843B]

By antiphrasis, Fame sings; and the impious crowd, mocking me,  
raises much laughter at my expense.

Many a stork behind my back clacks its beak at me.  
One fashions ass’s ears, another a dog’s, for me.

[15] The mill’s throng, the oven’s flock, the assembly at the church—  
these resound against me with abundant voices.

Though Ovid commended me, though Virgil’s Muse did,  
though Lucan’s trumpet did, scarcely would my fame be good.

Whomever infamy once blackens with dreadful stains  
[20] requires much water to wipe himself clean.

The Fates act like Neroes against me. [Note: [Col. 0844C] They rise against him cruelly.]  
The stars of heaven prophesy sorrow to me. The sky gives me grievous signs.

O pain! O shame! O burden! O mournful fates!

[Col. 0843C]

I am wretched, and I am wretched with no one to pity me.

[25] O good prosperity, where are you now? Now my lyre has turned  
to mourning; my lyre becomes tearful.

O evil sweetness, which, tasted suddenly, poisons—  
which now repays honey with bitter gall!

Happy is he who has not enjoyed prosperity,

[30] [Col. 0844A] for sorrow comes from prosperity alone.

Fortune gives no sweetness without her gall, nor whiteness  
without blackness; nor has there been a mountain without a valley.

To him to whom she gave much honey, she gave much poison as well.  
That gallish flavor first vomited honey.

[35] As one formed with a giant’s stature falls more heavily  
than a dwarf whose small frame is low;

as lead is heavier than a feather, and a stone than chaff,  
so falls more heavily the man who has borne many blessings.

Thus I, who had been sated with every prosperity,

[40] confess this to be true in every respect.

I discover the ambiguous faces of the deity—[Note: [Col. 0844C] Fortune has two faces: favorable and adverse.]  
I feel Fortune, once a mother, to be a stepmother.

[Col. 0844B]

I am wretched, and no compassionate person has pity on the wretched man.  
All fates turn for the worse for me.

[45] Fortune continually mixes poison for me,  
with which she thirsts [Note: [Col. 0844C] “Desires.”] to kill my head.

Nothing remains for the unfortunate man to do: I have perished. Therefore she cannot harm me  
further; no wounds injure one who is dead.

Alas, what shall I do? What shall I do? I shall weep. Is that enough?

[50] No, because the Fates prepare worse things for me.

What have I done to you, great Jupiter? What? Whence comes  
this thirst for harming me? I have borne no thunderbolts from heaven.

I did not seek Juno’s marriage-bed, nor did I wish to. Nor  
did I give savage weapons to my giant brothers.

[55] [Col. 0844C] Why do you harm me, cruel one? Why? Why? Speak—I do not know. You do not know.

Why then, high Jupiter, do you harm an innocent man?

He reeks too strongly of madness and lacks Solomon [Note: [Col. 0844C] “Solomon” for wisdom.]—  
he who harms the innocent and wishes to harm them.

For he is too angry, too proud, and vindictive,

[60] [Col. 0845A] who strikes an innocent man when a crime provides occasion.

Why do you persecute me? O how small a victory [Note: [Col. 0845D] Helmstedt manuscript: *prava*, “wicked.”]  
it is, to be able to injure a wretched man with many evils!

Stop. What wonder if Achilles defeats Davus [Note: [Col. 0845D] Helmstedt manuscript: *Darium*, “Darius.” Darius is said to have been of no reputation in the Trojan War because he lacked strength for fighting, whereas Achilles was strong and of great renown. Thus the manuscript gloss of the Helmstedt codex.]  
and if Hector tramples Thersites beneath his horse?

[65] For whenever an upright man strives to overcome a wretched man,  
the upright man strives to make himself like the wretched man.

I return to tears, of which I have abundance; their streams  
of salt water moisten my lips.

Anxiety is my food; tears are my drink; punishment  
[70] my bread; pain my wine; for me, to live is to die.

My pallor tells what I suffer, and emaciation gives it form;

[Col. 0845B]

my bloodless, shamefully white skin reveals it.

For the face confesses the disposition and striving of the mind,  
and that face announces outwardly what the mind does within.

[75] The countenance is the book and page of the inward condition.

Outward emaciation reveals inward bitterness. [Note: [Col. 0845D] It shows.]

Alas, wretched man, alas blind man, alas madman! The seeds of the world  
Draw angry dispositions down upon my fate.

The earth harms me, fire weighs heavily upon me, the water is injurious;  
[80] The air harms me with a more treacherous sorrow.

Thus the impious throng of the seven planets harms me.  
Every planet rages at my death.

Saturn bears a sickle, Jupiter lightning, Mars arms,  
[Col. 0845C] the sun heat, Venus dreadful poisons;

[85] Mercury bears a wand; the moon bears swift arrows.  
The sevenfold company stirs up sevenfold weapons.

Where shall I flee? Or what shall I do? Death blocks me on every side,  
Imperiously barring every path lest I flee.

Woe is me! Woe to the wretched man! Woe to him deprived of prosperity!  
[90] Woe to him who is granted knowledge of all that harms in the world!

Ever since our first mother broke the fasts imposed by the forbidden [Note: [Col. 0845D] Apple.] fruit,  
No one in this wretched world has been so wretched.

Neither mangled Tityus [Note: [Col. 0845D] Tityus, son of Jupiter by Elura, slain by Apollo’s arrows; vultures do not cease to devour his heart even in the underworld.] [Note: [Col. 0845D] Lacerated.], nor Tantalus amid the receding waters,  
Nor the boy who disastrously guided his father’s reins [Note: [Col. 0845D] Phaethon.].

[95] Niobe bereft; Job’s worms; Cadmus’s hissing creatures [Note: [Col. 0845D] Serpents.]:  
Compared with me [Note: [Col. 0845D] Ms. Helmst. *collata*, i.e. “compared.”], these flourish in prosperity.

[Col. 0845D] Who, then, unhappy man, suffers worse things? Who is that  
Tristan [Note: [Col. 0845D] Tristan was a certain knight who endured many evils. Thus the gloss in the Helmstadt manuscript at this passage.], who has borne more sorrows than I?

[Col. 0846A] I am overwhelmed by ocean and battered by savage waves.  
[100] May the sunken ship know no return from here.

The heedless vessel strikes upon reefs; the storm-tossed ship  
Endures innumerable gales.

If nature wished me to suffer such bitter things,  
It ought to have placed me in a worse [Note: [Col. 0846D] More grievous.] region—

[105] Either in icy Scythia, the land of snows [Note: [Col. 0846D] Scythia, the land of snow.], or at the sun’s rising,  
Or where the heat sets [Note: [Col. 0846D] Ms. Helmst. *concidit*, “falls.”] with its sun-bearing horses;

Or where the more treacherous four-cornered world is found,  
Or where the torrid zone is ever hot,

Or in some worse place, empty of people,  
[110] Where the report of my disgrace would be less widely known.

For wretches it is sweeter to live in a foreign land  
Than badly in their own, where every shame is exposed.

[Col. 0846B] I would rather that my disgrace be known to distant Indians  
Than to those made my neighbors by the place itself.

[115] Here among acquaintances, companions, and friends, miserable as I am,  
Because I trifle, I am oppressed by a teeming abundance of complaints.

I envy all who are better off. An envious mind  
Is always accustomed to be gnawed only by one better off.

I confess that all who flourish beneath the sun are better than I,  
[120] Though I should be Arthur [Note: [Col. 0846D] On this, the gloss of the Helmstadt manuscript: Arthur is said to have been a most worthy and honourable king of Britain. Beginning a contest with a certain beast, he lost his soldiers, but finally killed that same beast; yet he did not return home. Even after his death the Britons still await his coming. Hinnius therefore means that, if he were Arthur’s son, he would then be sufficiently despised.], whatever I may be thought to be.

I envy all; no one envies me. My mind grieves because  
Its pain here lacks the reciprocal exchange.

For the unhappy man lacks envy—indeed, most unhappy is he  
Who lacks every kind of prosperity too completely.

[125] What am I? What was I? Of what land? Where? By what name am I called? From where  
Born? Man or earth? I do not know—destitute of a mountain.

My lords, companions, acquaintances—and, what is worse, friends—  
Alas for the crime!—abandoned me in mid-sea.

While the west wind blew, I had many friends with me;  
[130] Now, as the north wind blows in a storm, it puts them all to flight.

As the singing nightingale flees leaves, melodious sound,  
Grove and woods when touched by cold,

So every friend, avoiding winter’s onset and dreadful clouds,  
Is absent in adverse circumstances.

[135] False love follows the delights of spring, but deserts  
The season of winter when the steersman has been taken away.

The ravenous vulture, black raven, and prophetic [Note: [Col. 0846D] Cunning.] crow  
Always stand ready for the gluttony of the belly.

[Col. 0847A] The honey-seeking creature [Note: [Col. 0847D] Bee.] seeks honey; the fly and wolf seek corpses; thus now [Note: [Col. 0847D] Ms. Helmst.: “The honey-seeking creature seeks honey; the fly and wolf, a corpse.”]  
[140] The mind prepares to pursue prey, not persons.

Cheap is that semblance of friendship which, at any breeze,  
The goddess, blind [Note: [Col. 0847D] Blind Fortune.] and bereft, changes with varied waves.

Had Euryalus and Nisus once been such men,  
Their everlasting love would not have endured.

[145] True love does not disdain an unhappy friend;  
True loyalty does not know how to follow only pleasant circumstances.

True loyalty shares both flowers and the great wrath of hail  
When borne amid the concussion of a storm.

Thus Scripture speaks of united companions  
[150] Whom true love has bound with a true bond.

In this alone adverse fortune prevails: it reveals friends.  
[Col. 0847B] It shows who is good and who bad—both kinds of loyalty.

As a furnace tests gold, the sea a ship, a blade chains,  
So a more grievous misfortune tests friendly hearts.

[155] For a single phoenix will sooner join companions,  
And wolves will sooner enjoy peace with sheep,

And old Arthur the Briton will sooner come [Note: [Col. 0847D] Ms. Helmst. *Britannis*, “to the Britons.”],  
Than a false friend bring help in adversity.

Job’s distress is surpassed when compared with mine,  
[160] Because he had a wife and three friends.

But I, abandoned, see neither her nor them.  
Apart from nothing, I am known to possess nothing.

If Codrus were here, I should now be poorer than he;  
[Col. 0847C] for he had nothing here. But I have more than nothing.

[165] So many things are mine that without me the queen would not lie down;  
If this were true, every poor man would lie down.

At every season fasting from prosperity,  
With death threatening too greatly, I lament harsher things.

Spring gave a promise, but summer brought me evils;  
[170] Autumn nourishes them, and cold winter feeds them.

By night and day evil makes me drink a bitter draught,  
So that none of my joys may thrive within me.

By day I complain, pour forth tears, belch sighs,  
Tear my cheeks, beat my breast, and rend my hair.

[175] Yet daylight conversation with a crowd is a consolation,  
And frequent reading lessens my punishments.

Night’s distress is far less than that of day,  
[Col. 0847D] which binds my heart in no small grief.

At night impious frenzy rages in me with excessive Furies [Note: [Col. 0847D] Ms. H. *imo*, “indeed.”],  
[180] And devours my heart with a deeper wound.

At night I groan and redouble my groans; the heap of sorrows  
Grows, and frequent hell-fire seethes my heart.

[Col. 0848A] Woe is me! My speech, my constant tale, is painful,  
While I speak sorrowfully with myself in such a voice.

[185] Wrath rages and pierces my heart with innumerable arrows [Note: [Col. 0847D] Ms. H. *lacerat*, “tears.”],  
And the troop of punishments rages in a wild storm.

I turn and turn again; the very soft bed  
Pricks my sorrowful limbs with sharp thorns.

Now the pillow is much too high; now it sinks far too low;  
[190] It cannot keep a middle measure.

Now I lower my head, now raise it; now I collapse upon my left side,  
Now upon my right; now I fall, now I rise;

Now this way, now that; now upward, now I turn below.  
[Col. 0848B] And now I turn my head where my feet ought to be.

[195] I cannot remain thus; I rise and turn the bed about.  
Thus now I turn my feet to where my head ought to be.

I cannot be thus [Note: [Col. 0848D] Ms. H. “stand thus.”]; I hurry and curse the servant  
Because he makes me fare badly with my bed.

In angry cries I call out to the innocent attendant:  
[200] “Come here, wretched Hugh! Come here, accursed one!

“What are you doing, Hugh? Are you lying down? What is this with my bed,  
That it is made badly every day? What is the reason [Note: [Col. 0848D] Cause, explanation.]?”

Then I beat him himself with dreadful [Note: [Col. 0848D] Ms. Helmst. *duris*, “harsh.”] slaps and fists,  
And so I repay the evil I suffer with a beating.

[205] [Col. 0848C] He turns and turns again, and strikes the feathers with his arms,  
And the boy now exacts revenge for what he had endured.

Then I lie down again. I think that I am sleeping. There is no point  
At which I can remain steady even for a single moment.

So Boreas is wont to tear away the leaves of trees [Note: [Col. 0848D] Ms. H. *evolvere*, “unroll.”];  
[210] So the wheel tosses mortals, and savage water the wheel.

Now burning heat, now cold freezes my limbs;  
Now watery, hostile sweat possesses them.

Then I groan. Then my eyes drink tears as their own draughts—  
Indeed they vomit them forth, a double spring watering my cheeks.

[215] If sleep steals upon me—which is rare—dreams play  
With my sick mind in manifold agitations.

[Col. 0848D] I am drowned in Ocean; I am valued at a trifling penny [Note: [Col. 0848D] *Taxor*, “I am valued.”].  
I often see armed gods running.

Little rivers flow; the sea dries up; Atlas falls;  
[220] And the bird shakes the two mighty worlds [Note: [Col. 0848D] Ms. Helmst. *fortis*, singular.].

I am like the fledgling whom Cadmus [Note: [Col. 0848D] A serpent.] gnaws upon an oak,  
The bird that calls for its mother with a dreadful cry.

[Col. 0849A] I am like a hungry man who dreams of golden roofs,  
And, though poor, of possessing clothes for his needs.

[225] I am like a peasant awaiting the rushing river,  
Who desires to go onward dry-footed when its waters have run off [Note: [Col. 0849D] A certain peasant, arriving at a great river, wished to wait until the stream had flowed away, so that he could cross dry-footed.].

I am like a gambler delayed by the deceptive die,  
Who, though he has lost, prepares to lose still more.

I am like a madman who, the more he is hurt, the more  
[230] He rages with clubs and a freer throwing of blows.

Ah, most unhappy man, who endures things beyond counting,  
Who bears upon his shoulders all [Note: [Col. 0849D] Ms. H. *crimina*, “crimes.”] too many things.

I suffer so many evils, so many punishments, that if anyone  
Compared the sand in number, the sand would yield to mine.

[235] Let the page be heaven, the leaves the scribe, the water  
[Col. 0849B] ink: they could not recount our evils.

I am wounded by things so grievous that I do not fear worse;  
[Col. 0850A] he who is supremely wretched cannot be pious.

Cursed be the day on which she conceived, and the day on which  
[240] My mother bore me; cursed be that day.

Cursed be the day on which I sucked the breast, and the day  
On which I cried in the cradle; cursed be that day.

Cursed be the day that would have transformed me from the womb of life into the grave—  
O God, cursed be that day!

[245] When my mother gave me her breasts, so that I might not see such great evils,  
She ought to have cut off my head at the throat.

For it is better for dead limbs to be hidden in a grave  
Than, while living, to suffer things worse than death [Note: [Col. 0849D] Ms. H. *deteriore*, singular.].

All things conspire against me. Merciful Father,  
[250] Come to the aid of a wretch—my hope, highest Father.

[Col. 0850B] All things conspire against me; you, *Kyrie eleison* (“Lord, have mercy”),  
Come to the aid of a wretch, highest Creator, *ymas* [Note: [Col. 0849D] What *ymas* means is not apparent. A complete distich is absent in the Wolfenbüttel manuscript, and I do not think it is Henry’s. Not only does the style conflict, but also the total number of verses—250—which completes each book.].

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849B] The first book ends; here the second begins.  
Weep, wretch. Weep with your palms, most wretched Henry;

Weep with your head and hard breast, wretch.

Cruel stepmother Ramnusia [Note: [Col. 0849D] Fortune.] burns  
To perpetuate me, her stepson, in dreadful evils.

[5] Fortune is more Neronian than any serpent [Note: [Col. 0849D] More cruel.].  
For a serpent flees; but she drives me away more often.

When will a favourable lot grant me prosperity?  
[Col. 0849C] Not today, nor tomorrow; perhaps, I think, yesterday [Note: [Col. 0850D] Irony.].

When chance has looked upon me with a flattering face,  
[10] Arno [Note: [Col. 0850D] The Arno is a river near Florence, flowing in winding bends.], hurry backwards; run back in your source.

How badly a tree bears fruit which has never flowered.  
Hope of harvest too is absent when the shoot dies badly.

O shame! O fear! O sorrow! O evil weariness of life!  
O constant companion, madness more than madness!

[15] What shall I do? You, my throng of evils, tell me this;  
For you are my aid and my counsel.

O God! Why does Fortune, with sudden turning,  
[Col. 0849D] grind all things in her ever-moving wheel [Note: [Col. 0850D] Turns.]?

Bad fate, worse fate, worst fate, malignant fate,  
[20] By shameful art changes [Note: [Col. 0850D] Changes.] her creature [Note: [Col. 0850D] Created being.].

[Col. 0850B] O Father, receive and restore to heaven  
This soul, which you release from wretched flesh, full of tears—

Kind parent, receive the soul which a troop of punishments scourges,  
Which Erinys harrows with Stygian horses.

[25] Which Alecto strikes, which Tisiphone too wearies,  
Which Fortune harms, and which Megaera strikes.

May pity therefore make you merciful, so that impious  
[Col. 0850C] Alecto, who wishes to tear the wretch apart, may cease.

And you also, most ready cause of frenzied pain,  
[30] Listen, faithless one, and stop the wheel of wickedness.

Headlong Fortune, with dreadful beatings, what is this—  
Why do you, treacherous one, afflict my head?

Where do you drag me, savage creature? Impious one, you make Croesus a Codrus,  
Nestor a Thersites [Note: [Col. 0850D] You make me foolish from prudent.], daring an uglier crime.

[35] Am I Scarioth [Note: [Col. 0850D] Judas.]? Am I Pontius? Why  
Have I deserved to suffer such severe scourges?

Fool, why are you mad? Why do you embitter this head, this head [Note: [Col. 0850D] Ms. H.: “Fool, why are you mad? Why do you embitter this head with punishments?”]?  
[Col. 0850D] Set a limit to your wickedness, faithless one; set a limit.

Do others fail you? Do you alone torment me alone?  
[40] But see what you do: vengeance rarely perishes.

Take care lest your troop of punishments shoot you with arrows;  
[Col. 0851A] for the arrow often strikes its own maker [Note: [Col. 0851D] Ms. H. *actorem*, “agent.”].

Alas, what are you doing? What are you doing? Why, faithless one, do you destroy me?  
Set a limit to your wickedness, faithless one. Set a limit.

Tell me what I have done. Answer, deceitful tongue.  
[45] Answer by him who sits above the stars.

If frenzied abundance of your kind were granted to us,  
Torn apart, you would shamefully be food for beasts.

What madness? Why do you rage? Why do you, mad creature, assail me?  
[50] Set a limit to your wickedness, faithless one; set a limit.

Deprived of such words, the goddess lent her ears.  
She spoke thus, and herself turns [Note: [Col. 0851D] Turns.] the wheel of wickedness:

“Why, wandering Muse, do you tear my fates with biting speech?  
[Col. 0851B] Whom has she made more wretched and more afflicted [Note: [Col. 0851D] More than you suffer.]?

[55] Are not the kingdoms of the world enclosed within my fist?  
Do not every clime tremble before my kingdom [Note: [Col. 0851D] Fear.]?

Greek and Hebrew, barbarian and Latin alike  
Fear me, entreat me, worship me, love me.

Do I not compel the powers of the world, and its lesser powers,  
[60] To bow their necks beneath my command?

Recently the German [Note: [Col. 0851D] Henry VI, son of the Emperor Frederick I; in 1191 he undertook an unsuccessful expedition into Apulia against Tancred, usurper of Sicily.], carried to the Sicilian shore,  
Lost his Ferica [Note: [Col. 0851D] Ms. H. *Pherisam*. This denotes Henry’s wife Constance, whom Tancred captured.] in play [Note: [Col. 0851D] In fighting.].

He lost knights, rooks [Note: [Col. 0851D] A term from the technical vocabulary of chess, here undoubtedly indicating military commanders.], foot-soldiers, and oxen [Note: [Col. 0852D] Ms. Wolfenbüttel: *minores*, “lesser pieces.”].  
He lost the *calphi* also [uncertain chess term]; scarcely does he depart safely.

[Col. 0851C] And Saladin [Note: [Col. 0852D] Saladin occupied Jerusalem and Palestine in 1187.], attacking too fiercely the banners of salvation,  
[65] Will find me to be his enemy [Note: [Col. 0852D] Ms. H. *senserat*, “had found.”] [Note: [Col. 0852D] Ms. H. *suum*, masculine.].

Why should I recount the ancients, whose ruin fame reports?  
I was mother to Pompey, then stepmother.

I gave Darius words of honey, then blows;  
[70] To Cyrus I gave an ingenious nurse, sweet at first, then bitter as gall.

You, whom fame does not mention, whom disgrace knows,  
Shamefully tear my anger apart with reproaches.

Why do you make threats [Note: [Col. 0852D] Ms. H. “Why do you threaten me”]? He is guilty of the crime of injured  
Majesty, and his entire stock shall pay for this.

Take heed what you do: not all poison has yet perished,  
[75] And my power has not yet ceased to be mine.”

[Col. 0851D] “What worse things can you do, harlot Fortune,  
Worst stepmother, Medea more cruel, fierce Hydra?

I have come to nothing [Note: [Col. 0852D] Ms. Helmst. *eveni*, “I have happened/come about.”]. My remaining breath now [Note: [Col. 0852D] Ms. H. *restat nec*, “nor remains.”]  
[80] Has no bones upon which your insults can have any force.

Do you think you harm me by death? That would be a cause of salvation for me.  
To be without death is a death to me twice over.

How gladly, at whatever hour God grants,  
I shall receive it. After this, dung in your mouth!

[85] Why, mad one, do you assume so many varying forms?  
Now you laugh joyfully, now you groan tearfully.

Now golden, now filthy, now black, now red;  
Now blooming, now made filthy with mud.

You are Proteus, and wandering. The wind moves your entrails,  
[90] [Col. 0852B] or the devil often moves your entrails.

You are always inconstant, wandering, changeable, harsh, blind,  
Unstable, frivolous, faithless, deaf, savage.”

Then she smiled: “O in how much night-dust  
Do the blind eyes of the human mind lie hidden [Note: [Col. 0852D] Ms. Helmst. *manent*, “remain.”].

[95] Have you not heard? Let each wise person [Note: [Col. 0852D] *Unusquisque* (“each one”) is to be formed by combining the two verses.] weigh his own words  
And think before speaking [Note: [Col. 0852D] Before he speaks.].

I operate under laws that have been imposed. If under laws, then  
Under just ones; if just ones, then lawfully. Therefore it is done rightly.

Does not each person thus use his own lawful art?  
[100] Every person uses what lot has granted him.

The soldier uses horses, the fisherman waters, and the cleric hymns;  
The sailor seas, boxers war, the poet metres.

[Col. 0852C] The rough peasant ploughs, the greedy merchant counts,  
The maiden gathers flowers, the foolish lover loves.

[105] But I, who am a goddess than whom none is more powerful in the world,  
Whom the circle of Ocean binds within its orb—

Am I not, most foolish man, to pursue my own art lawfully?  
Thus it is necessary that I turn you by casting you down.

Therefore see what you do. A wise man deliberates before  
[110] He acts. So you, wretch, think beforehand.

Ah, with how many bites does humankind embitter my deeds  
And harrow my work with its teeth!

If I extend riches to it with open fingers [Note: [Col. 0852D] To humankind.],  
I shall be extolled by imperial praises.

[115] [Col. 0852D] Then I am highest parent, then venerable queen;  
Then highest goddess; I myself am preferred to the god Jupiter.

But if by chance I close my withholding right hand,  
I myself am bitten with savage bites and stings.

[Col. 0853A] Then I am called perjured [Note: [Col. 0853D] More correctly, *perjurans*, “committing perjury.”], then a shameful adulteress;  
[120] Then they say that I have corrupted a priest.

But why, unhappy man, do you now tear me with sharp teeth  
And with your words?

You speak at your own discretion; for you shun the weight of law  
And disdain to speak reasonably.

[125] Yet he who contends unjustly, speaking only reproaches,  
Teaches one to defend an unjust cause and party.

Thus, when arguments fail him, the ignorant, talkative sophist  
Makes himself thunder with his own voice.

Thus also, when laws fail you, you resort to the aid  
[130] Of chatter, which you know well.

Therefore, if anything just adheres to your mind—which I do not think—  
State it; or, what I pray for more, be silent.”

Then I: “Mad Ramnusian, harlot, monster!  
Am I not permitted even to utter these words?

[135] You act and you speak. Faithless one, you tear me apart in deeds;  
After these wicked deeds, you reproach me [Note: [Col. 0853D] Cast up against me.]!

Now I know from experience that blame always falls  
Upon the wretch who has nothing with which to defend himself.

Whenever a dispute arises between eagles and swans,  
[140] Unjust blame is always assigned to the least.

Thus whenever Actaeon [Note: [Col. 0853D] The stag into which Actaeon was transformed.] and the king of beasts contend,  
They maintain that the weaker party upholds the worst rights;

And whenever German rage rages against Tuscans,  
[Col. 0853C] ruined lesser towns bear witness to the truth.

[145] You do the same to me. But if I could repel force with force,  
Either you would be silent, or your wrath would be more sparing.

Therefore insert your satires more cautiously, enemy of the gods,  
Or see to those things which ought to be kept silent for your own sake.

For he badly rebukes companions whom the same crime  
[150] Equally stains with the fault he strives to remove.

Thus Paris rebukes Aegides; thus that Lucius rebukes Catiline;  
Thus too the watery mother rebukes her backward-walking child [Note: [Col. 0853D] An allusion to the fable of the crab’s mother reproaching her child for walking sideways.].

Do not therefore endeavour to condemn in others what is in yourself,  
Lest shameful punishment fall upon your beard.

[155] For it is exceedingly foolish for anyone to condemn himself;  
[Col. 0853D] quarrelsome woman, take care not to do this.

You are flighty and sinister, headlong and mad;  
Lacking reason, you do not know how to keep measure.

You strike me and rage. You tear my limbs and assail my side [Note: [Col. 0853D] Ms. Helmst., “me, me.”],  
[160] and destroy all my breadth.”

Then she: “You will not gain a single penny from me,  
You who seek to adorn your mistress.

For the servant who struggles against his own lord  
Faithlessly kicks against his own goad.

[165] Let mortals learn to revere [Note: [Col. 0853D] Ms. H. *vereari*, “to fear/revere.”] their proper lords;  
For he who harms by deceit perishes by deceits.

Are you Alexander? Are you Caesar? Whence  
Such pride, or such unjust madness?

Who are you? Why do you rage? We know you—and where you came from,  
[170] What your origin is, and who your fathers were.

It suits you to vex fields with dreadful hoes,  
[Col. 0854B] because your stock demands rustic labour.

And who are you? Where do you come from? *Cro, cro* [Note: [Col. 0853D] The gloss of the Helmstadt manuscript substitutes *reoch, reoch*. Both seem to indicate a hissing sound.], madman—away!  
Groan forever, and hide yourself forever.

[175] Whatever you do, say, or suffer,  
It does not cause you to draw back what my right hand draws.

Thus I shall hold primacy and venerable sceptres,  
And according to my will I shall give you honey and gall.

You are a little ant, a small mouse, an empty *gnanus* [perhaps “fool”]?  
[180] What can you do to me, shameful *gnane*? Nothing.

I, the universal steward of things, care nothing for your insults or threats;  
[Col. 0854C] rather, I glory in my throne.

The powerful bird [Note: [Col. 0853D] A hawk or eagle.] cares no more for smaller birds than the lion for butterflies;  
Nor does greedy Polis [Note: [Col. 0853D] Constantinople.] care less for narrow Tibur [Note: [Col. 0854D] Rome. The sense is: Constantinople cares no less for Rome. Without harming the metre the sense would be clearer if the verse were arranged thus: “Nor does greedy Polis care less for narrow Tibur.”].

[185] Nor does the noble arch-flying bird [Note: [Col. 0854D] Eagle.] fear trembling cicadas  
More than I fear your empty-talking [Note: [Col. 0854D] Ms. Helmst. *vaniloquas*, “empty-talking,” feminine plural.] words and threats [Note: [Col. 0854D] The complete verse would be more correctly arranged thus: “Than I fear your words and empty-talking threats.”].

What can your derision do? Whoever is a scoffer  
Is himself customarily mocked by all crowds.

The screeching owl [Note: [Col. 0854D] Owl.] mocks the birds at night;  
[190] Does the rest of the flock tear it apart by day?

So those who mock others are themselves mocked.  
[Col. 0854D] Nothing is more common among peoples. Note!

Therefore be quiet, wretch! Wretch, then be quiet—be quiet!  
For you can endure light words, but deeds are heavy.”

[195] Then I: “I am angered by your mad words, Ramnusia,  
[Col. 0855A] while you cast insults upon me in your worthless verses.

While you rehearse my abuse in truth-speaking words,  
No wrath more savage than truth holds anything more grievous.

He who strikes an enemy with a sword has no need of words;  
[200] For a cruel blade sufficiently inflicts a wound.

Do you reproach me with my birth? Usurious monster!  
Hairy-faced, but shaven-headed behind!

You are not an ape. You are uglier. You are the ugliest thing—  
A thing I know not what, which I would prefer to be nothing.

[205] Though I be born of lowly rustic stock,  
A lineage does not lack every kind of nobility.

Not distinguished birth nor the illustrious name of forefathers,  
But virtue flourishes in true nobility.

Sweet honey often lies hidden in a slender reed;  
[210] The water of a modest spring tempers thirst.

You tremble at nothing. Why then? Bucephalus [Note: [Col. 0855D] Bucephalus. An ox is intended here.] is very often food for flies,  
And a wolf often becomes food for ants.

Nothing is so strong that it is not sometimes worn away;  
You can often see this even from what is weak.

[215] A ploughshare by earth, a stone by water, a gem by a thumb—what more?  
What is solid is often broken by what is soft.

You do not always turn Marius, nor always much-turned  
Apollonius. Another will be stronger—

One who, redeeming my reproaches, will fight in a hard contest,  
[220] And perhaps he will savagely take your head from you.”

[Col. 0855C] Then she: “I shall speak in peaceful discourse according to reason,  
If it pleases you and you wish to make peace with me.

[Col. 0856A] I should be despised too greatly if I always remained the same—  
Either good, evil, or holding between the two [Note: [Col. 0855D] Ms. Helmst. *tenens*, “holding.”].

[225] Everything that is frequent grows cheap through excessive use;  
Everything rare is usually more dear.

Among Indians, noble pepper is cheaper than pennyroyal;  
There a grass-green asp is cheaper than rocks [Note: [Col. 0855D] Ms. H. *jaspis* (“jasper”). For the sense and metre together, the verse would more correctly read: “Jasper among rocks.”].

A rough grey cloak is dearer to cold Goths,  
With which the savage right hand of the butcher strips a sheep.

[230] At Bologna [Note: [Col. 0855D] Perhaps Poland. A marginal gloss of the Helmstadt manuscript indicates that others read Pannonia.] a foot-soldier is held more renowned than a celebrated mounted warrior,  
Renowned and dreadful amid raging war.

You cannot complain so much yourself. I am often kind to you  
And, though never prodigal, generous with what is mine.

[235] Now I propose to be more merciful to you,  
[Col. 0856B] if it pleases you and you wish to make peace with me.”

“Far be it from me, wicked bitch, to make peace with you.  
Let sluggish, savage Brunellus [Note: [Col. 0855D] Brunellus: an ass so called by Nigel of Wireker.] make peace with you instead,

For you have no loyalty, no measure; in no order  
[240] Do you live, and frenzy is your companion in place of reason.”

Then she: “I do not refuse to stand with you before judgment,  
So that Justinian’s law may see this crime.

If you speak well, you possess what you lack: law and reason;  
If badly, then be quiet in accordance with my commands.

Unless, sluggish woman, you knew better than the laws,  
[245] The wheel which you turn in your orbit would stand still.

By law, madmen are forbidden to stand in judgment;  
Therefore law forbids you, since you are mad.”

Then she: “Go, savage man. Remember that you are my enemy.”  
[250] [Col. 0856C] “You too go; remember that you are my enemy.”

## THE THIRD LITTLE BOOK

[Col. 0855]

[Col. 0855C] The two books having been completed, let us join a third.

While I was recounting my lamenting elegiac [Note: [Col. 0855D] Ms. Helmst. *miserabilia* (“miserable”) for *elegiaca* (“elegiac”).] deeds  
And uttering hostile words against Fortune,

Behold, a shining, worthy woman, wiser than Solomon [Note: [Col. 0855D] More wise.],  
A gracious mother, stood before my sight.

[5] Her countenance rises; her form changes by turns;  
[Col. 0855D] Now heaven contains her, now more, now earth.

A company of seven, called *phrenesis*, accompanies her;  
She assigned its office to each one.

The first [Note: [Col. 0855D] Grammar.] cherishes boys; another [Note: [Col. 0856D] Logic.] syllogizes; another adorns  
[10] [Col. 0856C] discourse [Note: [Col. 0856D] Rhetoric.]; another measures [Note: [Col. 0856D] Geometry.] the ground;

This one shows the counting-board [Note: [Col. 0856D] Arithmetic.]; another sings like Philomela [Note: [Col. 0856D] Music.]; and the seventh maiden [Note: [Col. 0856D] Astronomy.] raises  
Her head high to the heavens.

The aforesaid goddess sat attended by these goddesses  
And, as though sympathizing with the sufferer’s just claim, said:

[15] “What Lethean cups has your mind drunk?  
[Col. 0856D] In what foreign place does your wandering mind slumber?

Certainly you are blind, and your mind likewise strays beyond its course [Note: [Col. 0856D] More correctly: “You are certainly blind. Your mind likewise strays beyond its course.”].  
You do not know even the little that learned school has taught.

Alas, how much you suffer. I grieve for your mind alone,  
[20] Because at this time your understanding has gone abroad.

If Hippocrates [Note: [Col. 0856D] Hippocrates.] were here, and all the medicine of Salerno,  
[Col. 0857A] not even so would your diseased mind be sound.

For medicine cannot drive out an inveterate illness;  
What has grown for long continues long in being.

[25] Alas, I grieve over this: that you are losing your mind and, in every  
Sense, becoming brutish—a man made into a beast.

What have you to do with tears? An abundance of tears  
Does not make a weak man share in his desire.

He who groans redoubles his losses; through grief he enlarges grief,  
[30] And dies alive by a double death.

What have you to do with unjust Fortune? You have always  
Suffered many chains of reproach because of her.

Do you wish her not to wander? Nature resists.  
Whoever would make her, whom nature made unstable and ever wandering, otherwise,

Sows among thorns while revoking nature’s laws.  
[35] The chattering frog cannot be torn from its marsh.

He who desires to take away nature sows a plant  
Whose fruit will come in Arthur’s time [Note: [Col. 0857D] When Arthur returns to Britain—that is, never.].

A breeze whirls you about too much; bitter things move you too much,  
And grief makes you excessively foolish.

[40] He who cannot endure prosperity joined to adversity  
Does not bear the stamp of a man and dishonours human dignity.

He uses sweetness ignorantly, not having used bitterness;  
For every good is known through its opposite.

[45] [Col. 0857C] Learn to endure what must be borne. Patience moderates anger,  
And the mind’s olive branch tames dreadful [Note: [Col. 0857D] Ms. Helmst. *duros*, “harsh.”] emotions.

Do you not remember how, when the tyrant urged him,  
Obedient Seneca died an innocent death?

Did not my Severinus [Note: [Col. 0857D] Boethius.], slain by unjust law,  
[50] Endure unbearable things in Pavia’s prison?

Did not lustful, verse-making master Naso,  
Driven from his homeland, die poor and exiled?

Why should I recount many whose guiltless life  
Endured Fortune’s unbearable blows?

[55] A forest of hairs would yield in number to those  
Whom illustrious life made immune from death.

One ought to bear harsh things. Harsh things ripen the mind;  
[Col. 0857D] and a well-ripened grape tastes more fully.

Through excessive heats one passes to cool shade;  
[60] Thus through its opposite man seeks sweet things.

For punishment comes the laurel; for death, a crown:  
Whence man labours, from there labour gives reward.

What are you doing, foul man? And what foul thing do you seek from the foul world?  
What clean thing will a foul world give you?

[65] Fool, do you think you will live through all ages? By thee! [Note: [Col. 0858D] An Italian formula of swearing. Ms. Helmst. partly.]  
[Col. 0858A] You have been made mad by your own credulity.

He certainly suffers from the grave sickness of a mad head  
Who thinks that he can live long in this world.

Your sense is absent and your understanding wanders;  
Your mind travels in Lethean waters.

[70] Tell me where are those things which Bologna once taught you?  
Tell me, I say, where are the things which I often gave you?

I cherished you greatly, taught you, often urged you,  
And often allowed you to see my secrets.

You were my vine; you were the shade of a new branch;  
[75] You often gave me strong hope of fruit.

I cultivated you with hoes, enclosed you with fence and protection,  
And removed stones and all harmful things from you.

The time for fruit has come; the vine itself has borne wild grapes,  
[80] [Col. 0858B] and in place of a rose a harsh thorn has grown for me.

Alas, the seed I sow in you falls among thorns;  
The thorn itself chokes your mind.

The thorn itself chokes what I say and advise, what I sow—  
like the sand that badly multiplies its seed.

[85] You are too much your own man, and too much trust yourself, fool;  
And you alone believe yourself a provident Cato.

You are too much a philosopher, more Platonic than Plato himself [Note: [Col. 0858D] A philosopher more distinguished than Plato himself.].  
Your mind often ranges beyond philosophers.

No one can, without labour, follow the Pythagorean horns—the letter Y [Note: [Col. 0858D] The letter Y.]—  
[Col. 0858C] with his right eye directed toward virtue [Note: [Col. 0858D] Ms. Helmst. *virtutum*, “of virtues.”].

[90] But the other fork is there: easy is the descent to Avernus,  
As the poet Virgil teaches in his far-speaking voice.

The tree of virtue is not climbed without sweat;  
Nor does the martial palm come without sweat.

[95] I praise you, but I do not praise you in this: that you lament  
That these perishable things have fled the world with swift steps.

Alas for your grief! Alas, why do you fear? Why grief? Why  
Do you weep? What things are yours, pitiable ash?

What did you bring with you at first into the world?  
[100] Naked you were at first, and naked afterward you shall be.”

Then I: “You speak marvellous things; but what sort of true wisdom is this  
[Col. 0858D] that you utter? This speech is too hard for me.

Who now is so gentle, so sweet, and so kind  
That this anger does not carry him excessively beyond measure?

[105] Now, when I see grain set beneath straw,  
When marsh-grass surpasses soft roses;

When fruit today prepares to consume its own flowers before them,  
A tree monstrous with abortive foliage;

When, a great wickedness, evil men are lifted on high  
[110] [Col. 0859A] and the good man is oppressed by a worse life—

Tell me: what character, what life, what order gave Nero  
The city, the city’s riches, and empire?

Behold—but I pass this over—many bear a name despite their virtue forbidding it;  
For them the shadow of the name is shame.

[115] Then she: “You are deceived, and ignorance of the law  
Does not excuse you; presumptuous man, you are very unlearned.

How difficult is this labour, and how great the mind’s effort:  
To know good men by true discernment.

False opinion often falsely calls good men wicked,  
[120] And conversely promotes evil men.

Not every bird clothed in a snowy garment,  
[Col. 0859B] even if it imitates one, is a true dove.

Often Lycaon, a goat, lies hidden beneath a lamb’s skin;  
And beneath pious Cato, faithless Nero himself.

[125] Conversely, as you well know, beneath rough coverings there lies hidden  
A soft rose dyed with blood-red colour.

And ancient literature recounts, in obscure words, the members  
Of both renowned leaders—Ithacan [Note: [Col. 0859D] Ulysses is called Ithacan.] and Philip’s offspring [Note: [Col. 0859D] Alexander the Great.].

You therefore see many things surrounded by counterfeit trappings  
[130] Which are far otherwise than they appear.

You grieve that unjust men have possessed the heights of power:  
That will be a long cause of grief to you.

You do not know what a wretched omen it is for mortals to be drawn upward  
[Col. 0859C] to high places. If you knew, you would wish to be silent about this.

[135] Changeful Fortune advances unjust men so that those whom  
She has made precipitately climb she may whirl down to the depths.

A swollen tower falls with a heavier crash,  
And a tall cypress strikes the earth more heavily.

In what great darkness of error the mind of man is blindly  
[140] Plunged, so that it reckons wickedness alone to be good.

Not fortunate is he who has nowhere to grow in honour, but he who has nowhere to decline to, nor any place whither he can fall.

Woe to you, woe to the mortal race, which always strives upward, only to fall with a more treacherous fall.

[145] Here swords, here cups, and both the savage enemy and the host mingle their own dreadful poisons within.

[Col. 0859D] Look at him to whom [Note: Julius Caesar.] lofty Capitols had so often offered triumphs, yet Fate bore him off as the servant of his own man.

Look at him whom [Note: Crassus.] Babylon, greedy for gold, made drink gold.

[150] And what bitter fates Caesar endured for his own people. [Note: Ms. Helmst.: “which.”]

Does not the fierce Macedonian tyrant, safeguarded from his enemy, perish among friendly hearts poisoned for him?

Why should I mention Darius? Why Cyrus? Or Nero?

[Col. 0860A] For honour always hangs upon a slender omen.

[155] Behold examples from the modern world, the ancient ones being set aside.

Nothing can be safer than poverty.

That one lion, that strength of faith, indeed that one wall and enemy [Note: Ms. H.: “hostile.”]—he alone was a terror.

Conrad, a fierce leader and the cause of our salvation, [Note: The Marquis of Montferrat, who had fought against the Saracens.]

[160] Why, because he was great, does he perish by treachery? [Note: Richard ordered her to be killed; see the gloss in the manuscript codex of Helmstedt.]

He who had lately broken the fortresses of reigning and mighty men,

To whom birth and wealth supplied great strength?

Recently that same man, beneath the miserable cloak of poverty,

The Englishman, confined and captive, paid the price for his deeds. [Note: King Richard of England, captured in 1192.]

[165] O blind mortal race! What, then, is safer than poverty?

Almost nothing. Nothing without dregs.

Go among the Spaniards; go among the dark Indians.

Go through ambushes. Go through every forest.

[Col. 0860B] Go through hostile battalions and troops of robbers:

[170] Provided that you are true, you will be safe though poor.

What will the unencumbered traveller do before a robber?

Glad and fearless, he will pour forth song to the stars.

What use are glittering necklaces? What, then, do tiaras avail?

What use is the sceptre? What honour? What purse filled to overflowing?

[175] Or offices? And what use is precious household property?

Nothing can be safer than poverty.

Then I said: “I should like to know, if it would not be too burdensome:

Will this world be one of a worse life?

Or will it put off as its own the sin which I love? Or will it stand yet more unhappily

[180] [Col. 0860C] in the condition in which it lies?”

“But tell me: whence, as I recall, you rightly reported above,

what clean thing will the unclean world give you?”

Then she said: “This scarcely bears even a shadow. The bright preludes of things cannot unravel the design.”

[185] Do we not come to silver from pure gold?

The next descent is from silver to bronze.

The third descent is from bronze to iron. What is there now?

In a still worse descent it has fallen into mud.

When mud fails, what will there be? We shall come to actual

[190] dung, and every man will stink in such a state.

Behold, you see amid what great filth this

[Col. 0860D] world is rotting; and for this very reason it cannot bear its name.

All things degenerate. All rush upon worse courses,

and the ship departs with its helmsman broken.

[195] The world loves, despises, impoverishes, pursues, abhors:

the worst things, justice, laws; wicked things, the good.

The world nourishes frauds, cherishes crime, excludes honourable things;

it flees what is right, violates compacts, desires shameful things.

[Col. 0861A] The very head of the world, the venal papal court,

[200] prostitutes itself, and the head enfeebles the remaining members.

See the sacred crime, more shameful than either age:

in a shameful market it is sold by contract.

Holy chrism, holy orders, holy altars, consecrated

gifts—what more? God himself is sold.

[205] O sacred transactions that defile sacred seats!

O sacred transactions that make heavenly temples into a marketplace!

Such is your world, if it is rightly called a world:

such a marketplace it sweats to possess. [Note: Ms. Helmst.: “strives.”]

Behold, moreover, that wandering throng of scholars is ashamed,

[210] yet they pursue the marketplace by selling themselves.

Outside the path of law—alas, such precious offspring—

[Col. 0861B] comes into a servile condition, a grief indeed.

Corrupted liberty flees; nor does reason allow that a talent of whatever sort should be called such.

[215] Behold, a wife, driven by desire, an abomination,

sells herself; and the same lot has befallen the unmarried woman.
