If chaste Lucretia were still what she once was, when a purse

is offered to her, bitterly she would yield to you.

Penelope, widow now of a mercenary life,

[220] will hear prayers at the sound of money.

A judgment is sold for all-destroying money—O grief!—

and abundance of wealth breaks the justice of judges.

A judge corrupted by a gift turns aside from truth,

and a pious treasure makes justice falsely speaking.

[225] Devouring luxury, lean envy, and the evil passion for possession—

[Col. 0862A] they lay waste resources, gnaw at what is best, burn hearts.

The flattering pest, under the smile of a feigned countenance,

can do everything, a delightful companion to satraps.

Behold, Pylades—crime!—plots against his own Orestes.

[230] And an unjust wife mocks her own husband. [Note: Read *subsannat*, “mocks,” and connect it with the preceding words. Perhaps the verse should more correctly be arranged thus: “She mocks her own husband, an unjust wife.”]

The instructed cleric, the unlearned soldier, and the fickle crowd; [Note: Read *indoctus*, “unlearned.”]

they neglect, abhor, and nourish laws, moderation, and evil.

Virtue migrates into exile, and vice triumphs;

it reigns and holds a great tribunal among the peoples.

[235] An unjust mind, smeared with I know not what blind poppy, sleeps,

and does not know its Creator.

Behold, once more he is crucified by the tongue throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0862B] Behold, once more God suffers dreadful scourges.

The hand of Vespasian rises again, and destroys every

[240] ocean that commits wicked deeds.

Creation, its tyrant inciting it, despises its Maker,

bereft by the deeds of its own sin.

Hence comes famine; hence grievous discord in kingdoms;

hence we are prey and food for Canaanites.

[245] Hence the carnal sword oppresses the spiritual,

and, with the roles reversed, the spiritual sword oppresses it.

Hence rapacious Atropos suddenly seizes the limbs,

nor allows the wretch to grieve and repent.

You see rightly, therefore, why proper connection binds

[250] these two words together: “unclean world.”

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0861]

[Col. 0861C] Here you should profitably learn the fourth book.

Thus far we have seen whence sorrow comes, and what nourishes sorrow,

after the treachery of evil had been discovered.

Now it is necessary that gentle medicine restrain the disease,

and make the enemy keep away from its enemy.

[5] First, strip away the mad storms of tears,

by union with which every good is destroyed.

For sorrow weakens strength where lamentation abounds,

and makes the sadness of evil tenfold.

If lamentation produces evils, then it must itself be evil;

[10] if evil, then harmful; if harmful, flee it.

Against grief take joys; restrain your desire;

and always think the end of evil near.

[Col. 0861D] A welcome hour will come, one not hoped for,

which will compensate former bitterness with honeycombs.

[15] One clear day repays the clouds of many days,

and dries the muddy ground which water has made.

Dismiss wandering Fortune; allow her to wander,

for she can never play with a steady face.

[Col. 0862C] Against Fortune be constant, be patient, be

[20] iron; let no adverse winter break you.

When Fortune smiles, groan; when she weeps, make merry;

let her herself be your omen for every season.

Fortune turns all things with the wheel by which all things are turned;

thus the great world perishes in a slight circle within a circle.

[25] Be firm in adversity, slow to do evil, slow to anger,

ready for service, grieved at every wicked deed.

Be your own pupil and another’s teacher; inwardly

be your own self, but outwardly be wholly another.

Seek virtue, but flee vice; seek what is honourable,

[30] and what is useful; flee what is shameful by fleeing it.

Honourableness, the treasure of the clergy, is to be embraced by you,

[Col. 0862D] and reason, alas now a rare companion among peoples.

Let your hand be neither sticky nor anointed with oil; rather,

holding the mean between the two, let it reject every excess.

[35] Run between laughing Democritus [Note: He always laughed.] and weeping Democenas. [Note: Gloss in the Helmstedt manuscript on this word: “Democenas was a certain philosopher who always wept.”]

Let a modest rod thereby balance your condition.

[Col. 0863A] Let honeycomb drip from your mouth, but let olive resound in your mind.

Let not your whole understanding be in your mouth.

Reject the unstable; pursue the steadfast; weigh transient things;

rebuke sinners; restrain the frivolous.

[40] Let words be fewer and deeds more; be sparing in praise, [Note: “Praises.”]

sparing in reproaches, lavish in every honour.

And if deeds are lacking, let kindly words not be lacking;

for a honeyed tongue produces many dear friends.

[45] Follow your betters, reverence fathers, instruct inferiors;

either spur on the young or anoint the old.

Flee the burden of drunkenness; despise the bow of greed;

where these hold sway, virtue is exiled thence.

Do not heed either the hisses of the crowd or gifts that turn back.

[50] Let nothing outside virtue be your concern.

[Col. 0863B] If stone should become ice, what is that to you? A pagan would be more useful to you than a hooked, key-bearing man, [Note: Curved, always drawing things to himself like a hook.]

Gold turns leaden. What is that to you? Even nectar turns sour;

and what a monarch refuses a tetrarch often does.

[55] Therefore put your trust in the goodness of God,

and let your own virtues rightly follow it.

You will be content with nature; life’s evils are stumbling blocks;

and let every one of your actions approve your counsel.

Let a worthless, deceitful friend be a playful companion for a time, [Note: Cheerful, pleasant.]

[60] always less in body, more in mind.

Search holy books, be gentle when asked,

[Col. 0863C] labour over laws, and utter nothing but what is just.

Give offence to few, service to all; take care lest

a wrinkled brow deny what the hand itself does.

He who poisons an offered kindness with a wrinkled brow

[65] displeases me more than the devil who gives it.

Give with a serene countenance, and make your dear friend serene;

by his face a man himself doubles his gift.

Promise nothing except what you have given, for often

the hand made gouty makes the tongue a balance.

[70] I would rather you were lame with gout than gouty in the hand in this manner.

Horses assist weak feet.

What you wish to give, give without hope of return,

lest the hooked hand take away what the open hand gave.

[75] [Col. 0863D] For the giver who becomes a taker represents a crab by walking,

and makes that crab his own disgrace.

Nor let grave anger, that worst counsellor,

incite you with angry words against your servants.

For it is a greater virtue to keep dependants mercifully,

[80] than to possess those whom higher rank itself makes.

Do not be talkative, nor mute in every conversation,

but strive to speak only for usefulness.

Recognize others in yourself: nothing is more useful,

and no one in the world can be more civilized.

[85] Let no pregnant distension of the belly be dear to you,

[Col. 0864A] for it is too wretched to have a body made of food.

No virtue is lesser than conquering one’s companion at table,

and making the purse equal to the sacred belly.

Let the vice of hypocrites, the contagion of Simon, which now

[90] every cleric loves, be hateful to you.

Take care not to accuse matters which abuse itself does not accuse,

lest you suffer the same thing by proceeding wrongly.

Do not always seek prosperity, nor always pleasant things:

honeycomb is not always licked sweetly by the mouth.

[95] Flowers do not hasten into the meadow at every season,

nor does green grass always purple the ground.

Make use of discernment, by which life becomes noble;

for no one can derive anything but what is discerning from the discerning.

For good things are drawn from the good, but evil from the wicked.

[100] [Col. 0864B] Sweet wines flow from a sweet vine.

A rose does not produce thorns, although it is the daughter of a thorn.

Nor do violets prick, nor does Paradise harm.

Let what is clean (*mundum*) be dearer to you than the world (*mundus*); let a friend be dearer

than a companion, than even the degree of blood relationship.

[105] Do not believe too much through foolish credulity;

for it has betrayed more men than Scariot betrayed.

Frederick of Iconium was not betrayed more in former times [Note: Christian Daumius understands this to refer to Frederick I Barbarossa, in his *Epistolae philologicae criticae*, p. 164.]

than his own men are now betrayed by suspicious credulity.

Endure very much; join remedies to diseases,

[110] so that abundant medicine may put abundant disease to flight.

[Col. 0864C] As different concerns seek different laws,

so trembling illness calls for different remedies.

Some illnesses require juices, some seed, some delight in bark;

for some foliage, for others roots, serve as medicine.

[115] Mallows cure the frenzied, wormwood the colicky;

dill treats the *empticus* [the ailment is uncertain], and spasm loves milk.

Thus not one sense performs one office alone,

but each flourishes in its own art.

One knows colours, another sounds, another tastes;

[120] one knows smells, another pleasant things.

You also, whom ugly vice wearies with excessive

weight, drink many cups of virtues.

Let victory over yourself be dearer to you than victory over another,

and strive to conquer yourself in battle more than others.

[125] Believe me: it is greater to subdue oneself by virtue

[Col. 0864D] than, in Samson’s manner, to lay low a thousand men.

Honour everyone with whatever services you can, and do not ask who he is;

for glad honour makes many illustrious men friends. [Note: Helmstedt: “dear.”]

Whoever earnestly seeks honour with constant steps,

[130] honour also seeks him with reciprocal steps.

Let the flattering parasite and the impious traitor

always, while you live, be equally in your affection.

For by natural law a flatterer is bound

to be a traitor through his smiles and adornments.

[135] [Col. 0865A] The pipe sings sweetly—if not for me, believe Cato—

while the lyre betrays birds with sweet-sounding song.

Let your tongue not become fox-like through overly crafty complaints;

for fox-like words produce doubtful trust.

I beg you not to boast of a hymn that belongs to another;

[140] lest a naked bird laugh in the assembly of birds.

Never attempt to paint a neck without a tail;

for to make a beginning without its end is harmful.

Be mute toward reproach, deaf toward murmurs, blind

toward vanity, lame on the path of foolish craft.

[145] Let not your own voice, but another’s, sing your praises;

for it rightly soils festive men with dung.

Let pride of character be more hostile to you as a stepmother

than the Soladine people who kill Christians.

[Col. 0865B] Let the taste of love be more bitter to you than usual; [Note: M. Helmstedt: “willow.”]

[150] for I know that you almost truly [Note: Ms. H.: “truly.”] love foolishly.

What have you to do with a brothel? What with a prostitute’s fosterling?

Do you trust a woman in labour? You are foolish—and a father.

That bastard child will counsel nothing honourable.

He who is born of adultery will always be an adulterer.

[155] Love makes hermits rather un-hermits, and itself becomes one:

make Hippolytus love, and in mind he will be Priapus.

For these reasons love, fasting from every fidelity, must be fled,

love which circles itself too much and purses itself;

therefore proscribe it with swords and clubs,

[160] [Col. 0865C] and flee it by fleeing—the only flight that puts it to flight.

Let no delay, companion of sloth, hold you back;

for one desiring every good thing thinks all things slow.

For delay blackens a gift and diminishes its merit,

but a swift hand magnifies small gifts.

[165] Do not think that only great men are to be feared:

there is a faithful companion and a loving friend.

It is a greater honour to fear Pylades and a dear comrade

than the king of Syria and imperial commanders.

Flee envy and the bites of the unjust sister,

[170] which with swift tooth sings against an illustrious work.

Nor let the origin of the human lot escape you:

an earthen pot, a clod of mud, and miserable ash.

[Col. 0865D] Alas, our flesh is grief, more fleeting than a fleeting flower,

which in a brief space becomes both child and old man.

[175] As fragile a web as the weaver-spider weaves,

so fragile a covering clothes brief life.

However excellent people may be in their own ranks, honour uprightness:

let excellence please you more than goodness.

He who delights in simplicity mixes Scottish dishes, [Note: The Scots were accustomed to mix all dishes together in one pot.]

[180] and makes greater and lesser equal with equal honour.

Much money corrupts illustrious characters;

if it is your guest, it is your enemy.

[Col. 0866A] Cultivated in character, sincere in mind, restrained

in actions, an example in speech, weighty in firmness,

[185] hard toward evil men, moderate toward good men; patient, mature, abundant:

endure, love, give—by mind, strength, and hand.

Against windy rage and strokes of lightning,

the gentle reed is stronger than solid oak.

In all things measured severity prevails,

[190] without which the great work of virtues will perish.

For to give wicked men is nothing other than to foster wickedness;

therefore one’s hand ought to be available only to the good.

Though they be obscure, do not despise the limbs of the body,

in which talent accomplishes more through smallness.

[195] The bee, enriching a temple with lamps and the palate with sweetness,

is small and serves a double purpose by its fruit.

[Col. 0866B] The hawk is small, yet overwhelms a flock of birds;

and the little viper puts the lofty ox to flight.

Let mockery, stripping the teeth from its enemy, be your perpetual enemy,

[200] and let deceit be the same against snares.

Be discerning and wise, courteous and honourable,

provident, attentive, vigorous: be watchful.

Reading the writings of the ancients, follow stern Cato,

obedient Seneca, and peaceable Probus;

[205] the Dulichian, Arastus, Cicero, Nestor, Titus—

in heart, counsel, conduct, speech, and action.

Put on the robe of virtues, and put off a tyrannical mind; [Note: Ms. H.: *Trutannam*. The gloss adds: “a jester.”]

[Col. 0866C] seek the good and despise evil.

Neither Hippocrates, nor Podalirius himself with his herbs,

[210] nor Apollo can pour forth all his learning.

They recount all remedies with wordy tongues;

if I attempted them singly, time would pass.

And where our palaces have walls cut off,

thus it pleases me to approach the purpose of my mind.

[215] Therefore join the remedies here spoken to your diseases,

and whatever you see as needing improvement in yourself.

Be an enemy to lawsuits, an enemy to frauds, an enemy to crime;

and be an enemy to all things that corrupt.

Be a friend to law, a friend to honour, a friend to what is honourable,

[220] and a friend in action to things that make men just.

Draw these precepts gladly with an attentive ear, though sick;

[Col. 0866D] drink them mingled together, and you will be well.

Although these things are good, I leave many better things aside,

which are not suited to your shoulders.

[225] Let these suffice for you. We cannot all do everything.

Receive what you are able to possess, whether you wish it or not.

He enjoys silver to whom shining gold is lacking;

and he plucks violets who cannot pick a rose with his nail.

Then, setting out upon her way, she said: “Keep these things, Henry,”

[230] and she ended her words thus: “Farewell,

O my other self, foster-child and guest of uprightness;

though far away, receive your Henry in your mind.

[Col. 0867A] No distant road divides steadfast love,

and that which divides it lacks wholeness.

[235] Neither mountain, plain, nor a beautiful stretch of sea

separates those whom one love joins.

How can a place be far away, such that love should abandon love?

Such a place is said to be one opposed to it.

Therefore concord grants that love may live, and one

[240] will makes two persons one in mind.

And you, not without reason, to whom the name of a flower clings,

Florentine, recover your former condition in mind.

I spare you because I spare your faults, illustrious flower,

[Col. 0868A] unless you bring your deeds to life by your own powers (*viribus*, evidently corrupted in the text). [Note: Ms. Helmstedt: “you damn.”]

[245] Receive the lyre of a thousand strings which I send forth,

I, an unskilled Orpheus in an art of song unknown to me.

Illustrious Florentine bishop, for whom I live, if I live,

kindly take thought for my condition.

I have endured heavy, heavier, and heaviest things: suffering,

[250] if art wishes, may exist in a fourth degree.

Therefore farewell, bishop. I am yours. This spirit,

after death, believe me, will be yours.

Living and dead, I shall always love you. Yet the love

of one living would be better than that of one dying. [Note: The last four verses exceed the thousand-verse total by which the author shortly before indicated that his Elegy had been written.]

[Col. 0867] Here ends the book of Henry Florentinus.

In the Helmstedt manuscript the following hexameter verses are added:

[Col. 0867B] Some assign the efficient cause in this way:

A poetic philosopher and leader produced this work,

who takes his name from you and is called Sangelsinus;

and he is believed to have been given the name Henry.

Henry taught true philosophy,

and dictated these four books set down above,

in the likeness of a poor man who is mocked everywhere,

showing many men excessively impatient

when they lose possessions or tremble in a weak body,

who, in their dealings with Fortune, utter most shameful words,

[Col. 0868B] and, weeping, would rather that their parents had begotten them;

but afterwards converted, they ask everywhere to be taught

and led by philosophy into the straight path,

which in these books gives very excellent instructions to all,

which benefit all people, old and new alike.

Therefore these books are good for you to learn from.

The priest Hugh dictated the verses aforesaid,

who had written this book with his own hands.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1191: LABORANS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 0867]

## NOTICE

(OUDIN, *Script. eccles.*, II, 1580)

Laborans, presbyter-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, called Laborans as his proper name, was first cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico and afterwards presbyter-cardinal of the title of St Mary across the Tiber. An outstanding philosopher and theologian, he published, as Cardinal Baronius states, in the year of the Lord 1182 a most elaborately prepared Collection of Canons. There also survives his work *On Justice and the Just Man*, addressed to Maio, the great admiral of Sicily; a book *On True Liberty*, addressed to Hugh, Archbishop of Palermo; a letter to Hugh against the Sabellians newly reviving; and another to Vivian, cardinal of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill, concerning appeals, which is read not complete but mutilated. A parchment codex of the Basilica of St Peter in the City contains all these works of Laborans, as Baronius reports in volume XII of the *Annals*.

[Col. 0869]

## CRITICAL INVESTIGATION OF THE COMPILATION OF DECREES PREPARED BY MASTER LABORANS, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. From a manuscript codex in the library of the most holy Vatican Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles.

(Augustine THEINER, *Critical Investigations into the Principal Collections of Canons and Decretals*, Rome, Urban College, 1836, quarto, p. 399.)

## [CRITICAL INVESTIGATION OF THE COMPILATION OF DECREES]

[Col. 0869A] Ever since J. M. Suárez, bishop of Vaison, first stated that Laborans had compiled a Collection of Canons, [Note: “Concerning Master Laborans, Cardinal Florentinus, so called because of his outstanding labour.” [Note: On the name Laborans see below the fragments from his own book *On Justice and the Just Man*, from which it is established that this was a family name and was not, as Suárez falsely supposed, bestowed upon the author because of his great labour.] It appears among his dissertations *On the Chronology of the Works of St Augustine*, *On the Completed Work against Julian*, and *On the Saffron Garment of Cardinals in Conclave*. Rome, 1670, quarto.] the curiosity and diligence of all who take pleasure in the history of canon law have been directed toward it. Yet since that distinguished man seemed content merely to persuade his most celebrated patron, Francis Barberini, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, that the greatest honour could thereby be added to the Roman purple and an increase made to legal learning if Laborans’s work were printed as soon as possible, he must be said to have accomplished very little in this matter.

Later Anthony Zaccaria of the Society of Jesus, easily foremost among scholars of literary history in these latter times, directed his mind chiefly to diligently seizing and bringing forth from the hiding places of libraries into public light whatever he saw might contribute anything to defending the authority of the [Col. 0869B] Apostolic See or increasing its splendour. He most carefully gathered all the materials which his predecessor had left as unknown. [Note: *On the Unpublished Collection of Canons Composed by Cardinal Laborans in the Twelfth Century*. See Galland’s *Sylloge*, II, pp. 766–800.] Accordingly, he not only discussed most accurately the life of this celebrated cardinal—demonstrating that he was highly acceptable to Pope Alexander III himself and was employed before others in managing all the affairs both of Church and state [Col. 0870A]—but also undertook a most diligent examination of the same cardinal’s works, so that he might refute the errors which Fabricius had attempted to spread abroad against Laborans.

Yet in describing Laborans’s most excellent work, namely the Collection of Canons, Zaccaria imitated the Ballerini brothers and, beyond an external description of the Collection, produced nothing that disclosed the plan and inner nature of the work itself, or at the same time showed how it is connected with other collections of canons, and especially with Gratian’s [Col. 0870B] *Decretum*. We therefore considered it fair that, since an opportunity had presented itself for us to examine the codex containing Laborans’s compilation—the only one known thus far—we should discuss the compilation itself somewhat more fully in this Dissertation.

### § I. Division of the Work

Laborans originally distributed the whole work into five books, each of which he divided into parts. The individual parts in turn contain a greater or lesser [Col. 0869C] number of rubrics or titles, which are called *capitularia*. Each *capitulare* bears its own heading and, in the manner of rubrics, presents more or fewer chapters according to the nature of the matters treated in the individual rubrics. Both the parts of the books and the *capitularia* of the parts are distinguished by numbers; these numbers are absent from the chapters. Although the chapters have headings, no brief summaries or indexes of contents are prefixed to them, such as are found in all earlier collections of canons and also in Gratian’s *Decretum*.

[Col. 0870C] The first book consists of eleven parts. The first has 16 *capitularia*, the second 12, the third 6, the fourth 18, the fifth 14, the sixth 51, the seventh 29, the eighth 14, the ninth 14, the tenth 24, and the eleventh 6.

The second book is divided into four parts, of which the first contains 23, the second 28, the third 40, and the fourth 21 *capitularia*.

The third book contains only two parts, [Col. 0871A] one having 10 and the other 6 titles.

The fourth book, more complete and extensive than the others, consists of twelve parts and has 25, 40, 40, 31, 25, 15, 19, 21, 22, 15, 4, and 18 titles.

Finally, the fifth book is composed of four parts, with 10, 8, 12, and 10 titles. To these five books a sixth was added in the manner of an epilogue. It has five parts, of which the first bears 10 titles, the second 14, the third 35, the fourth 7, and the fifth 13.

Each book has a preface, now shorter and now longer, explaining its subject and connecting it with what is treated in the preceding book. [Note: [Col. 0871B]

We here append these prefaces, since Zaccaria omitted them.

“Book One treats the varieties of ecclesiastical promotion.

“Book One has taught who may ascend to ecclesiastical ranks and in what manner. Book Two will now briefly teach, conversely, which persons, as often happens, and for what reasons, may or ought to be degraded from such exalted positions. Therefore the pestilential Simoniacal heresy is first to be noted, because by diabolical suggestion it first crept in against God’s Church; and every sin known to be committed deliberately, being mortal, brings upon both its supporter and its perpetrator—and nevertheless also upon its supporter—the danger of necessary degradation. But a venial sin, because repeated practice of it contrary to prohibition renders it criminal, such as drunkenness and gambling, does indeed lawfully occasion deposition, but not necessarily, unless it has taken root so stubbornly that it cannot be extirpated. Since, however, it is expedient that both these and the other grounds of deposition henceforth be made more fully and clearly evident from authentic texts.

“Book Three of this extract of decrees or canons indicates and explains, partly by examples and partly by canons, those who have been degraded and how their restoration may be granted.

“This Fourth Book teaches, both by examples and by venerable institutions, what discipline may be imposed without degradation. For it happens more often that a cleric is not degraded and a layman is not deposed, but that both one and the other [Col. 0871D] are struck with anathema or excommunication, stripped of a benefice, diminished by fasting, punished by loss of property, humbled by exile, subjected to custody in bondage, or afflicted by service to the court; they are mortified by abstinence and corrected in other ways, whether by canons, laws, or ecclesiastical discretion. The cases in which these things are done will be shown in their several divisions; but first, the distinction between anathema and excommunication.

“Book Five will, as briefly as it can, demonstrate the number and qualifications of persons required by a case, and the other matters especially required in it; it will clarify in what cases and by whom clerics or laymen can be convicted by claim or testimony, and other matters distinguished by titles. It will also assert first that judicial order must be observed in every cause, and will thus undertake its purpose:

“Not every cause is the same, nor is every judicial order the same. Yet judicial order must be observed in every case, since it is not fitting that anything be judged unheard. For the threefold subject-matter of causes entails a threefold judicial order. The point at issue in a lawsuit—the subject-matter, that is, of the first kind of litigation—is the cause for which the person summoned, attacked, or accused, whether he is or becomes such, is called into court. It is sometimes notorious or simply known, and sometimes unknown. It is deemed unknown even though known to the judge but not to others, or to others but not to the judge, or to others and to the judge but not judicially. I say that it is not judicially [Col. 0872C] known to the judge if the accused is not contumaciously absent but is before the law, and has neither been convicted by law nor freely confessed nor become notoriously known—that is, manifest by public report. For contumacy makes an absent accused person present. Hence, concerning the unlawful matter, above, Book IV, Part III, Title VII—C. 24, q. 3, c. 6, *Decrevimus*; Part XII, Title IX—C. 10, q. 1, c. 10; and, when the accused is before the court or law, it is judicially—that is, lawfully—known to the judge, namely sufficiently manifest to the judge and court for judicial sentence. Hence *Presbyter aut diaconus*, below, Title III—C. 13, q. 5, c. 2. Thus in the case of subject-matters known—or rather unknown—nothing has yet been established that should be struck by the sword of judgment. Indeed, absolutely nothing should occur without judgment, nor without provision for the general peace. Hence *Nos*, below, Title III—C. 2, q. 1, c. 22; *Cum quisque*, above, Book III, Part I, Title VIII—C. 23, q. 4, c. 19.

“But a subject-matter is called known when, under lawful examination, the person attacked has either been convicted in law or freely confessed; or when it has been made public by common certainty. This third kind is called notorious, as though known in fact and simply.

“These three subject-matters of causes—the first of which may be called established by proof, the second confessed, the third known of itself—differ from one another in nature, and so have differing judicial procedures in their execution. In proving the matter alleged, there must be five, or four, persons before the hearing of the court, distinct from one another and present to one another. These persons are: an elected judge; a qualified accuser or claimant; a lawful witness together with a lawful witness; the accused, defendant, or, more properly, the person proceeded against; and a suitable defender, if the person proceeded against wishes one—unless the case is criminal, capital, or concerns status. There no representative acts, nor does anyone defend. Hence, *Nullus*,” etc., C. 4, q. 4, c. 1, etc.]

At the end of the fifth book a brief note is added, again indicating the subject of the individual books [Col. 0871B] and explaining the nature of the sixth. Laborans explains the matter thus:

The sixth book is in part an epilogue of the preceding five books: it recalls the material of each to the capacity of understanding and, as an aid to [Col. 0872A] memory, presents it in brief compendium.

Therefore the subject of the first book will be promotion into the clergy and to clerical offices, and the modes of promotion.

That of the second: the deposition of those promoted and the causes of deposition.

That of the third: the restoration of those deposed and the modes of restoration.

That of the fourth: correction, without deposition, according to the variety of offences.

That of the fifth: the plurality, not to be descended from, of persons or other circumstances pertaining to a case.

The parts of the books make, as it were, different genera of things, or different species of a genus, or are caused by the weariness produced by copious multiplicity. Thus the first four parts of the first book differ as though by four genera, while the following seven are of one genus with the fourth, because [Col. 0872B] they concern the subject of promotion. The parts of the fifth and sixth books make, as it were, several species of one genus. But the divisions of the second, third, and fourth books were prompted by the weariness of multitude and extended plurality. Again, the first three parts of the first book, though they do not furnish the subject-matter, are nevertheless necessary for what furnishes it and for all that follows.

Moreover, the sixth book is an addition to the preceding books of certain matters, without knowledge of which ministers of the canons are sometimes thought rustic, contemptible, and ignorant.

### § II. On the Sources Used by Laborans and the Manner in Which He Arranged Them

[Col. 0873]

[Col. 0873A] In compiling a work of decrees of this kind, Laborans used no other collection of canons than Gratian’s *Decretum*. It must indeed seem remarkable that Laborans should have attempted to alter completely anew, and arrange in an entirely new order, the material of Gratian’s work—received with the highest applause as soon as it was published, used not only in the academies but also in the forum and the courts, and associated with the collections of Roman law. [Col. 0873B] Still more surprising is that he began to elaborate his own work scarcely thirty years after Gratian had completed the *Decretum*. Gratian compiled the *Decretum* in the time of Eugenius III (1145–1153); Laborans, however, as he himself indicates near the end of his work, brought his work to completion in 1182, after spending twenty years in its painstaking composition.

Yet, if we examine more carefully the character and nature of Gratian’s *Decretum* itself, we shall readily understand why he adopted this plan. We shall therefore first explain above all the order which Gratian followed, [Col. 0873C] and then endeavor to compare it with the order in which Laborans composed his work.

As everyone knows, Gratian divided his Collection into three parts. The first contains one hundred and one titles, which Paucapalea, the first to write glosses upon them, called “distinctions.” This first part concerns the law of persons and is arranged as follows.

1. It treats of laws in general—natural and positive, divine and human—of Roman law, custom, canon law, and the connection of the latter with civil law. Distinctions 1–14.

2. Of the origin and sources of canon law; the canons of councils and decretal letters of Roman pontiffs; [Col. 0873D] of councils themselves—when and by whom they are to be held—and of their authority; and of the holy Fathers and their authority. Distinctions 15–20.

3. Finally, the greater number of the distinctions in this part (from Distinction 21 through 79) concern ecclesiastical persons, their qualifications, rights, office, and consecration. This subject is further distributed as follows: D. 22, on the dignity and authority of the Roman Church and of the other principal Churches, especially those of the East. D. 23, on the ordination of ecclesiastical persons, from pope down to doorkeeper. D. 24, on the examination of candidates for ordination. D. 25, on the character and duties of ministers, beginning with the doorkeeper and proceeding to the bishop.

D. 26, on the character of the bishop: that he be the husband of one wife. [Col. 0874A] D. 27–32, on the chastity and continence of clerics in general. D. 33, on the qualifications of clerics, or irregularities: that bigamists, persons physically impaired, usurers, public penitents, gamblers, stage performers, madmen, demoniacs, those who take prostitutes as wives, and those who keep concubines are not to be admitted to sacred orders. D. 34, on the conduct of a bishop: that he avoid excessive intimacy with members [Col. 0874B] of his household, even relatives by blood, and not be distracted by hunting. Distinctions 35–38, on sobriety and the learning of clerics, lest they read pagan books.

D. 39–49, on the prudence bishops require in secular affairs, lest through their incompetence the Church suffer harm; on bishops’ inward adornment, namely that they be grave in gait and dress, temperate, hospitable, chaste, learned, not addicted to wine, not violent, not quarrelsome, not covetous, not neophytes, not criminal or vicious. D. 50, on the fall and restoration of clerics. D. 51–59 contain certain other matters already treated in part above in D. 33: for example, the qualifications and character of candidates for ordination; [Col. 0874C] that no one be promoted by a leap; that court officials, advocates, and judges not be ordained; that slaves manumitted by persons other than their masters not be ordained; nor persons physically impaired, bigamists, illiterate persons, public penitents, sons of priests, persons born of fornication or adultery, or persons baptized during illness; that monks not be ordained without their abbot’s permission; and that educated laymen not be suddenly ordained. D. 60–74 concern the status of persons who may be promoted: specifically, the manner of electing bishops, archbishops, and priests; those entitled to elect and consecrate; the non-repetition of orders; tonsure; and letters of credentials and dimissory letters. D. 75–80 concern the time and day for consecrating bishops, and likewise the times for ordaining other clerics; the Ember fasts [Col. 0874D] and their origin and rationale; intervals between ordinations; the age of persons to be ordained priests; and the ordination of the supreme pontiff by the cardinals alone.

Distinctions 81–89 are almost an epilogue to what preceded and discuss the requisite qualifications of persons admitted to the priesthood. Gratian here again treats of the need for a bishop-elect to be without crime; that clerics should not cohabit with women; that prelates be free from sin and not consent to the sins of others; of prelates’ vigilance over Church property and in defending the poor, miserable, and oppressed; of hospitality, especially necessary for bishops; of bishops’ care for widows and orphans; that they should not become merchants through covetousness; [Col. 0875A] and that bishops should administer their own household and their Church well. D. 90 concerns correcting litigious persons and not ordaining them. D. 91 and 92 concern church chant. D. 93, the obedience of subjects to their superiors. D. 94, the legate of the Roman pontiff and his authority. D. 95, that priests subject to bishops may celebrate the sacred mysteries in their presence.

Distinctions 96, 97, and 98 have no connection whatever with what precedes. For Distinctions 96 and 97 concern the position of laypersons in the Church: namely, that laypersons—indeed even emperors themselves—cannot ordain anyone or judge concerning ecclesiastical matters; but that laypersons, emperors, and other secular princes may assist churches by their prayers.

[Col. 0875B] Distinction 98, without any apparent rationale, concerns foreign and overseas clerics: that they are not to be received without the testimony of five bishops. This ought already to have been addressed above in Distinction 73, where letters of credentials and dimissory letters were under discussion. Finally, the last three distinctions, 99, 100, and 101, concern primates and their authority, and the proposition that no one is to be called “universal”; the pallium and its use; and the rule that one province is not to be divided into two.

Now, if anyone carefully examines the order observed by Gratian in arranging the subject matter of the first part, as we have set it out here, he will readily acknowledge that not everything coheres with everything else; indeed, that all has been stitched together without selection or design. The same appears repeatedly if [Col. 0875C] one considers the rationale and arrangement of the individual distinctions. For they often scarcely touch upon the subject they ought to discuss, and almost nowhere expound it fully. Even when Gratian sometimes seems to examine a matter more carefully and, citing all the decretals of pontiffs and passages from the holy Fathers that might serve to explain it, to establish the matter itself, he often seizes any occasion to depart from his subject and introduce other, wholly extraneous matters. A few examples will suffice. In Distinction 6, where he discusses the dignity of natural law, he also treats nocturnal emissions and whether they are imputed as sin. In Distinction 25, which concerns the conduct of those to be ordained, [Col. 0875D] after explaining in canon 3 that a bishop must be free from every stain, even venial, he treats purgatorial fire in canon 4. In Distinction 26, where he discusses the rule that bigamists are not to be ordained bishops, he asks whether the stain of bigamy is removed through baptism. While treating priestly continence in Distinctions 29, 30, 31, and 32, he raises a question concerning certain distinctions in positive law, maintaining that positive law must be considered in relation to causes, place, time, and person; and there he heaps together much concerning Manichaean superstitions.

[Col. 0876A] What he includes in Distinctions 34–49 ought rather to have been referred to Distinctions 25 and 26, where he confuses a very broad subject by an incredible mixture of alien matters. Nor is his arrangement any more correct in Distinctions 51–61, where he discusses various classes of persons who cannot be promoted to the priesthood: after briefly treating the sons of priests, he turns aside to another question, considering whether fathers’ vices harm their sons. Into what he sets forth in Distinctions 64 and 65 concerning the consecration of candidates for ordination, he mixes very many matters concerning the prerogatives of sees; and in Distinctions 79 and 81 he returns once more to the ordination of bishops, supplementing what he had elsewhere said: “Let it suffice that we have spoken of those to be ordained, of ordainers, and of the distinctions among the individual grades and their duties. [Col. 0876B] But because we have lingered somewhat over these matters, let us, by way of epilogue, bring to mind certain points connected with the preceding material. A candidate for ordination as bishop, as the Apostle writes, must be without crime,” etc.

No one can fail to see how poorly connected among themselves, and how ill arranged, are the matters he includes in Distinctions 91 through 101; we therefore believe that more than enough has been said regarding them.

No less than in the arrangement of subjects, such a lack of order and plan is found in the passages Gratian inserts into individual distinctions to connect their various chapters, as well as in the brief summaries prefixed to the chapters. These portions of Gratian and his *dicta*, as they are commonly called, are scarcely ever examined by those [Col. 0876C] who wrote glosses on the *Decretum*, since they are composed with little aptness or judgment. Johannes Andreae, called the trumpet and father of canon law, criticizes them everywhere and demonstrates that they are superfluous.

> [Note: [Col. 0875D] “It is no objection if you say that the Book of Decrees (*Decretum*) was approved by the pope, for that itself is not established. And even granted that it were established, the approval concerned [Col. 0876D] the compilation, not Gratian’s *dicta*, which we reject every day.” Commentary on chapter 2, *De rescriptis* (I, 3).]

It is certain that our Laborans understood well how much in Gratian’s work was open to criticism, and that chiefly for this reason he wished to arrange its entire subject matter in a new and better order. He must be said to have succeeded not only in the arrangement of subjects, but also in selecting both conciliar testimonies and those of the Fathers.

It will be worthwhile to set forth his method here briefly.

Laborans incorporated the whole subject matter of Gratian’s first part into the first book of his Collection, to which, in place of a preface, he added a preliminary discourse. In it he discusses generally the origin and development of law, and expounds certain more general principles. He treats alike of public law and ecclesiastical law, recognizing especially the canons of councils and pontifical decretals as, so to speak, the sources of ecclesiastical law. He then concludes with certain brief observations, explaining and setting forth, in the manner then customary in the schools, the end of all laws—which, he says, is no other than to make human beings better and more perfect—[Col. 0877A] as well as several other matters concerning the nature of laws. “Hence,” he says, “the end is to lead the human race back to its fatherland through the dispensation of duty. The author is divine prompting; the order is pontifical; the ministers are pontiffs and priests.”

After these preliminaries he undertakes the work itself. In the first part of Book I he discusses natural law and custom, their several kinds, and their connection. At the outset he explains the nature of law and says something of its force, authority, and use.

In the second part he treats of the origin of ecumenical councils, their number, the canon of sacred [Col. 0877B] Scripture, the authority to convene councils, when and by whom they ought to be celebrated, eulogiae to be brought to councils, bishops’ concern for councils and their statutes, decretal letters and apostolic enactments and their authority, and finally the authority of doctors.

The third part concerns the ministers of the canons; the origin of the priestly order of the New Testament; the primacy of the Roman Church; the rank and origin of patriarchal sees; and the subjection of the see of Constantinople and of the others.

In the fourth part and the following fifth, sixth, and seventh, he takes up the ordination of clerics. Beginning with the minor orders, he reviews every one [Col. 0877C] of them up to the priesthood. Since not a few were first laymen, then enrolled in the lower orders, and finally promoted to the priesthood, he discusses in the fourth part lay persons who may be admitted to the priesthood, and in the fifth those who desire to ascend from lower to higher orders.

He prefixes to each part a kind of introduction, in which he briefly declares what he will set forth. Thus he begins the fourth part:

> “Since a minister of the canons cannot be one who has not been enrolled among the clergy, and since a person designated as a cleric is not chosen from every class of laypersons, nor in any manner whatever, it must be seen whence and how he is to be chosen. For there are many classes of laypersons: free persons, [Col. 0877D] slaves, freedmen, curiales, and others.”

He begins the fifth part likewise:

> [Col. 0878A] “Having seen, with the rule of examination preserved, who may always, never, or only with difficulty clearly attain the clerical line, it must be seen, with the same rule remaining in force, who may always, never, or only with difficulty knowingly be assigned to the grades of sacred ministers. For there are several classes of such persons also: sons of priests, persons under obligation, and others.”

He then proceeds to bishops and begins his discussion in these words:

> “To the summit of episcopal excellence persons may not freely ascend from just any classes of humankind, nor from any except those whom the most provident rule of the canons indicates; persons held by crime, bigamists, and all whom we have determined are not to be admitted to the priesthood [Col. 0878B] or below may not aspire to the offices of this watchtower. Whatever removes acquired grades likewise prevents every grade from being acquired. Such persons will be discussed in the second book. But here, so that one may with some brevity more certainly rejoice to retain in memory, for the discernment and common benefit of ecclesiastical grades—especially the pontifical grade—what sort of person a bishop, priest, deacon, and every person to be set over as ruler of a Church ought and ought not to be, both the Apostle’s description and the enactments of the other Fathers will make this known.”

What he has concerning bishops he includes in Books VI and VII. In much the same manner as he had done above when discussing clerics, he enumerates the several qualities [Col. 0878C] with which a bishop ought to be endowed, and explains the whole matter with the utmost order and clarity; so that it ought far to be preferred to what Gratian had advanced on the same subject. For the matters Gratian had discussed confusedly Laborans gathered from every side, joined together as it were into one whole, and arranged with the greatest clarity. Thus he drew his chapters not only from the distinctions, that is, from the first part of the *Decretum*, but also from the second part, which, as is known, is divided into *causae* and very often treats matters which ought entirely to have been dealt with in the first part.

> [Note: [Col. 0877D] It is useful here to bring the entire sixth part of the first book into concordance with Gratian’s chapters, so that it may appear more clearly how Laborans used Gratian’s *Decretum*.
>
