The eighth part includes matters concerning the Roman pontiff. Thus he discusses his authority over patriarchs and the clergy at large. [Col. 0878D] There he also explains matters concerning the obedience [Col. 0879A] owed by subjects to prelates, the apostolic legation and its authority; and, after saying a little concerning the pallium, its origin, and use, he finally treats the authority of the Apostolic See and its authentic rescripts.

Following the natural order of things, in the ninth part he speaks of the promotion of clerics and the examination of candidates for promotion, adding what had to be said concerning intervals and terms between ordinations and the Ember fast.

He follows the same order in the tenth part, where he sets forth what concerns the election and deposition of clerics in the several orders. Beginning with the supreme pontiff, he proceeds down to clerics of the lower orders, adding monks also to them.

Finally, in the last part of this book, he explains what role laypeople have, or may have, in the election of clergy. He adds the constitutions of Emperors Louis, Henry, and Otto concerning the election of Roman pontiffs.

> [Note: [Col. 0879D] From Distinction LXIII, chapters 28, 29, 30, 31, and 32. Note that Laborans received two chapters—31 [Col. 0880D] and 32—which commonly occur under the designation *Paleae*.]

To these Laborans appended the following observation:

> “From these constitutions and the pact of Emperor Louis, therefore, it is inferred that the emperors renounced the privileges which, as we have set forth, Pope Hadrian granted to Emperor Charles and Pope Leo to King Otto concerning the election of the supreme pontiff. Hence it is clear that the election of the Roman pontiff belongs solely to the clerical order, and that the person elected is to be ordained without consulting the kings of the Romans. The same seems to be observed in the case of bishops: namely, that in their election [Col. 0879C] or ordination no layperson has any preeminence over clerics. Nevertheless, the founders of churches have free authority to elect their rulers.”

If, therefore, we compare Gratian’s order with that followed by Laborans, it will immediately be evident that the latter arranged everything more suitably and avoided that great and wearisome inconvenience into which Gratian too often fell, when he repeated precisely the same matters once and again in different parts of his Collection.

But in order that it may be clear that Laborans reshaped not only the first part of the *Decretum* into a better form, but also the other parts that follow it, it is worthwhile briefly to indicate here how Gratian distributed the second part of his work.

It is readily apparent to everyone that Gratian showed much greater prudence in composing this second [Col. 0879D] part of his work than in the first. For, by an excellent plan, he distributed the whole subject matter, comprising the diverse rights and duties both of clerics and laypeople, so that it was all completed in thirty-six *causae*. He proposed these in judicial form and divided them into various questions; all the questions were resolved by ecclesiastical decisions of pontiffs, councils, and holy Fathers. Yet, following the method of judicial proceedings and proposing arguments here and there for both sides, he often treats the matter itself so inartfully that questions sometimes [Col. 0880A] remain undecided or are expounded with such confusion that his definite opinion does not at all appear.

In the first *causa*, treating simony and simoniacal ordinations, he begins the second part of his work, attaching it to the first, in these words:

> “Thus far we have treated the election and ordination of clerics. Let us now proceed to simoniacal ordinations. And, so that it may readily become clear what the authority of the holy Fathers has decreed concerning this heresy, let a case be brought forward whose issue includes both persons knowingly consecrated by simoniacs and ordinations carried out through money.”

But here too Gratian again turns aside from the subject he had entered upon. Although he proposed to discuss simoniacal ordinations, he disputes at length concerning matters by no means relevant: namely, [Col. 0880B] the baptism of heretics, the nature of baptism, those ordained by false bishops, those who communicate with heretics, the remission of sins, whether the crimes of fathers harm their sons, the support of poor persons with provisions, and similar matters.

Since simoniacs are not infrequently deprived of benefices, indeed must even be deposed, Gratian proceeds in the second *causa* to the Church’s judicial procedure, introducing what he will say concerning courts, witnesses, accusations, and similar matters as follows:

> “Having briefly set these matters forth, let us come to those wrongs which the Church, armed with the severity of discipline, is prepared to punish, showing by what accusers or witnesses each person is to be convicted; by what judge each ought to be condemned or acquitted; by what remedy a case may be relieved if it has been vitiated; and whether, if the accusers fail, the accused must be compelled to purgation. And, that this may more readily appear, let an example be placed before our eyes, in which the authorities debating on either side may be distinguished and the judgment of the authority of the holy Fathers clearly indicated.”

In the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth *causae*, he continues the same subject and treats it more fully, though he nevertheless mixes in matters wholly extraneous, such as councils and their celebration.

In the seventh *causa* he entirely departs from what preceded, and discusses coadjutors for bishops and sick clerics, and whether, while a bishop is alive, another may be ordained in the same church.

[Col. 0880D] In the eighth *causa* he suddenly returns to simoniacal ordinations and raises the question whether it is lawful for a bishop to choose his own successor. The ninth *causa* concerns the ordinations of clerics, a subject he had discussed extensively in the first part.

In the tenth *causa* he takes up an entirely different subject: the administration of ecclesiastical affairs and how it is to be performed by bishops—a question likewise examined in the first part. But in *causa* XI he again returns to judicial matters and discusses the competent forum for clerics. Yet he does not remain sufficiently on that subject, for in *causa* XII he at once returns anew to [Col. 0881A] ecclesiastical goods, discussing clerics’ private property and wills. In *causa* XIII Gratian included certain ecclesiastical rights concerning tithes and burials, as well as prescription relating to those rights. In *causa* XIV many things are mixed which have no coherence: namely, that clerics ought not to litigate, even if summoned to court, over perishable goods, nor give testimony in matters of the Church; then, in the same place, he treats usury more fully. *Causa* XV coheres neither with the preceding nor the subsequent *causae*, and treats: 1) the rule that gifts are not to be received from clerics in return for advocacy rendered; 2) whether priests may be condemned on a woman’s confession; 3) whether bishops and ministers of the Church may hear causes on the Lord’s Day; 4) whether purgation ought to be imposed upon a person denying a crime; 5) [Col. 0881B] whether confession in judicial proceedings should be extorted through torture; 6) whether a bishop, on his own motion and without synodal examination, can condemn and depose priests; and 7) whether clerics confessing or convicted of crimes committed before ordination can perform the office of the order they received. He also discusses sons of priests. Such questions, although of the greatest importance, he does not treat sufficiently fully; and because they concern judicial proceedings, they would more conveniently have been discussed by Gratian above. Departing from this sequence of matters, in *causa* XVI he passes from clerics to monks, and in this and the following *causae* XVII, XVIII, XIX, and XX discusses monasteries and matters pertaining to monasteries. Yet he presents much confusedly, scarcely touches other matters of no less [Col. 0881C] importance, and inserts many alien and useless discussions of prescription and alienation of ecclesiastical goods, the right of patronage, benefices, and lay investiture. After asking in the final question of *causa* XX whether one may pass from one monastery to another, he again turns to the clergy. In *causa* XXI he proposes substantially the same question, but divided into two so far as clerics are concerned: namely, 1) whether a cleric may be enrolled in two churches; and 2) whether clerics may pass from their own church to another. Thus, beginning a discussion of clerics, he repeats much here that he had already treated fully in the first part: namely, clerics’ conduct, clothing, commercial dealings, and judicial proceedings.

[Col. 0881D] In *causa* XXII he disputes concerning oaths and perjury, where, without any apparent reason, he speaks of the habitual obedience clerics must not withhold from bishops. In *causa* XXIII he speaks of war, injury, and vengeance; proceeding further, he asks: 1) whether judges or officials who kill the accused sin; 2) whether evil persons are to be compelled toward good; 3) whether heretics ought to be deprived of their own goods and those of their church; and, finally, 4) whether clerics may bear arms. In the following *causa*, XXIV, he treats excommunication and interdict, and whether excommunication by a heretic is valid. Here he also discusses the origin and cause of heresies and schisms, and the principal sects of heretics, citing the celebrated passage from Isidore’s *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 5. *Causa* XXV deals wholly with privileges granted by the authority of Roman pontiffs especially [Col. 0882A] and, by a sudden leap, in *causa* XXVI he turns to matters concerning divination and diviners. Yet he mixes in many extraneous matters; and finally, in questions six and seven, asks: 1) whether a person excommunicated by a bishop may be reconciled by a priest without consulting that bishop; and 2) whether penance is to be imposed upon the dying. Having disposed of these, in *causae* XXVII, XXVIII, XXIX, XXX, XXXI, XXXII, and XXXIII he treats marriage and matters pertaining to marriage more fully and more correctly than any other subject, without turning to irrelevant matters, as we have observed him doing above.

Since many sins are committed in marriage and on account of marriage, the treatise *On Penance*, whether by Gratian himself or perhaps by another, is inserted among these *causae*, namely after the second question of *causa* XXXIII, where he had discussed at length penance to be imposed on married persons. There can surely be no doubt that Gratian was the author of this treatise; yet it appears altogether improbable that he inserted it here in an inappropriate place in his work. For he immediately continues *causa* XXXIII and, in the two remaining questions, examines: 1) whether intercourse between spouses is forbidden in time of prayer; and 2) whether a husband, without his wife’s consent, and conversely a wife without her husband’s consent, may vow continence. How far these matters differ from those contained in the treatise on penance no one can fail to see. Then *causa* XXXIV continues the subject of adultery, and the following *causa*, XXXV, passes [Col. 0882C] to consanguinity and affinity. Finally, in the last, or thirty-sixth, *causa*, he recalls certain omitted matters and treats: 1) the abduction of virgins by violence; and 2) whether an abductor may marry the woman abducted.

The third part of the *Decretum* follows the second, entitled *On Consecration*. Were it not for the unanimous testimony of the ancients, all of whom mention only this treatise *On Consecration* as the third part of the *Decretum*, nothing would be more likely than that Gratian prefixed another treatise, *On Penance*, to this treatise and separated them both from the second part. For each is arranged by the same method and composed in such a way that it seems not at all to have belonged to the second part. [Col. 0882D] But if we carefully consider the subject matter expounded in each and weigh the connection each has with Gratian’s *Decretum* as a whole, we are confident that it can readily be proved that the one entitled *On Consecration* is an epilogue to the first part, and the other, treating penance, an epilogue to the second part. But these matters too will become repeatedly clear if we first explain Laborans’s work more carefully.

In arranging the subject matter of the second and third parts of Gratian’s work, Laborans achieved even more than in the first book of his Collection. He distributed the entire matter, badly digested and heaped together by Gratian, so well and joined its several parts so aptly that everywhere it is evident [Col. 0883A] that he had laid down definite rules for his compilation and treated each subject in the places where it could most fittingly be brought into the method he followed in arranging the whole work.

Thus, in the second book of his work, he deals solely with the degradation of clerics. In its four parts, which contain titles 23, 28, 40, and 41, he enumerates all crimes for which clerics must be deposed. He arranged and ordered the entire subject so that he considers in sequence each matter pertaining to the clergy: doctrine, duties, the obedience clerics owe to their superiors, and finally their manner of life. With the greatest diligence and labor he sought out the chapters from the entire second part of the *Decretum*, [Col. 0883B] restoring to order and unity what he had found scattered here and there and confusedly heaped together.

In the following third book he discusses the restoration of the deposed, dividing this treatment in two: 1) restoration of persons deposed for manifest crimes; and 2) restoration for hidden crimes, the judgment of which can be reserved to God alone.

He also treats here of the mercy with which punishments ought to be imposed, and thus makes a transition to the fourth book, where he discusses ecclesiastical penalties and their use. He begins with excommunication, which he considers in the first three parts of the book. In the fourth part he then passes to sacrilege. He prefaces two passages borrowed from Gratian—one from Haimo, C. 20, q. 2, [Col. 0883C] c. 39, and the other from the Fourth Council of Toledo, C. 17, q. 4, c. 31—which concern sacrilege; to these [Col. 0884A] he adds the observation presented here, thereby making a transition to what follows:

> “Just as a collegium seems to be a diversity of persons gathered into one, so sacrilege is a plurality of sacred things hastily gathered into one; but in ordinary human speech it denotes the wickedness of such taking. More broadly, it is the injurious touching of a sacred thing, or of something assigned to it. Accordingly Arius was a sacrilegious person because, to Christ’s injury, he laid hold of Christ’s death. Likewise, anyone is sacrilegious who, in contempt of the Church, assaults a church building or any person assigned to the Church; and likewise one who wrongs clerics, monks, persons devoted to God, or pilgrims. And since sacrilege may be committed against persons, things, places, or times, the variety of such objects also produces a variety [Col. 0884B] of penalties for sacrilege.”

In expounding matters pertaining to sacrilege, he employs three parts, namely the fourth, fifth, and sixth. In the seventh he treats perjury and oaths. At the end of this part he adds certain small formularies and forms of swearing, several of which we append here because they are lacking in Gratian. Among these, however, the one especially to be noted is that prescribed during the schism of Octavian, which arose from the election of Alexander III.

> [Note: [Col. 0883C]
>
> “Oath against vexatious litigation, or oath of the plaintiff.
>
> “I, N., do not bring suit against N. with the intention of harassing him, but because I believe that I have a good cause. And throughout the entire suit, if at any point I seek proofs, I shall do this not on account of partiality, but in order to investigate the truth. So help me God, etc.
>
> “The defendant, however, swears thus against vexatious litigation:
>
> “I, N., believing that I am pursuing a good claim, have come to resist, not with the intention of harassment. And throughout the entire suit, etc., as above.
>
> “The following must also be added to the oath against vexatious litigation: each principal party shall swear—or those to whom the matter has passed in the midst of proceedings—that he has given absolutely nothing to the judges, or to any person, on account of this cause; that they have promised nothing, and will give nothing afterward, either themselves or through any intermediary person whatsoever. [Col. 0883D] Excepted are payments to their own advocates for legal representation, or to other persons to whom Roman laws have ordained that payments be made.”]

“I N. renounce and anathematize every heresy which exalts itself against the holy Roman and Catholic Church, and especially the schism and heresy of Octavian, Guy of Cremona, and John of Struma. I likewise declare their ordinations void; and from this hour forward I shall be faithful and obedient to blessed Peter, to the holy Roman Church, and to my lord Pope Alexander and his canonically succeeding successors; and I shall observe without fraud whatever command he gives me concerning this offence. So help me God and these holy Gospels of God.

“Oath upon the soul of an absent person.

“I N. received a mandate from N., which he has not subsequently revoked, namely that I should swear upon his soul that this statement or act was, is, or will be so. So help me God and these holy Gospels.—And [Col. 0884C] I N. swear upon the soul of N. himself that this was, is, or will be so. May God and these holy Gospels so help him.—A person who is to swear upon the soul of one present says to him: ‘Do you will and command that I swear upon your soul that this statement or act was, is, or will be so?’ And he replies: ‘I will and command it.’ Then the swearer says: ‘This statement or act was, is, or will be so, in truth. May God and these holy Gospels so help this man.’”—Book IV, part VII, title XVIII, fol. 151.

[lacuna]

In the eighth part he discusses the manner of excommunication and the manner of reconciling the excommunicated. At its conclusion he treats of heretics and, after adducing the well-known passage of Isidore, appends very weighty observations [Col. 0884C] [Note:

Laborans thus continues the treatise of St Isidore:

“Besides those sects of heretics which Isidore has identified, Augustine, in the book which he wrote to the deacon Quodvultdeus concerning almost all the heresies known to him, records others according to Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, or Philastrius, bishop of Brescia. Therefore, conveniently enough and [Col. 0884D] briefly, we set down here only their names, not their errors, lest an extended presentation of them perhaps produce weariness. They are: Saturnians, Sampseans, Elcesaeans or Elcesaeites, Sevandians, Ptolemaeans, Marcianists, Colorbasians, Heracleonites, Sinerians, Pepudians, named from a place, or Quintillians, from a certain Quintilla; Theodotians, Bardesanites, Valesians, Origenians—after Origen, not that expositor known to almost everyone; these are of indescribable practice—Melitians, Vadians, Semi-Arians, Massilians or Euchites or Euphemites or Martyrians or Sathanianists, Seleucians or Hermians, Proclinianists, Ascites, Passalorhynchites, who are also Dactylorhynchites, Rhetorians, Paternianists—of whom Isidore also speaks—or Maternianists or Venustianists, Abeliovites, or Abelian Abeloites. Others believed that, when Christ descended into hell, the unbelievers believed and all were thereby set free.

“These heresies, set out rather fully by Isidore in the aforementioned book, Father Augustine treats there at still greater length [Col. 0885B].

“And it should be noted that the Semi-Arians are, as it were, not complete Arians, since they proclaim that the Son is not of the same essence as the Father but like Him. These appear above to be called Tritheists, because, understanding three divinities just as they understand three persons, they consequently assert three gods. The Macedonians too—but by some they are rather called Semi-Arians—are so called because in part they agree with us, saying that the Father and Son are of one and the same nature and substance, or, more expressly, essence, which in Greek is called *ousia*; in part they agree with the Arians, saying that the Holy Spirit is merely a creature, although according to others He is the divinity of the Father and Son and has no substance of His own.

[Col. 0885C] “Moreover, it should be noted that those called Gnostics in Isidore are also Borborites in Augustine, as it were Cenosi; those who are Cherentians are Marinthians; those who are Apostolics are Apotactites; those who are Cathari are Novatians; those who are Pauliani are also Photinians and Archemonians, but in Innocent they are Paullianists; those who are Photinians are also Marcellians; those who are Marcellians are also Patripassians, Praxeans, Hermogenians, and Noetians; those who are Macedonians are also Pneumatomachians or Semi-Arians; those who are Donatists are also Donatians, Montenses, and Parmenianists; those who are Helvidians are also Antidicomarianites; and those who are Pelagians are also Coelestians, after Coelestius, Pelagius’s disciple.”—Book IV, part VIII, title XV, fol. 165.]

In the ninth, tenth, and eleventh parts he treats of marriage [Col. 0885A] and matters pertaining to marriage: adultery, divorce, consanguinity, and affinity. Yet he touches this subject only, so to speak, with the very tips of his lips; and he separates matters which Gratian had collected together in this section of his work, inserting them into earlier books of the compilation wherever occasion presented itself. Accordingly, he sets forth here only what he had not yet addressed elsewhere, so that these parts should be called merely a supplement to the matters already presented above.

Finally, in the twelfth part, the last of the whole book and the shortest of all, he embraces matters concerning the forensic immunity of clerics, the purgation of the accused, unjust judgments, and similar things; these prepare the way for the fifth [Col. 0885B] book of the work, which is wholly concerned with explaining the judgments of the Church.

[Col. 0886A] This book is divided into four parts. In the first, he discusses judicial procedure, the power of rendering judgments, and accusers in general; in the second, witnesses and advocates; in the third, judges and their authority; and finally, in the fourth, appeals [Note:

It seemed worthwhile to present here certain formulas then in use in the ecclesiastical court, which Laborans inserted into this and the first part of Book V. We have done so all the more readily because they contain at the same time matters of purely historical interest.

[Col. 0885D] “Form of an appeal after judgment.

“I, Adelmus, minister—though unworthy—of the holy Church of St Regina, appeal to the Roman See and seek the Apostles against the judgment unjustly pronounced against me by Lord Gualter, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, on the day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1105 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on Wednesday.

“Before judgment one should appeal thus: ‘I, A., unworthy minister of the holy Church of St Regina, perceiving that I am oppressed by Lord Gualter, archbishop of the holy Church of Ravenna, appeal to the Roman See and seek the Apostles.’—But before suit is commenced, thus: ‘I, Philip, by God’s mercy canon of the holy Church of Pisa, fearing, in this case which perhaps seems likely to be litigated before the said president between myself and Lord Villanus, archbishop of the same holy Church of Pisa, a judgment of the Pisan chapter prejudicial to me—or Pisan judges prejudicial to me, or Almachius as a judge prejudicial to me—appeal to the Roman See before the beginning of the suit and request letters dimissory.’

[Col. 0886B] “One or two persons shall appeal on behalf of many thus: ‘I, Peter,’ or ‘We, Peter and Anthony, syndics of the canons of the holy Church of Pisa, appeal to the Roman See and seek the Apostles against the judgment,’ etc. Or: ‘Perceiving that we are oppressed,’ etc., ‘we appeal to the Roman See and request the Apostles.’

“Appeals of this kind must be made in writing. On the first day, however, it is enough to appeal orally; on the second and thereafter, appeal must be made only in writing.”—Book V, part V, title V, fol. 226.

“Formula of accusation.

“According to the laws, an accusation should be written so as to state the month in which the crime was committed, the place, and the consul—or rather, in place of the consul, the emperor—the name of the accuser and accused person, the name of the person before whom the accusation is brought, and the day of accusation. No one is compelled to state the day or hour at which the crime was committed. In ecclesiastical [Col. 0886C] accusations, however, the name of the pope in whose time the crime was committed, and of him in whose time it is subsequently reported, together with the year of the Lord, is expressed in the written accusation. With these points observed, the accusation is framed thus:

“In the year 1100 from the Lord’s Incarnation, while Lord Pope Calixtus held the Apostolic See, in the second year of his apostolate, while the most victorious Henry reigned, in the fifth year of his kingdom and the first of his empire, in the month of May, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, I, Leo, dean of the Church of Freising, declare that I denounce Conrad, bishop of Freising, as guilty of adultery before the most holy Lord Pope Calixtus, because I say that he committed adultery with Teberga in the city of Freising, in the house of Gualdrada, in the month of July, while Lord Pope Gelasius occupied the chair of the blessed Apostle Peter, in the first year of his pontificate, while that most Christian ruler was emperor, in the eighth year of his reign and sixth of his empire. I, Leo the dean, subscribe my declaration that I have denounced the aforesaid Bishop Conrad as guilty of the aforesaid [Col. 0886D] crime.

“Otherwise: ‘In the year 1174 from the Lord’s Incarnation, on the second day before the Kalends of August, I, James, monk, accuse and denounce Peter, abbot of St Vincent’s, as guilty before Lord Pope Alexander, under the chapter of Pope Innocent, “If anyone [sells] prebends or a priory,” of the crime of simony committed at Coleaponis with Count Gislibert, Bernard of Fontanella, and the notary Alexander, in the year 1167 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the month of July, under the most glorious King William of Sicily. I, James the monk, declare that Peter, abbot of St Vincent’s, is guilty of the crime of simony, and promise that I shall prove it.’

“Otherwise: ‘I, Lucius, declare that I charge Seius under the Cornelian law concerning assassins, because he killed Maevius at Rome between the statue of Mars and the Mamertine guard-post, on the first day of July, while Alexander was pope or Frederick emperor. Likewise, declaring that I accuse the aforesaid Seius, I subscribe this written accusation.’”—Book V, part I, title VII, col. 3, fol. 242.]

This last part is the most complete of all. Laborans composed it with the highest skill in both ecclesiastical and civil law; consequently, it also contains a great many passages derived from Roman law.

Thus Laborans brought his work to an end. He did indeed add a sixth book; yet, as he himself observes in the preface, this book should be called only an epilogue of the preceding books, since it contains matters which in the others had either been omitted or could not conveniently be treated [Col. 0886B].

This book was excerpted from Gratian’s treatise [Col. 0887A] *On Consecration*. Corresponding to the five distinctions into which Gratian had divided it, Laborans divided it into five parts, presenting in summary nearly the same subject-matter. Thus, in the first part he deals with the consecration of churches and the celebration of Mass; in the second, with the sacrament of the Eucharist; in the third and fourth, with baptism and confirmation, where he also discusses catechism—that is, the instruction of children before baptism—and the exorcism of those about to be baptized. The final part is an appendix to the preceding ones and deals with holy-water sprinkling, the cross, and the veneration of images.

Moreover, in excerpting this final part of Gratian’s Decree, Laborans did not depart from his own distinctive and characteristic method of excerpting. For he very rarely retained Gratian’s sequence; he sought out chapters not only from the individual distinctions of this part, but also from the first and second parts of the Decree [Note:

We have considered it worthwhile to trace Laborans’s entire sixth book back to the chapters of Gratian’s treatise *On Consecration*.

Book VI, part I, titles I–X. D. 1, *De cons.*, cc. 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 31, 32, 26, 27, 28, 29, 46, 47, 49, 51, 52, 53. — D. 2, *De cons.*, cc. 14, 15, 6, 71. — D. 4, *De cons.*, c. 126. — D. 2, *De cons.*, c. 9. — C. 13, q. 2, cc. 24, 16, 17, 19, 21, 23, 29. — D. 1, *De cons.*, cc. 61, 37, 38. — D. 23, c. 25. — D. 1, *De cons.*, c. 39. — D. 23, c. 29. — D. 1, *De cons.*, c. 42. — D. 23, c. 32. — D. 1, *De cons.*, cc. 43, 44, 45, 46, 67, 68, 69, 70, 72, 73, 54, 55, 56, 71.

To this canon of Pope Pelagius II concerning the nine prefaces to be sung in Mass, Laborans adds a canon of the Synod of Piacenza, saying:

“To these ancient nine prefaces, at the council of Urban held at Piacenza, a tenth was added as follows:

‘It is fitting and salutary. Who, by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, conceived Thy Only-Begotten, and, with the glory of virginity remaining intact, brought forth the eternal light of the world, Jesus Christ our Lord.’”

Laborans adds: “Besides these ten, no others equally worthy of approval occur.”

There follow the most celebrated letters of Emperor Charlemagne to Alcuin concerning Quadragesima, Sexagesima, and Septuagesima, as well as an ancient fragment concerning the feast-day of saints. It appears to have Laborans as its author, and for that reason we give it here.

“Saints will have two robes: namely, the glorification of the body and the glorification of the soul. One precedes the other, namely the robe of the soul; for this is received on the day when the burden and weight of the flesh are laid aside. This day is called the birthday or feast-day of this or that saint. For then the holy man, dying to present misery, is born to eternal blessedness. ‘The day of death,’ he says, ‘is the day of birth’; and he is joined to the angelic choirs. And, as was anciently customary for a newborn child, a feast-day is celebrated for him on earth whose assumption causes joy in heaven; and, just as the other members rejoice with a bodily member, they do so not merely once, for the soul’s reception of the robe of joy, but a second time also, for its reception of the robe of blessedness in the body. Therefore the martyrology contains: ‘Of Agnes, the second [feast]’—understand: her glory is to be commemorated solemnly. This glory belongs to the second robe, because it will be conferred on the eighth day, that is, the last day; for which the sixth foot has ‘for the octave’ in its title. Therefore, for blessed Agnes and for all her other members, on the octave of their feast-day the holy Church already rejoices, gives thanks to divine mercy, exults, sings for joy, and keeps solemn festival. Thus the days of the elect’s laying aside [of the body] are also called their ‘deposition.’ But they are not called death or deaths, but only a placing, indeed from pain into refreshment. Likewise, they are called a departure, because one departing goes forth to meet the devout angels coming toward him. Accordingly, an octave seems to be celebrated for no one except on this ground: in view of his passage, so called, and because his flesh is to be raised again [Col. 0888B]. Hence no feast of Christ has an octave on this rationale. For Christ does not lie in the tomb awaiting resurrection. Accordingly, at the octave of the Lord’s Paschal resurrection, the introit was not sung, whereas at the octave of the feast-day of St Agnes and the others the introit is repeated. But because Christ is Lord of the universe, and the totality of things is signified by the number seven, Christ’s feast has seven days of celebration. The dedication of a church, however, has eight days: seven first for the Head, and then the first again, as the eighth, for the members.

“The Nativity of St Mary does not have an octave of the kind we have described, because it is not for the first robe, to which the second is added at the octave. Likewise neither the Annunciation of the Lord, nor the Hypapante, nor the Epiphany, nor the Beheading of St John, nor the Nativity of the Lord; for by being born of His mother He did not receive the first robe [Col. 0888C], but by dying the first and by rising again the second.

“Now every eighth day becomes the first in view of the day which follows it. But the Day of Judgment, which will come after the sevenfold course of this present age, because no other day follows it further, will be the eighth, and the gathering together of the eight beatitudes.”

Nevertheless, he distributed almost every chapter of the same treatise, separated from the others, here and there [Col. 0889A] throughout different parts of the compilation, as the nature of the subjects treated there demanded [Note:

. In this respect Laborans seems to us certainly more deserving of praise than blame.

Now, from the titles of the entire compilation, which Zaccaria made public in the dissertation mentioned above, one may perceive better than from anything else how Laborans rearranged the material of Gratian’s Decree into a new order and organized his compilation. We therefore refer the kindly reader to that dissertation.

§ III. On the manner in which Laborans arranged chapters taken from Gratian’s Decree.—Fragments from Laborans’s books *On Justice and the Just, to Maio, Great Admiral of Sicily*, and *On True Liberty, to Hugh, Archbishop of Palermo*.

[Col. 0889]

The method which, as we have shown above, Laborans followed required him to collect chapters from Gratian’s Decree from various places, excerpt them, and insert them in order into his compilation. Although for this reason he had very often to reverse Gratian’s sequence [Col. 0889B] and recast subjects borrowed from him into a wholly different form, he nevertheless not infrequently adopted entire distinctions or questions—with the exception of a few chapters—and suitably wove them unchanged into his compilation. Since we have already spoken often of this matter, we think that nothing remains to be said; instead, we shall explain the manner in which he connected the individual chapters of the titles.

Imitating Gratian, Laborans endeavoured, wherever it seemed suitable, to connect individual chapters by a brief note and to indicate the link of one with another by the word *unde* (“whence”). He not infrequently expressed these notes in Gratian’s own words [Col. 0890A], as he also did where he judged that Gratian’s so-called *dicta* ought to be received together with the chapters. Sometimes, however, he altered them slightly; he reduced some to a shorter and others to a fuller form. The historical events which Gratian mentions [Col. 0890B] Laborans narrates more accurately, and he adds others of greater importance.

For the most part he argues with extraordinary ingenuity and remarkable learning, and he applies such knowledge of both Roman and ecclesiastical law in these observations that nowhere can the practice of the courts of that age be more clearly known; and it is wonderfully evident that Laborans was highly experienced in the workings of those courts. Here we append only a few of these *dicta*, by which are illustrated passages not derived from Gratian: namely, C. 1, q. 1, c. II, concerning the promotion of heretics [Note:

“Now because, according to Leo and Innocent, such an ordination seems capable of being held both valid and invalid—since the Synod of Constantinople also at one time revoked as invalid ordinations validly performed through the fault of Maximus, in order utterly to blow away heretics—Innocent, Damasus, and Urban seem to invalidate and treat as if it had never existed whatever power Negzelon, as he was thought by the profane, received or conferred upon anyone by an order. Hence Daibert is shown to require ordination [Col. 0889D] as though he had not been ordained before. Augustine, however, speaks only of the validity of sacraments. For some sacraments are of necessity, others of dignity. Necessity is not subject to law, but law to necessity. Sacraments necessary for salvation, because they cannot be repeated when valid, ought not to be taken away or lost; rather, they are permitted to remain valid with penance. But sacraments of dignity, unless they are administered worthily, so that they are conferred by worthy persons, cease certainly to be dignities. This is not to diminish the truth of the mystery, but so that the office of the minister may cease.

“Again Damasus, Innocent, and Urban are met with this objection: ‘One who has once been consecrated,’ as St Gregory says, ‘must not be consecrated again.’ Likewise, sacraments administered by heretics in the form of the Church, as Augustine maintains, must not be repeated, lest an injury seem to be done not to a human being but to the sacrament. The answer is that Gregory’s statement is understood of those who have received priestly or episcopal consecration [Col. 0890B], [Col. 0890C] and who, when they return to the Church, either receive the effect of their anointing through the laying on of hands, or are commanded permanently to refrain from its administration. Likewise Augustine’s statement is understood of this same mystical anointing and of the sacrament of baptism. There are, however, other orders in the Church which are conferred without sacramental anointing, by episcopal blessing alone together with a certain distribution of vessels or vestments, such as the order of levites and those below it. Although these are ordained by heretics, nevertheless, when they return to the Church, if otherwise worthy, they are ordained by the Church in the title of the same rank which they had received; nor is the office repeated in them, since they are held to have received nothing from heretics.

“Yet it is astonishing that a heretic can confer greater things on anyone, and not lesser: give the priesthood and episcopate, but not the diaconate and what lies below it. If he cannot confer lesser things, how can he confer greater? Therefore either someone can be ordained deacon twice by a heretic, or he can be neither bishop nor priest.

[Col. 0890D] “Some make the following distinction. One heretic is ordained outside by a heretic; another is ordained within by a Catholic and subsequently becomes a heretic. He who becomes a heretic after his Catholic ordination is either reordained by a heretic or not. If he is reordained, then upon his return to the Church he neither receives a further order nor retains the one already received. Hence *Saluberrimum*, above, Book III, part II, title III. If he does not repeat the order, perhaps upon returning he retains the one already received, whether inside or outside, but is not to receive another. Hence *Si qui*, *Omnis cujuslibet*, Book II, part I, col. I; *Si quis haeretico*, above. He does indeed retain it unless he was ordained outside for the overthrow of the faith. Hence *Convenientibus*, part II, title XXIII.

“But one who is ordained outside, either by someone who had received the final laying on of hands in the Church or who had been advanced by the final anointing, receives the sacrament of order but not the execution of the order, that is, the power of the sacrament, because that power is no longer in the giver [Col. 0891A]. The order is not repeated in one thus ordained after his return; but, if necessary, he is confirmed by the priest’s blessing and the invocation of the Holy Spirit. Hence *Ordinationis*, title XVI; *Convenientibus*, title XXIII; *Ab excommunicatis*, above, part III, title III; *Quod quidquam*, above.

“Outside the form of the Church, however, no one receives the sacrament of orders any more than that of baptism. But if he receives orders from one who outside has been anointed with the final unction of promotion, and necessity or utility requires it, he shall be ordained as not hitherto ordained [Col. 0891B], because he has received neither the execution of order or power of the sacrament nor even the sacrament of order itself. Hence *Daibertus*, *Qui perfecte*, above. What then is Augustine’s statement: ‘Just as what he had outside is not restored to one returning, so what he received outside need not be repeated for one coming’? Above, chapter *Quod quidam*. But this man received nothing. Some, however, hold both possibilities: namely, that by one who has been last anointed outside both lesser and greater orders may be conferred, but that one is not to be reckoned as such—as was said concerning Maximus, who is nevertheless believed to have been canonically ordained—above, Book I, part II, title X, chapter *Propter*. For the Lord who recognizes tares with the wheat in the threshing floor will nevertheless say to those same tares: ‘I tell you, I never knew you.’ Likewise, he does not count the Jews, sons of Abraham, as sons of Abraham. He also says that they are not from God, although the Apostle says that all things are from Him, through Him, and in Him. The same Apostle also says: ‘Without charity I am nothing,’ although a reprobate creature without charity [Col. 0891C] exists. *Imperiali*, above, Book I, part VIII, title XIV: ‘But in all things regard must be had to what seems right to the most holy Church.’”—Book IV, part VIII, title XIII, col. 2, fol. 156.]

C. 16, q. 1, cc. 21 and 24, concerning the promotion [Col. 0891A] of monks to the clergy [Note:

PIUS, Pope. “Just as a regular canon may lawfully hold a parish, so also may a monk; and each, by dispensation of the Church, may be archdeacon or bishop, provided that each remains in his own order.”

“It should therefore be known that ecclesiastical history reports that monks were not clerics before the time of Popes Eusebius, Zosimus, and Siricius. Leo also says to Augustus, *Generaliter*, above, Book I, part VII, title XV, fol. 36.—C. 16, q. 1, c. 40.—Afterwards certain monks became clerics. Then, as time went on, some such clerics were promoted even to priests or deacons. Some were raised to the cardinals by Roman pontiffs, or, with the assent of their own abbot, were sought by the people and appointed by bishops [Col. 0891D] to minister to them. Monks brought forth from the cloister in such circumstances and in such a manner may preach among the people and publicly perform the other functions belonging to the priestly office; as may also these and all priests, because the same consecration in no way prevents them. For in consecrating each of them the bishop says individually: ‘May these hands be consecrated and sanctified, so that whatever they sacrifice may be consecrated, and whatever they bless may be blessed’; and the same subsequent episcopal blessing is bestowed upon them. Therefore, by the blessing of consecration all monk-priests, just like non-monks, have the power to preach and to perform every priestly office, but not all have the exercise of that power. Yet those who possess it possess it through appointment in the way we have stated. Thus monks—St Gregory, St Martin, and Augustine, bishop of the English—were permitted to preach to the people. Otherwise, no monks are permitted to do so unless divinely admonished. In this manner [Col. 0892A], as St Gregory relates in the *Dialogues*, St Benedict led the people of Monte Cassino to the faith and overthrew the altar of Apollo erected there. Likewise, an angel appeared in a dream to a certain Equitius and sent him to preach; when he complained of an impediment of the tongue, the angel touched his tongue with a lancet and cured him of that entire defect. It should also be known that monks, or others appointed to clerical—that is, administrative—office among the people, namely to the care of souls in secular churches, ought not to hold the governance of monasteries. Hence *Dudum*.”—C. 18, q. 2, [Col. 0892B] c. 27.—To Book IV, part IV, title XII, fol. 112.]

and C. 23, q. 8, c. 20, concerning bishops’ attendance with armies [Note:

“It is also read in the *Register* that St Gregory commanded the citizens of Tuscany to prepare arms against the Lombards and decreed pay for those who served as soldiers.

“But it is one thing to wish to kill enemies, which Gregory feared; another not to wish to be killed, either oneself or one’s own people, and therefore to wish to protect them with arms and surround them with shields, as Leo and Gregory himself endeavoured to do, and also the Apostle Paul, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles. Therefore priests may lawfully persuade those for whom the exercise of arms is permitted—or command any persons by their authority—to take up arms, so that they may be both a defence for the good and an instrument of vengeance. Hence *Nostri adversus*, above, title XXI.—C. XXIII, q. 3, c. 3.

“Again Nicholas means that it is blameworthy for bishops to go to military attendance or to camps without the consent of the Roman pontiff, because until then it had been a practice requiring correction among Gallican bishops [Col. 0892C], whether they possessed lands tributary to the emperor, perhaps bought or bestowed on churches by the benefaction of men, from which they must pay to Caesar what is owed to him—namely tribute or armed men, or attendance at court or labour on fortifications—or whether the bishop alone possessed revenues liable to obligation, such as tithes, first-fruits, and all offerings of the faithful. For if a bishop voluntarily goes on campaign to help the wretched, it is pious. If he is invited by a religious prince in order to assist him by sound counsels and prayers, it is worthy. But if he is summoned in order to render to the prince the service owed him, it is lawful. Yet he must by no means go unless permitted by the Roman pontiff. Hence *Quo ausu*, above, Book II, part II, title XIII.—C. 23, q. 8, c. 26; Book IV, part V, title XXIII, col. I, fol. 135.]

Sometimes he intermingled with his observations matters pertaining to the circumstances of his own life, which are not unpleasant. Thus, on C. 23, q. 4, c. 21, he recounts how, after completing his studies at Paris [Col. 0892A], while travelling through Germany, he was received as a guest, where he also [Note:

“It is also thought superfluous that prayer or any good work should be done in order that the predestined may be saved, since, just as things foreseen will necessarily occur, so the predestined will necessarily be saved. To this, if you consult Laborans, hear him himself and his host.

[Col. 0892D] ‘When I had successfully returned from my studies from the land of the Franks through Germany to the flourishing soil of my native Florentine country and to Pontormo, the noble castle of my birth in the valley of the Arno, which takes its name from the bridge nearest to it and the river Orma, I was received as a guest with becoming generosity by a pious man of blessed memory, who may have a palace in heaven. And when I wished at once that the necessities for myself, Laborans, and for my host should be procured at my own expense, the good host immediately said generously: “Far be it! For since I have bestowed hospitality on you, I have by the name of hospitality embraced together all necessities and added them to your rest.”’

“Thus, therefore, and indeed thus: since in the starry predestination a city is promised to the person who shall live, by the name of city every path to that city is included, and on the way aid is included: namely, the holiness of the predestined is the way, and the intercession of the Church is the aid. Hence *Ut obtineri*.”—C. 23, q. 4, c. 21; to Book IV, part V, title XX, col. 3, fol. 139.]

mentions the place in which he was born. In the margin, the manuscript’s copyist drew a small picture showing Laborans conversing with his host and preparing for travel. Ughelli, author of *Italia Sacra*, valued it so highly [Col. 0893A] that he intended to insert a copy of it in the work which he planned to publish, *On the Purple-Clad Men of Florence*.

Likewise, elsewhere he mentions a work which he had written *On Justice and the Just Man* for Maio the Great, admiral of Sicily [Note: [Col. 0893C] See the appendix to this Dissertation.], and another, *On True Liberty*, for Hugh, archbishop of Palermo [Note: [Col. 0893C] On c. 1, q. 7, c. 27. Book II, part I, title I, collation 4, fol. 63, Laborans here treats of simony, which he regards as the greatest of all crimes, and more grievous even than adultery. As testimony he invokes the words of Pope St Clement, reported by Gratian, c. 32, q. 7, c. 16: “What in all sins is more grievous than adultery? For it holds the second place in punishments, since the first belongs to those who stray from God, even though they have lived soberly.” Laborans then comments upon these words as follows:

> “Thus, almost nothing among sins is more grievous than adultery; yet adultery itself is lighter than simony or apostasy. But apostasy takes place within, goes forth, and is there completed. Adultery or simony takes place within, and there is consummated and remains. Therefore, among all sins existing within the Church, in the time of Clement B [as they suppose], none was considered more grievous than adultery. But now the simoniacal plague rages and has increased so abundantly that it has gone beyond adulterers to the chaste: it has polluted virgins, defiled the celibate, infected religious persons, and stained almost all the colleges of the world. Hence it is no wonder if now in the Church no crimes—not even those of Sabellius, being lesser both in their number [Col. 0894C] and in their power—can be compared with the immeasurable pestilence of this thousand-formed plague. Concerning this, the following is found in the little book which I composed, *On True Liberty*: Simony, among the unhappy persons for whom the grace of spiritual things [Col. 0894D] is saleable, is a notorious harlot. Her unchaste lover is thought to shudder at her; in public he always detests her and often condemns her in words. Yet he rejoices whenever a hidden opportunity presents itself, whether covertly through enormous clandestine contracts, or openly through raging, sophistical semblance of marriage, to be joined to her in those obscene unions. Therefore today the crime of simony is more grievous than adultery, since it more oppresses the goodness of worthy persons and is more immovably established within the bounds of the Church, being fortified by devices of ingenuity through the mass of its overgrown multitude and its powerful adherents.”

]. In these passages the author always gives his own name, namely Laborans. From this it follows that the name was proper to his family, and was not bestowed upon the author because of his great labour, as Suaresius wrongly maintains.

It may perhaps seem strange to someone that Laborans, while naming himself several times in his work, nowhere—not even once—mentions Gratian or the *Decretum* itself. This, however, can very easily be explained if we consider that Gratian’s *Decretum* was so universally known and familiar [Col. 0893B] that anyone, at first glance as it were, could perceive the connection between it and Laborans’s Collection.

As regards the method of division which Gratian employed in the *Decretum*, and which we mean when we speak of Gratian’s “parts,” Laborans employed it likewise, though he denoted it by another name, namely *collatio* (“collation”).

Moreover, he did not at all follow Gratian’s distribution, nor does he always and everywhere divide chapters into collations. He made collations only in those titles in which a larger number of chapters occurs. It is therefore clear that he did this in order that the chapters might more easily be cited and found. Hence he does not employ this method of division for a whole [Col. 0893C] part, as Gratian did with his parts, both in the distinctions and in the questions; nor, like Gratian, does he begin with the first chapter of a distinction or question and retain the same arrangement to the end. Laborans, moreover, does not distribute titles into collations very often [Note: [Col. 0894D] Here are the titles divided into collations: Book II, part I, collations 1, 2, 3, and 4. Part III, title XVI, collations 1 and 2. Book IV, part IV, title I, collations 1 and 2; title XXIII, collations 1 and 2. Part V, title XXII, collations 1, 3, and 4. Part VII, title XVIII, collations 1 and 2. Part VIII, title VIII, collations 1, 2, and 3; title IX, collations 1 and 2. Part IX, title VII, collations 1 and 2; title XXII, collations 1, 2, and 3. Part XI, title II, collations 1 and 2. Book V, part I, title VII, collations 1, 2, 3, and 4.], and where he does so, he uses fewer or more of them at discretion.

But that in which Laborans differs most from Gratian is chiefly this: he entirely neglected the questions into which the latter had divided the [Col. 0894A] second part of the *Decretum*; indeed, he had to neglect them if he wished to employ the division into books, parts, and titles. Yet because that Gratiansian arrangement offered no small advantage, Laborans tried to supply it in another way. In his *dicta*, by which, as we have seen, he connected individual chapters, he presents the factual case both of the preceding and of the following canon. Having set this forth, he introduces a division which he calls a *distinctio* (“distinction”). The difficulties which he raises he immediately resolves either by citing other canons or by his own observations, and he calls the answer a *solutio* (“solution”). Sometimes he adds: “it is resolved thus.” Not infrequently he opposes new difficulties to his solutions, indicating them sometimes as *contrarietates* (“contrarieties”) or *contrarium* (“the contrary”), and sometimes briefly with the word *contra* (“against”). The answers offered to these difficulties he calls the “solution of the contrary,” or, if he resolves the difficulty somewhat later, the “solution of the preceding contrary.” Nowhere does he mention this method of division in the text itself; he merely notes in the margin the words *distinctio*, *solutio*, or “solution of the preceding contrary.”

A few points remain to be said about the manner in which Laborans cites passages in his Collection, wherein he differs entirely from Gratian. It is his practice to append to certain passages parallel passages, which he calls “concordant” passages. We have chiefly observed this in the *dicta* composed by him, which often consist only of passages of this kind. The text of these passages is presented, either in part or in full, in some preceding or following book or part; [Col. 0894C] he therefore carefully indicates the book, part, and title in which it may be found. If it is in an earlier book, he indicates this by the word *supra* (“above”); if in a later one, by *infra* (“below”). He cites the passage itself, which he always calls a chapter, by its opening words; these always precede the number of book, part, and title. If parallel passages occur in the same book or part of a book, he never notes the book and part, but only the title. Yet he cites the chapters of titles which have collations [Col. 0895A] according to their collation; and in citing them he uses now the word *capitulum* (“chapter”), now *paragraphus* (“paragraph”). Laborans himself explains this method of citation at the end of the first book [Col. 0896A], as may be seen from the words appended in the note [Note: [Col. 0895C] Here are Laborans’s words:

> “Observe this in this and the following books: for finding concordances and contrarieties, the expression *supra* or *infra* is very frequently placed wherever needed; the abbreviated letter **l**, or **p** with a number, or **co** with two abbreviated **ll**’s, or **p** alone, and sometimes nothing at all. **L** means book; **P** with a number means part; **T** means title; **Co** with two abbreviated **ll**’s means collation. **P** alone means paragraph. If, therefore, **p** with a number is placed beneath it, the matter is understood to be in the same book in which the aforesaid expression occurs. If **t**, in the same part. If **co**, as stated, in the same title; but if the letter **p** stands alone, that is, without a number, it is situated in the same collation or title. If nothing is placed beneath *supra* or *infra*, that of which *supra* or *infra* is said is found in the same [Col. 0895D] collation or title in which the unqualified *supra* or *infra* occurs. But a concordance to which neither *supra* nor *infra* is appended is referred to the nearest *infra* or *supra*.” Fol. 57.].

§ IV. On the sources used by Laborans besides Gratian’s *Decretum*

[Col. 0895]

[Col. 0895A] Laborans could not have been unaware that Gratian, in compiling the *Decretum*, had used the collections of his predecessors, [Col. 0895B] especially those of Burchard, Anselm, and Ivo. There can therefore be no doubt that he too occasionally consulted them, particularly in order to obtain arguments which he might put forward in his concordances and contrarieties.

With regard to Burchard’s work, he extracted only four chapters from it, and specifically noted book and chapter—a practice which he followed in no other work that he cites [Note: [Col. 0895D]

Laborans cites Burchard’s *Decretum* twice in the text: in Book II, part III, title XIV, chapter 2, where he notes: “From Burchard, Book XIX, chapter *Qui per rixam*, which is chapter 101 of this book.” In a similar way he cites chapter 58 of Book XI of Burchard’s *Decretum* in Book II, part III, title XXVI, chapter 1, where he likewise notes: “Theodore in the Penitential, and B[urchard], Book XI.” As for Burchardian passages cited by Laborans in his *dicta*, they are these. On c. 28, q. 1, c. 11—Book II, part I, title VII:

> “The table of pagans, not that of Jews, is permitted to Christians, because it is not pagans but Jews who endeavour, by abusing the common Scripture, to seduce Christians. Yet, as is stated from the Council of Mainz in B[urchard], Book IV, in the chapter *Catechumenus* [Book IX, chapter 20], a catechumen ought not to share either food or the kiss with baptized neophytes—that is, novices—whose association might improperly, or not properly, form the catechumen.”

In almost the same manner Laborans cites below, Book VI, part V, title III, fol. 243, on chapter 29, Distinction III, *On Consecration*, chapter 35 of Book III of Burchard’s *Decretum*: “In B[urchard], Book III, from the Council of Elvira, chapter *Placuit picturas*, it is decreed that images are not to be adored, venerated, or made in church; but this has been abolished through lack of authentic authority and by the force of general custom.”]

; he also used the works of Anselm and Ivo only rarely. Some examples from them occur in the materials from Laborans’s compilation which we shall give in the appendix.

Moreover, we detect in Laborans certain passages which we have been unable to find in any other collection of canons, and which appear to have been collected [Col. 0895C] by Laborans himself. To the decretal letters of Innocent II—later ones than which are not found in Gratian’s *Decretum*—[Col. 0896A] he added some issued by Eugenius III and Alexander III.

[Col. 0896B] He produces only one letter of Eugenius III: it is found in Book V, part II, title IV, fol. 214, namely his decree *On the Oath against Calumny*, though defective at the beginning and end and lacking an inscription. Bernard of Pavia received the same decree, complete and bearing an inscription, into his compilation, and inserted it under *On the Oath against Calumny*, title XXIV of Book I; it likewise occurs in the collection of decretals of Pope Gregory IX [Note: [Col. 0896C] Chapter 2, *On the Oath against Calumny* (II, 7).].

From the decretals of Alexander III he added four to his Collection. Of these, the one addressed to Henry, archbishop of Reims, is likewise found in Bernard of Pavia’s collection [Note: [Col. 0896C] Chapters 5, 6, and 7, *On Appeal* (II, 20); and likewise in Gregory IX, chapters 5, 6, and 7, Book II, title XXVIII. The most celebrated Mansi reprinted this letter among the decretal letters of Alexander III. *Collectio amplissima conciliorum*, vol. XXI, p. 1081.]. The other three, however, we have been unable to find either in the registers of that pontiff or elsewhere [Col. 0896C]; we therefore append them here [Note: [Col. 0896C]

**ALEXANDER III TO THE DEAN AND CHAPTER OF SALISBURY**

> “When Hugh Buvet was present before us, he earnestly set forth before us and our brethren that Jocelin, your bishop, had long since canonically bestowed upon him the prebend of Britford, and that you had received him as a brother and canon. In support of this he produced letters of grant from the same bishop and from yourselves, together with testimony from certain other persons. On the other hand, our beloved son Master Gislebert, clerk of the aforesaid bishop and your canon, maintained that his father had possessed that prebend until his death and had never at any time resigned it. He further added that, even if it had been granted to him, he was then of such an age that he could in no way receive the cure of souls, since it is certain that the prebend has cure of souls and he is said to have been scarcely seven years old when it ought to have been granted to him. Since these and many other matters had repeatedly been advanced on both sides in our hearing, we, giving more careful consideration to the fact that his father, as each party acknowledged, had previously held the said prebend—so that it would be a pernicious example for him to succeed to it as if by hereditary right—and considering also that, when the prebend ought to have been granted to him, he was of an age at which he could not exercise the cure of souls, absolve the said bishop, yourselves, and your church from his claim in this matter, and impose perpetual silence upon him. By apostolic authority we decree that neither he nor anyone in his name may henceforth molest, or bring into suit, the said bishop, yourselves, or your church concerning this matter. We therefore decree, etc., [the text of] the instrument of decision.”  
> —Book IV, part III, title VI, fols. 98 and 99.

**POPE ALEXANDER III TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CASERTA**

> “Concerning what we have learned from your letters: namely, that the son of Adalard, bearer of the present letter, and the son of his sister are joined to the daughters of Stantio, sister of the late same Adalard, whom the said Stantio had begotten not by his own sister but by another woman whom he took after her—let it be made known to your prudence by these present letters that, if this is so, you ought not allow them to remain together, but they must rather be separated from one another. For such unions may be called cohabitations rather than marriages, since persons related by affinity in this manner, even in the third degree, [Col. 0897D] ought not to remain together.”  
> —Book IV, part IX, title VI, fol. 168.

**POPE ALEXANDER III TO THE ARCHDEACON AND CHAPTER OF BRINDISI**

> “V., bearer of the present letter and your parishioner, appearing in our presence, showed us by the assertion he made that his wife, having been seized by a long-lasting illness, was unable to render him the marital due, and frequently and most earnestly sought leave from him that she might become a nun. At length her husband, although rather imprudently and unlawfully, as he himself asserts, gave his consent in this matter. But after she had thus entered a monastery, the husband declared firmly in the presence of many that he would neither make a vow of chastity nor enter religious life. In the course of time he slept with his maidservant and, as he himself states, begot a daughter by her. Fearing the continuance of his sin and fearing relapse, he humbly requested us mercifully to grant him permission to take a wife who might care for him in his infirmity. Since, according to the enactments of the canons, when one spouse undertakes a state of conversion with the other’s consent, neither wife nor husband may worthily do so unless the other is converted likewise, although to some it may seem abhorrent that a woman should be recalled from the cloister to secular marriage, we will that you release the aforesaid woman from the monastery entirely, and that, setting aside every excuse, you restore her to him as his wife. For it is more tolerable that the aforesaid man should have such a wife than that he should range through many adulteries.”  
> —Book IV, part XI, title IV, fol. 196.]

.

Then, throughout the margins of the manuscript, canons of the Lateran Council [Col. 0897A] held under Alexander III in 1179 are written; among them there also appears a decretal letter of the same pope, addressed to Master Laborans, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico and legate of the Apostolic See—the author, that is, of the Collection discussed here. Yet John of Wales inserted the same decretal, mutilated and without its address, in his Collection of Decretals, commonly called the second among the ancient collections, chapter 2, *On Witnesses*, Book II, title XII. Gregory IX reproduces it again in chapter 20, *On Witnesses and Testimonies*, II, 20; but it bears a different address in each place: in John it is addressed to Cardinal Mark, [Col. 0898A] and in Gregory to Cardinal Matthew.

Moreover, since Laborans has so few materials not found in Gratian’s work, we may rightly say that the *Decretum* supplied him with the chief and almost entire substance of his Collection.

In the fifth book of our compilation, however, there are very many passages drawn from Roman law, namely from the *Digest*, the *Code*, and the *Novellae Constitutiones*; in gathering these Laborans far surpassed Gratian. Yet he seems to have drawn them not from some older collection of canons, but from the collections of Roman laws themselves.

§ V. On the merit of the Collection, especially when compared with Gratian’s *Decretum*

[Col. 0897]

[Col. 0897B] When we carefully consider the order and method followed by both Laborans and Gratian in compiling their collections of canons, no doubt can arise that Laborans surpassed Gratian in many respects. For everywhere we find that he set before himself a more definite and more complete method, and always kept it in view in arranging his materials, so that the whole work of Laborans seems capable of being easily reduced to definite headings, which cohere most closely with one another and bring the immense body of ecclesiastical laws [Col. 0898B] into definite classes, as it were.

Laborans is wholly intent upon making the system of his work altogether complete in every respect. Consequently he very often neglected the convenience of students; and, because he wished everywhere to append concordances and contrarieties, he was not infrequently compelled to insert titles or chapter-lists in which he did nothing but indicate chapters found elsewhere. We give several examples here, so that it may be apparent how much inconvenience this form entails [Note: [Col. 0898C]

We shall first give the titles as they occur in Laborans’s work, and then transcribe the rubrics of the same titles, which we take from the chapter-list preceding the part, so that it may be apparent that these titles indicate subjects which are certainly of greater importance and should have been treated more fully.

Book V, part V.

[Col. 0898D]

T. XI. *Quoniam*. *Si quis episcopus per*. Above, Book II, part I, title I, collation 1.

T. XII. *Quicquid*. In the same place: *Si quis episcopus prae*. In the same place, collation 3.

T. XIII. *Omnis cujuslibet*, Book II, part I, title I, collation 1. *Si qui presbyteri*. Title III, *Saluberrimum*, Book III, part II, title III.

T. XIV. *Ventum est*, Book I, part IV, title XI.

T. XV. *Sicut is*, Book II, part I, title I, collation 1.

T. XVI. *Qui in qualibet*, Book I, part IV, title XI.

T. XVII. *Pervenit*, Book II, part I, title I, collation III; *Statuimus*. Above, part IV, title VI. Other passages in the same place.

T. XVIII. *Quicunque sane*. *Eos qui*. *Praesentium*. Above, Book II, part I, title I, collation 1.

T. XIX. *Si quis dator*. In the same place, collation 3.

T. XX. *Patet Simoniacos*. In the same place, collation 4. *Sane quisquis*. Below, Book V, part I, title VI, collation 4.

The rubrics are as follows:

T. XI. Whether a layman too has simoniacally received the laying-on of hands, or …

T. XII. Whether, with or without the bishop’s knowledge, any of his clerics receives a price, unless voluntarily offered, whether for baptism, confirmation, or promotion, yet believing it ought to be received.

T. XIII. A person coming from heretics is not to be made a cleric.

T. XIV. A cleric coming from heretics is not to be promoted, but one promoted among them is to be counted among the laity.

T. XV. One who importunately intrudes himself.

T. XVI. On those rebaptized, and on those not baptized in church.

[Col. 0899C]

T. XVII. Anathema upon a bishop who grants tithes and offerings to a layman; upon the layman who receives them; and upon everyone who, though bound to render them, does not render them.

T. XVIII. On children for whom parental avarice has acquired prebends, and on adults for whom their own avarice or another’s has done so.

T. XIX. Whatever is received from the Church by simony must be restored to the Church, and what is received in return for something thus obtained must not be retained.

T. XX. On suppressing simoniacs through secular powers unless, after warning, they repent.]

At times he disposes an entire part of a book through citations, and gives the actual text of chapters only in one or two titles. He did this, for example, in the second part of Book IV, which runs as follows:

T. I. *Quamvis omnis*. Above, Book I, part IX, title IX: [Col. 0899D] *In singulis*, title X, *Optatum*. In the same Book, part VIII, title X.

T. II. *Ecclesiastica*, part IX, title II.

T. III. *Sacerdotes*, part VI, title IV.

T. IV. *Cum beatus*. *Quoniam*, title XX.

T. V. *Accedens*, Book IV, part I, title III.

T. VI. *Quisquis*, Book II, part IV, title XV.

T. VII. *Tanta*, Book I, part VI, title XLII.

T. XII. *Quidam clerici*, Book I, part VII, title VII. *Cum multae*, Book II, part III, title XVI. *Presbyteris*, below, title XXII. Other passages in the same place.

T. XIII. *Presbyter si for.*, Book III, part I, title II.

T. XIV. *Sicut*, Book I, part X, title XII.

T. XV. *Ante*. *Episcopus autem*, part IV, title IX.
