T. XXIV. *Clericos*. Above, Book I, part VIII, title II. *Placuit*, part X, title XVI. Other passages in the same place.

T. XXIX. *Quidam mon.* Above, Book II, part I, title XIV.

[Col. 0900B]

T. XXXII. *Hii qui*. Above, Book II, part III, title XXIV, collation 1.

T. XXXIV. *Episcopus qui*, Book I, part X, title XVIII. Other passages in the same place.

T. XXXV. *Episcoporum*, title XIX; *Consuluit*, title XXI.

T. XXXVI. *Sacerdos*, part VII, title II. Other passages in the same place. *Presbyteri*, Book II, part III, title IX.

T. XXXVIII. *Requiritis*, part I, title, collation I, 4.

The rubrics of these chapter-lists are:

I. If anyone transgresses the promise which he canonically makes to [Col. 0900C] his superior and to the Church before entering ecclesiastical orders.

II. A priest celebrates or communicates without a stole.

III. It is a crime for a priest, setting sacred Scriptures aside, to read comedies, etc.

IV. On rash assailants of prelates.

V. On those presuming to administer after they have lost their orders.

VI. Lay deposition also removes communion, if he deserves to be deprived of it.

VII. On those giving bad counsel to a bishop, and on his fickleness.

XII. What is due to a subdeacon and those above him who abstain from their wives; what to the wife, what to the child, what to the conniving bishop, what to the cleric with a concubine, and what to the concubine.

XIII. The discipline of a priest who has committed fornication and voluntarily confesses, because he quickly repents.

XIV. One who comes to the priesthood with a slight fault.

[Col. 0900D]

XV. If a deacon or someone above him gives himself up to drunkenness or gambling.

XVI. On one envious of the advancement of brethren; and likewise on an envious or contentious person.

XVII. One who despises the *agapetae* [women in spiritual companionship].

XXIV. One who receives and retains another bishop’s cleric against that bishop’s will, and one who is so retained.

XXIX. A cleric, monk, or layman who refuses to submit to his own bishop according to the tradition of the Fathers.

XXXII. If one serving at the altar, after a fall of the flesh, repents negligently or “swallows his vomit.”

XXXIV. If a bishop ordains someone unwilling, and if anyone refuses to be promoted by his own bishop.

XXXV. A predecessor is not to be set aside except in this way.

XXXVI. On providing a place for those deposed, and on their other penalty, or the absence of any other penalty.

XXXVIII. Whether sellers of doves may perform penance while remaining in orders.]

[Col. 0899A] Gratian acted very differently. Nowhere does he refer the reader to other passages in his work; rather, he recites the same canon twice, and often even three times, whenever it seemed necessary in several places. We think this too explains why Laborans’s work was received neither in the schools nor in the courts, while Gratian’s *Decretum*, because of the weight of its arguments and the abundance of ecclesiastical decisions—although they were arranged in an order less suitable than in Laborans—acquired the highest authority in both places.

Furthermore, the division into cases and questions which Gratian employed in the second part of the *Decretum* was especially suitable both for use in schools and for courtroom practice. Thus we cannot be surprised [Col. 0899B] that the *Decretum* held in canon law the same place as the book of the *Digest* in Roman law. Laborans, by contrast, entirely neglected this division and attempted to replace it with his concordances and contrarieties. Although he arranged the materials more systematically, [Col. 0900A] he made the use of his book exceedingly inconvenient and difficult. If one adds that Laborans did not correct all Gratian’s errors but indeed added not a few of his own, one can easily understand why Gratian’s *Decretum* was preferred to Laborans’s Collection and preserved unimpaired the authority which it had once obtained in courts and schools.

While we state these things, we gladly acknowledge that Laborans’s work is not only of the greatest importance for the history of canon law, and therefore deserves the highest praise, but also—what matters more—is extremely useful and timely for emending and correcting the text of Gratian’s *Decretum*. For he seems to have used the best manuscripts of Gratian’s work; [Col. 0900B] and, more surprisingly, he contains very many of those passages commonly called *Paleae*, which he not infrequently received from Gratian’s *Decretum* in continuous sequence together with other chapters, so that they must be said already to have existed in the manuscripts which he used. There is in no respect [Col. 0901A] any likelihood that they passed from Laborans’s compilation into Gratian’s *Decretum*—from a work, that is, which we rightly say lay wholly neglected and unknown—for no one who wrote glosses on Gratian’s *Decretum* mentions it, and no trace appears in the ordinary Gloss that the glossators ever used it.

This being so, we most willingly join our wishes to the desires of the most distinguished J. M. Suaresius, bishop of Vaison, and of the celebrated Zaccaria. Nothing do we desire more than that Laborans’s compilation of decretals should be published from the outstanding manuscript of the Vatican Basilica Library, so that it may provide a new aid for correcting Gratian’s *Decretum*.

[Col. 0901B] Meanwhile, in order to offer students of the history of canon law a specimen of this most excellent work, we have transcribed the preface, or Prelude, together with the first part of the first book, and also the entire third book, and have appended them to this dissertation. In transcribing them, however, we have omitted the text of those chapters which Laborans borrowed from Gratian, while carefully indicating the place where they occur in Gratian’s *Decretum*. Where Laborans does not give the text of chapters themselves but merely notes the place where he had inserted them, we have likewise appended the Gratiansian chapters, but have not distinguished them by numbers; we have done that only for those whose text Laborans gives. In all other respects we have altered absolutely nothing, so that wherever the Gratiansian chapters indicated by us are transcribed, a most complete [Col. 0902B] specimen of Laborans’s work is available.

# APPENDIX: Presenting Certain Specimens of the Collection Compiled by Laborans

[Col. 0901]

# PRELUDE TO THE VOLUME

[Col. 0901C]

Since, toward the eastern region, through the pleasant land of Eden, or the homeland of Paradise—which the first-created human lost by the deserved consequence of his own fault—the compassion of the Deity shows to the human race, wandering in the exile of an excessively calamitous pilgrimage after the tragedies of long duration and an unhappy age, the way by which it must return and which it must tread; and since it aids all who wish to return and freely grants fully effective help: the name of this way is moral conduct joined to the devotion of faith, namely the avoidance of evil and the pursuit of good. It begins with the rudiments of law and advances through its institutions.

Things that bear the name of law.

Law, then, is an enactment of nature, of nations, or of a people—as of the Rhodians—or of a city, a prince, or sovereign authority, which draws into a social bond by urging through hope, extending indulgence, or restraining through fear. Through hope, indeed, as: “Those who have done good shall live”; through indulgence, as: “Turn, and I shall turn”; through fear, as: “Every barren tree shall be cut down.” These and things of this kind are laws, or laws and rights, prohibitions and commands, because the tenor of all laws was promulgated to humankind so that they might hold fast to these things. Permission, for example, that a brave man seek a reward, makes the community rejoice through hope. But permission of what is unlawful, such as giving a writ of repudiation, makes the same community more gentle through indulgence. Exhortation, moreover, awakens a person to the one thing which he hopes for.

Civil law pertains to many [peoples], the law of nations to more, natural law to divine matters, while an enactment of will pertains to very many. The civil law of any single city is the enactment of that city or its ruler. The law of nations is that of many, or almost all, peoples. But natural law, implanted from the principle which is the efficient cause [Col. 0902C] of all things, resides in all living creatures. What the authority of Law and Gospel commends in it is called right, divine law, and does not lose the name of nature.

An enactment, law, and natural law are found to be the same by nature, though not the same in usage. For when *lex* applies its name to just provisions set down in writing by someone, it is narrowed within the compass of *ius*; and when *constitutio* grants its name only to an imperial or royal edict, it is brought within the circle of law and right.

Moreover, law and right are the same in usage, yet reduced from the general kind of right and law; as where, for example, passing through another’s field is said to be permitted, but not a right.

The species of the law of nations are military law and public law.

[Col. 0902D] Civil law is also called forensic law, and one of its species is Quiritary law. The species of Quiritary law are statute, plebiscite, senatorial decree, constitution or edict, and opinions of jurists. Yet all these are also designated by the name “law.”

The names of certain laws are, moreover, derived from the second or official names of their makers, such as consular or tribunician law; from a proper name, such as Cornelian and Falcidian law; from country or people, such as Rhodian law; or from some proportion, such as the *Satyra*.

There is another species of Quiritary law, not consisting in writing as those I have just mentioned do: namely custom or usage.

For custom is the practice which the long-standing authority of the ancestors has sanctioned for each person, according to his office and the end owed to that office, for the advancement of the commonwealth. An office, however, is permission granted for actions to be done in civic life. Although the acts of each person [Col. 0903A] according to the customs of a city are also called, by transferred name, an office. In the *Dicta ad stipulativum* the following is read:

Chapter 1. “All laws.” D. 1, c. 1.

Chapter 2. “General law,” etc. D. 1, cc. 2–5.

Chapters 3–9. D. 1, cc. 6–12.

The species of Roman law are statute and the other things mentioned above.

Chapter 10. D. 2, c. 1.

Chapters 11–17. D. 2, cc. 2–8.

Moreover, there is another kind of law, far more excellent than those before mentioned: namely, an enactment of ecclesiastical authority. It is certainly not secular law, but pertains to spiritual edification; it is called, by the specific name *canon*, that is, “rule”; it proceeds from the pious dispensation of the saints and of Christ and is not contrary to the teaching of nature. It contains four classes: institutions of the Lord, apostolic constitutions, decrees of popes, and enactments of councils; and in all these are contained the oracles of the prophets.

There are also the illustrious supports furnished by other Fathers and the glorious decisions or teachings of eminent [Col. 0903B] men.

Of decrees or canons, as likewise of laws, one kind is individual, pertaining to a single person or question—such as a decretal letter to a college or to an individual, and likewise a privilege, which is called a private law, as it were. Another is general, because it concerns many, and this too is particular; another is universal, because it concerns all.

Again, one is temporal, as: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles”; another perpetual, as: “Preach the Gospel in all the earth”; another local, as: “If clerics appeal to councils, let them not appeal except to African councils.” Below, Book IV, part IV, title XXVII, chapter *Presbyteri*. Another is occasion-specific, as: “Simon, give the tribute for me and for yourself”; another is at once temporal, local, and occasion-specific, as: “Marriages contracted within the third or fourth generation among the English are not to be dissolved.”

Likewise, of councils or synods, one is universal, as celebrated by all or by several nations; another provincial, celebrated either by the bishops of a single province and with the authority of the Roman pontiff, whether his legate is present, [Col. 0903C] or because its decrees or canons are promulgated by the authority of the primate or metropolitan who presides over the province.

Yet a provincial council is to be embraced by other provinces in similar cases; for, at the eating of the lamb, an Israelite who has not enough must invite his neighbour. Hence on writs, below, Book I, part II, title XII. There are other matters in the same place; *Novit*, Book IV, part I, title II. Nor should it be omitted that, among canons, an enactment of a council is more commonly called a “canon,” by a shortened use of the generic name; hence Nicaea, part II, title XXIII. By more common usage, a “decree” is a command, prohibition, or constitution of Roman pontiffs, whether confirmed in a council of bishops or in an assembly of cardinals. If it is written in epistolary form to an absent person, [Col. 0904A] it is called a decretal letter. If it is written in the form of a privilege, it is called a privilege, whether given to one present or granted to one absent. Yet the name *decree* is sometimes taken to mean the compilation of any canon and the teaching of the saints arranged under canons. Therefore every such item is also called a canon.

The cause of the enactment both of pontifical decretals and of synodal canons was Christ’s command: “Teach,” he says, “all nations whatever the Paraclete shall suggest to you.”

The subject is the reasonable rule of life and the way to the fatherland.

The office is, with measured discretion, to command and forbid, reward and punish, and likewise to grant indulgence or permission and to admonish. Hence:

Chapter 18. *Every law.*—D. 3, c. 4.

[Col. 0904B] Its end is to lead the human race back to the fatherland by the administration of office.

Its author is the pontifical order, by divine prompting.

Its ministers are bishops and priests.

The order followed is not that of those who composed them, which follows the times of their composition; rather, in the sequence of the present work it follows the order of the many matters selected individually for treatment, and of the books that concern them incidentally; and, within the books, the order of the titles.

The end of laws, moreover, is expressed in other words as follows.

Chapter 19. *They were made.*—D. 4, c. [uncertain].

Therefore a certain decretal and canonical teaching of the holy Fathers, though small, is a sampling from an immense body of material; nevertheless, it seems by no means useless in initiating, conducting, and concluding ecclesiastical affairs. It is divided into six books of this volume, all of which share in general a common instruction in ecclesiastical morality—a subject highly worthy, even in a small supply of arguments, for those wishing to exercise themselves in canonical debate and to resolve, through reason, the conflict of discordance that repeatedly arises. Although the individual books principally pursue individual purposes, they nevertheless interweave incidentally certain matters very necessary to their principal subjects. Thus the first book, intending to deal with the varieties of ecclesiastical promotion, frequently and not inappropriately appends elsewhere, as suitable to the places concerned, certain matters very useful to the whole volume. It begins thus: “Therefore the kind of canon.” But the titles of certain chapters are first arranged in the following order.

## TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST PART

I. What a law is; what sort it ought to be; when judgment is to be made concerning it or through it. II. The difference between natural law and other law. III. That something is not valid merely because it is done otherwise than the law permits. IV. That something is not valid merely because it appears contrary to natural law. V. That, because it is truly contrary, it is invalidated. VI. On bad custom. VII. On a sacrilegious constitution. VIII. On a constitution of less certain variety, or of certainty. IX. On a contrary constitution. [Col. 0905A] X. On a non-contrary constitution. XI. On custom opposed to law. XII. On custom not opposed to law. XIII. What custom must be cut away, how, and for what reason. XIV. Of two impossibilities, the lesser is to be chosen. XV. It is not permissible for anyone to sin so that another may not sin more grievously. XVI. The rule for mitigating rigor or not mitigating it, and how each is done.

To the Bishop of Pamplona.

[Col. 0905D] Title II, sole chapter.

Every law and constitution worthy of acceptance as an enactment follows natural law and draws its origin from the permission of nature as from its own streamlet. Natural law, indeed, is plainly earlier than all those things. But the law of custom began after the creation of man, and, it is believed, from the time of the city which Cain began to build. Yet even before the formation of man, irrational creatures themselves were not without knowledge of natural law. The law of constitution, however, began from the ordinances delivered by the Lord to Moses: “If you buy a Hebrew slave,” etc. Hence:

Chapter 1. *Moses.*—D. 7, c. 1.

It is more worthy by reason of its immovability, because, while other things change, it does not change. It is also superior in dignity. For whatever is contrary to natural law—whether the writing of vice has embraced it [Col. 0906A] or the custom of error has admitted it, as will be clear below in title VI and elsewhere—ought to be held invalid and void.

## TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS OF THE FIRST PART OF BOOK THREE

[Col. 0908A]

I. Examples of the restoration of those deposed. II. Canons restoring the deposed. III. Canons forbidding restoration. IV. Canons mediating between these discordant authorities and showing to which of the discordant views one ought rather to assent; and on penance. V. Canons forbidding those restored to rise higher. VI. Canons allowing them to rise higher. VII. Canons intending both. VIII. Canons yielding permission to those forbidden or to be forbidden. IX. Canons opposing some persons who have been permitted. X. Canons moderating opposition and the manner of restoring.

## HERE BEGINS BOOK THREE

The third book of this excerpt of decrees or canons judges and explains, partly by examples and partly by canons, the cases of those degraded and the manner in which their restoration is permitted.

Chapter 10. *A nobleman.* C. 2, q. 5, c. 14.

This, however, is not canonical censure, but a canonical permission of lawful censure in response to the severity of the accuser. Thus there is one popular kind of purgation, such as [the ordeal of] red-hot iron; another is canonical, such as that by oath alone. Hence “Mennas,” below, Book IV, part V, title V. Other matters there. The popular ordeal applies only to persons of servile status, or persons servilely suspected. For a freeborn person, canonical purgation alone applies, because you have both [rules] thus in Burchard, Book VI, “He who [accuses] a priest,” chapter 5; and “A nobleman,” above. Therefore, when a bad reputation does not attach to a freeborn person, canonical purgation is not to be demanded. Hence “But that,” below, Book V, part [uncertain], title VIII. Nor [is it to be demanded] if [the reputation] arises from the fabrication of enemies. Hence “What has been heard,” Book IV, part V, title V. But if it arises from a plausible suspicion, it shall be removed by purgation. Hence “A priest,” or there, and other matters there. If a cleric is defamed among the people, he should clear himself in the presence of the people. Hence “If a priest [is accused]”; “By counsel,” there. If, however, he is defamed only among the clergy, he should clear himself only before the clergy. Hence “Concerning a crime,” there. But a bishop ought to clear himself with twelve colleagues. Hence “By counsel,” there. A priest with seven, a deacon with three; a subdeacon and those below him may do so only with his own hand [by a simple oath]. Hence “If lawfully [accused]”; “If a priest [is accused],” there. This is the ordinary rule. But the number of hands by which each person should clear himself rests in the bishop’s discretion. Hence “By counsel,” there. If a person defamed [Col. 0911D] can establish his innocence but refuses, he shall remain suspended so long as he does not establish it. But if he cannot do so, suspension on account of inability shall endure equally with that inability; or, if perhaps he is equitable, let him remain until the adverse reputation subsides—as much as five years, whence perhaps is drawn: “If [it concerns] a bishop,” above.

Title II.

Title III, Chapters 1–6.

Of those whose rank is taken away, some are restored after canonically completed penance by a provident dispensation; others, because they do not repent worthily, [Col. 0912A] or because their penance does not appear in its fruits, or because no restoration granted them by the canons is found to have occurred, but rather one forbidden; or because, although they are free from crime, the sacrament would falsely represent an empty appearance—as in the case of twice-married men—the rank taken away remains irreparably lost.

Yet in the hand of the Roman pontiff are the finger and, in the finger, discernment; rigidity and flexibility. By the discriminating balance of his holy deliberation and providence, he can moderate the censures of the canons, so that mild things grow rigid and rigid things soften, harshness succeeds gentleness, and, where expedient—if indeed expedient, which perhaps has not yet occurred—dispensatory gentleness succeeds harshness. Hence “Dispensations,” above, part I, title VII. Other matters there.

[Col. 0912B] This dispensation is manifold in matters which the rigor of the canons does not admit, but promptly rejects or condemns. For it weighs proposed affairs according to the matters of office and according to the quantities of things. In the deliberation of administration, two considerations are set before the office of a dispenser: the attainment of advantage, which is utility and honorableness; and the avoidance of disadvantage, which is uselessness and baseness. Advantage or disadvantage is found in something of its own kind, either greater or lesser, and in advantage as compared with disadvantage. Of advantages, the lesser is always to be omitted so that the greater may result, if one of the two is necessary and both cannot occur. In disadvantages, by contrast, the lesser is always admitted so that the greater may be avoided, if one of the two is necessary and both cannot occur together. But if opposites alone are compared, the lesser good is omitted in order to avoid the greater evil, if one of the two is necessary. The magnitude of things or advantages, and conversely, is considered chiefly from the qualities of persons and the demands of times. Under the name “persons,” in rhetorical usage, we also include the people, and any number of persons bound together in the same purpose by one will. Therefore a “person” is one person or several. When it is one, he is either with several or alone. But when there are several, either the pest of tares can be uprooted without plucking up the wheat, in which case it may be called as though alone; or it cannot be uprooted without [uprooting] the wheat and destroying the general peace of the Church. [Col. 0912D] The canon does not apply to such a person; nor, conversely, is sentence to be given against him, but sentence is to be given only against the person alone, or as though alone, according to the canon, unless he is sustained by provident moderation. This moderation comes about through the variety of cases; when the causes for it cease, watchful rigor does not become lax. Severity is softened by the imminence of necessity, consideration of mercy, regard for the person, foresight of utility, and caution regarding the contrary. By the imminence of necessity: when, in the time of Pope Gelasius, the Italian Church was deprived of the ministry of all its clergy because of the deadly devastation of war and famine, so that many peoples lacked helpers for the governance of souls, that pontiff granted that clerics be chosen from monks and laymen, declaring: “Necessary [things],” above, Book I, part I, title XVI. Other matters there.

[Col. 0913A] I said that the canon does not apply to such a person, and conversely, because one canon is for the giving of sentence: it both states the cause of the sentence and legislates for the future, as: “Whoever does, or has done, this shall be suspended”; another canon is for a sentence already given: it both punishes the cause of sentence and speaks in the present, as: “We suspend him who has done, or will do, this.” The canons of the canons are known.

Title VI.

The sequence of disciplinary action in the clergy is understood to be straight, not inverted or crooked, so that one proceeds from mild measures to harsh ones and rises from the least to the greatest. Yet this medicinal operation accordingly applies lesser and gentler remedies, lest greater or harsher ones have to be applied. It touches with a word, lest it strike; it threatens with a look, lest it wound; but it also wounds mercifully, in order to set free. First, therefore, it appears that one who has transgressed should be rebuked or admonished as is expedient. Hence: admonition ought to intimate punishment. Below, Book IV, part IV, title VII, chapter *Unworthily.*—C. 12, q. 2, c. 21. Likewise: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him.” It follows that one who neglects rebuke should be excluded or suspended from his own office. “Besides this.” “If there are any,” part II, title XXXIX. Next, the contumacious person should be stripped of a benefice. Hence “If anyone”; “Them also,” title XXI. Next, the more contumacious person should be deprived of the rank of office. Hence “We decree,” above, Book II, part III, title XXVI, collection 1. Other matters there. Hear how the obstinate person is overwhelmed by the sword of anathema. Hence “So also a priest”; “None greater,” below, Book IV, part VIII, title VII, chapter *Let them be corrected.*—C. 24, q. 3, c. 17. Other matters there. But discipline is also carried out by another order of provident skill.

[Col. 0913] Here ends Book Three.

# A.D. 1048–1250: THE DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF VERDUN AND THE ABBOTS OF ST. VITON, BY LAURENCE OF LIÈGE AND HIS CONTINUATORS

Edited by Georg Waitz, Professor of Public Law, Göttingen.

(Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, XII, 486)

[Col. 0915]

## [EDITORIAL NOTICE]

Since in the twelfth century very many churches of Lotharingia possessed books written on the deeds of bishops and abbots, the men of Verdun also took care that they, who after the people of Metz had first attained such an honor, should not now be surpassed by others. Since, then, Bertarius’s continuation (*SS.* IV, p. 45 ff. [*Patrologia*, vol. CXXXII]) ends in the middle of the eleventh century, a monk of St. Viton named Hugh undertook to narrate the events of almost a hundred years, down to his own time. He persuaded a brother of his order from the monastery of St. Lawrence at Liège, then outstanding in literary learning, who had come to Verdun and, as it seems, was himself called Laurence, to undertake that task.

[Note: [Col. 0915] Compare Rainer’s book *On the Distinguished Writers of His Monastery*, in Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* IV, 3, p. 20 ff.; *Histoire littéraire de la France*, X, p. 99.]

[Note: [Col. 0915] The extant manuscripts do not state the author’s name with sufficient clarity. The manuscript numbered 1 below has no heading at all, and in the text of the preface it gives the letter L; the other, called 2, seems at this point to have changed L into I and prefixed to the letter written to Bishop Albero this rubric: “Letter of the monk John to Lord Albero, bishop.” But it is clear that this deserves little confidence, since the words “from the Liège monastery of Blessed Laurence” have been wholly omitted. In the sixteenth century both the Amiens transcript (*Archiv* VIII, p. 397) and Wassebourg, the distinguished writer on Verdun affairs, named Laurence; this name we may rightly retain.]

Nor did Laurence, although he lived at Verdun for only one year, refuse what was requested, being distressed that the deeds of illustrious men should be buried in oblivion.

[Note: [Col. 0916] Chapter 34; compare the Letter: “Before this year I was brought to the city of your governance.” Therefore Laurence came to Verdun not in 1140, as the author of *Histoire littéraire*, XII, p. 222, wrote, but in 1143 or 1142.]

He dedicated the book to Bishop Albero, with a prefatory letter in which he set out what he had been able to collect from every quarter concerning the history of Verdun omitted by Bertarius. Some of this he inserted here falsely out of zeal for the glory of his homeland, but some he drew from genuine records. Laurence nowhere indicated from what sources he drew the history itself, carried from the year 1018 (more correctly 1047) to 1144; but he openly declared that he had made it his aim to be “ready in all things to follow the better judgment of whoever should set it out better.” Nor did he wish to keep silent about wrongdoing, since “history ought to follow necessary truth,” while taking care not to “exaggerate anyone’s crime in words.”

[Note: [Col. 0916] Epilogue: “We ask that no one bring an accusation against us on account of this little work, because we believe that we have written only true things,” etc.]

And indeed cautious prudence was necessary, since he himself had to deal with the conflict between popes and emperors, in which the bishops of Verdun and the abbots of St. Viton had taken opposing sides. Since that conflict had then happily been calmed, he did not allow himself to be carried away by party zeal, though he did not wish to conceal his more favorable disposition toward the Church. Moreover, he had most of the events he narrated well established, having been informed by that Hugh and perhaps by other brethren of the monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0916] Chapter 32: “Hugh—at whose urging and from whose account we composed this whole little work.”]

Although Laurence sometimes made errors in the earlier years when recounting the public affairs of Lotharingia, he cannot be charged with such errors through the greater part of his book. Up to the end of the twelfth century he may be compared with Hugh of Flavigny, who treated nearly the same matters, although his book, which did not circulate widely, was unknown to Laurence. Thereafter, lacking altogether other records of Verdun history, we have no sure foundation upon which to assess his reliability. Yet it must be supposed that Laurence found at Verdun witnesses particularly knowledgeable about these periods; he used their assistance so as to compose a fairly accurate and full history of the Church. His rich, and at times more ornate, style also commends it to readers.

Furthermore, nothing is known of Laurence’s life, nor have we any information concerning the time of his death. Perhaps he subsequently revised the history written in 1144; perhaps he even undertook to continue it further. For although he plainly says that in 1144, the fourteenth year of Bishop Albero, he was occupied in writing the book and laid down his pen, he nevertheless once reports that Albero had held his see for fifteen years.

[Note: [Col. 0916] Epilogue; compare chapter 32: “Before these two years,” which was A.D. 1142.]

[Note: [Col. 0916] Chapter 32; compare what I have noted concerning this passage.]

Moreover, there survives a continuation carried far beyond Laurence’s own time, but it does not seem attributable to one writer. Its opening words refer to Laurence’s book in such a manner that you would think you were hearing him himself, and not another writer.

[Note: [Col. 0917] Chapter 1: “Of the praises of our pious and venerable Father Segard, from whom we departed not far above.”]

In this portion is narrated the elevation of St. Viton, the monastery’s patron, celebrated by Pope Eugenius in 1147—an auspicious event and one highly honorable to the monastery—which Laurence himself might have been moved to transmit to posterity and to celebrate in verses, though rough and unpolished. Alberic, however, who alone among medieval writers, so far as I know, excerpted Laurence, knew only the first and more important part of the book.

[Note: [Col. 0917] See on this matter Wilmans, *Archiv* X, p. 225. In the year 1131 also, with a few additions, Alberic seems to follow Laurence; but he reports nothing concerning the translation of St. Viton and Pope Eugenius’s journey to Verdun. Nor does he seem to have known the later continuation. For what is narrated in 1181 concerning the death of Bishop Arnulf he could have drawn from another source.]

Afterwards, the *Deeds of the Bishops and Abbots of Verdun* were continued further, apparently by two writers: one from A.D. 1156 to 1187, the other down to 1250. Others attributed these, together with the history for the years 1144–1147, to the same thirteenth-century writer. What especially prevents our agreeing with them is that the narrative is seen to break off completely twice.

[Note: [Col. 0917] In chapter 7 the earlier narrative had ended with the words: “Henry is succeeded by Albert, a man exceedingly vigorous.” What follows, “But when a dispute arose,” etc., plainly indicates another writer, who knew that Albert contended with Robert for the bishopric, but otherwise had learned nothing of his history down to 1208.]

We have therefore distinguished three parts of the continuation: the first, in our opinion, to be ascribed to Laurence himself; the other two written by monks of St. Viton, who equaled him neither in knowledge of events nor in elegance of style.

This work, already published by D’Achery (*Spicilegium* XII, p. 274 ff.; second edition, II, p. 241 ff.), Calmet (*History of Lotharingia* I, *Proofs*, p. 206 ff.; second edition, II, p. XVIII ff.), and in fragments by Bouquet’s continuators (XI, p. 249–251; XIII, p. 628–640; XV, p. 208), was to be reprinted by us. We therefore consulted the same manuscripts still extant in the public library at Verdun that we followed in preparing Bertarius’s edition.

1. The manuscript now marked no. 3, consisting of two parts (compare *SS.* IV, p. 39), contains, from fol. 248 onward, Laurence’s book, written in a thirteenth-century hand. We were generally able to follow it, though in representing individual words it often departs from the usage of the mid-twelfth century. For the scribe everywhere writes *e* for *ae* and *oe*, frequently *y* for *i* (*epytaphyum, antystes, archydiac., Sophya, Phylippus, Ytalia*), and similar forms. He also sometimes made errors, and once or twice omitted Laurence’s words.

[Note: [Col. 0917] Chapter 34: “But that house remains desolate [Col. 0918] until now,” etc.; words which perhaps did not seem quite appropriate to the time at which the manuscript was written. Yet the scribe found even these words in his exemplar, since he wrote the first words but immediately erased them. He also appears to have intended to supply in the margin, with a sign added, another passage in chapter 33 which is now lacking.]

The continuation was added, apparently in the same hand but with different ink.

2. Manuscript no. 36, of the thirteenth century, fol. 126 ff., contains the work of Laurence, attributed to John the monk. Although in this portion of the volume none of those alterations of the authentic text are found which occur in Bertarius’s history, nevertheless in certain places some additions have been made that can scarcely be ascribed to Laurence. Nor are the words themselves free from errors. Therefore there is scarcely reason to regret that, while occupied at Verdun, I was prevented from copying out the entire manuscript. At the end of Laurence’s work this subscription is read (fol. 147): “Peter of Flanders wrote me, but did not dictate me.” No continuation has been added; there follow: “The names of the bishops who came after Albero,” written in different hands.

3. The same volume, now in its first and older part, written in the twelfth century, contains fragments taken from Laurence’s history. These deserve high esteem, since they are closer to his own age and confirm the readings of manuscript 1 in most places, so that we may rely upon it with great confidence.

Supported by these aids, we did not wish to employ the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century copies preserved in the libraries of Paris (Archiv. VIII, p. 325), Amiens, and The Hague (ibid., p. 569); nor did we attach much importance to editions apparently taken from the same manuscripts. [Note: Another manuscript at Liège is attested by Miraeus, *De sanctis ecclesiasticis*, c. 362, p. 63. The same author says: “We once gave our manuscript copy of them as a gift to John Cordesius, canon of Limoges, when we were residing at Paris.”] Short fragments inserted by Wasseburg in his volumes of *Belgian Antiquities*, however, show that he himself used a very good copy of the work, which agrees especially closely with manuscript 3. [Note: *Le premier (le second) volume des Antiquitez de la Gaule Belgicque*, 1549, folio. The royal library at Hanover supplied me with this book, rarer in Germany.]

The same Wasseburg incorporated almost the entire narrative of Laurence and of the continuators into his own pages, furnishing and elucidating it with a continuous sort of commentary. Calmet, following him, added much of his own. Both appear indeed to have taken no small care in explaining the names of Verdun villages; yet they did not everywhere avoid errors with equal diligence. Some of these Roussel corrected, [Note: *Histoire ecclésiastique et civile de Verdun . . . , par un chanoine de la même ville*, Paris, 1745, 4to.] while leaving others untouched. Let confidence in the interpretations rest with those authors whom I have named at the several places. Moreover, I have cited whatever charters seemed to illustrate the deeds of the bishops here related.

There follow the Annals of Saint Vitonus, copied in a fifteenth-century hand in manuscript no. 3 of the Verdun library (cf. Vol. IV, p. 7), but undoubtedly drawn from an older source. They help establish the years of the bishops of Verdun and abbots of Saint Vitonus, but otherwise contain only a few matters worthy of record. Labbe copied and published part of them rather carelessly (*Bibl. nova manuscriptorum*, I, p. 400). What is printed in small type seems to have been drawn from a copy of the old annals which closely approaches the Annals of Saint Vincent at Metz, published in Vol. III, p. 153. With their publication, readers will rejoice with me that our collection has now admitted every writer on Verdun affairs surviving to us from the Middle Ages.

G. WAITZ.

[Col. 0919]

## THE DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS AND ABBOTS OF VERDUN BEGIN

[Note: Manuscript 2 has in red: “The letter of John the monk to Lord Albero, bishop.”]

## [LETTER]

[Col. 0919A]

Brother L. [Note: Manuscript 2 has a correction at “L.”; the words “of the Liège monastery of Saint Laurence” are absent there.] of the Liège monastery of Saint Laurence wishes the venerable A., [Note: A in manuscripts 1 and 2, i.e. Albero.] by God’s grace bishop of the people of Verdun, and his whole church, to live happily in Christ according to both the inner and outer person.

Having been brought before this year to the city under your governance, I found there above all that saying of Ecclesiastes (ch. 1): that all things under the sun tend toward destruction, and that there is no memory of those who came before. Mortality enfolds all things; it takes away from humankind and buries with their bones even the names—not only the deeds—of the mightiest kings and tyrants and, what is more grievous, of the holiest martyrs and confessors. Behold: your holy predecessors Sanctinus, Maurus, Salvinus, Arator, Pulcronius, Possessor, Firminus, Vitonus, and many others. At what time they lived, what wonders and deeds they performed while alive, we do not know today; and, alas for the shame of it, we endure an unworthy ignorance concerning our patrons, by whose merits we are made illustrious.

Even the very name of the most blessed Vitonus is almost in dispute and uncertain. Ancient records [Note: What these were is not known. Neither Bertarius (*SS.* IV, p. 41) nor Hugh of Flavigny (*SS.* VIII, p. 328) reports this.] call him *Videnus*, [Note: *vidennum* in manuscript 2.] a form more consonant with the vernacular tongue. Whatever is found concerning these persons is all uncertain and related as though through a mist, so that it can scarcely be judged worthy of belief. Indeed, some assert that the first of them, blessed Sanctinus, was one of the seventy-two disciples of the Savior. [Note: “of the Savior” is absent in manuscript 1.] But Bertharius, [Note: *bertarius* in manuscript 2.] who arranged their catalogue as best he knew, [Note: *cathalogum* in manuscript 1.] sets forth [Note: He gives two opinions about him: the first, and stronger, is in manuscript 2.] what is read in many places: that he was a disciple of Saint Dionysius of Paris and bishop of the Meldi, and that by the word of preaching he shone upon this city of Verdun through an angelic visitation. [Note: The words “angelic visitation” are absent in manuscript 2.] [Note: The other opinion, found in the Life of Saint Servatius, is that Sanctinus, bishop of the city of the Clavi, attended the council at Cologne, where the deposition of the heresiarch Effratha and the substitution of blessed Severinus were discussed. Which of these two opinions I should credit more, I can scarcely determine, except that some maintain—as both points are agreed—that two Sanctinuses at different times occupied the episcopal see of Verdun; the first of these they wish to have been either one of the Savior’s seventy-two disciples or that martyred bishop of the Meldi. Added in manuscript 2. At Orosius the town is not named; in editions of the *Historia miscella*, however, Lyons is read.]

The brethren of the monastery of Theologia say that six monks or abbots from their monastery were given as bishops to your church. [Note: “our” in manuscript 2 for “your.” Note: Paul, Gisloald, Gerebert, Armoinus, Bertalamus, and Abbo are meant; see Calmet, *Hist. de Lorraine*, I, p. 464. Elsewhere twelve bishops selected from the monastery of Theologia are mentioned; see Clouet, *Hist. ecclésiastique de la province de Trèves*, I, p. 583.] Yet Bertharius’s pious diligence deserves praise: from the very ashes and ruins of the burned city and church [Note: *ecclesia* in manuscript 2.] he drew forth, as best he could, at least the bare names of the predecessor bishops, [Note: *predescessorum* in manuscript 2.] or caused certain sparks of their deeds to shine for us. [Note: “for us” is absent in manuscript 2; manuscript 1 has *scintillant*, “they shine.”] For from him we have received even this very small knowledge of our bishops. Nor would I regard it as insignificant that the outstanding deeds of great persons are rescued from the destruction of oblivion through the service of writers.

Jerome relates [Note: Vallars edition, II, p. 13.] in the prologue to the Life of Saint Hilarion that Alexander the Great of Macedon—whom Daniel (ch. VIII) calls either the ram, the leopard, or the he-goat [Note: Manuscript 1 has *hyrcum*, “he-goat”; there also occur *Danyel*, *Achyllis*, and similar spellings.]—when he came to Achilles’ tomb, said: “Fortunate young man, who enjoy so great a herald of your merits,” meaning Homer, of course. Let these remarks have been made thus far so that the deeds of our fathers may be sought out by all our people in every direction and transmitted to the memory of posterity, in order that they may have those nearest to hand whom they may chiefly imitate. For every city embraces the examples of its own people more readily. Therefore, concerning the ancient condition of this city, we transcribe for you here, briefly gathered into one place, what we have found recorded in various writings.

The first item that occurs is from Roman history, which, while describing Gaius Julius Caesar’s ten-year war in Gaul, mentions this then very strongly fortified town in these words: [Note: Orosius, and the *Historia miscella*, from Caesar. What he here relates of Uxellodunum (Issoudun), Laurence applies to Verdun.]

> “Meanwhile Draptes and Lucterius,” undoubtedly leaders of the Gauls, “when they saw that Caninius [Note: *cavinium* in manuscript 1, here and below.] and the legions,” undoubtedly Roman, “were present in their territory, gathered forces from all sides and occupied the town of Verodunum. This town stood on the highest summit of a mountain; on two sides it was encircled by precipitous slopes and a sizeable river. Secure, moreover, in the middle of the descent by a most abundant spring, and safe within through a plentiful store of grain, it looked down upon the futile movements of enemies from afar. Caninius, doing what Roman foresight alone could do, defeated in a great battle the two leaders, who had been drawn into the plain with a very large part of their forces. For, after one of the leaders had been killed, he put the other to flight with very few men. None returned to the town; but Caesar was needed to attack it.
>
> “Accordingly Caesar, informed by messengers, hurried up; and, having surveyed everything, he saw that, if he attempted to storm it by force, his army would have to be destroyed as a game and spectacle for the enemy; that there was but one means of relief, if by some means the enemy could be cut off from water. Yet even this Caesar could not have accomplished otherwise. For the spring from which they drank issued from the middle side of the sloping mountain. Caesar ordered mantlets to be brought up near the spring and a tower to be built. At once a great sortie was made from the town. Since the Romans could fight without danger, although the defenders stubbornly resisted and repeatedly came forward, many nevertheless were slaughtered. Therefore an embankment and a tower sixty feet high were constructed, whose summit could be brought level with the spring’s position, so that missiles might be cast on equal terms, or the rolling masses of stones hurled down from above need not be feared.
>
> “But when the townspeople saw that not only their cattle but also the weaker ages of humankind were being exhausted by thirst, they filled tubs with pitch, tallow [Note: Corrected from *sepo* in manuscript 2.] and shingles. Then, having set them alight, they hurled them down the slope, themselves following them in a body from the whole town. When the engines were burning, Caesar saw that a serious and dangerous battle faced his men; he ordered cohorts to run swiftly around the town and suddenly raise a great shout on every side. Terrified by this, the townspeople, wishing to run back to defend the town, withdrew from attacking the tower and demolishing the embankment. Yet those who, protected beneath cover of the embankment, were digging tunnels to cut the channels of the spring, found the hidden courses of the water and, by dividing them into many parts, caused them to diminish and be consumed within themselves. The townspeople, when the spring had dried up, seized by utter despair, surrendered themselves.
>
> “Caesar, however, cut off the hands of all who had borne arms and left them their lives, that the punishment of wicked men might be more manifest even to posterity. For a displayed example of punishment greatly avails to check audacity, when the present pitiable appearance of the living both reminds the guilty and compels the ignorant to inquire. Having exhausted and demolished the Gauls, Caesar returned safely with the legions to Italy, fearing no subsequent Gallic uprising; for he knew with certainty that he had left none who either dared to rise or, if they did rise, need be feared.”

This is Roman history.

Thus the last battle Caesar fought in Gaul was at the fortress of Verodunum; from this one may reasonably infer how great already then were its fame and strength, since there the precipitous victory of fortunate Caesar lingered for so long amid delays beyond all the wars of Gaul; since its townspeople alone, after all the Gauls had been defeated, maintained the final act of war for liberty even against Caesar himself; and since, after they had been captured and subdued, Caesar, as history attests, feared no one else. Since we find no older testimony of Verdun’s antiquity, in order to mark this event by a definite date, the year then was, so far as can be gathered from histories, the seven-hundredth from the founding of Rome, the second year of the 182nd Olympiad, the fifty-second year before the Lord’s Incarnation.

It is, moreover, the common opinion of all that, during the days of your episcopate, while excavations were being made within the city for works, the very hidden channel of the now-exhausted water of which this passage speaks was found underground. Although the site has changed from antiquity, it is nevertheless readily apparent to anyone looking that it was as described here. We find that this town was then called *Veludunum* or *Veredunum*, both here and in other ancient writings; hence the present name Verdun remains. Indeed Antoninus, Caesar’s companion [Note: The itinerary of the emperor Antoninus is wrongly attributed to Antony, Caesar’s contemporary.], in his *Itinerary*, [Note: Wesseling edition, p. 364.] where he lists the cities, towns, and municipalities through which the course of public roads passed, calls this town the fortress of Verodunum.

It was also called the city of the Clavi, either because its wall was studded with nails, [Note: Compare Hugh of Flavigny, loc. cit., p. 292.] or because, as some relate, a hostile siege was obstructed and thus abandoned when the citizens threw iron nails outside the city. Although common opinion holds that the inhabitants of the place were called Clabi and the city Clabonia or Clabia after the people. But, to enumerate the other memorials of wars which we know to have fallen upon this town: under the emperor Marcian, this city and church are certainly believed to have been razed and overthrown by Attila, king of the Huns, who devastated all Gaul like a solitary wild boar from the forest. Blessed bishop Pulcronius is said to have lived at that time. [Note: Compare the Life of Saint Lupus of Troyes, *Acta Sanctorum*, July VII, p. 70.]

The Life of blessed Madelveus also relates that the church itself was burned in his time. [Note: Apart from Hugh’s account of Madelveus’s life, apparently drawn from an older book, only a brief notice of him occurs in Surius VII, 744; it does not contain this material. It is found in Hugh, p. 345.] Under Hildinus likewise, bishop of worthy memory, Hildinus’s own written lament bears witness to how King Charles gave the church of Theologia, together with other possessions, which had been taken from the church of Verdun, to a certain Adelelmus; and to the great evils the bishop endured in recovering it. So too does Pope Nicholas’s letter on behalf of Adelelmus. [Note: I sought this letter in vain; compare Calmet I, p. 638, II; Roussel, p. 132.] In the thirty-seventh year of Bishop Dado, fire consumed the city and the entire church. There books, the memorials of the holy fathers, and the records of the church’s affairs were burned. [Note: See the passage published in *SS.* IV, p. 38.] Certain writings recount that Boso Guntrannus, a tyrannical man, and this bishop Dado devastated one another by reciprocal killings, plundering, and fires.

There is also a charter of Bishop Dado, [Note: “bishop” in manuscript 2.] relating many notable things and confirming them concerning Hatto, Berhard, [Note: *berarhdo* in manuscript 1.] and himself, with respect to the ecclesiastical estate. [Note: See *SS.* IV, p. 37.] Under these bishops [Note: “the same” in manuscript 2.] came the incursion of the Northmen into Gaul; among other afflictions it severely troubled this bishopric, and, after churches had been burned, even martyred certain canons of Saint Vitonus and Saint Germanus, as we find also in an epitaph, whose ending is this:

> Your brother Haimo dies amid the slaughter of the devout;  
> He dies for the Lord and is present united with you.  
>
> On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March  
> The Northmen cut his throat; in heaven the martyr triumphs.

[Note: Manuscript 1 has *Haymo*, and likewise *epytaphyo* and very frequently *y* for *i*.]

Bishop Berhard [Note: *berardus* in manuscript 1.] restored eight canons in the ruined basilica of Saint Vitonus and reassigned its possessions to the church itself. In the first year of Bishop Bernuin, the most cruel people of the Hungarians invaded this bishopric, burned almost everything, and either killed or carried off the inhabitants. The Life of Saint Basolus reports that they were then divinely repelled from the monastery of Bellilocus, which is in honor of Saint Maurice. [Note: See *SS.* IV, p. 517, note.] A letter of the Verdun clergy concerning these misfortunes exists. [Note: It seems to have been lost, unless he means the letter addressed to the bishop of Verdun, published by D’Achéry and Martène, which sets out the origins and devastations of the Hungarians. On it see especially Roussel, p. CLI.]

Because Bertharius had omitted these matters in the episcopal deeds, your most devoted venerable Hugo, our monk, [Note: Perhaps *vestri*, “of your household,” should be read.] compelled me, unwilling though I was, with excessive insistence to gather them briefly here into one and transcribe them for your commendation. And because what follows from here to the time of Bishop Theoderic is found arranged by someone, [Note: *SS.* IV, pp. 45–51.] the aforesaid adviser of ours insistently required me to compile carefully from Theoderic himself down to the present time everything that had occurred. Where good things are related, I know that they will please all good people; but if the faults of some persons, which I could not pass over in weaving history, are recorded, I pray that no one be angry with me, since I have exaggerated no one’s crime in words and history was bound to follow necessary truth.

[Col. 0923] END OF THE LETTER.

## PROLOGUE TO THE FOLLOWING WORK ON THE DEEDS OF THE BISHOPS OF VERDUN BEGINS

[Col. 0923C]

We write, for the praise and glory of blessed Mary, ever Virgin Mother of God, the memorable and report-worthy events that occurred in this her bishopric of Verdun in peace and war. Since the deeds of the earlier bishops of this city, so far as they could be gathered, are contained in writing down to the times of Bishop Theoderic, we take the beginning of our account from Theoderic himself and shall carry it down to the present day. We rightly dedicate this little work to Lord Bishop Albero, since it was written about his predecessors and ends in him.

[Col. 0924C]

### 1.

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1048 [1047], according to Dionysius, [Note: Corrected in manuscript 2. Note: Hugh of Flavigny, *SS.* VIII, p. 406, seems more correctly to indicate the year 1047.] after the venerable Richard, Theoderic became bishop of this city of Verdun. [Note: “of this city of Verdun” is absent in manuscript 2.] He was the thirty-seventh from blessed Sanctinus, our first bishop, [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “first, as they relate.”] a man endowed with noble birth, character, and wisdom. A German by origin, [Note: *theuthonicus* in manuscript 2.] he had been a canon of the church of Basel, born to a very noble father named Gozelo. [Note: *gocelone* in manuscript 2.]

In the same year Waleran was appointed abbot of this monastery of Saint Vitonus after the abbot Richard of holy memory. He had long been a monk of that monastery, having formerly been count of Breteuil in France. [Note: Hugh of Flavigny, *SS.* VIII, p. 406, names Gelduin. Note: “Of Breteuil.”] For in the war which Duke Gozelo and his son Godfrey nobly fought at Bar against Count Odo, who was invading Lotharingia with all the forces of France, and in which Odo himself fell, this same Waleran had served under the said Odo. His heel was cut and he was seriously wounded; despairing of life, he was received by Abbot Richard and had then already spent ten years in the training-ground of the monastic order. He presided over this monastery for fifteen years; together with it he also undertook administration of the abbey of Aremar [Note: Moustier-Ramey.] as a gift from Count Theobald, son of the aforementioned Odo. There he is still buried and rests.

### 2.

In those days Duke and Margrave Godfrey, son of Duke Gozelo, had rebelled for a second time against Emperor Henry [Note: *henricum* in manuscripts 1 and 2.] because the duchy of the Moselle had been taken from him. He had held it jointly with his father, the duke, as protector after the death of Theoderic, duke of Bar, son of the most noble Duke Frederick and Beatrice, sister of Hugh Capet, king of the Franks. Theoderic’s son was the younger Frederick, who died in 1033 before his father, [Note: This seems to be an error; compare Stenzel, *Frank Kaisser*, II, p. 116.] in the first flower of youth. Frederick’s two daughters, nobly brought up after his death, were Beatrice, given by the king in marriage to Boniface, margrave of Italy, and Sophia, given to Count Louis of Montzon. [Note: *lodouvico* in manuscript 1.]

Because their father’s duchy fell to neither of them but was given by the king to Count Gerard of Châtenois in 1048, [Note: This occurred long after Frederick’s death; see Stenzel, loc. cit. Note: “Of Châtenois.”] Godfrey, who had been appointed their protector, seemed therefore to have taken up just arms against the emperor. The emperor had already, among many other acts, disinherited him in his court of the county of this city, which he had held from his predecessors; he had handed the county itself to Richard, bishop of the city, for him to transfer to another whom he judged suitable. For this reason the duke is said to have been hostile to the bishop.

Even earlier, in the time of Bishop Rambert, the knights of Bouillon, retainers of the father of that same duke, had overwhelmed and killed within the city the most noble count Louis of Chiny, son of Count Otto and father of another Louis, grandfather of our lord bishop Albero, because episcopal authority had placed him at the head of the aforementioned county of the city. The same hostility of the duke soon harassed Bishop Theoderic also, because he too had not recognized the duke’s lordship over the named county.

In the second year of his episcopate the duke himself and Baldwin, count of Flanders, entered this city with a strong force in 1047 and burned it out of hatred for Caesar, committing manifold slaughter. [Note: See Hermann of Reichenau, *Annals*, s.a. 1047, *SS.* V, p. 127.] The duke wished to preserve the city’s monasteries unharmed by fire; but suddenly a conquering flame seized the greater church of the Holy Mother of God and, despite the futile resistance of the duke and his troop of soldiers, consumed it utterly. A great treasure and written records of the church’s affairs were burned there. So great were the losses then suffered by the city itself and the church itself that many citizens and clerics fled the place and scattered elsewhere. Tradition says that twenty-four canons from that burned church then departed for Hungary because of poverty, and it is known that they never returned.

Therefore, fearing God’s wrath, the duke made peace with the bishop, restored the hundreds of jurisdictions and estates of the church that he had seized, and submitted himself to public penance. Nearly naked and barefoot, with knees and elbows bent, dragging himself along the ground in expiation, he proceeded from the upper part of the city to before the high altar of the church which he had burned. There too, it is said, he subjected himself to many blows. [Note: Compare Lambert’s *Annals*, *SS.* V, p. 154.] He also bestowed for rebuilding the church the villages under his jurisdiction of Pusvillare [Note: *pufuillare* in manuscript 1?] and Areium, [Note: Peuvillers (Puviller in Roussel) and Arey near Metz; Wasseburg and Calmet.] with their harbor and fishing-rights, and then many gifts besides—yet gifts far smaller than the injuries inflicted. He claimed the county of the city itself as though it were an inheritance legitimately derived from his fathers.

And although, while most hostile to the emperor, he burned the palace at Nijmegen, a work of marvelous craftsmanship, beyond repair; removed in war the most noble Albert of the castle of Longwy, [Note: He had governed Lotharingia before the above-mentioned Gerard.] whom the emperor had set over him as duke; and afflicted all Lotharingia with killings, burnings, and plundering in 1047—yet for the twenty-two years that he afterwards lived [Note: He died 24 December 1069.] he was kind to the people of Verdun alone. Through the venerable Ermenfrid, archdeacon of the church of Verdun, he succeeded in being reconciled with the king in 1049. Later he went to Italy, rendered noble service to Margrave Boniface, and, when Boniface died, married his wife Beatrice and betrothed their only daughter Matilda [Note: Matilda was daughter of Beatrice and Boniface.] to his son Godfrey. Thereupon both were margraves of Italy and dukes of Lotharingia.

At Beatrice’s urging, that same duke held within this city a general council of counts and princes and made many arrangements beneficial to the city and church; these were recorded also in ecclesiastical privileges. [Note: Compare Godfrey’s charter, copied from the register of the monastery of Saint Vitonus, in Wassebourg, fol. CCXLI; Calmet, *Probb.* I, p. 451.] When dying, he ordered that he be buried in the very church which he had burned. His son and successor Godfrey likewise, throughout the eight years that he held the duchy from 1069, was never troublesome but good to our people; and when dying, on 26 February 1076, he granted to the church of Verdun—where he rests—the estate of Gemmatium, [Note: Jametz in Roussel.] which was under his jurisdiction.

### 3.

In rebuilding from its foundations the church and the walls of the burned city, Bishop Theoderic’s great labor, concern, and industry shone forth; hence his memory is blessed among posterity. For this rebuilding work Wazo, venerable bishop of Liège, gave fifty pounds of silver. Count Frederick of Toul likewise transferred for the rebuilding and support of the church the usufruct of his forest of Argonne. [Note: Argonne.]

At that time Archdeacon Ermenfrid, endowed with wisdom, good character, and holiness, completed the church of Saint Mary Magdalene which he himself had already founded. From the gifts lavishly bestowed upon him by princes and faithful people because of his merits and services, he endowed it, according to his means, for the use of those serving God there. Above all, a venerable nobleman, advocate of the city, aided him in this rebuilding work. With his wife Bertranda, by devoted generosity, he offered the site on which the church was founded, many other allods, and in addition no small body of dependents. [Note: Manuscript 2 has *optulit*, “offered.”] He too rests there, beneath a fitting epitaph written concerning him. [Note: Manuscript 1 has *epytaphio*; manuscript 2, “with a worthy epitaph.”]

Moreover, Ermenfrid, through the renown of his religious devotion and also through his exhortation and friendship, drew after himself many clerics from distant lands and attached them to his own church and likewise to that of the Holy Mother of God. Through their diligence both churches flourished in every increase of possessions and religious life.

I shall not pass over one of these, the scholastic Martin. As he lay in the agony of death, unable to speak for two days already, he suddenly, to everyone’s amazement, solemnly began the morning praises of the Blessed Mother of God and sang them through without stumbling. Then, entering upon the office of the Mass, after the Communion had been solemnly sung, “Make your face to shine upon your servant,” [Note: Sung on Septuagesima Sunday.] he breathed out his spirit amid the sacred words, accomplished in good works.

[Col. 0928A]

### 4.

In these days Pope Saint Leo IX [Note: “saint” is absent in manuscript 2.], formerly bishop of Toul, came into Gaul and held a synod at Reims in October 1049, where, after dedicating his church, he translated the bones of blessed Remigius. At Ermenfrid’s own request, Bishop Theoderic honorably brought him thence to this city to consecrate the aforesaid church. That church was dedicated by the holy pope himself, with three archbishops present—Everard of Trier, Alinard of Lyons, and Hugh of Chrysopolis—and many bishops, in the third year of Lord Theoderic’s episcopate.

The pope, moved with pity for the ruins of the burned city and church, and for the clergy and people who prostrated themselves before him as soon as he arrived, issued to the church of the Blessed Mother of God a privilege in place of all the burned records of its possessions; [Note: See it in Mabillon, *De arte diplomatica*, supplement, p. 99, and Roussel, *Probb.*, p. 3 (Jaffé, *Regesta pontificum*, no. 3191).] likewise to the church he had consecrated [Note: In Calmet, I, *Probb.*, p. 423 (Jaffé, no. 3192).] and to the monastery of blessed Vitonus. [Note: Jaffé, no. 3190.]

Coming to Liège, he took with him Frederick, brother of Duke Godfrey and archdeacon of Saint Lambert. Frederick then became a monk, then abbot of Monte Cassino, and later the pope’s seventh cardinal-deacon. He was the third after that pope, after Victor, to sit in the chair of Saint Peter, being called Stephen by the Romans; Benedict and Nicholas succeeded him—the latter made certain privileges for us—and then Alexander and Gregory VII.

At the synod at Reims the pope had likewise deposed, on 5 October, Hugh, bishop of Langres, brother of Abbot Waleran, [Note: *walleranni* in manuscript 2.] on account of certain criminal charges. [Note: See Anselm’s history of the dedication of the church of Saint Remigius in Mabillon, *Acta*, VI.1, p. 721 ff.] But Hugh followed the pope as far as Rome, to experience his mercy. He entered the full synod over which the pope presided naked and barefoot, carrying with trembling hand the rods with which he was to be beaten, and singing in a tearful voice this antiphon:

> “The father gave the penitent son the first robe and likewise a ring; and, giving him shoes also, he celebrated a great banquet. We possess the first robe in the font, and the ring, the seal of faith.”

At the sight of him all burst into sobs, shed tears, and filled the synod with lamentations. The pope himself grieved more than the rest; and, as all interceded for the suppliant accused, he absolved him. Like a merciful father, he ordered the penitent son to be invested with the first robe and the ring of his lost episcopate, and to be shod again with the sandals of peace, provided only that his own church, which he had injured, or any other church should deign to receive him as bishop. Thus he deserved absolution from all. He began his return journey, fell ill while travelling, [Note: *itenerando* in manuscript 2.] requested and received from his companions, Cluniac monks, the monastic habit in the name of our monastery over which his brother presided, and died happily. He was entered among the deaths of our community.

5. But thereafter Bishop Theoderic suffered very many troubles from soldiers. For when he was asserting for himself, free from them, the city and bishopric which they had formerly oppressed, Count Rodulf of Crépy—stepfather of Philip, king of the Franks—again burned this city because the bishop refused him the twenty pounds yearly which he received from his predecessors in return for not attacking this region. Likewise Alo of the castle of Dun, a freeborn man, while the bishop was besieging and taking his stronghold at the village of Rouvre, which Alo had violently seized from the bishopric, set this city ablaze, taking advantage of the bishop’s absence and that of his fighting men. Yet both were checked and repulsed by the bishop’s skill in arms, and the property of the bishopric was restored to its freedom. Thus under this bishop the city was burned for the third time.

[Note: Col. 0929: *rodulphus* 1.]

[Note: Col. 0929C: Crépy.]

[Note: Col. 0929: *phylippi* 1; *philippi* 2.]

6. Moreover, the same bishop restrained by force of arms Count Manasses of the castle of Rethel from invading ecclesiastical property. He led an armed expedition against the castle of Sainte-Menehould, which was most hostile to him. Terrified by this threat, the inhabitants of the castle sent him the keys of the fortress while he was still on the road, humbly sought peace, and escaped the siege through their prayers. But the bishop, lest he bring back no trophy at all for the Church, turned the same expedition against the equally hostile castle of Santumnium, besieged it, took it, and destroyed it. Both castles belonged to the aforesaid Count Manasses. He likewise subdued Dudo, a freeborn man, and his brothers, sons of Haubert, when they rose against him; and, after fortifying a stronghold before Clermont, he took the castle itself from them.

7. Further, when Duke Godfrey the Hunchback had been murdered by treachery in Frisia in 1076, and was honorably buried in this city beside his father by Duke Godfrey III—his sister’s son, whom the dying duke had designated as heir—the bishop himself attempted to remove the county of the city from beneath the yoke of the Bouillon lordship, which seemed to have oppressed the city excessively. Accordingly, he took it away from Godfrey of Bouillon, who, after taking possession of the castle of Bouillon, succeeded to the duchy; he judged the moment opportune because the king and many leading men of the realm had risen in arms against him as a duke of doubtful legitimacy. He granted the county as a benefice to the most noble Count Albert of Namur, who was one of Godfrey’s enemies.

When this same Albert besieged the castle of Bouillon, claiming it as more properly his inheritance than that of the aforesaid Godfrey, the bishop came to his aid with all the forces of his bishopric. But the very warlike duke quickly came to the help of his enclosed men; gathering an army, he raised the enemy siege, killing many nobles. Then, greatly angered against the bishop, he captured Count Henry of Grandpré, who had first rebelled violently against him, released him from chains, and sent him as an enemy into the territory of Verdun. Henry promptly carried out his orders, committing many hostile acts against our people by sword, fire, and plunder.

The duke himself also fortified a castle in the town of Stenay, which was under his jurisdiction and projected into the borders of the bishopric; through it he pursued grave hostilities against our people. Therefore the bishop besieged it, having gathered auxiliaries from every side and the aforesaid Albert with all his men. But behold, the duke again came to help his own people, equipped with a strong force of warriors. The battle was exceedingly fierce, the clash most bloody, until both exhausted armies were recalled from the slaughter at the command of their leaders. This happened in the fortieth year of Theoderic’s episcopate, and many nobles fell there (perhaps 1086). Neither side gained the victory; but the bishop did not lift the siege: he received his men into tents, while the duke took his into the castle.

Then the duke sent very swift messengers and, through his brothers Eustace and Baldwin, summoned from all Germany and France an army to assist him. When the bishop received certain news that they were coming down upon him, he was frightened; he dreaded to make judgment by bloodshed and raised the siege, at the prompting, exhortation, and warning of that very messenger. This was Henry, the venerable bishop of Liège. His brother, Frederick count of Toul, and his brother’s sons Rainald and Peter—men who would later be renowned in the Jerusalem expedition—were then fighting there under Bishop Theoderic. Henry was dear and faithful both to our bishop and to Duke Godfrey: to the bishop because under him, in the church of Verdun, he had completed the first stages of his schooling and received the archdeaconry from him; to the duke because, seven years earlier, through his efforts, he had been raised from archdeacon of Verdun to bishop of Liège.

For when Emperor Henry III was campaigning against Duke Rudolf, who, having assumed the diadem, had taken the kingship in obedience to the Roman Church and had already occupied Saxony, Duke Godfrey, reconciled with the emperor, had come to his assistance with many soldiers. And behold, after Rudolf had been killed in 1080, while victory was being celebrated, noble envoys of the church of Liège arrived, seeking from the emperor’s gift and judgment a bishop for themselves. Then, through the action of the same duke, the imperial majesty bestowed upon the same envoys the office of bishop, offered to Henry the archdeacon in this city. The duke himself accompanied his beloved kinsman from there as far as Liège and assigned him as bishop to that city, where he shone among its former bishops with every distinction.

Theoderic, therefore, a true defender of liberty, fought for his country, as we have related, even beyond his strength. In this bishop’s time, on the Kalends of August, during the morning hour, lightning burst from heaven into the church, fell among the chanting clergy, and struck dead the priest Dominic, who was chanting the collect, and the subdeacon Alger, who was presiding over the choir; all the rest were terrified.

8. Let us say something also about his generosity and devotion. Once he went to Jerusalem, to the Lord’s sepulchre, and many times to Rome, to pray at the holy apostles or to conduct before the Apostolic See the affairs of the church entrusted to him. The generosity he displayed on his journeys appeared remarkable and praiseworthy both to the emperor of the Greeks and to the Roman pope.

When Gervase, archbishop of Reims, had come to visit him at Verdun accompanied by a great multitude of Frenchmen, Theoderic returned the courtesy of his hospitality: he came to revisit Gervase as far as the walls of Reims with a no smaller company of Lotharingians. From above the closed gates of Reims Gervase sang to meet him through two singers: “You have shaken the earth and troubled it” (Psalm 60 [Vulgate 59]). Theoderic answered in turn through two singers: “Heal its breaches, for it has been shaken” (ibid.). Then, celebrating Mass at Saint-Remi, he left there, in memory of himself, his chapel of great value when he returned home.

For his church he purchased at great price from Emperor Henry III the estate of Dura with all its appurtenances; also the castle of Miroalht with its forest, and the abbey of Juvigny, from Marchioness Matilda. To say nothing of other churches, he gave and confirmed to our monastery—that is, the monastery of Saint Vitonus—all the altars of churches which his predecessors had bestowed on us, together with the ban of Mount Saint Vitonus.

And because under Abbot Grimold, who presided over this place for fifteen years after Waleran’s death, religious observance was declining through the insolence of certain persons, and could not be corrected through him, Theoderic removed him and appointed in his place the venerable Rodulf, monk of Saint Agericus, distinguished in religious life, learning, and character. Rodulf, by his own efforts and through other worthy persons sought from his own church and that of Saint Agericus, introduced here the highest standard of order and very much good. Indeed the good reputation of their religious life attracted and joined to this church many diligent men even from distant lands; through their excellence this place has deserved to be ennobled and magnified down to the present. At that time the church of Blessed Agericus, from which this abbot had been taken, flourished so greatly with religious men that, during that same period, twelve abbots from among its sons were appointed to various churches, all men of great achievements.
