9. Let us come to the most grievous matter, in which, to our great sorrow, dangerous times detracted greatly from a bishop highly worthy of praise. The cause was as follows. In the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate, that sword-like strife between kingdom and priesthood had already arisen which engulfed the whole Roman Empire. Pope Gregory VII of Rome had excommunicated Emperor Henry for his many alleged crimes in 1076: namely, because of his wife Queen Praxedis, whom he had shamefully subjected to the fornications and insults of servants; because of various injustices and oppressions of churches; and especially because, contrary to the ancient sacred canons, he did not cease—although forbidden by anathema—to confer investitures of churches by staff and ring according to the custom of his predecessors.

But Henry, angered by this, broke into Rome with war in 1083, sacrilegiously seized the pope while he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass, and cast him into chains. The pope was then rescued by the duke of Apulia, but Henry drove him from Rome and, adding a second injustice, intruded into his chair a certain Wibert of Ravenna, a false bishop who had for seven years been disobedient, rebellious, and anathematized against the Apostolic See. Then the whole realm was divided against itself; every city was split into two parties, some defending the cause of the imperial court, others that of the holy Apostolic See, and each pursuing the opposing party. The Apostolic See struck all its enemies with anathema and excluded them from the sacred mysteries; the imperial court captured and exiled those hostile to it, depriving them of their offices. At last each party pursued its enemies with sword, slaughter, and fire.

Two parties arose also in this city. The bishop, badly influenced by his own people and excessively overborne either by love or fear of the prince, turned toward the emperor’s side. But the venerable Rodulf and his brethren zealously adhered to the Apostolic See. Hence their old, pious friendship was dissolved, so completely that the bishop drove the abbot himself and his brethren—after inflicting many injuries upon them—from this church. Yet the contrary consequences of their expulsion for righteousness’ sake soon turned to good. For the brethren, taken to Burgundy, were received like angels of God by Geronton, the venerable abbot of the church of Dijon, during the seven years for which that bishop survived; they were well treated in every respect. Through that occasion, a sisterly fraternity between our church and that church arose, worthier and firmer, we believe, than the ancient fraternity between Sabines and Romans.

The Apostolic See gave Abbot Rodulf a privilege to reconcile, in three bishoprics—Verdun, Metz, and Toul—all those returning to their senses from the Henrician schism. In those days Fulcrad, abbot of Saint Paul’s, with the consent of the aforesaid bishop, seized this abbey with certain of his followers. Under him this church lost three very precious cloths, two copes of great value, two silver candlesticks of six marks, the wine-market dues of the city, and the *pugillum* [a measure or milling due], as well as the churches of Marly and Métion, and many other things.

When this same bishop had sent Fulcrad and Dean Richer as envoys to seal the altar of Saint Michael, because that church wished to transfer itself from the bishopric of Verdun to that of Toul and, though summoned to a hearing, refused to come to Verdun, the household of that church dragged them out after attacking them and imprisoned them in chains at Bar. Consequently that town and church came to be burned in a hostile episcopal action.

But I should judge Dean Richer, of holy memory, and likewise among the clergy Engebert, Hairic, Gezo, and Boso, worthy of every praise for faith, zeal, and religious devotion. Through their persistence the ecclesiastical order then became so strong that all the clergy, under their leadership, attended reading, meals, the dormitory, and choir together, with no one excused; those unwilling, even the more noble, were compelled with greater strictness.

But when old age and excessive bodily infirmity had exhausted the bishop at last, and his final day pressed upon him, and no one was present to reconcile him to the Apostolic See, Abbot Rodulf sent two of his monks to reconcile him: Gerard, formerly an archdeacon, and Gerbert, later abbot of Saint Maurice. As they stood beside his bed, he immediately greeted them with gestures, since he could not speak, and asked for and received reconciliation. For as they set out, point by point, his offenses against the Apostolic See, at each point he appeared, with pleading eyes, hands, and beating of the breast like a penitent, to confess guilt and seek pardon. But when they put before him, “Confess your guilt concerning the monks of Saint Vitonus, whom you expelled,” he struck his breast repeatedly with both fists, groaned more deeply, and sighed more profoundly, so that all who saw burst into tears. Then, absolved by them, he shortly afterward gave up his spirit (1089, 28 April). They reported this satisfaction of his to the venerable Rodulf. Rodulf brought it before the synod presided over by the legate of the Apostolic See, Hugh, formerly bishop of Die and then archbishop of Lyons; his satisfaction was approved by all.

He held the bishopric for forty-three years: a man capable and praiseworthy in many respects, if only this stain had not been upon his glory at the end.

Henschel V, p. 507) says of this passage: “It seems to be the same as the right of measure or milling due, namely the payment which a lord exacts from vassals for the measuring of grain or its grinding in his mills.” Compare Honorius’s letters in the cited place: “the market of Mount Saint Vitonus, the toll, with the grain *pugillum*, the plea and correction of measures, tithes, etc.”]

10. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1088 [the note dates it 1089], Richer, dean of the church of Metz, a pious and honorable man, was elected after Theoderic. Since no other way was open to him, he was led to the imperial court and, contrary to the prohibition of the Apostolic See, received the episcopal staff from the emperor. He gave his brothers Albert, Bezelin, and John—most noble men—as hostages, that he would never depart from the emperor’s fidelity and communion. On returning, he was received with honor. But because he had incurred the offense of the Roman Church, he remained seven years without episcopal blessing, until Abbot Rodulf—whom, immediately upon his election, Richer had honorably recalled with all his monks—gave counsel and brought him to Lyons in Burgundy. There the aforesaid Archbishop Hugh, after Richer’s renunciation of the Henrician party, ordained him priest on Holy Saturday, 16 April 1093, and promoted him to the episcopate on the feast day, 17 April.

Returning from there with the favor and honor of the Apostolic See, he was received most fittingly by his fellow bishops Poppo of Metz and Pibo of Toul, through Rodulf’s agency, and by the whole city on the Sunday of the Mercy of the Lord, 1 May. As a messenger of peace and a saving star, he immediately calmed all things, ending the wars in the bishopric.

Henry of Grandpré alone still maintained his old hostilities. Since, like a robber, he secretly plundered whatever he could and immediately fled, he could not easily be crushed. When Peter, count and son of Frederick of Toul, one of the bishop’s barons, happened to reproach him for this at Châlons, Henry fiercely replied: “On such-and-such a day I shall come before Verdun. Meet me, if you dare, and let us match ourselves in the field.” Peter gladly accepted this; both pledged their faith and swore to one another that they would not fail.

The appointed day came, and Peter, armed with the bishop’s barons, awaited the promised enemy at Verdun. But Henry learned through certain intimate and familiar persons in the city, who brought him information concerning all our plans, what was happening; he postponed his arrival. Our men, thinking that he was doing the same, went out of the city and pretended to return home, as though they despaired of his coming. But when Henry heard from his usual informants that they had withdrawn to their own places, he immediately flew with his men to the area before Verdun, drove off booty from the neighboring villages, and began his usual retreat. Yet our men, who had feigned their return by stratagem, had already occupied by a cross-road the route by which the enemy would return. Armed citizens also followed the raiders closely. Thus the enemies were attacked from front and rear; a fierce battle began; many were killed, more wounded and captured, and the rest fled in terror with the count himself. It is reported that as many as six times twenty fighting men were captured, with such a quantity of horses and arms that our people were almost enriched by them.

Yet Henry did not cease attacking the church of Verdun until he incurred the judgment of a dreadful death. Having heard of the successes nobly achieved for Jerusalem by Duke Godfrey and his most renowned companions-in-arms in 1099, he resolved to undertake a second expedition after them. He came to Verdun and took the cross, intending to go; but, overtaken by God’s wrath and seized by madness, he miserably died there without accomplishing anything.

[Note: Col. 0935D: 1089. Hugh of Flavigny, p. 472.]

11. Dudo of Clermont also, who had ruined the property of the bishopric, was staying at Verdun without regard for the bishop’s gentleness; there he was captured by the clerics and shut in prison. Since the leading men and barons were indignant that this had been done by such a class of men, the clerics, by way of satisfaction, each carried a schoolbook for one stade before him.

[Note: Col. 0935: *clarofonte* 1.]

[Note: Col. 0935: *clericis*, corrected to *clericatis*, 2.]

[Note: Col. 0935D–0936D: A noteworthy matter, because it was a form of honorable amends observed at that time and in the preceding one. WASS.]

12. In the year of Richer’s consecration to the episcopate, Pope Urban held a synod at Clermont in Auvergne in 1095, to which Richer sent his gifts and envoys. At that synod, among many other acts, the aforesaid pope sent forth a proclamation through the whole Church of the West: soldiers were to vow their military strength to God and undertake an expedition to free the holy places of Jerusalem, which Saracen impiety had seized when the strength of the Byzantine Empire failed. At this proclamation all nations were stirred; renouncing the civil wars by which the kingdoms of West and North were oppressed, many nobles vowed their arms to God against the Turks for the holy places.

Among these, two brothers from our territory stood out: Duke Godfrey and Count Baldwin; likewise Baldwin of the castle of Rethel, nephew of the aforesaid Count Manasses. All three, one after another, became magnanimous kings after the Holy City had been recovered by arms. Godfrey himself, planning the holy journey in 1096, renounced the arms which he had raised against us, made peace with Bishop Richer, and gave in perpetuity to Holy Mary Mouzay and Stenay, with the castle which he had erected against us and all their appurtenances. The bishop gave him for the expenses of the holy expedition many weights of gold and silver which he had collected from the churches of the bishopric. Confirming the aforesaid allods to the Holy Mother of God, with priests from the whole bishopric standing in stoles, he pronounced anathema upon anyone who should thereafter take them away from the tables of the clergy of Verdun.

When Marchioness Matilda, widow of Duke Godfrey the Hunchback, claimed these same allods again as her paternal inheritance, the bishop once more redeemed them from that lady at great price at the synod of Guastalla through his envoys, Abbot Gerbert and the cantor Azelin. At that synod Pope Paschal, under anathema, confirmed them free from every bond of exaction and claim; Bishop Richer likewise, from his own see, confirmed them in perpetuity to the church of Verdun, renewing a similar excommunication against whosoever should attempt to take them away.

The county of the city also, over which discord had so often arisen, he received from the same duke and granted, as a favor to him, to his brother Baldwin. Baldwin, setting out upon the holy journey with his brother the duke, soon afterward returned it; and the bishop, softened by Count Theoderic of Bar’s gifts and services, handed it over to him upon the advice of his men, so that, because he seemed able greatly to help or harm the place through his position and strength, he might devote himself entirely to our advantage.

The same duke, when departing, caused the castle of Montfaucon, which he had built in the bishopric, to be demolished lest it do harm in the future. He also gave the castle of Bouillon with all its appurtenances to Saint Lambert at Liège, receiving from Otbert, bishop of that place, thirteen hundred marks of silver and a pound of gold for the undertaking of the holy journey.

Thus that illustrious lordship of Bouillon, happily begun with Count Godfrey, father of our bishop Adalbero and of the two dukes Godfrey and Gozelo, and also of the two counts Herman and Frederick—all of whom, with their numerous descendants, shone above others either by martial courage or religious devotion in the Church, and with their mother Matilda enriched this place above all mortals—ended more happily and more holy in this Godfrey, and was divided among many. For his duchy was first granted by imperial hand to the count of Limburg and afterward to the count of Louvain. Albert, brother of the bishop, claimed the lordship of Brie for himself under the protection of Marchioness Matilda, widow of Godfrey the Hunchback. The same Albert received from his brother Bishop Richer the bishop’s village of Rouvre, for his lifetime only and in usufruct only, so that he might assist him in conducting affairs; his descendants now unjustly claim it as their own.

Moreover, Duke Godfrey, with his glorious comrades-in-arms, crossed the Hellespont and took Nicaea, Bithynia, Asia, Pamphylia, Phrygia, and the great city of Antioch through countless labors of battle, siege, and hunger, and expelled the pagans in 1098. Advancing also into Syria and Judaea, he recovered the holy places and the Holy City by arms in the year one thousand one hundred from the Incarnation of the Prince of Life, and earned from God the kingdom of the Holy City in place of the duchy of Lotharingia—although he never permitted himself to be called its king, but only its advocate.

In the same year Pope Urban, successor of Victor and most ardent defender of ecclesiastical privilege against imperial violence, died a blessed death; so too did the venerable Abbot Rodulf, most steadfast supporter of the Apostolic See. Their successors in office and zeal were Pope Paschal and Abbot Lawrence.

13. Meanwhile, King Henry heard that Bishop Richer, having renounced him, had gone over to the Apostolic See. Angered, he demanded back the hostages given to him and cast one of them, John, into chains. The other two approached their brother, the bishop, asking him to free them from their hostage-status under the law of nations. Hemmed in on every side, and like Saint Martin—who under Maximus unwillingly entered into the wicked communion of bishops at Trier—he went to court, offered satisfaction to the emperor, entered into communion with him, promised him firm loyalty for the future, and so freed the hostages.

Returning, he suspended himself from the divine office for three years as one guilty before the Apostolic See. During that time our church did not communicate with him. When some maliciously reported this to him, he rebuffed them, saying: “Leave the servants of God alone, leave them alone; for they are better men than I.” Such was his humility and patience that he never himself inflicted injury upon anyone.

At length he sent Abbot Lawrence, Archdeacon Guy, and others to Rome as envoys for him, seeking communion and the favor of the Apostolic See. Pope Paschal first absolved the envoys from communion with their bishop, then gave them letters to Archbishop Hugh of Lyons for the bishop’s absolution. Richer came to Lyons, asked and received absolution from him who had consecrated him. Returning to Verdun, he did not enter until all the canons and monks had assembled at Saint Vitonus. He absolved them all alike for the communion which they had had with him while he was excommunicated, and compelled them to swear that they would keep faith with the Apostolic See.

Everything else prospered under Bishop Richer. In the eighteenth year of his episcopate, on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, 29 June 1107, he celebrated the solemnities of Mass in our monastery and, upon the altar, granted to those apostles and Saint Vitonus the allod of Paul’s Cross and the ban of Marculf’s Court by privilege; he commended to them his soul and body, and chose burial in their monastery. He then went to the church’s allod at Valdentia in the Vosges, fell ill, and was carried by boat down the Moselle to Trier. There Bruno, archbishop of the city, anointed him and fortified him with viaticum; he died in peace.

Bruno washed his body and most generously clothed it in his own pontifical vestments. Archdeacon Guy brought it back in a carriage, and Richard, bishop of Albano and legate of the Roman See, honorably buried him at Saint Vitonus, as he had directed, though the clergy opposed it, before the altar of Blessed Lawrence, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1107.

14. This Richard, formerly a canon of Metz [Note: [Col. 0939] “Mettensis” in witness 1, at this point.], had been expelled by the king and the Guibertines, together with his bishop Herimann [Note: [Col. 0939] “Herimann” in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 0939] “his” omitted in witness 1.], for the faith of the Apostolic See; and for that reason the Roman Church had so exalted him. His brother Arnulf was then our convert under Abbot Lawrence and afterwards died a monk. While he himself was still a knight, he had adhered so faithfully to the Apostolic See [Col. 0940A] [Note: [Col. 0939] “still” in witness 2.] that he sent to Abbot Lanzo of Saint Vincent [Note: [Col. 0939] “of Metz” is added afterwards in witness 2.]—who likewise had been expelled together with Bishop Herimann [Note: [Col. 0939] “Herimann” in witness 1.]—a certain Cono, who had been intruded by the Wibertines into his abbey, captured and bound, to Dijon in Burgundy. He built a cell at Bouzonville [Note: [Col. 0940C] Bouzonville.] from an allodial property under his own jurisdiction and gave it, with everything, to blessed Vitonus.

15. Before those days Manasses, archbishop of Reims, had died (A.D. 1106), and that church had chosen Richard, archdeacon of Verdun, as its pastor. His brother Count Henry of Grandpré [Note: [Col. 0940C] Grandpré.] had already died, and his other brother Baldwin, who after him had undertaken another expedition for Jerusalem, had been martyred by the Turks; Richard was then governing the county of Grandpré. Accordingly Pope Paschal, by letters and through his aforesaid legate, the bishop of Albano [Col. 0940B], instructed that same archdeacon to be ordained deacon by the bishop of Albano—for he was still a subdeacon—and then to be consecrated archbishop of Reims. But Richard obeyed nothing in these matters, and the unsuccessful legate departed.

Meanwhile, after Bishop Richer had died [Note: [Col. 0939] “After Bishop Richer had died, the clergy of Verdun chose the archdeacon as pastor for themselves”; deleted in witness 1. Witness 3 reads: “who, having gone from Metz, proceeded.”], the clergy of Verdun chose that same Richard as their bishop [Note: [Col. 0939] “chose” in witness 2.]. He preferred this election to the former one; brought to Metz, he received the pastoral staff from the king’s hand and, on his return, was received with acclamation together with the archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0939] “Trier” in witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 0939] Witness 3 omits “and” through “acclamation.”]. The king himself, with the imperial court, followed (May 1107), and was received on the same day with the applause of the whole city. On the third day [Note: [Col. 0939] Witness 3 reads “But on the third day.”], at Richard’s prompting, the same king besieged the castle of Clermont [Col. 0940C] and compelled it to surrender, because Guy from that castle was ravaging [Note: [Col. 0939] “was laying waste” in witness 3.] the possessions of the bishopric.

King Henry IV himself [Note: [Col. 0940C] Fourth as emperor, fifth as king.], then in the first year of his reign after his father’s death, proved an imitator of that dead father in attacking the Church. Although he, the son, had consigned his father, who had grievously risen against Holy Church, to custody, stripped him of the insignia of kingship, and persecuted him until his death, he nevertheless imitated that same dead man by attacking the Church [Note: [Col. 0939] “the death of his father” corrected to “the father’s death” in witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 0939] Witness 3 omits “King Henry IV himself” through “proved [to be].”].

Meanwhile Pope Paschal [Note: [Col. 0939] “the pope who had succeeded Urban” in witness 3.] held a synod at Troyes in France [Note: [Col. 0939] Omitted in witness 3.]. There, while dealing among other matters with the Guibertines [Note: [Col. 0939] “while dealing, among other things, with the Guibertines” in witness 3.], he is reported to have said: “Richard of Verdun, who has handed himself over to the royal court [Note: [Col. 0939] Witness 3 has the corrupted reading “h) t. se c. r.” for “who has handed himself over to the royal court.”], we hand over to Satan.” [Note: [Col. 0939] “Richard” in witness 2; the name occurs repeatedly.] He then notified the archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0941] “Trier” in witnesses 1 and 2.] and others that Richard was excommunicated.

In the following Lent, when almost all religious persons avoided communion with Richard and his clergy [Note: [Col. 0941] “and mocked him” in witness 1; omitted in witness 3.], he set out for the pope, having instructed his people to obtain absolution from the archbishop from communion with himself. He went to Rome and sought absolution from the pope. After many exchanges of words [Note: [Col. 0941] Witness 3 omits “and” through “exchanges.”], he finally heard this from the pope:

> “Unless you first renounce the investiture of the bishopric which you received from the hand of a layman—that is, the king—and unless you pledge that henceforth you will not concern yourself with it except by our permission, you cannot at all be absolved by us.” [Note: [Col. 0941] Witness 3 reads “afterwards.”]

In response Richard said that he wished to seek advice; he left the pope’s presence (A.D. 1108?), [Col. 0941B] and never returned [Note: [Col. 0941] “he left” in witness 2.]. Instead, threatening his followers that, if they thereafter regarded him as excommunicated, he would hand over them and all that they possessed to destruction, he departed Rome and, after gathering his men, returned home.

After his departure the pope sent this letter:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Lawrence, abbot of Saint Vitonus: greeting and apostolic blessing. Richard of Verdun, coming to us, made no satisfaction to the Church for his guilt [Note: [Col. 0941] Omitted in Wassebourg, fol. CCLXVII, where below it reads *non fecit* (“he did not do [it]”).]. Therefore he was neither received by us into communion nor absolved from the bond of excommunication. Wherefore we command your charity wholly to avoid his association, and to announce that both he and his supporters [Note: [Col. 0941] “and” omitted in Wassebourg; “supporters” is *factores* in witness 3 and Wassebourg.] are excommunicated by us, as also all who knowingly communicate.” [Note: [Col. 0941] The Wassebourg text omits “and all who”; the printed text is syntactically incomplete here.]

The clergy of Verdun, who from the beginning of Richard’s journey to Rome had been absolved by the archbishop, annulled that reconciliation when Richard returned, because, overcome by his favour or fear of him, they communicated with him while he was excommunicated. If anyone refused, he was oppressed by Richard’s faction until he yielded [Note: [Col. 0941] Witness 3 reads “until he ceased.”]. But Abbot Lawrence, full of regard for God, obeyed the Apostolic See in all things, as did all entrusted to him. Therefore discord between the two churches—that is, Saint Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Vitonus—flared daily and became worse day by day [Note: [Col. 0941] “daily” in witness 1.]. Their sons did not communicate with one another; and when the clergy, according to custom, celebrated their station at Saint Vitonus [Col. 0941D], the monks did not attend the clergy’s assembly as they had previously done. After the clergy had departed, the monks purified with holy water everything which they had touched.

16. Meanwhile Archdeacon Guy, who had gone to Rome as Richard’s companion but, while suffering from acute fevers, had been left behind sick at Bologna when Richard returned home, came back from Italy. He heard that the clergy of Verdun were communicating with Richard [Col. 0942A], and therefore feared for himself if he returned to Verdun; he turned aside elsewhere. For while ill in Italy and despairing of life, he had sought someone to provide him with the viaticum and the necessities of his soul, but found no one, since all avoided him as excommunicated. Unless he confessed his fault of communion with Richard and the clergy of Verdun, they threatened that after his death he would be buried on a dungheap.

At last, in order to be reconciled, under danger of death he vowed to God that he would never communicate with Richard or his supporters unless Richard had been absolved by the pope. Three canons of the church of Modena imposed this upon him while he was sick; afterwards the bishop of Parma, acting in the pope’s stead, imposed the same obligation [Note: [Col. 0941] “iddem” in witness 2.] upon him when he was well [Note: [Col. 0941] “then” in witness 2.]. Avoiding, therefore, communion with Richard [Col. 0942B] and the clergy of Verdun, he asked through friends that he might be permitted to enjoy his possessions among them without sharing their communion.

But [Note: [Col. 0941] “Set” in witness 2; it commonly writes *s*.] Richard and the clergy received this most harshly. By letters they ordered him, while he was at Metz, to come within forty days and make satisfaction for having avoided their fellowship. In the meantime Richard seized and dispersed all Guy’s property which he found at Verdun, and directed his followers to seize Guy wherever he might be found. Guy [Note: [Col. 0941] Omitted in witness 2.] approached Richard through relatives and friends, then through abbots and bishops, especially through his own archbishop [Note: [Col. 0941] “him” omitted in witness 1.]. But when he achieved nothing through them, he took letters from them in his support and returned to Rome.

Beyond Cluny he met Richard, bishop of Albano [Col. 0942C], and explained to him, on inquiry, the reason for his journey. The bishop kept him with himself, abandoning his own journey, and sent to Richard at Verdun admonitory and petitionary letters on behalf of Guy and Abbot Lawrence, whom Richard had deprived of his possessions and church. But after his messenger returned with the rejection of both letters and petitions, he sent Guy to the pope with his letters. The pope received and comforted Guy, kept him with himself for ten weeks, and finally sent him back with these two letters (A.D. 1109?):

> “Paschal [Note: [Col. 0941] The editor was unable to collate the remainder with manuscript 2.], bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbots and other clerics, to Count Raynald of Monzón, to Raynard of Toul, and to the other laymen [Note: [Col. 0941] Wassebourg, fol. CCLXVIII, reads “laymen”; witness 1 reads “clerics.”] of the archdeaconry of Guy: greeting and apostolic blessing. For love of Catholic unity [Col. 0942D], we have heard that your archdeacon Guy has been stripped of his possessions by Richard, invader of the church of Verdun. Therefore we commend him to your charity by these present letters. We command that, in churches belonging to monasteries, customary justice be rendered to him and that due obedience be paid to him by clergy and laity alike as archdeacon. Otherwise, until they obey, let them be deprived of divine offices and lose the tithes of their people. But you, sons, to whom God has given secular power and who uphold justice by arms, be his helpers for the reverence of Saint Peter, and restrain his adversaries manfully. We command the same concerning the venerable man, the abbot of Saint Vitonus, both to you and to the rest of the region of Verdun; for love of the same Catholic unity he has been deprived of his place and possessions. Know, moreover, that the aforesaid Guy has been ordained deacon by us.”

Guy delivered this letter to those to whom it was sent. There was also another:

> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Catholic brethren of the church of Verdun: greeting and apostolic blessing. Although you may not until now have read that Richard, occupier of your church, has been excommunicated by the holy Roman Church for his deserts, we nevertheless believe that you have certainly heard and know it. But now we notify all of you in writing that, knowing him to be excommunicated, you must in every way avoid his communion. We have learned that the abbot of Saint Vitonus and Archdeacon Guy have been deprived of their dignities and possessions for love of Catholic unity. Therefore we command, if you retain any obedience to blessed Peter and to us, that they be restored to their places and goods. But if you scorn to obey these present letters, we place your church under interdict from divine offices. Those, however, who recover themselves from the stain of this error [Note: [Col. 0943] Wassebourg reads singular *resipuerit . . . reconcilietur*: “who recovers … let him be reconciled.”], are to be reconciled to Catholic unity by the counsel of our fellow-brother, the archbishop of Trier, or of the aforesaid abbot. Know, moreover, that the aforesaid Guy has been ordained deacon by us. Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.”

17. Carrying these letters, Guy came to Verdun and concealed himself for several days at Saint Vitonus, attempting by persuasion to reconcile the minds of the clergy to himself. When he perceived that this was futile and that their stubbornness was increasing, he armed himself with a certain firmness of mind. Trusting that reverence for the Roman See would make him safe at least among the clergy, he entered the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in the morning—for by day he feared Richard’s armed men. On the feast of Saint James (25 July), with all the clergy gathered there, he stood at the altar, laid the letter upon it, and said in the vernacular:

> “If anyone here is Catholic, let him receive, read, and obey the letters of the lord apostolic.”

Immediately the clerics, who had conceived greater anger against him because they knew of his return, rushed tumultuously upon him. Although he clung to the altar and embraced the relics of the saints, they overthrew these and dragged him by the hair as far as the middle of the choir; they beat and kicked him. Wrenching himself from their hands, he fled into the court of Saint Mary Magdalene, a place especially revered by everyone because of the consecration of Saint Leo IX. They pursued him from behind and stirred the city against him with a disorderly outcry, as against a robber [Col. 0944A] [Note: [Col. 0943] “disorderly” in witness 1.]. There too, where he had thought himself safer because of the holiness of the place, he was seized, beaten, bound, led to Richard, and presented to him.

After insults and threats, Richard sent him to the castle of Grandpré. There he was plunged into a most confined dungeon and oppressed by hunger, nakedness, and chains. None of his friends was admitted to comfort him; only those were allowed in who brought cruel reports and instilled terror. Crushed by those who threatened every evil, Guy was compelled against his will to promise Richard and the clergy that he would make satisfaction according to their pleasure. He gave them his pledge, kissed them, and communicated with them for the moment; thus he escaped prison.

Once restored to liberty, he went to Richard, bishop of Albano, reported everything, and sought absolution from the forced communion with Richard [Col. 0944B]. On hearing this, Richard and the clergy of Verdun raged and sent threatening messengers, one after another, with letters ordering him to return. But Guy no longer rightly trusted himself to their hands; and since he found neither hearing nor justice with them anywhere, he sought from them a safe-conduct for his bodily safety; they promised it, and he named the escorts he wished. As these were not supplied, the entire business remained unaccomplished, and Richard bestowed Guy’s prebend [Note: [Col. 0943] “prey” in witness 1.] and dignity in the church of Verdun upon others.

The clergy composed accusatory letters against Guy, which he invalidated by strong arguments. He wrote an *Apologeticum* in his own defence, in which he depicted this entire tragedy in a lengthy discourse. The Roman Church received and honoured Guy as one who had served it well [Col. 0944C], and after the death of the venerable Richard assigned him the bishopric of Albano. But, it is said, Guy himself died before consecration.

18. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, King Henry IV, following in the footsteps of his faithless father, violently claimed for himself the investitures of churches, although the pope forbade this to him under anathema. He went to Rome with the appearance of intending to satisfy the pope. But after the third oath of faith, suddenly, in the church of Saint Peter—while others fled this crime—he himself seized Pope Paschal and the cardinals with his own hand. He stripped them of their pontifical vestments, intruded other cardinals into an unclean place [Note: [Col. 0943] “others” in witness 1.], wore them down, and bent them to his will by punishments and threats. By force he extorted from them in writing unlawful oaths and sacrilegious privileges: that the king should retain, according to custom, the investitures of churches and confer them by staff and ring, and that the pope should never excommunicate him for any offence whatever. He sent these throughout his whole kingdom to all his men and ordered them copied and observed.

As soon as Richard obtained this document [Note: [Col. 0943] Witness 1 may read “wrote” rather than “obtained.”], he brought it to Saint Vitonus, summoned the brothers, read it aloud, and reproached them:

> “Behold, behold to what your tribulations, to what your exiles—which you have endured for some thirty years—have come; behold, all things have been rolled into filth.”

Why should I report that some of his companions raised their mouths to heaven, spoke grandly of the king, proclaimed him both king and high priest—something not found to have been said even among any heretics—and argued that it belonged to his right to make or depose bishops? The assembly of brothers, hearing this—nor was the venerable Lawrence present—blushed and groaned; and because the tower of Roman faith had yielded, none of them opened his mouth even to mutter. They only watched to see what outcome so great a catastrophe would have.

Meanwhile Richard of Albano and Guy, afterwards pope and then archbishop of Vienne, together with other similar pillars of the Transalpine Church, united against this iniquity of Caesar [Col. 0945B]. Like men of courage, they urged one another to raise and support the tower of the Roman Church. They anathematized the violators of the Roman Church, condemned the grants that had been made—more properly calling them “evil privileges” (*pravilegia*)—and compelled the pope himself, who had granted them under violence, to join their judgment by condemning and anathematizing them.

19. Thus the kingdom on one side and the Church on the other each supported its own cause with all its strength. Since Richard and the clergy of Verdun defended the royal cause beyond measure, the whole storm in that same year fell upon Abbot Lawrence [Col. 0945C] and his church, because they alone among them dared to obey the Roman Church and not to communicate with the others. After Guy’s escape Richard and the clergy of Verdun directed every outrage against them. They publicly beat laymen who came to them out of devotion and ordered them not to come again. If fellow clerics had communicated with them out of devotion, they compelled them to renounce their brotherhood [Note: [Col. 0945] “confraternity” corrected to “brotherhood” in witness 1.], and over the communion given by the monks they imposed their own communion anew.

Finally, when Hairicus, a canon of pious memory and their most devoted confrater, who had supported them with many gifts, was at the point of death and asked them for the viaticum and likewise for burial, Richard sent a threat: if they did this, he would have the dead man buried nowhere except in a rubbish heap within his own house. They did the same to other clerics: they kept monks from communicating with them by locking the houses, and with insults drove the monks away from burials.

20. Meanwhile the feast of Saint Vitonus had come (9 November), at which the clergy customarily assemble for First Vespers and Mass when the bells have been rung. Since they had discovered [Note: [Col. 0945] “had discovered” in witness 1.] that, before their arrival, the monks were completing their own assembly so that they might not attend the clergy’s gathering [Col. 0946A] [Note: [Col. 0945] “those assembled” in witness 1.], they unexpectedly came upon them as they sang the hour of Vespers. The bells had not yet been rung, the hour was not yet fixed, and, because they were not yet expected, they found the choir-door shut. Indignant, they knocked and raised a tumultuous cry. Even so it was not opened, lest, by forcing themselves in, they disturb the brothers’ assembly—as they intended.

At last, when some of their party had opened the door, they pushed and pulled one of the lay brothers who had resisted opening it to them; in the sight of the monks, who grieved but did not dare to help, they tugged his beard and hair and beat his body. They then returned without celebrating Vespers, presented to Richard a student stained with blood, alleging that the aforesaid lay brother had inflicted this upon him, and immediately brought Richard with them, inflamed to vengeance by his own anger and theirs, while the entire city was stirred and gathered for the spectacle.

That evening and on the following day, after the order of brothers had been expelled from the middle of the cloister, Richard preached with his followers against the venerable Lawrence. After much had been said and heard, he forbade Lawrence the divine office by an abusive procedure. In conclusion he charged him with the crime of being rebellious against the emperor and himself, of not keeping faith, and, further, of spurning their communion. Therefore, as guilty toward both, he was worthy to lose all temporal possessions which he held from the emperor and, after him, from Richard himself.

Thus Richard violently deprived him of the possessions and authority of the abbey, inside and outside. He entrusted the keys of the treasury and library to the church’s rustics, and the custody of the cloister to clerics. Moreover, he forbade Lawrence and his men the market and public roads of the bishopric, so that some caught upon them were subjected to insults.

The venerable abbot yielded to such violence, moved elsewhere for a time, took some of those entrusted to him with him, and ordered the rest to follow. They carried out the command promptly, slipping away by daily flight [Note: [Col. 0945] “daily” throughout in witness 1.] and frustrating the clergy’s guard. The clerics did all they could to make the rest of them—only young men remained—communicate with them. Producing a letter from the archbishop of Trier urging ecclesiastical communion, and with Abbot Robert of Saint Hubert and many others pressing this peace upon them, they made them enter their communion.

Lawrence heard what had occurred and grieved. He sent letters ordering all of them to reject that communion and come out to him [Note: [Col. 0945] An edition adds “all who obeyed him to come to himself.”]. On the following night a certain Hugh, of ardent and worthy character, upon whom nearly all the rest depended—who had already been recaptured and bound after an earlier, second flight—escaped in a third flight with a companion named Riczo. The others who remained, bereft of him, deliberated on escape. The next day, carrying the cross before them and going in procession, they left the monastery, passed through the middle of the city, and escaped to their cell at Saint Paul’s Cross [Note: [Col. 0947C] Witness 13: “the cross.”]. The entire city lamented after them and denounced Richard’s condemnation; Richard himself too was deeply grieved. For it is related that he was being driven against them, even unwillingly, by certain clerics or monks, among whom Theodoric the primicerius is particularly named.

What need I recount concerning this man: how, after the clerics had been driven away and their houses broken open [Note: [Col. 0947] “broken open” in witness 1.], he seized the primicery, so that he twice lost it through canonical censure and seized it again through Caesarian violence; how, when his uncle Bishop Theodoric was at the point of death, he forbade him, in the presence of Herimann [Note: [Col. 0947] “Herimann” in witness 1.], bishop of Metz, to be reconciled to Catholic unity; or what things he then wrote to Caesar?

21. Abbot Lawrence gathered together the dispersed brothers [Col. 0947B]. He placed the senior brethren in suitable cells, but sent the younger men to Burgundy, where they were received with an affection beyond expression by Gerenton, venerable abbot of the church of Dijon, because of the brotherhood previously established. They remained there for the three years during which Richard survived. That church testifies and rejoices that it was advanced in every respect through them [Note: [Col. 0947C] On this matter, compare Abbot Lawrence’s *Apologeticum* in Wassebourg, fol. CCLXXVI; Bouquet, continuators, vol. XV, p. 207.]

22. So great a disturbance had arisen under Richard in the church of Verdun [Note: [Col. 0947] The account continues in witness 3.]; but no less was present in its territory. The cause of the wars from the beginning of his episcopate was as follows. His men from the castle of Dieulouard [Note: [Col. 0947] “Desluardo” in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 0947C] Dieulouard; concerning the place, see Roussel, p. 183 n.] had captured a citizen of Metz. While they held him prisoner, the people of Metz, indignant, besieged that castle, captured it, and demolished it. After Richard rebuilt it, he summoned Count Raynald, son of Theodoric, count of the city, to court, on the ground that, having been rewarded by the enemy, he had not come to the aid of the bishopric’s castle.

When Raynald did not come to the hearing, Richard convened an assembly of nobles and adjudged to him the county of the city. He handed it over to Count William of Luxembourg [Note: [Col. 0947] “William” in witness 3 and below.], because he seemed stronger than the rest. In payment for military service, for two hundred pounds, Richard also mortgaged to him Mouzay and Sathanac [Note: [Col. 0947] “Sathanac” in witness 3.], disregarding the excommunication pronounced concerning them by Bishop Richer. [Manuscript 3 corrects “bishop” to “predecessor” and adds: “without the emperor’s knowledge and against the resistance of the brethren of the church.”] [Note: [Col. 0947C] See above, chapter 12.]

Thus under Richard the church of Verdun lost Mouzay and Sathanac, and has lost them until now [Note: [Col. 0947] Witness 3 omits “Thus” through “has lost.”]. Thereafter Raynald defended the county of the city by arms as his own, while William claimed it for himself with Richard’s help. Everything was thrown into confusion by slaughter, fires, and plunder [Col. 0948A]; Raynald nevertheless was more severely pressed, alone against two. In the first onset of the war he lost the town of Saint-Mihiel [Note: [Col. 0948C] Saint-Mihiel.] and its castle, which was burned [Note: [Col. 0947] “was burned” in witness 1.] and destroyed. Then, through the daily assault of arms, his entire hereditary county fell into ruin, except castles and a few places fortified by nature, art, and men.

To capture these too, Richard summoned the emperor. The emperor assembled an army, besieged Raynald within Bar, demolished the castle, and carried him off captive [Note: [Col. 0948C] See the *Annals of Saint Vincent of Metz* for A.D. 1114, *SS.* III, p. 158.]. At last, through the intervention on his behalf of his most noble relatives from throughout the kingdom, the emperor released him from custody with all his men and sent him, as his kinsman, back to his own lands, receiving from him only homage.

But Richard, seeing everything adverse—the Roman Church hostile, Caesar unreliable, since he had freed from prison his own most formidable enemy, and Raynald himself devising new measures against him—and realizing that for seven years he had lived without episcopal blessing and under the anathema of the Apostolic See, lost heart and considered how to escape so many evils. Having collected much money, he vowed a journey to Jerusalem. First, before a full assembly of nobles, he summoned Abbot Lawrence to an apostolic hearing as one guilty against him. When Lawrence refused the summons because, having been stripped by Richard, he lacked the means to travel [Note: [Col. 0947] “having been stripped” in witness 3.], Richard promised him the necessities of the journey—yet, when Lawrence was about to depart, immediately denied them all.

Richard himself was subsequently summoned by Lawrence, that a legate and his monk might answer in his place before the Apostolic See. With great pomp, accompanied by Hugh, count of Troyes, he then set out for Jerusalem. On reaching Italy, he turned aside to Tivoli [Note: [Col. 0948C] “Tibur”; Pope Paschal stayed there in May and June 1114; see Jaffé, *Regesta*, p. 507.], where he had heard the pope was. While all his companions were admitted to the pope according to the custom for pilgrims, Richard alone fell prostrate upon the ground in the middle of the muddy street, before the gaze of the pope looking through the windows of the upper chamber [Note: [Col. 0947] Witness 1 reads *ecteras*; perhaps *ectetas* should be read; compare chapter 30.], and cried tearfully: “Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, merciful father!” [Note: [Col. 0947] “prostrate on the ground” is omitted in witness 3.]

Paschal, already informed of Richard’s journey by Archdeacon Guy [Note: [Col. 0947] “archdeacon” in witness 3.] and by the monk Rodulf, Abbot Lawrence’s messenger, nevertheless saw him thus and was moved with pity. Inclining to mercy, he said: “For your sake I shall return to Rome tomorrow. Come with me, and in the Roman court of cardinals I shall show you the mercy of the Lord according to their counsel.”

“But,” said Richard, “I give back to you the pastoral staff; only absolve me here, and do not compel me to go to Rome, for I absolutely cannot send this company of mine on to Jerusalem.” [Note: [Col. 0949] “Do not compel me” in witness 1.]

Why say more? When the pope refused to absolve him except at Rome, Richard left his presence sorrowfully and went on with his men. As the illness into which he had already fallen grew worse, he began to be carried in a litter. Then Richard, bishop of Albano, met him as he travelled and said in astonishment: “Who are you?”

With sighs Richard replied: “I am Richard of Verdun, wretched and exiled.”

Hearing this, the bishop was astonished and said: “What have you done with the lord pope?”

“Alas, alas! Nothing,” he said. “For I found no mercy, and behold, I die in my sins unless you quickly help me.”

When he had recounted what had happened, the bishop said: “I shall help you as I can. Wait for me here, so that, after I have spoken for you to the pope and the Romans, I may bring you the reconciliation I obtain.” Having said this, and after Richard had thanked him, he went on and hurried to Rome. Having obtained pardon for Richard, he quickly turned back to him. But pilgrims met him, announcing that Richard was already dead and buried [Note: [Col. 0949] “had already died” in witness 3.].

Richard died at Monte Cassino in the seventh year in which he had been elected bishop of the church of Verdun, though not yet consecrated; and the bishopric was vacant for three and a half years [Note: [Col. 0949] “and” is added afterwards in witness 3.]. [Note: [Col. 0949] Manuscript 3, in the same hand, adds: “This was the end of Richard, bishop-elect of Verdun. But when his men who had accompanied him on pilgrimage returned, he sent many silver vessels through Gozelo, his household servant and provost of his house, for the liberation and redemption of the castle of Sathanac and of Mouzay, strictly charging him to pay the aforesaid money to the said Count William of Luxembourg.”]

23. In those days Abbot Lawrence returned to the possessions from which he had been expelled and recalled his men. Through the archbishop he secured the return to himself of the treasure which he found had been taken from his church. The clergy too, certain of Richard’s death, sought absolution from the same metropolitan. Count William also came to peaceful agreement with Raynald, restoring to him the county of the city, although the townsmen themselves did not wish it. [Note: [Col. 0949D] Compare Wassebourg, fol. CCLXXI.]

Therefore the two of them hired strong forces of warriors to attack Verdun. But the burghers first sought a truce; once it had been granted, they attacked the enemies as they were withdrawing. A severe battle was joined on both sides, and Raynald was carried away wounded [Note: [Col. 0949] “severe” is feminine in witness 1.]

24. (A.D. 1117.) Meanwhile a certain Henry, endowed with letters and worldly wisdom and archdeacon of Winchester in England [Note: [Col. 0949] “Winchester” in witness 1.] [Note: [Col. 0949D] Winchester.], had come from there with Matilda, daughter of the king of the English, whom the king of the Romans had married. Being in her service, he obtained through her from the king himself the gift of the bishopric of Verdun. He sent envoys ahead to Verdun and, by gifts and promises, won the inhabitants’ hearts to his side [Col. 0950A], so that when he himself followed the envoys he was received by them with honour.

When they soon communicated with him, Abbot Lawrence and his men withdrew from their communion. Bruno, the metropolitan, also disapproved his election; Guy of Vienne, legate of the Apostolic See, likewise excommunicated him. Finally, after a year, the venerable Lawrence advised Henry to place himself in the hands of the Apostolic See. Henry set out for Rome; captured by imperialists on the way but escaping, he reached Milan. There he found John of Crema, a cardinal priest, and explained where he was going. John said that imperialists were active on that route; acting in the pope’s stead, he received and absolved Henry, had him consecrated bishop, and sent him back to his own people.

Before Henry returned, the king’s envoys had already arrived, the king ordering the people of Verdun to send Henry to himself. On arriving he found the city gates shut and their minds hostile, and withdrew to Hattonchâtel [Note: [Col. 0950D] Hattonchâtel.]. From there he threatened the city with arms. Therefore the city and clergy rose to depose him, accusing him of an unlawful intrusion before the archbishops who were legates of the Apostolic See and before the pope himself.

25. Meanwhile, after Pope Paschal died (A.D. 1118), the Roman Church made its apocrisiarius John Gaetan pope and named him Gelasius. Since the king was hastening to Rome, all were already afraid of him, and they fled even from his presence. The king arrived, rejected their elected pope, and intruded into the Roman see Maurice Burdinus, formerly bishop of Braga in Spain, then deposed. Gelasius fled this violence into Gaul and died at Cluny a year later (January 1119). The Romans substituted Guy of Vienne, who became Calixtus II.

Calixtus strengthened the ecclesiastical party and held a synod at Reims (October). Among many other decrees, he forbade under anathema the conferral of church investitures by staff and ring by laymen; and he consecrated as bishop of Liège Frederick of holy memory, whom God had glorified by so many signs. At this synod Henry prevailed against the accusations of his opponents through cardinals whom he had won to his side and received confirmation of the bishopric [Note: [Col. 0949] “of the bishop” in witness 1.]. Yet upon returning he was not received by his own people, except by Abbot Lawrence [Col. 0950D], who, though not himself favouring him, had received papal letters commending Henry.

Henry then shared his cause with Count Raynald, who himself was not received by the people of Verdun, and inflamed him against them. Both came to Verdun with great forces. When the citizens resisted and battle was fiercely joined, they entered the city and set fire to it; by this the churches of the Saviour, Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0951D] Saint-Pierre-le-Chairé; Roussel.], and Saint Agericus were burned, together with the greater part of the adjacent city. There was neither limit nor number to the slaughter and plunder.

On the following day the city was surrendered and secured in Raynald’s hand. Henry took his seat in the episcopal chair [Note: [Col. 0951] “chair” in witness 1.] and, in the tumult of the captured city, received by a clergy compelled to do so—not singing but lamenting, “We looked for peace, and it did not come, O Lord; we sought good things, and behold, trouble” (Jeremiah 14:19)—immediately proceeded to the solemnities of Mass, while the conflagration still smoked [Col. 0951B] and while the wound of the city and the ruins of his own flock, perpetrated under his leadership and for his cause, were still so recent.

At first light on the following day, the citizens, having placed ill-founded confidence in Raynald, fled to the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, as to a refuge of mercy. There Raynald besieged them, captured them, and stripped them of their possessions.

26. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1122, Pope Calixtus, having sent cardinals to the emperor—for he was his near kinsman by birth—settled that great discord which, from the time of Gregory VII, had troubled kingdom and Church: the emperor renounced the investitures of churches and the regalia of blessed Peter, and accepted reconciliation; and thus kingdom and Church rested from that plague. In the same year, because the men of Verdun had lamented in secret messages reaching the emperor’s ears how great were the evils they had suffered on his account [Note: [Col. 0951] omitted in 1.], the emperor entrusted the county of the city to Henry of Grandpré, commanding him to assist the citizens for his own sake. Henry, having spoken with the citizens and both taught and learned what was to be done, came with cavalry to Verdun in the morning and was admitted by false keys. While soldiers were running about amid such tumult, the bishop was roused from sleep; recognizing what had happened, he almost nakedly rushed out in shameful flight, swam across the Meuse, and hastened to Raynald. Raynald, having previously learned of the citizens’ and Count Henry’s scheme, had withdrawn to secure his own possessions, entrusting the defense of the city to the bishop.

Raynald, hearing these grievous tidings, immediately gathered a hostile force and came to Verdun. Henry and the citizens rushed to arms [Col. 0951D]; he fought and won, yet could not recover the city. Count Henry, lest he be inferior in forces, hired for pay the bravest men from Flanders and elsewhere; and when the enemy again attacked on two sides of the city [Col. 0952A], he most courageously repelled him and captured many of his men. Everywhere he harassed Raynald’s county, ravaging it with slaughter, fire, and plunder, and defeated him in open battle near the village of Oscara [Note: [Col. 0951D] Osche, three leagues from Verdun.].

Raynald then resorted to stratagem: he placed mercenary soldiers in the castle of Clermont, to harass the enemy by daily raids. Henry, in order to outwit the enemy’s art by artifice, instructed and warned his own mercenaries to draw those men out from Clermont to an engagement and weary them for a long time. Then, suddenly arriving, he vigorously attacked the already exhausted enemy with a strong force, drove them into the castle, followed them in, set fire to it, and led them all away, castle and all surrendered, most disgracefully taken by the throat like brigands.

Raynald, now despairing of arms, considered peace; and through the mediation of Frederick, count of Toul, he and Henry negotiated peace at Chalade [Note: [Col. 0951D] La Chalade, on the stream Biemme.]. Henry handed over the county of the city to him, on the condition that Raynald would not harm the citizens who supported Henry, while permitting Henry to despoil those whom he had captured. Thus at last the city rested under Count Raynald and Bishop Henry.

The bishop himself gave Raynald the castle of Dun and four estates of the bishopric: namely Rouveret [Note: [Col. 0951D] Rouveroy or Rouvret is a fairly common name. There is one in the duchy of Bar, another in the marquisate of Atton-le-Châtel, situated on the Meuse below Saint-Mihiel. ROUSS.], Malaudmont [Note: [Col. 0951D] Malaudmont near Commercy. ROUSS.], Mont Sainte-Lucie [Note: [Col. 0951D] The Mountain of Sainte-Lucie, apparently [Col. 0952D] that on which the Minims are today situated near Sampigny. CALM.], and the peasants [Note: [Col. 0951] “small estates,” ed. 2?] of Ernecourt and Dom-Remy [Note: [Col. 0951] “Domno R.” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0952D] Ernecourt and Dom-Remy.], as security for thirty pounds. To Peter of Mirevaux [Note: [Col. 0952D] Mirevaux.] he gave all that he possessed at Romméville [Note: [Col. 0952D] Romméville? WASS. and CALM.; ROUSS. doubts it.] and at both Azannes [Note: [Col. 0951] “both” spelled *utranque* in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0952D] Azane and Sommazane, in the parish of Til, deanery of Chaumont. ROUSS.], excepting four households [Col. 0952C], in return for assistance rendered to him.

Thereafter, considering himself secure, with his own wars and likewise those of kingdom and Church lulled to rest, he gave himself up to pleasure, contrary to the dignity of a bishop. Therefore God stirred up against him the minds of the populace, which assailed him in many seditions, and also of the clergy, who sent envoys even to the pope’s ears [Note: [Col. 0951] “peace” erased and “pope” corrected by hand in 1.], accusing him of incontinence, simony, and the squandering of Church property. The case of the venerable Lawrence carried especial weight. Before the ears of the most worthy Emperor Lothair, of the envoys of the Apostolic See, and of the pope himself, Lawrence lodged complaint against him: certain possessions of his church, taken from it by Henry’s predecessors during the discord between kingdom and Church, had not been restored to him, although he had repeatedly demanded them.

Henry, obstinate in mind, when summoned to the hearing of Pope Calixtus [Col. 0952D], did not come, nor did he restore to Lawrence the things taken away, as he had been ordered.

27. After Calixtus’ death (1124), Honorius succeeded him. Before him the clergy renewed their accusation, and Lawrence [Col. 0953A] renewed his complaint. Honorius summoned Henry by letter and ordered him to restore the stolen goods to the abbot [Note: [Col. 0953D] See the pope’s letters in Wassebourg, fols. CCLXXXIV–CCLXXXV; Bouquet, continuation XV, pp. 257–258.], suspending him in the meantime from the divine office. He was indeed suspended, but again fulfilled neither command. When the pope summoned him a second time, now more severely, Henry became afraid. Supported by gifts and by advocates offering excuses, he came to Rome, won over the cardinals, and appeared before the pope in court.

When the accusers, who were present, had also presented written articles of criminal accusation against him, the bishop’s advocates, so as to repel them as persons unworthy of a hearing, charged certain crimes against them. Since both parties broke out into abusive words and the dispute was drawn out without end, Honorius asked the venerable Lawrence, who was likewise present: “Father, what do you say concerning these crimes alleged against the bishop?” He replied, “Lord, I did not see them, but the people cry out.” The pope seized upon the words from his mouth; and because the cardinals favored the bishop and the dispute allowed nothing certain to be established, he could pronounce no judgment. He therefore entrusted the case for examination to Matthew, bishop of Albano, his legate stationed in Gaul [Note: [Col. 0953D] See the pope’s mandate in Wassebourg, fol. CCLXXXV; Bouquet XV, p. 269.].

Matthew summoned the bishop and the accusers to Châlons to appear before him [Note: [Col. 0953D] At the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary; Alberic [Col. 0954D], year 1129.]. There he, the bishop, and the accusers each called to the support of their cause the archbishop of Rheims, many other bishops and abbots, and learned and religious men. Henry first sought counsel from Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, of holy memory [Col. 0953C], upon whose counsels the kingdoms and churches of Gaul rest even today. Bernard advised that it was a most grievous thing to rule men forcibly against their will; and therefore, before the disgraceful accusation against him came to the public hearing of so many eminent men [Note: [Col. 0953] omitted in 1.], Henry ought to yield to all alone and renounce the bishopric, lest he incur public disgrace.

Henry accepted this counsel. Standing there, with Bernard speaking for him, he declared before the assembly [Note: [Col. 0953] “assembly” in 1.] that, since clergy and people had risen against him in their common hatreds, and especially those whom he had exalted and heaped with ecclesiastical honors had conspired for his disgrace and deposition, he did not wish to rule them against their will. Rather, lest he cause further scandal to the Church, he would now untie the long cords of contention [Note: [Col. 0954D] Compare Bernard of Clairvaux, Letter 48.]. Then he returned the staff, renounced the bishopric, and withdrew [Col. 0953D] in the thirteenth year after he had received it from the emperor’s hand. So that he might not depart in sorrow, the aforesaid abbot obtained on his behalf a sufficiently generous collection of ten marks from the leading members of the council, with which Henry redeemed his pledges [Col. 0954A] in that city. Many letters of both the pope and the Church of Verdun concerning his accusation or deposition survive.

28. The Church of Verdun, admonished by that same council to take instruction from past evils and set over itself a man supported by religious devotion, chose Ursio, abbot of Saint-Denis of Rheims, as bishop. Brought to Verdun, he greatly wished to manage pontifical affairs and the temporal jurisdictions of the land, but neither could nor knew how to do so. Instead, remaining at Saint-Viton, he lived the private life to which he was accustomed. His gentleness was soon despised by tyranny, and the bishopric suffered many injuries.

For he had gone to the royal court to obtain confirmation of his office; and behold, Count Raynald, devising lordship over the city for himself, unexpectedly [Col. 0954B] came to Verdun. He brought with him a large force of soldiers, masons, diggers, and craftsmen of every sort, with no small equipment. He cut down and rooted up the orchard of the episcopal residence; and because the site was very suitable, he built there a most costly, strong, and spacious tower. He stationed within it men most faithful to himself, and through it began to dominate the whole city and the entire bishopric. [Note: [Col. 0954D] The place where this fortress stood may still be seen, and the remains that survive retain the name Tour du Voué. CALM.]

Why should I recount the houses of clerics broken open and their goods carried away; the clergy themselves put to flight and thrown into confusion; and the people, in all these matters, not daring even to murmur? The same enemy waylaid the bishop himself as he returned from court and captured the clerics and retainers accompanying him. The bishop escaped by flight; and, as though he had lost Verdun [Col. 0954C], he did not return, lest he see what he could not bear to hear of, what he could in no way restrain.

Accordingly, the Church itself suspended itself from the divine office. Thus the people lost liberty, the clergy their bishop, and the Church the voice of divine psalmody; and all the glory of the people of Verdun seemed to have been removed. But behold, the blessed Mother of God shone forth most manifestly upon the desperate condition of her people. Her church, whose roofs had been thrown down by the previously mentioned storm of turbulent years, whose vault reeked with mud and admitted rain, whose chapel was uncultivated, whose altars stood neglected and lamps extinguished—this church she illuminated, made serene, glorified, and rendered renowned in all things by the splendor of heavenly miracles.

The order of the work demands that I insert here an account of the extent to which these miracles became famous [Col. 0954D], but the smallness of my talent cannot sustain such great matter for praise, especially since the venerable dean William, a man of more polished intellect and wisdom, has, as I have heard, described them in a worthier style [Col. 0955A]. [Note: [Col. 0955D] Wassebourg, fol. CCXC, laments the loss of this book.] Yet, since we are not of such merit that we can worthily praise the Mother of God in her miracles, let us at least offer some praise to him who, from the good treasure of his heart, has set forth in praise the accounts of her miracles [Note: [Col. 0955] “her praises” in 1.]. He is indeed a man worthy of much praise not only in this matter but in others as well. It is no small praise to be better among the good.

Who, among his own people and even among others, is more diligent than he in reading Holy Scripture, in seeking out the best books from every quarter, and in copying them? He now seems to be gathering for himself the famous library of Ptolemy Philadelphus or Eusebius Pamphilus, condemning the avarice which has seized the clergy of our age. Who among his own is more devout in frequenting God’s service by day and night? Who is more fervent [Col. 0955B] in showing hospitality? His house today appears to be a public hospice for the servants of God. A tree is known by its fruit, and a man by his pursuits; and concerning this man, on these grounds, we say: truly a good man, truly a good tree. For by the very proof of experience, both his root and the soil from which he sprang have appeared good.

His father, Gyezelo, in fruitful devotion gave to our monastery all that he possessed at Baroncourt [Note: [Col. 0956D] Baroncourt.], in fields, woods, a mill, and meadows. He also resolved to dedicate his body and soul in addition, and to profess himself a monk in the same monastery. But Abbot Lawrence, a man without avarice, by pious counsel turned his pious vow away from himself to the monastery of Saint Gorgonius at Gorze. For since this same Gyezelo had been advocate of that church [Col. 0955C], he ought to devote himself to the one to which, while serving the world, he had in some respects been indebted. The mother of the same dean, Helluildis [Note: [Col. 0955] Helluyldis in 1.], added to all these gifts of merit a distinguished silver chalice, which she gave to blessed Viton.

29. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1131, the glorious Emperor Lothair, who reigned after Henry, held at Liège, in mid-Lent (March), a great assembly of nobles to arrange the affairs of kingdom and Church. There Pope Innocent II also came, having been driven from Rome by Peter Leo, who had been intruded into his place, and sought and obtained assistance. Ursio, bishop-elect of Verdun, likewise came there. Since he regretted having undertaken the episcopate, and the people of Verdun regretted his election, he himself pleaded before the ears of that emperor [Col. 0955D] and pope the case of his incapacity; he requested release [Note: [Col. 0955] “he requested to be released,” ed.], and surrendered the episcopal insignia.

But those who were present there as heads of the Church and people of Verdun were immediately ordered by the emperor to choose from that great assembly the man they knew to be best and present him to him. After long deliberation, they chose as bishop Lord Albero, archdeacon of their church, son of Arnulf [Col. 0956A], count of Chiny. The court approved his election; the assembly of princes who knew him acclaimed it; and the imperial majesty confirmed it, granting him by the sceptre the temporalities of the bishopric. The pope also approved it. In order that all things might proceed canonically, he immediately sent the elected person back to the Church of Verdun, commanding that, when Albero should meet him at Paris with the assent and testimony of that church itself, and especially of the venerable Abbot Lawrence, then, after the public election by his own people had been seen, the pope should there confirm to him the spiritualities.

When the city and Church of Verdun heard the name of their chosen bishop, they rejoiced; they already conceived, as by a certain presage, hope of recovering liberty through him [Note: [Col. 0955] *spetie* in 1.]. They received him with joy and sent him to the pope at Paris in France, with the testimony of public assent [Col. 0956B]. There, on Holy Saturday of Easter (18 April), he was ordained priest; and on the feast day itself (19 April), he was consecrated bishop. He was then immediately dismissed with the honor and favor of the Apostolic See.

As he was returning, about eight men joined him on the road in the guise of pilgrims. One of the bishop’s party recognized, though uncertainly, from his face that the chief among them was Henry [Note: [Col. 0955] “Henry” added by the editor.], the emperor’s son-in-law and duke of Bavaria, and secretly informed the bishop. When questioned by the bishop, this same Henry secretly revealed who he was. He said that, under the guise of pilgrims, he had visited holy places and observed the customs of peoples and tyrants, and was now returning from them. He then placed himself in the escort of the bishop as far as Trier [Col. 0956C], where the emperor then was. The bishop, keeping the matter concealed, brought him with him to Verdun; and, after his own reception had been celebrated by all, escorted Henry as far as Trier, where he delivered him safe and sound to the emperor, who was overjoyed and gave thanks.

The duke also returned the bishop’s kindness: to each retainer who had accompanied him he gave a sword, one apiece, such as he had obtained as the best from royal princes. He invited the bishop’s cleric Peter, whose companionship he had used most frequently, to come to Bavaria; and when Peter came, he bestowed on him certain ecclesiastical insignia.

30. [Note: [Col. 0955] In the manuscript there is no division of chapters.] Meanwhile, those occupying the garrison of the Verdun tower were a great and diabolical snare [Note: [Col. 0955] “devil” in 1.] and evil to the entire city. It would take too long to recount how often they obstructed passing vehicles, wagons, and all the food-carrying loads [Col. 0956D] of common people and clergy, and the merchandise of travelers arriving or returning; how often they dragged them into the tower, seized some things at will for themselves, and compelled other things to be redeemed. So great was this oppression that the public traffic-route of the district, formerly running through the middle of the city, was then diverted; and our marketplace, once renowned, still endures the loss thereby inflicted.

Passers-by [Col. 0957A], even pilgrims of the blessed Mother of God flocking there from every side to seek her aid because of miracles they had heard of, were attacked from above by those men with stones and arrows. Therefore the lord bishop dealt with Count Raynald, asking him to remove the tower; or, since Raynald would not agree even to this, to restrain its garrison from such unlawful acts. Why recount how often he approached, warned, and begged him concerning this; how many promises and agreements he proposed; how he adjured him within the church of the holy Mother of God? Before him were brought all the shrines of saints from throughout the city; all monks and clerics and all the people lay prostrate before him. At the castle of Dieu-le-Wart [Note: [Col. 0957D] The same place as that above called *Deusluwart* in ch. 22.], in the presence of Lord Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate of the Roman See, and of many bishops [Col. 0957B] and nobles, the bishop cast himself at the count’s feet. Yet Raynald always resisted obstinately and denied every request.

Since the bishop found Raynald’s heart closed in every respect, he resorted to divine aid, entrusted the whole case to Christ and his Mother, and the outcome was favorable in every way. For the count, believing himself secure and supposing that the burgesses would dare nothing, since they had truly despaired, had entrusted the tower’s guard to only a few men, some of them foreigners and therefore of very little loyalty. One of these men was secretly approached by Albert, primicerius of the church, and thereafter by the bishop. Enticed by certain agreements, he promised to surrender the tower to them on an appointed day: the feast of Pentecost (3 June 1134).

Having given open signals [Col. 0957C], on that holy day after dinner he called his companions out of the tower onto the *ectetae*, the outer wall-platforms [Note: [Col. 0957D] Ducange, ed. Henschel VI, p. 934, considers that *zetas* should be read, that is, watch-platforms projecting over the walls. But Calmet cites a passage of Jerome, who uses this Greek word in his translation of Ezekiel 41:15–16: “At Rome,” he says, “they call *ecthetae* the balconies projecting from the walls of upper chambers, or *maeniana*, after the man who first devised them” (Works, ed. Vallars V, p. 504).]. He kept them there for a long while over a game of dice. At last, when they were fully absorbed in play, he rose with an angry expression, as though they were not conducting the game fairly toward him. He rushed away from them into the tower, shut them out while they continued playing—for there was no suspicion—and fastened the tower door with a very strong bar. From the summit of the tower he then displayed the signal of betrayal agreed upon with the bishop: he waved a linen head-covering.

The bishop saw it—for he was watching as he waited—and, as the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, he leapt up with all his zeal, ready to give soul and body for the liberty of his country and his flock. He had the signal for battle sounded from the church and rushed forward with the clerics and all the townspeople, whom [Col. 0957D] he had previously ordered, while keeping the matter secret, to be ready under arms at the appointed hour; the holy relics were brought along as well. With all their force they assaulted the tower. The excluded guards were attacked by all with stones, weapons, and every means of harm; resisting stoutly, they were at last overcome when fire was set to the wooden fabric of the tower [Col. 0958A], yielded, and surrendered to the bishop.

The bishop entered the captured tower with his men, and on its summit the victorious pledges of the Virgin’s virgins [Note: [Col. 0957] omitted in 1.] were raised as a triumph. They were celebrated with the highest outcry of rejoicing, even by pilgrims, whom the miracles then frequently occurring there drew in bands from every region. For in those very days the splendor of heavenly signs had become more renowned than usual, foretelling the victory itself and the fall of the tower—even, as common report interpreted it, through children prophesying it. The news immediately filled the entire land and threw Raynald into greater consternation than can be believed, especially because his own guards were being kept imprisoned in the dungeon of his own tower.

On the second day of Pentecost (4 June), he flew to the area before Verdun [Col. 0958B] and challenged them to battle. But the bishop called back his men, lest they rush in arms upon an enemy inflamed with fury, and kept them inside the walls. To harass the city from three sides, the enemy placed garrisons in three castles: Raynald himself at Ambly [Note: [Col. 0958D] Ambly, four leagues distant from Verdun.]; his son Hugh at the village of Eventron [Note: [Col. 0957] *eventonis v.* in 1; *Guentonis v.* in the edition.] [Note: [Col. 0958D] Watronville.]; and his chief officer Elias at Roset [Note: [Col. 0958D] Rosay, near Estain, WASS. Rosat is a castle in the parish of Rouvres, ROUSS.]. Having assembled armed forces, they maintained their posts, harassed the city with continual raids, devastated the bishopric, and imposed increasingly heavy ransom payments upon the villages.

The bishop necessarily hired armed forces and asserted the liberty of his people. He suddenly rose in arms against Elias at Roset, who was pressing the city more heavily; he set fire to the castle, captured the enemy himself with all the force of his followers, carried them off, and thrust them into the dungeon of the Verdun tower [Col. 0958C], which Elias himself had measured out for construction, all urging the bishop to do so.

Raynald [Note: [Col. 0957] “Reynaldus” in 1, in this place.], striving to repay like with like, hired Simon, duke of Moselle, many counts, and barons. Setting out with them from Ambly, he marched on Verdun. But behold: when they saw from afar the summit of the church of the glorious Virgin, their courage failed and shuddered under a divine influence. After seeking one counsel and then another, the duke and the other princes openly declared that they must not wage war against Christ and his Mother. They promised their allied forces in other wars, but declared that in this one they dared not participate. Thus, accomplishing nothing, they turned back toward their own lands; and Raynald, still breathing threats, gathered other armies.

Moreover, from the beginning of the capture of the Verdun tower, Raynald requested through Albero the metropolitan that the bishop [Col. 0958D] return his tower to him.
