When the bishop refused, Raynald again sought through his brother Stephen, bishop of Metz, with a thousand promises and agreements, that the bishop should allow him to hold it as an episcopal gift [Note: [Col. 0957] *sibi—dono* omitted in 1.]. When this too was refused, he begged through many mediators that the bishop should at least grant it, as an episcopal gift, to Count Albert of Chiny. Albert, because he was born of Count Otto, the bishop’s brother, and was the son-in-law of that same Raynald, was regarded as faithful to both men.

Furthermore, a great part of clergy and people advised, pressed, and urged the bishop in every way to do this, because of their severe distress and fear of worse things. But the most worthy bishop considered and kept in mind that, if the tower were returned, it would in the future become an instrument of tyranny for the destruction of the whole city and Church. He refused every request, declaring that he would rather die or endure exile in a long wandering through foreign lands than restore so great an enemy and scandal to the liberty of his flock. Although that flock, from evil fear, wished to receive the wolf coming to them in sheep’s clothing [Col. 0959B], he would nevertheless fight to remove from them that most savage enemy.

He therefore demolished the tower [Note: [Col. 0959] *everti*, “to be demolished,” in 1.], although clergy and people shrank from this through fear of the most formidable enemy; and from that point he began to surround the city with a wall, judging rightly that, once the tower was destroyed, the enemy would cease, its gain and cause for fighting having been removed.

31. But Raynald, after the tower’s demolition, the capture of his men, and the denunciation and withdrawal of his cause of war by leading men and friends, was sick with anxiety and carried beyond himself by anger and grief. Then suddenly he fell into a most severe illness and believed himself struck by God. Abandoning his threats, he considered peace and sent his brother Stephen, the bishop, to confer with Bishop Albero and seek a truce [Col. 0959C] in order to negotiate peace. Stephen came, fulfilled his instructions, and afterward became mediator of a most firm peace between his brother and our bishop. [Note: [Col. 0959D] Concerning it, compare Alberic under this year.]

Thus, through the efforts of the most worthy Bishop Albero, that most grievous enemy was removed from our necks; our city recovered peace, the Church the voice of divine psalmody, and both recovered the fullest liberty, which they had lost during three years in which evils reigned.

After this the bishop came with a strong force to the castle of Ambly, which had been exceedingly troublesome to the bishopric and was still held against him by certain malicious men. While he delayed briefly on the journey to take some food, infantrymen who had gone ahead attacked the same castle, broke in, stormed it, and set it on fire. When the soldiers accompanying the bishop immediately followed at the sight of this [Col. 0959D], the castle was destroyed; its plunder and every person within it were captured, bound, and carried away. Therefore a triumphal praise was celebrated to Christ and his Mother.

32. [Note: [Col. 0959] No chapter division in manuscript 1.] Nevertheless, through the exertions of this same bishop, the vigor of monastic order also flourished anew in certain places. [Col. 0960A] For the church of Saint Paul within the city had then become foul—torn apart, rent, and scattered—while the sons of Belial who inhabited it had plundered its lands and all its goods. I shudder to say to what enticements they were enslaved; how wickedly they withdrew, night and day, from the service of the Lord; how, though professed monks, they displayed themselves, to the disgrace of our holy order, not as most steadfast cenobites but as most loathsome sarabaites and wandering monks. Why should I recount how often their abbots and other monks more zealous for monastic discipline, sent by the bishop from other churches to correct them, fled the company of these pestilent men after being beaten by them or driven to every bitterness? How often, after the leaders of their wickedness had been admonished, rebuked, and even imprisoned, did they, [Col. 0960B] after every promise of amendment, immediately break out into greater abominations and draw the entire flock of their companions after them?

Therefore the bishop, like a faithful husbandman of the Church’s vineyard, after not three years but many periods of three years, after repeated diggings of correction and diverse baskets of manure—that is, encouraging admonitions—because this degenerate and barren planting gave no hope of fruitfulness, uprooted it with the pruning-iron, lest it occupy the land it possessed any longer. In its place he planted a new growth of clerics of the monastic order, which now springs up like the Paradise of God [Note: [Col. 0959] “of God on earth,” edition.]; Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, a great man in the Church, had assigned these men to him from among the professed members of his own order.

Yet, with everyone’s leave, I would say that, to pass over others, I am deeply grieved by the rejection of the monastic profession effected there, except that I know no other way had been open to this most worthy bishop for reforming the aforesaid monastery; for Abbot Laurence and all religious of our profession had declined to undertake the care of that place from the bishop’s hand. Accordingly, I must commend the vigilance of the diligent bishop in this matter too, because both they and all the faithful are one in Christ—especially since both the imperial majesty and the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0959D] Compare the fragment of Innocent II’s letter in Wassebourg, fol. CCXCIX.] ordered that this be done for the correction of evils, and since the abbots of that clerical order—the first, Roger, and the second, Theoderic, who presides there now—have improved that church in every respect [Note: [Col. 0959] “has improved,” manuscript 1.] and, with great care, recovered everything squandered by those men [Col. 0960D] [Note: [Col. 0959] “have recovered,” manuscript 1.], so that whereas twenty sarabaites [Note: [Col. 0959] “sarabaites,” manuscript 1.], not monks, could scarcely then support themselves from it, now nearly three hundred servants of God live there honorably. All this redounds to the praise of the industrious bishop. [Note: [Col. 0960D] Compare what Calmet, II, p. 106, has noted on this matter from the letters of Peter of Cluny, Bernard of Clairvaux, and Pope Innocent.]

[Note: [Col. 0959] Codex 2 adds: “Thus he wrote to the lord pope:

‘To his dearest father and lord I., supreme pontiff of the universal Church by the grace of God, A., unworthy minister of the Church of Verdun, sends sincere affection with humble obedience.

“The grace of God and yours, through the election of our church, consecrated me bishop, although my merits proclaimed me unworthy; and both before and afterwards it taught me how I ought to serve in the office entrusted to me. Among other things, it especially persuaded me to be vigilant concerning the ordering of the churches committed to my care. Therefore, watching over that ordering, which is very necessary here among us, according to my small ability, I found a church situated here near our city which, through the negligence and irreligion of the few monks living there, had been brought to such infamy that it was no longer called the house of God, but something like a brothel. What I did concerning it, I shall state as briefly and as certainly as I can.

“From its first establishment, the church, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostle Paul, had clerics through the times of nineteen bishops. But through their irreligion and [Col. 0961] negligence it fell into such poverty that what had formerly been sufficient for many could scarcely support one priest. A predecessor of mine named Wilfrid [“Wilfrid,” manuscript c.], a lover of religion, expelled those clerics for this reason and placed religious monks there. For a long time they persevered in religious fervor; they restored the church’s scattered goods and acquired very many more. But their successors gradually began to decline from that religious life, and, thus declining and luxuriously wasting the church’s property, they came down to our own times.

“Grieving over the excessive ruin of that church, which had been renowned from ancient times, I first met alone with the abbot of that place, and afterwards with the other abbots and religious. I laid before him many charges—not even to be named in the presence of your dignity [‘to be named’ corrected by a later hand from ‘named,’ manuscript c.]—which were truly reported of him; and I admonished him paternally to correct himself and his monks in these matters and to restore the ancient religious life in his church. He promised, for God’s sake and ours, to do whatever I wished; but because ‘the newly dyed jar will long retain the scent with which it was once imbued’ [“quod” (“which”) corrected by a later hand to “quo” (“with which”), manuscript c.; “odorem” (“scent”) added by a later hand, manuscript c.; Horace, *Epistles* 1.2.69], when he ought to have corrected [‘rebuked,’ manuscript c.] what he had done wrong, he increased his infamy daily.

“At length, after frequent but vain and useless admonitions, the persons of our church and the religious abbots assembled in our presence. They declared those monks to be a disgrace to their order and asked me to expel them and substitute other religious men. Compelled by their unceasing requests, I summoned religious men—abbots and clerics—to chapter, called that incorrigible abbot to account, and, having brought many charges against him concerning his evil conduct, obtained his confession of what he could not deny openly: namely, that he had despised himself and the form of the Rule [the printed reading is uncertain; an addition follows in manuscript c.] and committed many unlawful acts.

“Having taken the counsel of the religious, I ordered him under obedience to go to the church of Saint Vito in order to do penance among the religious; and, since he could not bear fruit in the church over which he presided, to allow fruitful men to enter. He agreed; but that very day, like one returning to his vomit, he refused to do what he had promised. When we heard this, the next day we came to that church with clerics and abbots, and also with two abbots of the order of Clairvaux [‘of Clairvaux’ corrected by a later hand from ‘of Clairvaux’s,’ manuscript c.], the abbot of Trois-Fontaines and that of Caladia. When we asked why he had not fulfilled the obedience he had accepted, he answered that he would not leave his cloister except by judicial sentence.

“Then the abbots and clerics, astonished at such impudence—that after accepting obedience he should demand a trial—brought forward, through one of them, namely the abbot of Saint Vito, the judgment of Saint Gregory concerning faithless abbots. When it had been read, all told me that, even if he were unwilling, I should confine him in the church and provide for the church so long desolated. Thus he was confined; and, after placing among the religious the few monks who had lived badly with him, I diligently sought monks to restore the church’s former condition—not only from our own houses or neighboring ones, but even from the Cluniac church—through our letters, through those of the lord archbishop of Trier, and also through those of the lord king. Since I could not obtain them, I placed there the poor of Christ from the church [an addition follows in manuscript c.] of Prémontré, who live praiseworthily according to the Rule of Saint Augustine.

“Moved by this, monks—not religious men, but those who fear for their own party in a similar matter—rage against us daily, complaining not so much about the expulsion of the aforesaid abbot, whose life they themselves plainly detest, as about the change of title. In this they slander us. For we do not change the title, but have restored the institution of the original foundation. Moreover, the abbot of that place is the bishop’s vicar; an office more fitting to an order of clerics than to monks. Therefore, with suppliant devotion, we beg your majesty to deign to confirm by the authority of your hand our action, which is praised by everyone except monks of this sort. May your life flourish long, to the honor of Holy Church.”’]

But just as he rooted out and destroyed violators of the Order of Saint [Col. 0961A] Benedict in this place, so also, with pious generosity, he was ready to build up and plant those preserving the same profession in their proper places. To the leaders of the Cistercian religion, by whom the Rule of Saint Benedict is observed more strictly, he offered the forest of Mangienne [Note: [Col. 0961A] Mangienne.] and urged them to build there an abbey [Note: [Col. 0961A] Later called Le Châtelet or Châtillon, situated near the village of Mangienne on the River Othain, about six leagues northeast of Verdun. ROUSS.]. Since the brethren of Caladia, occupied in building their own abbey, were insufficient for founding this one, the venerable Rannulf, abbot of the monastery of Claustrum [Note: [Col. 0962A] Himmerode near Trier.], received from the devout bishop the gift of this site, to develop into an abbey [Col. 0962A], and sent his brethren to prepare it. The undertaking was begun by them two years ago, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1142; it has already advanced so promisingly toward its future that the venerable assembly of Cistercians has decreed that an abbey shall be established there.

Let it be said, without offense to anyone, that in order that all these affairs of this place might proceed thus, our monk Lord Hugh, a man of most fervent zeal, at whose urging and report we composed this whole little work, [Note: [Col. 0961] “apud omnes” (“with everyone”) written twice in manuscript 1.] pressed, admonished [Note: [Col. 0963] “and” written twice in manuscript 1.] and entreated everyone and above all others. He now wishes the lord bishop to be piously reminded by our writing, that he may provide especially for this place, assist it, and bring it to completion, since it is his own alms, through which he may be received into the eternal tabernacles of heaven. Thus, just as some of our order have accused him of expelling the Order of Saint Benedict from the church of Paul, so those same persons may prove that he is ready in every respect worthily to care for, help, and bestow his resources upon those who keep the profession of Saint Benedict.

But why do I relate these very small matters concerning his generosity, as though there were not more? Why do I suppress in silence so vast a subject for praise—that God has not been silent concerning the praise of His Church in this time, and that, in this matter, He has been the worthy bishop’s helper by His counsel, [Col. 0963B] exhortation, and assistance? For, as Jeremiah lamented (*Lamentations* 4), long since among the older orders the gold had become changed, the finest color had perished, and the stones of the sanctuary lay scattered at the head of every street. Worldly glory, possessions, and wealth had infected the minds of both orders like the decay of poison; windy ambition and burning avarice afflicted these two orders of the Latin Church—rich in property but poor in virtues—with a double disease.

But behold: according to Ezekiel (chapter 1), amid this wind of vain ambition, this fire of inflamed avarice, and this dark cloud of faithlessness, coming from the cold north and enveloping all things, the radiance of divine mercy shone forth from [Col. 0963C] the midst; and from that radiance flashed those four living creatures of the heavenly Godhead [Note: [Col. 0963] “shall flash forth,” manuscript 1.], which, walking with straight feet, corrected the slipping feet of the ecclesiastical estate.

First, the holy Roman Church, through its apostolic leaders Gregory VII, Urban, and Paschal, drove simoniacal avarice from the holy Church as a profane thing, cut it down with the sword of blessed Peter against Caesar’s arms, and at length, after it had long resisted, killed it by great force. Thus there appears here, according to the Apocalypse (chapter 4), John’s first living creature, like a lion.

Then that Carthusian religious life, hitherto unheard of in the world [Note: [Col. 0963] “pure,” manuscript 1.], proceeded from the most holy school of the most reverend Bruno. By living in the flesh apart from the flesh in a manner unusual among mortals, he represents for us today angels upon earth, the apostle Paul in Paradise, [Col. 0963D] John the Baptist, and Paul the Hermit in the wilderness. You may therefore rightly call this religious life the flower of the world, and rightly declare it to be the living creature like an eagle flying into heaven.

[Col. 0964A] And so that we may have the living creature of the laboring calf, offered in sacrifice to God, and likewise that of the man wisely reasoning about divine and heavenly things, there followed those two cherubim spreading their wings in the midst of the Church and, with faces turned toward the mercy-seat, looking at one another [Note: [Col. 0963] “looking,” manuscript 1.]: that is, the two most illustrious orders, protecting the Church by their devotion and, with hearts turned to God, striving with one another in mutual charity. One of these, the Cistercian order, under Bernard, abbot of most holy name, restored the monastic order, now almost fallen, to the original standard of apostolic life. The other, shown beforehand by God both in merit and name (*Praemonstratus*), begun under Norbert, archbishop of Parthenopolis, shook the ecclesiastical order free from the mud of worldly vanity.

You might believe these [Col. 0964B] two orders to be the two prophets of the Apocalypse (chapter 11), sent by God near the end of the world and clothed in the sackcloth of penitence; the two olive trees of heavenly mercy and the two lampstands of divine grace. Thus they afflict themselves in every way; thus they water the world with the word of faith; thus they illuminate it by the light of their merits. With God’s cooperation and the help of all devout persons, they have now advanced so far that the Cistercian order, in this thirty-year period [Note: [Col. 0963] “three-year period,” edition.], has grown to seven hundred and more abbeys, great in name, worth, and number [Note: [Col. 0963] The reading of this word is not certain to me from codex 1; the edition reads “about two hundred.”], and has already begun to spread among the barbarian Sarmatians and the remotest Scythians [Note: [Col. 0963] “began,” manuscript 1.]; while Prémontré has grown in these twenty years to nearly seventy abbeys.

Our bishop received, planted, and fostered both orders in [Col. 0964C] his territories, so liberally that he granted land to the leaders of the Premonstratensian order for building three abbeys. Of these, the venerable Abbot Philip built two: the first, called Belle-Vallée [Note: [Col. 0963D] Belval in the diocese of Reims.], in the forest of Duellium [Note: [Col. 0963D] Duelle or Deuilly. CALM.]; the other beside Hatonchâtel, at a place called in Latin *piscina* (“pool”), but commonly Stanchia [Note: [Col. 0963D] L’Étanche.]. The third [Note: [Col. 0963] “Third,” manuscript 1.] was built by the hermit Herbert near the village of Arc [Note: [Col. 0963D] Arc-ville.], in the valley of Genesium [Note: [Col. 0964D] Genievaux near Hattonchâtel. CALM.].

Eustace also, a most reverend man and builder and father of the two monasteries of Monastery-in-Argonne [Note: [Col. 0964D] Moutier-en-Argonne.] and Chastle-place [Note: [Col. 0964D] Chatrices.], founded an abbey from the bishop’s gift on an island above the River Acra [Note: [Col. 0964D] Air?], upon episcopal freehold restored by Ulrich, brother of Guy the archdeacon, of whom I have related much. There now an elected abbot of the order of Saint Augustine, with eight canons, is advancing the place toward greater things [Col. 0964D]. All these establishments, still under construction, increase daily in resources and in the number of God’s servants. The knights of the Temple of Jerusalem also built a hospice near Hatonchâtel [Col. 0965A] [Note: [Col. 0965C] Apparently Doncourt-aux-Templiers near Hattonchâtel. CALM.], and certain other works are still being done.

The same bishop bestowed his best gifts on Saint Benedict: Aderard, son of Count Hugh of Risnel [Note: [Col. 0965C] Rinelle.], granted from his own property, on the border of the bishopric, land upon which a monastery of the Cistercian order [Note: [Col. 0965C] Saint-Benoît-en-Woëvre; compare fragments of the charter of donation in Wassebourg, fol. CCC.] was to be built. I cannot worthily recount how much this venerable bishop himself gave to these and all other servants of God from every quarter, beyond what has been mentioned; how much his entire reverend clergy, who became his co-workers in all these matters, added with most generous devotion; and how much all his people throughout the city and bishopric contributed and helped in every way. I venture to say in pious faith that all these people will still give more to these [Col. 0965B] servants of God. For one may see those people daily frequenting the servants of God and attending them with devout diligence, so that you might think simple doves were nesting in a rock, or ingenious bees were flitting about flowers to make waxen honey. The latter receive the former as a hen receives her chicks beneath her wings: they embrace and cherish them, and send them joyfully back to their own homes, glad at the favors obtained.

Nor shall we be silent concerning the worthy praise of the bishop in regard to his own church, that is, the church of the holy Mother of God: namely, how he enlarged or adorned [Note: [Col. 0965] A word is missing: “enlarged,” “adorned,” or similar.] its presbytery and nearly its entire fabric with two towers and a huge building, assigning to it all offerings of pilgrims made there and adding much from his own resources. This work, incomparable with any other of the age, is still growing [Col. 0965C] under the hands of craftsmen headed by Guarin, more learned than the rest, as Hiram of Tyre was under Solomon.

Nor should I pass over Constantius, an excellent keeper and servant of the church. Though very small in body, he was great in spirit and faith. Having acquired great wealth from a poor beginning, he spent it all upon the work of heavenly almsgiving. To say nothing of how many lepers [Note: [Col. 0965C] That is, lepers, commonly called *ladres*. CALM.]—abhorrent to others—he washed, clothed, and cared for in his home with his wife Officia, truly serviceable to God: he spanned the Meuse at Harenari [Note: [Col. 0965C] At the place called Pont des Raines, toward the Abbey of Saint-Nicholas-des-Prés. CALM. (with WASS); from whom Roussel, p. 254, dissents.] with a bridge, after floodwaters had destroyed it three times, twice in timber and once in stone; he laid out the public road to that bridge with a great embankment; he built hospitals for the poor, endowing them with assigned revenues; and finally, having exhorted others toward this work of the church, he himself began it first at great expense [Col. 0966A]. Thus faithful to city and church, and leaving a good example to posterity, he placed all his treasures in the treasury of heaven, borne there by holy almsgiving. [Note: [Col. 0965C] See Constantius’s epitaph in Wassebourg, fol. CCCIIII.]

Nor should this praise of the bishop be passed over: during the fifteen [Note: [Col. 0966C] Below, in Albero’s fourteenth year, Laurence testifies that he wrote; therefore this passage must have been subsequently added or altered, unless one supposes that the writer here counted years so as to reckon the first and last years in which he wrote as complete. But the words “Nor should this … be passed over” perhaps indicate a later addition.] years for which he has held the episcopate, he has spared his common people so much that he discontinued the debased striking of coinage [Note: [Col. 0965] “of coinage,” manuscript 1; “of his own coin,” edition.] immediately after his first year; and, introducing the money of Châlons, he has never afterwards permitted the coinage to be changed, lest the poor be burdened by it.

The church of Caladia, consecrated by this bishop and founded in this bishopric, has also grown into an abbey of the holy Cistercian order [Note: [Col. 0965] Written twice in manuscript 1.]. Under Abbot Gunter of holy memory, nearly [Col. 0966B] three hundred servants of God now serve there for the kingdom of heaven. It began under Bishop Henry, when Robert, a monk of our venerable monastery, first lived there as a hermit with two companions, after building a small church and a few little dwellings. When he was promoted to the abbey of Belle-Lieu and the place remained vacant, it was given by its noble owner, Walter the nephew, to the venerable Guy, abbot of Trois-Fontaines, with Bishop Henry’s consent and encouragement, and especially through the devoted effort [Note: [Col. 0965] “inserting,” manuscript 1.] and exhortation of the nobleman Hervey.

When that place had duly increased in resources and in the number of servants of God, Hervey joined their community in a remarkable example. Renouncing his wife, his only son, the world, and everything belonging to it, this excellent man compelled one of his servants to tie a noose around his master’s throat and drag him thus as though he were a robber from his home to the place of Saint Sulpicius [Note: [Col. 0965] “of punishment,” manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 0966C] The monastery of Caladia was dedicated to Saint Sulpicius.] for two miles, while all looked on in wonder, wept, and praised God in this act.

33. In the ninth year of the episcopate of the venerable Lord Albero, Laurence died a blessed death in 1140, after having happily presided as abbot over this monastery for forty years and three months. German by birth and language, and endowed with great learning and ability, he had distinguished himself from early youth at Saint-Airy in the training ground of monastic profession. There he flourished in our monastery under Abbot Rodulf; and during the exile of our community under that same Rodulf, as prior in the Burgundian monastery of Dijon under Abbot Gerenton of holy memory, [Col. 0967A] he abolished or altered many superfluities of tradition that he found there and introduced other, more honorable practices. Returning with our brethren, and after the death of the aforesaid Rodulf promoted from prior to abbot, he presided in all things holily, devoutly, and justly, and therefore advanced greatly both the community’s resources and its religious life.

Under him many nobles bestowed many gifts on our church. Among them Theoderic and Wideric, brothers of Count Frederick, granted the cell of Neuvillers [Note: [Col. 0967D] Neuvillers on the Moselle.] with all its dependencies. Count Raynald, their stepfather, also gave the cells of Alzeicourt and Nerli [Note: [Col. 0967D] Auzeicourt and Nesles. CALM.] to the holy Roman Church, so that this church might hold them by his gift for an annual rent of [Col. 0967B] twelve denarii. Pope Paschal and likewise Innocent then issued privileges providing that, since this house had twice suffered persecution for its loyalty to the Apostolic See, should persecution assail it again, it might find secure refuge under the protection of the Roman Church. The most noble Cunegund, wife of Maffrid, also offered Saint Vito many estates belonging to her in her own right. It would take too long to tell how many estates and gifts others gave, and by what resources and brethren the other cells were increased.

34. When Laurence died, the equally venerable Segard, his kinsman and a monk, became his successor in office, piety, and religious life. As prior he enclosed the brethren’s cemetery with a wall and improved the cloister. [Col. 0967C] As abbot, he had made at great expense a distinguished, vast, beautiful, and very costly shrine for the re-entombment of the bones of his blessed patron Vito, and he planned still greater things; but behold, God took him from us. For after two years of his blessed governance he rested in the Lord.

Under these leaders the name of this place flourished everywhere, its possessions spread and grew, and its religious life was vigorous. Yet I may justly pour out this complaint on my own behalf concerning them: I did not deserve either to see them or to enjoy their goodness, having been brought here after their deaths by Prior Rodulf, a venerable man. Of this Rodulf and Segard himself I shall worthily relate that both were kinsmen, compatriots, and contemporaries; both entered the monastery together on the same day and together professed the monastic life on the same day; and both likewise were consecrated abbots together by the bishop on the same day—Rodulf of Saint Vito and Segard of Saint Airy.

Segard, indeed, because he presided over obedient and disciplined men, acted well and prosperously in all things. Rodulf, however, because he ruled rebellious and contumacious men, conducted affairs well in all things, but not prosperously. For whatever works of piety and religious observance he enjoined upon them, they trampled underfoot abominably; they squandered prodigally the necessary resources [Col. 0968A] which he procured with care; they drove away through harassment and hostility the religious persons whom he had brought in for them; finally, having left him alone among them, they attacked him ruinously, provoked his heart day and night to extreme bitterness, and opposed him in everything.

Following the example of Saint Benedict, he fled such men; and he informed his beloved Segard, who went after him grieving, that he would more gladly endure every exile and death than preside over such people. When Segard called him back with him to Verdun, he began to protest that he would never return unless he were first released from the abbacy of such men. Segard secured his release from the unwilling bishop and honored him in every way as prior of his own monastery. That house [Note: [Col. 0967] The scribe of codex 1 wrote “That house,” but erased it, and thus omitted everything from “and so” to “thus driven out.”], however, [Col. 0968B] remains desolate to this day, like a shelter in a vineyard and a hut in a cucumber field, until the most worthy bishop provides for it as he did for the church of Saint Paul.

Indeed, if it is permissible to speak truth while preserving charity, I would judge that race of men alien to goodness: they could not endure even such a man as I found Rodulf to be—gentle, reasonable, and just—unless it be that they boast that by some fate they have been condemned so that, from the founding of their place onward, none of all their abbots has died among them; rather, each has died elsewhere, an exile driven out by them. Some of these men, driven out in this manner, are still alive today.

35. (1141.) The bishopric had rested from warfare for seven years; but behold, the storm of wars [Col. 0968C] thundered once more. Rayner of Baulny [Note: [Col. 0967] “of the bath,” manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 0967D] Baulny. ROUSS.], having fortified a new castle in fidelity to the bishopric, used it so that both he and his lord, Count Henry of Grandpré, inflicted every kind of harm upon ecclesiastical property. Moreover, this same Henry, while under the escort of Lord—or Count—Raynald, violently despoiled wealthy merchants of Huy travelling within the bishopric. The bishop and Raynald repeatedly summoned him to court to answer both for himself and for his man Rayner. But he despised law and hearing, took up arms, and made a first and a second raid through the bishopric, plundering and burning almost as far as Verdun. Yet, repulsed in arms, he unwillingly left victory to the ecclesiastical party on both occasions.

In order to intercept his raids, the bishop himself established a garrison at Bertincourt [Note: [Col. 0968D] Betincourt, three or four leagues northwest of Verdun. ROUSS.], having strengthened its defenses. Then, because this did not suffice, he besieged the castle of Baulny itself. Every day the fighting was extremely fierce on both sides; every day Henry’s soldiers, posted safely beyond the water, laid ambushes for our men.

But Hugh, son of Count Raynald, having one day left his own men with nearly two hundred knights, made for the castle of Vienne in order to attack Henry’s party. Behold, while on the road, he learned from messengers and from the very tracks of feet that hostile companies had passed in the direction of his own men. Following their trail, he fell unexpectedly upon them while they were badly but securely posted and unsuspecting; he captured about eighty of them and kept their horses with all the plunder [Note: [Col. 0969] Omitted in manuscript 1.]. A few escaped in flight to Vienne and reported the sad outcome to Henry, who lay ill there, grievously injured after falling from his horse and dislocating his shoulder. In fear they added that the enemy would soon come there; carrying him away in great distress, they fled to safer ground. Thus Vienne might at once have been taken as empty by our men, had they pursued.

[Col. 0969B] Henry, distrusting everyone and compelled by the loss of his nobler followers—nearly all of whom the episcopal force had captured—sought peace. As soon as he recovered, he came to Verdun, stood trial on every charge, and, submitting obediently, made restitution for all. First of all, he ordered the surrender of the castle besieged by the bishop. The bishop demolished it and jointly imposed an interdict that no one should ever dare restore its ruins.

36. In the fourteenth year of his episcopate (1144), the lord bishop vowed a journey to Jerusalem. He had conceived this vow with long-standing devotion and concealed it from his followers for fear of being impeded, so that his church saw him carry the cross in the customary manner before it heard that he was going. We then feared, not without reason, that the liberty he had restored to us would once again be taken away by tyrants during his absence. But God’s mercy came to our aid: at whose prompting Pope Celestine (1143–1144), Innocent’s successor at that time, and the entire Roman Church kindly obstructed the bishop’s devout vow, forbade him to go beyond Rome, and sent the worthy shepherd back to his abandoned sheep, whom wolves were already planning to attack.

Meanwhile a tremendous storm of winds arose and brought unheard-of destruction of forests, towers, and houses in these regions of Gaul. An unceasing wind and flooding rain were followed by barrenness of crops, and especially severe failure of wine. But when the bishop returned, to the joy of the Church, he immediately captured one wolf rising against his sheep and checked the other.

For Albert of the castle of Sainte-Menehould, which [Col. 0969D] had amassed innumerable plunderings from the bishopric, again pursued plunder and openly took up arms against the bishop. When the bishop pursued him with few men, and almost unarmed, the plunder was recovered; Albert himself was captured and carried away. Compelled to restore what he had plundered, he now hangs entirely in the bishop’s hands, pending an uncertain release. Robert of the castle of Conflans [Note: [Col. 0969D] Conflans.], likewise, who greedily sought the church’s goods by force of arms, was checked by many repulses, subdued, and compelled [Col. 0970A] to seek peace.

I would certainly ascribe it to no small grace of God that the honorable bishop so successfully restrained and checked these four tyrants like the four winds of heaven—Robert from the east, Albert from the west [Note: [Col. 0969] “and,” manuscript 1.], Raynald from the south, and Henry from the north—so that they might not burst upon his people with a destructive blast. Nor would I deprive of their praise the worthy bishop’s collaborators in all these matters, both in repelling evils and bringing about goods.

First among these from the clergy appear Albert, primicerius and archdeacon, a prudent man held in high esteem at the court of the two emperors Lothair and Conrad; William, dean of venerable memory; Richard, an archdeacon of elegant gifts and good promise, who bore the name of his mother’s kinsman, our bishop Richard of holy memory, [Col. 0970B] and of his uncle, another Richard, elected bishop of Verdun; Andrew, archdeacon, son of Peter of Miroalt [Note: [Col. 0969] “miroad,” manuscript 1.], who beyond all nobles of his time was faithful to the Church of Verdun; likewise John, archdeacon, at whose urging his brothers Rayner and Odard gave our church the freeholds of Chemeium with its church, Duncheium [Note: [Col. 0970D] Donchery. CALM. The other places are less certain.], Bruncurt, and Villare; Peter the cantor; Hugh the treasurer; and Emelin the scholasticus—all three men of outstanding wisdom and greatness of spirit—and all the rest of the clergy, endowed with every diligence and uprightness of character.

Here we reach the end of our subject and of the period, which is the year 1144 of the Incarnate Word: the seventh year of Conrad’s reign, [Col. 0970C] the first of Lucius’s pontificate, and the fourteenth of Albero’s episcopate among us. We implore divine mercy to remain with him to the end, so that the same mercy which advanced him to vindicate the liberty of Holy Church and has guided him in all things until now may inspire and assist him in everything: that he may wish, endeavor, be able, and accomplish the recovery of the goods taken from the whole Church committed to him, the restoration of those diminished, the preservation of those remaining intact, and the acquisition of others besides. Thus, having become a noble defender of the Church, he may become its distinguished promoter also, and thereby receive a double palm from Christ.

Moreover, we ask that no one construct an accusation against us from this little work. Although we believe we have written only what is true, whoever presents the truth more accurately, we are ready in every respect to follow the better judgment [Col. 0970D]. We have recorded good things for an example to posterity, but evil things as a warning to some, and we direct them to do the same for their descendants. Otherwise, just as we now fault our forebears’ negligence because they did not write down the deeds of their own time, which we therefore do not know, so they too may justly be blamed by their descendants if they do not write. For memory of the past has great power both to stir up the good and to restrain the bad. [Note: [Col. 0969] Here codex 2 ends; codex 1 continues in another hand.]

[Col. 0971]

## CONTINUATION
[Col. 0971A] 1. I fear that I should be taking away from the praises of our pious and venerable father Segard, from whom we have not long since digressed, that which, through the intervention of the grace of his merits and the ensuing effect of his good works, he deserved to have heaped upon him. Therefore let us turn our pen again to him. Thus, as abbot, he began with every effort to devote himself to the interests of the church, keeping watch both within and without, both personally and through the brethren joined to him. Finally, he began daily to concern himself with the honourable treatment of the most holy body of our venerable father Vito; and, having accumulated as much expenditure in gold and silver as he could, he resolved by every means to exalt it with great splendour. But, alas! soon struck by his final lot, after three years in office, with the goldsmith who had begun that work having died, that venerable father himself also [Col. 0971B] died not much later, in the year of the Lord 1143, and was buried in the chapter-house of this monastery. The venerable father Cono succeeded him in the administration.

Once ordained, Cono, impelled by great ardour of spirit, resolved with equal exertion to complete the work which his venerable predecessor had begun; and, God prospering him, he diligently strove to finish it honourably in every detail, as he had resolved. When at last this very laborious work had been completed, it had very often been resolved by many persons that, at a fixed time of year, the most blessed body should be transferred into so honourable a shrine, in the presence both of the lord bishop and of religious abbots or men of good repute, so that thereafter the anniversary of so great a translation might be solemnly observed each year. Yet, as is plainly clear and may be inferred from the outcome of the event, neither was divine cooperation present, nor did the will of the saint himself then support their wishes.

But as time went on, namely in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1147, when the expedition of Christians against the pagans went forth from the whole Roman Empire—

> A star, already seen beforehand, had foreshown it,  
> Scattering its light-bearing mane over the neighbouring realms;  
> This sign plainly signified the will on high:  
> that the Roman realms should bring the profane nations to ruin;  
> whither now the race of Christ’s worshippers hastens devoutly,  
> desiring with an avenging right hand to strike those  
> who strove to dishonour Christ’s mother—

[Col. 0971D] Lord Pope Eugenius came into France. Invited by many entreaties from the lord bishop of Verdun, Albero by name, to consecrate the principal church of the Blessed Virgin, [Col. 0972A] he entered the city on the Nones of November (5 November), while the whole city rejoiced. Having heard of the reputation of this saint, and that the solemnity of his sacred deposition was to be celebrated on the fifth Ides of the same month (9 November) [note: witness 1 reads *ydus*], he came with his cardinals and the lord bishop to this monastery. Received with due reverence and with laudatory acclamations, he saw the shrine prepared in a most honourable fashion, praised and blessed it, and himself, together with the lord bishop, transferred the venerable body into it, while an innumerable multitude of people stood by.

Immediately the venerable pope began to celebrate the divine offices; after the Gospel reading, ascending the pulpit with the aforementioned bishop and several others, he greatly extolled, among the other words of his holy sermon, the honour due to this saint. Finally, both he and the bishop enjoined upon the whole diocese that the saint’s feast should be celebrated with the greatest solemnity every year. O how countless was the throng of men and women present at this holy solemnity! Rushing eagerly and devoutly to kiss the most holy head, they joyfully testified—and marvelled as they testified—that they drew from it a wondrous fragrance; and very many wept.

> From this one must judge how great the honour due  
> to him whom Christ thus advanced to appointed honour:  
> that an apostolic man, leaving the toga-clad people,  
> came to these regions and blessed us with this gift,  
> when he revered the saint and with his own hands set him again in place,  
> and, after such an honour, established his feast for all ages.  
>
> Let none doubt that this counsel was ordained by God;  
> but He who wisely governs all things glorified the saint  
> as it pleased Him and as He had decreed.

2. Bishop Albero, a man of noble birth and approved merit, worn down by labour and weariness, broken by age and old age, resigned his bishopric. Avoiding tumults and crowds of people, he withdrew for rest to the cloister of Saint Paul at Verdun, of the Premonstratensian Order (1156). Having happily spent two years there in continual attendance on reading and prayer, full of days, he rested in peace in the year of the Lord 1158, and was committed to burial in the greater church of Blessed Mary.

[Col. 0972D] 3. Albero was succeeded in the government of the bishopric by Albert of Mercey [note: Marcey, near Longwy, between Verdun and Luxembourg, as Roussel, p. 259, supposes], a man of outstanding ability, flourishing in the study of letters. With diligent sagacity he cared for his flock and, insofar as human capacity allowed, rooted out the causes of error; he was ignorant of boastfulness and tireless in helping the poor. As he advanced toward old age, fleeing false and deceptive glory, he resolved to go to Clairvaux, so that, taking the habit there, he might sever the allurements of worldly life and all the pomp of the age, and, poor himself following the poor Christ, might acquire the riches of eternity.

But after preparing the conveyances for his journey and the other things necessary to him, leaving everything behind, he set out, rode in a carriage, left the city after bidding the people farewell, and came before the gate of the blessed Peter and Vito. Then suddenly, in a strange and marvellous way, a thing worthy of wonder happened. The carriage in which the venerable man sat came apart, its joints loosening and its axles breaking, so that it could not proceed another step on its journey. [Col. 0973B] The wise, prudent, and faithful man, having inspected and carefully considered the occurrence, judged that it had been brought about by divine providence. Yet he did not therefore, with his mind turned in the opposite direction, think that he ought to abandon his purpose; rather, interpreting the omen favourably, he entered the monastery of the blessed Peter and Vito [at the hour when the brothers are awakened for Matins by the lesser bell; note: added in the margin of witness 1], believing that the breaking-up of the vehicle had contained some omen that could have impeded the progress of his journey.

He also recalled the incident concerning Mark the Evangelist: when he was sent by blessed Peter to evangelize Alexandria and was leaving a ship by boat, [Col. 0973C] he broke his shoe. Taking this as a sign and giving thanks to God, Mark declared that his journey would be successful [note: see *Acts of Saint Mark*, *Acta Sanctorum*, April III, p. 348]. Our same venerable bishop Albert held that a similar thing had happened to himself. Having immediately requested the habit from Abbot Cono and received it, he proved by clear evidence that God had stood by him in His favour.

What vows he conceived there, how much devotion he displayed, and how purely he offered himself in sacrifice at the altar, was known and is known to God alone; and God, by the aforementioned memorials, declared that Albert had been most acceptable to Him. During the very short time that he survived, he began to devote himself to reading and prayer; and afterward, not long after receiving the habit, returning his votive thanks to God, he laid aside the burden of flesh in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1162 [Col. 0973D] (14 April), breathed out his spirit, and was buried before the altar of Saint Lawrence in our monastery. Richard, the elect, a nobleman surnamed the Child, succeeded him; for devotion’s sake he undertook an overseas journey (1162–1171). Arnulph, bishop, succeeded Richard (1171–1172).

[Col. 0974A] 4. We have also judged it fitting briefly to recount the deeds, most worthy of remembrance, of our venerable father Abbot Cono. Above many of his predecessors, he was very provident and solicitous in renewing and restoring this monastery. By various works of gold and silver, hangings, tapestries, books, and other ornaments, he greatly improved, dignified, and adorned this church. He obtained for this church from the bishop of Toul the altars—that is, tithes—of Flavigny and Neuville [note: Neuville]. Likewise, he deserved to obtain the altar of Valmé from the bishop and archdeacon of Châlons [note: witness 1 reads *chatal.*] [through the agency of the lord Gozwin, venerable prior of Chaude-Fontaine; note: added in the margin of witness 1]. He acquired an allod at the village of Saint-Amant for the church’s use.

And, since it is the custom of good men always to advance to better things, [Col. 0974B] after completing the work of the library, he raised stone towers from the foundations and brought their construction to completion [note: these are to be understood not as towers of the church, but as towers intended to fortify the monastery; Roussel, p. CLXII]. He also assigned to the brethren ten solidi at Nixéville on the day of his anniversary [note: in 1564 it is called Nixeville; Roussel, p. 454 n.].

Nor do I think it should be left unmentioned how much honour the lord pope showed him, and how much favour thereby accrued to him. When that lord pope had come to Rheims, according to custom, to celebrate a council [note: this appears to concern Eugenius, who held the Council of Rheims in 1148], and all the abbots and bishops had taken their places on their seats and benches, our venerable father Abbot Cono happened to arrive somewhat late. He entered the council clothed in sacred vestments, but had no seat on which to sit, and therefore sat upon the ground. When the lord pope [Col. 0974C] turned his eyes toward him, he said: “This is the man who, since I crossed the Alps, has shown us greater honour and more especial favour of reverence than all the Gauls.” At once, as a token of affection, he sent him the curule chair in which he himself was accustomed to sit. Cono humbly received it with thanksgiving and sat upon it.

From this his successors may see how great was the glory of the man whom the supreme pontiff wished thus to honour before all and above all. Therefore, being a man outstanding in many excellences under the discipline of regular strictness, he trained very many persons worthy of praise—his imitators and heirs, enriched by the rewards of the greatest merits—and formed them in holy morals and honourable conduct for the praise of God. These were James called of Bras, who became abbot of Saint-Airy; lord Bernacle [note: “Bernard” in the edition], claustral prior; lord Warin, prior of Flavigny; lord Gozwin, prior of Chaude-Fontaine; lord Gerbod, prior; lord Segard; lord Godfrey; lord Haimo; and many others whose names, by God’s mercy, we believe are inscribed in the book [Col. 0975A] of life. Our venerable father Cono died in the year of the Lord 1178 and was buried in the church.

5. Arnulph [note: concerning his genealogy Hermann of the *Miracles of Saint Mary of Laon* I.2, in Guibert’s *Opera*, p. 529, reports: “Count Ernulf of Waren begot Otto, count of Chiny; Otto begot Aubert; Aubert begot Count Aubert and Ernulf, bishop of Verdun.” Compare Alberic under 1168], a man distinguished in learning and character, having received the government of the bishopric, began diligently to conduct the business of his office and defend its rights. For he was shrewd in counsel and eloquent in speech.

In those days there arose a certain knight named Albert, surnamed Pichot, lord of Sainte-Menehould [note: witness 1 reads *manehylde*], a bastard and presumptuous practitioner of every wickedness. This gallows-bird and son of wrath began to harass the bishoprics of Verdun and Châlons, plunder their goods, despoil villages, and burn houses. Therefore Arnulph, bishop of Verdun, grieving for the calamity of his people, allied himself with princes from every quarter [Col. 0975B] and resolved to besiege the castle in which that minister of Satan was staying. Having assembled an army and arranged the battle-lines with their equipment of arms and the other necessities of war, they went there, pitched camp, and posted sentries.

After some days had passed, when they had already struggled in fiercer battles, the bishop was struck in the head by an arrow shot by an archer from the defensive works of the walls and died (1181, 14 August). The army, disturbed and dismayed by the loss of its leader, dispersed; each of the princes returned to his own home, not without sorrow. They conveyed the bishop’s body to Verdun and committed it to burial [Col. 0975C] in the greater church of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, in the year of the Lord 1181 [note: Wassebourg, fol. CCCXXVI, transcribed an epitaph, apparently of a later period, from marble]. Henry of Châtel succeeded him.

6. On the death of our venerable father Cono (1178), Richer, a man of remarkable simplicity, was elected abbot by the unanimous will of the whole chapter. For almost a year his blessing was deferred; then the venerable bishop Arnulph summoned and exhorted him to receive the sacrament of blessing according to custom and to carry out pastoral responsibilities with watchful care. But Richer, unable to endure the pastoral burden and labour, immediately renounced the abbacy.

After Richer, Peter of Brie was elected (1179). When he was being led, as was customary for an elected abbot, into the church to be enthroned in the pastoral seat, Bishop Arnulph, fearing that if Peter became abbot he would raise thorns of trouble against him, violently [Col. 0975D] confronted Peter, declaring that he belonged to the lordship of the count of Bar; and for this reason Peter was deprived of the honour of prelacy. Yet not much later he was made abbot at Saint-Pierre-au-Mont [note: the edition reads “was elected”; Saint-Pierre-au-Mont was then situated near Châlons-en-Champagne and is now within the city; CALM], [Col. 0976A] and, after a long time, having resigned his charge, returned to Saint Vito (1179).

Alestannus the Younger succeeded him, a very religious man (1180). In that same year he put off the human person—that is, died—and was buried inside the church beside the entrance to the chapel of Saint Christopher. Alestannus the Elder succeeded him, a man no less religious than his predecessor. After spending five years in pastoral care, he voluntarily resigned the administration of the abbey (1183). Living the remainder of his life at Bekenele, occupied with divine reading and constant prayer, he ended a blessed life by a more blessed death and was buried in the monastery of that place before the altar.

Thomas, abbot of Moiraumont [note: Maurimont], succeeded Alestannus the Elder, a man noble by nature and morals. He procured a black cope embroidered with gold, repaired suitably the ruins of the old refectory of the brethren, and renewed its roof and ceiling. Then Hugh, provost of Saint Vito, was raised to the abbacy in Thomas’s place [note: “of Maurimont” added in the edition]. Agitated by the spur of envy and inflamed by love of greed, he began with violent verbal reproaches to attack Thomas, abbot of Saint Vito [note: witness 1 has *lacessire*], to stir up enmities against him, and to entice Verdun persons with gifts and flattery, in order that he might remove Thomas from the office of prelacy and occupy his seat.

The abbot, free from fraud and ignorant of dark devices, unable to endure enmities and seditions, relinquished pastoral care lest, if matters worsened on his account, he might seem to be encouraging wrongdoing [Col. 0976C] and the monastery over which he presided might suffer loss of its property and honours. At length, after living well for some time at Neuvillers [note: either Neuvillers on the Moselle or, more probably, Neufville near Verdun], he died and rests buried in the church.

Hugh, abbot of Maurimont and formerly provost of this church, succeeded Thomas (1187). While he was abbot at Maurimont, he had the church screen and crypt built in costly and fitting workmanship. Once made abbot of this church, he acquired from Bishop Albert the altar of Bulainville [note: in the deanery of Souilly; Roussel], and had the larger vineyard, called the New Vineyard, planted and cultivated beside Scance [variant: witness 1 reads *scanciam*]. Later, however, when sedition arose from the very persons by whom he had been raised to the abbacy, divine judgment turned back upon him, and he began to be fiercely harassed. Thus he who had insulted his predecessor by stirring up conflicts was himself now subjected to like mockery by a similar fate. Since the disputes had been publicly stirred up and he neither could nor ought to resist, in the tenth year [Col. 0977A] after his ordination (1197) he resigned the prelacy.

After him Stephen, prior of Sainte-Marguerite and of Notre-Dame, a Cluniac monk, was elected and made abbot, at the request and urging of the noble lady Agnes, countess of Bar, sister of Louis, the illustrious king of the French. Having obtained the government of this monastery, he was one day standing in the presence of the said countess. Asked by her how he could remove the ruins of such great debts by which his church was burdened, he replied presumptuously in an irreverent and uncontrolled manner that he had the greatest confidence in the red tunic of Saint Vito. No sooner had he spoken than punishment followed the offence. Before the eyes of the ladies, barons, and all who were present, struck by a most violent paralysis for the mockery and insult [Col. 0977B] inflicted on the saint, he fell down, began to foam at the mouth, and tear himself with his nails. Thus chastised by the deserved vengeance, he remained permanently speechless, that fear might be instilled in others and an example given of the reverence due to saints. Seeing this, the countess ordered him to be lifted up and carried to a bed. Later he was brought back to this church; shortly thereafter he resigned the abbacy, returned to Notre-Dame, and, after residing there for some time, died.

7. Thus, contention having burst forth among princes who wandered on a trackless waste and not on the way, schism arose between kingdom and priesthood. And behold, while such strife was troubling the princes of the world, [Col. 0977C] Henry of Châtel [note: on his family, see Alberic under 1167] succeeded Arnulph (1181). Because he favoured the emperor’s party in counsel, aid, loyalty, and affection, he was struck with public excommunication.

Meanwhile Folmar, archbishop of Trier, after staying at Rome for some time on the business of the holy church and his own affairs, returned. Since, amid the storm-cloud of raging wars, he could not return to Trier, he arranged to celebrate a council at Rheims concerning the ordering of church affairs and the correction of abuses. Accordingly, when the clergy of Verdun had been summoned, Henry, who resisted the priesthood, was compelled by the judgment of the clergy to resign the bishopric. Having done this, he returned to Liège. There, after recovering the personate and prebend with which he had long before been endowed, he remained for some time [variant: *aliquot* in witness 1 for *aliquod*] and, overtaken by death, [Col. 0977D] closed his final day (1186). Albert, a very vigorous man, succeeded Henry.

Yet a dispute arose in the greater chapter between factions over the election of the bishop, because one party wished Albert the treasurer, while the other wished Robert of Grandpré, to be made bishop [notes: “treasurer,” “of,” and “Grandpré” are each corrected in witness 1]. Albert prevailed at the emperor’s court. Later, when sedition had arisen between the townsmen and outsiders, he was pierced by a lance wielded by a certain knight in defence of the city and died in 1208, on 25 or 26 July [note: see the epitaph in Wassebourg, fol. CCCXLII, who also gives a fuller account of the cause of death]. Robert the primicerius succeeded him.

8. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1197, our venerable father Louis, a man endowed with grace and good character and very zealous for the law of the Lord, succeeded Stephen and was appointed abbot of our monastery, while his venerable brother Albert was bishop. Louis found his church burdened by a multitude of debts and stripped of temporal goods, so that it was oppressed by borrowed money and the greater part of its revenues went to pay interest. Therefore, lest this church should thereafter be compelled to lose the greater part of its possessions, it was forced to sell to the nobleman Lord Thomas of Boulay the manor of Boulay [note: Boulay; CALM] with all its appurtenances—except [Col. 0978B] the village of Leimerfelt—and whatever our church possessed at Criemenges [note: the edition reads *Cimenges*].

Since he had assumed the church’s care while still young, he endured poverty in himself, avoided every superfluity, gradually began to advance through good works, and before long restored to good condition, with divine assistance [note: added above the line in witness 1], the church which the disorder and contention of previous men had reduced almost to nothing in religion and honour. Our aforesaid father, being esteemed and renowned among princes and magnates, obtained for this church the altars of Mont-Saint-Martin, Villers, and Baylod, and the church of Rohons [note: the edition reads *Reboris*], acquiring them from the men of Trier; and from the bishops of Verdun [Col. 0978C] he obtained the donation to this church of the altars of Rarecourt [note: Rarecourt; CALM] and Neuville with their dependencies.

And, since it is characteristic of good men always to advance to better things, he assigned adequate revenues for the use of the sick and infirm in the infirmary, and completely built a new almonry with a chapel. Having also acquired, at great expense, the advocacy [variant: *Advociam* in witness 1 for *Advocatiam*] of Chaude-Fontaine, he enlarged with wealth and revenues this priory, which could scarcely suffice for the maintenance of one monk. But since it would be long to recount individually all the ways in which he improved the church, repaired the priories, and restored our distant and nearby places to good condition, omitting many matters, he bought for five hundred pounds the advocacy of Mont-Saint-Vito from the nobleman Gobert of Apremont. [Col. 0978D] He also adorned our church with furnishings of gold and silver; had a silver panel suitably made before the high altar; raised the cloister from the foundations; repaired almost all the workshops; and, at the end of his life, began a handsome and costly new work in the monastery, in a part of which—namely, the chapel of the Blessed Virgin—he appointed that he should be buried [note: witness 1 reads *sepiliri*].

On the day of his anniversary [Col. 0979A] he also assigned to the brethren forty solidi charged upon one house in the market, ordering that half of this be spent on the anniversary of Abbot Richard of pious memory. In his time there flourished venerable and honourable persons through whom law, reason, discretion, religion, and honour flourished and prevailed in this church. Of these, three successively became abbots at Saint-Airy: Martin, a good and honourable man; after Martin, James, a man very religious and learned in letters; and after James, Nicholas, treasurer of this place. This Nicholas enclosed the abbey of Saint-Airy with a strong wall, rebuilt the court outside [note: witness 1 has *iiii* for *extra*] the circuit of the walls, and repaired and built barns [note: added in the margin of witness 1; the edition ends after “court … built”].

Nicholas of Chastes was made abbot in the monasteries of Waucourt and Hastière [Col. 0979B] [note: Vaussor and Hastières]. Moreover, religious men flourished in this church: Stephen called Tyecans; his brother Renard; Werner called Paganus; Hugh called of Belle-Lieu; Reynald; and likewise Hugh called Faber. Bearing the burden manfully upon their shoulders [variant: *supposito* in witness 1 for *suppositis*], they vigorously assisted our venerable father Louis in improving the church, with counsel and aid, loyalty and affection.

9. When Robert, a vigorous man, had been raised to the summit of the bishopric and was managing episcopal affairs vigorously and discreetly, two noblemen opposed him: Herbert [Col. 0979C] Dyvous [note: d’Yvois? XI, 261], dean of Rheims and canon [Col. 0980A] of Verdun, and Theoderic, dean of Verdun [note: compare the letters of Pope Innocent III]. They said that he was a novice and unlearned, unworthy of episcopal honour; and they harassed him so greatly that he was compelled to go personally to Rome [note: he is said to have attended the Lateran synod of 1215]. A date having been assigned to him by the supreme pontiff, he was compelled to resign the bishopric. When he had returned to Verdun, he laid aside his mortal clay within the prescribed term and was buried in the greater church (1216, 25 August).

After his death John of Apremont succeeded him, worthy of glory and honour. Burning with the spirit of devotion, he raised from the foundations the monastery called *in Prato* (“in the Meadow”) [note: Saint-Nicolas-des-Prés near the city; compare John’s charter of 1226 in Calmet II, p. CCCCXXXVII], together with certain buildings; he introduced canons and enlarged its revenues. After happily completing seven years at Verdun, he was translated to the bishopric [Col. 0980B] of Metz. Ralph [note: “of Corta,” according to the *Annals of Saint Vito*], cantor of Laon, succeeded him (1224), a gentle and mild man, who gave us the altar of Rarecourt. After completing twenty-one years in the government of the bishopric, he put off the human person and was buried in the greater church (1245, 21 April).

After Ralph’s death, Guy of Traînel received the honour of the bishopric. As he was coming to Verdun to be enthroned in the episcopal seat, he arrived at Hattonchâtel, was seized by a severe fever, and died. Thus joy was changed into grief; he was brought to Verdun and buried in the greater church. Guy of Mello succeeded him in the same year.

[Note: The life of Guy is narrated more fully in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre*, written by a contemporary, in Labbe, *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, I, p. 497 ff.; it is pleasing to add here the passages relevant to the present matter:]

The bishop Guy of Mello, of memorable recollection, succeeded. His deeds claim an all the more attentive hearer because they are known to have been more elevated and nobler in action. He was born in the diocese of Auxerre, of noble blood on both his father’s and mother’s side. His father was William of Mello, knight and lord of the castle of Saint-Prix in that diocese, a man devoted to every courtesy and generosity, a cheerful sharer of his own table, and a supporter of poor nobles. As is reported, because of the aptness of the designation to the fact and a certain special quality of goodness, he was called by many the “Bailiff of Peace.” Whenever he learned that discord had arisen among any of his neighbours, he devoted all his effort to restoring peace and never ceased to labour until he had recalled the discordant, if possible, to concord.

His mother drew her origin from the lineage of the lords of Mont-Saint-Jean and was not inferior to her husband in the distinction of ancient nobility. The bishop of whom we speak, born of these parents, was given from childhood to the study of letters. He made such progress that, first rooted in the foundations of grammar, he became a proficient student of the liberal arts; then, having acquired knowledge of both laws, namely canon and civil law, he afterward, whenever opportunity allowed, diligently studied Holy Scripture [variant: *existit* (“was”) in the edition, for *extitit*]. Yet his purpose in this respect was often hindered by the business of ecclesiastical affairs.

Adorning himself with the morals and learning proper to youth, he despised frivolities. With untrimmed limbs and uncombed hair, he did not concern himself with the grooming of his body, as noble young men customarily do [variant: *compositione* (“grooming”) in the edition, for *compositioni*]. Consequently he was less dear than the other children to his father. But the disposition of the Most High, who reserved him to become a bishop, so adorned his ungroomed state as time passed that the wise son became his father’s glory; his father changed the name “son,” and he was regarded as father and lord, while the sons of his mother were as though bowed before him.

For he was a man tall in stature, well-proportioned in body, great-souled in heart, an industrious augmenter of the church’s estate, a provident administrator of the public good, and a tireless protector of the people; modest in speech, devout in prayer, angelic at the altar. His melodiously resounding chant, like a sounding trumpet, filled the house of God and delighted the souls of his hearers with sweet sounds. Nor was he inferior in counsel in councils and assemblies of prelates; surpassing others in bodily beauty, [Col. 0981] he seemed by his venerable bearing and somewhat commanding look to exercise precedence.

If any matter had to be examined before him in judicial inquiry, or anything else ordered, he gave a ready and careful hearing to persuasions and arguments. Turning over and weighing in his mind what he had heard, he did nothing rashly. From the very beginnings of his discretion he had acquired the practice of maturing his affairs in so great a furnace of deliberation that many attributed this to his mildness; at times, though rarely, it happened that matters ended disadvantageously which could have been settled by prompt dispatch. Yet although he was diligent in affairs and in carrying matters through successfully, scarcely ever was the pressure of secular business so great that he did not give precedence to divine service at its appointed hour.

It was, as it were, his inborn custom to exercise the rigour of justice, reward those who deserved well, and punish wrongdoers, so that at times, not from the swelling pride of malice but from zeal for justice, he somewhat exceeded the gentleness of the rod; to feel compassion for the oppressed, spare suppliants, exalt the humble, humble the proud, and subdue rebels. Moreover, the Lord granted him this happiness: in all that he undertook for the honour of God and the rights of his churches, the Lord always gave him victory and directed his works with grace and favour.

### How he subdued the citizens of Verdun

In the thirty-second year of his life, or thereabouts, he was called by canonical election to govern the church of Verdun. Although he was not from its own body, he was consecrated bishop, while nevertheless retaining by dispensation the deanery of the church of Auxerre, which he had formerly held. He learned that the entire jurisdiction—both spiritual and temporal—over the city and citizens of Verdun belonged to the bishop; and that the bishops of Verdun, his predecessors, had long ago possessed it peacefully and in full right for a long time. But, through the negligence or weakness of certain bishops who had immediately preceded him, the shrewd citizens had usurped the city’s temporal jurisdiction and many episcopal rights. They had also created mayors and aldermen, through whom the city was then governed. Moreover, they had imposed public levies and tolls, from which, they said, they maintained the commonwealth and strengthened the city’s walls and fortifications.

Having summoned them before him, he, being prudent in mind, first, according to Gospel teaching, personally admonished and entreated them charitably in gentle words and kindly persuasions. Afterwards he caused them to be earnestly addressed through other great and wise men, asking that they restore to the church the jurisdiction it had thus usurped and the episcopal rights which they had withdrawn, and refrain from like presumptions. But they listened with deaf ears and refused to do this, putting forward, beneath a feigned sweetness of speech—as is the custom of the country—many excuses for their sins.

Compelled then to proceed by the royal road, he struck with the sword of excommunication those who had been canonically warned and, with proud eye, refused to obey his admonitions. They bore this sentence, aggravated—as the law required—to the point that ecclesiastical censure could go no further against persons, with obstinate minds; and, made more stubborn by correction, they went away less burdened by the obstacle.

Seeing their wickedness—for usury and deceit had flourished and still flourished among them from their ancient ancestors—he first took counsel, then, in solemn procession with all the clergy of the city, went out from the town and had Christ’s body carried outside. He placed the city itself and its inhabitants under a general interdict, leaving there only a few priests for the penitence of the dying and the baptism of infants. Suspecting that, if they could, they would gladly devise some evil against him, he withdrew into the castles and fortified places of the bishopric.

Provoked with the greatest indignation by this, they took up the spirit of rebellion and began wickedly to consider how they might unjustly crush the just man. Thus it came about that one day, after a common resolution among themselves and a publicly proclaimed edict, all who were capable of bearing arms and fighting, from youth to old age, went forth from the city under immense noise and pompous tumult, together with mercenary soldiers estimated at almost twelve thousand, to lay waste the bishopric’s territory. Among them, it is said, one of their leaders and chief men wore an episcopal mitre placed above his helmet, in mockery of pontifical honour.

On that same day the bishop, with some of his armed men, had gone out to the castle of Charny to seize, as is believed, livestock which the citizens had sent out from the city to graze [variant: “had released,” Col. 0981]. But when the enemy had been sighted from afar, his own company, which was not far away and for which he had sent, came [variant: “had come,” ed., Col. 0981] to him. When these had assembled—few in number, namely about three hundred men and, it is believed, no more, but men skilled in warfare and experienced in arms—the wary bishop, after brief counsel with them, seized a height, thereby enclosing adversaries untrained in war and positioned with the sun against them. He then attacked them with his men as prudently as powerfully. Almighty God, who taught the hands of His own servants for battle, defended his cause; and he defeated them not so much victoriously as miraculously. He trampled beneath his wrath the wickedly raised head of rebels in their crimes [variant: “and,” ed., Col. 0981]. Some were put to flight, others fell by the sword, and the rest were captured and led away; and the number of prisoners was far greater than that of those who captured them.

In this conflict he did not forget the ministry of the priesthood or pontifical moderation. He wounded no one mortally; rather, by encouraging and exhorting his men to fight, he aided the battle more by the service of his tongue than by his own hands. When victory had been won, he returned joyfully to the castle from which he had gone out.

After a few days had passed, the citizens, taught by the rod of correction—whom the admonitions of gentleness had been unable to bend shortly before—began to seek peace. Through the mediation of good men, the following agreement was reached: when they had restored every temporal jurisdiction and the rights of the church, they were to pay the bishop ten thousand pounds for losses and expenses. From that time he governed the city in tranquillity; he presided over it for only one year.

### How he was transferred to the church of Auxerre, etc.

After some interval of time had elapsed, Reginald of Sallingy, bishop of Auxerre, of good memory, having departed from this life, he was transferred to the church of Auxerre, in which, as stated above, he had retained the deanery. This occurred through both canonical election and postulation, with apostolic authority intervening, and amid great rejoicing of people and clergy. How he governed there [variant: “ruled,” ed., Col. 0983] and what he accomplished is sufficiently declared by the clear evidence of his works, some of which we shall briefly set down in writing. [lacuna]

But these matters also from the later part of his life pertain to our subject:

### How he went to the aid of Charles, king of Sicily

At the time when Manfred, the most wicked prince of damned memory, imitator of his father’s crime and son of the former emperor Frederick, had occupied the kingdom of Sicily, the patrimony properly belonging to Peter, and the duchy of Capua, he shamefully mistreated ecclesiastical affairs, destroyed churches, and drove prelates into exile. The supreme pontiff summoned the illustrious man Charles, son of the king of France, to receive this kingdom and free it from the hands of the aforesaid impious man. A general remission of sins was granted by the Apostolic See to all who went to his aid.

Inflamed by zeal for this devout pilgrimage, he went to Rome to assist Charles, being about to depart with apostolic permission. There he was received with honour and joy by the most holy father Clement IV, then presiding over the Roman Church, and by the cardinals. Entrusted with the office of legate in that expedition, he directed his course, by command of the same supreme pontiff, to the aid of Charles, who had been consecrated king (26 February 1266), accompanying that king and his army.

When they had already approached the city of Benevento, where the adversary stood with a warlike host of Germans, and the battle-lines on either side were on the point of engaging [variant: “was,” ed., Col. 0983], he stood, as one girded inwardly with divine arms and outwardly clad in military equipment, before the king’s army. After an address of saving exhortation to encourage them for the battle, he raised his armoured hand and, relying upon apostolic authority, absolved all from all sins, promising them immediate passage to their homeland, should any perhaps die after fighting with greater valour according to their strength.

Then, so that he might be proved a teacher by the example of his preaching, he seemed not to follow but to go before them into battle. He set the hearts of the beholders aflame with such ardour of courage that, rushing everywhere against enemies and swords, they seemed not to be attacking but raging. In this encounter, not forgetful of pontifical moderation, now breaking through battle-lines, now striking down the enemies’ horses with his sword, now shouting and encouraging, he made up by gesture and by the service of his tongue for what perhaps he feared to attempt against the persons of enemies because of the danger of irregularity—if one may believe that a valiant man in a just war and deadly conflict does not resist those striking with their hands.

Finally Manfred fell dead in battle; his men were either captured, fleeing, or slain by the sword. When the victorious conflict had been completed and the king himself had obtained peaceful rule and lordship over all Apulia, he remained with him for some time. Then, taking his leave, he revisited the apostolic thresholds. There he was received with joy and veneration by the pope and the brethren. After remaining for several days, he departed with the apostolic blessing and, the Lord making his journey prosperous, returned to his own country.

[Col. 0980C] When he wished to depose the twenty sworn men of the city, who had usurped for themselves the lordship [Col. 0981A] and jurisdiction of that city, he besieged the town, first compelling all the clergy to leave it and placing the city under interdict. During this conflict, the citizens within, and the bishop and raiders without, inflicted much damage upon churches and monasteries, both to movable goods and to buildings. Among these losses, the citizens utterly demolished the tower of Saint Paul together with its bells.
