This bishop Guy, I say, being unable to sustain for long the siege of the army, finally surrounded and enclosed the city with fortified positions of soldiers at three places, namely Charny, Dieue, and Watronville [Note: Charny, Dieue, and Watronville, villages nearly two leagues from Verdun, north, south, and east of the city respectively; Col. 0981]. During this time, one day—the Monday after the feast of Saint Bartholomew—the citizens went out from the city with a strong armed force, thirteen thousand men equipped for war. They vigorously attacked those who were inside the aforesaid fortified positions. Although the latter were scarcely three hundred in number, the citizens nevertheless defeated them and took almost three hundred of them prisoner. In this conflict one hundred men or more fell.

After this the citizens, greatly terrified and crushed, at last offered peace to the bishop. They gave ten thousand pounds for the citizens whom he held captive, surrendered to him all their jurisdiction, and the aforesaid twenty sworn men fell. Thus peace was restored between clergy and citizens [Note: Calmet, II, p. 303, testifies that the charter of peace was dated on the vigil of Saint Andrew—that is, 29 November—in 1246]. In that same year, about the Purification of the Blessed Virgin, this same bishop was transferred from Verdun to the bishopric [Col. 0983B] of Auxerre [variant: “altys.”, manuscript 1], while peace was not yet [variant: “nundum,” manuscript 1] firmly established.

10. When the venerable abbot Louis, worn out by old age, had resigned, in the presence of the reverend fathers, namely John of Metz, Roger of Toul, and Ralph of Verdun, William, abbot of Saint-Mansuy, was elected. He had become a monk of this place and had been made prior of Flavigny. He found that priory, its church and all its buildings, completely ruined and reduced to nothing.

Weighing in the balance of reflection that it would bring him disgrace if he remained inactive, but merit if he energetically devoted himself to improving the place, he invoked God—whose custom it is to bestow many things even upon those who do not ask—as his helper. He set his shoulders to so great a work and burden. Sustained by the divine arm, in the first year he restored from the foundations to the summit the timbers, ceilings, roofs, and carved work of the church together with the tower, having removed the rotten old coverings. He also repaired the chapter house [Col. 0984B] with the dormitory, and the refectory with its granaries, sufficiently, suitably, and honourably.

He also rebuilt from new, at great expense and with strength, the barn which had been enclosed and shut in with hedges; he improved the surrounding granges; and through his own diligence and labour, and through Duke Matthew of Lorraine, he restored to their proper place the tithes of Dynvas [Note: D’Ynvas, that is Einvaux or Neinvaux near the abbey of Belchamp. CALMET] and Chamont, which for forty years had been taken from the priory of Flavigny by the count of Lunéville [Note: Lunéville]. He also recovered almost half the village of Flavigny, which Duke Matthew of Lorraine had seized and made subject to his lordship, together with many other things. How beneficial he was to this place is declared by the very memorials of its possessions and buildings.

Therefore, because of these and other good works, he was drawn, against his will, to the abbacy of Saint-Mansuy. When transferred there, he found the church despoiled of both spiritual and temporal goods and burdened with heavy debts. He found almost all the church’s revenues submerged in a most profound flood of debts; and he found its chalices, book-covers, crosses, chasubles, and better copes pledged, so that delay in repayment of principal produced ever greater interest. He repaired the roof of the church, the carved work, and the enclosure of the court, and improved other buildings. Through his diligence and labour he reduced its debts, lightened its interest payments, redeemed everything that had been pawned, and increased revenues.

He acquired for the church of Blessed Mansuy the church of Clateigneis, with its appurtenances, from the count of Toul, and the altar-right from Roger, bishop of Toul. He also obtained from the same bishop the altar-rights of Germai and Bures, with their appurtenances, and many other things from which income to the annual value of one hundred pounds might arise. He did this within the eight and a half years during which he presided over that church.

This abbot William, I say, greatly increased the church entrusted to him not only in spiritual but also in temporal goods. With the consent of Ralph, bishop of Verdun, he made his prior James, called of Vignuoles—whose life and conduct he knew to be sufficiently ordered and honourable—abbot at Saint-Airy. This man, devout and gentle, though he ruled as abbot only briefly, acquired a good name for that place. For he was very gracious and performed many good works there.

11. Therefore, while our venerable father William was abbot, the sedition mentioned above, which was being waged between Bishop Guy of Melloto [variant: “Merloto,” manuscript 1] on the one side and the citizens of Verdun on the other, became so violent that the aforesaid bishop violently seized, wherever he could, our possessions, revenues, and goods. The count of Bar did the same from one direction, and the lord of Aspremont from another. Thus, as our goods were surrendered to plunder on every side, urgent necessity compelled us unwillingly to leave our house. Dispersed among our priories and elsewhere, we remained there in anxious mind until the dispute on both sides was calmed.

Meanwhile the citizens of Verdun, fearing that the bishop would station garrisons and guards in our towers, who would bar the citizens’ entrance and exit, proposed to demolish the towers lest they hinder them. Having assembled stonecutters by general proclamation, they began to undermine the towers with iron tools so that they might more easily throw them down. The memory of this deed will be able to pass down to posterity forever through visible monuments.

When our venerable father William saw this, his mind was grievously distressed, and he began to appeal to the citizens repeatedly and earnestly not to commit so great a crime. They would in no way comply with his request unless on the following condition: if, on account of the towers, the bishop inflicted any injury [Col. 0986B] upon them, the aforesaid abbot together with the chapter would be bound to them in two thousand strong pounds [variant: “bound,” manuscript 1]. Hostages having therefore been given and the agreement confirmed, the towers remained standing.

But the citizens caused the enclosure of the court, the gatehouse, and the carved and highly polished stones of the church—worth nearly three hundred pounds—to be carried away for the enclosure of their own walls and defensive works. Accordingly, the bishop, stirred to anger by these and like things, seeing that he could inflict no injury upon the city and its citizens, caused all Scantia from top to bottom and the whole upper suburb as far as Saint-Amant to be burned with fire, that he might at least thus satisfy his rage.

12. In his time, Frederick the emperor raged in proud and abusive fury against the Church of God, and with heretical deceit, by a serpent-like creeping, defiled almost the whole world. Pope Innocent IV came to Lyons in Gaul (1245), not because he timidly avoided hostile conflicts, but that he might resist more effectively and securely. Armed therefore with the shield of faith and relying on divine aid, he manfully opposed Frederick, lest falsehood overshadow truth, injustice prevail over equity, and perfidy overcome faith. Drawing the most powerful sword of Peter, he pronounced against him a sentence of excommunication.

After this, upon consultation with all the clergy, the aforesaid Frederick was deprived by judgment of the universal Church of the sceptre of imperial honour [Col. 0986D] (1246); and the landgrave was elevated to his throne, in order that he might bring the aid of the material sword to the Catholic faith, so that the insufficiency of one might be supplied by the other, since these two swords borrow mutual assistance from one another and ought mutually to impart alternating strength to each other. But he survived only a short time, and by his death brought grief and sorrow upon his followers.

When he was removed from the midst (1247), the nobleman William, most valiant knight and son of the count of [Col. 0987A] Holland, was raised as king. He fought many battles against King Conrad, son of the aforesaid apostate Frederick, captured several fortresses and castles, and endured innumerable plots and sufferings.

Pope Innocent, however, exposing himself to every danger for the protection of ecclesiastical liberty and dying, as it were, with the Church of God under persecution, began to drain the entire Church and the monasteries enormously by unprecedented and burdensome exactions. Thus he compelled every church and monastery to give him, in military subsidies, first a twentieth and then a tenth of all revenues and tithes; those who refused he struck with a sentence of excommunication. The cardinals on one side and the supreme pontiff on the other burdened [our church, added above the line in manuscript 1] with one thousand pounds [variant: “have burdened,” manuscript 1?, edition], both through the twentieth and tenth, and through pensions, procurations, and subsidies.

“But wonderful are the surges of the sea; wonderful on high is the Lord” (Psalm 92 [Vulgate 92; Hebrew/modern numbering 93], 6). He made its storm a breeze; and He who commands winds and sea commanded by His authority that the emperor should not rule. For He who is before the ages humbled him—He who humbles every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God. For Frederick had grievously oppressed the Church of God and given it over to trampling. Moreover, this Frederick, who had disturbed cities by a violent schism and shaken kingdoms, fell like Dagon. He was to share the lot of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, whose imitator he made himself by trampling churches in contempt of Christ and plundering their goods. When he had died, the lord pope returned to Milan [Col. 0988B] (1250).

[Col. 0987]

## Annals of Saint-Viton of Verdun

[Col. 0987B] **96. Passion of Saint Dionysius.** Saint Sanctinus, with Antoninus, set out for Rome at the command of blessed Dionysius after his martyrdom. Instructed by an angelic visitation, he turned aside to the city of the Clavi, which is called Verdun [Col. 0987C]. Preaching the word of God to the citizens, he converted many; and, after building and consecrating a church in honour of blessed Peter, he was elected their first bishop by the Christians whom he had converted.

**360.** In these times, after the devastation of the Huns, the churches flourished again. Pulchronius, disciple of Lupus, bishop of Troyes, was appointed fifth bishop of the church of Verdun.

**503.** Death of Saint Firminus, bishop of Verdun. Blessed Viton was appointed in his place by King Clovis and enthroned in the episcopal see.

**518.** The Annunciation of Saint Agericus.

**528.** Death of blessed Viton, bishop of Verdun.

**554.** Ordination to the bishopric of Saint Agericus. [Note: “ornatio” in the manuscript.]

**602.** Saint Agericus died; Caramerus succeeded him.

[Col. 0987D] **688.** Pippin, son of Ansegisel, began to reign. From his time blessed Madelveus lived on to the time of Charlemagne.

This Pippin, duke and illustrious prince of the Franks, together with his wife, the illustrious matron Plectrude, gave to the church of Saint Viton the village of Parida with its appurtenances, together with the spacious forest called the Nauca of Saint Viton, in the seventh year of King Childebert.

[Col. 0988B] **758.** Saint Madelveus, bishop of Verdun, died.

**771.** Peter was appointed bishop of Verdun.

**795.** Peter, bishop of Verdun, died; [Col. 0988C] Austrannus succeeded him.

**800.** Austrannus, bishop of Verdun, died; Herilandus succeeded him. [Note: These items must be added to those already published above from the older part of the same manuscript, IV, p. 7.]

**847.** Hildinus, bishop of Verdun, died; Hatto succeeded him.

**915.** The church of Saint Viton of Verdun was burned on the vigil of the commemoration of the saints. [Note: Thus in the manuscript; perhaps read “vigilia” (“vigil”).]

**920.** Dado, bishop of Verdun, died; Bernoynus succeeded him.

**941.** Bernoinus, bishop of Verdun, died; Berengarius, kinsman of Emperor Otto, succeeded him.

**952.** Clerics were expelled from the monastery of Saint Viton, and monks were substituted under Abbot Hubert. [Note: See the charter of Bishop Berengarius in Roussel, *Probb.*, p. 2.]

[Col. 0988D] **958.** Berengarius, bishop of Verdun, died; Wicfridus succeeded him. He founded the church of Saint Paul at Verdun.

**986.** Wicfridus, bishop of Verdun, died; Adelbero succeeded him.

**990.** Adelbero, bishop of Verdun, died; Heymo succeeded him. He founded the monastery of nuns of Saint Maurus.

[Col. 0989A] **1005.** Fingenius, abbot of Saint Viton, died; Richard succeeded him.

**1025.** Heymo, bishop of Verdun, died; Raymbertus succeeded him. He founded the monastery of Saint Agericus.

**1039.** Raymbertus, bishop of Verdun, died; Richard succeeded him.

**1046.** Richard, abbot of Saint Viton, died; Walerannus succeeded him. Richard, bishop of Verdun, died; Theodericus succeeded him.

**1048.** The city of Verdun was captured and plundered by Duke Godfrey and Baldwin, and, together with the monastery of Saint Mary, was burned.

**1049.** Blessed Odilo, abbot of Cluny, died. The church of Blessed Mary Magdalene was dedicated by [Col. 0989B] Pope Leo IX.

**1056.** Emperor Henry died; the boy Henry succeeded him.

**1060.** Abbot Walerannus died; Grimoldus succeeded him.

**1064.** The chapel of Saint Bartholomew, together with its precinct, was dedicated. The star called a comet appeared; in the same year Harold, king of the English, was killed, and William succeeded him.

**1069.** Duke Godfrey, son of Duke Gozelo, died; his son Godfrey, called the Hunchback, succeeded him.

**1071.** Ermenfridus, canon and builder of the church of Blessed Mary Magdalene, died.

**1075.** Duke Rudolf invaded Saxony.

[Col. 0989C] **1076.** Duke Godfrey the Younger died; Godfrey, called of Bouillon, succeeded him.

**1077.** Rudolf succeeded Abbot Grimoldus. A severe frost continued for four months.

**1078.** Abbot Grimoldus died.

**1079.** War in Saxony, where Duke Rudolf was killed by the younger Henry.

**1080.** The body of Lord Bishop Richard was translated and buried before the choir in the new basilica of Saint Mary.

**1082.** A great sedition arose between kingdom and priesthood. Because of it, the monks were expelled from the monastery of Saint Viton for seven years, namely until after the death of Theodericus, bishop of Verdun.

**1086.** War at Sathanacum.

[Col. 0989D] **1087.** William, duke of the Normans and king of the English, died. Victor was pope. Translation of Saint Nicholas to Bar.

**1088.** Theodericus, bishop of Verdun, died; Richerus succeeded him, and Urban became pope.

**1091.** Hermann, bishop of Metz, died.

**1095.** Consecration of Bishop Richerus. A council of bishops from almost the whole world, excepting those of Lorraine, Germany, and Bavaria, was gathered at Clermont in Auvergne.

**1097.** The star called a comet appeared.

**1098.** Pope Urban died; Pope Paschal succeeded him.

[Col. 0990A] **1099.** Abbot Rudolf died; Lawrence succeeded him. Jerusalem was captured by Duke Godfrey of Bouillon and the Christians.

**1106.** On the death of Emperor Henry the father, Henry succeeded him.

**1107.** Bishop Richerus died; Richard the elect succeeded him.

**1111.** The monastery of Saint Viton was deserted after Bishop Richard expelled the monks. Henry, son of Henry called king, came to Rome as though to make satisfaction to Pope Paschal; by treachery he seized him with the cardinals inside the church of Saint Peter and thrust him into a muddy place.

**1114.** The monks of Saint Viton returned to the monastery after Bishop Richard’s death. The bishopric was vacant [Col. 0990B] for three and a half years.

**1116.** Henry succeeded as bishop of Verdun.

**1117.** War before Verdun between Counts Raynald and William. Pope Paschal died; Gelasius succeeded.

**1118.** Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, died.

**1119.** Pope Gelasius died; Calixtus II succeeded.

**1120.** The city of Verdun was taken by Count Raynald, and the greater part of the city was burned and plundered, along with the monasteries of Saint Saviour, Saint Peter, and Saint Agericus.

**1122.** The citizens of Verdun delivered this city by treachery to Count Henry of Grandpré. Having possessed it for some time, he committed many evils there.

[Col. 0990C] **1124.** Peace was made between kingdom and priesthood.

**1125.** Pope Calixtus died; Honorius succeeded. Emperor Henry V died; Lothair, duke of Saxony, succeeded.

**1129.** Henry surrendered the bishopric. Orsio, abbot of Saint Dionysius of Reims, was elected.

**1130.** Pope Honorius died; Innocent succeeded. [Note: Thus in the manuscript, and often elsewhere.]

**1131.** Orsio resigned the bishopric; Archdeacon Adelbero was elected and consecrated at Paris by Pope Innocent on holy Easter Day.

**1132.** The tower of Verdun was captured and demolished.

**1138.** Emperor Lothair died; [Col. 0990D] Conrad succeeded him.

**1139.** Lawrence, abbot of Saint Viton, died; Segardus succeeded him.

**1142.** Abbot Segardus died; Cono succeeded him.

**1143.** Pope Innocent died; Celestine succeeded.

**1144.** Pope Celestine died; Lucius succeeded.

**1145.** Pope Lucius died; Eugenius III succeeded.

**1147.** Pope Eugenius placed the body of the most blessed father Viton in a new shrine on the day of his feast [Col. 0991A], and on the feast day of Saint Martin dedicated the church of Blessed Mary.

**1150.** Pope Eugenius died; Anastasius succeeded, and afterwards Adrian. The monastery of Saint Mary Magdalene and the greater part of the city were burned.

**1152.** Conrad, king of the Romans, died; Frederick, duke of Alsace, succeeded.

**1153.** War before Mouzon, where the men of Metz perished. Ascalon was captured by the Christians. Frederick, king of the Lorrainers, went to Rome to extend his imperial power.

**1156.** Ordination of Bishop Albert, two years before the death of Adelbero.

**1158.** Adelbero, bishop of Verdun, died.

**1161.** Pope Adrian died; Alexander [Col. 0991B] III succeeded.

**1163.** Albert, bishop of Verdun and monk of Saint Viton, died; Richard, called the Child, succeeded.

**1171.** Richard, bishop-elect of Verdun, died; Arnold succeeded. Saint Thomas, bishop of Canterbury, suffered martyrdom.

**1178.** Cono, abbot of Saint Viton, died. He ordered stone towers and the place called the Treasury to be built, and the shrine of Saint Viton to be completed. Richerus succeeded him.

**1179.** Richerus resigned of his own free will; the younger Allestannus succeeded. He died in the same year, and the elder Allestannus succeeded him.

[Col. 0991C] **1181.** Arnold, bishop of Verdun, died after being struck in the head by an arrow before the castle of Sainte-Menehould; Henry succeeded him.

**1182.** Pope Alexander died; Pope Lucius succeeded.

**1183.** The elder Allestannus resigned the abbacy; Thomas, abbot of Mureau, was appointed in his place.

**1186.** Pope Lucius died; Urban succeeded. Henry resigned the bishopric, and Albert was elected.

**1187.** Abbot Thomas resigned; Hugh succeeded. Pope Urban died, and Gregory succeeded; he died in the same year, and Clement succeeded.

**1189.** Emperor Frederick died; his son [Col. 0991D] Henry succeeded him.

**1190.** Pope Clement died; Celestine succeeded.

**1194.** A severe famine occurred, so that grain was sold at the price of four pounds.

**1197.** [Note: I have supplied these words, which are cut off in the manuscript.] Pope Celestine died; Innocent III succeeded. Abbot Hugh resigned his prelacy; Stephen succeeded him. Stricken with paralysis, he resigned the abbacy in the same year. Louis, [Col. 0992A] brother of Albert, bishop of Verdun, was elected abbot. Emperor Henry died; Philip succeeded him.

**1200.** Constantinople was captured by the Franks and Venetians, and they made Baldwin, count of Flanders, emperor.

**1208.** Philip, king but not yet emperor, was killed by the count palatine [lacuna]; Count Otto succeeded [lacuna]. After he had been consecrated, [the clause *mandatis Innocentii pape imperans*—“ruling/commanding in relation to Pope Innocent’s mandates”—is syntactically uncertain], he was excommunicated [lacuna], deposed from royal dignity, and Frederick, duke of Apulia, was raised to the empire. A great sedition arose at Verdun: citizens rose against clergy, clergy against citizens, and committed many evils. Finally Bishop Albert died, killed by a lance; Robert, the primicerius, succeeded him.

[Col. 0992B] **1216.** A general council was convened at Rome, and there Emperor Frederick took the cross. Pope Innocent died; Honorius succeeded.

**1217.** Robert, bishop of Verdun, died; John of Aspremont succeeded him. He founded the monastery of Saint Nicholas-in-the-Meadow. A fire occurred in this city of Verdun, from the steps of Saint Mary and from the gate of Ancelin Street to the bridge of Brachiolum, throughout the whole stretch from wall to wall.

**1222.** Saint Dominic, founder of the Order of Preachers, died.

**1224.** John, bishop of Verdun, resigned the bishopric and passed to the bishopric of Metz; Ralph of Torta succeeded him, cantor of [Col. 0992C] Laon [Note: “Lyons” in the text; Laon, Col. 0991D]. Louis, abbot of Saint Viton, ordered a silver panel to be made before the high altar. Pope Gregory admonished Emperor Frederick to set out for Jerusalem with his army, which had long before taken the cross, to destroy the enemies of the Christian faith.

**1226.** Pope Honorius IX died; Gregory succeeded.

**1227.** [lacuna] battle between Ralph, bishop of Verdun, and the citizens [lacuna].

**1232.** Saint Dominic, founder of the Friars Preachers, was canonized.

**1237.** On the eighth day before the Ides of March [8 March], Abbot Louis, worn out by old age, resigned the abbacy. He had begun the costly work of the monastery [Col. 0992D] and died in the following year. William, abbot of Saint-Mansuy and formerly a monk of Saint Viton, succeeded him by election. He was found most faithful in that costly undertaking, in constructing houses and a chapel, in the reliquaries of saints, in excellent and very large bells, and in acquiring landed estates, just as [Note: “sic” in the manuscript] his predecessor had been.

**1241.** Pope Gregory died; Celestine succeeded and reigned for eighteen days. The see was vacant for three years.

[Col. 0993A] **1243.** Innocent succeeded to the papacy.

**1245.** Ralph, bishop of Verdun, died; Guy de Triagnel succeeded him, but died in the same year. Guy of Melloto succeeded him. A great sedition arose between him and the citizens of Verdun; peace having been made, in the same year he passed to the bishopric of Auxerre. John of Aix succeeded him.

**1253.** Pope Innocent died; Alexander succeeded. John d’Aix, bishop-elect of Verdun and deacon, died. By provision of the lord pope, James, archdeacon of Laon, a Frenchman from the city of Troyes, succeeded him.

**1256.** James, bishop of Verdun, was transferred by papal command to the patriarchate of Jerusalem; Robert of Milan succeeded him.

[Col. 0993B] **1259.** Abbot William died. The see was vacant for eight years, while litigation continued between two elects, namely Dominic the provost and Ralph, prior of Mont-Saint-Martin; Ralph nevertheless prevailed. Because of this, the costly work on the monastery ceased, after many attacks [variant: “impitionibus,” manuscript] and injuries done by him to this church. Pope Alexander died; the aforesaid James, formerly bishop of Verdun and patriarch of Jerusalem, succeeded him as Pope Urban IV. He instituted the solemnity of the most holy sacrament.

**1264.** Pope Urban died; Clement succeeded.

**1265.** Charles, count of Anjou, brother of Louis, king of France, and leader of the Christian army, defeated Manfred, enemy of all Christendom.

[Col. 0993C] **1267.** Clement died; Gregory succeeded.

**1270.** Saint Louis, king of the Franks, died.

**1271.** Robert II, bishop of Verdun, died; Ulrich of Satanacum [Note: “Saranacho” is read in the manuscript; Labbé reads “Savinaco”], provost of Blessed Mary Magdalene, succeeded him.

**1272.** [“Pope Gregory died” is absent from the manuscript.] Pope Gregory died; Innocent succeeded.

**1273.** Ulrich, bishop of Verdun, died; after him the see was vacant for three years.

**1276.** [“Pope Innocent died” is absent from the manuscript.] Pope Innocent died; [“Pope Adrian succeeded” is absent from the manuscript.] Pope Adrian succeeded, and then John. Gerard of Grandson succeeded in the bishopric.

**1277.** Pope John died; Nicholas succeeded.

**1278.** Gerard of Grandson, bishop of Verdun, died; his brother Henry of [Col. 0993D] Grandson succeeded him.

**1281.** Abbot Ralph died; John succeeded him.

1286. Abbot John died; Theodoric succeeded. Henry of Grandson, bishop of Verdun, died; the see was vacant for four years.

1290. James of Revigny, *clericorum generalissimus* (“most general of the clerics”), succeeded to the bishopric of Verdun.

[Col. 0994A] 1292. Abbot Theodoric died; Gobert the almoner was elected; but Philip Dorne, prior of Corbigny, obtained it [Note: [Col. 0993] i.e. obtained the abbacy.].

1296. James II, bishop, died at the Roman curia, whither he had gone because of the dispute he had with the citizens of Verdun. John of Richericourt, called John of Aspremont, succeeded him.

1297. Abbot Philip died; Hugh of Reims succeeded.

1302. John of Richericourt, bishop of Verdun, died; Thomas of Beaumont succeeded.

1303. Hugh, abbot of Saint-Vitton, died; Baudocus of Failley, prior of Munau, succeeded.

1305. Abbot Baudocus died; Nicholas Maisel, cellarer, succeeded. Thomas, bishop of Verdun, died; Nicholas of Neuville-sur-Orne succeeded [Note: [Col. 0993D] Neuville-sur-Orne in Barrois territory.].

1312. Nicholas, bishop of Verdun, resigned the burden of his bishopric; Henry of Aspremont succeeded him.

1314. Henry of Luxembourg, emperor, died. In Italy he was poisoned by venom placed in the chalice while he was receiving the Eucharist and administering the blood of Christ [Note: [Col. 0993] *amnistratione* in the manuscript.].

1316. Nicholas, abbot of Saint-Vitton, died; Simon of Nancey, prior of Flavigny, succeeded him. There was a great famine and a very great mortality among humankind.

1318. Simon of Nancey, abbot of Saint-Vitton, died; Theobald of Bazel, prior of Munau, succeeded him.

1319. Theobald, abbot of Saint-Vitton, died; his kinsman Erard of Bazel succeeded him, and discharged the debts and pledges [Note: [Col. 0993] thus in manuscripts 1–2.] of his predecessors.

1325. The archdeacon of Trier, the king of Bohemia, the count of Bar, and the duke of Lorraine, with their retinues, appeared before Metz three times during the year. Because of this the whole country [Note: [Col. 0993] *patres* in the manuscript; edition: *patria*, “country.”] was burned.

1332. There were thunderclaps and flashes of lightning on the day after Christmas. The leading men of the city of Verdun were bound over by the city’s commune.

1336. The citizens of Verdun burned the village of Buzy [Note: [Col. 0993D] *Buxey*; Buzy.]; and, as they returned, many were killed and wounded by the men of Bar at the bridge of Way [Note: [Col. 0994D] Warcq, ROUSS.], and the bishopric of Verdun, through treachery [incomplete in the source; Note: [Col. 0993] thus in manuscripts 1–2.].

1340. Erard, abbot of Saint-Vitton, ordered two large half-bells to be made [Note: [Col. 0993] *capanas* in the manuscript.].

1346. The king of England defeated the king of France near Crécy [Note: [Col. 0994D] The battle of Crécy is meant.]; and there fell the king of Bohemia, the duke of Lorraine, and many other princes.

1349. Henry, bishop of Verdun, died; [Col. 0995A] Henry of Germiny was elected. He was not confirmed. Erard, abbot of Saint-Vitton, died; Bastiavus, prior of Chaudefontaine, was elected; but Raymond Dachic obtained the office through the favour of the Apostolic See.

1353. Gerard of Voudenay succeeded Abbot Raymond through the favour of the Apostolic See. He dissipated the goods of the monastery of Mary [Note: [Col. 0995] *maie* in the manuscript.], mortgaged its rents and revenues, pawned letters and charters of the utmost necessity, impoverished and stripped of their goods its people and dependants, reduced its revenues by a third, and inflicted losses of a further 26,000 francs and more. He reduced the monastery itself to such poverty that Matins was scarcely sung there twelve times in a year. May he who governs all things spare and forgive him [Note: [Col. 0995] *regit* (“rules”) appears to be missing in the manuscript.].

[Col. 0995B] 1381. Gerard of Vodenay, abbot of Saint-Vitton, died; John of Tric, prior of Flavigny, succeeded him.

1382. John of Tric, abbot of Saint-Vitton, died; Henry of Passavant, called le Champenoy, prior of Chaudefontaine, succeeded, and greatly reduced the pledges and debts of his predecessor.

1391. Henry, abbot and a good governor, died; Reginald Pallardelli, a monk of Saint-Michael’s, succeeded through favour of the Apostolic See.

1403. Leobald of Cusance, bishop of Verdun, died; John of Sarraponte, son of Sir John of Commercy, knight, succeeded. He suffered many injuries, unjustly and without cause inflicted upon him by robbers and by certain vassals of the bishopric of Verdun.

1413. A fire, neglected in the south bell-tower on the eve of Saint-Vitton’s feast, melted two of the larger bells; Abbot Reginald restored them in the following year.

1417. Abbot Reginald died; his nephew succeeded him. Stephen Burgundian, almoner of Saint-Vitton and a most faithful rector, died [Note: [Col. 0995] *died* is omitted in the edition, with the result that Stephen is called Reginald’s nephew.].

1420. John of Sarraponte was transferred to the bishopric of Châlons by an exchange made between him and Louis of Bar, cardinal bishop of Porto, duke of Bar, marquis of Pont-à-Mousson, lord of Cassel, and administrator of the bishopric of Verdun.

[Col. 0995D] 1430. When the smaller bell of Abbot Reginald broke, Abbot Stephen made a larger one from it. Louis of Bar, cardinal and bishop of Verdun, died; Louis of Harcourt, cantor of Verdun, succeeded.

1431. From the magnificent and costly old structure of the church of Saint-Vitton, begun by Abbots Louis and William, brought nearly to utter ruin, and lacking a roof, Abbot Stephen of Saint-Vitton took the better stones and began another new structure. He caused it to be completed on both sides as far as the southern portal of the common entrance, with its [uncertain: *verevis*] vaults and a suitable roof.

1436. The body of Abbot Louis was transferred from the old work to the new, beneath the altar of Saint Mary, at its head.

1437. The first four altars of the new work were dedicated on 27 May, the sixth day before the Kalends of June. When Louis, bishop of Verdun, obtained the bishopric of Toul, William, abbot of Saint-Theodoric near Reims [Note: [Col. 0995] *theoderi* in the manuscript.], succeeded to the bishopric of Verdun by apostolic authority.

[Col. 0996B] 1438. Severe famine.

1448. Abbot Stephen purchased four copper columns.

1449. By an exchange, William, bishop of Verdun, passed to the bishopric of Toul. Louis, bishop of Toul, returned to Verdun and governed it well.

1451. A mortality of epidemic disease in Verdun: 2,500 persons.

1452. Stephen, abbot of Saint-Vitton, died. John of Arency, chamberlain, was elected; but, after fifteen months had elapsed, he was deposed by the Apostolic See at the instigation of Lord Cardinal William Hugh, to whom the administration was granted. Nine months later Anthony of Sérières [Note: [Col. 0995] Senecey in the edition.], prior of Flavigny, obtained it from him by giving an annual pension of 400 gold ducats.

[Col. 0996C] 1454. Work on the new church of Saint-Vitton ceased.

1455. The same Lord Cardinal William died, as did his pension.

1456. Louis, bishop of Verdun, died; his kinsman William of Harcourt, provost of Montfaucon, succeeded.

1461. Charles, king of France, died; his son Louis succeeded. When the great bell of Abbot Stephen broke, Abbot Anthony restored it. He also purchased two silk copes woven with gold and silver. John of Arency died—formerly elected [Note: [Col. 0995] This appears to be the reading.] of Saint-Vitton, chamberlain and prior of Chaudefontaine.

1463. The lectern and the whole tomb [Col. 0996D] of the eight bishops of Verdun, who had rested from ancient times in the cemetery of this monastery of Saint-Vitton before the high altar, were restored.

1475. [Note: [Col. 0995] What follows was added in other hands.] Anthony, abbot of this place, died.

1476. Death of Charles of Burgundy at Nancy.

1481. Abbot Matthew died; Gerard succeeded [Note: [Col. 0995] I have omitted what was written after this year, in various sixteenth-, seventeenth-, and eighteenth-century hands, down to 1742.].

# A.D. 1124–1192. SAINT STEPHEN OF MURET, INSTITUTOR AND FOUNDER OF THE GRANDMONTINE ORDER, AND OTHER GRANDMONTINES

[Col. 0997]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ST. STEPHEN

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, II, 646)

Stephen I of Muret—so called from the place where he lived a solitary life for almost fifty years—first prior, institutor, and founder of the Grandmontine Order, was of noble Auvergnat lineage. He was the son of Stephen, viscount of Thiers or Tygier, and of Candida, a lady of no inferior birth.

When his father went to Italy, he took Stephen, then only twelve years old, with him. But when the boy fell ill, he was entrusted to Count Milo, archbishop of Benevento, likewise a native of Auvergne and a man of outstanding holiness. Stephen was trained under his discipline for twelve years. When Milo passed to the Lord, Stephen came to Rome, where he spent four years.

At that time Hildebrand, called Gregory VII, was elected pope; our Stephen was known to him. Stephen therefore obtained from him permission and a privilege to establish a new monastic order according to the Rule of St Benedict, which he had long observed among certain monks of stricter observance in Calabria. For Gregory VII certainly speaks thus in his diploma: “Why do you continually . . . . . . . petition the Apostolic See . . . . for authority to initiate the monastic order you have conceived, according to the Rule of St Benedict, which you have long experienced among the brethren of Calabria,” etc. See the sixth Benedictine century, part II, Preface, nos. 82 and 83, where Mabillon discusses these matters learnedly, as is his custom.

The diploma was granted in 1073, although the establishment of the Grandmontine Order is deferred until three years later. Many persons, abandoning the world, followed Stephen. He showed them the same rule of life, wrote a Rule, and left it for his brethren to observe. In it he perpetually forbade his disciples all eating of meat; care of, and association with, women; the possession of livestock or animals; and ownership of land, apart from the hermitages in which they lived.

Pope Urban, Pope Adrian, Alexander III, and Lucius III successively confirmed this Rule, securing the aforesaid order by very many favourable privileges. Yet the sons born in place of the fathers, because the Rule seemed too strict, repeatedly had it moderated by supreme pontiffs, especially by Pope Innocent IV at Lyons, after the General Council, on 15 November 1247; and finally by Pope Clement V at Avignon, on 20 April 1309.

St Stephen passed from the world to Christ in his cell at Muret, being only a deacon in the order of Levites, thus becoming an imitator of the other St Stephen, protomartyr and Levite. In the eightieth year of his age, full of miracles and holy works, he died on 8 February 1124, epact 3, with the seventh concurrent joined to the bissextile year, after living in the wilderness for nearly fifty years, lacking two months, as may be inferred from these verses:

> Stormy February had already completed eight days,  
> When Stephen’s light-bearing spirit sought the stars,  
> In the year one thousand, one hundred, and twice ten,  
> With four added, having won a kingdom in heaven.  
> Firm in his purpose, crucified with the Crucified,  
> Stephen served Christ, through whom he now lives.

In the same year, 1124, his body was brought to Grandmont on 25 June, the seventh day before the Kalends of July. Shortly before his death he had been visited by two cardinal legates of the Holy See, Gregory of the title of St Angelo and Peter Leonis, who learned his entire manner of life.

He was enrolled among the confessors in the catalogue of saints by Clement III, in a bull issued on 21 March, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of his pontificate, A.D. 1188. In that year Clement sent from his side the legate John, cardinal of the title of St Mark, with apostolic letters to Grandmont to proclaim the canonization of the same St Stephen, about the end of August. Stephen’s disciples had moved there from their first seat at Muret, because the canons regular of St Augustine of Limoges claimed that place as their own; it lay about three miles from Grandmont. Then, with solemn ceremony, the legate celebrated the elevation of St Stephen, in the presence of very many bishops, abbots, and religious men, sixty-two years after his death [Col. 0999], after many preceding miracles divinely wrought to declare his holiness.

[Note: [Col. 0999] In the papers of Dom de Ganière, preserved in the Royal Library, the following prelates are recorded as having been present at the canonization of Stephen of Muret, 30 August 1188, sixty-four years after his death: Henry of Bourges; Raymond, otherwise Rainaud, of Pamiers; Elias of Bordeaux; Saibrand of Limoges; W. of Poitiers; Elias of Saintes; Adhemar of Périgueux; Gerald of Cahors; and Bertrand of Agen.]

A fuller Life of him is preserved in manuscript in a codex of the Abbey of Grandmont.

[Col. 0999]

# LITERARY NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, by Benedictine religious, vol. XII, p. 416.)

1. We believe that we may rank among the writings of St Stephen the notable act by which he consecrated himself to God [Note: [Col. 0999] *Life of St Stephen*, in Martène, vol. VI, *Collection*, p. 1056; Mabillon, *Annals*, book LXIV, no. 112.]. It is too brief and too edifying not to be given here:

> “I, Stephen, renounce the devil and his pomps. I offer myself to God and place myself in the hands of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one God in three persons, living and true.”

Such was the act Stephen wrote after placing a ring upon his finger, as the sign of the covenant which he wished to contract with Jesus Christ. Then, putting it upon his head, he said:

> “Almighty and merciful God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God in three persons, who live and reign eternally: I, Brother Stephen, promise you that from this moment I shall serve you in this wilderness in the Catholic faith. For this reason I place this act upon my head and this ring upon my finger, so that, on the day of my death, this promise and this act may serve as shield and defence against the snares of my enemies. Restore to me, Lord, I beseech you, the wedding garment. Deign to place me among the children of your holy Church; and, when my soul departs from my body, clothe it in the garment of your charity and cause it to enter the hall of the wedding-feast of your Son, to reign with all your saints. Holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, I entrust to your Son and to you my soul, my body, and my spirit.”

2. St Stephen left his disciples a Rule divided into seventy-five chapters. At its head is a very moving prologue, in which appear the great principles of religion with which the author was imbued and thoroughly instructed. “All the rules of the various religious orders,” he says, “are only streams and not the source of religion; they are leaves and not the root. There is one which is the rule of rules and the origin of all the rest: the Gospel. There all the faithful have drawn, and will draw until the end of the ages, the means of observing God’s commandments and attaining perfection.”

He wishes his disciples to answer those curious to know what Rule they profess that they observe no other than that of the Gospel. If they were shown anything not conformable to it, he wishes his Rule to be corrected, though he assures them that he included nothing except on the advice of learned persons and people of great piety, after carefully consulting the Rules of the Fathers in order to conform to them.

This Rule contains many excellent statutes. Poverty and obedience are recommended in it (ch. 1) as the principal foundation of religious life. The fourth is notable for the legislator’s prohibition against his disciples possessing churches or receiving any remuneration for Masses. Secular persons are forbidden entry into their oratory on Sundays and feast days, since it is fitting that they attend the offices in their own churches. All trade and litigation are prohibited by the fifteenth chapter.

The fifty-fourth chapter, which entrusts care of temporal affairs to the lay brothers, occasioned disturbances in the Grandmontine Order that nearly overthrew it. The fifty-sixth shows the saintly founder’s charity toward the sick, for whose relief he commands even the church ornaments to be sold. Nevertheless, in chapter 57, he absolutely prohibits them the use of meat without any exception. Dom Mabillon [*Annals*, book LXIV, no. 113] believes that what induced St Stephen to prohibit meat even to the sick was his wish to avoid the reproach which the schismatic Greeks had made on this matter against Latin monks during the pontificate of Leo IX.

He prescribes a continual fast from the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until Easter, except on Sundays and Christmas Day, with this difference: during Lent the sole meal was taken after Vespers, while at other times it was taken after None. From All Saints’ Day until Christmas he prescribes the same abstinence as for Lent; in the other fasts he permits eggs and cheese.

The election of the prior of Grandmont was to be made through the participation of the whole order (ch. 60). Two religious from each monastery having assembled at the place of election, twelve were chosen—six clerics and six lay brothers—who elected the prior. This Rule was approved by several popes, some of whom altered different articles within it. It was mitigated in particular by Innocent IV in 1247, after the General Council of Lyons, and by Clement V in 1309 at Avignon.

The Rouen editor who published St Stephen’s Rule, and M. Baillet in the preface to his translation of the saint’s *Maxims*, assert that Stephen contented himself with instructing his disciples by word and example, never writing anything, and that the Rule was subsequently collected by his disciples, especially Peter of Limoges, and put into its present form by Gerard, seventh prior of Grandmont. But Dom Mabillon [Note: [Col. 0999] Vol. VI, *Annals*, book LXXIV, no. 91.]—or rather Dom Martène, in an addition to Dom Mabillon’s manuscript [Note: [Col. 0999] *Annals*, book LXIV, nos. 37 and 112.]—maintains that this claim is supported by neither reason nor authority, and that it is enough to read this excellent Rule attentively to be convinced that its true author is St Stephen, who reveals himself therein, both in the prologue and in chapters 9, 11, and 14.

It was formerly doubted whether St Stephen of Muret and his earliest disciples professed the [Col. 1001] Rule of St Benedict. Trithemius, Yepes, Haeftenus, Le Mire, Choppin, and many others maintained the affirmative; Father Mabillon followed this view in his preface to the second part of the Acts of the sixth century. Nevertheless, this opinion must be abandoned, following Father Mabillon himself [Note: [Col. 1001] *Annals*, book LXIV, nos. 37 and 112.]. Having examined more closely the grounds upon which it rested, he recognized their slight solidity and, ever guided by love of truth, changed his mind.

It is unnecessary here to set out the reasons showing that St Stephen of Muret followed neither the Rule of St Benedict nor that of St Augustine, but composed one of his own. The reader may consult what Dom Martène says on this subject in the preface to the sixth volume of his great *Collection*, where he discusses the origin of the Grandmontine Order. It is enough to say that, whatever the Rule of this holy founder may have been, his disciples made their age admire and marvel at them by their holiness. All writers who have spoken of them have said wonderful things. They were “angels,” in the expression of Peter of Celle (*Epistle* 8), who was convinced that the least prayer of these holy solitaries—or these angels, as he calls them—could obtain for him heaven’s assistance.

John of Salisbury, a contemporary author, depicts them [Note: [Col. 1001] *Polycraticus*, book VII, ch. 23.] as persons who, raised above the necessities of life, were victorious not only over cupidity and avarice but over nature itself. Stephen of Tournai (*Epistle* 2) speaks of them with no less praise. He calls them “good men,” a name given to mark their goodness and piety; hence the houses they inhabited were called *boni-hominiae*, “good-men’s houses.”

St Stephen’s Rule was printed at Dijon by Pierre Palliot in 1645, in a small duodecimo, under the title: *Regula S. Stephani confessoris auctoris et fundatoris ordinis Grandimontensis*—“Rule of St Stephen, confessor, author and founder of the Grandmontine Order.” Lipenius cites another edition, in sextodecimo, two years earlier, in the same city. Albert Barny, vicar-general of the Grandmontine Order, caused it to be printed in 1650, in an octodecimo volume at Paris by Jean Paslé; he appended the *Maxims* of St Stephen collected by his disciples, the constitutions and statutes made at the general chapter of the Order held in 1643, and finally the office of the holy founder. In 1671 the same Rule was printed at Rouen by Eustache Viret.

3. Besides St Stephen’s Rule, we have from him maxims and instructions which were collected only after his death by his disciples. M. Baillet [Note: [Col. 1001] Preface to the translation, p. 7.] maintains that the disciples of this saint:

> “Even wished this collection to be taken as the rule of their institute, which, in his view, had in fact no other rule at that time than the Gospel—that is, the common rule of all the disciples of Jesus Christ and the testament left to all his children. To tell the truth,” adds M. Baillet, “these maxims are nothing other than the maxims of the Gospel itself; and one may judge that St Stephen had no intention of giving another rule to his disciples, since, near the end of his days, he still exhorted them to persevere in the rule he had taken from the Gospel to guide them: *Tantum in regula, de Evangelio per me sumpta, perseveretis*—‘Only persevere in the Rule which I have taken from the Gospel.’”

Do not these words cited by M. Baillet appear to prove the opposite of what that celebrated critic maintains? If Stephen had given his disciples absolutely no rule other than that of the Gospel, would he have told them to persevere in the one he had taken from the Gospel? He would simply have told them to persevere in practising the Gospel. Therefore he had given them a Rule drawn from the Gospel: *per me sumpta de Evangelio*, “taken by me from the Gospel.” If St Benedict had told his disciples to persevere in the Rule he had taken from the Gospel—as he could have said with as much basis as St Stephen of Muret—would one have just grounds for concluding that he had given no particular Rule distinct from the Gospel?

Moreover, the very reply which St Stephen wished his disciples to make to those who might question or blame them concerning the kind of life they led is proof that they possessed a particular Rule. This reply includes part of the practices prescribed by the Rule which are not expressed in the Gospel, but which, far from being contrary to it, are highly conformable to it. Thus they were ordered to answer that, if what they did were not conformable to the Gospel, they were ready to correct and reform it.

The Rule of St Stephen, composed especially for his disciples and discussed above, must not be confused with the *Maxims* in question here. The latter are common both to his religious and to people who came from outside to consult him; that is, they contain not only practices proper and particular to St Stephen’s disciples, but also general instructions suitable for all the faithful. It is true that part of what is prescribed in the Rule occurs here among these 122 maxims; but several matters concern less the disciples of St Stephen than those who came for his advice, and many others belong to all the faithful. Indeed, one may say generally of these maxims what has been said of the *Ascetical Works* of St Basil the Great, as M. Baillet observes [Note: [Col. 1001] Preface, p. 14.]: although they appear principally to have in view the instruction of persons withdrawn from the world, scarcely one is not useful to all Christians, whatever their estate or condition.

William Dandina [Note: [Col. 1001] *Life of Hugh*, in Martène, vol. VI, *Amplissima Collectio*, p. 1155.] tells us that the *Maxims* of St Stephen of Muret were collected after his death by Hugh of Lacerta, the most celebrated of his disciples, who had often heard them from the lips of that holy man, at whose side he had always been during his lifetime.

M. Baillet [Note: [Col. 1001] Preface, p. 8.] wishes them to be considered according to the spirit that produced them, drawing them from their divine source, and according to the body in which they are clothed, so as not to confuse what belongs to St Stephen with what belongs only to his disciples:

> “On the side of the spirit,” he says, “they will be no small cause of admiration to those who, without stopping at the surface, wish to penetrate their depth. One will be surprised to find in them so much good sense and solidity, joined to elevation of mind and delicacy of thought. The very manner in which the saint presents great truths in their proper light, and the grace with which he accompanies them, gives more than a glimpse of a refinement of taste and a polish which renunciation of the world and the wild dwelling of woods and mountains had been unable to efface. One finds in them a savour, vigour, and even brilliance which one would scarcely think to demand elsewhere from a man humbled and, so to speak, smothered for so many years beneath mortifications of mind and body.”

There is reason to believe that these maxims, as we possess them, are only the smaller part of what might have been collected from them. Yet what remains displays a pleasing variety, with an air of novelty which gives an idea of the fertility and beauty of the author’s genius. Proof of this will be found from the first chapter, in the proposition the saint made to those who asked to be received among his disciples. He pleasantly told them that they would be shut up in a prison having neither opening nor door through which to leave it, and that they could return to the world only by the breach they themselves made in it. If such a misfortune befell them, he could not send after them to bring them back, because all who were there, like himself, had their legs cut off with respect to the world.

We should like to enlarge further and show, by other examples, the attractiveness and solidity found in the instructions which Blessed Stephen gave both to his disciples and to outsiders, whom his reputation drew into the wilderness of Muret. What light and force there are in what he said to the former regarding the advantages of religious life; the temptations by which the devil seeks to make them fall; the means of guarding against them; vainglory and its fatal effects; the ambition to command or teach others; the knowledge needed to serve God as he ought to be served; the mercy God shows to one entering religion; and the hundredfold promised in the Gospel to those who leave all things for Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 1003] See chapters 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, and 16.]! In every stroke one recognizes a man filled and penetrated by the Spirit of God, who pours forth the words of his wisdom like rain, in the expression of Scripture.

There, in chapter 17, he makes the sinner feel how dreadful it is to separate oneself from God; here, in chapter 18, he reassures the righteous person by showing what ought to be the ground of confidence. He teaches the faithful how they should cast the cares of this life upon the Lord (ch. 22). He makes them understand (chs. 20, 23) the sweetness of God’s commandments, how sweet and easy they are to observe; the limitless obligation laid upon them to love and serve God without end; and how they should possess the love of God and make it prevail over all other things (chs. 27, 42).

These maxims would have to be transcribed in full if we wished to set out all they contain that is useful and edifying on several important points of Christian morality. But we may say generally that few writings of this kind are as instructive, luminous, and exact as the collection of the *Sentences* of St Stephen.

The style of these maxims in no way corresponds to the beauty, precision, and solidity of the thoughts. This gives reason to believe that they lost much in passing through the channel of Blessed Stephen’s disciples, who did not render them with the same clarity, force, and beauty in which they received them from their holy founder. As for the method followed and the order in which they were arranged, it appears that no other was observed than to place them as they came to the mind of the person or persons who compiled the collection.

Two duodecimo editions of St Stephen’s *Maxims*, in Latin and French, appeared at Paris: the first in 1704, from Pierre-Augustin Le Mercier and the widow of Jean de Saint-Aubin; the second in 1707, from Jacques Vincent. The author of this translation was M. Baillet, so celebrated in the republic of letters. Those ignorant of Latin are truly obliged to him for providing them the means of reading instructions from which they may derive much profit. Even those who know the language will obtain aid from the French translation in understanding several obscure Latin passages whose sense is sometimes broken or suspended.

The learned translator remedied this defect by supplying what appeared to him to have been omitted by those who made the collection; by completing thoughts which did not seem to him finished; by sometimes determining or fixing a sense which appeared to be left suspended; and finally by explaining, through the addition of a few words or short phrases, what required some development. But, so as not to fail in the fidelity required by an exact translation, he took care not to let his additions be confused with the text of the original: he enclosed them in parentheses in order to distinguish them.

4. We find still some further maxims and instructions of Saint Stephen of Muret in a short Life of this saint composed under the direction of Stephen of Lisiac, fourth prior of Grandmont, according to the testimony of Bernard Gui. This Life, entitled *Sayings and Deeds of Saint Stephen*, is divided into sixteen chapters [Note: [Col. 1003] Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, p. 1043 ff.], which had been inserted into the Life of the holy founder of the Order of Grandmont written by Gérard Ithier. When Dom Martène published the latter’s work, he perceived this patchwork from the difference in style and for other reasons; he judged that these sixteen chapters had improperly been inserted into Gérard’s work after the forty-sixth chapter, and removed them in order to print them separately. Among the maxims reported in these sixteen chapters, some are the same, and in almost the same terms, as those found in the collection of one hundred and twenty-two. This may be seen by comparing the third chapter with the fifty-seventh of the collection, and the fourth with the sixty-third, in which are reported the counsels Saint Stephen gave soldiers concerning how they might be saved in their profession, the spirit in which they should undertake military exercises, and how they should serve God in the services rendered to their princes. But others in the sixteen chapters, especially in the eighth, are not found in the collection. This chapter bears the title: “Why he bestowed temporal goods upon prostitutes and actors.” Saint Stephen wished persons of this kind to be relieved in their bodily needs, so as to have an opportunity to procure for them the goods of the soul. “If,” he said, “the sinner who comes to us is received with harsh words, he will believe God to be cruel and will remain more attached to his sin; whereas he will listen more willingly to what is prescribed for the salvation of his soul if he first receives what is needed by the body.” The ninth chapter bears this title: “Why he avoided confraternities of secular persons.” Saint Stephen answered those who proposed such confraternities to him that all the good works which he and his disciples practised were shared with all people, and that they could add no further prayers to those which they said every day. Afterwards, when reporting these proposals privately to his disciples, he said that those who made them wished, without knowing it, under the specious pretext of a good, to make them guilty of simony. “But God forbid,” he added, “that we should sell the divine office. For it is the act of a hireling to pray when something is given, and to cease from prayers when nothing is given.” [Note: [Col. 1003] “Thus and thus they urge us, indeed unwittingly, under the appearance of goodness, to become Simoniacs; but far be it from us to sell the divine office! For it is the work of a hireling to pray when something is given, and to cease from prayers when nothing is given.”]

[Col. 1005] 5. Dom Montfaucon lists among the manuscripts of the library of Saint-Victor in Paris a letter of Saint Stephen: “Of Stephen, first father of the Grandmontines.”

[Col. 1005]

# LIFE OF SAINT STEPHEN, BY GÉRARD, SEVENTH PRIOR OF GRANDMONT

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, 1043, from two ancient manuscripts of Grandmont and a third, more recent manuscript of Marmoutier.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

Very many authors have celebrated in their writings the illustrious deeds of Saint Stephen, founder of the Order of Grandmont. Stephen of Lisiac, made fourth prior of Grandmont in the year 1141, seems to have been the first of all to undertake this task. For, according to the testimony of Bernard Gui, he caused the sayings and deeds of Saint Stephen to be written down. This work, indeed, has hitherto lain hidden in darkness.

Thereafter Gérard Ithier, who in 1188 was appointed, by unanimous agreement of the brethren, to succeed William of Trinhiac, the sixth prior, when he earnestly sought to have his most devout father enrolled among the saints, wrote his Life and miracles in a fuller style; and this work likewise had not hitherto deserved to see the light. A third Life, abridged from this one—or rather excerpts from Gérard’s work, not arranged very coherently—was compiled by certain brethren living in cells, apparently, as I conjecture, for their own use, sparing themselves the longer labour of committing the whole Life to writing. Philip Labbe, the learned priest of the Society, first published this Life without its author’s name in his *New Library*, in 1657. John Bolland and Godfrey Henschen received it from Pierre-François Chifflet and reprinted it under the name of Gérard, seventh prior of Grandmont, for the eighth day of February. For when they had compared the work of Gérard cited by Charles Frémon with the Life in their hands, and had found in it the very words of that work, they did not doubt that it could and ought to be attributed to him, although it contains only certain excerpts by a leisurely brother who, sparing himself the more extended labour, did not wish to transcribe the whole.

Fourth, the pious Charles Frémon of Tours, reformer of his order, composed the Life of Saint Stephen in French in order to encourage his brethren to follow in the footsteps of their lawgiver, and had it printed at Dijon in 1647. Fifth and finally, the most reverend Henri de La Marche de Pargnac, the last general superior of the order and abbot of Grandmont, published a similar work at Paris not long ago. Besides these authors, William Dandina, surnamed of Saint-Savin, who toward the end of the twelfth century wrote the Life of Hugh of La Certa elegantly and carefully, inserted into it very many things most worthy of notice concerning Saint Stephen, hitherto little known. Add to these Vincent of Beauvais, who likewise treats of Saint Stephen in book XXV, chapter 46 and following, of the *Historical Mirror*; Bernard Gui; Saint Antoninus, part II, title 15, chapter 21; and many others.

Thus, for the elucidation of the memory of Saint Stephen of Muret, nothing seemed wanting except that the writings of Stephen of Lisiac and of Gérard, seventh prior, should at last become public property. When I was once permitted to examine the library of the monastery of Grandmont, two very large codices came into my hands, bearing the name of Gérard, seventh prior. They were elegantly written and, unless my judgment deceives me, penned by the author’s own hand; from these we believe that the more recent manuscript of Saint Martin of Tours, Marmoutier, was copied. As I carefully turned over these manuscripts, I found in one of them, after chapter 46, sixteen further chapters inserted, followed by verses. Having read them with the greatest attention, I immediately conjectured that they were the sayings and deeds of Saint Stephen, first collected by order of Stephen of Lisiac. The somewhat different style and the matters treated in them, which agree admirably with “sayings and deeds,” as the title declares, confirmed this conjecture of mine. Then, since chapter 47 is most closely connected with the preceding chapter 46, no one can fail to observe that those sixteen articles were inserted there out of sequence, after the work had been completed.

Furthermore, since Gérard prefixed three prefaces to the Life which he composed, and only the third bears his name, I immediately concluded that the first two were by other authors, whose work he had interwoven with his own. Strong suspicion suggests to me that one of them was Stephen of Lisiac. For this reason we judged it worthwhile to publish those sixteen chapters separately.

Moreover, although Gérard professes that he recounts what he had learned from the truthful reports of certain trustworthy persons and had seen with his own eyes, it must nevertheless be admitted that he wrote the beginnings of Saint Stephen’s Life with little accuracy. For what he relates about Stephen’s journey to Benevento in the twelfth year of his age, and his residence there for the same number of years with Archbishop Milo, cannot in any way be reconciled with the duration of Milo’s episcopate, which lasted scarcely two years. For Milo was ordained in 1074 and had a successor in 1076, as we have shown in our notes. But since Milo had obtained the dignity of dean of Paris before Pope Gregory VII raised him to the see of Benevento, it seems far from improbable that Saint Stephen went to him in Paris in the twelfth year of his age, resided there with him, and devoted himself to sacred and humane letters; that he afterwards followed him to Benevento when Milo had become archbishop, Stephen then being in the twenty-second year of his age; and that, after Milo was called to heaven two years later, Stephen lived for some time in Rome with a cardinal.

## The first heading in the Life of Saint Stephen the Confessor, first father of the Order of Grandmont

[Col. 1005A]

Since it is the proper duty of faithful servants, whom the Lord has appointed over His household (Matt. [Col. 1006A] XXIV), to watch over their disciples lest they fall from the state of uprightness, wherein indeed the chief ground of salvation for those entrusted to their care is believed to lie: although pastoral charity does not seek [Col. 1007A] its own interests (I Cor. XIII), disciples must nevertheless always look upon the life of a good teacher, who can say with blessed Paul, “Be imitators of me” (I Cor. IV), so that they may afterwards take from it in all things the necessary pattern for their own conduct.

For Him through whose aid truth is disclosed by the Lord to the faithful, the faithful themselves ought to love above all visible things, both in word and deed. Certainly we, the brethren of Grandmont, may say this of Stephen, the most reverend first shepherd of our religious way of life. Although we came long ago to the light of faith, yet we cannot by any means pass along the straight path through this way of righteousness which we have undertaken unless we follow a guide who knows how to avoid every perilous turning. It is as when a sheep, clinging to the grass before it, disdains to follow [Col. 1007B] its shepherd who wishes to lead it to the richest pastures: it is either at some time devoured by wolves, or, thin and failing, bleating without knowing where it is going, remains shut out from the fold.

The discerning judgment of a shepherd is indeed the great salvation of all; a wise master is the glory of disciples. Likewise, the walls of a building are firm only when they do not depart from the foundation which the wise architect laid. Therefore, beloved brethren, after receiving faith, let it be our highest joy to have a good shepherd, whose miracles we continually behold with our eyes and uphold without failing. For what else are our revenues, or our extensive farming, or our great possession of livestock, or profits obtained through churches, from which so many brethren [Col. 1007C] gathered together are fed daily, except his pure faith? We receive the reward of his tears and fasts; every day we reap the fruits of the long poverty which he embraced without ceasing—as you see—wherever obedience transfers us, though we possess no temporal means of support and have no fear of want, since we await the Lord alone.

Therefore, as the proverb says, “Whose bread we eat, his praise we should uphold,” let us keep in mindful remembrance the Lord’s mercy and the steadfastness of faith of Stephen, our shepherd, in which through Christ’s grace we hope for eternal salvation. I pass over the fact that none of us, attempting to take up by any wisdom of his own this way of freedom, could do so unless it had been clearly shown beforehand by this Father and fenced on every side against every slavery to desire. Or, if anyone did attempt it, he would not know how to bring it to completion, as we see in many who do not persevere in the poverty they have begun. Hence we ought to venerate the memory of this patron more joyfully.

We say these things in order to make the brethren well disposed and attentive to reading what is set down in this writing concerning the aforesaid man, for the common cause: because what is wholly unknown cannot be loved. “Faith comes by hearing,” as the Apostle says (Rom. X), especially when faith must be given to the testimony of those disciples from whom we heard these things. For in truth they knew him from the beginning by sight and hearing, and [Col. 1008A] those who still survive bear witness by their deeds to the truth of their words.

Yet if many things have been added concerning the perfect man of God which not all of us can imitate but can only admire, listeners ought not therefore to neglect them; rather, they should embrace them more dearly, so that through them we may discern our own frailty more subtly and cleanse the sight of our minds in the examples of so great a Father. For each person advances toward God in proportion as, through another’s good qualities, he more carefully considers his own lowliness. This is the steadfast harmony of the members in the human body: hands and feet, although they see least of all, nevertheless love the eyes through which they are directed to what is necessary.

Let us likewise love the outstanding merit of the venerable Stephen, because such grace was divinely bestowed upon him for the benefit of us all. Whoever refuses even to hear the word of truth will scarcely, or never, preserve it by putting it into practice. This is said with reference to the person held in this folly. But let us give thanks to God, because such arrogance has been wholly removed from the brethren. Since, moreover, we have divided the treatise into chapters, we have set down the points briefly in the course of the reading, so that the sequence of the words may be understood more easily; and now we carry out our purpose.

## Another heading

Since the same grace has by no means been given to all people for knowing and loving their Creator, those undoubtedly have been accounted worthy of more celebrated remembrance who, more abundantly inspired by the divine Spirit, shone more clearly in conduct and doctrine and rendered greater service in [Col. 1008C] God’s Church. Out of their immense multitude we have before our eyes one man: namely, Saint Stephen, the first Father of the Order of Grandmont after the Lord, who, following in the footsteps of his Redeemer (I Pet. II), loved poverty of spirit so greatly that he wished to possess almost nothing on earth. We believe that an account of his virtues must be given, as it will be of benefit to some; yet the scantiness of our knowledge and slowness of our intellect are plainly unequal to the task.

Nevertheless, the austerity of his life proclaims his merits, and the pattern of conduct which he left to his followers bears witness to them. For who in our times listened more devoutly to the Lord saying in the Gospel, “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV)? Who more explicitly [Col. 1008D] put into effect this counsel of Jesus Christ: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI)? No deaf hearer of any evangelical perfection, no forgetful reader of any divine justification, he abandoned all things in order to gain Christ (Phil. III), so completely that he retained in the world neither livestock, nor landed property, nor revenues, nor profits, nor anything else from which necessities might be supplied to him.

Thus poor and naked in worldly goods, but endowed with the treasure of heavenly virtues, he placed faith and love in Him who said to His disciples, “Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat? or what shall we drink? or with what shall we be clothed? For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matt. VI). Without [Col. 1009A] anxiety or worldly preoccupation, he began first to seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness (Matt. VI). Hence it is not without reason to believe that he led a heavenly life upon earth and very frequently tasted the hidden manna, which no one knows except the one who receives it. Nor could he suffer excessive lack of bodily nourishment, having placed all his hope in God, as the Prophet says: “Cast your care upon the Lord, and He will sustain you” (Ps. LIV).

We, his disciples however unworthy, acknowledge that this has hitherto befallen us through his faith and merits; and we confidently believe and hope that it will always happen thus to all who follow the purpose of this poverty. For we know how faithful He is who says, “I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread” [Col. 1009B] (Ps. XXXVI). But how great a grace this man obtained in the sight of the Most High through the merit of his faith and the mortification of his flesh, we have undertaken to recount in a true report for the knowledge of those who gladly hear of the works of divine mercy. Yet the beginning must be taken from his birth and childhood.

Of those things which the Lord deigned to work through him in miracles and in discerning the thoughts of the brethren, however, we shall say little, lest truth perhaps seem a lie to unbelievers, while believers, from the few things they hear, may say that “all things are possible to the one who believes” (Mark IX).

## Another heading, of Gerald, venerable seventh prior of Grandmont, in the Life of Saint Stephen the Confessor

[Col. 1009C]

To all Christ’s faithful: greetings from the humble and unworthy minister, by divine permission, of the Church of Grandmont.

Do not wonder, beloved, nor think it foolish or tasteless that I presume to write to your whole community and to place my name at the beginning of this work. I do this not from boastfulness, vain glory, or any perverse intention, but with a good will and humble conscience, supported, as we believe, by divine grace in perfect charity. With that grace we desire, insofar as the Lord grants, faithfully to commit briefly to writing—if we can—how the blessed confessor Stephen, first founder of the Order of Grandmont, resolved from the earliest beginnings of his childhood to serve faithfully our Lord God; and his purpose and manner of life, abounding in praises most worthy [Col. 1009D] of him; his most holy character; and the miracles which God Almighty in His gracious kindness deigned to perform through Stephen’s glorious merits, as we have learned by the true report of certain trustworthy persons and have seen with our own eyes.

Let foolish liars, therefore, who bark and contradict the truth, come to their senses. Let them be silenced, I say, for the Lord is true (Rom. III), and all His ways are judgments and truth (Ps. CXVIII). He has done whatever He willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths (Ps. CXXXIV). And what wonder is this? He can do all things; He accomplishes whatever He wills. Therefore let unbelievers understand and perceive, and let the faithless blush, because God made blessed Stephen marvellous and, in making him marvellous, made him praiseworthy. Nor did He wish his holiness to remain longer concealed, though it lay hidden like a gem in the dung-heap of oblivion.

Let the faithful who fear the Lord rejoice and be glad—those who love truth, despise empty things, and disdain worldly things—because God has shown them the light of truth and the lamp that had been hidden beneath a bushel, though it [Col. 1010B] seemed to have been set upon a lampstand (Matt. V): that is, the blessed man Stephen, whom the all-powerful Lord God in His marvellous goodness wished to make known to all peoples.

Rejoice, I say, you men of Grandmont, for whom the Lord provided such and so great a shepherd, who faithfully showed you the way of truth, the path of righteousness, the rule of holy religion, the pattern of chaste living, the observance of vigils and fasts, the norm of right conduct, the discipline of correcting morals, and steadfastness in loving and embracing poverty. These are the works for which I urge you to rejoice and to which you ought to devote yourselves, because in these and other works of righteousness and faith he gave you an example. For he was [Col. 1010C] a lover of truth, a follower of righteousness, a founder of holiness and an establisher of an excellent and venerable religious life, a nourisher of chastity, and a preserver of most perfect virginity.

Therefore, beloved, I exhort you to imitate him as far as you can: by pursuing righteousness, preserving patience, loving true humility, enduring voluntary and necessary poverty, holding right faith, certain hope, and unfeigned charity. These are the works of true goodness and holiness with which your most holy Father, blessed Stephen, was adorned and crowned. If you listen to him and wish to follow his way, you shall eat the good things of the land of the living and see the King of glory in His beauty, when you come to the heavenly kingdom [Col. 1010D] with that blessed Stephen himself leading and showing the way, through the working of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

Here ends the heading of Gerald, venerable seventh prior of Grandmont, in the Life of Saint Stephen, most perfect confessor and hermit.

# HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF SAINT STEPHEN THE CONFESSOR

[Col. 1011]

## I. Of Saint Stephen’s parents—His father goes to Bari to pray

[Col. 1011A]

There was, then, in the region of Auvergne a most noble man named Stephen, lord and viscount of a certain town called Tiernium or Ternas; and his wife was named Candida. They had not received such names without reason. For they were to have a son who was to be crowned by the Lord with virginity and with the most prolonged affliction of the body, as with fragrant lilies and blooming roses. The event afterwards gave proof of this true presage.

For by divine direction a son was born to them, who remained always a virgin; and, as a sign of the crown he earned, he was called Stephen after his father’s name. His parents, following the custom of nobles, carefully brought him up; and when he had reached an age capable of understanding, they handed him over to be taught letters. They loved him all the more dearly because the boy began to appear both more beautiful in form and of good disposition.

As the boy grew and made ever greater progress in literary learning, his father was divinely inspired to hasten in prayer to the glorious body of blessed Nicholas, which had recently been translated to Bari from Myra, the metropolis of Lycia. [Note: [Col. 1011D] The author of this Life seems not to have known the true occasion of the pilgrimage of Stephen, viscount of Tiernium; for all authorities agree [Col. 1012D] that the body of Saint Nicholas was translated to Bari in 1087, and consequently some years after he had undertaken the pilgrimage.] At that time a multitude of faithful people from different parts of the world assembled there to seek pardon for their sins through the glorious intercession of so great a confessor.

Accordingly, when the father was choosing expenses and companions and wished to set out, he was greatly troubled by a very grave temptation: he feared that the boy might be weakened by the tenderness of his age or by the length of the journey. Yet he did not wish to leave him behind, because he loved him above all things and therefore could not bear to be without him. What more need be said? He hastened most joyfully with him to the most sacred relics, unaware what the Lord God had decreed to do with him. The boy was already twelve years old. But Almighty God willed and ordained that the boy should begin to serve Him at the age at which His own Son according to the flesh was brought by His parents to the Temple; and just as the boy Christ remained in Jerusalem, without Joseph and Mary knowing it (Luke II), so this boy was to remain on the journey, his father unaware and God so ordaining.

## II. Of the boy’s illness in the city of Benevento

[Col. 1012A]
