When, guided by Christ, father and son were happily returning after prayer had been made, so that the father might become more devout from being devout, they passed through the city of Benevento. Who could recount without sorrow what happened there? For there the boy fell ill, and the father’s joy in his little companion was turned to grief. Greatly distressed, he prayed, gave alms, and implored the aid of the all-powerful physician and of blessed Nicholas; but he received no sign of his son’s recovery. O a father’s love! O providence of the heavenly dispensation! The father seeks the boy’s health, but God provides another father for the boy.

## III. Of Milo, archbishop of the city of Benevento

[Col. 1012B]

At that time, in the same city, there was the most blessed Archbishop Milo, an Auvergnat by origin, who had known this man since childhood. Seeing that the boy did not recover, moved by his desire and affection for this most noble man, he asked him to leave his son with him. The father, entirely confident in Milo’s friendship and well aware of his prudence and integrity, entrusted to him as a most faithful man the most faithful pledge, the little boy whom he could not take home. With many prayers he begged him that, if the boy survived, he should have him educated, so that he might know the law of Him to whom he had already been offered while still small. Thus bereft of the pledge of his flesh, desolate and sorrowful, the father returned home.

But after a few days, through the working of divine mercy, the boy [Col. 1012C] was made well; and as though he had forgotten father and homeland, he was cheerful and joyful in a foreign land.

## IV. Of the boy’s instruction by the archbishop

The archbishop, therefore, greatly rejoiced and handed him over not only to be trained in sacred letters, but himself, like a pious father and faithful teacher, took special care to teach him goodness, discipline, and knowledge (Ps. CXVIII). Whenever the boy was free from school, he always had him sit beside him while he conducted his business, whether he was dealing with the affairs of his diocese or taking part in the cases and judgments of the Roman pontiff, for whom Benevento is a see and chamber. He was very frequently compelled to occupy himself with such business because truth, gentleness, and justice were plainly eminent in him. But, as the Apostle says, “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counsellor?” (Rom. XI).

## V. Of God’s providence toward the boy

[Col. 1013A]

That he might find a teacher of righteousness and have a spiritual father, his bodily father led his son to foreign nations, unaware of what he was doing. But He knew, who intended to make something great with and through the boy. For the boy went forth from his land, his kindred, and his father’s house (Gen. XII), so that among nations unknown to him he might learn a way of life; and afterwards a very great multitude of people would swiftly flock to him from Ur of the Chaldeans and Egyptian bondage, to the land of promise and the mountain of virtues (Gen. XI).

## VI. Of the religious men of Calabria, and their life and manner of living

At that time a certain religious community of righteous men flourished in the region of Calabria, all the richer in heavenly goods because it was removed from every concern for temporal things. It had so completely renounced livestock, possessions, and every worldly occupation that it possessed nothing by which its professed members might be drawn back into the turmoil of the age. And so that, with enlarged hearts, all who came to it might walk on the narrow way which leads to life (Matt. VII), none possessed anything as his own; rather, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, “All things were common to them, and distribution was made to each according to his need” (Acts IV).

Yet they had no servants except themselves, so that the greater took the place of the lesser and the superior became the servant. They had cast all concern for bodily support upon God alone. Living unanimously in the cloister, they kept, to the extent of their strength, in all things the obedience that restores humankind. And because they had crucified the world to themselves and themselves to the world, and gloried in the cross of Christ (Gal. VI), bearing witness to the truth by the preaching of their deeds, they found such grace with God and people that the grace of miracles overflowed and they did not lack the provisions of food and clothing sufficient for human nature.

The most wise Archbishop Milo continually commended this rule of life in the sermons which he delivered to the people. Whenever he could see any one of these Fathers, he set aside every other concern and gave himself wholly to him, in order that he might hear Christ speaking in His servant. [Col. 1013D] For he heard of their manner of life, by means of which he subsequently kindled clergy, laity, and other religious persons toward higher things, setting before [Col. 1014A] them the example of these men, who shunned every covetousness—which is the root of all evils (I Tim. VI)—and sought heavenly things alone.

## VII. How he desired to imitate the example of the aforesaid men

Since Stephen, now passing beyond the limits of boyhood, saw that this most holy man took such pleasure in this manner of life, he eagerly endeavoured to investigate the customs and practices of that religious life, in his desire to imitate them, and faithfully committed them to memory. For Christ the Lord had made His dwelling in Stephen’s breast; therefore, out of love for Him, Stephen desired to leave all things. But, being a most prudent youth and full of God, he carefully considered how he might accomplish this perfectly.

## VIII. Of his visit to the land of his birth and to his parents

[Col. 1014B]

Having been taught and brought up by Saint Milo, archbishop of Benevento, [Note: [Col. 1013D] Here the author seriously stumbles in what he relates about Stephen’s residence for twelve years with Milo, archbishop of Benevento, since it is certain that Milo occupied the see of Benevento for scarcely two years. This is evident both from the brief Beneventan Chronicle in our manuscript, where Milo’s ordination is recorded under the year 1074, his death in the following year, and the election of Roffred, his successor, in 1076; and from an instrument of Milo himself reported by Ughelli, in which Milo equates the first year of his episcopate with the year of Christ 1075. Mabillon considers that Milo was still alive in 1078, when, by the authority of Pope Gregory VII and by the testimony of Archbishop Milo—who [Col. 1014D] had formerly been dean of Paris and was appointed archbishop of Benevento by the Apostolic See—one John built the cell of Saint Florentius near Dol in Armorica, having had Milo as his intermediary with the pope in this matter. Yet Milo may have intervened some years before that cell was built; and Ughelli proves by utterly compelling arguments that Roffred, Milo’s successor, occupied the see in 1076.] for twelve years, he received permission from him and resolved in his heart to visit [Note: [Col. 1014D] The Life published by Bolland is silent concerning this visit to his parents.] his homeland and his parents. When they saw him, they rejoiced beyond measure and welcomed him as though he had risen from the dead.

After he had remained there for some time, he resolved, through God’s mercy, to return to the archbishop. Having entered Rome, he learned that the archbishop had already entered upon the way of all flesh. He then remained with a certain most prudent cardinal of the holy Roman Church, and for four successive years [Col. 1014C] entered and went out with him in the Roman curia. [Note: [Col. 1014D] If Saint Stephen remained for four successive years with a certain cardinal after Milo’s death, he could not have laid the foundations of his order before the year 1080.] He often heard Catholic men disputing concerning the practices of various religious orders and concerning the dispensations of the whole Church.

When he had been sufficiently taught about everything that concerns the salvation of the soul and also the sound counsel needed for the world, and when the conceived desire to serve God urgently pressed his mind toward execution in deed, he most devoutly asked the Roman pontiff, to whom he was well known, to allow him, for the remission of his sins—which, I think, were few—to observe somewhere the rule which he had learned to be kept in Calabria.

## IX. What was his standing with the Roman pontiff?

[The text is syntactically uncertain:] although he might do more than was required, if by reading, hearing, or inspiration from above it should happen to him to find the means whereby, at the Lord’s return, he might expect the first good and “a measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing” (Luke VI). The admirable Apostolic Father, marvelling at the devotion of this pious petition, considered the young man’s age and the severity of the rule. At first he was astonished; then, by promising Stephen ecclesiastical honours and immense benefices, he urged him to abandon both such a petition and such an intention. Perhaps he thought that through youthful inconstancy or some coming temptation Stephen would wish to enter upon so narrow and arduous a way.

But the more the pious Father, testing whether the spirit was from God, seemed to dissuade him from asking such things, the more fervent and insistent Stephen became in carrying out what he had proposed and obtaining what he requested.

## X. Of blessed Stephen’s confirmation by the supreme pontiff

[Col. 1015B]

Having therefore learned and tested his constancy, Christ’s vicar at last granted what he sought. By his apostolic authority and power, by which he surpasses all mortals, he enjoined upon him as penance and as the reward of virtue every good work he might perform. Then Stephen, rejoicing at the command of the supreme pontiff which he had so greatly desired, departed from the curia with his blessing. And, as though he already possessed the means of his future way of life, he judged it good to return to his homeland with this intention: that what he had left in body unwillingly and unknowingly, he might leave voluntarily and knowingly in mind and body.

## XI. Of his entry into Auvergne, or his homeland

Setting out, therefore, at the beginning of his youth [Col. 1015C] he returned to Auvergne. But after staying there only a little while, he secretly departed alone from his parents, brothers, kindred, and friends, who greatly rejoiced at his return.

## XII. Of his departure from his homeland and the visitation of divine grace
When he was leaving his native country, having left behind his parents, home, all his household, and his kindred, and knowing that he would never return, he looked back, to bid a final farewell; and suddenly, by divine power, all his bones were shaken, so that it seemed to him that all his joints were being dislocated and loosened. We therefore believe that this sign indicated his future holiness and goodness; hence he could truly say: “You have burst my bonds asunder, O Lord” (Ps. 115). Traversing and examining regions in many provinces, he most diligently considered those places better suited for serving God and doing penance. For he knew that, for those who seek and love God, a crowd of people and an abundance of possessions are harmful, whereas poverty and solitude are beneficial.

### XIII. On the discovery of the wilderness site near Muret

At last, after travelling through many wildernesses and solitary places, and committing to memory, from the lives of canons, monks, and hermits, those things worthy of imitation, he arrived, Christ leading him, in Aquitaine, at a wooded mountain not far from the city of Limoges, called Muret. There he found springs and rocks, a deserted and trackless land [Col. 1016A] which, offering its new guest very cold drink and a dwelling exposed to the winds, promised, by evident signs, affliction for the body and repose for the mind. Moreover, being wholly wild and barren, almost always wintry, unfamiliar to human beings but familiar to wild beasts, it could promise nothing else.

### XIV. On his entry into the wilderness

But one who has experienced God’s consolations does not fear trials; nor does one who frequently eats the bread of angels (Ps. 77) hunger overmuch for human bread. God’s servant, not ignorant of this, fervent and fearless in hope of him of whom it is written that “he was in the wilderness with the beasts, and angels ministered to him” (Matt. 4), approached a spring. Rejoicing in the solitude which he had found suited to his heart [Col. 1016B] for leading a poor life, he vowed that he would serve God there all the days of his life. With a certain ring—the only thing he possessed out of all the world’s substance—he betrothed himself, a most chaste virgin, to Christ, saying:

### XV. On his profession

“I, Stephen, renounce the devil and all his pomps, and I offer and render myself to God the Father, and to his Son and the Holy Spirit, the living and true God, three and one.”

And, writing out his profession, he placed it upon his head and said:

“Almighty and merciful Lord, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who, ever abiding the same, live and reign as the triune and one God: I, Brother Stephen, promise you that henceforth I shall serve you in this wilderness in the Catholic faith. [Col. 1016C] For this reason I place this charter upon my head and this ring upon my finger, so that on the day of my death this promise and this charter may be a shield and defence to me against the snares of my enemies. I beseech you, Lord, to restore to me the wedding garment; to deem me worthy to be numbered among the children of holy Church; and, most holy Father, when my soul departs from the body, to bring it, clothed in the garment of your charity, into your kingdom with all the saints, to the wedding feast of your Son—you who live and reign as God with your Son and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.”

He also said: “Holy Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, to your Son and to you I commend my soul, my body, and my understanding.” Having said these things, he never again returned to the world. Instead, making a small hut of brushwood, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076, in the thirtieth year of his age, he began to dwell in the wilderness, serving the Lord day and night in fasts, vigils, and continual prayers.

### XVI. On his food

From that day, indeed, his food was bread and water, with sometimes a small draught of rye gruel, which, less savoury than other gruels made from other flours, serves necessity in some fashion, not pleasure. In his old age, however—namely, from the thirtieth year of his religious life—he used a little wine for his stomach’s sake (1 Tim. 5), which the dryness and scantiness of food had excessively weakened. But throughout the whole period of his conversion he ate neither flesh [Col. 1017A] nor fat, whether healthy or sick.

Moreover, if anyone wishes to know how even that slender provision which sustained his body came to him, especially while he lived alone in the wilderness for a long time and did not go out into the world, let him recall how the prophet Obadiah, for God’s love, fed the prophets of the Lord hidden in a cave with bread and water (3 Kings 18). Let him know that the charity of neighbouring people, prompted solely by divine inspiration, likewise brought these things to this servant of God. He who sent Daniel, shut up in the lions’ den, a meal through Habakkuk (Dan. 14); who by the service of a raven and a widow freed Elijah from the hardship of hunger (3 Kings 17); who daily gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him (Ps. 146)—could not forget a man of such great faith, whom he had hidden in the hiding-place of his countenance from the disturbance of men (Ps. 30). Therefore, intent only upon heavenly things, he received bodily nourishment abundantly from the devotion of the faithful, but refreshment of mind and the anointing of the spirit from the grace of divine contemplation.

### XVII. On the iron cuirass which he wore

For how could he fail to taste that the Lord is sweet (Ps. 33), or fail to have the dripping drops of his sweetness (Ps. 71), when, chastising his body and reducing it to servitude by rigorous abstinence (1 Cor. 9), he also went armed for so long with an iron cuirass against the snares of the flesh and the wantonness of the mind (Eph. 6), until, with his whole body dried up, [Col. 1017C] he gained a complete victory over himself? To the height of this extraordinary perfection was added such spareness of clothing and hardness of bed that it seemed to all who considered the capacities of human nature to exceed a person’s strength.

### XVIII. On his clothing

The garments which he wore over the cuirass were at no time increased or diminished; rather, in winter and summer alike, they were always equal and the same, to ward off cold and heat.

### XIX. On his bed

The bed to which, after excessive weariness of his body, he withdrew for a little rest was so hard and opposed to repose that someone sleeping in it could be tormented rather than comforted. [Col. 1017D] It consisted of wooden planks set into the ground like a tomb, lacking every covering and every kind of bedding, except for the iron tunic which he always wore next to his bare flesh and the very mean garment with which he remained clothed over it. When he came to bed, he brought that garment with him; when he rose from bed, he carried it away with him. In his absence his bed was bare and empty; in his presence it was furnished with such mattresses and such linen sheets. But who would not marvel at this? Who would not be astonished? For, to speak truthfully, he was sparing in food, sparing in bed, sparing in sleep.

### XX. On his perseverance in divine offices

Apart from the regular obligations of the ecclesiastical office—namely, the Office of the day, of Blessed Mary, and of the faithful departed—from the first day when he came into the wilderness until the last day of his life, he celebrated most devoutly every day and night the Office of the Holy Trinity, with nine lessons and the canonical hours.

### XXI. On his genuflections

We cannot know the number of his genuflections, which he humbly performed by kissing the ground and striking it with forehead and nose; indeed, because of their exceedingly frequent repetition, we believe that he himself did not know it. Yet we know that, by the continual practice of these genuflections, he had developed calluses on hands and knees like those of a camel, and had bent his nose sideways.

### XXII. On his psalmody and prayers

[Col. 1018B]

He loved psalmody and familiar prayers so greatly, and possessed so effectually the grace of that most excellent contemplation in which God is more fully known, that, sometimes carried away by its sweetness and sometimes detained by the occupation of those prayers, he often went without bodily food for two or three days. And because a light once kindled could not remain hidden under a bushel (Matt. 5), the report of his holiness spread far and wide, and many came to him from every direction, desiring to hear admonitions for their salvation.

But if, for the sake of conversing with those whom he could not fail, without violating charity, to receive, he sometimes did not fulfil at the appointed hours or times what he was accustomed to do or say in prayer, [Col. 1018C] those things could be postponed, but not omitted. For after those who had come to him departed, whatever the hour might then be, before he ate or slept he made up, with all devotion, everything that he had necessarily interrupted from his customary prayers. Thus he often took no food until the following day, a true imitator of Christ’s disciples, who, because of those coming and going, had no leisure even to eat.

Accordingly, in the first year of his conversion, pure and rigorous in exacting discipline from himself, deprived of human companionship, he was alone in the wilderness. In the second year he received under his care and discipline a certain man from the world; another later followed him. For a long time he had only these two as companions, since others were afraid to undertake the austerity of his way of life. Yet he imposed upon no one his own rule of severity or measure of endurance. Rather, as he had begun—cruel and harsh to himself—so he was gentle and far more moderate toward others. For he knew that, according to the grace bestowed from heaven, one person is stronger than another, and that not all of us can do everything.

### XXIII. On the prudence he showed toward his disciples

He did not seek to kill his disciples’ bodies, but their vices. Therefore, like the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord appointed over his household (Luke 12), he granted them, with even balance, food, clothing, and the other necessities of human frailty. He demanded only this of them: that, loving [Col. 1019A] the Lord above all things, they should be able truly to say to the Lord: “For your sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Ps. 43). And after the number of his disciples had increased by God’s ordering, he did not become as one of them among them, but the least of them all (Luke 9).

### XXIV. On his humility

For, as is customary in religious life, while they sat at table in the refectory and ate, he humbly sat on the ground, reading the passions of the saints, the Lives of the Fathers, or another edifying Scripture, so that while receiving bodily food they might remember the saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4). For he had read—he had read, I say—and committed to memory: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you shall find grace before God” (Ecclus. 3); and this: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you shall be the servant of all” (Matt. 26).

### XXV. On his teaching given to his disciples

How prudently and carefully he taught his disciples and those who spoke with him, by living speech, through the sayings and examples of the saints, concerning the observance of religious life, maturity of conduct, and everything pertaining to the soul’s salvation—as is written in his sayings—we pass over in silence. For we hasten to those most evident indications of his holiness, to which greater faith should be given than to words. For who knows [Col. 1019C] the thoughts of human beings, except him who fashioned their hearts one by one and understands all their works (Ps. 32), or one to whom he himself wills to reveal them?

### XXVI. On his knowledge of the thoughts of his disciples

This man had received with such effect from that Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James 1), the privilege of this grace, that he told his disciples most openly what they were thinking and the temptations they suffered from the devil. Like a loving father, earnestly concerned for their salvation, he instructed them how to resist manfully evil thoughts and troublesome temptations.

### XXVII. How great was the power of his prayers with God

[Col. 1019D]

Moreover, whenever their weakness required it, he frequently helped them with his prayers, lest they be submerged by such waves in this great and wide sea. For his prayers had such power before the Lord that, with God cooperating, they could free those captured from the very jaws of demons and from the evil contrivances of human beings. To make this clear, let us briefly recount here two of the many miracles which the Lord deigned to perform through his faith and prayers.

### XXVIII. On a knight freed by him from a certain sin

A noble knight, then, was held guilty of a certain enormous sin. Once, while he stood with him among others who had come to visit, he spoke like one of the foolish. For he said: “I beg you, servant of God, do not pray to the Lord for me.”

Stephen, astonished, answered him: “What is this, brother? Why do you speak so?”

The knight said: “I love a certain sin so much that I do not at all wish either to hate it or to leave it. But I fear that this might happen to me if you pray for me. Therefore help others with your prayers, but by no means help me.”

Having said this, the knight of the devil went away rejoicing; but Christ’s faithful athlete remained sad and distressed. Entering the chapter-house, he struck the board and gathered the brothers; yet under the force of his tears he could scarcely make known to them why he had done this. At last, after revealing the knight’s words to them, [Col. 1020B] he commanded and urged them to strive with him in entreating the Lord for the most foolish knight. Without delay, the sinner returned; seeking pardon for the folly just described, he renounced his iniquity in heart and speech. In this deed one may surely recognize how great was Stephen’s charity: until he restored his erring neighbour to the way of truth, he did not cease to pour out prayers to the Lord with tears. There is another most splendid work of his faith, not unlike this one.

### XXIX. On the retainer of a certain man who was set free

For a certain man, sufficiently wealthy in worldly means, used to bring provisions which the faithful people charitably sent to Stephen, as he continually remained in the wilderness. But since he lived far from Stephen’s cell and could not reach it in a single day, he had arranged lodging on the way, where he stayed both going and returning. The master of that lodging knew that this servant of God possessed wealth; and therefore, at the devil’s instigation, he betrayed him to two robbers. To compel him to pay ransom, they hid with him in caves and hollows of the earth, holding him bound and captive.

After several days it was reported to the servant of God that his retainer had secretly been seized on the road by which he came to him, by unknown persons, and taken somewhere unknown. Hearing this, Stephen first had him sought most carefully in many places, but he could not be found at all. Then, when the brothers complained and grieved over this, he said: “Why are you anxious? I know him to whom it is manifest where the man is and how he fares. Let us therefore go barefoot into the oratory and implore the help of the glorious Virgin, mother of the Lord, in whose service he was captured. For there is no prison and no place from which she cannot at once restore him to us free.”

When this had been done, behold: at dawn on the next day, the treacherous host, the two robbers, and the man whom they had captured stood knocking at the door of the cell. The man who had been captured and bound was released and free; the thieves and betrayer were bound with chains. Seeing this and rejoicing greatly at the miracle, the brother porter privately informed the spiritual father, who at the usual hour was instructing his disciples. But Christ’s servant concealed the joy of his mind in his expression [Col. 1021A] and did not interrupt the discourse he had begun, offering the brothers an example that they should glory not in miracles but in the Lord alone. Then, after he had finished his discourse, he freed the thieves and betrayer from the bonds with which they were tied; and, giving thanks to God and to the most blessed Virgin Mary with the brothers, he allowed them to depart safe and free.

### XXX. On the great numbers of men and women who came to him

Many came to him, small and great, poor and rich. For his reputation was most renowned: he benefited everyone and harmed no one. His hand was not stretched out to receive and drawn back from giving; rather, he gave more willingly than he accepted. With cheerful mind and glad countenance he generously distributed spiritual and temporal nourishment to beggars; he reproved sinners; he consoled those grieved by their sins and showed them what they should do. He was kindly toward the righteous, compassionate toward the afflicted, merciful toward the needy; he was a father to all.

### XXXI. On the fragrance of a wonderful odour which proceeded from him

Those who spoke with him and stood near him sensed a fragrant odour proceeding from the man; many reliable witnesses of this still survive. This fragrance, certainly, not only testified—as those who experienced it acknowledged and proclaimed to others—that the author of all sweetness rested in him; it was also, so far as we are permitted to understand, a reward with which the most unimpaired virginity and the humility of soul and body conspicuous in him were endowed during his lifetime. [Col. 1021C]

It would take long to recount the patience with which, by fasting, vigils, and enduring cold and heat, he bore the Lord’s cross in heart and body; his charity, sobriety, discernment, and cheerfulness, by which he gave counsel to all in need and made himself approachable. God knows all these things. For throughout our narrative we have judged that those matters concerning him should remain unspoken which might perhaps cause the faith of our time to waver. Yet the holiness of his life gave forth such a fragrance that it could summon even the highest persons to know him.

### XXXII. On the coming of the Roman cardinals

[Col. 1021D] The most eminent cardinals, namely Gregory and Peter de Leo—between whom, as is known, there was later a schism over the primacy of the Roman papacy—had been sent by the supreme pontiff to Gaul. While they were performing their legation in the region of Limoges, they came together to this man of God. They carefully asked him first about the manner of life which he followed; then from whom he had learned it; whether he was a canon, monk, or hermit; and finally why he had begun to undertake the care of human beings on a dry and cold mountain, in barren and uncultivated land, without the aid of animals or any temporal possessions.

### XXXIII. On Blessed Stephen’s reply to the cardinals

He answered them humbly, as he was accustomed to answer all who spoke with him. First he mentioned his teacher, the venerable Milo, archbishop of the city of Benevento, turning over in his heart Christ’s saying: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (John 8). But when the cardinals heard him speak of so famous a man, they hesitated somewhat at his words. For they knew that the death of this most holy man had occurred long before.

Perceiving this, God’s servant said: “Do you doubt this, my lords? Certainly, if you were not in haste and were permitted to hear whether we speak truth, you would prove it immediately.” Then they promised that they would gladly listen to whatever he said, to his very last word.

### XXXIV. A Limoges abbot’s testimony to the aforesaid cardinals on behalf of Blessed Stephen

[Col. 1022B]

A certain abbot of Limoges who had brought them said to them: “Do not for a moment suppose that this servant of God utters a false word. He would sooner allow his head to be cut off than knowingly lie in any utterance.”

Then, beginning from the start, Stephen related to them in order how, in childhood, he had been brought by his father to Benevento; how he was educated there for twelve years by Saint Milo; and how he learned this rule. He also inserted many remarkable things about Milo’s life and teaching which they themselves knew. They therefore recognized that he spoke truthfully and gladly accepted whatever more he said.

Having thus answered all their questions—for he was always entirely ready to give an answer to everyone who asked concerning the faith and hope he possessed (1 Pet. 3)—he added at the end of his speech:

“Therefore, when we wished, by the grace of Christ leading us, to depart from the deceitful world, at the Roman pontiff’s court, where, with a certain cardinal, we had been since the passing of our most wise and holy teacher, Archbishop Milo, we undertook our penance as best we could. By his command and obedience, for the remission of our sins, we resolved to follow this way of poverty and lowliness.

“And if, because of our weakness, [Col. 1022D] we cannot imitate the holy and praiseworthy hermits whom we read to have devoted an entire week to divine contemplation without bodily food, nevertheless, because we have withdrawn somewhat from the public road and follow, however inadequately, the brothers who serve God in Calabria without livestock or possessions, we await his mercy at the last judgment, when Christ comes to judge the living and the dead.

“And behold, as you see, we do not wear the clothing of monks or canons, concerning which you asked us, because we do not presume to appropriate to ourselves titles of such holiness. For the institution of canons, which has the power of binding and loosing after the manner of the apostles, surpasses the authority of monks; and therefore, as we have said, we do not dare at all to usurp their life. For such great perfection is necessary for governing churches that we could scarcely, or never, suffice to imitate their perfect rulers; but their imperfect and useless rulers we must by no means follow. Nor ought we merely to expel greed from ourselves, but also everything from which it might arise. Indeed, even if it happened that we possessed churches, how could we undertake the care of others, we who are dead to the world and, with our limbs cut off from the world, lack feet for walking and a mouth for speaking? Thus we neither undertake nor can undertake even our own care; how much less that of others, as pastors of the Church do?

“We do not use the name of monks, because they have obtained a title denoting holiness or singleness, although all Christians can be called monks. Yet those are especially called monks who take further care of themselves [perhaps: *who do not take further care of themselves*], and think of nothing except God alone. [Col. 1023B] Nor can we imitate the life of hermits, because it especially belongs to the life of all hermits to avoid the tumult of the world and remain in their cells, so that they may devote themselves to prayer and silence.”

### XXXV. The cardinals’ exaltation of the righteous man

When they had heard these things, the cardinal-legates marvelled at his prudence and humble answer, and confidently said to all who were present: “We tell you, and testify, that nowhere have we found anyone like this man; for the Holy Spirit speaks in him.”

Turning to this soldier of Christ, they spoke as follows: “Man of God, if it is possible for you to persevere thus until the end, then certainly you will be numbered with the apostles in the kingdom of heaven; [Col. 1023C] for these are their footsteps.”

And so, having given him their blessing and shared prayers with him, they departed. If here we carefully and cautiously consider the dispensation of divine mercy, we may behold an evident miracle. For Christ willed that his servant, who at the beginning of his intention to do good had received a command from his apostolic vicar, should at the end of his religious life receive testimony to his holiness from apostolic men, the vicars of that vicar.

### XXXVI. Comparison

Here, with God’s permission, we can make a certain and most true comparison, so that his holiness and goodness may be better displayed and it may be seen how almighty God chose to make his holiness known by clear signs. Let us therefore recall the words written in John’s Gospel concerning John the Baptist, where it says that the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to John, to ask him: “Who are you?” And he confessed: “I am not the Christ.” They asked him: “Who then? Are you Elijah?” And he said: “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered: “No.” Therefore they said to him: “Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?” He said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said.” And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees (John 1).

Understand the correspondence of the words. Priests and Levites were sent: by whom? By the Jews, certainly. From where? From Jerusalem. To whom? To John, namely. For what purpose? To question him. About what? Whether he himself was Christ.

Likewise, these two legates were sent. But by whom? By religious men. From where? From the city of Limoges. To whom? To Blessed Stephen, certainly. For what purpose? To question him.

John was questioned in three ways: whether he was Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet. As you have heard, he denied all this out of humility, although he could truthfully have affirmed all these things of himself, if he had wished, according to the testimony of the Scriptures. For *Christ* means “anointed,” and he himself was anointed with invisible oil—that is, filled with the Holy Spirit—from his mother’s womb, according to Luke. This is the spiritual anointing of which it is said: “His anointing teaches you concerning all things” (1 John 2).

But the Lord Jesus, speaking of John to his disciples, says: “Elijah has already come, and they did to him whatever they wished; and, if you are willing to know it, John himself is Elijah” (Matt. 17). Elsewhere the Lord, speaking to the crowds, asked: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? I tell you: and more than a prophet” (Matt. 11).

Likewise, Blessed Stephen was asked whether he was a canon, monk, or hermit. As was said above, he avoided all this out of humility, lest he should appear before people, although he could most truthfully have professed all this of himself. For “canon” is interpreted as “regular,” and, insofar as he was able, he lived according to the rule of the Gospel, which is the head of all rules. A monk, moreover, is called one who is alone or guardian of himself; and he was alone because he had prepared for himself a place in spiritual solitude where he might dwell with God, so that he could truthfully say: “I fled afar off into solitude and remained there” (Ps. 54). This is the spiritual solitude of which it is said: “He shall sit alone and keep silence” (Lam. 3); this is the keeping of oneself from which one is called a monk, that is, guardian of oneself. Hence it is said: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4).

But most blessed Stephen sat alone—that is, rested—and became guardian of himself, because he retained for himself or his disciples absolutely nothing from all worldly goods except a little solitude, in which, indeed, he served God with his brothers. A hermit is so called from the wilderness; or he is an *anachorete*, that is, one withdrawn. [Col. 1024D] Who could ever be more withdrawn from the world than Blessed Stephen, who, as we have said, retained absolutely nothing for himself in the world? He had left everything whatsoever for God; he cultivated the wilderness, because there he faithfully performed an exceedingly rigorous penance day and night.

And just as it is said of John that, when they further asked who he was or what he said about himself—since he was not Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet—so that they might give an answer to those who had sent them, he said: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1), likewise these two legates asked Blessed Stephen, saying: “What then do you say about yourself?” (*ibid.*), since you confess that you are neither canon, monk, nor hermit, because the whole religious life is supported by these three orders or ranks. He answered them with the humblest reasoning, like John, as is written above: “Therefore, when we wished to depart from the deceitful world,” etc.

### XXXVII. Again, on his exaltation

Now therefore, beloved, observe and understand how divine goodness made its saint like greater and more worthy persons in word and deed. Yet we do not make him equal to John the Baptist, to whom Christ the Lord gave so great a testimony that among those born of women none greater than he has arisen (Matt. 11). Rather, it seems good to us that, by comparison with the deeds of so great a prophet, than whom, as is affirmed, none is greater, the deeds of Blessed Stephen, insofar as they can in some respect be compared with his, may shine more fully and brightly.

For we do not speak against the prophet’s dignity if we first set forth his sayings or deeds, and afterwards demonstrate Blessed Stephen, as far as we can, to be in some respect like him. For John the Evangelist says of the Lord Jesus Christ that, when he appears, “we shall be like him” (1 John 3).

Certainly, we know that John the Baptist was clothed in camel hair and that his food was wild honey and locusts. Stephen’s food, as we have said, was bread prepared with lye, or rye porridge, which he ate rarely; his clothing was an iron cuirass. Thus are shown the austerity of the prophet and the austerity of the holy confessor. Blessed be God in all things, who made both such men and could make them so. Amen.

### XXXVIII. On the perfection of his prayer and his confirmation of the disciples near the end

[Col. 1025C] On the eighth day after their departure, that is, on the day before the Nones of February, while he was as yet troubled by no pain, he began to withdraw from conversation about outward matters and to devote himself wholly to instructing his disciples and to prayer. For he knew through the Holy Spirit that the day of his death was near; and he wished to confirm them in the commitment to poverty for which they had come, and to obtain by his prayers before God that they might always wish to persevere in it.

While he was most fervently exhorting them to love God, cherish poverty, and observe the institutions which he had given them, it happened, by God’s providence, that they all stood before him with one accord and said:

### XXXIX. How the disciples complained to their spiritual father

[Col. 1025D]

“Most holy Father, while we were with you, God provided us with necessities for your sake; but after your death, how shall we be able to live? You take away all temporal things from us: from what shall we be sustained?”

To this the loving Father, most steadfast in the faith of Christ, replied:

### XL. His reply to the disciples

“I leave you God alone, to whom all things belong, and for whose love you left all things together with yourselves. If, loving poverty, you adhere to him steadfastly [Col. 1026A] and do not depart from this way of truth, he will grant you, according to his providence by which he wonderfully governs all things, whatever he knows to be expedient. But if—God forbid!—you withdraw from his love by loving temporal things, I do not wish to leave you that by which you may feed yourselves in fighting against him.

“Know for certain that I have completed almost fifty years in this solitude.

> [Note: At Col. 1025D, William of Dandina, in the *Life of Hugh of Lacerta*, says that Saint Stephen passed to heaven in approximately the forty-sixth year of his conversion.]

“Some of those years passed in great want, others in great abundance. Yet divine goodness always provided everything for me in such measure that in the time of want nothing necessary was lacking, nor in abundance did anything become superfluous. The same will happen to you if, avoiding all excess—for no one has condemned necessities [variant: *necessity has condemned no one*]—you persevere in this rule drawn from the Gospel.”

For four days he spoke to them much more fervently than usual about these matters and others written in the book of the Rule and in other volumes, so that they clearly recognized that the grace of speech had been doubled in him. On the fifth day, very early at dawn, a mortal pain seized his limbs. Then he had himself carried into the oratory, commanding the brothers to celebrate the divine office and earnestly to beseech the Lord by their prayers to receive his soul in peace.

### XLI. On the passing of Blessed Stephen the confessor

At length, Mass having ended, after holy anointing and after receiving the body and blood of the Lord, while the brothers wept and sang psalms, in the eightieth year of his age, in the order of the diaconate, on Friday, the sixth day before the Ides of February, saying, “Into your hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit” (Luke 23), [Col. 1026C] he happily passed to the Lord.

### XLII. Again, on his passing

Immediately the monks of Ambasiac—

> [Note: At Col. 1026D: In French, *Ambezac*, a village half a league from Muret, where there was a cell or priory dependent upon the monastery of Saint Augustine at Limoges.]

—with the chaplain of that same village and a great multitude of people, came knocking at the door of the cell, crying sorrowfully: “Good men, good men, do not conceal from us the death of Lord Stephen. Truly we know, truly we know, that our beloved Father is dead.”

But the porter, hearing this and wishing to keep them away from the burial, so that the brothers might worthily and most devoutly celebrate the obsequies of so great a funeral without disturbance, said to them, as though consoling them: “What is this? You say that he is dead? Rather, we believe him to be far better than usual.” [Col. 1026D]

### XLIII. The miracle of the boy of Ambasiac
To him the priest, who had come with the monks and the people, said: “Lord, we know well that he is dead. For in our village a certain boy, now at the point of death and having lost his speech since yesterday and the day before, was being watched by his mother as she awaited his end. Suddenly he burst out with these words: ‘I see a most radiant ladder, one end of which touches heaven and the other Muret; and many angels are descending by it in order to lead the soul of lord Stephen, most pleasing to God, [Col. 1027A] to glory.’ When his mother heard this, she was greatly astonished; leaving the house, she summoned me and the monks whom you see. Telling us the words which the boy had spoken, she led us into her house. When we came together before the boy and, at the woman’s prompting, asked him what he had said, both we and many others present heard the same thing from his mouth. He added: ‘Now I hear bells sounding everywhere through the churches and monasteries.’ Again he said: ‘This shall be the sign to you that I speak the truth: I shall now die and speak with you no more, but shall ascend with the most holy Father and the multitude of angels.’ Having said these things, he expired. Therefore we believe without doubt that what we say is true: namely, that the most glorious Father has departed.” O happy vision! And who could more fittingly bear witness to a virgin than a virgin? For both were virgins: the faithful servant of God, and the boy who saw and reported the vision. Moreover, another miracle powerfully shows how great this athlete of Christ’s merit was before God.

### XLIV. On the revelation of his death at the city of Tours and at Vézelay

For, by God’s wondrous ordering, his death was made known at Tours and Vézelay on the same day. These two places are so far distant from one another and from Muret that this could by no means have happened unless miraculously. Suitable witnesses to this fact were Limousin pilgrims who were there at that time for prayer, [Col. 1027C] and afterwards reported the certain truth of the matter to the brothers.

### XLV. How he revealed his death by night to a certain canon

[Note: [Col. 1027D] Saint Gaucher.]

On the following night he appeared in a vision to a certain canon, his familiar friend, adorned in rose-coloured clothing. Nor is it surprising that it was rose-coloured, since he had been a martyr of Christ. Rejoicing with him in his vision, the canon said: “My father, what is the reason for this splendid garment, which you have not worn until now?” He replied: “It is the sign of the Roman pontificate bestowed upon me by Christ.” To this the canon answered: “Blessed be God; for by such a pope the holy Church will rightly be governed.” Immediately on waking, he understood that Stephen had paid the debt of death. Rising swiftly, he chanted the entire divine office anew for the commendation [Col. 1027D] of his soul. For in mutual love they had agreed with one another that whichever of them lived longer should celebrate the other’s funeral rites.

### XLVI. On messengers sent to the Roman legates

Therefore, after the most holy body had been given burial, his disciples informed the aforementioned cardinals of his death by letter and messenger. When, at the council which they had convened at Chartres, the letters were delivered to them, they immediately announced his death to all. Before the whole assembly of archbishops, bishops, and other learned men, they spoke much good concerning his virtues and the purity of faith which they had investigated. [Col. 1028A] On hearing this, all present gave thanks to God; and, after the dismissal, the cardinals said: “We prayed for him; but now let us beseech him to pray for us to the Lord, because without doubt his holy merits can help us more than our intercessions can help him: for he lives with Christ in glory.”

### XLVII. On the election of lord Peter of Limoges as second prior

Thus bereft and orphaned of their devout Father, the brothers unanimously chose from among their community one man, Peter of Limoges, as their prior and spiritual Father. Formerly an honoured priest in the world, he was now, in religious life, an imitator of the paternal tradition and of the vow he had made, beloved and pleasing to God and men. [Col. 1028B] Under his government, while the Lord’s flock advanced in the growth of religious observance, the monks of Saint Augustine began to lay claim to the place of Muret, where they served God and had long served with their most holy Father.

### XLVIII. On the search for various places

But they preferred to surrender their cloak also to one who took away their tunic, rather than retain anything through which they might be drawn into lawsuits and the habit of litigation. They therefore took care diligently to seek another place where they might suitably establish the head of their religious order and serve God freely and peacefully. After assiduously traversing diverse places, but finding none suitable, they were at last enlightened by God and all unanimously adopted this wholesome plan: that the prior should celebrate Mass with all humility and devotion, and with all the brothers should supplicate the Lord from the depths of their hearts, that He might mercifully provide for them and not delay to show them what they sought. O wondrous clemency of God, worthy of everlasting remembrance! Envy may perhaps have contrived this lawsuit against God’s servants, but from the very circumstance by which it intended to oppress them, it enlarged them still more. For the immeasurable and ineffable providence of the heavenly dispensation had prepared for them from the foundation of the world a broader place, more suitable both in situation and in name for the observance of religious life; and they deserved to hear the name of that place from the divine voice itself.

### XLIX. On the revelation of the place of Grandmont

[Col. 1028D] While the prior, as had been agreed, was celebrating Mass, and while the *Agnus Dei* had been sung three times, and both he and all the other brothers were most fervently entreating the Lord, a certain heavenly voice was heard saying: “At Grandmont, at Grandmont, at Grandmont.” The prior and some of the brothers heard this most blessed voice. When Mass was ended, the prior asked the brothers whether they had heard the heavenly voice. One of them immediately said before all: “I heard it say three times, ‘At Grandmont,’” and another likewise testified. All then rejoiced abundantly, were consoled and greatly strengthened, and, because of the happiness of the glorious revelation, sought to marvel at, praise, and glorify the generosity of divine mercy. [Col. 1029A] And because at Grandmont Christ’s soldiers were always to fight against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, lest they lose heavenly things (Eph. VI), fittingly its name was heard there, where the victory won by Christ over the ancient enemy of the human race is celebrated daily.

### L. On the building of that place

They therefore went to the place disclosed by divine revelation—for it is quite near Muret [Note: [Col. 1029] Grandmont is only one league distant from Muret.]—and, by the command of Him to whom it belonged, built a church and dwellings with all speed. When these had been put together, however humbly, they returned to Muret, where some of the brothers had remained. Taking [Col. 1029B] the glorious body of their most holy Father, they carried it to Grandmont and, with few persons knowing, buried it beneath the presbytery before the altar.

### LI. Miracle concerning bread given to a certain knight

While the devout Father was still living, he distributed bread on the holy day of the Supper to Boso Dereses, a distinguished man. Boso kept it for a long time with reverence, gave it in pieces to many sick persons, and the divine power restored every one of them to health. By means of this one loaf many miracles were performed.

### LII. Miracle of a knight healed

Later a certain knight named Raymond de Plantadio had himself brought to that new planting of the Lord, so that he might deserve to be received into the brothers’ prayers. He had been so affected by the disease called paralysis that he had lost the use of one half of his body, and no limb on that side could function at all. Speaking to the prior as best he could, he asked to be taken into the church to the altar. One of his sons supported him on one side and the prior himself on the other, so that he was almost wholly carried. But after he had set his feet upon the stone beneath which the body of the most holy man lay buried before the altar, he cried aloud in a free voice: “Let me go; do not help me. For in this place where I have set my feet I have now been made whole. I tell you that some saint lies buried here, and that for his merits and love God has granted me health.” The prior rebuked him and strongly forbade both him and those [Col. 1029D] with him to say this. But the more insistently he prohibited it, the more strongly the man who had been healed cried out in joy: “Here I was made whole.” And he who, shortly before, could not proceed even from the church door to the altar without human assistance, now returned safe and sound to his own house through the aid of divine mercy alone. Thus he was made entirely well, so that thereafter no trace of that sickness remained in his body.

### LIII. On his disciple healed

Likewise, one of his disciples, who had lost his outward sight, prostrated himself and prayed at his tomb, and recovered his former vision.

### LIV. On the cloth which could not be burned

[Col. 1030A]

The cloth in which the sacred relics of his bones had been wrapped could not be burned, though the priest who had wrapped them in a more fitting cloth threw it into the fire once, twice, and again.

### LV. On the corrective words addressed to him by the second prior, after observing miracles following his death

Having observed these miracles, the prior feared that peace would be diminished for himself and the others, and that they would experience the sweetness of inward delight more slowly, if crowds of people, coming for the sake of miracles, frequented the place. He therefore came to the tomb of the man of God before the altar and, as a true lover of spiritual poverty, spoke to him as though he were living:

“Servant of God, you showed [Col. 1030B] us the way of poverty and taught us with all your effort to walk in it. Do you now wish, by your miracles, to call us back from the narrow and arduous way which leads to life to the broad and spacious way which leads to death? You preached solitude; do you now wish to gather markets and fairs in solitude? We are not led by curiosity to desire to see your miracles; we have sufficient faith in your holiness. Take care, therefore, henceforth not to perform miracles which exalt your holiness and destroy our humility. Do not provide for your own praise in such a way that you forget our salvation. This we command you; this we ask of your charity. But if you do otherwise, we tell you—and, by the obedience which we promised you, firmly declare—that we shall draw your bones out from there and scatter them in the river.”

Therefore, because pure faith and true charity love works more than signs, let us pass over the many miracles which, while he still lived, we heard from him and read had been performed, and which we see daily, with God cooperating, in the provision for all of us without possessions, livestock, or revenues. Let us instead follow him, with his help, through the example of holy conduct shown to us: him who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

### LVI. Miracle concerning Peter of Limoges, nephew of the second prior, healed through a vision

Peter of Limoges, a priest and revered brother of Grandmont, nephew of Peter of Limoges, second prior of Grandmont, flourished with the dove-like simplicity [Col. 1030D] and splendid bloom of virginity. He frequently overflowed with a stream of tears and diligently fulfilled the offices both of Martha and of Mary. By divine permission he began to suffer severely from illness. As he could scarcely endure the crushing weight of his bitter sickness, he humbly begged our most holy first Father Stephen, and his above-named patron, to beseech the divine clemency mercifully, so that it might temper his excessive pain and enable him somehow to bear it.

Then, through the grace of divine kindness, the sick man saw coming to him two radiant and glorious heavenly physicians: Stephen, servant of Christ, and Peter of Limoges, his paternal uncle. They brought a snow-white cloth, [Col. 1031A] with which they gently began to wipe his whole body from head to foot. As they did so, whatever they touched with the cloth was immediately healed. When this was done, they said: “He is wholly well.” Having said this, they vanished. Peter of Limoges, gladdened by the gift of perfect health, began affectionately to marvel at and praise the wondrous visitation of God and of the aforementioned Fathers. This miracle my faithful companion and most dear brother first disclosed to me himself, and afterwards, at my request, to the other brothers, with downcast and modest countenance.

### LVII. Likewise, another miracle concerning a certain woman

There was a man in the territory of Poitou with his wife, named Petronilla. They dearly loved our brothers of Alonia and very often gave them many good things, frequently visiting them and placing great faith in them and in blessed Stephen. They regarded these brothers as sons, because they remained barren and without offspring. Their custom was that each year, on the feast of blessed Stephen, they provided for the brothers for his love and honour; on that very day they came to them, bringing what was necessary. As they were travelling according to custom on his feast day, joyous and exultant with all their provisions, the woman rode trustfully upon a beast of burden. Suddenly the animal, by some unknown mishap, carelessly set down its foot and fell in a remarkable manner; immediately the woman fell [Col. 1031C] from the donkey and died.

Seeing that his wife was dead, her husband began to wail and cry out: “Alas for me, unhappy man! Alas for me, desolate! Alas for me, utterly abandoned! My wife is dead; I am alone and have no one to console or support me. O God, what shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I undertake? I do not know. If I return home, my neighbours will see me; they will hear me mourning and lamenting; and mocking enemies will say, ‘Where is your wife? Where has she remained? Where has she gone?’ And, sad and anxious, I shall be unable to answer them at all. If I remain here long, travellers on this road will encounter me and ask what has happened to me, and I shall be overcome with shame and distress. If I go on to the brothers, they will be distressed and grieve; their joy will turn to sorrow and their feast to sadness. And what shall I say? ‘My harp has been turned to mourning, and my organ to the voice of those who weep’ (Job XXX).”

While he wept, lamented thus, and was already despairing, he recalled that they were travelling for the honour and love of blessed Stephen. He therefore thought it good faithfully to seek his aid. Recovering his strength and coming to himself, he said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Through the merits of blessed Stephen, restore my wife to me, that I may praise you with her. Let the holiness of blessed Stephen now appear, for whose sake we your servants were making this journey. Lord, give us aid in this affliction; I beseech you, let her soul return to her body.” [Col. 1032A] And he said: “Holy Stephen of God, help me. Holy Stephen of God, hear me; pray for me. Let your glory and goodness now appear. If you can do anything, help me and restore my wife to me, because she has just died in your service.”

Having said these things, he approached his dead wife’s body with complete confidence and said: “Lady Petronilla, lady Petronilla, answer me. My lady, my beloved, my sister, answer me.” When he had said this, by divine ordinance she answered at his voice: “Alas, my lord, why were you troubled about me? Certainly I was well; I would have been much better.” Then her husband, filled with joy, took her up, raised her again, placed her upon the same beast of burden, and they came with joy and exultation to the place for which they were bound. [Col. 1032B] They told the brothers what had happened to them on the way, and together they praised the Lord, who saves those who hope in Him. Great joy came upon them that day and thereafter. A priest, venerable in life and conspicuous for the integrity of his conduct, truthfully related this marvellous sign.

### LVIII. Likewise, another miracle

We shall relate to your charity another miracle no less marvellous. In the time of lord Stephen of Liciac, the venerable fourth prior of Grandmont, a church was being built at Grandmont. One day, while workmen were carrying a large square stone upward to a height, they encountered Gerald, the master of the work. Unwillingly and unwittingly, through carelessness, they knocked him from the top of the scaffolding. He fell to the ground, was grievously crushed, and died; blood flowed from his eyes, ears, nostrils, and mouth. When the workmen saw this, they began to wail and cry loudly.

At that time lord Stephen was engaged in prayer. When he suddenly heard such a clamour, he was greatly alarmed. Rising at once from prayer, trembling and hurried, he went to the place where the covered body of the dead man lay lifeless. The masons and other workmen wept bitterly over him. Looking upon them, Stephen, being a man of great austerity and integrity, began to rebuke them, drive them from that place, and vehemently rail at them for weeping and crying out, saying: [Col. 1032D] “Go away, good men, impostors; flee from this place. This workman is not dead, but sleeping.” He drove them outside and shut the door.

Then, trusting and hoping in the goodness of the Lord and the merits of blessed Stephen, he called the brothers and gathered them in chapter, saying: “Brothers and my sons, today the enemy of humankind has attempted grievously to attack and wound us. Therefore I exhort and firmly command you to come barefoot, with groans and tears, before the altar of blessed Mary ever-virgin, and afterwards to the tomb of Saint Stephen.” They came with a terrible cry; they prayed and wept. Then Prior Stephen led them to the tomb of our blessed Father Stephen and began to rebuke him with a terrible voice, saying: [Col. 1033A] “Restore him—restore him quickly. Why have you afflicted us thus? Why have you allowed this? Quickly, quickly let your goodness, your power appear. If you can do anything—and we certainly believe that you can—help us, having pity on us.”

When he had completed the prayer, confident in God’s mercy, in the help of the Mother of God, and in blessed Stephen’s favour, he approached the dead man’s body with the brothers. Uncovering it, he took his right hand and, as if rebuking him, said: “Gerald, rise; rise, I say; work, and return to your work. Rise quickly, and do not delay.” At this command the man came to life, rose, and said: “Behold, lord, I am here, and I have and feel no ill at all.” The brothers who were present saw this, were afraid, wept for joy, praised [Col. 1033B] the Lord and blessed Mary, Mother of the Lord, and gave thanks to blessed Stephen.

Then the venerable Prior Stephen opened the door to the men whom he had driven out, saying: “Behold, your master Gerald remains healthy and sound. Return therefore with him to your work.” Seeing the man alive whom they had left dead, they were amazed and astonished, and began to cry out: “O Lord God, who alone doest great wonders, whose name is blessed for ever! For Thou dost not forsake those who seek Thee, O Lord. Behold, we see the great works and prodigies wrought through the glorious merits of blessed Stephen.” Then Stephen, the fourth prior and a man worthy of God, rebuked them, saying: “See that you keep silent; take care that none of you reveal this sign to anyone. For if you reveal it, vengeance shall be taken upon you.” Thus thereafter they completed the work with joy.

### LIX. Another miracle

We shall relate another miracle, no less wonderful, to the charity of all of you. In the time of this venerable prior there was at Grandmont a boy named Audoin, born of noble stock but given to excessive childishness. Because of his very tender youth, he was tolerated by the brothers. One day, wishing to play, the boy climbed onto a certain porch or gallery, laid himself across it, and began to swing himself to and fro. A certain priest named Guy, a religious man, saw him and feared that the boy might be endangered by such recklessness. He ran to rebuke him; but before he reached him, the boy fell by chance, was crushed, and died.

The priest ran to the spiritual Father and informed him. On hearing this, the latter hurried to the boy and found him already dead. Taking him in his arms, he carried him to the tomb of blessed Stephen, which at that time was kept in the cloister, and said: “Behold, Stephen, most loving man, behold your son; behold your disciple: as you see, he is now dead. Restore him to us—restore him—or certainly I shall cast you out of this place. See that you do not delay or linger. You see that we are sorrowful, afflicted, and distressed. Give us consolation and [Col. 1034A] honour to your name.” Without delay, after the prayer had been made, the youth recovered life. The prior rejoiced with the brothers because the young man had returned to life; then the Lord was praised and blessed Stephen extolled.

### LX. Likewise, another miracle

At the same time the brothers were working in the forest. While they were cutting timber, they needed to fell a tree in another direction; it trapped a certain brother named John. The aforementioned prior saw this, as he happened to be speaking there with a certain religious man. The brother was held fast by the tree, and his hand with his arm was being crushed. The brothers, together with the prior, cried: “What are you doing, blessed Stephen? Hasten to help this your disciple, who is at the point of death.” [Col. 1034B] When they had said this, he was immediately freed; they praised the Lord and gave thanks to blessed Stephen.

### LXI. Likewise, another miracle

In the Limousin territory, near our house of Puy-Gisbert, there was a man who earnestly loved the aforesaid house and bestowed many benefits upon the brothers living there. He had an aged mother, worn out by the multitude of her days. One day the old woman was seized by a fever. Her son then said to her: “Mother, command that I go to the priest, so that you may receive from his hand the body and blood of the Lord.” His mother replied: “Certainly, my son.”

The man went to the priest and brought him back with him. [Col. 1034C] When they arrived, they found her already dead. Then the priest said to him: “You see that your mother is dead and that my exhortation can profit her nothing. Prepare what you must do, and tomorrow, God willing, I shall return to you.” Having said this, the priest went away. The man began to be sorrowful and downcast because his mother had died without receiving Christ’s body and blood and without confession.

He then anxiously began to invoke the Lord’s name and to await the aid of blessed Stephen throughout that whole night. After doing this for a long time, he confidently approached his mother’s body and began to cry out with great force: “O mother! O mother!” She answered him: “What do you want, my son? Why have you disturbed me? Certainly I was well.” Her son, rejoicing and exulting, said to her: “O good mother, if it pleases you, I shall go again to the priest, that he may give you the body and blood of the Lord.” She replied: “Let your will be done.”

The man again went to the aforesaid priest, who brought the aged woman the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. After first making confession, she received communion and immediately died again. All who were present rejoiced, praised the Lord’s name, and magnified the merits of blessed Stephen, in whose honour, by God’s will, such a sign occurred. Every year, in memory and reverence of so great a miracle, this man was accustomed to bring a candle to the aforesaid house on Saint Stephen’s feast. Clerics and lay brothers who saw and heard these things [Col. 1035A] reported them to us truthfully.

### LXII. Likewise, another miracle

At a certain time lord Stephen of Liciac, the venerable fourth prior, was ill. At that time the relics of blessed Stephen’s body were hidden in a wooden vessel, unknown to very many of the brothers. As he was suffering severely from fever, he ordered that they should be placed in a stone sarcophagus. When it had been prepared, he commanded that the relics be brought before him, so that they might be laid away while he watched. He himself was severely afflicted by feverish pain. When the relics had been brought before him, to be honourably buried thenceforth in another vessel, the venerable prior was suddenly and entirely freed from the fever.

When the aforesaid lord prior perceived this, he cried out and said: “Why have you done this? I certainly thought that by occasion of this sickness you now wished truly to take me with you before Christ’s tribunal; and you have presumed to give me what I did not want. Know surely that henceforth I am ungrateful to you. You have prolonged what I desired, and given what I did not want. I do not care for your miracles; rather, I rejoice more in the works of your holiness. The unbelieving, weak, and sick need signs and wonders; the faithful, righteous, and firm in faith have no need of them. This sign would have been salutary for me if you had presented me before the Lord in the kingdom of heaven.” After this sign we shall tell another miracle, marvellous to relate.

### LXIII. Likewise, another miracle

[Col. 1035C]

A certain knight of Gascony, a kinsman of Gaillarda, wife of Pons, formerly lord of Bainac, was captured by William de Gordun in a military expedition. He was taken to the town of Domme and placed in prison in the house of a knight named Gerald. There he was heavily weighed down with chains, fetters, manacles, and iron weights. The prison doors and windows were shut, and he was grievously afflicted within. Tormented with severe pain and already despairing of his life, he hastened to have recourse to spiritual arms: he invoked the Lord’s name and blessed Stephen, earnestly begging with tears in every way that he might deign to free and hear him. [Col. 1035D] Thus constant in prayer, he never ceased day or night to call upon him.

What more need be said? Salvation is promised by the Lord to the one who perseveres. For the Gospel says: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. X). While this knight persevered in prayer and continually invoked the Lord’s name, asking that through love of blessed Stephen He might deign to grant him help from heaven, blessed Stephen was sent to him from above as a helper.

One night, while he was praying fervently and seeking help from blessed Stephen with loud cries, he was suddenly overcome by sleep and became as though dead. But blessed Stephen suddenly shook him and asked why he tormented him with such loud cries. When the knight, astonished, heard this, he said, as though awakening [Col. 1036A] from a heavy sleep: “Who are you, lord?” He replied: “I am Stephen, whom you have not ceased to invoke; and I have come here for this purpose, to attend to your deliverance.” The knight awoke and began to beg him more earnestly to deign to free him completely.

And what happened? The manacles fell from his arms, and one foot was freed from the fetters. Feeling himself free, he went to the prison door and found it locked. He then turned to the window, which he found open. Considering the depth of the valley above which that house stood, he feared to leap down. But afterwards, strengthened by the divine Spirit and returning to himself, he said: “It is better for me to die thus than to be shut up in prison again.” Immediately, trusting in the Lord’s goodness and blessed Stephen’s merits, [Col. 1036B] he made the leap and, through God’s mercy, escaped unharmed.

A certain young man met him and subsequently became his travelling companion. Before long they came to the Dordogne River and found a boat prepared for them by the Lord. Having crossed the river, they came by a successful journey to our house at Veyrassac. As they knocked at the gates, the brothers arose, according to custom, for matins. It was then made known to them that the knight had been freed by the Lord through blessed Stephen. The brothers came out to meet him with congratulations and brought him into the church. The knight told them what had happened and how God had wonderfully delivered him through blessed Stephen. The brothers therefore rejoiced at the miracle, sang praises, and gave thanks to the Lord. [Col. 1036C] Afterwards they led him to the guesthouse, where he remained for three days. Those who saw these things related them faithfully and truthfully to us.

### LXIV. Likewise, another miracle

At another time, a multitude of evildoers, with their leader named Lupard, entered the territory of the bishopric of Limoges to ravage it. What can I say? Men were captured, wives violated, and their children slaughtered. Thus, because their sins demanded it, the castle of Peyrat was then by chance captured by them. Among others, five men were seized and confined in an underground cave. Two of these men greatly loved blessed Stephen [Col. 1036D] and our order. As they were shut in by the evildoers, tightly bound with stocks and chains, and constantly guarded, they began to seek Saint Stephen’s favour.

One was named Peter, a familiar associate and servant of one of the houses of this order, called Bonavallis or Serra; the other was called Gerald de Montellio. These two, with the other three, fervently prayed to the Lord that, through the merits of blessed Stephen, He might deign to free them from their enemies’ hands. As they prayed most fervently from the heart, behold, blessed Stephen appeared to them in splendour and said: “Rise, do not be afraid, and follow me.” They answered: “Who are you, lord?” He said: “I am Stephen, [Col. 1037A] first shepherd of the Order of Grandmont.” Then, for joy, they began to weep and said: “O lord, O shepherd of the Most High, free us from these most cruel enemies of ours.” Then, taking them firmly, he led them through the midst of the camp in the sight of all; no one harmed, or could harm, any of them. Thus, made free through God’s mercy, they marvellously escaped through blessed Stephen.

### LXV. Likewise, another miracle

Again we shall tell another wondrous sign. There was a man in the Limousin territory named Reginald, who greatly loved blessed Stephen, lord Hugh, his other disciples, and our whole order. It was his custom each year to visit the house of Grandmont, [Col. 1037B] the house of Muret, and the house of La Plaine. Once, after he had visited the aforementioned places with all diligence and with his own wife, he was returning to the village in which he lived when he saw that village suddenly catch fire. Seeing it, he began to cry out: “O God, what shall I do? I am weary from the journey and cannot defend my house from this fire. Help me today, Lord. Remember that I love blessed Stephen, his order, and his disciples, from visiting whom I have now returned. Therefore, my Lord, I beseech you by your mercy that, for love of blessed Stephen and through his merits, You may deign at this hour to deliver my house with all its furnishings [Col. 1037C] from the fire-spewing flames.”

When he had completed the prayer, the fire never dared to harm that house, not even one straw. The people of the village also testified that, when the fire burned the houses adjoining that man’s house, it pursued and burned the straws of the other houses but wholly avoided, as though in fear, the thatch of that man’s house. When those standing by, both priests and other people, saw this, they praised the Lord, who through blessed Stephen’s merits had performed so great a miracle before them. Afterwards Reginald, the priests, and many others related this sign to the brothers of Entrefis and to the priest Geoffrey, who reported it to us truthfully and gladly. Later this man took the habit [Col. 1037D] of this order and persevered faithfully in it to the end, as we ourselves saw and knew.

### LXVI. Likewise, another miracle

In the time of the venerable Prior Peter Bernard, when the general chapter was assembled at Grandmont, the translation of the body of most blessed Stephen was celebrated in the presence of lord Gerald, bishop of Limoges, on the day after the feast of the Forerunner and Herald of the Lord and Saviour. There was a brother there named William, grievously afflicted by extreme deafness in both ears. When he saw the saint of God being transferred from the cloister to the church by the aforesaid prior and the whole community, he quickly approached the sarcophagus and found shoes in the sarcophagus of blessed Stephen. Taking them, he began to put his fingers [Col. 1038A] inside the shoes, draw out whatever he could find, and then place it in his ears. After doing this for a long time, full of good faith and most certain hope, he swiftly recovered the hearing that he had lost; and afterwards he himself related the matter in truthful speech.

### LXVII. Likewise, another miracle
Moreover, we have made known to your charity another miracle that must by no means be passed over in silence, which occurred in the time of Lord William, sixth prior of Grandmont, in the Gallic city of Sens. There was there a canon named Genulf, who loved our Order and Blessed Stephen with good faith and goodwill, and had faithfully caused the buildings of a certain house of our Order to be constructed at his own expense.
