Now when that city, as aforesaid, was being grievously consumed by a most violent fire [Col. 1038B], he entered his own house, full of faith and in no way doubting the mercy of God and the aid of Blessed Stephen, saying: “Now, I beseech you, Lord God, let the power and holiness of Blessed Stephen, first Father of the Order of Grandmont, appear, so that for love of him you may defend my house and everything within it, lest they be consumed by this fire; otherwise I shall be burned with it.”

The man stood trembling, and his servants said to him: “My lord, withdraw! The whole city is already catching fire and burning, and the flames are striving from every side to lick at this house; it certainly cannot escape so great a conflagration without being burned. At least provide safety and assistance for your own person, which is noble and worthy of every honor.” [Col. 1038C]

To them he said: “Now by this I shall know whether the Order of Grandmont is holy, whether the wonderful and astounding deeds of Saint Stephen which I have heard are true, and whether those things which I have gladly offered in that Order for love of him are pleasing to the Lord.”

And what more need be said? That city was devastated by the fire and utterly destroyed beyond belief; but the house of this canon alone remained unharmed and unburned, by divine ordinance and through the aid of Blessed Stephen. Thus indeed divine goodness made known its servant far and wide by many and countless proofs of miraculous signs.

### LXVIII. Another miracle

A certain woman presented eggs to the gracious Father. At his command she set them before him and before many others, both men and women, who had come to him for spiritual edification. [Col. 1038D] Immediately the holy man, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, separated some from the others with a rod and said to the woman: “If it pleases you, we shall keep these; but take those back home.”

The woman said: “Lord, do not reject this small gift from my poverty.”

He replied: “If you would not take it ill, I would explain to you the reason for this.”

She said: “Father, I shall not take it badly; indeed, I beg you to deign to make it known to me.”

He added: “Because these eggs are from your own hen, but those are from another’s; therefore we do not wish to keep them.”

At once she blushed and was astonished; she prostrated herself before him and humbly confessed her own fault before all present, affirming that his word was true. [Col. 1039A] Seeing and hearing these things, all who were present were greatly amazed and began to praise the Lord.

### LXIX. Another miracle

A certain woman, devoutly visiting the servant of God, said to him: “Father, I offer you this bread.”

He immediately asked her where she had obtained the bread. She replied: “I acquired it by my honest labor. For after my field had been stripped by harvest, I carefully gathered the ears which remained, and made this bread from them.”

Then the bread was divided and was found to appear bloody, causing the woman the greatest astonishment and horror. At once the spiritual man said to the stunned woman: “Because you presumed to take for yourself the remnants of the harvest which the divine law grants to the poor, therefore the just Judge has deigned to perform such a miracle for your terror and correction, and for that of others.” [Col. 1039B]

### LXX. Another

When the brothers of Muret, at the earnest request of Brother Amelius of La Croisille-Fontcrose, steward there, sent him by Giraud David the humble and precious table of the reverend Father—

> [Note: [Col. 1039] In the diocese of Poitiers, attached to the priory of La Quarte.]

—the messenger himself, out of faith and devotion, cut off a piece of the table and kept it for a long time as a relic. He often scraped a little from the wood, put it into water, and gave it to many fever sufferers to drink; and by God’s grace he immediately cured them all. He himself was also cured of fever by the same remedy.

Meanwhile it happened that the house at Orca, where the wood was, together with everything in it, was burned; but divine power wholly protected the wood, the linen cloth, and the white skin in which it was wrapped from the fire. [Col. 1039C] The greatness of this miracle gave Giraud David much comfort over the loss of his possessions.

But although a wondrous life shines with miracles, and although that outstanding hermit—than whom, according to the Lord’s testimony, none greater has arisen among those born of women—is read to have performed few or no miracles, one should not dwell excessively upon or glory in such things. For when his disciples gloried in the splendor of signs, the Master of humility said: “Do not rejoice because the spirits are subject to you; rather rejoice because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X). [Col. 1039D]

With all our strength we beseech the supreme King that, through the merits and prayers of so great a Father of ours, he may make us perpetual sharers in his blessedness. Amen.

### LXXI. Concerning a knight cured of an inextinguishable fire

In the territory of Limoges there was a knight, distinguished indeed by birth but not greatly resplendent in uprightness of conduct. It happened that, by divine judgment, he was scourged by an incurable disease: namely, an inextinguishable fire called “infernal.” This inextinguishable fire, because it did not cease until it had wholly consumed the material laid beneath it, mercilessly consumed the aforesaid knight’s foot—its flesh together with its bones—without any remedy intervening. [Col. 1040A]

The knight consulted many physicians and spent very much upon them, but could find no healing remedy for himself. At last he turned to the Lord, manifesting outwardly the inward contrition of his heart through abundant tears and the performance of good works. He had himself carried to the house of Grandmont, seeking not human but divine counsel and assistance.

Stephen of Liciac, then prior of that house, was summoned. The knight humbly prostrated himself at his feet, showed him the intolerable pain of his body, and indicated that he suffered no less in his heart, uttering words of great humility and weeping profusely, believing without doubt that he was so grievously scourged by the Lord because of his sins. [Col. 1040B]

When he saw this, the venerable Father was astonished and asked the knight what he sought. The knight humbly and tearfully replied that he sought recovery of health. The prior said: “Brother, we are not physicians, nor are we accustomed to provide any remedy of bodily medicine, either for ourselves or for others.”

The knight said: “Lord, deprived alike of human counsel and assistance, I flee to spiritual aid, asking that the most holy relics of the blessed man Stephen the confessor may mercifully be shown to me, the most wretched sinner among all wretches. For I believe that through the merit of his prayers, divine grace favoring me, I shall be delivered from this intolerable burning.”

But the prior, fearing that quiet would be diminished for himself and the other brothers and that they would experience less readily the sweetness of inner delight if crowds of people should frequently visit that place on account of miracles—he had often rebuked the blessed man severely, as though speaking to a living person, concerning miracles that he performed, threatening to have his bones taken out and thrown into the river unless he ceased from miracles—said to the knight: [Col. 1040C] “Brother, the bones of the blessed man Lord Stephen can scarcely, if ever, be seen by anyone. But go to other saints, at whose shrines miracles occur very frequently; and we shall gladly pray for you, that the Lord may grant what he knows to be necessary for you.”

The knight replied that he would by no means leave until the prior at least granted him permission to approach the tomb of Blessed Stephen. At length, overcome by the prayers of the knight and his companions, the prior granted him leave to approach the burial place of the most blessed man. [Col. 1040D]

Then the knight rejoiced exceedingly. Conceiving good hope of a future remedy, he was carried as quickly as possible by his companions’ hands to the tomb of the blessed man. Immediately he prostrated himself humbly before the tomb and prayed with tears and great devotion, hoping in the Lord that, through the merits of his servant whose body rested there, he might grant him a remedy for his intolerable pain and healing for his ulcer. Washing with water the stone beneath which the body of the most blessed man was buried, he poured that same water upon the ulcer. [Col. 1041A] At once the fire was extinguished, and the knight was healed both of the ulcer and the pain. He who previously could not go anywhere without human assistance now returned healthy and whole to his own home, aided solely by divine mercy. Thus restored to health, he thereafter persevered steadfastly until the end in devotion to God’s service and works of piety.

### LXXII. Another miracle

We shall relate to your charity yet another miracle that must not be passed over in silence, which miraculously occurred during his lifetime. One day, as a certain member of his household was, according to custom, bringing him bread from a certain village, he happened to encounter robbers lying in wait in the wood through which he was travelling, intending evil. [Col. 1041B]

When they saw the man leading a beast burdened with bread, they rejoiced greatly. Taking the bread from the animal, they placed it on the ground in order to refresh themselves with it. When the household servant saw this, he began to rebuke them, saying: “What is this that you are doing, wicked and perverse men? I am carrying this bread, which you violently and unjustly seize, to the blessed man Stephen. Therefore, on behalf of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the authority of his goodness, I forbid you to presume henceforth to touch this bread. If you do so, know for certain that you will without delay incur the wrath and indignation of almighty God.”

This man was faithful and had great confidence in the Lord and in Blessed Stephen. [Col. 1041C] The thieves said to him mockingly: “Even if God himself were here in person, we cannot leave this bread without eating it. Since yesterday and the day before, we have neither eaten nor drunk; we are tormented by incomparable hunger.”

And what more need be said? They drew their swords from their scabbards and wished to attack the bread and cut it into pieces, but they could not do so at all. Divine power was certainly present: it hardened that bread so greatly and rendered those robbers so weak that they could in no way cut or break it.

Seeing the miracles that were happening, the household servant began to cry out: “O wretches! O evildoers! Did I not tell you? I certainly now fear for you, lest fire come down from heaven [Col. 1041D] and consume you all. You did not believe me when I told you that this man to whom I carry this bread is good and holy. And since you were unbelieving, almighty God has willed in this event to show you, though unworthy, his holiness.”

The robbers, astonished and trembling, said to him: “We certainly know that we have sinned grievously. Therefore we repent before you with our whole heart. Lead us to the servant of God Stephen, so that through his merciful prayers we may deserve to obtain from God forgiveness for so great an offence.”

When the household servant saw that they repented from their whole heart, he encouraged them and led them to the man of God, drawing them after him with ropes like captives and wretches. When they came to the gate of the cell of the man of God, [Col. 1042A] he knocked and told the gatekeeper what had happened to him on the road. Then he entered with the robbers before the man of God, presented them to him, and recounted in order what had occurred.

On hearing this, the man of God summoned the gatekeeper and said: “Bring us some of the loaves that were taken from us.” Meanwhile the robbers, prostrate at his feet, begged forgiveness from him, asking him to pray to almighty God for them that he might pardon this offence. When the gatekeeper came with the loaves, the servant of God took them and, as if smiling, began to break them and offer them to the robbers, saying: “Now see, my children, how weak you were, since, as you claim, you could not break these fresh loaves.”

Nevertheless they sought pardon from him ever more urgently, with tears and all humility. [Col. 1042B] Being most gentle toward all, he spoke kindly to them, comforted them, and admonished them not to presume to do such things again, but to abandon the wicked business of robbery and plunder to which they had been devoted. Thus he dismissed them.

### LXXIII. Another miracle

At the same time, a man from Mont Cuculli, named Gerald, came to him. His wife had lain crippled in bed for a long time. He said to the man of God Stephen: “Servant of God, what am I to do? My wife is daily afflicted by grave illness, and I have not the means even to support her for one day. Excessive poverty distresses and confines me. Because of her grave illness, I cannot leave her even for an hour of the day in order to support both myself and her by any work. Therefore my neighbors often and persistently urge me to take her to Mont-Maurillien, so that there in the house of the poor she may have food and covering.” [Col. 1042C]

On hearing this, the man of God asked whether he had joined her to himself in lawful marriage, and what he had promised her in the hand of his chaplain when he took her as wife.

Sighing, the man replied: “Certainly, my lord, I, wretched and grieved, promised her in good faith that I would, to the extent of my strength, support her whether healthy or sick. Up to the present I have taken care to fulfill this faithfully as far as I could; but henceforth I shall be unable to do so, because want and poverty consume me.”

Blessed Stephen said to him: “See, son, lest, oppressed by any want, you presume to abandon her. Rather, hasten faithfully and truly to fulfill what you promised; otherwise you will by no means be able to attain eternal life. Consider carefully: if such illness afflicted you, would you wish her to abandon you? Hear what the Lord commanded in the Gospel: ‘What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another’ (Tobit IV). [Col. 1042D] Therefore take courage and be strong. For the Lord is the comforter and sustainer of the poor and the fatherless, and he will provide you with what is necessary, provided that you remain in truth and justice.”

After saying these and similar things to the man, he said: “Wait a little, until I return to you.” Entering the house, he brought him a loaf of bread and one coin, placed it in the man’s hand, and said to him: “Be at peace; go, and provide for your wife from this bread and this coin as long as it lasts. When it fails, return confidently to us.”

Thus he dismissed him. Returning to his own home, the man joyfully and exultantly told his wife what the man of God had said to him. When he opened the hand in which Blessed Stephen had placed one coin, the coin immediately multiplied so that his hand could in no way contain it. Coins fell from every side of his hand and multiplied before their eyes. [Col. 1043A]

Astonished and amazed, they praised the Lord’s name. As long as the woman lived, those coins never failed, but always supplied their need through the Lord’s bounty, just as is read concerning Elijah, sent to the widow of Zarephath, whose jar of flour did not fail and whose flask of oil was not diminished (III Kings XVII). After Blessed Stephen’s death, the man later recounted the whole matter faithfully and truthfully to the brothers at Muret, some of whom remain alive.

### LXXIV. Concerning the vision seen at Muret by Lord Hugh de Lacerta

One day, therefore, Blessed Hugh, disciple of Blessed Stephen the confessor, had come from Grandmont to visit his shepherd, Stephen of Liciac. Setting out with his companion Guy de Miliac and descending toward our house at Castenat, it happened that the bell of the church at Muret was rung by the brothers for Mass. [Col. 1043C]

Hearing it, the aforesaid Hugh said to his companion Guy: “Brother, let us enter the house at Muret, so that, God willing, we may attend the solemn celebration of Mass.”

He replied: “I am ready.”

Turning aside to that place, they entered in all haste the house of prayer and place of divine vision. The priest of that cell was alone with a single assistant, preparing himself for the office of Mass. When the aforesaid Hugh rose from prayer and attentively lifted his eyes toward the altar and the ministers of the altar, he suddenly saw Saint Stephen, clothed and radiant in deaconal vestments, ministering with all devotion and reverence at the altar and to the priest like a deacon. He also seemed to hear him proclaim the Gospel and afterward, as is the deacon’s custom, present the offering to the priest. [Col. 1043D]

At this sight, the aforesaid man of God Hugh became joyful, was bathed in tears, illumined by heavenly light, and rejoiced at so great a vision. In order that he might have most certain witnesses of this very famous vision and glorious visitation, he called one of the brothers who were in the church and asked him how many, or what kind of, ministers of the altar there were.

The brother replied: “Lord, there are only two: the priest alone with one assistant.”

After that brother had returned to his place, the same Blessed Hugh called another and asked him again and again the same question. That brother said to him: “Certainly, my lord, I see no one there except the priest alone with his companion.” [Col. 1044A]

He did all this so that he might be more readily believed when he later disclosed this famous vision to someone. For it is written in the divine law: “Every word is established by the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy XIX).

When these things had been done and the sacred solemnities of Mass had been duly and reverently conducted, Saint Stephen, the eminent confessor, shepherd and first Father of the Order of Grandmont, did not wish to dismiss without greeting the disciple whom he had greatly loved and whom he had illumined from heaven by so great and such a vision or visitation. Turning toward him with a cheerful countenance and joyful face, smiling upon him, he stretched out his hands and immediately disappeared.

We believe that by this stretching out of his hands the man of God Stephen summoned his disciple to the heavenly kingdom; for at that same time the most faithful Hugh faithfully departed to Christ. After leaving that place, he continued on his way with the aforesaid companion, joyful and rejoicing, comforted by such consolation and vision. [Col. 1044B]

Then Brother Guy addressed him as follows: “Tell me, I beseech you, my Father, you who are accustomed to reveal much to many, and who long ago deigned to embrace me, unworthy as I am, with much familiarity and love: what is this that you saw today? I certainly believe that the Lord deigned to reveal something to you. Take care, therefore, most loving Father, that your kindness does not strive to hide so great a vision from me, an unworthy sinner.”

He replied: “Certainly you do not know what you ask or what you seek from me. Go on quickly, and let us walk together. Cease from this foolishness; do not inquire nor think highly of what is not fitting.”

The brother again added: “I beg you, Father, do not delay, but disclose to me this vision which you saw. For while I was with you in church, I observed that you were more attentive than usual to the service of the altar. Why do you wish to conceal God’s gift and grace? For God’s love, tell me what and what kind of vision you saw.” [Col. 1044C]

When that most loving Father heard these and similar things from the brother, he charged him, saying: “By the power of the Holy Spirit, and at the peril of your soul, I forbid your brotherhood to presume to disclose to anyone, while I live, this vision whose explanation you ask of me.”

The other replied: “I promise you, by the salvation of my soul, that I shall reveal it to no one while you live.”

Afterwards that most holy Father faithfully disclosed to him in order the vision that he had seen, and added: “I know that I shall soon depart from the prison of my body and enter upon the way of all flesh, because my Master has called me to the wedding feast of the spotless Lamb, that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life [Col. 1045A] and be filled from the breasts of his consolation.”

After the death of the aforesaid Lord Hugh, Brother Guy took care to reveal this vision to the brothers. [Col. 1046A]

[Col. 1045]

## GERALD, BY THE GRACE OF GOD, SEVENTH PRIOR OF GRANDMONT

### I. Concerning the revelation of Blessed Stephen

For a long time after the death of Blessed Stephen, confessor of Christ, the Order of Grandmont had, by the bounty of divine grace, continued multiplied among the peoples in religious observance, holiness, and goodness, enjoying great peace, charity, honor, and no small prosperity. But in the last year of the pontificate of Lucius III, while Philip was reigning as king of the Franks and Henry as king of the English, a grave dissension arose in our Order itself, through our sins demanding it, God permitting it, and the enemy of humankind instigating it. [Col. 1045B]

Necessity therefore compelled the brothers, disputing among themselves, to hasten to the papal court. Alas, alas—sorrow upon sorrow! Those who had long been peaceful now became discordant; those who had loved one another became enemies; those who excelled in the power of holiness were reduced to disgrace and mockery by many.

What shall I say? Nearly all the friends of the Order wept, mourned, lamented, and were distressed because they saw and heard false speakers and enemies of truth uttering, chattering, and clamoring impious words against religious observance and brotherly charity. They feared that the Order would be overthrown, changed, or abandoned, when they saw its condition disturbed on every side, brothers running about and wandering through the world, some unwillingly and others willingly. The unwilling defended the Order; the willing acted against it.

And what more need be said? “The stones of the sanctuary were scattered at the head of every street. Those who were accustomed to feed on saffron embraced dung” (Lamentations IV). [Col. 1045C] Brotherly charity turned into hatred, truth into falsehood, goodness into weariness, holiness into reproach, sobriety into derision, humility into contempt, religious observance into loss, obedience into nothingness—almost every virtue into vice.

What then? The citizens of Jerusalem became citizens of Babylon; spiritual persons became fleshly, sensual, bestial persons. Against such persons the Apostle says: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not human beings? Are you not fleshly, walking according to man?” (I Corinthians III).

Who, I ask, could see and hear such things without ceasing from weeping, groaning, sobbing, sighing, and tears? O good Lord Jesus! O most merciful Redeemer of humankind! O eternal Shepherd! O most merciful Father! O most loving Savior! Why did you endure this? Why did you permit it? Why did you dispose that it should happen thus: that your people should be so wickedly slain by the devil’s poison, your house confounded, religious observance disturbed, and the venerable Order so treated and mocked, turned to loss and disgrace? [Col. 1045D]

Where, my Lord, where is your protection? Where is your promise: “I will not leave you orphaned” (John XIV)? [Col. 1046A] Why did you not visit us? Why did you not oppose our crimes? Why did you not blot out our wrongdoings? Alas, my Lord! Here understanding fails; here thought fails; here we have become ignorant; here we acknowledge our guilt; here we confess our sin. Therefore we ask forgiveness; mercifully and suppliantly we beseech from you, Lord, mercy and pardon.

Pardon, Lord, because you are powerful, merciful, gracious, gentle, devout, and kind; you who have mercy upon all and hate nothing that you have made, Lord, overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance. Spare, Lord, spare your people, and do not give your inheritance over to destruction (Joel II). Show mercy to your servants. Visit us with your salvation (Psalm CV), and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people (Exodus XXXII). If, Lord, we have spoken presumptuously in saying these things, “Do not remember our former iniquities; let your mercies swiftly come before us, for we have become exceedingly poor. Help us, O God of our salvation, and for the glory of your name, Lord, deliver us; be gracious to our sins for the sake of your name” (Psalm LXXVIII). [Col. 1046B]

Perhaps because of our iniquity and crime this partial blindness, this such temptation, has fallen upon your people: for some, as a test; for others, unto destruction—that is, for the good, unto good; but for the evil, unto evil. Or perhaps this occurred so that those who lay hidden in the Order, covering themselves by artful pretense beneath a sheep’s skin, might be recognized, and thus avoided, rejected, and despised; or so that those not predestined to be saved within the Order might depart; or so that the Order, through your mercy, might regain the peace and concord or the spiritual goods that it had lost.

Therefore, Lord, hear the voice of our supplication and attend to our prayers. You who opened the eyes of Hagar, your handmaid, open the eyes of our hearts and deign to reveal to us, your servants, what your holy will toward us may be, so that we may praise your name unceasingly, which is blessed for ever and ever. Amen. [Col. 1046D]

### II. Another notice to the brothers

Therefore, most beloved, hearing these things, be pierced with compunction; do not sin or be cast down. Rather, recall how almighty God, in a wondrous and inestimable manner, permitted the land of Jerusalem, at the time when these things happened among us, to be delivered into the hands of foreigners, and his people to be killed, captured, and tortured by them.

These things are found very often in the divine books: how the Father of mercies has allowed his own to suffer persecutions and tribulations from the beginning of the world until today. [Col. 1047A] What happened to righteous Noah? Did he not suffer the affliction of the flood? Did not faithful Abraham become an exile? Was not Moses, the gentlest of men, pursued by Pharaoh? Was not Israel, God’s people, persecuted by Pharaoh himself and the Egyptians? What did righteous David, whom the Lord of all found according to his own heart, suffer from wicked Saul? Again and again, what did the children of Israel suffer from Nebuchadnezzar and from the others by whom they were so often carried captive? What did the holy patriarchs suffer? What the prophets? What did the holy apostles, holy martyrs, and doctors of the holy Church suffer from unbelievers?

Recall the Lord himself of patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all the other faithful: in what manner he suffered for all, and from whom. Why should it be surprising, if he and his own suffered such great things, that he has allowed us to be afflicted—us who are sinners, fragile, bearing earthen vessels, and therefore weak and feeble? [Col. 1047B]

Do not then be astonished that it happened thus, because our Lord God permitted it so; and it is wonderful in our eyes. For from him comes every good gift and every perfect present. As you have heard, he allows his own in this world to be afflicted, tortured, and tormented, so that afterward they may be comforted, visited, rewarded, crowned, and glorified by him.

Therefore the Apostle says: “If we have been companions in sufferings, we shall also be companions in consolation” (II Corinthians I). And elsewhere: “Tribulation works patience; patience, tested character; tested character, hope; and hope does not disappoint,” etc. (Romans V). And elsewhere: “What the file is to iron, the furnace to gold, and the flail to grain, tribulation is to the righteous.”

Therefore, most beloved, endure patiently persecutions if they come, temptations if they assail you, tribulations if they meet you, necessities if they arise, saying with most blessed Job: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord,” etc. (Job I). [Col. 1047C] Comfort one another, then, with these words, and hear the apostle Peter saying: “If you suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed” (I Peter III).

Now act courageously; let your hearts be strengthened; and wait for the Lord, because he who comes will come and will not delay. Take care, therefore, that there be no more schisms among you. Choose the better spiritual gifts, for, as the Apostle says, “the servant of God ought not to quarrel” (II Timothy II). Rather, may there always and continually be peace, patience, joy, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, unfeigned charity, and fruitful humility. Adorned fittingly with these virtues, may you shine as lights in the world, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, holding fast the word of life and bearing with one another in the fear of Christ, imitating and following the footsteps and commands of our most blessed Father Stephen, whose memory is in blessing. In his mercy the Lord God made him wondrous and revealed him in our times, upon whom the ends have come, in the following manner. [Col. 1047D]

### III. Another account of the revelation of Blessed Stephen

When, as we have said above, this dissension had persisted grievously for almost three years, the brothers went very often to the papal court and returned with little or no success, until the time of Pope Clement III. After the confirmations of his predecessors Adrian, Alexander, and Lucius, Clement in turn confirmed the Rule and institutions, renewed the privileges, deposed the two priors who were then opposed to one another, and granted permission to elect a prior.

Having received this permission from him and completed their business, the brothers returned in peace and joy. By the pope’s command, a general chapter was assembled at Grandmont on the feast of Saint Michael, and the customary deliberation concerning the election of a prior took place. Yet there were those who endeavored to disrupt the process so that it would not happen. Some said one thing, others another; almost everyone sought his own prior. But “there is no wisdom, prudence, or counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs XXI). [Col. 1048A]

When divine goodness saw that their hearts were violently divided from one another, the consoling grace of the Holy Spirit was suddenly and truly present in their assembly. It kindled and inflamed their hearts intensely and turned them into unity. Thus there came to be great tranquility and exultation in the chapter, so that it seemed as if almighty God had descended among them.

Nearly all the brothers wept, comforted one another, rejoiced, and blessed the Lord with joy, perceiving that God’s presence had been there. O divine goodness! O ineffable mercy of God! O inexpressible sweetness of the Lord, how swiftly you dispose all things and bring every opposition back to your will! Who could so quickly reduce to unity and recall to concord minds that were discordant with one another, unless your present grace had been there? Truly, Lord, truly you say: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). [Col. 1048B]

To you be praise, glory, honor, power, and dominion, because you do not forsake those who seek you, Lord, nor those who place their confidence not in themselves but in you.

After they had thus been visited by the Lord and comforted for nearly half an hour, they unanimously agreed: “Let twelve brothers be chosen from among us—six clerics and six lay brothers—who, God willing, after prayer has first been made, may provide for themselves, for us, and for the good of the whole Order, and elect a shepherd.”

This was done; and, God willing and with the consent of the general chapter, Gerald was chosen as the seventh prior after Blessed Stephen. The faithful rejoiced and exulted; they rejoiced in divine praises. Obedience was promised to him by all. There were gathered there nearly five hundred brothers, lacking twenty: more than two hundred and twenty clerics, and two hundred and sixty lay brothers. [Col. 1048C]

After these customary matters had been completed, they deliberated concerning the revelation of Blessed Stephen. Counsel having been taken with Lord Elias, bishop of Bordeaux; Seibrand, bishop of Limoges; and Bertrand, bishop of Agen, who had then assembled at Grandmont; and letters having been received from them and from the other bishops, archbishops, abbots, and princes, Prior Gerald sent two of his disciples, Robert the priest and Brother William the lay brother, to the papal court with the aforesaid attestations.

Having courageously undertaken the business laid upon them, and with every success, guided by God and through the merits of Blessed Stephen, they came to Rome. Received by the supreme pontiff and by certain cardinals who were his friends, they presented the letters of attestation that they had brought with them. After these letters had been seen and read, the lord pope, with the cardinals, took care—God so ordering—to carry out this business faithfully. He believed that, if in his own time he could complete such a great work, he would obtain everlasting great reward from God through the merits of Blessed Stephen. [Col. 1049A]

Having taken counsel with his brethren, he sent the lord bishop of Palestrina, John, cardinal of Saint Mark and legate of the Apostolic See, giving him a privilege and command to proceed with all speed to Grandmont, canonize the saint of God honorably as was fitting, and add him to the catalogue of saints.

For us and our chapter, he also took care to send through our brothers the following privilege:

> **CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, GERALD, prior, and the brothers of Grandmont: greeting and apostolic blessing.**
Therefore, the phrase “the most holy Roman Church,” etc. See under Clement III, *Patrologia*, vol. CIV.

Having therefore received the lord pope’s letters and honorably welcomed back, as was fitting, our messengers, we rejoiced exceedingly [Col. 1049C], and, exultant and glad, rendered thanks to God as best we could, with worthy praises. Then the whole assembly of brothers, with great devotion, entreated and exhorted us, saying:

“Lord Father, your discernment knows how and in what manner the spiritual father, Lord Peter of Limoges, the second prior, addressed the first lord and venerable father, blessed Stephen; and, as though rebuking and threatening him, when he saw that God was working wonders and signs through Stephen’s merits, he forbade him to act thus, boldly saying: ‘What is this? What are you doing, most loving Father? Why do you wish, by performing your miracles, to exclude us, servants of your holiness, from this way of poverty and humility? Do not signs and miracles require crowds and assemblies [Col. 1049D] of people? And how shall we be able to remain in the secrecy of solitude if crowds come from every direction, having heard and seen your miracles? Do we not believe in your holiness? Certainly we believe. Why do you wish to trouble us? What have you to do with miracles? Stop, stop; beware, I say, of their pomp: you have nothing to do with them. Cease, my lord; or, if you do not, I certainly shall not love you, and I shall utterly expel you dishonorably from this place and cast you into some most vile and dishonorable place.’ These are the words which the beloved Father spoke to the blessed man Stephen, out of great religious devotion and humility.

“But now, if it please you, good Father, deign humbly to beseech him with pious prayers and bended [Col. 1050A] knees, that at the time of his revelation he may deign to visit and console us by certain signs. For you see in what bonds of blindness and unbelief the people of God are held; and unless they see signs and wonders, they certainly will not believe. Yet signs are given to unbelievers, not to believers. Let therefore your humility ask him that certain miracles may be performed and appear among God’s people, through his merits and prayers, by the divine gift.”

When we heard this, we rejoiced greatly; and exultant and glad, we said to them: “Come then, gather together, and let us go before the tomb of the blessed man and invoke the Lord’s name, so that he who begins to make him wondrous may deign to honor him with various miracles.”

Then all the brothers came and did not cease to persist in prayer [Col. 1050B], seeking God’s help and praising the name of the Lord, which is blessed for ever.

## IV. Of the miracle which occurred before the revelation of blessed Stephen

As the time of the revelation approached, behold, a certain blind old man was led to Grandmont from the parish of the village of Ambazac, seeking and requesting the help of the Lord and of Stephen, the man of God. And what then? He was drawn by his guide’s hands into the church; before our eyes and at our command, he was brought in and led to the altar. The brothers poured out prayer to the Lord for his healing; he was signed with the sign of the true Cross; immediately he was enlightened, recovered his sight, and rejoiced in his healing. He who had been unable to enter without his guide’s hand [Col. 1050C] departed seeing and rejoicing, without his guide’s help. This we saw; this we testify; and this testimony is true.

As the feast of St Augustine drew near, and after the recent death of the most illustrious Henry, king of the English [Note: [Col. 1049] He died in 1189 at Chinon and was buried in the church of Fontevraud.], the lord legate came to Grandmont at great speed and in swift course. Bishops and archbishops were accordingly summoned and gathered there: namely, Lord Henry, archbishop of Bourges; Rainaud, archbishop of Apamea, who at that time had come here as an exile from lands overseas; and Elias, archbishop of Bordeaux; likewise Seibrand, bishop of Limoges; William, bishop of Poitiers; Elias, bishop of Saintes; Adémar, bishop of Périgueux; Gerald, bishop of Cahors; and Bertrand, bishop of Agen; together with abbots, religious men, and an innumerable people [Col. 1050D].

Then also the clerics, who until that time had been in discord, returned to peace by God’s inspiration; and, in the sight of all those named above, humbly bowed their necks, as was fitting, beneath the yoke of obedience to our chapter, and were devoutly received by us and the brothers with the kiss of peace. When these things had been done, and all rejoiced and exulted in the Lord, we came to the place where the body of blessed Stephen lay buried with due honor.

Then, at the command and direction of the lord legate, it was raised from the earth and carried through the cloister with great devotion, amid burning candles and smoking censers. With the people going before and following, it was led into the church with [Col. 1051A] hymns and praises, and honorably placed above the altar of blessed Mary. Lord Henry, archbishop of Bourges and primate of Aquitaine, at the command and direction of the lord legate, prepared himself for the office of Mass in honor of St Stephen; and the singers solemnly began the antiphon, “The mouth of the righteous.”

Then we, having received leave from the lord legate, prepared ourselves with the ministers in another crypt to celebrate the solemnities of Mass in honor of blessed Stephen. While we were applying ourselves to the solemnities of Mass with every devotion and fear, and had entered the Canon after the *Sanctus*, behold, suddenly and unexpectedly a priest-brother named Simon came crying from the church. We had left him there to guard the body of blessed Stephen. Bringing with him [Col. 1051B] a boy, he said:

“Lord Father, lord Father, see and behold the signs and miracles which almighty God, in his wondrous omnipotence, has now deigned to work miraculously before our eyes through the blessed Stephen, our wondrous Father, in this boy.”

We, however, were greatly startled by so loud and sudden an outcry; nor was this surprising, since we were burdened and bound by so weighty a responsibility. Nevertheless, as best we could, we looked; and he who had broken silence in such a place under such necessity—a thing he would never have ventured to do unless amazement at the miracles compelled him—continued:

“Behold, lord, this boy whom you see was lame from his mother’s womb, mute, and with withered hands. Behold his father, whom I know, named Elias Valaris, and his wife, the mother of this boy, who [Col. 1051C] testify to this. For this reason they brought him here from the town of Limoges, of which they are citizens: that almighty God might visit him with healing through blessed Stephen. Behold, lord, behold: you see that he speaks freely; behold, he walks; he moves his hands as he wishes. This boy may now be about ten years old.”

As he spoke and said these things, we looked upon them for a long time in astonishment and wonder. In the joy of heavenly consolation and visitation, we raised our hands to heaven, shed tears, prostrated ourselves upon the ground, and praised almighty God with heart and voice as best we could. Together with those who had flocked to this spectacle, we blessed him. The boy spoke and walked, and God’s people rejoiced at these things. The boy was [Col. 1051D] handsome in appearance and fair of face.

We returned, exultant and consoled by the miracles, to the place in the Canon which we had left. As we hastened to continue the Canon according to custom, after the Lord’s Prayer had already been completed, behold, that same priest mentioned above came bringing another young man, older than the first, the son of a burgess of Limoges named Peter of Uzerche, and cried out:

“Lord, lord, behold a recent and no small miracle. This young man had a large and considerable swelling in his neck, which grievously afflicted him. He was unable to look upward or turn his face in any direction except together with his whole body, because his chin remained glued and joined to his body [Col. 1052A]. But his father, whom you see, came and offered him to blessed Stephen with tears, asking that he might grant him heavenly help—he who already shines forth in wondrous powers. While the father persisted earnestly in prayer and sought divine help, the swelling began to disappear and his chin to pull free from his breast. Then the boy, seized with great pain, again began to cry: ‘O God, because I am in pain, heal me for your love; heal me through the merits of him whose aid I seek.’ As the boy said this, he was immediately healed. Therefore now, my Father, bless God, who has visited us today.”

Behold, two miracles in a short time. At the priest’s words I trembled throughout, seeing God’s mighty works which had been done for the glory of the blessed man. Again we shed tears and prostrated ourselves upon the ground [Col. 1052B], raised our hands to heaven, and began to praise the Lord with hymns and praises. The people assembled and gathered to behold so great a miracle, praising the Lord’s name and the holiness of blessed Stephen.

## V. Of the healed girl

When the solemnities of Mass had been completed, there was at the doors a third miracle, miraculous and glorious. A certain girl from the village of Bersac had arrived with the others; from her mother’s womb she had had a bent and withered right hand. She came and prayed, standing in prayer for nearly half an hour. The hand which had been bent and withered was raised by God’s power, stretched out for signing herself, and its fingers separated from one another. God’s works were extolled by the people’s praises [Col. 1052C], and hymns and songs were sung by the clerics.

And what shall I say? The church was filled with cries. God’s mighty works were wondered at and exalted; blessed Stephen’s merits were venerated and praised; God’s present grace was recognized and received. Why? Because blind people were brought and enlightened; the lame, healed; the mute, made to speak; the possessed, freed; the insane, changed; the sick, cured; the dead, raised; and the deaf, helped.

Of this multitude of signs, we wish, if we can, to run through a few with the utmost brevity, lest the prolixity of words burden readers or hearers. For good and brief reading sometimes becomes useful instruction to readers; and the more prolix it becomes, the more burdensome it is. And [Col. 1052D] what more need be said? Although many signs have appeared by divine action, only a few are set down on this page: those which we have resolved to write for your affection and benefit as better, more certain, and more pleasing.

For on the day of St Stephen’s revelation, together with the night following, seventeen miracles became evident through God’s grace at work and through his merits. Some indeed we saw; others we did not see but believe upon hearing them. For Adémar, viscount of Limoges, as is reported, took with him to be cared for a boy blind from birth, whom blessed Stephen had divinely enlightened on the very day of the revelation. We heard this but did not see it, though we were present in that place. For we did not see everything done there on that day; and if we did not see it, shall we not believe? Far greater are the things [Col. 1053A] which we have heard than those which we have seen. Does not the Apostle say: “Faith comes from hearing” (*Romans* 10)? Therefore faith is to be given, especially to those who speak truth and obey truth.

For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not be unbelieving, but believing” (*John* 20). And again: “He who does not believe withdraws; and he who believes draws near.” Faith has great merit before the Lord if it is supported by good works. For there are certain invisible things which cannot at all be seen with the eyes of the flesh, but are truly beheld with the eyes of faith. Yet very many suppose that they see them, though they do not see them—as is the case with the Lord’s body. Bread and wine are placed upon the altar; they are consecrated by the priest through divine words. Neither color nor taste is changed in the outward created things, but inwardly [Col. 1053B] power is active in the substances of holiness. External eyes cannot see this at all, except the outward things which are placed there.

The inner—that is, intellectual—eyes must therefore be opened, that they may see and understand what lies hidden within. For outward things are seen with outward eyes, namely bread and wine; inward things are seen and contemplated with inward eyes, namely the body and blood of the Lord. These are the sacraments and proofs of true faith. For “faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing” (*Hebrews* 11).

Have we never believed unless we have seen? Hear then Isaiah—or rather, the Holy Spirit—speaking and threatening: “Unless you believe, you shall not remain” (*Isaiah* 7); and the Lord in the Gospel: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe” [Col. 1053C] (*John* 4). Believe, therefore, believe, that you may remain: seeing signs and wonders and hearing of marvels done in our times, through divine grace generously bestowed by the venerable merits of blessed Stephen. Do not harden your hearts, for God is able to do beyond what you can believe.

## VI. Another miracle

We shall further tell another precious and pleasing miracle which occurred at the time of his revelation. There was a woman at Limoges, mother of the wife of Elias Valaris, whom we mentioned above, and whose son was healed by God’s grace through a threefold miracle. This woman had been deaf for many years and could hear nothing at all [Col. 1053D]. When she saw her daughter and son-in-law return from Grandmont with their healed grandson, she asked her daughter where she had come from and what necessity had made her remain away from home for so long. Signifying the matter to her, the daughter told her what had happened.

Her mother said: “O good daughter, if it please you to go back again for my sake, perhaps almighty God, through his saint, and through the help of your labors and prayers, will deign to look upon and console me, wretched and unworthy as I am. I see that my grandson is wholly healed, but I cannot hear. Go back then, good daughter, I beg you, go back, my daughter, barefoot and clothed in a woolen garment, carrying a candle in your hands.”

The daughter came, approached the saint’s tomb, and gave herself to prayer. When she had prayed [Col. 1054A] and made an offering, she returned with complete confidence to her mother and found her already healed. She saw and heard that the woman whom she had left deaf was now rejoicing and hearing through the divine gift and the merits of blessed Stephen. Great joy and exultation arose in that house, both over the healed boy and over that old woman. Therefore the daughter again returned joyfully to Grandmont, to give thanks with praises to God and blessed Stephen, who through his merits had visited her house, and to make known to all the miracles which had occurred there.

Blessed and illustrious woman, who was able to be the bearer of tidings of divine works, and upon whom the Lord God, through the interceding merits of his glorious confessor, deigned to bestow such benefits! Such and so great miracles could never have remained hidden in so famous a town [Col. 1054B]. Accordingly, many signs were wrought in that same town at that time through blessed Stephen, God willing. A priest who heard and partly saw this related it truthfully to us.

## VII. Another miracle

While these feast-days were being celebrated and almost publicly proclaimed in that same town, a very poor girl heard of them. She had been lame in her mother’s womb. Hearing that God and our Lord were doing such things at Grandmont at the tomb of the blessed and holy man, she groaned and said:

“O Lord God, what shall I do, since I have no comforter to carry me there, because I am oppressed by the greatest need and poverty? But I know, Lord, that you are the comforter and helper of the poor. Be my helper and comforter in this tribulation of mine; and through the merits of blessed Stephen, if these things which I hear are true—and I believe that they are true—help me, your wretched handmaid. For here you are able to help me through him just as though I stood before his tomb. This is the confidence I have in you and in his powers. Therefore, Lord, show mercy to your handmaid through his holy merits.”

When she had completed her prayer, the Lord looked upon her petition and heard her; and, as she had asked, she was healed by the Lord through the intercession of blessed Stephen. Thus, assuredly, day by day his holy merits, signs, and wonders were spread abroad.

## VIII. Another miracle

[Col. 1054D]

At the same time there was a burgess in the same town of Limoges named Stephen, whose wife was called Matilda. They had a son named Stephen, lame from his mother’s womb for almost fourteen years. When they heard that God was performing signs and wonders at Grandmont through the goodness of blessed Stephen, they saddled an ass and placed the lame boy upon it with crutches, and began to come toward Grandmont with great confidence. While they were on the way, that animal, by I know not what chance, carelessly set down its foot and fell, and the lame youth’s crutches were broken.

When the lame boy saw this, he said to his mother: “Mother, now I know that I shall be healed [Col. 1055A] when I reach the tomb of blessed Stephen at Grandmont. The breaking of my crutches, by which I used to be supported, is the sign of my healing.” He said this almost as a prophet of his recovery.

When they came to the tomb of the holy confessor, they prayed and wept, and deserved consolation from the Lord. Before all our eyes, the boy who had been lame suddenly rose up and, raised by the Lord with blessed Stephen’s aid, began to walk joyful and glad. Taking him in our own hands, we placed him upon the altar. He ran swiftly from one corner of the altar to the other, with his hands raised to heaven. All who were there rejoiced; some wept for joy, others in gladness sang hymns and praises to God and proclaimed the merits of holy Stephen [Col. 1055B]. We kept this boy with us, given by his parents, to be cared for as testimony to so great a miracle.

## IX. Another miracle

Likewise a certain woman, Joanna Brugiola of Montgaudii—a place situated near the town of Limoges—came with a mute and crippled boy. The child was monstrous to behold. His mouth was twisted toward his left jaw, and his teeth were disordered in his mouth. It was no wonder that he could not speak; indeed, he could scarcely eat. His left hand was exceedingly bent and weak.

And what then? The mother prayed for the boy, supplicated by calling upon the Lord’s name, and sought the aid [Col. 1055C] of blessed Stephen. Having done this, she deserved to be heard by the Lord, with the aid of Stephen, the most reverend confessor; and immediately the mute boy spoke. The crowds were amazed, great fear fell upon them, and they blessed God, “who gave such power to human beings.” Filled with wonder and astonishment, they began to extol the holiness of the man of God.

As nearly everyone spread abroad the signs and wonders which were daily performed at Grandmont and in many places where the memory of his name was held, through God’s goodness and the blessed man’s merits, many began to come in throngs and processions from different provinces, that through his merits they might deserve to be heard by the Lord God in their necessities.

Among them came two young men holding a certain cloth in their hands [Col. 1055D]. When we asked where they were from, what they sought, or why they carried that cloth, they humbly replied: “Lord, are you not the prior of this house?”

I gave them this reply: “I am, my sons.”

And they said: “Lord, we were born in this province of Limoges. The reason why we bring this cloth here is as follows. Our father, who had survived until now, died this week under the pressure of a grave illness. But having heard of the signs and wonders of the blessed man Stephen, we began to invoke his power over our father, asking that God and our Lord, if the things we had heard about this man were true, might deign to help [Col. 1056A] and aid him through his merits, which are very many and great before God. When we had completed our prayer, without delay our father rose and came back to life. Behold, we have brought this cloth as testimony.”

When I heard this, I was greatly astonished and began to glorify the Lord’s name with the others who heard it. All were filled with amazement and astonishment at what had happened to them, because God adorned and made his saint honorable by such, as it were, manifest signs.

## X. Another miracle

After this wondrous miracle we shall recount another sign which occurred at the time of his revelation, by God’s mercy. Among the other sick persons who had gathered [Col. 1056B] was a young man from the village called Saint-Hilaire, near the monastery of Benevento, named Stephen [Note: [Col. 1055D] Benevento was a monastery of the Order of St Augustine, two leagues distant from the city of Limoges, [Col. 1056D] whose revenues were assigned to the church of Quebec in 1693.]. He had been blind from birth and was the only son of a most poor widow. While he persisted earnestly in prayer before the tomb of blessed Stephen with the others, anxiously begged God’s mercy, and invoked holy Stephen in loud cries that he might grant him help, divine power suddenly came, restoring to him, through blessed Stephen’s merits, the sight which, as he afterward told us, he had never possessed. Since he was poor and needy, we received and retained him in our house [Col. 1056C], to be maintained and cared for, for God’s love, for the honor of the glorious confessor Stephen, and as testimony to so great a miracle.

## XI. Another miracle

On the same day on which these things happened, a certain woman, who had lost her sight for almost eight years, happily recovered it, by God’s favor and the help of God’s saint, before our eyes and those of many others. At that very time, out of reverence for the miracle, we gave her a small gift of food.

For it was certainly the custom at that time with this saint of whom we speak that he granted more help and greater benefit to widows, orphans, virgins, children, and the poor than to the rich. This we certainly observed and proved in the working of his miracles, as well as another marvelous and miraculous thing [Col. 1056D]. For while only a few lights shone before him during the day, few or no signs or wonders were performed through him. But when a multitude of people came together, and a manifold abundance of lamps and candles was lit about him, so that almost the entire church inside and out shone solemnly with very many lights, then signs and wonders were divinely performed through him. When we observed this many times, seeing these things, we were filled with amazement and joy and exchanged refined words with one another, as was possible and fitting.

We certainly believe that almighty God wished to illumine him with such great honor because this saint, while he lived in the world, boldly and humbly concealed himself as much as he could from the knowledge and veneration of this world [Col. 1057A]. Very often, when crowds arrived or great gifts were offered to him by someone out of love for God, so that Christ’s poor who lived with him might be supported from them, he would see this and flee, saying in a tearful voice: “God, hide me; God, hide me.”

When the brothers said to him, almost rebuking and reproving him: “Why, lord, do you now flee when you ought to return—even if you had fled—when you see that you have been visited by the Lord?” he humbly answered them, as he was the gentlest and kindest of all, in peaceful words: “I fear, brothers, lest God—forbid it!—repay to me, unworthy as I am, merits which are almost small or nonexistent [Col. 1057B].” Thus indeed, thus certainly, he avoided and fled the abundance and flow of temporal things; and if at any time he could not do so in body, he did so in heart.

## XII. Another miracle

Let us recount still further some of the signs which we saw or heard. Among the wonders occurring at the time of his revelation, certain pilgrims came by chance to Grandmont to pray, returning from Rocamadour, where the memory of the blessed Virgin Mary is honored. They brought with them a woman with a withered hand. These people, as we heard, were natives of Normandy. When they had seen and heard the divine works then shining forth at Grandmont through the glorious merits of blessed Stephen, they urged the woman, saying [Col. 1057C]: “Quickly touch, in whatever way you can, with that withered hand, the place where the consecrated limbs of this saint rest buried.” When she did so, she was immediately healed.

## XIII. Another miracle

At the same time, a certain insane man named William was brought by his mother to Grandmont from the village of Saint-Martin in the land of Soudour, that almighty God might deign, through blessed Stephen the confessor, to restore to him reason and soundness of mind. When she had arrived, she remained for nearly three days at the memorial of blessed Stephen, praying and petitioning. Nevertheless, through the intercession of God’s saint, he attained his former soundness of mind; and afterward [Col. 1057D], joyful and exulting, he took part with our brothers in the vintage, helping and harvesting grapes soberly with them.

## XIV. Another miracle

Next we shall recount a miracle which we saw. The lord legate and the archbishop of Apamea were still at Grandmont. We happened to be discussing certain matters with the latter at the time or hour when this miracle occurred. Night had now approached as day departed; the people, with lamps lit, surrounded the tomb of the holy man; and a woman from the diocese of Limoges brought her son, lame from the womb, as best she could. She stood [Col. 1058A], prayed, and earnestly and resolutely begged blessed Stephen’s aid for her son.

When she had done this, her son immediately recovered the power of walking; his ankles and soles were strengthened; and the crowds were astonished. Then the people standing by pulled the rope of the cymbal, praising the Lord’s name because of so great a miracle. When we and the archbishop heard its sound, we came to the church, found the lame man walking, gave praise to God, and were led to the altar, marveling at this miracle.

The crowd brought another man, who had been blind and whom God had visited. He had prayed at the tomb and received sight. Therefore the Church rejoices, seeing God’s mighty works; God’s servant is praised; all the people rejoice together, seeing divine gifts and Stephen’s wonders [Col. 1058B]. The archbishop was amazed at the blind man who had been enlightened, almost deprived of breath by so great a wonder. On one side walks the lame man, who is now seen; the blind man sees the lights, things he had never seen before. These are two miracles performed in a short space, seen by all the people; therefore the Lord is praised and God’s saint exalted. Hence God’s praise arises and a psalm is sung to God, because the lame man walks and the blind man enjoys the light. Let us all praise the Lord for this double miracle, who has exalted his holy servant for ever.

## XV. Another miracle

There still remain miracles received by the Church of the Order of Grandmont during that period [Col. 1058C]. A certain girl was brought from the village called Nobiliacum, having no eyes by which all things might be seen. There were, as it were, little hard stones like crystals. Therefore she was brought to the saint and prostrated herself upon the ground. Thus the Church prayed for this handmaid of Christ, that she might see the light of the world and that Christ might hear her. Scales fell from her eyes, resembling crystals, and she saw what she had not seen before: God had then looked upon her.

Her name was Mary; she sees and is seen, as this was thus asked of us and thus reported to us. O new gifts of Christ! O new grace of Christ, which shines through the ages and gleams in the Church, where the saint is exalted and the righteous one acknowledged! Who has ever seen such things as are done in the church of the Order of Grandmont together with the other wonders? God’s servant is praised [Col. 1058D]; all the people applaud in hymns and songs, having seen such great miracles. Now therefore marvel, dearest children, giving honor to Stephen, the truly most holy Father.

## XVI. Another miracle

Henceforth let us recount another praiseworthy sign, which God and our Lord at that time wished to show his people, in honor of so great a Father and in praise of his own name. At the village of Solignac [Note: [Col. 1057] Solignac is a village two leagues distant from Limoges, where there is a monastery of the Order of St Benedict founded by St Eligius.], a boy named Otgerius was so grievously ill with fevers that he was in danger of death. When his father William and his mother Adema saw this, afflicted with overwhelming sorrow, they vowed him to blessed [Col. 1059A] Stephen; and he immediately recovered and became well.

A priest named Peter, who saw and heard this with many others, later faithfully related this sign to us. So too did another priest, named Guy, a brother of this order. One night, at the time of the revelation of blessed Stephen the confessor, he was guarding the saint’s tomb with the other brothers. An innumerable people of both sexes had come to pray. Among them was a woman with her blind daughter. With great confidence she poured out prayer to the Lord for her daughter, asking that, for the love and honor of blessed Stephen, he might restore her daughter’s sight, which she had lost for nearly eight years. Without delay, she immediately regained her sight, and the people who stood by and saw it gave thanks to almighty God and to St Stephen [Col. 1059B], the venerable confessor.

## XVII. Another miracle

Another brother, John of Belle-Arbre, truthfully told us that at that time a certain woman from his village, named Petronilla, came with her withered son, whose father had already died. When that brother saw him, he was moved with pity for him and, taking him from the crowd, confidently offered him to blessed Stephen to be healed. When he and another man named Aimeric, who happened then to be guarding the tomb of the man of God, had prayed for him, the Lord God visited him for the love of blessed Stephen. He was healed, and his mother received him from the brothers’ hands and went away rejoicing [Col. 1059C] and exulting with her healed son.

## XVIII. Another miracle

On the day of the revelation, a most noble knight named Eschivard was carrying through the cloister, with the others in procession, the reliquary in which were the relics of St Stephen’s body. Through Stephen’s merits he was vigorously healed of quartan fevers.

## XIX. Another miracle

Another knight, a nobleman named Josselinus, of the place called S. [reading uncertain], was miraculously healed of the same quartan fevers by the same confessor Stephen in that same year. Afterwards he came safely and joyfully to the blessed man’s tomb with his brother, the abbot of Solignac, to give thanks to Stephen and to the Lord Jesus Christ. Thus, far and wide, the Lord God [Col. 1059D] made his holiness known by diverse miracles.

## XX. Another miracle

While these wonders were daily and most plainly performed at Grandmont, at the tomb of so great a man, through his merits and by God’s ordering, and while the report of such great works spread rapidly through different regions, it happened that in a town called Porgeria a man named John Gormund was afflicted with a grave illness, nearly unto death, for almost a year. For, as he afterward told us, he could not bring his hand to his mouth or move his foot.

Hearing, therefore, of St Stephen’s powers and distinguished deeds, he began with his whole heart—for he could not do so with his mouth—to invoke the Lord’s name, asking that through the merits of the most illustrious confessor, blessed Stephen, he might deign to restore to him the grace of his former health [Col. 1060A]. He promised and made a vow that, once health and soundness had been received, he would afterwards hasten joyfully to Stephen’s memorial at Grandmont. And so it happened.

When his prayer was finished, he was immediately healed; and, as he had vowed, he came to Grandmont and, joyful and healthy, gave thanks to God and blessed Stephen before our seeing and rejoicing eyes. For the love of God and in honor of so great a miracle, we gave him one cloak.

At that time—that is, on the Nativity of the Virgin St Mary—five miracles involving blind persons, lame persons, and other sick people were wondrously performed before blessed Stephen’s tomb, by God’s power, through blessed Stephen’s intercession and the merits of the Mother of God, as we saw and heard [Col. 1060B].

## XXI. Another miracle
Then, on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, while we were earnestly occupied with the divine praises, behold, a great cry suddenly arose and was loudly raised in the principal church, where the relics of the body of the blessed confessor Stephen had been honourably entombed. Astonished by so great a cry, we promptly asked why such a loud and violent outcry was being made in the church. We learned that a certain mute man, whom his mother had brought to the holy man of God, namely Stephen, with great faith, was speaking correctly through his merits. Therefore, interrupting the divine praises because of the din of so great an outcry and in honour of the venerable miracle, we left the places of Matins and ran to the place where he who had been mute from birth was speaking. For the crowds had already brought him, with his attendants, before the altar of the Blessed Virgin Mary, praising and blessing the Lord, who through blessed Stephen had visited him. When we came there, we found him speaking and saying: “Give me something to drink, give me something to drink.” We therefore ran swiftly to the water flowing nearby and gave him drink—plainly as testimony to so great a miracle. This young man, as it seemed to us, had now almost completed his twelfth year.

## XXII. Another miracle

[Col. 1060D] In those days another young man, who had lain ill in bed for one year, was brought by his friends to the tomb of the holy confessor Stephen. While they prayed at his sepulchre, behold, suddenly that sick man was raised up by God’s power and began to walk without any human assistance. Before our eyes—for we were then present there, seeing and watching—he bravely and wonderfully climbed the stone steps built before the altar.

For this was a marvellous and incredible thing to relate: his arms were like dry wood, and likewise his shins; his hands and feet were large, his body exceedingly emaciated, and his face pale and greatly disfigured. Who could look upon him without being astonished? On the one hand [Col. 1061A] we pitied him; on the other, we rejoiced with him.

## XXIII. Another miracle

Nor should you yet be weary of hearing of the wonderful and glorious sign which almighty God, in his miraculous goodness, deigned to work through the blessed man Stephen at the village of Glutorum, in the same year of his revelation, namely on the feast of St Michael.

A fair, according to the custom of that village, was being held there. And behold, a certain man named Andrew was suddenly seized with fever at the fair itself. As he lay feverish almost to the point of death, and believed that he could live no longer, he summoned the priests and clerics of the Church, together with his other friends; and, having made confession, he fortified [Col. 1061B] himself with the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. He then ordered everything necessary for his funeral to be prepared. While the funeral rites were being arranged, as seemed appropriate, the sick man began to suffer grievously from excessive pain and was brought to the point of death.

When those standing by saw this, they took him from the bed and laid him on the ground upon straw, as is the Christian custom in dying. His hands were folded upon his breast, his eyes closed, and his breath almost wholly extinguished. Seeing that he was dying, he began, as best he could, to pray and invoke blessed Stephen in his heart, the first shepherd of the Grandmontine Order, asking him to bring aid to him; and promising that, if he did so, he would hasten swiftly to his tomb when restored to health.

What more need be said? Behold, this man who thus spoke [Col. 1061C] in his heart—for he could not speak with his mouth—was already thought dead by those around him. And behold, the pious and venerable confessor blessed Stephen appeared, in the form of a man of utmost whiteness: his beard was long and white, his garments white as snow, and his hair white; his face shone like the sun. He held in his hand a vial full of healing water. As the saint of God poured that water over the sick man’s body, he said to him, smiling as it were and rejoicing: “Do not fear, for you shall not now die, but shall be healed.”

Having said this, he disappeared; and immediately he who had been thought dead rose and was made well. He told those around him all that had happened to him, and all were astonished. Afterwards he came to Grandmont, [Col. 1061D] as he had promised the holy man, to visit his tomb. He truthfully recounted all these things to us in his own living voice, and told how, at the pouring out of that healing water, his body received such great refreshment that he seemed to himself to be in the paradise of God.

## XXIV. Another miracle

At this time a certain peasant youth from the little village called Boissi, filled with an evil spirit and with anger and indignation, violently pulled up and burned in the fire the crosses which our brethren of Exclusa had set round their wood as boundary markers. After doing this, he was seized by a demon, which began violently to agitate and grievously afflict him, so that he could recognize no one.

[Col. 1062A] When his parents saw this, they brought him, as best they could, to the memorial of blessed Stephen at Grandmont, so that God our Lord might, for Stephen’s sake, free him from the demon and restore his senses. By God’s will and the intercession of blessed Stephen, this was done. The young man, having recovered his senses and been freed from the demon, humbly sought and obtained from us and from our brethren pardon for the injury done to our brethren. He promised that he would thereafter presume to cause them no trouble. For he knew and openly confessed that God had handed him over to Satan to be scourged for so great a crime.

Thus indeed, thus certainly, you may observe, if you please, how almighty God severely avenges injury done to [Col. 1062B] his servants and does not permit their goodness and holiness to remain hidden for long.

## XXV. Another miracle

Let us next relate another miracle which must not be passed over in silence. In those days a young man named Peter de Schola fell ill at the village called St Hilary in the Limousin district. As he was in danger from a grave illness, he was brought to the point of death. When his neighbours and kinsfolk heard this, they gathered together to prepare his funeral rites. But his mother, overwhelmed by excessive grief, suddenly took a tow thread and approached her son, who lay [Col. 1062C] lifeless on the ground, seeing and hearing absolutely nothing. She measured him from head to foot so that a candle might be made from it for blessed Stephen, to whom she vowed him and for whose aid she humbly prayed; if the young man recovered, he would afterwards joyfully and exultantly carry it to the tomb of the man of God.

Thus the boy’s anxious mother sought help from blessed Stephen, saying that, if he restored her son to her, she would bring him, God willing, to his tomb; and all who stood by prayed likewise. They regarded him as dead and mourned him as one who had entered upon the way of all flesh. His mother had already despaired of his life and therefore wept as though bereaved and widowed.

What more? At his mother’s prayer the young man’s face came back to life. At cockcrow, those standing round saw and received the youth alive and [Col. 1062D] unharmed. Then all began to praise God and extol the holiness of blessed Stephen with worthy praises. Moreover, his mother spun a cloth for almost the entire year, which, when the year had elapsed, she carried on her head to the tomb of the holy man of God at Grandmont. We learned all these things from him, from his mother and cousin, and from others who had come with him to us at Grandmont.

## XXVI. Another miracle

In the town of Auveria there was a widow named Dea, whose son Belinus lay ill to the point of death. He suffered from a most severe disease of the throat, so that he could neither speak, [Col. 1063A] eat, nor swallow his saliva. His face and throat were exceedingly livid and shone almost like glass. He lay in his bed as though dead, and almost everyone despaired of his life.

His mother, deeply distressed and sorrowful, wept, lamented, wailed, and gave herself up to grief; as though driven mad, she tore the hair from her head, rent her clothes, and sought help from above. Yet she could not obtain a hearing for her son until she vowed him to blessed Stephen. Once she had vowed him to the saint of God and implored him to restore her son, without delay the young man began to call to his mother and say: “Good mother.”

She answered him: “I am here, my son,” and ran to him.

Then he said: “Good mother, three pilgrims will come this night [Col. 1063B] to lodge here. I beg you to receive them kindly and honourably, and have them conducted upstairs into the higher chamber with due honour. For St Stephen will come with them, and after cockcrow he will restore me to my former health. And do not delay in preparing here, before my bed, a place for Lord Peter the chaplain to rest.”

When he had spoken thus, he fell silent, unaware of what he had said—as he afterwards faithfully recounted to us at Grandmont before the altar, with his mother and the aforesaid priest Peter present, in the hearing of many of our brethren.

But when the young man’s mother heard these things from her son, with the often-mentioned chaplain and many others standing there, she was amazed and filled with joy because she heard her son speaking, though from yesterday and the day before yesterday she had been unable at all [Col. 1063C] to hear him. With confidence she began to await the coming of blessed Stephen and her most beloved son’s promise.

While they waited, marvelled with joy, watched attentively, and spoke together, after the cock had crowed once or twice as usual, the sick man suddenly ordered his mother to come quickly to him. She rose at once, hurried to him, and gently asked what he wished. He said:

“Good mother, behold, St Stephen, the illustrious confessor and first shepherd of the venerable Grandmontine Order, has now deigned to visit me in my misery, mercifully to pierce my throat with three of his fingers, and thus to heal me. If perhaps you doubt this, hasten and see. Certainly, by God’s favour and blessed Stephen’s intercession, [Col. 1063D] I have been made sound and whole, as though I had never had or suffered this sickness.”

Then the mother, having lit lamps, came with the priest Peter and the others present to her son, and carefully examined whether what he said was true. On careful investigation, she found that the coverings beneath which the youth lay were soaked with the discharge of the disease, and that there were three holes in his throat—two on the left and one on the right side of the throat.

Later at Grandmont, when the mother brought him with the aforesaid priest, many others, a cloth upon his head, and a candle in his hand, we saw the scars from these three holes, so that every word might stand, as it were, by the mouth of two or three witnesses (Deut. XIX). For at that time the general chapter was assembled at Grandmont, namely on the feast of St Michael. More than two hundred brethren who had gathered there saw and heard this sign; many of them shed tears for joy, and, as we saw and marvelled, they devoutly kissed those scars as though they were the footprints of their Father. As testimony of so great and famous a miracle, we ourselves presumed to insert our fingers into those scars.

When, as we said above, the mother found her son thus healed, astonished and filled with all wonder and exultation, she began to cry out and say with tears: “Come, come, see the mighty works and wonders of almighty God, which he has wrought upon my son through the merits of blessed Stephen. He has indeed looked upon the misery of his handmaid, freeing my son from death through his saint and restoring him to life.”

[Col. 1064B] Therefore the whole multitude of the people of the town of Auveria gathered in the house of this widow to see the signs and wonders which God had there wonderfully wrought through blessed Stephen.
