All marvelled at what they saw and praised God in heaven, who alone does great wonders. Amen.

## XXVII. Another miracle

Let not your charity yet be weary of hearing a clear sign, radiant with truth, which gloriously and manifestly occurred at the time of blessed Stephen’s revelation. In the village of Ambasiac there was a poor man named Stephen, who had a son named Peter, lame from his mother’s womb and now almost ten years old. When he wished to move, he crawled along the ground like some creeping thing.

When his father heard of the many signs and wonders done at Grandmont, at the urging and counsel of his neighbours he carried the boy to the tomb of the confessor blessed Stephen. But after staying there two or three days, compelled by hunger and, as though despairing of God’s goodness and blessed Stephen’s holiness, he returned with his son, gaining absolutely nothing because he remained unbelieving and, in contempt as it were, had refused to persevere.

When his neighbours and those who knew him saw that he had departed from the tomb of the man of God so swiftly and grievously, as though foolish and unbelieving, having neither hope nor faith in the divine works [Col. 1064D] continually performed there by God, they began sharply to rebuke him and say with complete confidence: “Return, wretched and miserable man; return with your son to Grandmont, and do not remain unbelieving. Therefore take up the courage of a faithful man; take your son and set him before the altar and the tomb of the man of God.”

The man believed the words of the faithful and brought his son to Grandmont, but secretly fled away, leaving him there. Thus abandoned by his unbelieving father, the lame boy remained continually at the church door, begging alms from those entering the sanctuary. As he persevered in knocking and, so far as he knew how to pray or had been taught by others, sought aid from above—asking that God our Lord might, through the merits of blessed Stephen, deign to **relieve** [the text prints *revelare*, apparently for *relevare*] the weakness of his body—the merciful and compassionate One heard his prayer: he who saves all who hope in him and wills all to come to the knowledge of truth, opening the bosom of his mercy and granting him perfect health, because his ankles and soles were strengthened.

The witnesses of this event are six hundred men and countless women who had known him before. We, moreover, so that we might be more fully assured and made more joyful by so great and precious a miracle, ordered him to be brought to us. We saw him standing upright and walking, and heard from his own mouth a truthful account of his former infirmity and then of the health which he had received from God through the merits of blessed Stephen. [Col. 1065B] These things we have seen; these things we have heard; these things we testify; these things we faithfully announce to your charity, so that you may believe the signs and wonders which you hear and, believing faithfully, may have eternal life. Amen.

## XXVIII. Another miracle

Since the Apostle Paul says, “Charity does not seek what is its own, but what belongs to Christ” (1 Cor. XIII); and the Lord says in the Gospel, “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark XVI); and the Apostle says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI); and the same Apostle, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (ibid.); therefore, dearest brethren, we exhort your love in every way in the Lord to prepare your hearts to hear [Col. 1065C] and believe, so that you may receive, believe, love, and proclaim with every confidence and kindness the things which you find written in this book concerning blessed Stephen, our most holy father.

Know for certain that, so far as we could, by God’s inspiration, as we said above, we have written what is true and most true. Nor have we wished to commit to this page all that ought to be written, or could be written, concerning him; for if it were written, perhaps it would not be believed. For many signs and miracles accomplished by God through his merits in different places and provinces, although in our own time we have heard of them from trustworthy persons after a juridical attestation had been made, we intend to pass over in silence; [Col. 1065D] but we commit a few of the more certain to this writing.

We have heard that in the diocese of Rodez God raised a certain boy through him. A wax image of this boy was brought to one of our houses called St Michael’s, where it is preserved and displayed in the church in memory of so great a miracle. We have also heard that he performed many signs in the diocese of Rodez, which, as it seems to us, should not be consigned to oblivion.

For the wife of a knight named Arnaud, lord of a certain town called Rupis-excisa, was healed through him in the following manner. In the month of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1192, the aforesaid woman, called Florence, flourishing in birth, nobility, and virtue, suddenly began to suffer fever [Col. 1066A] and to be oppressed by a grave illness. Her sickness increased day by day, so that neither physicians nor anyone else could help her. What more need be said? She was brought almost to death.

Seeing that she was dying, and as she herself, her husband, and the rest nearly despaired of her recovery, she was laid in ashes and haircloth, according to the Christian custom in dying. Then, as best she could, she spoke with her husband, saying: “Behold, my husband, as you see, I am dying and entering the way of all flesh. I beg you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to offer and vow me to blessed Stephen the confessor, the first founder of the Grandmontine Order.”

Then, at her words, her husband took a tow thread, measured her from head to foot, and began afterwards to cover the thread with wax. The woman meanwhile invoked blessed Stephen in her heart as best she could. While she persevered in prayer, blessed Stephen suddenly appeared to her, surrounded by a multitude of his disciples. Taking the woman’s right hand and smiling as it were, he said: “Rise quickly; for you shall not die, but shall be healed of this illness.”

No one saw or heard him but the woman alone. When blessed Stephen had raised her from the bed of her sickness, the woman rose sound and whole; and St Stephen disappeared. Her husband, seeing her rise, was overcome with astonishment and asked what this meant, saying: “Alas, my lady! Alas! How can this be? I thought you were now dying, but now I see you sound, whole, [Col. 1066C] and cheerful. What is this?”

Smiling, she replied: “Certainly, my lord, blessed Stephen, to whom you vowed me, has now deigned to come to his handmaid and to appear to me, an unworthy woman, with a multitude of his disciples. As you see, the good and holy man of God has left me sound and whole in peace.”

There was then great joy and exultation in that household and throughout the entire castle on that day and thereafter. Afterwards the woman visited our brethren who live in that province, on the border of her castle at Auram-Ventosam, and told them what had happened to her and how God had deigned to visit and heal her through blessed Stephen. She gave three solidi of Rodez currency, for them to bring to us at Grandmont to make a wax statue in memory of so great a miracle, to be set before the tomb of blessed Stephen.

## XXIX. Another miracle

In the same territory, near the castle called St Baudelius, there was a woman distinguished by nobility and lineage. She dearly and earnestly loved our brethren living at Auram-Ventosam and our Order. During the time of the revelation of blessed Stephen the confessor, her little son was seized by a grave illness and brought almost to death. When his noble mother saw this, she became anxious and tearful. The boy’s illness grew day by day, and the aforesaid lady grew more distressed and was sorely troubled by grief.

When she heard of the miracles of Stephen continually performed at Grandmont, she vowed him to Stephen the confessor; and immediately, by God’s will, the boy was restored to his former health. The brethren who saw and heard this truthfully reported it to us.

## XXX. Another miracle

In the Limousin district, near the village of St Junian, there were two men distinguished by lineage and nobility, one called Iterius and the other Peter. One day, as they were leaving the aforesaid village to transact their affairs, they encountered a fugitive knight named Gerald de Oratorio. He wished, with his companions, to invade that region in order to plunder it, should he chance [Col. 1067B] to find anything. When he encountered the aforesaid men, he rejoiced greatly, being one who supported himself and his followers by robbery.

He seized them, carried them into another territory, and shut them in prison, where they remained for almost two months, afflicted by hunger, starvation, and irons. Seeing themselves grievously tortured and tormented, and having now almost despaired of their safety and release, they began to cry to the Lord, asking him, through the help of the true Cross which was at Grandmont and through the merits of blessed Stephen the confessor, first father of the Grandmontine Order, to free them.

By God’s mercy, after they had persevered throughout that whole night, praying to God with heartfelt devotion, divine compassion came to them and freed them in the following manner through the power of the aforesaid life-giving Cross and through the merits of blessed Stephen. At daybreak, on the day before the vigil of St John the Baptist, the shackles suddenly fell from the hands of the aforesaid man Iterius; but they did not fall from the other man’s hands until, under God’s guidance, they came to our house at Castaneariis. There they were received by the brethren with joy and gladness in honour and reverence of so great a miracle, and rested for three days.

The brethren of that place promptly sent us word of this while we were holding the general chapter at Grandmont. When we heard it, we rejoiced exceedingly and arranged for brethren to go out [Col. 1067D] to meet them and bring them to us. When these men came with the brethren, they were honourably received by us and by the entire community at Grandmont. Taking from their hands the iron shackles with which they had been grievously bound, we joyfully offered them together with hymns and praises at the tomb of Stephen the confessor. There visitors may continually see those shackles hanging as testimony to so illustrious a miracle. All these things occurred in the fifth year of the revelation of the same blessed Stephen the confessor.

## XXXI. Another miracle

At the same time another miracle, no less marvellous and worthy of celebration, occurred. A pestilential and most cruel band, accustomed under its leader—called Mercator—to serve robbery and wickedness, entered the territory of the diocese of Limoges to plunder. While they were devastating almost the whole land situated near Grandmont and spreading throughout that region, some of them came to a village of St Saviour. There, treacherously seizing a cleric named Gerard, they carried him captive to the village of Ambasiac. Afflicting him with severe tortures, threatening him with harsh words and rebukes, and fastening iron shackles upon his hands, they bound him tightly to a post, intending, when morning came, to kill him with various tortures because one of their company had met a most cruel death at the aforesaid village.

[Col. 1068B] This cleric was a good and gentle man, and he had great faith in the Lord. Captured by such and so great a treachery of those evildoers, he could not believe that God would permit them to keep or torture him for long. Therefore, devoting himself eagerly to prayer and vigils throughout the whole night, he began with all his heart to invoke the name of the Lord and the help of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Then, with many entreaties and prayers, he began to invoke the most holy confessor blessed Stephen and earnestly begged him in these words:

“O blessed Stephen! O most holy confessor! O most loving Father! Quickly come now to the aid of your unworthy and wretched servant; come to my aid, I say, for, as you see, I have been captured near your tomb, where I, unworthy though I am, have seen with my own eyes many miracles very often wrought by divine generosity and goodness. Come now, lord: show mercy to your servant and free me from the cruelty of these evildoers, lest all who afflict me rejoice over me. Rise to help me and show the power which I truly believe you possess with God’s favour. For if you decree to free me and bring me safe to your tomb, I shall continually invoke your name and shall not cease to make known your mighty works.”

While he anxiously spoke these words and others like them throughout that night, as dawn was approaching, behold, those who were in that dwelling suddenly fell asleep. [Col. 1068D] As they lay like dead men, the grace of God and the help of blessed Stephen suddenly came. The cleric was freed, for the Lord granted him aid, and, we believe, blessed Stephen had asked that he be released from his bonds. He was indeed freed from the post, with no fastening hindering him; but the iron shackles still hung upon his hands.

Seeing himself free, he sought God’s help, that through blessed Stephen, his guiding leader, he might be led back to shelter. He left the house confidently, found the doors open, and divine mercy led him to our threshold. Praises are sung to the Lord, which our congregation chants, for the wretched man freed from the prison of the wicked. The hard shackles which he brought from the prison are broken and hung [Col. 1069A] at the tomb because of so great a miracle. Thus the Lord is praised, and Stephen the good shepherd, through whom divine grace wrought such great wonders.

## XXXII. Another miracle

In the fifth year of the revelation of blessed Stephen the confessor, a miracle occurred in the village of Anginiac in the Limousin district, in the following manner. There was a priest there named Gerald, distinguished by lineage and rank, chaplain of the church of St Martial the apostle situated in that place. Suddenly, I know not by what chance, he was afflicted with such deafness that, if every cymbal were struck or drums sounded at his ears, he could hear absolutely nothing, as the same priest afterwards told us before many witnesses at Grandmont.

When he saw that he had completely lost his hearing, he went to the church of St Martial, where there is a memorial of Stephen the confessor, to the altar of the Blessed Mary ever-virgin and of the same blessed Stephen the confessor. Having received as a relic a tooth of blessed Stephen—which we had given to that priest—he, clothed in linen garments and having washed his hands, made the sign of the cross and touched his ears all around, having great faith in the Lord and the blessed man Stephen.

On the following night, by God’s mercy and, as we believe, with holy Stephen’s aid and prayer on his behalf, he deserved to recover his hearing, so completely that, as he afterwards firmly told us, he heard twice as well as before.

## XXXIII. Another miracle

[Col. 1069C] At the same time another miracle occurred in the Cahors district near the village of Saliniac. There was a dependent of the brethren of Lassiaisseras and of Podio Girberti, named Arnaldus, whose son Bernard was seized with a severe fever in the month of August. Seeing his beloved son distressed by such great suffering, the father became anxious and did not know what to do. Nevertheless, he sent word of his son’s illness to a friend named Bernardus Constantini, who was then staying at the village of Sarlat. This Bernardus had given the boy his name when he lifted him as an infant from the sacred font of baptism.

Thus distressed, Bernardus Constantini hurried quickly to the bed of the feverish child. When he arrived, he found the young man entirely spent, neither seeing nor hearing, but cast down as though dead in haircloth and ashes, according to the Christian custom of ending life. [Col. 1069D] The boy’s father and those with him wept and lamented over the young man’s passing.

Bernardus Constantini began to console the boy’s father and the others in that house with these words: “Beloved brethren, take care not to weep or be disturbed by any grief. Rather, let us all pray together to almighty God, that for love of blessed Stephen the confessor of Grandmont he may restore this boy to his former health.”

These words pleased them all. They all vowed him to St Stephen the most holy confessor, making a candle [Col. 1070A] and placing it upon him, and saying: “St Stephen, illustrious confessor of God, help us today, so that this boy may live again. For if through you we regain him, we shall gladly bring him with this candle to your tomb at Grandmont.”

Meanwhile, while this was being done, the young man saw a vision in this fashion. A certain old man appeared to him, white-haired and with a long beard, clothed in our habit, and said to him: “Come with me to Grandmont, and there, at the tomb of Stephen the confessor, you shall be healed, by the Lord’s favour.” The young man followed him, as he thought, setting out along the road; but the man left him during the journey. Therefore the boy who had lain as though dead cried out in a loud voice, to the hearing and amazement of all present: “Alas! Alas! Where is the man who was leading me? I do not know where he has gone.”

Thus, while all those present saw and rejoiced, through God’s mercy and the prayer of blessed Stephen on his behalf, he was restored to life. Those standing by began to ask why he had cried out thus. He said to them: “I do not know whether I cried out or not; but it seemed to me that I was being led to Grandmont by a most holy man, who sometimes went away from me while we were on the journey. Perhaps this was why I was asking where he was going.”

When all who had gathered for the rites of his death heard this, [Col. 1070C] they were struck with manifold amazement and began to praise the name of the Lord and exalt blessed Stephen with loud voices and praises. Then the aforesaid Bernardus Constantini, the boy’s godfather, brought him with him to Grandmont, as he had vowed, to the tomb of blessed Stephen. Through their faithful account, in the hearing of very many people, by the generosity of divine grace, we learned all these things.

## XXXIV. Another miracle
In the same year in which these things occurred, that is, about the feast of St. Luke the Evangelist, a certain remarkable and astonishing miracle took place near the castle called Mont-Mauril. A great and abundant fire suddenly began to devastate the houses of the aforesaid castle. There lived there a man named Peter Soutarius, a dependent of a certain house of our order called Entrefis. [Col. 1070D] This man had a large house among the others being consumed by the fire, furnished and laden with very many utensils and goods; against it the fierce fire advanced, as though threatening utterly to burn and lay it waste.

When the aforesaid dependent saw the violent fire, he fearlessly hurried out of the house with the utmost speed, taking and carrying away none of all his possessions. He began to cry aloud and say: “Saint Stephen, eminent confessor and venerable founder of the Order of Grandmont, you know that throughout my life, insofar as I have been able, by God’s inspiration, I have loved you and have long faithfully served your sons and disciples.”

Then all his friends who stood by, and those who had come [Col. 1071A] to help him, began vehemently to rebuke and reproach him, saying with great indignation: “What are you doing, wretched and pitiable man? Do you not see the abundant fire, burning and devastating everything, coming to destroy you? Allow us, we beg you: let some enter to strip the house, and let others climb upon the roof, so that in this way, God willing, we may rescue your house and all your goods from the fire.”

But he, being a man of great faith and integrity, replied as though mocking and reproving them: “See, beloved friends, see that you do not do this. I trust in God that my house, with God’s help and Saint Stephen’s aid, cannot in any way now be burned or destroyed by this fire. Go away, go away; help others, but not me. There is another whom you neither know nor can see, who will help me and deliver my house from this fire.” Again and again he cried out loudly: “Saint Stephen of God, help me, your unworthy servant, and defend my house, which is yours, from this fire.”

At this cry the fire suddenly broke apart, fled, and was shaken; the house was left untouched by it. God was blessed, and Saint Stephen of God was extolled with great praises. Nor is this surprising, for the fire had devastated all the houses round about and had never been able to touch that house, because divine power had preserved it through blessed Stephen. Afterwards the man came with his son to Grandmont and offered praise and thanks to God and blessed Stephen for [Col. 1071C] the benefit of this miracle; and he faithfully and truthfully disclosed all these things to us.

### XXXV. Another miracle likewise

At the same time, about the feast of blessed Luke the Evangelist, a glorious miracle occurred in the village of Saint-Junien in the Limousin territory, in the following manner. Iterius of Mont-Valerii, whom we mentioned above, whom the Lord God Almighty in that same year had delivered from the prison-house by the power of the life-giving cross and through love for blessed Stephen the confessor, was suddenly seized by a lethargic illness and brought almost to death.

His household and all his kinsfolk wept because they saw him suffering from such a great and grievous sickness. [Col. 1071D] They had already despaired of his life and bodily recovery. What more is there to say? They sent messengers [Col. 1072A] to us, asking that through our prayers before God and blessed Stephen we might bring him help. On hearing of his bodily illness, we were deeply distressed, for he was our friend and kinsman, conspicuous also for birth and nobility.

Therefore, summoning the brethren together and making the matter known to them, we enjoined them to pray for him and seek help from the Lord, so that through the intercession of most holy Stephen the confessor, God our Lord might deign to grant him help from above. Afterwards we took care to send our messenger with all speed, carrying provisions necessary for the sick man.

When he hurried into the sick man’s house, he found him already laid upon ashes and haircloth, as is the custom for Christians [Col. 1072B] who are dying; his friends were wailing and weeping, making preparations for the funeral, while clerics chanted and sang psalms. He lay as though dead, seeing and hearing absolutely nothing. It was the vigil of All Saints.

Calling to him with a great cry and lament, the aforesaid messenger began to say: “Lord Iterius, behold, I am the messenger of the Lord Prior of Grandmont. I beg you, for love of him and for the affection which you bear toward him, to pour out in your heart—if indeed you cannot do so with your lips—a prayer to the Lord, that for the love and honor of blessed Stephen the confessor he may deign to release you from this illness.”

And what shall I say? At the voice and exhortation of this messenger, the sick man began to invoke him in his heart [Col. 1072C] and, as best he could, to make supplication to blessed Stephen. Then all who stood by likewise did not cease to pour out prayer to the Lord for him, and with continual prayer they entreated blessed Stephen to pray swiftly on his behalf. After all had continued in prayer for some time, the sick man was suddenly healed; his countenance was changed for the better and he became joyful. Thus no trace whatever of illness remained in his body. His friends, who had formerly been weeping, now rejoiced and congratulated him, and on that day and thereafter there was great joy and exultation in that house.

Afterward, restored to health and cheerful, he came to Grandmont to visit the tomb of blessed Stephen and offer him thanks for the twofold benefit of healing [Col. 1072D] and deliverance from prison, granted within a short space of time.

[Col. 1071]

# THE SAYINGS AND DEEDS OF ST. STEPHEN, written, as we conjecture, at the command of Stephen of Liciac, and inserted by Gerard of Iterius into the Life of the same saint composed by himself

## I. Here are briefly set forth and brought together the virtues of the conduct and holiness of blessed Stephen the confessor

[Col. 1071D]

Holy Stephen, therefore, first founder of the venerable [Col. 1072D] Order of Grandmont, beloved by God and men, and distinguished hermit, was adorned with the ornament of humility, virginity, truthfulness, obedience, abstinence, patience, faith, hope, charity, prudence, [Col. 1073A] justice, fortitude, temperance, and the other virtues, as we stated above.

He was, so to speak, small and great; humble and exalted; poor and rich. He set spiritual things before carnal things, eternal before temporal, sacrificed himself wholly to God, and left everything for him alone. Handsome in body but more handsome in heart; gracious in speech but more gracious in deed; noble by birth but nobler in holiness, he was a pattern of religious life, a rule of perfection, and a way of salvation. Devoting himself earnestly to vigils, prayers, sighs, groans, tears, genuflections, fasts, and almsgiving, he flourished and gave forth fragrance in spiritual life and wholesome teaching.

On the wings of holy contemplation he often flew upward; with ardent desire he dwelt [Col. 1073B] in heaven; he strove to fix his whole heart in the Lord. Divinely enlightened, he enlightened others; kindled from heaven, he kindled others; enriched to the marrow, he enriched others; filled to the depths, he made others drunk. Clothed day and night in an iron breastplate and everywhere armed with divine weapons, he manfully won the everlasting kingdom both for himself and for many others. Persevering most holily for almost fifty years in his purpose of holiness, he, a glorious soldier, passed on to the glorious King by a glorious end on the sixth day before the Ides of February.

That he was rightly called Stephen, and with how great glory and honor he is crowned, is testified and declared not only by the wondrous perfection of his own person, but also by the manifold evidence of his daughter, namely the religion of Grandmont. [Col. 1073C]

## II. On his charity, gentleness, long-suffering, and other virtues

This holy man, full of every goodness, continually pursued charity, gentleness, and long-suffering. He loved God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength. He was calm in manner and serene in countenance. He bore a peaceful face, a moderate appearance, a comely expression, a tranquil disposition, a cheerful spirit, and humble wisdom.

He always displayed good works more by deeds than by words: chastening his body with hunger, loving fasting rather than feasts, comforting the afflicted, committing his hope to God, frequently devoting himself to prayer, and preferring nothing to God’s love. What he believed he taught; what he taught he imitated. The last day was always before his eyes, and his mind continually meditated upon the heavenly commandments.

He prayed often because he had learned that the Lord must be asked without ceasing. He strove with all his power that none might be found second to him in good works. He was also very humane and kind toward God’s servants. He himself loved charity above all things and commanded everyone to preserve it. In every circumstance he remained steadfast, and he bore all adversities patiently. He feared others’ dangers as his own and judged the misfortunes of others to be his own.

He also continually considered the end of his life, fearing lest [Col. 1074A] that hour should seize him unarmed like a thief. Along with manual work he gave himself to reading, knowing that reading increases understanding and gives discernment, and that reading teaches what should be avoided. He was humble toward all and deeply grounded in humility, preferring himself to no one and accounting himself superior to none. He knew also that whoever is content with perfect humility will receive glory from it, and that the humbler one is, the greater the height of glory that will follow.

He had moderation in prosperity and patience in adversity; neither joy nor sorrow ever recalled his mind from Christ’s love. He soothed an angry man with patience and tempered the rage of one in fury by gentleness; and thus he mourned another’s misery as though it were his own. His step was simple, his movement pure, his bearing grave, his gait honorable, his fasting cheerful. For his soul appeared in the most modest habit of his body.

He was sparing in speech and gentle in expression; with sweet words he comforted the sad, indeed the afflicted. From his lips proceeded what would edify the hearer’s mind, and his speech proved useful to the people who heard it. He attributed none of the good things he had done to his own merits and never presumed upon his own powers; but always referring every work to God, he implored God’s help in all his actions.

He taught the good which he had learned, but put deeds before words, knowing [Col. 1074C] that what one teaches is not worthy of praise unless one joins deeds to words; rather, if one both teaches and does what one teaches, then one will be accounted glorious. Hence the Apostle says: “Lest, after I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9).

Moreover, he continually strove to repel the invisible enemy by prayers and petitions, fighting with his mouth, not a sword; with prayers, not a missile; with petitions, not iron. On every day and at every hour he begged for God’s protection, that after the light of this world he might be worthy to attain the prize. He gave temporal goods to the needy in order thereby to purchase the delights of paradise. He avoided pride, embraced humility, always sought God’s help, and continually prayed for a blessed end.

Who, seeing his humility at that time, would not immediately be pierced with compunction? Or what lover of money, beholding his humanity and frugality, his devotion also and zeal, would not at once stand amazed in admiration? For whatever good purpose he undertook at the beginning, he did not allow any business to entangle it until the end of his life. Preserving an unblemished and holy purpose, he altered in nothing the rule he had begun.

Under the habit of another he always served another; and whatever he could possess in the world he gave wholly to Christ. More and more he excelled in vigils, fasts, and charity. He was generous in almsgiving, diligent in vigils, devout in prayer, perfect in charity, overflowing in humility, eminent in teaching, ready in speech, cautious in conversation, most holy in conduct, bound by no chain of the world, prompt in service to God’s servants, solicitous for the ransom of captives, lavish in gifts to the needy, strong amid harsh sufferings, cheerful in good works, most steadfast in temptation, and most generous in hospitality. Secure amid reproaches, beneficent amid hatred, in prosperity as also in adversity he was always intent upon heaven.

For the enemy of the human race could find in him nothing that he might deceive by fraud or darken by pretense. He revealed sincerity of mind by serenity of face and displayed the compassion of his most merciful heart in gentleness of speech. Nothing was more merciful than his spirit; nothing more pleasing than his severity; nothing more severe than his pleasantness; [Col. 1075B] nothing more grave than his laughter; nothing whatever sweeter than his sadness.

If he saw a poor person, he supported him; if a rich person, he exhorted him to do good, calling God as witness that he did all these things for God’s name. For this most holy man wholly overflowed with the inward affections of charity. Bearing the Lord’s cross in mind and body, he had one concern altogether: to bring sinners back to the way of truth.

Whenever he found someone willing to hear God’s word, neither the matter of food nor that of sleep, neither cold nor heat, delayed him from this work of Christ. He wisely gave diverse counsels of salvation to different persons, introducing fitting enigmas into his words so that they might be heard more attentively, as though displaying honey enclosed in wax; thus he said to some:

## III. On certain counsels given  
[Note: [Col. 1075D] Compare chapter 57 of the *Sentences*, below.]

“Many people need this: that they should perform the good things which they do, especially while holding the conviction of their perdition. For whoever is held in some sin ought not, on that account, to cease from good works; rather, he should strive all the more eagerly to do as much good as he can. But let him believe without doubt and continually think in his heart, saying: ‘Lord God, I do these good things; nevertheless, I do not doubt that I shall be damned without end if I die in sin. I perform this good deed only with this intention: that I may deserve to rise from my iniquity.’

“And this, I say, is the useful conviction of perdition. For if a sinner continually meditates on such things, he will very quickly be delivered from wickedness through this thought; and the good things which he did while remaining in sin will be faithfully preserved for him by the Lord—things which he would not have had if he had then ceased to act.” [Col. 1075D]

## IV. What counsel he gave to soldiers wishing to go out for plunder  
[Note: [Col. 1076D] Compare chapter 63 of the *Sentences*.]

To soldiers seeking counsel concerning plunder he said this: “My brother, if you wish, when you proceed to plunder you may gain Christ. But let this be fixed at the outset in your heart: make this vow to the Lord—‘My God, I shall go there not in order to harm anyone; rather, I account myself solely your soldier upon this road, seeking safety for all residents [Col. 1076A] and strangers. Meanwhile, since compelled only by the necessity of your earthly lord you go there, run first as though a plunderer, and make all whom you see flee; or, if they are to be captured by others, seize them first, so that afterward you may be able to set them free. And behold: if you observe this, you are Christ’s monk hidden beneath a shield.’”

## V. Likewise, on a person making alms from plunder

“Take care not to make alms from plunder. For the sin is greater when it is offered to the poor—except only to those who complain—than when it was taken from those who possessed it. For you truly believed that you sinned in plundering, but you suppose that you are absolved by what you offered. Yet God accepts such a sacrifice as you would accept blood, if your only son had been killed [Col. 1076B] and it were offered you in a golden cup to drink.”

## VI. How he instructed clerics and learned men to act rightly

Moreover, he admonished clerics and learned men differently according to their knowledge and manner of life, not exalting himself through teaching but always humbling himself. Thus he is reported to have given the following reply to a learned man seeking counsel under temptation:

“My lord, have you ever thought in your heart of something which you judged to be right and which pleased you as you thought of it?”

“Certainly,” the other replied.

“Again, have you ever meditated in your mind upon anything which undoubtedly appeared altogether unjust to you?”

Again he said: “Yes.”

Finally the man of God said: “Then you have within yourself what you seek from another: do in deed what you discern in your mind to be right.”

Then the learned man aptly added: “You do not dwell here alone: the Lord and angels are your many companions.” [Col. 1076C]

## VII. How he formed religious men in righteousness

He also formed the conduct of religious men toward righteousness, suitably saying to them: “Take care, brothers, not to love the world. If you follow the age, you will never overtake it. If you flee from it, it will come after you, God compelling it.”

Further, he said to his disciples: “Although we cannot provide sufficiently for religious men, they must nevertheless be drawn to our guesthouse, for poverty itself is useful and our modest provision is honorable. Otherwise, if we send them elsewhere [Col. 1076D] to the lodging of a rich man, those who assist them will gain the profit that we have set aside. On the night on which they dwell with us, they are kept from the world in praise of God.”

## VIII. Why he bestowed temporal goods upon prostitutes and actors

Finally, he willingly expended his own material goods as well as spiritual goods upon prostitutes and actors, saying concerning this matter: “If a sinner who comes to us hears words of harshness, he will think God harsh and will cling more heavily to his iniquity. But he will more readily obey one who announces salvation to his soul if he first receives what his body needs. [Col. 1077A] For many sin in order to drive away their poverty, although through crimes they become poorer, not richer. Therefore, if spiritual things must be administered to them so that they may be freed from error, temporal things must much more be given them so that they may serve Christ, who mercifully—not ignorantly—waits for them to be converted.”

By this deed the wise may recognize how greatly blessed Stephen, following the Apostle Paul, went beyond what was required in healing the wounds of the man who fell among robbers (Luke 10). Yet with admirable charity he drew sinners back from iniquity, saying most kindly to them when he saw penitents somewhat afraid: “My brother, do not be frightened. You cannot overcome God so as to be more powerful in sinning than he is in forgiving. Your sins are small when you turn to [Col. 1077B] God. If they were equal to mine, you would be more heavily burdened. Certainly the Apostle Peter had not yet perfectly recognized the devil’s deceits when he asked Christ whether he should forgive a brother who sinned seven times; but Jesus multiplied forgiveness, taking no account of the disciple’s ignorance” (Matt. 18).

Such things he said to penitents; but toward the obstinate, and those defending themselves, he was strict, without however departing from moderation.

## IX. Why he avoided fraternities of secular people

Meanwhile, some asked him as a favor of friendship, for the redemption of souls and the benefit of the poor, to permit a gathering of people to be held there which is commonly called a “brothers’ feast” (*convivium fratrum*). Having carefully investigated it, as though entirely ignorant of it, he shrewdly asked how many times a year it was held. When they explained, as though instructing him, he guarded against avarice and, unwilling to lose his peace, firmly replied: “You urge us to establish an annual association, but we strive to observe one continuously. What else do we do every day but public works? Whatever goods we have are common to all. Know that we cannot add prayers longer than those of the brethren. What more, then, can we promise you, so that we may receive more of your goods, when we would give nothing else?” [Col. 1077C]

Afterwards he privately explained the people’s request to his disciples, saying: “In this and that manner they urge us, not realizing indeed that under the appearance of goodness we should become Simoniacs. But far be it from us to sell a divine office! For it is the work of a hireling to pray when something is given, and to cease from prayers when nothing is given.” [Col. 1077D]

## X. On the distribution of alms

We cannot explain how great was this man’s constant care for poor people outside the community. Casting his thought upon the Lord, he had resolved in his heart faithfully to place, in separate chests, each person’s alms as he received them from others, saying to those who gave: “Why do you burden us, brother?”

Thereafter he was diligent in returning gifts received from noble clerics to poor persons of the same rank. With discernment he knew what ought to be given to orphans, widows, and all others, lest he should be accursed for doing God’s work negligently.

## XI. On the distinction between alms

[Col. 1078A]

But what he received from the parish itself he bestowed upon the poor of the same parish where he lived, not upon outsiders. He gave this reason: “We have come here from elsewhere into the place of these poor people, receiving alms owed to them; if we are able, we ought to return them to those same persons.”

## XII. How he behaved toward the poor

Sometimes, when evening drew on and a multitude of noble men who had come to hear him had departed, a crowd of needy people remained with him. Then, most tenderly, he kissed paralytics as though they were brothers. To his disciples, who urged him not to go to them when tired, he replied: “Now that Christ has arrived, you tell me to withdraw, though today [Col. 1078B] I have remained with the powerful people of this world. Far be such disgrace from me, that I should not run to Christ! For Truth, which can neither deceive nor be deceived, would never have sent his poor people here in vain, unless he knew that we possessed something which could be given to them. Where now could we find so many messengers to send to them, as we should have had to do, if Christ had not brought them, he alone who knows how to choose?”

No poor person ever returned from him empty-handed. He continually recalled in his mind the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5); and also: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 33); and: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11).

For as it is said of blessed Job that his door stood open to every comer, so he too could proclaim freely with Job: “My door stood open to the traveler” (Job 31). He was a foot to the lame and an eye to the blind, a father of orphans and comforter of widows. He never denied his help, insofar as his resources allowed, to those shut in prison or worn down by illness; rather, mercifully caring for all the afflicted, he supplied assistance.

What blind person did he not call his own heir? What disabled person did his hand not support? His doors were besieged by the wretched; seeing Christ in them, he eagerly embraced them, and by giving them garments he believed that he clothed Christ’s limbs beneath the dress of the poor person. [Col. 1078D] He truly considered that he lost whatever almsgiving did not take up. He joyfully judged that he laid up in the safest place what the harsh necessity of the needy took from him.

Most devout in their needs, he increased the weight of his substance, so that the poorer he was in the world, the richer he might become toward God. He considered that sin cannot fail to occur every day; therefore daily alms, by which stains might be wiped away, ought not to fail. For this reason, dividing his money with his Lord, he rejoiced to associate his property with Christ, making Christ a sharer in his earthly possessions so that Christ might make him a coheir of heavenly kingdoms.

He entrusted his resources to Christ, that Christ might be their perpetual guardian, knowing that an inheritance entrusted [Col. 1079A] to God is neither carried off by the state, invaded by the treasury, nor overthrown by any lawsuit in court. He knew also that it is written that an inheritance is well laid up when it is preserved with God as its guardian.

For his counsels among his own people were nothing other than divine teachings: foundations for strengthening faith, nourishment for sustaining the soul, rudders for directing one’s course, and safeguards for attaining salvation. It is therefore fitting that religious persons should imitate and love him, that the people should honor him, and that the wicked should fear him, whom divine power so illumined that even beneath a lay habit he possessed gifts bestowed by God: teaching sweet as honey, seasoned by the Holy Spirit, salted with desire for Christ, and concerned for eternal blessedness. He was so religious and God-fearing that, forgetting the dignities [Col. 1079B] of the world, he shared all fellowship with the needy and the religious.

## XIII. Likewise, concerning the same man

Above all, though poor himself, he continually lent to the poor without interest; he was a comforter of widows and orphans, an imitator indeed of the widow of Zarephath (3 Kings 17). Often hungry himself, he distributed his own lawful substance to Christ’s members. If he saw a sick person, he comforted him mercifully. If he saw someone burning with love for God, he exhorted him to zeal. If anyone came to him sick, he was so cared for by his ministry that he desired neither the luxuries of cities nor a mother’s affectionate care.

He had so devotedly given himself to serving the weak that many healthy poor persons envied the sick. For Christ’s love he constantly cared for them, so that all the poor rejoiced to have him as their own father. He knew what the rich man clothed in purple had once failed to do for Lazarus, and by what recompense a proud mind was condemned (Luke 16). Therefore, showing himself more and more merciful toward all, he continually came to the aid of the afflicted with compassion.

For with whose pain did he not suffer, or at whose ruin did he not groan? What naked or ashamed person was not covered by his clothing? What hardships did he not endure for the hope of eternity—namely hunger and thirst? Persevering in such a purpose, he made himself for the future a vessel of election, useful to God and ready for every good work.

He shone in appearance [Col. 1079D] and was strong in virtue. He conducted himself as though he were about to die every day; therefore he subdued the resistant flesh by hunger, and, anticipating the cruel torments of avenging Gehenna, he became his own persecutor and torturer. If the circumstances of the time had permitted, he desired to become a martyr for the Creator’s name. But although a persecutor did not pierce him with his fist, he willingly imposed daily martyrdom upon himself.

Hunger served him in place of claws, thirst in place of flame, the calamity of the world in place of beasts, abstinence in place of the gridiron. Bound by a harsh law under the likeness of martyrdom, as though by a chain of rigid iron, he denied himself to himself so that he might gain Christ. He longed for him and thirsted for him with immense eagerness: for him who became man for love of humankind and descended from the Father’s bosom to earth to draw us to heaven.

Pouring out upon him all his toil and all his love, he cultivated the good soil of his heart by continual cultivation and unceasing exercises. Like a hungry and thirsty man, enduring a certain longing, he frequently lamented in a tearful voice the Psalmist’s saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and be at rest?” (Ps. 54). And: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41). And Solomon’s words: “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

Moreover, in all things he pursued gentleness and faith, and also perfect charity, which is the bond of spiritual edification. He strove to present himself as a sanctified vessel, so that he might receive God, its indweller, in the guest-chamber of his mind. [Col. 1080B] He was continually occupied with saving deeds, so that whenever the tempter approached, whenever the crafty enemy sought an entrance, he might always find the door of the saint’s breast closed against him.

According to the Apostle, he frequently prayed for all people, for kings and for those in high station, that they might lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and charity (1 Tim. 2), knowing, according to the same Apostle, that this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth (ibid.).

## XIV. On the exalted excellence of the righteous man

Why should I linger by saying more? In all his conduct, shining like Lucifer among the stars, he gleamed like a great lamp. For he always emulated the perfect in goodness, and always set before himself the virtues of others as examples. Slow to speak, according to the Apostle, and swift to hear (James 1), he was subtle in speech, lofty in humility, rich in alms, patient in charity, watchful in fasting, ready in expression, and burning with zeal for the holy Scriptures—truly a useful vessel in Christ’s house.

He was not slow to heed the words of the afflicted, ready for prayer, lavish in almsgiving, most generous in giving, cultivating gentleness, greatly rejoicing in poverty, holding fast to goodness, always embracing purity of heart, and preaching all things to all people. For him, to live was nothing other than to fear Christ with love [Col. 1080D] and to love him with fear.

O truly blessed enemy of the world, to whom the world was so greatly crucified, and he to the world! He was so wakeful in wisdom and gentle in mildness that he possessed the serpent’s prudence with discernment, yet did not lose the spirit of the simple dove. In his mind wisdom, a most sober dwelling-place, established the beauty of every virtue: a temple truly most worthy for the Lord to inhabit, cleansed by fasts, adorned by prayers, filled with purity, and trained by vigils.

Who could be so obstinate that, seeing his moderation, he would not immediately stand amazed in admiration? Or what arrogant person, considering his sober life, would not at once turn himself toward equity? In him daily grew a reputation that served the virtues. [Col. 1081A] He sowed among the people words of truth overflowing with the fruit of faith, seasoned with sufficient salt and infused, as it were, with aromatic ointments.

For, as a watchman appointed by the Lord, he preached the word with all authority. According to the Apostle, he persisted in season and out of season, reproving, beseeching, rebuking with all patience and teaching (2 Tim. 4), always making gracious either his address to the people concerning divine matters or his discourse in brotherly fellowship.

## XV. Likewise, concerning the same man
Surely, if he saw anyone wounded by harmful sins and pierced by the devil’s arrows, he at once applied the fitting remedies of discourse and the healing medicine of God’s word, [Col. 1081B] showing that against the wounds inflicted by the tempter, the wholesome poultice is confession. He also gently rebuked the breaches of discipline and transgressions of his own people from the honorable and right rule, and bore them patiently. In all his works there was marvelous discernment, and unchanging love toward all.

Thus Stephen was chaste in deed, Catholic in faith, lavish in charity, cautious in interpretation, most steadfast in faith, prompt in good works, most truthful in speech, just in judgment, provident in counsel, conspicuous in goodness, outstanding in charity: diligently serving God, correcting those who went astray, encouraging those corrected, rejecting the obstinate, and always loving the humble. There likewise abounded in him constancy of faith, purity of affection, [Col. 1081C] sincerity of peace, and the love of charity. With just zeal he urged the children of his teaching toward eternal life; he instructed them by exhortation, went before them by example, did what he taught and taught what he did, neither uttering one thing with his mouth while turning another over in his heart. Rather, he confirmed by work what he taught by word; as was his speech, such was his life, and as was his life, such also was his speech.

With the utmost goodness he governed those subject to him; with the utmost severity he subdued himself. He was not sufficiently terrible toward those under him, but was exceedingly austere in respect of sins: in himself he maintained strictness; toward others he displayed justice. He employed rigor in the examination of justice, mercy in determining judgment. Yet he always tempered the severity of discipline with mercy, knowing what is written: that one shall be judged in that wherein one judges (Matt. 7); that the powerful shall suffer powerful torments (Wis. 6); and that judgment will be most severe for those who preside (ibid.). [Col. 1081D]

Considering these things attentively in his mind, he maintained discernment in every action. He never behaved without restraint, but, carefully distinguishing all things, always preserved measure and moderation alike in discipline and modesty. Above all he loved the Lord with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength; then his neighbor as himself (Matt. 22). Persevering without weariness in the law of the Lord, he did not stain good morals by any harmful conduct. He regarded temporal life as exile and desired eternal life with every spiritual longing.

Guarding the actions of his life at every hour, he kept the eye [Col. 1082A] of his mind always fixed upon God. With diligent care he abstained from everything forbidden by the law, and recalled his soul even from harmful thought, knowing that a human being must also be judged for thoughts. Presuming nothing of himself, he ascribed the good done by himself to God’s gift. He invited even those who hated him to peace and recalled the discordant to concord. Always turning his counsel and work toward God, in every endeavor he begged for Christ’s aid.

His feet were always directed to proclaim peace, to proclaim good things; with honorable bearing and a gracious spirit he went his way. And, like the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord appointed over his household to give them food at the necessary time, he hastened by every means to refresh with spiritual food the people entrusted to him: teaching gently, instructing most effectively, and striving with all his strength to draw all away from the habit of sinning. [Col. 1082B]

Moreover, he was fervent in spirit, tireless in diligence, distinguished in manners, adorned with works, and conspicuous in every gracious quality; constant in prayer, vigorous in fasting, lavish in almsgiving. He stood between rich and poor in such a way that the poor looked upon him as a father and the rich as one set above them. For he paid attention not to the power of a person’s rank, but rather to excellence of conduct; and he honored each person more highly in proportion as that person had learned to live more holy a life.

Toward the needy and strangers he showed himself so solicitous that he believed with whole faith that Christ was truly in them, and rejoiced not so much that he was giving something to them [Col. 1082C] as that he was giving the same things to Christ himself. He ministered food to them, while his eyes looked upward to heaven. He provided them with nourishment and invoked Christ with confidence. He stretched out his arms in giving, undoubtedly awaiting recompense from on high.

For how great a mass of possessions Stephen scattered abroad, inflamed by the love of God, it is not ours to recount in full. What poor person was not reached by his almsgiving? What cleric was not refreshed by his resources? What pilgrim was not received into his hospitality? Or to what strangers did he not render his service? Seeking them out with the greatest care everywhere, he counted it his own loss if any weak or hungry person were sustained by another’s generosity. For, [Col. 1082D] joined with his whole soul to the Savior in most ardent faith, he rendered to him what he had received from him. Believing that he saw Christ in each of Christ’s servants, he rejoiced that whatever he bestowed upon them he had bestowed upon God, continually pondering what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). And: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3). And: “Make for yourselves friends from unrighteous mammon, who may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). And: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). Exercised in pursuits of this kind, holy Stephen was attended ever more abundantly by divine grace.

## XVI. On the Loftiness of His Speech and Learning

[Col. 1083A]

Among his other virtues, his speech also was richly seasoned with the salt of wisdom, knowledge, and consolation. He possessed Christ’s humility beyond measure, and charity in equal degree. He did not set a rich person before a poor one in honor, nor prefer a prince or nobleman to a lowly subordinate; rather, he showed himself stricter toward the former and more gentle toward the latter. Nor did he afflict his disciples in the manner of masters; rather, he loved them kindly and modestly with brotherly charity.

But what and how great was his evenness of mind and patience in bearing with the perverse? He was intent on bending unbelievers toward faith by persuasion, softening the ungrateful by service, answering opponents [Col. 1083B] gently, and humbly bearing with the proud. He was strong for every endurance, gentle in suffering injury, and ready in showing mercy. He gave resources to the needy, entrusting his money to Christ so that from him he might receive eternal rewards. He said that his possessions were not his own but belonged to the poor, whose stewardship he seemed in some sense to administer.

In short, by giving generously to the needy, he stored all his riches in heavenly treasuries; by righteous action he transferred all his household goods to paradise, conveying them there where he might receive the fruit of an eternal possession, hiding treasures there where he might live happily and gloriously without end. This same blessed man, moreover, was firm in Christ’s faith, just in work, prudent in judgment, perfect in humility, girded for devotion, most gracious in manners, most learned in understanding, peaceable in spirit, and most devout in heart. [Col. 1083C]

He continually maintained sincerity in his actions, purity in his heart, virtue in his work, and discipline in his manners. In simplicity he practiced innocence; in charity, concord; in humility, modesty; in administration, diligence; in helping those who labored, watchfulness; in supporting the poor, mercy; and in defending doctrine, constancy. His speech was always seasoned with charity and gentleness, and with it he illuminated the minds of his hearers like a most brilliant lamp.

O man truly worthy of imitation! O blessed seed of Abraham! O example of Stephen to be preferred above all others! Rightly, therefore, he is called a son of Abraham, since he follows the order of his father’s glorious dignity. Deservedly, I say, he is reckoned Abraham’s offspring: by faith, not lineage; by imitation, not descent; by devotion, not stock. Abraham’s blessing deserved a son; blessed Stephen, however, is transferred into the number of sons. The former offered his son to the Lord; the latter offered himself, more precious than every gift. Abraham indeed surrendered an heir; this man likewise surrendered an inheritance. The former gave the innocence of his offspring; the latter, all his possessions. Therefore likeness in duties must bring likeness in merits. Finally, Abraham offered the pledge that he possessed; Stephen committed to the Lord’s right and judgment everything that he could possess in the world. [Col. 1083D]

[Col. 1084A] But it would now take too long to go through the individual distinctions of his virtues in words, especially because this book, already filled beyond measure, demands its end and cuts off the discourse; and because the thinness of our speech, as though nearly exhausted by a long journey, gives way. This is not because it has exhausted all that ought to be told about blessed Stephen—for it has not, so to speak, reached even a hundredth part of the precious and greatest adornments of every good thing which the prerogative of heavenly recompense bestowed upon him—but because, like some high rock rising aloft and already grown to great size, by its very length it sets itself before the brow of its narrator.

We trust, not in our own merits but in his, that the work begun may faithfully and happily be brought through to its end, [Col. 1084B] if he himself may deign to intercede in heaven for us with Christ the Lord. Through that same Lord he deserved, by Christ’s gift, to work such great wonders on earth: our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

## The Verses on the Virtues of the Same Man Begin

Founder of the Grandmontine religious order,

After Christ Stephen crushed the head of ambition.

He was an Auvergnat, the glory of his native people;

the eternal King was the wise man’s protection.

A disciple of Christ, he was zealous in Christ;

a servant of the Most High, he was precious to the Most High.

He joined himself to the Lord; God anointed him inwardly.

[Col. 1084C]

He himself was a worshipper of God and a stern avenger upon himself.

He strove to serve the heavenly King and enjoy the trophy,

and labored to subdue the flesh.

A royal soldier, he toiled to conquer

the deadly wickedness of the world and prepared to fly upward.

Glorious against the black enemies, he was their bitter foe;

in deeds and words he stood opposed to evil-speaking.

He nourished the soul, knowing how to subject the flesh to it.

He vowed himself to the Lord and put away what must be removed.

He despised the riches of the city and grew in the summit of merits.

Full of justice, he was both rich and poor;

he was greatest and least, exalted and lowly.

Thus divine mercy made the man wonderful.

Happy in his blessed life, he was a happy hermit;

he was an angelic man, a friend of the divine law.

[Col. 1084D]

Prudent simplicity shone in the holy Father;

flourishing virginity gave forth fragrance in the devout Father;

inward nobility made him mature.

Though he possessed the distinction of lofty descent,

nobility of character made him still more honorable.

A virginal dove, he was far from the serpent;

a man full of the Lord, he was free from slippery sins;

a man pleasing to the Lord, he was made radiant by merits.

For a long time he fixed his washed heart wholly in heaven.

In Stephen shone the light of living reason;

in Stephen flourished the sweat of a mighty contest.

The Lamb taught him to avoid the dragon’s deceit;

the Lamb granted him strength to crush the lion.

With all his might he strove to placate the source of goodness

and, as far as he could, to overthrow the head of wickedness.

[Col. 1085A]

Joined in love to heaven, he rejoiced in the Prince alone.

The illustrious Prince, dearer than all things to his servant,

was for him blessed consolation and help,

and was the guardian of his lover at every hour.

The man of pure mind uttered abundant groans;

anxious and joyful, he poured out streams of tears.

A reprover of sin, he became a builder of the flock;

a planter of peace, he was an abolisher of strife;

a keeper of justice, he was a destroyer of deceit.

Desiring to become a divine man inwardly and outwardly,

he sought enduring things and despised things that pass away.

He lived for Christ and strove to die to the world.

He sought the kingdom and sacrificed himself to the King.

He cultivated bright things and shone with the light of virtues.

The Father’s diligence guarded against deeds of error;

[Col. 1085B]

the hermit’s goodness performed deeds of piety;

the warrior’s uprightness endured the weapons of the enemy;

the virgin’s integrity loved the King’s embrace.

He lacked the vice of dark duplicity,

for he shone with the ray of venerable simplicity.

He did not cease to trust in the counsel of the Godhead,

and, with exceeding desire, to be joined to the glorified.

Growing in his heart, he worshipped the King of mercy.

He was drunk with spiritual sweetness

and strove to become a companion in the imperial warfare.

The luxury of miserable brevity displeased him;

what the King gave him was that of perpetual newness.

He flourished in the nobility of manifold virtue,

[Col. 1086A]

and therefore deserved to enjoy the blessedness of paradise.

Simple and upright, refreshed with heavenly honey,

he fed many with both bodily fare and spiritual food,

and strove to clothe the naked.

He rendered to Christ what Christ bestowed upon him:

a praiseworthy shepherd, wondrous and venerable,

a vigilant seeker of the honor of the supreme Shepherd.

He would not what was impious; he willed the divine will.

With prudent heart he rejoiced in the Almighty.

To the glorious King he sang psalms with chaste heart.

To the wondrous Father he gave answering song with gentle heart.

To the festal King he cried aloud with living heart.

The praise of the Psalmist was the voice of his heart and mouth;

he answered it, and pleased the Lord in his mind.

His heart was steeped in divine nectar;

[Col. 1086B]

with the cry of his heart he filled the divine ears,

and the fragrance of his prayer smelled sweeter to God than incense.

Resolved at the Lord’s nod to obey the Lord,

the Rich One made him rich; the Wondrous One made him wondrous;

the Most High honored him and numbered him among the exalted.

The flower of hermits, thirsty for the gain of souls,

he abhorred what harms and hungered for what profits.

He rejected harmful things and sowed health-giving seed.

He soothed the fierce, rebuked the wanton,

bent the hard, and aided the oppressed.

Whomever the wolf was pressing, he urged to return to the sheepfold;

he burned for what abides and fled whatever flees.

[Col. 1085]

# BOOK OF THE SAYINGS OR REASONINGS OF SAINT STEPHEN, Founder of the Grandmontine Order, Commonly Called the Order of Good Men

(*Maxims of Saint Stephen, founder of the Order of Grandmont, called the Order of Good Men; translated from the saint’s originals by Adrien Baillet. Paris, 1707, duodecimo.*)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1085C]

Lord Stephen taught his disciples in many ways how they should answer those who asked them about their manner of life. He said to them:

“Brothers, do not be surprised if some disagree with your life and with your elders, since you differ from what they maintain and do not wish to follow them in what they do. Why, then, should you be surprised at them? Other religious persons, however, are not at all asked what Rule they observe. Their garment identifies certain ones: these are under the Rule of Saint Augustine, and among those the Order of Saint Benedict is observed. Thus, brothers, many will say to you: ‘What you observe is a novelty; it is neither an order nor the Rule of the doctors of holy Church.’ [Col. 1086C]

“But although the one who says this to you has clothing and the mark of religious life, I tell you firmly that he has denied his own life, being ignorant of what an order or Rule is. Answer him in this way.”

## THE BROTHERS’ ANSWER

“Since you condemn our life and conduct, show us in what respect; and we shall gladly amend it if you can demonstrate this to us by evangelical authority. Then, brothers, if he does not immediately answer you, begin to mention your observances to him in this manner:

“Does our pastor depart from order or Rule because, remaining in his cloister, he tends, with the help of divine grace, to the souls of the disciples [Col. 1087A] entrusted to him by God? Does our pastor cast us out from order or Rule because he preserves among us a community of all things, allowing no one, with God’s help, to possess anything as his own except only the love of God and service to others? Tell us, you who condemn our conduct, whether our pastor expels us from order or Rule because he does not permit us to return to the homes of the relatives we have left, nor wishes us, when they come to us, to disclose our poverty to them.

“Does our pastor exclude us from order or Rule because he does not allow us to enter castles or cities, unless a journey requires us to pass through them and we cannot go by another way? Does our pastor again cast us out from order or Rule because he does not permit us to visit markets and fairs, not wishing us to be traders or merchants? [Col. 1087B] Does our pastor cast us out from order or Rule because he does not allow us to have tithes, revenues, and large landed possessions, through which we would often have to contend in court with secular persons? Likewise, does our pastor expel us from order or Rule because he does not permit us to accept churches and the things belonging to them?

“Does our pastor exclude us from order or Rule because he commands us to live without the care of animals, so that we may serve God more freely? Again, does our pastor transgress order or Rule because he receives no women into his religious community and permits them neither to sleep in the cells [Col. 1087C] nor to work with the brothers? Does our pastor cast us out from order or Rule because neither he nor his disciples accepts pledges for appearances in court? Finally, does our pastor expel us from order or Rule because he allows us to recover none of the secular business that we have renounced, commanding us to remain in the wilderness as dead men, cast off from the world?

“Brothers, you may answer with words of this kind those who condemn your way of life. Whoever showed you how to withdraw still further from secular business, you would willingly believe on this point, whoever he might be, whether from within or without; but never believe anyone concerning worldly increase, whatever intelligence he may possess. For if the Son of God, coming to earth, had known a better way of ascending to heaven than poverty, he would have chosen it and walked by it. [Col. 1087D] Therefore love poverty, since Jesus Christ chose it as the better way. Yet do not suppose that I commend either myself or you in what I have said to you: God alone knows what we are like.

“There is no doubt, however, that this life is holy. If anyone disparages it, exalt it; if someone praises you, humble yourselves: for thus the holy apostle Paul acted. Know firmly that there is no Rule other than the divine commandments: whoever observes them is religious; whoever departs from them exists outside every order or Rule. For whatever is done without God is nothing.”

## CHAPTER I. What Should Be Said and Shown to a Novice Entering Religious Life

[Col. 1088A]

1. Just as Jesus Christ says in the Gospel, “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Luke 9), so our pastor spoke to those whom he received into his discipline. Whenever anyone, desiring to come to him, asked him for the charity [that is, admission] from him, he answered in this way before granting it:

“Brother, how will you be able to bear the burden that you wish to lay upon yourself? Look at the cross: it is very difficult to remain there. If you come here, you will be nailed to it and will lose the mastery you have over yourself—over your eyes, your mouth, and your other members. You will abandon your own will in eating, fasting, sleeping, waking, and many other things; [Col. 1088B] and what you love in the world will come to be hateful to you. Thereafter you will not return to the home of your relatives; and if they come to you, you will by no means show them your poverty.

2. “Will you be able, brother, to dig, carry wood and dung, and serve all the brothers? All this would be easy; but you will remain shut in such a prison, where there is no opening through which you may return to the world, unless you make one yourself. I shall not attend to your affairs, nor permit you to attend to your own. For I have cut off my feet from the world; and if I do not return for my own sake, I shall not return for yours. There is something further: perhaps I would send you into some woodland, and I would take the grain that you acquired by working with your hands and a wooden hoe, [Col. 1088C] and give it to those who keep watch over me here.

3. “Yet there remains something more dreadful: it is a hundred times better for you to be damned in the world than here. For one who falls from a greater height is hurt more severely; and if you fell from here into hell, you would be lower than all other lost persons. You may instead go to any of the monasteries, where you will find great buildings and delicate foods provided at their proper times. There you will find livestock and broad lands; here there is only the cross and poverty.”

4. By words of this kind the good man tested whether the candidate had a resolute heart for leaving the world. For he would have judged him a simoniac if he entered religious life on the promise of any earthly thing. Likewise, [Col. 1088D] after the candidate had come, if he asked for anything according to custom, and finally answered him: “I desire to come here in order to endure all this, not in order to increase but to diminish,” the pastor received him among the other brothers and instructed him jointly with them in such words as these:

## CHAPTER II. A Discourse to the Newly Converted on Grace, Justice, and the Guarding of the Whole Religious Life

1. Religious life is grace, justice, and guardianship. When God brings someone into it, he brings that person back into paradise. Just as the Lord forbade Adam what was not necessary for him, while granting him everything else, so he acts toward those who wish to stand in truth. So long as they are content with what is useful to them, they remain at rest. But when they stretch themselves toward other things, which are not expedient for them, they fall into tribulation and distress, as Adam did (Gen. 3). [Col. 1089A]

For the one who delights in God finds paradise everywhere and dwells in heaven; the one who separates himself from him finds hell in every place. Therefore a religious man ought, in everything that he says and does, to meditate upon the presence of God, who always sees him; and upon that of God’s angels; and also upon the devil, who wishes to draw him out of paradise. For the devil never departs from good, because he wishes utterly to destroy it, though he is wholly separated from it.

2. One who is watched so closely has great need to be circumspect and diligent. He must learn to speak, walk, sit, look, work, pray to God, and do everything else otherwise than he did in the world. Let him learn to speak in such a way that he places such a restraint upon his speech that whatever he says can always be true. For whatever word or statement a religious man speaks, unless it is fruitful for body or soul, for himself or another, is worldliness.

He ought to walk honorably and without noise, sit humbly, work with recollection, without murmuring and with moderation. When he sees something desirable, let him keep his eyes in prison, lest he fasten them there, but turn his gaze away. When he prays to the Lord, let him make no clamor; for God hears the voice of the heart. Whoever prays in such a way as to harm others excludes charity from prayer—and this is what God loves there more abundantly. [Col. 1089B]

3. In all these matters and the rest, he must take care, in relation to the brothers with whom he lives, not to provide a bad example by which they might be scandalized through him. Whoever does not change bodily gestures upon entering religious life is not likely to change the habit of his soul; rather, his mind will always remain in the vanity of the world. For outward composure sometimes reveals the inward state; and one who is worldly in words and deeds—how will he be religious in thoughts? It is easier for someone to restrain the limbs of the body at will than thought.

## CHAPTER III. On the First Temptation of Neophytes

The devil lays his first snares for a person coming to conversion in order to take away the good with which he came—namely, the faith he had in the world concerning the good that existed in religious life. The devil wishes first to take this away when he sees the brothers doing what is necessary for them. For a novice is more tempted by good things that displease him than by anything else. One who falls in his first actions and loses his weapons is not likely to overcome in battle; and he is very weak whom one weaker than himself throws down—that is, the devil. [Col. 1089D]

## CHAPTER IV. On the Conflict of a Religious Man with the Devil

A religious man ought to meditate on the fact that he has ascended a high mountain, where God has brought him to fight with the devil and defend God’s right, as though he were God’s champion. The wrestling match begins on the mountaintop, but the struggles take place along the slope: now one is above and the other below, then the reverse, and it is unknown who has been defeated. Yet at some time they will come to level ground, and then it will appear whose victory it has been.

The mountain is divine love, by which the world is despised. No one remains always in that love in the same manner, because he is continually assailed by the devil. Yet at least while wrestling with him on the slope—that is, through faith and good works—a person must defend the Lord’s right. Nor is it surprising, while such struggles occur, that the devil should sometimes be uppermost and the person greatly tempted. The Lord afterward consoles that person by his grace, and then he stands above. Yet at the end of the wrestling match—that is, at the end—[Col. 1090B] let the person keep his foot firmly upon the devil’s throat.

## CHAPTER V. On the Diversity of Temptations Suffered by One Newly Converted

While the world is loved by a person, the enemy draws him after himself at will. When someone abandons the world, the devil, left behind, pursues him in many ways. He is called the thousand-artificed one, and comes with different drinks in order to discover which the person has accepted. The one in which he learns that the person takes most delight he afterward withholds for a long time, in order to throw him down by it near the end. With greater treachery he permits a person to remain undisturbed in a good life for a long time. For there is greater safety when he attacks him more harshly at the outset. [Col. 1090C]

## CHAPTER VI. How a Religious Man Should Avoid the Devil’s Snares

1. For this reason, great discernment is necessary for avoiding the devil’s snares: he is always beside the good, never with the good. He is like someone who attends any counsel but is not with the counsel, wishing to ruin it. Likewise God, existing everywhere, is in an evil person, yet not with him, because he does not agree with him; as the Gospel says, “The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1). Indeed, the evil person’s punishment is increased because he rejects divine grace and does not see in himself the brightness of that grace, which shines everywhere for those who behold it. [Col. 1090D] Likewise the good person’s crown increases as he rejects the darkness brought to him by the devil.

2. The devil sometimes enters a person more sweetly than honey and the honeycomb, or any other bodily sweetness. For if, on first coming, he struck with such a sword that a person felt pain, that person would flee and would never carry out what the devil urges. The devil is also so cunning that he wishes some people to perform good works, provided that he can hold them in one sin, by which he may possess them in the end.
