When they return to their conscience, the devil says to them: “You will never be damned for this, since you perform these and these good works. Finally, if you have any doubt about it, you can at least confess at the end.” He does not wish to say to a religious man, “Commit this sin,” because he would be recognized.

3. Instead, he begins to advise him differently: “If you were there now, you would do this; you would keep more vigils, fast, and speak of God in that religious community, rather than here among these poor people, remaining all day in the distress of labor [Col. 1091A] like other secular laborers, and also under discipline. Or, if you were still in the world, you could often enough come here.” By a pretext of this kind he makes the man despise and hate the good to which he had come.

4. He also often invites him to something of which he knows with complete certainty that he will never be believed, solely in order to delay him by one moment from divine love. And since the devil thus labors to keep a person from ascending to heaven, from which he himself fell, without any benefit that he expects from it, should not a person who hopes for salvation strongly resist him and do what displeases him, solely because it displeases him? Each person ought to love God even if he knew that no other advantage would come from it, just as one who fights in the world does many things for no other benefit than to make his enemy angry.

5. To every counsel brought to him by the devil, let the disciple answer: “O enemy, I know well that you are foolish. Why do you speak with me? Do you not know how [Col. 1091C] I have acted? I have given myself away; I am not my own. If you wish to fight with me, go to my pastor, whose I am, and he will answer you. I am behind his shield, and God’s words, which he speaks to me, will protect me from all your darts. The more violently you come with evil thoughts, the more dishonored and defeated you will depart from us.”

6. Furthermore, the devil is so crafty that he brings certain people into religious life and afterward brings them back into the world, or keeps them disobedient in the cloister among the other brothers, so that they may have greater punishment. For the wicked person loses God much more by refusing to amend himself while among a righteous man than while among another person—as Judas did while with Jesus Christ. Otherwise God would see nothing more in a person there, if merely by changing from one fortress to some woodland a person became good without good works. But the Lord sometimes converts by his grace one whom the devil had brought there and counted as his own, giving him humility by which he treads upon all the devil’s snares. These are even denser than the threads of a spiderweb when great heat comes in summer. [Col. 1091D]

## CHAPTER VII. Again, on Avoiding the Devil’s Snares

7. There is another snare of the devil, difficult to discern and still more difficult to avoid. When someone has left the world and entered religious life with a good purpose, his acquaintances sometimes visit the place to which he has come. Then the devil begins to say to him under a pretext of good: “You ought to rejoice greatly, because so great a benefit has come to this community on your account. No one from your homeland ever came here until you came; indeed, even your father and mother would never have come if you had not been here.”

Whoever does not know the devil’s snares delights in what is said to him, and, thinking it true, falls into vain glory. Nor does this fault befall only the man visited by his parents, but also those who speak with secular people, imagining that good comes to the community because of themselves.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Vain Glory, Which Sometimes Takes from a Person the Faith He Ought to Have in the Lord, His Brothers, and Himself

1. Vain glory takes from a person the faith that he ought to have in himself, in the other brothers, and also in the Lord. For each person ought to believe, know, and recognize himself to be more sinful than the other brothers. If he is good, indeed, he sees his own sins better than those of others; and he ought to submit himself to all robbers and prostitutes, believing himself to be worse. Nor should he think that divine grace cannot reach as far as himself. For he thinks this when he despises others, who can rise from the sins in which they are, while he himself can fall from the good in which he stands. [Col. 1092B]

2. It is no great thing for him to subject himself to all brothers who are good, as he ought to believe them to be. He ought also to approve and love their humility, even more than his own, since he considers it better and greater. This is what a righteous man does after he has remained a long time in some community: the longer the Lord has dwelt in him, the more fully he understands and knows the office and work that all the others have in religious life. He finds each one’s proper place, considering himself to be nothing there except an impediment; and yet perhaps God provides for others through love of him. [Col. 1092C]

3. Vain glory takes all this faith away from a person, and divine faith besides, when it withdraws honor from the good that the Lord works solely through his grace, believing that it is done on its own account. For certainly everyone desires to be praised by another and desires that person to be grateful to him because he thinks in his heart: “This happens because of me.” Vain glory, according to its own estimate, possesses what it does not possess: great understanding, great power, prudent speech, and very many other goods. It is deceived more gravely by thinking that it possesses them when it has none of them.

For God causes many to be believed good for the benefit of others, though the only goodness found in them is as much as others believe. Yet those of whom such belief is held will perish unless they are good. [Col. 1092D]

4. But by such attraction and occasion God wishes to assist his own. So that no one may fall into this devilish snare, let him inspect the works he has done; and if he examines himself well, he will undoubtedly recognize [Col. 1093A] that he has deserved nothing but punishment. Thus let him believe that good comes into religious life because of others who have served God longer. But if any adversity occurs, let him blame himself for it.

5. For no speech or writing makes a person so near to God as knowledge of one’s own sins, from which His help is sought. And nothing is more acceptable to God in the righteous man whom He greatly loves than when the righteous man finds nothing in himself that pleases God, except what God works in him. Nor does the righteous man even wish to be helped or saved by God for any good of his own, except by His grace. Likewise the Son of God, who descended from heaven, knowing how one ascends there, said and taught that no one would ascend there except by humbling himself (Matt. XVIII). Yet [Col. 1093B] the greatest humility that can be had before God is, in the way a person ought to reflect, pride; for no one can judge himself so wretched that he is not worse still. And if anyone looks upon the humility of Jesus Christ, his own will be altogether nothing. But whoever possesses only as much as he is worth, God dwells in him and grants him what is His.

## CHAPTER IX.—Another discourse addressed to the newly converted

1. Many prefer to be condemned while teaching rather than saved while learning, wishing to be shepherds because they do not know how to be disciples. Yet this is what they ought first to know; like all those who have newly entered religious life, beginning to lead before they know how to follow. Let this one person now be present, and let us speak with him: “You who have recently come from the world, how do you [Col. 1093C] wish to teach what you do not know? Did you not abandon your own rule, which you might have taught us if we had sought you out, and come unasked to ours? Follow those before you, who know the road where you have not yet been; and rejoice greatly if you can follow them. For if you turn aside to the right or to the left, you will find briars and thorns, and robbers lying in wait for you.

2. “Remember also, while you were under your own power and government, by what paths you walked and how you governed yourself. You sought a guide because you did not know how to go; therefore you must follow him. For if you, being blind, go first, you will fall into a pit, and others following you will fall as well. Do you not know that no creature ever gained anything by governing itself? [Col. 1093D] A good angel became a devil when he wished to govern himself. Adam likewise, following him, went out of paradise.

3. “Such counsel is first necessary for a person: that he not take counsel from himself—that is, that he rely upon his own judgment—if he wishes to follow the Lord Jesus Christ; so that he may lose his own understanding and cast himself away, if he desires to find himself. He must also reduce himself to nothing if he wishes to imitate the Son of God, who emptied Himself. For it is necessary for a person to recognize this much good in himself: that no good is possessed by him unless God imparts and preserves it. And this is the first path by which God comes to a person: knowledge of one’s own ignorance.

4. “But perhaps, when the novice brother is restrained [Col. 1094A] from something that he says or does, he will consider the riches or power, the property or literary learning, that he had in the world. Let him now remember whether, because of any of these things, he had greater power to do evil or to depart further from God. If he can find this in his heart, let him repent that he ever possessed property or riches by which he assailed God. Would he judge himself richer because he had greater means in the world to do evil than some poor person? There are no riches or property except cleaving to God; but whoever is separated from Him, whatever he has is turned to his disgrace.

5. “Nor is it strange if the natural person, when he has newly come to conversion, wishes to govern [Col. 1094B] the members of Christ. For the Lord’s own disciples would gladly have taught Him, if He had wished to believe them; and they would have advised Him not to undergo death or suffering. Such is worldly counsel in the matter of religion as they offered to Jesus Christ Himself. And just as the disciples never understood the works of God, although they saw them, until they had passed through the distress occasioned by His death and He had given them the Holy Spirit, so a person long delighting in sins cannot understand the sweetness of God until he passes through the distress which the cross of Jesus Christ requires him to endure. For this reason the Lord had not given the apostles the Holy Spirit while He was with them: because afterward, when He gave it to them, His death pleased them, as did the grief they had suffered on account of it and because He had [Col. 1094C] bodily departed from them.

6. “And as wood which has remained in water, when recently drawn out, cannot burn brightly until it is dried, so a person, so long as he is full of the moisture of vices, cannot grow warm in divine love until he is dried. Nor can anyone see anything with closed eyes; yet eyes see nothing unless something else shines upon them. But when bodily light is joined to that which is in a person, then he can see. So it is in spiritual matters: when a person has some small share of them in himself, he understands what he hears from another. Therefore, when a worldly man is told concerning some small matter, [Col. 1094D] ‘Brother, this is an offense,’ he does not recognize it at all: he has so many greater offenses within himself which take the light away from him.

7. “But in proportion as the novice defends his worldliness, so one who has long stood in righteousness should defend his religious life by reasoning with him, teaching him by word and deed, and helping him spiritually and bodily according to his ability. For a person more readily believes one who does him good than another—unless he has demons within him. But whoever scarcely believes one who aids him in every way, how would he believe him if he did him harm? It is the height of pride for a person not to amend himself when corrected by another. Nor does a person cease doing something through forgetfulness after it has been pointed out to him, but because [Col. 1095A] pride takes memory from him; for humility always remains in fear of offending, whereas pride does not care what may be said to it.”

## CHAPTER X.—On the knowledge necessary for serving God reasonably

1. Whoever loves God more is wiser and more religious; but in no matter is knowledge so necessary to a person as for serving God reasonably. The Lord gives His faithful servant the furnishings and implements necessary for His love, just as a rich man equips his house with ornaments suited to it. And in nothing does a religious person offend so greatly as in this: that he does not understand what implements have been entrusted to him by God for carrying out His service [Col. 1095B]. Since he does not know them, he sometimes begins to work with furnishings not entrusted to him by God; then, wearied, he afterward abandons the task in shame, when he presumes upon a power not yet granted him, neglecting another exercise in which God would have had him engage.

2. For the Lord does not assign every virtue to one person; pride would cast him down if he could possess them at his own pleasure. God shows great mercy in refusing a person what he asks of Him, when He recognizes that it would be harmful to him—just as a mother does not wish to give an infant a knife with which he would cut himself. He gives one virtue to one person and another to another; and finally the entire [Col. 1095C] community of one religious order forms Jesus Christ.

3. God also wishes a righteous man to rejoice more in the good which he holds in common with others through faith and unity than in a virtue he possesses above them. For that virtue would profit him nothing without unity, just as sight profits the eye nothing once it has been severed from the head. The hearing of the ears pleases the eyes as much as their own seeing; and, because of the unity that is in the members, the eye walks, the foot sees, the mouth hears, and the ear speaks. If anything is necessary for one member, all the others aid it; yet if any one of them abandoned its proper office, it could by no means do this. Whoever ought to be a foot, hand, or other member [Col. 1095D] in the body of Jesus Christ and withdraws himself from it—God charges him with having dismembered it; and he is accused by all the other members because he departed from them and, insofar as he could, dishonored them. Yet the Lord is so wise that He puts another in his place; but no grace is repaid to the one who left, because thereafter the body of Jesus Christ will be honored.

4. Therefore each brother must test his own capacity, and discover by what part he can make his way to God. Just as a traveller, when he comes to a marsh, first tests it and, seeing that he cannot cross, turns aside by another route—because, if he fell into the mud, he would delay both himself and his companions—so a religious person must test how to order his body and soul [Col. 1096A], lest they injure one another. For neither can withhold from the other what is due to it without the loss being common to both. The body must keep watch, fast, and labor for the soul. For God by no means excuses from working according to his ability one whom He wishes to keep in righteousness, when bodily support is necessary to him, as it is to the other brothers. Someone may begin the contemplative life before he knows the active life; and when he examines himself, he is neither Martha nor Mary. For the freer he is from every work, the more evil thoughts he piles up; and one who does not know how to care for the lesser thing—that is, the ordering of the body—will scarcely manage the greater, namely the soul.

[Col. 1096B] 5. Therefore each person must carefully test how much food, sleep, and clothing will sustain him and enable him to remain in righteousness. For God is faithful, not cruel; and He wishes to be served in joy and fear, without complaint from body or soul. Whoever cannot endure and serve God with what is necessary to him would scarcely endure it if he lacked everything. Therefore it is better for each person to take sufficient food and be obedient than to fast beyond measure, despise others, and neglect God’s service. For exceeding measure is in no way abstinence; indeed, however one acts in this respect, let him blame himself for it.

## CHAPTER XI.—Another discourse on correction

[Col. 1096C]

1. When one brother corrects another in charity as far as he can, and the other grows angry, the corrector ought to believe that the anger which comes upon him is discipline for his own sin; and he should accuse himself because he did not know how to rebuke him in the manner and with the gentleness required for the other to receive it in peace. By this humility which he adopts, God will soften the other, if he is foreseen for good. Again, if the one who administered correction and blamed himself for the other’s anger is afterward rebuked and troubled on that account, he ought entirely to believe that he suffers that trouble for his own sin.

2. For truth is always sweet, and it is difficult to a person for no reason except the rust of vices which he has in himself. Thus a sick person, because of the [Col. 1096D] bitterness in which he is, finds food bitter which would be sweet to him if he were well; likewise, to an eye that does not see, nothing is bright. Therefore the false religious person cannot listen to righteousness, because he fears that he may be compelled to hold to it in his deeds; and one who cannot bear the word will scarcely perform the deed.

3. Someone is also so foolish that he prefers, in some discourse, to hear a rebuke of vices of which he is not guilty rather than of others that he has in himself, concerning which it would be better for him to be rebuked. And no one will receive any rebuke so well as when he first rebukes himself.

4. He who does not wish to be corrected by another does well if he is such a disciple that nothing is found in him for which he should be [Col. 1097A] rebuked. Discipline, however, does not bring rust into a person but removes it. Just as a rod does not put ashes into the lye but dislodges the ashes that were already there, causing the lye to become turbid, so the one who is displeased when rebuked had not thoroughly cleansed himself of what another finds in him.

5. Yet no one ought to desire either praise or blame from another. For one who knowingly does that for which he is reviled is foolish; and one who does good wishing to be praised for it is likewise foolish. But he who is displeased when blamed is pleased when praised.

## CHAPTER XII.—On the mercy God shows to one coming to religious life

[Col. 1097B] 1. God shows this mercy to one who comes to religious life with others: what he most fears and considers himself unable to bear He afterward turns into greater sweetness for him when he consents to righteousness; and likewise in all things done for God’s service. But in what is least feared, greater difficulty is sometimes found. Yet one who has not yet passed through it does not believe the person telling him so. He may observe this from the following example: the women going to the tomb and wishing to anoint the body of Jesus Christ were more anxious about rolling away the stone than about anything else (Mark XVI), and concerning this they first found an answer. But they did not find the body of Jesus Christ, which they certainly expected to be there. Likewise the disciples who [Col. 1097C] fled when the Lord told them that unless they ate His flesh and drank His blood they would not have eternal life (John VI)—if they had fled beforehand, they ought then to have returned, since in no matter could the Lord have spoken to them of greater mercy.

2. But truth is at first difficult for a person and afterward turns into everlasting sweetness; falsehood and sin please at first, and afterward a person falls into perpetual distress. Whoever finds the discipline of religious life difficult ought to consider the labor in which he was in the world and would bear the present one more lightly; indeed, he should consider also the suffering that Jesus Christ endured without sin. It is [Col. 1097D] not strange, therefore, if a person bears the miseries which he has deserved and deserves daily by sinning. But whoever remains in righteousness should say in his heart concerning the tribulation he suffers: “God, blessed be You, because You now defend me from that pleasure on account of which I might perhaps go to hell.”

## CHAPTER XIII.—A comparison between the unskilled soldier and the true religious person

1. An unskilled soldier is one who, without compulsion and without fear, leaves his fortification, where he stands safely, and goes out among the enemies who besiege him, so that he is captured by them. Likewise, a religious person remains safe as long as he is within his cloister, if he has made it out of himself; for there is no other cloister than for a person to shut himself in, so that the devil may find no opening [Col. 1098A] in him through which he can be besieged.

2. If a religious person hears of his friend fighting in the world against the worst enemy he has there, and wishes more that his friend may overcome and injure the enemy than that the enemy may injure his friend, he is not at all in religious life but wages war in the world, throwing stones and darts, because he has driven righteousness from his heart. Therefore it is good that no one hear reports from his homeland except as little as possible. And since one thus falls into the devil’s hands by thought alone, he would wholly fall if he went out into the world in body and soul.

## CHAPTER XIV.—How God is faithful to every person

1. God is so faithful to each person that He by no means [Col. 1098B] counsels him to damn himself for the salvation of others; rather, He commands him first to save himself, by loving the Lord above all things and doing good works; afterward, he should extend a hand to his neighbor and draw him with himself to the kingdom of heaven. Again, when God commands a person to love his neighbor as himself, He exceeds no measure, for He commands nothing in him to be loved except what is good; and the good belongs as much to the one who loves as to the one who does it. Why, then, should each person not love what is his own? Therefore, when a good person hears of another’s good works, he praises God in his heart, saying: “God, blessed be You; for this good is mine, and this person who labors for love of You works for me as for himself.”

[Col. 1098C] 2. Nor ought one living rightly to give thanks to God only when he hears of another’s good, but also when he hears of evil: over the good, let him rejoice because it is his; for the evil, let him be grateful to God, because He has protected him from that which he hears of, or from something worse. For no one killed him, nor did he kill another; no one took anything from him, nor did he take anything from another.

3. Indeed, nothing that is his can truly be taken from a righteous person. If he has bodily property, he does not count it as his own; no one can rob him of spiritual riches. Rather, they are increased when his temporal property is diminished, as in Job. For the more the Lord wishes a righteous man to be poor and afflicted for His sake, the more richly He endows him with spiritual goods—provided, however, that he patiently bears bodily [Col. 1098D] poverty.

## CHAPTER XV.—On God’s love for humanity

From this one can understand the great love God bears toward a person: whatever anyone does, bodily or spiritually, for his own true benefit, God counts it as done for Himself. But when he does what harms himself, God is angry with the person because he does not live for himself; and He is angrier because the person departs from Him for nothing. This true love which God shows to a person, and the great labor which He endured for him, ought above all things to bring him shame for his sins. For in return for the good which God bestows on a person, and because He speaks to him of his own advantage, the person renders Him [Col. 1099A] evil in return. For if any good is present, God alone performs it; so greatly does God love a person that He rejoices when His grace is willingly received from Him.

## CHAPTER XVI.—What the evangelical hundredfold is

A person wishes to possess temporal things both in order to rejoice in them and to live from them. One joy is had from a son, another from a wife, and so with each individual thing. But every joy derived from them God increases beyond number for the person who leaves the world for His sake and follows Him, whenever He enables him to overcome temptations that arise and protects him from others by which he would be cast down if they came. The joy derived from the victory achieved, and the strengthening of faith which the Lord then gives His [Col. 1099B] faithful servant concerning salvation, is called by Jesus Christ in the Gospel the hundredfold (Matt. XIX). For a good person rejoices more in what he does not have but hopes to have than an evil person does in the wealth of the world, even if it were all his own.

## CHAPTER XVII.—How dreadful it is to be separated from God

It is so dreadful to be separated from God that one could scarcely believe anyone would dare to depart from Him, unless he saw it daily and another told him of it. For God, through His grace, willed to share in human poverty and misery; but the human being is so proud and disdainful that he does not wish to share in His riches and glory.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On the faith the righteous person has in the Lord

[Col. 1099C]

For this reason, more than for any other, the righteous person believes that God will make him reign with Him forever in heaven: because the Lord so deigns to humble Himself that He deigns to dwell both in the righteous person, who is an earthen vessel, and in this world.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the human being’s love for God

A person can love nothing with his whole heart except God alone. For if someone loves anything else greatly, he will not forsake everything else for it without desiring something else. Thus the whole heart is not filled by that love, since it is still more captivated away from it; divine love alone fills it wholly, driving out desire from it.

## CHAPTER XX.—On the sweetness of God’s commandments

[Col. 1099D]

1. Everyone ought greatly to wonder at the sweetness of God’s commandments. If God said to a person: “I will not hear your prayer unless a great crowd hears when you ask Me, nor will I accept your almsgiving unless, when you give it, it is seen by many people,” it would be difficult for him always to assemble a crowd whenever he wished to do good. But since God commands good to be done in secret, it is much easier than if He said: “I will not accept it at all unless it is seen by everyone.”

2. Likewise, it is easier for someone to be poor and humble than proud and rich, according to the works which humility and pride require. Humility requires that possessed property be despised; pride, that [Col. 1100A] unpossessed property be amassed—and this is harder. Humility asks that one recline in the lower place, where anyone will arrive sooner when he comes to a wedding feast; pride wishes one to ascend to a higher place, and this is more laborious. For all these reasons Jesus Christ ought to be praised, because He did not say, “The wealthier, more eloquent, or nobler by birth will be greater in the kingdom of heaven,” but promised greater things to the lesser (Matt. XVIII), because it is easier to become lesser than greater.

## CHAPTER XXI.—Why a person is condemned

A person prefers to follow the devil and the hardships he advises rather than the Lord and the rest He commands; for this reason he will justly be condemned. For it is greater labor to lie than to tell the truth, [Col. 1100B] since a lie seeks to be hidden and covered lest it be recognized, while truth seeks to remain naked and uncovered. Jesus Christ counsels entry through the door into the sheepfold (John X); this is easier than what the devil suggests, that one should fall into it from above.

## CHAPTER XXII.—How believers place concern for this world upon the Lord

The Lord commands His faithful servants, in order that they may love Him more freely, to place upon Him the care of this world, and He will be their steward. He shows greater mercy by freeing them from it than if He said: “Provide whatever is necessary for you, and afterward love Me.”

## CHAPTER XXIII.—How the sweetness of divine commandments is understood

[Col. 1100C]

One may best understand the Lord’s sweetness to be great when His commandments are so sweet to some people that they cause them to hate what they love most in this world: wives, children, and other possessions. From this, too, one may know that the elect in the kingdom of heaven will never feel compassion for the lost, since even now in this life divine love makes the righteous forget those whom they loved according to the world.

## CHAPTER XXIV.—How a person can find the Lord

It would be much easier for a person, if he understood, because he can find the Lord [Col. 1100D] better near at hand than by going farther away to seek Him—namely, within himself, where he has Him nearer than anything else. But a person is so foolish that he prefers to seek joy and rest outwardly in nothingness rather than within himself, where he would find them. Nor does anyone wish to do freely what he certainly knows he would do unwillingly: that is, despise the world. But one whose every joy is hateful to him—that is, the Lord—will scarcely possess joy.

## CHAPTER XXV.—How a person should delight in Christ’s works, and how great is the power of patience

1. It is good to delight in Christ’s works. For He sent His disciples as lambs among wolves (Luke X); and if anyone else wished to fight wolves and overcome them, he would by no means choose lambs for [Col. 1101A] battle. But the Lord, for the sake of greater honor, preferred to overcome wolves with lambs rather than with bears or lions.

2. And because a lamb cannot carry a great burden, God relieved them of the care of the world, which would have been an impediment to them; and they won their victory through patience. For patience is such a virtue that whoever lacks it does not possess himself; and whoever does not possess himself—with what will he serve God?

## CHAPTER XXVI.—On the sweetness present in God’s words

1. Because of the sweetness present in divine words, it greatly pleases the righteous person that the [Col. 1101B] Lord has never given a person a limit to doing good. When the evil person accuses God because he does not know the day of his end, the good person praises Him and says in his heart: “God, how great a mercy You show, because You do not wish anyone to know his death, but to keep it always before him, so that each person may be more intent upon the repose of Your love!”

2. For it would not be consistent with God’s desiring so greatly that a person always serve Him if He granted him knowledge of his end, since the person separates himself from Him even when he does not know the day or hour. It so pleases the righteous person that God grants him no interruption in doing good. If someone said to him, “Remain for one day without doing good,” it would amount to saying, [Col. 1101C] “Depart from joy and stand in anger.”

3. For Christ’s cross is his rest. The evil person says, on the contrary: “I would turn to God if I knew the day of my end.” He is not to be believed in this: that he would serve God within himself if he knew for certain that he had another year to live, since he departs from Him while not even certain of one day’s life.

## CHAPTER XXVII.—That no one should set a term for performing God’s service

It is a great wonder, since God is always necessary to a person and always wishes and is able to help him, why the person does not always love Him. And since [Col. 1101D] a person wishes to be saved by God without end, and does not wish after a thousand years to be cast out of glory, it is unjust for anyone to set a term or interval for performing His service.

## CHAPTER XXVIII.—On speaking the truth

He who speaks truth should pray to God that He may grant him to speak it truthfully. For he speaks it falsely unless he holds in deeds what he declares with his mouth. Thus, when it is said in the Psalm, “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. XXIV), although the word of God is true, whoever speaks it lies unless he accords with God; nor is good good to him while it does not please him in his heart.

## CHAPTER XXIX.—How a person may take an example from evil in order to do good

[Col. 1102A]

In some matters there is great wisdom in taking an example from evil to do good, as in this: “A person planning some act of treachery or another sin takes great care that no one should know of it who might hinder it, though it would be necessary for him to do so.” Since such a person thus guards evil, one doing good ought certainly to take care not to boast of it, lest vainglory steal it from him.

## CHAPTER XXX.—How one who comes to religious life should follow the example of those who have gone before

1. Whoever comes to religious life, if he cannot take an example from the good another does [Col. 1102B], ought at least to take an example from the very evils in which he formerly lived, in this way: that he should bear for his own benefit as much care and labor as he endured for his harm.

2. A good person ought always to speak of God or with God: in prayer he speaks with God; with his neighbor, he speaks of God.

## CHAPTER XXXI.—Ignorance or blindness concerning sins

In nothing can anyone see his hindrances better than in the fact that he does not recognize them. For an abundance of sins prevents them from being seen; they are recognized only when they have been removed, just as darkness is recognized when someone has come out of it, though no one can see it while standing [Col. 1102C] in it.

## CHAPTER XXXII.—On the manner of hearing God’s word

He who hears the word of God, if his disposition is good, first accuses himself from what he hears. But if he has an evil will, he removes the accusation from himself by turning it upon another.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—How the perfect person should accuse himself in the good works he performs

It is more perfect for someone to accuse himself in the good he does than in the evil. For who does not know, when committing evil, that he is guilty? But when he does good, let him wisely consider how many evils he retains within himself, so that by considering his faults he may preserve his [Col. 1102D] virtues with humility.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—On the thought one ought to have concerning the sweetness of divine counsels

1. One ought greatly to consider how sweetly and without difficulty God counsels a person. For each person could more easily examine himself and inspect what he has within than examine another; for this reason the Lord commands it, because it is easier and more useful. The devil advises the opposite: that a person, abandoning his own eye which has a beam in it, should go to cleanse another’s. And many, by his counsel, prefer to go farther away and remain amid tumult while treating another’s eye rather than remain near and stand in peace while examining themselves. It is not likely that one who rebukes another for something of which he is [Col. 1103A] himself more guilty does so from charity, but from hatred, envy, or vainglory.

2. Therefore, whenever someone begins to murmur against another, the right counsel is that he return to himself and examine his own thoughts, words, and deeds. When he has examined himself well, he will see that the person against whom he murmured is running so far ahead of him that he will never be able to catch him; and it will please the Lord that he displeases himself.

3. It is also better for someone to be conquered and then conquer than to conquer and afterward be conquered. Thus soldiers in battle gain greater honor who first flee but afterward return and conquer their enemies than others who were pursuing but are afterward defeated.

## CHAPTER XXXV.—What anyone on God’s way ought to be like

[Col. 1103B]

1. Whoever is on God’s way must take care neither to be delayed by sloth nor to fall through pride. For no one coming to the field of harvest has his entire burden at the first ear of grain; nor did Saint Peter complete all his gain on the day he was crucified. He had long gathered ears of grain, but then he made up his bundle in full.

2. The first path by which one proceeds to God is fear of punishment, when someone fears the Lord so greatly that he abandons evil-doing through fear of hell; and this is good. But no one ought to remain in this through [Col. 1103C] sloth. It is better to love God and perform good works for love of righteousness, as Martha did, who received and served Jesus Christ because of the love she bore Him (Luke X).

3. Yet pride sometimes casts a person down from such good. Something more excellent than all these is to forget every care of the world and delight in God alone. This is perfect charity, from which no one will ever fall damnably once he has possessed it. Whoever has it loves God so much as seems to him impossible. For the more ardently the spirit embraces Him in desire, the more it seems to itself to lose Him, and that God is being removed farther from it [Col. 1103D].

4. For the Lord does not wish a righteous man in this world to be satiated with His love, but always to hunger and thirst for righteousness. And just as a father bringing his son an apple or something else withdraws it from the child who wants to take it, in order to stir him more strongly, so God withdraws Himself from those who love Him greatly, in order to kindle them more intensely; yet He always leaves them consoled by His grace.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—How a righteous person should receive alms

1. It is more perfect for a righteous person to receive alms to live on than to give them. For while someone is in the world and under his own power, he can sometimes do good [Col. 1104A] and evil as it pleases him: give alms, attend prayers, and do countless other things. But when he abandons both evil and the good which he is able to do for the sake of what is better, giving himself to the Lord, he cannot give alms so great or so acceptable to God.

2. For other almsgivers, however much property they offer, always retain something, whether themselves or something else. But once a person has left himself and cast himself at Jesus’ feet, in order to hear His words and do His will, the Lord does not command him to return again to Martha’s anxious activity—that is, to the good which he could do in the world. For the Lord praised Mary, sitting at His feet and hearing [Col. 1104B] His words, more than Martha, who was serving and thought that her sister was doing nothing. Yet Mary feared that the Lord might say to her, “Rise and help her”; but He did not say this at all. Rather, He defended her and said that this woman was doing what was better, while that one was doing good (Luke X).

3. Hence, when the good man whom God has chosen to praise for His sake receives bodily goods brought to him by secular people, he receives nothing belonging to another, but what is his own is restored to him. Nor does he think, “This man or that man provides for me”; rather, giving thanks to God alone, he prays for those who serve him. For God does, sustains, and provides all things for the sake of the good, even the wicked, who have no right in the members which they possess [Col. 1104C] because they depart from God—much less in other things—although they have power for their greater condemnation.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—On Christ’s poor

1. Christ’s poor, who have left themselves and made the greatest alms they could, possessing nothing of their own—not themselves or anything else—ought to rejoice more because they cannot give alms than if the power to do so were granted them again. For there is someone who loses God because of the good he can do and does: when he speaks of God or lavishly gives alms, which are good works, but performs them for vainglory. Others gain the Lord through the good which, as it seems to them, they neither do nor are able to do, like these poor [Col. 1104D] of Christ when they see others and wish to help them but cannot act because they have nothing. Therefore God counts it to them as though they had done everything, because of their good will; and perhaps, if they had resources, they would lose their good heart. For nothing produces good will so much as spiritual poverty.

2. But if these people who are free still seek how they may give alms again, they have not left themselves well; and it is as though they retained something from which to give them. For if they had left themselves well, they would have neither foot, hand, nor other member with which to give them.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—How a pastor ought to conduct himself toward those subject to him
1. Nevertheless, a pastor who is permitted to give something of outward goods [Col. 1105A] to the poor must then take every care not to harm inward goods; since every good that he does belongs in common to his disciples, he must carefully ensure that he does not take it away from them. For if some saw an alms being given, although it pleased them at the time, afterward they might be displeased when they themselves came to need something, and say in complaint: “Because our pastor gave this, we are now in want.” It is the nature of a wise man, therefore, that when he performs a good work, he takes the utmost care that it harms neither himself nor another.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—On the reward of the righteous who provide others with a good example.

Whoever sets forth a good example receives his reward from all his hearers, good and bad alike: from the good, because they follow him; from the bad, because they refuse to follow him, though they would do so of their own accord. But God reckons it to that man as though he had saved them all; for the peace not received by the hearers returns to the preacher, if he is faithful. [Col. 1105B]

## CHAPTER XL.—On counsel necessary for every person.

If anyone of his own accord abandons grave sins, he greatly pleases God. But if he has a blameworthy tendency to talk lightly, to anger, or something of that kind, it is more pleasing to God that he fight against the thing which continually pursues him. For this is to deny and abandon oneself.

## CHAPTER XLI.—On the difference between the punishments of hell and the joys of heaven.

[Col. 1105C] If a person destined for condemnation saw the infernal punishments and torments as they are, and as he is to suffer them, he would not draw toward himself any limb that he possesses: he would die there of terror. But one who is to be saved, if he saw the heavenly joys as they are and as he is to possess them, would immediately depart this life through their sweetness. For a bodily thing in this life cannot endure a spiritual reality so as to behold it.

## CHAPTER XLII.—How divine love ought to be held.

1. God has placed love in gold, silver, and the other earthly things, so that love for him might be dearer, and of greater merit, to those who possess it. For whenever anyone wishes to desire anything of this world, God gives him a choice, as though saying: “Choose what you prefer: either me, who am God, [Col. 1105D] or a temporal thing. If you choose me, I shall give you more than you can desire; if you choose something else, you will lose everything.”

2. Yet the Lord rightly grants a person whatever is necessary to him, and no one will ever be condemned on that account if he gathers together all the wealth that he can acquire, provided that in doing so he first harms neither himself nor anyone else. For the Lord ordains that wealth be spent in the manner in which it is gathered. Whoever gathers it perversely and unjustly spends it foolishly; but he who accumulates it justly, with God’s help, spends it for good.

3. Nor does anyone cease to be poor in spirit if he desires only that by which he can serve God; but he must not will in any part of his heart that, through anything he possesses, another should suffer loss, or that he himself should depart from God’s commandment. And whenever anyone wishes to sin, above all losses he ought to think this: “I shall never do this, for divine love would thereby be diminished in me.” By this fear he would be protected by God. He should also bear shame before sin, not sin before shame. [Col. 1106A]

## CHAPTER XLIII.—On the divine grace and goodness by which each person is visited.

1. God gives his good to each person under this condition, as though saying: “Assist me with this good as much as you can; and if you work according to your ability, I, who am God, shall complete what you cannot do. By my grace I shall save you, and I shall reckon it to you as though you had done everything. But if you do not serve me with what [Col. 1106B] I have entrusted to you, then, were I to entrust more to you, it would lead to your destruction.”

2. Therefore, in all things in which God gives someone more than others, he ought to consider the purpose for which God does this. If he has wealth, let him think that God has entrusted it to him in order to provide for God’s poor, and that God hopes and relies upon him concerning them. Therefore God allows them to be in want, so that the rich person may feed them for him, as he ought to believe. For all wealth, wherever it may be, always belongs to God.

3. When someone transfers it and gives it to a poor person, God looks there at nothing but the intention. No one can make such a mass of alms that it reaches heaven; but a good will penetrates all the heavens when an alms is given for this reason alone: that God may thereby be praised. And it is certain that the rich person gains more through the poor than the poor person through him. [Col. 1106C]

4. Likewise, whoever is strong for labor, or wise in speaking, should believe that others have merited his strength and wisdom, and that God gave them to him both for himself and for others. The same must be thought of each individual virtue.

5. For a good benefits a person when he removes it from himself, believing that God entrusted it to him so that by means of it he might serve others. Therefore he ought rather to believe that he may be condemned because of the virtues he possesses unless he guards them from pride and another profits by them. But everyone should draw evil near to himself in this way: whatever may happen to him, he should believe that he has deserved it. Then God will make him free from it, because he will accuse himself on its account. [Col. 1106D]

## CHAPTER XLIV.—How one should regard oneself.

A person can better see what is than what is not. Therefore let a person acknowledge that he is a sinner, and he will know the truth. Let him by no means think himself righteous, for he would be a liar. For the whole righteousness of a just person consists in believing that God alone possesses righteousness.

## CHAPTER XLV.—On the reward for an alms performed by someone.

1. After someone has been buried, he has no friend so good that he does not leave him and return home. But the demons that desire to seize the soul are not far away. Almsgiving alone never departs from him, if it has been performed by him. Rather, it goes before him and places the soul behind itself, preparing its shield against the demons that wish to rush upon it. Driving them back, it says to them: “Do you not see me here?” Then it says to the soul: “Do not be afraid.” Finally, when the devil comes before the Lord at judgment, he sets out his accusations, saying: “In such and such ways this soul performed my service.” Almsgiving answers: “Whatever it has done, I make it free from all its sins.” [Col. 1107A]

2. It is good, then, to acquire such a companion. But very avaricious is the person who denies bread and wine to Jesus Christ—things which are not his at all except for stewardship—since Christ himself gave his flesh and blood for humankind. Yet there are some who take greater concern for the seasoning of food alone, that it may be savory to them, than for their own soul; they dream that their hands are full of riches, but when they awaken and depart from this world, they find nothing but vanity. [Col. 1107B]

## CHAPTER XLVI.—On the difference between the fool and the wise man.

1. The wise man and the fool differ in many things, but especially in this. When the fool does good, he does not look there to the divine will but to his own. And when he wishes to give his alms to those who are not in great need and could do without them, God answers him in return: “What will you do with the wealth [Col. 1107C] which I entrusted to you? Where do you wish to take it? Help me here in this poor person, where I suffer more from hunger, cold, and misery, and lack one to care for me.” The fool answers: “Shall I help you where you would wish? Woe to him who should do that! Rather, I will go help you where you will show me no gratitude for it.”

2. He says this by his deeds. For the alms he gives would profit him nothing, as he thinks, unless he had lost it before giving it. This is what God answers him: “If you acted according to my pleasure, I would praise you and cause all my angels to praise you; but because you do this according to your own plan, you shall not have the very thing you seek.” Thus the fool builds upon sand; and however slight the rain of human praise may be, when someone says that he has done well, it carries away the whole building.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—Again, on the meditation of the wise man.

[Col. 1107D]

1. But a wise man sometimes reflects even upon any small thing: “I shall give this for my soul, but it is far too little. Yet, according to God’s will, if I can, I shall do it, lest it be wholly diminished.” But if what he wishes to give is great, then the prudent person takes every care not to lose it through an idle choice, saying in his heart: “God, where would you rather that I render this to you, or which of your members has greater need of it? For to that one I would wish to distribute it.”

2. While he asks this, almsgiving sweats, blossoms, and bears fruit in the wise man’s hand. And when someone gives his charity to a poor person of modest disposition, it is great compassion likewise to give it modestly [Col. 1108A] to him, taking care that he is not recognized. For God reveals the good that is concealed, causing that which is displayed to be forgotten.

3. Whoever, therefore, wishes to be honored should place his whole intention in the Lord, always laboring to increase his good.

## CHAPTER XLVIII.—On aiding the poor.

1. It is more perfect to assist other poor persons than one’s own relatives. Although Holy Scripture does not at all forbid help for relatives, but indeed permits it, nevertheless carnality draws a person toward that love by which the left hand takes something from the right hand. Jesus Christ forbids this.

2. Moreover, it is good to help all who ask for assistance—orphaned children, widows, and other [Col. 1108B] poor persons—beyond what they request; but it is much better and more acceptable to God to assist bodily and spiritually the one from whom the salvation of one’s own soul is sought.

## CHAPTER XLIX.—On the discernment necessary to complete a good work once begun.

1. At the beginning of a good work, no small deliberation is necessary; and great steadfastness is necessary while one performs it, lest one abandon it before it is completed.

2. For this reason, whoever desires to visit Jerusalem, or any saint, for prayer must first consider all the service which he ought to perform for his church in offerings and other matters while he is delayed in going to and returning from prayer; [Col. 1108C] that debt must be paid by him before he sets out. For in regard to any good which a person wishes to do, God by no means counsels him to commit an injury; rather, he forbids it. And this is the first justice: to avoid injustice. Therefore, before all else, he must discharge the debt owed to the church of which he is a son. Greatly deceived is the person who does a good work for nothing; and all do so who do not attend to the divine will in it. But certainly, in this way God will receive more gladly every good work he performs and the labor he endures in pilgrimage, because of the justice he has done toward his church; indeed, every divine office celebrated in it will be his.

3. Moreover, when he goes to prayers, he ought to think this, saying in his heart: “But where do I wish [Col. 1108D] to go? For I shall speak with that saint about nothing, nor will he say anything to me. God, I go there because he served you; therefore I too shall do likewise.” With this intention he may remain where he is; or, if he wishes, he may go there.

## CHAPTER L.—On the pride involved in abandoning one’s own cemetery.

1. This is the final pride committed at the end: when someone abandons his own cemetery and has himself buried in another. For then he renounces every good that he had received in his own church, where he came for counsel when he wished to amend himself and rise from vices.

2. For no pilgrim is more rightly a pilgrim than the one [Col. 1109A] who goes to his own church. In this too may be understood the mercy which God shows to the poor: namely, that they are buried where they ought to be.

## CHAPTER LI.—Why God is accustomed to conceal his secrets from sinners.

1. Very many sins are committed because of unbelief. For as often as someone wishes to commit sin, God’s commandment says to him in opposition: “Do not do it.” He is reproved by conscience, and when he sins, he disbelieves all this. For whoever perishes never believed in heavenly joys or infernal punishments, even though he hears them spoken of, reads them in Scripture, or proclaims them to others. For God no more wishes his enemies to know his secrets than a worldly person wishes his ill-wishers, and those by whom he is daily assailed, [Col. 1109B] to know his own.

2. But when it pleases God, he confirms his faithful servant in faith and in the love of good—sometimes more, sometimes less. And when that faith and love have departed from him, let him at least remember that he once possessed them; and God will lead him back to that state if he keeps himself from evil.

## CHAPTER LII.—On the person who received his good things in the present life.

Nothing is worse for a person than to have had all his good things in this life, and nothing is better than to have had all his evil things. For the person who has had all his good, however long it lasted, was only in passage, and will more grievously endure the afflictions in which he will remain eternally. But the other, who has passed through evils, receives good things with greater joy, and every labor he endured pleases him because of the rest in which he abides. This is what Abraham answered to the rich man who was tormented in hell: “Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, whereas you are tormented” (Luke 16). [Col. 1109C]

## CHAPTER LIII.—A consideration of the subtlety of divine judgment.

If one of the elect were to die before judgment and immediately rise again, and commit some sin for which he needed to be purified, then, dying, he would suffer in one moment of time a punishment as great and as long as another suffered for the same sin who remained in purgatorial fire for a thousand years or more. For otherwise God would need time in order to execute his justice; but he can do more than a human being can say or think. [Col. 1109D]

## CHAPTER LIV.—On the foolish anxiety of the fool.

1. A fool is anxious about what a good man is doing when he sees him remaining in one place and doing nothing. Yet from this he could observe that a laborer, even in the smallest plot of ground, continually finds something to do throughout the day, and need not be idle. Why, then, should anyone think this of one who abides with God and walks with God through heaven and earth in thought, as though he lacked work?

2. For a good man stands spaciously in any narrow place because of the charity that he has entertained; but an evil person cannot be contained by a whole kingdom, but remains cramped because of the anger he bears against another.

## CHAPTER LV.—On the difference of each person’s intention.

[Col. 1110A]

1. All works that are done are good or evil because of intention. Judas and the Jews, to the extent that they could, plotted Christ’s death, through which the world was redeemed; yet it profited them nothing, because their intention was perverse. Saint Peter and the other disciples grieved while the Lord was dying, and suffered no loss in that grief, because their understanding was good.

2. For this reason the image of the Cross is also made with Adam depicted at the feet of the crucified Christ. He signifies all the righteous who were in hell, awaiting Jesus’ death for their liberation; and that he himself should endure it pleased him greatly. Thus Adam raises his hands to the Lord in joy [Col. 1110B] because he is upon the cross. But the Mother of God and Saint John the Evangelist, who are painted nearby, were saddened by his passion, and their own salvation displeased them. So ignorant is humankind in this world!

## CHAPTER LVI.—What was Saint Paul’s infirmity.

Saint Paul’s infirmity was for him the key of his virtues. Just as a rich person stores his treasure in some secret, secure, and strong place, and afterward fastens the door lest some thief enter, so God acted in his beloved Paul. He placed within him treasures of wisdom and afterward fastened the door, carrying away its key. When the Apostle asked it of him, God refused to give it to him. For the treasure would be diminished if God healed him of his infirmity.

## CHAPTER LVII.—That no one should cease to do good while remaining in sin.

[Col. 1110C]

There is someone for whom it is fitting to do good while believing himself to be lost. Whoever is in a grave sin and unwilling to abandon it should not on that account cease to do whatever good he can. Rather, let him do it more urgently, with this intention, saying in his heart: “God, I perform this good, but I know with complete certainty that I shall be condemned without end if I am found in this sin. Yet I do good for this reason: that you may grant me to hate the sin.” By this faith God will draw him out of sin, and then he will recover all the good that he had previously done. Otherwise, if he thought himself to be saved while retaining the sin, he would be without hope. For there is hope that, by doing good, someone may await salvation from [Col. 1110D] God; but one has fallen away from hope who believes himself to be saved while doing evil.

## CHAPTER LVIII.—On the constant wrongdoing of the fool.

A fool who is trusted does worse upon the land than an invading army. For an army departs after a few days, but a fool devastates it for a long time. Hence Solomon says: “Woe to the land whose king is a child!” (Ecclesiastes 10).

## CHAPTER LIX.—How someone ought to leave the world.

1. All sins displease the Lord; but it utterly displeases him when someone sins in the hope of doing good.

2. For example, whoever wishes to do something excellent—namely, to leave the world, or anything else—and, in hope of this, first commits one of the grave sins, saying in his heart: “I shall leave at once all the sins [Col. 1111A] in which I remain,” then he virtually forbids the Lord to lead him to the good which he had intended. He acts as though someone rolled in mud when he wished to bathe; rather, he ought first to wash his feet, so that he might enter the bath without dirt.

## CHAPTER LX.—A discourse on usury.

1. Whoever receives usury sins; and likewise, in this manner, does the person who pays it. When someone, by his lack of moderation, incurs an expense which his means cannot sustain—whether in food, clothing, or other things—although he could maintain his life in some way from his own possessions, and afterward, because of that excess, goes to a moneylender, he sins in the payment which he gives him just as much as does the other who receives it. For no one would ever be in want if he remained moderate; one sin drives him into another. Nor will anyone be without want who always spends his income before he has it. [Col. 1111B]

2. Usury is sinned in many ways, but especially by the person who takes pledges. For after he has received them, toward the end of his life, he leaves them to his son or whomever he wishes. In doing this he says—indeed, his actions speak more forcefully than words—“Son, I shall die, and I have fought against God as long as I have lived. It is not enough for me; I shall leave you as my deputy, so that with this same usury you may fight against him.”

3. Of such a person it may be said that even after he is dead he is still a moneylender and continually lends his money at usury. For whatever is received beyond what was entrusted is usury. [Col. 1111C]

4. Again, someone claims as an inheritance his father’s sin: tithes which the father took away, or some other land. This avails him no more than if he claimed hell as an inheritance. Yet let him know without doubt that he has never been there; for if he had been there even for one moment, he would never wish to return there for all the wealth of the world.

## CHAPTER LXI.—On the wise man.

1. A wise man considers his words before uttering them. But the fool, who takes no thought for his reasoning, sometimes says when he hears of another’s good works: “God ought to be very grateful to this man, who has done so much good for love of him.” O fool, why do you say that God ought to be grateful to a person for good? Will God be grateful to a person because he sees with his eyes, speaks with his mouth, or walks with his feet? Rather, let the person give thanks to God because he has granted him to walk, speak, and see, and likewise because he allows him to perform good works. [Col. 1111D]

2. Again, the fool says of those who have overcome their enemies, capturing some and killing others: “These men have accomplished what was useful to them.” He is mistaken who says that a person works for his own benefit when he departs from God and obtains hell. Would not anyone judge himself deceived if even a single limb were taken from him? What then will become of the one who kills his own body and soul?

## CHAPTER LXII.—On justice.

[Col. 1112A]

Everything that a person spends ought to be something which he lawfully possesses as his own; otherwise, at least he should spend what he possesses more justly on bread. For alms are more often made from bread than from other things. And the person unwilling to abandon all evil at present should nevertheless abandon some part of it. This is how a wise man ought to instruct an evil person. When he cannot convert him entirely, he should show him how, even in that wickedness itself, he may do some good. He will believe him more readily in this than if he told him to abandon all evil.

## CHAPTER LXIII.—How a soldier ought to conduct himself on campaign.

1. It is a marvelous knowledge, and greatly pleasing to God, that when a person takes part in evil deeds, he should restrain himself from evil. This can be done as follows. A soldier going on campaign for his natural lord, from whom he cannot withdraw himself, if he wishes to cleave to God, should first say in his heart: “Lord God, I shall go on this campaign, but I declare that I shall be your soldier there, wishing to perform in it nothing except your service: to destroy evil and seek good, here and there, as much as I can.” [Col. 1112B]

2. With this intention let him begin to go, running ahead as though he wished to seize everyone. But those whom he sees, let him make flee lest they be captured; or, if another wishes to take them, let God’s soldier seize them first and then release them. Let him defend his companions from evil, and others too, as much as he can. Thus a monk may wear a shield about his neck and render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s (Matthew 22). [Col. 1112C]

3. But let everyone take utmost care not to make alms from plunder. For one sins more by giving it to the poor than by taking it from others. While taking it, he does not doubt that it is evil; but when he distributes it to the poor, he supposes himself thereby free. Thus he is received by God as though someone killed a son before his father’s eyes and afterward brought the father the blood to drink in a golden cup. It is also a greater sin to seize than to steal, because the pride is greater.

## CHAPTER LXIV.—On vengeance against enemies.

No one can avenge himself upon his enemy as well as by taking from him that by which he inflicts evil upon him. But if evil is returned for evil, wickedness is increased, and no one has thereby been avenged; rather, he has enlarged it. Surely no one avenges himself by something which increases more than it diminishes. But whoever returns good to his enemy for his evil then fully avenges himself on wickedness, because he destroys it by taking away its place where it dwelt—namely, the other’s mind, which may at some time be converted to good. Or if it is not converted, then the enemy’s infernal punishment is wholly increased, and in this he has been greatly avenged. [Col. 1112D]

## CHAPTER LXV.—How an offering at the altar is to be made.

1. The Lord says in the Gospel to everyone who wishes to offer: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and remember that your brother has something against [Col. 1113A] you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother” (Matthew 5). This ought to be understood in two ways. The person who has committed an injury must seek peace as a matter of strict justice; and he has not thereby attained great perfection—indeed, he would sin if he did not do it.

2. But when someone has been injured and afterward is ill-disposed toward the person who committed it, then it is perfection for him to seek peace. For Jesus Christ acted thus upon the cross: he first forgave his crucifiers before they asked it of him. Therefore we ought to believe that he likewise commands and wills this in that Gospel saying.

3. Again, if someone has injured another and asks forgiveness from him, but the other refuses in every way to forgive him, God turns the judgment for the wrongdoing upon this latter person. Nor does anyone entrust God not to forgive him for any other sin than when he refuses to forgive his own enemy. [Col. 1113B]

## CHAPTER LXVI.—How a person out of his mind should be cared for.

1. Sometimes a person’s brain is disturbed and his faculties are changed; he may deny, swear oaths, and know neither any good nor even himself. But if he should die in that disturbance, one ought not believe that he is therefore condemned, provided that before then, when he was well, he was not in grave sin but kept himself from evil and cleaved to God. For God is faithful and will judge him according to the memory of his soundness.

2. The following counsel would be necessary for one afflicted with this infirmity: no one should take him to saints, nor anywhere except where strictly necessary. For people laugh at this, and in churches they lose their prayer; moreover, he is beaten, his brain is wholly disturbed, his infirmity grows, and there is great sin. Rather, he ought to be kept more privately in some house, moderately protected from cold and heat, and his friends should pray for him. [Col. 1113C]

## CHAPTER LXVII.—That no layperson should reproach clerics vainly.

1. A layperson sometimes says, in defense of his own sins: “Why do clerics sin, when they know the Scriptures and God’s secrets?” But a wise man should answer him thus: “Friend, since you recognize the clerics’ guilt, you are wiser than he in this matter. Why, then, do you not take care not to do what you reproach in another? The Scripture of the heart, which God has placed in you, always shows you what you ought to abandon or do. Thus you sin knowingly, just as though you were a cleric.” [Col. 1113D]

2. Know with certainty that it will never profit you if another perishes and you follow him. For no one can devise a more foolish argument than that of the person who says to his pastor: “You will be held accountable if you lead me to destruction.”

## CHAPTER LXVIII.—On counsel given to each person.

1. A person very often complains more about that which would not benefit him, and which God would never demand of him, than about the rest for which he will be condemned. Such is the one who says: “I have no wealth with which to serve God or give alms.” [Col. 1114A]

2. But a wise man should show him that he is rich, saying: “Brother, since you are so poor, for what price would you give up a foot or any one of your limbs?” Perhaps he will answer: “For no price, sir.” Again: “For what wealth would you allow your eyes to be taken from you?” He will scarcely say: “For so much.” The wise man may say to him: “Then you are very rich, since you would not give what you possess for great wealth.” Therefore guard your limbs carefully, but love them only so far that you do not lose them eternally in hell.

## CHAPTER LXIX.—How religious persons should act when someone inflicts evil.

[Col. 1114B]

1. When someone inflicts evil upon religious persons, and they cry to God by reading curses against their wrongdoers, they virtually forbid the Lord to execute justice upon it. But God, who stood ready to take vengeance, answers them: “Then I shall depart, since you did not wait for me and have yourselves taken vengeance by cursing.”

2. First, the wrongdoer ought to be questioned why he did this. If he answered that he did it from need, the religious community should help him. But if he did it from pride, the entire convent of the cloister should pray God with all its heart to forgive him. Then either God would convert him, or without delay would execute his justice upon him.

## CHAPTER LXX.—That no one, pastor or disciple, may leave his cloister for the sake of prayer.

[Col. 1114C]

1. A pastor may send his disciple anywhere in order to maintain his religious community. But if a disciple goes to Jerusalem, or to any saints, for prayer, then by his own decision he renounces his life, not knowing the good for which he had come. For he cannot carry money there unless he has long stolen it from the others.

Finally, how will one go to Rome or elsewhere who has cut off his own feet?

2. At last, when the pastor and the whole community absolve the disobedient disciple in order that he may go there, it is not enough for them that he alone depart from God unless all together become participants in the sin. The disciple goes freely to hell, as he thinks, because they have absolved him. For if he were excommunicated, he would continually be afraid and perhaps return. [Col. 1114D]

3. But if the pastor sets out anywhere for prayer, he utterly pierces the cloister without restraint, telling all the others to do likewise.

## CHAPTER LXXI.—How the divine word should be heard.

When someone hears the Lord’s word, even though he cannot retain it all, he profits as much when it pleases him as he would be harmed if it displeased him. At least each person should strive to retain from it enough by which the soul may live until he hears God spoken of again, just as someone sitting at table takes enough food to reach another meal. For both body and soul must eat, and neither can live long once food wholly fails it. [Col. 1115A]

## CHAPTER LXXII.—On any good thing: how, or in what manner, it is done.

1. Everyone may observe this from many examples. Some measure their good by shaving it off; others heap it up; some also add increments. When a good is done grudgingly, and not with great willingness, it is done by shaving. When a good work is pleasing, to take pleasure and delight in it is an accumulation of good. Again, some are displeased, for greater perfection, because they did not do better: and behold, additions. Such accumulated, carefully considered, [Col. 1115B] and overflowing good a person ought to return to the Lord, who purchased him at the most precious price of his blood.

2. Evil likewise grows when it pleases, just as good does. Therefore it is a greater sin to kill one’s enemy than one’s friend. For everyone is angry over the killing of a friend, and God forgives him, because the person repents of it from the heart. But someone takes such pleasure in having killed his enemy that he can scarcely attain forgiveness for it. Even after he has undergone judgment for it, he then says in his heart: “God, blessed are you for bringing me to repentance from this sin. Yet I greatly enjoy that the man who harmed me is dead.” And while he thinks this, he has never been so far from repentance. [Col. 1115C]

3. For repentance consists in a person’s repenting—a thing which God alone gives to a person by his grace. When a priest imposes judgment, he first asks the sinner whether he brings repentance or whether the sin displeases him. If he answers, “I do not repent at all,” what judgment can he impose upon him until he repents? But if he says, “I repent,” he can judge him and grant penance, which God gives him—namely, that he may always repent of it.

## CHAPTER LXXIII.—On the greater labor someone suffers in a small good than if the good were great.

1. A person suffers greater labor in a small good than if the good were great. For a small good does not bring a person to the perfection of divine love, in which there is rest; but a great good causes him to arrive there. [Col. 1115D]

2. But if anyone asks what good is small or what great, whoever performs good works can see this in himself, for it is not expedient that another know it. If the good pleases him and he remains at rest while doing it, it is great; but if it displeases him and he remains in uneasiness, the good is small.

## CHAPTER LXXIV.—On the anger and anxiety of the wicked person, and the joy and sweetness of the just person.

An evil person weeps from anger and anxiety; but a good person weeps from joy, and sometimes from sweetness. The evil person does not wish to leave the tribulation in which he remains by dying, for he fears that his punishment in hell may be increased. But the just person wishes, from the sweetness in which he remains, to pass on in hope of something greater. Everyone may also know that great will be the joy when a person laughs with God, since it is so great now while he weeps. [Col. 1116A]

## CHAPTER LXXV.—On the difference between the just person and the wicked person.

1. A good person and an evil person are alike in many respects. Both can keep watch, fast, give alms, and do very many other good things; but the good person can forgive from the heart, whereas the evil person cannot. [Col. 1116B]

2. Suppose any very wealthy person were told: “Give one penny, or be killed.” He would easily give it in order to save his life. But if someone said to a poor person: “Give a thousand silver marks, or be hanged,” he might be hanged and would never give them, because he did not have them. So too the good person is so rich in goodness that he is not burdened when he forgives from the heart: he is so filled with forgiveness that he forgives before forgiveness is asked of him. But the evil person is so poor in good that he cannot do this at all, nor even believe that it may be done by a good person.

3. There is, however, someone who out of pride rejects forgiveness when it is offered him by a just person, saying: “I do not care that you forgive me.” But one who grants forgiveness to a person unwilling to receive it acts as though he blew coals upon his head and shoulders. The infernal punishment of one so proud and contemptuous is increased greatly. [Col. 1116C]

## CHAPTER LXXVI.—On the punishments suffered by the unjust.

1. From this one may understand how great the punishments will be that the wicked person shall suffer. For God wills that his faithful endure tribulations in this life for the redemption of their sins; and to their redemption he added his own death and his own labor. Since that death profits those who perish nothing, indeed rather increases their punishment, neither do they endure labor for their sins which God may accept; rather, insofar as they are able, they do such deeds, and the righteous guard themselves against them. It may therefore be known [Col. 1116D] that they will have great punishment; but the will to sin removes from them the fear of punishment.

2. God is so faithful that he prefers to be asked for something great rather than something small. But when something lesser is asked of him, namely the riches of this world, it is sometimes denied; whereas if anyone rightly asks him for the greater thing, he will undoubtedly give it—namely, his kingdom. And, in order to draw a person toward what is better, he sometimes withdraws what is worse.

3. Whoever endures in peace and joy when he lacks the necessities of life is not yet perfectly abstinent, though he does well. But abstinence is perfect when he has before him that which the body [Col. 1117A] desires, and restrains himself from using it. Yet abstinence is greater in this: that a person desires less of the things of this world.

## CHAPTER LXXVII.—On the greatness of good and evil

1. In the greatness of good there is sometimes a greatness of evil. For one who knows the Lord more fully—which is greatness of good—sins more grievously when he dissents from him. Therefore the devil’s sin was so great, because he knew the Lord so well; and next came Adam’s sin, because he stood in so great a good. Likewise, the more God grants each person his good things, bodily or spiritual, the greater an injury that person commits when he dissents from him. This too ought to inspire great fear in all people: that a kindly angel, because of [Col. 1117B] one evil thought, became a devil and fell forever. What, then, will become of the person who daily thinks and does evil?

2. A wicked person judges that he does a greater good for the Lord when he abstains from evil for a time than a good person does by continually performing good. For the more righteous anyone is, the more he despises all his good, although he cherishes more dearly than another what appears to be contrary to this. But it must be understood thus: whoever labors more for the Lord and strives more in good works is stirred by the Holy Spirit to such an extent that he regards the works he does as little, because he cannot make them better; and he seems to himself to be delayed, because he is unable to do all that the will of his [Col. 1117C] spirit suggests to him.

3. Thus the Lord makes a righteous man regard his good as little, lest he lose it; and yet he loves it so much that he in no way wishes to be separated from it. Whoever does not understand this has not deeply experienced divine love.
