## CHAPTER LXXVIII.—On the fear which a wise man has concerning divine goods

1. A righteous man fears more concerning the good things in which he stands, lest they accuse him before God, than concerning the crimes he committed while he was in the world. For each person knows well that crimes have been forgiven, provided that he repents of them and does not thereafter return to them. But a person can lose good things in many ways: if he despises another because of them, or judges that he possesses them of himself; [Col. 1117D] or if he believes himself worthy because God grants him to do them; or thinks that he ought therefore to be saved by God; or desires praise, so as thereby to take honor away from God; or does them for some reward other than that which he may have in this world.

2. A person is also condemned in many other ways because of God’s benefits, because of his sacred word, and because of the sacraments of holy Church, since a person approaches them while unworthy. For one who perishes through both good and evil, like false Christians, will suffer a greater punishment than one condemned solely for evil, like unbelievers.

3. And when the Lord protects his faithful servant from all snares that impede good, this is more pleasing to him and he praises him more for it than for forgiving him the crimes [Col. 1118A] which he committed in the world. For that very forgiveness would be condemnation for him unless he were defended by God, as in the Gospel concerning the servant who would not forgive another.

But God is so wise a guardian that he does not permit evil to be added to his good. Yet when someone attributes that good to himself, God hands him over to the enemy. Greatly deceived, indeed, is the person who is rejected because of his good.

## CHAPTER LXXIX.—On the rebuke of a fool’s words, and how a wise man should answer him

A certain fool says: “It would be enough for me to remain one year in religious life, only that the Lord might find me in good works at the end, and that I might be able to make confession.” But a wise man should answer him in this way: [Col. 1118B] “Brother, do you wish God to cast you out from his glory after a thousand years, or to save you forever?” Perhaps he will answer: “I desire salvation.” Therefore, since you wish to be saved by God without limit and without end, why do you wish to impose a limit or interruption upon your service of him?

## CHAPTER LXXX.—On the counsel given to everyone, that no one through folly should delay doing good

1. It is the height of folly for a person to delay confessing his sins, praying to the Lord, and giving alms until the end of life. For a person zealously and according to his ability opposes the Lord for thirty or forty years, and afterward wishes God to forgive him as quickly as possible. Yet he ought, at the very least, to labor as much to make peace as he labored to make discord; for one takes longer to wash something than to defile it.

2. Finally, in no work are such soundness and such strength necessary to a person as in praying to God and loving him with the whole heart. And when the body fails and memory diminishes, how will he pray to him and make confession? For when someone is very ill, he labors more merely to open his eyes than he would by walking for a whole day while well. Nor is it sound counsel when someone says: “I would pray to God, if I were not ill.” To one who has done well the Lord replies: “Why do you seek prayers other than me? I [Col. 1118D] am here with you, performing my office.” But if he has acted negligently, God says to him: “I know well how you acted while you were healthy.”

3. Indeed, it would not be beneficial for a person to have at his end even the means by which one alms might be made for him, or with which he might be wrapped. For one alms will benefit him more if he makes it while healthy than innumerable alms made after his death; and another will scarcely love him more than he loves himself.

4. A person is so foolish that he wishes everything he possesses, whether great or small, to be good. Yet concerning the soul, which governs everything, he says to works: “Let it belong to whomever it can”; for he hands it over into the enemy’s power when he does not guard himself at all from evil.

## CHAPTER LXXXI.—On hastening to do good

[Col. 1119A]

1. At every hour and at every age it greatly pleases God if someone turns to him. But when a person is young, his body vigorous, and his blood ardent, it wholly pleases the Lord if he begins to serve him, withdrawing his members from the evil they can do and turning them toward good. For then he becomes a living sacrifice, pleasing to God.

2. Therefore everyone ought to hasten to do good works, because one who loses a single prayer or another good will never afterward recover it, just as time past cannot return backward. Nor will a person render account to the Lord only for superfluous thoughts, vain [Col. 1119B] words, and evil deeds, but also for the good which he ought to do while committing evil. For whenever anyone fails to do what he knows pleases God, he sins grievously; and no one can do penance for this sin alone unless God forgives him through his grace.

## CHAPTER LXXXII.—On the severe temptation of any righteous person

1. Sometimes a severe temptation occurs to a righteous man in his prayer; and behold, when he says, “Lord God, help me,” his temptations increase. But the Lord answers him spiritually: “Now I am helping you. The more strongly you are tempted, the better I aid you, because I do not permit you to be conquered by temptations; nor can you otherwise be crowned unless you have contended lawfully. For what would consolation do for you now, until [Col. 1119C] you have passed through your straits and recognized how necessary I am to you?”

2. But God is faithful, and he does not wish to burden his beast of burden so heavily, even if he sees it strong, that its spine is broken; nor does he strike it in order to cast it down, but to bring it back into the way and make it go more swiftly.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII.—Again on the same subject

For this reason a righteous man is more strongly tempted than another: because temptations displease him more. He does not think more wickedly than others who follow an evil will; but the better he is, the more an evil thought displeases him, and he considers himself more guilty because of it than another does while committing evil deeds.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV.—Again on the same subject

[Col. 1119D]

1. In the same way God is pleased when a good man endures temptations as he is pleased when that man rejoices in the visitation of divine sweetness. This may be perceived by the following example. If someone has a wife and, while he is absent, another speaks with her of adultery, yet she does not consent, then when he returns he does not love her any less on that account; indeed, he is as pleased that she defended herself as he is delighted that he himself has come.

2. Likewise, if the soldiers of a fortress defend themselves against an army while their lord is absent, the lord, when he arrives, will be as pleased that they defended themselves as they will rejoice at his coming. Similarly, God is pleased when a good man [Col. 1120A] endures temptation and afterward rejoices in God himself.

## CHAPTER LXXXV.—How someone should sometimes be restrained from good

1. There is someone for whom it is better to be restrained from good than from evil. For it is unnecessary to say to a good man, “Beware of murder or other crimes.” If he is good, he avoids them as far as he can.

2. But when he does good, then the pastor by whom he is governed should sometimes say to him: “You could do this better,” so that the disciple may preserve humility all the more because he is rebuked and held back from the good itself.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI.—On recognizing the good of humility

1. In this may the good of humility be seen: no one is such a sinner that, if he humbles himself from the heart, God will not make him righteous. Humility therefore greatly increases the virtues of a righteous man, since it removes all the evils of a sinner. And it greatly pleases God when the righteous humble themselves, since he is so pleased with the sinner because that sinner is reconciled with him.

2. Pride, by contrast, destroys virtues when it enters into a good man. It may therefore be known that it makes evil people worse.

3. It ought greatly to please a person to live long in a good life. For God grants him many days with so much grace that, if any wicked person had one of them at the end of his life, he would without doubt be saved. Great, therefore, will be the reward of the faithful person who daily gains God’s kingdom, just as the wicked person acquires [Col. 1120C] hell.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII.—On the recollection of sins by which a religious man was once corrupted in the world

1. A religious person recognizes the sins in which he lived in the world in this way: on some day it happens that he weeps and accuses himself so greatly that God makes him free from all crimes. But after the good movement of his heart, he finds within himself innumerable sins on that very day on which he had wept, although after repentance he has not fallen into crime. From this he may understand the sins in which he lived in the world, when he was not at all at peace with God.

2. It is one thing to conquer oneself, and another to be conquered by oneself. One who tramples vices overcomes himself; one who is cast down by vices is conquered by himself.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—On the wonder of heavenly joys

1. This, along with other good things, will be wonderful in heavenly joy. All the elect will be present there together; none will precede another, although he was born and died earlier; nor will anyone think that he has arrived there late. For all will see together how they were present in the providence of God in the kingdom of heaven before the world was made.

2. They will also know how through their sin they lost that joy which God afterward restored to them through his grace. And just as they will praise the Lord because their salvation will lack an end, so they will praise him [Col. 1121A] because it never had a beginning in the sight of God.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.—How God is honored both in the reprobate and in the elect

1. God will be honored in the reprobate in the same manner as in the elect. Just as one power at war with another, if it can conquer the other in battle and put it into its prison, will receive as much honor in its conquered enemies as in the reward it gives its allies, so the punishment of some and the salvation of others will be praise to God.

2. But there will be something further: God will show mercy in those who perish—not to them, but in them he will show it to the rest. Just as, if someone destroys a wicked robber, he shows great compassion to the people whom that wicked man oppressed through destroying him, so the Lord will show mercy in the reprobate to his elect, because he will remove the former from the latter, so that they can no longer afflict them.

3. Jesus Christ showed this mercy to his disciples when he departed from them bodily and thereby removed Judas. For Judas would have vexed them greatly had he remained with them. But while God was bodily present, he allowed Judas to carry the common funds, so that the others might be unencumbered and the thief might be occupied with the nothing on which he had set his heart.

## CHAPTER XC.—On divine mercies toward the soul

[Col. 1121C] 1. Blessed is the person whose sins no one sees except himself and God. For this is one of the great mercies which God displays toward one who loves him. God does not wholly remove the vices a person has within himself while he lives in this world, but covers them as fire is covered by ashes; and no one sees them except God and the good man. But when God’s servant recognizes them, he disagrees with himself, and that discord is the beginning of peace.

2. Finally, God displays to the people the good which he places within him through his grace, and causes the righteous man to be praised for that which does not belong to him at all. Yet all honor belongs to the Lord; for no one would be judged good if another saw what he sometimes thinks.

[Col. 1121D] 3. For a person is often seen where he is not and not seen where he is: the body is seen in good works, but the heart is far from them. Therefore God shows great mercy by concealing human thoughts.

## CHAPTER XCI.—On God’s mercy and justice, which sometimes displease a person

1. Sometimes God’s mercy displeases a person, and sometimes his justice. Suppose that someone wicked is in some country, and the people say: “Why does God permit this man’s wickedness? He ought not to permit it.” But you who complain, what do you say about yourself? Have you never done anything foolishly? If you have, do you wish God to destroy you? You will answer me: “I do not.” Therefore, since it does not displease you that God endures you, why do you accuse his mercy in another, when you likewise need it? Human wickedness ought to displease you, but you ought to admire and praise God’s mercy with your whole heart.

2. In another way God’s justice displeases a person. Certainly everyone ought above all things to love God; but whoever does not do this should at least always be pleased with the love divinely bestowed upon him. Again, if he is not greatly pleased by it, let him take care that it does not displease him, and this will suffice for him. Someone will reply: “The love God shows me will never displease me.” Yet let him understand this: a person falls into this displeasure as often as he is displeased by the divine ordering and justice by which God wishes to hold him [Col. 1122B] in sickness, poverty, or the afflictions he sends him, so that he may abandon evil and do good.

3. Therefore this virtue is more necessary to a person than all others: that with an upright heart he agree with all divine actions and words, and rebuke none of them. But each person’s own works should displease him, because they are all useless; and he should praise those works which are God’s, from whom good things come.

4. Whoever does not know this should wholly accuse himself, for his sins obstruct him, so that he does not understand it. And in nothing can one better know oneself to be a sinner than in this: that one does not see God’s secrets, which are clearer than day [Col. 1122C] to those who live rightly.

## CHAPTER XCII.—On the great mercy which God shows to a righteous person

1. When God saves a righteous person who has long remained in a good life, he shows him as great a mercy as he shows a sinner who converts near the end of life. If someone asks how this can be, without the sinner’s salvation—which cost him no labor—being a greater mercy than that of the righteous person who labored long, we answer: “The salvation of the righteous is not only as great a mercy, but even greater. For it is certain that the righteous would have fallen into the same sins into which another fell, or worse ones, unless he had always been held by divine hands.”

[Col. 1122D] 2. For the corruption of vices is twofold in all people. Thus God shows his mercy to the righteous person when he protects him from sinning, grants him to live delightfully in works of righteousness, and afterward saves him through his grace. Is it not a greater power that the fire and heat of vices should not burn where they are present than if they had been entirely absent? At last the righteous person will be free from the punishment which another suffers for his sins, whether in this world or in purgatorial fire.

3. Behold another mercy: for this reason too God shows greater grace to the righteous person when he saves him than to another. For the more righteous one is, the greater is his need and the greater his desire for salvation. Someone who relieves a needy person [Col. 1123A] and gives a beggar what he desires shows greater mercy than if he relieved another who has no concern. But the wicked person has no desire or care for salvation; the righteous person sighs and weeps because he is absent from it. Therefore it is a greater mercy for God to fulfill his desire.

## CHAPTER XCIII.—On the exaltation of God’s riches

1. So great is the height of God’s riches that, if a person knew nothing further about him except that he had found written that God had once remembered the whole world in heaven, he ought to serve the Lord more for that memory alone than he serves him for all that God has done and daily does for human salvation.

2. Again, if God had said: “Those who do [Col. 1123B] my will I shall save without end,” and he were asked: “Lord, tell it to us,” but he did not tell it, and no one did it, then a person could have some excuse for sins committed through pride. He could say when he came to judgment: “I would not have done evil had I known that it displeased God.” But God has not hidden his will: first he announced it through the patriarchs and prophets; he himself, coming to earth, spoke it fully; and afterward the apostles and other teachers did so. He still speaks it to every person in conscience when he grants him discernment of good and evil.

3. Indeed, divine commandments are so full of sweetness that, even if God had not given them, a person ought reasonably to ask them of him and say: “Lord God, grant us to do this, because it will be easier for us to love one another and remain in peace.” Therefore, since God commands this, is not whoever refuses to do it exceedingly cruel and worthy of great punishment?

## CHAPTER XCIV.—How the body of Christ should be received

This might reasonably be said to one wishing to communicate: “Brother, do you wish to receive the body of Jesus Christ? Do you also wish God wholly to give himself to you? If you desire this, God is ready wholly to give himself to you on this condition: that you likewise wholly give yourself to him, since you desire to possess him wholly.” Consider also [Col. 1123D] in your heart whether God asks anything excessive when he says to you: “Give yourself wholly to me, and I shall give myself wholly to you.” And, brother, what you give him you will retain, and it will be yours. But what you retain and refuse to give him will be for destruction. For whoever loves his soul will lose it, and whoever loses it will gain it, as the Gospel says (Mark VIII).

## CHAPTER XCV.—On the necessary thought concerning the end

1. With this thought everyone ought to rise, lie down, and do all his works: always to say in the voice of his heart, “Lord God, defend me only today, that I may not depart from you. Yesterday, indeed, I did not restrain myself well; but today I shall amend myself in every way, since my end is at hand.” And, as though he held death before his eyes, he should daily do good works for the respite of one day, as though, so to speak, he kept one foot raised in readiness to pass into another world.

2. Finally, when he falls ill and knows that he will not live longer, after he has confessed and repented of his sins, let him turn his heart to the grace of Jesus Christ and to the love which Christ has for his members. Let him also remember the greater good which God granted him to do, and give thanks to him for it. At last, with the remembrance of good works, and also with faith and hope of salvation, let him depart from this world.

3. Yet it would be necessary for everyone to labor long toward this; and, that he might at least dare to die, everyone ought to wish to remain in righteousness. For one who loves God sometimes desires to depart out of a desire to see him, and no one ought to wish to die for another reason.

## CHAPTER XCVI.—On charity and the excellence of charity

1. True charity has its honor in heaven and a greater excellence, because God is its friend and it does not wish to degenerate. Of all things it sees bodily, it always desires less: cheaper clothing and poorer food, only that it may somehow pass the present day and often revisit the treasure of its bridal chamber, namely Jesus Christ, whom it has in its heart.

2. The king of this world values one penny more highly than charity values all the world’s riches; for it never wishes to have a better dwelling than heaven. It may also be said that it is greatly covetous, since the whole world cannot suffice for it. But whoever possesses it does not care that anyone should speak of him; he prefers to remain hidden and despised in this world, and observes divine commandments more fully. For adversity and poverty do not terrify him. But the heavenly King makes her beauty wonderful to all his citizens because she has abased herself: every angel knows better how to praise and honor God’s friend than all the people of the world.

3. Again, it greatly pleases true charity that God commands it to love its enemies, for it remains more at ease while loving them than if it hated them; and it wholly rejoices because God commands it to pray for its persecutors. Considering this too, the Lord will show the greatest mercy to those who suffer labors for him, since he wills prayers to be made for those who torment his other friends, and wills to have mercy on them.

4. These are the works and thoughts of true charity. But perhaps someone will say: “Who can possess it?” Without doubt, this is the way by which Saint Peter and the other elect ascended to heaven. But one who wishes to possess as much as one of them, and desires to be saved as they were, will he not do something of what they did? Let him at least do so much. Let him believe without doubt that [Col. 1125A] he ought to do it. If he believes rightly, he will turn away from evil and do good according to his strength.

## CHAPTER XCVII.—On the grace of Jesus Christ toward the elect

1. Whoever has his whole heart in the grace of Jesus Christ rejoices. For Abraham and the other Fathers of the Old Testament descended into hell when they died. If anyone could be saved by good works alone, Moses, Saint John the Baptist, and many others would never have descended there, and would have remained there forever unless God’s Son had delivered them from it.

2. Indeed, if all the works of all the righteous from the beginning of the world to the end had been done by one person, and the evil which others did were also good and all were his, [Col. 1125B] still it would not suffice for him to see heavenly glory for a single moment if God’s grace were absent. For no one can merit anything by his own powers except punishment. God would have done enough for the one who obeyed the Lord most fully if he merely freed him from the punishments of hell—and his mother as well—since all people have deserved them for the sins in which they are born.

3. This, then, is the highest counsel for all people: that everyone live as rightly as he can, awaiting the Lord. Let God himself do what pleases him, whether concerning punishment or salvation. Even if someone knew with absolute certainty that he would be damned, he ought not therefore to cease from God’s service.

[Col. 1125C] 4. Since Jesus Christ accomplished everything necessary for human salvation, and nothing was lacking on his part for a person’s salvation except the fault of each individual, why should anyone withdraw his service from him? Yet God is not cruel, but faithful, and he will save those who obey him. The good works which God works in a person are by grace, and salvation likewise; and from one grace God wills another to be hoped for. But whoever rejects the first—that is, good works—is not worthy of the second, that is, salvation.

## CHAPTER XCVIII.—On the honor of the righteous

God honors one who loves him in many ways. For it will be a greater honor to a person that God saves him by his grace alone than if he saved him [Col. 1125D] by that person’s good works. Would it not be more honorable to any poor person if a king went far away to seek him in a foreign land, brought him to his court, made him sit with himself, and appointed him lord of his kingdom, than if the poor person sought the king? Likewise, did not the sheep that was lost return more honorably to the house when the shepherd himself sought it and placed it upon his shoulders than if it had begun to come of its own accord and no one carried it? So it is a greater honor to a person that God is concerned for his salvation.

## CHAPTER XCIX.—On the dishonor of the reprobate

1. By this reasoning may also be understood the disgrace and dishonor of the reprobate. For they will lay blame upon nothing but themselves, since they condemned themselves by their own will. For God will never condemn anyone, nor does he have grounds to do so unless someone gives them to him; indeed, he gladly saves those who desire to follow him.

2. A person delights in God when God first delights in him; someone rests in God when God first rests in him; a person receives God when God is in him. For God can rest or delight in nothing except himself, nor can anything other than God receive God. If it were otherwise, God would have found some good other than himself, whereas all good is in himself.

## CHAPTER C.—On the security which ought to be had in the Lord alone

1. Security can be found in nothing except God. For those who hear the lives of the saints and the labors they suffered for the Lord say to themselves nothing other than that they must do likewise. Their sufferings are not redemptions except for themselves; indeed, they are terrors to one who refuses to imitate them.

2. Likewise, irrational creatures, which continually remain in the Lord’s ordering, ought to inspire a person with great shame and great fear, because he possesses reason and yet departs from divine ordering. Thus fear is found in all things.

3. But Jesus Christ alone says to one who loves him: “I did all my works for you; for you I was born and baptized; my death is your life; my resurrection [Col. 1126C] is your forgiveness; my ascension is your glorification.” It is therefore evident that all other things terrify a person, while God alone, who suffered for him and loves him most, makes him secure.

## CHAPTER CI.—On a question put by a disciple to the pastor

1. A disciple asked our pastor: “Lord, since you defend divine justice in so many and such great matters, for what reason did the Lord command the children of Israel to borrow treasure from the Egyptians and carry it away with them (Exod. XII)? It seems to be robbery.” He answered: “Brother, this was plainly just. The former had served the latter for a long time, and the latter had repaid the former’s service with evil. In just judgment God, the righteous judge, willed that they should carry away with them the wages of their labor which the others had withheld from them. There is also another, spiritual meaning: in the same way, the members of Christ received the treasure of Holy Scripture from the Jews who remained in Egypt, that is, in the darkness of this world.”

2. The same disciple asked him again: “Lord, you say that God loved the land of Jerusalem more than another, so much that he brought his friends there from other regions; he himself was born there of the Virgin, and in Scripture often calls it the land of promise. It is therefore surprising that he wished it to be such: for there are no beautiful meadows there, nor excellent springs, nor very rich rivers, but water in cisterns, and roughness and heat more than in many lands.” [Col. 1127A] The pastor resolved this question thus: “Brother, in this one may consider how admirable the divine ordering is. For this reason he removed bodily delight from it, so that his friends might delight in him alone, and his love might be for them meadow, spring, river, and every other refuge. For unless God knew another world to be better, he would never transfer his friends there; indeed, he would in no way deceive his own mother.

3. “But for heavenly joy he sometimes withdraws present joy, yet not so as to leave his friends sad and desolate in this world. Rather, God seems to will this because then he keeps his servants in greater rest when the world considers that they suffer labor; for he is more honored when he makes them rest amid afflictions. But sometimes, in order that unbelievers may be ashamed, he displays to the people the sweetness in which his friends bodily remain while they are tortured, as is read of the three boys, who blessed him in the fire of the furnace (Dan. III). Others, whom he does not so deliver bodily, so that the faithful may there take an example of patience, he consoles so greatly in spirit that those who torture them suffer greater labor than the servants of God who are tortured.”

## CHAPTER CII.—On divine sweetness

The Lord God is exceedingly sweet. Whenever someone wishes humbly to speak with him in prayer, God is present, ready to hear the person’s words. But if someone wished to speak privately with a powerful person of this world, it could happen that he would not speak with that person on the very day on which he came before him.

## CHAPTER CIII.—On saving instruction for everyone

You must understand this, whoever desires to speak familiarly with God: God will not hear you unless you are with yourself when you ask him. For how would your friend come to you if, when you invited him, you fled away first? Take care, therefore, that your heart does not depart from you through vain thoughts, and you will find God present in your prayer.

## CHAPTER CIV.—On a question asked by a certain disciple to his master while he was speaking about prayer, and on his answer

[Col. 1127D] 1. While the pastor was speaking about prayer, the aforesaid disciple asked him how one ought to remain in it. He answered with a discourse of this kind: In his prayer Moses raised his hands to God while Joshua, his minister, fought Amalek; and as long as he held his hands raised, his people prevailed; when his hands were lowered, that people was overcome. Finally Aaron and Hur supported his hands until the victory was achieved (Exod. XVII).

2. Elsewhere it is found that Mary Magdalene, coming to the Lord for the forgiveness of her sins, fell at his feet; and God forgave her because of the great love with which she was filled (Luke VII), for she loved him before she came there. Thus Moses raised his hands so that he might [Col. 1128A] love God more and pray better; Mary Magdalene bent herself at Jesus’ feet. Therefore, when someone is more private in his prayer, let him arrange himself in the manner by which he can love God more: whether sitting, standing, lying prostrate on the ground, or with bent knees.

3. Yet let him bring humility with him, without which the Lord will not hear him for his benefit. For when the disciples themselves, Saint James and Saint John, asked Jesus Christ without humility, he answered them: “It is not mine to give you to sit at my right hand or at my left, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matt. XX). Become different from what you now are through humility, and it will be given to you. For all the power of prayer consists in the greatness [Col. 1128B] of divine love; but divine love finds its place only in humility. Therefore Jesus Christ promised exaltation in the kingdom of heaven to humility, because he found nothing else on earth by which he might be loved.

4. In all works God also wills that time and place be observed—except in prayer. According to the time, he wills that one recite psalms, speak of God, listen to others speaking, and work; and likewise in other matters. For this reason God gave different commands, lest anyone grow weary in his service and so be able to pass from one thing to another for greater delight. But in every work he wills each person always to pray to him, saying in his heart: “God, [Col. 1128C] I do this alone so that I may be able to love you.”

5. To anyone wishing to undertake any action, the Lord says: “If you wished, I would go with you and help you in what you intend to do.” Then the person who loves the world answers: “Help another, but not me.” He says this by his actions whenever he departs from the divine commands; and because of the pride by which a person rejects God’s companionship, the Lord subsequently answers him in his prayer: “Because you did not wish to have me as a companion in that work, I now shall not receive your prayer.”

6. Discipline pleases the Lord in all works, but especially in prayer, in this way: when a good man prays to God concerning his own tribulation [Col. 1128D] or that of another, and finally brings his will into conformity with the Lord’s will, so that he neither dares to choose nor wishes to say, “God, accomplish it thus,” but places everything in God’s choice—then the righteous man remains under God’s discipline. Therefore his prayer is fitting, just as a faithful disciple remains obedient to his shepherd after denying himself and refusing to choose his own will.

7. Whoever has firm faith praises God alike for what God denies him and for what he grants him, in bodily as well as spiritual things. For as God provides resources so that a person may serve him through them, so he takes them away so that he may be loved more; and as one virtue gives assistance toward salvation to another virtue, [Col. 1129A] so he withdraws another virtue lest anyone fall into pride.

8. Every common good is better than a private one. Yet sometimes someone prays to God for a close friend—which is a good act—with the intention of considering that, through that prayer, he may be able to love the Lord more. For the more a person desires anything, the greater the longing with which he petitions the one able to help him in it. And in whatever way anyone can draw near to God, it is good for him: whether by praying for himself, for a friend, for an enemy, or for all in common.

## Chapter CV.—Another question put to the master by the aforesaid disciple

[Col. 1129B] Again the disciple asked his shepherd why the Scriptures say, “Praise God,” “Bless God,” when God has no need of human blessing. He answered him thus: “Holy Scripture commands nothing except for human salvation; and when it exhorts, ‘Praise God; bless God,’ all the benefit returns to the human being. For whenever anyone says with a good heart, ‘God, may you be praised; God, may you be blessed,’ the Lord immediately replies: ‘And you who praise me, may you be praised; and you who bless me, may you be blessed.’ This may be understood as God’s reply in this manner, because no one can bless God unless he has first been blessed by God and anticipated by his grace. Thus, since blessing comes wholly from God first, [Col. 1129C] when a person blesses God, he increases his own blessing and love.”

## Chapter CVI.—That it is more perfect to praise God than to ask him

1. It is more perfect to praise God than to ask him. For one who praises has obtained what he desires, and already performs on earth the service performed by angels in heaven; the one who asks is not yet secure, but remains in uncertainty.

2. If anyone lived rightly and always loved God, he would never need to ask him, but only to praise him; and God would undoubtedly grant him more than he himself knew how to request. Yet a person whose whole heart is in the Lord often considers this, saying in his spirit: “Lord [Col. 1129D] God, what could I ask of you? You have done for humanity far more than any creature could think: you have given yourself and all else to one willing to receive and desiring to do your will.” In this reflection the good man praises God, not knowing what to ask of him. But because of his frailty he cannot always remain in this contemplation, prayers again become necessary.

## Chapter CVII.—Another question of the aforesaid disciple to the master

1. “Again the same disciple asked where all the new songs are found that are continually sung in heaven. The shepherd said to him: “Jesus Christ taught his disciples in the Gospel what the new song sung in heaven is, saying to them: ‘I give you a new commandment, that you love one another’ (John 13). This is charity, which is called a new song because it renews a person and makes a child of light out of a child of darkness.”

2. “This charity is a new song for people on earth and also a new song for angels in heaven. For whenever they see any one of the elect ascending on high, they sing a new song over that person’s ascent. Even if they had nothing else by which to praise God, they would never come to an end through this alone, since they rejoice over one sinner doing penance, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Luke 15). They rejoice utterly on seeing him become a companion in their salvation, and knowing [Col. 1130B] that he will sin no more. And when, seeing the Son of God clothed in flesh and ascending into heaven, they marvelled and said, ‘Who is this King of glory?’ (Psalm 23), they marvel rightly for joy and sing a new song when the members follow the head.”

## Chapter CVIII.—On the honour of the righteous

1. The Lord will honour in many ways those whom he saves. For every evil they could have done but refused to do for God’s sake, they shall have their reward; and for the sins they committed, from which they turned back to God, they shall possess glory and honour. For the more anyone has sinned, the more the entire heavenly court will look upon him and say together: “Look at this man; marvel at this man, [Col. 1130C] who had deserved the whole of hell, but whom God afterward delivered from it through good warfare and manly combat.”

2. As a soldier, once victory is won, receives great honour for the blows by which he defended himself from his enemies, and is praised for the wounds he bore because they did not cast him down, so God’s friends shall receive honour in the virtues by which they defended themselves and in the sins that were in them but did not hurl them into condemnation. Then will be fulfilled what the Apostle says: “For those who love God, the Holy Spirit works all things together for good” (Romans 8). Yet God does not wish a person to consider his mercy or this honour in order to do evil, but in order to repent and, by doing good works, hope for salvation.

## Chapter CIX.—On the delight in which a righteous man sometimes abides

1. No one can understand, through Scripture or a sermon heard, the delight in which a good man abides unless he has experienced something of it. For he takes such delight in God’s service that, even if he knew truly that he would never be condemned for his crimes, he would by no means commit them. So pleasing are virtues to him. And because he has begun to live heavenward on earth, he often meditates in his heart on how sweet it will be when one known to them comes into the heavenly kingdom.

2. For as a soldier, when he comes to the king’s court and the nobles recognize him, rise, and invite him to sit down, rejoices in that reception, so the righteous man is pleased when he ascends into heaven and the angels, recognizing him, receive him joyfully because of the fellowship he had with them while he was in this world, sighing, weeping, and praising the Lord with them. [Col. 1131A] For this recognition alone, even if all else were absent, the good man strives to do good works.

3. The expectation angels have for a human being’s salvation may also be understood through another example. After a rich man has pledged himself to his bride, he makes known to his friends the day on which he wishes to celebrate his wedding. Gathering them to himself, he speaks in many ways about taking his wife, so that they may receive her honourably when she arrives; meanwhile, he has sent his betrothal gifts where she is staying. But a woman is exceedingly foolish if, for one apple offered to her by some servant-boy, she rejects the gift her bridegroom has sent and refuses to go to him. The human soul is Christ’s bride, whom he washed at the price of his blood. Above, where he is, he waits with his friends for her to be joined to him; below, on earth, he feeds her with his flesh and blood so that she may not die of hunger. Is not the unhappy soul therefore exceedingly foolish when, for some apple that will immediately rot—that is, worldly business—it turns itself over to falsehood, commits adultery with the devil, and rejects the garment of charity which Jesus Christ wishes to give it, so that wearing it, it may go forth to him? But the faithful soul loves [Col. 1131C] this garment so greatly that it would first allow its whole body to be cut to pieces rather than abandon it. Thus it is recognized by the angels when it comes among them, and is honoured.

## Chapter CX.—On the fall of the angel and the rest of the righteous

1. The devil found no rest in heaven, where all is rest, because there he dissented from God. Abraham and many others bore no punishment in hell, where torments are, because there they loved God. Hence it may be known that there is no rest except divine love.

2. The same thing happens daily: an evil person finds no good where good exists, while a good person finds it where it does not exist. Thus, when a servant of God assists any wicked person in the name [Col. 1131D] of Jesus Christ, receiving him in the name of a righteous person, he finds in him as much good for himself as he believes. But when an evil person looks at a good man, he finds no good in him because he believes none to be there—as Judas did in Jesus Christ. And this is why a person does not believe good to be in another: because he does not have it in himself. Yet no one can believe so much good to be in a righteous man who loves God greatly that there is not more. For if he is good, God dwells in him; and no one can comprehend the goodness of God.

## Chapter CXI.—Again, on the devil

1. If anyone considers why the devil fell so swiftly from heaven, he can clearly understand how he would act in the heights if the Lord allowed him, since [Col. 1132A] he killed the Son of God down on earth when he saw him clothed in flesh.

2. All the reprobate, moreover, who now follow him, knowing what befell him, plainly show by their deeds that, if they had then been angels in heaven with him, they likewise would have followed him. For all these reasons good people and angels praise the Lord: because, for their honour and so that they may better know the rest in which they abide, God willed that there should be devils and infernal punishments.

## Chapter CXII.—On the gift of the Holy Spirit

1. Jesus Christ did not give the Holy Spirit to the apostles while he was bodily with them on earth, because he himself comforted them and was their Paraclete. Had he then given it to them as he afterward gave it, [Col. 1132B] other believers might have thought, saying: “From now on we shall not have the Holy Spirit as the apostles had it, because Jesus Christ will no longer be bodily with us on earth as he was with them.” But on the day of Pentecost he sent it to them from heaven, so that from then on we may always await it.

2. And he imparted to them a savour in all their works; hence that feast may be called the seasoning of all other feasts. Divine works, although sweet, would have been tasteless to them unless the Holy Spirit came upon them. That God’s friends experience great sweetness in themselves may be known from this: they sweeten others’ bitterness when they touch them with the sweetness of their speech.

## Chapter CXIII.—On the feast of Pentecost

[Col. 1132C]

The feast of Pentecost may be compared to the holy day of Preparation, when the Son of God was shamefully driven out of Jerusalem, carrying the cross upon his neck. For this reason the heavenly Father honoured him so greatly on Pentecost that, through his own action, he was more praised and testified to by one of his disciples (Acts 2) than all unbelievers had dishonoured him. It is certain that through that disgrace he gained honour; such is patience.

## Chapter CXIV.—On the difference between good and evil

The good that is done is greater insofar as it is more pleasing; and evil is likewise greater. Yet no one desires evil so greatly that another does not desire good more strongly. This may be understood from the following example. No pleasure of sin or any wealth would make a person inwardly wish to be killed by another. But if anyone who loves God is told: “Either depart from the Lord or be killed,” he will endure death and cling to God. It may therefore be understood that he loves good more than another loves evil.

## Chapter CXV.—On the aid of the saints

This is how saints aid those who pray to them. When someone entreats blessed Mary or any saint, the Lord, receiving the prayer because of the good devotion, shows this within himself to that saint, as though saying: “For love of you, I have granted this mercy to the one entreating me.” Nor should it be believed that any new thing is communicated to God in heaven: [Col. 1133A] no good spirit knows anything unless God shows it. When the saints see in God the mercies he grants for love of them, they praise him with thanksgiving; and, seeing one thing, they immediately behold another. They have no need to ask, but to praise and love, as the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Psalm 83).

## Chapter CXVI.—On the reward of the righteous

1. No one in this world can know or praise God worthily. Whatever the prophets, apostles, and other saints have said about him may almost be called nothing, and a dishonour, compared with God’s riches. For he will give more to one of the elect than all have been able to conceive, much less to say. [Col. 1133B] Even in the present life a good person sometimes perceives so much of divine love that he cannot speak of it or put it into writing.

2. Since a person cannot fully know or express what he possesses within himself, what could he say worthily of God in view of God’s greatness? Indeed, even concerning a single member, if it is carefully examined, no one can explain why the mouth does not hear, why the eye does not speak, or why the ear does not see, when these three are in one head and are animated by one spirit. In this a wise person marvels at divine power; a foolish person cannot even listen so as to recognize that it is wonderful.

## Chapter CXVII.—On the mutual charity of the heavenly kingdom and its fulfilment

[Col. 1133C]

1. Charity will not be complete until it is in the heavenly kingdom. But then it will be fulfilled when each of the elect loves every other as himself, and all the others love him as themselves. Afterwards, angels and human beings alike will together turn their love toward the Lord and love him more than themselves. Yet God will never be surpassed: for he will love each of them more than all can know how to love one another or to love God. He will also give himself wholly to each one, not partially but entirely, just as many people look upon the sun and none hinders another, while each possesses the whole of it.

[Col. 1133D]

2. But human beings are very sluggish. If it were known with certainty that one of God’s apostles had descended somewhere and was speaking to the people, how many would run there! Why, then, do they not run where they all are? A man sufficiently instructed by good teachings should therefore strive to put them into practice, so that they may please him. For as honeycomb is sweeter to the person eating it than to one looking at it, so God’s word is sweeter to the soul that performs it than if it knew it merely by hearing or by writings and did not carry it out.

## Chapter CXVIII.—What a righteous man ought to be like in his meditations

It is good that a good man sometimes consider [Col. 1134A] what he will be in God’s kingdom; but it is especially good that he continually consider what he ought to be in this world while he lives. One does well who does not allow himself to be defeated by the devil, but he is not greatly perfect unless he defeats the devil. He does not allow himself to be defeated by the devil who guards himself from evil; he defeats the devil who removes others from the devil’s service, thereby attaining greater perfection. No perversity is greater than wishing to endure labour in order to go to punishment, and refusing to remain in peace in order to go to joy.

## Chapter CXIX.—On the mercy God showed Susanna

1. God showed great mercy to Susanna by defending her from being stoned; but he showed her greater mercy by protecting her from sin, lest she consent to the will of the false judges. For if she had been stoned without having sinned, she would have suffered no harm except before the people; but if she had sinned, she would have deserved hell.

2. For the former mercy God had no minister but himself, because he inspired the woman’s heart. It was therefore altogether greater; and it was also greater because the first mercy led her to the second. For the latter, however, he had Daniel as his minister, to whom he said: “Go and tell the Babylonians that Susanna has defeated them all, though they are all unaware of it: for she remained in truth, and they in falsehood.”

## Chapter CXX.—On the person whom God allows to depart from him in peace

[Col. 1134C]

1. No greater misfortune can befall a person than when God peacefully allows him to depart from him. God places thorns and hedges in the path of his elect when they wish to draw away from him, as the prophet says (Hosea 2), so that they may not be able to fulfil their wicked will in action. But to others, whom God foresees will not be saved, he sometimes permits prosperity on the way, by which heavier infernal punishments will come upon them. These depart from God in peace: those to whom the Lord allows, without any opposition, the fulfilment in this world of their evil desire.

2. It is not surprising if one who cannot see chooses the worse among things at hand. Those who love the world have no eyes except in the flesh; greed closes their spiritual eyes, and so they choose the worse. Good people choose better because they see and know it clearly. If someone stood in a street at midday, unable to look upon the brightness of the sun when the day was very bright, it could surely be said that he saw nothing. Thus he is altogether blind who does not behold God’s brightness, by whom the sun is illuminated. One who does not remember God or love his commands thinks that the Lord does not remember him or care for him. If he knew how the Lord beholds every evil that he thinks and does, he would never do it.

## Chapter CXXI.—On hearing divine teachings

1. Whoever is unwilling to fulfil divine teachings in works thinks, when he hears them proclaimed, that good is not as God says it is, but rather as he himself wishes to act.

2. Whoever wished to love God with his whole heart ought to rejoice more when wealth, power, or dignity in this world is granted to another than if it were granted to himself, because he ought to know that the other will make better progress through it, dispose of it better, and spend it for good. For another reason too, this should especially please him: every person who desires salvation ought rather to wish that another have the soul’s impediment—which exists in this world—and estrangement from God, than that he himself have it.

## Chapter CXXII.—A discourse on tithes

O unjust man, who withholds his tithes from the Lord, listen to the Lord’s right and claim in tithes. You work the earth, cast grain into it, and at last, when you have gathered it, store it up. Now understand how the Lord does there what is his own. He has his own earth in which you labour, and his own iron and wood with which you work. God gives there his own beasts to help you perform the labour. From whom do you have the grain you cast there, except from him? Are not your strength and arms his? After you have scattered the grain on the earth and mixed it with the dust, who would gather it from there for you, unless God exercised such care? He sends his rain and sun, his cold and heat, his dew and frost, and his temperate air: all these are necessary there. Finally, he makes its own husk for every grain of corn, so that it may grow and multiply. When harvest comes at last, how could you act unless God then sent his sun there for you? Even after you have harvested and threshed the grain, the Lord must send his wind to separate the grains from the chaff. Finally, unless you found sevenfold, or even more, [Col. 1136B] than you sowed, you would complain against the Lord and lament your labour. It is thus apparent that by just judgment nine parts belong to God, and the tenth is yours for the labour you endured there. Yet God is so merciful that he grants you the nine parts which are his by right, for all things necessary to you. Therefore render him the tenth; if you keep it, you turn every other profit into injustice.

[Col. 1135]

# The Rule of Saint Stephen, Confessor, Author and Founder of the Order of Grandmont

(Dijon, at the press of Pierre Palliot, printer, bookseller, and engraver to the king, under the sign of the Queen of Peace, before the Royal Chamber of Accounts, 1645.)

## Prologue.—On the unity and diversity of Rules

[Col. 1135C] My most beloved sons and brothers: although the way leading to life is hard and narrow (Matthew 7), the house of the Lord is nevertheless great, exceedingly broad and spacious, confined by no boundaries; and it is reached by that hard and narrow way. To that house of the highest Father, in which the Son testifies that there are many dwelling-places (John 14), there are diverse choices of ways, well-trodden directions of paths, and manifold ascents of steps, concerning which the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has set ascents in his heart” (Psalm 83). By these one goes from strength to strength, that the God of gods may be seen in Zion (ibid.). Although these diversities of ways have been commended in writing by different Fathers, so that there is called [Col. 1136C] the Rule of blessed Basil, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the Rule of blessed Benedict, they are not the origin of religious life but its branches; not the root but the foliage. For there is one first and principal Rule of rules, of faith and salvation, from which all others flow like little streams from one fountain: namely, the holy Gospel delivered by the Saviour to the apostles and faithfully proclaimed through them throughout the whole world. All the faithful who passed before us drank an inexhaustible draught from the fullness of this unfailing fountain, and left it to us who live today and to those who will come after us until the end of the world. This living fountain stands open to all, rejecting none; from it, according to the capacity of each, those who are able to receive, receive [Col. 1137A] (Matthew 19).

For in it we have certain things prescribed generally for all of us under fixed bounds of commandments. We also have in it special counsels granted for the highest perfection of our salvation, to the one to whom the Lord said: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (ibid.); and elsewhere: “Whoever leaves house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (ibid.). Wonderful, therefore, was the compassion of the highest Father and ineffable the ordering of heavenly providence: commandments were imposed upon us in obedience to which he who knows no secret is hidden knew human nature capable, provided it wished fully and diligently to direct itself toward its Creator. Hence it would rightly be judged guilty of disobedience if it presumed to pass them by with a deaf ear. But other things were given as counsels, whose observance appears so burdensome that many consider it almost beyond the capacity of human nature; yet those who transgress them are not condemned by the fault of disobedience. Such, then, are the Lord’s counsels: before a vow, freedom and choice; after a vow, they pass into law and obligation.

You must therefore take the greatest care, my brothers, lest, after freely putting your hand to the plough, you look back, lest perhaps Lot’s wife become a reproach to you [Col. 1137C] (Luke 17), and the washed sow, again entangled in mud, and the dog returned to its vomit (2 Peter 2); and lest you become an object of mockery and derision to all (Psalm 78), according to that Gospel saying: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14). Therefore offer God an evening sacrifice (Psalm 140), because “he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matthew 10). Thus, adhering to Christ, the true vine, as branches, take care to fulfil the commands of his Gospel as far as you can, by his gift. So, when those who ask what profession, Rule, or order you profess, you may not be ashamed to confess yourselves, whatever sort of observers you may be, of the first and principal rule of the Christian religion, namely the Gospel, the fountain and beginning of all rules: “For we all offend in many things” (James 3). You may also dare to say that you are subject to apostolic and canonical institutions and wish, insofar as possible, to follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers.

Nevertheless, if anyone among you, whether with good intent or not—for “not all obey the Gospel” (Romans 10)—questions the customs of your order, kindly answer everything he wishes to hear as you have received it from us. If, upon hearing it, he reasonably shows you that any of your traditions are contrary to the Gospel or opposed to the admonitions of the holy Fathers, I grant that they should be corrected according to the judgment of learned persons. I, a sinner, though of little understanding, have arranged them, with God’s help, according to what I received from learned and very devout men and learned through long application to the Fathers’ rules. I am therefore confident of you, brothers, in the Lord, that none will be able to accuse you of being exempt from any Catholic religious observance or unacquainted with any Rules of the aforesaid Fathers or other orthodox teachers, if, while you remain together according to the apostolic pattern, you have one heart and one soul in the Lord (Acts 4). Behold, [Col. 1138C] I believe you have tasted how sweet the Lord is (Psalm 33), and how good and pleasant it is, brothers, to dwell together in unity (Psalm 132). Let all things therefore be common among you; let there be mutual charity and a shared affection of love; and let none of you think that anything is his own, except that you love one another and obey one another.

# Rule of Saint Stephen

[Col. 1137]

## Bull of Pope Clement III Confirming the Rule of Saint Stephen

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest sons, the brothers of Grandmont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The order of reason requires, and the norm of ecclesiastical custom commends, that matters which bring uncertainty into the observance of Christian religious life should be clarified by the provident governance of the Apostolic See. Therefore, lest any question later arise concerning your Rule—which our predecessor Urban, of blessed memory, is known to have corrected, with the counsel and assent of the cardinals and many bishops of Italy, in the presence of members of your community, both clerics and lay brothers, who gave their assent for its confirmation and perpetual peace by the kiss of peace, as is more fully contained in his privilege—we have decided to insert it under seal in the present document, word for word. It is as follows:

## Chapter I.—On obedience

[Col. 1139A]

[Note: [Col. 1139D] These words and the other institutions of this religious order were removed by Innocent IV at the Council of Lyons.]

Whoever enters this religious order by God’s inspiration shall first promise obedience to God and to the shepherd who receives him, and to his successors; then to the brothers, both present and future. He shall also promise faithfully to observe this present Rule and the other institutions of this religious order until the end. On account of this profession which he is first to make to you, dearest brothers, gathered together in unity so that you may love God with one heart, we first command that you persevere steadfastly in obedience to God, to your shepherd, and mutually to the brothers, without murmuring or hesitation. For each ought to murmur only against himself, not against [Col. 1139B] another: both because of the multitude of temporal goods which he uses unworthily and because of the depravity of conduct for which he is held guilty.

Hesitation is opposed to the faith which brothers of this congregation ought to have in obedience to their shepherd, when he says: “Brothers, you will go to a certain poor place; but there are not yet books or buildings there.” If anyone hesitates on this account, he should be answered thus: “He is not skilled in religious life whom poverty frightens. For nothing makes a person so secure in divine love as poverty, especially one that pleases him from the heart. But one who loves the world thinks himself free when temporal honour or some revenue is given to him; whereas one who loves God thinks himself impeded by it. No one is so unencumbered as an obedient disciple, for he never holds himself back but always draws near to God. Obedience is better than sacrifices (1 Samuel 15), for whoever obeys sacrifices himself to God; and this is more pleasing to God than if he offered something else while retaining himself. Again, we can show more plainly on another evident ground how obedience is better than sacrifices: as the Apostle says, ‘Christ became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name’ (Philippians 2).”

Whenever a faithful disciple willingly fulfils a command of his shepherd or of the brothers, God forgives him his sins. Obedience also plants virtues and preserves those planted; for without obedience there is no saving good, since a disobedient person can do nothing that profits him unto salvation. Likewise, if in any part of his heart a religious man can find that he wishes to be exalted in temporal things, he has not yet wholly left the world. He has not left what he still finds in himself; nor should anyone merely cut himself off from the world, but uproot himself from it altogether, for the root would sprout if it remained there. Otherwise, he cannot be perfectly obedient until he withdraws from it completely and utterly denies himself [Col. 1140A] [Note: [Col. 1139D] From this word onward, it is certain that the remainder of this chapter [Col. 1140D] was removed by Innocent IV.]. It is also certain that whoever does not willingly wish to obey a human being in this world will unwillingly obey all the demons of hell; and it would be better for him to obey all the people of the world than one devil alone.

## Chapter II.—On not choosing one’s obedience

Besides all this, a disciple must take care never to choose what his shepherd is to command him. For if he made this choice, neither could profit by it. Indeed, let the brother know without doubt that if by his own choice he wishes to remain somewhere in order to have better food and clothing and live more luxuriously, perhaps without his shepherd’s knowledge, and follows his own will, then, if he should die there, his soul is to be feared for. For the Lord says: “He who loves his life shall lose it; and he who hates his life in this world shall keep it unto eternal life” (John 12).

Again, the disciple ought to love obedience so greatly and, for the will of his shepherd, hate his own will, that he says this to him: “Father, you send me there, where I remain at your command. Yet if I knew that it pleased you more for you to send me elsewhere, and that because I disliked it you refused to move me from there, I would by no means regard you as a provident shepherd for my soul. For you would be following my will, not I yours.” Therefore each person must love and more willingly do another’s will rather than his own, because in this he gains more. Likewise, whether a brother prays or does anything else, he must always be ready to obey, preferring nothing to obedience. For one who continually does the Lord’s will praises him without ceasing. God reveals his secrets to a person more through no virtue than through obedience, when it is understood from him subtly and without delay. But whoever imposes obedience must carefully consider the common good in doing so; here he especially needs discretion, lest he consider his own advancement more than that of others.

## Chapter III.—On the reward of obedience

It must most certainly be believed that whoever dies in obedience will not thereafter be judged; for the devil finds nothing by which he can hold an obedient disciple. Jesus Christ likewise will by no means judge the one who has judged himself and offered himself to him in order to bear his cross. Rather, together with him whom he will set at his right hand on the day of judgment, he will judge the rest (Matthew 25).

## CHAPTER IV. On Not Possessing Lands  
[Note: [Col. 1140D] This entire chapter was removed by Innocent IV.]

We wholly forbid you to possess any lands outside the boundaries of your own places, as persons who are strangers and have here no abiding city, but seek the one to come in heaven (Heb. XIII). For when you entered the wilderness, you left such possessions behind along with the other worldly things; and one must always stretch forward to what lies ahead.

For every person, once dead, needs only as much land as will contain his burial. Yet it would be a great marvel if, after being enclosed in his own grave, he took away the grave of another dead person lying beside him. Brothers, so too you ought to be dead as regards worldly business; for, as the Apostle says, “We must die to sin, that we may live to God” (Gal. XI). Does not as much land suffice you as is needed to make an enclosure in which to dwell? By “enclosure” I mean the very wood given to you within the limits of your habitation, where, lest your life be idle, you may carry on your labor and build your structures.

You should inflict upon those possessing lands outside your enclosure as much violence as one dead person inflicts upon another. Do you not know what a great stench comes from a dead person when he is dragged out of his grave? That stench is very slight, for it is not spread far and wide in comparison with the stench and disgrace that will proceed from you and be scattered and perceived through many provinces if, abandoning your purpose, you begin to acquire lands. For through you the name of God will be blasphemed, and people will say: “These men entered the wood under the appearance of humility, but now they are beginning to lift up their heads.”

He would indeed desire little who wished to have the whole earth and nothing else. Let a person wish to possess God, heaven and earth alike; then whatever exists will be his, as the Apostle says: “As having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (II Cor. VI). And again: “All things are yours; but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (I Cor. III). Certainly you possessed lands, but knowingly left them because they separated you from God. And because you could not possess the lands of your inheritance without wronging others, we greatly fear that, if you acquired others’ lands, you would thereby utterly offend God. For, as blessed Jerome says: “No one possesses this land through meekness, but through pride.”

If, however, you wish to have a sufficiency of land, possess absolutely none outside the enclosure or boundaries of your places. For all land is contiguous; and if you acquire any portion of land, you will then wish to have another adjoining it, and thus your desire will scarcely, or never, end. Rather, you will incur that curse which the Lord terribly threatens through the prophet Isaiah: “Woe to you who join house to house and couple field to field, up to the boundary of the place. Will you dwell alone in the midst of the earth?” (Isa. V). Therefore, brothers, leave lands behind, so that God may deign to draw you after himself into heaven.

## CHAPTER V. On Not Possessing Churches

For the reason already stated—namely, because you left churches and the things belonging to them behind, together with other worldly things, out of divine love—we wholly forbid you to recover them, so that you may imitate the Apostle who says: “Forgetting the things behind and stretching forth to those before me, I press toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Phil. III).

Moreover, do no more harm to peoples and churches, whether near or far away, than to the trees of the wood in which you dwell, if this can be avoided. Therefore, do not on any account accept a thirtieth-day, seventh-day, or annual payment, or any payment specifically offered to you for a Mass. Nor presume to impose penitential judgments upon laymen; such a matter does not belong to your purpose.

Again, on the holy day of Parasceve—that is, Good Friday—allow those who cannot go to their own churches that day to adore the holy cross in your churches. Nor ought you to refuse holy water from your churches to neighbors wishing to carry it to their homes. On Sundays and feast days, when they should attend the divine offices in their own churches, do not receive them if they frequently come to you to hear the solemnities of Mass. But if, at some time through God’s inspiration, they wish to visit you, they are not to be excluded from the divine offices.

Likewise, if you know that persons have been excommunicated by their bishops or priests for their own offenses, your church is not to be granted them until their own church receives them again. Otherwise, they would show less reverence and service to their own churches. If anyone wishes to give churches to you, do not accept them at all. For such perfection is required for the governance of churches that you could scarcely, or never, sufficiently imitate their perfect rulers; but imperfect and useless rulers you ought by no means to follow. You must expel from yourselves not only greed and envy, but also everything from which they may arise.

Indeed, if it should happen that you possessed churches, how would you care for others, when you are dead to the world and, as members cut off from the age, lack feet for walking and a mouth for speaking? Thus you cannot even care for yourselves—much less for others. Although another governs you and you govern no one else, you should nevertheless greatly rejoice if you could freely approach the presence of God.

## CHAPTER VI. On Not Possessing Animals  
[Note: [Col. 1141D] This was removed by Innocent IV.]

Since you left behind every kind of animal, together with other worldly goods, for the Lord’s sake, we wholly forbid you to recover them, so that the concern you would expend in buying, breeding, and selling them may be devoted to the service of God alone. For the freer you are from temporal concerns, the freer you will be to attain heavenly things. For, as Truth itself says: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX).

For this reason we especially forbid you animals of every kind: lest, if you should wish to be elevated temporally in this world through the acquisition of lands, churches, or anything else, a great abundance of livestock become for you an occasion and material of worldly exaltation. For nothing destroys religious life more violently than greed and an abundance of riches. And since you possess no broad pastures suitable for feeding livestock, if you had animals they might perhaps occupy others’ pastures; and there would be a great outcry from your neighbors, saying: “Would that these hermits had never come, for their manifold possession brings us manifold hindrance.”

## CHAPTER VII. That Love of Animals Diminishes Divine Love  
[Note: [Col. 1143D] This entire chapter was removed by Innocent IV.]

Likewise, if you had animals, you would undoubtedly love them; and in proportion to the love you bestowed upon livestock, so much would be withdrawn from your love of God. For just as the greatest heap of money becomes very small when divided into many heaps, so the human mind, the more it is divided among different loves, has the less divine love within it. Even when it is wholly gathered into itself, it is still very small for loving God; what then is to be said when it has been divided into various parts?

## CHAPTER VIII. That Those Who Would Ascend on High Should Be Unburdened

Whoever intends to ascend on high acts on useless advice if he burdens himself with a heavy weight when he should rather unburden himself. Since, therefore, you wish to ascend to heaven, why would you load yourselves with that burden from which you have been freed? Even if you were entirely unencumbered, it would still be a great wonder and a great mercy of God if you could ever ascend there. For, as the Gospel says: “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII).

Shall we permit you, who came here solely with the purpose of spiritual things and undertook to be sheep of the supreme Shepherd, to become shepherds for thieves and robbers? Far be it!

Moreover, you must take the greatest care that no one find in you an occasion by which he may compel you to leave your enclosure.

Finally, believe the heavenly Master who says: “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matt. VI).

## CHAPTER IX. On Avoiding Gain

So long as you can in any way live for one day without gain, do not presume to seek anything from outsiders.  
[Note: [Col. 1143D] “But you”: the remainder was removed by Innocent IV.]

But perhaps you will ask us how you can live after our death, since we forbid you churches, lands, animals, revenues, and even gain. To this we answer: “We leave you God alone, whose all things are, and for whose love you left all things together with yourselves.” If, observing this manner of life, you cleave steadfastly to him—not according to your own will, which is human and can err, but according to his ordinance, which is divine and cannot err—he himself, as a lord who has care for his servants, will undoubtedly supply everything necessary to you. For he says to his disciples: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). But if—God forbid—you depart from God and become transgressors of the present Rule, we would surely wrong him if we left either himself or his goods to you.

## CHAPTER X. That One Should Seek Rather from God Than from a Human Being

Yet we do not wholly forbid gain to you; rather, we shall tell you how you ought to seek it. Carefully consider from whom necessities ought preferably to be requested: from one who has, or one who does not have; from one willing to give, or one unwilling; from one who is near, or one far away.

If you return to the world to ask something from one of your friends, perhaps he will lack either the means or the willingness to give what you request of him. Moreover, you will readily become burdensome if you return to him frequently for this reason. If he does not grant your request, both you and he will be ashamed; and even if you suffer no other harm from it, you will nonetheless have to leave your enclosure, not without danger. If any friend visits you very often, you may nevertheless alienate him from yourselves if you ask him for his goods.

Ask, therefore, from the Lord, who is near to all who call upon him in truth (Ps. CXLIV), and who can and wills to give you far more than you yourselves wish to receive. Ask, I say, from the Lord who says to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XIV).

## CHAPTER XI. That God Never Fails Those Who Cleave to Him  
[Note: [Col. 1144D] This entire chapter was removed by Innocent IV.]

But perhaps there are people—and I know such people—who, with feigned piety, will say to you: “Your master has resolved, by an unusual practice, to live with you. It will continue, it will continue while he lives; but when he is dead, without lands, churches, revenues, animals, or even gain, you will not be able to remain long in the same vow.”

It will not be so; it will not be so, my brothers. Indeed, as I fear, because my sins demand it, God is deferring for you many spiritual and bodily goods until the future. If you do not believe me, the works themselves after my death will show this to you, if you persevere in this life. How could it happen that God should fail you if you cleave to him, when he fed you while you opposed him and loved the world?

## CHAPTER XII. That God Is a Provident Steward for the Truly Poor

Let poverty be your treasure and riches. Since worldly people love so greatly their riches, by which they go down to hell, you should love yours much more dearly—that is, the poverty by which you go to heaven. Likewise, if you desire to be rich according to the world, you will always be poor; if you desire to be poor according to God, you will always be rich. As the Psalmist says: “The rich have wanted and have suffered hunger, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. XXXII).

Therefore, most beloved brothers, appoint the Lord as your steward; and we say to you most firmly that your storehouse will never be empty so long as you entrust its keys to God. As the prophet says: “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Ps. LIV).

Again we tell you: do not seek alms so long as you can somehow live for one day. You well know the unity that ought to exist among you: namely, that both your poverty and your abundance should be common to all.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Permission to Beg

But if God, in order to test you, permits you to come to such poverty that food entirely fails, you may first make this known to the bishop in whose diocese the place of your habitation lies, saying: “Lord, we do not wish you to be unaware of the need that we suffer there.”

If he does not hear you in this matter, then, after you have fasted in the cell for two days, let two brothers more steadfast in religious life humbly go out to beg, going through mills and houses, asking alms door to door like other poor persons. When they have received enough alms for themselves and the other brothers to live for one day, let them return to the cell and distribute them to each person with thanksgiving.

In such begging, avoid intimate friends, lest your own need be added, as though a burden, to the poverty which they may perhaps then be suffering as you are; and lest, being unable to help you, they be afflicted more severely. You must always take care not to burden anyone. There are also certain things of little value which, if necessary, you may request from your neighbors—for example, straw, dung, and such things. If you can and it is necessary, do not delay to return something more valuable in exchange.

## CHAPTER XIV. That God Always Provides Necessities for Those Persevering in This Life
