Nevertheless, if you persevere steadfastly in this life, rarely or never will necessity compel you to return to the world in order to seek others’ goods. For when need is greater, God will provide what is necessary for you with greater watchfulness. If you make God alone your treasure by loving poverty, then, while he abounds, you will by no means lack.

Thus in all things strive, according to your ability, to share with God, so that you may be poor in this world, as he too was; and so you will be perpetually rich where he is eternally rich. Finally, we can strengthen you in the love and perseverance of this life by another consideration. Nearly fifty years have passed—some of them in great plenty, others in great scarcity—while I have remained in the wilderness under such a vow. Yet in times of abundance nothing ever overflowed to me, nor in times of want did anything necessary fail me. The same will happen to you if you faithfully keep these ordinances. Therefore, first seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you (Matt. VI).

## CHAPTER XV. On the Manner of Buying

When you wish to buy something, instruct one of your friends to bring it to you. If, after you have asked him to buy it, he wishes to give it to you, do not accept it at all.  
[Note: [Col. 1145D] “But perhaps to us”: the remainder of this chapter was removed by Innocent IV.]

But perhaps you will say to us: “We shall buy better if we go to the markets.” We forbid this to you. For it is much better to lose a little material property than, by returning to the world, to lose the soul. We tell you without doubt that, if you remain in righteousness, your means of support will never diminish on that account. For it is written: “Those who fear God lack nothing” (Ecclus. I); nor do those who love him in truth (Ps. CXLIV).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Manner of Selling

When necessary, you may exchange your own goods for others’. Yet if you can sell more dearly than you bought grain or any other thing acquired by you for your own expenses, do not do so out of any greed. For you would thereby become merchants. Rather, we command you to sell what you sell more cheaply, and to buy what you buy more dearly, so that you may always turn away from fraud.  
[Note: [Col. 1146D] Innocent IV reads: “we advise.”]

For the Apostle forbids anyone to defraud his brother in business (I Thess. IV).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Manner of Borrowing

Whenever you wish to borrow money or some other resource from anyone, do not accept it unless it is a movable item with a fixed time for repayment. Say this to the person lending it to you: “We shall repay when we have the means to repay.” But if he requires another agreement and a fixed term, accept it when no poverty compels you; for you have no revenues from which to repay. You could therefore sin if you appointed him a fixed day. Take care, then, to avoid lying and remain in truth; for “a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. I).

But if anyone wishes to give you resources as a loan, accept them when no poverty compels you.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Manner of Lending  
[Note: [Col. 1147D] The entire chapter was removed by Innocent IV.]

If any friend wishes to borrow your resources, do not lend him gold, silver, or grain when no need is being suffered by him and when he has conferred no benefit upon you. But if he wishes to borrow any of these from you, you may lend it to him; rather, give it to him, for the love of him who gave this to you—provided that you can give without harm to your religious life. In this way you will attain greater perfection. For if you lent someone your money and he meanwhile gave you some small thing, you might thereby become usurers. Take care, therefore, not to lend the aforesaid things; for it is not contrary to the Gospel if you do not lend but are willing to give.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Not Choosing Gifts

If anyone, moved solely by God’s grace and saying with benevolent charity that he wishes to give you something of his own according to your choice, asks you to select what you want most from two or more things, while promising to give what has been selected, it must by no means be yours to choose, but his. For this alone have you chosen: to be lowly in the house of God (Ps. LXXXIII). Answer him thus:

“God has inspired you with the will to give what you offer us; and because, without any request from us, he has given you both the willingness and the ability to do the good that you wish to do, he will not henceforth be troubled, but will show you what you should provide for us. For he alone knows what is necessary for us and for you.”

## CHAPTER XX. On Avoiding Confraternity

Do not on any account hold at your place the banquets which people call confraternities. But if, where you are not present and have sent no messenger, they establish a confraternity and afterwards bring you something from it of their own will, you may lawfully accept it and use it modestly according to your order.

But if they wish to come there, hold their feast in your places, and diminish the spiritual rest in which you ought to remain with God, do not permit this in any way. Nor presume to say psalms or celebrate any other divine office for money. For God hears prayer made from charity, while rejecting that which proceeds from greed.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Not Choosing Alms

Likewise, you may lawfully accept all alms which the Holy Spirit brings forth in human hearts, without your asking for or choosing them. Even for this reason alone, though all other reasons were absent, you should take care not to ask alms of laymen: for they will be more pleased when, without your asking or choosing, they give them to you than if they offered them while you asked and chose them. And the more this pleases them, the more gratefully it will be received by God.

You ought to desire of every person, as of yourselves, that they do the divine will. But if laymen gave you alms upon your solicitation, it would please them less; and the alms would diminish before God’s eyes in proportion as their good will diminished.

## CHAPTER XXII. That No One Is to Be Sent for a Promised Gift Unless Its Nature and Amount Are First Specified

Again, if someone says to you, “Send for my grain or other goods, and I shall give you some of it,” do not inquire into the quantity of the promised thing, lest you be guilty of greed; nor presume to send unless he himself specifies it to you.

If he subsequently asks you, “Why did you not send?” answer him thus: “We did not know the quantity of the promised thing, and therefore either you or we might have done wrong in this. For if we had sent for more than you intended to give us, you could have complained on that account; and if you gave us more, we would seem to have taken it away from you. But if we had sent for less, perhaps it would have displeased you; and therefore we did not wish to send.”

Finally, if he specifies the amount, you may lawfully send. Since you would accept this were he himself to bring it, it would seem prideful if you did not send. Yet always examine carefully in your hearts how you may avoid greed still more. And we tell you without doubt that you will consequently have even more temporal money, for “those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. XXXIII).

## CHAPTER XXIII. What Revenues May Lawfully Be Held  
[Note: [Col. 1148D] The entire chapter was removed by Innocent IV.]

If someone says to you, “I and my sons will give you such an alms annually from my land,” do not refuse it. Answer him thus: “So long as it pleases you, we shall accept this.”

Afterward, however, should the giver himself or his heirs withhold it, or should some plunderer take it from them, you may request it in this way: “We do not wish you to be unaware that you have received the alms which was given to us annually.” Having made this known, if he is willing to restore it to you, give glory to God. But if he is unwilling, do not demand it again—that is, do not contend with him in court—but give thanks to God because it pleased him to permit you to have it for so long.

We permit you to possess only such revenues: receive them so long as their possessors render them to you; when they withhold them, relinquish them patiently. Therefore, mindful of the counsel of Jesus Christ, who says, “Do not demand again what is taken from you” (Luke VI), never contend at law with laymen; rather, remaining in peace, cleave continually to God.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Not Having Charters for Litigation  
[Col. 1149A]

[Note: [Col. 1149D] The entire chapter was removed by Innocent IV.]

Likewise, we command you never to make a written instrument, for the purpose of litigation, concerning things given or to be given to you; nor presume even to litigate.

## CHAPTER XXV. What Is the Key of Our Religious Life

We shall now make you secure: if you persevere in this life, you will find no one who dares to drive you away. For what we shall tell you is the key of our religious life; if you keep it well, no enemy will find an entrance through which he may enter against you.

Wherever you build, if you cannot benefit someone, at least do not harm him; if you cannot do good to someone, at least do not do evil. And we tell you most firmly that those who at first hate you when you begin to inhabit deserted places will later love you and confer many benefits upon you. Yet we tell you this on the condition that you faithfully remain in this life. If you depart from God, would it not be just for all to persecute you?

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Rightly Paying Over an Alms of the Dead to a Just Complainant

Moreover, if someone at the point of death leaves you his resources, so that you may do good for him and pray for him, you may lawfully accept them. But after he has died, if you happen to hear a complaint that he committed an injustice against anyone, mercifully pay over the money left to you by the deceased to the person making the just complaint—provided that the dead person’s heirs refuse to restore it. For charity “does not seek its own, but the things of Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XIII).

## CHAPTER XXVII. That God Everywhere Prepares Hospitality for Humility

Again, we firmly affirm that many people will offer you many places with many entreaties, and will freely give you woods which they were unwilling to sell to others, if you humbly persevere in the purpose of this life. For God everywhere prepares lodging for humility, because humility itself is his lodging. Be humble, therefore, and heaven and earth alike will be yours.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Mills  
[Note: [Col. 1149D] This entire chapter was removed by Innocent IV.]

In fulfillment of the command that your association should harm no one, do not have mills in common with the people. For when neighbors abandon their accustomed mills and come to yours, those whose mills had previously existed will suffer loss on account of their association with you. For it is written: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV; Luke VI; Matt. VII).

## CHAPTER XXIX. That No Service Be Rendered for Temporal Things

Since you are bound to serve God alone, whose service is freedom, if the donors of the places in which you dwell demand that you render them service for those places, we command you rather to abandon the places themselves than to give them even the least thing that they ask with this intention.  
[Note: [Col. 1149D] Innocent IV has: “we advise.”]

Otherwise you would not be true pilgrims from this world, but, like other cultivators of fields, persons owing tribute.  
[Note: [Col. 1150D] What follows was removed by Innocent IV.]

Moreover, it would be unjust and simoniacal to render temporal service to the donor, rather than to God alone, in return for what someone offered to God by giving it to the poor, for love of whom he abandoned all that.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Requesting Woods

When necessary, you should request a wood suitable for your religious life first from its owner and then from all who have any right in it. When it has been given to you by all these persons, if you know anyone who lays claim to the wood, ask him for the right which he says he has in the wood, if perhaps you wish to build there.

For, as the Apostle says, you must, if possible, have peace with all people (Rom. XII). Yet you should demand no further improvement from the land on which you build except that it may somehow sustain you while you perform your penance there. For the poorer it is, the more diligently God will provide for you there, if you cleave trustfully to him. As the Lord says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV). When he asked his disciples, “When I sent you without purse, bag, and sandals, did you lack anything?” they said, “Nothing” (Luke XXII).

Earth is very small in comparison with heaven, and it would satisfy you only briefly if you loved it. Take care, therefore, not to exchange what is better for what is worse—that is, heaven for earth.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Not Conducting Lawsuits or Giving Testimony

Since, as the Apostle says, “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs, so as to please him to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II), we command you most firmly never to presume, on account of your own [Note: [Col. 1150D] This word, “your,” was removed by Innocent IV.] or another’s affairs, to litigate or contend in court with anyone; nor receive others’ cases or disputes into your hands. In short: whether you are present or absent, no lawsuits or such secular conflicts are ever to be conducted in your places.

Nor is it for you to bear testimony to anyone concerning matters which you have seen or heard in the world and from which disputes may arise. For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. III).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Seeking Permission from the Bishop

Furthermore, without the permission of the bishop in whose diocese you wish to build, do not presume either to bless water or to celebrate Mass in that place. Humbly entreat him to deign, at a suitable time, to visit that place in order to consecrate the church in honor of God and the cemetery for the burial of the brothers.

Moreover, request by devout prayers from that bishop, from the priest in whose parish you reside, and from all other possessors of them, the tithes of your labor. But once they have been given to you, you must by no means keep them; rather, you must faithfully give them to other poor persons.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That No Building Be Erected on Monks’ Property

Among these matters, we command you never to build structures on the property of monks. We do not say this in order to detract from the holiness of monks. Indeed, some of them will love you greatly and confer manifold benefits upon you; but the heads of monasteries are frequently changed, and what some grant, others later often wish to reclaim by demanding it back.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That Brothers Should Not Leave the Cell to Visit Sick Laypersons

If perhaps your father, or any lay friend near your cell, is gravely ill and wishes you to visit him so that he may confess his sins and settle his affairs in your presence, do not go to him, provided that clerics sufficient for his need are present with him. If, in presuming to go there, you die on the way, we shall by no means render an account of you to God on the day of judgment (Matt. XII).

For the supreme Master said to his chosen disciple who wished to bury his father: “Let the dead bury their dead; but you, follow me” (Matt. VIII). But if you know that someone near your dwelling is close to death, you must assist his need if other clerics are unable to assist him. Otherwise, through his death, you might perhaps incur eternal death.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That Brothers Should Not Leave Their Cells in Order to Provide for the Poor

You ought not leave your cells in order to provide for the poor. For no one can provide better for poor persons than Martha provided for God himself; yet Jesus Christ did not say to Mary, seated at his feet, “Rise and help her.” Rather, the Lord answered the one who thought that her sister was doing nothing according to that person’s own view: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke X).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Showing Hospitality for God’s Sake

Hospitality must be shown to guests out of charity. By gathering and retaining you will be in need; by giving and scattering you will abound. Let what you spend and give to guests please you; for as long as this pleases you, nothing will thereby diminish for you, but it will always be restored to you by God. For he says: “Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke VI).

Yet you spend nothing of your own, for the Lord brings you provisions and receives from you what has been brought. Hence the prophet says: “What we have received from your hand, O Lord, we have given to you” (I Chron. XXIX). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. XXV). Nevertheless, strive to show religious persons more honor and reverence than others. Therefore, as the Apostle says, “While we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. VI).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Bestowing Assistance upon the Poor

You ought to rejoice greatly whenever you do good to the poor. For in this world the Lord left the poor this inheritance: good people, to provide for them. You ought surely to give thanks to God when he sends his poor people to you. For you would not find so many messengers to send to so many poor persons, nor would you know how to choose them; but God chooses them and sends the chosen ones to you.

Therefore you should believe that the Lord does not deceive poor persons who ask you for alms. For if he knew that there was nothing present which you could give them, he would scarcely or never permit them to ask you for anything. Thus always give them at least a good word, if you happen to lack other things. For speaking with the poor is an honor to you; speaking with the rich you ought greatly to fear, since you can easily incur disgrace thereby.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Rewarding the Alms of the Poor More Generously

If poor persons bring you their small alms, do not reject them, but receive them joyfully. Yet carefully understand the sermon that they preach to you as they hand it over: since those who are poor give you what is theirs, you ought to give them what is yours more generously, especially if you have the means.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Not Receiving Women
We utterly forbid women to be admitted into this religious community; for since woman drew the first man away from the delights of Paradise [Col. 1152D], where will anyone be able to resist her? If David, most gentle; Solomon, most wise; and Samson also, most strong, were caught in a woman’s snare, who will not yield to her blandishments? Is not a man tempted by the devil through her even when she is absent? What, then, will he do when she is present? The Apostle teaches that this vice is overcome by fleeing from it, not by attacking it (Rom. VIII). Blessed Gregory likewise affirms that no one should presume, after a vow of continence, to live with women. They are therefore to be wholly separated from this religious community: they are not even to give assistance to the brothers’ work during the day, nor are they to enter the cells after sunset until morning. Moreover, no woman is ever to enter the cells alone at any hour of the day, unless accompanied by a companion of age.

### CHAPTER XL. That Men of Another Religious Order Are Not to Be Admitted.

[Col. 1153A]

We wholly forbid men of another religious order to be admitted into this religious community. For your customs differ greatly from theirs. You are accustomed to carry dung and wood, heat the oven, and make bread and many other things; for you have no servants except yourselves. When you do such things, they would often reproach you, saying: “In our religious order we would never concern ourselves with such lowly tasks.” Moreover, one who has never been in the discipline is more easily kept in it when he has newly left the world than one who, having once departed from it, is recalled to it. Furthermore, if after a long time, having examined your customs, they wished to return to the habit of their former religious order [Col. 1153B], the very shepherd to whose obedience they had formerly submitted could receive them as his own sheep; and they could leave you freely and without dispute. Therefore, lest disgrace should befall both you and them, they are by no means to be admitted. Hence Solomon says: “A heart entering upon two ways shall have no rest” (Ecclus. III). Hence James says: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas. I).

### CHAPTER XLI. What Sort of Men May Be Admitted.

Whoever is a secular man and wishes to join this congregation may lawfully be received by the prior of this religious community, even if he is bound to another religious order merely by a promise, so long as he remains clothed in secular dress [Col. 1153C].

### CHAPTER XLII. What Sort of Men Are Neither to Be Released nor Sought Out.

Conversely, if anyone, having received from the shepherd the gift of brotherhood and having fixed a definite time for coming, should afterwards wish to enter another religious order or remain in the world, the shepherd is not to seek him out. But if he asks the shepherd to release him from the promise already made, the shepherd is by no means to release him, but is to answer him briefly thus: “You will never have been sought by us.” He is not to be released in any other way, nor compelled to come, nor sought out by anyone after he has been received.

### CHAPTER XLIII. That a Solitary Man with His Own Cell Is Not to Be Admitted.

[Col. 1153D]

It is decreed by this religious community that whoever joins it must leave outside all landed possessions, submitting himself wholly to the will of the shepherd. We therefore command that no solitary man with his own cell be received; but, if it be the shepherd’s will, let him accept either the man without the cell, or the cell without the man, should it be offered.

### CHAPTER XLIV. That Men Under Twenty Years of Age, the Sick, and Lepers Are Not to Be Admitted.

Since Christ’s yoke must be undertaken through voluntary choice and prudent deliberation of mind, we command that no one under twenty years of age, nor any sick person, be admitted into this religious community unless he can come riding or walking on foot [Col. 1154A]. We also forbid the admission into our religious community of anyone manifestly known to be leprous. For he would cause scandal to Christ’s members and incur the curse of the Lord, who says: “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. XVII).

### CHAPTER XLV. That Simony Is to Be Entirely Avoided.

Furthermore, let the shepherd of this congregation keep himself and all his disciples wholly from every kind of simony; and, faithfully fulfilling the Lord’s command, “Freely you received; freely give” (Matt. X), let him, in receiving brothers, consider with the utmost discernment only God’s will and the salvation of souls.

### CHAPTER XLVI. That the Brothers Are to Remain in Their Cell.

[Col. 1154B]

Just as we read in the Gospel that Christ went up into the solitude of the mountain to be tempted by the devil (Matt. IV), so those who follow Christ seek wooded solitudes and absence from human beings, in order to cleave to him more freely through contemplation. And just as he himself did not descend from the mountain until the enemy had been defeated, so his imitators, while they are in battle and have not yet finished their course—which is throughout the whole time of their life—must not leave the solitude that they have chosen. For in this your life, and that of all hermits, must chiefly consist: that, avoiding the tumult of the world by the practice of continual prayer and silence, you may rest in your cells. For scarcely, or never, can he be truly religious who is shut in one day and permitted to wander about the next [Col. 1154C]. Even the apostles themselves, who abounded beyond others in the grace of the Holy Spirit, sprinkled dust upon their feet while they went through the world; and since the apostles, perfect men though they were and travelling through the world by God’s command, were sprinkled with the dust of earthly intercourse, you, being altogether frail, would be stained by the dust of sin if, contrary to your purpose, you wandered through the world. We therefore command you not to presume to roam through the world.

### CHAPTER XLVII. On Silence.

Silence is to be observed according to the prescribed places and times [Col. 1154D]. In these places—that is, in church, cloister, refectory, and dormitory—and also during these times, namely from Compline until morning, when chapter has ended, the brothers are to observe continual silence, unless some great necessity, which knows no law, should at times compel otherwise. For Isaiah testifies: “The work of righteousness is silence and peace” (Isa. XXXII). Whoever violates silence in the places or times mentioned above is to be subject to regular discipline.

But the other kind of silence, which consists in keeping silence about useless things and speaking what is necessary, must always and everywhere be observed by each brother with the utmost discretion. For Solomon says: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Ecclus. XXXVII). Therefore, if the steward of the place himself [Col. 1155A], or any other brother, corrupts himself and others by murmuring, slandering, lying, resisting obedience, or often repeating worldly and vain words, the other brothers, in the affection of brotherly charity, are to rebuke him for this the first, second, and third time. If he neglects humbly to correct even this slight habit of his, he is to undergo regular discipline.

### CHAPTER XLVIII. That the Brothers Are Not to Leave Solitude in Order to Preach.

Again we command you not to leave solitude in order to preach. For while you remain in the wilderness and guard yourselves against the world, you are a light upon a candlestick—that is, a good life shining upon the faithful people. For blessed Gregory says: “The life of a righteous person is a living sermon” [*viva praedicatio*].

### CHAPTER XLIX. That the Brothers Are Not to Leave the Wilderness in Order to Hear Preaching.

Moreover, we command you not to leave the wilderness in order to hear preaching. For it is clear that John the Baptist remained in the wilderness while Jesus Christ preached on earth; yet the Gospel does not say that John left it in order to hear the Lord’s preaching. If God had wished John to come to him and John had not come, he would undoubtedly have sinned in this; but it was not necessary for him bodily to go and hear the discourse of Jesus Christ. For he heard his voice spiritually in his heart [Col. 1155C], as he himself testifies in the Gospel, saying: “The friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John III). Yet do not suppose that I compare you with John the Baptist. Nevertheless, if, following his example, you cleave to God and do not wish to leave the wilderness, God himself will remain in you and teach you.

### CHAPTER L. That the Brothers Are Not to Confess Their Sins to Outside Men.

If any one of you incurs some sin—which God forbid!—he must carefully avoid confessing it to any outside man, however great that man’s holiness may be. If he presumed to do so, he would certainly be disobedient and unbelieving, and would say by his very actions: “I have no confidence either in my shepherd or in my brothers; therefore I seek counsel from outsiders about this.” But God forbids anyone to despise one of his little ones (Matt. XVIII). Furthermore, he is greatly deceived who defiles himself when he thinks that he is cleansing himself, and increases his sin by confessing it. Yet he would incur all these things if any of our brothers confessed his sin to outside men.  
[Note: From “But he would incur all these things” through “therefore” Innocent IV corrected the text; Col. 1155D.]

And all others likewise incur the same things who, after confession, do not abandon their sins. Therefore consult God, in the secrecy of solitude, concerning all your needs. Thus: “Confess your sins to one another [Col. 1156A], and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. V). For the reasons stated above, we command you to remain in your cells and, from there, to request what has been permitted—namely, the assistance of neighbors with their beasts in your work, when necessary—yet never to leave your cells on such a pretext. Therefore, dearest brothers, we have begun, by God’s permission, to lead our life in solitude and eremitical poverty; and, with his help, we must end it in the same condition.

### CHAPTER LI. That Brothers Going Out into the Portico Are to Conduct Themselves Properly.

When you are enclosed in your cells and can cleave to God alone, then you ought to sigh, groan, and weep for your own sins and those of others. But whenever you need to go out into the portico in order to speak with your visitors, show them a cheerful countenance and receive them joyfully. It is fitting that, since they come to you from afar and make, so to speak, their procession, you too should make yours and go out honorably to meet them [Col. 1156B].

### CHAPTER LII. That at Least Two Brothers Are to Go Out of the Cell Together.

Whenever necessity compels you to go outside the cell, we command you to go two by two, according to the Gospel’s institution, so that one may look after the other. “Woe to him who is alone, for if he falls, he has no one to raise him up” (Ecclus. IV) [Col. 1156C]. Also, on the journey, avoid the company of travellers as circumstances require, and avoid entering cities and castles, lest the outward eye see that by which the inward eye becomes blind.

### CHAPTER LIII. On Those Who Flee from This Religious Community.

If anyone falls away from this religious community through a diabolical suggestion, the shepherd may restore him, if he wishes to be reconciled, to the unity of the religious community upon fitting satisfaction. Nevertheless, this must be carefully observed: whatever the disobedient man acquired or built, however much it may be, is wholly to be cast away and rejected as a thing of perdition. Otherwise, if it were accepted, brothers still weak might take it as an example for themselves, saying: “Since this happened to him after his fall, let us do likewise.” Care must be taken that this does not happen [Col. 1156D].

### CHAPTER LIV. On the Care of Clerics and Lay Brothers.

[Note: This chapter, insofar as it speaks of the care of lay brothers (*conversi*), was removed by John II; Col. 1156D.]

We assign to clerics, free from every care of temporal matters, the best part, which the Lord especially praised in Mary, so that they may truly say: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XXV); and likewise: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. CXVIII); and again: “It is not right that we should leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts VI). Thus, devoting themselves solely to divine praises and contemplation, let them minister spiritual things to one another [Col. 1157A] and to the other brothers who confess their faults.

And lest the divine office be interrupted by conversation with secular persons or anxiety about external affairs, and lest their minds forget the sweetness of inward satisfaction—which blessed Gregory laments having happened to himself—we therefore entrust the temporal care of the cell solely to the lay brothers. In their labor and other tasks, they are to direct the other brothers, clerics and lay brothers alike, not by domination but by charity, so that humility, the guardian of all virtues, may remain unharmed. For the Creator of all was himself obedient to his creatures, namely Mary and Joseph, as the Gospel says: “And he was subject to them” (Luke II).

Nevertheless, it would be advantageous for all, clerics and lay brothers alike, never again to see the world, if that were possible, since they have left it. But because this cannot be done, we wish at least to keep the clerics in the repose of divine love. The lay brothers, however, are to go out to converse with outsiders both for the clerics’ sake and for their own. Clerics too sometimes go out when they are needed there. Yet it is great wisdom and great mercy, when they can rest in God’s secrecy, for them to remain there for the common benefit of all. For if their minds were occupied with temporal matters, they would undoubtedly provide less well for others in eternal things [Col. 1157B]. Whoever goes out must beware of taking delight in conversation with secular people; for the more he delights in it, the greater harm he will suffer. But if obedience permits, let him desire rather to remain continually in seclusion than to go out; for if God is not found within, he will certainly not be found without. Indeed, God is accustomed to reveal his secrets more often and more intimately to his friends in private than in public: for example, to blessed Mary in her chamber, to John the Baptist in the wilderness, to Peter, James, and John on the mountain, and likewise to John himself in exile [Col. 1157C]. The same is to be understood of the others.

### CHAPTER LV. On the Distribution of Food and Clothing.

Let the brother responsible for the cell distribute food and clothing to the brothers with prudent administration, as circumstances require, observing what is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “All things were common to them [Col. 1157D], and no one among them was needy; and distribution was made to each according as anyone had need” (Acts IV). Meanwhile, neither the steward himself nor any other brother is to request that some special food be prepared for him alone, nor even for all in common, except the steward alone. If anyone asks, he is not to be heard at all, unless perhaps he is sick; for the sick person is to be served with every humility.

Certainly, one who was rich in the world is very blameworthy if, in this religious community of poverty, he asks for anything other than poverty. Did he not have abundance enough of refined food and clothing? Why then should he desire more of such things? Especially one who was poor in the world: on what grounds would he seek riches in the wilderness which he could not possess in the world? For what delights has anyone come here, except to follow Christ by bearing the cross [Col. 1158A]? What indeed did the holy apostles and the holy Fathers in Egypt, whose footsteps we ought to follow, demand as customary except to persist in vigils, fasts, prayers, and labors? Finally, what revenues or estates did anyone voluntarily offering his whole self to God as a living sacrifice retain in the world in order to procure these things? Absolutely none.

### CHAPTER LVI. On the Care of the Sick, the Aged, and the Weak.

If a brother is unable to follow the community because of pressing and grave illness, he is to be placed in the infirmary. Then let the cell’s steward choose one brother, or more if necessary, who will patiently serve the sick man day and night; and they alone are to enter the house in which the sick person is [Col. 1158B]. Other brothers, whether living there or arriving from elsewhere, are not to presume to visit the sick man without the steward’s permission.

For when a brother has remained a long time in the discipline of religious life, has guarded himself from the world to the best of his ability with the help of God and his shepherd, and finally falls ill and is already approaching his end, then he especially requires greater protection, when his soul is to receive its reward. It is like runners: they exert themselves fully when they are near the place where their race will be completed; if they stopped beforehand, they would have labored in vain. For this reason it is beneficial for the sick disciple not to hear anything concerning worldly affairs from which his spirit might think vain thoughts. The fewer people he speaks with, the less he will hear from them [Col. 1158C]. He must always be strengthened in the Lord. And if he is wise, he will say to those speaking with him: “Let me remain in peace, and help me by your prayers, so that my heart may be able continually to cleave to God.”

If the cell does not have an abundant supply of what he needs, we command that the ecclesiastical ornaments assigned to God’s service be sold before the sick person should suffer want of anything he may lawfully request; for he is the temple in which God dwells. Since his father, mother, or any secular friend may not be permitted to enter him, the brothers must take the greatest care of him. No business of the religious community is to be preferred to service of the sick, except the divine office alone [Col. 1158D].

Likewise, humbly and diligently supplying the aged and weak with necessities, faithfully fulfill the command: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI); and also the Lord’s command: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. VII).

### CHAPTER LVII. On the Times for Fasting, the Hours for Meals, and the Kinds of Food.

From holy Easter until the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, we appoint that you take a meal twice daily: first after Sext, and again after Vespers, except on the fasts prescribed within this period. But from the Exaltation of the Holy Cross [Col. 1159A] until Easter, we command you to fast, except on Sundays and the day of the Lord’s Nativity. Again, from the aforesaid feast of the True Cross until the beginning of Lent, we appoint that you take food after None; and from then until the Lord’s Resurrection, after Vespers. Likewise, from the feast of All Saints until the Lord’s Nativity, and from Septuagesima until Easter, we command you to use only Lenten food. At other times, we permit you sometimes to eat eggs and cheese.  
[Note: Innocent IV added: “excepting altogether the weak and the sick”; Col. 1159D.]

For we command you always to abstain, whether healthy or sick, from flesh and blood, both of birds and quadrupeds.  
[Note: Innocent IV removed the text from “Nevertheless” to “No one is to request anything”; Col. 1159D–1160D.]

Nevertheless, because you have no fixed revenues from which the brothers’ daily meal can be prepared [Col. 1159B], let no one presume to demand food at fixed hours as something due; but receive with thanksgiving whatever, and whenever, the Lord himself—whom we appoint as your only steward—shall provide for you in his customary mercy. And if he frequently delays in giving you food, nevertheless give thanks to him, remembering the Apostle’s words: “Giving thanks always for all things, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God and the Father” (Eph. V).

### CHAPTER LVIII. On the Divine Offices.

We have judged it fitting to celebrate the divine offices gathered from certain holy authorities, which blessed Gregory and other holy teachers arranged in the holy Church [Col. 1159C]. It is not now necessary to speak of each of these separately, because our books contain fuller material on such matters.

### CHAPTER LIX. On the Brothers’ Mutual Service.

You must all constantly remember that you have left your servants, together with other worldly things, outside. Therefore each must honor the other, preserving the fraternity of religious life and taking precedence in showing honor; and “he who is greater” must become “as the younger,” and “he who is leader” as “the servant” (Luke XXII). Let each person gladly serve everyone in gentleness. For brothers living in obedience should, if possible, be served as angels; since it is credible that, if they persevere in this obedience, they will without doubt be saved and thus become equal to angels [Col. 1159D].

But if it seems absurd and unfitting to anyone that they should be described as angels when they are human beings and certainly sinners, let it be said more expressly: in such things, they are to be treated not only as angels but as God himself. For God declares through the prophet that he dwells in them, saying: “Heaven”—that is, the soul of the righteous—“is my throne” (Isa. LXVI); and in the Gospel: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. XXV); and again in the Psalm: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI). We say this not for your exaltation [Col. 1160A], but so that brother may humbly serve and obey brother out of love.

### CHAPTER LX. On the Election of the Prior.

When a prior is to be chosen, two brothers from each cell are to assemble at Grandmont, as two are customarily to come to the assembly. Those remaining in the same places are to promise with certainty that, upon the departure of the others, they will assent to the whole decision of the electoral assembly. When the assembly has gathered, after invocation of the Lord’s name, twelve faithful lovers of religious life—six clerics and six lay brothers—are to be appointed to elect the prior. Once they have heard from all that their election will be opposed by no one, they are to discuss it privately among themselves [Col. 1160B].

Such a shepherd is to be chosen as has previously been a faithful disciple of this religious community, so that, considering others by himself, he may know how to provide what is useful for each according to need. If, however, some of the twelve disagree in the election, the greater part is to prevail—that is, the part understood to be more faithful and sound, considering nothing except the common benefit. Those dissenting from the decision are to be excluded from the counsel and even from the assembly, so that everything may be done without them. Yet as many persons are to be added to the council from the same assembly as have been expelled, whether clerics or lay brothers, so that the election always consists of twelve.

### CHAPTER LXI. That No Outsider Is to Be Chosen Prior.

[Col. 1160C]

Do not presume to choose as prior for yourselves anyone who is outside your religious community, however eminent he may be in learning or holiness. For he would disagree with this way of life and would overturn you toward another. Rather, confidently choose one from your own assembly. Blessed Gregory himself commands this, saying: “When the shepherd of any congregation has died, let no outsider be chosen, but one from the same congregation, whom the harmonious society of brothers has chosen by its own will.”

Moreover, if God is with you, he himself will provide for you; but if you depart from him, you will never find a good shepherd. If all of you were evil, what other shepherd could succeed if no good man were found among you? Whatever shepherd you have will be wise, provided that he does not depart from this way of life. But if—which God forbid—he departs from it, he will undoubtedly be anathema, and so will everyone who agrees with him. Again we command you that your shepherd [Note: This was corrected by John XXII; Col. 1160D.] is never to be called abbot, but only prior. Moreover, do not permit any outsider whatsoever to take part in the election of your shepherd.

### CHAPTER LXII. On the Shepherd’s Stability.

Again, let your shepherd take every care never to leave the enclosure of Grandmont except when compelled by unavoidable necessity [Col. 1161A]. Let him know firmly that, so long as he remains bound by Christ’s chain and refuses to travel through the world, none of his disciples will dare to disobey him or remain in any of his cells against his command. For the Lord, by whose love the shepherd is bound, will keep the disciples bound as well. But if—which God forbid—he begins to travel through the world, we greatly fear that you will all follow him together, despise his commands, and fall into disobedience. He himself will not thereafter recover the honor which he possessed before God and human beings on the day when, leaving his enclosure, he presumed to travel through the world contrary to his vow. Hence blessed Gregory says concerning himself and the other shepherds of the Church: “We are, dearest brothers [Col. 1161B], we are the stones of the sanctuary, who ought always to appear in God’s secrecy, whom there is never any need to see outside.”

### CHAPTER LXIII. How the Prior Is to Conduct Himself toward His Relatives.

Likewise, because carnal affection for relatives commonly draws many religious persons far back from divine love and greatly dissipates the goods of churches, let the prior of this religious community carefully avoid giving anything to his own relatives, except the benefit of hospitality and some small gift of little value.

### CHAPTER LXIV. That What Has Been Renounced Is Not to Be Reclaimed.

[Col. 1162A]

The purpose and command of our religious community is that we are never to reclaim churches and things belonging to them, or any honors outside our religious community; nor lands, beasts, tithes, fixed revenues, markets, fairs, visits to relatives, lawsuits or judgments, whether for ourselves or for others, profit so long as we can in any way live for one day, and the other things which we have left for God’s love. Rather, in the wilderness, as dead men and cast away from the world, we are to persevere until the end.  
[Note: “Lands, etc.” were removed by Innocent IV; Col. 1161C.]

### CHAPTER LXV. On Perseverance in the Things Mentioned Above.

[Col. 1162B]

Therefore, dearest brothers, persevere steadfastly in the matters stated above. If your shepherd attempts to turn you from this path of truth toward another and does not in any way yield to your counsels, abandoning these institutions, we confidently command you by God’s authority to cast him wholly out of your fellowship as an apostate rather than depart from this path because of him. Hence the Lord himself commands in the Gospel: “If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you” (Matt. V). Whoever perseveres faithfully in this holy way of life until the end will undoubtedly be saved. Amen.

## THE CONFIRMATION FOLLOWS.

[Col. 1161]

That the Rule set forth above may remain inviolate for all time, we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of the present writing, as it was corrected by our predecessor Urban, as we have said above. We decree that absolutely no person may be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the fifth day before the Kalends of July [27 June], in the second year of our pontificate, in the year of the Lord 1188.

[Note: Col. 1161C]

It should be known that this Rule, issued by Saint Stephen the Confessor, founder of the said order, was examined, approved, corrected, altered, and modified by many supreme pontiffs, as appears from what follows.

Adrian III approved it in the year 1156.

Alexander III approved it in the year 1174.

Lucius III, in the year 1182.

Urban III approved it and added something to it in the year 1186.

Clement III examined it and approved it intact in the year 1188.

Celestine III examined it and was the first to alter something in it, in the year 1191.

Innocent III altered and corrected something in the year 1202.

Honorius III modified and corrected something in the year 1218.

[Col. 1162C]

Gregory IX modified and corrected something in the year 1234.

But among the others, Innocent IV, who at the Council of Lyons in the year 1247 read, corrected, and improved the whole Rule, first removed from Chapter I the words “and the other institutions of this religious community,” and in the same Chapter I added “those matters which pertain to the convenience and usefulness of the house.” He also removed the entirety of Chapters 4, 6, 7, and 9; and many other things were removed and corrected by the same Pope Innocent IV, as has been noted.

Clement V added and altered something at Avignon in the year of the Lord 1306.

John XXII also, at Avignon in the year 1317, decreed among other corrections to the aforesaid Rule that the monastery of Grandmont, recognized as the head of that order and formerly governed by a prior, should henceforth and forever be governed by an abbot; and he changed the manner of electing the most reverend general.

.

## STEPHEN OF LICIAC, FOURTH PRIOR OF GRANDMONT

[Col. 1163]

### NOTICE  
*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. II, col. 648)*

Stephen II of Liciac, a native of Limoges, governed at a time when the order was greatly expanded in the number of its houses. He also caused the deeds of Stephen the Confessor to be written and read aloud, as the Chronicle of Grandmont notes, where he is described as discerning, generous in almsgiving, powerful in deed and word, devout in prayer, assiduous in fasting, and as having happily presided over the flock. He died, as is thought, in 1161, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January]. His epitaph reads: “Here lies Lord Stephen, fourth prior, a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord; he lived as prior for twenty-three years.” So Pandulf of Garda and John l’Évêque state. In his time Henry II, king of England, enriched the monastery of Grandmont; and through the generosity of kings and princes, cells or priories were established in various places and made subject to the mother church of Grandmont, because of the reputation for piety possessed by the brothers of this monastery.

[Col. 1163]

## THE SAYINGS AND DEEDS OF SAINT STEPHEN OF MURET, BY STEPHEN OF LICIAC.

(See above, col. 1071, at the end of the Life of Saint Stephen of Muret by Bernard Itier. Compare Dom Martène’s prefatory notice to the Life of Saint Stephen.)

## PETER BERNARDI, ALSO CALLED PETER OF CORILO, FIFTH PRIOR OF GRANDMONT

[Col. 1163]

### NOTICE

*(Gallia Christiana nova, vol. II, col. 649)*

[Col. 1163A] Peter III Bernardi, of Boschiac, born of a noble family and brother of Bernard Aimeric of Bré, as is written in an old book of Saint Martial, was elected on the seventh day before the Ides of February [7 February] in the same year. He notified Henry II, king of England, of his election; the king wrote to him in the seventh year of his reign. He had first been a married knight, afterwards a monk, and finally was ordained priest: a man religious in life and conduct, a stern enemy of vices, and an outstanding imitator of his predecessor’s virtues. These and many further praises of him are mentioned in the Chronicle of Grandmont.

In the year 1165 the church of Blessed Mary of Grandmont was dedicated on 2 September. Peter, Patriarch of Bourges, consecrated the greater church, with Bertrand of Bordeaux, Gerald of Limoges, the bishops of Angoulême, Cahors, and Séez, and other bishops present. This Peter splendidly rebuilt the entire refectory of the abbey anew, with a stone vault. He likewise completed the church from the head end as far as the entrance to the clerics’ choir; it had formerly been begun and constructed from the lower end. During his tenure there took place a translation of the body of most blessed Stephen from the cloister into the church, in the presence of Gerald [Col. 1165A], bishop of Limoges, on the day after the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist, Christ’s forerunner. He resigned his office about the year 1167, having become corrector of Vincennes, and lived at least until 1191, as his letters prove.

[Col. 1165]

## LETTERS OF PETER BERNARDI.

(Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, p. 454 ff.)

Peter Bernardi, elected prior of Grandmont, informs Henry, king of England, of his election, to which he consented unwillingly. (February 1160.)

[Col. 1165B]

To the most excellent prince, Lord HENRY, by God’s grace king of the English, our duke of Aquitaine, most magnificent nourisher of the poor of Grandmont: Brother PETER BERNARDI, elected prior of Grandmont but a sinner, whatever a sinner’s prayer is worth.

The Holy Spirit, who blows where He wills, chose us—not because of works of righteousness which we had done, but according to His great mercy—though unworthy, to be the visible leader of His servants of Grandmont. [Col. 1165C] I frankly confess that I subscribed to this election, although canonical, not without opposition, and that I should still have resisted for two reasons. First, unless, trusting in the Lord and hoping in the power of His majesty, I believed that He Himself, who began a good work in us, would bring it forward, so that I might make my ways and my endeavours paths of the perfection begun—finding greater pleasure in being better than in being higher. Second, unless my brethren had declared that this election was pleasing to God and to Your Royal Highness, I should never have accepted the reins of so great an office.

My lord king, it has come to pass as God commanded; may He who is our Father, and we the work of His hands, strengthen us in every good work. Would that, as I can set forth this present letter, so I could lay open my mind to you! Oh, if you could read in my heart what God has deigned to inscribe there concerning love for you, with His own finger! You would surely know that no tongue, however learned, nor even a pen, suffices to express what it has pleased the Spirit of God to imprint upon the tablets of fleshly hearts. We remember your unspeakable benefits; and everywhere I shall proclaim that we have always found in the eyes of your majesty great familiarity, with familiarity favour, and with favour an abundance of kindness. Of these things, without doubt, your reward is great in heaven, according to the promise in the Gospel of Him who is faithful in all His words and who judges as done to Himself what is found to have been done to one of His least ones.

Therefore, preserving, as is our duty, a good will toward [Col. 1166B] the sceptre of your kingdom, we humbly seek a like good will from your sacred highness. I confess that we can do nothing in the desert; yet this little which we can do before almighty God, in whose hand are all powers, we devote for you and your royal blood: that you may receive increase in every virtue and graciously attain Him who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life. We shall continue this prayer for you in your Grandmont from this first day of our election, as the bearers of this letter will make known.

Given at Grandmont, in the month of February.

II. Reply of Henry II, King of the English, to Peter Bernardi, Prior of Grandmont.—He accepts his election gladly and commends himself to his prayers. (A.D. 1160.)

[Col. 1166C]

To the religious priest, eminent in the Word of glory, P. Peter Bernardi, prior of our brethren of Grandmont: Henry, by the grace of God King of the English, son and brother, wishes the rightful desires of a Christian prince.

“A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart.” You have brought forth two good things. First, when you gave your assent to your election, which we believe was made by God, since, as your messengers reported, we have learned that it was celebrated by the agreement—indeed the approval—of so many correctors and discerning men.

[Note: [Col. 1165D] In the Order of Grandmont, *correctores* were the superiors of monasteries, distinguished from the Prior of Grandmont, who alone was called “prior.” [Col. 1166D] After he was invested with the title of abbot, they were no longer called *correctores* but priors.]

Second, you promised continual remembrance of us in your prayers. It is enough if it is done; [Col. 1166D] I believe it will be done. Yet let it be continued through your prayers. We hope much in the Lord and in the power of His majesty; nor do we make light of your prayers. I pray that they may be offered without ceasing in your church to God for us, for your consolation, and for the joyful day of your coming to the seat of the general prior.

By these letters we make known to you that, even today, we remember that the tail and the head of the sacrifice were owed to God. We do not begin to do you good in order to cast off you who have deserved well of us. By God’s grace we take care to make the Church’s tunic now many-coloured and full-length. Only pray for me; and be not anxious about temporal things: the Lord will provide through our hands. I call my royal heart to witness that I keep before my eyes—and would that I always may—the immortal King of heaven and earth, who has given us a kingdom on earth and will give us one in heaven if we administer justly and wisely what we have received from His adorable right hand. But who do you think is the faithful and prudent servant? Would that I may so appear before Him that we may reign faithfully here and happily there. We also hope this, if, by making us sharers in your spiritual goods, you incline toward us the great mercy of the King of kings and Lord of lords.

Given at London by the hand of Master Thomas, our chancellor, in March, in the seventh year of our reign.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] This is Thomas, who afterwards became Archbishop of Canterbury and a martyr.]

III. Letter of Peter Bernardi, Corrector of Vincennes, to William, Prior of Grandmont.—He announces to him the killing of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. (A.D. 1171.)

[Col. 1167B]

To the reverend Father William, his general prior: Brother Peter Bernardi, formerly general prior, wishes him better things than he knows.

What shall we do for the soul of the King of the English, once our sister? Her face has been blackened beyond extinguished coals. Alas! he who founds our churches has violated the Church of Canterbury. Alas! if you knew what new and portentous news the court of the King of France brings, you would be struck dumb. For even the heavens are struck dumb [Col. 1167C] at this, with reproach concerning our embassy.

Both the most excellent prince and reverend father Lord Henry of France, full brother of the King of the French, duke and Archbishop of Rheims, and the reverend father William, Archbishop of Sens, wrote that Henry, King of England, had killed Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. Would that I had slept more deeply than usual when both the most holy pope and the reverend bishops of France sent me to this same Henry with the lord prior of the Carthusian house of Mont-Dieu.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] From this passage and another in the same Peter Bernardi’s letter to King Henry, it is clear that the agents of the reconciliation of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, with the King of the English were Peter Bernardi of Grandmont and Simon, priors of the Carthusian house [Col. 1168D] of Mont-Dieu. This has hitherto escaped scholars. From this one may infer how much men dead to the world and buried in the tomb of the cloister can accomplish—namely, what neither supreme pontiffs nor kings could accomplish—and how undeservedly religious men are called useless by secular persons.]

Would that they had left us wandering in solitudes, hidden in the caves and caverns of the earth of Grandmont! See how much compassion such impiety pours into my heart. Now my pen is overwhelmed. [Col. 1167D] Farewell; and write with me to that same king, if perhaps he may hear and turn back. I pray that prayer may be made without ceasing by our Church to God for me in my distress.

IV. Letter of William, Prior of Grandmont, to Peter Bernardi, Corrector of Vincennes and former Prior of Grandmont.—He consoles him over the death of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. (A.D. 1171.)

[Col. 1168A]

To the faithful servant of Christ and prudent father, Lord Peter Bernardi, our brother and corrector of Vincennes: Brother William, general prior, wishes him to recover good courage in the mercy of God.

Why are you disturbed by the bloody death of the reverend Father of Canterbury, and why do your thoughts rise into your heart? If, at the devil’s urging, you had lent hand or counsel to the parricide, you ought to grieve with the sorrow that works salvation. Certainly a cruel and bloody blow has been violently inflicted upon the holy Church of God in the murder of the holy primate. But what remedy is there? The innocent man who died is not so much to be lamented as [Col. 1168B] the man who killed him. For the slain remains a crown; for the killer, hell, which has already opened its monstrous mouth to swallow him alive.

What was reported to your fatherhood—that the most illustrious King of the English committed this crime—I could scarcely have believed, had not the dignity of the reporters intervened. But if it is so, the matter turns out badly for the king himself and for us, his servants; nevertheless, one must not despair on that account, for the bruised reed is not to be broken. Do not be disturbed as though you had done it. The righteousness of the righteous shall deliver him, but the wicked man shall fall in his own iniquity. If you do well, you shall receive. Just as leprosy clings to and defiles the body, so guilt clings to the one who commits iniquities. The impiety of the impious shall be upon him.

The righteous son shall not die in the iniquity of his father, [Col. 1168C] but shall surely live. The son shall not bear his father’s iniquity; nor shall you, dearest Father, bear that of your son, the King of England, if what is said is true—that he has so forgotten the justice innate to him. To please you, I shall write to him; but I think the letter will be weak, for in his eyes I am not a man of great merit. Yet I shall gladly do it, that he may return to the Lord. He sets great store by your holy eloquence. Therefore, through your diligence he must devoutly be approached, movingly admonished, and awakened in Christ Jesus by earnest exhortation.

V. Letter of William of Trahinac, Prior of Grandmont, to Henry II, King of the English.—On the killing of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. (A.D. 1172.)

[Col. 1168D]

To Henry, King of the English, who labours grievously, especially in the inward man: salvation in Him who gives salvation to kings, from Brother William of Trahinac, alarmed prior and sinner in your Grandmont.

Alas, my lord king, what is this that I hear concerning you? I do not wish you to be unaware that, from the day when we learned that you had fallen mortally, we dismissed the workmen of your devotion who were building the church of your house [Col. 1169A] of Grandmont, lest in anything we should share with you. For, when I considered the native goodness of your royal majesty and set it against the horrible crime of parricide of which you are accused, my soul could not persuade itself that this was true of you. If you are innocent, thanks be to God, who has given us, your servants, the desire of our heart. But if you are near to and a participant in the shed blood, take heed, and do not remain weak in the mire of so great a guilt.

Indeed, I do not know whether this most wicked crime was planned with your knowledge or not. Yet I write to you not without fear and trembling; for if you were a supporter—let alone the author—of so great a crime, I should neither wish nor dare to deal with you. But if, by some fate unknown to me, it has happened, I deeply grieve for you and for your good works brought to death; for it is written: “If the righteous man turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, none of his righteous deeds which he has done shall be remembered” (Ezek. XIV.26). [Col. 1169B]

I have no right, nor any dominion, over your will; and even if I had, I would by no means compel you. For the human mind is free-born: it prefers to be led rather than dragged. But if the prayer of a sinner has any force before you, I beg you: do not destroy the fruits of your good works; do not neglect your lost soul, for which Christ died. Turn and do penance for all your iniquities, and iniquity shall not be your ruin. If today you hear the voice of the Lord and do not harden your heart, the prayers of your servants of Grandmont, which we pour out [Col. 1169C] and offer with fastings, shall ascend to the Lord.

VI. Letter of Peter Bernardi, former Prior of Grandmont, to Henry II, King of the English.—On the killing of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury.

To Henry, King of the English, made utterly poor: poor and desolate Brother Peter Bernardi, former general prior of Grandmont, sends his tears to soften your heart.

As the proofs of your devotion are countless, so they are beyond telling, O most illustrious yet now impoverished crown of England, whose roses of glory have fallen. Surely we owe you something immense beyond measure, O king; therefore it is hard—indeed most hard—for the Christian commonwealth, and especially for us, to hear that the king [Col. 1169D] who could find no end in conferring good things upon us, who in his magnificence considered it too little unless he overwhelmed with innumerable benefits the people of Grandmont which was once his—our people, I should rather say—has been made alien to God and cast away by Him.

So much, I say, do we owe to your once splendid diadem as we cannot recount. But what have you to do with this song? To have begun well but failed in the way of God is to go backward. All who see it will begin to mock you, saying: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke XIV.30). But what is it to be praised here by men? He who strives to please them is not Christ’s servant; indeed, he is put to shame, because God has rejected him, and in heaven he is reprobated by God, from whose hand alone come the reward of our work and the crown of glory. [Col. 1170A]

We grieve when the soul is separated from the weak body. Can the true form of a man remain separated from God? The light of God’s countenance has been marked and sealed upon us. This light of grace, which alone grants serenity, is defiled and darkened by sin. Blinded by courtiers, the father is about to be dashed down a precipice by the seductiveness of their words: how can his sons allow him to perish through their condemnable silence? As the Lord lives, God will require the soul of such a father from these sons. If we keep silent, God will accuse us of wickedness, calling us dumb dogs unable to bark. He will judge us worthy of hanging with the dogs who guarded the Capitoline citadel.

What is this word that was spoken to the poor of Grandmont? How has it vanished? [Col. 1170B] You promised Father Simon, prior of the Carthusian brethren of Mont-Dieu, and me, that you were ready to place Lord Thomas, Bishop of Canterbury, second in your kingdom, provided that he showed before your people an appearance of humility toward you. He did a hundred times what you asked, and now he lies in the bosom of the earth. We have heard the voice of blood crying from the earth to God: How has the word fallen from the mouth of the king, a word holy and venerable in you?

Yet all such rich men are like this: if you do them any good, their gratitude is lighter than a feather; if there is any sin, they bear leaden wrath. Is this the funeral lament of a tragic actor (*parsinalis*, as printed) which the hoopoes of our wilderness have learned? In common and weak breasts all benefits are preserved as though written in sand upon the seashore; in those same [Col. 1170C] hearts injuries remain engraved as though in marble. That reverend Father Archbishop Becket had performed the office of chancellor before you without reproach: why has forgetfulness erased so great and so faithful a man? O glass-like favour of princes! What have we to do with the world? “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.” Rather, salvation belongs to Lord Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, because, killed by them, he washed his robe white in the blood of the spotless Lamb. Therefore he is blessed: because he was called, and because he was also brought into the wedding supper of the Lamb. O venerable hieromartyr! O blessed bishop! His soul possesses paradise, since he found salvation from [Col. 1170D] his enemies and from the hand of those who hated him without cause.

Good God! We have heard with our ears, and our fathers—Lord Prince Henry of France, peer of France, duke and Archbishop of Rheims; Lord William of the White Hands, Archbishop of Sens; Lord John of Bellesme of Poitiers; Lord Bernard, Bishop of Nevers, the fathers [or peers?] of France—have told us of the deed wrought by certain lost murderers, not by the King of the English: that wicked deed, unworthy of a man, still more of a kind, merciful, gentle king, well disposed toward everyone.

“It was enough,” they said, “for the magnanimous lion to have struck down the body of Lord Thomas, Primate of Canterbury, humbled before you, O England.” They report that a father solicitous for your royal welfare, O king, fell [Col. 1171A] beneath the swords of the wicked William de Tracy, Hugh de Morville, William le Breton, and Reginald Fitz-Urse. If you sent them, you too killed the man whom they killed. Far be this from the King of England. I do not believe that you planned so foul a crime. You bear the sword only for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.

While treating political matters, the Illyrian count Thaeroneus declares in his *Instruction and Inauguration of a King* that a king, at his institution and inauguration, undertakes and vows a perpetual obligation to live well and blessedly, and to observe right judgment. The great priest of God Jehoiada, when he preserved for the kingdom of Israel Joash, son of Ahaziah, saved until the proper time—whom his aunt Jehosheba had stolen away from among the sons of King Ahaziah while they were being murdered by that she-wolf Athaliah—placed upon [Col. 1171B] the young king both the diadem and the testimony. What is the testimony? The book of God’s Law, teaching that kings are especially bound, from the solemn day of their coronation, to practise the divine law.

Remember, lord, what happened to you, O king, when you were to be consecrated by the hands of the reverend father Theobald, Archbishop of Canterbury, on 20 December, and that you uttered this profession into the hands of the consecrating bishops: “I, Henry, by God’s permission to be King of England, profess and promise before God and the angels henceforth [to maintain] law, justice, and peace for the Church of God and for the people subject to me.” Consider, I pray, both what you promised and to whom. For it is written: “Make vows and fulfil them” (Ps. LXXV.12); and [Col. 1171C] again: “A foolish and faithless promise displeases God” (Eccles. V.3). Set your heart against yourself and ask it how and when you have fulfilled your vow. Is this how you have preserved justice, by not rendering to your own what is due? They say that you committed this dreadful and monstrous crime of parricide. We, though ignorant of the facts, already grieve for you, fearing what we should never wish to know.

“How the fine gold of your love has grown dim; the finest colour has changed!” You took care to build and endow our churches: how then, by striking the shepherd of the Church, have you scattered—and, incredible to say, slaughtered—the sheep of the Catholic flock?

The chief of the Peripatetics, in the *Ethics*, calls kings “living law.” I believe he spoke thus because kings customarily provide for the life of their subjects. Certainly he would not have greeted you in this way, but under the name of dead law, you who have brought your own to death. The son of the nations who do not know God stained Rome’s foundations with fraternal slaughter. But far be it from a son of Christian truth and protector of our houses to wash the cement of our foundations in paternal blood. [Col. 1171D] I hate and curse violent hands more than hairy ones.

Though a pagan, King Antigonus most wisely cursed a flatterer who urged him to act by right and wrong alike among his subjects and fellow-citizens: “Far be this from me,” he said. “To proceed thus belongs to tyrants; to kings belongs action according to the laws and institutions of government.” O saying worthy of the best king! The Greek sages called a king *basileus*, because they found him to be the base and firm foundation of the people. [Col. 1172A] But what kind of foundation of the people will you be judged? Is this how, radiant with a royal diadem, you support and bear your people—by removing from their midst your people’s and your own spiritual father? You will deservedly be called the shaken foundation of the people, already near collapse.

That blind Greek poet called kings shepherds. But who does not know that it belongs to a good shepherd to shear the flock, not swallow it? Yet you have dragged away, possessed, and killed. Who can see or hear of such iniquity being poured back upon the head of a king—and a Catholic king? He who in the days of Saul removed reproach from Israel called kings a shield in that funeral lament for Saul and Jonathan, the beloved princes: “The shield of the mighty has been cast away upon you” (II Kings I.21). Jerome, doctor of the holy Church, read the tenth verse of Psalm XLVI, in which David glories, “For the mighty gods of the earth are exceedingly exalted” (Ps. XLVI.10), as “the kings, the shields of the earth.” Granted this, I cannot discover among what kings I should place you. The righteous do not recognize you as one of their kind. Those kings cast shade over the heads of the people in the day of battle. But you, my lord king, not only turn your face from your own: you leave even those whom you have killed unburied before the sun’s eyes, so that it may endlessly behold those whom you oppress. [Col. 1172B]

I confess, and frankly my soul cannot persuade itself that this is true of you unless it had been reproached by the letters of those fathers, after I had undertaken my embassy, in which you had promised on oath to do enough as a king. You bestowed so many and such great benefits upon us; what will their value be? For behold, the stern prophet sent by God says: “God shall remember none of all the righteous deeds which you have done” (Ezek. XXXIII.13). In vain have you laboured in building cities and small cells in which few men dwell above rivers of shed blood, weeping when they remembered you, the zealot of our Zion. To build today and destroy tomorrow—what else is this but to take one’s own soul in vain?

When the divine prophet asked, “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps. XXIII.3), the Holy Spirit answered him: “He who is innocent in hands and clean in heart” (ibid.). If these two steps are necessary to attain heaven, and you can no longer find the first step, by what way will you arrive? It is necessary to depart from here. Where will you go? On the day on which Christ brought us life, [Col. 1172D] you pronounced that the life of His Christ was to be cut off. They reported this incredible thing; I do not believe it. O Lord God, who will believe our report?

All who receive these things will say of you: “Why have you sharpened your tongue like a serpent’s?” If you have thus fixed yourself in the mire of innocent blood, behold, you have become without crown and without substance. O most cruel lot of Angevin blood! O pitiable condition of the once flourishing kingdom of England! When the head aches, we feel the other members suffer. The king is the head of his people, and Christ is the head of the king. By harming the innocent and slaughtering the guiltless, you have fallen by a disaster so ruinous that a great crushing has been inflicted upon you, the head of the English. Who will heal you? Every fish stinks from the head. The people’s weakness flows down from the king, their head, because [Col. 1173A] he turns it where he will.

A man of consular rank, well and widely known, writes to Sempronius that among your own one may observe what is seen in bodies also: the disease that spreads from the head through the human body from a dead heart is most grave. What more is our flesh than worm, stench, and horror? When you, the heart of the Britons, have been choked by the crime of parricide, what can the people avail—and we, your poor hermit servants? That experienced man spoke truly who said: “As the king is, so is his people”; for the world is shaped after the king’s example. What an example, alas, do you give us—an example of an august king!

In the oracle of Testimony, the great and wise king of Israel placed two cherubim, made of olive wood and overlaid with gold, in order to teach that the supreme powers, ecclesiastical and temporal, serving God, should be adorned with love and kindness—the qualities represented by that kind of olive wood. Of what will posterity proclaim that you are composed? When Ahijah the Shilonite spoke with Jeroboam on the road, he called the king of Israel, burdened with the torn pieces of a new cloak, a lamp. What does this mean? A lamp is worthless unless it abounds in oil together with light. Thus a king, however much he shines with gold and jewels gleaming on his sceptre, is of little account unless he excels in love and beneficence. [Col. 1173B]

We too have heard, when we rose at midnight to pray, of the Bridegroom refusing to receive the five virgins who came late and had not taken oil with them, confounding them with the Gospel’s rejection: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV.12). Oil, frequently used in Scripture, is a symbol of royal mercy and magnificence. By relieving the miseries of the weak and of subjects, it closely resembles the oil which we see floating above other liquids. Hence, I think, kings are consecrated not with harsh wine or vinegar but with the oil of mercy, that from the day of their coronation they may learn indeed to exercise mercy with judgment.

For a lamp devoted to watchfulness to shine, it must be held upright. Thus kings, the lamps of peoples, ought to be magnificent, upright, most loving, and watchful for the welfare of their own. Now therefore you see the true lamp placed at the feet of kings in the word of God: because the light which was in you is darkness, and darkness is over all your land through the scandal which you have placed before all your people; [Col. 1173D] and you have seen this:

> And the shadows fall longer from lofty mountains.

Every vice of the soul bears a crime so much more conspicuous in itself as the person who sins is held to be greater. Jeroboam, because as King of Israel he displeased God more than any other Hebrew through the crime of idolatry, caused the people of Israel to sin by the worst and most scandalous example of his life. Indeed, as Hegesippus observes, an emperor’s complicity is set before the people like a law of shameful deeds. Every ruler is regarded as a kind of monarchy of his people; by the rudder or helm of his example, he turns them whither he wishes, whether to good or evil.

Have the ambassadors of the Three Magi never told you that when Herod was troubled, all Jerusalem too was troubled with him? The higher a tower, the heavier its fall; its ruin is more extensive, and the crash, noise, and terror of its fall greater. So kings—since their vices can escape no one—who have become towers of strength to the nations committed to them against the raging enemy, when they fall through corrupt morals and ruinous conduct, cause great ruin in the minds of their subjects.
