Christ, the Way, Truth, and Life, Prince of the kings of the earth, declared that this fearful saying, “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. XVIII.7), was to be feared not because of the evil deed of a little woman who followed Him, but because of the sin of an apostolic prince. How great—alas, how great—is this scandal which you have placed before your own? Manhu! [an exclamation, perhaps corrupt], what a man and how great a man you are; who are you, and what have you done? Do you see whether this crime befits a prince of your blood? [Col. 1174B] You have placed before the brethren of your redemption a stumbling-block, a stone of offence, and a rock of scandal. A master will render account for the trifles of his disciples, a lord for the insolence of his servants, a father for his children’s evil conduct; so too a king will render account on the day of judgment for his subjects’ transgressions. All their crimes, whether light or grave, are poured upon the heads of kings.

But if, inspired by God, you plan to avoid and erase a stain upon your name as bitter as it is disgraceful, those four assassins, notorious for their savagery, must be subjected to the final punishments and removed and exterminated from the bounds of human nature. Do not suffer them to live in your lands, lest this escape you: if, through your toleration or partnership with those four excommunicated men, you have ceased to live the spiritual life, I do not wish you to live the temporal life any longer. So great is my concern for the salvation of your diadem that I speak as one who would even wish to become anathema for you.

Would, indeed, that you had never done us good, because, when a father has been killed by a son, God—the Judge, righteous and strong, who arms His creation for His vengeance (Wis. V.18), “for with what measure you have measured, it shall be measured to you again” (Mark IV.24), and “he who has shed blood, his blood shall be shed” (Gen. IX.6)—will soon raise up the bitter zeal of your sons against the sceptre of your everlasting dominion. Yet may God grant that I prophesy falsely. Meanwhile prepare your soul for tribulation. “Jerusalem has sinned grievously; therefore she has become unstable” (Lam. I.8); [Col. 1174D] and there is no peace in the royal bones—that is, in the higher parts of the inward man—because of his sins (Ps. XXXVII.4).

When Solomon sets forth his case, he reveals that the mighty shall suffer mighty torments, because the eternal Judge will not fear anyone’s greatness (Wis. VI.7–8). Already the last of the apostles fears the judgment that “shall be most severe for those who rule” (ibid. 6). We do not stone you with this grave weight of words for a good work, but for blasphemy, execration, and falsehood—if the reported parricide is true. Zealous with zeal for the sons of the Lord God of hosts, the tongues of the thorns of our wilderness have been sharpened; they speak pointedly, not without a wound; but let them prick in such a way that those who must be pricked may be pierced unto salvation.

Let not my bitter complaints distress you, lest something worse happen. Stronger cleansing is necessary for the great discharge of ulcers; the surgeon’s hand, if too gentle with a small wound, makes the ulcer festering. A faithful physician does not heed his friend’s lamentable voice while cutting away a rotten limb, but acts for healing. My lord king, I want you to employ such speakers and advisers as fear to flatter vices as much as to detract from virtues. Let those sinful flatterers sell their oil somewhere other than before you; the pure image of kings does not wish its head to be fattened with the sinner’s oil. Even if sinful courtiers have nursed you, do not assent to them: their words have grown soft, but they themselves are darts.

Let the Samaritans—I mean the guardians of your soul—[Col. 1175B] offer oil and wine to pour into the wounds of your rebellious soul. Would that I too might become with them a fit minister of the New Testament in your presence, coming to you with harsh words and pouring in the wine of due rebuke until your heart is crushed; and this is to act mercifully by being severe in this kind of case.

While we address you, son of the Most High, neither wishing nor bound to flatter you, perhaps we shall stir your indignation against us. I fear nothing and do not make my soul more precious than myself. It is better for me, like that woman accused by two elders grown old in evil days, to fall into human hands without an evil deed, together with the slain Lord of Canterbury, than into the hands of the living God (Heb. X.31), which the Doctor of the Gentiles deemed fearful. Let our temporal goods perish through me, if only your soul, for which Christ died, the just for the unjust, does not lose eternal goods.

Two things forbid me from proceeding farther and lingering longer with you, imposing silence upon me. First, your majesty is fettered beyond my strength by affairs deserving execration and is too deeply entangled in them; I grieve that it has been mortally wounded by the shedding of innocent blood. Second, this contagious wound of excommunication inflicted upon your soul forbids me to deal with you, lest my soul, once yours, be infected by so pernicious a contagion, until you come to your senses. For Paul, writing to the Corinthians, commands under a holier title that one should not associate or even eat with the covetous or rapacious. [Col. 1175D] The disciple whom Jesus loved likewise, commending charity to the elect lady and her children, says: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine of charity, do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Hail’ to him; for he who says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (II John 10–11). But you, who know [Col. 1176A] that we ought to render mutual service to the parents of our souls, understand that we ought no longer to have fellowship with you unless you first put away your soul’s filth.

At Jerusalem there was the sheep-pool, where, when the water was stirred, whoever first descended into it was healed. At Rome too are the pools of Siloam, which is interpreted “Sent,” or “Apostle,” because the apostolic see is there and receives sinners to repentance. Go therefore to these pools of Siloam. But if the way is blocked by the arms of Emperor Frederick, go down into the Jordan of repentance; for those waters are indeed better than the rivers Abana and Pharpar of Damascus. Hasten; do not delay: delay is dangerous. Wash seven times. Once you have cleansed and restored the wretched and pitiable ruins of your soul by this sevenfold washing—confession, tears, fastings, satisfaction, discipline, pilgrimage to holy places, and almsgiving—redeem your sins.

Bring in the Church whom you have made a widow, that she may pray for you. We indeed do not cease praying for you night and day, that, by coming before His face in confession, you may return to the Lord, if perhaps you hear us and are healed by Him. Without this washing, forget us: you have nothing to do with us; He who feeds the birds of heaven will care for us. We neither await nor seek your letters. Write no more, because your name has been blotted from the book of the living; nor may we see your face, scorched by the lightning-flash of excommunication, lest, made participants in the curse, we be separated with you from the use of God’s grace, without which [Col. 1176C] we can do nothing.

If you wish to find us, return, return to our heavenly Father, in whom and through whom we live, move, and are (Acts XVII.28), and say to Him in a spirit of humility and a contrite mind: “I, who have acted wickedly, Father, against heaven and against your own, expect nothing more from you.” Thus have mercy on your soul by pleasing God. The people of Grandmont, groaning and seeking from God, who gives food to all flesh, the bread of grace for you, wait indeed until your change comes; in ashes and sackcloth they have made themselves obedient to God.

I say these things to you through our general prior and exhort you in Christ Jesus, my Lord, the strict Judge, who, although all things are naked and open to His eyes, declares that He will make an exact inquiry into our deeds with the lamps of Jerusalem, though she is beloved. What will He do to those whom He has rejected? “He will miserably destroy the wicked.” These are the words of the holy Gospel: “He who is of God hears God’s words” (John VIII.47).

GUILLELMUS DE TRAHINAC, SIXTH PRIOR OF GRANDMONT

[Col. 1177]

NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. II, col. 649)

[Col. 1177A] William I of Trahinac, also called of Aixe, of the diocese of Limoges, was appointed on the vigil of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary. Devoted to fasts, vigils, and prayers, he governed the priorate for eighteen years and three months. During his rule, a portion of the Lord’s Cross was received, as the following document attests:

“In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1174, while Pope Alexander III presided, Amalric VI was king of Jerusalem, Louis VII king of the Franks, and Henry II king of the English; in the time of Lord William, sixth prior of Grandmont, on the day before the Kalends of June, the life-giving Cross was received, which the aforesaid Emperor Manuel of Constantinople had bestowed, together with a golden reliquary, upon the aforesaid Amalric, husband of the emperor’s niece. The same King Amalric, enlightened by divine inspiration, sent that Cross with the same reliquary to Grandmont through the venerable Bernard, bishop of Lydda, where it was received with every honor and devotion by the aforesaid prior and all the brethren. Therefore, by the common counsel of the prior and brethren, it was decreed that, if anyone should presume either to remove or to take away from the place of Grandmont the whole Cross or any part of that Cross, let him be anathema. Amen.”

During William’s prelacy, at the prompting of the enemy of the human race, a serious dissension arose in the Order of Grandmont, to the grave detriment of the religious life [Col. 1178A] which had flourished until then, and to the scandal of very many. It raged for three years, until the time of Pope Clement III. This same William, I say, stoutly defended the liberty of the clerics of his house against the lay brethren, whose audacity went so far that, in a wicked act of violence, they not only committed him to prison but even presumed to depose him from the office of prior, Stephen having been intruded in his place. For this reason the bishop of Chartres and the abbot of Saint-Victor were delegated as judges by Lucius III; with the assistance of Audebert, count of La Marche, they restored William to his former dignity. Afterwards, when he had promised to resign, Pope Clement III decreed that both he and Stephen, appointed in his place, had forfeited their office of government, granting permission to elect another; concerning this, see the bull among that pope’s letters. Subsequently an agreement was made between the clerics and the lay brethren through Pope Innocent III. But William, at Rome—or, as others report, after returning from the curia—was called from this life on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December. Borne in funeral procession to Grandmont, he was buried among the priors beneath this brief epitaph:

“Here lies Lord William, most reverend sixth prior, a true Israelite, in whom there was no guile. He lived in the priorate eighteen years and three months.”

[Note: [Col. 1177B] In the year 1639 a lead coffin was found in which rests the body of Prior William, with this distich:

[Col. 1178B]

“Behold: William, the sixth prior, made an exile for the flock,  
rests with Christ in this tomb.”]

[Col. 1177]

## LETTERS OF WILLIAM OF TRAHINAC

(See above, among the letters of Peter Bernard, nos. 4 and 5.)

## GERARD ITHERIUS, SEVENTH PRIOR OF GRANDMONT

[Col. 1177]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. II, col. 649)

[Col. 1177C] Gerard Itherius succeeded William by the votes of the general chapter held on the third day before the Kalends of October, on the feast of [Col. 1178C] Saint Michael, in 1188; through his promotion tranquility was restored by the Lord to the brethren. In the first year of his administration this prior, at the earnest request of religious persons, procured the canonization and translation of the body of Saint Stephen, with the cooperation of Elias, bishop of Bordeaux, Sebrand, bishop of Limoges, and Bertrand, bishop of Agen. Two disciples of Gerard, Robert and William, were sent to the Apostolic See with letters from the aforesaid prelates, and also from other bishops, abbots, and princes. The bull was issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of Clement’s pontificate. Moreover, this prior devoted himself successfully to literary study out of zeal for monastic discipline; for he wrote the deeds of Saint Stephen, published in the book called the *Mirror*. His epitaph teaches us the following concerning him: “Here lies Lord Gerard, seventh prior; he remained in the priorate ten years and three months.” Afterwards, having been removed, he died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May; for while still living he had resigned the priorate, and he was honorably buried among the priors of Grandmont.

[Col. 1179]

## LIFE OF SAINT STEPHEN OF MURET, BY GERARD ITHERIUS

(See above, col. 1005.)

[Col. 1179]

## REVELATION OF A CERTAIN BROTHER CONCERNING THE DEPOSITION OF WILLIAM OF TRAHINAC, PRIOR OF GRANDMONT

About the year 1180.

(MARTÈNE, *Anecdota*, vol. I, col. 604, from a Vendôme manuscript about five hundred years old.)

[Col. 1179B]

### WILLIAM TO BROTHER WIDO

There is still living at Grandmont a certain brother, a priest, a religious man of good repute, formerly most intimate with Lord Prior William and with his predecessors. His name will be withheld. He is full of virtues, honorable in life and character, sparing in food and drink, slow to anger, slow to speak, gentle in speech, humble in all his conduct, righteous and pleasing before God and men, walking blamelessly in all the commandments of the Lord. For his practice is always to read psalms, or to pray, and to bend the knee before God, so that, being in every respect already worthy of God, he has, if it may be said, become like the angels while yet in mortal flesh, and ought to have been taken alive by the Lord into the heavenly kingdom.

This man [Col. 1179C] lay prostrate in prayer before the crucifix in the chapter-house, entreating God with all the desire of his heart. And behold, while he was awake and sighing for the attainment of the heavenly kingdom, a certain priest-brother, who had died not long before, appeared to him, clothed in exceeding brightness: his friend and companion, well known to us all, Bernard of La Roche by name. Lord Prior William had reared him from childhood, and virgin loved virgin exceedingly, as did Bernard in return, so that, while William still lived, Bernard carried one of his teeth in a comb-case as a relic. Thus, by divine disposition, it came about that those whom one love had bound together in life should be joined in death. For Lord William, prior of Grandmont, as is known to almost the entire world, because of the injury he suffered from his brethren, died in exile and pilgrimage at Rome and passed to Christ. The Church of us all knows the renown of his holiness and virtue, which frequent miracles also attest. The aforesaid Brother Bernard, journeying from the western regions to Rome in order to see William’s tomb, died there likewise. Here it is clearly shown how greatly he had loved William while living, whom he loved so greatly even in death that, by God’s ordering, he wished him to come from distant lands to himself and to be buried with him. For that brother was very gracious and lovable, and, as has been said, a blameless virgin, persevering from infancy in God’s service.

When the aforesaid priest saw him standing before the crucifix in a white robe, he was astonished. Yet he was not greatly [Col. 1180C] terrified, being a spiritual man accustomed to heavenly visions; but, raising his head a little from prayer and looking, he said: “Lord Bernard, are you that man?” He replied: “I am Bernard of La Roche.” Then the brother asked him, saying: “Lord, how is it with you?” He answered: “It is well with me, indeed, because I am saved; but I complain of Gerard, who would not have my name written in the Calendar. Yet I shall take vengeance upon him”—speaking, that is, of Gerard the prior, though unwilling to call him prior.

Afterward that holy priest asked him again: “Lord, tell me: how is it with Lord Prior William?” He answered: “Know [Col. 1181A] certainly that he is with the Lord Jesus Christ in the kingdom of heaven, and that God in heaven has crowned him before Himself.”

After these words he disappeared, and the brother rose joyfully from prayer. That priest related this vision to me in familiar confidence, and his testimony is true; but he does not yet wish it to be made public, lest perhaps it turn to hatred or vainglory for him. Yet I was unwilling to cover divine works in silence, but wished to commend them to memory in writing, especially because none of the faithful disciples of Lord Prior William ought to keep silent about the praises of his holiness, but should proclaim them, praise them, rejoice, and be glad. Farewell.

## [LIFE OF BLESSED HUGH LACERTA]

[Col. 1181]

## LIFE OF BLESSED HUGH LACERTA, DISCIPLE OF SAINT STEPHEN, FOUNDER OF THE ORDER OF GRANDMONT

By William Dandina of Grandmont, surnamed of Saint-Savin, his contemporary.  
(After 1157.)

(MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, VI, 1143, from a Grandmont manuscript written in the author’s own lifetime.)

[Col. 1181B]

1. Therefore Lord Stephen, the first father and founder of our entire religious order, through whom divine mercy made known to us, and through us to others, the light of truth, is shown and believed, on the reliable testimony of many, to have been a native of Auvergne. For when the holy man of God first fled the nobility of birth, attachment to possessions, the fleeting glory of the world, the varied pleasures of food, and the remaining allurements of laxity as though from a certain fire, he hastened with swift course to Muret, where, establishing himself, he dwelt as a new inhabitant. There, as the merits of religious life grew in conformity with his will, now free from every bond of the world, he embraced a lofty and harsh observance. Determining to bind himself by the rule of a more severe life, he began to endure hunger and vigils so greatly [Col. 1181C] that one would not doubt that he was cruel to himself. Spending the night in prayer, he ate once a day, most often only after sunset; sometimes he remained fasting for two or three days and was not refreshed until the fourth day. At times he took bread and salt, and a very little drink of water, utterly rejecting ointments. Concerning wine, moreover, we judged it better to say nothing than to say anything, especially since we have heard that he abstained from it altogether for thirty continuous years, except when he received the Lord’s communion on appointed days.

He was content in winter with as many garments as he wore in summer; what he used by day he also used by night. When he gave rest to his limbs, he used two planks joined together and a hair-shirt [Col. 1181D], with a cuirass always worn above it; sometimes he even lay upon the bare ground. His life, indeed, is sufficiently eloquently written elsewhere in places held and preserved with the highest honor, through the devotion of filial love. Finally, from the time when he entered the dry wilderness, desiring to serve Christ from the heart so as to receive abundant reward in heaven for his own merits and those of others, he became the father and servant of brethren [Col. 1182B] dwelling together. Living among them, he daily advanced in the work of God, preserving the pattern of that primitive Church of which it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; nor did anyone say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4).

2. In those days there was in Limousin a brother of blessed memory, Hugh by surname Lacerta, who, from the earliest years of childhood, surpassed his age in character and, according to what is written, “dwelt in the house of innocence.” Though born of lawful and distinguished parents, he despised and trampled underfoot the world, now as it were growing old, together with its desires. We must set forth for the edification of us all, lest we be found envious, both how greatly God endowed him with goodness and with virtue [Col. 1182C] while he yet flourished as a soldier in the world.

3. O praiseworthy man! O man beloved by all! Divine grace so chose him beforehand in infancy, so marked him out as one destined to benefit future generations, that God made him loved by his contemporaries in common speech, and he deserved to be called holy. While still a child, when he often came to church with his parents, he did not follow childish wantonness or boys’ heedlessness, but listened only to what was read.

4. When he had become a knight, he did not forget Christ’s poor, being himself to become poor. He gladly and carefully refreshed religious persons and all others whom he entertained with him, always in one house and at one table, at his own expense, as a generous giver. He distributed his goods as generously as he could to each according to need; he fed the hungry and furnished clothing to the naked; he visited and comforted orphans and widows, the sick and captives in their distress; and he diligently provided burial for deceased pilgrims and neighbors. What more need be said? He humbly supplied those who lacked hoes and the other necessities [Col. 1183A] for labor.

5. For, according to the teaching of our Master, no one is proclaimed perfectly abstinent except one who, when things he desires more strongly are set before him, tramples down and restrains his desire unharmed. This servant of God had bent himself to such abstinence that he very often went without things permitted to him and which he might freely have used. When various dishes of different kinds were set before him and his friends at table, he would then rise from it seeming somewhat sad, pretending that he suffered from a pain in the stomach or some other cause. Thus, after all had dined, he often remained alone without dining. Nor was he ever weary, as that military order commonly is, of his own food because it lacked varied and delicate dishes; content with what was given, he asked for nothing further.

[Col. 1183B]

6. In the castle where the servant of God lived, there came devoutly to church on Sundays a certain very poor man to pray. Family needs had stripped him so thoroughly of all possessions that he had scarcely anything except, I know not, some half-girdles with which he might cover his shameful parts. These seemed so patched together from other garments that one could scarcely, or never, discern what color they had formerly been. Beholding such things, as has been said, the soldier of God groaned and sighed, and for Christ’s sake desired with all his heart to have them; indeed, he hoped that they might suffice him for his whole life.

7. There was another man in the aforesaid place, poor only in possessions but, I believe, rich in virtues. With much sweat throughout the year, he gained a scant livelihood for himself and his household with a hoe. His dwelling was so poor and narrow that, carrying on his neck small branches of juniper and other low shrubs, he warmed himself at the very doorway near the threshold. The structure was hemmed in by such narrowness on every side that those dwelling there could with great difficulty get out. The aforesaid man thought that such a little lodging would be necessary for himself, in order to gain Christ, remembering the Scripture which says: “How narrow is the way that leads to life!” (Matt. 7:14).

[Col. 1183D]

8. It is worthwhile, and very necessary for our edification, to add to this account how the servant of God conformed himself in spirit not only to poor people but even to unclean animals. In the aforesaid castle, beneath a certain staircase, a filthy sow lay on a bed which it had made for itself from worthless straw and chaff. When the man of God very often saw it lying there at ease, he said sadly and in amazement to himself: “How do I live? What, wretched man that I am, do I endure for Christ?” For he was already so ready in Christ’s love that he would most gladly have accepted such a chamber, if the time of his religious life had permitted it.

9. It belongs to perfect life and highest wisdom to possess in the world what is related in the following chapter. This religious and devout knight, more obedient in all things and for all things to Christ than to the world, always strove to expend for good use, as far as he could, whatever he unwillingly acquired through military service. When, by his lord’s command, he was compelled to undertake military business, from which nevertheless he could not withhold his service because of the benefit received, he promised, desiring to cling to God, that he would do nothing there except serve Him: namely, on both sides to destroy evil and seek good. Yet, to render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, as if he wished to seize all, he sometimes began by being the first to depart. Thus, rendering to God the things that are God’s, he drove away those whom he did not wish to capture; but those whom others tried to hinder, he himself captured first, and then allowed them to go away safe and free in suitable places. Furthermore, he urgently demanded from his fellow-soldiers the share that fell to him [Col. 1184B], but with this intention: that those who had suffered loss might receive from him something not without gain.

Since the soldier of God thus ordered himself wisely in all things, he was judged dear and acceptable to God and to the people because of his zeal in religious conduct. At one time, therefore, while he silently debated with himself in his customary manner concerning contempt for the world, approving eternal life rather than the present and transitory life, it pleased him to leave his land and kindred and to live as a pilgrim in a foreign country. Accordingly, for some time he deliberated within himself where he should go and how this should be done. Making a vow to God, he resolved to go to Jerusalem, to serve Christ in arms, and never thereafter to return to his own home.

When the soldier of God, having found the appropriate time, arranged his expenses and gathered companions, had been pursuing his desired journey for many days, he was granted to find a fellow traveler, through the grace of God going before him, who would willingly supply him with necessities if he should lack means upon the road. This man was of a great family, very rich in gold, silver, and possessions, and provided with an exceedingly large household. As travelers customarily talked together about many matters, it happened that, in everyone’s judgment, Hugh was declared pre-eminent both in counsel and speech. When the rich man daily saw him thus exalted with so much grace, he so preferred him as friend and intimate that both refreshed themselves from one cup and one dish, and, leaving the counsel [f. companionship] of his own people, he enjoyed Hugh’s alone as his own. As they continued their journey with the proper pace of their undertaking [Col. 1184D], it happened that they arrived at Jerusalem sound and unharmed. Then, after refreshing their limbs weary from much exertion, they went through the holy places to pray, as opportunity allowed, bearing abundant offerings.

The soldier of God was moreover devoted to almsgiving, prayer, and frequent fasts, and obedient to all the commandments of eternal life according to his ability. For the sake of religious life he very often visited recluses and other religious persons, desiring both to be instructed by their preaching and refreshed by their presence. For nearly two years he rendered diligent service to Christ there, sometimes as a knight and sometimes as a pilgrim.

[Col. 1185A]

10. Meanwhile, circumstances arose compelling his wealthy companion to return home, for he was burdened with much business. Having explained this in order to the venerable man, he asked him, as his intimate and friend, to come back with him at once and as quickly as possible. Hugh replied: “I cannot at all do what you ask; for I came here in order to devote the remaining days of my life to God’s service.” Again the rich man said: “You are seeking an excuse not to grant what I ask. But since a long and laborious road remains for us, do not delay, sweetest friend, to comply with my words. I promise that, if you wish, I shall return here with you soon.”

Then, overcome by these entreaties, he consented, without further delay. The rich man promptly ordered what remained of his treasure to be prepared, so that they might have supplies of food and relieve their want of clothing. But as they went down to the sea [Col. 1185B], the man of God began to be saddened and troubled within himself about his return. It happened, however, that a pilgrim beautiful in face but more beautiful in faith was passing by the same way. Seeing him, he came up and said: “Brother, what is the matter? Why are you weeping?” Hugh said to him: “My lord, this and this has happened, and God has rejected both me and my service.”

The aforesaid pilgrim comforted him, as it were with a prophetic word: “My son and friend, do not mourn or be troubled. Perhaps the Lord is calling you back to other and more useful affairs, because, in order to draw someone on to a greater good, He sometimes overturns a lesser one.” Having heard and received this encouragement, he immediately and cheerfully boarded the ship with his companions in confidence. All together giving thanks to God, with favorable sailing, a gentle breeze, calm waves, moderate winds, a hanging sail, and a tranquil sea, they at last reached the harbor of safety.

[Col. 1185C]

11. When they had come ashore, it pleased him to return together with his companions and friends to his homeland, his own house, and his fields. Having come to them and settled among them, he attended to his household for nearly two years in a sufficiently honorable manner. Yet he devoted himself far more earnestly and fervently to works of mercy, being intent upon good works and especially zealous in hospitality. Though occupied with worldly concerns, he conducted earthly business, but, as later became clear in his life, more from obligation than from inclination. Now, when he was reaching his fortieth year, wearied by public business and worldly cares, he began utterly to detest the world and to seek within himself a place where he might be free for God alone.

[Col. 1185D]

12. At that time Lord Stephen had only recently received brethren, though few, into his discipline; he nevertheless kept watch, sometimes openly and sometimes secretly, to train them in the pursuit of holy conduct. As he grew for a long time in that wilderness in virtues and signs, some began afterward to leave the world and hasten to his instruction. His name therefore became known through neighboring places, and from that time he began to be visited by many. Those who brought him food for the body carried away from him in their hearts nourishment for eternal life.

This man, of whom our present discourse speaks, learned the renowned reputation of that venerable Father and, moved, as we believe, by the divine Spirit, entered the aforesaid wilderness, alone and with others, and many times presented himself before him. When the venerable Father perceived the request in his heart, he offered him, as was his custom, the gift of prayers through many words of consolation, but indicated that he could not remain with him. Thus, after consolation and conversation had ended, the soldier of God often withdrew to his own home, having been refused.

On another occasion he tested, through a priest sufficiently learned and well instructed in religious observances, whether so great blessings were present there as the reliable report of many had proclaimed—and as he himself also believed. Upon returning, the priest told him: “This Father about whom you inquire, both he himself and his disciples follow, as far as is permitted, the life of angels on earth.”

13. Not many days later the soldier of God again set out upon the journey to the desired wilderness for the same purpose. [Note: [Col. 1185] Compare chapter 1 of the *Sentences* of Saint Stephen, above.] When he presented himself before the man of God, he immediately declared what he sought:

“I know, lord, that my request does not escape you. I have often begged your charity, and often I have withdrawn from you rejected. Father and lord, I beseech you: I do not wish to return to the world, because I know it to be very unstable, and I fear that, because of the condition of my weakness, I may not be able to return here so easily as I do now. Behold, I am wholly prepared to turn to God, whom you preach and to whom you render devoted service with your followers. Therefore I beg you to grant me the habit of holy religious life.”

When the venerable Father saw the constancy of his request, he began to address him in these words:

“Brother and friend, you do not know what you ask. Your life is too delicate, wholly nourished amid pleasures. How will you be able to bear the burden which you wish to impose upon yourself? Look upon the Cross: it is very difficult to remain there. If you come here, you will be fastened to it, and you will lose the mastery you have over yourself—in your eyes, your mouth, and your other members. You will surrender your own will in eating, fasting, sleeping, and keeping vigil, and in many other matters. What you love in the world will come to be hateful to you. Thereafter you will not return to the house of your kinsfolk; and if they come to you, you will by no means show them your poverty. Can you, brother, be a digger, carry wood and dung, and serve all the brethren? All this would be easy; but you will remain confined in such a prison that there is no opening through which you may return to the world, unless you make one yourself. I shall not take care of you, nor permit you to take care of yourself. I have cut off my feet from the world; and if I do not return because of myself, neither shall I return because of you.

“One further thing remains. Perhaps I would send you into some wood, and I would take the grain which you had acquired by laboring with your hands and a wooden hoe, and give it to those who keep me here. Yet another, more terrible thing remains: it is a hundred times better for you to be damned in the world than here. For he who falls from a greater height is more seriously injured; and if from here you fell into hell, you would be lower than all the other lost. You may, however, go to any of the monasteries, where you will find great buildings and delicate foods appointed for their seasons. There you will find beasts and broad lands; here there are only the Cross and poverty.”

With these and many similar words the venerable Father tested the soldier of God, and then, after offering farewell, ordered him for the present to depart.

[Col. 1187B]

14. While the Father spoke thus, Hugh was filled with very great anxiety, and, as though he had lost all hope of salvation, he mourned without consolation—chiefly because the aid to salvation which he believed he could bear was deferred from him. Then he said again, as best he could: “O good man, good man! Exert all your strength in what you are doing; work at what you are working; let not your foot cease, let not your hand cease. But I, on the contrary, shall henceforth commit so much evil, both through myself and through others, that, by my deserved sins, I shall cast both myself and you into the depth of the abyss.”

Having spoken, he departed sadly and disappeared. Immediately the man of God rose, struck with great fear. Calling the brethren together, trembling and afraid, he told them all that he had heard from him and asked what counsel they would give regarding so perilous a matter. Meanwhile he prayed unceasingly for him, lest a long delay of testing should turn him away from the service of religious life.

The brethren are said to have given him this answer: “Hear, Father, our counsel, which may perhaps benefit our religious order. If this comes from God, you may test it in this way. Since by God’s goodness we have various supplies of food, order a portion from all our shares to be prepared, such as might suffice him for one day’s food and might be much better. If he remains with us because of all this, let God be praised for it; but if not, then from now on neither you nor we shall have it imputed against us at the judgment.”

When the aforesaid disciples had spoken thus, this counsel is known to have pleased both him and them. Then, summoning two of the disciples, he commanded them: “Go and say to him, ‘Trusting in Christ’s mercy, we make the sign that you may come and serve Him with us in fear and discipline.’” What the man of God commanded was at once accepted by the brethren.

On the following day the disciples were sent to go where they had been ordered. When they had entered his house, they immediately drew him aside with them and secretly explained all that the Father had commanded. The words of the commanding Father pleased him, and from that time fear entered into him, compelling obedience in all things. In that very hour, from the inmost marrow of his heart, he abandoned every hope he had placed in the world and renounced all that he possessed, because he had wholly chosen Christ as his master. No longer seeking wife, children of the flesh, riches, or worldly honor, [Col. 1188A] he devoted himself wholly to serving God alone. When supper had been made and he had sufficiently instructed them concerning the day and manner of his coming, the brethren went for a short time to sleep in his chamber.

In the morning, the soldier of God rose first. As he opened the lodging of the chamber for the brethren, an extraordinary fragrance immediately spread from it into his nostrils. While he wondered for a long time whence it came, he thought that it proceeded from the brethren’s labor and the sweat of their garments. Immediately returning to himself, he said: “Lord God, if I have ever found favor in your eyes, let such and so great a fragrance come forth from me, for your love, before I die.”

Then the brethren cheerfully and safely resumed their former journey. As they questioned one another uneasily about his coming, behold, the man followed them at the swiftest pace. When he reached them, he said: “Do not wonder, brethren and my lords, that I alone follow you. Perhaps you are uncertain about the day on which I promised to come to you, because you found me, when you arrived, so worldly and so delicately living. Why did you doubt this, you of little faith?” On hearing this, the astonished disciples answered that it was so.

Again he said to them: “But so that you may know it with certainty, behold, a traveler is coming toward you; ask him how I fare.” Immediately he departed. As they continued on their way, the traveler met them. When they asked him, “How does that man fare?” he answered: “What others scarcely obtain even at a price, he gains merely by a simple word.” Hearing this, the brethren rejoiced together exceedingly. Thereafter, when the evening hour of that day had been completed and the journey finished, they returned in peace to the Father and brethren.

[Col. 1188C]

Not long afterwards, the soldier of God left his land, kindred, friends, relatives, and—what was more difficult than all these—his own will, for the sake of the kingdoms of heaven. Taking with him one of his household servants as a companion, with the same intention and counsel, he set out for the place where the servant of God lived with his disciples. Arriving there, the disciple, humble and willing to learn, immediately approached the Father and master, that he might be trained in the holy form and teaching of religious life; and his desire was fulfilled as he wished.

[Col. 1188D]

15. Thus received and made a disciple, and joined within the congregation to the number of Christ’s poor religious servants, he immediately began to live and associate with God’s servants according to the vow, manner, and rule of poverty established under so great a Father. He attached himself especially to those who served God from the heart, engaging in fasts, prayers, and good works, meditating on the law of God day and night. As has been said, no one in that holy fellowship was permitted to possess anything as private property or to turn either to the right hand or to the left. There, having long been completely trained in pious habits and examples, and before he had attained the whole discipline of religious observances, he imitated the habit and conduct of the best brethren. In consequence he afterward became especially dear and acceptable to the venerable Father above the others.

He attended most diligently, above all others, fixed and attentive, at that Father’s frequent discourses on the word of God and the state of religious life, preserving the usefulness of the commandments and the discipline of life. Thus taught, there gradually and little by little sprang up in him so great a zeal of love for progress in religious life that no one, in his presence, dared to disparage it or say anything against it. And God’s grace, increasing in him, advanced daily so that he was always fully prepared to give an answer to those who asked concerning the state and rule of religious life.

Ordering his life in this way, he was loved by all the brethren with pure affection, drawing to himself the distinctive graces of each. He emulated this man’s gentleness, that man’s vigils, and another’s diligence in prayer; he followed one man’s continence and another’s cheerfulness; he admired one fasting and another resting upon the ground; he praised one man’s patience and another’s meekness. Considering all these things within himself, he strove to express in himself the good qualities of them all.

But his venerable Father and master, being a devout man who feared the Lord, rejoiced in his progress and advancement and gave thanks to the Lord. He did so chiefly because divine mercy had granted him such a disciple, one able to console and build up others by the word of God and the example of good works, and to provide sound counsel for their needs. Thus, a lamp lit, burning, and set upon a lampstand gave light to all who were in that house [Col. 1189C] of God. Concerning his intimacy, counsel, forethought, and goodness, the venerable Father gave much testimony in many matters, as the following words can demonstrate.

16. As that disciple daily increased in signs and virtues and became his master’s helper, the brethren—gathered together in charity, not envy—came to the Father and master, compelled by religious necessity. They addressed and earnestly exhorted him concerning the advantage and expansion of their church, the acquisition of cells, and the ordering of brethren; and, already knowing the firm purpose of the aforesaid disciple, they all worked together to have him sent out. To those asking with one consent and desire that this be done and accomplished, the Father replied:

“Why, brethren, why do you say this? Do you see that he is as necessary to you as to me? God has worked many benefits for us through him; and do you wish, therefore, to dismiss him from these things? For if we let him go from us, let us at the same time destroy the altar.”

For holiness, kindness, and wonderful humility were in him, and prayer, as the Lord commanded when he said: “Pray at every hour” (Luke 21). He never taught anyone to do anything which, if he could do it, he had not first done himself. Since that wilderness was growing day by day fervent in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the example of that same Father some began to be kindled with a desire for eternal life and humbly gave themselves, under his instruction, to the service of almighty God. For there his life, by holiness and teaching, had already become renowned among those dwelling far and wide.

17. At that time, compelled by ecclesiastical necessity, two men from the number of the cardinals, namely Gregory and Peter de Leo, were sent by the supreme pontiff of the Roman Church and came to Limoges. Afterwards they divided between themselves the care of that same place. Having learned and confirmed from the reports of many people the many praises of his life and manner of living, they came to visit him, each wishing privately to converse with him separately according to his own wish.

For many frequented his dwelling, since that man of God abounded in the teaching of heavenly grace. When the hour for conversation had come, he began to inquire into the purpose and way of each one, asking why such great and distinguished men had turned aside to such small and humble lodgings. When each explained, in answer to his inquiry, why he had come to him, and they discovered great wisdom in him, they immediately asked the brethren standing by to grant each of them, separately, however small an opportunity for more private counsel, and not to press him to leave them.

When they had withdrawn, the pastor called Lord Hugh to himself and ordered him to sit with him. When they were seated, the man of God said:

“My lords and friends, do not be troubled or astonished about this. I keep this disciple of mine and good son with me for this reason: whatever you say to me in private, I would afterwards tell him in full. For you can undoubtedly find as much counsel and goodness in him as in me. He is very prudent in counsel and faithful in what is entrusted to him.”

A matter very worthy indeed followed from that conversation, for, as they afterwards testified, they departed much more informed and wiser concerning the condition and customs of the Roman Church than when they had come.

18. At that time there was a certain retainer from Mortemar who was accustomed to carry charity to Muret, as to other places besides. He had a host at Bonnac, with whom he stayed whenever, travelling onward or returning, he could not reach his destination because he was tired and the hour was late. That retainer had already bestowed many benefits upon his host, both because of the reverence and love which he seemed to show toward the brethren, and because of the service and honour which he rendered him in his lodging.

For the host appeared to be a man of good character and orderly in all his actions; but, as the event later revealed, he was far other than he appeared. While his retainer was visiting the inn, he was secretly sold by him, for a price, to two robbers. They seized and bound him, dragged him away with them to the bank of the Vienne, and placed him under the strictest guard in certain hiding-places among the rocks.

Meanwhile certain men from Mortemar came to Muret to make a visit. When, after words of edification, they wished to depart, they began to ask the Father whether that man had ever been sent. He answered them, “No.”

After they had gone, others arrived and reported the same thing to the man of God. His household was bitterly weeping because he had now delayed longer than usual. On hearing this, the man of God withdrew and had all the brethren gathered to him. They, according to their custom, expected to hear from him something great and pleasing. But the servant of God immediately told them all that he had heard. It was uncertain whether the man was alive or dead.

While the brethren hesitated for an hour about what ought to be done, Lord Hugh stood in their midst and, through the spirit of prophecy, as we believe, declared that he was alive and had been betrayed by his host. Some testify that he possessed this spirit of prophecy, having been able to know him intimately.

On hearing this, the man of God rebuked him, saying:

“Brother, why did you ever presume to say such a thing? Would he return such and so great an evil to that man for such and so great a good?”

He immediately ordered messengers to be sent in every direction to seek him, and charged the brethren in so great a necessity to implore divine help by devout prayers.

One day, after dawn had come and the solemnities of the Masses had been completed, the porter went out to the gate and found that retainer holding his host and the robbers by the hand, their arms twisted and bound behind their backs and joined at the neck. They at once disclosed to the man guilty of the offence all the punishment of their guilt. Seeing this, the porter returned to the place where the man of God was speaking to the brethren about the Lord, and privately whispered in his ear what he had seen and heard outside.

On hearing it, however, the holy man did not rise from the sermon which he had begun; nor did he appear to rejoice at that very good news, nor to shorten his discourse more than usual. When the sermon had ended, the servant of God went out, as the matter required. Before his presence the wretches immediately stood, convicted and bound by their very prey.

When they had stood before him in silence for an hour, still bound, they were violently terrified and fell to the ground. Confessing at his feet the punishment due to their wickedness, they asked with loud groaning and wailing that pardon might be granted them. But he, compelled by excessive compunction, remained in his goodness. Calling the brethren, he ordered them to untie the cords binding their arms and raise them up, so that they might receive the blessing together. He was not forgetful of the Apostle, who teaches that our enemies ought to be satisfied with food and drink (Rom. 12). When they had been restored to themselves, he rebuked them for their wicked actions; and, peace having been restored among them, he admonished them henceforth to cease from such madness of cruelty. Thus he let them go to their own homes.

Then the brethren began together to rejoice and marvel, especially because it had happened to them just as that brother and disciple had foretold in his prophetic declaration.

19. On another day, some other persons, having a matter full of very great danger, came to the man of God at Muret. They had come together in order that it might be decided, for the restoration of peace, by the judgment of the aforesaid disciple alone. Therefore the pastor ordered him to come to him and carefully explained to him what evil and how great a loss he alone could extinguish.

He answered them: “I alone was not involved in the affair about which you ask.”

And they said to him: “My lord, it is as you say; but those who were then with you have long since completed the way of all flesh.”

“But whether they are dead,” he said, “I do not know. For I know this one thing: I was dead to the world before them. For just as they are now unable to bear testimony to you or to others about this or anything else, so neither can nor ought I to do so concerning the world.”

Therefore the pastor praised and blessed the aforesaid disciple because he had answered so prudently. Thus his answer became both his defence and a lesson from pupil to master.

20. For the good pastor was accustomed to confer with the brethren. On one occasion, when he sought their counsel concerning a certain necessity, they at length unanimously declared that, as the pastor himself had predicted, it would be good. But that disciple said the opposite:

“Good pastor, as it seems to me, it is not good as the others say.”

When the brethren heard this, they were greatly angered against him. Therefore the pastor rebuked him and moreover reproved him, making him ask many pardons in the presence of all the brethren.

But the pastor came to know and believe that that disciple alone had foreseen matters much better than he himself had arranged with all the others. Therefore he immediately said to him:

“Thus, my son, a good and faithful disciple draws his master to God and leads him back.”

21. That disciple remained with our Lord and master Stephen until his death, faithfully listening to him and questioning him about his teachings and the other commandments of our life, lest the spiritual seeds that proceeded from his mouth should perish without increase through the presumption and negligence of hearers. And God’s goodness chose this one man from so many thousands, who knew how humbly to receive what he heard and faithfully to reveal it in its proper time to future ages.

But since we have come to this point, let us hear together at least a few of their questions and answers.

22. [Note: [Col. 1191] Compare chapter 104 of the Sentences of Saint Stephen, above.]

When the pastor was speaking about prayer, the aforesaid disciple asked him how one ought to remain in it. He answered with a discourse of this kind:

“Moses, in his prayer, raised his hands to the Lord while Joshua, his minister, fought against Amalek. And as long as he held his hands raised, his people prevailed; when his hands were lowered, that people was defeated. At last Aaron and Hur supported his hands until the victory was achieved” (Exod. 17).

“Elsewhere it is found that Mary Magdalene, coming to the Lord for the remission of her sins, fell at his feet; and God forgave her because of the great love with which she was filled. For she loved him before she came there. Thus Moses raised his hands in order to love God more and pray more effectively; Mary Magdalene bowed herself at Jesus’ feet” (Luke 7).

“Therefore, whenever anyone is alone in private prayer, let that person adopt whichever posture enables him to love God more: sitting, standing, lying prostrate on the ground, or kneeling. Yet let him bring humility with him, without which the Lord does not hear him for his benefit. For when the disciples themselves, Saint James and Saint John, asked Jesus Christ without humility, he answered them: ‘It is not mine to grant you to sit at my right hand or at my left, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father’” (Matt. 20).

“Therefore become other than you now are through humility, and it shall be given to you. All the force of prayer lies in the greatness of divine love; but divine love finds its merit only in humility. Thus Jesus Christ promised exaltation in the kingdom of heaven to humility, because he found nothing else on earth by which he might be loved.

“In all works, God wills that time and place be observed, except in prayer. According to the proper time, he wills that someone recite psalms, speak of God, hear others speak, and labour, and likewise in other matters. For this reason God gave different commands: lest anyone become weary in his service, and so might move from one thing to another for greater delight. But in every work he wills that each person always pray to him, saying in his heart: ‘God, I do this only so that I may be able to love you.’

“To anyone wishing to do any act whatsoever, the Lord says: ‘If you wished, I would go with you and help you in what you intend to do.’ Then the person who loves the world replies: ‘Help another, but not me.’ He says this by his deeds whenever he departs from the divine commandments; and, because of the pride by which a human being rejects divine companionship, the Lord afterwards answers him in his prayer: ‘Because you were unwilling to have me as companion in that work, I will now not receive your prayer.’”

23. [Note: [Col. 1193D] The same work, same place, chapter 105.]

Again the disciple asked his pastor why the Scriptures say, “Praise God,” “Bless God,” when the Lord has no need of human blessing. He answered:

“Holy Scripture commands nothing except for human salvation. When it admonishes, ‘Praise God; bless God,’ all the benefit returns to the human being. For whenever someone says with a good disposition, ‘God, may you be praised; God, may you be blessed,’ the Lord immediately answers: ‘And may you who praise be praised; and may you who bless me be blessed.’

“From this reasoning one may understand that God answers me in this way: no one can bless God unless first blessed by God and anticipated by his grace. Therefore, since blessing comes entirely from the Lord first, when a human being blesses God, he increases his own blessing and love.”

24. [Note: [Col. 1193D] The same work, same place, chapter 107.]

Again the same disciple asked where all the new songs are found that are continually sung in heaven. The pastor said to him:

“Jesus Christ taught his disciples in the Gospel what the new song sung in heaven is, saying to them: ‘A new commandment I give you: that you love one another as I have loved you’” (John 13).

“This is charity, which is called a new song because it renews a human being and makes a child of light out of a child of darkness. This charity is a new song for human beings on earth; it is also a new song for angels in heaven. For whenever they see any one of the elect ascending on high, they sing a new song because of that person’s ascent. Even if they had nothing else for which to praise God, they would never come to an end because of that fact alone.

“For they rejoice over a sinner doing penance, as the Lord says in the Gospel (Luke 15); they rejoice completely when they see that person become a companion in their salvation and know that he will sin no more. And when they saw the Son of God clothed in flesh and ascending, they marvelled and said: ‘Who is this King of glory?’ (Ps. 17 [Vulgate numbering]). They rightly marvel in joy and sing a new song, because the members follow the head.”

25. [Note: [Col. 1194D] The same work, same place, chapter 101.]

The same disciple asked the pastor this:

“Since you defend divine justice with all your strength and so greatly, why did the Lord command the Israelites to borrow treasure from the Egyptians and carry it away with them?” (Exod. 12). “Is this not robbery?”

He answered:

“Brother, this was plainly just. For the Israelites had served God, while the Egyptians repaid them evil for their service. Therefore, by a true judgment, God the just judge willed that they should carry away with them the wages for their labour, of which the Egyptians had defrauded them.

“Spiritually, this means that likewise the members of Christ received from the Jews the treasure of Holy Scripture, while the Jews remained in Egypt—that is, in the darkness of this world.”

26. [Note: [Col. 1194D] The same work, same place.]

Again the same disciple asked him:

“Lord, you say that God loved the land of Jerusalem more than any other, so greatly that from other regions he brought his friends there; he himself was also born there from a Virgin, and in the Scriptures he frequently calls it the land of promise. It is therefore remarkable that he wished it to be such a land. For there are no beautiful meadows there, no excellent springs, no very rich rivers; rather, there is water in cisterns, roughness, and heat more than in many lands.”

The pastor resolved this question as follows:

“Brother, in this may be seen how lovable is the divine ordering. He removed bodily delight from that land so that his friends might delight in him alone, and so that his love might be meadow, spring, river, and every other refuge to them.

“For unless God knew that another world was better, he would never transfer his friends there. Indeed, he would in no way deceive even his own mother; but for the sake of heavenly joy he sometimes withdraws present consolation. Yet he does not do so in such a way as to leave his friends sad and desolate in this world. Rather, God wills to act thus, for then he keeps his servants in greater rest when the world considers that they are suffering labour.

“For they are more highly honoured when he causes them to rest amid straits. At times, however, so that unbelievers may be put to shame, he shows the people the sweetness in which his true friends abide while they are being tortured, as is read of the three children who blessed him in the fire of the furnace. Others, however, whom he does not console so bodily, he consoles in spirit, so that those who torture them suffer greater labour than the servants of God who are tortured, in order that the faithful may there take an example of patience.”

27. When the time came for the calling of the venerable Father, during that most holy sickness of his he lay for three days and three nights upon the breast of the aforesaid disciple, except when he attended to bodily necessities. For, as that disciple afterwards testified, while he was being instructed by him, he found in him almost every faculty and understanding doubled.

During those three days, as he instructed and consoled the brethren concerning our life and his own departure, they all stood around groaning and weeping, saying:

“Ah! Ah! Ah! Dearest Father and good shepherd, behold, we have left all things and followed you; we have come to you. Now tell us to whom you leave us, who will have care of us. What counsel, then, will you give us? Yet you permit us to have neither animals, landed possessions, tithes, churches, nor things belonging to churches—neither revenues nor gains—without the care of which this temporal life can scarcely or never be maintained.”

He said to them:

“Brethren, I leave you and commend you to that true God to whom all things belong and whom all things serve; whose nature is goodness, whose will is power, whose work is mercy; for whose love you have left all things. That gracious God will care for you as a good Lord, who knows well how to care for his servants. He himself will give you what is necessary—yet not what you might wish. For you are human beings, and in this you might sin.

“I tell you this on the condition that you remain in this life. But if you depart from life, I should wrong him if I promised you his things. For it is nearly fifty years since I came into this solitude: never afterward was bread so bitter that God did not give me what I could bear well; nor was it ever so abundant that everything God supplied was not wholly necessary. He will act likewise toward you if you remain in this life.

“Therefore I do not wish you to have animals, lands, tithes, churches, gains, or revenues, so that God may be more necessary to you. For when God is more necessary to you, you will love him more, if you are wise. What, then, can be lacking to one who has him who possesses all things?”

28. “I shall also give you another sound counsel, my sons, and command it: if you desire to have good and complete peace with your neighbours and other secular persons, beware entirely lest you covet what they possess. For if you attempt to seize their lands, vineyards, meadows, and the other things they own—choosing labour rather than rest, anger rather than joy, earth rather than heaven, nothing rather than all—there is no way for you to have complete peace with them.

“Moreover, henceforth beware altogether lest you possess anything which they may be able to covet: namely, animals, horses, mules, and oxen, which have no understanding, and the other things which you, being rational and obedient, cannot possess. For what agreement is there between Christ and Belial, or between light and darkness?” (2 Cor. 6).

“Let each person claim what is his own. Therefore, brethren, claim and seek what is yours, the things above, not those upon the earth” (Col. 3). “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11); “he who is able to receive it, let him receive it” (Matt. 19). That is: whoever does not persevere in this, having become disobedient, will not possess the kingdom of God. For the farther you withdraw from the world for Christ’s name, the nearer you will deserve to become to heaven.”

They said: “Lord, will you still help us?”

“If I could, certainly, brethren.”

28. But the brethren, made glad and secure by their father’s consolation, said to him again:

“Father and lord, many people say something else to us. They say: ‘While you live, we shall remain together; after you die, we shall not be able to survive unless we have animals.’”

He said to them:

“Brethren, those who tell you this are mistaken. Abbots say it, and other religious persons, and even learned clerics. I say that those who say this are mistaken; and the better the cleric, the more greatly he is mistaken—that God should lose his power because Stephen of Muret dies. It is therefore not worth the Lord’s while that I should die if he loses his power because I die.

“Rather, know firmly that he withdraws his benefits from you because of my sins. And after my death you shall see this: he will do for you so many and such great things that you will all marvel, provided that you remain in this most holy life, so that, if it were not seen every day, scarcely anyone would believe it.”

Thus the saying of the man of God was afterwards fulfilled among the brethren.

29. Then, asked by the brethren to speak to them the word of faith before he passed from this world to Christ, he immediately set forth to all a discourse on how they should worship God: God three in persons and one in the essence of divinity. He instructed them concerning charity: namely, that God should be loved with the whole heart and the whole mind, and that each person should do for his neighbour what he would wish done to himself by that neighbour.

He showed what humility is, since through humility one comes to that place from which the proud angel fell:

“This,” he said, “is the virtue that preserves the virtues once gathered together.”

He also repeatedly urged them, according to the Apostle’s teaching, to remember most diligently the good of hospitality, because through it some are known to have pleased the Lord, even by receiving angels as guests (Heb. 13). The Father added how, when the Lord comes in judgment, he promised this recompense to his faithful: that whatever they gave to one of his least ones, he would say had been given to himself.

Moreover, he exhorted them always to practise charity in works, because “love is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13), and whoever offends in one point is held guilty of both the law and the prophets (James 2). He continually recalled them to the remembrance and preservation of humility, that is, poverty of spirit, and urged them to keep God before their eyes. He declared and excommunicated avarice as altogether detestable, because it is called the root of all evils and the service of idols.

Thus he made the entire time of his illness fruitful and pleasant, satisfying the brethren in every respect, and sometimes relieving himself of his sickness by conversations concerning the spiritual life. As that illness increased day by day, on Thursday, before he departed from the body, he fortified his departure by receiving the body and blood of the Lord. Finally, lying upon haircloth, with eyes and hands always raised to heaven, on Friday before the altar of the Lord, he yielded his spirit to the Lord amid the words of prayer, in the very hands of that disciple.

It is therefore entirely clear to all who desire to know it that the glorious and in every way praiseworthy passing of Lord Stephen took place on Friday, in approximately the forty-sixth year of his conversion. This too is judged to have been no small merit: that the Lord received him with himself and with the thief on that day on which that same Redeemer and Lord had formed humankind, and redeemed condemned humanity on the cross; and that he who had always celebrated that most holy day in abstinence should, after the pressures of the world, be placed in glory on that most holy day.

Concerning the month and year in which he happily departed from the world, the following contains very good information:

> Cloud-bearing February had now completed eight days of light,  
> when Stephen’s light-bearing spirit sought the stars,  
> in the year one thousand, one hundred, and twice ten,  
> with four added, having gained for himself the kingdom of heaven.

Although the history, now written and clear, elsewhere fully sets forth his words and deeds, we have not heard all that was done in his Life; if we attempted to unfold it all in writing, we should undoubtedly fall silent concerning the task already undertaken. It is therefore necessary, since it is not within our ability or purpose, that from this point we begin to read about that disciple, whose pious life and good manner of living greatly benefit our religious observance.

30. Therefore, after the passing of the most eminent and memorable man, the lord of Muret—concerning whose life and teaching, as has been said, great volumes are preserved among us—Lord Hugh, with God’s help, was directed to Plania, Peter of Limoges of blessed memory succeeding. There, living a glorious and in every respect praiseworthy life, he became renowned far and wide among those dwelling there through signs and miracles.

For his aim was utterly to despise earthly things and to burn with all the striving of his mind for heavenly things alone. He was filled with divine learning, distinguished in religious observance, strong in uprightness of character, and remarkable in the working of signs. He was a despiser of the world, a lover of God and neighbour, and one for whom “to live is Christ and to die is gain” (Phil. 1).

He devoted himself to constant prayers, frequent fasts, and uninterrupted works of goodness. All who came to him out of charity he kindled with desire for eternal life. He also always took care, according to his ability, to relieve the need of poor people, pilgrims, widows, and orphans whenever they asked anything of him. He especially showed due reverence to all religious persons and ministers of God, and fraternally relieved their need from his own resources.

If he happened to see a noble person in need, he assisted him in necessities, according to his means, modestly and generously. Moreover, he maintained the adornment of religious life with great kindness, both in word and example, as he had learned it from his master and lord, blessed Stephen. He reproved the transgressions and breaches of discipline of his fellow disciples away from the straight rule, and bore with them as was fitting and necessary in such cases. Above all, he taught that no one’s heart should “turn aside to words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins” (Ps. 140 [Vulgate numbering]).

Furthermore, for the edification of others—not, God forbid, from boastfulness—he used to say of himself:

“For I, miserable man that I am, cannot labour much, fast, keep vigils, or do other things of this kind. But, as it seems to me, by his free mercy I know and am able to love God.”

He also encouraged his fellow disciples and brethren to practise virtues and to take care, with all diligence, to guard themselves from every vice and sin.

31. The goodness of Christ had bestowed upon him such grace that he knew the consciences of the brethren living with him, revealed to them by what temptations they were assailed, and declared what each suffered from wicked and unclean thoughts. Whenever he recognized anyone’s faults, he never spared them rebuke.

And so that no one might be able to despise his preaching, the multitude of signs which he performed in Christ’s name confirmed it. For, as we have learned, by his sight alone he restored sight to those who did not see; to the crippled, uprightness; to those afflicted with falling sickness, health; and by his prayers even the many diseased limbs of sufferers were restored to soundness.

We have not learned all his signs and deeds. But the few we recount we have learned from the reports of four of his most devout and truthful fellow disciples, who lived with him at different times: namely, Lord Peter, our most reverend prior, who was received by him with worthy honour for instruction, and who, because of reverence for his simplicity and humility, was held in the place of highest veneration; Guy of Miliac, who succeeded him first, as was fitting, in the care of their cell, so well taught by knowledge of religious observance and reverence, as well as by the bond of earlier familiarity; Bernard Bocard, who for some time lived with him in the closest intimacy through mutual conversation about our observances and the sweetness of spiritual love, so that they had bound themselves by the bond of immeasurable love; and Hugh of Monte, toward whom he was most warmly affectionate because of the justice and fidelity which he found in him, and from whom, at the very moment of his departure, he received the saving kiss of the Lord’s peace.

Since the reputation for holiness of the aforesaid man had grown greatly, many sick persons were accustomed to flock to him from different provinces in hope of recovering health.

32. At that time, then, as our elders relate, a certain cripple named Haarnac was said to have lain ill. From the loins downward he had fallen into such weakness of the limbs that, crawling on his hands with his loins dislocated, he dragged his body along the ground and, as he crept, resembled some sort of monster. For a long time he remained confined by this infirmity; and, in hope of eternal reward, he received from the holy monks dwelling there divine alms for his daily needs, since he was able to perform no work either for himself or for another [Col. 1199C].

When he had remained in that place in such misery through many years, and all hope of bodily health had entirely been given up for him, one day, through divine mercy, it came into his mind that he should somehow have himself carried to the man of God, where he had already heard that, through the working of our Lord Jesus Christ, the frequent manifestations of his virtues were daily being displayed. Encouraged by faith, and compelled by the greater necessity of his body, he tearfully begged his parents without delay to carry out his purpose. When his parents heard this and saw that for a long time he had made no progress whatever, they carried him and laid him before the dwelling of the man of God, so that he might at least be fed by those arriving there, since he could not support himself by his own labour [Col. 1199D].

As that sick man lay for several days at the door of the servant of God, feeling his way about as circumstances allowed, he was brought before the man of God by those carrying him. Scabs and decay had covered all his limbs; he was pitiable in appearance and horrible to behold, so that the people thought him near death. When the man of God looked upon him, he said to those who had carried him: “What do you seek? What do you want us to do for him?” For he did not yet know what they were going to ask of him.

They replied: “But we, lord, have heard and believed that by your prayers you are able to assist persons afflicted by calamities such as these. Behold this man whom you see: he is greatly wearied by his miserable life. For he has neither the means nor the strength to work, by which his misery might be relieved [Col. 1200A]. Therefore help him and have pity on him.”

When he heard this, the man of God immediately ordered him to be carried into the church and commanded those present to withdraw for a little while. He at once resorted to the fitting place for his accustomed assistance and gave himself to prayer with deep groaning. Meanwhile the sick man, with his feet and loins as contracted as they were, threw himself face down upon the pavement like a log and began with tears to call upon the Lord’s name, asking that, if He would not aid him in this necessity, He would at least hereafter deliver him from the fires of Gehenna.

After he had prolonged his prayer in this manner for an hour, the bitterness of his illness suddenly departed, and he realized that he had received the health he desired. Immediately, standing upright upon his feet, he bore witness before those outside to the miracle of the man of God, saying: “See, see, see what the man of God has done this day, as I myself bear witness and prove it” [Col. 1200B].

They ran up at once, astonished and amazed, saying: “How is it, brother?” They asked how this had happened. But he said: “That man of God has delivered me from my present misery.” He then returned to the servant of God and related all that had taken place. On hearing it, those standing around raised a cry to heaven, magnifying God.

But the man of the Lord, fleeing temporal honour, silenced them with a stern prohibition, saying: “Be silent, be silent. But if anyone asks you how this has happened, answer only that the Lord Jesus Christ, who works everywhere through His friends, has Himself worked in you, through His beloved blessed Maximus, such a great miracle in this place [Col. 1200C]. Now arise, and go give thanks to your restorer with a light and a votive offering.”

He delayed no longer. Having recovered both the strengthening of food and bodily vigour, he began to outstrip others with his own steps—he who had been carried by others while lying helpless and sick. From that hour all the sinews and limbs of his body were so restored that thereafter no signs whatsoever of his former dislocation remained. Truly, according to my understanding, I judge this power not inferior to that by which the Apostle Peter once raised the lame Aeneas at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple. But above all let our God be praised, who grants such power to His beloved ones that He deigns to work such things through them. [Col. 1200D] Amen.

53. A barren tongue fails when it wishes to recount the many reported powers of so great a man. The son of a certain matron at Brantôme suffered grievously from a contracted head. He had incurred such distress from this illness that his head clung to his left shoulder, and he could not see the sky unless he lay on his back. One night, as he lay exhausted by this same illness, it seemed to him that, if he were present with the servant of God, he would immediately recover his health.

When morning came and light was restored to the world, he did not shrink back in fear; rather, taking courage from his affliction, he rejoiced and said to his parents: “I seek the one who can heal my infirmity by touching me—the one who healed that cripple by prayer” [Col. 1201A].

His parents, understanding this to be a mystery of God, carried him as quickly as possible to the dwelling of the man of God. When the man of the Lord had him brought before him, he asked what he sought. Then, weeping and wailing in the voice he could manage, the young man began to beg him to deign to pray to the Lord for him and not allow him to return sick after he had devoutly sought his aid.

The man of the Lord, whose countenance was most kindly, said in a tearful voice: “Son and friend, what you ask of us is not ours to grant.”

But those who had come with him began to ask that he at least lay his hand upon him. Meanwhile the sick man, grievously afflicting himself with great weeping, gave continual expression to his pain in groans of lamentation. When he had done this for a long time and did not cease weeping in any way [Col. 1201B], the man of the Lord was moved in heart and had compassion on his suffering. Coming near, he took him by the hair, invoked the Lord’s name, and separated his head from his shoulder.
