Immediately he said that he wished to vomit. When he had been moved away, he raised his eyes and hands to heaven, and a stream of blood and corruption burst from his mouth. Spitting upon the ground, he began to groan heavily and to spit up, with blood, certain humours—what they were, I do not know—so that it seemed as though his throat were being cut by some instrument. A wasting discharge like bloody threads also hung from his mouth.

Then, with the bonds of his tongue and throat broken, he again lifted and raised his eyes and hands to heaven. Though his mouth was still bloody, he burst forth in this first clear utterance; for formerly he had been accustomed to produce speech that was empty and scarcely intelligible [Col. 1201C]: “I render you great thanks, Lord Hugh, good restorer, because you have been willing to help me in such misery.”

All who were present marveled and were amazed at such a miracle, and asked whether he had been able to speak. The man who had been healed spoke before them. The man of the Lord bore this calmly; keeping the sick man with lamps, he sent him away restored to health and refreshed with necessities, directing him to give thanks to God for the power and reverence of that neighbouring place.

Having returned home, he constantly proclaimed in many words the benefit he had received, judging with assured conviction that it had been done through the aid of God’s servant, who in his mercy, while living, extended many benefits to the neighbouring people.

[Col. 1201D] 34. But who could ever investigate and know how many powers were wrought through the servant of God? Still, we have thought that one memorable miracle, confirmed by the faithful, should not be passed over in silence. In a neighbouring castle—named Segur, though ancient usage had called it *Securum*—a certain young man, with a swollen throat and face, was afflicted day and night for a long time by unceasing pains.

His parents, deeply grieved and excessively distressed by the suffering of their child, had repeatedly sent their servants to pray at the holy places of the saints in the surrounding region, so that he might be healed. But those friends of God to whom he had been sent did not grant him a remedy for his illness, so that the miracles might proclaim to neighbouring peoples how great was the grace of power in the servant of God [Col. 1202A].

He was so near death that, with almost all use of food refused, matters had reached the point where, all hope of his present life being lost, his parents thought only of the requirements for his burial. While they lamented publicly, someone came and said: “For the affliction from which your son suffers, by the King of the Franks, if God wills, medicine is given to the sick. Therefore take him there; if he believes, he may find a remedy.”

Then, rejoicing with unexpected exultation, his parents came as quickly as they could to the man of God, to learn how what they had heard might benefit them and how they might approach the king. When the man of the Lord heard this, he ordered the sick man to come nearer. Stretching out his hand, he touched his throat in prayer and made upon his face the sign of the saving cross [Col. 1202B].

Meanwhile the sick man, opening his mouth and moving his lips a little, tried with moaning to implore the aid of his patron. Immediately, amid his groaning and suffering, as the patron laboured, the swelling of his throat and face began to lessen. At length, after returning home, within a short time he received in full the health he had desired. When his parents saw what had happened, they feared and glorified God, “who gave such authority to men” (Matthew 9). Amen.

35. Nor should this be left unmentioned: how the straw footstool of the man of God gave healing from a fistula to one near death. The son of a certain smith, in a neighbouring estate, had long suffered grievously from the affliction of a fistula [Col. 1202C]. His condition had indeed become so dangerous that physicians debated whether he could survive unless he were cut as swiftly as possible by their dreaded hand.

As the illness worsened, the evil fistula had nearly deprived him, through pain, of all sensation; he had been reduced to such a state that he could understand or do absolutely nothing. What wonder? He could not stand; he was never able to rise in his bed or even sit up; he could not move his foot or turn himself to the other side. His parents, loving him too carnally and without sound judgment, as is the custom among rustics, were deceived into bringing him daily charms and potions from diviners, soothsayers, and magical bindings.

But as these did no good, and no one could discover at all what the illness was, nothing improved; rather, it grew worse daily. Then in a nocturnal vision it seemed to him that, if he could obtain some straw from the footstool of the man of God and bind it upon himself, he would recover the healing immediately necessary [Col. 1202D].

When daylight came, he awoke from sleep with this faith, all fear removed. Compelled by pain, he promptly sought the aid of the oft-mentioned man and disclosed his vision to his mother, adding and affirming that he would be sick no longer if the pledge he sought—namely, the man of God’s straw—were brought to him.

When his mother heard him, she immediately arose and came to the dwelling of the man of God. There, as best she could, she sought help for her child with great weeping and groaning, with a sincere heart and great love for her son. Then, discreetly taking away what she wanted from the straw, she entered and placed what she had brought upon her son. To her intense amazement, as soon as it touched the sick man’s knee, the wound lost all power to cause pain. Every illness departed; the discharge flowing from his body dried up; new skin grew over it; and he was entirely restored to his former health [Col. 1203A], so that in the same hour he rose from his bed as though he had never suffered bodily injury anywhere.

His parents, astonished, marveled that he had so swiftly obtained a remedy through divine mercy and asked what this meant. He said: “I understand that I am very well, and I shall do whatever you command.” He then began to render them such service as he had been accustomed to provide before his affliction.

Then, rejoicing together and weeping for [Col. 1203B] joy, they gave thanks to the Almighty both for themselves and for him: through the help of God’s servant, He had made him sound in body and them glad concerning their child. He lived for many years afterward and continually proclaimed thanks to God because He had through His servant restored him to soundness.

See, see what the servant of God, while dwelling in the flesh, bestowed upon the faithful: those who sought his help were saved through him; those who brought pledges in fulfillment of vows were delivered by the aid that followed. Thus the man who believed that he would be healed by the straw footstool of the man of God was readier in faith than the woman suffering from the flow of blood who, in order to be healed, touched the hem of the Saviour’s garment (Matthew 9). But vigorous faith accomplishes all these things, as the Lord says: “Your faith has made you well” (Mark 10) [Col. 1203C]. Amen.

36. It would be fitting not merely to write, but even to recount, how many trials and distresses he removed from those living with him; in how many necessities he stood by them with his kindness; and how many troubles he restrained in them through his power. Yet, since an appropriate occasion presents itself, this should by no means be kept silent among the man’s virtues which now comes to mind.

Lord Bernard also, a venerable shepherd by God’s grace, experienced without doubt, while still under discipline, how great was the power of the man of God in his own need. For several days, through I know not what accident or neglect, he was consumed by a severe pain in one foot, finding rest neither by day nor by night. Yet amid the complaints of his torture, he chiefly lamented this one thing: that he could not fulfill his turn in the church office [Col. 1203D].

One day, when the servant of God saw him continually oppressed by pain, he said: “Do you not know why this is happening to you?”

He replied: “I do not know at all, my lord, whence this has come.”

He immediately revealed what he was suffering. Then the man of the Lord approached him with a cheerful, smiling face and, bringing the customary weapons of the cross, reverently made the sign upon the painful place as he touched it.

He then said: “We read in the divine page that there was a man of venerable life and yet more venerable merit whose body showed no sound part from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. A discharge of fluid and pus flowed constantly from his body [Col. 1204A]. Sick persons who wished to be healed were sprinkled from it and became well, so that there was no doubt that whoever deserved devoutly to touch or be sprinkled by it would thereby escape illness. Yet this man also repeatedly sought a remedy in this matter from almighty God, but did not deserve to be heard. From this we gather that God so wishes to preserve miracles in him and openly to declare to the afflicted, by a sign, how great his merit was.”

When he had finished these words, all pain utterly fled, and he restored Bernard to health. Restored by the power of the aforesaid servant of God, Bernard from that hour began to be most intimate with him, and remains well to this day as a testimony to the glory of the blessed man. Amen.

37. What, then, shall we say of epileptics, for whom a remedy was found as swiftly as it was faithfully sought from him? But because it would take too long to recount how many miracles he performed for them, let us relate one memorable miracle among many.

Two men—one living at Bre, the other at Rancum Balista—experienced in themselves that which had become widely known among many concerning the aforesaid servant of God [Col. 1204B]. We learned that for many years they had suffered from that affliction, so that, when they were seized by it, they could scarcely be held by several people. Indeed, through the attack and through vomiting the excesses of their bodies, they had lost both the strength of food and bodily vigour.

[Col. 1204C] Faith suggested to each of them that they ought to visit the dwelling of the venerable man. They were so moved by desire that they thought life itself intolerable if they delayed setting out to him. Without delay, although only partly recovered, they undertook their journey, coming with still slow effort to the footsteps of the servant of God. Seeking to test what they had heard about him, they begged with great weeping that he would grant them his grace.

When the servant of God asked what they wanted from him, they replied: “We can no longer remain in this life with that affliction.”

He said to them: “What is this that you are saying, brothers? God alone can do this for you.”

But they, lamenting their misfortune more and more, said to him: “We adjure you by almighty God and by the Day of Judgment, feared by all the guilty, to consent to what we ask [Col. 1204D]: before we depart, lay upon us in prayer the sign of the saving cross.”

Wearied by the importunity of their request, he prayed, tearfully made the sign of the cross for which they asked, and ordered them to depart. Having returned home, from that day and throughout the rest of their lives they remained free and untouched by that suffering, as if they had never endured it in their bodies. They thereafter lived a very happy life and gave thanks to the Lord among their neighbours because, through the merit of His servant, He had deigned to deliver them from so perilous an affliction, bearing before the people testimony to a miracle no less than to a benefit.

These things are marvelous and greatly astonishing in our days; but the life of the aforesaid man is reported to have been such that those who knew his manner of life ought not to wonder at his power [Col. 1205A]. We have undertaken to relate this one miracle concerning two men together because we learned that it had the same outcome and the same manner in both. Amen.

38. These things which we have learned concerning the servant of God, and which have remained hidden from us until now, are indeed greatly to be admired. For the true assessment of his life lay not only in the display of signs but in the power of his deeds.

The neighbouring cellarer and household brethren, whom the man of the Lord brightened by his visits, had made it their custom to gather there for various reasons whenever they knew that he was present. One day, while the man of the Lord was taking refreshment in the cell commonly called Chatenet with the other brothers, a man full of faith came to him from the nearby place named Solemniac. He was grievously afflicted by a headache, finding no rest day or night. By chance, at that same hour, the servant of God was sitting, as usual, in the portico and serving the people outside with words of edification [Col. 1205B].

The visitor, unwilling wholly to reveal his illness to everyone, could not find a way or place to approach him because of the crowd standing about and the confusion. Greatly anxious, he waited throughout the day. But when the crowd had dispersed toward evening, the servant of God remained alone with him in the portico. One of the visitor’s friends, who had seen him anxiously moving here and there all day [Col. 1205C], pointed out to him that he should approach the servant of God; for he had heard that the man had long been troubled by headache.

On hearing this, the sufferer immediately wept copiously and threw himself weeping upon the ground before him. In fear and groaning he wept violently, striking his head against the ground for a long time and showing himself a miserable groaning man. Then he suddenly stated what he sought: “My lord, I suffer such disturbance in my head that I scarcely know what I should say or do. Therefore I have come down to you, that you might offer me some counsel, insofar as you can, concerning this. For I know that you have done and can do far greater things. Therefore, insofar as you are able, have mercy upon me, lord!”

When the brothers standing around heard him, moved by his tears, they began to weep and earnestly begged the servant of God for him [Col. 1205D]. The man of the Lord answered: “My head hurts too.” He immediately raised his right hand to his own head and, after touching it, passed the same hand over the head of the sufferer with the sign of the cross.

As he touched the other’s head for some time, that affliction began in a wonderful manner to fade away of itself, as though its very withdrawal showed that it could no longer find a place in him. When this had been done, the man was dismissed by the servant of God to return home, restored from that hour with all speed to his former health. The brothers who were then present—and, as we believe, still survive—freely attest the truth of this miracle. We shall now add what and how great a miracle he was able to obtain by prayer in that same cell for another man. Amen.

[Col. 1206A] 39. At another time, we learned from the report of many that another man from the aforesaid place hastened to the servant of God in the same cell. Daily he was seized by a sharp torment with evil “pulses,” which rustic speech calls *ira dolens* (“painful wrath”), and by various torments so severe that his soul seemed about to be wrested from his body unless it were held back for an hour by divine mercy.

When he came to the man of God, he set out in order the whole course of his illness, humbly commending himself to his prayers. Having received permission to return, he began to improve on the road itself. He who had scarcely reached the man of God by several stages under the savage onset of his affliction returned home rejoicing, comforted by him and without any other restorative. From that hour he was restored for so long to the health he desired that he was sounder than he had been before that affliction [Col. 1206B]. Amen.

40. A certain householder in the village called Tiverius, near the cell of Planiac, had been deprived of the use of one eye and had long suffered severely; almost every aid of physicians had already failed him. Since he could find no remedy anywhere, yet prompted by faith, he hastened to the dwelling of the man of God.

When he stood before the servant of God, the pain in his badly seeing eye began violently to distress him. No longer with loud cries but with shrieks, he exclaimed: “Ah! Ah! Ah! my lord, I am about to die unless you immediately help me too, as I perish, with counsel and prayer” [Col. 1206C].

Addressing him in gentle speech, the man of God first sought to restrain the cries of the man in danger. Then he said: “But almighty God, who in His mercy heals all the infirmities of all people, can certainly heal yours too, if He wills.”

Having said this, the man of the Lord at once approached him and, stretching out his hand, devoutly made the sign of the cross upon his painful eye, then dismissed him to go home. Before he had left the enclosure of that place, he deserved to receive again, wholly and completely, the light he had greatly desired. With the eye from which he had long suffered—and by whose sole guidance he had earlier come—he himself chose the wider path without saying anything and was entirely certain about everything else.

[Col. 1206D] 41. Another man in the aforesaid village, having fallen into a similar affliction through some misfortune unknown to me, had for a long time suffered very grievously the loss of one eye, all hope of recovery abandoned. When he heard that the householder had recovered his sight, he hurried to him and asked how he could see. The first man immediately related the whole event in order.

The sick man said: “Would that the man of God might deign to reveal himself in such power that he would drive the affliction from my eye just as he drove the long discomfort of darkness from yours. Therefore, friend, you must go down with me.”

Then the man who had been made well went to the dwelling of the man of God, led the sick man with him, and devoutly begged the servant of God himself to help the wretched man. The man of the Lord immediately said to him: “What can we do in this matter, brother?”

The sick man replied: “Ah, ah, ah, lord! Only look upon the eye from which I suffer so greatly; I believe that this alone may suffice for me.”

“It will by no means fail,” he said, “that almighty God will do you good.”

The servant of God then left his portico and, beneath the open sky, carefully examined the painful eye. Having made upon it the sign of the cross, he immediately restored light, and the night of blindness departed from him. They at once returned home and began to praise and bless God, who saves those who hope in Him [Col. 1207A]. Amen.

42. Nor should it be left unmentioned what happened to a certain blind woman when she sought the help of the aforesaid man of God. A beggar woman [Col. 1207B] from a place quite nearby, deprived of the light of her eyes and unable to keep to the road unless another led her, was very devout and full of faith. With the other needy persons she used daily to come to his dwelling for alms. He used to give her some sustenance for the sake of eternal reward, in consideration of what she distributed to other poor people; and she often begged alms from others and distributed them thence to the other needy.

For she was not merely blind but was also deprived of the natural strength of one part of her body. Every day she ran to the dwelling of the aforesaid man in order to beg. One day, while on her way, she disclosed her thought to her guide: “If ever I deserve to speak alone with that blessed man, I believe that I shall immediately recover my health. For I trust [Col. 1207C] that he can restore light to my eyes, since he has been able to give guidance to the eyes of those sick men.”

After some time, she stood alone before him, begging and asking him only to stretch his hand over her face. The man of the Lord then closed her eyes and made the sign of the cross, saying: “Jesus Christ our Lord and Master, who applied clay to the eyes of the man born blind and restored light to him, He who is God, He who is almighty, can illumine you by the brightness of His power.”

He had not yet finished the words; the speech still hung upon his lips. While she prayed, her eyes suddenly opened, so that she clearly saw everything. Immediately she fell to the ground, weeping and groaning, praising and blessing God. When he asked what had happened to her, she answered: “Thanks be to God: according to your word, healing is present to me” [Col. 1207D].

The man of the Lord, wishing to test this, said: “Tell me, then, whom you now see before you.”

She replied: “Your face is grave and honourable, your beard snowy and long.”

He said: “You learned from another that you are now speaking with me.”

Holding a reed in his hand, he asked her what it was. “It is a rush,” she replied. Then he lifted his hand to his ear, and she immediately answered what he was doing. The man of the Lord, understanding that this was a divine mystery, took care to send her as quickly as possible to give thanks to blessed Maximus, as he did others.

Then he strictly commanded her: “Now be silent, but wait for me here a little.” Yet when he went inside, she did not wait for him at all [Col. 1208A]. As quickly as she could, she joyfully went outside and called for her boy. Exulting and weeping with joy, she no longer sought a guide for her way. Thus she was healed: she who had come blind, led by another, returned destined to be a guide for the blind. She lived many years afterward, continually giving thanks privately and publicly to almighty God because through His servant He had restored her to soundness.

This miracle was proclaimed by a faithful recluse; the people too proclaimed it, marveling at the woman’s faith and magnifying the glory of the good father of the household.

43. We must by no means remain silent, for the greater publication of the blessed man’s glory, about how sad and terrible divine vengeance came upon a certain judge when he swore falsely in the portico [Col. 1208B].

There is a neighbouring estate named Syncelly, where a certain familiar of the servant of God used to live. His judge, for unjust causes and pretexts, oppressed him by legal proceedings beyond the annual due, in order to seize his property; and he harshly harassed him without any order of equity. One day, filled with great fury, the judge is said to have told him among other things: “Whether justly or unjustly, while I am steward, you shall not remain in peace.”

Since the landholder could not escape his hands in any way, he took counsel and appeased the enraged man with gifts, compelling him to establish peace with him. At length the judge, bound by the favour he had received, promised, so that the frightened man would not distrust him, to strike the peace sought with his own hand in the hand of the man of God [Col. 1208C].

As they stood before him, the judge placed his hand in that holy hand, as he had said, declaring: “In this holy place, in the presence of my lord, I promise you in full faith, friend, that henceforward I will demand from you no more than I ought.”

But after not many days, that judge, as though forgetful of his pledge, brought an unjust claim concerning the inheritance of the man whom he had released from every injustice. Distressed by this, the landholder reluctantly gave him some of his own goods to secure peace. The judgment upon his perjury was immediately present: he swiftly became master of goods not owed to him, and his hand at once became weak and infirm [Col. 1208D].

Like Gehazi (4 Kings 5), he possessed money gained through violence, acquiring not only the leprosy of his soul but also never again having his own hand sound. Hear this, all who hold power: clothe yourselves in such a way that you do not despoil others; gather to your treasures only that by which you do not bring poverty upon your neighbours. Amen.

44. We judge it worthy of record that swift and profoundly divine judgment came upon one who, in arrogance, did not fear to wrong the servants of that same man. From the benefits and alms which the man of the Lord received from the people, filled with the grace of charity, he took care, like a father, to relieve as much as he could the need of our community. But especially toward his mother, as one weaned from her, he kept watch with more diligent and provident care than he did toward his daughters [Col. 1209A]. For he knew that great expense and excessive labour were required to support her there.

It happened one day that the man of the Lord, in his customary compassion, sent by his messengers many aids for this wretched life from the offerings of the devout to the shepherd at Grandmont and to the brothers. On the following day those who had been sent began to return to the dwelling of the man of God. As they were travelling a fairly long road and were wearied by the remoteness of their lodging, they found on their journey a meadow and a stream while riding.

One of them said: “What a pleasant place! Here is water and meadow; here we can refresh ourselves and rest for a little while, so that afterward we may complete our journey safely.”

All of them therefore turned aside together to that place [Col. 1209B]. As the place pleased their eyes, they immediately dismounted from their beasts, loosening their mouths from the bits and allowing them to graze. While they remained there, the owner of the place suddenly arrived, carrying an iron-tipped stake upon his shoulder. Furiously entering the meadow, he began to run here and there, striking the men severely and ragingly pursuing their animals.

The servants, terrified and taking flight, had their beasts leap across the open ground and run away, their halters torn apart. Greatly distressed, the servants gathered them as best they could beyond the boundary of the place, then came to the blessed man and reported that they had suffered this outrage most unjustly.

After the man had unjustly exhausted his rage, he was suddenly seized by madness, so that he could scarcely be restrained by several people [Col. 1209C]. He trembled, and meanwhile seemed entirely senseless, his face transformed and his eyes discoloured. Neighbours and relatives ran together from every direction, having heard that the disturbance had not been slight; finding those men unharmed, they asked what had happened.

“The man,” they said, “assailed the boys of the blessed man both by hand and tongue; therefore immediate vengeance is scourging him.”

His relatives then took counsel. Openly acknowledging the fault of his pride, they brought him bound to the servant of God in order to obtain a remedy for his health, devoutly entreating him on the man’s behalf. When the servant of God heard their words and understood what the wretched man had done, he immediately ordered him released from his bonds.

See a new miracle, unheard of in our own times: in that very hour he appeared so healthy and sound as though the enemy of human salvation had never possessed power over him [Col. 1209D]. Recognizing his guilt, he fell at the servant’s feet and began more and more to lament and be ashamed of his fault.

The man of the Lord immediately raised him from the ground and rebuked him for his deeds in these words: “Go, take heed, and never presume to do such a thing again. For God is a swift avenger of His servants. Do not make earth more precious than heaven: there one must live; here one must also come to an end.”

He departed healed, praising and blessing God. When countless people heard of this astonishing miracle, they raised mighty cries to heaven, saying: “Glory to You, Lord.” [Col. 1210A] Amen.

45. Not far from the dwelling of the man of God there was a village named [lacuna], in which the son of a certain knight lay grievously ill. He suffered so greatly that he barely breathed; his skin had become slack, and his bones could almost be seen. When his father, the knight, saw him pressed by extremity, he said to his servants: “That man of God, whom we believe to shine with many powers, as though set close beside our ear—whose merit with God has hitherto proved reliable on behalf of others—I must now test as faithful on behalf of my little son. Therefore let us all go with the boy to his dwelling, carrying assured faith in our hearts. For if he cannot obtain healing there, I shall henceforth believe that my son can be healed nowhere.” Immediately his faithful servants carried the child from the house in their own arms to the aforesaid servant of God; there, pouring out many tears and grievously afflicting themselves, they begged the holy man’s aid for the sick boy. When they had presented him to him as was customary, he immediately ordered the cloths in which he was wrapped to be removed, and then made the sign of the cross upon his bare flesh. The boy returned home restored from that illness, and, as a testimony to this saint’s miracle, remains safe and sound in this life to this day. Amen.

46. From a place near blessed Aredius, behold, there follows another account of a similar kind. The little son of a man of considerable means, who had not yet reached his fifth year, had long languished there, weak and wholly deprived of every power of movement. His father entirely did not know what to do for him, since he had already abandoned all hope of his recovery. And what wonder? For whether he was laid in his cradle or elsewhere, his people found him motionless where they had put him. If by chance you bent his foot or extended his hand, you would undoubtedly find them remaining thus, so that you might think that all his bones lay beneath the skin shattered into tiny pieces. But when the signs of the man of God had been proclaimed and reports of his powers gathered, he was brought by his parents to the man of God and presented to him as usual. They humbly begged him on behalf of their pledge, declaring also that no remedy remained for him.

[Col. 1210D] The man of God said to them: “Why do you groan and weep?” Then, when the wrappings had been removed, they told him how severely the boy had languished, begging him, for the love of God, merely to lay his hand upon the child’s bare flesh. Hearing this, the man of God put forth the right hand they sought, passed it in touch from the crown of his head over each limb down to his feet, and, taking a reed, began playfully to draw it back and forth over the boy’s belly. Then, extending it to him, he said to the sick child: “Take it, take it—eh! eh!” And he who had almost been dead, as though awakened from sleep, immediately raised his hand at the man of God’s voice, however faint it was, and took and held the reed extended to him. Those who had assembled, seeing the miracle, began to weep for joy.

[Col. 1211A] When this was done, the man of God had the boy wrapped up and ordered them all to return home with him. His parents immediately rose, lifted the child from the place where he lay, and went to their house, magnifying and praising God. They said: “For truly we have seen wondrous things today.” The boy, recovering from his sickness, grew and flourished, and thereafter lived for a long time, healthy and happy. We should reflect that, because of the great faith of the parents, they deserved to receive the complete restoration of their son. Hence we are given to understand that perfect faith can obtain everything which it perfectly desires, as the Lord says: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9). Amen.

[Col. 1211B] 47. Having thus recounted certain deeds performed through the blessed man for others, let us undertake to relate one memorable and precious miracle among many, in which divine grace worked at his word both for himself and for another man. At the same time, the servant of God and his porter were each suffering severely from violent fevers in his own cell. One day, when the man of God began to be feverish and greatly distressed, he went to his bed so that he might bear the pain somewhat more easily—a bed quite suited to such an illness. He was besieged by continual pain and burning heat, intolerable thirst, and extreme agony in his head.

While he lay sick and feverish there, a noise was heard at the gate. When he learned of it, the porter came to him as best he could, saying: “Up, up! Rise quickly—quickly, quickly, rise! Lord Geoffrey, Archbishop of Bordeaux, is here, desiring to see your face and to speak with you.”

> [Note: [Col. 1211] Letters addressed to him by St Bernard and Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, survive. He began to preside over the Church of Bordeaux in 1136.]

The porter reached him only slowly, for his limbs too had by then almost been consumed by the same affliction. Hearing this, the holy man smiled with disdain and said: “Truly wretched and very weak is the person who allows himself to be wearied by disturbances so empty and trifling. Brother,” he said, “I approve and desire that from now on we be no longer burdened by them.”

O wonderful and venerable thing! His word was immediately followed by the deed. In that same hour the man of God went out healed. The other man, who had been about to suffer severely from fevers nearby, likewise thereafter remained unharmed and secure. From this, dearest brethren, we are given to understand that charity knows how to possess nothing in distress. For he wished both himself and his neighbour to prosper for God’s sake, since otherwise the fullness of the law would not be present; for whoever loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law. Amen.

48. But what should we recount concerning other sufferers from chills and other sick persons, for whom healing was found as swiftly as it was faithfully sought? There would be much to say about each one separately; but because we hasten to other matters, we judged it better to be silent about them.

[Col. 1212A] For if all that individual persons receive secretly while asking in faith, and that the conscience of many keeps hidden, were publicly disclosed, we think that all the days of our lives would scarcely suffice to write it down. Yet among the other signs and benefits which the man of God bestowed upon those near him, the inhabitants and neighbours of that land were accustomed especially to recount one. As we have heard from our elders, hail had formerly been accustomed to ravage all the fields of that region. It fell so heavily that, when it came, it left nothing there. But after that day, when the man of God first set foot in that place, no storm ever fell there while he remained in the flesh. It came, indeed, as it had formerly been accustomed to come, [Col. 1212B] but passed by as though fearful and ashamed. Amen.

49. Moreover, why do we labour at his praise and glory, when we cannot accomplish it? He himself is his praise and glory, whose praise never departed from his mouth. It was surely fitting to divine condescension that he whose spirit was made wondrous in heaven should likewise be made wondrous on earth in his body by such signs. Such great marks of merit are believed of him that they not only cannot be fully explained in speech, but cannot even be comprehended by human subtlety.

Yet, since our discourse seeks the particular conclusion which we proposed to carry through concerning his life, before our little pages receive their end, we shall set out to narrate one more outstanding vision, which he himself, caught in ecstasy but with both the man’s eyes open, carefully beheld. The venerable brother Guy of Miliac was a most intimate companion of this aforesaid servant of God. At his admonition he received the habit of the same holy religious order, and was also excellently instructed and formed by him. Later, by the merit of his life and the greatness of his character, he obtained before others, as it is said, a special prerogative of intimacy with him. From his account we too learned what we now narrate, since the man of God often used to delight him with the secret of his heart and the familiar use of his speech.

At one time they both came together to Grandmont in order to visit our pastor. On the following day, after receiving the blessing, as they began to return at first light, they turned aside in haste to Muret in order to hear the solemnities of Mass and see the brethren. It was the feast-day of the dedication of the church of Muret. The brethren fittingly received the arriving visitors with kind and cheerful countenances, rejoicing greatly; and when Prime had been completed, the first priest devoutly and solemnly began the Introit of the Mass, as the reverence and order of so great a mystery required.

[Col. 1213A] It was the constant custom of this ever-memorable man to direct his eyes toward the altar at such an hour more intently and watchfully than at any other. For he had heard it written: “Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matthew 6); and: “Where the eye is directed, there the mind is fixed.” While the man of God was attending closely to this, he suddenly saw among the others one man in a deacon’s vestment and a white stole, busily engaged in the frequent ministrations. Moreover, his crown, temples, and beard had been shaved. He began to wonder greatly who he was, and was uncertain, for he knew that there were only two clerics present.

The man of God did not wait long, but immediately approached Brother Guy—through whom he wished to be made certain of this doubt—once, twice, and three times at different moments, and anxiously asked him how many clerics were present. Guy answered him each time in the same terms: “Lord, as I see, only two are present.” But we believe that he was not of equal merit, since, though asked so often, he did not deserve to see this.

[Col. 1213B] Certain of the matter, when the lesson from the book of Revelation had been read, he went at once rejoicing to the choir of clerics, where he remained standing for a long time until the divine mystery had been solemnly celebrated. When the hour had come to read the Gospel, behold, that deacon came with the priest to the lectern in order to proclaim it. He distinctly began it according to Luke and clearly pronounced it through to the end. From his voice and appearance the man of God drew an invincible proof: he firmly believed, from the true signs, that the man of whom he had so long been doubtful was Lord Stephen of Muret. For he had been accustomed to see him thus during his lifetime.

When the service had been performed in the customary manner, the venerable Father vanished from the eyes of the disciple who beheld him. On leaving the church, he immediately summoned the brethren, ordered the animals on which they rode to be brought, and began most urgently to hasten his companion so that they might depart. The brethren of the place said to him: “Father and brother—indeed, lord—this cannot be done, because you came in to us today and wish to leave today.” He replied: “Brothers and lords, it must be done thus.”

When the animals were ready, the brethren of that place took Guy aside and said: “We know most certainly that today the Lord has deigned to reveal some secret to him in [Col. 1213D] our house; and since this is not now the place for a longer conversation, come, brother: go on with great care.” He said to them: “I too am at this very moment considering the things you say.” They at once took leave of the brethren and set out on the road they desired. As they hurried along together, they began by turns to satisfy themselves on the way with accounts concerning God.

Finally, as intimate charity affords immense confidence among the hearts of all friends, Brother Guy did not forget and began to question the servant of God in this manner about what he had seen in the church: “Thanks be to God, and to your holy kindness, Father and lord, because you have always wished me—so unworthy, so unlearned—to be present at your great concerns, private as well as public. Yet, lord, there is one matter which I turn over within myself in great uncertainty, and which, dearest father, if it is fitting, I ask to learn from you. For I hold and firmly believe that today you saw some sign which, because of our sins hindering us, it was not granted us from above to see. I infer this because the brethren, greatly astonished, saw you remain in the church in an unusual manner.”

Then he, being a most eloquent man and unwilling to disclose publicly what he held within, quickly persuaded his questioning companion to be silent concerning what he sought, saying: “Indeed, it is not expedient for me to tell it, nor would hearing it greatly profit you.” “Can you, lord,” he said, “hide from me what I desire to know from you by asking?”

[Col. 1214B] Since Guy demanded this so insistently with a multitude of prayers and continual questioning, and in no way consented to cease, the man of God, at last constrained by his friend’s loving entreaties, answered that he would no longer conceal it. He said: “I shall tell you what you ask on this condition: that while I live, I never hear you speak of it again anywhere.” For he feared that he might be carried away by vain glory, and become inwardly blameworthy precisely for that whereby he might appear outwardly wonderful to people—following also the example of the Lord, who commanded his disciples concerning himself that they should tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead (Matthew 17). After Guy promised and gave his assurance, the man of God related the whole event in order, just as it had occurred.

There are also many other things worthy of remembrance which the grace of Christ is known to have worked through him. If they were committed to writing, unbelievers would judge them apocryphal. But having spoken thus far of his life, conduct, and manner of living, let us turn pen and hand alike to tell how he attained from this world the prize of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

50. Therefore, in the year 1157 from the Passion of the Lord, Brother Hugh of blessed memory, a good and true hermit, full of virtues and holiness, bestowing, as has been said, many benefits upon the sick and needy, departed in peace from this wicked world at Plagne, a place especially notable in his manner of life, when God called him.

[Col. 1214D] To that blessed and venerable man a long span of life had truly been divinely granted for the benefit of our religious order and its enlargement. For, as we have it in writing, he lived eighty-six years. Above all, it should be noted that, among the many marks of grace by which that man of God shone in his life, he was conspicuous to no small degree for the gift of sound and steadfast memory. Whatever is found faithfully written, or entrusted to human memory, whether from the sayings of our Father or from the other precepts of our way of life, is believed to have been revealed and made known wholly through him, just as he heard it from Lord Stephen, our master, and received it by heart.

[Col. 1215A] He devoted such attention also to hearing the divine Scriptures that he heard nothing spoken to the brethren which he did not retain, for he had memory in place of books. But to conclude all in brief: as with the other matters already said of him, though we have not been able to say everything, in those days no one anywhere was found his equal. Neighbours and those from farther away alike, rich as well as poor, came to see and hear him, and, seeing him, called him a “servant of God” (*Deicola*), a name bestowed upon him. Some loved him as a son and brother; they venerated him as a father. For he desired to show himself such to all, and to be worthy in God’s sight, humble in heart and wholly submissive to His will.

But since in saying this we have wandered a little from our purpose, let us now, free from these matters, gladly return to the order of the narrative.

51. At the time when the man beloved by God and human beings was about to depart from this present world, it pleased divine providence that certain of our elders, very devout men, should come together from different places on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, a Thursday, in order to visit and hear him, and to question him concerning what was useful for them. The man of God received them, as was his custom, with a kind and cheerful countenance, and was exceedingly glad and joyful at the sight of them. He spent that whole day with the brethren most pleasantly and happily; for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9).

[Col. 1215C] On the following day, however, around noon he was seized by a severe sickness, and immediately the harp of them all was turned to bitter mourning. Yet God, who hears the poor, did not wish the brethren living in neighbouring cells to be deprived of his funeral rites, since they had made use of the necessary benefits he provided while strong and well. Thus many gathered, by God’s will, in order that they might devoutly commend their own souls to that most holy soul departing from this world; meanwhile he might endure his sickness much more lightly through their visitation and fellowship, and they in turn might thereafter remain happier and better through his presence and instruction.

For ten days he continued sound in mind, with sight and hearing unimpaired. Nor was it without reason that he remained sick until the third day before the Kalends of May, that is, the twenty-seventh day of April. We believe that all this took place so that he might instruct the brethren, in a deeply symbolic sense, concerning the Decalogue of the Law; and so that, if through forgetfulness they had failed in any point of it, they and he might at least then be permitted, at his admonition, to correct it.

[Col. 1215D] Moreover, lest his preaching should be interrupted in any way, throughout all the days of his illness, lying in bed, he preached and heard the word of God continually and vigorously until his last day, except only at the hours he devoted to prayer. For he prayed often then, and wept abundantly and continuously because of his own experience. Amid those exhortatory words, he admonished and urged them to bear and support the brethren who were sick, weak, or less learned—not so that they might have a defence, but so that they might feel mercy toward one another. This he himself, while he still survived, taught lovingly and practised thereafter above all else that he had long before laid down concerning obedience and our rule.

[Col. 1216A] Now, however, with more abundant grace and more powerful speech, he recalled these things to the brethren present and asked them to observe them faithfully. The total number of brethren was fixed: namely, twice five priests and also eight lay brothers. Among them was one brother who, greatly trusting in Hugh’s goodness, secretly sought from his heart to be blessed by him, unknown to anyone. While he was thinking this, God, the searcher of hearts, who alone knows what the spirit desires, caused His friend alone to burst forth in these words in fulfilment of his desire: “Let Brother Guy of Champagne be blessed, and truly let him be blessed; and may God bless him!” Afterwards the brother recounted to the brethren in order all that he had silently sought. From this and other things of the kind it became plain to everyone that the servant of God possessed the spirit of prophecy, for even the words of thought sounded in his ears.

Those who had assembled then questioned him, saying: “Lord, what do you fear? What do you judge can do most harm to our religious order?” He replied: “New woods and novice brethren, above all things, I fear and judge can do most harm.”

For such was his purpose, both in health and sickness, that he always sought the things of Jesus Christ and remembered Him alone and no other; wholly forgetting, according to the Apostle, the things behind and stretching forward to what lay before him (Philippians 3). He did this especially for God: so that, with the bonds of the flesh broken, he might bring back to his Lord doubled the talent entrusted to him, and in that country might possess, so to speak, double things from the Lord who lends in return for the doubled talent.

[Col. 1216C] As the brethren awaited day by day his departure from the body, because it was then Saturday, he announced his approaching death in different words but with precisely the same meaning: “Tomorrow the Lord will do me good, and on Monday the soul will remain in me no longer.” And all occurred exactly thus.

When the ten days of illness had been completed and the day which he had foretold had come, the Almighty decreed to render him an everlasting reward. The bodily pain entered his vital parts, and he suddenly began to fail in his natural strength. It was morning. Knowing, therefore, that he was now near death, he instructed the brethren who had spent the night there, and all the others as well, to rise as quickly as possible for Prime and to pray with him far more earnestly and devoutly to gracious Jesus, in expectation of his departure.

[Col. 1216D] That night he had lain in the chapter-house, and there, after confession had been made and the reckoning completed, he was heard to speak no more. Until the Peace, he prayed and listened, facing the church, through the whole office of the Mass; and he received the kiss of the Lord’s peace from the peaceful brother Hugh Dumont. Since, at that very hour of the holy sacrifice, Gregory testifies that at the minister’s voice the heavens are held to open, the choirs of angels to be present at Jesus Christ’s command, things highest to be joined with things lowest, and earthly things united to heavenly, it is plainly proved—and may truly and catholically be understood—that through the kiss of peace he received full and perfect remission of all those matters concerning which he had shortly before made confession and, reciting the reckoning from memory, had deserved to complete.

[Col. 1217A] After this, the brethren keeping watch over him, looking at him more closely in the light, first realized that he had begun to die; they immediately announced this to the others in the church. Those who came at once stood around him where he was placed in their midst, chanting praises and thanksgivings in psalms and hymns for the commendation of his soul. As they continued to sing the psalms for some time, and only his breath still fluttered in his breast, they began to sing the fifteen psalms.

When the man of God, in whom there was then but the faintest breath, heard one of the fifteen—the psalm “I was glad”—being sung, he rose in the midst of them, held and kissed the Lord’s cross, gathered his breath, and, with whatever strength he had, lifted and opened his eyes before they had finished the words “into the house of the Lord.” He looked kindly and attentively in turn upon the brethren standing around him, as though greeting them. Then at last, with eyes and hands ever directed toward heaven, reclining upon ashes, before the Mass was ended, at that holy hour, amid joyful words and while so holy an assembly prayed, he yielded up, as we have received the account, his rejoicing spirit to Christ—the Lord of the house into which he had already been invited by the brethren. He rendered it indeed in a good old age, nourished in a holy manner of life.

52. Then great sorrow and fear gripped all who were present because of his death. But those more perfect and firmer in the observance of religion restrained themselves from tears through fear and reverence, suppressing the voices of those who wept. If faith forbade some to weep, emotion at least forced sighs from them, though they ought rather to rejoice because the Lord was now cherishing him in His bosom.

[Col. 1217D] So great was everyone’s exultation over his holy glory as was their devout lamentation over his death, since each found within himself both something over which to grieve and a reason to rejoice for Hugh. Those who were present testified to us that, once his body was lifeless, he seemed more alive than dead. The countenance of a waking man was surpassed in brightness by the face of one now asleep in Christ. No slightest blemish lay hidden in his other limbs, and his flesh appeared, in a sense, not that of an old man but wholly like that of a little child. Thus, in a certain glory of the future resurrection, if it is permitted to speak so, he seemed even to change the nature of the flesh.

O blessed and happy men, who, while he was on earth, enjoyed his conversations, shared his meals, were instructed by his teachings, refreshed by his presence, strengthened by his conduct and example, and further delighted by his signs and miracles. You are happier still, provided that you strive faithfully to observe what you heard from him. He marked out the way upon which you who remain should walk; he gave the faith of his words in his deeds, lest you think he preached anything superfluous. Having once accepted the cross enjoined upon him, he refused to lay it down; rather, fastened to it as to a commander, he always bore it in love and voluntary service, not in Cyrenian compulsion.

[Col. 1218A] Therefore, because he deserved to follow the sanctifier of the cross both in length of time and in the extent of labour, after the world’s weariness. These things have been said not for reproach but for emulation. Emulate him, therefore, in what is good.

53. Meanwhile the priest, standing at the Lord’s table, greatly exhausted and having long prayed for bodily health, had already offered the sacrifice to the Lord and was about to say the post-Communion collect. Since he did not yet know whether he should pray for the desired recovery or for Hugh’s departure, when he finally learned what had happened, he began the collect to pray for his departure.

[Col. 1218B] Nor is this place devoid of mystery; yet, because of our littleness and because we still suck at the breast before those more advanced, we have resolved to unfold it, especially for those who possess some share in the Lord’s sacraments. To pass over many things, the brethren also fully and attentively performed for him, both at his death and during his illness, as devoutly as they could, the other observances which the institution and rule of our holy religious order require according to ecclesiastical custom.

At last the brethren, mindful both of the will and command of their dearly beloved and good pastor, under whom our religious order then flourished, swiftly carried out what he had long before ordered them to do. With the holy priests of God, censers prepared and candles lit, they reverently uncovered the blessed man’s body with the honour due to it. When it had been uncovered, so great a fragrance of marvellous scent was suddenly diffused there that those present were filled with inestimable sweetness. From that sweetness it became clear to all that the author of sweetness had long made His dwelling in him, while his flesh, now dead, testified by this open miracle to all that his living spirit had always done.

[Col. 1218D] They received his inward parts, which immediately appeared purer than the fragrance of the aforesaid scent and than glass, for the protection of the place and the salvation of the homeland; and buried them there with great reverence in an edifice built there for worship with outstanding splendour. When these had been duly deposited with worthy veneration, the brethren divided his clothing among themselves as a heavenly treasure, except for his spades, which they secretly took as relics with the utmost devotion and preserve in their respective places to this day with the zeal of due reverence. From that place, from that day onward, many miracles were performed for the faithful, which through negligence were neither written down nor related to us.

54. Many who were present at this miracle are still alive, and attest with great tears of joy that, until his body had been sewn up and clothed in the garments in which, according to our custom, we bury our dead, the fragrance of that scent did not depart from their nostrils. This sign was accompanied by another venerable one, which we especially did not wish to omit, so that from this single instance the faithful might judge many others.

[Col. 1219A] A certain brother of ours, now heard of in connection with this matter, was present. Because of his remarkable suitability, he, together with the others, opened Hugh’s most holy body, devoutly received and buried that incomparable treasure, which the blessed man had long preserved for his own benefit and for the future benefit of posterity, making it openly available to all from himself. This brother had, I do not know by what accident, a hand cut and severely wounded, full alike of pain and pus. On the next day—or perhaps that same night—when he looked at it as usual in order to treat it, he found, trembling, that the bandage in which it was wrapped had suddenly been unwound. His hand was so sound, with only the scar remaining, as though it had never had any wound at all.

[Col. 1219B] Those who were present add certain other wonders in confirmation of these, of which it is not now the time to speak individually. When this had been completed, the surviving body, still placed in the midst, was guarded by the brethren with psalmody and prayer. They waited for night because they feared the neighbouring people, who, knowing that he had been guarded by them on other occasions, had formerly posted their guards at the exits of the roads, fearing that they might lose him as their heir and defender of the land. O pious and praiseworthy theft, which brought harm to absolutely no one!

When the sun had set, twelve brethren in number, or perhaps more, lifted the most holy body from that place with the honour and reverence fitting to it, at such an hour as they could manage. At the first twilight of night, as they had agreed among themselves to do, they took the road entrusted to them and hurried together with their holy pledge down the way leading to the fortress to which ancient antiquity had given the name Chalucium.

[Col. 1219C] On the preceding night, evildoers who hated the light had gone out, leading a certain peasant captive and heavily burdened with his poor household goods. When they learned this—for those bandits were travelling before their eyes—the brethren approached them and sent the captive, freed from their hands together with his humble burden, back to his home. What the man of God, while alive and still in the world, had been accustomed to do himself, he did not forget to do through his sons and brethren after his death.

He was therefore received with the highest veneration by the good pastor and the holy community, who came out to meet him, preceded even by very generous alms; and he was brought by them to Grandmont with great rejoicing. There, before the brethren, the aforesaid pastor offered sacrifice to God for the commendation of his bodily deposition. He was laid with his fathers and buried between Lord Stephen of Muret and Lord Peter of Limoges, with a sure marker set in place.

[Col. 1220A] O what grief among the surrounding peoples; what lamentation among Christ’s poor and the religious; above all, what a cry from orphans and widows, to whom he had extended the arms of charity and kindly aids of life! It cannot be told how great a multitude of people stirred from their own homes out of devotion to him. Many came from farms, villages, hamlets, and castles, and also from the city of Limoges. Returning from there, they announced to the crowds gathering that he had already been buried. In all these things it is plainly shown how acceptable he was to God and how dear to the people, and with what fervour of true faith, hope, and charity he lived in the holy Church—inasmuch as, by the Lord’s will, we are granted to know it.

For the Mass during which, by hearing it, he departed to the Lord was a sign of faith; the multitude of signs which he had already performed in the Lord was a manifestation of hope; and the freeing of the captive plainly declares the good of charity.

[Col. 1220B] This is more fully known to all who had been able to hear him speaking and see him present, and especially to those who were not ignorant of his religious way of life. But we, who did not deserve to see or hear him in the flesh, have nevertheless striven faithfully and carefully to commit to the pages of our book, according to our capacity, the few things written above which we could investigate, through the generosity of the Lord, “who gives abundantly and does not reproach” (James 1). In this too, dearest brethren, we have great confidence: although uncultivated and rustic speech cannot adorn this account for reading, that blessed man will make it shine through his splendid signs and miracles. We hope, moreover, to receive this one reward for our labour: that when these things are recited in praise and remembrance of this aforesaid righteous man, perhaps refreshment for sins may be granted both to us who pray and to you, as the poet says:

> “[Lacuna.] Perhaps even this one day it will be pleasant to remember.”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.203.)

The commemorated and most glorious day of his passing was celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of May, Monday, in the year 1157 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, as noted above; the thirty-second year from the death of Lord Stephen of Muret, our first father; and about the eighty-sixth year of the most blessed Hugh’s age. Adrian IV was then pope, by the providence of the Roman Church; the most glorious king of the Franks, Louis, was reigning—Louis who succeeded Louis in the kingdom—under our fourth prior, Stephen of Liciac, of good and most blessed memory, a most loving man.

[Col. 1220D] Therefore let us all rejoice in the Lord, who deigned to honour us with the fellowship of so great a man. May God Himself grant that we may be raised up by his intercessions, He who enriched us with his conduct and signs and instructed us on earth. May He, our Lord and Redeemer, who received His faithful servant from the earth in peace, help, govern, and guard us for his sake from this wicked world, lest we be defiled by evils.

[Col. 1221A] Behold, the day closes, the pen grows dull, the hand becomes sluggish, the tongue is impeded. Why then do we delay? Why do we strive to prolong matters further, when even the end of these things is wholly unknown to humankind? Truly, He who opened the mouth of the beast (Numbers 22) has opened and instructed ours: that same One who is our end and our beginning, Jesus Christ our Lord and God, to whom belong honour and glory, power and dominion with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, from eternity, now, and through all ages of ages. Amen.

Who said it? The Lord: this name remains to him.

For the Lord is the speaker of the saying, and none other than he.

Glory be to the Lord alone, who has accomplished all things.

I, William Dandina, improperly surnamed “of Saint-Savin” [Col. 1221B], a sinful brother and unworthy priest, humbly and supplicatingly beg you to pray for me.

Who could ever investigate or recount in due order the wonders of so great a man so as adequately to praise him? The venerable pastor mentioned above, who, by the Lord’s providence, had lived and been educated as his disciple and had been very intimate with him, used to tell us one miracle concerning him; it must by no means be omitted, so wonderfully full of humility is it understood to be. For Hugh, of blessed memory, then a novice, who, with God as author, served the Church of Angoulême in the episcopate, being certain of his miracles and goodness, which the Lord deigned to work through him [Col. 1221C], often used to come to him with such devotion, greatly desiring to be refreshed by his presence and instructed by his word, as though to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

One day it happened that the bishop came to him; and, when he had sat down as usual, worn out by distress, he said: “I, poor wretch, suffer such pain in my right shoulder that I am wholly unable either to raise it upward, bend it aside, or turn it in any other direction. It proceeds, I believe, from gout. My neck also, throat, and face, as you can see, have become swollen and livid from the aforementioned raging pain [Col. 1222A]. Therefore, for the love of God, lord, touch and feel with your holy hands the place where I am in pain.”

Hearing this, the man of God said in astonishment: “I greatly wonder why you speak thus, lord. My hands are indeed full of blood, while yours are consecrated and prepared for the mystery of the living God, and are filled with God’s gift and grace. What you seek from me, a sinner, ought both to be and can be granted, when need arises, through you, with the Lord at work, both to me and to others. For of you and such persons the Lord says: ‘They shall lay their hands upon the sick, and they shall recover’ (Mark 16).”

The bishop answered: “Certainly, if you say you hesitate because of the privilege and honour of the divine mystery, know that in your state you hold and possess no unequal share of the divine sacraments [Col. 1222B]. For if I, an unworthy sinner and unworthy priest, receive the Lord in the mystery with my unclean hands, you likewise receive that same Lord, and no other, in receiving and feeding the poor. For he himself said: ‘What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me’ (Matt. 25). And elsewhere: ‘He who receives you receives me’ (Matt. 10). There are also many other passages, which need not now be considered one by one.”

But the man of the Lord, seeing that the bishop persisted in his request, did not wish him to remain distressed any longer. Choosing instead the common good of both parties, he immediately took the bishop’s hand in his own and, with the sign of the cross, felt and treated it all the way along where it hurt. In this especially [Col. 1222C] preserving humility for himself and showing the holy bishop the reverence due to him. When this was done, the bishop who had come sick was healed without any delay.

It is pleasing to consider that, in this most gracious benefit, the devotion of the holy bishop greatly corresponds to the merit of the aforesaid man. We must therefore suppose that he was able to do this because he trusted more in the bishop’s power than in his own: for though he placed the bishop’s hand together with his own upon the painful place, he believed that through that hand he would obtain what he sought. Amen.

[Col. 1221]

# ITINERARY OF THE GRANDMONT BROTHERS, OR THE TRANSLATION OF THE RELICS OF THE HOLY SEVEN VIRGINS, COMPANIONS OF SAINT URSULA, FROM THE DIOCESE OF COLOGNE TO THE CHURCH OF GRANDMONT

*(Mémoires de la Société des Antiquaires de l’Ouest, vol. XVIII, p. 547.)*

## PRELIMINARY LETTER

[Col. 1221D] To all present and future brothers of the Order of Grandmont, their fellow servants and brothers [Col. 1222D], WILLIAM and IMBERT, everlasting salvation in Christ Jesus.

[Col. 1223A] Since, dearest brothers, through the care of illustrious men, many monasteries of God in various parts of the world are said to be adorned with the most holy relics of martyrs, confessors, and virgins more richly than with gems and gold, those who desire with their whole heart to love God and honour and venerate his saints are undoubtedly encouraged to do likewise. For it is evident that in churches where the bodies of saints lie buried in peace, not only cloistered men, but secular clerics also, are more diligent about the Lord’s office and gather more readily and pray more devoutly.

These are indeed benefits that come to faithful Christians from the presence and merits of those who shed their blood for Christ or endured a long martyrdom without the shedding of blood. Hence [Col. 1223B], if all things work together for good for those who love God, we believe that those especially do not lack the reward of the eternal and unchangeable good who, by the zeal of their diligence in acquiring such remains, offer to those who are and those who shall be a model of devotion and furnish matter for compunction.

One such man, indeed, is the venerable William, sixth prior of Grandmont, who was privileged to place in his own church and ours at Grandmont seven heavenly pearls from Christ’s diadem—that is, seven glorious virgins. Therefore, dearest brothers, we possess—yes, we possess—a mirror in which the failings of our frailty may be reflected; and we possess an everlasting reminder of divine praise. What [Col. 1223C] indeed do the marks of martyrdom, which we behold upon the virgins’ necks, cry out? What do the swords, which we ourselves saw among their sacred bones, signify [Col. 1224A], except that with one harmony of heart and voice we should all together praise the Lord upon well-sounding cymbals in his saints (Ps. 150), and that each of us should weep for his sins, saying with the Prophet: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall soak my couch” (Ps. 6). “Alas for me! Who will give water to my head, and to my eyes a fountain of tears?” (Jer. 9).

What, I ask, brothers, what shall we say at the Judgment, when we do not doubt that young girls attained the kingdom through the sword? Yet do not fear, little flock (Luke 12) of Grandmont; rather, rejoice and exult, serving God there with the whole world aware, since Christ has been pleased, through the provision henceforth made for you by your spiritual Father in return for the service bestowed upon his virgins, to give you the kingdom. But if you act otherwise [Col. 1224B], you will deserve punishment. These virgins will be witnesses against you if you cease to extol their merits in the proclamation of due praise; they will be your helpers by their glorious intercessions if you strive with all devotion to praise and glorify in them and for them their Bridegroom, your God.

O gift sent to you from heaven! O grace freely given! You have that by which the lukewarmness of your religious life may be rekindled, should it perhaps come upon you. You have that by which the fervour of your charity may increase. “The Dayspring from on high has visited you” (Luke 1). He has regarded your humility (ibid.), he who looks upon the lowly and knows the lofty from afar (Ps. 138) has regarded your humility, when he entrusted this deposit of your faithfulness to be kept. How he did this [Col. 1224C], at what time, and through what persons, must be committed to writing for the memory of posterity.

# ITINERARY OF THE GRANDMONT BROTHERS

[Col. 1223]

[Col. 1223C] In the year 1181 of the incarnate Word, under Alexander III, supreme and universal pontiff; Frederick, emperor of the Romans; in the second year of Philip’s reign, son of Louis, king of France; and under Richard, son of Henry, king of England, duke of Aquitaine: Gerald, abbot of Sieburg [Note: [Col. 1223] According to the conjecture of Baron de Roizin, this is the Abbey of Siegburg, an eleventh-century Benedictine foundation.], a man most eminent among the fathers of monasteries [Col. 1223D], came from the regions of Germany to Saint-Gilles and the Rock of … Amator, for the sake of prayer.

After completing his prayers, as he was returning to his homeland and German people, he turned aside to Grandmont, seeking the fellowship of the Order. For he hoped it would greatly benefit him to be supported by the prayers of brothers living in such a manner. He was honourably received, as so great a guest deserved to be received; and, in chapter before all the brothers of the whole Order, participation in the Order’s benefits, both in life and in death, was granted both to him and to his venerable companions—namely, William the monk and Master Guoderamnus, canon of Bonn.

[Col. 1224C] When these things had been carried out with great devotion, the aforesaid Prior William, who had bestowed this charity, knelt with the whole community of brothers and begged the abbot to obtain by his prayers, from the archbishop of that city and those having authority in the matter, the gift to the church of Grandmont, in which he had become a brother, of one of the sacred virgins martyred for Christ at Cologne [Col. 1224D].

Considering the affection behind this pious request, the holy man said: “Lord, if you send your brothers to us at Cologne, we grant you this: if we are ever able, God consenting, we shall do one of two things. Either the lord archbishop, who loves us greatly, will at our request give you one of the sacred virgins as you ask; or we shall send to your devotion one of those we have in our monastery.”

At this the prior was made joyful; and, trusting the man’s words, a day was appointed on which the brothers were to come to the aforesaid city [Col. 1225A]. The abbot then departed to return to his own place.

But as the days of the Lord’s Passion approached, when those who, God willing, were to carry away this precious treasure were due to set out, the brothers’ proposed journey displeased nearly all the brethren. The Prior alone [Note: [Col. 1225D] Lord Gerald Itherii in the Grandmontine mirror.—Manuscripts of the fonds de la Garde, 1590.] could not be turned from his undertaking by any discouragements. O devilish cunning! O craft of the ancient serpent, who transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11)! Even through those who perhaps feared both the danger of the journey and the toil of the undertaking for their brothers, he was trying to extinguish the devotion of the faithful and the honour of the saints. But there is no wisdom and no counsel against God. What has been predestined from eternity cannot be prevented by any art.

Therefore, by the command and with the blessing of the lord prior, four of us brothers—two priests and two lay brothers—set out for Cologne. We arrived there, indeed, on the Saturday before Palm Sunday, amid the severity of winter, the violence of snow, hail, and rain, the diversity of lands, and the discordance of language [Col. 1225B], in such safety; and we were received and provided for so honourably by the inhabitants of the city and natives of the country until after the Lord’s Resurrection, that none of us doubted, or could doubt, that all which was being done concerning us was by divine ordering.

That night we rested near the cloister of the major church, in the lodging of the aforesaid abbot; for he had so arranged matters with our Father. Since we did not find him there, in the morning we crossed the Rhine and proceeded to Sieburg, where he was happily celebrating the Sunday procession and feast day with his holy brothers. When he was told that we had arrived, he came out from the brothers’ choir to meet us in the church, receiving us joyfully and gladly with the kiss of peace. He led us aside into a small chapel, where we heard Mass privately.

First, therefore, refreshed by heavenly food, we were then led by the Father himself and certain most religious monks accompanying him to our lodging, to be refreshed with bodily food. The arrangement of the house, the cleanliness of the table, and the propriety of the servants attested the master’s propriety and prudence; not the abundance of dishes set before us [Col. 1225D], which ought not to be preferred to these. “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God shall destroy both it and them.” Propriety, however, is a virtue, as is prudence. Yet, unless charity excused our abundance, the frugality of monastic tables rightly reproved it. We afterward both heard and read that reproach in the pale and lean faces of the cloistered brothers, whom we observed to be most orderly in monastery, cloister, refectory, and their other workplaces. Nothing that we wished to see escaped our eyes; nothing that we asked about escaped our ears.

When the greater part of the day [Col. 1226A] had been spent in these matters and the hour for sleeping arrived, we went to bed. When the monks rose for Matins, we rose also and celebrated the morning office in our own manner. In the morning, after Mass had been celebrated, we entered chapter, where the abbot and the whole community received us and all the brothers of our Order into the benefits of their house, on the same condition on which they themselves had been received in our chapter. It was also jointly decreed that, every year, on the fifth day before the Nones of October, a service should be performed in our church for their departed brethren, and in theirs for ours [Note: [Col. 1225D] Note that on the fifth day before the Nones of October an anniversary for our brothers of Cologne is to be held at [Col. 1226D] Grandmont, on the feast of Saint Gereon. Manuscripts of the fonds de la Garde.].

When this had been done, the venerable abbot, mindful of his promise, delivered to us with the greatest reverence the body of Saint Albina, virgin and martyr, and [Col. 1226B] another body of a holy virgin whose name God knows. On her forehead appears the mark of martyrdom: the wound, namely, of an axe. He had promised one, but gave two, displaying the generosity of liberal men, who always bestow gifts more abundant than those they promise.

Greatly rejoicing, we bade farewell to the abbot and brothers and accompanied them with thanksgiving; with their blessing we departed, despite their wish to keep us with them throughout the whole week. Master Guoderamnus, who had come there to us and who, because of the privilege of our fraternity, had shown himself very kindly disposed toward us, departed with us and took us that night to his lodging at Bonn.

On the following day, after prayers had been exchanged with the canons of the church of Bonn, in which [Col. 1226C] he himself was a canon, and with certain enclosed nuns outside the city, we returned to Cologne to speak with the lord archbishop. He was sitting in a chamber of his palace, as was always his custom, surrounded by groups of clerics and barons. Having learned from Lord Guoderamnus’ report that we were present in the outer hall, he ordered us quickly admitted. Rising for us out of reverence for our Order, before all who watched in amazement, he kissed each of us and made us sit at his right hand.

Then he graciously received the letters of our Father, containing our petition, and the letters of Lord Peter, bishop of Tusculum, cardinal of the Roman Church and legate of Germany, the bishop of Liège, and the count of Flanders, asking him to hear us [Col. 1226D]. Having willingly received and inspected them, he ordered us taken to Saint Pantaleon, where his daytime meal was being prepared; for he wished to have us with him both at lodging and table. But God, who knew what was expedient for us, inspired him, after changing his plan, to send us to the nearby abbey of Saint Martin to avoid the crowd. And so it was done.

There we were gladly received, both out of reverence for the sender and because of the grace of hospitality. Since we had heard that there was an abundance of relics there, we begged the abbot of the monastery on bended knees, for God’s love, to impart to us something from the treasure entrusted to him [Col. 1227A]. He readily consented, like a man whose face, voice, and words displayed the appearance of holiness. Yet, wisely, he was unwilling to do anything in the matter without counsel. He ordered us to speak with him the next day, when we would receive what God meanwhile inspired him to give.
