After dinner we had to go to speak with the archbishop at Saint Pantaleon, as he had commanded us.

We therefore mounted horses, since he was almost a mile away, and, with our guide and interpreter, the aforesaid Guoderamnus, going before us, we first proceeded to the abbess of the Monastery of the Virgins. When she heard from the letters of our Father and brothers both our request and the manner of our religious life [Col. 1227B], God gave us such favour in her sight that she confessed she had never seen men whom she would more gladly help in such matters. She therefore ordered us to return to her in the morning. We asked and requested that one of us might celebrate Mass in the Monastery of the Virgins.

Then we came to the house of the venerable Master Armanus, dean of the Church of the Apostles. Endowed with learning and distinguished by maturity of character, he was a close friend of the lord archbishop and had seen us before him. The reason for our arrival was by no means hidden from him. Knowing that we were going to speak with the archbishop, he did not wish to speak much with us, but ordered us to return to him immediately after our conference with the archbishop. We believe [Col. 1227C] that he feared that, if he spoke with us too long at that time, we might return to our lodging by another route, and he would thus be deprived of the opportunity, divinely inspired in him, to do us good.

Continuing the journey we had begun, we again presented ourselves to the archbishop. At first he had been gracious to us, but the second time he became so much more gracious as he was freer from the business of those waiting upon him; for nearly the entire court of people had departed, since evening was already approaching. Carefully investigating the purpose for which we sought the bodies of the most sacred virgins, he learned from our answer—which he readily believed—that this was to be done not for temporal gain, but solely out of devotion. He spoke for a long time in German with certain of his clerics. When this had been done, he answered us most graciously in these words:

“We wish you to know, dearest brothers, that we formerly forbade under anathema anyone to dare carry an entire virgin’s body outside our diocese. Nevertheless, on account of the honour of your Order, of which we have heard much good from the report of our beloved son, the abbot of Sieburg, we have already broken our decree at his request, ordering him, trusting his word, to give you what he promised. We must yet break it further at the insistence of your prayers, because we wish to win the friendship of the brotherhood of your Order. Therefore, that we may forever enjoy the aid of your prayers in your church, we shall send to that church, as a gift and blessing [Col. 1228A] of our devotion, one most holy virgin, as you request.

“You shall remain with us throughout this week, for these are holy days and you must attend the divine offices. After the Resurrection, however, you shall set out on your journey, carrying back in peace the relics which in the meantime, by the favour of our permission, you can acquire through the city’s monasteries. You shall also have our messenger, who will guide you as far as you please.”

Hearing this, we gave manifold thanks to God and to him, as humbly as we could and knew how, for the consolation of such great favour. But because we wished to return, we objected that our Father and brothers would be troubled if they saw us remain so long. He objected in turn: “If it is right,” he said, “for you to ride on Maundy Thursday and Good Friday—which no other religious persons will do—you yourselves must judge.”

Thus convinced and silenced by the wise man’s speech, we returned with his blessing by the way we had come to the house of the aforementioned dean. Joyfully meeting us, he urged us in charity to spend the whole week with him. But when we said that we could not abandon the lord archbishop’s lodging, he turned charity into compulsion. As we were soon to read concerning the two who were going to Emmaus, that they compelled the Lord, so he seized us and compelled us.

A most beautiful house! It was surrounded on every side by a wall; within was a church, and beside it an orchard. So far as concerns things religiously conducted in the world [Col. 1228C], we saw there nothing disorderly, nothing that did not serve religion. That most holy man gave us books and priestly vestments, all very good; he gave us a gold and silver chalice and cruets, and the key of the church; he gave us an excellent small house and its key. And behold, with God guiding us—religious life found in the world, a wonderful thing—we were among them without reproach.

When morning came, we went to the Monastery of the Virgins as we had been commanded the day before. Brother William celebrated Mass at the high altar, one sacred body of a virgin, which the abbess gave us, having meanwhile been placed upon it. In that body there could be seen a very large nail, by which the holy virgin was believed to have been killed [Col. 1228D]. When Mass had been sung in the same church, we exchanged the gift of prayers; and, reverently receiving the sacred body, we hastened to our host, namely the abbot of Saint Martin. Mildly reproving us, as he was a most gentle man, because we had not returned to our lodging, he gladly began to recount what had happened to him in a vision during the preceding night.

## Vision of the Abbot of Saint Martin

“When I was in my bed,” he said, “during the night just passed, I began to consider what I could give you. For what I had heard the day before yesterday about your Order pleased me. While I was thinking on this, by divine inspiration—as the outcome proves—it came into my mind [Col. 1229A] to give you the head of one most glorious virgin, which I had long held in great veneration. Before I became abbot, I used regularly to celebrate the sacred mysteries of Mass before it. But after becoming abbot, I placed it in my chapel, where until now I have honourably kept it as an incomparable treasure.

“Yet while I was considering giving you the head, I repented of my resolve to give it and said in my heart: ‘What shall I do? Shall I give the head? How shall I be able to be without the head which I have loved so greatly and long held in such veneration, and for whose sake God has done such immense good things for me? Certainly, I shall not give it.’ Immediately correcting what I had said, I replied: ‘Indeed I shall give it, for holy is the place to which it will be carried; holy, as I hear, are the inhabitants of that place; there it will be guarded most holy [Col. 1229B] and accorded due honour.’

“Contending with myself and hesitating what to do in this manner, I fell asleep. In dreams I saw very white doves flying overhead, one of which fell at my feet. Stretching out my hand, I caught it and found its leg swollen and bound to its wing, so that it could neither walk nor fly. I loosed it, and it immediately shook itself free from my hands and flew away unharmed, joining the other flying birds, as though rejoicing and very glad at its release.

“Immediately upon waking, I clearly understood that the head of the virgin and martyr over which I had been thinking and hesitating wished to fly with her fellow martyrs and virgins as far as Grandmont [Col. 1229C], and there rest forever. Therefore, God willing, you shall have the head. Yet I tell you truly that you would by no means have had it, unless I had believed that this had been shown to me in the vision.”

Going to the chapel, when we saw the head and the mark of martyrdom on its forehead, who can recount the greatness of our joy and abundance of tears? God knows it, the source and origin of all mercy; and we knew it also, rejoicing at the vision we had heard, but more joyful still at receiving the gift. Having received the Father and brothers into the gift of our prayers, and been received by them, we went out with the head and were already mounting our horses, when behold, a monk—nearly eighty years old, a man of wholly praiseworthy life—brought the head of Saint Anathalia, virgin and martyr. It is covered with hair and marked with the sign of martyrdom [Col. 1229D], as is plainly evident to all who see it.

For the man of God, moved to compunction by the Father’s vision and touched by the brothers’ tears, wished that the virgin should receive in the church of Grandmont, as the principal part of herself, all the veneration she deserved. The virgin herself, moreover, would not allow another virgin to leave the monastery alone or proceed to foreign nations. She had accompanied her from England as far as Rome, and from Rome as far as Cologne. Perhaps they had agreed together that, as they had been companions through rivers, lands, and seas in the transient course of this present life, and had together been joined to their heavenly Bridegroom through an equal palm of martyrdom [Col. 1230A], so at Grandmont their heads should await reunion with the bodies which they had left elsewhere.

This seems to be confirmed both by the favour of the monk, who brought and gave the head unasked, and by the hair and wounds of martyrdom seen on both heads, which can arouse devotion in the undevout.

Enriched with such gifts, we returned to our church, to the dean’s house. Having reverently placed upon the altar the relics of the holy virgins—the three, namely, bodies and two heads—our Father and interpreter Guoderamnus left us. Reverence for the holy days and the approaching solemnity of Easter required him to return to his church and his own house. Yet he did not leave us orphans, nor did he abandon us desolate [Col. 1230B]. The dean, as it were, adopted us as sons: for six days he led us through the city’s monasteries, seeking relics of saints, and brought us back to our lodging to receive what was necessary for our bodies.

In this, indeed, he seems to me to display the likeness of the Gospel hen, which leads and brings back her chicks, calls and recalls them, supplies food, and preserves life. Thus this Father became guardian of both our lives, present and future: supplying nourishment to our bodies and devotion to our minds. May he be rewarded in the recompense of the righteous.

Going before us on foot, therefore, on Maundy Thursday he first led us to the church of Saint Mary in the Steps [Col. 1230C], where, at his request, we received from the repository of relics the larger bones of one virgin. Then he led us to the church of Saint Gereon, where more than six hundred bodies of martyrs from the Theban Legion rest in peace. When he asked that some small portion of that sacred multitude be given to us, they replied that all the saints’ tombs had been so firmly secured with iron bars that, unless they were broken open with great labour after fasts had first been ordered, they could have nothing at all.

Yet, not knowing how they could permit a man of such great rank to return without recompense for his labour, they conferred, by God’s inspiration, out of love for him and reverence for our Order. For some among them had kept small portions for themselves out of devotion when the bodies of the holy martyrs were enclosed [Col. 1230D]. These were collected and placed upon the altar; then, after prayers had been exchanged, they gave us relics of Saint Brandan and Saint Tran, and many very beautiful bones of the holy Mauri—all of them from the Theban Legion.

Returning thence exceedingly joyful, on Good Friday we crossed the Rhine [Note: [Col. 1229] “The river Rinch (Rhine).” Manuscripts of the fonds de la Garde.] and received at Saint Heribert’s in Deutz the glorious gift of the venerable Father Philip, archbishop: namely, Saint Essentia. Among her sacred bones are two iron plates joined together, resembling a knife, with which the most holy virgin appears to have been killed [Col. 1231A].

While the body was still upon the altar, we begged the abbot and monks, in God’s charity, to make for our church in particular some share of the monastery’s relics. After the prayers of mutual fraternity had been given and received, and after the prescribed day had been established on which service for their dead and ours should be performed annually, they charitably gave us relics of many martyrs and virgins, marked with their small labels. Taking up these pledges of the saints, we hastened gladly back to our lodging with very great joy.

There was in the city a certain householder, an elderly man, and his wife, a venerable matron. At their own expense they had rebuilt a monastery that was old and ruined. They possessed an entirely intact body of one glorious virgin and martyr, which they intended to send to Huy in the diocese of Liège [Col. 1231B], for a certain knight, the brother of this matron, had asked them to do so. They said—and truthfully maintained—that although this had often been attempted, it had never been possible to carry it there. There was no doubt that she wished to accompany to Grandmont those whom she had accompanied from childhood, and there await with them the second robe, having already received the first with them through the palm of martyrdom.

Therefore, after the dean, who had heard these reports, had celebrated the divine offices in the Church of the Apostles on that same Good Friday, he went to the old man’s and matron’s house, accompanied by us and his clerics. They earnestly begged her to deign to send to the church of Grandmont, as a most welcome and God-pleasing gift, the virgin who would not allow herself to be transported elsewhere [Col. 1231C]. Though for some time she refused, we heard their voices but understood none of their words. At length, following her counsel, they addressed the old man. Repeating again and again the arguments that they had already made to the matron, they accomplished absolutely nothing.

Then the dean said to us: “See, brothers, whether you can accomplish anything through yourselves, since we cannot obtain what we have asked.” But we, who were as barbarians to them as they were to us, did what we could, throwing ourselves at their feet. They did not understand our words, nor we theirs. Seeing this, the matron began to raise us from the ground [Col. 1231D]. The old man, however, went back inside the house; but not even so could he escape the dean’s prayers, for the dean knew that God loves persistence in asking.

Following him into the house, therefore, the dean promised them that they would effectively share in the prayers of the whole Order, both in life and in death. Esteeming this a great thing—by the working of him who said, “Give, and it shall be given unto you” (Luke 6)—they had a book brought, and, as the dean had promised, we gave them the benefits of the Order, while they gave us the virgin’s intact body. We then went to the church with the matron, reverently received the body, and departed joyfully with it without any difficulty.

On the next day [Col. 1232A], that is, Holy Saturday of Easter, the dean took us to the Church of the Apostles and gave us, delivering with his own hand from the shrine containing the virgins’ relics, the larger bones of one body. On that same day he himself gave us nearly two bodies of virgins, which had been found so recently that they had not yet been washed. A cellarer of a Cistercian abbey, a very learned and devout man, had given him these bodies for our purpose.

We ourselves saw this man and heard from his own mouth that, when these two bodies of virgins had been found, he came to the place where a demoniac had lain. They bound a small mass of that earth upon his chest, and he was healed. He then conceived such joy and recovered soundness of mind so fully [Col. 1232B] that he never afterwards wished to return to the world. Eager to become a monk, when the monk told us these things, he himself was devoutly awaiting, under probation, the monastic habit and observance.

That monk also told us of an Englishman who, together with others, was removing earth from above the virgins’ bodies. When they reached the bodies, he stole one small bone, bound it in his breeches, and intended to carry it to England. The following night, while he slept, his leg became so swollen that, waking in pain, he cried out. A woman of the household arose, lit a fire, and saw the man suffering terribly from the swelling of his leg. When she asked what this was or how it had happened to him, he confessed that he had stolen a little bone of the holy virgins which he had tied in his breeches [Col. 1232C]. Forced, therefore, he returned what he had voluntarily stolen; and when morning came, he was healed.

They also gave us relics of virgins at the monastery of Saint Pantaleon and in a certain newly built house of monks; they received from us the gift of prayers, and we from them.

Accordingly, having collected such relics of virgins and martyrs as we were able to obtain through the intervention and generosity of those whom we have mentioned above, and having most honorably placed and secured them in flasks, we set out on the Monday after the Lord’s Resurrection to return, with the archbishop’s blessing and with his servant, who attended to us and led us as far as we wished. Moreover, out of reverence for the relics and for the favor which God had bestowed upon us in his sight, the venerable dean Armanus came out of the city with us, showing us the most welcome familiarity of his condescension for nearly one mile; then, embracing and kissing each of us there, he departed from us in body, never to depart in spirit. We, by our day-stages, happily arrived with our happy merchandise at our cell of Brondello.

[Note: [Col. 1231] La Celle de Bronzeau, a monastery of the Order of Grandmont, situated in the parish of Saint-Léger-Magnareix (Haute-Vienne). TEXIER.]

We pass over in silence the benefits, honors, and consolations which, by God’s favor, we enjoyed on our journey out and back, lest they perhaps seem incredible to someone, or lest the sharpness of envious persons allege that this has been said from arrogance. We wished only to commit to writing matters which simply show how so great an abundance of relics could reach Grandmont, so that it may be believed that this was done by divine disposition alone—as is indeed manifest. From Brondello, therefore, we sent letters to our Father Prior and to the brothers in the following manner.

## Letter to the Brothers

Through the merits and intercessions of the holy virgins, and through the favor of your devotion, God granted us a prosperous journey both going and returning. We return, therefore, joyful and exceedingly rich; for we bring back with us from the treasury of the eternal King seven most precious pearls, that is, seven glorious virgins. One of them is called Saint Albina, virgin and martyr; another, Saint Essentia, likewise virgin and martyr; another, Saint Panafreta, virgin and martyr; another, Saint Secunda, virgin and martyr. We do not know the names of the others, but their Bridegroom knows them.

We also have relics of very many martyrs, and the head of Saint Anathalia, virgin and martyr, which is covered with hair and adorned with the mark of martyrdom. We also have another head of a glorious virgin and martyr, in which locks of hair may be seen, and on the forehead the mark of martyrdom—namely, the blow of an axe. We have, besides, relics of other virgins, which will be divided in portions among the individual churches of our Order; for so we have been commanded. With what honor, with what joy, and with what reverence the gifts of the heavenly King are to be received and kept by you, your prudence may judge. For tomorrow, before the third hour, our ladies will come to you, if God wills.

While the letter was still being read, by the ordinance of almighty God the venerable Father Saibrandus, bishop of Limoges, arrived. The coming of this most excellent Father was truly by divine disposition. For he had not intended to rest that night at Grandmont; wishing only to see the prior and brothers, he meant to leave at once. He was returning from the king of England and his son, the count of Poitiers, into whose favor he had honorably been restored after the estrangement which he had had with him concerning the bishopric. But when he heard that Christ’s virgins had now entered his diocese, he was made joyful; and, reading in the letter that they would come to Grandmont on the following day, he believed that God wished him personally to go out to meet them, and he remained.

Therefore, when morning came, clothed in pontifical vestments, he went out with the prior and the solemn procession of the brothers to meet the virgins. The cross of the Lord went before; incense gave forth fragrance in the censers; burning candles were carried; the people wept; the clerics sang; and the earth resounded with their voices. On the fourth day before the Kalends of May [28 April], receiving the relics of the virgins and martyrs with due honor, they bore them with wonderful devotion and humility as far as the church of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, etc.

PHILIP, by divine mercy Archbishop of Cologne, Prince-Elector of the Roman Empire and Chancellor of Italy, to the brothers of Grandmont.

PHILIP, by God’s grace humble minister of the holy Church of Cologne, to the venerable brothers in Christ, WILLIAM the prior and the whole convent of Grandmont: greeting and an ever-expanding love in Christ.

We willingly and with gladness of heart received your brothers, bearers of this letter, together with your letter, since we place firm hope and great confidence in you and in your Order: that we, who sail amid the waves of this age, performing many works upon this great sea, may through the aid of your prayers, with the Father of mercies as our pilot, be mercifully brought to the harbor of salvation; so that through Mary’s watchfulness Martha’s administration may be assisted.

Moreover, as a covenant and pledge of steadfast friendship and affection to be maintained mutually between us and you, we most willingly granted your petition, brotherly sharing with you the treasure of our Church. What we would scarcely have done for any emperors or kings, we have bestowed upon your charity with ready will, assigning you a fair and honorable portion of the most sacred relics. Therefore, in return for our devotion, repay us with a share in your prayers, and receive us into your full brotherhood, so that we may deserve to become sharers and participants in your good works and prayers. We shall receive this from your love as a most welcome gift, more precious than gold and topaz.

[Note: [Col. 1233] The itinerary transcribed above from three manuscript codices of the Library of Grandmont was collated with them by me, the undersigned secretary of the most reverend lord D., abbot and general superior of the whole Order of Grandmont, and it agrees with them. In testimony of this matter, the most reverend lord himself subscribed at Grandmont on the sixteenth day of May, in the year of the Lord 1602.

DE LA MARCHE, Abbot of Grandmont.

By command of D. Ant. DESTHÈVES.]

## About the Year of the Lord 1192: Ermengaudus

### Notice

(FABRICIUS, *Library of Middle and Lower Latin*, II, 107.)

Ermengardus, or Ermengaudus, a writer of the twelfth or thirteenth century. James Gretser published at Ingolstadt in 1614, quarto, this author’s little work against the Waldensians—mutilated at the end and containing only nineteen chapters—together with Bernard, abbot of Fontcald, and Ebrard of Béthune.

[Note: [Col. 1235] Pamelius, in Cyprian, Epistle 63.]

This trio of anti-Waldensian writers was then reprinted in the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 1644–1655, vol. IV, and in the Lyons edition of 1777, vol. XXIV. It ought also to appear again among Gretser’s *Works*, vol. XII.

## Here Begins the Little Work of Ermengaudus against the Heretics Who Say and Believe That This World and All Visible Things Were Made Not by God but by the Devil

(GRETSER’S *Works*, vol. XII, p. 223.)

### Chapter I. God Is the Creator of All Things

The heretics say and believe, in their secret assemblies, that this world and everything seen in it—namely, the heaven which we see, the sun, moon, stars, earth, all animals and human beings, the sea and fish, and all things seen or existing in it—were not made by almighty God, but by the prince of evil spirits. Very many authorities of the New Testament oppose these heretics and their malicious error.

It is found in the Gospel of Blessed John, who wrote against heretics maintaining such an error, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). From this it is plain that almighty God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—created and made all things visible and invisible, as the blessed Apostle Paul testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying: “By faith we understand that the ages were fashioned by the Word of God” (Heb. 11). Likewise, in the same Epistle: “He who created all things is God” (Heb. 3). Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, all the apostles and disciples, gathered together in one place, lifted up their voice unanimously, saying: “Lord God, you made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them,” etc. (Acts 14). Likewise, John says in the Apocalypse: “The angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth lifted up his hand to heaven and swore by him who lives for ages of ages, who created heaven and earth and all things that are in them,” etc. (Rev. 10). Likewise, in the same book: “Fear the Lord and give him honor, for the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth, sea and all things in them, and the springs of waters” (Rev. 14). Likewise, Paul said in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands” (Heb. 2). Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth,” etc. (Matt. 11). Likewise, John says of the same: “And the world was made through him,” etc. (John 1).

Let these New Testament authorities suffice for you, although many authorities in the New and Old Testaments and in the prophets are found testifying to the same thing: that God created and made all visible and invisible things. Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, Paul and Barnabas say: “Men and brothers, we proclaim to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living and true God, who made heaven and earth and all things in them, giving rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14).

### Chapter II. There Are Not Two Aeons

What the heretics say, that there are two gods—one almighty and the other evil—is contrary to all divine Scripture. For all divinely inspired Scripture of the New and Old Testaments, and of all the prophets, affirms one God only. For Blessed Paul says in the Epistle to the Ephesians: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all, who is above all and in all of us” (Eph. 4). Likewise, Mark says in the Gospel: “One of the scribes asked the Lord Jesus what was the first commandment of all. Jesus answered him: ‘The first commandment of all is: Hear, Israel: your God, God is one. And the second: Love the Lord your God with all your heart,’ etc. And the scribe said to him: ‘Well, teacher, you have spoken truly, because God is one, and there is no other besides him’” (Mark 12).

### Chapter III. The Mosaic Law Was Given and Promulgated by the True God

The heretics say: “The Law of Moses, which we call the Old Law, was not given by almighty God but by the prince of evil spirits.” Very many authorities of the divine Scriptures contradict this error. For the Lord says in the Gospel according to Matthew: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill” (Matt. 5). He who is the Son of God would not have said that he came to fulfill the Law if it had been given by the devil; rather, he would have destroyed it. Likewise, according to Luke: “When the days of Mary’s purification were completed according to the Law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the Law of the Lord, etc., and to offer a sacrifice, according to what is said in the Law of the Lord” (Luke 2). And again: “When they had completed all things according to the Law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own city Nazareth” (ibid.). It is certain and beyond all doubt that Christ, who is true God and true man, would not consent to the commandments of a devilish law being observed or fulfilled in himself.

Likewise, in the Gospel according to John the Lord says: “Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope. For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also, for he wrote of me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5). As though he said: Whoever does not believe and receive in faith the words of the old Law cannot believe or receive the words of the Gospel for his salvation. Likewise, in the Gospel according to Luke, when a lawyer asked the Lord what he ought to do in order to possess eternal life, the Lord asked him what was written in the Law. The expert answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, all your strength, and all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.” He said to him: “You have answered correctly; do this and you shall live” (Luke 10). For if the Law of Moses had not been given by God, Christ would never have promised life for observing it. Likewise, in the same Gospel, the Lord testifies: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them,” etc. (Luke 16). From this it appears that observance of the Law and the prophets does not allow a person to go to the places of infernal punishments.

Likewise, in the same Gospel, after Christ had risen from the dead, appearing to two disciples going to the village of Emmaus, he bore witness to the Law, saying: “Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and thus enter into his glory? And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24). If the Law had been given by the devil to Moses, Christ would never have taught and interpreted it to his disciples. Likewise, in the same Gospel Truth itself said: “It is necessary that all things written about me in the Law of Moses, the prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (ibid.). Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew, when the Pharisees asked why his disciples transgressed the traditions of the elders, the Lord says: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God said: ‘Honor your father and mother,’ and ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die’” (Matt. 15). This testimony is certainly from the Law of Moses. Christ said that this testimony was spoken and given by God; therefore, the Law was given by God.

Likewise, Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “I proclaim to you God, who made heaven and the world and all things that are in it; since he is Lord of heaven and earth” (Acts 17). The same Paul, in the same book, defends himself against the Jews before Felix, governor of Caesarea, concerning the matters of which he was accused, saying: “I confess this to you: according to the sect which the Jews call a heresy, I so serve God, my Father, believing all things written in the Law and the prophets” (Acts 24). Likewise, Paul says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Do you not know,” he says, “that the Law is sin? By no means! The Law indeed is holy and good, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good” (Rom. 7).

### Chapter IV. Moses Was Not a Magician

Likewise, there are certain heretics who assert that Moses was a magician, that almighty God did not speak to him, and that he did not give him the Law. Against this error Paul wrote in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “In many ways and by many means, God formerly speaking to the fathers in the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1). But Moses is one of the prophets to whom God spoke. He is also called “faithful in the house” (Num. 12), to whom God spoke. Likewise, in the same Epistle: “Every house is built by someone; but he who created all things is God. And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, as testimony to the words that were to be spoken; but Christ as a son in his own house. We are that house, if we hold fast unto the end the confidence and glory of hope” (Heb. 3). The Apostle testifies that Moses was not a magician, but a faithful servant in the house of God.

Likewise, Moses is called friend and faithful servant of God in many Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments and of the prophets. Thus Blessed Paul recalled him in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying: “By faith Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the pleasure of temporary sin, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of Egypt. For he looked to God’s reward” (Heb. 11). From this it appears most certainly that Blessed Paul did not distrust Moses, the Law of Moses, or the God of the Hebrews. Rather, he declared and believed in his heart that Moses was holy and good, the Law holy and good, and the God of the Hebrews almighty God.

### Chapter V. Marriage Is Lawful

The heretics, following the heretic Tatian, who condemned all marriage, say and believe that men and women joined together in marriage cannot in any way be saved. But many testimonies of the divine Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments oppose this error.

It is found in the Gospel according to Matthew that the Pharisees asked the Lord: “Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatever?” He answered them: “Have you not read that he who made human beings from the beginning made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’? Thus they are no longer two but one flesh. Therefore, what God has joined, let no one separate” (Matt. 19). But Christ came into this world in order to separate a man from every evil, and likewise a woman. Everything that prevents a person from eternal life is evil; but if the use of marriage were evil, Christ would never have forbidden separation, nor would he have consented to it—he who consented to no evil. Likewise, Mark says of the same matter: “From the beginning of creation God made them male and female,” etc. (Mark 10). Likewise, Luke says: “In the days of Herod, king of Judaea, there was a certain priest named Zechariah, of the course of Abia,” etc. “And they were both righteous before the Lord, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke 1). It follows, therefore, that since they were righteous, they will be saved. “And they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both had advanced in their days” (ibid.). It should also be noted that the lack of a child was not owing to the man, but to the woman, because she was barren. “And the angel of the Lord, appearing to Zechariah in the temple, said to him: ‘Do not fear, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. For your wife will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John,’” etc. “For he shall be great before the Lord, and shall be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (ibid.). Likewise: “How shall I know this? For I am old, and my wife has advanced in her days” (ibid.). Note that he said this because he did not believe the angel’s words on account of his wife’s old age, since she had passed the age of conception. Likewise: “They made signs to his father what he wished him to be called” (ibid.). The Evangelist would not call him father unless he had a son. No one can be a natural father unless he has a natural son. Likewise: “Zechariah, his father, was filled with the Holy Spirit” (ibid.). Behold a threefold affirmation of fatherhood. And the Gospel does not deprive them of being both righteous before the Lord on account of begetting a son, provided that they walk in all the commandments of the Lord, neither in the Old Testament nor in the New.

Likewise, in the Epistle to the Corinthians, the Apostle, giving counsel to faithful Christians, said: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. Let the husband render to the wife her due; likewise also the wife to her husband. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7). That is, do not abstain if the other does not consent. Likewise, in the same Epistle: “I say to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them to remain as they are, as I do. But if they do not have self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. But to those joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband” (ibid.). It follows: “If any man has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her,” etc. “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the faithful wife,” and conversely; “otherwise your children would be unclean. But now they are clean” (ibid.). The Apostle did not believe that a husband and wife, if they are faithful, lose their holiness by rendering the marital due, if their other works are good.

Likewise, the Apostle says in the same Epistle: “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (ibid.). The same Apostle says in the same Epistle: “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not give her in marriage does better” (ibid.). The Apostle would not have given these above-mentioned commands to his disciples or written these words to them if he believed that they were to be damned because of this marital act.

Likewise, the Apostle says in the Epistle to Timothy: “The Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, forbidding marriage” (1 Tim. 4). Note that the Holy Spirit openly revealed that some would depart from the faith, adhere to doctrines of demons, and speak lies in hypocrisy. Such persons forbid marriage. Likewise, in the same Epistle the Apostle says: “I wish younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no opportunity for reproach” (1 Tim. 5). Note that the Apostle did not believe that married persons had any occasion of condemnation because of this act.

We have also in the First Epistle of Blessed Peter. Blessed Peter the Apostle, who was established by God as prince of all the apostles and also head of the whole Church, as Christ says in the Gospel, “You shall be called Cephas,” and elsewhere, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16), after writing his instruction to faithful Christian men, wrote to women concerning how they should be subject to their own husbands, preserving humility and modesty: “Likewise, let women be subject to their husbands, so that, if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives,” etc. “For in this manner holy women of old, hoping in God, adorned themselves for their husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord; and you are her daughters when you do good,” etc. (1 Pet. 3). Here Blessed Peter indicates that husbands should not depart from wives, nor wives from husbands, because Abraham did not depart from Sarah his wife except through death; rather, by God’s ordinance he knew her and begot a son, as Elkanah knew Hannah and Joachim Susanna.

Likewise, Blessed Paul says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “I wish you to know that the head of every man is Christ, the head of woman is man, and the head of Christ is God. Man is not from woman, but woman from man. For man was not created for woman, but woman for man. Nevertheless, neither is man without woman nor woman without man, in the Lord” (1 Cor. 11).

Likewise, it is found in John, chapter 2, that our Savior, his Mother, and his disciples were invited and came to a wedding; and at that wedding he performed before his disciples the beginning of his signs, namely, turning water into wine. Therefore it is most certain that weddings are good, since it is not to be believed that Christ would have come if they were not good, nor that he would have performed a miracle there. Likewise, Paul says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “A woman is bound by the law of her husband for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband sleeps, she is freed from the law of her husband and may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Cor. 7). Likewise, Paul says to Timothy: “A woman shall be saved through bearing children, if she remains in faith, love, sanctification, and sobriety” (1 Tim. 2).

### Chapter VI. The Conception and Birth of John the Baptist Were Announced by a Good Angel

Likewise, they say that John the Baptist was announced not by a good angel but by a demonic one. Nor do they believe him to be good. But many Gospel testimonies are found against this error. Thus Blessed John wrote in his Gospel: “There was a man sent from God whose name was John. This man came for testimony,” etc. (John 1). Likewise, he testified in the same Gospel concerning Christ: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (ibid.). John also bore testimony about Christ: “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit of God descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit,’” etc. (ibid.). Likewise, in the same Gospel: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled” (John 3). Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew Christ commends John the Baptist himself, saying: “Amen, I say to you, among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11). Likewise: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? I tell you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare my way before you’” (ibid.). Whoever thinks evil or perversely of John is against Christ, the apostles, and the catholic faith.

We have in the Gospel that John the Baptist himself baptized Christ in the river Jordan, saw the Holy Spirit descending upon him in the form of a dove, saw the heavens opened, and heard the voice of the Father saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 4). If John had been announced by an evil spirit, as the heretics say, Christ would never have allowed himself to be baptized by him, nor would he have wished so great a sacrament to be initiated by him. Likewise, in Matthew, Christ himself approves him, saying to the Pharisees: “Amen, amen, I say to you: tax collectors and prostitutes go before you into the kingdom of God. For John the Baptist came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him; tax collectors, sinners, and prostitutes believed him. But you, seeing him, did not afterward repent so as to believe him” (Matt. 21). Behold, Christ declares of John the Baptist that John himself walked in the way of righteousness—the way by which one goes to the kingdom of God—and preached it. He would not have done this if he were evil or had been announced by an evil spirit. Likewise, in the Gospel according to John, concerning the commendation of John the Baptist: “You sent to John; he bears testimony to the truth. But I do not receive testimony from a human being; rather, I say this so that you may be saved. He was a burning and shining lamp; and you were willing to rejoice for an hour in his light” (John 5).

### Chapter VII. On Christ’s Incarnation, Birth, Passion, Death, Resurrection, and Whether He Truly Ate and Drank

There are certain heretics concerning Christ’s incarnation, among them those following the Condomanian heresy, who say that “Christ was not born of a woman; nor did he have true flesh, nor did he truly die, nor suffer anything; rather, he feigned his passion. Nor do they believe that he ate or drank, as though he had a phantom body; nor that he rose again.”

Against the error of those heretics who do not believe that Christ was born of a virgin woman, we have testimony in Matthew: “When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea” (Matt. 2). Likewise, in the same Gospel: “An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: ‘Arise and take the child with Mary his mother,’” etc. (ibid.). Likewise, in the Gospel according to Luke: “Joseph went up from Galilee to Bethlehem, the city, to enroll there with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant. And the days were completed for her to give birth; and she bore her firstborn son,” etc. (Luke 2). Likewise, in the same Gospel the angel of the Lord announced the birth to the shepherds, saying: “For behold, I proclaim to you great joy which shall be for all the people, because today there has been born to you a Savior, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David. And this shall be the sign to you: you will find an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and placed in a manger” (ibid.). Likewise: “When eight days were completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (ibid.). Likewise: “When Jesus was twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and when the days were completed, as they returned, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem; and his parents did not know,” etc. “And Jesus advanced in age and grace and the Holy Spirit before God and human beings” (ibid.). Likewise, Paul testifies in the Epistle to the Galatians that Christ was born of a woman when he says: “But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. 4).

We also have many testimonies concerning Christ’s conception, birth, circumcision, childhood, age, and youth. Likewise, John says concerning his birth: “For this I was born, and for this I came, to bear testimony to the truth” (John 18).

Testimonies concerning Christ’s incarnation against heretics who do not believe that Christ had true flesh, but that he assumed an aerial body.

But John wrote his Gospel against this error, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” etc. “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). Likewise, in the same Gospel: “The Jews asked Pilate, because it was the Preparation, that the bodies should not remain on the cross on the Sabbath,” etc., “that their legs might be broken. Therefore the soldiers broke the legs of the first and of the other who was crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; rather, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. And he who saw it bore testimony, and his testimony is true” (John 19). John says in his First Epistle: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus to have come in flesh is from God. And every spirit that divides Jesus is not from God,” that is, denies that he is a fleshly human being.

[Note: [Col. 1243D] That is, composed of true flesh.]

“And this is Antichrist” (1 John 4). Likewise, in the same Epistle: “And we know that the Son of God came, put on flesh for us, died, and rose from the dead for us” (ibid.). Likewise, John says in his Second Epistle: “Already many deceivers have gone out into the world, who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in flesh. This is the deceiver and Antichrist. Everyone who departs and does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have God. He who remains in the doctrine”—that is, in the apostolic faith—“has both the Father and the Son. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, but denies that Jesus Christ has come in flesh, do not receive him into your house, nor say ‘Greetings’ to him. For whoever says to him, ‘Greetings,’ shares in his evil works” (1 John 9–11).

Likewise, Paul says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined Son of God,” etc. (Rom. 1). Likewise, Peter says in his First Epistle: “Therefore, Christ having suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought, because whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins” (1 Pet. 4).

Likewise, against the same heretics who do not believe that Christ suffered or died: Matthew wrote against this error in the Gospel, saying: “Pilate handed Jesus, after he had been scourged, over to the Jews to be crucified. Then the governor’s soldiers, taking Jesus into the praetorium, stripped him and put a scarlet cloak around him; plaiting a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand,” etc. Likewise, in the same Gospel: “Then they crucified him,” etc. Likewise, in the same Gospel: “Then one of the soldiers, taking a spear, pierced his side, and blood and water came out” (Matt. 27). These things concern Christ’s passion and his death. The other Evangelists likewise testify to the same in their Gospels. Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles: “Peter, standing with all the apostles among the Jews, said: ‘Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God through words, mighty works, wonders, and signs, which God did through him in your midst, as you know—him, delivered up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, you afflicted and killed through the hands of the wicked; but God raised him up, having loosed the pains of hell’” (Acts 2). This testimony concerns Christ’s passion, death, and also resurrection, which all the apostles, remaining in the same place, bore witness to.

Likewise Peter, concerning Christ’s Passion, says in his First Epistle: [Col. 1245B] “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps,” etc. “When he suffered, he did not threaten; he bore our sins in his body upon the wood, by whose death we have been healed” (1 Pet. II). Likewise Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans, said concerning his death: “For when we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. V). The same, in the same epistle: “Christ Jesus, who died for us—indeed, who also rose again” (Rom. VIII); and many further testimonies on these matters are available.

Concerning Christ’s resurrection, against heretics who do not believe that Christ rose from the dead, Matthew says in the Gospel concerning Christ’s resurrection: [Col. 1245C] “The angel said to the women: Do not be afraid; I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here; he has risen, as he said” (Matt. XXVIII). Mark and Luke likewise testify to this in their Gospels. Likewise John says in the Gospel: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” But he was speaking of the temple of his body. “Therefore, when he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this,” etc. (John II.)

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Luke, affirming by testimony that Christ has human flesh: “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself; touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet” (Luke XXIV). Likewise [Col. 1245D] John, in the Gospel, concerning the resurrection of the flesh: “Jesus came, though the doors were shut, and stood in the midst of his disciples, and said to them: Peace be with you. Then he says to Thomas: Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing” (John XX).

There are certain heretics who do not believe that Christ ate and drank while he remained with his disciples before the Passion. But to overthrow this error we have, in the Gospel according to Matthew, testimony uttered by Christ himself, who is Truth, saying: “For John the Baptist came, neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and they say: He has a demon. The [Col. 1246A] Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say: Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matt. X). Likewise Luke bears testimony in the Gospel that he himself ate, saying: “A certain Pharisee asked him to eat with him” (Luke VII). It is altogether certain that he ate; otherwise he would not have been invited by anyone to eat.

Likewise in the same Luke: “A certain Pharisee asked him to dine at his house; and entering, he reclined” (Luke XI). The same writer testifies in the same Gospel: “And it came to pass, when Jesus had entered the house of a certain chief of the Pharisees, that he ate bread.” Likewise John in the Gospel: “Rabbi, eat” (John IV). His disciples said this to him when they came from Samaria, [Col. 1246B] bringing the food which they had bought, etc. If anyone objects that he said to them: “I have other food to eat which you do not know” (ibid.), this is true, because Christ himself used two kinds of food, namely bodily and spiritual; he said this concerning the spiritual food. Nor is it any less to be believed that the other evangelists testify that he used temporal food.

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew, when the disciples questioned him, saying: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” (Matt. XXVI), they said “for you,” not “for themselves,” “to prepare the Passover.” This establishes that he ate temporal food while he was with them. Likewise, there is testimony in the same Gospel [Col. 1246C] that Christ himself said: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will betray me” (ibid.). It is not to be believed that Christ himself dipped his hand in the dish unless he was eating. Mark and Luke testify to the same in their Gospels. These are testimonies concerning Christ’s eating before he suffered.

But after his Passion, Luke testifies in the Gospel that he ate before his disciples, saying: “Have you here anything to eat? And they offered him a piece of roasted fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, taking the remains, he gave them to them” (Luke XXIV). In the same place Luke testifies in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “And eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem” [Col. 1246D] (Acts I). Thus it is altogether certain and firm that, before he suffered, Christ used all human activities, as Paul testifies in the Epistle to the Philippians, saying: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and, being found in appearance as a man, humbled himself unto death” (Phil. IV). And let these things concerning Christ’s humanity suffice.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Man-Made Churches

Concerning ecclesiastical institutions, we read in the Old Testament that the Lord showed Moses on the mountain a tabernacle not made by hands, saying: “Go, [Col. 1247A] and make a tabernacle not made by hands like this one, in which I may dwell among them when I speak with you; in which gifts, libations, sacrifices, victims, and offerings brought by the Israelite people may be offered by the priests.”

Then Moses faithfully carried this out according to the Lord’s command. And after Moses, when the people of Israel entered the promised land, they brought it with them to Shiloh. In it was the ark of the covenant, within which were a golden vessel containing manna, the tablets of the covenant, and Aaron’s rod, which had put forth leaves.

Then, after a long time, Solomon, son of David, by the Lord’s command built a man-made temple in Jerusalem. There all the Israelite people gathered for worship and sacrifice, just as [Col. 1247B] their fathers had been accustomed to come to the former tabernacle, thus observing the legal commandments of the Lord until Christ’s coming.

But when Christ came, unwilling to destroy the law but to fulfil it, he wished to be presented there by his parents and, according to the law given by God and customary practice, to be offered. After this he is found to have come into the temple in his youth with his parents, when he was twelve years old (Luke II). Then, after thirty years of his age, he came to Jerusalem, as is found in the Gospel according to Matthew: “And he entered the temple and drove from the temple all those buying and selling, saying: My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. XXI). For Christ himself [Col. 1247C] testified that the temple was “the house of God and of prayer.” Likewise Mark gives the same testimony in the same words in his Gospel (ch. XI), and also records that he forbade anyone to carry a vessel through the temple. Luke likewise testifies in his Gospel in these words. John also wrote in his Gospel: “And Jesus found in the temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves,” etc. (John II).

It is found in the Gospels that Christ came to the temple many times, teaching the people there; and in it he performed many signs and miracles in healing the sick, as Matthew the Evangelist relates: “The blind and the lame came to Jesus, and he healed them” (Matt. XXI). We also have in the Gospels that, when Jesus travelled through the Israelite [Col. 1247D] cities preaching, he especially entered the synagogues of the Jews. There, teaching the people concerning the kingdom of God, he performed many signs and wonders, as Matthew says: “Jesus went round all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel, and healing every sickness and every infirmity” (Matt. IX). Likewise, in Matthew’s Gospel, he himself testifies, saying to you: “Every day I sat among you, teaching in the temple” (Matt. XXVI). John gives testimony in his Gospel in the same words: “I always taught in synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews assemble; and I spoke nothing in secret” (John XVIII).

If you object to us that he preached more often in other [Col. 1248A] places than in temples or synagogues, that is true; but because of the multitude of crowds coming to him, lest they impede the ministers of the temple and synagogues, or render their own vows and the duties imposed upon them less fully, he withdrew to mountains and other places.

But after his Ascension, the disciples, desiring to imitate Christ their Master and Saviour, so long as they remained in Jerusalem came daily to the temple to pray, as is found in the Acts of the Apostles: “Every day the apostles continued steadfastly and prayed with one accord in the temple” (Acts II). And again: “Peter and John were going up to the temple to pray, at the ninth hour of prayer” (Acts III). Likewise, in the same book, when Annas the chief priest [Col. 1248B] and all who were with him laid hands upon the apostles and placed them in public custody: “But an angel of the Lord by night opened the doors of the prison; and, bringing them out, said: Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life” (ibid.). From this arose the man-made house of prayer which we call a church.

When the apostles and their disciples had been expelled from Jerusalem and, by God’s will, scattered through diverse parts of the world, and when in all the cities of the Jews they saw buildings of synagogues, then passing among the Gentiles they found in their cities various temples of idols. In these [Col. 1248C] temples people offered their vows and sacrifices to the idols of demons, and gathered constantly in order to fulfil these observances. The apostles, guided by the Holy Spirit, formed the plan that, in order more easily to uproot them from so great an error and wickedness and to deliver them from diabolical bonds, they should command houses made by hands to be built in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. They showed that these should be built after the pattern of the temple, in which the faithful people might gather faithfully and devoutly for baptism, worship, sacrifice, hearing God’s word, and receiving all the sacraments of Christianity. In these houses—which, because of the congregation of the people within them, we call churches—the apostles appointed ministers, namely bishops, presbyters, and deacons, to accomplish Christ’s mystery, [Col. 1248D] as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “And when they had appointed presbyters for them in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed” (Acts XXIII).

From this we have that presbyters were first ordained in the Church of God by the apostles. We have deacons in the Epistle to the Corinthians; rebuking them, the Apostle called the house in which the faithful were assembled a church, saying: “Do you not have houses for eating and drinking? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you” (1 Cor. XI).

Likewise Paul says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “Let women [Col. 1249A] be silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but to be subject, as the law says. But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church” (1 Cor. XIV).

In this and many other passages the Apostle indicates that every house in which the faithful have assembled in order to participate in Christ’s sacraments is to be called a church.

Likewise John, in his final Epistle, threatening Diotrephes, wrote: “Therefore, if I come, I shall call attention to the works which he does, babbling against us with malicious words; and, as though these things were not enough for him, he himself does not receive the brethren, forbids those who do receive them, and expels them from the church.” Likewise Paul to Timothy: [Col. 1249B] “But if I delay, that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of the Lord, which is the Church of the living God,” etc. (1 Tim. III).

In these testimonies of the apostles written above, and in many others set down in this treatise, it is plainly shown that the house of God and house of prayer is called and understood to be a man-made church, in which Christ’s sacraments are performed by ordained ministers for the salvation of faithful Christians.

## CHAPTER IX. On Altars

But since all heretics count as nothing man-made churches, the altars within them, the sacraments performed in them by God’s ministers, and every ecclesiastical ornament [Col. 1249C], and say that these do nothing toward the salvation of souls, and despise them, we shall briefly set forth testimonies to overthrow this great and heinous error. First, concerning the altar, without which a man-made church ought neither to exist nor, perhaps, to be called blessed; on altars gifts, oblations, and sacrificial victims are offered for sins. In the Gospel according to Matthew we have that Truth itself instructs one who offers a gift, and teaches him how he ought to offer, saying: “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then, when you return, you shall offer your gift” (Matt. XVI). By this Christ himself indicates that the faithful [Col. 1249D] should have altars in churches on which they may offer gifts.

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Luke, Christ himself wished to be offered by his parents in the temple according to the Lord’s law, and sacrificial victims to be offered for him upon the altar in the temple, namely “a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons” (Luke II). From this it is understood that, just as Christ wished to be offered at the altar and to have a victim given for himself, so all faithful people throughout the regions of the world should have altars on which they offer to God gifts and oblations for their sins. Likewise Paul, concerning the same matter, instructing his disciples to have altars and serve God in them, and to become participants in God’s gifts through service at the altar, wrote: “Those [Col. 1250A] who serve the altar partake with the altar” (1 Cor. IX). Likewise, Paul, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, “offered in the temple, for himself and for the others who had been purified with him, victims upon the altar” (Acts XXI). He did not wish to despise altars or count them as nothing, but gave an example.

Likewise, in the Apocalypse (ch. VIII), John testifies that he saw an altar in heaven, upon which much incense—the prayers of the saints—was offered by an angel. Therefore Blessed John, because he saw a golden altar in heaven before God, wished that upon earth, in man-made churches, an altar made by hands, clean and purified, should be built.

Against the errors mentioned above we might introduce, as it were, a vast cloud of witnesses from the Old Testament, namely the Law, [Col. 1250B] the Prophets, and the Psalms. But because these heretics do not wish to answer—or give a reasoned reply—to the testimonies of the Old Testament Law and Prophets brought against them, since they are ignorant and would immediately be convicted, we did not wish to labour over these. We have done so only concerning the testimonies which we have gathered from the books of the New Testament; to these they can now have no just excuse for refusing to answer or give any account.

## CHAPTER X. On Ecclesiastical Chant

Likewise, heretics disapprove of the Church’s chant and praises, which clerics render to God their Creator from the New and Old Testament. Against this error we offer [Col. 1250C] the testimony of Paul, who says in the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking among yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing in your hearts to the Lord; always giving thanks for all things, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God and the Father” (Eph. V).

Likewise Paul, concerning the same matter, says to the Colossians: “Let the word of Christ dwell richly in you in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing to the Lord in your hearts with grace” (Col. III).

Likewise John saw in the Apocalypse twenty-four elders, who “fell before the Lamb, each having [Col. 1250D] golden bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints; and they sang a new song, saying: You are worthy, O Lord, to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us to God by your blood” (Apoc. V).

Likewise John says in the same book: “And the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing on their harps; and they sang, as it were, a new song before the throne of God” (Apoc. XIV). And elsewhere: “Having the harps of God, and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God,” etc. (Apoc. XV). Likewise John in the same book: “I heard a great voice of many multitudes in heaven saying: Alleluia: praise and glory and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just” (Apoc. XII).

## CHAPTER XI. On the Sacrament of Christ’s Body and Blood

[Col. 1251A]

After we have briefly treated, though unworthily, some rather than all of the testimonies that occur to us concerning the house of the Lord, which is the Church, let us bring forward divine authority against heretical perversity concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. This sacrament is worthier than all sacraments, and its consecration is celebrated in the house of the Lord, which is the Church of the living God, as Paul testifies (1 Tim. III).

Christ, seeing that death was imminent for him and wishing to commend to us the sacrament of his body and blood, took bread, gave thanks, blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples; likewise the cup. Thus Matthew the Evangelist says: “While they were dining, [Col. 1251B] Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, and said: Take and eat; this is my body. And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: Drink from this, all of you. For this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI).

Likewise Mark, concerning the same matter: “As they ate, Jesus took bread, and, blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, and said: Take; this is my body. And having taken the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, and they all drank from it. And he said to them: This is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many” (Mark XIV). Likewise Luke: “And having taken bread, [Col. 1251C] he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: This is my body, which shall be given for you; do this in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup, after he had dined, saying: For this cup is the new covenant in my blood, which shall be poured out for you” (Luke XXII). The evangelists indeed assert that the Lord took bread and gave it to his disciples, saying: “This is my body.”

Observe every detail: “He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it.” The Gospel does not say that the Lord took his body, blessed what he broke, and gave it to his disciples; rather, the evangelists testify that he took bread and, blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, saying: “This is my body; this is my cup of the new covenant [Col. 1251D] in my blood, which shall be poured out for you.”

But heretics say that the demonstrative pronoun *hoc*, “this,” refers not to the bread which he held in his hands, blessed, broke, and distributed to his disciples, but to his own body, which performed all these things. Their most wicked error arose from ignorance of the force of the pronoun. *Hoc*, “this,” cannot be referred back except to things [or: to those things] which have been mentioned. But in the handing down of this sacrament no mention of his body had yet been made; therefore what they assert is utterly false. Rather, just as flour, water, and salt, when these three have been mixed and baked, are no longer the flour, water, and salt which they formerly were, [Col. 1252A] but are truly pure bread and are called such, so the bread which Jesus Christ took into his hands after supper, once he blessed and broke it, is understood and believed to be Christ’s body, not bread. This is what Christ our Saviour and Redeemer gave to his disciples at supper, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.” The same reasoning applies to the cup, after he gave thanks, gave it to his disciples, and said to them: “Drink from this, all of you; this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be poured out for many for the remission of sins.” And he added: “As often as you do this, do it in remembrance of me.”

These words, spoken by Christ over this sacrament at supper, ought especially to be noted, as though they were his final testament. But when he said, “As often as you do this, do it in remembrance of me,” these words indicate that Christ did not wish this great and most holy sacrament to end there. Rather, he commanded his apostles, as his co-heirs, and their successors to perform this sacrament for ever after his Passion, resurrection, and ascension, in remembrance of his Passion and in hope of eternal salvation.

When the Lord Jesus had gathered his disciples, he promised them that he would give them his flesh under the appearance of bread and his blood under the appearance of wine, as is contained in the Gospel of Blessed John (John VI), [Col. 1252C] saying: “The bread which I shall give you is my flesh for the life of the world.” But when the Jews heard this, they disputed among themselves, saying: “How can he give us his flesh to eat?” Because of this dispute, and because he understood that they lacked spiritual understanding, he said to them with solemn assurance: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” And: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him on the last day.”

In these words it must be noted that no one can have eternal life unless he has eaten his flesh and drunk his blood, according to what he himself said. Yet Christ did not wish to deceive his disciples or allow his promise to be made void. At the Last Supper he gave his flesh and blood to his disciples under the appearance of bread and wine, so that they might eat without the mouth’s repugnance. But whatever words Christ spoke are altogether certain and true, and do not deceive in any respect. For he said many things that are true which, if another had said them, would seem neither true nor credible.

For he said: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John X). “I am the good shepherd” (John VI). “I am the living bread; I am the vine, and you are the branches” (John XV). “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). So great is the force and power of God’s word that everything [Col. 1253A] which he has said comes to pass; it never deceives or fails, as the Psalmist said: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII).

And this should be noted: the evangelist employed not the past tense but the present. Although he wrote after the Passion, he understood and believed that Christ is what Christ said he was, is, and always will be (Apoc. I). Thus the words which Christ spoke at supper before his disciples and taught them retain in themselves the same force that they had among the apostles in the sacrament of bread and wine—that is, of the Lord’s body and blood—and they will retain the same force, power, and efficacy in God’s ministers until the end of the age.

After our Lord Jesus Christ had heard of the Jewish dispute concerning his flesh and said to them, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life and eternal resurrection,” he added, so that the promise of eating his sacrament might not seem difficult and useless to them, but certain and most beneficial, and able in the present time to be received under the appearance of bread and wine—just as he gave it to them at supper and declared that his body was to be distributed: [Col. 1253B] “For my flesh truly is food, and my blood truly is drink” (John VI).

But there are certain heretics who believe that, by hearing God’s word, they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood—as though Christ, who knows all things, did not know how to say: “My word truly is [Col. 1253C] food, and my blood truly is drink,” substituting one word for another.

But when he said, “My flesh truly is food, and my blood truly is drink,” he did not say, “My flesh truly is hearing” or “understanding”; rather, by the working of spiritual grace, my flesh truly is food and my blood truly is drink.

And Christ said this properly. [Note: [Col. 1253] “Properly,” because we truly, really, and substantially eat the Lord’s body and drink his blood.] It is altogether certain that he said this concerning the sacrament of bread and wine which he bestowed on them at supper; and every day this sacrament is consecrated upon the altar in the Church of God by ordained ministers of God, with commemoration of his own words. But because he wished to show its benefit to those who rightly receive this sacrament, [Col. 1253D] he added: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John VI). And: “He who eats me shall himself live because of me” (ibid.).

This, then, is the power of this sacrament and the benefit of receiving it rightly: namely, that the faithful person remains in God and God in him. Such a person bears much fruit, as John testifies: “Because, without me,” as Truth itself says, “you can do nothing” (John XV).

But Blessed Paul, hearing, knowing, and believing the power and benefit of this great and most certain sacrament, wished to instruct his disciples by words [Col. 1254A] and deeds, withholding from them nothing useful for their salvation, so that it might always be held in memory by their successors. He wrote in the Epistle addressed to the Corinthians: “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that our Lord Jesus Christ, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: Take and eat; this is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. XI). And this should be noted: Christ commanded his disciples to perform this sacrament in remembrance of himself, and that they should hand it down to their disciples as they themselves received it from him, so that the memory of him and of his Passion might endure through this sacrament among the faithful for ever and ever. [Col. 1254B] (ibid.)

Likewise: “In the same manner also the cup, after he had dined, saying: This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me; for as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Therefore whoever eats this bread and drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (ibid.). But if, as heretics say, consecrated bread and wine have no dignity, why would the Apostle declare that one who receives the consecrated bread unworthily is guilty of the Lord’s body and blood? For if someone eats ordinary bread, he is neither called nor believed guilty of the Lord’s body and blood. Therefore the Apostle exhorts that, before anyone wishes to receive this sacrament of bread and wine, “let him examine himself”—that is, cleanse himself from his sins—“and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (ibid.).

Likewise, the Apostle gives the reason why one receiving it ought to be cleansed from sins when he says: “For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (ibid.).

Likewise, the Apostle, approving and affirming that this sacrament of bread and wine is the Lord’s body—which he had shown the Corinthians by word and deed—wrote in the epistle [Col. 1254D] sent to them: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not communion in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not participation in the body of the Lord?” (1 Cor. X). This does not depend on the merit of the consecrator, but upon the power and truth of the Holy Spirit: “For we, though many, are one bread, one body, all who partake of the one bread” (ibid.).

In this chapter the apostle Paul makes clear that he himself performed this sacrament which he had received from the Lord. The other apostles did likewise.
