Likewise the apostle Paul says in the same epistle: “When you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper; [Col. 1255A] for each one takes his own supper first to eat. And one indeed is hungry, while another is drunk” (1 Cor. XI). But to gather in one place, eat one’s own private food, give nothing to others, and become drunk—these actions are not eating the Lord’s supper. Rebuking the Corinthians, the Apostle asks: “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink,” namely ordinary food? “Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing?” (ibid.) I praise you in this, that you gather together in one place in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; I do not praise you in this, that you eat your own food and shame those who have nothing, but hunger because they have nothing to eat.

[Col. 1255B] From this it is apparent and evident that the disciples of the apostles, imitating them, carried out the celebration of this sacrament throughout the world, keeping it in remembrance.

And we say and believe—and the whole Roman Church, first founded by blessed Peter and Paul, says and believes—that every person who has no faith in this sacrament and in the other traditions of the apostles, such as baptism, confession and penance, and the other apostolic institutions performed in the present Church, is alien from the unity of the holy Church and the Catholic faith, separated from the fellowship of the holy faithful, namely [Col. 1255C] those who have gone before and those still living, and damned for ever and ever.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Sacrament of Baptism

After we have dealt, though unworthily, with the treatment of the body and blood of Jesus Christ as universally celebrated in the Catholic Church extended throughout the world, let us begin on baptism. Against the errors of heretics who corrupt the sacrament of baptism in water, let us bring forward, in refutation, such authorities of the New Testament as the Holy Spirit supplies us.

For some heretics say that this sacrament of baptism in water, without their laying on of hands upon the recipient, is of no benefit for attaining everlasting salvation either to adults [Col. 1255D] or even to infants. And this error, among the other errors in which they secretly wallow, is the greatest. We have in the Gospel that John the Baptist, in order to be Christ’s forerunner and true herald, was sent by almighty God to baptize in water, as the Baptist himself testifies, and John testifies in the Gospel: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven” (John III). And: “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: He upon whom you shall see the Spirit of God descending and remaining as a dove, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John I).

Likewise, at Christ’s baptism the heavens were opened, the Father’s voice was heard, and the Holy Spirit appeared [Col. 1256A] (Matt. IV). See the great and divine sacrament of piety. For the whole Trinity acted in Christ’s baptism and deigned to be present: the Father is heard, the Son is baptized, and the Holy Spirit appears in the form of a dove. When the Son of God was baptized, the heavens were opened. And because the institution and sacrament of baptism is of such great dignity, the Lord therefore says to Nicodemus in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III). Likewise: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God. What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit” (ibid.).

Hear, heretic: you must have two births, namely a fleshly and a spiritual birth. And, as the divine utterance testifies, whoever lacks spiritual birth cannot see the kingdom of God or enter it. But spiritual birth cannot be had unless fleshly birth has first been had. How then do you say that fleshly birth is evil, when spiritual birth follows from it—a birth which grants one to see the kingdom of God and enter it—since the spiritual birth cannot be had without the fleshly? For one who has not yet been born can never be born again. Therefore one must first be born and afterwards be born again.

We have in the Gospels that John the Baptist, inspired by the Holy Spirit, went into the wilderness and preached and administered repentance and baptism in water to those [Col. 1256C] who came to him. Therefore Christ, wishing to sanctify and confirm John’s baptism in water, came to him and deigned to receive from him baptism in water upon himself, giving all the faithful an example that they ought to receive the sacrament of baptism in water for the attainment of the salvation of their souls. In it they are cleansed from all sins, both original and actual. And it is the faith of the universal Church that, without this sacrament, everyone who despises it and refuses to receive it can in no way deserve or attain eternal life, as our Saviour Jesus Christ testifies in the Gospel of Blessed John, saying: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.”

[Col. 1256D] We also have in the Gospel that, before the Passion, his disciples, at his command, baptized those who believed in the Son of God; as it says: “When Jesus therefore knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples—he left Judaea” (John IV), etc.

But it should be known that John the Baptist baptized in the name of the Lord who had sent him. But our Lord Jesus Christ, because he was sent from heaven by the Father, bringing eternal salvation to the human race with himself, and teaching his disciples the use of the sacrament of baptism, sent them throughout the whole world and commanded them to preach the kingdom of God and to baptize, adding, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Col. 1257A] (Matt. XXVIII), etc. Thus, at the end of the Gospel of the blessed evangelist Matthew, appearing to his disciples on the mountain, he said to them: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them” (ibid.), etc. And he adds: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark XVI). From this authority we may rightly understand that the use of the sacrament of baptism benefits no unbeliever toward salvation, even if he receives it.

The heretics also say that this sacrament cannot benefit anyone unless he asks for it with his own mouth and heart. From this they advance the error that water baptism is of no benefit to little children.

But we have in the Gospel of blessed Mark that, after his resurrection, the Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1257B] appeared to his disciples and said to them: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature: he who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (ibid.).

In this passage he made no exception for adults or little children, males or women, when he says, “to every creature.” Therefore it is the faith of the Catholic Church throughout the whole world, wherever the name of Christ is celebrated and believed, that whether they are little children or grown persons, men or women, if they receive this sacrament of baptism, they are without doubt saved; and, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, they are cleansed and purified from all sins, whether original or actual, [Col. 1257C] unless they fall into the corruption of sin after the washing of baptism before they die.

Against the error of heretics who say that little children cannot be saved in baptism, blessed Paul said in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “If any believing brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away. And if any believing woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not put away her husband. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy” (I Cor. VII).

The Apostle says that the children of believing parents are clean and holy. Much more, then, ought it to be believed [Col. 1257D] that baptized little children, through immersion in water performed by the ministers of the Church and the invocation of the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, are believed to be cleansed and saved through the faith of their sponsors.

Hence we have in the Gospel of Matthew that the daughter of the Canaanite woman was made whole through her mother’s faith (Matt. XV). Likewise, we have in the Gospel that certain persons carrying a paralytic to Jesus, lying on a bed, could not approach him because of the crowd standing at the entrance of the house; so that they might place him before him, they lowered the paralytic through the tiles before him, that he might heal him. “But he, seeing their faith” (Luke V), gave health to the sick man through the faith of those carrying him. Likewise, when a royal official came to Jesus on account of his child, he heard from the Lord: “Go, and as you have believed, [Col. 1258A] let it be done to you; and his child was healed from that hour” (John V). Likewise, the deceased daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was raised by the Lord at her father’s request (Matt. IX). Likewise, when the son of a certain widow was being carried outside the city gate for burial, the Lord, moved by compassion at his mother’s weeping and lamentation, raised him and restored him to his mother.

And therefore, by these Gospel authorities and very many other testimonies contained in the apostolic Scriptures, the universal Church throughout the whole world believes and maintains that through the faith of sponsors, by the invocation of the Holy Trinity made by ministers of the Church, spiritual grace is bestowed in baptism by almighty God upon infants and little children. Paul testifies to this, saying: “I planted, Apollos watered, [Col. 1258B] but God gave the increase. Therefore neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III). And because the Apostle said, “God gives the increase,” every believer ought to believe that, whatever the character of the one baptizing with the invocation—that is, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—God gives increase, namely spiritual grace, to the recipient of this sacrament, whether little or grown.

Hence Peter said in the Acts of the Apostles: “Let every one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts II).

Likewise, you say, heretic, that a sinner cannot baptize. How then did the apostles baptize, who were sinners, as John testifies when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I)?

Likewise, you say that the Holy Spirit is not given through the ministry of a priest—a Spirit whom you falsely claim to give. How do you say that you give the Holy Spirit when you yourself oppose the Holy Spirit, so far as you are able? And when it belongs to God alone to give the Holy Spirit?

Likewise, it is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles that “the apostles laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (Acts VIII). It is not said [Col. 1258D] that they gave him; rather, through their laying on of hands, people received the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles: “Both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him; and the Holy Spirit came down upon him” (ibid.).

Likewise, concerning infants and little children we find in the Gospels that our Lord Jesus Christ approved such an age of childhood, when he said to his disciples, who were forbidding those bringing little children to him: “Allow the little children to come to me, and do not forbid them to come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX; Mark X; Luke XVIII). Whoever, therefore, does not believe that the baptism of little children and infants [Col. 1259A] avails for the salvation of eternal life believes against the Gospel and is like one who prevents little children from coming to Christ.

Likewise, we have in the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Corinthians that in the primitive Church the disciples of the apostles were baptized for the dead, believing that this contributed to the salvation of their souls. For the Apostle says: “If the dead do not rise, what shall those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead do not rise at all, why then are they baptized for them? Why also do we preach every hour?” (I Cor. 15.) [Note: On this passage of the Apostle and its true sense, see Bellarmine, *On Purgatory*, book I, chapter 6.] If, then, it was the faith of the primitive apostolic Church that the baptism of living persons on behalf of the dead conferred eternal salvation upon those dead persons—who had not heard it or received it, and therefore others were baptized for them—[Col. 1259B] how much more ought the faithful now to believe that little children baptized through the faith of sponsors will obtain eternal salvation and spiritual grace. And let this suffice concerning baptism.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the sacrament of penance

We have spoken of the sacrament of baptism, which is the first plank after shipwreck. Therefore, in the second place after baptism, we must speak of penance, a sacrament which we ought authoritatively to confirm against heretical perversity. John’s preaching begins from penance. For he says: “Repent: for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III). What the herald had said, Christ himself afterwards taught [Col. 1259C] at the beginning of his preaching, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV). And Peter, in the Acts of the Apostles, said to those who had been pierced in heart by his preaching: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts II). Likewise Peter: “Repent, therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts III).

But because in penance inward contrition of heart, confession by mouth, and worthy satisfaction imposed by the priest are necessary, let us bring forward examples of each. That inward contrition of heart is necessary, we have from the authority of the Psalmist, who says: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. L). For contrition is compunction [Col. 1259D] of heart arising from remembrance of past evils, as in the Gospel: “Peter remembered the word of Jesus, which he had said: Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times; and going outside, he wept bitterly” (Matt. XXVI). See how he was pierced in heart: remembering his past evil, he had recourse to tears.

Likewise, confession by mouth is necessary, and it is spoken of in two ways: confession of God and confession of sins. Confession of God is that of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father” (Matt. X). Confession of sins is that of which David says in the psalm: “Give thanks to [confess] the Lord, for he is good; for his mercy endures for ever” (Ps. CV). He called the Lord good and merciful, because if anyone confesses, he is ready to show mercy. For he foresaw his mercies from afar through the Holy Spirit when he said: “I shall sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Likewise: “I shall sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. C). Likewise: “Your mercies are many, O Lord” (Ps. CLVI). Likewise David: “I said: I shall confess against myself my injustice to the Lord” (Ps. XXXI). For confession is the abhorring of one’s own deed together with self-accusation. Hence: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII). And James, in the catholic Epistle: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray [Col. 1260B] for one another, that you may be saved” (James V). And the apostle Paul: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X). Here, from James’s authority, we have that we are to confess our sins. And he did not say, “Confess to God alone,” as the heretic says, but “confess to one another.” And that we ought to confess to priests, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go, and show yourself to the priest” (Luke XVII). And James: “Is any among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him” (James V).

That satisfaction is likewise necessary is found in the Gospel, where Luke says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke III). Note: to produce worthy fruits, [Col. 1260C] fruits worthy of repentance, means nothing other than to perform the worthy satisfaction imposed by the priest. Satisfaction is the sentence or judgment given by a priest to a penitent concerning sin. And this is the judgment of which it was said: “The Lord will not judge twice in the same matter” (Nahum I). And Paul: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI). And Peter: “Now is the time for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord” (I Peter IV).

And this is the power which the Lord gave to human beings, namely, the power of binding and loosing. For Truth itself says: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX). For just as, in the Old Testament, lepers were commanded to show themselves to priests, so that they might determine [Col. 1260D] who were clean and who unclean, so now the priest, in the exercise of his office, when he has heard the varieties of sins, knows who is to be bound and who loosed. Likewise, after Christ raised Lazarus, he said to his disciples: “Loose him” (John XI). The Lord willed that they should loose and show loosed the one whom he had raised. Thus God forgives sins through a minister. For when God forgives sins, and a human being forgives them, God does so in one way and the human being in another. God does so from himself, because by himself, when he wills, he forgives sins; human beings do so not from themselves, but by grace working in and through them. Thus it is true that God alone forgives sins, as [Col. 1261A] he himself says in the prophet: “I am he who blots out the iniquities and sins of the people” (Isa. XLII). Likewise: “He alone performs great wonders” (Ps. CXXXV). Nor is it denied that human beings also perform wonders, but not from themselves, as God does. Likewise: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII), because he is good from himself; yet we do not deny that there are good human beings. And so human beings forgive sins not from themselves, but God forgives through their ministry.

But you say that someone can be saved without confession, and you object that authority which says: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII). To this it must be said that the truly invisible priest, namely God, frees by contrition of heart from the guilt of eternal punishment the person who wishes to confess but cannot; but, while he is able, unless he confesses with his mouth, he does not absolve him. For it is certain that one who has a contrite heart wishes to confess; but he can abandon this good will. For while a human being is in this life, he does not will something that he cannot cease to will. And if, after losing this will, he should not wish to confess and then die, there is no doubt that he is condemned for the sin which he refused to confess. For no sin goes unpunished: either the human being punishes it, or God does. It is therefore apparent that God alone forgives sins, giving inner life through grace; and that the priest forgives not by giving inner life, but by absolving from the obligation of future eternal punishment through the satisfaction which he imposes. But your saying, “At whatever hour the sinner [Col. 1261C] groans, he shall be saved,” is said of those who, with the danger of death at hand, cannot have time for satisfaction. It is as though it said: At whatever hour in this life a sinner truly repents, he shall not perish in the life to come. Or it may be said of all: “At whatever hour he groans, he shall be saved,” because then the sinner’s salvation begins.

But after speaking of the matters to be considered in penance, we must say what penance is. Penance is to lament evils committed and not to commit again what is to be lamented. For one who so deplores deeds already done that he nevertheless commits others either does not yet know how to do penance or feigns it. Likewise, the person who still does what he has repented of is a mocker, not a penitent; nor does he seem to seek God in submission, but rather to mock him in pride. [Col. 1261D] Isaiah says to sinners: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I). The person who laments the past and does not again admit what is to be lamented is washed and clean. And this is true penance, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “There is greater joy in heaven among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need penance” (Luke XV). Not that anyone is righteous before God who has no need of penance, but “who do not need,” that is, who think that they have no need. And this is what heretics still retain from the arrogance of the Pharisees. They are those of whom Solomon says: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II). Let what we have said about penance suffice for the present subject.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the laying on of hands

[Col. 1262A]

After the treatment of penance follows the laying on of hands, which they call the “consolamentum.” The heretics presumptuously perform this laying on of hands among themselves, contrary to the Lord’s commands and the institutions of the apostles. We must first say how and by what persons it is performed, and what they think of it.

The manner of the “consolamentum” is as follows. The one called superior, bishop, or deacon is designated ruler of the other heretics subject to him. When they wish to perform the “consolamentum” for some man or woman, the one called “greater” and ordained, having washed his hands—as likewise all who wish to be present have washed their hands—holds in his hands the book of the Gospels and admonishes the person or persons who come to receive the “consolamentum” to place, in that “consolamentum,” all their faith and hope for the salvation of their souls in God and in the “consolamentum.” Then, placing the book upon their heads, they say the Lord’s Prayer seven times; and then, while all listen, he recites the Gospel of blessed John, beginning “In the beginning,” up to the place in the Gospel which says, “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I). [Col. 1262B] And thus that “consolamentum” is concluded.

Let us say by what persons it is performed: namely, by those who among them are called “ordained.” If they are absent, it is supplied by those called “consoled”; and if men are not present, women alone perform it for the sick.

Let us say what they think of it. In it, all those generally who are to be saved place their faith and hope; and they believe that through it they obtain forgiveness of all their sins and cleansing from their offences, without any satisfaction, if they immediately die. They believe that in it God gives them pardon not only for venial sins which they have committed, but also for crimes they have perpetrated. They also say that no one—adult or child, man or woman—unless he or she receives that “consolamentum” from their “consoled” persons, can obtain the heavenly kingdom and the fellowship of angels by any work, benefit, religious contemplation, or even martyrdom, even if, which is impossible, he or she abstains from all sins and offences [Col. 1262D] whatsoever.

They also believe that if the person who performs that “consolamentum” has fallen into any of the sins which they call “criminal”—such as eating meat, eggs, or cheese; killing a bird or any animal other than a creeping thing; or even those sins which the Roman Church calls “criminal,” such as murder, adultery, fornication, uncleanness, theft, false witness, perjury, and robbery—the “consolamentum” is of no benefit to those receiving it. For they say that one who has so fallen does not possess the Holy Spirit, and they believe that one who does not have it cannot give it to another. Indeed, they believe that such a person must receive that “consolamentum” again from someone else if he desires salvation, [Col. 1263A] and that this must be done universally for all fallen persons, both men and women, as stated.

But the Roman Apostolic Church judges all the aforesaid practices performed by heretics to be most evil and deadly errors, by many authorities, because they are not done by the persons by whom they ought to be done; nor were they instituted by Jesus Christ, by the apostles, or practised in their time. We also have in the Gospels that the Lord Jesus Christ, our Saviour, laid hands upon children brought to him and also upon the sick; he blessed them, and they were healed. We do not find that he bestowed this office on any disciple before his Passion, until he rose from the dead. But after the Resurrection he gave and granted only to ordained apostles the authority to baptize and to lay hands in the name of the Lord, so that those ordained by them might have the same authority of baptizing and laying on hands—namely, those whom God had chosen and whom they themselves had judged worthy. Hence we have in the Acts of the Apostles that, when Simon Magus offered money to blessed Peter and asked that such power to give the Holy Spirit be granted to him, so that whoever received his laying on of hands might receive the Holy Spirit, Peter answered: “You have neither lot nor part in this matter, because you have judged the gift of God to be obtainable with money. But ask God and repent of this great wickedness which has entered into your heart” (Acts VIII). Thus, rejecting him, he judged him unworthy of this divine office.

We also have in the same book that the apostles ordained priests and deacons [Col. 1263C] in all the cities where the name of our Lord Jesus Christ was celebrated and faithful Christians persevered, to perform these same divine sacraments. For example: “When they had appointed priests for them in every Church” (Acts XIV). Likewise, in the same book, when Paul wished to go from Asia to Jerusalem, passing through the churches in which he had ordained priests and bishops, he came to Miletus; and, sending to Ephesus, he called the elders of the Church and said to them: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to rule the Church of God, which he acquired by his blood” (Acts XX). And after our Lord Jesus Christ had chosen the apostles, and after his Ascension the apostles had appointed bishops, priests, and also deacons throughout all [Col. 1263D] the Churches for performing all the divine mysteries, granting to those ordained by them the same authority and tradition which they themselves had received from Christ—whoever acts or believes contrary to this apostolic tradition errs greatly and brings death upon himself. Hence the apostle James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all” (James II). Likewise Paul: “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (I Cor. V). And let this suffice against the persons of the heretics.

Likewise, against the manner of their “consolamentum”: heretics give that “consolamentum” to adults and children alike, men and women, something which was never done by the apostles or among their disciples, nor is it found to have been commanded by them. Likewise, upon those whom they wished to ordain as preachers, priests, or deacons over the people, the apostles laid hands only. Concerning others we find nothing in Holy Scripture except that they preached and baptized them with invocation of the Holy Spirit, as our Lord Jesus Christ had taught and commanded them, as it says: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). But he gave them the form and manner which is still constantly retained in the Church to this day. Hence one must wonder very greatly from whom such a custom of the heretics’ “consolamentum” had its beginning or took its origin; for it does not appear to derive from the prophets, Christ, [Col. 1264B] the apostles, or apostolic men who succeeded the apostles, since it differs greatly from the sayings, deeds, and writings of all these. Therefore it should be believed to belong to those of whom the apostle Paul wrote in his Epistle to Timothy: “A time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up for themselves teachers with itching ears, and indeed they will turn away from the truth” (II Tim. IV).

Likewise, these people are unwilling to believe or obey the sayings of the prophets, the traditions of the apostles, the practices of apostolic men, or even the writings of the holy Fathers. These heretics judge all persons, of whatever manner of life, who have not received that “consolamentum” from them to be damned. In this [Col. 1264C] they contradict the word of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said to his disciples: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn,” etc. (Luke VI). Therefore they may be among those of whom he added: “With what judgment you judge, you shall be judged; and with what measure you measure, it shall be measured back to you” (ibid.). Because they judge and condemn all others who are not of their party, their condemnation and judgment, God willing, shall be upon their own heads. Likewise, they do not attend to or obey the counsels of the blessed apostle Paul, who says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV). And elsewhere: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II).

## CHAPTER XV. On eating meat and certain other things

[Col. 1264D]

It is the belief of all heretics that no one who, after receiving their “consolamentum,” eats meat, cheese, or eggs can be saved unless he receives penance from them and is afterwards reconsoled by them. But let us endeavour to counter so great an error with testimonies from the Gospels, and also from the apostles’ Epistles and Acts.

For it is recorded in the Gospel that the Lord said to his disciples: “Into whatever house you enter, remain there, eating and drinking whatever is set before you” (Luke X). He made no exception of foods—meat or any other provisions—[Col. 1265A] but said universally: “Eat whatever is set before you.” Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew, he says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a human being, but what proceeds from the mouth; these are what defile a human being. For murders, adulteries, thefts, false testimonies, etc., proceed from the heart” (Matt. XV). Likewise, we have in the Gospels that the Lord Jesus Christ ate the flesh of the paschal lamb at supper with his disciples, as Luke plainly wrote in the Gospel: “The day of unleavened bread came, on which it was necessary to kill the Passover. And he sent Peter and John, saying: Go, prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it. But they said: Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover? etc. The Teacher says to you: Where is the guest room [Col. 1265B] where I may eat the Passover with my disciples? etc. And going, they found it as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. And when the hour came, he reclined, and the twelve with him; and he said to them: With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you that from now on I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God” (Luke XXII). The other evangelists wrote words similar to these (Matt. XXVI; Mark XIV). See how plainly the evangelists wrote that Christ ate the Passover; and that Passover, which had to be killed, was the paschal lamb concerning which the Lord had commanded Moses (Exod. XII). Christ ate the paschal lamb, and that lamb was flesh; therefore Christ ate flesh. Why, then, heretic, do you forbid the eating of meat?

[Col. 1265C] Likewise Paul says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: “Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking no questions for conscience’ sake. If any unbeliever invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for conscience’ sake. But if someone says: This has been sacrificed to idols, do not eat it, because of the person who informed you and because of conscience; and I mean not your conscience, but that of the other person” (I Cor. X).

Likewise Paul to Timothy: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (I Tim. IV). And we know and believe that Christ, who is the Word and Wisdom of God [Col. 1265D] the Father, came into the world, taking flesh from the womb of the Virgin, for no other purpose than the salvation of souls. He would not have done the things written above, nor ordered them to be done, if they involved judgment and condemnation for the souls of believers. Nor would the apostles, made imitators of Christ and endowed with spiritual wisdom, have acted, written, or eaten meat or other foods if they knew that it was a damnable sin for those who eat them. Likewise Paul to the Romans: “Receive the weak in faith, not for disputes about opinions. For one person believes that he may eat all things; but one who is weak should eat vegetables. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats. For God has received him. Who are you, to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own Lord. But he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand,” etc., to the end of the chapter (Rom. XIV). “But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not please ourselves” (Rom. XV). The Apostle calls weak in faith the one who judges and condemns a person for eating meat or drinking wine. It is a most evil error to judge God’s servant, when God says: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Luke VI).

But when he says, “It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine” (Rom. XIV), this is not a command but counsel given to those who wish to afflict their flesh lest they fall into the temptations of demons, provided that they do not believe that people are damned through eating meat. [Col. 1266B] Again, the Apostle says to the Colossians: “Let no one judge you in food or drink,” etc. (Col. II). And again the Apostle says to Titus: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is clean” (Titus I). Likewise: “Their mind and conscience are defiled” (ibid.). “Hear me, all of you, and understand: There is nothing outside a human being which, entering into him, can defile him; but the things which proceed from a human being are what defile a human being” (Mark VII).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the resurrection of the dead

After speaking about the eating of foods, let us speak about the resurrection of the dead. For heretics, imitating [Col. 1266C] the error of the Sadducees, deny the resurrection of dead bodies, that is, of human beings.

But let them hear Christ saying: “You err, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven. But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken to you by God, saying: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? He is not God of the dead but of the living” (Matt. XXII). Likewise, Matthew says: “The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose; and coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many” (Matt. XXVII). You hear, heretic, that bodies [Col. 1266D] arose.

Likewise, the Lord says in the Gospel according to John: “Do not marvel at this, for the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and they shall come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V). Likewise, in the same Gospel: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations shall be gathered before him; and he shall separate them from one another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats,” etc. (Matt. XXV).

The resurrection of the dead is confirmed not only by Gospel testimonies, but Paul also spoke much in his Epistles, disputing about the resurrection, to the Corinthians: “If Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen. And if Christ has not risen, then our preaching is empty, and your faith also is empty” (I Cor. XV).

But here the heretics object: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (ibid.). The Apostle did not say this of the substance of flesh and blood, but of the works of flesh and blood, as the Apostle explains in what follows: “Neither shall corruption possess incorruption” (ibid.).

The Apostle, seeing that the Corinthians had been deceived in this [Col. 1267B] error and wishing to make them certain concerning the resurrection, wrote to them: “It is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonour; it shall rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it shall rise in power. A natural body is sown; a spiritual body shall rise. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual one” (ibid.). Likewise Paul to the Thessalonians: “But we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve as also the rest do, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose, so also God will bring with him those who have slept. For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have slept. [Col. 1267C] For the Lord himself, with a command, and with the voice of an angel, and with the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first,” etc. (I Thess. IV). Likewise Paul to the Philippians: “But our commonwealth is in heaven, from which also we await the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working of his power” (Phil. I). Likewise Matthew says in the Gospel: “I tell you that many shall come from East and West and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the children of the kingdom shall be cast into the outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII). If there will be “weeping” of eyes there, which belongs to flesh, and [Col. 1267D] “gnashing of teeth,” which indicates bones, then there is a true resurrection of the very members which had fallen.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the invocation of saints and prayers for the departed

Against the perverse opinion of certain heretics, who assert that the saints and their prayers are of no benefit to those still living in the world and striving for Christ, nor that the departed are relieved by the benefits and prayers of the living, let us fortify our faith by the authorities of God’s Church and of all Catholic teachers.

At times the living pray for the dead, and the dead for the living, as is found in the Gospel according to Luke. Thus the rich man says to Abraham: “I beg you, Father, [Col. 1268A] to send him to my father’s house; for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments” (Luke 16). This rich man was buried in hell, and yet prayed for the living. What then is to be said of the saints, who have obtained mercy and desire—not their own salvation, but that of others—and rejoice in the salvation of the elect yet to come? And John says in the Apocalypse: “And another angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer in his hand; and much incense was given to him, that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne. And the smoke of the incense, from the prayers of the saints, ascended from the hand of the angel before God.” You hear that the saints pray; and if they pray, they pray either for themselves or [Col. 1268B] for others. They do not pray for themselves, because they have no need, nor do they require an increase of any virtue. Therefore they pray for others. And if for others, then either for the reprobate or for those to be saved. But not for the reprobate, for John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw beneath the altar the souls of those slain for the word of the Lord and for the testimony which they held; and they cried with a loud voice, saying: How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” (Apoc. 6). And the Lord says to Cain in Genesis: “The voice of your brother Abel’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. 4). And Paul says of Abel: “And through it, though dead, he still speaks” (Heb. 11). It is therefore clear [Col. 1268C] that they do not intercede for the reprobate, concerning whom they demand vengeance. Therefore they pray for those to be saved, whether living or dead; and if the dead pray for the living, it is evident that the living do so for the dead much more.

But there are three classes of the dead. Some are exceedingly good, who, at the very moment of dissolution, are joined to God in heaven and receive eternal joy without the struggle of punishment, as Peter, John, and others. Such persons cannot be aided by prayers, because they do not need aid. To them the Lord says: “Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10); and to the thief the Lord says: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). Again, some are exceedingly evil: those who, sinning unto death or remaining in grave crimes, have not been converted through repentance. And [Col. 1268D] these, on receiving the first death, receive also the second, of which John says in the Apocalypse: “He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death” (Apoc. 2), that is, eternal death. They cannot be delivered by the intervention of saints or by any benefit, because in hell there is no redemption, and God himself disdains to be entreated for such persons. Again, some are neither exceedingly good nor exceedingly evil, who, moved by repentance after their sins, have confessed their sins; but, before satisfaction has been completed, enter upon the way of all flesh. These are neither condemned nor immediately saved, but are punished while awaiting the salvation to be received. They are aided by prayers and benefactions, for God does not reject prayers for them, since they have not sinned unto death. Hence John says in the [Col. 1269A] First Epistle: “I write these things to you, that you may know that you have eternal life, because you believe in the name of the Son of God. And this is the confidence which we have toward him: that whatever we ask according to his will, he hears us. And we know that he hears us, whatever we ask. We know that we have the petitions which we request from him. He who knows his brother to be sinning a sin not unto death, let him ask; and he shall give life to one sinning not unto death. There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for that” (1 John 5). Again, there are those sinning unto death, concerning whom Jude says in the Catholic Epistle (v. 3): “For whom the storm of darkness has been reserved for ever.”

We have said for whom prayer ought to be made, and have also proved it by the authority of John. Again, that the prayer of the living [Col. 1269B] benefited the dead is evident in the Acts of the Apostles: “But when they had all been put outside, Peter, kneeling, prayed; and turning to the body he said: Tabitha, arise. And she opened her eyes, and, seeing Peter, sat up. Then, giving her his hand, he raised her; and when he had called the saints and widows, he presented her alive” (Acts 9). Again Martha says to Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11). Again, in the Book of Maccabees: “But the most valiant Judas, having made a collection, sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem for an offering of sacrifice for the sins of the dead, thinking well and religiously concerning the resurrection. For unless he hoped that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have seemed superfluous and vain to pray for the dead, [Col. 1269C] and because he considered that those who had received death in piety had an excellent grace laid up for them. Therefore it is a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins” (2 Macc. 12). And since among the ancients it was customary, and seemed right, to pray for the dead, because they could not immediately be saved but descended to hell in expectation, what shall we say of those who can immediately be saved?

Again, there are those who say that no one can be saved who does not repent except at the point of death, and that no prayer ought to be made for him. But let them hear what the Lord says to the thief, repenting at the last and unable to make satisfaction: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke [Col. 1269D] 23). Again: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 33). But you say that a sinner can be saved without repentance and satisfaction. In this it is observed that you seek to detract from divine power, when the Lord says in the prophet: “I am he who blots out the iniquities and sins of the people” (Isa. 43). But God does not blot out the sin of this sinner whom you affirm may be saved when he does not repent. Take care, therefore, that henceforth you do not presume to say anything so detestable.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Oaths

Let us discuss oaths, and set forth authentically from the treasury of the Scriptures which oath is lawful and which unlawful. Moses says in [Col. 1270A] Genesis: “The Lord spoke to Abraham, saying: By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing,” etc. (Gen. 22). Again Moses says to the people of Israel: “You shall fear the Lord your God, and you shall swear by his name” (Deut. 6). Behold, heretic, you hear the prophet Moses testifying to what God testifies in the Gospel, saying: “Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth” (Matt. 5). The Lord forbade swearing by creatures, he who swore by himself to Noah and Abraham. Hence Moses says: “You shall swear in the name of your God” (Deut. 10). Again: “You shall render your oaths to the Lord” (Matt. 5). And the Lord says: “You shall not swear falsely by my name” (Lev. 19). And Moses agrees with this saying when he says: “You shall not swear falsely in the name of the living Lord [Col. 1270B] God.” Again Abraham says to his servant: “Swear to me by the God of heaven.” Behold, Abraham wished an oath to be sworn by the Creator, not by a creature; he to whom the Lord had sworn by himself recognized that one ought to swear by him. Of this oath Zechariah says: “The oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would give to us” (Luke 1). And Habakkuk: “You shall surely raise up your bow: the oaths spoken to the tribes” (Hab. 3). And David in the Psalm: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain for ever” (Ps. 88). Again David: “He who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive,” etc. (Ps. 54). Again David: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent” (Ps. 109). Not only did he swear, but he did not repent of having sworn. This proves that that oath is not evil. For in the commendation of an act is indicated the certainty of the agent’s act.

Again, in the Book of Ecclesiasticus: “Therefore by an oath the Lord made him great among his people” (Ecclus. 44). Again, this is evident in Corinthians: “But I call God as witness upon my soul” (2 Cor. 1). Again: “I testify before God” (2 Tim. 4). Again Paul says: “Do not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherited the promises. For when God promised Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying: Unless I bless you with blessing, and multiply you with multiplication. And so, bearing patiently, [Col. 1270D] he obtained the promise. In this, God, wishing more abundantly to show to the heirs of the promise the immovability of his counsel, interposed an oath, so that through these two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope might have strongest consolation” (Heb. 6). Again Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles concerning David: “Therefore, being a prophet and knowing that God had sworn to him by an oath that one from the fruit of his loins would sit upon his throne, he spoke, foreseeing, of Christ’s resurrection” (Acts 2).

But you object, heretic, to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not swear at all, either by heaven or by earth” (Matt. 5). Here he forbids swearing by creatures, because a creature, rather than the Creator, ought not to be adduced as witness to an [Col. 1271A] oath. But if it is a sin to swear by the Creator, and God swore, then he sinned.

Again you object: “Let your speech be, ‘is, is’; ‘no, no’” (Matt. 5). Observe what this word, “I am, you are,” signifies. It manifests the divine essence, as the Lord says to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). Again the Lord says to Moses: “If they ask my name, you shall say to them: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (ibid.). Again in the Apocalypse: “I am Alpha and Omega” (ibid.). Behold, this word “is” manifests the divine essence, which properly is, and from which whatever is derives its being. And one who says “is” calls God as witness. And if he is false, by uttering “is,” he takes the name of the Lord God in vain, which the Lord forbids, saying: “You shall not take [Col. 1271B] the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. 20). But when the Lord said, “Let your speech be ‘is, is’; ‘no, no,’” he teaches that those whose lives agree should also have words that agree.

Again you object: “But if anything is more, it is from evil” (Matt. 5). Note that it is said, “it is from evil”; he did not say, “it is evil,” but “it is from evil,” that is, from unbelief. But hear, heretic: you ought to love your neighbor as yourself, as the Lord says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Again John says: “He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4). But you call brothers only those who consent to your [Col. 1272A] heretical perversity. This is by no means so, for every human being is your brother and your neighbor. If your neighbor is an unbeliever toward you, you ought, as far as you can, to call him back from unbelief by applying faith. Unless you do this, you do not will him to be saved, nor do you fulfill the divine commandment.

Again, John says concerning an oath in the Apocalypse: “And the angel, who held his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth, lifted his hand to heaven and swore by Him who lives for ever and ever, who created heaven and all that is in it, and earth and all that is in it, and sea and all that is in it” (Apoc. 10). Behold, you hear an angel as a competent witness, who swore and testified that God created all things; do you, heretic, contradict this statement? Do you believe [Col. 1272B] the angel sinned? Far be it! For the angels of God cannot sin, because they are confirmed and bound to the highest good. Let these things suffice for you, heretic, concerning oaths; for it would take too long to enumerate everything that occurs.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Killing a Human Being

Having explained with sufficient clarity the foregoing chapters, which ought to suffice, let us discuss killing. And how God does not kill. (The remainder is lacking in the parchment manuscript, unless perhaps death itself cut short the author’s thread, begun and woven to some extent.)

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1191: POPE CLEMENT III

[Col. 1273]

## NOTICE

(MANSI, *Councils*, vol. 22, p. 543)

Clement, the third of this name, a Roman by birth, formerly called Paulinus, was made pope from being cardinal-bishop of Palestrina, in the year of the Lord 1188, under Emperor Frederick, on the eighth day before the Ides of January. He immediately worked to advance and bring to completion the expedition to the Holy Land proclaimed by his predecessor, and confirmed the indulgence, decreeing that whoever took up the sacred cross for this cause should, by the authority of God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, be freed and absolved from all sins of which he had repented and confessed. Roger, recounting these things, also reports that this pope prescribed a fixed form of prayers to be said each day for the recovery of the Holy Land. Having made peace with the Roman senate on terms sufficiently unfavorable, he returned to Rome. From there he sent embassies to the kings of France and England, who were at war, and directed all his thought toward recovering the Holy Land, especially because Saladin had occupied the whole principality of Antioch. The Emperor and the Christian princes, assenting to his pious endeavors, took up arms; and the kings of France and England, the Duke of Burgundy, the Pisans together with the Venetians, and very many others followed the Emperor himself as he advanced with a great army. At that time William, king of Sicily, died childless. But Tancred, a kinsman of that same William, claiming the kingdom for himself, stirred up civil war. King Henry, on account of his wife Constance, the nearer heir of the kingdom, sent an army into Italy to expel him. Although he inflicted many losses on the rebels, he returned to Germany before the affair was settled. The pope, favoring Tancred, granted him investiture of the kingdom. NEUBRIGENSIS.

Thereafter he turned to ecclesiastical reform, built the monastery of St Lawrence outside the walls, and repaired the Lateran palace. Shortly after completing these things, he died on the fourth day before the Ides of April and was buried at Rome in the Lateran church, in the year of the Lord 1191, having governed the Church for three years, three months, and four days. In his time also, Emperor Frederick, after overcoming immense hardships in the expedition to the Holy Land, after defeating the Sultan of Iconium in battle, and while traversing lower Armenia, perished, swallowed up by the swift current of the river Caleph. He was succeeded by his son Henry, who had long before this time been made king of Germany.

[Col. 1273]

## YEAR 1187

[Col. 1275A]

### I. He confirms all monasteries belonging to the Camaldolese congregation and subjects them to the governance of the prior of that congregation.  
*(Pisa, 23 December.)*

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of the Camaldolese*, IV, Appendix, p. 159.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, . . . prior of Camaldoli and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

The authority of our office warns and invites us to concern ourselves with the condition of churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide beneficially for their peace and tranquillity. [Col. 1275B] For it is recognized as worthy and fitting to propriety that we, who by the Lord’s ordering have been appointed to their governance, should protect them from the wickedness of evil men and strengthen them by the patronage of blessed Peter and the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory—Paschal, Eugenius, Anastasius, [Col. 1276A] Adrian, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs—we decree and by the authority of the present enactment establish that no person whatsoever, cleric, monk, or layman, of whatever order or dignity, whether now or in the future, may divide from its subjection and unity in any way those congregations and places which have received the discipline and order of the Camaldolese hermitage or cenobium and which are today governed by it. For the sake of preserving unity, these places and congregations have seemed fit to be recorded under their individual names:

In the diocese of Arezzo: the monastery of St Saviour of the Berardingi; St Peter in Rota; St Mary in Agnano; St Quirinus in Rosa; the hermitage [Col. 1276B] of Fleri; the monastery of St Vivian; St Bartholomew in Anglare; near Bagno, the monastery of St Mary in Trivio; and, in Galliata, the monastery on the Island. In the diocese of Montefeltro: the monastery of Monte Hercules. In the diocese of Forlimpopoli: Aimeric’s hospital. In the diocese of Pesaro: the monastery of St Vincent and the hermitage of Sagoli. In the diocese of Bologna: the monastery of St [Col. 1277A] Michael the Archangel, near the castle of Britti, and St Felix. In the diocese of Florence: the monastery of St Peter of Luco and St Saviour near the city. In the diocese of Fiesole: the monastery of St Mary in Poplena and the church of St Margaret. In the diocese of Volterra: the monastery of St Peter in Fontiano, St Mary in Policiano, St Peter in Cerreto, and St Justus near the city. In the diocese of Pisa: the monastery of St Mary of Morrona, the monastery of St Stephen in Cintoria, and St Sabinus in Montione; in the city itself, the monasteries of St Michael, St Fridianus, and St Zeno. In the diocese of Lucca: the monastery of St Saviour in Cantiniano and St Peter in Puteoli. Likewise, in Sardinia, in the diocese of Torres: the monastery [Col. 1277B] of the Holy Trinity of Saccaria; the church of St Eugenia in Samanar; the churches of St Michael and St Lawrence in Vanari; the churches of St Mary and St John in Altasar; the church of St Mary in Contra; the churches of St John and St Simeon in Salvener; the church of St Nicholas of Trulla; the church of St Peter in Scano; the church of St Paul in Contrognano; and the church of St Peter in Olim. Likewise, in Tuscany, in the diocese of Chiusi: the hermitage of Vivi on Mount Amiata, with all appurtenances of the aforementioned places. Moreover, the estate of Majona, which you bought from Henry the provost and the other canons, with all its appurtenances; and the estate of Moncione, which you bought from the abbot of St Flora, as is contained in your charters, [Col. 1277C] and which was adjudged to you by justice and confirmed by the decree of our predecessor of good memory, Pope Anastasius.

Therefore, following the example of our aforesaid predecessor Alexander, we decree and by the authority of the apostolic see establish that all the above-mentioned monasteries with all their appurtenances shall remain for all time, as one body under one head—that is, under the prior of the Camaldolese hermitage—and persist in observance of that discipline under the prior, namely, who shall, by the Lord’s favor, be regularly elected by the abbots or priors of that congregation and by the hermits. Moreover, we decree that this congregation shall be fostered forever under the protection of the apostolic see in such manner [Col. 1277D] that no bishop may excommunicate any of these monasteries or prohibit it from divine offices without the consent of the prior or permission of the apostolic see.

Further, we establish that none may presume to exact or extort from you tithes of your lands, but that, according to your ancient custom, you shall have the free authority, by apostolic authority, to distribute them to your hospitals for the use of the poor. We also grant that, in appointing and removing the prelates of your community, you may without any opposition observe what is said to have been obtained hitherto from our predecessors. The brethren themselves shall be free to receive the sacraments of consecrations and ordinations from whichever Catholic [Col. 1278A] bishop they prefer.

Furthermore, following the example of our already mentioned predecessor Alexander, we confirm to you and your community, by apostolic authority and without prejudice to the right of the Church of Ravenna, the monastery of Urano.

We therefore decree that no one at all may, etc. If anyone therefore, etc.

To all, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St Mary across the Tiber, title of Calixtus. I, Melior, cardinal priest of SS John and Paul, title of Pammachius. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of SS Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of SS Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulf, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1187 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## YEAR 1188

[Col. 1278C]

### II. He confirms to the monastery of Vallis Regia the churches of Rengisvalle and Jovillare.  
*(Pisa, 5 January.)*

[HUGO, *Annals of the Premonstratensian Order*, II, Preface, p. 145.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, etc., to his beloved sons GALTER, abbot, and the convent of Vallis Regia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the office committed to us by divine providence requires us to love with sincere charity persons bound to religious life and to grant their just requests, we have examined the writings of our beloved sons Hugh, abbot, and of the general chapter of the abbots and brethren of the Church of Prémontré. The churches of Rengisvalle and Jovillare, which are your daughters because they sprang from your church, had been subject to that church from the beginning of their foundation and had rendered filial reverence during the tenure of three abbots in your church. But the abbot and brethren of Rengisvalle, because the brethren sent from the church of Prémontré had first come to their place—although they did not remain there because the place itself was too confined, but afterwards moved to your place—began to withdraw themselves from subjection to your church. They maintained that they ought by right to be subject only to the church of Prémontré. For the sake of peace, Philip, the former abbot of the church of Prémontré, of good memory, without consulting the abbot of Vallis Regia, ordained that both churches should be subject only to the church of Prémontré; and this was observed down to your time, son abbot. But after you raised this question in the chapter of Prémontré, the churches just mentioned were restored to you, and they were commanded henceforth to be subject to your church. That this act might not at any time be altered, it was afterward strengthened by sealed writings of Abbot Hugh and of the general chapter of the abbots and brethren of the church of Prémontré. We also, so that this may have perpetual force, have judged it right to confirm it by apostolic authority, as it was reasonably done and is more fully contained in those writings.

Therefore let no one whatsoever presume to invalidate this page of our constitution or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Pisa, on the Nones of January, in the sixth indiction.

### III. He receives the monastery of Vallombrosa under protection and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Pisa, 6 January.)*

[LAMI, *Monuments of the Florentine Church*, I, 552.]

[Col. 1279C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons FERTIUS, abbot of Vallombrosa, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

The authority of the apostolic see, over which, though unworthy, we preside, warns us to strive with prudent care for the welfare of all churches and to afford them apostolic protection lest they be exposed to the plundering or harassment of the malicious. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive under the protection of St Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery of Vallombrosa, where you are devoted to divine service, together with all monasteries subject to it, and fortify it by the privilege of the present [Col. 1279D] writing. We decree that every immunity and liberty granted to the said monastery by our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Victor, Gregory VII, Urban, Paschal, Innocent, Adrian, and Urban, shall remain firm, unimpaired, and perpetual to you, your successors, and the Vallombrosan congregation.

We add also that whatever possessions and goods the said monastery and the whole Vallombrosan congregation now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you, your successors, and the Vallombrosan [Col. 1280A] congregation. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Magnale, with its church and appurtenances; the church of Fosi, with the whole estate and its appurtenances; the hospital of Sprunzola, with its church and appurtenances; the hospital of Faventia, with its appurtenances; the monastery of St Salvi; the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Florence; the monastery of Struma; the monastery of Osella and of St James of Castello; the monastery of Passignano and of St Michael of Senis and of Alphiano; the monastery of Coltibuono, of Monte Pisis; the monastery of Montescalari and of Nerano; the monastery of Fiesole [Col. 1280B] and of Cappiano; the monastery of St Paul of Pisa; the monastery of Plaiano and of St Venereus in Sardinia; the monastery of St Angelo of Pistoia, of Pacciano, and of St Mary of Grato; the monastery of Vaiano, of Oppleta, and of Monte Piano; the monastery of Fonte Taona; the monastery of Musceto, of Monte Armato, and of St Cecilia; the monastery of St Reparata; the monastery of Forlì, of Trecento, of Crispino, of Razzolo, of Rivo Caesaris, of Cuneo, and of Turri; the monastery of Caprilla; the monasteries of Piacenza, Pavia, and Cremona; the monasteries of Cavanna and Novara; of Vercelli, Genoa, Tortona, and Turin; the monasteries of Brescia, Verona, and St [Col. 1280C] Vigilius; the monasteries of Bergamo, Milan, St Carpophorus, and Asti.

Certainly, no one whatsoever may rashly seize, detain, or harass with any vexations the lay brothers or monks of the said monastery or of the whole congregation. We likewise prohibit any bishop from pronouncing against you a sentence of excommunication or interdict, so that you, who have been received as special sons of the apostolic see, may not rashly be subject to another’s judgment. We further enact that none may presume to demand or extort from you tithes of the fruits which you gather anywhere by your own expense and labor, or of the nourishment of your animals.

You may also receive freely, without anyone’s prohibition, clerics and laymen, free and absolved persons, into conversion; bury with Christian burial those who have vowed to be buried among you; and receive, without prejudice to other churches, the offerings both of these persons and of other faithful people. By the authority of this present decree we also establish that, whenever a general or particular interdict is issued by the diocesan bishop under pressing necessity, you may celebrate divine offices in your monasteries with closed doors, without ringing bells, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, in a subdued voice, and only with your own brethren.

Moreover, in accordance with the common ordinance made in the general chapter of all the abbots of your order, you, son abbot, may transfer brethren from any monastery [Col. 1281A] of the congregation to the principal monastery, as you judge expedient for the salvation of souls, without anyone’s opposition. And because the apostolic see ought to give no occasion or favor for wrongdoing, we additionally establish that, if abbots or brethren of your congregation wish, on the pretext of the protection of the apostolic see, to live less regularly than monastic order or the custom of the Vallombrosan congregation requires, the abbot of Vallombrosa shall have free authority canonically to correct them. Nor may any brethren of the same congregation appoint an abbot for themselves without his consent, as is known to have been observed from the time of John, the first abbot of that congregation, of good memory.

[Col. 1281B] We therefore decree that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see. If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, presumes rashly to act against it, and, after a second or third warning, does not amend the offence by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of rank and office; let him know that he is guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be alienated from the most sacred [Col. 1281C] body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to stern vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. [Col. 1281D] I, Jacob, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulph, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran and vice-chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on 6 January, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## IV. He receives the monastery of St Michael of Orticaria under protection and confirms its possessions. (Pisa, 11 January)

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, IV, Appendix, p. 174.]

[Col. 1282A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of St Michael of Orticaria, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a speedy effect, and so that it may apply itself with the greater freedom to the observance of sacred religion and to other good works, the more graciously it perceives itself to be supported in its pious purpose by the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your [Col. 1282B] just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St Michael of Orticaria, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order which is known to have been established in that monastery according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the brethren of Pulsano, shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, etc. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms: the place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all [Col. 1282C] its appurtenances; the church of St James of Padio in the diocese of Pisa; the church of the Holy Cross of Corvo in the diocese of Luni, with all belonging to it. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any opposition. Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of that monastery shall be free, etc. Therefore we decree, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Hyacinth, [Col. 1282D] cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulph, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in place of the chancellor, on 11 January, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1189, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## V. He receives the church of St Michael of Arezzo under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Pisa, 13 January)

[Ibid., p. 162.]

[Col. 1283A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior of the church of St Michael, situated in the suburb of the city of Arezzo, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may attain a speedy effect, and so that it may apply itself with the greater freedom to the observance of sacred religion and to other good works, the more graciously it perceives itself to be supported in its pious purpose by the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of Pope Anastasius, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of St Michael, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the Camaldolese brethren shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favour, through grants of popes, gifts [Col. 1283C] of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances. We have thought fit to define the boundaries of its own parish as set forth in the authentic document of Jerome, formerly bishop of Arezzo: namely, all the people who now dwell, or shall dwell, in the suburb on either side of the road, from the house or *classaria* formerly called that of the son of Tiribald, by which one goes to St Peter Minor, as far as the house or *classaria* formerly called that of Morontus, by which one goes [Col. 1283D] to St Michael’s mill; and from the house or *classaria* formerly called that of Ardimannus Villanus, by which one goes to St Bartholomew, as far as the house or *classaria* formerly called that of Aricius Captapanus, by which one goes to the mill of the patrons of the aforesaid church, namely the sons or grandsons of Rainerius Gerzi.

Moreover, one half of the mill which is near the suburb, with all its appurtenances and revenues; the houses which you possess in the same suburb, with all their revenues; the square situated before that church, as contained in the charter of donation; whatever you possess in Albagnoro and Montagnoro; the lands which John, formerly prior, together with his mother, bestowed upon that church for the sake of piety; the lands which [lacuna] Iventone, with his wife and son, gave you; [Col. 1284A] whatever you bought from Mazagallus, or he himself gave you, and whatever his nephew Petrolus exchanged with you or gave you; the land which you bought from Filiastro; the land which Gerardinus bestowed upon you for the remedy of his soul, as is contained in the charter drawn up at the request of him and his sons; and the lands which you possess in the city of Arezzo.

We likewise confirm to you, your successors, and your church the holy oil for the sick and all things pertaining to the ecclesiastical office, except baptism, on solemnities, feast-days, and ordinary days alike, as they were granted to you by the aforesaid bishop. We also decree that the burial-place of that establishment shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving nevertheless the right of the mother church. Therefore we decree, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See, and in all things the obedience and reverence due to the Camaldolese prior, and the canonical right of the bishop of Arezzo. If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 1284C] I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulph, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in place of the chancellor, on 13 January, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## VI. At the request of Maurice, bishop of Paris, he confirms the abbeys of Hérivaux, Hermery, Mont-Évêque, and Gif. (Pisa, 15 January)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame of Paris*, I, 33.]

[Col. 1284D]

CLEMENT to MAURICE, bishop of Paris.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners, and bring to effect the vows which do not depart from the path of reason.
