Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, assenting to your petitions, we confirm to you by apostolic authority the abbeys of Hérivaux, Hermery, Mont-Évêque, and Gif, which you are said to have newly founded, just as you possess them canonically and without dispute, [Col. 1285A] and strengthen them with the protection of this present writing, decreeing that no person whatsoever may, etc.

Given at Pisa, 15 January, in the sixth indiction.

## VII. He receives the monastery of St Cassian of Carisi under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Pisa, 16 January)

[MITTARELLI, *Annals of Camaldoli*, IV, Appendix, 164.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [lacuna], abbot of St Cassian of Parisio, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just petitioners be granted what they seek, especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not forsake it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following in the footsteps of Pope Lucius, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery of St Cassian, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the monastery justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by God’s favour, through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order [Col. 1285C] known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. We have thought fit to specify the names of the possessions in their proper terms.

The estate of Carisi, with its court, jurisdiction, and all its appurtenances, together with the River Regulus; the church of St Michael of Monte-ruttulo, with all that it has and possesses; all that you possess in the castle of Pezole; the church of St Cerbonius, with all that you possess in the village and court of Applano; the right which you possess in the church of St Donatus, with all known to belong to it; all that you possess in Rocca and in the court of Valli; the right which you possess [Col. 1285D] in the church of St Justus; whatever you possess in the court of Alliga, and in the court and jurisdiction of Folliano, and on the hill of Monte Tusculi, and in the court of Aletreta with the church of St Andrew and all that you possess in that same village; the church of St Pontian, with its hill, village, and court; what you possess in the court of Legul and in the court of Fognano and in the court of the castle of Falfi; the church of St Peter of Libiano; the church of St Mary of Griciano, with all that you possess in Griciano and its court; all that you possess in the court of Monte Cuccari, the court of Monticlo, the court of Pava, the court of Casanova, the village of Padule, the court of Camuliano, the court of Palaja, and the court of Montezano; all that you possess in the court of Gavorano; the church of St Andrew of Ravi, with [Col. 1286A] all that it has and possesses; whatever belongs to you in that same court of Ravi; the church of St Germanus, with all that it possesses, situated in the court of Colle Maggiore; whatever you possess in the court and jurisdiction of Buriano; all that you possess in the court of Cumulo and in the court of Ceole; moreover, the tithes of all the lands which you are known to hold in the dioceses of Lucca, Pisa, and Volterra, as they were granted to you by John of Lucca, Azo of Pisa, and Gunfred of Volterra, bishops of blessed memory, and as you hold them peacefully.

You may also receive into conversion clerics and laymen fleeing the world, free and absolved, and retain them in your community without any opposition. But we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, from leaving your cloister without the permission of his abbot, save for the sake of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare [Col. 1286B] [lacuna]. Moreover, when a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, and in a subdued voice, [lacuna] etc. We further decree that no one within the boundaries of your parishes shall presume to build a new church or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop [lacuna] etc. We grant that [lacuna] of your monastery shall be free [lacuna]; no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, [Col. 1286C] saving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of deception or by violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

Therefore we decree that, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of St Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulph, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in place of the chancellor, on 16 January, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, [Col. 1287A] in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Clement III.

## VIII. To the bishops of Scotland.—He announces to them that Hugh, bishop of St Andrews, having been summoned by Urban and remaining contumaciously absent, has been deposed from the episcopate; and he urges the election of John. (Pisa, 16 January)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 544.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren JOCELIN, bishop of Glasgow, and MATTHEW, bishop of Aberdeen, and to his beloved sons ERNALD, abbot of Melrose, and BERTRAM, prior of Coldingham, greeting and apostolic blessing.

In order that matters which are transacted may not relapse into a scruple of doubt, it is fitting that they be entrusted to the record of letters and conveyed, by a public and truthful notification, to the knowledge of those whom they appear to concern. We recall that Pope Urban, our predecessor of blessed memory, commanded Hugh, formerly called bishop of St Andrews, regarding the controversy between him and our venerable brother John, bishop, to present himself before the apostolic presence on a specified day to answer in law, under pain of excommunication. But because, conscious of his deeds and fearing the outcome of judgment, he contumaciously refused to come, we, both for this reason and for many other matters which, as report increasingly spread, brought scandal upon the Church of God, judged him, with the counsel and assent of our brethren, to be permanently removed from the episcopate of St Andrews by authority of the Apostolic [Col. 1287C] See, and suspended from the exercise of episcopal office until such time as the Apostolic See should otherwise determine concerning him, releasing his subjects from the fealty by which they were bound to him.

Now, since the decrees of the holy canons forbid vacant churches to lack pastoral government for too long, we command your discretion by apostolic letters diligently to admonish, on our behalf, our beloved sons the chapter of St Andrews that they elect for themselves such a bishop and pastor as may worthily hold the dignity of episcopal office. But you shall especially endeavour, as far as lies within your power, to induce them to receive the aforesaid Bishop John—a man of good repute and, by reason of his integrity, acceptable to us and our brethren—as ruler and prelate of that church, without any scruple of difficulty. If you cannot all be present for carrying these matters out, two of you shall nevertheless carry them out.

Given at Pisa, 16 January, in the sixth indiction.

## IX. To William, king of Scots.—On the same subject. (Pisa, 16 January)

[Ibid., col. 545.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WILLIAM, illustrious king of Scots, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We consider that the eyes of the divine majesty are gravely offended if we leave unrestrained, to the injury of justice, the excesses of prelates which we cannot overlook without injury to conscience. Therefore, whereas Pope Urban, our predecessor of blessed memory, commanded Hugh, etc., as in the preceding letter, down to “strict.” Although we have the firm purpose, so far as we may with God, of attending to your honour and advantage, and although the Roman curia has hitherto deferred to the royal serenity in the affair of the aforesaid Hugh, not without the criticism of many, nevertheless, because indisputable report of his conduct has reached us, we could not further pass over his errors with our eyes closed in dissimulation. For this reason, we believe that nothing has been done in this matter which ought on any grounds to move the royal mind.

Yet we ask your devotion with all the prayer and affection in our power, and admonish you in the Lord, that you hold the aforesaid Bishop John—whom we and our brethren sincerely love because of his integrity—commended and acceptable to you for reverence toward the Apostolic See and ourselves; and, remitting any offence of indignation that may have been conceived, that you treat him in all things with royal clemency and kindness. We indeed believe that, through his diligence and probity, much advancement may, by the Lord’s authorship, accrue to you and to your kingdom; and it will be most pleasing to us if our prayers obtain their desired effect before royal ears.

Given at Pisa, 16 January, sixth indiction.

## X. To Henry, king of England.—On the same matter. (Pisa, 16 January)

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1288C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, illustrious king of the English, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When royal eminence receives petitions from the Apostolic See, it ought diligently to heed them and apply its authority and power to their fulfilment, since this is expedient for preserving churches in their condition and for the salvation of many; and it ought to attend to them with such greater strength and ardour that they may achieve the desired effect, as it is more certain that their devout reception and diligent execution concern equally royal glory [Col. 1288D] and salvation.

For this reason, we have thought fit confidently to send apostolic letters and petitions to your royal serenity on behalf of our venerable brother John, bishop of St Andrews, earnestly requesting, admonishing, and enjoining upon the height of your royal eminence, for the remission of all sins, that, out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, and in view of the persecution which he is known to have endured for a long time, you diligently admonish and induce our dearest son in Christ, William, illustrious king of Scots; and, if necessary, compel him by the royal coercive power by which you surpass him, and by the authority granted to your royal highness, to forgive, with every pretext removed, the resentment of all his indignation [Col. 1289A] against the bishop—a resentment conceived through the malice of certain whisperers—having regard to royal dignity and the salutary works of piety. And may he henceforth allow that bishop to possess peacefully and without molestation the diocese of St Andrews, which the supreme pontiff, with the common counsel and assent of the brethren, has confirmed to him in perpetuity; since he too stands ready to be obedient and faithful in all things to the royal majesty, insofar as shall accord with reason.

Given at Pisa, 16 January, in the sixth indiction.

## XI. To the clergy of the diocese of St Andrews.—On behalf of John, bishop of St Andrews. (Pisa, 16 January)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, col. 546.]

[Col. 1289B]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy of the diocese of St Andrews, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although in doubtful matters some may display their craftiness or malice, nevertheless, once the scruple and point of doubt have been removed and the traces of truth have appeared through clear indications, false paths must be entirely abandoned and the paths of rectitude must be sought and observed alike, lest—God forbid!—those acting otherwise and persisting in their obstinacy be inwardly destroyed by the eternal punishment of everlasting death after present scourges and deserved penalties.

Therefore, wishing in fatherly concern to provide for your salvation [Col. 1289C] and to make provision for your welfare and peace, we command and order your whole body by apostolic letters, and enjoin it upon you in virtue of obedience, that within fifteen days after receipt of these letters you humbly and devoutly receive our venerable brother John, your bishop, canonically appointed to the pontifical office, as your own father and pastor; and that henceforth, setting all hostility aside, you do not fail to render due reverence and obedience to his salutary admonitions and commands. Know that, after Hugh, who was formerly called bishop, was removed by the Roman Church from the dignity of your episcopate, or after his death while the aforesaid John, your bishop, yet survives, if perhaps [Col. 1289D] you have elected any bishop, we annul that election by apostolic authority.

But if, God forbid, at the prompting of the enemy of humankind, you have presumed to form any conspiracy against the same Bishop John, we decree that both you and the whole episcopate shall lie under sentence of interdict until, acknowledging your offence, you return to obedience to the command of Bishop John himself.

Given at Pisa, 16 January, sixth indiction.

## XII. To all bishops.—On the same affair. (Pisa, 16 January)

[Ibid., col. 547.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1290A] brethren JOCELIN, bishop of Glasgow, MATTHEW, bishop of Aberdeen, and RICHARD, bishop of Moray; and to his beloved sons ERNULF of Melrose, and the abbots of NEWBATTLE, HOLYROOD, STIRLING, and SCONE, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although you ought, even without admonition, to attend to matters which concern integrity and bring about the salvation of souls, and although we believe that you devote diligent effort to them as required by your office, we have nevertheless thought fit by apostolic letters to exhort your diligence to show greater concern in these matters, so that you may apply yourselves to these praiseworthy works with the greater fervour, as it will be more salutary for you to employ more exact diligence in them at apostolic exhortation.

It is certainly established, according to the apostolic rule, that certain prelates of churches ought to endure burning with those who are scandalized and to become weak with the weak. How many persecutions the Church of St Andrews has endured in these times, how many calamities and pressures it has suffered, and how grievously it has hitherto been disturbed and shaken under the shadow of the indignation of royal highness; moreover, how many and how great dangers and labours our venerable brother John, bishop of St Andrews, has undergone in preserving the liberty of the church entrusted to him and confirmed to him by us and by two of our predecessors—all these things are manifest to you, and it seems superfluous to impress them upon your ears.

Now, therefore, it is recognized to be most expedient that we take suitable concern both for the king’s welfare, for restoring the condition of the aforesaid church, and for securing peace for that bishop; and we regard your circumspection as suitable for strengthening us [or, perhaps, “as suitable”]. We command and order your discretion by apostolic letters that, after receiving our letters, you assemble together and, as becomes prudent and discerning men, approach the presence of our dearest son in Christ, William, illustrious king of Scotland, and diligently admonish and urgently induce him to remit the resentment of his indignation against the aforesaid bishop and not to despise in this matter the Roman Church, which has deferred to the royal serenity [Col. 1290D] for a long time. Rather, admonished by it and by you, as accords with royal glory and salvation, let him without delay obediently and humbly comply with salutary counsel, and allow the aforesaid bishop to hold the diocese of St Andrews in peace. For by the duty of royal dignity he is bound not to scatter churches together with their pastors, but to cherish them; not to despise them, but to love them; not to persecute them, but to protect them.

But if, to the peril of his own salvation—God forbid!—he judges that apostolic admonitions must be resisted, you shall declare a sentence of interdict, by apostolic authority and without obstacle of appeal, to be promulgated by you within twenty days, against the kingdom of his highness, his person, and all royal supporters. Moreover, those who have obeyed Hugh and given him support in his obstinacy after the Apostolic See permanently removed him from the diocese of St Andrews and pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him, [Col. 1291A] you shall strike with a like sentence. Publicly announcing this, you shall cause them to remain under excommunication and to be more strictly avoided by others until they return to the command of the Church, seeking the benefit of absolution from the same bishop.

Furthermore, you shall purify and sanctify, according to the custom of the Church, the altars and chalices at which the aforesaid Hugh celebrated while under excommunication. You shall also proceed together to the church of St Andrews and, after summoning the brethren together, enter the chapter-house and diligently inquire into the order and condition of the church. If you find that anything in that church has been altered or established by the aforementioned Hugh, you shall by our authority restore it to its due condition; and, if anything there requires correction, you shall effectively strive to reform it for the better. But if, God forbid, you find any of the canons hard and rebellious toward humbly and devoutly receiving their aforesaid pastor, you shall admonish them more urgently to render him the reverence and obedience due to a father and to desist from their wicked and damnable purpose. If they remain contumacious, suspend them alike from office and benefice, and bind them by the bond of excommunication, causing them to remain bound until they comply with ecclesiastical admonitions and commands. If you cannot all be present for carrying these matters out, [Col. 1291C] the remainder shall nevertheless carry them out.

Given at Pisa, 16 January, in the sixth indiction.

## XIII. He grants Maurice, bishop of Paris, authority, whenever prebends fall vacant, to assign them to suitable persons. (Pisa, 16 January)

[*Cartulary of Notre-Dame of Paris*, I, 33.]

CLEMENT to MAURICE, bishop of Paris.

Although it is our purpose, beyond the common duty by which we are bound to all, especially to wish to preserve the rights of our venerable brethren and bishops, nevertheless, because you ask, fearing the persistence of petitioners, that the granting of prebends which belongs to you be confirmed to you more abundantly, we have thought fit to admit your petition in this matter. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we decree that, just as it was lawfully open to your predecessors and to you from ancient times, so it shall also henceforth be free, whenever the said prebends fall vacant, to assign them to suitable persons, notwithstanding any letters which may hitherto have been procured from the Apostolic See to the prejudice of your right, and notwithstanding any investiture which is said to have been made by another on the occasion of such letters.

Given at Pisa, 16 January, in the sixth indiction.

## XIV. At the request of Maurice, bishop of Paris, he confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Paris. (Pisa, 18 January)

[Col. 1292A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MAURICE, bishop of Paris, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

“The more noble, etc.,” as in the bull of Innocent II for the same church. [Note: [Col. 1291D] See *Patrology*, vol. CLXXIX.] Also episcopal right in the following abbeys and in their parishes or all their parishioners: namely, in the abbey of Lagny; in the abbey of Fossés; in the abbey of St Magloire; in the abbey of St Victor; in the abbey of the Valley of St Mary; in the abbey of Sarneia; in the abbey of Hérivaux; [Col. 1292B] in the abbey of Hermery; in the abbey of Mont-Évêque; in the abbey of the nuns of Montmartre; of Edera, Kala, and Gif; and in the church above Argenteuil. Moreover, “the agreement, etc.,” as in the bulls of Innocent and Lucius II. [Note: [Col. 1292D] See above.]

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in place of the chancellor, on 18 January, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## XV. He grants Gerard, abbot of Vézelay, and his successors the use of sandals. (Pisa, 18 January)

[LAUNOIS, *Works*, vol. II, part I, p. 288.]

[Col. 1292C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GERARD and the convent of Vézelay, greeting and apostolic blessing.

For the increase of ecclesiastical splendour, insignia of dignities have been devised, which the most holy Roman Church distributes with fitting generosity to particular persons and grants to devout sons, as it judges worthy, both to receive and to retain. Therefore, moved by reverence for blessed Mary Magdalene, whose sacred body rests in your church, and by the merit of your devotion, we grant to you, son abbot, and to your successors the use of sandals within your churches, and confirm it by apostolic authority. Therefore let no one, etc.

[Col. 1292D] Given at Pisa, 13 January, in the sixth indiction.

## XVI. Privilege for the monastery of St Angel of Pistoia. (Pisa, 20 January)

[ZACHARIA, *Medieval Anecdota*, p. 237.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of the monastery of St Angel, situated in the suburb of Pistoia, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us which is known to accord with religion and integrity, it befits us readily to grant it and to bestow appropriate support upon the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your petitions; and, following the example of the pope, our predecessor of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St Angel, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that place according to God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the institution of the brethren of Vallombrosa shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that monastery justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the Lord’s favour, through grants of popes, gifts of kings [Col. 1293B] or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the farmstead purchased with money, with vineyard, woodland, and the men subject to its jurisdiction; likewise the enclosed lands, mills, all the *caufagium* [uncertain due or right], and the church of St. Mark, situated near the monastery, with its parish. The land of Muoso with its enclosure and all its appurtenances; the revenues from Guliano, and every right which you possess in that village, as is contained in the public instruments [Col. 1293C]; likewise we confirm to you by apostolic authority the tithes of your possessions, which you have hitherto held peacefully for forty years.

Moreover, let no one presume to exact from you tithes of your newly cultivated lands (*novalia*), which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, without prejudice to the sustenance of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, if free and unbound, and retain them without any opposition. Furthermore, we forbid any one of your brethren, after making profession in your house, to leave that place without his abbot’s permission, unless for the sake of a stricter religious life. No one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of authorization from the community.

[Col. 1293D] When a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices with closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We further decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who choose burial there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; while preserving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. When the abbot then in office dies, no one shall be placed over the house by any artifice of usurpation or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of them, in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St. Benedict, shall decide is to be elected.

[Col. 1294A] Furthermore, we ratify the ancient liberties and immunities and the reasonable customs conferred upon your monastery, as they have hitherto been observed, and by this present decree establish that they shall remain unimpaired for all time. By apostolic authority we also forbid anyone, within the boundaries of your parish—especially from St. Leonard’s as far as St. Christina’s—to presume in any way to build anew a chapel or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and of yourselves, without prejudice, nevertheless, to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We likewise forbid anyone to presume, without manifest and reasonable cause, to pronounce against you or your monastery a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict, or to impose new and unlawful exactions upon you or your people.

We decree, therefore, that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1294B] rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due reverence owed to the abbot of Vallombrosa. If, therefore, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly [violates] this page of our constitution, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus, have subscribed. [Col. 1294C] I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, James, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Radulf, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given at Pisa, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, [Col. 1294D] in the sixth indiction, in the year 1187 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

XVII. He commands Baldwin, archbishop of Canterbury, not to delay to demolish “whatever has been done concerning the construction of the chapel after the appeal made by the monks of Canterbury to the Apostolic See, or after the prohibition of his predecessor Urban III.” (Siena, January 26.)

[TWISDEN, *Hist. Angl. Script.*, I, 1528.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable B., archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more you excel in the Church of God through the gift of learning and the honor of religion, and the higher a summit of dignity you hold in the English regions, the more fitting it is that your charity should, with more vigilant care, restrain itself from injuries or oppressions of subjects; and, setting aside those things which tarnish the beauty of justice and extinguish the fragrance of good repute, should render the obedience and reverence due to superiors. We therefore wonder, not without cause, that, as is represented to us, after an appeal had been made to the Apostolic See and the prohibition of Urban, our predecessor of blessed memory, you have so heavily burdened the brethren of the church entrusted to you through your activities concerning the construction of a new chapel and many other matters, that it may be thought that they have received no benefit from the remedy of the appeal which was lodged—as the principles of law plainly require—and that you have not shown the honor due, as you ought, to your mother, the most holy Roman Church. [Col. 1295B]

Although it is our purpose, so far as we can with God’s help, to show deference to your brotherhood and to honor your person in all matters which it is our official duty to determine, nevertheless we can neither can nor ought, with a good conscience, to pass over with closed eyes both the pressures and the cries of these brethren. Therefore, by apostolic letters, and on the counsel of our brethren, we command your brotherhood strictly: setting aside every contradiction and pretext—even if it should happen that you are absent from your church—you are not to delay demolishing whatever has been done in the work of the chapel after the appeal to the Apostolic See or after the prohibition of our predecessor. You shall wholly revoke and render void [Col. 1295C] whatever has been done or improperly introduced concerning the establishment of canons and other matters connected with the chapel.

You shall also hold barred from office and benefice those who presumed to celebrate the divine offices in that chapel after the prohibition of our aforesaid predecessor, until they have rendered us fitting satisfaction. You shall restore the ministers of the convent whom you removed after the appeal was lodged, and whom that same predecessor restored. Likewise, you shall regard as absolved those whom you sought to excommunicate or suspend after the appeal; and you shall restore to their former state, after abandoning appeal and objection, all things attempted after the appeal to their disadvantage—namely, the seizure of their villages and possessions, their revenues [Col. 1295D] and other things which they possessed before the appeal, and likewise the taking away of other goods. Moreover, because according to the form of law nothing may be altered after an appeal, we will and command that, while judgment is pending, you shall make no effort whatsoever to alter anything affecting the status of the monastery to the detriment of these brethren. Otherwise it would be grievous and vexatious to us in every respect, and we could not calmly endure it without due correction.

Given at Siena, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth indiction.

XVIII. He confirms to Gunteram, bishop of Siena, the church situated on Mount Boniti. (Near San Quirico, January 28.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 548.]

[Col. 1296A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUNTERAM, bishop of Siena, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

By a common and special obligation we are moved to accede to your petitions and to grant them a fitting effect, so that we who are bound to hear all persons in their just requests may appear more especially favorable to you, in proportion as we love you and the church entrusted to you with a more abundant charity. [Col. 1296B] Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, willingly assenting to your just petitions, we grant and confirm to you and your successors, with the common counsel of our brethren, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of pious memory, the church at Montebonizzi, built by your predecessor Raynerius of blessed memory upon an estate which Count Guido of blessed memory formerly granted to St. Peter, and constructed by authority and concession of Pope Adrian, our predecessor of pious memory. We give you free authority—as our predecessors are known to have given it—to consecrate the same church without any opposition, and to place and freely ordain clerics there according to your judgment, [Col. 1296C] notwithstanding the retraction which our aforesaid predecessor Adrian is known to have made concerning this matter, led by a slight and vain error, on the ground that the place lies in the Florentine diocese. For the privilege of that predecessor of ours states that the aforesaid estate was granted by the said count, and was granted by that same predecessor to your predecessor, for building a church there, subject to an annual payment of one Byzantine coin.

[Col. 1296D] We establish, as our aforesaid predecessors are known to have established, that whoever from your diocese moves to that place shall in all spiritual matters answer only to you and your successors, and that you shall retain over them in every respect the authority which you previously possessed. Moreover, as a token of this our grant and confirmation, you shall pay one Byzantine coin each year to us and our successors. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our grant and confirmation, etc. If anyone, therefore, etc., ecclesiastical, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. [Col. 1297A] I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil, have subscribed.

Given near San Quirico, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1187 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

XIX. Privilege for the monastery of St. Mary of Florence. (Lateran, February 11.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar. Casin.*, II, 211.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the abbot of St. Mary of Florence and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1297B] Although, unworthy as we are, care for all churches has been entrusted to us and we are bound to exercise solicitude for all, we ought to assist more zealously those which are known to belong especially to the right of St. Peter. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions, and take under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, following the example of Pope Alexander, our predecessor of happy memory, the aforesaid monastery of St. Mary of Florence—known to belong especially to the right and property of the Roman Church—in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, establishing that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that monastery according to God and the Rule of St. Benedict [Col. 1297C] shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. Among these we have judged it fitting to specify the following by their proper names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Signa and one-third of the castle of Grumulo, with its church and appurtenances; the estate of Greve with the church of St. Martin and its other possessions; the church of St. Bartholomew with its estate, and the land of Berizo and of his wife Aza of Rodda. Further, his land at Patroio, or wherever situated, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Radda with its estate, churches, and all that belongs to it; the church of St. Martin at the place called Confluens, with its appurtenances; the church of St. Martin within the city, beside the aforesaid monastery, with houses, lands, and all its appurtenances; the church of St. Martin at Mensula with all its appurtenances; the estate of Monte-Domini with all belonging to it; the estate of Mandria with its appurtenances; the land of John, son of Teudus, with houses and the remaining possessions, as Maria and her son Donatus [Col. 1298A] bestowed them upon the monastery; the houses and lands of John, son of Buga; the church of St. Roch with the lands and houses around it; the castle of Vicli with its estate, churches, and all its appurtenances.

Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and your monastery whatever you lawfully possess from the donation of Boniface, brother of Benedict, formerly your abbot; and all tithes from Viclo, as you are known canonically to hold them by the concession of the bishop of Florence of happy memory, whose name is lost in a lacuna; and the tithes from your allod at the estate of Casaglia, of Tusci, and of Rocchetta, as you are known canonically to possess that tithe by the grant of Guido, formerly bishop of Volterra. We likewise judge that the free appointment of persons to your churches, which your predecessors and you yourselves are known to have possessed without challenge for the past forty years, should be confirmed to you by apostolic authority.

[Col. 1298B] Moreover, we forbid any bishop or his official to dare harass your churches or their clerics with unlawful exactions or vexations, or to presume to impose a sentence of excommunication upon you or of interdict upon your monastery without the command of the Roman pontiff or a legate dispatched from his side. Let no one presume to demand from you or your monastery tithes or first-fruits from your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce supporting your animals. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and the ordinations of your monks or clerics who are to be advanced to holy orders, from the bishop of Florence, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the grace and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide them freely and without any improper condition. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall provide what you request. [Col. 1298C] We further decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who choose burial there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may [Col. 1298D] rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of February.

XX. He takes the church of St. Mary of Grandgurgitis under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, February 13.)

[HUGO, *Ord. Praem. Annal.*, I, Preface, p. 600.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RADULPH, abbot of the church of St. Mary of Grandgurgitis, [Col. 1299A] and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Those choosing the religious life ought to receive apostolic protection, lest the assault of any rash person either turn them from their purpose or, God forbid, break the strength of their sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously grant your just petitions, take the aforesaid church of St. Mary of Grandgurgitis, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, establishing that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to God, the Rule of St. Augustine, and the institute of the Premonstratensian brethren, [Col. 1299B] shall be observed there inviolably for all time.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. Among these we have judged it fitting to specify the following by their proper names.

The place of Grandgurgitis itself, in which the aforesaid church [is situated]; [holdings from: reading uncertain] Bellelagia, Henry of Larges, Theodore of Plozoesc, and Gerard his brother; [Col. 1299C] the estate of Courdumaco, which Reimbald of Ferretis gave you with its appurtenances, with the consent of Louis, count of the same castle; the estate of Gerivillari with its appurtenances, part of which Richard of Gleire gave you; the estate of Burres with its appurtenances, which you hold from the abbess and chapter of des Balmes (*Baumes-les-Nones*) for five solidi to be paid annually to that church; the estate of Courdemaiche with its appurtenances, which Cetto of Eglingues gave you; the estate of Seneve, which Henry and his brother Billingus sold and gave you, with the consent of Louis, count of Saloerner; the alms of nineteen solidi which Reimbald of Euperpa gave you at St. Ulric’s, to be possessed in perpetuity; the alms of one meadow and two *mansi* of land at Estophum, which Richard Libranchet gave you; [Col. 1299D] the alms which Reiger of Bonchort gave you at Altoreille.

Let no one presume to demand or extort from you tithes from your newly cultivated lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce supporting your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, if free and unbound, and retain them without any opposition.

Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to leave it without his abbot’s permission; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of authorization from the community. We also prohibit anyone from personally granting, or in any way alienating, churches, lands, or any benefice bestowed upon [Col. 1300A] your church without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater or sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than as stated, we deem them void.

We add, moreover, that no canons or lay brothers (*conversi*), bound by profession to your house, may stand surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone without the consent of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, beyond the amount provided by the prudent determination of your chapter, except for a manifest benefit to your house. Should anyone nevertheless presume to do so, the convent, without whose leave and consent they acted, shall not be bound in any way to answer for these matters. Furthermore, in your cases it shall be lawful to produce suitable brethren as witnesses and, by their testimony, if it is right, both to repel violence and vindicate justice.

[Col. 1300B] To avoid the frequent presence of secular persons, you may, saving the rights of the diocesan bishop and parish church, build oratories on your granges and, when necessary, celebrate divine offices in them for yourselves and your household. No one may dare demand anything from you, whether under pretext of custom or in any other way, for chrism, holy oil, consecration of churches, ordination of clerics to be promoted to holy orders, the bringing of an abbot to the episcopal see, or any other ecclesiastical sacraments. [Col. 1300C] But if anyone presumes to act contrary to this, let him know that he will have a portion with Gehazi, whose deed he imitates in exacting shameful gain and payment.

We further decree that the burial-ground of that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and last will of those who choose burial there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while preserving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. Desiring also to provide henceforth, with paternal concern, for your peace and tranquillity, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone to commit theft or robbery, set fire, seize or kill a person, or rashly exercise any violence within the enclosures of your places or granges. [Col. 1300D]

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the Ides of February, in the third indiction [read: sixth], in the year [Col. 1301A] 1187 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary. I, Melchior, cardinal priest across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus, [and] of Saints John and Paul, etc. I, James, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Goffredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Radulf, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

XXI. He commands archbishops and bishops not to permit “the possessions of churches to be alienated by the priors and obedientiaries of the Cluniac brethren without the counsel of the abbot and convent, and transferred to laymen.” (Lateran, February 16.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 88.]

[Col. 1301B]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the archbishops and bishops in whose dioceses are situated priories and obediences of the Church of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is incumbent upon our office to correct acts undertaken, through the arrogance of prelates, to the prejudice of churches, lest, if we are negligent in providing for them, their condition suffer grave loss and we ourselves be reproved for negligence at the final [Col. 1301C] judgment. Since it has therefore reached the hearing of our apostolate that priors and obedientiaries of the Cluniac brethren, without the counsel of the abbot and convent, unlawfully alienate the possessions of their churches contrary to the institution of the Cluniac order, and, by transferring certain of them to laymen, do not hesitate to reduce the rent due, to the grave detriment of the churches: by the authority of the present letters we enjoin and firmly command your brotherhood that, when complaint reaches you, you diligently admonish the possessors of the goods of the aforesaid churches thus alienated, and, if necessary, compel them, by excommunication together with interdict and without appeal, to restore without difficulty possessions alienated to the prejudice [Col. 1301D] of the churches by the rash act of priors or other administrators, and not delay to make whole the rent unreasonably reduced.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the first year of our pontificate.

XXII. He takes the Church of Cammin under protection, on condition that Bishop Sifrid and his successors pay each year to the Apostolic See one *ferton* [Note: [Col. 1301D] A quarter of a mark.] of gold. (Lateran, February 24.)

[LUNIG, *Spicileg. eccles.*, Supplement, p. 6.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother SIFRID, bishop of Cammin, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 1302A] By the apostolic office imposed upon us by God, it is fitting that we provide with paternal care for our brethren and fellow bishops, both near and far away, and preserve their rights to the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord. For it is equitable and reasonable that those who are known to be more devoted to blessed Peter and his vicars, and who desire to be fostered by the patronage of the holy Roman Church, should be nourished at the breasts of that pious mother. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously grant your just petitions; we take under the protection of the prince of the apostles and our own the Church of Cammin entrusted to you, which belongs to the right of blessed Peter; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and peacefully possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God favoring, through concessions of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. Among these we have judged it fitting to specify the following by their proper names:

The city of Cammin itself, with its tavern and market, and all their appurtenances; the following castles—namely Demusin, Treboses, Chosow, Wolgast, Huzonim, Groswin, Piris, and Stargard—with their villages and all their appurtenances; Stettin; Prentzlow with market, tavern, and its appurtenances; Colberg with its saltworks-hut, toll, market, tavern, [Col. 1302C] and all its appurtenances; all Pomerania as far as the River Łeba, with markets and taverns; and the tithe of Fohri Sithen.

Moreover, since the city called Wollin, in which the episcopal seat formerly used to be, is stated to have been deserted because of the misfortunes of war, we establish that the seat itself shall be maintained in the church of St. John the Baptist near the city of Cammin, which is more populous and secure. We ratify the liberty by which that see, from its first establishment, has been subject to the Roman pontiff alone, as it has hitherto been observed, and decree that it shall remain inviolable for all time. Furthermore, we confirm by apostolic authority to you, and through you to the church itself, the tithes which it possesses both through the relinquishment of laymen and by other just means.

[Col. 1302D] Moreover, we establish that all clerics subject to your jurisdiction, both religious and others, shall render you due reverence and obedience in all things, unless they are exempt through privileges of the Apostolic See. We further forbid the episcopal goods, when you or any of your successors dies, to be alienated through the violence of the prince of the land or of any other person; rather, they shall be kept undiminished and entire for the person canonically appointed. By apostolic authority we likewise forbid laymen who build churches or oratories in your diocese to presume to place priests in them, or to remove canonically instituted priests, without the consent of the diocesan bishop.

[Col. 1303A] We add also, prohibiting that, if any church is built in that diocese, the bishop then in office shall confer upon it the gift of consecration unless beforehand a competent endowment for the adequate support of its ministers has been assigned by its founder or someone else. We further forbid anyone to receive persons placed under your interdict or excommunication into ecclesiastical office or communion without fitting satisfaction, unless perhaps danger of death is imminent and they cannot have your personal presence; in that case, after satisfaction has first been made, the bound person should be absolved by another according to the form of the Church. As acknowledgment of this protection and liberty received from the Apostolic See, you and your successors shall pay each year to us and our successors one *ferton* [Col. 1303B] of gold.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in the place of the chancellor, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord [Col. 1303C] Pope Clement III.

XXIII. He confirms to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, the monastery of Baumes. (Lateran, February 25.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 88.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1303D] The glorious and wonderful majesty of divine providence established diverse ranks and orders in its Church for this purpose: that, while inferiors render due obedience and reverence to superiors, unity might arise from diversity, and the administration of the several offices might be ordered rightly. As obedient sons of holy Church ought to be cherished in the bosom of their mother with the breasts of gracious consolation, so rebels and the proud—who through their misconduct incur, as it were, the sin of divination and the crime of idolatry—must be restrained more strictly by the disciplines of ecclesiastical severity.

Thus the monastery of Baumes, which, through the brethren gathered there, ought to have shone and flourished with the fragrance of good repute and the splendor of religious excellence, wasted away in their sins at the devil’s prompting because they followed the old man with his deeds. Consequently, it had been miserably diminished both spiritually and temporally. But when it pleased him who disposes all things from eternity to put an end to such great evils and mercifully call the place itself back to his service, he willed to fill the faces of those brethren with shame, so that by this means they might seek his name and return, even unwillingly, to the way of uprightness. [Col. 1304A]

Accordingly, justice leading the way, Pope Eugenius, our predecessor of happy memory, decreed that the aforesaid monastery of Baumes, with all its appurtenances, should be possessed in perpetuity by the Church of Cluny, and confirmed this by the protection of his privilege.

Therefore, following in the footsteps of Eugenius and Urban, Roman pontiffs and our predecessors, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and, through you, to your church the aforesaid monastery, as you possess it justly and canonically, with all that it now justly and canonically possesses or may hereafter acquire by just means, the Lord granting; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. This is upon the express condition that the monastic order there shall always be inviolably observed in future according to the Cluniac institution; and that, because of the rebellion, contumacy, and offence which the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Baumes committed against the holy Roman Church, whoever obtains the governance of that place through you shall never bear the title of abbot, but only that of prior.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever [Col. 1304C] may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, with the authority of the Apostolic See undoubtedly reserved. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, knowingly violating this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; and let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, [Col. 1304D] and become subject, at the last judgment, to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1305A] I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Suffredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Julian Prison. I, Ralph, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting as vice-chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March [25 February], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1305B] 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## XXIV. He takes the monastery of Cluny under protection and confirms certain property and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 25 February.)*

*[Bullarium Cluniacense, 89.]*

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Cluny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

The more especially your Church is subject to us directly, without intermediary, the more earnestly we are bound to provide for its [Col. 1305C] rights, lest in the passage of time it be burdened by unjust molestation concerning things which it is known reasonably to possess. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, after the example of Alexander and Urban, Roman pontiffs of happy memory, our predecessors, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been instituted in your monastery according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same [Col. 1305D] monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God granting, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid monastery is situated, with all its appurtenances. The priory of Saint Mary of Nazara, with all its appurtenances; the priory of the Holy Trinity of Lencona, with all its appurtenances, as your Church canonically possesses those priories. We grant you, in an authentic written instrument, the donation of the aforesaid priory of St. Mary, and by apostolic authority [Col. 1306A] confirm it to you and to that Church.

Moreover, of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, and of the produce of your animals, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you. You may also receive clerics or laymen, free and absolved, fleeing from the world for conversion, and retain them without any opposition. Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from departing it without his abbot’s leave, save on account of a stricter religious life; and no one shall dare retain a person who departs without the security of letters of common authorization. We decree, therefore, that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; yet the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken shall remain intact. Since tithes are known to have been granted to ministers of churches under both the Old and the New Law, we prohibit, under threat of anathema, any layman from presuming to demand or extort tithes from you. [Col. 1306B]

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those uses for whose governance and support they were granted, the authority of the Apostolic See being reserved in all things. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc. [Col. 1306C]

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 1306D] I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Saffredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Ralph, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting as vice-chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March [25 February], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## XXV. He confirms all possessions of the monastery of Cluny.  
*(Lateran, 25 February.)*

*[Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, 1453.]*

[Col. 1307A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of Cluny, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

The monastery of blessed Peter at Cluny, a model of monastic religion in modern times and an example in the regions of Gaul, was offered to the Apostolic See as its own proper right from the very beginning of its foundation. Accordingly, our fathers of holy memory—John XI, likewise John XIX, Agapetus II, [Col. 1307B] Benedict VI, likewise Benedict VII, Leo VII, likewise Leo IX, Gregory VI, likewise Gregory VII, Alexander II, Stephen, Victor III, Urban II, Paschal II, Gelasius II, Calixtus II, Lucius II, Eugenius III, Adrian IV, and Urban III, pontiffs of the Roman Church—endowed that place with the prerogative of singular affection and liberty, and protected all its goods and dependencies by the enactments of their privileges.

For it was established that all churches, cemeteries, monks, clerics, and all laypersons living within the boundaries—which run from the stream of Salnai, from the church of Rufiaci and the Cross of Lornant; also from the boundary of the mill of Tornesac, through the village called Varenna, together with the wood of Burserius; and likewise from the boundary called Perois as far as the stream of Salnai—shall remain under the jurisdiction and protection of the Apostolic See alone. Neither the priests nor even the parishioners of the place of Cluny itself shall be compelled to attend the synod or assembly of anyone other than the Roman pontiff and the abbot of Cluny. [Col. 1307C]

For the ordination of an abbot, monks, or clerics living within the aforesaid boundaries; for the making of chrism; and for the consecration with holy oil of churches, altars, and cemeteries, the monastery of Cluny may summon whichever bishop it prefers. No person whatsoever, other than the Roman pontiff or a legate dispatched from his side, shall excommunicate or place under interdict Cluniac monks wherever they live.

Moreover, we confirm by the page of this present decree the boundaries of the immunity of your place, which were established by our aforesaid predecessor Pope Urban II, so that no person, of whatever condition or power, may presume within their bounds to commit invasion, plunder, robbery, or homicide. The boundaries of the sacred ban are therefore these: toward Berziacum, the boundary is at the fork near Sarrata, whence one road leads to Cluny and the other to Masilles; on the road toward Bellumjocum, the boundary is opposite the cart-track above the mill of the Cluniac cellarer; on this side of Viengias, beyond Cluny toward Masilles, the boundary is at the fork whence one road goes to Masilles and another to Saint Mary of the Wood; above Rufiacum, the boundary is at the summit of the enclosed ground, at the fork [Col. 1308A] whence one road goes to Besorniacum and another to Quarella; toward Sergiacum, the boundary is within the cart-track, on this side of the place called ad Turgum; on the road toward the district of Chalon, the boundary is at the great oak above Marniacum; toward Brancedunum, the boundary is on the road above the wood called Bannedum; toward Trenorchium, the boundary is above the stream called Longa Aqua; between Banoscium and Donziacum toward Petrona or Zasiacum, the boundary is at the three beeches, where our wood of Cluny and the count’s wood are divided; toward Igiacum, the boundary is at Carmos, on Mont Moyen.

In the abbeys which, along with their abbots, were entrusted to the governance of the monastery of Cluny—namely Saint Martial of Limoges, the New Monastery at Poitiers, Saint [Col. 1308B] John of Angély, the monastery of Lézat, Moissac, Figeac in the district of Cahors; in Auvergne, Mozac, Thiers, and Menat; in the diocese of Auxerre, Saint German; in the Rouen abbey at Pontoise; and in the diocese of Thérouanne, Saint Wulmar—an abbot shall by no means be elected without the counsel of the abbot of Cluny.

In addition, we decree that in all priories and cells now subject to your governance without their own abbot, no one shall ever presume in future times to appoint an abbot. Rather, both those priories and cells, and all other things whatsoever in whatever places of which the Church of Cluny was invested at the time of the Council of Auvergne, celebrated by the aforesaid Pope Urban II, and concerning which no question was then raised, shall always be preserved to you and your successors in peace and quiet.

With respect to your altars, churches, and tithes, no bishop shall have power to impose any burden or harassment upon you; rather, as you have held some of them in part and others wholly with their permission, so you shall hold them in the future. Tithes belonging to your churches which are held by laymen, if reverence for your religious order can, according to God, withdraw them from those persons’ control, you may possess for the maintenance of yourselves and the poor. You shall henceforth hold in greater peace, without any opposition from bishops and episcopal officials, the tithes of your labours—those called *Dominicaturae*, for which bishops have been accustomed to trouble both you and other men of monastic religion—which are cultivated at your expense by the monasteries and by the dependants of your cells, and which you distribute to travelling brethren and to the poor. [Col. 1308C–D]

All churches located anywhere, as well as your chapels and cemeteries, shall be free and immune from every exaction, except the bishop’s customary procuration and jurisdiction over priests who offend against the dignity of their order. You or your brethren may also choose priests, provided that they receive the cure of souls from bishops or the bishops’ vicars without payment. If those bishops refuse, through perversity—may it not be so!—to confer it, then, through the kindness of the Apostolic See, the priests shall obtain permission to celebrate the offices. For consecrations of churches or altars, if the diocesan bishops are willing to provide them without charge, receive them from any Catholic bishop. Nor shall brethren of your cells wherever situated suffer suspension from divine offices on account of any interdict or excommunication; rather, the monks themselves, their servants, and those who have devoted themselves to monastic profession shall, with the church doors closed and diocesan authorities not admitted, celebrate the offices of divine service and perform the duties of burial. [Col. 1309A]

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God favouring, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

In Burgundy: the church of Villefranche, the church of Barberiaco, the monastery of Prims, and the church of Belna with its appurtenances. In France: the church of Mont-Desiderii, the church of Dompetra, and the church of Crispeium. In Provence: the monastery near Montpellier. In the diocese of Toulouse: the churches of Saint Columba. In Spain: Nazara, Saint Isidore, Saint Zoelus of Carrión, Saint Romanus of Peñis, Villaviridis, Villefranche, Valemviridis, Palumbarium, Bodinum, Vimeneria, Saint Martin of Nebda, Saint Vincent of Salamanca, Saint Columba of Burgos, and Cornilana, [Col. 1309B–C] which were granted directly to the monastery of Cluny.

Likewise, in the diocese of Nevers: the monastery of Albiniacum, which belongs to La Charité. In France: the monastery of Causiacum, which belongs to Saint Martin-des-Champs; and the collegiate church of Abbeville. Likewise, the church of Rue, which belongs to the monastery of Abbeville. In the diocese of Castres: the church of Saint Peter of Aliano. In the diocese of Tusculum: the church of Saint Mary of Pessulo [Pesculo]. In the diocese of Orvieto: the church of Saint Mary of Aquamola and the church of Saint Angelus.

We prohibit anyone from presuming to build a church or chapel within parishes belonging to the right of the monastery of Cluny without the assent of the abbot of Cluny, the authority of the Apostolic See being reserved in all things. [Col. 1309D] We further forbid anyone to sell, alienate in another manner, or pledge as security lands, other possessions, or the treasures of your churches; or for any of your brethren to stand surety for anyone, without the consent of your abbot and chapter, or of the greater and sounder part thereof. Should this be done, we decree that it is to be invalidated.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those uses for whose governance or support they were granted. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, [Col. 1310A] attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; and let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church.

**Teach me, Lord, to do thy will.**

I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint [Col. 1310B] Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St. Callixtus. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, James, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gofridus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. [Col. 1310C] I, Ralph, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting as vice-chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March [25 February], sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## XXVI. He orders that the election of the abbots of St. Benedict of Padilirone be conducted according to the privileges of the monastery of Cluny.  
*(Lateran, 26 February.)*

*[Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 1452.]*

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot, and the convent of Cluny, [Col. 1310D] greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having carefully examined the privileges granted by the Apostolic See to the monastery of Cluny, we have clearly learned that the monastery of Saint Benedict was entrusted by our predecessor Gregory VII, of good memory, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors, so that they should have it under their governance, custody, and authority and should devote their care to its administration. Further, on the death of the abbot of that place, their diligence should always ensure that a suitable person, worthy of this office, should be installed in the position of government according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; and that whatever ought to be instituted or corrected in the monastery for the growth and observance of monastic religion should be carried out jointly through their ministry and stewardship, while in all things the authority of the Apostolic See, to whose right that place belongs, remains intact. [Col. 1311A]

The same was ordained and confirmed by the successors of Gregory himself, our predecessors, and especially by Pope Calixtus of happy memory. In his confirmation he added that, in that same monastery of Saint Benedict, no abbot whatsoever should be elected without the counsel, provision, and command of the abbot of Cluny; and that no bishop should lay the hand of consecration or ordination upon the person elected without letters of recommendation from the abbot of Cluny. Otherwise, both the consecrator, as a transgressor of the apostolic constitution, shall be subject to a graver punishment, and the election or ordination of the person consecrated shall be held void until satisfaction has been made to the Apostolic See and to the same monastery of Cluny.

In the time of Pope Lucius, of blessed memory, our predecessor, Peter, then abbot of your monastery, both personally and through his brethren frequently complained to Lucius’s predecessors and to Pope Lucius himself that, without consulting that same Peter, the brethren of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Benedict had elected an abbot for themselves contrary to the foregoing tenor, and were withholding from him the obedience and reverence due to him. Therefore our predecessor Pope Innocent, of happy memory, instructed them by his letters that Abbot William, who had been elected and ordained without consultation with the abbot and brethren of Cluny, should proceed with honourable and discreet members of his community to the monastery and brethren of Cluny, and should humbly and devoutly render to that Abbot Peter the obedience and reverence which his predecessor Abbot Henry, of good memory, had rendered. [Col. 1311B–C]

As this was in no way carried out by them, and the brethren of Cluny persisted in their complaint, Pope Lucius himself commanded them in his writings that the aforesaid Abbot G., with honourable and discreet persons and with the privileges of his monastery, should appear before him after the octave of Saint Andrew had passed, so that, once the case of each party had been heard, he might, with the Lord’s help, restore peace between them. Although your brethren appeared before the said Lucius at that appointed time, he neither came himself nor could peace between the parties be restored through the brethren who had come.
