Therefore, since Lucius could no longer so manifestly fail the justice of the monastery of Cluny, he commanded and enjoined them by apostolic letters that Abbot G. himself, with honourable and discreet persons from among his brethren, should visit the monastery of Cluny without excuse or delay and humbly render to the aforesaid Abbot P. the obedience and reverence which his predecessors had rendered to the predecessors of that P.; and, if burdened by illness he could not perform this in person, he should perform it through the best persons of that monastery. [Col. 1311D]

We, therefore, following in the footsteps of our predecessors and following the example of the often-mentioned Lucius, by apostolic authority forbid any election of an abbot hereafter in that monastery of Saint Benedict unless it is made according to the aforesaid tenor of the privileges of the Apostolic See. If such an election is made, it shall be held void and without effect. [Col. 1312A]

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March [26 February], in the first year of our pontificate.

## XXVII. He assigns the monastery of Saint German of Auxerre to Abbot Hugh and the convent of Cluny.  
*(Lateran, 26 February.)*

*[BALUZE, Miscellanies, ed. Mansi, II, 177.]*

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot, and the convent of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more particularly your monastery belongs by right to blessed Peter, pertains immediately to our care and protection, and you and your predecessors—subject therein to the teaching of heavenly discipline—have through the infusion of the Holy Spirit spread more widely the fragrance of integrity and religion thus far observed in your order, the more readily we are bound to preserve its rights intact and benignly to admit the just petitions of your devotion. [Col. 1312B]

Accordingly, as was made known from the documents of S., formerly count of Blois, and A., his wife, and of Urban II and Paschal, Roman pontiffs of happy memory—transmitted under the seals of our beloved sons B., cardinal deacon of Saint Angelus, and S., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legates of the Apostolic See, to the presence of our predecessor Urban III, of good memory—the monastery of Saint German at Auxerre had so declined through the negligence of its overseers in regular observance, discipline, and temporal resources that its custody was entrusted to lowly persons. At the prayer of the aforesaid count, patron of the same monastery, and of Humbald, of good memory, then bishop of Auxerre, and of many others, our aforesaid predecessor Urban II, by prudent deliberation, granted it to blessed Hugh, then abbot of your monastery, and to his successors, to be reformed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and to be possessed perpetually in future under the order of the monastery of Cluny. Yet the monastery itself was not to lack an abbot’s oversight. [Col. 1312C]

That grant, and the donation of the aforesaid count, were later confirmed by Paschal and Urban III, our aforesaid predecessors. Following in their footsteps, we decree that the same grant shall stand ratified and confirm it by the page of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever shall be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, blessed Peter and Paul. [Col. 1312D]

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March [26 February], in the first year of our pontificate.

## XXVIII. He prohibits archbishops and bishops “from henceforth demanding any procurations from the Cluniac brethren, except when they come to their priories for purposes of visitation.”  
*(Lateran, 26 February.)*

*[Bullarium Cluniacense, 88.]*

[Col. 1312D]

[Col. 1313A] CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brethren, archbishops and bishops, in whose dioceses the priories and obediences of the Church of Cluny are situated, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By divine ordinance it is permitted to prelates of churches, while sowing spiritual things, to receive temporal things as a harvest, according to the saying: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (1 Tim. 5), provided that they do not become a burden to the churches committed to them. We have learned, however, that some of you, paying no due heed to this, [Col. 1313B] when making circuits of your dioceses, cause procurations to be furnished to you by the priories and obediences of the Cluniac brethren while lodging elsewhere, although, as they assert, they were prepared to receive you kindly in their own priories and to serve you with ready devotion.

Since it is unworthy and contrary alike to your honour to turn offices of ecclesiastical charity into a burden upon brethren subject to you, we strictly forbid by the authority of these presents that henceforth, unless you come to the aforesaid brethren’s priories for the purpose of visitation, you demand any procurations from them or inflict upon them any burden or annoyance in this regard. Know that, if you do otherwise, we shall, the Lord being the author, take care to forbid those brethren to provide procurations while you are lodged elsewhere. [Col. 1313C]

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March [26 February], in the first year of our pontificate.

## XXIX. He takes the monastery of Saint Mary of Flabémont under protection and confirms its goods.  
*(Lateran, 26 February.)*

*[HUGH, Order of Prémontré, Annals I, Preface, p. 551.]*

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of the church of Saint Mary of Flabémont, and his brethren, present and future, to be regularly appointed, for ever.

[Col. 1313D] “To religious desires,” etc. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Mary of Flabémont, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institutions of the brethren of Prémontré shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God granting, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

The place itself in which the church was founded, which from ancient times is commonly called Flabémont, together with the wood of Wathes. Rights of pasturage in the same meadows, waters, and woods; mast of oak and beech in those woods; timber both for building and burning and for all other uses. These were granted to you, in their respective portions of the entire territory of Baigneval, by Wido of Acrimonte and Wiardus Rufus of Daville; by Genoldus and Herbert of Saint Julian; by Wido, with the consent of Hugh, count of Vaudémont; by Guido and Herbert, with the consent of Olric of Gisnei; by Wiardus, with the consent [Col. 1314A–B] of the same Guido, from whom they held those things in fief; and also by Guido, with the consent of Olric of Posternis, his wife Esclamundia, and Walter of Deuilly, etc.

*(Here the pope gives a very lengthy list of all the possessions of the church of Flabémont; he then closes his bull by granting it the customary privileges and exemptions.)*

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St. Mary across the Tiber. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1314C] I, Melchior, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Sacerdos, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Cosmedin. I, Decamanus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Soffridus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Ralph, cardinal deacon of St. George at the Golden Veil.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting as vice-chancellor, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March [26 February], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, [Col. 1314D] in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement.

## XXX. Bull confirming the abbey of Blessed Mary of Hérivaux.  
*(Lateran, 2 March.)*

*[Gallia Christiana, VII, Instruments, 274.]*

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of the church of Blessed Mary of Hérivaux and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life of brethren, for ever.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps the onset of anyone’s rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, [Col. 1315A] beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Mary of Hérivaux, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of the brethren of Saint Victor of Paris shall be observed there inviolate for all time.

Moreover, whatever possessions and whatever goods that same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God granting, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances—lands, vineyards, meadows, woods, pastures, wine-cellars, and tithes. By the gift of Renaud, count of Clermont, and Matthew, count of Beaumont: Hérivaux, together with the wood and the plain adjoining that place, to the extent that you and your successors can cultivate it at your own expense and with your own animals, wholly free and immune from every secular exaction. The church of the village of Marly, with its appurtenances. By the gift of Odo Aprus: two setiers of grain annually at the Mill of Fort; and the right that at the same mill the brethren of that house, immediately after the first grinder, shall always grind free of milling-charge whatever is required for the brethren’s subsistence. [Col. 1315B–C]

By the gift of Count Renaud: three setiers of grain and three of mixed grain at the mill of Coye. By the gift of Alberic, knight: one setier of grain annually from his house at Fosses, whoever may possess it. By the gift of Gerard of Atrium: one mina of grain from the allod of Compens, of whatever kind of grain shall arise there. The tithe which the knight Guido, with the consent of the diocesan bishop, relinquished to your church. Sixty arpents of land from Rericus of Fosses, and thirty from Hugh the mayor of Luzarches, acquired by your church through purchase. A small wood adjoining your house. By the gift of Amaury of Villariobellum and his wife Elizabeth: certain vineyards and lands at Villariumbellum. Sixty and a half arpents of wood, which you hold from the aforesaid Rericus of Fosses under an annual rent of six denarii payable for each arpent. Six arpents of land, which the said Rericus gave to your church as a free and unconditional alms. [Col. 1315D]

The wood of Roissy, which you hold from Alberic, knight of Fosses, his sister’s son Hubert, and Odo of Bellofonte, under an annual rent of four denarii payable for each arpent of that wood. Twelve arpents of arable land and ten of woodland, which Hugh the mayor of Luzarches granted in perpetual gift in the territory of the village of Fosses. Also the exemption from ten solidi granted by the same Hugh to your church, [Col. 1316A] which your church had been bound to pay him annually for a certain wood. Moreover, the tithe which the same Hugh, with the consent of the diocesan bishop, relinquished to your church at Fosses and Marly; the tithe which Milo of Bellofonte, with the consent of his wife and heirs, relinquished at Bernerii; and likewise that which Malcerius, knight of Ballanval, relinquished to your church at Survilliers, with three setiers of grain, with the consent of the diocesan bishop. By the gift of Odo, mayor of Luzarches: one setier annually and four arpents of land for the soul of his wife. By the gift of Ralph, knight of Aquabona: two setiers of grain at Villariumsiccum. By the gift of the woman Brunisendis: two setiers of grain in the village of Marioli. By the gift of the woman Idonea [Col. 1316B] of Doemunt and her son Cunavus: a free hostise/tenancy at Villare, and two arpents of land for the soul of her husband Adam. One half of one fourth part of the tithe of Fosses, which Robert Bochardus, with the consent of the diocesan bishop, relinquished to your church.

No one may presume to exact tithes from you on the new lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your animals. You may also receive into conversion clerics or laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, from leaving it without his abbot’s permission, [Col. 1316C] or from retaining any private property through levity; and no one may dare retain one who has departed without the safeguard of letters of communal permission. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of that locality shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any trickery or deceit, or [Col. 1316D] violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater part of the brethren of sounder counsel, shall, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, determine should be elected.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept intact for the benefit and use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, canon of the Lateran, acting in place of the chancellor, on the sixth day before the Nones of March [2 March], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187 (which is now 1188), in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### XXXI. To all bishops: notification of the privilege of the brethren of St Mary of Reno, “that they may receive orders from whatever Catholic bishop they prefer.” (Lateran, 3 March.)

[Trombelli, *Memorie di Reno*, 436.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, all bishops to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it was long ago granted to our beloved sons Hugh, prior and our subdeacon, and the convent of St Mary of Reno [Col. 1317B] by the bishops of Bologna, and confirmed to them by apostolic privilege, that they may receive orders from whatever Catholic bishop they prefer, we both wish and ought to ensure that this liberty is preserved unimpaired for them in future times. Therefore, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Lucius and Urban, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, whenever one of them comes to you to be ordained, you shall ordain him by apostolic authority according to the tenor of his privilege, notwithstanding any opposition or appeal. We do not, however, wish that, because they have once or repeatedly received orders from someone, their ability to approach another or others should in any way be denied them.

[Col. 1317C] Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Nones of March [3 March], in the first year of our pontificate.

### XXXII. He confirms Sana villa to the monastery of Cluny. (Lateran, 5 March.)

[*Bullarium Cluniacense*, 92.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Hugh, abbot, and the convent of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily admit, and bring to their due effect, petitions which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, granting your just request, [Col. 1317D] we confirm to you by apostolic authority the estate of Sana, which the nobleman … Despire, through the hand of our venerable brother Theobald, bishop of Ostia, then your abbot, bequeathed to your monastery in his last will; and we strengthen this confirmation by the protection of the present document, as you possess it lawfully and without dispute.

Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of March [5 March], in the first year of our pontificate.

### XXXLI. To William, king of Scots—concerning the exemption of the churches in his realm. (Lateran, 11 March.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXII, 548.]

[Col. 1318A]

Although all who are subject to Christ’s yoke ought to find protection and favour at the Apostolic See, those whose faith and devotion it has most often experienced should especially be cherished by the safeguard of its protection, so that they may be drawn yet more strongly toward the favour of its choice and may submit to its reverence with more devoted affection, in proportion as they know that they have more surely obtained a pledge of its good will and grace. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, considering the reverence and devotion which, from times long past, we know you have shown toward the Roman [Col. 1318B] Church, we have determined by the present document that the Scottish Church, which is a special daughter of the Apostolic See, shall be subject to it without any intermediary.

The episcopal sees known to be within it are these: namely, the churches of St Andrews, Glasgow, Dunkeld, Dunblane, Brechin, Aberdeen, Moray, Ross, and Caithness. No one except the Roman pontiff, or a legate sent from his side, may pronounce a sentence of interdict or excommunication within the kingdom of Scotland; and, if such a sentence is pronounced, we decree that it shall have no force. We further add that henceforth no one who is not from the kingdom of Scotland, except one whom the Apostolic See has specially sent from its own body for this purpose, may [Col. 1318C] exercise the office of legate there. We also prohibit controversies arising in that kingdom concerning its possessions from being brought before the judgment of judges situated outside the kingdom, unless an appeal has been made to the Roman Church. If any documents obtained against the provisions of this liberty should appear, or should hereafter be obtained without mention of this concession, they shall create no prejudice for you or for the kingdom itself concerning the grant of this prerogative. Moreover, we hold valid the liberties and immunities granted to you, to the same kingdom, or to the churches established in it, by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and hitherto observed; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future [Col. 1318D] times.

Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe the page of our constitution and prohibition or oppose it in any manner. If anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Ides of March [13 March], in the first year of our pontificate.

### XXXIV. He takes the monastery of St Mary of Moncel under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, 16 March.)

[Hugo, *O.P.A.*, II, preface, p. 193.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Albert, abbot of St Mary of Moncel, and his brethren, present and future, professing the religious life: in perpetual remembrance.

It is fitting that apostolic assistance be available to those choosing the religious life, lest an assault of any rash person either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid!—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the aforesaid church of St Mary of Moncel, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of the present document. First, we establish that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that church according to God, [Col. 1319B] the Rule of blessed Augustine, and the institution of Prémontré, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods that church now lawfully and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by grant of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, donations of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself on which your abbey stands, which you hold from Anselm of Moncel through Count Theobald and with the assent of Wiburg, from whom he held it in fief; mills, two ploughlands of land, meadows, fishing rights, woodland, and the two men Giguard and Alberic, with their other appurtenances. A third part of the tithe of Moncel, both small and great; the right of user which Count Henry granted you in his wood, both for fuel and for constructing all kinds of buildings for your church, together with all pastures of the same wood; and a certain piece of land at Volliers, through Boso, formerly bishop of Châlons, with the assent of the aforesaid Ralph, who held it from him in fief. Land sufficient for clearing and cultivation by ploughs, marked by fixed boundaries, which Count Henry gave you in the wood of Luorico, [Col. 1319D] together with another piece of land from the adjoining woodland beyond the aforesaid boundaries, sufficient for making twenty mowings of meadow; land which the same count gave you in the same wood at the request of Master Hugh, situated between Lefrid’s spring and the hut and the road of …, together with woodland and other land … beyond the stream of Casum, as far as an arrow can be shot, for the concealment of the house, so that … of his shall neither claim from you any customary due nor make any exaction.

Four sextarii of grain—two of *tremeciatum* and two of *tremesagium*—which Guy, lord of Cytripeio, gave to your church at Casum, to be received every year from the land-dues of Moncel; twelve pence of rent, which Hersendis of Troam gave to the church of Casum at Pont, of which [Col. 1320A] six … and the other six Hugh of the same town … must annually pay to the prior of Casum. The grange of Vilo, located beside Bosemont, which you hold from Count Henry, from the abbot and chapter of Belle-Loc, with all its appurtenances, as the church of Belle-Loc had held it, excepting what that church had at …; on this condition, namely, that each year you must pay to Ralph of Blanciaco, cleric of the same count, three measures of grain by the measure of St Margaret—half wheat and half oats. On the death of Ralph and the count, however, you shall pay only two measures of grain by the aforesaid measure to the heir of the aforementioned count.

The house which you have in the marketplace at Vitry, given by Louis of the same [Col. 1320B] castle with Count Henry’s assent; two parts; three parts of the great tithe of Maweu; a third part of tithes, both great and small, which you hold freely within the parish of Boran-curiata, so that you owe nothing for … on your part; a third of the tithe, both great and small, which you hold at Libatiam; a third part at Blois; two sextarii of wheat which you have at St Veran from land-dues held by Simon; and a mina of wheat at Sapignecourt; six pence of rent for the soul of the wife of Odo of Cloes. All these things the aforesaid Simon, or those who held the aforesaid land-dues, were required to pay annually to your church.

The place of Avigneio, where the cloister of the sisters was built … [Col. 1320C] from the field of Peter Piguis as far as the meadow of Avigneio, together with that meadow, which Guy, lord of Dampierre, and his wife Helaydis gave you for the remedy of their souls, with the assent of their sons, namely Andrew and Milo; the meadow of the Island; the meadow called Arrandicampus; the tithe of all the grain from all their lands belonging to the lord of Moilen; the ploughs of his mills and his land-dues, except seed and coppice-wood; fishing rights from the bridge of Hauteville to Moilen; the right of user in all his woodland, except his protected grounds, both for fuel and for constructing all kinds of buildings for your church, with pasture for swine, livestock, [Col. 1320D] and animals in open country and woodland, without any customary payment or exaction by officials.

The two mills which you hold from Hilduin of Moilen and from … of Cosantia, knights, subject to an annual rent of twenty-four sextarii of grain, sixteen of wheat and eight of *tremesagium*, with the assent of Guy of Dampierre; the land which Guy of Habucort and his brother Berald gave you, located from Sabico of Horecourt …; the field at the boundary of the bridge of Neuville; half the mill of Guigny; free fishing rights from the customary course of the Marne to the division of the water of Sapignecourt; the liberty granted to your church by Guy, lord of Dampierre: namely, that if any of his men, free or servile, [Col. 1321A] should wish to join you and assume the religious habit, you may freely receive him together with his property, saving rent and land-dues; except that, in the case of knights, whether in life or at death, you may not be given the whole fief, but only a part, while preserving his homage. If any of these men should wish to sell you land, you may receive it, while preserving the customary due upon that land.

Eight solidi of rent which you receive at Ramerum, from the gift of your convert Milo and his son Peter, on the feast of St Remigius, from the hand of the reeve of the Isles at Dommartin; a third part of the tithe and sixteen pence of rent from nineteen sextarii of grain, half rye and half oats; a third part [Col. 1321B] of the tithe which you have in the village called Piper—namely, three sextarii out of eight in the year when you receive it with the abbess of Troyes; but when it is with Pagan, you owe a fourth part of the same tithe; in the year in which … receives it, you have nothing in that same tithe.

The alms of your convert Beliardis and of Milo Cose, sister of the same Beliardis; the land-dues and rent which you have, by gift of the aforesaid persons, at Grandeville and at Doenum. A third part of the great and small tithe which you have in the village called Mallyacum and at Roman …; a fourth part of the tithe which you have at Val-du-Puits; a sixth part of the same mill, with half its custody, which you have at the holding of Willerminus … [Col. 1321C] the small tithe which you have at …, which the chaplain receives for his chantry, while a third part of the small tithe there is retained for you.

The great tithe which you have at Vaspium in every third year, a third part of the small tithe annually, and whatever … held in the land-dues and rents of that same village, and whatever he held in land-dues, rents, and customary dues at Albeme; an annual rent of six and a half sextarii of wheat and six and a half sextarii of oats, which both Robert of Walsecourt, son of Waltica surnamed Britel, and his successors must pay every year on the feast of St Remigius to the brethren of Avigneio, from whom he received half the mills of Walsecourt under the same rent. Moreover, Robert and his successors shall be bound annually to pay the aforesaid monks the annual rent which the brethren of Avigneio had customarily paid every year to the monks of Hozecort, on account of their receipt of the same mills. Nevertheless, if those mills should be completely destroyed in any manner through Robert’s fault, the aforesaid brethren shall repair one half and Robert the other. New sureties shall be given every three years concerning the rent: two sextarii of wheat which Robert of Walsecourt gave you with his mother when he came to your conversion, and which the three men of Hautefont paid to that same Robert annually as rent for the land between the pond and the land of Blefia, with the assent of the lord [Col. 1322A] of Dampierre, from whom Robert held that land in fief.

The freehold which you hold from the church of St Mary of Vanno, and from Abbot Bartholomew and the chapter of St Paul of Verdun, subject to an annual rent of five solidi in Châlons currency, payable every year on the feast of St Remigius to that church of Walfno; the freehold which James of Graveria gave you at the stream beside the village called Loisis, rent reserved, with the consent of his lords from whom he held it, together with a certain house and one holding, as is contained in the authenticated document of the bishop of Châlons.

Half a meadow called Manbre, with half the arable land adjoining that meadow, which Guy, son of … [Col. 1322B] Rufus of Walsecourt, gave you with the assent of his brothers and of Hilduin Peter, for his sister, a convert in your church; the other half of that meadow with the aforesaid land, which … gave you with the assent of the aforesaid brothers of Hilduin Peter. In return for this concession your church released to the three aforementioned brothers half the mills of Walsecourt, which they had pledged to the same church for ten pounds of Troyes currency. The other half of those mills was retained by the aforesaid Galba, who held the freehold of Hescalaron, which Stephen of One gave you insofar as it belonged to him by right.

No one may presume to demand or extort tithes from you on the produce of your labour which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the sustenance of your [Col. 1322C] animals, although you pay to the lords of the estates, by reason of ownership, a rent or any allotted part of the crops.

You may also receive into conversion clerics and laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them without any opposition. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, from leaving it without his abbot’s permission; and no one may dare retain one who departs without the safeguard of letters of communal permission.

We also forbid churches, lands, or any benefice granted to your church to be personally bestowed upon anyone or alienated in any other way without [Col. 1322D] the consent of the entire chapter, or of its greater and sounder part.

If any gifts or alienations have been made otherwise than as stated, we judge them void. In addition, we forbid any canons or converts bound by profession to your house, without the consent of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, to become surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone beyond the amount … provided for by your prudent administration, unless for the manifest benefit of your house. If they should nevertheless presume to do so, the convent, without whose permission and consent they acted, shall not be bound to answer in any way for these matters. Moreover, it shall be lawful for you in [Col. 1323A] your legal cases to bring forward brethren qualified to testify, and through their testimony, as is right, both to repel violence and to vindicate justice. In order to avoid the frequent presence of secular persons, you may, without prejudice to the right of the diocesan bishop and parish church, build oratories in your granges, and there, when necessary, celebrate divine offices for yourselves and your household.

Furthermore, we decree that the burial-place of that locality shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. For chrism, holy oil, consecrations of churches, [Col. 1323B] ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, the bringing of an abbot to his see, or any other ecclesiastical sacraments, no one may dare demand anything from you, either under colour of custom or in any other manner.

If anyone presumes to act against these provisions, let him know that he shall have a portion with Gehazi, whose deed he imitates by exaction of a shameful reward. Moreover, wishing with paternal concern to provide in future for your peace and tranquillity, we prohibit by apostolic authority anyone from committing theft or robbery, setting fire, seizing [Col. 1323C] or killing a person, or rashly exercising any violence within the enclosure of your places or your granges.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept intact for the benefit and use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus. [Col. 1323D] I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of St Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St Callistus. I, Albinus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Melior, cardinal-priest of the title of St Cecilia. I, Rodulphus, cardinal-priest of the title of St Praxedes. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of St Clement. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of St Pudentiana, of the title of Pastor. I, James, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 1324A] I, Soffredus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Bobo, cardinal-deacon of St Sergius. I, John, cardinal-deacon of St Theodore.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on 18 April [Note: [Col. 1323D] For “18 April,” read “the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April” (17 March).], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### XXXV. He takes the church of St Mary of Reno under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Lateran, 17 March.)

[Trombelli, *Memorie di Reno*, 381.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons [Col. 1324B] Hugh, prior of St Mary of Reno, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for ever.

Although, unworthy as we are, the care and concern of all churches has been entrusted to us, we are bound to exercise pastoral concern for the condition of your church and, as the Lord has granted us, diligently to attend to your peace. Therefore, moved by your devout petitions and just requests, in order that you may be protected by apostolic defence from the assaults of wicked men, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own the church in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of the present document. We establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions or goods the same church now lawfully and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire by grant of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The place itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the church of St Andrew at Turicella; the church of St Domninus near Bagno; the church of the Holy Saviour. The possessions formerly belonging to Gerard of Sala, with tithes, [Col. 1324D] rents, and all their appurtenances; the hospital of Casaiola with its appurtenances; the church of St Praxedes, as it was granted to you by our predecessors of pious memory, Anastasius, Alexander, Lucius, and Urban, Roman pontiffs—saving the right and reverence of the cardinal who at the time shall hold that church. The church of St James called Casa-Dei, with its appurtenances. The bridge situated over the Reno near your church, with its possessions.

We hold valid and firm, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time, the liberties and immunities reasonably granted by Henry and Gerard, bishops of Bologna of good memory, to your church and to your other aforesaid churches: namely, that with all their goods, movable and immovable, they shall be wholly free and exempt from every condition, service, and tribute of those holding from the bishop, whether monks, clerics, laymen, or persons of whatever rank, great or small, save episcopal right. [Col. 1325A]

You may also receive into conversion clerics and laymen fleeing the world, free and unencumbered, and retain them in your church without any opposition. Moreover, we prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, from leaving it without his prior’s permission, except on account of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain one who departs without the safeguard of your communal letters. If any of these brethren has dared remain outside the cloister without the aforesaid permission and, after a second or third warning, should refuse to repent, the prior of the same place may pronounce against him, as against one professed to him, a sentence of excommunication. Furthermore, we confirm to you and your church by apostolic authority the tithes which you have held without disturbance for forty years and are now known to hold peacefully. We also prohibit anyone from imposing new and unlawful exactions upon you and your church; rather, we decree that it shall enjoy the liberty known to have belonged to it during the forty years elapsed up to the present time.

[Col. 1325C] We also decree that the burial-place of that locality shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved. Further, we grant you free authority to receive the ordinations of your clerics from whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, as the said bishops are known by authenticated documents to have granted us that very power. We confirm to you the tithes of your produce, coming from anywhere within the diocese of Bologna, as those tithes were granted to your church by the prudent foresight of the same bishops. Upon the death of you, the present prior of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful trickery or violence, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the part of the brethren of sounder counsel, shall, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, determine should be elected.

As a token of this protection and liberty received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay annually to us and our successors two solidi of Luccan currency.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, [Col. 1326A] or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be kept intact for the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, beneficial in every respect, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the bishop of Bologna.

If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to violate this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and [Col. 1326B] let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance.

But may all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of St Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal-priest of St Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Callistus. I, Albinus, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1326C] I, Melior, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, James, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gerard, cardinal-deacon of St Adrian. I, Octavian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Soffredus, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Via Lata. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Radulphus, cardinal-deacon of St George at the Golden Veil.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman [Col. 1326D] Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [17 March], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1187, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### XXXVI. He confirms the exemption from tithes to the abbots and brethren of the Premonstratensian order. (Lateran, 17 March.)

[Lepaige, *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*, 641.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots and brethren of the Premonstratensian order: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect the requests that do not depart from the path of reason. [Col. 1327A] Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring gladly with your just requests, we grant by apostolic authority to you and your successors that henceforth you shall pay no tithes on your new lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, firmly forbidding anyone henceforward to demand or presume to exact them from you. We also graciously grant you the tithes of your new lands which you possess in the parish of Firmitas, in the woodland which Gobert of Firmitas mercifully conferred upon you, retaining for himself and his heirs one half of the fruits, except the sheaves of the harvest; and, following the example of our predecessor Lord Urban, we confirm them by apostolic authority and strengthen them with the protection of the present document, [Col. 1327B] establishing that no person whatsoever, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [17 March], in the first year of our pontificate.

### XXXVII. He commands the prior of Faversham and Master Firmin to declare excommunicate those who have invaded the goods of the Church of Canterbury, if, after warning, they have not made reparation for the damage. (Lateran, 17 March.)

[Gervase, *Imaginatio*, in Twysden, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 1321.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior of Faversham and Master Firmin: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The detestable presumption of a horrible crime has profoundly stirred our mind by its atrocity, so that we may strike with the dart of due severity those who, like robbers, wickedly invaded the possessions of the Church of Canterbury, or who, breaking down walls, cruelly burst into the monks’ court enclosure and workshops and are known to have plundered their goods with sacrilegious audacity. Likewise, those who, inflicting violence upon the monks and their men, occupied the court despite their opposition. Therefore, since we can neither can nor ought to overlook the injuries done to the aforesaid brethren—whom we are bound to support in their right with greater kindness because they are pre-eminent in the English regions by greater distinction—we decree by the authority of these presents that those presumptuous persons who committed so monstrous a sacrilege, and their accomplices, shall remain under anathema until fitting satisfaction is made. [Col. 1327D] We command you by apostolic letters that, if after warning they refuse to make suitable satisfaction, you shall solemnly and publicly announce them, with opposition and appeal set aside, as excommunicated according to custom, and cause them to be cautiously avoided by all. You shall take especial care that—God forbid!—the apostolic command in this matter is not neglected through your idleness, for that would be grievous and wholly distressing to us, and we could not bear it with equanimity. If both of you cannot be present to execute these matters, one of you shall nevertheless carry them out.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April [17 March], in the first year of our pontificate.

### XXXVIII. He commands William, bishop of Worcester, the abbot of Tewkesbury, and the prior of the Holy Sepulchre of Warwick to judge between the canons of Kenilworth and the clerics of Gnosall. (Lateran, 23 March.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXII, 943.]

[Col. 1328A]

We have learned from the canons of Kenilworth that, when the dispute between them and the clerics of Gnosall concerning the church of Cule had been committed by the Apostolic See to our beloved sons, the abbots of Combermere and Darley and the archdeacon of Coventry, for canonical settlement, the procurator of R., knight of Stanford, who has the right of advocacy in that church, perceiving that the canons’ side was [Col. 1328B] being unjustly burdened—for the clerics wished, contrary to ancient liberty, to subject it to the jurisdiction of their chapel at Gnosall—appealed to the Apostolic See. But the judges, giving no heed whatever to the appeal lawfully interposed, proceeded to determine the dispute in the absence of the other party. Since those canons complain that their right is thereby greatly impaired, we command your discretion by apostolic letters that, having summoned the parties before you, you hear the case and, setting the appeal aside, settle it by means of justice.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XXXIX. He takes the church of Saint Piat of Seclin under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Lateran, 26 March.)

[BUZELINI, *Gallo-Flandria*, 297.]

[Col. 1328C]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost of Saint Piat of Seclin and his brethren, both present and those canonically to be appointed in the future, for ever.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just petitions be granted effect; especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and reason does not oppose it. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive the aforesaid church, in which you are [Col. 1328D] devoted to divine service, under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the safeguard of this present writing. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God granting, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church itself with its appurtenances, namely at Houptine, Lechin, Anquene [otherwise Ancoisne], Attiche, Martinsart, Watiessart, and Ploiek, with all their tithes, etc. [lacuna] The altar-right of Chemy, with the whole tithe [lacuna]; the altar-right of Godencourt, with [Col. 1329A] all the revenues which you have there and with arable land; the altar-right of Carnin with like revenues. The whole vill of Tumeries, with the altar-right, jurisdiction, land-rent, and the other revenues [lacuna]; the altar-right of Tourmegnies with land-rent and the other revenues; the altar-right of Los, etc. The altar-right of Croix with like revenues; the altar-right of Mesnil [lacuna]; the altar-right of Fressin [lacuna]; the altar-right of Wahegnies with all the revenues which you have there [lacuna]. Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority to that church the visitations of all churches belonging to the deanery of Lille, which are held at your church in honour of Saint Piat the martyr on the Friday of Pentecost, as is known to have been observed for the past forty years.

[Col. 1329B]

Moreover, by the gift of the nobleman Philip, count of Flanders, fifteen solidi, which he gave to your church for buying the bread and wine of which the sacrament of the altar is made.

Moreover, we hold valid the ancient liberties and immunities and the reasonable customs granted to your church and hitherto observed, and decree that they remain unimpaired for ever. Further, we altogether forbid new and unlawful exactions to be imposed upon you or your church by archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, or deans, or by any other ecclesiastical or secular persons.

We further forbid anyone, within the bounds of your parish, [Col. 1329C] to presume to build a new chapel or oratory without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, saving the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. Likewise, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from pronouncing against you or your church a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause. When, however, a general interdict is imposed upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, bells not rung, and in a low voice.

We also grant that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, [Col. 1329D] the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Clement, Pope III.

XL. He takes the Venetian church of Saint Saviour under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, 28 March.)

[CORNELIUS, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XIV, 117.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gregory, prior of the church of Saint Saviour at Rialto, and his brethren, both present and [Col. 1330A] future, professing the regular life, for ever.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. Following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Innocent, Eugenius, Anastasius, Lucius, Urban, and Gregory, Roman pontiffs, we receive the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in [Col. 1330B] that church according to God and the Rule of Saint Augustine shall be observed there inviolably for ever. Therefore, whatsoever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God granting, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The place itself where the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the houses and lands, vineyards, saltworks, and whatever rights you have at Clugia; the mill and lands which you have at Barbana; in the territory of Dese, the mill and estate, with vineyards, [Col. 1330C] woods, and its other appurtenances, as the noblemen Leonard, Philip, and Rigetus, sons of Gerard of Inginulfo, gave them to your church; the lands of Liguentia, Flumisello, Marsiliaco, and Sacco. We confirm to you by apostolic authority one half of the tithes paid by the parishioners of your church, as our predecessor of blessed memory directed and John Polanus, formerly diocesan bishop, granted you by his privilege, both for the clergy and for repairing the *sartatecta* [roofed buildings]. We grant the prior of your church full authority to pronounce a sentence of excommunication [Col. 1330D] against parishioners who presume to defraud you of half of those tithes, as our predecessors of happy memory—Adrian, Alexander, Lucius, Urban, and Gregory, Roman pontiffs—are known to have granted in their writings. We also grant you, as is known to have been granted by those aforesaid predecessors, that the prior of your house for the time being may freely furnish security for those tithes according to the custom of the land.

It shall also be lawful for you that no one of your brethren, after having made profession in that place, may leave the cloister without the permission of his prior. No one may dare retain a person who has departed without a guarantee in common letters. Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority the judgment reasonably pronounced by our venerable brother Henry of Grado, [Col. 1331A] patriarch, and Ildebrand of blessed memory, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles and then legate of the Apostolic See, in the controversy formerly long contested between you and Dominic, parish priest of Saint Bartholomew, concerning certain parish houses—namely the houses of the Giusti, Maurocenii, Gradonici, Greeks, Leonard Fradelli, and Dominic Aureus—which each party claimed to be within its own right, as is known to be contained in their authentic instrument made concerning it. We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may presume to oppose [Col. 1331B] the devotion and final wish of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. We decree that no one may dare, without your consent, to give or impose penance upon your parishioners in sickness, or receive them for burial, unless the right of our church established by the sacred canons is preserved. Upon the death of you, the present prior of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of subreption or by force, save one whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of the brethren, shall canonically provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of Saint Augustine.

Therefore we decree that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb [Col. 1331C] your church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and after a second or third warning should fail to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, acknowledge himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to divine vengeance. But may all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1332A] I, James, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Bobo, deacon-cardinal of Saint Angelus. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Clement, Pope III.

XLI. He grants the prior and chapter of Saint Saviour of Venice the power to appoint a steward. (Lateran, 29 March.)

[CORNELIUS, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XIV, 119.]

[Col. 1332B]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . the prior and chapter of Saint Saviour at Venice, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more commendably you apply yourselves to the service of the Creator, the more willingly we wish to assist you in those things which you justly request, and graciously to grant what befits your honourable standing. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, inclined by your prayers, by the authority of these presents we grant you free power to appoint for yourselves an administrator or steward (*oeconomus*), who may usefully transact your affairs and, where necessary, take an oath on behalf of your church. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this charter of our grant or rashly oppose it. [Col. 1332C] But whoever presumes to attempt this shall know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XLII. He releases the canons of the Venetian church of Saint Saviour from paying tithes. (Lateran, 29 March.)

[Ibid., p. 119.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . the prior and canons of Saint Saviour at Venice, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1332D] Since, by the Lord’s inspiration, you have professed a regular order, we wish, as we ought, to assist you by a common and special obligation and effectively to grant apostolic favour in the things which you justly request. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, by these present letters we grant that no layperson shall have power to demand or extort tithes from you on the produce of your own labours. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this charter of our grant or rashly oppose it. But whoever presumes to attempt this shall know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XLIII. He takes the monastery of Prémontré under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, 1 April.)

[LEPAIGE, *Bibl. Praem.*, 641.]

[Col. 1333A]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Abbot Hugh of the church of Prémontré and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

It is fitting that apostolic protection be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either recall them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, after the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Adrian, Alexander, and Urban, Roman pontiffs, we receive the aforesaid church of Prémontré, in which you are [Col. 1333B] devoted to divine service, under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God granting, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Col. 1333C]

The place itself where the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances: namely, the whole valley of Prémontré, exempt and free from every exaction and customary due; the valleys adjoining that valley; the slopes of the mountains, as far as the valleys extend; and the woodland in them, for your building works and necessities; the right to use dead wood in the forest of Vois; and pasture for your animals. You reasonably possess all these by the grant of Bartholomew, bishop of blessed memory, and Thomas, lord of Coucy; likewise everything which you hold from Ralph, nephew of the same Thomas, and from Ralph’s vassals and other men, by the grant of that same Ralph; provided that, in recognition of these things and of his grant, you freely relinquish to Ralph the jurisdiction [Col. 1333D] which you held in the vill of Sorny. Also, the ponds and mills of the aforesaid valleys, free from every tithe and exaction; woodland for your use from Halierpre as far as Humbert’s bridge, and on the other side through the middle of the valley of Rohard as far as the neighbourhood of Monand, etc.

By apostolic authority we decree that none of the ecclesiastical prelates shall subject your church itself, or its oratories in which there is no parish cure, to an interdict on divine worship unless by an express apostolic command. But when there is a general interdict upon the land, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, with bells not rung, excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, and in a low voice. [Col. 1334A] We also grant you, son Abbot, that whenever you judge churches of your order to require visitation, you may hear the confessions of brethren who wish to confess to you the secrets of their sins, and grant them the remedy of penance and absolution. By this present charter we further grant your devotion the power to bless sacerdotal vestments and altar-cloths, and, when abbots come and the bishop is absent, to pronounce the blessing at the conclusion of the chapter.

Furthermore, whenever it happens that the diocesan bishop is absent, or is negligent in his presence in correcting your wrongdoers, arsonists, and robbers, it shall be lawful for you, son Abbot, if the bishop neglects to correct them within forty days after you have complained [Col. 1334B] to him, to strike those wrongdoers, arsonists, and robbers of your property with the penalty of excommunication in the assembly of your abbots; and no bishop shall absolve them before due satisfaction. We further will that you may freely restore to their own houses fugitives or expelled members of your order after the appointed penance has been imposed, unless they are such persons as the manifest enormity of their crime ought to separate from the order. And, out of regard for charity, we command that no one presume to demand or extort from you tithes from the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the increase of your animals, although you pay to the lords of the estates some rent or whatever portion of the crops is due by reason of their ownership of the land. [Col. 1334C] In the parish churches which you possess, you may place four or three of your canons, one of whom you shall present to the diocesan bishop; he shall answer to the bishop in spiritual matters, but to you in temporal matters and observance of the order. We also forbid anyone personally to give away, or in any manner alienate, churches, lands, or any benefice granted to your church without the consent of the whole chapter, or of its greater and sounder part. If any gifts or alienations are made otherwise than has been stated, we decree them void.

Moreover, we add that no canons or lay brethren bound under the authority of your house may stand surety for anyone or borrow money from anyone, beyond an amount provided by the prudent judgment of your chapter, without the consent of the abbot and the greater part of your chapter, [Col. 1334D] unless for the manifest benefit of your house. If they presume to do so, the convent, without whose permission and consent they acted, shall not be bound in any way to answer for them. Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever, etc. But that all things be preserved entire, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, etc.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of April, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Clement, Pope III.

XLIV. He permits Lanfranc, bishop of Bergamo, to recover the possessions of the church alienated without the chapter’s consent. (Lateran, 7 April.)

[LUPI, *Cod. diplom. Bergom.*, II, 1387.]

[Col. 1335A]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable L[anfranc], bishop of Bergamo, greeting and apostolic blessing.

For this purpose we have been raised to the governance of the universal Church: that we should diligently attend to the welfare of churches, and, if we learn that anything has rashly been altered to their loss, restore it to its due condition [lacuna]. Understanding that the church entrusted to your care has, through its own insufficiently cautious administration, incurred a great loss of its goods, [Col. 1335B] we annul by the authority of these presents sales, exchanges, pledges, and other alienations, made to the detriment of the church from its possessions and other property without the consent of the chapter or of its greater and sounder part. By apostolic letters we grant your brotherhood that you may lawfully revoke them without impediment of any contradiction or appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XLV. To the same, he signifies that he has rescinded the alienations of goods made by his predecessor Girard without the chapter’s consent. (Lateran, 8 April.)

[Ibid., p. 1389.]

[Col. 1335C]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother L[anfranc], bishop of Bergamo, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As it is fitting that those things reasonably granted by prelates of churches should be preserved with due firmness, so we annul by the authority of the canons those things which were assigned to certain persons, to the detriment of the church of Bergamo, by G., your predecessor, contrary to the form of the canons and without the consent of the chapter or of its greater and sounder part; and we decree that they have no force. Furthermore, we command that the sentence which you judge should be canonically pronounced against holders of goods belonging to your church be held valid until suitable satisfaction. [Col. 1335D] Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this charter of our constitution or rashly oppose it. But whoever presumes to attempt this shall know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XLVI. He takes under protection the nunnery of Saint Mary of Moliana and confirms its possessions and goods. (Fragment.) (Lateran, 9 April.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 528, where the reader is referred to the privilege granted to the same convent in precisely the same words by Alexander III in 1172, on 6 October. See *Patrologia*, vol. CC.]

[Col. 1336A]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Clement, Pope III.

XLVII. He grants Lanfranc, archbishop of Bergamo, authority to punish disobedient clerics. (Lateran, 9 April.)

[LUPI, *Cod. diplom. Bergom.*, II, 1389.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother L[anfranc], bishop of Bergamo, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1336B] By the duty of the administration we have undertaken, we are obliged to provide as carefully as we can that ecclesiastical advantage may not perish through the efforts of certain persons pursuing their own wishes. Therefore, by these present letters we have thought fit to grant your brotherhood that, if any of your clerics, when matters concerning your church are being discussed by common deliberation, having been summoned by you refuse to appear on the pretext of dissension or any similar ground, you may, setting aside their appeal, ordain with the consent of those present whatever the welfare of the churches requires.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XLVIII. He assures the convent of Monte Cassino concerning money assigned by Abbot Peter of blessed memory for the brethren’s use. (Lateran, 10 April.)

[TOSTI, *Storia di Monte-Casino*, II, 213.]

[Col. 1336C]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . the convent of Monte Cassino, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we embrace with the arms of special love the monastery of Monte Cassino, in which you are devoted to divine services, and wish, as we ought, always to attend most carefully to its welfare, we rightly rejoice with you in its prosperity and wish to apply diligent effort to preserve what has been established by reasonable ordinance for its good. Thus, whenever you request of us matters bearing on the welfare of your whole community, we grant your petitions apostolic favour all the more readily because the aforesaid monastery looks in a special manner to our care and protection. Now, when the cloistered brethren of that monastery sometimes suffered a lack of clothing, Gentilis of Palearia, of blessed memory, who had chosen burial at that monastery, gave you, as we have learned, sixteen thousand *tarenes*, from pious concern and for the sake of his own salvation, for the provision of felt garments and for purchasing stout pelts every two years. But when Peter, your former abbot of blessed memory, had devoted the aforesaid money to another benefit of the monastery, in compensation he granted [Col. 1337A] twenty ounces of gold from Castellone and five from the church of Cinglis, to be disbursed to the brethren in perpetuity for the uses aforesaid. Therefore, since our assigned office requires us to ensure that what is prudently done is not undone by anyone’s rashness, graciously moved by your petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, after the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, and fortify by the safeguard of this present writing, the aforesaid twenty ounces of gold from Castellone and the other five from the church of Cinglis, assigned by the aforesaid abbot to the brethren’s uses, as is contained in the public instrument. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this charter of our [Col. 1337B] confirmation or rashly oppose it. But whoever presumes to attempt this shall know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, in the first year of our pontificate.

XLIX. He takes the Florentine church of Saint Lawrence under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Lateran, 12 April.)

[LAMI, *Ecclesiae Florentinae Monum.*]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Ildebrand, prior of Saint Lawrence in the city of Florence, and his brethren, both future and present, canonically appointed, for ever.

[Col. 1337C] A pious petition ought to be fulfilled by an effect corresponding to the will, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may assuredly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, receive the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatsoever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God granting, [Col. 1337D] shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the parish belonging to your church, as you have hitherto held it; the hospital situated beside the same church of Blessed Lawrence, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mark with all its appurtenances; the hill of Saint Lawrence with its tithes and appurtenances; the *citinas* of Saint Lawrence situated there nearby, with their tithes and appurtenances; the community of the Gate of Saint Lawrence; the church of Saint Bartholomew situated at Faltignano, with all its appurtenances and all the possessions which you hold in the same district; the church of Saint Andrew at Percussine; and whatever has been granted you by our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and confirmed to your church by their privileges, we likewise strengthen after the example of our predecessor Pope Lucius of happy memory. [Col. 1338A] We further forbid anyone, within the bounds of your parish, to build a new church or oratory without authority from the diocesan bishop and your consent, saving the privileges of the Apostolic See. We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; saving, nevertheless, the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the said church, take away [Col. 1338B] its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be preserved entire for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and maintenance they were granted, saving, nevertheless, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the bishop of Florence. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and after a second or third warning should fail to correct the offence by worthy satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour, acknowledge himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be cut off from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to divine vengeance. [Col. 1338C] But may all who preserve the rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, priest-cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1338D] I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, James, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Brother Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the second day before the Ides of April, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Clement, Pope III.

L. He grants the prior and Carthusian brethren that “whenever clerics or laymen of a lower religious order decide to enter the profession of their order, they may freely receive them.” He adds other privileges. (Lateran, 12 April.)

[*Privileges of the Carthusian Order* . . ., fol. 3.]

[Col. 1339A]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the prior and Carthusian brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.
