Moreover, we apostolically confirm for you, following the example of the same Urban and of Gregory of blessed memory, our predecessors as Roman pontiffs, the fourth part of parish tithes belonging to the clerics, which our venerable brother Henry, patriarch of Grado, with the assent of our venerable brother Mark, bishop of Castello, is known to have canonically granted you at the command of Urban, our predecessor of good memory, just as you possess it justly and peaceably. Because, however, from the fourth part assigned for the repair of the church, the aforesaid bishop permanently reserved one quarter for himself and his successors for the benefit of the mother church, and decreed that the other parts of that same fourth should be conferred upon you and [Col. 1366C] your successors under the common privilege granted to parish priests, priests, and clerics of other churches, for repairing the fabric of your church, its books, and other necessities; and because, from the fourth assigned to the poor, as plainly appears from the tenor of that bishop’s privilege, the same bishop decreed that three parts should be distributed to the poor of your parish, reserving the fourth for himself during his lifetime: we confirm by the page of this present writing that concession, as canonically made by the same bishop and confirmed by an authentic document. Moreover, we grant you and your successors full authority to make out instruments of security for your parishioners from whom you have received tithes.

[Col. 1366D] Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid church, or take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should fail to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and recognize himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed [Col. 1367A]; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary beyond the Tiber, title of Calixtus. [Col. 1367B] I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Rodulf, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, James, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. [Col. 1367C] I, Soffredus, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John Felix, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### LXIX. He commands the abbot of Saint Geneviève, the dean, and the cantor of Paris to compel [Manasses], bishop of Troyes, to “take regular canons from the church of Saint Lupus at Troyes and establish them in the church at Marigny.” (Lateran, 15 June.)

[Letters of Stephen of Tournai, ed. DU MOLINET, p. 411.]

[Col. 1367D]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of Saint Geneviève, the dean, and the cantor of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We wish it to come to your knowledge that our venerable brother, the bishop of Troyes, received from the Apostolic See an instruction, and was commanded once and again, to admit regular canons into the parish church at Marigny, while preserving all his rights, so that in it they might establish the order of religion according to the pious desire of the founders and serve almighty God under regular [Col. 1368A] discipline. But the said bishop could not be induced by love of religion, nor softened by apostolic commands, to turn from the harshness which he customarily displays in matters commanded by the Apostolic See to the kindness of charity, so as to grant the favor of his consent to the pious petition and commendable vow of the petitioner.

Therefore, by apostolic writings, we command your discretion diligently to admonish and endeavor to induce him, in accordance with what he has so often received by command, to take regular canons from the church of Saint Lupus at Troyes and establish them in the aforesaid church, with all the rights of diocesan jurisdiction preserved; through them the order of religion may be extended and increased, and he may satisfy both apostolic commands and the founder’s desire. But if, within thirty days after your admonition, he does not willingly do this, you shall compel him by our authority, without hindrance from appeal, to carry it out through ecclesiastical censure [Col. 1368B].

If all of you cannot be present for carrying these matters out, nevertheless two of you shall carry them out.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, in the first year of our pontificate.

### LXX. He commends the church of Saint Honoratus to the consuls of Grasse. (Lateran, 20 June.)

[Monuments of the History of the Fatherland, *Writers*, p. 468.]

[Col. 1368C] CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the consuls of Grasse: greeting and apostolic blessing.

You discharge the office of consul entrusted to you in accordance with the Creator’s good pleasure if you hold in reverence the Church of God and the men who render service to the Lord within it, and take care, with the power entrusted to you, to defend them from the injuries of others. Therefore we admonish and request your community in the Lord that you hold the church of Saint Honoratus and the persons dwelling in it under attentive protection, and take care to defend them from others’ injuries in such a way that it may profit you toward an eternal reward and that those churches may rejoice, through your protection, in enjoying the desired peace.

[Col. 1368D] Given at the Lateran, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the first year of our pontificate.

### LXXI. At the request of Archbishop Tribun, he receives the church of Ragusa under his protection and confirms its privileges. (Lateran, 21 June.)

[HORMAYR, *History of the Princely County of Tyrol*, I, II, 127.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother TRIBUN, archbishop of Ragusa, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Although unworthy, we have been placed, by the Lord’s ordering, upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See in order that we may love with brotherly charity our brother archbishops and bishops, whether near or far away, and strengthen by the privilege of the Apostolic See the churches committed to their governance. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Archbishop Tribun, we graciously assent to your just requests and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Innocent, Anastasius, Adrian, and Urban, Roman pontiffs, receive the church of Ragusa, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your [Col. 1369B] successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The site itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances. All parishes belonging by right to the church entrusted to you: namely, the kingdom of Zachlumia, the kingdom of Servulia—which is Bosnia—and the kingdom of Travunia; likewise the city of Cataro, and the sees of Rosa, Gudua, Antivari, Liciniana, Suacium, Scodra, Divaster, and Polatum, with their abbeys, churches, and parishes. We also confirm to you all possessions and whatever goods in churches, tithes, valleys, tenants, estates, fields, woods, mountains, hills, waters, meadows, or any other things, held by the aforesaid church of Ragusa justly and canonically by title of diocesan or proprietary disposition [Col. 1369C].

We also apostolically confirm to you and your successors the use of the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office and a sign of humility and justice—for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, as it is known to have been granted to your predecessors, on the feast of Blessed Blaise and on the principal feasts of your church. Your fraternity shall remember to use it only on those days, namely, the feast of Blessed Blaise and the principal feasts of your church, on which it is established that the Apostolic See granted its use to your predecessors. We decree that your successors shall forever receive the grace of consecration from us and our successors [Col. 1369D]. Moreover, we forbid anyone to presume to admit to the divine office or ecclesiastical communion those whom you have interdicted or excommunicated without suitable satisfaction, unless perhaps danger of death is imminent, so that, when they cannot have your presence, one who is bound may be absolved by another, after the required satisfaction, according to the form of the Church.

Furthermore, we decree that the liberties and immunities granted to your church by kings, princes, and other persons, both ecclesiastical and secular, and the ancient and reasonable customs hitherto observed, shall remain whole and unimpaired by this present decree.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person [Col. 1370A] to rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should fail to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and recognize himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to divine vengeance [Col. 1370B].

But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, John, priest-cardinal, at that time of Saint Mark, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary beyond the Tiber, at that time of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, at that time of Pammachius, have subscribed. [Col. 1370C] I, Radulf, at that time priest-cardinal of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Peter, at that time priest-cardinal of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Bobo, at that time priest-cardinal of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Alexander, at that time priest-cardinal of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal, at that time of Saint Peter in Chains, have subscribed. I, Jordan, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, at that time of Pastor, have subscribed. I, James, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. [Col. 1370D] I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, John Felix, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa, have subscribed. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, [Col. 1371A] on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Clement III.

### LXXII. He receives the church of Saint Lawrence at Florence under his protection and confirms its goods. (Lateran, 21 June.)

[LAMI, *Monuments of the Florentine Church*, III, 1785.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ILDEBRAND, prior of Saint Lawrence in the city of Florence, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed in perpetuity.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by an effect corresponding to the will, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of our predecessors as Roman pontiffs of revered memory—Nicholas, Alexander II, Alexander III, and Lucius—receive the aforesaid church of Saint Lawrence, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor [Col. 1371C], acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The parish belonging to your church, as you have held it hitherto; the hospital situated beside the aforesaid church of Blessed Lawrence, with all its appurtenances; the hospital-house built by Spina Petrioli in the parish of Saint Stephen in Pane, and bestowed upon the church of Saint Lawrence by his wife, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mark, with all its appurtenances; the hill of Saint Lawrence, bounded on one side by the land of Saint John and by two running roads, and on the other by Saint Romulus, with Saint Mary on the third side and the public road running alongside it on the fourth [Col. 1371D], together with its tithes and first-fruits; the abbacy of the Gate of Saint Lawrence, together with that congregation itself; the church of Saint Bartholomew situated at Faltignano, with all its appurtenances and all possessions you hold in that jurisdiction; the church of Saint Andrew at Percussina. Likewise, we confirm whatever has been granted you by the aforesaid predecessors, Roman pontiffs, and confirmed to your church by their privileges.

We also forbid anyone, without the authority of the diocesan bishop and your consent, to build anew a church or oratory within the boundaries of your parish, without prejudice to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. Moreover, we decree that the burial-place of that site shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; provided, however, that the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken are preserved [Col. 1372A].

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things shall be preserved whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the bishop of Florence. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second and third time [Col. 1372B], should fail to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and recognize himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. [Col. 1372C] I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marius, have subscribed. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary beyond the Tiber, title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Melior, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius, have subscribed. I, Radulf, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes, have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Bobo, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia, have subscribed. I, Alexander, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna [Col. 1372D], have subscribed. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains, have subscribed. I, Jordan, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, title of Pastor, have subscribed. I, James, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, John Felix, deacon of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa, have subscribed. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. [Col. 1373A] I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### LXXIII. Privilege for the church of Saint Ansgar at Bremen. (Lateran, 22 June.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 245.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost of the church of Saint Ansgar at Bremen and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Although unworthy, we have been raised by the providence of the heavenly ordering to the summit of the highest pontificate so that we may extend the gaze of our care to all the Churches of God and strengthen them with the protection of the Apostolic See against the attacks of evil men. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive your aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through grants of pontiffs, the liberality of kings [Col. 1373C] or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favor, acquire, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the site itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the estate called Spenchoph, with its appurtenances; the estate at Sluttere, with its appurtenances; the estate of Leste, with everything pertaining to it; the estate at Stenthorpe, with its appurtenances; the church with the ban (*bannum*) of Horne; the tithe of Swechusen; the tithe of Ascwarde; three Hollandish quadrants, which they hold by the gift of our venerable brother Hardwic, archbishop of Bremen; by the gift of the layman Theodoric [Col. 1373D], half a quadrant; by the gift of Alard the advocate, one plot and the rent of four plots; by the gift of Theodoric of Horst, the rent of one plot.

We decree, moreover, that the stipends assigned from the aforesaid estates to the poor who serve both the greater church and yours, as Saint Ansgar piously ordained, shall always be paid to them in full and without diminution.

Furthermore, by apostolic authority we grant you that, whenever the provostship or other dignities, prebends, or other benefices of your church fall vacant, you shall have, with the permission of the Apostolic See, free authority to elect suitable persons to them; nevertheless, the investiture of the aforesaid offices is reserved to the diocesan bishop. When a general interdict of the land is in force [Col. 1374A], you may celebrate divine offices with closed doors, excluding the excommunicated and interdicted, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. Moreover, since the pages of both Testaments state that tithes have been granted to ecclesiastical persons, we forbid by apostolic authority any layperson to presume to demand or extort tithes from you. We likewise forbid anyone to pronounce against you or your church a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without a manifest and reasonable cause, or to impose new and unlawful exactions upon you or your people.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person to rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things shall be preserved unimpaired and whole for the benefit in every respect of those for whose governance or support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time [Col. 1374B], should fail to correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor, and recognize himself or herself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer, and be subject at the final judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Mark. I, Laborans, priest-cardinal of Saint Mary beyond the Tiber, title of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, priest-cardinal of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian [Col. 1374D]. I, Octavian, deacon-cardinal of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Radulf, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Clement. I, Bobo, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Peter, priest-cardinal of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Jordan, priest-cardinal of Saint Pudentiana, title of Pastor. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore. I, Bernard, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary the New. I, Gregory, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Roman Church and acting chancellor, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1375A] 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### LXXIV. He announces to the brethren of the Order of Grandmont that he has removed both William and Stephen from the priorate. He grants them free discretion to elect a successor. (Lateran, 25 June.)

[New *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, col. 192.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the brethren of the Order of Grandmont: greeting and apostolic blessing.

No one should again fall into the scruple of litigation over matters settled by a judicial sentence after examination by the Apostolic See; it is fitting and consonant with reason that they be committed to writing for the memory of posterity and strengthened by the protection of an apostolic rescript. Certainly, when controversy concerning the resignation of William, formerly your prior, and the appointment of Prior Stephen—at the prompting of the persecutor of the Christian religion—had long been agitated among you, and certain of you, both clerics and lay brothers, were present before us, we ascertained by definite evidence that the said William had promised, under oath, that on a fixed day he would resign the office of prior before judges delegated by the Apostolic See; and that afterwards, on another occasion, he had orally resigned, without an oath, into the hands of our beloved son Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, then legate of the Apostolic See, and of our venerable brother the bishop of Périgueux, and of our beloved son the abbot of La Couronne.

But concerning the appointment of the other, namely Stephen, although his election could have been canonical after the said William’s resignation, we learned that serious scandal had arisen among some of you, namely among the clerics. Therefore, wishing through the prudence of apostolic governance to provide for your tranquillity and peace, so that henceforth, with God as author, every cause of dissension and dispute among you may be stilled, by the counsel and assent of our brethren we have judged that both William, who is known to have resigned, and Stephen are to be removed from the governance of the priory, for the sake of restoring peace and concord among you; and we grant you free power to elect a prior.

We also will and command that in future you observe without any contradiction the Rule of your order, as it is known that our predecessor Urban of blessed memory, with the counsel and assent of the cardinals and many bishops of Italy, corrected it—clerics and lay brothers from among you being present and, for its ratification and perpetual peace, exchanging the kiss of peace with one another in their presence—and as it is more fully found both in his privilege and in ours. In order that this sentence may remain inviolate and firm for all time, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it by the protection of the present writing. Decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe the page of our determination and confirmation, etc.

[Col. 1376A] Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXV. He informs Henry, Count of Champagne, of the settlement of the dissension among the brothers of Grandmont. (Lateran, June [?])

[Ibid.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the nobleman Count HENRY of Champagne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the other grave matters which, during our apostolate, have come to the Apostolic See to be made known from diverse parts of the world, the disturbance of the house of Grandmont has caused us no small grief. For who could hear without bitterness that a house celebrated for the renown of its religious life, friendly by its religious institutions to the unanimity of peace, had passed into so great a scandal of disturbance that, factions having been formed, they stood opposed on either side as battle-lines and contended with one another in judicial disputes—men whom it was fitting to preserve the observances handed down to them in religious silence?

Alas! The enemy has prevailed to such an extent that he has drawn them out from the shelter of cloistered custody and, after stirring up a tempest, scattered them into almost every wind and region. We, indeed, grieving from the inmost affections of our heart over so great a shipwreck of theirs, summoned our brethren and deliberated concerning the gathering together of their dispersion and the restoration of a bond of peace among them. At last, after careful deliberation and by the counsel of our brethren, we determined that the matter should be arranged in the following manner: “Clement, bishop,” etc., as above in the bull previously cited.

Therefore we admonish and exhort in the Lord the piety of your highness, which is accustomed to foster and defend religious places, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of sins: cause the companions of William, the former prior, who dwell in land subject to your jurisdiction, to be warned that they must return without any delay to the house of Grandmont; and arrange that the houses which they hold be restored without difficulty to the lay brothers, to be peaceably administered by them according to the statute of that order; and see to it, insofar as lies in your power, that our aforesaid ordinance is observed.

And since your prudence does not fail to know how hostile divisions are to religious observances, if you find any persons opposing our ordinance, withdraw from them all your favour in maintaining their opposition. But bestow kindly protection and defence upon those who humbly obey and return to fraternal unity.

Given, etc.

LXXVI. He confirms the Rule of Grandmont. (Lateran, June 27.)

[Ibid., col. 191.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the brothers of Grandmont, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The order of reason requires, and the rule of ecclesiastical custom commends, that matters which introduce doubt into the observance of the Christian religion be clarified through the provision of apostolic moderation. Therefore, lest any question concerning your Rule be raised in future—a Rule which our predecessor Urban of blessed memory is known to have corrected, with the counsel and assent of the cardinals and many bishops of Italy, clerics and lay brothers from among you being present and giving assent for its ratification and perpetual peace through the kiss of peace, as is more fully contained in his privilege and in this very document—we have judged it proper to insert it under seal in the present writing, word for word. It is as follows: “Whoever [observes] this religious order, etc., down to ‘shall be saved, amen.’”

That the aforesaid Rule may remain unimpaired for all time, we confirm it by apostolic authority, as corrected by our said predecessor Urban, as stated above, and fortify it by the protection of this writing; decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation.

Given at the Lateran, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXVII. He grants Bishop M[aurice] of Paris a privilege concerning procuration to be provided, when he and his archdeacons travel through parishes, by canons of regular churches. (Lateran, July 5.)

[Cartulary of Notre-Dame of Paris, vol. I, 64.]

[Col. 1377C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother M., bishop of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as it is certain that, by canonical ordinance, bishops are bound diligently to attend to visiting parishes, so that they may more readily and fully root out what ought to be rooted out and implant what they know ought to be implanted, so likewise it pertains to those who reside in dioceses to take fitting care to furnish visitors with the service of procuration, unless they can protect themselves by a privilege or some other reasonable ground. Nor ought bishops to be impeded by the obstacle of an appeal from carrying out the aforesaid office; nor should others be permitted the evasion of appealing in order that they may defend themselves against rendering procurations duly owed.

Moved, therefore, by this consideration and prompted by your just petitions, we have thought fit, by apostolic authority, to grant you, brother bishop, that when you visit your parishes and the regular canons established in the parochial churches of your diocese presume, by the evasion of an appeal, to deny procuration to you and to your archdeacons passing through there, as it is rendered by the other churches, you may—such an appeal being in no way an obstacle—place those canons and their churches under interdict, unless they show themselves exempt from furnishing that procuration by a special privilege granted them in this matter, or defend themselves by the general custom of the other parochial churches of the same diocese.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation and concession or, by rash presumption, to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Nones of July, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXVIII. He commands the abbot of Silvacane and the sacristan of Aix to protect the monks of Saint Victor of Marseilles against the wrongs of the canons. (Lateran, July 5.)

[The Antiquity of Marseilles, I, 525.]

[Col. 1378B]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of SILVACANE and the sacristan of Aix, greeting.

Our beloved sons, the abbot and brothers of the monastery of Marseilles, have shown us in a complaint laid before us that the provost and certain other canons of Marseilles and chaplains of parochial churches prevent the sons and descendants of those buried in their cemetery from burial in that monastery. Wherefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, having summoned [the parties] before you, etc., you restrain them from these and other vexations of the same monastery. [Col. 1378C]

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Nones of July, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXIX. He commands the bishops of Regensburg and Freising to defend the monastery of Aldersbach against the wrongs of Albert of Kam, who has arrogated to himself the advocacy of the monastery. (Lateran, July 9.)

[HUNDIUS, *Metropolis of Salzburg*, II, 60.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the bishops of Regensburg and Freising, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1378D] On behalf of our beloved sons the abbot and convent of Aldersbach it was represented before us that the nobleman Albert of Kam, although his brother has lost the right of advocacy over the monastery and its possessions by judgment, is wrongfully endeavouring to claim that right for himself; on this pretext he presumes to inflict many losses and injuries upon them. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your brotherhood that, if what is alleged is true, you restrain the said knight from unjust vexation of those brothers and compel him, by ecclesiastical censure and without regard to appeal, to restore what has been taken, as justice requires.

Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXX. To Henry, Archbishop of Bourges: monks and regular canons are not to dwell alone in towns. (Lateran, July 11.)

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus*, I, 631.]

[Col. 1379A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, archbishop of Bourges and primate of Aquitaine, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it was generally forbidden in the Lateran Council that monks or regular canons should live individually in towns or other populous places, there are some who, acting in the capacity of chaplains in parochial churches, dwell alone and do not fear to live in a secular manner, forgetful of their profession. Therefore, wishing to ensure that what was prudently established by conciliar deliberation is not rendered void for the private convenience of certain persons, by this letter we grant your brotherhood that you are not to delay diligently warning their abbots either to recall them to the cloister or to fulfil what is set forth in the decree.

But if the abbots should perhaps disregard your warning, carry out what we write by our authority, setting aside the obstacle of appeal. We also grant you by apostolic authority that, if monks or canons established in your diocese do not within three months present suitable chaplains to churches to which they have the right of presentation and to which you have the right of institution, you shall have free power, without awaiting their presentation any longer and with appeal set aside, to provide canonically for those churches. Yet this is to be so done that no prejudice may thereby arise against them in the future.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or, by rash presumption, to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth of July, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXXI. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Jesus of Nazareth (Monastery of Montearagón). (Lateran, July 18.)

[Ayusa, *Foundation of the City of Huesca*, p. 456.]

[Col. 1379D]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son . . . abbot of the monastery of Montearagón, belonging immediately to the Roman Church, of the Order of Saint Augustine in the diocese of Huesca, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Bearing toward your person and your monastery an affection of holy love, and wishing to favour you and that monastery with special favours and honour it with particular graces, we grant you and your successors—who have only the use of ring and pastoral staff—by the authority of the present letters, perpetual free power to use a white mitre embroidered with figures and adorned with precious stones, and other pontifical insignia; to give the blessing in the manner of bishops when bishops are not present, and also to bless and consecrate chalices and altars, altar-cloths, and other ecclesiastical ornaments for the use of your monastery; likewise to reconcile the church and cemeteries of that monastery; to carry and keep with you a portable altar and to celebrate divine offices upon it, and to have them celebrated in a suitable and honourable place.

Let no person whatsoever, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or, by rash presumption, to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles Saints Peter and Paul. [Col. 1380B]

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting vice-chancellor, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

LXXXII. He declares that the bishoprics of Lübeck, Schwerin, Ratzeburg, and Uxküll are suffragans of Hartwig and of the Church of Hamburg. (Rome, at Saint Mary the New, September 25.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 247.]

[Col. 1380C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HARTWIG, archbishop of Bremen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

By the office of apostleship laid upon us by God, we ought to love our brethren and fellow bishops, both near and far, with sincere affection of charity, and to preserve intact for the churches in which, by God’s will, they are known to serve their dignity and rights. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, gladly assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to you and to your Church the Church itself over which, by God’s will, you preside, with all its appurtenances, and also the bishoprics of Lübeck, Schwerin, Ratzeburg, and Uxküll, with all goods, both spiritual and temporal, as you possess them justly and without dispute; and we fortify them by the protection of this writing.

Decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or, by rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, the seventh day before the Kalends of October, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXXIII. He commands the abbots of Lübeck, Saint Paul of Bremen, and Stade that, if [Hartwig], archbishop of Hamburg, has lawfully appointed the abbot T. over the monastery of Ramsloh, they are to confirm him. (Rome, at Saint Mary Major, September 27.)

[Ibid., p. 248.]

[Col. 1381A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbots of Lübeck, Saint Paul of Bremen, and Stade, greeting and apostolic blessing.

When a dispute had arisen between our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bremen, and the beloved sons, the canons of Ramsloh, concerning the election of a provost in the church of Ramsloh, and each party asserted that the election belonged to itself, the archbishop, seeing that the Church was suffering no slight loss through lack of a rector, often took care to induce the canons to proceed to the canonical election of a provost. But when they passed over this matter as though by evasion, after ten months he appointed as provost in that church a certain T., a canon of Saint Peter at Bremen, a priest, a learned and honourable man, as is asserted, by the counsel of the synod assembled there.

Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command you diligently to investigate the truth concerning the appointment of the said T., confirming it without obstacle of appeal if you find that it ought by law to be confirmed. Moreover, compel Count B., by a sentence of excommunication, to restore what has been taken from the said provostship, without regard to any letters obtained from the Apostolic See, if any appear, that prejudice truth and justice. If all of you cannot take part in carrying these matters out, nevertheless let two of you carry them out.

Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the pontificate . . . . . .

LXXXIV. He confirms the bishopric of Uxküll to [Hartwig], archbishop of Hamburg. (Rome, at Saint Mary Major, October 1.)

[Ibid.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the archbishop of Bremen, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are bound to love our brethren and fellow bishops with special charity and to grant more graciously the apostolic favour to their just petitions. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions and confirm by apostolic authority to you, to your Church, and to your successors the bishopric of Uxküll, which you and the clergy entrusted to your care are said to have acquired in Ruthenia through the ministry of the priest Meinhard, a religious and discerning man. There, by the bestowal of the grace of the Holy Spirit and the sounding in the inmost minds of certain barbarians of the trumpet of sacred preaching, the faith of the Christian name is said to have put down such roots that he who had been the sower of the divine word in those regions deserved to become the shepherd and bishop of those souls. We likewise confirm the observances which you have there canonically established and ordained to endure in future times, and fortify all this by the protection of the present writing.

Let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or, by rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God, of his apostles Saints Peter and Paul, and of us.

Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, on the Kalends of October, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXXV. Privilege for the monastery of Osterholz. (Rome, at Saint Mary Major, October 6.)

[Ibid., p. 249.]

[Col. 1382B]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons EYLHARD, provost, and the brothers and sisters of Osterholz, professing the regular life, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever matters are sought from the Apostolic See that concern the protection and advancement of churches, it is fitting that we grant them with willing mind and bring to effect the requests that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves your persons and the church in which you are devoted to divine service, together with all goods, both ecclesiastical and secular, which that church justly and canonically possesses or may, with the Lord’s favour, acquire in the future.

And in particular, we confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion the estate of Schermbeck and the chapel belonging to that estate, as you possess them justly and without dispute, and fortify them by the protection of the present writing. Let no person whatsoever be permitted to infringe this our protection or confirmation or, by rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1382D] Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, on the day before the Nones of October, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXXVI. Privilege for the Church of Forcona. (Lateran, October 14.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, VI, 497.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ODORISIUS, bishop of Forcona, and to his successors in perpetuity.

Established, though unworthy, upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See . . . following the example of our predecessor, Pope Alexander of blessed memory, we receive [you] under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves. Decreeing . . . the castle of Collepaidoni with its church and its holdings . . . the church of Saint Justa with its chapel, men, and holdings . . . the church of Saint Marcian with its men and holdings . . . the church of Saint Silvester of Collebrinconio with its men, holdings, and chapels; the church of Saint Mary of Asserico with its chapel and holdings; the church of Saint Grisanctus with its chapel and holdings; the church of Saint Andrew of Stiffi with all its appurtenances . . . Tornamparte with its village church and its appurtenances; the city of Forula with two churches and their appurtenances . . . .

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic See. I, Albinus, presbyter cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Bobo, presbyter cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Alesius, presbyter cardinal of the title of Saint Susanna. I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. [Col. 1383B] I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquino.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting vice-chancellor, on the second day before the Ides of October, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

LXXXVII. He confirms donations made to the canons of the Church of Saragossa. (Lateran, October 14.)

[ARRUEGO, *Cathedral of the Bishopric of Saragossa*, 686.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the chapter of the Church of Saragossa, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to effect requests that do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, willingly assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this writing, the donation made for the rebuilding of your church by our venerable brother Peter, your bishop, and by yourselves, inasmuch as that donation has reasonably been made to the same church.

Decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or, by rash presumption, oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles Saints Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Ides of October, in the first year of our pontificate.

LXXXVIII. He confirms the laws of the Premonstratensian Order. (Lateran, October 15.)

[LE PAIGE, *Premonstratensian Library*, 643.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, abbot of Prémontré, and the other abbots and canons of the Premonstratensian Order, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1384A] Established, though unworthy, by the Lord’s disposition upon the lofty watchtower of the Apostolic See, we are compelled to be solicitous for the condition of each person and are bound sincerely to embrace those things that pertain to the increase of religion and the adornment of virtues, so that the peace of religious persons may be secure from every disturbance and preserved unharmed from the yoke of worldly oppression when fortified by apostolic protection.

Considering, therefore, how your religious community and order, resplendent with much glory of merits and fragrant with the grace of holiness, has extended its branches from sea to sea, we have judged that the order itself and all houses of the same order should be cherished by the safeguard of apostolic protection and fortified by the present privilege. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, after the example of our predecessors of happy memory, the Roman pontiffs Alexander, Lucius, and Urban, we strengthen by apostolic authority and fortify by the privilege of this writing all regular institutions and regulations which you have made by common consent, or by the consent of the greater and sounder part, as they are set forth below: namely, that the canonical order, which is known to have been established at the church of Prémontré in the white habit according to the Rule of Saint Augustine and the ordinance of Norbert of revered memory, formerly founder of the Premonstratensian Order, and of his successors, shall be observed inviolate in all churches of the same order for all time; and that the same observance, as well as the same books pertaining to the divine office, shall be kept uniformly by all churches of the same order, etc., as they stand in the privilege or diploma of Lucius III, down to the following words.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Henry, bishop of Albano. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, Laborans, presbyter cardinal of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of Saint Callistus. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Radulph, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 1384D] I, Albinus, cardinal of Saint Mary the New.

[Note: [Col. 1383] Either the bull is false, or the names of the witnesses have, by some chance unknown to me, been transferred into the copy from other letters. E.]

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting vice-chancellor, on the Ides of October, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

LXXXIX. In a letter to William, Archbishop of Monreale, he commands that the bishops of Syracuse abstain from the use of the pallium. (Lateran, October 19.)

[PIRRI, *Sicilia Sacra*, I, 624, where the following is prefaced to the fragment printed below: “I was altogether unable to find the original; nevertheless, in a manuscript book of privileges of the Church of Monreale among the monks of that same place I read this form:”]

[Col. 1385A]

To the venerable brother William, archbishop of Monreale.

We command that the bishop of Syracuse and his successors must henceforth entirely abstain from the use of the pallium.

Given at the Lateran, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of salvation 1188, in the first year of the pontificate.

XC. He confirms the privileges of William, Archbishop of Monreale, and grants him the use of the pallium. (Lateran, October 28.)

[MARGARINI, *Cassinese Bullarium*, II, 213.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, archbishop of Monreale, and to his successors canonically appointed.

Although the Lord Jesus Christ, in establishing his Church, gave his disciples authority over believers to bind and loose (John 20), he nevertheless wished one man in it, namely the blessed apostle Peter, to hold pre-eminence, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16). By this he gave all the faithful to understand that, just as there was one mediator between God and humankind, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), making peace between the things in heaven and the things on earth (Colossians 1), breaking down the wall of partition and making the two one (Ephesians 2), so also in his Church there should be one, from him and through him, over all, since he is the head of all; and that among the members there should be no diversity that was not reduced, through the authority and foresight of the one head, to the one truth of faith and the same rule of religion. This is also shown in the passage in which he is recorded to have received from our Lord the command both to strengthen his brethren (Luke 22) and to feed the Lord’s sheep (John 21).

From this power, therefore, which came to Saint Peter through the Lord’s institution, the most holy Roman Church, established and founded through the Lord Jesus Christ by that same blessed Peter, has obtained authority over all churches, so that everywhere what it established by its providence might be binding and firm. This too has been received and observed by all Churches spread throughout the whole world, so that through it there has been a distribution of dignities, and those matters that seemed to pertain to the worship of piety have been prescribed to Christ’s faithful and more carefully ordered. By the power given to blessed Peter by the Lord, he and his successors established bishops in the various regions of the world and apportioned dignities among the provinces. We also, who, though unequal in merits, have succeeded them at the Lord’s call, confirm by apostolic authority the metropolitan see established by our predecessor of pious memory, Lord Lucius, in the place called Monreale, for the great benefit of the Christian people.

For when our most Christian son in Christ, William, illustrious king of Sicily, fired by divine charity, had founded there a monastery for the glory of God and the salvation of himself and his parents, and had first offered it to blessed Peter and the Roman Church for this purpose, our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, with the assent of our venerable brother Walter, archbishop of Palermo, rendered it free and exempt from episcopal subjection. Thus, devoting royal care to raising royal buildings, he constructed within a short time for the Lord a church worthy of great admiration; he enlarged it with very strong castles and revenues, adorned it with books, sacred vestments, silver, and gold, and finally introduced a multitude of monks of the Cava Order. He raised that place so greatly in buildings and other resources that no comparable work has been accomplished by any king since ancient days; it fills with wonder those to whom even by report alone the things that were done have come.

Then, panting for a good work like a stag after springs of water, and counting as little whatever he had done through desire for eternal things, in accordance with what Wisdom says, “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclesiasticus 24), he earnestly requested from our predecessors Alexander and Lucius and from the brethren that the same place be endowed with metropolitan rank. This was especially because he had begun, and intended, to gather people there, who might provide the whole land, on that side, with an unconquerable defence against the assaults of all enemies.

Accordingly, Lord Lucius himself, after no small deliberation with the brethren and considering the common benefit hoped for from the advancement of that place, generously yielded to his desire and petition. Otherwise, where the king himself had been most generous from his treasury and resources, the pope might seem ungenerous in matters belonging to the duty imposed upon the sacred apostolate; and the king’s devotion would have been diminished by delay in proportion as it was fitting that he should be encouraged from good to better by the zeal of the supreme pontiff. This also appeared readily feasible in fulfilment of his desire, although it was unprecedented that two metropolitan sees should be so near one another. Yet, from this new foundation, although the right of the other was diminished, the monastery itself had already, through archbishops and bishops, been exempted from every episcopal right, both in itself and in all its places, and endowed with full liberty in all things, so that it was subject to no archbishop or bishop, but only to the Roman pontiff.

Therefore he consecrated you, venerable brother in Christ William, as archbishop of that place by hands that were, as it were, those of Saint Peter, and decreed that you be adorned with the dignity of the pallium. He received under the protection of apostolic guardianship the same church, founded by royal generosity in honour of the Lord our God and in memory of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, and confirmed it by the privilege which he issued.

First, moreover, he established that the monastic order known to have been instituted in that place according to the fear of God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the observances of the monastery of Cava, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions and whatever goods that church presently possesses by gift of the aforementioned king or of any other persons, or may in future acquire by grant of pontiffs, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired to that church.

[Col. 1387B] Among these, we have thought the bishopric of Catania should be designated by name. The same lord Lucius, with the common counsel of the brethren, and at the urgent request of the aforesaid king, ordained that it should be subject in perpetuity, by metropolitan right, to you and your successors as to its own archbishops. He also confirmed to you and your successors by apostolic authority the episcopal jurisdiction and all that you possess in the places listed below by concession of the brethren and fellow bishops; and decreed that these should remain firm and unimpaired for all time: namely, by concession of our venerable brother Gualterius, archbishop of Palermo, with the will, counsel, and assent of all his canons, and likewise with royal acquiescence, both the parish and the diocese of the castle of Corleone, together with the monastery of [Col. 1387C] Saint Mary Magdalene and other churches, with the tithes and other rights which the Church of Palermo had customarily received from the barons and other men of that castle and its dependencies, and with every parochial and episcopal right which it appeared to possess in that parish and diocese; likewise the church of Saint Sylvester, which had belonged to the lordship and proprietary right of the Church of Palermo, and which the aforesaid archbishop—as is contained in his authentic instrument—freely and voluntarily transferred to your church, with the counsel and assent of all his brethren, because it lay very near your church and was much more useful to it than to the Church of Palermo, together with all its holdings, villeins, [Col. 1387D] possessions, and rights; by concession of Nicholas of good memory, formerly first archbishop of Messina, with the consent of his whole chapter, all episcopal right which the Church of Messina ought to have in the monastery and all its appurtenances, which Margaret of illustrious memory, formerly the glorious queen, built out of devotion in the place called Maniachium, in the diocese of Messina, for the honour of God and the remembrance of the most blessed and ever-virgin, and which she obtained through the aforesaid archbishop as free and exempt from every due owed to the Church of Messina; by concession of Thomas, archbishop of Reggio, with the common consent of his chapter, all episcopal right, or whatever else belonged to the Church of Reggio, in the monastery [Col. 1388A] of Saint Saviour of Marcello, built by John Calomenus, formerly royal chamberlain, and in the monastery of nuns of Saint John Essocaliva, outside the walls of the city of Reggio, together with the cells, dependencies, possessions, holdings, and appurtenances of those monasteries, as is contained in the privilege of the aforesaid archbishop; by concession of Bartholomew, bishop of Agrigento, with the assent of his chapter, both the parish and diocese and the whole episcopal jurisdiction, together with all its tithes and other rights, which he possessed from the barons and other men of the castle of Batalarii and its dependencies, as is known to be contained in that bishop’s instrument; by concession of Matthew, bishop of Mazara, the parish, diocese, and episcopal jurisdiction, and all [Col. 1388B] tithes and other revenues which the Church of Mazara possessed in the township of Jati and the township of Calatrosi, together with all their dependencies, as is more clearly contained in the instrument of the aforesaid bishop; by concession of Roboam, bishop of Anglona, with the common consent of his chapter, in the Carbonense monastery, together with its cells, dependencies, and possessions, all episcopal right and whatever else the Church of Anglona possessed there, as is expressly indicated in that bishop’s instrument; by concession of Rinald, bishop of Bisignano, with the assent of his chapter, the church of Saint Mary of Macla, with episcopal jurisdiction and all its dependencies and appurtenances, as is shown in the same bishop’s privilege; and also the church of Saint Martin, [Col. 1388C] built by Peter Indulfus upon the holdings of the church, which Peter himself offered to that church, together with its holdings, possessions, and appurtenances.

Moreover, for the fullness of the pontifical office, we bestow upon your brotherhood, by the authority and generosity of the Apostolic See, the pallium, which you are to use within your church for celebrating the solemnities of Mass on the following days: the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ; the feast of Saint Stephen; the Octave of the Lord’s Nativity; Epiphany; Palm Sunday; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; Easter and the two following days; Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mother [Col. 1388D] of God; the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist; the commemoration of All Saints; the solemnities of all apostles; the principal feasts of your church; dedications of churches; consecrations of bishops; ordinations of clerics; and the anniversary day of your consecration. Take care, therefore, that the honour of this garment is preserved by modesty and the vigour of your deeds, so that the adornments of your character may accord with it; and, with God’s help, may you be distinguished more by good works than by such an ornament. Since the duty of pastoral care binds you, show the love you profess to your brethren; grounded in the virtue of humility, be neither lifted up by prosperity nor wearied by adversity. Let even your opponents, because of the Lord’s commandment, be joined to you by your affection [Col. 1389A] toward them; and, so far as lies in you, keep peace with all, and strive to bring the discordant back to peace. Let the breastplate of judgment shine upon your breast, joined in rational order to the shoulder-piece; and proceed before God and men in such a manner that you furnish the flock of the Lord entrusted to you with an example of virtue, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5), and may rejoice that they have such a ruler, through whom they are instructed in faith and urged toward upright works. Upon your death, or that of any of your successors, let no one be placed over that house by any cunning of stealth or violence, except one whom the monks of that place—or the better part of the sounder counsel from that body—if a suitable person be found among them, believe should be elected according to God and [Col. 1389B] canonical enactments. But if no suitable person can be found there and one must be chosen from elsewhere, the brethren of that place shall elect a monk who uses the customary food and clothing of the Rule. Since all these things were prudently done by our aforesaid predecessor, we also, wishing them to remain ratified and unshaken for all time, strengthen them by the protection of our privilege. We add also that the Church of Syracuse, which is known hitherto to have been subject to no one except the Roman pontiff alone, shall henceforth be subject to you and your Catholic successors by metropolitan right.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, [Col. 1389C] or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See. As a token indeed of your devotion, and to show that the same church was subject to the Roman pontiff alone, our aforesaid son the king, when he began to found it under the name of a monastery, established that one hundred tarenes should be paid yearly to the Roman pontiff. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, having been warned a second and a third time, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power [Col. 1389D] and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Theobald, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. [Col. 1390A] I, Laborans, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Calixtus. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the title of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Adelard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Bobo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Alexius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Jacinthus, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Octavian, [Col. 1390B] cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John Felix, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, John, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Theodore. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary Nova. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Aquiro.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November [28 October], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

[Col. 1390C] The sign of Pope Clement III.

**TEACH ME, O LORD, TO DO THY WILL**

**XCI. He confirms the judgment of the bishops of Equilio and Torcello regarding the reception of the bishop of Castello by the abbot of Saint Nicholas of the Shore on Ascension Day.** (Lateran, 31 October.)

[F. CORNELIUS, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, vol. XIII, p. 322.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother MARCUS, bishop of Castello: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things established by judgment ought to remain firm and to be fortified by apostolic strength, lest they be disturbed through the presumption and malice of anyone. We have learned that, when our venerable brethren [Col. 1390D] the bishops of Equilio and Torcello undertook, by our command and with appeal set aside, to determine the case pending between you and the abbot and monks of Saint Nicholas concerning the reception to be provided for you by that abbot and brethren on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, at the greater Mass, at the procession, and at the meal, they finally, having fully heard and understood the arguments concerning that reception, procession, and meal, and having sufficiently ascertained the truth of the matter by the confession of the abbot and monks of the same monastery, rendered a definitive judgment in your favour. Holding this judgment ratified and firm, we confirm it by apostolic authority and by the protection of this present writing, following the example of Urban, pope of blessed memory, our predecessor; decreeing [Col. 1391A] that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Kalends of November [31 October], in the first year of our pontificate.

**XCII. He orders to stand ratified the judgment issued between the churches of Saint Tryphon, Saint Nicholas de Praefecto, Saint Saviour de Sere, and the church of Saint Mary in the Campus Martius by Alexius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna, and John, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.** (Lateran, 4 November.)

[MARINI, *Diplomata pontificia*, p. 67.]

[Col. 1391B]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clerics of Saint Tryphon, Saint Nicholas de Praefecto, and Saint Saviour de Sere: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Matters settled by judgment or agreement ought, lest they relapse into the difficulty of renewed litigation or be disturbed by anyone’s malice, to be confirmed by apostolic authority in accordance with the petitioners’ request, which accords with reason. Therefore, assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the judgment promulgated by our beloved sons Alexius, priest of the title of Saint Susanna, and John, deacon of Saint Theodore, cardinals, by command of the Apostolic See, [Col. 1391C] as that judgment is contained in an authentic instrument. For greater security, moreover, we have ordered the text of the authentic instrument concerning the judgment promulgated to be inserted word for word:

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We, Alexius, by God’s mercy priest of the title of Saint Susanna, and John, deacon of Saint Theodore, cardinals, make known to all whom these letters may reach that, when the clerics of Saint Tryphon, Saint Nicholas de Praefecto, and Saint Saviour de Sere presented complaints in the presence of Lord Pope Clement III that the nuns of Blessed Mary in the Campus Martius were, by many devices, disturbing the status of their parishes, the lord pope entrusted this case to us for hearing. Therefore, with both parties appearing before us, we asked the sisters who had come why Abbess Agnes had not appeared or sent a sufficient representative. They replied that this case had been decided by a judgment of the rectors of the Roman fraternity, by command of Lord Pope Lucius, and confirmed by that same supreme pontiff; and that therefore there had been no need either for the abbess to come or for her to send a representative. When we heard this, lest we should seem to deny the record, we thought the instrument which had been shown to us privately should be read before the parties, since no defect appeared in it. But in the course of the instrument it was stated that, in the presence of [Col. 1392A] Lord Obicio, cardinal of Saint Clement, and Master Rainerius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian, this case had been examined most carefully; that it had been proved by suitable witnesses before Lord P. de Rustico, the judge whom the rectors had as assessor; and that it had been decided and settled by judgment by the rectors named below. This judgment reads as follows:

“In the name of the Lord. We, rectors of the Roman fraternity—namely P. [Peter], Christian of the basilica of Saint Peter; Guido de Papa of the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber; John, archpriest of Saint John of the Island; Gregory of the Lateran basilica; Jordan, priest and prior of Saint Mary Nova; Girard of Saint Nicholas de Marmorata; Bobo of the title of Saint Marcellus; the priest Jonathan of Saint Pantaleon; and the priest Ingo of Saint Mary in Transpadina—by the authority and command of Lord Pope Lucius, absolve you, Agnes, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary in the Campus Martius, from every petition, complaint, and molestation which P. Albertini, steward of the aforesaid churches, has brought or could bring against you on behalf of the aforesaid monastery concerning the houses listed below, situated within their boundaries: namely, from the house of Paul de Nuzo inward; from the house of Buccacanum inward; from the main road which passes before the tower of Armeldrigus Scorsasanti inward, on both sides of the road; from the house of Monachus inward; and from the house of Benencas de Romanello inward. Henceforth you and your successors may lawfully hold and possess these in perpetuity by parochial right, for the people and as their parish, and provide and administer to them all divine ministrations through your chaplain.”

When the clerics of the aforementioned churches heard this, they at once exclaimed that the instrument was wholly false: first, because they had never assembled before Lord Obicio, cardinal of Saint Clement, in this case; second, because no witnesses had been produced before the aforesaid judge; and third, because the rectors named in the instrument as having issued a judgment had never issued any judgment in their presence. Since both parties were noisily disputing with one another, we fixed a day for the abbess’s party to establish the authenticity of the instrument. In the meantime, we met separately and together with the rectors: namely Guido de Papa; Gerard, abbot of Saint Sabba, who was then archpriest of Saint Nicholas de Marmorata and a rector of the Roman fraternity; the priest Ingo of Saint Mary in Transpadina; Leo, archpriest of Saint Cecilia; and Rolland, archpriest of Saint Mary in Aquiro. We also met separately with the judge P. de Rustico and asked whether all these things had occurred as recounted above. The rectors answered without any hesitation that Lord Obicio had never been with them in this case, that no witnesses had been produced, and that they had rendered no judgment concerning it. Lord P., the judge, said the same and added that he had met with the rectors concerning this case only once.

When both parties had assembled in our presence on the appointed day and, by our command, had sworn against calumny, the abbess, having sworn against calumny and having been questioned by us, said that she had not been present at any judgment concerning this case, had neither produced nor caused witnesses to be produced in it, and, when she received the charter of the instrument, had not heard that a judgment had been rendered on the matter.

After this, the clerics’ party, having taken counsel with its advocates—Lord John, archpriest of Saint Magutus, and Lord Tholomaeus, legal advocate—produced witnesses for greater and clearer caution. The sworn priest Carisomus said that no judgment had been rendered in the dispute concerning the status of the parishes between the church of Blessed Mary in the Campus Martius and the churches of Saint Tryphon, Saint Saviour de Sere, and Saint Nicholas de Praefecto; that no witnesses had been produced by either party; and that P. Albertini, steward of the aforesaid churches, as stated in the instrument, acted in this case only on behalf of the church of Saint Tryphon. For all these reasons he said the instrument was false. He also said that they had never appeared before Lord Obicio in this matter and that the case had not been delegated to him.
