The sworn priest Girard said that, when he and his fellow associates had appeared before the rectors concerning the complaint over the status of the parishes which then existed, and still exists, between the church of Blessed Mary of the Campus Martius and the aforesaid churches, and perceived that the rectors were not proceeding as they ought, they appealed to Lord Pope Lucius. He committed the hearing of the case to Master Rainerius, cardinal deacon of Saint Andrew. He gave no judgment, nor were witnesses produced by either party in this case. Concerning P. Albertini and Lord Obicio, he said the same as the priest Carisomus. The sworn priest Peter said the same as the others: that the commission had been made only to Master Rainerius, that no judgment had been rendered, and that no witnesses had been produced. He added that, although the archpriest of Saint John of the Island was named Nicholas Buccalata, the instrument names John; that the archpriest of Saint Blaise, although named John, is written there as Peter; and that, although the priest Carisomus had never been archpriest, he is described there as archpriest. For all these reasons he asserted that the instrument was false. John Ranucius, the sworn usher, said the same concerning the absence of a judgment and witnesses, and concerning the commission made only to Master Rainerius. Regarding the appeal made to Lord Pope Lucius because the rectors were not proceeding as they ought, he said the same as the priest Girard. He also added that P., the judge of Lord Rusticus, had been appointed assessor by the rectors and not by Lord Pope Lucius, to whom the case had not yet been appealed; and concerning P. Albertini he said the same as the others.

When all this had been heard, both parties were repeatedly asked by us, as is law and custom, whether they wished to add anything new; by common consent and upon the advice of their advocates, they renounced their allegations. Therefore, after both sides had made this renunciation, as stated, and after the witnesses’ depositions had been read, published, and reviewed point by point in the presence of both parties, by the command and authority of Lord Pope Clement and with the consent and will of the cardinals, we rendered the following judgment:

“In the name of the Lord. We, Alexius, by God’s mercy priest of the title of Saint Susanna, and John, by the same mercy deacon of Saint Theodore, cardinals, delegated by Lord Pope Clement concerning the complaint about a false instrument pending between the church of Saint Mary of the Campus Martius on the one side, and the churches of Saint Tryphon, Saint Nicholas de Praefecto, and Saint Saviour de Sere on the other, concerning a certain false charter which Agnes, abbess of Saint Mary of the Campus Martius, and the nuns produced, by which they asserted that the rectors of the Roman fraternity had absolved them from every complaint and molestation made, as the charter stated, by Peter Albertini, steward of the aforesaid churches: namely, from the house of Paul de Nuso inward; from the house of Buccacanum inward; from the main road leading to the tower of Armeldrigus Scorzasanti inward, on both sides of the road; from the house of Monachus inward; and from the house of Benencasa de Romanello inward. Having heard and carefully examined the allegations of both parties, by the authority and command of Lord Pope Clement III and with the consent and will of the cardinals, we judge the aforesaid charter to be false and to lack legal force for all time. We order it to be handed over, cut up, to the clerics of the aforesaid churches; and whatever has been done by any person to confirm that false little charter, we annul and quash by the authority of Lord Pope Clement.”

This judgment was rendered in the presence of Agnes, abbess of the Campus Martius, and the nuns Odolina of Ravenna, Lucia, Scholastica, Theodora, Agnes, and Catherine; Peter de Rogata, procurator of the same monastery in this cause; and, on behalf of the churches, Octavian, archpriest of Saint Tryphon; Nicholas Justus, cleric of the same church; Romanus, archpriest of Saint Saviour de Sere; Leo, archpriest of Saint Nicholas de Praefecto; Carisomus, priest of the same church; Jordan de Malabranca; Conrad, his nephew; and Stephen, son of Conrad.

Therefore let no person whatsoever infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, by divine permission cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Bobo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Alexius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Jac[inthus], cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary Nova. [Col. 1395A] I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, on the day before the Nones of November [4 November], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III. Amen.

**XCIII. Privilege for the monastery of Monte Cassino.** (Lateran, 19 November.)

[TOSTI, *History of Monte Cassino*, II, 214.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons . . . abbot and the monks of Monte Cassino: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since free burial has been granted to you by the Apostolic See both in head and members, we have also thought fit, from the customary clemency of that See, to grant you—being known to be subject to it without intermediary—that whenever you happen to go out in procession for dead bodies, you may, by our permission, freely carry the cross, incense, and holy water according to the custom of the land, without objection or appeal from anyone. But if any persons wish to bring a case against you on the ground that you ought not to have such liberty, let them pursue their right in our presence.

Given at the Lateran, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [19 November], in the first year of our pontificate.

**XCIV. He receives the monastery of Monte Cassino under the protection of Saint Peter and the Apostolic See. He declares that this monastery is to be preferred above the others throughout the West. He decrees that its abbot shall hold a place superior to other abbots at assemblies and shall pronounce the first judgment.** (Lateran, 21 November.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar of Monte Cassino*, II, 216.]

[Col. 1395C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROFFRIDUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

We give thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is better than life, because He is glorious in His saints and merciful, and with ineffable goodness displays His powers wherever He wills. By the power of His favour He established most blessed Benedict as the father of all monks. He appointed him to be both lawgiver and practitioner of the monastic rule. By that saint’s merits He placed the monastery of Monte Cassino, in which Benedict lived most holily and died most gloriously, above all monasteries throughout the West, in His merciful kindness. Since, therefore, it is fitting that the Apostolic See should embrace in a special manner so celebrated and solemn a monastery, following the example of Roman pontiffs of blessed memory, our predecessors, we receive that monastery under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves and strengthen it by the page [Col. 1396A] of this present writing. Moreover, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of holy memory, the Roman pontiffs Urban and Calixtus, we declare that your monastery is to be preferred above all monasteries throughout the West. We decree that you and your successors shall sit above all abbots in every assembly of bishops or princes, and in judgments shall pronounce, before others of your order, the first judgment of law.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, having been warned a second and third time, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour, separated from the most holy body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and at the last judgment subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December [22 November], in the eighth indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

**XCV. He receives the church of Saint Michael of Nonantola under his protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.** (Lateran, 22 November.)

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of Nonantola*, II, 317.]

[Col. 1396C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SIGIFREDUS, archpriest, and all the canons of the church of Saint Michael situated near the castle of Nonantola, present and future, leading the canonical life: for perpetual remembrance.

The authority of the Apostolic See, which we serve although unworthy, admonishes us to provide with prudent care for the condition of churches and to grant them apostolic protection, lest they be exposed to the plundering or harassment of the malicious. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of Alexander and Urban, popes of happy memory, our predecessors, receive the aforesaid church of Saint Michael, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s assistance, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we think the following should be expressly named.

[Col. 1397A] The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances and lands both cultivated and brought under cultivation; likewise the church of Saint Mary de la Banzola; the church of Saint Lawrence; the church of Saint Saviour; the church of Saint Nicholas; the church of Saint Mary del Cantone; the church of Saint Senesius; the church of Saint Mary de Reduto; the church of Saint Peter de Rubiaro; the church of Saint Michael de Senaida; the church of Saint John de Gazo; the church of Saint Ambrose; the church of Saint John de Runco; the church of Saint Mary de Bagazzano; the church of Saint John de Panaro; the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian de Ravarino; and the church of Saint Agnes de Ronco de Praeposo. We also confirm the tithes granted to your church by Rodulph, abbot formerly of the monastery of Nonantola, of good memory, with the counsel and assent of his chapter: from the Claudia road to Portiola, from Mucia to the river Panaro, and beyond the Panaro to the Dark Ditch, of whatsoever and however much is or shall be cultivated by the men of the village on the aforesaid river or by the inhabitants of Nonantola; as is known to be reasonably contained in the privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Sergius, Alexander, and Urban, of happy memory. We likewise confirm the tithes of the lands lying in the estate of Sicco and Crepacore: namely, beside the stream flowing below the long bridge, above within the ditch called Rabiosa, and on the other side within Bisentulum and the ditch called Cenosa, insofar as you have reasonably acquired them. We confirm all these to you and your successors by apostolic authority, as you now possess them canonically and peacefully, decreeing and strictly forbidding that they be granted by anyone as a benefice to lay persons.

Moreover, the village called Salicetum, granted to the archpriest of that church because he is known, above the others, to bear responsibility and care for the celebration of divine offices, the reception of guests, the provision of lights and building works, and the division among the brethren of tithes and offerings, shall remain unimpaired to you and your successors. Further, lest suitable penance be denied to one contrite and humble of heart who wishes to make satisfaction for his offences, following the example of our aforesaid predecessors, we grant you free power, in cases of criminal offences committed by those who belong to the jurisdiction of the aforesaid monastery and are subject to no bishop, to bind and loose, provided that, if necessity arises, you act with the counsel of some religious and discerning bishop. We also hold ratified the ancient and reasonable customs, liberties, and dignities hitherto observed in your church, and decree that they remain unimpaired for all time; and by apostolic authority we forbid anyone to presume to burden you or that church with new or undue exactions.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb [Col. 1398A] the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the monastery of Nonantola. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, having been warned a second and third time, unless he correct his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Rodulphus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bobo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Alexius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. [Col. 1398C] I, Bobo, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary Nova.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Brother Moses, Lateran canon and subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting chancellor, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December [22 November], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

**XCVI. He receives the monastery of Saint Martin of Metz under protection and confirms its discipline and possessions.** (Lateran, 29 November.)

[*History of Metz*, III, Preface, p. 144.]

[Col. 1398D]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Metz and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: for ever.

It is fitting that those who choose the religious life should have apostolic protection, lest some assault of rashness either turn them away from their purpose or, which God forbid, weaken the strength of their sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of the apostolic see, the aforesaid monastery of blessed Martin of Metz [Col. 1399A], in which, by God’s authoring, you are devoted to divine service. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in the same monastery according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by the Lord’s favour, acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper [Col. 1399B] names:

The benefice of the church of Saint Martin, with its tithe, the whole tithe of the *perticae*, and [lacuna] of land; and the village itself, with the right of cattle and the hundred-court (*centania*); the benefice of the church of Hatrise (Hatrize), and one holding; the chapel of Valleroi; the chapel of Saint Julian with its churchyard; the allod of Wazumaitul, and the mill and land of Burtville (Burville) and of Boumont (Beaumont); the benefice of the church of Abba isvilla (Abbeville), the village itself with its ban-right, and the whole tithe of clearings and bees; the benefice of the church of Sauneio (Sauny); the benefice of the church of Vineolis (Vigneules), with the whole tithe of *perticae*, half the tithe beyond the stream, and the village itself [Col. 1399C] with its ban-right; the benefice of Saint Hilary of Metz; the benefice of the church of Otranges, one third of the village with its ban-right, the chapel of that place, and the tithe of *perticae*; the benefice of the church of Guelanges (Gueblanche), and two dayworks of land; the benefice of the church of Mayaco (Maye), of the church of Guen (Goin), and of the church of Faumacres (Famech), with the chapel of Morlanges; the benefice of the church of Celleio (Sailly), with its chapels; and at Juez the tithe of demesne land; the benefice of the church of Luceio (Lucy), with the whole tithe of labour and produce, and the village itself with its ban-right; the chapels, with their offerings, of Saint Christopher, Saint Mary of Buis (Bey), and Braconis Valley (Baronville); the village itself with its ban-right; the tithe, above the royal [domain], of clearings and resources; [Col. 1399D] likewise the tithe of demesne land at Scholanges, and the village itself with its ban-right; the benefice of the church of Buseio (Busy), with its chapels; the whole tithe of *perticae* and of the duke’s demesne land; the tithe from two houses situated in the churchyard, namely four denarii from them; and four denarii from two mills; two thirds of the offerings at the feast of All Saints, the Nativity of the Lord, and Easter; likewise two thirds of alms for the dead, within eight days after Easter, within thirteen days after the Nativity of the Lord, or on the very feast of All Saints; also four solidi and quarters of grain for one holding; a demesne meadow; and four solidi from clearing and from the tithe of swine-pasturage; and the whole tithe of the demesne land of Saint [Col. 1400A] Mary of Verdun; at Moulins, one holding with its ban-right; the jurisdiction of Mauridomus with its chapel; the whole tithe of mills, meadows, all the labour of the brethren, and clearings; the whole tithe of the brethren’s livestock, of demesne lands, and of the *accingiae* and *quartaria* coming into the abbots’ hands; likewise, at Busiacum, the whole tithe of the household’s livestock and of the royal fisc; and, as at Mauridomus, the tithe of *accingiae* and *quartaria* coming into the abbots’ hands, of the brethren’s labour, mills, and meadows, and four denarii for the stake of Chinel; the church of Condeto, with the chapels of Wormeranges and Saint German, and the village itself with its ban-right; fishing rights from Arnulf’s spring as far as Astat, and from Conis as far as Bruscas; and [Col. 1400B] at Vy sixteen measures of salt, six and a half solidi for one holding; also freedom in appointing or dismissing ministerials, and the whole tithe of the demesne land belonging to that church; and, for *angeria* service, thirty denarii in the village of Saint Martin, and in Vineolis and Otranges, for every holding; likewise, at Abbatisvilla, two solidi; in the other villages, as much for *angeria* as for rent, at the feast of Saint Martin; likewise freedom, both for the churchyard of the aforesaid church of Saint Martin and for all its granges, from every exaction and procuration of advocates; two solidi from the shepherd of Buseio; and likewise from Atrise, Famacres, Guelanges, Otranges, Guen, and Cerleio.

Furthermore, let no one presume to demand or extort tithes from you of your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense [Col. 1400C]. We also decree that burial in the monastery itself shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken remaining intact. On the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be put in charge there through any stratagem of intrusion or by force, except the person whom the brethren, by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall judge to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars [Col. 1400D] or churches, and ordinations of monks to be promoted to sacred orders, or of clerics belonging to the cells or churches of the same monastery, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the apostolic see, and is willing to provide these things freely and without impropriety. Otherwise, you may have recourse to whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Therefore we decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, claim for personal use things unjustly given, or harass it by rash or vexatious molestations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and [Col. 1401A] support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this text of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his office and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment.

But upon all who preserve the rights of that place [Col. 1401B], may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Rodulf, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Bobo, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Alexius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Susanna. [Col. 1401C] I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Octavian, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Blessed Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Aquino.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, on the third day before the Kalends of December [29 November], in the sixth indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

XCVII. He orders B[aldwin], Archbishop of Canterbury, to restore within forty days what he has taken from the monks of Canterbury. He forbids injury to the privileges both of the apostolic see and of the Church of Canterbury in the appointment of a new prior; otherwise, he declares that his legate R[adulf], cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, will employ severity. (Lateran, 10 December.)

[Gervase, *Chronicle*, in Twysden, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 1537.]

[Col. 1401D]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., Archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more you excel in the Church of God by the gift of learning and the honour of religion, and hold a higher summit of dignity in the English regions, the more it befits your charity, with more watchful concern, to restrain yourself from injuries or oppressions of your subjects and, putting aside those things that tarnish the beauty of justice and extinguish the fragrance of good repute, to show to your superiors the obedience and reverence due. Therefore we do not without cause wonder that, as has been represented to us, after an appeal was made to the apostolic see and after the prohibition of Urban, our predecessor of good memory, you have so increased your acts concerning the construction of the new chapel and many other matters to the distress of the brethren of the Church entrusted to you, that it may be thought that they have obtained no remedy from the appeal which they interposed, as the rule of law requires; nor do you appear to have rendered due regard to the honour of the most holy Roman Church, your mother. Although [Col. 1402B] it is our intention to show all possible deference in God to your brotherhood, and we have resolved to honour your person in all things incumbent upon us by office, nevertheless we can neither, with a good conscience, pass over with closed eyes the sufferings and cries of those brethren, nor ought we to do so. Therefore, with the counsel of our brethren, by apostolic letters we command and strictly order your brotherhood, setting aside objection and excuse—even if it happens that you are absent from the Church—not to delay to demolish whatever has been done in the work of the chapel after an appeal was made to the apostolic see or after the prohibition of our predecessor. You shall recall and utterly annul [Col. 1402C] whatever has been done or wrongly altered concerning the establishment of canons and other matters connected with the chapel. You shall keep excluded from office and benefice those who, after the prohibition of the aforesaid predecessor, presumed to celebrate divine offices in that chapel, until they offer us fitting satisfaction. You shall restore the ministers of the convent whom you removed after the appeal was lodged and whom that same predecessor restored. You shall likewise hold absolved those whom after the appeal was lodged you wished to excommunicate or suspend. And you shall restore to their former condition, with appeal and objection set aside, everything attempted after that appeal to their prejudice: namely, the seizure of their villages and possessions, their revenues and other things [Col. 1402D] which they had before the appeal, and likewise the taking away of other property.

Moreover, since by the form of law nothing is to be altered after an appeal, we will and command that, while the suit is pending, you make absolutely no attempt to alter anything concerning the state of the monastery to the detriment of those brethren. Further, by this command we order that you do not delay, within forty days after receipt of these letters, to restore to those monks everything which from the time of your promotion, whether after or before the appeal, you have unlawfully taken from them without legal process—churches, gifts, villages, possessions, revenues, or other property—together with suitable recompense for the fruits thereafter unlawfully received, and together with their due and free liberties and administration [Col. 1403A]. We also command those monks that, if since that time they have presumed anything contrary to your right and honour, they shall render you appropriate satisfaction, appeal set aside. Since the prior of the monastery has died in the prosecution of this case, we will and command that in appointing a prior you proceed in no way contrary to the privileges of the apostolic see, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the custom hitherto observed by the Church. If you have acted otherwise, you shall not delay, appeal set aside, to revoke it, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the apostolic see. Otherwise, we have commanded our beloved son R., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes, legate of the apostolic see, by apostolic authority [Col. 1403B] to compel you, all opponents, and the monks themselves if they prove rebellious, by ecclesiastical censure to do this, the obstacle of appeal being removed.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Ides of December [10 December], in the first year of our pontificate.

XCVIII. He receives under protection the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Frutino and confirms its observance, possessions, and privileges. (Lateran, 12 December.)

[D. Erasmus Gattula, *Supplement to the History of Monte Cassino*, vol. I, p. 200.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of Saint Nicholas in Trotino and his brethren, present and future, who profess the regular life: for ever.

[Col. 1403C] As often as [lacuna]. Whatever is recognized as befitting religion and honour, it is proper for us to grant willingly and to give fitting support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforementioned monastery of Saint Nicholas, which belongs to the right or provision of the monastery of Monte Cassino, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to the fear of God, the Rule of Saint Benedict, and the observance of the aforesaid monastery of Monte Cassino shall be observed there [Col. 1403D] inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by the Lord’s favour, acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their proper names:

The church of Saint Martin beside the monastery itself; the church of Saint James; the tower of Summosano with the church of Saint Mary; the tenement at Gardeto and Laterneto; the hamlet of Tocsano with the church of Saint Mary; the castle of Cerreto with the church of Saint Angel; the castle of Nepocsano with the church of Saint Martin; [Col. 1404A] the church of Saint Saviour in Rusticiliane; the church of Saint Sylvester; the church of Saint Scholastica; the church of Saint Mary in Camerone; the church of Saint Mary of Biensa; the tenement at Artesano and at Pucsatello; the tenement beside Salanellum with one mill in the sand-pit; a landed tenement of one thousand modii; the tenement at Velleri; and at Allano the portion of Gerard of Totonis Frum, from the castle of Velleri, with the church of Saint Angel also within that castle itself, and in various places one thousand modii of land; the hill of Festagiano with the church of Saint Sabinus; the hill of Varano with the church of Saint Juvenal; the church of Saint Peter at Allianum; the church of Saint Andrew; the church of Saint Felix at Tullianum with its appurtenances; at Calducso, the church of Saint Saviour with its hamlet; [Col. 1404B] the hill of Spoltino with its appurtenances; the hill of Botunto with the church of Saint Peter and all its appurtenances; and one site of a mill [lacuna]; the island of Ficu; a tenement at Arn[lacuna]; the hill of Ascutula, with two mills; the hamlet of Aven[lacuna]; a tenement in pla[lacuna] and at Sportellis; the tenement at Pacsano; and on the plain of Mortula, two thousand modii of land; the tenement at Paragano and Monteaureo; the tenement at Sorbellis and Grecana; the tenement at Cerritulo and Fontejano; the tenement at Nepocsano, at Vi[lacuna]o of Naretulo, and Moserano in Abruzzo; one fourth of Collerotundo; one fourth of Frundarolo; and twelve households of men, with the church of Saint Angel at Saldinum, and the churches of Saint Saviour and of the Holy Cross at Scilianum; the tenement of Oferano; one hundred modii of land at Roccha de Cameliano; the church at Cellas; the church of Saint Peter; and a tenement in various places of one thousand modii; the castle of Montino with its appurtenances; the estate of Cabiano with the church of Saint Nicholas and all its appurtenances; the castle of Oregnano with its entrance and exit; the church of Saint Mary and the church of Saint Peter with the appurtenances of Pacsano; and in Campo Nerino and Fageto, one thousand modii [Col. 1404C]; the tenement at Paterno and Ancarano; the castle of Carrusa; the church of Saint Angel with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin at Barano with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Donatus in Campo Nerino; the church of Saint Martin at Galegnano [Col. 1404D] with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Flavian at Torano with its appurtenances; at Colondelle, the church of Saint Saviour; and twelve households of men in the appurtenances of the castle of Cosenulis; the church of Saint Martin with its appurtenances; the church of Saint John at Gavanne with its appurtenances. In its same appurtenances, the church of Saint Felicity with its estate; a tenement at Pat. [uncertain, abbreviated in the source]; a tenement at Ripa Alta; the church of Saint Benedict of Cabiano with its appurtenances; the castle of Montorio by the sea with the church of Saint Saviour; at Tortoreto, the hill of Oddo with the church of Saint Liberator; the hill of Foreman with the church of Saint Angel; the hill of Tassello with its appurtenances and with one mill at Bibrata; the tenement of Laciano with the church of Saint Pardus; the tenement [Col. 1405A] at Ponesano, with the seashore and its fishing rights. In the district of Tor[lacuna] and its appurtenances, the gifts of Count Transmund [lacuna], with the church of Saint Paul; the church of Saint Vitalis with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Stephen at Cesule; the church of Saint Gervasius; the church of Saint Lawrence with the castle of Patemo; the church of Saint Angel in Cucero; the church of Saint Lawrence at Monianum with its tenements; the church of Saint Mary at Romeliano with its appurtenances; the castle of Casa Domnica with two mills; the entire estate of Antojano with the church of the Holy Cross; the church of Saint Peter at Opacum with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Flavian; the church of Saint John in the castle of Ripa; the church of Saint [Col. 1405B] John at Bacclianum, with the castles and appurtenances of Cacsiano; various tenements in the territory of Podio; the church of Saint Victoria; the churches of Saint Giles and Saint Rusticus with their appurtenances; the castle of Pharaone with its appurtenances, in the county of Penne. In the territory of Bassano, a certain tenement with one mill on the river Maone; the church of Saint John of Gaminaro with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary above that same church of Saint John; the church of the Holy Cross of Scafeniano; the hill of Saint Angel of Camarda with the churches of Saint Angel and Saint Sabinus, and two thousand modii of land in various places; the estate of Caeseriano with its tenements; the church of Saint Peter at Collealtum with one mill; the church of Saint Mary at Eubillos; an estate [Col. 1405C] at Albeto with its tenements; the tenement at Caesellejano, on the river Magone and stream of Temerino; the church of Saint Cassian, with its estate and all its appurtenances; the churches of Saint Peter and of the Holy Cross of Monte; the church of Saint Agnes; the church of Saint John; the church of Saint Andrew of Collegraeco, with its cells and appurtenances; the church of Saint Saviour of Castellis with its castle; the church of Saint Martin in the place called Caeselian and Pacsanum; the church of Saint Martin in the field of Jupiter; the church of Saint Peter in the place called Valdaresco, and at the stream Eutoso, and Saint Maurus, and Ficu Nereca near the boundary-river; the castle of Genestrule, with the church of Saint Nicholas; the hill of Pecsano, with three thousand modii of the lands of Roceto [Col. 1405D]; the churches of Saint Victorinus, Saint Saviour, and Saint Sylvester; the church of Saint Mary in the place called Genestrule; the church of Saint Saviour in Bifero with its appurtenances; the church of the Holy Cross in Cerreto; the church of Saint Martin in Solenianum; the island of Marnarolo with its tenements; the church of Saint Mary of Casaleneja with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Donatus [lacuna] with its appurtenances. At Termulis, the church of Saint Paul of [lacuna] Actico; the tenement of Petacsato with water and sea-fishing; the church of Saint George of Montecello in the territory of Ascoli; the estate of Morule with the church of Saint Saviour at the place called Ableto, and a tenement of two hundred modii by measure; the estate of Tolleman. with its tenements; the church of Saint Sabinus with its appurtenances [Col. 1406A]; in the place called Frisian., the church of Saint Vincent with its appurtenances and one mill on the little river; the castle of Pecsano with the church of Saint Saviour; the hill of Petra Capellata with the church of Saint Peter; the church of Saint Archangel in Poppleto with two thousand modii of land; the castle of Ancarano with the church of Saint Mary and one thousand modii of land in the March; the church of Saint Benedict at Salbuceto near the river Tisinus; the church of Saint Paratiada with its hamlet; the church of Saint Mary in the Woods, with its appurtenances; at Ajello, the church of the Holy Cross, the church of Saint Apollinaris, the church of Saint Valentine, the church of Saint Peter in Cerreto, the church of Saint Quiricus beside the river Menoccle, the church of Saint Peter in Lamentian. with its appurtenances, the church of Saint Mary [Col. 1406B] in Libiano, and the church of Saint Bartholomew in Campo Fullonis with its appurtenances.

Furthermore, no one may presume to demand or extort from you [tithes] of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, whether from the aforesaid [lacuna]. You may also receive clerics [lacuna], free and absolved, into conversion [the monastic life], and retain them without any opposition.

When a general interdict of the land has been imposed, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding those under interdict and the excommunicated, without ringing bells and in a low voice. Furthermore, we prohibit any of your brethren, after having made profession in that place, from leaving it without permission of his abbot, except for the purpose of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without letters of the community giving assurance. We also forbid secular persons to dare to trouble you or your churches by any vexations or exactions, or to exercise authority over you or those churches [lacuna], so that, undisturbed by [lacuna], you may devote yourselves to the religious purpose which you have undertaken and to divine offices. We decree that burial [lacuna] of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict.

Therefore we have decreed that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them [Col. 1406D], or harass it by any vexations; but that all shall be preserved intact for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see and the due obedience and reverence owed to the aforesaid monastery of Monte Cassino. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person in future, knowing this text of our constitution, rashly attempts to act against it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his offence by worthy satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his office and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the last judgment. But upon all who preserve [lacuna], may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1407A], so that they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of Saint Mary across the Tiber, of the title of Saint Callixtus. I, Pandulf, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, James, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. [Lacuna], cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Lacuna], cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, John of Saint [lacuna], cardinal [Col. 1407B]. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary the New.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, [lacuna], in the seventh indiction, in the year 1188 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

XCIX. He confirms the peace arranged by Peter, cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia, and Sofredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, between the Pisans and the Genoese. (Lateran, 12 December.)

[Tronci, *Memories of Pisa*, p. 152.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the consuls and people of the diocese of Pisa: for ever.

[Col. 1407C] Agreements are pronounced to no purpose among those in discord if they are not committed to writing for the memory of posterity and, in order to prevent a renewed dispute, every avenue for contesting them is not closed to the disputants. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, wishing to provide henceforth for your peace and tranquillity, we have thought fit to confirm for your devotion the agreement prudently confirmed between you and our beloved sons the consuls and people of Genoa and your cities, through our beloved sons Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, and Sofredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legates of the apostolic see. As it is contained in their authentic instrument, has been received by the parties without impropriety, and confirmed by oath, we decree by apostolic authority that it shall be observed inviolably in times to come. We have also thought fit to insert it, word for word, in the present document, in accordance with the authentic instrument of the aforesaid cardinals. Its text is as follows:

“Peter, by God’s grace cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, and Sofredus, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, legates of the apostolic see, to all God’s faithful dwelling in peace and love: the love of peace and love.

“Among the other matters which the supreme pontiff, as Father and shepherd of the universal Church, is bound by the duty of pastoral care to carry out, he is specially obliged to ensure that the cause of sedition [Col. 1408A] and scandal is entirely removed from the midst, and that tranquillity among Christ’s faithful is established by Christ’s grace and through his care. Moved by this consideration, and having special regard for the aid of the Holy Land, Pope Gregory of happy memory first, and subsequently Clement, the venerable Father of the universal Church appointed in his place, laboured most earnestly, personally and through those subject to him, so that the Pisans and Genoese, whom an unjust and dangerous turmoil of wars had long wearied, not without danger to themselves and others, might, with the Lord’s help, be fully restored through the good of peace. Accordingly, after earnest admonition, the Pisan consuls swore, as pleased the aforesaid Lord Pope Clement, that in all controversies pending [Col. 1408B] between the Genoese and Pisans they would abide by his commands, whatever he should impose upon them personally, or through specified messengers, or by his letters. And the noble and prudent men Nicolanus and Picchius, envoys of the Genoese consuls, immediately swore the same thing on behalf of those consuls. This having been done, they gladly gave one another the kiss of peace.

“The lord pope, acting with the common counsel of his brethren, immediately ordered the Genoese that one thousand of their citizens, chosen by the Pisans, should, as one man and on behalf of the whole people, confirm the peace in the same manner by oath. Likewise, he ordered the Pisans that one thousand of their citizens, chosen by the Genoese, should, as one man [Col. 1408C] and on behalf of the whole people, confirm it by oath in the same manner. By God’s grace this was happily accomplished. Accordingly, the supreme pontiff, exercising his customary paternal concern to impose an end upon the aforesaid suits and controversies, sent us—although unequal and unworthy—to establish a definite form in certain articles, with the common counsel of his brethren.

“By the special command of the apostolic see, we wholly annul in Sardinia the detestable form of commerce—indeed, usury—which you have been accustomed to disguise under the name *donnicalia*. We command you and the Genoese, under obligation of oath, neither to add anything to such previous contracts nor thereafter presumptuously to enter into new ones of that kind. You may, however [Col. 1408D], collect, without any deceit or fraud, what is owed to you from that kind of trade. We also command you Pisans not, by any device, to offer any impediment preventing the Genoese from holding peacefully and quietly all pledges and possessions which they have or ought to have in Sardinia, and especially the pledges of Bartolus, formerly king of Arborea, until they have received full satisfaction for the principal. We command you Genoese, under the same strict requirement, to observe this same rule concerning the pledges and possessions of the Pisans.

“We also strictly command you Pisans, under obligation of oath, neither personally nor through others to offer any impediment to prevent all the judges of Sardinia and ten of the greater and more powerful men in each judicature, after taking an oath, from promising complete security to the Genoese and all persons of their district, on land and water and wherever they have power and capacity; and to prevent them, whenever the Genoese lodge a complaint against their men, from causing full justice to be rendered to them. Nor may you hinder the aforesaid oaths of security from being kept firm and unimpaired on land and sea [Col. 1409A]. We further command you both, Genoese and Pisans alike, under obligation of oath, to promise each other free power and permission to sail through the sea wherever you wish, to put in at whatever port you wish, and from there to convey merchandise.

“[Col. 1409B] Moreover, we command you Pisans, under obligation of oath, not to prevent the Genoese from freely approaching your city, other places of your district, and your strongholds, and from trading among you as friends, saving decrees made without malice by either city. Concerning the remaining articles, we decree and command this to be observed: if either party considers itself wronged in any matter and wishes to seek justice, the party against whom the complaint has been lodged shall, plainly, without all deceit, malicious delay, or evil evasion, provide full justice to the complaining party before judges or arbitrators chosen by both parties. We command each party to cause its consuls faithfully and without fraud to put into execution [Col. 1409C], within forty days counted from the delivery of the judgment, whatever sentences the aforesaid judges or arbitrators shall pronounce. And so that what we have decreed may attain its due effect, we command that, from this day and within two months—or longer, should they wish—the Genoese from the city of Pisa and the Pisans from the city of Genoa shall choose judges or arbitrators, who, after taking an oath, shall promise faithfully to fulfil what we have said concerning the administration of justice.

“And so that what is set down at the end may be better committed to memory, and both this and all the foregoing may be observed more firmly under obligation of oath, we strictly command you Genoese and Pisans that henceforth you shall maintain firm and perpetual peace between yourselves, preserve it everywhere unshaken on land and sea [Col. 1409D], and make no deliberate attempt to harm one another in persons or property. We command that these oaths of peace be renewed every year by the chief consuls of the cities, and every sixth year, in the presence of and with the acclamation of the people, by three hundred suitable men chosen by the Pisans from the city of Genoa and another three hundred chosen by the Genoese from the city of Pisa—provided that they have not individually taken this peace specially—and by one public representative on behalf of the whole people.”

We likewise decree that the consuls or governors who for the time being shall be in either city shall require, receive, and cause to be rendered, without deceit or fraud, the aforesaid oaths of renewal. But if—may God [Col. 1410A] avert it!—an offence against the peace confirmed above should be committed abroad by the commune of either city against the other, the peace remaining in force, the offence shall be wholly redressed by the archbishops of the two cities and two learned men in law chosen by those archbishops, without deceit, fraud, or malicious delay. We decree that those jurists whom the archbishops choose with them shall assist them, working in good faith with the archbishops for the restoration of peace; and we decree and command that the consuls of the cities, according to what the archbishops shall ordain, shall diligently observe, fulfill, and carry into execution faithfully and in good faith.

“We also decree that the consuls of those merchants who are sent to different provinces shall swear [Col. 1410B] that they will in good faith do justice concerning the complaints brought before them, and will carry it into execution, and will apply diligence and effective effort to preserving peace inviolate, without any fraud.

“All the foregoing, on the part of the lord pope and by the authority by which we act at his command, we command and prescribe in this matter to you, the Pisan and Genoese consuls, and through you to the communities of your cities, whose representation you exercise in this matter by their command: that you observe it forever, inviolate, according to its good and plain meaning. And, so that this our determination and statute may obtain perpetual firmness and irrevocable force, we deliver it to you marked with the present writing and fortified by the protection of our seals [Col. 1410C].

“This sentence was issued and recited in the city of Lucca, in the court of the lord bishop of Lucca, in the presence of the same Lord William, bishop of Lucca; Alcherio Vecchii, podestà of Lucca; Donato de Ricottis and Locterio Bernardi, his counsellors; Bonfilio, public chancellor of the same city of Lucca; Forteguerra; Rolando Guarmignani; Jacobus de Cervasiis, jurists; Salamoncello; Ildebrandino, son of Malpilius; Borcaino Alteminello de Alteminellis; Batroso; Guido Uberti de Fralmo; and Ildebrando de Goltellis, distinguished consuls of Lucca; Gargosso de Alica; and many other noble fellow-citizens of Lucca and many others of the people of Lucca. Also present were the Pisan [Col. 1410D] consuls, namely Ugo Alde, viscount; Ildebrando Bambone; Vitale Gattabianca; Lambert, formerly of Rainerius Pandulphus; Philip, formerly of Vernagallus; and Pipino, formerly of Henry Frederick. Present also were the wise men of the city of Pisa, namely Bulgherino, viscount, formerly of Ugo; Uguccione, formerly of Lambert Bononis; Gaetano Burgundi; Bulso, formerly of Peter Albitonis; William, son of Gerard Seretti; and Ugo, formerly of Bernard Marignani, judge and notary. Present likewise were Nicola Ebriaco, Genoese consul; Nuecelone, indeed a wise man; and Guglielmo Caligopalli, public chancellor of Genoa. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, the sixth indiction, on the Nones of July.”

Therefore we decree that absolutely no person may be permitted [Col. 1411A] to infringe this page of our constitution and the page containing the sentence of our aforesaid brethren, or rashly to oppose it. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly presuming rashly to act against this page of our constitution, after a second or third warning does not amend his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance.

But upon all who preserve the aforesaid settlement and peace may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 1411B] so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Amen. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark, have subscribed. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St Mary across the Tiber, of the title of St Callixtus, have subscribed. I, Pandulphus, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, have subscribed. I, Alexander, cardinal priest of the title of St Susanna, have subscribed. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin, [Col. 1411C] have subscribed. I, Gratianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, John Felix, cardinal deacon of St Eustace by the temple of Agrippa, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal deacon of St Theodore, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of St Mary Nova, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Aquiro, [Col. 1411D] have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the second Ides of December, in the year 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Clement III.

### C. Privilege for Roffridus, Abbot of Monte Cassino.  
*(Lateran, 13 December.)*

[D. TOSTI, *History of Monte Cassino*, II, 214.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops in whose bishoprics are churches and other goods of the monastery of Monte Cassino: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the monastery of Monte Cassino is, among other monasteries [Col. 1412A], of great dignity and renown, and belongs directly, without any intermediary, to the Roman Church, it is fitting that we watch over its condition by a common and special obligation and preserve its rights with the zeal of pastoral care, lest we be reproved for insufficient diligence if we allowed its goods to be exposed to anyone’s violence or plundering. Moved therefore by this consideration, following the example of our predecessors, we have deemed it proper to grant to our beloved son R., abbot of Monte Cassino, by a privilege strengthened with the subscriptions of our brethren, that, against wrongdoers to his monastery, if the archbishops or bishops in whose bishoprics they live, when requested a second or third time, refuse or delay to do justice to them, he may freely have authority, by our [Col. 1412B] authority, to pronounce ecclesiastical sentence.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command and prescribe to your brotherhood that, concerning wrongdoers against the aforesaid monastery who are your parishioners, concerning whom the same abbot, his brethren, or their messenger shall lodge a complaint before you, you shall administer strict justice without delay or condition; or you shall firmly observe, all obstacle of appeal being removed, the sentence which the same abbot shall render against them under the indulgence of the Apostolic See, and shall order it to be observed by all until due satisfaction has been made. [lacuna]

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of December, in the first year of our pontificate.

### CI. Privilege for the Monastery of St Peter of Massa on Mount Nerone.  
*(Lateran, 15 December.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, II, 814.]

[Col. 1412C]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Milo, abbot of St Peter of Massa on Mount Nerone, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

“To religious desires,” etc. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of the present writing, the aforesaid monastery established in your territory and built on the freehold of blessed Peter, in which you are devoted to divine service. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order [Col. 1412D] known to have been established there according to God and the Rule of St Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions, etc., down to the words expressly set out: In the county of Cagli, the church of St Mary at Sorripule; the church of St Andrew at Petroniano; the church of St Christopher at Barbiano; in the county of Senigallia, the church of St Bartholomew with its appurtenances; in the county of Gubbio, the church of St Agatha at Capite; the church of St Mary at Villano; the church of St Mary at Belforte; and the church of St Sylvester at Testo, with their appurtenances.

Following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, Benedict and John, Roman pontiffs, we confirm to you whatever you appear to possess within the boundaries set down below in the present seventh indiction, and within these boundaries: on the first side, the land of Cagli; on the second, the Glaciata water; on the third, the Great Valley; on the fourth, the water called Partita; on the fifth, the Great Land; on the sixth, the land of Lucelana. We further grant and confirm to you the land which appears to belong to your monastery at Massa on Mount Nerone, saving, of course, the right and lordship of the Holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and to whose right all the aforesaid things belong. You shall receive consecrations of altars or churches and ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from whichever bishop you prefer, provided that he is Catholic, has the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to grant this to you without impropriety; otherwise, from whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall provide what is requested. [Col. 1413B] We also decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the gift and last will of those who resolve to be buried there—while preserving, nevertheless, the due rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are carried out.

Therefore we decree that no one whatever, etc. But if anyone, therefore, etc.

But upon all, etc. Amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Bacchus. I, Laborans, of St Mary across the Tiber, title of St Callixtus. [Col. 1413C] I, Pandulphus, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Bobo, cardinal priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, Alexander, cardinal priest of the title of St Sylvester. I, Jacobus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of St Mary Nova, [Col. 1413D].

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### CII.

At the request of Peter, bishop, he confirms all the privileges which the Roman pontiffs had formerly granted to the Church of Segni; among the places particularly enumerated are the following castles: Collis Medius, Mattelonicus, Gabilianus, Plumbinaria, Valmontonius, Lacus, and Mount Fortinius.—Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, seventh indiction, in the year 1188, in the first year of the pontificate.—Lucius III had long before granted all this to the same Bishop Peter by a very ample privilege, which is highly useful for determining the boundaries of the diocese of Segni (see *Patrologia*, vol. CCI, under Lucius III, no. 67).

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1237.]

[Col. 1414A]

### CIII. He confirms certain rights of the chapter of the Church of St Alexander of Bergamo.  
*(Lateran, 23 December.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 472.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Oberto, provost of the Church of Bergamo, and the chapter of St Alexander: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Since from the Apostolic See,” etc. Therefore, granting your just petitions, we grant you by apostolic authority free power to compel by ecclesiastical censure the priests who are ordained [Col. 1414B] to render fealty to that Church, as it has hitherto been maintained by custom that they ought to render that fealty. This was confirmed and established by apostolic protection by Anastasius and Adrian, our predecessors: if, after receiving orders, they should at once refuse to render it, they are to be excluded from the orders which they have received. Likewise, you may compel those who ought to come to that same Church for the principal Mass on Sundays and other solemnities to attend, as is contained in the decision of the supreme pontiffs Innocent and Eugenius and has hitherto been observed without dispute.

Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CIV. He receives the Church of Saints Felix and Regula at Zurich under protection and confirms its possessions.  
*(Lateran.)*

[NEUGART, *Codex diplomaticus Alemannicus*, II, 115.]

[Col. 1414C]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Walter, provost of the Church of Saints Felix and Regula at Zurich, and his brethren, present and future, to be canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just requests be granted; especially when the piety of petitioners assists their wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your [Col. 1414D] just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this writing, the aforesaid Church of Saints Felix and Regula, in which you are dedicated to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have considered it proper to state the following by their own names:

The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the church of Küsnacht [Chussennaco], [Col. 1415A] with a third part of its estate and the other things you possess there; the church of Schwamendingen [Swanligen], with every right you have in it; the tithes of the villages of Mediolani, Mure, Wittalicon, Henco, and of the city of Zurich. We also confirm to you and, through you, to your church by apostolic authority the right which the regular canons of the church of St Martin, situated on the estate of the provostship of Zurich, are bound to render to you each year, both in rent and in tithes and other revenues, together with all your other possessions which you possess justly and peacefully. We hold valid the liberties and communal rights, as well as the reasonable and ancient customs granted to your church by ecclesiastical and secular persons and hitherto observed; and we decree that they shall remain unimpaired in future times.

By apostolic authority we also forbid anyone to pronounce against you or your church a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without manifest and reasonable cause, or to impose new and undue exactions upon you or your men; nor may the advocate of your church enter your courts in any way unless with your consent or at your invitation. Upon the death of you, the present provost of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any artifice of surreption or by force, save the person whom the brethren collectively, or the sounder judgment of the greater part of the brethren, as has hitherto been observed, shall provide to be elected according to God. Nor shall anyone be instituted parish priest in your same Church [Col. 1415C] unless he is a canon who ought to be elected by you.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved entire for the benefit and use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the rights of the diocesan bishop. But if anyone, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the third day before the Kalends of [lacuna], in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1415D] 1188, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement.

### CV.

He writes to Isaac, emperor of Constantinople, that “by his edict his princes have been stirred up against Saladin; the chief among them were Frederick, the other emperor; Philip, king of the Franks; Richard of England; and Otto of Burgundy; that William, king of Sicily, after pacifying the sea against pirates, furnished provisions from Sicily and Apulia to those setting out; that the Frisians and Danes also equipped fifty triremes and twelve Flemish ships, which, crossing into Mauretania and turning toward the African shores, inflicted great injuries on the Saracens and plundered the city of Sylvina after taking it by force; that the king of Hungary made peace with the Venetians; and he asks him to support this war, now renewed, by whatever means he can.”

[See REUSNER, *Turkish Letters*, p. 16.]

## Year 1189

### CVI. He receives the Florentine Monastery of St Salvi into protection and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Lateran, 2 January.)*

[LAMI, *Monuments of the Florentine Church*, II, 995.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Gilbert, abbot of the monastery of St Salvi, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1416B] Apostolic protection ought to be at hand for those who choose the religious life, lest perhaps the assault of any rash person should either call them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of the present writing, the aforesaid monastery in which you are dedicated to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions and goods [lacuna] the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire by just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors.

Following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Urban, [Col. 1416C] Gregory, Innocent, and Alexander, Roman pontiffs, we decree that no archbishop, bishop, or other ecclesiastical or secular prelate, except the Vallombrosan congregation, may obtain any lordship over your church, as is known to have been established by those same predecessors. Moreover, just as the chapel of St Nicholas of Casa Arsa, which belongs to your right, is known to have been hitherto free from every yoke of the lordship of bishop and parish priest, so we decree that it shall remain free hereafter as well. We likewise confirm to you the right which you have hitherto held in the hospital of Capraria. We have also considered it proper to confirm to your monastery the Church of St James, situated [Col. 1416D] in the city of Florence, granted to your Church by Julius, once bishop of that city, of good memory, with the consent of the Florentine chapter, together with its burial ground and parish, and with the fixed boundaries expressly recorded in the charter which that bishop delivered to you and to the Church of St Silvius concerning its donation, after the example of our predecessor Urban of blessed memory. Moreover, we hold valid the liberties, ancient immunities, and reasonable customs granted to you and your monastery, as they have hitherto been observed, and decree that they shall remain unimpaired for all time.

You may also receive into your monastery clerics or laymen fleeing from the world, free and absolved, and retain them without any opposition; and, when necessary, bring them forward to give testimony in the causes of your monastery. We forbid anyone who, after making profession in that place, should presume to depart without the abbot’s leave, unless in pursuit of a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain one who has departed. We further prohibit anyone from daring, without the consent of the abbot and chapter, either to give monks or lay brothers to that monastery or to take them away, or to impose new or undue exactions on the said monastery or on your churches or men. By apostolic authority we additionally prohibit anyone from pronouncing against you, your monastery, its abbot, or your clerics a sentence of excommunication, suspension, or interdict without manifest and reasonable [Col. 1417B] cause. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars, and ordinations of clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, has the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to furnish them freely and without impropriety; otherwise you may have recourse to whichever bishop you prefer, who, relying on our authority, shall grant what you request. We also grant that the burial place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; while preserving, nevertheless, the canonical rights of those churches from which [Col. 1417C] the bodies of the dead are taken.

Indeed, no one may presume to demand tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the fodder of your animals. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of the same place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any artifice of surreption or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder judgment of a part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St Benedict.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but let all things be preserved unimpaired and entire for the benefit in every way of the use of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See. But if, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark. I, Laborans, cardinal priest of St Mary across the Tiber, title of St Callixtus. I, Pandulphus, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Albinus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Peter, cardinal priest of the title of St Lawrence in Damaso. [Col. 1418A] I, Hyacinthus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Octavianus, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, Bernard, cardinal deacon of St Mary Nova. I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Aquino.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and acting chancellor, on the fourth Nones of January, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1189, the seventh indiction, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### CVII. To all clerics established throughout Norway, he forbids “any of them to presume to go on campaign, except perhaps in order to administer penance and ecclesiastical sacraments to the dying and to dissuade evil deeds”; otherwise, the sentence pronounced against them by the archbishop of Nidaros is to be confirmed by him.  
*(Lateran, 28 January.)*

[THORKELIN, *Diplomata Arnamagnæana*, II, 11.]

[Col. 1418B]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all clerics established throughout Norway: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, the weapons of clerics are held to be prayers and tears, it is dangerous to you and utterly hostile to your profession [Col. 1418C] to involve yourselves in carnal wars, when you ought even to abstain from secular concerns, according to the Apostle’s saying: “No one serving as a soldier of God entangles himself in secular affairs,” etc. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we forbid your whole body that any of you, except perhaps in order to administer penance and ecclesiastical sacraments to the dying and to dissuade evil deeds, shall presume by any rashness to go on campaign. Otherwise, the sentence which, on this account, our venerable brother the archbishop of Nidaros shall pronounce against you, we shall hold confirmed by the Lord’s authority and shall command to be observed inviolably.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the second year [Col. 1418D] of our pontificate.

### CVIII. To the sisters of the Church of Langenhorst.  
*(Lateran, 10 February.)*

[NIESERT, *Münster Document Collection*, IV, 219.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, the nuns of the church of Langenhorst: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When matters concerning the protection and advancement of churches are sought from the Apostolic See, it is fitting that we grant them with willing mind and, in accordance with the petitioners’ wishes when consistent with reason, accomplish them with sympathetic disposition. A certain beloved son, Franco, vicedominus of the Church of Münster, informed us that, when a certain inheritance had devolved upon him by hereditary right, he built your monastery, in honour of St John the Baptist, on his own estate for the salvation of his soul. And because he saw very many churches in those parts burdened by the importunity of advocates, he ordained in your church that you should have free power to choose an advocate, in this manner: if the person so chosen should prove troublesome, you shall have free power to choose another, and the first advocate’s son shall not succeed to that office by hereditary right.

Therefore, assenting to the just petitions of that same vicedominus, we confirm that ordinance, as rationally made, by apostolic authority and fortify it with the protection of the present writing. We decree that no person whatever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth Ides of February, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CIX. To B[aldwin], Archbishop of Canterbury, he writes the same as above, except that he declares that not Radulph but John, cardinal priest of the title of St Mark and legate of the Apostolic See, will see to the execution of his orders.  
*(Lateran, 12 March.)*

[GERVASE, *Imaginatio*, in TWYSDEN, *Historiæ Anglicanæ Scriptores*, I, 1322.]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., archbishop of Canterbury: greeting and [Col. 1419C] apostolic blessing.

The more you pre-eminently possess in the Church of God the endowment of learning and the honour of religion, and hold a higher pinnacle of dignity in the English regions, the more it befits your charity, by more vigilant care, to refrain from injuries or oppressions of those subject to you and, laying aside those things which mar the beauty of justice and extinguish the fragrance of good repute, to render the obedience and reverence due to your superiors.
