CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, all bishops to whom these letters shall come: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1446D] Although we are bound diligently to provide for the peace of all churches, we ought nevertheless to give more watchful thought to the tranquillity and peace of those which belong to our jurisdiction and are known to pertain to the Roman Church without any intermediary. Accordingly, our beloved sons the provost and brethren of the church of St Nicholas of Stendal—which belongs to the jurisdiction of St Peter and is known to pertain particularly to us—have received, through the clemency of the Apostolic See, the concession that, if their diocesan bishop, repeatedly requested by them with due humility before prudent men as witnesses, does not grant them ecclesiastical sacraments freely and without any difficulty or improper impediment, they may request them from whichever Catholic bishop they prefer. Therefore, [Col. 1447A] by apostolic writ we command your brotherhood that, when you are requested by those brethren, you shall freely administer those sacraments by apostolic authority, all delay and appeal being set aside.

Given at the Lateran, 11 September, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CXXIX. He takes the monastery of Baumburg under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, 12 September.)

[HUND, *Metropolis of Salzburg*, III, 85.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son MARSILIUS, provost of the church of St Margaret at Baumburg, and to his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Whenever that is requested of us which is recognized as befitting honour and religion, it is proper that we grant it willingly and give suitable support to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, since Count Berengar of Sulzbach, in pious devotion, offered his allod at Sulzbach, in the territory of [Col. 1447B] Sulzbach, to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church under an annual rent of one Byzantine coin; and since, building there your church in honour of God and in memory of the blessed virgin Margaret, he assigned it to the order of regular canons: we, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Paschal, Honorius, Innocent, Lucius II, and Lucius III, take that place, because it belongs to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted there according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church presently possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter acquire, by the grant of pontiffs, the liberality of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

[Col. 1447D] The archdeaconry; the parish of St George; the church of St John at Fruchtlachingen; Frulestorf with its appurtenances; Funigen with its appurtenances; Varnaspacht with its appurtenances; Meglinger with its appurtenances; Windbret with its appurtenances.

We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are perhaps excommunicated or under interdict; while preserving, nevertheless, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken. The provost then in office may also, with the common counsel of the brethren, or that of their sounder part, elect before God an advocate whom he judges very useful and necessary to the place, [Col. 1448A] and remove him if he appears unsuitable, as was decreed and confirmed in writing by our predecessors of happy memory, Paschal, Honorius, Innocent, Lucius II, and Lucius III.

Upon the death of yourself, the present provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, in the fear of God, shall canonically provide to be elected. Further, after making profession, none of you may possess private property or leave the cloister without the permission of the provost or congregation. By the benevolence of the Apostolic See, we also permit and confirm to your charity and that of your successors that you may receive the ordination of [Col. 1448B] clerics and other ecclesiastical sacraments from good and religious bishops, if your own bishop is infected with simoniacal or another heretical perversity and does not possess the favour of the Apostolic See. As a token of the protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay one Byzantine coin every year to us and our successors.

Moreover, that you may serve our Lord Jesus Christ with freer minds, providing in every respect for your welfare, we decree that your servants who serve you in your court shall, without hindrance from the parish priest, hear the word of God and masses in your church, receive the sacraments, and be subject to the other divine laws. We grant to you and your successors the tithes of your newly cultivated lands, all opposition by episcopal officials being removed, [Col. 1448C] so that, by the Lord’s bounty, you may remain for ever undisturbed in the purpose you have undertaken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved intact and serve in every respect the use of those for whose governance and maintenance they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop in the aforesaid parishes subject to you. If, therefore, anyone in the future, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran, 12 September.

### CXXX. To the provost and brethren of St Nicholas at Stendal, he grants that they may minister in the parishes belonging to them, either personally or through chaplains. (Lateran, 13 September.)

[RIEDEL, *Codex diplomaticus Brandenburgensis*, I, V, 23.]

[Col. 1448D]

Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost and brethren of St Nicholas at Stendal.

[lacuna] Yielding to both your prayers and those of our beloved son, the nobleman Count Henry, founder of your church, we have thought fit by this present document to grant to you and your successors that, if the diocesan bishop, repeatedly and humbly requested before reputable persons as witnesses, does not, without any difficulty or improper impediment, confer the cure of souls of those parishes belonging to you upon suitable persons canonically presented by you, then by apostolic authority, with appeal set aside and without litigation, you shall hold that cure and freely minister in those parishes either personally or through your chaplains, until the bishop, reconsidering his obstinacy, admits those presented by you as he ought.

[Col. 1449A] Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 13 September, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CXXXI. To the provost and brethren of St Nicholas at Stendal, he permits them “to redeem tithes from the hands of laymen and freely assign them to their own use and that of their successors.” (Lateran, 13 September.)

[RIEDEL, ibid., I, V, 24.]

[Col. 1449B]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost and brethren of St Nicholas at Stendal.

[lacuna] By the authority of this present document we have thought fit to grant you permission to redeem from the hands of laymen the tithes belonging to your parishes, and freely assign them to the use of yourselves and your successors.

Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our grant, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 13 September, in the second year of our pontificate. [Col. 1449C]

### CXXXII. To Al., provost, and the brethren of St Nicholas at Stendal, he grants that “no one may hold a synod in their church, nor may any bishop or prelate presume to excommunicate them or place their church under interdict.” (Lateran, 4 November.)

[Ibid.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Al., provost, and the brethren of the church at Stendal: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[lacuna] Beloved sons in the Lord, favourably assenting to your just petitions, by the authority of this present document we grant that no one, against your will, may hold a synod in your church. We also prohibit by apostolic authority any bishop or prelate from presuming to excommunicate your persons or subject your church to interdict, [Col. 1449D] without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and of its legate.

Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted, etc.

Given at the Lateran, 4 November, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CXXXIII. To Count Ger. and all the people of Ragusa. (Lateran, 25 November.)

[FARLATI, *Illyricum Sacrum*, VI, 83.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the nobleman Count GER . . . and all [Col. 1450A] the people of Ragusa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When our venerable brother Ber., Archbishop of Ragusa, came to the Apostolic See, we received him kindly in view of his integrity, honourability, and learning, and graciously caused the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office—to be bestowed upon him. Therefore, sending him back to you with the favour of the Apostolic See, him whom we sincerely love with charitable affection in consideration of his discretion and integrity, we admonish and command and enjoin your whole community by apostolic writ to receive him kindly and devoutly, to render him due obedience and reverence, and reverently and [Col. 1450B] without resistance to observe his salutary admonitions and commands. In matters pertaining to God, strive to support him as the father and shepherd of your souls, with every meekness and devotion, and freely extend your favour, so that in the ministry he has undertaken he may make beneficial progress for you and for the Church entrusted to him, and so that you may unfailingly hope to receive from the Lord a reward for the observance of obedience and fidelity.

Given at the Lateran, 25 November, in the second year of our pontificate.

### CXXXIV. He takes the monastery of St Quintin near Beauvais under protection, and confirms its discipline and possessions. (Rome.)

[LOUVET, *Antiquities of Beauvoisis*, I, 477.]

[Col. 1450C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Peter, abbot, and the other brethren in the church of Blessed Quintin, situated near Beauvais, professing the canonical life, and to their successors who shall live according to the rule, in perpetuity.

The affection of pious intention ought to be fostered by zealous support, so that ecclesiastical advantage may gain strength and increase through the favour of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, after the example of Alexander, Roman pontiff of happy memory, our predecessor, take under the protection [Col. 1450D] of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are dedicated to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order, known to have been established in your church according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Augustine, shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now possesses justly and canonically, or may hereafter acquire, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following in their own terms:

The place in which the church itself stands, with all its appurtenances: namely, a whole and perpetual prebend in the church of Blessed [Col. 1451A] Beauvais; also, the annual revenues of prebends in that church, when they are vacated or transferred from one person to another, whether after resignation they return to the same person, for a full year and in full; a whole and perpetual prebend in the church of St Bartholomew; a whole and perpetual prebend in the church of St Vedast; a whole and perpetual prebend in the church of St Lawrence; a whole and perpetual prebend in the church of St Arnulf of Clermont, with the vineyard belonging to the prebend; a whole and perpetual prebend in the church of Blessed Mary of Mertol, with the vineyard belonging to the prebend; and a certain house within the walls of that same castle.

A tenth share of all the bishop’s [Col. 1451B] mills at Beauvais, for grinding grain; the thirteenth penny in all the bishop’s fulling-mills; the church of St Hippolytus; the wood of Le Parc, whatever names it may be designated by, for uses necessary to you: for baking the bread of your burgesses and your *Bolengarii*; for the enclosures and *escaratz* [as printed] of your vineyards and small gardens; and for thorns. Four asses for daily carrying what is needed for the fire, and in that same wood dead and cut timber lying upon the ground.

Land adjoining the island of the aforesaid church, and a mill and oven with the water which runs through that land, free of every outside authority. No one may presume to claim governance, lordship, or jurisdiction in the aforesaid borough and the land adjoining that church, except the Roman Church, without prejudice to the canonical right of the bishop of Beauvais. [Col. 1451C] Jurisdiction over the roads and meadows adjoining and extending from the land of your church lengthwise as far as the court of that church situated on this side of the monastery of St Just of Marais; breadthwise as far as the ditch which separates the meadows from the common pastures; and from the new ditch and the upper channel of the river as far as your court at Marais.

The parish of St Gervais of Bragella; the parish called Flagellatum of St Quintin, together with all jurisdiction over that village and land sufficient for three ploughs, with a portion of woodland; the church of Novovico, with mill and oven; the church of Fuscinae-villa; the altar-right of Temerii-villa; the altar-right of Audoeni-villa; the altar-right of Arione; the altar-right of Bussy; the altar-right of Medianville; the altar-right of Fredinville; the altar-right of Dudonis-villare; the altar-right of Novavilla Regis, with the entire small tithe and a third of the great tithe; [Col. 1451D] the altar-right of Hamenvillare; the altar-right of Monciaco; and the altar-right of Autoilo, with all the great and small tithe.

The land called Albert’s *mansionile*, free from every jurisdiction; rights of use in all the woods of Altiollo for the brethren living there; at Beauvais, the dues of two gates and the hide-duty; the cell of Blessed Mary of Gornaco with its appurtenances; one modius of wheat and one of oats, which the church of Ressonis pays you yearly; a sixth part of the entire tithe of the village of St Menelai; one modius of wheat at Gremeviller, owed to you by the canons of St Michael; half of Grandisvillare; four altar-rights held from you by monks; and the *mansionile* of Furnodo, free from every jurisdiction and vicariate.

In the diocese of Amiens: the church of Blessed Denis of Piccio with its appurtenances; the parish of St Martin with the whole great and small tithe; the parish of Sancet with the whole tithe; the church of Contey [Col. 1452A] with its appurtenances; the altar-right of St Martin and the chapel of Tilleio; the altar-right of Corcellis; half the tithe of Riveriis; the chapel of Ferreriis with the whole great and small tithe; and the *mansionile* of Vagella and Molaria.

In the diocese of Noyon: the altar-right of Partin with its appurtenances; in the church of Blessed Quintin of Vermand, one whole and perpetual prebend. [Col. 1452B] In the church of Blessed Mary of Nigella, one whole and perpetual prebend. In the diocese of Soissons: the cell of St Adrian with its appurtenances; likewise, lodgers settled on the land of the canons, exempt from every jurisdiction and exaction; at Reinvalle, a fourth part in all land-rents on every kind of seed.

In the archdiocese of Rouen: the altar-right of Spei, with presentation of the priest, a third part of the tithe, and one tenant. In the diocese of Troyes: the cell of St George with its appurtenances; likewise the canons’ court and the enclosure of that place, free by parochial right; also vineyards and lands sufficient for one plough, free from every tithe and exaction; in the church of Blessed Peter at Troyes, one [Col. 1452C] perpetual prebend; at Troyes, the gate called Belon’s; the church of St Mary of Druto with all great and small tithes, and with the oven and jurisdiction of that village; the chapel of Fontanis with the oven of that village and half of that village; the chapel of Auriniaco and a third part of the whole great tithe together with the entire small tithe; the land of Mariniaco, free from every tithe and jurisdiction; the parish of Maceriis with the whole small tithe, and in that parish the island of Granceae, free from every jurisdiction; the parish of Villenosse with all great and small tithes of that parish, your men free from every jurisdiction, and the mill; the chapel of Fontanellis and the tithe of that place; [Col. 1452D] the chapel of St James; half a modius of grain in the tithe of Loen; the church of St Andrew of Baldement with its appurtenances and the oven of that village and half the great tithe; and a third part of the tithe of Pars.

In addition, by apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from presuming, without evident and reasonable cause, to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or suspension, or an interdict in your churches, or to impose upon those churches new or undue exactions. Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of fraud or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to [Col. 1453A] God and the Rule of blessed Augustine. We likewise decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who have determined to be buried there, unless they are perhaps excommunicated or under interdict; while preserving, nevertheless, the right of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away or retain what has been taken of its possessions, diminish them, or harass it with any other vexations; but that all things be preserved intact and serve in every respect the use of those for whose governance and support they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 1453B] person knowingly attempts rashly to violate this page of our constitution, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office, know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed, be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Done at Rome, in the year 1189.

## YEAR 1190

[Col. 1453C]

### CXXXV. He confirms the judgment, approved by Otto, former bishop of Constance, concerning the right of foundation of the three churches of Chilcheim, Eimuotingen, and Matra. (Lateran, 6 February.)

[SCHOEPFLIN, *History of Zähringen-Baden*, IV, 130.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALGOTO, LUPULTO, and THEODRIC of Chilcheim: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever disputes arising over ecclesiastical matters come to lawful examination and, once brought before a court, having long been debated in the parties’ arguments, are lawfully settled by a definitive judgment through the discernment of prelates, it is proper and fitting that those judgments should be confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See, lest through anyone’s rashness they again fall into the entanglement of contention. Now, when a question arose between you and Abbot B. of Stein concerning the right of foundation of the three churches—namely Chilcheim, Eimuotingen, and Matra—you proved your claim by the lawful testimony of witnesses, and a judgment was lawfully pronounced in your favour, which Otto, of good memory, formerly bishop of Constance, confirmed. We therefore hold that same judgment ratified, since it was reasonably delivered and not suspended by a lawful appeal; and [Col. 1454A] we confirm it by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this writing. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 6 February, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXXXVI. To the abbot and convent of Cîteaux, he confirms the church of Schardeburg, donated by King Richard of England. (Lateran, 9 February.)

[HENRIQUEZ, *Rule*, p. 232.]

[Col. 1454B] CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Cîteaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant our assent to the just desires of petitioners and bring to fulfilment, by a corresponding effect, vows which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, favourably assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion the church of Schardeburg, with all its appurtenances and liberties, as the authentic documents made concerning it by Richard, illustrious King of England, testify—he having granted that church to you by pious gift as a perpetual alms, under the supervision of the abbots of the General Chapter—and strengthen it by the protection of this [Col. 1454C] writing. We decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, 9 February, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXXXVII. To the suffragans of the church of York, and to all abbots, priors, people, and clergy established throughout the province, he announces that Geoffrey, brother of Richard, King of England, has been recognized by him as Archbishop of York. (Lateran, 7 March.)

[RALPH OF DICETO, *Images of History*, in TWYSDEN, *Historiæ Anglicanæ Scriptores*, I, 653.]

[Col. 1454D]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the suffragans of the church of York, and to his beloved sons, all abbots, priors, people, and clergy established throughout the province of York: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Having learned from the letters of our dearest son in Christ R., illustrious King of England; of our venerable brother H., Bishop of Durham; of the beloved sons of the chapter of York; and of many religious communities of that diocese, that the same chapter of the church of York elected their beloved son Geoffrey, brother of the aforesaid king, by unanimous vote and common consent as father and archbishop; [Col. 1455A] and that our beloved son J., cardinal-priest of the title of St Martin and legate of the Apostolic See, as we have more fully learned from his letters, confirmed that election by the authority of the legation which he exercised in England; and further considering that the church of York, long deprived of a pastor’s guidance and having suffered much loss through the lack of a prelate, may be restored to a better condition through Geoffrey’s diligence and influence: we hold that election ratified, as it was made in concord and confirmed by our said legate, especially since Pope Alexander, our predecessor of pious memory, dispensed in his case; and, with the counsel of our brethren, we confirm it by the authority of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 1455B] Therefore we admonish your whole community and command you by apostolic writ to strive to render to him, as your prelate, without opposition, the reverence and honour which you have shown to his predecessors, so that thereby you may appear deservedly commendable before God and men.

Given at the Lateran, 7 March, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXXXVIII. To Milo, Archbishop of Milan, and his suffragans, he reports that he has ordered [Theobald], Bishop of Piacenza, to proceed severely against the consuls of Piacenza unless they desist from injuries against churches. (Lateran, 29 March.)

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 371.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable [Col. 1455C] brethren, the Archbishop of Milan and his suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The audacious and detestable presumption has recently come to the ears of the Apostolic See that the consuls of the city of Piacenza, rashly attacking churches, not only broke down their doors, but, after carrying off their keys, refused to return them until certain persons had given them security and firmly promised that they would dispose of none of the churches’ resources except what pertained solely to subsistence. Not content with these acts of rashness, they confirmed by oath that, unless, by the counsel of the city itself, they desist at the ringing of the bell before the Kalends of June, they will endeavour to take six hundred pounds from those churches.

Accordingly, although we sincerely love in the Lord the people of that city, as a people who particularly belongs to us, we nevertheless neither wish nor ought to allow their presumption in these matters to remain unpunished, lest, if ecclesiastical severity against them should prove weak or lax, others may be given an occasion for wrongdoing. We have therefore commanded our venerable brother, . . . Bishop of Piacenza, that, unless the aforesaid consuls promptly determine to desist from so criminal a design, as we have commanded them, he shall pronounce ecclesiastical censure against the consuls themselves and a sentence of interdict upon the whole city, excepting penitence and the baptism of infants.

[Col. 1456A] Wherefore, by apostolic writ we command your brotherhood to hold valid and firm the sentence which the aforesaid bishop shall pronounce against them on this account, and, insofar as lies in your power, to cause it to be inviolably observed, strictly forbidding your parishioners to presume for any reason to make any contract or commercial transaction with those Piacenzans.

Given at the Lateran, 28 March, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXXXIX. Privilege for the church of Thienen—he confirms to it the grants made by Archdeacon Albert. (Lateran, 30 March.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 992.]

[Col. 1456B] CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the provost and canons of the church of Thienen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although by the obligation of the office entrusted to us we ought, not without reason, to be solicitous for the tranquillity of all, yet a greater concern for maintaining the liberty of churches rightly moves us to solicitude, so that through the foresight of our disposition they may receive increase both temporally and spiritually, and that things well ordered and arranged within them may not be lost to them, but may be strengthened by the safeguard of apostolic confirmation. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, assenting to your petitions, we hold ratified the canonical ordering and disposition of that church, and its reasonable constitutions; and whatever has been conferred upon you and upon your church [Col. 1456C] by our beloved son Albert, archdeacon of Liège, son of the noble Duke of Louvain, as you justly and without dispute possess it, we confirm to you, and through you to your church, by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of the present writing, decreeing that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone shall presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXL. Privilege for the Church of Radesdorf.  
*(Lateran, May 25.)*

[DRONKE, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 412.]

[Col. 1456D]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CONRAD, provost of Saint John the Baptist at Radesdorf, and his brethren, both present and those canonically to be appointed in the future, in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that the effect sought by just petitioners be granted, especially where the piety assists and truth does not abandon the wishes of those who ask. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint John [Col. 1457A] the Baptist and Saint Cecilia at Radesdorf, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of the present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these, we have judged the following to be expressly named.

The site itself on which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Lawrence at Ussine, with the village itself and all its appurtenances; [Col. 1457B] Doftaha, Ingimaristat, Sulaha with their appurtenances; Geitinstat, Isileibes, Negilstete, with their appurtenances; Melre; Cledistete with all its appurtenances; Datinberch, Serlinges, Gozoldesdorf, Haselaha, together with the other villages and appurtenances of all the aforesaid villages.

Moreover, we hold ratified the liberties and immunities of your cloister courts, as well as the ancient and reasonable customs granted to your church and hitherto observed, and decree that they remain unimpaired in future times. By apostolic authority we likewise prohibit your advocate, whoever he may be at the time, from presuming to burden the place itself or its dependencies, or to harass them with any undue exactions, whether in the forests and woods [Col. 1457C] or in the newly cleared lands of your church; rather, he shall be content with those things granted to him in ancient times and belonging to his lawful jurisdiction.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved whole and intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, [Col. 1457D] does not amend his offence by due satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to divine vengeance at the last judgment.

But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1190 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1458A], and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### CXLI. He receives under protection the convent of Saint Cosmas at Tagliacozzo, and confirms its possessions and rights.  
*(Lateran, June 4.)*

[GATTULA, *Supplementum Historiae Cassinensis*, vol. II, p. 803.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ AUDOISA, abbess of the monastery of Saint Cosmas at Tagliacozzo, and her sisters, both present and those who shall in future profess the regular life, in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which is recognized as consonant with religion and honour, it becomes us to grant it with willing heart and to give suitable support [Col. 1458B] to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions, and, after the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of blessed memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of the present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and to those who succeed you. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named:

[Col. 1458C] The church of Saint Vitus with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint John of Camerata with its appurtenances; the right which you possess in the church of Saint Andrew at Clereto; half the offerings made in the churches and castles of Tagliacozzo on the feasts of Easter and the Nativity of the Lord, and half the offerings of the dead; the burial of the principal persons of the said castle; the burial-place of Podius Bufara, with half the offerings of the dead; the tithes of the mills in the valley of Saints Cosmas and Damian; and, in its river-bed, thirty sowing-modii of land; vineyards, lands, woods, houses, and small dwellings which you possess in the aforesaid castle; two mills; twenty-two feet of land, from which the men [Col. 1458D] of your monastery hold fiefs; the church of Saint Mary of Sorbo with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Cecilia with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Giles with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Nicholas with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter with its appurtenances, outside the aforesaid castle; the church of Saint John of Camerata on the hill of Palanga; and whatever you possess in the church of Saint Andrew.

Further, holding ratified and firm the renunciation promised before our aforesaid predecessor, which the noble Bartholomew of Tagliacozzo made, in the presence of many persons, concerning the evil customs which he exacted from your monastery, we prohibit by apostolic authority the said Bartholomew or his heirs from presuming at any time to enforce those customs upon [Col. 1459A] the monastery. We also decree that no bishop of the Marsi may exercise any jurisdiction over the same church, its nuns, or its clerics. Nor may any bishop or legate, unless specially sent from our side or that of our successor, under pretext of his legation burden you, your successors, your church, your men, or the servants dwelling in your church with any sentence of interdict or excommunication. No one, except the Roman pontiff or a legate sent from his side with our special mandate, may bind the nuns of your house or its clerics with the bond of excommunication or interdict. No bishop or other person may impose new or undue exactions upon your churches—especially the church of Saint Mary [Col. 1459B] of Sorbo, which is your own property—or exercise there procurations, tallages, or demands contrary to the ancient and reasonable custom hitherto observed there.

Furthermore, we grant you permission to redeem from lay hands the tithes belonging to your churches and to acquire them by any reasonable means available to you, prohibiting anyone from receiving those tithes from a lay hand without your consent.

We further decree that within the bounds of your parishes no one may build or erect a church, chapel, or altar opposite an altar without the consent of the diocesan bishop and yourselves, without prejudice, however, to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. [Col. 1459C] Moreover, none of your sisters or clerics, after making profession in that place, may leave the cloister through any frivolity without permission of her abbess; and no one may dare retain a departing person without letters of the community guaranteeing the matter. It shall, however, be lawful for the abbess then in office to pronounce the regular sentence against any one of her sisters who, without your knowledge or against your will, has departed from your church and, after a second or third warning, contemptuously refuses to return to the monastery.

The church of Saint Peter, situated in the castle called Falliacozzo, and its chaplains, shall remain in the same liberty which it possessed in ancient times and is known to possess now. We likewise will that the chapel of Saint Giles situated there remain in the same [Col. 1459D] liberty; also, half of the mill of John Frocta, which Lady Abbess Aduisa purchased from Lord Philip of Saint Donatus; half the wood at the head of the water; and the wood of the hill of Coci.

When there is a general interdict of the land, it shall be lawful for you to celebrate the divine offices in your monastery, behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a low voice. We further decree that abbesses in office may not diminish lands, churches, other possessions, or goods of your church without the common consent of your chapter, or of its greater and sounder part; nor may they henceforth give anything personally or in perpetuity as a benefice or precaria, or alienate it in any manner.

[Col. 1460A] We also forbid any of your nuns, clerics, or lay brothers to stand surety for anyone without permission of the chapter—or even the abbess herself to do so. If anyone does so, neither your church nor any of your places shall be bound by that suretyship. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, without any contradiction or appeal, from whatever bishop you choose: whether called by you to your church, or lawfully celebrating in his own church or another’s, provided that he is Catholic and enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, as has hitherto been observed.

[Col. 1460B] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, let all things be preserved unimpaired and whole, to benefit in every way those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the due right and reverence of the monastery of Cassino. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, shall rashly attempt to act against it, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct this presumption by due satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the wrong committed; let him be excluded from [Col. 1460C] the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment.

But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano, have subscribed. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark, [Col. 1460D] have subscribed. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mary, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia, have subscribed. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherds at Saint Pudentiana, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, John Felix, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. [Col. 1461A] I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the second day before the Nones of June, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1190 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Clement III.

### CXLII. Privilege for the Church of Trier.  
*(Lateran, June 4.)*

[GUENTHER, *Codex diplomaticus*, I, 470.]

[Col. 1461B]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son JOHN, elect of Trier, and his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The ineffable providence of Majesty has placed us in the eminence of the Apostolic See and entrusted to us the governance and care of all churches, in order that we may usefully provide for His body, which is the Church, and that we ought more attentively to uphold our brothers, the bishops, and the other prelates of churches in their rights. For they cannot truly be solicitous for the salvation of those subject to them and the governance of their subjects, nor can they apply themselves [Col. 1461C] more effectively to the fulfilment of their office, unless they perceive that we bestow more abundant honour upon them and love them with a more sincere affection of charity.

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, concurring with favourable assent in your just petitions, we deem your person and the Church of Trier, over which by God’s authority you are recognized to preside, to be under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves by a special prerogative. We confirm by apostolic authority to you and your successors, and fortify by the privilege of the present writing, all the dignities, honours, and liberties granted to that church by our predecessors John XIII, Benedict VII, Leo IX, Victor II, Innocent, Eugenius, and Adrian, Roman pontiffs of blessed memory, or by emperors or kings.

[Col. 1461D] We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors; namely, the church of Logenstein, the castle of Muncler, and the castle called Tris, with its ban and appurtenances, which the noble Count Otto is known to have granted to the aforesaid church with the assent and will of his wife Gertrude, Countess Palatine. We further decree that, as was ordained in the holy Council of Chalcedon, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. [Col. 1462A] I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd at Saint Pudentiana. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Tusculum. [Col. 1462B] I, John Felix, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Soffridus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Aquino [Col. 1462C].

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the second day before the Nones of June, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1190 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### CXLIII. At the request of Richard, king of the English, he entrusts the office of legate to William, bishop of Ely.  
*(Lateran, June 5.)*

[RALPH OF DICETO, *Imagines Historiarum*, in TWYSDEN, *Historiae Anglicanae Scriptores*, I, 656.]

CLEMENT, pope, to WILLIAM, bishop, greeting.

In accordance with the commendable desire and salutary petition of our dearest son in the Lord Richard, illustrious king of the English, [Col. 1462D] we have judged that the office of legate should be committed to your brotherhood by apostolic authority throughout all England and Wales, both within the archbishopric of Canterbury and that of York, and in those parts of Ireland in which the noble John, count of Mortain, brother of the same king, exercises jurisdiction and lordship.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of June, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXLIV. He receives the Carthusian brethren under protection and confirms their possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, June 6.)*

[*Privileges of the Carthusian Order*, fol. 3.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1463A] sons, the prior and Carthusian brethren, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the perfumes of virtue and the fragrance of saints, the balm of the reputation of your way of life is distinguished to us by its own scent. Since it separates itself from worldly vanity through stricter observances and shines with the splendid glory of merits, it deserves all the more honour from us. Care must also be taken more diligently and precautions adopted, lest the wickedness of anyone be able to disturb your holy peace.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by your humble supplication, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves your house with all its appurtenances and all the goods which you now reasonably possess, or which may hereafter be granted to you by pious donation or which you may acquire by other lawful means. [Col. 1463B] We fortify it by the protection of the present writing, decreeing that all shall remain secure and unimpaired to you, and that no one may unlawfully trouble you concerning them. We further strictly prohibit by apostolic authority new and undue exactions from being demanded of you by anyone, cleric or layman.

Moreover, by the present letters we grant that, whenever clerics or laymen decide to enter the way of life of your order, you may freely receive them with our permission, and retain them after they have made profession among you, saving nevertheless the privileges obtained from the Apostolic See concerning this matter. But if any privileged person, after the brethren have learned of the house from which he departed, remains among you for a year without being claimed [Col. 1463C], he may thereafter neither leave your order nor be forcibly recalled from it.

Likewise, for consecrations of churches and ordinations of clerics, if you do not have access to your own bishop or he refuses, when asked, to provide what he ought, you may request these from whatever bishop you choose; at your request he may come to your churches and, relying upon our authority, provide you with the sacred things necessary. You, beloved son prior, may also compel by sentence of excommunication those who, whether on behalf of the relief of the Holy Land or for any other causes, take occasions for wandering away from your order, if after warning they do not resolve to abandon that intention.

[Col. 1463D] Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our concession and constitution, or rashly oppose it. But if anyone shall presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXLV. He commends the Carthusian Order to archbishops and bishops.  
*(Lateran, June 6.)*

[Ibid., fol. 3b.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brothers, archbishops and bishops, [Col. 1464A] to whom these letters shall come, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since we hold our beloved sons, the Carthusian brethren, very dear and acceptable because of the merit of their religious life, we desire the mandate which we issue on their behalf to be carried out all the more effectively because those who persecute them on any pretext more grievously offend our Creator. Therefore, by apostolic letters we command and order your whole body that, if anyone presumes to act against the privileges granted to these brethren and, having been admonished, perhaps refuses to amend his conduct, you shall restrain him by ecclesiastical censure, notwithstanding any contradiction or appeal. Thus, through your diligence, those brethren may enjoy due peace; and you may appear worthy of commendation before God and men through zeal for justice and the aid of piety, notwithstanding any letters obtained from the Apostolic See through concealed fraud.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXLVI. He grants the priors and brethren of the Carthusian Order that “no prior or brother may have leave to appeal without the consent of his house’s chapter.”  
*(Lateran, June 7.)*

[Ibid.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all priors and brethren of the Carthusian [Col. 1464C] Order, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you are separated from all agitations of worldly tumults not only in mind and profession but also in places and dwellings, you must take the greatest care lest, for the sake of some temporal advantage, you again plunge yourselves into the storms of the world contrary to the purpose of your order; and lest, deceiving yourselves under the appearance of right, you rashly involve yourselves in litigious disputes in order to acquire temporal benefit or avoid temporal inconvenience.

Accordingly, desiring also to provide for your peace and tranquillity, we firmly prohibit any of your priors or brethren, on any rash presumption, from having leave to appeal without the consent and will of the chapter of his house, or of its greater and sounder part.

Moreover, whenever it happens that you celebrate your general chapter, as you are accustomed to do annually, if all are perhaps unable to assemble, whatever shall reasonably and prudently be ordained by the prior major of the order with the counsel of its greater and sounder part shall be held ratified and firm, and shall be observed without objection by all brethren of your order.

Therefore no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our prohibition or rashly oppose it. But if anyone shall presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed [Col. 1465A] apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CXLVII. He confirms two altars to the monastery of Eiham.  
*(Lateran, June 17.)*

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, IV, 29.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Eiham, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting that we readily grant assent to the just desires of petitioners, and, by bringing them to effect, fulfil requests which do not depart from the path of reason. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, concurring with favourable assent in your just [Col. 1465B] petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority to your devotion, and fortify by the protection of the present writing, the altar in the church of Roesbeke in the diocese of Thérouanne and the altar of Dorna in the diocese of Cambrai, which you have canonically acquired and justly possess without dispute.

No person whatsoever, therefore, may infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly oppose it. But if anyone shall presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the third year of our [Col. 1465C] pontificate.

### CXLVIII. He confirms the peace reconciled between the canons of Saints Vincent and Alexander of Bergamo.  
*(Lateran, June 21.)*

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IV, 472.]

CLEMENT, to his beloved sons ALDERAD, archdeacon, OBERTO, provost, and all the clerics of the Church of Bergamo, greeting, etc.

Things which, after discord and controversy between parties, have been settled by friendly concord through the adoption of better counsel ought, in accordance with the reasonable will of those who ask, [Col. 1465D] to be fortified by the authority of the Apostolic See, so that they may obtain inviolable stability and no one may in future presume rashly to oppose them. Therefore, assenting to your just petitions, we confirm by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of the present writing, the peace and concord and union of your college, prudently conceived between you, unanimously received, and committed to writing, as it was reasonably made, received, and preserved, with the assent of our brethren.

For greater security, we have judged that the text of the document itself should be inserted word for word: “In the name of Christ, in the year of the Lord 1190, on a certain day,” etc. See Ughelli, in the place cited.

We therefore decree that no person, etc. Amen.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 1466A] I, Albinus, bishop of Albano. I, Octavian, bishop of Ostia and Velletri, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark, have subscribed. I, Pandulf, cardinal-priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, have subscribed. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of Saint Peter in Chains, of the title of Eudoxia, have subscribed. I, Jordan, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd at Saint Pudentiana, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. [Col. 1466B] I, John Felix, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Susanna, have subscribed. I, James, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, have subscribed. I, Gratian, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian, have subscribed. I, Soffridus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Bernard, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary Nova, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Aquiro, have subscribed.

[Col. 1466C] Given at the Lateran through the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of the chancellor, on the ninth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1190 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

### CXLIX. Bull of the canonization of Blessed Malachy.  
*(Lateran, July 6.)*

[*Works of Saint Bernard*, ed. 1719, I, 697.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, all abbots assembling at the Cistercian chapter, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our Redeemer willed that the most holy Roman Church should be the head and teacher of all the faithful, so that, divine grace going before, those things which are everywhere to be done by the faithful may be ordered according to its disposition and command; errors may be corrected for the better; recourse may be had to its counsel in doubtful matters; and no one, however much he may glory in his merits, may alter what it has established. Otherwise, if indiscriminate liberty were granted to everyone to carry out whatever came to mind according to his own will, confused freedom—since persons’ vows differ according to their wills—would at times, without the balancing judgment of justice, suppress what ought to be commended to the scandal of others, and celebrate less worthy things with undeserved praise.

Accordingly, our beloved son Jordan, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd at Saint Pudentiana, at the request of some among you, took care devoutly to present to us the life of a certain holy man named [Col. 1467A] Malachy, who rests in the Lord at Clairvaux, written first by Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, together with the miracles which the Lord deigned to perform through him for the manifestation of his merits, supported by the testimony of many of your order, so that we might publicly declare to all, by apostolic authority, what the Church ought to judge concerning his merits.

Therefore, having seen the testimonies of so great men, and having diligently examined both his life and miracles, and moved also by the prayers and testimony of that cardinal, our beloved son the abbot of Casamari, and very many others, to whom we believed full credit should be given, we have judged, with the common counsel of our brethren, that the said holy man Malachy should be enrolled in the catalogue of saints. Through his merits we decree that the aid of the Redeemer, together with the intercessions of the other saints, should be sought by Christ’s faithful. We therefore will that your whole order and other faithful persons, by permission of the Apostolic See, devoutly render him the reverence due to saints and confidently enroll him among their number.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of July, in the third year of our pontificate.

### CL.

Clement III, in letters issued at Viterbo on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the third year of his pontificate, thus addresses the people of Fleury:

[Col. 1467C] “…desiring that the church of your monastery, dedicated in honour of Saint Benedict, may be frequented with fitting honours, to all Christ’s faithful who are truly penitent and have confessed, and who visit that church on the feast-day of the same saint and on his translations, etc.”

And he grants one hundred days of indulgence.

[SAUSSEY, *Annals of the Church of Orléans*, 201.]

### CLI. He receives the Church of the Holy Cross of Guingamp under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, September 1.)*

[MORICE, *Memoirs Serving the History of Brittany*, I, 717.]

[Col. 1467D]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JODOIN, abbot of the Church of the Holy Cross of Guingamp, and its brethren, both present and those who shall in future profess the religious life, in perpetual remembrance.

Pious petitions ought … to be fulfilled by bringing them to effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth more praiseworthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire force. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ the Lord, we willingly assent to your just petitions, and, following the example of our predecessors Innocent and Alexander, Roman [Col. 1468A] pontiffs of blessed memory, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of the Holy Cross of Guingamp, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of the present writing.

First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order recognized as instituted in that church according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Further, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God granting, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have judged the following to be expressly named:

[Col. 1468B] The place itself in which the aforesaid church is situated, with all its appurtenances; the land lying beside the river Trieux, with the borough and the other things pertaining to it; the church of St. Mandet near Guingamp, with three estates of land; half the tithe of the whole parish of Plomagor; four mills on the Trieux, given by Countess Havis; nine estates of Rivallon, free from every service; two measures of bread daily, which were given by . . .; half the mill of Colel before the count’s motte, given by Count Stephen; a fifth part of the estate of Sulbar with its meadow; half the estate of Guidamori, given by Geoffrey the steward; a third part of the estate of St. Mary of Lesquilli, which [Col. 1468C] Rogus gave, and a fourth part of the same estate, given by Count Stephen; the land between two streams which had belonged to Quiniou, son of Kaermaroc, given by Dongualus, son of Markoet; the church of Christ at Pleian with its appurtenances; the land of Corle and three arpents of land, given by Yvon, son of Conec; beside the borough of Holy Cross, the tithe of Porhic; the countess’s house by the Redon gate, which the countess gave; two mills of Chostella within Guingamp, given by the countess; the meadow and land on the south side of the stream that flows into the Trieux beside the Motte; the market-dues of Guingamp castle, given by Count Stephen; the island called Guirguenis; the church of St. Quirinus, situated in the wood called Meuc; half [Col. 1468D] the mill of Choesel, called the mill of Louhen; one mill on the Trieux at the place called the Rock of Suhart, given by Count Stephen; one mill of Chosel on the western side of the Trieux, above the borough of Holy Cross; three marks of silver in England, given by Count Stephen from the tithe held by Eudo, priest of Lambolia; and the church of Blessed Mary Magdalene near Montcontour, with all its appurtenances; four arpents of meadow beside the mill of Locon, given by Hamo son of Walter; and likewise two arpents of meadow beside your mill of Choesel, which the countess gave to your church; moreover four arpents of arable land between your church and Guingamp, [Col. 1469A] which the often-mentioned countess bestowed upon your church for planting a vineyard. The chapel of St. Geranus of Telerna and the island with its appurtenances; the chapel of Portal with its appurtenances; the church of St. Gildas of Ploetmagoer; the great estate of Tremeler Pordic with its appurtenances. We likewise decree that the people belonging to your Church of the aforesaid place of Holy Cross shall not be compelled to pay any undue or unlawful exactions or forced services.

Certainly, no one shall presume to demand or extort tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or on the produce of your animals. You may receive for protection clerics or laymen living in the world who are free and absolved, [Col. 1469B] and retain them without any objection. Furthermore, we forbid any of your brethren, after making profession in the same place, to leave it without the permission of his abbot, except for the sake of embracing a stricter religious life; and no one may dare retain one who departs without letters of authorization from the community. When a general interdict is in force, you may celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated and interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. We also decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted; the rights, however, of those churches [Col. 1469C] from which the bodies of the dead are taken being preserved. . . .

Upon the death of yourself, now abbot of the same place, or of any one of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any cunning of intrusion or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the greater and sounder part of the brethren, shall determine is to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of St. Augustine.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things remain entire for the benefit in every way of those for whose [Col. 1469D] governance they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, etc.

I, Clement, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Peter, cardinal-priest of St. Peter in Chains, etc.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Moses, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting as vice-chancellor, on the Kalends of September, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1190 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III.

## CLII. To the Abbot of St. Geneviève, the Dean, and the Cantor of Paris, concerning a prebend in the church of Meaux, founded by P[eter], formerly bishop of Tusculum, which is to be preserved according to the founder’s intention. (Lateran, October 17.)

[DU PLESSIS, *History of Meaux*, II, 77.]

[Col. 1470A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot of St. Geneviève, the dean, and the cantor of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since P., of good memory, formerly bishop of Tusculum, had bequeathed in his last will 150 pounds of Parisian money for the establishment of a prebend in the Church of Meaux, our beloved sons the abbot of St. Victor and Master N., formerly cleric of the aforesaid bishop of Tusculum, [Col. 1470B] to whom execution of the will had been entrusted both by the testator himself and by the Apostolic See, duly presented to our venerable brother the bishop and beloved sons of the chapter of Meaux a person for the title of the said prebend. They further ordained that whoever should obtain that prebend in the course of succession should be accounted a canon in choir and chapter with the same fullness of dignity and honour enjoyed by the other canons established of old; and that, after the death of that person, the church of St. Mary of Cagia should hold the revenues of that prebend for one year, without diminution, as it did those of the other prebends. But because certain persons were scheming, according to their own will, to prevent his being accounted a canon, while the aforesaid executors were unwilling to alter the stated arrangement on account of their opposition, letters on this matter came to us at the request of the aforesaid bishop and canons. And while the case was pending, etc. . . . You, having regard to the testator’s final will and unwilling that so great a benefit should henceforth be impeded by anyone’s cunning, approved the aforesaid arrangement in both points on which the dispute had long continued; and, confirming it by our authority, decreed that he should always be a canon with the fullness of dignity and honour enjoyed by the other canons established of old, and that the aforesaid church of Cagia should, upon the death of the holder, be bound to receive in full for one year the annual fruits of this prebend, as it does from the other prebends.

[Col. 1470D] Therefore, holding valid what you have done in this matter on reasonable grounds, etc. . . .

Given at the Lateran, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the third year of our pontificate.

## CLIII. Bull confirming the possessions of the church of St. Mary the Gilded at Toulouse. (Lateran, October 19.)

[Gallia Christiana, XIII, 26.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons B., prior, and the brethren of the church of Blessed Mary the Gilded: greeting and apostolic blessing.

A pious request should be followed by an effective fulfillment, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth more praiseworthily [Col. 1471A] and the requested benefit may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, giving grateful assent to your just petitions and considering the devotion which you are known to bear toward Blessed Peter and ourselves, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own your persons, together with all ecclesiastical and temporal goods which you now laudably possess or may hereafter, by God’s help, acquire by just means. In particular, we confirm to you and your church by apostolic authority, and strengthen by the protection of this present writing, the church of St. Mary Dealbata, the church of St. Peter and St. Martin, the church of St. Nicholas, the chapel of St. James, the chapel of St. Mary in the house of Branhanon, the church of St. Martial, the church of St. John of Savignac, the church [Col. 1471B] of St. Eleutherius, the church of St. John of Gorionis, the church of St. Amantius, the church of St. Peter of Quinto, the church of St. Salvius of Dalbs, the church of St. Sulpicius of Cella, and the church of St. Mary of Salvenes with their appurtenances, as you possess them justly and without dispute. We decree that, if you perceive yourselves to be burdened in any matter, you may freely appeal to the Apostolic See. Therefore no person whatsoever may rashly disturb your persons or goods, infringe this page of our confirmation and protection, or dare presumptuously to oppose it. But whoever presumes to attempt this shall know that he incurs the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter [Col. 1471C] and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the third year of our pontificate.

## CLIV. He grants the use of gloves to the provost of St. Mary’s, Magdeburg.

[LUDEWIG, *Reliquiae manuscriptorum*, II, 407.]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the provost of the church of Blessed Mary at Magdeburg.

Raised by the providence of divine appointment to the governance of the universal Church, we ought so to administer the ministry of the stewardship entrusted to us that the eyes of the Apostolic See may watch over the welfare and advancement of each person, and may especially urge toward the observance of good works those who strive under the regular discipline to render holy service to the Lord. Since the church entrusted to you by N., archbishop of Magdeburg of blessed memory, has by God’s grace been formed according to regular institutions, and canonical rigor and the regular observance of discipline have hitherto flourished there laudably through the Lord’s action, and since by its fragrance of praiseworthy integrity several churches have been founded in those regions, it especially behooves your care to guard against—may it never happen!—the purity of that religious life growing cold at the prompting of the enemy of humankind, and fraternal [Col. 1472A] charity and the observance of religion among you suffering loss in your time. Therefore, we earnestly admonish and exhort your discretion in the Lord, and by the authority of these presents enjoin you continually to stretch yourself toward the things that are before, to pursue the office of the administration you have undertaken with vigilant care, to instruct and exhort your subjects by wholesome admonitions, to correct what needs correcting, to build and to plant, so that God may be honoured in your actions and, through your diligence, vices may be cut away and the shoots of virtues propagated not only in your own church but also in the others transplanted from it, and likewise in all the houses of your order throughout Saxony, which by right ought to look to you.

The censure of the Apostolic See has customarily adapted its indulgence to the needs [Col. 1472B] and poverty of subjects, so that it, which is bound to provide for all, may seem to neglect neither anyone’s circumstances nor merits. Therefore, favourably following the report of your good conduct, we effectively comply with your desire and grant you the continual use of gloves, so that the hands which you have spiritually devoted to sacred uses may not be defiled by the touch of any impurity, but may be kept undefiled from heat and frost by the protection of a continuous covering, etc.

## CLV. He receives the monastery of St. Denis of Nogent under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.

[Bullarium Cluniacense, 92.]

[Col. 1472C]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons SIMON, prior of the monastery of St. Denis of Nogent, and its brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, forever.

It is fitting readily to give assent to religious desires, so that the devotion of the faithful may obtain a swift result and may apply itself all the more willingly to the observance of holy religion and to other good works when it feels itself graciously supported by the Apostolic See in its pious and blessed undertaking. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, granting favourable assent to your just petitions, we receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and our own, following the example of our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory, the aforesaid monastery of St. Denis of Nogent, in which you are devoted [Col. 1472D] to the Lord’s service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by God’s help, through the grants of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to state the following by their proper names:

The church of Blessed Hilary of Nogent, with its chaplaincies and appurtenances; the borough of St. Denis, free and exempt from every jurisdiction and exaction [Col. 1473A] of anyone; ovens; the fishery in the same town; mills; the wood of Croisillis; firewood from the count’s woods and timber for repairs to their own houses; the peasants around the water of Edulia and beyond the water, with their own homesteads; the tithe of the toll of the same castle; and, in all these matters, full lordship over the burgesses and peasants, except judicial combat; the church of St. Mary of Margon; two modii at Arcies; the church of Pierre-Fixe; the church of St. Martin of Brunelles; the church of Champ-Rond; the chapel of St. Mary Magdalene of Perraria; the church of Cidroerillo; the church of St. Andrew of Fretiniac; the church of St. Albin of the other Champ-Rond; the church of St. Peter of Harponvillier with its appurtenances; the church of St. Hilary of [Col. 1473B] Bellonville; the church of St. Anastasia of Nonvillier; the church of St. Martin of Universio with its appurtenances; the chapel of Oroneo; the church of Flacciac with its appurtenances; a house in the city of Chartres and all that you reasonably possess there; peasants at Roemville and whatever else you canonically possess in the parish of Chartres; the church of St. Peter of Bosvillette with its appurtenances, situated in the same parish; the church of St. Peter of Cetone, with its borough, mills, oven, peasants, and appurtenances; the church of St. Vulphacius with its appurtenances, and whatever you possess in the diocese of Le Mans; the church of St. Martin of Berzelis; the church of St. Peter of Brueria; the church of St. Owen [Col. 1473C] of Verreries; the church of St. Martin of Beloup with its appurtenances; the church of Gimagiis; the church of St. Mary of Bure; the church of Fadentivilla near Mauritania, with a certain portion of the tithe; the tithe of Burethe; the church of St. Peter and St. John of Mannis with an arpent of meadow; tithes at Cerbon; the church of Comblou; tithes at Corgon; the church of St. Martin of Loisel; the church of St. Praescetus; the church of St. Gervasius of Fannis; the church of St. Germanus of Loscio, with its chaplains and appurtenances—that is, the church of Blessed Mary, the church of St. Maentius, and the church of St. John—which are situated in the castle of Mauritania.

[Col. 1473D] The tithe of the toll of Mauritania with its oven; the tithe of pannage from Resnou, and firewood from the same wood and repair-timber for the houses of the monks of Loscio; whatever right you have in the church of St. Hilary beside St. Cerona; the tithe of Fesvallo; the tithe at Ortum Robur; the tithe at Lineroles; the tithe of Corbeon; and whatever right you possess in the parish of Sées, in cemeteries, first-fruits, burgesses, mills, fields, meadows, or other possessions—we confirm to you by the authority of the Apostolic See. You may also elect priests in your churches and present them to the diocesan bishop; if they are suitable, they shall receive the care of souls from him freely and without any improper payment, render him an account of their pastoral care, [Col. 1474A] and show you due subjection in temporal matters. Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbid any archbishop or bishop to pronounce a sentence of interdict or excommunication upon the aforesaid monastery or upon you, to exact any customary payments there, impose his hand on it for any cause of burden, or celebrate public masses or stations without your consent, so that, secure from every harassment of secular service and removed from every burden of worldly oppression, you may, by God’s permission, remain diligent and undisturbed in the observance of holy religion.
