But if violence should happen to be committed in your court, whether by shedding blood, insulting speech, or anything of that kind, the church should by no means on that account be prohibited [Col. 1474B] from divine offices.

We hold valid, and decree shall remain unimpaired in future times, the liberties and immunities, together with the ancient and reasonable customs, granted to your monastery and hitherto observed. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars and churches, the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide them to you freely and without any improper payment. Otherwise, you may approach any Catholic bishop whom you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. Furthermore, we decree that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated; the rights, however, of the churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken being preserved. The tithes of your churches held by laymen, if reverence for your religious order can, according to God, remove them from lay control, you may possess for the support of yourselves and the poor. We also command that all your churches, chapels, and cemeteries shall be exempt from every exaction, except the bishop’s customary procuration and his jurisdiction over priests [Col. 1474D] if they offend against the dignity of their order. We also forbid anyone within the boundaries of your parishes to presume to build a church or oratory without your consent, save only the privileges of the Roman pontiffs. We further decree that gifts and alienations illegally made within the past forty years from the possessions of your chapter and your houses, without the consent of that chapter or of its greater and sounder part, shall lawfully be revoked; and by apostolic authority we forbid their being made in such a manner hereafter.

We also confirm that the brethren of your cells, wherever situated, shall not suffer suspension of divine offices on account of any interdict or excommunication; rather, the monks themselves, [Col. 1475A] their servants, and those who have devoted themselves to monastic observance shall, with the church doors closed, [lacuna], with [persons] not admitted, celebrate the offices of divine service and perform the rites due for burial. We also grant you the right to receive, at your houses, laypersons or secular clerics who are free and absolved, unless they are excommunicated for specified crimes, for conversion or burial. No bishop shall have power to impose any burden or annoyance upon you in respect of your altars and churches; rather, whatever rights you have held in them, you shall hold canonically in the future. We also prohibit anyone from selling, otherwise alienating, or pledging as security the lands, other possessions, and treasures of your churches, or from standing surety for any of your brethren, without the consent of your chapter or its greater and sounder part; and if this is done, we decree it void. [Col. 1475B] Moreover, desiring henceforth to provide for your peace and tranquillity with paternal concern, we forbid by apostolic authority anyone within the enclosures of your houses, granges, or cemeteries to dare commit violence, theft, or sacrilege; set fire; seize or kill a person; or rashly injure anyone.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery and places subject to it, take away their possessions, rashly retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with any vexations; but let all be preserved whole for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the reverence due to the monastery of Cluny, to which it is spiritually subject. If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to violate this page of our constitution, etc.

## CLVI. He confirms for Maurice, bishop of Paris, this privilege: whenever the deanery is vacant, he is to receive its revenue.

[THEODORE’S *Penitential*, II, 640.]

CLEMENT TO MAURICE, bishop of Paris.

From an authenticated document exhibited to us, [Col. 1475D] we have learned that, when the dispute that had arisen between you and the canons of your church concerning the receipt of the revenues of the deanery during a vacancy had been entrusted by our predecessor Pope Alexander of happy memory to our venerable brother, the archbishop of Reims, cardinal of St. Sabina and then archbishop of Sens, the dean, cantor, and many canons of the same church met, within the day assigned to you and the canons by that archbishop, in your new house, in the archbishop’s presence. They confessed before the aforesaid archbishop that they had entirely renounced that case, had placed it at your discretion, and had jointly caused all the other canons in full chapter to do the same. [Col. 1476A] Therefore, wishing that no litigation may henceforth be improperly stirred up in this matter, we hold valid and confirm by apostolic authority the renunciation of those disputes, voluntarily made by your chapter before the aforesaid archbishop, hitherto observed, and contained in the document made about it by that archbishop; decreeing that no person whatsoever, etc.

## CLVII. At the request of Maurice, bishop of Paris, he orders the observance of the agreement concluded between Stephen, formerly bishop, and Theobald, archdeacon.

[THEODORE’S *Penitential*, II, 718, where the reader is referred to the privileges of Eugenius III and Alexander III granted on the same matter to the bishop of Paris. See *Patrologia*, vols. CLXXX and CC.]

## CLVIII. He writes to Maurice, bishop of Paris, that he is astonished that the archbishop of Sens sends the bishop’s parishioners “without his knowledge or request, to other judges, and sometimes even sets aside the determination of his own judgment.” He grants “that he may declare a sentence promulgated in this way void by operation of law, subject to appeal, and forbid the parishioners to answer before judges so appointed.”

[THEODORE’S *Penitential*, II, 563.]

[Col. 1476B]

CLEMENT TO MAURICE, bishop.

Since the authority of the canons makes clear what is owed to archbishops by metropolitan right, and since it is written that no one shall usurp another’s boundaries, we regard it as astonishing and quite blameworthy that our venerable brother the archbishop of Sens sends certain parishioners subject to your jurisdiction to other judges without your knowledge or request, and sometimes even overturns the determination of his own judgment. Since, indeed, this is found forbidden by canonical prohibition, saving the exception concerning an appeal, and since a sentence given by a judge who is not one’s own has no validity, we have thought fit by this letter to grant your brotherhood that you may declare such a sentence void by operation of law and forbid your parishioners to answer before judges appointed in this manner.

Therefore no one, etc.

## CLIX. At the request of Alfonso, king of Castile, he establishes an episcopal see in the city of Plasencia and confirms the diocese established by the king.

[FERNÁNDEZ, *History and Annals of Plasencia*, p. 23.]

[Col. 1476D]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, the illustrious ALFONSO, king of Castile: greeting and apostolic blessing.

God’s good pleasure is fulfilled in human actions when we see the hearts of princes applying themselves with all their strength to extend the worship of the divine name and crush the enemies of the Catholic faith. Hence we, who are bound by a certain hand of pastoral care to assist the pious desires of all, wish to induce them by more diligent exhortation to carry their intentions into effect, and to encourage them by granting what they request, in proportion as pious beginnings proceeding from a good intention may be hoped to reach a more praiseworthy outcome. Therefore, approving your royal intention in every respect, we establish by apostolic authority an episcopal cathedra in the city of Plasencia, which, in land acquired from the hand of the Ishmaelites by your prowess, you are known, through the prosperity granted by divine mercy, to have peopled. We also decree that the cathedral church shall have a diocese according to the royal disposition, so that the towns which, as this present writing specifies, are granted to it by your gift shall belong to it forever by diocesan right: namely Targellum, [Col. 1477B] Medelinum, Mons Fragorum, and Sanctacruz, with all their appurtenances. And so that this grant may remain whole and unimpaired in future times, we decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or dare presumptuously to oppose it. Whoever presumes to attempt this shall know that he incurs the indignation of almighty God and of his apostles, the blessed Peter and Paul.

## CLX. To Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig, he confirms the liberty which “Canute, king of Denmark, his kinsman, granted to him and his successors: that both reeves and peasants shall remain free and exempt from every burden imposed by the king or his officials; that in investigations and executions which formerly were customarily handled through royal officials they shall now answer to no one, but shall be subject to his own command; and that henceforth they shall be subject to no secular power.”

[See CYPRAEUS, *Annals of the Bishops of Schleswig*, 202.]

[Col. 1477C]

## CLXI. [Note: [Col. 1477C] Doubtful.] To Peter, abbot of Chartres. — He confirms the condemnation at Metz of charters obtained through false representation against the ancient liberty of the Church of Chartres, and confirms that church’s freedom. (Lateran, June 4.)

[MIRAEUS, *Diplomatic Works*, III, 368.]

[Col. 1478A]

CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the church of Chartres, and its brethren, present and future.

From sealed letters of Lord Stephen, bishop of Metz, and the convent of the same church, we have learned [Col. 1478B] that charters confirmed by the seals of Pope Benedict VIII, Pope Eugenius III, and the emperors Otto I and Conrad, and obtained through false representation against the ancient liberty of the Church of Chartres, have been condemned by judgment at Metz. We approve that this was done justly and canonically; we condemn forever the aforesaid charters and whatever may oppose your liberty; and we confirm, by apostolic authority and the protection of this present writing, that your church is free in every right belonging to a conventual church. We decree that no person whatsoever may dare presumptuously to oppose this confirmation.

Whoever presumes to attempt this shall be subject to divine vengeance [Col. 1478C] at the last judgment.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, in the second year of our pontificate.

[Col. 1477]

# DECREES OF POPE CLEMENT III

(MANSI, *Councils*, vol. XXII, p. 549.)

## I. To the abbot and archpriest of Montulan. — That they restore to the acolyte Gant. the benefice taken from him.

[Col. 1477D]

Know that we have received the complaint of the acolyte Gand., as did our predecessor Gregory, who is known to have written to you twice on his behalf. When G., a woman, sought him in marriage, you took occasion from this and, after an appeal had been made to the Apostolic See, deprived him less than reasonably of the benefice which he held from us. Therefore, because we are bound to grant apostolic protection to all who are unjustly burdened, we earnestly command your discretion, through apostolic letters, that, [Col. 1478D] if the matter is found to stand thus, you restore without delay to the said cleric the benefice so removed and allow him peaceably to retain it, so that he need not repeat his complaint to us. The sentence of the said abbot concerning the marriage shall not prevent him from holding the benefice, unless a care of souls is attached to it.

## II. To Odo, bishop of Veroli. — Concerning a certain marriage not to be dissolved.

We have received your letter, from whose tenor we have learned that, when the bearer of these presents had joined a certain woman to himself in marriage five years ago, and had slept with her in the same bed for three months, he was believed to have been hindered by sorcery so that he could not know her carnally. On this matter you received letters from the Apostolic See, stating that according to the custom of the Roman Church marriages of this kind were not to be separated. Therefore, having summoned them before you while they were living separately, you compelled them to return to common habitation. Although afterward they were in the same house and bed, and although the man had spoken many words to the woman, as was established to you, he nevertheless could not have carnal intercourse with her. Consequently, fearing that this same man might incur the guilt of homicide, you wished to consult us concerning what should be done in this case. Therefore, through apostolic letters, we command your discretion not to fail, for the stated reasons, [Col. 1479B] to compel the aforesaid husband and wife by ecclesiastical censure to live together.

## III. To the archbishop of Ancona. — Concerning a law established by the people of Ancona.

Furthermore, concerning that law—or error—which you say your citizens have established, namely that if anyone held for thirty years the possessions of some church and did not pay the stipulated rent, he should not on that account become liable for the rent of that possession, we can give you no certain answer until you take care to send us the constitution made by them, set out word for word.

## IV. To a certain bishop. — Concerning priests who have incurred the guilt of adultery, perjury, or false testimony.

[Col. 1479C]

From your brotherhood’s consultation we have learned that you wish to be instructed by the Apostolic See with certainty whether priests or others constituted in any sacred orders, who through a lapse of the flesh have incurred the guilt of adultery, perjury, false testimony, or have become entangled in the crime of homicide and lost the good of a right conscience, may, after performing worthy penance for what they have committed, be tolerated in their former rank or advanced to higher ones through the support of their merits. We answer your brotherhood that, if the crimes which we have mentioned are notorious or proved by due judicial process, the censure of the sacred canons does not permit such offenders, even after penance has been performed, to advance to higher ranks, but indeed commands that they shall not retain their former rank. But if the alleged crimes against someone are neither notorious nor proved by due judicial process, those who are guilty of them should be admonished and adjured under threat of divine judgment not to minister in the order they have received, lest it serve as testimony to their condemnation.

Since the most holy Roman Church, etc. And below: But others who cannot attain the honour of the priesthood because of the impediment of age—if it finds that this alone prevents them, although perhaps they ought not to have been admitted to such offices at that age—you ought patiently to tolerate without resentment [Col. 1480A] until that time. Those whom you then find qualified by the constitutions of the canons to undertake the burden of priesthood, provided nothing else prevents it, you should, by our authority, bind under the sentence of the aforesaid disciplinary measure if, after being admonished by you, they then scorn to be ordained priests.

## V. Rescript to a certain archbishop.

If a matrimonial case can be conducted through a procurator, you have thought it proper to consult us in your prudence. Here, however, we decree that a distinction must be made: if, in the matrimonial case itself, a criminal issue is being litigated, and criminal proceedings must on that account be brought by the opposing party, the matrimonial case ought to be concluded not through an intermediary but by the principal person himself, since, as the laws testify, one who is present must accuse one who is present and bind himself by the obligation of retaliation. But in a matrimonial case in which no criminal charge is involved, we believe that the procedure should be otherwise. Yet it would be safer, where the personal presence of the principals can be had, for the matter to proceed, with the persons themselves present, in both respects to the rendering of judgment.

### VI. To a certain archbishop.—On absolving those who, when summoned to judgment, refuse to come and are bound by the bond of anathema for their contumacy.

Your brotherhood has informed us that certain persons in your province, when at times summoned to judgment, disdain to come, and are bound by you or by one of your suffragans with the bond of anathema for their contumacy [Col. 1480C]. At length, returning to their senses, they offer themselves to justice and wish to confirm by the solemnity of an oath that they will obey the law. But the opposing party lodges an appeal in order that they may not be absolved from the sentence of excommunication before the case is decided. There are also others who, having been excommunicated, promise under oath to submit to justice; but after their absolution they abscond and appeal.

Concerning these matters, therefore, we have thought it necessary to answer your fraternity that the absolution of those aforesaid who received a sentence of excommunication because they refused to come to court cannot be impeded by a prohibition or appeal of the opposing party [Col. 1480D], provided that they furnish adequate and suitable security for obedience to the law. But those who promise on oath that they will submit to justice and evade it through the obstacle of an appeal may and ought to be compelled by you, unless they have pursued the appeal within a suitable time, to obey the equity of the law, as they swore.

### VII. To a certain bishop.—On consecrating an oratory.

The tenor of your letters has informed our apostolic office that a certain nobleman, C. of your diocese, having received the foundation-stone from your predecessor, built an oratory on his own estate; and when, at his request, you were ready to distinguish it with the gift of consecration, another nobleman appealed, as you believe [the text perhaps reads “he believes”], in order to prevent you from proceeding, out of hostility toward him [Col. 1481A]. Wishing, however, as befitted your brotherhood, humbly to defer to the appeal, you refrained from the consecration and fixed for him a time within which he ought to pursue the appeal. Since he has in no way pursued it, and a year has elapsed from the day of appeal, the said founder does not cease urgently to request from you the consecration of the said oratory.

Since it seems presumable that he appealed not truly for some grievance or oppression involving loss of his right, since he did not intend to proceed concerning the appeal within the time assigned to him—especially since, by common law, appellants are granted a year within which to conduct the suit individually or jointly—we, by apostolic authority, command you that, if you ascertain that matters have proceeded as the tenor of those letters states, then, when requested to do so, you shall render the aforesaid oratory illustrious with the gift of consecration, the appeal having ceased [Col. 1481B].

### VIII. To a certain bishop.—On appeals.

Although the remedy of appeal was devised for the relief of the oppressed, some clerics subject to your brotherhood, as we have learned, maliciously resort to the refuge of appeal. While they rashly evade examination by your court, it often happens [Col. 1481C] that not only they themselves but also others entirely free of such fault are drawn into secular judgment. Thus innocent persons are more extensively harassed by laymen as though they were vexatious litigants.

Therefore, wishing in pastoral concern to provide against so great an inconvenience to clerics and to take away from the laity an occasion for disparaging clerics or coercing them under their judgment, we have thought fit to answer your inquiry as follows. If a dispute involving any cleric subject to you is brought before your brotherhood, and the matter at issue is not worth forty solidi, we do not impose on you the obligation of deferring to a cleric who appeals from this matter to the Apostolic See. Rather, if you prefer, you may conclude the case without the impediment of an appeal [Col. 1481D], unless a manifest ground of suspicion against you has been shown.

### IX. To the bishop of Angers.—What has been decreed by the larger and sounder part of a council shall always prevail.

The prudence of your brotherhood, etc. And below: We have thought that the knot of the second question should be resolved by the authority of the Lateran Council: namely, that, unless something unreasonable—or, in the variant, something unreasonable indeed or less reasonable—should happen to be alleged and proved against someone, or by certain persons, whether more eminent or inferior, what has been established by the larger and sounder part of the council shall always prevail and obtain the due firmness of apostolic approval.

> [Note: Col. 1481. These words must be restored as they are read in Decree 44 below.]

Unless an ancient custom of the Church, hitherto observed and confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See, should suggest that something else is to be observed [Col. 1482A]. Thus, by the Lord’s gift, the audacity of the wicked will be restrained, and by His mercy the benefit of the Churches will be more widely extended.

### X. To the bishop of Segovia.—On Jews or Saracens converted to the Christian faith.

On your behalf we have been asked whether Jews or Saracens converted to the Christian faith may cohabit with their wives whom, while still in unbelief, they married despite being related to them in the second, third, or fourth degree; or whether, after their conversion, they may leave their wives and proceed to other marriages.

By the authority of the present letter we answer you [Col. 1482B] that converts to the faith of Christ of this kind, so long as their wives wish to remain with them, may, if they wish, retain them, whether the wives are converted or not. They are not, however, to be compelled to do so. But while those wives are alive and willing to remain, they ought not to contract marriage with others. If the wives withdraw out of hatred for the Christian faith, then, since, in the testimony of Gregory, an insult to the Creator with respect to the person who is left dissolves the right of marriage, they are not forbidden to marry others. Nor does it matter whether they contracted while related in the second or third degree when they were alien to the faith, since under the old law alone it was forbidden that they should uncover the nakedness of their sisters.

### XI. To . . . .—Reply concerning the vow of a certain count.

[Col. 1482C]

We have considered, etc. Moreover, concerning the vow which, you state, the count made—namely, that he should fast on bread and water every Friday—it does not appear that that redemption, consisting in the construction of an altar, is sufficient. For although making a vow is voluntary for everyone, vows once made must nevertheless be fulfilled lawfully as a matter of necessity. Finally, concerning what he promised for aiding the land of Jerusalem: exhort him diligently to go there himself in person, if possible; or, in fulfillment of his vow, let him supply suitable assistance to those going to Jerusalem.

### XII. To certain monks.—On churches subject to their presentation.

We could rightly be charged with too little concern [Col. 1482D] if we did not apply our attention to preserving those rights of your monastery which pertain especially to your provision [the text also reads “our provision”]. Therefore, wishing to provide with pontifical diligence for your rights and claims [the text has *justitiis*, perhaps corrupt for “claims”], we forbid by apostolic authority that anyone be ordained in churches subject to your presentation unless he has been presented by you. If anyone should be ordained without your presentation, let him be removed by you yourselves from the churches by apostolic authority, and let his ordination be held wholly void—unless perhaps, which God forbid, it is established that you maliciously delay the presentation of clerics.

### XIII. To a certain bishop.—On dissolving the marriage of a certain knight.

[Col. 1483A]

The tenor of your letters has made known to us that a certain knight, your parishioner, once swore that he would give a certain noblewoman to his son, who was of marriageable age, as wife. He gave her in marriage in the name of that son; thereafter he nourished the same daughter-in-law in his own house for more than four years. In the course of time, the wife of the said knight died; and he slept with the woman who had been given to his son, at the devil’s prompting. When this finally became public, he joined her to himself in marriage. You firmly forbade him to sleep with her any further [Col. 1483B], if he wished to provide for his own salvation.

Since you thought it proper to consult the Apostolic See concerning what ought to be done, approving your diligence, we command you by apostolic authority to forbid the aforesaid knight, under excommunication, ever again to presume to approach her carnally or dare further to have intercourse with her.

### XIV. To . . . .—On those who have contracted clandestine marriages contrary to a prohibition.

Although you are endowed with learning and competent in the matters on which you wished to consult us, yet, because in pastoral concern you seek our judgment for greater certainty [Col. 1483C], we commend your prudence in this regard and send you our reply in fulfillment of the duty of our office. Your discretion has asked us whether those who have contracted clandestine marriages contrary to a general annual prohibition, issued in your synod under excommunication, are to be separated; or whether marriages so contracted ought to be tolerated; or whether those who contract them are to be excommunicated until they have made satisfaction to the Church which they have injured.

Concerning this, we have thought it proper to answer your fraternity that, although marriages thus contracted may seem not to be marriages, the sacred canons are known to prohibit them for this reason: that if one of the contracting parties, having changed his intention, should publicly transfer himself to another vow, a judge would not be able to pronounce a sentence concerning a marriage which is uncertain [Col. 1483D]. But if the personal will of the parties concurs and lawful vows are present, although such a marriage may not have held from the beginning, it is nevertheless strengthened afterward by the subsequent lawful consent of both, and persons contracting in this way are to be tolerated unless the marriage has been accused.

But because they presumed to act against the Church’s prohibition and the general excommunication, they are to be publicly declared excommunicated by name for their contempt, until they have made satisfaction to the Church. Thereafter, with regard to the character of the persons and the time, penance is to be imposed upon them.

### XV. To the archbishop of Canterbury.—On not dissolving the marriage of the knight B.

[Col. 1484A]

From the letters of your brotherhood we have learned that the knight B. held the woman L. as his wife for twenty-five years. Now, wishing to separate from her, the said knight accused the marriage, asserting that they were related to one another in the seventh degree of consanguinity; and he stated that he would sufficiently prove this before you by suitable witnesses. He added that for this reason he had been bound by excommunication by G., your predecessor, in the first year of the marriage.

On the other hand, the said woman declared that his accusation ought not to be heard at all, because, as she said she could clearly prove [Col. 1484B], the same man had held her as his lawful wife for twenty-five years. Since you wished to consult us on this matter, we answer your inquiry as follows: if it is established to you that the said man held that woman as his lawful wife for twenty-five years, compel him, the appeal having been set aside, to keep her henceforth as his wife and to treat her with marital affection, imposing upon him by apostolic authority perpetual silence concerning the same dispute.

### XVI. To a certain bishop.—On two men who took two sisters as wives.

Our beloved son, your archpriest, informed us by his letters [Col. 1484C] that, when two men had taken two sisters as wives, one sister died without children. Her husband took another wife, by whom he fathered a son. In the course of time, the daughter of the other sister was joined in marriage to this son; and, still living with her, he has had sons and daughters by her who are still alive.

Since an unfavorable report has arisen concerning that marriage, the said archpriest sought apostolic counsel in his letters. Although the law of public decency forbids marriages of this kind, they have remained together so long that the accusers, if any appear, ought to be held suspect, since, although they were present, they are known to have remained silent through so long a period. Therefore we advise you that no accusation against that marriage is henceforth to be admitted [Col. 1484D]; rather, these persons are to be permitted to remain together, with the matter overlooked.

### XVII. To . . . .—On the marriage of H. and the woman R.

As we have learned from your letters and the tenor of the petition presented to us, a marriage between H. and the woman R. had formerly been confirmed by oath. A certain person asserted that they were related to one another by a degree of consanguinity. You therefore summoned the parish priest from whose parish the man and woman originated and strictly commanded him to investigate the truth of the matter diligently, and to order the accusers of this marriage on your behalf to appear for the accusation within the period [Col. 1485A] which that parish priest should appoint; otherwise they were not to be heard further.

Since the same accusers did not appear within the time appointed to them, the marriage was confirmed by the union of both parties. But afterward the uncle of the said girl, allegedly coveting her inheritance, came before you to accuse that marriage, bringing with him two witnesses whom the man and woman were prepared immediately to prove infamous. Since you seemed unwilling to acquiesce in their words, the same man appealed to our hearing.

Because contracted marriages must not be separated without great deliberation, nor disputes admitted against them, we command you that, if what we have stated is true [Col. 1485B], you reject as suspect the witnesses and accusers of that marriage; neither involve yourself in the matter nor permit, insofar as lies within your power, anyone else to admit them.

### XVIII. To a certain bishop.—William de Rimare ought not to divorce his second wife.

Count William de Rumaren [W. de Rimare], a nobleman and your parishioner, as you reported to us in your letters, secretly confessed to you that, after he had contracted marriage with a certain noblewoman, she, prompted by certain persons, alleged that consanguinity existed between herself and him, and sought a divorce through Richard, formerly archbishop of Canterbury [Col. 1485C]. Although the said count believed that no line of consanguinity connected her with himself, yet, resentfully bearing that his wife had despised him, he kept silent though he could have objected, and did not appeal to the Apostolic See [another reading: “did not wish to appeal”].

After the consanguinity had been proved and a divorce obtained by judgment of the Church, the said woman married a certain nobleman, while William himself joined another woman to himself in marriage. But, as you state, his own conscience reproaches him because, although he knew that no consanguinity existed between himself and his first wife, he allowed himself to be separated from her. Having been consulted by him, you diligently ask what he ought to do.

By this present letter we answer that, although he bears a scruple of conscience concerning his abandoned first wife [Col. 1485D], he nevertheless ought not to leave his second wife or deny her the conjugal debt. It is fitting, however, that you impose upon him a suitable penance because he consented to be separated contrary to his conscience; and let him experience that penance as imposed upon him, so that, if required, he is bound even in sorrow to approach his second wife for intercourse. Yet he should judge that he has lost the right of demanding from her the carnal debt.

### XIX. To a certain person.—On approving a certain election.

Concerning your question whether, if someone’s election has been annulled and he is again unanimously nominated for the government of the same Church [Col. 1486A], the second election ought to be confirmed: we wish your discretion to hold that, if the prior election was annulled not because of a defect in the person but because of the manner of election, his promotion in the same Church ought not to be impeded—unless perhaps it is established that some taint of simoniacal depravity intervened.

### XX. To William, king of Sicily.—On the oath of fidelity to be rendered by the king’s heirs to the Roman pontiffs.

The friendly simplicity of charity seeks to be obscured by no deceptive verbal devices, by no entanglements of ambiguities. It is therefore often necessary that statements which appear full of threats [Col. 1486B], and which, though harmlessly expressed, might generate scruples of ambiguity, should shine more clearly through a truthful explanation.

Accordingly, beloved son in the Lord, having heard that a question was raised in your presence whether it might be inferred from the tenor of our rescript that each of your heirs ought to render such an oath of fidelity to each of our successors; and having also understood the explanation of our beloved sons A., cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, and P., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, legates of the Apostolic See, which was sent to us under attestation of their seals: not wishing in any respect to differ from their sound interpretation, we have thought it right to inform your royal serenity that, since our intention is to impose nothing intolerable on you or your heirs [Col. 1486C], we answer you on this point as follows.

Your heirs who have sworn to us or to any one of our successors are not thereafter to be compelled to swear to another. Nevertheless, they shall at all times be bound, without any evasion, faithfully to observe toward our Catholic successors who have been set over them both the purity of homage and fidelity, just as if they had sworn it—unless homage has been remitted to one of them by the kindness of the Apostolic See, as it was remitted to your person. Yet he is not thereby to think himself exempt from the observance of fidelity.

Given at the Lateran.

### XXI. To the bishop of Absara [Absorense] and the abbot of Saint Andrew of Bergis.—On penance to be imposed upon a certain priest when it is uncertain whether a servant died through his fault.

[Col. 1486D]

> [Note: The material in brackets is lacking in the Decretals.]

It has come to the hearing of our apostolic office on your report that a certain priest, wishing to correct one of his household, attempted to beat him with the belt with which he was accustomed to gird himself. It happened that a knife slipped from the sheath attached to the belt and wounded him slightly in the back. Subsequently the wounded man lived for some time and had already recovered from the wound; but, struck by a more serious illness, as is believed, he entered the way of all flesh with sound mind [Col. 1487A] and due devotion.

Because it was doubtful whether he had died as a result of the wound, and because the same priest had been suspended from every office and benefice, you wished to consult the Apostolic See concerning what ought to be done. We therefore answer your prudent inquiry that, since in doubtful cases we must choose the safer path, you ought to command the said priest not henceforth to undertake ministry in sacred orders. Yet, after suitable penance has been imposed, you may permit him to be content to minister in minor orders. But if it is lawfully established to you that the man died from another illness, he may, with your permission, celebrate the divine offices as he was accustomed to do.

[Given at the Lateran.]

### XXII. To a certain bishop.—On one of his parishioners, not yet eleven years old, who had been given in marriage, though unwilling, to a certain German.

In response to what you informed us in your letters concerning a certain parishioner of yours, whom her stepfather joined in marriage to a certain German, we answer as follows. Although, when she was not yet eleven years old, she was at first given to him against her will and in resistance, nevertheless, because afterward she lived with him for a year or half a year and seems to have consented, she must be compelled to return to him [Col. 1487C]. Nor are witnesses henceforth to be admitted whom the said woman has named to prove that she did not consent to him, since delay for so long a time excludes such proof.

We therefore will and command that you do not omit, on this account, to compel both parties, the appeal having been set aside, by ecclesiastical censure to love one another again with marital affection—unless perhaps they should wish together to enter religious life. A penalty is to be imposed upon them because each of them has gone over to alien and unlawful concubinage.

[Given at the Lateran.]

### XXIII. To the bishop of Formola.—Replies to his questions.

[Col. 1487D]

The relatives of Ermengard, bearer of the present letter, as you informed us by your letters, produced witnesses under legal examination to establish that spiritual kinship had lawfully arisen between her and her husband; and you accordingly pronounced a sentence of divorce between them. But afterward the said E. confessed to you that she had not in truth been her husband’s comother before the sentence; after the separation, she contracted that spiritual kinship, and yet proceeded to a second marriage.

Because, therefore, acknowledging her guilt, she seeks our counsel concerning this matter, you asked us for an answer. We answer your brotherhood by this present letter that a judgment reasonably pronounced by the Church’s court is not to be abandoned merely because of the woman’s confession [Col. 1488A], unless the contrary should perhaps be lawfully proved. Finally, impose upon the same woman, who has confessed her fault to you, such a penalty as you judge should be imposed according to the character of the person and the gravity of the offense.

Martin married Bertha; Lothair married Teberga; Lothair received from the sacred font the son of Martin and Bertha; then, after Lothair and Bertha had died, Martin contracted marriage with Teberga. (Your brotherhood asks whether such persons ought to be separated from one another.) We answer your inquiry that, since according to the Lord’s word husband and wife become one flesh through marriage, it is clear that Teberga cannot be joined in marriage to Martin [Col. 1488B], who was her *compater*—that is, the spiritual co-parent of her husband—with whom Teberga is known to have become one flesh.

Concerning another person about whom you requested a rescript from the Apostolic See—whether a married man who, before contracting his marriage, carnally knew a close blood-relative of his wife, when both confess it and some people of the neighborhood are said to proclaim it, ought to be separated from his wife by judgment of the Church—we reply to your brotherhood as follows. If the truth cannot otherwise be made clear in an ordinary judicial proceeding, they ought not to be separated merely because of their confession or neighborhood rumor. For when some persons wish to collude against a marriage, they would readily rush into a confession of incest [Col. 1488C] if they believed that this would bring about the result they desire. Neighborhood rumor is not to be judged so weighty that, unless reasonable and trustworthy proofs are added, it can annul a well-established marriage.

Thirdly, your brotherhood asked us to resolve this question: whether a young man who consented to his betrothed by words in the present tense ought to have her as his wife, when the niece of that betrothed woman, coming forward to impede their marriage, alleged that she had previously been carnally known by the young man. When she produced witnesses concerning this, they said that they firmly believed that she had been the young man’s concubine and joined to him by carnal intercourse. They added that they had seen them wandering together over plains and woods, on roads and repeatedly along the road, and said that they had received the testimony of the neighborhood concerning this.

But, for greater certainty, because you believed this insufficiently proved, you summoned the woman who asserted that both she and the young man were bound by oaths. Separately examined, they confessed that they had carnally known one another, although the young man did not wish to be separated from the woman to whom he had been betrothed. Having understood the matters stated, we observe that the report of the neighborhood, the contrived stories of the woman and the young man, and their wandering through solitary places were proved by witnesses; and that they separately confessed under oath to carnal knowledge [Col. 1489A]. Especially since this is said not to be hidden but is openly reported by many, following the footsteps of our predecessors, and especially the decrees of Pope Alexander of blessed memory, we believe it more prudent and safer that they should not be joined in marriage but, their betrothal dissolved, should be separated from one another.

[Given at the Lateran.]

### XXIV. To Gottfried, patriarch of Aquileia.—On the absolution of excommunicated persons.

Since you desire that your brotherhood be more fully instructed in writing by the Apostolic See concerning matters that contain doubt, we—although unworthy, yet compelled by the office of administration entrusted to us to answer consultations—wish to resolve in this rescript the knots of each of your questions. We commend your prudence in this, since, though you possess knowledge of canon law and enjoy the counsel of prudent men, you nevertheless seek the counsel of the holy Roman Church, your mother, for greater clarity and to establish a pattern for others. In this you show yourself, as a beloved and prudent man, to possess the spirit of counsel and fortitude [Col. 1489B].

The tenor of the first question was this: whether an excommunicated person who has sworn to abide by the Church’s command, and to whom the bishop restores communion before absolution, may be communicated with by others, and whether the bishop ought to do this. To this question we answer that the oath-bound security which those now excommunicated give has been introduced more as a precaution according to the Church’s custom than from the rigor of the canons. It is not considered of such force that, unless the benefit of absolution follows, an excommunicated person should be restored to the communion of others. Especially since he has not obtained absolution from that oath, and it is established both that he was excommunicated and that he has not truly been absolved, the bishop cannot and ought not restore communion to him [Col. 1489C], nor may others communicate with him, unless after taking the oath he has been absolved according to the ecclesiastical form. For, according to the canons of the Apostles and the decrees of Pope Fabian, one who knowingly communicates with an excommunicated person must be deprived of communion; indeed, according to Isidore, he immediately incurs with him the penalty of excommunication [Col. 1489D].

Following the statutes of the canons, and especially those of Pope Alexander III, our predecessor of pious memory, we have thought that the second question should receive this answer: if public report says that someone struck a cleric, neither the bishop nor others ought to communicate with him unless he has lawfully cleared himself of the charge at the bishop’s discretion, or, for greater caution, has received the benefit of absolution.

Thirdly, your discretion asked whether, if a cleric struck by someone laid his complaint before his bishop [Col. 1490A], was prepared to produce witnesses, and, through the bishop’s intervention, made an amicable settlement and was reconciled with the person who struck him—although the bishop communicated with that person—others may communicate with him. We answer that, although the person who laid violent hands on the one he injured seems to have satisfied him, he nevertheless offended the grace of the Church; he is not recognized as having made satisfaction for this unless the ecclesiastical form introduced for absolving such persons, as stated above, is observed.

Moreover, we resolve the difficulty of the final question as follows: one who keeps a cleric captive, although he has not laid violent hands upon him, is guilty of a crime no less serious than one who has laid violent hands upon him. He is not to be restored to fraternal communion unless, as stated above, he has been absolved according to the Church’s form [Col. 1490B].

Given as above.

### XXV. To certain priests.—Replies to their questions concerning the “accusation of marriage.”

On behalf of your Church, we have been asked whether persons who offer nothing in their own voice concerning an accusation against a marriage ought to be admitted solely through the writing of a little document. To this we say that, except insofar as it creates a presumption, such a writing has no force in such matters toward rendering judgment unless some other lawful proof supports it.

Moreover, this was also added to the inquiry [Col. 1490C], and we reply that persons who attended the betrothal and remained silent when questioned are not later to be admitted if they wish to confess anything against the marriage, unless they wish to speak of matters which they truly learned afterward and concerning which it is established that they knew nothing at the time of the original inquiry.

We have not thought fit to append in the present letter the manner in which an oath is to be received from those who accuse a marriage or make some protest, nor after how many years persons are to be heard in an accusation of marriage. The form of such an oath is carefully set out and evident in almost all the canons; and, because of the variety of cases and differences of persons [Col. 1490D], no fixed limit of years can be prescribed for them.

Given at the Lateran.

### XXVI. To a certain bishop.—On penance to be imposed upon Greek priests if they seek its imposition for children accidentally smothered.

We have been asked whether public penance should be imposed upon Greek priests, who may lawfully use marriage, if they request it for children who have been smothered in bed. We answer this inquiry as follows. If, through their own action or deliberate negligence, children are found smothered in beds, they must abstain perpetually from the service of the altar, and a penance more severe than that imposed on laymen must be enjoined upon them—though not public [Col. 1491A], unless the matter has become public. They shall not only cease from the exercise of sacred orders; if they are not yet in those orders, they are not to be admitted to them.

But if children are found dead in cradles through negligence, and the matter has remained concealed, a penalty is to be imposed upon them at the discretion of the confessor, and, to deter others, they are to abstain for a time from the celebration of Masses.

[Given at the Lateran.]

### XXVII. To a certain bishop.—That he compel W. to return to his lawful wife.

From your letters we have learned that the bearer of these presents, named W., formerly took a certain woman of your diocese, namely Lucia, as his wife; and, through the instigation of the evil spirit, they lived in harmony for only a short time. The same W. also alleged that he had married her under compulsion, violence having been done to him and fear having intervened. But you, together with your chapter, frequently striving to restore peace between them by both threats and admonitions, compelled them, being rashly separated, likewise to be reconciled; finally the husband charged his wife with the crime of fornication [lacuna]. Yet after long delays and careful admonitions that they should cease from such litigation, since they could no further be calmed in this respect, and the husband again more expressly accused her of the crime of fornication, she herself, led by a spirit we know not what, was compelled publicly to confess that, because her husband refused to provide for her necessities and needs, she had been compelled to incur the aforesaid crime. And when you had more carefully warned her not, at anyone’s suggestion or upon wicked counsel, to allege against herself something so disgraceful, she asserted the same thing yet more plainly.

Now, having assembled your chapter and other discreet men, you, by their advice, firmly enjoined continence upon both parties, so that they should live chastely while separated from one another. And, having learned from certain reports that the said W. intended to take another wife, although you carefully warned him not in any way to attempt this, he nevertheless secretly contracted betrothal and rashly celebrated marriage with another woman outside the city. But when you endeavoured to investigate the act so that you might proceed accordingly, the aforesaid W., setting forth and explaining the course of events as they had occurred, is said to have appealed to our hearing.

Therefore, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if matters proceeded thus, you compel the aforesaid man, setting aside the appeal, by sentence of excommunication to return to his lawful wife; and, after imposing upon him penance for the adultery committed with the second woman, cause him to treat the first with marital affection. Moreover, do not delay in sending to the Apostolic See, suspended from office and benefice, the chaplain whom you ascertain to have celebrated the blessing with the second woman, together with testimony in your letters.

Given at the Lateran.

XXVIII. To a certain bishop.—Concerning a regular canon who, at the point of death, refused to surrender property of his own.

[Col. 1492A]

Regarding a certain regular canon of your diocese who, while at the point of death, although warned by his prior, refused to surrender the private property which he secretly possessed contrary to the Rule, and so ended his final day: you judged it necessary to ask us what should be done concerning him, since he has nevertheless been buried among the other brethren. Since indeed we do not believe that you are ignorant of what is laid down concerning such persons in the Rule of St Augustine, and what is known to have been forbidden in the Lateran synod, we plainly answer your inquiry by these letters: that canon was not only to be deprived of Christian burial, but also, if it can be done without very great scandal, he deserves to be cast out from that burial-place and buried outside the church cemetery; for, as is expressly contained in that synod, neither is absolution to be performed for him nor should he have burial among the brethren. This, however, is to be done whenever such a case happens among persons of this kind.

XXIX. To Provost Falc[...].—Against clerics who engage in warfare.

The following question was presented to our hearing on your behalf: whether clerics who are in no way ashamed, having laid aside clerical dress, to bear military arms, ought—if bodily injury is inflicted upon them, or if they ransom themselves from a captor—to enjoy that immunity of clerics by which one who rashly lays hands upon a cleric is marked as excommunicated by the law itself.

To this we briefly answer you: since one who commits an offence against the Church invokes her aid in vain, and since the law of secular princes supplies quite forceful arguments for this answer—where it is plainly laid down as void that a woman whose chastity has been attacked cannot bring an action for injuries if she was caught in the clothing of a prostitute—such clerics, if they have been warned three times by their prelates and refuse to lay down their arms, ought not to possess the privilege of clerics.

XXX. To the bishop of Sigüenza.—If the matter cannot otherwise be proved, witnesses are to be compelled even in a criminal case, etc.

[Col. 1492D]

It has come to us that in your bishopric it often happens that a cleric suffers enormous and intolerable injury at the hands of a layman, while many stand by and see; or that, in the presence of the people in church, human blood is horribly shed through the prompting of diabolical fraud. On this account, when the wrongdoers are brought into court, they deny that they committed so great a crime; and although the injured party wishes to prove the injury inflicted by the testimony of those who saw it present, [these persons themselves, although they know the truth, disdain] to bear witness to the truth. Thus ecclesiastical justice is defeated and the clerical order is held cheap. [It also frequently happens that many rashly lay violent hands upon a cleric and, impeded by numerous obstacles, cannot come to the Apostolic See; and because your brotherhood judged that we should be consulted concerning these matters], we answer your inquiry as follows: those who refuse to give testimony concerning ecclesiastical matters, if the truth cannot otherwise be discovered [although according to the strictness of the canons one witness’s testimony is not to be accepted], we wish, according to the custom of the Roman Church and out of reverence for the clerical order, to be believed upon their oath.

But those who, hindered by illness, cannot come to the Apostolic See for the benefit of absolution, you may absolve after receiving their oath, as is customary, on the condition that, once restored to their former health, they present themselves before the Apostolic presence. We believe that you may freely grant dispensation to women, children, and the elderly. Churches [Col. 1493B] polluted by the shedding of blood may be cleansed by summoning the clerics of the city, with a procession and sprinkling of holy water, as is written in the ordinal.]

But concerning those who inflict no enormous injury upon a brother, we have judged the matter to be left to the discretion of your brotherhood.

XXXI. [Note: [Col. 1493D] The same, with a few changes, also in Decree 10 above.] To the same.—Concerning Jews or Saracens converted to the Christian faith.

We have been asked on your behalf whether Jews or Saracens converted to the Christian faith may cohabit with wives whom, while they remained in unbelief, they married within the second, third, or fourth degree of relationship; or whether, after their conversion, they may leave their wives and enter into other marriages.

By the authority of these presents I answer that persons so converted to the faith, so long as their wives wish to remain with them, may, if they wish, retain them, whether those wives are converted or not; yet they are not to be compelled to do so. But while those wives live and wish to remain, they ought not to contract with others. If, however, the wives depart in hatred of the Christian faith, then, since—as Gregory testifies—an insult to the Creator dissolves the bond of marriage as regards the one who is left, they are by no means forbidden to take other wives. Nor does it matter whether they contracted marriage in the second, third, or fourth degree while they were in unbelief, since in the old Law it had only been forbidden [Col. 1493D] that they should uncover the nakedness of their sisters.

XXXII. To John, archbishop of Lyons.—Concerning conventual churches.

[In accordance with the duty of our office, it is fitting that we provide answers to questions submitted to the Apostolic See by our brethren and fellow bishops.]

We have learned from your letters that two conventual churches have been established in your diocese, each of which possesses a parish church with estates situated nearer to the other than to itself. They desire to exchange these churches; but because one of them, on account of the better revenues of the estates belonging to its church, demands that a fixed sum of money be added to it, so that equivalence in value may be attained, some have begun to doubt whether this may lawfully be done, [and for this reason you wished to consult the Apostolic See. Although we by no means think that the industrious discretion of your judgment is ignorant what ought to be done concerning this point, nevertheless we] answer your diligence as follows: since an exchange may be effected between the parish churches already mentioned considered in themselves, and since in an exchange of estates considered in themselves it is not forbidden, where one estate outweighs another, to make a monetary payment, a contract of exchange may be made between their estates, as may seem expedient, upon payment of a specified sum of money; provided, however, that [Col. 1494B] the contracts are in no way combined with one another.

XXXIII. To the archbishop of Saint-Marin (of Daran? ).—Concerning the removal of a plebanus elected by simony, and the right of patronage.

It was represented to us on your behalf [with great care] that, when four persons had been appointed by the chapter who were to elect a certain person as *plebanus* [parish priest], the friends of the man whose election was under consideration promised to pay money to one of the electors, or to all of them, while the man subsequently elected through the intervention of this promise knew nothing of it. Since you wished to consult us on this matter, we answer your concern as follows: unless it should be established that those who made such a promise did so maliciously through fraud and to the detriment of the person to be elected, even though he himself was unaware of the promise, the election, as having been obtained simoniacally through such depravity, is nevertheless wholly to be rejected.

[Furthermore, you asked us whether someone who becomes patron of his church through having built it is to be admitted with the clerics to the election of a *plebanus*, or wholly excluded from it, even if he has alleged, on the basis of long custom, that he ought to take part in the election. To this, indeed, we give the following answer: if anyone builds a church with the consent of the diocesan bishop, he thereby acquires the right of patronage. But in a conventual church the patron is not involved in making the election of a *plebanus*, but, after the election has been made, his consent is requested as a matter of propriety, unless the patron has otherwise obtained by his own jurisdiction that he ought to take part in conducting the election. It is otherwise, however, in a chapel where one priest is to be appointed: for he is chosen by the patron and presented to the bishop of the place for institution. The honour of a procession is likewise reserved to the founder on account of the foundation itself; and, if he falls into poverty, the Church provides him modest assistance, as is established in the canons.]

Finally, concerning what we find at the end of your letter, we judge this answer to be given: a person elected *plebanus*, priest, or any prelate of the Church, even if he has been rejected on account of depravity, ought not to obtain from his bishop any dispensation contrary to law.

[Given at the Lateran, 8 May.]

XXXIV. To Roffridus, cardinal priest of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino.—That he shall determine the matrimonial question between Robert and the woman B.

The tenor of your letters sent to us shows that [in the archpresbyterate of Saint Germanus] a matrimonial dispute was in progress between Robert and the woman B. [When she produced witnesses for the marriage, the man appealed to the Apostolic See. And when the case had been entrusted to our venerable brother, the bishop of Telese [of Theate], because that land was then disturbed by the king’s death [Col. 1495B] and the woman, fearing the evident danger of the roads to herself, was unable to appear before the judge, although she sent a messenger with an excuse, the bishop nevertheless] later absolved the same R., in the woman’s absence, from her claim. The same woman, however, [coming into our presence] obtained from us letters to you, that, after hearing the case, you should bring it to its due conclusion, [since it could not be determined before the aforementioned bishop because of the disturbance of the land.]

But the said R., summoned by you to the case, did not appear, alleging illness; yet because on the following night he presumed to unite another woman to himself, you pronounced a sentence of excommunication against him. He was at length later absolved from it, when he came before you in person and showed letters of the aforementioned bishop, by which it appeared that he had been absolved from disturbance by her [because he had not appeared before the bishop]. Since, therefore, [as you state, the same woman daily cries after you in tears,] producing her witnesses to prove that he publicly pledged her with a betrothal ring, you humbly ask to be instructed what you ought to do.

We answer your inquiry thus: notwithstanding such unlawful absolution as the bishop made, proceed in the case [after removing the impediment of appeal, and decide it by its due conclusion], strictly forbidding the same Robert, under penalty of excommunication, to have access to the woman whom [Col. 1495D] he has subsequently brought in, until the case has been decided. [Do not reject the witnesses whom the aforesaid B. may bring forward from her own relatives or from others, provided that they are otherwise suitable; for relatives are accustomed to know their own kinship better than strangers, whether by documents, witnesses, recitation of ancestors, or other evidence.]

XXXV. Concerning one who knew his wife’s kinswoman.

From the letters of your discretion we have learned that G., having sought a penance from you, confessed that he had betrothed a certain woman during her marriageable years; but while he was staying with her in her father’s house, he approached his betrothed’s sister and, at the devil’s prompting, carnally knew her. Afterwards, when he was compelled by his parents to take his betrothed as wife, he confessed to them that he had committed the aforesaid offence; yet the archdeacon of the place nevertheless compelled him by ecclesiastical censure to render carnal due to his betrothed. He asserts that he obeyed, though unwillingly.

Since, moreover, you are said to have forbidden him to have carnal access to either woman, and you wished to consult us as to what it is your office’s duty to do, we answer your inquiry as follows: on the confession of the man alone concerning this crime, he ought not in any way to abstain from his betrothed.

XXXVI. To Gilbert, bishop of Clermont.—Concerning an oath.

[Col. 1496B]

When we heard that before your consecration you had taken an oath to the canons, so detrimental to episcopal right and dignity that episcopal authority appeared thereby to be excessively weakened, you, prudent and discreet as you are, wished to consult us on this matter and humbly sought an apostolic remedy for this inconvenience. Therefore, wishing by the authority owed to our office to make provision, we answer your concern that unlawful oaths, given by you to the chapter of Clermont to the detriment of the bishopric, ought to bring you no impediment. And so that you may be secure and forewarned in this matter against the objections of detractors, we have judged that letters of our absolution should be granted to you as testimony.

XXXVII. To the bishop of Zaragoza.—Concerning penance to be imposed upon simoniacs.

You wished to consult us concerning regular canons or monks who obtained admission through simony, knowingly [and by their own contrivance]. But since many authorities expressly address this matter, we give no answer other than what has been decreed: that those who have been so admitted must wholly leave the place and go to solitary places or stricter monasteries, in which they may without interruption bewail so detestable an offence. But if money was given without their knowledge, compel them to renounce that place; and afterwards restore them to it, if they can remain there without scandal, or you may place them in some other house of the same order in order to serve there.

XXXVIII. To the consuls and people of Genoa.—Concerning the subdeacon D., who unwillingly killed a boy.

It has been represented to us that D., a subdeacon and bearer of these presents, was one day crossing a certain bridge and happened to stop upon it. He saw young men violently struggling with a certain boy in the river; moved by good zeal, lest the boy be suffocated in the water by them, he began mildly to rebuke them so that they should release him. But after releasing the boy, they attempted to drag that subdeacon himself to the river by his feet. When he was near the bank, he held himself as best he could so as not to fall headlong because of their violent pulling; nevertheless, a dislodged stone killed the very boy whom he had first wished to save.

Therefore, by apostolic writing we command your brotherhood that, if the matter stands thus, after suspending that subdeacon for a time from exercising the order he has received, according as seems fit to you, you thereafter permit him to minister in that order. But he shall by no means advance to higher orders, lest scandal be caused among God’s people, although in this respect he does not appear to have been at fault—unless perhaps a dispensation concerning the suspended orders be made for him on his entering a monastery or house of regular canons, and his ordaining bishop judges it proper.

XXXIX. To the archbishop of Cassino [Cassilian?].

[Col. 1497B]

This, etc., was reported to our hearing on your behalf. As to what your brotherhood asked of us—whether those begotten by bishops may be promoted to [ecclesiastical grades], if they are proven by learning and uprightness of conduct—let your discretion know that, provided they were begotten in lawful marriage and no other canonical obstacle stands in the way, they may lawfully be ordained in sacred orders and obtain benefices in the churches in which their parents preside or have presided.

XL. To the bishop of Livonia and his companions.—He grants that they may use foods set before them by unbelievers.

[Col. 1497C]

How praiseworthy it is, etc. And below. Granting your petitions, brother bishop, we concede by apostolic authority to you and your companions, when you go forth to preach Christ’s faith to pagans, that you may use, with moderation and thanksgiving and with observance of the distinction of times according to canonical enactments, those foods which are set before you by the unbelievers themselves. We further grant that any suitable men, monks, or clerics able to proclaim evangelical truth to the nations, having requested and obtained permission from their prelates, may, if they wish to join you, have by apostolic authority free power to carry this out without any opposition.

XLI. To a certain bishop.—Assailants of clerics and arsonists are to be absolved only by the Roman pontiff. A leprous priest is to be removed from office.

Your brotherhood judged that we should be consulted whether only those who, falling under canons of automatic sentence, have laid violent hands upon clerics are to be sent to the Apostolic See, and whether they can be released from that sentence otherwise than by the Roman pontiff. We therefore answer your brotherhood that not only those who rashly lay hands upon clerics but also arsonists, once they have been publicly denounced by ecclesiastical sentence, are to be sent to the Apostolic See for the benefit of absolution—and are to be absolved only by the Roman pontiff.

[Those, however, who presume to receive ecclesiastical benefices from lay hands are not customarily required to go to the Apostolic See for such an offence.]

Concerning a priest who, by divine judgment, has been afflicted with leprosy while holding the office of prelate in a parish church, we judge that you should be informed that, because of scandal or the murmuring of the people, he must be removed from the office of administration; yet, according to the means of the church, provision is to be made for him so long as he lives.

XLII. To the archbishop of Tours.—Concerning the cleric H.

[Col. 1498B]

When H., the bearer of these presents, as he showed us by his complaint, came into your presence at the time of ordination, your brotherhood conferred upon him, according to the custom of the country, the four minor orders. Not content with these, he rashly received the subdiaconate [on the same day, hiding himself among the others without your knowledge, and also the diaconate]. Since that cleric greatly exceeded the bounds in this act, we command your brotherhood to allow him to minister in the minor orders. But if he enters a religious house, and his life and conduct warrant it, his abbot may also dispense with him concerning the other orders.

XLIII. To the bishop of Abbeville [Albi?].—That he shall establish in certain churches as many religious persons as their revenues support.

It is known, etc. And below. For it has come to our hearing, as you have reported, that certain churches within your diocese and subject to your jurisdiction, in which secular clerics formerly served, have been transferred to regular observance. Yet in one where twenty clerics had formerly been maintained, scarcely seven or eight monks now live; and where there were ten clerics, only four or three monks have been established, although the possessions have not now been diminished, nor any other revenues from which the clerics used to be supported. You asked to be taught by our letters what you should henceforth do in these matters.

Therefore, lest God’s service in those churches remain any longer diminished through such a change, by the present letter we grant your brotherhood that, if the prelates to whom these churches belong neglect, after your admonition, to establish in them as many religious persons as can be honourably supported from their revenues, you may freely establish in them, without contradiction or appeal, as many religious persons of the same order as their revenues suffice to provide with necessities. You may also compel, by ecclesiastical coercion and with appeal set aside, any persons whom you find resisting to observe whatever you judge ought to be decreed concerning these matters.

XLIV. To a certain bishop.—Concerning acts done by the greater part of a chapter.

Your brotherhood, etc. And below. Your diligence believed, after careful consultation with us, that it should inquire what you ought to observe and establish by apostolic authority in this matter: in his church, a certain person—even the least among them—places the church itself under an interdict without your consent and that of the other canons, thereby both abandoning the service of that church and causing no small scandal among the people. Your discretion also added that you wished to obtain a rescript from the Apostolic See concerning the fact that certain clerics of the greater church, or of other churches established in your diocese, obstruct their ordinances and other reasonable statutes of the chapter [lacuna] under the pretext of canonical objection, and do not permit ecclesiastical order to proceed.

We answer the first point of the question: you ought by no means to observe an interdict imposed in a church by any canon without the assent of yourself and the brethren, nor should you permit others, especially contrary to justice, to observe such an edict. We judge that the knot of the second question is to be resolved by authority of the Lateran council: unless it happens that some reasonable objection is proved by one or more persons of greater or lesser rank, that which has been established by the greater and sounder part of the chapter shall always prevail and have its due force, with appeal set aside—unless an ancient custom of the church, hitherto observed and confirmed by authority of the Apostolic See, counsels that something else be observed. Thus, God granting it, the boldness of the wicked will be restrained and ecclesiastical benefit will be more widely extended.

XLV. To Walter, archbishop of Rouen.—Concerning the grant of a church which is not vacant.

It is known, etc. And below: On your behalf, there has been laid before us the question whether the appeal of persons is to be entertained who, because of a promise made to them concerning churches that are not vacant, understand that subsequently vacant churches ought to be conferred upon them and burst forth in an appeal after being passed over. To this we judge that your brotherhood should be answered: since promises of this sort were forbidden in the Lateran council, unless authority of the Apostolic See intervenes or some other reasonable ground stands in the way, the institution to vacant churches ought not to be delayed or in any way impeded on account of such an appeal.

XLVI. To the bishop of Astorga.—Concerning prebends.

[Col. 1500A]

In your church, as has come to our knowledge, it has been customary to establish one hundred canons and to confirm this establishment by the solemnity of an oath. Therefore, since that number has diminished with the passage of time, you raise the doubt whether, if laymen are counted who in your church are called by the title of canons, your statute concerning the establishment of canons can be fulfilled. To remove this uncertainty from your hearts, it seems to us that laymen ought not to be counted in the number of canons; nor ought you to refrain from completing with other suitable clerical persons the number of canons prescribed by our statute and strengthened by an oath. For our intention is not thought to have been anything other than that, whenever necessary, you should take care unanimously to find persons to make up the number, through whom you might fittingly serve God in divine offices through ecclesiastical orders. Moreover, we strictly forbid you henceforth to admit laymen as canons.

XLVII. To the elect of Alloc [uncertain].—Concerning penance to be imposed upon Count H.

We have gathered from your letters that a certain priest of your diocese, because he presumed to call himself the king’s son and, taking up arms, caused sedition and war in Provence, was seen to be beaten through the streets by order of our beloved son Count H.; afterwards, by the count’s command, he was delivered to the gallows and died. Since you stated that both the count himself and the other participants in this deed wish to make satisfaction for it, by this letter we answer that, if the said priest offended in such a manner and was killed while bearing arms, not while repelling injury but while inflicting it, it does not seem to us that his killers ought on this account to be compelled to approach the Apostolic See to obtain absolution. But you, who know better the merits of the persons, should impose upon them another suitable penance.

Furthermore, concerning the vow which you state that the count made—namely, to fast on bread and water every Friday—it does not appear that this suffices for the guilty man; the intervening words are corrupt in the supplied text (“e pretio illa sufficiat de altari constructo”). Although making a vow is voluntary, lawful vows must nevertheless be fulfilled of necessity.

Finally, concerning what he promised about aiding the land of Jerusalem, diligently exhort him to go there in person, if possible; or, in fulfilment of his vow, to provide suitable assistance to those going to Jerusalem.

At the end of your letters you asked us whether a certain baron of your diocese, who inflicted death upon a priest and afterwards entered the Cistercian order, can now, having become a monk, be absolved by your abbot. To this we briefly answer: where such an excommunication has preceded a man’s becoming a monk, he can obtain absolution only from the Roman pontiff or by his command. Nevertheless, by dispensation and by our authority, you may confer upon him the benefit of absolution and impose suitable penance for the offence.

XLVIII. To [...].—Concerning trial by combat.

The care of the government entrusted to us leads us to answer the inquiries of our brethren [as we ought], and, so far as human frailty permits, to remove from them scruples of doubt. Therefore, since your brotherhood judged that the Apostolic See should be consulted whether duels ought to be allowed in disputes concerning presentations to churches, we judge that your concern should be answered: you must tolerate them in no way, neither in this case nor in any other.

XLIX. To the chapter of Lucca.—Concerning a sentence of excommunication.

[Col. 1501B]

When Pope Clement, our predecessor of blessed memory, summoned L., M., M., and certain other clerics of Bari to come into his presence to answer to his archdeacon Bernard, whom they had grievously injured, and they scorned to come in accordance with the apostolic command, he had the bishop Vigilius pronounce against them a sentence of suspension. While, as is said, certain of them remained suspended under this sentence for three years, they obtained another ecclesiastical benefice. Since you wished to consult us whether they can reasonably retain the benefices thus obtained, we answer you by these presents that they may in no way retain either those benefices which they had before or those which they afterwards obtained. Therefore we have commanded our venerable brother, the bishop of Bari, not to delay depriving them of the benefices which they possess on account of such obstinacy and apostolic contempt; and those benefices are to remain in his hands until he receives our letters and command concerning what he ought to do in the matter.

L. To John, archbishop of Lyon [Lyons].—That he is not to admit the appeal of certain clerics.
