Since, in the Church of God, jurisdiction over subjects sometimes varies because of the diversity of orders and honours held by those possessing jurisdiction, and since our venerable brethren the bishops exercise the power granted them in rendering justice to their subjects and peoples, it happens that some persons, considering not justice but the freedom of their own will, seeking their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, evade the judgment and authority of bishops, usurping the refuge of appeal—a remedy known to have been instituted for the just protection of the innocent.

Now we have received the complaint transmitted to us by our venerable brother, the bishop of Langres: certain clerics of Guilan, compelled by no need of grievance and burdened by no weight of oppression, but solely under the pretext of shaking from themselves the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline, so that they may more freely revel in the liberty of their error and wicked purpose, appeal from his jurisdiction and, on the pretext of your judgment, which they boast that they wish to observe, evade the jurisdiction of their ordinary judge without reasonable examination.

But since both canon and civil law introduced recourse to appeal not for the defence of wrongdoing but for the remedy of those oppressed and unjustly condemned, an appeal of subjects of this sort is not, according to the decrees of the Lateran council, to be admitted when it is brought solely so that the due correction of prelates and of all who, by the Lord’s disposition, are called to share in the care of the churches may be evaded. It is recognized to be in the interest of all that each person’s rights remain inviolate. We therefore judge that your brotherhood should be warned by these letters, commanding you by apostolic writing that, whenever it should happen that one of the aforesaid clerics appeals from the said bishop to your hearing, you are not to grant him a hearing or admit his appeal before it is established to you that it was lodged “ab appellatione illius” (an uncertain phrase in the supplied text), or from a grievance, or from an unjust condemnation; otherwise, setting aside the appeal, send him back to the court of the aforesaid bishop, leaving him to that bishop’s just judgment in the examination of his case. Thus the contumacy of the wicked will be restrained, and the honour due to fellow bishops, through observance of fraternal reciprocity, will remain secure in its freedom.

LI. To the bishop of Zaragoza.—Concerning vacant prebends.

[Col. 1502C]

Since you, son P., provost, asked us what ought to be done when, upon a prebend becoming vacant in your church, several of those counted there burst forth in an appeal, expressly forbidding any proceeding to elect someone, we answer your inquiry as follows: if they have not pursued the appeal which they lodge within forty days, one must thereafter proceed, no appeal standing in the way, to the canonical election of a person suitable for service in the church.

LII. To Gerard, bishop of Bologna.—That masters’ and students’ lodgings are not to be rented to the injury of current tenants.

[Col. 1502D] From a rescript of letters of the late P. [Peter], bishop of Tusculum, of pious memory, it has come to our knowledge that, when he entered the city of Bologna during his legation, he found that the late W. [William], formerly bishop of Porto, had established there and, under excommunication, forbidden anyone to lease the lodgings of others by promising a higher rent, where they claimed them for themselves either from a vain-glorious desire to appear, through their expenditure, more powerful than others, or for the advantage of private gain. Therefore he, by prudent provision considering that the wickedness of such leasing bred a furnace of discord and no slight impediments to study, confirmed the aforesaid ordinance by the authority of the Apostolic See which he exercised as legate [Col. 1503A], decreeing that it be observed for all time under penalty of anathema: that no master or student, concerning the leasing of lodgings, should dare to approach a lodger to the injury and prejudice of the inhabitants, unless it were first established that the term of the lease had expired or that the tenants had given their willing consent to this.

Accordingly, we—who condemn detestable cunning, hostile to contracts made in good faith, not only among clerics but also among all persons, even merchants—decree to be valid the aforesaid ordinance made by the said bishop of Porto and subsequently confirmed by the bishop of Tusculum just mentioned, and confirm it by apostolic authority. We take care that you, brother bishop, and each of [Col. 1503B] all your successors shall have this present document read every year in the common assembly of masters and students, and that the aforesaid wickedness of an improper agreement be checked by a sentence of excommunication renewed annually. Let absolutely no one, therefore, infringe this document of our confirmation, etc.

### LIII. To the Archbishop of Sorrento (Surrentinum).—Concerning P. de Regali

After marriage had been contracted between P. and his wife A. [as P.’s own complaint made known to us, since they had lived together for two years and the said P. had had a son by that wife], the kinsmen of that same A. [wishing her to be separated from her husband], objected to the contracted marriage, asserting that the same A., at the first feeding with holy salt, had held the son of a former concubine of P. himself [Col. 1503C], [when she was first brought to him; and, for these reasons, coming before you, they said that she ought to be separated from her husband by your judgment. But your brotherhood, as we have learned, without hearing the case, forbade them marital intercourse, prohibiting P. himself from demanding the marital due from his wife.]

But, even if it were established before the Church that what we have said were true, the marriage contracted would not thereby be dissolved; indeed, that fact would scarcely constitute an impediment to contracting marriage. Therefore, by this apostolic writing, we command you to enjoin firmly upon the aforesaid P., by our authority, [Col. 1503D] that he treat the said A. with marital affection as his lawful wife, and freely demand and render the marital due. Whether it be established that A. did what was mentioned above before contracting marriage with P. or afterwards, provided nevertheless that, if she did it fraudulently in order to bring about the separation of the marriage, she receive punishment for her presumption, the marriage shall remain in its full force.

### LIV. To a certain bishop.—Concerning the subdeacon C., who unwillingly killed a boy

Having examined the letters which you sent to Urban, our predecessor of happy memory, we have fully learned that the bearer, the subdeacon C., when formerly of tender age and playing with a certain boy, threw [Col. 1504A] a stone and wounded that boy, not deliberately but accidentally. From this wound he was, with difficulty, treated by physicians and within a short time, as was believed, completely cured; nevertheless, after a year had elapsed, the wound subsequently opened. But because the physician employed to treat him is thought, through negligence or ignorance, or some other fault, to have exercised less than necessary care, the boy died as a consequence of that wound.

In reply to these matters, we command your brotherhood that, however the matter may have proceeded, you permit him to minister in minor orders. Concerning him, you will do well to decide regarding the benefice which you ask to be conferred on him through you, as his merits demand and as shall better commend itself to your judgment. But he is not to approach the service of the altar, since he appears to have furnished the occasion for the death of that boy.

### LV. To the dean of Cama Cen. . . . (of Tarvanne?).—Concerning the prohibition against imposing a new rent upon the churches of the diocese of Thérouanne

A complaint, exceedingly serious and most worthy of correction, has lately been laid before our hearing, which we cannot pass over in dissimulation with a clear conscience. For certain [Col. 1504B] ecclesiastical persons possess churches [as if they were parishes in the diocese of Thérouanne]; when these churches become vacant, they are unwilling to call anyone to their government unless they first impose a new rent upon those churches, or increase those rents contrary to the Lateran constitution, compelling the priest to be appointed [bishop] to provide security by oath or surety for payment of it [Col. 1504C], [and they even strive to appropriate a certain part of the revenues to their own uses. Hence it often happens that, without the diocesan bishop’s knowledge, or without his being consulted at all, they introduce priests into those churches at their own will. Therefore, since we have not wished, nor ought we to allow, the ordinances of the aforesaid council to be violated by anyone’s malice], we command and enjoin your discretion by apostolic writing that, [when you have been called upon in this matter, after summoning the parties before you], whatever you learn [Col. 1504D] has been attempted by anyone, since the time of the aforesaid constitution, against that constitution concerning those churches or their rents, you shall revoke as void [all objection and appeal having ceased], [entirely release the churches from increases of rent and restore them to their proper condition]. Priests whom you know have sworn unlawful oaths concerning these matters you shall cause to be absolved after imposing suitable satisfaction. Those also whom henceforth you learn to have acted in these matters contrary to the form of the canons, [without regard for any person, [perhaps: setting aside] the obstacle of appeal], you shall punish by canonical censure.

### LVI. To R., canon of Cologne, “learned in the medical art.”—He is advised not to proceed to the major sacred orders, because he has administered medicines to several persons who thereby incurred danger of death

[Col. 1505A]

It has come to our ears, as you have reported, that, although you are trained in the medical art, you have diligently administered medicines to several persons in the practice of that art; yet the outcome has often been contrary to your intention, and those to whom you thought you were applying a safeguard, after taking the medicines, incurred danger of death [Col. 1506A]. But because [as you assert] you desire to be promoted to sacred orders and wished to consult us on this point, we have judged it necessary to reply that, if your conscience seems in any way to reproach you concerning the foregoing, you should not, on our advice, ascend to the major orders.

[Col. 1505]

## LETTER OF RICHARD, KING OF THE ENGLISH, TO CLEMENT III, ROMAN PONTIFF, CONCERNING THE PEACE MADE BETWEEN HIMSELF AND KING TANCRED

(RYMER, *Foedera, Conventiones, Litterae inter reges Angliae et alios*, London, 1816, folio; vol. I, p. 68.)

[Col. 1505B] To the most reverend lord and most blessed Father CLEMENT, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, RICHARD, by the same grace king of England and duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, greeting and the affection of sincere devotion in the Lord.

The acts of princes obtain a more just outcome when they receive strength and favor from the Apostolic See and are guided by conference with the holy Roman Church. We have therefore judged it fitting to bring to the knowledge of Your Blessedness those matters recently concluded between us and the lord Tancred, illustrious king of Sicily, in a public and most necessary treaty.

Indeed, we have established with him brotherly affection and perpetual peace, which we have promised, on the oaths of our magnates, archbishops, bishops, and very many illustrious men [Col. 1505C], to preserve in inviolate faith toward him and his people, his kingdom, and the whole land of his dominion. Moreover, binding the pact of peace and friendship with him by a still closer bond, we have agreed, God willing, that a marriage shall be contracted between Arthur, the distinguished duke of Brittany, our dearest nephew and heir should we die without offspring, and his illustrious daughter. By the Lord’s gift it shall receive its due consummation when the illustrious girl reaches marriageable years; or, should the aforesaid lord King Tancred wish that, before she reaches marriageable years, she be handed over in betrothal as wife to our nephew, we have granted that our nephew will do this, if the holy [Col. 1505D] Roman Church decrees a dispensation in this matter.

As for the money which we received from the same lord King Tancred for that marriage, for the use of our nephew—namely, twenty thousand ounces of gold—if perchance, which God forbid, owing to the intervening death of either party, or through our fault or that of our nephew or of the other party, the marriage should not stand, we or our heirs are bound, having sworn concerning this, to restore it in full to the said lord King Tancred or to his heirs [Col. 1506B].

Therefore, that the terms of the peace concluded and the pledged marriage may be preserved with due integrity by us and our nephew, as we have affirmed to the said lord Tancred under the solemnity of an oath, we earnestly request Your Holiness and the holy Roman Church to undertake surety for us toward the lord King Tancred and his heirs, both for the perpetual observance of the peace confirmed and the consummation of the marriage, and, if from the aforesaid causes the marriage should not take place, for repayment of the money [Col. 1506C].

That the Roman Church may confidently undertake the burden of this surety together with us, by the testimony of these present letters we grant to you and to the holy Roman Church free authority stringently to constrain us and our heirs and our land, should we act contrary to the aforesaid peace or, if the marriage does not follow for the aforesaid causes, should we or our heirs refuse payment of the money.

Your Blessedness knows that it concerns the honor of both kingdoms that, through the Roman Church’s mediation, both the good of peace and that of marriage attain a fitting end; from this many benefits will result hereafter.

[Col. 1506D] Witnessed by ourselves, on 11 November, at Messina.

[Col. 1507]

## AGREEMENT BETWEEN LORD POPE CLEMENT III AND THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF ROME, CONCERNING THE REGAL RIGHTS AND OTHER DIGNITIES OF THE CITY. A.D. 1188

(MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, vol. III, p. 785.)

[Col. 1507A] To the most holy Father and lord, CLEMENT, by the grace of God supreme pontiff and universal pope, the Senate and People of Rome: greeting and faithful service with submission.

The dignity of the Roman Senate and People is strengthened into its best condition, and it contributes exceedingly to the commonwealth, if we bring to the memory of posterity, by the solemn recording of writings, the concord of peace firmly established between the most holy Church and the renowned City, lest perhaps through negligence or indolence the truth of so inestimable a peace perish with the lapse of time—a peace which, by the prerogative of its excellence, must be both cherished by all and observed for all time. For through the abundance of peace, with the aid of God the Father, defense grows, and the dignity of the Roman Church [Col. 1507B] and of the noble City is preserved uninjured. From it comes the fertility of the fields, which supplies the uses of human life with manifold advantage; through it, indeed, very many benefits and gains are produced for us and you and for all others who preserve it, while fitting destruction is prepared for our enemies and yours who deserve ill.

Accordingly, most merciful Father and lord in Christ, we have judged that the terms of this peace should be ratified for the perpetual remembrance of the matter by this present document of senatorial dignity, by decree of the most ample order of the sacred Senate and with the counsel of very many men, both wise and highly prudent; and that they should be settled with you as follows. Namely, at present we restore to you the Senate [Col. 1507C], the City, and the mint. Yet of the mint we shall have a third part, as is set forth below. Likewise, we restore St. Peter’s church free, and we restore free the bishoprics and other churches pledged for war, in this manner: from the third part of the mint which the Senate shall have, they shall be discharged each year until the whole sum for which they were pledged is paid; and as the principal diminishes, so shall the interest diminish proportionately.

We restore all royal rights, both within and outside the City, which we hold, except the Ponte Lucano; nevertheless, without repudiating what others hold, we shall not act against you concerning it. Likewise concerning the captains, saving what is written below concerning them. We shall defend all dignities [Col. 1508A] and honors of the City for your benefit and that of the Roman Church. Both we the senators and all senators who shall be from time to time shall swear every year fidelity and peace to you and your successors, as is customary. And we shall cause all those who have lost possessions, after receiving compensation as agreed, to make a renunciation thereof by public instrument to you and your successors and to the Roman Church.

And, however Tusculum may come to be destroyed, all its possessions and holdings, within and without, together with all their goods and property, shall nevertheless be in the right and power of the Roman Church. You, however, shall give the senators who shall be from time to time the customary benefices and *presbyteria* [Note: [Col. 1507] That is, the gifts which supreme pontiffs were accustomed sometimes to distribute among Roman magistrates.]; likewise, you shall give the customary *presbyteria* to judges, advocates, scriniaries appointed by the Roman pontiff [Col. 1508B], and officers of the Senate.

As for those who have lost property taken from them by the retinue of the Roman pontiff, by wrongdoers, or by the people of Tusculum in war, you shall make compensation, as you promised by the agreement, saving the exceptions made by you. While those exceptions remain pending, you shall observe the agreements made by you, as you agreed with them; and those who have lost property shall observe toward you the agreements made by themselves, as they agreed with you.

And every year you shall give one hundred pounds of good revenue for the restoration of the walls of this most excellent City—namely, from Tusculum, however it may come into our hands. Within [Col. 1508C] half a year you shall give us all the walls and charcoal-pits of the city and fortress of Tusculum, and of its suburbs, for demolition; and you shall never rebuild, nor cause to be rebuilt, those walls and works in your lifetime. There shall be retained and preserved, however, to you and your successors and to the Roman Church all possessions, holdings, and appurtenances of that same Tusculum, within and without, together with its inhabitants and their property.

But if from now until the Kalends of January the said Tusculum has not come into our hands, then you shall excommunicate the people of Tusculum and, through your faithful men from Campania and Romagna, compel them, with our assistance, to carry out concerning Tusculum what has been stated above. In return for this, we the senators shall swear peace and security to you and to the bishops, cardinals, and your whole curia, and to those going to the curia, staying there, and returning, saving the rights of the Romans, which they shall seek in good faith and without malice [Col. 1509A].

Moreover, in every district of all the regions of the City, you shall choose ten men without malice; we the senators shall have them swear this peace to you and your successors, together with the benefices which they were accustomed to receive from the Roman curia. And should more persons wish to swear this peace, we the senators shall permit it. If you summon the Romans to defend the patrimony of St. Peter, they shall go with the expenses which their predecessors were accustomed to receive from the Roman curia.

Concerning the captains, there shall remain safe to the City and People of Rome whatever has been agreed with them and permitted to Rome by writing and oaths, and by *plenariae*, *starariae*, and public criers; saving the ownership which the Roman Church has in the city of Palestrina, and saving the homage which the captains owe to you and the Roman Church. You shall not receive Tivoli to the detriment and injury of the City; but if we wish to attack the people of Tivoli, you shall not act against us. You shall have coin minted within the City, wherever you please; of this, you shall give a third part to the senators from time to time. If, at your command, we make war upon anyone, and someone acts against us on that account, you shall assist and defend us in this by your aid [Col. 1509B].

All the aforesaid things you and all the bishops and cardinals of the Roman Church, for yourselves and your successors, shall promise to observe forever to the Senate and People of Rome. And we the senators and the whole Roman People, for ourselves and our successors, shall promise forever to observe all these things toward you, your whole curia, and your successors. Let all these things be observed by both sides in good faith and without fraud. And that this settlement may stand inviolate for all time, we confirm it by decree of the Senate and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing.

[Col. 1510A] Therefore, by the authority of almighty God and by the edict of the most magnificent order of the Senate, we firmly command that no fellow citizen, friend, or faithful man of ours presume in any manner to act against these provisions, which have been written down and firmly established, if he desires to retain our love and good favor; otherwise, let him incur most grievously the wrath and hatred of the most ample Senate and the dread Roman People.

Done in the forty-fourth year of the Senate, in the sixth indiction, in the month of May, on the last day, by order of the senator-councillors: Angelo Ser Romano de Pinea, Bobone Stefano de Octaviano, Pietro Stefano de Transtiberim, Romano Senebaldo, Rainerio Rainaldi de Ramucio, Giovanni de Schinando, Cafaro Bartolomeo, Pietro [Col. 1510B] Nicolai, Fuscone de Berta, Bubone Donna Scotta, and Ilperino Domnici.

And of the senators: Stefano Contebraca, Pietro Berardi, Cencio Muti, Giovanni Cencio, Guido Bobone, Giovanni Leone, Giovanni Parentio, Gregorio Malebrancha, Guido Roffredo, Giordano de Ponte Sancti Petri, Oddone Caputferri Romano, Giovanni de Flajano, Pietro Giovanni Ada, Cencio de Gulferamo, Stefano Giudice, Nicola Buccaemazi, Gerardo Pietro de Gerardo, Giacinto de Tosto, Piscione Nicolai, Giovanni Sassone, Giovanni Guido de Papa, Pietro de Gerardo, Giovanni Bartolomeo, Giovanni Cencio, Benone Pietro de Octaviano, Vitale Paolo, Francone Stefano, Pietro Latrone, Cuntebrace, [Col. 1510C] Pietro de Gregorio, Pietro Berardi de Blanca, Rainone Buccaenuza, Ottaviano Giovanni de Octaviano, Giovanni Plage, Giovanni Buccaemazi, Giordano Oddone, Cencio de Bertranno, Silvestro Pietro Artonis, Giovanni the Scriniary, Bartolomeo Ciconnis, Nicola de Antonio, Giovanni Astulfo, Angelo Romano de Giovanni, Astaldo de Transtiberim, Giovanni Gulferamo, Matteo Mecuminpunga, Giacomo Oddone Francone. [Note: [Col. 1509C] Observe how many Roman nobles the one paternal designation distinguished one from another. The Guido Bobonis named among them was perhaps the paternal uncle [Col. 1510C] of Hyacinth, Cardinal Orsini, who three years later assumed the name Celestine III on the Roman throne; for his father was Peter Bobonis.]

## HENRY OF CHÂTEAU-MARÇAY, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

Historical notice. 211  
Second notice. 213  
Literary notice. 215  
**LETTERS OF HENRY.** 215  

EPISTLE I.—To Pope Alexander III.—Sent to preach the holy war, he announces that Henry, count of Champagne, has taken the cross, and commends his land or principality to the pontiff. 215  
EPISTLE II.—To Abbot Buscalon.—He wishes Buscalon to come to Clairvaux and asks him to meet him at Hautecombe, where Henry had been abbot. 217  
EPISTLE III.—To Pope Alexander.—He begs the pope not to appoint a bishop for the Church of Toulouse. 217  
EPISTLE IV.—To the same.—He asks the pope to deign to grant the bearer of this letter a bishop for the Irish. 218  
EPISTLE V.—To the King of the English.—He extols the king of England both for other reasons and because he had resolved to cover the church of Clairvaux with lead; for this purpose he sends him the dimensions of that church. 219  
EPISTLE VI.—To the same.—He says that at the first feast of St. Bernard he made mention of him and that his presence had been desired; he sends him a finger of St. Bernard. 220  
EPISTLE VII.—Which is from the lord of Cîteaux to Henry and the abbot of Morimond.—Henry and the abbot of Morimond are appointed by the lord of Cîteaux to visit the monastery of La Colombe. 220  
EPISTLE VIII.—To the community of Savigny.—He exhorts the Savigniacs to frugality, on account of the apparent present poverty of their house. 221  
EPISTLE IX.—To Pope Alexander.—He complains about the monks of Dol, who had forcibly extorted tithes from the monks of the House of God, of the Cistercian Order, and had even wounded some of them. 222  
EPISTLE X.—To the same.—He complains that the abbot of Dijon disregards the pope’s decrees for a certain house of the Order and asks him to lay a heavier hand upon the obstinate man. 222  
EPISTLE XI.—To the same.—He laments certain vices of Gaul which the cardinal of St. Chrysogonus had begun to uproot, and for that reason prays that his time for return be extended. 223  
EPISTLE XII.—To the Black Abbots of Flanders.—He endeavors to calm their agitated minds over the withdrawal of the abbot of Hans to a monastery of the Cistercian Order. 225  
EPISTLE XIII.—To the Bishop of Chalon.—He congratulates him upon his recent assumption of the episcopate of Chalon, and commends a certain matter concerning the monastery of Longivaux. 226  
EPISTLE XIV.—To Lord Hyacinth.—He excuses himself for not yet having shown him honor—by letter, I think. 227  
EPISTLE XV.—A petition to a prelate.—He commends his Order to him, especially the house of Al. 227  
EPISTLE XVI.—A petition to a bishop.—He commends to him the monasteries of his Order situated in the bishopric of León. 227  
EPISTLE XVII.—A petition to a prince.—He commends to him the monastery of Perosa. 228  
EPISTLE XVIII.—To . . .—He excuses himself because he cannot be present on the appointed day to settle the affair of Vallis-Lucentis. 229  
EPISTLE XIX.—Concerning the affair, to the abbot of Trois-Fontaines.—He entrusts his authority to him to resolve the affair of Vallis-Lucentis. 229  
EPISTLE XX.—A petition to the pope.—That he restrain foreign religious and nuns of Bellecombe, whose proximity obstructed the pasturage of the animals of Benediction-of-God. 230  
EPISTLE XXI.—To a prelate.—On the same subject. 230  
EPISTLE XXII.—To the pope.—That he alter the agreement, contrary to the institution of the Order, made by the brothers of Fontenay with the monks of Flavigny. 230  
EPISTLE XXIII.—A petition to a prince.—He complains [Col. 1513] of the vexations of the lord of Wangion-Rive. 231  
EPISTLE XXIV.—A petition to a king.—He commends to him the house of M. in Ireland. 232  
EPISTLE XXV.—A friendly letter to a companion. 232  
EPISTLE XXVI.—To the Bishop of Chalon.—A letter of congratulation. 233  
EPISTLE XXVII.—To the same.—That he support him in the election at Cîteaux. 233  
EPISTLE XXVIII.—To Louis, king of the French.—Concerning the Albigensian heretics. 234  
EPISTLE XXIX.—To all Christ’s faithful.—Concerning the acts performed by him and his companions during their legation against the Albigensians. 235  
EPISTLE XXX.—Sentence of Henry, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, issued in 1188 against the abbot of St. Sever, in favor of the monastery of the Holy Cross at Bordeaux, in which several councils are mentioned. 241  
EPISTLE XXXI.—Letter of Henry, bishop of Albano, to all prelates of the Church.—He exhorts them to moderation, humility, and penitence. 247  
EPISTLE XXXII.—Letters of Henry, bishop of Albano and apostolic legate, by which he summons the prelates of Germany, through the bearer, to an assembly for deliberation concerning holy wars against the Saracens, for the vindication of the cross and places consecrated by Christ’s feet. 249

XIX.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Mary of Florence. 1297  
XX.—Takes the church of St. Mary of Grandigurgitis under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1298  
XXI.—Orders archbishops and bishops not to permit the possessions of churches to be alienated by the priors and obedientiaries of the Cluniac brethren, without the counsel of the abbot and convent, or bestowed upon laymen. 1301  
XXII.—Takes the Church of Camin under protection, on condition that Bishop Sifridus and his successors pay yearly to the Apostolic See one ferton of gold. 1301  
XXIII.—Confirms to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, the monastery of Balma. 1303  
XXIV.—Takes the monastery of Cluny under protection and confirms certain goods and privileges. 1305  
XXV.—Confirms all the possessions of the monastery of Cluny. 1307  
XXVI.—Orders that the election of the abbots of St. Benedict of Padilirone be conducted according to the privileges of the monastery of Cluny. 1310  
XXVII.—Assigns to Abbot Hugh and the convent of Cluny the monastery of St. Germanus of Auxerre. 1312  
XXVIII.—Forbids archbishops and bishops henceforth to demand any procurations from the priors of the Cluniac brethren, except when they come to the priories for purposes of visitation. 1313  
XXIX.—Takes the monastery of St. Mary of Flabons-Mont under protection and confirms its goods. 1313  
XXX.—Bull confirming the abbey of Blessed Mary of Herivallis. 1314  
XXXI.—Makes known to all bishops the privilege of the brethren of St. Mary of Reno: that they may be ordained by whatever Catholic bishop they prefer. 1317  
XXXII.—Confirms to the monastery of Cluny the village of Sana. 1317  
XXXIII.—To William, king of Scots.—On the exemption of the churches in his realm. 1318  
XXXIV.—Takes the monastery of St. Mary of Moncello under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1318  
XXXV.—Undertakes the protection of the church of St. Mary of Reno, and confirms its goods and privileges. 1324  
XXXVI.—Confirms to the abbots and brethren of the Premonstratensian Order exemption from tithes. 1326  
XXXVII.—Orders the prior of Faversham and Master Firmin that, if invaders of the property of the Church of Canterbury, having been warned, do not make reparation for the losses, they are to declare them excommunicated. 1327  
XXXVIII.—Orders William, bishop of Worcester, the abbot of Tewkesbury, and the prior of St. Sepulchre of Warwick to judge between the canons of Kenilworth and the clerics of Gnosbale. 1328  
XXXIX.—Takes the church of St. Piat of Siclini under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1328  
XL.—Undertakes the protection of the church of the Holy Savior at Venice and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1329  
XLI.—Grants the prior and chapter of the Holy Savior at Venice authority to appoint an administrator. 1332  
XLII.—Exempts the canons of the church of the Holy Savior at Venice from paying tithes. 1332  
XLIII.—Takes the Premonstratensian monastery under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1333  
XLIV.—Permits Lanfranc, bishop of Bergamo, to recover church possessions alienated against the will of the chapter. 1335  
XLV.—Informs the same man that he has annulled the alienations of property made by Gerard, his predecessor, against the will of the chapter. 1335  
XLVI.—Takes the nunnery of St. Mary of Moliano under protection and confirms its possessions and goods. 1335  
XLVII.—Grants Lanfranc, archbishop of Bergamo, authority to punish disobedient clerics. 1336  
XLVIII.—Confirms to the convent of Monte Cassino the money assigned by Abbot Peter of blessed memory for the brethren’s needs. 1336  
XLIX.—Takes the church of St. Lawrence of Florence under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1337  
L.—Grants the prior and brethren of the Carthusians that, whenever clerics or laymen of a lower religious profession wish to enter the observance of their order, they may freely receive them. Adds other privileges. 1338  
LI.—Takes the monastery of St. Benedict of Gualdo under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1339  
LII.—Confirms the judgment pronounced in the presence of Urban III between the sisters of St. Hilary and the provost of Florence. 1342  
[Col. 1526]  
LIII.—Privilege for the church of St. John of Monza. 1342  
LIV.—Privilege for the church of St. Germanus. 1344  
LV.—Informs the consuls and people of Pisa that Peter, cardinal priest of St. Cecilia, and Soffredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata, have been sent to settle their dispute with the Genoese concerning Sardinia. 1346  
LVI.—Orders Tammo, bishop of Verden, the abbot of Lüne, and the master of schools of Verden not to allow a certain court to be taken from the nunnery of Leven by Hartwig, archbishop of Hamburg. 1346  
LVII.—Privilege for the church of Ravello. 1347  
LVIII.—At the request of Bishop Balderam, takes the church of Brandenburg under protection and confirms its goods and rights. 1348  
LIX.—Confirms the possessions and privileges of the chapter of Brandenburg. 1349  
LX.—Takes the church of St. Nicholas of Stendal under protection and confirms its goods and privileges, on condition that one ounce of gold be paid annually to the Roman Church. 1351  
LXI.—Confirms to the canons of the Roman church of St. Peter the privilege granted by Eugenius III. 1353  
LXII.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Gilbert of Neufontaines, in the diocese of Clermont. 1355  
LXIII.—Urges Joachim, abbot of Curatio, to complete the *Exposition of the Apocalypse* and the work of the *Concord*, and diligently to undertake their correction. 1357  
LXIV.—Takes the church of St. Mary of Viborg under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1358  
LXV.—Permits Absalon, archbishop of Lund, to enroll Ketil, formerly provost of St. Mary of Viborg, among the saints. 1360  
LXVI.—Approves the judgment rendered by Gerard, bishop, and Vitalian, archdeacon of Padua, between Mark, bishop of Castello in Venice, and the parish priests and priests of certain churches concerning certain tithes. Confirms the possessions of the church of St. Cantianus. 1361  
LXVII.—By apostolic authority confirms to the priests and clerics of St. Mary Mother of the Lord the portion of tithes granted them by Mark Nicholas, bishop of Castello; and decrees that the goods of that church remain safe and unimpaired. 1364  
LXVIII.—Receives the church of St. Cassian of Venice under St. Peter’s protection and, by apostolic authority, confirms its rights and revenues. 1365  
LXIX.—Orders the abbot of St. Geneviève, the dean, and the cantor of Paris to compel Manasses, bishop of Troyes, to admit regular canons into the church of St. Lupus at Troyes and establish them in the church of Marigniac. 1367  
LXX.—Commends the church of St. Honoratus to the consuls of Grasse. 1368  
LXXI.—At the request of Archbishop Tribunus, takes the Church of Ragusa under protection and confirms its privileges. 1368  
LXXII.—Takes the church of St. Lawrence of Florence under protection and confirms its goods. 1371  
LXXIII.—Privilege for the church of St. Ansgar at Bremen. 1373  
LXXIV.—Informs the brethren of the Order of Grandmont that he has removed both William and Stephen from the priorate. Grants them free discretion to elect a successor. 1375  
LXXV.—Informs Henry, count of Champagne, that the dispute among the brethren of Grandmont has been settled. 1376  
LXXVI.—Confirms the Rule of Grandmont. 1376  
LXXVII.—Grants Maurice, bishop of Paris, a privilege concerning the procuration to be furnished to him and to his archdeacons, when visiting parishes, by the regular canons of the churches. 1377  
LXXVIII.—Orders Abbot Silvecanus and the sacristan of Aix to protect the monks of St. Victor of Marseille against the injuries inflicted by canons. 1378  
LXXIX.—Orders the bishops of Regensburg and Freising to defend the monastery of Aldersbach against the wrongs of Albert of Kam, who had arrogated to himself the advocacy of the monastery. 1378  
LXXX.—To Henry, archbishop of Bourges.—That monks and regular canons should not remain alone in towns. 1379  
LXXXI.—Confirms the possessions of the monastery of Jesus of Nazareth on Mount Aragon. 1379  
LXXXII.—Confirms to Archbishop Hartwig and the Church of Hamburg that the bishoprics of Lübeck, Schwerin, Ratzeburg, and Woxull are its suffragans. 1380  
[Col. 1527]  
LXXXIII.—Orders the abbots of Lübeck, St. Paul of Bremen, and Stade that, if Hartwig, archbishop of Hamburg, has lawfully appointed Abbot T. over the monastery of Ramesle, they are to confirm him. 1381  
LXXXIV.—Confirms to Hartwig, archbishop of Hamburg, the bishopric of Woxull. 1381  
LXXXV.—Privilege for the monastery of Osterholz. 1382  
LXXXVI.—Privilege for the church of Furcone. 1382  
LXXXVII.—Confirms donations made to the canons of the church of Zaragoza. 1383  
LXXXVIII.—Confirms the laws of the Premonstratensian Order. 1383  
LXXXIX.—In letters to William, archbishop of Monreale, orders that the bishops of Syracuse refrain from using the pallium. 1384  
XC.—Confirms the privileges of William, archbishop of Monreale, and grants him use of the pallium. 1385  
XCI.—Confirms the judgment of the bishops of Equilio and Torcello concerning the reception, by the abbot of St. Nicholas of the Shore on Ascension Day, of the bishop of Castello. 1390  
XCII.—Orders to be ratified the judgment rendered by Alexius, cardinal priest of the title of St. Susanna, and John, cardinal deacon of St. Theodore, between the churches of St. Tryphon, St. Nicholas of the Prefect, Holy Savior of Sere, and St. Mary in the Field of Mars. 1391  
XCIII.—Privilege for the monastery of Monte Cassino. 1395  
XCIV.—Receives the monastery of Monte Cassino under the protection of Blessed Peter and the Apostolic See. Declares that this monastery is to be preferred to all others throughout the West. Decrees that its abbot is to take a place superior to other abbots in assemblies and to pronounce the first opinion. 1395  
XCV.—Takes the church of St. Michael of Nonantola under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1396  
XCVI.—Takes the monastery of St. Martin of Metz under protection and confirms its discipline and possessions. 1398  
XCVII.—Orders B[aldwin], archbishop of Canterbury, to restore within forty days what he has taken from the monks of Canterbury. Forbids injury to the privileges both of the Apostolic See and of the Church of Canterbury in the appointment of a new prior; otherwise, he indicates that R[adulf], cardinal priest of the title of St. Praxedes, his legate, will act with severity. 1401  
XCVIII.—Takes the monastery of St. Nicholas of Fruttino under protection and confirms its discipline, possessions, and privileges. 1403  
XCIX.—Confirms the peace negotiated between the Pisans and Genoese by Peter, cardinal priest of St. Cecilia, and Sofredus, cardinal deacon of St. Mary in Via Lata. 1407  
C.—Privilege for Roffridus, abbot of Monte Cassino. 1411  
CI.—Privilege for the monastery of St. Peter of Massa on Mount Nero. 1412  
CII.—At the request of Bishop Peter, confirms all the privileges formerly granted by Roman pontiffs to the Church of Segni; among the places especially enumerated are the following castles: Collis Medius, Mattelonicus, Gabilianus, Plumbinaria, Valmontonius, Lacus, and Mons Fortinius.—Given at the Lateran, 14 days before the Kalends of January, indiction VII, in the first year of the pontificate, 1188.—Long before, Lucius III had granted all this to the same Bishop Peter in a most ample privilege, which is highly relevant for determining the boundaries of the diocese of Segni. 1413  
CIII.—Confirms certain rights of the chapter of the church of St. Alexander of Bergamo. 1414  
CIV.—Takes the church of Saints Felix and Regula of Zurich under protection and confirms its possessions. 1414  
CV.—Writes to Isaac, emperor of Constantinople. 1415  

ANNO 1189.

CVI.—Takes the monastery of St. Salvius of Florence under protection and confirms its goods and rights. 1416  
CVII.—Forbids all clerics established throughout Norway “to presume to go on campaign, unless perhaps in order to administer penance and ecclesiastical sacraments to the dying and to dissuade men from evil deeds”; otherwise, the sentence pronounced against them by the archbishop of Nidaros is to be confirmed by himself. 1418  
CVIII.—To the sisters of the church of Langenhorst. 1418  
CIX.—Writes to B[aldwin], archbishop of Canterbury, the same things as above, except that he announces not Radulf but John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark, legate of the Apostolic See, as the one who will ensure execution of his commands. 1419  
CX.—Receives the monastery of Muri under St. Peter’s protection, confirms all privileges granted even by Pope Alexander, and adds new ones. 1421  
[Col. 1528]  
CXI.—Takes the monastery of St. Mary of Esrum under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1423  
CXII.—Grants the prior and brethren of Fonte Avellana authority to reform the condition of the monastery of St. Victor. 1425  
CXIII.—Informs Gerald, prior, and the brethren of Grandmont that he has commanded John, cardinal priest of the title of St. Mark and legate of the Apostolic See, publicly to declare Stephen, founder of the Order of Grandmont, enrolled among the saints. 1426  
CXIV.—Takes the church of St. Peter of Douai under protection and confirms its goods. 1427  
CXV.—Orders Pistor, bishop of Vicenza, to determine whether the sisters of St. Christina, after their church was destroyed, are building another church within the city of Treviso, against the bishop’s opposition; he is to restrain the nuns. 1429  
CXVI.—Takes the Church of Siena under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1430  
CXVII.—Confirms the monastery of Subiaco and its enumerated goods under the protection of the holy Roman Church; forbids anyone to construct fisheries or mills in the lake of the monastery without the abbot’s permission; directs that the bishop for church dedications and for the ordination of monks or clerics is to be sought from the Supreme Pontiff, while permitting them, should circumstances of the time not allow this, to receive these things from any bishop; forbids anyone other than the Apostolic See to exercise jurisdiction in that monastery; declares that the election of the abbot belongs to the monks and consecration to the Supreme Pontiff; decrees penalties against the disobedient; and grants a blessing to benefactors. 1432  
CXVIII.—Takes the Church of Ferrara under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. 1436  
CXIX.—Orders Eberhard, bishop of Merseburg, and Otto, bishop of Eichstätt, carefully to investigate the life and miracles of Otto I, bishop of Bamberg, and, unless they find impediments, declare him enrolled among the saints. 1438  
CXX.—Informs Otto II, bishop of Bamberg, of the mandate given to the bishops of Merseburg and Eichstätt. 1438  
CXXI.—Confirms to the monastery of St. Denis the church of St. Blaise of Grandiputeo. 1439  
CXXII.—Undertakes protection of the monastery of St. Matthew of the Castle, and confirms its discipline, goods, and rights. 1440  
CXXIII.—Absolves the whole chapter of Trier and all clergy and people established throughout the archbishopric from obedience, in spiritual and temporal matters, to Archbishop Fulmar and Provost R. 1442  
CXXIV.—Confirms to the monastery of St. Chrysogonus of Zadar the church of St. Martin. 1444  
CXXV.—Confirms to Master Herman and the brethren of the Hospital of Jerusalem the things which Philip, archbishop of Cologne, had given to the hospital of the Holy Sepulchre at Duisburg. 1444  
CXXVI.—Confirms to the canons of the church of St. Thomas of the Louvre at Paris the possessions bestowed by Count Robert. 1445  
CXXVII.—Grants privileges to the provost and brethren of the church of St. Nicholas of Stendal. 1446  
CXXVIII.—Orders all bishops, whenever requested by the brethren of the church of St. Nicholas of Stendal, to administer the sacraments without delay and without appeal. 1446  
CXXIX.—Takes the monastery of Baumburg under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1447  
CXXX.—Grants the provost and brethren of St. Nicholas of Stendal authority to minister, either personally or through chaplains, in the parishes belonging to them. 1448  
CXXXI.—Permits the provost and brethren of St. Nicholas of Stendal “to redeem tithes from the hands of laymen and freely assign them to their own use and that of their successors.” 1449  
CXXXII.—Also grants the provost and brethren of St. Nicholas of Stendal “that no one may hold a synod in their church, nor may any bishop or prelate presume to excommunicate them or place their church under interdict.” 1449  
CXXXIII.—To Count Ger. and the whole people of Ragusa. 1449  
CXXXIV.—Receives the monastery of St. Quentin of Beauvais under protection and confirms its discipline and possessions. 1450  

ANNO 1190.

CXXXV.—Confirms the judgment concerning the right of foundation of the three churches of Chilcheim, Eimuotingen, and Matra, approved by O[tto], formerly bishop of Constance. 1453  
CXXXVI.—Confirms to the abbot and convent of Cîteaux the church of Schardeburg, given by Richard, king of England. 1454  
[Col. 1529]  
CXXXVII.—Announces to the suffragans of the Church of York and to all abbots, priors, people, and clergy established throughout the province that Geoffrey, brother of Richard, king of England, has been recognized by him as archbishop of York. 1454  
CXXXVIII.—Informs Milo, archbishop of Milan, and his suffragans that he has ordered [Theobald], bishop of Piacenza, to proceed severely against the consuls of Piacenza unless they desist from injuries against churches. 1455  
CXXXIX.—Privilege for the church of Thena. Confirms to it the grants made by Albert, archdeacon. 1456  
CXL.—Privilege for the church of Rasdorf. 1456  
CXLI.—Undertakes protection of the nunnery of St. Cosmas of Taliacot and confirms its possessions and rights. 1458  
CXLII.—Privilege for the Church of Trier. 1461  
CXLIII.—At the request of Richard, king of England, entrusts the office of legate to William, bishop of Ely. 1462  
CXLIV.—Takes the Carthusian brethren under protection and confirms their possessions and privileges. 1462  
CXLV.—Commends the Carthusian Order to archbishops and bishops. 1463  
CXLVI.—Grants the priors and brethren of the Carthusian Order “that no prior or brother may be free to appeal without the consent of the chapter of his house.” 1464  
CXLVII.—Confirms two altars to the monastery of Eiham. 1465  
CXLVIII.—Confirms the peace reconciled between the canons of St. Vincent and St. Alexander of Bergamo. 1465  
CXLIX.—Bull of the canonization of Blessed Malachy. 1466  
CL.—Clement III, in letters given at Viterbo, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the third year of his pontificate, addresses the people of Fleury. 1467  
CLI.—Takes the church of the Holy Cross of Guingamp under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. 1467  
CLII.—Writes to the abbot of St. Geneviève, the dean, and the cantor of Paris concerning the prebend of the Church of Meaux, founded by P[eter], formerly bishop of Tusculum, which is to be preserved according to the founder’s will. 1470  
CLIII.—Bull confirming the goods of St. Mary the Golden of Toulouse. 1470  
CLIV.—Grants the provost of St. Mary of Magdeburg the use of gloves. 1471  
CLV.—Takes the monastery of St. Denis of Nogent under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. 1472  
CLVI.—Confirms to Maurice, bishop of Paris, the privilege that whenever a deanery falls vacant he may receive its revenue. 1475  
CLVII.—At the request of Maurice, bishop of Paris, orders the preservation of the agreement reached between Stephen, formerly bishop, and Theobald, archdeacon. 1476  
CLVIII.—Writes to Maurice, bishop of Paris, that he is astonished that the archbishop of Sens “sends his parishioners to other judges without his knowledge or consultation, and sometimes even condemns the determination of his own judgment.” He grants “that he may, by operation of law, publish a sentence promulgated subject to appeal, and prohibit parishioners from answering before judges thus appointed.” 1476  
CLIX.—At the request of Alfonso, king of Castile, establishes an episcopal see in the city of Plasencia and confirms the diocese established by the king. 1476  
CLX.—Confirms to Waldemar, bishop of Schleswig, the liberty which “Canute, king of Denmark, his kinsman, granted to him and his successors: namely, that both stewards and peasants are to remain free and exempt from every royal burden and from that of the king’s officials; and that in judicial inquiries and executions, which formerly used to be handled by royal officials, they are now to answer to no one, but are subject to his own command, and henceforth are subject to no secular power.” 1477  
CLXI.—To Peter, abbot of Hartes.—Approves the condemnation at Metz of charters, obtained by false suggestion against the ancient liberty of the Church of Harter, and confirms that church’s freedom. 1478  

## Decrees of Pope Clement III

I.—To the abbot and archpriest of Montulanum.—That they restore to the acolyte Gant. the benefice taken away from him. 1478  
II.—To Oddo, bishop of Veroli.—On a certain marriage not to be dissolved. 1478  
III.—To the archbishop of Ancona.—On a law established by the people of Ancona. 1479  
[Col. 1530]  
IV.—To a certain bishop.—On priests who have incurred the guilt of adultery, perjury, or false testimony. 1479  
V.—Rescript to a certain archbishop. 1480  
VI.—To a certain archbishop.—On the absolution of those who, summoned to judgment, disdain to appear and, because of their contumacy, are bound by the bond of anathema. 1480  
VII.—To a certain bishop.—On consecrating an oratory. 1480  
VIII.—To a certain bishop.—On appeals. 1481  
IX.—To the bishop of Angers.—What has been determined by the greater and sounder part of a council is always to prevail. 1481  
X.—To the bishop of Segovia.—On Jews or Saracens converted to the Christian faith. 1482  
XI.—To . . .—Replies concerning the vow of a certain count. 1482  
XII.—To certain monks.—On churches subject to their presentation. 1482  
XIII.—To a certain bishop.—On dissolving the marriage of a certain knight. 1483  
XIV.—To . . .—On those who contracted clandestine marriages contrary to a prohibition. 1483  
XV.—To the archbishop of Canterbury.—That the marriage of the knight B. is not to be dissolved. 1484  
XVI.—To a certain bishop.—On two men who took two sisters as wives. 1484  
XVII.—To . . .—On the marriage of H. and the woman R. 1484  
XVIII.—To a certain bishop.—That Will. de Rimare ought not to divorce his second wife. 1485  
XIX.—To a certain person.—On approving a certain election. 1485  
XX.—To William, king of Sicily.—On the oath of fealty to be rendered by the king’s heirs to the Roman pontiffs. 1486  
XXI.—To the bishop of Abserent and the abbot of St. Andrew of Bergis.—On penance to be imposed upon a certain priest, through whose fault it is uncertain whether a servant died. 1486  
XXII.—To a certain bishop.—On a female parishioner of his who, though unwilling, had been given in marriage to a certain German when she was not yet eleven years old. 1487  
XXIII.—To the bishop of Formolum.—Replies to his questions. 1487  
XXIV.—To Gotifred, patriarch of Aquileia.—On the absolution of excommunicated persons. 1489  
XXV.—To certain priests.—Replies to their questions concerning the accusation of marriage. 1490  
XXVI.—To a certain bishop.—On penance to be imposed upon Greek priests if they request that it be imposed upon them for children they have oppressed. 1490  
XXVII.—To a certain bishop.—That he compel W. to return to his lawful wife. 1491  
XXVIII.—To a certain bishop.—On a regular canon who, at the point of death, refused to resign his property. 1492  
XXIX.—To the provost of Falc . . .—Against clerics engaged in warfare. 1492  
XXX.—To the bishop of Sigüenza.—If the matter cannot otherwise be proved, witnesses must be compelled even in a criminal case, etc. 1492  
XXXI.—To the same.—On Jews or Saracens converted to the Christian faith. 1493  
XXXII.—To John, archbishop of Lyon.—On conventual churches. 1493  
XXXIII.—To the archbishop of Saint-Marino Tarantaise.—On removing a parish priest simoniacally elected and on the right of patronage. 1494  
XXXIV.—To Roffridus, cardinal priest of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino.—That he decide the matrimonial question between Robert and the woman B. 1495  
XXXV.—On one who had intercourse with his wife’s blood-relative. 1495  
XXXVI.—To Gilbert, bishop of Clermont.—On an oath. 1496  
XXXVII.—To the bishop of Zaragoza.—On penance to be imposed upon simoniacs. 1496  
XXXVIII.—To the consuls and people of Genoa.—On the subdeacon D., who unwillingly killed a boy. 1496  
XXXIX.—To the archbishop of Monte Cassino. 1497  
XL.—To the bishop of Livonia and his companions.—Grants them permission to use foods set before them by unbelievers. 1497  
XLI.—To a certain bishop.—Those who assault clerics or commit arson may be absolved only by the Roman pontiff. A leprous priest is to be removed from office. 1497  
[Col. 1531]  
XLII.—To the archbishop of Tours.—On the cleric H. 1498  
XLIII.—To the bishop of Abbeville.—That in certain churches he establish only as many religious persons as their revenues suffice to support. 1498  
XLIV.—To a certain bishop.—On matters done by the greater part of a chapter. 1499  
XLV.—To Walter, archbishop of Rouen.—On granting a church which is not vacant. 1499  
XLVI.—To the bishop of Astorga.—On prebends. 1500  
XLVII.—To the elect of Alloc.—On penance to be imposed on Count H. 1500  
XLVIII.—To . . .—On judicial combat. 1501  
XLIX.—To the chapter of Lucca.—On a sentence of excommunication. 1501  
L.—To John, archbishop of Ludim.—That he not admit the appeal of certain clerics. 1501  
[Col. 1532]  
LI.—To the bishop of Zaragoza.—On vacant prebends. 1502  
LII.—To Gerard, bishop of Bologna.—That lodging for masters and schools is not to be leased in a way harmful to tenants. 1502  
LIII.—To the archbishop of Sorrento.—On P. de Regali. 1503  
LIV.—To a certain bishop.—On the subdeacon C., who unwillingly killed a boy. 1503  
LV.—To the dean of Cama Cen . . .—That a new levy not be imposed upon the churches of the diocese of Thérouanne. 1504  
LVI.—To R., canon of Cologne, trained in the medical art.—Advises him not to advance to the higher sacred orders, because he has administered medicines to several persons who thereby incurred danger of death. 1505  

Letter of Richard, king of England, to Clement III, Roman pontiff.—On the peace made between himself and King Tancred. 1505  

Agreement between Lord Pope Clement III and the senators and people of Rome concerning the regalian rights and other dignities of the City. (1188) 1507  

[Col. 1531] **END OF THE TWO HUNDRED AND FOURTH VOLUME.**
